## Volume front matter

### Series title page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age down to the time of Innocent III;** a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully compared with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continually illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all the works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject treated below; expanded by works that are doubtful or apocryphal, and also by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each of the Fathers has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is easy for the reader to discover which Fathers have commented on the individual books of Scripture, and in which places of their works they have done so.

A most accurate edition, and one easily preferable to all others if the following qualities are weighed: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the modest price, and above all this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but now gathered for the first time in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and literary form.

**First Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great, edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the *Complete Courses* in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

# Historical-Literary Notice on John Cassian

*(Schoenemann, Bibliotheca, Leipzig, 1794, vol. II.)*

## Chapter I. The life of John Cassian

[Col. 0009A]

It is commonly believed, on the authority of Gennadius, that Cassian was a native of Lesser Scythia, one of the provinces of Thrace. Nevertheless, in more recent times there have been learned men who, on the basis of arguments that cannot be dismissed—especially the pleasantness and fertility that he himself praises in his homeland, as well as the elegance of the Latin language displayed in his writings—have maintained that his birthplace should be sought in Gaul, and specifically in Provence.

Whatever the truth may be, from an early age—he is generally believed to have been born around the year 350 or 360—he was, by an uncertain route, educated among the monks of Palestine in a monastery called Bethlehem, though distinct from the monastery of the same name founded later by Jerome. There he was first instructed in the doctrines of the Christian religion.

Having obtained a companion with whom he lived in the closest intimacy, a fellow countryman named Germanus, he resolved with him to visit the anchorites established in the desert of Scythi.

[Note: [Col. 0009D] Thus Cassian himself writes at the beginning of the *Conferences*. Others read *Scythiae*. The desert lay beside Lake Mareotis in Egypt, [Col. 0010D] which is also called Scetis, Scetica, Scetina, and Scetiaca, as well as Scythica, Scytica, and Scythiotica.]

This difficult journey was undertaken around the year 390. They penetrated into the interior of the Thebaid and spent seven full years among those austere holy men. What is more, in the same year in which they had returned to the monastery—397—they again entrusted themselves to this journey and remained hidden in that gloomy corner of the earth until the year 400. Judge, then, whether Cassian bears the name of hermit unjustly.

After leaving the desert once more, Cassian and his companion [Col. 0009C] journeyed to Constantinople. He attached himself to John Chrysostom and was ordained by him to the diaconate. Soon afterward, when Chrysostom had been driven from his see by a mob of depraved men, Cassian was sent on his behalf, in the year 405, with a delegation of the clergy of Constantinople to Innocent.

From that time until approximately the year 415, his history is obscure. Some say that he returned to the East and identify him with the presbyter Cassian who, in 414, was sent by Alexander, bishop of Antioch, to Rome to reconcile peace between the two Churches. Others, however, believe that he had already gone to Massilia, where he was raised to the dignity of presbyter and, from approximately the year just mentioned, became distinguished both for his life and for his teaching.

He became especially renowned for founding two monasteries, [Col. 0009D] one for men and the other for women. He himself directed their discipline, which he had arranged according to the rules of Palestine and Egypt, [Col. 0010A] and he strongly confirmed it both by his own example and by that of his writings, although the reputation he acquired through these publications could not remain entirely free from blemish.

For although he was a vigorous opponent of the Pelagians, he nevertheless promoted doctrines concerning original sin and grace by which he himself might have acquired the name of heresiarch, and which stirred serious agitation in Gaul and other provinces and provoked Prosper’s pen against their author. Nevertheless, whatever in others bore the appearance of heresy, he detested most intensely, and he crowned his achievements by attacking the Nestorian error with the greatest vigor.

The time of his death is uncertain, but one would not depart far from the truth by supposing that it occurred around the year 440.

## Chapter II. The writings of John Cassian

[Col. 0010B]

### 1. Twelve books *On the Institutes of the Coenobia*

These books were composed for Castor, bishop of Apt, at whose request they were written. Gennadius divides them into three parts. The middle part, or fourth book alone, contains the *Institutes*; the first part, consisting of three books, concerns the monk’s habit and the canonical manner of prayer and psalmody observed in the monasteries of Egypt; finally, the third part, contained in the eight later books, is entitled *On the Origin, Nature, and Remedies of the Principal Vices*.

Photius makes two books: one entitled *Institutes*, the other *On the Eight Capital Vices*. Guychins followed this division. Cassian himself recognizes only one continuous work of twelve books, which teaches the perfect monastic life through examples and precepts.

The time at which these books were written cannot be determined with precision. The authors of the Benedictine *Literary History of Gaul* hold only that they were written before the condemnation of the Pelagians by Innocent and Zosimus, that is, before the years 417 or 418.

### 2. Twenty-four Conferences of the Fathers

These were committed to writing at different times between the years 419 and 427. The first ten are addressed to Leontius, bishop of Fréjus, and Helladius, abbot of Saint Castor; the next seven to Honoratus, soon to be bishop of Arles; and the final seven to Jovinianus, Minervius, and other monks.

### 3. Seven books *On the Incarnation of Christ against Nestorius*

[Col. 0010D]

These were written around the year 430 and addressed to Leo, then a deacon and later bishop of Rome.

[Col. 0011A]

The work entitled *On the Spiritual Medicine of the Monk*, or *Medical Dose for Emptying the Passions of the Soul*, is falsely attributed to Cassian. Godefridus Tilmannus, a Carthusian, quotes it in a letter to John Gropper, archdeacon of Saint Gereon at Cologne, as having been translated by himself from Greek. It is a very short piece, which John Baptist Guesnay inserted in its entirety in book I, chapter 58, page 188, of his *Cassianus Illustratus*.

The *Theological Confession* and *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues* belong to the same class. It is wearisome to mention the others. Tidemont conjectured that the *Acts of Saint Victor the Martyr*, found in Ruinart, had Cassian as their author, but the authors of the *Literary History of Gaul* do not agree with him.

Cassian is also said to have composed a *Monastic Rule*, which no longer exists. The Benedictines just mentioned say that this is established by a letter of Castor, bishop of Apt, to Cassian. But we have learned that they transmitted this incorrectly. On the other hand, it has already been pointed out by others that the testimony of Benedict of Aniane concerns not a new and distinctive rule of Cassian, but rather an excerpt compiled from various passages of his *Institutes*.

Some have believed that Cassian wrote his works not in Latin but in Greek, and that they were later translated. They were refuted in this error long ago. Certain Greek works of Cassian do indeed exist in Photius’s *Bibliotheca*, codex 197, but they were translated from Latin, and not from Cassian’s own books, but from books that Eucherius of Lyons had abridged.

For Gennadius, chapter 63, tells us that Eucherius composed [Col. 0011C] a Latin epitome from the first four books of the *Institutes* and the first seven *Conferences*. Greek manuscripts of this kind still survive in various libraries—for example, in Caesarea, according to Lambecius, volume IV, page 167 (Kollar’s edition, pages 373 ff.), and volume V, page 276 (Kollar’s edition, pages 582 ff.); also in the Royal Library and the Paris library of the Jesuits, as Fabricius reports in his *Bibliotheca Mediae et Infimae Latinitatis* from Simon’s *Censura* concerning Dupin’s library.

Similar works were printed under the name of Athanasius by Montfaucon, in his edition of Athanasius’s works, volume II, part I, pages 366–386.

John Rosweyde, among the *Lives of the Fathers*, presents a book fourth in order, composed from Severus Sulpicius and John Cassian. In manuscript codices—of which he consulted a considerable number—it is sometimes attributed to Sulpicius and sometimes to Cassian.

John Baptist Guesnay therefore hesitates, in the lacunose passage “[lacuna].l. Eucherione,” whether this epitome may be attributed to Eucherius, or whether it should perhaps be referred to a certain Victor the African, of whom Cassiodorus writes in chapter 29 of the *Institutes* that he purged Cassian’s statements and added what was lacking. But Cassiodorus’s words seem to signify not so much an epitome as a correction of errors.

## Chapter III. Editions of the works of John Cassian

### I

The first four books of the *Institutes* and the work on the causes and remedies of the eight vices were printed, if Fabricius’s report is true, by the Venetian presses in 1481.

A certain edition is the Basel edition of 1485, reprinted there by Amerbach in 1497 and at Lyon in 1516. The *Conferences* were added in the Venetian edition of 1491, reprinted at Bologna in 1521 and at Lyon in 1525. All these works, rendered together in paraphrase by Dionysius the Carthusian, appeared at Cologne in 1540.

The seven books against Nestorius were first, as far as I remember, published separately by the Basel printer Cratander in 1534. His edition was reproduced by the Paris booksellers in 1545 and 1569, and Josua Simler reproduced it, with several notes added, in 1572.

Afterward came the first collected edition of the works, from the Henricpetrine press, together with the works of John Damascene, in 1559, again in 1569, and a third time in 15[5].

A learned man was now needed who would remove, partly through comparison of manuscripts and printed codices and through sound judgment, the errors that the hands of copyists could hardly have failed to introduce in such an author, and who would partly clarify obscure and difficult passages and warn readers about the author’s errors. Yet the character of these books was not such as to attract and engage just anyone skilled in textual criticism; men nourished by monastic studies and eager to advance them had rather to be awaited.

I believe that Cardinal Antonio Carafa, who was highly deserving of the Church’s gratitude for his learning, thought he had found such a man when he recommended Cassian to Henry Cuychius, a professor at Louvain and later bishop of Roermond. At the same time, however, he urged the celebrated critic and man distinguished for the reputation of his refined learning, Peter Ciacconius, a priest of Toledo, to apply his hand to purging the same work.

Although the latter perhaps obeyed unwillingly, both men complied with Carafa’s wishes and authority concerning the manner in which he wanted them to discharge the editor’s role. Cuychius issued a new edition of Cassian, corrected according to Belgian codices and furnished with useful notes, at Antwerp from the Plantin press in 1578.

Ciacconius, however, did not live to see printed the recension he had prepared from eight manuscript copies in the Vatican Library. He died in 1581. Dominicus Basa, a Roman printer, had it printed from his autograph in 1588—unless the year 1580 should rather be regarded as the true date of birth of this edition, which was later furnished with a new title bearing the year 1588.

Certainly the year 1580 is attached to the dedicatory epistle that the same printer prefixed to Gregory XIII. From this we learn at least with certainty [Col. 0012D] that Ciacconius himself did not wish to undertake the responsibility of publishing this author, but sent his labors to the cardinal.

The Roman edition was reprinted at Lyon in 1606 and at Rome in 1611. I do not recall a separate reprinting of the Cuychian edition.

From both editions Alardus Gazaeus, a Vedastine monk at Arras—of the Abbey of Saint-Vaast, of the Order of Saint Benedict, at Arras—easily produced a single edition. In most respects he followed Cuychius, but did not neglect Ciacconius, other earlier editors, or even some new manuscript codices.

He added a continuous commentary of his own, useful to religious of every order but especially to Benedictines. Thus equipped, this edition appeared at Douai in 1616, in three octavo volumes, and afterward deserved to be reprinted repeatedly in various places, most recently at Leipzig in 1733.

What follows is a chronological record of the individual editions.

# Fifteenth century

## 1485

Basel, folio. *Cassian, On the Institutes of the Coenobia, the Origin, Causes, and Remedies of the Vices, and the Conferences of the Fathers.*

At the end:

> Here end the twenty-four Conferences of the holy Fathers, written by John the hermit, who is also called Cassian. Printed at Basel in the year of the Lord 1485.

The text is preceded by an alphabetical register of subjects and memorable sayings, in which references are made to individual books and chapters.

On the reverse of the title page one reads:

> Who and what sort of author he was; what books he wrote; to whom he wrote; and what subjects he treated: a brief commendatory exposition ending with these words:
>
> “Therefore, so that the works of this distinguished man, Cassian, worthy of such high commendation, might more easily be obtained by all who wished to read them, they have recently been collected into one body in the illustrious city of Basel, after the most accurate correction of the same works and an ingenious, highly useful, and previously unseen division; each work with its own heading, printed in polished letters, as can clearly be seen, for the commendation of the fruitful art of printing, for the benefit of all who diligently read these books, and for the glory and honor of our Savior Jesus Christ, who is blessed forever, in the year of his birth 1485.”

Sixty hexameter verses on the same subject were added on the second page of the ninth gathering of the register. They begin:

> “Let Romulus’s world serve the imperial command of Caesar,”

and end:

> “The sayings of Abraham: on the law of mastering the flesh.”

These two lines serve as their epigraph:

> “If you wish to know what books this work contains,  
> Read through the following verses to learn what each contains.”

The volume was printed in large Gothic type, though relatively slender and pointed, in two columns, without folio numbers or catchwords. The gatherings are signed. The titles of the books also appear in capital letters along the upper edge, and small initials occur in the chapters.

We observed one nearly unique feature in the type: the syllable *is* at the end of words is written by means of a straight perpendicular line, slightly bent toward the left at the top.

The same edition was formerly held by the library of the Duke de La Vallière. Fabricius, moreover, praises in his *Bibliotheca Mediae et Infimae Latinitatis* a Venetian edition of 1481, which I shall nevertheless regard as belonging to the realm of fable until I am taught otherwise.

## 1491

Venice, folio. *John Cassian, On the Institutes of the Coenobia; and his Conferences of the Fathers.*

Maettarius cites it in volume I, part II, page 538, from the catalogue of the Menars Library, page 19, no. 161. It was also present in the Pinelli Library.

## 1497

Basel, by John Amerbach; quarto. *John Cassian, On the Institutes of the Coenobia*, etc., as in the first edition.

At the end:

> Here end, etc. Printed at Basel by Master John Amerbach, in the year of the Lord 1497.

And below:

> Thanks be to God.

The first Basel edition is reproduced word for word in small Gothic type, in two columns.

# Sixteenth century

## 1516

Lyon; octavo. *The Life and Twelve Books of John the Hermit, who is also called Cassian*, namely: four books *On the Institutes of the Coenobia*, and eight books *On the Eight Capital Vices*.

Catalogue of the Bodleian Library. The authors of the *Literary History of Gaul*, volume II, page 224, report that this edition was printed by Simon Bevilaqua, a Lyon printer.

## 1521

Bologna, at the shop of Benedict Hector; octavo. *The work of John the Hermit, who is also called Cassian, on the Institutes of the Coenobia, the Origin, Causes, and Remedies of the Vices, and the Conferences of the Fathers.*

Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris, volume I, page 382, no. 772.

## 1525

Lyon, by Jacob Myt.; octavo. The same books. The Maurist Fathers are the sponsors of this notice in the *Literary History of Gaul*.

## 1528

At the end: Haguenau.

[Note: [Col. 0013] That is, Hayn (Grossenhain) in Upper Saxony, as the Benedictines correctly state: “at Hayn, in Upper Saxony.”]

By John Secerius, in the month of March; quarto. *The Conference of Cassian of Constantinople, deacon, on Free Will.*

Eight gatherings, printed in a handsome Roman type, like Justin two years earlier in the same place. It also appears in the catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris.

This Conference is the twenty-third in the complete work. The editor removed its final chapter, however—as the Maurist Fathers just mentioned point out—and substituted seventeen chapters compiled from other *Conferences*. Thus, if the title were to be accurate, it should have been *Treatise on Free Will from Cassian’s Conferences, especially Conference XXIII*.

## 1540

Cologne, from the workshop of Melchior Novesianus; folio. *The twelve books of John Cassian on the Institutes of the Coenobia and on the Capital Vices, together with two books containing the Twenty-four Conferences of the Holy Fathers, rendered in paraphrase by Dionysius the Carthusian.*

Added is the *Ladder of Paradise* of Saint John Climacus, in Latin, translated by the monk Ambrose.

Catalogue of the Bodleian Library, the Royal Library of Paris, and the Casanatense Library.

## 1542

[Col. 0014D]

Lyon, at the shop of Jacob Giunta; octavo. *The Conferences of the Fathers. The work of John the Hermit, who is also called Cassian, on the Institutes of the Coenobia, the Origin, Causes, and Remedies of the Vices, and the Conferences of the Fathers.*

The author’s life is added.

Catalogue of the Casanatense Library. Also the catalogue of the Library of Saint-Jacques at Liège, 1788, page 190.

## 1559

Basel, from the Henricpetrine press; folio. *Several works of John Cassian together with the works of Saint John Damascene.*

[Col. 0015A]

Some time earlier, namely in 1548, the works of John Damascene had been issued from the same press. It seems beyond doubt that this edition is a reprint of that one, although it did not include Cassian, as appears from its title in the catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris, volume I, page 357, no. 382.

## 1572

Zurich, folio. *The seven books of John Cassian on the Incarnation of Christ against Nestorius the heretic, addressed to Leo, bishop of the city of Rome*, included among *The Latin Writings of the Ancients on the One Person and Two Natures of Christ*, edited by Josua Simler, page 17.

Cassian’s life and notes on his books are added from page 47.

## 1575

Basel, from the Henricpetrine press, in September; [Col. 0015B] folio.

**ΤΑ ΤΟΥ ΜΑΚΑΡΙΟΥ ΙΩΑΝΝΟΥ ΤΟΥ ΔΑΜΑΣΚΗΝΟΥ ΕΡΓΑ** — “The works of the blessed John Damascene.”

*The complete works of John Damascene that actually survive, most of them not previously seen.*

Also:

*Several books of John Cassian the Hermit, on a subject not entirely dissimilar; the list of all the works, both of this author and of the other, will be found on the reverse page, and the subject of each individual work in the preface.*

There was also added to the works of John Damascene and Cassian a triple index, compiled with the greatest care, of memorable subjects and expressions, and of the passages of Sacred Scripture that are explained and cited in these works.

All of Cassian’s works are included: the four books *On the Institutes of the Coenobia*, beginning at folio 903; the eight books *On the Eight Capital Vices*, beginning at folio 932; the twenty-four *Conferences of the Fathers*, beginning at folio 990; and the seven books against Nestorius, beginning at folio 1239.

Marcus Hopperus of Basel wrote the preface, an epistle to Thomas a Planta, bishop of Chur or of Upper Rhaetia, dated Basel, the Kalends of August 1575. But he says nothing about the method by which either he or the earlier editors treated the author.

## 1560

Rome, octavo. *The Lives of the Fathers of John Cassian, excerpted from his Institutes of the Renunciants and his Conferences*, in the *Lives of the Saints* of Aloysius Lippomano, entire part II.

## 1578

Antwerp, from the workshop of Christopher Plantin; octavo.

*The four books of the Monastic Institutes of the holy John Cassian the Hermit; the eight books on the Capital Vices; the twenty-four Conferences of the Holy Fathers; and the seven books on the Incarnation of the Word.*

Now at last, after various editions, corrected according to the authority of numerous manuscripts and purged with incredible labor of many thousands of errors—a fact that can easily be recognized from the corrections appended below at the end.

Censorial notes have also been added to certain passages, together with an explanation of obscure words and statements, as well as two very full indexes.

The *Rules of the Holy Fathers*, taken from a very ancient manuscript codex of the monastery of Affligem, have also been added.

By the work and scholarship of Henry Cuychius, licentiate in sacred theology, later bishop of Roermond.

In a letter to Hermann, count of Rennenberg, provost and archdeacon of the Church of Saint Savior at Utrecht, and so forth—dated Louvain, from the monastery of the White Ladies, on the Kalends of March 1578—the editor complains at length of the misfortune of the age, caused partly by the enormous carelessness in copying books and partly by the arrogance and corruption of the books themselves.

For that reason, he considers it a worthy service among those whom the Christian commonwealth possesses as cultivators of the Lord’s vineyard that some should devote all their zeal to restoring, purifying, reading, and mastering the monuments of the holy Fathers with the help of ancient manuscript codices.

To prevent him from seeming to have said this without cause, he turns to praising and commending the Fathers. But then, returning to his subject, he says:

> Since, however, partly through the injury and decay of time, partly through the carelessness of copyists, and partly also through the insolent recklessness of heretics, the labors of these men have in many places been disfigured and sprinkled with numerous errors, and since many passages are found scattered throughout them that are gaping, distorted, mutilated, confused, and, as it were, like a broom that has come apart, care must therefore be taken that they be restored as accurately as possible to their original purity and integrity from the oldest and best manuscript exemplars.
>
> This consideration moved me also and persuaded me that I would be performing a worthwhile service, and one by no means unwelcome to all devotees of sacred learning, especially to lovers of monastic perfection, if I devoted some labor to purifying and illuminating John Cassian.
>
> The authority of the most illustrious and distinguished cardinal, Lord Antonio Carafa, which has the greatest weight with me, caused me to do so. For, in letters sent to me from Rome, he wrote that he would find this pleasing and that it would not be without benefit to the Christian commonwealth; he also explained what he especially wished to be done in revising this author.
>
> Let others judge what we have accomplished in this matter. I venture to assert only this: if anyone compares this edition with the earlier editions that we received a few years ago from Basel and Lyon—leaving aside the older printed codices, in which nearly everything is mutilated and incomplete—he will discover that a new face, a new form, and a new appearance have been given to this writer. This will become clear from the preface that follows immediately and from the corrective notes appended at the end of the work.
>
> There are, in fact, two kinds of notes by which he has assisted Cassian in accordance with the goal he set himself. Some he calls corrective notes; in these he explains the variant readings of the manuscripts and the reasons for the emendations. To these he has further added an explanation of the Greek-Latin words that occur here and there in Cassian and whose meaning seemed somewhat obscure.
>
> Others are called censorial notes. These he intended as a kind of antidote and amulet against certain more obscure passages and errors found both in the thirteenth Conference and in others. In the manner of digressions, they treat each point more fully.
>
> It must be kept in mind that both in the preface to the entire edition and in the warning prefixed to those censorial notes he professes—and constantly maintains and attempts to establish with arguments—that these errors should be attributed not so much to Cassian himself as to the persons holding the Conferences, whose opinions Cassian reports.

As for the rest, although he had found the division of chapters adopted from earlier editors not entirely consistent with the manuscript exemplars, he nevertheless did not wish to alter it rashly. He did, however, divide the books on the Incarnation, which had not yet been divided, into chapters.

He added indexes: one of the holy sayings explained by the author, and another of notable and memorable subjects.

## 1588

Rome, from the Vatican press; octavo.

*Twelve books of John Cassian the Hermit on the Institutes of the Renunciants, and twenty-four Conferences of the Holy Fathers, purged of almost innumerable errors with the assistance of very ancient codices and restored to their original integrity.*

Added are interpretations of certain obscure expressions arranged in alphabetical order, and observations on ambiguous and less secure passages that might offend a devout reader.

Furthermore, there are two indexes of testimonies from Sacred Scripture that Cassian either explains or cites in a form different from that of the Vulgate edition. Finally, there is an index of memorable subjects.

The *Rule of Saint Pachomius*, translated into Latin by Saint Jerome, has also been added, much more accurately corrected than previously.

The printer Dominicus Basa dedicated the edition to Gregory XIII, Supreme Pontiff, in a letter dated Rome, the intercalary Kalends of the year 1580. Both in this dedication and in his preface to the reader, he indicates that this work was undertaken and completed chiefly through the efforts of Cardinal Antonio Carafa.

In the latter place he explains this more openly, claiming that Carafa had supplied him with a copy of the already published codex, enlarged with the manuscript marginal notes of Peter Ciacconius, so that he would not lack the authority of the man through whose work this undertaking had been initiated.

He then adds that Peter Ciacconius, at the urging of the said cardinal, purged Cassian of innumerable errors and restored him to his former splendor, adding notes but, out of modesty, refusing to disclose his name. Basa therefore says that, aided by Ciacconius’s codex, he is publishing Cassian both more accurately corrected and richer, since he had found many additions written again by Ciacconius’s hand that could make the book more distinguished.

But we detected no such additions—although he speciously directs readers to learn of them by comparing the two editions, the old and the new—apart from the *Rule of Saint Pachomius*.

This preface is followed by another, also addressed to readers, which from the preceding account can clearly be understood to belong to Ciacconius. Let us therefore reproduce the very words in which he describes his work:

> The Vatican Library, he says, placed eight very ancient copies of Cassian before us, some of them written with the greatest accuracy. From comparison of these, innumerable passages have been restored in this edition. But it was not our plan to mark them, for the volume would grow beyond all bounds. It is enough here to have stated that we preserved the reading of the ancient codices with such conscientiousness that, whenever their variation occurred, we did not neglect it.

[Note: [Col. 0017D] These words, written in the same round type as the preceding words, can scarcely be reconciled with them in any satisfactory way.]

> In addition, we have explained more fully, in alphabetical order, the Greek words that this author freely uses and certain Latin words, for the benefit of less learned readers, adducing the passages from which we believe Cassian drew them.
>
> We carefully sought out all the testimonies of Sacred Scripture and marked them in the margin. Those taken from the edition of the Septuagint, or occasionally differing from our Vulgate, we printed separately in the form of an index, lest they should be thought corrupt; and we joined to them the Greek text from which they had been transcribed, taken from a very ancient book of the Vatican Library and other exemplars of venerable antiquity.
>
> We also added a second index containing passages incidentally explained in these books.
>
> Finally, we stated in the preceding letter that an antidote had been supplied against certain less familiar statements of this author.

Cassian did indeed write, at the urging of Leo I, Supreme Pontiff, splendid books on the Incarnation of the Lord against Nestorius. But because no manuscript copy existed in the Vatican Library according to which they could be corrected, and because they differed greatly from the purpose we had adopted—namely, to form a truly religious man—we omitted them, adding the Rule of Saint Pachomius, and so forth.

Such is the statement of the editor. If he was Ciacconius, we regret that he did not, as the preceding editor had done, openly declare what critical service he had rendered to Cassian. We understand, however, that Antonio Carafa prescribed for him the same method of treating Cassian that he had indicated to Cuychius as pleasing to him.

The chief purpose of that method seems to have been to warn readers about passages that breathed of Pelagianism. What Cuychius did in his censorial notes, this editor attempted to do through observations placed last, before the indexes. He gathered into eleven propositions all the passages that might generate suspicion of Pelagianism. To these he added a few other statements of Cassian requiring a pious interpretation, without regard to the order of the books or Conferences.

These observations are preceded by explanations, under the name of annotations, of the Greek words used by Cassian. They are likewise arranged alphabetically, but are fuller and more numerous than those of Cuychius, who had attached these explanations to his corrective notes.

There was also added an index of the passages of Sacred Scripture cited according to the Septuagint version.

[Note: [Col. 0017D] Cassian, he says, cites almost all his testimonies of Sacred Scripture from the Vulgate edition, which he declares to be the better translation and to have been rendered according to the Hebrew truth. But because he had absorbed the Septuagint interpreters, which were then in everyone’s hands, it happens that he cites certain passages—especially from Proverbs, which perhaps had long since been fixed in his memory—according to their translation. We have gathered these passages, most of which had gone unnoticed by others or had been corrected less carefully, together with any others that differed somewhat from our Vulgate edition, into the form of an index, and so forth.]

The Greek texts from which these passages were taken were added from the most ancient book of the Vatican Library and other more accurate exemplars.

# Seventeenth century

## 1606

[Col. 0019A]

Lyon, octavo. *Twelve books of John Cassian on the Institution of the Renunciants, and twenty-four Conferences of the Holy Fathers.*

It appears in the catalogue of the British Museum. From the title it is evident that this is a reprint of the Roman edition, which Gazaeus also confirms in the preface to his own edition.

## 1611
## 1611

Rome, printed by the Apostolic Chamber; in octavo. *The twelve books of John Cassian the Hermit on the Institutes of the Renunciants; the twenty-four Conferences of the Holy Fathers; the seven books on the Incarnation of the Word, with annotations and observations.* Added were the Rule of Saint Pachomius; the Rules of the Holy Fathers; Saint Prosper of Aquitaine’s book *On the Grace of God and Free Will*; and observations on ambiguous passages: [Col. 0019B] all much more accurately corrected than in previous printings. Catalogues of the Royal Library of Paris and the Casanatense Library.

## 1616

Douai, from the printing house of Balthasar Bellerus; in octavo, in three volumes. *The complete works of John Cassian the priest, whom some call a hermit and others an abbot. Newly revised, purged, and furnished with very extensive notes.* To these were added other short works on the same subject, a list of which the following page will display. Edited and prepared by Dom Alard Gazaeus, a Vedastine coenobite of the Benedictine Order.

The second volume consists of two parts, one of which begins with the preface to Conference XVIII, on page 881, which is the title page itself. The list of contents of both volumes appears here immediately after the title.

The first volume contains: [Col. 0019C] the twelve books *On the Institutes of the Coenobia*, with commentaries and notes; the Rule of Saint Pachomius, formerly translated into Latin by Saint Jerome, now also illustrated with scholia and notes; *Cassian’s Flowers*, or the more notable sayings collected from his works; and John Cassian’s seven books *On the Incarnation of Christ*.

The second volume contains: John Cassian’s twenty-four *Conferences of the Fathers*, illustrated with commentaries and notes; Denis the Carthusian’s *Catholic Doctrine*, substituted for Conference XIII; Saint Prosper of Aquitaine’s book *On the Grace of God and Free Will against the Collator*; the annotations, or censorial notes, of the Right Reverend Henry Cuychius, Bishop of Roermond, on the books of John Cassian; the statutes of two congregations, or general chapters, of the Order of Saint Benedict; the observations of Peter Ciacconius, priest of Toledo, [Col. 0019D] on John Cassian; and four indexes. The first is an index of passages of Sacred Scripture, according to the Vulgate edition, explained throughout this work; the second, of certain passages according to the version of the Seventy Interpreters; the third, of certain subjects and words occurring in Cassian’s text; and the fourth, of the commentaries and notes.

Also prefixed to the second volume are Saint Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury’s *Divine Poem on the Life of Monks*, and *Praise of the Monastic Life*, by an unknown author. Furthermore, what was worked on or taken care of in this latest edition—matters which the editor himself refers to six points—we shall present in his own words.

### I

First, I did not think it necessary to labor greatly over purging or reforming the Author’s text, since Cuychius and Ciacconius, men of the greatest learning and accuracy, who devoted vigorous effort to this matter, had left it to us sufficiently corrected and clarified. Nevertheless, I compared it with several printed and manuscript copies, and occasionally corrected or examined certain passages which they had overlooked or treated less fully. I also brought in the paraphrase of Denis the Carthusian and thereby shed additional light; yet I sometimes warned the reader—without prejudice to the authority of so great a man—that this paraphrast had departed from the author’s mind and meaning, leaving the matter to the reader’s judgment.

### II

I added almost continuous annotations. In them I not only explained certain Greek, barbarous, or less familiar words and expressions, but also examined, with as much ease and clarity as I could manage for the understanding of younger readers, more obscure statements and theological questions relating to the monastic institution, including many very useful matters that arose incidentally. From these, many commonplaces on monastic affairs may be drawn for daily and familiar use.

I freely admit, meanwhile, that I was sometimes assisted both by Cuychius’s notes and by those of Ciacconius. For the public benefit I therefore incorporated them with my own, while nevertheless attributing each contribution to its author and claiming nothing belonging to another. Nor did I forget the apt saying of Pliny to Vespasian: “It is generous and full of an honorable modesty to acknowledge through whom we have advanced.”

### III

Furthermore, I carefully observed the ancient rites and institutions of the early monks, both in the performance of divine offices and in their other ascetic exercises; and, as though painted on a panel, I placed them before the diligent reader for closer inspection and contemplation. From these, likewise, as from commonplaces, the student of monastic antiquities may understand through what authors and observers such rites and monastic observances—on which a large part of regular discipline depends—have been handed down to us as if from hand to hand.

### IV

But I especially had this in view, and for this principal reason devoted myself to Cassian: to explain, for the benefit and service of my fellow soldiers and brothers—namely, the coenobites of the Benedictine Order, to which God by his grace willed me to belong—as many and as important Rules of our most holy Father Benedict as lay within my power, with God’s help and as opportunity presented itself; and to refer and restore numerous passages of his work to Cassian’s writings, as to their prototype.

From this it plainly appears with what care and with how pious and diligent an emulation our most holy Father Benedict sought to imitate the ancient monks, to follow in their footsteps, and by his example and instruction to urge his own coenobites to imitate them.

### V

In addition, I illustrated and strengthened Cassian’s more notable sayings throughout with similar sayings and praises of the Holy Fathers Basil, Jerome, Augustine, Gregory, and others. I collected some of the choicer and briefer ones from them, like brighter little stars, and arranged them together at the end of the work, so that younger readers might more easily commit them to memory and fix them more firmly in their minds.

### VI

Finally, so that nothing in the course of this work might delay, offend, or in any way mislead the reader, I decided to add, besides our own annotations, the other observations and censorial notes of Cuychius and Ciacconius, and to place them in due order at the end. Thus, forewarned by these antidotal notes, anyone may afterward pass through Cassian without stumbling and need desire nothing further for the perfection of the work or the security of his soul.

I strongly recommend and advise that these observations be carefully read in advance by those who are not especially versed in such matters, but who wish to handle usefully and profitably the books of the *Conferences* and the other most useful works customarily read, as has been said, by the Holy Fathers, Benedict, Thomas Aquinas, and others. He therefore appended his notes immediately to the individual chapters, everywhere learned and full of practical value.

The preface is preceded by his dedicatory letter to Philip Caverellius, then superior of the Vedastine monastery at Arras, dated from his own residence and the provostship of Saint Michael, on the feast of the Apparition, 1615. Cuychius’s preface was also added. The entrance to both volumes is covered with congratulatory and anagrammatic poems addressed to the editor, including one in the second volume furnished with its own commentary. The title was printed from an engraved copperplate.

## 1617

Lyons, at the expense of Laurence Durand; in folio. *The Lives of the Fathers by John Cassian, excerpted from his books on the Institutes of the Renunciants and the Conferences.* In Heribert Rosweyde’s *Lives*, p. 563.

## 1628

Cologne Agrippina, at the expense of Anthony Hierat; in folio. *The four books of John Cassian, priest of Massilia, on the Institutes of the Coenobia, etc.; all from the revised edition of Alard Gazaeus.* In *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. V, part II.

## 1628

Arras, from John Baptist and William Riverius, under the sign of the Good Shepherd; in folio.

A new edition, again revised by the same editor and purged of the errors that had crept into the earlier one; rendered more illuminating by commentaries increased by a third; and further enriched with a new commentary on the books *On the Incarnation*, which had previously been lacking.

Besides what is promised in the title, the individual works have also been arranged in a new order. Thus, immediately after the *Institutes*, the *Conferences* follow, together with Denis the Carthusian’s *Doctrine* [Col. 0021D] and Prosper’s book *On Grace*. After these are inserted Pope Celestine’s letter, in defense of Prosper and Hilary, *On the Grace of God*, addressed to certain bishops of Gaul; likewise the canons of the Second Council of Orange, concerning free will, around the time of Pope Leo I; and Saint Prosper’s letter to Augustine.

Then, after Cuychius’s and Ciacconius’s observations, there is read a final annotation on Cassian’s doctrine, excerpted from Diego Álvarez, book I, disputation 2, section 3, *On the Aids of Divine Grace and the Powers of Free Will*. Finally, the seven books *On the Incarnation*, the Rule of Saint Pachomius, and the *Flowers* from Cassian are presented, up to the indexes; excluded from this body are those items which, although contained in the first edition, are absent from this new table of contents.

The text is marked by notes chapter by chapter [Col. 0022A] as in the first edition, and the notes are printed in double columns. There are two title pages: one typographical and the other engraved in copper.

## 1642

Paris, from Laurence Cottereau; in folio. *The complete works of John Cassian, with the commentaries of Alard Gazaeus, etc.* Catalogues of the Royal Library of Paris and the library of Cardinal Joseph Renato Imperiali.

## 1677

Lyons, from the Anissons; in folio. *The complete works of John Cassian from the edition of Alard Gazaeus.* In *Bibliotheca Maxima Patrum*, volume VII, p. 17 and following.

As the title indicates, this is a carefully printed second edition of Gazaeus. We infer from the brilliance of the type and the notable Wetstein device printed on the title page that it was produced by the Amsterdam press. The paper, however, is rough and raw.

# III. Manuscripts

Here it is permissible to record only those manuscripts which Cuychius used, since he not only did not think it right to conceal from readers where and on what grounds he altered the text—something he did only when all the manuscript copies agreed—but also voluntarily supplied variant readings about which he himself would not venture to decide, so that others might exercise their judgment. There are six in number, though he did not undertake to describe them.

1. The manuscript of Affligem Abbey in Brabant.

2. The manuscript of the regular canons at Corsendonck in Brabant.

3. The manuscript of the Bethlehem monastery of the regular canons near Louvain.

4. The manuscript of the regular canons at the Wood of the Lord Isaac near Nivelles.

5. The Plantinian manuscript.

[Col. 0023B] Would that Ciacconius, too, had at least identified in this manner the eight Vatican manuscripts which he professes to have collated.

# IV

Finally, we must mention a book whose stated purpose was indeed to present Cassian, after the labors of all earlier editors, in a more correct, fuller, and enlarged form, but whose author by no means won among scholars the favor he had hoped for.

Here is the title:

*Saint John Cassian Illustrated; or, A Chronology of the Life of Saint John Cassian, Abbot, and of the Monastery of Saint Victor, founded by him at Massilia, foremost among Western coenobia in antiquity, from the year of Christ 420. By the work and study of Father John Baptist Guesnay of Aix, theologian of the Society of Jesus.* Added is a list of the saints, illustrious men, abbeys, priories, cells, and churches dependent upon that monastery. Also included is a glossary of difficult subjects and words in the commentaries on Saint Cassian. Lyons, at the expense of Anthony Cellier, 1652, in quarto.

Take care, however, not to expect here anything resembling the work which Chiffletius undertook under the same title for Paulinus of Nola. What concerns the monastery is satisfactory enough, as might be expected from an author long engaged in these matters and richly supplied with ancient documents [Note: [Col. 0023D] Shortly afterward the same author produced a work entitled *Massilia Gentilis et Sacra*, which appeared at Lyons from the same bookseller in 1657, in folio.]. But what he relates about Cassian’s life consists of inventions born of an imagination playing with itself, and long ago rejected by everyone.

You will understand best from his own words what new material he introduced concerning Cassian’s doctrine. Guesnay admits that it would be ungrateful not to praise the work of Cassian’s editors; nevertheless, Cassian had not yet been restored to such dignity that it was no longer conceded that several further things of this kind might quietly and obscurely perish, and that he required additional eyes and hands.

He therefore hoped that Cassian would now emerge much more correct, fuller, and more enlarged than ever before. “For in these controversies,” he says, “I seem able to profess without rashness that I ought to be considered a sufficiently suitable witness, although in other respects I neither fail to recognize nor deny my own weakness. Since the matter concerns writings depending chiefly upon ancient codices and papers, I have spent more than twelve years in the most assiduous study of them and have discovered archives of exceptional richness, furnished above all with documents that faithfully and fully explain the beginnings of the monastery of Saint Victor at Massilia and of its patriarch and founder, Saint Cassian.”

It is easy to gather and judge in what respects the work is enlarged from the addition of the commentaries which we have undertaken to publish. In the first commentary we have faithfully collected from Cassian’s writings and arranged in many chapters the life and glorious deeds of Saint Cassian, scarcely touched upon by the older historians and for the most part unknown.

Then we added a second commentary in which the extremely rash presumption of certain people is most clearly refuted. They arrogated to themselves the sole right to pass judgment and decide concerning the writings of the ancients, to such an extent that, apart from what Saint Prosper rightly refutes and proves erroneous, they wished either at will and unjustly to cut away a large part of Cassian’s excellent works, or to deny that they were really his as they now exist, reducing them by their own censures and empty commentaries to the lowest classes of worthless writers.

We also added at the end of this volume I (?) a second commentary on his glory, composed in a new manner, as a kind of summary of the entire work, preserving the order of events and times, so that it might be evident to all how greatly the Church honored and esteemed this man for his holiness and learning.

We also wished to investigate unusual paths and to abandon the well-trodden ways of interpreting his statements according to the custom of other Doctors in explaining the remaining Fathers; nor did we wish to measure them, as some ignorant men do, by the length or brevity of the discourse, by ambiguity, inflection, or alteration of words.

The work consists of two books. The first, in sixty-four chapters, presents an image of Saint Cassian, or an idea of the religious life; the second treats, in twenty-nine chapters, of his glory and blessedness. From these titles of the books the author may seem to have sufficiently disclosed his purpose.

Whatever is useful in them is contained for the most part in the eight final chapters of the first book. We shall give their titles here:

- Chapter 57: “On Cassian’s Writings. Which works of Cassian are genuine and authentic?”
- Chapter 58: “Which are doubtful and spurious?”
- Chapter 59: “In what place, at what time, and in what language did he write?”
- Chapter 60: “Religious discipline is illustrated by the outstanding Institutes and examples of the same, and public piety is greatly advanced.”
- Chapter 61: “The Conferences, first published at Massilia and then elsewhere at different times, arouse immense movements of the spirit.”
- Chapter 62: “Has that same Cassian who flowed from his source, sound in doctrine and free from erasure, reached us intact?” This is asserted against Baronius.
- Chapter 63: “Did Cassian have favorable and kindly interpreters and defenders?” Here a long series of theologians is listed who attempted to interpret in a better sense what Cassian had stated less cautiously; and it is clear that the Society of Jesus has at all times presented itself as the patron of this interpretation.
- Chapter 64: “Catholic Doctors can err without the stain of heresy.”

Here is the end of his entire disputation and defense, which he directs in the words quoted above against all who do not admit that Cassian everywhere teaches orthodox doctrine:

“We ought reasonably to interpret the statements of Catholics in as favorable a sense as we can; but the statements of heretics we should judge, in the fullest hostility toward them, according to their heresy.”

[Col. 0025]

# PREFACE OF THE RIGHT REVEREND HENRY CUYCHIUS

[Col. 0025A] I have no doubt, benevolent and candid reader, that this study and labor which we have expended in elucidating Dom John Cassian and in purging and revising him, on the authority of ancient manuscripts, of countless errors that had crept in either through the carelessness of scribes and printers or for other reasons, will be disapproved by many who accuse this Author of ours of heretical contamination.

For Pope Gelasius, in Distinction XV, chapter “Sancta Romana,” numbers the works of John Cassian among the apocrypha. And blessed Prosper composed a book against the thirteenth Conference, which is almost entirely sprinkled with the remains of the Pelagian heresy, and entitled it *Against the Collator*.

Yet just as it cannot be denied that several obscure passages and errors are found both in that thirteenth Conference and in most of the others—errors which we have noted at the end of the entire work and against which, lest an unwary reader stumble, we have appended censorial notes, as it were antidotes and amulets—so we firmly maintain that these errors should be attributed not so much to Cassian himself as to the Collators whose opinions he says he reports.

This is chiefly demonstrated by the very preface placed before the *Conferences*, in which he promises to narrate faithfully not his own institutions but those of the Holy Fathers and the anchorites. Accordingly, in chapter 10 of Conference XX, after recalling of the abbot Theonas that, having separated from his wife, he had given himself over to the anchoritic life, he added:

“First I ask this of the reader: whether he approves or disapproves of this, let him grant that I am in every way free from slander, and let him praise or blame the author in this deed of his. For I, who have not pronounced my own opinion on this matter but have embraced the history of what happened in a simple narrative, ought justly, as I claim nothing for myself from the praise of those who approve the deed, so not to be struck by the ill will of those who disapprove it.”

Although he did not give this warning everywhere when he reports the errors of the Collators, he nevertheless seems to have removed all suspicion of error from himself when, at the very beginning of the entire work, he promised to narrate not his own opinions but those of the men whom he introduces as speakers, with the same fidelity in which he had received them from them.

I pass over the fact that the *Conferences* themselves frequently contain discordant, divergent, and conflicting opinions concerning the grace of Christ. Some, excluding grace, refer almost everything to free will; others, on the contrary, exalt grace in such a way that they seem to exclude free will. This contradiction of opinions may be detected not only in Conference XIII, as blessed Prosper observed, but also from time to time in the others.

For in chapter 10 of Conference III the abbot Paphnutius speaks as follows:

“By this it is clearly proved both that the beginning of our salvation comes through the Lord’s call, when he says, ‘Go out from your land,’ and that the completion of perfection and purity is likewise granted by him, when he says, ‘And come into the land which I shall show you’: that is, not a land which you can know by yourself or discover by your own effort, but one which I shall show you when you are not only ignorant of it but not even seeking it.”

And in chapter 12:

“No righteous person is sufficient for himself to obtain righteousness, unless divine mercy, moment by moment, places beneath the one who is stumbling and falling the support of its hand.”

To these may be added what is found in several subsequent chapters of that Conference, as well as what the abbot Daniel says in Conference V, chapter 15, and the abbot Serenus in Conference VII, chapter 20.

Since all these passages and many similar ones directly contradict what the abbot Chaeremon is said to have thought about the grace of Christ in Conference XIII, I cannot persuade myself that John Cassian—who, as the books he wrote on the Incarnation of Christ testify, possessed the highest intellectual skill both in refuting the opinions of heretics and in establishing and confirming our own—supported opinions so mutually opposed and contradictory.

He would have possessed an extremely small capacity for sound judgment if he had either failed to notice this conflict of opinions evident in the *Conferences* or had not guarded himself against it.

Furthermore, in these books on the Incarnation of the Word, which he wrote toward the end of his life at the request of Saint Leo, archdeacon of the city of Rome—who was Cassian’s contemporary and later became the first Roman pontiff of that name—he disputes against a certain Pelagian bishop of Antioch, as is clear from chapters 6 and 7 of the sixth book and chapter 31 of the final book.

He attacks and refutes this man’s errors with arguments so choice and powerful that it is plainly evident from them that Cassian in no way supported the Pelagian sect.

Nor can we tolerate the claim made by some that he was rejected, sent away, or expelled by blessed Chrysostom because of suspicion of this error, especially since they produce neither clear evidence nor certain documents for their suspicion. Chrysostom himself, moreover, because of the heresies concerning free will that were spreading in his time, sometimes extols its powers so highly that he might appear unfair toward the grace of Christ, although the matter is otherwise.

Therefore, since the cause of Cassian’s departure is wholly uncertain, and since the conclusion of the seventh book *On the Incarnation* plainly shows that Cassian always venerated Saint Chrysostom as his excellent and most approved teacher, I judge it rash to suspect anything sinister or uncertain concerning him.

Either he was expelled from the Church of Constantinople or Jerusalem by heretics, as Volaterranus reports; or the desire for solitude drove him to withdraw into Narbonese Gaul, in which Massilia is situated, a province unknown to him, where he founded two monasteries, one for men and the other for women; or finally, he migrated to Massilia because of his studies in the liberal disciplines and his moral seriousness.

The Romans likewise, in preference to a journey to Athens for the pursuit of learning, used to seek the Massilian school. For moral seriousness and maturity, as well as honorable studies, flourished in that city to such an extent that Plautus, in the *Casina*, called the customs of the Massilians excellent and most approved.

Marcus Tullius also wonderfully commends the same studies and customs, in several places and especially in his speech for Lucius Flaccus. These are his words:

“Nor do I pass you over, Massilia, who knew Lucius Flaccus as a soldier and quaestor. I would rightly say that the discipline and gravity of this state ought to be preferred not only to those of Greece but, I scarcely know whether, to those of all nations. Although so far removed from all the regions, disciplines, and languages of the Greeks, and although, at the ends of the earth, it is washed by the waves of barbarism and surrounded by the peoples of Gaul, it is governed by the counsel of its nobles in such a way that everyone can more easily praise its institutions than imitate them.”

Other works of Cassian himself testify how correctly he thought about the grace of Christ. In them he sets forth not what others believed, as in the *Conferences*, but his own judgment; this too we have noted in the first two censorial notes.

Among those works in which he speaks from his own judgment, besides the four books of the *Monastic Constitutions* and the eight books *On the Capital Vices*, we must count his seven books *On the Incarnation of the Word*. No one who reads them carefully and compares their thread of discourse with his earlier works will doubt that they were published and written by Cassian himself.

I pass over for the moment the fact that Trithemius and Gennadius, who composed catalogues of illustrious men, also number these books among Cassian’s works.

The earlier books appear to have been written with the purpose of handing down to posterity in them a certain complete and definitive form of a pious, religious, and monastic life. They are therefore worthy never to be put down by the most religious, because of the holy and salutary doctrines and examples they contain.

We have the most authoritative witnesses to this in Saint Benedict, Dominic, Thomas Aquinas, Denis the Carthusian, Ignatius, the first founder of the Society of Jesus, and others distinguished for the holiness of their lives and their monastic perfection. Delighted beyond measure by reading this Author, they devoted all their effort to learning his precepts, institutions, and *Conferences*, and applying them to practice.

The other books circulated under Cassian’s name—such as the *Theological Confession*, which some attribute to him, and the book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, which is entitled Cassian’s among the Dominicans of Liège—and any others that may be found, have been omitted by us, both because Gennadius and Trithemius do not attribute them to Cassian and because they do not bear the mark of his style.

It remains for me to explain in what language Cassian wrote, Greek or Latin. I see that this too has been questioned by some, because of the authority, as I suppose, of Trithemius, although one need not labor greatly to resolve the question.

Cassian himself gives us clear evidence in the preface to his *Conferences* that he wrote in Latin. There he addresses Bishop Leontius and his brother Helladius in these words:

“May your prayers obtain from him who judged us worthy either to see them, to be their disciples, or to share their company that he may grant us a clear memory of these traditions and an easy mode of speech with which to declare them; so that, explaining them as holily and completely as we received them from the Fathers themselves, we may in a certain sense present them incorporated in their own institutions, and, what is more, present them to you speaking in the Latin tongue.”

And in chapter 15 of Conference III, when he cites the Apostle’s words, “Our sufficiency is from God,” he says: “It can be expressed less literally in Latin but more clearly: ‘Our ability is from God.’”

Although, in recalling and citing passages of Sacred Scripture, he generally follows the reading of the Seventy-Two Interpreters, and although many obscure Greek and Greek-Latin words frequently present themselves during reading—in connection with which we have appended a catalogue and interpretation after the end of the entire work—nevertheless, because he wrote near Massilia, where his memory is still celebrated, and not in Greece, and because he wrote to the Latin bishops of Gaul, he ought to have used no language other than Latin, in which they were versed and in which he himself, now living near the Massilian school, had become practiced.

Nor has anyone ever heard of a translator of Cassian, nor has any Greek copy, whether manuscript or printed, so far as we have been able to see, ever been brought to light.

As for Cassian’s own text, we have rescued it from almost countless errors and corruptions by collating ancient manuscript copies and the paraphrastic translation of Denis the Carthusian, which agrees with manuscript codices in many passages, as may be observed from the censorial notes whose tables we present after the end of the work.

The division into chapters, which in many places differs in the manuscripts from that found in printed copies, generally agrees with Denis’s paraphrase. Nevertheless, we judged that we ought not rashly to depart from the division hitherto found in printed books, except that we divided the books *On the Incarnation*, which had previously been undivided, into chapters.

To all this we added two new indexes collected by us from Cassian’s entire work: the first, of passages of divine Scripture explained by the Author; the second, of notable and memorable matters.

It remains, kind and candid reader, for you to receive this labor of ours with the same candor with which we offer it, and to use it happily for the honor of God, the welfare of the commonwealth, and the salvation of your soul.

Farewell.

From our monastery of the White Ladies at Louvain, on the Kalends of March, 1578.

[Col. 0029]

# PREFACE OF ALARDUS GAZAEUS

[Note: [Col. 0029C] Before you begin reading the devout work of this eloquent and holy author, whom the ancient Fathers esteemed so highly—especially our Father Benedict, and the divine Thomas, the sun of the theological schools, so that they scarcely ever laid him aside—I do not doubt that you will wish to know who that Alardus Gazaeus is who has illuminated Cassian for you with such brilliant commentaries.

To satisfy this desire of yours, I think I may appropriately place before you the following words from Ecclesiasticus 11: “Do not praise a man for his appearance, nor despise a man for his outward look: the bee is small among flying creatures, and its fruit has the beginning of sweetness.” By these words the Wise Man teaches us to judge not according to outward appearance but according to fruit. A splendid face and appearance often conceal a baser spirit; and the Apostle Paul, in answer to those who spoke against him, saying, “His letters indeed are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible,” considered it fitting to reply: “Let him who is such a one consider that what we are in word by letters when absent, such also are we in deed when present” (2 Cor. 10). That is to say, although small in body, he was nevertheless magnificent in work and speech.

The comparison of the Wise Man in Ecclesiasticus beautifully illustrates this. For neither the eagle with its great wings, nor the phoenix with its long life, nor any other larger bird deserves the praise merited by the smallest of all flying creatures, the little bee, which produces by its artful work in the honeycomb a fruit that is the beginning and measure of every sweetness. For, as the Philosopher teaches, the first thing in each genus is the measure of the others; and honey is here called the beginning of sweetness because it is the measure of all sweet things. Thus the Greek word properly signifies not only the beginning but also the primacy of sweetness.

Our Alardus Gazaeus likewise, among the flying creatures—by which name understand contemplative souls suspended in continual reflection upon divine things—was indeed small and slight in body and outward appearance, and, as they said of the Apostle, “weak in bodily presence and contemptible in speech,” because of the humility of spirit by which he avoided every display of himself. Yet in mind, and in deed and writing—as you see here, reader—he was truly strong and weighty, so that his fruit holds the beginning and primacy of sweetness in this kind of commentary, offering you, from his flower-laden workmanship, reflections sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.

Alardus was the eldest of the brothers who were also distinguished among the flying creatures of heaven and renowned through the writings they published. Angelinus Gazaeus, a priest and religious of the Society of Jesus, was outstanding for varied learning and piety and was also celebrated for his sacred poetry. Nicolaus Gazaeus, a disciple of Saint Francis, was commendable for the distinguished sermons he published. Our Alardus, however, though physically smaller than they, was superior to them and to many others in the sweetness of his writings. From early childhood he entered the Order of our holy Father Benedict at the monastery of Saint Vedastus in Arras, and lived there blamelessly until his sixtieth year. His health was generally weak, yet, struggling against it with constant courage of spirit, he remained continually occupied in studies of great importance.

He also held major offices in the administration of temporal affairs, not without praise; yet even amid that administration he devoted himself to the beloved studies of learned contemplation with an intensity scarcely credible. Death carried him away while he was absorbed in this literary occupation, although he had first left these monuments of his intellect to benevolent readers. When you have examined them, excellent reader, pray well for the soul of your Alardus, and wish that among the inhabitants of Paradise he may forever taste the fountain of eternal sweetness which here, like an ingenious bee, he has fashioned for you as this honeycomb of sweet reflections. Farewell.

—Prefatory notice of the Leipzig editor.]

[Col. 0029A] Behold, we are printing again Cassian, so often printed and reprinted, and publishing him once more in a somewhat newly arranged form. Many, I know, will be astonished; some will accuse us of useless labor, others perhaps of rashness, because, after editions so recent and widely circulated, we seem to be undertaking the same work again, repeating what has already been done, or rolling the stone of Sisyphus.

To pass over earlier and more ancient editions, not many years ago—namely, in the year of Our Lord 1578—the Reverend Master Heinrich Cuychius, a theologian of Louvain and afterward bishop of Roermond, published from the Plantin press the works of John Cassian, purged of many errors. He also added to certain passages highly learned critical observations, together with explanations of some obscure words and statements; these additions are now commonly handled and circulated by many people.

Shortly afterward Peter Ciaconius, a priest of Toledo commended by Baronius (*Martyrologium*, 14 May), published another edition, which he enlarged and illuminated with new observations, censures, and other additions. We have received it as first published at Rome in 1588 and later brought here, a few years ago, from the Lyon edition in 1606.

Why, then, this new and so premature edition? Who, at first sight, would not attack it or regard it with suspicion, when it intrudes itself upon editions so recent that they have scarcely ceased sweating from the press?

There is also the fact that the Author himself might seem to some either suspect or less worthy of esteem because of that ancient and widely known controversy concerning the grace of God and the free will of man, as well as for other causes that are not unknown. Hence it might perhaps seem preferable for him to remain hidden rather than to come forth so often into public view.

Why, then, has such great labor again been expended on printing and polishing him? I hope, however, for fairer judges and critics—men who know Cassian himself well and who have accurately recognized what has been achieved in this edition beyond the others. Before explaining that, I thought it appropriate first to say a little about the Author and then about the work. These points, gathered both from Cassian himself and from other writers, will contribute considerably to his commendation and will at once inform and delight the reader’s mind with some knowledge of antiquity and historical truth.

There is much worthy of notice in the encomia of distinguished men, which we shall append to this preface. His very name and surname, his origin, order, office, dignity, and finally the title of sanctity attributed to him by certain writers—all these matters deserve to be considered in order and explained to some extent.

First, as regards his name, the initial observation is that the ancients more commonly called him by his surname than by his personal name. For Gennadius, Cassiodorus, and others call him only Cassian [Cassiodorus, *On Divine Institutions*, ch. 29; Sigebert, under the year 427], although, on the authority of Saint Prosper, it is clear that he was called John as his proper name, and Cassian by surname. Trithemius and others likewise used this designation.

In the second place, he is described as a Scythian by nation. In contrast, Honorius calls him an African [Honorius of Autun, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Cassian], perhaps because he thought that Scythia was situated in Africa, whereas others place it in Asia [Pliny, book 5, chapter 9, and book 6, chapter 17; Pomponius Mela, book 1; see Ortelius’s maps].

This would provide an occasion for saying more about the Scythian people and region. Omitting what does not pertain to our present purpose, however, I think that from this designation—confirmed by the testimony of many—I may draw a not implausible conjecture: namely, that our Cassian, converted to the faith and Catholic religion through the work of Saint Chrysostom, placed himself at Chrysostom’s service and under his discipline [Baronius, vol. 5, under the year of Christ 400].

For concerning the conversion of the Scythians, brought about and completed through Blessed John Chrysostom, Theodoret records the following (*Ecclesiastical History*, book 5, chapter 30):

“When he saw,” he says, “that the Scythian nation was held entangled in the snares of Arian teaching, he diligently endeavored to rescue it from them. To capture this prey he devised the following means. He ordained as priests, deacons, and readers several men who spoke the same language, and assigned them a single church. Through their ministry he reconciled many who had fallen into error to the Church.”

And in the following chapter:

“When he learned that the Scythians called Nomads, who lived beside the Danube, eagerly desired salvation but had no one to quench their thirst with the streams of saving doctrine, he sought out men who imitated apostolic labors and placed them in charge of instructing those people.”

So far Theodoret.

When these statements are compared with the testimony of Gennadius and others, and weighed in the balance of reason, scarcely anyone can justly hesitate to accept one of the following alternatives as established: either that Cassian, born of the Scythian people, was brought over to the orthodox faith among his own countrymen through the work and efforts of Saint Chrysostom, as stated; or—what is more—that he was ordained and appointed by the same man, whose disciple he had become, to convert his nation together with other priests and deacons. But I shall speak of this discipleship and ordination later.

For now, so far as we can, let us adhere to the order and chronology of events. No one can doubt that, before entering the discipleship or discipline of Chrysostom, Cassian had spent a long period—perhaps from the very years of childhood—among monks, both Egyptian and Palestinian. He was instructed by them in the first rudiments of both the Christian religion and monastic formation, and thus embraced the monastic life and became a monk.

He himself states this most expressly in several places. First, in the preface to Bishop Castor, to whom he dedicated the twelve books *On the Institutes of the Coenobia*. Among the reasons he gives for being less able at that time to respond adequately and accurately to Castor’s wish that he recall and explain the institutions of the monks whom he had observed in Egypt and Palestine, he offers this second one:

“For the things,” he says, “which, from our childhood, while established among those same men and encouraged by their daily exhortations and examples, we either attempted to do, learned, or perceived by sight, we are now scarcely able to retain in their entirety, having been separated for so many years from their company and from the imitation of their way of life.”

He speaks no less openly in the first chapter of the Eleventh Conference, where he begins as follows:

“When, residing in a coenobium in Syria, after the first beginnings of faith and after our progress had advanced to some degree, we began to desire a greater grace of perfection, we immediately resolved to go to Egypt and, penetrating even the most remote desert of the Thebaid, to visit the many saints whose glory fame had spread throughout the world, if not in the hope of imitating them, at least in order to know them. Thus, after completing our voyage, we arrived at an Egyptian town called Thennesus.”

So far there.

Again, throughout many chapters of Conference 17, he clearly shows how anxious Germanus and Cassian were to return to their coenobium, and how carefully Abbot Joseph relieved them of this concern. Cassian therefore adds in chapter 31 of the same Conference:

“Although afterward we were somewhat careless about our promise, nevertheless, when the number of seven years had been completed, we gladly fulfilled our pledge. For we hastened back to our coenobium at the very time when we were confident of obtaining permission to return to the desert, and so forth. We restored our former affection; and at last, when the thorn of our pledge had been completely drawn out, while they too accompanied us with joy, we returned to the hidden solitude of Scetis.”

From all this it is perfectly clear that John Cassian, when he was scarcely more than a boy, embraced the Christian faith and monastic life among monks and was bound by the laws of monastic obedience [see the note on Conference 11, chapter 1]. He did so in a coenobium in Syria, which elsewhere he more explicitly calls the Bethlehemite monastery, at that time a celebrated institution. He frequently mentions it elsewhere as well [*Institutes*, book 3, chapter 4; book 4, chapter 31], together with his renunciation of the world, his profession, and the monastic formation he received there.

In that coenobium he seems to have formed a particularly close friendship and fellowship with Germanus, a monk of the same profession and monastery, although perhaps older and more advanced in age. From this it followed that, after scarcely two years had passed there—whether from a desire for greater perfection or for some other reason—they obtained permission from their elders to leave the monastery and together undertook a long and extremely difficult pilgrimage. They visited many of the deserts of Egypt, Scetis, and other regions, and held familiar conversations and meetings with many holy and especially revered Fathers who lived in remote and hidden places and were renowned for their sanctity. With great eagerness of mind and devotion they discussed divine matters, especially those relating to the attainment of perfection in the monastic life.

Thus Cassian later found both the occasion and the subject for writing the *Conferences of the Fathers*. By the term “Conferences” he intended nothing other than the familiar meetings and conversations he had held with those Fathers, and the salutary instructions he had privately received from them. This is made certain and indisputable by many passages in the *Conferences*.

In the first chapter of the First Conference, he writes of this pilgrimage and of his inseparable companionship with Germanus:

“When, together with the holy Abbot Germanus, with whom from the very beginning of our training and the rudiments of spiritual warfare there was afterward such an inseparable companionship, both in the coenobium and in the desert, that everyone used to say, to signify the equality of our fellowship and purpose, that one mind and soul dwelt in two bodies, I went into the desert of Scetis seeking Abbot Moses and desiring to be established by his instruction. We likewise sought from that same abbot, with abundant tears, a word of edification, and so forth.”
