Again, in chapter 1 of the Sixteenth Conference, when Abbot Joseph asked whether they were biological brothers, they replied:

“Not by carnal but by spiritual brotherhood were they bound, and from the beginning of their renunciation they had always been joined by an inseparable union, both in the pilgrimage undertaken by them for the sake of spiritual warfare and in their devotion to the coenobium.”

In chapter 1 of the Eleventh Conference they relate that, from the coenobium in Syria—the Bethlehemite monastery, namely, in which they lived—they went to Egypt, penetrated the most remote desert of the Thebaid, and from there met or visited many Fathers in the farther regions of Egypt.

Finally, in chapter 5 of the same Conference, Germanus says the following to Abbot Cheremon on his own behalf and Cassian’s:

“At least this should be gained from so great a labor of travel: that we have hastened here from the beginnings of the Bethlehemite coenobium, out of desire for your instruction and love of our progress.”

So far he.

Although it cannot be determined with certainty how much time they spent on this distant journey, since it is nowhere expressly stated, nevertheless, because they declare in the final chapter of Conference 17 that they completed seven years in the region and desert of the Thebaid alone, it is reasonable to conclude that a considerable period was devoted to the remainder of their pilgrimage. It should therefore not seem surprising that, because of his long and continuous association, companionship, and residence with anchorites and hermits, Cassian was also given the title of hermit by many.

“But how,” someone may ask, “and for what reason did Cassian and his Germanus, after so long a pilgrimage, come into the power and familiarity of John Chrysostom and become enrolled among his disciples?”

Although I have no certain information about this, I would believe that it happened for one of two reasons, or perhaps for both. Either Chrysostom, having learned more accurately of their sanctity and the fervor of their religion, summoned them to himself so that through their teaching, counsel, and work he might recall to a sounder mind certain Origenist monks who at that time were causing various disturbances in the East [Baronius, under the year 403]—a course he greatly desired to pursue—while Theophilus of Alexandria was deciding that they should be treated more harshly.

Hence hostilities and great disagreements broke out between these Fathers. Or rather, because at that same time two factions of monks in Egypt and Palestine—the Anthropomorphites and the Origenists—were contending with one another in mutual hatred and disputation, Germanus and Cassian, lest by inclining toward one side or the other they should be led into error, may have fled for refuge to Blessed Chrysostom, patriarch and chief teacher of the Eastern Church and standard-bearer of truth. In this way, following the Apostle’s words (Gal. 2), they took care for their faith and salvation, lest they should run or had run in vain. Received kindly by Chrysostom and confirmed in Catholic doctrine, they afterward remained in his service and under his discipline.

Whatever the circumstances may have been, Cassian certainly was a disciple of Saint Chrysostom. This is testified not only by Trithemius and others; Cassian himself openly acknowledges and professes it. Indeed, he attributes whatever he knew to Chrysostom’s generosity at the end of his work *On the Incarnation* (book 7, chapter 31), where, among other distinguished statements about Chrysostom, he says:

“Finally, may he himself commend to you these things also which have been written by me. For what I have written, he taught me; and therefore believe that this work is not so much mine as his, because a stream derives from its source, and whatever is thought to belong to the disciple ought wholly to be referred to the honor of the teacher.”

Cassian wrote these and other words about Chrysostom to the people of Constantinople with great praise, honoring the memory of his teacher with a profoundly grateful and devoted spirit.

But let us now come to the fourth honorary title attributed to him in the praises mentioned above: that of deacon, or diaconate.

Whether that devout Father had perhaps begotten Cassian in Christ, among his Scythian people, through salutary and orthodox teaching, or whether, as a wise teacher, he had certainly chosen him as a disciple and pupil of his doctrine, he judged him, as bishop, worthy of this office and ministry. Besides the assertions of Gennadius and Trithemius, Cassian himself gratefully acknowledges this in the passage cited above, where he recalls that he was adopted by John of blessed memory for the sacred ministry and offered to God.

The deacon Theodore of Rome likewise confirms it in his dialogue with Palladius. Why should we not go a step further and, when we hear that Cassian was ordained deacon by John, patriarch of Constantinople, understand him to have been not merely initiated into the order and office of the diaconate but also raised and advanced to the dignity of archdeacon?

Why, indeed, should he not also be said to have been ordained subdeacon by the same man, unless “deacon” is being used antonomastically—that is, to mean archdeacon, or first among the deacons? For in former times, unlike today, it was not the custom of the Church for priests to serve as archdeacons. Rather, from the entire order and number of deacons, a very few, and those the most suitable, were chosen as archdeacons. They served the bishop or pontiff immediately, like eyes serving the head, and watched more diligently on his behalf in the house of God.

Thus we read of Laurence, the celebrated martyr and levite of the Roman Church; Vincent in Valencia; Aldebert in Utrecht in more recent memory; and others elsewhere. If such men had been promoted to the honor of the priesthood, they would have ceased to be or to be called deacons or archdeacons.

It seems that, through the prerogative of this dignity—namely, the archdiaconate—together with the other endowments and virtues that accompanied it, Cassian eventually achieved such standing that he was selected from among the leading clergy of the Church of Constantinople to undertake a mission on Chrysostom’s behalf.

An authoritative witness to this is that same ancient writer Theodore. Among the other embassies sent on behalf of Chrysostom, who had been driven into exile, from the Church of Constantinople to Pope Innocent of Rome, he describes this embassy of the priest Germanus and the deacon Cassian in fourth place, beginning as follows:

“After Palladius, the priest Germanus and the deacon Cassian, men of great religion, brought letters from the entire clergy of John. They stated that the Church itself had suffered tyranny, its bishop having been forcibly expelled by soldiers and sent into exile,” and so forth.

Pope Innocent likewise, writing back to the clergy and people of that same Church of Constantinople, began as follows:

“From the letters of your charity which you sent through Germanus the priest and Cassian, and so forth.”

Baronius, discussing this embassy and the other envoy, Cassian the deacon, writes:

“Cassian is mentioned”—he says, “in the letter of Pope Innocent to the clergy of Constantinople. We think that this Cassian is the one whose work is the *Conferences of the Fathers*. For Gennadius also records that this same man was ordained deacon by John Chrysostom. Thus anyone who wishes to maintain that this Cassian was a different person must assert that there were two disciples of John Chrysostom with the same name and office—two Cassians, both deacons.”

So Baronius, confirming that the Cassian who acted as Chrysostom’s envoy and the Cassian who wrote the *Conferences* were one and the same.

To this I add, by the same reasoning, that there would have to be not only two Cassians but likewise two priests named Germanus, disciples and contemporaries of the same Chrysostom. Otherwise one would have to admit that one was the companion and colleague of that Cassian who acted as Chrysostom’s envoy, while the other was the companion and associate of our author of the *Conferences* during his pilgrimage and monastic profession. Who could accept this when no authority or memory from antiquity supports it?

[Col. 0036A] From these facts, I believe, you can easily perceive, reader, how empty and futile is the opinion of certain people who have written that Cassian, after being ordained deacon by Saint Chrysostom, was expelled and sent away several years later. They offer no reason or probable argument for this suspicion, especially since no ancient writer is known to have branded Cassian with such a mark.

Let them tell us, I beg, when he was expelled by Chrysostom himself—he who is known to have remained in Chrysostom’s service even after his exile and to have acted as his envoy to Pope Innocent; he who praised the memory of Chrysostom after his death with such great commendations and encomia; he who, many years after Chrysostom’s death, gave so illustrious a testimony of his affection and respect for him that he left no trace whatsoever, not even the slightest, of any suspicion of hostility.

Cardinal Baronius wisely observed that the occasion of this error arose because, when Cassian was found to have been expelled with other clergy of the same Church on behalf of John Chrysostom, people carelessly or thoughtlessly imagined that he had been expelled by John himself. In fact, however, he became an exile with the others not from Chrysostom but for Chrysostom and on his account.

Let us proceed to other matters.

After completing that embassy, what did Cassian do? Where did he turn after he had subsequently been deprived of so great a father and patron as Chrysostom? Baronius summarizes the matter in a few words:

“After this, Cassian went to Egypt, where he began to cultivate the monastic life; from there he drew the subject for writing the *Conferences of the Fathers*. There is an extant letter of Isidore of Pelusium to Cassian, written when he was undertaking the profession of the monastic life, in which Isidore especially admonished him that he must restrain his tongue.”

Baronius uses this style of expression as though he wished to indicate that only after completing the embassy on behalf of Chrysostom did Cassian go to Egypt and begin to cultivate and profess the monastic life.

Taken precisely in this sense, however, and without support from any other author, that opinion cannot stand alongside Cassian’s own words. We have already shown, with the clarity of midday, that Cassian cultivated the monastic life not only before the embassy but long before any knowledge of or association with Chrysostom—indeed, from the very rudiments of his childhood—and openly professed it both in the coenobium and in the desert.

Nevertheless, it is quite possible, and very easy to believe, that after completing his embassy and after Blessed Chrysostom died not long afterward, Cassian, overcome by grief and weariness with human affairs, and stirred by the memory and revived desire for the former companionship and society of the holy Fathers, returned once more to Egypt and Palestine. There he cultivated the monastic life among the monks, absorbed more deeply in his mind the teaching he had received in his early years, and committed it to memory, later setting it down in written works.

This, it may be believed, is what Baronius intended. Yet he can scarcely be excused for expressing it in such a way that he seems to indicate that Cassian began only then.

As for the letter of Isidore of Pelusium, in which Cassian is seriously admonished to restrain the license of his tongue, I agree with Baronius that it was written to our Cassian the monk—especially since it is established that Isidore was Cassian’s contemporary and a fellow disciple of the same teacher, Chrysostom. I do not, however, believe that it was written at the time and age proposed by Baronius, but much earlier, when Cassian was still a young man living in that Bethlehemite coenobium.

It would have been excessively unbecoming and incongruous for Cassian, already advanced in age and distinguished both by the office he had held under Chrysostom and by the highly honorable embassy he had undertaken to the supreme pontiff—indeed, a man illustrious and conspicuous for his religion—to be admonished, like a child, about silence and the restraint of his tongue. Anyone can easily judge this from the very context of the letter.

As for the reason or occasion on which Cassian finally crossed from Egypt or Palestine into Gaul, reached Massilia, the noble trading center of Narbonese Gaul, I know of no writer who has reported it. Nevertheless, I think it should be attributed to the calamity of that period and to the wickedness of the heretics.

For in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 416, that Bethlehemite monastery in which Cassian had professed the monastic life was invaded, plundered, and almost destroyed by the Pelagians, with the connivance of John, bishop of Jerusalem—so it is believed, out of hatred for Saint Jerome, who was still alive—as Baronius reports in his *Annals*. Innocent, pope of Rome, wrote letters to Jerome on this matter.

Because of these disturbances, it seems entirely credible that Cassian, returning from that long pilgrimage and unable to remain there safely and peacefully, turned toward the regions of Gaul and finally, by God’s providence, chose Massilia as a seat and dwelling place of piety and religion.

From this, I suspect, arose the opinion of certain writers who said that Cassian, driven out of the Church of Jerusalem by the heretics, crossed over to Massilia. That he settled at Massilia, however, and afterward remained there for a long time until the end of his life, is clearly declared not only by the commendations of Gennadius and Trithemius but also established with complete certainty by the testimony of Cassian himself and of Saint Prosper.

For Cassian himself indicates, both in his prefaces and elsewhere, plainly enough that, while already living in the western regions of Gaul and the Gallic provinces, he committed both the *Institutes* and the *Conferences* to writing, dedicating them to several Gallic bishops known and familiar to him. Prosper, moreover, testifies that Cassian was regarded at Massilia as an eminent and eloquent writer.

Since Prosper elsewhere indicates that Cassian belonged to the priestly order when he was engaged in writing the *Conferences*, it is reasonable to conclude that, earlier, in view of his piety and learning, he had been admitted and ordained to the priesthood—just as Gennadius and Trithemius also relate—either by the bishop of Massilia or by some other bishop of Gaul. Hence Pope Gelasius calls Cassian a priest of Gaul.

Afterward, as he burned more intensely each day with a growing zeal for advancing piety and religion and securing the salvation of souls, and as he had led many Christians of both sexes in those regions to pursue the path of evangelical perfection by word and example, the same authors report that he founded two monasteries near Massilia, one for men and the other for women. There he laid distinguished and solid foundations for establishing and transmitting to later generations the regular and monastic discipline.

Accordingly, the title of abbot and coenobiarch was afterward deservedly bestowed upon him—unless one prefers to refer it to the ancient custom by which elder or holier anchorites were habitually called *abba* in Syriac or *father* in Latin, the terms being used interchangeably. Cassian likewise commonly calls his Germanus “abbot.”

Nor should we pass over the related and closely connected, no less honorary, title *domnus*, which appears in the inscription of Castor’s letter: “To DOMNUS Cassian, abbot of Massilia.”

Although this word is less purely Latin, it had been customary in the Church for many centuries and was regularly applied to very distinguished men and, at times, even to saints. Apart from the testimony of this letter and the very ancient litanies of the Church—which call the supreme pontiff *domnus apostolicus*—there are many other testimonies from the ancient Fathers.

The first is that of Evodius, bishop of Uzalis, in the books *On the Miracles of Saint Stephen* preserved by Saint Augustine. There he frequently calls the protomartyr Saint Stephen *domnus Stephanus*, and speaks of “my lord of Uzalis,” meaning the leading man of that place.

The second is Saint Benedict, chapter 63 of the Rule, where he establishes the following concerning the title of the abbot:

“Let the abbot—because he is believed to represent Christ—be called DOMNUS and ABBOT, not by his own assumption but in honor and love of Christ.”

The third is Gregory of Tours, who, speaking of Saint Martin in book 10, at the end, says: “Lord Martin.”

Finally, there is Gregory the Great, who in several of his letters calls honored men and women *domni* and *donnae*.

It therefore appears that, according to the ancient usage of speech, the word *Dominus* was customarily attributed to God alone as His proper title, whereas *domnus* was used commonly for saints or distinguished men—not only bishops but also men of lower rank, and especially abbots.

In former times this seemed to accord with Christian modesty and simplicity: out of reverence for the divine majesty, since one commonly says of God, “Thus says the Lord,” and similar expressions, they called God alone *Dominus*, while they more willingly called honored human beings *domni*, using the shortened form—*domnus* being formed from *dominus* by syncopation—rather than *domini*. This is attested by that verse well known to our ancestors:]

Say “the heavenly Lord,” but call a mortal “Domnus.” There remains one final title of sanctity, with which our Cassian too is adorned by the praises of not one person only, but of many. For Peter of Equila expressly lists him in his catalogue of the saints and designates him “Saint Cassian, priest and confessor.” Gennadius likewise honors him with the title of sanctity in these words:

“Saint Eucherius also gathered into one volume certain little works of Saint Cassian, written in an expansive style, recasting them in a dignified course of expression.”

Trithemius likewise affirms that he died at Marseilles, not without a reputation for sanctity. But what Dionysius Richelieu, the Carthusian, thought of Cassian and his holiness, he openly shows in the prefaces to his paraphrase, when he repeatedly calls him “the venerable, most devout Father, worthy of eternal remembrance,” and at other times “the most illustrious and foremost teacher of all religious.” But what eulogy could be more splendid and distinguished than that of Castor, bishop of Apt—who had commissioned Cassian to write the *Institutions*—when he greets Cassian as “Domnus,” adorned with the special glory of sanctity and worthy of remembrance in every respect?

Who, then, would dare to withdraw faith from so many and such distinguished witnesses, or begrudge our Cassian the title of sanctity [Col. 0039B] attributed to him, or mock it? I am truly surprised that Doctor Cuychius, when he placed the letter “D.” followed by a point before John Cassian in every inscription, as a mark of honor or title, did not make clear whether he intended it to signify *Divus*, *Domnus*, or *Dominus*—unless he knew that among Christian writers it was a familiar and ordinary practice for *Divus* to be marked by that sign without ambiguity. Since, however, I have not found it in the older copies, I thought it better to omit it, without any disparagement of the Author or of anyone else.

I do not write this as though I dared to enroll our Cassian in the register of the divine and blessed, or to pronounce with certainty upon his sanctity. Rather, I have thought it appropriate to bring forward and present to the reader what serious and learned men have thought about him, so that each judgment may be weighed according to its own merit and significance [Col. 0039C]. For, unfortunately, this praise of sanctity has been greatly diminished and obscured among Catholics by certain errors with which Cassian seems to have been stained—whether in truth or in the opinion of many—and thereby a considerable blemish has been inflicted upon him. Yet it is certainly very difficult to determine from his writings with certainty whether he himself really held such views and wrote in accordance with his own judgment, as is commonly charged against him, or whether he merely reported and expressed the opinions of others in his writings.

I think that, moved by this ambiguity, Pope Gelasius, in the council held at Rome, included Cassian’s works among the apocrypha, chiefly because in the Thirteenth Conference and elsewhere he had spoken about the grace of God and the free choice of man [Col. 0039D] in the manner of the Pelagians, and had been convicted of this by Prosper of Aquitaine in a special work published against him. Because of this warning and rebuke by Saint Prosper, Cassian’s writings came to be read more cautiously, and indeed were corrected by some. Above all, the *Conferences* themselves—for Cassiodorus also warned his monks about this matter—were found to have been amended by certain persons, lest, although otherwise most useful and salutary for all religious who labor in the pursuit of perfection, anyone should happen to draw poison from them instead of medicine.

For it is not believable that the holy Fathers Benedict, Dominic, Thomas, and others would have held Cassian’s *Conferences* in such high esteem, and would have recommended them so strongly and without scruple [Col. 0040A], unless they had found them cleansed and purified of at least their principal errors. Saint Eucherius of Lyon, then a presbyter of that Church, seems to have been the first of all to accomplish this. While making a concise collection of Cassian’s works, he reduced what seemed useful to an epitome, as was noted above from Gennadius.

What Eucherius undertook in Gaul, Victor undertook in Africa, as Cassiodorus testifies:

> “Victor, bishop of Martyritanus in Africa, purified Cassian’s sayings in this way, with the Lord’s help; and he added what was lacking, so that the palm in these matters may rightly be awarded to him. We believe that he should quickly be sent to us from the regions of Africa, among others.”

Thus Cassiodorus. Baronius, however, thinks that Victor was disappointed in his hope and did not receive what he expected from Africa. For Ado, bishop of Vienne, says that Cassiodorus himself prepared this work, when, speaking of Cassian, he writes:

> “Cassiodorus the Senator of Ravenna, wishing to purify his errors, was not able to do so fully in every respect.”

Finally, Dionysius the Carthusian seems to have accomplished something of the same kind in his paraphrase, when in certain places he omitted erroneous opinions and substituted and inserted true, Catholic, and orthodox doctrine. You see, reader, how much labor learned men have expended in thoroughly purging this work and adapting and polishing it in every respect for the benefit of its readers.

Moreover, lest these matters—which seem in some degree to detract from Cassian and his writings—should offend the minds of the less learned, turn them away from reading and handling his works [Col. 0040C], or make them more sluggish, I have thought it necessary to give the reader a serious warning about them.

First, concerning the censure or decree of Gelasius: it must not be understood as though the pontiff had entirely condemned the writings—or, as he calls them, the little works—of Cassian and all the others named there, or had altogether forbidden them to be read. Rather, he did not wish them to be read publicly in the Church or to possess canonical authority, because certain errors had been mixed into them or because their authors were somewhat suspect.

This is clear both from the word *ἀπόκρυφον* (*apokryphon*), which signifies nothing other than something hidden, concealed, or secret, and from the decree itself, in which the pontiff plainly distinguishes three classes or orders of books. In the first class he lists the canonical and authentic books [Col. 0040D]—namely, sacred Scripture and the works of the holy Fathers—which the Catholic Church receives and approves and publicly uses in ecclesiastical offices.

In the second class he places the apocryphal books. These he forbids to be read and proclaimed publicly in the Church, but he does not in any way prohibit their private reading or their reading outside the Church. Cassian’s little works are named among many others in this class.

In the third place, finally, he sets the books of heretics and schismatics, which are utterly condemned and rejected by the Church. What Catholic, then, ever hesitated to read, or discouraged the reading of, the works of those ancient authors—Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, Arnobius, Lactantius, Victorinus, and others—because the same decree placed them among the apocrypha? Especially since what they got wrong, and therefore what must be avoided, has for many centuries been clearly known and established [Col. 0041A].

Or by what reasoning did the most holy men, Doctors Benedict, Cassiodorus, Dominic, Thomas, Dionysius, Ignatius, and others themselves embrace and venerate Cassian with such devotion, and recommend him to others for embracing, turning over, and frequent reading—both by their example and in their writings and many encomia—if they had not judged him to be a most useful, indeed a foremost, mirror of monastic life, and, apart from a few blemishes, an otherwise beautiful body of work commendable in every respect?

Yet I seem to see before me an acute adversary standing on the opposite side: that Prosper, bishop of Rhegium, who, as has been said, published a special book against the *Collator* and sharpened his pen against Cassian—though he suppressed his name—and severely attacked his Thirteenth Conference.

What shall I say here, friendly reader? Should I, with Gennadius of Marseilles, excuse Cassian by attacking or disparaging Saint Prosper, a man beyond all exception and a most approved teacher of the Church? Far be it from me. Cassian is certainly a friend; but truth is a greater friend.

No sane person will deny that Cassian erred seriously in this matter and proved deserving of much criticism, because, among other sayings of the anchorites, he undertook to record that Conference of Abbot Chaeremon, which is wholly darkened by the soot of Pelagian doctrine, and published it in such a way that he himself seemed to favor Pelagius and oppose Saint Augustine. This was especially dangerous at a time when Augustine’s writings on the grace of God and the free choice of man, published against the Pelagians, were being rashly and imprudently misrepresented and called into question by certain Gallican presbyters who nevertheless professed to be Catholics—and Cassian was counted among them [Col. 0041C].

At such a time nothing could have been more harmful or more ill-timed than the written work of that Conference, which, under the appearance of honey, offered poison: harmful to the author’s reputation, injurious to Saint Augustine, and finally dangerous to souls. For this reason alone Cassian rightly incurred both the censure of Gelasius and the criticism and reproof of Prosper.

Prosper did not think that he had to engage in combat with Abbot Chaeremon, whom Cassian introduces in that Conference discussing the grace of God and free choice [Col. 0041D]. Rather, he says, the contest was with Cassian himself, who had published such teaching in a manner that he was altogether believed to have approved and adopted it; it would have been with Chaeremon only if the latter had refuted his own opinions by denying them or corrected and dispelled them.

Yet it can be proved by several arguments, without prejudice to a sounder judgment, that Cassian did not really hold such views, nor write in accordance with his own opinion, but merely reported what others had said.

First, in several places—especially in his *Institutions*, where he discusses the necessity of God’s grace and the weakness of free choice—he speaks so piously and so Catholicly that he plainly demonstrates himself to have been entirely alien to the error of Pelagius. Since Doctor Cuychius has treated this argument fully in his preface, which we shall append to this one, I consider it unnecessary to explain it at greater length [Col. 0042A].

Furthermore, Saint Prosper himself, Cassian’s opponent, not only remembers him honorably in his *Chronicle*, but, while refuting him in his little work, nevertheless acknowledges him as a Catholic teacher. He speaks of Cassian and the other critics of Saint Augustine in these words:

> “Yet, since they have not been separated from fraternal fellowship, their intention should be tolerated rather than their correction despaired of, until the Lord, through the leaders of the Church and the legitimate ministers of his judgments, restores order to those matters which have been disturbed by the pride of a few and the ignorance of others.”

Prosper writes this in the epilogue of that work. From it you understand that Cassian was counted among Catholic teachers.

But a much more certain argument seems to arise from the fact that, after composing the *Conferences*, Cassian—at the advice and encouragement of Leo, archdeacon of the Roman Church and later supreme pontiff—published a clear and highly useful commentary on the Incarnation of the Lord against Nestorius. In the same work he vigorously attacked Pelagius as the father of the Nestorian heresy.

Cassian himself testifies in the preface that he completed the books of the *Conferences* before beginning to write these books on the Incarnation, when he begins as follows:

> “The little books of the spiritual Conferences having long since been completed…”

The same is confirmed by the eulogy of Gennadius, where he says of Cassian:

> “Finally, when asked by Leo, archdeacon of the city of Rome and afterward its bishop, he wrote seven books against Nestorius on the Incarnation of the Lord; and while writing them at Marseilles, he brought his life to an end, during the reigns of Theodosius and Valentinian.”

Who could believe that Leo, that most holy and most wise man, would have chosen anyone other than Cassian for that work unless he knew—or most certainly believed—that he was orthodox in every respect, sound in his judgment concerning matters of faith, and consequently most hostile to the Pelagians no less than to the Nestorians?

Cassian proved this in reality when he willingly undertook the commission and applied himself to the work with every effort. He showed himself a fierce enemy both of Pelagian and of Nestorian doctrine, and a vigorous defender of Catholic truth. Therefore, if in his earlier writings he had sinned through human imprudence, he wiped that stain away by becoming sounder and more cautious through a worthy correction.

To make this still more certain for you, listen, if you please, to what he himself writes in Book I of *On the Incarnation*, chapter 4, concerning a certain presbyter Leporius, notorious among the Pelagians but finally recalled by Cassian’s admonitions to a sounder mind and the Catholic faith. Gennadius likewise supports and bears witness to Cassian’s account:

> “Leporius,” he says, “then a monk and now a presbyter, who, proceeding from the teaching—or rather the depravity—of Pelagius, was in Gaul an advocate of that heresy and was among its first or greatest defenders, was admonished by us and corrected by God. He condemned his badly formed conviction so magnificently that his correction is scarcely less worthy of admiration than the uninjured faith of many. For the first thing is never to fall into error; the second is to repudiate it well.”

These and other things Cassian writes about the conversion of Leporius the Pelagian, which he himself brought about.

Again, in another book—Book VII of *On the Incarnation*, chapter 21—he attacks Nestorius as the offspring of Pelagius:

> “Because thorns and thistles, springing up from their roots, reveal their stock by their nature and, by the very fact of what they are, indicate from where they arise, so you also, thorny offspring of the Pelagian heresy, display in your growth the same thing that your father is said to have possessed in his root. For that Leporius…”

These and many other things Cassian wrote against Pelagius and Pelagius’s offspring, Nestorius. Through them he left abundant testimony to his stable and sincere judgment in the Catholic faith, and finally cleared himself of every suspicion of error.

But enough of these matters.

I now see that I am being asked what work has been undertaken or completed in this latest edition. Although this is something the reader ought rather to judge than I to recount, I shall nevertheless indicate it briefly, both to discharge my obligation and with due modesty.

First, I did not think it necessary to labor greatly over purifying or reforming the Author’s text, since Cuychius and Ciaconius—men of great learning and accuracy—have left it to us sufficiently corrected and clarified, having worked vigorously on this matter. Nevertheless, I compared it with several printed and manuscript copies, and from time to time corrected or examined certain passages which they had overlooked or treated less fully. I also made use of the paraphrase of Dionysius the Carthusian and thereby brought additional light to the text. At the same time, while respecting the authority of so great a man, I occasionally pointed out that this paraphraser had departed from the Author’s mind and meaning; the matter is left to the judgment of the reader.

[Col. 0043C] **2.** I added almost continuous annotations. In them I not only explained certain Greek, barbarous, or less familiar words and expressions, but also clarified more obscure statements. I likewise examined, as far as I could with ease and clarity suited to the understanding of younger readers, a number of theological questions relating to the monastic institution—questions that arose incidentally and are highly useful. From them many commonplaces concerning monastic matters may be drawn for daily and familiar use.

I honestly admit that I was sometimes assisted by the notes of both Cuychius and Ciaconius. Accordingly, for the public good, I interwove them with my own notes, while still assigning each observation to its proper author and claiming nothing foreign as my own. Nor have I forgotten that saying of Pliny, written aptly to Vespasian in the preface to his *Natural History*:

> “It is generous, and full of honorable modesty, to acknowledge through whom we have advanced.”

[Col. 0043D] **3.** I carefully observed the ancient rites and institutions of the earlier monks, both in the performance of the divine offices and in their other ascetic exercises. I have presented them to the reader, as though painted on a panel for closer inspection and contemplation. From these materials, as from commonplaces, the student of monastic antiquity may likewise learn through which authors and observers such rites and monastic practices—containing so large a part of regular discipline—have been handed down to us, as it were from hand to hand.

[Col. 0044A] **4.** Above all, I pursued this aim, and devoted myself to Cassian especially for this reason: in order to serve and oblige my fellow soldiers and brothers of my Order—namely, the Benedictine cenobites, among whom God in his grace has willed that I be enrolled—I wished, with God’s help and as opportunity arose, to explain from Cassian as many and as important difficulties of the Rule of our most holy Father Benedict as lay within my power. I also wished to refer and restore many passages of the Rule to Cassian’s writings, as to their prototype.

From this it is plainly evident how carefully, and with how pious and diligent an emulation, the most holy Father Benedict strove to imitate the ancient monks and follow in their footsteps, and how by his example and instruction he encouraged his own cenobites to imitate them.

**5.** In addition, I have frequently illustrated and strengthened Cassian’s more distinguished statements by similar sayings and eulogies of the holy Fathers Basil, Jerome, Augustine, Gregory, and others. I have also selected some of the shorter and more choice passages from them, gathered them together like brighter little stars, and arranged them in order at the end of the work, so that younger readers may more easily commit them to memory and fix them more firmly in their minds.

**6.** Finally, lest anything in the course of this work should delay, offend, or in any way lead the reader into error, I thought it appropriate, besides my own annotations, to add other observations and critical notes by both Cuychius and Ciaconius, placing them likewise in their proper order at the end. Fortified by these antidotes, anyone may henceforth pass through Cassian without stumbling and desire nothing further concerning the perfection of the work or the security of his own mind [Col. 0044C].

I strongly advise and urge those who are not yet sufficiently practiced in these matters, but who wish to handle profitably and beneficially the books of the *Conferences*—otherwise most useful books, which, as has been said, were customarily worn smooth by the holy Fathers Benedict, Thomas Aquinas, and others—to read these observations carefully beforehand.

You have, reader, what, with God’s help, I have endeavored to accomplish in this edition of the work. How much labor it has cost me, you will judge better than I can while I remain silent. But I shall regard it as a great reward if, by the goodness of Almighty God, I may succeed in contributing something fruitful and spiritually useful to my brothers, the members of the Benedictine family, and to the *κοινοβία* (*koinobia*, communities), through this little work; and if I may deserve to bring even two small coins from my poverty into the sacred treasury of the house of God (Luke 21).

Come, then, most beloved brothers in Christ—for I address you above all, since this labor and effort of ours has been expended chiefly for you—come, I say, and receive with open arms Cassian, prepared for you with much labor and dedicated and entrusted to you with great devotion of mind. Receive him as a welcome guest; embrace him with cheerful countenance and grateful heart, this most eloquent man, commended by such great eulogies and praises.

And what Saint Benedict asks of you—as a father from his children, a teacher from his disciples—and what the other holy Fathers have taught and urged by their example, exhortation, and the manifold fruit they received from reading Cassian [Col. 0045A], do this:

> “Turn him over by night; turn him over by day.”

Set him before you as a mirror of monks—indeed, as a living portrait of monastic life. Recognize in him the true and perfect monk, depicted with living colors in the utmost precision and complete in all his parts. Finally, learn from him the instruction of the whole of regular discipline, and the true path and method of attaining perfection, handed down, practiced, and trodden by the holy Fathers and the ancient monks.

But remember how great is the difference between doers of the law and hearers, or readers. For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified (Romans 2).

Permit me, therefore, to admonish you in the words of the Apostle James:

> “Be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves. For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he will be like a man observing the face of his birth in a mirror: he observed himself, went away, and immediately forgot what he was like. But the one who has looked closely into the law of perfect freedom and has remained in it, not becoming a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work—this person will be blessed in his deed” (James 1).

This truly apostolic saying, worthy of being written in letters of gold, brought to my mind the thought of alluding to it in these extemporaneous verses, adapted to the understanding of younger readers, and of adding them to this preface as a kind of crown. In them I address and admonish first myself, and then the other monks who share my condition:

> Why do you vainly boast, monk, of wearing the cowl?  
> It is not the garment that makes the monk; practice itself does that.  
>   
> The monk’s name is nothing, nor a sure knowledge  
> Of the ways that should adorn the monk; practice itself is of help.  
>   
> Practice possesses merit; practice claims for itself  
> The rewards of the eternal kingdom; practice carries one to the stars.  
>   
> Do you wish, with the name of monk, to wear a true cowl?  
> Love a practice worthy of the monk’s name.  
>   
> But if you desire to learn a true practice worthy  
> Of the monk’s name, this book teaches it.  
>   
> For what else are the customs and examples of the Fathers of old  
> Than the monk’s mirror and certain rule?  
>   
> Learn, then, what the surest practice of a monk is,  
> From the example of the ancient Fathers who went before.  
>   
> Yet learning is little unless action and practice follow;  
> Prove by your deeds that you have learned what you know.  
>   
> Surely the man who swells with pride while looking at himself in a mirror  
> Immediately departs, forgetful of what his face was like.  
>   
> Thus contemplation devoid of works and holy practice  
> Brings nothing except the empty name of monk.

Farewell, most beloved brothers in Christ, and judge this fraternal admonition fairly and kindly.

[Col. 0045]

# TESTIMONIES OF DISTINGUISHED MEN CONCERNING JOHN CASSIAN

[Col. 0045C] **Saint Prosper of Aquitaine in his *Chronicle*, under the year 436:**

> “John the Monk, surnamed Cassian, is regarded at Marseilles as a distinguished and eloquent writer.”

**The same author in his little work against the *Collator*:**

> “We shall report especially the definition of one man, who undoubtedly excelled all of them in the study of the sacred Scriptures.”

And a little later:

> “Accordingly, in the book whose heading is *On the Protection of God*, he introduces a certain man of the priestly order, who excels among those with whom he has dealt in the practice of disputation, introducing a certain abbot discussing grace and free choice.”

**Castor, bishop of Apt, in his prefatory letter to Cassian:**

> “Castor, etc., to Father Cassian: Domnus adorned with the special glory of sanctity, worthy of remembrance in every respect, and distinguished by the splendor of learning.”

**Saint Benedict, in chapter 24 of the Rule:**

> “At all times, whether it has been a day of fasting or a day of eating, as soon as they have risen from the evening meal, let all sit together, and let one person read the *Conferences*, or the Lives of the Fathers, or certainly something that will edify the hearers.”

And below:

> “But if it has been a fast day, after Vespers have been said, let them immediately come to the reading of the *Conferences*, as we have said. After four or five pages have been read, or as much as the hour permits, when all have come together, during this interval of reading…”

[Col. 0046C] **And in chapter 73:**

> “For those who hasten toward perfection of life, there are the teachings of the holy Fathers, whose observance leads a person to the heights of perfection. For what page, or what word of divine authority, in the Old and New Testament, is not a most direct rule for human life? Or what book of the holy Catholic Fathers does not resound with the exhortation that we should reach our Creator by a straight course? Moreover, what else are the Conferences of the Fathers, their institutions and lives, and the Rule of our holy Father Basil, than examples and instruments of virtue for monks who live and obey well?”

**Gennadius, presbyter of Marseilles, in his *Catalogue of Distinguished Men* [Note: [Col. 0045D] Honorius of Autun has the same material, except that he asserts that Cassian was an African rather than a Scythian, and inserts below the titles or subjects of the individual Conferences [Col. 0046D].]:**

[Col. 0046D]

> “Cassian, a Scythian by nationality, ordained a deacon at Constantinople by John the Great, bishop, and a presbyter at Marseilles, founded two monasteries, one for men and one for women, which still exist today. With experience as his teacher, he wrote in a plain and balanced style—or, to put it more clearly, finding words through understanding and moving his language through action—about matters necessary to the profession of all monks: on the habit of the monk; on the canonical manner of prayer and psalmody, which is observed day and night in the monasteries of Egypt, in three books; one book of *Institutions*; eight books on the origin, nature, and remedies of the eight principal vices, composing one book on each individual vice.
>
> “He also arranged the *Conferences* while living with the Fathers of Egypt. Finally, when asked by Leo, the archdeacon and afterward bishop of the city of Rome, he wrote seven books against Nestorius on the Incarnation of the Lord; and while writing them at Marseilles, he brought his life to an end, during the reigns of Theodosius and Valentinian.”

**Saint Fulgentius:**

Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, as the author of his life writes, was inflamed by spiritual meditation when reading the admirable lives of the Egyptian monks in both the *Institutions* and the *Conferences*. He decided to sail to those lands for two reasons: either to lay aside the title of abbot there and live in humility under a Rule, or to submit himself to the laws of stricter abstinence.

**Cassiodorus to his monks of the Vivarium monastery, in Book 1 of *On the Institution of Divine Reading*, chapter 29:**

> “Read diligently and listen frequently to Cassian the presbyter, who wrote on the institution of faithful monks and says that the eight principal vices must be avoided from the very beginning of the holy profession. He presents the harmful movements of the soul so appropriately that he first makes a person see his own excesses and then compels him to avoid them—excesses that previously, through the confusion of darkness, he did not recognize. Nevertheless, he was rightly blamed by Saint Prosper concerning free choice. Therefore we warn you that when he exceeds the mark in such matters, you must read him with caution.”

**The same author in his exposition of Psalm 69 [Note: [Col. 0047D] That is, the psalm beginning, “O God, come to my aid,” and so forth.]:**

[Col. 0047C]

> “The most eloquent Cassian celebrates this passage in his Tenth Conference, discussing its usefulness at great length and with such honor that the monks would not begin anything without first repeating this verse three times.”

**John Climacus, step 4 of his *Ladder*:**

> “From obedience humility is born; from humility discernment, as the great Cassian discussed most beautifully and profoundly in the discourse he wrote on discernment.”

**Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, Book X, chapter 29, speaking of Pelagia, the mother of Saint Aredius:**

> “She founded a monastery in which not only the Rules of Cassian but also those of Basil and the other abbots who established monastic life are celebrated, while the blessed woman supplied each person with food and clothing.”

**Photius, bishop of Constantinople, *Bibliotheca*, codex 197 [Note: [Col. 0047D] From the translation of Father Andreas Scotus.]:**

> “The Rules of the Egyptian monks by Cassian the monk [Note: [Col. 0047D] This is how he titled Cassian’s books, which he saw translated into Greek.]; *On the Eight Vicious Thoughts*; a little book of three Conferences.
>
> “I have read a little book containing two books of Cassian the Monk, a Roman by nationality—one of them dedicated to a certain bishop Castor, who had requested that it be written by him.

[Note: [Col. 0048D] “Or was he called Roman because he lived among the Latins at Marseilles? For Gennadius says that he was a Scythian by nationality.” Thus Scotus. I think this is an error, or an addition by someone else.] In it he prescribes forms and rules according to which the monks in Egypt live, distributed among those communities which, from the origin of the word, they call *coenobia*.
>
> “The other book, also dedicated to the same man, derives its title from those eight vicious thoughts: gluttony, lust, avarice, anger, envy, acedia, vainglory, and pride. These teachings are exceedingly useful—more useful, perhaps, than any others—for those who desire to enter the religious life.
>
> “Indeed, such power and almost divine force reside in them that even to this day, if a community of monks is governed according to this form and by these precepts, it truly flourishes for a time and is seen to be a workshop of virtue, shining before the others. But the community that rejects these teachings, equipped only with a few remnants of virtue, is tossed about as though in the waves, or even suffers shipwreck. Therefore it is advantageous to despise nothing that is taught there [Col. 0048B].
>
> “For these teachings are an exposition and explanation of the Lord’s law and of evangelical discipline. Moreover, the expression corresponds to the subject matter itself, so that it not only offers clarity but is also endowed with the power to impress itself easily and without force upon people’s minds, indeed to penetrate them and draw them toward its own purpose.
>
> “Everything is so wisely, skillfully, and appropriately balanced and formed that even the second book is not without tropological interpretations. It contains much that charms and attracts, as well as much that both inspires fear and terror and possesses the power to stir repentance.
>
> “We read that a third little book was added to these. After the death of Bishop Castor, Cassian dedicated it to the superior of that monastery, for whose sake those earlier books and Rules had been sent. This little book resembles those we have already counted. For it teaches first of all what discernment is, and so forth. See the rest in the same author.”

**Rabanus, on chapter 38 of the Rule of Saint Benedict:**

> “As Cassian also says: ‘While the brothers are being refreshed, holy readings should be read,’ and so forth.”

**Burchard, bishop of Worms, Book VIII, chapter 77, from the Council of Mainz, canon 6:**

> “The nuns established in the monastery shall come every day to the chapter and to the Conferences, and shall diligently observe the Rule established for them by the holy Fathers.”

In nearly the same words, canon 59 of the Second Council of Chalon is quoted in Ivo, part VII, chapter 95 [Col. 0048D]. It commands that the nuns come every day to the Conference.

**Peter Damian, cardinal and bishop of Ostia:**

Peter Damian, Book V of his letters, letter 19, where he discusses the clothing of monks and clerics:

> “But if this seems doubtful to you, at least lend an ear to the testimony of your own side. Read the Conferences of the Fathers, which Eucherius, bishop of Lyon, endeavored to abridge in polished language. And if you do not wish to believe us, at least believe his writing [Col. 0049A]. For under that teacher we wrote this page.”

**Saint Dominic [Note: [Col. 0049D] In Surius, 5 August.]:**

As it is read in his life, Saint Dominic, striving to imitate the footsteps of the perfect and to press on toward the heights of virtue, undertook to read diligently the book entitled the *Conferences of the Fathers*. He took care to grasp what he read with understanding, to feel it with affection, and to carry it out in practice. For from it he learned purity of heart, the way of contemplation, and the perfection of all the virtues.

**Vincent of Beauvais, bishop, *Historical Mirror*, Book XX, §18 [Note: [Col. 0049D] Saint Antoninus, archbishop of Florence, has the same account, part II of his *History*, title 10.]:**

> “At that time, during the reign of Honorius, there flourished an illustrious, prudent, and eloquent man, John the Hermit, also called Cassian. He wrote many things, among them accounts of the Fathers found in Egypt, and he set forth their teachings and rules in books addressed to many people.”

And below:

> “Certainly his little works contain much edification for souls and shine with lucid language. Among the many little works of the ancients, I do not think I have read anything more useful for those striving toward spiritual progress and the summit of perfection. For our blessed Father Dominic, as it is read in his life, diligently read the book entitled the *Conferences of the Fathers*, understanding it attentively, searching out in it the paths of salvation, and attained the great summit of perfection.
>
> “For this book treats of purity of heart, of the vices, and of the perfection of all the virtues. Its frequent reading, with the assistance of grace, advanced the disciple of Christ to great purity of heart, to the citadel of contemplation, and to the perfection of the whole spiritual discipline.”

**Saint Thomas Aquinas [Note: [Col. 0050D] In Surius, in his life, 7 March.]:**

> “This too is worthy of remembrance in the holy man: whenever he had leisure, he was accustomed willingly to read something in the Conferences of the Fathers, lest, through speculation on subtle matters, his affections should grow somewhat cold, and so that he might more easily gather and raise himself again to the contemplation of divine things. In this he followed Saint Dominic, who is known to have taken great delight in reading that book and to have been stirred and advanced toward a high perfection of life.”

How willingly and frequently Saint Thomas himself cites Cassian in his *Summa Theologica*, and draws arguments from him or confirms his conclusions by his authority, the reader will see, if he wishes, in my annotations, where he will find not all, but certainly most, of the relevant passages.

**John of Torquemada, cardinal, treatise 107 on the Rule of Saint Benedict, discussing the words quoted above from chapter 42:**
This, he says, has been rightly and most holily established, because in this way the monks can draw from that reading material for edification and devotion, by which they may be advanced toward the heights of contemplation during the time of silence. And for this purpose the books of the *Conferences* and the lives of the holy Fathers were rightly chosen, since they contain the teaching of every kind of perfection, edification, and holiness.

### B. Dionysius the Carthusian

What Dionysius the Carthusian thought of John Cassian and his writings he sufficiently demonstrated in the prefaces to his paraphrase. In the first, indeed, he reckons John Cassian and John Climacus among the venerable and most devout Fathers worthy of eternal remembrance. In the second, prefixed to the *Conferences*, he calls him the most illustrious Father. In the third, prefixed to the Eleventh Conference, when comparing him with other ecclesiastical Doctors whose writings are more obscure and difficult, he says:

“Among books of this kind are reckoned and stand out the volumes of the most illustrious Father and foremost Doctor of all religious persons, John Cassian.”

### John Trithemius, in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*

John Cassian, a Scythian by nationality, formerly a hearer and disciple of blessed John Chrysostom, bishop of Constantinople, and ordained deacon by him, was expelled by him after some years, I do not know for what reason. He was then consecrated priest at Massilia and founded two monasteries, one for men and one for women, in which the fervor of regular discipline continued for many years. With experience as his teacher, he wrote several short works, in which even through the translator the beauty of expression can be perceived. Among them are said to be:

[Column 0050C] Seven books *On the Incarnation of the Lord against the Heretic Nestorius*, written at the request of Leo the archdeacon, later bishop of the city of Rome.

Four books *On the Institutes of the Monks*.

Eight books *On the Eight Principal Vices*.

Twenty-four *Conferences of the Holy Fathers*.

In these *Conferences of the Holy Fathers* there is a useful and necessary instruction for monks. But because he is censured in certain respects by blessed Prosper concerning free choice, his short works are counted among the apocrypha. At length he died at Massilia, after publishing many books, not without a reputation for holiness, while Theodosius and Valentinian were reigning, in the year of the Lord 435.

### Peter, Bishop of Equilium, commonly called de Natalibus, in the *Catalogue of the Saints*, Book VII, Chapter 59

Saint Cassian the priest, of whom Brother Vincent and Gennadius speak, flourished in the time of the Emperor Honorius. He was an illustrious and eloquent man, also called the Hermit. Expelled by heretics from the Church of Constantinople, he was ordained priest at Massilia in Gaul and founded two monasteries, one for men and one for women, and so forth.

[Note: Raphael Volaterranus has “the Jerusalem Church” (*Anthropology*, Book XIV).]

### Cardinal Bellarmine, of pious memory, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

John Cassian, formerly a deacon of Saint John Chrysostom, later going to Gaul and settling there, was ordained priest at Massilia. He wrote in the Latin language:

Three books *On the Monastic Habit and on the Canonical Manner of Praying and Chanting the Psalms*.

One book *Of the Institutes*.

Eight books *On the Origin and Remedy of the Eight Principal Vices*.

Twenty-four *Conferences of the Fathers*.

Seven books *On the Incarnation of the Word*.

After completing this work at the request of Leo, later supreme pontiff, he ended his life while Theodosius the Younger and Valentinian were reigning, as Gennadius testifies in his book *On Illustrious Men*. All these works survive and may usefully be read, except the Thirteenth Conference and a few others, which are marked in the Roman edition.

### John Maldonatus, theologian of the Society of Jesus, on Luke 24

Cassian was a Catholic and good author; but no body is so beautiful that it is without a blemish.

### Hieronymus Platus, theologian of the same Society of Jesus, *On the Good of the Religious State*, Book II, Chapter 25

John Cassian, a Scythian by birth and, in style, supremely Latin, first a disciple of Chrysostom and later the builder of a monastery at Massilia, undoubtedly explained in practice, when establishing and governing it, everything that he had committed to writing from his meetings and conversations with the holy Fathers. Everyone knows how much perfection those writings contain.

### Antonius Possevinus, theologian of the same Society of Jesus, in the *Sacred Apparatus*

John Cassian the Hermit wrote twelve books *On the Institutes of the Renunciants* and twenty-four books of the *Conferences of the Holy Fathers*, and he wrote them in Latin, whatever some may have thought otherwise, whether Trithemius or Dionysius the Carthusian. For Cassian himself, in the first book of his *Institutes*, chapter 3; in Book V, chapter 16; in *Conference* 23, chapter 8; and very often elsewhere, when he says that he followed a more accurate translation of the Bible, means our Latin Vulgate.

Lest you complain, reader, that something has been taken from you concerning antiquity, behold: we offer you certain verses from that age, by an unknown author, printed in an ancient codex before the paraphrase of Dionysius the Carthusian. They briefly summarize the contents of each of Cassian’s books.

[Column 0051D]

If you wish to know which books this work contains,

and what each contains, read through the verses written below.

[Column 0052A]

Behold, divine [Note: “Divine” is used in the manner of legal writers for the emperor, namely Maximilian I, to whom he dedicated these verses and presented the book. I infer this from certain indications of that old and first edition of the year 1497.] one, the little books long sought by you,

fulfilling my promise, I have gathered into one body.

Those which one man’s voice, whose author was the renowned Spirit,

offered to the Church, to its divine mother, as a gift,

which she watches over for her own use without end.

Finally, I ask you to behold twice six books

in their present body, in the order that follows.

The first teaches what the monastic habit ought to be.

The second gives the rule and manner of chanting the psalms.

The third describes this same matter more fully,

and the fourth instructs new pupils in each detail.

The remaining eight, which you still see left over,

contain within themselves the number of the same number of vices.

Each book pursues its own monstrous subject in its own composition,

showing what it is and what must be avoided concerning it.

[Column 0052B]

These are accompanied by twice twelve books

of the *Conferences of the earlier Fathers*, in celebrated discourse,

in a twofold form. Hear what each of them offers you that is honorable.

For the first Moses teaches, above all, in the first two,

what the appointed end ought to be, or what it will be.

He commands the brothers to live discreetly above all things.

Paphnutius then teaches the monk to abandon the world.

Resist the allurements of the body, Daniel being your teacher.

Serapion again identifies the eight plagues of the vices.

Abbot Theodore speaks of the death of the saints.

The wickedness of Satan and the wandering mind are attacked by Serenus,

and much is handed down concerning evil spirits.

In two Conferences Isaac exhorts the brothers

to pray purely, with simplicity of heart.

What is perfect, what is chaste, and what can be prepared

and preserved with God as guardian, we are taught

in three Conferences of the teacher Cheremon.

But Nesteros the abbot speaks to you

of divine knowledge of the supreme truth

and of spiritual gifts.

Joseph dictates the strongest laws of friendship,

and further shows what the true definition is.

Then Piamun treats of three kinds of monks.

John’s many salutary Conferences speak

of the end of the common life and of the anchoritic life.

Pynufius establishes rules for purging sins.

Theonas grants permission to live with greater indulgence

during the season of the Fifty Days, and resolves this question:

why do apparitions of the night come upon us,

and why do we often do the evil that we do not wish to do?

[Column 0052D]

All the traditions of the elders are concluded

by the sermons of Abraham concerning the subduing of the law of the flesh.

[Column 0053]

## LETTER [Note: From an ancient codex of the monastery of Elnon, Saint-Amand.]

### Of Saint Castor, Bishop of Apt, to the Lord Cassian, Abbot of Massilia (G, S)*

To the Lord adorned with the special glory of holiness and worthy of remembrance in every respect, distinguished also by the beauty of learning, namely Father Cassian: Castor, the refuse of those living in the world (1 Corinthians 4), offers whatever humble services we can.

Reasonably, Father, pedagogues provide support for those who are irrational and without speech; for although a measure not equal for all is found to flourish under oppressed humanity, nevertheless the result is that, for those who are proved to have been subdued, it subdues the benefit. For we cannot all do everything, since we are not all capable of knowing and contending in every matter. Anyone who does not hesitate to steal away those better goods that he has learned to grasp rightly incurs, deservedly, the loss of his own goods [Perhaps: “earnestly strives”]. Such men must be pressed by long practice and nourished by various works, through which the discernment of others is supplied. For sometimes a presumptuous man falls through his own rashness, when what is suited to necessary uses is distributed by his inappropriate ingenuity according to uncertain measures.

But we simpletons can easily be persuaded through negligence of what is unsuitable. Therefore, dearest Father, we anticipate you with whatever charity we can, so that, in your pious and inexhaustible abundance, you may assist us, who are unable to offer anything to the wise, and may not delay in rousing us novices, enticed by the refinements of worldly pomp, through those exercises in which your pre-eminent mind and limbs have grown strong.

We know you especially as experienced in the teaching of the Eastern monasteries, and above all of those in Egypt and those founded in the Thebaid—especially since places distinguished by the Lord’s nativity have also been illuminated by your presence. Since you are therefore filled with the discipline of every Catholic pursuit, it is fitting that you should not pass by us, who are poor in knowledge. We ask your fatherhood not to refuse to apply, in plain speech to our rough monastery, the institutions of the monasteries that you saw flourishing and being established throughout Egypt and Palestine, and whose observance you decreed must be maintained as they had been handed down there by the Fathers. Pouring forth the abundant words of your eloquence with their honeyed sweetness, do not delay in watering our hearts, long parched, so that from them the fruits of righteousness may be able to sprout after barrenness has been cast away.

Hence I think that, if it should be possible for us to make any progress, you too would deserve a greater reward: if obedience to your fatherly labor should render the minds of the sluggish in some degree capable of service.

Farewell, father of God’s servants, and remember us.

[Column 0053]

# JOHN CASSIAN, ABBOT OF MASSILIA, TWELVE BOOKS ON THE INSTITUTES OF THE MONASTERIES (C)

## Preface, TO BISHOP CASTOR

[Column 0053A]

The history of the Old Testament relates that the most wise Solomon, after receiving from God exceedingly great wisdom and prudence and breadth of heart like the immeasurable sand of the sea (1 Kings 4), so that by the testimony of the Lord no one like him had existed in former times and none would arise after him, when he desired to build that magnificent temple for the Lord, requested the assistance of the foreign king of Tyre. The latter sent him Hiram, the son of a widow, and through his service and direction he completed whatever, prompted by divine wisdom, he was planning that was excellent in the temple of the Lord or in the sacred vessels (1 Kings 7).

If, then, that ruler, higher than all the kingdoms of the earth, and that nobler and more excellent offspring of the Israelite race (1 Kings 7), together with that divinely inspired wisdom which surpassed the disciplines and institutions of all the Eastern and Egyptian peoples, did not disdain the counsel of a poor foreign man, then you too, most blessed [Note: “Pope,” or *pappas* in Greek, was originally a word taken from the speech of boys or infants babbling and calling their fathers by a childish stammer (Coelius Rhodiginus, Book XI of the *Ancient Readings*, chapter 21). Hence *papazein* in Homer (*Odyssey* VI), or *papizein* (Onuphrius, *On Ecclesiastical Words*), and *papissare* among comic writers, mean to address one’s father gently in the manner of infants. Following this example and in a kind of imitation of it, the first Christians, because of evangelical simplicity and modesty, began to call the spiritual father by this affectionate word, “pope.” From this it came to be transferred into a title of dignity, and only more honored clerics came to be distinguished by this name (Baronius, notes on the *Martyrology*, 10 January), as Walafrid Strabo observed in Book VII of *On Ecclesiastical Matters*: “Pope is the name of a certain fatherhood, and it is appropriate to the dignity of clerics.” Later, however, ecclesiastical usage began to make this designation peculiar to bishops, so that all bishops, and they alone, were called popes, as is clear from the letters of Saints Cyprian, Jerome, Augustine, Sidonius, and others. In this sense, therefore, Cassian here, and in the other preface to the *Conferences of the Fathers*, calls Castor “pope,” that is, father or bishop, as Dionysius the Carthusian explained. In later centuries, however, the usage of the Church established that the name “pope,” like the epithet “most blessed,” should be attributed only to the Roman Pontiff (Bellarmine, Book II *On the Roman Pontiff*, chapter 31). When certain schismatic bishops arrogantly appropriated the name “pope” to themselves out of hatred for the Roman pontiff, Gregory VII decreed in a Roman synod in 1077 that the name “pope” should be unique throughout the Christian world, and that no one might attribute this title either to himself or to another. Concerning this, see more in Baronius and others. But who this Castor was, and of what place he was bishop, since Cassian did not expressly say, was not easy to discover or determine with certainty. At last, however, this was revealed by the prefatory letter in an ancient manuscript codex that we later received on loan from the monastery of Elnon, or Saint-Amand, prefixed to these books of the *Institutes*. Although it is found nowhere else and is obscured by many errors and erasures, we nevertheless judged that, insofar as possible, it should be cleansed of them and restored to its integrity, placed before this work, and brought forth from darkness. In its title this Castor is expressly called bishop of Apt, and the letter is said to have been written by him to Cassian. He was bishop of Apt, that is, of the city of Apt-Julia in Narbonensian Gaul (Pliny, Book III of his *History*, chapter 4), one of the suffragans of the archbishop of Aix, or of Turin, as Anto-Demochares reports (*On the Sacrifice of the Mass*, chapter 30). That this Castor was a man conspicuous for holiness and endowed with notable zeal for piety and religion is shown both by the letter just mentioned and by this elegant and eloquent preface of Cassian.]

—then you, Pope Castor, intending to build a true and rational temple for God, not from insensible stones but from a congregation of holy men, not temporal and corruptible but eternal and unconquerable, and wishing to consecrate to the Lord the most precious vessels—not vessels cast from a great quantity of gold or silver, which the Babylonian king, after their capture, would devote to the pleasure of his concubines and princes (Daniel 5), but holy souls shining with the integrity of innocence, justice, and chastity, bearing within themselves the King Christ dwelling there—you deem me, needy and utterly poor in every respect, worthy to be admitted to a share in so great a work.

[Note: This refers to the province of Apt, which above is called *experte coenobiorum*, that is, “without monasteries,” or “empty of monasteries.” For Bishop Castor himself is here said to have founded the first monastery. Hence it is also called below a new monastery. In some copies, instead of *experte*, the reading was *ex parte*, two words that make no sense.]

Since you wish the institutions of the Eastern, and especially the Egyptian, monasteries to be established in your province, which is without monasteries, and since you yourself are perfect in every virtue and in knowledge, so filled with all spiritual riches that, for those seeking perfection, not only your speech but even your life alone is more than sufficient as an example, you ask and command me, who am without speech and poor in language and knowledge, to contribute something from the poverty of my understanding toward fulfilling your desire. You command me, although I arrange in an unskilled style the institutions of the monasteries that we saw being observed throughout Egypt and Palestine, just as they were handed down to us there by the Fathers, not seeking elegance of language, in which you yourself are supremely learned, but wishing the simple life of the saints to be explained in simple speech to the brothers in your new monastery.

As much as the pious ardor of your desire urges me to obey this request, so much do the many burdens of my anxieties deter me, although I am willing to comply. First, because the merits of my life do not match it so completely that I can trust myself to be able to comprehend in spirit and mind matters so difficult, obscure, and holy. Second, because what we attempted to do, learned, or perceived by sight from childhood, when we were placed among them and stirred by their daily exhortations and examples, we can no longer retain in its entirety, having been separated for so many years from their companionship and imitation of their way of life. This is especially true because the knowledge of these matters cannot be handed down, understood, or retained in memory through idle meditation and verbal instruction: it rests entirely upon experience.

And just as such things cannot be handed down except by one who has experience, so they cannot even be perceived or understood except by someone who has labored to grasp them with equal zeal and sweat. Yet unless these matters have frequently been examined and refined through continual conferences with spiritual men, they quickly slip away again through the negligence of the mind.

Third, because even what we can remember, however inadequately—not according to the merit of the subject but according to the condition of the present time—cannot be suitably explained by an inexperienced speaker. In addition, men noble both in life and illustrious in speech and knowledge have already labored over many short works on this subject—Saint Basil and Jerome, I mean, and several others—[Note: He expressly names two most celebrated Doctors of the Church, Basil and Jerome, who flourished shortly before his own time. The former in the East and the latter in the West greatly illuminated and propagated the monastic institution by their writings and their deeds. The former, namely Saint Basil the Great, archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, was earlier, or older, than Saint Jerome. He flourished under the Emperor Valens and died under Gratian, as Jerome himself testifies in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. Among his distinguished works are the *Rules*, or monastic institutions, of two kinds: some are discussed at greater length, others explained more briefly and concisely. In both, monks propose various questions concerning matters pertaining to the monastic and perfect life, and Saint Basil answers them one by one. The Rule of Saint Basil translated into Latin, or rather paraphrastically explained, by Rufinus seems to have been compiled from the former, with much omitted and changed. It is commonly circulated among the four Rules of the Holy Fathers approved by the Church; Saint Benedict also mentions it at the end of his Rule, as do the Seventh Synod and Pope Innocent II, cited by Gratian. All Greek, or Eastern, monks are likewise said to serve under the Rule of Basil.]

—of whom the earlier, in response to brothers asking about various institutions or questions, answered not only in eloquent speech but also in abundant discourse supported by testimonies from the divine Scriptures.

[Note: Saint Jerome the priest and pre-eminent Doctor of the Church was flourishing and writing in the fourteenth year of the Emperor Theodosius, as he himself testifies at the end of his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. He died under the Emperor Honorius, in the year of the Lord 422 according to Prosper’s *Chronicle*, or 420 according to Baronius. His writings, famous throughout the world, contain many matters relating to the instruction of monks, partly drawn from and worked out by his own genius, as is said here, and partly translated from Greek. To assist the reader’s interest and convenience, I shall briefly indicate here a list of them.

In the first volume:

Letter 1, to Heliodorus, in which he urges him to embrace the solitary life.

Letter 2, to Nepotianus, on the life of clerics; there he also lucidly explains many matters relating to the condition of monks.

Letter 3, in which he reproves certain monks who were greedy for wealth.

Letter 4, to the monk Rusticus, for whom he prescribes a way of life and describes the duty of a true monk.

Letter 8, to Demetrias, on preserving virginity, which is especially appropriate to monks and nuns.

Letter 13, to Paulinus, entitled *On the Instruction of a Monk*.

Letter 22, to the virgin and religious woman Eustochium, in which he lists three kinds of Egyptian monks and recounts their customs and institutions.

Letter 27, to the same Eustochium, in which he describes the life of her mother Paula, filled with holiness and religious devotion, and conveys much about the nuns whom she instructed.

Letter 47, in which he also says something about the vow, tonsure, and enclosure of nuns.

The lives of the hermits Paul, Hilarion, and Malchus the captive monk are full of excellent teachings and instruments for monks.

In the second volume:

Book I *Against Jovinianus*, in which there is much about the excellence of chastity and virginity over marriage.

Near its end, Book II contains some material on the duty of a monk and praise of the desert.

In the third volume:

Letter 103, in which he vehemently urges Paulinus, who was slow to give away and distribute his possessions for Christ and who postponed the matter from day to day, to fly naked to the naked Christ.

In the fourth volume:

His commentary on the passage from Jeremiah: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth” (*Lamentations* 3). There coenobites are compared with anchorites, and the contemplative life is preferred to the active life.

These are the principal passages in Saint Jerome’s own genuine works in which monks and monastic institutions are discussed.

In the works that he translated into Latin from Greek authors, which Cassian also mentions here, I find nothing else relating to the monastic institution except the life of Saint Anthony, written in Greek by Saint Athanasius and, according to Baronius’s opinion (Baronius, vol. III, year 358, and *Martyrology*, 17 January), also translated into Latin by Saint Jerome; and the Rule of Saint Pachomius the abbot, which, God willing, we shall append to this work, elucidated with scholia and notes. Saint Jerome himself testifies in the preface prefixed to that Rule that he translated it from Greek into Latin. A Rule of Monks is indeed circulated under Saint Jerome’s name, as is another Rule of Nuns. The former, however, was not composed by Jerome himself but excerpted and compiled from his writings; it is also said to have been approved by Pope Martin V. The latter has been removed by more discerning scholars from the catalogue of Saint Jerome’s works and cast aside as spurious and falsely attributed to him.]

Another author not only published books worked out by his own genius but also translated works composed in Greek into Latin speech. After such abundant rivers of eloquence, I could rightly be accused of presumption if I attempted to add even a trickle of this sort, unless the confidence inspired by your holiness encouraged me to do so, together with your promise that these trifles, whatever they may be, would either be acceptable to you or that you would assign them to the congregation of brothers dwelling in the new monastery.
