If anything should perhaps have been expressed by us less cautiously, may they read it with piety and sustain it with more generous indulgence, seeking rather the faithfulness of my speech than elegance of expression.

Therefore, most blessed pope, unique model of religion and [Column 0058A] humility, encouraged by your prayers, I shall undertake, according to the strength of my ability, the work that you impose upon me. I shall make known to the rough monastery and to those thirsting for truth those matters that our predecessors left entirely untouched, since they attempted to describe what they had heard rather than what they had experienced.

I shall not undertake to weave together an account of God’s wonders and signs. Although we have heard many things from our elders, some of them incredible, and have even seen them fulfilled before our own eyes, I shall pass over all these matters, since for readers they contribute nothing more than admiration and no further instruction in the perfect life. Instead, I shall endeavor faithfully, insofar as the Lord assists me, to explain only their institutions and the rules of the monasteries, and especially the origins, causes, and remedies of the principal vices, which they identify as eight, according to their traditions.

My purpose is not to discuss the wonders of God but, according to what we received from our elders, to say a little about the correction of our conduct and the completion of the perfect life.

In this also I shall strive to satisfy your commands: if I should discover that anything in these regions has been established not according to the pattern founded by the most ancient constitution of our elders, but has been diminished or added according to the judgment of each individual founder of a monastery, I shall, according to the rule of the monasteries founded in ancient times throughout Egypt or Palestine, either add or remove it in faithful speech [Alternative: “cut it away”].

[Note: The old reading is: “For you must by no means believe,” and so forth.]

I shall certainly not believe that anything more reasonable or more perfect could have been found in the new constitution of the western regions of Gaul than those institutions in which the monasteries founded by holy and spiritual Fathers at the beginning of the apostolic preaching have endured down to our own time.

I shall nevertheless presume to introduce this moderation into the work: whenever I find that practices established according to the Egyptian rule are impossible in these regions, whether because of the harshness of the climate or because of the difficulty and diversity of customs, I shall temper them to some extent by the institutions of the monasteries maintained throughout Palestine or Mesopotamia. For if a reasonable measure of what is possible is preserved—*gnōmē* (γνώμη), that is, judgment or discretion—the perfection of observance is the same even where ability is unequal.

# BOOK ONE

[Column 0059]

## CHAPTER ONE. On the Habit of a Monk

[Column 0059B]

[Note: On the occasion of these words, you should be advised, reader, that various authors assign more titles to these twelve books. Their wording differs, but their meaning is the same, or at least points toward the same subject.

Some entitle them all *On the Institutes of the Renunciants*. Thus Ciaconius, I believe, following the Vatican copies; the Lyons edition, and so forth.

Others call them *On the Institutes of the Monasteries*. Thus Saint Thomas commonly does in his *Summa Theologica*, as do the Basel edition, Cuychius, and others.

Others divide them under several particular titles, namely:

[Column 0059C]

Four books *On Monastic Institutions*.

Eight books *On the Principal Vices*. Trithemius, Cuychius, and others.

Others follow Gennadius in this way:

Three books *On the Monastic Habit and on the Canonical Manner of Prayer and Psalmody*.

One book *Of the Institutes*.

Eight books *On the Origin and Remedy of the Eight Principal Vices*.

Finally, others call them the twelve books of the *Institutes*, and by this title distinguish the *Institutes* from the *Conferences*.]

Since we are about to speak of the institutions and rules of monasteries, from what more suitable beginning, with God’s gift, could we take our start than from the very habit of monks? We shall then be able to explain their inner cultivation after we have first depicted their outward adornment before the eyes of our readers.

## CHAPTER TWO. On the Belt of a Monk
Therefore [Note: Although all Christians, in a general sense, are called soldiers of Christ—whose armor the Apostle describes in Ephesians 6 in these words: “Take the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day and, having completed everything, to stand firm. Stand therefore, with your loins girded in truth, clothed with the breastplate of righteousness, and with your feet shod in readiness for the Gospel of peace; taking up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the wicked one, and take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God”—nevertheless, religious deserve this title much more particularly, since by three vows, as by a triple sacrament, they are devoted and bound to this spiritual warfare. The weapons of this warfare, according to the same Apostle, are not carnal but powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds, for destroying arguments and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and for taking every understanding captive into the obedience of Christ (II Corinthians 10); and this is achieved especially through the vow and practice of obedience. For this reason monks are called by the Greek Fathers (Basil, *On the Solitary Life*, and Epistle 63) ἀσκηταί (*askētai*), that is, “fighters” or “exercisers,” because their entire exercise and way of life ought to be, as it were, a training ground of virtues, whereas other people train themselves in warfare, commerce, forensic cases, and so forth. Hence Saint Basil calls his sermons on monastic matters “ascetical,” and monasteries themselves were formerly called *asceteries*, as workshops and dwellings of spiritual exercises. Saint Benedict likewise, at the beginning of his Rule, addresses the monk as a soldier in these words: “To you, therefore, my speech is now directed—whoever, renouncing your own will and wishing to serve under Christ the true King, take up the strongest and most glorious weapons of obedience”; and in chapter 1 he says that coenobites serve under a rule or an abbot.]

the monk, as a soldier of Christ stationed perpetually in the battle line, must always walk with his loins girded [Luke 12]. [Note: Saint Basil discusses similar matters at greater length in the *Longer Rules*, chapter 22, and in the *Monastic Rule* translated by Rufinus, chapter 12. There he likewise reviews the examples of Elijah, John, Peter, and Paul, and adds this further reason why monks ought to be girded or belted. “We see,” he says, “that the Lord commands Job to gird himself. For this is, as it were, a sign of a vigorous spirit prepared and equipped for action: ‘Gird your loins like a man,’ he says (Job 38).” It is also clear that the use of a belt was familiar to the Lord’s disciples, since they were forbidden to have bronze in their belts. These are Basil’s words.

To these examples other similar ones from Scripture could be added: Elijah, who, with his loins girded, ran before Ahab (III Kings 18); Elisha, who said to his servant Gehazi, “Gird your loins, take my staff in your hand, and go” (IV Kings 4); the angel Raphael, who appeared to the younger Tobias girded and ready, as it were, for a journey (Tobit 5); and our Savior, who, when he wished to wash the apostles’ feet at the Last Supper, is said to have girded himself with a tunic (John 13).

The same point is made by the similar statements about girding and belting the loins: Luke 12, “Let your loins be girded”; Ephesians 6, “Stand with your loins girded in truth”; and I Peter 1, “Therefore, with the loins of your mind girded, hope in the grace that is being offered to you.” To have one’s loins girded or belted, in the literal sense, means nothing other than to be ready and equipped, as is gathered from these words of Luke 12: “Truly I tell you, he will gird himself, and passing by, he will minister to them.” The peoples of the East used long garments; therefore those who were about to minister or undertake a journey gathered up their clothing and tightened it around their loins with a belt, so that it would not impede them.

Saint Gregory, however, interpreting the matter morally, understands chastity to be signified by girded loins. “We gird our loins,” he says, “when by continence we restrain the wantonness of the flesh” (*Homily 13 on the Gospels*). Cassian had both meanings in view, as will become clearer from what follows (the final chapter of this book and Book II, chapter 1). He teaches that the ancient custom of wearing a belt, girdle, or sash was customary and prescribed by rule among those Egyptian monks, for two reasons; and by their example he seeks to commend it to other monks: namely, so that they might show themselves girded and equipped with the spiritual weapons mentioned above, especially with the belt of chastity as with a military girdle, and so that they might always be ready and prepared for every task imposed or about to be imposed.

Hence Saint Basil universally commends the use of a belt to monks (as cited above). Saint Jerome also assigns a linen girdle to the monks of Tabennisi (in the preface to the Rule of Saint Pachomius). Palladius calls them belts (Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 7), and adds that Pachomius prescribed this noteworthy and unusual rule for them: when they came to the sacred assembly on Saturday and Sunday, as was customary, they were to loosen their belts, remove their sheepskin or *melote*, and approach wearing only the *cuculla*—so that, in my view, they might display greater and particular reverence and a more decorous dress. Sozomen and Nicephorus confirm the same.

Saint Benedict, too, our holy Father, following everywhere in the footsteps of the earlier monks, did not omit this prescription concerning the monastic belt, which he had received from them. For when he decrees in chapter 22 of the Rule that monks are to sleep clothed and girded with belts or cords, he gives this reason: “so that they may always be ready, and, at the signal, rising without delay, hasten to anticipate one another for the Work of God.” He thus sufficiently indicates that during the day—and with still greater reason—they ought to be girded.

Accordingly, John the Deacon writes in the *Life of Saint Gregory* that Gregory preserved, in the narrowness of his belt—which did not exceed the measure of one inch—the appearance of the regular discipline formerly established by Saint Benedict. In describing Benedict’s life, he had praised the Rule as well. By these words he intimates that the use of a sash or belt was customary among the Benedictines—a practice that many who remain faithful to ancient traditions still retain today—and that from its narrowness and measurement, as from a certain indication, Saint Gregory was long after his death, when his body was transferred elsewhere, recognized and identified as a professor or monk of Saint Benedict’s institution. “Especially,” he says, “since that same venerable teacher Gregory sent the monks of his own monastery, certainly bound to the Rule of Benedict, into Saxony” (John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 80). These are his words.]

This is how those also walked who in the Old Testament established the beginnings of this profession [Note: Namely, of the monastic profession. For this reason Saint Jerome frequently calls them monks of the Old Testament. In Epistle 4 he says: “The sons of the prophets, whom we read of as monks in the Old Testament (IV Kings 6), built themselves huts beside the streams of the Jordan, and, abandoning the crowds of the cities, lived on coarse meal and wild herbs.” And in his letter to Paulinus: “Our leader is Elijah, our Elisha; our commanders are the sons of the prophets.”

Isidore teaches the same in Book II of *Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 15, where he calls Elijah, Elisha, and the other prophets leaders of monks. Cassian likewise says below (*Conference* 18, chapter 6), using another expression, that those Fathers and prophets “prefigured the outlines” of the monastic profession. He derives the metaphor from painters, who first prefigure and sketch out a future image by drawing its lines, and afterward add its colors and ornaments. In this way those prophets and anchorites, wandering in deserts, needy, afflicted, and so forth, sketched and prefigured the life and profession of the monks and anchorites of the New Testament.]

—namely Elijah and Elisha, as Scripture’s authority demonstrates. Thereafter, we recognize that the chief founders and authors of the New Testament—John, Peter, and Paul, together with the other men of the same order—walked in this manner.

The first of these, who had already prefigured the flowers of virginity and examples of chastity and continence in the Old Testament, was sent by the Lord to rebuke the messengers of Ahaziah, the sacrilegious king of Israel. Because the king, hindered by illness, had sent to consult Beelzebub, the god of Ekron, concerning his recovery, the prophet met the messengers and denied that the king would rise from the bed on which he had fallen. When they returned to the king and reported the prophet’s sentence, he asked them what sort and appearance the man had who had met them and spoken these words. “He was,” they replied, “a hairy man, girded around his loins with a leather belt.” From this dress the king immediately recognized the man of God and said, “It is Elijah the Tishbite” (IV Kings 1). By the sign of the belt and the appearance of his rough and unkempt body, he unmistakably recognized the man of God, since, amid the countless thousands of the Israelite people among whom he lived, this distinctive mark of his own dress clung to him perpetually.

Concerning John also, who came forth as a most sacred boundary between the Old and New Testaments, the end and beginning of each, we learn from the Evangelist’s account (Matthew 3): “John himself had a garment of camel’s hair and [Note: Although the Jews in Palestine used woolen belts (the author of the *Incomplete Work on Matthew*, chapter 3), John nevertheless preferred to use a leather belt—that is, one made of rawhide or hairy skin—both in imitation of Elijah and in order to obtain bodily affliction and mortification even through the belt. Thus Saint Jerome, in his letter to the virgin Demetrias, says among other praises of the elder Demetrias, who visited the holy places: “She marveled at the way of life of Elijah and John the Baptist, each of whom tightened and mortified his loins with a leather belt.” Writing likewise on Matthew about John the Baptist, he says: “The leather belt with which Elijah too was girded is a symbol of mortification.”

Following this example, Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, writes that monks in Africa were accustomed to use a leather girdle (Baronius, vol. IX of the *Annals*, year 938). Blessed Dorotheus the anchorite confirms the same in his first teaching, which concerns Renunciation, where, speaking of himself and the monks of his time, he says: “We also have a leather belt around our loins. This is a sign that we are girded for every task, so that we may be ready as quickly as possible; for whoever is about to work first girds himself, and only then undertakes the task. It is also a sign of the mortified body. For we must mortify our desires, especially those that arise from the loins. Concerning these the Apostle said: ‘Put to death, therefore, what is earthly in you: fornication, impurity,’ and so forth (Colossians 3).” These are his words.

Nevertheless, some other monks used a linen belt. Saint Jerome testifies this concerning the Pachomians in the preface to the Rule of Saint Pachomius: “Each one had a little linen girdle.” Others preferred a woolen belt, because Christ is believed to have used such a belt. Wool was the common material for belts among the Palestinians, and Christ did not depart from their common custom and dress. Hence Saint Jerome commends a woolen belt to Marcella, who lived in Palestine: “Let the belt be woolen and entirely simple and pure; let it be able to tighten the garment rather than tear it.”

We also read of some who were girded with a cord. Besides those Egyptians whom Cassian discusses in chapter 6 of this book, Paulinus of Nola describes other monks (Epistle 7) as girded not with a belt but with a rope. Saint Francis, the contemptuous of the world and outstanding lover of poverty, chose this sort of belt—woven from cords—as the most humble and suitable for the lowliest servants, for himself and his brothers.

As for the Benedictines, there is also a constitution of Pope Clement V concerning their belts and other articles of dress, in these words: “Let no one presume to wear a belt, knife, or spurs with ornamentation, or to ride with a saddle excessively decorated with nails or otherwise excessively costly, or with a bridle having iron fittings for adornment.”]

a leather belt around his loins [Matthew 3]. When Peter had been thrust into prison by Herod and was to be led out to execution the following day, an angel appeared to him and commanded: “Gird yourself and put on your sandals” (Acts 12). The angel of God would not have instructed him to do this if he had not observed that, because of the restoration afforded by the night’s rest, he had loosened the limbs that were usually tightened by his belt.

When the prophet Agabus found Paul at Caesarea on his way up to Jerusalem, where he was soon to be bound by the Jews, he took Paul’s belt, bound his own hands and feet with it, and, by this bodily gesture, prefigured the injuries of Paul’s future passion. He said: “Thus says the Holy Spirit: The man whose belt this is will the Jews bind in Jerusalem and deliver into the hands of the Gentiles” (Acts 21). The prophet could not have spoken and said, “the man whose belt this is,” unless Paul had been accustomed to fasten it continually around his loins.

## CHAPTER III. On the Monk’s Garment

[Note: After the belt, with which it is fitting for the monk, as a soldier of Christ, to be girded, the Author treats of the monk’s garment. In it he chiefly requires and commends the following conditions, using the example of the monks of old.

The first condition is that it not be excessive, but sufficient to cover the nakedness of the body and ward off the severity of cold. Thus Saint Basil, in the Rule translated by Rufinus (chapter 12), citing the same saying of the Apostle as Cassian, says: “The Apostle sufficiently established a rule for such necessities in a brief statement: ‘Having food and clothing, let us be content with these.’ He shows that we need only the garment by which we are covered, not a variety of clothing or ornament.” The first use of clothing itself indicates the same thing, since it is said that God made leather tunics for the first human beings. Such clothing was sufficient to cover their shame.

Yet because progress in our clothing also seems to require that we be warmed and protected, its use should be regulated for both purposes, so that nakedness may be covered and the force of cold, or whatever else causes external harm, may be kept away. Saint Benedict likewise says: “Let garments be provided for the brothers according to the character of the places where they live and the climate; for more are needed in cold regions, fewer in warm ones” (Rule, chapter 55).

The second condition is that it be plain, not costly or arranged for pomp and display; concerning this, Blessed Basil in the same place, Augustine in chapter 23 of his Rule, and Benedict in the passage cited above give instruction.

The third is that it be respectable and clean, not deliberately filthy. Saint Jerome urges this in more than one place. Writing to Nepotian, he says: “Ornament and filth must alike be avoided, for the one suggests luxury, the other glory” (Epistle 2). And to Eustochium: “Let the garment be neither too clean nor dirty, and marked by no peculiar variation, lest a crowd of passersby stop to meet you and you be pointed out with a finger” (Epistle 22). In the *Epitaph of Nepotian* he says: “His dress followed the custom of the province, distinguished neither by cleanliness nor by filth” (Epistle 3). The author of the *Life of Saint Bernard* says: “He always favored poverty in clothing, never filth; for he used to say that these were signs of the mind, either of one who is negligent or of one who seeks human glory outwardly” (Book III, chapter 2).

The fourth condition, which the Author touches on here and which amounts almost to the same thing, is that the garment not be singular or marked by some unusual peculiarity, as Saint Jerome says. Cassian here reports that the ancient monks rejected and condemned this fault of singularity, both in other matters and especially in clothing. Saint Pachomius, at the direction of an angel himself, forbade anyone to introduce into clothing and dress anything new or different from the others for the sake of adornment (Rule, article 55).

There will be other occasions to discuss the clothing of monks. As for why religious persons wear a distinctive and particular dress, different from that of secular people, Saint Basil gives two reasons in Question 22 of his *Longer Rules*. The first is to indicate their particular profession and state, or condition of life. “The ordinary dress of a Christian,” he says, “is understood to be that which is suitable according to his purpose and profession. Just as one dress belongs to a soldier and another to a senator, by which it is understood either that this man is a senator or that he is a soldier, so a monk should also have clothing suited to his profession.”

The second reason is that religious persons may be compelled, even against their will, to live religiously. “If someone,” he says, “sees an obscure person striking or publicly beating another, shouting shamefully, or spending his time in taverns or brothels, he will not easily observe or take note of such a person, knowing that he behaves similarly in the rest of his life. But if someone sees a person who professes the religious life do even some small thing contrary to what is fitting, everyone observes it, rebukes him, and turns it into a reproach against religion. Thus religious dress is like a tutor for the weaker, so that it may keep them, even against their will, from dishonorable and indecent conduct.” These are Saint Basil’s words.

Why religious persons change their clothing when they make their profession will be discussed elsewhere (Book IV, chapter 5).

As for the monastic garments that Cassian mentions here, Saint Jerome has gathered the whole equipment of the Egyptian monks into a brief summary, which it will be useful to reproduce here. He writes:

“They have nothing in their cells except a *psiathium* and two *lebitonaria*—a type of sleeveless garment among the Egyptian monks—and one already worn out for sleeping or working; a linen cloak; two *cucullae*; a goatskin, which they call a *melote*; a little belt; sandals; and a staff as a companion for travel.”

These are Saint Jerome’s words in the preface to the Rule of Saint Pachomius.]

The monk’s garment, too, must cover the body only, remove the shame of nakedness, and blunt the severity of cold—not nourish the seeds of vanity or pride, as the same Apostle teaches: [Note: The Vulgate version reads: “Having food and coverings, let us be content with these” (I Timothy 6). The Greek word is σκεπάσματα (*skepasmata*), “coverings” or “protections,” which has a broader meaning than garments, as is well known. For *sképasma* is a general term that includes not only clothing with which we are dressed but also a dwelling by which we are covered and protected, in accordance with Ecclesiasticus 29, which corresponds to the Apostle’s statement: “The beginning of human life is water, bread, clothing, and a house protecting shame.”

For this reason Cassian argues that it is less accurate for other Latin translators to render the passage, “Having food and clothing.” This is true whether one considers the force of the word *sképasma* or the moral instruction that the Apostle seems deliberately to imply through this general term—an instruction explained here by the Author and by Saint Basil in the passage cited above.

Since the Apostle intended those words to name explicitly the things necessary for all human beings generally, and intended them simply and absolutely rather than only with respect to particular purposes—and since food and clothing unquestionably occupy the chief place among them—Saint Jerome and others therefore often read and cite the passage in this way: “Having food and covering,” or “clothing,” attending more to the Apostle’s meaning and the common understanding than to the precise force of the Greek word (Epistle 22 to Eustochium; Book II *Against Jovinian*; and Epistle 26). From this also arose the custom in many religious orders that, when religious persons about to make their profession are asked what they seek, they answer: “Food and clothing” (Cassian, Book VII, chapter 29).

It should also be observed here that some people use this passage of Cassian and several others to prove that these books were written by him in Latin, not in Greek, as some have thought (Ciaconus, in his preface). For when he shows that the Apostle’s statement is better translated from Greek into Latin in this way than as it appears in certain Latin copies, he indicates rather clearly that he is writing in Latin, not Greek.]

“Having food and coverings, let us be content with these” (I Timothy 6). “Coverings,” he says—not “garments,” as the expression is not properly rendered in certain Latin copies—that is, things that cover the body only, not things that flatter with the glory of clothing. They should be so plain that no novelty of color or style makes them conspicuous among other men of this profession; so far removed from studied refinement that they are not, in turn, discolored by deliberately affected neglect. Finally, they should be so separated from the adornment of this world that in every respect they remain common to the dress of God’s servants.

[Note: This is a noteworthy statement, which we shall later list in its proper place among the more select passages at the end of the work. It corresponds to the eighth degree of humility assigned by Saint Benedict: “If a monk does nothing except what the common Rule of the monastery or the examples of his elders encourage” (Rule, chapter 7). Another similar statement is: “Whatever is done without the permission of one’s spiritual father will be counted as presumption and vainglory, not as a reward” (chapter 49).]

For whatever is presumed by one or a few among the servants of God, and is not held universally and in the Catholic manner by the whole body of the brotherhood, is either excessive or proud, and must therefore be judged harmful, displaying more the appearance of vanity than of virtue. Accordingly, those practices that we do not see handed down either by the holy men of old who laid the foundations of this profession or by the Fathers of our own time, who to this day preserve their institutions through succession, we too ought to cut away as excessive and useless.

Therefore [Note: *Cilicium*, from which *cilicina vestis* is derived, was named from the Cilician peoples, among whom cilicia were first made (Varro, Book II *On Agriculture*, chapter 11). It is a rough and coarse garment woven from the shorn hair of camels or goats. Its frequent and varied use is mentioned and commended in the sacred writings.

First, it was used in mourning and lamentation over death or some calamity. Thus the patriarch Jacob, when he saw the tunic of his son Joseph, is the first of all recorded as having put on cilicium (haircloth) and mourned his son for a long time (Genesis 37). So did David at the funeral of Abner (II Samuel 3), and Mordecai in the Book of Esther, chapter 3.

Then, and especially, it was used as a sign of repentance, either to perform or proclaim repentance, to avert God’s vengeance, to mortify the flesh, and to signify contempt for the world. In this way David, Ahab, Jehoram, the Ninevites, many prophets, and others are read to have been clothed in cilicia, or sackcloth.

Finally, it was used to obtain victory, deliverance from enemies, and other benefits from God, as in Judith 8 and Esther 4.

It should be observed that although *saccus* is used for *cilicium* in many passages of Scripture—hence Cassian in this passage says that the Ninevites were covered with the roughness of cilicium, whom Scripture says were clothed in sacks—and although wherever the translator renders *cilicium* in the Old Testament, the Hebrew is *sac*, a word also used among the Germans, from which the Greeks and Latins borrowed the name σάκκος (*sakkos*, “sack”), nevertheless elsewhere the two seem to be distinguished clearly.

Cilicium was worn inwardly and directly over the naked body, for the sake of affliction and mortification of the flesh; sackcloth, however, was worn outwardly as a humble and shameful dress, especially by princes and illustrious persons. This can be proved by two examples.

Concerning King Ahab, IV Kings 2 says that he covered his flesh with cilicium, fasted, slept in a sack, and walked with his head bowed. Here four acts of repentance are distinguished individually. Concerning Jehoram, IV Kings 6 says: “When he had torn his garments, all the people saw the cilicium with which he was clothed next to his flesh.” You will never find this said of a sack; rather, Scripture says that someone was covered, clothed, girded, belted, and so forth—actions generally performed outwardly.

In the New Testament, John the Baptist, the first herald of repentance, likewise first adopted the garment suitable to his preaching, namely cilicium as a symbol of repentance: “He had a garment of camel’s hair,” says the Evangelist (Matthew 3). It is therefore clear that his garment was cilicium woven from camel’s hair, not the hide of a camel or of any other animal, as the Apostle says concerning certain people in Hebrews that they wandered about in *melotes*, in goatskins. More will be said about them below.

Following this example, and for the same reasons, cilicium was customary among Christians at all times, especially among monks and hermits, as is clear from Saint Basil, chapter 69 of the Rule, and from the Lives of the Saints.

The use of cilicium, however, was not the same among all. Some were covered and content with this garment alone and wore no other outer dress. Cassian does not approve this practice here, and says that it was displeasing to the Egyptian monks because of the danger of display and vainglory, and also because it made a person less fit and ready for manual labor. Others concealed it beneath other clothing, as religious persons and devout Christians commonly do today. This practice is in no way to be condemned; indeed, the Author sufficiently indicates near the end of the chapter that it is most salutary. See also the fuller discussion of cilicium and cilicium bedding in the notes on *Conference* 1, final chapter.]

they utterly rejected the cilicium garment as something conspicuous and noticeable to everyone, which, precisely for that reason, could confer no spiritual benefit and could even foster the vanity of pride, and which was unsuitable and unfit for the necessary work in which a monk ought always to proceed energetically and efficiently.

If we have heard that certain people wrapped in this garment proved themselves worthy of approval, we must not for that reason establish the rule of monasteries or disturb the ancient decrees of the holy Fathers. A few presumptuous people, privileged by other virtues, are not thereby thought incapable of being reproved even for practices they have taken up contrary to the Catholic rule.

The judgment of the few ought not to be set above or allowed to prejudice the general constitution. We must give unquestioning faith and complete obedience in all things to those institutions and rules—not those introduced by the will of a few, but those that the antiquity of so many ages and the multitude of holy Fathers have transmitted to posterity by harmonious determination.

Nor should it prejudice us, as an example for daily conduct, that either the sacrilegious king of Israel, surrounded by troops of enemies, is said to have worn cilicium inwardly beneath his torn garment (IV Kings 6), or that the Ninevites, to soften the sentence of God pronounced against them through the prophet, were covered with the harshness of cilicium (Jonah 3). The former is shown to have worn it secretly next to his body, so that no one could have known it unless the garment above had been torn. The latter displayed their covering of cilicium at a time when everyone was mourning the city’s impending destruction and was wrapped in the same garment, so that no one could be accused by anyone of ostentation [Alternative reading: “of ostentation”].

For unless the difference is excessive, inequality is not offensive.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Hoods of the Egyptians

Furthermore, certain features of the Egyptians’ dress are suited not merely to the care of the body but also to the formation of character, so that the observance of simplicity and innocence may be maintained even in the very quality of their clothing.

[Note: A *cucullus*, or *cucullio*, or, less correctly in Latin, *cuculla*, is a kind of garment or covering that surrounds and protects the head and shoulders. Hence *cucullatus* means “dressed in a *cucullus* or *cuculla*” (Saint Ambrose, final sermon; Sidonius, Book VII, Epistle 16; Peter of Cluny, Book III, Epistle 28).

The Egyptian monks used *cuculli*, Cassian says, not so much for bodily care as as a symbol of monastic simplicity and innocence. Blessed Dorotheus also testifies to this in the passage cited above: “We also wear the *cucullus*, which is a sign of innocence and purity. Little children wear a *cucullus*, not mature men. We therefore wear the *cucullus* so that we may be children in malice, as the Apostle exhorts: ‘Do not be children in your understanding; but be children in malice.’”

Sozomen, speaking of these same monks in Book III of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 13, says: “They covered their heads with a covering which they usually call a *cucullus* (κυκούλλιον), thereby showing that they led a life as simple and sincere as that of children nourished with milk, whose heads they wrap in such a tiara so that they may be covered and warmed at the same time.” Nicephorus adds that the covering or hood was pointed (Book IX, chapter 14 of his *History*).

Palladius writes in chapter 37 of the *Lausiac History* that the Tabennesiot monks under the abbot Pachomius had *cucullae* marked with the figure of a purple cross. As noted above, they were accustomed to approach communion wearing only the *cuculla*. In chapter 41 he says that consecrated virgins, too, in his time were accustomed to use *cuculli*.

Saint Jerome names a *cuculla* in the Testament of Hilarion. He writes: “Leaving him all his possessions—namely, the Gospel, a sackcloth tunic [Note: The phrase “sackcloth tunic” means a sack or cilicium, discussed above. See Sidonius, Book VII, Epistle 16, and Peter of Cluny, Book III, Epistle 28, *Treatise 21 on the Rule of Saint Benedict*], a *cuculla*, and a little cloak.”

Monks generally call it a *cuculla*, not a *cucullus*. Saint Benedict does so as well in chapter 55 of his Rule, where he assigns a double or twin *cuculla*: one shaggy for winter, the other simple and light for summer.

Turrecremata commented on this passage that different people understand *cuculla* in different ways: “Some,” he says, “namely the Transalpines, call *cuculla* a long and ample garment without sleeves, as Pope Clement seems to understand it in the first Clementine on the state of monks; but they call *floccus* a garment with long sleeves. Others call *cuculla* the garment that elsewhere is called *floccus*, namely a garment closed on every side, with a hood and long sleeves.” These are his words.]

They wear very small *cucullae*, hanging only as far as the juncture of the neck and shoulders and covering nothing but the head, continually by day and night, so that they may be constantly moved—by imitating the covering itself—to preserve the innocence and simplicity of little children.

Having returned to the infancy of Christ, they sing at every hour with devotion and strength:

“Lord, my heart has not been exalted,  
nor have my eyes been lifted up;  
I have not walked in great matters,  
nor in things too wonderful for me.  
If I did not think humbly,  
but exalted my soul,  
as a child weaned from his mother” (Psalm 131).

## CHAPTER V. On the Colobia of the Egyptians
[Note: [Col. 0068C] *Colobium* should, according to its Greek derivation, be written with a single *l*, not a double one (Alcuin, *Book on Divine Offices*, chapter 35). It is a tunic lacking sleeves, with the arms protruding beyond it: from Greek ἀπὸ τοῦ κολόβου, which means “short,” “mutilated,” or “maimed.” Cassian’s *colobia*, however, which the Egyptian monks wore, were not entirely without sleeves; rather, the sleeves ended below the elbow (Sophronius, *Spiritual Meadow*, chapters 92, 120, and 124), or, as he himself says, reached almost to the ends of the elbows, rather than leaving the arms bare as far as the shoulders, as Cuychius thought. Concerning these garments Sozomen, assigning another, tropological or moral, explanation, writes in Book III, chapter 13, that the Egyptian monks had κειτῶνας ἀχειροδωτούς, that is, tunics without sleeves, so that by this sign they might show that their hands were entirely removed from inflicting injury and insult (the same is said by St. Dorotheus in the passage cited above). Similar to these *colobia* in sacred vestments are the dalmatics, or little tunics, that we see (Alcuin, cited above, chapter 37). Concerning these Anselm, the compiler of decretals, quotes the following as though from Eusebius, although it is uncertain from which work: “From Saint Sylvester and his presbyters the use of *colobia* began, and Mark, Julius, and Liberius used them in succession. After these, however, the *colobia* were changed into dalmatics.” Thus he. The *colobium* is also elsewhere called *libitonarium* or *levitonarium*, as Isidore testifies in Book XIX, chapter 22, of the *Etymologies*: “The *libitonarium*,” he says, “is a *colobium* without sleeves, such as the monks of Egypt wear.” Saint Jerome also mentions it in the preface to the Rule of Saint Pachomius. It was also called *lebeton* or *lebitum*, with the same meaning; hence in the Life of that same Pachomius we read: “They had so restricted themselves in the poverty of clothing that they never used another *lebeton*, except when necessity compelled them to wash the dirt from their garment. The *lebeton* was a linen garment in the form of a *colobium*, which monks nowadays wear throughout the Thebaid and Egypt.” The same work also contains, among the Institutions of Pachomius preserved by Palladius in the *Lausiac History*: “At night they are to have linen *lebitones*, girded up.”

Why those monks, in the austerity of that desert, used linen *colobia* rather than woolen ones could have had several obvious causes: either because linen garments, being cheaper and more contemptible, were also more suitable and convenient in those hot regions; or because they had received this practice from apostolic example and tradition. Certainly Eusebius, in Book I, chapter 24 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, writes from Hegesippus that James, the brother of the Lord, never wore a woolen garment but used only a linen cloth. Cassianus indicates another reason, and a moral one: by that linen clothing, or covering, they signified that they had been mortified to every earthly way of life and were dead to the world, since the bodies of the dead are customarily wrapped in linen; and Christ, who died for us, is likewise read to have been wrapped in a clean linen cloth (Matthew XXVII). Cassianus appears to have this in view on the basis of the Apostle’s sayings that he cites. Linen also has this symbolic meaning because, in order to be made into cloth, it is softened, beaten, twisted, and in its own way mortified through many processes. It is also plausible that they wished to use linen garments because of their cleanliness and whiteness, to signify the innocence and purity that they pursued, in accordance with Ecclesiastes, chapter IX: “At all times let your garments be white.”

As for the color of the *colobia* or of other garments, it does not seem worthwhile to investigate the matter too curiously; for it is clear that those poor men and hermits, who cultivated the utmost poverty, could use no garments other than the simplest and cheapest, and that they did not all universally and perpetually use one identical habit. Rather, according to differences of place, time, means, or the varying tradition of their ancestors or elders, they used different garments. In the first place, Philo describes those Alexandrian *therapeutae*—that is, the most ancient monks, disciples of the apostles—as dressed in white. “When,” he says, “the men in white had assembled, joyful yet filled with the greatest gravity,” and so forth (*On the Contemplative Life*, supplementary book). Clement of Alexandria also testifies that Egyptians generally wore white, according to a distinctive national custom; and he especially commends to Christians white garments as natural, undyed, and, as his translator says, not subjected to the fuller, preferring them to all dyed garments (*The Paedagogue*, Book II, chapter 10, and Book III, chapter 11; *The Cloak*).

On the other hand, there is much that teaches us that monks formerly used black garments. First, Tertullian testifies that Christians devoted to the more perfect life wore the *pallium* in the manner of philosophers, and he congratulates himself on this designation in a special book that he published on this subject. That the philosophical cloak, once transferred to Christians, was black is suggested by Saint Jerome in Letter 23, where, speaking of Christians who were mocked by pagans—and sometimes even by pseudo-Christians—because of their cheaper clothing, he says: “Because we do not use silk garments, we are called monks; if the tunic is not white, immediately comes the cry from the street: ‘Impostor and Greek!’”

This is established much more clearly by ancient history (*Acta Sanctorum*, volume VI, chapter 9). For in the Life of the holy martyrs Galaction and Episteme, who suffered under Decius, the author says that those clothed in a black cloak were like angels—namely, those who separated themselves from the world and from the things of the world, preserved virginity, and chose a life like Christ’s.

The Fathers also commend this black and dark garment as especially customary for monks and nuns. Saint Jerome, in Letter 15 to Marcella, says: “She suddenly consecrated herself to the Lord after putting on a darker tunic.” Augustine, in Letter 199 to Ecdicia, indicates that the dark garment, which he calls *nigella*, was then the distinctive sign of those professing continence. Finally, Saint Bernard writes in his book to his sister: “The black garment signifies humility of mind.” And Peter of Cluny, writing to Bernard, says: “It seemed to those great Fathers that this black color of which we are speaking was more suited to humility, more suited to penance, and more suited to mourning. Since the monk must devote his entire life to these practices, they determined that color should be joined to conduct and garments to virtues by whatever kinship they could establish,” and so forth.

To this may be added the fact that, from the color of their garments, Benedictines are called “black monks” in canon law and commonly among canonists. Raphael Volaterranus, in Book XXI of his *Anthropology*, and the Cassinese Chronicle, Book IV, chapter 115, testify that Saint Benedict himself used this color. The Cassinese Fathers likewise confirm it in their declaration on the Rule, chapter 55, in these words: “For this reason a varied custom and color of garments has arisen in the monastic state; but we have adopted the black color, following our most blessed father Benedict, who, as we read, used black.” Thus they.

It should also be observed that Saint Basil, in Letter 1 to Gregory of Nazianzus and in the more fully discussed Rules, Question 22, says much about the monks’ habit but nothing about its color, except that the habit should be of one color and uniform. Cassianus likewise says nothing about color throughout this entire book in which he describes the monks’ habit. Hence Saint Benedict, thoroughly imbued with the examples and institutions of those ancient monks and hermits, warns his cenobites in chapter 55 of the Rule not to complain about the color or thickness of their garments, or matters of this kind—that is, not to grumble or murmur—but to use, he says, whatever can be found in the province where they live, or whatever can be obtained more cheaply.

As for what was established in later centuries concerning Benedictine garments, their colors, and their other conditions, this is discussed more fully in the famous Constitution of Clement V, whose words deserve to be recalled:

“Lest anything unbecoming creep into the Lord’s field—that is, into the sacred order of the Black Monks—or anything vicious grow disastrously amid the crop; but rather that flowers of honor and fruits of uprightness may flourish there in abundance: forbidding them every disordered or elaborate adornment or display in clothing, as well as any notable excess in food, drink, riding, or bedding, we decree that their outer garment, nearest to their habit—that is, to the *floccus*, *cuculla*, or *scapular*, as the gloss says—namely, the gown, shall be black, brown, or white, according to the custom ordinarily observed among them in the region where they live. Nor shall moderation be exceeded in the quality of the cloth; nor shall anything more costly or finer be sought, but only what can usefully be found,” and so forth.

Where the glossator comments on the words “black, brown, or white”: “By permitting these three colors, he prohibits all the others, including mixed colors, a point that many do not consider. Therefore, when the Rule says—namely, that of Saint Benedict, in the passage cited above—that monks are not to complain about color, it does not mean that they may use every color; for certain colors are forbidden even to secular clerics (*On the Life and Honesty of Clerics*, chapter *Clerici*, Book III of the Decretals, title I). Rather, it means that they should not complain among the permitted colors that one is more fixed, more beautiful, or better than another.”

The glossator then adds the reason why those colors are permitted rather than others: “These colors can be obtained from wool without dye, and therefore are more approved.” I thought it worthwhile to report these matters here on account of the occasion.]

Clothed also in linen *colobia*, which scarcely reach the lower ends of the elbows, they leave their hands bare for the remainder of their length, so that the cutting off of the sleeves may suggest that their actions and works in this world have been cut away, and the linen garment may teach that they have been mortified to every earthly way of life. Through this they hear the Apostle saying to them every day: “Mortify your members which are upon the earth” (Colossians III). The habit itself also bears witness to the words: “For you are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians III). And again: “I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me. The world is crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians II).

## CHAPTER VI. On Their *Rebrachiatoria*

[Note: [Col. 0071B] This is an obscure passage, made still more obscure rather than clearer by the use of many words that are nearly synonymous to explain the same matter; each of them must therefore be explained (see Nicephorus, Book IX, chapter 15). I interpret the double cords woven with a woolen under-thread as small ropes or bands woven of woolen thread, hanging here and there beneath the armpits. By these the monks girded and tightened their lower and looser garments around the chest and loins, as Cassianus himself explains. This is what the French call *trousser les vestemens*, “to tuck up the garments,” just as Franciscans restrain their garments with a belt or cord so that they do not impede them when working or traveling. *Resticula* is a diminutive of *restis*, that is, “rope,” as is well known. *Subtegmen*, or, as Junius’s *Nomenclator* prefers, *subtemen*, is the thread that passes beneath the warp or is woven into the warp; hence it is also called *trama*, because it passes through the web. In French, *trame* or *traime du tisserand* (“a weaver’s weft”). *Succinctorium* is the same as *succingulum*, by which garments were gathered and girded up, as has been said.

Among poets, *redimiculum* means a band hanging from a woman’s or priest’s headdress; the Greeks call it ταινία, “a ribbon.” Virgil, *Aeneid* IX:

“And the sleeves of the tunic, and the bands of the headdress.”

And Ovid, *Metamorphoses* X:

“The bands hang down upon her breast.”

Isidore, however, explains it more appropriately for this passage as follows: “The *redimiculum* is what we call a *succinctorium* or *bracile*. Descending along the neck and let down from the sides of the neck, it surrounds the hollow beneath both arms and girds from either side, so that by constricting the garment’s width it fits the body and, joining it together, arranges it. In common speech this is called *bracile*, as though *brachiale*, although now it is a belt not for the arms but for the loins.” Thus Isidore (*Etymologies* XIX, near the end of chapter 22). From this I conclude that Cassianus’s *rebrachiatoria* mean the same as Isidore’s *bracile* or *brachiale*, although *brachialia* properly denotes ornaments of the arms, just as *frontalia* denotes ornaments of the forehead and *tibialia* those of the shins.

Cassianus was not content with these terms, but also added the Greek word ἀναβολάς, which in many older manuscripts is written *analaboys*. Dionysius the Carthusian has *anabore*; both forms are corrupt and barbarous (see Suidas, under ἀναβολή). Ἀναβολή means the same as “delay” or “suspension,” as is well known, and in this sense agrees suitably with those synonyms. Others read ἀναβόλαια or ἀναβολάδια, with the same derivation and meaning, although Isidore (*Etymologies* XIX, cited above) explains *anaboladium* as a linen covering for women, by which the shoulders are covered, and which the Greeks and Latins call *sindon*.

A related word, *analabus*, appears in Blessed Dorotheus, in the First Instruction, but with a meaning far different from these. Speaking of the monks’ garments and explaining their purposes and mysteries, he says: “Our habit is this: a tunic without sleeves, a leather belt, an *analabus*, and a *cucullus.” He explains below what an *analabus*, or *anabalus*, is: “The *analabus* is placed in the form of a cross. We carry the sign of the cross upon our shoulders, in accordance with the words: ‘Take up your cross and follow me.’” Again, below: “We also have an *analabum*, that is, a scapular hanging from the shoulders, which is the cross.”]

They also wear double cords woven with a woolen under-thread, which the Greeks call ἀναβολάς, while we may call them *succinctoria*, *redimicula*, or, more precisely, *rebrachiatoria*. Descending over the upper part of the neck and dividing at the sides of the neck, they surround the hollows beneath both arms and gird them on either side, so that, by constricting the garment’s width, they draw it toward and join it to the body. Thus, with their arms tightened, they are made unimpeded and ready for every work, striving with all their strength to fulfill the Apostle’s command:

“These hands have ministered not only to me but also to those who are with me; nor did we eat anyone’s bread without payment, but working night and day in labor and weariness, so that we might not burden any of you” (Acts XX). And: “If anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat” (II Thessalonians III).

## CHAPTER VII. On Their *Mafortes*

After this, pursuing both the humility and the cheapness of the garment, as well as economy, they cover their necks and shoulders with a narrow little cloak, which

[Note: [Col. 0072B] In the plural, *mafors* or *mavors* in the singular; elsewhere *maforte* or *mavorte*. Concerning it Isidore says: “In Greek, *stola* is so called because it is placed over another garment; in Latin it is also called *ricinium*, because one half of it is thrown backward; in common speech it is called *mavortem*.” Thus he (*Etymologies* XIX, chapter 25). The translator of Sozomen calls it a *humerale* (*Ecclesiastical History* III, chapter 13). Saint Jerome also mentions it in Letter 22 to Eustochium, where he reproaches certain virgins who wore a looser *mavorte* in these words: “And the hyacinth-colored cloak, flying as a *mavorte*, over the shoulders.” It is also called *maphorte* or *mavorte* in the Acts of the Martyrdom of Saint Paul the Apostle, attributed to Linus, where the veil of Plautilla, called a *maphorte*, is mentioned as having been presented to Paul. Likewise, in the Acts of the holy martyrs Fausta and Evilasius, a fragment of which Bede quotes in his *Martyrology* for September 20, we read the following about the *maphorte*: “He ordered Fausta to be scourged naked and without a *maphorte*, imprisoned, and her head pierced,” and so forth.

Cassianus gives a sufficiently clear picture of what a *mafors* or *mavors* was: a narrow cloak with which they covered their necks and shoulders. It seems not unlike the little cloak that abbots and certain other religious persons now wear, which the Italians also call a *maforetta*, with a closely related name.]

are called *mafortes* both in our language and in theirs, and thus

[Note: [Col. 0072C] Some read *planetae*; Dionysius explains it as *planicae*. It seems to me that *planetica* is a diminutive of *planeta*, which in sacred vestments is otherwise called a *casula*, as though “little house,” because in ancient times it covered the entire person like a house. Garments of this kind—*planetae*, or *casulae*, entirely closed and rounded—still exist in certain monasteries. By analogy with this, *planetica* or *planica* was called a broad and splendid garment, arranged for pomp and display and surrounding the entire person in the manner of a *planeta* or *casula*. Some think it was derived from the verb πλανάομαι, “to wander” or “to stray,” because by its length and breadth it flowed in every direction and seemed, as it were, to wander about. Hence Isidore says: “The Greeks wish *casulae* to be called *planetae*, because they wander about with wandering edges, like the stars called *planetae*, that is, ‘wandering,’ which move about in their wandering motion” (*Etymologies* XIX, chapter 24).

Cassianus therefore rightly sets the *planeta* against the *mavorte*, since the latter is a simple and narrow little cloak. Isidore likewise forbade *planetae* and *birri* to his monks in his Rule, as Ciaconius has noted.

Furthermore, *birrus* and *birrum* are found in both masculine and neuter forms. Coelius Rhodiginus discusses it in his *Ancient Readings*, Book XVI, chapter 10: “The Greeks write that it was a Roman garment, and the historian Martianus confirms this in Book IV. *Birrus* and *tunica* are names of garments.” But not everyone agrees about what kind of garment it was. Some explain *birrus* as a silk or costly garment, as Zonaras and Theodore do when interpreting canon 12 of the Council of Gangra, which Gratian quotes in Distinction 30 in these words: “If any man should think that it is suitable to the holy purpose—that is, to continence—to wear a cloak as though he possessed righteousness by it, and should reproach and judge those who respectfully wear *birri* or another common garment that is in ordinary use, let him be anathema.”

Others more probably believe that the *birrus* was a kind of shorter cloak, also commonly used by ecclesiastics at that time; and that this canon was issued against certain Eustathian monks who, dressed in long cloaks in the manner of philosophers and glorying and taking pride in that habit as a mark of holiness or wisdom, despised and condemned other ecclesiastics who wore *birri* or some other shorter garment.

That such a habit was also clerical and ecclesiastical, and was used not only by lower clergy but also by bishops, is shown especially by the Acts of the martyr Saint Cyprian. There we read that, when he was already about to be beheaded, he first removed his *birrus*—or, as other Acts have it, his *lacerned birrus*—then stripped off his dalmatic or tunic, remained in a linen garment, and in that condition awaited the executioner.

From this Cardinal Baronius concludes (*Annals*, year 261) that it was an ancient custom of bishops first to put on, over their ordinary garment, a linen garment, commonly called a rochet; then a loose, sleeved tunic, otherwise called a dalmatic; and finally a short cloak, or *birrus*, covering only the shoulders and arms. We see those who are promoted from religious orders to that dignity using a similar habit today.

Saint Augustine further testifies that clergy in Africa were accustomed to wear a linen tunic and a *birrus*, while bishops wore a more costly *birrus*. For in Sermon 50 *On Various Matters*, where he regulates the discipline of his clergy, he says: “Let no one give a *birrus*, a linen tunic, or anything else except for the common fund. From the common fund I will receive what is for myself.” Shortly afterward he says: “Bring me an expensive *birrus*; perhaps it suits a bishop, although it does not suit poor Augustine, born of poor parents.” Thus Augustine.

It is also known from Gregory of Tours (*History* II, chapter 1) that Saint Brictius, bishop, when falsely accused, carried burning coals in his *birrus* to the tomb of Saint Martin to prove his innocence; yet the *birrus* remained entirely unburned and unharmed. The same custom also prevailed in the Eastern Church, namely, for bishops to wear a *birrus* over their tunic, as we may gather from what Palladius writes about Saint Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria (*Lausiac History*, chapter 51, as Baronius cites it above), saying that he withdrew dressed in a tunic and *birrus*.

It is certain from Saint Augustine’s statement quoted above that the *birrus* could be either cheap or costly, according to each person’s choice. Flavius Vopiscus, in his Life of the Emperor Carinus, testifies that the more expensive *birri* were those of Arras and Canusium, writing among other things: “The requested Arras *birri* were given; Canusian *birri* were given.” By these words he indicates that the people of Arras in Gaul had shamefully squandered costly *birri*, or βήρους, as some think it should be read, for the disgraceful uses of actors.

The same point is relevant to Saint Jerome’s statement against Jovinian: “Now you walk adorned with linen and silk garments and the clothing of Laodicea” (Book II, chapter 13). Marianus adds in his scholia: “Soft and luxurious linen garments were made among the people of Arras and Laodicea; some peoples of lower Germany, such as the town of Lille and the province of Holland, are still distinguished by this glory.”

Suidas calls them ἀτραβάτικας χλαμύδας, for which Robert Stephanus corrected the reading to ἀτρεβάτικας. Sulpicius Severus, when attacking the luxury of certain ecclesiastics, likewise mentions a stiff *birrus* and a flowing *lacerna* (*Dialogues* III, chapter 14).

Understand, therefore, that the *birri* or *byrri* referred to here were costly and sumptuous garments, which the Egyptian monks rejected in their avoidance of expense and ostentation, covering their heads instead with cheap *mavortes*. Otherwise, in form, shortness, and shape, the *birrus* differed little or not at all from the *mavorte*. Hence in French *birretum*, a diminutive of *birrus*, means a small cap, just as the *mavortes* worn by the Egyptian monks, to avoid the expense of *birri*, were also coverings for the head.]

they avoid at once the cost and the ostentation of *planeticae* and *birri*.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the *Melote* and the Goat’s Skin

[Col. 0073A]

The last of their garments is a goat’s skin, which

[Col. 0074A] [Note: [Col. 0074A] *Melotes*, or *melota*, is a Greek word signifying a sheep’s or goat’s skin removed from the body together with its wool, or a garment fitted and made from such skins. For μῆλον in Greek means “sheep” in Latin (Nicephorus, Book IX, chapter 15).

Saint Jerome, in the Life of Hilarion, calls it by another name, a leather *ependytes*; others interpret this as a *paenula*, others as a tunic. The Apostle writes that certain fathers of the Old Testament went about in such skins, or *melotes*—that is, wandered about like fugitives or strangers (Hebrews XI), undoubtedly referring to the prophets, especially Elijah and Elisha, the heir of his cloak. For the Septuagint calls Elijah’s cloak μελώτην in III Kings IX and IV Kings II. Hence he himself is called “a hairy man” in IV Kings I, which should be understood not so much of his beard and hair as of his clothing. Thus Saint Jerome says in Letter 28: “Elijah, carried up to heaven in a fiery chariot, left his *melote* on earth.”

Following this example, Saint Antony is also said to have possessed a *melote*. As he was dying, he said: “Give the *melote* and the worn cloak on which I lie to Bishop Athanasius; he himself had brought it new” (Athanasius, *Life of Saint Antony*).

With the same desire to imitate them, Sozomen, in Book III, chapter 13, records that the Egyptian monks wore skins, which he calls διφθέραι, that is, leather *paenulae*, or shaggy leather cloaks. He explains the reason for this garment in these words: “Following the example of Elijah the Tishbite, they clothed themselves in skins, so that each of them, continually recalling the prophet’s virtue through the skin thrown around his body, might struggle vigorously against sexual desires.” Thus he.

In the Rule of Saint Pachomius preserved by Palladius we also read the following provision: “Let each man have a worked white sheepskin; without it they are neither to eat nor sleep” (*Lausiac History*, chapter 38). Saint Jerome likewise confirms this in the preface to the same Rule.

Finally, it can plainly be inferred from the Dialogue of Saint Gregory the Great that our holy father Saint Benedict also used a *melote* (Book II, chapter 7). Gregory relates that when Saint Maurus, at the abbot’s command, walked upon the water to rescue a boy from it, and Saint Benedict attributed the miracle not to his own merits but to the boy’s obedience, the boy intervened as an arbiter in this friendly contest of mutual humility and said: “When I was being drawn from the water, I saw the abbot’s *melote* above my head, and I thought that it was he who was pulling me out of the water.” Thus the passage.

It may seem strange that Cassianus appears to have called the *melote* a *pera*, or bag, not only here but also in *Conference* 11, chapter 3: “When we had received a bag and a staff, as is customary there for all monks who are traveling.” Isidore likewise interprets *pera* as *melote*: “The *melotes*, which is also called a *pera*, is a goat’s skin hanging from the neck and girded down to the loins,” and so forth (*Etymologies* XIX, chapter 34).

Despite this, I incline to the opinion that *pera*, here and elsewhere, has been put for *paenula* through the fault of scribes or copyists; and therefore that the text should read: “the *melotes*, which is called a *paenula*” (chapter 10). For who could believe that those monks abstained from footwear so religiously or scrupulously because they thought it forbidden by the Lord’s command, as will be said below, yet regarded a bag as a *melote* and as an ordinary garment, when in those same passages and Gospel sayings a bag is forbidden together with sandals (Matthew X and Luke II)?

Especially since, among reputable authors both sacred and secular, *pera* signifies nothing other than a pouch or sack in which shepherds or travelers commonly store their daily food or provisions. It is understood in this sense in Luke’s Gospel: “Do not carry a purse or a bag.” Likewise in Luke XXII: “When I sent you without a bag and a staff,” and elsewhere.

Concerning the *paenula*, Niccolò Perotti says the following, which Ambrose Calepinus also repeats and which sufficiently shows that the *paenula* agrees with the *melote*: “The *paenula* is a thick and cheap garment that is put on over the tunic in cloudy and rainy weather in place of a cloak, to keep rain away from the body. If it was made from skins, it was called *scortea*.” Martial writes of it in Book XIV:

“You may set out upon the road beneath an entirely clear sky;

yet a leather cloak should never be absent against sudden showers.”

And there is more of this kind in those authors and others.]

is called a *melotes* or a *pera*; they also carry a staff, in imitation of those who prefigured the outlines of this vocation in the Old Testament (see above, chapter 2). Concerning them the Apostle says:

“They wandered about in *melotes* and goat skins, needy, afflicted, and distressed—men of whom the world was not worthy—wandering in deserts and mountains, and in caves and caverns of the earth” (Hebrews XI).

This garment of goat skin signifies that, after every form of carnal wantonness has been mortified, they must stand in the utmost gravity of virtue, with nothing wanton, heated, youthful, or restless remaining in their bodies.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Staff

[Note: [Col. 0075C] Saint Jerome testifies in the preface to the Rule of Saint Pachomius, and in the Life of Hilarion, that the monks of the Thebaid had a staff as a companion for travel. Saint Antony also, according to the same Jerome, was accustomed to carry a staff; hence he is usually depicted equipped with one. If the reader seeks moral interpretations, he may find many of them, entirely consonant with Cassianus’s statements, in Peter Berchorius, who gathers and explains, aptly and ingeniously though in a rough style, various moral meanings of the staff from different passages of Scripture (*Dictionary*, under “Staff”). Pagninus likewise offers other sufficiently similar material concerning the staff and its meanings (*Isagoge* I, chapter 18).]

That these same men carried a staff is also taught by Elisha, who was one of them, when he says to his servant Gehazi, sending him to raise the son of the woman: “Take my staff, and go quickly; place it upon the boy’s face, so that he may live” (IV Kings IV). The prophet would certainly not have given it to him to carry unless he himself had been accustomed to carry it continually in his own hand.

The carrying of the staff spiritually admonishes them never to walk unarmed amid so many barking dogs of vices and invisible beasts of spiritual wickedness. Concerning these, blessed David asks to be delivered when he says: “Do not hand over, O Lord, the soul that confesses you to the beasts” (Psalm LXXIII). Rather, they must blunt their assault by the sign of the cross, drive them far away, and extinguish those raging against them through constant remembrance of the Lord’s Passion and imitation of his mortification.

## CHAPTER X. On Their Sandals
Footwear, however, as though forbidden by the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0075D] Namely, by the passage expressed in Matthew and Luke in these words: “Do not carry a purse, nor a bag, nor sandals” (Matt. 10; Luke 9). Those monks understood these words in such a way that they concluded that the use of footwear had been forbidden to the apostles and their followers—that is, to monks and those devoted to the more perfect life—and that they therefore ought to walk barefoot and unshod. Thus, according to their custom, capacity, and simplicity, they were accustomed to interpret the words of Scripture too rigidly and literally, as the saying goes, that is, according to the sound of the words; and this was also the custom of the first Christians, who embraced whatever they heard from the Gospel, either out of fervor or simplicity, as a commandment, without considering the distinction between counsels [Col. 0076B] and commandments. Yet this opinion seemed insufficiently solid and probable to more prudent men. For even if it were truly said that this commandment had been imposed on the apostles for a time—that is, at the beginning of their preaching—it would not follow that it was perpetual, especially since Christ appears to have revoked it later, on the night of the supper, when he said to them: “When I sent you without purse and sandals, etc.” (Luke 22), as St. Chrysostom notes in Homily 9 on the Epistle to the Philippians. Still less should it be extended to others as though it were a universal commandment. Nor is it credible that Christ himself or the apostles always went entirely barefoot, since John the Baptist said of Christ in Matthew 3: “He is mightier than I; I am not worthy, stooping down, to loosen the strap of his sandals.” Mark, moreover, as though wishing to prevent what Matthew had written from being wrongly understood, wrote that sandals had been permitted to the apostles: “But shod with sandals.” By these words he indicates that Christ [Col. 0076C] wished, or at least permitted, the apostles to be shod with sandals. Hence the angel also said to the apostle Peter in Acts 12: “Put on your sandals,” where the Greek has σανδάλια [sandalia, “sandals”]. For this reason St. Augustine, in Book 2, chapter 30, of *On the Harmony of the Gospels*, and others judge that only those kinds of footwear were forbidden to the apostles which covered the entire foot and were properly called ὑποδήματα [hypodēmata, “footwear” or “shoes”]; whereas sandals were permitted to them according to the custom of that region, since they covered only the sole of the foot, leaving the upper part bare and uncovered. Augustine indicates that this kind of footwear was called both *sandalia* (sandals) and *soleae* (sandals or soles). Since, therefore, Christ and the apostles, as is probable, used sandals according to the custom of that people, especially the custom adopted by the poor, the Lord did not wish his disciples, when setting out to preach, to change their sandals or to be anxious about procuring shoes; thus, by this dress as well, they might display humility, penitence, and contempt for worldly goods. Accordingly, those monks, moved by this example and reasoning, when they read in the Gospel that footwear had been forbidden to the apostles but sandals had not, adhered simply to the words of Scripture and also attended to the spiritual or moral meaning touched upon here. They religiously abstained from footwear as though it were forbidden by the Gospel commandment, and, rejecting its use, wore sandals—or, as Cassian puts it, fortified their feet with *caligae*. By these and the following words he clearly indicates that he understands *caligae* as sandals, that is, coverings for the feet rather than the shins, in accordance with the passage of Scripture mentioned above. (See Baronius, vol. 1 of the *Annals*, year 57, and Molanus, *On Paintings and Images*, chapter 82.) St. Gregory of Nazianzus also testifies that, in former times, many monks customarily walked without shoes, either barefoot or wearing only soles, in imitation of the same practice [Col. 0077A]. In *Oration 1, On Peace*, when listing the exercises of monks, he includes bare feet resembling those of the apostles [Col. 0077B]. St. Jerome likewise indicates this without obscurity when he taunts the apostate monk Jovinianus [Col. 0078A] in these words: “Formerly you were barefoot [Col. 0078B]; now you are not only shod, but even adorned.”]

rejecting footwear as forbidden by the Gospel commandment [Col. 0076B], whenever bodily weakness, the morning cold of winter [Col. 0077A], or the heat of the noonday sun [Col. 0078A] requires it, they merely protect their feet with *caligae*. They interpret the use of these as signifying either the Lord’s permission, or this: that if, while situated in this world, we cannot be entirely freed from the care and concern of this flesh, nor prevail in being wholly released from it, then at least we should discharge the body’s necessity through a light occupation and slight involvement, and should not allow the feet of our soul—which must always be ready, unimpeded, for the spiritual race and for proclaiming the peace of the Gospel, with which we run after the fragrance of Christ’s ointments (Song 1), and concerning which David says, “I ran in thirst” (Ps. 61), and Jeremiah, “But I did not grow weary in following you” (Jer. 17)—to be entangled in the death-dealing cares of this age. By these cares I mean thoughts directed not toward supplying nature’s necessity, but toward excessive and harmful pleasure. We shall fulfill this if, according to the Apostle, we do not make provision for the flesh in its desires (Rom. 13). Although they use these *caligae* lawfully, therefore, since they have been permitted by the Lord’s command, they nevertheless do not allow them to remain on their feet when they approach to celebrate or receive the sacred mysteries. They judge that even in the literal sense the command spoken to Moses, or to Joshua the son of Nun, must be observed: “Loosen the strap of your sandal, for the place on which you stand is holy ground” (Exod. 3; Josh. 5).

# BOOK TWO  
## ON THE CANONICAL FORM OF NIGHT PRAYERS AND PSALMS

[Col. 0077]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0077B]

[Note: [Col. 0077C] Namely, bodily and spiritual, concerning which above (Book 1, chapters 2 and the last): bodily, so that the monk, girded up, may be more ready for every use and external work; spiritual, that is, through the mortification of the members in which the seeds of lust are contained.]

Thus, once the soldier of Christ has been girded with this twofold belt of which we have spoken, let him now learn what form of canonical prayers and psalms was established in ancient times by the holy fathers in the regions of the East. Concerning their character, however, and how we may pray without ceasing according to the Apostle’s teaching (1 Thess. 5), we shall explain in their proper places, when we begin to set forth the *Conferences* of the elders, as far as the Lord grants us to do so (*Conference* 9, chapters 3, 6 and following, and *Conference* 10, chapter 7).

## CHAPTER TWO  
### On the diversity of the number appointed for chanting psalms throughout the various provinces

For we have discovered that in other regions many men, according to the capacity of their minds, possessed indeed, as the Apostle says (Rom. 10), zeal for God, but not according to knowledge, and had established for themselves various patterns and rules concerning this matter [Note: [Col. 0077C] He sometimes calls it a *type*, or canon; at other times a rule [Col. 0077D] or constitution; and at other times a method and arrangement. St. Ambrose likewise understands the word in this sense in Letter 68, when he says: “It is possible to find some pattern by which the discord of the brethren may be removed.”].

Some judged that twenty or thirty psalms should be recited each night, and that these same psalms should be extended by antiphonal melodies and the addition of certain musical embellishments [Col. 0078C]; others attempted to exceed even this measure; some prescribed eighteen. Thus, in different places, we found different canons established, and we saw almost as many patterns and rules in use as the monasteries and cells we observed. (See below, chapter 8 of this book.)

There are some who thought that the number should likewise be adapted to the very daytime offices—namely, Terce, Sext, [Col. 0079A] and None, so that [Note: [Col. 0077D] The reason why, in the daytime offices, he here and elsewhere omits Prime, as we call it, and names only Terce, Sext, and None (Book III, chapters 3 and 1), seems to be that at that time Prime either was not in use among Easterners, as will be said more fully below, or was joined with Lauds and reckoned under the single name of the morning solemnity or morning office. At that time these three canonical hours were properly called daytime hours. For Vespers were in some sense intermediate, since they were celebrated in the last part of the day, when the day was completed, being completed, and ending; while Compline was to be celebrated at the beginning of the night, when the first shadows of night were already deepening, as St. Basil testifies in the Longer Rules, question 37.

Moreover, in order to understand the nature of these hours, three points necessary to know should here be noted concerning their names (Bellarmine, Book I, *On Good Works in Particular*, chapter 11). First, the names of the canonical hours properly correspond to the hours in use among the ancients, which are called unequal and ancient. They began with sunrise: thus the first hour was the first from sunrise, the second was the second from that same sunrise, and so on. They are called unequal because the ancients divided the artificial day throughout the year into twelve hours, and the night into the same number; necessarily, therefore, in summer the daytime hours were longer than the nighttime hours, and conversely in winter the nighttime hours than the daytime hours.

Second, the offices of the three hours—Terce, Sext, and None—were to be celebrated regularly and canonically at those very hours. Since those unequal hours are no longer in use, the times to be understood are those corresponding to them in our reckoning. This may easily be done if one observes at what times sunrise, sunset, and noon occur. For the unequal sixth hour, which is the sixth hour of prayer, always falls at noon. The unequal third hour always falls at the time midway between sunrise and noon. The unequal ninth hour falls at the time midway between noon and sunset, that is, at three in the afternoon. It is therefore called the hour of Terce, or the office of Terce, because it must be celebrated at the third hour from sunrise; the office of Sext because at the sixth hour; and the office of None because at the ninth hour.

Third, the canonical and lawful time for discharging the offices of these hours is not after the hours themselves have ended and been completed, but after they have begun to elapse and while they are still elapsing; that is, it is not at their boundary or end, but throughout their entire span, course, or passage. This is proved from the fact that the office of morning Lauds is not to be celebrated once the twelfth hour of the night has been completed—that is, once the sun has already risen—but during the running twelfth and final hour, and therefore at dawn, as we shall teach below.
