By the same reasoning, the office of Prime must be celebrated not after the first hour has elapsed but while it is elapsing, that is, shortly after sunrise; and consequently the same must be said of the offices of Terce, Sext, and None: they are to be celebrated during those hours while they are elapsing, before they have been completed. This is substantially Bellarmine's account. Why these hours rather than others are assigned to the divine offices will be said below in its proper place (Book III, chapter 2).]

[Note: [Col. 0079C] That is, so that at each third hour from sunrise they might offer three psalms to the Lord in each of the daytime offices, and thus make the number of psalms equal to the number of hours; or so that, according to the number or increase of the hours, they might likewise increase the number of psalms: that is, three psalms at Terce, six at Sext, and nine at None, which is properly to make the number of hours and psalms equal.]

they might judge the number of psalms and prayers also to be made equal according to the measure of the hours at which these services are rendered to the Lord. Some preferred to assign the number six to each assembly during the day.

Therefore I think it necessary to bring forward the most ancient constitution of the fathers, which is still observed throughout all Egypt by the servants of God, so that the inexperienced infancy of the new monastery in Christ may be instructed rather by the ancient institutions of the most ancient fathers.

## CHAPTER THREE  
### On the observance of a uniform rule throughout Egypt, and on the choice of those appointed over the brethren

[Col. 0079B]

Thus, throughout all [Note: [Col. 0079D] Egypt, a region very well known in Scripture, situated west of Judaea, is a part of Africa—or, as others prefer, of Asia. It is divided into two parts. The lower part is also called the Delta, from the triangular shape formed by the Nile as it divides to the right and left and encircles the region. The author seems to designate this part by the name Egypt, since he distinguishes it from the Thebaid, which is called Upper Egypt.

As for the monasteries and monks of Egypt, whose rites and observances in divine offices and canonical prayers Cassian is undertaking to explain here, it should be known that St. Anthony, in the time of the emperor Constantine the Great and at the beginning of the fourth century, restored and renewed the monastic discipline first founded and established in the regions of Egypt by St. Mark the Evangelist, but later weakened and almost extinguished by the violent storms of persecution. In doing so, he in a certain sense laid the first foundations of the communal life, and in a short time gathered together so great a multitude of monks that the deserts of the Thebaid and of all Egypt were filled with monasteries.

Among other things, St. Athanasius writes the following about them: “There were monasteries on the mountain, like tabernacles filled with divine choirs singing psalms, reading, and praying; and his discourse”—that is, Anthony’s—“had so inflamed the minds of all with zeal for fasting and vigils that, eagerly awaiting the hope of the future, they continually labored to show mutual charity and mercy to those in need. Thus they seemed to inhabit an immense region separated from worldly society and filled with piety and justice,” and so forth. These words plainly agree with what Cassian says in this chapter about the works and exercises of the Egyptian monks.

St. Chrysostom describes how greatly the Egyptian desert had been adorned by those gatherings of holy monks in these words: “If anyone now comes to the solitudes of Egypt, he will see that whole desert as more worthy than any paradise, and innumerable choirs of angels shining in mortal bodies. The sky does not gleam with such varied choirs of stars as the Egyptian desert is marked and illuminated by the countless tabernacles of monks and virgins.” Thus Chrysostom (*Homily 8 on Matthew*).

Moreover, not all the monks living in Egypt belonged to the same class, had the same institution, or possessed the same degree of perfection in life. Some, departing from Anthony’s institutions, adopted another way of life. Hence St. Jerome, writing about them in his letter to Eustochium, says that in his time there were three classes of monks in Egypt: the first, cenobites, that is, those living in common; the second, anchorites; and the third, which he calls the worst, not unlike those whom St. Benedict calls Sarabaites. But more will be said about these elsewhere (see *Conference* 18, chapter 4 and following).]

Egypt and the Thebaid, where monasteries are not established according to the arbitrary choice of each person who renounces the world, but either continue to exist or are founded to endure even to the present day through the succession and traditions of the elders, we observed that the legitimate form of prayer was retained in the evening assemblies or night vigils. No one is permitted to preside over an assembly of the brethren—or even over himself—before he has not only become detached from all his possessions, but has also learned that he is not his own master and has no authority over himself.

Thus, a person renouncing the world, however richly endowed with possessions and wealth, must seek residence in a coenobium so that he may not flatter himself in any way on account of what he has left behind or brought into the monastery. He must obey everyone in such a way that he recognizes that, according to the Lord’s saying (Matt. 18), he must return to his former infancy, claiming nothing for himself on account of age or length of years, which he considers to have been foolishly spent and lost in the world [Col. 0080B]. Rather, because of the level of his rudimentary training and the newness of his service, which he recognizes himself to bear in Christ’s army, he should not hesitate to submit even to those younger than himself.

He is also compelled to undertake a habit of work and toil in such a way that [Note: [Col. 0080D] It was the institution and custom of nearly all the ancient religious communities that they devote themselves to manual labor and, by working with their own hands, provide daily sustenance both for themselves and for guests and travelers who came to them. St. Jerome testifies in his letter to the monk Rusticus that the monasteries of the Egyptians maintained this custom, accepting no one without the labor of work. St. Basil likewise confirms it at length in his *Longer Rules*, chapters 37 and 38; St. Augustine in Book 1, chapter 31, of *On the Customs of the Catholic Church*; and our own Cassian in numerous passages.

St. Benedict also wished his cenobites to be occupied in labor at appointed times, and he distributed the daytime hours free from the work of God, or divine office, in such a way that some were devoted to reading and meditation and others to manual labor. He also urged that the brethren should not be saddened if necessity or poverty required them to gather crops themselves. “For then,” he says, “they are truly monks, if they live by the labor of their hands, as did our Fathers and the Apostles.”

Cassian seems to refer the reason for this institution and custom to the Apostle’s command in 1 Thessalonians 4: “Work with your hands, as we commanded you”; and in 2 Thessalonians 3: “If anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat.” Yet it is clear that these and similar commands are common to all Christians and do not bind religious persons more than others; and, more to the point, that they are not absolute but conditional, as they say (see St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* II–II, question 187, article 3).

For the Apostle nowhere commanded people absolutely to work, but under a condition: either to obtain the necessities of life, if they cannot be obtained in another way, which is the point of “Whoever does not work, should not eat”; or to avoid theft and to give alms, according to Ephesians 4: “Let the one who stole steal no longer, but rather labor, working with his hands, so that he may have something to give to the one in need”; or to avoid scandal and giving offense to others, according to 1 Thessalonians 4, so that “you may walk honorably”—that is, without scandal—“before those who are outside,” namely, among unbelievers; or finally to avoid idleness and overcome temptations of the flesh, according to Ecclesiasticus 33: “Send your servant to work, lest he be idle; for idleness has taught much wickedness.”

It follows that those who can obtain their livelihood elsewhere, and avoid theft, scandal, idleness, and similar things without manual work and bodily labor, are in no way bound by the Apostle’s command to undertake such work—unless they have bound themselves to manual labor by a vow or by their own rules and institutions, as those ancient monks did.

St. Jerome touches upon two reasons why they established such a rule in the passage cited above. The first was poverty and the necessity of obtaining food. They could not otherwise support themselves, since they possessed no estates or properties left to them, and brought nothing with them into the monasteries (Bellarminus, Book 2, *On Monks*, chapter 42), as Cassian testifies in Book 4, chapter 4. Nor could alms have sufficed for them, since in one place, under a single abbot, there lived at least three thousand monks, as St. Augustine writes in Book 1, chapter 31, of *On the Customs of the Catholic Church* [Col. 0082B].

The second reason was to avoid idleness and, as St. Jerome puts it, to prevent the mind from wandering among dangerous thoughts. St. Benedict also alleges this reason (in the passage cited above). Since those ancient monks were not clerics but all laymen, except for the abbot and a few others, as we shall show elsewhere, and since most of them were also entirely uneducated, they were not sufficiently occupied; therefore, in order to flee idleness, it was necessary for them to work.

Cassian suggests other reasons directed toward much the same end, namely, the mortification of the body and the exercise of humility: “So that,” he says, “he may be able to forget the arrogance and pleasures of his former life and acquire humility of heart through the hardship of labor.”

Add to this the relaxation of the mind through the alternation and variety of spiritual and bodily exercises. Cassian likewise discusses this in chapter 11 of this book: “Every form of chastisement is always endured with greater equanimity, and labor is undertaken without weariness, if some alternation or any change of work intervenes.”

The great Anthony, taught by divine instruction, perceived and thoroughly understood this. As we read in the *Lives of the Fathers*, while he was living in the desert he was once overcome by weariness of solitude and is said to have cried out: “Lord, I desire to be saved, but my thoughts trouble me.” Immediately he saw an angel in monastic dress, at one moment sitting and working, at another bending his knees in prayer, then rising again to work and weaving baskets. From him he received this instruction: “You too do likewise, and you will be saved.” Strengthened by this oracle and obedient to it, he found the salvation he was seeking.

But let this suffice for now, since elsewhere we shall have to discuss manual labor at greater length (Book 10 of the *Institutes*, chapter 7 and following).]

preparing daily food with his own hands, either for his own use or for the needs of those who arrive, so that he may forget the arrogance and pleasures of his former life and acquire humility of heart through the hardship of labor.

Therefore [Note: [Col. 0082C] See what sort of person ought to be chosen as abbot; St. Benedict discusses this in chapters 2 and 64 of the Rule, where Turrecremata may be consulted. Note also the similar text in Canon Law, title “On Election,” chapter *Cum in magistrum*, where it says: “The one who has not assumed the form of a disciple ought not to be taken as a master; nor should one be placed in authority who has not learned to be subject.” Thus Pope Zosimus writes to Hesychius, chapter 1: “For if secular offices confer the chief place not upon one who has entered merely the threshold of service, but upon one tested through many stages and at appropriate times, who is so arrogant and shameless as to desire immediately to be a leader in the heavenly army—which must be weighed with greater care and tested like gold in repeated fires—when he has not first been a recruit, and wishes to teach before learning?” Pope Celestine likewise writes to the bishops of Gaul, chapter 3: “Whoever desires to be a teacher must first be a disciple, so that he may teach what he has learned.” Ruricius says in Book 2, Letter 25: “Everyone must first learn before teaching, for the teacher’s arrogance is usurped too hastily unless he has first undertaken the service of a disciple.”]

no one who is to preside over a congregation of brethren is chosen before the person who is to be appointed has learned through obedience what ought to be commanded to those who will obey, and has acquired through the institutions of the elders what he ought to hand down to those younger than himself.

They rightly declare that governing or being governed is the mark of a wise person, and they define it as the supreme gift and grace of the Holy Spirit. For they say that no one can establish salutary commands for those who obey unless he has first been instructed in every discipline of virtue; nor can anyone obey an elder unless he has been perfected in the fear of God and in the virtue of humility.

Therefore we see different patterns and rules being used throughout the other provinces, because we often dare to preside over monasteries despite lacking the instruction of elders, and, professing ourselves abbots before disciples, establish whatever pleases us. We are more ready to demand observance of our own inventions than to preserve the tested teaching of our predecessors.

But while we wish to explain what form of prayer ought above all to be observed, impelled by our eagerness for the institutions of the fathers, we have prematurely anticipated the narrative that we had reserved for its proper places. Let us now return to our subject.

## CHAPTER FOUR  
### That throughout Egypt and the Thebaid the number twelve is observed for the psalms

[Col. 0083A]

Thus, throughout all Egypt and the Thebaid, as we have said, [Note: [Col. 0083A] It seems worthy of careful consideration that in this chapter and those following Cassian reports that it was established among those monks not by human invention but through an angelic ministry from heaven that twelve psalms should be sung both at Vespers and in the night office.

For the rites and institutions of those ancient monks in the celebration of the divine office, which are being discussed here, may be understood more clearly and easily if we gather them together briefly here and present to the reader in summary what Cassian relates about them, scattered and at length, throughout this entire book and partly also in the following one.

First, it was their custom to assemble together in the choir, or oratory, twice each day: namely, at Vespers, when the day had been completed, as St. Basil says (*Longer Rules*, question 37), which they called the lamp-lighting hour, because they then lit lamps as daylight faded, as will be said below (Book 3, chapter 3). They called this the evening solemnity, or synaxis. Then they assembled around midnight, at which time they celebrated the night office, or the nocturnal solemnity and synaxis.

Second, at each assembly and office, both evening and nocturnal, twelve psalms were sung. They had learned through a remarkable miracle from an angel that this number was to be observed. Thus they completed the evening office, which we now call Vespers, with twelve psalms, and likewise their nocturns, or night office.

Third, these psalms were sung sweetly and recited in a clear or sonorous voice by a single reader—or cantor—who rose in the midst of the brethren (chapters 5 and 10). St. Benedict likewise requires such readers or cantors (chapter 18 of the Rule), namely, those who edify their hearers. To prevent the cantor from becoming exhausted, others succeeded him in turn—three or at most four—dividing the twelve psalms among themselves so that, if there were only two, each sang six; if three, each four; and if four, each three psalms (chapter 11).

Fourth, there was meanwhile complete silence. The others sat on the ground, their entire attention fixed on the words of the one singing, and singing mentally rather than vocally, so that neither a yawn, nor a cough, nor a clearing of the throat, nor any noise could be heard. Indeed, no one other than the singer seemed to be present (chapters 10 and 12).

Fifth, they did not run through every psalm, especially the longer ones, continuously and in a single stretch all the way to the end. Rather, after every ten or twelve verses they paused briefly at certain breaks and devoted themselves to a short prayer or meditation.

Sixth, each psalm did not end with the verse customary among Latins, “Glory be to the Father, etc.,” but with another brief prayer. After the end of the twelfth psalm, “Alleluia” was answered (chapters 5 and 11).

Seventh, once the psalms had been completed, two readings followed: one from the Old Testament and one from the New, except on Sundays and Saturdays, when both readings were taken from the New Testament (chapters 7 and 11).

Eighth, after these had been completed, all fell on their knees, giving thanks to God. Then, once everyone had risen, the abbot or priest presiding over the congregation, as though gathering together and offering to God the prayers and petitions of all the brethren, brought the office to an end with a public prayer. From this, it seems, the name and use of Collects in the ecclesiastical office arose. On this, see Durandus, *Rationale*, Book 4, chapter 15 [Col. 0084A].

In this manner they celebrated the offices they called evening and nocturnal. For, as far as can be gathered from Cassian’s account, they do not seem to have had other ordinary and canonical night offices, since in this book, where he discusses the rites and offices of the Egyptians, he makes no mention of Lauds, Matins, or Prime, or of Compline. Indeed, in chapter 12 he seems in a certain way to excuse them on the grounds that they had such a short or moderate office of nocturnal psalmody, namely, because of the excessive constancy of their prayers, labors, fasts, and vigils, which he calls the unparalleled rigor of their discipline in Book 3, chapter 1.

Ninth, after the psalms and night vigils had ended, each monk returned to his cell and, during the remaining part of the night, devoted himself both to prayer and to manual labor, keeping watch until, at the coming of dawn, daytime work and activity succeeded the work and meditation of the night (chapters 2, 13, and 14).

Tenth, the remaining daytime offices—Terce, Sext, and None—were performed privately by each monk in his own cell, and at each one he recited three psalms with a prayer. They also interspersed these continually with other private prayers and devotions, so that they spent the entire day until evening in these offices, without meanwhile being free from manual labor, but devoting themselves equally to prayer and work.

They did not assemble together more than once a day, as has been said, except on Saturdays and Sundays, when they customarily gathered at the third hour in the church or oratory, where they celebrated the divine mysteries (chapters 2 and 3 of Book 3). Let this suffice concerning the monks of Egypt and their rites and exercises.]

the number twelve is observed both in the evening solemnities and in the nocturnal solemnities, with only this provision: that two readings, one from the Old Testament and one from the New, follow it. This form, established in ancient times, has therefore remained undefiled through so many centuries in all the monasteries of those provinces down to the present day, because the elders affirm that it was not established by human invention but was delivered to the fathers from heaven through the instruction of an angel.

## CHAPTER FIVE  
### On the number twelve for the psalms, received through the tradition of an angel
For when, in the beginnings of the faith, only a few indeed, but the most approved, were counted under the name of monks, who, having received the rule of life from the evangelist Mark of blessed memory—who was the first bishop of the city of Alexandria—[Note: Saint Mark the Evangelist, sent to Egypt by Blessed Peter, preached in Alexandria the Gospel that he had written, and was the first to establish and govern the Alexandrian Church. To the many people in that region—both Jews and others converted to the faith and inflamed with a more ardent zeal for perfection—he handed on the norm of monastic life that he had received from the apostles and that Saint Luke records as having been observed by the first believers in Jerusalem (Acts 4). Eusebius gives especially clear testimony to this in book 2 of his Ecclesiastical History, chapters 15 and 16. There he demonstrates with many arguments that the life, customs, and institutions of those same monks, and not of others, had at that time been accurately described by Philo the Jew in a short work entitled *On the Theoretical, or Contemplative, Life of Suppliants*, in which he honors them with this twofold designation, calling them θεραπευταί (*therapeutaí*) and ἱκέται (*hikétai*). He calls them θεραπευταί—that is, worshipers, or attendants—either because they worshiped God with the greatest devotion or because they diligently cultivated and cared for their souls, curing them of the diseases of vice. He calls them ἱκέται—that is, suppliants—from their principal duty, which is to pray to and praise God.

Saint Jerome supports this interpretation in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, where, speaking first of Saint Mark, he reports among other things: “Mark, having taken up the Gospel that he had completed, went to Egypt; and, being the first to announce Christ at Alexandria, he established the Church there, with such learning and restraint of life that he compelled all the followers of Christ to conform to his example. Finally, Philo, the most eloquent of the Jews, seeing that the first Church at Alexandria was still observing Jewish practices, wrote, as though in praise of his nation, a book about their way of life.” Thus far Jerome.

Later, speaking again of Philo, he added: “Philo the Jew, an Alexandrian by nation and of priestly descent, is included by us among ecclesiastical writers because, when writing a book about the first Church of the evangelist Mark at Alexandria, he devoted himself to praising our people. He records that they existed not only there but also in many provinces, and he calls their dwellings monasteries. From this it is apparent that the first Church of those who believed in Christ was such as monks now strive and desire to be: nothing belonging to anyone individually; no rich person and no poor person among them; estates divided among the needy; devotion given to prayer and psalmody, as well as to learning and continence—just as Luke reports the first believers at Jerusalem to have been.” Thus far Saint Jerome.

Saint Epiphanius expresses the same view in *Heresy* 29, speaking of this work of Philo: “When he enumerates their monasteries in the neighborhood around Lake Mareotis, he speaks of none other than Christians.” Cassian too confirms the same point here with no little clarity, when he recalls and extols the austerity and holiness of those monks whom he asserts were instructed by Saint Mark. For how could he have learned these things except from that book of Philo, from which Eusebius, Jerome, and others drew the same descriptions?

As for Philo’s commending among those ascetics—whom he describes under the name of the Essenes—the observance of the Sabbath, the reader will not find this surprising if he considers that, at the beginning of the nascent Church, many Jewish observances continued for some time among Christians, indeed even among the apostles, as their Acts testify (Josephus, book 2 of *The Jewish War*, chapter 7, and book 8 of the *Antiquities*, chapter 2). For this reason Saint Jerome wrote with good judgment: “Philo, seeing that the first Church was still observing Jewish practices,” and so forth.

For the rest, whether Philo’s Essenes and those of Josephus are the same is not a question for this place (see Bellarmine, book 2 *On Monasticism*, chapter 5).]

not only retained those splendid practices that we read the Church, or the multitude of believers, originally celebrated in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 4)—namely: “The multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul; nor did any of them say that anything he possessed was his own, but everything was common to them. For as many as owned fields or houses sold them, brought the proceeds of what they had sold, and laid them at the apostles’ feet; and distribution was made to each according as he had need”—but had heaped upon them practices much more sublime.

For, withdrawing into the more secluded places of the suburbs, they led a life disciplined by such strict abstinence that even to those who belonged to an external religion the profession of their way of life seemed astonishingly arduous. They devoted themselves by day and night with such fervor to the reading of the divine Scriptures, to prayer, and to manual labor that the appetite for food—or even the memory of it—would interrupt their fasting only on the second or third day; and they took food and drink not so much because they desired them as because they needed them. Even then they did not take them before sunset, so that they might join the hours of daylight to the practice of spiritual meditation, and the care of the body to the night; and they accomplished other practices far more sublime than these. Of these matters even someone who has learned less from the reports of the natives can be instructed by ecclesiastical history. [Note: Namely, Eusebius of Caesarea, book 2, chapters 15 and 16; Sozomen, book 1, chapters 12 and 13; Palladius, *Lausiac History*; Cassiodorus, *Tripartite History*, book 3, chapter 1; Nicephorus, book 1, chapter 16, and book 9, chapter 14.]

At that time, therefore, while the perfection of that primitive Church still remained inviolate among its successors, fresh in their memory, and while the fervent faith of the few had not yet grown lukewarm through being dispersed among the multitude, the venerable fathers, taking thought for posterity with watchful care, came together to deliberate what form of daily worship ought to be established throughout the whole body of the brotherhood [Note: *Corpus* is well known sometimes to mean a fellowship, assembly, or corporate body; it is frequent and familiar in Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 39, and in *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 3. Nor is this surprising, since the Apostle also says: “We are many, one body,” and “we were baptized into one body” (1 Corinthians 10 and 12). Thus *the body of the brotherhood* here means the community, or the entire assembly of the monks. It is called a brotherhood because they called one another brothers and loved one another with fraternal charity. A little later he calls it “the fullness of the brothers.”], so that they might transmit to their successors an inheritance of piety and peace, complete and free from every dispute.

They were naturally afraid that some disagreement or variation in the daily solemnities among men united in the same worship might eventually produce a harmful seed of error, rivalry, or schism. Since each man, in accordance with his own fervor and forgetful of human weakness, thought that the practice ought to be established which he judged easy in view of his own faith and strength, while giving little consideration to what was generally possible for the fullness of the brothers, among whom the weaker must necessarily constitute a very large part, they strove, each according to his own spiritual capacity, to establish an enormous number of psalms in different ways. [Note: It may be gathered first from Scripture that psalmody, or the singing of psalms, held the foremost place in ecclesiastical assemblies from the very beginning of the Church. Paul says in 1 Corinthians 14: “When you come together, each of you has a psalm.” And in Ephesians 5: “Be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and songs.” He repeats the same words in Colossians 3.

Observe in these words three things that are chiefly contained in the divine office: namely, psalms, readings, and songs. Amalarius, in book 4 of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, derives this from certain statements of Blessed Jerome: “In the readings, both the longer readings that are read at the nocturnal vigils and the shorter ones that are said at the other hours and are called chapters, we praise God and proclaim him. Every praise of God is called a hymn in the broad sense. Antiphons, responsories, and metrical hymns, however, are plainly songs, because they are varied by musical notes in a higher voice.”

“If, therefore, in the Apostle’s words we understand by ‘hymns’ the readings, chapters, and prayers, and by ‘songs’ the antiphons, responsories, and metrical praises of God that we commonly call hymns, we have all the offices of divine praise.” Thus writes Radulphus of Tongeren.

Second, the perpetual use in the Church of reciting and singing psalms can be proved by many examples and authorities of the Fathers; it will suffice to mention a few. Tertullian, at the end of *On the Veiling of Virgins*, says: “How great a punishment will those deserve who remain unveiled amid psalms and whenever God is mentioned!” Eusebius, in book 2 of his *History*, chapter 17, shows from Philo that those first monks, or Alexandrian Therapeutae, whom Saint Mark had established near Alexandria, exercised themselves day and night in singing psalms and hymns to God.

Saint Athanasius, near the end of his *Apology for His Flight*, clearly indicates that psalmody was customarily celebrated in the Church. Explaining how, when Arian soldiers burst into the Church to seize him, he escaped the hands of his enemies, he says: “I remained in the chair; I ordered the deacon to recite a psalm, and after the recitation everyone was to go home,” and so forth.

Saint Chrysostom, in Homily 6 *On Repentance*, asks and marvels why, above all the writings of the Old and New Testaments, all Christians so loved the Book of the Psalms of David and wished to have it alone continually on their lips: “In churches keeping vigil,” he says, “David is first, middle, and last. At dawn, are the melodies of hymns sought? David is first, middle, and last. At funeral processions for the dead, he is first, middle, and last. In holy monasteries, among choirs of angelic ranks, David is first, middle, and last. In the communities of virgins imitating Mary, he is first, middle, and last,” and so forth.

Saint Jerome, in the *Epitaph of Paula*, says: “In the morning, at the third, sixth, and ninth hours, in the evening, and at midnight, they sang the Psalter in order.”

Saint Augustine, in book 9 of the *Confessions*, chapter 7, writes that Ambrose instituted the singing of psalms and hymns in the Church at Milan, according to the custom of the Eastern Fathers, and that this practice spread from there to the other Churches of the West. Cardinal Bellarmine explains that this should not be understood as though psalmody or ecclesiastical singing had been unknown before the time of Ambrose (book 1 *On Good Works*, chapter 16). The Fathers cited above testify to the contrary. “But perhaps,” he says, “Augustine is speaking not of singing absolutely, but of the singing of the whole people. Previously only one person sang the psalm, while the others listened, as is clear from Cassian. Hence Jerome’s statement in his letter to the monk Rusticus: ‘Say the psalm in your order.’ Perhaps the clergy alone also sang, as we see done now. Ambrose, however, to alleviate the grief of the people during the persecution of Justina, instituted that the entire people should sing. Chrysostom did the same on a similar occasion at Constantinople, as Socrates reports in book 6 of his *History*, chapter 8.

Finally, Cassian, here and throughout nearly this entire book and the next, teaches in many chapters that the ancient Fathers in the East made especially frequent use of psalms in the divine offices, completed a fixed number in each office, and continued—some more, some fewer—until, through the instruction of an angel sent from heaven, the number twelve was prescribed for all to observe in the nocturnal and evening offices.

As for the claim made by some that Damasus instituted the singing of psalms by day and night, Baronius declares it false (Baronius, volume 4, page 429), since it is certain that from the beginning the Church had both daytime and nighttime psalmody accompanied by singing. Perhaps Damasus prescribed some particular form, or perhaps Saint Jerome revised the Psalter of the Septuagint translators and entrusted it to the Western Churches to be sung.

On the benefits of psalmody instituted in the Church, see Radulphus of Tongeren and Bellarmine in the places cited above.]

while some sang fifty psalms, others sixty, and some, not even content with this number, judged that it ought to be exceeded, so that among them there was a holy diversity of pious rivalry according to the rule of religion. In this way the time of the most sacred evening solemnity would arrive while the question was still being debated by those who wished to celebrate the daily rites of prayer. [Note: We learn from this passage, as well as from many other testimonies of antiquity and from examples of holy Fathers and monks, that the psalms of David in the divine offices, or canonical hours, were formerly sung not while sitting, as most people do, but standing. It seems appropriate to cite some of those examples here.

First, Philo, speaking of those therapeutics, or Alexandrian monks established by Saint Mark, says in *On the Contemplative Life*: “There are hymns to be sung during the sacred rites by those who are standing.” Again: “At night they sang hymns standing until dawn.” There he calls psalms hymns, as Cassian also does below.

Athanasius, in his book *On Virginity*, says: “Rise at midnight and recite psalms, as much as you can, standing.” Saint Basil, in his letter to the Neocaesareans, says: “After confessing to God, they finally rise from contemplation and are assigned to psalmody.”

Chrysostom, in Homily 14 on the First Epistle to Timothy, says: “When before dawn the rooster sends forth his voice, everyone, with reverence and having shaken off sleep, rises when awakened by his superior; they stand before the sacred choir and immediately sing the holy hymns with outstretched hands.” He is speaking of the monks of Syria, who sang not only standing and erect but also with their hands outstretched. Cassian likewise testifies below that this was done by the Egyptian monks (chapter 7).

Finally, the angel in question himself observed and taught this very practice of standing. He prescribed the manner of singing psalms to those Egyptian Fathers by his own example, when he rose in the midst of the brothers with whom he was sitting in order to chant the psalms.

If someone objects that, in this same passage and in chapter 11, those monks are said to have celebrated psalmody not standing but sitting, the answer is immediately available from the same passage: those Fathers were not actually reciting the psalms but merely listening to one person who was singing, and, as the text says here, they remained silent, wholly intent on the words of the singer (chapters 11 and 12). Thus both facts are established by this passage: the singer stood, while those who were not singing sat down.

From this arose the custom that is still observed: when someone reads sacred Scripture, the lives of the saints, the martyrology, chapters or lessons, or anything of that kind, the reader himself reads standing, while all the others listen sitting. Hence Sidonius Apollinaris calls them μεσοχοροί (*mesochoroí*), that is, “those standing in the middle of the choir” (book 1, letter 2).

From these facts we understand that the angel left the Fathers two instructions through this action of his. First, that they should chant twelve psalms in both the evening and nocturnal offices, a matter discussed below. Second, that they should sing standing and erect, and that those who sang should stand. The monks thereafter decided to retain and observe this custom and practice.]

one man rises to sing psalms to the Lord in the midst of the assembly. When all the others were sitting—as is still the custom in the regions of Egypt—and concentrating with their whole heart on the words of the singer, he sang eleven psalms, separated by interruptions of prayer, in uninterrupted verses and with an even cadence. He completed the twelfth with the response “Alleluia,” and then suddenly disappeared from the eyes of everyone, bringing the questioning and the ceremonies alike to an end.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Custom of Twelve Prayers

From that time the venerable council of the Fathers, understanding that a general rule had been established for the communities of the brothers through the instruction of an angel, not without the Lord’s dispensation, resolved that this number should be observed both in the evening [Col. 0089A] and in the nocturnal gatherings. [Note: Saint Benedict too judged that the number twelve of the psalms in the nocturnal vigils—which those holy Fathers had learned from the angel and received after being warned by the remarkable miracle related above—should be retained at all times for the daily night vigils, or nocturnal office, which we improperly call “matins,” and should be sung by his monks. On Sundays and feast days, however, he added canticles for the third nocturn.

This can be seen in chapter 18 of the Rule. After arranging the order of the daytime psalmody, he states: “Let all the remaining psalms that are left be divided equally among the seven night watches”—that is, the entire week—“distributing the longer ones” (as is customary among us), “and let twelve psalms be assigned to each night.” Every effort should be made so that the entire Psalter of one hundred and fifty psalms is sung every week, and so that on Sunday it is always begun again at the vigils. For, he says, the monks show themselves exceedingly negligent in the service of their devotion if they sing less than the Psalter with its customary canticles over the course of a week, since we read that our holy Fathers energetically completed in one day what we, lukewarm as we are, should wish to complete in an entire week.

By these words he seems to allude to those holy Fathers and monks of whom Cassian writes in chapter 2 of this book. They competed in pious rivalry when establishing the number of psalms for the daily offices, or solemnities, as he calls them: some sang fifty, others sixty, while still others, not even content with this number, judged that it ought to be exceeded.

Saint Benedict’s other, allegorical interpretation of this institution—namely, of the number twelve of the psalms to be sung at night—was skillfully expressed by Durandus of Mende in these words:

“Blessed Benedict arranged the office of the night in another manner, though he did not disagree with the Church’s foregoing arrangement or contradict it in any respect; rather, he established something particular within his own order. He instituted that ‘O God, come to my assistance’ be said once, and ‘O Lord, open my lips’ three times, in honor of the Unity and the Trinity. Then he prescribed the psalm ‘O Lord, how they have increased,’ because, rising from sleep, one says in it: ‘I slept and took my rest,’ and so forth” (Psalm 3).

“Then, in the first nocturn, he instituted that six psalms and four readings, with an equal number of responsories, be sung; and the same number in the second. By this he signified the contemplative and active life. For the number six of the psalms signifies the active life, in which it is appropriate to exercise the six works of mercy if one wishes to attain the perfection of the contemplative life, which is signified by the four Gospels and likewise represented by the four readings.

The number four among monks expresses square stability and evangelical perfection in the saints; or the fourfold sense of Scripture, on account of the chariots of Amminadab: the historical, allegorical, tropological, and anagogical senses.

In the third nocturn he instituted that three canticles be sung in praise of the Trinity, from whom we believe and hope that the perfection of life is given to us together with charity,” and so forth (Durandus, book 5 of the *Rationale*, chapter 3; and from him John Selethus in his *Explanation of the Office*, chapter 23).

Thus far Durandus. John Selethus, his abridger, followed him as well.

As for why Saint Benedict and others prescribed fewer psalms in Vespers, or the evening office, than in the nocturnal office, rather than twelve in both, the reason seems to have been that Compline was instituted and introduced after Vespers in their place. Radulphus of Tongeren rightly observed in his book *On the Observance of the Canons*, proposition 14, that the office of Compline is not as ancient as the offices of the other hours.

Saint Ambrose does seem to indicate the time of Compline somewhat obscurely in book 3 *On Virgins*. But explicit mention is first found among the Greeks in the more extensively discussed Rules of Saint Basil, question 37. Among the Latins, both the name and the time of Compline are first found in chapter 16 of Saint Benedict’s Rule.]

To these they added two readings—one from the Old Testament and the other from the New—as though they had been handed down by themselves and were extraordinary additions, intended only for those who wished to possess the memory of the divine Scriptures and diligently devoted themselves to it through constant meditation. [Note: Someone might suppose that “the Sabbath day” here is synonymous with Sunday, because of the conjunction “or,” by which the one seems to be explained by the other, and because the Jewish Sabbath was changed among Christians into Sunday. But it is sufficiently clear from other passages of Cassian considered together with this one that this is not the case. There the Sabbath is joined with Sunday in such a way that the two are clearly indicated to have been different days, not one day; and both days were held in equal honor by the Egyptian monks and observed with nearly the same ceremonies.

On both days they recited readings from the New Testament, as a sign of evangelical preaching, as stated here; on both days they ended their fasts (book 3, chapter 9); and on both days they likewise went to the meal without psalmody (book 3, final chapter). On both days they solemnly assembled in church to pray, offer sacrifice, and receive Communion (book 3, chapter 2).]

But on the Sabbath or Sunday they recite both readings from the New Testament: one from the Apostle or the Acts of the Apostles, and the other from the Gospels. Those who care about reading, or about the memory of Scripture, do the same throughout the entire period of the Pentecost. [Note: Here the author calls the period of fifty days from the Lord’s Resurrection until the coming of the Holy Spirit *Quinquagesima*, which the Greeks call *Pentecost*. He uses the word again with the same meaning in book 2, chapter 18, and in *Conference* 21, chapter 8.

Rabanus calls this the Paschal Quinquagesima, to distinguish it from the other Quinquagesima, which precedes Lent. In another place he noted the following about both:

“It should be noted that Pope Telesphorus established that fasting should begin at Quinquagesima among the Romans, so that for seven weeks before Easter we might chastise the body with fasts; and he wished the other seven weeks after Easter until Pentecost to be released from fasting in gladness, so that we might spend the first Quinquagesima in repentance for our sins, in order to obtain mercy, and in the second, devoting ourselves to praises and prayers, strive to arrive at the promised grace of the Holy Spirit.” Thus far Rabanus.]

## CHAPTER VII. On the Discipline of Prayer

[Col. 0091A]

These prayers, then, they begin and conclude in the following manner: when the psalm has ended, they do not immediately collapse into genuflection, as some of us in this region do, who, before the psalm has properly ended, hasten to prostrate ourselves in prayer, seeking the swift completion of the service.

[Note: That is, hastening or striving toward the end or acceleration of the divine office, as he says below—not “toward the celebration of the Mass,” as Dionysius has it. For *missa*, here and frequently in Cassian, does not mean the liturgical sacrifice called the Mass, but a sending away or dismissal (*missio* or *dimissio*) that took place after the divine office, psalmody, or prayer had been completed, for which the monks had assembled, whether by day or by night. Thus Cicero used *collecta* for the collection of a contribution; Saint Cyprian used *remissa* for the remission of sins; others used *proba* for proof, and similar formations. The use of *mittere* and *missum facere* for “to dismiss” is also very common.

Accordingly, the “night dismissal” mentioned in the heading to chapter 13 means nothing other than the dismissal that took place at night after the public prayer had been completed, when, at a given signal, each monk returned to his cell. Again, in the title of chapter 15, “the dismissal of the prayers” means the dismissal from prayer itself. Likewise, in Book III, chapter 7, the man who comes rather late to the oratory is ordered to wait outside for the dismissal of the whole congregation. And in chapter 8: “Content with the sleep granted to us from the dismissal of the vigils until the coming of daylight.” In these passages, the dismissal of the vigils or of the congregation is the dismissal itself from the vigils and congregation, once they had been completed and each person was permitted to return to his own place.

Again, in Book XI, chapter 15, “the dismissal of the catechumens” is the dismissal by which the deacon, after the Gospel had been read in the sacrifice of the Mass, ordered the catechumens to leave before the priest began the awesome mysteries. Saint Benedict likewise understood *missa* in this sense in his Rule (chapter 17), when, after prescribing the office, he adds: “And let the dismissals be made,” or “let the dismissals take place”—that is, “when the office is completed, let the brothers be dismissed.”

Hence, as Cuychius says, most learned men think that the Mass was so called from the two dismissals that formerly took place in the Eucharistic sacrifice. At the first, the catechumens and those whom either their own judgment or that of the Church considered unworthy of communion in Christ’s body were dismissed; at the second, when the minister said among the Greeks, “Dismissal for the people” (*λαοῖς ἄφεσις*), and among the Latins, “Go, the dismissal is made” (*ITE, MISSA EST*), the whole people were dismissed. The Mass, then, was named from this twofold sending away or dismissal, by the principle whereby the whole is named from a part.

An indication of this is that formerly, on penitential days, when public prayer continued after the sacrifice had been completed and the people remained present, the deacon did not say, “Go, the dismissal is made,” but instead said, “Let us bless the Lord” (*Benedicamus Domino*). This is still observed today in Lent, Advent, and on weekdays. On this subject it will be useful to hear the *Micrologus*, who reports the following in chapter 46 of his book *On Ecclesiastical Observances*:

“Appropriately, on feast days, ‘Go, the dismissal is made’ (*ITE, MISSA EST*) is said, because at such times the general assembly is customarily celebrated, and through this announcement it is accustomed to receive permission to depart. For the daily solemnities of the Mass, however, people do not assemble universally, but religious persons do, who devote more attention to spiritual than to worldly concerns and who, when permitted, also attend the other offices each day. Therefore it is appropriately announced to them after Mass that they should not depart immediately, but should bless the Lord.”

Ecclesiastical custom also seems to support this assertion. For when we say, “Go, the dismissal is made,” we turn toward the people and order them to depart; but when we say, “Let us bless the Lord,” we turn not toward the people but toward the altar—that is, toward the Lord—and exhort ourselves not to depart but to bless the Lord.

Thus far the *Micrologus*, in a passage highly useful for clarifying this and other places and for understanding the word *Mass*. If desired, see Durandus, Book IV of the *Rationale*, chapter 57.]

Thus, while we are trying to go beyond the limit that was established in ancient times by our predecessors, we count the number of psalms still remaining and press on toward the end, thinking more about the refreshment of our wearied bodies than seeking the usefulness and benefits of prayer.

Among those monks, however, it is not so. Before they bend their knees, they pray for a little while, and they spend the greater part of the time standing in supplication. Then, after this, they briefly fall upon the ground, as though merely adoring the divine mercy, and rise again with the utmost speed; then, standing upright once more with their hands extended, in the same manner in which they had previously prayed while standing, they devote themselves more earnestly to their prayers.

[Note: Observe the various gestures and bodily postures of the ancient monks in the celebration of the divine offices and in the offering of prayers. Four principal ones are noted here. At times they stood while praying and singing psalms—that is, upright on their feet, with their hands also raised and extended upward; at times they bent their knees; at times they fell upon the ground and lay prostrate; and finally, at times they sat on the lowest seats.

As for the first and second forms of prayer, tradition shows that both had been customary in the Church from the time of the apostles, and that Christians were accustomed sometimes to adore standing and sometimes with their knees bent. A distinction of times was nevertheless maintained according to the character of the divine mysteries commemorated on those occasions. For just as on Sunday, which is consecrated to the Lord’s Resurrection, so also during the period of the Fifty Days—from Easter to Pentecost—antiquity taught that the faithful should pray publicly only while standing; at other times they were to bend their knees, as will be explained more fully below.

Some think that it was also the custom of the Jews to pray standing, because in several passages those who pray are said to stand. Mark 11: “And when you stand to pray, forgive whatever you have against anyone.” Luke 18: “The Pharisee, standing, prayed thus within himself.” Yet other passages make it clear that the more usual practice was to pray with the knees bent. Scripture says of Solomon: “He had fixed both knees upon the ground and had spread out his hands toward heaven” (1 Kings 8). Christ also is said to have prayed with his knees bent (Luke 21). Stephen, kneeling, cried out with a loud voice (Acts 7). Peter, kneeling, prayed and said, “Tabitha, arise” (Acts 9). After Paul had said these things, he knelt and prayed with them all (Acts 20 and 21).

Moreover, the verb “to stand” in Sacred Scripture does not always signify a bodily posture, but sometimes merely presence. Matthew 16 says: “There are some standing here”—that is, present. Therefore, “to stand for prayer” does not mean to pray while standing, but to be present for prayer, or to devote oneself to prayer. Thus Saint Cyprian says in his book *On Prayer*: “When we stand for prayer, we ought to keep watch and devote ourselves to prayer with our whole heart.” Saint Benedict, in the same spirit and sense, says: “Let us stand for psalmody in such a way that our mind agrees with our voice,” whereas shortly before he had said: “When we attend the divine work.”

We therefore stand for prayer or psalmody whenever we are engaged in prayer or psalmody, whether standing upright, kneeling, sitting, or lying down, says Doctor Navarrus in Book I of his *On Prayer*, chapter 4.

As for the third bodily posture, prostration upon the ground, an example was given by the twenty-four elders whom John saw falling before the One seated upon the throne and adoring the One who lives for ever and ever (Revelation 4). The royal Psalmist also invited us to this posture when he said: “Come, let us adore and fall prostrate before God,” and so forth (Psalm 94). A legion of Christian soldiers imitated this practice; under Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, they prayed to God in this manner and obtained the destruction of their enemies and deliverance for the Roman soldiers who were suffering in the greatest danger.

Justin Martyr also testifies that this was the prayer-custom of the ancient Church: kneeling, striking the breast with the hands, and rolling the face upon the ground, or having it rolled upon the ground.

As for sitting, which we have placed fourth among the gestures or postures of those who pray and sing psalms, although Tertullian testifies that worshiping while seated is outside the discipline, the example of the ancient monks under discussion here teaches the contrary. The Author records that they used this variety to remove weariness and relieve bodily weakness, praying and singing psalms now standing, now prostrate, now seated. The common practice and observance of the Church in the performance of its offices has continued to approve this same variety.

From this perspective one should understand and interpret Cardinal Turrecrematus, who, in commenting on the passage of the Rule cited above, noted that, according to Saint Benedict, the discipline of psalm-singing consists in three things: “the reverence of posture, the watchfulness of attention, and the discipline of singing.” By “the reverence of posture” he meant not only an upright bodily posture, but also kneeling, prostration, sitting, and every suitable, appropriate, and reverent bodily disposition according to the time and the requirements of the office.]

For they say that one who remains prostrate upon the ground for too long is attacked not only by thoughts but also more severely by sleep. Would that we, too, did not know this to be true by experience and daily habit! We so often desire to prolong this same bending of our limbs, lying prostrate upon the ground not so much for the sake of prayer as for the sake of refreshment.

When the one who is to gather the prayer has risen from the ground, everyone rises together, so that no one dares either to bend his knees before that man bows down or to linger after he has risen from the ground. Otherwise, he might be thought not so much to have followed the conclusion of the one who gathers the prayer as to have performed his own.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Prayer That Follows the Psalm

We also observed something in this province which we never heard anywhere throughout the East: when one person sings at the conclusion of a psalm, all those standing join in with a shout, “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.” In the East, however, after the psalm has ended, a prayer follows, recited by the one who sings, while everyone remains silent.

[Note: It should be read in this way, as Baronius also read and cited it under the year of the Lord 325. The meaning requires this, since the Author intended to point out the difference between the Eastern and the Latin or Western rites. The difference consists in the fact that among the Easterners and Egyptians, such as those monks were, the verse “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit”—which he calls the glorification of the Trinity—was not said at the end of the psalms, as is customary in the Latin Church, but at the end of the antiphons.

It will nevertheless be worthwhile to hear Baronius discussing this verse, its ancient institution, and the addition “As it was in the beginning,” and so forth. He says:

“We think it should first of all be noted that this hymn of glorification, as it was called by our ancestors, was by no means—as some suppose—invented by the Council of Nicaea. Rather, from the time of the apostles themselves, when the faithful were baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, they began to glorify together those three persons of the most holy Trinity in such a hymn. Saint Basil affirms this at length on the basis of the tradition of the ancestors, without any written document, when he writes to Amphilochius concerning the Holy Spirit.”

Thus Baronius indicates that in the Church of God this glorification began to be sung by the faithful from the time when the Gospel was proclaimed by the apostles and when, as we have said, holy baptism was administered by their command in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. He further teaches at length that this practice was handed down to the faithful without written record, and he observes that it should be recited as the Church received it from the Lord.

Baronius adds later:

“As for the decrees of the Council of Nicaea, just as one must in no way say that the hymn of the glorification of the most holy Trinity was first invented by that council, so we do not think that it was decreed by the council that it should be sung at the end of every psalm. Indeed, if the great council had established this, it would have prescribed a uniform rule for all the Churches alike—as it did in other matters—and no one would ever have dared to depart from it even by the breadth of a finger. Yet we see that different Churches had different customs in this matter and differing rites.

For Cassian says: ‘We also observed this practice in that province: when one person sings at the conclusion of a psalm, all those standing join in with a shout, “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.” We never heard this anywhere in the East; rather, after the psalm had ended, the one who sings follows with a prayer, while all remain silent. But they customarily conclude the antiphon only with this glorification of the Trinity.’”

Thus far Baronius. From this and many other considerations, the letter attributed to Jerome and addressed to Damasus is plainly exposed as fictitious and is rightly rejected by learned men who have examined Jerome’s writings more carefully. It contains these words:

“Your client therefore begs that this voice of those singing psalms may be sung day and night in your Roman See, and that the authority of your Apostolate may command it to be joined at the end of every psalm, whether at the morning or evening hours: ‘Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit; as it was in the beginning,’ and so forth.”

For if Cassian says that he nowhere heard in the East that “Glory to the Father” was said at the end of the psalm, how could Jerome have instructed Damasus about such a form of psalm-singing on the basis of Eastern practice, when the same letter previously asserts that this form of psalm-singing had prevailed both in the Western and in the Eastern Church? Nevertheless, those who accepted the letter as genuine believed that Damasus had established the practice at Saint Jerome’s prompting.

Thus, although the custom of singing this hymn of glorification by the faithful had prevailed throughout the Church before the Council of Nicaea by apostolic tradition, as we have seen, it received an addition at a later time and on another occasion, though with a different rite. When the Arians blasphemously asserted that the Son had been made by the Father in time and that there had been a time when he did not exist, the holy synod decided, in opposition to this heresy, to add to the ancient hymn of glorification the following appendage:

“Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, as it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.”

Thus far Baronius, whose discussion seemed to me highly appropriate for clarifying this passage of Cassian. See more on the subject in John Durandus, *On the Rites of the Church*, Book III, chapter 15.]

But they customarily conclude the antiphon only with this glorification of the Trinity.

[Note: Two matters concerning the antiphon deserve attention here: first, its antiquity and institution; second, its etymology and meaning.

Most writers trace the original origin and institution of antiphons to Blessed Ignatius of Antioch, bishop and martyr. Socrates reports that Ignatius saw choirs of angels praising the Holy Trinity with hymns and antiphons. “For this reason,” says Durandus, “the Greeks first composed antiphons and ordered that they be sung in the choir with the psalms.” Among the Latins, Saint Ambrose was the first to institute antiphons, according to Isidore, imitating the example of the Greeks. From that time their use spread throughout all the regions of the West. Thus it is written in the Chronicles that Saint Ambrose was the first to transfer the rite of antiphons from the Greeks to the Latins.

As for etymology and meaning, the Greek word *ἀντιφωνή* signifies in Latin nothing other than a reciprocal voice, or a reciprocal and alternating song. The word “antiphon” derives from *ἀντιφωνεῖν*, “to call back,” or to respond in turn and from the opposite side. Thus an echo is called *ἀντίφωνος*, “resounding in return” or “answering back.”

Isidore therefore asserts that antiphons are so called because two choirs sing together alternately, exchanging the melodies in turn and reciprocally—like, he says, two seraphim and the two Testaments crying out to one another. For this reason, Durandus says, clerics who sing antiphons do not turn their faces toward the altar, but face one another.

In this sense, however, “antiphon” acquires a general meaning, embracing hymns and other parts of the ecclesiastical office. Saint Benedict even calls the invitatory an antiphon. The psalms themselves, when recited or sung alternately by several persons, may also be called antiphons in the general sense, as can be gathered from Isidore.

Consequently, it does not seem entirely clear from the story of Saint Ignatius what sort of antiphons are meant, since the interpreters of both Socrates and Nicephorus variously call the praises of the Holy Trinity sung by the angels “hymns” and “antiphons.”

In the stricter ecclesiastical usage and ordinary manner of speaking, however, antiphons are called sacred songs or chants that are placed before the psalms sung at the canonical hours. For the most part antiphons are joined to psalms, although they are sometimes sung separately.

Cassian therefore indicates above that antiquity observed a twofold use of antiphons. First, they were inserted among the psalms of David in the canonical office and sung with a certain modulation and melody. Durandus derives their function and etymology from this practice in the following words:

“They are called antiphons in relation to psalmody, to which they respond, just as responsories relate to the history; hence an antiphon is said to be so called as though it were ‘sounding before the psalm.’”

Durandus would have spoken more accurately if, instead of “before,” he had explained the term through *ἀντί* as “against” or “from the opposite side.”

Amalarius also seems to have had and suggested the same relation in Book IV of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 7, and he explains it tropologically as follows:

“An antiphon is called a reciprocal voice. The antiphon begins with one member of one choir, and to its harmony the psalm is sung by two choirs; for the antiphon itself joins the two choirs together.”

A little later he says:

“It seems to us to be the power of love that joins together the works of two brothers. The psalms refer to works; the antiphon refers to that love by which each person offers his work to his brother.”

So far Amalarius, together with what follows in the same sense.

From all this it is easy to gather that there are two etymologies, or analogies and relations, of the word “antiphon.” One refers to the singers themselves, who alternate and exchange the melody among themselves, as Isidore and others have noted; the other refers to psalmody, or the singing of Davidic psalms, to which the antiphons respond as though from the opposite side, like voices and chants of another kind. In the same way, responsories respond to histories—that is, to readings—as Durandus explains.]

## CHAPTER IX. On the Character of Prayers

Since the established order has consequently advanced us to the manner of the canonical prayers, although we reserve a fuller treatment of them for the *Conferences of the Elders*, where we shall discuss them more fully when we begin to speak in their words about their character and continual practice, I nevertheless think it necessary, given the place and the course of the narrative, to touch briefly upon them here as the opportunity has presented itself.

In the meantime, we are shaping the movements of the outward person and laying down, as it were, certain foundations of prayer, so that later, when we begin to discuss the condition of the inward person, we may construct the heights of his prayers with less effort.

We are taking particular care beforehand that, if the end of our life should come upon us and prevent us from arranging, God willing, the account we desire to set forth, we may at least leave you in this work the beginnings of a matter so necessary—beginnings for which, because of the ardor of your desire, everything seems too slow. Thus, while the intervals of our stay here are granted to us, we may at least sketch for you for a little while certain outlines of prayer, by which especially those who live in monasteries may be instructed to some degree.

At the same time, we are looking ahead for the sake of those who may encounter only this book and may not be able to reach the other one, so that through the instruction contained here concerning the character of prayer they may be formed, at least in part. Just as they have been instructed concerning the clothing and outward dress of the human person, so they may also know how they ought to present him for the offering of spiritual sacrifices.

For these little books that, with the Lord’s help, we are now preparing will be more suitably adapted to the observance of the outward person and to the ordering of monasteries. The other books, however, will pertain more properly to the discipline of the inward person and to perfection of heart, and to the life and teaching of the anchorites.

[Note: *Ἀναχωρέω* means “I withdraw,” and *ἀναχώρησις* means “withdrawal.” From this the anchorites received their name: they were people who, out of devotion to piety, withdrew from human society and concealed themselves in solitude so that they might devote themselves more freely to the contemplation of divine things.

Saint Jerome says in Letter 22 to Eustochium: “Anchorites, who live alone in deserted places, are so called because they have withdrawn far from human beings.” Justinian, in Novel 5, writes that they were also accustomed to be called *ἡσυχασταί*, that is, people living in quiet and silence. Others call them hermits; Cassian frequently calls them solitaries. He treats their origin and discipline especially in Conference 18.]

## CHAPTER X. With What Silence and Brevity the Egyptians Gather Their Prayers
When, therefore, they come together to celebrate the aforesaid solemn observances, which they call *synaxes* [Note: The word *synaxis* is frequent among ecclesiastical writers, both Greek and Latin, and indeed has a twofold meaning. First, it denotes an assembly or congregation of the faithful—as here, of monks—for prayer, psalmody, the celebration of the sacred mysteries, or hearing the word of God. The word *synaxis* derives from συνάγειν, “to collect” or “assemble.” Cassian renders it in Latin by various terms, calling it in different places a *collecta*, assembly, gathering, congregation, canonical office or prayer, solemnity, celebration, and canonical Mass. In this same sense Saint Benedict says in chapter 17 of the Rule: “Vespers’ synaxis is concluded with four psalms together with their antiphons”; that is, the solemnity or course of Vespers, says Turrecrematus. At other times *synaxis* denotes the sacred communion of the Eucharist, and the holy Fathers frequently use the word in this sense (John Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book IV, chapter 14; Basil, *Short Rules*, chapter 71), either because this sacrament is customarily celebrated and received when Christians gather together, or because it is a sign and sacrament of peace and union.], all are enjoined to maintain such complete silence [Note: A remarkable and singular example of the regular silence to be observed in choir and in the divine offices. Saint Benedict also treats this in chapter 52 of his Rule, and Innocent III in chapter *Cum ad monasterium*, *De statu monachorum*. John Climacus recounts how severely the ancient Fathers punished those who violated sacred silence in a place of prayer: “While we were often standing at prayer, the holy Father noticed some people talking to one another. He set them before the doors of the church and ordered them for seven days to prostrate themselves before everyone entering and leaving” (Step 4). Pachomian monks maintained a lesser severity and strictness concerning silence, their Rule decreeing: “If it happens that anyone speaks or laughs during psalmody or prayer, or in the middle of a reading, he shall unfasten his belt and, with bowed neck and hands lowered, stand before the altar and be reproved by the head of the monastery. He shall do the same in the assembly of the brothers when they have gathered together to eat.”], that, although so immense a multitude of brothers has gathered together, no human being seems to be present except the one who rises and chants the psalm in the midst. Especially when the prayer is concluded, no spitting is heard, no clearing of the throat causes a disturbance, no cough interrupts, no sleepy yawn is drawn out through loosened lips and gaping mouths, no groans or sighs that might disturb those standing are uttered, and no voice is heard apart from that of the priest who concludes the prayer [Note: “Apart from” means “unless it is” or “except for” the priest, and so forth. The priest—or the abbot—concluded the prayer or office with a brief prayer in which he was said to gather together the vows and prayers of all; hence the name *Collecta*, as noted above, and this also demonstrates its antiquity. It is called *Collecta*, as the *Micrologus* explains (*On Ecclesiastical Observances*, chapter 3), because the priest, who acts as ambassador for the people before the Lord, gathers together and concludes all their petitions in that prayer. Those prayers, however, seem more specifically to be called *Collectae* which are said among the Romans over the assembly of the people—that is, over the people gathered together—when the people assemble in order to proceed from one church to another to celebrate a station. This is what he says. Yet *collecta* also means an assembly of the faithful or of monks in Cassian, and the collection of money to be distributed to the poor, which used to take place in such an assembly, as will be said elsewhere. From this passage we likewise infer that the abbots, or fathers, of those monks were for the most part priests or presbyters; this is also clear from many of the *Conferences*, especially Conference 4, chapter 1, and Conference 18, chapter 15. That this was customary, though not universal, will be shown more suitably elsewhere.], unless perhaps something has escaped through the barriers of the mouth in an excess of spiritual emotion, or something has imperceptibly stolen into the heart, when the spirit has been inflamed by an immoderate and intolerable fervor, and the burning mind, unable to contain within itself what it feels, attempts to exhale it through some ineffable groan from the innermost chambers of the breast.

But if someone, while appointed to pray, petitions with a cry, or emits from his throat any of the things we have mentioned, or is especially overtaken by yawning, they declare that he sins in two ways. First, he is guilty with respect to his prayer, because he offers it to God negligently. Second, by his undisciplined noise he also interrupts the attention of another who might perhaps have been able to pray more intently. Therefore they prescribe that the prayer be concluded quickly, lest, if we linger over it, some excess of spittle or phlegm interrupt the fervor of our prayer. For this reason, while it is still burning, it must be snatched swiftly, as it were, from the jaws of the enemy. Without doubt, since he is always hostile to us, he is most aggressively present when he sees that we intend to offer prayers to the Lord against him. Then he hastens to draw our mind away from the intention of supplication by stirring up thoughts or various bodily humors, and thereby strives to cool it from the fervor with which it began. Accordingly, they judge it more beneficial that prayers should be brief but very frequent [Note: He means the prayers which those monks, while one person chanted psalms in the oratory and the others listened, silently conceived and offered to God out of devotion and fervor, as though shooting them up into heaven; hence they are also called “ejaculatory” prayers. He also seems to refer to those prayers—which we call *Collectae*—with which each office, whether by day or by night, was concluded, as may be observed from several chapters of this book (chapters 7, 10, 11, and 12). Both kinds were brief rather than lengthy, for the excellent reason expressed here. Saint Augustine also noted the custom of those monks in his letter to Proba, writing: “It is said that the brothers in Egypt have frequent prayers, but that these are nevertheless very brief and, as it were, shot out rapidly, lest that alert and upright attention, which is most necessary to one who prays, should vanish and grow dull through prolonged delay. Thus they themselves sufficiently show that this attention, just as it must not be blunted if it cannot endure, so, if it endures, must not be broken too quickly. Far be much speaking from prayer; but let there be much petition if the fervor of attention persists. For to speak much is, in prayer, to pursue an unnecessary matter with superfluous words; but to pray much is to knock at the one whom we beseech with prolonged and devout stirring of the heart. More is often accomplished by groans than by words, and more by tears than by speech.” Thus Saint Augustine. Saint Benedict’s admonition in chapter 20 of the Rule agrees with this: “Therefore prayer should be brief and pure, unless perhaps it is prolonged by the inspiration of divine grace. In the community, however, prayer should be altogether brief; and when the prior gives the signal, let all rise together.” Turrecrematus says that this should not be understood of the canonical prayer, which has fixed chapters, verses, and psalms, for that must in no way be shortened, but of private prayer, by which each person prays individually in the assembly or oratory, as they customarily do at the end of the religious office while prostrate or bowed down, continuing some prayer until the signal given by the superior. He says that this prayer is to be shortened so that, when the signal has been given, all may rise together. That practice too was received from Cassian and from the example of the monks of old. The author reports in chapter 7: “When the one who is to gather the prayer”—namely, the superior or senior—“has risen from the ground, all rise together, so that no one dares either to bend his knees before that man has bowed down, or to delay when he has risen from the ground; nor may anyone be thought to have followed the conclusion of the one who gathers the prayer more than he has celebrated his own.” Saint Benedict does not prohibit private prayer in church after the divine office has been completed; indeed, he strongly commends such prayers and forbids their interruption, as does Saint Augustine in his Rule. Thus he says elsewhere: “When the Work of God has been completed, let all depart in the deepest silence, and so forth, so that a brother who perhaps wishes to pray for himself—that is, secretly within himself—and privately may not be hindered by another’s misconduct. But if someone perhaps wishes to pray for himself more secretly, let him simply enter—that is, without noise—into the oratory and pray, not with a loud voice, but with tears and attention of heart.” Explaining how he had earlier said that all should depart, he concludes: “Therefore, whoever is not engaged in a similar work”—namely, prayer or meditation—“must not be permitted to remain after the Work of God has been completed—that is, to remain in the oratory—lest another suffer hindrance.” See Turrecrematus.], so that by beseeching the Lord more frequently we may continually cling to him; and so that, by their concise brevity, we may avoid the darts of the devil lying in ambush, who is especially intent on inflicting them upon us when we pray.

## CHAPTER XI. By what discipline the psalms are chanted among the Egyptians

For this reason they do not strive to conclude even the psalms themselves, which they chant in the congregation [Col. 0100A], in a continuous recitation; rather, according to the number of their verses, they divide them by two or three interruptions, inserting prayers, and complete them distinctly and in separate portions. They take delight not in the multitude of verses, but in the understanding of the mind [Note: This is the apostolic teaching in 1 Corinthians 14, which urges that we should strive to pray and sing not only with the spirit but also with the mind. Many understand “spirit” as external speech and the voice, which consists of air and breath; thus praying and singing with the spirit means praying and singing with the voice, or, in another scriptural expression, honoring God with the lips (Isaiah 29; Matthew 15). Lactantius defines speech in this way in book IV, chapter 8, of the *Institutes*: “Speech is breath brought forth with a voice signifying something.” In other scriptural passages as well, “spirit” is used for “voice,” as in Psalm 31: “There is no deceit in his spirit,” and in the last psalm: “Let every spirit praise the Lord.” Others understand “spirit” as the devout affection by which a person burns toward God and the worship of God, as in Luke 11: “How much more will your heavenly Father give the good spirit to those who ask him!” and Ephesians 6: “Praying at all times in the spirit.” They interpret “mind” as intellect or understanding.
