In this sense, to sing with the spirit is to sing devoutly and piously; to sing with the mind is to grasp with the mind and understanding what we sing, and to consider it attentively. The Apostle therefore admonishes us, and by his example urges us, to strive, as far as we are able, to pray and sing not only devoutly—with pious affection and fervor—but also attentively and intelligently, so that we may grasp, at least to some extent according to our capacity, what we pray and sing. He adds the reason: “For if I pray with the tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is without fruit.” That is, the affection is raised toward God and refreshed by spiritual sweetness, but the mind is not refreshed by the nourishment and food of spiritual understanding, because it does not understand what it says. This, then, is what the holy and wise monks pursued with all their strength—that is, with all their zeal and the exertion of their minds: they strove not only to pray and sing with the spirit, meaning with voice and affection, but also with the mind, penetrating and receiving through meditation and rumination the meaning and mysteries of the psalms. This is the best and most perfect manner of praying and singing. Therefore, as has been said, they did not recite whole psalms continuously and in one uninterrupted flow to the end, but after every ten or twelve verses they paused briefly at certain divisions and short intervals, turning over in their minds what had been said and recited.]; and they pursue this with all their strength: “I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the mind” (1 Corinthians 14).

Therefore they consider it more beneficial that ten verses should be sung with intelligent understanding than that the whole psalm should be poured out with the mind confused. Such confusion is sometimes produced by the haste of the singer, who, considering the measure and number of the remaining psalms to be chanted, does not strive to reveal to the hearers the distinctions of meaning, but hastens to reach the end of the synaxis. Finally, if one of the younger monks, either through spiritual fervor or because he has not yet been instructed, begins to exceed the proper measure of chanting, the senior checks the singer’s progress [perhaps: “interrupts it”] by clapping his hand upon the seat where he is sitting, and by this causes all to rise for prayer. In every way he takes care that the seated brothers do not become weary through the excessive length of the psalms, so that the one who chants may not only lose the fruit of understanding for himself, but also suffer harm through those whom the excessive length of his singing has caused to become disgusted with the synaxis.

They also carefully observe among themselves that, when “Alleluia” is sung responsorially, no psalm is recited except the one whose title is prefixed with the inscription “Alleluia” [Note: The psalms which bear “Alleluia” in their title number twenty: namely, Psalms 104, 105, 106, 110, 111, 112, 113, 114, 115, 116, 117, 118, 134, 135, 145, 146, 147, 148, 149, and 150. For this reason the holy Fathers Jerome and Augustine call them “Alleluia psalms,” and they give no other reason for this inscription than that these psalms contain, above others, a distinctive and festal praise of God, which the title itself indicates. *Alleluia*, composed of two words, means “praise God with jubilation, joy, and song,” or “rejoice in God.” Hence in heaven, where all things are joyful, there is perpetual *Alleluia* (Revelation 19). In the Church it is sung only in joyful seasons, and has been so sung since the apostolic age, as Saint Augustine testifies in his commentary on Psalm 106. Saint Epiphanius, in book 1, chapter 20, of his work on the prophet’s life and death, says that the custom of singing this word in the Church came from the prophet Haggai, who was the first of all to sing “Alleluia” when he saw the new construction of the Temple; he relates this to the prophecy of Tobit, chapter 13, although many of the psalms listed above, bearing the title “Alleluia,” were already considered to have existed before their time (Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 10). It should be noted that some psalms are headed by “Alleluia” twice; some people wish the second occurrence to belong to the end of the preceding psalm. Augustine rejects this, saying: “Wherever, after the number of a psalm, whether once or twice, we find ‘Alleluia’ written, according to the most widespread custom of the Church it must be assigned to the psalm whose number it precedes.” It also appears that Saint Benedict instituted, in imitation of the practice of those ancient monks, that after the twelfth psalm—which is the last of the second nocturn—the *Alleluia* should be sung on weekdays outside Septuagesima, and after the canticles on Sundays (Rule, chapters 9 and 11).].

They divide the aforesaid number of twelve psalms in such a way that, if there are two brothers, each sings six; if three, each sings four; if four, each sings three. They never chant fewer than this number in the congregation; and therefore, no matter how large the gathering, no more than four brothers ever sing in the synaxis.

## CHAPTER XII. Why, while one sings, the others sit in the synaxis, and with what diligence afterward they prolong their vigils in their cells until daylight

They lighten the canonical number of twelve psalms, which we have mentioned, by such bodily repose that, while celebrating these same congregational solemnities according to custom, all of them, except the one who has risen into the midst to recite the psalms, sit on very low seats and attend with complete concentration of heart to the voice of the singer [Note: Here you see that seats were already in use in the churches or oratories of the monks. It also follows that the monks were accustomed at times to sit during the divine offices. This is also clear from the Rule of Saint Benedict. In chapter 9 he decrees that on weekdays, while all sit on benches during the nocturns, three lessons are to be read in turn by the brothers from the lectern; after the third lesson, “Glory be to the Father” is to be said, and when the cantor begins it, all are immediately to rise from their seats in honor and reverence of the Holy Trinity. In chapter 11: “With all sitting in an orderly fashion and in their places on the benches,” and so forth. Thus Tertullian’s reproach does not appear to apply quite adequately here (*On Prayer*, chapter 12, and Pamelius’s notes there), where he seems to condemn or disapprove of sitting in the choir and during ecclesiastical offices, as noted above—unless it refers to those who pray or sing while sitting out of irreverence, carelessness, and sloth, or who fail to observe the proper distinctions and variations in divine offices; that is, who sit when they ought to stand or kneel. No one will deny that this is outside discipline, that is, contrary to the institution of the holy Fathers. For Saint Benedict also commands (Rule, chapter 50) that brothers even when traveling must perform the Work of God, that is, the divine office, at the appointed hours, kneeling with godly fear. See Navarrus, *On Prayer*, chapter 4.].

For they become so exhausted by fasting and the labor of the entire day and night that, unless they are assisted by this kind of refreshment, they would not even be able to complete this number while standing. They allow no time at all to pass free from labor [Note: These statements should be understood appropriately and hyperbolically. For it is certain that an exception must be made for the time spent on the divine offices, and that which had to be allotted to meals, sleep, and other necessities.], for they strive not only to perform with all diligence by their hands the tasks permitted by the light of day, but also carefully seek out kinds of work which not even the deepest darkness of night can prevent, believing that they will attain a purer contemplation of spiritual things through the vision of the mind in proportion as they remain longer intent upon work and labor. Accordingly, they regard the moderate number of canonical prayers as divinely regulated [Note: This refers to the number of twelve psalms, instituted by the teaching and command of an angel for both the evening and nocturnal offices, as mentioned above (chapters 5 and 6). Let certain uninstructed and troublesome people consider this—those who think that whole days should be spent in psalmody and song, as though nothing else had been entrusted to us. For from the example of the ancient monks and the institution of our own Rule (Rule, chapter 48), it is clear that there are three things in which the monk’s life ought to consist: prayer, reading, and manual labor. The hours of the day should therefore be distinguished and distributed so that some are devoted to reading, some to prayer, and some to work. Thus Isidore says concerning these three in his *On the Highest Good*: “The servant of God ought without interruption to read, pray, and work.” Turrecrematus says concerning that passage of the Rule: “It must be considered that, from what has already been said about the distribution of the hours of the day among reading, labor, and prayer, it is clear how greatly those depart and rashly deviate from the intention and institutions of the Rule of the most blessed Father Benedict who spend entirely in prayer the time assigned to reading and labor. This is what some do who, putting their own judgment before the correctness of the Rule and the prudence of the holy Fathers, have so prolonged the divine office in certain monasteries, with reading neglected and labor abandoned, that they occupy almost the whole day with it. How plainly they act contrary to the mind of the most blessed Father and his Rule can easily be seen by anyone who has read even a little of his Rule.”]. It preserves for those more ardent in faith a span in which their tireless course of virtue may extend, while nevertheless ensuring that excessive length does not produce disgust in weary and weakened bodies.

Therefore, when the canonical prayers have been completed according to custom, each person returns to his own cell. He is permitted to inhabit it either alone or with only one other person—someone joined to him by a partnership in work, by discipleship and training in discipline, or, at any rate, by similarity of virtues. There each one again celebrates the same office of prayer more zealously, as a private sacrifice, and none of them thereafter relaxes into the rest of sleep until the daylight arrives and daily work succeeds nocturnal labor and meditation.

## CHAPTER XIII. Why one ought not to sleep after the nocturnal Mass

[Col. 0103B]

This labor—namely, that daily work should succeed nocturnal labor and meditation, as stated at the end of the preceding chapter [Note: This is the labor referred to at the end of the preceding chapter: “Daily work should succeed nocturnal labor and meditation.”]—they carefully maintain for two reasons, besides the reason that, striving with all their industry, they believe they are offering God a sacrifice from the fruit of their hands. If we seek perfection, it is fitting that we too should observe it with the same diligence.

The first reason is [Note: See with what zeal and concern those devout monks and lovers of purity strove to guard against the nocturnal illusions and pollutions customarily brought about by the devil’s activity. For this reason no one was allowed to return to sleep during the time remaining after the nocturnal Mass (as this chapter’s title has it), that is, after the nocturnal Office; rather, all were continually to devote themselves to prayer or work. Saint Benedict, emulating this practice, likewise decreed (Rule, chapter 8) that during winter the time remaining after the vigils—that is, after the nocturnal office commonly called Matins—be given by the brothers to meditation.] that the jealous enemy, envious of our purity—which he always especially watches and persistently attacks—might perhaps contaminate the purification acquired through the psalms and prayers of the night by some deception of sleep. After the satisfaction which we have offered for our negligences or ignorances, and after we have implored pardon for our confession with abundant groans, he hastens to defile us if he finds a time of rest, striving especially to overthrow and weaken our confidence when he sees us turning more fervently toward God through the purity of our prayers. Thus at times he attempts in that briefest hour to dishonor those whom he was unable to wound throughout the whole night (see Conference 22, which concerns nocturnal illusions).

The second reason is that, even if no such shameful deception of the devil should arise, the pure sleep intervening between the offices would immediately generate sluggishness in the monk who is soon to awaken, introducing a torpid lethargy into the mind and dulling its vigor throughout the whole day. It would blunt the keenness of perception and drain the richness of heart which could preserve us, throughout the day, more cautious and stronger against all the enemy’s snares.

For this reason they join private vigils to the canonical vigils [Note: These are the private vigils which he mentioned above (in the preceding chapter): private and spontaneous prayers, meditations, and spiritual exercises, which those devout monks, after completing the vigils or nocturnal offices and withdrawing to their cells, practiced privately out of devotion together with manual labor, as far as human frailty allowed. They did this so that no time might be lost without fruit or spiritual enjoyment, and so that sleep might not steal upon those who were idle or unoccupied. Thus they continually practiced manual labor privately in their cells, so that meditation on the psalms and on the other Scriptures might never be entirely omitted. The author repeats and emphasizes this in book III, chapter 2. Saint Jerome, speaking in his letter 18 about the monastery and monks of Bethlehem, says: “In Christ’s village all is rusticity; outside the psalms there is silence. Wherever you turn, the plowman holding the plow sings ‘Alleluia’; the sweating reaper diverts himself with psalms, and the vine-dresser, trimming the vines with his curved pruning hook, sings something of David.” Saint Augustine says in chapter 17 of *On the Work of Monks*: “They can easily sing divine songs while working with their hands, and console the labor itself as though with a divine chant. Do we not know what vanities, and often even what indecencies of theatrical stories, craftsmen give to their hearts and tongues while their hands do not cease from work? What, then, prevents a servant of God, working with his hands, from meditating on the law of the Lord and singing to the name of the Most High—provided that he reserves times for learning those things which he is to recall by heart?” These are the words of the holy Fathers. From them I conclude that prayer, especially mental prayer, is not always prevented by external or manual work; and that it is not only permissible but also pious and salutary to meditate on something devout while working, or to recite psalms and other prayers, provided that the work is not of a kind that excludes all attention (Saint Thomas, II, question 83, article 14; Navarrus, *On Prayer*, chapters 18 and 21). For some internal attention and reverence are required in every vocal prayer, even free and spontaneous prayer, as is gathered from the well-known saying of Jeremiah: “Cursed is the one who performs the work of God negligently” [Jeremiah 48; in the Hebrew, “deceitfully”; in the Septuagint, ἀμελῶς, “negligently”]. As Saint Benedict says: “If, when we wish to make some request of powerful human beings, we do not presume to do so except with humility and reverence, how much more must we plead with all humility and devout piety before the Lord God of all!” If this applies even to private and spontaneous prayer, it must be observed much more in public and prescribed prayer, such as the canonical hours and ecclesiastical offices. We shall discuss this matter more fully below, in a passage very similar to this one (book III, chapter 2). Moreover, mental prayer or meditation cannot lack attention, since attention itself is the very essence of prayer (Sotus, book X *On Justice*, question 5, article 5). It is therefore self-contradictory to pray mentally without paying attention, as is obvious in itself: as soon as the mind begins to wander, it ceases to pray. Thus it is only vocal prayer that can lack attention, when the tongue gives sound without the mind because the thought has drifted elsewhere.], following them with even greater care, so that both the purification acquired through psalms and prayers may not be lost and a more attentive vigilance, destined to guard us more carefully throughout the day, may be prepared by nocturnal meditation.

## CHAPTER XIV. How they practice manual labor and prayer together in their cells

For this reason they carry them out together with the addition of work [Col. 0105A], lest sleep creep upon them as upon idle people. Just as almost no time of leisure is allowed among them, so there is no end to spiritual meditation. Exercising together the virtues of body and soul, they make the service of the outer person equal to the benefits of the inner person. They fasten the weights of work, as it were a tenacious and immovable anchor, to the slippery movements of the heart and the unstable fluctuation of thoughts, so that the heart’s volatility and wandering, attached within the enclosure of the cell, may be held as in a most secure harbor. Thus, being intent only upon spiritual meditation and the guardianship of thoughts, the vigilant mind is prevented not only from falling into consent to any evil suggestion, but also from being overcome by every superfluous and idle thought. The result is that no one can easily discern which depends upon which: whether they practice unceasing manual labor because of their spiritual meditation, or whether, because of the constancy of their work, they acquire so distinguished a progress of spirit and so great a light of knowledge.

## CHAPTER XV. By what rule of modesty each person returns to his own cell after the prayers have been concluded, and what rebuke is imposed upon anyone who acts otherwise

When the psalms and the daily gathering have been completed, as we mentioned above [Note: An example of religious modesty and silence in the oratory, cell, cloister, and dormitory; we shall say more about it in Conference 14.], none of them dares to remain even for a short time or converse with another. Nor does anyone presume to go out of or leave his cell for the whole day, or to abandon the work he is accustomed to perform there, except when they have been summoned to perform some necessary task. They complete such tasks after leaving their cells in such a way that no conversation whatsoever takes place among them. Each person carries out the work assigned to him while reciting from memory a psalm or some Scripture, and thus gives neither opportunity nor time not only to harmful plotting or evil counsels, but even to idle conversation, being continually occupied in spiritual meditation through the work of both mouth and heart.

This was established and observed with the greatest wisdom; the angel also dictated it to Saint Pachomius in these words: “No one shall dare to enter another’s cell.” Saint Benedict likewise wished it to be observed that no brother should join himself to another at unsuitable hours. Such are the hours during which the brothers ought to be engaged in reading or manual labor, says Turrecrematus. The same principle applies to the rule that no one may enter the workshops of the workers without permission, except those appointed over such workshops and work. Saint Basil therefore decreed: “If anyone comes unseasonably into the kitchen or storeroom, except those designated or those responsible for the discipline of this order, let him be deprived of the blessing.” Saint Pachomius, nearly a contemporary of Basil, likewise says: “Only the superiors shall go to the workshops of the various crafts, so that they may receive what is necessary.”

The strictest observance is maintained so that no one may be found to have stood together with another, especially the younger brothers [or: “a younger brother”], even for a moment, or to have withdrawn anywhere with him, or to have held one another’s hands. If any are found to have committed something contrary to the discipline of this rule, they are declared guilty of no light offense, as stubborn and transgressors of the commandments; moreover, they cannot escape suspicion of conspiracy and evil counsel. Unless they purge this offense by public penance before all the brothers gathered together, none of them is permitted to take part in the brothers’ prayer.

## CHAPTER XVI. That no one may pray with one who has been suspended from prayer
Certainly, if anyone has been suspended from prayer for any offense committed, no one at all is permitted to pray with him until [Note: [Col. 0105D] He uses the same expression in Book III, chapter 7. What sort of penance this was he explains in Book IV, chapter 16, in these words: “When all the brothers have assembled in the synaxis, he shall lie prostrate on the ground and ask pardon for so long, until the solemnity of the prayers has been completed; and he shall obtain it when, by the abbot’s judgment, he has been ordered to rise from the ground.” Saint Benedict has similar provisions in chapters 43 and 44 of his Rule.] his reconciliation and pardon for the offense have been publicly granted by the abbot before all the brothers, after he has performed penance prostrate upon the ground.

For this reason they separate and withdraw themselves with such strict observance from sharing in his prayer, because they believe that the person suspended from prayer is, according to the Apostle’s sentence, handed over to Satan: [Note: [Col. 0105D] It is sufficiently evident that one suspended from prayer is here understood as one who has been excommunicated. For, according to the Apostle’s sentence, the person said to be handed over to Satan is the one who is cut off from the body of Christ, that is, from the Church, and excluded from the communion of the faithful; and thus is in a certain sense left to the power and tyranny of the devil, just as the Church leaves convicted heretics to secular authority. Hence Augustine says: “Every Christian who is excommunicated by priests is handed over to Satan.” How so? “Because outside the Church is the devil, just as Christ is in the Church; and therefore the one removed from ecclesiastical communion is, as it were, handed over to Satan.” Thus he shows that those whom the Apostle then declares to have been handed over to Satan were excommunicated by him (1 Cor. 1 and 5). Augustine’s words are from *On the Words of the Apostle*, sermon 68.

Those suspended from prayer were therefore considered excommunicated and consequently handed over to Satan. In this respect Saint Benedict, as I believe, imitated this passage of Cassian (chapters 24, 25, and 44), expressing more distinctly two kinds of suspension: one for more serious offenses, by which a person is suspended both from the table and from prayer—something he declares to be equivalent to being excommunicated and handed over to Satan according to the Apostle’s terrifying sentence; and another for lesser offenses, by which a person is excluded only from participation at the table.

Moreover, since according to evangelical teaching the penalty of such suspension, or excommunication, is to be inflicted upon no one unless he has refused to listen to the Church (Matt. 18), no one should therefore be excommunicated for any grave and deadly offense unless the sin of disobedience is joined to it—namely, that the person refuses to hear the Church, that is, to obey the Church or an ecclesiastical superior lawfully issuing a command. It is therefore reasonable to think that none of the brothers was suspended from prayer, or excommunicated by those fathers with that excommunication which, for the sake of distinction, we call the greater excommunication, unless he had been judged guilty of a serious offense and nevertheless refused to expiate and amend it through the regular and prescribed penance and satisfaction, as the Author says.

Only then was he considered suspended from prayer, from the oratory, and from the divine offices, so that neither he with the others, nor the others with him, were permitted to pray in common. Accordingly, chapter 25 of Saint Benedict’s Rule must be explained in this sense, where it says: “But that brother who is held by the guilt of a serious offense shall be suspended both from the table and from the oratory; none of the brothers shall associate with him in any way,” and so forth. For if this passage concerned a true ecclesiastical sentence of excommunication or suspension, as the following words plainly indicate—“Remaining in the grief of penance, knowing that terrible sentence of the Apostle who says, ‘Such a one has been handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh,’” and so forth—it would necessarily be understood that the “serious offense” meant disobedience or contumacy, which alone is sufficient for imposing excommunication, as chapter 23 clearly indicates when it says:

“If any brother is found to be contumacious, disobedient, proud, murmuring, or in any way opposed to the holy Rule and its precepts, or to be a despiser of the elders, let him be admonished once according to the command of our Lord,” and so forth.

Alternatively, it may mean a more serious and deadly offense to which disobedience has been added or joined. Yet it is not required that the offense be mortal in itself or by its nature; it is sufficient that it be mortal because of the force of the command or prohibition, when the gravity of the matter and a just cause recommend or permit this. Whenever, whether by law or by a human authority, something is lawfully commanded or prohibited under penalty of excommunication, failure to obey such command or prohibition is understood to be a mortal sin, even if its transgression would otherwise, and in itself, not be mortal.

From this one must form a judgment concerning those offenses which the Author mentions in the preceding chapter and concerning others like them.

From the argument of this passage, moreover, two conclusions worthy of knowing and noting may be drawn. First, abbots and other superiors of monasteries have the power to suspend their monks not only from prayer—that is, from the divine offices and from external fellowship and association with the brothers—but also to cut them off from the body of Christ, which is the Church, and to hand them over to Satan. Saint Benedict rightly calls this a terrifying sentence (chapter 25), because it not only deprives a person of external communion but undoubtedly also affects the soul, subjecting it to the tyranny of the devil and making it liable to him, so that the person may rightly be called the devil’s beast or slave.

Second, observe the ancient strength and rigor of monastic discipline, by which contumacious monks were sometimes suspended from prayer—that is, excommunicated—by their abbots and superiors, even though these may perhaps not have been priests. For abbots, even if they have not received the abbatial blessing and are not priests, can and do possess such authority over the monks subject to them, provided that they have been lawfully instituted and confirmed. But enough on this.] and if anyone, moved by ill-considered compassion, should dare to join in his prayer before he has been received by the elder, he makes himself a partner in his condemnation—voluntarily handing himself over to Satan, to whom the other had been consigned for the correction of his guilt—and incurs an especially grave offense by mingling with him in either conversation or prayer. For by doing so he supplies the offender with greater fuel for insolence and nourishes the delinquent’s contumacy toward worse things. By offering him such pernicious consolation, he will make his heart grow increasingly hardened and will not allow him to humble himself because of the offense for which he had been separated; and thus the offender will either attach little importance to the elder’s rebuke or think deceitfully about satisfaction and pardon.

## CHAPTER XVII

### That the person who awakens the brothers for prayer ought to summon them at the appointed hour

[Note: [Col. 0108D] That is, the person responsible for awakening or summoning the brothers to the nocturnal office, as deacons customarily do in certain monasteries. This chapter should also be compared with chapter 47 of Saint Benedict’s Rule, entitled “Of announcing the hour of the work of God.” There Abbot Smaragdus likewise reports the following constitution of a certain ancient Father:

“Whoever has been appointed to this task—that is, whoever has been found suitable for it, with an attentive and energetic mind—must arrange the hours according to the abbot’s disposition, so that the work of God is not delayed. He must not presume to awaken the brothers for the vigils at whatever hour he pleases, but must invite the whole congregation to the office of prayer in such a way that he is found careless in neither respect: neither allowing the appointed hour of the night to pass because he is overcome by sleep, nor anticipating it by hurrying.”

Thus far Smaragdus.

And lest anything seem relevant here to the instruction of the younger brothers and to the clarification of our purpose, I would also add what is found in chapter 11 of the same Rule and bears upon this very subject. There, after Saint Benedict has prescribed how the vigil, that is, the nocturnal office, is to be conducted on Sundays, he adds:

“This order of the vigils is to be maintained at all times, in summer and winter alike, on Sunday, unless perhaps—God forbid—we rise later than we should; in that case something must be shortened from the readings or the responsories. Yet every precaution must be taken to prevent this from happening. If it should occur, the person through whose negligence it happened must make worthy satisfaction to God in the oratory.”

Here Turrecrematus, explaining how something is to be shortened from the readings or responsories, says:

“Not in number, certainly, since twelve must always be recited, but in length, so that they are said more briefly than they ought to be. The brevity of the responsories, however, is not to be understood as a reduction in number, so that fewer than twelve are said, nor as a reduction in length, so that they are said more briefly, but with respect to the musical note: they are to be said more quickly, with shorter notation.”] The person entrusted with summoning the religious assembly, or with responsibility for the synaxis, must not presume to awaken the brothers for the daily vigils indiscriminately, whenever he pleases, or according to the time at which he happens to wake during the night, or according to whatever circumstance arising from his own sleep or sleeplessness may constrain him. Although long-established custom compels him to wake at the appointed hour, he must nevertheless diligently and frequently determine, by observing the course of the stars, the time fixed for the congregation and summon them to the office of prayer, lest he be found careless in either respect: either by allowing the appointed hour of the night to pass because he has been overcome by sleep, or by anticipating it through rising too early and hastening to sleep, so that he may be thought to have served not the spiritual office or the rest of everyone, but merely to have satisfied his own need for rest.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### That from Saturday evening until Sunday evening the knees are not to be bent

We must also know [Note: [Col. 0109B] The Author borrowed this expression from chapter 28 of Matthew. It signifies the evening that immediately precedes Sunday. In this sense some interpret “dawning toward the first day of the week” as meaning “inclining toward the immediately following Sunday” (Walafrid, *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 25; Amalarius, Book I, chapter 26).] that from Saturday evening, which dawns into Sunday, until the following evening, among the Egyptians [Note: [Col. 0109C] Here first observe the ancient practice of bending or kneeling at certain times during the ecclesiastical offices, which Saint Benedict also mentions in chapter 50 of his Rule.

Two periods are designated here during which the knees are not bent. The first is, as the Author says, from the evening of Saturday that dawns into Sunday until the following evening. We commonly call this the period from First Vespers until Second Vespers of each Sunday; or, if one prefers, until the evening of Sunday, so that the second Compline is also included.

The second period extends through all the days of the Quinquagesima, which we commonly call the entire Paschal season—that is, from Easter to Pentecost. Here it is called the Quinquagesima, as we noted elsewhere (above, chapter 6).

Tertullian writes that this practice was once commonly observed by all Christians, in chapter 3 of *On the Crown of the Soldier*: “On Sunday we consider it unlawful to kneel in worship; we enjoy the same exemption from the day of Easter until Pentecost.”

Likewise, in canon 20 of the Council of Nicaea—or canon 29 according to Turrianus—it was decreed in the commonly circulated editions that on Sunday and during the days of Pentecost, or the Paschal Quinquagesima, the knees are not to be bent in prayer, but that all should pray standing in every place and bow. See canon *Quoniam*, *On Consecration*, distinction 3. The same regulation is found in precisely the same words in canon 20 of the Council of Carthage.

Saint Ambrose says in sermon 61, *On Pentecost*: “Your Holiness ought to know why we observe this holy day of Pentecost, and why the number of these fifty days constitutes for us a continuous and uninterrupted festival: throughout this whole period we neither prescribe fasting as an observance nor bend our knees in supplication to God; but, as we customarily do on Sunday, standing upright and rejoicing, we celebrate the Lord’s Resurrection.”

Saint Jerome writes in his *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*: “On Sunday and throughout all of Pentecost, neither to worship on one’s knees nor to break the fast, along with many other practices not written down, has been claimed by reasonable observance” (chapter 4).

The same author writes in the preface to his letter to the Ephesians: “Paul remained at Ephesus until Pentecost, a time of joy and victory, during which we do not bend our knees or bow to the earth; but, rising with the Lord, we are lifted up to the heights.”

Finally, Pope Alexander III states the following in his Decretal: “On Sundays and other principal feast days, or between Easter and Pentecost, the knees should by no means be bent, unless someone wishes to do so privately out of devotion” (*Decretals*, Book II, chapter *Quoniam*).

The author whom Justin records as answering these questions explains more fully the cause and rationale of this institution and custom:

“If kneeling in prayers commends sinners to God more than praying while standing, and if it moves divine mercy more powerfully, why do those who pray on Sundays and from the days of Easter until Pentecost not bend their knees? And whence did such a custom arise in the Church?”

That author then answers:

“Because it is fitting for us to preserve an enduring remembrance of both things: of our own fall through sin and of the grace of Christ our Lord, through which we have risen from our fall. Therefore, kneeling for six days is a symbol and sign of our fall through sins; but the fact that we do not bend our knees on Sunday is a sign and representation of the Resurrection, through which by Christ’s grace we have been freed from sins and death. This custom began in the time of the apostles, as the blessed Irenaeus, martyr and bishop of Lyons, says in his book *On Easter*. There he also mentions Pentecost, during which we do not bend our knees, because it has equal authority with Sunday” (Justin, *Questions*, 4.115. See Turrecrematus on the canon *Quoniam*, *On Consecration*, distinction 3).

These are Justin’s words.

In the same sense Rabanus writes about this Quinquagesima, which he calls the Paschal Quinquagesima and which possesses a special rite and privilege:

“For this reason all the days of the Quinquagesima after the Lord’s Resurrection are celebrated, with penance relaxed, in joy alone, on account of the figure of the future resurrection, when there will no longer be labor but the rest of joy. Therefore during these days the knees are not bent in prayer, because, as one of the wise men says, the bending of the knees is an indication of penance and mourning. Hence throughout these days we observe the same solemnity that we observe on Sunday, during which our ancestors handed down that neither fasting was to be undertaken nor the knees bent, out of reverence for the Lord’s Resurrection” (*On the Instruction of Clergy*, Book II, chapter 4).

So far Rabanus.

From these statements three features peculiar to this Quinquagesima may be gathered. Although they are sufficiently well known, it will not be out of place to note them here. First, throughout this period the *Alleluia* is sung and used with great frequency, as a sign of joy and exultation. Saint Benedict discusses this in chapter 15 of his Rule, and Turrecrematus there as well. Second, the knees are not bent during the offices, or canonical hours, as stated here, as though the whole period were an unbroken Sunday or feast day. Third, there is no fasting until the vigil of Pentecost, except from devotion. Concerning this, see the canons in Gratian, distinction 4, chapter *Post Pascha*. But more will be said about these matters in the twenty-first Conference, entitled “On the Relaxation of the Quinquagesima,” especially chapters 12 and 20.] the knees are not bent; nor is the rule of fasting observed throughout all the days of the Quinquagesima. The reason for these matters will be explained in its proper place in the *Conferences of the Elders*, when the Lord commands it. (Conference 22.) For now, we intend only to pass briefly through the causes, lest the volume, by exceeding the prescribed limit, either burden the reader with boredom or weary him with labor.

# BOOK THREE  
## ON THE CANONICAL ORDER OF THE DAILY PRAYERS AND PSALMS

[Col. 0111]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0111B]

### On the nocturnal order of prayers and psalms observed throughout Egypt

The nocturnal order of prayers and psalms maintained throughout Egypt I believe, by God’s gift, to have been explained as far as the weakness of our understanding has allowed. We must now discuss the solemnity of Terce, Sext, and None [Note: [Col. 0111B] The reason he does not mention Prime among the hours, or daily solemnities, was indicated above and will be explained more fully below, in chapter 4 of this book.] according to the rule of the monasteries of Palestine and Mesopotamia [Note: [Col. 0111B] In the preceding book the Author discussed the monks of Egypt and their canonical order of nocturnal prayers and psalms (chapter 2). He now undertakes to speak about the monks of Palestine and Mesopotamia and about their offices.

Their founder was Saint Hilarion, as Saint Jerome testifies in his Life:

“For at that time there were not yet monasteries in Palestine, nor had anyone in Syria known monks before Saint Hilarion. He was the founder and teacher of this way of life and discipline in that province. The Lord Jesus had the old Antony in Egypt; in Palestine he had the younger Hilarion. Therefore, following his example, innumerable monasteries began to exist there, and all hastened to him in rivalry to draw from him the precepts of heavenly life. Seeing this, he praised the Lord’s grace and urged each one toward progress of soul” (Sozomen, Book III, chapter 13; Cassiodorus, *Tripartite History*, Book VI, chapters 12 and 28).

These are Saint Jerome’s words concerning Hilarion.

Saint Basil, moreover, in Letter 79, testifies that in his own time very many monks lived in Egypt, Palestine, Syria, and Mesopotamia. He describes their customs and manner of life as follows:

“I found many indeed at Alexandria, and not a few throughout the rest of Egypt; then also others in Palestine, Coele-Syria, and Mesopotamia. I admired in them both their moderation in maintaining their diet and their endurance in their labors. I was astonished at the vigor of their prayer when I observed how, neither overcome by sleep nor diverted by any other necessity of nature, they always preserved their lofty and unconquered spirit amid hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness. They themselves paid no regard to the body, nor did they tolerate care being shown to them by others; but, as though they lived in another person’s flesh, they demonstrated by their very works what it means to be a stranger in the affairs of this life and to have one’s manner of life in heaven.”

These are Basil’s words.

Sozomen writes similarly about the monks of Palestine in Book VI, chapter 32 of his *History*, and lists by name many of them distinguished for holiness.

Palestine is that region of Syria which the Hebrews call *Philistiim*. It lies west of Judaea and extends to the Mediterranean Sea, as Josephus reports in Book I, chapter 12 of the *Antiquities*.

Mesopotamia is a region of greater Asia and Syria situated between Babylonia and Arabia and between the two most famous rivers, the Tigris and the Euphrates. Hence it received its name, as though from the Greek *mesos potamōn* (μεσὸς ποταμῶν), “between the rivers,” and from the Hebrew *Aram Naharim*, that is, “Syria of the rivers.” It was made famous by the arrival of the patriarch Abraham, when he fled from Ur of the Chaldeans and stayed there at Haran, or Charan, until, by God’s command, he journeyed as a pilgrim to Palestine (Pliny, Book V, chapters 12 and 13; Gen. 24; Deut. 23; Judg. 3).] as we stated in the prologue, moderating the perfection of the Egyptians and the inimitable rigor of their discipline by the institutions of these communities.

## CHAPTER II

### That among the Egyptians, without distinction of hours, the entire day is continually devoted to work, prayers, and psalms
For among them (that is, among the Egyptians) [Note: [Col. 0112B] I mean the canonical offices, namely Terce, Sext, and None, as is clear from the preceding chapter. What then, you may ask, is it permissible to celebrate or recite the offices, that is, the canonical prayers, while doing something else—or, while reciting them, to do something else? Navarre treats this question in his work *On Prayer and the Canonical Hours*, chapter 13 (nos. 47 ff.; book II, chapter 14). Among other things, he adduces this example [Col. 0112C] of the Egyptian monks on the affirmative side: they performed not only private and spontaneous prayers, which were discussed in the preceding book, but also the offices, or canonical hours—Terce, Sext, and None—simultaneously with manual work, or privately while working in their cells, as is stated here.

First, Navarre declares that he wishes, indeed earnestly desires, that he might see this question—so daily and so important—decided by one who could not err, namely, by the Roman pontiff. He then explains the entire matter through several conclusions and reconciles various opinions of theologians that appear to conflict.

But in order to resolve this difficulty more briefly, and insofar as seems appropriate and sufficient for this place and our purpose, we must note first that the question concerns the private recitation of the office, as those monks recited it, not the same office being publicly sung. For it would be exceedingly incongruous and irreligious to perform manual labor publicly in church [Col. 0112D] during the divine office, and there is no doubt about this. Hence Saint Thomas (II-II, question 187, article 3, in the body of the article) seriously warns that what Augustine says in *On the Work of Monks* (chapter 17)—namely, that those working with their hands can easily sing divine songs, following the example of craftsmen who give their tongues to stories while nevertheless not withdrawing their hands from their work—cannot be understood of those who sing the canonical hours in church. Rather, he says, it is understood of those who recite psalms or hymns as private prayers.

Second, we must note that attention during the canonical hours and divine offices—in fact, during every vocal prayer—can be of several kinds. One kind of attention is directed to the words, so that they may be pronounced correctly; another to the meaning of the words, so that it may be grasped by the mind; another to God, so that the words of the prayer may be directed to him; and another, finally, to the matter for which we pray (Saint Thomas, II-II, question 83, article 13; Cajetan, at that place; Azorius, book X, chapter 2; Soto [Col. 0113A], book X, question 5, article 3; Leonard Lessius, book II, chapter 37). At least one of these kinds of attention is required and is sufficient in every prayer, whether spontaneous, obligatory, or commanded.

Moreover, each kind of attention may be either actual or virtual, confused or distinct. Attention is called virtual when it derives its force from a preceding actual attention, or from the will and intention to attend. For example, someone begins to recite a psalm and intends to pay attention; afterward, however, he is unwillingly distracted by various thoughts. Nevertheless, the entire psalm is recited attentively through the force and efficacy of that first intention by which he wished to recite the psalm with an attentive mind. He is considered to persist in that intention so long as he does not voluntarily become distracted or depart from it through a contrary act.

Third, we must note that the external acts, or external activities, of which we are speaking here are of three kinds. Some require careful and serious attention and presence of mind, such as reading, writing, painting, conversing with another person, listening to someone speaking, and similar activities. Others require neither the highest attention nor none at all, but a moderate degree—for example, getting out of bed, putting on or removing one’s clothes, building a fire, and so forth [Col. 0113B]. Others, finally, require little or virtually no attention, such as walking, traveling, picking a flower, looking out over gardens or meadows, and so forth.

A certain and general rule cannot be given as to which acts belong to one category or the other. The matter must therefore be left to the judgment of a good man, whose task is to consider not only the nature of the external activity but also the person’s manner and aptitude. Someone might be so attentive to the recitation of the hours while putting on his clothing that he would not sin at all; conversely, someone might be so intent upon walking or traveling that, if he recited the hours while maintaining that degree of attention, it would be sinful, at least venially, Navarre says.

With these points established, and in order—as the saying goes—to meet the proposed question at the threshold (Navarre, in the place cited above, no. 50), I say first: It is certain that acts or external activities of the first kind are incompatible with attention to prayer. Consequently, a person who knowingly and willingly occupies himself with such acts or activities while reading or singing the office does not satisfy the obligation of ecclesiastical office; indeed, he incurs mortal guilt. For the Church, in the Lateran Council, strictly commands that the divine office be celebrated with equal diligence and devotion (Book III of the *Decretals*, title “On the Celebration of Mass,” chapter *Dolentes*). The gloss refers the word *diligently* to the duty of the mouth, that is, to external pronunciation; and *devoutly* to the duty of the heart, that is, to the interior affection and attention of the mind. It is obvious, and experience teaches, that activities of this sort obstruct every form of due attention.

Second, I say that those acts or activities of the second kind, which require at least moderate awareness and care, consequently conflict with attention to the hours in such a way that the hours can scarcely be recited while preserving that attention. Therefore, whoever performs such acts during the canonical prayers can scarcely be excused from sin, at least venial sin.

For this reason Anthony judges that a cleric who recites the canonical prayers while dressing, putting on his shoes, or occupying himself with other external activities deserves reproach and scarcely fulfills the obligation, because he deliberately involves himself in acts that turn him away from attention [Col. 0113C] (Part II, title 9, chapter 3). Cajetan, however, Soto, and Navarre deny that he sins at all, or at most that he sins only lightly; hence they also allow that he satisfies the obligation. Such activities, they say, being light, easy, and customary, do not entirely impede or exclude the attention of mind that prayer requires, especially when greater care, diligence, and desire to attend are applied.

Here it is useful to hear Soto, who discusses these matters carefully, so that no one may think I am saying these things on my own. “No one,” he says, “should be judged to be deliberately distracted from attention unless the following conditions are present: namely, that while reciting the hours he is occupied with another task which by its nature is opposed to attention to prayer—for example, if someone at that time reads, writes, paints, or does something of that kind [Col. 0114A] that requires attention.

“Therefore, if while praying someone washes his hands, dresses himself, or does something else that does not demand so much awareness, although he acts improperly against the dignity of prayer and perhaps sins venially, he does not thereby act against the obligation mortally. I say ‘perhaps venially,’ because it is not always a sin. Indeed, in our order we are commanded to recite the office of the Blessed Virgin when rising from bed; and, as the ancient arrangement of the dormitory indicates, the brothers began it while dressing, so that the evil imaginings that commonly arise at the very moment of awakening might be driven away.

“Again, it is required that a person who does or thinks something extraneous to attention in prayer should recognize that, through it, he is slipping away from that attention. Thus, even if he voluntarily and deliberately thinks about something else—as Cajetan rightly says in his *Summa*—so long as he does not notice that he is being distracted, he is always regarded as wandering inadvertently.” Thus far Soto (*On Justice*, book X, question 5, article 5).

Saint Basil supports this view in Homily 5, *On the Martyr Julitta*, where he teaches that one should pray in every place and at every time, and among other things says: “Are you putting on your tunic? Give thanks to the benevolent giver. Are you wrapping yourself in a cloak? Cause your more intense love for God to increase within you, since he has freely bestowed coverings, and so forth.”

Saint Dominic is also reported to have said, according to Cajetan (on II-II, question 83, article 13), that prayer attentively pronounced by someone rising from bed is a common and salutary medicine for resisting perverse thoughts.

Add to this that in the Missals certain formulas of prayer are prescribed for priests about to offer sacrifice, to be recited while they put on the sacred vestments, while they wash their hands in the middle of Mass, and while they remove their vestments at its conclusion. Likewise, in the pontifical books many psalms are prescribed for bishops to recite with their ministers while they are being vested in pontifical garments.

It is now clear from what has been said what must be said about acts of the third kind. These conflict so little with the attention due even during the canonical hours that they may be performed while reciting the hours without sin, even when no special reason intervenes, as Navarre likewise teaches [Col. 0114C] (in the place cited above, no. 50).

Thus we should understand those holy monks in the following way: they celebrated and completed those canonical offices privately, together with the addition of work, as is stated here—that is, they worked with their hands in the meantime. Yet they did not perform just any activities, but those that least impeded the attention due to prayer, and with which they had become so accustomed that they could perform them with no attention or consideration, or at least with very little. Such activities included weaving baskets, digging gardens, sowing seeds, planting or uprooting herbs, hoeing the soil, arranging garden beds, and other tasks mentioned by Saint Jerome in his letter to the monk Rusticus.

Or, what I consider more likely, those monks celebrated and completed the offices with the addition of work, not because they worked and recited the office simultaneously and at the same time, but because they alternated and successively joined prayer to work, and work to prayer, at intervals, so that prayer continually followed work and work followed prayer.

Finally, Navarre gives a warning that deserves particular attention and can also be inferred from what has been said: the recitation of the hours is worthy of greater praise—and, other things being equal, certainly more pleasing to God, more religious, and more fruitful—the less it is carried out with external occupation of the hands, feet, eyes, or other senses; “so that,” he says, “we may be wholly intent upon it in mind,” in accordance with the rightly understood saying of our Redeemer: “When you pray, enter into your room, and, having shut the door, pray” (Matthew 6).

He added the qualification “other things being equal” both because of the example of the monks under discussion and because of other arguments that might be raised concerning the public recitation of the hours, or the public celebration of the divine offices in church. Such public celebrations are indeed superior to private ones, other things being equal—that is, when devotion, attention, and the other circumstances are equal—although they require greater occupation of the senses [Col. 0115B].

These, then, are the offices that we are compelled to render to the Lord at fixed divisions of the hours and intervals of time, summoned by the warning [Col. 0115A] [Note: [Col. 0115B] That is, by the striking or sound of a superior, or of another person calling someone to the work of God, or to the divine office. Saint Benedict also discusses this in chapter 47 of the Rule, “The Announcement of the Hour for the Work of God.” It appears from this passage, and even more clearly from book IV, chapter 12, that instead of the bell we now use they employed a striking at the doors of each individual. For there we read: “When they hear the sound of one striking the door and knocking on the cells of the various brothers, inviting them, that is, to prayer or to some task, each one hastens from his lodging.” But more will be said elsewhere about this striking and about the instruments by which they were summoned to the divine office (see the scholia on the Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 2).] of the one who calls us, and throughout the entire day they are voluntarily celebrated continually together with the addition of work.

For their manual labor is so constantly carried on privately in their cells that the meditation of the psalms and of the other Scriptures is never entirely omitted. Mingling prayers and petitions with it at every moment, they spend the whole day in these offices that we celebrate at appointed times.

Consequently, apart from their evening and nocturnal assemblies, they have no public solemnity during the day, except on the Sabbath or the Lord’s Day, when they gather at the third hour for the sake of Holy Communion.

[Note: [Col. 0115B] That the Egyptian monks customarily assembled solemnly in church on the Sabbath and the Lord’s Day to celebrate and receive the divine mysteries is plainly evident both from this passage and from other passages in Cassian. It is also clear that this custom prevailed among all Christians, especially in the East, from Clement, who says in book VII of the *Constitutions*, chapter 24: “We keep the Sabbath and the Lord’s Day as festivals, because the former is a memorial of created nature, the latter of the resurrection.” The historian Socrates confirms the same in these words: “Whenever the weekly festivals occurred, namely the Sabbath and the Lord’s Day, on which assemblies are customarily held in churches, etc.” (book VI, chapter 8). But this matter will also be treated below, where the fast of the Sabbath is discussed (chapters 9 and 10).]

For what is offered continually is greater than what is rendered at intervals of time; and [Note: [Col. 0115C] Saint Jerome’s opinion in book I *Against Jovinianus* is plainly similar: “It is a greater grace to offer what one ought not to offer than to render what one is required to render.” Neither statement, however, should be expounded in such a general way that the words are taken exactly as they sound and appear to imply, but specifically, according to the authors’ intention and the requirements of the passages. In this way, the scope and meaning of both statements are nearly the same.

Saint Jerome is speaking there about virginity and virgins, whom he says are loved more by Christ than married women because, as he says, they freely offer what has not been commanded of them—that is, they offer and consecrate their virginity to God, which is not a precept but a counsel. It is a greater grace and perfection to observe the counsels, which few do, than merely to observe the precepts, which are required of everyone.

Cassian is likewise speaking here, as is clear from what precedes, about private prayers, meditations, and other exercises of piety. Those devout monks interspersed or inserted these among their manual activities and spent the entire day without any interruption or rest, as he said shortly before. Thus, in addition to the functions—that is, the canonical offices—owed by canonical compulsion, or regular institution, they offered God voluntary gifts—that is, spontaneous and private offices of devotion and supererogation—so that they would not be free from God’s service for even a moment. This is certainly better and more pleasing to God than satisfying only the offices that are owed and prescribed at their appointed times. For, he says, what is offered continually is greater than what is rendered at an interval of time.

Accordingly, the voluntary gift is not here separated from the canonical and obligatory functions; rather, it is presumed to be joined with them. Whoever performs works that are not commanded, out of charity and as he ought, also performs the works or offices that are commanded or obligatory—as those monks undoubtedly did. In this way he gives more than the person who performs only what is commanded or obligatory. For the precepts are included within the counsels, not opposed to them.

Nothing, therefore, can be inferred from this against the common teaching concerning a vow and a work performed by virtue of a vow. Other things being equal, such a work is certainly better, more pleasing to God, and more meritorious than if it were performed [Col. 0116C] without a vow, provided that it is not performed under compulsion or from servile fear. In that case Cassian’s statement, “The voluntary gift is more pleasing,” is simply true. But Cassian does not seem to have understood it in this way when he was speaking of those monks who performed everything promptly and devoutly and supplied more than they were bound to supply.] more pleasing is the voluntary gift than the functions [Col. 0115B] that are rendered under canonical compulsion. For this reason David, exulting, gloriously offers something more when he says: [Col. 0116A] [Note: [Col. 0116C] “Voluntary” is opposed to sadness and compulsion, but not to necessity or obligation, which arises from a vow or a precept. Saint Augustine speaks of this in his letter to Armentarius: “Happy is the necessity that compels us to better things.”

Nevertheless, Cassian seems here to understand “voluntary” as what is done spontaneously, without any obligation arising from a vow or precept. This is indeed better and more pleasing to God when it is added, out of the fervor of charity, to other works and obligatory and necessary offices, and offered beyond what is required, as was said above. Here the Gospel saying applies: “These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others” (Matthew 25).] “I will sacrifice to you voluntarily” (Psalm 53); and, “May the voluntary offerings of my mouth be pleasing to you, Lord” (Psalm 118).

## CHAPTER III. That throughout the entire East the solemn celebration of Terce, Sext, and None is concluded with only three psalms and prayers; and why these spiritual offices have been assigned more particularly to these hours

Accordingly, in the monasteries of Palestine and Mesopotamia, and throughout the entire East, the solemn celebrations of the hours mentioned above are concluded every day with three psalms. Thus both the constancy of prayer may be offered to God at appointed times and the necessary tasks of work, once the spiritual services have been completed with due moderation, may in no way be impeded [Note: [Col. 0116C] Saint Cyprian says similarly near the end of his book *On the Lord’s Prayer*: “In the celebration of prayers we find that the three youths, strong in faith and victorious in captivity, observed with Daniel the third, sixth, and ninth hours.” Saint Jerome says likewise in his commentary on Daniel, chapter 6: “The Church’s tradition understands three times at which the knees must be bent before God.”]

For we know that at these three times the prophet Daniel also poured out prayers to the Lord every day, with the windows of his upper room open (Daniel 6).

[Note: [Col. 0116D] Besides the ancient Fathers, Rupert, Isidore, Hugh of Saint Victor, and other more recent writers treat explicitly of these and other mysteries and meanings of the canonical hours, which Cassian touches upon here. They offer various reasons why these times have been assigned more particularly to religious offices—that is, why the divine offices are performed at these times or hours. Three reasons, however, appear to be primary: the first concerns the benefit of creation, the second the benefit and mystery of redemption, and the third the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity.

First, the canonical hours were instituted so that we might commemorate the benefit of creation every day and render perpetual praise and thanksgiving for it to the Creator of all things, as the weekday hymns of Vespers clearly show (Bellarmine, book I *On the Goodness of Works*, chapter 13). There are seven daytime hours because God created heaven and earth and everything contained within the compass of heaven in seven days.

An eighth hour is added, namely the nocturnal office, on account of the hope and expectation of the resurrection, which is customarily signified by the eighth day. The Lord himself indicated that the resurrection would occur at night in Luke 17: “On that night there will be two in one bed; one will be taken and the other will be left”; and in Matthew 25: “At midnight a cry was made: Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him.”

The second reason, and the most important one given by the Fathers—Clement, Basil, Cassian, and others—is the preservation of the memory of our redemption and restoration. For it is known that the principal mysteries of our redemption and of the Lord’s Passion were completed at these hours. On this subject there are those memorable verses, which I quote for the benefit of younger readers and which they should commit to memory:

> These are the reasons for which we sing psalms at the seven hours:
>
> Matins binds Christ, who cleanses sins.
>
> Prime fills him with spittle; Terce gives the cause of death.
>
> Sext binds him to the cross; at None his side is pierced in two.

Vespers lays him down; Compline restores him to the tomb. But in these same hours we also profess the memory, and grateful remembrance with praise, of the other benefits and mysteries of our restoration—for example, the Incarnation, Nativity, Resurrection, sending of the Holy Spirit, calling of the Gentiles, and so forth—which Scripture and antiquity record as having occurred at the appointed times corresponding to the offices of the Hours.

[Col. 0117C] The third reason is that, in honor of the most holy Trinity, we should praise God at every third hour and profess the mystery of the Trinity, which is the foundation of our faith, at each group of three hours. St. Cyprian intimates this reason in these words:

> In the celebration of prayers we find that the three boys, together with Daniel, observed the third, sixth, and ninth hours—namely, as a sacrament of the Trinity, which was to be manifested in the last times. For when the first hour advances to the third, it displays the completed number of the Trinity; likewise, when the fourth advances to the sixth, it declares the other Trinity. And when the seventh is completed by the ninth, the perfect Trinity is reckoned by groups of three hours.

(*On the Lord’s Prayer*, near the end.)

Thus Cyprian indicates that at each ternary of hours, both by day and by night, God was publicly and solemnly praised in the church, to signify and honor the mystery of the Trinity. For the ancients were accustomed to divide the entire day into four parts, each consisting of three hours; [Col. 0117D] likewise, they divided the night into four watches, each containing three hours. And just as, among the twelve nocturnal hours, every third hour was regarded as especially important—namely, the third, sixth, ninth, and twelfth, at which the four night watches ended—so also among the daytime hours the third, sixth, ninth, and twelfth, the last of which was commonly called the vespertine hour, were generally assigned to the more important tasks and therefore were regarded as more distinguished, since they divided the day into four equal parts, as has been said.

Cassian therefore rightly maintains that these times, or hours, were regarded as more important and distinguished in ordinary human usage; but, all the more because they were illuminated and consecrated by so many mysteries, they were deservedly assigned by the Church more especially to divine services. Nor without reason have these times been specially assigned to religious offices. For in them the fulfilment of the promises and the sum of our salvation were accomplished.

[Note: [Col. 0118A] In undertaking to discuss the daytime Hours, or offices, and to explain their mysteries, reasons, or meanings, the author begins with Terce, omitting Prime for the reason indicated above and to be explained more fully in the following chapter. Because of the dignity and eminence of its mystery, this Terce is commonly called among the Italians the “golden hour.” In canon law, however, it is called the sacred hour, *Distinction* 44, final canon, where it is said that clerics or religious laypeople ought not to begin banquets before the sacred third hour of the day (in Gratian, from a council of Pope Martin). It seems to have been called sacred because it was dedicated to the sacred solemnities of the Mass, as John Durandus aptly conjectures in *On the Rites of the Church*, book III, chapter 8.

Two principal mysteries of this third hour are commemorated in Scripture and celebrated by the Fathers. One concerns Christ’s Passion; the other, the sending or coming of the Holy Spirit. Concerning the first mystery, St. Clement says in book VIII, chapter 40, of the *Apostolic Constitutions*: “Offer your prayers at the third hour, because at that hour the Lord received Pilate’s sentence.” St. Ignatius likewise asserts in his eighth letter to the Trallians: “At the third hour Christ receives his sentence from Pilate.” St. Athanasius, in *On Virginity*, says: “Let the rising sun find a book in your hand; after the third hour receive Communion, because at this hour the wood of the cross was brought forth.”

Concerning the other mystery, which the author explains here, Tertullian says in *On Fasting*: “In Luke’s commentary, the third hour of prayer is also indicated, at which those who had been initiated by the Holy Spirit were thought to be drunk.” St. Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*: “For at the third hour the Holy Spirit descended upon the disciples, fulfilling the grace of the promise.” St. Basil, Sermon I, *On the Institution of Monastic Life*: “Indeed, the coming of the Holy Spirit also took place around the third hour of the day, as we learn from the Acts. At that time, when the Pharisees mocked the disciples because of the effective power of those various tongues, Peter denied that they were drunk, since, as he said, it was the third hour.”

Likewise, in the *Longer Rules*, question 37:

> The third hour is appointed for rising to prayer and for all the brethren to assemble together, although they may be occupied in different places with different tasks. This is so that, reminded of the gift of the Spirit, which was given to the apostles around this hour, they may all with one and the same mind worship him and ask him to make them likewise worthy to receive sanctification, and so forth.

St. Jerome, in his commentary on Daniel VI: “At the third hour the Holy Spirit descended upon the Apostles.”

Thus far the holy Fathers have discussed separately and distinctly the twofold mystery of the third hour. Rabanus embraces both together in these words:

> The office of the third hour is performed because Christ’s Passion began at the third hour, when the Lord was crucified by the tongues of the Jews. After his Resurrection, on the day of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles at the third hour.

(*On the Institution of the Clergy*, book II, chapter 4.)

Rupert of Deutz likewise says in book I, chapter 3, of *On the Divine Offices*:

> The third hour shines forth as distinguished for a twofold reason. At that hour the Lord Jesus was crowned with thorns and crucified by the tongues of the Jews, in accordance with the words: “The sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Psalm LVI). For, when Pilate was judging, they confirmed an evil decision for themselves by crying out stubbornly: “Crucify, crucify!” (Luke XIII). The Spirit, moreover, who had not been given for the remission of sins before Jesus was glorified, was poured out upon the newly born Church in tongues of fire, and the Lord’s promise to the disciples was fulfilled: “But you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now” (Acts I).

[Col. 0118A] The Holy Spirit, promised long ago through the prophets, is first shown to have descended upon the apostles at the third hour, while they were engaged in the office of prayer. For when the unbelieving Jewish people, astonished and mocking because of the utterance of the languages that flowed from them through the infusion of the Holy Spirit, said that they were filled with new wine, Peter stood among them and said:

> Men of Israel, and all you who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and listen to my words: These men are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is the third hour of the day. But this is what was spoken through the prophet Joel: “And it shall come to pass in the last days, says the Lord, that I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams. Indeed, upon my servants and upon my maidservants in those days I will pour out my Spirit, and they shall prophesy” (Acts II; Joel II).

All these things we see fulfilled at the third hour, and the coming of the Holy Spirit foretold by the prophets arriving upon the apostles at that same time (Colossians II).

[Col. 0119B]

[Note: [Col. 0119C] With regard to Sext, the author touches upon two particular sacraments or mysteries. One likewise concerns the Lord’s Passion; the other concerns the calling of the Gentiles, represented and announced to the apostle Peter by the vessel lowered from heaven, full of every kind of animal. Both mysteries are also asserted and commended by the Fathers in the same passages cited above. There they all affirm without hesitation that Christ was crucified around the sixth hour, and that the office of Sext was instituted in his memory.

The Evangelist John plainly and explicitly reports this in chapter XIX: “It was the Parasceve of Passover, about the sixth hour. And Pilate said to the Jews: ‘Behold your king.’ But they cried out: ‘Take him away, take him away, crucify him.’” A little later: “Then he delivered him to them to be crucified.” Besides the authors mentioned above, including our Cassian, and countless others, the Church confirms this judgment in the office of the Cross and in its prayers (see John Durandus, cited above).

The other mystery, concerning the calling of the Gentiles, which was demonstrated to blessed Peter when he was in an ecstasy of mind at the sixth hour, is admirably explained here. Cyprian also agrees in *On the Lord’s Prayer*: “At the sixth hour Peter, ascending to the upper room, was instructed by both the sign and the voice of God, who warned him to admit all people to the grace of salvation, since previously he had hesitated concerning the cleansing of the Gentiles.” St. Jerome likewise says in his commentary on Daniel VI: “At the sixth hour Peter, wishing to eat, went up to the upper room for prayer.” For more on the other mysteries of the sixth hour, see the authors who treat of the ecclesiastical offices.]

At the sixth hour the spotless victim, our Lord and Savior, was offered to the Father; and, ascending the cross for the salvation of the whole world, he washed away the sins of the human race. And [Note: [Col. 0119D] The Apostle’s words to the Colossians are as follows:

> And you, when you were dead in trespasses and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, he made alive together with him, forgiving you all trespasses, blotting out the written decree that stood against us, which was contrary to us, and removing it from our midst by fastening it to the cross. He stripped principalities and powers, exposed them openly, and triumphed over them in himself (Colossians II).

Here the Apostle calls the “written decree” that guilt, or debt, by which Adam had made himself and his descendants liable to eternal death through eating the forbidden tree, in accordance with God’s decree and sentence: “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die” (Genesis II).

In this passage *to expose publicly* means to disgrace someone and set him before everyone as an example and spectacle, just as victorious generals customarily lead captives through the city in triumph. So Christ, victorious on the cross, stripped the demonic powers of their spoils and, triumphing over them in himself, exposed them confidently and publicly, displaying them to all as shamefully defeated. Thus, in the previous year, the emperor led the duke of Saxony and the Landgrave around as a trophy and displayed them to the people, as Adam Sasbout says, in a striking and universally known example.]

Having stripped principalities and powers, he exposed them publicly, and freed all of us, who were liable and bound by the unbreakable debt of the written decree, removing it from our midst and fastening it to the trophy of his cross.

At that same hour, while Peter was in an ecstasy of mind, the calling of all the Gentiles was divinely revealed to him through the lowering from heaven of the evangelical vessel, together with the purification of all kinds of animals contained in it. A voice from heaven said to him: “Rise, Peter, kill and eat” (Acts X). It is clearly understood that this vessel, lowered from heaven by its four corners, signifies nothing other than the Gospel.

Although, because of the fourfold account of the Evangelists, it appears to have four beginnings, there is nevertheless one body of the Gospel, embracing together the humanity and divinity of the same Christ, as well as his miracles and Passion. It is beautifully said not “a linen cloth,” but “something like a linen cloth.” Linen is an indication of mortification (Psalm XV). Since, therefore, the Lord’s death is undertaken not according to the law of human nature but by the choice of his own will, it is called “something like a linen cloth.” For although he died according to the flesh, he did not die according to the spirit, since his soul was not abandoned in hell, nor did his flesh see corruption.

[Col. 0120B] Again he says: “No one takes my soul from me; rather, I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again” (John X).

Thus, in this vessel of the Gospels sent down from heaven—that is, written by the Holy Spirit—all the nations who were formerly considered unclean because they stood outside observance of the Law are brought together through the belief of faith, so that they may be beneficially offered in sacrifice [Perhaps: “be turned away from the worship of idols”] and advance toward salutary food. They are conveyed to Peter by the Lord’s voice, with Peter purifying them.

[Note: [Col. 0120C] The author gives three reasons why None was instituted among the canonical hours and honored by ecclesiastical office.

First, in memory of Christ’s most sacred death and his descent into hell. All the Evangelists testify that Christ expired on the cross at the ninth hour; and it is a constant tradition of the Church that at that same time his soul descended into hell in order to free the Fathers. Thus, according to the testimony of blessed Clement, we pray at the ninth hour because then everything was shaken and trembled at the crucified Lord, horrified at the audacity of the impious Jews and unable to endure the Lord’s insult.

Tertullian, in the passage cited above, says: “The oppression must be observed up to that hour”—that is, abstinence or the Lord’s affliction must be observed—“at which the world, darkened from the sixth hour, performed a mournful office when the Lord died, so that we too may then return to joy, when the world recovered its brightness.”

St. Cyprian says: “The Lord was crucified at the sixth hour and at the ninth washed away our sins with his blood. In order that he might redeem and give us life, he then completed his victory through his Passion.”

St. Athanasius says: “At the ninth hour you will again be engaged in hymns and glorifications; with tears and confession of your sins you will beseech God, because at this hour the Lord, hanging upon the cross, gave up his spirit.”

[Col. 0121A] St. Basil, Sermon I, *On the Institution of Monastic Life*: “Moreover, the ninth hour recalls the memory of the Lord’s Passion, which he accepted for the sake of our life.”

Rabanus Maurus says:
