> The ninth hour is consecrated because at it the Lord, praying for his enemies, commended his spirit into the hands of the Father. The faithful, therefore, ought to commend themselves to God with devout prayer, recognizing that their Head commended his own soul to his Father, so that, joined with him in his body, they may be able to enter with him into the everlasting kingdom.

(*On the Institution of the Clergy*, book II, chapter 6.)

Rupert of Deutz says:

> At the ninth hour we rightly cry out in praise of God, when the Lord, crying with a loud voice, gave up his spirit; when the thief was admitted into paradise, and when forgiveness was dedicated to those who truly repented and confessed, however late. Then also, when his side was pierced, the sacraments by which the Church was to be formed flowed forth: the blood by which we are redeemed and the water by which we are washed.

(As cited above.)

The second reason for the institution and observance of the ninth hour is here assigned from the distinguished conversion of Cornelius the centurion. At this hour he was warned by an angel to summon Peter; instructed by Peter in the mysteries of the faith and baptized with his entire household, he consecrated the firstfruits of the calling of the Gentiles.

The third reason and prerogative of the ninth hour comes from the example of the apostles Peter and John, who are said in Acts to have gone up at the ninth hour of prayer— in Greek, ἐπὶ τὴν ὥραν τῆς προσευχῆς τὴν ἐννάτην, that is, “to the hour of prayer, which was the ninth.” This is what the repetition of the Greek article signifies: it clearly shows both that the ninth hour was consecrated to prayer and that there were other hours of prayer besides the ninth.

Hence St. Basil says in the *Longer Rules*, question 37: “That the ninth hour is necessary for us as a time of prayer, the apostles themselves demonstrated in Acts, where it says that Peter and John were going up into the temple at the ninth hour of prayer.” St. Jerome likewise says in his commentary on Daniel VI: “The Church’s tradition understands the third, sixth, and ninth hours.” And below: “At the ninth hour Peter and John were going to the temple.”]

At the ninth hour, penetrating the regions below, he extinguished the impenetrable darkness of Tartarus with the flashing of his own brightness. Breaking its bronze gates and crushing its iron bars, he carried with him safely to heaven the captivity of the saints, which had been held shut in the darkness of merciless hell; [Note: [Col. 0121C] This alludes to the passage in Genesis where, after the first parents had been expelled and excluded from paradise, God is said to have placed before the paradise of delight the Cherubim and a flaming, turning sword, to guard the way to the tree of life.

In place of “flaming sword,” St. Jerome frequently reads *flaming sword* (*romphaea flammea*). Thus, in Letter 3 to Heliodorus: “That flaming sword, the guardian of paradise, and the Cherubim presiding at its gates, have been extinguished and unlocked by Christ’s blood.” And in Letter 25: “Christ had not yet broken open the gate of paradise; his blood had not yet extinguished that flaming sword and the whirling of the Cherubim presiding there.”

Hence Abraham is said to have been in the place of refreshment, yet still among the dead. Again, in his commentary on Amos IX: “God placed the Cherubim and the flaming sword, which turns, to guard the way to the tree of life, so that the one who had been expelled from paradise might not enter it unworthily.” St. Gregory likewise says in the *Moralia*: “After the sin of the first man, a flaming sword is said to have been placed at the entrance to paradise; it is also called turning, because at some time the moment would come when it could be removed” (*Moralia*, book XII, chapter 7).

These sayings of the holy Fathers fit this passage well. Moreover, John writes in the Apocalypse, chapter II: “These things says he who has the sword sharp on both sides.” For a *romphaea* is a long sword sharpened on both sides, called in Latin a *framea*. Hence St. Jerome elsewhere reads *framea* in place of *romphaea*. He says:

> At its guardianship—namely, that of paradise—the Cherubim, that is, the multitude of knowledge, and the burning *framea* were placed, so that they might guard the way to the tree of life, lest Adam, while still in sin and not yet recognizing his transgressions, should eat from it and die the death of impenitence, despair, and pride.

(On Isaiah, chapter 65.)

Isidore says in *Etymologies*, book XVII, chapter 5:

> A *framea* is a sword sharpened on both sides, which people commonly call a *spatha*. It is also called a *romphaea*. A *framea* is so called because it is made of iron.

So he. I would rather say that the term derives from *flammea*, “flaming,” or *ignea* and *ignita*, “fiery” or “burning,” as shown above from St. Jerome and Gregory.]

And when the fiery *romphaea* had been removed, he restored the ancient inhabitant to paradise through a pious confession.

At that same hour Cornelius the centurion, persevering in prayers with his customary devotion, learned through an angel speaking with him that his prayers and almsgiving had been remembered before the Lord. At the ninth hour the mysteries of the calling of the Gentiles were openly disclosed to him, the same mysteries that had been revealed to Peter in an ecstasy of mind at the sixth hour (Acts X).

In another passage, Acts of the Apostles narrates the same time as follows: “Peter and John were going up into the temple at the ninth hour of prayer” (Acts III).

These passages clearly prove that, with good reason, these hours were consecrated by holy and apostolic men to religious observances and ought likewise to be observed by us. Unless we are compelled, as though by a law, to discharge these duties of piety at least at the appointed times, we spend the entire day, entangled in forgetfulness, idleness, or occupations, without interrupting it for prayer. [Al.: “without interpolation of prayer.”]

[Note: [Col. 0122B]

Concerning Vespers, or the office of Vespers—which here is called the vespertine sacrifices foreshadowed in the old Law—four matters are here to be noted:

1. Its antiquity, or institution approved by the Fathers.
2. The reason for this institution.
3. The time at which the vespertine office is to be celebrated.
4. The manner or form of the office.

As to the first, besides St. Clement and Basil in the passages cited above, the Council of Laodicea, held twelve hundred years ago, remembers this vespertine hour in canon 18, where it says that “supplications and prayers should always”—that is, daily—“be celebrated at None and at Vespers.”

Chrysostom, in Homily 59 *To the People of Antioch*, speaking of the daily prayers of monks, says: “They celebrate prayers at Terce, Sext, None, and Vespers; and, dividing the day into four parts, whenever each part is completed, they worship God with psalmody and hymns.”

Jerome, in his letter to Eustochium on the preservation of virginity, says: “Everyone knows the third, sixth, and ninth hours, as well as dawn and Vespers.” And in Letter 27, *On the Death of Paula*: “In order, they sang the psalter in the morning, at the third, sixth, and ninth hours, in the evening, and at midnight.” So much for antiquity.

The reason for the institution of the vespertine hour, or vespertine office, is here assigned as threefold. The first is for the memory and imitation of the evening sacrifice of the ancient Law, which foreshadowed the sacraments and mysteries of the new Law.

Isidore says in book I, chapter 20, of *On the Ecclesiastical Offices*:

> The vespertine office is the conclusion of the day; it is the setting of the day and of the alternating light, and its solemn celebration comes from the Old Testament. For it was customary at this time to offer the sacrifices of the ancients and to burn spices and incense upon the altar. The witness to this is that royal singer who had exercised a priestly office, saying: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight; the lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Psalm CXL).

Rabanus repeats the same words in book II, chapter 7, of *On the Institution of the Clergy*.

It should further be noted that in the old Law there were two evening sacrifices, and both were daily: one bloody, namely the sacrifice of an unblemished lamb, discussed in Exodus XXIX; the other bloodless, namely the offering of incense upon the golden altar, discussed in Exodus XXX and Numbers XXVIII. The Psalmist referred to the latter in the verse just quoted, and Isidore followed him.

But why does the prophet wish his prayer to be like the evening sacrifice rather than the morning sacrifice, when both the offering of incense and the slaughter of the lamb took place morning and evening—hence it is also said here that morning and evening sacrifices were offered every day? Bellarmine gives the reason: either David sang this psalm in the evening, just as the Church also customarily sings the same psalm at Vespers; or the evening sacrifice was nobler because it was a figure of the sacrifice of the Cross, which took place in the evening.

The second reason why the Church honors the evening hour of prayer is here suggested: namely, the memory of the Lord’s Supper, which our Lord Jesus Christ celebrated in the evening with the holy apostles, wondrously making his flesh from bread and his blood from wine and instituting it as the Church’s perpetual and solemn sacrifice.

Hence Isidore, in the passage cited above:

> In the New Testament also, in the evening, while the Apostles were dining, the Lord and Savior handed over the mystery of his body and blood, so that the very time might indicate the evening sacrifice of the age.

The third reason, finally, is the memory and remembrance of the bloody sacrifice—that is, of the Lord’s Passion—which, as is said here, took place on the following day toward evening. In it the Lord Jesus, the supreme priest and also the true unblemished lamb, offered himself to God the Father as a propitiation for our sins. He also hung upon the cross until evening, at which hour he was taken down from the cross, as the gloss notes in chapter I of *On the Celebration of Mass*.

In the office of the Cross the Church sings: “In the evening hour he is taken down from the cross.”

St. Gregory Nazianzen, in Oration 42, *On Easter*, referring to both sacrifices, says:

> At the end of the ages Christ’s Passion took place; in the evening also, dispersing the darkness of sin, he imparted the Sacrament to the disciples.

Isidore adds above:

> Therefore, in honor and memory of such great mysteries, it is fitting that at these times we should appear before God’s presence and resound in his worship, offering him the sacrifice of our prayers and rejoicing together in his praises.

There is considerable controversy, however, concerning the canonical or proper time of Vespers—that is, at what hour Vespers ought to be sung. Among others, John Durandus should be consulted, for he has written about these matters carefully (*On the Rites of the Church*, book III).

The common opinion is that the vespertine office should be celebrated before sunset, as the Roman Church has been accustomed to celebrate it. This can be proved both by authority and antiquity and by reason.

By authority, first, there is blessed Chrysostom, who in the passage cited above writes that monks divide the day into four parts and celebrate Vespers—the praises of Vespers—in the fourth and final part of the day. This final part is not the indivisible endpoint of the day, namely sunset itself, but a span of three hours, from the ninth hour—which for us is three o’clock in the afternoon—until the end of the twelfth hour and sunset, according to the ancient division of the day, just as the other parts likewise consisted of three hours, as has often been said.

Therefore, the entire three-hour span after None, or the ninth hour, that is, after three o’clock, up to the setting of the sun, is the ancient and canonical time of Vespers.

There is also Theodoret, who in *The History of the Holy Fathers*, chapter 2, writing about Julian and his companions, says: “Before sunset they all assembled in the atrium and together offered evening hymns to the Lord.”

Finally, to omit others, there is our Cassian, who in this book, and particularly in this chapter on the Daytime Hours—or, as the title has it, *On the Canonical Manner of the Daytime Hours*—treating the matter expressly, includes Vespers among them, as does St. Benedict in chapter 16 of the Rule, where he recalls the seven daytime hours, or daytime offices.

Now, as regards the reason or form of the vespertine office, which was the fourth point under consideration, one must first remember what the author reported in the preceding book (book II, chapters 4 and 5): namely, that the singing of twelve psalms at Vespers was instituted among the Egyptian Fathers not by human invention but through angelic instruction from heaven. The Council of Tours, held a thousand years ago, also remembers this institution (chapter 19).

Why, then, did St. Benedict and others prescribe not twelve but far fewer psalms—perhaps only four or five—in the vespertine office? We noted the reason in that same place (book II, chapter 6): Compline was later instituted and added to the canonical hours in place of, and as a kind of compensation for, that number, as Radulphus of Tongeren notes in *On Canonical Observances*, proposition 14, with Bellarmine’s approval.

Second, St. Benedict’s constitution concerning the office of Vespers should be noted. He says:

> The vespertine assembly is to conclude with four psalms and antiphons. After those psalms, a reading is to be recited. Then the responsory, the Ambrosian hymn, the verse, the Gospel canticle, the litany, the Lord’s Prayer, and let the *missae* be made.

(Chapter 17 of the Rule.)

In the following chapter he says: “Every day Vespers is to be sung with the modulation of four psalms,” and so forth.

These passages expressly enumerate the parts of the vespertine office: four psalms; the Reading, that is, the chapter; the responsory, whether short or long; the Ambrosian hymn, that is, a hymn composed by Ambrose or by another in imitation of Ambrose—for this, see Radulphus of Tongeren, propositions 13 and 14; the verse, that is, the short versicle sung after the hymn; the Gospel canticle, that is, the canticle of blessed Mary, the *Magnificat*, which is contained in the Gospel (Luke VIII); the litany, that is, “Kyrie eleison”; and the Lord’s Prayer, “Our Father.”

Finally, “let the prayers be said”—that is, according to Turrecremata, the Collects.

Smaragdus adds:

> What he says elsewhere, “And it is completed,” he expresses in this clause, “And let the prayers be said.” For the prayers of the office, which have been completed by us, have been sent to God, since they have been celebrated in his honor. In another sense, the prayers or Collects said by the priest at the end of the service are called *missae*, that is, “sent” or “transmitted” to God. They are sent by the priest but received by God. Hence the Levites—that is, the deacons—when some solemnity has been celebrated in the Church, cry out to the people in a raised voice: “Go, the dismissal is made”—that is, “The solemnity is completed, and through the ministry of the priest it has now been sent to God.”

So he.

Third, the difference between secular clergy and religious, especially Benedictines, should be observed regarding the number of psalms at Vespers. This difference also concerns moral instruction. John Beleth, the abridger of Durandus, explains it as follows:

> At Vespers we sing five psalms, because we are imperfect, on account of the five senses, so that what has been committed through the five bodily senses may be completely forgiven through the singing of five psalms. Monks, however, show themselves more perfect in that they say only four. For whatever is square remains the same, firm, and solid, no matter in which direction it is turned. In the same way, the perfect person remains always the same and unmoved, wherever or whenever he may be.

So he.

Thus far concerning Vespers—indeed at considerable length, but necessarily so in proportion to the subject, since the entire rationale and understanding of the ecclesiastical office, or canonical Hours, depends upon it. I therefore trust that this extended treatment will not prove burdensome to the reader.]

What, then, is to be said about the evening sacrifices, which the Mosaic Law also sanctions as being offered continually in the Old Testament? For we can prove from the fact that morning holocausts and evening sacrifices were offered every day in the Temple without ceasing, even though with figurative victims (Num. 28), that David sings:

> Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight;  
> the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice (Ps. 140).

In this passage, a more sacred interpretation may also be understood of that true evening sacrifice which was either handed over by the Lord and Savior in the evening, while the apostles were dining, when he inaugurated the Church’s most holy mysteries; or that sacrifice in which he himself was offered to the Father on the following day—namely, as the evening sacrifice at the end of the ages—by the lifting up of his hands, for the salvation of the whole world. The extension of his hands upon the cross is very appropriately called a lifting up. For he lifted all of us, who were lying in hell, up to heaven, in accordance with the statement of his promise:

> And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself (John 14).

[Note: [Col. 0125B] Immediately after the office of Vespers, the Matutinal solemnity, or Matutinal office, is incidentally mentioned here; by this name Lauds are understood in this passage. For most of the ancients call these Matins, or the Matutinal Office, and count them among the daytime hours. Radulphus of Tongeren, proposition 14, explains their close affinity and analogy with the office of Vespers in this way:

“Vigils are canonical hours in themselves, having no equality with the others. But Lauds and Vespers have equality with each other; likewise Prime and Compline with each other; and Terce, Sext, and None with each other. They have an equal and similar order and manner of performing the office.”

That Lauds and Vespers ought to be performed in the same manner is established by two canons found in the Decrees, distinction 12, final chapter, and in the section On Consecration, distinction 5, chapter *Convenit*. The first is from the Council of Braga, which says:

“It has pleased all by common consent that one and the same order of psalmody be maintained in the Matutinal and Evening offices, and that neither diverse private customs nor monastic usages be mingled with the rule of the Church.”

There, the Matutinal office means what we call Lauds. Therefore, the order of psalmody ought to be the same in both, because both begin in the same way. In both there are five psalms, and in both these ought to have five antiphons. In both are said the chapter, hymn, verse, Canticle with antiphons, and prayer or collect with similar commemorations.

He speaks of monastic custom because in the Benedictine office there are five psalms at Lauds but only four at Vespers. Lauds also begin with the *psalmus directus* [direct psalm]; otherwise the offices are performed equally.

The second is from the Council of Agde, which says:

“It is fitting that the order of the Church be observed equally by all. Therefore it must be established that, just as everywhere after the antiphons the collations are said by bishops or priests, and morning or evening hymns are sung every day, and at the conclusion of Matins and Masses the chapters are said after the hymns, so the people, after the prayer has been completed, are dismissed at evening by the bishop with a blessing.”

Thus far the council. And “after the antiphons,” says Radulphus, means after the psalms recited antiphonally at Lauds and Vespers; “collations” means the readings that we call chapters.

Thus far Radulphus, a learned and careful man. That this text of ours concerns the Matutinal solemnity which we call Lauds is clear from the fact that it says that the following psalm is customarily sung daily at it:

> My God, to you I keep vigil from the dawn,

a psalm commonly sung at Lauds in the solemn or festal office, as is well known.]

The Matutinal solemnity also instructs us through the fact that the following passages are customarily sung daily at it:

> O God, my God, to you I keep vigil from the dawn (Ps. 62).

And:

> In the morning I will meditate on you (ibid.).

And:

> I anticipated the dawn and cried out (Ps. 118).

And again:

> My eyes have anticipated you at dawn, that I might meditate on your words (ibid.).

It was also at these hours that the evangelical householder hired laborers for his vineyard (Matt. 20). For he too is described as having hired them first thing in the morning; this time indicates our Matutinal solemnity. Then came the third hour, thereafter the sixth, after that the ninth, and finally the eleventh, in which the candle-light [alternative reading: *lucernaris*] hour is marked.

[Note: [Col. 0125D] According to Dionysius’s paraphrase, the *lucernaris hora* [candle-light hour] is understood as the evening hour, which is designated in Matthew by the eleventh hour. As was said, the ancients divided the entire day, from sunrise to sunset, into twelve equal parts, which they called hours, just as Christ says in John, chapter 11: “Are there not twelve hours of the day?” These hours were equal on a given day, but unequal on different days—that is, longer or shorter—as all days are unequal among themselves, and still more so at different seasons of the year, for example in summer and winter.

Thus the first hour was the first after sunrise; the second was the second after the same sunrise, and so on. “The last hour of the day was consequently the twelfth, with which the eleventh, already completed, coincides”; this is how the eleventh hour is understood in Matthew. For it is plainly inferred from the words “These last have worked one hour” that those laborers began to work after the eleventh hour had elapsed and worked until the end of the twelfth.

Cassian compares the Evening office with the work of those who were called into the vineyard at the eleventh hour. Therefore, according to this reckoning of the hours from sunrise, the evening hour, or the hour of the Evening office, is the twelfth hour as it begins or is in progress, as has been said, or the eleventh hour already completed, designated in that passage of Matthew.

It is also called the candle-light hour because candles were then lit, specifically for the Evening office, when the light of day was failing, especially in darker places such as oratories. Hence the Evening office itself, or part of it, is at times called by the Fathers the office of the candles.

Concerning this, St. Basil writes to Amphilochius, chapter 29:

“It seemed good to our Fathers not to receive the benefit of the evening light in silence, but, as soon as it appeared, to give thanks.”

“But who was the author of the thanksgiving at the candle-light hour, we cannot say.” Thus Basil, implying that this custom was received and observed from no other source than apostolic tradition.

St. Chrysostom likewise writes concerning Psalm 118:

“At sunset, which we also call the candle-light hour, one ought to pray, because then we give thanks to God for the passing of the day.”

St. Epiphanius calls those psalms “candle-light psalms” which were customarily sung after sunset (*Compendium of Doctrine*, book 3, at the end).

St. Jerome likewise writes in his letter to Laeta, among other instructions concerning the education of a little girl who was to be dedicated to God:

“Let her become accustomed, when the lamp has been lit, to offer the evening sacrifice.”

Finally, Isidore says in chapter 6 of his *Rule for Monks*:

“At the Evening offices, first the Candle-light office, then two psalms, one responsory, and Lauds, a hymn, and a prayer are to be said.”

From these testimonies of the holy Fathers we conclude that the Candle-light office belongs to our Vespers and was so called from the lighting of the candles. But enough of this, which has been discussed only incidentally because of the candle-light hour.]

**CHAPTER IV. That the Matutinal solemnity, which we call the solemnity of Prime, was not established by ancient tradition but invented in our own time**

It must nevertheless be understood that this Matutinal office, which is now observed especially in the western regions, was first established in our own time as a canonical function in our own monastery, where our Lord Jesus Christ was born of the Virgin and graciously accepted the growth of human infancy; there, by his grace, he also strengthened our own infancy—still tender and nursing—in religious life.

[Note: [Col. 0126D] Concerning the Matutinal solemnity which we now call Prime, it may reasonably be doubted whether it is as ancient as, and of the same institution as, the other hours or ecclesiastical offices. For Cassian explicitly teaches in this passage that this Matutinal office, which is observed chiefly in the regions of the West, was first established in his own time and, apparently, in his own monastery at Bethlehem, before he migrated from there to Marseilles in the province of Gaul.

Hence, in chapter 6 of the same book, he calls it a new institution and solemnity. And whenever he discusses the daytime offices and solemnities of monks, he names only Terce, Sext, and None, omitting Prime, as can be seen in book 2, chapter 2, and in this book, chapter 1, and elsewhere.

Nor do St. Basil, Chrysostom, Jerome, or any others earlier than Cassian mention Prime, although they often mention the other hours, as Cardinal Bellarmine observes in book 1, *On Good Works*, chapter 11.

For this reason Radulphus of Tongeren writes that Prime and Compline were added after the institution of the other hours. In proposition 14 he says:

“The holy Fathers observed five hours through psalmody: namely, the Vigils of the night, Vespers, Terce, Sext, and None. Then, because Scripture frequently joins morning and evening, Matutinal praise was added. It was also established by many bishops that clergy and people should pour out prayers and supplications to God morning and evening, together with the *Pater Noster* and the Creed. Therefore two other Hours, Prime and Compline, were introduced for this purpose, each with prayers, the Lord’s Prayer, and the Creed.”

Thus he writes (*Radulphus of Tongeren, On Canonical Observance*, proposition 14).

Durandus, however, argues against this opinion (*On the Rites of the Church*, book 3, chapter 7). First, he cites St. Clement, whose words are these in book 8, chapter 40, of the *Apostolic Constitutions*:

“Offer your prayers at dawn, at the third hour, the sixth, the ninth, in the evening, and at cockcrow; at dawn giving thanks because the Lord has enlightened us, having driven away the night and brought in the day.”

Second, he cites St. Athanasius, in his book *On Virginity*, where he says:

“At sunrise let the book be seen in your hands after Terce,” and so forth.

Third, he cites St. Basil, *Longer Rules*, question 37:

“For this reason these times have necessarily been selected by us, because in each of them a particular remembrance of God’s benefits toward us occurs. At Matins, therefore, let the first movements of our soul and mind be consecrated to God, and let us not admit concern for any matter before we have delighted ourselves in the thought of God, as it is written: ‘I remembered God, and I was delighted’ (Ps. 76). Nor should we move the body to perform any task before doing what is said: ‘To you, Lord, I shall pray; in the morning you will hear my voice; in the morning I shall stand before you’ (Ps. 5),” and so forth.

Fourth, he cites St. Jerome, letter 7 to Laeta:

“Let her become accustomed, following this example, to rise at night for prayers and psalms, to sing hymns in the morning, and at the third, sixth, and ninth hours,” and so forth.

There Victorius interprets “in the morning” as the hour of Prime.

But, with due respect to Victorius and Durandus, those testimonies of the holy Fathers do not seem so clear and explicit that they compel us to depart from Cassian’s opinion, which has also been approved by the judgment of others, or to withdraw confidence from it, since he says so explicitly that the office of Prime was first established in his own time.

For the Fathers cited are not speaking of the Prime now under discussion, but of the Matutinal solemnity—that is, of Lauds—which used to be sung at dawn and in the morning, or in the early morning, that is, at daybreak and before sunrise, as has been said.

Moreover, if Cassian is examined more carefully, he distinguished two, or a double, Matutinal solemnity, and included both Lauds and Prime under the name Matutinal. One was before sunrise, at cockcrow; the other after the sun had already risen (Azorius, *Moral Institutions*, book 10, chapter 2, question 6).

He says that the other Matutinal office was instituted and observed from ancient times: it was completed together with the nocturnal psalms and prayers, that is, it was celebrated immediately after the end of the nocturnal office, at dawn. This is what we commonly call Lauds. It is clear that these were formerly performed at first light and before sunrise from their weekday hymns.

Concerning this Matutinal office he writes at the end of the preceding chapter, where he says that the following psalm is customarily sung in it every day:

> O God, my God, to you I keep vigil from the dawn;

and:

> In the morning I will meditate on you.

The other Matutinal office, which he discusses in this chapter, was recently introduced in his own time and in the monastery just mentioned, in order to awaken or shake off the sluggishness and sleepiness of certain people who, after completing the nocturnal Vigils and morning Lauds, returned to bed and indulged in sleep for too long; for they had no other office or assembly to attend before Terce, as is stated here.]

Until that time, we find that, once the Matutinal solemnity—which in the monasteries of Gaul is customarily celebrated after the nocturnal psalms and prayers have been completed, following a short interval—had been completed along with the daily Vigils, the remaining hours were assigned by our elders to bodily refreshment.

But when some abused this indulgence and prolonged the postponement of sleep—for nothing requiring them to leave their cells or rise from their beds before Terce summoned them to any assembly—and when, to the detriment of their work, they became sluggish through excessive sleep at a time of day when they ought to have been engaged in certain duties, especially on those days when more burdensome weariness arose from their keeping watch from the evening hours until near dawn, the complaint of certain brothers fervent in spirit, who were far from indifferent to this kind of negligence, was brought before the elders.

After lengthy discussion and careful deliberation, they decreed that, until sunrise—when, without inconvenience, either a reading could be prepared or manual labor undertaken—the exhausted bodies should be allowed refreshment; after that, all alike, summoned by the observance of this religious practice, should rise from their beds. Once three psalms and prayers had been celebrated, according to the pattern established in antiquity for the observance of Terce or Sext, on the model of a threefold confession, they were to bring sleep to an end and begin their work, both in equal measure and with moderation.

Although this pattern may appear to have been devised incidentally and established recently for the reason we have mentioned, it nevertheless supplies, in the literal sense, the number designated by blessed David, although it also possesses a spiritual meaning:

> Seven times a day I have praised you for the judgments of your justice (Ps. 118).

[Note: [Col. 0129A] St. Basil, *Homily 11 on the Hexaemeron*; Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 94; Jerome on Amos, chapter 5; Augustine, book 11 of *The City of God*, chapter 31; and Gregory, book 1 of the *Moralia*, chapters 11 and 12, and book 35, chapters 6 and 7, discuss the spiritual or mystical meaning of the number seven (see Navarrus, *Commentary on Prayer and the Canonical Hours*, chapter 5).

However, we may also understand “spiritual meaning” in the figurative sense, namely, that a definite number is taken for an indefinite one. This is frequent in Scripture: “seven times a day” means the same as “often,” “daily,” or “frequently,” as we indicated above. In the same way the statement “His praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. 33) is explained, because seven is the number of fullness and totality, as the same Fathers explain (see below, book 8, chapter 12).

St. Augustine says in the passage cited:

“The whole of the odd numbers is represented by three, and the whole of the even numbers by four, from which the number seven is composed. Therefore it is often used for the whole, as in: ‘The righteous man falls seven times and rises again’—that is, however often he falls, he will not perish.”

He wished this to be understood not of sins but of tribulations leading to humility. Likewise, “Seven times a day I shall praise you” is said elsewhere in another form: “His praise shall always be in my mouth.”

Many such examples are found in the divine authorities, in which the number seven is customarily used for the totality of any matter.]

This number, although it also has a spiritual meaning, is nevertheless most plainly supplied according to the literal sense:

> Seven times a day I have praised you for the judgments of your justice (Ps. 118).

[Note: [Col. 0129C] This praise and example of the Psalmist especially establish and commend those solemn prayers and divine praises instituted in the Church, which we call the canonical hours. Although in that verse the number seven signifies nothing other than the frequent repetition of divine praise—as “seven times a day” is understood in the same way as the frequent falling mentioned in Proverbs 24, “The righteous man falls seven times”—the Church nevertheless appears not without reason to have established the use of the canonical hours from this passage.

For when she wished her children to praise God as frequently as that devout and holy king had done, she appropriately designated seven hours during which clerics, or ecclesiastical persons, should devote themselves to divine praises, both for a more exact imitation of that example and because of the perfection and mystical significance of the number seven, discussed below.

Hence St. Ambrose, book 7 on Luke, commenting on chapter 11, “Which of you shall have a friend?” says:

“If that David—so holy a man, and one occupied with the responsibilities of kingship—praised the Lord seven times a day, always attentive to the morning and evening sacrifices, what ought we to do, who must pray all the more because we sin more frequently through the frailty of body and mind?”

Thus Ambrose (see Basil, *Sermon 1 on the Institution of Monastic Life*).

There are, however, two opinions concerning this number of seven canonical hours. Some, and nearly all of the more ancient writers, include in this number only the daytime hours, that is, those customarily celebrated or recited during the day: Matins, or morning Lauds; Prime; Terce; Sext; None; Vespers; and Compline.

They separate Vigils, or the nocturnal office—which we improperly call Matins—from this number and place it separately, because they understand the artificial day to be signified in that verse. This day begins at dawn—called by the French *aube du jour*, as if “the whitening of the day”—and ends as night approaches.

Cassian undoubtedly understood the number in this way. In this book he treats of the daytime offices, just as in the preceding book he treated of the nocturnal offices, as he himself states. Hence, in the preceding chapter he first lists the three hours that were then more commonly celebrated, namely Terce, Sext, and None; then he adds the evening sacrifice, that is, the office of Vespers; and finally he mentions the Matutinal office, at which the psalm is sung:

> O God, my God, to you I keep vigil from the dawn,

which takes place at Lauds.

Since, therefore, he counts six daytime hours, and says in this chapter that another Matutinal solemnity—that is, Prime—was added to them, so that the number seven designated by the Psalmist might be completed properly and according to the literal sense, it follows that he placed the Vigils, or nocturnal offices, outside this number.

But St. Benedict refers this number much more clearly and explicitly to the daytime offices alone in chapter 16 of the Rule, whose title is “How the Divine Offices Are to Be Performed during the Day.” Corresponding to this title, he says:

“As the Prophet says, ‘Seven times a day I have praised you.’ We shall fulfill this sacred number of seven if we perform the offices of our service at the times of Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline. For concerning these daytime hours the Prophet says, ‘Seven times a day I have praised you.’ But concerning the nocturnal Vigils the same Prophet says, ‘At midnight I rose to give thanks to you.’ Therefore at these times let us offer praises to our Creator for the judgments of his justice: at Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline; and at night let us rise to give thanks to him.”

Thus St. Benedict. These words are cited verbatim from the Council of Agde, book 3 of the Decretals, title *On the Celebration of Masses*, chapter 1.

According to this interpretation, it must be admitted that there are eight canonical hours. One nocturnal hour is commended by the verse, “At midnight I rose,” and seven other daytime hours are designated by the other verse, “Seven times a day I have praised you”—namely, during the artificial day, as it is called.

Others, however, think that both the nocturnal and daytime offices are included in the number seven. They therefore maintain that the natural day is signified, and that the nocturnal office, or nocturnal Vigils, is counted together with Lauds as one hour (Bede, *On the Meditation of the Passion of Christ*; Isidore, book 1, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*; Rabanus, book 2, *On the Institution of Clergy*; Rupert, book 1, *On the Daytime Office*; Gloss on chapter 1, *On the Celebration of Mass*).

According to this interpretation, Turrecremata says, all the canonical hours are reduced to the number seven, which is a sacred number. Thus David’s statement, “Seven times a day I have praised you,” is understood of the natural day: one praise occurs during the artificial night, and the other six during the day belonging to that night—namely, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, the eleventh hour, which is Vespers, and the twelfth hour, which is Compline.

Thus he writes, alluding to that passage of Matthew 20 mentioned above.

The resolution of this difficulty depends on the question whether the nocturnal offices are separated from morning Lauds. For if we separate the nocturnal offices from Lauds, there are undoubtedly more than seven canonical hours. But if we join the nocturnal offices to Lauds, there are only seven.

Therefore, following Durandus, I think the times must be distinguished. For there was a variety of ecclesiastical custom concerning the nocturnal offices (Radulphus of Tongeren, proposition 14, *On Canonical Observance*; Durandus, *On the Rites of the Church*, book 3, chapter 3; Bellarmine, book 1, *On Good Works*, chapter 11).

In some places among the ancients, three nocturnal offices were celebrated at three distinct hours, that is, during the three watches of the night. Hence St. Jerome says in his letter to Eustochium (letter 22):

“One must rise two or three times during the night.”

Rupert, book 1, *On the Divine Offices*, and St. Thomas, lecture 6 on chapter 14 of the First Epistle to the Corinthians, report more explicitly that this custom was observed in ancient times by some.

Elsewhere all the nocturnal offices were customarily celebrated together, but especially at midnight, in accordance with the verse:

> At midnight I rose to give thanks to you (Ps. 118).

For the holy Fathers cited above prescribe this time.

Finally, elsewhere the nocturnal offices are joined with morning Lauds and celebrated in the fourth watch, which is also called Matins.

That this was the ancient custom of the Roman Church is testified by Amalarius in the preface to his book *On the Order of the Antiphonary*. Among other things, he reports that he asked the teachers of the Roman Church whether there ought to be any interval between the nocturnal office and the Matutinal office, that is, Lauds; and the answer was that there should be none, but that Lauds should be begun immediately with the verse:

> O God, come to my assistance.

Those, therefore, who recited the nocturnal offices separately at midnight, or pronounced each nocturnal office separately in the three watches of the night, after the manner of military watches, certainly had more than seven canonical hours.

Whereas, when the nocturnal offices began to be recited together and continuously—as is now done almost everywhere—so that the nocturnal office and Nocturns include Lauds, there are only seven canonical hours.

In this way the statements brought forward on both sides by different authorities can be reconciled.]

For with this solemnity added, we are undoubtedly shown to say the Lord’s praises seven times a day by holding these spiritual assemblies seven times a day.

Finally, since this pattern, proceeding from the East, has thus far been propagated with great benefit, it appears not to have been admitted in certain very ancient monasteries of the East, which by no means allow the most ancient rules of the Fathers to be violated.

**CHAPTER V. That after the Matutinal prayers one ought not to return to sleep**

Since some, being ignorant of the reason why this solemnity was established or introduced in this province, [Note: [Col. 0131C]

What he taught in the preceding book (chapters 12 and 13), by the example of the ancient monks and with the strongest arguments, was that monks striving for perfection ought not, after the night Mass—that is, the night office—to return to bed or indulge in sleep, but should rather devote themselves to prayer and meditation and keep watch. He now teaches that this must be observed much more strictly after the morning Lauds. Accordingly, he censures and reproves those who, once the morning hymns—that is, Lauds—have been completed, return again to sleep, and who therefore hasten to finish Lauds so early and prematurely that, once they have been completed, they may again have the opportunity to sleep. The blessed Benedict also appears to have adopted this institution. For in chapter 8 of the Rule he decrees that, in winter—from the Kalends of November until Easter—according to a reasonable calculation, they are to rise at the eighth hour of the night, so that they may rest a little longer than half the night and rise when digestion is complete. The time that remains after the Vigils is to be devoted to meditation by those brothers who need to read or study something from the Psalter or the lessons.

[Col. 0131D]

From Easter until the aforementioned Kalends of November, however, the time for celebrating the Vigils is to be so regulated that, after the briefest possible interval—during which the brothers may go out for the necessities of nature—Matins, which are to be celebrated at daybreak, immediately follow.

In explaining and elucidating this chapter, which is by no means easy and is known to few, it will not be irrelevant to linger here for a while, as the opportunity and our purpose permit, and to examine and explain each of its parts somewhat more attentively and precisely.

First observe that, concerning the celebration of the Vigils, or nocturnal office, the holy Father established a double arrangement, corresponding to the two divisions into which he divided the entire year: namely, from the Kalends of November until Easter, and from Easter until the Kalends of November. But for the celebration of Lauds he establishes only one arrangement: namely, that they are regularly to be celebrated at the beginning of daylight—that is, at dawn or the twilight of day—in both winter and summer.

During the former period, winter, he advises that they should rise at the eighth hour of the night, so that they may rest a little longer than half the night, and so forth. But the question arises: how is this eighth hour to be understood, since not all nights are equal, indeed since all are unequal, just as the days are?

Turrecremata replies that, when the holy Father says that they are to rise at the eighth hour so that they may rest a little longer than half the night, he plainly indicates that the eighth hour is after midnight; consequently, it must not be understood according to the sequence of the nocturnal hours of each particular month, but according to their proportion to the time of the Kalends of November. This, he says, is what the holy Father means by “according to a reasonable calculation,” namely, one derived from the Kalends of November. Thus far Turrecremata.

Yet these matters are more obscure than can readily be made clear and satisfactory to everyone. It must therefore be noted that unequal hours are being discussed here, and that the meaning of this passage must be derived from them.

An unequal hour is one-twelfth of the artificial day or night. For, as was said above, in former times every artificial day and every night was divided into twelve equal portions, which writers call unequal and ancient hours. They are called ancient because their use existed among all the ancients. They are called unequal—not because the hours of a single day or night were unequal among themselves, for that would be false, since we have said that every day and night was divided into twelve equal parts—but because, since artificial days and nights are unequal except at the equinoxes, the hours of a longer day or night are longer than those of a shorter day or night.

For just as the nights are longer in winter, so their parts, that is, their twelve hours, must also be longer than in summer; and conversely, the longer the daytime hours are in summer, the shorter the nocturnal hours are.

The Jews used these unequal hours, as is clear from the sacred Scriptures; so did the Romans, the Italians, and nearly all antiquity, as both histories and the books of mathematicians testify. (See here Smaragdus’s Commentary.)

D. Benedict therefore understands “the eighth hour of the night” to mean the hour which, when the nocturnal hours are counted from sunset to sunrise, is numbered eighth at whatever season it may be, and which therefore falls in the second or third hour after midnight—whether those hours are longer, as in winter, or shorter, as in summer. (At the end of chapter 16 of the Rule.)

Here, however, another objection arises, which the same Turrecremata raises elsewhere. “It seems,” he says, “that the statement, ‘At midnight I rose’ [Col. 0132D] (Psalm 118), and so forth, contradicts what is said in chapter 8: that in winter they are to rise for the Vigils at the eighth hour, so that they may rest a little longer than half the night.”

The answer is that “middle” is said in two ways: either with equal distance from the extremities, or by being situated between the extremities. In the Prophet’s statement, “the middle of the night” means the middle by being situated between the extreme parts of the night. According to this meaning of “middle,” when one rises at the eighth hour, one rises at midnight.

So far Turrecremata. St. Thomas supports this interpretation in the Third Part, question 51, article 4, where, explaining the words of Gregory—who says in Homily 21 on the Gospel that Christ rose at midnight—he says: “Not indeed in a night divided into two equal parts, but within the night. For that dawn,” he says, “may be called both part of the night and part of the day, because of the likeness it has to each.” Thus St. Thomas.

Explaining why the blessed Benedict allows so much time for rest—that is, for repose and sleep—he says: “so that, having digested,” that is, with the food already digested and discharged, and having become lighter because freed from the burden of food, they may rise watchful and alert to perform the divine office devoutly, in accordance with the saying of D. Jerome (Epistle 4): “When you rise at night for prayer, let not indigestion produce a belch, but emptiness.”

He continues: “The time that remains after the Vigils”—that is, after the nocturnal office—“is to be devoted by those brothers who need something from the Psalter or the lessons,” that is, who need to read, investigate, or prepare something from the Psalter or the lessons. Turrecremata says that this time is to be devoted to meditation, that is, spent in it.

Here Abbot Smaragdus, the commentator on the Rule, says:

“He does not command them here to sleep, as some wish, but to keep watch; not indeed to rest in bed, but to devote themselves to meditation. For it is written: ‘On my bed I sought him, but I did not find him’ (Song of Songs 3). For Christ the beloved is not found in the bed of carnal pleasures, but in holy labors, sacred watchings, and frequent prayers; he is not found in the torpor of sleep, but in the prayer of watchfulness and in the compunction of prayer.”

Thus Smaragdus, who then cites the passage of Cassian that we are presently discussing.

St. Hildegard also agrees in her explanation of the Rule. From the words already quoted she infers:

“It must be noted that both in summer and in winter—that is, whether there are three lessons or only one—the brothers did not return to bed for rest either after the nocturnal office or after Matins. Rather, in both seasons they so regulated the nocturnal watch after midnight that, while already singing Lauds, they saw the coming day. Because this was a properly arranged regulation, they were not burdened by it but rejoiced. For, after resting for more than half the night and then being roused, a person who subsequently remains awake is not weakened in his strength by these vigils, as has been said.”

Thus far Hildegard.

As for the other part of the year, namely summer, which our D. Benedict extends from Easter until the aforementioned Kalends of November, he establishes that the time for celebrating the Vigils is to be regulated—that is, accelerated or delayed according to the season—so that, after the briefest possible interval, during which the brothers may go out for the necessities of nature, Matins, that is, the morning Lauds, may follow at daybreak.

By these words he seems to imply that, because the summer nights are short, not only is the nocturnal office itself to be shortened, as is done, but also the interval of time that remained after the nocturnal office had been completed, until Lauds began at daybreak.

From this we learn, first, that in ancient times, by an old institution and also according to the Rule of D. Benedict, Lauds were separated from the nocturnal office by an interval of time, and may still be separated from it—especially in private office—since they are distinct hours and distinct offices, as was said above. Hence the nocturnal Vigils are counted among the nocturnal hours, while Lauds are morning and daytime offices and are counted among the daytime hours. (Durandus, book V of the *Rationale*, chapters 3 and 4; Radulphus, *De canonica observantia*, proposition 14; Navarrus, *De oratione*, chapter 34.)

Second, it follows that the rite and custom we now follow—rising for the nocturnal office, or Matins as we call it, before midnight—is not regular, that is, not conformable or consistent with our Rule. Nevertheless it is not for that reason to be condemned, since such accidental matters are easily changed according to differences of times, places, and persons.

This is especially so because the practice seems to have arisen for two prudent reasons. First, because of the lengthening or increase of the divine office, especially of the lessons, antiphons, and so forth, with the additional offices of the Blessed Virgin and of the dead, as well as the many appendices and additions of psalms, prayers, and commemorations newly established over the course of time. To complete these more conveniently and healthfully, especially on more solemn days, it seemed preferable to rise for the nocturnal office earlier than midnight.

Second, this diversity and variation has the consequence that God is praised continually and at every hour, both nocturnal and diurnal, and that no part of the night is empty of divine praise, since different people have chosen different parts and watches of the night for themselves, without entirely omitting any of them. For many at the present time who recite the office privately observe the first watch of the night; religious men generally occupy the second and third; the fourth is commonly occupied by cathedral and collegiate churches. Thus, if not by the same persons, certainly by different servants of God, divine praises are celebrated during each of the nocturnal watches, as Thomas Waldensis observed in book 38 of *The Sacramentals*, chapter 24. See Navarrus, *De oratione*, chapters 3 and 4.]

Once they have completed the morning hymns, they return again to sleep, thereby falling into the very fault for the suppression of which this solemn observance was instituted by our elders. For they hasten to complete it at an hour that gives the more negligent and less watchful an opportunity to sleep again.

This must by no means be done, as we explained more fully in the preceding little book when describing the Egyptian synaxis, lest the purification acquired through humble confession and prayers before dawn be polluted either by some arising excess of natural humors, corrupted by the enemy’s deception, or interrupted by the intervening refreshment even of pure and simple sleep, which breaks the fervor of our spirit and, making us lukewarm through the torpor of sleep, thereafter carries us inactive and sluggish through the whole day.

To avoid this, the Egyptians, although they habitually rise at fixed times even before cockcrow, once the canonical office has been celebrated, extend their Vigils until daylight.

[Note: [Col. 0134C] That is, after the morning office, or nocturnal office, has been completed and the brothers have been dismissed, as was said above.]

[Note: [Col. 0134C] That is, they continue in prayer and meditation while still keeping watch. Concerning these voluntary vigils and their many benefits, especially for the preservation of chastity, which is also commended here, several testimonies of the holy Fathers agreeing with this passage should be noted.

St. Hilary, on Psalm 118, “I remembered your name in the night, O Lord”: The Prophet knows that at night we must remember the divine name; he knows that then above all we must retain the observance of God’s law, when impure desires creep into the mind, when the goads of vice agitate the body after recently consumed food. Then the name of God must be remembered; then his law must be kept, establishing chastity, continence, and the fear of God. He knows that at this time especially the Lord must be prayed to, entreated, and won over, saying elsewhere: “Every night I wash my bed.” The mind must not be relaxed in the dangerous leisure of nocturnal wakefulness, but must be occupied with prayers, entreaties, and confessions of sins, so that when the body’s vices are given the greatest opportunity, those same vices may then especially be broken by remembrance of the divine law.

St. Ambrose, on the same verse of the Psalm: When bodies are heated by sleep and food, the vigor of the mind is also loosened by drowsiness and relaxed by sleep. Then the desire for impure intercourse creeps in; then the mind is disturbed and does not shrink from the filth of uncleanness; the purity of chastity is not considered, nor is the glory of modesty recalled. It was night when Judas betrayed Christ, and when Peter denied him. Therefore, especially at that time, God’s ordinances must be recalled in the mind, his commandments reread, and so forth.

St. Jerome, Epistle 10, to Furia: “The burning arrows of the devil must be restrained by the rigor of fasts and vigils.” And Epistle 22, to Eustochium: “When you rise at night for prayer, let not indigestion produce a belch, but emptiness.” A little later: “Be a cicada of the nights; wash your bed every night; keep watch; and become like a sparrow in the wilderness. Sing with the spirit; sing also with understanding.”

John Climacus, *The Ladder*, step 19: “A wakeful eye purifies the mind; immoderate sleep dulls and blinds the soul. The ever-watchful monk is the enemy of fornication, while the drowsy monk is its companion. Vigils break the fire of lust and free one from dreams. An eye suffused with tears and a tender heart raised up for its own protection observe thoughts with the greatest caution, consume the foods of the furnace’s fire, tame the passions, restrain and repress the tongue, and drive away fantasies. The watchful monk fishes for thoughts and, through the tranquility of night, can readily examine and capture them. As soon as the sound of the trumpet has sounded its alarm, the monk who loves God turns eagerly to prayer and says joyfully and cheerfully, ‘Well done! Well done!’ But the negligent monk says, ‘Woe is me! Woe is me!’ Farmers gather their wealth from the threshing floor and the winepress; monks gather their riches and knowledge especially through evening and night prayers and the exercises of the mind. When the day is ended, the merchant counts his profits; when the psalmody is ended, the monk, sitting down, reckons his gain.”

These are the testimonies of the holy Fathers; more may be found in John Durantus (book III, chapter 4). See also what is noted below on chapter 8.]

They extend their vigils after this, so that the morning light, when it arrives, may find them established in this fervor of spirit, and may preserve them more fervent and watchful throughout the whole day, receiving them prepared for the conflict and strengthened against the devil’s daytime struggle by the exercise of nocturnal vigils and spiritual meditation.

## CHAPTER VI  
That nothing was changed by the elders from the ancient order of the psalms when the morning solemnity was established

We must also know that nothing was altered by our elders, who judged that this same morning solemnity ought to be added, from the ancient custom of the psalms; rather, the office was always celebrated in the nocturnal assemblies in the same order as before.

[Note: [Col. 0135C] What we now call Prime, or the office of Prime, to distinguish it from Lauds, because it ought to be celebrated at the first hour of the artificial day, that is, after sunrise, as the hymn indicates: “Now the star of daylight has arisen,” that is, the sun; likewise the collect: “O God, who have brought us to the beginning of this day,” and so forth.

Prime, which according to the opinion of the Fathers was added in Cassian’s century to the other hours, or hourly prayers, was nevertheless established in such a way that nothing at all was taken from the nocturnal office; rather, the same number and order of psalms were retained. This is what is meant here when it says that the office—the “Mass”—was always celebrated in the nocturnal assemblies in the same order.]

For the hymns which in this region they adopted for the morning solemnity, at the end of the nocturnal Vigils, which they customarily finish after cockcrow and before dawn, they sing in the same way even today: namely, Psalm 148, whose beginning is “Praise the Lord from the heavens,” and the psalms that follow. But Psalm 50, Psalm 62, and Psalm 89 were, as we know, assigned to this newly established solemnity.

[Note: [Col. 0135D] They were newly established among them for Prime, as was noted above.]

Finally, even today throughout Italy, once the morning hymns have been completed, Psalm 50 is sung in all the churches. I have no doubt that this custom derives from that practice.

[Note: [Col. 0135D] Here he calls the psalms “hymns,” as is clear from the following words, and not inappropriately. For among the Hebrews the Psalter is entitled the Book of Hymns. Dionysius, however, translates the term as “psalms” for ease of understanding, since according to common usage ecclesiastical hymns are distinguished from the psalms of David, as is well known.]

## CHAPTER VII  
That anyone who does not arrive for the daytime prayer before the first psalm is finished may not enter the oratory; but that at the nocturnal office a delay is excusable until the end of the second psalm

Anyone who does not arrive for prayer at Terce, Sext, or None before the psalm that has been begun is finished may no longer

[Note: [Col. 0135D] We would rightly be accused of neglecting the oratory if we passed over its meaning in silence. The testimonies of the holy Fathers should therefore first be noted, since they explain and commend the use and institution of the oratory.

D. Augustine, Epistle 121, to Proba: “In the oratory, apart from the worship of praying and singing psalms, absolutely nothing is to be done, so that the work continually devoted to it may correspond to its name.” Again, in chapter 5 of the Rule: “In the oratory no one is to do anything except what it was made for; hence it received its name.”

Hugh of St. Victor aptly observed here that the Lord of all not only reserved certain persons for himself to serve as ministers, namely, the ministers of the Church, but also reserved tithes from material goods for the support of ministers, solemn days from time, and certain places for himself in particular, to serve him. Among these is the oratory, that is, a place dedicated to prayer.

Following St. Augustine, the blessed Benedict says in chapter 52 of the Rule: “Let the oratory be what it is called, and let nothing else be done or stored there.” Turrecremata explains that “done” means “conducted or performed,” and “stored” means “placed or set up.” In the oratory not only is nothing to be done except what it was made for; nothing is even to be stored there for safekeeping except what pertains to divine worship.

Second, it should be noted that the place where the faithful customarily assemble for prayer and sacrifice has been called by various names among both Greeks and Latins. The more common and celebrated names are: church, oratory, house of God, *Dominicum*, basilica, temple, and sanctuary.

Concerning the name “church,” Walfridus Strabo says in *Ecclesiastical Affairs*, chapter 6: “Church” is a Greek name and means an assembly or gathering. It may mean the universal unity of the saints joined in one faith and love, whence it is called the one and catholic Church; or the holy fellowship of individual places, whence many churches are spoken of. Yet the very house in which a multitude of the faithful gathers either to learn or to celebrate divine things is also called a church.

The Apostle suggests examples of this when he says: “That he might present to himself a glorious church, not having spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5); and, “As I teach in all the churches of the saints” (ibid.); and, “Let women keep silence in the church” (ibid.); and many similar passages.

Every one of the elect is also called a house and temple of God, as the Apostle confirms by his own and by prophetic examples: “The temple of God is holy, which you are”; and, as the Lord says, “I will dwell in them and walk among them,” and so forth. Peter likewise says: “You, as living stones, are being built into spiritual houses,” and so forth.

Thus, just as one church exists within the Church, so many houses and temples exist within the house and temple of God. So far Walfridus.

Churches are also often called by the Greeks *euktēria* (εὐκτήρια), and by the Latins *oratoria*, as was seen above from St. Augustine and Benedict. Eusebius too, in book 2 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 16, quoting Philo, says that in each place where the first monks lived near Alexandria there were sacred buildings consecrated to prayer:

“There is,” he says, “in almost every estate a building called a *semneion* (σεμνεῖον), that is, a venerable or august temple, or a *monastērion* (μοναστήριον), which in Latin may be called a solitary and separated place. There, separated and withdrawn from others, they perform the sacred mysteries of the devout life and of august virtue,” and so forth.

Tertullian writes in the *Apologeticus*, chapter 39, that people assemble in the Church, first for prayer, second for reading, and third for exhortation.

Origen, in Homily 2 on Exodus, calls the churches of Christians houses of prayer, in accordance with what the Lord said in Matthew 21 and Luke 19: “My house shall be called a house of prayer.”

Sometimes it is also called *Dominicum*, in Greek *Kyriakón* (Κυριακόν). Thus, in canon 28 of the Council of Laodicea: “It is not permitted to hold love-feasts in the *kyriaka*” (οὐ δεῖ τὰς ἀγάπας ἐν τοῖς κυριακοῖς ποιεῖν).

In this same sense St. Cyprian says in his book *On Works and Almsgiving*: “Do you come to the *Dominicum* without a sacrifice?” And Rufinus, in book 1 of his *History*, chapter 2, has the elder say: “If you believe these things to be so, rise and follow me to the *Dominicum*.”

Eusebius gives the following reason for this name in his *Oration on the Praises of Constantine*: “He took care that sacred buildings and temples should be dedicated and consecrated to the one God of all and Lord of all things. Hence the temples consecrated to him also received the name of the Lord, a name bestowed upon them not from human beings but from the Lord of all himself; and for that reason they were called *Dominica*.” Thus Eusebius. Walfridus says nearly the same in the passage cited above, chapter 7.

At other times *Dominicum* means the sacrifice of the Mass itself. Hence the frequent expression in the Acts of the Holy Martyrs, “to celebrate the *Dominicum*,” which is equivalent to “to celebrate Mass.” (See Baronius, volume 2 of the *Annals*, and his notes on the Martyrology.)

It is also called a basilica. Thus the words of the Council of Laodicea are rendered in Latin by Gratian: “It is not permitted to hold an agape in basilicas or churches” (*Decretum*, Distinction 42, canon *Non oportet*). St. Jerome likewise says in the epitaph of Marcella that “she celebrated the basilicas of all the Apostles and martyrs with secret prayers.”

As for the origin of the name “basilica,” Isidore says in book 15 of the *Etymologies*, chapter 4:

“Basilicas were first called the dwellings of kings. Hence they have their name. For *basileus* (βασιλεύς) means ‘king,’ and basilicas are royal dwellings. But divine temples are now called basilicas because worship and sacrifices are offered there to God, the King of all.”

See Baronius’s notes on the Martyrology for 5 August, and Durandus, book 1 of *On the Rites of the Church*, chapter 1. Amalarius, book 3 of *On the Offices*, chapter 2, and Walfridus, chapter 6, say similar things.

Concerning the designation “temple,” Isidore likewise says:

“The name ‘temple’ is general. For the ancients called any large places temples. They are called temples as if they were broad covered places. But a place marked out toward the east was also called a temple because of contemplation.”

Thus Isidore.

The sacred place was by no means called *delubrum* or *fanum* by our forefathers, although some more recent writers have used these words—improperly, indeed I might say abusively—since they are more appropriate to the temples of the pagans. It is certain that our Fathers abstained from them. Thus Baronius.

Finally, the same place is also called a sanctuary, either because sacred things are kept there, such as the relics of the saints, or because the sacraments are administered there, by which a person is sanctified, as Turrecremata says (on chapter 52 of the Rule). He also demonstrates by many arguments how greatly the place of the oratory ought to be honored and revered.

But these remarks on the various names of the oratory, offered by way of occasion, are sufficient.]

dare to enter the oratory or join those singing psalms; rather, standing outside the doors, he awaits the dismissal of the assembly until everyone has gone out; then, having prostrated himself on the ground in penitence, he obtains pardon for his negligence or lateness, knowing that he cannot otherwise expiate the fault of his indolence. Nor may he be admitted to the solemnity that will follow three hours later unless he hastens to make immediate satisfaction for his negligence with genuine humility.

In the nocturnal assemblies, however, a delay is allowed until the second psalm, but only on condition that, before that psalm has been completed and the brothers prostrate themselves in prayer, the latecomer hastens to insert and join himself to the assembly. If he is even slightly late beyond the appointed limit, he is undoubtedly to be subjected to the rebuke and penitence described above.

[Note: [Col. 0137D] “The dismissal,” that is, the sending away of the brothers after the office has been completed. Thus St. Fructuosus also says, according to Smaragdus: “Anyone who does not arrive for the daytime prayers by the first psalm is not to dare to enter the oratory with the others, but is to be assigned to penance” (on chapter 43 of the Rule).

As for the nocturnal hours, D. Benedict took a different view, and with no less prudent reasoning. Concerning the punishment of those who are negligent and arrive late for the work of God, or divine office, he establishes the following:

“If anyone arrives at the nocturnal Vigils after the Gloria of Psalm 94—which, for this very reason, we wish to be drawn out and recited slowly—he is not to stand in his place in the choir, but last of all, either in the place which the abbot has separately appointed for such negligent persons, so that he may be seen by him or by everyone, until, when the work of God has been completed, he makes public satisfaction through penitence” (chapter 43 of the Rule).

And lest the holy Father seem to have established this contrary to the custom of the ancients without reason, he adds:

“We have judged that they ought to stand last or apart for this reason: so that, being seen by all, they may be corrected by their very shame. For if they remain outside the oratory, there may perhaps be someone who returns to bed, or sleeps, or at least sits outside, or occupies himself with stories. Let no opportunity be given to the evil one; rather, let him enter inside, so that he may not lose everything and may amend what remains.” (See also the Rule of St. Pachomius, article 2.)

Concerning the daytime hours he immediately adds:

“During the daytime hours, anyone who arrives at the work of God after the verse and the Gloria of the first psalm—which is said after the verse, that is, after the end of the first psalm—is to stand last according to the rule mentioned above, and is not to presume to join the choir of those singing psalms until he has made satisfaction, unless perhaps the abbot has granted permission. Even then, the offender is to make satisfaction for this fault.”

Thus D. Benedict imitated Cassian’s, or the ancient monks’, institution in this matter. (See here the declaration of the Cassinese Congregation, the Council of Basel, session 21, section 2, and the Council of Aachen, canon 131.)

As for the statement, “Even then, the offender is to make satisfaction,” Abbot Smaragdus explains it as follows: he is received into the choir by the abbot’s permission in such a way that, even after the appointed course—that is, after the office has been completed—he, as the offender, still makes satisfaction for the negligence he has committed, until he receives pardon from the abbot and is subsequently granted complete and peaceful remission. Thus Smaragdus.]

[Note: [Col. 0138B] That is, with his whole body prostrate on the ground as a sign of penitence, and not rising before the abbot has dismissed him and pardon has been obtained.

Thus, in book 2, chapter 16: “If anyone has been suspended from prayer for any fault whatsoever, no one at all is permitted to pray with him before his reconciliation has publicly been granted by the abbot before all the brothers, after he has prostrated himself on the ground in penitence and received forgiveness for his offense.”

Again, in book 4, chapter 16: “If anyone accidentally breaks an earthen jug, he is not to remove his negligence except by public penitence. With all the brothers gathered in the assembly, he is to remain prostrate on the ground and ask pardon until the solemnity of the prayers has been completed, obtaining it when, by the abbot’s judgment, he is ordered to rise from the ground.”

The blessed Benedict, an imitator of this institution, established two such forms of prostration, one for more serious faults and another for lesser ones (chapter 44 of the Rule). Concerning the former he says:

“He who is excommunicated from the oratory and the table for more serious faults is to lie prostrate before the doors of the oratory while the work of God is being celebrated in the oratory, saying nothing, but with his head placed on the ground he is to lie prostrate at the feet of all who leave the oratory. He is to do this until the abbot judges that satisfaction has been made. When he comes at the abbot’s command, he is to throw himself at the abbot’s feet; then at the feet of all the brothers, that they may pray for him.” (See Smaragdus on this passage.)

And so forth.

Here Turrecremata notes that this form of satisfaction for more serious faults contains and prescribes four parts. First, he says, there is prostration before the doors of the oratory at the feet of the abbot and of the departing brothers. Second, there is prostration at the feet of the abbot and at the feet of the brothers, together with a request for their prayers, when the offender is summoned to the chapter meeting. Third, there is his reception or station in the humble place assigned to him in the oratory, together with abstention from beginning the psalms, lessons, or responsories. Fourth, there is prostration on the ground at the end of the hours, or of the divine office, until the abbot releases him from this satisfaction.

The form of satisfaction for lesser faults is prescribed as follows, with Turrecremata commenting and explaining:

“Those who are excommunicated”—that is, separated—“from the table alone are to make satisfaction in the oratory, as was partly said in the preceding form: namely, although they remain in their place in the oratory, they are not to intone a psalm or antiphon, nor recite the lessons. Likewise, at the end of the hours they are to throw themselves on the ground, as was ordered above, and are to do this until the abbot commands it—that is, they are to continue doing it until the abbot blesses them, giving a sign or word of blessing.”

Thus Turrecremata in his exposition of the Rule.]

[Col. 0139A]

He obtains pardon for his negligence or lateness by penitence on the ground, knowing that he cannot otherwise expiate the fault of his indolence. Nor is he to be admitted to the solemnity that will follow three hours later unless he first hastens to make immediate satisfaction for his negligence with genuine humility.

In the nocturnal assemblies, however, a delay is allowed until the second psalm, but only on condition that, before that psalm has been completed and the brothers prostrate themselves in prayer, the latecomer hastens to insert and join himself to the assembly. If he is even slightly late beyond the appointed limit, he is undoubtedly to be subjected to the rebuke and penitence described above.

## CHAPTER VIII  
What duration and order are to be observed for the Vigils celebrated on Saturday as evening falls
Indeed [Note: Here and elsewhere, “vigils” refers to the nighttime prayers and assemblies at which these monks, and other monks following their example, customarily remain awake through the night and keep watch like spiritual soldiers or sentries stationed upon the walls of Jerusalem. Hence St. Jerome, explaining in his commentary on Daniel 4 the words, “And behold, a watcher and a holy one descended from heaven,” says: “For ‘watcher,’ Theodotion used the Chaldean word *Hir*, written with the three letters *Ain*, *Jod*, and *Res*. It signifies angels, because they are always watchful and ready for God’s command. Therefore we imitate the angels’ duties by frequent all-night vigils.” The same author writes in Letter 55, to Riparius: “When you say that Vigilantius curses vigils, he acts contrary to his own name, wishing that Vigilantius might sleep, and not hearing the Savior say: ‘So, could you not watch with me for one hour? Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation. The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak’ (Matthew 26). And elsewhere the prophet sings: ‘At midnight I rose to confess you because of your righteous judgments, O Lord’ (Psalm 118). We also read that the Lord spent the night in prayer in the Gospel (Luke 6), and that the apostles kept watch all night while confined in prison, so that, as they sang psalms, the earth was shaken, the jailer believed, and the magistrates and the city were terrified (Acts 16). Paul says: ‘Persevere in prayer, keeping watch in it’ (Colossians 4). And elsewhere: ‘Frequently in vigils’ (2 Corinthians 11). Let Vigilantius, then, sleep, and while sleeping with the Egyptians let him be strangled by the destroyer of Egypt.” Thus far St. Jerome, richly supplied with Scripture and examples.

The recently cited John Climacus likewise speaks excellently of the vigils and nighttime exercises of monks in these words: “Among earthly and mortal kings who stand in attendance, some are lightly equipped and almost naked; others carry fasces, others shields, others swords. There is a great and incomparable difference between the first and the others. Some are, properly speaking, relatives and closest intimates of the king; the others are servants and ministers—and some are arranged in one way, some in another. Let us now examine more diligently how we too attend upon God, our king, in evening and daytime assemblies and prayers. Some, during evening vigils, wholly free from worldly care, extend pure hands in prayer. Others attend with the chanting of psalms. Others devote themselves more to reading. Some, through manual labor, valiantly fight against sleep despite their weakness. Others exercise themselves in meditation on death, striving through such reflection to acquire compunction. Of all these, the first and the last devote themselves to daytime watchings; the second are closer to the monastic life; the third walk on a lower path.
