Yet God accepts and esteems the offerings of all according to the devotion and virtue of those who offer them.” Thus he speaks of the monks of his own time (*The Ladder*, step 10).] Accordingly, in winter, when the nights are longer, the elders regulate throughout the monasteries until the fourth cockcrow the vigils celebrated each week from the evening that ushers in the Sabbath, so that, after the watchings of the entire night, they may refresh their bodies for approximately the remaining two hours and not languish in the torpor of sleep throughout the whole day, being content with the brief rest of this period as compensation for the entire night.

[Note: Above he said simply, “Before cockcrow” and “After cockcrow.” Here he adds a number: “Until the fourth cockcrow.” This gives occasion to say something about the crowing of the cock, or cockcrow, its rationale and significance, from both profane and sacred authors, since this contributes to understanding not only this chapter but also many passages of Holy Scripture.

Pliny, book 10, chapter 21, says: “Next [that is, after peacocks], these nocturnal watchmen too are conscious of glory, whom nature produced to rouse mortals to their work and break their sleep. They know the stars and distinguish by their crowing the three divisions of the day. They go to roost with the sun, and at the fourth military watch call men back to care and labor. They do not allow the sunrise to steal upon the unwary, but announce the coming day by their crowing, and their crowing itself by the clapping of their sides.” Thus he.

Cicero, book 2 of *On Divination*: “Democritus explains in excellent words why cocks crow before daylight: when the food has been driven from the breast, distributed and regulated throughout the whole body, they utter their song, satisfied with rest; in the silence of night they delight their throats, as Ennius says, and then with song and clapping beat their wings.” Suidas, under εὐφωνεῖν [elsewhere εὐφώνη]: “Who persuaded this most vocal bird within the house to count the hours of the night?” St. Basil, Homily 8 on the *Hexaemeron*: “Let the familiar domestic bird rouse you to finish your work, crying out in its piercing voice and by its song proclaiming the sun’s still distant approach; awakening with travellers in the morning, it leads the farmers forth from their houses to their labors and harvest.”

St. Ambrose most elegantly celebrates this property of the domestic cock in the morning hymn, or the hymn customarily sung at Morning Praises on the Lord’s Day—of which he himself is the author, as St. Augustine also testifies, *Retractations*, book 1, chapter 21. In it he describes in these verses the many benefits and advantages which cockcrow ordinarily brings to humanity:

> Now sounds the herald of the day,  
> Wakeful through the depths of night;  
> A nocturnal light to travellers,  
> Dividing night from night.  
>
> Roused by this, the day-star  
> Looses heaven from its darkness;  
> Roused by this, every band of error  
> Abandons its harmful course.  
>
> At this the sailor gathers strength,  
> And the waves of the sea grow calm;  
> At this the very Rock of the Church,  
> At its crowing, washes away his fault.  
>
> Let us therefore rise vigorously:  
> The cock rouses those who lie down,  
> Rebukes the drowsy,  
> And convicts those who deny.  
>
> At the cock’s crow hope returns;  
> Health is restored to the sick;  
> The robber’s sword is sheathed;  
> Faith returns to the fallen.

Almost every verse contains a distinct benefit of cockcrow. First, the cock is called the herald of day because by the proclamation of its song it announces the approaching day; thus Aurelius Prudentius, imitating Ambrose, expressed it likewise in his hymn at cockcrow (*Tuesday at Lauds*):

> The bird, herald of day,  
> Foretells the approaching light.

Secondly, the cock is wakeful through the depths of night because, in the dead of night, when deep sleep possesses other living creatures, it keeps watch and at fixed, appointed hours gives its cry. Hence Virgil says of it (*Aeneid* 4): “The bird, the watchman, had foretold the day by its song”; and Ovid says (*Metamorphoses*): “There no wakeful bird, with the songs of its crested beak, summons the dawn.”

Thirdly, it is also a nocturnal light to those on the road, so far as its function and office are concerned, because it indicates the night-hours to those travelling by night, just as daylight indicates them and announces the passage of time to travellers by day (see Cochlaeus, exposition of this hymn). Finally, it is said to divide night from night because by its crowing it separates the earlier part of the night from the later, through a certain mark and seal of discernment and understanding implanted in it by divine providence, by which it breaks into song with utmost regularity at those same times of night, as though the divider and mediator of the night. Hence the Lord not undeservedly asks concerning it in blessed Job: “Who gave the cock understanding?” (Job 38). There Venerable Bede says: “God gave the domestic cock such awareness that, when the time of night has passed, mindful as it were of the approaching light, it announces by its crowing that it is returning to the world.”

Ambrose himself, in prose, so paraphrastically explains the remaining verses quoted above in book 5, chapter 24 of the *Hexaemeron* that no other interpreter is necessary: “The cock’s crow is pleasant in the night; nor is it only pleasant, but useful also. Like a good fellow-dweller, it rouses the sleeper, admonishes the anxious, consoles the traveller, proclaiming the progress of the night by its musical signal. At its crow the thief abandons his ambushes; at its crow the day-star itself, that is, the morning star, rises awakened and lights heaven; at its crow the fearful sailor lays aside his sadness, and every storm and squall, repeatedly stirred up by evening winds, grows calm. At its crow the devout man springs up to pray and resumes also the task of reading; finally, at its crow, the very Rock of the Church, that is, the apostle Peter, washes away the fault which he had incurred by denying three times before the cock crowed. At its cry hope returns to all, the sick person’s distress is relieved, the pain of wounds decreases, the burning of fevers is mitigated, faith returns to the fallen, Jesus looks upon the wavering, and corrects those who have gone astray. Finally, he looked upon Peter (Luke 22), and immediately error departed: denial was driven away and confession followed.” Thus far St. Ambrose.

From all this it is quite clear why the author here says “the fourth cockcrow,” and what the fourth cockcrow is: namely, the nocturnal one; for this, not the daytime crowing, is under discussion. I think the expression is used by allusion and with reference to the ancient custom by which the span of every night—that is, twelve hours—was divided into four watches. The first began at sunset and ended at the third hour of the night; the second extended from the third to the sixth hour; the third from the sixth to the ninth; and the fourth, properly called the morning watch, from the ninth hour until sunrise, or the end of dawn, which was the twelfth and last hour of the night (Jerome, Letter 139 and Psalm 89; Augustine on Numbers 5; see also Durandus, *On the Rites of the Church*, book 3, chapter 5).

Christ designated these four parts of the night, or watches, by other names: “For you do not know when the Lord will come: in the evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or in the morning” (Mark 13). What he calls here “at midnight” and “at cockcrow,” Luke 12 calls coming “in the second watch” and “in the third watch.” Thus the second watch is the same as midnight, and the third watch the same as cockcrow. What is here called “morning,” Mark, chapter 6, calls “the fourth watch of the night”; this is the fourth cockcrow mentioned here. For cocks customarily crow at fixed spans and intervals of the night, as though at fixed and appointed guard-watches; the author therefore seems to have fitted four cockcrows to the four watches, calling that the fourth cockcrow which corresponds to the fourth watch, just as the third corresponds to the third, and so on.

Indeed, in the preceding verses of St. Ambrose one may easily observe that some things refer to the first or second, some to the third, but most to the fourth and final cockcrow, which they utter as day dawns. This is the cockcrow also under discussion in this chapter and the preceding ones, since this is indicated to be the time of the morning office, that is, Lauds; Prudentius likewise entitled his hymn *At Cockcrow*. Holy Scripture, however, mentions only a twofold cockcrow: the first after the sixth hour of the night, that is, around midnight and the third watch; the second after the tenth or eleventh hour, that is, in the fourth watch (Matthew 26). This is also the sense of Tobit 8: “It came to pass about cockcrow that Raguel ordered his servants to be summoned,” and so forth, which is subsequently explained as “before day dawned” and “before it was light.”

Hence Jansenius, in *Evangelical Harmony*, chapter 133, explains how the statement in Matthew 26, Luke 22, and John 13—that the Lord said to Peter, “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times”—is to be understood, whereas Mark writes, “Before the cock has crowed twice, you will deny me three times” (Mark 14): “The three Evangelists,” he says, “speak of that crowing of the cock which people especially observe, from which the last part of the night, formerly called the fourth watch, is called cockcrow. For cocks ordinarily crow in the night chiefly twice: once not long after midnight, and a second time when two or three, or approximately that many, hours of night still remain, when they persist in crowing until the time called *conticinium* [the silence of the birds]. From this second crowing the fourth watch of the night is called cockcrow. Mark, therefore, writing an exact history of what happened to Peter, as he had heard it from Peter, mentions both crowings of the cock; but the other three Evangelists mention only the later crowing, as the principal one, from which a part of the night is called cockcrow.” Thus he.

There is therefore no discrepancy, but complete harmony and agreement among the Evangelists concerning cockcrow. Peter denied Christ three times before dawn, the time properly called cockcrow, as Matthew, Luke, and John write; and, what is the same thing, he denied Peter three times before the cock crowed twice—once at midnight and again before dawn—as Mark writes (see Maldonatus on Matthew 26). St. Jerome is to be understood in this way when, writing on Isaiah 21, he says: “The apostle Peter, before the cock crowed—that is, at the second crowing—denied the Lord three times; this is understood as midnight. But after the night had advanced and day began to draw near, when the darkness of midnight had been overcome and the cock, herald of light, sounded, he wept bitterly, understood his sin, and at that time could say: ‘Weeping will linger until evening, and joy until morning’ (Psalm 29).” But enough has now been said on cockcrow and the crowing of the cock for the occasion of this passage.]

[Note: “From the evening that ushers in the Sabbath,” that is, beginning at vespers—or, paraphrastically, as Dionysius puts it, during the night following Friday. Among the Hebrews, observance of the Sabbath began in the evening, that is, at sunset, and ended in the evening. It should be observed here that those monks had a special ceremony and observance, different from that of others, both for the Sabbath night and for the Sabbath day (Leviticus 23). They held the nighttime vigils much longer and more solemnly, so that they spent almost the whole night sleepless and awake, partly occupied with private prayers and partly with the nighttime and canonical offices. Only two hours toward the end of the night were granted them for obtaining brief sleep and rest, until, as dawn approached, they were summoned to the Morning Psalms, that is, the Morning Praises. The Author gives the reason for this in chapter 9. They celebrated the Sabbath day as a feast according to the custom of the Eastern Church, nor did they fast on that day as on the others, as will be shown more fully below (chapters 5 and 6).]

Hence it is also fitting for us to observe this practice with all care: namely, being content with the sleep granted us after the Mass of the vigil until the coming of daylight—that is, until the Morning Psalms—we should spend the whole remainder of the day in work and necessary duties. Otherwise, compelled by the fatigue and exhaustion of the vigils to recover during the day the sleep we withheld from the night, we might seem not so much to have deprived the body of rest as to have exchanged the time of rest and nighttime refreshment. For frail flesh cannot be deprived of the rest of the entire night in such a way that throughout the following day it can maintain an unshaken watchfulness without drowsiness of mind and torpor of spirit. That watchfulness will rather be hindered than helped by this, unless, after the Mass of the vigils, it has tasted at least a little sleep.

Therefore, if at least one hour of sleep, as we have said, is granted before daylight, we shall gain the benefit of all the hours of the vigils that we spent in prayer, giving nature what belongs to it and having no need to recover during the day what we withheld from the night. Whoever attempts not reasonably to withhold a part from this flesh, but to deny it everything—and, to put it more accurately, wishes to cut off not superfluities but necessities—will certainly restore the whole to the flesh. For this reason the vigils must be compensated with greater interest if they have been prolonged until daylight through inconsiderate and irrational excess.

Therefore they distinguish the vigils into three divisions of offices, so that the labor, divided by this variety, may relieve the body’s exhaustion with a kind of pleasure. When they have sung together three antiphons while standing, they afterward sit on the ground or on very low seats and respond to three psalms while one chants them; each psalm, however, is offered by individual brothers in turn as they succeed one another. While they remain seated in the same repose, three readings are added. Thus, by diminishing bodily labor, they perform their vigils with greater concentration of mind.

[Note: These are three antiphons—for one should read “three antiphons,” as Dionysius and other manuscripts have it—three psalms, and three readings, as he explains shortly afterward. From this passage one may infer what nighttime office those monks had and by what rite and manner they performed it. First they had three antiphons, that is, pleasing chants handed down to them by their elders, which they sang with some melody while standing upright, as among us the invitatory is ordinarily sung with Psalm 94. Then, sitting on the ground or on very low seats, they sang three psalms: one began and led, and the others sang in response. This custom was widespread and familiar, as is clear from St. Basil’s Letter 63. Finally, Cassian says, “they added three readings,” whereas among the Egyptian monks only one would chant the psalms while the others listened in silence.

Although this office seems exceedingly brief in comparison with the office of other monks, who had twelve psalms together with the other parts during their daily vigils, as has been shown in its proper place, it follows either that those antiphons and readings were very lengthy, or that they were sung very slowly, solemnly, and at length, or that the remaining time of night was devoted to other private prayers and meditations. For, as the Author says, after the vigils of the whole night they reserved only one or two hours for the body’s restoration and rest, lest they should either collapse from excessive fatigue and sleeplessness or be burdened by sleep during the day.]

## CHAPTER IX. Why vigils were appointed when the Sabbath dawned, and why throughout the whole East the fast was presumed to be released on the Sabbath day

[Col. 0144B]

From the time of the apostolic preaching, when the Christian religion and faith were founded, it was therefore established throughout the whole East that the vigils should be celebrated when the Sabbath dawned. For when our Lord and Savior had been crucified on the sixth day of the week,

[Note: That is, on Friday. Among the Hebrews, “Sabbath” signifies both the whole week and the seventh day of the week. When it signifies the whole week, the first day is called the first of the week, the second the second of the week, the third the third of the week, and the following days in the same manner. St. Jerome writes in his letter to Hedibia, question 4: “The first day of the week is to be understood as the Lord’s Day, because the whole week is divided into the Sabbath and the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth days of the week, which the pagans call by the names of idols and the elements.” Thus Cassian, in book 4, chapter 19, called the second day “the second of the week,” meaning Tuesday.]

his disciples, still overwhelmed by the fresh shock of his Passion, remained awake throughout the whole night, granting their eyes no sleep or rest. For this reason, from that time until today, the solemnity of vigils assigned to that night has likewise been observed throughout the whole East.

[Note: That is, the Sabbath night, or the night preceding the Sabbath day. On that night the Easterners, especially the monks, watched and kept vigil longer and more solemnly than on other nights, for the reason given here.]

[Note: That is, the fast is dissolved and relaxed, or, to come closer word for word, the brethren are released from fasting. The reader may wonder that those monks did not fast, but positively broke the fast on the Sabbath day, although on the other five days they fasted until evening, and Christians commonly fast on that day as on Friday—that is, abstain from eating meat. But he should know that on this point the judgment and custom of the Eastern Church differed from those of the Western Church.

For the Easterners and Greeks did not fast at all on Saturdays, not even in Lent. They did so on the basis of a tradition and a certain apostolic canon which forbade clergy to fast on the Sabbath under penalty of deposition and laypeople under penalty of excommunication. Thus St. Ignatius, writing to the Philippians, says: “If anyone fasts on the Lord’s Day or on the Sabbath, with one exception”—namely, the Paschal Sabbath—“he is a murderer of Christ” (see *Conference* 21, chapter 27).

Writers trace the reason for this to certain heretics who arose especially in the East in the first ages of the Church. Some denied Christ’s resurrection and, in contempt of it, spent in mourning and fasting the Lord’s Day, upon which Christians customarily rejoice in its remembrance. Others said that the God of the Hebrews, maker of the world and author of the Law, was evil, and that Christ had come to destroy him; consequently they fasted and mournfully observed the Sabbath day, which was joyful and holy to the Jews because of God’s rest from his works, in insult to the Creator, as Epiphanius relates, *Heresies* 41 and 42. In hatred and detestation of these people, therefore, the orthodox Easterners considered fasting on the Sabbath, no less than on the Lord’s Day, unlawful or unfitting, lest they appear to agree with or imitate those heretics. In the Latin and Western Church, however, fasting on the Sabbath was introduced and observed from the very times of the apostles for other reasons, which we shall explain in the following chapter; it is still observed, though imperfectly. Of it Gregory VII says, in Gratian, distinction 5: “Because the Sabbath day was held in honor among the Fathers by abstinence, we admonish that whoever desire to be participants in the Christian religion abstain from eating meat on that day.”]

Therefore the release from fasting after the labor of the vigils, established on the Sabbath day by those same apostolic men, is not without reason presumed throughout all the Churches of the East, in accordance also with that saying of Ecclesiastes which, although it has another mystical meaning, is not inconsistent with this one: that we are commanded to allot an equal share of solemnity to both days, that is, to the week and to the octave, when it says: “Give a portion to these seven, and indeed to these eight” (Ecclesiastes 11).

[Note: He designates the seventh day, that is, the Sabbath, by the name “the week,” and the eighth day, that is, the Lord’s Day, by the name “the octave,” alluding to the rather obscure passage of Ecclesiastes which in the Vulgate reads, “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight,” whereas the Author translates from the Septuagint. The Easterners therefore granted a share of solemnity to both days because they observed the Sabbath day and the Lord’s Day with almost equal worship and solemnity—not with Jewish superstition, as did the heretical Ebionites, but with a Christian and religious understanding and rite.

As for the mystical meaning that the Author assigns to the same saying, St. Jerome interprets “Give portions to seven and to eight” (Ecclesiastes 11; Ezekiel 40; Psalm 118) as meaning that one should believe both Testaments (*Against the Luciferians*, chapter 8). Explaining this more fully in his commentary, he says: “In Ezekiel, seven and eight steps are read as the ascent to the temple. And after that ethical psalm, namely, the hundred and eighteenth, there are psalms of five steps, by which we are first instructed in the Law, and, after the number seven has been completed, ascend through the octave to the Gospel. We are therefore commanded to believe in both Testaments, the old as well as the new, with equal veneration. The Jews gave a portion to seven, believing in the Sabbath, but did not give one to eight, denying the resurrection on the Lord’s Day. Conversely, the heretics Marcion and Manichaeus, and all who tear apart the Old Law with rabid mouths, give a portion to eight, accepting the Gospel, but do not assign the same to the number seven, rejecting the Old Law. Let us therefore believe in both Covenants. For we cannot now comprehend in our minds the fitting torments and fitting punishment reserved for those who dwell upon the earth—Jews and heretics—who deny one of the two.”

Thus far St. Jerome’s mystical and allegorical interpretation. St. Gregory also gives other mystical interpretations in book 35 of the *Moralia*, chapter 7, writing as follows: “By the number seven he expressed the present time, which is conducted through seven days. By the number eight he signified perpetual life, which the Lord revealed to us through his resurrection. He rose, of course, on the Lord’s Day; and since that day follows the seventh day, namely, the Sabbath, it is found to be the eighth from creation. Well, then, is it said: ‘Give a portion to seven and also to eight, because you do not know what evil will be upon the earth.’ It is as though it were plainly said: Dispose of temporal things in such a way that you do not forget to desire eternal things. For one must provide for the future by doing good, since one does not know how great a tribulation will follow from the future judgment,” and so forth.

The genuine and literal meaning of the same saying seems to be the one given by Franciscus Titelmannus, with the preliminary observation that “seven” and “eight” are dative cases, as is clear from the Greek, where the article τοῖς (*tois*)—the dative plural—is placed before both. He says: “The sense of the sentence is: Give a portion to those seven and also to those eight, or to groups of seven and eight; that is, distribute and scatter what you have among all who happen to meet you, whether they are seven or eight. Do good to as many as and to all those to whom you are able.” Thus he writes, with what follows.]

“Give a portion to these seven, and indeed to these eight” (Ecclesiastes 11).

[Note: That is, not so that they might agree and share with the Jews in the celebration and superstition of the Sabbath.]

For this release from fasting must not be regarded as participation in a Jewish festival, especially in the case of those who are shown to be entirely alien to every Jewish superstition; rather, it pertains to the restoration of the weary body mentioned above. For after fasting continuously on five days throughout all the weeks of the year, the body easily grows weary and fails unless it is refreshed by at least two intervening days.

## CHAPTER X. How it came about that the Sabbath is fasted on in the City

[Col. 0147A]

Some people in certain Western cities, ignorant of the reason for this moderation [Col. 0148A] [Note: [Col. 0147A] The Author brands the Latins and Westerners with the mark of ignorance, but on what grounds he does so, he himself must see. The Romans—for by the name “the City” he appears to designate Rome, as though by antonomasia—and other Western Christians were not ignorant of the reason for that moderation, that is, for the relaxation of the fast on Saturday among Easterners; nor did they condemn it, provided it was done without superstition. Rather, moved by other and more serious causes and considerations, they judged it more appropriate to fast on Saturdays.

First, we fast on Saturday, or at least abstain from meat, in order to distance ourselves as far as possible from Judaism. For the Jews do not fast but [Col. 0147B] feast on Saturday. The Ebionites and other heretics imitated them by observing the Sabbath in a Jewish manner; concerning these, see Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* III.21 (Bellarmine, *On Good Works in Particular* II.18), and Epiphanius, under the heresy of the Audians (*Heresies* 41 and 42). To this pertains Canon 9 of the Council of Laodicea: “On not Judaizing on the Sabbath.”

Second, we fast in memory of the Lord’s burial, since on Saturday he lay dead and enclosed in the tomb. This reason is touched upon in canon 26 of the Council of Elvira and by Blessed Augustine in Letter 86: “On Saturday,” he says, “Christ’s flesh rested in the tomb, just as God on that same day rested from all his works” (Psalm XLIV). Hence arose a diversity in the royal vesture, so that some—especially the peoples of the East—preferred to relax the fast in order to signify rest; others, on account of the humility of the Lord’s death, fasted, as did the Roman and certain other Western Churches, and so forth.

Third, we fast in order to imitate the Apostles and the other disciples of the Lord, who, together with the Mother of God and the holy women, remained in mourning and sorrow not only on Friday but also on Saturday. This reason [Col. 0147C] Pope Innocent I of Rome gives to Decentius, bishop of Gubbio: “The clearest reasoning demonstrates that one ought to fast on Saturday. For we celebrate the Lord’s Day on account of the venerable resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ not only at Easter, but also throughout each weekly cycle we repeatedly observe an image of that day. But if we fast on Friday because of the Lord’s Passion, we ought not to pass over Saturday, which appears to be enclosed between the sorrow and joy of that time. For it is certainly established that during those two days the Apostles were both in mourning and, because of fear of the Jews, hidden away and fasting.” Thus Innocent.

These considerations prove not only the reasonable custom of the Roman Church, but show that it ought to be approved even more on the basis of the practice of the Eastern Church. Augustine also reports another reason for the Saturday fast in Letter 86: namely, that when the Apostle Peter was about to contend with Simon Magus at Rome on the Lord’s Day, he fasted on the preceding day, together with the whole Church that was in the City, because of the great danger of that temptation; and, he says, after achieving so prosperous and glorious a result, he maintained the same custom thereafter, and certain Western Churches imitated him.

Cassian, however, who in this matter is excessively attached to the customs of the Greeks, or Easterners, mocks and rejects this reason as weak. He argues that Peter’s example was exceptional, arising from necessity and from the occasion of Peter’s contest with Simon Magus; from it one ought not to infer a general and perpetual law requiring fasting on Saturday. This argument might perhaps have some force if there had not been other, more serious, and likewise general causes, mentioned above, for which the Roman Church adopted and established the Saturday fast. Those causes are not inconsistent with—indeed, it is more than credible that this occasion, too, was added on the basis of the example and precedent of the Apostle Peter.

Moreover, it was not only the Roman Church and those neighboring it that were accustomed to think and practice this same thing concerning the Saturday fast, as Cassian appears to indicate, but also more distant churches. Saint Augustine bears witness to this in Letter 97 to Jerome; among them was the Church of Hippo in Africa. When Augustine’s mother, Saint Monica, went from there to Milan and found that people did not fast on Saturday, she was consequently uncertain what to do and consulted Saint Ambrose. He gave her this reply: “When I am in Rome, I fast on Saturday; when I am in Milan, I do not fast. So you, too, wherever you happen to come to a church, observe its custom, if you do not wish to be a cause of scandal either to anyone else or to anyone on your account.” When Augustine reported this to his mother [Col. 0148B], she gladly embraced it (Augustine, Letter 118 to Januarius).

Similarly, when Lucinius Boeticus consulted Saint Jerome on this matter, Jerome wrote back that the custom of each church ought to be observed (Jerome, Letter 28). His words are especially appropriate here:

“Regarding the Sabbath, about which you ask whether one ought to fast, and regarding the Eucharist, whether it should be received daily—as the Roman and Spanish Churches are said to observe—Hippolytus, a most eloquent man, did indeed write, and various writers have published excerpts from different authorities. But I think I should briefly remind you that ecclesiastical traditions, especially those which do not injure the faith, ought to be observed as they have been handed down by our predecessors; nor should one custom be overturned by the contrary practice of another.

Would that we could fast at all times! For in the Acts of the Apostles we read that the Apostle Paul and the believers with him did so during the days of Pentecost and on the Lord’s Day (Acts XIII, 20 and 27). Yet they are not to be accused of the Manichaean heresy, since bodily food ought not to be preferred to spiritual food.”

Thus Jerome.] and especially in the City, therefore think that the relaxation of the Saturday fast [Alt. “of the fast”] ought by no means to be presumed [Note: [Col. 0148C] Or, as another reading has it, “that the relaxation of the fast ought not to be presumed,” that is, that the fast on Saturday ought not to be relaxed, as was done among Easterners], because they assert that the Apostle Peter fasted on that very day against [Col. 0149A] Simon [Note: [Col. 0148C] Concerning this conflict and contest between Blessed Peter and Simon Magus at Rome, apart from this passage of Cassian, there are many testimonies of ancient writers that most certainly demonstrate that the history is true and authentic, not fabricated or legendary, as Calvin maintains.

The oldest of these, Clement of Rome, narrates the event in Peter’s person and gives a full account of it; Hegesippus does the same in Book III of *The Destruction of Jerusalem* (Clement, *Constitutions* VI.9, II.2). Arnobius likewise, writing *Against the Gentiles*, says: “They”—that is, the Romans—“saw Simon Magus’s flight and the fiery chariots, blown apart by Peter’s mouth at the name of Christ, vanish. I say, they saw the man who trusted in false gods, and who, betrayed by those same gods whom he feared, fell by his own weight and lay there with his legs shattered” (Arnobius II; see Baronius, volume I, year 68).

Eusebius tells the same story in Book II of his *History*, where these words occur at the end of the narrative: “When the divine word had already reached the Romans”—through Peter’s preaching, of course—“Simon’s mad power was extinguished, and the man himself was quickly and utterly overthrown.”

Saint Epiphanius, in Heresy 21, says: “Simon is found to have paid nature’s debt in the city of the Romans, when that wretched man collapsed and died in the midst of the city of the Romans.”

Saint Jerome, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Peter, testifies that after his episcopate of the Church of Antioch he went to Rome to overthrow Simon Magus.

Sulpicius Severus expresses the same view: “That celebrated contest of Peter and Paul against Simon was exceedingly remarkable. When Simon, supported by two demons, flew up by magical arts in order to prove himself God, the Apostles’ prayers drove away the demons; he fell to the ground in the sight of the people and was torn apart.

Finally, Saint Augustine, writing to Casulanus, testifies on the basis of many reports that the Saturday fast was instituted at Rome on that occasion, saying: ‘This indeed is the opinion of many, although many Romans say that it is false’ (Letter 86).” The material cited above follows.

By these words Augustine does not signify that the opinion concerning Peter’s contest with Simon is uncertain, as Calvin supposed [Col. 0149C], but rather that the cause of the Saturday fast is uncertain, as Cardinal Bellarmine correctly observed (*On the Roman Pontiff* I.23). For although it is certain—as the cited authors and many others unanimously relate—that Peter contested Simon at Rome and overcame him, no one before Augustine relates that this occurred on the Lord’s Day, that the preceding day was observed by fasting, or that the Saturday fast was instituted for that reason. It is concerning this fast, and the differing opinions of many about it, that Augustine argues in that Letter.

Elsewhere, however, Augustine clearly confirms that Simon was destroyed and killed through the work of Blessed Peter, when he says: “In the city of Rome, Blessed Peter the Apostle destroyed Simon Magus by the true power of almighty God” (*On Heresies* I). By these words he left no room for doubting that this contest took place.] Magus. (Acts VIII). From this it becomes still clearer that Peter did not do this as a matter of canonical custom, but rather because of the immediate necessity of the contest. Indeed, in that case, too, for this same matter Peter appears to have imposed on his disciples not a general but a special fast; and he certainly would not have done so if he had known that the fast was ordinarily observed by canonical custom. Undoubtedly he would likewise have been prepared to impose it on the Lord’s Day if the occasion of the contest had fallen on that day; yet a canonical rule of fasting would not immediately have been promulgated on that account. It was not a general observance that established it, but the reason of necessity that compelled it to be done once.

## CHAPTER XI. How the solemnity of the Lord’s Day is observed differently from the custom of other days

[Col. 0149B]

Yet this, too, must not be overlooked: on the Lord’s Day only one Mass is celebrated before the meal [Note: [Col. 0149C] We have already observed several times that Cassian understands by this one Mass the service performed for the assembly of the monks for divine worship, and the Author himself indicates as much here. Nevertheless, there is nothing to prevent the sacrifice of the Mass from also being included in this assembly, since it was especially for this reason that the monks gathered in the church.

Notice also that no mention is made here of None. The implication is that they took their meal at Sext, that is, after the office of Sext, or at midday, as was customary on the Lord’s Days, while on other days they fasted until None. Saint Benedict followed this practice in chapter 41 of his Rule: “On Wednesday and Friday let them fast until None; on the other days let them dine at Sext.” Thus on the Lord’s Day they celebrated one Mass before the meal, because they gathered in the church only once and continuously performed the divine office there; on other days they performed it privately at the appointed hours, namely Terce, Sext, and None, with intervals between, as stated in chapter 2 of this book.] In it they devote something more solemn and earnest to psalms and prayers, or readings, out of reverence for the Sunday assembly or communion, and they regard Terce and Sext alike as completed within it. Thus nothing is diminished from the service of prayers, since readings are added; nevertheless, the brothers appear to be granted a certain difference or relaxation out of reverence for the Lord’s resurrection.

This relaxation, more than at other times, seems to temper the observance of the entire week; and, because this particular difference is interposed, it makes the same day, as a feast day, once again eagerly awaited with greater solemnity, and makes the fasts of the coming week less burdensome through anticipation of it. For any fatigue is always endured more calmly, and labor is undertaken without weariness, if some alternating change or any kind of alteration in the work intervenes.

## CHAPTER XII. On which days, when supper is provided for the brothers, a psalm is not recited as they come to eat, as is customary at meals

[Col. 0150B]

Finally, even on those days—that is, [Note: [Col. 0149D] He calls Saturday and Sunday “days of rest,” or “times of rest,” because on both days the Easterners rested and abstained from work (Palladius, *Lausiac History* 7). They regarded both as feast days and festive occasions, and held sacred assemblies both on Saturday and on Sunday, as stated above. Nevertheless, there is no doubt that, apart from Saturdays and Sundays, other periods of rest and solemn days also existed among them, on which they did not fast but could eat the midday and evening meals, as on Saturdays and Sundays, with the same ceremony and distinction from other days that are mentioned here.] Saturday or Sunday, or other times of rest, when both the midday and evening meals are customarily provided for the brothers—a psalm is not recited at evening: that is, neither when they come to supper nor when they rise from it, as is customary at solemn meals or at the canonical breaking of the fast. Customary psalms ordinarily precede and follow this meal [Col. 0151A]; but they come to supper after a simple prayer, and, when they rise from it, conclude it again with prayer alone. The reason is that this meal is an extraordinary one among the monks, and not all are required to assemble for it, except visiting brothers who have arrived, those whom bodily weakness brings, or those whom their own desire invites.

[Note: [Col. 0150C]

It was an ancient custom of the monks to place psalms or hymns before and after meals; hence they were called “customary” or “habitual” psalms. This was done following the example of Christ, who is said to have sung a hymn with his disciples after the sacred meal: “And after singing the hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives” (Matthew XXVI, Mark XIV). The Greek expression is καὶ ὑμνήσαντες (*kai hymnēsantes*), that is, “when they had sung praise to God.” According to Augustine on Psalm LXXII, this Greek expression encompasses three things: praise, praise of God, and song—or praise accompanied by singing.

Some think that Christ sang one of the customary Jewish hymns (Walfrid, *On Ecclesiastical Matters* 25; Radulph of Tournai, proposition 13). For the Evangelists speak as though they meant a familiar hymn: “After singing the hymn.” Paulus Burgensis writes that the Jews were accustomed to recite seven psalms in place of thanksgiving, namely from Psalm 112, which begins, “Praise the Lord, you servants,” through Psalm 118.

Others think that Christ composed some new hymn. Maldonatus reports this view (*Commentary on Matthew* XXVI). Chrysostom, explaining Matthew’s words, says: “Let all those who rise like swine, eating simply in drunkenness, hear this, when they ought to give thanks and bring the meal to an end with a hymn.”

Philo the Jew, in his book *On the Contemplative Life*, reports that the first Alexandrian ascetics sang hymns at table: “Before they recline, they stand together in a single orderly line, raising their hands and eyes toward heaven—raising their eyes because they have learned to contemplate heavenly things, and their hands because they are unstained by gifts and illicit gain—and they pray that the banquet may be pleasing to God. When the prayers have been completed, the elders recline,” and so forth.

Further on he says: “Then he”—the presiding officer—“rises and is the first to sing a hymn in praise of God, either newly composed by himself or taken from one of the ancient poets. The others then imitate the presider in orderly fashion, while all listen attentively and quietly, except at the end of the hymn and its final clause; then everyone raises his voice,” and so forth.

Saint Jerome, writing about the Egyptian monks in Letter 22 to Eustochium, says: “After the ninth hour they come together; psalms resound, and the Scriptures are read according to custom. When the prayers have been completed and everyone has sat down,” and so forth. “Then they rise together, and after the hymn has been sung, they return to their stalls,” that is, to their cells (see Eusebius, *History* II.10).

But, to mingle something playful with serious matters and season spiritual austerity with the sweetness of a little joke—which the Greeks call εὐτραπελία (*eutrapelia*, “wit” or “good-humored playfulness”; Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* IV.8)—I recall on this occasion some very charming and memorable verses that I remember reading in an old manuscript. In them the customary blessing of the table and thanksgiving, both on fasting days and on nonfasting days, are distinctly expressed and identified by the opening verses of the psalms from which they are taken.

Thus a certain brother, who perhaps did not love fasting, versified them in his own way:

> I love “Let them confess,” for in the evening I proclaim the meal.  
> I hate “He made a memorial,” for in the evening it takes away the meal.

For when there is no fast, the thanksgiving begins with the verse: “Let all your works give thanks to you, O Lord,” and so forth. When there is a fast, it begins with the verse: “He made a memorial of his wonders,” and so forth.

He embraced both blessings in a limping verse:

> Twice the Eyes will eat; only once will they Eat.

That is, on nonfasting days the blessing begins with the verse: “The eyes of all hope in you, O Lord,” and so forth [Col. 0152B]; whereas on fasting days it begins with the verse: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied,” and so forth. Thus wrote that witty versifier.] 

## BOOK FOUR. ON THE INSTITUTES OF RENUNCIANTS

[Col. 0151]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0151B]

On the canonical manner of psalms and prayers that ought to be maintained in the daily assemblies throughout the monasteries, we now proceed, as the order of our narrative invites us, to the institution of the one who renounces this world. We shall endeavor to set out briefly, as far as we can in speech, the conditions under which those who desire to turn to the Lord are received into monasteries.

We shall combine some elements from the rules of the Egyptians and some from those of the Tabennesiots [Note: [Col. 0151D] Tabenna is an island in the River Nile where Saint Pachomius founded a notable monastery, which was the head and, as it were, the metropolis of the other monasteries of his institution, as Palladius and Sozomen testify (Palladius, *Lausiac History* 38, *Life of Pachomius*; Sozomen, III.13). The monks who followed Pachomius’s institutes were called Tabennesiots and Tabennesians. Saint Jerome briefly describes their manner of life and institutions in the preface to the Rule of Pachomius, which he translated into Latin and which we shall also append at the end of this work.] whose coenobium in the Thebaid [Col. 0151C] is the more populous by comparison with all others, and the stricter in the rigor of its way of life in proportion to its numbers. Indeed, more than [Note: [Col. 0151D] Saint Jerome, Sozomen, Nicephorus, Palladius, and others testify that seven thousand monks lived under the Rule of Saint Pachomius at one and the same time. Yet they did not live in one coenobium or under one abbot, as Cassian says here. Saint Pachomius founded and organized several monasteries in Egypt and the Thebaid.

But in the coenobium of Tabenna, which is under discussion here, Saint Pachomius presided. It was the largest of all and the head of the others, as stated above; from it they also received their prefects and abbots. It is recorded that no more than thirteen or fourteen hundred monks lived under Pachomius in that coenobium. This number was distributed, in accordance with the prescription of the angel who dictated the monastic Rule to him, into twenty-four classes or ranks, corresponding to the number of Greek letters. Each class was given a name suited to its character and condition: for example, the simpler and more modest were called ι and ο, the crafty and difficult ζ and ξ, and others were designated by the names of other letters, according as the form of each letter seemed aptly to express the manner of life and character of each class. “Only the spiritual understand what was signified,” says Palladius.

Accordingly, what is asserted here about five thousand brothers living in that one coenobium under one abbot seems not to refer to the time of Pachomius but to a later period, when it is credible that the monastic community had grown to such a number. Saint Jerome also writes in his Letter to Eustochium that approximately five thousand monks lived in separate cells at the same place, Nitria (Letter 22.14).] five thousand brothers [Col. 0152B] are governed under one abbot. Such obedience is found there, with so large a number of monks subject in every age to their elder, that among us one man could scarcely either obey another for a short time or preside over him.

## CHAPTER II. That among them they persevere in the coenobia until extreme old age

How their such long perseverance, humility, and submission continue for so long, and by what discipline they are formed, so that they persevere in the coenobium until [Note: [Col. 0152D] “Bent old age,” which makes people stooped and decrepit; they are called *silicernii* because, with their bodies bent, they look upon the stones—that is, the ground. We shall discuss elsewhere the longevity and extreme old age of the monks and anchorites of antiquity (Conference 3.1).] bent old age, I think we ought first of all to touch upon [Col. 0153A]. [Note: [Col. 0153A] It may be unclear to what these words should be referred: whether to the perseverance, humility, and submission mentioned above, or to the institution or examination discussed in the following chapter, which he also mentioned shortly before. The meaning would then be that the examination and probation carried out among the Tabennesiots at the time of entry were so thorough that there was nothing comparable to the examination, probation, and year-long training in Cassian’s monasteries.

The former interpretation, however, appears both more immediate and more suitable. For he wishes to signify that their constancy, humility, and obedience were so great from the very beginning of their training—that is, from their first formation and novitiate—that it is not surprising that they reached the highest perfection in extreme old age. ## CHAPTER III. By what examination the person to be received into the coenobium is tested
Therefore, anyone who seeks to be received into the discipline of the coenobium is not admitted outright, but only after keeping watch at the doors for ten days or more and demonstrating the evidence of his perseverance and desire, as well as of his humility and patience. And when he has prostrated himself at the knees of all the passing brothers, and has been deliberately rejected and despised by everyone, as though he wished to enter the monastery not for the sake of religion but under compulsion,

> **[Note: [Col. 0153B]** Saint Pachomius received this practice of testing and carefully examining those who wished to become monks, and of not admitting them hastily, from the angel who dictated his Rule, and handed it on to his Tabennesiot monks. For article 26 of that Rule, in the version of D. Jerome, reads as follows:
>
> “If anyone comes to the door of the monastery wishing to renounce the world and be numbered among the brothers, he shall not have permission to enter. Rather, the father of the monastery shall first be notified, and he shall remain outside before the door for several days. He shall be taught the Lord’s Prayer and as many Psalms as he can learn, and he shall carefully give proof of himself, lest perhaps he has done something and, disturbed, depart after a time; or lest he be under some authority and unable to renounce his parents and despise his own possessions. If they see that he is suitable for everything, then he shall be taught the remaining disciplines of the monastery: what he ought to do and whom he ought to serve, whether in the assembly of all the brothers, in the house to which he is to be assigned, or in the order of eating. Once instructed and perfected in every good work, he shall be joined to the brothers. Then they shall strip him of his secular clothing and dress him in the monks’ habit. He shall be handed over to the doorkeeper, so that at the time of prayer he may bring him into the presence of all the brothers; he shall sit in the place assigned to him. The clothing that he brought with him shall be received by those appointed for this matter, brought into the storeroom, and placed under the authority of the monastery’s superior.” Thus far the Rule.
>
> Other Fathers who composed monastic Rules followed this institution as well, such as the patriarchs of the monks, D. Basil and D. Benedict, as may be seen in their respective places (Basil, *Longer Rules*, ch. 10; Benedict, Rule, ch. 58).
>
> But, to return to our Author: because testing is directed toward profession, and reaches its conclusion and completion in it, he therefore treats in this book, with little distinction, both of the testing that constitutes an initial renunciation and of profession, in which renunciation of the world is properly and perfectly made. Hence the particular title of this book was taken: *On the Institutions of Those Who Renounce*, that is, of those who profess monasticism, or the monastic life, as has been said.
>
> It will therefore be useful to note here, in summary, what the institutions of those who renounced the world were among those ancient monks: that is, what rites, procedure, and method governed both testing and profession—or, in D. Benedict’s language, what was the discipline for receiving brothers.
>
> The first institution was that someone coming to the monastery to be received was not immediately granted entrance. Instead, he was ordered or permitted to keep watch for several days outside the doors or at the entrance of the monastery, so that his willingness, humility, perseverance, and the like might be tested. Palladius supplies numerous examples of this in the *Lausiac History*; but one especially memorable example is that of Paul the Simple, which I leave for the reader to examine and admire.
>
> D. Benedict followed the trace of this institution when he established three stages of testing, as Turrecrematus noted: “The first,” he says, “is at the monastery gate, for four or five days; the second is in the guest cell, for two months; the third is in the novices’ cell, for ten months.”
>
> The second institution was the removal of the old clothing and the putting on of new clothing. Cassian, Pachomius, Basil, and Benedict speak of this in the passages cited above. This rite is extremely ancient and was received from the tradition of the apostles, as will be said below. From it, the practice arose that novices should wear a religious habit, though one distinct from the habit of professed monks.
>
> The third was that a novice was not permitted to bring any possessions whatsoever into the monastery—not even money to be contributed for the monastery’s common use—as is stated in chapter 4. This was distinctive among those monks, since most other monks, even from the time of the apostles, contributed to monasteries whatever they possessed in the world when they became monks (Acts 4), as will be said below.
>
> The fourth was that a brother who had been received should be tested for a full year under obedience and the discipline of the monastery. This is to be understood of adults or adolescents, not of children or minors. This period of testing, or novitiate, was granted by the holy Fathers both for the benefit of the convert—that is, the novice—and for that of the monastery, “so that he may test its way of life and it may test his,” as Pope Innocent III says (*De Regularibus*, chapter *Ad Apostolicam*). Hence D. Benedict, in addition to the three stages of testing mentioned above, included a full year and several days.
>
> The fifth was that during this period the humility and obedience of the novices and juniors should be tested and exercised in every possible way. Cassian discusses this from approximately chapter 4 to the end of the book, especially in chapter 10, where he says:
>
> “The rule of obedience is observed with such strictness that the juniors, without the knowledge or permission of their superior, not only do not dare to go outside their cell, but do not even presume on their own authority to satisfy a common and natural necessity. Thus they hasten to fulfill everything that he has commanded, as though it had been issued from heaven by God, without any questioning. Sometimes, even when things impossible for them have been commanded, they receive them with such faith and devotion that they strive with all their strength and without any hesitation of heart to accomplish and complete them,” and so forth.
>
> The sixth was that, once the annual testing had been completed, novices who appeared capable and suitable were joined to the assembly of the brothers—that is, admitted to profession. I mean a profession identical in substance with that which novices make today, namely, of the three vows: poverty, chastity, and obedience.
>
> Cassian mentions profession and vows in general in chapter 33, where he says that Abbot Pynuphius declared very severe punishments prepared for those who had carried out the discipline of the Rule lukewarmly and negligently, and who had failed to offer God the appropriate fruits of holiness according to what they had professed, or according to what people believed of them. “For,” he says, “according to Scripture, it is better not to vow than to vow and not fulfill.”
>
> In the following chapter he says that a monk ought to resemble a crucified man, who not only does not walk where he wishes or do what he wishes, but can neither walk nor do anything unless he is moved by another. Again, in chapter 38, he says that a monk who has professed perfection commits no small sin if he pursues what is imperfect.
>
> He speaks equally clearly and explicitly about each of the individual vows, so that he plainly indicates that all who embraced monasticism were bound by those three vows—if not explicitly, at least tacitly and interpretatively—according to the institution of the holy Fathers and common observance.
>
> Nothing more explicit or precise could be said about the vow of poverty than what is found, among other places, in chapter 36: “that you may persevere to the end in this nakedness which you have professed before God and his angels.” He teaches that this poverty, or nakedness, was strictly observed by them in chapter 3 and those that follow.
>
> He supplies clear evidence of the vow of continence and chastity both in that comparison between a monk and a crucified man, where he says that monks, crucified through fear of God as though by certain nails, ought to be dead not only to bodily vices but, in a certain sense, even to the elements themselves (chapters 34 and 35), and also in his statement that they most carefully observed the practice whereby juniors, especially, disclosed all their thoughts, even their most secret ones, and the devil’s suggestions, or fiery darts, to an elder (chapters 8 and 9).
>
> Hence D. Basil, in *Longer Rules*, disputation 15, seriously warns that those who do not wish to undertake the monastic life together with a profession of virginity must be dismissed altogether. And in the preface to his *Monastic Constitutions* he says:
>
> “Therefore, whoever wishes to be free from the bonds of the world flees marriage as though it were a kind of snare; and, having abandoned it, consecrates his life to God and professes chastity, so that he no longer has the possibility of returning to marriage.”
>
> As for obedience, Cassian discusses its bond and observance throughout almost this entire book, as is clear from what has been said and will become clearer below. In particular, in chapter 12 he teaches that they valued the virtue of obedience and placed it above all other virtues to such an extent that they judged everything else ought to be postponed to it, and preferred to suffer every loss rather than violate this good in any respect.
>
> You have here, reader, the principal rites and conditions of both monastic testing and profession observed among the Tabennesiot, or Pachomian, monks. Consult the Author for a fuller explanation of them.]**

## CHAPTER IV. Why they do not wish the possessions of one who is enrolled in the community of monks to be applied to the monastery’s uses

And for this reason they do not consent to receive from him even money that could benefit the uses of the coenobium.

> **[Note: [Col. 0156D]** With great zeal for perfection, those Pachomian monks, pursuing the highest poverty and accustomed to live solely by the work of their hands, as has been said elsewhere (*Book III*, chapter 3), allowed no possessions or money whatsoever to be brought into the monasteries by those whom they received—not even for common use—so that they might apply themselves more diligently to manual labor (Sozomen, book 3, chapter 3; Nicephorus, book 9, chapter 14; Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 38; see *Conferences*, 24.10).
>
> That they could live solely by this is clear from Cassian’s statement in chapter 14 of this book concerning certain monks: each day one of them contributed so much income from his own labor and sweat to the monastery that from it he could support not only his own small needs but also have enough left over for the needs of many.
>
> Yet the institution and custom of other monks and religious communities were not the same. From the very beginnings of the Church, the first religious persons brought the prices of their possessions to the apostles’ feet, and the proceeds were distributed to each according to his need (Acts 4).
>
> Such was also the practice of the ancient monasteries: they accepted whatever those becoming monks wished to contribute for common use. Hence they were said to offer themselves and their possessions to God. Thus D. Augustine says in chapter 3 of his Rule: “Those who had possessions in the world when they entered the monastery should willingly wish that they be held in common.”
>
> Saint Benedict likewise, as is read in the *Life of Saint Placid*, did not allow the possessions of his monks to be diverted elsewhere than to his monasteries, so that from them he could support many servants of God. And in chapter 58 of his Rule he decrees that the person to be received should first distribute whatever possessions he has to the poor, or contribute them to the monastery by a formal donation.]**

First, lest, puffed up by confidence in this offering, he should in no way deign to make himself equal to the poorer brothers; and then, lest through this pride he should never descend to the humility of Christ, and, being unable to persevere under the discipline of the coenobium, should leave and later, having cooled from the spiritual fervor with which he had been inflamed at the beginning of his renunciation, attempt to recover and demand, in a sacrilegious spirit and not without injury to the monastery, what he had brought in.

They had frequently been taught by many experiences that this must be observed in every respect. For in less cautious monasteries, some who had been received in their simplicity attempted, after a great blasphemy, to demand back what they had brought in and what had been distributed for the work of God.

> **[Note: [Col. 0157B]** The question is why it is a grave blasphemy, and what sort of blasphemy it is, to demand back possessions contributed to a monastery.
>
> **Answer:** This can be understood in two ways: first, of professed monks; second, of novices who had not yet professed but were still under probation. For, as has been said, the Author treats both indiscriminately in this book.
>
> If it is understood of professed monks, as the preceding words appear to indicate—“what he had brought in at the beginning of his renunciation, inflamed with spiritual fervor”—then it is certain that a monk who demanded back possessions contributed and incorporated into the monastery could do so only with immense blasphemy, that is, injury and irreverence toward God and the sacred place. This is especially true if he did it out of contempt or detestation of divine worship and religion, as apostates do (see Saint Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* II–II, questions 13 and 14). Such a crime also pertains to sacrilege. Hence he said above: “attempt to recover and demand, in a sacrilegious spirit and not without injury to the monastery.”
>
> But if it is understood of novices who had not yet professed or been bound by a vow, then either they had donated and contributed their possessions absolutely to the monastery, as persons legally free to do so, or they had not done so absolutely but under the condition that they would remain and profess in the monastery.
>
> If absolutely, then undoubtedly it was a grave or great blasphemy—that is, injury and irreverence, indeed sacrilege in the strict sense—to claim for oneself or demand back possessions consecrated or dedicated to God, following the example of Ananias. Gratian confirms this with many canons (*Decretum*, 17.4 and 19.3, chapter *Quae semel*, from the Council of Chalcedon, chapters 2, 3, 4, and 21).
>
> Reason also teaches that this is the moral precept of Leviticus 27: “Whatever has once been consecrated shall be most holy to the Lord”—that is, it shall remain perpetually sanctified and may not be converted to other uses, as Saint Thomas explains (*Summa Theologiae* II–II, question 88, article 11).
>
> If under a condition, it was still considered a grave blasphemy among those religious men and holy Fathers to demand back or take away possessions contributed to the monastery, because this displayed a certain contempt for divine honor and religion.
>
> In later centuries, however, the Church, taught by many experiences because of the more serious inconveniences and dangers to souls that arose or could arise from such donations by novices, decreed at the Council of Trent:
>
> 1. No renunciation or obligation of a novice, even one made under oath or in favor of any pious cause, shall be valid unless made with the permission of the bishop or his vicar within the two months immediately preceding profession; nor shall it be understood to take effect unless profession follows.
>
> 2. Before profession, apart from the novice’s food and clothing during the period of probation, nothing whatsoever may be given to the monastery from his possessions by his parents, relatives, or guardians under any pretext, lest he be unable to depart because the monastery possesses all or most of his property and he cannot easily recover it if he leaves.
>
> 3. Rather, the holy synod commands, under penalty of anathema, both those who give and those who receive that this must not be done in any way.
>
> 4. If they leave before profession, everything that belonged to them must be restored.
>
> 5. Nevertheless, by these provisions the synod did not intend to alter the pious institution of the clergy of the Society of Jesus.
>
> Thus far the Council (*Session 25*, chapter 16, *De Regularibus*).]**

## CHAPTER V. Why those who renounce the world, when received into monasteries, lay aside their own clothing and are dressed in other clothing by the abbot

For this reason, when someone has been received, he is stripped of every former possession so completely that he is not even permitted to retain the clothing with which he is covered. Instead, he is brought into the midst of the assembly of the brothers, stripped of his own clothing, and dressed by the hands of the abbot in the monastery’s clothing,

> **[Note: [Col. 0158C]** Thus D. Benedict says in the passage cited above: “The brother who is to be received shall be stripped in the oratory of the possessions in which he is clothed and dressed in the possessions of the monastery” (Rule, chapter 58).
>
> Blessed Dionysius the Areopagite counts this change of clothing, among the other rites of monastic profession transmitted and instituted by the apostles, in *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 6, and explains its meaning in these words:
>
> “The laying aside of the former garment and the assumption of another signifies that migration from the middle life”—that is, from the common life of secular people—“to perfection, just as in divine regeneration”—that is, baptism—“the changing of the shining garment signifies advancement from the purified life to the contemplative and illuminating state.”
>
> D. Jerome follows the same reasoning when instructing the monk Paulinus: “You change your tunic when you change your mind,” and so forth (Letter 13). In other words, it is not enough to change one’s tunic unless one also changes one’s mind for the better.
>
> In Letter 4, to the monk Rusticus, he rebukes certain monks who, after renouncing the world, had changed nothing of their former way of life except their clothing and the profession of their words.
>
> Cassian suggests another reason: namely, that by laying aside and removing one’s clothing, the renunciation of all possessions professed by monks may be signified (see the Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 26). Through this, he says, the monk is to recognize that he has been stripped not only of all his former possessions, but also, with every worldly pride laid aside, has descended to the poverty and want of Christ, and so forth.]**

so that by this he may recognize that he has been stripped not only of all his former possessions, but also, with every worldly pride laid aside, has descended to the poverty and want of Christ. He is now to understand that he will be supported not by resources acquired through worldly skill or preserved from his former faithlessness, but will receive the provisions of his service from the holy and pious generosity of the monastery. From that source he will henceforth be clothed and fed, recognizing that he possesses nothing; and, nevertheless, learning according to the Gospel saying not to be anxious about tomorrow, he must not be ashamed to be made equal to the poor—that is, to the body of the brotherhood—among whom Christ is numbered and whose brother he was not ashamed to call himself (Matthew 6). Rather, he should glory in having become a member of Christ’s household.

If, as time passes, they see that he can remain there and that he persists in the same fervor with which he began, they give the clothing to the needy. But if they discover that some fault of murmuring or any minor act of disobedience has arisen in him, they strip him of the monastery clothing with which he had been dressed, put back on him the old clothing that had been set aside,

and drive him out. he is not immediately permitted to mingle with the assembly of the brothers. Rather, he is assigned to an elder who lives apart, not far from the entrance of the monastery, and whose responsibility is to care for travelers and newcomers. He offers them every attention of welcome and hospitality.

After he has served there for a full year and has performed his service among the travelers without any complaint, having thereby been instructed in the first lesson of humility and patience and having been recognized through long practice in these qualities, he is to be joined to the congregation of the brothers. He is then handed over to another elder who presides over ten juniors—hence called deans; more will be said about them elsewhere—whom he has received from the abbot to instruct and govern together.

## CHAPTER VIII. With what initial practices juniors are exercised so that they may advance toward overcoming every desire

His principal concern and instruction will be this: to introduce the junior and enable him, in due course, to ascend even to the highest summits of perfection. He must first teach him to overcome his own will. By diligently and carefully exercising him in this matter, he will deliberately command him always to do what he perceives to be contrary to his disposition.

For, taught by many experiences, they assert that a monk—and especially a junior—cannot restrain even the pleasure of his own desire unless he has first learned, through obedience, to mortify his own will.

> **[Note: [Col. 0160D]** The first discipline of a monk is the mortification of his own will. “The purpose of the coenobite,” says Abbot John, “is to mortify and crucify all his own wills”; and he asserts that this perfection can be fulfilled by no one except a coenobite (*Conferences* 19.8).
>
> D. Jerome likewise says in Letter 4, to the monk Rusticus:
>
> “Do not do what you wish; eat what you are ordered to eat; wear what you are given; fulfill the task assigned to your work; submit to one to whom you do not wish to submit; come to your bed tired; walk and sleep; and before your sleep is complete, be compelled to rise.”
>
> D. Benedict also commends and inculcates this abandonment, or mortification, of one’s own will in many places, especially chapters 4, 7, 49, and 58. See D. Bernard, sermon 3 *On the Resurrection*, where he says much against one’s own will (D. Basil, *Monastic Institutions*, chapters 46 and 50).]**

They therefore declare that a person cannot prevail over or extinguish anger, sadness, or the spirit of fornication; that he cannot maintain true humility of heart, lasting unity with the brothers, or firm and enduring concord; and that he cannot even remain long in the coenobium unless he has first learned to overcome his own will.

## CHAPTER IX. Why juniors are commanded to conceal nothing of their thoughts from their elder

Having established these practices, they hasten to imbue and shape those whom they initiate for perfection, as though with elementary lessons and syllables. Through these practices they discern with complete clarity whether they are founded upon a false and imaginary humility or upon a genuine one.

To enable them to attain this easily, they are instructed not to hide at all in their hearts any troubling thoughts through a destructive confusion, but to disclose them to their elder as soon as they arise.

> **[Note: [Col. 0161B]** On the need to disclose evil thoughts to an elder or spiritual father, see the notes on *Conferences* 2.10.]**

They are not to entrust anything concerning the judgment of those thoughts to their own discernment, but are to believe that whatever the elder’s examination has considered and declared is either evil or good. In this way the crafty enemy cannot prevail in any respect against the young man as one inexperienced and ignorant, nor deceive by any trick the person whom he sees to be protected not by his own discernment but by that of his elder. Nor can he persuade him to conceal from his elder his suggestions—whatever fiery darts he may cast into the young man’s heart.

For the exceedingly subtle devil cannot otherwise mock or overthrow the junior unless he has enticed him, either through arrogance or through shame, to conceal his thoughts. They declare that it is a general and evident sign of a demonic thought if we are ashamed to disclose it to our elder.

## CHAPTER X. How great the obedience of juniors is, even in matters subject to natural necessity
After this [Note: [Col. 0161C] Thus St. Jerome, speaking of the Egyptian coenobites: “The first bond among them,” he says, “is to obey their elders and to do whatever they command” (Letter 22). Sulpicius, in the first Dialogue on the virtues of St. Martin: “The chief virtue there, and the first, is obedience; nor is anyone received into the monastery on arrival unless he has first been tested and proved, and is prepared never to refuse any command of the abbot, however arduous, difficult, or unworthy of endurance.” St. Augustine, discussing monks in Book I, chapter 31, of *The Morals of the Catholic Church*: “These men”—the fathers of monasteries—“with no arrogance, give counsel to those whom they call their sons, with great authority in commanding and great willingness on their part to obey.”] such a strict rule of obedience is observed [Col. 0162B] that the juniors, without the knowledge or permission of their superior, dare not merely leave their cell, but do not even presume on their own authority to satisfy their common and natural necessity.

[Note: [Col. 0161C] Similar statements are read throughout the writings of the holy Fathers. I have thought it worthwhile to cite some of them here, for greater clarity concerning this passage and as a commendation of perfect obedience. St. Basil, in *The Monastic Constitutions*, chapter 23, says: “Just as sheep obey their shepherd and enter whatever path he wishes, so those who are pious worshipers of God ought to obey their superiors, without scrutinizing their commands too inquisitively, whenever those commands are free from sin.” St. Jerome, in his letter to Rusticus the monk: “Fear your superior as a lord, love him as a parent; believe whatever he commands to be conducive to salvation; and do not sit in judgment on the decision of your elders, whose duty it is to obey and fulfill what has been commanded.” Gregory the Great, Book II, chapter 4, on *1 Kings*: “True obedience neither examines the intention of superiors nor distinguishes among commands; for whoever has subjected the whole judgment of his life to an elder rejoices in this alone: that he does what is commanded him. Whoever has learned to obey perfectly does not know how to judge.” St. Benedict, in his Rule (chapter 5), which the same St. Gregory testifies to be full of discretion and wisdom, describes true obedients in these words: “As soon as anything has been commanded by a superior, they do not know how to delay in doing it, as though the command had been issued by God himself.” Of such people the Lord says: “He obeyed me at the hearing of the ear” (Psalm 17 [18]). Finally, St. Bernard, in *On Precept and Dispensation* (chapter 6): “Whether God or a human being acting as God’s representative has delivered a command, it must certainly be obeyed with equal care and received with equal reverence—provided that the human being commands nothing contrary to God.” And again: “It is a sign of an imperfect heart and altogether weak will to scrutinize too carefully the statutes of elders, to hesitate over each injunction, to demand an explanation for everything, and to harbor suspicion concerning every command whose reason is hidden; and never to listen willingly except when one happens to hear what one may perhaps have wished to hear, or what either evident reason or undoubted authority has shown may or must be done otherwise.” Thus St. Bernard. By these and other praises of the holy Fathers it is clearly demonstrated that the obedience which is perfect and most acceptable to God is that by which a person obeys simply, without first examining the command, and does not wish to know why this or that has been commanded by a superior, being content with the fact that it has been commanded (Cassian has similar remarks in chapter 41 below). The only exception must always be a command that plainly contains sin; in such a case examination would be superfluous, since it is clear that one must obey God rather than human beings (Acts 5).]

Thus they hasten to fulfill every command given by him as though it had been issued from heaven by God, without any examination, so that sometimes even [Note: [Col. 0162D] By “impossible” understand not only what appears impossible to someone because it is very burdensome and difficult—as St. Benedict seems to understand the word in chapter 68 of the Rule, entitled “If impossible tasks are imposed on a brother”—but also what is genuinely impossible, exceeding human strength, or in itself unlawful; such things are also called morally impossible (see St. Thomas, I, q. 13, art. 5, ad 3). ## CHAPTER XI. What food is considered most luxurious among them

Passing over likewise that arduous and sublime form of abstinence [Col. 0164A] in which it is counted the height of luxury if a herb seasoned with salt, which they call *lapsanium*, is diluted with water and served to the brothers as food [Note: [Col. 0164B] Thus again in chapter 22 below: “Among them, a dish consisting of leek leaves, *lapsana*, roasted salt, olives, and tiny salted fish, which they call *maenidia*, is regarded as the greatest pleasure.” I think *lapsanium* is derived from *lapsana*. For *lapsana* is a wild vegetable, as Pliny testifies in Book XX, chapter 9, of the *Natural History*. Hence the proverb *lapsana vivere*, “to live on lapsana,” meaning to live on meager and poor fare. *Lapsana*, or *lapsanium*, was therefore a kind of relish made from vegetables seasoned with salt and diluted with water, and was regarded among those monks as a great delicacy. Thus in the *Life of St. Pachomius* (chapter 8) we read: “For they were accustomed to eat lapsana—that is, wild vegetables—and other herbs without oil.” *Lipsanum*, or in the plural *lipsana*—lest anyone confuse these words—has an entirely different meaning in ecclesiastical usage, namely sacred objects or the relics of saints. ## CHAPTER XII. How, at the sound of someone knocking at the door, they leave no task undone in their eagerness to respond quickly

Accordingly, while they sit in their cells and devote equal attention to work and meditation, whenever they hear the sound of someone knocking and striking the doors of the various cells [Note: [Col. 0164C] It may be inferred from this that the doors of the individual cells were customarily struck with a wooden mallet or some similar instrument, and that the monks were thereby summoned either to the divine office or to manual labor, as we noted above (Book III, chapter 2), where Cassian calls the person who performed this duty the *compulsor*. The custom is still observed among us at the funerals of deceased brothers, as we shall explain elsewhere.
