I think that the following passage of the Emperor Leo in his *Panegyric on St. Chrysostom* also refers to the same practice: “While they were still hesitating, the watchman awakened them for the morning hymns by blows upon the wood” (see the scholia on the Rule of St. Pachomius).], summoning them, of course, either to prayer or to some task, each one rushes competitively from his cell [Note: [Col. 0164C] That is, from their rooms or cells. St. Benedict, describing true obedients and plainly imitating this passage, says: “Therefore such men, immediately abandoning what is their own and forsaking their own will, at once leaving unfinished what they were doing and with their hands empty, follow by the swift foot of obedience the voice of the one commanding through their deeds; and, as though in a single moment, the command of the master and the completed work of the disciple are speedily and simultaneously accomplished in the haste inspired by the fear of God, by those who are moved by love to advance toward eternal life” (Rule, chapter 5). Turrecrematus comments: “Concerning this degree of obedience it is read in the *Lives of the Fathers* that Abbot Silvanus had twelve disciples, one of them named Mark, whom he loved more than the others because of the excellence of obedience that was in him. When some people told him that the others were saddened by this, he led them through the brothers’ cells and, knocking at each door, called them; but no one came out. Finally he called Mark, who immediately came out, leaving unfinished the letter he was writing. When Silvanus saw this, he said to them: ‘There is why I love him.’ They replied: ‘Indeed, you should love him more, because he is loved more by God’” (Book III, no. 143). So far Turrecrematus. The example is reported somewhat more fully in the *Lives of the Fathers*, where this is added: when the abbot entered Mark’s cell—for Mark was a scribe—he found the gathering of pages on which he had been writing, and discovered that at the moment he was called he had left unfinished the letter O that he was forming, doing so solely in order to fulfill obedience. Thus it is recorded there. Cassian’s intention in this passage, and likewise St. Benedict’s in the passage cited above, is sufficiently shown by the style of both.] so that the one engaged in writing does not dare to finish the letter [Col. 0165A] he has just begun, but springs up with the greatest speed at the very moment when the sound of the knocking reaches his ears. He does not insert even as much delay as would be required to complete the outline of the initial stroke he has begun; instead, abandoning the unfinished lines of the letter, he hastens with his whole energy and zeal to practice the virtue of obedience rather than pursuing the saving of time or profit from the work.

They prefer obedience not only to manual labor, reading, silence, and the quiet of the cell, but even [Col. 0166A] [Note: [Col. 0165B] They judged religious obedience preferable to all the moral virtues for many reasons (St. Thomas, II–II, q. 104, arts. 3 and 4; q. 186, art. 8). First, because through obedience one consecrates one’s own will to God, and this is rightly preferred to all human goods. Nothing is greater or dearer to a human being than the freedom of one’s own will, or the power to live according to one’s own judgment. A religious abandons this freedom when, for God’s sake, he subjects himself entirely to another’s will; and this is surely greater and more difficult than abandoning wealth, honors, or bodily pleasures (see Jerome Platus, *On the Good of Religious Life*, Book II, chapter 5). Those are external goods, which even pagans have sometimes abandoned in pursuit of knowledge of natural things. But the power to live according to one’s own judgment and will is a spiritual good proper to human beings as such, and no philosopher ever thought it should be despised or abandoned. Hence St. Gregory, Homily 32 on the Gospels: “Perhaps it is not difficult for a person to leave his possessions; but it is exceedingly hard to leave himself. For it is less to deny what one has, but very much indeed to deny what one is.” Therefore to abandon and deny this very thing for God’s sake is a greater perfection and merit than to abandon wealth, honors, or the allurements of the flesh.

A second reason is that through obedience the acts of all the other virtues become meritorious. “All works of virtue,” says St. Thomas, “are meritorious before God because they are performed in order to obey the divine will.” For even if someone endured martyrdom or distributed all his possessions to the poor, these deeds could not be meritorious unless he directed them toward fulfilling the divine will—which certainly belongs to obedience—just as they could not be meritorious if performed without charity, which cannot exist without obedience. Thus St. Thomas. See also Leonard Lessius, Book II of *On Justice*, chapter 46, doubt 5. Since charity is the queen of all the virtues, obedience is certainly next to it and most like it: both unite one with God, and both cause one to will and reject the same things as God. The only distinction is that charity does so in the manner of a friend, while obedience does so in the manner of a subject. For this reason theologians also call obedience the form of the other virtues, since the actions of all of them are directed toward this one end: the fulfillment of the divine commands.

A third reason is that the vow of obedience contains the other vows within itself, as the same St. Thomas says. For although a religious is bound by vow to preserve chastity and poverty, these too fall under obedience. Thus, although obedience is a particular virtue, it has a general force, since it embraces everything belonging to religious life. Let the reader remember that above I spoke of religious obedience—that is, obedience confirmed by a vow in the religious state. This includes not merely the ordinary and common virtue of obedience, which concerns only the obligation of a command, but also the virtue of religion, by which God is properly worshiped, and which, by universal agreement, holds first place among the moral virtues. [Col. 0166B] In this sense it is said that obedience is better than sacrifice (1 Kings 15), insofar as it is contained under religion, says Cajetan (in the passage cited above in his commentary on St. Thomas); and it belongs to the superior act of religion, namely devotion. In this sense it is rightly preferred to sacrifices, because, as Gregory says, “through sacrifices another’s flesh is slaughtered, but through obedience one’s own will is slaughtered” (Book IV of the *Morals*, chapter 121)—that is, it is offered and consecrated to God.

I also said that obedience should be preferred to the moral virtues, not to the theological virtues, again following the teaching of St. Thomas. “The virtues,” he says, “by which one cleaves to God in himself, namely the theological virtues, are superior to the moral virtues, by which something earthly is despised in order to cleave to God.” In addition to what has been said about the excellence of religious obedience, I would also like to bring here a notable passage from the *Lives of the Fathers*, where the privilege of coenobitic obedience is splendidly commended above the other virtues and even above the various states of human life, and adorned with distinguished praises (Book V, pamphlets 14 and 19). It reads as follows:

“One of the Fathers related that he had seen four orders in heaven. The first order consisted of sick people who gave thanks to God. The second consisted of those who practiced hospitality and diligently served the sick. The third consisted of those who lived in solitude and did not see human beings. The fourth consisted of those who subjected themselves for God’s sake to spiritual Fathers in order to obey them. The order of the obedient wore a golden necklace and a crown, and had greater glory than the others. I said to the one who was showing me all these things: ‘How does this order, which is small, have greater glory than the others?’ He replied: ‘Because those who practice hospitality do this according to their own will. Likewise, those who withdraw into the desert have departed from the world according to their own judgment. But this order, which has devoted itself to obedience, has cast away all its own wills and depends upon God and the command of its spiritual Father; therefore it has greater glory than the others.’

“And shortly afterward: ‘Therefore, children, strive to acquire some trace of this virtue. Obedience is the salvation of all the faithful. Obedience is the mother of all virtues. Obedience is the discoverer of the kingdom of heaven. Obedience opens the heavens and raises human beings from the earth. Obedience dwells with the angels. Obedience is the food of all the saints; for through it they were weaned, and through it they attained perfection.’”

Thus it is recorded there. See more in John Climacus, *The Ladder*, step 4, which concerns obedience, and in the most holy Father Ignatius of Loyola, in his letter on obedience, truly more than golden and worthy of every acceptance.]

They prefer obedience to all the virtues to such an extent that they judge everything else must be set aside for it and are content to undergo every loss, provided that they do not appear in any way to have violated this good.

## CHAPTER XIII. How criminal it is considered if anyone calls even the most insignificant thing his own

[Note: [Col. 0166D] Here we have the vow and practice of poverty, customary and perpetual even among the monks of ancient times, since it is no less essential and necessary to the religious state than the vows of chastity and obedience. To this virtue—voluntary poverty—those monks undoubtedly bound themselves by a vow, if not an explicit one, then at least an implicit one, when they professed their desire to become monks and undertook the monastic life, as was shown above. They observed it so strictly and religiously that they were not permitted to retain, possess, or claim as their own and private property any object whatever, however small, as is stated here. More will be said about this below.]

Among the rest of their institutions, I think it superfluous even to mention that no one was permitted to possess a small chest, no one a private [Note: [Col. 0167A] *Sportella* and *sportula* are both diminutives of *sporta*, a wicker vessel formerly used for carrying food and also money. Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book XX, chapter 9: “*Sportula* is a diminutive of *sporta*; and *sporta* is so called because it carries something out, or because it is made from *spartum*.” Hence Saul’s words to his servant: “What shall we bring to the man of God? The bread in our bags is gone, and we have no *sportula* to give to the man of God.” There *sportula* is taken to mean some gift, the container being used for the thing contained, as has been noted in the margin. Among the Romans, *sportulae* were called the gifts or food allowances distributed by wealthy men to those who had accompanied them in the performance of their duties or had paid their respects to them at home while wearing the toga (Alexander ab Alexandro, Book V, chapter 24). By a similar analogy St. Cyprian calls *sportulae* the fixed stipends or subsidies given each month to certain clerics and priests; those who received such allowances were therefore called *sportulantes* (Cyprian, Letter 34; Baronius, under the year 253). Cicero uses *sportella* for a certain type of confectionery in his letter to Papirius Paetus, when he says: “You must unlearn your little baskets and your pastries.” Here, however, *sportella* properly means a small wicker basket, just as *cistella* means a small chest. It is clear in itself why the author mentions these receptacles: money and other private possessions were ordinarily stored in them, and he wished to signify how completely those monks were removed from every fault of ownership and embezzlement, since they did not even have a little chest or box in which to hide a coin or anything private for themselves.] basket, nor anything of such a kind that, retaining it as his own, he ought to secure it with his personal seal [Note: [Col. 0167C] That is, with a signet ring or a private key. More will be said about these below (chapter 15).].

We know them to have been naked in every respect, so that, apart from [Col. 0168A] [Note: [Col. 0167C] St. Jerome, as I have reported elsewhere on another occasion, describes the clothing and entire equipment of the Tabennesiot monks as follows: “They have nothing in their cells except a *psiathium* and two *lebitonaria*—a kind of sleeveless garment among the Egyptian monks—and one worn garment for sleeping or working; also a linen cloak, two hoods, and a goatskin, which they call a *melote*, a little linen belt, sandals, and a staff as a companion on journeys.” Thus Jerome calls the *lebitonaria* *colobia*, which has the same meaning, and the linen cloak a *maforte*, and he adds hoods, which the author here omits.

Concerning the *colobium*, *maforte*, sandals, and *melote*, we have spoken in Book I. The *psiathium*—also called *psiathus* and *psiathius*, as is evident from Collation 18, chapter 1, and other passages—is understood as a mat or covering made of rush, papyrus, or straw; the French call it a *natte*. The *Life of St. Pachomius* says: “After entering the monastery and praying, he came to the kitchen and found the brother in charge of the kitchen working on *psiathoi*”—that is, mats, as the common people call them—and so forth. St. Ambrose, on 1 Corinthians 14: “Let them sit and discuss: the elders in dignity in chairs, those next in rank on benches, and the last on the floor upon mats.” Gregory of Tours, *Life of the Fathers*, chapter 11: “He had no bed made of hay or straw, except only that which is customarily made from woven rods of rush, which the common people call mats.” The Rule of St. Benedict, chapter 55: “The bedding should be sufficient: a mat and a blanket,” and so forth. Peter of Auvergne, Letter 20 of Book I: “Prepare the ancient work of the monks, mats on which you may sleep either always or often.” The same author, Letter 50 of Book II: “He himself sat upon the monastic mat that lay beside his seat.” The Egyptian monks therefore used the mat or *psiathium* as a bed and covering, and at other times as a seat, as can be seen in Book V, chapter 35, and in the first Collation, chapter 23, where they are sometimes said to have sat upon and sometimes to have lain upon *psiathia*.

As a passing addition, Caelius Rhodiginus writes (Book VII of the *Ancient Lessons*, chapter 23, and Book XXVIII, chapter 2) that among the Greeks the first seat in tribunals, the presiding chair, was customarily called πρῶτον ξύλον—that is, “the first wood”; lower seats or humbler benches were called *psiathia*.] they possessed only a *colobium*, *maforte*, sandals, *melote*, and *psiathium*, they had nothing more. Yet even in other monasteries, where certain relaxations are granted more freely, we see this rule still observed with the greatest strictness, [Note: [Col. 0168B] You can see, reader, with what zeal and fervor those true monks and coenobites embraced the perfection of coenobitic life, which received its name from the perfect common ownership or sharing of all things and the complete renunciation of private property. How deeply they recoiled from the vice of ownership is shown by the fact that no one dared to say, even in words, that anything was his own; indeed, it was considered a great crime and severely punished if someone, without even thinking about ownership, said “my book,” “my tablets,” and so forth.

They had learned from their predecessors to abstain from such expressions, lest they display even the slightest appearance of ownership and lest they depart from the pattern of apostolic institution. For concerning the first coenobites, the disciples of the apostles, we read in Acts 4: “No one claimed that any of his possessions was his own, but everything was held in common.” The holy Fathers who founded religious orders and monasteries adopted this institution and practice, and diligently commended it in their Rules and monastic constitutions, so that no one should call anything his own but rather ours—that is, common property (Trithemius, *On Monastic Property*, chapter 6; Basil, *Monastic Institutions*, chapter 21; Augustine, chapter 2 of the Rule; Chrysostom, Homilies 58 and 59, and Book III *Against the Critics of the Monastic Life*; Basil, *Longer Rules*, chapter 32). Hence among them the familiar saying: “Let ‘mine’ and ‘yours’ not be heard among ascetics; let them be far from monasteries.”

St. Benedict likewise, to omit others, following everywhere in the footsteps of the earlier monks and concerned to eradicate the vice of ownership from his coenobites, first commands that everything be common to all, as it is written; then he adds: “Let no one call or presume to call anything his own.”

For the rest, let no one go astray on this account and suppose that a religious or coenobite always commits a mortal sin when he says “my book,” “my robe,” and so forth, since the entire force of words depends upon the mind and intention of the speaker. One must consider in what sense and with what attitude something is called “mine,” “yours,” or “his.” If a religious person calls something his own with the intention of having, possessing, or using it as private property, there is no doubt that he sins mortally and commits the crime of ownership against the vow of poverty. It is otherwise if he calls something his own by reason of an administration entrusted to him, or merely with respect to its use and for as long as it pleases his superior. Still less is there fault if he says it inadvertently or absent-mindedly, through a customary manner of speaking, especially since for a long time that perfect common ownership or sharing of all things—even as regards use—has ceased to be observed so strictly among coenobites, and no religious person is found without certain private items granted for his use, even by decree of the sacred Council of Trent, session 25, *On Regulars*, chapter 2.

Accordingly, although those holy and perfect monks are greatly to be praised and commended who recoiled from the vice of ownership with such zeal that they did not dare even in words to call anything their own, others are not therefore to be reproved or blamed if, with knowledge joined to zeal, they religiously say “my book,” “my tunic,” and so forth, without any sense or affection of ownership, but merely by reason of use or of a lawful administration granted to them. But to explain these matters more fully is not the purpose of this place. See Navarrus, *Commentary on Regulars*, Book II.]

so that no one would dare even to say in words that anything was his own, and it was considered a great crime for “my book,” “my tablets,” [Col. 0169A] “my stylus,” “my tunic,” or “my sandals” to have proceeded from a monk’s mouth [Note: [Col. 0169B] A *graphium* was a bronze or iron stylus with which people formerly wrote on wax tablets; we still use one for such writing tablets.]. For this, if such a word happened to escape his mouth through inadvertence or ignorance, he had to make satisfaction by performing an appropriate penance.

## CHAPTER XIV. Although much money is amassed from the work of each individual, no one nevertheless presumes to exceed the frugal sufficiency that has been established
And although each of them contributes to the monastery every day such substantial income from his own labor and sweat that it can sustain not only his own modest allowance but even provide an abundance for the needs of many, nevertheless none of them is puffed up by this, nor does he flatter himself because of the considerable profit and sweat of his work. Beyond the two *paxamacia* [Note: A *paxamacia*, or, as others read it, *paximacium*, was a small loaf of about six ounces; two *paxamacia* were assigned to each monk as his daily measure of food. These two together did not amount to a full pound, as can be seen in *Collation* 2, chapter 19, and *Collation* 12, chapter 15. Palladius, in the *Life of Paul the Simple*, calls them *paxamidia*: “Antony brings loaves and places four *paxamidia* on the table; he soaked one for himself, for they were dry.”]—which are scarcely sold there for three denarii—[Note: It may seem remarkable that two *paximacia*, weighing at least a pound of bread or approximately that, could be obtained in that desert solitude for three denarii, or even less—unless one attributes this to the fertility of Egypt, of which Pliny says in *Natural History* XVIII.10 that it was called “the common granary of the world.” For this denarius, here and often in Cassian, does not mean the silver coin which the Romans called a denarius (Mark 12; Luke 21), because it was worth ten asses; rather, it signifies a small as, that is, a bronze coin worth one-tenth of a silver denarius. In Greek it is called λεπτόν (*lepton*), “the small coin,” and in French a Tournois denier, or little denier (Jansen, *Harmony of the Gospels*, chapter 121). For the Author’s words clearly indicate that he means the smallest coin when he says, “They are scarcely sold for three denarii,” that is, “they are sold”; as though he were saying, “at the very lowest price,” which even the poorest desert-dwellers could easily pay from the proceeds of their manual labor. Certainly this would not have been the case if he meant a silver denarius.] no one presumes to claim anything more for himself.

Among them [Note: What a private undertaking is among monks will be explained below (chapter 16).] no one has any desire for a private undertaking—something which it is shameful to mention, and which, if only we did not even know how to do it in our monasteries—not in practice, I say, nor even in thought. And since he regards the monastery’s entire storehouse [Note: *Entheca* signifies a granary, storehouse, pantry, or repository of treasure. Pope Gelasius uses this word in Gratian, *Decretum* XII, question 2, chapter *Vobis enim*. Thus the *entheca* of the monastery is what we commonly call the common fund of the monastery’s goods; below it is called the sacred common treasury (chapter 20). Each coenobite believes it to be his substance, as the Author says, because he is nourished and provided for by the common goods, as though they were his own, enjoying them under the abbot’s direction and disposition, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “As having nothing, yet possessing everything” (2 Corinthians 6). Here one should note the remarkable statement of Navarre concerning the goods of a monastery: “The goods of a monastery are common to its religious members, but not in such a way that individuals may claim a definite portion of the common goods as their own, or some particular item—for example, this garment or this book—or even a fixed use of them; as a common estate belongs equally to several heirs appointed jointly, or as purchasers contribute equally to the price. Rather, they are common to all as a whole, because all have in common within the monastery’s common fund the use of, and right to, food and clothing, as brothers and members of a household; but no one has a definite portion, nor a definite use. Their use is common, necessary rather than excessive, and always dependent upon the judgment of the superior. In this religious differ from secular canons, among whom the individual claims one thing and the chapter or college another in the common goods.” So Navarre, *Commentary 2 on Religious Persons*, no. 65, and *Commentary 4*, no. 23.] of the monastery as his own substance, and, as master of all things, devotes all his care and concern to everything [Note: *Dependat* is used for *impendat*, “expends,” as Dionysius translated it. Lucan, Book VIII, said *dependisse caput felicibus armis*—“to stake one’s life on fortunate arms”—meaning to expend or pour out one’s life in order to obtain victory.], in order to preserve the virtue of the nakedness he has embraced—a virtue which he strives to guard perfectly and inviolably to the end—he considers himself so much a stranger to everything and alien to all things that he behaves as a pilgrim and regards himself as an inhabitant of this world, a dependent and servant of the monastery, rather than presuming himself master of anything.

## CHAPTER XV. On our excessive eagerness to possess.

[Col. 0170B] [Note: Let whoever reads understand, and let whoever has ears to hear listen.]

What shall we wretched men say to this? We live in monasteries, placed under the care and supervision of an abbot, [Note: To carry personal keys with the intention of concealing something from the abbot or superiors, or of withdrawing it from their disposition and claiming it as one’s own, is undoubtedly the sin of proprietorship, contrary to the vow of monastic poverty. Hence the Fathers call it theft and sacrilege (see Basil, *Monastic Constitutions*, final chapter). Augustine says in chapter 17 of his Rule: “If anyone conceals a thing given to him, let him be condemned as a thief.” Saint Caesarius says in his Rule: “No one shall have a private cell, cupboard, or any locked enclosure.” The Cassinese monks state in chapter 22 of the Rule: “No brother may have keys to chests, benches, or anything else without permission,” except the cloister prior, to whom alone they allow the power to apply a lock to a bench or chest that may be opened with a key, and so forth. It should be noted that this Rule makes an exception for the prior; by the same reasoning, other superiors and officials who have some administrative responsibility are also excepted. They necessarily have keys for safeguarding money, documents, and other possessions, as the learned Father Julius Nigronus wisely observes in his ascetical writings (*On the Second Rule of the Society of Jesus*). He adds: “All storerooms and workshops should likewise be locked—wine stores, clothing stores, pantries, libraries—and it is sometimes necessary for the cupboards within them to be secured with locks. The keys to these storerooms are kept and guarded by their custodians.” This is what he says, together with what follows.] yet we carry personal keys, and, having trampled underfoot all the shame and disgrace of our profession, [Col. 0171A] we are not ashamed to wear openly on our fingers even rings with which we mark and seal our stored possessions [Note: These are signet or seal rings, which the ancients used not only to seal letters and epistles with an impressed seal, but also to lock the doors of houses, chests, and boxes in place of keys (see Durantus, *On Ecclesiastical Rites* II.9; Coelius Rhodius, *Ancient Readings* VI.12). Indeed, they used them even to guard the keys themselves more securely, as Pliny reports in *Natural History* XXXIII.1, comparing the conditions of his own time with ancient customs: “What was that life of the ancients, what innocence, in which nothing was sealed? But now even food and drink are protected from theft by a ring; and it is not enough even to have sealed the keys themselves. When people are weighed down by sleep or dying, their rings are removed.” So he says. Clement of Alexandria likewise says that the ring given at betrothal as a pledge and always worn by the wife on her finger was not worn so much for adornment as so that, with that same ring, she might seal the things kept at home (*Paedagogus* III.11). Some monks devoted to private property therefore concealed and wore such rings on their fingers in order to guard their possessions more carefully, as the Author indicates. Their projecting bezel, or gem, served in place of a key.]—rings with which we seal away not only little chests or baskets, but not even chests or cupboards suffice for storing the things we accumulate or have reserved after leaving the world.

And sometimes we become so inflamed over things that are most worthless and of no value, claiming them solely as our own, that if anyone presumes to touch one of them even with a finger, we are filled with such anger [Note: “Be filled with anger” (*suppleri iracundia*) is used for “be filled with wrath,” a scriptural expression meaning “to become exceedingly angry” (Ecclesiasticus 39; Luke 4; Acts 5 and 13). Elsewhere we read “be filled with grief” (*suppleri dolore*) in *Collation* 9.26 and 18.11; “be filled with fury” (*suppleri furore*) in *Collation* 16.18; and “be filled with darkness” (*suppleri caligine*) in Book 10, chapter 2.] that we cannot restrain the agitation of our hearts even from our lips or from the whole expression of our bodies.

But setting aside our own vices, and consigning to silence those things which are not even worthy of mention, in accordance with the saying, “Let not my mouth speak of human works” (Psalm 16), let us rather continue, in the order of our narrative, with the virtues that exist among them and that we too ought to pursue with every effort. Let us now set forth the rules and patterns briefly and in outline, so that, when we later arrive at certain actions and deeds of the elders which we intend to commit carefully to memory, we may strengthen what has been arranged in our exposition with the strongest testimonies, confirming everything we have said by their examples and the authority of their lives.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the rules governing various corrections.

[Col. 0172A]

If, then, anyone should accidentally break a clay *gillon*, which they call a *baucal* [Note: Who would understand *gillo* unless Cassian had explained it to some extent? From his explanation we infer that it was a pottery drinking vessel, also called by another barbarous word, *baucalis* (Junius, *Nomenclator*). The Spanish call it a *congilon*, the Italians a *boccale* or *boccalium*, and the French a *flascon*. The Greek word βαυκάλιον (*baukalion*) occurs in Aphrodisius’ *Problems* and means a small vessel with a narrow mouth and a swollen body, suitable for drinking or preserving liquid. The barbarous and vernacular words derive from it.] he shall expiate his negligence only by a public penance. With all the brothers assembled in the synaxis, he shall remain prostrate on the ground and ask forgiveness until the service of prayers has been completed; he shall obtain it only when, by the abbot’s judgment, he is ordered to rise from the ground.

In the same way anyone shall make satisfaction who, summoned to some task or to the customary assembly, arrives late; or who, while chanting a psalm, stumbles even slightly. Likewise, if he answers excessively, harshly, or obstinately; if he performs an assigned service carelessly; if he murmurs even lightly; if, preferring reading to work or obedience, he carries out the appointed duties sluggishly; if, after the synaxis has been dismissed, he does not hasten quickly back to his cell [Note: “The congregation” means after the service has been completed. Elsewhere: “after the congregation’s Mass,” “after the Mass of prayers,” “after the canonical Mass has been completed,” and similar expressions.]; if he stops with someone even briefly, or withdraws somewhere for a moment; [Note: This is because such conduct is alien to religious purity and modesty. In some religious communities it is strictly forbidden for one person to touch another. The Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 53, says: “No one shall speak to another in the darkness; no one shall sleep with another; no one shall hold another’s hand” (see above, Book 2, chapter 15).] if he has held another’s hand; if he presumes to converse even briefly with one who is not a cohabitant of his cell [Note: Thus two or more persons sometimes lived together in the same cell. Cassian confirms this in *Collation* 20.1–2, where he calls the inhabitants of the same cell *syncellites*. See also the annotations on this subject in *Institutes* II.12 and V.37.]; [Note: The suspension from prayer and prohibition of prayer have been discussed above (Book 2, chapter 16).] if he prays with one who has been suspended from prayer; if he sees a parent or a secular friend [Al. “tries to see”] or speaks with them without his elder’s permission; [Note: According to Navarre, it belongs to the vice of proprietorship in a monk to send or receive letters without the consent or permission of his superior, although it may also be referred, for another reason, to the sins of disobedience or incontinence. It is disobedience insofar as he secretly violates the command of obedience; it is incontinence if it tends toward a violation of chastity (Navarre, *Commentary 2 on Religious Persons*, no. 13, and *Counsel* 73, “On Religious Persons”). An exception is made for letters permitted in certain cases by common law (chapter *Ex parte* and chapter *Olim*, *On Accusations*) or by the statute of the congregation. Hence the holy Fathers strictly prohibited this practice. Saint Basil, cited by Smaragdus—although I have not yet been able to locate the passage—says: “No monk may receive any gift, including letters, or presume to give one without the abbot’s order” (*Letter* 2). Saint Jerome, among the instructions on religious life given to Nepotian, says: “Frequent little gifts, handkerchiefs, ribbons, offered and tasted foods, and flattering, sweet little letters have no place in holy love” (*Letter* 48). Elsewhere he bitterly laments the wicked dealings, through secret letters, of a certain deacon Sabinianus with a consecrated virgin. Saint Augustine says in his Rule: “Whoever has advanced so far in evil as secretly to receive letters or any gift from someone—if he voluntarily confesses this, let him be forgiven, and let prayer be offered for him. But if he is discovered and convicted, let him be corrected more severely according to the judgment of the superior” (chapter 14 and sermon 3, *On the Common Life of Clerics*). He then gives the reason why nothing may be secretly, that is, without the superior’s permission, be received: “Since the brothers of this congregation have renounced not only their resources but also their own wills at the very time of receiving their ordination, and have submitted themselves through their promised obedience wholly to the power and commands of others, in Christ and for Christ, it is certain that they ought to have, possess, give, or receive nothing without the superior’s permission.” Thus Augustine. Finally, Saint Benedict says in chapter 54 of the Rule: “Under no circumstances may a monk receive or give letters, blessed loaves, or any little gifts, either from his parents or from anyone else, or from one another, without the command of his abbot.” See Turrecremata on this passage.] if he attempts to receive someone’s letter or to reply without his abbot.

This far, and in such and similar offenses, spiritual correction proceeds. But the remaining offenses, which are tolerated among us as though indifferent—though we sustain them even more reprehensibly—are open insults, manifest contempt, arrogant contradiction, unrestrained and undisciplined wandering, familiarity with women, anger, quarrels, hostility, and disputes; [Note: A “private undertaking,” mentioned above as well (chapter 14), is something a person works for himself—that is, for his own advantage or profit, not for the common good—or something he presumes to do on his own authority or rashly, contrary to or apart from the abbot’s intention. Hence Saint Augustine says in chapter 16 of his Rule: “Let no one work for himself, but let all your works be done for the common good, with greater zeal and more fervent enthusiasm than if each of you were working for yourselves.” For charity, of which it is written that it “does not seek its own” (1 Corinthians 13), is understood in this way: it places common things before private things, not private things before common. Therefore, the more carefully you attend to the common matter rather than your own, the more you should know that you have advanced. Saint Benedict likewise guards against this by ordering that the brothers’ beds be frequently inspected by the abbot, lest a private undertaking be found there; and if one is found anywhere, the offender is to undergo the most severe discipline (chapter 15 of the Rule).] the presumption of a private undertaking; the contagion of avarice [Note: The vice of avarice is treated fully and expressly in Book 6 of these *Institutes*]; affection for and possession of unnecessary things not possessed by the other brothers; extraordinary and furtive eating; and things of this kind [Note: In this chapter Cassian distinguishes lighter offenses from graver ones, listing several examples of each and also recalling the different penalties and corrections established and applied by those Fathers for each category. The lighter offenses receive spiritual correction; the graver, corporal correction—of which he again makes two kinds: one involving blows or scourging, the other expulsion from the monastery. He describes spiritual penance as follows: when someone has been publicly corrected for negligence and lies prostrate on the ground before the brothers in the synaxis—that is, in the assembly or oratory—until, after the prayer or service has been completed, he obtains forgiveness from the abbot (see above, the notes on Book 3, chapter 7). It is called spiritual in contrast to corporal because it does not touch the body but is imposed for the contrition of the spirit and the humiliation of the mind. Saint Benedict, our holy Father, admirably imitated and reproduced this ancient institution of the monks, so that he seems to have transferred almost this entire passage of Cassian into his Rule. In chapter 70 he prescribes public rebuke: “Let those who sin be corrected in the presence of all, so that the others may have fear,” which is taken from the Apostle, 1 Timothy 5. He prescribes prostration and a plea for forgiveness even for lighter offenses in chapter 44: “Those who are excommunicated only from the table for light offenses shall make satisfaction in the oratory until the abbot commands otherwise; and they shall always do this until he gives his blessing and says, ‘It is enough.’” And in chapter 46: “If anyone, while laboring at any task—in the kitchen, cellar, service, bakery, garden, or any craft—or in any place at all, commits an offense, breaks or loses something, or exceeds the proper bounds in any way, and does not immediately come before the abbot or the congregation, but voluntarily makes satisfaction and discloses his offense, then, once it has become known through another person, he shall be subjected to more severe correction,” and so forth. Again, in chapter 71: “If a brother is corrected for any very small reason by the abbot or by any superior in any manner, or if he perceives even slightly that the mind of any superior is angry or disturbed against him, however mildly, he shall immediately, without delay, remain prostrate on the ground before that superior’s feet, making satisfaction until the disturbance is healed by his blessing. If anyone refuses to do this, he shall either undergo corporal punishment or, if he is obstinate, be expelled from the monastery.” Here you see both forms of corporal correction mentioned by Cassian and also prescribed by Saint Benedict. For a fuller explanation of this passage, it will be useful briefly to note the five or six stages of regular discipline or correction to be exercised toward those who commit grave offenses, which interpreters derive from chapters 23, 28, and 65 of Saint Benedict’s Rule. The first stage is private admonition by the elders; the second, public rebuke and correction; the third, the burning of excommunication, if the guilty person understands what excommunication means, or otherwise corporal punishment, namely, a penalty of blows or fasts; the fourth, the common prayer of all the brothers for his conversion and correction; the fifth, deposition, or deprivation of honor and office; the sixth and final stage is the cutting iron, that is, the sentence of separation from the body of the monastery. This, says Turrecremata, may be imposed either by enclosure or imprisonment, or by complete expulsion from the monastery.]—are corrected not by the spiritual rebuke we have described, but either by blows or by expulsion.

## CHAPTER XVII. By whose authority it was instituted that sacred readings should be recited in monasteries while the brothers eat, and how much silence is observed among the Egyptians.

That sacred readings should be recited in monasteries while the brothers eat [Note: Cassian frequently uses *type* for a rule, institution, custom, or manner of acting. The Cappadocian monks from whom he says this pattern or custom of reading at table, or during meals, originated were undoubtedly those whom Saint Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia and an outstanding promoter and interpreter of monastic life in the East, had as disciples and instructed with those truly golden Rules or monastic institutions. They were mentioned in the preface to this work (Baronius, under the year 363, toward the end). Saint Basil’s institution of sacred reading during meals is not so much explicitly stated as presupposed in his *Shorter Rules*, question 180, which we shall cite shortly. Other Fathers cited below also commend it, including Saint Benedict: “The reading of the brothers while they eat must not be absent” (chapter 38 of the Rule). Not content with this, he expressly prescribes the manner of reading and the office of the reader: “Nor may whoever happens to seize the book presume to read there; but the one who is to read for the whole week shall enter on Sunday,” that is, to read, well prepared in what he is about to read, as Turrecremata says. “After entering, following Mass and Communion, he shall ask all to pray for him, that God may ward off from him the spirit of pride,” and so forth. Having received the blessing, he shall then enter to read.] we should understand as having proceeded not from the Egyptian custom [Col. 0175A] but from that of the Cappadocians.

There is no doubt that they [Note: Both reasons for instituting sacred reading at table are equally approved and commended by the Fathers, as may be seen in Turrecremata, tractate 101 on the Rule of Saint Benedict, where he assigns three reasons for this institution; but the first and second seem to concern spiritual exercise. The first reason, then, is that while the body is refreshed, the soul also, or inner person, may be fed and refreshed with its own food, namely the word of God or salutary teaching (Sidonius, Book IV, letter 9). On this subject there is a very ancient decree of Pope Eutychian in these words: “Let sacred reading be recited, so that those dining may rejoice that they are refreshed not only with bodily food but indeed with the nourishment of the heavenly word” (*Roman Penitential*, title V, chapter 2). Saint Augustine likewise touches on this reason in his Rule for clerics (chapter 7): “When you come to table, until you rise from it, listen without tumult or disputes to what is customarily read to you; let not the throat alone take food, but let the ears also hunger for the word of God.” Abbot Smaragdus also says (on the Rule of Saint Benedict, cited above): “Therefore reading must not be absent from those who eat, so that, attending to sacred reading, the brothers may eat their bread in silence, according to the Apostle (2 Thessalonians 3). For as the body is refreshed with bodily food, so the soul must be refreshed with spiritual food. Therefore, when seated at table, let them be silent, and let reading be done daily and at every meal while food is taken, so that both persons—the outward with food and the inward with the word of God—may be refreshed; for it is written: ‘Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God’ (Matthew 4).” Thus he.

The second reason is that our mind, intent upon sacred reading, may be drawn away from greed and excessive pleasure in food and from the vices consequent upon them. Thus Saint Basil, having proposed this question, “With what disposition or attention ought we to hear what is read while we recline at table?” (in the place cited above), replies: “With much greater delight than that with which we eat or drink, so that it may appear that the mind is not distracted toward bodily pleasures, but takes far greater delight in the words of the Lord”; as did the man who said, “Sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Psalm 118). Thus Basil.

The third reason, given here by Cassian, is that idle and harmful conversations, detractions, and disputes, which are commonly generated at banquets, may be avoided. Hence this decree is read in the African council in Burchard and in the Third Council of Toledo, chapter 7: “Out of reverence for God and the priests, this holy synod universally decrees that, because idle tales are often introduced at table, reading from the divine Scriptures shall be included in every priestly meal. By this means souls are built up for good and unnecessary tales are prohibited” (Book II, chapter 169; Gratian, distinction 44). Possidius, bishop of Calama, says in the *Life of Blessed Augustine*: “At table itself he loved reading or discussion more than feasting and drinking; and, against the pestilence of human custom, he had this written there:

‘Whoever loves to gnaw at the life of the absent with his words,
let him know that he is forbidden this table.’

“And therefore he admonished every guest to abstain from superfluous and harmful tales and detractions.” Thus he. Conversely, Saint Bernard (*Apology to Abbot William*) sharply rebukes certain monks of his own time because they entirely neglected this religious institution received from their elders and occupied themselves while eating only with vain and idle talk. “O how far,” he says, “we are from the monks who lived in Antony’s days! For when they visited one another in charity, they received from one another the bread of souls with such eagerness that, utterly forgetting bodily food, they often passed the whole day with their stomachs fasting, but not their minds. And this was the right order, when service was first rendered to the worthier part. This was supreme discretion, when that which was greater received more. This, finally, was true charity, when souls, for love of whom Christ died, were refreshed with such care. But when we come together into one—as I use the Apostle’s words—it is no longer to eat the Lord’s supper (1 Corinthians 11): for now there is no one to seek or to offer heavenly bread. Nothing is said of the Scriptures, nothing of the salvation of souls; but trifles, laughter, and words cast into the wind are produced. During the meal, as much as throats are fed with dishes, so much are ears fed with gossip; wholly intent on it, one cannot know moderation in eating. Meanwhile dish is set upon dish,” etc. Saint Bernard states this no less elegantly than aptly for the present passage.

Cassian further suggests here that this reason for sacred reading at table, as the weightier and more necessary one, ought rightly to be preferred to that spiritual exercise or meditation for which the mind is usually less fit at mealtime and which is practiced only by a few more perfect persons. For he says that sacred readings are customarily recited to brothers while they eat not so much for spiritual exercise as to restrain excessive and idle conversation, etc.] wished to establish this not so much for spiritual exercise as to restrain excessive and idle conversation, and especially the disputes which usually arise at banquets, because they saw that these could not otherwise be restrained among them. Among the Egyptians, and especially among the Tabennesiots, such complete silence is observed by everyone [Col. 0176A] that, when so great a number of brothers sit down together for the purpose of eating, no one dares even murmur except the one [Note: It is evident from this that the brothers in one refectory were divided into distinct groups of ten, or *decanies*, and that each decany had its own dean or overseer sitting among and presiding over it. Saint Jerome also indicates this in his letter to Eustochium: “Each decany proceeds to table with its own father, and they serve in turn each week” (*Letter* 22; see above, the note on chapter 10).] who presides over his decany. Yet if he notices that something needs to be brought to or removed from the table, he indicates it by a sound rather than by his voice.

[Note: This is a notable passage concerning the silence to be observed by monks at table. Saint Jerome also mentions it in *Letter* 22, describing the customs of coenobites: “There is no noise during eating; no one speaks while he eats.” Saint Benedict likewise legislates in chapter 38 of his Rule: “Let the greatest silence be observed at table, so that no one’s whisper or voice may be heard there except that of the reader. The things necessary for those eating and drinking shall be supplied to one another by the brothers in such a way that no one needs to ask for anything. If anything is nevertheless needed, let it be requested by the sound of some signal rather than by voice.” Commenting on this passage, Abbot Smaragdus wisely notes that what is prescribed here is not simply silence, nor just any kind of silence, but absolute silence: “There is a difference between silence and absolute silence. Absolute silence exists where no voice and no whisper is heard. Ordinary silence exists where people speak, but softly and silently. Thus in the Gospel (John 2), Martha called Mary quietly—that is, secretly and in a subdued voice—saying, ‘The Teacher is here and is calling you.’ The Rule speaks of the first kind of silence when it says (chapter 42): ‘At all times let the monks strive for silence’; of the second when it says: ‘At table and during the night let absolute silence be observed.’” Smaragdus then discusses the signs and gestures used to preserve silence according to the prescriptions of the Rule, which the Author mentions here and whose use still continues in well-ordered monasteries. Thus Saint Fructuosus says: “If something is lacking at table, the one in charge shall give a sign or gesture and indicate to the server what needs to be brought to or removed from the table.” Elsewhere he says: “If anything necessary is wanted at table, no one may dare to speak, but he shall give the servers a signal by making a sound.” This is what he says. The ancient use of such signs can also be demonstrated from the Rule of Saint Pachomius, translated into Latin by Saint Jerome, where the thirteenth article reads: “If anything necessary is wanted at table, no one shall dare to speak, but he shall give the servers the sound of a signal.” Nicephorus mentions the same signs in Book 9, chapter 14. The following is related in the *Life of Saint Odo of Cluny* concerning the custom of the Cluniacs: “Whenever necessity demanded that something be requested, various signs were repeatedly made among them to accomplish what they wished; these, I suppose, grammarians would have wished to call signs of the fingers and eyes. Their system had grown so thoroughly among them that, even if deprived of the service of the tongue, the signs themselves would have been sufficient to indicate everything necessary.” This is found there (see John Moschus, *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 67). Pope Innocent III also strengthened and confirmed this institution of the holy Fathers and the law of silence at monks’ tables in the famous decree beginning *Cum ad monasterium*, “Concerning the Status of Monks”: “In the oratory, refectory, and dormitory, continuous silence shall always be observed.”]

Such discipline of silence is maintained among those who eat that, with their cowls lowered below their eyes—so that their unrestricted gaze might not have the opportunity to wander inquisitively—they look at nothing beyond the table and the foods placed upon it or taken from it. Thus no one observes how, or how much, another is eating.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How unlawful it is to taste any food or drink outside the common table
Before or after they receive the regular common meal, the strictest care is taken that no one presume to indulge his mouth with any food at all outside the common table [Alternative reading: “or drink”], so that, when they walk through gardens and orchards and apples hang attractively and abundantly from the trees, presenting themselves not only to the breasts of those passing by but also, fallen upon the ground, offering themselves to be trampled underfoot, and lying ready to be gathered, they may easily entice those who see them to consent to desire, and by their availability or abundance provoke even the strictest and most abstinent to long for them: it is regarded as sacrilege not only to taste anything from these, but even to touch them with the hand, unless it is openly displayed to all while they are eating together and publicly distributed for consumption through the steward’s administration and the service of the brothers.

> **Note:** R. P. Julius Nigronus (*In Reg. Soc. Jesu*) aptly observes that this chapter does not seem to correspond to its heading and title, because no mention of drink is made here, as in the heading itself. Hence he suspects that a textual error has entered and that one should read *potusve* (“or drink”) rather than *penitus* (“at all”). This is so, first, because the word *penitus* seems superfluous in this passage and is also absent from Dionysius the Paraphrast, as well as from Smaragdus, who cites this testimony, though in abbreviated form (*In Reg. D. Benedicti*); and, second, because a copyist’s error could easily have occurred owing to the similarity of the words. Thus the Egyptian monks allowed themselves no food or drink outside the canonical times, that is, outside the regular common meal.

> The Author places this instruction elsewhere also among the precepts of the more perfect life, which clarifies the ambiguity of this passage. Thus he says (*Book V, chapter 20*): “The monk who desires to advance to the struggles of inward combat must first impress this precaution upon himself: that, overcome neither by the pleasure of any drink nor by the enjoyment of any food, he should never allow himself to take anything outside the table before the proper hour of the regular common meal; and even after the meal has ended, he should not permit himself to presume upon any quantity of food from it.” Again, elsewhere (*Book IV, chapter 12*), after listing lesser faults, he explains the graver ones, among which he has these words relevant to the present subject: “An extraordinary and furtive eating of food is corrected not by that admonition which we have called spiritual, but either by blows or by expulsion.”

> St. Augustine likewise prohibited this in his Rule (*chapter 9*): “When someone cannot fast, nevertheless let him not take any food outside the hour of dinner, except when he is ill.” And St. Benedict says in chapter 43: “Let no one presume to take any food or drink before the appointed hour or afterward.” The same principle is found in the Rule of St. Pachomius (*article 43*), where we read: “Let no one keep in his cell anything to eat except what he has received from the steward.”

> Finally, Cassian above (*Book IV, chapter 16*) reported that the ancient Fathers considered the vice of furtive eating so serious that, if they found anyone guilty of it, they corrected him not merely by the admonition with which lesser offenses were punished, but either by blows or by expulsion. Understand this according to the regulation of Pachomius: namely, if anyone should dare to possess or secretly eat anything furtively and without the knowledge of the superior, apart from what he had received from the superior or, with the superior’s permission, from the steward. Concerning this, you have a notable example in the second Conference of Serapion, chapter 13.

> We also read that this same offense, as a crime involving personal property, was prohibited under severe penalty by St. Isidore of Seville: “Let no contamination of furtive eating defile anyone, nor any shameless or private appetite outside the common table. For whoever tastes anything either secretly or outside the common table shall be subject to the sentence of excommunication.”

## CHAPTER XIX. How the daily services are rendered to the brothers throughout Palestine and Mesopotamia

So that we may not seem to have omitted anything concerning the institutions of the monasteries, I think it useful to mention briefly how the daily services are also rendered to the brothers in other regions. Throughout Mesopotamia, Palestine, Cappadocia, and the whole East, the brothers take turns each week in performing these duties, so that, according to the number of the monastery, a corresponding number of ministers is appointed.

> **Note:** Something concerning these regions was said above (*Book III, chapter 1*).

> **Note:** Cappadocia is a region in Greater Asia, bordering Galatia and Pamphylia on the west, Lesser Armenia on the east, Cilicia on the south, and the Euxine Sea on the north. Its capital, or metropolis, first called Mazaca and later Caesarea by Claudius Tiberius, was the city in which St. Basil, himself a Cappadocian, served as bishop (*Pliny, Book VI, chapter 3; Strabo, Book XII*).

> **Note:** St. Jerome also mentions this institution as having been observed among the Pachomian, or Tabennesian, monks. In the preface to the Rule of St. Pachomius he writes: “Let them go together to work, or let them succeed one another in the weekly service in due order.” And in Letter 22, speaking of the Egyptian monks: “Each group of ten goes to the table with its father; they serve in turn each week.” Likewise St. Benedict says in chapter 35: “Let the brothers serve one another, and let no one be excused from kitchen duty except one who is occupied by illness or by some matter of great importance, because thereby greater reward and charity are acquired” (see Turrecremata there).

> The same rule was established, though somewhat more briefly and obscurely, for regular canons in the Council of Aachen (*chapter 123*): “In turn, in the refectory and in the other common necessities, let them perform the duty of brotherhood for one another.” Hence the brothers who discharge this weekly ministry are called *hebdomadarii* or *septimanarii*, and expressions such as “to leave the week” and “to complete one’s week” occur in St. Benedict. “The one leaving the week,” he says, “shall clean the utensils on Saturday.” Likewise: “Those leaving the week shall recite this verse: ‘Blessed are you, O Lord,’ etc.”

> Our predecessors commonly had weekly ministers of various kinds, as John Molanus notes (*Book I on Canons, chapter 15*). There is a weekly minister in the divine office, whose duty it is, during his week, to begin all the Hours, chant the chapters and Collects, and celebrate the principal Mass. There was also a weekly reader at table, concerning whom an entire chapter appears in the Rule of St. Benedict. Finally, among the monks there were weekly ministers, or *hebdomadarii*, serving and assisting both in the kitchen and at the table; these are the ones under discussion here.

> In this office, as Abbot Regino reports elsewhere (*Book II*), Carolomannus, the illustrious prince of Austrasia, offered an outstanding example of humility and patience. After abandoning and despising his earthly kingdom for Christ’s sake, he withdrew into the monastery of Monte Cassino and bound himself to the strict discipline of St. Benedict. It happened that he was appointed weekly minister for kitchen duty. Since he made many mistakes through ignorance, the cook, inflamed with wine, slapped him three times; he endured this with a calm countenance. But when a companion disclosed his rank, he was thereafter treated with great reverence.

> St. Bernard also writes of St. Malachy that, while he was in the monastery of Ibiacum, he performed kitchen service in his turn, even though he was a bishop, and served the brothers as they reclined at table.

They hasten to fulfill these duties with such devotion and humility that no servant renders his service to the harshest and most powerful master with greater zeal. Indeed, not content with these services alone, which are discharged according to canonical rule, they even rise at night and, by their diligence, assist those specially charged with this care; they strive secretly to anticipate and complete the tasks that those men are required to perform.

Each person who undertakes one of these weekly turns remains in service until the Sunday supper. When it has been completed, the ministry of the entire week is concluded in this manner: when the brothers assemble to sing the psalms that they customarily chant before retiring, those who are to take over wash the feet of all the brothers in order, earnestly seeking from them, as the reward of the labor of the entire week, this blessing: that, after they have fulfilled their duty, a prayer uttered by all the brothers may follow, interceding either for their errors or for sins committed through human weakness, and commending to God, like a rich sacrifice, the complete service of their devotion.

Then, on the second day of the week, after the morning hymns, as others again take their place, they hand over the utensils and vessels with which they have served. Those who receive and guard them do so with such vigilance and care that nothing belonging to them may be diminished or lost. They believe that, even for the smallest vessels, they will have to give an account as of sacred objects, not only to the steward who is present but also to the Lord, should anything be diminished through their negligence.

You will be able to recognize the character of this discipline, and the faith and care with which it is observed, from a single testimony that I shall offer by way of example. Just as we strive to satisfy your eagerness—since, desiring full knowledge of everything, you wish even those things you know very well to be repeated for you in this little book—so we fear exceeding the limits of brevity.

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning three lentil seeds found by the steward

During the week of a certain brother, the steward happened to see three lentil seeds lying on the ground as he passed by. They had slipped from the hands of the weekly minister, who was hurrying to prepare them for cooking, together with the water in which they were being washed. The steward immediately consulted the abbot about the matter. The brother was judged to be a defrauder and squanderer of the sacred property, and he was suspended from prayer. He was not released from the guilt of this negligence until he had cleansed it through public penance.

> **Note:** Here *lenticula* means a small lentil (*lens*), a well-known type of legume, very similar to the lentil but belonging to its own kind; Pliny discusses it in *Book XVIII, chapter 12*. Esau sold his birthright for a dish, or reddish stew, made from it (*Genesis 25*). There is another *lenticula olei*, or small oil vessel, discussed below (*chapter 25*).

> **Note:** That is, a defrauder or squanderer, which is more serious than a negligent person, as Dionysius explained. He calls the monastery’s goods and property “sacred property”: utensils, food, furnishings, and everything belonging to the use of the monastery and the monks. They are rightly called sacred because they have been dedicated and consecrated to God.

> St. Basil gives three noteworthy and highly relevant instructions concerning their careful management and custody (*On Monastic Institutions, chapter 55*). First he asks: “How should those who work take care of the tools or utensils with which they work?” He answers: “First, they must use them as vessels of God, or as things already consecrated to God.” Second he asks: “What if something from them should perish through negligence or be destroyed through contempt?” He answers that the one who treats them with contempt should be judged sacrilegious, while the one who loses something through negligence also incurs a similar crime, because everything assigned to the use of God’s servants is undoubtedly consecrated to God. Third he asks: “What if someone wishes to lend something of his own to another, or to receive something from another?” He answers that such a person is to be regarded as insolent and reckless. These, says Basil, are the proper duties of those who preside and administer the property.

> In the same way, St. Benedict warns (*Rule, chapter 31*) that the cellarer should regard all the monastery’s vessels and its entire property as though they were consecrated vessels of the altar. Understand this not as equality but proportionally, as Turrecremata says: that is, according to the degree and order proper to each among sacred things. For there are many categories of sacred things, as St. Thomas notes (*II–II, question 59, article 3*), among the lowest of which are the goods of churches and monasteries. Again, in the following chapter, St. Benedict decrees that if anyone handles the monastery’s property carelessly or negligently, he should be corrected; and if he does not amend, he should undergo regular discipline.

For they believe not only that they themselves do not belong to themselves, but also that everything belonging to them has been consecrated to the Lord. Therefore, if anything has once been brought into the monastery, they decree that it must be handled with every reverence as something sacred.

They procure and administer everything with such faith that they confidently believe they will receive a reward from the Lord even if they move something regarded as contemptible, small, and worthless from one place to another or put it in a more suitable location; if they fill a small vessel with water; if they offer it to someone to drink; or if they remove a slender straw from the oratory or cell.

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning the spontaneous service of certain brothers

We have known brothers during whose week such a severe shortage of firewood occurred that there was absolutely no means of preparing the customary food for the brothers. Until wood could be purchased and brought in, it had been ordered by the abbot’s authority that they should be content with what is called *xerophagy*—that is, dry and uncooked foods—and this had been agreed upon by everyone, so that no one could hope for any cooked dish.

Yet, as though they would otherwise be deprived of the fruit and reward of their labor and service if, in their turn, they did not prepare food for the brothers according to custom, they imposed upon themselves so much voluntary work and concern that, in those dry and barren places where wood cannot be found at all unless it is cut from fruit-bearing trees—for no wild thickets are found there, as they are among us—they ran through the extended wilderness and traversed the desert stretching toward the Dead Sea.

> **Note:** That is, they used dry and uncooked foods. For *xerophagia* (*ξηροφαγεῖν*, “to eat dry foods”) means to eat dry fare, to use drier foods, or even to eat raw and uncooked foods, as can be inferred from this passage. The abbot therefore ordered them to be content with xerophagy because there was no wood available for cooking their food.

> Hence Tertullian interprets *xerophagia* as “dry foods,” Epiphanius as “the eating of dry things,” and Rhenanus as “dry nourishment.” This was a form of abstinence, or stricter and more austere fasting, in which one abstained not only from meat and wine but also from fish and other brothy or succulent foods. One ate only bread and salt—properly understood by the term “dry foods”—and raw herbs, and drank water.

> It is clear that this kind of xerophagy had been customary among Christians from the time of the apostles (*Baronius, under the year of Christ 34; Book on Contempt of the World, supplement 8; Jerome, On Ecclesiastical Writers, under Philo, Book II of the History, chapter 16*). The earliest ascetics, or Therapeutae of Alexandria, whose customs and institutions Philo describes, and whom St. Jerome declares to have been Christians and disciples of St. Mark, provided an example of this abstinence, especially during the holy days of the Lord’s Passion. As Eusebius reports from Philo, during those days they did not taste wine at all; indeed, they ate neither meat nor any kind of food that contained blood. Their only drink was water, and they used salt and hyssop as relish and bread as food.

> There is also an apostolic decree of Blessed Clement, the pontiff, in *Book V, chapter 19 of the Apostolic Constitutions*, which permits the use of only bread, salt, and vegetables during fast days and teaches abstinence from meat and wine. It confirms the same teaching with many passages of Scripture in chapter 21 of that book, and records its practice in Blessed Peter in *Book VII of the Recognitions*.

> Tertullian likewise (*On Fasting, chapters 1 and 9*) demonstrates the very ancient religious observance of xerophagy and abstinence from wine by the examples of Daniel and his companions, Elijah, David, Samuel, Aaron, the Apostle Paul, and his disciple Timothy.

> The Council of Laodicea, held a thousand years ago, likewise decreed in canon 50: “δεῖ πᾶσαν τὴν τεσσαρακοστὴν νηστεύειν ξηροφαγοῦντας”—that is, “We must fast throughout the whole forty-day period, using xerophagy.”

> Finally, Epiphanius provides abundant testimony to this observance. His words appear near the end of Book III *Against Heresies*: “During these six days”—namely, Holy Week—“all the peoples continue in the eating of dry foods, using at that time bread, salt, and water until evening.”

> There were also special forms of xerophagy among heretics, observed by them with great scrupulousness. Tertullian, after being drawn into the Montanist sect, stubbornly defended them against the Catholics (*as above, chapter 1*) and describes them in these words: “They”—namely, the Catholics—“accuse us because we observe xerophagies, drying our food of every kind of meat and broth, and even of the more vivid fruits, so that we may neither eat nor drink anything of a vinous nature.”

> By these words he seems to indicate that the Montanists’ *xerophagia* was such that they ate not merely dry or raw foods, but only foods without juice and thoroughly dried—every bit of moisture having been pressed and extracted even from fruits and vegetables. Catholic writers, however, mention and commend only the use and eating of dry foods, not of foods without juice.

They gathered in their bosoms and garments the slender sticks and little thorns that the wind had scattered here and there, and by this voluntary service prepared all the customary food, so that nothing was lacking from the usual provision. They rendered these duties to the brothers with such faith that, although they could honorably have been excused either by the shortage of firewood or by the abbot’s command, they did not wish to use that permission as an excuse for failing to obtain the fruit and reward of their labor.

> **Note:** Concerning this desert and the Dead Sea, see the notes on Conference 6, chapter 1.

## CHAPTER XXII. Concerning the Egyptian practice established for the brothers’ daily services

Let what has been said stand as applying, as we stated earlier, to the practice of the entire East. Among the Egyptians, however, who devote the greatest care to manual labor, there is no mutual weekly rotation, lest, under the pretext of this duty, everyone be prevented from following the regular work. Instead, responsibility is entrusted to one highly approved brother, either the cellarer or the person in charge of the kitchen, who performs this work continuously for as long as his strength or age permits.

He is not wearied by any great bodily labor, because among them neither the preparation nor the cooking of food requires such extensive care, since they make use chiefly of xerophagy or *homophagy*, and among them, once each month, cut leek leaves, *lapsana*, roasted salt, olives, and small salted fish, which they call *maenidia*, are a very great delicacy.

> **Note:** *Lapsana* was discussed above (*chapter 11*). Let the reader observe how far the delicacies of the ancient monks differed from ours, and consult St. Bernard’s *Apology to Abbot William* concerning them.

> **Note:** Most manuscripts have *menominia*, a word unknown in Latin. For it, Ciaconius conjectured *maenidia*, not implausibly. For *μαινίς* or *maena* is a sea fish, commonly called a herring (*Aristotle, Book VI on Animals*), whose diminutive is *μαινίδιον*, “little herring,” according to Theodore Gaza. Pliny calls them *manae* (*Book XXXII, chapter 11*), and Caelius Rhodiginus discusses them (*Book XX of Ancient Readings, chapter 6*).

> **Note:** In the Author’s view, there seems to be little difference between xerophagy and homophagy, as can be gathered from what has been said. For *ὡμοφαγία* means raw and uncooked foods, or the eating of such foods. Hence *ὡμοφάγος* means one who eats raw things. Such were the vegetables or legumes that the Egyptian monks used as relish, seasoned only with salt or moistened with water and at times even eaten uncooked and raw.

> St. Jerome writes of these monks (*Letter 22*): “I say nothing of their food and drink, since even sick monks use cold water, and to have received anything cooked is considered luxury.” Of Hilarion he writes that from his twenty-fourth to his twenty-seventh year he ate dry bread with salt and water—this was xerophagy. From his twenty-seventh to his thirtieth year, however, he was sustained by wild herbs and the raw roots of certain shrubs—properly speaking, homophagy.

> Finally, in the *Life of St. Pachomius* (*chapter 43*), when Pachomius asked why the cook had not cooked vegetables or legumes for the brothers for several months, the cook replied: “Because whatever I cooked was not eaten by the brothers, since everyone abstains”—for only the boys received some cooked food—“and therefore I did not cook any stew.”

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning the obedience of Abbot John, through which he advanced to the grace of prophecy

Since this book concerns the formation of one who renounces the world, through which formation he may be introduced to true humility and perfect obedience and thereby ascend to the heights of the other virtues, I think it necessary to explain, by way of example as we promised, certain deeds of the elders who excelled through this virtue. From a very large number, we shall select only a few, so that for those striving after higher things these examples may provide not only encouragement toward a perfect life but also a model for their purpose.

Accordingly, for the sake of the brevity of this little book, we shall present two or three from the countless multitude of the Fathers.

> **Note:** His outstanding holiness was honored by the testimony of eminent men (*Baronius, in the Martyrology under 27 March and in the Annals under the year 388*). St. Jerome writes about him to Ctesiphon against the Pelagians; St. Augustine in *On the Care to Be Shown for the Dead*, chapter 17; Theodoret in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, chapter 24; Sozomen in Book VI, chapter 28; Palladius in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 43; and others, including Sidonius Apollinaris (*poem 16*).

> The emperor Theodosius the Great sent two embassies to him, hidden in the desert but renowned for the spirit of prophecy, to consult him about the uncertain outcome of wars against tyrants; in both cases he received from him a definite announcement of victory. Augustine relates the first embassy (*City of God, Book V, chapter 26*), and Rufinus the second (*Book II, chapter 9*), as does Cassiodorus (*Tripartite History, Book IX, chapter 45*). This John is different from Abbot John in the Scetian desert, who will be discussed below (*chapters 27 and 40*).

We shall begin with Abbot John, who lived near Lycon, a town of the Thebaid. Because of the virtue of his obedience he was exalted even to the grace of prophecy, and he became so renowned throughout the world that, by his own merit, he was rightly made illustrious even among the kings of this world.

> **Note:** The Thebaid, or Thebais, as it is called here, was a region of Egypt adjoining Ethiopia. It took its name from Thebes, a very powerful city and the metropolis of the entire region. St. Jerome, in his *Book on Hebrew Questions*, considers the Thebaid to be the region formerly called the land of Goshen, where the patriarch Jacob lived with his sons after coming to Egypt (*Genesis 45–46*). The town of Lycus, or Lycopolis, was situated in its farthest part. Hence Pliny says (*Book V, chapter 9*): “Lycon, where the mountains end the Thebaid,” and among its prefectures he names Lycopolitis as the last.

For while he lived, as we have said, in the farthest parts of the Thebaid, the emperor Theodosius did not presume to march against the powerful tyrants until he had been encouraged by John’s oracles and answers. Trusting in them as messages delivered to him from heaven, he carried back triumphs from wars that had seemed hopeless and from his enemies.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning the dry wood which the same Abbot John did not cease to water at the command of his elder, as though it were to grow

This blessed John served his elder from his youth until he reached full and mature manhood, for as long as the elder remained in this manner of life. He clung to his service with such humility that his obedience itself inspired the old man with the greatest astonishment.

The elder wished to discover more clearly whether this virtue arose from true faith and deep simplicity of heart, or whether it was affected and, in a sense, compelled, being displayed merely before the face of the one who commanded. He therefore frequently imposed upon him many superfluous, unnecessary, or impossible tasks.

I shall mention three of them, by which those who wish to know may see either the integrity of his mind or the completeness of his submission.

The old man took from his woodpile a branch that had long before been cut and prepared for use as firewood. Since the opportunity to use it for cooking had been delayed, it lay there not only dry but almost rotten from age. He fixed it in the ground in the young man’s presence and ordered him to water it twice each day with water brought from elsewhere, so that, taking root through daily moisture and coming back to life as an ancient tree, it might spread its branches, offer beauty to the eyes, and provide shade for those sitting beneath it in the intense heat.

The young man received this command with his customary reverence, without considering its impossibility, and carried it out day after day. He continually brought water from a distance of nearly two miles and never ceased to water the wood. Throughout the entire year, neither bodily illness, nor a festival or solemnity, nor any pressing necessity that could honorably have excused him from fulfilling the command, nor finally the harshness of winter was able to prevent him from observing it.

The old man silently and secretly examined his diligence day after day. When he saw him preserve the command entrusted to him, as though it had been issued by God, with a simple affection of heart and without any change of expression or examination of its reason, he recognized the sincerity of his humble obedience.
