At the same time, he pitied the long labor that the young man had devoted throughout the year out of his zeal and devotion.

Approaching the dry branch, he said, “Well, John, has this tree put down roots, or not?”

When John said that he did not know, the old man, as though investigating the truth of the matter and testing whether it was already standing upon its own roots, pulled up the branch in his presence with a slight effort. Throwing it aside, he ordered him to stop watering it from that time forward.

> **Note:** Sulpicius relates a similar example in the first Dialogue concerning the virtues of St. Martin, except that in his account the watered branch blossomed in the third year and produced fruit, which the abbot brought to the church and displayed to the brothers, saying: “Behold the fruit of obedience.”

## CHAPTER XXV. Concerning the single vessel of oil thrown down by Abbot John at the command of his elder

Thus the young man, trained daily by exercises of this kind, grew in the virtue of obedience. The grace of his humility shone forth, and the sweet fragrance of his obedience spread throughout all the monasteries.

Some brothers came to the old man under the pretext—indeed, with the intention—of being tested and edified. They marveled at the submission they had heard about. The old man suddenly called John and said, “Climb up, take the small oil vessel, and throw it down through the window.”

He quickly went up and, throwing the vessel through the window, let it fall to the ground to be smashed. He gave little thought to or reconsideration of the absurdity of the command, the need of the day, the weakness of his body, the scarcity of supplies, or the narrowness and difficulties of the barren desert, where, even if money were available, the lost vessel could not be found or replaced.

> **Note:** *Lenticula* is an oil vessel, or ointment jar, which the Greeks call *φακός* or *φακή*. Gellius uses *guttum* in the masculine gender (*Attic Nights, Book XVII, chapter 8*), while Isidore calls it *lenticulum* and thinks the word derives from *linire*, “to anoint,” because kings and priests were anointed with such vessels (*Etymologies, Book XX, chapter 7*).

> Ludovicus Vives thinks that *lenticula* derives from *lentitudo*, “slowness,” because oil drips slowly from it (*On the City of God, Book XVI, chapter 37*). Others more plausibly derive *lenticula* from the shape and resemblance of the legume discussed above (*chapter 20*). Apuleius describes such a vessel as follows: “Also an oil flask which he carried, of lentil-shaped form, with a rounded circumference and a rounded swelling,” and so forth.

> Pliny likewise says (*Book XVIII, chapter 13*): “There are two kinds of lentil in Egypt: one rounder and blacker; the other of its own shape.” Hence the name *lenticula* was transferred, with various applications, to vessels formed and named after the shape of a lentil. It is also called an oil *lecythus* in 3 Kings 17. In Scripture, however, *lenticula olei* seems to be the more usual expression and almost a special term for the anointing of kings. Saul, Jehu, and Hazael are said to have been anointed with it (*1 Kings 10; 1 Kings 19; 4 Kings 9*). David alone was anointed by Samuel with an oil horn (*1 Kings 16*), not without a mystery, concerning which St. Gregory writes in Book IV of his commentary on the Books of Kings, chapter 4.

> Ciaconius also noted that *lenticula* is sometimes used of a vessel for water. For in 1 Kings 26, where David is said to have taken from Saul’s tent the spear that was at his head and a cup of water, the Septuagint has *φακὸν ὕδατος*, that is, “a lentil-shaped vessel of water.” St. Ambrose interpreted it similarly in *On Duties*, Book III, chapter 5: “David took the spear that was at Saul’s head and the lenticula of water.”

> To illuminate this passage of Cassian, it will also be useful to note a similar event concerning the same subject, namely, an oil flask, which St. Gregory relates among the miracles of our most holy Father Benedict (*Dialogues, Book II, chapter 28*). It is similar in the virtue of the master, though not in the obedience of the disciple; for, as the Philosopher says: “Things opposed, when placed side by side, become more clearly visible.”

> Gregory writes: “At the time when a shortage of food was severely afflicting Campania, the man of God had distributed everything to the various needy people of his monastery, so that almost nothing remained in the storeroom except a small amount of oil in a glass vessel. Then a subdeacon named Agapitus arrived, earnestly asking that a little oil be given to him. The man of God, who had resolved to give everything on earth in order to reserve everything in heaven, ordered that this small amount of oil which remained be given to the petitioner.

> “The monk who was in charge of the storeroom heard the command, but delayed carrying it out. When Benedict shortly afterward asked whether what he had ordered had been given, the monk replied that he had not given it, because if he gave it away, absolutely nothing would remain for the brothers.

> “Then, angered, Benedict ordered the others to throw through the window the glass vessel in which the small amount of oil seemed to remain, so that nothing might remain in the cell through disobedience. This was done. Beneath the window there was a great precipice, rough with masses of rock. The glass vessel was thrown down upon the rocks, but remained unbroken, as though it had not been thrown at all; it could neither be shattered nor spill its oil. The man of God ordered it to be lifted up and, as it was, intact, given to the petitioner.

> “Then he summoned the brothers and publicly rebuked the disobedient monk for his lack of faith and his pride.” This is Gregory’s account.

## CHAPTER XXVI. How Abbot John obeyed his elder when he tried to roll a huge stone that not even many men could move

Once again, when others wished to be edified by this example of obedience, the elder called him and said, “Hurry, John, and roll that stone over here as quickly as possible.”

Immediately he tried to roll the enormous stone, which a large crowd of men could not even move, applying now his neck and now his whole chest to it. He exerted such force and effort that the sweat of all his limbs not only soaked his entire garment but also moistened the stone itself against his neck.

Here too he paid little attention to the impossibility of the command or the deed, out of reverence for his elder and the sincere simplicity of his obedience. He believed with complete faith that the old man could command nothing useless or without reason.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Concerning the humility and obedience of Abbot Mucius, who did not hesitate to carry out the command of his elder by throwing his little son into the river

[Col. 0186B]

Hitherto, let what has been said about Abbot John, out of much material, suffice; now I shall relate the memorable deed of Abbot Mucius.

[Note: Mucius here seems to be someone other than that Mut(i)us or Patermutius whose remarkable conversion, deeds, and many miracles Rufinus recounts in *The Lives of the Fathers* (see *Lives of the Fathers*, book II, chapter 9, new edition). He first approached the Church as a pagan and brigand; after being instructed by priests, he soon withdrew to the desert, where he lived as a solitary, not in a monastery, as this Mucius did. Nor is anything said there about a young son brought into a monastery and cast into a river out of obedience.]

This man, desiring to renounce the world, kept watch for so long before the monastery gates that by his immovable perseverance, contrary to the whole custom of the monasteries, he secured admission with his little son, who was about eight years old. When at last they had been received, they were immediately handed over to different superiors and separated in their dwelling places, so that, through the continual sight of the boy, the father might remember, amid all the property and carnal affection that he had renounced and cast away, that at least his son remained to him; and so that, just as he knew he was no longer rich, he might also cease to know himself as a father.

To test more fully whether he was moved more strongly by natural affection and love for his own flesh and blood, or by the obedience and mortification of Christ—which every person who renounces the world ought to prefer for love of him—the boy was deliberately neglected. He was dressed in rags rather than clothing and was so covered and defiled with filth that, whenever his father saw him, he could offend rather than delight his paternal eyes. He was also exposed to blows and slaps from various people, which the father often saw being inflicted, even gratuitously, upon the innocent child before his eyes, so that he never saw the boy’s cheeks except stained with the dirty traces of tears.

Although the child was treated in this way every day before his eyes, the father’s heart, for love of Christ and through the power of obedience, always remained rigid and unmoved. He no longer considered the boy his son, since he had offered him together with himself to Christ; nor did he grieve over the injuries inflicted upon him. Rather, he rejoiced that he saw him enduring them by no means fruitlessly. He paid little attention to the child’s tears, being concerned instead with his own humility and perfection.

When the superior of the monastery perceived the strictness of his mind and his immovable rigor, he wished to test his steadfastness completely. One day, seeing the child crying, he pretended to be angry with him and ordered the father to pick him up and throw him into the river.

[Note: A truly remarkable example, and one more to be wondered at than imitated. But which is more astonishing: the one giving the command or the one obeying? That an abbot could give such an order—that a father should throw his son into a river, something nature and reason recoil from—and that the father should wish to obey this command, and should be commended for it as an outstanding example of obedience. Yet since God himself approved it by his testimony and revealed to that same abbot that through this obedience the work of Abraham had been fulfilled, as Cassian says—plainly through a certain resemblance and singular imitation—no one can doubt that the abbot gave the order by divine inspiration, not that it should actually be carried out (for he sent brothers to prevent it), but, as we said above, in order to test the man’s steadfastness, devotion, and obedience, to set him before others as an example, and to make the merit of obedience before God evident to all.

The other man, moved by the same Spirit, wished to obey without delay or hesitation, as though the command had been given to him by God himself. This was either because he thought the command had not been given simply and absolutely for him to carry out, but for the testing and proving of his obedience, as has been said; or because, to use Cassian’s words (chapter 26), “out of reverence for his superior and sincere simplicity of obedience, he believed with complete faith that the elder could command nothing useless or irrational.”

The same judgment should be applied to other similar examples, in which almighty God approved and confirmed simple and prompt obedience—obedience that does not scrutinize the commands of superiors—by astonishing miracles.

I wish to relate here one still more remarkable example, which I mentioned above (chapter 24), recorded by Sulpicius in the passage cited earlier. “When a certain man,” he says, “having renounced the affairs of the world, began to seek admission into a monastery of great discipline, the abbot began to set many things before him: that the labors of this discipline were severe, that his own commands were harsh and could not easily be fulfilled by anyone; that he should rather seek another monastery where he could live under easier rules; and that he should not attempt to undertake what he could not accomplish.

But the man was not moved at all by these threats. Rather, he promised such complete obedience that, if the abbot ordered him to enter fire, he would not refuse to enter.”

When the master heard this profession, he did not hesitate to test the man who had made it. By chance, a kiln was burning nearby, fired with a great blaze and prepared for baking bread. Flames poured out from the opened furnace, and within the hollow of the chimney the fire raged with full force. The master therefore ordered the newcomer to enter it. He did not delay in obeying the command, but entered the midst of the flames without hesitation. The flames, immediately overcome by such bold faith, yielded before him, just as they once had before the Hebrew children. Nature was defeated; the fire fled; and he who was thought likely to burn found himself, as though sprinkled with cool dew, marveling at his own condition.

But what is strange, Christ, if that fire did not touch your novice—so that the abbot did not regret giving a harsh command, nor the disciple regret obeying it? On the very day when he had arrived, he was found perfect when tested in weakness; deservedly happy, deservedly glorious, proved by obedience and glorified by suffering.”

Sulpicius writes this elegantly (*First Dialogue on the Virtues of the Monks of the East*, chapter 13). More examples of admirable obedience may be found in John Climacus, fourth degree, which concerns obedience.]

Then the father, as though this command had been given to him by the Lord, immediately seized his son, carried him swiftly in his arms to the riverbank, and prepared to throw him in. The deed would certainly have been completed through the fervor of his faith and obedience, had not brothers deliberately been stationed in vigilance along the riverbank. They seized the boy after he had been thrown—or rather, when he was already in a sense within the river channel—and prevented the completion of the command, which had been fulfilled by the father’s obedience and devotion, from being carried through in the deed itself and to its final outcome.

## CHAPTER XXVIII  
### How it was revealed to Abbot Mucius that he had performed the work of Abraham, and how, after that abbot’s death, the same Father Mucius succeeded him in governing the monastery

His faith and devotion were so acceptable to God that they were immediately confirmed by divine testimony. For it was at once revealed to the superior that, through this obedience, he had fulfilled the work of the patriarch Abraham.

[Note: That is, he had expressed and imitated Abraham’s obedience, faith, and steadfastness through a similar deed. Concerning this the Apostle says in Hebrews 11: “By faith Abraham offered Isaac when he was tested, and was offering his only-begotten son, in whom he had received the promise.” The same point is illustrated by a similar example in *The Lives of the Fathers*, in the passage noted above:

A certain man had entered a monastery, leaving three sons in the world. After three years, with the abbot’s permission, he went into the city to bring them to the monastery, and found that two of them had already died; only one remained. Taking him, he brought him to the abbot, who at that time was in the bakery. The abbot embraced the child and said to his father, “Do you love him?” He answered, “Yes.” Again he said to him, “Do you love him completely?” He replied, “Yes.” Hearing this, the abbot said to him, “Then take him, if you love him, and throw him into the oven, which is now burning.” The father took his son and threw him into the burning oven. Immediately the oven became like dew. Through this deed he gained glory at that time, like the patriarch Abraham. So it is told there.]

After a short time had passed, that same abbot of the monastery departed from this world to the Lord. He placed Mucius over all the brothers and left him as his successor and abbot of the monastery.

## CHAPTER XXIX  
### On the obedience of the brother who, carrying ten baskets, sold them publicly at the abbot’s command

We shall not be silent about a brother known to us who belonged, according to the order of this world, to a very distinguished family. He was born to a count who was exceedingly wealthy, and had also received a considerable liberal education.

[Note: For the term *count* and its various meanings and the several ranks of counts, one should consult the interpreters of Civil Law. It will suffice to note that before the time of the Emperor Constantine the Great, those were called counts who accompanied consuls, proconsuls, and provincial governors in the conduct of public affairs, as their administrators and assistants; they also administered justice with them as assessors (Baronius, notes on the *Martyrology*, 31 May). From the time of the Emperor Constantine, however, after the Roman Empire had been transferred to Constantinople, those were called counts whom the emperor selected from among the magistrates as associates in the administration of the empire and adorned with the greatest dignities and offices. They were of three ranks: first, second, and third, as Eusebius writes in *The Life of Constantine*, book IV, chapter 1. Numerous titles concerning these counts occur in the Theodosian Code, book XII.]

When he left his parents and hastened to the monastery, the superior immediately commanded him, in order to test the humility of his mind or the fervor of his faith, to carry ten baskets—although there was no need for them to be sold publicly—on his shoulders through the streets and sell them.

[Note: Among the occupations or manual labors of the ancient monks, baskets are frequently mentioned. They wove them from willow, rush, esparto grass, or similar material and supported themselves by selling them, thereby procuring food and other necessities (see above, chapter 13). Witnesses include St. Jerome, in his letter to the monk Rusticus and in the *Life of Hilarion*; Palladius in the *Lausiac History*; Cassian here and elsewhere; and Sozomen, book VI, chapter 29.]

A condition was added by which he would be kept at this task for a longer time: if someone wished to buy all of them together, he was not to yield, but was to sell them individually to those who asked for them.

He fulfilled this with complete devotion. Trampling underfoot every shame and embarrassment for the name and desire of Christ, he placed the baskets upon his shoulders, sold them at the fixed price, and carried the money back to the monastery. He was not at all frightened by the novelty of such a lowly and unfamiliar task, nor did he consider the indignity of the matter, the splendor of his birth, or the humiliation of selling, while through the grace of obedience he desired to attain that humility of Christ which is true nobility.

## CHAPTER XXX  
### On the humility of Abbot Pynuphius, who, leaving a celebrated monastery presided over by a priest, sought a distant monastery where he might be received as a beginner, out of his desire for subjection

The limited scope of this little work constrains us to hasten toward its conclusion, but the excellence of obedience, which holds first place among the other virtues, does not permit us to pass over in complete silence the deeds of those who became illustrious through it.

[Note: In what sense and for what reason obedience holds first place among the other virtues has been explained above (chapter 12).]

Accordingly, balancing both considerations appropriately—that is, serving both brevity and the desires and usefulness of earnest readers—we shall add one more example of humility. It was carried out not by a beginner but by a perfected monk and an abbot, and through its lesson it can instruct the younger and also encourage the older toward the perfect virtue of humility.

We therefore saw Abbot Pynuphius,

[Note: Peter calls him *Punificus* in his *Catalogue*, book XI, chapter 56; Dionysius and our manuscripts have *Pinuphius*. The twentieth Conference, concerning the end of repentance, belongs to him, as may be seen there.]

who, although he was a priest of a great monastery in Egypt, not far from the city of Panephys,

[Note: This is how the name of this city is written by Ptolemy and in the Vatican manuscripts, says Ciaconius. It is a town in Egypt, also mentioned by Cassian, *Conference* 7, chapter 26.]

and was honored and revered by all because of his life, age, or priesthood, saw that he could not practice the humility he desired in accordance with the ardor of his mind, nor find any means by which to extend the virtue of the subjection he longed for.

[Note: He calls it a “vast monastery,” as I think, both because of the extent of its site and because of the number and multitude of its monks; for, according to St. Augustine (*On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, book I, chapter 31), as many as three thousand monks sometimes lived in a single monastery. Indeed, St. Jerome writes of an innumerable multitude in his letter to Eustochium. If the monks lived in separate cells, as they now do among the Carthusians, according to Jerome; or at least two or three together, as the Rule of St. Pachomius preserved by Palladius states (*Lausiac History*, chapter 38), it is easy to estimate how great an area and expanse they occupied.

As for the priest, it should be noted that, since formerly both hermits and cenobites generally lived far outside the cities and at a distance from other people, and could not assemble at the churches of bishops or parish priests, most monasteries had their own abbot who was a priest, from whom they received the sacraments. St. Augustine indicates this in the passage cited above and in Letter 81 to Eudoxius, whom he calls both priest and abbot. Epiphanius likewise says in his letter to John of Jerusalem that he ordained Paulinian, the brother of St. Jerome, priest of the Bethlehem monastery:

“Because the multitude of brothers living in the monastery complained that they had no one to celebrate the Lord’s sacraments for them, since the holy priests Jerome and Vincent, out of modesty and humility, were unwilling to perform the sacrifices due to their office or to undertake this part of the ministry, which is the chief salvation of Christians.”

Jerome himself writes in Letter 27 that, when the holy widow Paula was visiting the holy places, she met the holy and venerable Bishop Isidore amid innumerable crowds of monks, many of whom had been elevated to priestly and Levitical rank.

Sozomen, in book VI of his *History*, records that many fathers or abbots of monks were priests and names them individually. Palladius likewise reports that there were eight priests in the monastery of Nitria, but that as long as the first priest lived, no other offered the sacrifice, judged, or delivered a discourse; they merely sat silently with him.

Augustine (*On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, book I, chapters 31 and 33) teaches that monks had a priest as superior not only in the desert but also in cities such as Rome and Milan. He was undoubtedly a priest so that he could celebrate the sacraments in the monastery and administer them to the others.

The same may also be inferred from many of Cassian’s *Conferences*, especially Conference 18, chapter 15, where Abbot Paphnutius is said to have been a priest of the Scetian desert.

It may also not improbably be inferred from the Rule of St. Benedict, chapter 46, where he advises that hidden sins be confessed to the abbot: “If the soul’s sin is hidden, let him disclose it only to the abbot or to spiritual elders who know how to heal their own wounds and not uncover and publish those of others.” Turrecrematus explains this as sacramental confession, which is made only to priests. Hence a certain glossator wrote in the margin there, on the basis of the argument, that the abbots in the time of St. Benedict were priests, and consequently that Benedict himself was one.

I have nevertheless warned above that this was not perpetual, and that many were called abbots in those times—that is, fathers of monks or anchorites—who were not priests, but merely monks by profession and laymen by rank. Besides other evidence that we have reported elsewhere (*Conference* 2, chapter 5; *Conference* 3, chapter 1), this can be proved both from the Decree of Pope Sylvester preserved by Gratian, which reads:

“To the pontiff, the priest; to the priest, the deacon; to the deacon, the subdeacon; to the subdeacon, the acolyte; to the acolyte, the exorcist; to the exorcist, the lector; to the lector, the doorkeeper; to the doorkeeper, the abbot; to the abbot, the monk: in every place let them render service.”

(*Epitome of Canon Law*, distinction 93, chapter “From the Subdeacon.”)

Here one sees a gradation made from superiors to inferiors, with the abbot placed below the doorkeeper, as a layman below a cleric, as the gloss notes there (§ “Hence it is,” at the end of question 16, distinction 1).

It can also be proved from a letter of St. Jerome (*On the Work and Humility of the Monk*), where he relates that the monks of Scetis once assembled to find a priest who might celebrate the solemn Mass for them, as Gratian also reports (*Decree*, book II, chapter 1, concerning the age and qualifications of those to be appointed).

In later centuries, however, it is clear that the name “abbot” passed into the name of a dignity, as may be gathered from the chapter “We Decree,” concerning judgments. It was long ago established by ecclesiastical laws (*Clementine, Let No One in the Field*, concerning the status of monks) that not only abbots but also conventual priors, and even all monks, unless prevented by a legitimate impediment, should at the appropriate time be promoted to holy orders and the priesthood.

But these matters belong elsewhere.]

Therefore, secretly fleeing from the monastery, he withdrew alone into the remotest parts of the Thebaid. There, laying aside his monastic habit and putting on secular clothing, he sought the monastery of the Tabennesiots, which he knew to be stricter than all the others. He believed that there he would either remain unknown because of the distance of the region or easily be concealed because of the size of the monastery and the multitude of its brothers.

He remained for a very long time before the gates, repeatedly falling at the knees of all the brothers and begging with the greatest insistence to be received. At last he was admitted amid great contempt, since he was an aged and decrepit man who had spent his entire life in the world and, in the final stage of life, was asking to enter a monastery, when he was no longer even capable of serving his own pleasures. They declared that he was not seeking this for the sake of religion, but was compelled by hunger and poverty.

He was therefore assigned the care and cultivation of the garden, as an old man fit for no other work. He carried out this task under a younger brother who kept him under his authority. He submitted to him so completely and cultivated the desired virtue of humility with such obedience that he performed daily not only the tasks belonging to the care and cultivation of the garden, but also every duty that was difficult, degrading, or regarded by all as abhorrent.

He also carried out many tasks at night, rising secretly and doing them under cover of darkness, without any witness or knowledge, so that no one could discover who had performed the work.

After hiding there for three years, while brothers throughout Egypt were searching for him, he was finally seen by someone who had come from the regions of Egypt. Because of the lowliness of his clothing and the disgraceful nature of the task he was performing, he could scarcely be recognized. Bent down over the ground with a hoe, he loosened the earth around the vegetables and then carried manure on his shoulders and placed it at their roots.

When the brother saw this, he remained for a very long time uncertain whether he recognized him. At last he approached more closely, examined not only his face but also the sound of his voice, and fell at his feet. At first, in the sight of all, he caused the greatest astonishment: why, they wondered, was he doing this to someone who among them was regarded as the lowest, like a novice recently come from the world? Then they were struck with even greater amazement when he immediately revealed his name, which was also well known among them and held in high regard.

All the brothers asked his forgiveness for their former ignorance, since they had counted him for so long among the younger and least important members. They brought him back, unwilling and weeping, to his own monastery. He grieved that, through the envy of the devil, he had been deprived of the way of life and humility he had so long desired and had at last found, and that he had not been allowed to end his life in the subjection he had undertaken.

They watched him with the greatest care, lest he should again slip away from them in some manner and flee elsewhere.

## CHAPTER XXXI  
### How Abbot Pynuphius, after being brought back to his monastery and staying there for a short time, fled once more to the regions of Syria

After he had remained there for a short time, he was again inflamed by the same desire and ardor for humility. Taking advantage of the silence of night, he fled so far that he no longer sought a neighboring province, but distant, unknown, foreign, and widely separated regions.

He boarded a ship and arranged to travel toward Palestine, believing that he would hide more safely if he carried himself to places where even his name had never been heard.

When he arrived there, he immediately sought our monastery, which was not far from the cave in which our Lord Jesus Christ was pleased to be born of the Virgin.

[Note: A more poetic term for “cave” (see *Conference* 17, chapter 5). Virgil writes in the tenth *Eclogue*:

“It is certain that in the forests, among the lairs of wild beasts,  
I would rather endure.”

As for the matter at hand, those who have visited the region of Jerusalem report that the stable in which Christ our Lord was born was a cave, in which a manger had been cut into the rock. This is also confirmed by the testimony of the holy Fathers, who commonly call it a cave situated in the suburbs of Bethlehem. Hence St. Jerome writes, among other things, in Letter 18 to Marcella: “With what words, with what voice, shall I describe the cave of the Savior and that manger in which the little child cried? It is to be honored more by silence than by the lowest expression.”]

He remained hidden there for only a very short time. In accordance with the Lord’s saying (Matthew 5), like a city set upon a mountain, he could not remain concealed for long. For some brothers who had come from Egypt to the holy places for the sake of prayer immediately recognized him and, by their earnest entreaties, brought him back to his monastery.

## CHAPTER XXXII  
### What instructions Abbot Pynuphius gave to the brother whom he was receiving into his monastery

Because we had formerly been intimate with this old man in our monastery, after these events we diligently sought him in Egypt. We intend to insert into this little work the exhortation he gave to a brother whom he was receiving into his monastery in our presence, since I think it can provide useful instruction.

[Note: The author reports the notable prayer or exhortation delivered by Abbot Pynuphius to the novice whom he was receiving, and continues it through the remaining chapters of this book. An abbot could appropriately imitate it when receiving or admitting novices. Cassian mentions this exhortation in *Conference* 17, chapter 5.]

[Note: We discussed this testing and watching before the monastery gates above (chapter 2 of this work). Palladius reports similar examples of testing in the case of Paul the Simple and Macarius, who, coming to Pachomius in a pretended habit and asking to be admitted, waited seven days before the gates.]

“You know,” he said, “for how many days you kept watch before the gates before you were received today. You must first understand the reason for this difficulty. For it can greatly benefit you on the path you desire to enter if, once you understand its reason, you approach the service of Christ accordingly and as you ought.”

## CHAPTER XXXIII  
### That just as great reward is owed to the monk who labors according to the teaching of the Fathers, so punishment is likewise assigned, and that therefore no one should be readily admitted to the monastery

For just as immense glory is promised in the future to those who faithfully serve God and cleave to him according to the rule of this teaching, so the gravest punishments are prepared for those who have carried it out coldly and negligently and have failed to offer the fitting fruits of holiness in accordance with what they professed—or what people believe them to be.

[Note: Let the reader observe, both from this chapter and from those that follow, the name of monastic profession, and infer from it that monastic profession was made even by the monks of ancient times, at least tacitly and interpretatively; and that its force or obligation, together with the punishment for violating it, is expressed here. This should be noted against the heretics of our own time.

If anyone asks whether the form of religious life in that age was the same as it is now, there can be no doubt that it was very similar. For in the earliest times of the Church monks professed not only poverty, chastity, and obedience, as is clear from Philo (*On the Contemplative Life*), but were also bound by the obligation of a vow to observe these things perpetually, so that abandoning that state was considered plainly unlawful and wicked.

The only difference, if there was one, is that these monastic vows did not yet possess such authority—or, as theologians call it, solemnity. Perhaps at the beginning vows were made explicitly, and, as is more likely, publicly; but, by the common understanding and consent of all, that profession was so attached to the religious state that even if no profession had been made in words, the obligation of professing that state was nevertheless understood to have been assumed along with the state itself—just as now the vow of chastity is understood to be attached to sacred orders.

This may be understood from a passage of St. Basil (*Letter to Amphilochius*, chapter 19), where he says that those who devoted themselves to the monastic way were accustomed tacitly to accept celibacy.

This continued for as long as that ancient piety and modesty were sufficient to keep people in their duty. With the passage of time, however, as human wickedness increased, it seemed more prudent and safer to require from those who wished truly to be considered religious or monks an explicit promise of chastity, poverty, and obedience, as St. Basil also decrees in the same place and as other founders and legislators of religious orders established. Tacit profession was not thereby excluded, but was circumscribed by certain conditions in the sacred canons; hence it receives the same firmness and obligation as explicit profession.]

For it is better, according to Scripture (Ecclesiastes 5), that no one make a vow than that he make one and fail to fulfill it; and, “Cursed is the one who does the work of God negligently” (Jeremiah 48).

[Note: Other manuscripts read, “According to the judgment of Scripture.” This saying is found in Ecclesiastes, chapter 5, in these words: “If you have made a vow to God, do not delay to fulfill it; for he is displeased by an unfaithful and foolish promise. It is much better not to vow than, after making a vow, not to fulfill what was promised.”]

Therefore we kept you away for so long—not because we do not desire with all our heart to embrace your salvation and that of everyone, nor because we do not wish to go out even from a distance to meet those who desire to turn to Christ, but lest, by receiving you rashly, we should make ourselves guilty before God of levity and make you yourself liable to a heavier punishment if, having been readily admitted at present and not understanding the burden of this profession, you should afterward abandon it or become lukewarm.

For this reason, you must first understand the very cause of renunciation. Once you have examined it, you will be more clearly instructed by its meaning about what it is fitting for you to do.

## CHAPTER XXXIV  
### That our renunciation is nothing other than mortification and the image of the crucified man

[Note: The term *renunciation*, like *self-denial*, is taken from the Savior’s words in Matthew: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 10). And in Luke: “Anyone among you who does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14). What self-denial or renunciation is—these words are synonymous—is discussed at length in the third Conference, where the three kinds of renunciation are treated.]

Renunciation is nothing other than a sign of the cross and of mortification. Therefore you must know that today you have died to this world, to its deeds, and to its desires, and that, according to the Apostle, you have been crucified to this world and this world to you (Galatians 6).

[Note: In Galatians, chapter 6, the Apostle says, “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.” St. Gregory explains this as follows (*Morals*, book V, chapter 5): “The world was crucified to him because he no longer loved it, since it was dead to his heart; but he had also crucified himself to the world, because he strove to present himself to it in such a way that it could not desire him, as though he were dead.” And further: “Since Paul neither sought the glory of the world nor was himself sought by the glory of the world, he glories that he and the world were crucified to each other.” Thus Gregory.

In this chapter and the next, a beautiful comparison is made between the monk and a man fastened to a cross, a comparison highly worthy of reading and practice. Caesarius—not the bishop of Arles, but the Cistercian monk—explains this comparison aptly and consistently with this passage (*Book VIII*, chapter 10), as follows:

“There is a twofold crucifixion of religious persons: that of the inner man through compassion for another, and that of the outer man through the mortification of one’s own flesh. The cross is so called from torment; the monk’s cross is the rigor of his order, because of vigils and prayers, fasts and punishments, silence and manual labor, continence of the flesh, and the harshness of clothing and bedding.

Who are Christ’s? Those who can say with the Apostle (Galatians 2), ‘We have been crucified with Christ’; those who have crucified their flesh—that is, fastened it to the cross—while fighting against the vices of their deeds and the desires of their passions. The two plural genitives are not to be taken instrumentally but passively, since they are mortified through virtues in the discipline of the flesh.

The three nails by which the monk’s body ought to be fastened to the cross are the three virtues through which, according to Jerome, martyrs are made: obedience, patience, and humility. Obedience without murmuring should fasten the monk’s right hand; patience without pretense, his left. Love of heavenly freedom should drive in the nail of obedience; fear of the punishment of Gehenna, the nail of patience.

True humility should fasten his feet, so that he submits himself for Christ’s sake not only to superiors but also to his brothers, and can say with the Psalmist (Psalm 118), ‘I have been humbled exceedingly, Lord,’ and in another psalm (Psalm 65), ‘You have placed men over our heads.’

The two feet signify a twofold pride, of the mind and of the body. Although pride is the head of all vices, it is not inappropriate that it should sometimes be signified by the feet, which are the lowest parts of the body; for what we hate and despise greatly, we trample underfoot. Thus Joshua commanded the children of Israel to place their feet upon the necks of kings.”

In this way he depicts the monk in the likeness of a crucified man.]

Consider, then, the conditions of the cross, under whose sacrament you must henceforth live in this world, because you no longer live, but he lives in you who was crucified for you (Galatians 2).

Therefore, in the same condition and form in which he was suspended on the cross for us, we too must live in this life, so that, according to David (Psalm 118), “fastening our flesh with the fear of the Lord,” we may keep all our wills and desires fixed—not in the service of our own lust, but in his mortification.

In this way we shall fulfill the Lord’s command: “Whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10).

But perhaps you will say: How can a person continually carry his cross, or how can someone who is alive be crucified? Listen briefly to the explanation.

## CHAPTER XXXV  
### That our cross is the fear of the Lord
Our cross is the fear of the Lord. Just as a crucified person no longer has the power to move or turn his limbs anywhere according to the impulse of his mind, so we too must apply our wills and desires—not according to what is pleasant and attractive to us at the moment, but according to the law of the Lord, wherever it binds us. And just as one fastened to the cross does not now contemplate present things, nor think about his own affections, nor stretch himself out in anxious concern for the following day, nor is moved by any desire to possess; is inflamed by no pride, rivalry, or envy; does not grieve over present injuries; no longer remembers past ones; and, while he still breathes in the body, considers himself dead to all the elements, directing the gaze of his heart to the place where he does not doubt that he will soon depart—so we too, crucified by the fear of the Lord, must be dead to all these things: not only to bodily vices, but also to the elements themselves, fixing the eyes of our souls upon the place where we ought to hope that we shall depart at every moment. In this way we shall be able to keep all our desires and carnal affections mortified.

[Note: On how monks are said to be dead to the world, see the explanation in Conference 24, chapter 9.]

**CHAPTER XXXVI. That our renunciation is of no benefit if we become entangled in the very things we renounced**

Beware, therefore, lest you ever take up again any of the things that, when renouncing them, you cast away, and, contrary to the Lord’s prohibition (Matthew 24), returning from the field of evangelical labor, you be found putting on again the tunic from which you had stripped yourself. Do not turn back to the lowly earthly desires and pursuits of this world; and, contrary to Christ’s command, do not descend from the roof of perfection and presume to take anything from the things that, after renouncing them, you had abandoned.

Beware lest you remember your parents or your former affections and, recalled to the cares and anxieties of this age, become, according to the Savior’s saying, unfit for the kingdom of heaven by putting your hand to the plow and looking back (Luke 9). Beware lest, when you have begun to acquire some knowledge of the Psalms or of this profession, you gradually become elated and attempt to revive the pride that you are now beginning to trample underfoot with the ardor of faith and complete humility; and, according to the Apostle’s saying (Galatians 2), by rebuilding what you destroyed, make yourself a transgressor. Rather, persevere to the end in the nakedness that you professed before God and his angels.

Persevere also in that humility and patience with which, in order to be received into the monastery, you remained for ten days at the gate, imploring admission with many tears. Indeed, do not merely remain in them, but make progress and grow. For it is exceedingly miserable that, when you ought to advance from your beginnings and first steps and strive toward perfection, you should begin to fall from those very beginnings into lower things. For it is not the one who begins these things, but the one who perseveres in them to the end, who will be saved (Matthew 10 and 24).

[Note: The author alludes to the passage in Matthew 24, where the Lord, speaking of the destruction of Jerusalem and the calamity of the Jews, says: “Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains; and let the one who is on the roof not come down to take anything from his house; and let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his tunic.” Saint Hilary also interprets this passage mystically and morally, as Cassian does here. In this sense it is truly said that a monk is forbidden to descend from the roof of perfection and take anything from the things he renounced when he abandoned them; or to return from the field of evangelical labor in order to put on again, like a tunic—that is, to clothe himself again in—the external and temporal goods from which he stripped himself. It will be useful here to hear the Fathers explaining the passage.

Hilary writes in his Commentary: “The roof is the ridge of a house, and the exalted perfection of the whole dwelling. Whoever, therefore, has stood at the completion of his house—that is, in the perfection of his heart—must not descend, out of desire for lower worldly things. And whoever is in the field, that is, engaged in the performance of the commandment, must not return to his former cares, on account of which he will leave behind the tunic of his former sins, by which he was previously covered.”

Saint Jerome encourages Licinius to perseverance by piling up many such sayings, as though they all pointed to the same thing: “I beseech and exhort you,” he says (Letter 28), “with a father’s affection, that you who have left Sodom (Genesis 19), hastening toward the mountains, do not look behind you; do not let go of the plowshare (Luke 9), or of the Savior’s fringe, or of his locks moistened by the dew of night (Song of Songs 5), which you once began to hold; do not descend from the roof of your former virtues in search of garments; do not return from the field to the house (Matthew 24); do not, with Lot (Genesis 13), love the plains and the pleasant gardens, which are not watered from heaven, like the holy land, but from the muddy river Jordan, after it has changed its sweet waters by mixing them with those of the Dead Sea. Many begin; few reach the summit. Those who run in the stadium all run, but one receives the prize (1 Corinthians 9). Yet we are told: ‘Run in such a way that you may obtain it’ (1 Corinthians 9).”

Saint Augustine, in his Letter to Hesychius (Letter 80), says: “In tribulations one must beware lest anyone, overcome, descend from spiritual exaltation to a carnal life; or lest one who had been making progress by stretching forward to what lies ahead, fail by falling back into what lies behind.” See more on the same subject in Book VII, chapter 27.]

**CHAPTER XXXVII. That the devil always lies in wait for our end, and that we must continually watch his head**

For the crafty serpent (Genesis 3) always watches our heels—that is, he lies in wait for our end and tries to trip us until the end of our life. Therefore it will be of no benefit to have begun well, nor to have undertaken the first steps of renunciation with complete fervor, if an appropriate end does not likewise commend and complete them, and if the humility and poverty of Christ that you have now professed before him are not guarded by you to the end of your life in the same manner in which you undertook them.

To enable you to fulfill this, continually observe his head—that is, the beginnings of his thoughts—and immediately report them to your elder.

[Note: “His” means the serpent’s, that is, the devil’s. Isidore appropriately says concerning this passage: “The devil is a slippery serpent; if one does not resist his head, that is, his first suggestion, he slips wholly into the innermost heart without being perceived” (Isidore, Book II, On the Supreme Good, chapter 1).]

[Note: This salutary teaching and warning of the holy Fathers, intended for the instruction and protection of the young or novices against diabolical suggestions, was discussed earlier (Book I, chapters 8 and 9), and more will be said elsewhere.]

In this way you will learn to crush his destructive beginnings, if you are not ashamed to reveal any of them to your elder.

**CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the preparation of one who renounces the world for temptations, and on the few whom one ought to imitate**

Therefore, according to the saying of Scripture (Ecclesiasticus 2), when you have gone forth to serve the Lord, stand in the fear of God and prepare your soul not for rest, security, or delights, but for temptations and distress. For through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14). The gate is narrow and the way is constricted that leads to life, and few are those who find it.

Consider, therefore, that you have become one of the few and the chosen, and do not grow cold through the example and tepidity of the multitude. Live as the few live, so that you may deserve to be found with the few in the kingdom of God. For many are called, but few are chosen (Matthew 20 and 22); and it is a little flock to which the Father has been pleased to give the inheritance (Luke 12).

Know, therefore, that it is no light sin for someone who has professed perfection to pursue what is imperfect.

[Note: Religious profess perfection, not because they are immediately bound to be perfect, but because through their vows they are established in a state of perfection (Saint Thomas, *Summa*, II–II, question 186, articles 1 and 2; Navarre, *Commentary on the Regulars*, commentary 1, numbers 9 and 10). By this very fact they are obliged throughout their lives to strive and aspire toward perfection as their proper end, namely by observing the evangelical counsels, which are the essential vows, and the constitutions of their religious order, which are the most suitable instruments for attaining perfection, in accordance with Matthew 19: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give it to the poor, and come, follow me.” Consequently, as is said here, a religious commits no slight sin if he abandons or relaxes his zeal or desire to attain perfection—much more so if he determines this within himself and says: “I do not wish to strive toward perfection or make progress in it.” Saint Jerome is to be understood in this way when he writes to Heliodorus: “You promised that you would be perfect. For when, after abandoning military service, you castrated yourself for the sake of the heavenly kingdoms, what other life did you pursue than the perfect life?”]

This state of perfection is reached by these steps and in this order.

**CHAPTER XXXIX. The order in which one ought to ascend to perfection**

[Note: The fear of God will be treated more fully in several places. See Book XII, chapter 31; Conference 3, chapter 18; Conference 11, chapters 6 and 8; and, if you wish, consult Turrecremata’s treatise 59 on the Rule of Saint Benedict, where he discusses the fear of the Lord at length and devoutly.]

The beginning of our salvation and its safeguard, as I have said, is the fear of the Lord. Through it, those who are being instructed in the way of perfection acquire both the beginning of conversion, the cleansing of vices, and the preservation of virtues. When it has penetrated the human mind, it produces contempt for all things, forgetfulness of one’s parents, and horror of the world itself. Through contempt for and deprivation of all possessions, humility is acquired.

[Note: Here he enumerates ten acts or duties of humility, which generally agree and coincide with the twelve degrees of humility assigned by Saint Benedict (Rule, chapter 7). By these degrees that ladder must be raised which appeared in Jacob’s dream, on which angels were seen ascending and descending. More will be said elsewhere about humility and its degrees (Book XII). I add only this: three signs of humility mentioned here—namely the sixth, seventh, and eighth—are numbered among Saint Benedict’s degrees of humility in the very same words, as may be seen there. Hence I suspect that this passage was borrowed from that source.]

Humility, however, is demonstrated by these signs:

First, if one has all one’s wills mortified within oneself.

Second, if one has concealed nothing from one’s elder—not only of one’s actions, but also of one’s thoughts.

Third, if one commits everything not to one’s own judgment but to his judgment, and eagerly and gladly listens to his admonitions.

Fourth, if one preserves obedience, gentleness, and steadfastness in patience in all things.

Fifth, if one not only inflicts injury on no one, but does not grieve or become saddened even by an injury inflicted upon oneself by another.

Sixth, if one does and presumes nothing that is not encouraged either by the common rule or by the examples of one’s superiors.

Seventh, if one is content with every kind of lowliness and judges oneself, in everything commanded, to be like a bad and unworthy laborer.

Eighth, if one declares oneself lower than all others not merely with the surface of one’s lips, but believes it with the innermost affection of one’s heart.

Ninth, if one restrains one’s tongue and is not loud in speech.

Tenth, if one is not ready and quick to laugh.

By these and similar signs true humility is recognized. Once it has truly been possessed, it will immediately lead you by a higher step to charity, which has no fear. Through charity you will begin to guard, without any labor and as though naturally, all the things that previously you observed only with the pain of fear—not now from consideration of punishment or of that fear, but from love of goodness itself and delight in virtue.

[Note: He appears to allude to these verses:

“The good hate sin because they love virtue;

the wicked hate sin because they fear punishment.”

But he refers especially to the Apostle John’s saying: “Perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4), namely servile fear.]

**CHAPTER XL. That a monk should not seek examples of perfection from many, but from one or a few**

[Note: The reader should remember that this concerns novices and beginners, not those more advanced and already perfect. The abbot Pynuphius was forming and instructing a novice by this lengthy speech, or exhortation, as is clear from what precedes (chapter 32 of this book). He teaches such novices and beginners that, while they are still inexperienced and do not possess enough judgment and prudence to reject evil and choose good—that is, to distinguish virtues from vices—they should not employ many teachers from whom to seek examples for imitation and for ordering their lives. Rather, one or certainly a few truly religious persons should be proposed for imitation, since it is much easier to be formed by the example of one than by that of many; conversely, it is extremely easy for the young to be corrupted or made worse by the example of many. “The imitation of the wicked is easy,” says Saint Jerome (Letter 7, *To Laeta on the Education of Her Daughter*), “and those whose virtues you cannot attain, you will at least imitate in their vices.”

Regarding those who are more advanced and prudent, however, the matter must be understood differently, according to the judgment of blessed Antony, which the author reports in the following book. He teaches that a monk should by no means seek every kind of virtue from one person, however eminent. “One,” he says, “is adorned with the flowers of knowledge; another is more firmly fortified by sound judgment; another is grounded in the gravity of patience; another excels in humility; another in the virtue of continence; another is distinguished by the grace of simplicity,” and so forth.]

To reach this more easily, while living in a community you should seek examples of imitation and perfect life from a few—indeed, from one or two—not from many. For, apart from the fact that a tested and thoroughly refined life is found among only a few, this further benefit follows: in attaining the perfection proposed here, namely the cenobitic life, one is more diligently imbued and formed by the example of a single person.

**CHAPTER XLI. What those established in a cenobitic community ought to tolerate and endure**

[Col. 0200A]

To enable you to attain all these things and remain perpetually under this spiritual rule, you must necessarily observe these three things in the community, so that, according to the Psalmist’s saying (Psalm 37), “I, like a deaf man, did not hear, and like a mute who does not open his mouth; I became like a man who does not hear and who has no reproaches in his mouth”—you too may proceed as deaf, mute, and blind.

Without considering the one who has rightly been chosen for you as an example of perfection, you should, like a blind man, not see anything you observe that contributes little to edification, lest, encouraged by the authority or conduct of those who do such things, you be led toward what is worse and toward what you had previously condemned.

If you hear someone disobedient, rebellious, slanderous, or doing something contrary to what has been handed down to you, do not be offended or overturned into imitating him by such an example. Rather, like a deaf person who has heard none of these things, pass them all by completely.

If insults or injuries are inflicted upon you or anyone else, remain unmoved and, like a mute, listen without answering in kind, always singing this verse of the Psalmist in your heart:

“I said: I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue. I placed a guard over my mouth when the sinner stood against me; I was mute and humbled, and I was silent even from good things” (Psalm 38).

[Note: Here, as though in a picture, you have four characteristics or conditions of the true monk: he must be deaf, mute, blind, and foolish. These are to be understood morally, not literally or physically; there is no need to point this out.]

But above all cultivate this fourth quality, which adorns and commends the three mentioned above: make yourself foolish in this world, according to the Apostle’s saying (1 Corinthians 3), so that you may be wise. In other words, distinguish and judge nothing among the things commanded to you, but always offer obedience with complete simplicity and faith, judging that alone to be holy, useful, and wise which either the law of God or the judgment of your elder has prescribed for you.

Grounded in such training, you will be able to endure perpetually under this discipline and will not be turned away from the cenobium by any temptations of the enemy or by any factions.

**CHAPTER XLII. That a monk should not hope for the good of his patience from another’s virtue, but from his own long-suffering**

You should not, therefore, base your patience on the virtue of others—that is, possess it only when no one has provoked you, since preventing this from happening does not lie within your power—but rather on your own humility and long-suffering, which depend upon your own choice.

**CHAPTER XLIII. Recapitulation of the exposition by which a monk can ascend to perfection**

[Col. 0201B]

So that all these things, which have been set out in a fuller discourse, may be more easily impressed upon your heart and remain most firmly fixed in your understanding, I shall gather from them a brief summary, by which you can commit the whole to memory through a concise account of the commandments.

[Note: *Breviarium*, a term also common among ancient Latin authors, means a compendium or summary, or a concise and abridged work; in Greek, *epitomē* (ἐπιτομή) or *anakephalaiōsis* (ἀνακεφαλαίωσις). Suetonius writes of Augustus: “He also made a summary of the whole empire: how many soldiers were everywhere under the standards, how much money was in the treasury and the treasuries, and how much remained in taxes.” The same author writes of Caligula: “When the steward presented him with a summary of the accounts.”

In the same or a related sense, *breve* and *brevis* are used substantivally, in the masculine and neuter genders. Thus the common people use *breve apostolicum* for an apostolic brief; and Saint Benedict likewise (Rule, chapter 32) advises the abbot to keep a brief inventory of the monastery’s goods and utensils, which Turrecremata interprets as a note or memorandum.

Since the opportunity has arisen to speak of the Breviary, it may be useful, for the benefit of the younger members, to note that the book we have in hand, which contains the divine office, is called a Breviary for several reasons. First, because it contains all the Psalms, in which all the principal mysteries of divine Scripture and the chief works and benefits of God are briefly expressed in the form of praise, as Dionysius says in Book III of *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*. Second, because it contains the most select passages from the whole of the Old and New Testaments; third, selected teachings of the Fathers; fourth, the principal deeds of the saints; fifth, brief prayers called collects, most of which were composed by the supreme pontiffs; and sixth, certain hymns composed by the Fathers (Leonard Lessius, Book II, *On Justice and Right*, chapter 37, doubt 8).

It is therefore rightly called a Breviary, because it is an admirable compendium of all these things. In the same way Tertullian (*On Prayer*, chapter 1) calls the Lord’s Prayer “a summary of the whole Gospel.” But these remarks about the Breviary have been added incidentally and by way of occasion, since nothing is more familiar to us.]

Listen, then, to the order by which you can ascend to the highest perfection without any labor or difficulty.

According to Scripture, the beginning of our salvation and wisdom is the fear of the Lord (Proverbs 1). From the fear of the Lord arises salutary compunction. From compunction of heart proceeds renunciation—that is, nakedness and contempt of all possessions. From nakedness humility is produced. From humility the mortification of the will is generated. Through the mortification of the will, all vices are uprooted and wither. Once the vices have been expelled, virtues bear fruit and increase. Through the growth of virtues purity of heart is acquired. Through purity of heart the perfection of apostolic charity is possessed.

**BOOK FIVE. ON THE SPIRIT OF GASTRIMARGIA**

**CHAPTER ONE. The transition from the institutions of the cenobiums to the struggle against the eight principal vices**

With God’s help, this fifth book is now forged for us. For, after the four little books that have been arranged concerning the institutions of monasteries, we now undertake the struggle against the eight principal vices—first, *gastrimargia*, which is interpreted as the desire of the belly or gluttony; second, fornication; third, *philargyria*, understood as avarice, or, to express it more precisely, love of money; fourth, anger; fifth, sadness; sixth, *acedia*, which is anxiety or weariness of heart; seventh, *cenodoxia*, which signifies vain or empty glory; and eighth, pride.

As we enter upon this contest, most blessed Pope Castor, we now need your prayers more earnestly, so that, first, with the Lord strengthening us, we may suitably investigate their natures, so subtle, hidden, and obscure; second, adequately explain their causes; and third, be able to set forth appropriate cures and remedies for them.

[Note: Thus he includes the four preceding books under one title, *On the Institutions of Monasteries* or *of Cenobiums*. Gennadius and others distinguish them by their own titles. Others, however, designate them under one and the same heading, *Monastic Institutions*, and thus separate the twelve books of the *Institutions* from the books of the *Conferences*, as has been said elsewhere (on Book I, chapter 1).

The Greek Photius mentions these books in his eulogy and highly commends them, as may be seen at the beginning of this work.

Several preliminary observations should be made concerning the principal or capital vices that Cassian now begins to discuss. First, “capital vice” is understood in two ways. *Capital* derives from *caput*, “head,” and the head is a member of an animal that is the source of the direction of the whole animal. Metaphorically, every directing principle is called a head; hence people who direct and govern others are called their heads.

A capital vice may therefore be understood in one way from *head* in its proper sense, and in that sense a capital vice is one punished by capital punishment (Thomas, *Summa* I–II, question 34, articles 3 and 4; II–II, question 5, 48; John Azor, *Moral Institutions*, Book IV, chapter 12).

That is not how “capital vice” is understood in this treatise, which deals with capital vices. They are called capital because they are like springs or heads of the other vices, from which, as from a corrupt root, every kind of vice, shame, scandal, and corruption flows. This is not to be taken as though each capital vice were the cause and origin of all the others, but because each one is the head and cause of many others. Hence numerous vices arising from each capital vice are assigned to it and called its daughters.

Second, it should be noted that Cassian (here and in Conference 4, chapter 2) posited eight capital or principal vices because he lists pride as the eighth and, as it were, highest among them. He explains the reason for this order and relation of the vices in Conference 5, chapter 10, in these words:

“These eight vices, although they have different origins and dissimilar effects, are nevertheless connected—at least the first six—by a certain kinship and, so to speak, a chain. Thus the excess of the earlier becomes the beginning of the next. From abundance of *gastrimargia* fornication arises; from fornication, love of money; from love of money, anger; from anger, sadness; and from sadness, *acedia* necessarily grows.”

And later:

“Therefore, in order to overcome *acedia*, sadness must first be conquered; to drive away sadness, anger must first be thrust out; to extinguish anger, love of money must be trampled down; to uproot love of money, fornication must be restrained; to overthrow fornication, the vice of *gastrimargia* must be chastised; and, by this reasoning, for pride to be excluded, *cenodoxia* must be strangled.”

Thus Cassian. Saint Gregory, however, in Book XXXI of the *Moralia*, chapter 31, discusses only seven capital vices, since he did not wish pride to be counted among them but placed it as queen and common mother of all vices, because of its general influence over all vices and sins. Saint Gregory speaks of the seven capital vices and their mother, pride, in this way:

“The vices that tempt us, serving in an invisible battle against us under the pride that reigns over them, advance in some cases like commanders and follow in others like an army.”

And shortly afterward:

“For when pride itself, the queen of vices, has completely seized the conquered heart, it immediately hands it over to the seven principal vices, as to certain commanders, to be devastated. The army follows these commanders, because from them undoubtedly arise the troublesome multitudes of vices. We can show this more clearly if, by enumerating them individually as we are able, we identify the commanders and the army. Pride is indeed the root of all evil, concerning which Scripture says: ‘Pride is the beginning of every sin’ (Ecclesiasticus 10). Its first offspring, the seven principal vices, proceed from this poisonous root: vainglory, envy, anger, sadness, avarice, gluttony, and lust.”

You see, reader, that Saint Gregory enumerates the seven capital vices differently from Cassian and in almost the reverse order, comparing them to commanders or tribunes serving under pride as a kind of empress or queen. He then explains the armies of each commander or capital vice—what we commonly call their daughters—in these words:

“Each of these has its own army against us. From vainglory arise disobedience, boasting, hypocrisy, quarrels, obstinacy, discord, and presumptuous innovations. From envy arise hatred, whispering, detraction, rejoicing in one’s neighbor’s adversity, and grief at his prosperity. From anger come quarrels, swelling of mind, insult, shouting, indignation, and blasphemies. From sadness arise malice, rancor, faintheartedness, despair, sluggishness regarding the commandments, and wandering of mind toward unlawful things. From avarice proceed treachery, fraud, malice, perjury, restlessness, violence, and hardness of heart against mercy. From gluttony are propagated foolish merriment, buffoonery, uncleanness, excessive speech, and dullness of understanding in matters of comprehension. From lust arise blindness of mind, lack of consideration, instability, rashness, self-love, hatred of God, attachment to the present age, and horror or despair regarding the future.”

Saint Gregory says these and other things about the order and comparison of these vices, which it would take too long to report here. Yet this should not be omitted: of these seven vices, two are and are called carnal—namely gluttony and lust—because they are exercised in the flesh or body and are completed through the carnal pleasure of the external senses. The remaining five are spiritual, since they pertain to the soul and are completed without any action of the body. Other things being equal, the former are the greater disgrace, while the latter are the greater guilt.

Finally, these vices are called capital not because they are always mortal. No one would say that a slight desire for glory or a slight stirring of the mind toward anger is mortal. Rather, they are called capital, as has been said, because they are like springs or heads of the other vices, from which all the rest gush forth abundantly.]

**CHAPTER TWO. That the causes of vices, although they dwell in everyone, are unknown to everyone, and that we need the Lord’s help to reveal them**

The causes of these passions, once they have been disclosed through the teachings of the elders, are immediately recognized by everyone. Before they are revealed, however, although we are all devastated by them and they dwell in all human beings, they are unknown to everyone.

Nevertheless, we trust that we shall be able to explain them to some extent if, through your intercessions, that word of the Lord spoken through Isaiah (Isaiah 45) is directed also toward us:

“I will go before you, and I will humble the powerful of the earth; I will break the bronze doors and shatter the iron bars, and I will open for you hidden treasures and secret things.”

Thus may the word of God that goes before us first humble the powerful of our earth—that is, these harmful passions that we wish to conquer, which claim the most savage dominion and tyranny for themselves in our mortal body—and make them submit to our investigation and exposition. May it break down the doors of our ignorance, shatter the bars of the vices that exclude us from true knowledge, and lead us into the secrets of our inner being. Then, according to the Apostle (1 Corinthians 4), may it reveal to us, once enlightened, the things hidden in darkness and disclose the counsels of hearts.

Thus, penetrating the dreadful darkness of the vices with the purest eyes of the soul, may we be able to expose and bring them forth into the light, and disclose their causes and natures both to those who have been free from them and to those who remain bound by them. Then, according to the prophet (Psalm 65), after passing through the fire of the vices that terribly consume our minds, may we immediately pass unharmed also through the waters of the virtues—that is, through those that extinguish the vices—and, sprinkled with spiritual remedies,

[Note: This is an uncommon word. The Basel manuscript has *irrigati* (“watered”), while Dionysius has “sprinkled with the dew of spiritual remedies.”]

may we deserve, through purity of heart, to be brought to the refreshment of perfection.

**CHAPTER THREE. That our first struggle must be against the spirit of *gastrimargia*, that is, the desire of the belly**
Therefore [Note: [Col. 0205A] *Gastrimargia* properly means “madness of the belly”; *γαστρίμαργος* means “gluttonous,” “a devourer,” “devoted to the belly” (Billius). Isidore of Pelusium says: “*Gastrimargia* is the madness concerning the belly.” *Gastrimargia* is an irrational preoccupation with the belly. St. Gregory (Book I, Letter 184) interprets it as “the belly’s gluttony”; Cassian and Dionysius interpret it as “the desire of the palate,” attending more to the thing itself than to the etymology of the name [Col. 0205B]. Aristotle also used this word in Book V of the *Ethics*, as did Clement of Alexandria in Book II of the *Paedagogus*, chapter 1, and John Climacus in Step 14. Latin authors were content with the word *gula*, “gluttony.” But Cassian thought that this word did not sufficiently express the whole force of *gastrimargia*; hence he preferred to use the Greek term. This vice is contrary to the virtue of abstinence and embraces every disordered desire for, and use of, food and drink. Cassian calls it “the spirit of gastrimargia” in the title of this book, just as he calls the other vices treated in these books “the spirit of fornication,” “the spirit of avarice,” “the spirit of vainglory,” “the spirit of pride,” and so forth. Most of these phrases and designations are taken from Sacred Scripture, as will be shown in their proper places. Against this vice, the Author says that our first contest must be undertaken; and St. Gregory confirms this in Book XXXI of the *Moralia*, chapter 26, giving the following reason:

“No one grasps the palm of spiritual combat who has not first conquered within himself, through the affliction of the belly’s desire, the incitements of the flesh. For one does not rise to the struggle of the spiritual contest unless the enemy placed within us—namely, the appetite of the palate—has first been subdued. If we do not overthrow what is nearer to us, we pass vainly on to attack what lies farther away. For a battle against external enemies is waged in the field to no purpose if a treacherous citizen is held within the very walls of the city.”

And further on he applies to this the passage written about Nabuzardan, commander of the Babylonian army: “The chief of the cooks destroyed the walls of Jerusalem.” For what, he says, does Scripture signify by the walls of Jerusalem (Jeremiah V; 2 Kings XXV), except the virtues of the soul that strives toward the vision of peace? Or whom is the chief of the cooks to be understood as representing, except the belly, which cooks serve with the greatest diligence? Thus the chief of the cooks destroys the walls of Jerusalem, because, when it is not restrained, the belly destroys the virtues of the soul. Thus far St. Gregory.

John Climacus should also be consulted in Step 14 of his *Ladder*, where he admirably describes this vice of gluttony, or *gastrimargia*. He questions it as though it were a beast ruling over the human race, and introduces it as answering with a striking personification:

“Tell us,” he says, “O excessively violent mistress of all mortals, from where do you prepare an entrance into us? And what do you usually prepare after your entrance? And what is your way out from us—namely, how are we freed from you?”

But, provoked by these insults, it answered us tyrannically, bloodthirstily, and fiercely:

“Why do you assail me with curses, when you are subject to me? Or how do you seek to separate yourselves from me, when I am joined to nature? My door is naturally food; habit is the cause of my insatiability. The material of my disturbance is the habit I have mentioned, together with the soul’s apathy and forgetfulness of death. Do you ask how to learn the names of my offspring? I shall enumerate them, and they will multiply beyond the sand. Hear, nevertheless, the names of my firstborn: my firstborn is the inciter of fornication; the second after him is the author of hardening; sleep is the third. A sea of thoughts, waves of defilements, and the depth of hidden and unknown impurities proceed from me.

“My daughters are sloth, talkativeness, boldness, buffoonery that provokes laughter, contradiction, stiffness of neck, slowness to hear, insensibility, arrogance and swelling, rashness, love of the world, unclean prayer, followed by waves of thoughts; and sometimes calamity as well, beyond all hope and expectation, which is necessarily followed by despair, more bitter and grievous than all the rest.

“The memory of sins attacks me, but does not overcome me. The thought of impending death wages war against me. Yet there is nothing among human beings that perfectly overcomes me. Whoever possesses the Paraclete intercedes against me, and when he has been entreated, he does not permit me to work wickedly. But those who have not received even a taste of him are wholly carried away by the allurements of my sweetness and pleasantness.”

Such is the passage in Climacus, in which the nature and properties of gluttony are vividly depicted; more will be said about them below.]

Thus our first contest must be undertaken against *gastrimargia*, which we have said is the desire of the palate. And since we are first going to speak about the manner of fasting and the quality of foods, we shall once again have recourse to the traditions and regulations of the Egyptians, whose superior discipline of continence and perfect rule of discernment no one is unaware of.

## CHAPTER IV. The testimony of Abbot Antony, teaching that each virtue should be sought from the person who possesses it in a distinctive degree.

For there is [Note: [Col. 0206B] Concerning blessed Antony, the celebrated anchorite, among other writers both Greek and Latin, Sozomen writes briefly as follows (Book I of the *History*, chapter 13): “Whether Egyptians or others were the founders of this devout—that is, monastic—life, this at least is agreed by all: Antony, that great monk, brought this mode of life to its highest point by perfect rules of piety and exercises suited to it.” At that time, while he was living in the deserts of Egypt amid great renown and fame, Emperor Constantine, because of the splendor of his virtue, made him his friend, sent him honorably written letters, and earnestly urged him to write to him concerning anything he needed, and so forth.

The Roman Martyrology says of him (17 January): “In the Thebaid, [the feast] of Saint Antony, abbot, father of many monks, most illustrious in life and miracles; his deeds were recounted by Saint Athanasius in a distinguished volume.” There Cardinal Baronius says in his notes: “Saint Athanasius wrote his excellent acts, which Evagrius—not the Pontic Origenist, but he who later presided over the Church of Antioch—translated into Latin, as Saint Jerome testifies in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Evagrius. Jerome himself performed the same task at the request of Pammachius, as he declares in writing to him in Letter 101, *On the Best Method of Translating*.
