We believe this to be the version now at hand; and since, as he himself says, in translating it he rendered not words by words but meanings by meanings, according to his custom, perhaps this is why Pope Gelasius testifies that he did not so much translate as write the *Life of Antony*, when he says: ‘We receive with all honor the Lives of the Fathers—Paul, Antony, Hilarion, and all the hermits—which the most blessed Jerome nevertheless composed’ (in Gratian, Distinction 11, chapter *Sancta Romana*).” Thus Baronius, and what follows (see Bellarmine, Book II *On Monks*, chapter 5).

These remarks seem to hold that the life of blessed Antony, written in Greek by Saint Athanasius, was first rendered into Latin by Evagrius and then by Saint Jerome, and that this is the very version now at hand—that is, as I suppose, the one commonly and widely circulated and found at the end of the works of Saint Athanasius, though it bears the title of a translation by Evagrius. But the Reverend Father Heribert Rosweyde, theologian of the Society of Jesus, shows in his notes on the *Life of Antony* in his outstanding work on the *Lives of the Fathers*, recently restored and illustrated by him, that Baronius’s opinion is improbable and conceived through a misunderstanding of Saint Jerome’s Letter 101. I leave his reasons to be consulted in that work, since mention of Antony’s life and its translator has arisen here only incidentally from Baronius’s note.] an ancient and admirable saying of blessed Antony that a monk who, after undertaking the cenobitic life, strives to attain the heights of a more exalted perfection, and who, having grasped the test of discernment, is already able to stand by his own judgment and [Note: [Col. 0207B] That is, to the summit and perfection of the anchoritic life, which is like a citadel and pinnacle of religion.] to reach the stronghold of the anchoritic life [Note: [Col. 0207B] By this saying of blessed Antony, the Author teaches that one who strives toward perfection and who, as he says, having grasped the test of discernment, is already able to stand by his own judgment—that is, who is so endowed with the gift of prudence and discernment that he can test everything and hold fast only to what is good (1 Thessalonians V)—ought not to propose to himself the examples of all the virtues for imitation from one person alone. Rather, he should examine many people and observe in each what is best and most perfect. For it is clear that no mortal excels in every virtue: one surpasses another in prudence, another in courage, and another in some other virtue, or is himself surpassed, according as each has exercised himself more or less in this or that virtue.

That same great Antony handed down this excellent instruction not only in words but also in example and practice. For, as St. Athanasius relates, he so vied with the better gifts of all the brothers that, like a most prudent bee, he drew out the particular graces of each. He followed one man’s continence, another’s cheerfulness, this man’s gentleness, another’s watchfulness; he imitated another’s diligence in reading. He admired one who fasted and another who rested on the ground; he praised one man’s patience and another’s meekness. Retaining toward himself the reciprocal charity of all, and watered by every part of the virtues, he returned to his own dwelling. There, considering everything within himself, he strove to reproduce in himself the good qualities of all. Thus Athanasius speaks of St. Antony (Theodoret, *History of the Holy Fathers*, chapter 5).

The most holy Abbot Publius likewise exhorted his cenobites to try continually to derive benefit from one another: one should imitate another’s gentleness; the other, in turn, should strengthen his own gentleness through zeal for this man; one should learn watchfulness from another; and another should teach him the austerity of fasting. Finally, all should become both disciples and teachers to one another. For he said that in this way, by taking from one another’s lives what they lacked, they would form the most perfect accumulation of virtues.

St. Jerome likewise, after various instructions, adds the following to the monk Rusticus (Letter 4):

“Through all these things the exhortation tends toward this end: to teach you that you must not be left to your own judgment, but must live in a monastery under the discipline of one father and in the fellowship of many, so that you may learn humility from one, patience from another; let this man teach you silence, and that one meekness, and so forth.”

And in his Letter to Eustochium (Letter 22), recalling the institutions of the Egyptian monks, he relates how they observed the virtues, various gifts, and perfections of one another and proposed them to themselves for imitation:

“After the hymn has been sung,” he says, “they return to their stalls—that is, their cells. There, until evening, each one speaks with his companions and says: ‘Did you see that man, and that one? How great is his gravity! How profound his silence! How measured his walk!’ If they see someone ill, they console him; if someone is fervent in the love of God, they encourage him to pursue it.”]

should by no means seek all kinds of virtues from one person, however eminent. One is adorned with the flowers of knowledge; another is more firmly strengthened by the practice of discernment; another is grounded in the gravity of patience. One is distinguished by the virtue of humility, another by continence, and another is adorned by the grace of simplicity. One surpasses the others in greatness of spirit, another in mercy, another in watchfulness, another in silence, and another in zeal for labor.

Therefore, a monk who desires to store up spiritual honey, like a most prudent bee, ought to gather each virtue from those who possess it more familiarly [Col. 0207B] and carefully store it in the vessel of his own heart. He should not investigate what anyone lacks, but should contemplate only what virtue that person possesses [Col. 0208A] and diligently pluck it. For if we wish to borrow all things from one person, examples suitable for imitation will either be difficult or certainly impossible to find.

For although we do not yet see Christ to be all things in all, according to the Apostle (1 Corinthians XV) [Note: [Col. 0208B] These words refer to the Apostle’s statement in Colossians III: “All things and in all, Christ.” By “all things” are understood the things that pertain to the renewal of the human being, which the Apostle discusses there—justice, holiness, and the qualities he immediately enumerates. Christ is said to be all these things in all, that is, in every kind of human being, not only causally, as God is the principal cause, but also meritoriously, through the merit of his passion. In this sense he is also said below to have been made for us by God “wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption” (1 Corinthians I). But because this renewal, or newness, of the human being begins in this life through grace and justification, yet is not fully and absolutely perfected and completed until the future, through the complete reformation and glorification of soul and body, Cassian says that Christ does not yet appear to have become all things in all—that is, perfectly and absolutely.], nevertheless in this way we can find him—that is, in parts—in all. For it is said of him that he was made for us by God “wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption” (1 Corinthians I). Therefore, when wisdom is found in one person, righteousness in another, holiness in another, gentleness in another, chastity in another, humility in another, and patience in another, Christ is now divided among the individual saints, member by member.

But when all these persons come together into the unity of faith and virtue, he is restored into a perfect man [Note: [Col. 0208C] Here again he alludes to the Apostle’s words in Ephesians IV: “Until we all attain to the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.” Here, however, he interprets “the perfect man” as Christ himself, although it is evident that the words refer to us: the Apostle says that at the general resurrection of all we shall come forth—or escape—as perfect men, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, and so forth, because “when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part shall be done away” (1 Corinthians XIII).], completing the fullness of his body (Ephesians IV) in the structure and distinctiveness of each member.

Until that time comes when God is all things in all [Note: [Col. 0208D] St. Jerome skillfully and appropriately explains what it means for God to be all things in all, and when that time will be, in words that illuminate this passage of Cassian (Letter 147, vol. III):

“What the Apostle says (1 Corinthians XV), ‘That God may be all in all,’ must be understood in this sense: our Lord and Savior is not now all things in all, but is a part in each. For example, in Solomon there is wisdom; in David, goodness; in Job, patience; in Daniel, knowledge of future things; in Peter, faith; in Phinehas and Paul, zeal; in John, virginity; and in others, other qualities. But when the end of all things has come, then he will be all things in all, so that each of the saints will possess all virtues, and Christ will be wholly in all.” Thus St. Jerome.], God can, in the present, be in all in the manner we have described—that is, through the several virtues—even though he is not yet all things in all through their fullness. For although the goal of our religion is one, the professions by which we strive toward God are different, as will be discussed more fully in the *Conferences of the Elders* (see Conferences I, 18 and 19).

Therefore, the pattern of discernment and continence should be sought more particularly from those in whom we see these virtues flowing more abundantly through the grace of the Holy Spirit—not because anyone can acquire alone those things that have been divided among many, but so that in those goods of which we are capable we may strive to imitate those who have obtained them in a more distinctive degree.

## CHAPTER V. That a uniform rule of fasting cannot be observed by everyone.

Therefore [Note: [Col. 0209B] St. Basil likewise treats this matter in chapter 10 of his *Rule for Monks* (in Rufinus’s translation, and in the *Longer Rules*, Question 19). He asks what the measure of continence—that is, temperance or abstinence—is, and answers:

“As regards food, it should be according to what necessity demands, whether age, labor, bodily strength, or physical condition; accordingly, the amount and quality of food should also be moderated. For it is not possible for all the brothers to observe one order, measure, or rule. Those who are healthy, however, can all maintain the same measure in abstinence. But changes should be made for individuals in whom some cause of difference exists, with the foresight and provision of those entrusted with the responsibility of dispensing these things.”

St. Benedict says in chapter 40:

“Each one has his own gift from God: one in this way, another in that” (1 Corinthians XII).

“And therefore the measure of food is established by us with some scruple. Those to whom God grants endurance of abstinence should know that they will have their own reward. But if the needs of the place, labor, or the heat of summer demand more, it should lie within the prior’s discretion, provided that he considers in all things that satiety or drunkenness does not creep in.”] a uniform rule concerning the manner of fasting cannot easily [Col. 0210A] be observed, because neither is the same strength present in all bodies, nor are fasts acquired solely through the rigor of the mind, as are the other virtues. And therefore, since they do not consist in mental strength alone but participate in the capacity of the body, we have received the following definition concerning them [Note: [Col. 0209C] It is clear from this passage that the Fathers and monks of both sexes had different practices of fasting: some stricter and more austere, others less austere, according to the unequal condition of their bodies, their age, or their sex. Some prolonged their fasts for entire weeks—that is, fasted for whole weeks; others observed three-day or two-day fasts; others fasted through the entire Forty Days without food or drink; finally, some were content with legumes or vegetables alone, and others with a small quantity of bread, dry bread—that is, without a relish or side dish. Such examples may be found in Epiphanius at the end of his book *Against Heresies*, in Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, in Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 28 and following, and also in the *Lives of the Fathers*, recently illustrated with excellent notes and observations by the Reverend Father Heribert Rosweyde, theologian of the Society of Jesus, where countless examples of this kind are reported.

This is relevant to what Philo the Jew writes about the Alexandrian monks (*On the Contemplative Life*), and what Eusebius of Caesarea quotes from him (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 16):

“None of them takes food or drink before sunset. Some, whose souls are more ardently possessed by the desire for knowledge, scarcely remember food once in three days. Others, as though invited by the allurements of wisdom—which supplies the wholesome precepts of virtue so abundantly and copiously—are so delighted by them, and derive such pleasures from them, that they easily endure twice as long a period of fasting, and scarcely taste the necessary nourishment after six full days.”

To this may be added St. Augustine, who writes the following about the cenobites of his own time (*On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, Book I, chapter 31):

“I have learned that many practice fasts utterly incredible—not merely refreshing the body once each day toward evening, which is everywhere most customary, but very often spending three continuous days or more without food or drink.”] namely, that the time, manner, and quality of meals differ according to the unequal condition, age, or sex of bodies, while the rule of mortification is one for all as regards continence of mind and strength of spirit.

For it is not possible for everyone to prolong fasts for whole weeks, or even to postpone the taking of food for three or two days. For many who are already worn out by illness, and especially by old age, cannot tolerate fasting without distress even until sunset. [Note: [Col. 0210B] A legume is anything that grows from the sowing of the earth in pods. Varro says in Book I of *On Agriculture*: “Legumes are pulled up from the earth, not cut down like grain; because they are thus gathered, they are called *legumina*.” Isidore says in *Etymologies*, Book XVII, chapter 4: “They are called *legumes* from *legere*, ‘to gather,’ because the ancients gathered the best things; or because they are gathered by hand and do not require cutting.”

There are many kinds of legumes, among which beans, lentils, peas, chickpeas, chickling vetch, and lupins appear more agreeable for human use. Soaked legumes are those merely moistened or diluted with water. Thus in the *Lives of the Fathers* one often finds *infundere panes*, “to soak” or “moisten bread.” In Book III, number 4: “He soaked the bread in water, saying: ‘While this bread is being soaked …’” In Book V, booklet 4: “He soaked the bread and sat down to eat.”

St. Jerome also relates that monks commonly used legumes and vegetables. In Letter 22 he says: “They live on bread, legumes, and vegetables, which are seasoned only with salt.” And in the *Life of Hilarion*: “From his twenty-first to his twenty-seventh year, for three years he ate half a *sextarius* of lentils moistened with cold water, and for another three years dry bread with salt and water. From his twenty-seventh to his thirtieth year, he supported himself on wild herbs and the raw roots of certain shrubs.” Thus Jerome.

Lentils, which are counted among legumes, and *lapsana*—that is, a wild vegetable familiar as food to the Egyptian monks—were mentioned above (Book IV, chapters 20 and the last). St. Benedict also grants the brothers a third dish of legumes (Rule, chapter 39).

Besides these serious matters, I am reminded of the amusing reply of a certain monk who, when asked what he had eaten that day, answered, “Vegetables with peas”; when asked what he had eaten the day before, “Peas with vegetables”; when asked what he had eaten two days earlier, “Peas and vegetables”; and finally, when asked what he had eaten four days earlier, “Vegetables and peas.” In this way he indicated that this was the monks’ daily, or at least very frequent, fare. See another example in Caesarius, Book IV, chapter 79; Basil, *On Holy Virginity*; and Jerome, Letter 10 to Furia.

As for the reason why the eating of legumes is here called weakened or enervated, I do not understand it sufficiently unless the expression is metonymical, because legumes weaken and debilitate the body and its strength rather than strengthen them; or unless it is by comparison with other, stronger foods—that is, foods that nourish more and [Col. 0211A] strengthen the body, such as meat and fish. For Basil and Jerome testify that legumes are otherwise hot and flatulent by nature. Jerome’s position concerning the eating of legumes and vegetables, and the difference between them, is as follows:

“Avoid all hot foods among foods themselves. I am not speaking only of meats, concerning which the Chosen Vessel gives the judgment: ‘It is good neither to eat meat nor to drink wine.’ But even among legumes, those that cause wind and heaviness should be avoided; and you should know that nothing is so beneficial to Christian youths as eating vegetables. Hence he says elsewhere: ‘Let the weak person eat vegetables’; and the heat of the body should be moderated by colder foods. Again, elsewhere (*Against Jovinianus*, Book II): ‘The preparation of vegetables, fruits, and legumes is easier; it does not require the skill and expense of cooks, and it sustains the body without care; taken in moderation, it is digested more easily.’”]

The consumption of soaked legumes does not suit everyone in its weakened form [Col. 0211A]; nor is the frugality of plain vegetables suitable for all; nor is a restrained portion [Note: [Col. 0211A] That is, a thin and frugal portion, bound by the laws of a fixed measure [Col. 0211B] that it would not be permissible to exceed. Macrobius says in Book II of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 1: “But when heroes sit down to restrained banquets.” Tertullian says in *On Fasting*: “Now, if one rashly considers the rule of such restrained nourishment,” and so forth; in some copies this is wrongly read as “nourishment chastised by God.” St. Jerome says in Book II *Against Jovinianus*: “The sick person does not recover health otherwise than through thin food and restrained nourishment,” which is called *λεπτὴ δίαιτα*, “a slender diet.”

Cassian, again, in the final chapter of Book I, according to the reading of some, says *castigatum modum*, “a restrained measure,” meaning a just and suitable one. The meal of dry bread was called in Greek *ξηροφαγία*, that is, “the eating of dry things,” such as bread alone with salt, without any other relish; this did not, however, exclude water. They used water in two ways: both to soak or pour over the bread and to drink. Thus in Palladius’s *Life of Paul*, Antony is said to have placed four *paxamidia*—that is, loaves—on the table and soaked one for himself; “for they were dry,” he says.]

a restrained meal of dry bread is granted to everyone. One person does not feel satisfied with two pounds in quantity [Note: [Col. 0211B]

A considerable difficulty arises here concerning the bread-pound: how many ounces did it contain among those Fathers? For the Author appears to imply here that one pound consisted only of six ounces. “One pound,” he says, “or six ounces,” as though one pound and six ounces were the same. To explain this, something must be said about the pound and what sort of pound is meant both by Cassian and by St. Benedict in the Rule.

Those who have written about measures and weights distinguish two kinds of pound: a measuring pound and a weighing pound. Galen asserts that the Romans used both, as Georgius Agricola testifies (*Galen, On Compound Medicines*, Book I; Agricola, *On Weights and Measures*). Among the Romans, the pound was a kind of measure divided by certain intersecting lines into twelve equal parts, which they called ounces. To distinguish this measure from weight, they called it a measuring pound, or a pound-measure; the other, by which things are weighed—that is, weight itself—they called a weighing pound, or a pound by weight. Its parts were likewise called ounces.

It follows that there are two kinds of ounces: measuring ounces and weighing ounces. The measuring ounces are parts of a measuring pound, just as the weighing ounces are parts of a weighing pound. The difference between measuring ounces and pounds and weighing ounces and pounds is that the latter place before our eyes the heaviness of bodies, whereas the former indicate bulk, size, or capacity, as the same Galen teaches.

It is evident that the weighing pound, and consequently weighing ounces, are meant when a bread-pound is discussed. For the question concerns the weight or heaviness of this pound. Thus, in St. Benedict (chapters 39 and 40), the measure of food is understood in one way and the measure of drink in another. The measure of food, insofar as bread is concerned, is understood as a weighing measure—that is, bread of one pound, or one *pondo*. But the measure of drink, called a *hemina*, is not understood as the weight of the drink itself, or as drink of a particular weight, but as a measuring measure or measuring vessel that contains and measures the drink, or as the drink contained in the vessel, which may be called the measured measure. Thus the measure of drink is considered not by its heaviness or weight but by the capacity of the vessel, as is sufficiently well known.

Moreover, they again distinguish two kinds of weighing pound: one of sixteen ounces, which they call the mercantile or zygostatic pound, and which the Gauls call the royal or Parisian pound; merchants and all shopkeepers who sell weighed goods use it. The other is the Roman pound of only twelve ounces, formerly customary among the Romans and most frequently mentioned by writers (Budaeus, Book II *On the As*; Junius, *Nomenclator*).

Thus St. Epiphanius, who wrote a book on measures and weights, says: “A pound consists of twelve ounces.” Isidore says in *Etymologies*, Book XVI, chapter 24: “An ounce is so called because by its unity it binds together—that is, comprehends—the totality of smaller weights. It consists of eight drachms, that is, twenty-four scruples.” This is therefore regarded as the legitimate weight, because the number of its scruples measures the hours of day and night, or because, when counted twelve times, it makes a pound and is completed by twelve ounces. Hence it is a type of perfect weight, because it contains as many ounces as the year has months. It is called a pound because it is free and encompasses within itself all the aforesaid weights. Thus he writes.

With these points established, let us come to our purpose. As far as Cassian is concerned, I do not think that any other pound should be understood than the ancient pound, customary and known to everyone—namely, one of twelve ounces. Cassian himself sufficiently indicates this in *Conference* II, chapter 19, where Abbot Moses approves and commends a measure of bread consisting of two *paximacia*, which he calls small loaves and says scarcely weighed one pound. But if the two loaves together had not weighed twelve ounces or thereabouts, that measure would certainly not have been, as he calls it, a most equitable arrangement, or a sufficiently just measure that could suffice for everyone without any relish. Hence some, on the contrary, infer from that passage that each *paximacium* was one pound, or twelve ounces; but we shall refute this in that same place.

Palladius confirms the matter more clearly in chapter 28 of the *Lausiac History*, where he speaks of Paul the Simple:

“Antony brings and places on the table four *paxamidia*”—this is his term for what others call *paximacia*—“of six ounces, and he soaked one for himself,” and so forth.

“Of six ounces,” he says; and this must certainly be understood of each *paxamidion* or *paximacium*. For who would say that four *paxamidia* together and collectively amounted to only six ounces? Therefore four *paxamidia* weighed twenty-four ounces, that is, two pounds of bread; from this it follows that each pound consisted of twelve ounces.

But what shall we say about the present passage of Cassian, where he appears to confuse a pound and six ounces, or to take them as the same thing? I admit that at first sight this is how it appears, and that any sufficiently attentive reader would judge so at a glance. But since it is clear from what has been said that the Author held a different view, reason requires us to interpret his words, as far as possible, conveniently and consistently.

I therefore think that the word *sive*, “or,” is not explanatory here but rather adversative, as dialecticians say, standing for “indeed,” or with “even” or something similar understood. The sense would be: some are content with a pound of bread—indeed, even with half a pound, or, what amounts to the same thing, six ounces. This sense is both true and clear, and consistent with what has been said.

For we heard above that Antony himself was content with a single *paxamidion*, that is, half a pound of bread weighing six ounces. And in the *Life of Paul the First Hermit*, St. Jerome relates that at Antony’s arrival a raven brought a whole loaf of bread—that is, a loaf of one pound. When he saw it, Paul said:

“Behold, the Lord has sent us a meal, truly kind, truly merciful. For sixty years now I have always received half a loaf of bread; but at your arrival Christ has doubled the rations for his soldiers.”

And in the *Life of Hilarion*, the same Jerome says:

“From his thirty-first to his thirty-fifth year, he had six ounces of barley bread and a small quantity of boiled vegetable without oil as his food.”

Likewise, for Abbot Dorotheus in Egypt, six ounces of bread and a small bunch of vegetables constituted a meal, as Sozomen testifies (Book VI, chapter 29). More examples can be found in the *Lives of the Fathers*.

But anyone who rejects this interpretation of ours must necessarily admit one of two things: either that this passage is corrupt—although I find it consistent in all copies, both manuscript and printed—or else that those monks had two different bread-pounds, one of six ounces and another of twelve ounces. Who would accept this without any support from antiquity?

[Col. 0213B] Now let us approach Saint Benedict (for whose sake and with whose teaching in view this discussion has also been undertaken). His regulation concerning the daily portion of bread to be distributed to the brothers reads as follows:

“One weighed pound of bread shall suffice for the day, whether there be one meal or both dinner and supper. But if they are to sup, a third part of that same pound shall be reserved by the cellarer and returned to those who are to sup. If greater labor should perhaps have been undertaken, it shall be within the abbot’s judgment and authority, if expedient, to increase something, while above all gluttony is removed,” etc. (Chapter 39 of the Rule).

Here two things may be considered. First, the quantity is defined and fixed at a specific measure, namely one weighed pound—*propensa*, that is, hung, weighed, or measured out, as Smaragdus explains. I, however, understand *propensa* as meaning hanging forward and overflowing, that is, ample and abundant, not scanty or diminished, in accordance with the words of Luke 6: “They will give into your lap a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing.” In Plautus also, *propensa munera* means “large gifts.”

Second, the abbots are granted the power to increase this amount, if expedient. As to the first point, it should be noted that various opinions have been held concerning the pound of bread prescribed by Saint Benedict, and that among different people it has had, and still has, different weights.

Turrecrematus, the commentator on the Rule, judges as follows:

“We believe that the weight of this pound of bread is greater than that of the Florentine pound, which is said to contain only twelve ounces, because the latter would not suffice for two meals. Moreover, this division of the pound of bread would more properly and usefully be divided into several loaves, so that a third part could be reserved in a whole loaf for the brother’s supper.”

So he writes.

Abbot Smaragdus, in the same place, cites a certain master of monks, whom he does not name, who says:

“A half-loaf weighing a pound shall suffice each brother for the day, according to the pattern of divine provision, since the crow prepared half of the heavenly bread for Paul, the servant of God, to eat each day. Therefore, when they take their meal at the sixth hour in summer, or at other times, a third quarter-loaf of that Lord’s bread shall be removed by the cellarer from each person’s allowance—that is, from his portion or provision—and set aside in the cellar, so that in the evening, before them, a raw relish may be brought to the tables—that is, lettuces or garden herbs dressed with vinegar and oil. When he says ‘one weighed pound of bread,’ it is understood to mean previously weighed or measured.”

This is what Smaragdus says. When he speaks of “a half-loaf weighing a pound,” this agrees sufficiently with the Rule as far as the pound is concerned. But as to the half-loaf, which he says weighs a pound—as though a whole loaf ought to weigh two pounds—he seems to allude rather inappropriately to the example of Paul the hermit. It is not plausible that half of a one-pound loaf was brought to him each day; rather, it was half a loaf, that is, half a pound, as we explained above. At Antony’s arrival, the provision was doubled: a whole one-pound loaf was supplied. The two men humbly disputed over its division until, having seized the loaf from opposite sides and each pulling it toward himself, each retained his own portion in his hands (Jerome, in the same place).

For who could believe that two exceedingly abstinent hermits, worn out by old age, consumed two pounds of bread at a single little supper and divided it between them by pulling against each other, equally or nearly so?

But let us also hear the opinions of others. The Cassinese monks, in their declaration on the words of the Rule, “One pound of bread” (Chapter 39), say:

“Since the weight of the pound, as we have received it from our monastery of Monte Cassino, is thirty-three and a half ounces, so that scarcely could one brother eat that much bread in a single day, we wish our custom to be maintained: namely, that as much bread as is sufficient be placed before him.”

Thus they establish the pound of bread at thirty-three ounces and a half. James Brolius, a monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, noted in his *Supplement to the Antiquities of Paris* that this weight, as truly Benedictine—that is, prescribed by Saint Benedict and received from the monastery of Monte Cassino—was retained by many monasteries of the Benedictine order in France.

Leo of Ostia, in the first book, chapter 14, of his *Cassinese Chronicle*, reports that in the year of the Lord 774 the emperor Charlemagne sent a letter to Theodemar, abbot of Monte Cassino, asking him to send several brothers from the monastery of Saint Benedict who could restore in the regions of Gaul the regular discipline that had died out there. Theodemar did so, sending him also the Rule and the hymns that were then sung in that monastery according to the tradition of the Rule. He likewise sent in writing the weight of the pound of bread and its measure, as well as the measure of the cup that the servers were to receive in the mixed drink, and every custom that was then observed in that place.

This is what Leo of Ostia says in the cited passage.

[The margin notes: “The weight of Saint Benedict’s bread was four pounds.”]

The letter of Abbot Theodemar, appended to the end of that Chronicle, in which he fully satisfied Charlemagne’s request, contains among other things the following:

“We have also sent the weight of four pounds, according to the equality of which weight the bread ought to be made, so that, in accordance with the sacred text of the Rule, it may be divided into four quarters of one pound each, since that weight, instituted by the Father himself, has been found here.”

This is found there, along with other matters concerning the measure of drink, which will be reported elsewhere.

To this may be added the first addition to the *Capitularies of the Kings*, chapter 57, where it is decreed that the pound of bread given to monks is to be weighed at thirty solidi, counted in denarii, before it is baked. I understand this to mean that the pound of bread—that is, the monks’ daily portion—ought to weigh thirty solidi—that is, asses, Turonian at least if not Parisian, or 360 denarii—that is, to be worth that amount; from this its size and weight may be estimated (see Budé, book 5 of the *Treasury*).

I believe that Andreas Quercetanus also had this and similar evidence in view in his notes on the life of Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, where it is said: “He was sustained by half a pound of bread.” He writes:

“There are two kinds of pound: the Roman pound of twelve ounces, and the mercantile pound of sixteen; but the Benedictine, or monastic, pound is much greater than these, and the half of it, which the writer of Odo’s life reports as having sustained him, proves this. For Benedict, prescribing in chapter 39 of the Rule the measure of food for his monks, says: ‘One weighed pound of bread shall suffice for the day,’ etc. It is established that many monasteries in Gaul, living under the rule of their father Benedict, retained this measure.”

So he writes.

But enough has now been said about the pound of bread among the Benedictines, and about its differing interpretations, as well as its varying weight and measure among different people, on the basis of various writers. Each person has shown sufficiently that he is rich in his own opinion; yet no one has been able definitively to determine and explain what the legislator’s intention was.

As for the second part of Saint Benedict’s regulation, we must first listen to that venerable man, Peter of Cluny. Refuting sharply and with great force the serious and bitter objections of the Cistercian monks against the Cluniacs, whom they accused of violating the Rule and transgressing their vow, he teaches that in these and similar provisions of the Rule one must attend not so much to the words themselves as to the mind of Benedict, the devout father and legislator, and interpret them piously according to the judgment and opinion of superiors (Letter 28, book 3).

From his excessively long and elaborate discussion, I thought it appropriate to extract and set down here those passages that principally concern our subject and clarify the place under discussion. In them he both rebukes and skillfully instructs his opponents concerning the measure of bread and drink, which they had misunderstood:

“For if a weighed pound of bread should not suffice a monk for the day; if he should take even a little above a pound, or something else instead of a pound; unless he returns an entire third part to the cellarer, and not to someone else, to be given back to him for supper; if at the first meal he should eat more or less of the pound than would leave a third part to be kept—that is, so that neither more nor less than a third part remains for the one who has eaten—are we therefore condemned, excluded from paradise, and thrust into hell as perjurers and sons of perdition?

“What will you say about those who travel outside the monastery, and, going about in various places out of necessity for the monastery, remain away from it for a long time? Will they always be able to weigh their bread? Will they always and everywhere be able to have the monastery’s cellarer with them, to whom, whenever they have eaten twice, they may entrust a third part of their pound to be received for that supper, and avoid eating bread from elsewhere?”

And further on:

“Not so, not so did the saint think, who is said to have been filled with the spirit of all the just. Not so did he think. But hear what he did think. ‘If greater labor,’ he says, ‘should perhaps have been undertaken, it shall be within the abbot’s judgment and authority, if expedient, to increase something, while above all gluttony is removed,’ so that indigestion may never creep upon a monk, because nothing is so contrary to every Christian as gluttony, as our Lord says: ‘See that your hearts are not weighed down with gluttony’ (Luke 21).

“In saying this, what else did he do but preserve necessity and cut away vice, while judging that all such matters should lie within the abbot’s authority? And do not all his words concerning the measure of drink also support this understanding of ours? We would gladly pass over them for the sake of brevity; but since his intention and discernment can be recognized especially from them, we must set them down” (Chapter 39 of the Rule).

“‘Each person,’ he says, ‘has his own gift from God: one in this way, another in that’ (1 Corinthians 7). Therefore, with some scruple, a measure of food is established by us for others,” etc.

He says that different gifts are given by God to different people, and therefore establishes the measure of food for others with scruple. Yet, in establishing it, he commands nothing. Rather, he believes that the measure he sets forth can suffice for the brothers; but if labor, heat, or any necessity should demand more, he places the matter within the prior’s authority, cutting away only what is superfluous and vicious in his customary manner, and therefore warning that satiety and drunkenness must be avoided in everything.

So he writes. Finally, after a little more, he concludes:

“This is what that holy man understood; this is what he wrote. For this reason he wished neither to define nor to command anything else. Instead, according to the character of places, times, customs, infirmities, and various circumstances, he decreed that food, drink, clothing, and, finally, all things necessary both for bodies and for souls should be given to his subjects by their fathers, intent solely upon the salvation of their souls and anxious to secure it whether by giving, withdrawing, sparing, or correcting” (Chapter 40 of the Rule).

He shows this in almost every passage of his Rule; and he says it especially in the chapter mentioned above, where he asks whether everyone ought to receive necessities equally:

“As it is written, ‘It was distributed to each according to what each had need of’ (Acts 4). Here we do not mean that there should be favoritism toward persons—far be it from us—but consideration of infirmities. Let the one who needs less give thanks to God and not be saddened. Let the one who needs more humble himself because of his infirmity, and not exalt himself because of the mercy shown him. Thus all the members will be at peace.”

This reasoning is supported by the rule of charity, which extends to everything and makes all things right through its own rectitude. Thus blessed Augustine, writing in his book *On the Customs of the Catholic Church against the Manichaeans*, says:

“Those who are able therefore abstain—although they are innumerable—from both meat and wine, for two reasons: either because of the weakness of their brothers or for the sake of their own freedom” (this refers to the Apostle’s passage in Romans 14 concerning the avoidance of scandalizing the weak).

“Charity is guarded above all; food is adapted to charity, speech to charity, dress to charity, and one’s countenance to charity. They come together into one charity and conspire toward charity. To violate it is considered a sacrilege, as though it were to violate God. They know that Christ and the apostles commended it, so that if this one thing is absent, everything is empty; but if it is present, everything is full” (Chapter 34 of the Rule).

Thus far Peter the Venerable, and Augustine as cited by him.

Although I have been somewhat lengthy in recounting these passages, I trust that I have not been burdensome to religious readers, since nothing more suited to our purpose, nothing more explicit, effective, or precise, could apparently have been brought forward. It seemed to me a matter of religious duty not to omit even one iota or one stroke.

Nevertheless, I would like to summon another defender of the same opinion: John Bertelius, abbot of Luxembourg, a dialogist on the Rule of Saint Benedict, sometimes serious and sometimes humorous. His words concerning the passage of the Rule are these:

“As for what Benedict says about a pound of bread being given to each religious, and about the leftovers being preserved by the cellarer for those who are to sup, I do not know whether Benedict understood it quite as justly as the words of the Rule seem to sound. For otherwise the man of God would not have cared for Christ’s poor; and it could rightly and justly be objected that whatever the religious leave on the table ought to be given to them—not, however, through their own hands, as some think and wish. But I think Benedict understands the passage as follows: a portion of bread should be kept for those who are to sup, and it should be such that, in relation to dinner, it does not exceed at supper the aforementioned pound. For in the preceding and following chapters he proclaims nothing else than that care must be taken for the poor and for guests.”

This he says, more subtly than elegantly (Dialogue 18).

From all this, then, to bring this discussion to an end, I briefly gather three reasonable and just grounds that may—and rightly should—have moved the most holy Father Benedict, as well as his successors, the fathers and superiors of the same order, and the congregations themselves, to judge that so large and abundant a daily portion and measure of bread—namely, two, three, or four pounds—should be granted and distributed to the brothers.

The first reason, which Saint Benedict mentions, arises from consideration of the labors and tasks in which the monks were engaged:

“If greater labor,” he says in the passage cited above, “should perhaps have been undertaken, it shall be within the abbot’s judgment and authority, if expedient, to increase something,” etc.

Turrecrematus says that this should be understood not only of labor in the fields and manual work—occupations to which, because of poverty and the necessity of food, the monks devoted themselves in Saint Benedict’s time and for many years afterward—but also of labor in the divine offices, as on solemn days, when the monks customarily worked much harder by reciting the office more solemnly.

So he writes.

Bertelius likewise says in the passage cited above:

“He calls it greater labor when bodies are so exhausted that weakness consequently follows, making perseverance in spiritual matters difficult; and when prudent administrators of affairs, according to the character of the condition and status involved, judge that the labor exceeds what is customary.”

The second reason concerns the support and relief of the poor: namely, so that several poor people might be fed and refreshed from the leftovers of the brothers’ table, and larger alms might be given, since whatever religious people leave on the table ought to be distributed to the poor, as we have already heard from Bertelius.

The Louvain doctors judged that this generosity in almsgiving was akin to hospitality and almost essential to the order (in their response to the questions of the monks of Aulne).

The third reason concerns increasing the merit of monks who voluntarily abstain, for God and the salvation of their souls, from things placed before them, contenting themselves with a smaller measure than what is available to them, knowing [Col. 0217B] with the Apostle (Philippians 4) how to be filled and how to hunger, how to abound and how to suffer want.

This was the notable teaching of Saint Pachomius. As has been said elsewhere, when he entered a monastery subject to him and saw that nothing cooked had been prepared for the brothers in the kitchen, he became severely angry, even though the cook offered an excuse, because the brothers were eating nothing cooked that had been set before them.

“Do you not know,” he said, “that it is always glorious to abstain from what is present? For if someone restrains himself, out of regard for God, from something that lies within his power, he receives a great reward from God. But if he restrains himself from something that he has no permission to use, he is known to be restrained by a kind of necessity; and therefore, because his abstinence is compelled and fruitless, he seems to await his reward in vain.

“Finally, when several foods have been placed before them, if the brothers use them more sparingly for God’s sake, then they place their greatest hope in God. But concerning foods they do not see, and for which no opportunity at all is given them to partake: how is a reward granted for frugality?”

So it is related in the *Life of Saint Pachomius*. But enough of this.

Another is burdened by a meal of one pound, or six [Col. 0213A] ounces; nevertheless, in all [Col. 0214A] these cases there is one aim of abstinence: that no one, in proportion to the measure of his [Col. 0215A] capacity, should be overburdened by the glut of satiety. For not quality alone, but also the quantity of foods, dulls the keenness of the heart; and, when the mind is fattened together with the flesh, it kindles [Col. 0216A] the harmful, fiery tinder of vices.

## Chapter VI. That the Mind Is Intoxicated Not by Wine Alone

[Col. 0217A]

[Note: [Col. 0217C] Saint Jerome, Letter 10: “Some who seek a chaste life collapse halfway along the road because they concern themselves solely with abstaining from meat and load their stomachs with vegetables, which are harmless when consumed moderately and sparingly. And in Book 2 against Jovinianus: Even with the cheapest foods, satiety must be avoided; for nothing so overwhelms the soul as a full belly, swollen and shifting from side to side, breathing out in belches or by the expulsion of intestinal winds.”]

A stomach replenished with any kind of food produces the seeds of lust and cannot successfully regulate the reins of discernment,

[Note: [Col. 0217C] Hence Saint Chrysostom (Homily 44 on John): “Nothing is more destructive than gluttony. It makes the intellect dull and thick, blinds the carnal understanding, and does not allow it to perceive anything. And elsewhere he says elegantly: Just as a cargo ship that begins to carry more than its size permits is weighed down by the mass of its load and sinks, so the nature of our body, if it receives more food than it can bear, unable to withstand the weight of what has been ingested, sinks into the sea of destruction and destroys its sailors, its helmsmen, and the cargo itself together with the people” (In the homily against lust).]

suffocated by the weight of food. For it is not only the drunkenness caused by wine that usually intoxicates the mind; excess in every kind of food also makes it unsteady and wavering, and strips it of every contemplation of integrity and purity.

For the Sodomites, the cause of their overthrow and lust was not drunkenness from wine but satiety from bread. Hear the Lord rebuking Jerusalem through the prophet (Ezekiel 16):

[Note: [Col. 0217D] The Vulgate reads (Ezekiel 16): “Behold, this was the iniquity of your sister Sodom: pride, fullness of bread, abundance, and leisure for her and her daughters; and she did not extend her hand to the needy and poor.” It should be noted here that four or five vices are attributed to Sodom as the causes of its destruction and overthrow. Yet, when compared with the sins of the Jews, these are considered much smaller and lighter: namely, pride; gluttony, which the prophet calls fullness of bread; abundance of riches, that is, avarice; freedom from good works, which he calls leisure; and lack of compassion toward the poor and needy. Of these vices the author here expressed only two, those suited to his purpose.]

“For what did your sister Sodom do wrong, except that she ate her bread in fullness and abundance? And because through fullness of bread they had been inflamed with an unquenchable ardor of the flesh, by God’s judgment they were burned from heaven with sulfurous fire” (Genesis 19).

If the mere excess of bread, through the vice of satiety, drove them into so precipitous an abyss of crimes, what must be thought of those

[Note: [Col. 0217D] That is, those who, although strong and healthy, nevertheless do not abstain from meat and wine, but instead abuse them immoderately and voluptuously. Concerning the avoidance of meat and wine, especially their immoderate use, by adolescents and young men, Saint Jerome writes much splendidly throughout Book 2 against Jovinianus, including the following (Chapter 6): “Suppose that the eating of meat is common to all nations, and that whatever is commonly produced is everywhere permitted. What does that matter to us, whose citizenship is in heaven? We who stand above Pythagoras, Empedocles, and all the followers of wisdom are not bound to the one by whom we are born, but to the one by whom we are reborn; we subdue by fasting the rebellious flesh that drags us toward the incitements of lust. The eating of meat, the drinking of wine, and the fullness of the belly are a breeding ground for lust. Hence the Comic poet says: ‘Without Ceres and Liber, Venus grows cold.’”

“And in Letter 22 to Eustochium, after many preceding remarks, he concludes as follows: ‘If, then, my advice can have any value, if experience deserves belief, this is the first thing I advise and entreat: let Christ’s bride flee wine as poison. These are the first weapons of the demons against youth. Wine and youth are a double fire of pleasure. Why should we add oil to the flame? Why should we supply fuel for the fire to a body already burning?’ etc.

“And elsewhere (in chapter 5 of his letter to the Galatians) he confirms the same advice, saying: ‘Although some think I should be criticized in the book I wrote on preserving virginity because I said that adolescents ought to flee wine as poison, I will not regret that opinion. For there we condemned the use of wine rather than God’s creature; and we removed the license from youth, which is burning with the natural heat of its age, lest under the pretext of drinking a little it should drink more and perish.’

“Again, elsewhere (Letter 10 to Furia), he speaks in the same vein: ‘Neither the fires of Etna, nor the land of Vulcan, nor Vesuvius and Olympus burn with such heat as young marrow filled with wine and inflamed by rich foods.’”

Thus far Jerome.]

On the occasion of this passage, however, it seems appropriate to discuss at greater length abstinence from meat and wine insofar as it concerns religious people and monks.

First, it is clear that such abstinence is commended in many ways:

1. By the authority of Scripture;

2. By the example of the apostles;

3. By the example of the ancient monks and hermits;

4. By the rules and institutions of the holy Fathers;

5. By the decrees of the supreme pontiffs;

6. Finally, by examples of divine punishment inflicted on transgressors of this kind of regular abstinence in the Old Testament.

### I

Daniel speaks of himself as follows:

“In those days I, Daniel, mourned for three weeks. I did not eat desirable bread; meat and wine did not enter my mouth” (Daniel 10).

In the New Testament, John the Baptist is commended. He fed on locusts and wild honey, Jerome says (Book 2 against Jovinianus), not on meat (Matthew 3); and the desert dwelling and the cradle of monasticism began with such foods.

Augustine likewise says (Sermon 65, *On the Seasons*):

“John, the forerunner of the Lord, is nourished in the wilderness by locusts and wild honey; he is not fed with the flesh of animals or with the delicacies of birds. He abstained not only from meat but also from bread and wine. Hence the Savior says: ‘John the Baptist came neither eating bread nor drinking wine’” (Luke 7).

And the Apostle, writing to the Romans, says:

“It is good neither to eat meat nor to drink wine, nor to do anything by which your brother is scandalized or weakened” (Romans 14).

From these words Baronius concludes (in the year of Christ 57) that in that flourishing primitive Church it was a distinctive practice neither to eat meat nor to drink wine. Although the faithful could lawfully use these things as much as they wished, many were nevertheless offended because they regarded the practice as unusual; and the Apostle warns that account must be taken of this scandal.

### II

Many examples likewise prove that the apostles abstained from meat and wine. To establish this concerning Peter, the chief of the apostles, Gregory Nazianzen readily persuades us in his *Oration on the Love of the Poor*, where he writes that Peter was accustomed to drive away hunger with lupine beans purchased for a small coin.

Concerning James, the brother of the Lord, Hegesippus, as cited by Eusebius, affirms that he never used meat as food or wine as drink (Book 2 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 22).

Clement of Alexandria says the following concerning Matthew:

“Matthew used seeds, berries, and vegetables, without meat.”

The interpreters also report that blessed Paul was an abstainer from wine (Acts 21; Baronius, year 58).

It is likewise clear that Saint Timothy was accustomed to abstain from wine, from the Apostle’s words:

“Do not continue drinking only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses” (1 Timothy 5).

“See,” Jerome says (Letter 22, cited above), “for what reasons the drinking of wine is permitted: so that by it pain of the stomach and frequent illness may be treated. And lest we perhaps flatter ourselves concerning our illnesses, he commands that only a little be taken, more as a physician’s prescription than an apostle’s, although the Apostle is also a spiritual physician, lest Timothy, overcome by weakness, be unable to complete the course of preaching the Gospel,” etc.

### III

To these examples may be added those of the ancient monks and hermits. Eusebius, drawing on Philo, reports that the first Christians, whom he calls the Therapeutics—that is, worshipers or caretakers—established by Saint Mark the Evangelist near Alexandria, took food only in the evening and abstained from meat and wine.

The same is attested by Saint Epiphanius in Heresy 29, concerning the Nazarenes, and by Saint Jerome in his book *On Illustrious Men*, in the section on Philo (Bellarmine, Book 2 *On Good Works*, chapter 5).

Saint Athanasius also admits that the monks of his time practiced the same discipline. Thus, in the *Life of Antony*, he writes:

“He took bread and salt, and very little water as a drink. As for meat and wine, I think it better to remain silent than to say anything, since such foods were not even customary among very many of the monks.”

Saint Jerome imitated him in that letter in which he describes his austerity in the desert:

“I say nothing about the foods and drink on which I lived at that time, since even sick monks use cold water, and to have received anything cooked is considered luxury.”

And further, speaking of the Egyptian cenobites and their customs:

“They live on bread, legumes, and vegetables seasoned only with salt; only the old men receive wine,” etc.

Saint Augustine reports similar things in Book 1, chapter 31, *On the Customs of the Catholic Church*. Finally, anyone who reads the Lives of the saints, especially those of hermits—Antony, Hilarion, Serapion, and others—will readily recognize that they consistently observed abstinence from eating meat and drinking wine.

[Col. 0219D] IV

Now, to come to the rules of the holy Fathers, the Rule of Saint Pachomius, dictated by an angel, establishes the following in article 22:

“No one shall touch wine or a fish-sauce, except in the case of the sick” (see our scholion in the same place).

If even fish-sauce was forbidden to them, meat was forbidden all the more.

Saint Basil, in his *Monastic Constitutions*, chapter 26, indicates plainly enough that the regular eating of meat was unlawful for his monks. Nevertheless, it was sometimes permitted to dip a morsel of bread into broth made from salted meat or to take some of that stew. For he says:

“That very tiny fragment, cast into so great a quantity of water or vegetables, if chance so brings it, is in no way an indication of delicacy; rather, it is the most rigorous and truly sweetest self-restraint of those devoted to piety.”

So Basil writes.

The *Rule of Monks* attributed to Saint Jerome—although it is not Jerome’s, but was compiled by someone from his opinions—contains much concerning the abstinence from meat that monks should especially practice (Volume 9).

More explicit and solemn, however, is the constitution of our most holy Father Benedict (Chapter 12 and following), by which he forbade his cenobites to eat meat, excepting the weak and the sick. He did so in two places.

First, in chapter 36 of the Rule, where he says:

“Let the eating of meat be granted altogether to the weak and very infirm for their restoration. But when they have recovered, let all abstain from meat in the customary manner.”

Again, in chapter 39, he says:

“Let the eating of the flesh of quadrupeds be altogether abstained from by everyone, except by the very weak and the sick.”

Here Turrecrematus observes (Treatise 104 on the Rule) that although the holy Father names only the flesh of quadrupeds, the prohibition nevertheless extends to the flesh of two-legged animals, namely birds. Since the flesh of birds is sweeter, more delicate, and more expensive, when he forbade the less delicate flesh, he must certainly be understood to have forbidden the more delicate and expensive flesh as well. It is customary among the saints to include the greater under the lesser.

So he writes.

Abbot Smaragdus, writing on the same passage of the Rule (chapter 39), adds the following after the words of the Rule:

“Hence Aurelius says: ‘Meat is never to be taken as food. Let chickens and all fattened birds not be served in the community. Let them be provided only for the sick, and let it be permitted to receive them.’

“Hence Fructuosus says: ‘No monk is permitted either to eat or to taste meat—not because we judge God’s creature unworthy, but because abstinence from meat is considered useful and suitable for monks. Nevertheless, the proper measure of compassion toward the necessities of the sick and toward those traveling far away must be preserved, so that the sick may be sustained by eating birds, and those assigned to a distant journey, if they are summoned or invited by a prince or bishop, may not fear to taste meat as a mark of blessing and obedience, while retaining their customary abstinence in other respects. But if any monk violates this and, contrary to the sanction of the Rule and the practice of the elders [or: the ancient practice], presumes to eat meat, he shall be subjected to confinement and penance for six months.’”

This is found there. Gratian placed this constitution, although in abridged form, among the canons, *On Consecration*, distinction 5, chapter “Carnem”; Smaragdus preserved and reported it here in full.

### V

It should further be noted that this same constitution prescribing abstinence from meat for monks was approved and confirmed by Pope Innocent III in *Extra*, *On the Status of Monks*, chapter “Cum ad monasterium,” where he establishes many rules concerning the matter:

1. No one at all is to eat meat in the refectory.

2. Nor, on certain solemnities—as was sometimes done, apparently, is the convent to leave with the abbot, leaving a few people behind, so that they might eat meat outside the refectory; for on those days regular discipline ought especially to be observed with greater diligence.

3. Nor are they to think that eating meat outside the refectory is permitted to them.

The weak and sick, who require bloodletting or some medicine, are to receive whatever they need, both meat and other things, appropriately—not separately in their rooms, but all together in the infirmary.

4. Nevertheless, out of indulgence, the abbot may sometimes call in some of the brothers, now these and now those, and provide for them with himself in his room more fully and generously.

This is what is found there.

It should also be known that Pope Benedict XII, in his Benedictine constitution (chapter 26), seems to have acted with great moderation concerning this abstinence from meat and to have considerably mitigated and relaxed it. Interpreting both Saint Benedict’s Rule and the aforementioned constitution of Pope Innocent III, he establishes the following:

“Because the observance of moderation and sobriety tends toward the advancement of salvation, and because we wish the provisions concerning the eating and abstinence from meat handed down in the regular institution of blessed Benedict, and established in the constitution of Pope Innocent III, our predecessor of pious memory, to be firmly observed, we decree and ordain that throughout the entire year all regulars of the same order or religious institute shall abstain everywhere from eating meat on Wednesday and Saturday, from the first Sunday of Advent until Christmas Day, and from Septuagesima Sunday until Easter Day, unless the necessity of a genuine illness should perhaps persuade the abbot or another proper superior to dispense someone,” etc.

From this it follows, first, that at the present time Benedictines are bound, apart from the Church’s fasts, to abstinence from meat only on the days and during the seasons expressed and prescribed in this Benedictine constitution. Even during those times, however, abbots or superiors may sometimes dispense them for a just reason. The Glossator also made this point in his commentary on that chapter of Innocent III, concluding:

“Thus you have it: the abbot may dispense from the monastic Rule with regard to eating meat.”

Second, it follows that this constitution of the Rule neither did nor does possess the force of a precept, nor does it bind under pain of mortal guilt, even outside the case of illness and the other exceptions, unless it is violated contemptuously. In that case, the penalty of confinement or imprisonment prescribed by that canon applies (the chapter “Carnem” cited above).

Saint Thomas teaches this, followed by Cardinal Turrecrematus and others (Saint Thomas, *Quodlibet* 1, article 20; Turrecrematus, cited above).

It might, however, be objected against the foregoing, and certainly it is remarkable that St. Hildegard understood the matter differently and considered that St. Benedict prohibited the eating of quadrupeds, but not of birds. For, explaining those words of the Rule—“Let the eating of meat be granted altogether to the sick and weak for their restoration” (Rule, chap. 36)—she says:

> He wishes “meat” to be understood as including both that of quadrupeds and that of birds, excluding no meat that human beings customarily eat. But when they have recovered, let all abstain from meat in the customary manner—that is, from the meat of quadrupeds, because healthy people did not customarily eat them or their juices, but the sick did. Healthy people, however, ate the meat of birds, since it is clean and does not arouse burning lust in those who eat it. And again below: “Let the eating of the meat of quadrupeds be entirely abstained from by everyone” (chap. 39). Here, she says, he is silent about birds because he does not prohibit their consumption to the healthy. For that same Father, because in his time the monks’ way of life was still undeveloped and almost unfamiliar, avoided prohibiting the eating of meat to them in every respect. Thus, so that they might eat birds, he permitted it to them.

This is Hildegard’s view. Nevertheless, despite these considerations, it is certain that the differing judgment and authority of the supreme pontiffs, of other holy Fathers, and of the interpreters of the Rule must carry greater weight. They understood the Rule and the mind of St. Benedict in such a way that they interpreted the eating of meat, both of birds and of quadrupeds, as having been simply prohibited by him, as is clear from what has been said. Custom itself also—which is usually the best interpreter of laws—and the practice of the monasteries of this order confirm the same conclusion. On these matters, see the distinguished note of Jacobus du Breul, monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris, on Aimonius’s *De Gestis Francorum*, book V, chapter 10, where he adduces arguments on both sides.

Finally, by way of a concluding flourish, I shall append a few examples of certain monks who, through contempt for and violation of regular abstinence, both from meat and from wine, incurred the severe vengeance of divine punishment, so that, frightened by these examples, we may observe it more religiously. Blessed Odo, the first abbot of Cluny, related two truly terrifying examples to his disciple John, who wrote his life, in the following manner (*Apud Surium*, vol. VI, 18 November, book III of the *Life of Blessed Odilo*, chap. 2):

> “During those days,” he says, “two brothers died a very sudden death, though not in the same place or at the same time. One of them came to his sister’s house and said that he was extraordinarily hungry. His sister immediately replied that she had a large supply of fish and that he might eat whatever he wished and whenever he wished. He, almost indignantly, said that he was disgusted with fish, which he had used continually for so many years, and that he could no longer eat it. Then his sister said: ‘Look, we have meat at hand; eat as much as you like.’ So he ordered a shoulder to be roasted. But meanwhile, impatient of delay, he put a piece of it onto the coals and, when wine had been brought, greedily thrust it into his mouth. At once heavenly vengeance appeared. The piece, rashly swallowed, stuck in his throat and could neither be swallowed nor rejected; it strangled the man and forced the unhappy soul to depart.

> “The other came in the morning to his father’s house and asked whether they had anything that they could set before him to eat. When they said that it was not yet time to eat, he replied angrily: ‘What! I rode all night to complete what I had been ordered to do, and you are forcing me to fast? Bring me whatever you have.’ They told him that they had fish. But the wretched man, driven on by still sharper goads of anger and swollen with disdain, cast his eyes around him and saw a flock of hens at his feet. Immediately, in a kind of fury, he seized a stick, struck one of them that pleased him, and said with raging mouth: ‘This will now be a fish for me.’ Those who were present then said to him, not without embarrassment: ‘Perhaps, Father, you are permitted to eat meat?’ But he replied: ‘Birds are not meat. For they have the same origin as fish and are of the same nature as they, as one of our hymns says.’ At these words everyone fell silent. Then a roasted hen was set before him. When he had taken a morsel from it, he could neither force it down into his stomach nor spit it out; he was suddenly taken from their midst.”

Thus far the account. Peter of Cluny also relates this same example in book VI, letter 17, where he expressly proves by many arguments that the eating of meat was forbidden to the Cluniacs. For a third example, which concerns abstinence not from meat but from wine—a practice observed on certain days in some monasteries—see Peter Damian, book VI, letter 32. But enough of this for now.]

Those who, [Col. 0219A] with vigorous bodies, presume upon the consumption of meat and wine in excessive abundance [Alternative reading: freedom], taking not as much as weakness requires, but as much as the desire of the soul suggests.

## CHAPTER VII. That bodily weakness cannot hinder purity of heart

[Col. 0221A]

Bodily weakness does not hinder purity of heart, [Col. 0222A] provided that one takes only what the frailty of the flesh, not what pleasure, demands.

> **Note:** [Col. 0222C] “Those overcome,” not “men,” as some read it, thereby producing a contrary or altogether different meaning, alien to the author’s intention. For he means nothing other than that those who abstain from foods that are not more abundant—as the Plantin edition also erroneously reads—but more substantial, as Ciaconius correctly emended it, that is, foods of greater juice and nourishment, are more easily overcome by temptation than those who observe due measure and proportion in their use, or who use their customary and permitted foods moderately.

We have seen those more easily overcome who abstained entirely from more substantial foods, [Col. 0222C] which moderate use permits according to necessity, and those who denied themselves everything out of love of self-restraint, than those who took such foods on the pretext of illness while preserving the measure of sufficiency. Bodily weakness also possesses the palm of self-restraint, provided that, even when the flesh’s weakness has been granted food, a person still deprives himself of the restoration he needs and permits himself only as much eating as strict temperance judges sufficient for maintaining life—not as much as appetite desires.

More substantial foods, just as they promote bodily health, do not take away purity of chastity if they are consumed with moderation. For whatever strength is received by eating them is expended through the exertion and weakness of illness. Therefore, just as the virtue of frugality is taken away from no condition of life, so the consummation of integrity is denied to none.

> **Note:** [Col. 0222C] A more suitable epithet than “more abundant,” as Dionysius and most other manuscripts have it. Physicians call foods “more nourishing” or “more substantial” when they contain more nourishment, a pleasant flavor, and better juice. Concerning such foods, the School of Salerno says: “More substantial, because they contain more bodily substance; more nourishing, because they are more suitable for eating and more agreeable to the palate or stomach.” Hence Tertullian, speaking of foods, joins “more agreeable” and “more nourishing” (*On Fasting*, chap. 5). St. Jerome likewise writes in his letter to Eustochium: “To abstain from wine and more nourishing foods.” Cicero similarly uses *esculenta* adjectivally when he says: “To choose from among those things which are nourishing” (*On the Nature of the Gods*, book II), that is, suitable for eating. Hence the proverb: “Everything is edible to the besieged.” From the Greek: ἅπαντα βρωτὰ τοῖς πολιορκουμένοις, “everything is edible to the besieged”—that is, to those who are extremely hungry and worn down by hunger, as those who have long been under siege commonly are, no food is not pleasant.

## CHAPTER VIII. How it is permissible to desire and take food

It is therefore a most truthful and thoroughly approved judgment of the Fathers that the measure of fasting and self-restraint consists solely in frugality of quantity and discipline, and that this is the common goal of perfect virtue for all: that we restrain ourselves from the foods which the necessity of sustaining the body compels us to take, even while we remain in the state of desiring them. For although someone may be physically weak, he will possess perfect virtue equal in every respect to that of the strong and healthy if, with firmness of mind, he chastises desires that bodily frailty does not require. For the Apostle says: “And [Col. 0223C]

> **Note:** [Col. 0223C] St. Gregory reasons from this same principle in *Morals*, book XXX, chapter 18: “What,” he says, “is forbidden in desire is permitted in necessity. But often, when we unwisely yield to necessity, we serve our desires. At other times, when we strive too immoderately to oppose our desires, we increase the miseries of necessity. Thus it is necessary for each person to hold the citadel of self-restraint, so that he may kill not the flesh but the vices of the flesh.” St. Gregory says this very aptly in the present passage (*On True Virginity*). St. Basil agrees, writing as follows:

> “Since the vehicle of the body is innate in us, we ought to bring it along the course of virtue neither by loosening the reins too much nor by restraining them again immoderately. Therefore it is fitting to examine carefully both the condition and constitution of our bodies and the qualities of our foods, so that to a vigorous and healthy body we may apply the reins, while through hunger and colder foods we restrain the excess of heat; but to one that is aged and growing cold we should supply food and drink as assistance for sustaining its strength.”

> And again in the same place:

> “Just as it is grave and dangerous to incline toward gluttonous excess, so to wear down the body through excessive abstinence and render it useless is altogether irrational. For abstaining from the pleasures of the stomach is not desirable in itself, but because it contributes to the acquisition of virtue. If, however, through immoderate hunger we neglect the very purpose for which we choose abstinence, we act contrary to our intention. For once the instrument has been broken and crushed, we can neither cling to God through the practice of reading and prayer nor perform the human duty of benevolence toward our brothers. Therefore care must also be taken of the body—not for its own sake, but so that we may use its service in the pursuits of philosophy, that is, the contemplative life.”

Thus far St. Basil. Moreover, St. Augustine explains how care of the body in food and drink should be exercised without pleasure, in these words:

> “You have taught me, O Lord, to approach food as I would medicine. But while I pass from the discomfort of want to the repose of satiety, a snare of concupiscence lies in wait for me in that very transition. For the transition itself is pleasure, and there is no other route by which one passes than the route along which necessity compels one to pass. And although health is the reason for eating and drinking, dangerous pleasure attaches itself like a handmaid and often tries to go before it, so that what I say or wish to do for the sake of health may instead be done for its sake; yet the measure of the two is not the same. What is enough for health is too little for pleasure. And it often becomes uncertain whether the body’s necessary care is still asking for assistance or whether the deceptive service of pleasurable desire is supplying it. At this uncertainty the unhappy soul rejoices and prepares in it a defense of excuse, glad that it does not appear what is sufficient for the moderation of health, so that, under the pretext of health, the business of pleasure may be concealed.”

So excellently Augustine (*Confessions*, book X, chapter 31).

“Make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Romans XIII). He did not therefore forbid care of the flesh in every respect, but denied that it should be exercised in the sphere of desires. He removed the flesh’s pleasure-seeking attentiveness, but did not exclude the care necessary for maintaining life: the former, lest indulgence of the flesh should cause us to fall into harmful preoccupation with desires; the latter, lest the body, corrupted through our own fault, should be unable to perform spiritual and necessary functions.

## CHAPTER IX. On the measure of disciplines to be undertaken and the remedy of fasting

The full measure of self-restraint must therefore be determined not only by consideration of time, nor merely by the quality of foods, but above all by the judgment of conscience.

> **Note:** [Col. 0224C] St. Jerome writes to Nepotian: “Impose upon yourself only as much fasting as you can bear. Let your fasts be pure, chaste, simple, moderate, and not superstitious.” Thus Abbot Moses says in *Conferences*, conference 2, chapter 22: “The general measure of self-restraint is that, according to the capacity of one’s strength, whether of body or of age, each person should allow himself as much food as the sustenance of the flesh, not the desire for satiety, requires.” And in the following chapter: “This is the balanced equality and measure of self-restraint approved also by the judgment of the Fathers: that daily hunger should accompany daily nourishment, preserving the soul and body alike in one and the same condition, permitting neither collapse through the weariness of fasting nor burdening of the mind through satiety. For such frugality is enjoyed that sometimes, after evening, one neither feels nor remembers having been refreshed.”

Each person ought to impose upon himself as much frugality as the struggle with bodily weakness demands. The canonical observance of fasts is indeed useful and must be observed in every respect; but unless a frugal restoration of food follows it, it cannot reach the goal of integrity. For the hunger of long fasts, followed by bodily satiety, produces rather a temporary weariness than purity of chastity. Integrity of mind is joined to hunger of the stomach. Whoever is not content to maintain a constant equality of self-restraint does not possess a perpetual purity of chastity. Although rigorous fasts are emptied of their value when excessive relaxation follows and immediately collapse into the vice of gluttony:

> **Note:** [Col. 0224D] St. Jerome takes this position first in his tenth letter, where he says: “A sparse diet and a stomach always hungry are preferable to three-day fasts. And it is much better to take a little every day than to take enough at rare intervals. The best rain is that which descends gradually upon the earth; a sudden and excessive downpour overturns the fields headlong.” And again, book II *Against Jovinian*: “What sort of fast,” he says, “or what sort of restoration after fasting is it, when we stuff ourselves with yesterday’s feasts and our throat becomes a channel of latrines, while, wishing to acquire the reputation of a prolonged fast, we devour as much as the night of scarcely another day can digest? Therefore it should be called not so much fasting as gluttony and a foul and burdensome digestion.”

A rational daily restoration with moderation is better than a difficult and prolonged fast undertaken at intervals. Immoderate hunger knows how not only to weaken the steadfastness of the mind but also to deprive prayers of their efficacy by enervating them through bodily weariness.

## CHAPTER X. That abstinence from food alone cannot suffice to preserve purity of mind and body

To preserve integrity of mind and body, abstinence from food alone is not sufficient unless the other virtues of the soul are also joined to it.
