Humility must therefore first be learned through the virtue of obedience, contrition of heart, and weariness of body. Not only must possession of money be avoided, but the desire for it must also be eradicated from the roots. For it is not enough not to possess money—a state which often results even from necessity—but one must not even accept the will to possess it if it should happen to be offered.

The fury of anger must be crushed, the dejection of sadness overcome; vainglory, that is, empty glory, must be despised; the arrogance of pride trampled underfoot; and the mind’s own unstable and wandering movements restrained by continual remembrance of God. Our heart’s slippery wandering must be brought back to the contemplation of God as often as the subtle enemy, attempting to seize the mind from that contemplation, has crept into the hidden recesses of our heart (see John Climacus, steps 14 and 15).

## CHAPTER XI. That the desires of the heart are not extinguished except by the complete eradication of vices

It is impossible to extinguish the fiery incitements of the body before the fuel of the other principal vices has also been cut out by the roots. We shall discuss these separately in distinct books at their proper place, with the Lord’s help. For now, however, our purpose is to discuss *gastrimargia*, that is, the desire of the stomach, against which our first struggle is directed.

> **Note:** [Col. 0225C] A sensible judgment, confirmed not merely by reason but also by experience. Similar is that saying of St. Jerome: “The belly heated with wine easily foams over into lust.” And in Letter 22 to Eustochium: “Chastity cannot be secure except through abstinence. Without Ceres and Bacchus, Venus grows cold.” Likewise another saying of Cassian in *Conferences*, conference 5, chapter 10: “Fornication is joined to gluttony by a special partnership.” Also that of Climacus (step 14): “Whoever, while obeying his belly, wishes to overcome the spirit of fornication is like one who tries to extinguish a fire with oil.”

No one, therefore, will ever be able to restrain the impulses of burning desire if he cannot bridle the desires of the stomach. The chastity of the inner person is discerned by the perfection of this virtue. For you should never expect that someone can wrestle with stronger adversaries whom you have seen overcome by weaker ones in a lesser conflict.

> **Note:** [Col. 0225D] “One,” not in species, as is well known, but in connection and a certain mutual conspiracy, concurrence, or coherence, as is clear from what precedes and follows. Thus Acts IV says: “The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and one soul.” For all the virtues assist one another and provide mutual support, while each one drives away certain hindrances of the others. For example, abstinence moderates the appetite, and thus helps the other virtues that could be hindered or violated through, or on account of, the appetite. The same applies to the rest. All also look toward one and the same general end, namely, human perfection, or the perfect integrity of mind and body, as the Author calls it. On the connection of the virtues, however, see what follows.

All the virtues have one nature, although they appear to be divided into many species and names, just as gold also has one substance, although it appears distinct in many different kinds of ornaments according to the skill and intention of artisans. Therefore:

> **Note:** [Col. 0226C] “To possess perfectly,” he says. For the old and common axiom that all the virtues are connected must be understood of perfect virtues, or virtues possessed and practiced perfectly; Cassian appears to have this in view. Thus the Fathers teach (St. Thomas, *Summa theologiae* I–II, question 65, article 1; Jerome, book I *Against the Pelagians*; Augustine, letter 29). Among them St. Gregory says in *Morals*, book XXII, chapter 1: “One virtue without the others is either nothing or imperfect. For, to speak of the first four virtues, prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice are perfect in proportion as they are joined to one another; separated, they can in no way be perfect. For prudence is not true if it is not just, temperate, and courageous; nor is temperance perfect if it is not courageous, just, and prudent; nor is fortitude complete if it is not prudent, temperate, and just; nor is justice true if it is not prudent, courageous, and temperate.”

No one, therefore, will be proved to possess any virtue perfectly if he is recognized as having been defeated in one part of them. For how can someone be thought to have extinguished the raging heats of desire, which are kindled not only by bodily instigation but also by a fault of the mind, if he could not mitigate the barbs of anger that erupt from the intemperance of the heart alone? Or how can someone be thought to have blunted the wanton impulses of flesh and soul if he could not overcome the simple vice of pride? Or how is he to be believed to have trampled underfoot the lust implanted in the flesh if he was unable to renounce the desire for money, which is situated externally and alien to our substance? And by what reasoning will he triumph in the war between flesh and soul if he was not able to cure the sickness of sadness?

However lofty a city may be in the height of its walls and the strength of its closed gates, it will be laid waste by the treachery of a single postern, however tiny.

> **Note:** [Col. 0226D] I think *posterula* has been placed for *posticum*, *posticulum*, or, if one prefers, “a rear gate” or “little rear gate.” Properly speaking, a gate is an entrance to a city, town, or other place fortified with rampart and ditch. Hence the diminutive *portula* or *posterula*, as it were “a rear gate.” Gates of this kind, smaller than the main gates, are seen in certain towns; they are opened only on particular occasions or in cases of necessity. Nevertheless, cities sometimes come to be betrayed and captured through them, as is plainly established by examples from ancient and more recent times, and as the Author suggests here. Dionysius incorrectly and inattentively wrote “by the opening of a post,” for posts are not opened, but doors or gates.

For what difference does it make whether the pernicious enemy enters the innermost parts of the city through lofty walls and broad gate-openings or through the hiding places of a narrow tunnel?

> **Note:** [Col. 0227B] A *cuniculus*, or, in the plural, *cuniculi*, is a trench secretly dug beneath the ground, through which soldiers unexpectedly break into an enemy’s fortress or city, or which they blow up and overthrow with ignited gunpowder. Hence the expression “to fight with tunnels,” ὑπονόμοις πολεμίζειν, is used metaphorically of one who conducts an affair not by open force but deceptively and by trickery. By contrast, one who acts openly is said to act “with engines.” Cicero, *For the Agrarian Law*: “What was being openly sought is now secretly attacked through tunnels.”

## CHAPTER XII. That the spiritual contest must also take its pattern from the bodily contest

“He who competes in the contest will not be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (II Timothy II). Whoever wishes to extinguish the natural appetites of the flesh should first hasten to overcome the vices situated outside nature.

> **Note:** [Col. 0227C] That is, non-natural vices, such as avarice, envy, and acedia. He contrasts these with the natural appetites of the flesh, namely lust and gluttony, which have their primal and innate roots and fuel in our nature and are therefore called natural. This comparison of the vices is discussed more fully in the fifth *Conference*.

For if we wish to experience the force of the apostolic saying, we must first recognize what the laws and discipline of worldly contests are, so that by comparing them we may finally understand what the blessed Apostle wished to teach us by this example as we compete in the spiritual contest. For in those contests which, according to the same Apostle, prepare a perishable crown for the victors, this custom is observed: whoever strives to prepare himself for a glorious crown adorned with the privilege of exemption, and desires to undertake the contests of the perfected athlete, must first display the character of his youth and the strength of his elementary training in the Olympic and Pythian contests.

> **Note:** [Col. 0227C] In ancient times four kinds of contests were celebrated among the Greeks with great crowds and elaborate ceremony: the Olympic, Pythian, Isthmian, and Nemean games (Alexander ab Alexandro, *Genialia*, book V, chapter 8). Concerning them, see Budaeus in the *Pandects* and Coelius Rhodiginus, *Various History*, book X, chapter 3. The Olympic contests, or games, were held at the city of Olympia in the territory of Pisa in Elis, a region of the Peloponnese, in honor of the impure idol called Olympian Jupiter, recurring every fifth year with a great gathering from all Greece; from them the Olympiads took their name. The Pythian games were held in honor of Apollo Pythius, so called from the serpent Python, pierced by his arrows; Ovid describes the story in the *Metamorphoses*. In these and similar games and contests, competition took various forms: running, wrestling, boxing, jumping, and others. Hence the contestants were called athletes, agonists, boxers, runners, or gymnasts. Not everyone was admitted to such contests; candidates had to be tested and approved under specific conditions, as is said here: they could not be slaves, disgraced, idle, or marked by any other dishonor. By this example and analogy the Author teaches what spiritual athletes must be like as they strive in the stadium of the spiritual life for an incorruptible crown.

In those contests, younger men who wished to devote themselves to these disciplines were examined to determine whether they deserved or ought to be admitted, both by the judgment of the person presiding over those contests and by that of the entire people. When someone had been carefully examined and was first found to be stained by no disgrace of life; second, found not to have been judged base under the yoke of slavery and thereby unworthy of this discipline or of association with those who practiced it; and third, found to display worthy evidence of skill and strength, demonstrating, in competition with younger men of his own age, both the ability and the vigor of his youth; and when, having progressed through the wrestling of the ephebes, he had been permitted by the presiding judge to compete with fully grown men already tested by long experience; and when, by constant struggle, he had proved himself not merely equal to their virtue but had also often won the palm of victory among them—then at last he would deserve to advance to the distinguished contests of the games, in which permission to compete is granted only to victors and to those adorned with the rewards of many crowns.

> **Note:** [Col. 0228B] According to Suidas, among the Athenians *ephebes* were called those up to the age of eighteen; they bore that name for two years and were then enrolled in the civic register. The word *ephebe* is derived as if from ἐπὶ ἥβης, that is, “from youth,” because one is already in youth, having reached the years of puberty. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I: “When I was at Athens among the groups of ephebes.” The contests of the ephebes were those in which the young customarily trained themselves; hence *ephebeia*, places established for training the young. On these matters see Alexander ab Alexandro, *Genialia*, book III, chapter 21, and Vitruvius, book V.

If we have understood the example of the bodily contest, we must also recognize, by comparison with it, what the discipline and order of the spiritual contest are.

## CHAPTER XIII. That unless we are freed from the vice of gluttony, we can in no way reach the contests of the inner person

We too must first demonstrate our freedom by subjecting the flesh.

> **Note:** [Col. 0228C] The Vulgate reads: “For by whatever a person is overcome, by that he is also enslaved.” A corresponding saying is found in the Apostle Paul, Romans VI: “To whom you present yourselves as servants for obedience, you are servants of the one whom you obey, either of sin leading to death or of obedience leading to righteousness.” When Sacred Scripture speaks of freedom and slavery, it forms several elegant antitheses. The first contrasts freedom with slavery, Romans VI: “Having been freed from sin, you became servants of God.” Conversely: “When you were servants of sin, you were free from righteousness.” The second appears in I Peter II: “As free, yet not using freedom as a veil for wickedness, but as servants of God.” Here he contrasts true freedom, which is joined to service of God, with false and empty freedom. The third appears in the words cited above: “You are servants of the one whom you obey, either of sin leading to death or of obedience leading to righteousness.” From this we also learn that there is one freedom of the spirit and another of the flesh, and similarly one slavery to righteousness and another slavery to sin. The latter is the most wretched and shameful slavery, of which St. Augustine says: “O most wretched slavery!” (*Tractates on the Gospel of John*, tractate 41). “Often, when people suffer under wicked masters, they ask to be sold, seeking not to have no master but to change masters. What can the slave of sin do? Whom can he appeal to? To whom can he ask to be sold? Then, when a human slave is worn down by his master’s harsh commands, he sometimes finds rest by fleeing. But where can the slave of sin flee? Wherever he flees, he drags himself along with him. An evil conscience does not flee from itself; there is nowhere for it to go, and it follows itself—or rather, it does not depart from itself, for the sin it commits is within.” Thus Augustine. Philosophers also recognized this slavery and its shamefulness. Diogenes used to say that between slaves and wicked masters there was no difference except in name, except that slaves served masters while masters served their desires. Horace sings the following about the pleasure-loving man (*Satires*, book II, satire 7):

> For a harsh master presses hard upon his mind,  
> Applies sharp spurs to the weary man, and turns him against his will.

“For by whatever a person is overcome, by that he is also enslaved” (II Peter II). And everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin (John VIII). When the examination of the one presiding over the contest finds that we are stained by no disgrace of shameful desire, and when we have not been judged by him to be servants of the flesh, dishonorable, and unworthy of the Olympic contests against the vices, then we shall be able to enter into contest against our peers—that is, against the desire of the flesh and the movements and disturbances of the soul.

> **Note:** [Col. 0229D] That is, against those who are noble and glorious, such as the Olympic contests and victories were, not against things slight or ordinary. Above he calls this “the wrestling of the ephebes,” that is, a childish contest.

For it is impossible for a person with a full stomach to experience the contests of the inner person; nor is someone worthy of being challenged by stronger battles if he can be overthrown in a lesser conflict.

## CHAPTER XIV. How the desire of gluttony can be overcome

We must therefore first trample underfoot the desire of gluttony, and reduce the mind to such a degree—not only by fasts but also by vigils, reading, and frequent contrition of heart—that, remembering how it may have been deceived or defeated, it groans, now inflamed by horror of vices, now by desire for perfection and integrity. This must continue until, occupied and possessed by such cares and meditations, it recognizes the restoration of food itself as granted not so much for pleasure as imposed upon it like a burden, and perceives it as assigned to the body because necessary rather than to the soul because desirable.

Held by this discipline of mind and continual contrition, we shall blunt the wantonness of the flesh, which grows more insolent through the fostering of food, and its harmful goads. Thus we shall be able to extinguish the furnace of our body, which the king of Babylon continually kindles for us by supplying occasions of sin and vices.

> **Note:** [Col. 0229D] The king of Babylon, that is, the devil, who is compared to the king of Babylon on account of pride and the incentive to lust. Cassian likewise uses the same allusion and metaphor in book VI, chapter 17: “May the furnace of our flesh, which the Babylonian king never ceases to kindle with the incentives of carnal suggestions, be extinguished as the dew of the Holy Spirit descends into our hearts.” See there further material from St. Jerome.

We shall be able to extinguish these things by the abundance of tears and weeping of heart, by which we are burned more fiercely than by naphtha and pitch, until, through God’s grace, when the spirit of his dew breathes into our hearts, the heat of carnal desire can be utterly quieted.

> **Note:** [Col. 0230D] Naphtha, according to Pliny (*Natural History*, book II, chapter 105), is a kind of liquid bitumen, or a seepage of bitumen, found in great abundance around Babylon. It has such an affinity with fire that flame leaps into it from whatever direction it is seen. Common people call it Medea’s oil; others maintain that it is petroleum, or rock oil. From it a nearly inextinguishable fire is made, which the Greeks call “Greek fire.” The Author alludes to the words of Daniel, chapter 3: “The king’s servants did not cease feeding the furnace with naphtha, tow, pitch, and brushwood.” On this passage St. Jerome writes: “Sallust says that naphtha is a kind of fuel among the Persians, by which fires are especially nourished. Others think that the olive pits discarded with the olive dregs, when dried, are called naphtha. Hence in Greek it is also called πυρίνη, from πῦρ, that is, fire, because it nourishes fire.” Thus Jerome.

This, then, is our first contest, our first trial, as it were, in the Olympic games: to extinguish the desire of the stomach and of gluttony through the desire for perfection. For this reason, not only must the excessive appetite for food be trampled underfoot through contemplation of virtue, but even food that nature requires must be taken, with anxiety of heart, as contrary to chastity. Thus the course of our life must be ordered so that there is no time when we feel ourselves called back from spiritual pursuits more than when the frailty of the body compels us to descend to its necessary care.

When we submit to this necessity, serving the needs of life rather than the desire of the mind, let us hasten to withdraw from it as quickly as possible, as from something that draws us away from salutary pursuits. For we shall never be able to despise the pleasures of present foods unless the mind, fixed upon divine contemplation, takes greater delight in the love of virtues and the beauty of heavenly things. Thus a person will despise all present things as transitory when he has fixed the gaze of his mind inseparably upon things immovable and eternal, contemplating already in his heart, while still placed in the flesh, the blessedness of his future dwelling.

## CHAPTER XV. That a monk must always be intent on guarding the purity of his heart
[Note: [Col. 0230D] Almost the same comparison is found in *Collation* I, chapter 5.]

It is as though someone, hastening to strike with the keenest vision of his eyes, which are aimed like a weapon, at enormous prizes of virtue marked out on high by certain small indications, knowing that the immense palm of glory and the rewards of recompense consist in hitting them, must turn the sharpness of his eyes away from every other sight and direct it to the place where he sees the fullness of the recompense and reward established. He would unquestionably lose the palm of his skill and the reward of virtue if the aim of his contemplation swerved even slightly.

## CHAPTER XVI. That, following the custom of the Olympic contest, a monk cannot engage in spiritual battles unless he has first won the carnal ones

Thus, when the desire of belly and throat has been overcome with this aim [Col. 0231A], and we have neither been declared servants of the flesh nor branded with the disgraceful mark of vices, we shall be judged worthy, as in the Olympic disciplines, of engaging in the contests that follow. Once such lessons have been given beforehand, we shall be thought capable of confronting spiritual wickednesses also—wickednesses that deign to contend only with those who are victorious and with those who deserve to struggle in the spiritual arena.

For this is, as it were, the most solid foundation of all struggles: [Note: [Col. 0231B] Saint Gregory establishes this at length in *Morals* XXX.26: “No one gains the palm of the spiritual contest who has not first conquered in himself the incitements of the flesh by afflicting the desire of the belly. For one does not rise to the conflict of the spiritual arena unless the enemy placed within us—the appetite of gluttony—is first tamed; because, if we do not overthrow what is nearer to us, we plainly proceed in vain to attack what is farther away. It is useless to wage war against external enemies in the field if an ambushing citizen is within the very walls of the city. The mind of the combatant itself is also driven back from the encounter of the spiritual contest under the grave disgrace of confusion when, weak in the battle of the flesh and pierced by the swords of gluttony, it is overcome. For when it sees itself overthrown by small things, it is ashamed to fight greater ones.

“Some, however, ignorant of the order of combat, neglect to tame gluttony and already rise up to spiritual wars. They sometimes do many things of great strength; but, while the vice of gluttony rules, through the enticement of the flesh they lose everything they have done bravely. And, while the belly is not restrained, all virtues together are overwhelmed by the desire of the flesh. Hence, when Nebuchadnezzar conquered, it is written: ‘The chief of the cooks destroyed the walls of Jerusalem’ (4 Kings 25). For what does Scripture signify by the walls of Jerusalem except the virtues of the soul that tends toward the vision of peace? Therefore the chief of the cooks destroys the walls of Jerusalem because, while it is not restrained, the belly destroys the virtues of the soul.

“Hence Paul was taking strength away from the chief of the cooks warring against the walls of Jerusalem when he said: ‘I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified’ (1 Corinthians 9). He had also said beforehand: ‘So I run, not as uncertainly; so I fight, not as one beating the air.’ For when we restrain the flesh, by the very blows of our abstinence we strike not the air but unclean spirits; and when we subject what is within us, we give battle to adversaries placed without.” Thus far Saint Gregory, with whom Isidore agrees in *On the Highest Good* II: “No one,” he says, “can attain the perfection of virtues unless he has first tamed gluttony.”] that the incentives of carnal desires should first be destroyed. No one who has not conquered his own flesh can fight lawfully. And whoever does not fight lawfully will assuredly be unable to contend in the arena, to earn the glory of the crown, or to merit the reward of victory. But if we are defeated in this contest [Col. 0231B], proved to be servants of carnal desire and therefore bearing neither the insignia of freedom nor of strength, we shall immediately be driven away from the conflict of spiritual contests as unworthy slaves, not without the mark of disgrace. For everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin (John 8).

And the blessed Apostle will say to us, together with those among whom fornication is named: [Note: [Col. 0231D] There is a double reading of this sentence. The Greeks, whom Cassian follows here (*Collation* 3.17 and [Col. 0232B] 1.14), read εἴληφε, “has apprehended,” in the past tense. Following this reading, Saint Cyprian, *To Quirinus* III.91, says: “Temptation has not seized you except as human temptation.” In this way the sense of the passage is: You have no reason to glory or applaud yourselves as though you had accomplished something great, as though you had endured a great contest and, having already defeated the enemy, were awaiting triumph. “Temptation has not apprehended you except as human,” that is, light and easily overcome, in accordance with the same Apostle’s statement: “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh” (Romans 6). For you have not yet encountered the more serious battles of spiritual wickedness. You have not yet, as he writes to the Hebrews, resisted unto blood (Hebrews 12).

But the Latin translator seems to have read εἰληφέτω, “let it apprehend.” The other Latin authors followed this version, and Cassian’s authority, although he rejects it, cannot diminish theirs. It also fits better with what precedes: “Whoever thinks that he stands, let him take heed lest he fall. Let no temptation apprehend you except what is human.” As Saint Gregory says (*Pastoral Rule* I.11), it is as though he were plainly saying: “To suffer temptation in the heart is human; to be defeated in the contest of temptation is demonic.”

And in *Morals* XXI.3 he says: “Human is the temptation by which we are often touched in thought even against our will, because that unlawful things should sometimes enter the mind comes to us from ourselves, from the burden of corruptible humanity. But the temptation is demonic, not human, when the mind binds itself by consent to what the corruption of the flesh suggests.” Hence he says again: “Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body” (Romans 6). He did not forbid sin from being in the mortal body, but from reigning there, because in corruptible flesh it can fail to reign, but it cannot fail to be present. Thus far Gregory.]

“Let no temptation apprehend you except what is human” (1 Corinthians 10). For we shall not deserve, through strength of mind acquired by us [Col. 0232A], to experience the more serious battles of heavenly wickedness if we have been unable to subject our fragile flesh, which resists our spirit.

Some, not understanding the Apostle’s testimony, have put the optative mood in place of the indicative: “May no temptation apprehend you except what is human.” But it is clear that he speaks this not with the feeling of one expressing a wish, but of one declaring or reproving.

## CHAPTER XVII. That the foundation and basis of the spiritual contest are established in the struggle against gluttony

Do you wish to hear of a true athlete of Christ [Note: [Col. 0232D] He calls the law of the contest the rules that must be observed by the Christian soldier, or spiritual athlete. From the Olympic and secular contests he previously transferred and adapted these rules to the spiritual and religious arena (chapters 12 and 13). The first is that the vices of flesh and gluttony must be subdued; without this, no one is considered fit to endure the more serious contests against spiritual enemies, as we showed above from Saint Gregory (chapters 3 and 16).] fighting according to the lawful rules of the arena? “I,” he says, “so run, not as uncertainly; so fight, not as one beating the air; but I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest, while preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified” (1 Corinthians 9).

You see how he established the entire burden of his struggles in himself—that is, in his flesh—as upon a very firm foundation, and placed the outcome of the battle solely in the chastisement of the flesh and the subjection of his body. “I therefore so run, not as uncertainly.” He does not run uncertainly who, seeing the heavenly Jerusalem, keeps fixed the goal toward which the unbending speed of his heart must be directed. He does not run uncertainly [Col. 0233A] who, forgetting what lies behind, stretches himself toward what lies ahead, pursuing the appointed prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus. Directing the gaze of his mind continually toward him and hastening toward him with every preparation of his heart, he confidently proclaims: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4).

Because he knew that, after the fragrance of Christ’s ointments, he had run tirelessly with the swift devotion of his conscience, and had overcome the contest of the spiritual arena by chastising the flesh, he confidently adds: “From now on a crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day.” And to reveal to us a similar hope of recompense, if we wish to imitate him in the course of this contest, he added: “And not to me only [Col. 0233B], but also to all who love his appearing”—declaring that we shall share his crown on the day of judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0233C] He indicates a twofold coming of Christ: one spiritual and inward, by which he comes through grace into the souls of the devout; to this he refers the Apostle’s words, “to all who love his appearing” (2 Timothy 4); and another external and visible coming. The latter is again twofold: namely, his coming in the flesh and his coming in judgment. Thus Saint Bernard (*Sermon 3 on Advent*) says: “The Lord’s coming to human beings is threefold: to human beings, into human beings, and against human beings. To human beings through incarnation and birth; into human beings through justifying grace; against human beings through the severity of judgment.”

Innocent III (*Sermon 2 on Advent*) makes four comings of the Lord, though in such a way that the final two refer to the twofold judgment, particular and universal. The first is in the cloud of flesh, the second in the dew of grace, the third in the whirlwind of death, and the fourth in the fire of judgment.]

If, then, by chastising the body we wish to obtain victory in the contest, let us love Christ’s coming—not only that coming which will appear even to those unwilling, but also the coming that daily visits holy souls. Concerning this coming the Lord says in the Gospel: “I and my Father will come to him, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John 14). And again: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will enter in to him, and I will dine with him, and he with me” (Revelation 3).

## CHAPTER XVIII. Through how many kinds of contests and palms the blessed Apostle rose to the crown of the highest arena

[Col. 0234A]

Nor does he describe himself as having completed only the course of the contest when he says, “So I run, not as uncertainly”—which refers particularly to the intention of his mind and the fervor of his spirit, with which he followed Christ with all his ardor, singing with the Bride: “I will run after you in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song of Songs 1); and again: “My soul has clung to you” (Psalm 62). He also testifies that he conquered another kind of struggle when he says: “So I fight, not as one beating the air, but I chastise my body and bring it into servitude” (1 Corinthians 9).

This properly refers to the pains of continence, bodily fasting, and affliction of the flesh. By these he describes himself as a vigorous boxer of his own flesh [Col. 0234B], showing that he did not exercise the blows of continence against it in vain, but obtained the triumph of the battle through the mortification of his body. Having chastised it with the blows of continence and crushed it with the caestus of fasts, he bestowed upon the victorious spirit the crown of immortality and the palm of incorruption.

[Note: [Col. 0233C] This should be read “with the caestus,” not “with the heats of fasting,” as Dionysius rendered it, so that the metaphor may remain consistent and continuous. Up to this point the Author has compared the athlete and the spiritual contest with the secular and worldly contest.

The caestus was a kind of club, consisting of leaden balls attached to leather thongs, with which boxers fought and battered one another. Virgil writes that Dares and Entellus fought in this manner in *Aeneid* V, calling it “to join battle with the savage caestus.” Sidonius says, “to contend with the caestus” (*Poem* V). Tertullian, discussing Greek contests (*Against the Gnostics* 6), says: “There are contests and wounds of various kinds: fists batter, heels ram, caesti tear, and whips lacerate.”

Saint Ambrose, on Psalm 36, says: “In the secular arena there are some who wrestle in a simple and lawful manner, contending only with the binding of the body; they are called athletes. Others mingle slaughter and the scattering of dust with the entanglement of their limbs, every license for striking being granted them; these are called παμμάχοι, ‘all-fighters.’ Others contend with caesti against one another and are bloodied by their torn heads; these are called πυκταί, ‘boxers.’” Thus Ambrose. The word *caestus* is derived from *caedere*, “to strike,” and is written with the diphthong.

Accordingly, as Cuychius says, fasts are metaphorically called here certain spiritual caesti, by which the flesh is subdued, beaten down, and tamed as though with thongs and leaden balls. *Cestus*, without the diphthong, is a belt or girdle—the bride’s girdle which the bridegroom would loosen on the first night.]

[Note: [Col. 0234C] Saint Ambrose treats this subject eloquently and at length in the cited passage, where he shows that the Apostle experienced all the kinds of contests mentioned above and triumphed over them all.]

You see the lawful order of the struggle and contemplate the outcome of the spiritual contests: how the athlete of Christ, having obtained victory over rebellious flesh and having in a manner placed it beneath his feet [Note: [Col. 0234C] He alludes to the Roman custom of triumphing. The triumph was the greatest of all honors granted by the Roman people, bestowed only upon generals or commanders who had won a notable victory over enemies (Zonaras II; Alexander ab Alexandro, *Genial Days* VI.6). The triumphators rode in an ivory and gilded chariot drawn by four white horses, their heads crowned with gold, while the defeated enemy commanders followed the chariot with their necks loaded with chains. Thus, preceded by the Senate, they ascended to the Capitol and the temple of Capitoline Jupiter. After a white bull had been sacrificed, they returned home in the same procession.

Cicero, discussing and enlarging upon such a triumph in *Against Piso*, asks: “What, after all, does that chariot contain? What of the defeated commanders before the chariot? What of the images of cities? What of gold? What of silver? What of ambassadors on horseback and tribunes? What of the soldiers’ shouting? What of that whole procession? What of being carried through the city?”] is carried in as a sublime triumphator.

Therefore he does not run uncertainly, because he trusted that he would immediately enter the holy city, the heavenly Jerusalem. Thus he fights—with fasts, that is, and bodily affliction—not as one beating the air, that is, extending the blows of continence in vain. Through the chastisement of his body he struck not empty air, but the spirits that inhabit it. For the one who says “not as one beating the air” shows that, although he does not beat empty and void air, he nevertheless beats certain beings in the air.

And because he had overcome these kinds of contests and advanced enriched by the rewards of many crowns, he rightly begins to undertake struggles against stronger enemies. Having triumphed over his former adversaries, he confidently proclaims: “Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6).

## CHAPTER XIX. That the athlete of Christ is never without a battle so long as he dwells in the body

[Col. 0235B]

[Note: [Col. 0235C] This is a notable statement, one to be fixed in the memory. It agrees with the saying of blessed Job: “The life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job 7). If this is true of every human being, it is much more especially true of the Christian, and most especially of the religious and monk, whom we have elsewhere shown to be called particularly an athlete, or ascetic—that is, a boxer and soldier of Christ (Book I, chapter 2).

Saint Chrysostom discusses at length how the monk’s contest is perpetual and its palm, or reward, manifold, in Homily 54 (*To the People of Antioch*, on the life of monks), as does Saint Ephrem in an exhortation to piety, where he says: “The warfare of soldiers is short; but the monk’s struggle lasts always, until he departs to the Lord.” See the scholia of G. Vossius there.]

For the athlete of Christ who dwells in the body, the palm of struggles never fails. The more he grows through the successes of his triumphs, the stronger an order of struggles follows him. For once the flesh has been subjected and conquered, how many companies of adversaries, how many armies of enemies, stirred up against the victorious soldier of Christ by his triumphs, rise against him! This happens lest Christ’s soldier, growing sluggish through the leisure of peace, begin to forget the glorious contests of his struggles and, relaxed by the inactivity of security, be deprived of the rewards and merits of his triumphs.

Therefore [Col. 0235C], if we desire to ascend through increasing virtue to these degrees of triumph [Col. 0236A], we too must enter upon the struggles of battle in the same order and first say with the Apostle: “So I fight, not as one beating the air, but I chastise my body and bring it into servitude” (1 Corinthians 9). Then, having overcome this conflict, we may again say with him: “Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6).

Otherwise we shall in no way be able to contend with them, nor shall we deserve to experience spiritual battles, having been cast down in the carnal conflict and crushed in the struggle against the belly. Rightly, therefore, the Apostle will say to us reproachfully: “Temptation has not apprehended you except what is human” (2 Corinthians 10).

## CHAPTER XX. That a monk must not exceed the time for taking food if he wishes to reach the struggles of the inner contests

[Col. 0236B]

A monk who desires to reach the struggles of the inner contests must first prescribe this precaution for himself: conquered by no pleasure of drinking or eating, he must not permit himself to take anything outside the table before the lawful and common hour of the meal [Note: [Col. 0235C] That is, before the time properly appointed for the fast, or, as he says elsewhere below (chapter 24), before the fixed hour of the fast. And in *Collation* 5.11: “The breaking of the fast must in no way be presumed before the canonical hour.”

For Cassian and other ecclesiastical writers frequently use *station* for fasting. Thus Tertullian, in *On Prayer* 14, says that after receiving the Lord’s body the station is not dissolved—that is, the fast—and that the term *station* is taken from military usage, namely from the stations of soldiers. Saint Ambrose explains the origin of the term more clearly in Sermon 25: “Our fasts are our camps, which defend us from the devil’s assault. They are therefore called stations, because by standing and remaining in them we repel lurking enemies.”

In Sermon 24 he gives this explanation of the Lenten fast: just as the people of Israel, freed from the yoke of Egyptian captivity, reached the promised land through forty stations or encampments, so we reach the desired feast of Easter by approximately the same manner and number of fasts, which, he says, are our encampments.

Thus Ambrose. From Tertullian, however, it does not seem that *station* signifies every kind of fast, but rather a fast established and prescribed by law. For in *On Fasting*, distinguishing appointed stations from voluntary fasts, he says: “They accuse us because we observe our own fasts, because we often extend our stations until evening,” and so forth.

Hence Rabanus, *On the Institution of the Clergy* II.18, says: “It is called both fasting and a station. Some distinguish fasting from a station. Fasting is abstinence on any day, not according to law but according to one’s own will; a station is the observance of appointed days or periods—of days, such as the fast on the fourth and sixth days, commanded by the old law, namely the apostolic law; of periods, such as the fasts of the fourth, fifth, seventh, and tenth months, and the observance of Lent, which is observed throughout the world by apostolic institution.” Thus Rabanus on the distinction between stations and fasts.

Cassian, however, seems to use *station* indiscriminately for any fast, even a voluntary one. In chapter 24 of this book he calls the daily station the daily fast shortly afterward, and says that it is customarily broken at the arrival of a guest. In *Collation* 21.29, joining the two terms, he calls it a station of fasting. The two kinds of stations, or fasts, will be discussed below (chapter 24).]

Nor, once the meal has ended, should he permit himself to presume to take even the smallest amount from it. Similarly, he must observe the canonical time and measure of sleep. For the dissipations of the mind must be cut away with the same diligence with which the vice of fornication is severed.

For whoever [Col. 0236C] could not restrain the excessive desires of gluttony [Note: [Col. 0236D] That is, disordered desires, which Saint Gregory expresses in *Morals* XXXI.27 as follows:

“The vice of gluttony tempts us in five ways. Sometimes it anticipates the time of need; sometimes it does not anticipate the time, but seeks more luxurious foods; sometimes, whatever food is to be taken, it demands that it be prepared with excessive care; sometimes it is in accord with both the quality and the time of the food, but exceeds the measure of moderate nourishment in the quantity consumed; sometimes it sins still worse in the very heat of its immense desire.

“Jonathan incurred the sentence of death from his father because, in tasting honey, he anticipated the appointed time for eating (1 Samuel 14). The people led out of Egypt perished in the wilderness because, despising manna, they asked for meat, which they considered more luxurious (Numbers 11). The first sin of Eli’s sons arose because, contrary to ancient custom, the priest’s servant wanted to receive from the sacrifice not meat cooked in the customary manner, but raw meat prepared with greater care (1 Samuel 2). And when it is said to Jerusalem, ‘This was the iniquity of your sister Sodom: pride, fullness of bread, and abundance’ (Ezekiel 16), it is plainly shown that she lost salvation because, with the vice of pride, she exceeded the measure of moderate nourishment. Esau lost the glory of his birthright because, in the great heat of desire, he craved a worthless food, namely lentils (Genesis 25). By preferring them even to the sale of his birthright, he showed how eagerly he yearned for that appetite; for it is not the food but the appetite that is at fault.” Thus Gregory.

From these Saint Thomas derives five kinds of gluttony (2.2, question 148, article 4), contained in this verse:

“Too early, luxuriously, excessively, ardently, studiously.”

Gluttony is committed “luxuriously” when unusual or exceptional foods are desired, more expensive than one’s state permits—for example, if a religious refuses to eat anything except partridges, pheasants, and so forth. This is excess with respect to the substance of the food.

“Studiously” refers to excess in seasoning and preparation—for example, if a monk refuses to eat unless the food is prepared with much sugar or fruit juice. See Turrecremata, treatises 102 and 103 on the Rule of Saint Benedict, and Father Leonard Lessius, *On Justice* IV.3.

Bernard should be consulted on these matters in his *Apology to Abbot William*, where he sharply and remarkably censures the luxury of monks in food, especially in preparing eggs and fish, tasting and seasoning wines, and so forth.

“Excessively” indicates excess in the quantity of food, when more is eaten than nature requires; this is the most frequent form.

“Too early” concerns the taking of food, when the time for eating is anticipated.

“Ardently” occurs when the proper manner of eating is not observed—for example, when someone eats raw, insufficiently chewed, or harmful foods greedily, or eats more often than is proper.

Cassian, below (chapter 23), and again in *Collation* 5.11, assigns only three forms or kinds of gluttony from those just mentioned: the first, second, and fourth. Saint Gregory does the same in his commentary on 1 Kings, chapter 3.]

how will he be able to extinguish the heat of carnal desire? And whoever could not restrain the small passions that lie openly before him, how will he be able, by disciplined discretion, to fight hidden passions that rankle without any human witness? Hence the strength of the soul is tested in every movement and in every desire. If it is defeated in the smallest and most obvious desires, each person’s conscience bears witness to what it will endure in greater, stronger, and hidden matters.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the monk’s inner peace and spiritual abstinence

We must not fear an adversary from outside; [Note: [Col. 0237D] Thus Saint Jerome, Letter 22 to Eustochium:

“Greed does not shake us, pride does not inflate us, ambition does not delight us; we can easily do without other vices. This enemy is shut up within us. Wherever we go, we carry the enemy with us.”

Earlier, Saint Gregory Nazianzen, in Oration 16, says:

“I do not know how I have been joined to the body, how I can be both the image of God and wallow in the mire; how, when it is healthy, it provokes me to war, and when it is oppressed by war, it afflicts me with sorrow; how I love it as a fellow servant and hate and shun it as an enemy; how I flee it as a bond and fear it as a fellow heir. If I strive to weaken and destroy it, I no longer have a companion and helper with which to undertake noble things. But if I treat it more gently as a companion and helper, I find no means of escaping its rebellious assault and of not falling away from God, weighed down by fetters that either drag me to the ground or hold me there. It is a gentle and placid enemy, a treacherous friend. O wondrous union and estrangement! What I fear, I embrace; what I love, I dread. Before waging war, I make peace; before enjoying peace, I become estranged from it.”

John Climacus says similarly in *The Ladder*, step 15:

“I do not know by what manner or method I should bind this friend of mine and judge it as I judge the others. Before I bind it, it is released; before I judge it, I am reconciled with it; before I punish it, I am bent toward it. How shall I bind the one whom I received by nature in order to love? How shall I be freed from the one to whom I am bound forever? How shall I destroy the one that rises with me? What rational word shall I speak to it, when by nature it lies through a thousand arguments and persuasions?

“If I conquer it by fasting, I am again handed over to it as to a neighbor. If, ceasing to judge it, I overcome it, I am thrown headlong against it, lifted up in heart. It is at once a co-worker and an enemy, a helper and an adversary, an ally and a plotter. If it is indulged, it attacks; if it is afflicted, it becomes weaker. It grows wanton through rest, but again it cannot endure blows and lashes,” and so forth.]

an enemy is shut up within us. An inward war is waged in us every day. Once it has been defeated, everything external will be rendered weak, and all things will be peaceful and subject to Christ’s soldier. We shall have no adversary to fear from outside if what is within us has been subjected to the spirit through victory.

Nor should we think that this fast from visible foods alone can suffice for the perfection of the heart and the purity of the body, [Note: [Col. 0238C] For what does it profit, Saint Jerome says (Letter 14 to Celantia, near the end), to make the body thin through abstinence if the spirit swells with pride? What praise shall we deserve for the pallor of fasting if we are livid with envy? What virtue is there in not drinking wine while becoming drunk with anger and hatred?

“Then abstinence is excellent, then the chastisement of the body is beautiful and magnificent, when the spirit fasts from vices.”

Saint Leo, in a sermon on Saint John the Baptist, says:

“There are two kinds of abstinence and of the cross: one bodily and the other spiritual—the latter being what is here called the soul’s fast. One consists in abstaining from drink and banquets and restraining the appetite of the throat from pleasures and the softest delights. The other and more precious and sublime kind of abstinence and cross consists in governing the movements of the mind, calming its disturbances with the tranquility of moderation, restraining the impulses of anger and pride like a savage beast, fighting daily against one’s vices, reproving oneself with the conscious authority of virtue, and, as it were, engaging in dispute with oneself; bringing evil thoughts under control, renouncing one’s own wishes, and abstaining from speech and action by which the mind is harmed, as from harmful foods,” and so forth.]

unless the fast of the soul is joined to it as well. The soul too has its harmful foods, by which, when fattened, it is driven toward the precipices of lust even without an abundance of food.

Detraction is its food, and a very sweet one. Anger too is its food, though by no means a light one; yet it feeds the soul for a time with that wretched nourishment and at the same time casts it down by a deadly flavor.

Envy is food for the mind, corrupting it with poisonous juices and never ceasing to torment it continually with misery at another’s prosperity.

Vainglory, that is, empty glory, is its food. For a time it caresses the soul with a pleasurable dish, but afterward it leaves it empty, stripped and naked of every virtue, barren and useless with respect to all spiritual fruits, so that it not only causes the merits of immense labors to perish but also brings upon it greater punishments.

Every desire and every unstable wandering of the heart is a kind of nourishment for the soul, feeding it with harmful foods but leaving it deprived thereafter of heavenly bread and solid food.

If, then, with as much strength as we possess, we abstain from these through a most sacred fast, we shall maintain a useful and beneficial observance of bodily fasting [Col. 0239B]. For bodily labor joined to the contrition of the spirit will present to God, in pure and clean recesses, a sacrifice most acceptable to him and a worthy dwelling place of holiness.

But if, while fasting bodily, we become entangled in the most destructive vices of the soul, bodily affliction will profit us nothing, since the more precious part has been polluted—namely, that substance by which we become a dwelling place of the Holy Spirit. For it is not so much corruptible flesh as a clean heart that becomes a dwelling and temple of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, while the outer person fasts, the inner person must likewise abstain from harmful foods. The blessed Apostle urges that the inner person be presented clean to God, so that it may deserve to receive Christ as a guest within itself, in these words: [Note: [Col. 0239C] The Apostle calls the soul the “inner person” (Ephesians 3), and the body the “outer person” (2 Corinthians 4): “Though our outer person is corrupted, yet the inner person is renewed day by day.” On this terminology see Saint Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* I, question 75, article 4.]

“that Christ may dwell by faith in your hearts in the inner person” (Ephesians 3).

## CHAPTER XXII. That we must practice bodily continence for this reason: so that through it we may reach spiritual fasting

Let us therefore understand that we undertake the labor of bodily continence [Col. 0240A] so that by this fasting we may reach purity of heart. Otherwise our labor is undertaken in vain if we endure it tirelessly while contemplating the goal, yet cannot attain the goal for which we endured such afflictions.

[Note: [Col. 0239C] The paraphrast says: “It is more praiseworthy to abstain from the forbidden foods of the soul, namely vices, than to fast bodily from voluntary and less harmful foods.”]

Indeed, it would have been better to abstain from the soul’s forbidden foods than to fast bodily from voluntary and less harmful foods.

In the former there is the simple and harmless reception of God’s creature, which in itself contains no sin [Note: [Col. 0239D] “In those,” namely in the forbidden foods of the soul—that is, vices and sins—not “in that,” as some copies have it, and wrongly. For what could “that” refer to? Dionysius translates and explains thus: “But in that, namely in the soul’s eating of harmful foods, or its reception of vices, there is first the destructive devouring of one’s brothers.”]; but in the latter there is first the destructive devouring of one’s brothers, concerning which it is said: [Note: [Col. 0239D] Thus the Septuagint, Proverbs 20: Μὴ ἀγάπα καταλαλεῖν, ἵνα μὴ ἐξαρθῇς, “Do not love slander, lest you be uprooted.” Saint Jerome also cites it this way in his letter to Celantia (Letter 14) and in *Apology 3 against Rufinus*. The Vulgate instead has: “Do not love sleep, lest poverty overwhelm you.”]

“Do not love to slander, lest you be uprooted.”

And concerning anger and envy blessed Job says: “Anger kills the foolish, and envy slays the little one” (Job 5). [Note: [Col. 0239D] Ecclesiasticus 30 expresses the same thought in different words: “Jealousy and anger shorten one’s days, and anxiety brings old age before its time.” Saint Gregory explains in approximately the same way why the angry person is compared with a fool and the envious person with a little one (*Morals* V.33).]

It should also be noted that the one who becomes angry is judged a fool, and the one who envies is judged a little one [Col. 0240B]. The former is rightly judged a fool because, driven voluntarily by the goads of anger, he brings death upon himself; the latter, while he grows livid with envy, proves himself little and inferior. For by envying he testifies that the person whose prosperity torments him is greater than he is.

## CHAPTER XXIII. What the monk’s food ought to be
Therefore the food should be chosen not only that it may moderate and lessen the heat of burning desire, but also that it may be easy to prepare, and that its lower cost may make it more convenient to eat; and it should be something common to the fellowship and ordinary use of the brothers.

[Note: Saint Basil likewise advises: “In every place, food necessary for life should be sought with careful judgment; and elaborate seasonings’ seductive appeal and the enticements of pleasure should be rejected” (*Monastic Institutions*, chapter 10). Jerome, Book II *Against Jovinianus*: “Let us not take such foods as we shall either digest with difficulty or regret having eaten, since they were obtained and wasted with great labor. Vegetables, fruits, and legumes are easier to prepare; they require neither the skill nor the expense of cooks; they sustain the human body without anxiety; and, taken in moderation, they are digested with less effort.” And below: “Epicurus, the advocate of pleasure, filled all his books with vegetables and fruits, and says that one ought to live on cheap foods, because meats and elaborate banquets are prepared with immense care and misery.” See Saint Bernard, *Apology to William, Abbot*.]

For gluttony has three forms: one compels a person to anticipate the canonical hour of eating; another delights merely in the stuffing and saturation of the belly with any foods whatsoever; the third takes pleasure in more carefully prepared and more appetizing dishes.

[Note: “Canonical” means regular, fixed, and established by the elders. Above he said, “before the legitimate station” (chapter 20). And below: “the legitimate time for breaking the fast,” namely, the time appointed for ending the fast. Again, chapter 24: “Until the appointed hour of the fast, the rule of eating was observed.”]

Therefore, against it the monk must maintain a threefold discipline: first, he must await the legitimate time for ending the fast; second, he must not yield to satiety; third, he must be content with any food, however cheap.

[Note: The Author lists only three kinds of gluttony here and elsewhere (see Conference V, chapter 11). Yet the other two kinds listed above (chapter 20 of this work) can easily be reduced to these. Excess in the quantity of food and in the manner of eating is contained under stuffing and saturation of the belly; excess in the substance and quality of food is contained under the third kind expressed here.]

Whatever is presumed upon beyond custom and common usage, the most ancient tradition of the Fathers has marked as contaminated by the disease of vanity, glory, and ostentation. Nor have we known any of those whom we clearly saw to excel deservedly in knowledge and discernment, or whom the grace of Christ placed before all others for imitation like brilliant lights, to have abstained from eating bread, which among them is regarded as cheap and readily available. Nor have we ever seen any of those who, departing from this rule and setting aside the use of bread, pursued a meal of legumes, vegetables, or fruits counted among the most approved, or even regarded as having obtained the grace of discernment or knowledge.

[Note: Thus Abbot Moses says in *Conferences* II, chapter 19: “When they examined the abstinences—that is, the practices of self-denial—of various people who continually sustained their lives either solely on legumes, or only on vegetables, or on fruits, they placed above them all a meal consisting only of bread,” and so forth.]

For they decree not only that a monk ought not to seek foods unusual among the rest, lest his course, exposed before everyone as though on an open stage, should become empty and vain and waste away through the disease of vainglory; they also declare that he ought not readily to make known to anyone the common austerity of his fasts, but should conceal and hide it as far as possible.

When brothers arrive, they judged it more commendable to offer the virtue of kindness and love than the strictness of abstinence, and to display the ordinary rigor of one’s practice, without considering what our will, advantage, or ardor of desire might demand, but placing first and gladly fulfilling what the visitor’s rest or weakness requires.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How, in Egypt, we saw the daily fasts broken without distinction upon our arrival

[Note: He frequently says, and in many places shows, that he had lived first in the monasteries of Syria or Palestine before proceeding to the solitudes of Egypt.]

When, desiring to learn the judgments of the elders in the regions of Syria, we had gone to the province of Egypt, and there marveled that we were received with such great eagerness of heart that, unlike the practice in which we had been trained in the monasteries of Palestine, the rule of eating was not observed until the appointed hour of the fast, but our daily fast was broken everywhere we went except on the legitimate Wednesdays and Fridays, one of the elders, when we asked him why their daily fasts were passed over so indiscriminately, replied:

[Note: This means except for the fasts of Wednesday and Friday, which he calls legitimate because they were sanctioned by the law and precept of the Church—as was noted above from Rabanus—and had been received and observed at those times as a common practice among the faithful. For there exists an apostolic canon, number 68, by which it is commanded with equal strictness that one fast “the Forty Days, and Wednesday, and Friday” (τεσσαρακοστὰς καὶ τετράδα καὶ παρασκευήν, that is, Lent, Wednesday, and Friday). Lest anyone interpret this canon as referring only to Wednesday and Friday of Holy Week, on the ground that the word *parasceve* seems to signify only that day, it should be noted that the Greek Fathers customarily called every Friday *parasceve*; just as the Roman order calls every Sunday “the day of Easter,” as the compiler of liturgical antiquities perceptively observed (in Gratian, *On Consecration*, distinction 3, chapter “Fasting”).

There is also an Apostolic Constitution preserved by Clement, Book V, at the end, in these words: “We command you to fast on Wednesdays and Fridays.” Saint Ignatius likewise says in his fourth letter to the Philippians: “Do not neglect to fast on Wednesdays and Fridays, distributing the remains of your food to the poor,” and so forth.

That this was also received as a practice throughout the whole Church is attested by Tertullian in his book *On Fasting*, when he says: “Why do we call Wednesday and Friday of the week stations?” and so forth. See Bellarmine, Book II *On Good Works*, chapter 22; Jerome on Galatians 4; Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 51; and Socrates, Book VII, chapter 22. He calls fasts *stations* according to his custom because on those days fixed and appointed fasts were observed, as has been said.

Finally, Clement of Alexandria says in Book VII of the *Stromata*: “The faithful know the enigmas of the fast of these days, Wednesday, I mean, and Friday.” Here he calls their mysteries the mystical and hidden causes and reasons for the fast. From these testimonies it is clear that these fasts derived from no other source than apostolic tradition and institution.

Saint Augustine, writing to Casulanus, gives the reason for this institution in these words: “Why, then, does the Church fast especially on Wednesday and Friday? The reason appears to be that, when the Gospel is considered, the Jews are found to have held a council on that Wednesday—which is commonly called Wednesday—to put the Lord to death. Then, after one day had intervened, on the evening of which the Lord ate the Passover with his disciples—which is the end of the day we call Thursday—he was handed over during that night, which already belonged to Friday, the manifest day of his Passion.” A little later he says: “The Lord suffered, as no one doubts, on Friday; therefore Friday is rightly devoted to fasting, for fasts signify humility.” Thus Augustine.

From the testimonies of antiquity just cited it is clearly gathered that at the beginning and in those earliest times the fasts of these days were complete: not merely abstinence from meat, but also the practice of taking only one meal, and that at the ninth hour of the day—which for us is three o’clock in the afternoon—was observed by the Christian people. Gradually, however, as the fervor of charity grew weak, they came through the relaxation of spirits and the indulgence of Mother Church to mere abstinence from meat—the fast called imperfect—which is now observed weekly on Friday and Saturday. Finally, we see that the Wednesday fast was entirely neglected in the Western Church, or changed into the Saturday fast.

Since, therefore, in former times the whole Church fasted on these days—Wednesday and Friday—in accordance with apostolic institution, it is not surprising that those monks observed these fasts so religiously that they would not break them even for visiting brothers or pilgrims, nor anticipate the hour, as they were accustomed to do on other fast days, on which they did not feel themselves bound so strictly, especially when an occasion arose to show charity or hospitality.

From this ancient observance there followed that praiseworthy custom by which, in many religious orders and monasteries, abstinence from meat is practiced on Wednesday just as on Friday and Saturday at every time of the year, so that at least some trace of that religious and ancient observance might be retained among monks (see Turrecremata, chapter 104 on the Rule of Saint Benedict). This custom Pope Benedict XII strengthened and confirmed by a special [word uncertain in the supplied text] in these words: “We decree and ordain that throughout the entire year, on Wednesday and Saturday, and from the first Sunday of Advent until Christmas Day, and from Septuagesima Sunday until Easter Day, all regulars of the same order or religious community shall everywhere abstain from eating meat, unless the necessity of a genuine illness should perhaps persuade the abbot or another proper superior to dispense someone.” Thus far the constitution (*Benedictine Constitution*, chapter 26).

I think it is clear why no mention is made here of Friday, since it is common to all Christians throughout the whole year to abstain from meat on Friday, but not likewise on Saturdays. For in some churches, on account of the joy of the Lord’s Nativity, others are permitted to eat meat between Christmas and the Purification (Paludanus, Book IV, distinction 15, question 4, article 4, conclusion 2), as Molanus noted (*On the Martyrology*). But this constitution forbade it to Benedictine monks. Concerning the ancient observance and fast of Saturday, more has been said elsewhere (Book III, chapter 10).]

Wherever we went, the daily station was broken except on the legitimate Wednesdays and Fridays.

[Note: Here *station* is used for a daily and therefore voluntary fast, whereas Tertullian—and Rabanus following him—understood the word only of fixed and prescribed fasts, or days of fasting, as the meaning of the term would seem to require, as we noted above.

It should also be observed from Tertullian himself (*On Fasting*, chapter 10), and from others, that such stations in the primitive Church were of two kinds, or had a twofold use and observance. Sometimes the station, or fast, was observed until evening; sometimes only until the ninth hour. Tertullian testifies that the former was customary in Lent, and the latter on Wednesday and Friday of each week outside Pentecost—that is, outside the Paschal season. Epiphanius likewise confirms this concerning those two days: “Throughout the whole year this fast is observed in the same holy Church, on Wednesday, I mean, and on the day before the Sabbath, until the ninth hour, except during Pentecost alone—that is, throughout the entire fifty days, during which neither knees are bent nor a fast imposed” (*Compendium of the Faith*).

Concerning the first kind of stations, or the practice of fasting until evening, many examples and testimonies from antiquity exist. Eusebius writes from Philo concerning the early ascetics of Alexandria: “None of them takes food or drink before sunset” (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 16).

Such fasts were customary not only among monks but also among other Christians, as is known from the Fathers. Saint Basil, in Sermon 1 *In Praise of Fasting*, speaking of the customary manner of fasting, says: “You wait for evening in order to take food; yet you spend the whole day in the courts,” and so forth. Athanasius writes of Saint Antony that he ate once a day, after sunset. Jerome says the same of Hilarion, and elsewhere writes elegantly: “From Easter to Pentecost, dinners are changed into lunches,” indicating conversely that before Easter—that is, in Lent—lunches were changed into dinners, because lunch was omitted and one ate only in the evening.

Hence Saint Ambrose says in Sermon 34: “I ask you, those of you who eat lunch during Lent: are you not guilty in conscience?” Augustine, in Sermon 52 *On Time*, warns that during Lent, except on Sundays, no one should presume to eat lunch. Saint Bernard, in Sermon 3 *On Lent*, testifies that the monks of his own time and community broke their other fasts at the ninth hour, but that the Lenten fast was not broken before evening even by other Christians: “Until now,” he says, “we alone have fasted until the ninth hour; now, until evening, all kings and princes, clergy and people, noble and common, rich and poor alike will fast with us.”

From all this it is clearly demonstrated that what Tertullian writes in the same place (*On Fasting*, chapters 1 and 10)—that in the Roman Church fasts were prolonged not until evening but only until the ninth hour—is false, since it is established that in Lent fasts were customarily broken only in the evening. Those who committed to writing the ecclesiastical observances practiced especially at Rome also report that this custom was observed from ancient times (the *Micrologus*, chapter 49, and others).

From this custom it is still observed today that in Lent the fast is not broken until after Vespers, but in other fasts at the ninth hour—that is, after the office of None. Saint Benedict also took account of this observance in chapter 41 of his Rule, where he says: “From the Ides of September until the beginning of Lent, the brothers shall always eat at None. In Lent, however, until Easter, at Vespers.” But enough concerning this.]

One of the elders, when we asked him about it, replied:

[Note: Cassianus teaches more than once that a monk may relax something of the severity of his customary fast when guests arrive, in order to refresh the guest, as in *Conference* 21, chapter 14, and *Conference* 24, chapters 20 and 21. Blessed Prosper agrees in Book II *On the Contemplative Life*, at the end.]

[Note: That is, on the five weekdays: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday. For the Easterners did not fast on Saturday, any more than on Sunday, as has been shown elsewhere. Yet among these fasts some were legitimate—that is, binding by law and precept—such as the Wednesday and Friday fasts, which were observed much more strictly, as ecclesiastical fasts ordinarily are. The others were voluntary, or established by monastic rules with unequal obligation; these could more readily be relaxed at the discretion of the elders, chiefly for two reasons: first, to render the office of charity and kindness to visiting brothers or pilgrims; second, to conceal from outsiders the austerity of their life and avoid the danger of vainglory, as the Author indicates at the end of the preceding chapter. In the same way, monastic or regular fasts are now from time to time relaxed for similar reasons by the authority and permission of superiors. Saint Benedict, however, explains how far this should be done on the arrival of guests in chapter 53 of his Rule, where he treats of receiving guests: “Let the prior break the fast for the sake of guests, unless perhaps it is an especially important fast day which cannot be violated. But let the brothers continue the custom of fasting”—that is, keep and observe it, says Turrecremata. “For although the prior breaks the fast out of kindness for the guest, the community ought not violate the fast, but preserve the customs and ordinances of religious life.” Thus, from Cassian’s account, we must also understand that those Egyptian monks and cenobites were not all accustomed, upon the arrival of any guest whatever, to break even their daily fast; rather, one or two of the elders did so, or those to whom the abbot or elder had given consent.]

“Fasting is always with me; but you are about to leave me immediately, and I cannot keep you continually with me. Although fasting is useful and continually necessary, it is nevertheless an offering of voluntary service; but the necessity of the commandment requires that the work of charity be fulfilled. Therefore, since I receive Christ in you, I must refresh him. When I send you away, I shall be able to compensate in myself, by a stricter fast, for the kindness shown for his sake.

“The children of the bridegroom cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them; but when he has departed, then they may fast lawfully” (Luke 5).

## CHAPTER XXV. On the continence of a certain elder who ate so frugally six times that he preserved his hunger

When a certain elder was encouraging me, while I was eating, to take a little more, and I had already said that I could not, he replied:

[Note: The good elder ate so sparingly and lightly that he nevertheless invited his guests to eat and was still hungry after his sixth meal. Palladius similarly writes in the *Lausiac History* of the presbyter Isidore that, although each day he took only as much food as was sufficient to sustain the body, he nevertheless earned great praise for temperance from everyone because he never rose satisfied from the table.]

“I have already set the table six times for different visiting brothers, and, while encouraging each one, I have eaten with them all—and I am still hungry. Yet you, eating for the first time today, say that you cannot?”

## CHAPTER XXVI. On another elder who never took food alone in his cell

[Note: John Moschus gives a similar example in the *Spiritual Meadow*, concerning certain Scetian monks: “I saw there elders who never took food unless someone came to them. Among them was a certain elder named Ammonius, who lived near me. Knowing his custom, I came to him every Saturday so that he would take food because of my arrival. They all generally had this practice: whenever anyone approached, regardless of the hour, they allowed him to pray; while he prayed, they themselves set the table and immediately took food.” Thus far the account (chapter 54).]

We saw another man living in the desert who testified that he had never indulged himself by taking food alone. Even if no brother came to his cell for five entire days, he continually postponed his meal until, going out on Saturday or Sunday to attend church for the sake of the devout assembly, he found some traveler. He would then bring him back to his cell and eat with him, taking bodily nourishment not so much for his own need as for the sake of kindness and for the brother’s benefit.

Thus, just as they know how to break their daily fasts without distinction when brothers arrive, so when the brothers depart they compensate by greater continence for the meal granted on their account, exacting the taking of the smallest amount of food by a harsher mortification through a reduction not only of bread but even of sleep itself.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Praise of Abbots Paesius and John

[Note: Ciaconius corrected the reading to “to the elder,” which is more Latin; but our manuscript and other codices read “with the elder Paesius.” Dionysius calls him Phesius. Palladius, in the *Lausiac History*, writes of a certain Paesius and his brother Isaiah; but whether he is the Paesius discussed here cannot be established with certainty.]

While the elder Paesius was living in a vast desert, the elder John, who was superior over a large coenobium and a multitude of brothers, came to him. As though to an extremely old companion, he asked what he had done during all the forty years in which he had been separated from him and had been entirely undisturbed by the brothers.

“Never,” he replied, “has the sun seen me eating.”

And he said: “Nor has it seen me angry.”

[Note: This is not, as I think, the Egyptian anchorite of the Upper Thebaid, famous for prophetic inspiration and older than Cassian, whose excellent virtues are commemorated in the preceding book (Book IV, chapters 23 and following); rather, it is another man of the same name and profession, who likewise became famous for holiness in the desert of Scetis, or Scete (Peter, *Catalogue*, Book III, chapter 157). He is also mentioned below in chapter 40, and Cassian attributes to him the nineteenth *Conference* (see the notes there, chapter 1). That conference concerns the end of the coenobite and the hermit and explains why, after leaving the desert, he entered the coenobitic life.]

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The notable teaching of the same Abbot John when he was dying

When the same elder, cheerful as though he were migrating to his own home, was already at his last breath, and anxious brothers surrounded him and earnestly begged him to leave them some memorial instruction, like a kind of hereditary legacy by which they might more easily reach the summit of perfection through a brief rule, he sighed and said:

“I have never done my own will, nor have I taught anyone what I had not first done myself.”

## CHAPTER XXIX. On Abbot Machetes, who never slept during spiritual conferences but always fell asleep during worldly stories

We saw an elder named Machetes, living at a distance from the crowds of brothers, who had obtained from the Lord through prolonged prayers this grace: whenever a spiritual conference was being held, day or night, he was never completely relaxed by the dullness of sleep. But if anyone attempted to introduce a word of detraction or some idle remark, he immediately fell asleep, as though the poison of slander could not reach even the pollution of his ears.

## CHAPTER XXX. The same elder’s judgment that no one should judge another

When this same elder was teaching us that we ought to judge no one, he added that there had been three matters in which he had examined or reproved the brothers: namely, when some allowed the uvula to be cut off, when they possessed a cloak in their cells, and when they blessed oil and gave it to secular people who requested it. He said that he himself had fallen into all these things.

[Note: The *uva* here is not the fruit of the vine, but a certain membrane hanging at the innermost part of the mouth, or at the end of the palate, around the throat, as can be seen in a person with his mouth open (Caelius Rhodiginus, Book IV *Ancient Readings*, chapter 14). It is so called because it hangs down round like a grape and varies with moisture; it regulates the voice and sometimes swells into the shape of a grape with severe inflammation and pain. Hence the poet Serenus:

“Delicate throats grow sick when the force of cold
has entered their mouths, or when air, driven by winds,
turns and a heavy blast infects the very uvulae.”

This illness has two names. If it has an elongated form, it is called *columella*, from its resemblance to a little column; but if it becomes rounded into a globe, the Greeks call it σταφυλή, and the Latins *uva* or *uvula*. Pliny frequently mentions it in his *Natural History* (Book XX, chapter 18, and elsewhere). It seems likely that those monks, being prone to this disease because of their frequent and daily drinking of water, used to have the uvula cut away. Cornelius Celsus discusses this operation in Book IV, chapter 12.]

“For when I contracted the disease of the uvula,” he said, “I was debilitated by it for so long that, compelled both by the necessity of the pain and by the encouragement of all the elders, I finally allowed it to be cut away. Because of this illness I was also compelled to have a cloak.”

[Note: Among the Romans, the *sagum* was a military garment worn over armor, as can be gathered from Cicero’s eighth *Philippic*; in Greek, σάγος. Among Cassian and those monks, however, it was a kind of blanket or rough cloak, which sick people sometimes wore beyond the ordinary custom, as though compelled to do so; this is what is suggested here. Saint Jerome likewise attributes a *sagum* to the rustic Hilarion (*Life of Hilarion*).]
