“I was also forced to bless oil and give it to those who begged for it—something I abhorred above all else, since I judged it to arise from great presumption of heart. When many secular people suddenly surrounded me, I was so constrained that I could not escape them in any other way than by their using great force and entreaties to extort from me that I place my hand, marked with the sign of the cross, upon the vessel they offered. Thus, believing that they had obtained blessed oil, they finally released me.

“From this it became plainly clear to me that a monk becomes bound by the same causes and vices in which he has presumed to judge others.”

[Note: Saint Bernard gives excellent advice on this matter when writing on the *Song of Songs*: “Beware,” he says (Sermon 4), “of being either a curious investigator or a rash judge of another’s manner of life. Even if you discover that something has been done wrongly, still do not judge your neighbor; rather, make excuses for him. If you cannot excuse the deed, excuse the intention; suppose ignorance, suppose surprise, suppose accident. But if the certainty of the matter permits no such explanation, nevertheless persuade yourself and say within yourself: ‘The temptation was exceedingly violent; what would it have done to me if it had likewise been given power over me?’” See John Climacus, Step 10.]

“Therefore, each person ought to judge only himself and carefully and cautiously guard himself in everything, not scrutinizing the conduct and life of others, in accordance with the Apostle’s command: ‘But you, why do you judge your brother? He stands or falls before his own Lord’ (Romans 14). And again: ‘Do not judge, so that you may not be judged. For with the judgment by which you judge, you will be judged’ (Matthew 7).

“Besides the reason we have mentioned, it is also dangerous to judge others because, being ignorant either of the necessity or of the reason by which they do those things at which we take offense—things they may perform rightly before God or with pardon—we discover that we have judged them rashly. In this way we commit no slight sin by forming an improper opinion of our brothers.”

## CHAPTER XXXI. The rebuke of the same elder when he saw brothers who had been sleeping during spiritual conferences awaken at the narration of an idle story

[Col. 0247C]

This same elder demonstrated by the following signs that the devil is always the patron of idle stories and the adversary of spiritual conferences. For when he was discussing necessary and spiritual matters with certain brothers, and saw them sinking into a kind of Lethean sleep, unable to drive the weight of sleep from their eyes, he suddenly introduced an idle story. When he saw them immediately awaken for its amusement and prick up their ears, he sighed and said:

[Note: Lethean sleep, or sleep among the poets, is not called so from *lethal*, meaning deadly or death-bearing, but from the river Lethe in the underworld, which they imagine produces stupor and deep forgetfulness of all things. Virgil writes in Book VI of the *Aeneid*:

“They drink at the stream of Lethe
the carefree waters and long forgetfulness.”

Saint Jerome likewise writes in Book I *Against Rufinus*: “According to the tales of the poets, I had to drink from the Lethean pool, lest I be accused of knowing what I had learned.” Lethean sleep, therefore, properly means heavy and profound sleep, which is also usually forgetful. Yet the Author seems to take it in the sense of *lethal*, since below he uses the same meaning and synonymous words: “they were plunged into deadly sleep.” He calls the sleep and drowsiness deadly either because it makes a person resemble death—or one who is dead—in accordance with Persius:

“Fool, what is sleep except the image of cold death?”

or because it gradually brings death to the soul when someone refuses to hear salutary admonitions and falls asleep amid vanities. The Wise Man speaks of this sleep: “How long will you sleep, sluggard?” (Proverbs 6). The Apostle says in Ephesians 5: “Rise, you who sleep; arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you”; and in Romans 13: “It is already the hour for us to rise from sleep,” and so forth.]

“Until now we were speaking about heavenly matters, and the eyes of all of you were weighed down by deadly drowsiness. But when an idle story was introduced, we all awoke and shook off the torpor of the sleep that had mastered us. From this, then, consider who was the adversary of that spiritual conference and who is the introducer of this fruitless and carnal tale. For the adversary is most clearly seen to be the one who rejoices in evil and never ceases either to encourage the latter or to oppose the former.”

## CHAPTER XXXII. On letters burned before they were read

[Col. 0248B]

I think it is no less necessary to recall the deed of a brother who was intent upon the purity of his heart and exceedingly solicitous for divine contemplation. After fifteen years, when several letters from his father, mother, and many friends had been brought to him from the province of Pontus, he received a large bundle of letters and, turning them over for a long time within himself, said:

[Note: Pontus is understood both as the sea and as a region. The region of Pontus, or province of Pontus, as it is called here, is part of Asia Minor along the Pontic or Euxine Sea, which separates Asia and Europe; it includes Cappadocia, Armenia, Colchis, and other provinces (Strabo, Book VII; Ptolemy, Book V, chapter 6). Marcion, the arch-heresiarch, came from Pontus. When Tertullian argues against him, he vividly depicts this region, his homeland (*Against Marcion*, Book I, chapter 1).]

“What a multitude of thoughts the reading of these letters will cause me! They will drive me either into empty joy or into fruitless sadness. For how many days will the remembrance of those who wrote them call my mind away from the contemplation to which I have devoted it? After how long a time will this confusion conceived in my mind be dispersed, and with how much labor will this state of tranquility have to be restored, if my spirit, once disturbed by affection for the letters, should begin, by reviewing their words and faces—those whom I abandoned so long ago—to see them again, dwell with them again, and occupy itself with them in heart and mind?

“It will certainly profit me nothing to have left them bodily if I begin to behold them in my heart, and if I, who renounced this world and rejected their memory as though dead, should revive it and admit it once more.

“Turning these thoughts over in his heart, he resolved not only not to open any letter, but not even to untie the bundle itself, lest, by reviewing the names of those who had written or recalling their faces, he should cease from the attentiveness of his spirit. Thus, just as he had received it bound, he handed it over to the fire to be burned.

“Go,” he said, “thoughts of my homeland; burn together, and do not try to recall me any further to the things from which I fled.”

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the resolution of a question which Abbot Theodore obtained through prayer

[Col. 0249B]

We also saw Abbot Theodore, endowed with the highest holiness and perfect knowledge, not only of practical life but also of the Scriptures. This knowledge had been given him not so much by the study of reading or by worldly learning as by purity of heart, since he could scarcely understand or pronounce even a very few words of the Greek language.

[Note: Two Theodores are mentioned, both distinguished by the praise and holiness of the monastic life. One was not, as Baronius erroneously states in the *Martyrology* (January 7), a disciple of Saint Antony, but of the anchorite Ammonas, as is clear both from the life of Antony written by Saint Athanasius and from Palladius (*Lausiac History*, chapter 8), Sozomen (Book I of his *History*, chapter 14), and others. The other was a disciple of Saint Pachomius, whose deeds are recounted in his life and in the *Lives of the Fathers*. Saint Nilus discusses the same man in his book *On Prayer*.

To which of the two the saying reported here should be attributed is not sufficiently certain. I nevertheless think it should rather be attributed to the latter, because he was more renowned for the gift of doctrine and wisdom commended here and succeeded Saint Pachomius in governing the monastery of Tabennisi. Hence this Theodore is called “abbot.” Gennadius writes of him in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 8: “Theodore, the successor of Abbot Pachomius, distinguished for holiness and remarkable for doctrine, is commended in the book of *Conferences of the Fathers* published by Cassian in many ways. After Pachomius, he vigorously governed his monasteries at the highest summit of perfection. He wrote several exhortatory and elegant letters to other monasteries on concord and unity and on persevering in one’s purpose of heart and study, and, renowned for miracles, he rested in the Lord.” Thus Gennadius (*Tripartite History*, Book I, chapter 11).

From this I conclude that this is the same Theodore whose learned discussion is found in the sixth *Conference*, “On the Death of the Saints.” See the notes there.]

When he was seeking an explanation of an exceedingly obscure question, he persisted tirelessly in prayer for seven days and nights, until the Lord revealed to him the solution of the question he had posed.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. The teaching of the same elder, by which he showed with what devotion a monk can attain knowledge of the Scriptures
Therefore, while certain brothers were admiring the exceedingly brilliant light of his knowledge and asking him about certain meanings of the Scriptures [Col. 0250B], he said:

[Note: [Col. 0249C] This statement, if it is to be true, requires a sound interpretation. At first sight it seems to contain two errors: first, that Sacred Scripture is in itself sufficiently easy and clear, and has no need of commentary or interpretation; second, consequently, that a monk—or anyone wishing to attain knowledge of the Scriptures—has no need of another teacher or interpreter, nor need to apply himself to the study and reading of commentaries, but should ask and await from God [Col. 0249D] an understanding of them through prayers, purification of the heart, and so forth. Both of these positions are false and erroneous, and close to the doctrine of the heretics of our time, who maintain that Sacred Scripture is easy and clear in every respect, indeed clearer than all the commentaries of the holy Fathers.

As to the first point, the royal prophet openly contradicts it; he frequently bears eloquent witness to the difficulty and obscurity of the law and of divine Scripture. Psalm 118: “Give me understanding, and I shall search out your law.” In the same psalm: “Make your face shine upon your servant, and teach me your statutes.” And again: “Open my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law.” Explaining these words, Saint Jerome says in his letter to Paulinus on the formation of a monk (Letter 13): “If so great a prophet confesses the darkness of ignorance, how much more do you think that little ones, and those scarcely weaned, are surrounded by the night of ignorance?” [Col. 0250B]

Peter, chief of the apostles, also contradicts it, saying: “Understanding this first, that no prophecy of Scripture is made by private interpretation; for prophecy was not at any time brought forth by human will, but holy men of God spoke under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter 1). The holy eunuch of the queen of Ethiopia likewise contradicts it. When he was reading the prophecy of Isaiah and Philip asked him, “Do you think you understand what you are reading?”, he wisely replied: “And how can I, unless someone show me?” (Acts 8).

The holy Fathers and Doctors of the Church also contradict it (see Baronius, volume 1 of the Annals, year 34; Bellarmine, book 3, On the Word of God, chapter 1). Jerome, in that celebrated letter to Paulinus which is prefixed to the Bibles, goes through the individual books of Scripture and shows that there are many great difficulties in all of them. He severely rebukes those who, trusting in their own cleverness or holiness, presume that they can read, interpret, and understand the sacred books without a teacher or interpreter. Saint Ambrose says in Letter 44, to Constantius: “The divine Scripture is a sea, containing within itself profound meanings, the depth of prophetic riddles,” and so forth.

Saint Chrysostom says: “There is not even a syllable or a tiny mark in the sacred writings in whose depths there is not some great treasure. Therefore we must be guided by divine grace and, illumined by the Holy Spirit, approach the divine utterances” (Homily 21 on Genesis; see also Homily 40 on John).

Saint Augustine says in book 12 of the Confessions, chapter 14: “Wonderful is the depth of your utterances, whose surface, behold, is before us, flattering the little ones; but wonderful is the depth, my God, wonderful the depth: it is fearful to gaze into it—the fear inspired by honor, and the trembling of love.” Elsewhere he says: “So great is the depth of Christian writings that I would make progress in them every day if I attempted to learn them alone, from the beginning of youth to the most advanced old age, with the greatest leisure, the utmost diligence, and better intelligence—not because such difficulty is encountered in reaching what is necessary for salvation, but because, once someone has held fast to the faith without which one cannot live piously and rightly, so many things remain for those who advance to understand, things obscure under so many and such varied coverings of mysteries; and so great a height of wisdom lies hidden not only in the words but also in the matters that must be understood, that even the oldest, sharpest, and most ardent in their desire to learn experience what the same Scripture says in one place: ‘When a man has finished, then he begins’” (Ecclesiasticus 18). This is Augustine’s statement (To Volusianus, Letter 2).

Gregory likewise says in the same sense: “Many things in it are so clear that they feed little ones; some, however, are expressed in more obscure sentences so that they may exercise the strong, in order that, when understood with labor, they may be more pleasing. Some things in it are so closed that, while we do not understand them, recognizing the weakness of our blindness, we may advance more toward humility than toward understanding. For there are certain things that speak of heavenly matters in such a way that they are open only to those heavenly citizens who remain in their homeland, and are not yet disclosed to us while we are pilgrims,” and so forth (Homily 17 on Ezekiel).

The second statement also, if understood simply, is shown to be erroneous and alien to sound doctrine, both by the examples and authority of the holy Fathers and by reason. Rufinus writes thus of Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus in book 11 of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter 9: “Both were noble, both educated at Athens, both colleagues for thirteen years. Setting aside the books of all secular Greeks, they devoted themselves solely to the volumes of divine Scripture, and they pursued their understanding of them not through presumptuous reliance on themselves, but through the writings and authority of their predecessors, who themselves were known to have received from the apostolic succession the rule for understanding.”

Saint Jerome says similarly of himself in the preface to his Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians: “From my youth,” he says, “I have never ceased either to read or to question learned men about what I did not know, nor have I regarded myself as my own teacher.” Again, recently, chiefly for this reason, he says, he went to Alexandria to see Didymus and to ask him about all the matters in Scripture that were doubtful to him.

And in his letter to Pammachius he says, among other things: “When I was young, I was carried along by a wonderful eagerness to learn; nor, contrary to the presumption of some, did I teach myself.” And below: “My head was already being sprinkled with gray; it was more fitting for me to be a teacher than a pupil. Nevertheless I went to Alexandria, listened to Didymus, and I thank him in many matters: what I did not know, I learned; what I knew, I did not lose because he taught me. People thought that I had finished learning: I went again to Jerusalem and Bethlehem. At what labor, and at what price, I acquired Barabbas as a teacher by night!” and so forth.

On Daniel, chapter 12, he says: “The most ignorant people especially claim for themselves the understanding of Sacred Scripture without the grace of God and the teaching of their predecessors.” And in that letter to Paulinus he teaches with great elegance, through many testimonies, examples, and arguments, that no one can enter the path of the sacred Scriptures without a guide going before him. Clement of Alexandria also taught this in the fifth book of the Stromata.

Similarly, Abbot Moses says in Cassian, Conference 2, chapter 11: “Although all the arts and disciplines discovered by human ingenuity, and which serve no purpose beyond the conveniences of this life, can be touched with the hand and seen with the eyes, nevertheless no one can properly grasp them without the teaching of an instructor; how foolish, then, to believe that this one discipline alone has no need of a teacher, when it is invisible and hidden, and can be perceived only with the purest heart. Its error produces not temporal loss, nor something easily repaired, but the ruin of the soul and everlasting death.” He is speaking of divine philosophy, that is, of the understanding of the Scriptures and of matters pertaining to salvation.

Saint Augustine sings a similar tune in the book On the Usefulness of Believing, addressed to Honoratus (chapter 7, volume 6). Since Honoratus thought that he could read and understand the sacred books without outside assistance, Augustine says: “Is that really so? Though you had received no training in poetry, you would not dare approach Terence’s Maurus without a teacher. Asper, Cornutus, Donatus, and countless others are required if any poet is to be understood; yet you rush upon the holy books without a guide and dare to pass judgment on them without an instructor.” And in chapter 17: “If every discipline, however lowly and easy, requires a teacher or instructor in order to be learned, what could be fuller of rash pride than to refuse to learn the books of the divine mysteries from their interpreters?” Thus far Augustine.

To these authorities theological reasoning must also be added. For to wish to attain sacred doctrine and the understanding of Scripture without a teacher or instructor would truly be to tempt God (Thomas Aquinas, Second Part of the Second Part, question 97, articles 1 and 2). One tempts God when, without necessity or serious cause, having abandoned natural and ordinary means, one seeks from God effects that can come about through the use of secondary causes—that is, through our work and study and through other aids—as when a sick person refuses to use natural and available remedies while expecting health from God.

Saint Augustine also touches on this reasoning in the prologue to his book On Christian Doctrine, where he says: “Let us not tempt the Lord in whom we have believed, lest, deceived by such tricks and perversity of the enemy, we should refuse even to go into the churches to hear and learn the Gospel, or to read the book, and should expect to be snatched up into the third heaven, whether in the body or outside the body, as the Apostle said, and there to hear unspeakable words which it is not lawful for a man to utter; or there to see the Lord Jesus Christ and hear the Gospel from him rather than from human beings. Let us beware of such temptations, full of pride and peril, and let us rather remember that the Apostle Paul himself, although struck down and instructed by a divine and heavenly voice, was nevertheless sent to a man [Col. 0252B] so that he might receive the sacraments and be joined to the Church,” and so forth.

Cassiodorus expresses the same view in the preface to his Institutions, referring to this very passage of Cassian. He writes: “I do not fail to recall that the most eloquent Cassian, in the fifth book of the Institutions—so I think it should be called, not of the Conferences—said that a certain old man, a simple man, had been questioned about a very obscure passage of Sacred Scripture and, through very frequent prayer, had come to know it by heavenly illumination, so that, suddenly filled with divine inspiration, he explained the most difficult matters to those who asked him, although he had not previously learned them from human teachers.”

There is a similar statement by Augustine (in the place cited above), which he records in his books On Christian Doctrine: a certain barbarian servant, uneducated in letters, was said, through frequent prayers, suddenly to have read the book entrusted to him as though he had been educated through long meditation at school. On this matter he himself says afterward: “Although these may have been astonishing miracles, and all things are acknowledged to be possible for believers, we should nevertheless not frequently display such things, but should remain more safely within the practice of ordinary instruction, lest, when we boldly seek what is above us, we should seem to incur the guilt of tempting God against the Lord’s command, which says in Deuteronomy: ‘You shall not tempt the Lord your God’ (Deuteronomy 6). And again in the Gospel: ‘An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign,’ and so forth” (Matthew 12).

Therefore let us pray that what is closed may be opened to us, and let us in no way withdraw from the study of reading. Thus far Cassiodorus.

The decree of the Council of Trent concerning the interpretation of Scripture also bears on this matter, in these words: “To restrain wandering minds, the synod decrees that no one, relying on his own judgment in matters of faith and morals pertaining to the edification of Christian doctrine, may twist Sacred Scripture to his own meanings and dare to interpret that Sacred Scripture contrary to the meaning which holy mother Church has held and holds—for it is her task to judge the true meaning and interpretation of the sacred Scriptures—or contrary to the unanimous agreement of the Fathers, even if such interpretations were never at any time to be published. Those who act contrary to this shall be declared so by the ordinaries and punished with the penalties established by law.” Thus it is stated there (Council of Trent, session 4; see Melchior Cano, On Theological Places, book 7, chapter 3).

With all these points carefully considered, we must now see in what sense Theodore’s statement is true. It should be observed that he does not absolutely say that a monk wishing to attain knowledge of the Scriptures ought not to devote his efforts to books of commentators—that is, to the explanations of the holy Fathers. Rather, he adds that the monk must study and devote himself to piety and to the cleansing of the heart, especially from carnal vices, and that he must labor first and chiefly at this rather than at turning over and repeatedly reading many books and commentaries. This is entirely true, since the first and immediate disposition for reading and understanding Scripture [Col. 0253B] and sacred doctrine is purity of heart, according to Wisdom 1: “Wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins.”

This kind of expression is also familiar in divine Scripture. When it prefers one thing to another, it ordinarily does not affirm the one and deny the other absolutely; rather, it affirms the former without qualification and denies the latter without qualification. Thus in Hosea 6, when the Lord says, “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,” he does not deny that he desires sacrifice, which he himself instituted and commanded to be offered to him; he says rather that he prefers mercy to sacrifice. Likewise in John 7: “My teaching is not mine,” that is, it is not mine as much as it is the Father’s, from whom I received it.

In this sense the words that follow here, whether they are Theodore’s or Cassian’s, should be excused and explained—especially the statement that the reading of the Sacred Scriptures alone is fully sufficient for contemplation of true knowledge, and that it does not need instruction from commentaries. These words seem to signify nothing other than that knowledge of the Scriptures is acquired more through prayer and purity of mind than through assiduous study, just as Saint Thomas, the Angelic Doctor and chief of theologians, testified concerning himself that he had advanced more through prayer than through study or the teaching of others (Leander, in his Life of Thomas).

Saint Bernard likewise, as we read in his Life, confessed that whatever he knew in the Scriptures, and whatever he spiritually perceived in them, he had received chiefly by meditating and praying in the woods and fields. He used to say jokingly and pleasantly among his friends that he had never had any teachers in this matter except oaks and beech trees. Hence, in Letter 106, he says: “Believe one who has experienced it: the woods will teach you something more than books; trees and stones will teach you what you cannot hear from teachers.” Thus Bernard.

Nor will anyone depart from sound meaning and truth who understands these and similar statements not of a mere and simple knowledge of divine matters, but of a knowledge that also affects and moves the will with a holy sense of piety, continually stirs those who possess it toward better things, and edifies others—a knowledge joined with love of God and neighbor and with the gifts and fruits of the Holy Spirit.

Of this Cassian says elsewhere (book 6, chapter 18): “It is impossible to possess spiritual knowledge without purity of chastity. For it does not enter a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins, as Scripture testifies (Wisdom 1); nor is it obtained by the effectiveness of study, however assiduous and intense. Rather, it comes from God and from his most holy Spirit, whom we must win for ourselves through holy prayers and a humble preparation of the heart.” Hence the Apostle James admonishes: “If anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask it of God, who gives abundantly to all” (James 1), and so forth.

Finally, it may be said that they are speaking of those who, outside the common and ordinary law, are enlightened by God through a supernatural gift of knowledge and wisdom and understand the meanings of the sacred writings with no teacher other than the Holy Spirit—such as the prophets and apostles, and many holy men whom the Greeks call θεοδίδακτοι (*theodidaktoi*), that is, “taught by God.” Of these the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 12: “To one through the Spirit is given a word of wisdom, to another prophecy, to another the interpretation of utterances.”

Whatever exercise and daily meditation on the law ordinarily bestow on others, the Holy Spirit suggested to them; and, as it is written, they were θεοδίδακτοι, that is, “taught by God,” says Jerome in the letter to Paulinus cited above.

In this way Saint Antony is said, without any knowledge of letters, to have retained the divine Scriptures in memory by hearing them and to have understood them through prudent reflection (see his Life, chapter 38). And that barbarian Christian servant, ignorant of letters, obtained knowledge of them through three days of prayer, so that he read through the book placed before him, to the astonishment of those present, says Saint Augustine in the passage cited above.

Peter Damian, in book 6 of his letters, letter 17, mentions several other holy men who were distinguished in doctrine without much study, being taught by God. Among them Saint Benedict is named by Saint Gregory (Book 2 of the Dialogues, chapter 1) with the notable praise “knowingly ignorant and wisely unlearned”—that is, despising human knowledge but sufficiently illumined by heavenly doctrine.

It is plausible that Saint Abbot Theodore also received such a gift, as may be inferred from this passage, from the preceding chapter, and from Cassiodorus’s statement. Yet this is an extraordinary mode, granted to few, and the examples of the few are more to be admired than imitated. Happy indeed are those to whom that gift has been divinely granted; but those who attain it through much labor and study are not unhappy, since, as the Apostle testifies, “Each will receive his own reward according to his labor; for we are God’s fellow workers” (1 Corinthians 3).

Therefore, as in other matters, so also in this one, two extremes must be avoided and the middle course maintained. The extremes are either to expect knowledge of divine mysteries and the Scriptures from God alone and from our prayers, or to expect it from our own work, study, and labor alone. The middle course is to join and employ both, as is clear from what has been said. But more will have to be said about these matters in Conference 14, which belongs to Abbot Nesteros.]

“A monk who wishes to attain knowledge of the Scriptures [Col. 0251A] ought by no means to devote his efforts to books of commentators, but rather to keep all [Col. 0252A] the industry of his mind and the attention of his heart directed toward the cleansing of carnal vices. Once these have been expelled, immediately [Col. 0253A] the eyes of the heart, the veil of the passions having been removed, will begin naturally to contemplate the mysteries of the Scriptures.

“For they were not proclaimed to us by the grace of the Holy Spirit so that they might be unknown or obscure to us; rather, they are made obscure because the veil of sins, covering the eyes of the heart through our fault, darkens them. When these eyes have been restored to their natural soundness, the very reading of the Sacred Scriptures alone is abundantly sufficient for contemplation of true knowledge, and they have no need of instruction from commentators—just as these bodily eyes need no instruction for seeing, provided only that they are free from the discharge or darkness of blindness.

“For this reason such great diversity and error [Note: [Col. 0254D] A little earlier he said ‘commentators.’ Thus Claudianus, in book 2 of On the State of the Soul, calls Jerome especially ‘the chief of the interpreters.’ Severus likewise, in the first dialogue, calls Origen ‘a most skilled interpreter of the sacred writings.’ Finally, Vincent of Lérins says in the Commonitorium: ‘The teachers who are now called interpreters, whom this same Apostle sometimes also calls prophets, because through them the mysteries of the prophets are disclosed to the peoples.’] have arisen among the interpreters themselves: most of them, rushing to interpret [Col. 0253B] without applying diligence to the purification of the mind, have been unable to grasp the light of truth. Because of the grossness or uncleanness of their hearts, they have formed differing and contradictory opinions either contrary to the faith or contrary to one another [Col. 0254A].”

## CHAPTER XXXV  
### The rebuke of the same old man when he came to my cell in the middle of the night

When this same Theodore unexpectedly came to my cell in the dead of night, secretly investigating with a father’s concern what I, still an inexperienced anchorite, might be doing alone, he found me, immediately after the evening service had ended, beginning to restore my weary body and lying down on a mat. Drawing deep sighs from his heart and repeatedly calling me by name, he said:

“How many, O John, at this hour are conversing with God and embracing and retaining him within themselves—and you are deprived of so great a light, dissolved in sluggish sleep!”

And since the virtues and grace of the Fathers have moved us to turn aside to a narrative of this kind, I think it necessary to commend in this volume the memorable work of charity [Note: [Col. 0255C] Dionysius calls him Arthebius; Peter, in his catalogue, testifies that he was made bishop from an anchorite, and describes his life in this summary, from which one may understand what a great man he was (Peter de Natalibus, book 11, chapter 58): “Arthebius, bishop of Pamphylia [or, Panephysia], was unwillingly and reluctantly raised from the anchoritic life to the aforesaid episcopal see. Yet while living in the episcopate he did not abandon the life of the desert; indeed, continually intent on fasts and prayers, he diligently administered his pastoral care, and often visited the desert dear to him, visiting the holy anchorites and Fathers in person and with his blessings.” Thus he. Cassian, Conference 11, chapter 2, calls this same man Archebius bishop of Panephysis and commends his virtues. Sozomen (book 6, chapter 30) and Nicephorus (book 11, chapter 37) also number Arsesius among the more celebrated monks, call him great and illustrious, and write that he grew old in monastic philosophy and presided over monks. Hence I am almost led to think that Arsesius should be read here in place of Archebius; but [Col. 0255D] I prefer to await the judgment of others.] which we experienced through the kindness of the great man Archebius, so that the purity of continence, joined to the work of charity, may shine more brightly, distinguished by a beautiful variety. For the offering of fasting then becomes pleasing to God when it has been brought to completion by the fruits of charity.

## CHAPTER XXXVI  
### Description of the desert at Diolcos, where anchorites dwell

When [Note: [Col. 0255D] The monks and monasteries of Palestine have been discussed elsewhere (book 3, chapter 1). On them see also Sozomen, book 6, chapter 32; Nicephorus, book 11, chapter 39; and, before these, Saint Basil, Letter 39.] therefore, we had come from the monasteries of Palestine to the Egyptian town called [Note: [Col. 0255D] Cassian elsewhere calls it a town, and elsewhere a village, Conference 18, chapter 1: “We reached the village called Diolcos, situated above one of the seven mouths of the Nile.” Nicephorus, book 11, chapter 35: “Around the narrow passages of land in Egypt, called *diolkoi* (διολκοί) because ships are transported across them, Piammon and John were especially famous and leaders of many brothers,” and so forth (see Saint Jerome, in his letter to Eustochium). In this same place Sozomen records that several holy monks lived, book 6, chapter 29; Palladius gives a fuller account of their life in the *Lausiac History*.] Diolcos, very inexperienced, and had there marvelously seen a very large crowd bound by the discipline of a coenobium and an excellently ordered community of monks—which is also the first order [Col. 0255B] [Note: [Col. 0256C] Cassian frequently mentions two orders, or two kinds, of monks, here and elsewhere. One is that of the coenobites, that is, those living together and in common, which he calls the first order of monks because it began in the very origins of the Church under the apostles. Such were the first Christians, the disciples of the apostles, of whom it is said in Acts 4: “The multitude of believers were of one heart and one soul; nor did anyone say that anything was his own, but all things were common to them.” The other is that of the anchorites, or solitaries, which he rightly calls more excellent, because the anchoritic or eremitic life is the summit and pinnacle of the religious life. Hence the Fathers commonly teach that no one should pass to the anchoritic life unless he has first been carefully trained and tested in a coenobium. The author also indicates this in the present chapter (Augustine, book 1, On the Morals of the Catholic Church, chapter 31; and Castan, Conference 1, Conference 18 throughout. See the notes on chapter 17 of book 8; Jerome, Letter 4 to Rusticus).]—we hastened, urged on by the praises of all, with keenest eagerness to see the other order as well, which is regarded as more excellent, namely, that of the anchorites (see Conference 18, chapter 5).

“For these men, after dwelling for a very long time in coenobia, carefully instructed in every rule of patience and discernment, having likewise acquired the virtue of humility and nakedness, and having completely destroyed the whole multitude of vices, penetrate the deepest and most secret recesses of the desert in order to engage in the fiercest battles with demons.

“Having learned, then, that men of this way of life lived near the bed of the Nile River, in a place surrounded on one side by that river and on the other by the vastness of the sea, which makes it an island—habitable for no one except those seeking solitude as monks, for the salinity of the soil and the barrenness of the sands prevent it from being suitable for cultivation—we hastened to them with the greatest desire. We were exceedingly astonished at the labors they endure, in contemplation of their virtues and in love of solitude.

“For they are constrained by such a great scarcity of water that they distribute it with such care and scrupulousness that no one among the most frugal preserves and rations even the appearance of the most precious wine with greater economy. They bring it from the bed of the aforementioned river for their necessary uses, three thousand paces or more away; and that distance, divided by sandy hills, is doubled by the extreme difficulty of the labor.

[Note: [Col. 0256C] On this, see the note to Conference 24, chapter 2.]

## CHAPTER XXXVII  
### The kindness of Abbot Archebius is commended
Having seen these things, when the ardor of imitating them had inflamed us, and when the aforementioned Archebius, a man of the highest proven virtue among them, had drawn us to his cell out of kindness, he discovered our desire and pretended that he wished to leave that very place. He offered us his cell as though he were about to move away, asserting that he would do so even if we were not present. We, inflamed by our desire to remain there and readily placing unquestioning faith in the assertions of so great a man, gladly accepted the cell with all its furnishings and utensils.

Thus, having achieved his purpose through a pious stratagem, he left the place after a few days, in order to acquire the materials needed to build another cell. Returning afterward, he constructed another for himself with the greatest labor. Not long afterward, when other brothers arrived and likewise wished to remain there, he deceived them by the same charitable lie and handed it over to them with all its equipment. He himself, indefatigable in the work of charity, built a third little cell for himself in which to live.

> [Note: It is quite evident, both from this chapter and from other passages, that at that time two classes of people customarily lived in monasteries. Some had professed the monastic life and were bound by vows to live there perpetually under obedience; these were monks both in fact and in name. Others lived in monasteries only temporarily, not so much in order to become monks as to exercise themselves in piety and other virtues, or even in studies. They were bound by no vows and could leave the monasteries whenever they wished (Basil, *Monastic Institutions*, chapter 49, and *Shorter Rules*, chapter 292). Cassian speaks here of these persons, as does Chrysostom near the end of book III *Against the Detractors of the Monastic Life*, where he urges his fellow citizens to send their sons to monasteries; indeed, even though married, to go there themselves and remain for some time. In this way our Cassian and his companion Germanus, visiting monasteries and monks’ cells, would repeatedly stay in them for a time, so that they might enjoy longer the conversation and company of the holy Fathers and commit their teaching, institutions, and examples to memory.]

> [Note: Cassian attributes lies to this holy man; this is not surprising, since he himself, along with certain others, held that a “dutiful lie”—which he here calls a “lie of charity”—was not only permissible but praiseworthy and sometimes necessary, as will become clearer from the Conferences. Yet Saint Augustine vigorously attacked this opinion as false and contrary to Holy Scripture in the two books he wrote On Lying; the entire later school of theologians agrees with him and teaches that every lie is a sin, and that one must never lie, even in order to benefit oneself or another as greatly as possible. For, Augustine says, a lie must not be thought to be no sin merely because we may sometimes benefit someone by lying: we can also benefit someone by stealing, if the poor person to whom something is openly given experiences an advantage while the rich person from whom it is secretly taken experiences no disadvantage. Moreover, since lying is one thing and speaking obscurely or amphibologically is another—for someone who uses amphibology or a tacit restriction does not intend to assert what is false as true, or to deny what he knows or believes to be true, which is properly what it means to lie, namely, to go against one’s mind or intention—that good hermit could easily be excused from a lie properly so called. In reality, he willingly left his cell to those who came and afterward built another for himself; and again, when others arrived, he was prepared to yield it to them. In the same way, a prudent reader can easily excuse from the charge of lying the other example related in chapter 39, although one need not be excessively anxious about this matter. We must not immediately believe that everything we read about holy men, whether in Scripture or elsewhere, was therefore permissible or ought to be imitated, since it is clear that they did not live without sin, at least venial sin. Among such sins are the so-called dutiful lies, which Saint Augustine nevertheless teaches are not the least of sins and must be carefully avoided by those who are perfect. It should also be noted here that these words, which appear to support lying, were deliberately omitted by Dionysius the Carthusian, who endeavored to present Cassian’s teaching cleansed of every error. He likewise omitted the material in which Abbot Joseph discusses the same license to lie at greater length, from chapter eight to the end of the seventeenth Conference. On the other hand, I discovered in our manuscript a certain addition inserted at this point after the words “asserting that he would do so even if we were not present.” It continues as follows: “The charity of a servant of God ought to be praised; but the example of lying, which is always a sin, ought to be rejected. For blessed Augustine and the other Fathers affirm with many assertions that the children of God—namely, children of truth—must in no way lie.” The context sufficiently indicates that these words are not Cassian’s, since they agree neither with what precedes nor with what follows, and they are found in no other copies. They therefore seem first to have been written in the margin by someone wishing to point out this error concerning lying, and afterward, through the ignorance or carelessness of some scribe, to have entered the text itself. More will be said about this in the seventeenth Conference.]



> [Note: Palladius tells a similar story about a certain Abbot Dorotheus in the Lausiac History, chapter 2. “He,” Palladius says, “spent the entire day—and indeed the very heat of midday—in the desert near the sea gathering stones; continually building and making cells from them, he gave them to those who could not build, constructing one cell each year.” Rufinus, in Lives of the Fathers, book II, chapter 23, and Palladius, chapter 70, relate another similar story about Ammonius. The frequent mention of a cell and little cell in these books and in the Conferences plainly seems to require that we make some remarks about it. A cell (*cella*, from which the diminutive *cellula*) is so called because things that we wish to keep hidden (*celare*) are concealed in it. Any place in which something is stored for preservation is called a cell. Cicero says in On Old Age: “The wine-cellar, oil-cellar, honey-cellar, and fruit-cellar of a good and diligent master are always well stocked” (Festus Pompeius, book III; Isidore, book XV of the Etymologies, chapter 3). Virgil likewise called the honeycombs’ chambers cells when he says of the bees: “They fill the cells with nectar” (Georgics IV). Among the pagans, moreover, the *cella* was the more sacred part of a temple, into which it was not lawful for just anyone to enter; in Greek, an *adyton* (ἀδύτον, “inaccessible place”). Thus Gellius records that Scipio came to the Capitol and ordered Jupiter’s cella to be opened (Attic Nights, book VII, chapter 1). In ecclesiastical usage, however, cells were initially called the small houses or modest dwellings of monks or anchorites, in which, hidden away in remote and solitary places, they devoted themselves to prayer, contemplation, and other exercises. Saint Jerome mentions them in letters 22 and 27 to Eustochium, as well as in the preface to the Rule of Saint Pachomius. Later certain holy men also began to have cells in cities and outside cities. As a result, when brothers gathered together and were placed under their discipline, humble and contemptible cells everywhere grew into large and splendid monasteries. Hence even now many coenobies retain the ancient name and are called cells, as Molanus noted in the Martyrology (on November 6 and 27, and in the Annals of the Saints of Belgium, October 9, and elsewhere). Saint Benedict also uses the word *cell* in one place to mean a dormitory, when he says: “Let a lamp burn continually in the same cell until morning” (chapter 22). In canon law, two kinds of monks’ cells are distinguished. Some are within the enclosure of the monastery but outside the common dormitory. The canon of the Council of Agde forbids these to be indiscriminately assigned to individual monks, much less constructed by them on their own authority; they are to be granted only to the sick or to elderly monks who have served long and have been approved. Others are the cells of hermits or anchorites, established outside cities in deserted or remote places. Boniface VIII speaks of these in the chapter *Privilegium*, on the meaning of words, in the Sixth Book of the Decretals (in Gratian, 18, question 2, chapter *Nullus*). There he explains that by cells he understands secluded and solitary places, separated from human society and specially assigned to contemplation and the service of God. The chapter *Unicum*, on the Excesses of Prelates, in the Sixth Book, also decrees that religious, including mendicants, may go to such cells with the permission of their superiors. It should further be noted concerning the cells and little cells of monks that, according to the practice and institution of the ancient Fathers, they customarily were and ought to be assigned one to each monk. For although we find that the ancient monks sometimes lived several to a cell—Palladius reports this of the Tabennesiots—we learn that it was much safer and more convenient, and also more frequent and customary, for each to live separately. First, Philo says this of the Alexandrian Therapeutae: “Each has a sacred little house where, alone, he devotes himself to the mysteries of the holy life” (On the Contemplative Life). To prevent anyone from interpreting these as shrines rather than cells, Philo himself writes that, in addition to these individual cells, they possessed a common *semneion* (σεμνεῖον, “sacred place”), where on appointed days and hours they gathered to celebrate the praises and liturgies of God (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book II, chapter 10). Second, the Rule of Pachomius, article 61, says: “No one shall dare enter another’s cell”; and article 65: “No one shall store anything in his cell without the superior’s order” (see also articles 43 and 45). Third, Saint Jerome says in letter 22 to Eustochium, speaking of the Egyptian coenobites: “They remain separate, but with their cells joined together.” And below: “They go around the cells of each one.” In letter 27 he says: “Whose cell did he not enter?” Fourth, Cassian not only indicates in this chapter that Archebius possessed a cell of his own, which he nevertheless willingly yielded to outsiders who came, but also says above, speaking of Abbot Theodore: “When he had unexpectedly come to my cell” (chapter 35), and the same point is indicated in many other places. Fifth, Saint Benedict, when he forbids a brother to join himself to another brother at unsuitable hours (chapter 48 of the Rule). Sixth, Justinian’s fifth Novel concerning monks, which says: “Let the monks, certainly, have one house and one refectory, but separate bedrooms”—that is, one for each—“and each his own sitting room.” Seventh, the Second Council of Tours, which decreed the same in these words: “Nor shall they [the monks] be permitted to have common cells in which two remain together; rather, they shall sleep separately.”]



## CHAPTER XXXVIII. The same Archebius, by the labor of his hands, discharged his mother’s debt.

I think it worthwhile to commit to memory another work of charity by this same man, so that the monks of our own regions may be instructed by the example of one and the same man not only in the rigor of continence but also in the most sincere affection of love. He was born, indeed, of a family that was not undistinguished, but from his earliest years he fled to the monastery situated nearly four miles from the aforementioned town, rejecting both the affection of this world and that of his parents. There he spent his entire life in such a way that, throughout the whole fifty years, he not only never entered or even saw the village from which he had departed, but never saw the face of any woman, not even that of his own mother.

Meanwhile, his father was overtaken by death and left a debt of one hundred solidi.

> [Note: The *solidus*, also called the *stater*, was among the ancient Greeks and Romans a gold coin. It was so called because it was struck at its proper weight, not at half-weight or one-third weight, as were the *semisses* and *tremisses* (Coelius Rhodiginus, book X of Ancient Readings, chapter 2; Budaeus, On the As; Isidore, book XVI of the Etymologies, chapter 24; on chapter 3 of Ezekiel). Hence Isidore says: “Among the Latins the solidus is also called the *sextula*, because an ounce is completed by six solidi. The common people call it a solidus because it seems to lack nothing. For the ancients called what was whole *solidum*.” Such is his statement. Authors disagree, however, about the value of the solidus. Some equate the solidus and the stater with the Hebrew shekel, which weighed four drachmas, according to Saint Jerome; the Spanish call these *reales*, the Italians *giulii*, that is, five French *asses*. Others judge a solidus to be worth five florins, or French carolus coins; on that valuation one hundred solidi would amount to five hundred florins. There is also a silver solidus of more recent coinage, which is called an *as* or *assis* and is well known to the Germans as a *Stüber*.]

Although this man was entirely free from every disturbance—for he was an exile from all his paternal possessions—he learned that creditors were nevertheless harassing his mother severely. Then, softened by consideration of filial duty, he recognized that he had a mother and hastened to assist her in her distress, without relaxing anything of his established discipline; previously, while his parents were prosperous, he had, according to evangelical rigor, regarded himself as having neither father nor mother on earth. He hastened to assist her in her distress,

> [Note: This example teaches us that religious persons may and ought to assist their parents—that is, their father and mother—when they are placed in extreme or serious necessity, provided the substance of their state and profession remains intact. On this matter see Saint Thomas and Navarre (Saint Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* II–II, question 101, article 4; Navarre, commentary 3 on Regulars). Two things in particular should be observed and imitated in this example. First, that the monk, or abbot, worked with his own hands in the monastery for about a year in order to assist his afflicted mother, and in this way paid the entire debt. Second, that he did so without impairing his profession or diminishing his customary austerity—or, in Cassian’s words, without allowing anything of the rigor of his commitment to suffer diminution under the pretext of pious necessity. In this connection see Saint Basil, *Constitutions of Monasticism*, chapter 21, where he teaches how a monk ought to conduct himself toward secular parents and relatives, and how he ought to lay aside excessive familiarity, care, and anxiety regarding them.]

without relaxing anything of his established discipline. Remaining within the monastery’s enclosure, he asked that his usual daily task be tripled. There, laboring throughout an entire year by day and night alike, he paid the amount of the debt to the creditors by the sweat of his labor [prepared?], and freed his mother from every harassment. Thus he lifted the burden of debt from her without allowing anything of his established rigor to be diminished under the pretext of pious necessity. He guarded his accustomed strictness so carefully that he did not refuse his mother the work of filial duty, though for the love of Christ he had previously rejected her, now recognizing her again for the sake of that same piety.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. By what stratagem an old man provided the abbot Simeon with manual work when he was idle.

When our very dear brother Simeon, who was completely ignorant of the Greek language, had come from the regions of Italy, one of the elders, wishing to perform toward him, as a stranger, an act of charity under the appearance of mutual recompense,

> [Note: That is, an exchange and repayment, since Simeon would provide the service of writing and in return receive provisions. What he says below, “to purchase it under the guise of a debt,” has the sense of “repayment.” Dionysius has “recompense.” On the word *redhibitio* (“restoration” or “repayment”), see more in book IV, chapter 4, and Conference 21, chapter 33.]

asked him why he was sitting idle in his cell. He inferred from this that Simeon would be unable to remain there much longer, both because of the wandering produced by idleness and because of a shortage of necessities. He was certain that no one could endure the struggles of solitude unless he were content to procure his own food by the labor of his hands. When Simeon replied that he neither could nor was capable of performing any of the tasks that the brothers practiced there,

> [Note: A *librarian hand* is a hand accustomed to writing books, or skilled in writing, or the skill of writing itself. Among the Romans, *librarii* were those who copied books for publication for a fee or price. At Rome they had their shops on the Argiletum, and these shops were also called *librariae*. Hence Martial says to his book:

> “You prefer to dwell in the Argiletan shops,
>
> when my bookcases are empty for you, little book.”

> Saint Jerome calls his copyists *librarii* in his letter to Heliodorus (letter 42, where see Macianus’s scholia); they are also called amanuenses or tabularii. He writes to the subdeacon Niceas as follows: “For those uncultivated men of Italy whom Ennius calls *Cascos*, and who, as Cicero says in the *Rhetorica*, sought their livelihood in a barbarous manner, before the use of paper or parchment, used either smoothed wooden tablets or tree bark to exchange written messages with one another. Hence they called the carriers of such messages *tabellarii*, and their writers *librarii*, after the books of trees.” Such is Jerome’s account. Regarding books of trees, note that in ancient times, and in their original meaning, *libri* were called the bark of trees, which was divided into several very thin strips or sheets. Such were the sheets stripped from papyrus plants in Egypt and used in place of paper (Isidore, book VI of the Etymologies, chapters 12 and 13). Hence Pliny says: “At first people wrote on palm leaves, then on the bark of certain trees” (book XIII, chapter 11). Since books—that is, the thinner bark of trees—formerly supplied the place of paper, as stated, the codices that used to be assembled from them were also called *libri*. Usage prevailed so that, although the material changed and other kinds of writing material had already been discovered, the ancient name remained, and books came to be called those things assembled from many sheets prepared from whatever material. They are also called *codices*, from the *codices* or *caudices* of trees, that is, trunks, from which the ancients used to make wooden tablets for writing and cover them with wax.]

except for the work of a copyist, if only a Latin book were of any use in the region of Egypt, then at last the old man found an opportunity by which he could purchase the desired work of charity under the guise of repayment and said: “This opportunity has been provided by God. For I have long been looking for someone who would write out the Apostle for me in Latin. I have a brother bound by military service, and highly educated in Latin, to whom I wish to send something from the Holy Scriptures for his reading and edification.”

> [Note: That is, that he should copy Paul’s letters in Latin. When the name “the Apostle” is used without qualification, the Apostle Paul is ordinarily understood by antonomasia, just as Saint Thomas commonly cites Aristotle simply as “the Philosopher.” Here we see an ancient and praiseworthy practice of monks: writing and copying books, especially sacred books, on parchment. Saint Jerome mentions this practice in his letter to the monk Rusticus, where, listing various exercises with which monks ought to occupy themselves, he says among other things: “Let books be written, so that the hand may work for food and the mind be filled by reading.” Saint Chrysostom also mentions it when writing about the monks of his own time:

> “After they have celebrated the morning prayers and hymns, they turn to the reading of the Scriptures. Some are trained to copy books; each, taking the dwelling assigned to him, works continually in silence, with no one causing disturbance and no one saying anything.”

> Cassian also clearly implies the same custom in book IV, where he says: “He who is engaged in the work of a copyist must not dare to finish the letter he has begun when he hears it; but, leaving the lines of the unfinished letter at the very point at which the sound of the one who knocks has reached his ears,” and so forth. Palladius mentions it in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 39, which we shall cite elsewhere, and Sophronius in chapter 171 of the *Spiritual Meadow*. Trithemius testifies that this exercise was exceedingly familiar and customary among Benedictine monks in book *On Illustrious Men of the Benedictine Order*, chapter 6. There, recalling their various exercises and occupations according to each person’s ability and capacity, he says: “Some who were suited to it wrote books, while others brought to fair copy from notes the works published by more learned men; some skillfully bound written codices together; others corrected them; the rest adorned them with red minium.” Such is his statement. There is likewise a splendid testimony concerning the copying of books in Gaspar Brusch, where, while recounting the beginnings of the monastery of Fulda and the distinguished deeds of its first abbot, Sturm, he inserts these words about him (in the first century of *German Monasticism*): “The pious teacher had four hundred disciples of monastic discipline, apart from the younger men and those assigned to humbler duties—namely, cultivating the land, planting trees, ringing bells, and other such tasks. For the more advanced brothers, occupied in copying authors in both languages and the monuments of every discipline and profession, laid the foundations of so great a library, one that shortly afterward would rival that famous library of Philadelphia.” Such is his statement. Yet there is no need for testimonies of this kind, since as many witnesses to the practice exist as there are manuscript codices carefully preserved, as they should be, as a great treasure in libraries, especially those of illustrious monasteries. It is nevertheless lamentable that by far the greatest abundance and wealth of these books has perished through the ravages of war, and especially through the fury and wickedness of heretics, to the great loss of the entire Christian commonwealth (Josephus, book XII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 2). Monks were moved to this writing or copying for three reasons. First, to avoid idleness, as is clear both from this chapter and from what we have noted elsewhere concerning manual labor (on chapter 4 of book II and book X, chapter 22). Second, to obtain and earn food and necessities when the monastery’s goods and resources were insufficient, as is also suggested in this chapter and in Jerome’s words. Third, as a punishment and satisfaction for offenses. Hence one brother, at the end of a book he had copied, placed this verse as a conclusion:

> “This book is finished; now I am freed from punishment.”

> At an opportune moment there also appeared here a charming poem on the same subject, rhythmic in the ancient manner, by a certain monk of the monastery of Saint Vedast, whose first and last names are given. It was found in the archives of our library at the end of a very ancient manuscript codex, and seemed worthy of being brought from the darkness in which it had lain into the light, for the reader’s enjoyment and benefit. From it we may recognize both that the ancient custom of copying books had flourished for many centuries in this celebrated monastery and that the candor and simplicity of that period ought to be piously tolerated and excused. Thus sings that distinguished poet:

> “I, Rodulphus, called a monk only by name,
>
> not by merit, but trusting in Christ, the bishop,
>
> wrote out this book, full of heavenly doctrine.
>
> Let no one begrudge me if I gain profit from the book:
>
> for I certainly possess a great pledge on its account.
>
> What pledge, you ask? What pledge? You will know at once.
>
> When I write a book, Vedast from the highest heaven
>
> looks down from the skies; he also notes how many letters
>
> I shall draw with my pens, how many furrows
>
> shall be plowed across the page,
>
> how many leaves shall be torn here and there
>
> by sharp points.
>
> Then, favoring our work and our labor, he says:
>
> ‘As many letters, as many furrows, and finally as many points
>
> as there are in this book, so many sins I now forgive you,
>
> and Christ gives you this power perpetually.’
>
> Nor will this labor benefit you alone, brother;
>
> let a great share of the labor be given to whomever you wish.
>
> This is the reward of the work that holy Vedast,
>
> the excellent and kindly father,
>
> gives to the writers themselves.
>
> For this reward I diligently wrote out this book.”

> So writes Rodulphus de Monchy. Recently, while we were at Bruges, we unexpectedly saw, not without joy, even an image of this monument of antiquity. In the collegiate church of Saint Salvator there hangs a panel of ancient painting depicting Blessed Mary and Saint Vedast in the background, with the life and miracles of Saint Vedast shown in the little windows or surrounding panels. In one of them Saint Vedast is seen, his head flashing with rays, receiving a book above from the hands of a monk kneeling at his tomb, and congratulating him in these words. How useful and pleasing to God this work of writing was is confirmed by a remarkable miracle, which Caesarius of Cistercium records in these words (book XII of the *Examples*, chapter 47): “A Premonstratensian monk had written many books with his own hand, awaiting the reward of his labor in heaven. When he had died and had been buried in a notable place, his tomb was opened after twenty years, and his right hand was found so whole and so lifelike that it seemed to have been freshly cut from a living body, while the rest of the flesh had been reduced to dust.” Such is his account; he adds that, as proof of so great a miracle, the same hand is preserved in the monastery to this day.]

Simeon gratefully accepted this opportunity as though it had been offered him by God. The old man, too, gladly embraced the pretext by which he could freely carry out this act of charity. He immediately brought him not only all the necessities of life under the pretext of payment for the entire year, but also the parchment and implements needed for writing. In return he received the completed codex, which was useful for no practical purpose—for everyone in that region was entirely ignorant of the language—apart from the fact that he had acquired it through this subtle arrangement and at considerable expense. In this way the other man, without shame, could receive the necessities of food as the rightful reward of his labor and work, while the old man could fulfill the generosity of his piety as though compelled by a debt. He thus secured a more abundant reward for himself, the more generously he had supplied the foreign brother not only with the necessities of food but also with the instruments of work and the opportunity to work.

## CHAPTER XL. Concerning the boys who, while carrying figs to a sick man, died of hunger in the desert without tasting them.

Since, however, in a place where we had proposed to say something about the rigor of fasting and continence, affection and works of charity seem to have been mixed in, let us return to our subject and insert into this little work a memorable deed performed by boys in age but not in understanding.

For when certain figs from the region of Mareotis in Libya, like something never before seen in that place, had been brought to Abbot John, the steward

> [Note: Libya, or the region of Libya, bordered Egypt and lay near Alexandria, according to Pliny (book V of the *Natural History*, chapter 9). Part of it is Libya Mareotis, or Mareota. Saint Jerome distinguishes two Libyas: one is Cyrenaica, concerning which Acts 2 says, “the parts of Libya near Cyrene”; the other is near Ethiopia, concerning which Jeremiah 46 and Ezekiel 30 speak (Saint Jerome, *On Hebrew Places*).]

> [Note: The desert, or wilderness, of Scetis—also called Scythis or Sceti—and the monks living there are frequently mentioned by Palladius, Evagrius, Cassian, Sozomen, Nicephorus, and others. Sozomen, book I, chapter 14, and the *Tripartite History*, book I, chapter 11, indicate that Lake Mareos, or Marea, Scetis, and Nitria were neighboring or nearby regions.]

of that church in the desert of Scetis, who at that time administered the church’s property entrusted to him by the blessed priest Paphnutius,

> [Note: This Abbot Paphnutius was a priest in the desert of Scetis, where he lived to an advanced age. Because of his devotion to solitude he was surnamed Bubalus and Cephala. Cassian mentions him in several places, especially in the third Conference, which he attributes to him. Palladius also mentions him in the *Lausiac History*, chapters 62 and following, as does Nicephorus, book IX, chapter 4. There was another Paphnutius, much earlier than Cassian, an illustrious confessor and bishop of the Upper Thebaid. Under the persecution of Maximian he lost his right eye and had one knee severed, yet while still alive he attended the Council of Nicaea with the others under the reign of the great Emperor Constantine, who also held him in great honor. Rufinus speaks of him in book I of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 4.]

he immediately sent them by two young men to an old man who was ill in the inner parts of the desert. He lived eighteen miles from the church.

> [Note: Above he called them figs; now he calls them fruits. *Fruit* is a general name for every produce that comes from trees. Pliny likewise calls a fig a fruit in book XIII, chapter 7, where he tells remarkable stories about the Egyptian fig, and in book XII, chapter 5, concerning the Indian fig.]

When they had received the fruit and were making their way to the aforementioned old man’s cell—a thing that even the elderly very easily experience there—a very dense fog suddenly arose, and they lost the path of the direct route. Though they wandered throughout the whole day and night across the trackless vastness of the desert, they could not find the sick man’s cell. Exhausted both by the length of the journey and by hunger and thirst, they fell upon their knees and gave up their spirit to the Lord while engaged in prayer.

Afterward, when they had long been sought by the signs of their footprints—such marks are impressed in those sandy places as though in snow, until drifting fine sand once again covers them—they were found to have preserved the figs untouched, just as they had received them:

> [Note: True Israelites and true monks, and, as Cassian says, boys in age but not in understanding, who, for the virtue of obedience, chose rather to lose their souls—that is, their temporal life—than to betray the trust committed to them, namely, the fruits entrusted to their care. The text should therefore preferably be read *to lose* rather than *to betray*, so that it corresponds to Christ’s words: “Whoever loses his life for my sake will save it” (Matthew 10 and 16; Luke 9). Someone loses his soul for Christ who, out of love for him, chooses to meet death rather than violate either his commands or his counsels. Yet whoever loses it in this way truly rather finds and preserves it for eternal life, as the Truth testifies. Indeed, I am persuaded, according to Saint Thomas’s teaching (II–II, question 124, article 5), that these men may truly and properly be called martyrs. For not only faith, but every act of virtue joined with true faith and religion, can be the cause of martyrdom. It follows that whenever someone endures death for any virtue, he must altogether be regarded as a martyr. Saint Thomas proves this also by the example of Saint John the Baptist, whose martyrdom the Church celebrates, although, as he says, he suffered death not for denying the faith but for condemning adultery. In Theodoret (Ecclesiastical History, book V, chapter 26; in the Martyrology, January 1), a certain monk who placed himself between gladiators and was killed by them is counted among the martyrs. Saint Chrysostom likewise asserts in a homily that someone is truly a martyr who, though he could be cured of an illness by magical arts, nevertheless prefers to die rather than offend God in this way (Homily 3 on the First Epistle to the Thessalonians). Finally, those who willingly faced death while ministering to people afflicted by plague are also recorded as having been regarded in the place of martyrs. Concerning them Eusebius says in book VII of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 16: “Why, then, should we not ascribe the praise and palm of martyrdom to those distinguished young men, sons of obedience, who chose to sacrifice their lives rather than obedience and endured death with such steadfast courage in order to preserve it inviolate? And why should we not joyfully applaud that saying of David: ‘Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints’” (Baronius, in the Martyrology, January 1 and February 28; see Conference 2, chapter 6). For the rest, I leave the certain and definitive judgment on this matter to the judgment of Holy Mother Church.]

choosing, that is, rather to surrender their lives than betray the fidelity owed to what had been entrusted to them, and preferring to lose their temporal life rather than violate the old man’s command.

## CHAPTER XLI. The saying of Abbot Macarius concerning the observance of the monk, whether as one who will live for a very long time or as one who dies every day.

Yet one [Note: The historian Socrates commemorates two Macariuses, famous for holiness and contemporaries, in these words: “At that time there were among the monks two men beloved of God, both named Macarius, one from Upper Egypt, the other Alexandrian; both distinguished in many respects, for their abstinence, way of life, character, and the miracles performed by their hands. For Macarius the Egyptian drove away so many diseases and expelled so many demons that a whole book is filled with his deeds. He was reverend and severe toward offenders. Macarius the Alexandrian, however, although like the Egyptian in every respect, differed in this: he appeared more cheerful toward those who consulted him, and with a joyful countenance drew young men into the monastic life.” Thus far Socrates (*Hist.* IV.18; also *Tripartite History* VIII.1; Sozomen, III.13; Palladius, *Lausiac History* 19 and 20; Suidas, s.v. “Macarius,” final part of book III, chapter 2; Rufinus, *History* II.4, and *Tripartite History* VII.39). Since Cassian does not specify which Macarius gave the saying he reports, I would not rashly assert which one it was. Other sayings of Abbot Macarius are likewise reported in Conference 5, chapter 12, and Conference 24, chapter 13.] of blessed Macarius is set before us as a salutary command, so that the saying of so great a man may close the little book on fasts and continence. He says that a monk ought to devote himself to fasting as though he were going to remain in the body for a hundred years; but that he ought to restrain the movements of his soul, forget injuries, reject sorrows, and disregard pains and losses as though he were going to die every day. In the former matter, prudent and useful discretion is needed, making the monk always proceed with equal strictness and not permitting him, under the pretext of bodily weakness, to fall from difficult heights into the most dangerous precipices. In the latter, salutary greatness of soul is needed, capable not only of despising what appears prosperous in the present world, but also of not being broken by adversity and sorrow, and of disregarding them as small and worthless, keeping his mind’s gaze continually fixed upon the hour when he believes himself to be summoned every day and at every moment.

# BOOK SIX. ON THE SPIRIT OF FORNICATION

[Col. 0265]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0265B]

[Note: Since two of the capital vices are carnal, as was stated from St. Gregory (see Conference 5, chapter 4; Book V, chapter 1), lust is placed second among them, and rightly so. For, as St. Jerome testifies in Letter 146, gluttony is the fuel and mother of lust: when the belly is distended with food and irrigated with wine, sexual pleasure follows, and the order of the vices corresponds to the order of the bodily members. Hence Cassian elsewhere says (Conference 5.10) that fornication is joined to the vice of gluttony by a special alliance. For just as gluttony pursues, in a disordered way, the good of the individual in food and drink, so lust pursues, in a disordered way, the good of the species in sexual pleasures, says St. Thomas (I–II, q. 84, art. 4). For this reason Scripture often joins these two vices together. Hosea 4: “Fornication, wine, and drunkenness take away the heart.” Ecclesiasticus 19: “Wine and women make the wise apostatize.” Proverbs 20: “Wine is a luxurious thing.” Ephesians 5: “Do not be drunk with wine, in which is lust.” The Author calls it the “spirit of fornication,” following the language of Scripture, which uses “spirit” in various senses, sometimes for good and sometimes for evil, and applies the term repeatedly both to virtues and to vices. For Isaiah enumerates and names the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit as seven spirits (Isaiah 11), and in the Apocalypse they are called “seven spirits sent into all the earth” (Apocalypse 5). Daniel prays in a spirit of humility and with a contrite heart (Daniel 3). The Apostle likewise commends a spirit of gentleness and meekness (I Corinthians 4; Galatians 6). Conversely, and as though by a certain antithesis and antonymy, Scripture speaks of the spirit of pride (Zechariah 4), the spirit of fornication (Hosea 4 and 5), the spirit of stupor—that is, sleepiness or acedia (Isaiah 29), the spirit of dizziness—that is, error (Isaiah 19), and the spirit of jealousy—that is, anger or envy (Numbers 5). When “the spirit of fornication” is mentioned, “fornication” is understood generally as the vice of lust, which is opposed to chastity and is called by the Apostle, in Galatians 5, ἀσέλγεια (*aselgeia*), meaning unrestrained lust. That this vice belongs among the capital vices, whose causes, effects, and remedies Cassian discusses in these books, is also taught by St. Gregory, Book XXXI of the *Moralia*, chapter 31; reason likewise demonstrates it, since several other vices plainly flow from lust as from a fountain (St. Thomas, II–II, q. 153, art. 4). Accordingly, St. Gregory (in the passage cited above) enumerates eight daughters of lust: blindness of mind, rashness, inconsideration, inconstancy, self-love, hatred of God, attachment to the present age, and dread of the future; St. Thomas explains their reason and order (art. 5).

The same Gregory beautifully describes the nature of this vice and the manner of conquering it (Book VI on II Kings, chapter 15), explaining what was said concerning Amalek to the people of Israel: “Do not spare him, and do not desire anything belonging to him; but kill man and woman, child and infant, ox and donkey, sheep and camel.” Who, he asks, spares Amalek, except one who retains something of wantonness either in thought, speech, or the flesh? Many do not commit shameful deeds, but do not restrain their tongues from shameful speech; many avoid lust in action, but do not avoid it in thought; some do nothing shameful, but desire in their hearts what they reject in action. Thus he spares Amalek who retains the blandishments of wantonness in speech, intention, or thought. He says, “Do not spare him,” because nothing from so wicked a vice should be kindled in the mind or permitted to burn in action. “Do not desire anything belonging to him,” so that it may be completely uprooted from thought. Who are the men who must be killed, except the persuasive impulses toward shamefulness? They are men because they violently suggest evil and pour seeds of depravity into corrupted minds. The women are the mind’s desires, which are placed beneath those movements to produce wicked offspring. Who are the children and infants except those generated by the intercourse of the Amalekite men and women? For if the movement of an evil suggestion is received in the mind as an adulterer, desire is impregnated like a prostitute; if it is allowed to bring forth, the movements of lust are generated not only in the mind but also in the flesh. When they are born, they are children, because they do not yet inflict violence upon the flesh by provoking it. They are infants when they are nourished by a slight and negligent thought. The milk of the children, therefore, is the thought of impurity; for if the shameful movement is not fed by thought, the children are killed as though their milk had been denied them. The prostitute mother supplies this milk, because when the heat of desire precedes the mind, it is stirred as though from the foul abundance of the heart, so that worse offspring of these movements may be nourished in the flesh.
