What, then, is denoted by the ox but the deceitful counsel that suggests carnal pleasure on the precedent of the ancients who pleased almighty God amid works of the flesh? By the sheep is signified the life of the innocent, that is, the simulation of innocence. Some, when they consider the form of the human body, the characteristics of both sexes, and the lust implanted in the limbs, think that they may licitly use this as a natural good. It is therefore like a sheep, because something is suggested to the incontinent as though it were good, although it is clearly proved not truly to be good. The camel chews the cud but does not divide the hoof; so there is a certain thought of lust that begins as though from reason but is not brought to completion by discernment. Some who have professed continence, when overcome by carnal desire, trust that they can be saved in married life. What is the donkey except the open wickedness of fornication? For the devil drives some into the open abyss of fornication, while he deceives others through frauds. Thus all Amalek is ordered to be destroyed, because those who resolve to live chastely must retain nothing within themselves of the flesh’s blandishments.

Elsewhere Gregory says (Book XXI of the *Moralia*, chapter 9): “Blessed Job, defining the crime of lust, says: ‘It is a fire consuming even unto destruction.’ For the guilt of this crime not only stains unto defilement, but devours unto destruction. And because, however many other good works there may be, if the crime of lust is not washed away, they are overwhelmed by the enormity of this offense, he adds: ‘And it uproots all good growths.’ For the growths are the soul’s good works. Yet if the flesh dominates it in perverse order, the fire of lust burns up everything well produced. No works of justice or piety are clean before the eyes of almighty God when they are shown to be defiled by the contagion of corruption.” Such are these and other observations of St. Gregory, the keenest censor and investigator of vices and morals.]

According to the tradition of the Fathers, our struggle against the spirit of fornication is longer and more prolonged than any other, and is conquered completely by very few [Note: How difficult, prolonged, and dangerous is the struggle that we must continually wage against the spirit of fornication—that is, lust or carnal desire—St. Jerome expressed in these words (Letter 10 to Furia): “Avarice is trampled by many and laid down together with the moneybag. A curse-filled tongue is corrected by the silence imposed upon it. Bodily adornment and clothing are changed within the space of a single hour. All other sins are external, and what is outside is easily cast away. Lust alone, implanted by God for the procreation of children, goes beyond its proper bounds, overflows into vice, and by a certain law of nature breaks out into crime. It is a great virtue and requires vigilant diligence to overcome what you were born with; to live in the flesh but not according to the flesh; to fight with yourself every day; and, like Argus, as the fables relate, to watch the enemy confined within you with a hundred eyes.

This is what the Apostle expressed in other words: ‘Every sin that a man commits is outside the body; but he who commits fornication sins against his own body’ (I Corinthians 6). Elsewhere (Letter 21 to Eustochium): ‘Avarice does not shake us in this way, pride does not inflate us, ambition does not delight us; we easily do without other vices. This enemy is enclosed within us; wherever we go, we carry our enemy with us.’ Again in the same place, emphasizing the same difficulty by his own example and experience, and recalling how many troubles he had suffered from this domestic enemy even amid the greatest austerity of life, he says: ‘Oh, how often, when I was in the desert and in that vast solitude, scorched by the sun and providing monks with a dreadful dwelling, did I think I was present amid the pleasures of Rome! I sat alone because I was filled with bitterness; my misshapen limbs bristled beneath the sackcloth, and my squalid skin was covered with the foulness of an Ethiopian body. Every day there were tears, every day groans; and whenever approaching sleep overcame me as I resisted, I dashed against the bare ground my bones, which scarcely clung to it. I, then, who had condemned myself to such a prison for fear of Gehenna, the companion only of scorpions and wild beasts, often found myself amid choirs of girls. My face was pale from fasting, and my mind burned with desire in a cold body; before a man already half-dead in his flesh, only the fires of lust were boiling. Thus, deprived of every aid, I would lie at Jesus’ feet, water them with tears, wipe them with my hair, and overcome my rebellious flesh by weeks of fasting. I remember that, crying out, I frequently joined day to night, and did not cease beating my breast until, when the Lord rebuked it, tranquility returned,’ and so forth.”

Agreeing with Jerome, Augustine says: “Among all the struggles of Christians, only the battles of chastity are hard: there is daily combat and victory is rare. For chastity has received a formidable enemy, one resisted every day and always feared” (*On the Honorable Woman*, chapter 2). Palladius likewise writes in the *Lausiac History* that Abbot Pachon or Pachonius—not Pachomius of Tabennisi—desired to be torn apart by the teeth of beasts because, after forty years in solitude and amid fasting and other austerities, he had been unable to conquer this enemy, although he had never succumbed to it (Lausiac History 29). The same author also relates that Moses, once a robber and later a hermit, had been unable by any severity of fasting to subdue the wantonness of the flesh, although his former life had been little restrained. Indeed, even after he had joined six years of fasting to prolonged vigils, long prayers, and many tears, he achieved nothing until, after enduring many other labors, he finally obtained some rest—though Satan still raged—through the blessing of his spiritual father, the holy Isidore.]

It is a monstrous war, and although it begins to attack the human race from the earliest time of puberty, it is not extinguished until the other vices have first been overcome. [Note: Thus Abbot Serapion says in Conference 5, chapter 4: “Spiritual vices require a simple medicine of the heart; but carnal vices reach health only through a twofold cure. Therefore, for those who pursue purity, it is greatly beneficial first to remove from themselves the very materials of these carnal passions, by which either their occasion or their recollection may be generated in the still-sick soul. A double illness requires a double treatment. From the body, therefore, lest desire attempt to break forth into action, the images and enticing material must necessarily be removed; and from the soul, lest it conceive desire even in thought, more attentive meditation on the Scriptures, vigilant care, and withdrawal into solitude must be sought.”]

For this is a twofold assault, armed with a double vice, rising to battle; and therefore it must likewise be resisted by a double line. Just as it acquires strength from a disease compounded of flesh and soul, so it cannot be defeated unless both fight against it together. Mere bodily fasting is not enough to acquire or possess the purity of perfect chastity unless it has been preceded by contrition of spirit and persevering prayer against this most unclean spirit; then there must be continual meditation on the Scriptures, joined to spiritual knowledge, as well as labor and manual work that restrain and recall the unstable wanderings of the heart. Above all, true humility must have been firmly established, without which no vice can ever be completely conquered.

## CHAPTER II. On the Principal Remedy against the Spirit of Fornication

The correction of this vice proceeds principally from perfection of heart, from which the Lord’s words indicate that the poison of this disease also emerges. “From the heart,” he says, “come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies” (Matthew 15), and so forth. The heart, therefore, must first be cleansed, since it is known to be the source from which the fountain of life and death flows. Solomon says: [Note: From the Greek text: ἐκ γὰρ τούτων ἔξοδοι ζωῆς, “for from these are the outlets of life.” The Vulgate version has: “because from it life proceeds.” St. Bernard, in his sermon on the threefold guardianship of the hands, tongue, and heart, says: “There is a watch over the heart, to which the Wise Man rightly exhorts us to devote all guardianship, namely because from it life proceeds. I think that this guardianship consists especially in two things: namely, that the mind should vigilantly and attentively watch over the flocks both of its affections and of its thoughts.”]

“Guard your heart with all vigilance, for from it are the issues of life” (Proverbs 4). The flesh serves the will and command of the heart; therefore fasting must be practiced with the utmost care and restraint, lest flesh filled with an abundance of food, resisting the soul’s saving commands, become insolent and cast down its ruler, the spirit. But if we place the entire burden only in disciplining the body, while the soul does not likewise fast from the other vices and is not occupied with divine meditation and spiritual pursuits, we will by no means be able to ascend to the most sublime height of true integrity, because that which is principal within us is attacking the purity of our body. [Note: For this reason the Lord severely rebukes the Pharisees, saying: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who cleanse what is outside the cup and dish, but within you are full of plunder and uncleanness. Blind Pharisee, cleanse first what is inside the cup and dish, so that what is outside may also become clean.” Origen says here: “This saying instructs us to hasten to be just, not merely to appear just. He who strives to appear just cleanses what is outside and takes care of what is seen, but neglects the heart and conscience. He who strives to cleanse what is inside—that is, his thoughts—will consequently also make clean what is outside” (*Treatise 25 on Matthew*).]

Therefore, according to the Lord’s teaching, we must first cleanse what is inside the cup and dish, so that what is outside may also become clean (Matthew 23).

## CHAPTER III. How Much Solitude Contributes to Overcoming the Vice of Fornication

[Col. 0270A]

Moreover, [Note: So too Abbot Serapion says in Conference 5, chapter 4: “In the other vices, human company does no harm; indeed, it contributes greatly to those who sincerely desire to be free from them, because in the presence of many people they are more readily reproved, and while they are more frequently exposed when provoked, they reach healing more quickly.”] the other vices are usually cleansed through human contact and daily exercise, and are in a certain sense cured by the exposure that accompanies a fall; for example, the sickness of anger, sadness, and impatience is healed by meditation of heart, vigilant care, the company of the brothers, and continual provocation. When these vices are stirred up, they are exposed more often and reproved more frequently, and so reach healing more quickly.

This disease, however, requires bodily affliction, contrition of heart, [Note: That is, flight from secular people, and especially from women. Thus St. Jerome, in his book against Vigilantius, at the end, refutes the objection of Vigilantius, who criticized monks’ flight into solitude: “Why,” you will say, “do you go into the desert?” Precisely so that I may not hear you or see you, so that I may not be moved by your fury, so that I may not endure your battles, so that the eye of the prostitute may not capture me, and so that a most beautiful form may not lead me into illicit embraces. You will reply: “This is not fighting, but fleeing; stand in the battle line and resist the adversaries, armed, so that after you have conquered, you may be crowned.” I confess my weakness: I do not wish to fight with the hope of victory, lest I ever lose the victory. If I flee, I have avoided the sword; if I stand, I must either conquer or fall. Why is it necessary to abandon certainties and pursue uncertainties? Death must be avoided either with a shield or with one’s feet. You who fight can both be overcome and conquer. When I flee, I do not conquer in what I flee; rather, I flee so that I may not be conquered. There is no security in sleeping beside a nearby serpent. It may happen that it does not bite me, but it may also happen that at some point it does bite me.” St. Jerome expresses this elegantly and shrewdly; what follows will be cited elsewhere (see Conference 19, chapter 16; Book V, treatise 2).

The same point is made by what is read in the *Lives of the Fathers*. Abbot Antony said: “He who sits in solitude and is at rest is delivered from three battles—that of hearing, speech, and sight—and has only one battle, that of the heart.” Likewise, while Abbot Arsenius was still in the palace, he prayed to the Lord, saying: “Lord, direct me toward salvation.” A voice came to him, saying: “Arsenius, flee from human beings and you will be saved.” Afterward, when he had departed for the monastic life, he prayed again, saying the same words, and heard a voice saying to him: “Arsenius, flee, be silent, and remain at rest; for these are the roots of not sinning.” Thus far the text.]

and also solitude and withdrawal, so that, once the pernicious fever of its heats has subsided, it may reach complete health. Just as it is often useful for those suffering from a particular illness that harmful foods not even be presented to their eyes, lest the sight of them give rise to a deadly desire, so quiet and solitude contribute greatly to driving away this particular disease. The sick mind, undisturbed by diverse images, reaches a purer contemplation and can more easily uproot the destructive fuel of desire from its very foundations.

## CHAPTER IV. The Difference between Chastity and Continence, and Whether Both Are Always Possessed Together

Let no one suppose from this that we deny that continent persons can be found among those living in a community of brothers; we readily acknowledge that this can happen. [Note: Thus Abbot Chaeremon says in Conference 12, chapter 10: “It is not chastity but continence when some resistance of pleasure’s adversity still remains.” More observations on this matter are recorded there.]

For it is one thing to be continent—that is, [Note: Ἐγκρατῆ, ἐγκρατής: that is, “continent”; ἐγκράτεια, “continence,” discussed by Aristotle in Book VII of the *Ethics*. I do not know why Cuychius, in the Plantin edition, printed εὔκρατον, which means “well-tempered” or “well-constituted”—in body, not in mind; this differs greatly from *encratia*. The Basel copy is still more faulty, reading εὐκράτην. The Apostle uses the word ἐγκρατῆ in his letter to Titus, where among the other qualifications of a bishop he commands that he be continent (chapter 1); St. Jerome translates it *abstinentem*, “abstinent,” while others render it “temperate.”] ἐγκρατῆ; it is another thing to be chaste [Col. 0271A] and, so to speak, to pass into a condition of integrity or incorruption, [Note: Ἁγνός, “chaste, pure, undefiled,” for which Cuychius has ἄκιον, meaning “uncorrupted”; but, if the etymology of the noun is considered, this adjective is more suitable for wood than for a human being. The Basel manuscript has ἀκόν, more erroneously (see Conference 12, chapter 11; Aristotle, Book VII of the *Ethics*; St. Thomas, II–II, q. 155, art. 1).

As to the matter itself, Cassian here distinguishes between continence and chastity. He says that many are continent, but very few are chaste, incorrupt, or virginal. He uses continence, or ἐγκράτεια, as the Philosopher does in the *Ethics*, for firmness of mind, or a firm resolve by which one restrains oneself within the good of reason against the impulses of desire that drive one toward sexual pleasures. Thus he describes as continent those who extinguish and restrain the assault of the flesh—which they endure either rarely or daily—whether through fear of Gehenna or desire for the heavenly kingdom.

He explains chastity as integrity and incorruption, and says that to be chaste is to pass into a condition of integrity and incorruption. This virtue, he says, is granted only to those who remain virgins either in flesh or in mind. By these words he indicates that under the name and condition of chastity two classes of people are included: one consisting of those who are incorrupt in mind and body and contaminated by no lust, who are properly called virgins; the other consisting of those who, although they have experienced some stain of corruption or lust, nevertheless, as he says, have reached a similar state of purity through prolonged labor and diligence, and feel the goads of the flesh not so much through an assault of shameful desire as merely through the movement of nature. Thus he himself says (see below, Conference 18). This is why he uses the distinction “virgins either in flesh or in mind.” Such people are called chaste and virgins in mind because they have washed away and cleansed the stain of the mind through repentance; yet they are not properly virgins, because virginity presupposes and requires perfect integrity and incorruption of mind and body, as will be said below.]

which is called ἁγνόν; this virtue is granted especially to those who remain virgins either in mind or in flesh, [Note: No Catholic doubts that John the Baptist remained a virgin, since it is clear from the Gospel that he lived in the desert from infancy to the end of his life in the greatest austerity and holiness (Matthew 3; Luke 1). Therefore the Church sings in his praise:

“O supremely blessed, and lofty in merit,  
knowing nothing of a stain upon snow-white purity.”

St. Jerome, Book II against Jovinianus, and St. Augustine, in his final treatise on John, also testify that the evangelist John was a virgin. Augustine says that Christ loved John more than the other apostles for this reason: he had neither taken a wife nor ceased to live most chastely from early boyhood.]

as were both Johns in the New Testament; [Note: Concerning Elijah, Jeremiah, and others, St. Jerome writes to Eustochium (Letter 22): “Elijah was a virgin, Elisha was a virgin, and the sons of the prophets were virgins; and it is said to Jeremiah, ‘And you shall not take a wife’” (Jeremiah 16). In the preface to Jeremiah he also testifies that Jeremiah was a virgin. Concerning Daniel, John of Damascus asserts that, because of his outstanding virtue of chastity, Daniel himself and the three young men were preserved unharmed both from the fierceness of the lions and from the fire (Book IV of *The Orthodox Faith*, chapter 25).]

in the Old Testament as well, Elijah, Jeremiah, and Daniel are known to have been virgins. Those who, after experiencing corruption, have reached a similar state of purity through prolonged labor and diligence, preserving integrity of mind and body, and who feel the goads of the flesh not so much through an assault of shameful desire as merely through the movement of nature, will also rightly be counted among them.

We say that this state can be attained only with the greatest difficulty amid the crowds of human beings. Whether it is also impossible, however, let no one expect to learn from our judgment; let each examine the matter through the scrutiny of his own conscience.

We do not doubt, nevertheless, that many are continent who extinguish and restrain the assault of the flesh—which they endure either rarely or daily—whether through fear of Gehenna or desire for the heavenly kingdom. The elders declare that such people may not be completely overwhelmed by the incentives of vice, but that they cannot always remain entirely secure and unwounded. For anyone engaged in a struggle, although he may frequently defeat and overcome his adversary, must nevertheless sometimes be thrown into confusion.

## CHAPTER V. That the Assault of Fornication Cannot Be Conquered by Human Effort Alone

Therefore, if we desire, with the Apostle, to contend lawfully in the spiritual contest (I Timothy 4), let us hasten to overcome this most unclean spirit with the full concentration of our mind, [Note: The Author speaks piously and in a Catholic manner in this and the following chapter about the necessity of grace and divine assistance, and about the weakness of nature or free will in acquiring and preserving the virtue of continence and overcoming the assaults of the flesh (see Book XII of the *Institutes*, chapter 9, and several following chapters). Hence it appears that if he seems elsewhere to have held a different view, he was speaking not so much from his own opinion as from that of others. In these *Monastic Institutes*, as also in the books on the Incarnation of the Word, he set forth his own judgment. In the *Conferences*, however, he reports the opinions of those Fathers whom he introduces as speakers. This was the opinion of Dom Cuychius. Whether it is in fact so, I leave to be weighed and examined from the *Conferences* themselves and from St. Prosper’s book against the *Collator* (see also the notes on Book XII, chapter 14).]

not trusting in our own strength—for human effort cannot accomplish this—but hastening with the Lord’s assistance. For the soul must be attacked by this vice until it recognizes that it is waging a war beyond its own strength [Note: Abbot Chaeremon also emphasizes this at length in Conference 12, chapter 4. John Climacus likewise says (Step 15): “Let none of those who exercise themselves in chastity suppose that they have acquired it through their own labors or diligence; for it is impossible for anyone to overcome his nature. Wherever nature has been overcome, there one must recognize that he who is above nature has arrived.” For without any controversy, what is inferior is destroyed by what is more powerful.] and acknowledges that it cannot obtain victory through its own labor or effort unless it is supported by the Lord’s aid and protection.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Special Grace of God Necessary for Attaining Chastity
And indeed, although in all progress in the virtues and in the conquest of every vice grace and victory belong to the Lord, in this matter above all there is a peculiar benefit and special gift of God. This is most clearly declared, according to the judgment of the Fathers and by the experience of its purification, to those who have been deemed worthy to possess it.

[Note: Concerning this peculiar gift and special assistance of God, the following points are necessary for a correct and Catholic understanding. First, continence is both a gift of God and nevertheless placed within human choice and power. Heretics in our time affirm one of these propositions—namely, that it is a gift of God—but deny the other. Hence they conclude that no one ought to vow continence, because no one knows whether he possesses the gift of continence (Bellar[mi]ne, book II, *On Monasticism*, chapter 31).

Second, insofar as the present subject is concerned, the gifts of God are of two kinds. Some are given to a person without his cooperation, such as strength, health, beauty, the gifts of prophecy, tongues, and miracles, and all the dispositions infused by God. It is certain that such gifts are not within our power and do not depend upon human choice, so that anyone who wishes may possess them. Another class of gifts consists in divine assistance: with its help we can and do will the good, which without it we cannot do. Thus faith, hope, love of God, perseverance, and victory over temptations are said to be, and truly are, gifts of God, because unless God by his grace first anticipated us by stirring us up, and assisted us by directing, protecting, and cooperating with us, we could accomplish none of these things. Nevertheless, these very acts depend upon human choice and lie within our power, because God does not work them in us without our consent and cooperation; and although he assists, he does not compel or necessitate, and on his part he is always ready to help.

We therefore say that continence belongs to this class of gifts. Third, it should be noted that, just as with faith, repentance, perseverance, and other good acts, so also with continence two kinds of grace, or assistance, must be distinguished. One is sufficient assistance, which is given to everyone, at least according to place and time; this is called the gift of continence in the first act. The other is efficacious assistance, by which it comes about that we actually remain continent; this is the singular or special gift, which is not given to everyone, and is called the gift, or sufficient assistance, in the second act. For just as only those possess the gift of faith who actually believe, and only those possess the gift of perseverance who actually persevere, so only those possess the gift of continence who actually remain continent. It is certain that such persons are not many, much less are they all. Of this gift it is said: “Not all receive this word, but those to whom it is given” (Matthew 19).

Nevertheless, it remains true that everyone can remain continent, because sufficient assistance for continence and for obtaining grace is denied to no one. Therefore it is within our power to possess the efficacious gift of continence, if we are willing on our part to cooperate and to employ suitable means, or remedies, as Saint Jerome teaches in his commentary on Matthew 19. “It has been given,” he says, “to those who asked, who wished, who labored in order to receive it.”

The remedies that we must employ on our part are chiefly three: prayer, fasting, and flight from, or avoidance of, women. Since temptations of the flesh arise either from the suggestion of the devil, from an excess of food and drink, or from the sight and association of women, prayer must be employed against the first. Since no one can be continent unless God grants it (Wisdom 8), he must certainly be asked to grant it. Thus the Apostle both asked the Lord against the thorn of the flesh and received the answer: “My grace is sufficient for you” (2 Corinthians 12), so that he might always depend upon God and always devote himself to prayer.

Hence the Church teaches us, with particular care and devotion, to pray in the litanies: “From the spirit of fornication, deliver us, O Lord.” Saint Jerome gives his Sabina this admonition: “Let your prayers be frequent, so that all the arrows of thought with which youth is usually struck may be repelled by such a shield.”

Saint Augustine, in the *Confessions*, where he lays before God the various temptations by which he was tormented before his conversion, writes among other things (book VI, chapter 11): “I did not consider the medicine of your mercy for healing that same infirmity—namely, incontinence—because I had not experienced it, and I believed continence to be the work of my own powers, of which I was not conscious, since I was so foolish that I did not know, as it is written, that no one can be continent unless you grant it. And surely you would grant it if I knocked at your ears with inward groaning and cast my care upon you with steadfast faith.”

And elsewhere (book X of the *Confessions*, chapter 19): “My whole hope is only in your exceedingly great mercy. Give what you command, and command what you will.” You command us to be continent. “And when I knew,” someone says, “that no one can be continent unless God grants it, this itself was wisdom: to know whose gift it is” (Wisdom 8). Through continence, indeed, we are gathered together and brought back into unity, from which we had scattered into many things. For he loves you less who loves something with you that he does not love for your sake. O love, which always burns and is never extinguished! O Charity, my God, kindle me. You command continence. Give what you command, and command what you will. Thus Augustine.

Under prayer is also included the use of the Sacraments, especially that of the most holy Eucharist. For this is “the Grain of the chosen and the wine that makes virgins flourish” (Zechariah 9). Hence Saint Cyril, in his commentary on John (book IV, chapter 17), says: “When Christ dwells within us, he quiets the law of our members when it rages; he strengthens devotion and extinguishes the disturbances of the soul.”

And Saint Bernard, in his sermon on the Lord’s Supper, says: “That Sacrament works two things in us: it diminishes sensation in lesser matters and removes consent altogether in graver sins. If any of you no longer feels the movements of anger, envy, lust, or other things of this kind as often or as bitterly, let him give thanks to the body and blood of the Lord, because the power of the Sacrament is at work in him.”

Against the second cause there is the chastisement of the body through fasts, vigils, hair shirts, scourging, and other practices of this kind, always employed by holy and religious people, following the example of the Apostle who says: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude” (1 Corinthians 9). According to Blessed Gregory of Nazianzus (*On the Praise of Saint Cyprian*), Blessed Justina also employed this remedy after her prayers, when the magician Cyprian was tempting her to lust: “She fortified herself with the medicine of fasting and lying upon the ground, so that she might obscure the beauty of her appearance as though it were a treacherous thing, and thus withdraw the fuel from the flame and consume the torch of lust; partly also so that by her humility she might render God favorable and inclined to hear her. For God is won over by nothing so much as by the affliction of body and soul, and mercy is commonly repaid in turn with tears.”

Saint Jerome, in his tenth letter, says: “The burning arrows of the devil must be quenched by the rigor of fasts and vigils.” And later: “Why do we need to boast of chastity, which cannot prove itself without its companions and appendages, continence and moderation? The Apostle mortifies his body and subjects it to the authority of his soul, lest he himself fail to practice what he commands to others; and is a young woman, whose body is inflamed by food, secure in chastity?”

Finally, against the third cause, the sight of women and excessive familiarity with them must be avoided. Concerning this Saint Ambrose writes, in speaking of the patriarch Joseph’s flight: “When he was approached by his master’s wife, she could hold him by his garment, but she could not seize him in spirit; he did not even endure her words for long. He judged it a contagion, lest the provocations of lust pass through the adulterous woman’s hands.”

We have indicated other remedies elsewhere, where we discussed the immediate suppression of obscene thoughts or their disclosure to one’s spiritual father. When these and similar remedies have been employed on our part, that peculiar assistance of God and special gift of continence will not be lacking; by it we may preserve continence easily and joyfully, as is clear from what has been said.]

For in a certain manner it is to go out from the flesh while remaining in the body; and, while enclosed in fragile flesh, it is beyond nature not to feel the goads of the flesh. Therefore it is impossible for a human being to soar on his own “wings,” so to speak, to so lofty and heavenly a reward, unless the Lord’s grace has raised him from the mire of earth by the gift [or: led him out] of chastity.

[Note: There are many praises of this kind by the holy Fathers, in which virgins are compared with angels or even preferred to them. Cyprian (*On the Conduct of Virgins*) addresses virgins consecrated to God as follows: “You have already begun to be what we shall be; you already possess in this world the glory of the resurrection; you pass through the world without concern for the world; when you persevere as chaste virgins, you are equal to the angels of God.”

Chrysostom, in Homily 18 on Genesis, says: “In what respect did Elijah, Elisha, and John, lovers of true integrity, differ from the angels? In none except that they were constituted by mortal nature. For in every other respect, if one examines carefully, they will be found disposed no differently from those blessed spirits; and the very fact that they appear to be of an inferior condition ought to be counted to their great praise. For consider how great their courage and discipline of life must have been, since they were inhabitants of earth and possessed mortal nature, yet were able by strength and effort to reach that virtue.”

Basil, in his book *On Holy Virginity*, says: “Those who preserve continence are certainly angels, who, while living in corruptible flesh, protect and illuminate the life of mortals. They are angels not from some lowest order, but certainly most illustrious and noble. Those angels, free from the bonds of flesh, preserve their integrity in heaven, inviolable in place and nature, and established before God, the supreme King of all. But these, while for a long time resisting the enticements and pleasures of the flesh on earth and continually overcoming the devil’s temptations, preserve before the eyes of the Creator, by outstanding virtue, an incorruption equal to angelic purity.”

Finally, to omit others, Saint Bernard writes in Letter 41: “What is more beautiful than chastity, which makes one clean from seed conceived in impurity, a member of the household from an enemy, and, finally, an angel from a human being?” A chaste human being and an angel do indeed differ from one another, but in happiness, not in virtue. Although the chastity of the angel is happier, that of the human being is nevertheless recognized as stronger. Chastity alone, in this place and time of mortality, represents a certain state of immortal glory; alone among the solemnities of marriage it claims for itself the likeness of that blessed resurrection in which they neither marry nor are given in marriage, providing, in a certain sense, on earth an experience of that heavenly way of life.”

Saint Jerome has similar statements, as does whoever was the author of the sermon *On the Assumption of Blessed Mary*, and Augustine in book *On Holy Virginity*, chapter 13.]

For human beings who are carnal are equaled to spiritual angels in the imitation of their manner of life by no virtue so specifically as by the merit and grace of chastity. Through chastity, while still dwelling on earth, they possess, according to the Apostle (Philippians 3), citizenship in heaven—what the saints are promised they will possess in the future after laying aside carnal corruption, they already possess here in fragile flesh.

[Note: This refers to the Apostle’s statement to the Philippians (3:20): “For our citizenship [Greek: Ἡμῶν γὰρ τὸ πολίτευμα] is in heaven.” The Latin version has: “But our conversation is in heaven.” Jerome elsewhere reads (in his commentary on Zechariah, chapter 3): “Our municipal citizenship is in heaven.” And in his first letter to Heliodorus, alluding to this, he says: “Then you will receive citizenship with Paul.” Tertullian too, in book III *Against Marcion*, added the Greek word, saying: “Jerusalem, which the Apostle assigns as our mother above, and declares our πολίτευμα—that is, our citizenship—to be in heaven.”]

## CHAPTER VII. An example from the worldly contest, according to the Apostle’s discourse

Hear what the Apostle says:

[Note: The Author returns to the comparison drawn from the Apostle (1 Corinthians 9) between our spiritual struggle and contest and the secular and worldly contest, and between the contestants in each kind of contest, which he explained in the preceding book (chapter 12). The Apostle establishes this comparison in two things, namely running and fighting, to which our life is compared. Running has regard to the prize that we hope for, which the Apostle calls “the prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 3); fighting, or contest, has regard to the present adversaries by whom we are attacked and drawn back from the spiritual course—namely, the world, the flesh, and the devil, with whom we are perpetually engaged in conflict and struggle in this world. By this comparison the Author chiefly intends here to teach that the soldiers of Christ, or spiritual athletes, ought to be chaste and alienated from, and free of, every corruption of mind and body. He explains this more clearly in the following chapter.]

“Everyone who competes in the contest exercises restraint in all things.” Let us inquire what he means by “all things,” so that by comparison with the bodily contest we may acquire instruction for the spiritual contest.

Those who strive to compete lawfully in this visible contest do not have the freedom to consume whatever foods the appetite of desire may suggest, but only those which the discipline of the contests themselves prescribes. And they must abstain not only from forbidden foods, drunkenness, and every kind of excess, but also from all idleness, leisure, and sloth, so that through daily exercises and continual training their strength may increase.

They also become so alienated from every anxiety and sadness, from worldly business, and even from marital affection and activity, that apart from the exercise of their discipline they know nothing else and are not at all entangled in any worldly concern. They hope only from the one who presides over the contest to obtain the sustenance of their daily life, and they seek the glory of the crown and worthy prizes in praise of victory.

They guard themselves so purely from every pollution of intercourse that, when preparing themselves for the contests of the arena, they cover the regions of their loins with leaden plates, lest perhaps, deceived by some nocturnal illusion during sleep, they diminish the strength acquired over a long period. By applying the rigidity of the metal to their genital members, they are able to restrain obscene fluids. They understand beyond doubt that they will be defeated, and will no longer be able to complete the contest they have undertaken once their strength has been removed, if a deceptive image of harmful pleasure should corrupt the chastity they have taken precautions to secure.

[Note: On the various laws and customs of athletes, see, if desired, Alexander ab Alexandro, and much material in Budaeus, *Pandects*. On the use and efficacy of lead for restraining the assaults and discharges of Venus, see Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXXIV, chapter 18; also book III of the *Genialia*, chapter 9, and book V, chapter 8; and Coelius Rhodiginus, *Ancient Readings*, book XV, chapter 6.]

## CHAPTER VIII. On the comparison with the purification of those who are about to compete in the earthly contest

Therefore, if we have understood the discipline of the worldly contest, by whose example the blessed Apostle wished to instruct us, teaching how great its observance, diligence, and vigilance are, what must we do? With what purity must we guard the chastity of our body and soul—those who must daily eat the most sacred flesh of the Lamb, which even the precepts of the old law do not permit an unclean person to touch?

[Note: Leviticus 7, according to the Septuagint. He cites the same passage again in *Conferences* 22, chapter 5. The Vulgate text differs somewhat: “The polluted person who eats of the flesh of the sacrifice of peace offerings that has been offered to the Lord shall perish from among his people,” and so forth. There “soul” is understood as “person.”]

For in Leviticus it is prescribed as follows: “Every clean person shall eat the flesh.” And: “Any person who eats of the flesh of the sacrifice of salvation, which belongs to the Lord, while uncleanness is in him, shall perish before the Lord.”

How great, therefore, is the gift of integrity, without which even those who lived under the Old Testament could not take part in the typical sacrifices; and those who desire to obtain the corruptible crown of this world cannot be crowned!

## CHAPTER IX. How great a purity of heart we must always prepare before the eyes of God

Therefore, with all vigilance, the hidden places of our heart must first be cleansed. What those people desire to attain in bodily purity, we must possess even in the secret places of conscience. In that conscience the Lord, the judge and president of the contest, sits and continually watches for the struggle of our running and contest, so that we may not allow, even through careless thought, those things to take shape within which we dread admitting openly; and so that we may not be polluted by secret connivance in matters that shame us before human knowledge.

Whatever may escape the notice of human beings cannot escape the knowledge of the holy angels or of almighty God himself, from whom no secrets are hidden.

[Note: *Agonothetes*, or *agonotheta*, is the person who presides over a contest or who proposes prizes for the contestants. Saint Jerome also attributes this title to Christ (book I, chapter 7), when discussing virginity against Jovinianus: “The agonothetes proposes the prize, invites one to the race, holds in his hand the prize of virginity, shows the purest spring, and cries out: ‘Let the one who thirsts come and drink. Let the one who can receive it receive it’” (Matthew 19).

The Apostle referred to the same idea in the passage cited above (Hebrews 12), urging us to look to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, as the president and rewarder of our contest. Runners and contestants in the stadium customarily look toward the overseer and agonothetes, who watches them present and encourages them by proposing a prize. A notable example of this is found in Athanasius’s *Life of Saint Antony*.

When Saint Antony had long wrestled with demons and had been grievously tormented by them, at last a ray of light shone upon him, restoring him, and he understood the presence of the Lord. Drawing long sighs from the depths of his heart, he spoke to the vision that had appeared to him, saying: “Where were you, good Jesus? Where were you? Why were you not present from the beginning, so that you might heal my wounds?” And a voice came to him saying: “Antony, I was here; but I was waiting to see your contest. Now, because you did not cease fighting bravely, I shall always assist you.” What follows there may also be read. These are Athanasius’s words.]

## CHAPTER X. What is the sign of perfect and complete purity

[Note: Cassianus repeatedly inculcates this teaching in several places, as in chapter 20 of this book, where he concludes: “This, then, is the end of integrity and the perfect proof of it: that when we are at rest no tickling of pleasure should creep upon us,” and so forth.

And in chapter 22: “We must hasten to this point, and fight against the movements of the soul or the incitements of the flesh until the condition of the flesh fulfills the necessity of nature without arousing pleasure.”

Again, in *Conference* 12, chapter 7, where he enumerates the degrees of chastity: “The third is that one should not be moved to desire even slightly by a woman’s appearance; the fourth, that while awake one should not endure even a simple movement of the flesh; the fifth, that when the memory of human generation, or the logic of discussion, or the necessity of reading has introduced it, the mind should not be touched by the subtlest assent to a pleasurable action, but should contemplate it with a calm and pure gaze as though it were merely some work and service necessarily contributed to the human race,” and so forth.

“The sixth degree of chastity is that even while asleep one should not be deceived by seductive fantasies of women.”

Thus far Cassianus, both according to his own judgment and that of others. Yet these and similar statements seem at first to conflict with the Apostle’s declaration (2 Corinthians 12): “There was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet me. For this I besought the Lord three times, that it might depart from me,” and so forth.

Elsewhere he again laments in himself such movements of the flesh, which resist or anticipate reason, in these words (Romans 7): “I see another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin. Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” That is, from the body subject to death and to the impulses of sin.

And yet who could doubt that so great an Apostle attained perfection of purity and chastity? Second, the very grave authorities and testimonies of the holy Fathers, especially Augustine, also seem to conflict with this teaching, for they commonly assert that the movements of the flesh cannot be completely extinguished in this life.

Thus Augustine, in book V *Against Julian*: “Who could doubt,” he says, “that concupiscence can be diminished but cannot be consumed?” And Saint Gregory, in his commentary on First Kings (book V, chapter 11, and book VI of the *Moralia*, chapter 27): “It cannot indeed be taken away from the flesh that the law of the flesh should not move the members; but the violence of the movement can be removed from the flesh, so that movement remains, while all the obscenity of pleasure is taken away from that same movement, and it becomes a simple movement in which there is no shameful lust.”

And later: “When divine grace perfectly rewards those who practice abstinence, it removes from their bodily movements the goads of every obscenity, but leaves them the movements themselves, so that they may always be tempted but never overcome, since what greatly displeases them is taken away. It weakens what it leaves behind in such a way that it does not permit it to prevail over those who are victorious.” Thus Gregory.

To this may be added the definition of the Council of Trent (Session V), which says that concupiscence remains even in those who have been baptized, and that it has been left in us for the contest—that is, the struggle—yet in such a way that, when we do not consent but bravely resist through the grace of Christ Jesus, it cannot harm us; indeed, it contributes greatly to the crown.

The Author treats this opposition of flesh and spirit at length and expressly in the fourth *Conference*, which is entitled *On the Concupiscence of the Flesh and of the Spirit*, and in *Conference* 23, on the Apostle’s statement: “I do not do the good that I desire,” and so forth.

To reconcile these passages, Cassianus must be interpreted piously, insofar as this can be done. It is known that he was especially devoted to piety. First, he may mean that a perfect person, by the action of God’s grace, can reach such a degree of chastity that, once established in it, he scarcely, or scarcely at all, feels the goads of concupiscence, as though its incitements had been entirely extinguished. Abbot Chaeremon indicates this (*Conference* 12, chapter 12), when he says: “Great and wondrous are those things, known to no human beings except those who have experienced them, which the Lord in ineffable generosity bestows upon his faithful while they are still established in this vessel of corruption.” Of these the Prophet says (Psalm 138): “Wonderful are your works.”

And shortly afterward: “Who would not be astonished at the works of God, when he has perceived that the fire of lust, which he previously believed to be natural and, as it were, inextinguishable, has cooled to such a degree that he does not feel himself aroused even by a simple movement of the body?” Thus he.

No one who has even lightly touched upon the deeds of the saints doubts that this gift was granted to some. Cassianus praises such a gift in Abbot Serenus (*Conference* 7, chapter 2, and *Conference* 12, chapter 7), and we have noted other examples in the same place.

Furthermore, although Cassianus seems to wish to abolish every movement of the flesh even in those who are asleep, he himself nevertheless indicates clearly enough that in perfect men too some awareness of such movements remains, and he does not think that this detracts in any way from the perfection of chastity.

For in that very *Conference* in which he is so severe against the goads of the flesh (*Conference* 12, chapter 11), he says: “As for your assertion that this unavoidable disturbance of the flesh occurs because urine, when it has filled the bladder by continual dripping, arouses the quiet limbs: although this disturbance, which such a necessity sometimes causes even during sleep, does not at all prejudice true followers of purity in their attainment of it, it should nevertheless be understood that, if the limbs have been disturbed in this way, they are restored to their proper repose by the authority of chastity, so that they settle down not only without any itching, but even without the slightest recollection of lust.”

And again, at the end of the same *Conference* (chapter 16): “This is the consummation of chastity: that no delight of lust should touch a monk who is awake, and that no illusion of dreams should deceive one who is at rest. But when, through the carelessness of the sleeping mind, a movement of the flesh creeps upon one who is asleep, just as it was aroused without any tickling of pleasure, so also it should settle down without any bodily itching.”

Thus far Abbot Chaeremon, or Cassianus speaking in his person. He therefore acknowledges that even in perfect men, whether awake or asleep, there is a movement of the flesh and members, but stripped of and empty of delight, pleasure, and consent.]

The evident sign and complete proof of this purity will therefore be that either no deceptive image appears to us when we are at rest and relaxed in sleep, or, if one does intrude, it is unable to arouse any movements of concupiscence.

[Note: The paraphrast says: “Although such a movement—namely, of the genital organs in sleep—is not considered fully culpable,” and so forth. The subject here is movements or motions that occur to those who are at rest, that is, asleep and relaxed in slumber, as a result of some dream or illusion. This is clear both from the preceding words and from the following chapter.

So too Abbot Chaeremon, cited above (*Conference* 12, chapter 11): “Although this disturbance, which such a necessity sometimes causes even during sleep, does not at all prejudice true followers of purity in their attainment of it.”

Likewise, concerning nocturnal illusion (*Conference* 12, chapter 7): “Although we do not believe this deception to be subject to sin, it is nevertheless an indication that concupiscence still lies hidden in the depths.”

Moreover, involuntary movement or tingling of the flesh, whether it occurs in sleep or while awake, is purely natural and arises from the body’s condition and disposition, or from the quality of food or drink, or from the necessity of nature. It not only does not constitute sin but also provides an occasion for merit if the will resists it and gives no consent.

Hence Saint Augustine, book I *On the City of God*, chapter 25: “If that disobedience of concupiscence which still dwells in dying members moves according to its own law, contrary to the law of our will, how much more is it without guilt in the body of one who does not consent, if it is without guilt in the body of one who is asleep!” Thus Augustine.

Such movement or itching of the flesh can, however, be voluntary either in itself or in its cause, and to that extent it has the character of sin insofar as it is directly or indirectly voluntary against or outside the law of uprightness. Since it is generally a beginning or predisposition toward pollution, its indication must be taken from this. Accordingly, what will be said about pollution in the *Conferences* should be consulted.]

For although such a movement is by no means considered to entail the full liability of sin, it is nevertheless not yet a sign of a perfectly purified mind, nor a manifestation of a vice thoroughly refined away, since this illusion operates through deceptive images.

## CHAPTER XI. From what vice nocturnal illusion proceeds
[Note: [Col. 0280D] Dionysian paraphrase: The kind of distractions of thought in which we wander more carelessly by day is shown during the quiet of night. Moreover, nocturnal illusions and emissions, and their causes, are treated more fully in Collation 22, chapter 5 and following.]

For the quality of one’s thoughts, which is guarded too carelessly amid the distractions of the day, is tested during the quiet of night.

[Note: [Col. 0280D] Saint Augustine laments with groaning in the books of his *Confessions* (Book 10, chapter 30) these nocturnal illusions and mockeries of dreams, which remain to him from the acts and thoughts of his former life and recur from time to time; and he seeks to be delivered from them: “The images of such things,” he says, “still live in my memory, where my habit fixed them; and they meet me while awake, indeed without power, but in sleep not only so far as pleasure, but even so far as consent and an act very like the real thing. And the illusion of the image has such force in my soul and in my flesh that false visions persuade me while asleep of what true things cannot persuade me while awake. Am I not then myself, O Lord my God? Yet there is so great a difference between myself and myself in the moment in which I pass hence into sleep or return thence hither. Where then is that reason which, while awake, resists such suggestions and remains unmoved if the things themselves are presented? Is it shut up with the eyes? Is it put to sleep with the bodily senses? And whence is it that even in dreams we often resist, mindful of our purpose, and remaining most chastely in it, granting no assent to such allurements? Yet the difference is so great that, when it happens otherwise, on waking we return to the repose of conscience and, by that very difference, find that we have not done what we nevertheless grieve to have been done in us in some manner. Is not your hand, almighty God, able to heal all the languors of the soul and, by your more abundant grace, to extinguish even the wanton motions of my sleep? You will increase more and more in me your gifts, O Lord, so that my soul, freed from the birdlime of desire, may follow me to you; so that it may not rebel against itself; and so that, even in dreams, it may not only fail to perpetrate those shameful corruptions through animal images unto an emission of the flesh, but may not even consent to them. For it is no great thing for the Almighty, who are able to do above what we ask or understand, that nothing of this sort—even so little as can be restrained by a nod—should be pleasing, even in the chaste affection of one asleep, not only in this life but even at this age.”

Thus Saint Augustine, no less learnedly than devoutly, speaks of nocturnal illusions and dreams that not infrequently afflict pious minds. Note here the great difference, to be discussed elsewhere, between a waking and a sleeping person in such illusions or allurements of the flesh. But when he says at the beginning that such images of shameful things, recurring from time to time in dreams, move one not only to pleasure but even to consent and an act very like the real thing, this must be understood thus: a person sometimes appears to consent not only in imagination but even by a process of intellect and reasoning, although he does not truly consent, because he has no completely free use and power of reason, as Saint Thomas teaches, First Part, question 84, article 8.]

And therefore, when some such illusion has intervened, it should not be considered the fault of sleep, but rather negligence during the preceding period and the manifestation of a disease lying hidden within. The night did not first give birth to it; rather, the restoration brought by sleep drew it out from the innermost recesses of the soul to the surface, exposing the hidden fevers of passion that we contracted by feeding on harmful thoughts throughout the entire day. In the same way, bodily illnesses are not usually acquired at the time when they appear to emerge; rather, they are acquired through the negligence of an earlier period, when someone, imprudently nourished by foods contrary to health, accumulated within himself harmful and deadly humors.

## CHAPTER XII. That purity of the flesh cannot be attained without purity of heart

[Col. 0281B] Therefore God, the creator and maker of the human race, knowing above all the nature and correction of his handiwork, applied the remedy there from which he knew the causes of the disease principally arose:

[Note: [Col. 0281D] Saint Jerome writes aptly on this passage of Matthew: The difference between *pathos* (πάθος) and *propathos* (προπάθεια), that is, between passion and pre-passion, is that passion is counted as a vice, whereas pre-passion, although it bears the guilt of an initial impulse, is nevertheless not held as a crime. Thus, whoever sees a woman and has his soul titillated has been struck by pre-passion; but if he consents and turns the thought into an affection, he has passed from pre-passion to passion, and what is lacking in him is not the will to sin but the opportunity. Therefore, whoever looks at a woman in order to lust—that is, if he looks so that he may lust and intends to act—is rightly said to commit adultery with her in his heart.

Saint Augustine, moreover, admonishes his Regular clergy in his Rule as follows: “Even if your eyes are cast upon some women, let them be fixed upon none. For when you go out, you are not forbidden to see women; but it is criminal either to desire them or to wish to be desired by them. Women are desired, and desire is aroused in them, not only by touch and affection but also by sight. Do not say that you have chaste minds if you have immodest eyes, because an immodest eye is the messenger of an immodest heart,” and so forth.]

“Whoever,” he says, “looks at a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5).

[Note: [Col. 0282B] On restraining the wantonness or lasciviousness of the eyes, Saint Jerome—or the author of the passage—writes in chapter 4 of Jeremiah’s Lamentations: “When, through negligence, the eyes have opened an entrance to temptation, the troubled mind will scarcely find tranquility unless the gaze of divine mercy comes to its aid. Hence blessed Job says: ‘I have made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think about a virgin’ (Job 31). For in order to preserve the thoughts of his heart chastely, he made a covenant with his eyes, lest he first look carelessly upon what he would afterward love unwillingly. For the flesh draws downward with great force; and once the appearance of beauty has been fastened to the heart through the eyes, it is scarcely released except by the hand of a great struggle. Therefore, lest we turn over anything slippery in thought, we must take precautions, because one ought not to look upon what one is not permitted to desire. Thus, in order that the mind may be kept pure in its thoughts from the wantonness of its pleasure, the eyes must be lowered, as though they were robbers dragging us toward guilt. For Eve would not have touched the forbidden tree (Gen. 3) unless she had first looked upon it carelessly. For it is written: ‘The woman saw that the tree was good for food, beautiful to the eyes, and desirable to behold; and she took of its fruit and ate.’ From this, then, we should consider how carefully we ought to restrain our sight from unlawful things, we who live as mortals, if even the mother of the living came to death through her eyes. Hence also, speaking in the voice of Judea, which by desiring external things in her manner of life lost the good things within, the prophet says: ‘My eye has plundered my soul’ (Lam. 4). By desiring visible things, she lost invisible virtues. Thus, she who lost her inner sense through outward sight suffered the plundering of her heart through the bodily eye. Therefore, in order to guard purity of heart, we must also maintain discipline over the external senses. For however great the gravity with which the mind may be strong, the bodily senses nevertheless make childish commotion outwardly; and unless they are restrained by the weight of inward seriousness and, so to speak, by a helpful ardor, they drag the weakened mind toward every frivolous and trivial thing.” Thus he himself.]

He notes the wanton eyes, but he censures not so much the eyes themselves as that inward sense which misuses their service in seeing. For the heart is sick and wounded by the dart of lust when it sees in order to desire, twisting to the service of evil works the benefit of sight rightly granted to it by the Creator, and bringing forth, on the occasion of contemplation, the disease of desire hidden within itself.

Therefore a salutary command is given to that inward sense, through whose fault the worst disease proceeds on the occasion of sight. For it does not say, “Guard your eyes with all vigilance”—although they certainly ought to have been guarded above all if the effect of desire proceeded from them, since the eyes provide the soul with nothing more than the simple service of seeing—but it says:

[Note: [Col. 0283B] Saint Basil, in the *Longer Rules* (Question 5), says: “With all vigilance we must guard our heart, and we must not allow continual thought of God to slip from our minds, nor permit the memory of the things wonderfully made by him to be defiled by futile thoughts. Rather, we must constantly strive to carry within our minds, as an indelible mark, a devout thought of God impressed there by continual and perfectly pure remembrance. For this is the way by which love toward God is ordinarily acquired; and while it moves us to observe God’s commandments, it is in turn itself preserved and made stable forever by those same commandments. The Lord himself teaches that this is so: at one time he says, ‘If you love me, keep my commandments’ (John 14); at another: ‘If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love.’ And, to move us still more effectively: ‘Just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in his love.’” Thus Basil, and what follows. See, in the same sense, Saint Bernard’s forty-sixth sermon in the *Parva Quadragesimalia*.]

“Guard your heart with all vigilance” (Prov. 4)—the medicine being applied especially to that which can everywhere misuse the ministry of the eyes.

## CHAPTER XIII. That carnal thoughts, as soon as they arise, must immediately be driven away

This, then, will be the first safeguard of this purification: when the memory of the female sex has insinuated itself into our mind through the subtle cunning of the devil’s suggestion,

[Note: [Col. 0283C] “Previously introduced,” that is, introduced beforehand. See Collation 19, chapter 16. The meaning is made somewhat clearer by Dionysius in his paraphrase: “When the memory of the female sex occurs to our mind through the subtle cunning of diabolical suggestion, let us hasten to expel it swiftly from our hearts, even if it was first introduced through the recollection of our mother, sisters, relatives, or certainly holy women. Otherwise, if we linger over it too long, although we may have suffered no harm because of the sex of our relatives or holy persons, nevertheless, through that occasion, the mind may subtly roll and plunge toward those persons through whom the devil can insert harmful thoughts into the heart.” So he writes.

For the devil is accustomed to occupy and hold our mind with harmful images and fantasies of the female sex by repeatedly introducing and thrusting upon it the thought or recollection of one’s mother, sisters, or holy women. Once these have been admitted into the mind, since we are less cautious about them, we gradually descend toward harmful thoughts of other women or of shameful things, unless we repel that first suggestion of diabolical cunning as quickly as possible.]

first bringing forward the recollection of our mother, sisters, relatives, or certainly holy women, let us hasten to thrust it as quickly as possible from our inner recesses [senses]. For if we linger over it too long,

[Note: [Col. 0283D] That is, conceived in the mind or admitted into the mind.]

[Note: [Col. 0283D] Namely, the devil, as is gathered from what precedes and follows. He is called the enticer of evils because he always entices and provokes toward evil. Hence he is also called Satan and the tempter (Matt. 3 and 4; 1 Thess. 3).]

once the occasion of sex has been gained, the enticer of evils may subtly roll and plunge the mind,

[Col. 0284A] toward those persons through whom he can insert harmful thoughts. Therefore we must continually remember that commandment: “Guard your heart with all vigilance”; and, according to God’s principal commandment, carefully watch the harmful head of the serpent (Gen. 3)—that is, the beginnings of evil thoughts, by which the devil attempts to creep into our soul—lest, if his head penetrates our heart through negligence, his remaining body, namely, the assent of pleasure, should slip in. If this is admitted, it will undoubtedly kill the captivated mind with its poisonous bite.

We must also extinguish the sinners arising from our earth—that is, carnal sensations—at the dawn of their rising, and, while they are still little,

[Note: [Col. 0284B] He alludes to the words of Psalm 136: “Daughter of Babylon, miserable one: blessed is he who will seize and dash your little ones against the rock!” Commenting on these words, Saint Augustine writes: “Who are the little ones of Babylon? Newly arising evil desires. When desire is born, while it is still little, before it gains strength, dash it down. But you fear that, once dashed down, it may not die? Dash it against the rock; and the rock is Christ” (1 Cor. 10).

In the same way Saint Jerome, admonishing the virgin Eustochium, writes these words (Letter 22): “I do not want you to allow a thought to grow. While the enemy is small, kill him; let wickedness be crushed in the seed, lest the weeds grow.” And shortly afterward: “Because it is impossible for the innate heat of the marrow not to rush into a person’s thoughts, he is praised and proclaimed blessed who, as soon as he begins to think of filthy things, immediately kills them and dashes them against the rock.”

Saint Benedict also placed among the instruments or exercises of good works (Rule, chapter 4): “To dash the evil thoughts that arise in one’s heart against Christ and to reveal them to one’s spiritual elder.” In these words he included two singular remedies and antidotes against perverse and harmful thoughts. The first is to suppress their beginnings or first movements and to resist them manfully as they arise: this is to crush the serpent’s head and dash the children or little ones of Babylon against the rock. The second is to reveal them to a superior or spiritual elder.

Cassianus also speaks elsewhere of this (Book 4, chapter 9), reporting that among the Fathers and ancient monks it was the custom and discipline for the younger monks first to be instructed not to conceal entirely in harmful confusion any itching thoughts in their hearts, but immediately, as soon as they arose, to reveal them to their elder; nor were they to entrust anything concerning their judgment to their own discernment, but were to believe that something was evil or good according to what the elder’s examination had investigated and pronounced. In this way the crafty enemy could not prevail in anything against the young monk as one inexperienced and ignorant, nor deceive by any trick the one whom he saw fortified not by his own discernment but by that of his elder. Whatever suggestions or fiery darts he might cast into the young monk’s heart, he could not persuade him to conceal them from his elder.

See Collation 2, chapter 11 and following, where the usefulness of revealing and disclosing thoughts to elders is treated more fully and confirmed by a remarkable miracle. See Turrecremata, treatise 29 on chapter 21 of the Rule of Saint Benedict.

To these two remedies a third may also be added—or rather, the first and chief remedy—which Cassianus expresses in these words below, in chapter 23 of this book: “If we consider God to be not only the daily and nightly observer and knower of our secret actions but also of our inward thoughts, and if we believe that we shall render an account to him for everything that occupies our heart, just as we shall for our deeds and works.” More on this below, at chapter 21.]

let us dash the children of Babylon against the rock (Ps. 136). Unless they are killed while they are still most tender, when they have grown up through our connivance they will rise against us with greater strength for our destruction; or at least they will be conquered only with great groaning and labor.

For while our spirit, strong indeed, guards its house while armed, fortifying the recesses of its heart with the fear of God, “all its possessions will be at peace” (Luke 11)—that is, the rewards of labors and the virtues acquired over a long period. But if one stronger comes upon him and conquers him—that is, the devil, through the assent of thought—he will take away his armor in which he trusted—that is, the memory of Scripture or the fear of God—and divide his spoils, scattering the merits of his virtues through every kind of contrary vice.

## CHAPTER XIV. That we should not strive to compose praise of chastity, but explain its effect

[Col. 0285B]

To pass over all the passages inserted in the sacred Scriptures in praise of this virtue—for it is not my purpose to compose a panegyric of chastity, but to explain, through the traditions of the Fathers, its character, how it should be acquired and guarded, and what its end is—I shall set down only one statement of the blessed Apostle Paul, by which it may be evident how, when writing to the Thessalonians, he placed it above all virtues, commending it with such noble wording.

[Note: [Col. 0285C] Not simply and absolutely, but according to the considerations and prerogatives that he explains in the following chapter. For individual virtues possess their own excellences of different kinds, by which they both surpass and are surpassed by one another; hence what appears superior in one respect may be inferior in another.

The passage could indeed be explained differently from Saint Thomas. For, when asked whether virginity is the greatest of the virtues, he answers (2–2, question 152, article 5) that it is the most excellent virtue in the genus of chastity, because, he says, it surpasses widowhood and marriage. For this reason Saint Cyprian (Book on Virginity) calls it “the flower of the ecclesiastical shoot, the honor and ornament of spiritual grace, the more illustrious portion of Christ’s flock”; but he does not call it absolutely the most excellent, since it is clear that it cannot be equated with, much less preferred to, the theological virtues, religion, or martyrdom. The former explanation, however, is more consistent with this passage and the author’s intention, as is evident to anyone who examines it.]

## CHAPTER XV. That the virtue of chastity is specially called sanctity by the Apostle

“This,” he says, “is the will of God, your sanctification.” And lest he leave us in doubt or obscurity as to what he wished to call sanctification—whether justice, love, humility, or patience—for sanctification is believed to be acquired through all these virtues—he goes on to state and clearly designate what he specifically wished to call sanctification.

[Note: [Col. 0285D] *Sanctification*, in Greek ἁγιασμός (*hagiasmos*), is used for holiness or sanctity, just as *justification* is used for justice. Although holiness is generally understood as every virtue or a combination of virtues, in this passage the Apostle quite probably uses it for a particular and distinctive virtue opposed to lust, namely chastity. Cassianus demonstrates this by two arguments.

First, the Apostle immediately adds, as an explanation: “That you abstain from fornication, that each of you may know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honor,” and so forth. By these words he plainly indicates what that sanctification consists in, namely abstaining from fornication, which is the proper function of chastity.

Second, shortly afterward he adds this as the reason: “For God has not called us to uncleanness but to sanctification.” By this antithesis he indicates that holiness is opposed to uncleanness and is nothing other than purity of heart, which will be discussed below.]

“This,” he says, “is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from fornication, that each of you may know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of desire, like the Gentiles who do not know God” (1 Thess. 4).

[Note: [Col. 0286C] Some understand “vessel” to mean each man’s wife, or the body of his wife (Augustine, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 8). In their favor is a passage very similar to this, 1 Peter 3: “Granting honor to the woman as to a weaker vessel.” Others, including Cassianus, interpret it as each person’s own body.

This is how the word is understood in 1 Samuel 21: “And the vessels of the young men were holy.” In the same way they explain 2 Corinthians 4: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels,” that is, in this fragile body. This interpretation appears more plausible, both because the Apostle’s statement is general and concerns all the faithful, not merely married people, and because the words added here in paraphrase seem intended to explain and clarify what precedes. To possess one’s vessel—that is, one’s body—in sanctification and honor means nothing other than abstaining from fornication and every unlawful pleasure, and avoiding all uncleanness of the flesh, which everyone acknowledges to be the proper work of chastity.]

See with what praise he pursues it, calling it the honor and sanctification of the vessel, that is, of our body. Therefore, conversely, whoever is in the passion of desire remains in disgrace and uncleanness and is alienated from sanctification.

Third, shortly afterward he again declares it to be sanctity: “For God has not called us to uncleanness but to sanctification.” Thus,

[Col. 0286B] “whoever rejects these things rejects not man but God, who has also given his Holy Spirit in us” (ibid.). He joined inviolable authority to his command when he said: “Whoever rejects these things”—that is, the matters concerning sanctity that I have just stated—“rejects not man,” that is, me, who command these things, “but God,” who speaks through me and who has appointed our heart as a dwelling place for his Holy Spirit.

You see in what simple and pure words, and with how many commendations and praises, he has exalted it: first, by attributing sanctification specifically to this virtue; second, by asserting that through it the vessel of our body must be freed from uncleanness; third, by declaring that, once disgrace and dishonor have been cast aside, it will remain in honor and sanctification; and finally—what is the highest reward of perfect recompense and blessedness—by indicating that through it the Holy Spirit will become the inhabitant of our breast.

## CHAPTER XVI. Another testimony of the Apostle concerning the same sanctity

[Col. 0287A]

Although the discourse is tending toward the end of the little book, I shall nevertheless add another similar testimony of the same Apostle that has been omitted. For, writing to the Hebrews, he says:

[Note: [Col. 0287B] Cassianus proves by another testimony of the Apostle the prerogative of chastity discussed in the preceding chapter: namely, that holiness and sanctification are attributed to it specifically and that, under the title of sanctity, it is adorned in a distinctive way and above the other virtues.

Here the Apostle calls sanctity what he earlier called sanctification, using in both places the same Greek word, ἁγιασμόν (*hagiasmon*). That it is the same purity of heart of which the Lord says, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5), is sufficiently indicated by the concluding clause, “without which no one shall see God,” a statement to which the Apostle was referring.

Thus, in other passages of Scripture, especially in the apostolic writings, holiness or sanctity is understood as chastity or purity of mind and body: for example, 1 Corinthians 7, “that she may be holy in body and spirit”; Ephesians 4, “that she may be holy and immaculate”; and Romans 6, “present your members to serve justice for sanctification.”

This same concluding clause also contains another prerogative of chastity and purity, one especially proper and fitting to it: namely, the capacity or aptitude to see and contemplate God. For just as nothing so clouds and dulls the eyes of the mind as shameful conduct and the unclean pleasure of the flesh, so chastity, especially virginity, purifies them above all and makes them fit for contemplation. In this respect the vision of God holds the chief place—namely, that vision by which God is seen in his essence, which Scripture calls seeing him “as he is” and seeing him “face to face” (1 Cor. 13).]

“Pursue peace,” he says, “with all, and sanctity, without which no one shall see God” (Heb. 12). Here also he plainly declared that without sanctity—which he ordinarily calls integrity of mind or purity of body—God cannot be seen at all, since he likewise adds, explaining the same meaning: “lest there be any fornicator or profane person, as Esau.”

## CHAPTER XVII. That hope of a loftier reward should increase the guarding of chastity

[Col. 0287B]

Therefore, the more sublime and heavenly the reward of chastity is, the more grievously it is assaulted by the ambushes of its adversaries. For this reason we must apply ourselves more earnestly not only to bodily continence but also to contrition of heart, with the continual groaning of prayers,

[Note: [Col. 0287C] A beautiful allegory drawn from the history of Daniel (Dan. 3), concerning the three youths cast into the burning furnace. When they remained untouched and unharmed, as though sprinkled with heavenly dew, praising and blessing God, “the flame enveloped many servants of the king of Babylon who were tending it.”

Saint Jerome also touched upon this allegory in Letter 8, writing: “Against young men and girls our enemy exploits the ardor of youth, and he inflames the wheel of our birth; thus fulfilling what Hosea says: ‘All are adulterers; their hearts are like an oven’ (Hos. 7), hearts which are extinguished by God’s mercy and by the coldness of fasting. These are the fiery darts of the devil, which both wound and inflame at once, and which are prepared by the king of Babylon for the three youths. He sets fire to a furnace forty-nine cubits high, himself also possessing seven weeks for destruction, which the Lord commanded to be observed for salvation.

But just as there the fourth figure, appearing like a son of man, diminished the immense heat and taught the flames, amid the fire of the burning furnace, to lose their warmth—to threaten one thing to the eyes and offer another to the touch—so, in the virginal soul, the heat of youth is extinguished by heavenly dew and the chill of fasting, and the companionship of angels is obtained within the human body.” Saint Jerome expresses this elegantly and most appropriately for the passage.]
