so that the furnace of our flesh, which the king of Babylon does not cease to kindle with the incentives of carnal suggestions, may be extinguished as the dew of the Holy Spirit descends into our hearts.

## CHAPTER XVIII. That chastity rests upon humility, and knowledge upon chastity

For, as the elders say, chastity cannot be grasped

[Note: [Col. 0288B] “Humility,” says Saint Bernard (*On Consideration*, Book 5), “is the good and stable foundation of the virtues.” Saint Augustine likewise writes (*On the Words of the Lord*, Sermon 10): “Do you intend to build a great structure of height? Think first about the foundation of humility.”

Humility may be called the foundation of chastity in a particular and special way, and for two reasons. First, true humility causes us to turn to God to obtain and preserve the gift of continence and chastity, according to Wisdom 8: “I knew that I could not be continent unless God granted it; I approached the Lord and entreated him.”

Second, humility teaches that one must not glory in chastity or virginity except in the Lord, lest we resemble those foolish virgins (Matt. 25) who, as Saint Gregory says (*Homily 12 on the Gospels*), “while seeking outward praise for their virginity, neglected to have oil in their vessels,” and therefore deserved to be excluded from the wedding of the heavenly Bridegroom.

Thus the same Gregory rightly says (*Morals*, Book 6, chapter 23) that there is no chastity of the flesh which humility of mind does not commend—that is, which does not make worthy of merit and value before God. Saint Bernard likewise says: “Virginity is praiseworthy, but humility is more necessary. The former is counseled; the latter is commanded. Without humility, I dare say, even Mary’s virginity would not have pleased.” And below (*Sermon 1 on ‘He Was Sent’*): “Although she pleased because of her virginity, she conceived because of her humility.”]

unless the foundations of humility have first been laid in the heart. In the same way, they declare that one cannot reach the fountain of true knowledge until the root of this vice has taken hold in the innermost parts of our soul. They affirm that integrity can indeed be found without the grace of knowledge, but that it is impossible to possess spiritual knowledge without integrity of chastity.

[Note: [Col. 0288D] He calls it spiritual knowledge: knowledge of spiritual and saving realities joined with piety, as stated elsewhere (Book 5, chapter 33). The Wise Man denies that it enters into a malicious soul or dwells in a body enslaved to sins (Wis. 1). Human knowledge, however, separated from uprightness and purity of mind, can certainly exist among evil and wicked people; concerning this the Apostle says, “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Cor. 8).]

For the gifts are diverse, and the grace of the Holy Spirit is not granted equally to everyone,

[Col. 0288B]

but according to how each person has rendered himself worthy and suitable through his own zeal or diligence.

[Note: [Col. 0288D] This passage is somewhat difficult and inclined toward Pelagianism unless it is properly understood. Therefore, reader, consult the annotations of Cuichius and Ciaconius placed at the end of the work; I consider it unnecessary to add anything to them.]

Finally, although perfect integrity is believed to have existed in all the holy Apostles, the gift of knowledge nevertheless overflowed more abundantly in Paul, because he prepared himself for it by careful zeal and diligence.

## CHAPTER XIX. The statement of Saint Basil, bishop, concerning the quality of his virginity

[Col. 0289A]

A stern statement is attributed to Saint Basil, bishop of Caesarea:

[Note: [Col. 0289B] I have not yet been able to discover where the author obtained this statement of Saint Basil. Something similar is nevertheless found in Basil’s commentary *On True Virginity*, addressed to Laetoius, bishop of Melitene.

The occasion and meaning with which that most holy and chaste man may have uttered it can perhaps be inferred from his letter to his disciple Chilo. In that letter he admits that he preserved the integrity of his body immaculate from every lust, but that he did not maintain the purity of his mind equally untainted in youth. In this matter he seems to complain against himself when he says: “Women even presented themselves to be seen by these eyes of mine, and my integrity of chastity was tempted by their exceptional elegance and beauty. Indeed, I avoided the crime of fornication, but I stained the flower of virginal purity by a secret thought of the heart.”

These are his own words about himself. By them he strictly—but nevertheless truly—defined true virginity as consisting in the perfect integrity and incorruption of mind and body, and on this basis he wrote that distinguished commentary *On Virginity*.

Saint Gregory Nazianzen, moreover, in his funeral oration in praise of the same Basil, declares that Basil was a most perfect devotee of virginity in these words: “Who, then, honored virginity more than Basil, or established the purity of the flesh as though by law, not only by his own example but also in those whom he instructed?” and so forth.]

“I know no woman,” he says, “and I am not a virgin.”

By this he understood that incorruption of the flesh consists not so much in abstaining from women as in integrity of heart, which truly and perpetually preserves the body’s uncorrupted sanctity either through fear of God or through love of chastity.

## CHAPTER XX. From what perfect integrity of soul may be recognized
Therefore, this is the end and perfect proof of integrity: [Note: [Col. 0289C] The author seems to attribute great perfection to the condition in which pollution occurs during sleep without any stimulation of the flesh, but solely from the necessity or weakness of nature. On this matter, see more in Conference 12, which concerns chastity, and Conference 22, concerning nocturnal illusions. [Col. 0289D] To these passages one may add this excellent encomium of John Climacus on perfect chastity and purity, which agrees with the present passage: “Chastity is familiarity with incorporeal nature. Chastity is Christ’s delightful lodging and the earthly shield of the heart. Chastity is the extraordinary denial of nature and the striving of mortal, corruptible flesh toward incorporeal and spiritual substance. He is chaste who, through love, has excluded love and quenched fire with the Spirit’s fire. He is modest who, not even in dreams, feels any movement or alteration of his condition. He is modest who, even in dreams, has always possessed perfect insensibility toward the form and variety of bodies. The end of perfect and consummate chastity is this rule: that we regard animate things as we regard inanimate things, and are affected by rational bodies as by irrational ones.” And below: “This is the sure sign of true chastity: to remain unmoved by those phantasms which we see in sleep.” Thus far he (Step 15).] if, while we are sleeping, no stimulation of pleasure steals upon us, and, without our awareness, obscene discharges are emitted as a necessity of nature. Just as to cut these off and eliminate them altogether and forever is beyond nature, so to reduce them to the unavoidable and exceedingly rare necessity of nature [Col. 0290A] is the mark of the highest virtue—a necessity that ordinarily assails a monk only once in two months. This, however, is said according to our own experience, not according to the judgment of the elders, by whom even this interval of the time mentioned was considered exceedingly short. Otherwise, if we explain the matter in the way we learned from them, we might seem to be describing things as unbelievable or impossible to those who, through their negligence or less diligent application, have had less experience of this purity.

## CHAPTER XXI. How we can retain the state of perfect purity.

We shall therefore be able to maintain this state perpetually and never exceed the natural measure or the period described above [Note: [Col. 0290B] Namely, the period of two months mentioned in the preceding chapter, so that pollution occurs no more than once in two months, without illusion, shameful dreaming, or stimulation of the flesh; this he called the state and proof, or indication, of perfect purity.] if [Note: [Col. 0290B] Thus Saint Benedict says in chapter 7 of the Rule, concerning the first degree of humility: “Let a man always consider that God regards him from heaven, that his deeds are seen by the divine gaze everywhere, and that they are reported to God by the angels at every hour.” The prophet demonstrates this to us when he presents God as always present in our thoughts, saying: “God searches hearts and kidneys” (Psalm 7). And again: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain” (Psalm 138). He also says: “You have understood my thoughts from afar, and the thought of man will confess to you” (Psalm 75). Other Fathers agree with this. Saint Ignatius to the deacon Geron: “Remember God, and you will not sin” (Epistle 9). Clement of Alexandria, Book 3 of the *Paedagogue*: “It is possible for someone never to fall for this one reason: if he considers God always to be present to him” (chapter 5). Saint Jerome on Ezekiel: “The remembrance of God excludes every crime” (Book 7, chapter 22). Saint Ephrem, *On Virtue*: “Nothing is worse or more grievous than to fall into forgetfulness of God. For by continuous remembrance of God the shameful passions of the soul withdraw, like sorcerers when the governor approaches; and thus the soul becomes a pure dwelling of the Holy Spirit. But where the remembrance of God is absent, darkness with stench rules, and every wicked deed is practiced” (Volume 2, *On Virtue*, chapter 10). Saint Basil, *Long Rules*: “For example, whenever a blacksmith forges some adze or axe, if he constantly remembers from whom he received the agreement to make that instrument, keeps in mind the form and size prescribed by him, and directs his work according to the will of the one who commissioned it, he completes his work excellently and without dispute. So too the Christian, if he directs all his actions, whether great or small, toward the will of God, unquestionably and admirably completes that work and at the same time preserves continually in his mind the memory of the one who commanded him to do it. He will truly be able to say: ‘I set the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand, that I may not be shaken.’ He also fulfills Paul’s command: ‘Whether you eat or drink, or whatever else you do, do everything for the glory of God’ (1 Corinthians 10). ‘Everything that we do,’ says Saint Basil in his treatment of the vices of the flesh, ‘will be seen as though displayed in sections on a painted panel—not only what has burst forth into action, but also the thoughts inscribed on the tablet of the soul without producing any outward deed’ (*On True Virginity*).] we consider God to be the daily and nightly observer and knower not only of our secret actions but also of all our thoughts, and believe that we shall render an account to him for everything that occupies our heart, just as for our deeds and works.

## CHAPTER XXII. To what degree the integrity of our body can be brought, and what sign indicates a mind thoroughly purified.

We must therefore hasten toward this goal and fight against the movements of the mind and the incitements of the flesh until the condition of the flesh fulfills the necessity of nature without arousing pleasure, expelling its accumulated excess without any irritation or harm and without provoking a struggle against chastity. But as long as the mind, while still asleep, is deceived by the vision of images, let it know that it has not yet been thoroughly purified for the complete perfection of chastity.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Remedies by which the perfect purity of our heart and body can be preserved.

[Col. 0291B]

Therefore, so that these illusions may not steal upon us even while we sleep [Col. 0292A] [Note: [Col. 0291B] John Climacus confirms this teaching in Step 15, where he discusses the various causes of pollution and the remedies for it; and Abbot Theonas does so in Conference 22, where this matter will be treated more fully.], a consistently equal and moderate fast must always be maintained. [Note: [Col. 0291B] Dionysius the Paraphrast: “Whoever exceeds the measure of austerity must also exceed the measure of relaxation. Held back by this inequality—that is, intemperance—he would unquestionably be prevented from reaching the most level state of the tranquility described above, now weakened by excessive emptying and hunger, now swollen by an excess of food.” The same point is made elsewhere in different words, Book 5, chapter 9; Conference 2, chapters 16 and 22; and Conference 21, chapter 22.] For whoever exceeds the measure of strictness must necessarily also exceed the measure of relaxation. Held back by this imbalance, he will undoubtedly be recalled from that most level state of tranquility: now weakened by excessive emptiness, now swollen by overly abundant food. With the alteration of nourishment, the quality of our purity must also necessarily be altered. Furthermore, constant humility and patience of heart must always be practiced, together with vigilant caution throughout the day against anger and the other passions. For wherever the poison of rage takes up residence, the fire of lust must also necessarily penetrate.

Above all, vigilant care during the night is necessary. [Note: [Col. 0292B] Such concern was especially strong among the Egyptian monks. Cassian writes that, precisely in order to avoid nocturnal pollution, they were not permitted after the night office and the morning praises to return to sleep, but had to devote themselves to prayer or manual labor (Book 2, chapter 13, and Book 3, chapter 5): “Lest,” he says, “the jealous enemy, envious of our purity, which he always especially plots against and continually attacks, contaminate by some dream-illusion the purification we have acquired through the nocturnal psalms and prayers.”] For just as the purity and vigilance of the day prepare chastity during the night, so the vigils of the night provide the heart and the daytime discipline alike with the firmest foundation and strength.

# BOOK SEVEN. ON THE SPIRIT OF LOVE OF MONEY

[Col. 0291]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0291C]

[Note: [Col. 0291C] Cassian assigns avarice—calling it *philargyria*—third place among the capital vices, for the reason explained elsewhere (Conference 5, chapter 11). After the two preceding vices, gluttony and lust, have been overcome, all Christians must enter into combat against it, but especially religious and monks, who profess by their own particular vow of voluntary poverty, as by a military oath, that they directly confront and oppose this vice. He calls this a foreign war—not because it is not inward and spiritual (for Saint Gregory also numbers it among spiritual vices [Book 31 of the *Moralia*, chapter 31], namely those fulfilled by the pleasure of the mind rather than the flesh), but because of its object, which is an external good, namely wealth, pursued by avarice. It is also foreign in comparison with the other vices, which seem to possess in us principles that are in some way innate and inborn, as the author shows regarding anger and desire (see Conference 5, chapters 4 and 8, and chapters 2 and 3 of this book).] Our third struggle is [Note: [Col. 0291D] *Philargyria*, as the etymology of the name indicates and the author himself explains, is love or desire for money, or wealth—in other words, disordered love. Hence the avaricious person is called *avidus aeris*, “greedy for bronze,” according to Isidore (Book 10 of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1). By money, or bronze, we mean not only coins but everything whose value is measured by money, as Aristotle teaches in Book 4 of the *Ethics*, chapter 1. Cassian took the word *philargyria* from the Apostle in Colossians 3 and 1 Timothy 6, where it is used for avarice, φιλαργυρία (*philargyria*), and preferred to retain it from Greek because the Latin word for avarice did not seem fully to express its force. Among the Greeks it is also called πλεονεξία (*pleonexia*), “the pursuit of having more” (Ephesians 5). Aristotle calls it ἀνελευθερία (*aneleutheria*), because it is an illiberal thing, unworthy of a free person. Among religious people this vice is commonly called proprietorship, or rather the vice of proprietorship, since it is not true ownership but usurped or assumed ownership; those afflicted by it are called proprietory monks. No one doubts that this vice is mortal in its kind, since it directly contradicts the vow of poverty. Its gravity is evident also from the fact that the holy Fathers commonly call theft, robbery, sacrilege, the most wicked vice, and the plague of religion.] against *philargyria*, which we may call love of money: a foreign and unnatural war, taking its beginning in the monk nowhere else than in the idleness of a corrupt and sluggish mind, usually because he made a bad beginning in his renunciation and was lukewarm in his love toward God. For the impulses of the other vices seem to have principles implanted in human nature as though innate, and to be in some way embedded in the flesh, almost as old as birth itself; they anticipate the discernment of good and evil. Although they seize a person first, they are nevertheless conquered through prolonged labor.

## CHAPTER II. How destructive the disease of *philargyria* is

This disease, however, arriving later and coming from outside into the soul, can be guarded against and rejected all the more easily; but once neglected and admitted into the heart, it becomes more destructive than all the others and is more difficult to drive out. For it becomes the root of every evil, producing many sources of vices.

## CHAPTER III. What usefulness we derive from the natural vices

[Col. 0293B] [Note: [Col. 0293C] Thus most manuscripts and printed editions begin this third chapter under the foregoing title with these words. Ciaconius, however—I do not know whether on the basis of Vatican codices—begins only with the words: “Nor do I say this in order to make the word ‘nature’ …” *For example* is placed here in the sense of “that is,” or “namely.” He explains what he had said above: that other vices seem to possess principles in us as though innate and to be in some way embedded in the flesh, and so forth.] For example, do we not see simple movements of the flesh not only in children, in whom innocence still precedes discernment of good and evil, but even in infants and nursing babies? Although they possess in themselves not even the beginning of any lust, they show that movements of the flesh are present in them through a natural impulse. [Note: [Col. 0293C] Thus Saint Augustine says in Book 1 of the *Confessions*, chapter 7: “I saw and observed a jealous child: he could not yet speak, yet he looked pale and bitterly at his fellow nursling.” These natural movements, whether of anger or lust, are not properly vices, since they are free from all guilt when they occur without the judgment of reason and the consent of the will, as in infants and sleepers; still more so in those who resist and struggle against them, as the same Augustine teaches in Book 1 of *The City of God*, chapter 25. See Conference 5, chapter 4.] Do we not likewise observe fierce goads of anger already active in little children? Before they know the virtue of patience, we see them stirred by injuries and even perceive them recognizing insults directed at them in jest. Sometimes, although they lack the strength, the will to take revenge is nevertheless present, incited by anger.

Nor do I say this in order to turn the word “nature,” or the condition of nature, into a fault, but to assert that of these movements which arise from us, some were implanted in us for our benefit, while others are introduced from outside through negligence and the choice of an evil will. For the carnal movements mentioned above were beneficially implanted in our body by the Creator’s providence for the renewal of offspring and the propagation of posterity, not for the perpetration of the crimes of fornication and adultery, which are condemned even by the authority of the law.

[Note: [Col. 0293C] Nemesius aptly said in *On the Nature of the Human Being*, chapter 21: “Anger is the bodyguard of reason.” Saint Basil likewise says in his homily *On Anger* that anger was given to human beings by God so that, obeying commanding reason like an armed soldier obeying his general, it might serve as a kind of sinew of the soul, supplying courage and steadfastness for accomplishing things well and properly. “It restrains,” he says, “the soul softened by pleasure and behaving wantonly, as though with some piece of iron, and makes it sterner and stronger instead of soft and slack. For if indignation and anger against injustice are absent, one cannot pursue it with the hatred it deserves.” Lactantius likewise says in *On the Anger of God*: “Just as God equipped the human body with many and varied senses necessary for the use of life, so he assigned various emotions to the soul, by which the ordering of life might be maintained. As he gave lust for the sake of producing offspring, so he gave anger for the purpose of restraining wrongdoing. But those who do not know the boundaries of good and evil use lust for corruption and pleasures, and anger and passion for doing harm, becoming angry with those whom they hate, whether equals or even superiors” (*On the Anger of God*, chapter 18).] Do we not also understand that the goads of anger have been most beneficially bestowed upon us, so that, becoming angry at our own vices and errors, we may instead devote ourselves to virtues and spiritual pursuits, showing all love toward God and patience toward our brothers?

We also know how great is the usefulness of sadness, which, when transformed into the opposite disposition, is counted among the other vices. For it is entirely necessary in relation to the fear of God, but extremely harmful in relation to the world, as the Apostle teaches when he says: “Godly sadness produces repentance leading to steadfast salvation, but worldly sadness produces death” (2 Corinthians 7).

## CHAPTER IV. That we may say that certain natural vices are present in us without injuring the Creator

[Note: [Col. 0294C] Saint Basil, in the passage cited above, after much discussion of the good and usefulness of anger, concludes: “Thus benefit is drawn from anger by good men. But every one of the other faculties will likewise be called good or evil according to the manner in which the person who uses and possesses it employs it. If someone uses the appetitive part of the soul for bodily pleasure and the most impure actions, he will certainly be abominable and impious. But if someone turns it toward the love of God and our Lord Jesus Christ and the desire for eternal goods, he will be happy and blessed. Therefore, beloved brothers, I beg you, do not make those things which have been granted for your salvation by the supreme God and author of all things an occasion of sin for yourselves. Thus anger, when dispensed by reason at the proper time and in the proper manner, produces courage, patience, and steadfastness; but when handled contrary to right reason, it becomes fury and madness. Therefore the psalm admonishes us: ‘Be angry and do not sin.’ Isidore of Pelusium says similarly: ‘For this reason anger has been implanted in us—not so that we too may sin, but so that we may restrain sinners; not so that it may be a turbulent movement and disease, but so that it may be medicine for vicious affections. We, however, change the medicine into poison when we misuse it for things that are improper’ (Isidore, Epistle 239). See Lactantius, Book 6 of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 19.] Therefore, if we say that these movements were implanted in us by the Creator, it does not follow that he is blameworthy if we choose, by abusing them wickedly, to turn them toward harmful purposes, and if we prefer to grieve over unprofitable and worldly gains rather than over salutary repentance and the correction of vices—or if, certainly, instead of using anger beneficially toward ourselves, we become angry with our brothers contrary to the Lord’s prohibition. For if someone were to turn iron, supplied for necessary and useful work, toward the killing of innocent people, this would not defame the maker of the material, since what he provided as suitable and necessary for right living had been used by another to cause harm.

## CHAPTER V. On the vices contracted through our fault beyond the natural movement

[Col. 0295A]

Nevertheless, we say [Note: [Col. 0295B] Dionysius: “Nevertheless, we say that certain vices grow or arise in us without any preceding natural occasion or cause, solely through the choice of a corrupt and perverse will, such as avarice and envy, which are contracted from outside, since they possess in us no principles arising from natural instinct,” and so forth. Thus Abbot Serapion says in Conference 5, chapter 3: “There are two kinds of these vices: some are natural, such as gluttony; others are outside nature, such as *philargyria*. And in chapter 8: That *philargyria* is outside nature is clearly seen from this: it is not proved to have an original beginning in us, nor is it conceived from matter that reaches the participation of soul or flesh and the substance of life.”] that certain vices grow in us without any preceding natural occasion, through the choice of a corrupt and evil will alone, as is the case with envy and even with *philargyria*. Since they possess in us no principles arising from natural instinct, they are contracted from outside. Yet although they are so easy to guard against and so readily avoided, they make the mind they occupy and possess miserable, and scarcely allow it to reach the remedies of health: either because those wounded by them do not deserve to be cured by swift medicine, since they could have ignored, avoided, or overcome them with the greatest ease; or because those badly founded are unworthy to receive the structure of virtues and the summit of perfection.

## CHAPTER VI. How difficult it is to drive out the disease of *philargyria* once received

For this reason, let no one regard this disease as trivial or contemptible. Just as it can be avoided with great ease, so, if it takes possession of anyone, it scarcely permits him to reach the remedies of health. For it is a receptacle of vices and the root of every evil, becoming an inextricable fuel for wickedness, as the Apostle says: [Note: [Col. 0295C] The author retained the Greek word, for which the Latin translator used *cupiditas*, “desire,” and Saint Ambrose used *avaritia*, “avarice.” Here, however, the word is not πλεονεξία (*pleonexia*), as elsewhere—a word with a broader meaning than love of money—but φιλαργυρία (*philargyria*), which signifies nothing other than love of money. This should be noted, lest anyone think that the Apostle is speaking of desire for glory, power, or some other kind of object. By “evils,” moreover, the Apostle intended to include both evils of punishment and evils of guilt. As regards evils of guilt, avarice, or desire for wealth, is called the root of all such evils—that is, sins—for two reasons. First, wealth provides the means, support, and, as it were, nourishment and fuel for carrying out every vice and evil desire, like the root of a tree, which supplies nourishment to the whole tree, as Saint Thomas says (1–2, question 84, article 1). “We see,” he says, “that through wealth a person acquires the ability to commit any sin and to carry out the desire for any sin, because money can assist a person in obtaining any temporal goods, as it is said in Ecclesiastes 10: ‘Money obeys everything.’ Hence wealth is called ‘mammon of iniquity,’ because it provides the material for many iniquities; indeed, it is an incentive to every iniquity, as Saint Ambrose explains in his commentary on Luke 16. Second, every kind of sin commonly sprouts from this desire as from a root, since for the sake of money people dare to commit anything—perjury, robbery, murder, sacrilege, and what not? There is no sin to which the desire for wealth does not at some time impel a person:

> What do you not compel mortal hearts to do,
>
> Accursed hunger for gold!

Thus the poet sings (Virgil, Book 3 of the *Aeneid*). Hence Ecclesiasticus, in the passage cited above, says: “Nothing is more wicked than the miser.” And again: “Nothing is more unjust than to love money; for such a person even sells his own soul”—that is, for the sake of wealth he despises God’s commands, ready to do or suffer anything in order to obtain it. We have an especially clear example of this in Judas, Christ’s disciple, who, through desire for money, sold his Lord and handed him over to be killed (Saint Leo, sermon *On the Passion of the Lord*). Therefore avarice is rightly counted among the capital sins, which are like the fountains and roots of many others. Hence Saint Gregory enumerates the daughters of avarice in this way (Book 31 of the *Moralia*, chapter 31): “From avarice arise betrayal, fraud, deceit, perjuries, restlessness, acts of violence, and hardening of the heart against mercy.” As regards evils of punishment, avarice is also called the root of all evils because it plunges its devotees into every kind of calamity and misery, not only in the future age but also in the present. The Apostle suggests this reason when, among the many evils proceeding from the root of avarice, he lists temptation, the devil’s snare, many useless and harmful desires, many sorrows, and finally destruction and perdition (see Saint Thomas, 2–2, question 119, article 9). See also Saint Gregory, Book 15 of the *Moralia*, chapter 11. Nor should we omit what Prudentius sang about avarice in his *Psychomachia*, that is, the struggle of the soul against such vices (chapter 5):

> It seizes the whole race of humankind; it occupies
> all mortals with destruction. For no vice
> throughout the earth is more violent, one that wraps
> the age of the worldly people in such disasters
> and condemns them to Gehenna.”] “The love of money is the root of all evils” (1 Timothy 6), that is, the love of money.

## CHAPTER VII. By what vices *philargyria* is generated, and of how many evils it is the parent

When this vice has taken possession of the monk’s relaxed and lukewarm mind, it first troubles him over a small sum and describes for him certain just and apparently reasonable pretexts [Note: [Col. 0296D] He calls them “colors,” meaning pretexts or excuses which proprietory and avaricious monks commonly put forward to cloak their desire and avarice. See Saint Basil, *Monastic Constitutions*, chapter 35, and Climacus, Step 16.] for which he ought either to keep some money for himself or to acquire it. For he complains that what is supplied in the monastery is not sufficient [Col. 0296B] and can scarcely be endured even by a healthy and robust body. What is to be done if poor health of the flesh should arise and nothing private has been put away to support the illness? [Note: [Col. 0296D] That is, a portion, allowance, stipend, or whatever is supplied by the monastery to each monk for food and clothing.] The monastery’s provision is too meager, and its negligence toward the sick is extreme. If he has nothing of his own with which care can be given to the body, he will have to die miserably. Even the clothing supplied is insufficient unless he arranges to obtain something else for himself.

Finally, he cannot remain for long in the same place or monastery. Unless he has prepared for himself the expenses of travel and the cost of an overseas passage, he will not be able to move away whenever he wishes; constrained by the necessity of poverty, he will have to endure continually a laborious and miserable life without any progress, always poor and naked and, not without disgrace, supported by another’s property. Thus, after entangling his mind in thoughts of this kind, he considers how he might acquire at least one denarius. Then, without the abbot’s knowledge, he anxiously seeks some private work to undertake. When he secretly sells it and finally obtains the desired coin, he is tormented more intensely and urgently by the question of how to double it—where he should deposit it or to whom he should entrust it, uncertain as he is. Then he is weighed down by even greater anxiety about what he should buy with it and by what kind of transaction he might double it (see John Climacus, Step 7).

When this too has turned out according to his desire, a greedier hunger for gold grows, and the more money is added to the profit, the more violently that hunger is aroused. [Note: [Col. 0297C] The maxim, expressed by the poet in other words (Juvenal, Satire 14), is:

> The love of money grows as the money itself grows.

This agrees with Ecclesiasticus: “The miser will not be satisfied with money” (Ecclesiasticus 5).] For with the increase of money the madness of desire increases. Next, he promises himself a long life, bent old age, and various prolonged illnesses, which cannot be endured in old age unless a larger sum has been prepared in youth. Thus the unhappy soul is bound in serpentine coils, seeking to increase the badly accumulated material with still worse care, itself giving birth to a disease with which it will be inflamed more fiercely. Entirely possessed by thoughts of profit, [Col. 0297C] it considers nothing else with the gaze of its heart except how it may acquire money, by which it may escape as quickly as possible from the discipline of the monastery, showing loyalty to no one whenever some hope of money begins to shine.

[Note: [Col. 0297C] Here you have most of the daughters, or offspring, of avarice or *philargyria*, enumerated above by Saint Gregory.] For its sake he does not shrink from committing a crime of lying, perjury, or theft; he does not shrink from breaking faith [Col. 0298A] or from being inflamed by the destructive fury of anger. If he should fall away from some hope of gain, he does not fear exceeding the bounds of honesty or humility. In every respect, as the belly is a god to others, so gold and the hope of profit become a god to him.

Therefore the blessed Apostle, seeing the harmful poisons of this disease, declared not only that it is the root of all evils but also that it is service to idols, saying: “Avarice [Note: [Col. 0297C] Saint Thomas says that avarice is compared to idolatry by a certain likeness, because just as idolatry subjects itself to a creature, so does the miser—but not in the same way (2–2, question 118, article 5, reply to objection 4, and commentary on Ephesians 5, lecture 3). Idolatry subjects itself to a creature in order to offer it divine worship; the miser subjects himself to a creature by desiring it immoderately for use (Philippians 3; Saint Jerome, Epistle 22). The miser is therefore an idolater, not in faith and worship but in affection, because he is more devoted to gold than to God, just as the glutton is devoted to his belly. Hence it is said of gluttons: “Their god is their belly.” Among the pagans, Pluto and Bacchus were likewise counted among the gods, since the former is the god of the avaricious and the latter of the pleasure-seeking. Innocent also illustrates and explains the same judgment of the Apostle in his little book *On the Misery of the Human Condition* as follows: “According to the Apostle, avarice is service to idols, because just as the idolater serves an image, so the miser serves his treasure. The idolater diligently magnifies the worship of idolatry; the miser diligently piles up his heap of money. The idolater worships the image with complete diligence; the miser guards his treasure with complete care. The idolater places his hope in idolatry; [Col. 0298C] the miser places his hope in money. The idolater fears mutilating the image; the miser fears diminishing his treasure.” Thus Innocent. Saint Ambrose gives another explanation: “Just as idolatry strives to take glory away from the one God, so that he alone may not possess what belongs properly to him and alone bear the name of divinity, so avarice extends itself over God’s things, so that, if it were possible, one person alone might seize for himself the creature which God made common to all” (commentary on Colossians 3). Elsewhere he says again: “Avarice is compared with idolatry because it appropriates and stores up for itself the things that belong to God. What God granted commonly for everyone’s use, avarice denies when it retains its possessions for itself precisely so that others may not use them.” Saint Augustine gives yet another explanation: “The avaricious wish to enjoy money and to use God, because they do not spend money for God but worship God for the sake of money” (*The City of God*, Book 11, chapter 25). See more on this in Conference 12, chapter 2.] which in Greek is called φιλαργυρία (*philargyria*), is service to images” (Colossians 3).

You therefore see to what degree this madness grows step by step in degradation, so that by the Apostle’s voice it is even pronounced service to idols or images. It does so because, abandoning the form and image of God—which a person devotedly serving God ought to have preserved unstained in himself—he preferred to love and protect, in place of God, the images of human beings impressed upon gold [Col. 0298B].

## CHAPTER VIII. That *philargyria* impedes all the virtues

[Note: [Col. 0298D] Dionysius puts it more clearly: “Through such increases of aversion and vice.” At this point Saint Augustine’s statement, highly appropriate to the passage, comes aptly to mind: “I openly confess before your charity, in the presence of the Lord our God, who is witness over my soul: ever since I began to serve God, just as I have found none better than those who have advanced in monasteries, so I have found none worse than those who have fallen in monasteries. Thus I think it is written in the Apocalypse: ‘Let the righteous become more righteous, and let the one who is filthy become filthier still’” (Revelation 22). Thus Augustine (Epistle 137).] Increasing through such stages of decline into something worse, he soon retains no virtue of humility, charity, or obedience—not even, I do not say the virtue itself, but its shadow. He is indignant at everything and murmurs and sighs over every task. With no reverence remaining, he is driven like an exceptionally stubborn horse toward a precipice, unbridled. He is not content with his daily food or customary clothing, and declares that he will no longer endure these conditions. He proclaims that God is not present only there, nor is his salvation confined to that place alone [Col. 0298C]. Thus, unless he transports himself somewhere else more quickly, he laments bitterly that he will immediately perish.

## CHAPTER IX. That a monk who has money cannot remain in a coenobium
Therefore, having money as the provision for his instability [Note: *Viaticum* means food or money that travelers carry with them, or equipment for undertaking a journey; hence Cicero, *To Atticus*: “I should like you to see how much travel money and equipment will be sufficient.” The author therefore calls money set aside for wandering about, or for leaving the monastery whenever he pleases, the “provision of instability.” From this chapter and those that follow we learn that the vice of love of money (*philargyria*), or proprietorship, is the beginning of apostasy and defection from one’s state.]—money in whose protection he has fashioned for himself something like wings—he is now insolently prepared to migrate, and answers every command defiantly; behaving as though he were a foreigner and an outsider, he neglects and despises whatever he observes to require correction. Though he secretly possesses hidden money, he complains that he does not even have shoes or clothing, and is indignant that these are given to him too slowly. If, perhaps through the superior’s dispensation, some of these things should first be distributed to someone known to possess absolutely nothing, he burns with still greater goads of anger and thinks that he is being despised as an outsider. Unwilling to apply his hands to any task, he criticizes everything that the monastery’s necessity compels to be done (see Turrecremata, *Treatise* 93 on the Rule of St. Benedict).

Then he diligently seeks occasions on which he ought to be offended or angry, lest he appear to leave the discipline of the monastery merely because he has been lightly provoked. Yet he is not content to migrate alone: lest he be thought to have deserted it through his own fault, he does not cease corrupting by secret whisperings as many as he can. If the severity of the season, the journey, or the voyage should block his passage, throughout that entire period he sits with a suspended and anxious heart and does not cease sowing or stirring up sorrows, finding no other consolation or excuse for his fickleness in his departure than the disgrace or stain of the monastery.

## CHAPTER X. What labor the deserter of the monastery, who formerly murmured at the lightest tasks, undergoes because of his love of money

Thus, increasingly inflamed by the torches of his money, which, once possessed, never permit a monk either to remain in a monastery or to live under the institution of the Rule, he is driven onward. [Note: Dionysius adds the substantive understood here: “And when proprietorship, like a savage beast, has separated him from the company of the brothers and made him a wanderer through the abandonment of his companions,” etc. Here he uses *proprietorship* for *philargyria*, since this is the monks’ own form of love of money, as stated above. The author seems to have had in mind the words of the patriarch Jacob mourning his son: “A most savage beast has devoured my son Joseph” (Genesis 37). Some interpret this “most savage beast,” morally and not inappropriately, as proprietorship and avarice, which devour and destroy the sons of Jacob—that is, monks, spiritual Israelites and those who overcome the devil’s snares.]

And when, having separated him from the flock’s company like some savage beast, it has made his breast exposed to prey [Note: “Woe to the solitary,” says Ecclesiasticus, “for when he falls, he has no one to lift him up and protect him” (Ecclesiasticus 4), while our adversary “prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 3). You have two examples of this in St. Gregory (*Dialogues* II.25): one of a monk who, leaving the monastery, encountered on the road a dragon that wanted to devour him unless the brothers came to his aid; the other of another monk who, likewise intending to flee the monastery, saw a black dog that was about to devour him (see *Register* IX.38), but was freed by the brothers’ prayers and brought back to a sounder mind.] and rendered him easy prey by depriving him of fellowship, it compels him, who previously disdained to perform the monastery’s light tasks, to labor tirelessly day and night in the hope of profit. It does not allow him to observe the appointed times of prayer, the measure of fasting, or the rule of vigils; nor [Note: That is, honorable occupations and regular exercises, such as private prayers, readings, meditation, discussions, mutual services, and other exercises by which monks are occupied at intervals and in rotation.] does it permit him to fulfill the duties of honorable occupations, provided only that he can either satisfy the madness of avarice or meet his daily needs—believing that, by acquiring it, he is extinguishing the fire of desire, while in fact kindling it.

## CHAPTER XI. That, for the sake of guarding money, the companionship of women is sought

From this point some, having fallen down a precipitous cliff, are carried by an irrevocable ruin toward death. Not content to possess alone the money they had either never possessed or had reserved through an evil beginning, they seek the companionship of women who will guard what they have wrongly amassed or retained. They entangle themselves in such great and harmful occupations that, having descended to the depths of hell, while refusing to obey the Apostle’s command that those who have food and clothing should be content with them (1 Timothy 6)—with the frugality that the monastery provided—they fall instead, by wishing to become rich, into temptation and the devil’s snare, and into many foolish and harmful desires that plunge a person into destruction and perdition (ibid.). For the love of money—that is, *philargyria*—is the root of all evils. By desiring it, some have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows.

## CHAPTER XII. The example of a lukewarm monk bound by the snares of the love of money

I know a certain man who claims to be a monk and, worse still, flatters himself about his perfection. Having been received into a monastery, he was warned by his abbot not to return to those things that he had renounced and abandoned, but to free himself from *philargyria*, the root of all evils, and from earthly snares. The abbot saw that he was grievously oppressed at every moment by his former passions, and admonished him that, if he wished to be cleansed of them, he should cease desiring what he had not even possessed before, [Note: St. Jerome also mocks and sharply rebukes such monks in his letter to Heliodorus, in these words: “Let others add coin to coin and, cramming the wealth of matrons into their purses, pursue it through acts of service. Let monks be richer than they were as laymen; let them possess, under poor Christ, wealth that they had not possessed under the wealthy devil; and let the Church sigh for them as rich, although the world previously held them as beggars.” St. Augustine likewise admonishes his regular clerics in his Rule not to seek in the monastery what they could not have had outside it, nor to think themselves happy because they have found food and clothing such as they could not find outside; nor to lift up their neck because they are associated with people whom they had not dared approach outside. Rather, they should have their hearts lifted up and should not seek earthly and vain things, lest monasteries begin to be useful to the rich rather than to the poor—if the rich are humbled there and the poor puffed up there (*Rule*, chapter 4). St. Bernard says similar things in Homily 4 on *Missus est*.] and, fettered by their bonds, could plainly never reach the purification of his vices. He did not hesitate to answer him with a fierce expression: “If you have the means to support many people, why do you forbid me to have them as well?”

## CHAPTER XIII. What the elders contribute to the younger in the uncovering of vices

Let no one think these things superfluous or burdensome. [Note: Germanus the abbot says correspondingly in the Nineteenth Conference: “For no one doubts that the person who has first discovered, with the testimony of his conscience, the causes and origins of the illnesses of the sick can discuss the remedies for their diseases most correctly,” etc. (*Conference* 9.13). St. Gregory of Nyssa teaches the same in his letter to Laetoïus, where he requires knowledge of the disease before medicines are applied. St. Chrysostom also declares that the best physicians are those who investigate the causes of diseases (*Homily 5 on Penance*). For this reason Galen wrote and entitled a book *On Recognizing and Curing the Diseases of the Soul*.]

For unless the kinds of wounds have first been set forth and the origins and causes of the diseases investigated, neither can suitable medicinal treatment be applied to the sick nor the perfect preservation of health be conferred upon the strong. These matters, and many more like them, are customarily brought forward for the instruction of the younger by the elders, who have experienced innumerable cases and downfalls of various kinds in the Conference. Often, when we recognized many of these things in ourselves, as the elders explained and revealed them, we were treated without the shame of our embarrassment, as though we ourselves too were being afflicted by those same passions [Alternative reading: “they were being afflicted.”]. At the same time, silently, we learned both the remedies and the causes of the vices attacking us—remedies and causes that we had concealed or passed over, not out of fear of the body of the brotherhood [Note: Dionysius the paraphrast explains this in clearer syntax: “What we concealed and passed over by not describing it—not through fear of the community of the brothers,” etc. Cassian calls the brotherhood itself, or the assembly of monks, “the body of the brotherhood,” as in Book I, chapter 3, and frequently elsewhere, as noted above.]—but so that perhaps a book falling into the hands of those who seem less instructed in this purpose might not disclose to the inexperienced what ought to be known only by those who labor and hasten to attain the summit of perfection.

## CHAPTER XIV. The threefold disease of the love of money

[Note: Dionysius has *avarice* in place of *health*, paraphrasing the term. Hence one might suspect that *illness*—that is, spiritual disease, which he interprets as avarice—should be read here. Yet there is no reason for such a suspicion, since *health* is an ambiguous and intermediate term by which both soundness and weakness are signified, as Gellius notes (*Attic Nights* XII.9). Thus Cassian frequently uses it for illness or disease of the soul. To come to the matter itself: here three forms of the disease of *philargyria*, or avarice, are described, by which three kinds or orders of monastic proprietors, or of those afflicted by the vice of proprietorship, are designated. The first order consists of those who desire in the monastery the wealth and other advantages that they did not possess even in the world; that is, those who were poor before becoming monks but wish to become rich and wealthy in the monastery. St. Jerome speaks of such men in his letter to Heliodorus: “Monks are richer than laymen” (Jerome, Letter 1). Likewise, speaking in the person of such people in his letter to Nepotianus, he says: “Born in a poor home and a peasant’s hut, where I could scarcely satisfy my growling stomach with millet and coarse bread, now I disdain fine flour and honey” (Jerome, Letter 2). Similar are the passages quoted above from St. Augustine (chapter 12 of this book). Cassian compares such monks to Gehazi, servant of the prophet Elisha, who, for the benefit of Naaman’s cure, dared on his own authority and out of desire to ask for silver and garments wholly unsuited to his status and condition. The second order consists of those who presume to seek again in monasteries, appropriate, and claim for themselves the wealth that they rejected or left behind at the beginning of their conversion and renunciation. He says that they resemble Judas the betrayer, who, after leaving everything with the other apostles and following the Lord, was later driven by the goads of avarice to the point of selling and betraying the Lord to the Jews (Matthew 18). He assigns the third place to those who do not wish to strip themselves of all goods and possessions but want to reserve some portion for themselves, following the example of Ananias and Sapphira. Although they appeared willing to embrace the common life, after selling the field they owned they secretly retained part of the price for themselves. Consequently, immediately exposed and rebuked by the Apostle Peter and struck invisibly by God, they died (Acts 5). Thus the first ask for what they did not have; the second reclaim what they had; the third retain a portion of what they had. See *Conference* 5.11, where these three kinds of *philargyria* are likewise listed. St. Bernard also discusses them in his treatise *On the Way of Living Well*, sermon 48.]

This disease of the soul is therefore threefold, and all the Fathers condemn it with equal abhorrence. The first is the one whose corruption we described above: deceiving the wretched, it persuades them to gather what they had not possessed even when they lived in the world. The second compels them to take up again and desire what they had cast aside at the beginning of their renunciation. The third, contracted through an evil and corrupt beginning and starting from imperfection, does not allow those whom it has once infected with this lukewarmness of mind—frightened by fear of poverty and distrust—to strip themselves of all the world’s possessions. By retaining the money or property that they ought, as those who renounce the world, to have cast aside, it prevents them from ever reaching evangelical perfection.

We also find examples in the Holy Scriptures of these three downfalls, condemned with no light punishment. For [Note: The story of Gehazi, servant of the prophet Elisha, is clear in 2 Kings 5. When Naaman the Syrian had been cured of leprosy and departed from Elisha, Gehazi, seeing that his master had accepted nothing from him, secretly followed him and, as though sent by Elisha, asked that a talent of silver and two changes of clothing be given to him. When he had received them, he hid them. As he stood before Elisha, Elisha said to him: “Where have you come from, Gehazi?” He replied: “Your servant went nowhere.” But Elisha said: “Was not my heart present?” etc. “Now you have received gold and clothing; but the leprosy of Naaman shall cling to you and to your offspring forever.” And he went out from him leprous, like snow (2 Kings 5). St. Hilarion joined this example to that of Simon Magus. As St. Jerome relates, after Hilarion had freed a prominent man possessed by a legion of demons, the man, once cured, came to the monastery after not much time with his wife and children, bringing many gifts as though to repay the favor. The holy man said: “Have you not read what happened to Gehazi and Simon? One accepted a price; the other offered one so that he might sell the grace of the Holy Spirit and purchase it” (Acts 8). When the man, whose name was Orion, said through tears, “Accept them and give them to the poor,” Hilarion replied: “You can distribute your own things better, since you travel through the cities and know the poor. I have left my own possessions; why should I desire another’s? No one distributes more wisely than the one who keeps nothing for himself.” To Orion, sad and lying on the ground, Hilarion said: “Do not grieve, my son. What I am doing, I am doing for myself and for you. For if I accept these things, I will offend God, and the legion will return to you.”]

Gehazi, wishing to acquire what he had not previously possessed, not only did not deserve to possess the prophetic grace that he should have received from his master by a kind of hereditary succession; rather, on the contrary, he was covered with eternal leprosy by the curse of the holy Elisha (2 Kings 5). Judas, however, wishing to take up again the money that he had cast aside when he followed Christ, not only fell into the betrayal of the Lord and lost the rank of apostle, but also did not deserve to end his very life by an ordinary death; [Note: This is how all the manuscripts read, and the Plantin edition followed them. Ciaconius, however—perhaps from the Vatican manuscript, as he usually does—and others read “he ended it by a violent death,” with the same meaning but a great difference in a single word. Yet the former reading prevails in antiquity, in the number of copies, and in probability. Although this new and unusual expression may seem strange, it appears to have been more customary in Cassian’s time. In the second *Conference*, chapter 5, he writes that the old man Heron, who had thrown himself into a well after being deceived by a shameful illusion of the devil, was counted among the *biothanati*. The word is written *βιοθάνατος* (*biothanatos*), or, as in Tertullian (*On the Soul* 57), *βιαιοθάνατος* (*biaiothanatos*), from *βιαίῳ θανάτῳ* (*biaiō thanatō*), “violent death.” This Greek word nevertheless passed into Latin, including among pagan and earlier writers, who use *biothanatus* in Latin and call those who die not a natural but a violent death *biothanati*. The historian Lampridius uses the word in his *Life of Elagabalus*: “The Syrian priests had foretold that he would be *biothanatus*.” Tertullian, *On the Soul*: “The *ahori* and the *biaeothanati* are invoked.” The *ahori* are those carried off by a premature or untimely death. Concerning the seven sons of St. Symphorosa, completed by martyrdom, Bede writes: “The next day Hadrian ordered their bodies to be thrown into a deep pit. The priests of the temples gave that place the name ‘To the Seven *Biothanati*’” (Bede, *Martyrology*, June 27). Pagans used to call Christians *biothanati* as an insult, both because they were liable to punishment by violent death and, as the Apostle says, were “appointed to death” (1 Corinthians 4), and because the Gentiles believed that the souls of the *biothanati*, that is, those who died violently, were not admitted to the dwelling places of the blessed, as Servius writes on *Aeneid* IV. Moreover, *biothanatos* refers not only to one killed by another but also to one who kills himself, or takes his own life, who is called in Greek *αὐτοθάνατος* (*autothanatos*). Thus Judas the betrayer is said to have ended his life by a *biothanatos* death, because he laid violent hands upon himself and, driven to despair, hanged himself. Isidore’s comic explanation—that *biothanatus* means “twice dead”—may be mentioned in passing (*Etymologies* X, letter B).]

and he ended it by a *biothanatos* death (Matthew 26). Ananias and Sapphira, meanwhile, having reserved part of what they possessed, were punished with death by the apostolic word (Acts 5). [Note: On this passage and on the death of Ananias and Sapphira, see below, chapter 25.]

## CHAPTER XV. How one who renounces badly differs from one who does not renounce

Concerning those who say that they have renounced this world but, once again overcome by distrust [Note: Dionysius: “Overcome by distrust.” A charming example of this is related in the *Lives of the Fathers*: “A certain brother renounced the world and gave to the poor what he had, but retained a little for himself. He came to Abbot Antony. When the old man learned this, he said to him: ‘If you wish to become a monk, go to that village, buy some meat, place it upon your naked body, and come here.’ When the brother had done this, dogs and birds tore his body. When he reached the old man, the holy Antony asked whether he had done what he had been told. When he showed his lacerated body, St. Antony said: ‘Those who renounce the world but wish to possess money are torn apart by demons in precisely this way.’”] are afraid to be stripped of earthly goods, it is mystically commanded in Deuteronomy: [Note: The Vulgate text reads: “Who is the fearful man and fainthearted? Let him go and return to his house,” etc. A similar passage occurs in Judges 7: “Whoever is fearful and timid, let him return.”]

“If there is any man who is fearful and fainthearted, let him not go out to war; let him go and return to his house, lest he make the hearts of his brothers fearful, as his own heart has been terrified” (Deuteronomy 20).

What testimony, I ask, could be clearer than this? Does Scripture not plainly prefer that those undertaking this profession should neither claim for themselves its beginning nor its name, rather than, through a corrupted exhortation and example, turn others away from evangelical perfection and weaken them through faithless fear?

They are therefore ordered to leave the battle and return to their house, because no one can fight the Lord’s battles with a divided heart. “A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways” (James 1). And, reflecting on the Gospel parable of the man who goes out with ten thousand to fight a king coming against him with twenty thousand, they should, while he is still far away, ask for peace (Luke 14)—that is, they should not even undertake the beginning of renunciation, rather than, after carrying it out lukewarmly, entangle themselves in greater danger. “It is better not to vow than to vow and not fulfill” (Ecclesiastes 5).

It is beautifully described here that one comes with ten thousand and the other with twenty thousand. For the number of vices attacking us is greater than that of the virtues fighting on our behalf. “No one can serve God and Mammon” (Matthew 6). [Note: In Matthew 6 it says: “You cannot serve God and Mammon.” *Mammon* is a Syriac word that signifies riches among the Syrians, just as *πλοῦτος* (*ploutos*, “wealth”) does among the Greeks. To serve Mammon does not mean merely to possess riches, for the patriarchs possessed riches but did not serve them. Rather, one serves riches who sets his heart upon them, gathers them by right and wrong, appropriates them contrary to God’s law or to his own vow, or places his happiness in them—that is, who has Mammon in place of God. Thus the Apostle calls avarice the service of idols, as will be said below.]

Nor is anyone who puts his hand to the plow and looks back fit for the kingdom of God (Luke 9). [Note: The Gospel text reads: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.” This is a metaphor drawn from farmers or plowmen, who, holding the plow-handle in their hand, always keep their eyes fixed upon the furrow so that it may be straight. A good plowman cannot be one who looks behind him. Just as one is unfit for plowing if, having put his hand to the plow, he looks back—for the person who wishes to plow properly must always look ahead—so whoever undertakes a state of better and religious life but looks back, that is, turns his mind toward the care of worldly affairs, is not fit to attain the kingdom of God. He puts his hand to the plow who embraces the institution of monastic life; he looks back who turns his mind toward his former worldly concerns and secular business, desiring to return to them or involve himself in them. Hence the Apostle, using another but similar metaphor, says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Timothy 4). “Those who run in the stadium abstain from everything” (1 Corinthians 9). Elsewhere, speaking of himself, he says: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the goal, the prize of the heavenly calling in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 3). Related to this is what the angel said to Lot in Genesis: “Save your life; do not look behind you, lest you also perish” (Genesis 19). There is also the terrible example of his wife, who, when she looked behind her, was changed into a pillar of salt. On this St. Augustine writes in Book XVI of *The City of God*: “For what else does the prohibition against those who were being delivered looking back signify, except that one must not return in mind to the former life from which, by grace, we have been regenerated and stripped, if we wish to escape the final judgment?” The poet Sedulius likewise sang elegantly (*Book I*, lines 121 ff.):

> As Lot fled the chaos of Sodom, his wife, while looking back,  
> > Remained in astonishment, changed into a statue of salt,  
> > Transformed into her own punishment; for no one,  
> > Looking back while avoiding the guilty dangers of the despised world,  
> > Will be saved; nor should the plowman,  
> > Performing worthy work, turn his face toward what lies behind him.

The Lord likewise reminded us of this example in Luke 17, saying: “In that hour, let the one who is on the housetop, with his belongings in the house, not go down to take them; and let the one who is in the field likewise not return backward. Remember Lot’s wife.” Finally, in Ezekiel, the holy living creatures did not turn back when they moved forward, but each one walked straight ahead (Ezekiel 1). St. Gregory says there: “The holy living creatures walk straight before their faces because they no longer look with any desire upon what they have left behind, and, with their eyes fixed upon the eternal things they desire, they place the foot of good works beneath the gaze of their contemplation,” etc. See St. Basil, *Monastic Constitutions*, chapter 21, and Prosper, *On the Promises*, part I, chapter 16.]

## CHAPTER XVI. Under what pretext those who refuse to strip themselves of their possessions defend themselves
They therefore attempt, by invoking a certain authority of Holy Scripture, to introduce once again into themselves an opportunity for their former avarice. Interpreting it with an even more defective understanding, they strive to corrupt the sentence of the Apostle—or rather of the Lord—and to distort it according to their own desire. They do not accommodate their life or their understanding of Scripture to its meaning; instead, they force Scripture to serve the desire of their own lust. They want Scripture to agree with their opinions, and say that it is written:

> “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20).

[Note: The adverb *magis* (“more”) is redundant in Latin; but since the Greek reads μακάριον μᾶλλον, “more blessed,” it seems that the translator read μακαριώτερον, “more blessed.” Moreover, although none of the Evangelists mention that this was said by the Lord and our Savior, Saint Paul asserts it in Acts 20: “You ought,” he says, “to remember the word of the Lord Jesus, for he said: ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’” Since this expression is found explicitly in none of the Evangelists, it must be counted among those things of which the Lord says in John 16: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.” John himself says at the end of his Gospel: “There are also many other things that Jesus did; if they were written down one by one, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written.” From these words it follows that the Lord did and said many things that were not written by the Evangelists.

Thus Pope Innocent III, in a certain Decretal, confirms the apostolic traditions from this very passage in these words: “Certainly we find that many things, both of the Lord’s words and of his deeds, were omitted by the Evangelists, which the Apostles are read either to have supplied orally or to have expressed in action. For Paul says in the Acts of the Apostles: ‘You ought to remember the word of the Lord Jesus, who said: “It is more blessed to give than to receive.”’ None of the four Evangelists recorded this.” Thus the pope.

But, you will ask, where did Paul receive this word of the Lord? The Gloss commonly called the Ordinary replies that Paul received it either from the other Apostles, or through a revelation of the Holy Spirit, or by reasoning it out from other statements of Scripture that signify the same thing, such as: “Give to everyone who asks of you”; and: “Lend, expecting nothing in return” (Luke 6). So Sixtus of Siena, *Bibliotheca*, book II.

Yet the Apostle sufficiently indicates that this is a saying of Christ uttered by Christ himself, not something revealed to Paul alone, nor something deduced from other sayings in which no comparison is made between the giver and the receiver. Rather, it was first received from Christ and afterward repeated and spread abroad by Christian speech.

Although this saying may seem paradoxical to avaricious and grasping people, who have hands more ready to receive than to give, it is nevertheless entirely certain, even according to human philosophy and ordinary understanding. For, speaking absolutely and with all other circumstances equal, it is more blessed to give than to receive, and happier is the one who gives than the one who receives. Giving denotes a certain power and abundance; receiving, however, denotes want and deficiency. As Saint Thomas says, “Giving and receiving stand to one another as acting and being acted upon” (*Summa theologica* II-II, question 117, article 4, reply to objection 3). No one doubts that acting is nobler than being acted upon.

Hence even avaricious people consider themselves happier because they possess enough to give than because they are able to receive. Indeed, they seek only to need nothing that they must receive from another.

A comparison must nevertheless be made between persons and things of the same kind if this saying is to remain true. As regards persons—that is, human beings—if human beings are compared with God, it is better to be loved by God than to love God, and better to receive a gift from him than to transmit it to others. For, as Saint Dionysius the Areopagite says, a creature is more perfected by receiving from God than by giving (*On the Divine Names*, book IV).

As regards things, temporal things must be compared with temporal things, and spiritual things with spiritual things. For if spiritual things are compared with temporal things, it is more blessed to receive spiritual things than to give temporal things. But it is more blessed to give spiritual things to human beings than to receive them, and to distribute temporal things—of which Paul was speaking—than to receive those same things.

Some people, however, whom Cassianus rebukes here, abused this saying and foolishly inferred from it, against religious poverty, that it was better to retain their possessions than to distribute or abandon them. Their reasoning was as follows: “It is more blessed to give than to receive; therefore it is better to retain what is yours, so that you have something to give, than to abandon it and thus be forced to receive or beg from elsewhere.”

Cassianus answers this argument only by setting against it various testimonies and authorities from Scripture. Yet this is not to solve the argument, but to evade or pass it by. Saint Jerome, writing against Vigilantius, who thought and reasoned in this way, demolishes and refutes the argument as follows:

> “As for your assertion that those do better who use their possessions and gradually distribute the proceeds of their estates to the poor than those who sell their possessions and give everything away at once, the answer will be made not by me but by the Lord: ‘If you would be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me.’ He speaks to the one who wishes to be perfect, who, together with the Apostles, abandons his father, his boat, and his net. The man whom you praise is at the second and third level, which we also accept, provided that we know the first is to be preferred to the second and third.”

This is Saint Jerome, *Against Vigilantius*, chapter 5.

A shorter answer, more appropriate to the form of the argument, is to deny the inference made by Vigilantius and the others. For, with all other circumstances equal, as has been said, it is more blessed to give all one’s possessions at once for Christ, as religious do, and afterward to receive a little for food and clothing, than to give little and receive nothing. “It is good,” Augustine says, “to distribute to the poor with proper administration; but it is better, with the intention of following Christ, to give everything at once and, freed from anxiety, to live in Christ.”

Therefore truly blessed is the person who, by the profession of monastic life, gives everything for Christ at once and in a single act: one who gives more than even the richest and most generous person in this world can give, since he strips himself of every ownership, right, and power over all the things that he possesses or could possess. “He gives more who gives the tree together with its fruits than one who gives only the fruits,” says Saint Anselm (*Book on Similitudes*, chapter 8).]

[Col. 0307A]

By their utterly perverse interpretation of it, they think that the Lord’s saying is deprived of its force—the saying that reads:

> “If you would be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.”

[Note: Saint Bernard, in his declamation on this passage, says: “These are the words that persuaded the whole world to despise the world and to embrace voluntary poverty; these are the words that fill monasteries with monks and deserts with anchorites.” Athanasius writes that when Saint Antony heard this Gospel being read in church, he immediately sold the possessions he had and distributed them to the poor, as though the passage had been read specifically for him. Saint Bonaventure reports the same regarding Saint Francis.

It should also be noted that these words of the Lord contain two evangelical counsels: poverty and obedience. The words “Go, sell all that you have, and give to the poor” clearly exhort and counsel poverty, and require it to be perfect and absolute. For when one says “all,” nothing at all is reserved. When the Lord commands that it be sold, he signifies a renunciation that is perpetual and irrevocable, as occurs through a vow.

The final words, “And come, follow me,” indicate obedience. For Christ himself explained what it means to follow him when he said in Matthew 26: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.” It is as though he were saying: The one who comes after me and follows me is the one who denies himself—that is, renounces his own will and affections—and subjects himself entirely to the judgment and will of another for God’s sake.

Perfect following of Christ consists in self-denial, that is, in perfect obedience; and this necessarily includes a vow by which a person denies himself so completely that he cannot turn back. For it is not perfect self-denial to obey another for a time and afterward cease to obey. Therefore the Lord adds in the same passage: “And let him take up his cross.” As Cassianus aptly observes in book IV, chapter 35: “The true and perfect monk must be like one crucified. One who has been crucified not only does not walk where he wishes or do what he wishes; he cannot even walk or work unless moved by another.”]

They suppose, by means of this interpretation, that they ought not to cast away their riches. They declare themselves happier if, supported by their former possessions, they distribute to others from their surplus. While they are ashamed to accept, for Christ’s sake, the glorious nakedness which the Apostle accepted, they are unwilling to be content either with the work of their hands or with the frugality of the monastery.

What remains for them is either to learn how to deceive themselves and, while clinging to their former riches, to recognize that they have in no way renounced this world; or, if they desire to test the monastic profession in reality and in practice, to scatter and cast away everything, reserving nothing of the things they have renounced, and, together with the Apostle, to glory in hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Renunciation of the Apostles and of the Primitive Church

[Col. 0309A]

As though the Apostle likewise could not have been supported by his former possessions—he who testifies that he had not been of low status even in the order of this world, when he declares himself, from birth, to have possessed the dignity of a Roman citizen (Acts 22); and as though those who, while living in Jerusalem, owned fields or houses, sold everything, kept nothing whatever for themselves from it, brought the proceeds, and laid them at the feet of the Apostles (Acts 4), could not have supported their bodily needs from their own resources, if the Apostles had judged this to be more perfect or had themselves found it more beneficial.

[Note: The Apostle Paul disclosed that he was a Roman citizen when necessity compelled him to do so—not to escape death, but to preach the Gospel more widely and, after completing his ministry, to ennoble the Roman Church by a glorious martyrdom.

When he had been bound at Jerusalem by the tribune and was about to be scourged, he said to the centurion standing nearby: “Is it lawful for you to scourge a Roman citizen, and one who has not been condemned?” When the centurion heard this, he went to the tribune and reported it, saying: “What are you about to do? For this man is a Roman citizen.” The tribune approached and said to him: “Tell me, are you a Roman?” He replied, “Yes.” The tribune answered: “I acquired this citizenship for a large sum.” Paul said: “But I was born to it” (Acts 22).

Elsewhere also, in Acts 16, when Paul and Barnabas had been sent to prison and were then asked to leave, Paul said: “They have beaten us publicly without condemnation, though we are Roman citizens, and have thrown us into prison; and now they are sending us away secretly?” Considering this and other actions which Paul undertook in his defense before Felix and Festus, Saint Augustine says: “The Apostle Paul was not looking after his transitory life, but after the Church of God, when, against those who had conspired to kill him, he caused their plan to be reported to the tribune. It therefore happened that an armed soldier escorted him to the place to which he was to be brought, so that he would not fall into their ambush. For he did not hesitate to invoke the Roman laws, proclaiming himself a Roman citizen, since at that time Roman citizens could not be afflicted with scourging.” This is Augustine, *Letter 50*.

But, you will ask, in what way does Paul say that he was born a Roman citizen? Certainly in no other way than that he had earlier declared publicly to the Jews that he was born at Tarsus in Cilicia: “I am,” he said, “a Jewish man, born at Tarsus in Cilicia.” Shortly before this he had also declared himself a citizen of Tarsus. For Tarsus, the metropolis of Cilicia, had obtained municipal status from the Romans. The inhabitants of municipalities were called Roman citizens not merely in the manner of colonists; they could also participate in honorary offices, as Gellius reports in book XVI, chapter 13:

> “Municipes are Roman citizens from municipalities, using their own rights and their own laws; they share with the Roman people only in honorary office, from which office they appear to have received their name; they are bound by no other obligations and by no law of the Roman people.”

Thus blessed Paul was a Roman citizen by hereditary right, and in this way he was “born” one. Cicero likewise distinguishes two classes of Roman citizens: some born citizens, others granted citizenship (*Against Catiline* II).]

They preferred to cast away all their possessions at once and to be supported by their own labor or by the contributions of the nations. Regarding their support, the holy Apostle writes to the Romans, commending to them his ministry in this matter and subtly urging them to make such a contribution:

> “But now I am going to Jerusalem to minister to the saints. For Macedonia and Achaia have been pleased to make some contribution for the poor among the saints who are in Jerusalem. They have been pleased to do so, and they are their debtors. For if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual things, they ought also to minister to them in material things” (Romans 15).

To the Corinthians also, showing similar concern for them, he urges them to prepare more carefully, before his arrival, the contribution which he intended to send for their needs:

> “Now concerning the collection for the saints: as I directed the churches of Galatia, so you also must do.
