On the first day of every week, let each of you put something aside and store it up as he has prospered, so that collections may not take place when I come. And when I arrive, I will send those whom you approve by letter to carry your gift to Jerusalem” (1 Corinthians 16).

To encourage them to make a more generous contribution, he adds:

> “And if it is appropriate for me to go also, they will go with me”—that is, if your offering is such that it deserves to be conveyed with my own accompaniment.

To the Galatians also, when he shared the ministry of preaching with the Apostles, he testifies that he had made the same agreement with James, Peter, and John: although he undertook the preaching of the Gentiles, he would by no means neglect concern and care for the poor who were in Jerusalem—those who, for Christ’s sake, had renounced all their possessions and voluntarily embraced poverty:

> “When they saw the grace of God that had been given to me, James and Cephas and John, who were reputed to be pillars, gave the right hand of fellowship to me and Barnabas, so that we should preach among the Gentiles, and they among the circumcised; only that we should remember the poor.”

He testifies that he fulfilled this with every concern, saying:

> “The very thing I was eager to do.”

Who, then, are happier? Those who, recently gathered from among the nations and not yet strong enough to climb to evangelical perfection, still clung to their possessions—in whom the Apostle recognized great fruit (Acts 15), provided only that, recalled from the worship of idols, fornication, things strangled, and blood, they had embraced Christ’s faith together with their possessions?

[Note: That is, they retained their possessions and estates, did not place them in common, and did not distribute them to the poor all at once.

That even the first Christians were permitted to retain and enjoy their temporal goods, unless they had bound themselves by a voluntary vow and private devotion to preserve poverty and lead a common life, is clearly gathered from the words of the Apostle Peter to Ananias: “While it remained, did it not remain yours? And after it was sold, was it not in your power?” (Acts 5). By these words he plainly indicated that Ananias, although a Christian, had been free not to sell his field and, even after selling it, not to offer the price to the Apostles or place it in common, unless he had voluntarily and freely professed this.

Hence we understand that what is narrated in Acts 4 about the first Christians living in Jerusalem—that no one called anything his own, but everything was held in common—was a matter of counsel, not of command, and was not observed by all Christians elsewhere.

Even in the earliest beginnings of the Church there were two classes of Christian people, as Cassianus indicates here. Some voluntarily and freely professed a common life and renounced all ownership of things; these are the people described in Acts 4. Others retained their possessions; concerning them the Apostle says in 1 Timothy 6: “Command the rich in this present age not to be proud; to give readily.”

For this reason the practice of collections always existed in the Church—collections such as are mentioned here—namely, that on Sundays money was gathered at the assembly of Christians from the wealthier members and distributed to the poor. This was done according to the will and devotion of those who contributed, as can be gathered from the many passages of the Apostle cited in this chapter.]

Or those who, obeying the evangelical saying and carrying the Lord’s cross daily (Matthew 10), wished to retain nothing of their own possessions?

When the blessed Apostle himself was bound with chains and imprisoned, or hindered by the hardships of travel and therefore unable, as he was accustomed, to obtain the customary means of sustenance by the work of his hands—

[Note: This is an obscure and uncommon expression, meaning “being unable” or “not being sufficient to procure his customary food”; or, as Dionysius translates it: “Since he could not obtain his daily food for himself by his own hands.”]

—he declares that he received assistance for his needs from the brothers who had come from Macedonia:

> “What was lacking to me, the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied” (2 Corinthians 12).

And writing to the Philippians, he himself says:

> “You yourselves know, Philippians, that in the beginning of the Gospel, when I departed from Macedonia, no church shared with me in the account of giving and receiving except you alone, because even when I was in Thessalonica you sent something for my needs once and twice” (Philippians 4).

[Note: That is, no church maintained with me a common account of what was given and received, because no church exchanged temporal things with me in return for the spiritual things it had received. The account of what was received is what is commonly called revenue; the account of what was given is what is called expenditure or outlay.

They had made an account of what was received because they had received spiritual things from him; they had not made an account of what was given because they had not in turn bestowed anything of their goods upon him. Consequently, they had not shared with him—that is, they had not made the account of giving and receiving common and equal. In French, this is expressed as *tenir compte de la recette et des mises réciproquement*, “to keep a reciprocal account of receipts and expenditures.”]

According to the opinion of these people, which they have conceived with lukewarm minds, will they therefore be happier than the Apostle because they are found to have shared their possessions with him? No sane person will dare say such a thing.

## CHAPTER XVIII. If We Wish to Imitate the Apostles, We Must Not Live by Our Own Definitions but Follow Their Examples

Therefore, if we wish to obey the evangelical command—

[Note: He means the evangelical command found in Matthew 19: “If you would be perfect, go, sell all that you have,” and so forth, which he mentioned in chapter 16. Or he may mean the evangelical saying about carrying the Lord’s cross, namely, through voluntary poverty and obedience.

Here and elsewhere he frequently uses “command” for an evangelical counsel, following the custom and practice of the first believers, who did not distinguish very carefully between evangelical commands and counsels. Inflamed by the fervor of devotion, they embraced whatever belonged to evangelical teaching as though it were a command and strove to observe it, as is evident in those who first believed in Jerusalem after the Lord’s Ascension.

Nevertheless, Athanasius in the *Life of Saint Antony* and Basil in his address to the rich also call the words “Go, sell all that you have and give to the poor” a command of the Lord. They understand it as a conditional, not an absolute, command, because it was not given to everyone, but only to those who desire to be perfect, and under this condition: “If you would be perfect,” and so forth.]

—and to be imitators of the Apostle and of that entire primitive Church, or of those Fathers who in our own times succeeded them in virtue and perfection—

[Col. 0311C]

let us not rest content with our own definitions, promising ourselves evangelical perfection in this lukewarm and wretched condition. Let us follow their footsteps and not try to deceive ourselves. Let us seek the discipline and institution of the monastery in such a way that we truly renounce this world, retaining nothing of the things we have despised because unbelief draws us back. Let us acquire our daily food not from money stored away, but by our own labor.

## CHAPTER XIX. The Sentence Pronounced by Saint Basil, Bishop, against Syncleticus

A saying is reported to have been pronounced by Saint Basil, bishop of Caesarea, against a certain Syncleticus who was torpid with the lukewarmness described above. He said that he had renounced this world, yet had retained some of his own possessions, unwilling to support himself by the work of his hands or to obtain true humility through nakedness, the hardship of labor, and submission to the monastery:

> “You have lost a senator and have not made a monk.”

[Note: Ciaconius rightly and skillfully restored this Greek word from the Vatican manuscript, since it had previously been read corruptly as *Syncletium*, as Dionysius also rendered it, whether through error or carelessness, as did the others—as though it were the proper name of the person to whom Saint Basil said this.

For συγκλητικός in Greek means “senator,” just as συγκλητός means “senate.” The Greek words reported by Ciaconius both support the reading and possess an elegance equal to that of the Latin. They are:

> καὶ τὸν συγκλητικὸν ἀπώλεσας, καὶ μοναχὸν οὐκ ἐποίησας.

“And you have lost the senator and have not made a monk.” He had lost the senator because he had laid aside his senatorial dignity in order to become a monk; yet he had not made a true monk because he was unwilling to undergo monastic poverty.

In the *Lives of the Fathers* the same saying is reported as follows: “You have ceased to be a senator and have not made yourself a monk.” From this (*Book V*, booklet 6) it is clear that the word *Syncleticus* was added unnecessarily, and therefore was rightly removed in this edition. Since *Syncleticus* means the same as “senator,” it would be tautological to say: “You have lost the senator Syncleticus and have not made a monk.”]

## CHAPTER XX. How Disgraceful It Is to Be Defeated by Avarice

Therefore, if we desire to fight the spiritual contest lawfully, let us also drive this destructive enemy from our hearts. To overcome it requires no great virtue; but to be defeated by it is disgraceful and full of dishonor.

To be struck down by a powerful enemy, although there is pain in the defeat and groaning in the loss of victory, nevertheless brings the defeated person a certain consolation from the strength of his adversary. But if the enemy is insignificant and the struggle weak, then, beyond the pain of defeat, a more shameful confusion and a disgrace heavier than the loss are inflicted.

[Note: Avarice is a shameful and dishonorable vice. Hence Aristotle rightly called it ἀνελευθερία, “illiberality” or “lack of freedom” (*Nicomachean Ethics* VII), because nothing is more alien to a free person. Cicero likewise says in one place that nothing is so narrow and so mean-spirited as loving money (*On Duties* II).]

[Note: This entire chapter is overflowing with excellent sayings worthy of being committed to memory. At the end of the work we shall arrange them, together with other choice passages, in order.]

## CHAPTER XXI. How Avarice Is to Be Overcome

The complete victory and perpetual triumph over it will be this: that, as it is said, the monk’s conscience should not be stained even by a coin of the smallest denomination.

For it is impossible that one who has once been defeated by the desire for a small stipend, after that desire has taken root in his heart, should not immediately be consumed by the fire of a greater longing. The soldier of Christ will remain victorious and secure, and will be free from every assault of desire,

[Note: This is a phrase peculiar to Cassianus. Dionysius renders it: “He will be immune from every attack of covetousness.”]

only so long as that most wicked spirit has not sown the beginnings of this desire in his heart.

Therefore, since in every kind of vice the serpent’s head must generally be watched over—

[Note: That is, it must be observed or guarded against, as he says below, where he calls the devil a serpent, just as in the preceding book. The serpent’s head is watched and guarded against, and, according to the Vulgate version, crushed, when his suggestions are resisted firmly and without delay.]

—in this matter especially it is necessary to take careful precautions. If it is admitted, growing strong through its own material, it will kindle still more violent fires for itself.

Therefore not only must the possession of money be avoided; the very desire must also be driven completely from the soul. For it is not so much the effect of avarice that must be avoided as its affection and inclination, which must be cut out by the roots. It will be of no benefit not to possess money if the will to possess remains in us.

## CHAPTER XXII. How Someone Who Possesses No Money Can Nevertheless Be Judged Avaricious

It is entirely possible for someone who possesses no money nevertheless not to be free from the disease of avarice, and for him to gain no benefit from the benefit of nakedness—

[Note: That is, from the profession of poverty. No greater nakedness can exist than that of the religious state, which not only brings about poverty but also completely strips and deprives every monk of possession, ownership, and dominion over all things. Thus he cannot call his own not only a field or a house, but, as Cassianus says elsewhere, not even a garment, a stylus, or a pen (*above*, book IV, chapter 13).

Saint Gregory explains the benefit of this nakedness in these words. Although they apply in their own way to all Christians, they properly and more especially refer to religious:

“Whoever comes to the contest of faith takes up a struggle against evil spirits. Yet evil spirits possess nothing of their own in this world. Therefore we must wrestle naked with the naked. For if a clothed person wrestles with a naked person, he is more quickly thrown to the ground because he has something by which he can be held. For what are all earthly things except a kind of clothing for the body? Therefore, whoever hastens to battle against the devil should cast off his garments, lest he succumb.” This is Gregory, *Homily 33 on the Gospels*.

For perfect nakedness, however, it is not enough to abandon possessions and estates or to be without them; one must also lay aside every affection for them and every desire to possess them, as Cassianus teaches here. For avarice consists not so much in possession as in love of riches or money, as the very name indicates. Hence throughout Scripture, where the Greek has φιλάργυροι, the Latin has *cupidi* or *avari*, “covetous” or “avaricious,” as though they were greedy for bronze or money, as noted above (Luke 16; 1 Timothy 3; 2 Timothy 3).]

—because he was unable to cut away the vice of covetousness, taking pleasure in the good of poverty but not in the merit of virtue, and being content with the burden of necessity, though not without dejection of heart.

Just as the Gospel pronounces those who have not been stained bodily to have committed adultery in their hearts—

[Note: Matthew 5: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” Just as the mere desire for another man’s wife makes a person guilty before God of fornication and adultery, so the mere affection for and desire for money—or, as we commonly put it, the mere affection for ownership—makes a monk guilty of avarice and possessiveness.]

—so it is possible for those who are not burdened by the weight of money to be condemned, in affection and mind, together with the avaricious. The opportunity to possess was lacking for them, not the will; and before God the will is always accustomed to receive a greater crown than necessity.

We must therefore hasten, lest the benefits of our labors perish in vain. It is wretched to have endured the outcome of poverty and nakedness, yet to have lost their fruits through the fault of a vain will.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The Example of Judas

Would you like to know how destructively and harmfully this tinder, unless carefully cut out, bears fruit toward the ruin of the person who conceived it, and how it sprouts into branches of every kind of vice? Consider Judas, counted among the number of the Apostles. Because he was unwilling to crush the deadly head of this serpent, see how it killed him with its poison and entangled him in the snares of desire, driving him into the crime of a precipitous fall, so that it drove him to sell the Redeemer of the world and the author of human salvation for thirty pieces of silver.

He would never have fallen into so wicked a deed of betrayal if he had not been infected with the disease of avarice. Nor would he have become sacrilegiously guilty of the Lord’s denial [alternative reading: killing] unless he had previously been accustomed to plunder the money-box entrusted to him.

[Note: Judas, distressed by the loss and waste of the ointment poured out by Mary Magdalene, indignantly uttered these words: “Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and the money given to the poor?” The Evangelist adds: “He said this not because he cared about the poor”—that is, not because he was concerned for them or anxious about them—“but because he was a thief, and, having the money-box, he used to take what was put into it” (John 12).

He calls Judas a thief because, as is stated here, he was accustomed to plunder the money-box entrusted to him by the Lord—that is, to steal from it and secretly take something for himself, as though it were his own private fund, from the money and alms sent or contributed to the Lord by pious and devout people. Judas had been appointed their treasurer and steward.

He was therefore indignant and murmured because he grieved over the profit he had lost—the profit he could have obtained by stealing from the sale of the ointment and its price.

But, you will ask, why did the Lord entrust the money-box to him when he knew that Judas was untrustworthy and would thereby obtain an opportunity for avarice and his own destruction? The Author suggests one reason in the following chapter: so that, at least by being satisfied with an abundance of money, Judas might put an end to the excesses of his desire. An opportunity was given him to cure his avarice and moderate his covetousness; but he turned this opportunity to his own destruction, God permitting it by his hidden judgment, so that it might be shown in Judas how dangerous the handling of money and the abundance of riches are.

Second, the Lord wished by this benefit, as by many others, to bind Judas to himself, draw him to his love, and restrain him, as far as lay within him, from committing the crime. He had entrusted him, as though to one especially faithful and dear, with the care of the household, just as prudent masters commonly choose as stewards those whose faithfulness and integrity they trust most.

Third, some think that the common money was entrusted to Judas because he was the least of the Apostles and the least spiritual among them. In this way Christ may have wished to teach that such business should rather be entrusted to those who are less suited to better and higher things, just as the Apostle instructed the Corinthians: “If you have secular lawsuits, appoint as judges those who are of no account in the Church”—that is, in the assembly of the faithful—“to judge them” (1 Corinthians 6).

The chief and most important reason, however, was the dispensation of our salvation. For this reason divine providence wished and had to permit Judas’s wickedness and blindness, so that the Scriptures might be fulfilled and Christ the Lord, betrayed by him, might die for the salvation of all.]

## CHAPTER XXIV. How Avarice Cannot Be Conquered Except by Nakedness

This is a sufficiently monstrous and evident example of the tyranny which, once it has taken possession of a soul, as we have said, allows it to observe no rule of honesty and cannot be satisfied by any addition of profit. The end of this madness is achieved not through riches but through nakedness.

When Judas had received the money-box, assigned to the relief of the poor and entrusted to his authority, so that at least the abundance of money might satisfy him and make him set a limit to his desire, the abundance of it inflamed him with an even more plentiful fuel for covetousness. He then preferred not merely to plunder the money-box secretly, but to sell the Lord himself.

[Note: Saint Jerome, in the epitaph for Paula, writes: “Lest the habit of possessing more give room to avarice, which is satisfied by no riches; the more it has, the more it seeks; and it is diminished neither by abundance nor by poverty.” In his letter to Paulinus he writes: “There is an ancient saying: To the avaricious person, what he has is as lacking as what he does not have. To the believer, the whole world is wealth; but the unbeliever needs even a single coin.”]

For the madness of this desire surpasses every mass of riches.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the End of Ananias, Sapphira, and Judas, Which They Suffered When Driven by Avarice
Finally, the prince of the Apostles, instructed by these examples, knowing that one who possesses even something of covetousness cannot control its reins, and that its end does not rest in a small or a large sum, but solely in the virtue of [Note: That is, religious poverty, as stated above (Chapter XII), by which the naked monk—that is, stripped and divested of all temporal goods and attachment to them—follows the naked Christ, as Saint Jerome admonished his monk Rusticus (Letter 4). Concerning this nakedness, John Climacus likewise says in Step 16: “Nakedness is the laying aside of all cares for material things, security of life, the freedom of a traveler from every impediment, estrangement from sorrow, and fidelity to the commandments; the naked monk is lord of the whole world”; and other things that follow.] nakedness, [Note: Saint Luke reports (Acts V) that Ananias and Sapphira, after hearing the rebuke and censure of the Apostle Peter, immediately fell down and died, and were carried to the tomb. But the difficulty is whether Peter truly and effectively killed them and inflicted death upon them, as is said here. For the Fathers speak about this matter in different ways.

Origen thinks that Ananias’s death should not be attributed to Peter, but that Ananias could not endure the severity of Peter’s words, especially these: “Why has Satan tempted your heart?” and that, having heard them, he fell dead from excessive horror and anguish of spirit. “Hearing these words,” he says (Treatise 8 on Matthew), “he therefore fell and expired because he did not endure Peter’s rebuke; but he was so punished by torments within himself that he even died.”

Saint Jerome seems to hold the same view when, refuting Porphyry’s slander, he says (Letter 8 to Demetrias): “The Apostle Peter by no means invoked death upon them, as the foolish Porphyry slanders him; rather, by the prophetic spirit he announced God’s judgment, so that the punishment of two men might be instruction for many.”

Dionysius Carthusianus teaches that Ananias and his wife Sapphira were struck by an angel. Cassian, however, says in this passage that Peter inflicted death upon them; elsewhere he states more explicitly that they were put to death by the apostolic mouth (Chapter 19 above). By these words he indicates that they were killed by Peter—that is, by Peter’s word and command—as the physical and instrumental cause, in the language of the philosophers.

Augustine, or whoever was the author of the book On the Miracles of Scripture, appears to support this view, saying (at the end of Book III, volume III of his works): “Behold how great is apostolic power in Christ: Peter rebuked Ananias while he was still alive, and by the mere command of his word bound him in death; and by the same power of command he released Tabitha, who had been bound by the bonds of death.”

Saint Gregory also indicates this same manner of killing, saying that Peter took life from both husband and wife by rebuking them, while he restored it to Tabitha by praying. Hence (Dialogues II.30–31) he concludes that the saints perform miracles in two ways: sometimes through prayer, sometimes through authority. “That they display miracles in both ways,” he says, “Peter bears witness, for he raised the dead Tabitha by praying. But he delivered Ananias and Sapphira, who were lying, over to death by rebuking them.” For it is not recorded that he prayed at their destruction, but only that he rebuked the guilt they had committed. “It is therefore clear that sometimes they perform such things by authority, and sometimes by petition.” This is Gregory’s statement. He subsequently reports two miracles of our holy Father Benedict, one performed by authority and the other by prayer.

It is therefore evident that both manners may be admitted, both of killing and of speaking, since each rests upon firm reasons and authorities. Thus Peter may be said to have inflicted the penalty of death either physically and effectively through his apostolic mouth—that is, by his word—as by a kind of spiritual sword or efficacious instrument, which he used as God’s minister, as occurs in the Church’s sacraments; or only improperly and morally, both because, as Saint Jerome says, he announced by the prophetic spirit the divine judgment that was immediately to follow, and because God, assenting to Peter’s sentence, immediately punished by sudden [Col. 0317B] death those whom Peter, by divine revelation, convicted as guilty.

Nor was there uniform agreement among the ancient Fathers as to whether this death was only bodily and temporal, or also spiritual and eternal. Cassian presents the view that they were punished with everlasting death in these words (Conference 18.7): “The blessed Apostle did not permit the aforementioned leaders of the new crime to be cured by repentance or by any satisfaction, but cut down the most destructive shoot by swift death.” Yet elsewhere (Conference 6.11) he seems to think and speak differently, as we shall report later.

Saint Basil and Bede incline toward the same opinion, thinking that they perished eternally. Basil’s words are these: “But what of Ananias? Is he found to have committed any other crime except that one for which he was punished so harshly? Where, then, does it appear that he deserved so severe a penalty? He had sold his property, brought the price, and laid it at the apostles’ feet; nevertheless, because he had secretly and maliciously appropriated part of it, for that reason he was put to death at that very moment together with his wife. He was not considered worthy to hear anything about repentance for the sin committed; nor to receive even enough time to grieve and be pierced in heart, however slightly; nor, finally, to obtain any delay in which to return to himself.” This is Basil’s statement.

On the other hand, there are no fewer serious authorities who think differently: namely, that Ananias and Sapphira repented of their sin at the very moment of death and consequently suffered only temporal death, through which they were purified and escaped everlasting death. Thus Origen, speaking of them (Treatise 8 on Matthew), says: “They were worthy in this world to receive their sin, so that they might leave this life purer, cleansed by the chastisement inflicted upon them through ordinary death.”

Saint Augustine also seems to hold this view (Against Parmenianus III.1), when, speaking of the Corinthian whom Paul handed over to Satan “for the destruction of the flesh” (1 Corinthians V), he says: “What, then, was the Apostle doing, except providing for the salvation of the spirit through the destruction of the flesh—whether by some punishment or bodily death, as Ananias and his wife fell before the feet of the Apostle Peter, or through repentance, since he had been handed over to Satan, destroying within himself the criminal desire of the flesh, and so forth?”

Peter Damian likewise writes in his book On Contempt for the World: “Because Ananias and Sapphira were inexperienced and newly come to the faith, and in the very beginning of their faith had sinned in a certain simplicity, they were punished, as we believe, by bodily death alone, through a judgment indeed strict but merciful.”

Cassian expresses the same opinion in Conference 6.11, speaking in the person of Abbot Theodore: “We find that some have received, for lighter offenses also, the same sentence of death for the present by which those whom we have mentioned as authors of sacrilegious transgression were punished. So it happened to the man who had gathered wood on the Sabbath, and to Ananias and Sapphira, who, in the error of unbelief, had secretly kept back something small from their possessions—not because the weight of their sins was equal, but because, having been found presumptuous in a new transgression, they were obliged to provide others with an example both of sin and of punishment and terror. Thus anyone who afterward attempted such things would know that, according to the same pattern by which they were condemned, he too would have to answer at the examination of the future judgment, even if punishment were deferred in the present.” Such is his statement.

This opinion, as more consonant with piety and divine mercy, is preferred by Baronius and other ecclesiastical writers (Baronius, volume I, year of Christ 34).]

Ananias and Sapphira, whom we mentioned above, because they had kept something back from their property, he punished with death, so that the destruction which Judas had voluntarily brought upon himself for the crime of betraying the Lord, they might suffer for the lie prompted by covetousness (Acts V). How great a similarity of crime and punishment appears here as well! In the one case betrayal followed covetousness; in the other, falsehood followed it. There truth was betrayed; here the crime of lying was committed. Although the outward effect of their deeds appears different, the same end is found in both. For he, fleeing poverty, desired to take back what he had cast away; they, lest they should become poor, attempted to retain something from their property, which they ought either faithfully to have offered to the Apostles or to have distributed entirely among the brethren. Therefore in both cases condemnation to death follows, [Col. 0317B] because both crimes sprang from the roots of covetousness. If, then, so severe a sentence was passed upon those who did not desire the property of others, but attempted to spare their own, and who had no wish to acquire but only the will to reserve, what should be thought of those who desire to gather money they never previously possessed, and who, while displaying nakedness before human beings, are proved rich before God in the affection of desire?

## CHAPTER XXVI  
### How Covetousness Inflicts Spiritual Leprosy upon the Soul

Those who, in imitation of Gehazi (2 Kings V), [Note: Concerning spiritual leprosy, it will be useful to set down here some noteworthy observations from Peter Berchorius. “Just as bodily leprosy,” he says (in the Moral Dictionary, under “Leprosy”), “arises from various causes, so spiritual leprosy—that is, sin—is generated in various ways. Leprosy sometimes arises from corruption of the blood, phlegm, choler, or melancholy. According to these four causes, we may understand four kinds of spiritual leprosy: simony, pride, avarice, and uncleanness. For leprosy may signify the horror of simony, the swelling of pride, the burning of avarice, and the stench of uncleanness.”

After much else, concerning the leprosy of avarice, which is at issue here, he adds: “Third, I say that a person becomes spiritually leprous through the severity of avarice. For just as a leper is heavy and weighed down, and feels itching and burning in his flesh, so the avaricious person is heavy, inclined toward earthly and temporal things, and continually inflamed by the burning of avarice. Hence avarice is properly the leprosy called elephantiasis, which is generated from a thick, earthy, melancholic humor; and for this reason it is compared with the elephant, a heavy, weighty, melancholic animal, which, once it has fallen, cannot rise.” This and other things follow.] are known to be leprous in spirit and mind, having been sprinkled with the contagion of an unclean leprosy because they covet the fleeting money of this world. Through it he left us a clear example: every soul polluted by the stain of covetousness is sprinkled with the spiritual leprosy of vices and is judged unclean before the Lord under an everlasting curse.

## CHAPTER XXVII  
### Testimonies from Scripture by Which the Person Desiring Perfection Is Taught Not to Take Back What He Renounced

[Col. 0318B]

Therefore, if, out of a desire for perfection, you left everything and followed Christ, who said to you (Matthew XIX), “Go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me,” why do you look back after putting your hand to the plow, so that you may be declared by the voice of that same Lord (Luke IX and XVII) unfit for the kingdom of heaven? [Note: This is a moral allusion to the passage in Luke XVII: “On that day, whoever is on the housetop, with his possessions in the house, must not come down to take them; and whoever is in the field likewise must not turn back.” Saint Ambrose explains this as follows (Book 8 on Luke): “If someone has climbed to the summit of his house and of exalted virtues, he must not approach the earthly works of this world.”

Augustine likewise says (Questions on the Gospels II.41): “He is on the housetop who, having risen above carnal things, lives spiritually as if in the open air. The possessions in the house are the carnal senses, by which many, using them to investigate the truth that is grasped by the intellect, have gone completely astray. Therefore the spiritual person must beware lest, on the day of tribulation, delighted once more by the carnal life that is nourished through the senses, he descend to the possessions of this world.”]

Established upon the height of the evangelical roof, why do you descend to take anything from your house, namely, from those things you formerly despised? Set in the field and engaged in the practice of virtues, why do you run back and strive to clothe yourself again with the substance of the world from which, by your renunciation, you stripped yourself? If, however, poverty overtook you and you had nothing to leave behind, you ought all the less to acquire what you did not previously possess. For this reason you were prepared by the Lord’s favor in such a way that you might hasten to him more freely, impeded by no snares of money.

Nevertheless, let no one in need be discouraged; [Note: Saint Augustine explains this skillfully in his commentary on Psalm 103, teaching that no one is so poor and needy that he cannot leave many things for Christ if he embraces evangelical poverty. He interprets the verse of the psalm, “There the sparrows will build their nests,” so that these sparrows, being small birds, signify the poor and insignificant who, hearing in the Gospel (Matthew XIX), “Go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me,” embraced it with their whole heart and resolved not to be joined to wives, not to be worn down by care for children, and not to have private dwellings to which they would be tied, but to enter upon a kind of common life.

“But what,” he asks, “did these sparrows leave? They seem to be the little sparrows of this world. What did they leave? What great thing did they leave? One man converts: he leaves his poor father’s hut, scarcely one bed and one chest. Let us not mock him; let us not say to him, ‘You left nothing.’ Let him not be proud who has left much.

“We know that Peter was a fisherman when he followed the Lord. What could he have left? Or his brother Andrew, or the sons of Zebedee, John and James, who were also fishermen? And yet what did they say? ‘Behold, we have left everything and followed you.’ The Lord did not say to him, ‘Have you forgotten your poverty? What did you leave, so as to receive the whole world?’ He left much, my brothers; he left much. He not only left whatever he had, but also whatever he desired to have. For what poor person does not swell with hope of this world? Who does not daily desire to increase what he possesses? That desire was cut off. It was moving toward infinity; it received a limit. Was nothing left? Peter truly left the whole world, and Peter received the whole world. ‘As having nothing, yet possessing everything’ (2 Corinthians VI).”

So speaks blessed Augustine. Saint Bernard says similar things in his Declamation on the words, “Behold, we have left everything.”]

For there is no one who does not have something to leave. Whoever has cut out at the root the affection of possessing the world’s goods has renounced all the world’s possessions.

[Note: Dionysius joins this chapter and the three following chapters together in a single continuous treatment, since they are brief. Concerning this nakedness, or religious poverty, in addition to the material already cited above, one may consult Isidore of Pelusium, Book II, Letter 161.]

## CHAPTER XXVIII  
### How Victory over Covetousness Can Be Won Only through Nakedness

[Col. 0319B]

This, then, is perfect victory over covetousness: that we do not allow the smallest spark of any coin to remain in our heart, certain that afterward we shall have no power to extinguish it if we have nourished within us even the slightest material for this spark.

## CHAPTER XXIX  
### What Monastic Nakedness Consists In

We shall not otherwise be able to preserve this virtue undefiled unless we remain in the monastery and, according to the Apostle, [Note: We discussed this statement elsewhere (Book I, chapter 3). Saint Thomas further noted two reasons given by the Apostle in his commentary why we ought to be content with these two things, food and clothing: one drawn from the beginning of our life and condition, the other from its end. “As to the beginning,” he says, “because we brought nothing into this world”; Job I: “Naked I came from my mother’s womb.” “As to the end,” because we cannot take anything away with us. Psalm LXXV: “They have slept their sleep, and all the men of riches have found nothing in their hands.” Job XXVII: “When the rich man sleeps, he will take nothing away with him; he will open his eyes, and find nothing.”] having food and clothing, we shall be content with these (1 Timothy VI).

## CHAPTER XXX  
### Remedies against the Disease of Covetousness

[Col. 0320B] [Note: Condemnation, whether eternal or temporal, concerning which see above (Chapter 25). The holy Fathers commonly use the example and dreadful end of Ananias and Sapphira to deter monks from the vice of private ownership and embezzlement.

Thus Saint Basil says in Sermon 1 on the Institution of Monks: “If it is our intention, by emptying ourselves of vices, to form the character of our souls according to the likeness of God and thereby acquire everlasting life for ourselves, we must take the greatest care that we do nothing unworthy of our profession and do not become subject to a judgment like that of Ananias. At the beginning, Ananias could have refrained from promising and vowing his little property to God; but after, moved by desire for human glory, he consecrated to God by his profession whatever he had among his goods, in order to arouse people’s admiration of himself by such an extraordinary deed. Then, craftily diverting some portion of the price, he provoked against himself the indignation of God, whose minister Peter was,” and so forth.

Saint Ambrose likewise says in Sermon 59: “An example has been set forth in Ananias for all avaricious people, so that whoever is guilty of the same crime may, on the day of judgment, be struck by the sentence of the same punishment. Avarice is therefore a great evil, indeed the source of all evils, as the Apostle says: ‘The desire for money is the root of all evils’ (1 Timothy VI).

“Saint Benedict says similarly in Chapter 57 of the Rule, speaking about the craftsmen of the monastery: ‘If any of the craftsmen’s products are to be sold, let those through whose hands the transactions are to be conducted take care that they do not presume to commit any fraud; and let them always remember Ananias and Sapphira, lest perhaps they suffer in their souls the death which those others endured in the body, or which all who commit any fraud regarding the monastery’s possessions may suffer.’”

Commenting on this passage, Turrecrematus says: “These things are clear and ought to be carefully noted by those who handle the possessions of monasteries, so that they may recognize how great a danger it is to handle the monastery’s property unfaithfully and fraudulently. Clearly miserable is the person who passes by deaf to the thunderclap of so great a lightning bolt.”

Smaragdus likewise says in the same place: “The death which monks suffer in their souls by committing fraud is worse and more severe than the bodily death suffered by Ananias and Sapphira. Bodily death is common to all and temporal, whereas the death of the soul belongs to the wicked and is eternal. The former separates the soul from the body; the latter separates it from the Creator. The former sends the body to the grave; the latter sends the soul to hell.” So he says.

For a fuller illustration of this passage, there will appropriately be added here some commendations and examples of the holy Fathers, by which it is shown how greatly they detested in monks the vice of private ownership and covetousness.

Saint Jerome writes in his Letter to Eustochium (Letter 22.14) that a monk was once found in a monastery at Nitria who, when he died, left behind one hundred solidi, which he had acquired by weaving linen. Accordingly, after the monks had held a council—for about five thousand lived in that place in separate cells—some said that the money should be distributed to the poor, others that it should be given to the Church, and some that it should be sent back to his parents. But Macarius, Pambo, Isidore, and the other Fathers, with the Holy Spirit speaking through them, decreed that the money should be buried with the dead man, while everyone cried out: “May your money be with you for destruction!” (See also Sermon 5, attributed to Augustine, To the Brothers in the Desert; and Caesarius, Book IX of Miracles, chapter 65.)

John the Deacon writes that blessed Gregory later did the same thing in a similar case (Book I, chapter 15 of his Life); Gregory himself also records it (Dialogues IV.55). Hence Innocent III, in that celebrated decree beginning “When [he comes] to the monastery,” legislated concerning the state of monks as follows: “If private property is found in anyone’s possession at death, it is to be buried with him outside the monastery in a dung heap as a sign of perdition, according to what blessed Gregory says he did” (Book III of the Decretals, and so forth, title “Concerning a Certain Matter”).

The same Saint Jerome reports another notable example in the Life of Hilarion: “Saint Hilarion especially detested monks who, through a certain lack of faith, reserved their possessions for the future and took care over expenses, clothing, or any of those things that pass away with the world. Finally, he drove from his sight one of the brothers who lived about five miles away, because he found him an excessively cautious and fearful guardian of his little garden and discovered that he possessed a small amount of money. Wishing to reconcile himself with the old man, he frequently came to the brothers, especially to Hesychius, in whom Hilarion took the greatest delight.

“One day, therefore, he brought a bundle of green chickpeas, just as they were in the field. When Hesychius had placed it on the table in the evening, the old man exclaimed that he could not endure its stench and asked where it came from. When Hesychius replied that a certain brother had brought the first fruits of his little field to the brothers, he said: ‘Do you not perceive the most horrible stench? Does not avarice stink in the chickpeas? Send them to the oxen; send them to the brute animals, and see whether they will eat them.’

“When he had placed them in the manger according to the command, the oxen, terrified and bellowing more than usual, broke their bonds and fled in different directions.” Thus far Saint Jerome.

See Saint Augustine, Sermon 1 on the Common Life of Clerics, where he speaks about one of his priests who had retained something for himself contrary to his profession and, when he was dying, had made a will concerning it.]

Therefore, keeping the condemnation of Ananias and Sapphira (Acts V) constantly before us, let us shudder at reserving anything from those things which, when we renounced them, we vowed utterly to reject. Let us also fear the example of Gehazi (2 Kings V), who, because of the crime of covetousness, was punished with the leprosy of eternal [reading uncertain: “eternal” or “everlasting”] punishment; and let us beware of acquiring what we did not previously possess. Moreover, fearing either the merit or the end of Judas, let us avoid with all our strength taking back any money which we once cast away from us.

Above all, considering the condition of our fragile and uncertain nature, let us beware lest the day of the Lord, coming like a thief in the night, find our conscience stained even by a single coin (1 Thessalonians V). Let us beware lest he, nullifying all the fruits of our renunciation, cause the saying spoken in the Gospel to the rich man to be directed to us also by the Lord’s voice: [Note: The avaricious person is called foolish, as was Nabal in the Old Testament, who refused to give David, when he was in need, something from his abundance. For Nabal signifies “fool,” and truly the avaricious person displays great folly by gathering through wicked labor things which he may perhaps never enjoy.

For this reason the Holy Spirit indicates that this is almost a perpetual and certain punishment inflicted upon the avaricious: that they are frustrated in their expectation, as is said here, “The things you have prepared—whose will they be?” Thus David says: “He will leave his riches to strangers” (Psalm XLVIII). And again: “He stores up, and does not know for whom he will gather them” (Psalm XXXVIII). Solomon likewise says: “I saw great and grievous folly: riches preserved to the harm of their owner” (Ecclesiastes V). Job noted the same thing: “When he has possessed whatever he desired, he will not be able to enjoy it” (Job XX).

Hence Saint Ambrose, commenting on that passage in Luke, says: “In vain does the man gather wealth who does not know how to use it. He is like the man whose barns, bursting with new harvests, were being filled with overflowing fruits, while he prepared receptacles for those fruits without knowing for whom he was gathering them. For those things are not ours which we cannot take away with us. Virtue alone accompanies the dead; mercy alone follows us, and obtains eternal dwelling places for the dead.” This is Saint Ambrose’s statement.]

“Fool, this night they demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke XII). Thinking of nothing concerning tomorrow, let us never allow ourselves to be torn away from the discipline of the cenobium.

## CHAPTER XXXI  
### How No One Can Conquer Covetousness Except by Persevering in a Cenobium, and How One Can Remain There

Without doubt, we are not permitted to fulfill this, or even to remain under the rule of our institution, unless first the virtue of patience—which proceeds from no other source than humility—has been firmly established in us. Patience knows how to inflict no disturbances upon anyone; humility, however, knows how to tolerate with greatness of spirit the disturbances inflicted upon it.

# BOOK EIGHT  
## ON THE SPIRIT OF ANGER

[Col. 0321]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0321C]

In the fourth contest [Note: Our manuscripts read: “In the fourth place the deadly poison of anger enters the contest,” and so forth. The Basel edition has: “The fourth contest also is that of anger, which is a deadly poison,” and so forth. Dionysius the paraphraser says: “In the fourth contest we must uproot completely from the inner recesses of our soul the deadly poison,” and so forth.

As for the reason for this order—why anger is placed fourth among the capital vices, immediately after covetousness—we have reported it elsewhere from the author himself (Book V, chapter 1). Yet one need not labor greatly over this, since neither Saint Gregory nor Saint Thomas nor others observe this order; rather, they reverse it, led by other considerations.

Here, however, it must first be explained what anger is and how it differs from irascibility; second, whether it is a capital vice; and third, what offspring and daughters it has.

Regarding the first point, observe that anger in a human being is twofold. One kind exists in the sensitive part, from which the irascible appetite receives its name, and which human beings share with brute animals. The other is proper to human beings and exists in the rational part—that is, in the will. It is nothing other than a movement of the soul desiring vengeance. Hence the ancients defined it as “a desire to avenge oneself” or “an appetite for vengeance” (Augustine, On the City of God XIV.15; Saint Thomas, II–II, question 158, article 1; Aristotle, Rhetoric I.2; Seneca, On Anger, chapter 3; see Lactantius, On the Anger of God, chapter 17).

This anger is generally joined with the anger of the sensitive part and with bodily movement. For the higher part is rarely moved without the lower and sensitive part also being moved.

Anger, insofar as it is a vice or sin, is an immoderate or disordered desire for vengeance. For not every desire for vengeance is simply unlawful, but only an immoderate one—whether it exceeds the proper measure in a just cause or proceeds from an unjust cause. An unjust cause is wishing to avenge one’s own and personal injury; this, precisely because it is personal, must never be avenged. A just cause for vengeance exists when either God’s honor is defended, as when Phinehas and Moses became angry, or when it is expedient for those with whom we are angry.

Anger therefore becomes vicious and evil when it excludes the order of reason, says Saint Thomas (article 2, in the place cited above), that is, when it does not preserve the measure prescribed by reason. This occurs in two ways. First, on the side of the object, when an unjust vengeance is desired—for example, if someone wishes to punish, or desires that someone be punished, who has not deserved it, or beyond what he has deserved, or not according to the lawful order, or not for the proper end, which is the preservation of justice and correction of fault. In this respect the sin is mortal by its nature, because it is contrary to charity and justice toward one’s neighbor.

Second, it occurs on the side of the movement itself, when someone boils over immoderately, either inwardly or through some outward sign, even though otherwise he desires a just vengeance.

In these two general ways anger passes into the vice contrary to gentleness, which Aristotle calls ὀργιλότης (*orgilotēs*) and which is called *iracundia* in Latin. This latter term, however, is more commonly used for the vicious habit of becoming angry, and is distinguished from the act or movement of anger itself, which is called ὀργή (*orgē*) in Greek.

Hence Cicero says in the Tusculan Disputations IV: “Irascibility differs from anger as anxiety differs from anguish. For not all are anxious who are sometimes distressed, nor are the anxious always distressed; and there is a difference between drunkenness and habitual drunkenness, as there is between being a lover and being in love.” Seneca likewise says almost in the same words (On Anger, chapter 4) that anger differs from irascibility as a drunken man differs from a habitual drunkard, and a frightened person from a timid one. An angry person may not be irascible, and an irascible person may sometimes not be angry.

Besides Cassian, Saint Gregory also counts anger, or irascibility, among the capital vices, as has been said elsewhere; and rightly so. For it is well known that a great many other vices and evils arise from anger as from their head and source. For this reason Saint Gregory lists six offspring, or daughters, of anger (Book V, chapter 1): “From anger,” he says, “come quarrels, swelling of mind, insult, shouting, indignation, and blasphemy.”

For if anger is internal, it gives birth to swelling of mind and indignation; if external, it is either in the mouth, and thus produces shouting, insult, and blasphemy, or in deed and action, and thus quarrels arise from anger, together with all the injuries that follow from quarrels and are inflicted upon one’s neighbors. But see these matters explained more fully in Saint Thomas and in Leonardus Lessius (Book IV, chapter 4, On Justice).]

the deadly poison of anger must also be completely uprooted from the recesses of our soul. For when it takes its seat in our hearts and blinds the eye of the mind with harmful darkness, [Note: Saint Gregory seems plainly to have imitated this passage in Book V, chapter 31 of the *Moralia*, where he lists these same harms of anger and confirms them from almost the same passages of Scripture, with some others added.

“Through anger,” he says, “wisdom is lost, so that one does not know what ought to be done or in what order, as it is written: ‘Anger rests in the bosom of a fool’ (Ecclesiastes VII), because it removes the light of understanding when, by disturbing the mind, it confuses it.

“Through anger life is lost, even if wisdom seems to be retained, as it is written: ‘Anger destroys even the prudent,’ because a confused mind cannot accomplish what it is able to understand prudently.

“Through anger justice is abandoned, as it is written: ‘The anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God’ (James I), because when the disturbed mind inflames the judgment of reason, it considers everything suggested by fury to be right.

“Through anger the grace of social life is lost, as it is written: ‘Do not associate with an angry man, lest you learn his ways and take a stumbling-block for your soul.’ And again: ‘Who can dwell with a man whose spirit is quick to anger?’ (Proverbs XXII). For he who does not restrain himself by human reason must necessarily live alone like a beast.

“Through anger concord is broken, as it is written: ‘An angry man produces quarrels, and an irascible man pours out sins’ (Proverbs XXIX). The irascible man pours out sins because he makes even evil people worse, provoking them carelessly to discord.

“Through anger the light of truth is lost, as it is written: ‘Let not the sun go down upon your anger’ (Ephesians IV), because when anger brings the darkness of confusion upon the mind, God hides from it the ray of his knowledge.”

This is Saint Gregory’s statement. It will be useful for elucidating certain passages of Scripture frequently cited throughout this book.]

we shall be unable to acquire either the judgment of sound discernment, or the insight of honorable contemplation, or maturity of counsel; we shall be unable to participate in life or hold fast to justice, and we shall not even be capable of spiritual and true light, because “my eye is troubled because of anger” (Psalm XXX).

Nor shall we become participants in wisdom, even though, in the opinion of all, we may be pronounced wise, because “anger rests in the bosom of fools” (Ecclesiastes VII).

Nor shall we be able to attain the life of immortality, even though, by human judgment, we may be considered prudent, because “anger destroys even the prudent” (Proverbs XV, according to the Septuagint).

Nor shall we be able to maintain the restraints of justice with the mind’s discerning judgment, although everyone may regard us as perfect and holy, because “the anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God” (James I).

Nor shall we in any way be able to possess that dignity of character which is usually familiar even to the men of this world, although we may be thought noble and honorable by the privilege of our birth, because “an angry man is dishonorable” (Proverbs XI, according to the Septuagint).

Nor shall we be able to attain maturity of counsel, although we may appear serious and endowed with the highest learning, because “an angry man acts without counsel” (Proverbs XIV, according to the Septuagint).

Nor shall we be able to remain free from harmful disturbances or without sins, even if no unrest is inflicted upon us by others, because “an angry man produces quarrels, but an irascible man [Note: “Digs out.” Two manuscripts in my possession and most printed editions likewise read *effodit*. Nevertheless, the text seems to require complete restoration from Saint Gregory as *effundit*, “pours out,” just as Dionysius translated it, and as John Turrecrematus rendered it in his twenty-fifth treatise on the Rule of Saint Benedict, where he cites this entire chapter in detestation of the vice.

This reading is according to the Septuagint version. The Vulgate has: “An angry man provokes quarrels, and he who is easily moved to anger will be more prone to sin.” There is no difficulty there. Ciaconius nevertheless thinks that Cassian combined one testimony from two passages of Proverbs, taking the first part from chapter XV and the latter from chapter XXIX. He should be consulted in his notes.] digs out sins” (Proverbs XV and XXIX, according to the Septuagint).

## CHAPTER II. On those who say that anger is not harmful if we become angry with offenders, since God Himself is also said to become angry

[Col. 0325A]

We have heard certain people attempt to excuse this soul-destroying disease in such a way that they eagerly diminish it by an even more detestable interpretation of the Scriptures, saying that it is not harmful for us to become angry with offending brothers, since, they say, God Himself is said to rage and become angry against those who either refuse to know Him or knowingly despise Him—as in the passage: “And the Lord was angry with fury against His people” (Psalm 105); or when the Prophet prays, saying: “Lord, rebuke me not in Your fury, nor correct me in Your anger” (Psalms 6 and 37). They do not understand that, while wishing to grant human beings an opportunity for this deadly vice, they mix the passion of the flesh into the immensity of the divine nature and the source of all purity.

> **Note [Col. 0325B].** It would be a perverse and detestable interpretation of Scripture to suppose that, when Scripture attributes anger, indignation, fury, and zeal to God, God becomes angry in the same way as human beings, and to imagine that these movements of the mind—which the Greeks call πάθη (*pathē*), the Latins *perturbationes* (“disturbances”), others *affectiones* or *affectus* (“affections” or “feelings”), and others, more expressively from the Greek, *passiones* (“passions”)—can occur in God, and consequently to argue that anger is not vicious or blameworthy. “For the anger and zeal of God,” says Saint Augustine (*On Psalm 78* and book 15 of *The City of God*, chapter 25), “are not disturbances of God, as certain people charge Him on the basis of Scriptures they do not understand; rather, by the name ‘anger’ the punishment of iniquity is understood, and by the name ‘zeal’ the exacting of purity, lest the soul despise the law of its Lord and, fornicating, perish away from its God.” Thus these things are turbulent through the very feeling involved in human affliction, but tranquil in God’s ordering, of whom it is said: “But You, Lord of hosts, judge with tranquillity.” Thus Augustine. In this way Cassian refutes the argument that could be put forward in defence or excuse of anger, and which he says was raised by some: “God is frequently said in Scripture to become angry; therefore it is permissible to become angry, at least with sinners.” Everyone can see that there is an evident ambiguity here concerning anger, since the anger of God is of a different nature and kind from human anger. Whatever, however, may be the force of this argument, it is certain that not every anger is vicious and unlawful, since not only other holy men but also Saint Paul (Acts 23), Saint Peter (Acts 8), and Christ Himself (Matthew 22 and 23; Mark 3) are reported to have been angry. See Lactantius in his book *On the Anger of God*, where he raises the question: “If God becomes angry, why did He forbid man to become angry?” He answers it (chapter 25) in such a way that he seems to think that God becomes angry, not metaphorically but literally, like human beings—which is false. More on this below.

[Col. 0326A]

For if, when these things are said of God, they are to be understood according to a literal, fleshly, and gross meaning, then He also sleeps when it is said: “Arise; why do You sleep, O Lord?” (Psalm 44). Elsewhere it is said of Him: “Behold, He shall neither slumber nor sleep who keeps Israel” (Psalm 121). He therefore also stands,

and He sits, when He says: “Heaven is My throne, but the earth is the footstool of My feet” (Isaiah 66).

> **Note [Col. 0326B].** God is said to sit in heaven, and heaven to be God’s seat, because, like a king seated in heaven as upon a throne and manifesting His majesty and glory, He governs His kingdom—that is, the whole universe—“reaching from end to end mightily and ordering all things sweetly” (Wisdom 8).

He measures heaven with a span and encloses the earth in a handful (Isaiah 40).

> **Note [Col. 0326B].** Isaiah 40: “Who has measured the waters in His fist and weighed the heavens with a span?” Saint Jerome says there: “In calling it a fist and a span, he uses the words of human custom, so that through our words we may learn God’s power.” Since a span signifies an extended hand and a fist a contracted one, it is aptly said here that God measures the heavens with an extended hand and encloses the globe of earth and water together in a fist. Yet if heaven is considered as a globe and sphere, it may also rightly be said to be weighed with a span. Hence the diversity of the versions, concerning which Saint Jerome himself may be consulted in that passage.

And He becomes heavy with wine, when it is said: “And the Lord arose like one sleeping, like a mighty man overcome with wine” (Psalm 78).

> **Note [Col. 0326C].** A harsh metaphor and a very crude comparison for expressing the terrible vengeance of the angry God, like a drunken man saturated with wine, who mixes everything together with shouting and blows.

Yet He alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light (I Timothy 6)—to say nothing of the ignorance

> **Note [Col. 0326C].** Isaiah 58: “Why have we fasted, and You have not looked upon us? We have humbled our souls, and You have not known?” Matthew 25: “I do not know you.” I Corinthians 14: “If anyone is ignorant, he shall be ignored.” For God’s knowing means approving, and His not knowing means rejecting, says Saint Gregory (*Morals*, book 28, chapter 7). Hence among theologians there is the term “knowledge of approval,” by which God is said to know or acknowledge what He approves, and not to know what He does not approve.

and forgetfulness

God is said to forget us when He acts toward us as though He had forgotten us; conversely, He is said to remember when He acts toward us as though He had previously forgotten us and later remembered us—that is, when He hears us as we pray and shows that He wills us well.

which we frequently read attributed to Him in the holy Scriptures; then there are the features of bodily members, which are described as though He were a figured and composite human being,

namely, hair, head and nostrils, eyes and face, hands and arms, fingers, belly, and feet. ## CHAPTER IV. How we should understand the human affections and members that we read ascribed to the immutable and incorporeal God

Thus, since these things cannot be understood literally without unspeakable sacrilege concerning Him who is defined by the authority of the holy Scriptures as invisible, ineffable, incomprehensible, inestimable, simple, and uncompounded, neither can the disturbance of fury and anger be fitted to that immutable nature without enormous blasphemy.

> **Note [Col. 0327C].** There were certain heretics of exceedingly crude understanding who attributed a human appearance to God and believed God to be corporeal and composed of human members, because God is portrayed in sacred Scripture in human form and both human members and the bodily actions of members are very often attributed to Him. They were therefore called *anthropomorphites*, from the Greek term, because they imagined God to be ἀνθρωπόμορφον (*anthrōpomorphon*), that is, endowed with human form (Socrates, book 6, chapter 7; Sozomen, book 8, chapters 11 and 12; Nicephorus, book 11, chapter 14). Concerning them Saint Jerome says in Letter 61: “The anthropomorphites, in rustic simplicity, believe that God possesses the members that are written of Him in the divine books” (Jerome, Letters 61 and 65). Augustine, in his book *On Heresies*, says that the anthropomorphites were so called because they imagined God in carnal thought, in the likeness of the image of corruptible man. Epiphanius attributes this to their rusticity, sparing them the designation of heretics (Epiphanius, *Heresy* 20). Thus Augustine. Sozomen writes that some Egyptian monks were deceived by this error around the year 400, among them Serapion, otherwise a most holy man who had spent fifty years in the desert; yet, being simple and uneducated, he could scarcely be recalled from this foolish belief except through the efforts of Blessed Paphnutius and the prayers and exhortations of other monks, as Cassian reports (*Conferences*, 10.2 and following). This error was rejected by the holy Fathers and rightly condemned by the entire Church, since it is clear not only from Scripture (John 4) but also from natural reason that God is spirit, incorporeal, incomprehensible, invisible, and free from all matter and corporeal form (Saint Thomas, *Summa*, part I, question 3, article 1; Lateran Council, chapter *Firmiter*; Damascene, *Orthodox Faith*, book 1, chapter 12). Hence the Author rightly concludes that, just as the members and bodily actions attributed to God in Scripture must be understood not according to the letter and sound of the words but mystically and symbolically, to signify His incorporeal and spiritual powers and operations, which are in some way similar to those performed by us through such members and affections, so also anger, fury, hatred, and similar things are not attributed to God in the manner and sense in which they are attributed to man, but must be understood tropically and figuratively.

For we must understand by such expressions of members the divine effects and God’s immense operations, which cannot be communicated to us except through these familiar terms for members. Thus, by the expression “mouth,” we are to understand His conversations, which are customarily infused mercifully into the secret perceptions of the soul; or we may recognize that He spoke likewise through our fathers and prophets. By “eyes,” we are to understand the immensity of His insight, by which He surveys and perceives everything, so that we may know that nothing of what is done, is to be done, or is thought by us escapes Him. By the designation “hands,” we are to understand His providence and operation, by which He Himself is the Creator and Maker of all things. His arm signifies the marks of His power and government, by which He sustains, regulates, and governs all things. And, to say nothing of the rest, what does the white hair of His head signify except the longevity and antiquity of the Godhead,

[Col. 0328B]

which exists without any beginning and surpasses all times and creatures?

> **Note [Col. 0328B].** Thus Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book 1, chapter 14: “Since we find many things spoken corporeally of God in sacred Scripture symbolically, mystically, and signifyingly, we must know that, because we ourselves are surrounded by a coarse garment of flesh, we are quite unable either to understand or to express God’s divine, subtle, and immaterial operations unless we use images, forms, and significant words according to our custom. Whatever, therefore, is said corporeally of God is said symbolically; yet it possesses a higher meaning, for the Godhead is simple and has no form.” Thus he. See also Gregory, *Morals*, book 32, chapter 4. He then explains in detail how the human members, senses, actions, and affections attributed to God are to be understood mystically. At the end of the chapter, however, he warns that this applies when such things are understood as being said of God according to the divine nature; for of Christ our Lord and Saviour, according to His human nature, they are said truly and properly, not figuratively or tropically. “For He,” he says, “assumed the whole man for our salvation: soul, intellect, and body, together with the properties of human nature and its natural and innocent affections. Therefore these things are attributed to Christ and man not allegorically but according to the truth of the matter.”

Thus, when we read of the anger or fury of God, we must not understand it

> **Note [Col. 0328D].** The adverb *non anthropopathōs* is used not only by the Greek Fathers but also by Saint Jerome (*On Jeremiah*, chapter 32), to signify that God is not angry in the manner of human beings, because He does not undergo the affection or movement of anger—called *pathos* (πάθος) by the Greeks—which is wont to arise in human beings, but displays only its effect. For God is said to be angry and enraged when, without any disturbance, He does what human beings do under the impulse of fury: that is, when He strikes, destroys, and annihilates. Hence Saint Jerome (*On Ephesians*, chapter 4): “Fury and anger, although they are often spoken of in God (according to: ‘Lord, rebuke me not in Your fury, nor correct me in Your anger’ [Psalm 6]), are not to be reckoned disturbances of mind as they are in us, because in Him all things are measured and ordered; and the punishment by which sinners are corrected is called by our terms. But if we become angry, we are disturbed and, seized by fury, cease to be ourselves.”

ἀνθρωποπαθῶς (*anthrōpopathōs*), that is, according to the abasement of human disturbance,

[Col. 0329A]

but in a manner worthy of God, who is free from every disturbance. We must understand it, namely, in such a way that through these expressions we may perceive Him as the judge and avenger of all that is wickedly done in this world, and, fearing in these verbal signs the terrible retributor of our deeds, may fear to commit anything against His will.

Human nature is accustomed to fear those whom it knows to be indignant and whom it fears to offend, just as, among certain very just judges, avenging anger is usually feared by those who are stung by some guilt in their conscience—not because such a disturbance exists in the minds of those who are going to judge justly, but because those who fear in this way experience the feeling that proceeds for the execution of laws, the examination of justice, and the weighing of equity. Yet however great the gentleness and mildness with which this may be expressed, those who are to be punished according to their deserts judge it to be severe fury and most savage anger.

It would be a long task, and not part of the present work, to explain everything that is figuratively said of God in the Scriptures through human modes of expression. What has been said here concerning the present need, against the vice of fury, should suffice, so that no one may thereafter through ignorance draw upon himself an occasion of disease and everlasting death from the very place where the remedies of holiness, immortality, life, and salvation are sought.

## CHAPTER V. What degree of gentleness is fitting for a monk

Thus the monk who is striving toward perfection and earnestly desires to engage lawfully in spiritual combat should be free from every vice of anger and fury, and should hear what the chosen Vessel commands him:

> **Note [Col. 0329B].** This sentence has both a varied reading and a varied interpretation. The Greek manuscripts, reversing the order, place “anger” and “indignation”; in Greek the first part reads: πᾶσα πικρία, καὶ θυμός, καὶ ὀργή (*pasa pikria, kai thymos, kai orgē*). See Basil, *On the Institution of Monks*, chapter 78. Saint Jerome reads: “All bitterness, fury, and anger,” and distinguishes them in this way: Bitterness is opposed to sweetness, which is why bitter people are commonly so called. Fury is beginning anger, boiling up in the mind—indignation. Anger, of which bitterness and fury are forms, seeks vengeance after the fury has subsided and wishes to harm the one whom it thinks has done the injury. Thus Saint Jerome. But, adhering with Cassian to the Vulgate reading and elucidating the individual parts of this sentence somewhat, it is certain that these words designate different degrees and affections of anger. Bitterness, or *amarulentia*, Greek πικρία (*pikria*), properly means sadness clinging to and fixed in the mind through the continual and prolonged remembrance of an injury inflicted or received. Those are called bitter who retain for a long time the sadness conceived from an offense and consequently the anger that seeks a remedy for sadness (Saint Thomas, on this passage and *Summa* II–II, question 158, article 5). Hence Ecclesiasticus 21 says: “There is no understanding where there is bitterness.” And the gloss on Matthew 5, explaining “Blessed are the meek,” says: “Meekness is a sweetness of mind that is not overcome by bitterness.” Saint Benedict calls this “the evil zeal of bitterness,” which separates from God and leads to hell (*Rule*, chapter 72); here, however, this evil zeal also includes envy, as will be said in its place. Anger, or ὀργή (*orgē*), is the disordered desire for vengeance itself—not merely natural but voluntary—which includes many kinds of anger, as will be said below. Indignation is the contempt and disparagement of the person against whom we are angry, as though he were unworthy of our suffering such a thing from him. Joined to this is mental swelling, by which the angry person exalts himself and prefers himself to the other (Leonard Lessius, *On Justice*, book 4, chapter 4). Anger causes the offended person to regard and exalt himself as great, and the offender as worthless and contemptible. Hence Saint Gregory lists both among the daughters of anger, as we noted above. Clamor is the voice of angry people shouting without judgment or shame (*Morals*, book 5, chapter 1, and this book, chapter 1). Concerning it Isaiah 5 says: “I expected him to make judgment, and behold, iniquity; and justice, and behold, a cry.” Blasphemy—that is, cursing, whether against God and the saints or against one’s neighbours—also arises from anger and is numbered among the daughters of anger. Hence Saint Jerome, in the passage cited above, says: “After bitterness, fury, and anger, clamor and blasphemy are rightly also forbidden among us, because one who has once been overcome by fury must burst into clamor and, roaring turbulently, be tossed here and there like a leaf in the wind, saying: ‘O injustice of things! O unjust judgments of God!’ and other such words as those who have lost the judgment of their mind through the fury of indignation commonly utter.” These and other things are said by Saint Jerome. Since it would have been lengthy to enumerate everything, the Apostle added: “With all malice,” including the remaining vices under this name. Saint Gregory, however, understands malice as an interior evil or perverse will to harm, distinguishing it from the exterior vices named previously. Thus he writes (*Pastoral Care*, part 3, chapter 10): “When the eminent Doctor was urging patience upon his disciples, saying, ‘Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, clamor, and blasphemy be taken away from you,’ as though all exterior things had already been well ordered, he turns to interior matters when he adds: ‘With all malice.’ For it is useless to remove indignation, clamor, and blasphemy from the outside if malice, the mother of vices, rules within. And it is useless to cut wickedness away from the branches outside if it is preserved within at the root, where it will multiply and return.” The Apostle used another similar sentence in Colossians 3, expressing nearly all the same individual vices belonging to anger, though in a different order, in these words: “But now put away from you all of them: anger, indignation, malice, blasphemy, shameful speech,” and so forth.

“For,” he says, “let all anger, indignation, clamor, and blasphemy be taken away from you, together with all malice” (Ephesians 4).

> **Note [Col. 0330C].** Cassian seems by these words to wish to exclude all anger and to place it among the vices. This appears to be supported both by the Apostle’s statement just explained and by other passages of Scripture. Yet if what precedes is compared with what follows and examined more carefully, it is sufficiently clear that he did not wish to condemn absolutely and without qualification all anger, but only the vice of anger—that is, vicious or disordered anger—and that he especially commends meekness, the moderator of anger, to monks striving toward perfection. For in these books he is dealing with capital vices, as is well known and as the title indicates; therefore he deals with anger only insofar as it is a vice and sin. Hence he does not say that a monk must be free from all anger, but from every vice of anger and fury; and below he teaches (chapters 7 and 8) that we should become angry with our vices and defects, and in chapter 7 he praises David because he was moved by holy indignation against the bitter suggestion of Abishai (II Samuel 16). Therefore it should be carefully observed and committed to memory, following the teaching of Saint Gregory (*Morals*, book 5, chapter 33), that one anger is aroused by impatience, while another is formed by zeal for justice: the former arises from vice, the latter from virtue. For if no anger arose from virtue, Phinehas would not have appeased the assault of divine judgment with the sword. Because Eli did not possess this anger, he aroused the movement of heavenly vengeance implacably against himself. Of this anger the Psalmist says: “Be angry and do not sin” (Psalm 4). Those who wish us to become angry only with ourselves, and not also with neighbours who offend, certainly do not understand this correctly. If we are commanded to love our neighbours as ourselves, it follows that we should be angry with their errors just as with our own vices. Saint Gregory says these and other things to the same effect. Here the reader should first observe that in the final words quoted, Cassian—or those who misunderstand Cassian and think that it is permissible to become angry only with ourselves or our own errors, and not also with neighbours who err and offend—is silently reproved, since the reason is the same in both cases. For if we become angry with ourselves because of an offense against God, why should we not become angry for the same reason with neighbours who offend God? Secondly, from the preceding words we learn that anger is of two kinds: one good and consonant with reason, the other evil and vicious. Anger is good and praiseworthy, first, when we strongly resist the devil and his suggestions and crush the serpent’s head at its very beginning, as was said elsewhere. Thus Christ angrily repelled the tempter, saying: “Go, Satan; for it is written,” and so forth (Matthew 4).
