Second, when we are angry with ourselves—that is, with our depraved affections, desires, and vices—and, as Cassian says (below, chapters 7 and 8), indignantly rage against the wanton movements of our soul and bring forth fruits worthy of repentance. Third, when we are moved toward offending brothers or neighbours by zeal for justice or charity and either correct them fraternally or punish subjects in accordance with our office. Scripture commonly calls this kind of anger the zeal of God. Because of it, not only Moses, Phinehas, Samuel, David, Elijah, and other holy men are greatly commended, but Christ the Lord Himself repeatedly displayed it: when He looked around at the Jews with anger and was grieved over the hardness and blindness of their hearts (Mark 3); when He drove the buyers and sellers from the Temple (Matthew 21 and John 2); when He attacked the Pharisees and scribes with that bitter and repeatedly uttered denunciation and curse: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees!” (Matthew 23 and Luke 11); and when He rebuked the Apostle Peter so harshly for trying to dissuade Him from His Passion: “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling-block to me” (Matthew 16). I omit the other examples of the saints whom Scripture records as having been angry in a holy and beneficial way. There is therefore a kind of anger that is good, useful, and necessary, which we either assume or admit according to reason; it must consequently be called a virtue, not a vice. Neither the Apostle nor Cassian excludes or condemns it, but they condemn vicious and disordered anger, which suppresses the judgment of reason or does not obey it. This happens in many ways, both on the part of the object and on the part of the movement or impulse of anger, as has been said. On the part of the object, anger is evil and sinful: first, if someone desires or takes unjust vengeance, for an illegitimate reason or against one who has not deserved it; second, if he desires just vengeance—that is, vengeance for a just cause—but more severe than the fault deserves. This is called cruelty or savageness of spirit in exacting punishment. Concerning this Seneca says in book 2 of *On Clemency*: “I shall call those cruel who have a reason for punishing but no moderation,” as in the case of Phalaris, who, they say, was savage not indeed against innocent people, but beyond the human and probable measure. To this belongs what Saint Benedict—whose statements relevant to the matter I gladly adopt—ordains concerning boys, or, as he calls them, infants, up to their fifteenth year: that diligent discipline should be applied and maintained, but, he says, “with all measure and reason.” For anyone of more mature age—that is, over fifteen—who presumes in any way to strike someone without the abbot’s command, or who becomes violently inflamed against the infants without discretion—that is, exceeds the proper measure—must submit to regular discipline, because it is written: “What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to another.” Third, anger is sinful if someone exacts punishment by private authority or without legitimate power and according to the proper legal order. Vengeance belongs to the judge as God’s minister and is therefore forbidden to private persons. Romans 12 says: “Do not avenge yourselves” (Greek ἐκδικοῦντες, that is, taking vengeance), beloved, “but give place to wrath. For it is written: Vengeance is Mine; I will repay.” Fourth, anger is sinful if punishment is not imposed with a right intention—namely, so that the neighbour may be corrected, justice and discipline maintained, and both the offender and others restrained from injury in the future—but from hatred and ill will, that is, with the intention that harm should come to him. For that is the act of hatred and contrary to love of neighbour. This is the sense in which we commonly speak of anger when we say that it is unlawful to become angry: hence ordinary anger is called a movement of the mind wishing evil upon another because of an injury received and seeking vengeance for pain. But one also sins in various ways on the part of the movement or impulse of anger itself, when it either boils over excessively or lasts longer than is fitting. For this reason Saint Gregory (*Morals*, book 5, chapter 32) distinguishes and depicts four kinds or degrees of anger in these words: “It should be known,” he says, “that anger kindles some people more quickly and abandons them more easily, while it moves others slowly but holds them longer. Some resemble reeds set alight: while they resound with their voices, they give forth, as it were, certain sounds of their kindling; they quickly produce a flame, but immediately grow cold into ash. Others are like heavier and harder pieces of wood: they are slow to catch fire, but once ignited they are more difficult to extinguish, and because they are slower to flare into harshness, they preserve the fire of their fury longer. Others, which is worse, both catch the flames of anger quickly and lay them aside slowly. Some, however, are slow to receive these flames and quick to lose them. In these four modes the reader clearly recognizes that, in relation to the good of tranquillity, the last approaches it more closely than the first, while in evil the third surpasses the second.” Thus Gregory. See Damascene, book 2 of *On the Faith*, chapter 16, and Saint Thomas, *Summa* I–II, question 46, article 8, and II–II, question 158, article 5. Cassian, moreover, distinguishes three kinds of anger on another basis in *Conference* 5, chapter 11, as may be seen there. From what has been said it is easy to understand in what sense the Apostle wished all anger to be excluded and removed from us, since there are so many and varied kinds of anger and so many sins. In the same sense Cassian said that no anger at all should be excepted for us as necessary or useful. He intends nothing different from the Apostle; otherwise he would contradict himself and his own writings, since he himself makes several exceptions. But because in these books he is engaged in portraying the true and perfect monk in vivid colours and in urging and inflaming all monks toward the pursuit of perfection, in which the highest achievement of the religious state consists, he took every measure to propose and inculcate those things that belong to evangelical perfection and that most befit and adorn a monk—above all, that he should strive, as far as he can, to restrain, tame, and mortify the depraved movements of his soul, especially anger and irascibility; that he should display meekness, modesty, and patience in all things; and that he should always maintain a peaceful and tranquil spirit. The abbot John, a true and perfect monk and hermit, taught this by his example. When another elder said to him, “The sun has never seen me eating,” he replied, “Nor has it seen me angry,” as Cassian reports (*Conferences*, book 5, chapter 27). Saint Augustine offers this salutary teaching to the same effect in Letter 149: “It is much better for us not to become angry with anyone even justly than, by becoming angry as though justly, to slip through the hidden ease of anger into hatred of someone. When receiving unknown guests, we commonly say that it is much better to endure a bad person than perhaps, through ignorance, to exclude a good one while taking care not to receive the bad. But with the affections of the soul the opposite is true: it is incomparably safer not to open the inner chamber of the heart even to anger that knocks justly than to admit an anger that will not easily withdraw and will proceed from a splinter to a beam. For it boldly and shamelessly grows more quickly than one might think.” Thus Augustine.

When he says, “Let all anger be taken away from you,” he made no exception whatsoever for any anger as necessary or useful to us.

> **Note [Col. 0332D].** Saint Gregory, commenting on Job 36, “Let not anger overcome you, so that you oppress anyone,” says: “Everyone who must correct the vices of another ought first to examine himself carefully, lest, while avenging the faults of others, he himself be overcome by the fury of vengeance. Very often the savagery of anger devastates the mind under the pretext of justice; and while it appears to rage through zeal for righteousness, it fills out the madness of fury and thinks that whatever anger wickedly dictates is justly done. Hence it often exceeds the proper measure of vengeance, because it is not restrained by the measure of justice. It is fitting that, when we correct the faults of others, we should first measure our own, so that the mind may first cool from its own kindling and first reconcile within itself the impulse of its zeal with tranquil equity. Otherwise, if we are dragged by abrupt fury to punish vices, we sin by correcting sin; and, while pursuing guilt in judgment, we rage by striking immoderately. In the correction of vices, indignation should be beneath the mind, not above it, so that it may follow in service rather than precede by domination the execution of justice; and so that it may fulfil a recognized judgment as its servant, not rush ahead as its master. It is therefore rightly said: ‘Let not anger overcome you, so that you oppress anyone’; for if the one who attempts to correct is overcome by anger, he oppresses before he corrects. When he is kindled more than he should be under the pretext of just vengeance, he is driven without restraint into savage cruelty.” Thus Gregory. Isidore has similar remarks in book 3 of *The Supreme Good*, chapter 40. See Saint Thomas, *Summa* II–II, question 33, article 5.

And if it is necessary, he should hasten to care for his offending brother in such a way that, while trying to provide a remedy to one suffering perhaps from a slight fever, he does not, in anger, entangle himself in the worse disease of blindness. For the one who wishes to heal another’s wound must remain entirely free from every disease and sound, lest the evangelical saying be applied to him:

> **Note [Col. 0333C].** A proverb commonly repeated in different words: “Physician, heal yourself,” customarily directed against those who chastise and attack the vices of others while themselves dripping with hidden vices, says Erasmus (*Chiliades* 2, century 5). In the same sense, and almost in the same words, the Jews mocked Christ crucified, saying: “He saved others; let him save himself” (Matthew 27; Luke 23). There is a similar proverb cited by Plutarch from a certain tragedy; Suidas attributes it to Euripides:

> Ἄλλων ἰατρὸς, αὐτὸς ἕλκεσι βρύων.
>
> A physician to others, but himself teeming with sores.

“By healing others, while himself covered with ulcers.” Considering this proverb, St. Gregory Nazianzen, in Oration 1, *Apologeticus de fuga sua*, says: “We must take care not to depart far from the proverb, attempting to heal others while we ourselves are covered with ulcers.”

The Apostle likewise uses a similar maxim in Romans 2 to prick and reproach the Jew, and anyone who acts contrary to his own teaching:

“You who teach others, do you not teach yourself? You who preach against stealing, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege? You who boast in the law, do you dishonor God through transgressing the law?”

And at the beginning of the same chapter:

“Therefore you are inexcusable, O man—every one who judges. For in judging another, you condemn yourself, since you do the very things that you judge.”

See St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* II–II, question 33, on fraternal correction.

“Physician, first heal yourself”; and, seeing the splinter in his brother’s eye, let him not see the beam in his own eye. Or how will he see to remove the splinter from his brother’s eye, when he carries the beam of anger in his own eye? (Luke 4; Matthew 7).

[Note: St. Augustine, *On the Sermon on the Mount*, book 2, chapter 30: “We must watch carefully and piously, so that when necessity compels us to rebuke or reprimand someone, we first consider whether the fault is one that we have never had, or from which we are now free. If we have never had it, let us consider that we too are human and could have had it. But if we have had it and no longer have it, let the common weakness of humanity touch our memory, so that mercy, not hatred, precedes that rebuke or reprimand—whether it proves effective for the correction of the person on whose behalf we act, or for his ruin (for the outcome is uncertain); nevertheless, we should be secure in the single-mindedness of our eye.” Thus Augustine.

Pagan writers also gave this warning, as Horace, book 1 of the *Satires* (Satire 3):

“While you are bleary-eyed and salving your own faults,  
why do you see so sharply into the faults of your friends,  
as either the eagle or the Epidaurian serpent?”

And Marcus Tullius: “He who is prepared to speak against another ought himself to be free from every fault.”

The same point is made by St. Jerome: “That is true correction among friends: while not seeing our own purse, we examine the wallet of others, as Persius says.”

Here Jerome alludes (*Letter* 91) to Persius:

“No one tries to descend into himself alone—  
but the wallet is seen hanging on the back before him.”

[Note: St. Augustine, in his commentary on Psalm 25, writes: “If you become angry with your servant because he has sinned, lest you yourself sin also, become angry with yourself” (see St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* II–II, question 46, article 7). Elsewhere, on Psalm 4: “I want you to be angry, but not so that you sin. But if you are not to sin, with whom should you be angry except yourselves? For what is a repentant person other than someone angry with himself? To receive pardon, he demands punishment from himself.”]

## Chapter VI. On the unjust or just arousal of anger

[Note: Understand this as St. Gregory explains it (*Moralia*, book 5, chapter 33): “Anger through vice blinds the eye of the mind, but anger through zeal disturbs it. For zeal itself for uprightness, because it agitates the mind with unrest, immediately obscures its keenness, so that in its agitation it does not see the higher things which it had previously seen well in tranquillity.” And below: “But when the mind is moved by zeal, the greatest care must be taken lest anger, which is taken up as an instrument of virtue, dominate the mind; lest it go before as mistress, rather than, like a handmaid ready for service, never depart from the rear of the plough.” See St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* II–II, question 158, article 1, reply to objection 2.]

Every anger that boils up from whatever cause blinds the eyes of the heart and, imposing upon the sharpness of its sight the beam of a more powerful disease, does not allow it to behold the Sun of righteousness.

It makes no difference whether a sheet of gold, lead, or any other metal is placed before the eyes: the preciousness of the metals does not alter the kind of blindness.

We have, in fact, been given a useful function of anger, and it is beneficial and salutary for us to receive it only for this purpose: when we angrily rage against the lustful movements of our heart, and are indignant that the things we are ashamed to do or say before men have arisen in the hidden places of our breast—while we tremble with complete fear before the presence of the angels and of God himself, whose eye penetrates everywhere and all things, and from whom the secrets of our conscience can in no way be hidden.

[Note: St. Jerome writes that St. Hilarion, while still very young and living in the desert, restrained the wanton movements of the flesh with holy and austere indignation:

“The devil tickled his senses and suggested to his adolescent body the customary fires of pleasure. The young soldier of Christ was compelled to think about what he did not know and to turn over in his mind the pageantry of something whose experience he had never had. Thus, angry with himself and beating his breast with his fists—as though he could drive out his thoughts by killing them with his hands—he said: ‘I shall make you, little donkey, stop kicking. I shall not feed you with barley, but with straw; I shall wear you out with hunger and thirst; I shall load you with a heavy burden, so that you will think about food rather than lust.’” (*Life of Hilarion*)]

## Chapter VII. In what respect anger is necessary for us alone, and by what examples of blessed David anger may be healthily employed

[Note: There is an iambic poem of considerable length against anger in Gregory Nazianzen, teaching that one should be angry with anger itself when it is stirred up in us contrary to or apart from reason. It begins:

“I am angry with anger, the demon concealed within;
for this alone is righteous bile among them all
(if it is necessary to endure something that the mind can bear).”

Explaining this, Billius says: “Since matters are so arranged by custom that scarcely anyone can be found in whom the passion of anger does not sometimes arise, this alone must be considered just: anger conceived not against those who have inflicted some injury upon us, but against anger itself.”]

Or certainly, when we are moved against this very anger because it has crept into us against our brother, we become angry and drive out its deadly instigations; we do not allow it to maintain harmful hiding places in the recesses of our breast.

The prophet also teaches us to be angry in this way. He had driven anger so far from his own feelings that he preferred not to repay even his personal enemies, although they had been delivered into his power:

[Note: Augustine teaches that this can be understood in two ways. “Either,” he says, “‘Be angry and do not sin’ (Psalm 4): even if a movement of the spirit arises which, because it is the punishment of sin, is no longer within our control, at least reason and the mind, regenerated inwardly according to God, should not consent to it; or, do penance—that is, be angry with yourselves for past sins, and cease to sin thereafter.” This latter interpretation was also approved by Cassian.

Isidore of Pelusium gives four interpretations of the same saying in one of his letters (*Letter* 239, book 2, according to Billius’s translation):

“This passage, ‘Be angry and do not sin,’ seems to me to have several meanings.

“First, it may be understood absolutely and definitively, or as a form of advice; for example: ‘Be angry—and why are you angry? Therefore do not be angry, so that you may not sin.’

“Second, it may signify this: since the passion of anger is violent and can extraordinarily carry away the soul—for it often outruns reason and arises almost against our will—quiet it by reason or subsequent reflection, not bursting out into vengeance but ending in gentleness and mercy.

“Third, it may mean: ‘Be angry with this passion, which is troublesome and hostile to you, and especially with pleasure, and you will not sin.’ For if it finds you weakened and lax, it will overcome you without difficulty; but if it finds you watchful and sober, and angry with it, it will depart at once.

“Fourth, it may also be explained as an imperative. For when we avenge our own injuries, we exceed the proper measure in taking revenge; but when the matter concerns divine glory or the vindication of those who suffer injury, then we feign fear and calmness and become mute and sluggish, so that there is scarcely any difference between us and stones. Therefore, he says: ‘Be angry justly, but do not sin’—that is, do not conceal the sins of others of which you are aware, nor abuse this aid to avenge private injuries.”

Thus he writes, with a few omissions.]

“Be angry,” he says, “and do not sin” (Psalm 4).

When he had desired water from the cistern of Bethlehem and had received it from brave men who had fetched it through the midst of the enemy ranks, he immediately poured it out upon the ground. Thus, becoming angry and extinguishing the passionate desire of his appetite, he offered it to the Lord and did not satisfy his longing, saying:

“May the Lord be gracious to me, that I should not do this. Shall I drink the blood of these men who went at the risk of their lives?” (2 Samuel 23).

[Note: St. Ambrose, commending this remarkable example of mortification in his book *On Saint Jacob*, chapter 1, writes:

“Whom shall we choose from among men as better and stronger than holy David? He could not take for himself the water he had desired from the well of Bethlehem, which was shut off by the enemy army, but he could restrain his desire. For although we do not find that others lacked water—that is, although there was so large an army, and although the king could have obtained water from many other springs—he suffered an irrational desire and longed for water surrounded by the enemy, from which it could not be brought without the greatest danger.

“Therefore he said: ‘Who will give me a drink from the well that is in Bethlehem by the gate?’ When three men were found who broke through the enemy camp and brought the water he had desired so greatly, he recognized that the water had cost him the danger of others and poured it out to the Lord, lest he seem to drink the blood of those who had brought it. This shows that desire anticipates reason, but reason resists desire.”

Thus Ambrose, in agreement with this passage.]

Or when Shimei, in David’s hearing, hurled stones and curses at King David before everyone, and Abishai, son of Zeruiah and commander of the army, wished to avenge the royal insult by cutting off Shimei’s head, blessed David was moved by holy indignation against this terrible suggestion, yet preserved the measure of humility and the firmness of patience with unshaken gentleness, saying:

“What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Let him alone, and let him curse. For the Lord has commanded him to curse David. Who then can say, ‘Why have you done this?’ Behold, my son who came from my body seeks my life; how much more this son of Benjamin! Let him alone, and let him curse, according to the Lord’s command, if perhaps the Lord will look upon my affliction and repay me good for this cursing today” (2 Samuel 16; 19).

[Note: How did the Lord tell Shimei to curse David (2 Samuel 16)? Who is wise enough to understand? He did not say it by command, in which case obedience would be praised; rather, because by his just and hidden judgment he inclined Shimei’s will—which was already evil through its own fault—toward this sin, Scripture therefore says that the Lord told him.

For if Shimei had obeyed a command, he would have deserved praise rather than punishment, as we know from the fact that he was later punished. Thus Augustine, *On Grace and Free Will*, chapter 20.

It is said that God inclined Shimei’s will to curse David, not by inciting or compelling him, but by permitting it, although he could easily have prevented it. Moreover, because he allowed Shimei’s perverse will—which was inclined toward many crimes—to undertake and carry out this one act among the many to which it was prepared, he did so in order to punish David. Similarly, when the devil asked permission to afflict Job, God granted him not everything he desired but only what was limited by these words (Job 1): “Behold, all that he has is in your hand; only do not stretch out your hand against him.” See Bellarmine, *On the Loss of Grace*, book 2, chapter 13.]

## Chapter VIII. On the anger we should take up against ourselves

[Note: St. Augustine writes similarly in his commentary on Psalm 25: “If you become angry with your servant because he has sinned, lest you yourself sin, become angry with yourself” (see St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* II–II, question 46, article 7). Elsewhere, on Psalm 4: “I want you to be angry, but not so that you sin. But if you are not to sin, with whom should you be angry except yourselves? For what is a repentant person other than someone angry with himself? To receive pardon, he demands punishment from himself.”]

We are therefore commanded to be healthily angry, but with ourselves and with the evil suggestions that approach us; and not to sin—that is, not to bring them to a harmful completion.

Finally, the following verse explains this same meaning more clearly:

[Note: Basil on this passage: “Correct in the time of rest, upon your beds, the evil plans you devise during the day, and conduct an examination of yourselves. Why did he speak not of words and deeds but of evil thoughts? He said this by way of emphasis: if evil plans must be corrected, the soul must be pierced with remorse much more because of deeds and words.” Thus Basil, whose view is also supported by Cassian.

That David was accustomed to recall and mourn his sins at night in his bed, because of the opportunity provided by nocturnal solitude and silence, is clearly inferred from the words of Psalm 6: “Every night I will wash my bed; I will water my couch with my tears.” See St. Jerome below, on Ephesians 4.]

“Whatever you say in your hearts, feel remorse upon your beds”; that is, whatever you think in your hearts when sudden and slippery instigations arise, remove all the noise and disturbance of rage by the moderation of reason; and, as though placed in the bed of rest, correct and amend these thoughts with the most salutary remorse.

Finally, the blessed Apostle, using the testimony of this verse, after saying, “Be angry and do not sin,” added:

[Note: Cassian gives three interpretations of this saying. He accepts the first and second but rejects and refutes the third.

The first is allegorical: by the sun is understood the Lord Christ, the true Sun of righteousness rising from on high, of whom Wisdom 5, Malachi 4, and Amos 8 speak, and who “enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1). He is said to set upon our anger when, because of the excess of anger, he withdraws from us and removes the rays of his grace.

The second is tropological: by the name “sun” is signified our mind, or the light of reason within us, which is like the sun and light, according to Luke 11: “See, therefore, that the light which is in you is not darkness.” It is metaphorically said to set and become dark when anger takes possession of and blinds the judgment of reason, placing a person, so to speak, outside himself, so that, walking as if in darkness and blind night, he does not know what he is doing or where he is going, according to the poet:

“‘Anger obstructs the mind, so that it cannot perceive the truth.’

“St. Gregory also confirms this interpretation (*Moralia*, book 3, chapter 31): ‘Through anger the light of truth is lost, as it is written: “Let not the sun set upon your anger”; for when anger inflicts the darkness of confusion upon the mind, God hides from it the ray of his knowledge.’

“The third is literal, referring to the physical and visible sun, the great luminary whose rising and setting distinguish days and nights. But, as I said, Cassian excludes this interpretation at the end of the following chapter, and St. Jerome seems to support him. He writes on this passage:

“‘If we understand this simply of the sun that is seen by bodily eyes, we sin when we become angry and our anger persists after the sun has set. But we do not sin when, for example, from the first hour until the eleventh, we remain angry and do whatever indignation, fury, and anger suggest. Nothing could be more absurd than this interpretation, as though someone could not rage from sunrise to sunset in crimes so great that he could not expiate them with tears throughout his entire life; or as though anger had more room during the day, when night is naturally a rest from fury and, as sleep follows, even if we are angry, we postpone our anger until the day.’

“Therefore, since the true sun, just as it sets upon evil prophets, according to the words, ‘The sun has set upon your prophets at midday’ (Amos 8), also sets upon all sinners, never granting them the light of its rising, the Apostle now commands us not to do such things when overcome by fury that the sun may set for us and the governing principle of the heart be enveloped in darkness.”

Thus far St. Jerome.

Yet, with due respect to so great a man and also to our Cassian, the true and proper meaning of this passage seems to be that expressed by the words taken in their proper sense—namely, that it concerns the physical and visible sun, which is properly said to set upon our anger when we retain anger against our neighbor even after sunset and await an opportunity for revenge.

This is a figurative expression and, as it appears, a proverbial saying familiar among the people. The Apostle wished to warn us that, if during the day we have been stirred up or angered against someone, we should at least make every effort to be reconciled with him before evening and sunset; laying aside all anger and ill will, we should return to mutual concord and friendship.

It does not follow that it is permissible, or that it is not sinful, to become angry or to carry anger through to its completion—that is, to take revenge—before sunset or even at night. Rather, the opposite is implied: anger must be laid aside immediately and without delay, and reconciliation must be restored.

It is as though someone said to a wounded or sick man, using the same phrase: “See that the sun does not set upon your wound, or upon your illness, without medical care.” This does not mean that he should wait until evening before going to or summoning a physician; rather, it means that he should do so as soon as possible. But if he cannot do so sooner, he should at least do it before sunset, lest the wound or illness grow worse.

Nor does St. Jerome entirely reject this interpretation. After what has been said, he adds:

“Some think that this should be understood simply, in the same way as the passage from Psalm 4 from which it seems to have been taken: ‘Whatever you say in your hearts, and upon your beds feel remorse’—that is, whatever you sin during the day, in deed, speech, or thought, cleanse it during the night by the coming of repentance, and let your anger be brief; let it not be deferred until the following day.”

And in Letter 36, referring to this same passage, he says:

“What shall we do on the day of judgment, upon whose anger the sun has set not for one day but for so many years?”

St. Chrysostom likewise explains these words:

“Let not the sun set upon your anger”—that is, “Let this departing sun not leave you as enemies.”

St. Ambrose agrees, writing in his commentary on the Psalms:

“Another physician says: ‘Let not the sun set upon your anger,’ lest, while you delay for a long time, he come who is accustomed to awaken a body warmed by sleep”—namely, the devil—“and stir you up, implant thoughts in you, and plunge into the hidden places of your breast, saying: ‘Avenge your injury. Recognize that you are a man; it is a woman’s weakness not to take revenge. So, your servant was supposed to despise you? Your brother to deceive you? Your friend to mock you?’”

Ambrose plainly explains the Apostle’s saying of the physical sun, whose setting ends the day and brings on night. He also suggests why anger should not be retained until sunset: lest, during the interval of night, after rest, we be provoked by the devil with sharper goads to seek revenge.

Finally, Prudentius sang in praise of Concord or Patience:

“Anxious pardon hastens to precede the setting of the light,  
lest the sun, conscious of enduring anger, leave it behind.”

Nor should I omit the most eloquent and weighty defender of this interpretation, Isidore of Pelusium, who explains and supports it so fully in one of his letters (*Letter* 189, book 2) that nothing more could be desired. He writes:

“Since anger has broken the reins of reason, which performs the function of a charioteer, and commonly drives the mind of a human being off course beyond the boundaries of nature, Paul devised for this kind of fall not merely the best but also the swiftest remedy, using these words: ‘Let not the sun set upon your anger.’

“That is: before the sun inclines toward setting, recognize your nature, extinguish your fury, restrain your arrogance; embrace kinship and closeness, which rule even wild beasts, lest the intervening night make the disease incurable.

“For then, having found a suitable opportunity, the devil inflames what has happened, rushes toward revenge, incites hostility, provokes accusations, creates a memory of injuries, and produces countless evils from them.

“That Paul commanded those who disagree to be reconciled with one another as quickly as possible, in order to cut off these things, is clear from what he immediately adds: ‘Do not give place to the devil.’ He secretly makes small emotions great and renders things that can easily be cured scarcely, or even not at all, curable.”

Thus he writes.

Finally, concerning this passage, I wish to note two other salutary teachings.

The first is that of St. Antony, who, as St. Athanasius reports in his *Life*, recommended that the Apostle’s saying, “Let not the sun set upon your anger,” be retained through constant meditation. He interpreted it as meaning not only that the sun must not set upon anger, but also that it must not set upon any human fault, lest the moon at night or the sun by day ever depart as witnesses of our sins.

The second is that of St. Benedict (*Rule*, chapter 13). As Turrecrematus and Smaragdus note, he most devoutly established that, at the final part of Matins—that is, of Lauds and Vespers—the prior, or the person serving in the office of the weekly priest, should recite the Lord’s Prayer aloud.

He says this should be done because of “the thorns of scandals”—that is, disagreements and quarrels, injuries or contentions, which are the causes of scandals. Like thorns pricking and tearing the mind through anger and hatred, they should be removed so that the brothers, having been admonished, persuaded, and compelled by the promise and condition contained in the Lord’s Prayer—“Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors”—may cleanse themselves of the vice of hatred, anger, or any other passion, and each forgive his brother from the heart.

Thus cleansed—that is, corrected of his vices—he may either proceed in the morning to perform the work of obedience or in the evening to celebrate the nocturnal vigils.

Turrecrematus explains why the entire Lord’s Prayer is not recited aloud in the same way at the other hours: evening is the end of the day and the beginning of night, while Matins is, conversely, the beginning of the day and the end of night. Therefore he especially wanted the Lord’s Prayer to be said aloud at these two hours, so that the brother, having been admonished, would not pass through day and night without being reconciled with his brother.

At the other hours it is not prescribed to be said in this manner because it often happens that one brother becomes angry with another and is stirred against him by an impulse of fury. Although he may not immediately restrain his mind, he should nevertheless be given time to seek pardon. Therefore the holy Father judged it sufficient if the sun did not set upon his anger.

Thus he writes.]

“Let not the sun set upon your anger, and do not give place to the devil” (Ephesians 4).

If it is harmful for the Sun of righteousness to set upon our anger, and if, when angry, we immediately give place to the devil in our heart, how does he earlier command us to be angry, saying, “Be angry and do not sin”?

Does he not plainly say this: “Be angry with your vices and your fury, lest, while you connive at them, Christ, the Sun of righteousness, begin to set because of your anger, with your minds darkened; and lest, when he departs, you give place to the devil in your hearts”?

## Chapter IX. Of which sun it is said, “Let it not set upon your anger”

God plainly speaks of this sun through the prophet:

“But for you who fear my name, the Sun of righteousness shall rise, and healing shall be in his wings” (Malachi 4).

Again, it is said to set upon sinners and false prophets, and upon those who become angry, in the middle of the day, as the prophet says:

“The sun has set upon them at midday” (Amos 8).

Or certainly, according to the tropological meaning, let the mind—that is, νοῦς (*nous*), or reason—which deserves to be called the sun because it examines all the thoughts and judgments of the heart, not be extinguished by the vice of anger. Otherwise, when it sets, the darkness of disturbances, together with its author, the devil, will occupy the whole perception of our heart; and, possessed by the darkness of anger, we will be like people walking in blind night, not knowing what we ought to do.

[Note: Among the Greeks, νοῦς (*nous*) is understood in various ways: as the spirit, or rational faculty—that is, the mind, reason, or understanding. In 1 Corinthians 14: “I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the mind” (Ψαλῶ τῷ πνεύματι, ψαλῶ δὲ καὶ τῷ νοΐ).

Aristotle, in the *Ethics*, book 6, under the word νοῦς, writes: “Body, soul, mind”—σῶμα, ψυχή, νοῦς—parts of the human being.

According to Suidas, Pythagoras said that the human spirit is divided into three parts: νοῦς, φρένες, and θυμός. Νοῦς and θυμός are found in the other animals, but φρένες only in human beings. Lactantius seems to have understood νοῦς as imagination (*Divine Institutes*, book 7, chapter 12):

“Mind and soul are not the same. For one is that by which we live, another that by which we think. In those who sleep, the mind, not the soul, is lulled to rest; in the insane, the mind is extinguished, but the soul remains. Therefore they are called not lifeless but demented. The mind, then—that is, intelligence—is increased or diminished according to age.”

St. Basil (*Monastic Constitutions*, chapter 3): “Just as the body sees through the eye, so the spirit sees through the mind (νοῦς), which is akin to it.”

St. Ambrose (*Letter* 28): “Νοῦς is the vigor of the soul, claiming authority over soul and body for itself, like a ruler.”

St. Jerome, on Nahum 3: “Here you should not understand ‘sense’ as spirit and mind, which in Greek is called νοῦς, but as αἴσθησις”—that is, sensation.]

We have therefore set forth, though in a longer discourse, this interpretation of the Apostle’s passage, handed down to us through the teachings of the elders, since it was necessary to explain how they understood anger. They do not allow anger to penetrate their heart even for a moment, observing in every respect the Gospel saying:

“Whoever is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment” (Matthew 5).

But if it were permissible to be angry until sunset, harmful disturbances could satisfy the fullness of fury and the agitation of vengeful anger before this sun reached the place of its setting.

## Chapter X. Those whose anger is brought to an end not even by the setting of this sun

What shall I say about those—and I cannot say it without shame on my own account—whose implacability is brought to an end not even by this setting sun, but who prolong it for many days and preserve resentment of spirit against those with whom they have become angry, while denying that they are angry in words, although their conduct and actions clearly show that they are deeply indignant?

For they neither address them with appropriate speech nor converse with them with their customary friendliness. They think they are not sinning at all because they do not seek revenge for their agitation. Yet because they either do not dare or are unable to express and exercise their revenge openly, they turn the poison of anger back upon their own destruction, silently digesting it in their heart and consuming themselves in silence. They do not immediately drive away the bitterness of sadness by strength of spirit, but digest it over the passage of days and gradually mitigate it as circumstances allow.

[Note: *Rancor* properly denotes a kind of stench and heaviness of odor arising from age and decay. Hence *rancid* means rotten or foul-smelling—something corrupted by excessive age and having acquired a fetid odor and unpleasant taste. Metaphorically, the word is transferred to the mind when it signifies long-standing anger, hatred, or hostility.

Thus St. Jerome writes in Letter 36: “Having laid aside old resentment, let us prepare for God a clean dwelling place in our breast.”]

## Chapter XI. Those who conceal or disguise their anger sin no less than if they revealed it

As though the end of every act of revenge did not lie here, and as though someone had not fully satisfied his own fury or sadness if, at the instigation of anger, he has accomplished whatever lies within his power.

This is also done by those who restrain their impulses not from a desire for peace but from a lack of power to take revenge. They can do nothing further to those with whom they are angry except refrain from speaking to them with their customary friendliness.

[Note: St. Gregory, in the passage often cited, says:

“Sometimes anger, disturbing the mind, introduces silence as though by judgment; and, because it does not express itself outwardly through the tongue, it is inwardly the less forgiving. Thus an angry person withdraws his conversation from his neighbor and, by saying nothing, says how alienated he is.

“Sometimes this severity of silence is practiced as part of the administration of discipline, provided that the form of discretion is carefully maintained in the depths of the heart. But sometimes, when an inflamed spirit is restrained from its customary conversation, over time it becomes entirely separated from love of its neighbor; sharper goads come to the mind, and causes arise that aggravate the matter more grievously. Then, in the angry person’s eye, the splinter becomes a beam, when anger is changed into hatred.”]

It is as though anger were to be moderated only in the outward effect of the deed, and not rather torn out from the hidden places of our breast, lest, darkened by its shadows, we be unable to admit either the light of salutary counsel or the light of knowledge—and lest, while the spirit of anger dwells within us, we be unable to become a temple of the Holy Spirit.

Fury restrained in the heart does not offend the people standing before us, but it excludes the most brilliant radiance of the Holy Spirit just as surely as if it had been expressed openly.

## Chapter XII. That not even momentary anger may be retained
Or how could the Lord wish it to be retained even for a moment, when he does not even permit the spiritual sacrifices of our prayers to be offered, if we know that someone else harbors any resentment against us? He says:

> “Therefore, if you bring your gift to the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; and then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5).

**[Note: [Col. 0341C]** Many things could be brought forward in support of this evangelical teaching, things handed down by various interpreters no less devoutly than learnedly. I shall set down here only a few, sufficient for this passage.

First, this saying is exceedingly effective in urging the pursuit of reconciliation, since it teaches that fraternal charity and concord are more pleasing to God than sacrifices and offerings—indeed, that sacrifices, and consequently all our other works, are not acceptable to God if mutual charity is lacking. Therefore, reconciliation must be pursued above all if charity has been injured; indeed, the sacrifice must be postponed and deferred so that we may be reconciled to the offended brother.

Hence Saint Gregory says: “Behold, he does not wish to receive a sacrifice from those who are at odds; he refuses to accept a holocaust. Consider, therefore, how great is the evil of discord, on account of which even that by which guilt is forgiven is cast aside” (Gregory, *Homily 8 on Ezekiel*).

This saying is useful not only so that the one who has injured another may seek reconciliation as quickly as possible, but also so that the one who has been injured—that is, who has suffered an offense—may readily forgive the brother who seeks reconciliation, lest he delay and obstruct the honor due to God and the sacrifices to be offered to him.

Second, a brother is said to have something against us when he has a just complaint against us because he has received some injury from us. Hence it does not say, “If you have something against your brother,” but, “If your brother has something against you.” “For,” says Augustine, “he himself has something against us if we have injured him in some way. We, however, have something against him if he has injured us; in that case there is no need to go to him for reconciliation. For you will not ask pardon of the one who has injured you; you need only forgive him, just as you desire the Lord to forgive you for what you yourself have done” (Augustine, Book 1 of *The Sermon on the Mount*, chapter 20).

Thus the person who has been injured by another is not commanded to be reconciled with his brother before the offering, although it is a mark of great perfection if an injured person induces his brother to enter into reconciliation with him. But even if it is not necessary for the injured person to seek reconciliation, it is nevertheless necessary for him to forgive the injury before the offering.

For being reconciled to a brother, or to one’s neighbor, is one thing; forgiving a brother is another. Reconciliation, on the part of the one who caused the injury, requires satisfaction for the injury; on the part of the injured person, it requires pardon and forgiveness.

Third, this saying should not be understood as though we must always go to our brother. That is indeed a holy counsel, and when charity demands it and place and time permit, it is also a necessary command. Usually, however, we should go to him by our affections or actions rather than by our feet: by affection, forgiving any injury we have received from him and releasing our hatred; by action, making satisfaction for any injury he has received from us. The former is a command of charity; the latter, a command of justice.

Finally, what is said here about the ancient sacrifices of the Jews—which were still in force when Christ spoke these words—is to be understood all the more of the sacrifice of the Eucharist. Therefore, if reconciliation had to be sought before the offering of the legal sacrifices, much more must it be sought before the offering of our Eucharistic sacrifice, especially since this is the sacrament and symbol of union and concord (see Saint Bernard, *On Precept and Dispensation*, chapter 26). Hence it is called both *communion* and *synaxis*. “For we, though many, are one body, because we partake of the one bread” (1 Corinthians 10).

Moreover, praises, thanksgivings, prayers, almsgiving, and absolutely all good works that we offer to God and refer to his honor are, in a certain sense, sacrifices. Thus by this saying we are taught that the sacrifice of praise, prayer, and other works cannot please God unless we offer them to him after having been reconciled and while living in concord with our brothers.]

How, then, can we be permitted to retain sorrow against a brother—not to mention for several days, but even until this sunset—when we are not permitted to offer our prayers to God if that brother has even the slightest thing against us? The Apostle commands us: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5), and, “Lifting up pure hands in every place, without anger or disputation” (1 Timothy 2).

It follows, therefore, either that we must never pray while retaining such poison in our hearts, and so remain subject to this apostolic or evangelical command by which we are ordered to pray continually and everywhere; or, if we deceive ourselves and presume to pour out a prayer contrary to his prohibition, we must recognize that we are offering the Lord not prayer, but defiance in the spirit of rebellion.

## CHAPTER XIII. On fraternal reconciliation

Since we often disregard brothers who have been injured and saddened, or at least despise them by saying that they are offended not through any fault of ours, the physician of souls and knower of hidden things, wishing to uproot the occasions of anger completely from our hearts, commands us not only, when we have been injured, to forgive and be reconciled with our brothers, retaining no memory of injury or offense against them; he also commands us, if we know that they have something against us, whether justly or unjustly, likewise to leave our gift—that is, to restrain our prayers—and hasten first toward their satisfaction. Thus, after bringing about the brother’s healing, we may carry the gifts of our prayers undefiled.

For the common Lord of all does not take such delight in our services that what he gains in one person he should lose in another, with sorrow prevailing. Whenever one of his servants suffers loss, he suffers a single deprivation, since he desires and awaits the salvation of all his servants in the same manner.

**[Note: [Col. 0343B]** Cassian seems (see *Conference* 16, chapter 16) to have understood that passage of Matthew to mean that, whether we know our brother or neighbor to have something against us justly or unjustly—that is, to be hostile to us in mind—we should immediately approach him for the sake of reconciliation and placate him. But, as is easy to observe here and elsewhere, he often confuses counsels with precepts. For what is commanded here is one thing; what is counseled is another: satisfaction is required of the one who caused the injury, whereas forgiveness or pardon of the fault is required of the one who was injured, as has been said. But it is a counsel of perfection, not a precept, to seek reconciliation from one who is unjustly angry, since we have done him no injury. Since all Christians are invited to this perfection for many reasons, religious persons, who profess themselves zealous for perfection and, as it were, its candidates, are invited to it much more; they ought to fulfill all righteousness (Matthew 3 and 5), and their righteousness ought to exceed that of secular persons by as much as their state is higher and holier.

On this consideration Saint Benedict, in chapter 71, also decreed that if any brother is reproved in any manner by the abbot or by any prior whatsoever, for any very slight cause, or if he perceives even slightly that the mind of any prior is angry or disturbed with him, however mildly, he should at once, without delay, lie prostrate on the ground at his feet, making satisfaction, until that disturbance is healed by a blessing.]

**[Note: [Col. 0343C]** This is a harsh and highly hyperbolical statement if, in accordance with what was said above, it is understood generally of a brother who has something against us, whether justly or unjustly. Saint Augustine, cited above, and the other Fathers did not understand it in this way. It should therefore be taken with a grain of salt and explained as follows: our prayer will be equally ineffective whether the brother or neighbor is hostile toward us, or we are hostile toward him—or, as the author explains in the words that follow, whether we preserve against him, with a swelling spirit, the bitterness of indignation.

Because of this obscurity and the difficulty that could arise from this chapter, Dionysius seems to have passed over this passage in silence, beginning with the words, “For the common Lord does not take such delight in our services,” and so forth.]

Thus, when a brother has something against us, our prayer will be equally ineffective as if we were preserving bitterness against him with a swelling spirit of indignation.

## CHAPTER XIV. How the old law also uproots anger not only from its outward effect but from thought itself

**[Col. 0344A]**

But why linger any longer over the evangelical and apostolic commands, when even the old law—which seems to contain some degree of concession—takes precautions against the same thing, saying: “You shall not hate your brother in your heart” (Leviticus 19); and again: “You shall not remember the injury done by your fellow citizens” (ibid.); and again:

> “The paths of those who retain the memory of wrongdoing lead to death” (ibid.).

**[Note: [Col. 0343D]** Dionysius the Carthusian omitted this statement, although it is found in all printed and manuscript copies—perhaps because it does not appear in the commonly circulated Bibles. It is taken from Proverbs 12 according to the Septuagint, as it is cited here in the margin. In the Vulgate edition, the corresponding statement reads: “In the path of justice is life, but the way that turns aside leads to death.”

As for the remembrance and forgetfulness of injuries, which is under discussion here, the words of John Climacus should be noted. “The remembrance of injuries,” he says, “is the completion of fury, the guardian of sins, hatred of justice, destruction of virtues, poison of the soul, the mind’s continual worm, confusion of prayer, severing of supplication, estrangement from charity, a nail fixed in the soul, an unpleasant sensation loved in the sweetness of bitterness, a perpetual sin, a never-sleeping iniquity, wickedness admitted every hour, a dark and most troublesome vice.

“And further: ‘The solitary monk who preserves this remembrance within himself is a serpent nesting in its lair, carrying deadly poison everywhere with it. Whoever casts it out finds forgiveness; whoever clings to it is deprived of mercy. Some have exposed themselves to labors and pains in order to merit pardon, but the man who forgets an injury has easily surpassed them. For the saying is entirely true: Forgive quickly, and you will be forgiven abundantly. Forgetfulness of injuries is a sure sign of true and genuine repentance. Whoever holds onto enmities and thinks that he is repenting is like one who thinks he is running in his dreams.’”

So he writes (*Step 9*).]

You see that there too wickedness is cut away not only from action but also from hidden thoughts, since hatred and not merely the repayment of injury, but the very memory of it, are commanded to be uprooted from the heart.

## CHAPTER XV. He notes those who cast the causes of their impatience upon others

**[Col. 0344B]**

Sometimes, overcome by pride or impatience, when we wish to correct our undisciplined and disordered conduct, we complain that we desire solitude, as though there we would immediately find the virtue of patience, with no one to provoke us. We excuse our negligence and say that the causes of our agitation are generated not by our own impatience but by the fault of our brothers.

**[Note: [Col. 0344C]** An outstanding example of this matter, and one highly appropriate to this passage, can be found in the life of Saint Ignatius of Loyola published by Maffei. It will not be out of place to relate it here.

When Ignatius saw one of the brothers, who was irritable by nature and consequently broke out into bitter words, withdrawing from the company of the brothers at an unsuitable time, he addressed him gently: “Why do you not place yourself among the brothers at the appointed hours?” When the man pleaded the anger of his nature and his bile, Ignatius replied: “No, you are greatly mistaken. These and similar vices are conquered not by fleeing but by resisting.”

This is relevant to what John Climacus writes about certain solitaries: “Once, when I was sitting for some necessary reason near the cell of certain solitaries, I heard them inside quarreling among themselves, like partridges, with the greatest bitterness and fury, and leaping most insolently upon the person who had injured them as though he were present. I piously and faithfully warned them not to remain any longer in solitude if they did not want to become demons instead of human beings.”

And further: “If we examine more carefully, we shall notice that most of those driven by the torches of anger readily fast, keep vigils, and seek the repose of solitude. For the intention of the most cunning demon—and what he seeks above all—is to persuade them, under the seemingly reasonable pretext of penitence and mourning, to pursue those things that can give this disease greater strength.”

So he writes (*Step 8*).]

But by turning the causes of our error upon others, we shall never be able to reach the goal of patience and perfection.

## CHAPTER XVI. How the tranquility of our heart ought to depend not upon another’s power but upon our own

The whole of our correction and tranquility, therefore, must not be placed in another’s power, since it is not subject to our control; rather, it must depend upon our own condition. Thus, in order that we may not become angry, this must proceed not from another’s perfection but from our own virtue, which is acquired not through another’s patience but through our own forbearance.

## CHAPTER XVII. With what discipline we ought to seek the desert

**[Note: [Col. 0345C]** Abbot John confirms this teaching in Cassian (*Conference 19*, chapter 10), and the other holy Fathers agree with him. They teach that no one should pass to the eremitical life unless he has first diligently exercised himself in a coenobium, because the desert, or solitude, being the summit and culmination of the religious life, does not confer perfection but presupposes it.

After Saint Jerome had reviewed various disadvantages and dangers of solitude and solitary life, he wrote: “In solitude pride quickly creeps in; and if he fasts for a little while and sees no human being, a man thinks himself important, forgetting who he is and from where and to where he has come. Within, his heart wanders; outside, his tongue wanders,” and so forth. He immediately adds:

“What, then? Do we criticize the solitary life? Not at all, since we have often praised it. But we want soldiers of this kind to emerge from the training ground of monasteries—men whom the harsh beginnings of the desert do not frighten; who have given proof of their way of life over a long period; who have been the least of all, so that they might become first of all; whom neither hunger nor satiety has ever overcome; who rejoice in poverty; whose clothing, speech, expression, gait, and teaching are lessons in virtue.”

Thus Saint Jerome (*Letter 4, to the monk Rusticus*).

Likewise Saint Benedict, at the beginning of his Rule, describing the anachoretic life and those for whom it is suitable, says: “The second kind is that of the anchorites, that is, hermits—those who are no longer novices, aflame with the first fervor of conversion, but who have learned through long testing in the monastery how to fight against the devil, instructed already by the support of many. They are well equipped to leave the fraternal battle line for single combat in the desert, and, without the consolation of another, are now capable, with God’s help, of fighting safely against the vices of the flesh and of their thoughts” (see Saint Bernard, Sermon 3 on the Circumcision).]

Moreover, those who seek the desert ought to be perfect and cleansed of every vice. They should enter after their vices have been thoroughly burned away in the fellowship of the brothers—not as a refuge from faintheartedness, but to pursue divine contemplation and the desire for a higher vision, which can be grasped by the perfect only in solitude.

For whatever vices we carry into the desert still uncured will be found there hidden within us, not abolished. Solitude knows how to unlock the purest contemplation for those whose conduct has been corrected and to reveal, through the clearest vision, knowledge of spiritual mysteries. But it is also accustomed not only to preserve the vices of those who are less thoroughly corrected, but even to magnify them.

A person seems patient and humble to himself only so long as he has no association with anyone. But when an occasion for agitation arises, he immediately returns to his former nature. The vices that lay hidden promptly emerge from him; like unbridled horses, nourished for a long time in idleness, they burst more violently and fiercely from their barriers, racing toward the ruin of their own driver.

Indeed, when human exercise and practice cease, vices grow more savage within us unless they have first been purged. We lose through the carelessness of security even that semblance of patience which, while mingling with our brothers, we seemed to possess—at least out of respect for them and concern for public opinion.

## CHAPTER XVIII. That even those who are not provoked by human beings are often impatient and irritable

**[Note: [Col. 0346C]** The style of Dionysius is both clearer and fuller: “All venomous kinds of serpents and wild beasts, when they remain in their lairs and solitude, are harmless; yet they cannot simply be called harmless because at that time they harm no one.” So he writes.

From this it is inferred that *harmless* should be read here, although others—and perhaps more correctly, including the Basel copy and some manuscripts—read *harmful*, in this sense: “As though they did not remain harmful, nor could they be declared harmful because they harm no one.” Both statements are true. Such animals are harmless in act so long as they remain in solitude or in their lairs; nevertheless, they remain harmful in their natural inclination and tendency, because they are always ready to cause harm. For this reason, as Dionysius says, they cannot simply be declared harmless.

The latter reading, however, seems to fit the preceding words better. It relates to what he said above: “The vices that lay hidden emerge from him, and like unbridled horses,” and so forth.

Thus Abbot John writes (*Conference 19*, chapter 12): “We must know that if we withdraw into solitude or hidden places while our vices are not yet cured, their effects are merely restrained, not extinguished. For the root of all sins, which had not been uprooted, lies hidden within us—indeed, it even spreads,” and so forth.]

As though all the venomous kinds of serpents or wild beasts, when they remain in solitude and in their dens, did not continue to be harmful, yet could not therefore be pronounced harmless because they harm no one. Solitude does not grant them this through an inclination toward goodness, but through necessity. When they obtain an opportunity to injure, they immediately bring forth and reveal the poison and savagery of soul concealed within them.

Therefore, for those who seek perfection, it is not enough not to be angry with a human being. We remember that, while dwelling in solitude, anger similarly crept over us against a pen, when its thickness or thinness displeased us; against a knife, when with its dull edge it cut sluggishly and performed the incision slowly; and against a flint, when, as we hurried to our reading, a spark of fire happened to come from it too slowly. The movement of indignation entered us so deeply that we could not otherwise digest or vent the disturbance of our mind except by uttering curses against lifeless materials—or, in truth, against the devil.

Therefore, merely for the purposes of perfection, it will not be enough for people against whom anger might arise to be absent. If patience has not first been acquired, the disposition to anger can similarly be exercised even against mute objects and tiny things. Remaining in our heart, it will not allow us either to possess a constant state of tranquility or to be free from our remaining vices—unless perhaps we think that some benefit or remedy is gained from our agitations, because inanimate and mute things do not answer our curses or anger and therefore do not provoke the intemperance of our heart to blaze into a greater madness of fury.

**[Note: [Col. 0347B]** Saint Augustine elegantly observed this very point in these words: “The ancients defined anger as nothing other than a desire for revenge, although a person sometimes becomes angry even with inanimate things, when there is no sense of revenge—for example, when in anger he strikes a badly writing pen or breaks a reed. Yet even this more irrational response is still a kind of desire for revenge, and, so to speak, a sort of shadow of requital: that those who do evil should suffer evil” (Book 14 of *The City of God*, chapter 15).

In his letter to Nebridius he says: “Anger, in my opinion, is a turbulent appetite to remove those things that impede ease of action. Thus we are often angry not only with human beings but also with a pen while writing, striking and breaking it; gamblers with their dice, painters with their brush, and each person with whatever instrument he thinks is causing him difficulty.” Doctors also affirm that through such continued practice bile increases; when bile has increased, we become angry again easily and almost without any cause (To Nebridius, Letter 131).

So Saint Augustine.

Explaining the cause of this kind of anger and agitation, Saint Thomas says: “Since there are in a human being both reason and imagination, the movement of anger can arise in a human being in two ways. In one way, it arises from imagination alone, which announces an injury; thus some movement of anger arises even toward irrational and inanimate things, according to the likeness of the movement found in animals against anything harmful. In another way, it arises from reason announcing an injury; thus, as the Philosopher says in Book 2 of the *Rhetoric* (chapter 3), anger toward insensible things and the dead is in no way possible—both because they do not suffer, whereas the angry chiefly seek suffering in those with whom they are angry, and because revenge against them is impossible, since they are not capable of committing an injury” (I–II, question 146, article 7).]

## CHAPTER XIX. On cutting away anger according to the Gospel

**[Col. 0347B]**

Therefore, if we desire to attain that highest divine reward of which it is said, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5), anger must be cut away not only from our actions but also uprooted from the innermost parts of the soul.

For it will be of little benefit that the fury of anger is restrained in speech and not brought into action if God, who is not unaware of the secrets of hearts, perceives that it remains present in the hidden recesses of our breast.

**[Note: [Col. 0347D]** “Already the axe is placed at the root of the trees,” or “of the tree” (Matthew 3; Luke 3). The author seems to apply this morally, as is his custom, adapting it to his purpose: he calls the internal anger hidden in the breast the root, while its fruits are the acts that emerge in word and deed.]

For the evangelical teaching commands that the roots of vices be cut off rather than their fruits. Once the sources that nourish them have certainly been torn out, they will no longer sprout; and thus the mind will be able to remain continually in all patience and holiness, when these things have been uprooted not from the surface of conduct and actions but from the hidden chambers of thought.

Therefore, to prevent murder, anger and hatred are cut down, without which the crime of murder can in no way be committed.

**[Note: [Col. 0347D]** All interpreters understand this of eternal death. For among the Hebrews, one was said to be liable or subject to judgment when he was worthy of death. But they were speaking of bodily death, whereas Christ was speaking of the death of the soul.

Yet since it is clear that not every anger is a sin, and since Christ himself, as well as the Apostles and other holy men, is sometimes read as having been angry, as was shown above, this statement requires a sound interpretation. Not everyone who becomes angry in any manner, nor everyone who calls another “worthless” or “foolish,” is immediately condemned. Rather, it is the person who becomes angry and speaks in such a way that he desires or wishes to inflict death, or any serious harm or injury, upon the other.

The Lord was speaking in relation to the murder under discussion. He calls “anger” not every desire for revenge, as philosophers define it, but specifically that which tends toward murder (Maldonado, on Matthew, chapter 5; Leonard Lessius, Book 4 of *On Justice*, chapter 4).

He was dealing with the commandment, “You shall not kill.” In explaining it, he taught that not only external murder is a deadly sin in divine judgment, but also the hidden anger by which someone desires the death or serious harm of his neighbor, as Saint Thomas explains (II–II, question 158, articles 3 and 5). Consequently, not only the one who actually killed, but also the one who killed by will alone, is guilty of murder before God—just as a little earlier he had said that not only the one who actually committed adultery, but also the one who desired to commit it, is an adulterer.

In this sense, neither Christ nor the Apostles were ever angry. For although Peter seems to have killed Ananias and Sapphira in anger, it must be believed that he did so not through anger but through religious zeal and zeal for justice, and not as a private person but as a minister of God, as we have shown elsewhere.

It is useful here to consider Saint Thomas, who explains these matters more fully and precisely. He says:

> “The degrees of anger that the Lord sets forth”—namely, in Matthew 5—“do not pertain to different kinds of anger; rather, they are understood according to the progression of a human act, in which something is first conceived in the heart. With regard to this he says, ‘Whoever is angry with his brother.’
>
> “The second stage occurs when it is manifested externally through certain outward signs, even before it bursts into action. With regard to this he says, ‘Whoever says to his brother, Raca,’ which is an exclamation of an angry person.
>
> “The third stage occurs when the sin conceived inwardly is brought into action. The effect of anger is injury to another under the aspect of revenge. The least of injuries is that which is done by speech alone. With regard to this he says, ‘Whoever says to his brother, Fool.’
>
> “Thus it is clear that the second adds something to the first, and the third to both. Therefore, if the first is a mortal sin in the case under discussion—namely, when someone desires the killing of his neighbor or any serious harm, as he explained in article 3, response to objection 2—then this applies all the more to the other stages.

“Accordingly, corresponding matters relating to condemnation are assigned to each. For the first, judgment is mentioned, which is the lesser penalty, since, as Augustine says (*The Sermon on the Mount*, chapter 19), there is still room for defense in judgment. For the second, the council is mentioned, in which judges deliberate among themselves about the punishment by which the person should be condemned. For the third, the fiery Gehenna is mentioned, which is certain condemnation.”

So Saint Thomas (II–II, question 158, article 5, response to objection 3).]

> “Whoever is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment; and whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (Matthew 5; 1 John 3).

That is, when he is so angry that he desires in his heart that the other should perish, although it is known that he has shed none of his blood with his own hand or weapon before human beings, he is declared by the Lord to be a murderer in the disposition of anger. For the Lord will repay each person with reward or punishment not only according to the outcome of his actions but also according to the desire of his will and aspiration, in accordance with what he himself says through the prophet:

> “I am coming to gather all their works and their thoughts, together with all nations and languages” (Isaiah 66).

And the Apostle says:

> “Their thoughts accusing one another or also defending them on the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings” (Romans 2).

**[Note: [Col. 0349C]** This is the corrected Vulgate edition. The older editions, however, read in the genitive, “the thoughts accusing one another,” and so forth, after the manner of the Greeks, who use genitives in place of ablatives because they lack ablatives. Moreover, *accusing* and *defending* are forensic terms. The sense is that, as our conscience bears witness and judges, some of our thoughts charge and accuse certain deeds as evil, while others defend and excuse them as good; accordingly, some of our thoughts assume the role of accuser, others that of defendant. This testimony of conscience, together with the thoughts or reasonings, λογισμοῖς (*logismois*), which accuse or defend, will occur especially at the last judgment; for then that accusatory and exculpatory power of conscience will disclose itself most fully, when God judges those things that are now hidden from human beings.]

**[Note: [Col. 0349B]** This statement explains the preceding one. In the Savior’s words, “to be angry with one’s brother” is the same as “to hate one’s brother,” according to the Apostle’s meaning—namely, when someone becomes angry in such a way that he desires in his heart that the other should perish, as Cassian says here, that is, that he wishes him dead.

Such a person is unquestionably a murderer before God and consequently liable to eternal judgment, even if he inflicts no actual harm. Hence Saint Jerome, referring to this passage, writes in Letter 36: “Since murder often arises from hatred, whoever hates is a murderer in intention, even though he has not yet struck with the sword.”

And Cassian says here: “Therefore, so that murder may not be committed, anger and hatred are cut away, without which the crime of murder can in no way be committed”—indicating that the words which follow refer to murder.]

**[Note: [Col. 0349B]** From this, Jerome says, we learn that not only works but also thoughts will be judged on the day of judgment. Concerning them it is said: “Now their thoughts have surrounded them,” when the Lord will judge the hidden things of human beings according to the Gospel of Jesus Christ. Thus what the Apostle writes will be confirmed by the truth of judgment: “Their thoughts accusing or defending one another on the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings” (Romans 2:7), so that all our thoughts, gathered together at one time, may bear witness to the just Judge, while either our conscience accuses us or makes satisfaction for the offense—whether our sins are more numerous than our good works, whether they are old or new, and whether they have been erased by repentance or renewed by fresh crimes.]

## CHAPTER XX. In the Gospel’s statement, “Whoever is angry with his brother,” and so forth, whether the addition **WITHOUT CAUSE** is to be accepted

**[Col. 0350A]**
It must nevertheless be understood that in some copies one finds: “Whoever is angry with his brother without cause will be liable to judgment”; [Note: Most Greek codices read: πᾶς ὁ ὀργιζόμενος τῷ ἀδελφῷ αὐτοῦ εἰκῇ, that is, “everyone who is angry with his brother rashly, undeservedly, without cause” (Matthew 5). Among the Greeks Chrysostom follows this reading (In comment.), and among the Latins Augustine (Sermon 1 on the Sermon on the Mount); from this they infer that not all anger is forbidden, but only unjust and irrational anger. Yet neither the Latin translator followed this reading, nor Cassian alone; St. Jerome also rightly criticized it and asserted that εἰκῇ, as superfluous, ought to be erased from the books. “For,” he says, “if we are commanded to offer the other cheek to one who strikes us, to love our enemies, and to pray for those who persecute us, every occasion for anger is removed. Nor is one free from sin who becomes angry even when injured and wronged by another. For just as no one may, on a just cause, kill anyone by private authority, so no one may, on a just cause, become angry—namely, in such a way as to wish evil upon another or avenge an injury, which is to return evil for evil. Nor is it an objection that someone may occasionally become angry without sin, or even say ‘Raca’ or ‘fool.’ First, what is not prohibited here are the initial impulses of anger, which are not under our control, but deliberate and complete anger, to which consent is added. Moreover, neither is this kind of anger—by which someone is angry or offended at a person’s fault—prohibited; to indicate this, some think the saying should be understood as: ‘Whoever is angry with his brother,’ that is, not with the person’s fault but with the person, whom he ought to love fraternally because he is a brother. Thus we should understand the Lord to be speaking of anger that conflicts with brotherly love. Hence St. Augustine (Book I of the Retractions, chapter 19, and Book XIV of The City of God, chapter 9) advises that we must consider what it means to be angry with one’s brother, since one who is angry at his brother’s sin is not angry with his brother. And elsewhere he says: ‘No sane person condemns becoming angry with a brother so that he may be corrected.’ For impulses of this kind, arising from love of the good and holy charity, should not be called vices, since they follow right reason.]

“Without cause” is superfluous and was added by those who did not think that anger should be cut off even when there were just causes; [Note: St. Augustine, in his hundredth letter, says: “Anger steals in because no angry person thinks his anger unjust. Thus, as anger grows old, it becomes hatred, while the sweetness—as it were—of justified grief holds it longer in the vessel, until the whole contents turn sour and corrupt the vessel. Therefore it is far better that we do not become angry with anyone even justly than that, by becoming angry as though justly, we should easily slip into someone’s hatred through the hidden power of anger.” Gregory likewise says in one of his letters (Book VII, chapter 26): “Once anger has taken possession of the mind, it considers even what it does cruelly to be just.” And elsewhere (Book XXXI of the Morals, chapter 31): “Anger’s conquered heart is accustomed to encourage itself as though from reason, saying: ‘What is being done against you cannot be endured calmly; indeed, to tolerate these things patiently is a sin. For if they are not resisted with great exasperation, they will thereafter be heaped up against you without measure.’ See St. Thomas, I–II, question 46, article 4, where he teaches that anger exists together with reason, or with the judgment of reason. Hence the Philosopher says in the Book of Problems (Section 3, problem 2) that those who are very drunk, as though possessing no judgment of reason, do not become angry, whereas those who are slightly drunk do, as though possessing the judgment of reason, though impeded. Anger is said by the Philosopher (Book VII of the Ethics, chapter 6) to exist together with reason because it desires another’s evil under the aspect of just vengeance. Thus it regards in its object a certain image of justice, so that it seems to imitate punitive justice. For just as justice desires the neighbor’s evil under the aspect of just vengeance, so anger does so under the appearance and image of just vengeance. The difference is that justice is governed by true prudence, whereas anger is governed not by prudence itself but only by its image.]

although certainly no one who has been moved without reason would say that he is angry without cause.
