Therefore it appears to have been added by those who did not understand the purpose of Scripture, which intends to cut away every fuel of anger and to leave no occasion for indignation at all—lest, while we are commanded to become angry when there is cause, an opportunity to become angry without cause should also be introduced to us. [Note: This sentence must be understood in the same way as the similar passages explained above, namely, of ordinary anger, or the feeling of a mind wishing another ill in order to avenge itself. Such anger is always a sin, contrary to patience or gentleness, even in a judge who justly punishes the guilty.]

For the end of patience consists not in becoming angry justly, but in not becoming angry at all. [Note: St. Augustine seems to have understood it in this way (as cited above, Book I of the Retractions, chapter 19): the person is said to become angry εἰκῇ, rashly and without cause, who sins by becoming angry, that is, who, while angry, intends evil for his neighbor or hates him.]

I know that some interpret the expression “without cause” in this way: namely, that the person becomes angry without cause to whom, while angry, it is not lawful to seek vengeance. Nevertheless, it is better to hold to the reading as it is found written in many recent copies and in all the ancient ones.

## CHAPTER XXI. Remedies by which we can eradicate anger from our hearts

Therefore the athlete of Christ, properly engaged in the struggle, must uproot the impulses of anger completely. [Note: Cassian suggests several remedies against anger, or irascibility, collected from what he has so far said about this vice. For further remedies, see St. Basil, in his homily on anger; Cassian likewise, Conference 16, chapter 27, and Conference 18, chapters 12 and 13, where Abba Piammon discusses the acquisition of patience; St. Gregory, Book V of the Morals, chapter 31; and among more recent authors, Turrecremata, Treatise 3 on the Rule of St. Benedict, and Fr. Leonard Lessius, On Justice and Law, Book III, chapter 2, and Book IV, chapter 4.]

The perfect medicine for this disease will be, first of all, to believe that it is in no way lawful for us to become angry, whether for just or unjust causes, [Note: 0351B] knowing that we shall immediately lose the light of discernment, the firmness of right judgment, moral integrity itself, and the restraints of justice, if the chief light of our heart is darkened by the darkness of anger. Then, too, we must know that the purity of our mind will immediately be disturbed, and that it cannot possibly become the temple of the Holy Spirit while the spirit of anger dwells within us. Finally, we must consider that we are in no way permitted to pray, or to pour out prayers to God while angry.

Above all, keeping before our eyes the uncertainty of the human condition, [Note: “A person easily despises everything if he has considered that he is going to die,” says St. Jerome in his Letter to Paulinus (Letter 103). Hence Ecclesiasticus 39: “Remember the last things, and cease—or you will cease—to be hostile.” St. Macarius is also said to have said that a monk ought to devote himself to fasts as though he would live forever, but restrain the movements of his soul and forget injuries as though he were going to die every day, as Cassian reports in Book V, at the end (see also Climacus, Step 6, which concerns remembrance of death).]

we should believe daily that we shall depart from the body. Then nothing will be gained for us from sexual continence, nothing from renouncing all possessions, nothing from despising wealth, nothing from the labors of fasts and vigils, since, solely on account of anger and hatred, punishments are promised to us by the Judge of all for eternity.

# BOOK NINE. ON THE SPIRIT OF SADNESS

## CHAPTER I

[Note: Cassian assigns sadness, or the spirit of sadness, fifth place among the capital vices and names it immediately after anger, for the reason he expressed elsewhere (Conference 5, chapter 10): sadness springs from anger, and therefore, in order that sadness may be driven away, anger must first be expelled. St. Gregory also seems to support him here, in Book XXXI of the Morals, chapter 31, where, explaining the order and kinship of the capital vices, he says: “From anger sadness arises, because the disturbed mind, by agitating itself disorderly, confuses itself through its very agitation; and when it has lost the sweetness of tranquillity, nothing feeds it except the sorrow that follows from disturbance.” Yet Cassian understands sadness in one way and Gregory in another. Cassian distinguishes sadness from acedia, and therefore treats them separately and distinctly in this book and the next; but St. Gregory calls acedia sadness, and indeed more appropriately, as St. Thomas asserts (II–II, question 35, article 3, reply to objection 4), as will become clear from what follows.

It may seem strange that Cassian, in this series of capital vices, did not name envy, although it is certainly a capital vice and is counted among the capital vices by St. Gregory and other teachers. Indeed, Cassian himself joins and compares it with the principal vices in several places (Book V, chapters 21 and 22; Book VII, chapter 5; Conference 18, last chapter). St. Thomas suggests one possible reason in these words (II–II, question 37, article 4): “Perhaps envy is not set down as a capital vice, neither by Isidore in his Book on the Supreme Good nor by Cassian in his book On the Institutes of the Coenobia, because envy manifestly arises from vainglory.” At first sight it seemed incongruous to call envy a capital vice when it is considered one of the daughters of vainglory, itself a capital vice. But St. Thomas replies that there is no incongruity in one capital vice arising from another, provided it is such that many other vices also usually arise from it, as they do from envy. For according to St. Gregory (Book XXXI of the Morals, chapter 31), “The capital vices are joined to one another by such kinship that one is produced only from another. For the first offspring of pride is vainglory; and when it corrupts the oppressed mind, it immediately gives birth to envy, because, while the mind desires the power of a famous name, it wastes away lest someone else should be able to attain it.” Thus Gregory.

It could indeed be said that envy is included under the name of sadness, since it is sadness at another’s good. But Cassian does not seem to have understood it in this way, as can be gathered from the whole treatment of this book (chapter 3 and the last chapter) and from other passages. For he does not usually call envy simply sadness; and when he lists the causes of sadness here, he makes no mention of envy or of the cause of envy.

Therefore, in order that we may understand what he means by sadness and how he distinguishes it both from envy and from acedia, it should be noted that John of Damascus distinguishes four kinds of sadness (Book II of the Orthodox Faith, chapter 14), which in Latin are called acedia, distress, envy, and compassion. “Acedia,” he says, “is sadness that induces silence and failure of speech; distress is sadness that weighs down and imposes a burden; envy is sadness arising from another’s goods; compassion is sadness at another’s evils.” Thus Damascene (St. Thomas, I–II, question 35, article 8).

Of these four kinds, only the second—namely, distress, which Cassian treats here under the name of sadness—is taught to be subdued and conquered by the spiritual combatant, that is, the monk. It is nothing other than disordered anguish, grief, or affliction of mind arising from the apprehension of some evil inflicted or some good taken away: for example, when someone is deprived of an expected good, or loses a good previously possessed, or is unexpectedly oppressed by evil, and is consequently cast down in spirit and depressed as though by a heavy weight, when he ought instead to be raised from such depression by patience, confidence, and hope of better circumstances.

Hence, to shake off such a heavy burden, the Psalmist rouses himself and cries out: “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you disturb me? Hope in the Lord” (Psalm 41), and so forth. The Apostle James likewise advises that the one who is sad should pray (James 5), that is, raise and lift up to God the mind depressed by grief.

From this it follows that the sadness under discussion is nothing other than impatience, which has a very close and almost inseparable association with anger. This vice is opposed to patience, whose task is to strengthen the mind in adversity by moderating the griefs ordinarily produced by adversity, so that through them one does not depart from the rule of reason or do anything unbecoming—for example, in the death of parents or friends, in exile, losses, illnesses, insults, and other evils of this kind. Such things ordinarily bring great griefs, which often drive a person from the citadel of reason and from the duty of virtue, impel him into many evils, and sometimes even induce despair.

Sadness, therefore, or impatience, is the subject of this book, as it is called; and it is rightly counted among the capital vices, since it is the cause of many evils and sins, as experience has shown. Hence Isidore, in the passage cited above, says that from sadness arise resentment, faintheartedness, bitterness, and despair. The difference between sadness understood in this way and acedia is evident in itself, and will become clearer from the following book.]

In our fifth contest, the stings of devouring sadness must be blunted. [Note: He calls sadness “devouring” not only with respect to the body and bodily life, to which it brings great harm above all other passions of the soul, as experience attests (St. Thomas, I–II, question 37, article 4), but also, in its own way, with respect to the soul, as can be gathered from what follows (chapter 3), where he says that the soul is devoured by the most ravenous bites of sadness. Scripture gives much testimony concerning the bodily harm contracted from sadness. Proverbs 17: “By sorrow of mind the spirit is cast down; a joyful mind makes life flourish, and a sad spirit dries up the bones.” Ecclesiasticus 30: “Drive sadness far from you; for sadness has killed many, and there is no benefit in it.” And chapter 38: “Better is death than a bitter life, and death hastens from sadness.” Although all these statements apply and are true of every kind of sadness, they apply especially and principally to this second kind, as stated above, by which the mind is oppressed with distress because of adversity or calamity; it is cured and driven away by no better medicine than patience.]

If it gains the power to conquer our mind through each successive attack and through uncertain and varied circumstances, it separates us moment by moment from the vision of divine contemplation [Note: Concerning these and other harms of sadness or impatience, see St. Gregory in the Pastoral Rule, Part III, chapter 10.] and utterly weakens and depresses the mind, cast down from every state of purity. It does not allow us to complete our prayers with the customary liveliness of heart; it does not permit us to apply ourselves to the remedies of sacred reading; it does not allow us to be tranquil and gentle toward the brethren; and it makes us impatient and harsh in every work or religious duty. Having lost every wholesome counsel and with the constancy of the heart disturbed, it makes us as though mad and drunk, breaking and overwhelming the mind with punitive despair.

## CHAPTER II. By what precaution the disease of sadness is to be cured

Therefore, if we desire to labor lawfully in the contests of spiritual combat, this disease must also be cured by us with no less vigilance. [Note: Interpreters note that this sentence is not found in the Hebrew. St. Thomas refers it to the body, Cassian to the soul, which in Scripture is frequently understood by the designation “heart.” St. Chrysostom referred it to both in these words (Letter to Olympias): “Sadness of souls is a cruel torment, an insatiable pain, and worse than judgment with judgment and vengeance. For it is like a poisonous worm, killing not only the flesh but the soul itself; and like a moth reaching not only to the bones but to the heart, and a perpetual executioner,” and so forth.]

For just as the moth harms clothing and the worm wood, so sadness harms a man’s heart. The divine Spirit expressed the force of this harmful and most destructive vice quite clearly and precisely (Proverbs 25).

## CHAPTER III. What comparison may be made with the soul that is devoured by the bites of sadness

A garment touched by the eating of moths can no longer have any value or honorable use; likewise, wood bored through by worms deserves to be assigned no longer to the adornment of even an ordinary building, but solely to the burning fire.

Thus, too, the soul devoured by the most ravenous bites of sadness will be useless either for that priestly garment which, according to the prophecy of holy David, is accustomed to receive the ointment descending from heaven first upon Aaron’s beard and then upon the hem of the garment, in accordance with the words: [Note: St. Jerome writes elegantly and at length on this psalm (Book I of On the Divine Offices, chapter 22). Rupert is more concise and more suited to our purpose, as follows: “What is that garment? The holy Catholic Church. For Aaron’s beard—Aaron being interpreted as ‘mountain of strength’—Aaron’s beard, I say, signifies Christ’s apostles and apostolic men, strong and perfect. The royal and priestly ointment is the Holy Spirit, whose fullness is in the head, namely Christ; from there it descends first upon the apostles, as upon the beard, then upon the whole Church, and down to the Church’s farthest members, as upon the hem of the garment.”]

“Like ointment on the head, which ran down upon Aaron’s beard, which ran down to the hem of his garment” (Psalm 132); nor will it be able to belong to the structure and adornment of that spiritual temple whose foundations Paul, a wise architect, laid, saying: “You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you” (1 Corinthians 3). The bride describes the character of its timbers in the Song of Songs: [Note: St. Jerome, drawing from Origen: “The beams of our houses are cedars, and our ceilings are cypresses” (Origen, Homily 2 on the Song). The Vulgate version reads: “The beams of our houses are cedars, our paneling is cypress.” Pliny discusses cedar and cypress in Book XVI of Natural History, chapter 4. They are very hard, decay-resistant, and fragrant trees, as is asserted here.]

“Our beams are cypresses; the timbers of our houses are cedars” (Song of Songs 1). For this reason such kinds of wood are chosen for the temple of God: they are fragrant, imperishable, and incapable of succumbing either to the corruption of age or to the eating of worms.

## CHAPTER IV. From where and by what means sadness arises

[Note: He investigates the causes of sadness and distinguishes several of its kinds from them; but he lists them somewhat more clearly in the last chapter of this book and in Conference 5, chapter 11.]

Sometimes it is accustomed to follow upon the preceding vice of anger, or to arise from some desire [Note: Dionysius paraphrases: “Or from the desire for profit, when someone sees himself deprived of the hope of, or attainment of, those things that he had conceived in his mind.” Cassian frequently uses indeptus, “obtained,” passively for adeptus, “having obtained”; likewise Plautus in the Trinummus used adipiscitur passively: “Wisdom is acquired not by age but by talent.” He also uses the same verb, indipisco, actively (in the Aulularia), from which comes the passive indipiscor, and hence the participle indeptus.] or some profit that has not been obtained, when someone sees that he has fallen away from those things conceived in his mind with a certain hope.

Sometimes, however, even when there are no causes by which we are provoked to fall into this corruption, at the subtle instigation of the enemy we are suddenly so depressed by grief that we cannot receive even the arrival of our dear and necessary companions with our customary friendliness. Whatever they say in suitable conversation seems to us intrusive and superfluous, we give them no gracious reply, and the bitterness of gall takes possession of every recess of our heart.

## CHAPTER V. That disturbances are stirred up in us not through the fault of others, but through our own

[Note: He taught the same thing in the preceding book, chapter 16 and following.]

Thus it is most clearly proved that the stimuli of disturbances are not always stirred up in us through the fault of others, but rather through our own fault, since we carry hidden within ourselves the causes and seeds of offenses and vices. When the rain of temptations has watered our mind, these immediately burst forth into shoots and fruits.

## CHAPTER VI. That no one falls through a sudden collapse, but perishes by gradually declining through a long process of injury

[Note: This is the very truth expressed by St. Chrysostom, although it may seem paradoxical: “No one is harmed except by himself.” By harm he means not bodily harm but harm to the soul, that is, sin, which no one commits unless he wishes to. See Conference 6, chapters 4 and 9.]

For no one compelled to sin by another’s fault is ever forced to do so if he does not have stored-up material for wrongdoing in his own heart.

[Note: This is what the title of this chapter means: “That no one falls through a sudden collapse,” and so forth. Hence the proverb: “No one suddenly becomes utterly wicked.” Abba Theodore makes the same point at greater length in Conference 6, chapter 17, whose similar title is: “That no one collapses in a sudden ruin.” His words are: “No fall should ever be thought to have come about through a sudden collapse; rather, the person has either been deceived at the beginning by a corrupt formation, or has fallen through prolonged negligence of mind, as the virtue of the soul gradually declined and vices thereby slowly increased. Before collapse comes ruin, and before ruin comes an evil thought. In the same way, a house never suddenly falls to the ground from a single blow unless its foundations have been weakened by some ancient defect or the supports of its roof have gradually been corrupted by the long negligence of its inhabitants, as tiny drops first penetrate them; then, when they have been opened up and weakened to a greater extent through prolonged neglect, the storm of rain and showers pours in abundantly.” And so forth.]

Nor should anyone be thought to have been suddenly deceived when, after seeing a woman’s beauty, he fell into the abyss of shameful desire. Rather, hidden and latent diseases deep in the marrow were then brought to the surface by the occasion supplied by sight.

## CHAPTER VII. That the company of the brethren should not be abandoned in order to seek perfection, but that patience should continually be cultivated

Therefore God, the Creator of all, knowing above all how to heal his own workmanship, and because the roots and causes of offenses lie not in others but in ourselves, commanded us not to abandon the company of the brethren or avoid those whom we have injured or whom we think have offended us. Instead, he commands us to conciliate them, knowing that perfection of heart is acquired not so much by separating from people as by the virtue of patience. [Note: “Perfection is born from patience,” says St. Gregory (Book V of the Morals, chapters 13 and 14): “For the person who is truly perfect is not impatient with the imperfection of his neighbor. Whoever, unable to bear the imperfection of others, abandons patience bears witness against himself that he has not yet progressed to perfection.” Hence the Truth says in the Gospel (Luke 21): “By your patience you will possess your souls” (see Conference 19, chapter 9 and following).]

When firmly possessed, patience can preserve us as peacemakers even with those who hate peace; [Note: That is, if patience has not been acquired or obtained.] but if it is not ready at hand, it continually causes us to disagree even with those who are perfect and better than we are. Opportunities for disturbances, on account of which we hasten to abandon those with whom we live, cannot be absent from human society. Therefore we do not escape the causes of sadness on account of which we separate from our former companions; we merely change them.

## CHAPTER VIII. That if we have corrected our conduct, we can live in agreement with everyone

We must therefore take care to hasten rather to correct our vices and amend our conduct. If these have undoubtedly been corrected, we shall find it easy to live not only with human beings but even with wild animals and beasts, according to what is said in the Book of blessed Job: [Note: Gregory wishes it to be read pacificae, “peaceful,” rather than pacatae, “pacified.” He offers a moral reason for this that is irrelevant here. Bede and the Vulgate likewise read pacificae. There are many examples of saints with whom wild animals were not merely pacified and peaceful but also subject and obedient at their command, found throughout the Lives of the Fathers and of the saints preserved by Surius.]

“For the beasts of the earth will be at peace with you” (Job 5). We shall not fear offenses coming from outside; [Note: Passive scandal, which is inflicted upon us from outside, that is, by others, is either the scandal of the weak, who through ignorance think that something lawful is unlawful and are offended when they see it done; hence St. Jerome says (On Matthew 18): “The one who is scandalized is little; the greater do not receive scandals.” Or it is the scandal of the Pharisees, who, through their own wickedness, interpret for the worse things that ought to be interpreted for the better. Such things do not occur among the truly religious and perfect, and still less do active scandals, by which one’s neighbor is led into sin or confirmed in sin. (St. Thomas, II–II, question 43, articles 5 and 6.)]

nor can any scandals be inflicted upon us from outside if their roots have not been received and planted within us. “Great peace have those who love your law, O Lord, and there is no scandal for them” (Psalm 118).

## CHAPTER IX. On another kind of sadness, which brings despair of salvation

There is also another, more detestable kind of sadness, which inflicts upon the delinquent not correction of life or amendment of vices, but the most destructive despair of the soul. [Note: This is the worst kind of sadness, by which someone is either driven to despair, as Cain and Judas were, or rushes headlong into graver sins, as did those who say through Jeremiah: “We have despaired; we will follow our thoughts, and each of us will do the perversity of his evil heart” (Jeremiah 18); and those of whom the Apostle speaks in Ephesians 4: “Having despaired, they gave themselves over to indecency, for the practice of every impurity, in greed.” For this reason the same Apostle writes to the Colossians in almost the same words as to the Romans: “Fathers, do not provoke your children to indignation, lest they become fainthearted” (Colossians 3), that is, lest they be cast down in spirit, lose heart, and through impatience with their grief become worse because of excessive severity. In 2 Corinthians 2 he advises that some consolation be given to the Corinthian who had been excommunicated and publicly rebuked: “Lest,” he says, “such a person should be swallowed up by excessive sadness.” Following this teaching of the Apostle, St. Benedict likewise (chapter 7 of the Rule) requires the abbot to show the same concern for the excommunicated and delinquent, so that he should send elders who, as though secretly, console the offending brother—that is, the brother who has offended—and urge him to make satisfaction in humility, and console him lest he be swallowed up by excessive sadness; but, as the Apostle says (2 Corinthians 2), charity should be confirmed in him, and everyone should pray for him. Also relevant is what St. Augustine writes in Book XII of On the Literal Meaning of Genesis (chapter 33): “That which Jacob says to his sons (Genesis 44), ‘You will bring down my old age with sadness to the underworld,’ seems to show that he feared this above all: that he might be so disturbed by excessive sadness that he would not go to the rest of the blessed but to the underworld of sinners.” For sadness is no small evil of the soul, since the Apostle was so concerned for someone lest he be swallowed up by greater sadness (2 Corinthians 1). Thus Augustine.

Moreover, says St. Thomas (I–II, question 37, article 2), a person is said to be swallowed up by sadness when the power of the evil that causes grief so completely affects the mind that it excludes all hope of escape, and in this way it also weighs down and swallows him. Some things follow one another when they are spoken metaphorically, although they seem contradictory if understood literally. Thus St. Thomas teaches that there is no contradiction when sadness is said both to swallow and to weigh down the mind, since these expressions are metaphorical, not literal. John of Damascus likewise calls distress “that which weighs down,” as was seen above. The Psalmist also appropriately joins these ideas when he first prays: “Let not the tempest of water drown me” (Psalm 68), that is, let not the greatness of troubles and misfortunes overwhelm and oppress me, which is to weigh down. Then he adds: “Nor let the deep swallow me.” Finally: “Nor let the pit shut its mouth over me,” which is the extremity of evils. For those who fall into a pit, says St. Basil (in the Scholia), have a little hope of escape from danger as long as the mouth of the pit remains open; but when even this is closed, all hope of safety is abandoned.]

This was what Cain did not do after his fratricide: he did not repent, nor did Judas, after his betrayal, hasten to the remedies of satisfaction. Instead, his despair dragged him to the hanging noose.

## CHAPTER X. In what respect sadness alone is useful to us

Therefore only one kind of sadness should be judged useful to us: when, inflamed either by repentance for sins, or by desire for perfection, or by contemplation of future blessedness, we conceive it. Concerning this the blessed Apostle says: [Note: The Apostle’s complete sentence gives a fuller meaning, as follows (2 Corinthians 7): “Although I made you sad in the letter, I do not regret it; and if I did regret it, seeing that the letter made you sad, though only for a time, I now rejoice—not because you were made sad, but because you were made sad unto repentance. For you were made sad according to God, so that you might suffer no loss through us. For sadness according to God produces repentance leading to lasting salvation, whereas worldly sadness produces death.”

Here, by antithesis and in direct opposition, two kinds of sadness are distinguished: one good and one evil; one according to God and one of this world; one producing eternal salvation and the other producing death. St. Bernard calls the latter worldly and the former spiritual (Sermon 11, On the Manner of Living).

St. Thomas gives the following account of the reason and origin of both in his commentary: “It should be understood that sadness and joy, and generally every affection, are caused by love. A person is sad because he lacks what he loves. The kind of love determines the kind of sadness caused by love. There are two kinds of love: one by which God is loved, from which arises sadness according to God; the other by which the world is loved, from which arises sadness of this world. The love by which we love God makes us willingly serve God, diligently seek God’s honor, and delightfully devote ourselves to God. Because sin hinders us from serving God, the love of God causes sadness over sin, and this is sadness according to God.” Thus St. Thomas. See also St. Augustine, The City of God, Book XIV, chapter 7.]

“As for sadness according to God,” he says, “it produces repentance leading to lasting salvation, whereas worldly sadness produces death” (2 Corinthians 7).

## CHAPTER XI. How useful and godly sadness is distinguished from diabolical and deadly sadness

But that sadness which produces repentance leading to lasting salvation [Note: “Lasting,” ἀμετακίνητον, that is, fixed, immovable, or perpetual. Other codices read ἀμεταμέλειτον, that is, not to be regretted, or never repented of. There is here a beautiful antithesis between repentance and impenitence, made all the more elegant because μεταμέλεια gives rise to ἀμεταμέλειαν.] is obedient, approachable, humble, gentle, agreeable, and patient, since it descends from the charity of God. It extends itself tirelessly toward every pain of body and spirit through contrition and the desire for perfection; and, in a certain sense, joyful and invigorated by the hope of progress, it retains all the sweetness of friendliness and forbearance. It possesses within itself all the fruits of the Holy Spirit, which the same Apostle enumerates: “The fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, continence” (Galatians 5).

The other kind of sadness, however, is extremely harsh, impatient, hard, full of resentment and fruitless grief, and destructive despair. It breaks and withdraws the person whom it has embraced from industriousness and salutary sorrow; being irrational, it interrupts not only the efficacy of prayers but also empties all the spiritual fruits mentioned above, which the former kind of sadness knows how to produce.

## CHAPTER XII. That apart from the salutary sadness generated in three ways, every sadness must be rejected as harmful
Therefore, apart from that sadness which is undertaken either for salutary repentance, [Col. 0360A] or for the pursuit of perfection, or from desire for future things, [Note: [Col. 0359B] St. Basil, in the *Shorter Rules*, Question 192, asks: “What is sadness according to God, and what is sadness according to the world?” He answers: “Sadness according to God is when we are saddened over neglected commandments or transgression, according to what is written: ‘Sadness has taken hold of me because of sinners who abandon your law.’ [Col. 0359C] Sadness according to the world, however, is when we are saddened on account of something belonging to human affairs or pertaining to the world.”] every sadness, as worldly and bringing death, must equally be rejected and driven completely from our hearts, just as the spirit of fornication, or of avarice, or of anger.

## CHAPTER XIII. Remedies by which we can drive sadness from our hearts

We can expel this most destructive passion from ourselves in such a way that we continually occupy our mind with spiritual meditation and raise it up through hope for the future and contemplation of the promised blessedness. In this way [Note: [Col. 0360B] He gathers and reviews the various forms of vicious sadness arising from the various causes mentioned above; nevertheless, he reduces and refers them to two headings, or kinds, in *Conference* 5, chapter 11, where he says: “There are two kinds of sadness: one generated either by anger coming to an end, or by inflicted loss and frustrated and defeated desire; the other descending from irrational anxiety or despair of the mind.”] we shall be able to overcome every kind of sadness—whether that which descends from preceding anger, or that which comes upon us through loss of profit or the infliction of harm, or [Col. 0360B] that which is generated by an injury inflicted upon us, or that which proceeds from irrational confusion of mind, or that which brings lethal despair upon us—when, always rejoicing and remaining steadfast through the vision of eternal and future things, we are neither cast down by present circumstances nor elated by prosperity, contemplating both as things that perish and soon pass away.

# BOOK TEN. ON THE SPIRIT OF ACEDIA

[Col. 0359]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0359C] [Note: [Col. 0359C] Ciaconius, from the Vatican manuscript: “Our sixth contest is against that which the Greeks call ἀκηδίαν (*akēdian*).” Dionysius: “Our sixth contest is against the vice which the Greeks call acedia.” Thus acedia is placed sixth among the capital vices, and follows sadness because, as Cassian says elsewhere (*Conference* 5, chapter 10): “From sadness acedia necessarily sprouts.” First, then, we must consider what concerns the derivation of the name, and then what concerns the thing itself.

*Acedia* ought to be written with a single *c*, not with two, as many ineptly write and pronounce it. It is a Greek word, ἀκηδία, as the author here indicates, which in Latin means a kind of carelessness or negligence; for κῆδος in Greek signifies care or labor. Hence it is called *acedia* in Latin, the Greek η being changed, as usually happens among Latin speakers, into a long *e*. This is why its second syllable is lengthened by reputable authors, as in the Mantuan’s eleventh poem of Book II of *On the Calamities of the Times*, where he depicts acedia thus:

> Thus acedia, with a false expression, deceives the human being,  
> Diminishing hope and weighing down courage, and mocking  
> The future rewards of labor; it teaches that the thunderbolt  
> And Tartarean fires are to be despised, and that Phlegethon  
> Is feared in vain.

[Col. 0360C] Yet because the Greek η sometimes passes without alteration into the Latin long *i*, some properly pronounce and write the word with a Latin *i* in the second syllable, *acidia*; just as we commonly say *paracletus* for the Holy Spirit, although some, not altogether ineptly, pronounce *paraclitus*, [Col. 0360D] lengthening the penultimate syllable, as Franciscus Philelphus explains elegantly in *Letters*, Book XIII, Letter 47.

Hence the opinion of those who think *acidia* is a Latin word derived from *acidus, -a, -um* is crude and untenable, because it supposedly so depresses a person’s spirit that he wishes to do nothing; just as things that are sour are cold, and just as cold things are not easily moved, so a person suffering from acedia becomes sluggish through excessive sadness (St. Thomas, *Summa theologica* II-II, Question 35, Article 1). Although the matter may indeed be so, it does not follow that *acidia* is derived from *acidus*, since both the authority of the Greek derivation and the length of the syllable plainly oppose this.

Moreover, in sacred writings *acedia* generally signifies sadness, weariness, sluggishness, and anxiety, as is said here (Toletus, *On Mortal Sin*, chapter 58). Thus in Psalm 118, where we read, “My soul has slumbered from weariness,” the Greek has ἀπ’ ἀκηδίας (*ap’ akēdías*), from which the verb *acediari*, “to be afflicted with weariness,” is derived and is also used in Scripture. Ecclesiasticus 6 says: “Bend your shoulder to wisdom and carry her; and do not become weary in her bonds.” And in chapter 22: “Withdraw from a fool, and you will not become weary in his folly,” where the Greek reads: καὶ οὐ μὴ ἀκηδιάσῃς ἐν τῇ ἀπονοίᾳ αὐτοῦ, “and you shall certainly not become weary in his madness.”

As for the matter itself, it must first be noted that acedia, just as was said above concerning anger and sadness, is understood in two ways. First, it is a certain passion in the sensitive appetite that so oppresses the spirit that it brings sluggishness even to the limbs, as well as negligence or aversion toward work—whether that sadness concerns a real evil or an apparent one. In this sense Damascene (*On the Orthodox Faith*, Book II, chapter 14) places acedia as the first kind of sadness and says that it is a sadness that produces silence and loss of voice: λύπη, he says, ἀφωνίαν ἐμποιοῦσα, “sadness producing voicelessness.”

By these words he seems to mean that silence and loss of voice follow from acedia: the spirit is so absorbed and occupied by languid collapse that it cannot bring forth its voice, but, hindered by a kind of confusion and obscuration of itself, is held back and constricted so that it cannot utter speech. [Col. 0361B] St. Thomas, explaining this more subtly (*Summa* II-II, Question 35, Article 8), says: “Acedia is especially said to cut off the voice because, among all outward movements, the voice expresses the inward conception and affection most fully—not only in human beings but also in other animals, as is said in the first book of the *Politics*.”

Thus, consequently, under “voice” all outward movements are understood, and acedia likewise makes a person sluggish and slow with respect to them. In another sense, acedia is understood as sadness, weariness, or aversion of the will, that is, of the rational appetite; and it is almost always joined with sadness in the sensitive appetite. It is understood in this way when the capital sins are discussed, among which it is counted. Thus Cassian in this book, and St. Thomas in the *Summa* (II-II, Question 35, Articles 2 and 5), commonly treat acedia as existing partly in the will and partly in the sensitive appetite.

Second, it must be noted that acedia in this sense, and insofar as it has the character of sin, is still understood in two ways. First, generally and broadly, it is sadness concerning spiritual good insofar as that good is burdensome and laborious to us. In this sense it is not a special vice or sin, but a certain condition and depravity inherent in and common to all vices. Second, acedia is understood properly and strictly as sadness of the will concerning divine spiritual good pertaining to charity. In this sense it is a particular vice distinct from others, and is placed among the capital sins both by Cassian and by St. Gregory and others.

For greater clarification, St. Thomas should here be heard at greater length, as he subtly and accurately explains the character and difference of both senses in these words (Article 2, cited above):

“Since acedia is sadness concerning spiritual good, if spiritual good is understood generally, acedia will not have the character of a special vice, because, as has been said, every vice shuns the spiritual good of the contrary virtue. Similarly, it cannot be said that acedia is a special vice insofar as it shuns spiritual good because that good is laborious, burdensome to the body, or prevents its pleasure, since this would not distinguish acedia from carnal vices, by which a person seeks bodily rest and pleasure.

“Therefore it must be said that there is a certain order among spiritual goods. For all spiritual goods found in the acts of individual virtues are ordered toward one spiritual good, namely divine good, concerning which there is a special virtue, charity. Hence it belongs to each virtue to rejoice in its own spiritual good, which consists in its own act. But it belongs especially to charity to possess that spiritual joy by which one rejoices in divine good. Similarly, the sadness by which one is saddened over the spiritual good found in the acts of individual virtues does not belong to any particular vice, but to all vices. But to be saddened over divine good, in which charity rejoices, belongs to the special vice called acedia.”

Thus far St. Thomas. [Col. 0362A] From this it is clear, first, what acedia means when strictly understood, as the scholastics understand it, and what it means when understood more generally, as the Fathers usually understand it. By the name *acedia* they mean weariness and sluggishness of spirit in carrying out pious works, a weariness that arises from lack of divine love and of that spiritual joy.

Hence St. Gregory (*On 1 Kings*, Book I, chapter 14) describes it thus: “Acedia is the languid collapse of both the inner and outer person from the praiseworthy exercise of the virtues.” “Both persons” means the inner and outer person—that is, spirit and body. St. Bernard says: “Acedia is the sluggishness of the mind that neglects to begin good things or to complete what has been begun.”

Second, it follows that the sin of acedia is contrary to the virtue of charity. For it is directly opposed to spiritual joy in divine good, which we possess in some manner through grace and hope; that joy is an act and effect of charity. Thus the Apostle says in Romans 14 that the kingdom of God is joy in the Holy Spirit. And in Galatians 5 he counts this joy among the fruits of the Holy Spirit, which proceed from charity.

Third, it follows that this sin is mortal in its kind, unless it becomes venial because the act is imperfect and not fully deliberate. On this point St. Thomas again says (Article 3):

“A mortal sin is said to be one that takes away spiritual life, which exists through charity, by which God dwells in us. Therefore that sin is mortal in its kind which, according to its proper character, is contrary to charity. Such is acedia. For the proper effect of charity is joy in God, whereas acedia is sadness concerning spiritual good insofar as it is divine good. Therefore acedia is mortal in its kind.

“But it must be considered in all sins that are mortal in their kind that they are not mortal unless they reach their perfection. For the completion of sin lies in the consent of reason. Thus, if sin begins in the sensual appetite alone and does not reach the consent of reason because the act is imperfect, it is venial. For example, in the category of adultery, desire that remains in the sensual appetite alone is venial sin; but if it reaches the consent of reason, it is mortal sin.

“Likewise, the movement of acedia in the sensual appetite alone sometimes arises from the flesh’s resistance to the spirit, and then it is venial sin. At other times it reaches reason, which consents to flight from, horror of, and detestation of divine good, with the flesh prevailing entirely against the spirit; then it is clear that acedia is mortal sin.”

Thus far St. Thomas. When acedia is said to be mortal in its kind, this condition is understood: that it be perfect acedia—that is, that a person deliberately and with the full judgment of reason shudder at and reject divine good, rather than experiencing this only on the part of the sensual appetite and bodily weakness. Therefore the same doctor, citing this passage of Cassian, admits that even in holy and perfect men, such as the anchorites and hermits discussed here, imperfect movements of acedia may sometimes arise; nevertheless, they do not reach the consent of reason and consequently are not mortal sins, [Col. 0362D] but only venial.

He further adds another condition (*ibid.*, response to objection 3), which is presupposed if acedia is to be mortal: namely, that acedia concern divine good to which one is bound by command to adhere. This means that the weariness or aversion of acedia must concern things commanded and necessary for salvation, and must do so under mortal guilt—for example, if a cleric omitted the reading of the canonical hours out of weariness, or a monk cast off his habit out of weariness with his profession.

“For it will not be the sin of acedia if someone is saddened because he is compelled to perform works of virtue to which he is not bound. And if one is bound only under venial obligation, it will be no more than venial acedia.”

Fourth, it follows that under the name *acedia* a certain twofold evil or sin is understood, or that one sins through acedia in two ways. Acedia is either sluggishness and laziness in undertaking and beginning the good, [Col. 0363A] or weariness, aversion, and sadness in persevering.

Those sin in the first way who undertake good works—fasts, prayers, and similar practices—lazily, slowly, and with sadness; those who shrink from the labor involved in learning, teaching, or doing what belongs to their vocation. Those sin in the second way who interrupt good works already begun out of weariness and aversion.

If what is omitted or interrupted is commanded or otherwise necessary for salvation, and if this relaxation or omission occurs with the full consent of reason, rather than being merely an unconsidered impulse or the weakness of human frailty—against which one must struggle and resist—then such acedia becomes mortal sin. Otherwise it is venial, as has been said.

Finally, St. Gregory rightly also counts acedia among the capital vices (*Morals* XXXI, chapter 31), and enumerates its six daughters—that is, the sins or vices which ordinarily flow from acedia as from a source or head, or which adhere to it through close kinship. He says:

“From sadness—for he considers sadness identical with acedia, as has been said—arise malice, rancor, faintheartedness, despair, sluggishness concerning the commandments, and wandering of mind toward unlawful things.”

Here, according to St. Thomas (Article 4), malice is hatred and detestation of spiritual good itself; rancor is aversion toward those who exhort others to spiritual goods; faintheartedness concerns spiritual goods insofar as they are difficult, and is usually a venial sin; despair is despair of attaining blessedness, which is the gravest sin against the Holy Spirit; sluggishness concerns observance of God’s commandments, which belong to common justice; and wandering of mind concerns other unlawful things that provide pleasure.

Moreover, Isidore, in Book II of *On the Highest Good*, says that from sadness arise rancor, faintheartedness, bitterness, and despair. Concerning acedia he says (chapter 37) that seven things arise from it: idleness, drowsiness, restlessness of mind, bodily agitation, instability, talkativeness, and curiosity.

But, St. Thomas says, these can be reduced to those listed by Gregory. For the bitterness which Isidore says arises from sadness [Col. 0363C]—which he distinguishes from acedia only conceptually—is a certain effect of rancor. Idleness and drowsiness are reduced to sluggishness concerning the commandments, since a person is idle with respect to them by omitting them all, and drowsy by fulfilling them carelessly. The remaining five things that he says arise from acedia belong to wandering of mind around unlawful things.

This much may be said, following the teaching of St. Thomas, about the nature and gravity of the sin of acedia and its daughters or effects, leaving aside the other matters that an industrious reader may seek in him and in his interpreters. In general, what has been said about the capital vices must also be observed specifically of acedia: they are not always mortal simply because they are capital, but are called capital because they are, as it were, heads and sources of many other vices. Thus, although acedia is judged mortal by its nature or kind, it often becomes venial when one of the conditions mentioned above is absent.]

Our sixth contest is with what the Greeks call ἀκηδίαν, which we may call weariness or anxiety of heart. [Col. 0363A] [Note: [Col. 0363D] Elsewhere he says (*Conference* 5, chapter 10): “Sadness is familiarly joined to acedia, and pride to vainglory.” He is referring to the sadness discussed in the preceding book (*above*)—that is, impatience, which is itself a form of sadness in the general sense used by Damascene, and is called distress—or to the sadness of this world which, according to the Apostle, “produces death” (2 Corinthians 7), and to which acedia also belongs. For it is not sadness according to God, which is set in opposition to the sadness of this world, says St. Thomas. For this reason St. Gregory also rightly calls acedia sadness (II-II, Question 35, Article 3; Book II of *On the Highest Good*, chapter 37).

Isidore, moreover, distinguishes sadness from acedia only conceptually: “If, in this vice, aversion from a good that is judged difficult and laborious is considered—such as fasting, praying, obeying, and similar things—it is called sadness for that reason. But if one considers the turning toward an undue rest that is judged easy and pleasant, it is called acedia for that reason.” Thus this vice is named in two ways, namely sadness and acedia. So much from him.]

This is akin to sadness, and is especially experienced by wandering and solitary monks, and is a more hostile and frequent enemy to those living in the desert, [Note: [Col. 0364A] By “wandering and solitary” he means those monks, or anchorites, who roam in the wildernesses and are not tied to one fixed place, often moving from one region to another either in pursuit of greater austerity or to avoid praise and empty glory—not for pleasure or out of a desire to wander. Such men are called *Gyrovagi* and *Sarabaites*, as may be seen in the *Lives of the Fathers* and also in Cassian’s *Conferences*. St. Bernard should also be consulted in his treatise *On the Passion of the Lord*, where he makes this vice peculiar to religious and solitary persons, as does Abbot Serapion in *Conference* 5, chapter 9.

Bernard’s words are these: “There are some who indeed perform good works, whether through compulsion, necessity, or habit, but are moved to do them without any eagerness; this vice is properly called acedia. Religious people are afflicted by this vice above all, for very few secular people, even if they possess the vice, recognize it. Bound as they are to the world, they can scarcely grasp the name of a spiritual vice, although this vice is counted among the seven principal ones.

“The vice of acedia casts a certain sluggishness over the soul, so that all spiritual exercises seem tasteless to those afflicted and are changed into oppressive weariness. Concerning this weariness the psalm says: ‘My soul has slumbered from weariness’; and elsewhere: ‘Their soul abhorred every kind of food, and they drew near to the gates of death.’

“For the soul of the good is sometimes afflicted by this vice to such an extent that it abhors every kind of food—that is, every spiritual exercise—so that it does not wish to pray, read, meditate, or carry out manual work. Indeed, they even draw near to the gates of death: they become so weary of life itself that they desire death to end it, saying with holy Job: ‘My soul is weary of my life.’”

This is Bernard’s account.]

and, [Note: [Col. 0364C] From this same statement St. Thomas raises an objection (II-II, Question 35, Article 1, response to objection 2), by which it might appear that acedia is not a sin: “No bodily defect that occurs at appointed hours has the character of sin; but acedia is of this sort,” for Cassian says in the tenth book *On the Institutes of the Monasteries*: “Acedia especially troubles the monk around the sixth hour, like a certain fever,” and so forth.

He answers the objection as follows: “It must be said that the passions of the sensitive appetite can in themselves be venial sins and can incline the mind toward mortal sin. Since the sensitive appetite has a bodily organ, it follows that through some bodily change a person becomes more disposed to a particular sin. Therefore it can happen that, according to certain bodily changes occurring at particular times, certain sins assail us more strongly.

“Every bodily defect in itself disposes one to sadness. Therefore those fasting around midday, when they are already beginning to feel the lack of food and are being oppressed by the heat of the sun, are more strongly attacked by acedia.” So says St. Thomas.

John Climacus, in the thirteenth step, expresses the same thought not inelegantly: “In the morning the physician first visits those who are languishing, but acedia visits monks around midday.”]

especially troubling the monk around the sixth hour, [Col. 0364A] like a fever coming on at its appointed time, and bringing upon the sick soul the fiercest heats of its attacks [Al. “accessions”] at the customary and appointed hours.

Finally, some of the elders [Note: [Col. 0364D] The Fathers variously explain the “noonday demon,” as well as the other dangers or harms that threaten us and are expressed in that verse of Psalm 90: “You will not fear”—first, “the terror by night”; second, “the arrow flying by day”; third, “the business that walks in darkness”; fourth, “the attack and the noonday demon.”

St. Augustine, in his explanation of this psalm, says: “Temptations of ignorance are the terror by night; sins of knowledge are the arrow flying by day, for by night ignorance is understood, and by day manifestation. Some sin in ignorance, others sin knowingly. Those who sin in ignorance are overthrown by the terror by night; those who sin knowingly are struck by the arrow flying by day.

“When these things occur in more serious persecutions, until one reaches what is like midday, whoever falls in that heat falls as if struck by the noonday demon.” And below: “There was then a great heat of persecutors; whoever fell in that temptation fell as if struck by the noonday demon.”

Thus Augustine suggests that those words signify a threefold temptation: the first, light and hidden, by the terror at night; the second, light and manifest, by the arrow flying by day; the third, grave and open or manifest, by the attack and the noonday demon—that is, by the attack of the noonday demon, especially as occurs in tyrannical persecution. It is clear here that a fourth member, or fourth kind of temptation—grave but hidden, designated by “the business that walks in darkness”—is lacking, so that the division may be complete, though I do not know why St. Augustine omitted it.

St. Jerome also seems to agree with this interpretation of the noonday demon in his *Apology against Rufinus* (Book II, chapter 4), where he aptly calls Arius, the most notorious heresiarch, a “noonday demon.” During the age of Constantine, when the Church was like a brilliantly splendid and flourishing midday, Arius disturbed it greatly, attacking it not through hidden machinations but openly and with incredible boldness, and almost throwing the entire Christian world into confusion.

St. Bernard offers another interpretation in Sermon 6 on the same psalm. By the terror at night he understands the temptation of faintheartedness; by the arrow flying by day, the temptation of vainglory; by the business walking in darkness, the temptation of ambition or avarice; and by the noonday demon, the temptation to do an evil work under the appearance of good (see Matthew Delrio, *Magical Investigations*, Book II, Question 27).

The same St. Bernard says elsewhere (*Moral Sentences*): “There are four robbers who steal from us the best things. The dullness of understanding, which takes from us knowledge of the truth, is the robber called by the Psalmist ‘the business in darkness.’ The unruly wantonness of the flesh, which snatches away the merit of integrity, is called the noonday demon. The boasting of a favorable breeze of approval, which takes away the fullness of holiness, is called the arrow flying by day. The love and desire for this life, which steals away the reward of eternity, is called the terror by night.” Thus far St. Bernard.

Those ancient anchorites of whom Cassian speaks here called acedia, or the temptation of acedia, the noonday demon because it attacked monks most strongly around the sixth hour—that is, at midday—when, fasting and hungry, they grew weary of or resented the longer period of hunger and abstinence, as was explained above from St. Thomas.] declare that this is the noonday demon mentioned in Psalm 90.

## CHAPTER II. How acedia creeps into a monk’s heart, and what losses it brings upon the mind

[Note: [Col. 0365D] Various effects of acedia are recounted here, or, which is the same thing, the serious and manifold temptations to which a monk afflicted with acedia, or possessed by the spirit of acedia, becomes subject. They may be listed more briefly and in nearly the same order as follows:

1. Horror of the place or monastery in which he lives;  
2. Weariness of the cell and enclosure;  
3. Disdain and contempt for the brothers living with him or nearby;  
4. Inertia and slowness in working;  
5. Wandering outside the cell;  
6. Neglect of sacred reading;  
7. Sighs and groans that he is making no progress there;  
8. The opinion that he would be more useful to himself and others elsewhere;  
9. The desire to preside over others for their benefit and the gain of souls;  
10. Hatred of monastic discipline and subjection;  
11. Impatience with hunger, solitude, prayer, and mortification;  
12. Drowsiness and frequent dozing;  
13. Superfluous visits and conversations;  
14. Long and useless journeys;  
15. Dangerous familiarities;  
16. Desire and concern for relatives.

Cassian explains these matters at greater length in this and the following chapters. John Climacus, a most devout man and an exceptionally subtle critic of vices, imitating him, presents nearly the same characteristics of acedia as if displayed in a chart, in these words (Step 13):

“Acedia is relaxation of the spirit, dissolution of the mind, neglect of the monastic life, hatred of one’s profession. It also urges one to leave the cell, making some sound, or crash, or noise of feet. Whoever mourns for himself does not know acedia; it calls worldly people blessed. It slanders God as harsh and merciless. It is weak in psalmody, feeble in prayer, iron-hard in service, lazy in manual work, and rebellious in obedience.

“The common monastery resists acedia; but for the solitary man it is an inseparable companion, and it will not leave him before death. Every day, as long as he lives, it will attack him. When it sees the anchorite’s cell, it smiles and, approaching, pitches its tents beside it.

“In the early morning the physician visits those who are languishing, but acedia visits monks around midday. Acedia suggests receiving guests and begs that alms be given through the labor of one’s hands; it eagerly urges one to visit the sick, reminding one of him who said in the Gospel: ‘I was sick, and you visited me.’

“It commands those afflicted with some sadness and the fainthearted to set out; being itself fainthearted, it suggests consoling the fainthearted. When we stand at prayer, it reminds us of some necessary matter and employs every device so that it, itself irrational, may drag us away by some supposedly reasonable rope.

“For three hours the spirit of acedia produces horror, headache, fever, and dizziness. But when the ninth hour arrives, it recovers somewhat; when the table is set, the monk leaps from his bed, and when the time of prayer returns, his body again begins to grow heavy. It plunges those standing at prayer into sleep and, through untimely yawning, tears the verse from their mouths.”

This is Climacus’s account, and everyone can see how closely it approaches Cassian’s words. Moreover, all these and the other effects of acedia can easily be reduced to the six daughters listed by St. Gregory, as was shown above.]

When acedia has besieged the pitiable mind, it generates horror of the place, weariness of the cell, and disdain and contempt even for the brothers who live with him or at a distance from him, as though they were negligent and less spiritual. [Col. 0366A] It also makes him lazy and inert regarding every task within the boundaries of his dwelling. It does not allow him to remain in his cell or devote himself to reading. [Note: [Col. 0366D] St. Thomas also clarifies this passage when it is raised as an objection, responding: “It belongs to humility that, when a person considers his own defects, he does not exalt himself. But it does not belong to humility, but rather to ingratitude, to despise the goods one possesses from God; and acedia follows from such contempt. For we are saddened by things that we regard as evil or worthless. Thus one ought to exalt the goods of others while nevertheless not despising the goods divinely provided—that is, bestowed—upon oneself, because otherwise they would become a source of sadness.”]

He more and more frequently groans that, although he has spent so long there, he is making no progress, and he complains and sighs that he has no spiritual fruit, until he has been joined to the company of others. He grieves that he is empty of every spiritual gain and stands in that place to no purpose, since, although he could govern others and benefit many, he has edified no one and won no one through his instruction and teaching. [Col. 0367A]

He magnifies monasteries that are absent and far away, describing those places as more useful for progress and more suitable for salvation. He depicts the fellowship of the brothers there as pleasant and full of spiritual conduct. By contrast, he portrays everything at hand as harsh, claiming not only that the brothers living in the place provide no edification, but that even bodily sustenance cannot be obtained without immense labor.

Finally, he thinks that he cannot be saved if he remains in that place, and that he will perish if he stays any longer in the cell; therefore he must carry himself away from it as quickly as possible. Then he arouses such weariness of body and hunger for food [Note: [Col. 0367C] This means around midday. Since the ancients, as has been said, divided the entire span of the day from sunrise to sunset into twelve equal parts, which they called hours, the sixth hour from sunrise necessarily fell at midday, and the fifth was the hour immediately before midday. Hence even today the sixth hour in the ecclesiastical office is called midday or noon.

I think Climacus had this in mind above when he said (Step 13) that the spirit of acedia sometimes generated horror, headache, fever, and dizziness in those anchorites and solitaries for three hours. That is, while they were fatigued by hunger and labor around midday, many of them continued to abstain and waited for food for three more hours, until the ninth hour, or three in the afternoon; the weaker ones did not do so, but acedia overcame them. Hence horror, pain, and dizziness were generated in them.]

in the fifth and sixth hours that he seems to himself exhausted and weary, as though he had completed a long journey and undergone the heaviest labor, or as though he had postponed eating for two or three days of fasting.

Then, anxious, he looks around in every direction. He sighs because no brother is approaching him; he goes out of and enters his cell more frequently; and he repeatedly gazes at the sun, as though it were hurrying more slowly toward setting. Thus, through an irrational confusion of mind, as though the earth were filled with darkness, he becomes idle and empty with respect to every spiritual activity, and thinks that no remedy for so great an assault can be found except the visit of some brother or the comfort of sleep alone.

[Col. 0367C] Next, the same illness suggests that he offer the brothers polite and necessary greetings and visit the sick, whether they are nearby or farther away. [Col. 0368A] It also dictates certain pious and religious duties: that he ought to inquire after his parents, whether male or female, and hasten more frequently to greet them; that it would be a great work of devotion to visit more often that religious woman devoted to God, especially if she lacks all support from her parents; and that, if she needs anything, it would be most holy to provide it, since she is neglected and despised by her own parents. It says that more effort of devotion ought to be spent on these matters than on sitting uselessly and without any progress in one’s little cell.

“O cell, storehouse of heavenly merchants, in which indeed is stored the sum of those wares by which possession of the land of the living is purchased! O cell, wondrous workshop of spiritual exercise, in which the human soul restores within itself the image of its Creator and returns to the purity of its origin; where dulled senses return to the subtlety of their keenness, and where, in place of corrupted nature, the unleavened bread of sincerity is found. [Col. 0368D] O cell, wholly a spiritual dwelling-place! For you make the proud humble, the gluttonous temperate, the cruel compassionate, the angry gentle, and the idle fervent in divine love. Saint Bernard likewise speaks excellently and most aptly to the present passage:

“Cell and heaven have a kinship, because just as heaven and cell seem to have some kinship with one another in name, so also in piety. For heaven (*coelum*) and cell (*cella*) seem to derive their names from *celare*, ‘to conceal’; and what is concealed in heaven is also in cells; what is done in heaven is also in cells. What is this? To be free for God, to enjoy God. When this is performed piously and faithfully, according to order, in cells, I dare to say that the holy angels of God regard cells as heavens and take equal delight in cells and in heaven. For when heavenly things are constantly enacted in a cell, heaven is brought close to the cell both by the likeness of the sacrament, by the affection of piety, and by the effect of similar works. Nor does the praying spirit—or even the spirit departing from the body—find the way from cell to heaven long or difficult. For one often ascends from cell to heaven; hardly ever does one descend from cell to hell. The dying man hardly ever, or never, descends from cell to hell, because hardly anyone who is not predestined for heaven perseveres in it until death. For the cell cherishes, nourishes, embraces, and brings to the fullness of perfection the child of grace, the fruit of its womb, and makes him worthy of God’s converse; but it quickly rejects and casts away what is alien or substituted.”

Such are the words of Saint Bernard, together with what follows, which is most worthy of reading.] in silence, and through the constant perseverance, meditation, and contemplation of the cell. Thus Saint Thomas (*Commentary*, lesson 1): piously and suitably according to the Vulgate reading, so far as morals are concerned. Ambrose and all the Latins read, as does Cassian, “the one to whom he has proved himself,” that is, “into whose military service he has entered.” But from the Greek it ought rather to be translated: “the one who has proved him,” that is, “the one who has selected and enrolled him for spiritual service.”]

## CHAPTER IV. That acedia blinds the mind to every contemplation of virtue

The blessed David elegantly expressed all the disadvantages of this illness in a single verse: [Note: [Col. 0369D] The holy Fathers note that the Hebrew has *distillavit*, “my soul has wept” or “dripped with tears because of anxiety.” Origen read it in this way, as though the Septuagint had translated it ἔσταξεν ἀπ’ ἀκηδίας, “it dripped because of acedia,” rather than ἐνύσταξεν, “it became drowsy.” The meaning nevertheless comes to the same thing: sorrow or grief of spirit ordinarily draws out tears, just as it raises vapors into the brain, from which sleep arises. We see infants sleep deeply after they have cried, and adults, when they are in mourning, become overcome by sleep. Hence Luke 22: “He found them sleeping because of sorrow.” *Acedia* is sorrow concerning a good work, whether one is beginning it or completing it, as has been said. Spiritually, therefore, the soul is said to drip—that is, to fail and, in failing, to become drowsy—when through acedia it grows numb from its former fervor and strength of spirit and develops a distaste for good work.] “My soul became drowsy,” he says, “because of weariness” (Psalm 118), that is, because of acedia. He quite properly said not that the body, but that the soul, became drowsy. For the soul wounded by the dart of this disturbance truly grows drowsy with regard to every contemplation of virtue and every perception of spiritual realities.

## CHAPTER V. That acedia is of two kinds in the struggle

[Col. 0369B]

Therefore the true athlete of Christ, who desires to fight the contest of perfection lawfully, must hasten to drive this illness also from the hiding places of his soul, and must struggle on both fronts against this most wicked spirit of acedia, [Note: [Col. 0370C] These are the two kinds of acedia, as Abbot Serapion observed in Conference 15, chapter 11: “One casts those who are burning with zeal into sleep; the other urges them to abandon and flee the cell.” Saint Bernard expresses it with slightly different words: “There are two kinds of acedia. One compels the monk to be sluggish in the work of God and to become drowsy; the other makes him wander here and there and urges him to flee from the company of the brothers with whom he lives” (*On the Order of Life*). Others also call these two principal effects, or daughters, of acedia sleepiness and instability—that is, abandonment of and wandering away from one’s place or cell. ## CHAPTER VI. How deadly are the effects of acedia

For whoever acedia begins to overcome in any part, it will either allow him, as an inert and sluggish man, to remain in his cell without any spiritual progress, or, once driven from it, will thereafter make him unstable and wandering, sluggish for every work; [Note: [Col. 0370C] These are the beginnings of the wicked monks whom Saint Benedict calls Sarabaites and Gyrovagues in chapter 1 of the Rule. Its example is found in Scripture in Exodus 10 and Numbers 11, where the children of Israel, wandering and idle in the desert, thought of nothing but the melons of Egypt and the pots of meat.] For the mind of an idle man knows how to think of nothing except food and the belly, until at some point it finds the companionship of a man or woman languishing in equal tepidity and becomes entangled in their affairs and needs; and [Col. 0370B] thus little by little becomes so ensnared in harmful occupations that, as though bound by serpent coils, [Note: [Col. 0370D] Elsewhere he said: “The unhappy soul bound by serpent-like knots” (Book VII, chapter 7). Coils are revolutions or circles that do not return upon themselves. Hence serpents are said to form coils when, contracted into a ring, they imitate certain circles. Virgil, *Aeneid* II:

“They bind him with enormous coils, and already

There he is speaking of the two serpents that had attacked the idol-sacrifice.] it can never afterward disentangle itself for the perfection of its former profession.

## CHAPTER VII. The Apostle’s testimonies concerning the spirit of acedia

[Note: [Col. 0370D] Against acedia and its offspring—which Scripture calls idleness and sluggishness—the author proposes and very earnestly inculcates manual labor as the best and exceedingly necessary remedy. He says that it was received from the teaching and example of the apostles and thereafter retained and practiced by the ancient Fathers and monks, especially the Egyptians, through continual use and observance (Bonaventure, *On Poverty*, Book II, chapter 3; II-II, question 187, article 3).

“First, as regards doctrine, he carefully examines the Apostle’s precepts drawn from both Epistles to the Thessalonians, both in this chapter and in those that follow, and adapts them in a particular way to monks, although the Apostle delivered them commonly to all Christians and they apply equally to secular persons and religious. For their explanation, besides what has been said elsewhere on this matter, one should note from Saint Thomas that manual labor is undertaken for four reasons and directed toward four ends. ‘First,’ he says, ‘and principally, to obtain sustenance; hence it was said to the first man: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread.” Second, to avoid idleness, from which many evils arise; hence Ecclesiasticus 33 says: “Set your servant to work, for idleness has taught much wickedness.” Third, to restrain concupiscence, insofar as the body is disciplined by it; hence II Corinthians 6 says: “In labors, in fastings, in vigils, in chastity.” Fourth, it is ordered toward giving alms; hence Ephesians 4 says: “Let the one who stole steal no more, but rather let him labor, working with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something to give to the one in need.”

“Thus, insofar as manual labor is ordered toward obtaining sustenance, it falls under the necessity of the precept, to the extent that it is necessary for that end. Therefore whoever has no other means by which to live is bound to work with his hands, whatever his condition. This is signified by the Apostle’s words: “If anyone is unwilling to work, let him not eat”; as though he said: one is bound to work with his hands by the same necessity by which one is bound to eat—namely, in order to sustain life. The same reasoning applies to those who have no other lawful means of living. For no one is understood to be able to do what he cannot lawfully do. Hence the Apostle is not found to have commanded manual labor except to exclude the sin of those who were acquiring their food unlawfully.

“Saint Thomas adds shortly afterward: ‘It should nevertheless be understood that under manual labor are included all human occupations by which people lawfully earn their sustenance, whether they are performed with the hands, the feet, or the tongue. Watchmen, runners, and others who live from their labor are understood to live by the work of their hands. Since the hand is the instrument of instruments, every operation by which someone may lawfully earn his sustenance is understood as the work of the hands.’

“Yet insofar as manual labor is ordered toward removing idleness or disciplining the flesh, it does not in itself fall under the necessity of the precept, because the flesh may be disciplined and idleness removed in many other ways than through manual labor. The flesh is disciplined by fasts and vigils, and idleness is removed by meditation on the Holy Scriptures and divine praises. Therefore religious persons are not bound to manual labor for these reasons, any more than secular persons are—unless, perhaps, they are bound to it by the statutes of their order. Thus Jerome says in his letter to the monk Rusticus: ‘The monasteries of the Egyptians maintain this custom, that they receive no one without work or labor, not so much because of the necessity of food as for the salvation of the soul, lest they wander through destructive thoughts.’

“Insofar as manual labor is ordered toward giving alms, it does not fall under the necessity of the precept except in the case where someone is obliged to give alms and could not otherwise obtain the means to assist the poor. In that case religious and secular persons alike would be bound to perform manual labor. Thus far Saint Thomas, with such clarity and solidity of doctrine that nothing clearer, more explicit, more precise, or more suitable to the present subject of manual labor could be said.”]

The blessed Apostle, as a true and spiritual physician, hastens to prevent this illness, which arises from the spirit of acedia, with the salutary medicines of his precepts—either because he already saw it beginning to spread or because, through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, he foresaw that it would arise among monks. Writing to the Thessalonians, he first acts like a most skilled and consummate physician, [Note: [Col. 0372C] Ciaconius’s note on the word *suscepti* seems not to be omitted. “Cassian,” he says, “calls the sick *suscepti*, those whom a physician has undertaken to treat.” Thus the person who is called Ambrose, in the commentary on chapter 1 of the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, says: “What physician does not rebuke his patient (*susceptum*) for treating himself carelessly, lest the care of his medicine remain fruitless?” Saint Ambrose, Sermon 27: “If we faithfully entreat the physician of our souls, and do not reject his precepts as suitable patients (*suscepti*).” Tertullian, *Against the Valentinians*, chapter 16: “Here, I suppose, he confirms the patient (*susceptam*) and cleanses her from every injury of suffering.” The term also referred to clients whom patrons had undertaken to protect. Servius, commenting on *Aeneid* VI, on the words “or fraud fastened upon a client,” says: “He wishes to indicate false advocates, who are patrons of clients, whom we now call *suscepti*.” Augustine, Letter 59 (Conference 6, chapter 10): “Then bishops, as advocates, offer their clients (*susceptos*), through the laying on of hands, to the most merciful power.” The work concealed under Augustine’s name, *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*, question 102: “If the advocate is of bad character, will judgment be pronounced against his client (*susceptum*)?” Ambrose likewise, Sermon 93: “The efficacious advocate’s presence will be of help to the extent that the client’s (*suscepti*) faith has been devout.” Thus far Ciaconius, diligently and accurately. Cassian also uses this word in the former sense in chapter 14 of this book, and in the latter sense in Conference 6, chapter 10.]

soothing the illness of his patients (*susceptorum*) with the gentle and mild treatment of his word. Beginning with charity, and praising them in that respect, he continues until the deadly wound, softened by a gentler remedy and with the swelling of indignation laid aside, can more easily endure harsher medicines. Thus he says:

“Concerning fraternal charity, we have no need to write to you. For you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another. Indeed, you do this toward all the brothers throughout Macedonia” (I Thessalonians 4).

He first applied gentle soothing remedies of praise and made their ears calm and ready for the treatment of salutary speech. Again he adds:

“But we urge you, brothers, to abound more.”

He still caresses them with the gentle softness of his words, lest perhaps he find them not yet fit to receive a perfect cure. What is this that you ask, Apostle—that they should abound more in charity, concerning which you had just said: “Concerning fraternal charity, we have no need to write to you”? And why is it necessary for you to tell them, “We urge you to abound more,” when they need no writing from you concerning this matter—especially since you give the reason why they do not need it, saying: “For you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another”? You add a third and greater point: they have not only been taught by God, but also fulfill in deed what they are taught. “Indeed, you do this,” he says, not toward only one or two, but “toward all the brothers”; and not merely toward your fellow citizens or acquaintances, but “throughout Macedonia.” Tell us, then, at last: why do you put this first with such insistence? Again he says: “We urge you, brothers, to abound more.” And only after long delay does he break into what he had been preparing: [Col. 0373A]

[Note: [Col. 0373C] To the many and various illnesses—or vices—of acedia, which are related to and accompany one another and which are enumerated in this chapter, the Apostle opposes an equal number of remedies (I Thessalonians 4 and II Thessalonians 3), and Cassian applies the antidotes and contrary medicines drawn from the Apostle.

“The first illness is restlessness, which Saint Gregory calls ‘the wandering of the mind toward unlawful things’ (*Morals* XXXI, chapter 31): ‘We hear that some among you are walking restlessly.’ The antidote is: ‘Make it your aim to be quiet,’ that is, to act calmly and without disturbance and not to trouble the quiet of others.

“The second evil is curiosity: ‘doing nothing, but acting inquisitively.’ The antidote is: ‘to conduct your own affairs,’ that is, for each person to attend to his own vocation and work and not interfere in the affairs of others.

“The third illness is idleness: ‘doing nothing.’ The antidote is: ‘to work with your hands.’
