“The fourth evil is giving scandal to others, which is signified by ‘walking dishonestly’ or ‘disorderly.’ The antidote is: ‘to walk honorably before those who are outside,’ that is, to live without scandal among unbelievers or, in Cassian’s application, among secular persons. Unbelievers were scandalized when they saw Christians wishing to live on the possessions of others, just as secular people are scandalized when they see monks wandering about and idle.

“The fifth illness is greed or desire for the possessions of others, from which theft arises. The antidote is: ‘to desire nothing belonging to anyone else.’ And Ephesians 4 says: ‘Let the one who stole steal no more, but rather let him labor,’ and so forth.”]

“And make it your aim to be quiet.”

He has stated the first cause. Then he introduces the second:

“And to conduct your own affairs.”

Then the third:

“And to work with your hands, as we commanded you.”

The fourth:

“And to walk honorably before those who are outside.”

The fifth:

“And to desire nothing belonging to anyone else.”

Here it becomes clear what that hesitation, which he had delayed introducing with such extensive preambles, was bringing forth in his heart. “Make it your aim to be quiet”—that is, remain in your cells and, becoming restless through various rumors, which are commonly generated by the desires or conversations of idle people, do not bring restlessness upon others as well. “And conduct your own affairs”—do not seek, through curiosity, to investigate the actions of the world, nor, examining the conduct of various people, devote your work not to your own correction or the pursuit of virtue, but to the detraction of the brothers. “And work with your hands, as we commanded you”—so that those things might be done which he had earlier warned them not to do: that is, so that they might not be restless, concern themselves with the affairs of others, walk dishonorably before those who are outside, or desire anything belonging to another. Now he adds: “And work with your hands,” [Note: [Col. 0374C] The Apostle did not command everyone, absolutely, to work with their hands or to practice a mechanical trade, but those who are in need and are not occupied with other better and higher exercises or duties, as can be gathered from what has been said.] “as we commanded you.” For he clearly showed that idleness was the cause of those things which he had condemned above. No one can be restless or concern himself with the affairs of others except one who refuses to persist in the work of his own hands.

He also introduced the fourth illness, which arises from this very idleness: namely, that they should not walk dishonorably, saying: “And that you walk honorably before those who are outside.” No one can walk honorably even among secular people who is not content to remain within the enclosure of his cell and devote himself to the work of his hands. Rather, he must become dishonorable while seeking the necessities of life, practicing flattery, pursuing even the latest rumors, and seeking occasions for disputes and stories through which he may prepare for himself an entrance and the opportunity to penetrate the houses of various people.

“And to desire nothing belonging to anyone else.” One who does not take pleasure in obtaining the substance of his daily sustenance through the pious and peaceful labor of his own work cannot help yearning for the gifts and presents of others.

Do you see how many and how serious and shameful causes are generated by the single fault of idleness?

Finally, these same people whom he had cherished in the First Epistle with the gentle touch of his words, he now attempts in the Second to heal with certain harsher and caustic medicines, as though they had not advanced through milder remedies. [Note: [Col. 0374C] Cuychius calls these *caustica medicamenta*. In Greek, καυστικὰ φάρμακα are bitter and severe medicines, such as incisions and things possessing a caustic—that is, burning—power. Hence καυτήριον, *cauterium*, is the instrument by which putrid flesh is burned. See more at Conference 6, chapter 11.] He no longer precedes them with any soothing treatment of mild words, nor with any tender or gentle expression such as “We urge you, brothers,” but says:

“We command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to withdraw yourselves from every brother who walks disorderly” (II Thessalonians 3).

There he asks; here he commands. In the first passage there is the affection of one who entreats; in this one, the severity and threat of one who charges. “We command you, brothers”: because you previously despised our entreaties, at least now obey our commands.

He makes the command itself terrifying not by a bare word, but by an adjuration in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, lest they again despise it as though it had been spoken merely in a human voice and regard it as requiring little observance. Immediately, [Note: [Col. 0374C] Saint Benedict likewise teaches the abbot to observe this procedure toward brothers who offend, are excommunicated, or are incorrigible (chapters 27 and 28; see Turrecremata): “With every concern, let the abbot care for offending brothers, because the physician is not needed by the healthy but by the sick” (Matthew 9). “Therefore he must use every means, like a wise physician,” and so forth. In the following chapter he says: “If a brother, frequently corrected for any fault and even excommunicated, does not amend, let a harsher correction be applied to him—that is, let the punishment of blows proceed against him. If this does not correct him, then let the abbot act as a wise physician. If he has applied fomentations, the ointments of exhortations, the medicines of the divine Scriptures, and finally the burning of excommunication or the wounds of rods, and sees that his skill has accomplished nothing, let him also apply what is greater: his own prayer and that of all the brothers for him, so that the Lord, who can do all things, may work salvation in the sick brother. If he is not healed even in this way, then let the abbot use the knife of excision, as the Apostle says: “Remove the evil one from among you”; and again: “Let the unbeliever depart,” lest one dead sheep contaminate the whole flock.”]

as a most skilled physician, he attempts to cure with the incision of spiritual steel those putrid members to which he could not bring a remedy by gentle medicine:

“Withdraw yourselves,” he says, “from every brother who walks disorderly and not according to the tradition which they received from us.”

Thus he commands them to withdraw from those who refuse to devote themselves to work, and, as though they were members corrupted by the putrefaction of idleness, to cut them away, lest the illness of sloth, like a deadly contagion, corrupt even the healthy parts of the members as its decay spreads.

And when he is about to speak of those who refuse to work with their hands and to eat their bread in quiet—those from whom he likewise commands withdrawal—observe with what reproaches he brands them from the beginning. First he calls them disorderly and says that they do not walk according to his tradition: in other words, he designates them as rebellious, since they refuse to walk according to his instruction, and as dishonorable, that is, [Note: [Col. 0375C] He seems to refer to the saying in Ecclesiastes, chapter 3: “Everything has its time; a time to be silent and a time to speak,” and so forth. Likewise there is a time to go outside—that is, to visit brothers or the sick—which he here calls the suitable and appropriate occasion for going out and visiting, an occasion that disorderly people and those unconcerned with propriety do not observe, since they do not know how to preserve decorum in everything. Hence the verse:

“Rustic offspring knows not how to observe measure.”]

not seeking an honorable and fitting opportunity for going out, for visiting, for speaking, or for the time. For anyone who is disorderly must necessarily be subject to all these vices.

“And not according to the tradition which they received from us”: here he marks them as rebellious and in some way contemptuous, because they disdain to keep the tradition they received from him and do not wish to imitate what they remember their teacher to have taught not only in word but also to have completed in deed.

“For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us.”

He greatly intensifies the immense accumulation of their reproach when he asserts that they fail to observe what remains fixed in their memory and what they learned to imitate not only through instruction in words but also received as an incentive through the example of his deeds.

## CHAPTER VIII. That one who refuses to be content with the work of his hands must necessarily be restless

[Col. 0375C]

[Note: [Col. 0375C] After the Apostle’s teaching and command concerning manual labor, cited above from II Thessalonians 3 as something to be undertaken in order to avoid idleness and other sins, the author proceeds to present the example of that same Apostle. What the Apostle Paul taught in word and writing, he also demonstrated in deed and left attested in several places. That he did this at Thessalonica is clear from the testimony cited here. He himself also affirms that he did the same later, while staying at Ephesus, when he testifies to them in these words: “You yourselves know that these hands ministered to the needs of myself and those who were with me” (Acts 20). And writing to the Corinthians he says: “We labor, working with our hands” (I Corinthians 10).]

“For we were not restless among you.”

When he wishes to prove by the exercise of work that he was not restless among them, he sufficiently indicates that those who refuse to work always become restless through the vice of idleness. [Note: [Col. 0375D] That is, “we received food.” Among the Hebrews, everything pertaining to sustenance is understood under the name “bread.” Thus Luke 14: “When Jesus had entered the house of a Pharisee on the Sabbath to eat bread,” that is, to have lunch or dinner. And I Samuel 14: “Cursed,” Saul says, “is the man who eats bread before evening.” By naming bread he understood every kind of food; hence Jonathan, after tasting honey, was regarded as liable to the curse (Augustine, *On the Work of Monks*, chapters 3 and 4). The Apostle denies that he ate anyone’s bread for nothing—that is, freely, through gratuitous generosity, or idly, doing nothing, as the French say, *pour néant*—for two reasons. First, because he ate his bread in the sweat of his face, or, as he adds himself, “in labor and weariness, working night and day”; and second, because food was due to him by reason of his evangelical ministry. For one who lives from the Gospel does not eat bread for nothing, even if he does not work with his hands: he receives what is owed to him, as he himself shortly indicates when he speaks of his authority: “Not as though we had no authority,” and so forth.]

“Nor did we eat anyone’s bread without paying for it.”

In each word the Doctor of the Gentiles heightens the force of his interpretation. The preacher of the Gospel says that he did not eat anyone’s bread without paying for it, although he knew that the Lord had commanded that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel (I Corinthians 9), and again: “The laborer is worthy of his food” (Matthew 10). Since the one who preached the Gospel, performing such a sublime and spiritual work, could take food for himself by the authority of the Lord’s command without charge, what shall we do, to whom not only has no preaching of the word been entrusted, but only the care of our own soul?

[Col. 0376B] [Note: [Col. 0376D] Saint Jerome uses the same argument to deter the monk Rusticus from idleness and to urge him to practice manual labor at the appropriate time and intersperse it with spiritual exercises. He says: “Do some work, so that the devil may always find you occupied. If the Apostles, though having authority to live from the Gospel, worked with their hands so as not to burden anyone, and provided relief for others, from whom they were entitled to reap material things in return for spiritual ones, why do you not prepare what will benefit your own use? Weave, perhaps, a basket from rushes,” and so forth. Saint Augustine likewise presses the same argument in the book he wrote *On the Work of Monks* (chapters 2, 3, and 4), against certain lazy and sluggish monks who rejected manual labor under a vain pretext. Isidore of Pelusium writes in the same vein, Book I, Letter 49 (above, at chapter 7, and below, at chapter 11). See more on this matter in other places.]

“But in labor and weariness, working night and day, so that we might not burden any of you” (II Thessalonians 3).

He further intensifies the additions to his correction. He did not simply say, “We did not eat anyone’s bread without paying for it,” and stop there. For then it might have seemed that he had been supported by his own idle expenditure and stored-up money, or by the contributions or gifts of others, though not of these particular people. But he says, “in labor and weariness, working night and day,” that is, sustained specifically by our own labor.

And this, he says, we did not do according to our own preference or for pleasure, as though rest and bodily exercise invited it, but because necessity and lack of food compelled us to do it with no small bodily exhaustion. For not only throughout the whole day, but also during the night, which appears to have been granted for bodily rest, I pressed on incessantly with this manual work out of concern for food.

## CHAPTER IX. That not only the Apostle, but also those who were with him, worked with their hands
Yet he does not testify that he alone had conducted himself in this manner among them, lest this practice perhaps seem neither extensive nor general if it were handed down only in his own example; rather, he asserts that all who were with him and had been assigned to the ministry of the Gospel—that is, Silvanus and Timothy, who write these same things with him—worked at similar labor.

[Note: Since the Apostle here speaks throughout in the plural, it is likely that he is speaking not only in his own person but also in that of his companions, Silvanus and Timothy, who were his fellow workers in the Gospel and whose names appear in the title of both Epistles to the Thessalonians. It should also be believed that the other apostles at times practiced manual labor when place and time permitted. For, apart from the fact that blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, returned with the other apostles to fishing after the Lord’s resurrection—where St. Gregory says, “To resume after conversion an occupation that had existed without sin before conversion was not culpable” (Homily 24 on the Gospels)—the Apostle likewise testifies concerning St. Barnabas (I Cor. IV and IX) that he shared manual labor with him, for the same end and purpose: “So as not to cause any hindrance to the Gospel of Christ.” And in Clement, among the Apostolic Constitutions (Book II, chapter 67), we read: “You who are young men in the Church, take care diligently to minister in all necessary matters; devote yourselves to your work with complete holiness, so that at all times you may provide both for yourselves and for those in need, and may not burden the Church of God. Indeed, we too, while occupied with the word of the Gospel, do not neglect our spare occupations; for some among us are fishermen, others craftsmen of theatrical scenery, others farmers, and we are never idle.” Thus far Clement. For Sila and Silvanus, see also Baronius’s note on the Roman Martyrology, July 13.]

In the phrase, “so that we might not burden any of you,” he also imposes great shame upon them. If the man who preached the Gospel, commending it by signs and mighty works, does not dare to eat bread for nothing lest he burden anyone, how can those who daily presume to remain idle and disengaged fail to regard themselves as burdensome?

## CHAPTER X  
### That the Apostle worked with his own hands for this reason: to provide us with an example of working

“Not as though we had no authority, but in order that we might give ourselves to you as a pattern for imitation” (II Thess. III).

He discloses the reason why he imposed so much labor upon himself: “In order,” he says, “that we might give ourselves to you as a pattern for imitation”—so that, if perhaps you should consign to oblivion the doctrine of words repeatedly impressed upon your ears, at least you might retain in your memory the examples of conduct placed faithfully before your eyes. He reproves them severely also in this respect, when he says that he undertook this labor and the bodily toil of day and night for no other reason than to provide an example, and yet they were unwilling to be instructed, although for their sake he had imposed such toil upon himself without being compelled by necessity.

Indeed, he says, although we had authority, and although the means and possessions of all of you were open to us, and I knew that our Lord had promised me the right to use them, I nevertheless did not exercise this authority, lest what I might rightly and lawfully have done should provide others with an example of harmful idleness. Therefore, while preaching the Gospel, I preferred to support myself by my own hands and labor, so that for those who wished to walk along the path of virtue I might also open the way of perfection and provide, through my labor, a pattern of conduct.

[Note: The Apostles sometimes labored with their hands to provide themselves with food out of necessity and want; at other times they did so by way of supererogation—that is, from spontaneous choice—as St. Thomas teaches (II–II, q. 187, a. 3, ad 5). “Necessity,” he says, “arose when they could not obtain food from others,” especially at the beginning of their preaching, when they preached among unbelievers who had not yet been converted. “Supererogation,” however, is evident from the fact that the Apostle says he did not use the authority he possessed to live from the Gospel.

The Apostle practiced this supererogation for three reasons. First, to remove occasions of boasting from the pseudo-apostles, who preached for temporal advantages alone. Hence he says in II Corinthians XI: “What I do, I will continue to do, in order to cut off the opportunity of those who seek an opportunity, so that in the matter of which they boast they may be found to be like us”; for if Paul had accepted support on account of the Gospel, those who preached not from piety but for profit would have boasted that they were like Paul.

Second, to avoid burdening those to whom they preached. Hence he says in II Corinthians XII: “What is it in which you were inferior to the other churches, except that I myself did not burden you?”

Third, to give an example of working and seeking food by one’s own labor to the idle and to those accustomed to live off others, of whom there were many at Thessalonica. This is signified by the words: “So that we might give ourselves to you as a pattern for imitation,” that is, so that by our example we might likewise urge you to work and labor.

St. Augustine, moreover, holds that the Apostle did not always and everywhere work with his hands, but did so when he had leisure from preaching the word. At other times he not only accepted what was offered by those who gave it, when necessity required this, but also instructed others by letter to do the same—as when he writes to the Galatians: “Let the one who is instructed in the word share all good things with the one who instructs him” (Gal. VI); or when he ordered a collection among the churches of Macedonia and others for the brethren living in Judea, who were afflicted by great want.]

## CHAPTER XI  
### That, preaching not only by example but also by words, he admonished them to work

[Col. 0378B]

And lest he should appear to have instructed them only by silently working and wishing to teach them through examples, without also training them by admonitions and precepts, he adds: “For even when we were with you, we gave you this command: that if anyone is unwilling to work, neither should he eat” (II Thess. III).

He continues to emphasize the idleness of those who, knowing that he had worked with his own hands as a good teacher for the sake of instruction and doctrine, nevertheless disdain to imitate him. He magnifies his own diligence and care, saying that he had not merely handed this example down to them while present, but had also continually proclaimed it in words: namely, that if anyone is unwilling to work, neither should he eat.

[Note: It is not my practice to explain each individual sentence of Scripture cited by Cassian, except insofar as his exposition absolutely requires it, or insofar as a passage contains something distinctive relevant to us and to our purpose. Yet I cannot pass over this sentence of the Apostle, upon which the entire discussion of manual labor principally rests.

First, it should be observed that the Apostle does not say, “If anyone does not work, he should not eat,” but, “If anyone is unwilling to work.” For there are many who would wish to work but cannot, either because of weakness of strength or because they cannot find work. Thus, when those people in Matthew were asked why they stood idle all day, they immediately replied, “Because no one has hired us” (Matt. XX). The Fathers sometimes cite the passage in the form, “If anyone does not labor, neither should he eat,” but only incidentally and in passing.

Second, the words that follow—“neither should he eat”—can bear two meanings. Some explain them as a prohibition: no one should give him anything to eat, so that, compelled by necessity, he may work even unwillingly. But since it is not within everyone’s power to judge whether someone wishes to work or not, others prefer to explain the words assertively in this manner: “If anyone is unwilling to work, he is not worthy to eat; therefore, if he is consumed by hunger, let him blame his own inactivity and idleness,” just as the Lord, conversely, said: “The laborer is worthy of his food” (Matt. X).

Cassian touches upon both meanings, the first in the following chapter and the second in chapter 19, at the end of section 3. St. Thomas asks whether this is a precept or a counsel (Commentary on the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians). He answers that something can be commanded in two ways: absolutely and conditionally.

What is in itself necessary for salvation, he says, is commanded absolutely; these are works of virtue, which properly fall under a precept. Something is commanded conditionally when a circumstance arises in which the precept cannot be observed without manual labor. A person is commanded to sustain his body, for otherwise he is his own murderer. Genesis II says: “Eat from every tree of paradise.” Therefore, by precept a person is bound to nourish his body, and likewise to do everything without which the body cannot live. Thus, whoever has no other lawful means of sustaining his body—whether through property or through lawful business—is bound to work, lest he steal. It is therefore a precept when he cannot otherwise live. Thus far St. Thomas.

From this we understand that the precept of working, insofar as it is natural, obliges in two ways: absolutely or in a particular circumstance. In the first way it does not bind individuals but the commonwealth, as is well known, because, according to the same St. Thomas (II–II, q. 187, a. 3, ad 1), individuals are not each bound to those precepts of the natural law that concern the good of many. It is sufficient that one person devote himself to one office and another to another—for example, that some be craftsmen, some farmers, some judges, and so on—according to the Apostle’s words in I Corinthians XII: “If the whole body were an eye, where would be the hearing? And if the whole body were hearing, where would be the sense of smell?” and so forth.

In this respect, therefore, it is not fitting for religious to work with their hands. Their office in the commonwealth is not to labor in this way, but to pray, chant psalms, preach, and perform similar duties.

In the second way, however, individuals are indeed bound by this precept, but secular persons are no less bound than religious. For in whatever circumstance or necessity arises, individuals are obliged to work with their hands; certainly secular persons are bound no less than religious. On this matter, see Cardinal Bellarmine, Book II On Monks, chapter 42.

Finally, it should be remembered here what was also noted above from St. Thomas: by manual labor, or work of the hands, every bodily work is meant, whether mechanical or liberal, whether it is performed only with the hands, with the feet, with the tongue, or in some other manner. It is called bodily work, or work of the hands, because the hand is the principal instrument by which we act. Consequently, religious who chant in choir, preach, teach, and so forth can plainly be said to labor with their hands. Let heretics therefore consider how not only wickedly but also incompetently they direct this sentence of the Apostle against monks, especially mendicants.]

## CHAPTER XII  
### That the Apostle, not content with a mere admonition, also added authority and a precept

[Col. 0379A]

He no longer addresses them with the counsel of a teacher or physician, but attacks them with the severity of a judicial pronouncement. Resuming his apostolic authority, he delivers sentence against the contemptuous as though from a tribunal—using that authority which, when writing with threats to the Corinthians, he asserted had been given to him by the Lord. He warned them, while they remained in sin, to hasten to correct themselves before his arrival, commanding them as follows: “I beg you that, when I am present, I may not be compelled to act boldly against some with that authority which the Lord has given me among you” (II Cor. X). And again: “For if I should wish to boast somewhat of the authority which the Lord has given me for your edification and not for your destruction, I shall not be put to shame.”

With this authority, I say, he pronounces: “If anyone is unwilling to work, neither should he eat.” He does not hand them over to the carnal sword, but by the authority of the Holy Spirit forbids them the substance of this life, so that, if they should remain unwilling to consider the punishment of future death and should still wish, through love of idleness, to persist in disobedience, they may at least be compelled, constrained by natural necessity and fear of present destruction, to accept salutary precepts.

## CHAPTER XIII  
### On the words, “For we hear that some among you walk disorderly”

After so much evangelical severity, he now explains the reason why he had prefaced all these things: “For we hear that some among you walk disorderly.”

[Note: He walks disorderly who does not perform what is his own duty and disturbs others who are performing theirs. Concerning this, blessed Benedict says in chapter 48 of the Rule: “The seniors should take care lest a brother who is acediosus be found—one who gives himself to idleness or idle conversation and is not attentive to reading—and who is not only useless to himself but also distracts others.” Turrecrematus explains this as meaning “he draws outward,” that is, he draws others away from reading or work.

Smaragdus, explaining the same passage, says: “Acediosus” means tedious, anxious, empty-minded, or frivolous: one who, moved by weariness of mind or lifted up by levity of spirit, neither permits himself to read nor allows others to devote themselves to reading. He is found to be useless to himself in his wandering and opposed to others who are reading. He loves idleness and idle conversation and therefore draws both himself and others away from sacred reading—that is, he separates and disturbs them.]

“Walking disorderly, doing no work, but acting as busybodies.” He is not content to declare that those who refuse to devote themselves to work are corrupted by one disease alone.

[Note: Cassian appears here to have suffered a lapse of memory, or an error may have entered the text. For it is not in the First Epistle to the Thessalonians, but in the Second, and in the same chapter from which the Apostle’s preceding words are cited here—unless perhaps he is referring to what is found in the First Epistle: “Correct the disorderly” (I Thess. II), where the Greek is ἀτάκτους, that is, “disorderly.” But since he has not mentioned this sentence earlier and immediately adds, “and not to walk according to the tradition,” he seems certainly to have in mind the sentence of the Second Epistle, which he had also cited above: “We command you in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to withdraw yourselves from every brother walking ἀτάκτως, disorderly, and not according to the tradition that they received from us” (II Thess. II).

Moreover, the verb ἀτακτεῖν is a military term and means to place oneself outside the ranks or withdraw from the army. Thus ἄτακτοι, that is, “disorderly,” are those who walk disorderly because they cannot keep themselves within the order of ecclesiastical or monastic discipline, withdraw themselves from the cloister, and refuse to submit to common laws. This is what soldiers called ἄτακτοι do in the army.]

For in the earlier Epistle he calls them disorderly and says that they do not walk according to the tradition they had received from him; he also defined them as restless and as eating bread for nothing. Again here he says: “We hear that some among you walk disorderly” (II Thess. III). And he immediately adds the second disorder, which is the root of this restlessness: “Doing no work”; and then a third disease, which grows from the former like a little branch: “But acting as busybodies.”

## CHAPTER XIV  
### That discourse cuts away many vices

He therefore hastens to apply a suitable correction to so many sources of vice. Laying aside the apostolic authority he had used shortly before, he again assumes the heart of a devoted father and a merciful physician. Like a father addressing his sons and dependents with wholesome counsel, he administers remedies for their health, saying: “But we command and exhort such persons in the Lord Jesus…”

[Note: In a few words the Apostle gathers together two nearly connected vices and their antidotes, mentioned above: he opposes quietness to curiosity and work to idleness. One works “with silence,” that is, in silence and quiet, who, unconcerned with the affairs of others, diligently attends to his own work or duty.]

“…that, working quietly, they eat their own bread.” Like a most skilled physician, he has treated the causes of so many ulcers that arise from the root of idleness with one salutary command to work. Knowing that the other unhealthy conditions sprouting from the same source must likewise be extinguished immediately, he has removed the principal origin of the disease.

## CHAPTER XV  
### On extending kindness even to the idle and negligent

Nevertheless, like a most discerning and provident physician, he desires not only to heal the wounds of the sick but also to provide fitting precepts for the healthy, by which their continual well-being may be preserved. He says: “But you, do not grow weary in doing good” (II Thess. III)—you who follow us, that is, our ways, fulfilling by imitation the examples of work handed down to you, and in no way following their idleness and inactivity.

[Note: Similarly Galatians VI: “Let us not grow weary in doing good, for in due time we shall reap, if we do not fail.”]

“Do not grow weary in doing good”—that is, if they perhaps neglect to observe what we have said, do not cease to extend your kindness toward them in the same way. Thus, just as he corrected those who were weak, lest, dissolved in idleness, they should devote themselves to restlessness and curiosity, so he warns those who are healthy not to withdraw from the wicked the kindness which, by the Lord’s command, we are ordered to extend to good and bad alike. If some wicked persons should refuse to convert to sound doctrine, they must not cut it off [variant: conceal it] from them; rather, they should continue to do good to them and support them, both by words of consolation and correction and by their customary benefits and kindness.

## CHAPTER XVI  
### That we ought to correct those who offend, not out of hatred but out of love

Yet, lest some, encouraged by this leniency, should disdain to obey his precepts, he interposes apostolic severity: “But if anyone does not obey our word through this letter, mark that person, and do not associate with him, so that he may be put to shame” (II Thess. III).

[Note: The words of the text are: “Do not associate with him, so that he may be put to shame.” Shortly before, the Apostle had said the same thing in other words: “Withdraw yourselves from every brother who walks disorderly”—that is, avoid his conversation and companionship, so that, covered with shame, he may come to his senses when he sees himself avoided by everyone. And in I Corinthians V: “If the one who is called a brother is a fornicator, or covetous, or a reviler, or a drunkard,” and so forth, “with such a one do not even eat.”

Interpreters ask whether these words signify excommunication—that is, whether the Apostle intended those whom he commanded the faithful to avoid to be excommunicated. The question concerns true and canonical excommunication, or ecclesiastical censure, by which a person is cut off from the body of Christ, which is the Church, or from communion with the faithful. This question would have little bearing upon the purpose of our work unless it shed some light upon the excommunication prescribed by our holy Father Benedict in the Rule for both grave and lesser offenses.

Interpreters, both Greek and Latin, acknowledge excommunication here (Chrysostom, Theophylact, Augustine, Book On Faith and Works, chapter 2, St. Thomas, and Cajetan in their commentaries); but the question concerns the mode and kind of excommunication. It is inferred that the greater excommunication is not signified because the Apostle does not hand these people over, nor command them to be handed over, to Satan, as he does the incestuous Corinthian mentioned in the Epistle to the Corinthians, and likewise Hymenaeus and Alexander, the heretics mentioned in I Timothy I. Rather, he merely decrees that they are to be avoided, since their sins were not so outrageous that they deserved to be cut off from the body of Christ and cast outside the Church, though they were nevertheless such that the faithful rightly ought to avoid them.

It is likewise inferred that the lesser excommunication is not signified by these words, since that form excludes a person not from the company of the faithful but only from the use and participation of the Church’s sacraments. It remains, therefore, that the Apostle signifies a kind of excommunication intermediate between the greater and lesser excommunications, which today we call ecclesiastical censures.

By this excommunication the Apostle intended nothing other than that those subject to such grave sins and scandals should be avoided by the other faithful, for two reasons. First, lest they infect others with their diseases and vices: “Bad company corrupts good morals” (I Cor. XV), and in the same chapter: “Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump?” Second, so that, affected by shame, they might come to their senses—that is, return to a sounder mind and better conduct—as stated above.

St. Chrysostom acknowledges and laments that this manner of excommunication, by which those who were to be avoided by the faithful were publicly and by name denounced, had already fallen out of use in his own time, at least among the common people of the faithful. Cajetan rightly observed that it had persisted in monasteries (Commentary), just as it still persists today, when some are separated or deprived on account of offenses from the oratory, from the society of the brethren, from the table, or from the common portion, as prescribed in the Rule of St. Benedict (chapters 24 and 44).]

He warns them, out of reverence for himself and for the common good, what they ought to observe and with what apostolic caution they should keep his commands. He immediately adds the gentleness of a most indulgent father and likewise teaches them what affection, in the love of brotherhood, they ought to retain toward those previously mentioned. “Do not regard him,” he says, “as an enemy, but correct him as a brother.”

He mingles paternal compassion with judicial severity and tempers the sentence issued with apostolic rigor by gentle mercy. He commands that the one who has scorned obedience to his precepts be marked and that no one associate with him; yet he does not command these things out of hatred, but with a view to fraternal love and their correction. “Do not associate with him, so that he may be put to shame”—so that the person who was not corrected by my gentle commands may, at least, shamed by the public separation of all of you, eventually begin to be recalled to the path of salvation.

[Note: Cajetan infers from this that it is lawful to admonish, instruct, and exhort excommunicated persons concerning those things that pertain to salvation. Hence St. Benedict also diligently admonishes and inculcates how the abbot ought to be concerned for excommunicated persons and send seniors to console the wavering brother and urge him toward humble satisfaction (chapter 27), and so forth. We noted this above on another occasion.]

## CHAPTER XVII  
### Various testimonies by which the Apostle commands that one ought to work, or by which he is shown to have worked himself

In the Epistle to the Ephesians he likewise commands this very work, saying:

[Note: St. Jerome writes concerning this passage: “Because those who live amid the affairs of this life are compelled, for the sake of food and necessary uses, either to buy or sell certain things and to pursue profits from commerce—and because it is difficult even for those who are free from other passions, namely fornication, idolatry, adultery, and murder, not to be held by this vice—he therefore now warns the Ephesians not to incur the crime of theft under the pretext of gain, calling everything that is acquired to another’s loss theft.

Nor does he say, ‘Let him work more diligently, laboring with his hands at what is good, so that he may not be in need, have food, and cause trouble to no one,’ but, ‘Let him labor, working with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something to share with the one in need.’ Therefore, whoever labors only so that he himself may not be in need, and withdraws the hand that he ought to extend to others, has not fulfilled the Apostle’s command, even if he applauds himself.” Thus far Jerome.

St. Thomas teaches that the phrase ‘what is good’ can be understood in two ways. First, as a nominative with a parenthesis: ‘Let him work at what is good,’ that is, at a good and honorable matter. Second, without a parenthesis and as an accusative: ‘Let him work with his hands, and indeed not at something unlawful, but at what is good’; that is, let him practice a good occupation and not seek food through a disgraceful trade, but through an honorable one.]

“Let the one who stole steal no longer; rather, let him labor, working with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something to share with the one suffering need” (Eph. IV).

In the Acts of the Apostles, too, we find that he not only taught these same things but also fulfilled them in practice. For when he came to Corinth, he would not allow himself to stay anywhere except with Aquila and Priscilla, because they practiced the same trade which he himself had been accustomed to practice. Thus we read: “After these things Paul departed from Athens and came to Corinth. And finding a certain Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, with Priscilla his wife, he went to them because they were of the same trade; and he stayed with them and worked. For they were craftsmen of the tentmaking trade” (Acts XVIII).

[Note: Scenofactoria, or scenefactoria, is a Greek-Latin term. For σκηνή, scena, properly means “tent”; hence among the Hebrews the dedication of tabernacles, from the likeness of dwellings, was called σκηνοπηγία, says Isidore (Etymologies XVIII, chapter 42).

According to some, therefore, the art of scenofactoria meant the art of weaving curtains (Coelius Rhodiginus, Ancient Readings, Book VIII, chapter 8; Bede in his commentary). More accurately, however, it meant sewing tents or military shelters from hides, for soldiers to use in camp. Tacitus writes of these: “The entire army was kept beneath hides.” Those who practiced this craft were called σκηνοποιοί, scenopoei, makers of tents or military shelters.

Concerning the Apostle Paul’s craft, Origen writes: “Paul was by trade a maker of tents” (Homily 17 on Numbers). A little farther on he says: “Just as those men, from fishing for fish, became fishers of men, so this man was transferred from making earthly tents to constructing heavenly tents.”

St. Chrysostom writes elegantly concerning the same matter: “This maker of tents did not travel through Sicily and Italy alone, but throughout the whole world, preaching the word of God, while at the same time he did not interrupt his craft, but even then sewed hides and presided over his workshop. Nor did this offend patricians or nobles, and rightly so. For it is not arts and studies but fabricated doctrines that ordinarily make teachers contemptible.” Thus Chrysostom (Homily 2 on the Epistle to the Romans).]

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### That the Apostle worked as much as he judged sufficient for himself and for those who were with him

Then, proceeding to Miletus—

[Note: Dionysius reads, “From Miletus.” Miletus, or Miletum, was a very famous city of Caria, situated by the sea. Pliny discusses it in Book V, chapter 29.]

—and from there sending to Ephesus and summoning to himself the presbyters of the Church of Ephesus, he gave them instructions about how they ought to govern the Church of God in his absence and said:

“I coveted no one’s gold or silver. You yourselves know that these hands ministered to all that was necessary for me and for those who were with me. In all things I have shown you that, by laboring in this way, you ought to receive the weak and remember the word of the Lord Jesus, for he himself said: ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive’” (Acts XX).

He left us a weighty [variant: great] example of his conduct, testifying that he had worked not only to provide what was sufficient for the needs of his own body, but also what could suffice for the uses of those who were with him—namely, for those who were occupied every day with necessary ministries and therefore could not similarly provide food for themselves by their own hands.

Just as he said that he had worked among the Thessalonians to give them a pattern for imitation (II Thess. II), so here too he presents a similar point, saying: “In all things I have shown you that, by laboring in this way, you ought to receive the weak”—whether weak in mind or in body. That is, we should hasten to refresh them by our own labor and expense, obtained through the sweat of our work, not from an abundance stored up or from money laid aside, and not even from the generosity or resources of another.

[Note: Ephesus was the metropolis of Lesser Asia and once a very celebrated commercial center. There stood the famous temple of Diana, which Luke mentions in Acts XX.]

## CHAPTER XIX  
### How the saying “It is more blessed to give than to receive” should be understood

He also says that this itself is the Lord’s command: “For he himself,” he says—that is, the Lord Jesus—“said: ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive’” (Acts XX).

[Note: We explained this sentence elsewhere (Book VII, chapter 16). Cassian applies it aptly and elegantly to the truly poor monk who nevertheless gives to others from his own work; for this reason he proclaims him blessed in two ways, namely in poverty and in generosity.]

That is, the generosity of the one who gives is more blessed than the poverty of the one who receives, provided that the gift is not made from money preserved through faithlessness or distrust, nor from treasures hidden by avarice, but from the fruit of one’s own work and pious sweat.

Therefore it is more blessed to give than to receive, because, although the giver may be as poor as the one who receives, he nevertheless hastens, by his own labor and pious diligence, to procure not only what is sufficient for his own need but also something to give to the needy. He is adorned with a double grace: he possesses the perfect nakedness of Christ through the rejection of all his possessions, and he displays, through his own labor and affection, the munificence of a rich man. The one honors God from his just labors and offers him a portion of the fruits of his righteousness; the other, dissolved in the torpor and inactivity of idleness, proves by the Apostle’s judgment that he is unworthy even of bread (II Thess. III), presuming to remain idle contrary to the Apostle’s prohibition, not without the guilt of obstinacy and sin.

[Note: The monk, namely, who labors for others and gives to them, although he himself is extremely poor, as will be explained below.]

## CHAPTER XX  
### On the idle brother who urged others to leave the coenobium

We knew a brother—if anything further might be gained from this instruction, we would disclose even his name—who, while living in a coenobium, was compelled by necessity to deliver the prescribed daily measure of work to the steward, lest he should be led toward or disturbed by the greater amount of work performed by someone who labored more earnestly as an example.

[Note: St. Jerome testifies that this was customary and prescribed among the Egyptian monks in his letter to Eustochium: “The work of the day is fixed; when handed over to the decanus, it is brought to the steward, who himself returns an account to the Father of all each month with great trembling” (Letter XXII).

St. Augustine likewise writes in Book II of On the Morals of the Catholic Church, chapter 31: “They perform those tasks by which the body can be nourished and the mind cannot be hindered from God. They hand over their work to those whom they call decani, because they are placed over groups of ten, so that concern for his body may touch none of them, whether in food or clothing, and so forth.” These decani, arranging everything with great diligence and providing whatever that life required because of bodily weakness, nevertheless also render their account to one whom they call Father.]

When he saw a brother enter the coenobium who, moved by the fervor of faith, wished to undertake a little more work, and could not recall him from this intention by secret persuasion, he would persuade him by evil counsels and whisperings to leave the place.

[Note: It may seem astonishing that such a monk could be found among the most holy and religious monks and anchorites—one who would so corrupt others by his wicked persuasions and counsels and drive them from the monastery merely to protect his own negligence. But why should this be surprising, when Judas the betrayer was found among the apostles, and compelled Christ to say: “Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” (John VI)—not by nature, but by wickedness. See more on this matter in Conference 18, chapter 16.]

To carry him away more easily, he pretended that he himself had long been offended for many reasons and wished to depart, if only he could find a companion or assistance for the journey. After drawing the other into agreement through secret disparagements of the monastery, he would arrange with him the hour at which he ought to leave the monastery and the place where he should go ahead and await him. Then he himself would remain there as though he were about to follow immediately.

But once the other, ashamed of his departure, no longer dared return to the monastery from which he had fled, the wretched instigator of his flight would remain in the coenobium.

[Note: This is how it appears in the Plantinian edition. The Basel edition and others instead read: “The enticer of the flight,” which has the same meaning. For illex means one who entices or lures.]

Let this one example of this kind of person suffice, for the caution of beginners, so that it may be made clearer how many evils idleness engenders in a monk’s mind, according to the judgment of Scripture (Eccles. XXXIII), and how “bad company corrupts good morals” (I Cor. XV).

## CHAPTER XXI  
### Various testimonies from Solomon against acedia
What the most wise Solomon also most clearly notes in many passages concerning this vice of idleness, saying as follows: “He who pursues idleness will be filled with poverty” (Proverbs XVIII)—whether visible poverty, that is, or invisible poverty, by which every idle person, entangled in various vices, must necessarily be held, and must always remain a stranger to contemplation of God and to spiritual riches, concerning which the blessed Apostle says: “For in all things you have been enriched in him, in every word and in every knowledge” (I Corinthians I).

Concerning the poverty of the idle person it is also written elsewhere: “[Note: This is from the Septuagint version. For the Vulgate has only: ‘Slumber will be clothed in rags.’] ‘And every drowsy person will be clothed in a torn and ragged garment’” (Proverbs XXIII). Without doubt, such a person will not deserve to be adorned with that garment of incorruption concerning which the Apostle commands: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans XIII); and again: “Clothed with the breastplate of righteousness and charity” (I Thessalonians V); and concerning which the Lord also speaks to Jerusalem through the prophet: “Arise, arise, Jerusalem; clothe yourself in the garments of your glory” (Isaiah LII).

Whoever, overcome by the sleep of idleness or acedia, has preferred to be covered not by the labor of his own industry but by the rags of inertia—rags cut away from the perfect fullness and body of the Scriptures—will fit to his sloth not a garment of glory or beauty, but a disgraceful covering of excuse. Those who have been dissolved by this sluggishness commonly refuse to support themselves by the work of their hands, which the Apostle constantly practiced and commanded us to practice. Instead, they use certain testimonies of Scripture by which they place a kind of veil over their inertia, saying that it is written:

“[Note: That is, strive to provide for yourselves by working—not so much the food that perishes as the food that endures. For the Lord does not forbid care for bodily food; rather, he teaches that care for spiritual food must be preferred to it: the former is to be attended to incidentally, while the latter is to be sought with the whole heart. Thus certain people, incompetently, understood from this passage (Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 10) that one ought not to labor for bodily food, abusing these words as a pretext for their laziness, although Paul taught the contrary both by word and by deed, as was seen above. The monk mentioned below seems to have belonged to this kind of folly; Abbot Sylvanus restored him to a sounder mind by an act no less witty than prudent. Concerning him, the following is found in the *Lives of the Fathers*:

‘A visiting brother came to Abbot Sylvanus on Mount Sinai and saw that the brothers were working. He said to them, “Why are you working for food that perishes? Mary chose the better part.” Then the old man said to his disciple Zacharias, “Give him a book to read, and put him in a cell that has nothing in it.” At the ninth hour the brother looked along the road, wondering whether the old man might call him to eat. When the ninth hour had passed, he came to the old man and said, “Have the brothers not eaten today, Abba?” When the old man admitted that they had, the brother said, “Why did you not call me?” Abbot Sylvanus then said to him, “You are a spiritual man and have no need of this food; but we, being carnal, need to eat, and therefore we work. You have chosen the better part: you read every day and do not wish to receive carnal food.” When he heard this, he began to repent and say, “Forgive me, Abba.” Sylvanus replied, “Then Martha is necessary for Mary; for the sake of Martha, Mary also is praised.”’ Thus far the passage there (*Book V*, booklet 10, new edition).] ‘Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which endures unto eternal life’ (John VI); and, ‘My food is to do the will of my Father’ (John IV).”

But these testimonies are certain rags cut from the solid fullness of evangelical teaching. They are taken up in order to cover rather the disgrace of our idleness and shame than to warm and adorn us with that precious and perfect garment of the virtues which, in the Book of Proverbs, the wise woman—clothed with strength and beauty—is described as having made for herself or for her husband. Concerning her it is subsequently said: “She is clothed with strength and beauty, and she shall rejoice in the latter days” (Proverbs XXXI).

Concerning this disease of inertia Solomon again says:

“[Note: The Vulgate edition has: ‘The way of the lazy is like a hedge of thorns.’ A similar passage is found in Proverbs XXIV: ‘I passed through the field of a lazy man and through the vineyard of a foolish man; and behold, nettles had entirely filled them, and thorns had covered their surface.’ See St Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XX, chapter 22. Following him, Abbot Smaragdus applies his words to a lazy and negligent monk as follows: ‘What does it mean,’ he says, ‘to pass through the field of a lazy man, except to inspect the life of a negligent monk and consider his works? Nettles or thorns fill it, because earthly desires and the prickings of vices sprout in the heart of negligent monks’ (*On the Fourth Chapter of the Rule of St Benedict*).

Elsewhere, likewise adhering to Solomon’s sayings, he writes: ‘Sluggishness is called laziness or slowness. Hence those who are found slow and lazy in a good work are called sluggish. Through this vice, which nourishes all evils, they grow; and because it nourishes all good things so that they may not advance, all good things lie in a wickedly drowsy rest. For concerning this vice Solomon says: “Sloth sends sleep upon a person” (Proverbs XIX). Sloth sends sleep upon the torpid mind because, when it finds a person lukewarm and slow in good works, it closes his eyes and binds his hands, so that he may increase in evil.’

Again, through the same Solomon it is said: ‘Because of the cold the lazy man would not plow’ (Proverbs XX). For the lazy man does not plow because, bound by the torpor of sluggishness, he pretends not to do the good things he ought to do. While he fears small evils, he neglects to perform great good works. Concerning this lazy man it is rightly added: ‘Therefore he will beg in summer, and nothing will be given him,’ because he who does not labor in good works in the present age, when the time of recompense arrives, fasts with an empty mind from the reward.

By contrast, the same Solomon says of the ant in Proverbs XXX: ‘The ant is a weak people, yet it prepares its food in the harvest.’ What is signified by the ant except the strenuous life of monks? For, in comparison with the lovers of this world, they appear small, like ants, through the grace of humility. In the present life, as in a harvest, they do not cease gathering the fruit of good works, by which they may rejoice in the future.’ Thus Smaragdus excellently describes two classes of monks (*Prologue to the Rule*). St Gregory has similar material in *Pastoral Care*, Part III, chapter 16.] ‘The paths of those who do nothing are paved with thorns’ (Proverbs XV), that is, with those and similar vices which the Apostle said above spring from idleness.”

And again: “Every idle person is in desires” (Proverbs XXI). Concerning these the Apostle said: “And [Note: That is, ‘that you may covet,’ as Cassian and many Latins interpret this passage in accordance with the commandment of the Decalogue: ‘You shall not covet your neighbor’s property,’ and so forth. From this it may also be inferred that Cassian wrote not in Greek but in Latin. For the Greek words require another sense: *μηδένος χρείαν ἔχητε*, that is, ‘have need of no one,’ or ‘be in need of nothing,’ although the former sense almost follows from the latter. For just as poverty arises from idleness, so from involuntary poverty there often arises coveting of other people’s possessions, according to Proverbs XXIII: ‘Desires kill the lazy man.’] desire nothing that belongs to another” (I Thessalonians IV).

And finally: “For idleness has taught many evils” (Ecclesiasticus XXXIII). The Apostle clearly enumerated these in the passages we explained above, saying: “Doing nothing, but acting inquisitively” (II Thessalonians III). To this vice he added another: “And take pains to be quiet” (I Thessalonians IV). Then: “To attend to your own affairs, and to walk honorably before those who are outside, and to desire nothing that belongs to another” (ibid.). He also identifies such people as disorderly and rebellious, commanding that the diligent be separated from them: “Withdraw yourselves,” he says, “from every brother who walks disorderly and not according to the tradition which they received from us” (II Thessalonians III).

## CHAPTER XXII. How in Egypt the brothers work with their own hands in such a way that they not only satisfy their own needs but also provide for those who are in prison.

[Col. 0388B]

Thus the Fathers instructed throughout Egypt, [Note: “Idle,” that is, free from manual work, as is understood from the whole discussion of this book. For they would not be altogether idle if they were occupied with other spiritual matters; as was that man who said of himself: “Then I am least idle when I am idle.” But this is not now under discussion.

But, to the point: after the Apostle’s example and the other testimonies of Scripture by which manual work is commended against the vice of acedia, the Author at last sets forth the example of the ancient monks, especially the Egyptians, who applied themselves to manual work with such diligence and assiduity that they seem to have held this kind of exercise among the chief and primary institutions of monastic life—yet without neglecting either the divine praises or other spiritual exercises. There are many testimonies of the holy Fathers on this subject; to set down some of them here for the illustration of Cassian’s meaning will neither be inappropriate nor, I hope, unwelcome to the reader.

Epiphanius writes the following concerning all monks as doing precisely this: “They labor with their own hands in order also to impart to the needy; and thus, in the monasteries severally, both in the region of Egypt and everywhere else, they labor for righteousness like bees, holding the wax of their handiwork in their hands, while in their mouths they have drops of honey, and with their own hymn-bearing voice praise the Lord of all according to their understanding.”

St Basil, in chapters 5 and 6 of his Monastic Constitutions, earnestly commends manual work to his monks, and teaches that a monk ought to exercise himself in employments fitting the dignity of his order—namely, all those, he says, from which every suspicion of shopkeeping and deceit is absent, and which do not entail prolonged distractions of the mind or dishonest gain; and which can be completed while the monks remain within the monastery, lest, by pursuing the labors of such work more eagerly than is proper, we weaken the powers and industry of the mind in the meditation of virtue. In this, the following must be observed: both that the work is completed and that one nevertheless does not depart from quiet (see the same author, *Longer Rules*, questions 41 and 42; see also Chrysostom, homilies 57 and 59 *On the Monastic Life*).

St Jerome confirms the same point, writing generally of the Egyptian monks to the monk Rusticus (*Letter* 4): “The monasteries of the Egyptians maintain this custom: they admit no one without the labor of work, not so much for the necessity of subsistence as for the salvation of the soul, lest the mind wander amid harmful thoughts,” etc. And in his letter to Eustochium (*Letter* 22), where he treats of their cenobites and their daily works, he says: “The work of the day is fixed; when it has been delivered to the dean, it is carried to the steward, who himself, every month, renders an account of it to the father of all with great trembling.”

In the Rule of St Pachomius in Palladius (*Lausiac History* 38), the angel who dictated it prescribes that strong tasks be assigned to the strong, while weak and light ones are assigned to those who exercise themselves more—namely, in spiritual matters—and are weaker. Palladius himself, speaking of another monastery (see articles 35 and 100 of the same Rule), in which there were three hundred monks, writes that they practiced every craft and even built monasteries: one worked at tilling the field, another in the garden, another in the bakery, another in a workshop for bronze, another in building, another in sewing shoes, another in fine writing, another in weaving large baskets, another in making baskets and little baskets.

But what is related in the *Lives of the Fathers* concerning Serapion and his monks (*Lausiac History* 39), with Sozomen attesting the same (*Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter 28), is altogether astonishing and almost incredible. There we find this: “Serapion was the father of ten thousand monks. All of them, from their own labors—which they especially undertook for the wages of their hands at harvest time—contributed the greater part to the aforesaid father and assigned the remainder to the uses of the poor. This custom belonged not only to them but to almost all Egyptian monks: at harvest time they hired themselves out for wages to reap the crops, and each procured, more or less, eighty bushels of grain from those wages, of which they offered the greater part for the use of the poor. Hence not only are the needy of that region itself fed, but ships laden with grain are sent to Alexandria, to be distributed to those shut up in prison and to other pilgrims and needy persons; for there are not enough poor people within Egypt to consume the fruits of their mercy and generosity.” Thus far the passage there, which plainly agrees with what Cassian here relates.

St Augustine also supports this, writing among other institutions of cenobites: “Indeed, whatever remains over from what is necessary for food—for very much remains over from manual work and from the restriction of meals—is distributed to the needy with as much care as it was not procured by those who distribute it. For they make no effort whatever to have these things abound for themselves; rather, they do everything possible to ensure that what has abounded does not remain with them, so much so that they even send laden ships to places inhabited by the poor.” There is no need to say more on so well-known a matter. Thus St Augustine, who elsewhere also recalls this monastic institution: “I call God to witness upon my soul that I would rather work with my hands for a certain time each day, as is established in well-regulated monasteries, and have fixed hours for reading and praying, than suffer the most tumultuous perplexities of other people’s lawsuits,” etc.

You will find many other examples and testimonies both in Palladius and in Sophronius’s *Spiritual Meadow*. From them all it is clear that those ancient monks—the Egyptians of whom Cassian speaks here, the Cappadocians or Basilians, and others—did not practice the labor of their hands or manual work wholly freely and at their own pleasure. Rather, as we have elsewhere observed (book II, chapter 3), they were bound and obligated to it by their own Rules and by the Institutes of the holy Fathers, both because of the lack of food and necessary things, and in order to avoid idleness and harmful thoughts, as St Jerome explained, and for other reasons set forth elsewhere. It is therefore not surprising that Cassian so strongly urges manual work as a matter altogether necessary and essential to monasticism when he is speaking of monks who were admitted to monasteries and monastic communities under this law and condition: that, among the other exercises of monastic discipline, they should also be occupied with manual work and devote a good part of their time to it.

This institution and obligation flourished for a long time and in most religious communities or orders of monks, especially in the East, as the Author here indicates, so long as the Fathers judged it expedient both for obtaining subsistence and avoiding idleness, before monks were taken up into ecclesiastical orders, into the public celebration of the divine offices, and into ecclesiastical duties. Yet one should not suppose that all ancient monks or religious labored with their hands—that is, practiced mechanical works—and obtained their livelihood from them. For neither the first monks in Jerusalem under the Apostles nor those Alexandrians instituted by St Mark the Evangelist are recorded as having received a law concerning manual work, as is clear from Acts II and IV, from Philo’s book *On the Contemplative Life*, and from Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 16).

Sulpicius likewise writes concerning St Martin’s monastery in chapter 7 of his Life: “No one there possessed anything as his own; all things were brought together in common. No one was permitted to buy or sell anything, as is customary with most monks. No craft was practiced there except by copyists; that task, however, was assigned to the younger men, while the elders gave themselves to prayer.” Thus he; and here you see that only the younger men labored by writing, and this not to procure food—for they were permitted to sell nothing, but lived from the goods they had brought—but in order to avoid idleness.

Indeed, St Augustine, in the work he wrote against certain idle monks who denied that one ought to work with one’s hands, teaches that there are four kinds of monks who may lawfully, by evangelical right, live without manual labor and use the assistance and offerings of others. In the first place he puts those engaged in preaching evangelical doctrine or teaching the word of God. For the Lord, according to the Apostle’s testimony, ordained that these should live by the Gospel (I Corinthians IX), that is, obtain their sustenance from the people. In the second rank he places those who serve at the altar—that is, administer the sacraments or perform other ecclesiastical ministries—because Paul had written of them in the same Epistle to the Corinthians: “Do you not know that those who work in the sanctuary eat the things of the sanctuary, and that those who serve the altar share with the altar? Thus the Lord ordained” (ibid.; see St Thomas, 2–2, question 187, article 3, reply to 3). He assigns third place to sick monks suffering from continual or frequent illness, concerning whom he says in chapter 16 of that book: “On account of bodily infirmities, which cannot be wholly absent, the Apostle not only permits the needs of the saints to be supplied by the faithful, but also most beneficially exhorts this.” Finally, in fourth place he reckons those who had been rich in the world and distributed their goods to the poor or contributed them to a monastery. He judges concerning them thus: “If they too do some manual work in order to remove an excuse from the lazy who come from a humbler life and from this sort of employment, they act much more mercifully than when they left all their possessions to the needy. But if they do not wish to do so, who would dare compel them?” etc. Thus far St Augustine concerning the monks of his time.

But what is now to be thought concerning the Benedictines? Are they also bound to manual work by their Rule? I for my part believe that our most holy father Benedict, a most careful and devoted imitator of the ancient monks, wished them to imitate the ancients in this matter also, and accordingly imposed upon his cenobites the same law of labor and work, though not absolutely, but insofar as necessity required, both for procuring subsistence and for avoiding idleness. Turrecremata confirms this, and it can be shown by many arguments (chapter 48 of the Rule).

For first he commands that the daytime hours remaining after the divine office be so divided that some are devoted to reading and meditation, others to manual work: “At fixed times the brothers ought to be occupied in manual labor; at fixed hours also in divine reading.” Then, according to the differing seasons of summer and winter, he prescribes so exactly the different hours during which the brothers ought to be occupied with manual work that he leaves no doubt of his intention and this law of working. He then adds: “But if the necessity of the place or poverty requires them to be occupied personally in gathering the crops, they are not to be distressed, because then they are truly monks when they live by the labor of their hands, as did our fathers and the Apostles.” Here Turrecremata says: “Our fathers here means either the patriarchs and prophets, or those most approved in the monastic order, such as Paul the first hermit, Antony, Hilary, Sylvanus, and so forth, all of whom procured their food by the labor of their hands.” Thus he.

Again, in chapter 57 of the Rule, Benedict commands craftsmen, if there are any in the monastery, to practice their crafts in all humility if the abbot orders it; then he directs how and by whom the works or products of the monks are to be sold. To this may be added what occurs in chapter 46: “If anyone, while working at some task, in the kitchen, in the storeroom, in a service, in the bakery, in the garden, in some craft, or in any place whatever, commits a fault or breaks something,” etc. But it is also plainly proved that he did not impose manual work absolutely, since he gives no causes for this institution except the two aforementioned ones: namely, necessity and the avoidance of idleness. He indicates the former by the words, “If the necessity of the place or poverty requires it,” etc.; the latter at the beginning of the chapter, where, having set forth the proposition, “Idleness is the enemy of the soul,” he infers: “And therefore at fixed times the brothers ought to be occupied in manual labor.” But when causes are removed or cease, the effect ought to cease. For necessity and want have been removed by sufficient provision and enrichment of monasteries; and the occasion for idleness and sluggishness has been removed by monks’ advancement to ecclesiastical orders, the public celebration of the divine office, the study of theology, and other more serious and holier occupations.

Hence neither in the decrees of the popes, especially Innocent III and Clement V, which make provisions concerning black monks—that is, especially Benedictines—and their reform, nor in the constitution of Benedict XII, which collected and renewed nearly all decrees relating to this order, is there any mention of manual work to be performed by monks. This is a clear sign that the obligation of manual work has been extinguished, except insofar as it belongs to natural law, concerning which we have spoken above, or is justly and beneficially imposed by prelates.

And lest anyone think that I am the first author and defender of this opinion, there fittingly presents himself that Abbot Peter of Cluny, deservedly called Venerable for his religious life and learning, who discussed this argument excellently and solidly. For in a certain letter (book III, letter 28), replying to Cistercian objections against the Cluniacs, he gives and refutes the following as the eighth objection: “Manual work, which the holy hermit fathers and ancient monks always practiced, by which the Apostles themselves supplied food for themselves and others, and concerning which God, punishing the sin of the first man by this penalty also, said: ‘In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread’ (Genesis III); concerning which David also said: ‘Because you shall eat the labors of your hands, you are blessed, and it shall be well with you’ (Psalm CXXVII)—this you have so cast aside that neither all these authorities can compel you to work, nor the obedience which you promised, according to the Rule, to render to God can draw your delicate hands, softened by idleness, out to work.”

Although he replies to this objection at considerable length, I have judged his whole reply altogether necessary for elucidating this passage: “Concerning manual work, which you added in the foregoing chapters, we have most sufficient reasons which, while demonstrating that your objections are wholly invalid, both utterly repel them and approve and maintain what is done among us. And, that this may be most plainly evident, let us consider not only what the Rule commands concerning manual work, but also why it commands it. ‘Idleness,’ it says, ‘is the enemy of the soul. And therefore at fixed times the brothers ought to be occupied in manual labor; at fixed hours likewise in divine reading.’ You have heard, behold, that it commands work; observe, as we said, why it commands it. It declares idleness to be the enemy of the soul, and therefore strives to exclude it by reading as well as by the labor of the hands, lest it be able to harm the soul whose enemy it is known to be. Tell me, then: if the same can be accomplished by other exercises of good works, does it not seem to you that the Rule is well observed? If, I say, monks can always occupy the whole span of the day with other good works—for many other good works besides manual work can be found—when they are commanded to work solely in order that they may not be idle, do they not remain wholly free from violation of the Rule when they do these things? Certainly they do, whether adversaries wish it or not. By whatever good exercise idleness is banished, the Rule is kept; no one who does these things is rightly called a transgressor, and the imputation of blame is utterly rejected.

“Unless there were works other than farming acceptable to God, the Lord would by no means have said to the Jews: ‘Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which endures unto eternal life’ (John VI). If bodily works were indeed to be preferred to spiritual exercises, Mary would by no means have chosen to sit at the Lord’s feet and hear his words without ceasing, idle from other works; she would by no means have allowed her sister alone to minister; nor would the Lord have said that she had chosen the better part. Therefore, if the mind is occupied in praying, reading, singing psalms, religiously fulfilling duties imposed upon it, or doing any other such good things, the Rule, as we have said, is perfectly observed, since in doing these things the monk is proved not idle but well occupied.

“And, to offer an example: we read that St Maurus, a disciple of Blessed Benedict himself, sent by him into these parts of Gaul to build cenobitic communities according to his teaching, maintained this custom in the monastery he had built in the diocese of Angers: because all necessities were supplied to them without their own labor, they omitted manual work and were exercised, as we have said, in spiritual exercises, so as not to be idle; and thus, by always doing good works, they best preserved the Rule recently handed down to them by the Saint. If Blessed Maurus had understood that they were acting contrary to the vow of their profession, since he could in no way have been mistaken in understanding this matter, he would never have allowed his monks to live so. Nor would God have deigned to work such wonderful and manifold works through him, or restore life to the dead at his prayers, if he had appeared to be a violator of his vow and had either refused to work with his hands through laxity or disdained it through pride.” Thus far Peter of Cluny, than whose words nothing clearer or more solid could have been brought forward for elucidating the question proposed.

Turrecremata also adds his support, in the place cited above, warning that the statement of the holy Father, that then they are truly monks if they live by the labor of their hands, should not be understood to mean that those who live not by the labor of their own hands but from others’ goods or benefices, while occupied with reading and contemplation, are not to be called truly monks. For the most holy father Benedict himself, as Blessed Gregory relates in the second book of the *Dialogues*, remained for three years in a cave, sustained by things supplied by the monk Romanus; though sound in body, he is not recorded to have procured his food by the labor of his hands. Rather, those who live by the labor of their hands are called truly monks because in this they imitate the ancient Fathers, from whom the discipline of the monastic order seems to have flowed, among whom it was almost an established custom to live by the labor of the hands. Thus he.

But let the reader remember that above I said, “unless it is justly imposed by prelates.” Since, according to the unanimous opinion, a religious is bound to obey in matters according to the Rule, and manual work belongs to the Rule of St Benedict not merely indirectly or, as they say, reductively, but is also expressly and plainly contained and prescribed in the Rule, there can be no doubt that a prelate, for a just cause or an arising necessity, can employ his Benedictine cenobites—especially the younger and stronger ones—in certain honorable crafts or manual works, particularly lest they grow sluggish in idleness or wander about while free from the divine office and other spiritual and holier activities; or even as a penalty and punishment for faults (see St Thomas, opusculum 9, chapter 5; and 2–2, question 187, article 3; Navarrus, *Commentary* 2 *On the Rules*, no. 27). In this way monks who formerly committed faults are customarily exercised and punished by copying books and manuscripts, a task requiring much labor and skill, and by other laborious works, as has been noted elsewhere (book V, chapter 38). But enough on these matters. See also what we noted on chapter 3 of book II.] do not permit monks to be idle in any way, and especially not young men, [Note: Dionysius, or whoever the paraphraser was, reverses the meaning, if he does not overturn it, when he says: ‘Measuring and directing their attention in this exercise more toward progress in heart, patience, and humility than toward diligence in the work.’ So he. But without any comparison or opposition, the Author is simply indicating that those ancient Egyptian Fathers carefully observed in their monks and novices whether they diligently applied themselves to the manual work assigned to them, and from that readiness and diligence in work drew a strong argument and judgment concerning each person’s true conversion of heart and progress in the virtues, especially humility and patience.
