St Benedict likewise says: ‘Then they are truly monks if they live by the labor of their hands, as did our Fathers’ (chapter 40 of the Rule), and so forth.] measuring the disposition of their hearts and their progress in patience and humility by their diligence in work. They not only refuse to accept anything from anyone for the use of their own sustenance, but also, from their labors, refresh not only visiting and traveling brothers; they even send through the regions of Libya—[Note: Libya, bordering Mareotis in Egypt.] regions afflicted by barrenness and famine—and through the cities to those wasting away in the squalor of prisons an immense supply of food and nourishment. They believe that, through such an offering, they offer themselves to the Lord in a rational and true sacrifice from the fruit of their hands.

## CHAPTER XXIII. How, because of idleness, there are no monasteries of monks in the regions of the West.

For this reason we see no monasteries in these regions founded with such a great multitude of brothers, because they are not supported by the resources of their own work, so that they can remain there continually. And even if the generosity of another can somehow supply them with sufficient food, nevertheless the pleasure of idleness and the wandering of the heart do not allow them to persevere in one place for long.

Hence this is the judgment established in Egypt by the ancient Fathers: “[Note: That is, to be attacked by one demon, as Dionysius explained—namely, by the spirit of acedia. The word ‘demon’ and ‘spirit’ is here used metonymically for the vices themselves, of which it is the author and persuader. It tries to turn the person who is working away from his labor and work unless it is resisted firmly. Hence St Jerome diligently admonishes the monk Rusticus: ‘Do some work, so that the devil may always find you occupied’ (*Letter* 4). A golden saying, never to be consigned to oblivion.] A working monk is assaulted by one demon; [Note: That is, he is exposed to countless vices, according to the saying of Ecclesiasticus: ‘Idleness has taught much wickedness’ (Ecclesiasticus XXXIII). ‘Much’ means ‘all’ or ‘every kind.’ ‘Idleness,’ says Basil, ‘is the beginning of every evil; no one is unaware of this’ (Basil, *Hexaemeron*). Chrysostom, writing on Matthew, says: ‘I greatly desire that you be occupied with good works; for idleness is like a certain teacher and origin of all vices’ (*Homily* 36).

St Augustine, or the author of the sermons *To the Brothers in the Desert*, says: ‘Through it we are frequently inflamed to lust; through it we are stirred to pride; through it we are led toward the glory of the world; through it we are tempted to feed delicately; through it we are suffocated by luxurious clothing; through it we are drawn to excessive sleep; through it we are led to worldly speech. No one will ever be a citizen of heaven if he loves idleness’ (*Sermon* 16).

Again, in the same place: ‘If anyone is weary of praying or singing psalms, let him not delay working with his hands, considering that, as long as David was engaged in warfare, lust did not insult him; but after he remained idle at home, he labored under adultery and committed murder (II Samuel XI). While Samson fought with the Philistines, he could not be captured by his enemies; but after he slept in a woman’s lap and remained idly with her, he was immediately captured and blinded by his enemies (Judges XVI). While Solomon was occupied in building the Temple, he did not experience the assault of lust; but as soon as he withdrew from the work, he felt lust’s attack and, failing through the instigation of a woman, worshiped idols and the golden calf in the chamber (I Kings XI). Keep watch, therefore, my brothers, and do not fail, for you know that you are neither holier than David, nor stronger than Samson, nor wiser than Solomon.’ Thus far the passage there.] but the idle person is ravaged by countless spirits.”

## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning Abbot Paul, who every year burned all the work of his hands after setting fire beneath it.

Finally, [Note: Since he names Abbot Paul in the following chapter as well, without distinction, and indicates that he was the equal and contemporary of Abbot Moses, he plainly seems to be speaking of the same man in both places (see col. 7, ch. 26). Yet since several anchorites of this name existed, men renowned for holiness, it is difficult to discover or determine which of them the Author intended to designate. Ciaconius interprets this inattentively and without sufficient consideration as referring to that first Paul the hermit, whose life St. Jerome wrote (in the Notes on Cassian); Cassian also speaks of him in Conference 18, chapters 5 and 6. But that Paul died long before Cassian’s time—namely, in the sixth year of the emperor Constantius, which was the year of the Lord 342—and no one except Antony alone knew of him, and that only shortly before Paul’s death, after he had spent nearly a hundred years in the desert, as the same Jerome reports (Baronius, Martyrology, 10 January; Palladius, Lausiac History, 28; Sozomen, book I, chapter 13; Nicephorus, book VIII, chapter 40; Tripartite History, book I, chapter 11; Baronius, Martyrology, 7 March). There was another Paul, surnamed “the Simple,” a disciple of that same Antony, who was wonderfully tested by him in the virtue of obedience, humility, and abstinence, as may be seen in Palladius; so that he could rightly be called the most approved of the Fathers, just as he is called here. But since he had become a monk already at the age of sixty and had been received among St. Antony’s first disciples, he must also have flourished in the time of the emperor Constantine the Great; consequently, he does not seem to have been able to reach the age either of Cassian or of Abbot Moses, who is mentioned below.

A third Paul, therefore, presents himself: [Col. 0395C] Sozomen and others assert that he was contemporary with a certain Abbot Moses, and that he lived the monastic life at Phenue, a mountain in Scetis, or Scythia, as father of five hundred monks (Sozomen, book VI, chapter 29; Nicephorus, book XI, chapter 36; Palladius, Lausiac History, 23). But what Cassian relates here seems in no way to suit him, since other writers, on the contrary, expressly state that he did no work, but devoted himself to continual prayers and offered God three hundred prayers each day, as though paying a kind of tribute. This could be understood in the sense explained by Peter of Equilium, book IV, chapter 60, where he speaks of this Paul in these words: “Who each day neither took food nor worked with his hands until he had paid God three hundred prayers, kneeling, which he counted out by means of pebbles, and so forth.” But the reliability of this interpretation must rest with its author.

Other abbots and hermits named Paul, distinguished for proven holiness, are also mentioned; perhaps this event should be attributed to one of them, although it is not explicitly recorded by other authors. In any event, whichever of these men he may have been, I certainly think that he was none other [Col. 0395D] than the one who is mentioned in the following chapter and in Conference 7, chapter 26, together with Abbot Moses as his contemporary. His exceptional purity and chastity are likewise reported there—he would not even look at a woman—as are miracles performed even after his death. The Author also mentions him in Conference 9, chapter 1.]

Abbot Paul, the most approved of the Fathers, [Col. 0395A] while dwelling in a more extensive desert called Porphyrio, had an adequate supply of food for his nourishment and sustenance from the fruits of palm trees and a small garden, [Note: [Col. 0395D] Pliny mentions the island of Porphyrion in book V, at the end of the book. But whether this is the same as this desert, I have not sufficiently established. Cassian again mentions this desert in Conference 24, chapter 4, in these words: “Those who dwelt in that desert of Calamus, or Porphyrion.” Palladius calls it Porphyritis: “To the holy Pityr, an anchorite who sat in Porphyritis,” he says, and so forth. Eusebius of Caesarea likewise says in Ecclesiastical History, book VIII, chapter 18: “It happened in a certain place of the Thebaid called Porphyritis, which had already received its name from the vein of porphyry stone found there.”]

and could not undertake any other work by which he might support himself, because his dwelling was separated from the towns and inhabited land by seven day-stages, or even more, of that desert, [Note: [Col. 0395D] That is, a journey of seven days. For a *mansio* means a journey of one day, even in Pliny, book XII, chapter 14: “The frankincense-bearing region extends for eight stations from the lofty mountain”; or it means the stations of soldiers or of travelers. Hence St. Jerome’s treatise on the forty-two stations of the children of Israel (volume III), by which, after changing camps, they came from Egypt to the Promised Land, as is read in Exodus and Numbers.]

and more would have had to be paid for the cost of transport than the value of the price of the work performed; [Note: [Col. 0396B] The palm is a noble tree, common in Syria and Egypt, producing dates, so called because of their resemblance to fingers. It alone among trees always retains the same leaves and remains perpetually green; hence it was called *aeiphyllos* (ἀείφυλλος), “ever-leaved,” by the ancients. It was also dedicated as a sign and ornament of victory, because it does not yield to weights but rises the higher the more it is pressed down (St. Ambrose, Sermon 24; Basil, Homily 5 on the *Hexaemeron*; Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book III, chapter 6; Caelius Rhodiginus, *Ancient Readings*, book V, chapter 6).

Hence Isidore says in *Etymologies*, book XVII, chapter 7: “The palm is so called because it is the ornament of the victorious hand, or because its branches are spread out in the form of the human palm. It is a tree distinguished by victory, clothed with a tall and graceful shoot and with long-lasting leaves, preserving its foliage without any replacement.”

Moreover, the use of palm trees was varied and familiar to those ancient monks, for the palm supplied them with food, clothing, and material for various kinds of work (Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue 1 on the Eastern Monks*, chapter 7; Sophronius, *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 115; Nicephorus, *History*, book XIII, chapter 11). Besides the example mentioned here, St. Jerome likewise bears witness to this concerning that first Paul the hermit, whose life he described, saying: “The palm provided him with food and clothing.” And below: “He clothed himself with woven palm leaves.” Athanasius likewise says of St. Antony: “Although the palm was modest, he was refreshed by it as by some consolation.” Sozomen, book VI of his *History*, chapter 29, says of the anchorite Dorotheus: “At night he wove palm leaves by twisting them together and made baskets from them, by which he supplied himself with food.” And concerning Stephen, below (chapters 28 and 30): “Nevertheless, he did not cease to work, and to weave and fold palm leaves with his hands.” Other examples may be found in Palladius’s *Lausiac History*. Pliny discusses the nature of the palm and its leaves, fruits, and varieties at greater length in *Natural History*, book XIII, chapter 4.]

he continually imposed upon himself a daily task, gathering palm leaves, as though he were to be sustained by them thereafter. When the work of an entire year had filled his cave, he burned every year, after placing fire beneath it, what he had produced with such painstaking care, [Col. 0396A] thereby demonstrating that without manual labor a monk could neither remain in a place nor ever ascend to the summit of perfection. He did this even though the necessity of obtaining food in no way demanded it, undertaking it solely for the purification of his heart, the firmness of his thoughts, perseverance in his cell, and the overcoming and defeating of his own acedia.

## CHAPTER XXV. The words of Abbot Moses that he spoke to me concerning the remedy for acedia.

When, at the beginning of my stay in the desert, [Note: [Col. 0396D] Three anchorites named Moses, conspicuous for holiness, are mentioned. The first was that Ethiopian who, having become a celebrated anchorite from being a fugitive and robber, converted many robbers and led them over to the monastic life. His deeds are related both in the *Lives of the Fathers* (book III, chapter 21) and by Palladius (*Lausiac History*, 22), Sozomen (book VI, chapter 29), and others (Nicephorus, book XI, chapter 36). But this is not the man intended here, for he preceded our Cassian by a considerable period, as may be gathered from Ecclesiastical History.

The second was Moses the Egyptian, who first led a solitary life in the desert and became famous for signs and virtues; afterward, at the request of Mauvia, queen of the Saracens, he was made a bishop. Concerning him, see Socrates, book IV, chapter 29; Theodoret, book IV, chapter 22; and Sozomen, *History*, book VI, chapter 38.

Finally, the third was Moses the Libyan, who was both abbot and priest and, according to Palladius (*Lausiac History*, 88), a man of great gentleness and endowed with the greatest charity. I am led to believe, by the following arguments or conjectures, that it was this Moses, and no other, who is intended here. First, shortly above (chapter 22), the Author specifically mentioned the monks of Libya, as though he intended to speak particularly about them. Then, in Conference 7, chapter 26, he joins Moses with that Abbot Paul mentioned above (chapter 24), as being of the same age and likewise his contemporary, saying: “A sufficiently evident and clear proof of this matter also occurred in our own times, in Abbot Paul and Moses, who dwelt in a place of this desert,” and so forth. Finally, Sozomen also makes that Libyan Moses contemporary and of the same age as Abbot Paul, and associates him with the other monks of Libya.

The first Conference, which concerns the monk’s intention and goal, and the second, on discretion, also seem to be attributable to this Moses.] I had said to Abbot [Col. 0397A] Moses, supreme among all the saints, that on the previous day I had been afflicted most severely by the sickness of acedia and had been unable to free myself from it by any other means than by immediately running to Abbot Paul, he said to me:

“You did not free yourself from it; rather, you made yourself more devoted and subject to it. For it will attack you afterward more severely, as a deserter and fugitive, when it sees that you, having been overcome in the struggle, immediately fled from the conflict. Unless henceforth, once the battle has been joined, you choose to dispel its onrushing heats for a while, not by abandoning your cell or through the torpor of sleep, but rather by learning to triumph through endurance and combat, it will attack you more severely.”

From experience, therefore, it has been proved [Note: [Col. 0397B] St. Thomas also supports this opinion and explains it in a notable commentary (*Summa theologiae* II–II, question 35, article 1): “Sin must always be fled, according to Ecclesiasticus 21: ‘Flee sin as from the face of a serpent.’ But the assault of sin must sometimes be conquered by fleeing and sometimes by resisting. By fleeing, when continual thought increases the incentive to sin, as happens with lust; hence it is said in 1 Corinthians 6: ‘Flee fornication.’ By resisting, when prolonged thought removes the incentive to sin, which arises from some slight apprehension. This occurs in acedia, because the more we think about spiritual goods, the more pleasing they become to us, and acedia consequently ceases.” Thus St. Thomas.

John Climacus agrees with this teaching when he discusses acedia (*Ladder*, step 13): “The strong shine forth most in the time of acedia. For nothing prepares so many crowns for the monk as acedia. If you consider it more carefully, you will find it attacking those who stand with weariness in their feet and persuading those who sit to lean against the wall. Let this tyrant also be bound by the memory of sins, struck down by manual labor, dragged along by attentive thought of future blessings, and, when it is present as is fitting, questioned: ‘Tell us, you sluggish and dissolute one, who wickedly begot you, who are your descendants, who are those attacking you, and who is your slayer?’ Let it answer those questioning it in this way: ‘Those who yield to me through the quiet of solitude—I dwell with them. But among those who are truly obedient, I have nowhere to lay my head. The things that gave me my name are many. Sometimes it is insensibility of soul; at other times, a kind of forgetfulness and oblivion of heavenly things; sometimes also, the immense burden of labors. My roots are changes of place, which occur together with me: disobedience to one’s spiritual father, forgetfulness of the future judgment, and sometimes even abandonment of one’s profession. My adversaries, by whom I am now held bound, are psalmody joined to manual labor and the remembrance of death. But what utterly kills me is prayer joined to the firmest hope of future blessings.” Thus Climacus.

Bernard also agrees in Sermon 12 on the *Song of Songs*: “When you feel yourself afflicted by torpor, acedia, or weariness, do not therefore despair or cease from spiritual endeavor; instead seek the hand of him who helps, begging him to draw you along, after the example of the bride, until grace once again rouses you and makes you more ready and more vigorous to run, so that you may say: ‘I ran in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart’ (Psalm 118).” And elsewhere: “When you begin, sadness will fill your heart; but if you persevere, your sadness will be changed into joy. Then the affection will be purified and the will renewed—or rather, newly created—so that everything that at first seemed difficult, indeed impossible, will be accomplished with great sweetness and eagerness.”]

that the assault of acedia is not to be avoided by fleeing, but overcome by resisting.

# BOOK ELEVEN. ON THE SPIRIT OF VAINGLORY.

[Col. 0397]

## CHAPTER I.

[Col. 0397C] [Note: [Col. 0397C] The Author himself offers a certain explanation in Conference 5, chapter 10, of why he placed cenodoxy, or vainglory, seventh in the order of the capital vices: cenodoxy has a great affinity and a particular connection and bond with pride, which is placed last as the most savage beast, more monstrous than all the preceding ones. “For,” he says, “the abundance of cenodoxy produces fuel for pride.” But it is entirely different from those six vices and is not bound to them by a similar association. For it not only derives no occasion for its generation from any of them, but is also aroused in the opposite way and order. When those vices have been uprooted, this one bears fruit more vigorously, and it sprouts and grows more energetically through their death. Thus Cassian (*Institutes*, book XII, chapter 1).

We leave the examination and discussion of this reasoning—which is not without difficulty—to its proper place. St. Gregory, moreover, who, as has already been said several times, makes pride the queen and mother of all vices, consequently places vainglory, which arises immediately from it, as the first capital vice (book XXXI of the *Morals*, chapter 31; St. Thomas, I–II, question 84, article 4, and II–II, question 131, article 4). He enumerates the capital vices in this order:

“The root of all evil is pride. From this poisonous root arise its first offspring, namely seven principal vices: vainglory, envy, anger, sadness, avarice, gluttony, and lust.”

John Climacus approves and follows this order more closely in step 21 of his *Ladder*. Speaking there similarly about cenodoxy, he says: “When most people discuss the vices, they define vainglory separately from pride; hence they say that there are eight principal and primary vices. But Gregory the Theologian and many other teachers have taught that these seven are the principal ones, and I follow them above all. For who has conquered vainglory and yet been proud?” This Gregory, it should be believed, is none other than Gregory the Great, the first Roman pontiff of that name, rightly honored by the title “Theologian.”

Although Gregory of Nazianzus, who bore the same name and was much older than the Roman Gregory, was customarily called “the Theologian” among the ancients by a special title because of his singular knowledge of divine matters, no mention of this division and distinction of the capital vices is found in his writings, so that no one could reasonably consider him the author of this opinion. It is therefore also clear that those are mistaken who place John Climacus before St. Gregory the Great, since Climacus cites Gregory and declares that he follows Gregory’s opinion rather than the differing view of Cassian and others concerning the number of capital vices. But these remarks have been made in passing, prompted by the mention of Gregory here.]

Our seventh contest is against the spirit of cenodoxy, [Col. 0398C] which we may call vainglory or empty glory, [Col. 0399A] [Note: [Col. 0399B] It is certain that “empty glory,” which the Greeks call *kenodoxia* (κενοδοξία), is understood here as the desire for vain glory. For glory itself, properly speaking, is not a vice or sin, but the object of sin. The Apostle uses the Greek word in Philippians 2, where he says: “Do nothing through rivalry or through empty glory (*kenodoxia*), but in humility,” and so forth. Likewise in Galatians 5: “Let us not become desirous of empty glory.” St. Jerome says (in *On the Priesthood*, and Homily 43 on Vainglory and Ambition): “The Greek has one word, *kenodoxoi* (κενόδοξοι), which the Latin translator expressed by a circumlocution of three words.” Hence the verb *kenodoxein*, that is, “to be led by empty glory,” appears in Chrysostom.

Suidas defines it less fully and accurately: “*Kenodoxy* is a certain empty opinion about oneself.” For cenodoxy is not named from opinion, but from affection or appetite for glory. Hence it is defined as an inordinate appetite for glory.

Here we should first note the difference among four honorific goods that are closely related and are commonly confused: fame, praise, honor, and glory. Fame is the opinion of many people and the report concerning someone’s life and character. It is of two kinds, good and bad; but bad fame is usually called not fame but infamy (St. Thomas, II–II, question 103, article 1, reply to objection 2). Honor is a certain acknowledgment of excellence in someone, or the offering of reverence as a testimony to that excellence, especially excellence of virtue and wisdom. Praise is speech that manifests the excellence and perfection of some good; we praise when we express someone’s virtue or perfection in words. Cicero says (*On Invention*, book II) that glory is “famous knowledge joined with praise,” or “frequent report concerning someone joined with praise.” Thus it embraces both opinion and praise and consequently also fame, since good fame consists in praise.

Second, we should note that cenodoxy is not simply called an appetite for glory. For desiring glory is not in itself evil, but indifferent, just as desiring riches is indifferent. Rather, it is an inordinate appetite for glory—that is, one alienated from right reason, deviating from and disagreeing with the order and prescription of reason—or, which amounts to the same thing, an appetite for empty and vain glory (Augustine, *City of God*, book V, chapter 12).

According to St. Thomas (II–II, question 132, article 1), glory can be called vain for three reasons. First, on the part of the thing for which someone seeks glory—for example, if someone seeks glory for what he does not possess, or seeks more glory than he deserves, or seeks glory for something unworthy of glory, such as some fragile or perishable thing. Second, on the part of the one from whom someone seeks glory—for example, from a human being whose judgment is uncertain, especially from those unable to judge matters rightly. Third, on the part of the one who desires glory, namely, when he does not refer his desire for glory to its proper end, such as the honor of God or the salvation of his neighbor. Thus St. Thomas.

Third, it follows from these considerations that cenodoxy, or the desire for vain glory, properly understood, differs both from pride and from ambition, although it appears closely related and joined to them. It differs from pride—which St. Gregory considers its first offspring and daughter—because pride desires excellence, whereas cenodoxy desires the manifestation of that excellence among others. It differs from ambition as glory differs from honor. Glory consists in the fame of one’s name and in the opinion and praise of others; honor, in offices, dignities, signs of reverence, and other testimonies of excellence (St. Thomas, question 163, article 8; Augustine, book V on the *Song of Songs*, chapter 19).

Nevertheless, although these things stand thus according to philosophy and their proper definitions, in common understanding and speech, when vainglory is established as a capital vice, ambition is also understood by that name.

Fourth, vainglory is numbered among the capital or principal vices, including by St. Gregory, as was seen above (chapter 3), not because it is always a mortal fault, as will be said below, but because it is the mother and parent of many other vices, which arise from it as from a poisonous root and are reduced to the number seven. St. Gregory assigns these seven daughters: disobedience, boasting, hypocrisy, quarrels, obstinacy, discord, and presumption of novelties. St. Thomas explains their rationale.

Aristotle also treats cenodoxy in book IV of the *Ethics*, chapter 3 (article 5), where he sets three neighboring and almost connected vices against magnanimity: presumption, ambition, and cenodoxy.]

we can call it multiform, varied, and subtle, so that it can scarcely be guarded against or even seen through and detected by the keenest eyes.

## CHAPTER II. That cenodoxy assails the monk not only in the carnal part but also in the spiritual part.

[Col. 0400A]

[Note: [Col. 0400D] Dionysius explains the “carnal part” as the sensory part, which is otherwise called concupiscence, sensuality, or the flesh; consequently, he understands the “spiritual part” as the higher, or rational, part of the soul. But this is far from the Author’s meaning, which he himself explained so clearly in Conference 5, chapter 11, that no other interpreter is needed here. He says:

“Although cenodoxy is multiform and manifold and is divided into various species, it nevertheless has two genera. The first is that by which we are exalted because of carnal and manifest things; the second is that by which we are inflamed with a desire for empty praise because of spiritual and hidden things.”

Thus, in this passage, to be assailed in the carnal part means to be exalted because of carnal and manifest things; and to be assailed in the spiritual part means to be puffed up with a desire for empty praise because of spiritual and hidden things. See what was noted above from Chrysostom.]

For it assails the monk not only in the carnal part, like the other vices, [Col. 0401A] but also in the spiritual part, insinuating itself into the mind with more subtle wickedness; so that those who could not be deceived by carnal vices [Note: [Col. 0401B] Dionysius clarifies this in a simpler style suited to his audience: “Thus those who could not be overcome by carnal sins are wounded more severely by vainglory arising from their spiritual progress.” These words aptly correspond to what John Climacus writes about cenodoxy in the twenty-first step, where he depicts it as follows:

“Cenodoxy is the dissipation of labors, the destruction of efforts, the ambush of treasures, shipwreck in harbor, and an ant in the threshing floor which, although small, lies in wait for all labors and fruits. The ant waits until the grain is completed, but cenodoxy waits until riches have been gathered; the ant rejoices in stealing, while cenodoxy rejoices in dissipating. The spirit of despair rejoices when it sees vices multiplying; cenodoxy, when it sees virtues multiplying.”

And below:

“Cenodoxy rejoices in every practice. For example, if I fast, I glory vainly; if I wear splendid clothing, I am overcome by that plague; if I dress more poorly, I glory again; if I speak, I am conquered by it; if I remain silent, I am again overcome. Whichever way you throw this [ [Col. 0401D] Vegetius calls the *tribulus* in book III an iron spur with a four-sided form which, whichever way it falls, always presents a hostile spike.] it remains standing with its spike upright.” Thus he.]

are wounded more severely by spiritual successes. It is therefore more pernicious in combat in proportion as it is more obscure and difficult to guard against. The assault of all the other vices is more evident and open; when the instigator has been rigidly refuted in each case by contradiction, it withdraws weakened, and the defeated adversary subsequently attacks its victor with less strength.

[Note: [Col. 0401C] Here again the paraphraser—or whoever the author may be—stumbles when he renders the passage as follows: “Moreover, when the spirit of vainglory has attempted to tempt a man through carnal sin,” and so forth. I ask you, reader: who has ever heard of the spirit of vainglory tempting a man through carnal sin? And what resemblance does this have to the Author’s meaning? Once one absurdity is granted, several others necessarily follow.

The illness discussed here, namely cenodoxy, strikes the mind through carnal exaltation—not as the paraphraser interprets it, but as the Author himself expressly stated above. For to be assailed here through carnal exaltation is the same as to be assailed above in the carnal part, that is, to be exalted because of carnal and manifest things.]

But when this illness has struck the mind through carnal exaltation and has been driven back by the shield of a response, it again attempts, as a kind of multiform wickedness, to stab and slaughter the victor under the appearance of virtues, [Col. 0402A] changing its former character and guise.

## CHAPTER III. That cenodoxy is manifold and multiform.

For the other vices, or disturbances, are said to be uniform and simple, but this one is manifold, multiform, and varied, confronting the warrior from every direction and meeting the victor on every side. It appears in clothing, in appearance, in gait, in voice, in work, in vigils, in fasts, in prayer, in withdrawal, in reading, in knowledge, in silence, in obedience, in humility, in patience, [Note: [Col. 0401D] “The soldier of Christ” means especially the monk, or more generally every Christian. Cenodoxy does wound the soldier of Christ, but not always with a fatal wound; for cenodoxy, or the desire for glory, should not be judged mortal. Indeed, theologians teach that it is usually and by its nature venial, unless it becomes mortal by reason of its matter, its end, or another sin that is sometimes involved in the affection for vain glory (St. Thomas, above, article 3).

It becomes mortal by reason of its matter if someone glories in mortal sin, drunkenness, fornication, an injury, an insult inflicted on a brother, and so forth. Concerning these things Proverbs 12 says: “They rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things.” Or, as St. Thomas says, it becomes mortal when someone glories in something false that is contrary to divine reverence, according to Ezekiel 28: “Your heart has been lifted up; you have said, ‘I am God.’” And 1 Corinthians 4 says: “What do you have that you have not received? But if you have received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?”

Such also was Herod. When the people had acclaimed him as he arrogantly harangued them in the theater, saying, “The voice of a god, and not of a man” (Acts 12; Josephus, *Antiquities*, book XIX, chapter 8), the angel of the Lord immediately struck him because he had not given honor to God; he expired, consumed by worms.

It becomes mortal by reason of its end when human praise is desired for a mortal end—for example, if someone desires to be praised, or praises himself, in order to attain a carnal end such as fornication, or something similar—or when he refers his intention to vainglory as his ultimate end, for the sake of attaining or retaining which he is prepared to transgress, or actually transgresses, some divine commandment. Such were many of the leaders of the Jews, of whom John 12 says: “They loved the glory of men more than the glory of God”; and chapter 5: “How can you believe, who receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that is from God alone?” (St. Thomas, in the passage cited above).

There is no doubt that in these cases cenodoxy, or vainglory, is a mortal sin and that it wounds, injures, slaughters, stabs, trips up, and destroys the soldier of Christ, as the Author puts it; that it brings sudden and miserable shipwreck upon those sailing with a favorable wind; and, finally, that it brings ruin and destruction.

Nevertheless, although outside these cases and in its own kind it is considered a venial sin, it always destroys the merit of a good work performed in a state of grace. For no one merits eternal life by sinning, says St. Thomas (above, article 3, reply to objection 1). Therefore a virtuous work loses its power to merit eternal life if it is performed on account of vainglory, even if that vainglory is not a mortal sin.

For this reason cenodoxy can also be said to wound, trip up, and destroy a person, since every sin, even venial sin, is a kind of wound and illness of the soul. This teaching is confirmed in Matthew 6, where the Savior seriously warns us: “Take care not to perform your righteousness before men, in order to be seen by them; otherwise you will have no reward with your Father who is in heaven.”

It is as though he said: “You will indeed have a reward with the people for whose favor you act, just as he says shortly afterward concerning the Pharisees: ‘They have received their reward,’ that is, the empty glory among men that they sought. But with your heavenly Father you will have no reward, since you do not act for his sake. For it is just that each person should receive his reward from the one for whom he labors, and that one labor should have not two rewards but one.”

For, as Chrysostom says (*Commentary on Matthew*), “What will you receive from God, when you have given nothing to God? For what is done for God is given to God and received from him; but what is done for men is poured out upon the winds.”

Because of this danger—the danger, namely, of vainglory and the loss of reward—St. Hilarion, as Blessed Jerome writes in his Life, when in the sixtieth year of his life he saw a large monastery, the multitude of brothers living with him, and the crowds of people bringing to him those afflicted by various illnesses and unclean spirits, so that every kind of person filled the surrounding solitude, wept daily and remembered his former way of life with an extraordinary longing. When the brothers asked him what was wrong and why he was wasting away, he said:

“Again I have returned to the world, and I have received my reward in my lifetime. Now the people of Palestine and the neighboring provinces think that I am someone of importance,” and so forth.

Jerome then adds: “Let others marvel at the signs he performed; let them marvel at his incredible abstinence, knowledge, and humility. I marvel at nothing so much as his ability to trample upon glory and honor. Bishops, priests, groups of clerics and monks, Christian matrons—a great temptation—and also powerful men and judges would gather so that they might receive from him bread or oil blessed by him. But he thought of nothing except solitude,” and so forth.]

attempts to wound the soldier of Christ, [Col. 0403A] and, like some exceedingly dangerous reef concealed beneath swelling waves, brings sudden and miserable shipwreck upon those sailing with a favorable wind, precisely when it is neither guarded against nor foreseen.

## CHAPTER IV. How cenodoxy attacks the monk from the right and from the left.

Therefore, one who wishes to proceed along the royal road by the weapons of righteousness, which are on the right and on the left, must, according to apostolic discipline, pass through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute (II Cor. VI), and steer his course along the path of virtue with such caution amid the swelling waves of temptations—while discretion guides us and the Spirit of the Lord fills our sails—that, if we turn even slightly to the right or left, we may know that we shall soon be dashed against destructive rocks.

Hence, through the most wise Solomon, we are warned:

> Do not turn aside to the right or to the left (Prov. IV).

[Note: The wording of the text is: “Do not turn aside to the right, nor to the left.” According to the Author’s interpretation, he turns aside to the right who is elated by virtues or by prosperous successes; he turns aside to the left who glories in sins and evil deeds. Isidore, however, expresses the matter negatively, though toward the same end (Book III, *On the Highest Good*, chap. 23): “He does not turn aside to the right who attributes the good he does not to himself but to God; nor does he turn to the left who does not presume upon divine indulgence as a license to sin.” This is what the Prophet says: “This is the way; walk in it; do not turn aside to the right or to the left.”

St. Jerome illustrates this statement by bringing together other scriptural sayings that seem to contradict it, such as that passage in Ecclesiasticus X: “The heart of the wise man is at his right hand,” and so forth. And in the Gospel (Matthew V and VI), he says, it is commanded that “the left hand should not know what the right hand of the wise man is doing.” And when we are struck on the right cheek, we are not commanded to offer the left cheek to the striker, but the other right cheek. For the righteous person has no left side in himself; everything in him is right. And when the Savior comes to judge, the lambs will stand at his right, while the goats will be on his left (Matt. XXV). And in Proverbs it is written: “The Lord knows the right-hand ways; but those that are crooked are on the left” (Prov. IV).

Therefore, the wise person always thinks about the age to come, which leads to the right; but the foolish person thinks about the present age, which is placed on the left. Following this, that same philosopher and poet says:

> The right-hand road, which leads beneath great Dis’ walls;  
>   
> By this way lies Elysium for us; but the left  
>   
> Inflicts punishments upon the wicked and sends them to impious Tartarus.

Our own Firmianus likewise, in his distinguished work *The Institutions* (Lactantius, Book VI, chapters 3 and 4), recalls the Pythagorean letter and discusses most clearly the right and the left—that is, virtues and vices. Nor should we think that the saying, “Do not turn to the right or to the left” (Prov. IV), contradicts this brief statement. There the right-hand side is understood as the good; here, however, it is not so much the right as the turning aside toward the right that is condemned, lest we become wiser than it is necessary for us to be: virtues stand in the middle, and every excess is a vice. Thus far St. Jerome, in explanation of that saying.]

That is: do not flatter yourself because of your virtues, nor become elated by favorable successes and spiritual attainments; and do not, by turning toward the left-hand path of vices, seek glory for yourself in them, according to the Apostle, to your own confusion.

[Note: Hence St. Jerome writes to Nepotianus (Letter 2): “Fine clothing, like filthy clothing, must likewise be avoided, because the one suggests indulgence and the other glory.” The same author writes to Paulinus (Letter 4): “Do not seek humility of clothing with a swollen heart.” And elsewhere (Letter 13): “Let filthy garments be signs of a pure mind, and a cheap tunic prove contempt for the world—provided only that the mind does not swell and that clothing and speech do not disagree” (chap. 17). To this belongs Tertullian’s statement in the *Apologeticus*: “Behold, with muddy feet Diogenes tramples upon Plato’s proud couches with a pride of another kind.”]

Since the devil could not generate vainglory in him under the appearance of a close-girt and clean garment, he attempts to implant it under the appearance of a dirty, unkempt, and cheaper one. He whom he could not bring down through honor, he trips up through humility; him whom he could not exalt through the adornment of knowledge and eloquence, he crushes through the gravity of silence. If he fasts publicly, he is assaulted by the glory of vanity. If he conceals the fast in order to avoid glory, he is struck by the same fault of elation. To avoid being stained by the contagion of vainglory, he avoids celebrating prolonged prayers in the sight of the brothers; yet even when he practices them secretly, with no one aware of what he is doing, he does not escape the thorns of vanity.

## CHAPTER V. By what comparison the nature of vainglory is illustrated

Our elders aptly describe the nature of this disease as resembling an onion and other bulbs: when one covering has been stripped away, another is found beneath it, and they are found to be covered as many times as they have been stripped.

[Note: Manuscripts read: “In the manner of an onion and a leek.” Hence I think that the error found in the Dionysian codex should not be tolerated, where the reading is: “By the arrangement of sluggishness,” in two truncated words joined together. This must be attributed not to the Author but to scribes and printers.]

## CHAPTER VI. That vainglory is not completely extinguished by the benefit of solitude

[Col. 0404B]

Even in solitude, vainglory does not cease pursuing one who has fled the company of all mortals for its sake.

[Note: See the examples of Saints Antony, Hilarion, and Benedict in their respective authors.]

And the more completely someone has avoided the whole world, the more fiercely it attacks him. It tries to exalt one because he is exceptionally patient in work and labor, another because he is exceptionally prompt in obedience, another because he surpasses the rest in humility. One is tempted through knowledge, another through reading, another through the length of his vigils. Nor does this disease attempt to wound anyone in any other way than through his virtues, setting snares of destruction precisely where the rewards of life are being sought.

[Note: Hence St. Chrysostom—or whoever was the author of the *Imperfect Work*, homily 13—asserts that the vice of vainglory is more dangerous than all other vices: “Although all evils afflict the servants of the devil,” he says, “the desire for vainglory afflicts the servants of God more than it afflicts the servants of the devil.”

St. Augustine, *Confessions*, Book X, chapter 38: “Speech proceeding from the mouth, and deeds that become empty before human beings, contain a most dangerous temptation arising from the love of praise. This love attempts to draw together, for a private kind of excellence, the votes begged from others; and when it is reproved by me in myself, by that very act of reproving it, it tempts me more gravely. Often a person glories even more vainly in his contempt for vainglory; therefore he no longer glories in the contempt of glory itself, for when he glories inwardly, he does not despise it.”

And in the following chapter: “There is also, within, another evil of the same kind of temptation, by which those who please themselves become empty, even if they please or displease others and do not seek to please them. Those who greatly please themselves displease you—not merely because of good things as though they were good, but because of your good things as though they were their own; or even because they regard them as yours, but as arising from their own merits; or even as arising from your grace but not on account of their merits—yet they do not rejoice together with others, but envy them. Amid all these dangers and labors of mine, you see the trembling of my heart, and I feel that my wounds are more often healed by you than inflicted upon me.”

Thus Augustine speaks to God while humbly exposing his own weakness.]

For those who wish to walk along the road of piety and perfection, the enemies lying in wait do not conceal the snares of deception anywhere except on the very road along which they walk, according to that saying of blessed David:

[Note: See this saying explained somewhat more fully in Book XII, chapter 9.]

> On this road on which I walked, they hid a snare for me (Psalm XIV),

so that, on this very road of virtues along which we advance toward the prize of the heavenly calling, we may fall, elated by our successes, and, with the feet of our soul bound, collapse, fettered by the snares of vainglory. Thus it happens that, although we could not be overcome in combat with the adversary, we are conquered by the height of our own triumph; or, in yet another form of deception, that by exceeding the measure of continence or of our own capacity, we lose the perseverance of our course when bodily weakness intervenes.

## CHAPTER VII. That when vainglory has been cast down, it rises again to the battle with greater force

All vices grow weak once overcome; after being defeated day by day, they become weaker, and are diminished and cooled either by place or by time. Alternatively, because they conflict with opposing virtues, they are more easily guarded against or avoided. But this vice, once cast down, rises again to the struggle with greater force; and when it is thought to have been extinguished, it grows stronger through its very death.

Other kinds of vice generally attack only those whom they have defeated in combat; but this one pursues its own conquerors more fiercely. The more powerfully it has been struck down, the more violently it attacks through the elation produced by that very victory. This is the enemy’s subtle strategy: to make the soldier of Christ fall by his own weapons, when it could not overcome him with hostile arms.

## CHAPTER VIII. That vainglory neither cools in the desert nor with age

As we have said, other vices sometimes become quiet even through the benefit of place. When the material, opportunity, or occasion for sin has been removed, they tend to grow sluggish and diminish. But this vice enters the desert with the one who flees, and it knows neither how to be excluded by place nor how to wither when external material has been removed. For it draws strength from nothing other than the successes of the virtues of the person whom it attacks.

Other vices, as we have stated, are sometimes softened and disappear as time passes; but longevity, unless it is grounded in diligent effort and prudent discretion, not only does not harm this vice, but knows how to pile up greater fuel for vanity.

## CHAPTER IX. That vainglory is more dangerous when mingled with virtues

Finally, the other disturbances conflict with the virtues opposed to them and wage open battle, as in broad daylight; they are therefore more easily overcome and avoided. But this vice, inserted among the virtues and mixed into the battle line, fights as though in blind night and more cruelly deceives the unsuspecting and unwary.

## CHAPTER X. The example of King Hezekiah: how he was cast down by the weapon of vainglory

Thus, indeed, we read that Hezekiah, king of Judah, a man approved by the testimony of Holy Scripture as perfect in every respect of righteousness, after innumerable praises of his virtues, was cast down by a single weapon of elation.

[Note: A distinguished testimony concerning Hezekiah, king of Judah, is found in IV Kings, chapter XVIII: “Hezekiah, son of Achaz, king of Judah, did what was good in the sight of the Lord, according to all that David his father had done. He destroyed the high places, broke the statues, cut down the sacred groves, and so forth. He trusted in the Lord God of Israel; therefore after him there was none like him among all the kings of Judah, nor among those who were before him. He adhered to the Lord and did not depart from his footsteps; he carried out his commandments, which the Lord had given to Moses. Hence the Lord was with him, and in everything he undertook he acted wisely.” Thus far the text.

This should not be understood to mean that Hezekiah was considered holier than David, who preceded him, or than Josiah, who followed him. The meaning is that, among the kings, there was none like him with respect to certain particular matters. For just as star differs from star in glory (I Cor. XV), so human being differs from human being with respect to particular gifts or deeds by which one excels others.

Accordingly, Scripture and history commend different people above others for particular virtues: Abraham and Peter for faith; Joseph and John for chastity; Job and Tobias for patience; Moses and David for gentleness. Among martyrs courage excelled; among virgins, chastity; and in others, other virtues. Thus the Church can rightly sing even of any confessor: “No one was found like him who kept the law of the Most High” (Eccles. XLIV), namely, as St. Thomas says (I–II, question 65, article 2), because of the excellence of some particular virtue, which nearly everyone possessed in greater measure than another.

Therefore, when it is said of Hezekiah that “there was none like him among all the kings of Judah,” this should be understood with reference to certain particular deeds—deeds admirable and unusual—that he performed. Of these, the following are especially recalled in sacred Scripture:

1. He destroyed the high places, broke the statues, cut down the sacred groves, and broke the bronze serpent that Moses had made (IV Kings XVIII). The reason is added: “For until that time the children of Israel burned incense to it” (IV Kings XIX and Isaiah XXXVIII).

2. At his prayer, the angel of the Lord struck down in one night 185,000 men from the army of King Sennacherib.

3. Again at his prayer, the sun moved backward ten lines by which it had descended on the sundial of Achaz.

4. Moved likewise by his tears, the Lord added fifteen years to the natural limit of his life (IV Kings XX and Isaiah XXXVIII).

In these and similar admirable deeds, none of the kings could be said to have been like him. There were indeed three kings who greatly pleased the Lord through religion and piety, because they led their peoples to repentance and to the worship of the one true God, destroying idolatry: David, Hezekiah, and Josiah. In their praise Ecclesiasticus XLIX says: “Except David, Hezekiah, and Josiah, all committed sin.” This is understood either of the sin of idolatry in themselves or in others, since it is clear that neither David nor Hezekiah can be excused from other sins.]

And he who, by a single weapon of elation, had obtained such astonishing victories—who by one prayer had been able to procure the destruction of 185,000 men from the Assyrian army, when an angel ravaged it during the night—was overcome by vainglorious boasting (IV Kings XIX).

[Note: That is, he was overcome by the vice of ostentation and vainglory, which St. Bernard says (Sermon 34 on the *Song of Songs*) is signified by “the arrow that flies by day”: “The arrow flying by day is vainglory, for fame flies, and therefore by day, because it arises from works of light.” Bernard is presumably alluding to Virgil’s line:

> Flying Fame, than which nothing is swifter.

What, then, was the specimen of elation or ostentation in Hezekiah that this Author passes over briefly? St. Gregory, treating the same subject, explains it from Scripture and recounts it in *Moralia*, Book VIII, chapter 36. After vividly depicting the behavior of ostentatious and vainglorious people, he adds:

“Certainly their life was represented by the universally known fault of Hezekiah, who, after he had struck down 185,000 enemies by one prayer and in the space of a single night, through the angel’s blow; after he had brought the sun, already near its setting, back into the higher regions of the heavens; after he had prolonged into a longer span the life that was already being shortened as its end approached—when he received the messengers of the king of Babylon, showed them all the possessions he had. But immediately he heard from the prophet’s voice: ‘Behold, the days are coming, and everything that is in your house will be carried away to Babylon; nothing will be left, says the Lord.’

“Thus, surely, hypocrites, after they have grown great through mighty virtues, because they neglect to guard against the snares of evil spirits and do not wish to remain hidden in those same virtues, make their good things the property of their enemies by displaying them; and by betraying them, they suddenly lose whatever they have worked at for so long.”

Gregory’s words most aptly illustrate this passage of Cassian. (See Isidore, Book III, *On the Highest Good*, chapter 23.)]

To pass over the lengthy catalogue of his virtues, whose repetition would take too long, I shall say only this:

[Col. 0408A]

[Note: Until now, “forbidden” had been read here, even in the Plantinian and Lyon editions, although everyone can see that “announced” must be read, as the manuscripts also show. For the prophet Isaiah announced, not forbade, the term of life to King Hezekiah when he was sent to him in his illness and said: “Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live” (IV Kings XX; Isaiah XXXVIII).]

After the term of his life had been announced and the day of his death fixed by the Lord’s decree,

[Note: How fifteen years were added to Hezekiah after the term of life and the day of death had been announced by the Lord’s decree, as the Author says, St. Gregory also explains admirably in his treatment of the passage in Job: “You have appointed his limits, which cannot be exceeded.”

“If,” he says, “Almighty God added fifteen years of life to King Hezekiah, when he allowed him to die, then he knew beforehand that he would die. In this matter a question arises: how could it be said to him through the prophet, ‘Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live,’ when, after the sentence of death had been pronounced against him, life was immediately added to him because of his tears?

“But through the prophet the Lord declared the time at which he deserved to die; through the generosity of his mercy, however, he postponed his death to that time which he himself had foreseen before the ages. Thus the prophet was not false, because the time of death was made known at which that man deserved to die; nor were the Lord’s decrees overturned, because the fact that, through God’s generosity, the years of his life would increase had also been fixed before the ages. The period of life that was unexpectedly added outwardly had been established inwardly in divine foreknowledge without increase.”

Thus far Gregory (*Moralia*, Book XII, chapter 2).]

he deserved by one prayer to exceed the limits of his life by fifteen years,

[Note: IV Kings XX: “The Lord brought back the shadows by the lines along which they had already descended on the sundial of Achaz, backward by ten degrees.” And Isaiah XXXVIII: “Behold, I shall bring back the shadow of the lines by which it descended on the sundial of Achaz in the sun, backward by ten lines.” And the sun returned by ten lines through the degrees by which it had descended.

Although there can be no doubt about the truth of this miracle—namely, the sun’s retrogression or backward movement for the sake of King Hezekiah—the interpreters nevertheless hold differing views about the manner and means by which it occurred.

Some think that the sun moved backward instantaneously, that is, within an extremely brief interval of time, by ten degrees or hours, which were indicated by the lines of the sundial—as commonly happens on sundials—from the tenth hour to the first hour of the artificial day; then it resumed its daily course and gradually proceeded toward sunset. Thus thought the Chaldean Paraphrast.

Others think that the lines of the sundial did not indicate whole hours but half-hours. Thus the day was extended by only ten hours: five in its backward movement toward the east and five in its return to the same point from which it had moved backward.

Cassian seems to have held one of these two views when he says that the day was doubled for the entire world, with only two hours still remaining, since among the ancients each artificial day and each night was divided into twelve equal parts or hours, as has often been said.

The third and more probable opinion is that each line or degree indicated a whole hour, that is, the span of one hour. Accordingly, this day was increased by twenty hours—not merely doubled but almost tripled—since it was illuminated for thirty-two hours while the sun remained above the horizon.

This is the opinion of Blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, who is to be believed above the others, since he undoubtedly learned such mysteries and secrets from the Apostle Paul. Speaking of this miracle in Letter 7 to Polycarp, bishop, he says:

> “A certain day was made greater, with perpetual light, by almost three times its usual length; and the heavens, moving backward within the twenty hours of the course they had already completed, retraced that course, and then, in another ten hours, completed the whole course again by a new mode.”

This miracle rightly terrified the Babylonians at that time and subjected them, without a battle, to Hezekiah, who was thought to be equal to God.

Thus far St. Dionysius. From this it is clear how empty and futile is the opinion of those who think that this miracle appeared only on the sundial of Achaz or Hezekiah, since it was seen not only in Judea but also in Chaldea. Hence the king of Babylon sent messengers to Hezekiah with gifts, both to congratulate him on his astonishing recovery and to inquire about the portent that had occurred over the earth, as is recorded in II Chronicles, chapter XXXII.]

when the sun, which in its course toward sunset had already illuminated ten degrees, returned, driving away by its renewed return the lines that the shadow had occupied as it followed the sun’s departure. By this unheard-of miracle he granted the whole world a doubled day, contrary to the fixed laws of nature.

After such great and unbelievable signs, after such immense proofs of virtue, hear how he was struck down by his successes, as Scripture tells:

> In those days Hezekiah became sick unto death, and he prayed to the Lord, and he heard him and gave him a sign—

namely, the sign that we read was given concerning the sun’s return through the prophet Isaiah in the Fourth Book of Kings.

[Note: Hezekiah did not show the gratitude, religion, and devotion of spirit that he owed for such great benefits received from God. Rather, “his heart was lifted up,” that is, it was raised up in pride. For “the beginning of every sin is pride” (Ecclesiasticus X). From this he incurred a threefold mark of guilt:

1. Ingratitude, because he did not give God glory for the victory and the flight of Sennacherib, and perhaps attributed it more to his own merits than to God’s favor, according to the Hebrews. For this reason he fell into the most serious illness, in which he was sick unto death.

2. Boastfulness, ostentation, and vainglory, when, delighting in the embassy and congratulations of the king of Babylon, he showed the envoys his treasures and all the splendor of his kingdom (IV Kings XX; Isaiah XXXIX).

3. Neglect of charity toward the salvation of his neighbors. For, as Cyril says (*Book III on Isaiah*), when those who had come from Babylon arrived, Hezekiah ought to have explained in an illustrious account the assistance of Almighty God, provided at various times, and the splendor and magnificence of these astonishing events, so that they too, admiring the divine excellence and the invincible power of the Lord more greatly through his words, might return to their homeland enriched by knowledge of God—for in this way he could also have benefited others, since they would report what they had learned. But he did nothing of the sort. Rather, he fell into human boastfulness and valued his glory not from those deeds by which he had been honored by God, but from the wealth of his kingdom, and so forth.]

“But he did not repay him according to the benefits he had received, because his heart was lifted up; and wrath came upon him and upon Judah and Jerusalem. But afterward he humbled himself because his heart had been exalted, both he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem; and therefore the wrath of the Lord did not come upon them in the days of Hezekiah” (IV Kings XX).

How destructive and how grave is the disease of elation! Such righteousness, such virtues, such faith and devotion—virtues that had deserved to alter nature itself and the laws of the whole world—perish through a single act of elation. Thus, with all his virtues consigned to oblivion as though they had never existed, he would immediately have incurred the Lord’s wrath, unless he had appeased it by recovering humility. He who had fallen from so lofty a summit of merits because elation drove him down could ascend again to the lost height only by the same steps of humility.

Would you like to learn another example of a similar downfall?

## CHAPTER XI. The example of King Uzziah, overcome by the stain of the same disease

[Col. 0410A]

Uzziah, the great-great-great-grandfather of the king we have mentioned,

[Note: “Great-great-grandfather” is written incorrectly, or at least loosely, in place of “great-grandfather,” who is the father of a grandfather. For the father of King Hezekiah was Achaz; his grandfather, Jotham; his great-grandfather, Uzziah, also called Azariah; his great-great-grandfather, Amasias; and finally his great-great-great-grandfather, Joas, as is clear from the history of the Kings (IV Kings VIII, XV, XVI; II Chronicles XXIV and following; IV Kings V).]

also praised throughout by the testimony of Scripture, after the great praises of his virtues and the countless triumphs he achieved through the merit of his devotion and faith, learn how he was cast down by the elation of vainglory.

[Note: When he wished to usurp the office of the priests. Concerning him Suidas writes, in agreement both with Scripture and with this passage: “Uzziah, king of Israel, was pious, but, elated by prosperity, he foolishly wished to sacrifice to God by himself—something permitted only to priests. And when he had burned incense in the temple, he immediately became a leper. His face was covered with leprosy in the temple of the Lord, and therefore they dragged him out.”

Suidas should have said more precisely “king of Judah” rather than “king of Israel,” since after the separation of the ten tribes under King Rehoboam, the kings of Israel are distinguished from the kings of Judah, among whom Uzziah is the thirteenth. There is an excellent homily by St. John Chrysostom on “Uzziah’s heart was lifted up” (Volume I).]

“And the name of Uzziah went forth, because the Lord helped him and strengthened him. But when he had become strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction, and he neglected the Lord his God” (II Chronicles XXVI).

You see another example of a most grievous downfall, and you see that two men so just and so perfect were destroyed by their triumphs and victories. Hence you see how dangerous the successes of prosperity ordinarily are: those whom adversity could not break are struck down more violently by prosperity if they are unwary; and those who escaped the dangers of death in combat and battle succumb to their own trophies and triumphs.

## CHAPTER XII. Various testimonies against vainglory

Therefore the Apostle warns:

[Note: In one word, κενόδοξοι (*kenodoxoi*, “vainglorious”), as noted above (on chapter 1 of this work). Relevant here is St. Basil’s question 25 in the *Shorter Rules*, in these words:

“When the Apostle says in one place, ‘Let us not become desirous of vainglory,’ and elsewhere, ‘Not serving to the eye, as pleasing human beings’ (Eph. VI), who is desirous of vainglory, and who is pleasing human beings?”

“Response: I consider the person desirous of vainglory to be one who does or says something merely for the sake of worldly glory, or of the glory that arises for him from those who see or hear him. But the person who pleases human beings is anyone who does something according to the will of some human being in order to please him, even if what he does is blameworthy.”]

> Do not become desirous of vainglory (Gal. V).

And the Lord, rebuking the Pharisees, says:

[Note: St. Jerome, writing to Eustochium on the preservation of virginity (Letter 22): “You must also avoid this, lest you be seized by the burning of vainglory. How,” Jesus says, “can you believe, when you receive glory from human beings?” See what sort of evil this is: whoever possesses it cannot believe. But let us say: “For you are my glory” (Psalm III), and “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord” (I Cor. I).

St. Augustine, *The City of God*, Book V, chapter 14: “This vice is so hostile to pious faith—if the desire for glory is greater in the heart than fear or love of God—that the Lord said: ‘How can you believe, who receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that is from God alone?’ That this kind of desire for glory has hindered the faith of many is shown by John, chapter XII: ‘Many even of the rulers believed in him; but because of the Pharisees they did not confess him, lest they be expelled from the synagogue, for they loved the glory of human beings more than the glory of God.’”

Thus Augustine. See Cajetan, *Jentaculum* 10, question 2, where he teaches that the Lord’s words signify a twofold impediment to faith: one positive, namely, desiring and seeking the empty glory of human beings; the other privative or negative, namely, not seeking the glory of God—that is, heavenly and everlasting glory. For the glory of God and the glory of human beings cannot coexist more harmoniously than the wisdom of God and the wisdom of human beings, of which one is foolishness to the other. Therefore, whoever pursues one must necessarily despise the other.]

> How can you believe, who receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that is from God alone? (John V)

Of these things blessed David also speaks with a threat:

> For God has scattered the bones of those who please human beings (Psalm LII).

[Note: That is, those who abandon the fear of God in order to win the favor of human beings and carnal friends.

There are two ways in which we may please human beings. First, when we strive to please people solely in order to seek their favor and approval. This is indeed a sin, especially if, for that reason, we are not afraid to displease God—that is, to offend God. Concerning this the Apostle says in Galatians I: “If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ.”

Second, we please human beings for God’s sake, by removing from ourselves every scandal and everything that could offend others. This is not so much pleasing human beings as pleasing God. Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Be without offense to Jews and Greeks, as I also please everyone in everything, not seeking my own advantage but that of many, so that they may be saved” (I Cor. X).

Therefore St. Jerome concludes (in his commentary on Galatians V): “If it is possible for us to please God and human beings at the same time, we should please human beings as well. But if we please human beings only by displeasing God, we must please God rather than human beings.”

The same author writes in his Letter to Pammachius (Letter 26): “The first virtue of a monk is to despise human judgments and always to remember the Apostle’s saying: ‘If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ.’”]

## CHAPTER XIII. The ways in which vainglory assails a monk

It also tends to tempt the minds of beginners and of those who have not yet advanced sufficiently either in strength of character or in knowledge,

[Note: Caesarius gives an amusing example of this in the following words:

“Once, when certain clerics in a secular church were singing loudly—that is, noisily rather than devoutly—and raising their tumultuous voices aloft, a religious man who happened to be present saw a demon standing in an elevated place, holding a large and long sack in his left hand. With his right hand stretched wide, he gathered the singers’ voices and put them into the same sack. When they had finished singing and were boasting among themselves as though they had praised God well and powerfully, the man who had seen the vision said to them: ‘You have sung well, since you have sung a full sack.’ When they were astonished and asked why he said this, he explained the vision to them.”

Thus far Caesarius of Citeaux, *Book IV of Miracles*, chapter 5.

Relevant also is what St. Augustine writes in *Confessions*, Book X, chapter 33: “When I recall the tears that I poured out at the singing of the Church in the early days of my recovered faith, and now, when I am moved not by the singing but by the things that are sung, when they are sung with a clear voice and most fitting musical expression, I acknowledge the great usefulness of this institution. Yet when it happens that the singing moves me more than the thing that is sung, I confess that I sin grievously, and then I would rather not hear the singer.”]

either because of the sound of their voice, namely, that they sing the psalms more melodiously, or because they are emaciated in flesh,

[Note: That is, their bodies have been reduced or made thin by fasting, or are gaunt. For St. Gregory says (Homily 32 on the Gospel): “Vainglory sometimes lies in wait nearby for abstinence of the flesh. For when thinness is observed in the body and pallor in the face, virtue is exposed to praise; and it pours itself outward all the more swiftly the more it emerges before human eyes through exhibited pallor.”

As for what follows in the text, “or more well-groomed in body,” the paraphrast seems to take it as an explanatory expression for the same category, not as a disjunction. He renders it as though it were one member: “or because they are of a thinner body, as though the thinner were more neat or delicate.” Yet it seems more likely that two members are distinguished here, that is, two kinds of people, and that “more well-groomed” means either more handsome, or fatter and stronger. For a person is certainly not called “well-groomed” when reduced to skin and bones, but when well supplied and well cared for.]

or more well-groomed in body,

[Note: Such was the monk who served St. Benedict at table and said within himself in proud thought: “Who is this man whom I attend while he eats, for whom I hold the lamp and perform service? Who am I that I should serve this man?” The man of God turned toward him and rebuked him, saying: “Mark your heart, brother. What is it that you are saying? Mark your heart” (Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book II, chapter 20).

A similar story is told about Brother Leonardo by Bonaventure in the *Life of St. Francis*.]

or because they have wealthy or noble parents, or because they have despised military service and honors. Sometimes it even persuades someone that dignities and wealth—which perhaps could never actually have been obtained—would have been very easy for him to acquire if he had persevered in the world, inflating him with vain hope even concerning uncertain things and concerning possessions he never owned; as though he had despised them, it exalts him with the glory of vanity.

## CHAPTER XIV. How it suggests that the clerical rank should be sought after
[Note: [Col. 0412B] Dionysius puts it somewhat more clearly: “Sometimes, however, he implants an inclination toward the clerical rank and a desire for the priesthood or diaconate.” For it is rather improper to say that he “implants the clerical rank,” instead of an inclination or desire for the clergy. Moreover, for restraining such inclinations and the premature desires of certain monks who prematurely seek and aspire to the clerical state and ecclesiastical orders, the Church has wisely provided that no monk be ordained without the permission of his superior. For, says the pontiff, “it is more honorable and safer for subjects, while rendering due obedience to their superiors, to serve in a lower ministry than, to the scandal of their superiors, to seek the dignity of higher ranks” (*De tempore ordinationis*, chapter “Ad aures”; Council of Trent, Session XIV, chapter 1, *De reformatione*). Hence Saint Benedict likewise decrees in chapter 62 of the Rule: “If an abbot wishes to have one of his monks ordained priest or deacon, let him choose from among them one who is worthy to exercise the priesthood; but once ordained, let him beware of conceit or pride,” and so forth.

“From this passage we may also infer that monks in former times, although initially regarded by their profession and condition as laymen, as we have noted elsewhere, nevertheless were customarily admitted and promoted to the clerical state and to sacred orders. Thus Saint Jerome, admonishing the monk Rusticus how he should prepare himself for this, writes (*Epistle* 4): ‘If the desire for the clerical state pricks you, learn what you may teach, and offer Christ a reasonable sacrifice [*hostiam*; the printed *hospitem* is evidently corrupt]; do not be a soldier before you are a recruit, nor a master before you are a disciple.’ And below: ‘Act and live in the monastery in such a way that you may deserve to be a cleric; let no impurity stain your youth, so that you may come forth to Christ’s altar like a virgin from the bridal chamber, and have a good reputation outside, so that women may know your name but not your face.’ And in *Epistle* 27 he relates that Bishop Saint Isidore met the widow Paula of Rome as she visited the places of the Holy Land, with innumerable throngs of monks, from among whom he raised many to the priestly and Levitical ranks.”]

Yet sometimes he implants the clerical rank and the desire for the priesthood or diaconate. If he had attained it even unwillingly, he depicts him as destined to accomplish so much with holiness and austerity that he could have offered the other priests examples of holiness, and thereafter would have won over many—not only by the example of his conduct, but also by his teaching and speech—

[Note: [Col. 0415C] This is the little fox which, according to Saint Bernard (*Sermon* 64 on the *Song of Songs*), deceives many who, concerned for the salvation and conversion of others, neglect their own salvation. As the saying goes in Plautus: “to sow another’s field and abandon one’s own.” Germanus, an abbot and companion of our Cassian, confessed to Abbot Abraham that he and Cassian had suffered from, or been tempted by, this fault, in these words (*Conference* 24, chapter 1): “Moreover, we nourished our minds with the hope of empty joys, believing that we would gain the greatest fruit from the conversion of many who, as though by our example and admonitions, would be guided onto the way of salvation.” He himself rebukes and refutes this foolish opinion—or rather, as he calls it, this diabolical illusion—in the following way: “All who are rather weak must necessarily become entangled in these illusions and losses: although they are uncertain even of their own salvation and still need the instruction and teaching of another, they are driven by diabolical illusions to convert and govern others. And even if they are able to gain some profit from the conversion of certain people, through their impatience and disordered conduct they lose whatever they have acquired. For what the prophet Haggai describes will happen to them: ‘He who gathers wages puts them into a pierced purse’ (Haggai 1). Truly he stores his gains in a pierced purse who dissipates, through the intemperance of his heart and the daily distraction of his mind, whatever he seems to acquire through the conversion of others. Thus it will happen that, while they believe they can prepare further gains through instructing others, they will be deprived even of their own correction.” Thus far he.

“In the same sense Saint Gregory writes in Book XXXI of the *Moralia*, where he discusses each of the capital vices: ‘Empty glory,’ he says (chapter 32), ‘usually exhorts the conquered heart as though from reason, saying: You ought to seek greater things, so that, in the measure that you wish to surpass many in power, you may also be able to benefit many.’ See also the same author, *Pastoral Care*, chapter 1; Saint Bernard, *Sermon* 64 on the *Song of Songs*; and what we noted on chapter 1 of Conference 24.”]

He also makes him, while living in the desert or in his cell, travel mentally and inwardly through the houses and monasteries of various people, and acquire the conversions [or, perhaps, “ways of life”: *conversationes*] of many through the stimulus of an imagined exhortation. Thus the unhappy soul is deceived by such vanity as by a most profound sleep. Often, enticed by the sweetness of such thoughts and filled with these images, it is unable even to contemplate the actions or brothers immediately before it, while it delights in clinging to those things which, awake, it has dreamed through the wandering of its thoughts, as though they were real.

## CHAPTER XV  
### How vainglory intoxicates the mind

I remember a certain old man, when I was staying in the desert of Scetis (see Conference 1, chapter 1). When he approached the door of a certain brother’s cell in order to visit him, and heard him muttering something inside, he stopped for a little while, wishing to discover what he was reading from Scripture—or, as is customary, reciting from memory while working. When the most devout investigator had carefully applied his ear and listened inquisitively, he found that the monk was so carried away by the assault of this spirit that he believed himself to be delivering an exhortatory sermon to the people in church.

When the old man had paused and heard him finish his discourse—

[Note: [Col. 0416C] The earlier printing had it incorrectly: “to have conducted a discussion.” Dionysius reads, “to have finished his sermon,” that is, the exhortatory address which the monk was evidently rehearsing, preparing himself for it in the manner of deacons—imaginarily, not in reality, acting as a deacon.]

—and then, changing his office again—

[Note: [Col. 0416C] The old and customary division of the Mass is into the Mass of the catechumens—that is, those being instructed in the faith but not yet baptized—and the Mass of the faithful. The first part of the Mass, from the entrance through the offertory, was called the Mass of the catechumens, because catechumens and public penitents were permitted to be present during it; once it was completed, they were dismissed from the church while the faithful remained. The remaining part of the celebration of the Mass, at which only the faithful could be present, was called the Mass of the faithful.
