Saint Augustine refers to this in *Sermon* 237, in these words: “Behold, after the sermon the dismissal is made for the catechumens; the faithful remain.” After the Gospel and the Creed had been read, or the sermon had ended, and before bread and wine were offered on the altar for consecration, the deacon in the Latin Church publicly proclaimed: “If anyone does not communicate, let him withdraw,” as Saint Gregory reports in Book II of the *Dialogues*, chapter 23; or in this form: “If anyone is a catechumen, let him go outside,” as Isidore and Durandus note (*Isidore, Etymologies*, Book VI, final chapter; Durandus, *Rationale*, Book IV, chapter 2; Demochares, Book IV, chapters 32 and 38). Thus in the Greek liturgy of Chrysostom: ὅσοι κατηχούμενοι παρέλθετε, “All you who are catechumens, depart.”

Hence Alcuin writes in his book *On the Divine Offices*: “The canons call it the Mass of the catechumens because after the reading of the Gospel the sacred mysteries begin to be celebrated, at which no one except the baptized may be present. Then, when the deacon cried out, these catechumens were sent outside.” Thus far Alcuin.

For this reason the deacon was said to celebrate the Mass for the catechumens—that is, to send the catechumens away or dismiss them with some solemn admonition or exhortation. The monk in question eagerly desired this office in his youthful zeal and was trying to imitate it.]

—as though celebrating the Mass for the catechumens in the manner of a deacon—

[Col. 0417A] only then did he knock at the door. The monk came out, met the old man with the customary reverence, brought him inside, and, troubled by the awareness of his thoughts, asked how long ago he had arrived, lest he had been made to suffer an injury by standing too long at the door.

[Note: [Col. 0417C] He asks how long before—that is, how long ago—the old man had arrived, or how long he had stood before the door, and whether he had endured exposure to the weather or the discomfort of waiting outside. Meanwhile the monk had been occupied with another thought, his anxious conscience reproaching him over whether the elder had heard him acting as a deacon.]

The old man humorously and graciously replied: “I have only just arrived, at the moment when you were celebrating Mass for the catechumens.”

## CHAPTER XVI  
### That vices cannot otherwise be cured unless their roots and causes are known

For this reason I judged it necessary to insert these matters into this little work—

[Note: [Col. 0417C] “Assaults,” that is, temptations. The author uses similar reasoning in Book VII, chapter 13: “Let no one regard these things as superfluous or burdensome. Unless the kinds of wounds have first been set out, and the origins and causes of diseases have been investigated, neither can appropriate medical treatment be applied to the sick, nor perfect protection of health be provided to the strong. For elders who have experienced innumerable cases and disasters of various kinds customarily bring these and many other matters before the younger in their conferences.” He repeats the same point in Book XII, chapter 4.]

—so that, instructed not only by reasoning but also by examples concerning the force and order of the assaults by which the wretched soul is torn apart, we may be more cautious in avoiding the snares and manifold traps of the enemy.

[Col. 0417B] For the Egyptian Fathers bring these matters forward so indiscriminately that, by their accounts, they reveal and expose all the struggles of the vices—both those which the younger men are suffering and those which they will suffer—as though they themselves were still enduring them. Thus, when they explain the illusions of every passion, all who are beginners and fervent in spirit may recognize the secrets of their own conflicts; and, contemplating them as in a mirror, may be taught both the causes of the vices by which they are assailed and their remedies.

[Note: [Col. 0417D] Dionysius reads: “so that the younger, fervent in spirit, may recognize the secrets,” and so forth.]

They may also be instructed, before the struggles of the future arrive, how they ought to guard against them, confront them, or engage them in battle. Just as the most experienced physicians not only cure present diseases but also, through their discerning skill, anticipate future ones and forestall them with prescriptions or health-giving potions, so these true physicians of souls—

[Note: [Col. 0417D] That is, diseases of the soul. The author frequently uses *valetudo* for illness or weakness, since the word may also be understood negatively, as Gellius testifies (*Attic Nights*, Book XII, chapter 9). Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 5: “The angel, intervening, troubled the pool” (John 5); “those who complained of illness,” that is, those who were held by some infirmity.]

—by spiritually anticipating the illnesses of the heart that are about to emerge, as though with a certain heavenly antidote, do not allow them to grow in the minds of the younger. They disclose to them both the causes of the passions that threaten and the remedies of health.

## CHAPTER XVII  
### That a monk ought to avoid women and bishops

Therefore this has been the enduring opinion of the Fathers from ancient times down to the present, an opinion which I cannot state without confusion, since I was unable to avoid either my own sister or the hands of a bishop: that a monk ought by all means to flee women and bishops.

[Note: [Col. 0417D] I think no one will read these words without some astonishment or hesitation. First, what connection do they have with the present treatise? Even though it is certainly true that monks, if they love chastity, ought to flee the company of women, to such an extent that Saint Jerome does not permit a monk to live even with his mother (*Epistles* 4 and 47), what does this have to do with cenodoxia, or vainglory? Further, what comparison or affinity is there between women and bishops, so that a monk should avoid both in the same way? (See Conference 19, chapter 16, with the notes.)

It seems to me that this statement was uttered by those holy Fathers on occasion and hyperbolically. For bishops, when they sometimes lacked clergy, would summon monks from their cloisters and cells and appoint some of them bishops or other governors of churches, as was shown above. Many monks, stimulated by ambition or cenodoxia, eagerly abandoned their cells, frequented cities, sought popular favor, and tried to insinuate themselves into the bishops’ favor, goodwill, and companionship, so that they might be promoted more quickly to the clerical state and ecclesiastical ranks.

The elders and holier monks detested this depravity and expressed that judgment with considerable exaggeration and hyperbole. They turned it into a proverb: if monks truly wished to be monks, they ought to avoid the company of bishops just as they avoided that of women. Both could draw monks away from their cells and from the pursuit of contemplation; from both came the same danger and the same opportunity for wandering—through women toward lust, through bishops toward ambition and cenodoxia. The present author also hints at this not obscurely when he adds: “For neither permits him,” and so forth.

Saint Jerome seems to have noted the same matter in his letter to Paulinus (*Epistle* 13), where, addressing every monk under a single appellation, he says: “If you wish to be what you are called—a monk, that is, one who is alone—what are you doing in the cities, which are certainly not the dwellings of the solitary but of the many?” And elsewhere (*Epistle* 1 to Heliodorus): “Interpret the word ‘monk,’ that is, your name. What are you doing in a crowd, when you are alone?”—that is, when by your proper name and designation you profess solitude.]

For neither permits the man whom he has once bound to his intimacy to devote himself any longer to the quiet of his cell or to cling, with the purest eyes, to divine contemplation through the vision of holy things.

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### Remedies against the evil of cenodoxia

Therefore let the athlete of Christ, who desires to fight the true and spiritual contest lawfully, hasten by every means to overcome this many-shaped and varied beast.

[Col. 0419A] We shall be able to escape this evil, which confronts us on every side like a manifold wickedness, by the following remedy: by remembering David’s saying, “The Lord has scattered the bones of those who please men” (Psalm 25).

First, let us never permit ourselves to undertake anything for the purpose of achieving vanity or vainglory. Then let us strive with equal vigilance to preserve the things we have begun well—

[Note: [Col. 0419A] Saint Gregory likewise admonishes us (*Homily* 12 on the Gospels) to fear, with great caution, even the good deeds we perform, lest through what is rightly done by us we seek human favor or approval; lest the desire for praise creep in, and what is displayed outwardly be deprived of its reward inwardly. Saint Benedict also gives a similarly devout warning in chapter 49 of the Rule: whatever each person wishes to add beyond the customary measure of his service and offer to God during Lent, he should disclose to his abbot and do it with the abbot’s prayer and consent. For, he says, what is done without the permission of the spiritual father will be attributed to presumption and vainglory, not to reward.]

—lest the disease of cenodoxia, once it has crept in, empty out all the fruits of our labors.

[Note: [Col. 0419B] The same point appears in Book I, chapter 3: “Whatever is presumed by one or a few among the servants of God, and is not observed in a Catholic manner throughout the entire body of the brotherhood, is either superfluous or arrogant, and therefore must be judged harmful, displaying more the appearance of vanity than of virtue. Consequently, since we see no examples of these practices handed down either by the ancient saints who laid the foundations of this profession or by the Fathers of our own time who, through succession, preserve their institutions down to the present, it is fitting that we too cut away such things as superfluous and useless.”

Likewise in Book V, chapter 23: “For whatever is presumed beyond custom and common practice, the most ancient tradition of the Fathers marks as polluted by the disease of vainglory and display.” In these and similar statements the vice of singularity is condemned, especially among religious. Saint Bernard also counts it among the degrees of pride, whereas Saint Benedict, conversely, places its opposite among the degrees of humility (chapter 7 of the Rule): “Let the monk do nothing except what the common Rule of the monastery or the examples of his elders encourage.”]

Whatever in the conduct of the brothers is not accepted or practiced as common usage, let us avoid with every effort as devoted to boasting; and let us shun those things which can make us conspicuous among the others—

[Note: [Col. 0420B] Dionysius reads: “and from which human praise is acquired, as though we alone possessed such things.” Supply: “as though we alone possessed them.”]

—as though praise among men belonged to those who alone performed them.

For by these signs above all it will be shown that the deadly contagion of cenodoxia has clung to us. We shall be able most easily to escape it if we consider not only that we shall utterly lose the fruit of whatever labors we undertake with the purpose of cenodoxia—

[Note: [Col. 0420B] How cenodoxia makes people guilty of a great crime, that is, mortal sin, was explained above (chapter 12).]

—but also that, having become guilty of a great crime, we shall pay eternal penalties like sacrilegious persons. For we shall be convicted by him who knows hidden things of having preferred human beings to God and the glory of the world to the glory of the Lord: in insult to God, we chose to perform for the sake of men the work which we ought to have done for God’s sake.

# BOOK TWELVE  
## ON THE SPIRIT OF PRIDE

[Col. 0419]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0419B] [Note: [Col. 0419C] At last we have reached the final contest, in which the spiritual combatant must fight against the spirit of pride. The author counted pride among the capital vices and placed it in eighth position, as though in the final battle line, as the first and most capital—or, as he calls it, principal—enemy. He appears to have imitated the order of military discipline, in which the strength of the army and the commander himself, as its chief, usually stand in the rear line.

Saint Gregory, however (*Moralia*, Book XXXI, chapter 31), placed pride outside the class and number of the capital vices, as has often been said, setting it, as the mother and queen of all vices, in a higher and more eminent position. Saint Thomas reconciles and explains the two opinions, which are based on different methods and considerations, in this way (*Summa theologiae* II–II, question 161, article 8):

“Pride,” he says, “may be considered in two ways: in one way in itself, insofar as it is a particular sin; in another way, insofar as it has a certain influence over all sins. The capital vices, however, are posited as particular sins from which many kinds of sins arise. Therefore some, considering pride insofar as it is a particular sin, numbered it among the other capital vices. Gregory, however, considering its universal influence, which it exercises over all vices, did not number it among the other capital vices; rather, he placed it as the queen and mother of all vices.”

Hence he says in Book XXXI of the *Moralia*, chapter 31: “Pride itself, the queen of vices, when it has completely seized the conquered heart, immediately hands it over to the seven principal vices, as to certain commanders of its own, to be devastated by them; and from these the multitudes of vices arise.”

Thus far Saint Thomas, citing the words of Saint Gregory.

Pride is said to derive from the verb *supereo*, for *superbire* means the same as going above oneself or above others, or going beyond one’s measure and condition, in accordance with Psalm 130: “I have not walked in great matters, nor in things too wonderful for me.” Hence Isidore writes (*Book on the Highest Good*, chapter 38): “He is called proud because he wishes to appear above what he is; for whoever wishes to overstep what he is is proud.” Anselm writes in *On Similitudes*: “Pride is so called because one walks above what one ought.”

Hence theologians define pride as a perverse or disordered desire for one’s own excellence or eminence. Thus Augustine writes (*City of God*, Book IV, chapter 3; *Sermon on the Words of the Lord*, sermon 53): “The love of excellence is called pride.” But the scholastics speak more fully. For not every love of excellence is to be condemned under the name of pride, but only a disordered love or desire—that is, one contrary to the order and rule of reason.

Such love can be ordered and upright in only two ways. First, when we are concerned for our own excellence and praise for the honor of God and the benefit of our neighbor. Regarding the first, the Apostle says: “Let him who glories, glory in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1). Elsewhere, speaking of divine revelations (2 Corinthians 12), he says: “For such a one I will glory; but for myself, nothing except in my infirmities.”

Again, when recalling his own praises for the benefit of others, he says: “I have become foolish”—namely, by recounting these things which I have suffered—“you compelled me. I ought to have been commended by you; for I was inferior in nothing to those who are exceedingly great apostles, although I am nothing.” Therefore, to pursue a good reputation and one’s own praise for these reasons is not the vice of pride.

Nor, again, is it counted as pride when someone desires his own excellence in what is good: for example, to burn with love of virtue and learning, and to desire to excel in both, provided that he seeks the means more than the end—that is, the virtues themselves and praiseworthy learning more than glory and praise. For this love of praise is not yet disordered, since the Apostle urges it in these words: “Finally, brethren, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are chaste, whatever things are holy, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report—if there is any virtue, if there is any praise, think on these things” (Philippians 4).

And again: “Do what is good, and you will have praise from it” (Romans 13)—that is, from human authority. For he is not speaking only of the praise that is to come, concerning which he says elsewhere: “Then each one will receive praise from God” (1 Corinthians 4).]

Outside these cases, love of one’s own excellence will be disordered and will therefore bear the name of pride. We shall now explain in how many ways this occurs. They are carefully enumerated by St. Gregory (Moralia, Book XXIII, chapter 7), whom all the later scholastics followed. “There are four kinds,” he says, “by which every swelling of the arrogant is displayed: when they think that they possess some good from themselves; or, if they believe it was given to them from above, they suppose that they received it on account of their own merits; or, at any rate, when they boast that they possess what they do not possess; or when, despising the rest, they desire to appear uniquely to possess what they do possess.” Thus Gregory.

The first kind of pride, therefore, is to attribute some good, whether of soul or of body, to oneself alone, and not to acknowledge that it has been received from God. Against this the Apostle says: “What do you have that you have not received? But if you have received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4). This was the pride of the devil, by which he wished to ascend into heaven and be like the Most High. Such also was the pride of those men who wished to be worshiped as gods, such as Alexander of Macedon, Nebuchadnezzar in Babylonia, Herod in Judaea, and many others.

The second kind of pride is to admit, indeed, that the good things we have received are from God, and yet to think that they were given in such a way that we acquired them through our own merits, efforts, and labors. Against this pride the Apostle cries out: “Not from yourselves, not from works, lest anyone should boast” (Eph. 2). And the Old Testament says: “Take care lest you forget the Lord your God; and after you have eaten and been filled, your heart be lifted up, and you say in your heart: ‘My strength and the might of my hand have provided all these things for me’” (Deut. 8). Such was Uzziah, or Azariah, the king, who, when he had been strengthened, became proud in heart and neglected the Lord his God (4 Kings 15, and 2 Chron. 26), and so forth.

From this pride the Pelagian heresy also arose, as did that of the Donatists. Against them Augustine often employs the saying of Jeremiah: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm” (Jer. 17).

The third kind of pride is to attribute to oneself a good that one does not possess, or to attribute to oneself less than one possesses. Such was the Laodicean bishop against whom the Lord speaks in the Apocalypse: “You say, ‘I am rich and have grown wealthy and lack nothing’; and you do not know that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked” (Rev. 3).

The fourth kind of pride occurs when, despising the others, we wish to appear uniquely to possess the good that we possess, and on that account place ourselves above others. It is in this respect that the Pharisee is reproved who, as Gregory says, descended from the Temple without justification because, attributing the merit of good works to himself as though he alone possessed it, he preferred himself to the praying publican (Luke 18). See more in St. Thomas. The degrees of pride will be discussed below (chapter 25).

The eighth, and final, struggle against the spirit of pride is ours.

[Note: The reason Cassian placed the disease of pride last in the conflict of the vices was stated above, and he himself suggests it in the words that follow shortly afterward: it is a most savage beast, more monstrous than all the preceding ones, attacking the perfect above all and so forth. Pride is therefore called the last disease because it is overcome last, after all the other vices, and is conquered with the greatest difficulty even by the perfect, whom it attacks most fiercely. St. Prosper elegantly expressed this both in prose and in verse (*Book of Epigrams*) as follows:

> By the vice by which man was first overcome,  
> He wins his final battle.  
>   
> For when he has conquered every sin,  
> The danger remains lest the mind, conscious of doing well,  
> Should glory in itself rather than in the Lord.  
>   
> By that same fraud of the Evil One  
> Through which man was first driven into death,  
> The final battles are waged against him.  
>   
> When at last he has taken lofty palms  
> And bright crowns,  
> And has brought the enemy beneath his feet,  
> He wishes to assign the triumph  
> To his own virtue,  
> Not to the Lord, whose gift and work it was.  
>   
> In this one thing the victor always conquers—  
> He who is not conquered;  
> When He deigns to lend His hand, no one falls.

Isidore, *On the Supreme Good*, Book II, chapter 38: “Pride,” he says, “just as it is the origin of all sins, is likewise the ruin of all virtues; for it is first in sin and last in conflict. It is first either at the beginning, when it lays the mind low through sin, or finally, when it casts it down from the virtues. Hence it is also the greatest of all sins, because through virtues as well as through vices it destroys the human mind.”]

Although pride is last in the conflict of the vices and is placed at the end of their order,

[Note: For, as Ecclesiasticus says (chapter 10): “The beginning of every sin is pride.” And Tobit, chapter 4: “In it every destruction began.” Pride is called the beginning of every sin for two reasons: first, because among both angels and human beings the first sin of all was pride, as will be shown below; second, because from pride, as from a fountain and source, every kind of sin flows and springs forth.

This happens in two ways, as St. Thomas explains. First, directly, or in itself, insofar as other sins are ordered toward the end of pride, which is one’s own excellence; whatever is desired in a disordered way can, and generally does, refer back to this. Second, indirectly and, as it were, accidentally: pride removes the obstacle when a person casts aside the divine law, by which he was restrained from sin. Once the barrier and restraint have been removed, he rushes headlong into every sin, according to Jeremiah 2: “You have broken your yoke; you have burst your bonds; you said, ‘I will not serve.’”

In this sense every sin is said to contain a tacit pride, an interpreted contempt of God, although not all sins are committed from formal and explicit contempt; some are committed from ignorance and others from weakness (St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* I–II, question 24, article 2; and II–II, question 162, article 2; Leo Lessius, Book IV, chapter 4).

In this sense also St. Prosper’s statement is to be understood: “Pride is the beginning, the end, and the cause of all sins,” because pride is not merely itself a sin; rather, no sin could, can, or will exist without pride (*On the Contemplative Life*, Book V, chapter 2).

Nor is this contradicted by the statement in 1 Timothy 6 that desire is the root of all evils. Avarice is called the root of all evils because every kind of sin can be committed through this desire, and in fact many sins are committed in this way, since riches provide the opportunity and capacity to fulfill every sinful desire, just as a root provides nourishment to a tree, says St. Thomas (I–II, question 84, articles 1 and 2).

“For one must consider,” he says, “that in voluntary acts, such as sins, there is a twofold order: that of intention and that of execution. In the former order, that is called first which has the character of an end, or of a final cause. The end in acquiring all temporal goods is that a person may possess through them a certain singular perfection and excellence. Therefore, in this respect, pride, which is the desire for excellence, is called the beginning of every sin. But in the order of execution, that is called first which provides the opportunity to fulfill every sinful desire and has the character of a root—namely, riches. In this respect, therefore, avarice is said to be the root of all evils.” Thus St. Thomas (*Book II of the Sentences*, distinction 41).

Peter Lombard, however, resolves this matter somewhat differently, explaining in what sense both pride and desire are called the root of all evils. “Both statements,” he says, “are rightly understood if the two expressions are understood to include the kinds of individual sins, not the individual instances of those kinds. For there is no kind of sin that does not sometimes arise from pride, nor any that does not at some time descend from desire.

“There are some people who become proud through desire. As Augustine says, there is a person who would not be a lover of money unless he thought that through it he would become more excellent; and therefore, in order to excel, he desires greater wealth. In such a person desire arises from pride. There is also someone who would not love excellence unless he thought that through it he would possess greater wealth; therefore he strives to excel because he loves possessing riches. In him pride—that is, the love of excellence—arises from desire.

“It is therefore clear that desire sometimes arises from pride, and pride sometimes from desire; and consequently it is rightly said of both that each is the root of every evil.” Thus far he (*On the Literal Interpretation of Genesis*, Book II, chapter 13).

In another way St. Prosper reconciles the two statements, that of Ecclesiasticus (Ecclesiasticus 10) and that of the Apostle (1 Timothy 6), comparing pride and desire with one another as follows:

“Since the Holy Spirit, who spoke through the prophet, also spoke through the Apostle, and cannot be inconsistent with himself, we must carefully consider why the one wished to call pride the beginning of sin, while the other wished to call desire the root of all evils. Or perhaps the Apostle Paul interpreted the prophetic statement, as he often does? For whether he speaks of the beginning of every sin or of the root of all evils, he signifies one and the same thing.

“Moreover, desire and pride are so completely one evil that neither can the proud person be found without desire nor the desirous person without pride. The devil himself, in whom pride holds dominion, desired both his own power and the destruction of humanity; and the human being, through his desire for the forbidden tree and his longing for likeness to God, displayed the diseased impulse of desire.

“From pride arise heresies, schisms, detraction, envy, loquacity, boasting, disputes, hostility, ambition, arrogance, presumption, vanity, restlessness, lying, perjury, and other things of this kind. But who would doubt that these also proceed from desire, when all who have been corrupted by all those diseases I have named are considered desirous?

“Again, since desire makes people gluttonous, intemperate, drunkards, greedy, rapacious, fornicators, adulterers, defilers, incestuous, and criminal, how can such people become so without pride, when the commandments of God cannot be despised without pride—those commandments that prohibit all the evils I have listed above?

“Therefore, if we wish to complete the course of our struggle, let us first beware of desire and pride—not two evils, but one, from which all evil acts take their beginning. For without pride, which is called the beginning of every sin, what sins could even be begun? Or without desire, which is the root of all evils, what evils could be committed, since without a root all things are either reckoned as nothing or are dead?

“Furthermore, if I cannot commit any sin unless I consent to an evil pleasure, which is characteristic of desire, and despise the commandments of God, which is the evil of pride, how does every sin not proceed from desire, which is the root of all evils, and from pride, which is called the beginning of every sin?”

Thus far St. Prosper (*On the Contemplative Life*, Book II, chapter 4), taking pride and desire in a broad sense, insofar as in every sin there is a certain contempt of God’s commandments, as has been said, and a certain disordered movement of desire; in this way every sin proceeds both from pride and from desire. See the notes on chapter 6 of Book VII.]

Nevertheless, in origin and in time it is first: a most savage beast, more monstrous than all the preceding ones, attacking the perfect above all and, with an especially cruel bite, devouring those who have already been placed almost at the summit of perfection.

## CHAPTER II. That there are two kinds of pride

[Note: Another division of pride is into spiritual and carnal pride. He calls that pride spiritual which assails spiritual persons and the perfect; carnal pride is that which assails the carnal—that is, the imperfect. St. Gregory also recognizes and explains the same distinction in these words (*Moralia*, Book XXXIV, chapter 19):

> It must be understood that this very exaltation of which we are speaking possesses some people through secular things and others through spiritual things. One swells with gold, another with eloquence; one with the lowest and earthly things, another with the highest and heavenly virtues. Yet the same thing is enacted before the eyes of God, although, when it enters human hearts, it is concealed from their sight beneath different coverings.

Thus Gregory; and the abbot Smaragdus says similar things in chapter 4 of the Rule of St. Benedict.]

There are two kinds of it: one, the kind we have mentioned, by which spiritual and lofty men are assailed; the other, which also embraces beginners and carnal persons. Although both kinds of pride puff one up with a harmful self-exaltation toward God as well as toward human beings, the first is especially directed toward God, while the second properly concerns human beings. With God’s favor, we shall pursue its origin and remedies as far as we can in the later chapters of this little work (chapter 24). For now, our purpose is to say a little about the former kind, by which, as we have stated, the perfect are especially tempted.

## CHAPTER III. That pride takes away all virtues

There is no other vice, then, that so drains away all the virtues and strips and deprives a person of all justice and holiness as does the evil of pride:

[Note: These words provide an occasion for investigating what kind of sin pride is. From this passage of Cassian—and indeed from the entire treatment in this book—it can be gathered clearly enough that pride is by its nature, or according to its kind, a mortal sin, as St. Thomas also confirms (article 5, cited above).

He teaches, however, that this must be understood of complete pride, by which a person is so exalted that he despises God, or refuses to be subject to the divine law, or, because of this contempt, transgresses God’s law or the commands of superiors (Leonard Lessius, Book IV, chapter 4).

For if we speak of incomplete or imperfect pride, this is not always a mortal sin. “Just as,” he says, “in other matters that are sins by their kind—such as fornication and adultery—there are certain movements that are venial sins because of their imperfection, since they precede the judgment of reason and occur without its consent, so it also happens with pride that certain movements of pride are venial sins when reason does not consent to them.

“Moreover, complete pride is judged not only a mortal and death-dealing sin, but also, according to the common opinion of theologians, the greatest and most serious of sins” (Navarre, chapter 23, no. 8). This must not be understood as though it were the gravest among every species of sin, since hatred of God is more serious; rather, it belongs to the class of the gravest sins, for the reason given by the same Angelic Doctor (article 6).

Since two things are considered in sin—conversion toward a changeable good, which is material in sin, and aversion from the unchangeable good, which is the formal and completing aspect of sin—pride is not, on the side of conversion, the greatest of sins, because the eminence that the proud person disorderedly desires does not have the greatest opposition to the good of virtue. But on the side of aversion, pride has the greatest gravity, because in other sins a person turns away from God either through ignorance, weakness, or desire for some other good; whereas pride turns away from God precisely because it refuses to be subject to God and to his rule.

Hence Boethius says that although all vices flee from God, pride alone opposes God. For this reason it is also said expressly in James 4: “God resists the proud.” Thus far St. Thomas.]

In this sense, therefore, pride is said to drain away all the virtues, strip away all justice and holiness, corrupt them with deadly destruction, and cast them down and slaughter them through a most grievous ruin, and so forth, as stated here.

As a kind of general and pestilential disease, it is not content merely to weaken one member or part of the body; rather, it corrupts the entire solid body with deadly destruction and attempts to cast down and slaughter those already established at the summit of the virtues through a most grievous ruin.

[Note: In the same sense, and almost in the same words, St. Gregory says in the thirty-fourth book of the *Moralia*, chapter 18:

> Other vices attack only those virtues by which they themselves are destroyed: anger attacks patience, gluttony attacks abstinence, and lust attacks chastity. But pride, which we have called the root of vices, is not content with the extinction of one virtue; it rises against every member of the soul and, like a general and pestilential disease, corrupts the entire body, so that whatever is done when it has invaded—even if it appears to be virtue—is done not for God but solely for empty glory. For when pride breaks into the mind, it seizes the city as a kind of tyrant captures a besieged city; and the richer the person it has captured, the harsher it becomes in its rule. For the more extensively a work of virtue is performed without humility, the more widely pride dominates.

Thus St. Gregory, an imitator and approver of Cassian.]

Every other vice is contained within its own limits and end. Although it also grieves other virtues, it nevertheless principally aims against one and specifically oppresses and attacks it. To make what we have said clearer: gluttony—that is, the appetite of the belly, or the desire for food—corrupts the rigor of temperance; lust contaminates chastity; anger ravages patience. Thus a person devoted to one vice may not be entirely deprived of the other virtues, but, with only that virtue truncated which succumbs to the opposing vice that attacks it, may retain the rest, at least in part.

But when pride has possessed the unhappy mind, like some most savage tyrant, it captures the highest citadel of the virtues and utterly destroys and overturns the entire city. It levels and mingles with the ground the once-lofty walls of holiness and thereafter permits no image of freedom to remain in the soul subjected to it. The richer the soul it captures, the more completely it strips it, through a most cruel plunder, of all the resources of the virtues and subjects it to the heavier yoke of slavery.

## CHAPTER IV. That on account of pride Lucifer was made a devil from an archangel
And so that we may recognize the power of his most grievous tyranny, let us consider that angel who, because of the excess of his splendor and beauty,

> **[Note: [Col. 0425D]]** *Lucifer*, in Greek φωσφόρος (*phōsphoros*, “light-bearer”), is understood in Scripture in three ways. First, *lucifer* is the morning star, which astrologers call Venus when it precedes the sun; when it follows, it is called *Hesperus*. Job 38: “Do you bring forth the morning star at its appointed time?” And Psalm 109: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you,” that is, before the origin of the world, or before every creature.
>
> Second, Lucifer is also called Christ the Lord, or his teaching and knowledge. 2 Peter 1: “Until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts.” Hence in Revelation 22 he is called “the bright morning star”; and in the blessing of the Paschal candle the Church sings: “May the morning star find these flames; that morning star, I say, which knows no setting,” and so forth.
>
> Finally, Lucifer was the name given to the first angel, on account of the singular splendor both of the nature and of the grace in which he had been created, and of his excellence above the other angels. Nevertheless, because of his pride, he was cast into everlasting darkness and dragged many other heavenly spirits into the same ruin, depriving them of the heavenly homeland. Thus Isaiah 14 says: “How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose in the morning,” and, “Your pride has been thrust down to the underworld.” (See St. Bernard, *Treatise on the Degrees of Humility*, in many chapters; St. Thomas, *Summa*, I–II, q. 63, a. 7.)
>
> St. Gregory expressly teaches that this Lucifer was the first of all the angels—that is, of the heavenly spirits—and the most excellent, the most eminent of the highest order or hierarchy, in *Moralia* XXXII, chapters 24 and 25; he gathers and confirms this from many passages of Scripture.
>
> First, in Job 40 he is called *Behemoth*—by which name the fallen first angel is represented—“the beginning of the ways of God.” For, says Gregory, “when God was creating all things, he made this one first, whom he made more eminent than all the angels.”
>
> Then Ezekiel 31 says: “No tree in paradise was like him, nor was any equal to his beauty, because he made him beautiful with many thickly clustered branches.” By the trees of paradise are signified the hosts of angelic spirits, who, although created sublime, were nevertheless neither set above nor made equal to him.
>
> Again, Ezekiel 28 says of the same one: “You were the seal of the likeness of God, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty.” The fallen angel is called, Gregory says, “the seal of the likeness of God,” so that, the more subtle he is in nature, the more fully the likeness of God is believed to have been expressed in him.
>
> And again, in the same passage of Ezekiel: “Every precious stone was your covering: sardius, topaz, jasper, chrysolite, onyx, and beryl, sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald.” He names nine kinds of stones because there are nine orders of angels. This Lucifer is described as having been covered with them, because he possessed them as a garment for his adornment; and while he surpassed their brightness, he was brighter by comparison with them.
>
> Finally Gregory adds: “Still contemplating the height of his principality, the same prophet continues” (Ezekiel 28): “You were an extended cherub, protecting, on God’s holy mountain; you walked perfect among the stones of fire.” For *cherub* is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge”; and therefore he is called a cherub, because there is no doubt that he surpassed all others in knowledge. He “walked perfect among the stones of fire,” because among the hearts of the angels, kindled by the fire of charity, he appeared glorious with the glory of the Creator. These and other things St. Gregory says to the same effect.]

was called Lucifer,

> **[Note: [Col. 0426D]]** St. Thomas teaches that Lucifer’s first sin was pride (I, q. 63, a. 2), following the judgment of the ancient Fathers, although Scotus opposed it. Indeed, there could have been no other sin in the angels than pride, from which envy subsequently followed. The Fathers explicitly affirm this.
>
> St. Jerome, Letter 45: “Satan,” he says, “fell from the height of archangelic dignity for no other reason than pride, which is contrary to humility.”
>
> St. Augustine, *City of God* XII, chapter 6: “When the cause of the misery of the evil angels is sought,” he says, “it reasonably presents itself that they turned away from him who supremely is and turned toward themselves, who are not supreme; and what is this vice called other than pride? For pride is the beginning of every sin.”
>
> Why only pride and envy can exist in angels is explained by St. Thomas: these alone are purely spiritual vices, and the vices that can occur in a spiritual and angelic nature must be of that kind. For although certain other vices are called spiritual, according to Blessed Gregory (*Moralia* XXXI, chapter 31), by comparison with carnal vices—namely gluttony and lust, which are fulfilled by carnal pleasure—they cannot absolutely and purely be called spiritual, because they either have bodily objects or presuppose and include bodily passion.
>
> The object of avarice is money. Anger, like desire, involves a certain passion; hence it cannot exist in demons except metaphorically. Sloth is a kind of sadness by which a human being is made slow to spiritual acts because of bodily labor, which does not apply to demons. It is therefore clear that only pride and envy are purely spiritual and can belong to demons—provided that envy is not understood as a passion but as a will resisting another’s good.
>
> So says St. Thomas. He adds two points relevant to understanding this, and they must not be omitted. First, when it is said that only pride and envy belong to demons, this is to be understood with respect to affection. With respect to guilt, he says, all sins can occur in demons, because when they induce human beings to every sin, they incur the guilt of every sin. But with respect to affection, only those sins can exist in evil angels toward which a spiritual nature can be disposed. A spiritual nature cannot be disposed toward goods proper to the body, but only toward those that can be found in spiritual things.
>
> The second point is that under envy and pride, insofar as they are attributed to demons, all the vices and sins that derive from them are included: hatred of God, blasphemy, hatred of human beings,

> **[Col. 0427D]** and so forth.
>
> Since it is therefore established that Lucifer’s first sin, and the first of all sins, was pride, the holy Fathers rightly call pride (*Gregory, Moralia* XXXV, chapter 22) a diabolical vice, the clearest sign of the reprobate, and the mark of the city of the devil, who is called “king over all the children of pride” (Job 41).
>
> Hence the Apostle, in 1 Timothy 3, forbids a recent convert to be appointed, “lest, being lifted up with pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil”—that is, into the same condemnation as the devil—clearly suggesting that pride is the devil’s vice, just as, conversely, humility is the proper virtue of Christ and of those who belong to him.
>
> Accordingly, St. Augustine, *City of God* XIV, chapter 13, teaches that the two cities, that of Christ and that of the devil—that is, the society of the righteous and the society of the wicked—and their two leaders, Christ and the devil, are distinguished above all by these marks, pride and humility. It is better to hear him establish this in his own words:
>
> “What is especially commended in the City of God, and to the City of God as it journeys in this world, is humility; and it is especially proclaimed in its king, who is Christ. Conversely, Scripture teaches that the vice opposed to this virtue, exaltation, especially dominates in his adversary, who is the devil. This is plainly the great distinction by which the two cities are separated: one is the society of devout human beings, the other of the impious; each together with the angels belonging to it, in one of which the love of God preceded, and in the other the love of self.”
>
> So Augustine. St. Gregory agrees in *Moralia* XXXIV, chapter 23, writing as follows:
>
> “Because our Redeemer rules the hearts of the humble, while this Leviathan—that is, the devil—is called king over the proud, we clearly recognize that pride is the most evident sign of the reprobate, whereas humility is the sign of the elect. When, therefore, the character of each person is recognized, under which king he serves is discovered. For each person carries, as it were, a title of his work by which he readily shows under whose ruling power he serves. Hence the Gospel says: ‘You will know them by their fruits’” (Matthew 7).]

and not by any other vice do we find him cast down from heaven, wounded by the dart of pride from that blessed and exalted station among the angels, and fallen into the regions below. If one act of self-exaltation could bring down from heaven to earth a being adorned with such virtue and such a prerogative of power, the magnitude of his fall shows with what vigilance we, surrounded by the weakness of the flesh, ought to guard ourselves. But we shall be able to learn how to avoid the most destructive poison of this disease if we follow out the causes and origin of his fall. For illness can never be cured, nor can remedies be applied to serious diseases, unless their origins and causes have first been investigated by careful inquiry.

And so, exalted as though he did not need divine assistance in order to persevere in this purity,

> **[Note: [Col. 0428B]]** There is a major question among theologians whether, and in what sense, Lucifer desired to be “as God” or “like the Most High.” From this it may be understood how great and of what kind Lucifer’s pride was, as well as that of the spirits who followed him. I would more willingly have passed over this question, since it is subtler and more extensive than the scope of our undertaking permits, had the Author’s statements here and elsewhere not required some explanation.
>
> There are three more notable opinions on this matter. St. Thomas reports two of them in these words:
>
> “Without any doubt the angel sinned by desiring to be as God. But this can be understood in two ways: either by equality—some say, by parity—or by likeness. In the first way, he could not desire to be as God, because by natural knowledge he knew this to be impossible. But in this he desired to be like God: he desired as the ultimate end of blessedness that to which he could attain by the power of his nature, turning his desire away from supernatural blessedness, which is the grace of God. Or, if he desired that likeness to God which is given through grace, he wished to possess it through the power of his nature, not through divine assistance according to God’s arrangement.”
>
> These words of St. Thomas, somewhat obscure, can be explained more clearly as follows. The angel desired to be like God in this respect: that by his own nature he should be blessed, resting in the excellence of his nature as his ultimate end and proper happiness, while neglecting or failing to consider the supernatural blessedness toward which he ought to strive through God’s grace.
>
> For as soon as God, the Creator of all things, had created this heavenly and most noble nature of the angels, Lucifer observed and magnificently contemplated the beauty, nobility, and extraordinary dignity of his own nature, by which he surpassed all created things. He then began to exalt himself and became captivated by such admiration and love of himself that he neither considered that he had received these gifts from God nor aspired to a further and perfected supernatural blessedness, as though content with his own lot and sufficient to himself.
>
> It is sufficiently clear from Cassian’s words that this was his opinion, when he says: “He judged himself to be like God, since he needed no one, just as God needs no one; relying on the power of free choice, he believed that through it everything could be supplied to him abundantly.” These words should not, however, be understood as though Lucifer really and explicitly felt and judged himself to be like or equal to God—for so great, crude, and obvious an error could not suddenly enter an angelic mind full of wisdom—but because he conducted himself, absorbed in admiration and contemplation of himself and withdrawn from remembrance of God, as though he really felt and judged this way. Hence the Apostle could justly address him with the words: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4).
>
> Hence Ezekiel 28 says: “Your heart was lifted up because of your beauty.” This signifies the beauty Lucifer possessed, not one that he desired.
>
> Nevertheless, other words of the same Lucifer in Isaiah 14 seem to signify something greater and higher: “I will ascend into heaven; I will exalt my throne above the stars of God,” and so forth.
>
> The second opinion, therefore, is the one St. Thomas touched on above: that this angel, namely Lucifer, desired and presumed upon supernatural blessedness, or the beatific vision of God, by the powers of nature alone, or through the power of his own nature. The Author’s words could be bent toward this interpretation: “Relying on the power of free choice, he believed that through it everything could be supplied to him abundantly which pertained to the perfection of virtues or the eternity of supreme blessedness.”
>
> Yet against this it could be objected, first, that it is scarcely, if at all, credible that so great an error could have entered an angelic mind—that it could have thought supernatural blessedness attainable by the powers of nature—since natural and supernatural things differ entirely in kind; indeed, the notion seems contradictory. For if supernatural blessedness is above nature, how could it be acquired by natural power?
>
> Second, it is sufficiently evident that a rational or intellectual creature is more likely to applaud and flatter itself over present and acquired things than over future things still to be acquired: the present are enjoyed, whereas the future cause anxiety. It therefore seems more probable that Lucifer first became proud of his present state before thinking about future blessedness.
>
> Third, this opinion might seem to favor Pelagianism, so that the first angel, rather than Pelagius, would be called the originator of this error, since he attributed grace and glory to the powers of nature. Yet the holy Fathers never made this charge, nor do they even mention it; and I do not know whether Pelagians themselves, or their Semi-Pelagian supporters—of whom we shall speak below—would have admitted it.
>
> The third opinion is that the demon truly desired equality with God, or an equal degree of dignity, together with equal worship and authority. For Ezekiel 28 says of Lucifer: “You said, ‘I am God’”; and in Matthew 4 Satan wished to be worshiped as God: “If you will fall down and worship me.”
>
> But this opinion is not approved by St. Thomas, as was seen above. Nevertheless, we can reconcile it with the others. St. Thomas and the others are speaking about the beginning of the devil’s sin, whereas this final opinion concerns its consummation.
>
> For in Lucifer’s sin we can consider three stages: its beginning, its development, and its consummation. The beginning could not have been that intolerable pride by which he wished to be equal to God. Rather, it was complacency and disordered delight in his own excellence, together with turning away from God, though still without contempt or hatred of God. Its development followed, when he came to believe that he was sufficient to himself and had no need of divine assistance. Finally, he reached the point of thinking that he ought to be subject to no one; and at last he came to despise God and to wish himself to be regarded and worshiped by all as God. It is of this final and consummate pride that the last opinion speaks.
>
> St. Augustine explains this development in *City of God* XIV, at the end, where he teaches that the love of self even to contempt of God built the city of the devil, just as, conversely, the love of God even to contempt of self built the City of God.]

## CHAPTER V. That the seeds of all vices spring from pride

> **[Note: [Col. 0430D]]** This means pride, as Dionysius has it; or, more precisely, as it seems to me, that thought or consideration of one’s own excellence of which he said above: “This thought alone became for him the first cause of his ruin.” For from that thought or consideration of his own excellence arose pride, which was Lucifer’s first ruin, or first sin, as has been said. From it pride then spread both to the other angels—represented by the third part of the stars in Revelation 12, which the red dragon dragged down with his tail into the abyss—and to the first-created human being, that is, the first man formed from the clay of the earth. Divine Scripture also declares pride to have been his first sin, making pride the beginning of every sin and destruction in Ecclesiasticus 10 and Tobit 4.
>
> Although these passages could be referred to the angel’s sin, which absolutely was the first of all sins, as has been said, it is more credible that Ecclesiasticus and Tobit were referring to the first sin of our first parents, which was more widely known than the sin of the angels (Bellarmine, *On the Loss of Grace* III, chapter 4; St. Thomas, I–II, q. 163, aa. 1–2).
>
> St. Augustine explains this very thing in elegant words and thoughts in *City of God* XIV, chapter 13, writing as follows:
>
> “In secret, however, they began to be evil, so that they might fall into open disobedience. For one would not arrive at an evil deed unless an evil will had preceded it. What, then, could be the beginning of an evil will except pride? For pride is the beginning of every sin. But what is pride except a desire for a perverse exaltation? Perverse exaltation is this: when the soul abandons the one to whom it ought to cling as its principle, it somehow makes itself its own principle and becomes one to itself. This happens when it is excessively pleased with itself, when it withdraws from that unchangeable good which ought to please it more than it pleases itself.
>
> “This withdrawal is voluntary. For if the will had remained steadfast in love of the superior and unchangeable good, from which it was illuminated so that it might see and inflamed so that it might love, it would not have turned away from that good toward self-pleasure, becoming thereby darkened and chilled, so that either she believed the serpent to have spoken the truth, or he preferred his wife’s will to God’s command, thinking himself only lightly blameworthy if he did not abandon his companion in life even in companionship in sin. For that evil deed—that transgression by which they ate the forbidden food—would not have been committed by those who were not already evil; nor would that bad fruit have been produced except by a bad tree.” So Augustine.
>
> Other Fathers agree. St. Prosper, *On the Contemplative Life* II, chapter 19:
>
> “It seems to me that they would not have eaten from the forbidden tree unless they had desired it; nor would they have desired it unless they had been tempted; nor would they have been tempted unless they had been abandoned; nor would they have been abandoned by God unless they had first abandoned God; nor would they have abandoned God unless they had become proud and miserably desired the likeness of God.”
>
> St. Fulgentius, *On the Incarnation and Grace* II, chapter 20: “Because the first man was cast into pride through the devil’s persuasion, he lost humility.”
>
> St. Gregory, *Moralia* IV, chapter 9: “He had made two creatures to understand him, namely the angelic and the human; but pride struck both and broke them from the condition of their innate uprightness.”]

This is the cause and origin of the first [variant: principal] ruin, the chief disease.

> **[Note: [Col. 0431D]]** The disease in question is pride. Through him—namely Lucifer, or the first angel, cast down from heaven because of pride—it again spread, and then, through the serpent, that is, by spreading itself, entered the first-created human being, Adam, and so forth.
>
> Dionysius reverses the meaning when he renders it: “Which, spreading through that first-created man who was cast down by it,” contrary to the Author’s intention and the testimony of all the copies. The Author intended to signify that Lucifer, whom he had discussed in the preceding chapter, was first overcome and cast down by the disease of pride; then, through him—that is, through his operation and instigation—Adam, the first-created human being, fell into the same disease, namely pride; and finally all vices sprang from it and spread throughout the entire human race.]

Through him who had been cast down by it, this disease spread again into the first-created human being and brought forth the weaknesses and seeds of every vice.

> **[Note: [Col. 0432A]]** Although it is established both by Scripture and by the teaching of the holy Fathers that Adam’s first sin was pride, as has already been said, it is not so straightforward or easy to explain what that pride was, and of what kind, or in what it consisted.
>
> Cassian seems to have thought the same about Adam as about Lucifer: namely, that Adam desired and presumed upon the glory of divinity—that is, the glory of eternal happiness—by which he would become like God, or at least obtain an extraordinary likeness to God through freedom of choice and his own effort, that is, through the powers of nature alone.
>
> And indeed God clearly showed that Adam had sought an extraordinary likeness to God through pride when he said of him: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil,” plainly reproving the excellence he had sought and claimed.
>
> St. Thomas establishes this divine excellence and likeness sought by Adam in two things (II–II, q. 163, a. 2). First and principally, in knowledge of good and evil; secondarily, in the ability, freedom, and power to act.
>
> “The first man,” he says, “sinned principally by desiring likeness to God with respect to knowledge of good and evil, as the serpent suggested to him—namely, that through the power of his own nature he should determine for himself what was good and what was evil to do, or even that he should foresee by himself what good or evil would befall him. Secondarily, he sinned by desiring likeness to God with respect to his own power of action: namely, that through the power of his own nature he should act so as to attain blessedness.”
>
> St. Augustine, an advocate of the same teaching, writes in *On Genesis against the Manichaeans* II, chapter 5:
>
> “We see,” he says, “that sin was persuaded through pride. For this is the force of the statement, ‘You shall be like gods.’ What else is understood here than that they were persuaded not to wish to be under God, but rather to be in their own power without the Lord; not to observe his law, as though they envied themselves the ability to rule themselves; not to need his inward light, but to use their own providence, as though by their own eyes to discern good and evil, which he had forbidden? Thus they were persuaded to love their own power excessively,” and so forth.
>
> And in Tractate 4 on the First Letter of John: “Adam, placed in paradise, despised God’s command and raised his neck, as though desiring to be in his own power and refusing to be subject to God’s power.”]

For when he believed that by the freedom and ingenuity of his own will he could acquire the glory of divinity, he also lost the glory that he had obtained through the grace of the Creator.

## CHAPTER VI. That pride is last in the order of the struggle, but first in time and origin

[Col. 0432A]

Thus it is most clearly established by the examples and testimonies of Scripture that the stain of pride, although later in the order of the conflicts, is earlier in origin, and is the beginning of all sins and crimes.

> **[Note: [Col. 0432D]]** Thus he also said above, in chapter 1: “Although this disease is last in the struggle with the vices and is placed at the end of the order, it is nevertheless first in origin and time,” and so forth. There are further notes there from St. Prosper and Isidore.

> **[Note: [Col. 0432D]]** He repeats what he said above in different words (chapter 3): that every vice is confined within its own bounds and destroys one virtue opposed to it, whereas pride corrupts all virtues. St. Thomas explains why pride, though a particular sin, is nevertheless said to corrupt all virtues:
>
> “A sin can corrupt a virtue in two ways. First, through direct opposition to the virtue; in this way pride does not corrupt every virtue, but only humility, just as any other particular sin corrupts a particular virtue opposed to it by acting contrarily. Second, a sin corrupts a virtue by abusing that very virtue; and in this way pride corrupts every virtue, insofar as it takes from the virtues themselves an occasion for pride, as it does also from any other things pertaining to excellence.” So St. Thomas (II–II, q. 162, a. 2, ad 3).
>
> The saying of St. Augustine in the *Rule* (chapter 4) has the same bearing: “Every other iniquity is practiced in evil works in order that they may be done; but pride even lies in wait for good works, that they may perish.” See there Umbert’s notable commentary, with its excellent comparison of pride with the other vices. Elsewhere Augustine says again: “The other vices are to be feared in sins; but pride even in right actions, lest things laudably done be lost through the desire for praise itself.”
>
> St. Gregory has similar remarks in Homily 12 on the Gospels, which may also be referred to *cenodoxia*, or vain glory, the first daughter and attendant of pride; to it this too may be applied:
>
> *And the daughter lightly follows her mother’s path.*

Nor, like the other vices, does it merely destroy the virtue opposed to it—namely, humility alone; rather, it is the destroyer of all virtues at once. Nor does it attack only ordinary and insignificant people; it attacks especially those who stand at the summit of strength.

According to Habakkuk, “his foods are choice.” He desires to overthrow Job, and after devouring Judas, he sought authority to sift the apostles.]

Therefore blessed David, although he guarded the secrets of his heart with such vigilance that he could confidently proclaim to the one who knew the secrets of his conscience:

> **[Note: [Col. 0433C]]** Trithemius noted that in these two verses of Psalm 130, also cited by St. Benedict in chapter 7 of the Rule in praise of humility, four kinds of exaltation are designated, which the Apostle John calls by one name, “the pride of life.”

## CHAPTER VII. That pride is such a great evil that it deserves to have God himself as its adversary
How great is the evil of pride, that it should deserve to have as its adversary not an angel, nor other virtues opposed to it, but God himself? [Note: This refers to the statement just cited, “God resists the proud,” attested and confirmed by two apostles, Peter and James (1 Peter 5 and James 4), so that this word, greatly celebrated and universally known among the holy Fathers, may rightly stand on the testimony of two such witnesses. Hence Saint Basil, in the Shorter Rules, responding to the question “How can a proud person be healed?” (Question 35), answers: “If he believes the statement of the one who said, ‘The Lord resists the proud.’” Saint Ambrose, on Psalm 118: “Scripture says, ‘The Lord resists the proud.’ As though he had undertaken the defense of his own dishonor, he has accepted a special contest against pride—as if he were saying, ‘This is my adversary, who provokes me; this confrontation belongs to me.’” Jerome, to Antonius (Letter 45): “See, brother, what sort of evil it is that has God as its adversary.” Hence the arrogant Pharisee is rejected, while the humble publican is heard (Luke 18). Augustine, in Book 3 of *On Christian Doctrine* (chapter 23): “There is scarcely a page of the holy books in which it does not resound that God resists the proud.” Finally, to omit others, Isidore of Pelusium, in one of his letters (Book 1, Letter 164): “God resists the proud, since from the beginning he also opposed their leader.” Consider, therefore, how great a thing it is to have God as an enemy and adversary, and the ancient enemy as an ally. These are the words of the holy Fathers.

Saint Thomas, moreover, noted that this statement was taken from the ancient Scripture, namely either Proverbs 3:34, where the Septuagint translators expressly have: “The Lord opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (*Κύριος ὑπερηφάνοις ἀντιτάσσεται, ταπεινοῖς δὲ δίδωσι χάριν*). Saint James has the same words in Greek; the Vulgate renders them: “He will mock the mockers, but will give grace to the meek”; or else from Proverbs 29:23, where it is said: “The proud person is followed by humiliation, and glory will receive the humble in spirit.” Certainly the apostle James plainly testifies that he received this from another author when he says, “For this reason it says”—that is, Scripture, or, as Saint Thomas says, the Holy Spirit speaking in it—“God resists the proud,” and so forth. The Fathers cited above say, “The Lord resists the proud,” following the ancient Greek version.]

It should indeed be noted that he did not at all say of those who are entangled in the other vices that they have God resisting them—that is, that God opposes the gluttonous, the fornicators, the angry, or the avaricious—but only the proud (James 4). For those vices are either directed back merely upon each individual who sins, or appear to be committed against their fellow participants—that is, against other human beings. Pride, however, reaches God in a special way, and for that reason rightly deserves to have him specifically as its opponent.

## CHAPTER VIII. How God extinguished the devil’s pride through the power of humility

Therefore God, the Creator and physician of the universe, knowing that pride is the cause and beginning of diseases, undertook to heal opposites by means of opposites, [Note: A proverbial saying: “Contraries are cured by contraries,” or, according to Hippocrates, “The remedies for contraries are contrary remedies.” Saint Jerome mentions this in his Letter to Algasius (Letter 121). Saint Gregory states it more explicitly: “Just as in the art of medicine hot things are cured by cold and cold things by hot, so our Lord opposed contrary medicines to sins: continence to the lustful, generosity to the grasping, gentleness to the angry, and humility to the proud,” as he says in Homily 32 on the Gospels.] so that what had fallen through pride might rise again through humility. He says, “I will ascend into heaven” (Isaiah 14); this one says, “My soul has been humbled to the earth” (Psalm 43). He says, “I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14); this one, though he was in the form of God, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death (Philippians 2). He says, “Above the stars of God I will exalt my throne” (Isaiah 14); this one says, “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matthew 11). He says, “I do not know the Lord, and I will not release Israel” (Exodus 5); this one says, “If I should say that I do not know him, I shall be a liar like you; but I do know him, and I keep his commandments” (John 8). He says:

“My rivers are mine, and I made them” (Ezekiel 29); [Note: Thus from the Greek: “The rivers are mine, and I made them” (*Ἐμοί εἰσιν οἱ ποταμοὶ, καὶ ἐγὼ ἐποίησα αὐτούς*). Saint Jerome likewise cites it in his commentary on Isaiah 50 and elsewhere several times. Yet in his Commentary on Ezekiel he once translates it, “The river is mine, and I made myself”; and later, “The river is mine, and I made it,” or, “My rivers are mine, and I made them.” These are the words of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who is there called the great dragon. Under his figure they are attributed to Lucifer, who, like Pharaoh, forgetting his Creator, wished to be like the Most High.]

this one says, “I can do nothing of myself, but my Father, remaining in me, himself does the works” (John 5, 14). He says:

“All the kingdoms of the world and their glory are mine, and I give them to whomever I wish” (Luke 4); [Note: The words of the Gospel text cited by Gregory are as follows: “I will give you power over all these kingdoms, and their glory, because they have been handed over to me, and I give them to whomever I wish.”]

this one, though he was rich, became poor, so that by his poverty we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8). He says:

“Just as eggs that have been abandoned are gathered, so I gathered the whole earth, and there was no one who moved a wing, opened his mouth, or chirped” (Isaiah 10); [Note: Saint Gregory omitted this passage, as well as the other that follows from Isaiah. These, however, are the words of the exceedingly proud Assyrian king Sennacherib, which are likewise figuratively referred to the devil, the prince of the proud.]

this one says, “I have become like a solitary pelican; I have kept watch and become like a solitary sparrow on the roof” (Psalm 101). He says:

“With the sole of my feet I dried up all the channels of the embankments” (Isaiah 37); this one says, “Do you suppose that I cannot ask my Father, and he would at once provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matthew 26).

[Note: Saint Gregory treats and illustrates this passage somewhat more fully and explicitly in Book 34 of the *Moralia*, chapter 22. After prefacing it with these words: “For this the only-begotten Son of God assumed the form of our weakness; for this the invisible one appeared not only visible but also despised; for this he endured the mockeries of insults, the reproaches of derision, and the torments of suffering, so that the humble God might teach human beings not to be proud. How great, then, is the power of humility, for the sake of teaching which alone he who is great beyond all estimation became small even unto suffering? Since pride provided the origin of our destruction, humility was found to be the instrument of our redemption.”

A little later he adds: “The former says, ‘I will ascend into heaven’ (Isaiah 14); the latter says through the prophet, ‘My soul is filled with evils, and my life has drawn near to hell’ (Psalm 38). The former says, ‘Above the stars of heaven I will exalt my throne’ (Isaiah 14); the latter, after the human race had been expelled from the seats of paradise, says, ‘Behold, I am coming quickly, and I will dwell in your midst’ (Zechariah 1). The former says, ‘I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north’ (Isaiah 14); the latter says, ‘I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people’ (Psalm 21),” and what follows.

There he cites nearly the same passages of Scripture that Cassian cites here, and many more besides, setting them against one another. Finally he concludes as follows: “The former teaches the minds subjected to him nothing other than to seek the summit of exaltation, to rise above all equals through the swelling of the mind, to pass beyond the fellowship of all human beings through lofty arrogance, and even to raise himself against the power of the Creator, as is said of them by the Psalmist: ‘They have passed into the purpose of their heart; they have thought and spoken wickedness; they have spoken iniquity on high’ (Psalm 72). The latter, coming to spittle, blows, slaps, a crown of thorns, the cross, the spear, and death, admonishes his members, saying: ‘If anyone serves me, let him follow me’ (John 12). Since, therefore, our Redeemer rules the hearts of the humble, while this Leviathan is called the king of the proud, we clearly recognize that pride is the most evident sign of the reprobate, whereas humility is the sign of the elect. When, then, one recognizes what each person possesses, one discovers under which king he serves.”]

If we have perceived the cause of the original ruin and the foundations of our salvation—by whom and in what manner each was established or brought forth—we may learn from the example of either that ruin or this one how we ought to avoid so terrible a death as pride. [Note: The reference is to the fall of Lucifer, mentioned above, and to the humility of Christ the Savior. Saint Basil also teaches that Christ’s example has been set before us as a remedy for pride, in these words (Homily on Humility):

“We discover that the whole dispensation of the Lord instructs us in humility. When he was an infant, he was immediately placed in a cave, not on a bed but in a manger. Then he was brought up in the dwelling of a carpenter and a poor mother, subject to his mother and to her husband. He was taught by listening, though he had no need of instruction; yet by asking questions and through his questions he displayed an admirable wisdom. He submitted to John, and the Lord received baptism from a servant. He neither resisted the fury of his adversaries nor unleashed his ineffable power against anyone, but as though yielding to those more powerful than himself. He was made to stand before the chief priests in the form of an accused man; he was led to the governor and submitted to his judgment. He was spat upon by servants and by the lowest boys; he was handed over to death, and to the most shameful death according to human judgment.”

These and other things are said by Basil.

Augustine, in Book 9, chapter 5, of *On the Trinity*, says: “It benefits us to believe and to hold firmly and unshakenly that the humility by which Christ, God, was born from a woman and was led by mortals through so many insults to death is the supreme medicine by which the swelling of our pride might be healed, and the profound mystery by which the bond of sin might be loosed.”]

## CHAPTER IX. How we too can overcome pride

[Column 0437A]

Therefore, [Note: This means by that safeguard of humility of which Saint Antony was assured. He seemed to see the world sprinkled and filled with snares, so that one could scarcely place a foot anywhere without danger. When he asked who could escape them, he heard that the truly humble person could do so: by humbling himself and pressing himself down even to the ground, he could crawl beneath the stretched-out snares; or he could trample the pleasures of the world underfoot as things despised (Athanasius, *Life of Saint Antony*).

There is, however, a third way of escaping the snares, especially those of pride: breaking through them. How? By the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. The Apostle commands us to put on the armor of God (Ephesians 6)—*πανοπλία*, that is, the entirety of the weapons, as Ambrose says; or “all the armor,” as Jerome explains—so that we may be able to stand against the devil’s stratagems. Among these weapons, both defensive and offensive, he mentions the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.

This is what the Author now does: against the stratagems and snares of demons, by which they attempt to trip our steps, we are to take up the sword of the Spirit—that is, the word of God—and, armed with the sayings of divine Scripture, which impress upon us the weakness of our powers and our need for divine grace, we are to break through and scatter, as with a two-edged sword, the hidden and creeping movements of pride.

John Climacus taught this by a notable example, particularly appropriate to this passage, in Step 21, where he introduces an old man, highly experienced in spiritual combat, relating the following about himself:

“When I was sitting in a certain assembly,” he said, “the demons of vainglory and pride came and sat beside me, one on either side. One of them struck my side with his little finger and urged me to say something concerning contemplation, or to speak of any work I had performed in the desert. When I drove him away from me, saying, ‘Let those who devise evil against me be turned back and put to shame’ (Psalm 6), immediately the one who was on my left said in my ear, ‘Well done! You have become great indeed, since you have conquered my most shameless mother.’ To him I replied, taking up the following verses: ‘Let those who say to me, “Well done!” be immediately turned back in shame.’”

This is what he says. Then he explains in what sense he called vainglory the mother of pride; we shall discuss that elsewhere.

From what has been said, then, you have three useful ways to commit to memory for escaping the devil’s snares: first, submitting oneself and, as it were, crawling beneath them through the practice of humility; second, trampling them underfoot through abstinence; third, breaking through and scattering them through the word of God. A fourth may be added, self-evident in itself: avoiding the place where the snares are—that is, the objects and occasions of sins.

In this sense Saint Augustine, commenting on Psalm 141, “On this path where I walked, they hid a snare for me,” noted that snares cannot be set on the Lord’s path itself, but beside the path, as it is said in Psalm 139: “Beside the way they placed a stumbling-block for me.” Hence Ecclesiasticus, chapter 9, also says: “Do you not know that you walk in the midst of snares?” What does “in the midst of snares” mean? “On the way of Christ.” For there are snares on the right and on the left; in the middle is the way of justice.

When it is said, “They hid a snare on the path,” this must be understood as referring to their opinion, not to reality. Since they are outside the way but think that they are on the way, they place snares beside the way, thinking that they are placing them on the way. The just person, however, not turning away from the way of justice either to the right or to the left, escapes all the snares.]

we shall be able to escape the snare of that most wicked spirit if, in each virtue in which we sense that we have made progress, we say the apostolic words: “Not I, but the grace of God with me”; and, “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15); and, “It is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure” (Philippians 2). The very Author of our salvation also says: “Whoever remains in me, and I in him, he bears much fruit; for without me you can do nothing” (John 15). And: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it keeps watch in vain” (Psalm 126). And: “It is vain for you to rise before the light” (ibid.), because “it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Romans 9).

## CHAPTER X. That no one can obtain the perfection of virtues or the promised blessedness by his virtues alone

For no one’s will, however willing, nor anyone’s running, however active, can be so adequate that, surrounded by flesh resisting the spirit, he can reach the reward and crown of such perfection, integrity, and purity, [Note: To exclude every occasion of pride and arrogance, the Author now digresses for several chapters into the subject he has often touched upon elsewhere: the grace and divine assistance necessary for us both to overcome temptations and escape the devil’s snares, and to attain perfection and blessedness.
