As for the wording of the text, he says, “No one’s will, however willing, or running”—as Ciaconius reads it from the Vatican manuscripts—or “however fervent and desirous”—as Cuychius reads it from a manuscript—“can be so adequate,” and so forth.

These words can bear two meanings, one Catholic and true, the other erroneous and false. The Catholic meaning is the one expressed by the title of this chapter: no one, however eagerly striving and aspiring to the summit of perfection and the reward of blessedness, can reach or merit it by his own powers without divine assistance and the help of grace. This is evident in itself, since such goods are supernatural, and all our merits depend upon God’s grace—indeed, are themselves his gifts—as the Fathers of Trent teach (Session 6, chapter 16), following Saint Augustine in many passages.

The erroneous and Semipelagian meaning would be that a human being can, from himself, will well and run well—that is, possess a good will or conceive a good purpose—and perform or begin many good works by the powers of nature, thereby advancing or at least becoming disposed toward justification and perfection, but cannot reach perfection and salvation unless divine mercy and grace confirm, complete, and bring that good purpose to fulfillment within him. More will be said on this matter below.]

unless he is protected by divine mercy, so that he may deserve to arrive at what he greatly desires and toward which he runs. For every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights (James 1). “What do you have that you have not received? And if you have received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4).

## CHAPTER XI. He confirms this very point by the example of David and the blessed thief

[Column 0439A]

For if we remember either that thief who was brought into paradise on the basis of one confession (Luke 23), [Note: The thief’s confession, joined with a petition, is found in Luke 23: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom,” or, in Greek, *ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ σου*, “in your kingdom.”

This is a brief but complete confession of faith. In a few words he confessed Christ’s royal power, his divinity, and his resurrection: his royal power in “when you come into your kingdom”—that is, already reigning or already having obtained the kingdom; his divinity when he calls him Lord, and such a Lord and king as is able also to forgive sins—for that is what it means for God to remember us; and finally his resurrection. He would not have asked one whom he saw so close to death to remember him unless he had believed that he would rise again and reign after his resurrection.

In Letter 7, written to Laeta, Saint Jerome proves that no one’s salvation should be despaired of by the example of the thief, who was converted on the cross and deserved to be with Christ in paradise that very day. Saint Cyprian likewise did not hesitate to assert that he was a martyr and baptized in his own blood (*Sermon on the Lord’s Supper*).

Saint Gregory writes most beautifully and appropriately for the illumination of this passage about this thief:

“Let us consider what sort of man he came to the gallows, and what sort of man he departed from the gallows. He came guilty of a brother’s blood; he came bloodstained, but on the cross he was changed by inward grace. The one who had inflicted death upon his brother proclaimed the life of the dying Lord, saying, ‘Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom’ (Luke 23).

The nails had fastened his hands and feet to the cross, and nothing in him remained free from punishment except his heart and tongue. By God’s inspiration he offered him everything free that he found within himself, so that, in accordance with what is written, he might believe with the heart unto justification and confess with the mouth unto salvation.

The Apostle testifies that three virtues above all remain in the hearts of the faithful, saying: ‘But now there remain faith, hope, and charity.’ Filled suddenly with grace, the thief both received and preserved all three upon the cross.

He had faith, for he believed that the Lord would reign, though he saw him dying alongside himself. He had hope, for he asked entrance into his kingdom, saying, ‘Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom.’ He also held charity vividly in his death: he rebuked the other thief, his fellow criminal, who was dying under the same sentence for a similar crime, for his iniquity, and proclaimed to him the life he did not know, saying, ‘Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same condemnation? And we indeed justly, for we are receiving what our deeds deserve; but this man has done nothing wrong.’

He who came to the cross guilty—behold what sort of man departs from the cross through grace. He confessed the Lord whom he saw dying with him in human weakness, while the apostles denied him whom they had seen performing miracles by divine power.”

This is Gregory’s account (Book 18 of the *Moralia*, chapter 25). See more in Conference 13, chapter 9 and following.]

we understand that he attained such blessedness not by the merit of his running, but by the gift of the merciful God. [Note: Not, indeed, by the merit of his former life, but by the merit of that good confession—which itself, however, was also a gift of the merciful God (see Conference 13, chapter 13), who wills his gifts to be our merits, as Saint Augustine says (*On Grace and Free Will*, chapter 7).

It is sufficiently clear from what has been said that the thief’s confession did not arise from the mere power of free will, as the Author appears to suppose, nor, likewise, did David’s example, which he next introduces. Rather, it was drawn forth and expressed from true and living faith—that is, faith formed by charity—which is known to be meritorious of eternal life (Pope Celestine, Letter to the Bishops of Gaul, chapter 12; Council of Trent, Session 6, chapter 16). The Apostle says: “With the heart one believes unto justification, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation”; for Scripture says: “Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame” (Romans 10; Isaiah 28).]

Or if we recall that two exceedingly grave and monstrous crimes of King David were wiped away by one word of repentance, [Note: David’s adultery and murder—namely, the killing of the innocent Uriah—in which many deformities and grave circumstances may be considered. Nevertheless, these grave and enormous crimes were erased by one statement of repentance, that is, by the single word, “I have sinned.” This was not uttered from the powers and capacity of nature or free will, as was said above, but by divine grace and inspiration, and through true contrition; and the crimes were removed with respect to guilt, though not with respect to temporal punishment.

When the prophet Nathan reproached him for his sin in God’s name, David was immediately struck with remorse and repentance and said, “I have sinned against the Lord.” Nathan then replied, “The Lord has also taken away your sin; you shall not die.” From these words the Fathers infer that the remission of sin preceded the confession itself, but did not precede inward contrition, in which there were simultaneously hatred of sin, love of God, and the intention to confess and make satisfaction.

Hence Psalm 31 likewise says: “I said, ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord’; and you forgave the iniquity of my sin.” Saint Gregory comments: “Consider how swift is the saving speed of forgiveness, how great the commendation of God’s mercy: pardon accompanies the penitent’s desire before repentance reaches punishment; remission reaches the heart before confession breaks forth in speech” (Gregory on Psalm 31).]

here too we shall not find that the merits of his labor were made equal to the remission of so great a crime, but that God’s grace abounded. Having received the occasion of true repentance, God consumed such a mass of sins through the full confession of a single word.

If we also examine the beginning of the calling and salvation of the human race, by which we are saved not from ourselves [Note: Thus the Apostle says in Ephesians 2: “By grace you have been saved through faith; and this is not from yourselves, for it is the gift of God; not from works, so that no one may boast.” “Not from works” means works preceding faith.

The Greek scholia of Photius express the sense as follows: “Not from works, so that no one may boast—not because he did not wish to save through works, but because no one can be saved from works except through faith and with faith.” He therefore excludes works preceding faith, lest people should think that they had been called to grace by their virtues without faith, since without faith they possess only the empty name of virtue.

Thus also the Council of Trent (Session 6, chapter 8), explaining the same statement of the Apostle, says: “When the Apostle says that a human being is justified by faith and freely, these words must be understood in the sense that the perpetual consensus of the Catholic Church has held and expressed: namely, that we are said to be justified by faith because faith is the beginning, foundation, and root of all justification and of human salvation, without which it is impossible to please God and to attain fellowship with his children.

“We are said to be justified freely because none of the things that precede justification—whether faith or works—merits the grace of justification itself. For if it is grace, then it is no longer from works; otherwise, as the same Apostle says, grace is no longer grace” (Romans 11).]

nor from our works, according to the Apostle, but by God’s gift and grace (Ephesians 2), we shall clearly be able to perceive how [Note: The attainment of perfection must be attributed less to our will and labor than to God’s grace and mercy, since our good will itself, and whatever good it is able to perform, comes from God as its principal and primary cause, according to James: “Every good gift and every perfect gift comes down from the Father of lights,” and so forth.

Hence Augustine, in chapter 32 of the *Enchiridion*: “Although unquestionably, if a human being is of an age to use reason, he cannot believe, hope, or love unless he wills to do so, nor reach the prize of God’s heavenly calling unless he runs willingly, how then is it not of the one who wills or runs, but of God who shows mercy? It is because the will itself, as it is written, is prepared by God.

“Otherwise, if it was said, ‘It is not of the one who wills or runs, but of God who shows mercy,’ because it results from both—from human will and from God’s mercy—so that we understand it in this way: ‘Human will is not sufficient if God’s mercy is not also present; therefore God’s mercy alone is not sufficient if human will is not also present’—then if it is rightly said, ‘It is not of the human will but of God’s mercy,’ because human will alone does not accomplish it, why is it not conversely rightly said, ‘It is not of God’s mercy but of human will,’ because God’s mercy alone does not accomplish it?

“Since no Christian will dare to say, ‘It is not of God’s mercy but of human will,’ lest he plainly contradict the Apostle, it remains that the statement, ‘It is not of the one who wills or runs, but of God who shows mercy,’ is rightly understood in this way: everything is attributed to God, who both prepares the human will so that it may be helped and helps it once prepared.

“Good will precedes many gifts of God, but not all; and in those gifts which it does not precede, it is itself also included.”

This is Augustine’s teaching.]

the summit of perfection is not of the one who wills or runs, but of God who shows mercy (Romans 9): he does not make us victorious over vices by compensating us according to the merit of our labors or running, nor, by matching the exertion of our will, does he enable us to climb so arduous a summit of integrity with the flesh that we use subjected to us. [Note: Similar passages may be found in Book 6, chapter 6; Conference 3, chapter 10 and following; Conference 12, the penultimate chapter; and Conference 13, chapter 6.]

For no affliction of this body and no contrition of the heart can be proportionate to the acquisition of that true chastity of the inner person, so as to obtain by bare human labor—that is, without God’s assistance—a virtue of purity such as is innate in the angels and native to heaven. For every effect of goodness flows from the grace of the one who, with multiplied generosity, has given such enduring blessedness and such immeasurable glory to our small will and our brief and limited running.

## CHAPTER XII. That no labor can be compared with the promised blessedness

[Column 0441B]

For every length of the present life, when compared with the eternity of the glory to come, vanishes; and all pains, when contemplated in light of that immeasurable blessedness, are driven away and, like smoke reduced to nothing, melt away, appearing nowhere, like ash. [Note: This passage is aptly answered by the decree of the Council of Trent concerning the merit of good works and the nature of merit. The final portion of that decree reads as follows:

“Nor should it be omitted that, although the sacred writings attribute so much to good works that Christ even promises that the one who gives one of his least ones a drink of cold water will not lack his reward (Matthew 10), and the Apostle testifies that our present momentary and light affliction produces in us, beyond all measure, an eternal weight of glory (2 Corinthians 4), nevertheless let it be far from a Christian to trust or glory in himself rather than in the Lord. His goodness toward all human beings is so great that he wishes their merits to be his gifts” (Council of Trent, Session 6, chapter 16).]

## CHAPTER XIII. The tradition of the elders concerning the manner of attaining purity
Therefore it is now time to present the judgment of the Fathers in the very words in which they transmit it—namely, of those who did not depict the way of perfection and its character with verbal boasting, but rather, possessing it in reality, practice, and spiritual virtue, handed it down through their own experience and most certain examples. They say, then, that no one can be cleansed from carnal vices to purity unless he understands that all his labor and effort, and the goal of such great perfection, cannot suffice [Col. 0442B]; nor can he recognize that perfection is grasped only through God’s mercy and assistance, being instructed not so much by the teaching of the one who transmits it as by affection, virtue, and personal experience.

For in attaining such magnificent and lofty rewards of purity and integrity,

[Note: [Col. 0441D] He notes the principal and most customary means of acquiring and preserving purity and holiness, [Col. 0442B] which nevertheless do not suffice by themselves; indeed, they themselves cannot be performed without God’s special assistance, of which we have treated elsewhere and shall treat more fully in another place. Moreover, what is taught both here and in the preceding chapters concerning the attainment of perfection, although at first sight everything appears sound, pious, and Catholic—as it truly is, if understood in a sound and Catholic sense—nevertheless, according to the Author’s mind and understanding, it is not as it appears on the surface. For under the name of perfection an error lies concealed; as the saying goes, a serpent lies hidden in the grass. This is the beginning of the error into which Cassian and his fellow presbyters of Marseille fell: they ascribed perfection to divine grace, but its beginning or commencement to our will. Hence the error of the Massilians and Semi-Pelagians was so called because it approached the heresy of Pelagius only in some respects. This will be explained more clearly in the notes to the thirteenth Conference.

For the present it will be enough to observe that the clerics of Marseille—among whom Cassian was regarded as the chief—although otherwise Catholic and religious men, nevertheless appeared, under the Catholic name, to support the heretic Pelagius. They acknowledged grace as necessary for attaining perfection in the virtues and eternal happiness, as Cassian teaches here, but not for the beginning of justification and salvation. For they said that certain beginnings of good will either were or could be derived from us, from the powers of free choice alone, without any inward movement or prompting of Christ’s grace. By these beginnings we would start to wish to act well, to be converted, healed, and saved; and on account of them God’s grace would then be granted to us so as to advance, perfect, and bring to completion such efforts and pious desires.

Thus these were their expressions and formulas of speech: that the beginning of salvation comes from us, but perfection from God; that God’s grace is in turn preceded by us, and is given only to those who spontaneously and by their own initiative ask, seek, and knock, without any prior movement of God or assistance of grace; that our efforts and labors are useless and vain unless they are aided and advanced by God; and similar statements.

Against this opinion, above all, Saint Augustine composed, in addition to the other books and treatises published against Pelagius, his final work at the request of Hilary of Arles and Prosper of Riez, bishops in Gaul: namely, the book *On the Predestination of the Saints*, and another *On the Gift of Perseverance*. In these he effectively taught that there is no beginning of good will, faith, justification, or salvation except from God.

Prosper himself then, in a particular book published against the *Collator*, sharply and incisively refuted the opinion of Cassian and the Massilians expressed and set forth in the thirteenth Conference under the persona of Abbot Chaeremon. Thereafter Pope Celestine I, moved by this controversy, imposed silence on the Massilians in a letter written to the bishops of Gaul, declaring their assertions erroneous and foreign to Catholic truth; whereas he approved the contrary doctrine of Saint Augustine, Prosper, Hilary, and the other Fathers (*Tome I of the Councils*, Binian edition).

Finally, when even this did not quiet the Massilians, under the pontificate of Pope Felix IV, as Severinus Binius notes, a synod was assembled at Orange in the year of our Lord 429. In several canons the articles of the Massilians were explicitly and formally refuted and rejected, while Catholic doctrine was asserted and defined. All this, with God’s help, we shall pursue and explain at greater length in the annotations to the aforesaid thirteenth Conference.]

however great a labor of fasting, vigils, reading, and severe withdrawal into solitude may have been expended, it cannot be worthy to obtain these things by the merit of one’s diligence or labor. For human labor can never compensate for a divine gift by its own efforts, unless what is desired has first been granted through divine mercy.

## CHAPTER XIV. That God’s assistance is granted to those who labor.

[Col. 0444A]

I do not say this in order to nullify human efforts or to attempt to turn anyone away from diligence and earnest labor. But I firmly define—not on my own authority, but according to the judgment of the elders—that perfection cannot be attained at all without these things, while no one can bring it to completion by these alone, without God’s grace.

[Note: [Col. 0443B] Here, as in the preceding passages, he understands “perfection” as the completion of a good work in any class of virtue—that is, perfect faith, charity, chastity, holiness, and so forth—in order to distinguish it from the beginning, or beginnings, of good works, which elsewhere (*Conference* 13, chapter 12) he calls “seeds of the virtues,” implanted in us by nature. By these he means good thoughts, good wills, and pious desires conceived by the powers of nature, or free choice, concerning every kind of virtue. This was the error of the Massilians, as has been stated.

The meaning, therefore, is that perfection—namely, of a good work, or, if you prefer, Christian or evangelical perfection, which primarily and essentially consists in charity, and secondarily or instrumentally in the possession and combination of the other virtues—cannot be obtained without these things, namely, human efforts, diligence, and labor. These, however, suffice of themselves to begin or conceive a good work; but for perfection divine supernatural assistance is necessary. See *Conference* 11, “On Perfection.”

That this is the Author’s meaning is manifestly gathered from other passages when compared with this one. For in *Conference* 13, chapter 9, he asserts the same thing in other words, saying: “But that it may become more evident that even through the good of nature, which has been bestowed by the Creator’s kindness, the beginnings of good wills sometimes arise, although, unless they are directed by the Lord, they cannot reach the completion of the virtues, the Apostle bears witness, saying: ‘To will is present with me; but to perform I do not find’” [Rom. 7:18].

It is still more evident from the following chapter, where he gives examples from every class of virtue, even faith in Christ and perseverance in goodness; and he says that we can desire all these things by the powers of free choice, but that this willing is too weak to accomplish them in practice unless grace comes to our aid. Nevertheless, he says that through this desire we can obtain grace for their completion.

Again, in chapter 11, he says: “When God sees us inclining toward the desire for good, he comes to meet us, directs us, and strengthens us,” and so forth. He continues the same argument in chapter 12 and finally concludes: “It cannot, therefore, be doubted that the seeds of the virtues are naturally present in every soul, implanted through the Creator’s gift; but unless they are stirred up by God’s assistance, they cannot advance to the growth of perfection, because, according to the blessed Apostle, ‘neither is he that plants anything, nor he that waters, but God who gives the growth.’” Thus he draws the Apostle to his own meaning.

But against this opinion the holy Fathers fight with the greatest force and reject it as Pelagian. Saint Augustine, *To Boniface*, book II, chapter 8: “If the desire for good begins in us without God’s grace, that beginning itself will be a merit, to which assistance would come as though by obligation; and thus grace would not be given freely, but would be given on account of our merit.”

And in book I, chapter 19, to the same Boniface: “You said,” he writes, “that one is always aided by God’s grace, as though a person who had undertaken a good work by his own will, without any grace of God, were divinely aided in the work itself—on account, evidently, of the merits of his good will—so that grace would be repaid as something owed rather than given freely. Thus grace would no longer be grace, but that very teaching which Pelagius himself was compelled to condemn in the episcopal judgment at Palestine: that God’s grace is given according to our merits.”

Saint Prosper, *Against the Collator*, chapter 6: “How do you fail to see that you fall into the condemnation whereby, whether you wish it or not, you are proved to say that God’s grace is given according to our merits, when you affirm that some good work must first proceed from human beings, on account of which they obtain grace?”]

[Note: [Col. 0444B] To these words Dr. Cuychius applied his censure, which, together with the others proposed in the preface, we shall append to this work, for the learned reader to examine and read. By it he attempted not only to elucidate the difficulty of this passage, but also to vindicate and clear Cassian entirely of the charge of error in this matter. For he judges that Cassian’s statements in this chapter—that God bestows his grace only upon those who labor and sweat, while it belongs to us to offer God an occasion of good will, by which, being moved, he pours out his gifts upon us—must be understood not of unbelieving or ungodly persons, but of those reborn and justified, or established in the state of grace. These, cooperating and laboring with the indwelling grace of the Holy Spirit, advance from virtue to virtue and make themselves fit and capable to receive greater gifts of God; thus this interpretation does not exclude divine assistance, which is presupposed in every disposition and preparation for grace.

But this exposition of Dr. Cuychius, though pious and Catholic, nevertheless does not seem suited to this passage, and is not approved by other theologians. For it is most certainly evident, both from the Author himself and from others, that he had no intention or opinion other than that of the Massilians discussed above, which he himself expressed and published more fully and openly in Conference 13 under the name of Abbot Chaeremon: namely, that the beginning of good will comes from us, and that a person can by his own powers dispose and render himself fit to receive God’s grace. Although he does not teach this here as openly as in that Conference, which Saint Prosper accordingly undertook to attack, he nevertheless intimated it not so obscurely that a moderately attentive reader cannot readily see it from many arguments:

1. From chapter 10 through chapter 19 he speaks quite honorably of God’s grace and highly commends it against Pelagius, but does so in such a way as to ascribe only perfection to it, making no mention of beginnings. Here lies a mystery which Cuychius failed to notice. Because Cassian speaks so magnificently, both in this book and elsewhere, of grace and its necessity, Cuychius thought him free from the Massilian error.

2. From chapter 10 onward he repeatedly presupposes in us good will, effort, labor, and a desire for salvation before every grace and before the divine mercy, as he calls it.

3. He requires that grace only advance our efforts and labors, not also arouse them.

4. Among the beginnings of good will which he attributes to us, he includes not only faith and prayer but also many other works: bodily affliction, fasts, vigils, solitude, and so forth. Thus he openly makes grace follow our works and subjects it, as it were, as their handmaid—something condemned by the Council of Orange (canon 6).

5. Here and in that Conference, chapter 9, he uses precisely the same style and manner of speaking, saying that grace is given to those who ask, found by those who seek, and opened to those who knock—namely, by their own movement and capacity of free choice. The sixth canon of the Council of Orange condemns this in the very words borrowed from him, as we shall shortly quote.

Indeed, these words are still more severe and explicit. He asserts that God’s mercy and grace are conferred only upon those who labor and sweat, who will and run; whereas in that Conference, chapters 12, 13, and 15, he acknowledges that God’s grace sometimes precedes us and that we sometimes precede God’s grace, as, God willing, we shall see there. Let Dr. Cuychius therefore see on what grounds he excuses Cassian here, reproves him there, and defends here an opinion conceived and expressed in the same words which he condemns there. For from what can it be inferred that Cassian thought differently here than there, when each person is justified or condemned by his own words? Mark XII. “But,” he says, “Cassian here sets forth his own opinion, as he also does in the books *On the Incarnation*; in the Conferences, however, he reports the opinions of those whom he introduces as speakers.” Yet it has already been shown that the opinion expressed in this passage is the same as that more diffusely and clearly explained in Chaeremon’s Conference and attacked by Saint Prosper and other Fathers. Let Cassian’s opinion, therefore, stand as he himself expressed it and as the Fathers judged it, lest, while we strive too zealously to excuse or defend him, we represent the most illustrious doctors of the Church—Augustine, Prosper, Hilary, and the rest—as slanderers, or suspect that the supreme pontiffs Celestine, Leo, and Gelasius, as well as the Council of Orange convened in this cause, were blind or exceeded due bounds. These matters have been spoken and written from zeal for investigating the truth, without prejudice to the sounder opinion and subject to the judgment of holy Mother Church.]

For just as [Col. 0445A] we say that human efforts cannot grasp perfection by themselves without God’s assistance,

[Note: [Col. 0445C] It is remarkable that Cassian, here as elsewhere, forgetful of himself or inconsistent with himself, should have asserted contrary things. For below he says in explicit words that we are sometimes drawn to salvation by God even against our will, as we shall prove there from the Scriptures. And in Conference 13, chapter 11, he says that our will is preceded by God, though that it sometimes precedes him. If it is preceded by God, then God’s grace and mercy are not conferred only on those who labor and sweat. More explicitly, in chapter 17, drawing this conclusion from the preceding matters, he says: “By these examples, therefore, which we have drawn from the records of the Gospel, we may most clearly observe that in diverse and innumerable ways and by inscrutable paths God procures the salvation of the human race, inviting the course of some who will and thirst to a greater ardor, while restraining even some unwilling and reluctant persons,” and so forth. Again, in chapter 18 of the same Conference, he says that God receives some who willingly run, but draws others who are unwilling and resisting, compelling them to a good will. If he draws the unwilling and resisting to a good will, how does he confer grace only upon those who labor and sweat?

See, reader, how great is the force and prerogative of truth: even while truth itself is silent, the falsehood opposed to it fights against itself and destroys itself. But, to make the truth of this passage clearer, something should be said concerning the proposition common among the scholastics: “God’s grace is not lacking to one who does what lies within him.” For both the title of this chapter—“That God’s assistance is granted to those who labor”—and especially the words of the context, “For he is ready, when we offer him merely the occasion of a good will, to confer all these things,” seem to signify this.

I find two explanations of this statement among Catholic doctors, leaving aside the Pelagian or Semi-Pelagian explanation, discussed above, which subordinated the grace of justification and the gift of faith to the powers and merits of free choice. The first is the explanation of those who maintain that a person doing what lies within him by the powers of nature alone is infallibly given, by God and according to a certain law, the helps of prevenient grace through which he advances to the grace of justification—not on account of any merit in the person acting thus, but because of Christ’s merits. Saint Thomas at times seems to have followed this explanation, and is therefore commonly invoked in its support. For in question 14 of *On Truth* he says: “If someone brought up in the woods followed the guidance of natural reason in seeking good and avoiding evil, it must be held with complete certainty that God would either reveal to him by interior inspiration the things which must be believed, or direct to him a preacher of the faith, as he sent Peter to Cornelius.” Here the Holy Doctor plainly teaches that if that person does what lies within him, following the dictate of natural reason in seeking good and avoiding evil, he will most certainly be enlightened by God and come to faith and grace. The same is taught by many other scholastics, cited by Father Leonardus Lessius in his particular treatise *On One Who Does What Lies within Him*, where he also defends and upholds this same explanation (*On Efficacious Grace*, book 10 and appendix).

But the other explanation of the same Saint Thomas is much more probable and safer: he teaches that the axiom is to be understood of one doing what lies within him, not indeed by the faculty of nature alone, but by God’s assistance and inspiration. For in I–II, question 112, article 3, he expressly teaches that a person’s preparation, considered as proceeding from free choice, has no necessity for obtaining grace, but it does when considered as proceeding from God who moves. Accordingly, there is no preparation or disposition on the part of human free choice and natural faculty for obtaining grace unless God moves and arouses it.

And in lecture 3 on Romans, chapter 3, speaking of those who have not yet heard the preaching of the Gospel, he says: “It must be said that, according to the Lord’s statement in John 17, those who have not heard the Lord speaking either in person or through his disciples have an excuse for the sin of unbelief. Yet they will not consequently receive God’s benefit—that is, be justified from the other sins which they either contracted by being born or added by living wickedly—and are deservedly damned on their account. But if any of them had done what lay within him, the Lord, according to his mercy, would have provided for him by sending him a preacher of the faith, as he sent Peter to Cornelius in Acts 10 and Paul to the Macedonians in Acts 16. Nevertheless, this very fact that some do what lies within them by turning to God comes from God moving their hearts toward good: ‘Turn us, O Lord, to yourself, and we shall be turned’ [Lam. 5:21].” Thus far Saint Thomas, briefly setting forth the meaning of that axiom.

Adopting his opinion, Cardinal Bellarmine, in book VI of *On Grace and Free Choice*, chapter 6, replies to an argument brought against him from the same axiom that this dictum of the schools is correctly explained by Saint Thomas (I–II, question 106, article 6; and question 112, article 3, reply to 1) and Saint Bonaventure (*Sentences*, book II, distinction 28, article 2, question 1). They teach that grace is not denied to one doing what lies within him when a person does what lies within him by cooperating with God’s grace, by which he is moved. For grace is not due to one who does what lies within him by the powers of nature alone, but punishment is—not because he acts by the powers of nature alone, but because, for one or two good moral works that he may perhaps perform, he will without doubt commit very many mortal sins.

Certainly, those who teach that a person is prepared for grace by doing what lies within him through the powers of nature alone either think that he can by his own powers desire and ask God for grace—and this is the Pelagian heresy, as was proved above from the Council of Orange and other cited testimonies—or else they think that a person can by his own powers keep all the moral precepts and lead an innocent life according to reason, and by this moral holiness induce God to grant him a special assistance through which he will finally attain faith and grace. But this too is the Pelagian heresy, sufficiently and more than sufficiently refuted in the preceding book, to say nothing of the fact that no such person can be shown from history. For it could readily be demonstrated that Catos, Socrates, and others like them, judged holiest among the pagans, were covered with many vices. So the most illustrious Bellarmine, than whose statements nothing more exact or lucid can be adduced. But enough, indeed more than enough, on these matters for the purpose at hand. If you seek more, consult Didacus Alvarez, book VI of *On the Helps of Divine Grace*, disputation 56, where he treats this question at length and refutes that first explanation.]

so we declare [Col. 0446A] that God’s mercy and grace are granted only to those who labor and toil; or, to use the Apostle’s words, are bestowed upon those who will and run, according to what is also sung in the eighty-eighth Psalm in the person of God: “I have laid help upon one who is mighty, and I have exalted one chosen from among my people” (see the second annotation of Master Cuychius at the end of the work).

[Note: [Col. 0447C] Against this excessively unrestricted assertion, several canons were issued in that Council of Orange mentioned above. They reject the same assertion and affirm the contrary truth.

First, canon 3 says: “If anyone says that the grace of God is conferred through human invocation—that is, invocation made by human powers—and not that grace itself causes us to invoke it, he contradicts the prophet Isaiah, or the Apostle who says the same thing: ‘I was found by those who did not seek me; I appeared openly to those who did not ask me’” (Isa. 65; Rom. 10).

In canon 4 those are condemned who said that God awaits our will by which we may wish to be cleansed, but that it is not also effected in us, through the infusion of the Holy Spirit and his operation in us, that we should wish to be cleansed.

Finally, canon 6 defines the same point more explicitly in these words: “If anyone says that divine mercy is conferred upon us who believe, will, desire, strive, labor, watch, study, ask, seek, and knock, without the grace of God, and does not confess that it is through the infusion and inspiration of the Holy Spirit in us that we believe, will, or are able to perform all these things as we ought; and if he subordinates the assistance of grace to human humility or obedience, and does not agree that it is a gift of grace itself that we should be obedient and humble, he resists the Apostle who says: ‘What do you have that you have not received?’ and, ‘By the grace of God I am what I am’” (1 Cor. 4 and 15).

By these canons, which employ Cassian’s own words, his manner of speaking and opinion are manifestly excluded. Augustine also condemns this manner of speaking as belonging to the Pelagians, or to those who favor them, in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 23, in these words: “Let them observe,” he says, “how those who think that it comes from us, rather than being given to us, that we should ask, seek, and knock, are deceived; and who say that this is how grace is proclaimed to be given on account of our merit, so that it follows when we ask and receive, seek and find, and knock and it is opened to us. They do not wish to understand that even this—that we pray, that is, ask, seek, and knock—is itself a divine gift. For we receive the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (1 Cor. 2).

Blessed Ambrose saw this, for he says: “To pray to God is also a gift of spiritual grace, as it is written: ‘No one says, “Lord Jesus,” except in the Holy Spirit’” (1 Cor. 2). Thus far Saint Augustine, also citing Saint Ambrose as supporting his position.

From these words it is clear how the Savior’s statement is to be understood, the statement from which Cassian derived his assertion: “Ask, and you shall receive; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you” (Matt. 7; Luke 11), and so forth. We are not commanded to ask, seek, and knock as though we could perform these things from ourselves, without the assistance of grace; rather, by consenting to divine inspiration and calling, and cooperating with assisting grace, we are made capable of asking, seeking, and knocking as we ought, according to the Psalmist’s words: “I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me, for he will speak peace to his people who turn their hearts toward him” (Ps. 84).

It must therefore be admitted, in accordance with the Savior’s statement, that grace is given to those who ask, seek, and knock; but no one asks, seeks, or knocks unless first stirred up and assisted by God. Consequently, our asking, seeking, and knocking is not merely unworthy, as Cassian says; it cannot exist in us at all unless it is inspired, begun, and brought to completion by God. For this was the common opinion and manner of speaking of the Massilians and Semi-Pelagians, as we noted above: “Our efforts are fruitless unless they are assisted.”

Against them Saint Bernard speaks excellently in his little book *On Grace and Free Choice*: “The efforts of free choice toward good are futile if they are not assisted, and nonexistent if they are not stirred up.” Thus we are to understand that grace is necessary both for beginning and for completing.]

We say, in accordance with the Savior’s statement, that grace is indeed given to those who ask, opened to those who knock, and found by those who seek (Matt. 7); but our asking, seeking,

[Note: [Col. 0448C] By this reasoning Cassian and the other Massilians thought that they avoided Pelagius’ error. Pelagius boasted that the merits of free choice were worthy of receiving grace, so that grace might be granted to us for acting more easily; he also said that by our own powers we could worthily and justly merit eternal glory. The Massilians, however, attributed to our efforts and works only a certain impetratory and congruous merit—one that was not sufficient in itself to obtain grace and salvation by the rigor of justice, unless God’s mercy came to our aid and perfected our efforts.

Yet it was precisely on this account that the Fathers convicted and judged them to have fallen into the Pelagian dogma: namely, that grace is given according to our merits, with God first looking upon and considering our merits—that is, our efforts and labors—and then, on account of them, granting us his grace, not indeed by condign merit or justice, but nevertheless by a certain congruity. This is certainly enough to empty grace of its character as pure and unmerited grace, as we shall show more fully, with God’s favor, in the thirteenth Conference.]

and knocking are not worthy unless God, in his mercy, gives what we ask, opens what we knock at, or causes what we seek to be found.

[Col. 0448A]

For he is ready, when we offer him merely the occasion of a good will, to confer all these things. Indeed, he desires and awaits our perfection and salvation more than we do.

And to such an extent did blessed David know that the outcome of his work and labor could not be obtained by his own diligence alone that he repeatedly begged the Lord to direct his works, saying: “And direct the work of our hands upon us; yes, direct the work of our hands” (Ps. 89). And again: “Confirm, O God, what you have worked in us” (Ps. 67).

## CHAPTER XV. From whom we should learn the way of perfection.

[Col. 0449A]

Therefore, if we wish to attain the true perfection of the virtues in deed and practice, we ought to submit to those teachers and guides who, having grasped it not by dreaming about it in empty talk but by reality and experience, can likewise teach us and direct us toward it, and demonstrate by the surest path how we may reach it; and who testified that they had arrived at it by faith rather than by the merit of their labors [Col. 0450A]. To them, moreover, the purity acquired in their hearts conferred this special quality:

> [Note: [Col. 0449A] The saints and those truly humble, the more they are enlightened by the ray of the inner light, the more they recognize and lament even their slightest offenses and their smallest failings; and the more they advance, the less they think they have advanced. Therefore, when they compare themselves with others, they judge themselves beneath and lower than everyone. For this is the character of humility: to look upon one’s own evils and upon the good things of others. Conversely, the disposition of pride is to attend to one’s own good qualities and the evils of others.

> Hence Saint Benedict includes among the degrees of humility (chapter 7 of the Rule): “Not only to declare with the tongue that one is lower and more insignificant than everyone, but also to believe this with the innermost affection of the heart.” But how can a humble monk believe and declare, without lying or pretense—indeed, without any falsehood—that he is lower and more insignificant than everyone? Saint Thomas explains this (II–II, question 161, article 3): “In a human being,” he says, “two things can be considered: namely, what belongs to God and what belongs to the human being. Whatever pertains to defect belongs to the human being; but whatever pertains to salvation and perfection belongs to God,” according to Hosea 13: “Your destruction, Israel, is from yourself; from me alone is your help.” Humility properly regards the reverence by which a human being is subjected to God; therefore every person, in respect of what is his own, ought to subject himself to every neighbor in respect of what belongs to God in that neighbor [Col. 0449C].

> Again, in another article (article 6, reply to objection 1), he says: “Someone can, without falsehood, believe and declare himself lower than everyone in respect of hidden defects that he recognizes in himself and the gifts of God that lie hidden in others.” Hence Augustine says in *On Holy Virginity*: “Consider others inwardly superior to you, to whom you are outwardly better.” Similarly, without falsehood someone can confess and believe that he is useless and unworthy for everything by his own powers, so that he refers his entire sufficiency to God, according to 2 Corinthians 3: “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God.”

> Thus Saint Francis used to affirm that he was the greatest of all sinners for two reasons: first, because if God had bestowed such grace upon others, they might perhaps have used it better and become holier; second, because if he were abandoned by God, or were not protected by him, he would be liable to more numerous and more grievous sins. See Bonaventure’s *Life of Saint Francis*.

> Furthermore, holy men call themselves sinners when they consider the infinite holiness and perfection of God’s justice, in comparison with which all human justice is injustice, purity is filth, and light is darkness. Hence David says in Psalm 142: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight.” And Job, chapter 25: “Can a human being be justified when compared with God, or can one born of woman appear clean? Behold, even the moon does not shine, and the stars are not pure in his sight; how much less a human being, who is rottenness, and a son of man, who is a worm?”

> In addition, the saints reckon that they have upon their conscience many serious past sins in which they wasted a large part of their lives, and therefore they call themselves sinners. Thus Paul, because he had been a persecutor, an insolent man, and a blasphemer, acknowledged and said that he was the first of all sinners (1 Timothy 1).

> Finally, because the saints were uncertain about the remission of their past crimes—for they had no certainty that they were in a state of grace—they were always fearful for themselves and strove to do penance as sinners and obtain pardon from God. For they knew the salutary teaching of Ecclesiasticus: “Blessed is the person who is always fearful” (Ecclesiasticus 5); and, “Do not be without fear concerning a pardoned sin.”

> Saint Bernard presses this argument in sermon 37 on the *Song of Songs*: “If we clearly knew in what condition God holds each one of us, we ought certainly to withdraw neither above nor below that condition, acquiescing in the truth in all things. But now, because he has made darkness his hiding place, and the word is hidden from us, so that no one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred, it is certainly more just and safer, in accordance with the counsel of Truth itself, that we choose for ourselves the lowest place, from which we may afterward be led upward with honor, than that we presume upon a higher place, from which we may soon have to withdraw in shame.

> “There is therefore no danger, however much you humble yourself, however much you regard yourself as less than you are—that is, less than Truth regards you. But it is a great evil and a dreadful danger if you exalt yourself even slightly above the truth, or prefer in your thought even one person whom Truth perhaps judges your equal, or perhaps your superior.” Saint Bernard says this and more in that passage.

> Finally, even the saints and the perfect call themselves sinners because of the frequent venial sins into which they repeatedly fall. “The just person falls seven times a day” (Proverbs 4), that is, frequently. They do not regard these sins as small and trivial, but as very serious and hateful, because they perceive that such sins diminish the ardor of charity and retard the progress of the spiritual life. Hence Ecclesiasticus, chapter 7, says: “There is no just person upon earth who does good and does not sin.” And the Apostle John, that beloved disciple, says: “In many things we all offend; if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1).]

so that they might recognize themselves as increasingly humbled by sins. [Note: [Col. 0450C] Saint Gregory, *Dialogues*, book 3, chapter 34: “There are two kinds of compunction, because the soul that thirsts for God is first pierced by fear, and afterward by love. At first it afflicts itself with tears, because, when it recalls its evils, it fears that it will suffer eternal punishments for them. But when this fear has been consumed by the long anxiety of sorrow, a certain security arising from the hope of pardon is born, and the mind is inflamed with love for heavenly joys. The one who previously wept lest he be led to punishment afterward begins to weep most bitterly because he is delayed from the kingdom.” He says similar things in homily 22 on Ezekiel. See Collation 9, chapter 26.]

For their compunction over sins increased each day in proportion to the progress of their purity of soul; and they continually drew sighs from the depths of their hearts because they felt that they could in no way avoid the blemishes and stains of sins impressed upon them through the manifold minutiae of their thoughts. And [Note: [Col. 0450D] These words, whether understood according to the author’s intention or according to the truth of the matter, should not be taken as though those holy Fathers did not recognize the merits of good works, or did not understand that eternal life was promised to them by God as the reward and recompense of their labors. Rather, they paid greater attention to and consideration of their defects and weaknesses than to their perfections and merits. For this reason they thought and spoke of themselves so humbly, expecting the recompense of the future life not from their own merits but from God’s mercy and grace—just as Christ taught us to think and speak after doing good works, lest the good works we have done be corrupted by pride.

> Luke 17: “When you have done all that was commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were obliged to do.” The author also seems here to allude to the Apostle’s words in Romans 6: “The wages of sin is death; but the grace of God is eternal life.” There eternal life is not called the wages of good works, as eternal death is called the wages of sin. Hence heretics infer that the works of the just are not meritorious of eternal life. See Bellarmine, book 3, *On Justification*.

> But Saint Augustine, explaining the reasoning of that statement, writes as follows (Letter 505): “Eternal life, which will be possessed without end at the end, is therefore given in return for preceding merits; yet because the same merits for which it is given were not acquired by us through our own sufficiency, but were produced in us by grace, it is itself also called grace—not for any other reason than that it is given freely; nor because it is not given for merits, but because the merits themselves for which it is given were also given.”

> And below: “When the Apostle had said, ‘The wages of sin is death,’ who would not most fittingly and consistently have judged that he should add: ‘But the wages of justice is eternal life’? For just as death is owed as the wages of sin, so eternal life is owed as the wages of justice. But the blessed Apostle, fighting with the greatest vigilance against human pride, says: ‘The wages of sin is death.’ Properly ‘wages,’ because it is owed, because it is duly repaid, because it is rendered according to merit. Then, lest justice exalt itself on account of human merit, just as human merit is unquestionably evil when it is sin, he did not state the contrary by saying, ‘The wages of justice is eternal life,’ but said: ‘The grace of God is eternal life.’”

> And again, in the same letter: “O human being, if you are to receive eternal life, it is indeed the wages of justice, but for you it is grace, for whom justice itself is grace. It would be returned to you as something owed if justice, to which it is owed, came from you.” Thus far Saint Augustine.

> From this we learn that the Apostle could rightly have said, “The wages of justice is eternal life,” just as he said, “The wages of sin is death”; but he did not wish to say this, in order to avoid the danger of human pride and to prevent anyone from thinking that we possess justice from ourselves in the same way that we possess sins from ourselves. Thus eternal life is called grace, not because it is not the reward of merit or the recompense of those who serve Christ, but because we have even our merits from grace and not from ourselves apart from grace.

> In this way, then, those holy anchorites and truly humble in heart whom Cassian here commends, understanding that our merits do not come from ourselves but from God’s grace, proclaimed that they hoped for the recompense of the future life not on the basis of the merit of their works but from the Lord’s mercy: partly from humility, which does not recognize its own merits, and partly because, on account of the uncertainty of their own justice and perseverance to the end, they placed their entire trust in God’s mercy alone. Yet they did not lack merits because they did not recognize their merits; nor did they fail to receive the recompense of the future life because they received it from God’s mercy.

> See the Council of Trent, session 6, chapter 16, where the nature of merit is carefully explained and where it is shown how eternal life is truly called both grace and reward; and likewise canon 16 of that session, which decrees: “If anyone says that the just ought not to expect and hope from God, through his mercy and the merit of Jesus Christ, for eternal recompense for good works performed in God, if they persevere in good conduct and in keeping the divine commandments to the end, let him be anathema.”]

for this reason they proclaimed that they hoped for the recompense of the future life not from the merit of works [Col. 0451A] but from the Lord’s mercy, claiming nothing for themselves from such great watchfulness when compared with others, since they ascribed even this watchfulness not to their own industry but to divine grace. Nor did they flatter themselves on the negligence of the inferior and lukewarm; rather, by contemplating those whom they knew truly to be free from sin and already enjoying eternal blessedness in the kingdom of heaven, they continually sought humility. Thus [Note: [Col. 0452C] He notes three considerations by which humility is prepared and the danger of exaltation avoided. The first is consideration of divine grace, by which we are what we are and without which we can do nothing pertaining to salvation; this is the consideration that the author chiefly inculcates here. The second is consideration of our weakness, worthlessness, and misery, both in soul and in body, which are so great that each seems to be nothing other than a reservoir of every misery and evil. All bodily misery flows into the body, and all spiritual misery into the soul. Hence each person may rightly say to himself the words of Ecclesiasticus 10: “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” The third is consideration of the purity and perfection of the blessed spirits, free from every stain of sin and enjoying the beatific vision.]

by this consideration they both avoided the ruin of pride and always found what they should strive toward and what they should lament. They understood that, impeded by the burden of the flesh, they could not attain the purity of heart they desired.

## CHAPTER XVI  
### That we cannot approach even the labor of attaining perfection without God’s mercy and inspiration

Accordingly, following their traditions and instructions, we must hasten toward it by devoting ourselves to fasts, vigils, prayers, and contrition of heart and body [Col. 0452A], lest we empty all these practices of their meaning by this very disease. For we must believe not only that we cannot possess perfection itself through our own industry or labor, but also that we cannot perform even those practices that we undertake for its sake—that is, our labors, efforts, and disciplines—without the help of divine protection, and of his inspiration, correction, and exhortation, which he is accustomed graciously to pour into our hearts, either through another person or by visiting us himself.

[Note: [Col. 0452C] Here you have four aids of divine grace by which God turns and recalls our will from evil, arouses it toward the good, and strengthens and confirms it in the good. In the following chapter he also recalls and commends these individually from many verses of the Psalms, so that, by the example of such a great king and prophet, we may acknowledge God’s benefits and aids toward us with humble and grateful hearts.]

## CHAPTER XVII  
### Various testimonies clearly showing that we can accomplish nothing pertaining to our salvation without God’s help

[Note: [Col. 0452D] Everything here consists of plain, devout, and salutary teaching, most worthy of being read and put into practice.]

Finally, the Author of our salvation instructs us about what we ought not only to feel but also to confess in each and every thing we do [Col. 0452B]. “I cannot do anything of myself,” he says; “but the Father, who remains in me, himself does the works” (John 14). He says this in the person of the assumed human nature: that he can do nothing from himself. And we, who are ashes and earth, should we think that in matters pertaining to our salvation we do not need the Lord’s help?

Let us therefore learn to proclaim daily with the saints, recognizing in each matter both our own weakness and his assistance: “I was thrust, overturned, that I might fall, and the Lord received me. The Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become my salvation” (Psalm 117). And: “Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell. If I said, ‘My foot is shaken,’ your mercy, O Lord, was helping me. According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Psalm 93).

When we see our heart strengthened in the fear of the Lord and in patience, let us say: “The Lord became my stronghold, and he led me out into a broad place” (Psalm 17) [Col. 0453B].

When we understand that our knowledge has increased through the progress of our works, let us say: “For you illuminate my lamp, O Lord my God; illuminate my darkness. For in you I will escape temptation, and in my God I will leap over a wall” (ibid.).

Then, when we feel that we have acquired strength for endurance and are directed more easily and without labor along the path of the virtues, let us say: “O God, who girds me with strength and has made my way blameless; who makes my feet like those of a deer and sets me upon high places; who teaches my hands for battle” (ibid.).

When we have obtained discernment, by which, strengthened, we can strike down our adversaries, let us proclaim to God: “Your discipline corrected me to the end, and your discipline itself will teach me. You enlarged my steps beneath me, and my footprints were not weakened” (ibid.).

And because we have been so strengthened by your knowledge and power, let us confidently continue with the words that follow and say: “I will pursue my enemies and overtake them, and I will not turn back until they fail. I will crush them, and they will not be able to stand; they will fall beneath my feet” (ibid.).

Again, remembering our weakness and recognizing that, surrounded by fragile flesh, we cannot overcome such bitter enemies of the vices without his help [Col. 0454A], let us say: “In you we will gore our enemies with the horn, and in your name we will despise those who rise up against us. For I will not trust in my bow, and my sword will not save me. For you saved us from those who afflicted us, and you confounded those who hated us” (Psalm 43).

“But you also girded me with strength for war, and you cast down beneath me all who rose up against me. And you gave me the backs of my enemies, and you destroyed those who obeyed me” (Psalm 17).

And, reflecting that we cannot conquer by our own weapons, let us say: “Take up arms and shield, and rise to my aid; draw the sword and close the way against those who persecute me; say to my soul, ‘I am your salvation’” (Psalm 34). “You made my arms like a bronze bow, and you gave me the protection of your salvation, and your right hand received me” (Psalm 17) [Col. 0454B].

“For our fathers did not possess the land by their sword, and their arm did not save them, but your right hand and your arm and the light of your face, because you were pleased with them” (Psalm 43).

Finally, as we attentively review all his benefits with thanksgiving—whether we have fought, or obtained from him illumination of knowledge, or the discipline of discernment, or whether he has armed us with his weapons and strengthened us with the belt of strength, or given us the backs of our enemies and granted us the power to crush them like dust before the face of the wind—let us cry out to him with the innermost affection of our hearts:

“I will love you, O Lord, my strength. The Lord is my stronghold and my refuge and my deliverer. My God is my helper, and I will hope in him; my protector and the horn of my salvation and my defender. Praising him, I will call upon the Lord, and I shall be saved from my enemies” (Psalm 17).

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### That we are fortified by God’s grace not only in our natural condition but also in his daily dispensation

[Note: [Col. 0454D] Consider the matters for which thanks ought daily to be given to God’s grace. The Apostle frequently and earnestly exhorts us to render such thanksgiving to God. Ephesians 5: “Give thanks always for all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God and the Father.” When he says “for all things,” he intends not so much persons as things themselves—that is, whatever goods they understood themselves to possess, of whatever kind or order. Another statement makes this clearer, 1 Thessalonians 5: “Give thanks in all things.” For one who says “in all things” clearly means that he is speaking of things, certainly good things, and permits nothing to be excluded from them.

> Again, Colossians 3: “Whatever you do in word or deed, do everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to God and the Father through him.”

> The holy Fathers commend the same practice. Chrysostom, homily 26 on Matthew: “The Apostle says: ‘Be grateful.’ For the memory of benefits and perpetual confession of thanks is the best guardian of benefits. Therefore those revered and salutary mysteries that we celebrate in every gathering of the Church are called the Eucharist, that is, thanksgiving.”

> Augustine, *Soliloquies*, chapter 18: “I will recall to my mind all the good things, O Lord, that you have done for me from my youth throughout my whole life. For I know that ingratitude greatly displeases you. It is the root of all spiritual evil and a certain wind that dries up and burns every good thing, blocking the fountain of your mercy over a human being. Through it, dead evils arise, and living works die.”

> And in *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 11: “The worship of God consists chiefly in this: that the soul not be ungrateful to him. Hence, in that truly singular sacrifice, we are admonished to give thanks to the Lord our God.” See Saint Bernard, sermon 52 on the *Song of Songs*.]

We should therefore give him thanks not only because he made us rational, or endowed us with the power of free choice, or bestowed upon us the grace of baptism, or granted us the knowledge and assistance of the law, but also for those things that his daily providence confers upon us: namely, that he frees us from the plots of our adversaries; that he cooperates with us so that we may overcome the vices of the flesh; that he protects us from dangers even when we are unaware of them; that he fortifies us against the fall of sin; that he helps and enlightens us, so that we may be able to understand and acknowledge this very help of ours—which some people wish to interpret as nothing other than the law— [Note: [Col. 0455C] He is referring to the heretics known as Pelagians, whose view was that we needed no other help from God than the law or knowledge of the law. Saint Jerome mentions this in book 1, chapter 9, against the Pelagians, and in his commentary on Jeremiah, chapter 25. Saint Augustine likewise says in *On the Grace of Christ*, against Pelagius, among other things: “The very help of grace by which natural possibility is said to be assisted, he placed in the law and in the teaching which he admits is also revealed to us by the Spirit.” And again against the same people: “Let them read and understand; let them look and acknowledge that God works in human hearts not through the law and teaching sounding outwardly, but through an inner, hidden, wondrous, and ineffable power—not only true revelations but also good wills.”]

that, because of our negligences and sins, we are secretly pricked by his inspiration; that, visited by his condescension, we are most salutarily corrected; [Note: [Col. 0455C] We are drawn unwillingly—not because we believe or love God unwillingly or under compulsion, for those notions involve a contradiction, but because God makes willing and obedient those who were unwilling, rebellious, and obstinate, both through external objects, fears, dangers, and exhortations, and especially through his inner movement and efficacious grace. By this grace he moves and persuades human hearts in a manner suited to their dispositions, so that he persuades them, as Saint Augustine says (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 8).

> We are therefore drawn unwillingly, not in the composite sense but in the divided sense, as the dialecticians say. In this same sense the Church prays in a certain secret prayer that God, in his mercy, compel even our rebellious wills toward himself; and in Luke 14 the Lord says to his servant: “Compel them to enter.” This compulsion signifies not violence or necessity but diligent and vehement exhortation, according to the ordinary manner of speaking in which we say that we are compelled when we are earnestly asked and invited.

> Thus the Bride prays in the *Song of Songs* (1): “Draw me after you; we will run after the fragrance of your perfumes.” And Hosea 11: “I will draw them with the cords of Adam,” that is, not by force, as oxen are accustomed to be dragged, but, as he immediately explains, “with the cords of charity.”

> We are indeed said to be drawn in ordinary speech not only when we are compelled and driven, but also when we are led and invited, and even when we are attracted by pleasure. Saint Augustine beautifully teaches this in tractate 26 on John, explaining how the Father draws people to Christ: “A great commendation of grace: no one comes unless drawn. What are we to say here, brothers? If we are drawn to Christ, then we believe unwillingly; then force is applied, and the will is not aroused. Someone may enter a church unwillingly, approach the altar unwillingly, receive the Sacrament unwillingly; but he cannot believe unless he wishes to.”

> And below: “Do not imagine that someone is drawn unwillingly: the soul is drawn by love. Nor should we fear that people who weigh words and are especially remote from divine realities will criticize us on account of this evangelical word of the Holy Scriptures and say to us: ‘How do I believe willingly if I am drawn?’ I say: it is too little to go willingly; you are also drawn by pleasure. What is it to be drawn by pleasure? ‘Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the desires of your heart.’ And there is a certain pleasure of the heart for which that heavenly bread is sweet.

> “Moreover, if poets were permitted to say, ‘Each person is drawn by his own pleasure’—not by necessity but by pleasure, not by obligation but by delight—how much more strongly ought we to say that a human being is drawn to Christ when he delights in eternal life?”

> Again, below: “You show a green branch to a sheep and draw it; nuts are shown to a child, and he is drawn.” And shortly afterward: “If, then, these things, which are revealed among earthly delights and pleasures to those who love them, draw them, will Christ, revealed by the Father, not draw? For what does the soul desire more strongly than truth?” Thus far Augustine.]

that we are sometimes even drawn by him unwillingly toward salvation; and finally, that he directs our free will itself, which is more readily inclined toward vices, toward better fruit and bends it toward the way of the virtues by the visitation of his prompting.

## CHAPTER XIX  
### That this faith concerning God’s grace was handed down by the ancient Fathers

[Note: [Col. 0456C] Humility toward God consists in acknowledging God’s benefits, giving thanks for them, and subjecting oneself to the divine will. The Apostle Peter calls this “being humbled under the powerful hand of God” (1 Peter 1), and, for God’s sake, also submitting one’s head to human beings—that is, to superiors—as ministers and instruments of God.

> Saint Bernard says in one of his sermons: “The whole sum of humility seems to consist in this: that our will be subject, as is fitting, to the divine will,” as the Prophet says: “Will not my soul be subject to God?” (Psalm 61). “I know, indeed, that every creature, whether it wishes or not, is subject to the Creator. But voluntary submission is sought from a rational creature, so that it may voluntarily sacrifice to the Lord and confess his name—not because he is terrible and holy, nor because he is omnipotent, but because he is good.

> “This submission, however, must be threefold: we must entirely will what we are certain God wills, and similarly detest what we are certain he does not will. But when it is uncertain whether he wills or does not will something, we should neither will it completely nor refuse it entirely.” Thus Saint Bernard.]

This is properly humility toward God; this is the sincere faith of the most ancient Fathers, which has remained undefiled among their successors even to the present day. To this faith [Note: [Col. 0456D] That is, miracles worthy of apostolic men and corresponding to the virtues and miracles of the apostles. The paraphrast expresses the point somewhat more clearly: “When apostolic signs, frequently displayed through holy men, bear certain testimony to the faith—not only among us but also among unbelievers.”]

apostolic miracles, manifested through them time and again, give indisputable testimony, not only among us but also among the faithless and unbelieving [Col. 0457A]. Retaining in a simple heart the simple faith of fishermen, they did not conceive it in a worldly spirit through dialectical syllogisms or Ciceronian eloquence; rather, through the experience of a sincere life, through the purity of their conduct, through the correction of their vices, and—to put it more truly—through visible proofs, they discovered that it inheres in the very nature of perfection. Without this faith, neither devotion toward God, nor purification from vices, nor correction of morals, nor the consummation of the virtues can be attained.

## CHAPTER XX  
### Concerning the man who, because of blasphemy, was handed over to an exceedingly unclean spirit
[Col. 0457B] I knew a certain man from among the brethren—would that I had never known him, since after these things he had allowed himself to be burdened by the rank of my order [Note: [Col. 0457C] Namely, the priesthood, into which Gennadius and Trithemius write that Cassian was ordained at Marseilles; hence above (ch. 17) he said that he could not escape the bishop’s hands, lest he be ordained by him. From this it may be inferred that, out of humility, he was in a sense ordained against his will, just as St. Epiphanius reports that St. Jerome’s brother Paulinianus was ordained by him, and Possidius reports the same of St. Augustine. Dionysius, however, says incorrectly—and according to his own interpretation, not the author’s, unless there is a corrupt reading in the manuscript—“He allowed himself to be burdened by the later rank of the order.” By “burdened,” Cassian means “loaded down” with the rank of the priesthood, perhaps with the apostle James III in mind: “Do not become many teachers, knowing that you will receive a greater judgment.” Thus St. Jerome also interprets clerical office in Epistle 62 not as an honor but as a task.] who confessed to a highly reputable old man that he was being assailed by a most serious vice of the flesh. For, contrary to the course of nature, he was consumed by an intolerable ardor of lust for suffering disgrace rather than inflicting it. Then, as a spiritual and true physician, he at once perceived the inner [Note: [Col. 0457D] Some manuscripts read: “As a spiritual man and inner physician.”] cause and origin of this illness [Note: [Col. 0457D] We are taught here that one sin is very often the cause of another sin (St. Thomas, *Summa* I–II, q. 87, a. 2); and it follows that certain things are sins in such a way that they are also punishments for sins, since a subsequent sin is the punishment of a preceding one. For, just as here blasphemy or pride was the cause of lust, so lust was the punishment of blasphemy or pride. Hence St. Gregory says in Homily 11 on Ezekiel: “The sin which is not quickly erased through repentance is either sin, or the cause of sin, and at the same time the punishment of sin. For everything committed first is sin; but if it is not quickly wiped away by repentance, almighty God, in a just judgment, permits a mind bound by sins to fall also into another fault, so that the person who did not wish to cleanse by weeping and correction what he had done may begin to heap sin upon sin. Therefore sin that is not dissolved by the lament of repentance is at once sin and the cause of sin, because from it arises that by which the sinner’s mind is still more tightly bound. But the sin that follows from sin is at once sin and the punishment of sin, because, as blindness increases, it is generated in retribution for the earlier fault, so that the very growth of vices is already, as it were, punishment in the sinner.” Thus far Gregory. He then teaches that sometimes one and the same sin is both sin and the punishment of sin, and at the same time the cause of sin. He confirms this with many testimonies and examples from Scripture.]. Sighing heavily, he said: “The Lord would never have permitted you to be handed over to so wicked a spirit unless you had blasphemed against him in some way.” When the man learned this, he immediately fell face-down at the old man’s feet on the ground, struck with the greatest astonishment, as though he saw the secrets of his heart disclosed by God; and he confessed that in thought he had blasphemed against the Son of God. From this it is evident that a person possessed by the spirit of pride, or who is blasphemous toward God, is deprived of the integrity of perfection, as one who inflicts injury upon the one from whom the gifts of purity are to be hoped for, and does not deserve the sanctification of chastity.

## CHAPTER XXI. The example of Joash, king of Judah, showing what he deserved because of pride

We read something of this kind in the Book of Chronicles [Note: [Col. 0458C] He was the son of Ahaziah, son of Joram, son of Jehoshaphat. 4 Kings XI and 2 Chronicles XXIV. There was another Joash, king of Israel—that is, of the ten tribes—who began to reign while this Joash was still alive, 4 Kings XIII and 2 Chronicles XXV.]: Joash, king of Judah, was brought to the kingship at seven years of age by Jehoiada the high priest, and, as long as that priest lived, he was praised in every respect according to the testimony of Scripture. Hear what Scripture records about him after Jehoiada’s death, and how, lifted up by pride [Col. 0458B], he was handed over to a shameful affliction:

“After Jehoiada had died, the princes of Judah entered and [Note: [Col. 0458C] St. Jerome, in his *Hebrew Questions* on this passage, noted: “They worshiped him as God; and he yielded, flattered by their attentions, so that he allowed himself to be worshiped as God.” This agrees with Cassian’s words.] worshiped the king. He, flattered by their attentions, consented; and they abandoned the temple of the Lord, the God of their fathers, and served the sacred groves and carved images. And great wrath came against Judah and Jerusalem because of this sin” (2 Chronicles XXIV).

And a little later:

“When the year had revolved, the army of Syria came up against him, and entered Judah and Jerusalem. They killed all the princes of the people, and sent all the spoil to the king at Damascus. And although only a very small number of Syrians had come, the Lord delivered an immeasurable multitude into their hands, because they had abandoned the Lord, the God of their fathers. And against Joash also the Syrians carried out shameful judgments, and when they had departed they left him in great illnesses” (2 Chronicles XXIV) [Note: [Col. 0458D] St. Jerome likewise interprets this as: “Inflicting shameful judgments upon him,” either because they did shameful things to him, or because, while killing his sons, they reproached him for the crime he had committed against Zechariah (*Hebrew Questions*, in the passage cited above). Cassian follows the former interpretation, meaning that King Joash, because of his pride and arrogance, came to such misery that he was defiled by the Syrians, impure men, through foul and shameful lust. Josephus and others, however, mention nothing of this kind, but only that Joash suffered a very serious illness and was killed by his own men; nor do the Greek interpreters say anything other than: καὶ ἐν Ἰωὰς ἐποίησαν κρίματα—“and they executed judgments upon Joash” (Josephus, Book IX of the *Antiquities*, ch. 8; Suidas, under “Joash”).].

Do you see to what disgraceful and filthy afflictions pride deserves to be handed over? For the one who, lifted up by arrogance, allowed himself to be worshiped as God was, according to the Apostle, handed over to shameful passions and to a debased mind, so that he might suffer what is not fitting (Romans I) [Note: [Col. 0459B] He applies here the Apostle’s statement in Romans I, where he says that the pagan philosophers were handed over to pride and ingratitude, and repeats three times that they were handed over by God: first, to the desires of their hearts, for impurity; second, to shameful passions—that is, shameful, dishonorable, and infamous lusts; third, to a debased mind, so that they might do what is not fitting.
