Thus he says that King Joash, lifted up by arrogance, was handed over by God to shameful passions and to a debased mind. Yet the case was very different from that of those philosophers. They were handed over so that, willingly and spontaneously, they might do what is not fitting; Joash, however, was handed over so that he might suffer it even unwillingly. God handed them over to foul desires, not by thrusting or driving them forward, but by abandoning them and withdrawing the help of his grace, in accordance with Psalm LXXX: “I let them go according to the desires of their hearts; they shall walk in their own inventions.” But, according to the author’s interpretation, God handed King Joash over to shameful passions by failing to defend and protect him from the impure mockery of his enemies, so that he might suffer what is not fitting. Here *ut* (“so that”) signifies not cause but result, as it often does elsewhere in Scripture.].

And because, as Scripture says [Note: [Col. 0459C] St. Jerome says: “Whoever attributes to himself the good that he does, even if he seems to perform no evil with his hands, has already lost the innocence of his heart, in which he has placed himself before the giver of gifts. Therefore his Creator abhors him as guilty, since he sees him ungrateful for his benefits” (see above, on chapter 6).], “everyone who exalts his heart is unclean before God” (Proverbs XVI, according to the Septuagint), this man, puffed up with the swelling of his heart, is handed over to be mocked by the most shameful confusion, so that, humbled in this way, he may recognize himself as unclean through the filth of the flesh and the consciousness of an impure passion—something which, in the elation of his mind, he had refused to recognize. Thus the shameful contamination of the flesh may reveal the hidden uncleanness of his heart, which he had contracted through the evil of pride, and by the manifest pollution of his body he may be proved impure, since, through the elation of his spirit, he had not perceived that he had been made unclean.

## CHAPTER XXII. That every proud soul is subjected to mockery by spiritual wickedness

[Col. 0460A]

It is therefore clearly proved that every soul possessed by the swelling of pride is handed over to intellectual Syrians—that is, to spiritual wickedness—and becomes entangled in the passions of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0459C] Just as King Joash is said to have been handed over to the Syrians, by whom manifest and shameful vices and sins are symbolically signified, or to the evil spirits whom he calls intellectual Syrians and spiritual wickedness, as the Apostle says, “spiritual wickedness in heavenly places” (Ephesians VI). For “Syrian,” or “Syria,” is interpreted as “subtle,” “deceiving,” or “their curse”; such epithets suit both demons and vices.], so that, humbled at least by earthly vices, it may recognize itself as carnally polluted and unclean. Previously, raised up by the torpor of its mind, it could not understand that it had been made unclean in God’s sight through the elation of its heart. In this way, once humbled, a person may depart from his former torpor, and, cast down and confounded by the disgrace of carnal passions, may thereafter hasten more ardently to devote himself to spiritual fervor [Note: [Col. 0459D] It has already been proved by many examples, from the beginning of the world, that pride is such a great evil that, in order to cure it, God often permits a person to fall into other sins, especially shameful and dishonorable ones, so that, recognizing his misery, he may be humbled. St. Augustine asserts this generally of more serious sins in Book XIV of *The City of God*, chapter 13: “I dare say that it is useful for the proud to fall into some open and manifest sin by which those who had fallen through pleasing themselves may come to displease themselves. For Peter was more healthily displeased with himself when he wept than pleased with himself when he presumed.” The sacred psalm also says: “Fill their faces with shame, and they will seek your name, O Lord” (Psalm LXXXI)—that is, they will seek to please you by seeking your name, they who had pleased themselves by seeking their own. Cassian teaches the same thing here particularly and specifically concerning the sin of lust, as does St. Gregory in Book XXVI of the *Moralia*, chapter 12, where he says: “Pride has often been the seedbed of lust; for while it raised their spirit as though to a height, the flesh plunged them into the depths. First they are secretly lifted up, but afterward they fall publicly; while they swell inwardly through hidden movements of the heart, they fall outwardly through open lapses of the body. Thus, thus, the elated deserved to be struck by a just retribution: because by their pride they set themselves above human beings, by their lust they are reduced to the likeness of beasts. ‘Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them’ (Psalm XLVIII). As though by a feather of knowledge they had been lifted on high—those of whom Paul said: ‘Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their reasoning’ (Romans I). And how they fell into the pleasure of beasts, or worse than beasts, he adds: ‘God handed them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity.’ Behold: the flesh plunged down those whom proud knowledge had lifted up, and they were cast beneath the place from which they seemed to rise above others.” Thus far Gregory.

St. Thomas also excellently illustrates and confirms the same doctrine in these words (*Summa* II–II, q. 162, a. 6, ad 3): “Just as in syllogisms leading to an impossibility a person is sometimes convicted by being brought to a more evident absurdity, so also, in order to convict the pride of human beings, God sometimes punishes them by permitting them to fall into carnal sins. Although these may be lesser sins, they contain a more manifest shame. Hence Isidore says in Book II of *On the Supreme Good*, chapter 21, that pride is worse than every vice, either because it is assumed by the highest and foremost persons, or because it arises from an act of justice and virtue and its guilt is felt less. Lust of the flesh, however, is conspicuous to everyone because it is immediately shameful in itself; yet, by God’s dispensation, it is less serious than pride. But the person held by pride, without perceiving it, falls into lust of the flesh, so that, humbled by this, he may rise from his confusion. From this the gravity of pride is also evident. For just as a wise physician allows a sick person to fall into a lesser illness as a remedy for a greater one, so the greater seriousness of the sin of pride is shown by the very fact that, as its remedy, God permits people to fall into other sins.].

## CHAPTER XXIII. That perfection cannot be attained except by the virtue of humility

[Col. 0460B]

It is therefore plainly shown [Note: [Col. 0460D] Humility is the foundation of all virtues, as will be explained more fully below (ch. 31). Hence St. Gregory says: “Whoever gathers virtues without humility is like one who carries dust into the wind” (*Homily 7 on the Gospels*; *Book on the Degrees of Humility*).] that no one can attain the end of perfection and purity except through true humility [Note: [Col. 0461B] Not fictitious or feigned humility—that is, no humility at all—but true humility. Humility is the virtue by which a person, through the truest knowledge of himself, regards himself as contemptible, says St. Bernard. Hence St. Jerome also writes in his Epistle to Celantia (Epistle 14): “Hold nothing more excellent than humility, nothing more lovable. For it is the chief preserver, and, as it were, the guardian of all virtues. Nothing makes us so acceptable to human beings and to God as being great in the merit of our life and lowly in humility; therefore Scripture says: ‘The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God’ (Ecclesiasticus III). And the Lord speaks through the prophet: ‘Upon whom shall I rest, except upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?’ (Isaiah LXVI). Yet pursue humility—not the humility displayed and pretended by bodily gesture or a broken tone of voice, but that expressed by the pure affection of the heart. For it is one thing to possess virtue and another to possess the likeness of virtue; one thing to follow the shadow of things and another to follow the truth. Much more deformed is the pride that hides beneath certain signs of humility. I do not know how it is that vices are more shameful when they conceal themselves under the appearance of virtues.”], which, first offering it to the brethren, he also presents to God in the inner chamber of his heart, believing that without his protection and the help which he supplies at every moment, he cannot possibly obtain the perfection that he desires and toward which he runs with all his strength.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Whom spiritual pride afflicts, and whom carnal pride afflicts

Thus far, concerning spiritual pride, which we have said afflicts those who are perfect, let it suffice that we have spoken as far as the feebleness of our understanding has been able, by God’s gift [Note: [Col. 0461C] What Cassian calls spiritual pride, and how he distinguishes it from carnal pride, was discussed above (ch. 2), and can also be understood sufficiently from this chapter.]. This kind of pride is known and experienced by few, because not many strive to attain perfect purity of heart, so that they may be able to reach these levels of combat; nor is there any cleansing from the preceding vices, whose nature and remedies we set forth at the beginning of the individual books. It usually afflicts only those who, having conquered the higher vices, are already almost placed at the summit of the virtues [Col. 0462A]. Since the most subtle enemy could not overcome them through a carnal fall, he tries to cast them down and overthrow them through a spiritual ruin, seeking by this means to strip them of all the rewards of their former labors, acquired with great toil.

But us, who are still entangled in earthly passions, he does not deign to tempt in this way; rather, he overthrows us by a coarser—and, so to speak, carnal—elation. Therefore, concerning this form of pride, by which people like us, especially the minds of the young and of beginners, are most often endangered, I think it necessary, in accordance with my promise, to say a few things.

## CHAPTER XXV. Description of carnal pride

[Col. 0462B]

This, then, is the pride of which we have spoken [Note: [Col. 0461C] He describes carnal pride and lists several of its degrees. In this connection it seems worthwhile, and entirely consistent with our purpose, to set out here the twelve degrees of pride enumerated by St. Bernard, directly opposed to the twelve degrees of humility which St. Benedict proposes—not so much as things to be counted as to be climbed—in chapter 3 of his Rule. St. Bernard explains them most beautifully in Treatise 29.

The first degree of pride is curiosity, which he teaches is detected by these signs: “If you see a monk in whom you previously had good confidence beginning to let his eyes wander, holding his head erect and keeping his ears pricked up, recognize from the movements of the outer man that the inner man has been changed.”

The second is levity of mind, consisting in a person’s readiness to judge the deeds of others and to blurt out anything whatsoever: “A monk,” he says, “who neglects himself and looks curiously at others, while he looks up to some as his superiors and looks down on others as inferiors, sees in some what he envies and in others what he mocks. Thus, as the mind is made light by the mobility of the eyes, it now raises itself on high through pride and now sinks into the depths through envy: in the one case wicked, in the other vain, and in both proud.”

The third degree is foolish joy. For it is characteristic of the proud always to seek pleasant things and to avoid sad ones, according to the saying: “The heart of fools is where there is joy” (Ecclesiasticus XVII). Thus the monk who has already descended two degrees of pride, having arrived through curiosity at levity of mind, when he sees the joy he always seeks interrupted by the frequent sadness that he derives from another’s prosperity, impatient of his own humiliation, flees to the counsel of false consolation. You will hear such a man groaning or see him weeping either never or rarely; clowning appears in his gestures, cheerfulness on his face, vanity in his walk. He is inclined to joking and quick and ready to laugh.

A little later: “For just as a bladder swollen with collected air, if pierced with a tiny hole and squeezed, crackles as it deflates, while the air, not released all at once but expelled in a narrow stream, produces a series of sounds, so the monk, when he has filled his heart with vain and clownish thoughts and, because of the discipline of silence, finds no fuller outlet for the wind of vanity, expels it through bursts of laughter amid the narrowness of his throat.”

The fourth is boastfulness. Whoever reaches this degree is full of words, says Bernard, and the spirit of his belly constrains him. He hungers and thirsts for listeners to whom he may boast of his vanities, pour out everything he feels, and make known what kind and how great he is. When an opportunity for speaking is found, if the conversation turns to literature, old and new materials are produced, opinions fly, and inflated words resound. He anticipates the questioner, answers the one who has not asked, asks and answers himself, and cuts short the unfinished words of his interlocutor, and so forth. If the discussion concerns religion, visions and dreams are immediately brought forward, and so forth.

The fifth degree is singularity, by which a person does something unusual or conducts himself in an unusual manner so that he may be esteemed above others. Thus it is not enough for him that the common rule of the monastery or the examples of the elders encourage him. Nor does he strive to be better than he appears; he does not desire to live better, but to appear to live better, so that he may say: “I am not like the rest of humanity” (Luke XVIII). He takes more pleasure in one fast that he undertakes while the others are dining than if he had fasted seven days together with the others. One private little prayer seems more suitable to him than the entire psalmody of a single night, and so forth, very beautifully.

The sixth is arrogance [Col. 0462D], by which a person attributes more to himself than he possesses and considers himself superior to others in knowledge, virtue, prudence, and so forth. As Bernard says, he believes what he hears, praises what he does, and does not consider what he intends; and although in every other matter he trusts himself more than others, concerning himself alone he trusts others more than himself. Whatever he recognizes as having been praised in him, he arrogantly attributes not to the ignorance or goodwill of the person praising him, but to his own merits.

The seventh degree is presumption, which the Latins also call overconfidence. By it a person trusts so much in his own industry or strength that he considers himself equal to everything and undertakes things that exceed his powers. For, says St. Bernard, whoever thinks himself superior to others, how can he not presume more about himself than about others? He sits first in assemblies, responds first in councils, approaches without being summoned, intervenes without being sent, rearranges what has been arranged, and repairs what has been done. Whatever he himself has not done or arranged, he considers neither correctly done nor beautifully ordered. He judges those who judge and prejudges those who are going to judge. If, when the time comes, he is not promoted to the priorship, he considers his abbot either envious or deceived. If some ordinary obedience [or office] is assigned to him, he becomes indignant and disdains it, thinking that he ought not to be occupied with lesser matters, since he feels himself suited to greater ones.

The eighth is the defense of sins. Excuses for sins are made in many ways. The person who excuses himself either says, “I did not do it”; or, “I did it, certainly, but I did it well”; or, “If I did it badly, it was not very badly”; or, “If it was very badly, it was not with a bad intention.” If he is convicted even concerning that intention, like Adam and Eve, he tries to excuse himself by another’s persuasion.

The ninth is simulated confession, which is much more dangerous than bold and stubborn defense. For when some people are accused of more obvious faults, knowing that they would not be believed if they defended themselves, they subtly discover an argument for defense by answering with words of deceitful confession. As it is written: “There is one who wickedly humbles himself, while his inward parts are full of deceit” (Ecclesiasticus XIX). His face is lowered, his body is prostrated, and, if he can, he forces some tears from himself; he interrupts his voice with sighs and his words with groans.

And below: “A glorious thing is humility, which even pride itself seeks to cloak itself with, lest it become contemptible.” Yet this evasion is quickly detected by a superior if he is not lightly swayed by this proud humility, by which the offender seeks more to conceal his guilt or postpone his punishment. For the person whose confession is feigned, if questioned with even one slight insult or a small punishment, can no longer either pretend humility or conceal the pretense: he murmurs, growls, becomes angry, and is shown not to remain at the fourth degree of humility but to have fallen into the ninth degree of pride, and so forth.

The tenth is rebellion, by which a person refuses to obey his superiors or despises their commands. “Bold-faced,” he says, “and then shameless, he falls by rebellion into the tenth degree, all the worse because he does so all the more desperately. He who had previously despised the brethren while secretly arrogant now, openly disobedient, despises even his master.”

The eleventh is freedom to sin. Through it the monk, expelled from or having left the monastery, since he no longer fears his master or respects the brethren, takes pleasure in fulfilling his desires all the more securely because he is all the freer, desires from which he had been restrained in the monastery both by shame and by fear.

Finally, the twelfth degree is the habit of sinning, when a person, having entirely cast away the fear of God, plunges into every kind of sin and persists in it—as apostates commonly do, who are described here—and at length, bound by the habit of evil custom, rolls down into the depths of evil.

“After,” says Bernard, “the terrible judgment of God has allowed the first crimes to go unpunished, experienced pleasure is willingly repeated; once repeated, it becomes seductive; as desire revives, reason falls asleep; habit binds; the wretched person is dragged into the depths of evil and handed over captive to the tyranny of vices. Absorbed in the gulf of carnal desires, he forgets both his own reason and the fear of God and says in his heart, like a fool: ‘There is no God’ (Psalm XIII). Now he uses permitted things indiscriminately as though they were lawful; now his mind, hands, and feet are not restrained from conceiving, committing, or investigating unlawful things,” and so forth.

These remarks on the degrees of pride are drawn from St. Bernard, from whom Turrecremata, Trithemius, and others likewise took them. The reader may consult the rest in Bernard himself, and will not regret having done so.

But so that these things may be more evident to the less learned, and may be seen more clearly as though painted on a tablet and almost touched with the hands, since, according to the Philosopher, “Things set beside their opposites shine more brightly,” it seemed worthwhile, and in keeping with our purpose, to present here to the religious reader a pair of ladders: one of humility and the other of pride, distinguished by their respective degrees, set against and opposite one another, roughly written and sketched [Col. 0464A], and to illuminate both with several sayings from Scripture and the holy Fathers written alongside them.

First, as reason requires, we shall present the ladder of humility, consisting, according to St. Benedict’s teaching, of its twelve degrees. But since it would be excessively long and unnecessary to write here the same degrees together with the whole text of chapter 7, where St. Benedict proposes and explains them, we shall note them briefly and summarily, first in the words of St. Benedict himself, then in those of St. Thomas Aquinas, and finally in the not-to-be-despised verses of Abbot Trithemius, who expressed the same degrees concisely and poetically.

With regard to St. Thomas, however, I have found that his text, in this passage, is plainly corrupt. He does indeed enumerate the same degrees, and in the same number as St. Benedict, and explains their rationale; but he does not give them in the same order, rather in precisely the reverse order. He calls the twelfth what St. Benedict calls the first, and the first what he calls the twelfth, and so on, as can be seen both in the first argument of the question cited and in the body of the article. It is therefore evident that his text is corrupt, both because it plainly conflicts with the Rule and the words of St. Benedict, about which he discusses and raises the question (*Treatise 59 on the Rule*): “Whether the twelve degrees of humility are suitably distinguished according to Blessed Benedict”; and because John Turrecremata, who transferred almost the whole of that text of St. Thomas into his own commentary, reads it in the opposite manner and reports St. Thomas’s words in such a way that they agree perfectly with St. Benedict. But now let us approach the ladders.

## THE LADDER OF HUMILITY

Religious reader, I propose to you and to myself two ladders [ [Col. 0464D] At the end of this volume you may see a graceful picture of both ladders—the ladder of humility and that of pride—which Gazaeus included in his edition.], although roughly constructed: one of humility and the other of pride; one described by St. Benedict and the other by St. Bernard, our two patrons who urge humility and hate pride; each distinguished by its own degrees set opposite the other: the former upright, so that we may ascend; the latter thrown down, so that we may not descend; the former reaching toward heaven, the other toward hell. If we are of sound mind, it is ours to choose the good and reject the evil. May God grant this to me and to you.

Jacob saw a ladder standing on the earth, whose top touched heaven; and he also saw the angels of God ascending and descending by it, and the Lord leaning upon the ladder, and so forth (Genesis 28).

St. Benedict, chapter 7 of his Rule:

“Divine Scripture cries out to us, saying: ‘Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.’ In saying this, it shows us that every exaltation is a form of pride.”

And below:

“Therefore, brothers, if we desire to reach the summit of the highest humility and wish to arrive quickly at that heavenly exaltation—which is ascended through the humility of the present life—then, by our ascending actions, we must erect that ladder which appeared in Jacob’s dream, by which descending and ascending angels were shown to him. We understand that this descent and ascent mean nothing other than descending through exaltation and ascending through humility. The ladder itself, when erected, is our life in this world, which, when the heart is humbled, is raised by the Lord to heaven. We call the sides of the ladder our body and soul, into which divine calling has inserted various degrees of humility or discipline, to be climbed.”

And at the end of the same chapter:

“Therefore, after all these degrees of humility have been climbed, the monk will soon arrive at the love of God, that love which casts out fear. Through it he will begin to observe without any labor, as though naturally and from habit, all the things he previously observed not without fear—not now from fear of Gehenna, but from love of Christ, from the good habit itself, and from delight in virtue, which the Lord will deign to display by the Holy Spirit to his laborer, now cleansed from vices and sins.”

St. Gregory, Book II of the *Dialogues*, chapter 37: “This is the way by which Benedict, beloved of the Lord, ascended to heaven.”

St. Bernard, in his treatise on the degrees of humility:

“Humility is the virtue by which a human being, through the truest knowledge of himself, regards himself as contemptible. This belongs to those who, having arranged ascents in their hearts, advance from virtue to virtue—that is, from degree to degree—until they reach the summit of humility. There, placed as it were in Zion, that is, in contemplation, they behold the truth. For, he says, the lawgiver will give blessing: because he who gave the law will also give blessing; that is, he who commanded humility will lead to truth.”

And below:

“Blessed Benedict arranges this law, by which one is restored to truth, in twelve degrees: just as one comes to Christ through the ten commandments of the law and the twofold circumcision, in which the number twelve is completed, so, after climbing these twelve degrees, one apprehends the truth. Moreover, what else does the fact that the Lord appeared above leaning upon that ladder shown to Jacob as a type of humility suggest to you, except that the knowledge of truth is established at the summit of humility?”

In the same place:

“‘Come,’ says the Savior. Where? ‘To me,’ the truth. By what way? ‘Through humility.’ With what result? ‘I will refresh you.’ But what is the refreshment that truth promises to those ascending and gives to those who arrive? Is it perhaps love? For, as blessed Benedict says, after climbing all the degrees of humility, the monk will soon arrive at this.”

In the same place:

“Firmly setting down the foot of grace and gently drawing along my own foot, which is weak, I shall ascend securely by the ladder of humility until, clinging to truth, I pass over into the breadth of love.”

Finally, farther below:

“David seems to have proposed two ways to you when he says: ‘Take away from me the way of iniquity, and graciously grant me your law,’ and so forth. Yet you should know that there is one way, which he nevertheless calls by different names according to its difference from itself: the way of iniquity for those descending, or the way of truth for those ascending. For the degrees of those ascending to the throne and those descending are the same; the way of those ascending to the city and those departing is the same; and there is one door for those entering the house and those leaving it. Finally, by one ladder Jacob saw angels ascending and descending.

“What is the point of this? Clearly, if you desire to return to the truth, you need not seek a new way that you do not know, but the known way by which you descended. Following your own footsteps with corresponding steps, you should climb through the same degrees of humility by which you descended through pride, so that what was the twelfth degree of pride for one descending may be the first of humility for one ascending; the eleventh may be found to be the second; the tenth, the third; the ninth, the fourth; the eighth, the fifth; the seventh, the sixth; the sixth, the seventh; the fifth, the eighth; the fourth, the ninth; the third, the tenth; the second, the eleventh; the first, the twelfth. Once these degrees of pride have been found—or rather recognized—in yourself, you will no longer labor to seek the way of humility.”

Thus far St. Bernard.

## THE LADDER OF PRIDE

You notice, I believe, benevolent reader, that the ladder of pride is inverted and overturned: its feet are at the top, while its head and summit are at the bottom. By contrast, you see the ladder of humility erected, looking toward heaven, indeed touching it. Do not think that this was done rashly or by chance [Col. 0466A]. Lucifer, the father of pride, inverted and overturned his own ladder when, with the order of nature and reason inverted and overturned, he turned away from his creator and toward himself, swelling more and more within himself, and gradually, as though by degrees, rolled down into the depths. Thus, turning backward, he descended with his ladder into the abyss by the very way in which he ought to have ascended; and the sons of pride, his imitators, likewise roll down into the same abyss by a similar progression.

“He is king over all the sons of pride” (Job XLI).

“How have you fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose at dawn?” and so forth. “Your pride has been brought down to the underworld” (Isaiah XIV).

“Core, Dathan, and Abiron descended alive into hell” (Numbers XVI).

“In his presence all who descend into the earth will fall” (Psalm XXI).

“Let not the foot of pride come against me; there all who work iniquity have fallen. They have been driven out, and they could not stand” (Psalm XXXV).

“Let death come upon them, and let them descend alive into hell” (Psalm LIV).

“In it every destruction began” (Tobit IV).

And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You will descend as far as hell. Matthew 11.

St. Jerome, Letter 45:

> “Satan fell from the angelic height for no other reason than pride opposed to humility. For this reason Scripture says: ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ See, brother, what an evil it is to have God as one’s adversary; because of it the arrogant Pharisee is rejected in the Gospel, while the humble Publican is heard.”

St. Augustine, *The City of God*, Book XIV, chapter 13:

> “What could have been the beginning of an evil will except pride? For pride is the beginning of every sin. But what is pride except a desire for perverse exaltation? Perverse exaltation is to abandon the one to whom the mind ought to cling as its principle, and somehow make oneself one’s own principle and become it. This happens when one takes excessive pleasure in oneself. One takes such pleasure in oneself when one falls away from that unchangeable good which ought to have pleased one more than oneself.” [Col. 0466C]

St. Gregory, *Morals*, Book IV, chapter 9:

> “Almighty God had made two creatures capable of knowing him, namely the angelic and the human; but pride struck both and broke them away from the state of their innate uprightness.”

St. Bernard, in his treatise *On the Degrees of Humility*:

> “Compare, if you wish, the first two degrees of pride with the highest two degrees of humility, and see whether curiosity is not restrained in the last and levity in the penultimate. You will find the same correspondence in the others, if you compare them with one another.”

And below:

> “It must be understood that all the degrees which I have divided into twelve can be gathered into only three: in the six higher ones, contempt of the brethren; in the following four, contempt of the master—that is, of superiors; and in the remaining two, contempt of God is brought to completion.” [Col. 0466D]

Finally, Bernard concludes this treatise with great self-abasement and humility:

> “Perhaps you say, brother Godefrid, that I have ultimately presented something other than what you sought and what I myself promised, since, instead of describing degrees of humility, I seem to have described degrees of pride. To this I reply: I could teach only what I have learned. I did not think it fitting for me to describe ascents, since I know more about descending than ascending. Let blessed Benedict set before you the degrees of humility which he first arranged in his own heart; I have nothing to set before you except the order of my own descent. Yet, if it is examined carefully, perhaps a way of ascent may be found in it.

> “If, for example, as you were traveling toward Rome, you encountered a man coming from there and asked him the way, what better guide could he give you than the route by which he had come? As he names the castles, villages, cities, rivers, and mountains through which he passed, announcing his own journey, he foretells yours, so that as you travel you recognize the same places which he passed on his way. [Col. 0467C]

> “Likewise, in this descent of ours you may perhaps find ascending steps, which, as you ascend, you will read more clearly in your own heart than in our book. Amen.”

“Hell enlarged its soul and opened its mouth; and the strong, the exalted, and the glorious shall descend to it.” Isaiah 5.

Carnal pride, when it has taken up residence in the monk’s mind together with a lukewarm and badly undertaken beginning of renunciation, prevents him from descending from his former worldly swelling to the true humility of Christ. It first makes him disobedient and harsh; then it does not allow him to be gentle and approachable. It does not permit him to become equal to the brethren and common among them; nor does it allow him, in accordance with the command of God and our Savior, to be stripped of earthly possessions and made naked.

Since renunciation is nothing other than a sign of mortification and the cross, and since it cannot begin or be established upon any other foundations than these—that one should know oneself to have been spiritually slain with respect to the actions of this world, and should also believe that one will die bodily every day—it does the opposite. It makes him hope for a long life, lays before him many and prolonged illnesses, and fills him with confusion and shame. If, having become naked, he begins to be supported by the possessions of others rather than his own, it persuades him that it is much better for his food and clothing to be supplied from his own substance rather than another’s, according to the saying—for in their dullness and lukewarmness of heart they were sometimes unable even to understand how it had been spoken—“It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20). [Col. 0467A] See above, Book X, chapter 18. [Col. 0467B]

## CHAPTER XXVI

### How one who is badly founded slips daily into a worse condition

> **Note:** Dionysius: “Thus defeated by such sloth of mind and recalled by diabolical unbelief from the spark of faith which they had used and kindled at the beginning of their conversion, they begin,” and so forth. This chapter chiefly concerns novices, whose instruction and discipline are discussed extensively and expressly throughout the fourth book of these *Institutes*. See St. Bernard, Sermon 63 on the *Song of Songs*. [Col. 0467C]

Thus beset by such distrust of mind, and recalled by diabolical unbelief from the spark of faith with which they had seemed to burn at the beginning of their conversion, they begin to guard more carefully the money which they had previously begun to distribute, and preserve it with more vehement avarice, as though, once squandered, they could not restore it. Or, what is worse, they take up again the things which they had previously cast away. Or, which is the third and worst kind of wickedness, they gather things which they had not even possessed before. Having left the world, they are proved to have acquired nothing more than the name and designation of monk. [Col. 0467C] [Col. 0468A]

> **Note:** The three kinds of love of money are explained elsewhere; here they are touched upon only briefly (Book VII, chapter 14). Into these forms monks—especially novices, the inexperienced, and the carnal—gradually fall when overcome by the spirit of pride. [Col. 0467D]

Upon these beginnings, therefore, founded badly and viciously, the entire structure of vices must thereafter arise. Nothing can be built upon such wretched foundations except what will cast down the miserable soul in an even more lamentable ruin.

## CHAPTER XXVII

### An explanation of the vices generated by the disease of pride

When the mind has been hardened by such passions and has begun in detestable lukewarmness, it must daily advance toward worse things and bring the rest of its life to a more deformed end. While it takes pleasure in its former desires and, according to the Apostle, is overcome by sacrilegious love of money,

> **Note:** Love of money in a monk is called sacrilegious for two reasons, one general and one specific. In the general sense, expressed here by the Author, love of money—or avarice—is, according to the Apostle (Colossians 3; Ephesians 3), “the service of idols,” that is, a kind of idolatry, in the sense explained elsewhere (Book VII, chapter 7). Every idolatry and superstition is therefore called sacrilege. Hence the sacrifices of idols are called by Augustine and other Fathers “sacrilegious sacred rites,” and agreements with demons “sacrilegious agreements” (Sidonius, Book III, Letter 12; St. Thomas, *Summa theologica* II-II, question 99, article 3; Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, Book I, chapter 21; Augustine, *Confessions*, Book VIII, chapter 2). In the specific sense, it violates the vow of monastic poverty; such a violation also belongs properly to sacrilege, as St. Thomas teaches. [Col. 0468C]

—as the Apostle likewise declares concerning it, “which is the service of idols” (Ephesians 5; Colossians 3). [Col. 0468B] And again: “For the love of money is the root of all evils,”

> **Note:** The manuscripts read, and better: “can never,” etc. For *for* is superfluous and leaves the sense suspended or obscured. [Col. 0468D]

> **Note:** The Apostle speaks of avarice in this way in two places. First, Ephesians 5: “Know and understand that no fornicator, or unclean person, or covetous person (which is the service of idols) has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.” In Greek: *πλεονέκτης, ὅς ἐστιν εἰδωλολάτρης* (*pleonektēs, hos estin eidōlolatrēs*)—“the covetous person, who is an idolater,” or “worshiper of idols.” Thus our Translator seems to have read the neuter article *ὅ* (*ho*) instead of *ὅς* (*hos*), and *εἰδωλολατρεία* (*eidōlolatreia*) instead of *εἰδωλολάτρης* (*eidōlolatrēs*). [Col. 0468C]

> “Again, in Colossians 3, he says: ‘Put to death your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and avarice, which is the service of idols.’ In Greek: *καὶ τὴν πλεονεξίαν, ἥτις ἐστὶν εἰδωλολατρεία* (*kai tēn pleonexian, hētis estin eidōlolatreia*)—‘and covetousness, which is idolatry.’ In both passages it should be noted that the terms are not *φίλαργυρον* (*philargyron*) and *φιλαργυρίαν* (*philargyrian*), as this Author seems to suggest or assume, but *πλεονέκτην* (*pleonektēn*) and *πλεονεξίαν* (*pleonexian*), which have a broader meaning, as stated elsewhere. Since, however, they are often taken as equivalent, Cassian has confused them here. Other matters concerning these same Apostolic statements may be found noted elsewhere.” [Col. 0468D]

—so that he can never receive in his heart the simple and true humility of Christ (1 Timothy 6), when he either boasts of the nobility of his birth, or is puffed up by the dignity of the world—which he has abandoned bodily but not mentally—or is exalted by the money which he retains for his own ruin. Through these things he is no longer content to bear the yoke of the monastery, nor to be trained by the discipline of any elder.

> **Note:** Here there appears to be a solecism, unless “proud” or something similar is understood; no other noun precedes to which *contentus* could refer, except “the mind hardened by passions” at the beginning of the chapter. The paraphraser noticed this and used other words: “He no longer consents,” he says, “to bear the yoke of the monastery.” [Col. 0468D]

nor does he submit to the discipline of any superior. For whoever has been seized by the disease of pride not only refuses to observe any rule of subjection or obedience, but does not even admit into his ears the teaching of perfection. Spiritual disgust thickens in his heart to such an extent that,

> **Note:** Spiritual conferences are frequently mentioned here. Among the ancient monks, such meetings were customary even for those living in solitude. They will be discussed in their proper place. [Col. 0468D]

whenever a spiritual conference happens to arise, [Col. 0468C] he cannot keep his gaze fixed in one place; rather, his stupid glance wanders here and there, and his eyes are fixed in directions other than the proper one, sideways and obliquely. [Col. 0469A] Instead of salutary sighs, saliva is drawn from his dry throat; throat-clearing is repeatedly provoked without any interruption of phlegm; his fingers play and flutter about, making marks and figures as though writing. All the members of his body are moved here and there, so that while the spiritual conference is taking place he thinks himself seated either upon swarming worms or upon the sharpest spikes. Whatever the simple conference offers for the edification of its hearers, he believes has been said as an insult directed against him.

Throughout the time in which the examination of the spiritual life is being discussed, he is occupied with his suspicions. He does not seek what he ought to take from it for his own progress; instead, with anxious thought he searches for the reasons why each point was said, or silently conjectures what objection he might raise against it. [Col. 0469B] Thus he is unable to grasp anything of what has been arranged most beneficially or to correct himself in any respect.

And so the spiritual conference not only benefits him in nothing, but becomes harmful to him and a cause of greater sin. For since, according to his conscience, he suspects that everything has been said against him, he is hardened by a more obstinate resistance of heart and is driven more fiercely by the goads of anger. Then follow a raised voice, a harsh manner of speaking, bitter and turbulent replies, an upright and restless gait, an easy tongue, and an insolent manner of speaking, never friendly to silence—except when he has conceived some resentment against a brother in his heart. [Col. 0469C]

> **Note:** St. Gregory, *Morals*, Book XXXIV, chapter 20: “Sometimes the proud do not reveal at all the insolent things they feel, and those whose talkativeness can scarcely be restrained sometimes fall silent solely because of the bitterness of inward resentment. Withdrawing the words of their insolence through the pain of their mind, although they are accustomed to speak wrongly, they are worse when silent; for when sinners hear something concerning correction, they angrily suspend even the words of their reply” (Gregory, *Morals*, Book V, chapters 29 and 31, and elsewhere). [Col. 0469D]

Thus his silence is not a sign of compunction or any humility, but of pride and indignation. It is not easy to discern which of the two is more detestable in him: that unrestrained and petulant cheerfulness, or this dreadful and venomous silence. In the former there are untimely speech, light and foolish laughter, and the unbridled, undisciplined elation of the heart; in the latter, silence full of anger and poison, conceived for the sole purpose of prolonging, through silence, the resentment stored up against a brother—not so that it might display the virtue of humility and patience.

And since, possessed by this swelling, he easily brings sadness upon everyone and disdains to humble himself in order to make satisfaction to an injured brother, he also rejects and despises the satisfaction offered to him by that brother. [Col. 0469D]

He is not merely unmoved or softened by any satisfaction from his brother; he is even more indignant that the brother has forestalled him in humility. Thus salutary humility and satisfaction—which ordinarily put an end to diabolical temptations [Lipsius, in the margin: “intentions”]—become for him the occasion of a more violent conflagration. [Col. 0470A]

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### Concerning the pride of a certain brother

I heard in this region—something which I shudder and am ashamed to recount—of a certain young man who, when his abbot reproved him for beginning to exceed the humility which he had retained for only a very short time after his renunciation, and for becoming inflated with diabolical pride, replied with the utmost insolence:

“Did I humble myself for a time for this purpose—that I should always remain subject?” [Col. 0470B]

At this utterly unrestrained and wicked answer the elder was so stupefied, and all his speech was so cut off, as though he had heard these words spoken by that ancient Lucifer himself rather than by a human being, that he could utter no word at all against such insolence, except groans and sighs from his heart. He silently turned over within himself only this saying about our Savior: “He who was in the form of God humbled himself, becoming obedient”—not, as that man said, possessed by a diabolical spirit and swelling, “for a time,” [Col. 0469D] but “unto death” (Philippians 2). [Col. 0470D]

> **Note:** That is, temporarily, as Dionysius explained in *On Precept and Dispensation*, chapter 24—as though monastic profession and obedience were temporary rather than perpetual. St. Bernard was asked a similar question: whether a change of abbot gave any support to those wishing to leave their monastery—that is, whether at the death or translation of a superior the subjects, or monks, received greater freedom, so that they might more freely depart at that moment, before another had been appointed. He replies in the negative. “The promise of profession,” he says, “does not take its limit from the abbot’s life, but bears witness to his presence.” For one who professes, therefore, the measure of his life is his own, not another’s.

## CHAPTER XXIX

### Signs by which carnal pride is recognized as present in the soul

To summarize more briefly what has been said about this kind of pride, gathering together as far as we can certain of its signs, so that we may in some manner express its features for those who thirst for perfection through the movements of the outward person, I think it necessary to repeat these matters briefly. Thus we may more concisely recognize by what indications we can distinguish and detect it, so that when the roots of this passion have been stripped bare and brought to the surface, and have been seen and examined with our own eyes, they may either be uprooted more easily or avoided. [Col. 0470C]

The destructive disease can then be completely turned aside when vigilance is not adopted too late, after its harmful heats and dangerous impulses have already gained mastery, but when, recognizing its preceding lines, so to speak, we forestall it through prudent and discerning foresight. For, as we have said, the condition of the inner person is recognized from the movement of the outward person. [Col. 0470D]

> **Note:** St. Gregory, imitating Cassian, gives similar, indeed nearly identical, signs of pride in the place cited above: “In all who swell with proud thought there is shouting in speech, bitterness in silence, dissipation in cheerfulness, fury in sadness, impropriety in action, propriety in appearance, a raised posture in walking, and resentment in reply. Their mind is always strong for inflicting insults, weak for enduring them, sluggish in obeying, yet importunate in provoking others; lazy in doing what it ought to do and is capable of doing, but ready for what it ought not and cannot do” (*Morals* XXXIV, 20). [Col. 0471B]

> “St. Prosper also discusses these signs, or indications, of both carnal and spiritual pride at length in Book III, chapter 8, of *The Contemplative Life*, distinguishing them individually. He begins as follows: ‘Let us now see by what indications pride can be detected, so that, just as it became clear above that no sin can be committed without it, so here its signs may shine forth, by which it can be shown that it must be avoided.’ [Col. 0471C]

> “‘Set aside those whom even their dress and gait reveal to be proud: their raised neck, grim face, fierce eyes, and terrible speech openly proclaim pride. Possessed by the desire to rule, they forcibly subject to themselves as many as they can, confuse human and divine laws, swell with honors, direct everything indiscriminately, rejoice in their crimes, and, corrupted by the disease of pride, do not recognize that they themselves are held captive by it.

> “‘I pass over these, in whom pride reigns so openly that it neither deigns nor is able to conceal itself. I point out only those worthy of pity, and declare their examples to be avoided: those who, already converted and making some progress, are secretly taken captive by pride; whom it deceitfully and tyrannically casts into the depths of evil and continually tramples down so that they may never rise from there.

> “‘It makes a place for the devil in the hearts of such people. It familiarly opens an unguarded breast to him when he comes. It receives him as he enters. It establishes for those it has captured a right to live wickedly. It strips of every virtue those whom it has once invaded. Whatever remains in them that could resist vices, it destroys, lest it should perhaps grow strong against it.

> “‘Hence those whom the purulent corruption of a proud mind has infected do not observe the commands of their elders. When rebuked for their negligence, they pass judgment on them; they either rebel insolently or murmur; they dispute about the higher place; they shamelessly desire to be preferred to better men; they mock and ridicule the simplicity of spiritual brothers; they brazenly parade their own opinions; they disdain services offered to them; they stubbornly seek what has been denied; they put birth before character; they look down arrogantly upon their juniors; they do not believe that anyone can be compared with them; they disdain being made equal to their elders; they set themselves above them through the mere swelling of their minds. [Col. 0471D]

> “‘They do not preserve reverence in service, modesty in speech, or discipline in conduct. They have obstinacy in intention, hardness in heart, and boastfulness in conversation; they are deceptive in humility, biting in jest, obstinate in hatred, impatient of subjection, followers of power, hateful to all good people; sluggish in good works, late in fellowship, harsh in service, ready to speak about what they do not know; prepared to undermine others, inhuman in everything upon which brotherly society depends; rash in daring, clamorous in speaking, disdainful in observing, presumptuous in teaching, and disgracefully savage in laughter.

> “‘They are burdensome to their friends, hostile to quiet, ungrateful for benefits, puffed up by services, and imperious toward their subjects. These are the signs of rampant pride, by which God is offended and departs, abandoning proud hearts.’

> “These words of St. Prosper, though lengthy, are so beautiful and rich that I could not refrain from enriching and supplementing this passage of Cassian with them, for the greater detestation of pride.” [Col. 0472C]

By these signs, therefore, the carnal pride of which we spoke is revealed. At first, there is shouting in its speech, bitterness in its silence, loud and unrestrained laughter in its cheerfulness, irrational sadness in its seriousness, resentment in its reply, and ease in speaking, with words bursting forth everywhere without any restraint of heart. [Col. 0471A]

It is without patience and alien to charity; bold in inflicting insults, fainthearted in enduring them, and difficult to obey—except in matters where its desire and will have anticipated it. It is implacable in receiving exhortation, weak in cutting away its own wishes, extremely hard in submitting to those of others, and always striving to impose its own definitions, while never agreeing to yield to another. [Col. 0471B]

Thus it becomes incapable even of salutary counsel and believes its own judgment preferable to that of its elders in everything.

## CHAPTER XXX

### One who has grown lukewarm through pride desires also to preside over others

When the man whom pride has once possessed has fallen down through these degrees of descent, [Col. 0472A]

> **Note:** The degrees of pride are degrees of those descending, just as, conversely, the degrees of humility are degrees of those ascending: the former are directed toward descent, the latter toward ascent. There are fifteen Davidic psalms called “Songs of Degrees,” that is, songs of ascents, according to the Hebrew expression *anahaboth* and the Greek *ἀναβαθμῶν* (*anabathmōn*), or songs of those who ascend upward through the degrees of humility (Augustine on Psalm 119). To signify this, we presented above the ladder of humility standing upright and the ladder of pride overturned, so that the degrees of those ascending and descending might correspond to one another. For just as through the degrees of humility one always ascends upward from the first to the last, so by an equal course and as though by an intervening slope one always descends lower through the degrees of pride, until at last one reaches the depth of evils, as is clear from what has been said. [Col. 0472C–D]

—he now abhors the discipline of the monastery. As though the companionship of the brethren were holding him back from perfection, and the fault and hindrance of others were keeping him from the good of patience and humility, he desires the residence of a solitary cell. Or else, as though he were going to win many others and build a monastery, he eagerly hastens to gather those whom he ought to teach and instruct. From a wicked disciple he becomes an even more detestable teacher.

For when, through such swelling of heart, he has fallen into a most destructive lukewarmness and harmful tepidity, and has become neither a true monk nor a secular person, what is worse is that he promises himself perfection precisely from this wretched state and manner of life.

## CHAPTER XXXI

### How we can overcome pride and attain perfection

[Col. 0472B]

Therefore, if we desire the summit of our building to rise complete and pleasing to God, let us hasten to lay its foundations not according to the desire of our lust, but according to the discipline of the strict Gospel. These foundations can be nothing other than the fear of God and humility, which descends from gentleness and simplicity of heart. [Col. 0473A]

> **Note:** By the summit of the spiritual building—that is, of the spiritual life, which consists in acquiring and practicing virtues—the author establishes two foundations: fear of God and humility, although these can be reduced to a single foundation, humility. For according to St. Benedict, the first degree of humility is to keep the fear of God always before one’s eyes and entirely avoid forgetfulness, and so forth (*Rule*, chapter 7). [Col. 0472D]

> “The fear of God is called the foundation of the spiritual life, according to Ecclesiasticus 27: ‘If you do not hold yourself steadfastly in fear, your house will quickly be overthrown.’ Explaining this statement, St. Bernard says in his sermon *On the Gifts of the Holy Spirit*: ‘Every building of virtue tends toward ruin if it loses the protection of this grace.’

> “In the same sense the fear of God is called the foundation of the spiritual building, in the words ‘The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom,’ Psalm 110 and Proverbs 1. Explaining this, St. Thomas teaches (II-II, question 19, article 7) that it can be understood of both servile and filial fear, though in different ways.

> “Servile fear is called the beginning of wisdom because it prepares a place for wisdom and leads to wisdom, but does not remain in it. For something is often called the beginning of a thing not because it shares anything with that thing whose beginning it is called, but because it is its external cause or the means by which that thing is brought to perfection. Thus wine is called the fuel and beginning of lust, not because it is itself something of lust, but because it provokes lust.

> “Accordingly, St. Basil explains that saying from Proverbs concerning this fear in his commentary on Psalm 32, and Augustine treats it in Tractate 9 on the First Epistle of John. The same fear is referred to in the statement of Ecclesiasticus, according to the declaration of the Council of Trent (Session VI, chapters 6 and 8): ‘The fear of the Lord drives out sin’ (Ecclesiasticus 1). The same also applies to Isaiah 26: ‘Because of your fear, Lord, we conceived and brought forth the spirit of salvation.’

> “Holy or filial fear, however, is called the beginning of wisdom as its first effect, says St. Thomas. Since it belongs to wisdom that human life be regulated according to divine principles, the beginning must therefore be made by revering God and submitting oneself to him. In this way one will consequently be regulated according to God in all things.

> “Cassian therefore rightly said in the final chapter of Book IV of these *Institutes*: ‘According to the Scriptures, the fear of the Lord is the beginning of our salvation and wisdom’ (Proverbs 9). From the fear of the Lord arises salutary compunction. From compunction of heart proceeds renunciation—that is, nakedness and contempt of all possessions,” and so forth. [Col. 0473B]

> “Concerning the other foundation, humility, St. Bernard says in Book V of *On Consideration*, at the end: ‘Humility is a certain good and stable foundation of the virtues.’ St. Augustine likewise says in Book I of *The Words of the Lord*, Sermon 10: ‘Do you consider building a great structure of exaltation? Think first about the foundation of humility.’ And below: ‘Dig this foundation of humility within yourself, and you will reach the summit of charity.’ [Col. 0473C]

> “Humility is called the foundation of the virtues (St. Thomas, II-II, question 161, article 5, reply to objection 2), not directly and principally—for in that sense faith alone is the foundation of the supernatural virtues, according to the Apostle’s statement that ‘whoever comes to God must believe that he exists,’ and so forth—but dispositionally, insofar as it removes the impediment to the virtues, namely pride, and renders a person subject to God and ready to receive the influx of his grace, which is the seed, origin, and preservation of the virtues.

> “St. James suggests both points when he says: ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ If God resists the proud, he does not give them grace. Pride therefore obstructs the influx of divine grace and consequently the pursuit of virtue, which cannot stand without the help of grace. Humility, however, attracts, receives, and gathers that influx.

> “Hence St. Augustine says in Sermon 27 on *The Words of the Lord*: ‘Water flows together into the humility of the valley; it runs off from the swellings of the hill.’ And in Sermon 157 *On Time*: ‘See a great miracle: God is high. You raise yourself up, and he flees from you; you humble yourself, and he descends to you. Why is this? Because the Lord is exalted and regards the lowly in order to raise them up; but he knows the proud from afar’ (Psalm 137), in order to bring them low.” [Col. 0473D–0474B]

Humility, however, cannot be acquired without nakedness.

> **Note:** That is, renunciation, abandonment, and contempt of all temporal possessions, as stated elsewhere (Book VII of the *Institutes*). [Col. 0474B]

While this nakedness is absent, neither the good of obedience, nor the strength of patience, nor the tranquility of gentleness, nor the perfection of charity can in any way be attained. Without these, our heart cannot at all become the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit, as the Lord declares through the prophet Isaiah 66:

> “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest except upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?”

> **Note:** In St. Jerome, according to the Hebrew truth, it is read: “Upon whom shall I look except upon the poor and lowly one, contrite in spirit and trembling at my words?”—as it is also read in the Vulgate edition. From the Septuagint, Jerome likewise translates it: “And upon whom shall I look except upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” Nevertheless, the Fathers frequently cite it in the form: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest?” and so forth (Gregory, *Morals*, Book V, chapter 31; Bernard, Homily 1 on *Missus est*). [Col. 0474B–C]

Or, according to the manuscripts that express the Hebrew truth:

> “Upon whom shall I look except upon the poor and lowly one, contrite in spirit and trembling at my words?” [Col. 0473B]

## CHAPTER XXXII

### How pride, the destroyer of all virtues, can be extinguished through true humility

[Col. 0474A]

Therefore the athlete of Christ, who desires to be crowned by the Lord after contending lawfully in the spiritual combat, must hasten by every means to extinguish this exceedingly savage beast as well, since it devours every virtue. He must be certain that, while it remains in his breast, he can not only fail to be free from every kind of vice, but that even if he appears to possess some virtue, it will perish from this poison.

[Note: St. Gregory, Book XXIV of the *Moralia*: “The vice of pride must be cut away from its very root, so that when it secretly arises it may then be cut off watchfully—not strengthened by advancement or made more powerful through habit. For each person finds it difficult to detect pride that has become established in him, because the more we endure this vice, the less we see it. Thus pride is generated in the mind just as darkness is generated in the eyes. The farther it spreads, the more severely it constricts the light. Therefore exaltation gradually grows in the heart; and when it has extended itself more widely, it completely closes the eye of the oppressed mind, so that the captive soul can both suffer the form of exaltation and yet be unable to see what it suffers.”]

For in no way can the structure of the virtues rise up in our soul unless the foundations of true humility have first been laid in our heart,

[Note: The same author, Book IV, chapter 18. St. Augustine to Dioscorus: “Unless humility both precedes and follows everything good that we do—being set before us as something at which we look, placed beside us as something to which we cling, and imposed upon us as something by which we are restrained—then, when we are already rejoicing in some good deed, pride snatches the whole thing from our hand. Thus, just as that most renowned rhetorician, when asked what he thought ought first to be observed in the rules of eloquence, is said to have answered, ‘Delivery’; and when asked what should come second, answered, ‘The same delivery’; and when asked what third, said nothing other than, ‘The same delivery’: so, if you were to ask me, and however often you were to ask me, about the rules of Christian religion, I would answer nothing other than ‘Humility,’ even if necessity should compel me to mention other things.”]

which, firmly established, may be strong enough to support the summit of perfection and charity. Thus, as we have said,

[Note: Concerning this passage, I cannot refrain from adding, as a conclusion to this treatise on humility and pride, two further distinctions and divisions of the degrees of this virtue, in addition to the division and arrangement of the twelve degrees of humility assigned by St. Benedict and previously demonstrated on his ladder.

The first is that of the Ordinary Gloss on Matthew 3: “For thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” Perfect humility, it says, has three degrees. The first is to submit oneself to one’s superior and not to prefer oneself to one’s equal; this is sufficient. The second is to submit oneself to one’s equal and not to prefer oneself to one’s inferior; this is called abundant. The third degree is to subject oneself to one’s inferior; in this consists all righteousness.

The other distinction is that of St. Anselm in his *Book of Similitudes*, chapter 99 and following, where he numbers seven degrees of humility and explains them at length. The first is knowledge of oneself, specifically with regard to sins and culpable defects. The second is sorrow for one’s sins and defects. The third is confession of them, both in the sacrament and elsewhere when reason requires it. The fourth is that we not only confess that we have sinned, but persuade others of this and wish to be believed. The fifth is that we patiently endure having this said about us. The sixth is patiently to endure being treated contemptuously or punished on account of one’s fault. The seventh is even to desire this and rejoice in it.

From these degrees of humility it is not difficult to gather and establish the contrary and opposed degrees of pride, proceeding in reverse order: the first degree of pride, namely, is judged to be that which is opposed to the seventh and highest degree of humility, and so on successively.]

let us first exhibit true humility toward our brothers with the innermost affection of our heart, in such a way that we are in no respect willing to grieve or harm them. This we will be utterly unable to fulfill unless true renunciation,

[Note: Renunciation and its three forms are treated fully in the Third Conference, chapter 3 and following.]

consisting in the stripping away of all possessions and in nakedness, has been founded in us through the love of Christ. Then the yoke and submission of obedience must be accepted with a simple heart and without any pretense, so that no will at all may live in us apart from the abbot’s command. This cannot otherwise be observed except by one who has judged himself not only dead to this world but also ignorant and foolish, carrying out without any examination everything commanded him by the elders,

[Note: We discussed this matter elsewhere as well, in Book IV.]

believing their commands to be sacred and promulgated by God.

CHAPTER XXXIII. Remedies against the illness of pride.

[Col. 0475B]

When we have established ourselves in this condition, that truly tranquil and immovable state of humility will undoubtedly follow.

[Note: A Gloss on Philippians 2: “Considering one another superior to themselves”: “We should not interpret this as though we merely pretend to consider it so, but should truly judge that there may be something hidden in another by which he is superior to us, even if the good in us by which we seem superior to him is not hidden.” This is from Augustine, Book LXXXIII, Question 71.

Chrysostom, Homily 33 on Genesis: “Let us not show honor only to those who are older than we are in age, or even to those who are our equals; for it is not humility to do what necessity requires you to do. True humility exists when we yield to those who seem inferior to us and revere those who seem more unworthy than we are. If we judge wisely, we will consider no one inferior to us, but will say that we ourselves are surpassed by all human beings. And I say this not merely of us, who are immersed in countless sins; even if someone is conscious of having accomplished many good deeds, unless he feels within himself that he is the last of all, none of all his good works will benefit him.”]

Thus, judging ourselves inferior to everyone, let us endure with the greatest patience everything inflicted upon us, even if it is insulting, painful, or harmful, as though it had been imposed by our superiors. (See examples in John Climacus, fourth degree.) These things will not only be endured by us very easily but will even be judged small and insignificant if we continually recall in our minds either the sufferings of our Lord or those of all the saints, considering that we are assailed by injuries so much lighter as we are farther removed from their merits and manner of life. Let us likewise consider that we shall soon depart from this world and, when this life quickly ends, shall soon become their companions.

For this contemplation is deadly not only to pride but, in general, to all vices. After this, let us hold this same humility toward God with the greatest firmness. This will be fulfilled by us when we recognize that, without his help or grace, we are able to accomplish nothing pertaining to the perfection of the virtues; and when we truly believe that even the very fact that we have deserved to understand this is his gift.

[Col. 0477]

THE COLLECTION OF THE TWENTY-FOUR CONFERENCES OF JOHN CASSIAN, ABBOT OF MASSILIA, DIVIDED INTO THREE PARTS. (C)

THE FIRST PART, COMPRISING THE FIRST TEN CONFERENCES OF THE FATHERS WHO DWELT IN THE SCYTHIAN DESERT.

Preface, TO LEONTIUS THE BISHOP AND HELLADIUS

[Col. 0477A]

The debt promised to the most blessed Pope Castor in the preface to those books which, with the Lord’s help, were arranged in twelve volumes on the institutions of monasteries and the remedies for the eight principal vices has, insofar as the weakness of our intellect was able, been repaid. Let them judge with fairness what assessment either his or our examination has made of this matter, and whether, amid things so profound and sublime, things which, as I believe, had not previously been brought into the service of writing, we have offered anything worthy of your knowledge and of the desire of all the holy brothers.

But now, since the pontiff mentioned above has left us and departed to Christ, I have believed that these ten Conferences of the supreme Fathers—that is, the anchorites who dwelt in the Scythian desert—should be dedicated above all to you, most blessed Pope Leontius and holy brother Helladius. He had ordered them to be written down in a similar style, burning with an incomparable zeal for holiness, without considering how greatly, because of the abundance of his charity, he was burdening my weak services with so great a weight.

[Note: No one is unaware that the Conferences are so called from *conferre*, “to confer.” Thus Abbot Smaragdus, on chapter 40 of the Rule of St. Benedict: “A conference is a confession, conversation, and discussion, in which, while some confer about the divine Scriptures by asking questions, others offer suitable answers; and thus things that had long lain hidden become clear through discussion.” Isidore, Book III of *On the Highest Good*, chapter 15: “Although reading is useful for instruction, when discussion is added it provides greater understanding. For it is better to discuss than to read. Discussion produces teachability: when questions are proposed, hesitation about matters is removed, and often a hidden truth is established through objections. For what is obscure or doubtful is quickly made clear by discussion.” So Cassian thought it appropriate to title these works “Conferences,” meaning familiar meetings and conversations in which he and his companion Germanus discussed spiritual matters, especially those relating to the perfection of monastic life, with the Fathers—or with more illustrious anchorites—in various places. They diligently sought out and recorded their teaching, admonitions, instructions, and rules. It is certain, on the abundant testimony and commendations of Cassian himself and others presented at the beginning of the work, that Cassian later committed these to writing while living near Massilia, at the urging of many bishops and religious men. Hence St. Prosper also called him “the Conferencer.”

There are twenty-four Conferences in all, but they are arranged in a general sequence and divided into three parts. They are distinguished by places, times, and persons, and likewise by their own prefaces and introductions. The first ten were held in the Scythian, or Scetic, desert and dedicated to the bishops Leontius and Helladius. The next seven were conducted in the solitude of the Thebaid and addressed to Honoratus and Eucherius, whether bishops or abbots is uncertain. The remaining seven were held in the more remote parts of Egypt and addressed to the monks, or abbots, Jovinianus, Minervius, Leontius, and Theodore; they were sent to the brothers living in the Stoechades Islands (in the preface to Conference 11).

Moreover, that such spiritual conferences were very common among the monks of antiquity, both coenobites and anchorites, is evident not only from these celebrated Conferences of Cassian, which by the author’s eloquence wonderfully delight and move the minds of readers and contain the whole teaching of the spiritual life, but is also confirmed by the testimony of the holy Fathers (see below, Conference 2, chapter 2). Athanasius recorded this in the *Life of St. Antony*, where he recalls an exhortation of that most holy Father delivered to brothers gathered together. St. Jerome likewise writes about the monks of Egypt in Letter 22 to Eustochium, among other things:

“After the ninth hour they gather together; psalms resound, the Scriptures are recited according to custom; and when the prayers have been completed and all have taken their seats, the one whom they call ‘Father’ takes the middle place and begins to speak. While he is speaking, such silence is made that no one dares look at another or clear his throat. The praise of the speaker is found in the tears of those who listen; silent tears roll down their faces, and grief does not even break out into sobs. But when he begins to proclaim the coming kingdom of Christ and the future blessedness, you may see everyone, with a restrained sigh and eyes raised to heaven, saying within himself: ‘Who will give me wings like a dove, and I shall fly away and rest’ (Psalm LXV)? After this the assembly is dismissed, and so forth.”

Many other examples occur in the *Lives of the Fathers*, in the *History of the Saints* by Theodoret, in the *Teachings* of Dorotheus, and in the *Lausiac History* of Palladius. From these it is clear that this practice of spiritual conferences was solemn and perpetual among the religious of antiquity. Cassian likewise mentions it in Book V of the *Institutes*, chapters 20 and 21.

Nor should we pass over what Basil writes about it in the *Longer Rules*, chapter 54: “It is worthwhile,” he says, “that at fixed times and in designated places assemblies should sometimes be held by those who preside over gatherings of brothers. In these meetings they should mutually communicate and confer with one another both about matters that have happened to them contrary to reason and about difficult dispositions and characters requiring treatment, as well as about how they have conducted themselves in managing each case. Thus, if something has at some time been done less correctly by anyone, it may be judged with greater authority, after the weighty opinion of many has been brought to bear; and, conversely, if something has been done correctly, it may likewise be confirmed by the testimony of many.” Thus Basil. See also Rule of St. Pachomius, article 7, and the scholia there (see Lorenzo Giustiniani, *On Monastic Discipline and Perfection*, chapter 15).]

I have believed that these Conferences of the supreme Fathers—that is, the anchorites who lived in the Scythian desert—should be consecrated especially to you, most blessed Pope Leontius and holy brother Helladius.

[Note: We discussed the title “pope” in the prologue to the *Institutes*. For it Dionysius has “O most blessed bishop Leontius.” This Leontius was the blood brother of Bishop Castor, to whom the preceding books were dedicated, and was likewise a priest, as is clear from what follows (see Conference 9, chapter 1). Indeed, he may also have been a bishop, as one may infer from the title itself and from that honorific designation, formerly given to bishops rather than inferior clergy; perhaps he was also the successor of his own brother Castor in the Church of Apt. Photius, however, calls him an abbot, saying that he governed the monastery on whose account the earlier books of the *Institutes* were written by the Author.

These facts are easily reconciled: the same man could have been both bishop and abbot—that is, governor of a monastery—for many holy bishops were also fathers and heads of monasteries of monks or regular clergy, as is known of St. Augustine and St. Martin, bishop of Tours. We shall note more about this same Leontius and about Helladius, who is also named here, later, in our remarks on Conference 9, chapter 1, where the reader may consult them. Whether this Leontius is the same as the one to whom the final Conferences were dedicated, I confess that I have not investigated very thoroughly.]

The one of you claims this debt by hereditary right, being joined to the man mentioned above by brotherly affection, by the dignity of the priesthood, and—greater than these—by the fervor of a holy zeal. The other did not undertake to follow the sublime practices of the anchorites, as some have done, through his own presumption, but, under the prompting of the Holy Spirit, grasped the legitimate path of teaching almost before he had learned it, choosing to be instructed not so much by his own inventions as by their traditions.

Now that I am stationed in the harbor of silence, an immense sea opens before me, so that I dare to commit to the memory of writing something concerning the practice and teaching of such great men. For the fragile boat of my intellect must be tossed amid dangers of navigation all the more profound inasmuch as anchoritic life is greater and more sublime than coenobitic life, and the contemplation of God—which those incomparable men were always intent upon—is greater and more sublime than the active life practiced in communities.

It is therefore your task to aid our efforts with pious prayers, lest either such a holy subject, which must be conveyed in speech that is unskilled but faithful, should suffer harm in our hands, or our rusticity be overwhelmed by the abysses of the same subject. Accordingly, let us pass from the external and visible observance of monks, which we arranged in the earlier books, to the invisible habit of the inner person; and from the manner of canonical prayers let our discourse rise to the unbroken continuity of that perpetual prayer which the Apostle commands (1 Thessalonians 5). Thus whoever, through reading the earlier work,

[Note: This alludes to the history of the patriarch Jacob, who is said to have had two names. First he was called Jacob, which means “supplanter.” Alluding to this, Esau, deprived of his father’s blessing, said: “Rightly is his name called Jacob; for he has supplanted me these two times.” But after he wrestled with the angel and received a blessing from him, he was called Israel instead of Jacob, that is, “a man seeing God,” or “a mind seeing God,” according to the interpretation of the ancients; see St. Jerome, *Hebrew Questions*.

Accordingly, the truly devout monk who, by reading the preceding books, has learned to supplant and overcome carnal vices, and who by this has earned the name of the intelligible—that is, spiritual—Jacob, or “supplanter,” will now, through reading the Conferences that follow, be advanced to a higher contemplation and theory, so that he may also become worthy of the name Israel, that is, “one who sees God.”]

has already earned the name of that intelligible Jacob by supplanting carnal vices, may now, receiving not so much my institutions as those of the Fathers, likewise be instructed in what he must observe at this summit of perfection, as he passes, through the vision of divine purity, to the rank and—as I may put it—the dignity of Israel.
