May your prayers obtain from him who has judged us worthy either to see these men, to be their disciples, or to share their company, that he may grant us a full memory of their teachings and an easy facility of speech, so that, explaining them as holily and completely as we received them from the men themselves, we may present them to you as though they had in some way been incorporated into their own *Institutes*—and, what is greater,

[Note: From this testimony of the Author it is clearly understood that he wrote these Conferences in the Latin language, not in Greek, as some have thought; the same was proved in its proper place concerning the books of the *Institutes* (see among the commendations). Let Trithemius explain where he learned that John Cassian published the books of the *Institutes* and the Conferences of the Fathers in Greek, and that Dionysius the Carthusian translated them into Latin with the same elegance of expression, as his words seem to imply. Dionysius certainly professes in explicit terms, in both prefaces, that he translated both the *Institutes* and the Conferences not from Greek but from a more obscure style—though still Latin—into a clearer and easier one. He should therefore be called not so much Cassian’s translator as his paraphrast. For, according to Quintilian, Book I, chapter 5, a paraphrase is a clearer explanation and freer interpretation of the same thought in another form of speech, even in the same language, adding or changing certain elements so as to explain more fully and clearly what another has said. Such is the paraphrastic exposition of Themistius on Aristotle (see Sixtus of Siena, Book III of the *Bibliotheca*, under “Paraphrase”). For this reason, up to now I have deliberately abstained more carefully than before from using the words “translated” or “rendered” when speaking of Dionysius, lest I seem to support Trithemius.

Nevertheless, it is certain that Cassian’s books, although first published by him in Latin, were later translated into Greek by others. Ciaconius writes in his preface that several Conferences and the eight later books of the *Institutes* exist translated into Greek in the Vatican Library, although they were probably reduced to an abridgment rather than rendered in full. Photius seems to have read such a version, since he mentions no more than two or three Conferences (Photius, *Bibliotheca*, chapter 177).]

we may exhibit them to you disputing in the Latin tongue.

We wish above all to warn the reader of both these Conferences and the preceding books that, if he should happen to think that anything in them is impossible or harsh in relation to his own condition and purpose, or to ordinary practice and life, he should measure it not according to the capacity of his own strength,

[Note: This passage most aptly agrees with St. Augustine, Book I of *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, chapter 31. There, extolling anchorites with marvelous praises, he says: “I shall say nothing of those who, entirely withdrawn from the sight of human beings, content with bread alone and water, inhabit the most deserted regions, enjoying communion with God, to whom they cling with pure minds, and being supremely blessed in the contemplation of his beauty, which cannot be perceived except by the understanding of the saints.” And below: “This most excellent height of holiness—who would not spontaneously consider it worthy of wonder and honor? And if someone would, how could it be perceived by our prayer?”]

but according to the dignity and perfection of those who speak, first conceiving in his mind their zeal and purpose. For they are truly dead to this worldly way of life and are bound by no affection for carnal parents or by any ties to secular actions.

Next, let them also consider the character of the places in which they dwell: they are established in a vast solitude, separated from the company of all mortals, and therefore possessing an illumination of the senses; they contemplate or speak of things that, according to the condition and mediocrity of their accustomed experience, may perhaps seem impossible to the inexperienced and uneducated.

If anyone nevertheless wishes to give a true judgment about these matters and desires to test whether they can be fulfilled, let him first hasten to embrace their purpose with similar zeal and manner of life. Then at last he will discover that what seemed beyond human ability is not only possible but also exceedingly sweet. But now let us hasten to their Conferences and institutions.

FIRST CONFERENCE, Being the First of Abbot Moses. ON THE AIM AND END OF THE MONK.

[Col. 0481]

CHAPTER I. On the habitation of Scetis and the purpose of Abbot Moses.

[Col. 0481C]

When we were in the desert of Scetis, where the most approved fathers of the monks dwelt and the perfection of all the saints resided,

[Note: So most manuscripts read. But St. Antony, the Basel edition, and others have: “In the desert of Scythia.” This desert, as has been said elsewhere, was in Egypt near Lake Mareotis, made famous by the great multitude of holy Fathers who frequented it, and was called by various names. It is written as Scetis, Scetic, Scetina, Scetiac, and also Scythic, Scythiac, and Scythiotic (Socrates, Book IV of the *History*, chapter 8).]

we desired to visit Abbot Moses,

[Note: Elsewhere “Moses.” Since three anchorites renowned for holiness are remembered under this name, as we noted elsewhere (Book X of the *Institutes*, final chapter), the Libyan Moses, who alone was Cassian’s contemporary, seems unquestionably to be intended here. Photius also mentions this Moses and the two Conferences held with him, in the following words, from the translation of Father Andrew Scott:

“We read a third little book added to these, which he entitled after the death of Bishop Castor and dedicated to the governor of that monastery, on whose account those earlier Rules had been sent. This little book is similar to those already listed. It teaches first what discretion is; then that it is greater than the other virtues, as well as from what source it arises and how it is often granted from heaven. Finally, by testimonies from Scripture, it proves that everyone should disclose his thoughts to an elder. It further adds what the aim and end should be of those who are tested in religious exercises. In addition, it introduces a certain Moses, a man of admirable virtues, teaching in such a way that he confirms his doctrines by placing the works themselves, so to speak, before the eyes.” (These five chapters appear in Conference 2.)

This is what Photius says about Abbot Moses and his Conferences—briefly and confusedly, indeed, but in keeping with the arrangement and disposition of the books that had then come into his hands, translated into Greek and reduced to an abridgment, as indicated above, or according to the way in which what he read remained in his memory.]

who burned not only with active virtue but also with contemplative virtue,

[Note: Ciaconius aptly wrote the following note on this passage: “The theoretical life is so called because it consists in contemplation, just as the active life consists in action. In all printed books the reading formerly appeared corrupt as ‘he burned with theoretical virtue’; but in the Vatican manuscript it correctly reads: ‘they were fragrant with the theoretical life.’ The subject had been flowers. Philosophers frequently mention the practical and theoretical lives (Aristotle, Book I of the *Ethics*, chapter 5, and Book IX, chapter 4). Cicero, *Letters to Atticus*, Book II: ‘Since there is so great a controversy between your friend Dicaearchus and my friend Theophrastus, that your man greatly prefers τὸν πρακτικὸν βίον—that is, the practical life—to all others, while this man prefers τὸν θεωρητικόν—that is, the contemplative life.’ Among Christians, it is well known that the practical and theoretical lives are represented in Martha and Mary.”

Cassian wrote these terms in Greek and explained them more fully in Conference 14, chapter 1. This is what Ciaconius says. But, with due respect, there is no reason why *theorica* should be criticized as though it had been written incorrectly in place of *theoretica*. It is used adjectivally not only by Cassian in several places—such as Conference 19, chapter 5, where he calls sublimity “theoretical,” and chapter 9 of the same Conference, where he speaks of “theoretical purity,” and again Conference 23, chapter 4, where he calls something “theoretical clarity”—but also by St. Jerome in his commentary on Lamentations 3, where he discusses theoretical purity in almost the same words Cassian uses in the passage just mentioned.

What, then, prevents one from saying *theorica vita*, “the theoretical life,” just as one says “theoretical purity”? Yet *theorica*, or *theorice*, is also used substantively by the same Jerome in the same passage, where he says: “There is therefore one and only one *theorica*, that is, the contemplation of God.” Niccolò Perotti, in the *Cornucopia*, says: “An art requiring no action, but content with the understanding of the thing whose study it pursues, is called *theorice*, that is, speculative.” Thus he. *Theoretica* too is sometimes an adjective and sometimes a noun, as in Conference 14, chapter 2, where contemplation is called *theoretice*.]

and, wishing to be founded upon his instruction, sought him out together with the holy Abbot Germanus. With him, from the very beginning of my training and the rudiments of spiritual warfare, I subsequently enjoyed such inseparable companionship both in the coenobium and in the desert that everyone, to signify the equality of our fellowship and purpose, would say that one mind and soul dwelt in two bodies.

[Note: Thus they generally called monks, or anchorites, especially those venerable for age or holiness, using the term in a somewhat broader sense. It is common in the *Lives of the Fathers* and in Palladius’s *Lausiac History*. In some manuscripts, however, only this is read: “Together with the holy Germanus,” as Cuychius observed. This was Cassian’s companion and colleague, who was likewise his constant companion both on the embassy undertaken to Rome on behalf of Chrysostom and on the journey to the solitudes of Egypt. Cassian elsewhere calls him a priest and introduces him in these Conferences conversing with and questioning those Fathers and anchorites. More on this matter below, at chapter 9.]

Together with him, therefore, we asked the same abbot for a word of edification, with many tears. We knew very clearly the rigor of his spirit: unless he was approached by those who sincerely desired and sought with complete contrition of heart, he would by no means consent to open the door of perfection, lest, if he displayed it indiscriminately to those unwilling to enter or thirsting for it only lukewarmly, he should seem, by revealing to the unworthy and to those who received them with disgust things that ought to be known only by those desiring perfection, to incur either the vice of vainglory or the crime of betrayal.

At last, worn down by our prayers, he began as follows.

CHAPTER II. On the question of Abbot Moses, who asks what the monk’s aim is, or what his end may be.

All arts and disciplines, he said, have a certain *scopos*, that is, a fixed aim, and a *telos*, that is, their proper end.

[Note: [Col. 0483D] Some read these words in Latin, others in Greek, as Ciaconius reports from the Vatican manuscript. This abbot distinguishes here between *skopos*, or aim, and *telos*, that is, the end of every art and discipline. For he calls *scopos* the very directing of oneself toward something—that is, the choice, direction, and arrangement of means suitable for attaining the end. He elucidates and confirms this distinction by the threefold example of the farmer, merchant, and soldier; by their analogy he shows that the religious profession too has its own aim and its own proper end. If one attends to the proper meaning of the words, *scopos* is properly the mark of archers, or the target toward which arrows are directed [Col. 0484C]. Hence Jerome, Book I *Against the Pelagians*, chapter 5: “The Apostle says that he has not yet apprehended and is by no means perfect, but, like an archer, directs his darts toward the object set before him and the mark; the Greeks more expressively call this *skopos*, lest an arrow turning aside show the archer to be unskilled.” *Finis*, however, properly means the boundary or extremity of anything, in Greek *telos*. Yet this distinction between end and aim is very often confused. For *scopos* too is metaphorically taken for the end toward which we direct our mind and purpose. Hence the proverbial expressions “to hit the mark,” “to miss the mark,” and the like. The end of intention—that is, the intention of the agent— is also objectively called the aim; thus we say that the end and aim of the physician is to heal, and of the orator to persuade.]

Looking toward this, the diligent practitioner of each art willingly and calmly endures all labors, dangers, and losses. For the farmer, neither avoiding the scorching rays of the sun nor the frosts and ice, tirelessly cleaves the earth and repeatedly subjects the stubborn clods of the field to the plow, while maintaining his *scopos*: to clear it of every thorn and free it of every weed, pulverizing it through cultivation until it resembles loose sand [Col. 0483C–0484A]. He is confident that he will attain the end—that is, the harvest of abundant fruits and luxuriant crops—by no other means than through his labor and sweat, so that thereafter he may either pass his life in security or increase his possessions.

He also willingly empties granaries filled with grain and entrusts the seed to decaying furrows through persistent labor, not feeling the present diminution because he is contemplating the future harvest [Lips. in the margin: “compensation”]. Those, too, who practice commercial trade do not fear the uncertain dangers of the sea or dread any perils, while they are spurred on toward the end of profit by hope of gain. Likewise, those inflamed by ambition for worldly military service, when they look toward the end of honors and power, do not notice the hardships [Lips. in the margin: “exiles”] and dangers of their journeys, nor are they broken by present sufferings and wars, while they desire to attain the dignity they have set before themselves.

Our profession, therefore, also has its own *scopos* and its own end, for which we undertake all labors not merely tirelessly but gladly. For its sake the hunger of fasts does not weary us; the exhaustion of vigils delights us; continuous reading and meditation upon the Scriptures does not satisfy us; even unremitting labor, nakedness and deprivation of everything, and the dread of this immense solitude do not deter us. For its sake you yourselves undoubtedly rejected the affection of your parents, despised your native land and the pleasures of the world, and crossed so many regions [Col. 0484B–C], so that you might come to us, rustic and uneducated men living in this squalor of the desert [Col. 0484C].

[Note: *Idiotes*, or *idiota*, properly means a private person, one who holds no public office. Hence the Greeks say *idioteuein* for “to live a private life.” Among the Latins, however, it is used for an uneducated, inexperienced, or ignorant person [Col. 0484D], as here. Explaining the word, Festus says: “*Idios* means ‘one’s own’; from it comes *idiotes*, an unlearned and useless person, as though useful only to himself and not to many.” Cicero uses it in the seventh book *Against Verres*: “Something that could delight not only that talented and intelligent man, but even any one of you whom he calls *idiots*.” The Apostle uses it in the same sense in 1 Corinthians 14: “The one who occupies the place of an *idiota*”; and Luke in Acts 4: “Unlettered and *idiotae*.” It is familiar, moreover, for holy men—even those who are most wise and perceptive, such as this anchorite Moses—to profess themselves ignorant and uneducated out of profound humility and true self-knowledge. They follow the example of the blessed Apostle Paul, who judged that he knew nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified (1 Cor. 2); not because he knew nothing else, but because he conducted and presented himself to everyone as though he knew nothing other than the cross of Christ, as St. Thomas says in his Commentary. How this can be done without falsehood or pretense may be understood from what was said in the preceding book (Book XII, chapter 15) about true humility.]

For this reason, he said, answer me: what is your aim or end, which prompts you to endure all these things so willingly?

## CHAPTER III. Our Answer

When he persisted in eliciting our judgment concerning this question, we replied: “All these things are endured for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.”

## CHAPTER IV. Moses’ Question Concerning the Proposition Just Stated

To this he said: “You have spoken well and cleverly concerning the end. But what our *scopos* must be [Lips. in the margin: “what”]—that is, the aim to which we must cling continually if we are to attain the end—you ought above all to know” [Col. 0485A–B].

[Note: [Col. 0485D] The abbot proceeds to show that the end of religion, or of the religious state, is one thing and its aim another. He admits that the end is eternal life, or the kingdom of heaven, as they had professed; but he teaches that its aim is purity of heart. That end, however, is ultimate, general, and common to all, both monks and others. The proper and distinctive end of religion and religious persons, and its primary end, is the perfection of charity, as the same abbot teaches in chapter 7, and St. Thomas in 2–2, question 186, articles 1 and 2. Hence religion is defined as the state of persons tending toward Christian perfection through the vows of poverty, continence, and obedience. This perfection consists in a person, having put away every impediment to divine love, being consecrated to God’s service and adhering to him through love and charity. Hence Blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 6, says that those called servants of God are united, through pure service and servitude to God, to beloved perfection [Col. 0486C]. The secondary end, moreover, is purity and rectitude of mind, consisting in the acquisition and exercise of the other virtues. Hence the Apostle says in 1 Timothy 1: “The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, and a good conscience, and unfeigned faith” (St. Thomas, as above; Turrecremata, treatise 5 on the Rule of St. Benedict) [Col. 0486D].]

When we had simply confessed our ignorance, he continued:

“In every art and discipline, as I have said, there comes first a certain *scopos*, that is, an aim of the soul or an unceasing intention of the mind. Unless someone preserves this with complete diligence and perseverance, he cannot reach the end of the desired fruit. For, as I said, the farmer, whose end is to live securely and abundantly through the yield of fertile crops, maintains this *scopos*: to cleanse his field of every thorn and empty it of all unfruitful weeds. He is confident that he will not otherwise attain the abundance of peaceful rest unless he first possesses, through a certain method of labor and hope, that which he desires to obtain in practice.

“The merchant, too, does not abandon his desire to acquire merchandise, by which he may accumulate wealth more profitably, because he would desire profit in vain unless he had chosen the path by which he might pursue it. Those who desire to be honored with particular dignities in this world first determine to what office or rank they must devote themselves, so that by the legitimate path of hope they may also attain the end of the dignity they desire.

“Thus, the end of our way is indeed the kingdom of God. But what our *scopos* is must be diligently investigated. If it is not similarly known to us, we shall wear ourselves out striving in vain, because for those who travel without a road the labor of the journey produces no progress.

“When we were astonished at this, the old man added: ‘The end of our profession, as we have said, is the kingdom of God, or the kingdom of heaven. Our aim, however—that is, our *scopos*—is purity of heart, without which no one can reach that end. Fixing the gaze of our direction upon this aim, as upon a definite line, we direct our course along the straightest path [Lips. in the margin: “let us direct”]. If our thought should turn aside from it even slightly, we must immediately return to contemplation of it and correct our thought again with perfect straightness, as though bringing it back to a certain rule. By continually recalling all our efforts to this one mark, it will at once expose whether our mind has deviated even slightly from the direction we have established [Col. 0486A–B].’”

## CHAPTER V. That We Must Aim at a Certain Mark, Proven by Another Example

“Just as those skilled in handling weapons of war, when they wish to display their expertise before the king of this world, strive to hurl darts or arrows at a very small target painted with prizes, certain that they can reach the desired prize only along the line of their aim—and that they will obtain it only when they have succeeded in hitting the intended *scopos*—so, if that mark should happen to be removed from their sight, however far the aim of inexperienced men may wander from the straight path and fail, they will nevertheless not realize that they have departed from the direction of the trained line, because they have no definite sign either to prove skill in aiming or to expose error. Therefore, after they have uselessly discharged their throws into empty air, they cannot determine in what they have gone wrong or by what they have been deceived. No indication accuses them of how far they have departed from the direction, nor can any line of discipline teach them where they should correct or recall themselves: their gaze is *passivus* [Col. 0486C].

[Note: That is, wandering, uncertain, and inconsistent. The word is familiar to Tertullian (*Against Marcion*, Book I), as Ciaconius notes; indeed, it is almost peculiar to African writers. Tertullian uses the neuter noun *passivum* of God and *passivum convictum* for what is common and indiscriminate. He says to a Valentinian that he claimed his nobility from the *passivitas* of life (*On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 24). In the same book he calls certain disciples *passivi*, that is, inconsistent, wandering about indiscriminately, and attached to no single teacher. The First Council of Carthage, canon 2, says: “Let no profane person dishonor the dignity of the martyrs, nor call the bodies of the martyrs *passive bodies*.” There *passive bodies* means any corpses of the dead or slain. In chapter 8 of the same council one reads of *passive communion*, that is, indiscriminate communion freely permitted to anyone without distinction [Col. 0487C]. St. Augustine, *Against Adimantus*, chapter 24, says: “If this was said so that bread should not be kept for the following day, the Roman vagabonds whom they call *passives* fulfill it more completely: after satisfying their bellies with the daily food supply, they either immediately give away what remains or throw it away.” St. Jerome likewise uses the term in his commentary on Ezekiel 16, where he speaks of *passive lust*, that is, wandering and promiscuous lust, not bound by marital laws. In Hosea 4 he contrasts *passive religion* with the austerity of true religion. James Billius, a very learned man, further noted (*Sacred Observations*) that these words do not derive from the adverb *passim*, as Rhenanus thought, but are translated from Greek: what the Greeks call *empatheia* is *passivitas* in Tertullian, and what they call *empathēs* is *passivus* in Tertullian and Jerome—that is, wanton and devoted to one’s own pleasures.]

“So, too, the end of our purpose, according to the Apostle, is eternal life, as he says: ‘Having your fruit unto sanctification, but the end eternal life’ (Rom. 6) [Col. 0487A].

[Note: The Vulgate reads *in sanctificationem*, to which the Greek corresponds: εἰς ἁγιασμόν (*eis hagiasmon*). Chrysostom, in agreement with Cassian, explains it by apposition: “Your fruit is sanctification.” Following him, St. Thomas says in his Commentary: “You have your fruit in sanctification, that is, sanctification itself—the carrying out of holiness through good works—is your fruit,” and so forth. In these words the Apostle distinguishes between the fruit of the pious—which our abbot calls the *scopos*—and the *telos*, that is, the end. From this distinction he took his starting point above [Col. 0488C].]

“Thus our *scopos* is purity of heart, which he rightly called sanctification, without which the aforementioned end cannot be attained. It is as though he had said in other words: ‘Having your *scopos* in purity of heart, but the end eternal life.’

“The same blessed Apostle teaches us elsewhere about this aim, expressing the very name—that is, *scopos*—with precision, saying: ‘Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the appointed goal for the prize of the upward call of the Lord’ (Phil. 3) [Col. 0488C].

[Note: In the received text of the Apostle, and in most copies of this passage, the preposition *ad* is added: *ad bravium*, “toward the prize.” Our manuscripts also have it, as does the Greek: ἐπὶ τὸ βραβεῖον (*epi to brabeion*), and it better suits this passage. For here *destinatum* is used substantively, like the Greek *scopos*. It is not joined to *bravium* but stands by itself, so that *ad destinatum* means “according to the aim,” as the Greek conveys; or “according to the purpose,” as it is explained here—that is, according to the resolve, intention, or gaze of the mind. Tertullian also reads it in Latin as “according to the aim” in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 23 [Col. 0488D].]

“This is expressed more clearly in Greek: κατὰ σκοπὸν διώκω (*kata scopon diōkō*), that is, ‘I pursue according to the aim.’

[Note: Here the Author again clearly shows that he writes in Latin, not Greek, since he cites the Greek text to illuminate the Latin meaning.]

“It is as though he had said: ‘By this aim, through which I forget what lies behind—that is, the vices of the former person—I strive to reach the end, the heavenly prize.’

“Whatever, therefore, can direct us toward this *scopos*, that is, purity of heart, must be pursued with all our strength. Whatever draws us away from it must be avoided as harmful and destructive. For its sake we endure and undertake everything. For its sake parents, homeland, dignities, riches, the pleasures of this world, and every delight are despised, so that purity of heart may be preserved perpetually.

“Therefore, once this aim has been set before us, our actions and thoughts will always be directed with perfect correctness toward attaining it. If it is not continually established before our eyes, it will not only render all our labors equally empty and unstable, forcing them to be expended in vain and without any benefit [Col. 0487B–C]; it will also stir up all manner of diverse and contradictory thoughts. For a mind that lacks a place to which it may return and a principal object to which it may cling must change from hour to hour and moment to moment according to the variety of attacks, continually being transformed by external events into whatever condition first presents itself.”

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning Those Who Renounce the World but Strive for Perfection without Charity

This is why we have seen some people despise the greatest resources of this world—not only many talents of gold and silver but also magnificent estates—and afterward become agitated over a knife, a stylus, a needle, or a pen [Col. 0488A].

[Note: A *scalper*, or *scalprum*, is an instrument by which something is cut. Such is the surgical instrument used to excise decayed flesh or open a vein, properly called a *scalpellum*. The word is also used more broadly for any scraping instrument, such as the implement used to clean earwax, which I think is meant here. The stylus was discussed elsewhere (Book IV of the *Institutes*, chapter 13).]

“If they kept fixed contemplation of a pure heart, they would certainly never allow themselves to be disturbed over small matters, since they had preferred to cast away their possessions entirely lest they be overcome by such disturbances over great and precious wealth. Indeed, some people often guard a book with such zeal that they will not allow it even to be read lightly or touched by anyone [Col. 0488B]. Thus they encounter occasions of impatience and death precisely where they are being instructed to acquire the rewards of patience and charity.

“Although they have scattered all their riches for the love of Christ, they nevertheless retain their former affection of heart in regard to trifling matters and sometimes become suddenly angry on their account [Col. 0488B].

[Note: That is, suddenly and quickly. Similar examples occur in Book IV of the *Institutes*, chapter 15.]

“Since they do not possess apostolic charity, they become barren and unfruitful in everything. Foreseeing this in the Spirit, the blessed Apostle says: ‘And if I distribute all my possessions to feed the poor, and if I deliver my body to be burned, but have not charity, it profits me nothing’ (1 Cor. 13).

“From this it is clearly proved that perfection is not immediately attained through nakedness, nor through the deprivation of all possessions, nor through the rejection of dignities, unless that charity is present [Lips. in the margin: ‘unless that charity is at hand’] whose members the Apostle describes in truth and which consists solely in purity of heart. For what else is it ‘not to be jealous, not to be puffed up, not to be provoked, not to act wrongly, not to seek what is one’s own, not to rejoice over iniquity, not to think evil,’ and the rest, than to offer God a perfect and most pure heart at all times and preserve it untouched by every disturbance?”

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning the Purity of Heart That Must Be Desired

Everything, therefore, must be done and desired for this reason. For this reason we must pursue solitude; for this reason we must undertake fasts, vigils, labors, bodily nakedness, reading, and the other virtues. We must understand that we should accept these practices so that through them we may prepare and preserve our heart unharmed by every harmful passion, ascend by these steps toward the perfection of charity, and not, because of these observances, fall into sadness, anger, or indignation if we happen to be prevented by some honorable and necessary occupation from fulfilling the strictness of our customary discipline [Col. 0489A–B].

[Note: That is, the customary austerity and regular observance. St. Bernard’s statement in his book *On Precept and Dispensation* aptly illuminates this passage. Speaking of the institutions and regular observances and austerities of the holy Fathers, which must sometimes be relaxed or interrupted either when necessity demands or when charity invites, he says: “These things were discovered and instituted not because it was unlawful to live otherwise, but because this way was more expedient; and plainly for no other purpose than the gaining and preservation of charity. As long as they serve charity, they stand fixed and immovable and cannot be changed, not even by those set over them, without offense. But if, on the contrary, they should at some time appear opposed to charity, to those alone who have been granted the ability to see and entrusted with the responsibility to provide—is it not clearly most just that what was invented for charity should also, for charity, where it seems expedient, be omitted, interrupted, or perhaps changed into something more useful? Just as it would undoubtedly be unjust if statutes established solely for charity were observed against charity.” This is St. Bernard’s statement [Col. 0489C–D].]

“For the gain from fasting is not as great as the loss caused by anger; nor is the benefit obtained from reading as great as the harm incurred through contempt of a brother. Therefore, we ought to practice the things that follow—fasts, vigils, the anchorite life, meditation upon the Scriptures—for the sake of the principal *scopos*, that is, purity of heart, which is charity, and not disturb this principal virtue because of those practices. If this virtue remains whole and unharmed within us, it will do no harm if, because of necessity, something among the practices just mentioned is omitted. Indeed, it will not help to have done everything if we have failed to attain this principal end, for whose sake everything must be done [Col. 0489B].

“Why does someone hasten to construct and prepare for himself the tools of any art? Not so that he may possess them uselessly, nor so that he may place the hoped-for benefit of their fruit in the bare possession of the instruments, but so that through their service he may effectively acquire the skill and end of the discipline for which they are aids [Col. 0489D–0490A].

[Note: A splendid statement, worthy—as the saying goes—of being marked with a white stone. It embraces the whole substance of this chapter and pleased St. Thomas, the chief and teacher of theologians, so much that he used it in several places in his *Summa* to support his conclusions, while in turn illuminating it through his own conclusions (2-2, questions 184 and 189, articles 7 and 8).

It contains two principal points. First, Christian and monastic perfection consists in charity. For, as St. Thomas says, each thing is called perfect insofar as it reaches its proper end, which is the ultimate perfection of the thing (2-2, question 84, article 1; see also Bellarmine, Book II *On Monasticism*, chapter 2). Charity, however, is what unites us to God, who is the ultimate end of the human mind: “Whoever remains in charity remains in God, and God in him,” as it says in 1 John 4. Therefore, Christian perfection is especially [Lips. in the margin: “substantially”] measured according to charity. Hence the Apostle says to the Colossians: “Above all these things have charity, which is the bond of perfection,” because charity in some way binds all the other virtues into the unity of perfection. This is St. Thomas’s teaching [Col. 0490C].

The second point is that fasts, vigils, reading and meditation upon the Scriptures, nakedness—that is, poverty—and the other austerities and exercises of religion are not perfection itself, nor do they immediately make a person perfect; rather, they are instruments of perfection. For, as he says, “the end of this discipline”—that is, monastic discipline—“does not consist in these things; rather, through them one reaches the end.” In other words, as was said above, “we strive to ascend toward the perfection of charity by these steps.” These practices are called instruments of perfection, especially the three evangelical counsels—poverty, continence, and obedience—which belong to the substance of the religious state because they are the most suitable and useful means of attaining the perfection of charity. They remove all impediments to divine love, which the Apostle John lists in these words: “Whatever is in the world is either the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, or the pride of life” (1 John 3). Through continence the desire of the flesh is removed and restrained; through poverty, avarice, or the desire of the eyes; through obedience, pride. This is what theologians teach: perfection consists essentially and primarily in charity and observance of God’s commandments, and secondarily, almost dispositively or instrumentally, in those evangelical counsels and the other virtues [Col. 0490D].]

“Therefore, fasts, vigils, meditation upon the Scriptures, nakedness, and deprivation of all possessions are not perfection but instruments of perfection, because the end of that discipline does not consist in them; rather, through them one reaches the end.

“Whoever, therefore, is satisfied with these exercises as though they were the supreme good, fixes the intention of his heart on them alone, and does not extend every effort of virtue toward attaining the end for which these practices must be desired, will labor at them in vain. He possesses the instruments of that discipline but is ignorant of the end in which all its fruit consists.

“Whatever, therefore, can disturb the purity and tranquility of our mind, however useful and necessary it may seem, must be avoided as harmful. By this rule we shall be able to escape all the aberrations and wanderings of errors [Al.: “all dispersions of earthly wanderings”] and reach the desired end along the line of certain direction [Col. 0490B].”

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the Principal Effort Directed toward Contemplation of Divine Things, and the Comparison of Mary and Martha
Here, then, our principal effort must be directed, and this immovable orientation of the heart must be pursued continually:

> [Note: [Col. 0490D] If not in act, then at least in power, or virtual intention. For the weakness of this mortal life does not permit our mind always to think of God and divine things, and without interruption to be carried toward him through affection or contemplation and to cling to him, as is well known [Col. 0491B] and is explained more fully below (Chapters 12 and 13). Moreover, Dionysius, in order to avoid this difficulty, deliberately omitted the word “always,” although it is found in all the manuscripts.]

—that the mind may always cling to divine things and to God—everything different from this, however great it may be, must nevertheless be judged secondary, or even of the lowest rank, or certainly harmful.

> [Note: [Col. 0491B] The phrase is rather obscure, though familiar to Cassian, as is clear from Conference 7, chapter 5. Dionysius sheds some light upon it in these words: “The figure of this principal action,” and so forth. The reference is to what he said shortly before: the principal effort and immovable orientation, or intention, of continually clinging to God and divine things. This is indeed the principal and primary act of charity. Its figure, that is, its type, is beautifully represented by Martha and Mary, the sisters of Lazarus, because it is commended in Mary’s example and preferred to Martha’s service. Hence the Fathers commonly distinguish, from the comparison of the two sisters Leah and Rachel in the Old Testament, and Mary and Martha in the New, two kinds of life, or a twofold life, in the Church of God: the one contemplative, corresponding to Mary and Rachel; the other active, corresponding to Martha and Leah (St. Thomas, II–II, question 1, article 1). St. Gregory, Book VI of the Moralia, chapter 28: “What,” he says, “is signified by Mary, who sat and listened to the Lord’s word, except the contemplative life? What is signified by Martha, occupied with outward service, except the active life? Yet Martha’s care is not censured, whereas Mary’s is even praised, because the merits of the active life are great, but those of the contemplative life are greater.” He says similar things about Leah and Rachel in Homily 14 on Ezekiel. On the same subject, see St. Basil, Ascetical Constitutions, chapter 2; St. Jerome, on chapter 3 of Jeremiah; Augustine, Sermon 27 on the Words of the Lord according to Luke; Theophylact and Bede, on chapter 10 of Luke; and Bernard, Sermon 3 on the Assumption of the Blessed Mary.]

This state or activity of the mind is also beautifully represented in the Gospel by Martha and Mary. For while Martha was engaged in a holy service, since she was serving the Lord himself and his disciples, and Mary, intent solely upon spiritual teaching, clung to Jesus’ feet, which she kissed and anointed with the ointment of a good confession, she was nevertheless preferred by the Lord because she had chosen the better part, the part that could not be taken away from her (Luke 10).

For when Martha, occupied with pious anxiety and the demands of her service, was laboring and, seeing that she alone could not manage so great a ministry, asked the Lord for her sister’s assistance, saying:

> [Col. 0491B] [Note: [Col. 0491D] Ciaconius, on the basis of the Vatican manuscript, and others read: “Do you approve that my sister has left me to serve alone?” Others read: “Does it please you that my sister,” and so forth.]

“Do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her, therefore, to help me.”

Certainly, she was summoning her not to an ignoble task, but to a praiseworthy ministry. And yet what does she hear from the Lord?

“Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things.”

> [Note: [Col. 0491D] He cites it in the same way in Conference 23, chapter 3: “But few things are necessary, or even one.” The Greek corresponds more closely: ἑνὸς δέ ἐστι χρεία, “there is need of one thing.” The common translator renders it: “But one thing is necessary.” What that one thing is which Christ calls necessary has been variously explained. Some interpret it as one simple kind of food, as though Martha were being reproved for occupying herself with preparing many dishes, when only one, and that easily prepared, was needed. Thus Basil, in the Monastic Constitutions, chapter 2. St. Augustine, in Sermon 27 on the Words of the Lord, interprets “one thing is necessary” as God himself, who alone is necessary and sufficient for us; the many other things are not necessary. Hence the well-known saying attributed to Blessed Francis: “My God and my all.” Others, such as Abbot Moses here, understand “one thing is necessary” as attention to heavenly teaching and devotion to divine things. He calls it theoria below, that is, knowledge and contemplation of God—not bare and simple contemplation, but joined with pious love and affection, through which the soul is said to cling to God and be united with God, because “whoever clings to God becomes one spirit with him” (1 Corinthians 6). And the Psalmist says: “But it is good for me to cling to God” (Psalm 72). Mary cared for this one thing: to hear Christ’s word, to be nourished by his teaching, and to rest in his love, according to the saying in the Song of Songs, chapter 3: “I found him whom my soul loves; I held him, and I will not let him go.”]

“Few things are necessary, or even one; Mary has chosen the good part,

> [Col. 0492A]

which will not be taken away from her.”

You see, then, that he placed the principal good

> [Note: [Col. 0492D] Theoria is contemplation, or, as Lactantius explains it, vision. Thus he writes in Book VII of the Institutes, chapter 9: “Since man’s condition is upright, he seeks his origin, and, as though despising earthly lowliness, strives upward, because he understands that the highest good must be sought on high. Mindful of the condition in which God made him distinguished, he looks toward his Maker. This vision Trismegistus most correctly called θεωρία, a vision that is found in no mute animals.” Thus far Lactantius.]

solely in theoria, that is, in divine contemplation. Hence, although we declare the other virtues necessary and useful, we nevertheless determine that they must be considered secondary, because all of them are ordered toward attaining this one thing.

For when the Lord says, “You are anxious and troubled about many things, but few things are necessary, or even one,” he placed the supreme good not in active work, however praiseworthy and abundant in fruits, but in contemplation of him [Lipsius, in the margin: “of himself”], which is truly simple and one. He declares that few things are necessary for perfect blessedness, that is, for theoria, which is at first maintained by contemplating a few holy things. From their contemplation, the person who is still making progress [Lipsius, in the margin: “advanced”] ascends to that which is called “one,” namely, the vision of God alone; and, with God’s help, reaches it. Thus, having surpassed even the marvelous actions and ministries of the saints, he is nourished thereafter by the beauty and knowledge of God alone.

“Mary, therefore, has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.” This must be examined more carefully. For when he said, “Mary has chosen the good part,” although he says nothing about Martha and does not seem in any way to censure her, nevertheless, by praising Mary,

> [Note: [Col. 0493B] St. Gregory, Book VI of the Moralia, chapter 28: “Martha’s care,” he says, “is not censured, whereas Mary’s is praised, because the merits of the active life are great, but those of the contemplative life are greater. Mary’s portion is said never to be taken away, because the works of the active life pass away with the body, whereas the joys of the contemplative life become stronger in the end.” [Col. 0493C] On this comparison of the active and contemplative lives, see the conclusions of St. Thomas, II–II, question 182.]

he declares the latter to be inferior. Again, when he says, “which will not be taken away from her,” he shows that Martha’s portion can be taken away. For bodily service cannot remain continually with a person; whereas he plainly teaches that Mary’s devotion cannot be brought to an end.

## CHAPTER IX. The question how the functions of the virtues do not remain with human beings

> [Note: [Col. 0493C] It seems worth observing that in these Conferences Cassian is found to have spoken personally only once or twice (Conference 17, chapter 3); otherwise, he always spoke through his companion Germanus, who conversed with those Fathers and asked questions and received answers in his own and Cassian’s name. In this respect Cassian displayed an example of religious modesty and silence: although himself the younger and merely a deacon, even if perhaps more learned and experienced, he yielded the duty and honor of speaking to his elder and presbyter and kept silent while he spoke (see Conferences 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, and 12). He was doubtless mindful of the apostolic saying: “If anyone thinks he is religious, not restraining his tongue but deceiving his heart, his religion is worthless” (James 1). He was also mindful of the salutary teaching he had received from a most holy man, who was likewise a disciple of St. John Chrysostom and his fellow disciple (Baronius, in the Martyrology, 4 February). There is extant a letter of Isidore of Pelusium, a man distinguished for holiness and learning, to Cassian (Book I, Letter 309), written when Cassian had begun to profess the monastic life. Isidore seriously admonished him that the tongue must be restrained, especially in a monk who was still young and a novice (see our preface to the Lessons). “For it befits a teacher to speak and teach; it befits a disciple to be silent and listen,” says St. Benedict in chapter 1 of his Rule.]

Germanus: Since we were deeply troubled by this, we said: “What, then? Will the labor of fasting, the diligence of reading, and works of mercy, justice, piety, and kindness be taken away from us and not remain with their authors? Especially since the Lord himself promises the reward of the heavenly kingdom for these works, saying: ‘Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink,’ and so forth (Matthew 25). How, then, will these things be taken away, since they bring those who perform them into the kingdom of heaven?”

## CHAPTER X. The answer that it is not their reward, but the action, that will cease

> [Col. 0494A]

Moses: Nor did I say that the reward of a good work would be taken away, since the same Lord says: “Whoever gives one of these little ones only a cup of cold water in the name of a disciple, truly I tell you, he will not lose his reward” (Matthew 10).

> [Note: [Col. 0493D] There are three kinds of actions or works of the active life that will cease in the life to come. The first consists of those concerned with bodily necessity, such as eating, drinking, sleeping, and so forth. The second consists of those concerned either with mortification of the flesh, such as fasting and vigils, or with a remedy for concupiscence, such as marriage. The third consists of those concerned with assisting one’s neighbor, such as works of mercy. All these will certainly cease in the future age and in the life of the blessed, because there will be no bodily necessity, no weakness or struggle of the flesh, and no need among one’s neighbors. A more precise and truly theological explanation of this passage should be sought in St. Thomas, II–II, question 181, article 4, where he asks whether the active life remains after this life and answers that the active life has its end in external actions, “which, if they are referred to the repose of contemplation, already belong to the contemplative life. In the future life of the blessed, the occupation with external actions will cease; and if there are any external actions, they will be referred to the end of contemplation. For, as Augustine says at the end of The City of God (Book XXII, final chapter): ‘There we shall rest, and we shall see, and we shall love; we shall love and praise.’ And in the same book he says beforehand that there God will be seen without end, loved without weariness, and praised without fatigue. ‘This gift, this affection, this action, will be in all.’” Thus far St. Thomas. Elsewhere (I–II, question 67, article 1) he teaches that the moral virtues do not remain in the future life with respect to what is material in them. “For,” he says, “in the future life there will be no place for the desires and pleasures of food and sexual relations, nor for fears and boldness concerning the dangers of death, nor for the distribution and sharing [Lipsius, in the margin: “or exchanges”] of things that serve the uses of the present life. But with respect to what is formal in them, they will remain most perfectly in the blessed after this life, insofar as the reason of each will be perfectly right concerning what pertains to that state, and the appetitive power will be moved wholly according to the order of reason in matters pertaining to that state. Hence Augustine says (On the Trinity, Book XIV, chapter 9) that prudence there will exist without any danger of error, fortitude without the burden of enduring evils, and temperance without resistance from desires: so that prudence consists in preferring or equating no good with God; fortitude, in clinging to him most firmly; temperance, in taking pleasure in nothing harmful through defect. As for justice, it will be clearer what act it will have there, namely, being subject to God, because even in this life it belongs to justice to be subject to one’s superior.” Thus far St. Thomas.]

But I say that the action required by bodily necessity, by the struggle of the flesh, or by the inequality of this world will be taken away. For diligence in reading and the austerity of fasts are beneficially practiced only in the present, for the cleansing of the heart and the chastisement of the flesh, until “the flesh desires against the spirit” (Galatians 5). We sometimes see even in the present that these practices are taken away from those who are exhausted by excessive labor, bodily illness, or old age, and that no human being can practice them continually.

How much more, then, will these things cease in the future, when “this corruptible body has put on incorruption,” and this body, which is now animal, has risen as spiritual, and the flesh has ceased to be such that it desires against the spirit? Concerning these matters the blessed Apostle also speaks plainly.

> [Note: [Col. 0494D] The present author here interprets “bodily exercise” as fasting and other austerities and practices by which the body is chastened and mortified. Yet this commentary does not please Chrysostom, whose words are these: “Some say that the Apostle spoke of fasting here, but they are certainly mistaken. For fasting is not bodily exercise, but spiritual. If it were bodily, it would nourish the body; but now it mortifies and weakens it.” Chrysostom himself understands the expression as referring to the exercise of athletes, which consists in running, wrestling, boxing, or some other activity, to which the Apostle frequently alludes and from which he draws comparisons, as is clear from 1 Corinthians 9, Philippians 3, and 2 Timothy 2. Such exercise is “profitable for a little,” that is, only slightly profitable, because it is useful merely for bodily health and strength.]

“Bodily exercise,” he says, “is profitable for a little; but piety”—which is undoubtedly understood as charity—“is profitable for all things, having the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come” (1 Timothy 4).

That which is said to be profitable “for a little” is plainly declared neither to be practiced for all time nor, by itself, to be capable of conferring the highest perfection upon one who labors. “A little” can refer to both matters: either to the shortness of time, since bodily exercise cannot be coeternal with a human being in either the present or the future; or certainly to the smallness of the benefit gained from carnal exercise, since bodily affliction produces certain beginnings of progress but does not itself produce the perfection of charity, which has the promise of the present and future life.

And therefore we consider the exercises of the works mentioned above necessary, because without them one cannot ascend to the heights of charity. These works also, which you mention,

> [Note: [Col. 0495C] St. Augustine says similarly in Sermon 27 on the Words of the Lord: “Let us consider,” he says, “our occupations concerning many things. Ministry is necessary for those whose bodies are to be restored: why is this? Because there is hunger. Mercy is necessary for the miserable. You break bread for the hungry because you found someone hungry. Take away hunger: for whom do you break bread? Take away pilgrimage: to whom do you show hospitality? Take away nakedness: for whom do you prepare clothing? Let there be no illness: whom do you visit? Let there be no captivity: whom do you redeem? Let there be no quarrel: whom do you reconcile? Let there be no death: whom do you bury?” [Col. 0495D] “In that future age these evils will not exist, and therefore neither will these ministries.” St. Jerome, on chapter 3 of the Lamentations of Jeremiah, and Gregory, Book VI of the Moralia, chapter 28, write in the same sense.]

the works of piety and mercy are necessary in the present age, while unequal diversity still holds sway. Their activity would not even be expected here if a very large proportion of the poor, needy, and sick did not abound:

> [Note: [Col. 0495D] This must not be understood as though the division of dominions and possessions, or inequality among human beings, were itself unlawful and unjust. Rather, misery and poverty among the needy and poor frequently result from the force and injustice of the powerful and rich. Yet such conditions also often arise without sin, as is well known, from misfortune or accidental circumstances, or because this division of possessions arose from sin or had its occasion in sin (St. Thomas, II–II, question 66, articles 1 and 2). Thus, in the chapter “Dilectissimis,” in Gratian, XII, question 1, Clement I says: “The common use of all things in this world ought to have belonged to everyone; but through iniquity one person said, ‘This is mine,’ and another, ‘That is mine.’ Thus division arose among mortals, because through human iniquity or greed an occasion was given for right reason to judge that division should be made, whereas before sin all things were held in common.”]

—the inequality created by human iniquity, namely, by those who seize for their own use the things granted to all by the common Creator, yet do not retain them for use.

Therefore, as long as this inequality rages in the world, this action will be necessary and beneficial to the person who practices it. It restores to a good disposition and pious will the reward of an eternal inheritance; but in the future age, when equality reigns, it will cease, since there will no longer be inequality on account of which these things must be practiced. Instead, all will pass from this manifold, that is, active, work to the charity of God and the contemplation of divine things, with perpetual purity of heart. Those who, already established in this age, have chosen with every effort and strength to devote themselves to the purification of knowledge or of the mind will then devote themselves to that same end without impediment. They assign themselves, while still placed in the flesh of corruption, to the service in which they will remain once corruption has been laid aside, arriving at the promise of the Lord and Savior, which says:

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5).

## CHAPTER XI. The perpetuity of charity

> [Col. 0496B]

And why are you surprised if the duties described above will pass away, when the holy Apostle also describes the higher gifts of the Holy Spirit as passing away, while designating charity alone as remaining without end?

“Whether prophecies,” he says,

> [Note: [Col. 0496C] Prophecies will be brought to an end in the homeland, because prophetic knowledge is obscure and enigmatic. Hence it is also compared to a lamp shining in a dark place. Tongues will cease—not the bodily tongues of the blessed, which will not cease continually to praise the holy name of the Lord, but the gift of tongues by which certain people in the primitive Church spoke in various languages (Acts 2). For in the future life everyone will understand every language; hence it will not be necessary to speak in various languages. Knowledge will be destroyed—not with respect to its habit or the things known, but with respect to the act and manner of knowing characteristic of this life, which proceeds through species abstracted from phantasms. That manner is not suited to the future life. Thus the well-known saying of St. Jerome in his letter to Paulinus, placed before the Bibles, is explained: “Let us learn on earth which of our knowledge will remain with us in heaven.” Knowledge of known things will remain in the blessed, but it will be of another kind and manner from the knowledge of this life (St. Thomas, I–II, question 89, article 5, reply to objection 1; the Master of the Sentences, Book III, distinction 31).]

“be brought to an end, or tongues will cease, or knowledge will be destroyed” (1 Corinthians 13).

But concerning charity:

> [Note: [Col. 0496D] Ἐκπίπτει, “falls away,” as most manuscripts read. Charity is said never to fall away—not because it cannot once be lost, as heretics interpret it, but because it remains in the blessed, whereas faith, hope, and many other gifts of the Holy Spirit listed by the Apostle will be brought to an end. Thus St. Thomas says that the Apostle’s meaning is: “Charity never falls away, because just as it exists in the state of this life, so it will remain in the state of the homeland, and with increase,” according to Isaiah 31: “The Lord has spoken, whose fire is in Zion,” that is, in the Church militant, “and whose furnace is in Jerusalem,” that is, in the peace of the heavenly homeland.]

“charity never falls away” (ibid.).

For all gifts are granted for a time according to use and necessity, and, once their dispensation has been completed, they undoubtedly pass away at once.

But charity will never be interrupted. For it not only operates beneficially in us in the present world; in the future also, once the burden of bodily necessity has been cast aside, it will remain far more effective and excellent, never to be corrupted by any defect, but through perpetual incorruption to cling to God more ardently and more intensely.

## CHAPTER XII. The question concerning the perseverance of spiritual contemplation

Germanus: Who, then, enclosed in fragile flesh, can remain so continually fixed upon this theoria that he never thinks of a brother’s arrival, of visiting the sick, of manual labor, or of showing kindness to strangers and visitors? Finally, who is not interrupted by the provision or care of the body itself? We desire to be taught how the mind can cling inseparably to that invisible and incomprehensible God, and in what manner this can be done.

## CHAPTER XIII. The answer concerning the direction of the heart toward God, and concerning the kingdom of God and of the devil

> [Col. 0497B]

Moses: To cling continually to God and to be inseparably joined to his contemplation, as you say, is impossible for a human being enclosed in this frailty of the flesh. But we must know where we ought to fix the intention of our mind and toward what orientation we must always recall the gaze of our soul. When the mind is able to attain that orientation, it should rejoice; when it finds itself distracted from it, it should grieve and sigh. It should feel that it has fallen away from the highest good as often as it discovers itself separated from that vision, judging even a momentary departure from the contemplation of Christ to be fornication.

When our gaze has strayed even slightly from him, let us turn the eyes of our heart back toward him and recall the focus of the mind as along the straightest line. For everything depends upon the soul’s withdrawal.

Therefore, once the devil has been expelled and the vices no longer reign in the soul, the kingdom of God is consequently established in us, as the Evangelist says:

“The kingdom of God does not come with observation, nor will they say, ‘Look here,’ or ‘Look there.’ For behold, the kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17).

> [Note: [Col. 0497D] This saying has been interpreted in many different ways. Here the abbot says that the kingdom of God is within us when we possess knowledge of it. Others think that “within us” means “in our power,” just as Deuteronomy 30 says: “This commandment which I command you today is not above you or far from you; rather, the word is very near you, in your mouth, so that you may do it,” and so forth. Others explain “the kingdom of God within us” as Christ dwelling in our hearts through faith. Others say that the kingdom of God is within us because we possess within us the image of God, according to which we were made. Finally, others say that the kingdom of God is within us through a foretaste, participation, and certain experience of it, which we perceive in the mind, and because, as the Apostle says, “the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God” (Romans 8). Gregory Nazianzen, cited by St. Thomas in the Catena Aurea, gives this interpretation. It also seems to have pleased this abbot, as is clear from what follows.]

“Within us” can mean nothing other than knowledge or ignorance of the truth, and either friendship with vices or friendship with virtues. Through these we prepare a kingdom in the heart either for the devil or for Christ.

The Apostle also describes the character of this kingdom, saying:

“For the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 14).

Therefore, if the kingdom of God is within us, and if the kingdom of God is righteousness, peace, and joy, then whoever dwells in these things is undoubtedly in the kingdom of God. Conversely, those who live in injustice, discord, and sorrow that produces death are established in the kingdom of the devil, in hell, and in death.

By these signs the kingdom either of God or of the devil is distinguished.

Indeed, if we consider with the lofty vision of the mind the state in which the heavenly and supernal powers live, which truly are in the kingdom of God, what other state should we believe it to be than perpetual and unending joy? For what is so proper to true blessedness, and so fitting, as continual tranquility and everlasting joy?

And so that you may be instructed more surely that what we say is so, not by my conjecture but by the authority of the Lord himself, hear him describing most clearly the quality and state of that kingdom:

“Behold,” he says, “I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things will not be remembered, nor will they rise upon the heart; but you will rejoice and exult forever in the things that I create” (Isaiah 65).

And again:

“Joy and gladness will be found in her, thanksgiving and the voice of praise; and there will be month after month, and sabbath after sabbath” (Isaiah 51).

And again:

“They will obtain joy and gladness; sorrow and groaning will flee away” (ibid.).

And if you wish to know more clearly about that fellowship and city of the saints, attend to what is addressed by the Lord’s voice to Jerusalem itself:

“I will make your visitation peace, and your overseers righteousness. Iniquity will no longer be heard in your land, devastation and destruction within your borders; salvation will occupy your walls, and praise your gates. The sun will no longer be your light by day, nor will the brightness of the moon illuminate you; but the Lord will be your everlasting light, and your God your glory. Your sun will no longer set, and your moon will not wane; but the Lord will be your everlasting light, and the days of your mourning will be completed” (Isaiah 60).

And therefore the blessed Apostle does not declare every joy generally and without qualification to be the kingdom of God, but specifically and particularly only that joy which is in the Holy Spirit (Romans 14). For he knows that there is also another reprehensible joy, concerning which it is said:

“This world will rejoice” (John 16),

and:

“Woe to you who laugh, for you will mourn” (Luke 6).

> [Note: [Col. 0498D] Observe the three meanings of the kingdom of heaven: active, passive, and local.]

The kingdom of heaven must indeed be understood in three ways.

First, as that by which the heavens—that is, the saints—will reign over other subjects, according to the saying:

“You are to be over five cities, and you over ten” (Luke 19).

There is also the saying addressed to the disciples:

“You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19).

Second, it may mean that the heavens themselves begin to be ruled by Christ, when God begins to be all in all, with everything subjected to him (1 Corinthians 15).

Or, finally, it may mean that they will reign with the Lord in heaven.

## CHAPTER XIV. The perpetuity of the soul

Therefore, while still established in this body, let each person now know that he is to be assigned to the religion or service of which he has made himself a participant and worshiper in this life. Let him have no doubt that in that everlasting age he will also be a companion of the one whose servant and associate he has now chosen to be, according to the Lord’s saying:

“If anyone serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also will my servant be” (John 12).

For just as the kingdom of the devil is received through agreement with vices,

> [Note: [Col. 0499C] “Zabulus,” that is, the devil. See what is noted below, on chapter 21 of this Conference. To this I add the following passage from St. Cyprian, speaking of the patience of Job: “How many arrows of Zabulus were sent against him. And Zabulus arms the wife” (Cyprian, On the Good of Patience).]

so the kingdom of God is possessed through the practice of virtues, purity of heart, and spiritual knowledge.

Where the kingdom of God is, there undoubtedly is also eternal life; and where the kingdom of Zabulus is, there unquestionably are death and hell. Whoever is in that kingdom cannot praise the Lord, according to the Prophet’s saying:

“The dead will not praise you, nor all those who descend into hell”—namely, the hell of sin—“but we,” he says, “who live”—not in vices or for this world, but for God—“will bless the Lord from now and forever” (Psalm 113).

“There is no one in death who remembers you; and in hell”—the hell of sin—“who will confess to the Lord?” (Psalm 6).

That is, no one.

For no one, even if he professes himself a Christian or a monk a thousand times, confesses to the Lord while he sins. No one who admits what the Lord abhors remembers God, nor does he truly profess himself the servant of the one whose commands he contemptuously and rebelliously despises.

The blessed Apostle declares that the widow who lives in luxury is in this death:

“The widow who lives in luxury is dead while she lives” (1 Timothy 5).

There are therefore many who, while living in this body, are dead and lie in hell, unable to praise God. Conversely, there are those who, although dead in body, bless and praise God in spirit, according to the saying:

“Bless the Lord, spirits and souls of the righteous” (Daniel 3),

and:

“Let every spirit praise the Lord” (Psalm 150).

In the Apocalypse, the souls of those who were slain are said not only to praise God but also to intercede (Revelation 6).

In the Gospel, too, the Lord speaks more clearly to the Sadducees:

“Have you not read what was spoken by God when he said to you, ‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? He is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Matthew 22).

For all live to him.

Concerning them the Apostle also says:

“For this reason God is not ashamed to be called their God; for he has prepared a city for them” (Hebrews 11).

For because…

> [Note: [Col. 0499C] [The supplied text ends here.]]

Others omit the word *animae* (“souls”) and read *otiosi* (“idle”) instead of *otiosae*, namely, “the dead,” or “the spirits of the dead.” But the present text appears more perspicuous. Three errors, or heresies, concerning human souls separated from the body are here noted.

The first error is that, after separation from this body—that is, after death—souls remain idle and insensible, indeed devoid both of understanding and of every affection. The second is that human souls are not immortal, but either perish together with their bodies or are dissolved into nothingness. The third is that even the souls of the just are not immediately transferred after passing from this life into blessedness, but await the final judgment and the resurrection of their bodies. Something must be said separately about each of these three errors.

As regards the first, Cassian speaks rather ambiguously in this chapter, both concerning the senses he attributes to separated souls and concerning the condition of their life. On the former point, he seems to attribute to the rational soul the senses and affections of this life, since he repeatedly insists that the souls of the dead are not deprived of their own senses, indeed that they lack none of these affections either—that is, hope and sadness, joy and fear. Later, however, as though explaining himself, he concludes that the mind, stripped of this bodily grossness—that is, of the body—recovers its intellectual powers in a better state and receives them purer and more refined rather than losing them. By these words he plainly indicates that the senses and affections of the separated soul which remain are not bodily and animal, but only spiritual and intellectual.

For a fuller clarification of this doctrine, the words of Saint Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book XII, chapter 33, should first be noted:

> Whoever denies that the soul bears a likeness to the body and to bodily members altogether may deny that the soul is what, in dreams, sees itself walking, sitting, moving here and there by foot, or even being carried along in flight; for this does not happen without some likeness to the body.

By these words Augustine seems to imply that the human soul has some likeness to its own body and therefore also possesses certain senses resembling bodily senses. But it is highly ambiguous what likeness he understands. He repeats the same point in Book IV of *On the Soul and Its Origin*, chapter 17, where he also seems to place sensation in the souls of the dead (Volume VII).

There is also cited under Augustine’s name, from the book *On Spirit and Soul*, the statement that the soul, departing from the body, takes with it sensation, imagination, understanding, the concupiscible appetite, and the irascible appetite (Volume I of Augustine’s Works, chapter 16). Likewise, from the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*:

> We believe that only man has a substantial soul—that is, subsisting in itself—which, when stripped of the body, lives and retains its senses and organs in a living condition.

Cassiodorus speaks in the same way in his book *On the Soul*, saying (chapter 8):

> The soul, separated from the body, still sees, hears, imagines, and remembers.

Finally, Peter Lombard, referring to this passage of Cassian in Book IV, distinction 44, says:

> In Cassian’s books it is read that they are not idle and are not devoid of all sensation, since that rich man declares that he is tormented by the flame in hell. Hence it is proved that the souls of the dead are not only not deprived of their own senses, but are deprived of none of these affections either—namely, hope, sadness, joy, and fear—and that, from what is reserved for them in that universal examination, they already begin in some measure to taste beforehand.

Thus he himself reports Cassian’s words.

Moved, as I think, by these authorities, Saint Thomas discusses this question in several places: “Whether all the powers of the soul remain in the soul separated from the body?” In the *Summa* he resolves it as follows:

> It must be said that all the powers of the soul are related to the soul alone as to their principle. But some powers are related to the soul alone as to their subject, such as the intellect and will; and these powers must remain in the soul when the body has been destroyed. Other powers, however, exist in the united whole—that is, in the composite, namely, the human being—as in their subject, such as all the powers of the sensory and nutritive parts. When the subject has been destroyed, an accident cannot remain. Therefore, when the united whole—that is, the composite—has been corrupted, such powers do not remain actually, but remain only virtually in the soul, as in their principle or root. Thus it is false that some say that such powers remain in the soul even when the body has been corrupted. And it is much more false that they say the acts of these powers also remain in the separated soul, since none of the operations of such powers occurs except through a bodily organ.

So Saint Thomas (*First Part*, question 77, article 8; *Commentary on Book IV of the Sentences*, distinction 44, question 3, article 3, question 1; and *Quodlibet* 7, article 8).

To the authority from the book *On Spirit and Soul*, he replies that the book has no authority, since it is not Augustine’s; concerning this, see Bellarmine, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Augustine. He adds, however:

> It can nevertheless be said that the soul takes such powers with it, not actually but virtually.

Understand this of bodily senses, imagination, and the concupiscible and irascible appetites; for it is certain that the intellect and will remain actually in the separated soul. Intellectual memory, moreover, is in reality the same as the intellect and differs from it only conceptually. Of this it was also said to the rich man buried in hell: “Remember, son, that you received good things during your life” (Luke XVI), and so forth.

Similarly, the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* is not by Saint Augustine but by Gennadius of Massilia, who is not highly authoritative among ecclesiastical writers. Yet he too explains himself correctly when he says (chapter 19):

> Man consists of only two substances, soul and body: the soul with its reason, and the body with its senses. Yet the body does not move these senses apart from the soul’s association with it. The soul, however, retains its reason even without the body.

Hence Saint Thomas infers (*Quodlibet* 7, article 8):

> Therefore, when the flesh has died, the sensory powers do not remain.

To Cassiodorus he replies that, just as the operations of the will are named after the passions that exist in the sensory appetite because of a certain likeness, so the operations of the intellect are named after the operations of the senses because of a likeness. Cassiodorus speaks in this way.

Cassian can be explained in the same manner when he says that the separated soul is not without these affections—namely, joy and sadness, hope and fear. For just as the souls of the blessed rejoice in their rewards, so it is certain that the souls of the damned are saddened by their punishments and torments and fear them as well, as is clear in the case of the rich man. Such passions, however, do not belong to the sensory appetite, but to the intellectual and rational appetite. Since hope belongs neither to the blessed nor to the damned, it can be attributed only to souls existing in purgatory, as can faith. For they hope for and believe in the eternal and blessed life which they do not yet possess.

As regards the second error, two errors arose against the immortality of the rational soul. The first was that of the Sadducees, who denied the soul’s immortality and therefore also denied the resurrection (Matthew XXII; Saint Thomas, *First Part*, question 75, article 6). The other was held by certain Arabs who, as Eusebius of Caesarea says (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book VI, chapter 30), asserted that human souls died together with their bodies at one and the same moment of time and were utterly extinguished, but that at the time of the resurrection of all flesh they would recover life again together with their bodies. See Augustine, *On Heresies*, number 23.

Against both errors, Scripture, the Creed, and the Church’s definition plainly teach that the immortality of the human soul must be held with certain faith, apart from both philosophical and theological arguments. See Pererius, Book IV on Genesis, question 2.

Cassian adduces here several passages of Scripture to which these could be added:

> The souls of the just are in the hand of God, and the torment of death shall not touch them.

Wisdom III.

> Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul.

In both the Apostles’ Creed and the Nicene and Constantinopolitan Creeds, we profess the resurrection of the flesh, or of the dead, and eternal life—something that presupposes that our soul is immortal.

Accordingly, Saint Jerome, commenting on that passage of Matthew XXII, which the Author also cites here, says:

> To prove the eternity of souls, he gives an example from Moses—that is, from the books of Moses: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus III). Immediately he adds: “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living.” Once he has proved that souls remain after death—for it could not be that he was the God of those who in no way continued to subsist—the resurrection of bodies is consequently introduced, since with their souls they performed good or evil deeds.

Finally, there was the explicit definition of the Church in the last Lateran Council, session 8, where this manner of speaking is also condemned: “The soul is immortal according to faith, but mortal according to reason or philosophy.” Certain people who were excessively devoted to philosophy used this expression.
