As regards the third error—that the souls of the saints, separated from their bodies, do not see God or enjoy heavenly blessedness, but are kept until the day of the final judgment in certain hidden receptacles where they neither see God nor can be called blessed except in hope—Tertullian first taught this in several passages. Then Vigilantius, whom Saint Jerome rebukes (*Against Vigilantius*):

> You say that the souls of the apostles and martyrs have taken their seats either in Abraham’s bosom, or in a place of refreshment, or beneath God’s altar, and cannot be present at their tombs or wherever they wish. They are, evidently, of senatorial rank, so that they are confined not among murderers in a most dreadful prison, but in free and honorable custody, on the islands of the blessed and in the Elysian fields.

The Greeks followed these men, as is clear from the Council of Florence, session 1, and finally the sectarians of our own time—Luther, Calvin, and others. See Bellarmine, *On the Blessedness of the Saints*, Book I, chapter 1 and following. He treats this controversy fully and accurately and establishes the affirmative position as Catholic truth through many testimonies of Scripture and authorities of the holy Fathers, so that nothing further seems capable of being added or required. I therefore leave the reader to consult him and will propose only two or three supports for this doctrine.

The first is the testimony of the Church, when it says of Saint Gregory and other holy confessors: “O God, who hast bestowed upon the soul of thy servant Gregory, or N., the rewards of eternal blessedness,” and so forth.

The second is the authority and definition of the two ecumenical councils, Florence and Trent. For this very point was defined at the Council of Florence, in its final session, where the Greeks, at last restored to unity with the Church, profess together with the Latins, by decree of Pope Eugenius (*Decree of Union*), that the souls of those who, after receiving baptism, incurred no stain of sin whatsoever, and also those who, after contracting a stain of sin, were purified either in their bodies or, after being stripped of their bodies, as stated above, are immediately received into heaven and clearly behold God himself, triune and one, as he is—though with one person seeing him more perfectly than another according to the diversity of merits. But the souls of those who depart in actual mortal sin, or in original sin alone, immediately descend into hell, though they are punished with unequal punishments.

At the Council of Trent, those who deny that the saints, enjoying eternal happiness in heaven, are to be invoked are condemned (Session 25, on the invocation of the saints). See the rest in Bellarmine and Scotus, Book IV, distinction 45, question 1, article 3, where he also expounds and explains most of the passages of Scripture cited here by Cassian.]

Since the souls of the dead are neither idle after separation from this body [Col. 0501A] nor insensible, the Gospel parable concerning the poor Lazarus [Col. 0502A] and the rich man clothed in purple also demonstrates this (Luke XVI). One of them attains the most blessed abode—that is, Abraham’s bosom [Col. 0503A]—as his place of rest; the other is consumed by the intolerable heat of eternal fire.

If we also attend to what is said to the thief, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII), what else does it plainly indicate except that souls retain not only their former understanding but also enjoy, in due alternation, conditions corresponding to the merits and deeds of each? God would never have promised this to him if he had known that, after the separation of the flesh, his soul would either be deprived of sensation or dissolved into nothingness. For it was not his flesh that was to enter paradise with Christ, but his soul.

Indeed, that most depraved distinction of the heretics must be avoided—or rather detested with utter horror. Since they do not believe that Christ could be found in paradise on the same day on which he descended into the lower regions [Col. 0503B], they make the following distinction: [Note: Theophylact also reports this erroneous interpretation and wicked distinction in his Commentary. The abbot rightly says that it must be detested, both because it contradicts Catholic doctrine and because it renders Christ’s statement entirely feeble and senseless, as though he had said: “Truly I tell you today.” What purpose would “today” then serve, and what emphasis would it have? Did the thief not see that the Lord was speaking on that very day? See Bellarmine, Book I, *On the Blessedness of the Saints*, chapter 3.]

> “Truly I tell you today,”

and, inserting a distinction, they conclude:

> “You will be with me in paradise,”

so that this promise is understood as being fulfilled not immediately after the passing from this life, but after the coming of his resurrection.

They do not understand that, before the day of his resurrection, he said to the Jews, who believed that he, like themselves, was confined within human anxieties and carnal weakness:

> “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III).

By these words it is plainly proved that the souls of the dead [Note: Understand this to mean not bodily but spiritual senses, which he below calls intellectual powers. For when the soul is separated from the body through death, all its sensory powers perish with the body, while only understanding and the rational faculty remain to it, as has been said.] are not only not deprived of their own senses, but are deprived of none of these affections either—namely, hope and sadness, joy and fear—and that they already begin to taste something of what is reserved for them in that universal examination [Col. 0503C]. Nor, in accordance with the opinion of certain unbelievers, are they dissolved into nothingness after passing beyond this temporary sojourn; rather, they subsist more vividly and cling more intently to the praises of God.

Indeed, setting aside for a little while the testimonies of Scripture concerning the nature of the soul itself, let us discuss briefly a few matters according to the modest measure of our understanding. Is it not beyond every absurdity—not merely folly but madness—to suspect even slightly that the more precious part of man [Note: He refers to the statement of the Apostle in 1 Corinthians XI: “A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God.” But the statement in Genesis II is more explicit, where it is said that God created man in his own image and likeness. Concerning this image and likeness of God in the human soul, see the Master, *Sentences*, Book II, distinction 16; Saint Thomas, *First Part*, question 93; and Pererius, Book IV, *Commentary on Genesis*.], in which the image of God, according to the blessed Apostle (1 Corinthians XI; Colossians III), and his likeness consist, becomes insensible once it has laid aside this bodily burden in which it is now enclosed? This is the very part that contains within itself the whole power of reason and, through its participation, makes even the mute and insensible matter of the flesh itself sentient.

For it necessarily follows—and the order of reason itself contains this conclusion—that when this mind has been stripped of the bodily grossness by which it is now dulled, it restores its intellectual powers to a better condition and receives them purer and more refined rather than losing them.

The blessed Apostle knows this to be so truly that he even desires to depart from this flesh, so that through its separation he may be able to cleave more earnestly to the Lord, saying: [Note: The desire for immortality or eternity implanted in the rational soul, which the Apostle suggests in these words, is a great argument for its immortality. From this even pagan philosophers recognized and affirmed that the human soul is immortal: Plato in the *Phaedo*; Aristotle, Book II of *On the Soul*.]

> “I have a desire to depart and to be with Christ, for that is much better” (Philippians I),

because:

> “While we are in the body, we are away from the Lord. Therefore we are confident and willing rather to be away from the body and present with the Lord. For this reason we strive, whether absent or present, to please him” (2 Corinthians V).

Thus he declares that the soul’s dwelling in this flesh is a pilgrimage away from the Lord and an absence from Christ, while he confidently maintains that its separation and departure from this flesh is a presence with Christ.

And more clearly still, concerning this same most vigorous state of souls [Col. 0504C], the same Apostle says:

> “But you have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and the company of many thousands of angels, [Note: That is, the society or fellowship of the saints or elect, whose names are written in the book of life and who are also called the firstborn, in Greek *prōtotokoi* (πρωτότοκοι). As Theophylact explains, all human beings are indeed sons of God by creation; but by adoption the firstborn are the chosen sons whose names are written in heaven. Others wish the firstborn to mean those who pleased God through faith in earlier ages, such as the holy patriarchs and prophets. Still others mean the holy apostles, who first and more abundantly received the gifts of grace, through whom these gifts were transmitted to later generations, according to Romans VIII: “We ourselves have the first fruits of the Spirit.” So Saint Thomas.] and the church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, [Note: The Author has omitted the following words, which precede those that follow in the Apostle: “And to God, the judge of all.” Then comes: “And to the spirits of the righteous,” and so forth. Three readings are found here. Some read: “And to the spirit of the righteous made perfect,” meaning that you have approached the Holy Spirit who makes people perfect in righteousness; for all righteousness and perfection come from the Holy Spirit. So Saint Thomas, who seems to favor this reading in his Commentary. Another reading is: “And to the spirits of the righteous made perfect,” as it was also read in ancient Latin editions. Hence Gagneius thinks that our translator read in Greek πνευμάτων, “of spirits,” and understood it as referring to the Judge, so that the meaning would be that Christ is judge of all, including the spirits of the righteous and perfected—that is, their souls. But the current Vulgate and corrected Latin version has: “And to the spirits of the righteous made perfect,” as it is also given here. The meaning is therefore that Christians have approached, through faith and charity, the spirits—that is, the souls—of the righteous and perfected, and have become sharers with the holy souls in eternal happiness; or, as Saint Thomas has it, that we may have fellowship with the spirits of the saints, who are righteous and perfected. As the Author presents it here, this statement serves not only to prove the immortality of souls, which is the principal subject here, but also to confirm that Catholic doctrine according to which we believe that the souls of the just, once fully purified, are immediately received into heaven and enjoy the beatific vision of God, contrary to the opposing error mentioned above.] and the spirits of the righteous made perfect [Col. 0505A]” (Hebrews XII).

Concerning these spirits he says elsewhere:

> “Furthermore, we had fathers of our flesh as instructors, and we respected them. Shall we not much more submit to the Father of spirits and live?” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XV. On the Contemplation of God

The contemplation [Note: Various concepts of God and methods of meditation. On these, see Saint Gregory, Homilies 17 and 18 on Ezekiel.] of God is conceived in many ways. For God is known not only through admiration of that incomprehensible substance of his, which nevertheless remains hidden as yet in the hope of the promise, but he is also discerned through the greatness of his creatures, through consideration of his justice, or through the assistance of his daily providence.

This occurs when we survey with the purest mind what he has done with his saints throughout the successive generations; when with trembling heart we marvel at his power, by which he governs, orders, and rules all things, and at the immensity of his knowledge and the eye from which the secrets of hearts cannot be hidden; when in fear we consider that the sand of the sea and the number of its waves have been measured and known to him; when, amazed, we contemplate the drops of rain, the hours and days of the ages, and all things past and future standing before his knowledge.

It occurs when we consider his unspeakable clemency, by which he sustains with tireless patience countless crimes committed beneath his gaze at every moment; when we behold the calling by which, without any preceding merits, he has chosen us through the grace of his mercy; and finally when, with a kind of excess of wonder, we observe how many opportunities of salvation he grants to those who are being adopted [Lipsius in the margin: “adopted”], since he ordained that we should be born in such a way that from our very cradles the grace and knowledge of his law would be handed down to us; since, conquering the adversary within us, he rewards us with eternal blessedness and everlasting prizes for the assent of a good will alone; and finally since he undertook the dispensation of his Incarnation for our salvation and spread the wondrous mysteries of his works among all nations.

There are also innumerable other contemplations of this kind which arise in our perceptions according to the quality of our life and the purity of our heart. Through them God is either seen by pure eyes or held fast.

Certainly, no one in whom anything of carnal affection still lives will retain these contemplations continually, because the Lord says:

> “You cannot see my face; [Note: This is a moral exposition of that statement, also found in Saint Gregory, *Morals*, Book XVIII, chapter 38. There, treating Job XXVIII—“It is hidden from the eyes of all living”—he says: “Whoever sees Wisdom, which is God, dies completely to this life, so that he is no longer held by its love. No one who still lives according to the flesh has seen her, because no one can embrace God and the world at the same time. For whoever sees God dies precisely insofar as, either in the intention of his heart or in the effect of his works, he is separated from the pleasures of this life.” Hence it is also said to the same Moses: “For man shall not see me and live”; as though it were plainly said: “No one ever sees God spiritually while living according to the flesh.” Thus the Apostle Paul, who, as he himself testifies, had known God’s invisible things only in part, declared himself already wholly dead to this world, saying: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians VI). So Gregory gives a moral exposition of those words of Exodus together with our Collator. The genuine and literal meaning of the statement, however, is that no one in this life sees or has seen God—that is, clearly and intuitively beholds the divine essence, as the blessed behold it in heaven. See Saint Thomas, II–II, question 180, article 5. For, as blessed Gregory says in the same place: “As long as one lives here in mortality, God can be seen through certain images, but he cannot be seen through the appearance of his very nature.” But this does not apply to the present passage.] for man shall not see me and live” (Exodus XXXIII),

that is, while attached to this world and to earthly affections.

## CHAPTER XVI. A Question Concerning the Mobility of Thoughts

[Col. 0506B]

Germanus: What, then, is the reason that, even when we are unwilling—and indeed even when we are unaware—they cling to us so subtly and secretly that it is exceedingly difficult not only to drive them away but even to understand and detect them? Can the mind ever be found empty of them and never be assailed by illusions of this kind?

## CHAPTER XVII. The Answer: What the Mind Can and Cannot Do Regarding the State of Its Thoughts

Moses: [Note: Saint Bernard discusses excellently the manifold variety of thoughts by which our mind is assailed in Book *On Conscience*, chapter 5. Among other things he says: “The manifold variety of thoughts is recognized. Some inflate the heart, others exalt it, others disturb it, others scatter it, others confuse it, others stretch it, others bind it, others defile it, others contract it, and others corrupt it. They inflate it as proud thoughts, exalt it as vain thoughts, disturb it as envious thoughts, scatter it as angry thoughts, confuse it as sluggish thoughts, stretch it as ambitious thoughts, bind it as gluttonous thoughts, defile it as lustful thoughts, contract it as timid thoughts, and corrupt it as malicious thoughts.” When these have been excluded, the mind is purified if it is continually exercised in holy thoughts, as it is written: “Holy thought will guard you.”]

It is impossible for the mind not to be assailed by thoughts; but it is possible for everyone who is striving to receive or reject them [Lipsius in the margin: “possible for one striving through the grace of God”]. See Cuychius’s third annotation after the end of this work.

Therefore, just as their arising does not depend entirely upon us, so their approval or choice rests with us [Col. 0507A]. Yet from what we have said—that it is impossible for the mind not to be visited by thoughts—it does not follow that everything must be attributed either to the assault or to those spirits who strive to force thoughts upon us. Otherwise free choice would no longer remain in man, nor would the effort of our correction depend upon us [Lipsius: “of correction”].

But, I say, it depends to a great extent upon us that the quality of our thoughts be amended and that either holy and spiritual thoughts or earthly and carnal ones take shape in our hearts. For this reason frequent reading and continual meditation of Scripture are sometimes practiced, so that from them an occasion for spiritual remembrance may be supplied to us. For this reason the Psalms are sung repeatedly, so that continual compunction may thereby be provided for us. For this reason assiduous vigils, fasts, and prayers are practiced, so that the weakened mind [Col. 0507B] may not savor earthly things but contemplate heavenly things.

When these practices cease again because negligence has crept in, [Note: Saint Gregory, *First Book of Kings*, chapter 14: “He cannot prevail in avoiding shameful thoughts who does not have honorable thoughts within himself. Since we are always thinking, we must seek good things so that we may not think evil things.”] the mind, soon compacted by the squalor of vices, must incline toward and collapse into the carnal part.

## CHAPTER XVIII. A Comparison of the Watermill and the Soul

[Note: Saint Bernard explains the same likeness and comparison between the human heart, or rational soul, and a watermill excellently in his *Most Devout Meditations*, chapter 9. He says: “Just as a mill turns rapidly and refuses nothing, but grinds whatever is placed upon it, while, if nothing is supplied, it consumes itself, so my heart is always in motion and never rests; whether I sleep or keep watch, it dreams and thinks whatever comes before it. And just as a mill destroys sand when sand is put into it, pollutes when pitch is put into it, and is clogged by straw, so my heart is troubled by bitter thought, stained by impure thought, and disturbed and wearied by vain thought. Thus, when my heart does not care for future joy and does not seek divine help, it is drawn away from love of heavenly things and occupied with love of earthly things. When it slips away from the former and becomes entangled in the latter, vanity receives it, curiosity leads it on, greed attracts it, pleasure seduces it, lust defiles it, envy torments it, anger disturbs it, and sadness afflicts it. Thus it is submerged in all vices through miserable disasters, because it abandoned the one God who could have been sufficient for it.” So Bernard, along with what follows.]

The activity of the heart is not inappropriately compared to mills which the channels of water, rushing with precipitous force, drive forward by their revolving motion. When turned by the force of the water, they can in no way cease from their work; but it lies within the power of the person in charge to determine whether they grind wheat or crush barley or darnel. For without doubt they must grind whatever is put into them by the person entrusted with responsibility for that work.

In the same way, the mind, driven about through the movements of the present life while torrents of temptations surge upon it from every side, cannot remain empty of the floods of thoughts. But what kinds of thoughts it should either admit or prepare for itself will be determined by its own diligence and application.

For if, as we have said, we continually return to meditation on the holy Scriptures and raise our memory toward recollection of spiritual things, desire for perfection, and hope of future blessedness, the thoughts that arise from this must cause the mind to dwell upon the matters we have meditated on. But if, overcome by laziness or negligence, we occupy ourselves with vices and idle conversations, or become entangled in worldly cares and superfluous anxieties, then consequently there will arise from this, as though generated [Note: “Darnel,” or *zizanium*, which in Greek is called *aira* (αἴρα) by Suidas, is a blight of wheat and barley, caused by excessive moisture in the soil and continual rains; in Latin it is called *lolium*. Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book XVII, chapter 10 (Homily 50), says: “Darnel is what poets always call the unlucky *lolium*, since it is useless and barren.” Saint Basil, however, in the *Hexaemeron*, seems to distinguish these somewhat when he says: “For what is called *lolium*, and the other adulterated seeds that commonly mix themselves with edible crops, which Holy Scripture (Matthew XIII) customarily calls *zizania*, do not arise from transformed wheat, but are born from their own origin and beginning and retain their own kind.” In sacred literature, *zizania* is metaphorically used of the evil seeds of doctrine, conduct, or thoughts—as here. Hence Saint Jerome, Letter 22 to Eustochium: “Do not allow a thought to grow: kill the enemy while he is small; let wickedness be struck down in the seed, lest the darnel grow.”], some kind of species of darnel, and will likewise supply our heart with a harmful activity [Col. 0508B]. According to the saying of the Lord and Savior, wherever the treasure of our works or of our intention is, there our heart must necessarily remain (Matthew VI).

## CHAPTER XIX. On the Three Sources of Our Thoughts
We must know above all that [Note: [Col. 0508C] One may ask why he posited only three sources of our thoughts, since good angels also often introduce good and beneficial thoughts into us, as is well known. St. Thomas answers briefly (Part I, question 111, article 2) that good thoughts are attributed to a higher source, namely God, even though they are brought about through the ministry of angels.] there are three sources of our thoughts: namely, from God, from the devil, and from ourselves.

Thoughts are from God when, in the illumination of the Holy Spirit, he deigns to visit us, raising us toward more exalted progress; and when, through the most salutary compunction, he chastises us in those matters in which we have acquired too little or, acting sluggishly, have been overcome. Or they are from God when he discloses to us heavenly mysteries and turns our purpose [Col. 0508C] toward better actions and our will toward them, as when King Ahasuerus, chastised by the Lord, [Note: [Col. 0508D] Various opinions about who King Ahasuerus was may be found in Bellarmine, *On the Word of God*, book I, chapter 7, and in Serarius’s *Commentaries on the Book of Esther*. How he is understood to have been chastised by the Lord can be gathered partly from Scripture (Esther VI) and partly, as it were, from Josephus’s commentary (*Antiquities*, book XI, chapter 6). The text of Scripture reads as follows: “That night the king spent sleepless, and he ordered the histories and annals of earlier times to be brought to him. When these were read in his presence, they came to the passage where it was written how Mordecai had reported the plot of Bagathan and Thares, the eunuchs who had sought to kill King Ahasuerus. When the king heard this, he said: ‘What honor or reward did Mordecai receive for this loyalty?’ His servants and ministers replied: ‘He received no reward at all,’ and so forth. Josephus’s commentary, however, says: ‘God mocked Haman’s evil hope and, foreseeing what was to come, took delight in future events. For he deprived the king of sleep that night,’ and what follows. Thus the Author here indicates that Ahasuerus was chastised by the Lord: when those sleeplessnesses were divinely sent upon him, and the records of the annals and histories were read aloud before him, he recalled Mordecai’s former loyalty and service in exposing the plot, and, by God’s inspiration, began earnestly to consider rewarding him worthily, as was proper. From this followed the reversal and abolition of the most cruel sentence against the Jews that Haman had procured. Furthermore, Aulus Gellius, book V, chapter 18, and Isidore, *Etymologies*, book I, final chapter, explain the difference between histories and annals. From these Baronius reported the following (*Annals*, first preface): ‘The ancients distinguished annals from history by this difference: history properly treats the deeds of its own times, which the author either saw or could have seen, and indicates not only what was done but also by what means and with what purpose. In annals, by contrast, the writer generally commends to written record year by year ancient events, which his own age did not know. So much for him.’] was prompted to examine the books of annals; remembering Mordecai’s services, he exalted him to the highest rank of honor and immediately revoked the most cruel sentence concerning the destruction of the Jewish nation (Esther VI).

Or thoughts are from God when the Prophet says, “I will hear what the Lord God will speak within me” (Psalm LXXXIV). Another says, “And the angel who was speaking within me said” (Zechariah I). Or when the Son of God promises that he will come together with the Father and make his dwelling among us (John XIV). And he says, “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew X). Likewise the chosen vessel says, “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (II Corinthians XIII).

[Note: [Col. 0509C] Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book II, chapter 4, speaking about demons: “All wickedness is brought about by them, as are impure disturbances. They are indeed permitted to make suggestions to a human being, but they cannot compel him. For it is in our power to accept or not to accept their suggestion.” Thus Damascene. St. Thomas, in the passage cited above, says: “Demons cannot introduce thoughts by causing them inwardly, since the exercise of the cogitative power is subject to the will. Nevertheless, the devil is called the kindler of thoughts insofar as he incites one to think or to desire what has been thought, by way of persuasion or by stirring up passion. He can stir up such passions in the sensitive appetite and thereby move the will, but not by necessity, since the will always remains free either to consent to or to resist the passion. The devil therefore introduces thoughts into us in two ways: either by altering the phantasy, or imagination, and presenting various persuasive objects to it; or by arousing passion in the sensitive appetite, through which the will is enticed. The devil can do both, if God permits it; yet he cannot compel the will or move it efficaciously unless it itself freely consents.”]

A succession of thoughts arises from the devil when he attempts to overthrow us both through the pleasure of vices and through hidden snares, displaying evil deceitfully as good with the subtlest cunning and transforming himself for us into an angel of light (II Corinthians XI). Or when the Evangelist reports: “And supper having taken place, [Note: [Col. 0510C] St. Augustine, *Tractate 55 on John*: “This sending is a spiritual suggestion; it does not occur through the ear but through thought. For diabolical thoughts are introduced and mingled with human thoughts.”] the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas, Simon Iscariot, that he should betray the Lord” (John XIII). And again: “After the morsel, Satan entered into him” (ibid.). Peter also said to Ananias, “Why has Satan tempted your heart, that you should lie to the Holy Spirit?” (Acts V). And that passage which we read as having been foretold in the Gospel and, much earlier, by Ecclesiastes: “If the spirit of one in authority rises against you, do not leave your place” (Ecclesiastes X). Likewise what is said to God against Ahab in the Third Book of Kings, in the person of an unclean spirit: “I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets” (III Kings XXII). [Note: [Col. 0510C] How thoughts can arise from us when the Apostle says, “We are not sufficient to think anything of ourselves, as though from ourselves” (II Corinthians III), see the note of Master Cuychius at the end of the work.]

Thoughts arise from ourselves when, naturally, we remember what we are doing, have done, or have heard (see Cuychius’s fourth annotation after the end of the work). Concerning these blessed David says, “I have considered the days of old, and I have had the eternal years in mind; and I meditated during the night with my heart, and I was troubled, and I searched my spirit” (Psalm LXXVI). And again, “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain” (Psalm XCIII). In the Gospel, too, the Lord says to the Pharisees, “Why are you thinking evil things in your hearts?” (Matthew IX).

## CHAPTER XX. He teaches, by the comparison of a tested money-changer, how our thoughts are to be discerned.

[Col. 0510B]

We must therefore continually observe this threefold method, and examine with keen discernment all the thoughts that arise in our heart, first investigating their origins, causes, and authors, so that we may consider what sort of response we ought to make to them according to the merit of those who suggest them, [Note: [Col. 0510C] Concerning this word and its meaning, there is scarcely anything that can be added to the notes of Cuychius and Ciaconius; I have therefore thought it appropriate to transcribe both of them here. Cuychius’s note runs as follows:

“Among the Greeks, trapezitae are those whom in Latin we may call money-changers, bankers, or mint officials; they are so called from money or silver—not because they engrave or gild silver vessels, for that belongs to craftsmen, but because money was examined and deposited with them, sometimes at interest and sometimes without charge. Their shops were called banking-houses. Among the Greeks they receive the name τραπεζίται from a table, for τράπεζα means ‘table.’

“It is also clear from the Gospel that among the Jews there were trapezitae, or money-changers, appointed by decree of the priests in the temple at Jerusalem, who lent money under security. Since, through their continual use of money, they could very well distinguish counterfeit and foreign coins from sound and approved currency, the name trapezitae was consequently extended in general to all who possess skill in judgment and rightly and prudently distinguish gold from orichalcum, wheat from weeds, truth from falsehood, and good from evil. John Cassianus uses the word in this sense.”

This is Cuychius’s note. Ciaconius added the following:

“Trapezita is called in Latin nummularius; mensarius may be rendered literally. For τράπεζα [Col. 0511A] means ‘table,’ and money-changers carried on their business at a table; hence, when our Lord entered the temple, he overturned the tables of the money-changers (John II). Among the Gentiles also their profit was little approved, since it generally consisted in lending at interest.

“There were, however, other trapezitae whose art was to distinguish genuine coin from counterfeit. These were popular favorites. Pliny writes of them in Book Thirty-Three, chapter nine:

‘Thus the art of testing denarii was made so pleasing to the people by statute that they dedicated entire statues to Marius Gratidianus throughout the neighborhoods. And it is remarkable that in this one of all the arts vices are learned, and the model of a false denarius is examined, while a counterfeit is bought for several genuine denarii.’

“These men are also commended by the Lord, as Cassianus does here, and as nearly all the sacred doctors report. Saint Jerome, in his letter to Numerius and Alexander (Letter 152), says:

‘Let him know that I gladly hear that saying of the Apostle: “Test everything; hold fast what is better” (I Thess. V). And also the words of the Savior: “Be approved money-changers”: so that if a coin is counterfeit, and does not bear Caesar’s image, and has not been stamped with the public mint-mark, it may be rejected; but whatever clearly presents the face of Christ should be stored in the purse of our heart.’

“Origen, in volume XIX on John, says:

‘Those who observe that command of Jesus, “Be approved trapezitae,” and the teaching of Paul, “Testing everything, hold fast what is good.”’

“Clement of Alexandria also writes near the end of Book I of the *Stromata*:

Εἰκότως ἱερὰ γραφὴ τοιούτους τινὰς ὑμᾶς διαλεκτικοὺς ὄντως θέλουσα γενέσθαι παραινεῖ, Γίνεσθε δὲ δόκιμοι τραπεζίται, πάντα μὲν ἀποδοκιμάζοντες, τὸ δὲ καλὸν κατέχοντες.

“That is:

‘With good reason Scripture, wishing you to become such truly dialectical people, exhorts you: “Be approved trapezitae, testing everything but holding fast what is good.”’

“Alluding to this, Saint Jerome says in his letter to the Ephesians, chapter IV:

‘With all diligence we must read the Scriptures and meditate day and night on the law of the Lord, so that, as approved trapezitae, we may know which coin is genuine and which counterfeit.’

“Saint Ambrose also alludes to it in Book I on Luke, chapter 1, and Book IX, chapter 10; as do Basil on Isaiah, chapter I, and Clement in Book II, chapter 21 of the *Apostolic Constitutions*.

“But, to mention this in passing, that saying is not found anywhere in the whole New Testament. I therefore adopted the opinion that it had been taken from the Gospel according to the Hebrews, from which the most ancient authors—Ignatius, Clement, Origen, and others—inserted certain passages into their writings, as Saint Jerome several times testifies in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers* (at the beginning of chapter 20, volume I), and Jerome himself in his commentary on Isaiah, chapter XL.”

Thus far Ciaconius. I embrace his conjecture more readily than the one noted above by Cuychius. Moreover, Baronius notes that the Gospel according to the Hebrews (A.D. 99) was the Gospel of Saint John translated into Hebrew, which Eusebius mentions at the end of Book III of his *Ecclesiastical History*—and in which those words may perhaps have been contained, since they are absent from the Greek and Latin texts—or, more probably, the Hebrew Gospel of Matthew used by the Nazarenes. For Saint Epiphanius calls it the Gospel according to the Hebrews (*Against Heresies* 30), as does Saint Jerome, who translated it into Latin, although those words have nevertheless dropped out of his version.

There is, however, no contradiction in supposing that the saying under discussion was a word or command of the Savior, as Origen and Jerome affirm, even if it is expressed in no Gospel. For, as Pope Innocent III says, many things concerning the Lord’s words and deeds are found to have been omitted by the evangelists, although the apostles are read either to have supplied them orally or to have expressed them by their actions (*Decretals*, Book II, *On the Celebration of Masses*, chapter “Cum Marthae”). Paul says in the Acts of the Apostles:

‘You must remember the word of the Lord Jesus, who said: “It is more blessed to give than to receive.”’

None of the four Evangelists recorded this. Thus Innocent. (See also Melchior Canus, *On Theological Places*, Book III, chapter 3 and following.) That saying, therefore, may have been received from apostolic tradition, even though it was omitted by the Evangelists.] so that, in accordance with the Lord’s command, [Col. 0511A] we may become approved trapezitae. [Note: [Col. 0512A] Here he identifies four defects, or vices, of coins or currency of every kind—defects also specified by imperial laws and to be examined by money-changers. He teaches us spiritually to imitate and observe the industry and skill with which they investigate and distinguish such defects when we examine our own ideas and thoughts, and likewise any counsels, doctrines, or suggestions introduced to us either externally or internally.

“The first duty of a good trapezita, or money-changer, is to test whether a coin is of sound currency—for example, whether it is genuine gold or orichalcum; [Col. 0512B] or genuine silver or shining tin. On this subject there is an imperial constitution of Gratian and Theodosius, Book III, chapter *On Old Coins* (see Cassiodorus, Book VII of the *Variae*, letter 32).

“Second, he must test whether it is pure—that is, whether it has been adulterated by no admixture of another metal. Concerning this, the Julian law on embezzlement decreed that no one should add anything to or mix anything into public gold, silver, or bronze (*Digest*, Book 48, title 13, law 1). The Cornelian law states the matter more explicitly: whoever adds any adulterant to gold or casts counterfeit silver coins is to be held liable for forgery (*Digest*, Book 48, title 10, law 9). Hence money is called *aerosa* when it contains a large admixture of bronze (Covarruvias, volume I, final chapter).

“Third, he must test whether the coin bears the true image of the lawful prince, or instead the mark or figure of some tyrant. Coins of this sort are properly called *paracharagmata* or *paratypa*, and those who make them *paracharactae*; they are discussed in the aforesaid law of Gratian and Theodosius. Ulpian calls them rejected coins, from which the emperor’s face is absent.

“Finally, he must test whether the coin has its proper and due weight, and has not been worn away or clipped. Valentinian and Valens treat this in their law *On Old Coins*. I have wished to record these points for the benefit of the curious reader; they can also assist spiritual understanding and instruction, as will become clear below.] whose highest expertise and discipline consist in testing which is the purest gold and, as it is commonly called, [Note: [Col. 0512C] *Obrizum*, or *obryzum*, χρυσίον ὄβρυζον, is gold that has often been smelted and purified; it is also called completely pure. Isidore, Book XVI, chapter 17 of the *Etymologies*, thinks that *obrizum* was so called because it shines with its brilliance, since it is of the finest color; the Hebrews call it *Ophaz*, and the Greeks καθαρόν, ‘pure.’ Pliny, however, writes in Book XXXIII, chapter 3:

‘The more gold has been exposed to fire, the more it improves in quality; and fire is the test of gold, so that it glows with a color like fire. For this reason it is called *obrizum*.’

Pagninus says in the *Treasury of the Sacred Language* that *obrizum* was derived from *Ophir*, as though *ophirizum*. Ophir was a place exceedingly rich in the finest gold, which was customarily brought to Solomon, III Kings IX (Saint Jerome, letters 133 and 140; Theodoret on Daniel X. See Pererius’s commentary on Genesis, Book III).] *obrizum*, or what has been insufficiently purified and smelted by fire; and not to be deceived by a bronze or base coin if it imitates a precious coin beneath the appearance of shining gold, but with the most prudent discernment to distinguish not only coins that display the faces of tyrants, but also those that bear the image of a genuine king without having been lawfully struck. Then he must carefully inquire, by the judgment of the balance, whether anything has been diminished from their lawful weight. [Note: [Col. 0512D] Saint Gregory treats this same comparison most beautifully in Book XXXIII, chapter 37 of the *Moralia*. Although he is speaking specifically about heretics, his words agree most aptly with this passage. He writes:

‘The more the mind of the elect clings to the inward light, the more subtly it sees how it ought to distinguish virtues from vices. What wonder is it that we do spiritually what we see money-changers perform bodily every day? When they receive a coin, they first examine its quality, then its image, and finally its weight, lest either bronze be hidden beneath the appearance of gold, or what is truly gold be dishonored by the image of a rejected coin, or what is both gold and correctly imaged be lightened by an incomplete weight.

‘When, therefore, we observe the remarkable deeds of unknown people, we ought, like skilled money-changers, to place them upon the balance of our mind, so that discernment may first examine the gold, lest vice conceal itself under the appearance of virtue, and what is done with a corrupt intention be masked by the appearance of righteousness. If the quality of the intention is approved, the image impressed upon it must next be sought: whether it derives from approved moneyers—that is, from the ancient Fathers—and whether it is in no way corrupted by comparison with their way of life.

‘When the quality of the intention has been recognized and the correct image has been confirmed by example, it remains to investigate whether its weight is complete. For a good work that shines through signs and miracles, if it does not possess the fullness of perfection, must be carefully weighed by vigilant caution, lest, while an imperfect thing is accepted as perfect, it turn to the harm of the one who accepts it.

‘How, then, do the preachers of Antichrist possess the genuine quality of a coin, when in what they do they do not know the force of a right intention, because through these things they seek not the heavenly homeland but the summit of temporal glory? How do they not differ from the image of the coin, when by persecuting the righteous they disagree with all the piety of the righteous? How do they display in themselves the weight of integrity, when they have not only failed to attain the perfection of humility, but have not even reached its first threshold?

‘From this, from this, let the elect learn how to despise the signs of heretics, whose actions plainly oppose everything that is remembered as having been done by the pious Fathers.’

These are Saint Gregory’s words concerning the examination of the conduct and actions of heretics. From them a general teaching may be derived concerning the careful examination of the other actions and thoughts of human beings, which are under discussion here.] All these things we too must observe spiritually, as the Gospel teaching demonstrates by means of this example and name. First, whatever may have slipped into our hearts, or whatever doctrine may have been introduced into us, must be most carefully investigated: whether it has been purified by that divine and heavenly fire of the Holy Spirit, or whether, belonging to Jewish superstition or descending from the swelling pride of secular philosophy, it merely presents piety on the surface.

We shall be able to fulfill this if we put into practice the apostolic saying, [Note: [Col. 0513C] Several points should be noted concerning this saying. First, it applies to matters concerning which it is doubtful whether they come from God or not, as Saint Thomas teaches (*Summa theologiae* II–II, question 189, article 10, reply to objection 1): just as it may be doubtful to those entering religious life whether a person who offers himself to religion is led by the Spirit of God or approaches hypocritically, so they ought to test whether the person approaching is moved by the divine Spirit. But for someone entering religious life there cannot be doubt whether the intention to enter religious life that has arisen in his heart comes from the Spirit of God, whose work it is to lead a person into the right land.

“Second, by ‘spirit’ may be understood any doctrine of a private person, or any suggestion, inspiration, revelation, or impulse of mind and will toward doing or avoiding something. The question here concerns all such things in general: whether they come from God, and therefore whether, following the example of money-changers, they ought carefully to be tested, examined, and investigated. I said ‘of a private person,’ for we are not to test whether the spirit of Sacred Scripture, the Catholic Church, the Roman Pontiff, general councils, or the mutually concordant holy Fathers and doctors comes from God—that is, whether it is true or false—since they contain complete and certain truth; rather, they are to be embraced with all reverence.

“Third, it must be understood that this task of judging spirits and testing them does not belong to everyone, but to those who preside, or to those who, as the Apostle says, ‘through practice have their senses trained for the discernment of good and evil’ (Heb. V), and who possess the gift of discerning spirits, discussed below. This gift is not given to everyone, although, insofar as it is useful, it is given to those who ask and flee to God. Therefore, whoever lacks it, or lacks wisdom, should ask God, who gives generously to all and reproaches no one, as the Apostle James says (James IV).

“Fourth, just as gold is tested and examined by fire or by the Lydian stone, called χρυσίτης, or by other suitable tests, so this certain rule must be observed in testing spirits: we should embrace as true, catholic, and salutary that doctrine, suggestion, or inspiration which is consonant with Sacred Scripture, general councils, the definitions of the pontiffs, and the opinions of the Fathers, and which is also found to agree with the piety and practice of the Church. “The statement that follows—‘And he deserved to be condemned to eternal death’—is quite harsh and insufficiently authoritative as the opinion of this anchorite, since both the historical text and the consensus of interpreters rather suggest that Achan truly and sincerely repented, openly acknowledged his sin, and thus, by a public and humble confession, gave glory to God. He said:

‘For he has commanded his angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways; they will carry you in their hands, lest you ever strike your foot against a stone’ (Psalm XC; Matthew IV). [Note: [Col. 0515C] Although the devil corrupted this Scripture by a malicious interpretation, attempting to apply to Christ, God and man, what had properly been said of a righteous man—that is, a mere human being—as the text here says, his argument therefore appeared to have greater force. He seemed to reason no less plausibly than vigorously from the lesser to the greater: ‘It is written concerning any righteous man: “God has commanded his angels concerning you,” and so forth; therefore it is much more so concerning Christ, who is not merely a righteous man but also the Son of God.’

“Yet beneath this subtle and deceptive argument the unwary sophist forged several irresistible arguments against himself and repeatedly slew himself with his own sword. If he was the Son of God—or rather, because he was the Son of God—he did not need the protection of angels; and because he was righteous, he could not tempt God, for then he would not be righteous (see Vincent of Lérins, chapters 37 and 38). If tempting God is foreign to a righteous man, how much more is it foreign to the Son of God!

“Thus Saint Chrysostom, or whoever was the author of the *Opus imperfectum* on Matthew, says:

‘Truly, the Son of God is not carried in the hands of angels; rather, he himself carries the angels. And if he is carried in the hands of angels, it is not so that, as one who is weak, he may not strike his foot against a stone, but for honor, as a lord. O devil, you read that the Son of God is carried in the hands of angels, but you did not read that he treads upon the asp and the basilisk. You put forward the former as a proud man, but conceal the latter as a cunning one’ (*Homily* 5).] Thus, by a crafty appropriation, he turned the precious utterances of Scripture and twisted them toward an adverse and harmful meaning, so that he might present us with the image of a tyrant’s face beneath the appearance of deceptive gold—or when [Note: [Col. 0516B] All printed and manuscript copies read *paracharaxismis*, although it clearly seems that one ought to read *paracharagmīs*, as Ciaconius noted, or *paracharagmatis*, that is, counterfeit coins, marked with a false stamp, as stated above. (See Molanus, *On Images*, chapter 13.) I shall likewise append here the serious and useful notes of both Cuychius and Ciaconius on this word, lest I seem unwilling to honor their scholarship or to serve the public benefit. (See Didacus Covarruvias, in the place cited above.) Cuychius writes as follows:

‘*Paracharaxima*, or *paracharagmata*, are counterfeit and false marks or coins; those who mint such currency are called *paracharactae*. For παραχαράσσειν means “to counterfeit” and “to stamp falsely.” Thus the most cunning demon and his heretical agents produce many works that indeed present an outward appearance of piety, but are intended for deception and illusion. Many examples of such works may be seen in Cassianus, in the first two Conferences.’

Ciaconius writes:

‘*Paracharaxismum*, or, as I believe it should be read, *paracharagmum*, is false money, called in Greek παράχαραγμα. Hence *paracharactae* are those who mint false coins. Thus, in Book IX of the Theodosian Code, title *On False Money*, law 8: “Those guilty of false money, whom the common people call *paracharactae*, are liable to the charge of treason.” Cassianus likewise reports in the second Conference, chapter 9, that *paracharagmum* was a common word; and I have no doubt that he took it from Origen. Origen writes in the third homily on Leviticus:

‘Our Lord Jesus Christ alone can teach you such an art, by which you can distinguish what money bears the image of the true king from what is counterfeit and, as the common expression has it, formed outside the mint—what indeed bears the king’s name but does not preserve the reality of the royal image.’

“What the Latin translator renders ‘formed outside the mint’ I believe was παράχαραγμα in Greek, for I have not had the opportunity to see those homilies in Greek. The same author writes in the third homily on Psalm XXXVI:

‘The speech of all heretics is not approved money; it does not possess the Lord’s figure in its entirety, but is counterfeit and, so to speak, formed outside the mint, because it has been composed outside the Church.’

“That *charagma* signifies the image impressed upon a coin is shown by the author whom they call the author of the *Opus imperfectum*, in homily 38 on Matthew, where he writes:

‘A coin that does not have Caesar’s *charagma* is rejected.’

“If I judge correctly, Cassianus declined *paracharagmum* with a Latin ending, as he did other Greek nouns. This is Ciaconius’s note.] he tries to deceive us with counterfeit coins, suggesting some work of piety that ought to be undertaken—one that, not proceeding from the lawful currency of the elders, leads under the pretext of virtues toward vices, whether by immoderate and unsuitable fasts, excessive vigils, disordered prayers, or inappropriate reading, deceiving us and drawing us toward a harmful end.

“Or when he persuades us to undertake pious intercessions and visitations by which he may drive us from the spiritual cloisters of the monastery and the seclusion of friendly quiet; or suggests that we assume the concerns and cares of religious and abandoned women, so that, entangled beyond escape in such snares, a monk may be stretched out under the burden of harmful preoccupations.

“Or certainly when, under the pretext of edifying many and out of love for spiritual profit, he urges us to desire the holy office of the clergy, through which he may tear us away from the humility and strictness of this profession. Although all these things are contrary to our salvation and profession, they are nevertheless easily able to deceive the inexperienced and unwary because they are covered by a kind of veil of mercy and religion.

“For they imitate the coins of the true king, because for the moment they appear full of piety; but they have not been stamped by lawful moneyers—that is, by approved and catholic Fathers. They do not come from the authoritative and public workshop of their teaching, but have been secretly manufactured by the fraud of demons and are thrust upon the inexperienced and ignorant, not without their harm.

“Although these things may at present seem useful and necessary, if afterward they begin to be contrary to the firmness of our profession and in some way weaken the whole body of our commitment, they ought to be cast away and cut off from us, like a necessary but scandalizing member that seems to perform the work of the right hand or foot. It is better to remain sound and firm in the other matters without one member of the commandment—that is, without one activity or fruit—and to enter the kingdom of God as one who is weak, than, while retaining the completeness of the commandment, to fall into some scandal that through a harmful habit separates us from the rule of strictness and the discipline of the undertaking we have embraced, and brings us into such ruin that, making no compensation for future losses, it causes all our former fruits and the entire body of our work to be burned in the fires of Gehenna (Matthew XVIII).]

The kinds of such deceptions are also elegantly expressed in Proverbs:

‘There are ways that seem right to a man, but their ends will come into the depths of hell’ (Proverbs XIV). [Note: [Col. 0517C] The Vulgate reads: ‘There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end leads to death’ (Proverbs XIV and XVI). Cassianus has joined together two passages from Proverbs. The first is from chapter XIV, which Saint Jerome quotes in Book I *Against the Pelagians* in this form: ‘There is a way that seems to men to be right, but its ends descend into the depths of hell.’ The second is from chapter XVI, which the same Jerome cites in his commentary on Isaiah II and in Book II, chapter 1 of *Against the Pelagians*, as follows: ‘There are ways that seem right to a man, but their ends look toward the depths of hell.’]

And again:

‘The wicked person does harm when he mingles with the righteous’ (Proverbs XVI), [Note: [Col. 0517C] The Septuagint reads: πονηρὸς κακοποιεῖ ὅταν συμμίξῃ δικαίῳ, μισεῖ δὲ ἦχον ἀσφαλείας, ‘The wicked person does harm when he mingles with the righteous, but he hates the sound of security.’ The corresponding sentence in the Vulgate is very different: ‘He will be afflicted by evil who gives surety for a stranger; but whoever avoids snares will be secure’ (Proverbs XI).] that is, the devil deceives when he is concealed beneath the appearance of holiness. ‘But he hates the sound of protection,’ that is, the force of discernment that proceeds from the words and admonitions of the elders.

## CHAPTER XXI  
### The Deception of Abbot John

In this way we also learned that Abbot John, who lives at Lycus, had recently been deceived. [Note: [Col. 0517C] This John and the town or village of Lycus were discussed in Book IV of the *Institutes*, chapter 23.] For, when his body had been exhausted and weakened and he had postponed eating for a two-day fast, as he approached the following day for nourishment, [Note: [Col. 0517C] Most copies, with Dionysius, read: ‘The devil came.’ Our manuscript, however, also supports the reading of the Plantin edition, and it is quite common among the Fathers to designate the devil by the name *Zabulus*. Saint Cyprian, in his letter to Demetrianus, writes: ‘Why do you fall through him and with him into the ruin of the devil?’ Some copies, as Pamelius reports, read: ‘Why do you fall into the ruin of Zabulus?’ Morelius gives this explanation: ‘The variation arose because in the Doric language, which is very close to Latin, ζα is used in place of διά, which belongs to the Attic language; for example, Ζαβάλλω for διαβάλλω, ζάκορος for διάκορος. Thus *Zabulus* is used for *diabolus* in imitation of the Doric form.’

Saint Hilary likewise writes in his commentary on Matthew, chapter IV: ‘The first power of Zabulus, entirely crushed in temptation, is indicated.’ Saint Ambrose, Book *On the Faith*, chapter 8, says: ‘What wonder if Arius imitates his author and usurps what is unlawful, although what his father Zabulus himself did not do, this man dares to do with more intolerable sacrilege? Zabulus confessed the true Son of God; Arius denies him.’

I have already noted that Cassianus above, in chapter 20, speaks of the kingdom of Zabulus for the kingdom of the devil. See also Caelius Rhodiginus, *Ancient Readings*, Book II, chapter 10. Finally, in the hymn of Saint Michael the Church sings: ‘Michael, who crushes Zabulus by his strength.’

*Zabulon* in Sacred Scripture, however, is the tenth son of the patriarch Jacob by Leah, and hence the tribe of Zebulun; but this has nothing to do with *Zabulus*.] Zabulus came in the form of a dark Ethiopian, threw himself at his knees, and said: ‘Forgive me, for I imposed this labor upon you.’

And so that great man, perfect in the practice of discernment, understood that he had been deceived by the devil’s cunning under the appearance of an inappropriately practiced abstinence, and had been burdened with such a fast that he was adding unnecessary exhaustion—indeed, harmful to the spirit—to a body already fatigued: [Col. 0518B] he had been deceived, that is, by a counterfeit coin, while reverencing in it the image of the true king and insufficiently investigating whether it had been lawfully struck. [Note: [Col. 0518C] That is, falsely and counterfeited. Peter Damian also uses the same word elsewhere, although perhaps in corrupt form, where he says: ‘If the standard of the coin itself has been rubbed away or worn down after it has been impressed upon the metals, it is found to be not a coin but a *paracharaximus*’ (Book II, letter 1 to a cardinal bishop).] [Note: [Col. 0518C] The fourth task or duty of a good trapezita, or money-changer, is the examination of the coin’s weight, mentioned above. The need to observe this also in spiritual examination is taught excellently both in this chapter and in the following one.]

The final duty of this approved trapezita, which we said concerned the investigation of weight, will be fulfilled by us in this way: whatever our thought has suggested should be done, [Note: [Col. 0518D] Ciaconius reads *scripulum* from the Vatican manuscript. ‘For,’ he says, ‘a *scripulum* is a small weight, namely the twenty-fourth part of an ounce. It is also called *scriptulum* or *scribulum*, a word derived from *scribo*, following the usage of the Greeks, who call such a weight γράμμα or γραμμή, that is, a “letter,” because just as a letter among them is one twenty-fourth of the alphabet, so a *gramma* or *scripulum* is one twenty-fourth of an ounce.’

It is also called *scrupulus* and *scrupulum* with the same meaning, and metaphorically for care and anxiety; in this sense it may also be understood here.] let us reconsider it with every scruple [Lipsius, in the margin: *scrupulo*], place it upon the balance of our breast, and weigh it with the fairest equilibrium: whether it is filled with ordinary honesty; whether it is heavy with the fear of God; whether it is sound in meaning; whether it is lightened by human ostentation or by some presumptuous novelty; whether the weight of its merit has not been diminished or gnawed away by empty vainglory.

Then, immediately submitting these things to public examination—that is, comparing them with the deeds and testimonies of the prophets and apostles—we should either accept them as complete and perfect, and equivalent to those standards, or reject them with every precaution as imperfect and harmful, and not consonant with their weight.

## CHAPTER XXII  
### The Fourfold Method of Discernment
It will therefore be necessary for us to exercise this discernment in the fourfold manner we have described: first, so that the material of the true gold—or of the counterfeit gold that deceives us—may not escape our notice; second, so that we may reject as counterfeit coins and false imitations those very thoughts which pretend to be works of piety, since they contain the false image of the king without having been lawfully stamped; and likewise those which, in the most precious gold of the Scriptures, display not the face of the true king but that of a tyrant, through a corrupt and heretical interpretation, so that we may discern and reject them in the same way; or those whose weight and value the rust of vanity gnawing at them prevents from being brought into conformity with the standard of the elders, so that we may refuse them as light and defective coins, of insufficient weight.

[Note: [Col. 0519C] Anacephalaeosis—a recapitulation—of what precedes.]

[Note: Elsewhere, “to be in conformity.” Here Cuychius says: “Things conform to the standard (*exagium*) of the elders when they are approved after examination by their judgment. For the term *exagium* seems to be derived from the Greek ἐξαγέομαι, which, among other meanings, signifies to relate, expound, examine, and comment.” The paraphrase of Saint Dionysius is not far from this view: “to be made equal to the acts of the elders.” Thus Cuychius. But Ciaconius takes it otherwise: “We would not know what *exagium* was unless the marble tablet in the Colonna palace at Rome had taught us. It is inscribed: ‘By the authority of Turcius Apronianus, *vir clarissimus*, prefect of the City, calculation has shown, utility urging, that, with the custom of bargaining by fingers removed, livestock ought to be sold by standard weight rather than by fingers concluding the bargain; so that, once the animal has been weighed, with the head, feet, the *saevum lactaneum*, and the subjugular butcher’s portion ceded, the remaining meat, with skin and entrails, may benefit the seller, the trustworthiness of the weight being established under public observation; so that both buyer and seller may know how much the flesh of the slaughtered animal weighs,’ etc. Therefore, something is made equal by *exagium* when it is required and examined against the reliability of a public weight.]

Lest, by falling into that which the Lord’s command urges us with all our strength to avoid, we be defrauded of all the wages and merits of our labors, we are warned: “Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where rust and moth destroy, and where thieves break in and steal” (Matthew VI).

Whatever we do out of consideration for human glory, let us recognize, according to the Lord’s judgment, that we are storing up treasure on earth. Consequently, like something hidden in the ground and buried in the soil, it will either be plundered by various demons, consumed by the devouring rust of vainglory, or eaten away by the moths of pride, so that it may yield no benefit or profit to the one who stored it up.

All the hidden recesses of our heart must therefore be continually searched, and the traces of whatever enters them must be examined with the keenest investigation, lest some intellectual beast—whether a passing lion or dragon—should secretly leave there harmful footprints, thereby opening an approach, through negligence in our thoughts, to the other things hidden in our breast. Thus, plowing the soil of our heart hour by hour and moment by moment with the Gospel plow—that is, by continual remembrance of the Lord’s cross—we shall be able both to destroy the lairs of the harmful beasts within us and to drive out the hiding places of venomous serpents.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the teacher’s discourse according to the merit of his hearers

When the old man saw us astonished at this and inflamed with an insatiable ardor by the words of his account, he paused for a little while, out of admiration for our eagerness, and then added:

“Since, my sons, your assiduity has drawn us into so long a discussion, and since a kind of fire, on account of your eagerness, supplies our conversation with more ardent feelings, so that from this very fact I plainly perceive that you truly thirst for the teaching of perfection, I wish to say a few things to you about the excellence or grace of discernment, which holds the citadel and primacy among all the virtues, and to approve its excellence and usefulness not only by examples from daily life but also by the ancient conferences and judgments of the Fathers.

“For I frequently remember that, when certain men asked for such a discourse with groans and tears, I too desired to contribute some instruction to them but was utterly unable to do so. Thus not only my understanding but even my speech failed me, so that I could not find a way to send them away with even slight consolation. From these indications it is clearly recognized that the grace of the Lord inspires the speech of those who are discussing matters according to the merit and desire of their hearers.

“Since the very short space of night that remains does not allow us to complete what is still to be said, let us rather devote it to bodily rest, to which all of it must necessarily be paid if even this small amount is denied. Let us reserve the complete order of the account for the undivided examination of the coming day or night.

“For it is fitting that the best counselors concerning discernment should first reveal their diligence of mind in this matter and prove, by this indication and by their patience, whether they are—or can be—capable of it. While treating of the virtue that gives birth to moderation, they must not incur the vice contrary to it, namely excess, and violate by their deeds and conduct the force of the reason and nature they cultivate in words.

“Therefore, may this good of discernment, about which we intend to inquire further insofar as the Lord grants it, first benefit us in this respect: that, while we discuss its excellence and moderation—the first virtue known to belong to it—it may not permit us to exceed the proper measure of either discussion or time.”

Having said this, blessed Moses brought our conference to an end. He urged us, still eager and hanging upon his lips, to take a little sleep.

[Note: We have said something about *psiathia* in Book Four of the *Institutes*, chapter 13. It is indicated both here and elsewhere (Conferences XVII.3 and XVIII.11) that among those anchorites these had a twofold use: they served as a seat and as a bed for taking sleep, though they slept on them in such a way that they seemed more like people sitting than lying down. This occasion also suggests the following observation: formerly religious men were accustomed either (1) to lie upon the ground, or (2) upon beds of rushes or straw, or (3) upon haircloth.

“Chameunia,” that is, sleeping on the ground, is exemplified by Saint Jerome in Letter 22, where, recalling his manner of life and austerity in the desert, he says: “My misshapen limbs recoiled beneath sackcloth, and a squalid skin had overlaid the swarthiness of Ethiopian flesh; every day there were tears, every day groans; and whenever approaching sleep overcame my resistance, I battered against the bare ground my bones that scarcely clung together.” The same author writes of Hilarion: “Upon bare ground and a bed of rushes he lay until death.”

He also mentions chameuniae in chapter 41 of Isaiah and associates them with fasting and restraint in food. Saint Gregory Nazianzen, in Oration 11, says among other things of his sister Gorgonia: “O tender limbs prostrate upon the ground and surpassing themselves contrary to nature.” Saint Athanasius, in the *Life of Saint Antony*, writes: “He gave his limbs over to rest upon woven rushes”—the Greek has *psathiō*—“and used haircloth; sometimes he even lay upon the bare ground.”

Sidonius Apollinaris, poem 16, praises Bishop Faustus:

> Gathering brief sleep upon a cold turf.

Paulinus, Book IV on Saint Martin:

> But whenever his eyes had yielded to brief sleep,  
> Bare earth spread beneath him was sufficient for delicate slumber.

As for a bed or mat of rushes or straw, we have just heard of it from Athanasius and Jerome. Since it was spread upon the earth, it is called *stratura* in Justinian’s Fifth Novella, where the translator renders it “a mattress spread upon the ground.” What Cassian calls a *psiathium*, Sidonius, Letter 24 of Book IV, calls a bed containing no feathers; Gregory of Tours, in the *Book of the Lives of the Fathers*, calls it a mat.

Hence Peter of Cluny, Book III, Letter 20, says: “Prepare the mats, the ancient work of monks, upon which you may always, or frequently, sleep.” The same author, Book II, Letter 50, writes: “He himself sat upon the monastic mat that stood next to his seat.” Saint Benedict, chapter 55 of the Rule, says: “The bedding of the beds should be sufficient: a mat and a blanket,” and so forth.

The same subject is addressed in chapter 50 of the Rule of Saint Pachomius: “Let no one sleep apart from”—that is, outside—“his reclining little chair.” The ancient Rule of the Nuns, chapter 32, preserved by Saint Jerome, says: “Therefore, dearest sisters, I wish you to spend each night in your cells upon a short and hard bed, not upon feathers or anything soft, but either upon straw or rushes, or rather in wooden boxes than in little beds, so that your limbs may dread rather than desire a bed spread for them,” and so forth.

There are many examples of lying or sleeping upon haircloth. Would that we might imitate them! I shall mention only a few of the older and more illustrious. First there is the example of Saint Antony mentioned above; then that of Saint Martin, who, as Sulpicius reports, gave up his spirit to God while lying upon his famous bed—namely, ashes and haircloth.

There is also the example of Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, concerning whom Victor of Utica writes in Book III of *The Vandal Persecution*: “While holy Eugenius mourned the hardships of our persecution, and wore down his aged body with the roughness of haircloth, lying upon the bare ground and soaking his sackcloth bed with showers of tears,” and so forth.

Finally, there are examples among women as well: Paula, the most noble Roman matron, of whom Saint Jerome writes in her epitaph, Letter 27: “Even in the most serious fever she had no soft bedding for her little bed, but rested upon the hardest ground spread with small haircloths—if indeed that can be called rest which she joined day and night to almost unceasing prayers.”

Moreover, besides the examples given above, it was also customary for monks to die in haircloth and ashes. This is taught by the following words of Sulpicius, Letter 3 on the death of Saint Martin, concerning Saint Martin when he was already near death: “Through the entire night, in prayers and vigils, he compelled his weary limbs to serve the spirit, lying upon that famous bed of his, in ashes and haircloth. When his disciples asked him to allow at least some humble bedding to be placed beneath him, he replied: ‘It is not fitting, my sons, for a Christian to die except in ashes. If I leave you any other example, I myself have sinned.’”

Peter the Venerable makes the same point explicitly in his account of the death of the monk Gilbert: “It happened, not long afterward, that he came to his end through the illness he had contracted. And when, as is the custom of Christians, especially monks, he had been laid out by the brothers upon haircloth and ashes and was awaiting the hour of his calling, the brothers of the monastery came to commend his departure to God in their prayers and surrounded him on every side with psalmody,” and so forth (Peter the Venerable, Book I of the *Miracles*, chapter 4).

In chapter 19 of the same book he says: “In the middle of the house there is a place capable of holding one body, prepared for this purpose, so that the brothers likewise, arranged in ashes and haircloth, may give up their spirit to God there.”

In Book II, chapter 22, concerning the funeral and burial in the monastery of Cluny of Matthew, bishop of Albano, he writes: “With these final words, after he had brought all his speeches to an end, he reclined upon his bed, and shortly afterward was transferred from there by the brothers to haircloth sprinkled with ashes.” He had often previously asked the brothers not to permit him, by any accident, to die except in ashes and haircloth, in the Christian manner, and so forth.]

He therefore instructed us to lie down upon the very same *psiathia* on which we had been sitting, placing *embrimia* beneath our heads in place of pillows. These were made from thicker papyrus sheets fitted into long, slender bundles.

[Note: This is a barbarous word, as are many others used by those monks. Its meaning, however, is sufficiently explained here. Ciaconius says that he read it in Metaphrastes, in the *Life of Euthymius the Abbot*, as the Greek *embrymium*. Cuychius’s conjecture is less probable.]

Bound together at regular intervals of one foot, these now provide the brothers sitting in the Synaxis with a very low seat in place of a stool; at other times, placed beneath the necks of those sleeping, they provide the head with a support that is not excessively hard but pliable and suitable.

[Note: More usual than *fulmentum*, as Ciaconius has it, although the word is also used by reputable authors.]

These objects are especially useful and suitable for the needs of monks, not only because they are somewhat soft and can be prepared with little labor and at little cost, since papyrus grows everywhere along the banks of the Nile—

[Note: The Nile is a river of Egypt, one of the greatest rivers in the whole world (Pliny, Book V, chapter 9; Strabo, Book XVII; Genesis II). Some call it Gihon. It has seven mouths through which it discharges itself into the Egyptian sea, and divides and embraces Lower Egypt on both sides, determining its boundaries in such a way as to form a triangular shape of land. Hence, because of its resemblance to the Greek letter Δ, they called it the Delta.

According to Pliny (Book XIII, chapter 11), papyrus is a little tree that grows especially in the marshes of Egypt or in the still waters of the Nile, where its waters, having overflowed, become stagnant and the depth of the pools does not exceed two cubits. The inhabitants use its roots in place of wood; from its trunk they weave boats; from its inner bark they make cloth, mats, garments, coverings, ropes, and other things of this kind.

From this shrub they also prepared sheets of writing material, cut with a needle into extremely thin and broad strips, called *phyllirae*. They were better in proportion as they were nearer the middle of the papyrus, and from the name of the shrub they too received the name papyrus. The ancients used them for writing. Later, the kind of paper now commonly used by human beings was invented; it is made from crushed linen rags, yet it retains the ancient name of papyrus.]

—but also because, when they must be removed or moved, they are made of light material and are easy to handle.

Thus, at last, following the old man’s instruction, we settled down for a burdensome taste of sleep, both inflamed with joy at the conference that had been so carefully arranged and suspended in expectation of the promised discussion.

# THE SECOND CONFERENCE

Which is the second conference of Abbot Moses.

## ON DISCERNMENT

[Col. 0523]

### CHAPTER I

After we had tasted the morning sleep, and, rejoicing that the light had at last dawned upon us, had begun to ask again for the promised account, blessed Moses began as follows:

[Note: This is the second conference of Abbot Moses, the substance of which Photius likewise summarized in a few words (Photius, *Bibliotheca*, codex 197).]

“Since I see you inflamed by such ardent desire that I cannot believe even the smallest moment of rest has benefited your bodies—the moment I had withheld from spiritual conversation and preferred to devote to the restoration of the flesh—I too, observing your fervor, feel a greater concern. For, in fulfilling my obligation, I must show a correspondingly greater devotion, the more attentively I see you seeking it, according to the saying:

[Note: This follows the version of the Septuagint translators. The Vulgate reads: “When you sit to eat with a ruler, diligently consider what is set before you, and put a knife to your throat,” and so forth (Proverbs XXIII). The Fathers offer various explanations of this saying, both literal and proper and mystical and spiritual (see Delrio, *Adagialia*, part 2). Among the mystical interpretations is the one followed by the Author here: he teaches that a teacher must satisfy his disciples with proportionately greater concern insofar as he notices their greater fervor and attention. Saint Ambrose likewise almost follows this interpretation in Book I of *The Duties*, chapter 22, where he proves from this passage that thanks should be returned when someone has received a benefit from another, and that we should imitate the nature of the earth, which is accustomed to return the seed it receives in greater abundance than it received it.]

“‘When you sit down to dine at the table of a powerful man, understand wisely what is set before you, and put your hand to it, knowing that you must prepare such things’ (Proverbs XXIII, according to the Septuagint).

“Therefore, since we are going to speak about the good of discernment and its virtue, into which the discourse of our nocturnal conference entered and which brought our discussion to an end, we think it appropriate first to establish its excellence by the judgments of the Fathers. Once it has become clear what our elders thought and pronounced concerning it, we shall then bring forward the ancient as well as more recent ruins and falls of many who, because they had attained less of it, were cast down in a destructive collapse. Insofar as we are able, we shall reconsider its usefulness and benefits, so that, after these matters have been examined, we may be more effectively instructed when we consider how we ought to cultivate and seek it, recognizing the weight of its merit and grace.

“For it is no ordinary virtue, nor one that human effort can readily grasp, unless it has been bestowed by a divine gift and grace. Indeed, we read that the Apostle numbers it among the noblest gifts of the Holy Spirit:

“‘To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another the gift of healings in one Spirit’ (1 Corinthians XII).

“And shortly afterward:

[Note: Saint Thomas explains these gifts of the Holy Spirit—or what are called gratuitously given graces—brilliantly, both in his commentary and in the *Summa Theologica* (I–II, question 112, article 4).
