By “discernment of spirits” he understands knowledge of the human heart and its secrets. “Just as prophecy,” he says, “is given for knowing and manifesting contingent future events, which only God can know, so discernment of spirits is given for manifesting the hidden things of hearts, which God alone searches, so that a person may discern by what spirit someone is moved to speak and act—for example, whether by the spirit of charity or of envy—according to 1 John IV: ‘Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God.’”

Saint Ambrose appears to take the expression somewhat more broadly when he says: “Discernment of spirits enables one to understand and judge whether what is said belongs to the Holy Spirit or to the worldly spirit.” But the abbot here takes it in the broadest sense, as the judgment of discernment that the Apostle calls “the discernment of good and evil” (Hebrews V), or the capacity to distinguish between truth and falsehood, good and evil, what should be sought and what should be avoided. This is nothing other than true Christian prudence, which Saint Augustine defines in Book I of *On Free Choice of the Will*, chapter 13, as knowledge of things to be sought and avoided, and in the *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 30, as knowledge of good, evil, and indifferent things.]

“‘To another, discernment of spirits’ (1 Corinthians XII).

“Then, after completing the entire catalogue of spiritual gifts, he adds:

“‘But all these things are accomplished by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one as he wills’ (ibid.).

“You see, therefore, that the gift of discernment is not earthly or insignificant, but the greatest reward of divine grace. Unless a monk attains it with complete dedication and possesses, by a reliable method, the discernment of the spirits that arise within him, he must wander like one moving through blind night and dreadful darkness, not only falling into dangerous pits and precipices—

[Note: The Lyon edition reads: “Not only falling into perilous pits and steep places.”]

—but also frequently stumbling on level and straight paths.”

### CHAPTER II. The usefulness of discernment demonstrated from a conference of Abbot Antony

[Col. 0525B]

“I remember, then, that when I was still in the years of childhood, I was in the region of the Thebaid, where blessed Antony lived.

[Note: The Thebaid has been discussed elsewhere (Book IV of the *Institutes*, chapter 3). It is also frequently mentioned in the life of blessed Antony written by Athanasius.]

“The elders had gathered to him in order to seek perfection.

[Note: This was a customary formula of conversation among those Fathers and anchorites. Not only was the great Antony frequently present at such meetings, but he also strongly commended them. For Athanasius, recalling an exhortation of Antony delivered to the brothers at such a gathering or conference, says that he began with these words: “The Scriptures are sufficient for the whole discipline of the commandments; but it would also be very good if the brothers should console one another through mutual conversation.” And he continued: “You, therefore, as to a father, report what you know; and I shall tell you, as to sons, what I have acquired through long years.” A similar example of a conference may be found below, in chapter 11.]

“The conference continued from the evening hours until daylight, and this question consumed most of the night. For a very long time they sought to determine what virtue or practice could always preserve a monk unharmed from the snares and deceptions of the devil, or at least lead him by a straight path and steady step to the summit of perfection.

“As each person expressed his judgment according to the capacity of his mind, some placed this virtue in the pursuit of fasting and vigils, because by these the mind, weakened and brought to purity of heart and body, would more easily be united to God; others placed it in nakedness and contempt for all possessions, since, if the mind were entirely stripped of them, it would reach God more freely, as though no retaining snares held it back; others judged withdrawal, that is, seclusion and the solitude of the desert, to be necessary, because one dwelling there could address God more familiarly and cling to him more intimately; some defined the duties of charity—that is, of human kindness—as the things to be pursued, because the Lord appears to promise especially in the Gospel that these will gain the kingdom of heaven, saying:

“‘Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink,’ and so forth (Matthew XXV).

“When they had concluded that a surer approach to God could be prepared by these various virtues, and a very large part of the night had been consumed in this inquiry, blessed Antony finally said:

[Note: This is the distinguished judgment of blessed Antony concerning prudence or discernment. Blessed Basil agrees with it in the *Monastic Constitutions*, chapter 95, in these words: “Prudence must intervene in every action that is undertaken. When prudence is removed, there is nothing of any kind which, though it may seem good, does not fall into vice if it is done at the wrong time or without moderation. But when reason and prudence determine the suitable time and measure for good things, it is astonishing how much fruit their use produces both in those who give and in those who receive” (see Saint Thomas, I–II, question 61, articles 1 and 3, and II–II, question 188, article 7).]

“‘All these things you have mentioned are indeed necessary and useful to those who thirst for God and desire to reach him; but the innumerable falls and experiences of many people do not allow us to attribute the principal grace to any of them. For we have often seen some people devoting themselves with the greatest severity to fasting and vigils, withdrawing wonderfully into solitude, and pursuing the renunciation of all their possessions so rigorously that they would not permit even enough food for a single day or a single coin to remain for themselves. We have seen others fulfilling the duties of human kindness with complete devotion. Yet they were suddenly deceived, so that they could not bring the work they had undertaken to a fitting conclusion, and they ended their supreme fervor and praiseworthy way of life with a detestable end.

“Therefore, we shall be able to recognize clearly what principally leads to God if we investigate more carefully the cause of their ruin and deception. For although the works of the virtues mentioned above abounded in them, the single defect of discernment did not allow them to persevere in them to the end.

“Nor is any other cause of their fall discovered except that, having received too little instruction from the elders, they were entirely unable to acquire the method of discernment. Discernment, by avoiding both extremes, teaches a monk always to walk along the royal road. It does not allow him to be exalted on the right by the excess of the virtues—that is, to exceed the measure of proper restraint through the foolish presumption of excessive fervor—nor does it permit him, seduced by relaxation, to turn toward the vices on the left; that is, under the pretext of governing the body, it does not allow him to grow sluggish through the contrary tepidity of the spirit.

“This is discernment, which in the Gospel is called the eye and lamp of the body, according to the Savior’s saying:

[Note: “What the eye is to the body, the intellect is to the soul,” says Chrysostom. Saint Gregory, Book XXVIII of the *Moralia*, chapter 13, writes: “What is expressed by the eye except the intention of the heart, which anticipates its action? Before it exercises itself in action, it already contemplates what it desires. And what is designated by the term ‘body’ except each action, which follows its intention as a seeing eye? The eye is therefore the lamp of the body because, through the ray of a good intention, the merits of an action are illuminated. ‘If your eye is simple, your whole body will be full of light,’ because if we intend rightly through simplicity of thought, a good work is produced, even if it may appear less good. ‘But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark,’ because when something right is done with a perverse intention, even if it is seen to shine before human beings, it is nevertheless darkened before the judgment of the inner judge.” Thus Gregory.]

“‘The lamp of your body is your eye. If your eye is simple, your whole body will be full of light; but if your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark’ (Matthew VI). For discernment itself distinguishes all the thoughts and actions of a person and sees through and examines everything that must be done.

“But if this eye is evil in a person—that is, if it is not supported by true judgment and knowledge, or if it has been deceived by some error or presumption—it will make our whole body dark. In other words, it will render the entire vision of our mind and all our actions obscure, wrapped in the darkness of the blindness of vices and disturbances.

“For he says: ‘If the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness be!’ No one can doubt that, when the judgment of our heart has gone astray and has been possessed by the night of ignorance, our thoughts and works, which proceed from the deliberation of discernment, become entangled in still greater darkness of sins.”

### CHAPTER III. On the error of Saul and Ahab, by which they were deceived through lack of discernment

Finally, Saul—

[Note: Saul was the first person chosen and anointed by God as king of the Israelite people. Reader, consult the history, from which you may learn how highly obedience is valued by God, so that it is preferred to all sacrifices and burnt offerings. Saint Gregory, commenting on Saul’s excuse, writes: “This often happens in monasteries, when a subject who is less religious presumes to add something to the commands of his spiritual superiors, despises the regular and common life, and follows the judgment of his own will. While he tries to improve his life by choosing rather than by obeying, what else does he show than that he is coloring open disobedience with the appearance of virtue?”]

—the man who first obtained the kingdom of the people of Israel by God’s judgment, because he did not possess this eye of discernment, became dark in his whole body and was himself deposed from the kingdom. Deceived by the darkness and error of this lamp, he judged his sacrifices more acceptable to God than obedience to Samuel’s command, and incurred the cause of his offense precisely in that by which he had hoped to reconcile the divine majesty to himself.

The same ignorance of discernment compelled Ahab, king of Israel, after the triumph of that most exalted victory which had been granted to him by God’s favor, to believe that his mercy was better than the strict execution of the divine command and than what seemed to him a cruel order. Softened by this consideration, he preferred to temper a bloody victory with clemency; but because of his undiscerning mercy, he became dark in his whole body and was condemned to irrevocable death.

[Note: The history is found in 1 Kings XX, where Ahab, contrary to God’s command, spared the common enemy, the king of Syria, with an ill-considered and disordered clemency. The prophet pronounced a sentence of death against him: “Your life shall be for his life.”]

### CHAPTER IV. What the Holy Scriptures report concerning the good of discernment

This is the discernment that is called not only the lamp of the body but also the sun by the Apostle, according to the saying:

[Note: Here the abbot interprets “sun” as the light of discernment or reason in the Apostle’s words: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Ephesians IV). Cassian likewise gives this interpretation in Book VIII of the *Institutes*, chapter 9. We have shown there that Saint Jerome also approved this interpretation.]

“‘Let not the sun go down upon your anger’” (Ephesians IV).

This is called the governance of our life, according to the saying: “Where there is no governance, they fall like leaves.”

It is rightly called counsel, without which Scripture’s authority permits us to do nothing at all. Thus we are not even allowed to drink the spiritual wine that gladdens the human heart (Psalm CIII) without its moderation, according to the saying: “Do everything with counsel; drink wine with counsel.”

And again:

[Note: The Vulgate edition reads: “Like a city lying open and without a surrounding wall, so is a man who cannot restrain his spirit in speech” (Proverbs XXV).]

“‘Like a city whose walls have been demolished and which is not surrounded, so is a man who does anything without counsel’” (Proverbs XXV, according to the Septuagint).

The testimony and image of this comparison, likening him to a demolished city without walls, shows how harmful the absence of counsel is to a monk.

In this lies wisdom; in this lies understanding and perception. Without them, neither can our inner house be built nor can spiritual riches be gathered, according to the saying:

[Note: The Vulgate text reads: “A house shall be built by wisdom, and it shall be strengthened by prudence. By knowledge the storerooms shall be filled with every precious and beautiful substance” (Proverbs XXIV).]

“‘When a house is built with wisdom, it is raised again with understanding; with perception the storerooms are filled with all precious and good riches’” (Proverbs XXIV, according to the Septuagint).

This, I say, is solid food, which cannot be received except by the perfect and strong, according to the saying:

“‘Solid food belongs to the perfect, those whose senses, through habitual exercise, are trained to distinguish good and evil’” (Hebrews V).

Its usefulness and necessity for us are demonstrated to such an extent that it is even joined to the word of God and its virtues, according to the saying:

“‘For the word of God is living and effective, sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart’” (Hebrews IV).

These words most clearly declare that no virtue can be perfected or remain perfect without the grace of discernment. Thus the judgment both of blessed Antony and of all the Fathers has established that discernment is what leads the monk to God with firm steps and without fear, continually preserves the aforementioned virtues unharmed, and enables him to climb to the lofty heights of perfection with less fatigue. Without it, many who have labored with great dedication have been unable to reach the summit of perfection.

For discernment is the generative source, guardian, and moderator of all the virtues.

### CHAPTER V. On the death of the old man Heron

[Col. 0529A]

And so, in order that this same definition, proclaimed long ago by Saint Antony and the other Fathers, might also be confirmed by a recent example, as we promised, recall what happened only a few days ago before your own eyes:

> [Note: Palladius (Lausiac History 32) mentions a certain monk named Heron, known to him, who, after great labors and distinguished exertions, as he himself says, was seized by arrogance and self-exaltation and was cast down. But whether he is the same Heron as the one discussed here I cannot determine with sufficient certainty. For that Heron seems to have been similar to this one in intelligence, character, and even austerity of life; but not in his end. He is said not to have thrown himself into a well, but to have recovered from a serious illness and later, after confessing his sins, to have fallen asleep.]

We remember the aged Heron, who, after living in this desert for fifty years and maintaining the strictest discipline of continence, had pursued the solitudes of the wilderness with astonishing fervor, beyond all who dwelt here. How, then, and by what means, after such great labors, was he deceived by the ambusher, and, falling into a most grievous ruin, struck everyone living in this desert with mournful sorrow? Was it not because, possessing too little of the virtue of discretion, he preferred to be governed by his own decisions rather than by the counsels and conferences of the brothers and the institutions of the elders?

Indeed, he always observed an unvarying discipline of fasting with such rigor, and continually pursued the seclusion of solitude and his cell so strictly, that not even reverence for the Paschal day could ever obtain from him that he join the brotherhood in sharing a meal. While all the brothers were kept in the church for the annual solemnity, he alone could not be brought into their company, lest by partaking of even the smallest amount of legumes he should seem to have relaxed his purpose in the slightest.

Deceived by this presumption, he received the angel of Satan as though he were an angel of light with the greatest reverence, and obeyed his commands with submissive service. He threw himself headlong into a well whose depth the eye could not reach, believing without hesitation the promise of his supposed angel, who had assured him that, on account of the merits of his virtues and labors, he could no longer be subject to any danger.

To demonstrate the truth of this by the clearest proof of his own survival, he cast himself into the aforementioned well in the dead of night, intending, of course, to prove the great merit of his virtue by emerging unharmed. After he had been drawn out through the immense labor of the brothers, already almost drained of blood, and was about to end his life on the third day, he remained—what was worse—in such obstinate adherence to his deception that not even the experience of his own approaching death could persuade him that he had been deceived by demonic trickery.

Therefore, in consideration of the merits of such great labors and of the number of years during which he had persevered in the desert, it was only with the greatest compassion and humility, and through the efforts of those who pitied his destruction, that it could scarcely be obtained from the presbyter and abbot Paphnutius that he not be counted among the *biothanatoi*—those who died a violent death by their own act.

> [Note: Cassian also discusses the same man in the *Institutes*, Book V, chapter 40, and again in Conference 3, which is attributed to him as well, and in Conference 18, chapter 15, where he relates his extraordinary patience. Palladius mentions him in the *Lausiac History* (sections 37, 38, and 78), as do Nicephorus, Book IX, chapter 14, and others. He is regularly called both presbyter and abbot, so that no one may suppose him to be that Paphnutius, the famous bishop of the Upper Thebaid in ecclesiastical history, who lived long before Cassian’s time, as we have noted elsewhere.]

> [Note: As we have observed elsewhere (*Institutes*, Book VII, chapter 14), the Gentiles formerly called martyrs *biothanatoi* as an insult, because they had been killed, or were destined to be killed, by violent death. Among Christians, however, *biothanatoi* properly meant those who voluntarily brought death upon themselves or laid violent hands upon themselves. From this passage we learn that, according to the institution of the ancient Fathers and ecclesiastical discipline, it had been forbidden that their memory should be celebrated in sacred rites or that offerings should be made for them. Ecclesiastical canons also exist on this matter, by which such persons are judged unworthy of the customary commemoration and offerings for the dead. Thus the First Council of Braga, chapter 24 (in Gratian, 23.5, canon “Placuit”), states: “It has been decided that for those who voluntarily inflict death upon themselves, whether by the sword, poison, throwing themselves from a height, hanging, or by any other means, no commemoration whatsoever be made in the offering on their behalf, nor may their bodies be accompanied to burial with psalms.” The Second Council of Orléans, chapter 14, likewise says: “We decree that the offering for the dead who were killed in some crime ought to be received, provided that they are not shown to have inflicted death upon themselves with their own hands.”]

> [Note: Two ancient rites and services customarily performed for the dead from the earliest times of the Church are touched upon here: the offering, or sacrifice offered on their behalf, and their memory, or commemoration, in the sacrifice. To illuminate this passage, it will be useful to record several testimonies from antiquity concerning both.

> As regards the sacrifice, it should first be observed that it was offered especially on certain fixed and appointed days. First, on the day of death or burial, which is chiefly under discussion here; this practice derived from apostolic tradition. Saint Clement, in his First Epistle, testifies that the Apostle Peter commanded that funeral rites for the dead be celebrated with hymns, prayers, and readings. Blessed Dionysius the Areopagite confirms the same in *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 7.

> Hence Saint Cyprian, in Epistle 60, reports that it had been decreed at the Council of Carthage that if a brother—that is, a Christian—had appointed a cleric as guardian, no offering should be made for him, nor should a sacrifice be celebrated for his repose. Saint Augustine, discussing the funeral of his mother, Saint Monica, says in *Confessions*, Book IX, chapter 11: “In those prayers which we poured out to you, when the sacrifice of our redemption was offered for her, her body having already been placed beside the tomb,” and so forth.

> Second, sacrifice and prayers for the dead were customarily offered on the anniversary of death; hence the practice of anniversaries was received in the Church. Tertullian says in *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 3: “We make offerings for the dead on the annual day.” And in *On Monogamy*: “For her soul let him pray; let him offer on the annual days of her repose.” Saint Gregory Nazianzen, in his Oration for his brother Caesarius, speaks of “offering annual honors and commemorations.”

> Finally, Saint Isidore of Seville, nine hundred years ago, established that this annual rite for the dead should be observed in his monasteries, using these words in the final chapter of his Rule: “For the spirits of the dead, let sacrifice be offered on the second day after Pentecost, so that, having been made participants in blessed life and more fully purified, they may receive their bodies on the day of the resurrection.”

> It should be noted that in Saint Isidore’s time—approximately four hundred years before Saint Odilo, who first instituted a general commemoration of all the faithful departed—the annual celebration of deceased brothers was customarily held not on the fourth day before the Nones of November but on the day immediately following Pentecost.

> Moreover, in our own time, in certain monasteries this anniversary is transferred to the Monday after the feast of the Holy Trinity. I think that this is what Isidore calls “the second day after Pentecost,” counting the entire octave of Pentecost as one day.

> Third, the commemoration of the dead was celebrated with greater solemnity not only on the anniversary but also on the third, seventh, thirtieth, and fortieth days (Onuphrius, *On the Rite of Burial*). In the churches of the West, the fortieth day was especially celebrated in memory of the deceased. Thus Saint Ambrose, in his funeral oration on the death of the Emperor Theodosius, says: “We recently lamented the death of this emperor, and now we celebrate the fortieth day, with the emperor Honorius standing beside the sacred altars; for just as holy Joseph performed the rites of burial for his father Jacob for forty days, so he has paid the proper honors to Theodosius his father.”

> He immediately adds the following about the diversity of this rite: “Some have been accustomed to observe the third and thirtieth day, others the seventh and fortieth,” and so forth. Likewise, in his Oration on the Faith of the Resurrection, he says: “Now on the seventh day we approach the tomb, for that day is a symbol of the future rest.”

> Alcuin also discusses the third, seventh, and thirtieth days for the dead in *On the Divine Offices*, in the penultimate and final chapters, and explains the reason for this institution. Yet he errs in failing to distinguish the *tricenarium* from the thirtieth day. The *tricenarium* is said to have been instituted by blessed Gregory, and the Masses celebrated for it are therefore called Gregorian Masses. For in *Dialogues*, Book IV, chapter 55, Gregory reports that he ordered a sacrifice to be offered for a certain deceased brother for thirty consecutive days, so that not a single day would pass on which the saving Host was not offered for his absolution.

> This was something different from the celebration of the thirtieth day. The latter was not observed continuously for thirty days but only on the thirtieth day after death. It is much older than Gregory, since it is mentioned by Palladius in the *Lausiac History* (section 23), by Saint Ambrose, as we have just heard, and by other ancient writers.

> Let this suffice concerning the offering, or sacrifice, made for the dead—not because the sacrifice does not benefit them every day, or because their memory ought not to be kept daily in the sacrifice, but because on those particular days it was celebrated with greater solemnity.

> As for their memory, or commemoration, which is also at issue here, it should be known that, according to the custom of the ancient Church, the names both of those for whom the offering was made and of orthodox bishops, living as well as dead, were customarily recited during the sacrifice of the Mass from the sacred tablets called *diptychs* and *ptychs* (δίπτυχα καὶ πτυχά). These were two tablets: the names of the living were written on one and those of the dead on the other.

> Hence Saint Cyprian, in Epistle 10, says that their names were offered—that is, recited—in the offering of the divine sacrifice. The following passage of Dionysius the Areopagite, *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 3, also belongs here: “And when all have greeted one another, the mystical recitation of the tablets takes place.” In Greek the words are “of the sacred tablets” (ἱερῶν πτυχῶν).

> The same subject is involved in what Theodoret (Book V, chapter 34), Nicephorus (Book XIV, chapter 26), and others write concerning the name of blessed John Chrysostom, which had been erased and was subsequently restored to the sacred *diptychs*. Likewise, Damascene, in Book III *On Images*, near the end, relates from the monk Isidore that Theophilus, patriarch of Alexandria, because of the sin of having forbidden the public recitation of Chrysostom’s name in church, could not die until an image of Chrysostom had been brought to him and he had reverently worshiped it.

> Add to this Augustine, who writes in *Confessions*, Book IX, chapter 12, that as the day of her departure approached, his mother Saint Monica had neither requested nor cared about anything except that she be remembered at the altar of God, whom she had served without allowing a single day to pass.

> There is also extant a letter from certain Egyptian bishops to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, in which the sacred *diptychs* are explained in these words: “He also placed the name of Dioscorus in the venerable diptych, which contains the names of the bishops who have passed to heaven in pious memory and which are reread, according to the sacred rules, during the celebration of the holy mysteries,” and so forth.

> Finally, Pope Innocent, in his First Epistle to Decentius, commands that the names of those for whom the offering is made be recited during the sacred mysteries—namely, within the canon and not beforehand. The same practice appears in the liturgy of Chrysostom, where the recitation of the names is repeated not merely at the beginning, as in Dionysius the Areopagite and in the Mass of Saint James, but also around the consecration. (In the *Epistle of the Illustrious Men concerning the Council of Chalcedon*.)

> A trace of this practice has remained in our own canon, where the ancient manuscripts read: “Remember, Lord, the names of your male and female servants”; and again, for the dead: “Remember also their names,” and so forth. Alcuin observed this long ago in chapter 32 of the same work. Explaining the sacred canon, he says: “After the words in which it is said, ‘In the sleep of peace,’ it was the custom of the ancients, as the Roman Church still does today, for the names of the dead to be immediately recited from the *diptychs*, that is, the tablets; and after the recitation of the names, the following words were added: ‘For them, namely those whose names are remembered, and for all who rest in Christ, grant a place of refreshment,’” and so forth.

> The *Micrologus* teaches the same in *On Ecclesiastical Observances*, chapter 23. See also Durantus, *On the Rites of the Church*, Book II, chapter 43.]

would be judged unworthy of the memory and offering made for those who have gone to their rest.

## CHAPTER VI. The downfall of two brothers through lack of discretion

What shall I say about those two brothers who lived beyond that desert of the Thebaid where blessed Antony had once dwelt? Moved by insufficiently cautious discretion, they traveled through the vast expanse of the wilderness and resolved to take no food at all except what the Lord himself should provide for them.

> [Note: This was a clear tempting of God, contrary to Deuteronomy 6 and Matthew 3: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God.” Discussing this kind of temptation, Saint Thomas says (*Summa*, I–II, question 97, article 1): “When, because of some necessity or benefit, someone entrusts himself to divine assistance in his petitions or actions, this is not tempting God. For it is said in the Second Book of Chronicles 20: ‘Since we do not know what we ought to do, this alone remains for us: to direct our eyes toward you.’ But when this is done without any necessity or benefit, it is interpretatively to tempt God. Thus, concerning Deuteronomy 6, ‘You shall not tempt the Lord your God,’ the Gloss says: ‘He tempts God who, having something he can do, without reason exposes himself to danger, testing whether he can be rescued by God.’

> “A similar example might be proposed here, involving two young monks, which Cassian relates in *Institutes*, Book V, chapter 40. While carrying fruit entrusted to them by their abbot to a certain old man laboring in the desert, they could not find his cell and preferred to perish from hunger on the road rather than touch the fruit.

> “But there is a great difference between the two examples. Those young men had been ordered and strictly warned to carry the fruit intact to the old man, because in that region it was rare and choice. Although they could have conveniently interpreted the command according to *epieikeia* (ἐπιείκεια), and have judged that such an extreme necessity released them from the obligation, they were not bound to do so—especially since, given their youth, they had sound reason either to think otherwise or to set their lives below the merit of obedience and fidelity to the deposit or commission, as the passage says.

> “These men, however, were moved by no command and no suitable reason not to eat food unless it had been sent by God—unless they wished either to test God’s benevolence or power, which is to tempt God, or to display to others the excellence of their sanctity, which is a form of great presumption and arrogance.”]

When certain Mazices saw them wandering through the deserts from a distance and already wasting away from hunger—

> [Note: Ptolemy places the Mazices, or Μάζικες, in that part of Egypt or Africa where Cassian lived. Palladius mentions them as a barbarous and savage people in his account of Arsacius (*Lausiac History* 7), although he calls them Mazici. Nestorius, in Evagrius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book I, chapter 7, and Nicephorus, Book XIV, chapter 13, also mention them. In the *Lives of the Fathers* (Book IV, chapter 15), the people of the Mazices are described.]

—the Mazices [Lipsius in the margin: “Marzites” or “Marzitos,”] a people almost more savage and brutal than all other nations—for whereas the desire for plunder drives some nations to shed blood, these people were impelled solely by the ferocity of their minds—came toward them with loaves of bread, contrary to the natural savagery of their race.

One of the two brothers, with discretion coming to his aid, received the bread with joy and thanksgiving, as though it had been placed before him by the Lord. He judged that food had been divinely supplied to him, and that it had not happened without God’s providence that men who always delighted in human blood should now, when the brothers were exhausted and wasting away, offer them the substance by which life is sustained.

The other, refusing the food as though it had been offered to him by man, was consumed by the exhaustion of starvation.

Although the beginnings of both men’s conduct arose from a blameworthy conviction, one of them, when discretion came to his aid, is acknowledged to have corrected what he had conceived rashly and imprudently. The other, persisting in foolish presumption and utterly ignorant of discretion, brought upon himself the death which the Lord had wished to avert. He did not believe that it had happened through divine inspiration that the fierce barbarians, forgetting their own savagery, had offered them bread instead of swords.

## CHAPTER VII. The deception of another, which he suffered through lack of discretion

What shall I say also about the man—whose name, since he is still alive, we do not wish to mention—who, after receiving a demon in the radiance of an angel and being repeatedly deceived by his countless revelations, believed him to be a messenger of righteousness?

> [Note: Since the demon commonly appears in various forms, he is also frequently said to have appeared in the form or likeness of a good angel, and in this way deceived or attempted to deceive many. The Apostle therefore rightly said: “Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light” (2 Corinthians 11:14).

> In the *Lives of the Fathers*, the devil appeared in this way to the anchorite Abraham while he was praying at night and filled his cell with a marvelous brightness. He likewise appeared to Simeon Stylites, whom he attempted to persuade to mount a fiery chariot, like another Elijah.

> To another monk the devil appeared transformed into an angel of light and said to him: “I am the angel Gabriel, and I have been sent to you.” The monk replied: “See to it that you have been sent to someone else, for I am not worthy that an angel should be sent to me.” The devil immediately disappeared. Thus far the *Lives of the Fathers* (Book V, booklet 15).

> The devil also presented himself in the appearance of an angel to Saint Elphege, bishop of Canterbury, as Osbert, bishop of that same church, writes in his Life. He appeared similarly to Saint Oswald, bishop of Worcester, according to Surius (volumes II and V). Caesarius of Cistercian reports many other examples in Book III, chapter 14, and Book V, chapter 47. Saint Peter Damian does so in Book VI, Epistle 21.]

For, in addition to these revelations, a light also shone in his cell every night without the service of any lamp. At last the demon ordered him to offer to God his son, who lived with him in the monastery,

> [Note: But the Lord did not choose this sacrifice, and the reasoning in the two cases is entirely different. Saint Augustine says in *The City of God*, Book I, chapter 26: “When God commands, and makes it unmistakably clear that he commands, who could call obedience a crime, or accuse dutiful submission? Yet it does not follow that anyone who resolves to sacrifice his son to God acts without sin simply because Abraham did this commendably.

> “A soldier who, obedient to the authority under which he has been lawfully placed, kills a man is not guilty of homicide under any law of his city; indeed, unless he did so, he would be guilty of deserting and despising his command. But if he had done it on his own initiative and authority, he would have fallen into the crime of shedding human blood. Thus the very reason for which he is punished if he acts without orders becomes the reason for which he is punished if, when ordered, he fails to act. If this is so when an emperor commands, how much more when the Creator commands!” Such are Augustine’s words.]

so that by this sacrifice he might in no respect be found inferior to the patriarch Abraham in merit.

He was so completely seduced by this persuasion that he would immediately have carried out the parricide in deed,

> [Note: *Parricida*, or *paricida*, referred not only to one who killed a parent but also to one who killed an equal—that is, any human being (Festus). Thus *parricidium* meant not only the killing of a father or parent but also the killing of an equal; or, according to others, the accomplishment of a killing.

> The ancient law of King Numa Pompeius indicates this in the following words: “If anyone knowingly and deceitfully gives a free man over to death, let him be a parricide” (Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book X, letter P).

> The Pompeian law on parricide likewise provides that one is liable for parricide not only if he kills his father or mother but also if he kills a brother, sister, paternal or maternal cousin, son, daughter, grandson, daughter-in-law, or other relatives.

> Saint Cyprian says similarly in *On Jealousy and Envy*: “Hence unspeakable parricides occurred, when the unjust Cain was jealous of the righteous Abel.”]

had not the boy, seeing him sharpen a knife—something he did not ordinarily do—and investigating the cords with which he was preparing to bind him for sacrifice as though he were about to offer him, fled in terror at the omen of the future crime.

## CHAPTER VIII. The fall and deception of a Mesopotamian monk

It would take too long to relate the deception of yet another Mesopotamian monk, who, after displaying in that province a continence scarcely imitable by anyone, and after spending many years shut away alone in his cell, was finally so deceived by demonic revelations and dreams that, despite the great labors and virtues by which he had surpassed all the monks living there,

> [Note: Antiochus, a Palestinian monk celebrated for holiness of life and learning, relates this same example—or certainly one extremely similar—in one of his homilies. One hundred and twenty-nine of his homilies survive in the *Bibliotheca of the Holy Fathers*; the eighty-fourth says:

> “There was a certain monk on Mount Sinai who gave so renowned an example of his continence that he lived enclosed in a little cell for many years. Finally, deceived by the devil through manifold revelations and dreams, he fell into Judaism and submitted to circumcision of the flesh.

> “For a long time the devil had repeatedly shown him certain true things in dreams and, as though offering bait, had lured his clouded mind. At last he displayed before his eyes a great crowd of Apostles, martyrs, and Christians of every kind, covered in the densest darkness and every form of disgrace. On the opposite side he presented Moses, the prophets, and the Jewish people—otherwise hateful to God—shining in an exceedingly bright light and passing their life in joy and gladness.

> “When the wretched man had seen this, he immediately arose, abandoned that holy mountain, and traveled as far as Palestine. He went straight to Mara and Libyas, the refuges of the Jews. After he had recounted to them the demonic apparitions that had seemed to him to be real, he was circumcised, professed Judaism, took a wife, and, in full public view, produced doctrines against the Christians, becoming a defender of Jewish superstition.

> “I saw this man, as did many of the monks; for it was scarcely four years before his death, by which he was miserably destroyed. After suffering for some time from a discharge of catarrh and wasting away from the gnawing of worms, he expired.

> “When I and several other monks saw him, we were seized with great fear and mourned him with lamentation. It was truly a most pitiable spectacle. This man had grown wholly gray in monastic discipline and had grown old, worn down by labors; and now he joked with women, defiled and polluted himself by eating unclean flesh—that is, Jewish food—spoke obscene and immodest words, blasphemed Christ, and inflicted intolerable insults upon the Holy Spirit. Yet the Jews who were without the Law called this man, in his condition, a second Abraham.

> “Thus far Antiochus concerning the monk deceived by the demon and fallen into Judaism.

> “Whether this was the same monk, or another, as the Mesopotamian monk whose deception and fall are related in this chapter may reasonably be doubted. The style and the whole structure of the narrative appear to present the same story, except that Antiochus describes the monk’s pitiable death and dreadful divine punishment more fully and explicitly.

> “On the other hand, the circumstances of place and time contradict this identification and clearly show that the two monks were different. This monk is described as a Sinaitic monk (Galatians 4:25; Sinai is a mountain in Arabia), whereas the other is said to have been a Mesopotamian. The latter was either earlier than or contemporary with Cassian; this one lived nearly two hundred years later.

> “Antiochus, who relates the event and testifies that he saw the apostate monk, lived during the reign of the Emperor Heraclius, around the year 620. Hence Baronius places this example in the year 614, the fifth year of Heraclius. Cassian, however, lived under the reigns of Theodosius and Valentinian, under whom he also died, in the year 435, according to Trithemius.

> “How, then, could Cassian have related what, according to Antiochus’s account, occurred almost two hundred years after Cassian’s death? It therefore remains that Cassian designates one monk and Antiochus another, though both were brought to Judaism and circumcision through a similar fall and demonic deception.”]

he miserably fell into Judaism and the cutting of the flesh—[Lipsius in the margin: “circumcision”]—

> [Note: That is, he circumcised himself according to Jewish custom. The Apostle could rightly have addressed him with the words spoken to the Galatians, who had been deceived by a similar error and had fallen into Judaism and circumcision: “Are you so foolish? Having begun with the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh”—that is, by a carnal ceremony? “Have you suffered so many things in vain—if indeed it was in vain?” (Galatians 3:3–4).

> Again, in chapter 5: “Behold, I, Paul, say to you that if you receive circumcision, Christ will profit you nothing. I testify again to every man who receives circumcision that he is under obligation to keep the whole law. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any power, but faith working through love.”

> The heretical Ebionites were like this, as Saint Jerome testifies in his commentary on Galatians 5: they asserted that circumcision and the law were to be observed together with baptism and the Gospel (Epiphanius, *Panarion*, heresy 30).

> It is not inappropriate to use “cutting of the flesh” for circumcision. For in Philippians 3 the Apostle calls it not circumcision but “the cutting,” as a term of contempt, saying: “Beware of the cutting.” He did not consider it worthy to call it circumcision, as Saint Jerome observed.]

For, wishing to lure him by the habit of visions into believing the deception that was to follow, the devil had for a long time revealed the most truthful things to him as a messenger of truth. Finally, he showed him the Christian people, together with the leaders of our religion and faith—namely, the Apostles and martyrs—as dark and horrible, wasted away in every kind of emaciation and deformity.

Opposite them he displayed the Jewish people, together with Moses, the patriarchs, and the prophets, exulting in the highest joy and shining with the most brilliant light. He persuaded the monk that, if he wished to become a participant in their merit and blessedness, he should hasten to receive circumcision as well.

No one, then, would have been deceived so lamentably by such visions if he had made the effort to understand the rule of discretion. The falls and experiences of many therefore demonstrate how dangerous it is not to possess the grace of discretion.

## CHAPTER IX. The question of acquiring true discretion

At this Germanus said:

“From both recent examples and the definitions of the ancients, it has become abundantly clear that discretion is, in a certain sense, the fountain and root of all virtues. We therefore desire you to explain how it is to be acquired, or how one may recognize whether it is true and from God or false and diabolical.

“Then, according to the evangelical parable which you discussed in the previous conference (Conference 1, chapter 20), by which we are commanded to become approved money-changers, may we be able to discern the coin upon which the image of the true king is impressed, and detect what has not been stamped with the legitimate image. Thus, using the ordinary expression you employed yesterday in the conference, we may reject it as counterfeit (*paracharagmos*), equipped with that skill which you explained at sufficient length and in full, and which you declared that the spiritual and evangelical money-changer must possess.

> [Note: This is the command of the Lord which he mentioned elsewhere: that we should be good, or approved, money-changers. Concerning this saying, in addition to the other authors cited there, Saint Clement says in Book II of the *Constitutions*, chapter 34:

> “Be like skilled bankers. For just as they separate counterfeit coins but keep the genuine ones, so the bishop ought to retain what is free from faults, but either remedy what is defective or, if the illness is incurable, expel and cut it off quickly, and not trust everyone.”

> Damascene likewise says in Book IV of *The Orthodox Faith*, chapter 18:

> “If we wish to gather something useful from those who are outside, this is not contemptible. Let us become approved money-changers, storing up genuine and pure gold but rejecting what is counterfeit. Let us take excellent sayings, but cast ridiculous gods and foreign tales to the dogs.”]

“For what benefit is there in recognizing the merits of its virtue and grace if we do not know how we ought to seek or acquire it?”

## CHAPTER X. The answer: how true discretion is possessed
Then Moses said: “True discernment is acquired only through true humility.”

[Note: Saint Benedict places among the degrees of humility, in fifth place (chapter 7), that a monk should conceal from his abbot none of the evil thoughts that come into his heart. Among the instruments of good works (chapter 4) he likewise places this: “As soon as evil thoughts come into one’s heart, to dash them against Christ and disclose them to one’s spiritual elder.” We have treated this matter elsewhere.]

The first proof of this humility will be that all things—not only what must be done, but also what is thought—are submitted to the examination of the elders, so that no one, trusting his own judgment, may rely on his own judgment in anything, but may yield entirely to their decisions and learn from their tradition what he ought to judge good or evil.

[Note: Photius also recalls this teaching of the ancient Fathers in his account of Cassian. Cassian is certainly full of frequent commendations and inculcations of this doctrine and discipline. Thus elsewhere he reports that the Fathers of Tabenna considered it greatly conducive to laying the foundations of the spiritual life firmly that younger monks should disclose their temptations, and even their thoughts, to a superior or elder as quickly and spontaneously as possible:

“They are instructed,” he says (*Institutes*, Book IV, chapter 9), “to conceal absolutely no troublesome thoughts in their hearts through a destructive shame, but, as soon as such thoughts arise, to disclose them to their elder; and not to entrust anything concerning their judgment to their own discernment, but to believe that something is evil or good according to what the elder’s examination has discussed or pronounced. Thus it comes about that the cunning enemy cannot prevail in anything against the young monk, as against one inexperienced and ignorant, nor deceive him by any trick, when he sees that the monk is protected not by his own discernment but by that of his elder. Nor can the enemy persuade him to conceal from the elder the suggestions or fiery darts that he has cast into his heart.”

Thus elegantly Cassian—or, in Cassian, the ancient Fathers—argued concerning the prompt disclosure of thoughts; and their teaching is entirely consonant with the present passage. To the same point belongs that admonition of Saint Antony reported by Athanasius in the *Life of Saint Antony*: “It is a great road to virtue if each person observes what he does, or reports all the thoughts of his mind to the brethren. For no one can sin when he is going to report to another whatever he has done wrong, and when he must undergo the shame of bringing disgraceful things into the open,” and so forth.]

This discipline will teach the young man to walk by the straight path not only along the true road of discernment, but will also preserve him unharmed from all the enemy’s deceptions and ambushes. No one can be deceived if he lives not by his own judgment but by the example of his elders. Nor can the cunning enemy mock his ignorance when the monk does not know how to conceal, through a destructive shame, any of the thoughts arising in his heart, but either rejects them or admits them after the mature examination of the elders.

As soon as the evil thought has been disclosed, it withers; and before the judgment of discernment has been pronounced, the most hideous serpent, as though dragged into the light from a dark and subterranean cave by the power of confession, and thus exposed and disgraced, departs. For his harmful suggestions dominate us only so long as they are concealed in the heart.

And so that you may grasp the force of this statement more effectively, I shall relate to you an incident involving Abbot Serapion, which he frequently proposed to the younger monks for their instruction.

[Note: Three anchorites of this name became renowned for holiness. The first was that great Serapion who, from being an anchorite, was ordained bishop of Thmuis by Athanasius, as Athanasius himself testifies in his letter to Dracontius. There survives a letter of Athanasius to this same Serapion against those who were beginning to murmur that the Holy Spirit was a creature, as well as a commentary on blasphemy against the Holy Spirit and another letter concerning the death of Arius. Saint Jerome discusses the same man in *On Illustrious Men* and in his letter to Magnus (Letter 84), as do Socrates in Book IV, chapter 18, of his *History*, the *Tripartite History* in Book I, chapter 1, and Nicephorus in Book IX, chapter 14, and Book XI, chapter 43.

The second was Serapion Sindonius, or Sindonites, so called because he wore nothing except a sindon, of whom Palladius relates wonderful things in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 83.

The third, finally, was Serapion of Arsinoe, abbot of ten thousand monks and also a priest. He is discussed by the same Palladius in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 76, and by Peter in his *Catalogue*, Book III, chapter 217. I am entirely convinced that this is the Serapion meant here, and that the fifth Collection, bearing his name and concerning the eight principal vices, was held with him. The first Serapion lived long before Cassian’s time. The second is neither called an abbot nor reported to have presided over monks.]

## CHAPTER XI. The words of Abbot Serapion; the withering of disclosed thoughts; and the danger of confidence in oneself

“When I was still a little boy,” he said, “and was living with Abbot Theon, I had acquired, through the enemy’s assault, the following habit: after I had eaten with the old man at the ninth hour, I would secretly conceal a *paxamacium* in my bosom every day and eat it secretly in the evening without his knowledge.

[Note: Three Conferences are ascribed to him as having been held with him: the twenty-first, on the relaxation of the Fifty Days; the twenty-second, on nocturnal illusions; and the twenty-third, on the Apostle’s saying, “For I do not do the good that I will,” etc. He was called Theon, Theona, or Theonas. Cassian likewise mentions him in Conference 21, chapter 9, and Palladius in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 50: “We saw,” he says, “another man, not far from the city, in the wilderness, named Theonas, a holy man shut up alone in a small dwelling, who had practiced silence for thirty years,” etc. Sozomen mentions the same man, Book VI, chapter 28; Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 34; and the *Tripartite History*, Book I, chapter 8. Sophronius also mentions him in the *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 27. There was another Theonas—lest anyone perhaps suppose him to be the same man—bishop of Alexandria, of whom Eusebius speaks in the *Chronicle* and in Book VII, the final chapter, of his *History*; Nicephorus Callistus in Book VI, chapter 34; and Bishop Nicephorus in the *Chronicle*.]

[Note: Elsewhere called *paximacium*, concerning which we have spoken above and shall speak below (*Institutes*, Book IV, chapter 14; Collection 2). It is also read as *paxamidium* in the *Life of Paul the Simple*, and in Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 28; and as *paximas* and *paxamadium* in the *Lives of the Fathers*. Cuychius says (chapter 19 and Collection 12, chapter 15) that it signifies bread baked twice, probably on the authority of Suidas, who says: παξαμᾶς δίπυρος ἄρτος, that is, “a twice-baked loaf.”]

Although I committed this theft continually, through the combined force [alternative reading: indulgence] of pleasure and the incontinent persistence of a desire that had once arisen, yet, once my deceitful appetite had been satisfied, I would return to myself and suffer more severely over the crime of theft than I had rejoiced over eating the food.

And when I was compelled each day, with sorrow in my heart, to complete this most burdensome task, imposed upon me like the bricks by Pharaoh’s taskmasters (Exodus 5), yet could not free myself from their most savage tyranny, and was ashamed to disclose the clandestine theft to the old man, it happened by God’s providence—since he wished to rescue me from this yoke of captivity—that certain brothers came to the old man’s cell under the pretext of seeking edification.

When the meal was over and a spiritual conference had begun, the old man answered their questions and discoursed on the vice of gluttony and the domination of hidden thoughts. He explained their nature and the most terrible force they possess so long as they remain concealed.

Struck by the power of this conference and terrified by my accusing conscience, I thought that these matters had been spoken because the Lord had revealed the secrets of my heart to the old man. At first I was moved to secret groans; then, as compunction of heart increased, I burst into open sobs and tears. I brought out the *paxamacium* that I had furtively taken to eat as a habitual vice,

[Note: A somewhat similar but, in its outcome and mournful conclusion, terrifying example of a monk who pretended to fast with the brethren while secretly eating is found in Saint Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book IV, chapter 38, in these words:

“There is still among us Athanasius, a presbyter from Isauria, who in his own days tells of a terrible event that occurred at Iconium. There, he says, there was said to be a monastery called Thongolaton, in which a certain monk was held in high esteem. He was seen to have good morals and to be composed in all his conduct; but, as the outcome revealed, he was far different from what he appeared to be.

For while he displayed himself as fasting with the brethren, he was accustomed secretly to eat, and the brethren were entirely unaware of this vice. But when illness overtook his body, he was brought to the point of death. As he lay dying, he had all the brethren who were in the monastery summoned to him. Since they believed that such a man was dying, they expected to hear from him something important and delightful.

But he, afflicted and trembling, was compelled to reveal to what enemy he had been handed over, as he was forced to depart. For he said: ‘When you thought that I was fasting with you, I was secretly eating. And behold, now I have been handed over to a dragon to be devoured. It has bound my knees and feet with its tail; then, putting its head into my mouth, it draws out my spirit as it drinks it.’

After saying these words he immediately died, and the dragon whom he had seen did not wait to see whether he could free himself through repentance. From this it is plainly evident that he saw the enemy to whom he had been handed over and disclosed him only for the benefit of those who heard him, but did not escape him. Thus Saint Gregory.”]

I drew it from my bosom, which knew of and harbored my theft, and placed it before everyone; lying prostrate on the ground, I confessed how I secretly ate it every day. With abundant tears I begged them to implore the Lord for the forgiveness of my most harsh captivity and to obtain my release.

Then the old man said: “Take courage, child. Your confession has freed you from this captivity, even though I have said nothing.

[Note: The power and efficacy of confession; concerning this there is another similar and memorable example in John Climacus, *The Ladder*, Step 4, which concerns obedience.]

Today you have triumphed over your adversary and conquered him, striking him down more powerfully by your confession than you had previously been cast down by him through your silence. Since you never refuted him by your own or another’s answer,

[Marginal reading in Lipsius: “reproof”]

you had until now allowed him to dominate you, in accordance with that saying of Solomon (Ecclesiastes 8):

[Note: Saint Jerome renders this same sentence from the Hebrew as follows. The old translation, however, has: “Because sentence against evil people is not pronounced swiftly, without any fear the hearts of the children of men are filled within them to do evil.”]

‘Because no contradiction is made at once against those who do evil, therefore the heart of the children of men is filled within them to do evil.’

Therefore, after this disclosure of yours, that most wicked spirit will no longer be able to trouble you, nor will that most hideous serpent henceforth claim a hiding-place in you, having been dragged from the darkness of your heart into the light by a saving confession.”

The old man had not yet finished speaking when, behold, a lighted lamp came out of my bosom and filled the cell with such a sulfurous odor that, because of the intensity of the stench, we could scarcely remain there.

The old man resumed his admonition: “Behold, the Lord has visibly confirmed the truth of my words to you, so that you might see with your own eyes that the instigator of this passion has been driven from your heart by a salutary confession, and might understand that the exposed enemy will never again have a place in you, since his expulsion has been openly manifested.”

Thus, according to the old man’s statement, it was indeed so: through the power of that confession, the domination of that diabolical tyranny was extinguished in me and put to rest forever. The enemy never again tried to force even the memory of this desire upon me, nor did I ever afterward feel myself assailed by the instigation of that secret appetite.

We also read this meaning beautifully represented in Ecclesiastes:

[Note: The Greek translation differs somewhat at this point from our Vulgate, which reads: “If a serpent bites in silence, one who secretly slanders is no better than it.” The Greek, however, renders the sentence in Latin approximately as it is expressed here: “If a serpent bites without noise or hissing, there is nothing more for the enchanter.” For this reason Saint Jerome gives this sentence a twofold meaning according to his two translations.

The first is: the serpent and the slanderer are alike. For just as the serpent, biting secretly, injects poison, so the man who secretly slanders pours the venom of his heart into his brother, and has nothing more than the serpent.

The second meaning is this: if the serpent who is the devil bites someone and, without anyone knowing, infects him with the poison of sin; if the one who has been struck remains silent and does not repent, and refuses to confess his wound to a brother and teacher, then the teacher who possesses a tongue for healing cannot easily help him. If the sick man is ashamed to confess his wound to the physician, medicine cannot heal what it does not know. Thus Saint Jerome.

The present abbot followed this latter meaning, as it agrees with that translation and with his purpose; and the Greek Fathers also support it. Thus Olympiodorus explains this passage: “If the serpent of sin bites in silence—that is, if the sinner does not wish to confess the crime he has committed—he who receives him with holy incantation can provide him no salvation so long as he refuses to confess his sins.”

Saint Gregory of Neocaesarea agrees with this in his *Metaphrase*: “Those who charm cannot heal the hidden bite of the serpent.” For the hidden bite of the serpent is sin concealed by the sinner; and that bite cannot be healed by those who charm, however prudent they may be—that is, by spiritual men and priests—until it comes into the open through confession.]

“If a serpent bites,” he says, “without hissing, there is no advantage for the enchanter” (Ecclesiastes 10). He indicates that the bite of a silent serpent is destructive: if, through confession, a suggestion or diabolical thought is not disclosed to an enchanter—that is, to a spiritual man who is accustomed to heal the wound immediately by the spells of Scripture and to draw the serpent’s harmful poisons from the heart—he will be unable to come to the aid of one who is in danger and near destruction.

By this means, then, we can most easily attain knowledge of true discernment: by following the footsteps of our elders, presuming neither to do anything new nor to make decisions according to our own judgment, but walking in all things according to the way their tradition or the integrity of their life has formed us.

Strengthened by this discipline, anyone will reach not only the full measure of discernment but will also remain entirely secure from all the enemy’s snares. For the devil drags and leads a monk to death through no other vice so headlong as when, having neglected the counsel of his elders, he persuades him to trust in his own judgment, decision, or teaching.

Indeed, although all the arts and disciplines discovered by human ingenuity—those that serve no purpose beyond the temporary conveniences of this life—can be handled with the hands and seen with the eyes, nevertheless no one can properly master them without the teaching of an instructor.

[Note: Saint Jerome earnestly admonishes his monk Rusticus in these words: “For my part, I approve that you should have the companionship of holy men, and that you should not teach yourself or enter without a teacher upon a road that you have never traveled. Otherwise you would immediately have to turn aside in one direction or another, exposing yourself to error, and walk more or less than necessary, so that you might either become exhausted by running or fall asleep through delay.”

In that celebrated letter to Paulinus he likewise severely criticizes certain people who boast that they possess knowledge of the divine Scriptures without teachers. “Farmers,” he says, “masons, workers in metal, cutters of wood, wool-workers, fullers, and all the others who manufacture various furnishings and cheap products cannot be without a teacher in what they wish to do. Physicians promise what belongs to physicians, and craftsmen practice the work of craftsmen; only the art of the Scriptures is one that everyone everywhere claims for himself,” and so forth.

Again, in his letter to Pammachius concerning the errors of Origen, he writes among other things (Letter 65): “When I was a young man, I was carried along by an extraordinary zeal for learning, and I did not, according to the presumption of certain people, teach myself.” He later adds that he continued to do the same even when his head was becoming white and people thought that he had reached the end of his learning.

Similarly, Saint Augustine says in his one hundred and twelfth sermon *On Time*: “Just as a blind man scarcely walks along the right road without a guide, so a man scarcely walks along the right path without a teacher.”]

How foolish, then, it is to believe that this one discipline does not need a teacher, when it is invisible and hidden, and can be perceived only by the purest heart; when error in it produces not temporal loss, nor a loss that can easily be repaired, but the destruction of the soul and everlasting death!

For it entails a daily and nightly struggle not against visible but against invisible and merciless enemies; and it is a spiritual battle not against one or two, but against innumerable hosts. Its fall is therefore more destructive in proportion as the enemy is more hostile and the encounter more hidden.

For this reason the footsteps of the elders must always be followed with the greatest care, and everything that arises in our hearts must be brought to them, the veil of shame having been removed.

## CHAPTER XII. An account of the shame on account of which we are ashamed to reveal our thoughts to the elders

Germanus: The occasion of that destructive shame by which we try to conceal evil thoughts and fear to disclose them in a salutary confession arises chiefly from this circumstance: we know that there was a certain man, considered pre-eminent among the Fathers in Syria, who was afterward moved by a certain indignation and severely reproached a certain brother among the elders who had disclosed his thoughts in a simple confession.

Thus it happens that, while we suppress our thoughts within us and are ashamed to make them public to the elders, we cannot obtain the remedies of healing.

## CHAPTER XIII. The answer concerning the shame that must be trampled down and the danger of one who does not sympathize with the afflicted
Moses: Just as not all young men are alike in spirit, fervor, discipline, or good character, so not all old men can be found alike in perfection or excellence. [Col. 0542C]

[Note: Saint Jerome: “For it is not age but virtue that should be considered in a man.” And Cicero, in *Cato Maior*: “Neither white hair,” he says, “nor wrinkles suddenly confer authority; but a life rightly lived yields the final fruits of authority.” Let those elders take heed who boast in religion solely under the title of old age, as though they were more religious because they are older: [Col. 0542D] this abbot Moses certainly censures them severely. For what Saint Jerome says (*Letter* 13) is praiseworthy: “It is not having been in Jerusalem, but having lived rightly in Jerusalem.” The same may be said of religion and religious people. Old age is indeed venerable and honorable, especially in religion; but, as the Wise Man just cited says, it is not because it is long-lasting or reckoned by a number of years, but because “the senses of man are gray hairs” (*Wisdom* 4)—that is, mature, prudent, and trained to discern good and evil, as the Apostle says (for this is true gray hair, which adorns the mind)—“and an unblemished life is the age of old age” (*Hebrews* 5). “Gray hair,” says Chrysostom (*Homily 7 on the Epistle to the Hebrews*), “is venerable when a person does what is fitting for gray hair; but when an old man behaves like a youth, he will be more ridiculous than young men.” Hence the Apostle seriously admonishes old men to be sober, chaste, prudent, and sound in faith, love, and patience (*Titus* 2). Seneca aptly said (*Letter* 4) that those men can scarcely be called old in whom childhood, already completed, nevertheless remains—which is worse, childishness.]

For the riches of old men are not to be measured by the whiteness of their heads, [Col. 0543A] but by the diligence of their youth and the rewards of their past labors.

[Note: There is an excellent passage in Ecclesiasticus, embracing and linking together several statements directed toward the same point; therefore it should be quoted here in full: “Three kinds of people my soul hates, and I am greatly burdened by their soul” (the Septuagint has: “And I was greatly burdened by their life)”): a proud poor man, a lying rich man, and a foolish and senseless old man. What you did not gather in your youth, how will you find it in your old age? How beautiful is the judgment of gray hair, and for elders to know counsel! How beautiful is wisdom in the aged, and understanding and counsel in those who are honored! The crown of the aged is extensive experience, and their glory is the fear of God.”]

“For what you did not gather in your youth,” he says, “how will you find in your old age?” (*Ecclesiasticus* 25). For old age is venerable, not because it is long-lasting or reckoned by a number of years. “For the senses of man are gray hairs, and an unblemished life is the age of old age” (*Wisdom* 4). Therefore we should not imitate or follow the footsteps of all elders whose heads are covered with gray hair and whose only recommendation is the length of their life; nor should we accept their traditions and instructions, [Col. 0543C]

[Note: Such were those truly religious elders, worthy of reverence—and indeed admiration—not so much for their gray hair as for their virtue. John Climacus says of them in *The Ladder*, step 4: “Many were found among those holy men who were admirable in action, contemplation, strictness, and humility. You would see in them a dreadful and angelic spectacle: elders venerable for their gray hair, with faces more august, running about here and there like children, always ready to obey, and acquiring for themselves the greatest glory through humility. I saw men there who had spent nearly fifty years in the contest of obedience. When I begged them to teach me what consolation they had gained from that labor and what progress they had found in it, some said that they had already reached the abyss of humility, through which they always excluded and overcame every battle; others said that they had perfectly stripped themselves of every sense of labor and pain through insults and reproaches. I saw others of those men, forever worthy of remembrance, with an angelic appearance and venerable gray hair, who had reached, with the greatest eagerness, the deepest innocence and a simplicity completely filled with wisdom, sought through steadfast purpose and God’s assistance—not some irrational and tasteless condition, such as occurs in worldly old men (whom people commonly call doddering), but a state in which outwardly they were entirely gentle, gracious, peaceful, and joyful, having nothing feigned, negligent, [Col. 0544B] or adulterated in their words or conduct—a quality found only in the few; inwardly, however, they sought God himself and the superior with the manner of children, while directing the eye of their mind against demons and vices with courage and the utmost firmness.” Thus he describes elders who are truly religious and worthy of imitation and obedience. On the honor and veneration to be shown to elders according to the rule of Saint Benedict, see Turrecremata, treatise 50 on that Rule.]

but those whom we have found to have marked out their lives commendably and with the greatest excellence in their youth, and to have been formed not by their own presumptions but by the traditions of their elders. For there are some—and, more grievously, they are the greater number—who, growing old in the tepidity that they acquired from adolescence and in sloth, seek authority for themselves not through maturity of character but through the multitude of their years (see *Conference* 24, chapter 1). Against such people that reproach of the Lord is very properly directed through the Prophet: “Strangers have devoured his strength, and he did not know it; moreover, gray hairs were spread over him, and he did not know it” (*Hosea* 7). These men, I say, have been advanced as examples to the younger not by the integrity of their life, nor by any strictness of this commendable and imitable vocation, but solely by their long years. Their gray hair the most cunning enemy places before the younger as a prejudicial authority, [Col. 0544C]

[Note: Saint Jerome, on chapter 1 of the Epistle to the Galatians: “Nor did she, in Pythagorean fashion, consider whatever I had answered to be right; nor did authority, prejudged without reason, prevail with her.” Thus Jerome. “Prejudged authority,” therefore, means authority wrongly presumed on account of old age alone. For just as a case is called prejudged when it has been condemned by a presumed opinion before judgment has been rendered, so here authority is called prejudged when foolish and irreligious old men claim it for themselves solely on the pretext of old age. The devil also repeatedly abuses this authority to deceive the young, as is said here.]

and by its fraudulent subtlety hastens to overturn and deceive even those who could have been stirred toward a life of perfection by admonitions of their own or of others; leading them either into harmful tepidity or into deadly despair through their teachings and institutions. Wishing to present you with examples of this matter, but omitting the author’s name—lest we too commit something similar to the man who publicized the faults of a brother revealed to him—I shall briefly set forth only the event itself, which may provide you with necessary instruction.

[Note: You have this example, and others of the same kind worthy of reading, in the fifth book of the new edition of the *Lives of the Fathers*, in the fifth treatise, which concerns fornication. See a similar account in Palladius, *Lausiac History*, in the Life of Moses.]

When, therefore, one of a group of young men, by no means indolent, had gone to an old man whom we knew very well for the sake of his progress and healing, and had simply disclosed that he was being troubled by carnal incitements and the spirit of fornication, believing that he would find consolation for his labors through the old man’s prayer and remedies for the wounds he had received, the latter rebuked him with the bitterest words. He declared him wretched and unworthy, and said that he should not even be counted as a monk, since he could be tickled by such a vice and desire. By these contrary censures he wounded him so severely that he sent him away from his cell utterly cast down in despair, deeply sorrowful, and overwhelmed by deadly sadness.

[Note: “By the goads of incitements.” Thus Sidonius (*Letters* 6.1) speaks of “the incitements of carnal vices”; Ambrose, in book 6 of the *Hexaemeron*, of “the incitements of oils,” and in his commentary on Psalm 118, of “the incitements of sins.” Jerome, writing to Nepotianus and Rusticus, speaks of “the incitements of puberty,” “carnal incitements,” and “the goads of incitements.” Moreover, *incentor*, *incitement*, and *incentive* are not derived from *incendo*, as Isidore maintains (*Etymologies* 10, letter I), but from *incino, incinere*, meaning to sing with some modulation, or to sing to someone as into his ear, to soothe or encourage him—as soldiers are accustomed to be encouraged to battle by the sound of trumpets. Hence the frequentative *incanto*, “to enchant.” Thus *incentive* means the same as encouragement or provocation, and *incentor* means an encourager or instigator, not one who burns, except metaphorically (Gellius, *Attic Nights* 4.13).]

When, in such grief, he was no longer thinking about a remedy for his passion but, in deep reflection, about fulfilling the desire he had conceived, [Col. 0544D] and when he was visited by Abbot Apollo,

[Note: He was famous and celebrated among the earliest and most distinguished anchorites. He lived in the time of Julian the Apostate, was the father of five hundred monks, and was renowned for the glory of his miracles. Palladius describes his life and admirable deeds at considerable length in *The Lausiac History*, chapter 52. Sozomen mentions him in book 6, chapter 20; following him, Nicephorus in book 11, chapter 34; and Cassiodorus in the *Tripartite History*, book 8, chapter 1. His name was Apollo or Apollos, indeclinable—as the Apostle also names a certain minister of the Church “Apollo” (*1 Corinthians* 3:16), not “Apollinem,” apparently to suppress the memory of that profane and notorious Apollo, the Pythian or Delphic god. Sophronius also mentions Apollo, abbot of a coenobium, in *The Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 184. There was also an anchorite named Apollonius, not obscure, about whom Palladius writes in *The Lausiac History*, chapter 66, and Nicephorus in book 11, chapter 35. Some wrongly confuse him with this Apollo, improperly attributing to him what is reported about Apollo. (Vincent, *Historical Mirror*, book 15; Antonius, part 2, title 15, chapter 10; Peter, *Catalogue*, book 4.)]

the most excellent of the elders, Apollo, observing from the young man’s expression and downcast appearance the labor and intensity of the struggle silently revolving in his heart, sought the cause of such disturbance. Although the young man could not give even an answer to the old man when he addressed him gently, the elder perceived more and more that he was not without reason seeking to conceal the cause of such sadness in silence, since he could not disguise it even in his expression. He therefore began to inquire more insistently into the causes of his hidden grief.

Pressed by these questions, the young man confessed that he was going to the village so that, since according to the judgment of that old man he could not be a monk and could no longer restrain the goads of the flesh or obtain remedies against the assault, he might marry, abandon the monastery, and return to the world. [Col. 0545B]

The elder Apollo soothed him with gentle consolation, asserting that he too was daily troubled by the same goads and agitations of incitements, and that therefore the young man ought not to collapse entirely into despair or be astonished at the ardor of the assault, which was overcome not so much by the labor of striving as by the Lord’s mercy and grace. He asked only for a respite of one day, begged the young man to return to his cell, and hurried with all speed to the monastery of the aforementioned old man.
