When he had drawn near it, he stretched out his hands and poured forth a prayer with tears: “Turn,” he said, “O Lord, who alone are the gracious and hidden physician, judge of secret powers and human weakness, the assault of that young man against this old man, so that he may learn, even in his old age, to accommodate himself to the weaknesses of those who labor and to sympathize with the frailty of the young.”

When he had concluded this prayer with a groan, he saw [Col. 0545C]

[Note: It is well established from many examples that the devil commonly appears in the form of an Ethiopian, or black man. See above, *Conference* 1, chapter 24; Athanasius, *Life of Saint Antony*; the *Lives of the Fathers*, in the Life of Macarius; Victor of Utica, book 1 of the *Vandal Persecutions*; Gregory the Great, *Dialogues* 2.4 and 4.18; and Peter of Cluny, book 1 of *Miracles*, chapter 8. But it is amusing and worth remembering that Palladius reports the following in the Life of Abbot Apollo mentioned above: “When he had withdrawn from the world at the age of fifteen, spent forty years in solitude, and practiced every virtue there, he later seemed to hear the voice of God saying to him: ‘Apollo, through you I shall destroy the wisdom of the wise in Egypt and the prudence of the nations. For you will beget for me a special people, zealous for good works.’ In response he said: ‘Take arrogance away from me, Lord, lest, lifted up above the brotherhood, I be deprived of every good work.’ Again the divine voice said: ‘Place your hand upon your neck, and then lower it and bury it in the sand.’ When he had immediately placed his hand upon his neck, he seized a little Ethiopian and buried him in the sand while he cried out and said: ‘I am the demon of pride.’” Thus far Palladius. And in truth this form suits the demon, whether because of his nature or even his choice, or because of God’s ordering and will, which the analogy of the name itself signifies. For “Ethiopian,” *Aethiops*—in Hebrew, *kusi*, that is, “black”—and in Greek, Αἰθίωψ, is interpreted as “one who burns” or “one who is burned.” Let him consider how well these meanings suit the demon.]

a dreadful Ethiopian standing opposite that man’s cell and directing fiery darts against him. When the old man was immediately wounded by them, came out of his cell, and ran here and there like a madman and a drunkard, unable to contain himself in it as he went out and came back in, he began to hurry along the same road by which the young man had departed.

Abbot Apollo, seeing him driven about as though he had become insane, understood that the fiery missile of the devil which he had seen shot from him had been fixed in the old man’s heart, and that it was producing in him, through intolerable burning, this confusion of mind and disturbance of the senses. Approaching him, he said: “Where are you hurrying, and what causes are troubling you so childishly and restlessly, making you forget the gravity appropriate to old age?”

The old man, confounded by the guilt of his conscience and his shameful agitation, believed that the burning of his breast had been detected and that, with the secrets of his heart exposed to the elder, he dared give no answer at all to his questions. Apollo said: “Return to your cell, and understand at last that until now you were either unknown to the devil or despised by him, and were not counted among those against whom he is daily stirred to fight and wrestle because of their progress and efforts. After so many years spent in this profession, you were unable not merely to repel one of his darts directed against you but even to endure it for a single day. The Lord allowed you to be wounded by it so that at least in your old age you might learn to sympathize with the weaknesses of others and to accommodate yourself to the frailty of the young. By your example and experience you were to be taught this: when you received a young man suffering under a demonic assault, you not only failed to encourage him with any consolation, but, having cast him down into destructive despair, you handed him over to the enemy’s hands, so far as lay in you, to be mournfully devoured by the very enemy who certainly would not have attacked him with so violent a conflict—an attack which he had disdained to direct against you until now—unless, envying his future progress, the enemy had hastened with his fiery darts to anticipate and corrupt the virtue he saw within the young man’s soul; plainly understanding that he was stronger, since he judged it worthwhile to fight against him with such violence.

“Learn, then, by your own example, to sympathize with those who labor, and never to terrify those in danger with destructive despair or to embitter them with the harshest words. Rather, restore them with gentle and soothing consolation. According to the command of the wisest Solomon, rescue those being led to death and do not hold back from redeeming those being killed (*Proverbs* 24). Following the example of our Savior, do not break the bruised reed or extinguish the smoking flax (*Isaiah* 42; *Matthew* 12). Ask the Lord for that grace by which you too may confidently be able to say in deed and truth: ‘The Lord has given me a learned tongue, that I may know how to sustain the one who has fallen by a word’ (*Isaiah* 50).

“For no one could withstand the enemy’s snares or extinguish or restrain the carnal passions burning with a kind of natural fire, unless God’s grace either helped our frailty or protected and fortified it. Therefore, now that the purpose of this salutary dispensation has been fulfilled—by which the Lord wished either to free that young man from his destructive passions or to teach you, through the intensity of the assault, the duty of compassion—let us together entreat him to command that this scourge, which the Lord has deigned to inflict upon you for your benefit, be removed. For he himself causes grief and again heals; he strikes, and his hands heal (*Job* 5). He himself humbles and exalts; he kills and gives life; he leads down to the underworld and brings back (*1 Kings* 2). May he extinguish, by the dew of his Spirit, the fiery darts of the devil which, in my judgment, he permitted to be inflicted upon you.””

Although the Lord again removed this temptation at a single prayer of the old man with the same speed with which he had allowed it to be inflicted, he nevertheless taught by clear experience that the faults of anyone who has revealed them ought not merely not to be reproached, but that the pain of one who is suffering ought not even to be lightly disregarded.

Therefore, let neither the ignorance nor the levity of one or a few people deter us [Lipsius, in the margin: “you”] from or exclude us from that salutary way and tradition of the elders that we have mentioned. The most cunning enemy abuses their gray hair for the deception of the young. Rather, everything should be revealed to the elders without any covering of shame, and from them we should confidently receive either remedies for our wounds or examples of conduct and life. In these we shall experience equal aid and a similar effect, [Col. 0548A] if we attempt to pursue nothing at all according to our own judgment and presumption.

## CHAPTER XIV. The Calling of Samuel

Finally, this judgment is so clearly approved by God that we find the same instruction deliberately inserted even in the Holy Scriptures: although he had preferred the boy Samuel by his own judgment [Lipsius, in the margin: “chosen by his own judgment”], the Lord did not wish to instruct him through the discipline of divine conversation by himself, [Col. 0547D]

[Note: It is well established that this is God’s perpetual—or at least ordinary—way: although he can enlighten everyone either directly or through angels, he nevertheless prefers that human beings be taught and instructed by human beings. He does this either to establish mutual charity among them, as among members, or to exercise and commend humility by subjecting one person to another. Moses confirms this here through the example of the boy Samuel. At his first calling, the Lord himself did not wish to instruct him, but allowed him once, twice, and even a third time to return to the elder Eli. The Lord called Samuel to his own conversation, yet wished him to be formed by the instruction of one who was older in age but inferior in holiness, so that, taught by him, Samuel might finally answer the God who was calling him: “Speak, Lord, for your servant hears.” A similar example shines forth in the centurion Cornelius (*Acts* 10). When an angel appeared to him, the angel could certainly have revealed to him directly all the mysteries of the faith; this would have been more convenient and shorter for both parties. Yet he sent him to Peter: “Send,” he says, “for Simon; he will tell you what you must do.”]

but allowed him to return to the old man once and again. He wished the one whom he was calling to his own address to be instructed by the teaching of that man who had offended God, provided that he was an elder; and he preferred the one whom he had judged most worthy of his calling to be formed by the instruction of an elder, [Col. 0548B] so that both the humility of the one called to divine service might be tested and an example of this submission might be offered to the young (*1 Kings* 3).

## CHAPTER XV. The Calling of the Apostle Paul

When Christ himself called and addressed Paul, although he could at once have opened the way of perfection to him, he nevertheless preferred to send him to Ananias and commanded him to learn the way of truth from him, saying: “Rise and enter the city, and there you will be told what you must do” (*Acts* 9).

[Note: Saint Bernard rightly marvels at this (*Sermon 1, On the Conversion of Saint Paul*, *Acts* 9), and, interpreting that city in a religious sense as religion itself, exclaims: “O wisdom, truly ordering all things sweetly! You send the one to whom you speak to a human being to be taught your will, so that the usefulness of social life may be commended, and so that, taught through a human being, he himself may learn to help human beings according to the grace given to him. ‘Enter the city,’ he says. You see, brothers, that it was not without divine assistance that you entered this city of the Lord of hosts in order to learn the divine will.” Saint Augustine confirms the same point. After recalling these examples of Paul and Cornelius, he adds most appropriately (*Preface to On Christian Doctrine*): “Everything could certainly have been done through an angel, but the human condition would have been degraded if God had not wished to minister his word to human beings through human beings. Moreover, charity itself, which binds human beings to one another by the bond of charity, would have no opportunity to pour out souls into one another if human beings learned nothing through human beings.”]

Thus he too sends him to an elder, and judges him to be instructed by the elder’s teaching rather than by his own, lest what had rightly been done in Paul provide posterity with a harmful example of presumption, as each person persuaded himself that he too ought to be formed by the teaching and instruction of God alone rather than by the instruction of the elders.

The Apostle himself teaches that this presumption is utterly to be detested, not only by his writings but also by his actions and example. He declares that he went up to Jerusalem solely for this reason: to compare with his fellow apostles and predecessors, in a kind of private and domestic examination, the Gospel that, with the accompanying grace of the Holy Spirit and with the power of signs and wonders, he preached to the Gentiles: “And I conferred with them,” he says, “the Gospel that I preach among the Gentiles, lest perhaps I should be running, or had run, in vain” (*Galatians* 2).

Who, then, could be so presumptuous and blind as to entrust himself to his own judgment and discernment, when the Chosen Vessel testifies that he needed the consultation of his fellow apostles? Hence it is most clearly established that the Lord reveals the way of perfection to no one who, while possessing the means by which he can be instructed, despises the teaching or institutions of the elders, making light of the utterance that must be guarded with the greatest care: “Ask your father, and he will declare it to you; your elders, and they will tell you” (*Deuteronomy* 32).

## CHAPTER XVI. The Pursuit of Discernment

Therefore, by every effort the good of discernment must be acquired through the virtue of humility, which can preserve us unharmed from either extreme. For there is an old saying:

[Note: In the Basel and Dionysian manuscripts this saying is not found in Greek, but only in Latin. Dionysius explains it as follows: “Extremes are equal,” that is, equally harmful. I would rather say, “Both are vicious and harmful,” which is explained more fully in chapter 22, where the disadvantages of excessive fasting and excessive eating are shown to be almost equal. Faustus of Riez translated this saying, whether Greek or spoken by Greeks, into Latin in book 1 of *On Grace and Free Will*, and adapted it to his subject as follows: “Almost every extreme, because it does not know how to maintain discernment and distinction, incurs equal guilt.” Again (chapters 1 and 17): “When, between these positions, one attributes everything to labor and the other judges everything to be assigned to grace, the Greek saying is fulfilled in both: ‘Extremes are equal’; there is similar impiety, and wickedness is shown to be equal, whether everything is attributed to grace alone or everything to labor alone.” So far Faustus. In Margarinus, however, the text is incorrectly printed (*Theological Library* 4, edition 3): “Extremes and inequalities are similar wickedness, and impiety is shown to be equal,” and so forth, as may be inferred from the earlier saying and the whole treatment of his book. This saying, or proverbial expression, seems to have been taken from Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* 2.6, where he teaches that most moral virtues consist in the mean, that is, between two extreme vices. Related to it is the famous saying of the ancients: μηδὲν ἄγαν, *mēden agan*, “nothing in excess,” discussed by Stobaeus in discourse 21, and another saying of Cleobulus preserved by the same author: ἄριστον μέτρον, *ariston metron*, “measure is best.” Alluding to these, Saint Jerome admonishes the young virgin Demetrias in *Letter* 8: “We do not command you to undertake immoderate fasts or excessive abstinence from food, by which delicate bodies are immediately broken and begin to grow ill before they have laid the foundations of holy conduct.” It is also a saying of the philosophers: μεσότητες ἀρεταί, ὑπερβολαὶ κακίαι, *mesotētes aretai, hyperbolai kakiai*, “virtues are mean conditions; excesses are vices,” which may be rendered in Latin: “Virtues are moderate conditions; what exceeds measure and proportion is counted among vices.” Hence one of the Seven Sages said: μηδὲν ἄγαν, that is, “nothing in excess”—a saying that became so famous that it was expressed even in a comic verse. “You should fast in such a way that you do not tremble and can scarcely breathe, and that your companions must either carry you or drag you along; rather, let the appetite of the body be broken without causing you to do less than usual in reading, psalmody, or vigils.” The same author says in his commentary on Isaiah, book 14, chapter 52: “For vices and disturbances do not follow one another in alternation, as is said of virtues, in which there are neither ὑπερβάσεις, *hyperbaseis*, ‘excesses,’ nor ἐλλείψεις, *elleipseis*, ‘deficiencies’—that is, neither too much nor too little, but everything is tempered.” Thus Jerome. To the same point are the following words of Isidore of Pelusium, *Letters* 3.131: “Just as the proper proportion of the limbs is the standard of bodily beauty, so the outer limit of spiritual exercise consists in the mean of the virtues. For if extremes degenerate into vice, as certain wise men have declared—and hence they have defined virtues as mean conditions—the Wise Man rightly also admonished: ‘Do not be excessively righteous.’” So far Isidore (*Letters* 19 and 6). Add to these the words of Horace (*Satires* 1.1):

“Virtue is the mean withdrawn from vices on either side.

There is a measure in all things; finally, there are fixed boundaries,

Beyond or short of which the right cannot stand.”

Elsewhere, with a celebrated epithet, he commends the golden mean. Finally, there is the widely known proverb: “Measure is the fairest virtue.”]

ἀκρότητες ἰσότητες, that is, “extremes are equal.” For excessive fasting and gluttony arrive at one and the same end, and the immoderate continuation of vigils overwhelms a monk with an equal loss to that by which the torpor of the heaviest sleep envelops him. For anyone weakened by excessive abstinence must necessarily be brought back to the condition in which the negligent person is held through carelessness. Thus we have often seen those whom we observed not to have been overcome by gluttony fall through immoderate fasting, and, because of bodily weakness, collapse into the very passion that they had conquered.

Irrational vigils and all-night watches have likewise cast down those whom sleep could not overcome. Therefore, according to the Apostle, we must pass onward by the weapons of righteousness that are on the right and on the left (*2 Corinthians* 6), with proper moderation; and we must proceed between the two extremes while discernment governs us, so that we neither permit ourselves to be led away from the path of abstinence handed down to us nor, through harmful relaxation, fall again into the desires of the throat and belly.

## CHAPTER XVII. Immoderate Fasts and Vigils

For I remember that I often rejected the appetite for food so completely that, after postponing a meal for two or three days, not even the memory of that food disturbed my mind. Again, through the devil’s assault, sleep was so removed from my eyes that for many nights and days I begged the Lord to pour even a little sleep into my eyes. I found myself more seriously endangered by my disgust for sleep and food than by the struggle against drowsiness and gluttony.

Therefore, just as we must hasten lest we fall through the appetite for bodily pleasure into harmful dissolution, and lest, before the appointed time, we presume either to indulge in food or to exceed its proper measure, so the nourishment of food and sleep must be taken at the proper hour, even when we shrink from it.

[Note: That is, we must take careful precautions and make every effort. *Festinare* does not always mean “to hurry,” but sometimes “to tremble,” “to be disturbed,” or “to be anxious and troubled.” Sallustius: “The senators, hastening in the greatest poverty.” Gellius (*Attic Nights* 10.14), drawing on Varro, teaches that *properare* and *festinare* are different: *festinare* is said as though from *fessum esse*, “to be wearied.” For one who is exhausted by many things that must be hurried at once no longer merely hurries but is in a state of agitation.]

Both battles arise through the adversary’s action, and immoderate abstinence trips a person more destructively than unrestrained satiety. From the latter, with salutary compunction intervening, one can ascend to the measure of strictness; from the former, one cannot.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The Question Concerning the Measure of Abstinence and Nourishment

[Col. 0551A]

Germanus: What, then, is the measure of abstinence by which, maintaining an even moderation between the two extremes, we may pass unharmed between them?

## CHAPTER XIX. The Best Daily Measure of Food
Moses: [Note: [Col. 0551A] See Book V of the *Institutes*, chapter 5.] We know that this matter was frequently discussed among our predecessors. For when they examined the dietary practices of various men who lived continually on legumes alone, or only on vegetables, or on fruit, they preferred to all these a meal consisting solely of bread, the most equitable quantity of which [Note: [Col. 0551A] Alternatively, “dry bread,” that is, without relish. Water was not excluded.] they fixed at two small loaves, whose weight was certainly scarcely one pound.

[Note: [Col. 0551A] This is an ambiguous expression. It may be doubted whether he intends each loaf to have weighed approximately one pound, or whether he means two loaves together. Some think that each *paximacium* was one pound in weight, and understand the words of Abbot Moses accordingly, as referring to separate small loaves. But that this should be understood not of each loaf individually, but of the two together, can be established by many arguments if the matter is carefully considered, as the Reverend Father Leonard Lessius learnedly shows in his notable little book *On the Preservation of Health*. First, Moses wished to state how much the whole daily measure of bread weighed—the measure consisting of two *paximacia*—not how much each individual loaf weighed, since the subject was the daily measure. Moreover, in chapter 21 he plainly indicates that this measure was quite small and difficult to maintain when no relish was included. But if the two *paximacia* amounted to two pounds of bread per day, that measure would certainly not have been small or difficult to maintain, especially for old men. For who, after eating such a quantity of bread, would not have had enough, or would be said to have eaten moderately or little? Nor is there any contradiction in the fact that Germanus, speaking below in his own name and that of Cassian, says that he considers this measure—namely, one pound—not at all a form of abstinence, since they could scarcely consume the whole of it. For he was either speaking of the stricter continence or abstinence that was not common and customary for everyone, or else he certainly understood the stated measure of bread together with some relish or dish, which Abbot Moses excludes, as may be seen there. Furthermore, the two *paximacia* did not satisfy hunger to such an extent that some did not prefer to fast for two days rather than eat daily with the others—namely, so that they might take a doubled portion and satisfy their appetite, as the same Abbot Moses reports in chapter 24, where he also condemns the practice. But what person, especially one devoted to spiritual exercises, would eat four pounds, or forty-eight ounces, of dry bread at one sitting? Finally, as the same abbot reports in chapter 11, when Abbot Serapion was still a young man, after taking two *paximacia* with the others at the ninth hour, he was still hungry, and therefore stole a third, which he later ate secretly. But what young man would eat three pounds of bread at one meal? From these considerations, then, it appears certain that each *paximacium* weighed only six ounces, and that the two together weighed approximately one pound (*Epiphanius, On Measures and Weights*). Hence it is understood that among those Fathers it was customary to allow each person to eat approximately twelve ounces of bread each day—a measure that could generally be sufficient for everyone. For among the ancients a pound consisted of twelve ounces, not sixteen as among us (see the note on Book V, chapter 5). Thus Abbot Moses is reported by Palladius (*Lausiac History*, chapter 22) to have taken nothing but twelve ounces of dry bread during the six years he was shut up in his cell. Saint Hilarion, according to Jerome, from his thirty-first to his thirty-fifth year had as food only six ounces of barley bread with a little-cooked vegetable (*Saint Jerome, Life of Hilarion*). Finally, in the *Life of Paul the Simple*, the same Palladius reports that Saint Antony brought four *paxamidia*—that is, *paximacia*—of six ounces each and placed them on the table, moistening one for himself (for they were dry loaves), but three for Paul the Simple. Here it should be noted that he says “of six ounces,” which, as we have explained elsewhere, must be understood of each *paximacium* or loaf. Nor is it surprising that Antony placed three *paxamidia* before Paul and reserved only one for himself, since Paul had already remained fasting for an entire week, as is clear from the story itself. From these facts it is likewise evident with what discretion and moderation the most holy Father Benedict treated his coenobites (*Rule*, chapter 39). In addition to that daily pound of bread—the measure established and maintained by the Fathers—he allowed them two cooked dishes, on account of their differing infirmities, so that those who could not eat from one might be nourished by the other. In this matter he seems to have followed the distinguished example and teaching of Saint Pachomius. For, as we read in his *Life* (chapter 13), Pachomius entered a certain monastery and, after prayer, went to the kitchen. There he found a brother in charge of the kitchen making *psiathoi*, which ordinary people call mats. He said to him: “Tell me, brother, how long has it been since you cooked vegetables or legumes for the brothers?” He replied: “Nearly two months.” Saint Pachomius said: “Why did you wish to act contrary to the commandment, so that such a benefit to the brothers should be neglected?” The brother replied with humble self-justification: “I had indeed wished, venerable Father, to perform my service every day; but since whatever I cooked was not consumed by the brothers, because they all practice abstinence—for only the boys take some of the cooked food—I did not cook any dish, lest what had been prepared with so much labor should be thrown away. Instead, so that I would not be idle, I chose to weave *psiathoi* with the brothers, knowing that one of those assigned to me could suffice for this work, so that he might prepare small foods, namely olives and herbs, for the brothers’ meal.” When Pachomius heard this, he said: “And how many *psiathoi* are there that you say you have made?” He replied: “Five hundred.” He said: “Bring them all here, so that I may see them.” When they had been brought, he immediately ordered them to be burned by setting fire beneath them. Then he said to them: “Just as you have despised the rule entrusted to you concerning the provision for the brothers, so I have consumed your labors indiscriminately in the fire, so that you may learn how harmful it is to tear down the institutions of the Fathers, which have been provided for the salvation of souls. Do you not know that it is glorious always to abstain from things that are available? For if anyone, in consideration of God, restrains himself from something that lies within his power, he receives a great reward from the Lord. But from something whose use he is not permitted, a person is evidently restrained by necessity; and therefore it is useless to expect a reward for forced and unprofitable abstinence. Finally, when several foods have been served, if the brothers use them sparingly for God’s sake, they place the greatest hope for themselves with God. But concerning foods that they do not see and have no opportunity to consume, how can a reward be granted for frugality? Therefore, so great a benefit to the brothers ought not to have been interrupted on account of the small expense.” Thus far the account.] They fixed the measure at two *paximacia*—small loaves which most certainly weighed scarcely one pound.

For it ends in such frugality that sometimes, after evening has come, a person neither feels nor remembers that he has eaten.

If one of the brothers arrives, we should eat it together with him, adding nothing more than usual to our customary practice; and by this arrangement the arrival of a brother, which ought to be most welcome to us, will not cause us distress. In this way we fulfill the duties of kindness without relaxing anything of the strictness of abstinence. [Col. 0557A] If no one arrives, we may freely take this portion also, as something owed to us from the canonical measure. Such frugality will prevent the stomach from being burdened in the evening, since one *paximacium* has already been taken at the ninth hour. The opposite commonly happens to those who, believing that they practice stricter abstinence, postpone the entire meal until evening. For the recent consumption of food does not allow a delicate and unencumbered state of mind to be maintained either in evening or in nocturnal prayers. Thus Eusebius, drawing on Philo, writes concerning those Alexandrian ascetics instituted by blessed Mark the Evangelist (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 16): “None of them takes food or drink before sunset. For they judge that the study of divine wisdom in which they are immersed deserves the light, whereas bodily needs rightly claim only darkness. Thus they grant the whole day to the former, but only a small portion of the night to the latter.” Saint Antony likewise, according to Athanasius, ate once a day after sunset, sometimes remaining in this way for two or three days and only eating again on the fourth day. Jerome reports the same of Hilarion, and, writing to Paulinus among other instructions for a monk, says: “Let his food be poor and taken in the evening” (Letter 13). From the Ides of September until the beginning of Lent, however, they should always eat at the ninth hour. From these words Abbot Smaragdus concludes that according to the Rule one should fast daily from the Ides of September—that is, from the Exaltation of the Holy Cross—until Lent, with the fast broken at the ninth hour, whereas in Lent it should not be broken until evening. With such fare blessed Moses has nourished us at the table of a twofold instruction: by the present instruction of his words he has shown not only the grace and virtue of discretion, but also, in the discussion that preceded it, the method, purpose, and end of renunciation. He has made clear as daylight what previously, moved only by spiritual fervor and zeal for God, we pursued with our eyes almost closed; and he has made us realize how far during that time we had strayed from the purity of heart and the path of discretion, since even the disciplines of all the visible arts in this world cannot exist without a defined purpose or be attained without contemplation of a certain end.

# THIRD COLLATION, WHICH IS THAT OF ABBOT PAPHNUTIUS. ON THE THREE RENUNCIATIONS.

He argues the contrary both from the Vatican copies that he used and from Sozomen and Palladius—together with the other ecclesiastical historians, Baronius the author of the *Sacred Annals*, Suidas, and all the others—among whom he is everywhere named and written *Paphnutius*, not *Pafnutius*, just as in Greek Παφνούτιος (*Paphnoutios*). Among them, to mention a few of the earlier examples, Saint Paul the first hermit extended his life to nearly one hundred fifteen years, spending approximately one hundred of them in the desert, as Saint Jerome writes. From his youth this man had devoted himself to the schools of the coenobiums with such ardor that, after spending only a short time in them, he was equally enriched both by the good of obedience and by knowledge of every virtue. For through the discipline of humility and obedience he put all his own desires to death; by this means all vices were extinguished and all the virtues established by the institutions of the monasteries and the teaching of the most ancient Fathers were perfected. Then, inflamed by an ardent desire for higher progress, he hastened to penetrate the hidden places of the desert [Col. 0559B], so that he might be more easily and inseparably united to the Lord, to whom he had thirsted to cling while living among the throngs of the brothers, once no human companionship remained to hold him back. There again, surpassing even the virtues of the anchorites by the ardor of his desire and by his pursuit of that continual and divine contemplation, he avoided the sight of everyone, penetrating the remoter and inaccessible places of solitude and concealing himself there for a long time. Thus he was thought to delight in and enjoy the daily companionship of angels, since even the anchorites themselves could discover him only with difficulty and very rarely. And because of the merit of this virtue [Note: [Col. 0559D] Namely, the virtue of solitude and contemplation, and because of the excellence of it. Cuychius says that the *bubalus* is a wild ox, black in color, with very strong legs and short hair and tail, possessing long, curved horns (Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 15). For this reason, since the animal is extremely wild, it seems that Abbot Paphnutius was given the nickname “Bubalus” because of his wild and solitary life, as may be inferred both from this chapter and from chapter 15 of Collation 18. Something similar, incidentally, is read concerning Saint Thomas Aquinas. When he was teaching in the schools under Albert the Great, his companions called him “the mute ox” because of his excessive silence and a certain Pythagorean silence. I remember that I once playfully composed these verses for his portrait:

“Behold the mute ox, whom the foolish crowd called so,  
whose bellow resounds in the farthest East.”] they gave him the nickname “Bubalus.”

## CHAPTER II. On the discourse of the same old man and our reply

[Col. 0560A]

Wishing to be instructed under his guidance, and also driven by the goads of our thoughts, we arrived at his cell as the day was already growing late. After he had remained silent for a little while, he began to commend our purpose: namely, that after leaving our homeland and traveling through so many provinces for the love of the Lord, we were striving to endure the poverty and desolation of the desert and to imitate the strictness of their way of life—a strictness that even those who had been born and raised in the same necessity and poverty could scarcely endure. We replied that we had come to his teaching and guidance for this reason: so that we might in some measure be imbued with the instruction and perfection of so great a man, which we had perceived to be present in him through innumerable examples—not so that we might be burdened by praises of qualities that were not in us, or, through that elation of spirit with which the enemy’s suggestion sometimes tickled us even in our own cells, be puffed up by his very words. Therefore we asked rather that those things be infused into us by which we might be pricked with compunction or humbled, not those by which we might flatter and exalt ourselves.

## CHAPTER III. Abbot Paphnutius’s proposition concerning the three kinds of calling and the three renunciations
Then blessed Paphnutius said:

> There are three orders of vocation,

and we should know that there are likewise three renunciations necessary for a monk established in any order of vocation.

[Note: [Col. 0560C] That is, three ways by which we are called and drawn to the worship of God, contempt for the world, and the pursuit of perfection; he explains these in the following chapter.]

[Note: [Col. 0560C] Lest anyone think that the three kinds of renunciation are opposed to the three vocations and correspond to them in the same order—namely, the first to the first, the second to the second, and the third to the third—and therefore that one would suffice without the others, he says that these three renunciations are required simultaneously and equally in every kind of vocation, so that someone may truly be and be called a perfect monk. Hence this conference is concerned with the three renunciations and is inscribed with that title.

As for the word *abrenuntiatio*—lest anyone criticize its barbarism or novelty—although no mention of it is found among classical pagan authors, Saint Clement, Roman bishop, nevertheless uses it in the *Apostolic Constitutions*, book 7, chapter 4, where he gives the formula of renunciation still used in baptism; Ambrose uses it in chapter 2 of his letter to the Colossians and in book 1, chapter 2, *On the Sacraments*; and Augustine in Letter 38.

The word *renuntiatio*, used by Tertullian, Cyprian, Jerome, Ambrose, and Augustine, is employed by Quintilian in book 10 with the same meaning as the Greek word ἀποτάσσεσθαι, used by the Greek Fathers Dionysius the Areopagite, Basil, and Cyril. It means to bid a final farewell, or to dismiss completely, cast away, or renounce.

The Greek and Latin Fathers seem to have borrowed this formula of expression not from the formulas of jurists, as some believe—among whom *renuntiatio* means the cession or refusal of something that had entered into a pact or promise—but rather from Luke 14: “Everyone among you who does not renounce all that he possesses,” and so forth.

It should also be remembered, as we have noted elsewhere, that there are two kinds of renunciation, or abrenunciation. One is common to all Christians and takes place in baptism; concerning it see Saint Clement and Ambrose in the passages cited above, Dionysius the Areopagite, *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 1, Tertullian, *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 5, Cyprian, Letters 7 and 54, and other Fathers. The other belongs properly and specifically to apostles and monks; this is the one under discussion here, whose three parts or degrees are explained in this conference.]

First, we must carefully investigate the reason why we have said that there are three orders of vocation. Once we recognize that we have been called to the worship of God by the first degree of vocation, we should proportion the conduct of our life to its sublimity. For it will be of no benefit to have begun nobly if we do not also display an end corresponding to our beginnings. But if we recognize that we have been drawn away from worldly conduct by the final order, then, the less promising the beginning of our religious life appears because of this, the more earnestly we must strive, with spiritual fervor, to impel ourselves toward a better end. We must also know the second reason for the threefold renunciation in every respect, because we will be able to attain perfection in no way if we either remain ignorant of it or, knowing it, fail to strive to complete it in practice.

## CHAPTER IV. Explanation of the Three Vocations

Thus, so that these three modes of vocation may be disclosed by a precise distinction, the first is from God, the second through a human being, and the third from necessity.

The first is from God whenever some inspiration sent into our heart sometimes awakens us, even while we are asleep, to desire eternal life and salvation, and urges us by a most salutary compunction to follow God and cling to his commandments. Thus in the holy Scriptures we read that Abraham was called by the voice of the Lord away from his native land, from the affections of his whole kindred, and from his father’s house, when the Lord said: “Go out from your land, and from your kindred, and from your father’s house” (Genesis 12).

[Note: [Col. 0561D] That is, called by God. Athanasius likewise reports this in his *Life* of him, in almost the same words.]

We know that blessed Antony was called in this way: he received the occasion of his conversion from God alone. For when he entered a church and there heard the Lord preaching in the Gospel, “Whoever does not hate father, mother, children, wife, and lands, and even his own life, cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14), and, “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you possess, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me” (Matthew 19), he received this command of the Lord as though it had been directed especially to him, with the deepest compunction of heart. Immediately renouncing everything, he followed Christ, provoked by no exhortation or teaching of human beings.

The second mode of vocation is the one that we said occurs through a human being, when we are inflamed with a desire for salvation either by the examples or by the admonitions of certain holy people.

[Note: [Col. 0561D] Two soldiers whom Saint Augustine mentions in *Confessions*, book 8, chapter 6 and following, were called and inflamed with a desire for salvation and perfection in this way. They came from the court of the emperor Theodosius. When they happened upon the written *Life of Blessed Antony*, they began, while reading it, to marvel and become inflamed; finally they burned with such zeal that, in the very place where they had stopped, they abandoned military service in the world and began a new military service in the service of God.

When Potitianus had recounted this to Augustine in familiar conversation, and had also described at greater length the practices of Antony—whose name had previously been unknown to Augustine—as well as the communities of Egyptian monasteries and their customs, which, as he himself says, were fragrant with the scent of God, that event placed such sparks, or rather torches, in Augustine’s breast that he could find no rest in mind or conscience until he too resolved to renounce the world and cling to the heavenly life.

Thus Antony’s example drew those two soldiers to salvation, the two soldiers drew Augustine, and Augustine in turn drew many others.]

We too regard ourselves as having been called by the grace of the Lord, since we were stirred by the admonitions and virtues of the aforesaid man and devoted ourselves to this pursuit and profession. In the same manner we read in the holy Scriptures that the children of Israel were freed from the oppression of Egypt through Moses (Exodus 14).

[Note: [Col. 0562C] Saint Bernard gives an example of this vocation in Paul the first hermit. Saint Jerome writes that Paul entered a cave by chance while fleeing the persecution of Decius and Valerian; after hiding there for some time, he began also to take pleasure in solitude. What he had first done from necessity he afterward did by choice, and he maintained it throughout his life. See Jerome above, in the *Life of Paul*.

The anger of the young man Arcadius, whom the holy man Arsenius was educating, likewise provided the occasion that led Arsenius to flee the world and devote himself entirely to God’s service. Thus, while he was caring for the health of the body, he found the salvation of the soul, far more desirable.

There was also another Paul, surnamed “the Simple,” who, having discovered his wife in adultery, abandoned both her and his house and went straight to Antony’s school. There he advanced in a very short time to the perfection of the highest holiness.

More remarkable still is what is read about the most holy and famous abbot Moses. When he was a pagan and a robber, he climbed onto the roof of a convent of virgins in order to plunder it. Falling asleep on the roof, he saw a certain king who urged him at last to desist from his crimes. Moved by this, he immediately received baptism and then embraced the monastic life. In it he attained such holiness that, among his other miracles, he even commanded the sun to stand still, like another Joshua.

You will find a similar example of Moses the Ethiopian mentioned below, in chapter 5; another of Evagrius in Sozomen, book 6, chapter 30; and another, still more marvelous, in Sophronius, *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 78. See also Metaphrastes, May 8; Baronius, volume 4, year 383; Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 28; Nicephorus, book 8, chapter 40; Cassiodorus, *Tripartite History*, book 1, chapter 11; and Peter, *Catalogue*, book 5, chapter 48.]

The third mode of vocation, however, is the one that proceeds from necessity. Those who are bound to the wealth or pleasures of this world are compelled, when sudden trials arise—trials that threaten the dangers of death, strike them through the loss and confiscation of their possessions, or wound them through the death of loved ones—to hasten, at least unwillingly, to the Lord whom they scorned to follow when circumstances were prosperous.

We find the necessity of this vocation very frequently in Scripture. We read that, because of the merits of their sins, the children of Israel were handed over by the Lord to their enemies; then, because of the savage cruelty of their domination, they turned back and cried out to the Lord. “And the Lord,” it says, “sent them a savior, Ehud, son of Gera, son of Jemini, who used both hands as though they were his right hand” (Judges 3). Again: “They cried out to the Lord, who raised up for them a savior and delivered them, Othniel, son of Kenaz, the younger brother of Caleb” (ibid.). And concerning such people the Psalm says: “When he slew them, then they sought him, and they returned and came to him at dawn; and they remembered that God was their helper, and that God Most High was their Redeemer” (Psalm 77). Again: “They cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their distresses” (Psalm 106).

## CHAPTER V. That the First Vocation Does Not Benefit the Sluggish, nor the Last Harm the Zealous

Although the first two of these three modes may appear to rest on better beginnings, we nevertheless sometimes find perfect and most fervent men in spirit arising even from the third degree, which seems the lowest and lukewarm. They become like those who began the service of the Lord with an excellent beginning and spent the rest of their lives with praiseworthy fervor of spirit.

Conversely, we very often see many from that higher degree grow cold and fall back into a blameworthy end. Accordingly, just as it did not harm the former that they appeared to have been converted not by their own choice but under the compulsion of necessity—for the Lord’s kindness had provided them with this very occasion for compunction—so it was of no benefit to the latter that they had had more exalted beginnings in their conversion, because they did not strive to bring the rest of their lives to a fitting conclusion.

[Note: [Col. 0563D] Saint Macarius says in one of his homilies (Homily 32) that this often happens: God harasses a person with hardships and tribulations so that someone who clings too intensely in mind and desire to earthly things, when he sees everything turning out unhappily for him, begins to reason with himself in this way: “Since I cannot obtain in the world what I wanted, behold, I am leaving the world and going to God, so that I may serve him alone.” Thus he comes to give thanks for his adverse fortune, whose occasion drove him to the sweetest service of God.

John Climacus says something similar, calling this a practice of God: sometimes he catches people by a benevolent deception and leads them, deceived or thinking of nothing less, into the way of salvation. His words are these (*Ladder*, step 1): “Let us not despise certain people who renounce the world without wise deliberation, because the Spirit sometimes deceives souls piously. Such renunciation often ends in a better outcome than renunciation that was deliberate, just as seed falling from a farmer’s hand sometimes sprouts more abundantly where he does not intend it than where it was deliberately sown.”

“I have seen some go to a monastery not with the right intention but compelled by necessity; afterward they were captivated by the great wisdom of the abbot and the peaceful conduct of the monks. Later they received from God the light of grace and attained a lofty state.” Thus Climacus agrees with what Paphnutius says here.]

For nothing was lacking to abbot Moses, who lived in the place of this desert called Calamus, for attaining the merit of perfect blessedness merely because he had been driven to the monastery by fear of death, which threatened him on account of the crime of murder. He embraced the necessity of conversion in such a way that, readily transforming it into an act of the will, he reached the highest summits of perfection.

[Note: [Col. 0564D] That Ethiopian, namely, concerning whom see Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 22; Sozomen, book 6, chapter 29; and Nicephorus, book 11, chapter 36.]

[Note: [Col. 0564D] Calamus was a place of solitude in Egypt, where Paul the hermit also lived. Cassian mentions it again in Conference 7, chapter 26, and Conference 24, chapter 4.]

By contrast, nothing benefited many others—whom I should not name individually—from having begun the service of the Lord with a better beginning, since afterward, as laziness and hardness of heart took hold, they fell into harmful lukewarmness and the abyss of death.

We see this same matter clearly displayed in the vocation of the apostles. What benefit did Judas receive from voluntarily accepting the most exalted rank of apostleship, being called in the same manner as Peter and the other apostles, when he completed the glorious beginning of his vocation with the pestilential end of greed and love of money and, as a most cruel murderer, advanced all the way to the betrayal of the Lord (Matthew 26)? Or what harm did it do Paul that, having suddenly been struck blind (Acts 9), he appears to have been drawn, almost unwillingly, onto the way of salvation? He afterward followed the Lord with such fervor of spirit that, completing the beginning imposed by necessity through voluntary devotion, he brought his life, distinguished by so many virtues, to an incomparable and glorious end.

Everything, therefore, depends on the end. Someone dedicated to the beginnings of an excellent conversion may nevertheless be found inferior through negligence, while someone drawn by necessity to profess the name of monk may become perfect through the fear of God and diligence.

## CHAPTER VI. Explanation of the Three Renunciations

We must now discuss the renunciations, which both the tradition of the Fathers and the authority of the holy Scriptures show to be three, and which each of us ought to fulfill with every effort.

The first is that by which we reject bodily all the wealth and resources of the world. The second is that by which we reject our former habits, vices, and dispositions of mind and flesh. The third is that by which, calling our mind away from all present and visible things, we contemplate only the future and desire the things that are invisible.

We read that the Lord commanded Abraham to accomplish these three together when he said to him: “Go out from your land, and from your kindred, and from your father’s house” (Genesis 12).

First he said, “from your land”—that is, from the resources and earthly riches of this world. Second, “from your kindred”—that is, from the former conduct, customs, and vices that have clung to us from our birth and are related to us as though by a certain affinity and blood relationship. Third, “from your father’s house”—that is, from every memory of this world that presents itself to the eyes.

For concerning the two fathers—namely, either the one whom we must abandon or the one whom we ought to seek—David sings in God’s person: “Listen, daughter, and see, incline your ear, forget your people and your father’s house” (Psalm 44). For the one who says, “Listen, daughter,” is certainly a father; and when he urges her to forget that father’s house or people, he nevertheless testifies that the one whose house or people she is urged to forget had been the father of his daughter.

This is fulfilled when, having been put to death with Christ to the elements of this world, we contemplate, according to the Apostle, not the things that are seen but those that are not seen: “For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4). Coming forth in heart from this temporal and visible house, we direct our eyes and mind toward that house in which we shall remain perpetually.

We shall fulfill this when, walking in the flesh, we begin to serve the Lord not according to the flesh, crying out in deed and power the saying of the blessed Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3).

[Note: [Col. 0565B] Tertullian likewise uses *municipatus* in *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 13, for the Greek πολίτευμα, rendered in our version as “citizenship” or “conduct.” The same occurs in book 3 of *Against Marcion* and in *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 12: “The Apostle,” he says, “indicates that our mother is above, declaring that our πολίτευμα, that is, our citizenship, is in heaven,” and so forth. Hilary, however, reads in book 1 of *On the Trinity*: “Our expectation is in heaven.”]

The three books of Solomon are appropriately applied to these three renunciations.

[Note: [Col. 0565B] Origen discusses these three books—which without controversy are attributed to King Solomon—and their mystical meaning, sequence, and correspondence extensively and quite suitably for this passage in his first homily on the *Song of Songs*. From Jerome’s version, the following is found there:

“According to this teaching of the wisest Solomon (Ecclesiastes 1), the person who desires to know wisdom must begin with moral instruction and understand what is written: ‘You desired wisdom; keep the commandments, and the Lord will give it to you.’ For this reason the teacher who instructs the first human beings in divine philosophy placed the book of Proverbs at the beginning of his work. In it, as we have said, the moral subject is taught, so that when someone has progressed in understanding and conduct, he may also come to the discipline of natural understanding. There, distinguishing the causes and natures of things, he recognizes that the vanity of vanities must be abandoned and that he must hasten toward eternal and perpetual things.

“Therefore, after Proverbs comes Ecclesiastes, which teaches, as we have said, that all visible and bodily things are fleeting and fragile. When the student of wisdom has discovered that this is so, he will undoubtedly despise and reject them; and, renouncing the whole world, so to speak, he will strive toward the invisible and eternal things taught through spiritual senses in the Song of Songs, though under certain veiled figures of love.

“For this book occupies the final place so that one comes to it only after one’s conduct has been purified and one has learned the knowledge and distinction of corruptible and incorruptible things. Through these preparations, one cannot be offended by any of the figures by which the heavenly love of the bride for the bridegroom—that is, the love of the perfected soul for the Word of God—is described and formed.”

And shortly afterward:

“I therefore believe that this threefold form of philosophy was also prefigured in those holy and blessed men for whose most holy instruction the supreme God wished to be called the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob (Genesis 26 and 32).

“Abraham represents moral philosophy through obedience, and so forth. Isaac likewise possesses natural philosophy, both when he digs wells and when he examines the depths of things. Jacob holds the contemplative position, since he was named Israel because of the contemplation of divine things, saw the armies of heaven, and perceived the house of God and the paths of the angels—that is, the ladders extending from earth to heaven (Genesis 28).

“Therefore we rightly find these three blessed men setting up altars to God, that is, consecrating the progress of their philosophy, so that they might teach that these things should be attributed not to human arts but to the grace of God. They also dwell in tents, thereby showing that the person who studies divine philosophy ought to possess nothing as his own on earth but should always advance—not so much from place to place as from knowledge of lesser things to knowledge of perfect things.

“You will also find many other things in the divine Scriptures that indicate, according to this same pattern, the order that we have said is contained in Solomon’s books.

“Therefore, if someone has fulfilled the first stage, represented by Proverbs, in correcting conduct and keeping the commandments, and if afterward, having discovered the vanity of the world and perceived the fragility of transitory things, he comes to renounce the world and everything in it, then he will consequently come also to contemplate and desire the things that are invisible and eternal. Yet to reach these things we need divine mercy, if perhaps, having perceived the beauty of the Word of God, we may be kindled with a saving love for him, so that he himself may deign to love such a soul, in which he has perceived a desire for himself.”

Thus far Origen.]

Saint Jerome, the interpreter of that homily, imitating him, writes similarly in his commentary on Ecclesiastes:

“Solomon, according to the number of the names, produced three volumes: Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs. In Proverbs he teaches the little child and, as though concerning duties, instructs him through maxims; hence his speech is frequently addressed to his son.

“In Ecclesiastes he instructs the mature man, so that he may not think anything in the affairs of the world to be everlasting, but may recognize everything we see as fleeting and brief.

“Finally, in the Song of Songs, he joins the already perfected man, prepared after trampling upon the world, to the embraces of the bridegroom. For unless we first abandon vices, renounce the pageants of the world, and prepare ourselves unencumbered for Christ’s coming, we cannot say: ‘Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.’”

This is Saint Jerome’s teaching. Saint Basil, Ambrose, Theodoret, Gregory the Great in their prefaces to the *Song of Songs*, and Isidore of Seville in his *Allegories of Sacred Scripture* offer similar and corresponding interpretations.]

Proverbs correspond to the first renunciation, since through them the desire for carnal things and earthly vices are cut away. Ecclesiastes corresponds to the second renunciation, since there everything done under the sun is pronounced vanity. The Song of Songs corresponds to the third, since in it the mind, transcending all visible things, is joined to the Word of God through contemplation of heavenly things.

## CHAPTER VII. How the Perfection of Each Renunciation Is to Be Sought

[Col. 0566B]

Therefore it will be of little benefit that we have undertaken the first renunciation with the utmost devotion of faith, [Col. 0567A] if we do not fulfill the second with the same diligence and the same ardor. And once we have attained this as well, we shall also be able to reach that third renunciation, by which, having gone forth from the house of our former parent—whom we remember to have been our father from the beginning of our birth, according to the old man and our former way of life, when we were by nature children of wrath, as were the rest (Eph. II)—we turn the whole gaze of our mind toward heavenly things.

Concerning this father, too, Jerusalem—which had despised the true God as Father—is told: “Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite” (Ezek. XVI). And in the Gospel: “You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father” (John VIII).

When we have abandoned him, migrating from visible things to invisible, we shall be able to say with the Apostle: [Col. 0567B] “We know that if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have a dwelling from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (II Cor. V). And that which we mentioned shortly before: “Our citizenship is in heaven; from there also we await the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will reform the body of our lowliness, conforming it to the body of his glory” (Phil. III). And that saying of blessed David: “For I am a sojourner upon the earth and a pilgrim, like all my fathers” (Pss. XXXVIII and CXVIII), so that, according to the Lord’s word, we may become like those of whom the Lord spoke these things to the Father in the Gospel: “They are not of this world, just as I am not of this world” (John XVII). And again, to the apostles themselves: “If you were of this world, the world would love what was its own; but because you are not of this world, and I chose you out of this world, therefore the world hates you” (John XV).

We shall then deserve to attain the true perfection of this third renunciation, when our mind, dulled by no contagion of fleshly heaviness but polished by the most exact refinement, stripped of every earthly affection and quality through unceasing meditation on the divine Scriptures and through spiritual contemplation, has passed over to those invisible things to such an extent that, intent upon what is heavenly and incorporeal, it does not perceive itself to be surrounded by the frailty of flesh and the body’s condition. It will be carried away into such an ecstasy that it will not merely fail to receive any sounds with bodily hearing or be occupied with looking upon the forms of passing human beings, but will not even see with the eyes of the flesh the masses of trees standing nearby or the enormous objects placed before them. [Col. 0567D]

[Col. 0568A] No one will grasp the truth and power of this except the one who has learned these things through experience as his teacher—one whose Lord has so withdrawn the eyes of his heart from all present things that he regards and sees them not as things that will pass away, but as though they already did not exist, dissolved into nothing like empty smoke. Walking with God like Enoch, and transferred from human intercourse and conduct, he will not be found in the vanity of the present age.

This is also commemorated as having happened to him bodily, when the reading from Genesis says: “And Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, because God transferred him” (Gen. V). The Apostle likewise says: “By faith Enoch was transferred, so that he would not see death” (Heb. XI).

[Note: [Col. 0567D] There were two Enochs, or Henochs: one, the son of Cain, in Genesis IV; the other, the son of Jared, of the line of Seth, and the seventh from him, in Genesis V. The latter is the one under discussion. Three notable prerogatives are handed down concerning him in Scripture. The first is that he “walked with God,” or “before God”—a Hebrew expression by which his singular devotion toward God and holiness of life are indicated (Augustine, *City of God* XV.19). To walk with God, or before God, is the same as to walk in the way of the Lord or in his commandments, or to please God, as the Septuagint translators rendered it: “He pleased God.” Hence God also said to Abraham: “Walk before me, and be perfect” (Gen. VII). The second is that he was transferred by God. For Scripture says: “And he did not appear, because God took him” (Gen. V); and Ecclesiasticus XLIV: “Enoch pleased God, and was transferred into Paradise,” etc. The third is that he is still alive and has not yet died, nor is he believed to die until the consummation of the age. The Apostle says plainly to the Hebrews: “By faith Enoch was transferred, so that he would not see death” (Heb. XI). From this it is clearly inferred that Enoch has not yet died, though he will eventually die, because according to the general sentence of God: “It is appointed for all human beings to die once” (Heb. IX; Gen. II). See St. Thomas on the Epistle to the Hebrews, and Pererius on Genesis.]

Concerning that death the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever lives and believes in me will never die” (John XI). [Col. 0568B]

Therefore, if we desire to attain true perfection, we must hasten, so that just as in body we have despised parents, homeland, the riches of the world, and pleasures, so also in heart, abandoning all these things, we do not return through any desire to what we have left behind. This is like those who were led out through Moses: although they did not return bodily, they are said to have returned in heart to Egypt—having abandoned the God who had brought them out with such mighty signs and worshiping the idols of Egypt that they had despised, as Scripture recalls:

[Note: [Col. 0568D] The author appears to cite these words as Scripture, although they are not found in the Vulgate edition, nor have I been able to find them in another author.]

“And they returned in their hearts to Egypt, saying to Aaron, ‘Make gods for us to go before us.’”

Let us not also be condemned together with those who, dwelling in the wilderness after eating the food of heavenly manna, desired the foul-smelling food of vices and the food of sordid baseness, and let us not appear to murmur in the same way with them: “It was well with us in Egypt, where we sat beside pots of meat and ate onions and garlic, cucumbers and melons” (Exod. XVI; Num. XI).

Although this figure was enacted earlier in that people, we see it being fulfilled every day even now in our own order and profession. For everyone who, after renouncing this world, returns to his former pursuits and is recalled to his former desires proclaims in deed and mind the same thing with them, saying: “It was well with me in Egypt.” I fear that as great a multitude as that of the transgressors whom we read existed under Moses may be found among them. For although six hundred thousand armed men were counted as having gone out of Egypt, no more than two of them entered the promised land [Col. 0568D] [Col. 0569A] (Num. XIV).

[Note: [Col. 0569C] That is, we must be diligent, provident, and laborious, as above, *Conference* I.17, and again below in the following chapter: “Therefore we must hasten.”]

Therefore we must hasten, taking examples of virtue from the few and exceedingly rare, because, according to the figure we have mentioned, in the Gospel also it is said: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX and XXII).

Our bodily renunciation, then, and our migration, so to speak, from Egypt to another place, will benefit us nothing if we are likewise unable to attain the renunciation of the heart, which is more exalted and more useful. For concerning the bodily renunciation we have mentioned, the Apostle declares: “If I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and deliver my body so that I may be burned, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (I Cor. XIII).

Blessed Paul would never have said this unless he had foreseen in the Spirit that some, after distributing all their possessions for the nourishment of the poor, would nevertheless be unable to reach evangelical perfection and the arduous summit of charity. For, retaining in their hearts their former vices and lack of self-control, whether pride or impatience ruled them, they would take no care to cleanse themselves of these things, and for that reason would not reach the charity of God, which never fails.

Having thus become inferior through this second degree of renunciation, they grasp still less that third degree, which is undoubtedly more exalted. Consider this point more carefully as well: he did not simply say, “If I distribute my possessions.” He might perhaps have seemed to speak of someone who, not yet fulfilling the evangelical command, had still kept something entirely for himself from those possessions, as some lukewarm people do. [Col. 0569C] But he says: “If I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor”—that is, even if I have perfectly renounced these earthly riches.

[Note: [Col. 0569C] St. Jerome speaks beautifully to this point, which is the chief foundation of the religious state, in Letter 8 to Demetrias: “It is the mark of apostolic eminence and perfect virtue to sell everything, distribute it to the poor, and thus, light and unencumbered, soar with Christ to heavenly things. A careful stewardship has been entrusted to us, although freedom of choice has been left to every age and every person in this matter. ‘If you wish,’ he says, ‘to be perfect.’ I do not compel or command; it is yours to choose, if you wish to be crowned in the contest and struggle. And let us consider how wisely Wisdom has spoken: ‘Sell what you possess.’ To whom are these things commanded? Surely to the one to whom it was said, ‘If you wish to be perfect.’ He does not say, ‘Sell part of your goods,’ but ‘all.’ And when you have sold them, what follows? ‘Give to the poor’—not to the rich, not to relatives, not for luxury, but for necessity.” Thus far St. Jerome. It is amusing, moreover, that a certain monk is said to have done the following (Socrates, Book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 18): persuaded by this Gospel saying, he sold the Gospel book that alone he possessed and distributed the price to the poor, saying, “I have sold that very book which says, ‘Sell everything you possess and give to the poor.’” We have noted more on the same subject elsewhere (*Institutes* VII.16). [Col. 0569D]]

To this renunciation he added something greater: “And if I deliver my body so that I may be burned, but do not have charity, I am nothing.” It is as though he had said in other words:

If I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, according to that evangelical command in which it is said (Matt. XIX), “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me”—renouncing in such a way that I reserve absolutely nothing of these things for myself; and if I add martyrdom and the burning of my flesh to this distribution, so that I deliver my body for Christ; and yet I am impatient, or angry, or envious, or proud, or inflamed by the injuries of others, or seek what is mine, or think what is evil, or do not patiently and willingly endure everything that can be inflicted upon me—then the renunciation and burning of the outward person will benefit me nothing, while the inner person is still entangled in its former vices.

This is because, despising the simple substance of this world in the fervor of my first conversion—a substance defined as neither good nor evil, but morally intermediate—I have not likewise taken care to cast away the harmful powers of my vicious heart, nor to attain the Lord’s charity, which is patient and kind, does not envy, is not puffed up, is not provoked, does not act wrongly, does not seek its own, does not think evil, and bears and endures all things (I Cor. XIII), and finally, which [Col. 0569D]

[Note: [Col. 0569D] What, then? Can the person endowed with charity never sin? Far be it from us to think so. Paphnutius did not mean this, for it is plainly refuted by the Christian faith (Council of Trent, Session VI, chapters 13 and 14, and canon 23), by reason, and by daily experience. No one in this mortal life is supported by such stability or endowed with such perfection of charity that he ought not to consider the Apostle’s saying addressed to him: “Let the one who stands beware lest he fall” (I Cor. X). The same Apostle warned even those who were more advanced and perfect of this danger when he wrote to the Galatians in chapter VI: “Brothers, if a person is overtaken in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted.” How, then, does charity never allow its follower or possessor to fall through the overthrow of sin? It does so in the sense and meaning in which the Apostle says that charity does not act wrongly and is not puffed up (I Cor. XIII), etc.; by these words is signified what charity effects and accomplishes so long as it is present and possessed. It does not follow from this that the person who has charity cannot become proud or do anything wicked. Rather, while it is possessed, charity prevents the mind from swelling with pride or acting wrongly at the same time. In this respect it differs greatly from faith, knowledge, and the other gifts of God, since, as the Apostle says, “Knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up” (I Cor. VIII).

This is the sense in which St. Prosper should be understood when he says in Book III of *The Contemplative Life*, chapter 13, that charity, joined inseparably to God, is subject to no change through vice—not because the person who has once received charity cannot be changed for the worse, but because, just as a flame is said always to rise upward although it can be extinguished, since, while it exists, it does not cease seeking higher things, so charity, as long as it possesses the human heart, does not allow a person to be separated or driven away from God by that kind of sin which separates from God, namely mortal sin.]

…never allows its follower to fall through the overthrow of sin.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Particular Riches in Which the Beauty or Ugliness of the Soul Consists

[Col. 0570C]

We must therefore hasten with every effort so that our inner person also casts away and scatters all the riches of its vices that it accumulated in its former way of life—riches that continually cling to body and soul and are properly our own. Unless they are cast away and cut off while we still remain in this body, they will not cease to accompany us even after our departure.

For just as virtues, or charity itself, which is their source, acquired in this age, make their lover beautiful and splendid even after the end of this life, so vices transmit the mind, as it were darkened by gloomy colors, infected to that perpetual dwelling. [Col. 0571C]

[Note: [Col. 0571C] For how vices, or sins, obscure our minds, as it were—that is, metaphorically—with dark colors, see St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, Prima Secundae, question 86, where among the effects of sin he places the stain contracted by the soul when it is deprived of the brightness of natural light and the splendor of divine grace. Hence Scripture frequently teaches that a person is defiled by sins and, by metonymy, calls sin itself defilement, filth, and stain. Deuteronomy XXXII: “They sinned against him, and are not his children in their filth.” Isaiah IV: “When the Lord has washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion.” Ezekiel XXXVI: “I will pour clean water over you, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements.” Ephesians V: “That he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle.”]

For the beauty or ugliness of the soul is produced by the quality of virtues or vices. From these a certain color is drawn, which either makes it so radiant and beautiful that it deserves to hear from the Prophet, “The king will desire your beauty” (Ps. XLIV), or makes it black, foul, and deformed, so that it itself confesses the stench of its ugliness and says, “My wounds have become foul and corrupt because of my foolishness” (Ps. XXXVII).

The Lord himself says to it through Jeremiah VIII: “Why has the wound of the daughter of my people not been bound up?” For this reason, these are our particular riches, which remain continually with the soul and which no king and no enemy can either bestow upon us or take away.

[Note: [Col. 0571D] These are, specifically, the sins and vices contracted in this age and stored up in the soul as in a chest, through guilt and stain. They are riches, I say, but evil ones, as the following chapter explains; and they are our riches because we contract and accumulate them from ourselves, that is, by the choice of our own will, according to the saying: “Your destruction is from yourself, O Israel.” To this may be referred Paul’s statement in Romans II: “According to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the just judgment of God, who will repay each one according to his works”; and James V: “You have stored up wrath for yourselves in the last days.” A treasure is, in fact, an accumulation of both good and evil things. Hence among the Greeks: θησαυρὸς κακῶν, “a treasure of evils.” [Col. 0572D]]

These are our particular riches, which not even death itself will be able to separate from the soul. By renouncing them we can attain perfection; or, if bound to them, we can be punished with eternal death.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Threefold Kind of Riches

[Col. 0571C]

In the sacred Scriptures, riches are understood in three ways: evil, good, and intermediate.

Evil riches are those of which it is said, “The rich have lacked and hungered” (Ps. XXXIII), and, “Woe to you who are rich, because you have received your consolation” (Luke VI). To cast away these riches is the highest perfection. In contrast to them are those poor whom the Lord’s voice praises in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V). And in the Psalm: “This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him” [Col. 0572A] (Ps. XXXIII). And again: “The poor and needy man will praise your name” (Ps. LXXIII).

There are also good riches, the acquisition of which is a matter of great virtue and merit. The righteous person who possesses them is praised together with them, as David says: “The generation of the upright will be blessed; glory and riches are in his house, and his righteousness endures forever and ever” (Ps. CXI). And again:

[Note: [Col. 0572D] St. Jerome also explains these as spiritual and heavenly riches, as this abbot does. He says (Letter 39): “We may indeed understand as our particular riches those which do not come from another’s property or from plunder, according to the saying, ‘Honor the Lord from your just labors’ (Prov. III). But the better interpretation is that we should recognize as our particular riches the hidden treasures which neither a thief can dig through nor a violent robber seize. Thus the Lord says in Matthew: ‘Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth, where rust and moth destroy, and where thieves dig through and steal. But store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves neither dig through nor steal.’”]

“The redemption of a man’s soul is his particular riches” (Prov. XIII).

Of these riches it is said in the Apocalypse that the person who lacks them is reproachfully poor and naked: “I am beginning to vomit you out of my mouth,” he says, “because you say, ‘I am rich and prosperous, and I need nothing,’ and you do not know that you are wretched and pitiable and poor and blind and naked. I advise you to buy from me gold refined in the fire, so that you may become rich, and to put on white garments, so that the shame of your nakedness may not appear” (Rev. III). [Col. 0572B]

There are also intermediate riches—that is, things that can be either good or evil. According to the will or character of those who use them, they can be transferred to either side. Concerning these the blessed Apostle says: “Command the rich of this world not to be high-minded or to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in God, who gives us all things abundantly for enjoyment; to do good, to give readily, to share, to store up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may apprehend the true life” (I Tim. VI).

The rich man in the Gospel, however, retained these riches and did not distribute them to the needy. The poor Lazarus, laid before his gate, desired to be filled with the crumbs from his table; yet that rich man was assigned to unbearable fires of Gehenna and eternal burning (Luke XVI).

## CHAPTER X. That No One Can Be Perfect in the First Degree of Renunciation Alone

[Col. 0572C]

In abandoning these visible riches of the world, therefore, we cast away not our own but another’s possessions, even though we boast that we acquired them either by our own labor or received them by inheritance from our parents. For, as I said, nothing is ours except that which, possessed in the heart and clinging to our soul, can be taken away from us by no one at all.

Concerning those visible riches, however, he rebukingly speaks to those who retain them as though they were their own and refuse to share them with the needy: [Col. 0573A]
