[Note: [Col. 0573C] The Fathers likewise interpret “another’s” as temporal things, and “our own” as spiritual things (Cyprian, *On Works and Almsgiving*; Augustine, *Questions on the Gospels* II.35). He calls temporal riches “another’s” because we do not possess them with full right, since in the briefest moment either they can be taken from us or we can be taken from them. Moreover, the Lord grants them to human beings not as their own property, but to be lawfully administered through them as stewards. He calls spiritual and heavenly goods “our own” because we were created for their possession, and they correspond to us according to what we most essentially are—namely, rational beings. They alone make us blessed, and they cannot be taken from us unless we are willing.]

“If you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?” (Luke XVI).

Clearly, then, not only does daily experience teach that these riches are another’s, but the Lord’s judgment itself signifies this by the very name. Concerning visible and most worthless riches Peter says to the Lord: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what, then, will there be for us?” (Matt. XIX).

They are nevertheless known to have left nothing more than very worthless and worn-out nets.

[Note: [Col. 0573D] The opinions of the holy Fathers agree with this. St. Jerome says in Letter 34: “The Apostles boast that they left everything and followed the Savior. Certainly, apart from nets and a boat, we do not read that they left anything; nevertheless, they are honored by the testimony of the future Judge because, in offering themselves wholly, they left everything they had.” Augustine, Letter 89, Question 4: “Nor will it be counted against me less because I was not rich. For neither were the Apostles, who did these things first, rich; but the person who leaves both what he had and what he desired to have leaves the whole world.” Gregory the Great, *Homilies on the Gospels* V: “Perhaps,” he says, “someone may say silently to himself: At the Lord’s word, what or how much did these two fishermen leave, who possessed almost nothing? But in this matter, dearly beloved brothers, we ought to weigh affection rather than wealth. The person who retained nothing for himself left much; the person who abandoned everything, however little, left much. Certainly we possess what we have with love, and we seek what we do not have out of desire. Peter and Andrew, therefore, left much when both abandoned even their desires to possess. The person who renounced his desires together with his possessions left much. Those who followed him, therefore, left as much as those who did not follow him could have desired. See similar material in St. Bernard, *Declamations* on the words ‘Behold, we have left everything’ (Matt. XIII).]

Unless all these things are understood within this renunciation of vices—which is truly great and supreme—we shall find that the Apostles left nothing precious, nor shall we understand that the Lord had anything for which he would bestow upon them such great glory of blessedness that they deserved to hear from him: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (ibid.).

If, then, those who perfectly renounce these earthly and visible possessions cannot, for definite reasons, reach that apostolic charity [Al. “glory”], nor climb with unencumbered vigor to that third degree of renunciation, which belongs to very few and is so much more exalted, what judgment ought those form about themselves who, not even perfectly embracing the first degree—which is very easy—and retaining the ancient filth of their money together with their former unbelief, think they may boast merely in the name of monks?

The first renunciation, therefore, which we have discussed, concerns another’s things, and for that reason by itself is insufficient to confer perfection upon the person who renounces, unless he proceeds to the second, which truly concerns the renunciation of our own things. Once we have attained this through the expulsion of all vices, we shall also climb the heights of the third renunciation. Through it we shall despise in mind and spirit not only everything that is done in this world or possessed individually by human beings, but even the fullness of all the elements, which is thought magnificent, regarding it as subject to vanity and soon to pass away.

We shall look, according to the Apostle, not at the things that are seen but at those that are not seen: “For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (II Cor. II). Only then shall we deserve to hear that supreme saying addressed to Abraham: “Go into the land that I will show you” (Gen. XII).

By this it is clearly shown that unless someone fulfills those three higher renunciations with the utmost ardor of mind, he cannot reach this fourth stage, which is granted to the person who renounces as a reward and recompense: namely, that he deserves to enter the promised land, no longer producing thorns and thistles of vices, but possessed in this body after the expulsion of all passions through purity of heart.

It will not be his own virtue or industry that shows this land to him; rather, the Lord himself promises that he will show it: “Go,” he says, “into the land that I will show you.” This plainly proves both that the beginning of our salvation comes from the Lord’s call, when he says, “Go out from your land,” and that the completion of perfection and purity is likewise granted by him, when he says, “Go into the land that I will show you”—that is, not a land that you can know or find by yourself or through your own industry, but one that I will show you when you neither know it nor seek it.

From this it is plainly inferred that just as, urged on by the Lord’s inspiration, we hasten toward the way of salvation, so, led by his instruction and illumination, we arrive at the perfection of supreme blessedness.

## CHAPTER XI. Germanus’s Question Concerning Human Free Will and the Grace of God

[Col. 0574C]

**Germanus:** In what, then, does free will consist, and to what is our own industry—which makes us praiseworthy—to be credited, if God both begins and completes in us everything that pertains to our perfection?

[Note: [Col. 0574D] An old refrain, or quibble, of the Pelagians: “Where do freedom of choice and the basis of merit consist if everything pertaining to our salvation and perfection is to be attributed to divine grace?” On this question see St. Jerome, *Against the Pelagians* I.3 and III.2; Augustine, *On Grace and Free Will* I; and Bernard, *Third Treatise on the Same Subject*. The matter will be treated more fully in *Conference* XIII.]

## CHAPTER XII. Paphnutius’s Response Concerning the Dispensation of Divine Grace While the Freedom of Choice Remains

[Col. 0575A]

**Paphnutius:** This would rightly trouble you if in every work or discipline there were only a beginning and an end, [Col. 0575D] and there were not also some intervening middle.

[Note: [Col. 0575D] Here Paphnutius appears to respond to that question as though he wished to attribute the beginning and end of our salvation and perfection to divine grace, but the middle—that is, progress or the intermediate course—to the powers of our free will. St. Cuychius, however, maintains (*Annotations* 5, at the end of this work) that Paphnutius intended nothing else than that the beginning of our justification comes from God alone, as does the gift of perseverance to the end; but that the progress or increase of grace, righteousness, holiness, and perfection, as a middle between the extremes—which is why he calls it “the middle”—must be attributed jointly to our free will and to divine grace. It follows that Paphnutius intended rather to rebuke the foolish or uninformed question of those who seemed to attribute only the beginning and end of our salvation and perfection to God.]

Thus, just as we recognize God to work the occasion of salvation in various ways, so it is ours to serve the occasions granted by the Divinity, either with greater or lesser earnestness (see Cuychius’s fifth annotation at the end of the work).

For just as the offer, “Go out from your land,” belonged to God who called, so Abraham’s obedience belonged to the one who went out. And just as the action of the one who obeyed was involved in the statement, “Go into the land,” so the addition, “that I will show you” (Gen. XII), belongs to the grace of God who commands or promises. [Col. 0575B]

Yet we must be certain that, even when we exercise every virtue with tireless efforts, we can never attain perfection by our own diligence or zeal. Human assiduity, by the merit of its labors, is not sufficient to reach such exalted rewards of blessedness unless we attain them with the Lord cooperating with us and directing our heart toward what is beneficial.

Therefore, praying with David, we ought to say at every moment: “Perfect my steps in your paths, so that my footsteps may not be moved” (Ps. XVI); and, “He established my feet upon a rock and directed my steps” (Ps. XXXIX). In this way, our free will—which is more readily carried toward vices either through ignorance of the good or through the allurements of the passions—may be turned by that invisible ruler of the human mind toward the pursuit of virtues instead.

We read this proclaimed most clearly in a single verse by the Prophet: “I was pushed and overturned so that I might fall”—in which the weakness of free will is signified—“but the Lord received me” (Ps. CXVII). Again, the Lord’s assistance is shown to be joined always to it: when he sees that we have stumbled, he sustains and strengthens us, as it were, by the extension of his hands, lest we collapse entirely through free will.

And again: “When I said, ‘My foot has slipped,’”—namely, through the slippery power of free will—“your mercy, O Lord, was helping me” (Ps. XCIII). Here again he joins God’s assistance to the instability of his will, because he confesses that the preservation of his foot from slipping was due not to his own industry but to the Lord’s mercy.

And again: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart”—sorrows that arose in me through free will—“your consolations rejoiced my soul” (ibid.). Coming into my heart through your inspiration and opening to me the contemplation of the future goods that you have prepared for those who labor for your name, they not only removed all the anxiety from my heart but also brought me the greatest joy. [Col. 0576A]

And again: “If the Lord had not helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell” (Ps. XCIII). He testifies that through the perversity of free will he would have dwelt in hell, unless he had been saved by the Lord’s help and protection.

For the steps of a human being are directed by the Lord, not by free will. And when the righteous person falls, he is not utterly cast down by free will alone. Why? Because “the Lord supports him with his hand” (Ps. XXXVI).

This is to say most plainly: No righteous person is sufficient in himself to obtain righteousness unless divine mercy continually places beneath him the support of its hand when he stumbles and falls, lest, having collapsed through the weakness of free will, he perish utterly when prostrate.

## CHAPTER XIII. That the Direction of Our Life Comes from God

[Col. 0576B]

The holy men have never testified that by their own industry they obtained the direction of the path on which they walked as they strove toward advancement in virtue and toward perfection. Rather, they prayed for it from the Lord, saying: “Direct me in your truth” (Ps. XXIV), and, “Direct my way in your sight” (Ps. V). And, “Make known to me the way in which I should walk” (Ps. CXLII).

Another, not only by faith but also through experience and, in a certain sense, by the very nature of things, declares that he has discovered this for himself: “I know, O Lord, that the way of a human being is not his own, nor is it in a person who walks to direct his steps” (Jer. X).

The Lord himself also says to Israel: “I will direct him,” he says, “like a flourishing fir tree; your fruit has been found in me” (Hos. XIV). [Col. 0576C]

## CHAPTER XIV. That Knowledge of the Law Is Granted through the Lord’s Instruction and Illumination

They also desire to obtain knowledge of the law itself daily, not through the labor of reading but through God’s instruction and illumination, saying to him: “Show me your ways, O Lord, and teach me your paths” (Ps. XXIV). And, “Open my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law” (Ps. XVIII). And, “Teach me to do your will, for you are my God” (Ps. CXLVI). And again: “You who teach human beings knowledge” (Ps. XCIII).

## CHAPTER XV. That the Understanding by Which We Can Recognize God’s Commandments, and the Affection of Good Will, Are Granted by the Lord

[Col. 0576D]

The blessed David himself also asks the Lord to grant him that understanding by which he may recognize God’s commandments—commandments that he certainly knew had been written down in the book of the law—saying: “I am your servant; give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments” (Ps. 118). He certainly possessed an understanding once granted to him by nature, and he also had readily available knowledge of God’s commandments, which were recorded in the law. Yet, in order to grasp this knowledge more fully, he entreats the Lord, knowing that what has been implanted through the nature of his creation cannot possibly suffice unless, through the Lord’s daily illumination, his understanding is enlightened by the same Lord to comprehend the law spiritually and to recognize his commandments more clearly. The chosen Vessel himself also proclaims this more explicitly when he says: “For it is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish, according to his good pleasure” (Phil. 2). And again: “Understand what I say, for the Lord will give you understanding” (2 Tim. 2). What could have been said more clearly than his declaration that both our good will and the completion of our work are brought to fulfillment in us by the Lord? And again: “For to you it has been granted for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him” (Phil. 1). Here too he declared that the beginning of our conversion and faith, as well as endurance of sufferings, is granted to us by the Lord.

Understanding this, David likewise prays that the same thing may be granted to him through the Lord’s mercy, saying: “Confirm, O God, what you have wrought in us” (Ps. 67). He shows that the beginnings of salvation, conferred by God’s gift and grace, are not sufficient for him unless they are brought to completion by that same mercy and by his daily assistance. For it is not free will but the Lord who releases the bound; it is not our strength but the Lord who raises up those who have been crushed; it is not diligence in reading but the Lord who gives sight to the blind—what is said in Greek as follows:

> Κύριος σοφοῖ τύφλους

that is, “The Lord makes the blind wise” (Ps. 145).

[Note: Thus the Greek interpreters understand the psalm verse concerning the illumination of the mind and the conversion of the will, so that “to illuminate” means “to make wise” (the Septuagint). The Hebrews understand it both of spiritual blindness and illumination and of bodily blindness and illumination (Jerome, on Isaiah 54).]

It is not our prudence but the Lord who protects the strangers (Ps. 145); it is not our strength but the Lord who raises up, or supports, all who fall (Ps. 144). We say this not so that we may abandon our zeal, labor, and diligence as though expending them uselessly and superfluously, but so that we may understand that without God’s help we can neither strive nor make our efforts effective in attaining so immense a reward as purity, unless the Lord’s assistance and mercy are bestowed upon us. “The horse is prepared for the day of battle, but from the Lord comes help” (Prov. 21), because “a man is not mighty by strength” (1 Sam. 2); and “a horse is a false hope for salvation” (Ps. 32), so that “whoever glories may glory in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1).

Therefore, with blessed David, we must always sing: “My strength and my praise”—not free will, but the Lord—“and he has become my salvation” (Ps. 117). The teacher of the nations also knew this. He declares that he was made fit for the ministry of the New Testament, not by his own merit or labor but by God’s mercy: “Not that we are sufficient to think anything of ourselves, as though from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Cor. 3).

[Note: Here is another singular and evident argument proving that Cassian wrote these Conferences not in Greek but in Latin, as Cuychius and Ciaconius also noted. For if he had written in Greek, he would simply have expressed the Greek word used by the Apostle, ἱκανότης, and would not have raised a question about comparing Latin words with one another by preferring one to the other. As for how “Our fitness is from God” may be said less elegantly in Latin but more expressively than “Our sufficiency is from God,” I leave it to grammarians to weigh and examine. To me the opposite seems more likely: “Our sufficiency is from God” appears less perhaps to be Latin, but nevertheless more expressive if the force of the words is considered, than “Our fitness is from God.” But because he had earlier quoted the Apostle’s words in this form—“Not that we are fit to think anything,” and so forth—he therefore says that it is more expressively stated, “Our fitness is from God,” so that the words correspond to one another. The Vulgate version now reads: “Not that we are sufficient,” to which the following words appropriately correspond.]

This may be expressed less elegantly in Latin but more clearly as: “Our fitness is from God.” Finally, it follows: “He who also made us fit ministers of the New Testament” (2 Cor. 10).

## CHAPTER XVI. That faith itself is granted by the Lord

The apostles felt so strongly that everything pertaining to salvation had been bestowed upon them by the Lord

[Note: In order to demonstrate more fully the necessity of divine assistance and the weakness of free will, Paphnutius teaches that Christian faith itself—which is the beginning of salvation—is not possessed by us from ourselves, that is, solely through the powers of free will, but is infused by God and is God’s gift. The Apostle expressly affirms this when he writes to the Ephesians, chapter 2: “By grace you have been saved through faith; and this is not from yourselves, for it is God’s gift.” Besides other Fathers, blessed Augustine vigorously defended and confirmed this teaching against the Pelagians in many places, especially through almost the whole book *On the Predestination of the Saints*. So too did blessed Prosper, in Book I of *On the Calling of the Nations*, chapter 23, where he brings together many testimonies of Scripture on this matter. To these was added the authority of the Council of Orange, canon 5 and those following, where it is defined against Pelagius that, just as the increase of faith, so also its beginning, and faith’s very inclination to believe, are God’s gift. Those are condemned who either say that the beginning of faith is naturally present in us or affirm that, through the power of nature, we can assent to the preaching of the Gospel without the illumination and inspiration of the Holy Spirit. The Fathers of that same council explain this position more fully in its final chapter, asserting that we ought to believe that, through the sin of the first man, free will was so inclined and weakened that thereafter no one could believe in God unless grace and divine mercy preceded him. They make this clear through various examples and testimonies from Scripture. Following this teaching, the Fathers of the Council of Trent, session 6, canon 3, condemn with an anathema anyone who says that, without the prevenient inspiration and assistance of the Holy Spirit, a person can believe as he ought. To believe as one ought means to believe as is expedient for salvation: to assent to the mysteries of faith proposed to one as revealed by God—that is, because of divine revelation, which is the formal reason for believing. Therefore, a heretic or unbeliever, because he does not assent to the mysteries of faith on account of divine revelation but on account of other motives or human reasons, does not believe with Christian, certain, and infallible faith, but with human faith. Accordingly, he does not believe as one ought and as is necessary for salvation. For this reason, to exclude such human faith, the councils added the phrase “as one ought.”]

that they even asked that faith itself be supplied to them by the Lord, saying: “Lord, increase our faith.” They did not presume that its fullness lay within free will, but believed that it would be conferred upon them as God’s gift.

Finally, the same author of human salvation teaches us how unstable and weak our faith itself is, and how entirely insufficient it is for itself unless strengthened by the Lord’s help. He says to Peter: “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has demanded you, to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for my Father that your faith may not fail.” Another man, perceiving this occurring in himself and seeing, as it were, his faith being driven amid the waves of unbelief toward the rocks of a disastrous shipwreck, asks the same Lord for help for his faith and says: “Lord, help my unbelief” (Mark 9).

Thus evangelical and apostolic men felt that everything good is brought to completion with the Lord’s help. They confessed that they could not preserve even their own faith unharmed by their own powers or by the freedom of their will, and therefore asked the Lord either to assist it in them or to grant it to them. If Peter’s faith needed the Lord’s help so that it would not fail, who could be so presumptuous and blind as to believe that he does not need the Lord’s daily assistance to preserve his own faith? Especially since the Lord himself plainly expressed this very point in the Gospel, saying: “Just as a branch cannot bear fruit of itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me.” And again: “For without me you can do nothing” (John 15).

How foolish and sacrilegious it is, then, to attribute anything concerning good actions to our own diligence rather than to God’s grace or assistance is plainly demonstrated by the Lord’s declaration that no one can produce spiritual fruits without his inspiration or cooperation: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1). Zechariah likewise says: “If there is anything good, it is his; and if anything excellent, it is from him” (Zech. 9).

And therefore blessed Paul consistently asks: “For what do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4).

## CHAPTER XVII. That the moderation and endurance of temptations are granted to us by the Lord

[Col. 0580A]

Blessed Paul likewise declares that the full measure of endurance by which we can withstand the temptations inflicted upon us rests not so much upon our strength as upon God’s mercy and moderation:

“Temptation has not seized you except what is human. But God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Cor. 10).

[Note: This is how it is now read in the Vulgate edition. But in certain older copies the reading is *apprehendat* (“may seize”), as in the Greek εἴληφεν. Cyprian, in Book III to Quirinus, has: “Temptation has not overtaken you except what is human.” Cassian argues that this reading is true and genuine in Book V of the *Institutes*, chapter 16, in these words: “Some, not understanding this testimony of the Apostle, have substituted the optative mood for the indicative, namely: ‘May temptation not seize you except what is human’; whereas it is clear that the Apostle speaks rather in the manner of one declaring than of one expressing a wish.” So he himself says. It is therefore surprising that here he disagrees with himself and follows another reading. As for the phrase that follows—“but with the temptation he will also provide a way out” (Greek ἔκβασιν)—blessed Jerome cites this passage in the same way in chapter 2 of Jonah. Cyprian, however, has: “He will provide with the temptation also the ability to escape.” Since ἐκβαίνειν means “to proceed beyond” and “to advance,” the Vulgate translator also correctly rendered it: “He will provide progress with the temptation.”]

The same Apostle teaches that God also adapts or strengthens our minds for every good work and works in us what is pleasing to him:

“Now may the God of peace, who brought out of darkness the great shepherd of the sheep, Jesus Christ, by the blood of the eternal covenant, make you fit in every good thing, accomplishing in you what is pleasing in his sight” (Heb. 13).

He also prays that this may come to pass for the Thessalonians, saying:

“May our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and gave us everlasting consolation and good hope in grace, encourage your hearts and strengthen you in every good work and word” (2 Thess. 2).

## CHAPTER XVIII. That perseverance in the fear of the Lord is conferred upon us by the Lord

[Col. 0580A]

Finally, the prophet Jeremiah plainly testifies, speaking in God’s person, that the fear of God itself—by which we may hold fast to him firmly—is infused into us by the Lord. He says:

“And I will give them one heart and one soul, so that they may fear me all their days; and it shall be well with them and with their children after them. And I will make an everlasting covenant with them, and I will not cease doing good to them; and I will put my fear in their hearts, so that they may not depart from me” (Jer. 32).

[Note: Isaiah numbers the fear of the Lord among the gifts of the Holy Spirit in chapter 11. This is understood not only of filial fear, by which one fears offending God and being separated from him through that offense, but also of servile fear, by which one is restrained from sin—not insofar as it is servile, that is, insofar as it contains an inclination to sin, but insofar as it is a kind of fear through which a person is restrained from the act of sin by the threatened punishment appointed for it. The Apostle teaches in Romans 8 that this fear is not evil in itself, but indeed is God’s gift. When he says, “You have not again received the spirit of slavery in fear,” he indicates quite clearly that this fear proceeds from the Holy Spirit and that it was at some time given by him to certain people, namely, to the Jewish people when they received the law itself. Again, in 2 Timothy 1, when he says, “For God has not given us the spirit of fear,” he means the spirit that had formerly been given to the Jews. The same is intended by Isaiah 26: “Because of your fear, Lord, we conceived and gave birth to the Spirit of salvation.” Finally, this fear is commended among God’s gifts to such an extent that, according to the interpretation of some, it is called “the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 111 and Prov. 2; Council of Trent, session 6, chapter 6 and canon 2). Thus blessed Augustine and Bede interpret it.]

Ezekiel likewise says:

“And I will give them a new heart, and I will place a new spirit within them; and I will remove the heart of stone from their flesh, and I will give them a heart of flesh, so that they may walk in my commandments and keep my judgments and perform them; and they shall be my people, and I shall be their God” (Ezek. 11 and 36).

## CHAPTER XIX. That the beginning and completion of good will come from the Lord

[Col. 0581A]

From these things we are most clearly taught both that the beginning of good will is granted to us when the Lord inspires it—whether he draws us toward the way of salvation by himself, through the exhortation of some person, or through necessity—and that the perfection of the virtues is likewise bestowed by him.

[Note: A similar and explicit statement by Abbot Chaeremon in Conference 13 agrees with this. Blessed Prosper strongly commends it as the basis and foundation of the whole argument against the Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians. It reads as follows (chapter 3): “Not only the beginning of good actions but also of good thoughts is from God, who inspires in us the beginnings of holy will and grants the strength and opportunity to carry out the things we rightly desire,” and so forth. Yet the same speaker appears to have departed from or deviated from this Catholic position throughout his subsequent argument and Conference on the protection of God and free will. Hence he was rightly rebuked by blessed Prosper and censured by Pope Gelasius and others, as will be seen elsewhere, God willing.]

But it is ours to carry out the exhortation and help of God either more sluggishly or more zealously, and accordingly to merit either rewards or punishments fully deserved, because we have either neglected or sought, through the devotion of our obedience, to conform to his dispensation and providence, which have been conferred upon us through his most benevolent graciousness.

[Note: Understand “ours” not as excluding grace but as presupposing it. The former is Pelagian, the latter Catholic, as is clear from what was said in Book XII of the *Institutes* (chapters 13 and following), and will become clearer throughout the thirteenth Conference, where this argument is treated carefully. Therefore, if we wish to interpret the matter in a Catholic way, what is ours must not be separated from what is God’s—as though we could assent and cooperate with him who calls us from ourselves, or by our own powers, without God’s special and supernatural assistance, and thereby merit eternal life. That was the error of the Pelagians or Semi-Pelagians. It is called ours because it depends upon our consent and cooperation with divine grace.]

This is clearly and openly described in Deuteronomy:

“When the Lord your God brings you into the land that you are entering to possess, and he destroys before you many nations—the Hittite, the Girgashite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite—seven nations more numerous and stronger than you—and when he delivers them to you, you shall strike them down to destruction; you shall not make a covenant with them, nor shall you enter into marriages with them” (Deut. 7).

Thus Scripture declares that their being brought into the promised land, that many nations being destroyed before them, and nations more numerous and stronger than the people of Israel being delivered into their hands are works of God’s grace. But whether Israel strikes them down to destruction or preserves and spares them, whether it makes a covenant with them, and whether it avoids or enters into marriages with them, Scripture testifies to be their responsibility.

[Note: These two things are so joined together in the work of our justification and salvation that we must assign their respective parts to each, though the greater place belongs to divine grace. Blessed Prosper explains this excellently in these words (*On the Calling of the Nations*, Book II, chapter 26): “Indeed, God’s grace takes precedence in all acts of justification: persuading through exhortations, warning through examples, frightening through dangers, stimulating through miracles, giving understanding, inspiring counsel, enlightening their hearts, and filling them with the affections of faith. But human will is also added and joined to it. It has been aroused by these aforementioned aids so that it may cooperate within itself with the divine work and begin to bring to merit what it conceived through heavenly seed as an inclination toward action. If it fails, it has its mutability to blame; if it progresses, it has the assistance of grace. This assistance is supplied to all in countless ways, hidden or manifest. What many reject is attributable to their wickedness; what many accept belongs both to divine grace and to human will.”]

By this testimony it is plainly distinguished what we ought to ascribe to free will and what to the Lord’s dispensation or daily assistance: it belongs to divine grace to provide us with opportunities for salvation, favorable outcomes, and victory; but it is ours to carry out the benefits granted by God either more zealously or more sluggishly.

We see this principle expressed with sufficient clarity also in the healing of those blind men. That Jesus passed before them belongs to the grace of divine providence and graciousness. That they cried out and said, “Have mercy on us, Lord, Son of David” (Matt. 20),

[Note: This occurred only with the cooperation of God’s grace, of which faith itself is also a gift, as was shown above. The fact that the blind men cried out, “Have mercy on us, Son of David,” so that they might be enlightened by Christ, or that only one of the ten lepers who had been cleansed returned to give glory to God, did not occur without God’s special assistance, movement, and inspiration. A fuller treatment of this matter should be referred to the thirteenth Conference.]

belongs to the work of their faith and belief. That they receive sight in their eyes is the gift of divine mercy. But that, even after receiving any gift, both God’s grace and the power of free will continue is also shown by the example of the ten lepers who were healed together (Luke 17). When one of them, through the good use of his will, returned thanksgiving, the Lord, seeking the nine and praising the one, showed that he continually retains the concern of his assistance even for those who forget his benefits. For this too is a gift of his visitation: that he either receives and approves the grateful person or seeks out and rebukes the ungrateful.

## CHAPTER XX. That nothing in this world occurs without God

Nevertheless, we must believe with unshakable faith that absolutely nothing in this world occurs without God. We must confess that everything is done either by his will or by his permission, so that what is good is believed to be accomplished by God’s will and assistance, while what is contrary to the good occurs by his permission. For, on account of our wickedness and hardness of heart, divine protection abandons us and permits the devil or disgraceful bodily passions to dominate us.

We are taught this most clearly by the words of the Apostle, who says: “For this reason God delivered them over to dishonorable passions” (Rom. 1). And again: “Because they did not approve of having God in their knowledge” [Lipsius, in the margin: “acknowledge God”], “God delivered them over to a reprobate mind, to do things that are not fitting” (ibid.).

The Lord himself also says through the Prophet:

“My people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not attend to me. Therefore,” he says, “I let them go according to the inventions of their heart; they shall walk in their own inventions” (Ps. 80).

## CHAPTER XXI. Germanus’s objection concerning the power of free will

Germanus: This testimony most clearly demonstrates free will, where it says: “If my people had listened to me,” and, “My people did not hear my voice.” For when he says “if they had listened,” he shows that it was within their power either to consent or not to consent. How, then, can our salvation not be placed in our own hands, since he himself has granted us the ability either to hear or not to hear?

## CHAPTER XXII. Paphnutius’s reply: that our free will always needs the Lord’s assistance

[Col. 0583B]

Paphnutius: You have indeed carefully considered the words, “If they had listened to me,” but you have paid no attention to who it is that speaks to those who listen or do not listen. Nor have you considered the words that follow, which certainly are not without purpose: “I would have humbled their enemies at once and laid my hand upon those who afflicted them.”

Therefore, let no one twist what we have brought forward to prove that nothing is done without the Lord and, by a perverse interpretation, use it to defend free will in such a way as to attempt to remove from human beings God’s grace and daily providence. This would be done by appealing to the words, “My people did not hear my voice,” and again, “If my people had listened to me, if Israel had walked in my ways,” and so forth. Rather, let him consider that, just as the people’s free will is demonstrated by their disobedience, so God’s daily providence toward them is shown by his crying out, as it were, and warning them.

For when he says, “If my people had listened to me,” he clearly shows that he had previously spoken to them. This is something the Lord is accustomed to do not only through the law written in letters but also through daily warnings, according to what is said through Isaiah: “All day long I have stretched out my hands to a people who do not believe in me but contradict me” (Isa. 65).

Thus both points can be established from the testimony that says: “If my people had listened to me, if Israel had walked in my ways, I would have humbled their enemies at once and laid my hand upon those who afflicted them.” For just as free will is demonstrated by the people’s disobedience, so God’s dispensation and assistance are declared at the beginning and end of the verse itself, when he testifies both that he had spoken first and that he would afterward humble their enemies if he had been heard by them.

By the things we have brought forward, we do not wish to remove human free will, but to prove that it requires God’s assistance and grace at every day and every moment.

Having been instructed by these discussions, Abbot Paphnutius sent us from his cell shortly before midnight, not so much cheerful as pierced in heart. Through his Conference he bestowed this chief benefit upon us: although we had believed that, after completing the first renunciation—which we were striving to fulfill with every effort of virtue—we had reached the summits of perfection, we began to recognize that we had not yet even begun to dream of the heights of monks. For, although we had been instructed by the Fathers in the second renunciation, which takes place in coenobia, we realized that we had not previously even heard of the third renunciation, in which all perfection is contained and which surpasses the other two in many ways.

# FOURTH CONFERENCE, Which is that of Abbot Daniel. ON THE DESIRE OF THE FLESH AND THE SPIRIT

[Col. 0583]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0583C]

Among the other men of Christian philosophy, we also saw Abbot Daniel, equal in every kind of virtue to those who lived in the desert of Scete, but more especially adorned with the grace of humility. On account of the merit of his purity and gentleness,

[Note: I do not think this was Daniel the Stylite, that is, the “Column-Dweller,” of whom Sozomen speaks in Book III, chapter 13, and from him Nicephorus in Book XV, chapter 22, and Book XVI, chapter 6, as do Cedrenus and others in the reign of the emperor Leo the Great, and Damascenus in the third Oration on Images (Baronius, volume VI of the *Annals*, year 460, and in the *Martyrology*, 11 December). For that Daniel was a disciple not of Paphnutius but likewise of Simeon the Stylite; nor is he said to have lived in the desert of Scete, or Scythia, but near Antioch in Syria, on a column for approximately twenty-nine years. Another Daniel is also mentioned, a disciple of Abbot Arsenius, whose excellent sayings and deeds are recorded in the *Lives of the Fathers*. There was also a third Daniel, an Egyptian abbot and priest, of whom Sophronius speaks in chapter 114 of the *Spiritual Meadow*, and Peter of Equilinum in Book VI, chapter 123 of his *Catalogue*. Finally there is the fourth, the one discussed here: a disciple of Abbot Paphnutius and himself a priest, whom Paphnutius had chosen as his successor. But, since God disposed otherwise, Daniel departed this life first, as is related here.]

the blessed Paphnutius, the priest of that same solitude, advanced him—although he was much younger in age—to the office of deacon.

[Col. 0584C]

For blessed Paphnutius rejoiced so greatly in his virtues that, knowing him to be his equal in the merits and grace of his life, he hastened to make him his equal also in priestly rank. Since he could not bear to see him remain longer in an inferior ministry,

[Note: A similar example is given by Abbot John, as the author relates in Book IV of the *Institutes*, chapter 29. Because of the singular and astonishing test of obedience that he had imposed upon the monk Mucius, John, when near death, placed him over all the brothers as his successor and left him as abbot of the monastery. On this occasion one might raise the question whether an abbot or superior may choose and appoint his own successor. But this question seems to require greater investigation and more difficult treatment than can conveniently be given here in accordance with the purpose of this work. I therefore leave it to be discussed elsewhere (see, among other additions, those at the end of the work).]

and wished to provide himself with the worthiest possible successor, he advanced him, while still alive, to the honor of the priesthood. Yet Daniel did not abandon his former habit of humility. While Paphnutius was present, he never claimed anything for himself from the addition of the higher rank, but, whenever Abbot Paphnutius was offering the spiritual sacrifices, he remained, as if still a deacon, in the ministry of his former office.

[Note: Observe that “spiritual sacrifices,” that is, the mystical offering of the Eucharist or the sacrifice of the Mass, were frequently celebrated even among those anchorites. It is called a spiritual sacrifice both because Christ himself, in a spiritual and ineffable manner, is offered and received as priest and victim, and because he makes those who are carnal spiritual.]

Yet, although blessed Paphnutius was such a great man that he possessed among his many gifts even the grace of foreknowledge, this hope and choice of a successor was frustrated. For not long afterward he sent on to God the man whom he had prepared as his successor.

## CHAPTER II. He asks from what source the sudden change of mind arises—from ineffable joy to the deepest dejection of spirit

This blessed Daniel, then, when we asked why at times, while sitting in our cell, we were filled with such great cheerfulness of heart, with a kind of ineffable joy and an abundance of the most secret feelings, so that I will not say that speech could follow it, but that not even thought itself could keep pace; why pure and ready prayer, and a mind full of spiritual fruits, felt that its effective and easy prayers reached God even during sleep; and, again, why, when there were no apparent causes, we were suddenly filled with such great anxiety and oppressed by an irrational kind of sorrow, so that we felt not only ourselves withering under such sensations, but even the cell growing dreadful, reading becoming distasteful, and prayer itself being uttered unsteadily, waveringly, and, as it were, drunkenly; so that, although we groaned and struggled, our mind could not be restored to its former direction, and the more intently it was brought back to the contemplation of God, the more violently it was carried away by a slippery excess into unstable wanderings, becoming so barren of every spiritual fruit that it could be awakened from that kind of deadly sleep neither by desire for the heavenly kingdom nor by fear of the threatened gehenna—he replied as follows:

## CHAPTER III. Reply to the question proposed

[Col. 0586B]

[Note: [Col. 0585C] The cause of spiritual desolation is threefold; here he calls it sterility or dryness of the mind, while elsewhere he calls it lukewarmness or tepidity.] Our predecessors handed down to us a threefold explanation concerning this sterility of mind of which you speak. For it proceeds either from our negligence, from the assault of the devil, or from the dispensation and testing of the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0585D] St. Gregory noted this cause in *Moralia* X, chapter 7. “Often,” he says, “we entertain in our minds certain impure or unlawful things whenever we are free from prayer. But when the mind has raised itself to the practice of prayer, it suffers the images of those things to be beaten back—things under which it had previously lain willingly in idleness; and, as though the soul were now unable to lift its face toward God, it is ashamed because it is polluted within by the stains of impure thought. Often we willingly occupy ourselves with worldly cares, and afterward, when we devote ourselves to prayer, the mind by no means rises to heavenly things, because the weight of earthly anxiety has plunged it into the depths; and the face is not shown clean in prayer, because it is stained with the mud of lowly thought.” Thus Gregory. See John Climacus, step 28, which concerns Prayer.]

Negligence is involved when, through our own fault, having first grown lukewarm, we conduct ourselves incautiously and carelessly; and when, through sluggishness and indolence, we feed upon harmful thoughts, we make the soil of our heart produce thorns and thistles. When these have begun to sprout in it, we consequently become sterile and are deprived of every spiritual fruit and contemplation.

[Note: [Col. 0586C] You have a striking example of this in the *Lives of the Fathers* (Book II, chapter 29), related there in connection with Macarius, in these words. One night a demon, in the guise of a monk, knocked at his door and said: “Rise, Abba Macarius, and let us go to the assembly, where the brothers gather for the vigils.” But he, filled with God’s grace, understood the devil’s deception and said: “O liar and enemy of truth, what fellowship or association have you with the assembly and congregation of the saints?” The demon replied: “Are you unaware, Macarius, that no assembly and no gathering of monks takes place without us? Come, then, and you will see our works there.” Saint Macarius said: “The Lord rebuke you, unclean demon.” Then, turning to prayer, he asked the Lord to show him whether what the demon boasted was true. He therefore went to the assembly, where the brothers were celebrating the vigil, and again in prayer begged the Lord to show him the truth of this matter. And behold, he saw throughout the church certain little black Ethiopian boys running here and there, as though being carried about in flight. These Ethiopian boys ran about mocking each of the brothers who were engaged in prayer and psalmody. If they pressed two fingers upon someone’s eyes, he immediately fell asleep; but if they thrust a finger into someone’s mouth, they made him yawn. Again, after the psalm, when the brothers had prostrated themselves for prayer, they went around to each one. Before one lying in prayer they appeared as women; before another, as builders, or as people carrying something, or engaged in various other activities. Whatever the demons had fashioned as if in play, the praying men turned over in the thoughts of their hearts. Yet when they began to do any of these things before certain brothers, they were violently repelled and thrown down, so that they dared neither stand before them nor pass by them. Others they rode upon their necks and [Col. 0587B] backs. When Saint Macarius saw this, he groaned bitterly and, shedding tears, said to the Lord: “Look, O Lord; do not be silent, nor be appeased, O God, but arise, and let your enemies be scattered and flee from your face,” and so forth. After the prayer, in order to investigate the truth, he summoned the brothers one by one privately and asked them whether, during prayer, they had entertained thoughts of building, of undertaking a journey, or of various other things that he had seen being imagined for each of them by the demons. Each of them confessed that the thoughts in his heart had indeed been as he alleged. Then it was understood that all those vain and [Col. 0587C] superfluous thoughts which each person conceived in his heart during the psalms or prayers were produced by the demons’ deception and instigation; but from those who guard their hearts with all vigilance the grim Ethiopians are driven away. For a mind joined to God and especially intent upon him during the time of prayer admits nothing alien and nothing superfluous. Thus far the account. Similar examples occur in Athanasius’s *Life of Saint Antony*, in Saint Jerome’s *Life of Hilarion*, and also elsewhere in Saint Gregory, *Dialogues* II, chapter 4, and in Caesarius of Cistercian, *On Miracles* V, chapter 5.]

The assault of the devil occurs when, even while we are devoted to good pursuits, the adversary penetrates our mind by cunning subtlety, and either draws us away unknowingly from our best intentions or does so against our will.

## CHAPTER IV. That the cause arising from God’s dispensation and testing is twofold

[Note: [Col. 0587C] That is, of divine providence, which was assigned above as the third cause of spiritual desolation.]

The dispensation or testing of the Lord has two causes.

[Note: [Col. 0587C] Saint Gregory explains this cause of spiritual desolation, arising from divine arrangement and testing, elegantly and at length. Among other things he writes the following (*Moralia* II, chapter 27): “It happens that this grace sometimes withdraws itself beneficially, and shows the presumptuous mind how weak it is in itself. For then we truly learn from where our good qualities come, when we feel that we have, as it were, lost them, because they cannot be preserved by us. Accordingly, for the instruction of humility, it often happens that, at the moment when temptation breaks in, such folly strikes our wisdom that the troubled mind does not know how to confront impending evils or how to prepare itself against temptation. Yet by this very folly the heart is prudently instructed, because in the place where it is foolish for a moment, it afterward becomes wiser with greater truth and humility; and wisdom is possessed more securely precisely where it seems to be lost. Sometimes, while the mind raises itself in elation by understanding sublime things, it grows sluggish through heavy dullness in lowly and contemptible matters, so that the one who swiftly penetrated the heights suddenly finds even the depths closed to him. Yet this very dullness, while it withdraws understanding from us, preserves it; for while it humbles the heart for a moment, it strengthens it more truly to understand sublime things. Sometimes, while we rejoice that we do everything with the gravity of deliberation, when an emerging circumstance presses upon us, we are swept away by sudden haste; and we who believed that we had always lived in an orderly manner are suddenly ravaged by profound confusion. Nevertheless, through this very confusion we learn not to attribute our plans to our own strength; and we are restrained toward gravity all the more maturely the more we return to it as though we had lost it. Sometimes, while we rejoice that we know great things, we grow numb through the blindness of sudden ignorance; but in proportion as ignorance momentarily closes the eyes of the mind, they afterward open more truly to knowledge, so that, taught by the scourge of his blindness, a person learns from whom he has knowledge.” Such are Saint Gregory’s words, with others of the same kind.]

The first is that, having been abandoned by him for a little while, we may humbly contemplate the weakness of our mind and not become proud in any way over the former purity of heart that was granted to us by his visitation; and, recognizing that we have been abandoned by him, may understand that by our groans and efforts we cannot recover that former state of joy and purity; [Col. 0587B] and may learn that the former cheerfulness of our heart was bestowed upon us not by our own exertion but by his gracious favor, while the present state must again be sought from his grace and illumination.

[Note: [Col. 0588C] Saint Bernard confirms this from his own experience and that of others (*Sermon 9 on the Song of Songs*): “Those who make a practice of prayer,” he says, “have often experienced what I am saying. Often we approach the altar with a lukewarm and dry heart and apply ourselves to prayer; but as we persist, grace is suddenly poured in, the breast grows rich, and an inundation of devotion fills the inward parts; and if there is anyone to press upon them, they will not delay to pour forth abundantly the milk of the sweetness they have conceived.” Elsewhere—namely, in *Sermon 22 on the Song of Songs*—he gives the following counsel to those placed in such anxiety: “If you feel yourself affected by torpor, listlessness, or weariness, do not therefore despair or cease from spiritual practice; but seek the hand of him who helps, begging him to draw you along after the example of the bride, until, when grace again arouses you, you run with greater readiness and eagerness and say: ‘I have run the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart.’ While grace is present, therefore, take delight in it, but do not suppose that you possess God’s gift by hereditary right, as though you were so secure of it that you could never lose it; otherwise, when he perhaps suddenly withdraws his hand and removes the gift, you may collapse inwardly and become sadder than you ought. Therefore, do not be secure on the day of your strength; cry out to God with the Prophet: ‘When my strength fails, do not forsake me’ (Psalm 70).”]

The second cause is that our perseverance, the steadfastness of our mind, and our desire may be proved, and it may be revealed with what intention of heart and persistence in prayer we seek the visitation of the Holy Spirit, who has abandoned us. At the same time, recognizing with what labor this spiritual joy and gladness of purity, once lost, must be sought, we may strive more carefully to guard and hold fast what we have found. For whatever is believed capable of being easily restored is, in a certain sense, usually guarded less carefully.

## CHAPTER V. That our exertion and diligence are powerless without God’s help

By these things it is clearly proved that God’s grace and mercy are always at work in us, producing what is good. When that grace withdraws, the effort of the one who labors is powerless; and however much the mind strives, without his help it cannot recover its former state. Thus what is written is continually fulfilled in us: “It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Romans [Col. 0589A] IX).

Yet this grace sometimes does not refuse to visit the negligent and relaxed with that holy inspiration of which you speak, and with an abundance of spiritual thoughts. It inspires the unworthy, awakens those who sleep, illuminates those besieged by the blindness of ignorance, and mercifully reproves and chastises us, pouring itself into our hearts so that, stirred even in this way by its compunction, we may be prompted to rise from the sleep of inertia.

Finally, [Note: [Col. 0589C] The same most gracious Bernard explains this very sweetly in his ninth and tenth sermons on the Song of Songs, where he speaks of the spiritual kiss, the breasts of the bridegroom and bride, the fragrance of spiritual ointments, and similar matters.] we are often suddenly filled, during these very visitations, with fragrances surpassing every sweetness of human composition, so that the mind, loosened by this delight, is carried into a kind of spiritual ecstasy and forgets that it dwells in the flesh.

## CHAPTER VI. That it is useful for us sometimes to be abandoned by the Lord

[Col. 0589B]

Blessed David understood that this withdrawal, or, so to speak, abandonment by God, was so useful that he did not choose to pray never to be abandoned by God in any respect. For he knew that such a request would be unfitting either for himself or for human nature as it advances toward any degree of perfection. Rather, he prayed that it might be moderated, saying:

[Note: [Col. 0589C] That is, completely and altogether. In Greek, ἕως σφόδρα, that is, “even exceedingly,” as Ciaconius reads below. Saint Ambrose aptly explains here the difference between being abandoned by God and being abandoned by him completely or altogether, using David as his example: “Since no one can be perfect without God’s favor, nor safe, he ought to pray that God not abandon him completely. Above, David prayed not to be abandoned, saying: ‘Do not abandon me, O Lord my God’; here he says: ‘Do not abandon me altogether,’ that is, ‘exceedingly.’ Above, perhaps, because he was still imperfect and placed amid great disturbances, he feared being abandoned; here, being already stronger, he does not fear being abandoned so that he may be tested, but asks not to be abandoned completely. God often abandons those whom he wishes to have tested; but he abandons completely those whom he forsakes. He completely abandoned Judas; but he did not abandon holy Job, into whose estate he granted the adversary tyrannical power and over whose body he gave the devil authority, but not over his soul. For if he had given authority over his soul, he would have abandoned him completely,” and so forth.]

“Do not abandon me altogether” (Psalm 118). As though he were saying in other words: I know that you customarily abandon your saints beneficially, in order to test them. For they cannot otherwise be tested by the adversary unless they have been abandoned by you for a little while. Therefore I do not ask never to be abandoned by you, because it is not good for me to be without either the awareness of my weakness, by which I may say, “It is good for me that you have humbled me” (Psalm 118), or the exercise of battle—which I certainly could not have if divine protection were always and uninterruptedly joined to me.

For the devil would not dare to test one supported by your defense, alleging and reproaching either me or you with the calumnious charge that he commonly brings against your athletes:

[Note: [Col. 0589D] Hence the devil—meaning “accuser” or “slanderer”—is called this in Revelation 12: “The accuser of our brothers has been cast down, who accused them before the sight of our God day and night.” “By day he accuses,” says Blessed Gregory (*Moralia* I, chapter 9), “when he suggests that we use prosperity badly; by night he accuses when he demonstrates that in adversity we lack patience.”]

“Does Job worship God for nothing? Have you not fenced him in, and his house and all his possessions round about?” (Job I).

Rather, I ask you not to abandon me completely, which in Greek is said—

[Note: [Col. 0589D] Ciaconius and our manuscripts read ἕως σφόδρα. The Greek text of that verse literally means “even exceedingly,” for which the Latin translator rendered “altogether.” The former Latin reading, however, corresponds better to the Latin exposition that follows: “to excess.” These words occur alone in certain manuscripts—the Basel manuscripts—and in Dionysius, with the Greek omitted. Moreover, from this passage also everyone can see that these Collations were written in Latin, not Greek.]

μέχρι πρὸς ἀγαντεῖον, that is, “to excess.” For just as it is useful for me if you abandon me somewhat, so that the constancy of my desire may be proved, so it is harmful if, on account of my merits and offenses, you allow me to be abandoned too greatly. No human virtue can endure by its own steadfastness if it is left for too long in temptation without your help, and it will immediately succumb either to the power or to the conspiracy of the adversary, unless you yourself, who know human strength and govern its struggles, do not permit us to be tested beyond what we can bear, but with the temptation also provide a way out, so that we may be able to endure it (1 Corinthians X).

We read that something similar was mystically signified in the Book of Judges, chapter III, concerning the extermination of the spiritual nations that oppose Israel:

[Note: [Col. 0590C] He calls those nations spiritual because, under the names of those nations expressed in Scripture, spiritual vices by which the minds of the faithful are attacked are mystically signified. Concerning them, see Saint Jerome and the other interpreters of the Hebrew words.]

“These are the nations that the Lord left, in order that he might train Israel through them and that they might learn the practice of fighting against their enemies.”

And again, shortly afterward:

[Note: [Col. 0590C] Not so that God, who knows all things, including future things, might come to know them, but so that they themselves might know—and that by their own conscience they might either glory or be convicted—whether they obeyed God’s commandments, and so forth, says Saint Augustine (*Question 17 on Judges*). For God, who knows all things, does not need any experiment or testing in order to foresee or know something; but he is said metaphorically, and with regard to the effect, to tempt, test, or try: first, because he acts as though he were tempting or investigating something unknown; second, because he brings into the knowledge of others what he himself knows. Thus he said to Abraham, ‘Now I know that you fear the Lord’ (Genesis XII), that is, ‘I have caused you to be known as one who fears.’ As for this passage, something similar is also read in secular histories concerning Scipio Nasica, who did not wish Carthage, the rival of the Roman Empire, to be destroyed, lest the Roman people, freed from such an enemy, should grow torpid through leisure and indolence. Concerning this Saint Augustine, arguing against the pagan Romans in Book I of *The City of God*, chapter 30, writes: ‘You do not desire peace and abundance in every kind of resource so that you may use these goods honorably—that is, moderately, soberly, temperately, and piously—but so that an endless variety of pleasures may be sought through mad extravagance, and so that, amid favorable circumstances, those evils may arise in your morals which are worse than raging enemies. But that Scipio, your chief pontiff, that man whom the judgment of the entire senate considered excellent, fearing this calamity for you, did not wish Carthage, then the rival of Roman power, to be destroyed; and when the decision was made that it should be destroyed, he opposed Cato, fearing that security would become an enemy to weak minds and, seeing that terror was necessary for citizens who were like wards, as a suitable guardian. Nor did his judgment deceive him: the truth of what he said was proved in reality,’ and so forth.”]

“God dismissed them, in order to test Israel through them, whether they would obey the commandments of the Lord, which he had commanded their fathers through the hand of Moses, or not.”

God did not preserve that battle because he begrudged Israel its peace, nor because he was ill disposed toward it, but because he knew it to be most useful. While Israel was continually oppressed by the attacks of those nations, it would never feel that it did not need the Lord’s help; and therefore, always persisting in meditation upon and invocation of him, it would neither be relaxed by inertia nor lose the practice of warfare and the exercises of virtue. For often those whom adversity could not overcome are cast down by security and prosperity.

## CHAPTER VII. On the usefulness of the battle that the Apostle places in the struggle between flesh and spirit

[Note: [Col. 0591B] See the sixth annotation of D. Cuychius at the end of the work.]

We read in the Apostle that this battle has also been beneficially implanted in our members (Galatians V).

[Note: [Col. 0591B] The Apostle expresses the same thing in other words in Romans VII: “I delight in the law of God according to the inner man; but I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members.” The same point is made by Matthew XXVI: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” The pagans also seem to have experienced this in their own way. Hence Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VII:

“My mind advises one thing; I see and approve the better;

I follow the worse.” [Col. 0591C] What is meant by flesh and spirit, or by the law of the members and the law of the mind, is explained clearly and fully below (chapters 10 and 11). The entire discussion of this passage aims at making us understand that this inward war—the desire of the flesh against the spirit and of the spirit against the flesh—which provided this Collation not only with its principal subject but also with its title, is useful and salutary for us, and has therefore been left and, in a certain sense, implanted within us by divine dispensation or providence. This must nevertheless be understood of the flesh not according to its original condition, in which Adam and Eve were created, but of flesh corrupted by sin, although cleansed through baptism. For the holy Council of Trent (*Session 5, decree on Original Sin*) defined, according to the teaching of the holy Fathers, that concupiscence, or the tinder of sin, as it is called, remains in the baptized. This concupiscence, Augustine says (*On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, final chapter), “having been left for the struggle, cannot harm those who do not consent but fight against it manfully through the grace of Christ Jesus; indeed, whoever has fought lawfully will be crowned.” The same council declares that, when the Apostle sometimes calls this concupiscence “sin” (Romans VI and VIII), the Catholic Church never understood him to mean that it is truly and properly sin in the reborn, but that it is called sin because it arises from sin and inclines toward sin. Thus far the council. From these statements we understand that the opposition of flesh and spirit arises from the inclination left after sin toward those things that are advantageous and congenial to each part. For the flesh desires what belongs to it [Col. 0592A] and is vehemently inflamed toward those things; the spirit, on the contrary, seeks spiritual things and what accords with truth and moral goodness. Yet one may ask how the act of desiring can be attributed to the flesh when it properly belongs to the soul. Saint Thomas answers (*Commentary on this passage* and I–II, question 70, article 41), following Saint Augustine, that the flesh is said to desire insofar as the soul, affected according to the flesh, desires; just as the eye is said to see, although rather the soul, or the person, sees through the eyes. Thus the soul desires through the flesh when it seeks things that are pleasurable according to the flesh. The soul desires in itself, however, when it delights in things belonging to the spirit, such as works of virtue, contemplation of divine things, and meditation upon wisdom, according to Wisdom VI: “The desire for wisdom leads to the everlasting kingdom.” But you may say: If the flesh desires through the spirit, how does it desire against the spirit? He answers that the desire of the flesh obstructs the desire of the spirit. For when the soul is occupied with and affected by sensible and lower things, which belong to the flesh, it is drawn away from higher things, which belong to the spirit. (See the notes below on chapter 13.)]

“For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. These two are opposed to each other, so that you do not do whatever you wish.”

Here you have the battle—

[Note: [Col. 0592B] How Abbot Daniel understands this battle, or the desire of the flesh against the spirit, as implanted and in a certain sense inwardly rooted in our members and body through divine providence, is learnedly explained by D. Cuychius in his critique, which the reader should not fail to consult at my recommendation. The passage from Saint Augustine that he cites should also be consulted, *Against Julian* V, especially chapter 5, where Augustine reports, among other things, that there were certain heretics called Paterniani and Venustiani, similar to the Manichaeans, who said that the devil had made the human body from the loins to the feet, while God had placed the upper parts above it, as upon a base. They claimed that nothing was required of human effort except that the soul—which they said dwelt in the body and stomach—be kept clean; and if the pubic region were smeared with every stain of wrongdoing, that did not belong to their concern. Thus they shamefully assigned that region to serve lust alone, attaching to it the title of a power proper to itself. These were the defenders of impurity; and that Julian shamelessly charged Augustine with favoring and defending them in his writings. Refuting this slander, Augustine says: “According to the Catholic faith, I attribute the whole person—namely, the whole soul and the whole body—to God, the supreme and true Creator; but I say that the devil created neither human nature nor any part of it, but corrupted nature. Against that diabolical wound, which must be healed by God’s aid until we are completely freed from it, we must fight. Nor can the soul, by which the body lives, be kept clean—to the extent that a person is clean in this life—if it consents to the desires of the flesh for committing crimes and every kind of impurity.” These words of Augustine I have wished to insert here to expand Cuychius’s elucidation.]

This battle is, in a certain sense, inwardly rooted in our body through the Lord’s dispensation. For whatever is generally present in everyone without exception—what else can it be judged to be except something attributed to human substance itself after the fall of the first man, as though naturally, and found congenitally and concretely in all? How can we not believe that it was implanted by the Lord’s will—not to harm us, but to provide for us?

He describes the cause of this battle, that is, of flesh and spirit, as follows:

[Note: [Col. 0592D] The conjunction “so that” often signifies not a cause but an outcome and consequence, as Chrysostom (Romans X) and Damascene observed in many passages of Scripture; hence they do not always call it causal, but consequential. Examples include Matthew II: “So that what was said might be fulfilled,” and John XII: “He blinded their eyes, so that they should not see,” and XIII: “So that Scripture might be fulfilled”; Romans I: “He handed them over to dishonorable passions, so that they might do what is not fitting.” This appears to be the proper and genuine sense of the Apostle’s words cited here. For the flesh does not desire against the spirit for this purpose—that is, with the end or intention—that we may not do whatever we wish; rather, from the opposition of flesh and spirit it follows that we do not do whatever good we might wish to do, as the Apostle says in Romans VII: “For I do not do the good that I wish, but I do the evil that I do not wish.” But the abbot here takes this particle in such a way that it denotes a final cause. He wishes the cause of this war and battle between flesh and spirit to be that we cannot do the good things we wish to do, namely, for our exercise and struggle, just as Scipio wished Carthage to remain standing in order to keep the Romans faithful to their duty. Nor does this abolish free will. For, says Saint Thomas, freedom of choice concerns those things subject to choice; but not everything within us is simply subject to our choice, though it may be so in a qualified sense. We can avoid this or that movement of desire or anger; but we cannot avoid every movement of anger or desire in general because of the corruption of the tinder—that is, the inclination toward evil left by sin. This matter will be treated more fully in Collations 13 and 21 (in the Commentary). Saint Thomas also wisely and acutely distinguishes, in this matter concerning desires, four kinds of people, none of whom does whatever he wishes, though for different reasons. The intemperate, he says, who deliberately follow carnal passions, according to Proverbs II, ‘They rejoice when they have done evil,’ do what they wish insofar as they follow their passions; but insofar as their reason protests against them and disapproves of them, they do what they do not wish. The incontinent, who intend to abstain but are overcome by passions, do what they do not wish insofar as they follow those passions against their intention (Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* VII, chapter 4); thus the intemperate do more of what they wish. The continent, who would wish not to desire at all, do what they wish when they do not desire; but since they cannot refrain from desiring altogether, they do what they do not wish. The temperate do what they wish insofar as, in a subdued flesh, they do not desire; but because the flesh cannot be subdued completely without offering some resistance to the spirit—just as wickedness cannot grow so great that reason does not protest—when they sometimes desire, they do what they do not wish, though they do more of what they wish. Thus Saint Thomas.]

“So that,” he says, “you do not do whatever you wish.”

Therefore, what God arranged could not be fulfilled by us—namely, that we do not do whatever we wish—if fulfilled, what else can it be believed to be except harmful? Yet this battle, implanted in us by God’s dispensation and urging and compelling us toward a better condition, is in a certain way useful; once it is removed, a contrary and undoubtedly harmful peace will follow.

## CHAPTER VIII. The question: what is the meaning of the third will added in the Apostle’s passage after the opposing desires of flesh and spirit?

Germanus: Although a certain understanding seems to shine before us in this matter, we still cannot yet see the Apostle’s meaning with complete clarity. We therefore wish this to be explained to us more openly. Three things seem to be indicated here: first, the battle of the flesh against the spirit; second, the desire of the spirit against the flesh; third, our will, which is placed, as it were, between the two, concerning which it is said: “So that you do not do whatever you wish.” Although, as I said, we can gather certain suspicions of the meaning from what has been set forth, nevertheless, since the occasion of this Collation has presented itself, we wish something clearer to be discussed for us.

## CHAPTER IX. Daniel’s answer concerning the understanding displayed by the questioner

Daniel: To discern the divisions and lines of a question [Col. 0594A]

[Note: [Col. 0594C] For one who correctly and clearly distinguishes the parts of a question or inquiry shows that he has grasped, at least in part, what he is seeking, according to Aristotle’s saying: “One who knows nothing doubts nothing and distinguishes nothing.”]

is a part of understanding, and a very large part of intelligence is knowing what you do not know. Therefore it is said in Proverbs XVII:

[Note: [Col. 0594D] Here Ciaconius supplied the words from the Septuagint: “Wisdom will be reckoned to the fool who asks for wisdom.” He confirms this from the following words and from Justin, who cites it in this form in his letter to Zenas and Serenus. Nothing of the kind is found in the Vulgate edition; instead it has: “Even a fool, if he keeps silent, will be considered wise,” and so forth.]

“Wisdom will be reckoned to the fool who asks for wisdom.” For although the person who asks does not understand the force of the question proposed, nevertheless, because he inquires prudently and understands that he does not understand, this very fact is reckoned to him as wisdom, since he has prudently recognized what he did not know.

According to your division, therefore, three things seem to be named by the Apostle here: the desire of the flesh against the spirit, and that of the spirit against the flesh. Their mutual opposition appears to have this cause and explanation: “So that,” he says, “we cannot do what we wish.”

[Note: [Col. 0594D] A fourth—supply, “thing”—is expressed in the Apostle’s words. They had said that three things were named by the Apostle in that passage; but they had failed to notice a fourth, which the abbot here points out: namely, the cause and explanation of this battle between flesh and spirit, expressed in the words that follow. On this cause, see what we noted above in chapter 7.]

A fourth cause, therefore, remains, which you entirely failed to see: namely, that we do what we do not wish. [Col. 0594B] It is therefore now necessary for us first to recognize the force of the two desires—the desire of the flesh and that of the spirit—and then to examine what our will is, which is placed between them. After that, we must likewise discern what may not belong to our will.

## CHAPTER X. That the word “flesh” is not used with only one meaning
[Note: [Col. 0594D] Isidore of Pelusium (Book IV), a contemporary and fellow student of our Cassian, designates only two meanings of “flesh” in a certain letter (Epistle 477), though nearly all the remaining meanings are contained under them: “The word ‘flesh,’” he says, “is used in Scripture in two ways. Sometimes it is understood of nature, sometimes of affection and corruption. An example of the former meaning is: ‘A spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have’ (Luke 24). Of the latter: ‘Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God.’” So much for him. Yet the division and distinction given here is fuller and more precise.]

We read that the word “flesh” is used in Holy Scripture in many ways. Sometimes it signifies the whole human being, that is, one consisting of body and soul; as where it says (John 1): “And the Word became flesh”; and (Isaiah 40 and Luke 3): “All flesh shall see the salvation of our God.” Sometimes it signifies sinful and carnal people; as there (Genesis 6): “My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh.” At times it is used for sins themselves; as there (Romans 8): “But you are not in the flesh, but in the spirit.” And again (1 Corinthians 15): “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God.” It follows: “Nor shall corruption possess incorruption.” Sometimes it signifies kinship and relationship; as there (2 Samuel 5): “Behold, we are your bone and your flesh.” And the Apostle (Romans 11): “If somehow I may provoke my flesh to emulation and save some of them.”

We must therefore inquire according to which of these four meanings we ought here to understand “flesh.” For it is clear that it cannot possibly mean what is stated in “And the Word became flesh,” or in “And all flesh shall see the salvation of God.” Nor can it mean what is said, “My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh”; for, just as there it refers abruptly to a sinful person, so here “flesh” is not used when it is said (Galatians 4): “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh.” For he is not speaking of substantial things, [Col. 0596A] but of actions, which struggle in one and the same person, either together or separately, with a certain succession and alteration of time.

## CHAPTER XI. What the Apostle names “flesh” in this passage, and what the desire of the flesh is
