[Note: [Col. 0595C] From the Apostle’s words, “The flesh desires against the spirit,” and so forth, the Manichaeans once attempted to establish that there are two natures in a human being: one good, created by God, and another evil, proceeding from the Devil as its author, which, dwelling in the flesh, desires through the flesh against the spirit. But they devised this not only impiously but also incompetently. For it is precisely the same soul that desires through the flesh according to the carnal appetite and through the spirit according to the rational appetite. It is established that the human soul possesses a twofold appetitive power: one without reason, which we call the sensitive appetite because it concerns the pleasures of the senses; and another which participates in reason, which we call the will (Augustine, To Quodvultdeus; Gregory, *Morals*, Book XXXII, chapter 10). Once healed and renewed by grace, this latter desires spiritual goods under the direction of the spirit. It is therefore the same soul which, according to its different powers, fights against itself. Accordingly, when the abbot says here that “flesh” and “spirit” do not signify the substance of a human being, understand this as meaning not substance simply, but substance insofar as it is carnal or spiritual—that is, insofar as it obeys the sensitive and carnal appetite, or the spiritual, rational one. The meaning is the same whether one says “flesh,” “soul,” or “a human being insofar as carnal.”

Moreover, Saint Augustine writes not only that the same soul, seething with different movements according to different and contrary appetites, experiences this division, but also that the rational power itself does so. For he teaches that the same human will quarrels, disputes, and fights with itself when, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, it wholly desires to cling to eternal goods, but, under the weight of carnal habit, still wishes to enjoy earthly advantages and pleasures. Thus he describes the difficulties and uncertainties that he himself suffered at the beginning of his conversion in Book VIII, chapter 5, of the *Confessions*:

“My will was held by the enemy, and from it he had made a chain for me and bound me. For from a perverse will arose lust; and when lust is served, habit arises; and when habit is not resisted, necessity arises. By these links, as it were, interwoven with one another—for which reason I called it a chain—a harsh bondage held me. But the new will, which had begun to arise in me, by which I wished to serve you freely and wished to enjoy you, O God, the only certain joy, was not yet strong enough to overcome the former will, strengthened by long age. Thus my two wills, one old and the other new, the one carnal and the other spiritual, struggled with each other and, by their discord, tore my soul apart. Thus, through my own experience, I understood what I had read: how the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh.”

These words of Augustine may illuminate what is discussed in the following chapter concerning a certain intermediate will between the desire of the flesh and that of the spirit.]

Therefore, in this passage we must understand “flesh” not as a human being—that is, the substance of a human being—but as the will and worst desires of the flesh; and “spirit” likewise not as some substantial entity, but as the soul’s good and spiritual desires. The blessed Apostle himself clearly expressed this meaning earlier, saying: “I say, walk by the spirit, and you shall not fulfill the desires of the flesh. For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh.” [Col. 0596B]

[Note: [Col. 0596D] Since the movements of the spirit are contrary to the movements of the flesh, as has been said. The flesh urges us toward shameful things, while the spirit invites us toward honorable things; this is later explained in a long and elaborate antithesis. It makes no difference whether “spirit” is understood as the Holy Spirit, which seems to fit the Apostle’s context better, or as the human spirit, insofar as it has been healed by the Holy Spirit and is ruled and governed by him. For, says Saint Thomas (*Summa Theologiae* I–II, question 70, article 4), the Holy Spirit moves the human mind toward what accords with reason, or rather toward what is above reason; but the appetite of the flesh, which is the sensitive appetite, draws toward sensible goods, which are below the human being. Thus, just as upward and downward movement are contrary in natural things, so in human works the works of the flesh are contrary to the fruits or works of the spirit.]

But these are opposed to one another, so that you do not do whatever you wish (Galatians 5). Since both desires—the desires of the flesh and of the spirit—are in one and the same human being, an internal war is waged daily within us. The desire of the flesh, rushing headlong toward vices, rejoices in pleasures belonging to present repose. Opposed to these, the desire of the spirit wishes so completely to cling to spiritual pursuits that it even longs to exclude the necessary uses of the flesh, desiring to devote itself continually to those pursuits and unwilling to devote any care at all to the flesh’s weakness.

The flesh delights in luxury and lust, [Col. 0597A] while the spirit does not yield even to natural desires. The flesh desires to be satisfied with sleep and filled with food; the spirit is so nourished by vigils and fasts that it does not wish to admit sleep or food even for the necessary uses of life. The flesh wishes to abound in every kind of wealth; the spirit is content not even to possess the daily substance of a small loaf of bread. The flesh desires to shine with baths and to be surrounded daily by crowds of flatterers; the spirit rejoices in the filth of squalor and the desolation of an inaccessible wilderness and dreads the presence of all mortals. The flesh is comforted by honors and human praise; the spirit rejoices in persecutions and insults inflicted upon it.

## CHAPTER XII. What our will is, which is placed between the desire of the flesh and that of the spirit

[Col. 0597B]

Between these two desires, [Note: [Col. 0597B] He posits a certain will, or state of the soul, as a kind of middle position between the two desires, namely those of the flesh and of the spirit. In this state the soul is disposed in such a way that it wishes to satisfy and obey both equally: that is, to enjoy earthly and eternal goods at the same time, to sleep, as the saying goes, on both ears, and now serve the flesh, now the spirit.

Scripture calls this depraved and divided, or partitioned, affection “tepidity,” because what is lukewarm lies midway between hot and cold water; and in many passages Scripture censures and detests it as wicked, absurd, and impossible. 1 Kings 18: “How long will you limp on both sides? If the Lord is God, follow him; but if Baal, follow him.” Proverbs 13: “The sluggard wills and does not will.” Matthew 6: “You cannot serve God and Mammon.” Luke 6: “No one can serve two masters.” Luke 9: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.” 2 Corinthians 6: “What partnership is there between righteousness and iniquity? Or what fellowship between light and darkness? What agreement between Christ and Belial? Or what harmony between the temple of God and idols?” 1 Timothy 2: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs.” Revelation 3: “Would that you were cold or hot,” and so forth.

Such was Augustine at the beginning of his conversion, as was seen above (Chapter 11), drawn now in one direction and now in another by a wavering will. The venerable Bede interprets Zacchaeus as having been spiritually disposed in a similar way: “He sought to see the Savior entering Jericho, but could not because of the crowd” (Luke 19), because he wished to share in the grace of faith that the Savior brought to the world, but his ingrained habit of vices prevented him from attaining his desire.

Finally, Saint Gregory, portraying such useless servants, says (*Homily 9 on the Gospels*): “There are many within Holy Church—of whom this servant bears the likeness—who are afraid to undertake the paths of a better life, yet do not fear to lie inert in the sluggishness of their own torpor”; and so forth. To shake off this torpor, division, and tepidity of the will, he suitably teaches that this struggle of the flesh and spirit has been implanted and left within us for our great benefit: so that, awakened by the constant contest and conflict of both sides, the soul may compel itself, raise itself above itself, and strive with all its effort and persistence toward the summit of perfection, because “the kingdom of God suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew 11).]

the will of the soul, situated in a certain blameworthy middle position, is neither pleased by the disgraceful acts of vices nor reconciled to the pains of virtues. It seeks to be restrained from carnal passions in such a way that it is altogether unwilling to endure the necessary pains without which the desires of the spirit cannot be possessed. It wishes to obtain bodily chastity without disciplining the flesh, to acquire purity of heart without the labor of vigils, to abound in spiritual virtues while the flesh rests, to possess the grace of patience without suffering any insult, to exercise the humility of Christ without the loss of worldly honor, to pursue the simplicity of religion together with worldly ambition, to serve Christ with human praise and favor, and to proclaim the strictness of truth without causing even the slightest offense to anyone.

Finally, it wishes to attain future goods without losing present ones. Such a will would never allow us to reach true perfection, but would place us in a certain most hideous tepidity, making us like those who are rebuked and chastised by the Lord in the Apocalypse: “I know your works, that you are neither hot nor cold.” [Col. 0598B]

[Note: [Col. 0598B] Saint Gregory says in the *Pastoral Rule* (Part III, chapter 35): “The hot person is one who both takes up good pursuits and brings them to completion; the cold person is one who neither begins what must be completed. And just as one passes from cold through lukewarmness to heat, so also from heat one returns through lukewarmness to cold. But just as before lukewarmness there is coldness under hope, so after coldness lukewarmness is in despair. For the person who is still in sins does not lose confidence in conversion; but the person who has grown lukewarm after conversion has removed the hope that could have been entertained concerning a sinner. Everyone is therefore to be either hot or cold, lest he be vomited out as lukewarm: either, if not yet converted, he should still give hope of his conversion, or, if already converted, he should burn with zeal for virtues. Let the lukewarm person not be vomited out—the person who, from the heat he had proposed, returns through torpor to harmful coldness.” So Gregory.

Cassian also vividly depicts the vice of tepidity and the conduct of lukewarm monks—against whom this passage is directed above all—in Book X of the *Institutes*, chapters 2 and 3. Add to this Saint Bernard’s Sermon 6, where he compares the two kinds of monks:

“You can observe,” he says, “in nearly all religious communities men filled with consolation, overflowing with joy, always cheerful and happy, fervent in spirit, meditating day and night on the law of God, frequently looking up to heaven and lifting pure hands in prayer, careful guardians of conscience and devoted followers of good works. For them discipline is lovable, fasting sweet, vigils brief, manual labor delightful, and finally the whole austerity of this way of life seems a refreshment. [Col. 0598D]

“By contrast, one can find fainthearted and remiss men, failing under the burden, needing the rod and the spur. Their slack joy is fainthearted sadness; their brief and infrequent compunction, animal thought; their way of life lukewarm; their obedience without devotion; their speech without watchfulness; their prayer without the attention of the heart; their reading without edification. In short, as we see, scarcely are they restrained by fear of hell, scarcely controlled by shame, scarcely curbed by reason, scarcely corrected by discipline. Does their life not seem to you to approach hell itself, when, with understanding resisting affection and affection resisting understanding, they are forced to lay their hand to the works of the strong, though they are by no means sustained by the food of the strong—plainly companions in tribulation, but not in consolation,” and so forth. See the same author, Sermon 63 on the *Song of Songs*.]

“Would that you were cold or hot; but because you are lukewarm, I am about to vomit you out of my mouth” (Revelation 3)—unless these wars rising on both sides shatter this most lukewarm state.

For when, in serving this will of ours, we wish to relax ourselves a little into this remission, immediately the goads of the flesh arise, wounding us with their vices and passions. They do not allow us to remain in that quality of purity in which we delight, but drag us along the cold path, full of thorns, toward the pleasure that we dread. Conversely, if, inflamed by fervor of spirit, we wish to extinguish the works of the flesh and attempt, without any consideration for human weakness, to devote ourselves wholly to immoderate pursuits of virtue, the weakness of the flesh, intervening, recalls and restrains the spirit from that blameworthy excess.

Thus, as the two desires oppose one another in alternating struggle, the will of the soul—which neither wishes to surrender itself entirely to carnal desires nor to labor sweatily in the exertions of virtue—is in a certain manner tempered by a just moderation. This conflict between the two excludes the more destructive will of the soul and places a kind of balance of equity on the scales of our body. It distinguishes the boundaries of spirit and flesh by a just judgment and allows neither the mind, inflamed by the ardor of the spirit, to preponderate on the right, nor the flesh, pierced by the goads of vices, to outweigh it on the left.

While this struggle is usefully agitated within us day after day, we are salutarily compelled to come to that fourth thing which we do not wish: to acquire purity of heart not through idleness or security, but through continual sweat and contrition of spirit; to retain chastity of the flesh through strict fasts, hunger, thirst, and vigilance; to obtain direction of heart through reading, vigils, continual prayer, and the squalor of solitude; to preserve patience amid tribulations through practice; to serve our Author amid blasphemies and an abundance of insults; to pursue truth amid the hatred and enmities of this world, if necessary.

When such a struggle is waged in our body, drawing us away from this idle security and summoning us to the labor and pursuit of virtues that we desire, the middle path of equity is admirably maintained. The lukewarm judgment of our will is tempered by the most moderate warmth: on one side by the fervor of the spirit, on the other by the coldest rigor of the flesh. The desire of the spirit does not allow the mind to be dragged toward unrestrained vices, nor does the weakness of the flesh permit the spirit to be lifted toward irrational desires for virtue. Otherwise, on the one side all kinds of fuel for vices would spring up, or on the other the chief disease of pride, arising from exaltation, would pierce us with the heavier weapon of pride.

Instead, the just balancing of these struggles preserves a healthy and moderate path between the two virtues, teaching the soldier of Christ always to walk along the royal road. Thus, whenever, through the tepidity of this most sluggish will of which we have spoken, the mind has inclined more strongly toward the desires of the flesh, the desire of the spirit restrains it, refusing to yield to earthly vices. Conversely, if through excessive fervor, by an excess of the heart, our spirit has been carried away toward impossibilities and rash undertakings, the weakness of the flesh draws it back to a just judgment. Thus, transcending the most lukewarm state of our will, our spirit proceeds by the most advantageous moderation and along a level path, with industrious exertion, on the road to perfection.

We read that something similar was arranged by the Lord in the construction of that tower, in the Book of Genesis, where the sudden confusion of languages restrained the sacrilegious and wicked attempts of human beings (Genesis 11). [Note: [Col. 0599C] Genesis 11: “The Lord descended to see the city and the tower which the sons of Adam were building, and he said: ‘Behold, they are one people, and there is one language for all of them; and they have begun to do this, nor will they desist from their plans until they complete them in action. Come, therefore, let us descend and confuse their language there, so that each one may not hear the voice of his neighbor.’ [Col. 0599D] And so the Lord divided them from that place throughout all the lands, and they ceased to build the city.”

Thus the confusion of languages and discord of speech restrained human beings’ rash and wicked attempts. In the same way, the internal discord of our own parts benefits us both by humbling the elevation of our mind and for the other effects mentioned above.]

For even there a harmful agreement against God—or rather against those who had begun to assault his divine majesty—would have continued, unless, by God’s providential arrangement, a diversity of language opposing them to one another had compelled them, through discord of speech, to advance toward a better condition; and unless the beneficial and useful disagreement had recalled to salvation those whom a destructive agreement had encouraged toward their own ruin, teaching them, through the intervening division, to perceive human weakness, which in their earlier arrogant and harmful conspiracy they had not known.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the usefulness of hesitation arising from the struggle of the flesh and spirit

[Note: [Col. 0599D] He gathers from what has been said several benefits that arise for us from the struggle and disagreement of flesh and spirit.

The first benefit is salutary hesitation and delay, by which the evils we have conceived in our minds are carried out more slowly, since we are hindered by the weight of the body, and by which we are more easily recalled from them when repentance follows. Hence the poet:

“Delay; small delays have great advantages.”

The second is an easier excuse before God and the attainment of pardon on account of human weakness and frailty. On this ground the Psalmist so often moves and implores divine mercy, saying: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak,” and so forth—a thing the angels cannot say, since, being incorporeal, they have no excuse of weakness, as is said here.

The third is greater caution and vigilance, so that, never secure against an enemy, especially a domestic one, we may watch over and protect ourselves more carefully. For who, with an enemy present, and a most hostile one at that, would not beware and fortify himself?

The fourth is humiliation, by which even spiritual and perfect men are salutarily humbled because of the weakness and impurity of the flesh that they suffer against their will, lest they be lifted up by their virtues and divine benefits. For if the Apostle Paul was given a thorn in his flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet him, lest the greatness of revelations should exalt him (see John Climacus, *The Ladder*, step 15), what wonder if this happens to others? These two benefits are pursued in Chapter 15 and those that follow (2 Corinthians 12).

Nevertheless, although the author rightly infers from these considerations that the struggle of flesh and spirit is, at least in some respect and in a certain sense, good and useful to us for many purposes, and that it therefore remains in us by divine providence or disposition even after baptism, for the contest, as has been said, it must nevertheless be admitted that the desire of the flesh against the spirit is, in itself and simply speaking, evil and vicious—not because it is a sin in the strict sense of the word, but because it is a vice and defect of nature opposed to natural order and equity, according to which it is fitting that inferior things be subject to superior things. For, contrary to this order, through the desire of the flesh the lower part of the soul resists the higher, that is, reason; it does not obey the law of the mind; it struggles against the spirit; and, what is worse, it draws toward sin.

Thus the Apostle expressly calls it evil in Romans 7, when he says: “Evil lies close at hand for me, but I do not find how to accomplish the good.” By this evil lying close at hand nothing else can be understood than the desire of the flesh, which the Apostle there calls the law of the members and the law of sin resisting the law of the mind (see Bellarmine, *On the Loss of Grace*, Book VI, chapter 14).

Saint Augustine also teaches this carefully against the Pelagians and confirms it with many arguments and testimonies of the ancient Fathers in Book II *Against Julian*, writing, among other things, that the law of sin which is present in the members of a human being and resists the law of the mind—the condition in which the flesh desires against the spirit—imposes the necessity of fighting even upon the baptized. “And against what,” he says, “unless against evil—not against substance, but against a vice of substance—which, through God’s grace regenerating us, is not imputed, and which, through God’s grace assisting us, must be restrained?”]

To such an extent, however, [Col. 0601A] does useful hesitation arise for us from this diversity of struggle, and salutary delay from this conflict, that, while bodily solidity resists and we are held back from carrying out what we wickedly conceive in our minds, we are sometimes corrected and brought into a better condition, either by subsequent repentance or by some amendment that usually arises when the execution of an act is postponed and further reflection intervenes.

Finally, those whom we understand to be unimpeded by any obstacle of the flesh in fulfilling the desires of their wills—namely, demons and spiritual wickednesses, even though they have fallen from a more exalted order of angels—we regard as more detestable than human beings. Since the possibility of fulfilling their desires lies immediately at hand, they do not delay to complete, by an irreversible evil, what they have once wickedly conceived. [Note: [Col. 0601C] This does not mean that they possess a judgment and will wholly inflexible and immovable, as some maintain (Saint Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* I, question 64, article 2), but that they are held back by no impediment or delay of the flesh from immediately carrying out what they have conceived in their minds.]

For just as their mind is swift in devising, so their substance is nimble and unimpeded in accomplishing; and while an easy readiness to perform whatever they wish is available to them, no salutary deliberation intervenes to correct the evil they have conceived.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the incorrigible wickedness of spiritual evil powers

[Note: [Col. 0601C] The Fathers teach that angels, whether good or evil, are spiritual and incorporeal substances: Saint Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* I, question 51; Dionysius the Areopagite, *Celestial Hierarchy*, chapter 2, and *On the Divine Names*, chapter 4; Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 2, *On Theology*; Chrysostom, Homily 22 on Genesis; Damascene, Book II of *The Orthodox Faith*, chapter 3; and Gregory the Great, *Morals* VIII, chapter 9. The Council of Lateran, in the chapter *Firmiter*, defined the matter as follows: “From the beginning of time God created both creatures from nothing, the spiritual and the corporeal, namely the angelic and the worldly.” There the spiritual creature is set in opposition to the corporeal.

The abbot teaches differently in Conference 7, chapter 13, where he admits that angels are indeed of a spiritual nature, but not wholly incorporeal. Saint Augustine also seems to have held this view in several passages, where, following the opinion of the Platonists, he attributes certain spiritual things—that is, aerial bodies—to both angels and demons.]

For a spiritual substance, not bound by any solidity of flesh, does not admit an excuse for the evil will that has arisen within it; so it excludes pardon for its wickedness. It was not provoked externally to sin by any struggle of the flesh, as we are, but was inflamed by the vice of its evil will alone; and for that reason its sin is without pardon and its sickness without remedy. [Col. 0603A]

[Note: [Col. 0601D] Damascene, in the passage cited above: “An angel is incapable of repentance because he is incorporeal. But man obtained repentance because of the weakness of his substance.” And in the following chapter: “What death is to human beings, a fall is to angels. For after their fall there is no place for repentance for them, just as there is none for human beings after death.” This must not be understood as though angelic nature were by nature incapable of restoration in comparison with human nature, or irreparable by its Creator; rather, it was most just that, just as the course of human beings—in which they can merit, advance, or repent—ends with death, so the course of angels, by the ordinance of the Creator, should end with their fall. Thus it occurs not so much because of the diversity of natures as because of God’s most just ordinance that an angel cannot be restored after a fall.

Two causes of this divine ordinance are touched on here—why, that is, after his fall and first sin the devil was immediately condemned and deprived of every hope and remedy for obtaining pardon and restoration. Saint Gregory also set them forth in Book IV of the *Morals*, chapter 9, by which this whole passage is most aptly illustrated. “God had made two creatures capable of understanding themselves, namely the angelic and the human; pride struck both and broke them from the state of their innate rectitude” (see Saint Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* I, question 64, article 2). “But one had a covering of flesh; the other bore nothing weak from flesh. For an angel is spirit alone, whereas a human being is both spirit and flesh. Therefore the Creator, in his mercy and in order to redeem, ought to bring back to himself that creature which evidently had something of weakness in the commission of sin; and he ought all the more to reject the apostate angel, since, when he fell from the strength to persevere, he bore nothing weak from flesh. Hence the Psalmist, when he called the Redeemer merciful toward human beings, also expressed the very cause of mercy, saying: ‘And he remembered that they are flesh’; as if to say: The more he saw their weakness, the less he wished strictly to punish their sins.”

There is yet another reason why fallen human beings had to be restored while the proud spirit could not be restored: the angel fell through his own pride, but the human being was overthrown by another’s. Saint Augustine offers a third reason in chapter 29 of the *Enchiridion*: why God willed to restore human rather than angelic nature—because, when one human being sinned, the whole human race perished in him, whereas when one angel fell, not all the rest fell. “It therefore pleased God, the Creator and Governor of the universe, that, since not the whole multitude of angels had perished by forsaking God, that part which had perished should remain in everlasting perdition; while that which had remained with God after the other had forsaken him should rejoice, secure in the certain knowledge of its happiness, which would always endure. But the other rational creature, existing in human beings, because it had wholly perished through sins and punishments, both original and personal, should, once restored from its portion, make up the loss which that diabolical fall had inflicted upon the society of angels.” Thus Augustine.

Against the first reason advanced by Saint Gregory, someone may perhaps object that, in the state of innocence, the human being had flesh wholly subject and obedient to the spirit, indeed then no less inclined toward good than it is now toward evil. Why then is the human fall attributed to the weakness of the flesh, and why do Gregory and the other Fathers assign this consideration as the reason for exercising mercy toward human beings rather than angels? Answer: although in the state of innocence there was no rebellion of flesh against spirit in human beings, nevertheless flesh, or the sensitive appetite, by its own nature or natural motion tended toward its sensible and corporeal object. Therefore it required the command and restraint of reason, as well as the assistance of divine grace, to keep it in its duty and within its limits. In this respect, then, the human being—being composed of two parts—was weaker, more inclined to sin, and therefore more worthy of pardon than the angel, who had no such object or occasion of sin except his own will, being wholly incorporeal and spiritual. See Saint Prosper, Book I of *The Contemplative Life*, chapter 3, and Fulgentius, *On Faith*, chapter 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0603D] [ [Col. 0603] This note is printed at the foot of column 603, but its callout letter, a, does not appear in the text.] We have expressed these two benefits together with two others above. See Cassian, Book XII of the *Institutes*, chapters 20, 21, and 23, and the notes there (Chapter 13).]

For just as it fell without any earthly matter tempting it, so it can obtain neither indulgence nor an opportunity for repentance. From these considerations it is clearly gathered that the conflict of flesh and spirit, which is aroused within us against each other, is not only not harmful, but also confers great benefit upon us.

## CHAPTER XV. How the desire of the flesh against the spirit benefits us

First, it immediately reproves our laziness and negligence. Like a most diligent tutor, it never allows us to depart from the line of strictness and discipline; if our security has exceeded, even slightly, the measure of suitable severity, it immediately goads and rebukes us with the scourges of its incentives and recalls us to a fitting moderation. [Col. 0603B]

Second, when, with God’s grace granting it, we have seen ourselves kept free for a long time from genital pollution, so that we believe we will no longer be troubled even by the simple stirring of the flesh, and, as though we did not carry the corruption of the flesh, we have become elated in the secret places of our conscience, the flesh again visits us with its flow, quiet and simple though it may be; it humbles and blunts us and reminds us by its goads that we are human beings.

In a certain way, although in the other kinds of vices—and indeed in those that are more serious and more harmful—we are accustomed to fall with greater indifference and are not so easily moved to compunction at committing them, in this matter our conscience is humbled in a special way. Through this illusion it is also stung by the memory of passions that we had neglected. It clearly understands that it has been made impure by natural incentives, whereas, though it was even more impure through spiritual vices, it did not know this.

Returning at once to correcting its former negligence, it is warned that it must not trust in the successes of its former purity, since it sees that it lost that purity after turning aside even a little from the Lord. Nor can it possess the gift of this purification except through God’s grace alone. The experiences of the matter itself teach us, as it were, that if we delight in attaining purity of heart perpetually, we must continually pursue the virtue of humility.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the incentives of the flesh, through which, unless we were humbled, we would fall more grievously
We should therefore believe that the elation arising from this purity would become more destructive than all crimes and vices, and that, because of it, we would gain no benefit from whatever integrity of chastity we possessed. This is testified by those Powers of whom we spoke above [Note: [Col. 0603D] The angelic Powers—that is, the evil angels, or demons—who were cast down from heaven solely on account of pride; see above, chapter 14. This term is used in two ways when applied to angels: 1. Generally and indiscriminately, for any order of angels, as here; for it is the common opinion that angels fell from every order. Thus Matthew 24: “And the Powers of heaven will be shaken”; or, as Mark has it in chapter 13: “The Powers that are in the heavens will be shaken.” Origen, Chrysostom, Bede, and others teach that the angels of heaven are called “Powers” [Col. 0604D]; similarly, in the Preface of the Mass, heaven and the Powers of heaven are mentioned. 2. Specifically, for a definite order or choir of angels distinct from the others, which, according to Dionysius the Areopagite, is the second and middle order of the second hierarchy [Col. 0604C], or, according to Gregory, the first of the third hierarchy (see Conference 8, chapter 15). Thus 1 Corinthians 15: “When he has abolished every principality, power, and virtue”; and 1 Peter 4: “Angels, authorities, and powers having been subjected to him.”], who, although they are believed to have had no such ticklings of the flesh [Col. 0604B], were cast down in perpetual ruin from their lofty and heavenly station solely because of the elation of their hearts. We would therefore be utterly without remedy, lukewarm as we would be, since we would have no indicator of our negligence dwelling either in our body or in our own consciences; nor would we ever strive to attain the fervor of perfection. Indeed, we would not maintain even strict frugality or continence, unless this increasing tickling of the flesh humbled and checked us, and made us solicitous and attentive also to the purification of spiritual vices.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Lukewarmness of Eunuchs

Finally, among those who are eunuchs in body, we generally find this lukewarmness of spirit present [Col. 0604C] [Note: [Col. 0604D] “Eunuchs” in body are those whom Matthew says were born eunuchs from their mother’s womb, or those who were made so by men. Eunuchs in spirit, but not in body, are those who castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven—that is, through spiritual castration, namely, by a vow of perpetual continence. What is said here about such eunuchs and their characteristics is likewise repeated and explained more clearly in Conference 7, chapter 12.], because, as though released from this carnal necessity, they consider themselves to need neither the labor of bodily continence nor contrition of heart. Relaxed by this security, they never hasten either truly to seek or to possess perfection of heart or even purification from spiritual vices. This condition, descending from a carnal quality, becomes animal, which is undoubtedly a worse state; for it is the very condition that, passing from coldness to lukewarmness, is marked as more detestable by the Lord’s own voice.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Germanus’s Question: What Difference Exists between the Carnal and the Animal Person

**Germanus:** The usefulness of the struggle that arises between flesh and spirit has, as it seems to us, been expressed with such clarity that we believe it has somehow been made palpable to us with our own hands. For this reason, we likewise wish this matter to be explained to us: what difference exists between a carnal and an animal person, or how an animal person can be worse than a carnal one.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the Three States of Souls

**Daniel:** According to the definition of Scripture [Note: [Col. 0605C] He distinguishes three states of the soul, although in reality and according to common understanding the carnal and animal states differ little or not at all. He seems, however, to establish the carnal state of the soul chiefly in the uncleanness and pollution of the flesh, even when involuntary, as the following makes clear.], there are three states of souls [Col. 0605B]: the first carnal, the second animal, and the third spiritual (see Augustine, *On Eighty-Three Questions*, question 4, §67). We read that these are designated by the Apostle as follows.

Of the carnal person it is said: “I gave you milk to drink, not food, for you were not yet able; indeed, even now you cannot, for you are still carnal” (1 Corinthians 3). And again: “For where there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal?” (ibid.).

The animal person is likewise described: “The animal person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him” (1 Corinthians 2). Of the spiritual person, however, it is said: “The spiritual person examines everything, but he himself is judged by no one” (ibid.). And again: “You who are spiritual should instruct such people in a spirit of gentleness” (Galatians 6).

[Note: [Col. 0605C] This word is derived from *anima* (“soul”), not from *animal*. In Greek it is ψυχικός (*psychikos*), that is, “animal,” from ψυχή (*psychē*), “soul.” Hence Tertullian, after becoming a Montanist, entitled his book *Against the Psychics*, that is, “Against the Animal People,” maliciously attacking Catholics by this name because they did not observe three Lents according to the custom of the Montanists [Col. 0605D]. Further, Saint Thomas explains most clearly in his *Commentary* what an animal person is, in these words:

“It must be considered that the soul is the form of the body. Accordingly, the powers proper to the soul are understood to be those that are acts of bodily organs, namely, the sensory powers. People are therefore called animal because they follow such powers, among which are the apprehensive and appetitive powers. Thus a person may be called animal in two ways.

“First, with respect to the apprehensive power. In this sense, a person is called animal according to perception when— as the Gloss says—he judges about God according to bodily images, the letter of the law, or philosophical reasoning, all of which are received according to the sensory powers.

“Second, a person is called animal with respect to the appetitive power, when he is affected only by those things that accord with sensory appetite. Such a person is said to possess an animal life; as the Gloss says, he follows the unrestrained wantonness of his soul, which the directing spirit does not contain within the bounds of the natural order. Hence Jude’s Catholic Epistle says: ‘These are the people who separate themselves, animal, not having the Spirit’ [Col. 0606C].

“Second, it must be considered why such people cannot perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God; and this is clear both with respect to animal perception and with respect to animal life. The things with which the Holy Spirit enlightens the mind are above human perception and reason, according to Ecclesiastes 3: ‘You have shown a multitude of things above human perception.’ Therefore they cannot be grasped by one who relies solely on sensory cognition.

“The Holy Spirit also kindles the affection to love spiritual goods while despising sensible goods [Col. 0606D]. Therefore a person who lives an animal life cannot grasp such spiritual things, because the Philosopher says in Book 4 of the *Ethics* that each person’s end appears to him according to what kind of person he is. Proverbs 18 says: ‘A fool does not receive the words of wisdom unless you tell him what lies in his heart.’ And Ecclesiasticus 22 says: ‘He who tells a fool wisdom is speaking to one who is asleep.’”

Thus far Saint Thomas, following his customary manner: not in sublimity of expression, but in the teaching of the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual things (1 Corinthians 8).]

Therefore we must hasten, so that when, by renouncing the world, we have ceased to be carnal—that is, when we have begun to separate ourselves from secular conduct and to cease from that manifest pollution of the flesh [Col. 0605C]—we may strive with all our strength immediately to attain the spiritual state. Otherwise, perhaps flattering ourselves because we seem [Col. 0606A] [Note: [Col. 0606D] Augustine, *City of God*, Book 13, chapter 24: “Divine Scripture, although these two things—body and soul—from which a human being lives are joined together, nevertheless calls each individually by the name ‘human being’: the soul the inner human being, and the body the outer human being, as though there were two human beings, although both together are one human being. See also the same author, *On the Trinity*, Book 12, chapter 1.] according to the outward person, to have renounced this world or abandoned the pollution of carnal fornications, as though by this we had attained the summit of perfection, we may thereafter become more remiss and sluggish in cleansing ourselves from the other passions. Held between the two states, we would be unable to attain the stage of spiritual progress, thinking that it was fully sufficient for our perfection to appear, in our outward person, to have withdrawn from the conduct and pleasures of this world, or to be free from carnal corruption and intercourse.

And so, having been found in that lukewarm state—which is judged the worst—we should know that, according to the Lord’s judgment, we will be vomited from his mouth, for he says: “Would that you were hot or cold! But because you are lukewarm, I am about to vomit you from my mouth” (Revelation 3) [Col. 0606B].

Nor without reason does the Lord declare that those whom he had already received into the inward parts of his charity, having become harmfully lukewarm, must be vomited out with a certain convulsion of his breast. Although they could in some way have offered him a salutary substance, they preferred to be torn from his inward parts. They thus became worse than those who were never brought as food to the Lord’s mouth, inasmuch as what we cast out under the compulsion of nausea we detest as more loathsome. For whatever is cold, even when received by our mouth, is changed into warmth and taken in with salutary sweetness; but what has once been cast out because of the harmful defect of lukewarmness, we cannot endure even to look at from a distance, much less bring it to our lips, without great horror.

It is therefore rightly declared to be worse, because a carnal person—that is, a secular or pagan person—more easily approaches a salutary way of life and the summit of perfection than one who has professed to be a monk but, without undertaking the way of perfection according to the rule of discipline, has once departed from that fire of spiritual fervor [Col. 0607A]. For the former, humbled at least by bodily vices and recognizing himself to be unclean through carnal pollution, will at some time, when pierced with compunction, run to the fountain of true purification and the summit of perfection. Shuddering at the icy state of unbelief in which he finds himself, he will, kindled by the ardor of the spirit, more easily hasten toward perfection.

But the person who, as we have said, once began with a lukewarm beginning to misuse the name of monk, and who did not undertake the path of this profession with the humility and fervor he ought to have shown, becomes infected with this miserable disease and, as it were, relaxed within it. He will thereafter be unable either to conceive anything perfect by himself or to be instructed by another’s admonitions. For he says in his heart, according to that saying of the Lord: “I am rich and wealthy, and I need nothing.”

To him the following will consequently be applied: “But you are wretched and miserable, poor and blind and naked” (Revelation 3) [Col. 0607B]. He has become worse even than a secular person in this respect: he does not recognize himself as wretched, blind, naked, or worthy of correction, nor does he recognize that he needs anyone’s admonition or instruction. For this reason he does not admit even any exhortation from the saving word, failing to understand that the very name of monk weighs him down and lowers him in the judgment of everyone. Since everyone believes him to be holy and venerates him as a servant of God, he must necessarily undergo a more severe judgment and punishment in the future.

Finally, why should we linger any longer over matters that experience has sufficiently shown and proved to us? We have frequently seen cold and carnal people—that is, secular persons and pagans—arrive at spiritual fervor; but we have never seen the lukewarm and animal arrive at spiritual fervor [Col. 0607C].

We read that the Lord detests such people through the prophet to such an extent that spiritual persons and teachers are commanded to withdraw from admonishing and instructing them, and not to spend the seed of the saving word, as though on barren and fruitless soil occupied by harmful thorns. Instead, they are to disregard that soil and cultivate new ground—that is, to transfer all the cultivation of instruction and the urgency of the saving word toward pagans and secular people. It is written thus:

“Thus says the Lord to the man of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem: Break up new ground for yourselves, and do not sow upon thorns” (Jeremiah 4).

[Note: [Col. 0607D] Tertullian, in his book *Against the Jews*, reads: “Renew newness for yourselves, and do not sow among thorns.” Elsewhere, however: “Renew a renewal for yourselves,” and so forth. Saint Cyprian, Book 1 of the *Testimonies against the Jews*: “Renew newness among yourselves, and do not sow among thorns.”]

## CHAPTER XX. On Those Who Renounce the World Badly

Finally—and it is shameful to say this—we see that many have renounced the world in such a way that they are proved to have changed nothing more in their former vices and habits than their secular status and clothing [Note: [Col. 0607D] Saint Jerome likewise portrays and rebukes in the colors of his own time certain monks of that period. In Letter 4 he says: “I have seen some who, after renouncing the world—in clothing only and in the profession of their speech, not in their actions—changed nothing of their former way of life: their household property was increased rather than diminished; the same services of servants, the same preparation for banquets; gold was eaten from glass and earthenware plates [ [Col. 0607D] He calls things made of gold and things purchased at great price “gold,” says Marianus.]; and amid crowds and swarms of attendants they claim for themselves the name of solitaries. Those who are poor and of slender means, yet consider themselves learned, proceed into public like dishes in a procession, to display a dog-like eloquence. Many cannot do without their former occupations and business dealings; changing only the names of their shops, they conduct the same commerce, pursuing not food and clothing—as the Apostle commands in 1 Timothy 6—but greater profits than worldly people.” Saint Jerome says these and other things consistent with this passage.], as to be shown to have altered nothing else in their former vices and customs (see Conference 3, chapters 3, 6, and following).

For they desire to acquire money, which they did not previously possess; or at least they do not cease to retain what they had; or, more grievously, they even desire to increase it, maintaining under this pretext that it is just for them to continue feeding either their servants or their brothers, or else reserving it under the pretext of gathering communities, which they presume they can establish as abbots [Note: [Col. 0608D] Ciaconius restored this passage, also corrupted in the Plantin edition by the addition of superfluities (as I failed to notice in the earlier edition), in these shorter words, supported by the Basel printing and several manuscripts, though there is some variation in them. Some have: “They retain [their goods] under the pretext of gathering a community, when they presume that they can be established as abbots.” The Basel edition and others: “whom they presume that they can establish as abbots.”] [Col. 0608B].

If they truly sought the way of perfection, they would strive with all their strength to accomplish this instead: stripped not only of money but also of their former affections and every distraction, they would place themselves, as solitary and naked men, under the authority of the elders, so that they would take no care not only of others but even of themselves.

The opposite occurs: while they hasten to preside over brothers, they themselves are never subject to elders. Beginning from pride, while they wish to instruct others, they do not deserve either to learn themselves or to do what ought to be done for God. It is necessary that such people, having become blind guides of the blind, fall together into the pit, according to the Savior’s saying (Matthew 15).

Although this pride is one genus, it has two forms. One continually feigns seriousness and gravity [Lipsius in the margin: “severity,” “serenity,” or “truth”]; the other dissolves in unrestrained freedom into foolish guffaws and laughter. The former delights in silence, whereas the latter disdains being confined by silence; it is not ashamed to speak indiscriminately, even about incongruous and foolish matters, while it is ashamed to be judged inferior or less learned than the others.

One, because of elation, seeks the office of cleric; the other despises it, judging it incompatible or unworthy of his former dignity or of the merits of his life and birth. Let each person’s own examination investigate and weigh which of these should be judged worse.

One thing is certain: it is the same kind of disobedience [Col. 0609A], whether someone violates the command of an elder because of eagerness for work or because of a desire for idleness; and it is equally harmful to overturn the monastery’s statutes for the sake of sleep or for the sake of vigilance. To disregard the abbot’s command in order to read is as serious as to disregard it in order to sleep. Nor is it a different fuel of pride to despise a brother for fasting than to despise him for eating, except that those vices are more destructive and farther removed from remedies which seem to emerge under the appearance of virtues and the image of spiritual things than those which plainly arise from carnal pleasure [Lipsius in the margin: “will”].

The former, like openly exposed and manifest illnesses [Lipsius in the margin: “illness”], are both reproved directly and cured. The latter, however, while concealed under the pretext of virtues [Col. 0609B], persist untreated and make those whom they deceive sicker in a more dangerous and desperate manner.

[Note: [Col. 0608D] Saint Gregory says: “It must be known that evil is never to be done through obedience, but that sometimes the good being done ought to be interrupted through obedience” (*Moralia*, Book 35, chapter 13) [Col. 0609C]. For the tree in paradise was not evil, which God forbade man to touch; rather, so that the well-created human being might grow through the greater merit of obedience, it was fitting that God should prohibit him even from something good, so that the virtue of his action would be the more genuine because, abstaining from what was good, he showed himself more humbly subject to his Creator. Thus Gregory.

For this reason the truly obedient are described by Saint Benedict (*Rule*, chapter 5) [Col. 0610C]: they immediately leave behind what belongs to them and abandon their own will; then, with empty hands and leaving unfinished what they were doing, they follow the voice of the one commanding with the foot of obedience, and so forth.]

## CHAPTER XXI. On Those Who, Disregarding Great Things, Occupy Themselves with Small Ones

Now consider how ridiculous it is that, after the initial fervor of renunciation by which some abandoned household property, extensive wealth, and worldly military service and brought themselves to monasteries, we see them so devoted to those things that cannot be completely cut off and that necessarily remain in this way of life, however small and worthless they may be, that their care for these things surpasses their former passion for all their possessions (Conference 3, chapter 3).

It will certainly profit them little to have despised greater wealth and property [Col. 0609C], because they have transferred the affection for them—on account of which such things ought to be despised—to small and insignificant objects. For by retaining the vice of greed and avarice [Col. 0610A], which they cannot exercise toward costly objects, around cheaper materials, they prove that they have not cut off their former passion but merely exchanged it.

Although the psathi, basket, little sack, book, mat, and other similar things are extremely cheap, they are nevertheless possessed by the same desire as before, being bound to them by excessive care. They guard and defend these objects with such rivalry that they are not ashamed to become agitated against a brother on their behalf and, what is even more disgraceful, to quarrel [Note: [Col. 0610C] See Book 7 of the *Institutes*, chapter 14. The rest is clear and deserves not so much explanation as reading.].

Still suffering from the sickness of their former greed, they are not content to possess, according to the common number and measure, those things which the use or necessity of the body compels a monk to have. Here too they reveal the avarice of their hearts [Col. 0610B]: either they take greater pains to have what they need than the others do, or, exceeding the proper measure of care, they guard such things with special attention and protect them from being handled by others, although they ought to be common to all the brothers.

As though only the difference between metals, and not the passion of greed itself, were harmless; as though it were wrong to become angry over great possessions but not wrong to do the same over cheap ones; and as though we had cast away more expensive materials for any other reason than to learn more easily to despise cheaper things.

For what difference does it make whether someone exercises the disturbance of greed toward broad and magnificent wealth or toward cheaper objects? The only difference is that he should be judged more blameworthy because, having despised the greatest things, he is bound to the smallest.

Therefore this renunciation does not attain perfection of heart [Col. 0610C], because, although it possesses the wealth of a poor person, it does not cast off the will of a rich one.

# FIFTH CONFERENCE

That of Abbot Serapion

## ON THE EIGHT PRINCIPAL VICES

[Col. 0609]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0609D]

In that gathering of the most ancient elders there was a man named Serapion [Note: [Col. 0609D] The Arsinoite Serapion, of course, reputedly abbot and priest of ten thousand monks, whose remarkable example as a young man is still recounted in Conference 2, chapter 10. Palladius also mentions him in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 76, where he is numbered among the chief and most illustrious inhabitants of the desert. Hence Saint Jerome says in Letter 27: “Why should I recount the names of Macariuses, Arsenii, Serapions, and the other pillars of Christ?” (*Catalogue*, Book 3, chapter 17). Petrus Equilinus says that this man sold the book of the Gospel, which was all he possessed, in order to help a poor person; Socrates recounts the event in Book 4, chapter 18. Others, however, attribute this to another Serapion, namely Serapion Sindonius, as may be seen in the *Lives of the Fathers*, Book 1, chapter 22.], a man especially endowed with the grace of discernment [Col. 0610D]. I consider it worthwhile to commit his conference to writing. When we urged him to discuss something about the attacks of the vices, so that their origins and causes might be disclosed more clearly, he began as follows.

## CHAPTER II. Abbot Serapion’s Account of the Eight Principal Vices

[Col. 0611A]

There are eight principal vices that afflict the human race: first, *gastrimargia*, which means gluttony of the belly; second, fornication; third, *philargyria*, that is, avarice or love of money; fourth, anger; fifth, sadness; sixth, *acedia*, that is, anxiety or weariness of heart; seventh, *cenodoxia*, that is, vainglory or empty glory; eighth, pride.

[Note: [Col. 0611C] We noted in Book 5 of the *Institutes* why eight principal vices are posited, when Saint Gregory and others enumerate only seven capital vices. Cassian also entitled eight books *On the Principal or Capital Vices*, treating each of them separately and individually in its own book. We dealt with these matters sufficiently there; to repeat them here would be superfluous.]

## CHAPTER III. On the Two Kinds of Vices and Their Fourfold Mode of Actualization

There are therefore two kinds of these vices. Some are natural, such as *gastrimargia*; others are contrary to nature, such as *philargyria*.

[Note: [Col. 0611C] There is a threefold division or distinction of the capital vices. First, some are natural and others contrary to nature. Second, some are carnal and others spiritual. Third, some are aroused by internal causes and others by external causes.

Gluttony and lust are called natural both because they were contracted from the very beginning through the disobedience of our first parent and implanted in our nature, and because they tend toward the preservation of nature, though in a disordered way. Gluttony concerns the preservation of nature in the individual, whereas lust concerns its preservation in the species. They are also called carnal because they are completed through carnal action and pleasure, as the following chapter explains.]

Their actualization, however, is fourfold. Some cannot be consummated without carnal action, such as *gastrimargia* and fornication; others are completed without any bodily action, such as pride and *cenodoxia*. Some receive the causes of their agitation from outside, such as *philargyria* and anger; others are aroused by movements within, such as *acedia* and sadness.

[Note: [Col. 0611D] The two divisions given above—the second and the third—are contained within this fourfold distinction. Moreover, *efficientia* here does not mean efficacy or the power of producing something, but an act, consummation, or execution, as will be clear from what follows.]

## CHAPTER IV. Recapitulation Concerning the Passion of *Gastrimargia* and Fornication, and Their Cure
And so that we may make these matters clearer not only by a brief discussion, insofar as we can, but also by testimonies from Scripture, [Note: That is, according to the natural tendency and inclination of corrupted and vitiated nature (which is otherwise called the tinder, stimulus, or goad of sin), not with respect to guilt and its particular kinds.] gluttony and fornication, [Col. 0612A] since they are naturally implanted in us, sometimes arise without any incitement of the soul, through the mere instigation and itching of the flesh; yet they require material from outside in order to be brought to completion, and thus [Note: Hence they are also called carnal by St. Gregory, Book XXXI of the *Morals*, chapter 31, where, out of the seven capital vices, he says that five are spiritual and two carnal—namely, greed of the belly and lust. (St. Thomas, *Summa* I–II, question 72, article 2, and question 73, article 5.)] reach their effect through bodily action. For each person is tempted by his own desire; then, when desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and when sin has been brought to completion, it produces death (James I). For [Note: Among the other sins of Adam and Eve there was also a certain disordered desire and appetite for the forbidden fruit, which is here called gluttony, that is, the vice of the appetite. For the woman saw that the tree was good for food, beautiful to the eyes, and desirable to behold; and she took of its fruit and ate, and gave it to her husband, who ate, Genesis III. For when Adam saw the beauty of the fruit and heard from his wife that it was of the sweetest taste, he desired to eat it most eagerly. But since the Apostle says, “Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived” (1 Timothy II), how is Adam here represented or supposed to have been deceived? St. Augustine answers in Book XIV, chapter 11, of *The City of God*: “Because she accepted as true what the serpent had said to her; but he did not wish to be separated from his one companion, nor from communion in sin; and for that reason he was not less guilty, but sinned knowingly and deliberately. Hence the Apostle does not say, ‘He did not sin,’ but, ‘He was not deceived.’ For he plainly shows that he himself sinned when he says, ‘Through one man sin entered into the world.’ And shortly afterward, more explicitly: ‘After the likeness of Adam’s transgression.’ He wished those to be understood as deceived who did not think that what they were doing was sin; but Adam knew it. And what need is there to say more? Even if, by believing, they were not both deceived, by sinning they were both captured and entangled in the devil’s snares.” Thus Augustine.] neither could the first Adam (Genesis III) have been deceived through gluttony unless, having the material of food readily available, he had illicitly abused it; [Note: Christ is called the second and last Adam, 1 Corinthians XV: “The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam a life-giving spirit. The first man was of the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly.”] nor is the second tempted without the enticement of some material, [Note: *Illicitatio* and *illicitamentum* mean the same as *incitamentum*, “incitement,” from the verb *illicio*. He uses the same word again in chapter 6. Christ is therefore said to have been tempted by the enticement of material because of the mention and suggestion of making bread from stones, when the devil said: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread” (Matthew IV).] when it is said to him, “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread” (Matthew IV). It is also evident to all that fornication cannot be accomplished except through the body, [Col. 0612B] as God says concerning this spirit to blessed Job: “His strength is in his loins, and his power is over the navel of his belly” (Job XL). Therefore these two in particular, which are completed through the service of the flesh, require, beyond that spiritual care of the soul, a more particular bodily continence. For the mere intention of the mind is not sufficient to blunt their goads—as it can sometimes be against anger, sadness, and other passions, which the skill of the mind knows how to conquer without any affliction of the flesh—unless bodily discipline is also added, accomplished through fasts, vigils, and laborious exertion, together with removal from place; for just as they are generated by the fault of both soul and body, so they cannot be overcome except through the labor of both (Gregory, Book XXXI of the *Morals*, chapter 31). And [Note: Since the Apostle in the fourth chapter of Galatians—which is what is indicated here—enumerates only fifteen or seventeen works of the flesh, how can it be true that he declared all vices generally to be carnal? The answer may be given in two ways. First, by “flesh” one may understand the carnal person; hence “works of the flesh” means whatever a person does insofar as he is carnal. A carnal person is one who lives according to himself, that is, according to love of himself. St. Augustine carefully notes this in Book XIV, chapters 2 and 3, of *The City of God*, and proves it with arguments suited to this passage: “Among the works of the flesh, which the Apostle called manifest and condemned after enumerating them (Galatians V), we find not only those that pertain to the pleasure of the flesh, such as fornications, uncleanness, lusts, drunkenness, and revelries, but also those by which vices of the soul are demonstrated, though they are alien to the pleasure of the flesh. Who would not understand idolatrous servitude, sorceries, enmities, quarrels, rivalries, angers, dissensions, heresies, and envies as vices of the soul rather than of the flesh, since someone may abstain from the pleasures of the flesh because of idolatry or the error of some heresy, and yet even then, although he may seem to restrain and curb the lust of the flesh, he is convicted by apostolic authority of living according to the flesh, and is shown to perform damnable works of the flesh by abstaining from the pleasures of the flesh?” And shortly afterward: “Why, then, does the Teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth call all these and similar things works of the flesh, unless he wishes, by that manner of speech in which the whole is signified by a part, that the human being himself be understood by the name ‘flesh’?” Thus far Augustine. Second, I answer with St. Thomas (*Commentary on Galatians* V) that sin may be called carnal in two ways: with respect to its completion, and in this sense only those are called carnal which are completed in the pleasure of the flesh—namely, lust and gluttony; or with respect to its root, and in this sense all sins are called carnal, insofar as the soul is weighed down by the corruption of the flesh, as Wisdom IX says. Through this corruption the intellect is weakened, so that it can more easily be deceived and is hindered from its perfect activity. Hence vices follow from it, such as heresies, sects, and other things of this kind; and in this way it is said that the tinder of sin is the beginning of all sins. Thus St. Thomas.] although the blessed Apostle declared all vices generally to be carnal, since he numbered enmities, angers, and heresies among the works of the flesh (Galatians V), nevertheless, in order to gather more carefully their cures and natures, we distinguish them by a twofold division. For among these [Note: St. Augustine indicates the same distinction in the passage cited above, chapter 4.] we say that some are carnal and others spiritual. We call those carnal which particularly concern the tinder and sensation of the flesh, which the flesh so enjoys and feeds upon that they even stir tranquil minds and sometimes drag them, against their will, into assent to its desire. Concerning these the blessed Apostle says to certain people: “We all once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the will of the flesh and of our thoughts, and were by nature children of wrath, even as the others” (Ephesians II). But we call those spiritual which arise from the impulse of the soul alone and not only contribute nothing pleasurable to the flesh, but also afflict it with the most grievous languors, while nourishing only the soul, in its miserable delight, with the food of a wretched pleasure. Therefore the former require the simple medicine of the heart, while the carnal require, as we have said, a twofold cure for their restoration to health. Hence [Col. 0614A] those who pursue purity gain great benefit by first removing from themselves the very materials of these carnal passions, through which either an occasion for them or a recollection of them may be generated in the soul, which is still sick. For a twofold illness requires a twofold cure. From the body, therefore, so that desire may not attempt to burst into action, the alluring image and material must necessarily be removed; and for the soul, so that it may not conceive desire even in thought, more diligent meditation on Scripture, watchful solicitude, and withdrawal into solitude should usefully be applied. [Note: Cassian says similarly elsewhere (Book VI of the *Institutes*, chapter 3): “The other vices are also usually cleansed through human interaction and exercise, and are in a certain manner cured by the very offense of falling: anger, sadness, and impatience, for example, are healed through meditation of the heart and watchful solicitude, as well as through the frequent and continual provocation of the brothers. While they are more often stirred up and more frequently reproved, they reach health more quickly. But this vice requires bodily affliction and contrition of heart, as well as solitude and withdrawal,” and so forth.] In the other vices, however, human companionship does no harm; indeed, it contributes greatly to those who truly desire to be free from them, because they are more strongly reproved through frequent association with people; and while they are more frequently provoked and revealed, [Col. 0614B] they arrive at health through a swift remedy.

## CHAPTER V. How Our Lord Alone Was Tempted without Sin

Therefore, although our Lord Jesus Christ is declared, according to the Apostle’s statement, to have been tempted in every respect according to our likeness, he is nevertheless said to have been tempted [Note: The Apostle’s words in Hebrews IV: “For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses, but one tempted in every respect according to our likeness, without sin.” (See Conference 22, chapter 10 and following.) The phrase “according to our likeness” means “in likeness,” or “after our pattern,” and “as we are”; “without sin” means without sin properly so called, because he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth, 1 Peter II. Thus he willed to be tempted while nevertheless not being led into any sin by the temptation; or “without sin” may be understood in an improper sense, that is, without concupiscence, the tinder and goad of sin; or, as St. Thomas explains it, without the slightest movement of sin. He did not possess that law in his members warring against the law of his mind and taking him captive under the law of sin (Romans VI), which the Apostle also subsequently calls “sin” (Romans VII), because it arises from sin and inclines toward sin, as was stated above (Conference 4, chapter 7) from the Council of Trent. How, then, someone may ask, is Christ said to have been tempted in every respect according to our likeness? First, according to the interpretation of many, Christ is said to have been tempted in every respect, that is, afflicted in every way in which we human beings are accustomed to be afflicted. In Scripture, temptation often means the suffering of evils by which a person’s steadfastness and patience are tested. Ecclesiasticus XXXIV: “What does he know who has not been tempted?” James I: “Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations,” and so forth. And again: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested,” and so forth. Christ, therefore, was tempted in every respect because he experienced all the evils of this life that are common to the whole human race, such as hunger, thirst, weariness, pain, sadness, fear of death, and death itself. Second, if being tempted means being solicited to sin—as this abbot understands it when discussing Christ’s temptations—Christ is said to have been tempted in every respect because he experienced whatever he could experience, that is, whatever was suitable to his person and condition and consistent with the end he had set before himself, namely, the redemption of humanity. Thus he was tempted by the devil in every respect, that is, in every way in which it was possible and fitting for him to be tempted, but only through external suggestion. He could not be tempted internally, whether by the devil, by the flesh, or by the world. For interior temptation does not occur without some pleasure and movement of concupiscence, which exists only in sinful flesh—that is, flesh wounded by sin and not completely healed. It was not fitting for Christ to assume such a nature, but rather one free and immune from every contagion of sin, lest he himself, according to the nature assumed, should require a redeemer and liberator. St. Gregory clearly teaches and explains this doctrine in these words (*Homily 16 on the Gospels*): “It must be known,” he says, “that temptation proceeds in three ways: suggestion, pleasure, and consent. When we are tempted, we usually fall into pleasure or even consent, because, having been propagated from the sin of the flesh, we carry within ourselves that from which we endure our conflicts. But God, who was incarnate in the Virgin’s womb and had come into the world without sin, endured no contradiction within himself. He could therefore be tempted through suggestion, but the pleasure of sin did not wound his mind; and therefore all that diabolical temptation was external, not internal.” So too Damascene, Book III of *The Orthodox Faith*, chapter 20: “The Evil One suggested from outside, not through thoughts,” and so forth. Christ heard the devil proposing to him the sins of gluttony, vainglory, and pride, and their advantages; nor is there any need to believe that he thought nothing about these matters. Nevertheless, no appetite, however slight, was aroused in him toward them, whereas in us these things are never, or only very rarely, separated so that we think about them without some affection.] “without sin” (Hebrews IV), that is, without the contagion of this passion, having in no way experienced the goads of carnal desire by which we must be pierced even unknowingly and unwillingly; for there was in him no likeness of human generation or conception, as the archangel announced the manner of his conception: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke I).

## CHAPTER VI. On the Manner of the Temptation by Which the Lord Was Tempted by the Devil

[Note: Below he says: “In these three vices,” namely, gluttony, cenodoxia—that is, vainglory—and pride. St. Gregory likewise explains Christ’s threefold temptation in nearly the same way (*Homily 16 on the Gospels*) and compares it with Adam’s temptations, except that he places avarice third instead of pride; but improperly and abusively, as can be gathered from Gregory’s own words, using avarice for the desire or appetite for exaltation, which is nothing other than pride. This does not, however, exclude the possibility that the temptation of avarice or philargyria was also joined to it, as will be said below; St. Thomas admits this as well (Part III, question 41, article 4). Gregory’s words are as follows: “The ancient enemy rose up against the first man, our parent, with three temptations, for he tempted him with gluttony, vainglory, and avarice; but by tempting him he overcame him, because he subjected him to himself through consent. He tempted him through gluttony when he showed him the fruit of the forbidden tree and persuaded him to eat. He tempted him through vainglory when he said, ‘You will be like gods.’ And he tempted him through the advancement of avarice when he said, ‘Knowing good and evil.’ For avarice concerns not only money but also exaltation. It is rightly called avarice when exaltation is sought beyond measure. For if the seizure of honor did not belong to avarice, Paul would never have said of the only-begotten Son of God, ‘He did not regard equality with God as a thing to be seized’ (Philippians III). In this way the devil drew our parent into pride, by stirring him up to an avarice for exaltation. But in the same ways by which he struck down the first man, the tempter was defeated by the second man. He tempts through gluttony when he says, ‘Command that these stones become loaves of bread.’ He tempts through vainglory when he says, ‘If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down.’ He tempts through avarice for exaltation when he shows him all the kingdoms of the world and says, ‘All these I will give you, if you fall down and worship me.’ But he is overcome by the second man in the same ways by which he boasted of having overcome the first, so that, captured at the very entrance by which he had held us when he entered, he might depart from our hearts.” Thus far Gregory. St. Thomas also follows and explains the same order of temptations in Part III, question 41, article 4. St. Augustine, however, does otherwise in Treatise 2 on the First Epistle of John.] For he too had to be tempted in those passions, possessing the incorrupt image and likeness of God, in which Adam was tempted while he still remained in that inviolate image of God—namely, gluttony, cenodoxia, and pride—not in those vices into which Adam was entangled after the transgression of the commandment, when the image and likeness of God had been violated and he had already fallen through his own fault. Gluttony is represented by his presuming to eat from the forbidden tree; cenodoxia by the words, “Your eyes will be opened” (Genesis III); and pride by the words, “You will be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Genesis III). In these three vices, therefore, we read that the Lord and Savior was also tempted. Gluttony, when the devil said to him, “Command that these stones become loaves of bread”; cenodoxia, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down”; pride, when, showing him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, he said, “All these I will give you, if you fall down and worship me” (Matthew IV). Through this example he taught us that, just as he was assailed along the same lines of temptation as Adam, so we too should learn how to overcome the tempter (see Conference 24, chapter 17). Therefore one is called Adam and the other Adam (1 Corinthians XV): the former first toward ruin and death, the latter first toward resurrection and life. Through the former the whole human race is condemned; through the latter the whole human race is liberated. The former was fashioned from rough and untouched [Col. 0616B] earth; the latter was born from the Virgin Mary. [Note: Some copies read *hujusmodi* (“of this kind”) instead of *hujus* (“of this one”), and I think this is more correct, so that the reference is to Christ. If it referred to Adam, it should say *illius* (“of that one”), not *hujus* (“of this one”), since the immediate preceding subject is Christ. The meaning, therefore, is: Just as it was fitting—that is, congruent and consistent with reason—for Christ, the new Adam, to take upon himself and endure those same temptations mentioned above, namely of gluttony, vainglory, and pride, by which the first Adam had been assailed and cast down, so it was not necessary for him to experience another temptation, namely that of the flesh or lust, which the first Adam would not have experienced in the state of innocence.] Therefore, just as it was fitting for him to undergo temptations of this kind, it was not necessary for him to go beyond them. For he who had conquered gluttony could not be tempted by fornication, which proceeds from gluttony’s abundance and root; even the first Adam would not have been cast down by it unless, first deceived by the devil’s allurements, he had admitted the passion that generates it. For this reason the Son of God is not said to have come absolutely in sinful flesh, but in the likeness of sinful flesh (Romans VIII): although true flesh was in him—eating, drinking, sleeping, and truly receiving the piercing of the nails—he did not have the real sin of that flesh—the sin incurred through transgression—but only its semblance.
