For he did not experience the fiery goads of carnal desire, which rise up even against our will, nature itself now administering them; rather, by sharing in the nature, he assumed a certain likeness of it. For while he truly fulfilled everything that belongs to our condition, and [Note: Natural and harmless infirmities, namely. There are certain human infirmities that, although they have arisen from the fault and transgression of our first parents, do not of themselves impel or draw one toward guilt, but rather provide material for the exercise of virtue, such as hunger, thirst, weariness, and mortality. Christ fittingly assumed infirmities of this kind, which are truly harmless; hence, as sacred Scripture attests, he hungered, thirsted, became weary, and died for us. There are other passions that are natural if we consider fallen nature, but unnatural if we consider its rectitude and original institution. They proceed not only from the fault and transgression of our first parents but also provide an occasion and path toward guilt, or are connected with guilt, such as inclination toward evil, slowness toward good, ignorance, the tinder of sin or concupiscence, and sensuality. It was not fitting for Christ to assume these (Damascene, Book III, chapter 20, *On the Orthodox Faith*). For he who came to take away sins ought certainly not to be subject to any fall, stain of sin, or tinder that provokes guilt; he should be not only, as God, *anamártētos* (ἀναμάρτητος), that is, impeccable, but also, as the human mediator, redeemer, and high priest, “holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners,” as the Apostle says in Hebrews VII, lest the familiar saying, “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke IV), rightly be directed against him. Moreover, the passions of the first kind, which, although they arise from guilt, do not incline toward guilt, are of two sorts. Some are common to the whole human race and accompany the whole of human nature; others are personal and particular, affecting not all human nature but certain individual persons, such as various kinds of disease, blindness, deafness, deformity, and things of this kind. Since Christ had come to repair and restore human nature generally and without distinction of persons, it was fitting for him to assume only natural, not personal, infirmities. Hence he did not contract diseases or bodily deformities, which usually arise in human beings through some impediment of nature or by accident.] he bore all human infirmities, he was consequently thought to be subject also to this passion, [Col. 0617B] so that through these infirmities he might seem also to bear in his flesh the condition of this vice and sin. Finally, the devil tempts him only in those vices in which he had also deceived the first man, supposing that, as a man, he too might similarly be mocked in the others if he perceived him cast down in those by which he had overthrown the former. But he could not introduce into the second contest the second disease [Note: Namely, lust, which had sprouted in human beings from the root of the principal vice, gluttony, and so forth.], which had sprung from the root of the principal vice, after having been defeated at the first attempt. For he saw that Christ had in no way assumed the initial cause of this illness, and it was pointless to hope for the fruit of sin from one whom he clearly saw to have received none of its seeds or roots. Although Luke, who places that last temptation—“If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down” (Luke IV)—second, could be understood in such a way that this is the passion of pride, while the temptation that Matthew places third, in which the devil shows him all the kingdoms of the world in an instant and promises them to him, may be understood as the passion of philargyria—that is, after he had failed to tempt him with fornication following his victory over gluttony, he moved on to philargyria, which he knew to be the root of all evils; and after being defeated there as well, he dared not impose any of the vices that followed, since he knew that they sprang from that root and tinder. He then moved on to the final passion of pride, knowing that even the perfect can be assailed after all the vices have been conquered; through it he remembered that he himself, when he was Lucifer, and many others had fallen from heaven without any incitement from preceding passions. [Note: The evangelist Luke (in the same passage) places the second temptation reported by Matthew not second but last. Hence interpreters ask which evangelist preserved the order of events and times. For the evangelists, like the other sacred writers, do not always observe the chronological order of events in their narratives. Most agree, however, that Matthew records Christ’s temptations in the order in which they occurred, while Luke did not follow that order, as can be gathered with some clarity from the Gospel text. First, St. Cajetan says that although Luke recounts Matthew’s third temptation second and his second temptation last, he does not say which of them came first; consequently no chronological order of these temptations can be derived from Luke. Matthew, however, explicitly explains their order in time when he says, “Again the devil took him up onto a high mountain.” For after he had once said, “Then”—that is, after the first temptation had been completed—“the devil took him into the holy city,” and afterward added, “Again he took him onto a mountain,” he clearly showed by “again” that he took him onto the mountain second, having first taken him into the holy city. Thus Cajetan. There is another argument as well. After Christ said to the devil, “Go, Satan,” the Evangelist adds, “Then the devil left him.” It is very likely that the devil, terrified and defeated immediately by Christ’s words, departed at once; those words, moreover, were spoken on the mountain and nowhere else. As for conduct and the present passage, St. Thomas also noted this (in the work cited above, response to objection 5): the evangelists appear to have followed a different order because sometimes one proceeds from vainglory to desire, and sometimes conversely, which agrees suitably with our text.] According to this order, therefore, which we have said is described by the evangelist Luke, the very enticement and pattern of the temptations with which the most cunning enemy attacked either the first or the second Adam also correspond most elegantly. To the former he says, “Your eyes will be opened”; to the latter he shows all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. There he says, “You will be like gods”; here, “If you are the Son of God” (Genesis III; Matthew IV).

## CHAPTER VII. On the Completion of Cenodoxia and Pride without Bodily Service

And so that we may discuss the effects [Note: That is, the execution or completion of the other vices, as above.] of the other passions as well—the account of which was necessarily interrupted by our exposition of gluttony and the Lord’s temptation—in the same order that we had proposed, cenodoxia and pride are often completed without any bodily action [Note: Cenodoxia and pride are spiritual, not carnal, vices, because they do not require bodily action; hence they are especially characteristic of the devil, as is envy. On this matter see St. Augustine, *The City of God* XIV, chapter 3.]. For what need have they of bodily action, when the will alone to seek praise and attain human glory abundantly brings about the ruin of the captive soul? Or what bodily effect did that ancient pride of Lucifer have [Note: We treated this at considerable length in Book XII, chapters 3 and 4.] except that he conceived it solely in mind and thought, as the prophet recalls (Isaiah XIV): “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of God I will set my throne. I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High’”? Just as he had no one to incite this pride, so thought alone brought it to the completion of its crime and perpetual ruin, even though no works of the tyranny he had desired followed after it.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Philargyria, Its Being Outside Nature, and the Difference between It and the Natural Vices

Philargyria and anger, although they are not of the same nature—for the former is outside nature, while the latter seems to possess in us an original seed [Col. 0619C] [Note: Namely, the irascible appetite, which was given to human beings as an attendant of reason and an avenger of desire, as Damascene says in Book II, chapter 16, of *The Orthodox Faith*.]—nevertheless arise in a similar manner: they generally conceive the causes of their agitation from outside. Indeed, those who are still weaker frequently complain that they have fallen into these vices through irritation or the prompting of certain persons, and blame the provocation of others for having driven them headlong either into anger or into philargyria. That philargyria is outside nature is clearly evident from the fact that it is not proved to have an original beginning in us, nor is it conceived from material that enters into participation in the soul or flesh and into the substance of life. Nothing, it is certain, comes to the use or necessity of common nature except daily food and drink; all other materials, however zealously and lovingly they may be preserved, are nevertheless shown by the very use of life to be foreign to human need. Therefore, existing outside nature, it attacks only lukewarm and badly grounded monks. [Note: Because it concerns a good external to human nature, namely riches, by which it is aroused and agitated. See Book VII of the *Institutes*, chapters 2 and 3, where it is called a foreign war, and “outside nature,” since it takes its beginning in the monk from no other source than the idleness of a corrupt and lukewarm mind, usually from a poorly begun renunciation—that is, conversion—and from love toward God founded in lukewarmness, as is said here of its assault upon badly grounded monks.] But those things that are natural do not cease to attack even the most proven monks, including those living in solitude. And this is shown to be so true that [Note: Caelius Rhodiginus gives an amusing example of this matter (*Ancient Readings*, Book XX, chapter 23), speaking of Themistocles, the Athenian commander, who, while touring the islands subject to his authority, collected money here and there. He approached the Andrians and pressed them more aggressively, saying, “I bring you two gods: force and persuasion.” They, no less wittily, replied that two other great gods also dwelt among them: poverty and impossibility, which prevented money from being paid to him. Plutarch is also the source for the report that, when money was brought into the territory of the Lacedaemonians, those who imported it were punished with death, since this oracle had been given to the kings Alcamenes and Theopompus: “The love of money will destroy Sparta.” Hence among the ancients that Laconian custom was praised: as brevity in speech, so frugality in material things; indeed, the state stood for more than five hundred years without the use of money. King Agesilaus, who first introduced its use, was badly regarded by his people and earned very poor credit among them.] we even recognize that some nations are entirely free from this passion, that is, philargyria, because they never acquired the disease of this vice through use and habit. We also believe that the earlier world, which existed before the Flood, remained for a very long time ignorant of the madness of this desire. [Note: That is, the first age of the world, from Adam to the Flood, when most people were either farmers or shepherds; their flocks were their only wealth, and they lived through exchanging them. Hence the word *pecunia* (“money”) is derived, according to Cassiodorus (*Variorum*, Book VII, letter 32), from the hide of cattle (*pecus*).] In each of us who truly renounces the world, this desire is also rightly proved to be extinguished without any labor, when, after casting away all his possessions, he chooses the discipline of the monastery in such a way that he does not permit even a single denarius to remain for himself. We can find many thousands of witnesses to this, people who, after dispersing all their possessions in a very brief moment, uprooted this passion so completely that they are no longer even slightly assailed by it. Nevertheless, those who fight constantly against gluttony cannot be secure unless they contend with great vigilance of heart and abstinence of body.

## CHAPTER IX. That Sadness and Acedia Are Not Generated by Any External Provocation, as the Other Vices Are

[Note: What Cassian understands by sadness and acedia should be examined in their proper places and treatments (Books IX and X of the *Institutes*).] Sadness and acedia, as we said above, are not generally generated by any external provocation. For [Note: Cassian himself says similarly in Book X, chapter 1: “Acedia is related to sadness and is more commonly experienced by those who are wandering and solitary; it is a more hostile and frequent enemy to those living in the desert.”] they are known frequently and most bitterly to afflict those who are solitary and established in the desert, mixed with no human companionship whatsoever. Anyone who has lived in solitude and experienced the battles of the inner person will easily confirm the truth of this through experience itself.

## CHAPTER X. On the Agreement of the Six Vices and the Kinship of the Two That Differ from Them
Although these eight vices have different origins and produce different effects, the first six—namely, gluttony, fornication, avarice, anger, sadness, and acedia—are nevertheless connected with one another by a certain kinship and, so to speak, by a chain, in such a way that the excess of the preceding becomes the beginning of the following.

> **[Note: Col. 0621B]** Understand this as applying for the most part; it often happens otherwise, and indeed in the reverse order. On this subject there is a most excellent discussion by John Climacus, which I have thought necessary to reproduce here in full:
>
> “Some people,” he says (*Step* 31, “On Discernment”), “asked me to judge a matter difficult to decide, one that surpasses all the people of our age and is contained in none of the books that have come into our hands. They said: ‘What are the particular origins of the eight principal vices? Or which of the three most principal vices is the beginning and offspring of the other five?’
>
> “I frankly confessed my ignorance in so ambiguous a matter, but I heard this from most blessed men: the mother of fornication is the desire of the belly; the mother of acedia is vainglory. I again begged those men worthy of everlasting remembrance to teach me which of the eight vices were born from which, and from what lineage each derived its origin.
>
> “They, instructing me gently and most peacefully, without any vice of self-exaltation, said that there is no order or rational arrangement in foolish matters, but complete perversity and instability. Those blessed men persuaded me of this by true examples and arguments, bringing forward many pieces of evidence. We have inserted some of them into this work, so that from them we may now understand other matters very clearly.
>
> “For example, untimely laughter sometimes arises from fornication, but sometimes from vainglory, when someone inwardly and shamefully glories in himself; at other times it is produced by indulgence. Much sleep sometimes arises from indulgence, sometimes from fasting, when those who fast become puffed up; at other times from acedia, and at other times from nature. Excessive talk sometimes takes its beginning from vainglory, sometimes from gluttony. Acedia, again, sometimes arises from indulgence and from contempt of the fear of God. Blasphemy is properly the offspring of pride; yet it sometimes also arises from judging one’s neighbor in the same matter, or from the wicked envy of demons. Hardness of heart sometimes originates in satiety, but often also in insensibility and in a corrupt affection. This affection, in turn, arises through many other channels—through fornication, vainglory, avarice, and gluttony. Malice, again, arises from fear and anger. Hypocrisy begins especially when someone is excessively pleased with himself, governs himself by himself, and does not live according to another’s direction.
>
> “Moreover, contraries are generated by contraries.” Thus far Climacus.

To this I would also like to add this statement of the Lord Thomas, which concerns this subject (*Summa theologiae* I–II, q. 48, art. 3), on the order and comparison of vices:

> **[Col. 0622B]** “Sin lacks order on the side of aversion—namely, aversion from the immutable good, God—for on this side it has the character of evil. Evil, however, according to Augustine (*On the Nature of the Good*), is the privation of measure, form, and order. But on the side of conversion—namely, conversion toward the creature—it regards a certain good; and therefore on this side it is said to possess order” (*Tom. VI, ch. 4*).

Thus writes Saint Thomas, indicating that certain vices have toward other vices an order and relation of principality like that which the head has toward the other members; for this reason they are called capital or principal vices.

The excess of the preceding therefore produces the beginning of the following: from the abundance of gluttony fornication necessarily sprouts; from fornication, avarice; from avarice, anger; from anger, sadness; and from sadness, acedia. Consequently, we must resist these in a similar manner and by the same method, and must always begin our struggles against the following vices from the preceding ones.

The harmful breadth and height of any tree dries up more easily if its roots, on which it depends, have first either been exposed or cut away. Likewise, the troublesome waters will continually dry up when their generating spring and flowing channels have been stopped with diligent care.

Therefore, in order for acedia to be conquered, sadness must first be overcome; in order for sadness to be driven away, anger must first be expelled; in order for anger to be extinguished, avarice must be trampled down; in order for avarice to be uprooted, fornication must be restrained; and in order for fornication to be overthrown, the vice of gluttony must be disciplined.

The remaining two—vainglory and pride—are likewise joined to one another by the relation that we described above concerning the other vices, so that the growth of the first becomes the origin of the other.

> **[Note: Col. 0622C]** The same Climacus confirms this opinion in several places, and certainly in passages worthy of notice. In *Step* 21 he says:
>
> “When most people discuss the vices, they usually define vainglory separately from pride, and therefore say that there are eight principal and primary vices. But the theologian Gregory, along with many other teachers, has handed down that there are seven, and I follow them above all. For who has conquered vainglory and has been proud? Their difference from one another is like that naturally existing between a child and a man, and between wheat and bread: the one is the beginning, the other the end.”
>
> By these words he plainly signifies that cenodoxia, or vainglory, is related to pride as a child is related to a man and wheat to bread—that is, as a beginning or origin is related to an end, since a man comes from a child and bread from wheat.
>
> Again, in the same place, after recounting the words of an old man who had called cenodoxia the mother of the spirit of pride, he adds:
>
> “When I asked him how vainglory is the mother of pride, he replied: ‘Praises elevate and inflate the mind. But when the soul has risen to exaltation, pride then takes hold of it, lifts it all the way to heaven, and casts it down to the abyss.’”
>
> And at the end of the same chapter:
>
> “A worm, when it has grown, is often carried upward after receiving wings; so perfected vainglory gives birth to pride, which is the guide, chief, and completion of all evils.”
>
> Again, in *Step* 22 he introduces this remarkable personification of cenodoxia and pride:
>
> “I discovered,” he says, “that this seductress, pride, had come with me headless, carried upon the shoulders of her mother, cenodoxia. Binding both of them with the bond of obedience and beating them with the whip of lowliness, I compelled them to tell me how they had entered me.
>
> “When they were compelled, they said: ‘We have neither beginning nor birth, for we are the rulers and mothers of all vices. A little contrition of heart, beginning from submission, attacks us; but we do not allow ourselves to be subjected to anyone’s authority, and therefore we also stir up rebellions in heaven.
>
> “‘To hear the whole matter at once: we are the mothers of everything opposed to humility; for everything that supports humility is exceedingly hostile to us. We are often accustomed to follow disgrace, obedience, lack of anger, forgetfulness of injuries, and service.
>
> “‘Our offspring are spiritual falls, anger, detraction, bitterness, shouting, rage, blasphemy, hypocrisy, hatred, envy, contradiction, and preferring to be governed by one’s own direction rather than another’s. Obedience is the one and only thing in which all the efforts of our strength fail.
>
> “‘Therefore, under compulsion, we tell you: if you always accuse yourself before the Lord from the innermost affection of your heart, you will despise us as spiders. For, as you see, pride is the horse that cenodoxia mounts. But holy humility and continual self-accusation will laugh both at the horse and at its rider, singing most sweetly the triumphal song: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified”’ (Exod. 15), and so forth.”

Thus far John Climacus, a man highly spiritual and exceptionally experienced in such matters.

But opposed to this stands the teaching of the Lord Gregory, who establishes pride as the mother and queen of all vices and calls cenodoxia, or vainglory, its first offspring:

> **[Col. 0623C]** “The first offspring of pride is vainglory,” he says (*Morals* XXXI, ch. 31), and so forth.

To this both Holy Scripture, reason, and the authority of all theologians give support (Saint Thomas, II–II, q. 132, art. 4), as we have shown elsewhere (*Institutes* V, ch. 1, and XII, ch. 1).

It must therefore be considered how these opinions can be reconciled. Cajetanus, in his commentary on Saint Thomas at the place cited above, solves this knot subtly and, as is his custom, rather obscurely, in the following way:

> **[Col. 0623D]** “It must be noted that an end and the means to the end have one relation according to the order of intention and another according to the order of execution. For health is prior in intention to medicine, but in execution medicine is applied before health is acquired.
>
> “Therefore, since pride and vainglory stand to one another as end and means, excellence—which is the end of pride—is prior in intention to appearance—that is, the manifestation of excellence before others—which is the end of vainglory.
>
> “But according to the order of execution, we first seek to appear, so that, once we have become manifest and distinguished, we may attain excellence. The proud seek to display themselves as endowed with virtue, power, or ability, so that, once they are seen, they may be loved and honored. Once loved and honored, they are considered distinguished. Those who are considered glorious are close to being exalted to dignities and positions of excellence. Thus glory is a means for acquiring excellence, and through this it arises from pride, as a means arises from an end.
>
> “Nevertheless, glory also arises from excellence as a property arises from its subject, since we consider it of little value to excel unless this comes to the knowledge of others, in accordance with the saying: ‘Your knowledge is nothing unless another knows that you know it.’
>
> “Both of these forms of proximity, connection, and dependence exist on the side of things considered in themselves. Therefore, speaking according to the things themselves, vainglory stands in relation to pride [the precise wording is uncertain in the supplied text], although from our perspective pride sometimes arises from vainglory.”

So speaks Cajetanus, more or less.

From this we understand that pride may be called the mother of cenodoxia, and conversely, but in different respects. Since the object of pride is one’s own excellence, while the object or end of cenodoxia is the manifestation of that excellence, it is naturally prior to desire excellence—which belongs to pride—to desire the manifestation of that excellence—which belongs properly to cenodoxia.

Yet because the manifestation of our excellence and perfection can cause us subsequently to become more proud, and through it to seek dignities and offices, cenodoxia is also not improperly called the mother and origin of pride. In this way the statements found in Climacus should be understood. Thus Cajetanus responds to the objection brought against him from this passage.

For the excess of cenodoxia gives birth to the fuel of pride.

But these two vices are completely opposed to the preceding six, and are not bound to them by a similar alliance. They not only do not receive from those six any occasion for their generation, but are also aroused in the contrary way and order. For when those six vices have been uprooted, these two bear fruit more vigorously; they sprout and grow more actively through the death of the others.

Accordingly, we are attacked by these two vices in a different manner. We fall into each of the six vices when we have been overcome by the vices preceding them; but into these two we are in danger of falling when we are victorious, and especially after triumphs.

All vices, therefore, just as they are generated by the growth of those preceding them, are purified by the diminution of those preceding vices. For this reason, in order that pride may be excluded, cenodoxia must be suffocated. And thus, whenever the preceding vices have been overcome, the following ones will come to rest; and when the preceding vices have been extinguished, the remaining passions will wither away without effort.

Although these eight vices, as we have said, are connected and intermingled with one another in this way, they are nevertheless more specifically divided into four pairings and unions: fornication is joined to gluttony by a special exchange; anger to avarice; acedia to sadness; and pride is familiarly joined to cenodoxia.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Origin and Nature of Each Vice

Let us now discuss separately the kinds of each vice.

> **[Note: Col. 0624B]** Cassian, *Institutes* V, ch. 23:
>
> “Gluttony has a threefold nature. One kind compels a person to anticipate the appointed hour of eating; another rejoices only in the stuffing and saturation of the belly with every kind of food; the third delights in more carefully prepared and more appetizing foods.”
>
> So far Cassian. Hugh of Saint Victor likewise indicates three kinds of gluttony, or of gula, and excellently admonishes that a threefold caution or discipline must be used against them. He depicts monks devoted to the vices of the belly in a remarkable manner in these words:
>
> “There are three forms of discipline in eating: first, discipline regarding what one eats; second, discipline regarding how much one eats; third, discipline regarding how one eats.
>
> “Discipline regarding what one eats means that one should neither seek excessively expensive and delicate foods, nor demand excessively rare and unusual foods, nor desire food prepared too lavishly and elaborately. In the first case luxury is censured, in the second curiosity, and in the third superstition.
>
> “There are some whose throats suffer from a sufficiently ridiculous infirmity: they cannot swallow anything except rich and delicate foods. Whenever plain or frugal food is offered to them, they immediately allege indigestion, dryness of the chest, blockage of the head, or some similar excuse.
>
> “Others energetically reject the delicacies and luxury of foods, but then despise the use of ordinary foods with no less—and no more tolerable—insolence. They seek new and unusual kinds of food, so that often, for the sake of one man’s belly, a crowd of servants runs through all the neighboring villages and can scarcely restrain the insolence of a single appetite, whether by pulling up unknown roots from distant desert mountains, dragging a few little fish from the depths of the lowest pools after careful searching, or gathering branches at an untimely hour from dry thickets.
>
> “I cannot readily see what vice agitates such people unless it is that, through a certain insolence of mind, they take pleasure in having many people occupied in their service, or because, through the swelling of self-exaltation, they wish to appear as different from everyone else in merit as they are different in food.
>
> “Others apply an excessively superstitious zeal to preparing food, devising infinite varieties of boiling, frying, and seasoning. They desire food sometimes soft, sometimes hard, sometimes cold, sometimes hot, sometimes boiled, sometimes roasted, sometimes seasoned with pepper, sometimes with cumin, sometimes with salt, according to the custom of pregnant women.
>
> “Such people should certainly not only be censured but also ridiculed, since, like tavern-keepers, they stretch out their palate at every moment to stimulate their taste.
>
> “To cure these vices, therefore, the rigor of discipline is necessary, restraining such insolence of the appetite within a fixed limit, so that it does not spread itself toward the desire for excessive delicacies, novelties, or superstitious preparations of food.”

Thus far Hugh Victorinus, also cited on this subject by Turrecremata (*Treatise* 103 on the Rule of Saint Benedict), with the additional testimony of Saint Jerome (*Letter* 2 to Nepotianus), in which he sharply attacks that third kind of gluttony and gluttonous people:

> “What benefit is there in refusing oil while seeking troublesome and difficult foods—figs, pepper, nuts, dates, fine flour, honey, pistachios? The whole cultivation of gardens is disturbed so that we may not eat ordinary bread.”

There are three kinds of gluttony. The first urges the monk to hurry toward eating before the appointed and lawful hour; the second rejoices in filling the belly and devouring every kind of food; the third desires more carefully prepared and exceedingly delicate foods.

These three strike the monk with no slight loss unless he strives to free himself from all of them with equal diligence and vigilance. For just as the breaking of the fast must in no way be presumed before the canonical hour, so the greed of the belly and the costly and elaborate preparation of food must likewise be cut away.

From these three causes different and most grievous diseases of the soul are produced.

> **[Note: Col. 0626C]** Here again *health* is used for *illness*, as frequently in Cassian and in Tertullian’s *On Baptism*, as we have noted elsewhere.

From the first arises hatred of the monastery, and from this hatred there gradually grows a horror of and inability to endure the same dwelling; this will undoubtedly soon be followed by departure or very rapid flight.

From the second arise the burning goads of luxury and lust.

The third also weaves inextricable snares of avarice around the necks of its captives, and never allows the monk to be established in the complete nakedness of Christ.

We can detect traces of this passion in ourselves by the following indication. If, while detained at a meal by one of the brothers, we are not content to eat the food with the flavor with which it has been seasoned by the person who offers it, but demand, with troublesome and unrestrained insistence, that something be poured over it or added to it, then we reveal this vice.

This must not be done at all, for three reasons. First, the monk’s mind must always be engaged in the exercise of endurance and moderation and,

> **[Note: Col. 0626C]** “I have learned,” says the Apostle, “in whatever circumstances I am, to be content” (Phil. 4)—that is, I have learned to be satisfied with what is present and with what is at hand.

according to the Apostle, must learn to be content with the circumstances in which it finds itself. No one will be able to restrain either the hidden or the greater desires of the body if, offended by the taste of a little insipidity, he has been unable to discipline the delicacies of his throat even for a moment.

Second, it sometimes happens that the particular food we request is unavailable at that moment, and we bring shame upon the need or frugality of our host by publicly revealing a poverty which he preferred to be known to God alone.

Third, the flavor that we ask to have added may sometimes displease others, and, while wishing to satisfy our own appetite and desire, we may be found to inflict an injury upon many. For this reason this freedom must be disciplined in us by every means.

> **[Note: Col. 0626D]** Fornication—that is, lust—has several forms, among which are simple and properly called fornication (Saint Thomas, II–II, q. 154, art. 1). Here, however, the kinds of fornication are certain common and general ways in which the sin of lust is committed, as is clear from the examples marked in the text.

There are three kinds of fornication. The first is completed through the sexual union of the two sexes. The second occurs without the touch of a woman; for this reason Onan, the patriarch Judah’s son, is read to have been struck by the Lord, and in Holy Scripture it is called uncleanness (Gen. 38). Concerning this the Apostle says: “To the unmarried and the widows I say that it is good for them if they remain as I am. But if they cannot contain themselves, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn” (1 Cor. 7).

The third is conceived in the soul and mind. Concerning this the Lord says in the Gospel: “Everyone who looks at a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5).

The blessed Apostle declares that these three kinds must be extinguished in the same way:

> “Put to death, therefore, your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust” (Col. 3), and so forth.

And again, concerning two of them, he says to the Ephesians:

> “Fornication and uncleanness must not even be named among you” (Eph. 5).

And again:

> “Know this: no fornicator, or unclean person, or avaricious person, who is an idolater, has an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (ibid.).

Since these three are to be avoided by us with equal vigilance, their similar and single exclusion from the kingdom of Christ warns us away from them alike.

> **[Note: Col. 0626D]** The same author, *Institutes* VII, ch. 4, and XII, ch. 26.

There are three kinds of avarice. The first does not allow those who renounce their riches and possessions to be stripped of them. The second persuades us to reclaim with greater greed what we have scattered or distributed to the needy. The third compels us to desire and acquire what we did not previously possess at all.

> **[Note: Col. 0626D]** Gregory of Nyssa (*On the Powers of the Soul* IV, ch. 13) and Damascene (*On the Orthodox Faith* II, ch. 16), followed by Saint Thomas, differ somewhat here. They establish three kinds of anger.
>
> They call the first *ὀργή* (*orgē*) and *χολή* (*cholē*). Saint Thomas calls it choleric or bilious anger, which has a beginning and quickly passes.
>
> They call the second *μῆνις* (*mênis*). Saint Thomas calls it madness, describing it as anger that persists and grows old; in Latin this is called *simultas*, hostility or resentment.
>
> They call the third *χόλος* (*cholos*). Saint Thomas calls it fury, describing it as anger that waits for the time of revenge (II–II, q. 152, art. 3).

There are three kinds of anger. One burns inwardly; in Greek it is called *θυμός* (*thymos*). Another breaks out into speech, action, and deed; it is called *ὀργή* (*orgē*). Concerning these the Apostle says: “But now put away from yourselves all anger and indignation.”

The third is not discharged fervently at once like the others, but is stored up for days and periods of time; it is called *ἄλυς* (*alys*; alternatively *μῆνις*, *mênis*).

> **[Note: Col. 0627C]** Cuychius thought this should be corrected in this way. “For *ἄλυς*,” he says, “signifies great and prolonged anxiety of mind. Hence *ἀλυσθαίνω*: ‘I am anguished, exhausted, tormented.’ Nor would it be inappropriate to read *μανία* (*mania*), which appears in the Plantinian copy, since *mania* signifies that insanity in which the mind is deprived of tranquility and stability.”
>
> “This is Cuychius’s view. Ciaconius, however, using the Vatican copies, reads: ‘which is called *μῆνις* (*mênis*).’ This reading seems more probable and more consistent with the rest of the text. For Damascene derives *mênis* from *παρὰ τὸ μένειν*—that is, from the fact that it remains and is not discharged at once, but is stored up for days and periods of time, as stated here. Hence Suidas says: ‘*Mênis*: abiding and persistent anger.’ Others say *ὀργὴν πεπαλαιωμένην*—that is, hatred or anger grown old.”

All these forms must be condemned by us with equal horror.

> **[Note: Col. 0627C]** Elsewhere he more distinctly enumerates four kinds of sadness arising from different causes (*Institutes* IX, chs. 4 and 13).

There are two kinds of sadness. One arises either when anger comes to an end, or from damage inflicted and from a desire that has been obstructed and frustrated. The other descends from an irrational anxiety of mind or despair.

There are two kinds of acedia. One drives those who are burning with it toward sleep; the other urges them to leave and flee from their cell.

> **[Note: Col. 0627C]** These matters are treated more fully in *Institutes*, chs. 3 and 5. He distinguishes the kinds of pride in the following chapter; that discussion had been omitted here.

Although cenodoxia is multiform and manifold and is divided into different kinds, it nevertheless has two forms. The first is that by which we exalt ourselves over bodily and visible things; the second is that by which we are inflamed with the desire for vainglorious praise on account of spiritual and hidden things.

## CHAPTER XII. In What Respect Cenodoxia Is Useful

**[Col. 0627B]**

Vainglory is therefore usefully assumed by beginners—but only by those who are still being stirred by carnal vices—in the following respect: if, for example, at the time when they are being strongly driven by the spirit of fornication, they bring to mind either the dignity of the priestly office or the opinion of everyone, by which they are believed to be holy and pure, and thus judge the impure impulses of desire to be shameful and unworthy either of their reputation or of that order, they may at least by this consideration turn away from them, restraining the greater evil by the lesser.

> **[Note: Col. 0627D]** This seems capable of being understood in two ways.
>
> First, cenodoxia may be taken properly as the vice or sin of vainglory. In this sense someone may overcome the temptation of the flesh through cenodoxia or vainglory when, in order not to incur disgrace and in order to be considered chaste and continent, he abstains from the wicked act toward which he was otherwise being strongly driven.
>
> Saint Gregory often warns that we are attacked at one time by several enemies (*Homily* 12 on Ezekiel): while one openly displays itself in front, another secretly lies in ambush behind. In this sense cenodoxia can be said to be usefully assumed by beginners—that is, by novices or the imperfect—insofar as it is less evil to succumb to cenodoxia than to the temptation of lust.
>
> Yet this is not to cast down the temptation, but to be cast down and prostrated by the temptation. For, as Saint Augustine says, carnal desire is not healed by another desire (*Book IV to Boniface, against two Pelagian letters*, ch. 4). The Apostle also says that evil must not be done so that good may result (Rom. 3).
>
> In another way, cenodoxia may here be taken improperly—not for the vice or sin itself, but for a certain form or appearance of it. Thus someone may abstain from fornication through fear of disgrace and dishonor, or out of consideration for his priestly dignity or religious status, or because of the shamefulness and unworthiness of the sin. This indeed occurs among beginners and the imperfect.
>
> For those who are more advanced, though not yet perfect, attend to higher and more elevated reasons: offense against God, the loss of divine grace and eternal goods, God’s benefits—especially the redemption and passion of Christ—the love owed to God, and other matters of this kind.

It is therefore in this respect that cenodoxia is usefully assumed by beginners, namely by those who are still being urged on by carnal vices. If, for example, at the time when they are being pressed by the spirit of fornication, they bring to mind either the dignity of the priestly office or the opinion of everyone, by which they are believed to be holy and immaculate, and thus avoid the impure impulses of desire as shameful and unworthy either of their reputation or of their rank, then by this consideration at least they restrain the greater evil by the lesser.

> **[Note: Col. 0628C]** Although it is not a sign of great perfection when someone drives away the spirit of fornication through fear of disgrace or brings to mind the dignity of the priestly office or the opinion of everyone, it is nevertheless not properly the vice of cenodoxia, nor is it any sin if someone abstains from sin for this reason, as is clear from what has been said. Accordingly, the author speaks improperly when he says that in this way the greater evil is checked by the lesser.

For it is better for someone to be troubled by the vice of cenodoxia than to fall into the heat of fornication, from which after the fall he may either be unable to recover or may recover only with difficulty.

One of the prophets elegantly expressed this meaning as if speaking in the person of God:

> “For my sake I will hold back my fury, and with my praise I will bridle you, so that you may not perish”—

that is, so that, while you are held by the praises of cenodoxia, you may not fall headlong into the depths of hell and be irreversibly submerged in the completion of mortal sins.

Nor is it surprising that this passion should possess such power that it can restrain someone rushing into the pit of fornication, since the experience of many has very frequently shown that, once it has corrupted someone with the plague of its poison, it makes him so tireless that it prevents him from feeling even two-day or three-day fasts.

We also know that some people in this desert have often confessed that, when they lived in the monasteries of Syria, they could endure five days without food without difficulty, whereas now they are driven by such intense hunger from the third hour that they can scarcely postpone their daily fasts until the ninth.

On this matter the abbot Macarius gave a beautiful answer to someone asking why he was troubled by hunger from the third hour in the desert, when, while living in a coenobium, he had often gone for entire weeks without eating and had not felt hunger:

> **[Note: Col. 0628D]** I do not yet know to which Macarius this saying should be attributed. A similar account is found in Sophronius in these words (*Spiritual Meadow*, ch. 155):
>
> “There were two secular brothers in Constantinople, both very religious and both great fasters. One of them came to Raithu, renounced the world, and became a monk. After some time his secular brother also came to Raithu to see his brother the monk.
>
> “While he stayed with him, the secular man saw his monk brother eating at the ninth hour. He was scandalized and said to him: ‘Brother, when you were living in the world, you never ate before sunset.’
>
> “The monk then said to him: ‘Indeed, brother, when I was in the world, my ears nourished me, for the vainglory and praise of men refreshed me greatly and made the labor of fasting easier.’”

Macarius replied:

> “Because here there is no witness to your fasting to nourish and sustain you with his praises. There, the finger of men and the nourishment of cenodoxia fattened you.”

This image of what we have said—namely, that when cenodoxia intervenes, it excludes the vice of fornication—is expressed very suitably and distinctly in the Book of Kings. There we read that Nabuchodonosor, king of the Assyrians, went up against the people of Israel, who had been taken captive by Necho, king of Egypt, and transferred them from the borders of Egypt to his own region—not in order to restore them to their former liberty and native land, but to lead them away to his own territories, carrying them farther away than they had been when they were captive in the land of Egypt (4 Kings 23 and 24).

This image may also suitably be applied here. Although it is more tolerable to serve the vice of cenodoxia than that of fornication, it is nevertheless more difficult to depart from the domination of cenodoxia. A captive carried away, in a certain sense, over a longer distance will return with greater labor to his native soil and ancestral freedom. The prophetic rebuke is therefore rightly directed at him:

> “Why have you grown old in a foreign land?” (Baruch 3).

Someone is rightly said to have grown old in a foreign land when he is not renewed and transformed from earthly vices.

> **[Note: Col. 0629C]** The same author, *Institutes* XII, chs. 2 and 24. See the notes there.

There are two kinds of pride: the first is carnal, the second spiritual, and the latter is more destructive. It attacks especially those whom it finds to have progressed in certain virtues.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Varied Assault of All the Vices

Although these eight vices assail the entire human race, they do not attack everyone in the same way. In one person the spirit of fornication occupies the chief place; in another, fury rides supreme; in another, cenodoxia claims tyrannical rule; in another, pride holds the citadel.

Although it is certain that everyone is attacked by all of them, each of us struggles in a different manner and order.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Establishing the Struggle Against the Vices According to Their Assault
Therefore we must take up the battle against these vices in such a way [Note: [Col. 0629C–D] Here is commended the particular examination by which one strives to discover the vice toward which one inclines more, whether by nature or by bad habit, and into which one falls more frequently. On this St. Chrysostom says in Homily 73 to the people: “I ask each of you that, if not before, at least henceforth, when he has recognized which fault vexes him more than the others, he should strive to cut it off from his soul, and, using a certain devout reflection as though a spiritual sword, free himself from the vice.” And in Homily 82 on John: “Let us therefore learn both to review our vices and to correct them in due time: one this month, another the next; and so in succession let us become better [Col. 0629D]. For thus, ascending as it were by certain steps, we shall reach heaven by Jacob’s ladder.”]

that each person, examining which vice most greatly assails him, should undertake his principal struggle against it, fixing all the care and concern of his mind upon attacking and watching it; directing against it the arrows of daily fasts; against it, at every moment, hurling the frequent sighs of his heart and volleys of groans; devoting to it the labors of vigils and the meditations of his heart; continually pouring out tears of prayer to God; and especially and unceasingly asking him for the extinction of this assault.

For it is impossible for anyone to obtain triumph over any passion before he has understood that he cannot achieve victory in the struggle by his own diligence or labor, although, in order to be cleansed, he must nevertheless remain day and night in complete care and concern. And when he has felt himself freed from it, let him again survey the hidden places of his heart with similar attention and discover which of the remaining vices he has found to be more savage; then let him bring all the spiritual weapons of his warfare especially against it. Thus, having always overcome the stronger enemies, he will easily and swiftly obtain victory over those that remain. For his mind will be made stronger by the progress of its triumphs, and the battle that follows against weaker enemies will make the outcome of the succeeding struggles more ready for him.

This is what customarily happens among those who, before the kings of this world, have been accustomed to fight beasts of every kind, in contemplation of the rewards. This kind of spectacle is commonly called a *pancarpum*.

[Note: Ciaconius noted that the *pancarpum* was a type of spectacle in which men hired for that purpose by payment fought with beasts of every kind, as is suggested here. The heretic Secundinus once used this word while mocking St. Augustine, who accepted the Old Testament literally: “Perhaps, after the contest of Dares and Entellus, you wished to watch Jacob and his *pammachia*? Or were you planning to see the number of the Amorites, or a *pancarpum* in Noah’s ark?” Thus he referred to what we read in Genesis VI: “You shall therefore take with you all food that may be eaten, and you shall store it with you, and it shall be food both for them and for you.” He calls this a *pancarpum*. Augustine replies: “By the name *pancarpum*, which is customary in theatrical entertainments because of beasts of every kind, you harass Noah’s ark, which, through every kind of animal, prefigured the future Church from all nations” (*Against Secundinus*, ch. 23), and so forth.

Emperor Justinian likewise writes in Novel 105: “[Note: Ciaconius quotes Greek here, but it is corruptly printed; I have therefore substituted the Latin.] It will fill the people with great pleasure to see such a spectacle—a so-called *pancarpum*—like a grove arranged with the fruits of every tree, in which men fighting with wild beasts, and seeking the reputation of boldness, as well as beasts struck down by them, [and so forth].”

If someone asks why that hunt in which men fought with beasts of every kind was called a *pancarpum*—a word meaning “every fruit”—I might say that it happened by transference. Since they called a dish (*lanx*) filled with every kind of fruit and carried into the temples of the gods a *pancarpia*, they also, by transference, called wreaths woven from various flowers *pancarpiae*, although they contained no fruit, as Festus Pompeius testifies. Hence they called a hunt composed of every kind of beast a *pancarpum*. Thus Ciaconius, omitting a few details.

Cuychius gives a somewhat different explanation, though aiming at nearly the same point: “Perhaps,” he says, “the name was derived from the fact that those who emerged victorious were given *pancarpiae*, that is, crowns composed of various and nearly every kind of flower.”

From what has been said, the distinction between *pancarpum* and *pancarpia* is sufficiently clear. The terms *eucarpus* and *eucarpia* are also used with the same or a related meaning (Tertullian, *Against the Valentinians*, ch. 12).]

These men, I say, when they have seen beasts that are more savage either in bodily strength or in the fury of their wildness, take up the struggle of their first encounter against them. Once these have been destroyed, they overthrow the rest—those that are less terrifying and less violent—with an easier outcome.

So too, when we have overcome the stronger vices and weaker ones have succeeded them, perfect victory will be prepared for us without any danger. Yet one must not suppose that, while fighting principally against one vice and, as it were, negligently watching for the attacks of the others, one can thereby be more easily wounded by an unexpected blow. This will certainly not happen. For it is impossible that someone who has armed the attention of his mind against the assault of any vice out of concern for the cleansing of his heart should not also possess a general horror of the other vices and a similar vigilance against them.

How, indeed, will he deserve to obtain victory over the passion from which he wishes to be freed, if he makes himself unworthy of the reward of purification through contagion with other vices? But when the principal intention of our heart has undertaken a particular battle against one passion, he will pray more attentively for that passion, entreating with special concern and zeal that he may deserve to watch it more carefully and thereby obtain swift victory.

That we ought to practice this order of battles, but nevertheless not trust in our own strength, the Lawgiver also teaches us in these words:

“You shall not fear them, because the Lord your God is in your midst, a great and terrible God. He himself will consume these nations in your sight, little by little and in stages. You will not be able to destroy them all at once, lest perhaps the beasts of the earth multiply against you. And the Lord your God will deliver them before you and kill them until they are utterly destroyed” (Deuteronomy VII).

## CHAPTER XV. That we can do nothing against the vices without God’s help, and that we must not become elated by victory over them

[Col. 0631C] He likewise warns us that we must not become elated by victory over them:

“After you have eaten and been filled, built beautiful houses and dwelt in them, and possessed herds of cattle and flocks of sheep, gold and silver and an abundance of all things, let your heart not be lifted up, and do not forget the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery, and was your leader through the great and terrible wilderness” (Deuteronomy VI).

Solomon likewise says in Proverbs:

[Note: The Vulgate reading is: “When your enemy has fallen, do not rejoice, and when he has been overthrown, do not let your heart exult.”]

“If your enemy has fallen, do not rejoice; and when he has been overthrown, do not become elated, lest the Lord see it and it displease him, and he turn away his anger from him” (Proverbs XXIV).

That is: lest, perceiving the elation of your heart, he withdraw from your enemy’s assault, and, abandoned by him, you begin again to be troubled by the passion that, through God’s grace, you had previously overcome.

[Col. 0631D] The Prophet would not have prayed, saying, “Do not deliver the soul that confesses you to the beasts, Lord” (Psalm LXXV), unless he had known that, because of the swelling of the heart, some people are handed over again to the same vices which they had overcome, in order that they may be humbled.

[Note: Gregory, *Moral Works* XIX, ch. 17: “Those who overcome vices perish when they grow proud of their victory, as the enemy himself falls upon them. Eleazar struck down an elephant in battle; but he fell beneath the very creature he had destroyed (1 Maccabees VI). Whom, then, does this signify—the one whom his own victory crushed—if not those who overcome vices but, by growing proud beneath the vices they have subjected, succumb to them? For one dies, as it were, beneath the enemy whom he has overthrown when he becomes elated over the fault he has overcome.”]

Therefore we ought to be certain, instructed both by the actual experience of things and by the innumerable testimonies of Scripture, that we cannot overcome such great enemies by our own strength unless we are upheld by God’s help alone, and that we must refer the sum of our victory to him every day.

[Note: [Col. 0631D–0632D] “Let us be upheld,” he says, “by the help of God alone,” and rightly so. For although free will cooperates—for, as the Apostle testifies, “we are God’s fellow workers” (1 Corinthians V)—we are not upheld by our own will; rather, it itself must be upheld by God’s help. Moreover, that a human being cannot overcome any temptation by the powers of nature alone, without God’s help, is the settled teaching of Catholics against the Pelagian heretics and the ancient tradition of the Church. On this see Bellarmine, Book II, *On Grace and Free Will*, ch. 7. Cassian confirms the same doctrine with many testimonies of Scripture in *Institutes* XII, chs. 16 and 17, and *Conference* 3, ch. 17 and final chapter.]

Thus the Lord also admonishes us through Moses:

“Do not say in your heart, when the Lord your God has destroyed them in your sight: ‘Because of my righteousness the Lord has brought me in, so that I might possess this land,’ when these nations have been destroyed because of their wickedness” (Deuteronomy IX).

“For you will not enter to possess their lands because of your righteousness or the uprightness of your heart; rather, because they acted wickedly, they were destroyed as you entered.”

I ask: what could have been said more plainly against our pernicious opinion and presumption, by which we wish to attribute everything we do either to free choice or to our own diligence?

“Do not say in your heart,” he says, “when the Lord your God has destroyed them in your sight: ‘Because of my righteousness the Lord has brought me in, so that I might possess this land.’”

Did he not express this clearly to those whose eyes of soul are open and whose ears are ready to hear? When the battles against carnal vices have gone well for you, and you see yourself freed from their filth and from the conduct of this world, do not attribute this to your own virtue or wisdom, inflated by the outcome of the battle and by victory; do not believe that through your labors, zeal, and freedom of choice you have obtained victory over spiritual wickedness or carnal vices. Beyond doubt, you could not have prevailed over them in the slightest degree unless the Lord’s help had fortified or protected you.

## CHAPTER XVI. The meaning of the seven nations whose lands Israel received, and why in one place seven nations and in another many nations are mentioned

[Note: More will be said about these matters below, in chapter 22.]

These are the seven nations whose lands the Lord promises to give to the children of Israel when they have gone out from Egypt. Since all these things happened to them in figure, according to the Apostle, we ought to accept them as written for our admonition. Thus it is said:

“When the Lord your God has brought you into the land which you are entering to possess, and has destroyed many nations before you—the Hittite, the Girgashite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite—seven nations much more numerous than you and stronger than you, and the Lord your God has delivered them to you, you shall strike them down to complete destruction” (Deuteronomy VII).

The reason they are said to be much more numerous is that there are more vices than virtues.

[Note: The reason is obvious: the good is constituted by a perfect cause, whereas evil arises from individual defects, as is commonly stated among philosophers. Moreover, several vices are opposed to a single virtue, and the vices themselves also oppose one another. See Augustine, Letter 29.]

And therefore, although seven nations are counted in the catalogue, in the account of their conquest they are mentioned without assigning a number. For it is said: “And he has destroyed many nations before you.”

[Note: St. Gregory, *Moral Works* XXXI, ch. 31, left this number and multitude of vices and vicious passions to be understood under the name and likeness of commanders and an army:

“The vices that test us, which in an invisible battle serve the pride ruling over them against us, advance in one case like commanders and follow in another like an army. For not all faults enter the heart with equal force. While the greater and fewer approach an unguarded mind first, the lesser and innumerable pour into it in troops.

“Pride itself, the queen of vices, when it has fully seized a conquered heart, immediately hands it over to the seven principal vices, as to its commanders, to be laid waste. An army follows these commanders, because from them without doubt arise the troublesome multitudes of vices.”

Gregory then shows that the seven commanders are the seven capital vices, each of which has its own army. We shall present this shortly below.]

For the people of carnal passions that proceeds from this sevenfold fuel and root of vices is more numerous than Israel. From it spring murders, quarrels, heresies, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies, banquets, drunkenness, slanders, entertainments, filthy speech, lies, perjuries, foolish talk, buffoonery, unrest, rapacity, bitterness, shouting, indignation, contempt, murmuring, temptation, despair, and many other things that it would take too long to enumerate.

Although we judge these things to be trivial, let us hear what the Apostle thought of them and what judgment he pronounced concerning them:

“Do not murmur,” he says, “as some of them murmured and perished by the destroyer” (1 Corinthians X).

And concerning temptation:

“Let us not tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him and perished by serpents” (ibid.).

Concerning slander:

“Do not love to slander, lest you be uprooted” (Ecclesiasticus XVIII).

And concerning despair:

“Having become despairing, they handed themselves over to indecency for the practice of every kind of error, in uncleanness” (Ephesians IV).

That shouting, like anger, indignation, and blasphemy, is condemned, we are taught most clearly by the words of the same Apostle, who commands:

“Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy be removed from you, together with all malice” (Ephesians IV);

and many other similar things.

Although these are much more numerous than the virtues, once those eight principal vices have been conquered—from whose nature it is certain that they proceed—all the others immediately become quiet and, together with them, are destroyed in a common and perpetual annihilation.

[Note: Gregory, in the same work, enumerates almost the same kinds and offspring of vices, but in reverse order and in much greater number, and he seems clearly to have imitated this passage:

“From vainglorious disobedience arise boasting, hypocrisy, quarrels, obstinacy, discord, and presumptuous innovations. From envy arise hatred, whispering, slander, rejoicing at one’s neighbor’s adversity, and distress at his prosperity. From anger arise quarrels, swelling of mind, insult, shouting, indignation, and blasphemies. From sadness arise malice, rancor, faintheartedness, despair, sluggishness concerning the commandments, and wandering of the mind toward unlawful things. From avarice arise betrayal, fraud, deceit, perjuries, unrest, violence, and hardness of heart against mercy. From gluttony arise foolish joy, buffoonery, uncleanness, excessive talk, and dullness of understanding. From lust arise blindness of mind, lack of consideration, inconstancy, rashness, self-love, hatred of God, attachment to the present age, and fear—or despair—of the future.

“Since, therefore, the seven capital vices produce such a multitude of vices from themselves, when they come to the heart they drag along with them, as it were, the troops of a following army.”

Thus far St. Gregory.]

For from *gastrimargia* arise banquets and drunkenness; from fornication, filthy speech, buffoonery, entertainments, and foolish talk; from *philargyria*, lies, fraud, thefts, perjuries, the pursuit of shameful gain, false testimonies, violence, inhumanity, and rapacity; from anger, murder, shouting, and indignation; from sadness, rancor, faintheartedness, bitterness, and despair; from acedia, idleness, drowsiness, importunity, unrest, wandering, instability of mind and body, verbosity, and curiosity; from vainglory, quarrels, heresies, boasting, and presumption concerning innovations; from pride, contempt, envy, disobedience, blasphemy, murmuring, and slander.

That these plagues are also stronger, we plainly perceive from the struggle against nature itself. For the pleasure of carnal passions or vices fights more powerfully in our members than the pursuits of virtue, which are acquired only through the greatest contrition of heart and body.

But if you also contemplate with spiritual eyes those innumerable troops of enemies whom the blessed Apostle enumerates when he says:

[Note: Some supply only the particle “only” or “merely,” so that the meaning is: “Our struggle is not merely against flesh and blood, but also, and especially, against demons,” and so forth. Others supply nothing and interpret it as follows: although the struggle we have with flesh and blood, considered in itself, is serious and burdensome, it is nevertheless, when compared with the struggle against demons, slight and almost nothing, so great are the strength and deceitfulness of demons. Others explain it as referring to the more perfect, for whom, once the flesh has been subdued and the impulses of anger and desire overcome, a great struggle remains against the rulers of darkness. Flesh and blood are weaker enemies; demons attack us more gravely and more fiercely in proportion as we become holier and more observant of chastity. Finally, others understand “flesh and blood” to mean mortal human beings, as Christ says to Peter: “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you,” that is, no human being (Matthew XVI).]

“Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians VI);

and that passage concerning the righteous man in Psalm Ninety:

[Note: St. Jerome and Bernard also interpret this as referring to spiritual enemies.]

“A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand”—

you will clearly see that they are far more numerous and stronger than we are, being carnal and earthly, since they have been granted a spiritual and aerial substance (see Conferences 7 and 12).

## CHAPTER XVII. Germanus’s question concerning the comparison between the seven nations and the eight vices

Germanus: How, then, are there eight vices that attack us, when Moses counted seven nations that oppose the people of Israel? Or in what way is it advantageous for us to possess the lands of the vices?

## CHAPTER XVIII. Serapion’s answer: how the number of eight nations is completed according to the eight vices

Serapion: Everyone’s settled judgment is that there are eight principal vices that attack the monk. Since these are figuratively named under the designation of nations, not all of them are now listed because Moses—or rather the Lord through him—was speaking in Deuteronomy to those who had already gone out from Egypt and had been freed from one exceedingly powerful nation, namely, the Egyptians (Deuteronomy VII).

This figure is also found to apply most correctly to us, since we have been released from the snares of the world and are known to have been freed from *gastrimargia*, that is, the vice of the belly or gluttony. We are now engaged in a similar struggle against the remaining seven nations, the first—that has already been conquered—not being counted. Its land, moreover, is not given to Israel for possession; rather, by the Lord’s command, Israel is ordered to leave it forever and depart from it.

For this reason fasts must be moderated in such a way that, through excessive abstinence—which has brought on bodily collapse or weakness—it is not necessary to return again to the land of the Egyptians, that is, to the former desire of the throat and the flesh, which we cast away when we renounced this world.

This is what those suffered figuratively who, having gone out into the wilderness of the virtues, again desired the pots of meat over which they had sat in Egypt.

[Note: St. Jerome, *Against Jovinianus* II, ch. 10: “The people of Israel had been expelled from Egypt and were to be brought into the land of promise flowing with milk and honey, yet they desired the Egyptian meats, melons, and other things (Exodus XVI; Numbers XI). ‘Would that we had died, struck down by God in the land of Egypt, when we sat beside pots of meat.’ And again: ‘Who will feed us with meat? The fish that we ate freely in Egypt come to mind, and cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic. But now our soul is dry; our eyes see nothing except manna.’ While scorning the food of angels, they sighed for Egyptian meats.”]

## CHAPTER XIX. Why the single nation of Egypt is to be abandoned, whereas the seven are ordered to be destroyed

The reason why the nation in which the children of Israel were born is not ordered to be utterly destroyed, but only its land to be abandoned, whereas the other seven are ordered to be destroyed completely, is this: however ardently we may be inflamed in spirit when we enter the wilderness of the virtues, we will never be able to be free from the proximity, instruction, and—so to speak—daily association of *gastrimargia*.

For the natural and inborn affection for food and nourishment will always live [Lipsius, in the margin: “flourish”] in us, even though we hasten to cut off its excessive appetites and desires. These cannot be destroyed in every respect, just as they ought to be avoided by a certain turning away.

For concerning this it is said:

“Do not provide for the flesh in its desires” (Romans XIII).

Since, therefore, we retain the affection for this care of the body—which we are commanded not to cut off in every respect, but to exercise without desires—we plainly do not destroy the Egyptian nation, but separate ourselves from it through a certain discretion. We do not think about excessive or luxurious feasts, but, according to the Apostle, are content with daily food and clothing (1 Timothy VI).

This is also commanded figuratively in the Law:

“You shall not abominate the Egyptian, because you were an immigrant in his land” (Deuteronomy XXIII).

For necessary nourishment is not to be denied to the body without either injury to the body itself or sin against the soul.

But the impulses of those seven disturbances, as wholly harmful, must be completely expelled from the recesses of our soul. Concerning them it is said:

“Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy be removed from you, together with all malice” (Ephesians IV).

And again:

“But fornication, and every uncleanness, and avarice must not even be named among you, nor indecency, nor foolish talk, nor buffoonery” (Ephesians V).

We can therefore cut off the roots of these vices that have been superimposed upon nature, but we will by no means be able to cut off the use of *gastrimargia*.

[Note: Here *gastrimargia* is taken improperly—or rather abusively—as including the necessary nourishment and care of the body; likewise, above *cenodoxia* was used for every desire for human glory, including a lawful and reasonable desire.]

For however far we may have progressed, we cannot cease to be what we were born to be. That this is so is shown both by the life and conduct of us insignificant people and by those of all the perfect. Even when they have cut away the impulses of the remaining passions and seek the wilderness with the whole fervor of their mind and the nakedness of their body, they nevertheless cannot be freed from the provision of daily food and the preparation of their annual bread.

## CHAPTER XX. The nature of *gastrimargia*, compared to an eagle

[Note: Dionysius puts it more simply: “The figure of gluttony,” and so forth. Concerning the nature of the eagle—its very high flight and its voracity, which are discussed here—see Pliny, Book X, ch. 3.]

The figure of this passion, by which even the most spiritual and exalted monk must necessarily be constrained, is very suitably represented by the likeness of an eagle.

Although it has been raised by the loftiest flight above the height of the clouds and has hidden itself from the eyes of all mortals and from the face of the entire earth, it is again compelled by the necessity of its belly to descend to the bottoms of the valleys, come down to earthly things, and become entangled with dead and decaying corpses.

The evidence makes it entirely clear that the spirit of *gastrimargia* cannot be cut away or extinguished completely, as can the other vices, but that its barbs and excessive appetites can only be blunted and restrained by strength of soul.

[Note: Concerning the vice of *gastrimargia*, or gluttony, and its importunity and violence above those of the other vices, St. Gregory writes consistently in *Commentary on 1 Kings*, ch. 11:

“Of the serpent it is said in Genesis that it was more crafty than all the animals. If the likeness of this serpent is sought among the vices, what is more similar than the violent movement of *gastrimargia*, that is, gluttony? The movement of lust, the crime of theft, the desire for shameful gain, the impulse of anger, the worldly bitterness of sadness, the sluggishness of acedia, the appetite for vainglory, and the swelling of pride are plainly detestable. But the vice of gluttony is more deceitful in proportion as it is more hidden. For it presents food to the body as though it were necessary; yet, while it abundantly refreshes the flesh, it plunges the sword of lust into the mind. It persuades us to do what is not a sin; but from the point at which eating is received as though it were not a sin, the soul is subjected to the sin of lust. Hence the serpent is shown in paradise approaching the woman to deceive her through the vice of gluttony: it suggested one thing but obtained another, so that, while it displayed something to be eaten, it brought unexpected death. This serpent therefore signifies the appetite of gluttony, because it creeps in under the appearance of just necessity and spreads the poison of impious pleasure.”

And in *Moral Works* XXX, ch. 28: “It must be understood that pleasure in food so disguises itself under necessity that scarcely anyone, however perfect, can distinguish it. For while necessity demands that a debt be paid, pleasure supplies the means of satisfying desire; and gluttony rushes all the more securely into ruin the more safely it hides itself under the honorable name of fulfilling necessity.”]

## CHAPTER XXI. The persistence of *gastrimargia* argued against the philosophers

[Note: [Col. 0637D–0638C] Palladius, *Lausiac History* 83, relates a similar—or certainly the same, though somewhat differently told—story of Serapion Sindonites in these words: “He [Serapion], in the course of his frequent journeys, came to Greece; and when he had remained three days at Athens, there was no one to give him bread. When the fourth day came, he was very hungry. For involuntary hunger is a serious matter, having unbelief as its ally. Standing over the city’s mound, where those who were lowly and despised in the city gathered, he began to lament vehemently and tearfully, crying: ‘Men of Athens, bring help!’ All who wore cloak and cap ran to him and said: ‘What is the matter? Where are you from, and what are you suffering?’ He replied: ‘I am Egyptian by birth; but since I have been away from my true homeland, I have fallen among three creditors. Two have indeed withdrawn from me after their debt was paid, having no ground on which to summon me; but one does not leave me.’ Eagerly seeking the creditors so that they might satisfy them, they asked him where they were: ‘Who is troubling you? Show him to us, so that we may bring you help.’ Then he said to them: ‘Avarice, gluttony, and fornication have troubled me. I have neither gold nor any other possession, nor do I indulge in the luxuries that nourish this disease; consequently they no longer trouble me. But I cannot get away from gluttony. For I have eaten nothing for four days now, and my belly continues to trouble me, demanding its customary debt, without which I cannot live.’ Then certain philosophers, suspecting that he was a beggar, gave him a coin. He put it, when received, in a baker’s shop and, taking bread, departed. Then the philosophers recognized that he was truly endowed with virtue; and after they had given the baker the price of the bread, they recovered the coin.”]

The nature of this vice was elegantly expressed by one of the elders in a dispute with philosophers who, because of his Christian simplicity, thought they could harass him as though he were a rustic. He represented it under the following form of a problem:

“My father left me liable to many creditors. I paid the others in full and was freed from all their demands; but I cannot satisfy one of them by making a daily payment.”

When they, not understanding the force of the question proposed, begged him for an explanation, he said:

“By my natural condition I was bound to many vices. But when the Lord inspired me with a desire for freedom, I renounced all of them as most troublesome creditors, abandoned this world, and likewise cast away from me all the property that had come to me by inheritance from my father. I satisfied them and was completely freed from them. But I was in no way able to be free from the goads of *gastrimargia*.

“For even though I reduced it to a small and most insignificant amount, I do not escape the force of its daily compulsion. I must continually be pressed by its demands, pay an endless kind of debt through constant service, and impose upon myself its inexhaustible levy.”

[Note: That is, to pay the daily debt, or to supply the nourishment that is owed. “*Indictio*,” says Ciaconius, was a type of assessment or tribute imposed upon estates or persons, as Asconius Paedianus and Paulus write in *I. Quaero. De Usufructu Legato*. Here, however, it seems to be used more generally for an exaction. The subject is the importunity of the belly, which demands daily food as though a perpetual and inexhaustible tax were owed to it. Hence St. Gregory, *Moral Works* XXX, ch. 26, commenting on Job XXXIX, “He does not hear the cry of the tax collector”: “Some wish the belly to be understood by the tax collector in this passage. For it demands a certain debt from us, since by nature it seeks to have the daily fruit of human labor supplied to it. Therefore abstinent men—who are represented here by the word ‘wild asses’—when they restrain the violent desires of gluttony, disregard the words of the shouting tax collector.”]

Then the philosophers, who had previously despised him as an idiot and rustic, declared that he had thoroughly mastered the first parts of philosophy, namely, ethical discipline. They were greatly amazed that he had been able by nature to attain what no secular education had given him, although they themselves, through much labor and lengthy study, had been unable to reach such things.

This is sufficient to have said specifically about *gastrimargia*. Now let us return to the exposition of the discussion about the general knowledge of the vices that we had begun.

## CHAPTER XXII. Why God foretold that ten nations would be conquered by the people of Israel
When the Lord spoke to Abraham about things to come—which you did not at all ask about—it is not written that he enumerated seven nations, but ten, whose land he promised would be given to his offspring (Genesis 15).
