[Note: Namely, the Kenites, Kenizzites, Kadmonites, Hittites, Perizzites, Rephaim, Amorites, Canaanites, Girgashites, and Jebusites. Of these ten nations and peoples, whose lands God promised to give to Abraham’s descendants, only seven are mentioned and promised to the Jews in Exodus 3 and Deuteronomy 7. The remaining three passed by inheritance to others. One was the portion of Esau, Abraham’s grandson, from whom came the Idumeans; the other two were the portions of the sons of Ammon and Moab, who were sons of Lot, Abraham’s nephew. For Abraham’s sake God likewise handed over these two nations to them to be subjected and their lands possessed (Abulensis, on Deuteronomy 7, question 1). Hence, too, in Exodus 2 the children of Israel were forbidden to fight against the Idumeans, Ammonites, and Moabites.]

This number is clearly completed when idolatry and blasphemy are added—vices to which the impious multitude of the Gentiles and the blasphemous crowd of the Jews were subject before the knowledge of God and the grace of baptism, while they dwelt in intellectual Egypt.

[Note: Dionysius has shed some light on this rather obscure passage by means of the following paraphrase: “This number ten”—that is, the number of vices morally represented by those ten nations—“is clearly completed when idolatry and blasphemy are added” to the eight principal or capital vices discussed in this Conference. To these two sins were subject the impious multitude of the Gentiles and the blasphemous crowd of the Jews, dwelling in spiritual Egypt—that is, in this wicked age—before the knowledge of God and the grace of baptism. Thus Dionysius interprets intellectual, or spiritual, Egypt as the present wicked age. Yet it seems more likely that the vice of gluttony, or gastrimargy, should be understood here from the preceding allegory of the nations.]

But if someone renounces it, departs from it by God’s grace, and, having likewise conquered gastrimargy, reaches the spiritual wilderness,

[Note: That is, if, having become victorious over gluttony, he proceeds to the pursuit of virtue or to the soul’s spiritual condition and rest.]

he will undertake battle against only seven nations, having been freed from the assault of three.

## CHAPTER XXIII. How it is useful for us to possess the lands of the vices

The command that we should beneficially possess the territories of these destructive nations is understood as follows:

[Col. 0639B] Each vice has its own station in our heart. By claiming it for itself, it drives Israel—that is, contemplation of sublime and holy things—from the recesses of our soul and never ceases to oppose them. For virtues cannot dwell together with vices: “What partnership is there between righteousness and iniquity, or what fellowship between light and darkness?” (2 Corinthians 6).

But when the vices have been defeated by the people of Israel—that is, by the virtues fighting against them—the place that the spirit of lust or fornication had occupied in our heart will thereafter be held by chastity; the place seized by anger will be reclaimed by patience; the place occupied by sorrow producing death will be possessed by salutary and joy-filled sorrow; and the place trampled down by pride will be honored by humility. Thus, when each vice has been expelled, the virtues opposed to them will possess their places—that is, their affections.

[Note: Saint Jerome reports this interpretation of the name “Israel” as received and commonly circulated from the ancients, though he does not wholly approve it in his Hebrew Questions, where, among other things, he writes: “But that interpretation found in the Book of Names, which renders Israel as ‘a man seeing God,’ or ‘a mind seeing God,’ worn smooth by almost everyone’s speech, seems to me to have been interpreted not so much truthfully as forcefully,” and so forth. See the note on Book 7 of On the Incarnation, chapter 9.]

These are rightly called the children of Israel—that is, souls seeing God. When they have expelled all the passions of the heart, they should be regarded as having recovered their own possessions rather than invaded those belonging to others.

## CHAPTER XXIV. That the lands from which the Canaanite peoples were expelled had been assigned to the descendants of Shem

For, as ancient tradition teaches,

[Note: Saint Clement mentions this tradition in Book 1 of the *Recognitions*, where he teaches that God restored to the children of Israel the land of Canaan, which their ancestors had left to them by hereditary right and which they were to recover and possess by the right of return. Hence he calls it both their ancestral soil and their paternal inheritance. Saint Epiphanius agrees with him in *Panarion*, heresy 66, where he records the following: “Noah, saved from the Flood, together with his wife, his three sons, and as many daughters, alone divided the whole world among his three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth, casting lots at Rhinocorura. Rhinocorura”—or, as it is sometimes written, Rhinocolura—“may be interpreted as Neel, and the inhabitants call it by that name. In the Hebrew language it signifies ‘lots,’ since Noah cast lots there for his three sons.” And later: “The lot fell to Shem in the broad region of Palestine, Phoenicia, and Coele-Syria,” and shortly afterward: “When the lots had thus been divided, Noah summoned his three sons and decreed under oath that no one should invade or defraud his brother of his lot. But Canaan, the son of Ham, being greedy, invaded the land of Palestine and occupied it. It was called the land of Canaan because he dwelt there, having abandoned his own lot, which seemed to be filled with excessive heat. Sitting in the land of Shem, now called Judea, he fathered these sons: the Amorite, Girgashite, Merezite, Jebusite, Hivite, Arucite, Cethrite, Asevaite, Samarite, Sidonian, and Philistian.” Finally he adds: “In the days of Naasson, leader of Judah, and in the days of Joshua son of Nun, the children of Shem received their own land—not through injury, but by just judgment.” Thus far Epiphanius. He means that the children of Shem—that is, the Israelites or Jews, called out of Egypt—recovered by just war and lawful right their ancestral and native land, namely Judea, which also includes Palestine, assigned to them by lot, and expelled or subdued the Canaanites.]

these same lands of the Canaanites, into which the children of Israel are brought, had once been allotted to the children of Shem in the division of the world. Later, the descendants of Ham possessed them through the injustice of seizure, by force and power.

In this, too, God’s perfectly just judgment is demonstrated: he expelled the former from places belonging to others, which they had wrongfully occupied, and restored to the latter the ancient possession of their fathers, which had been assigned to their lineage in the division of the world.

This figure is also plainly applicable to us. For the Lord naturally assigned possession of our heart not to vices but to virtues. After Adam’s transgression, however, when the vices—like the Canaanite peoples—grew insolent and drove the virtues from their own region, then, when through God’s grace they have been restored to it by our diligence and labor, they should be regarded as having recovered their own lands rather than occupied those belonging to others.

## CHAPTER XXV. Various testimonies concerning the meaning of the eight vices

The eight vices are also signified in the Gospel as follows:

“When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it wanders through dry places, seeking rest, and does not find it. Then it says: ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ And when it comes, it finds it empty, swept, and decorated. Then it goes and takes with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself; and entering in, they dwell there. And the last state of that person becomes worse than the first” (Luke 11).

[Col. 0640C] Just as there we read of seven nations, apart from the Egyptians from whom the children of Israel had departed, so here seven unclean spirits are said to return, apart from the one who is first said to have gone out of the person.

Solomon likewise describes this sevenfold fuel of the vices in Proverbs:

[Note: Text of the Vulgate edition: “An enemy is recognized by his lips, when he has conceived deceit in his heart. When he lowers his voice, do not believe him, for there are seven wickednesses in his heart.”]

“If your enemy pleads with you in a loud voice, do not consent to him, for there are seven wickednesses in his soul” (Proverbs 26).

That is: if the spirit of gastrimargy, having been conquered, begins to flatter you through its abasement, as though asking you to relax something and grant it a concession beyond the measure of continence and the standard of proper strictness that you have begun to observe, do not yield to its submission. Nor, when the assault seems to smile upon you and you appear to have become somewhat quieter, freed from bodily impulses, should you return to your former laxity or your earlier desires for gluttony.

For through this the spirit that you had conquered says: “I will return to my house from which I came” (Luke 11). The seven spirits of the vices that immediately proceed from it will then be more severe for you than the passion that had first been overcome; they will soon drag you into worse kinds of sin.

## CHAPTER XXVI. That, once the passion of gluttony has been conquered, labor must be devoted to acquiring the other virtues

Therefore, while we apply ourselves to fasting and continence, we must hasten, immediately after conquering the passion of gluttony, not to allow our soul to remain empty of the necessary virtues, but to occupy all the recesses of our heart with them more diligently. Otherwise, when the spirit of lust returns, it will find us empty and unoccupied; and, no longer content to prepare an entrance for itself alone, it will bring with it into our soul this sevenfold fuel of the vices,

[Note: That is, the seven capital vices, from which the others arise and by which they are nourished. The author alludes to the parable that begins in Matthew and Luke: “When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person,” and continues: “Then it goes and takes seven other spirits more wicked than itself; and entering in, they dwell there, and the last state of that person becomes worse than the first.” These words signify nothing other than that those who are excellent—whether religious or secular—if at some time, having despised divine grace, become wicked, ordinarily become exceedingly wicked. It is as though, in place of the one unclean spirit that was previously in them before they became good, seven spirits enter them.

We experience this every day: no heretics are worse than those who, although once good Catholics, despise divine grace and the simplicity of the Catholic faith, disdain it as though it were the lightest food, and, wishing to sit beside pots of meat, become heretics—that is, having lost the faith, they return to Egypt, from which they had departed through faith.

Nor are there worse Catholics than those who, although once extremely devout, did not hold firmly to what they possessed. Thus Augustine said most truthfully (Letter 137) that he had seen neither better people than those who had advanced in monasteries nor worse than those who had fallen away from monasteries.

“They turned,” says David (Psalm 77), “into a crooked bow”—that is, into the condition of a hard bow, disobedient to the hand. If it happens to be bent back, it either breaks through its own force and momentum or is certainly transformed into a worse shape than the one it had before it was drawn.

This is what the learned Maldonado says. It agrees perfectly with the teaching of this chapter and confirms it; I have cited it for that purpose, and I hope no one will find it tedious.]

and make our final state worse than the first.

For afterward the soul will be more disgraceful and unclean, and will be punished with a heavier penalty, if, while it boasts that it has renounced this age, it is dominated by the eight vices than it formerly was when it lived in the world,

[Col. 0642A] even though it had not professed the discipline or taken the name of a monk.

[Note: Here we see an ancient practice of monastic profession, which we have mentioned more than once elsewhere (Book 4 of the *Institutes*, chapter 33). You may understand from this that among the monks of old there was not only the practice of obedience and monastic discipline but also a vow, which is understood by profession.]

These seven spirits are said to be worse than the first one that had gone out because the desire for gluttony—that is, gastrimargy—would not in itself be harmful if it did not admit other, more serious passions: fornication, avarice, anger, sorrow, and pride. There can be no doubt that these are harmful and deadly to the soul in themselves.

Therefore no one will ever be able to attain the purity of perfection if he hopes to acquire it through this one form of continence alone, namely bodily fasting, unless he understands that he must practice (*exercere*) it [Lipsius, in the margin: *exhibere*, ‘perform/offer it’] for this purpose: so that, with the flesh humbled by fasts, he may more easily begin the contest against the other vices, while the flesh does not grow insolent through the gluttony of satiety.

## CHAPTER XXVII. That the order of the battles is not the same as the order of the vices

It must nevertheless be understood that the order of the battles is not the same for everyone. For, as we have said,

[Note: He repeats and impresses upon us that most beneficial instruction by which he previously warned (chapter 14) that each person must examine and investigate which vice he is especially subject to, whether by nature or by bad habit, and must labor particularly to conquer and correct it: “Let each person,” he says, “investigate the vice by which he is most afflicted and begin against it the principal battle,” and so forth.]

we are not all attacked in the same way. Each of us must undertake the struggle according to the character of the battle by which he is principally assailed. Thus one person must first engage in conflict against the vice placed third, another against the fourth or fifth, and so on, according to the vices that hold the chief place in us. As the manner of the assault requires, so must we establish the order of our battles; according to this order, the outcome of victory and the triumph that follows will also lead us to the purity of heart and fullness of perfection.

Thus far Abba Serapion has discoursed to us on the nature of the eight principal vices. He has so clearly laid open the kinds of passions hidden in our hearts—their causes and affinities—which daily devastated us and which we previously could neither fully recognize nor distinguish, that we seem to behold them, as it were, placed before our eyes in a mirror.

# SIXTH CONFERENCE, WHICH IS THAT OF ABBOT THEODORE

## ON THE DEATH OF THE SAINTS

[Col. 0643]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0643A]

In the region of Palestine, near the village of Thecue,

[Note: Saint Jerome calls it a town; Epiphanius places it in the tribe of Zebulun (*Book on the Life and Death of the Prophets*). Jerome writes in his preface to the prophet Amos: “Thecue lies six miles to the south of holy Bethlehem, which gave birth to the Savior of the world. Beyond it there is no village, not even the rustic huts—like ovens—which the Africans call *mapalia*. So vast is the wilderness, stretching as far as the Red Sea and the boundaries of Persia, Ethiopia, and India. And because [Note: *humi* is used adverbially, or means ‘ground.’] absolutely no crops grow in the dry and sandy ground, everything is filled with shepherds, so that the multitude of flocks may compensate for the barrenness of the land.” The prophet Amos was also one of these shepherds, “unskilled in speech but not in knowledge,” and so forth.]

which was privileged to give birth to the prophet Amos (Amos 1),

[Note: Ciaconius argues that “Dead Sea” has been mistakenly written for “Red Sea,” inferring this from Jerome’s words quoted above, where he says that this vast wilderness extends as far as the Red Sea and the boundaries of Persia, Ethiopia, and India. For the Dead Sea was not very far from Bethlehem. He therefore suspects that some words have been wrongly added here and proposes that the passage should read: “The wilderness is exceedingly vast, stretching in a very wide expanse as far as Arabia and the Red Sea.”

But, on the other hand, much weakens and renders improbable Ciaconius’s conjecture or opinion. First, all copies, both printed and manuscript—as many as I have been able to see—consistently read “Dead Sea,” not “Red Sea”; although they differ in other respects, they agree on this. Second, it is expressly added here: “where the streams of the Jordan enter and end.” This can in no way suit the Red Sea, from which the Jordan is exceedingly remote in every direction, as is evident from merely looking at a geographical map. Thus there is no reason why the Jordan can be said to enter or end in it, as is stated here. Finally, Cassian indicates that the Dead Sea lies on one side and Arabia—namely Arabia Petraea, which extends as far as the Red Sea—on the other, forming the desert in which the ancient Israelites wandered for forty years. It is therefore clear that Jerome’s words quoted above do not conflict with this. For the same exceedingly vast wilderness, which according to Cassian lies near the Dead Sea, extends on the other side, namely southward, as far as the Red Sea and the boundaries of Persia, Ethiopia, and India, as Jerome says. Jerome also mentions this same wilderness in Letter 129; and in his Hebrew Traditions he writes of the Dead Sea: “The Valley of Salt, as is written in this same passage, in which there were formerly pits of bitumen, was after God’s wrath and a rain of sulphur changed into the Dead Sea, which the Greeks call λίμνη ἀσφαλτίτης, that is, ‘the lake of bitumen’” (*Hebrew Traditions on Genesis* 14). The historian Justin, speaking of Judea in Book 30, says: “In that region there is a lake which, because of its immobility, is called the Dead Sea.” Josephus, Pliny (Book 4, chapter 13, and Book 5, chapter 10), and Solinus call it Lake Asphaltitis. So he says. Others think that it is called the Dead Sea because its waters are so salty and bitter that no living creature can survive there; hence it is also called the Salt Sea and the Sea of Salt.]

there is an immense wilderness extending as far as Arabia and the Dead Sea,

[Note: Arabia is a region of Greater Asia between Judea and Egypt, famous for Mount Cassius, which some assert to be Sinai, where Moses received the Law (Pliny, Book 5, chapter 11, and Book 6, chapter 28). Ptolemy and others distinguish three Arabias (Book 5, chapter 17): one called Felix, or εὐδαίμων, “fortunate,” because it produces frankincense and is exceedingly fertile. It extends southward in the form of a peninsula between the Persian and Arabian Gulfs and is otherwise called Sabaea. The second is Arabia Petraea, that part of Arabia adjoining Egypt and Judea, extending above Palestine to Mount Cassius and the Red Sea. Strabo calls it Nabataea (Book 16). The third is the desert, also called Scenitis, from σκηνή, “tent,” because its wandering people, without permanent buildings, live in tents. It is bounded on the south by Felix Arabia and on the north by Syria and part of Mesopotamia.]

where the streams of the Jordan enter and end,

[Note: The Jordan, Judea’s most delightful and pleasant river and one especially well known from sacred Scripture, rises from two springs at the foot of Lebanon. Jerome writes in his Hebrew Questions: “Dan is one of the springs of the Jordan; the other is called Jor, which means ρεῖθρον, ‘a stream.’ When the two springs, not far apart, join into one little stream, it is thereafter called Jordan.” Pliny adds (Book 5, chapter 15): “After many winding turns, near the mouth of the Arnon it flows, as if unwillingly, into the Dead Sea, or Lake Asphaltitis, a lake terrible by nature; mingled with it, it loses both its name and its very clear, healthful waters, which are corrupted by the mixture. When the fish with which the Jordan abounds taste them, they either float back up at once or die.”]

[Note: There is remarkable variation here among both printed and manuscript copies. Some read: “The streams of the Jordan end, and they extend in a vast expanse into the ashes of Sodom.” Others: “The streams of the Jordan end, and the channels of its bed come to an end, and the ashes of Sodom extend in a vast expanse.” Dionysius the Paraphraser has: “As far as Arabia and the Dead Sea, where the streams of the Jordan enter and end, and the ashes of Sodom extend very widely.” Finally, some place the words in parentheses: “(Where the streams of the Jordan enter and end, and the ashes of Sodom)”—followed by “stretched out in a vast expanse,” so that “stretched out” refers to the immense wilderness. Baronius reads and cites the passage in this way in his *Annals* (volume 5, year 410, at the end).]

and the ashes of Sodom stretch out over a vast expanse.

[Note: The story of the destruction of Sodom by fire sent down from heaven because of its abominable lust is well known (Genesis 19). The region lies between Palestine and Arabia and was called Pentapolis from its five cities, among which Sodom and Gomorrah held first place (Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book 14, chapter 3). When four were consumed by fire, only little Zoar was spared for Lot’s sake. The whole valley indeed was struck from heaven; yet its smallest and outermost part, or shore, remained bleak and dissolved into ashes, whence the name “ashes of Sodom.” On this shore, too, are seen trees witnessing to divine vengeance; although their fruit appears beautiful to look upon and ripe, when touched or lightly pressed by the hand it exhales foul smoke and crumbles into ashes. But the inner and much larger part of the whole valley was submerged after the conflagration and covered with very thick, dense waters issuing from the very ground; this is called the Dead Sea. Josephus discusses this more fully in Book 5, chapter 5 of *The Jewish War*; likewise Tertullian in the poem *On Sodom*, and Orosius in Book 1.]

[Col. 0645A] Another reading has “stretched out” in the masculine plural, referring to “ashes.”

[Note: This passage derives considerable authority from the fact that the memory of these monks is recorded in ecclesiastical calendars under May 28 in the following words: “At Thecue in Palestine, the holy monks and martyrs who were killed by the Saracens in the time of Theodosius the Younger; the inhabitants gathered their sacred remains and held them in the highest veneration.” Baronius says that this should be understood of the monks whom Cassian mentions here.]

Monks of the highest way of life and holiness had been dwelling there for a very long time when they were suddenly killed by marauding Saracen brigands.

[Note: Concerning the Saracen people and their origin, Nicephorus writes in Book 2, chapter 47 of his *History*: “The Saracen people, first receiving their name from Ishmael, who was the son of Abraham, were called Ishmaelites by the ancients, after the name of their first ancestor. But, in order to remove from themselves the stain of illegitimate birth and the mark of slavery—for his mother Hagar was a slave—they called themselves Saracens, as though they derived their descent from Sarah, Abraham’s wife. Nevertheless, tracing their lineage from that source, they follow the same way of life as the Jews. They practice circumcision as the Jews do, abstain from pork, and observe many of their other institutions,” and so forth (Jerome, *Hebrew Questions* and Letter 124).

Jerome also mentions the Saracens’ invasion and ravaging of Egypt, Palestine, and the neighboring provinces, during which those holy monks were killed. In Letter 82 to Marcellinus he says that he barely escaped them, writing: “This year, when I had completed three books”—namely, on Ezekiel—“a sudden invasion of barbarians occurred, of whom your Virgil says (*Aeneid* 4): ‘the Barcaeans wandering far and wide.’ Holy Scripture says of Ishmael: ‘He dwelt in the presence of all his brothers’ (Genesis 16). Thus they swept through the borders of Egypt, Palestine, Phoenicia, and Syria, carrying everything along like a torrent, so that only through Christ’s mercy were we able to escape their hands.”

Saint Augustine also records the same calamity at about the same time in Letter 122 to Victorianus, where he laments the disasters inflicted by those barbarians throughout nearly the whole world: “The whole world is afflicted by such great calamities that scarcely any part of the earth remains where things such as you have written are not committed and mourned. For a short time ago, even in those deserts of Egypt where monasteries lived in seclusion from every disturbance, brothers were killed by barbarians.” Thus Augustine.

Other persecutions by the Saracens and massacres of monks perpetrated by them are also reported, but these occurred either elsewhere than in Palestine or long before Cassian’s time. On these matters see Baronius’s notes on the *Martyrology*, January 14, February 19, and May 16.]

Although we knew that the bodies had been taken with the greatest veneration by the bishops of that region and by the entire Arab populace and deposited among the martyrs’ relics,

[Note: Here we have striking confirmation, from the testimony and example of antiquity, of the veneration of sacred relics, especially those of holy martyrs (Damascene, Book 4 *On the Faith*, chapter 16). It was also mentioned above from the Roman Martyrology, and Saint Jerome vigorously defended and commended it against Vigilantius (Homily 5 on Psalm 39).

Origen writes: “We usually call them relics when the spirit is separated from the body; for, since the greater part of the human being is assigned to the spirit, the remaining part of the body is called relics.” Ambrose writes on Psalm 36: “Relics are called the remains of a dead person. They are called relics because they appear to survive the person’s death. What remains is preserved for the resurrection.”]

so that countless people, coming from two towns, entered into a most serious dispute with one another, and their contest over the holy spoil proceeded even to armed conflict. They contended with pious devotion over which of them had the more rightful claim to possess their burial place and relics:

[Note: Other copies read: “the tombs for the relics.” Here you see how eagerly and ambitiously Christian peoples sought the relics of the holy martyrs. Gregory of Tours reports a similar dispute and contest between the people of Poitiers and Tours over the removal of Saint Martin’s relics (*History*, Book 1, chapter 43). Another such dispute may be seen in Saint Jerome’s *Life of Hilarion*, which concludes: “Even today you may see a remarkable contest between the Palestinians and Cypriots, the former contending that they possess Hilarion’s body, the latter that they possess his spirit. Yet great signs occur daily in both places, more abundantly perhaps in the garden of Cyprus, because he may have loved that place more.”]

some boasting of their proximity to the monks’ place of residence, others of the closeness of their origin.

We, however, stirred by the offense of our own brothers—or of certain brothers who were by no means unaffected in this matter—

[Note: Ciaconius interprets “being scandalized” as “suffering scandal” or “having been scandalized,” which theologians call passive scandal. Thus Hilary writes on Matthew, canon 30: “Peter, responding in the fervor of his faith, said, although the others were being scandalized, that he would never be scandalized.”]

and asking why men of such merit and such great virtue had been killed by brigands, and why the Lord had allowed so great a crime to be perpetrated against his servants, handing over men admired by all into the hands of the impious, we went in sorrow to the holy Theodore,

[Note: I am entirely convinced that this is the same Theodore whom Cassian mentions in Book 5, chapters 33 and following. He calls him an abbot endowed with supreme holiness and perfect knowledge, not only in practical life but also in knowledge of Scripture—a knowledge imparted to him not so much by devoted reading or worldly learning as by purity of heart. Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 8, identifies him as a disciple and successor of Saint Pachomius in governing the monks whom Pachomius had instituted. Cassian also praises him in many ways in the book of the *Conferences*. This must unquestionably refer to the present Conference, since nowhere else in these Conferences is he mentioned, much less praised.

Cuychius notes that in the oldest copies the Conference of Abbot Theodore is placed after both Conferences of Abbot Serenus. This also agrees well with Photius’s account, in which the Conference of Abbot Serenus is mentioned third. Dionysius Carthusianus, however, places Theodore’s Conference here with us.]

a man distinguished in practical conduct.

He was staying at Cellia,

[Note: Cellae, or Cellia, was a place in the Egyptian desert named from the monks’ cells, which were numerous and scattered throughout it. Sozomen, discussing Nitria and its monks and monasteries in Book 6 of his *History*, chapter 31, writes: “They call this place Nitria because it is near a village where natron is collected. A considerable multitude of people practiced monastic discipline there. There were about fifty adjoining monasteries, some containing communities, others housing men who lived separately from the rest. When one travels farther into the inner desert, there is another place about seventy stadia from Nitria called Cellia. It contains very many monks’ cells scattered about, which is why it received that name. They are so far apart that those who live in them can neither see nor hear one another.”

Sozomen says this, and Nicephorus gives a somewhat fuller account in Book 2, chapter 38. In the margin, his translator added this noteworthy scholium: “Today, on Mount Athos, there are twenty-two distinguished monasteries of Greek monks belonging to the order of Saint Basil. Each year they pay the Turkish tyrant six thousand Turkish obols in tribute from their vineyards and olive groves. Christians call the mountain ἅγιον ὅρος, that is, ‘Holy Mountain’; the Ruthenians call it Suvata Hora.”

Thus far the scholium. To return to Nitria: Saint Jerome also mentions the monks of Nitria in Letters 22 and 27, where he calls it “the Lord’s town of Nitria, in which the filth of many is daily washed away by the purest natron of virtues” (Sulpicius, *Dialogue on the Virtues of the Eastern Monks*). Marianus explains in his scholia: “Nitria is spiritually interpreted as having been named from natron, because of the flocks of holy monks dwelling there, who cleanse people from the filth of sins with the purest natron of virtues. For natron has a cleansing power, as Jeremiah indicates when he says: ‘Though you wash yourself with natron,’ and so forth.”

The desert of Scetis, or the Scetian desert, has been discussed elsewhere several times. See the First Conference, chapter 1.]

a place situated between Nitria and Scetis. It is five miles distant from the monasteries of Nitria, while an eighty-mile stretch of desert intervenes between it and the Scetian wilderness where we were staying.

When we had poured out to him our complaint concerning the death of the men mentioned above, wondering at God’s great patience—why he had allowed men of such merit to be killed in this way, men who ought by the weight of their holiness to have tried to free others from such a temptation, yet had not even rescued themselves from the hands of the impious—

[Col. 0648A] or why God had permitted so great a crime to be committed against his servants,

[Note: From this arose the occasion and title of the present Conference, *On the Death of the Saints*, whose entire subject is to teach why God allows holy men to be harassed or killed by the impious.]

## CHAPTER II. Abbot Theodore’s answer to the question proposed
Blessed Theodore replied:

> This question commonly disturbs the minds of those who possess little faith or knowledge and suppose that the merits of the saints, or the rewards that are not bestowed in the present but reserved for the future, should be repaid within the short span of this temporal life.  
>
> **[Note: [Col. 0647C–0648D]]** This question was widely known in those times and on everyone’s lips because of the evils pressing in everywhere and the barbarians ravaging far and wide. Cassian was not the only one to discuss it; on the same occasion Saint Augustine also addressed it in the aforementioned letter to Victorianus, who had asked, among other things: “Why were servants of God killed by the sword of the barbarians, and maidservants of God led away captive?” Augustine teaches that this question should be answered humbly, truthfully, and devoutly, as follows:
>
> “However much justice we preserve, however much obedience we offer to the Lord, can we possibly be better than those three men who were cast into the furnace of blazing fire in order to preserve God’s law? Yet read what Azariah, one of the three, says there. Opening his mouth in the midst of the fire, he said: ‘Blessed are you, Lord God of our fathers, and your name is praiseworthy and glorious forever, for you are just in all that you have done to us,’ and so forth; ‘for in truth and judgment you have brought all these things upon us because of our sins, because we have sinned and have not obeyed your law,’ and the rest that follows in the prayer of Daniel, or rather of Azariah, Daniel 3.
>
> “Then he adds: ‘You see clearly, brother, what sort of men they were—how holy and how strong in the midst of tribulation, although they were being spared and the flame itself feared to burn them—and yet they confessed their sins, for which they knew that they were rightly and justly humbled, and they did not remain silent. Can we possibly be better even than Daniel, concerning whom the Lord says through the prophet Ezekiel to the prince of Tyre: “Are you wiser than Daniel?” (Ezekiel 28)? Nevertheless, read also Daniel’s prayer and see how, while he was in captivity, he confesses not only the sins of his people but also his own, and says that by God’s justice he had come to that punishment and disgrace of captivity because of them. For it is written: “And I set my face,” and so forth.’
>
> “He continues through Daniel’s entire prayer, found in chapter 9, and finally adds: ‘Read these things faithfully, preach them faithfully, and, as far as you can, beware and teach others to beware lest anyone murmur against God amid these temptations and tribulations. You say that good, faithful, and holy servants of God were killed by the sword of the barbarians. But what difference does it make whether fever or steel released them from the body? In his servants the Lord considers not by what occasion they depart, but what kind of people they depart to him as—except that prolonged sickness is a greater punishment than a very swift departure. Yet we read of the same prolonged and dreadful sickness, such as Job endured, whose righteousness God himself, who cannot be deceived, bears witness to.
>
> “‘That captivity of chaste and holy women is indeed most grievous and greatly to be lamented; but their God is not captive, nor does he abandon his captives if he recognizes them as his own. Those holy men whose sufferings and confessions I have recalled from the Scriptures were led away by enemies and placed in captivity, yet they said what we read written down, so that we may learn that God’s captive servants are not abandoned by their Lord.’”
>
> Augustine says these and other things in the same sense. He treats the same subject more fully in the books *On the City of God*, written on the same occasion (see chapters 9 and 14 of book 1 of *The City of God*). There are, moreover, many other reasons besides that divine correction and punishment of sins—even in just and holy people—for which God permits them to be afflicted in this life by various hardships and calamities, to be harassed by the impious, and even to be put to death. It would be lengthy to enumerate them here and unnecessary, since they are encountered throughout the Scriptures and have been explained by the Fathers. The present author also touches upon most of them in this conference and elsewhere, where he discusses patience and related subjects. Among other Fathers, see Saint Chrysostom’s first homily *To the People*, where he lists ten or more reasons.
>
> But we, who do not place our hope in Christ in this life alone—lest, according to the Apostle, we be “more pitiable than all human beings” (1 Corinthians 15), since, receiving none of the promises in this world, we should also lose them in the future because of this unbelief—must not be led astray by their opinions. Otherwise, ignorant of the judgment of the true definition and wavering and fearful, we shall be shaken by temptations when we see ourselves delivered over to the same things, attributing either injustice or negligence concerning human affairs to God—which is itself a wicked thing to say—because he does not protect holy and upright men in temptation, nor repay good things to the good and evil things to the evil in the present. Thus we might deserve to be condemned along with those whom the prophet Zephaniah rebukes: “Those who say in their hearts, ‘The Lord will not do good, nor will he do evil’” (Zephaniah 1); or certainly we might be found among those who are said to blaspheme God with complaints of this sort: “Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and such people please him”; or, “Where is the God of justice?” (Malachi 2). We might likewise add the blasphemy described in what follows: “It is useless to serve God; what profit is there in keeping his commandments and walking mournfully before the Lord? Therefore we now call the arrogant blessed, since those who commit impiety have been enriched, and they have tempted God and been saved” (Malachi 3).
>
> Therefore, in order that we may escape this ignorance, which is the root and cause of this most perverse error, we must first know what is truly good and what is evil. Then, holding to the true definition of the Scriptures rather than the false opinion of the crowd concerning these matters, we shall not be deceived by the error of unbelieving people.

## CHAPTER III. Of the three things that exist in this world: good, evil, and the intermediate.

Everything that exists in this world belongs to three categories: good, evil, and the intermediate. We must therefore know what is properly good, what is evil, and what is intermediate, so that our faith, strengthened by true knowledge, may remain unshaken in every temptation.

Nothing, then, among merely human things should be believed to be the principal good except virtue of soul alone. Through sincere faith it leads us to divine things and makes us continually cling to that unchanging good.

**[Note: [Col. 0649C–0649D]]** Virtue is called the principal good, not because it is the highest and only good, as the Stoics maintained, but because it is the chief good of a human being in this life and especially worthy of pursuit. Yet virtue itself is not to be sought for its own sake, but for the sake of the highest good, which is God, or eternal blessedness (Augustine, book 9 of *The City of God*, chapter 4; Lactantius, book 3 of the *Institutes*, chapter 22).

Conversely, nothing should be called evil except sin alone, which separates us from the good God and joins us to the evil devil.

**[Note: [Col. 0649D–0650D]]** Saint Augustine, book 1 of *The City of God*, chapter 8: “Divine Providence has chosen to prepare in the future good things for the just, which the unjust will not enjoy, and evils for the impious, by which the good will not be tormented. But he willed temporal goods and evils to be shared by both, so that goods might not be desired too eagerly because the wicked are also seen to possess them, nor evils shamefully avoided because the good are often afflicted by them. What matters greatly is how one uses things that are called prosperous and things that are called adverse. For by these temporal goods the good person is not lifted up, nor is he broken by evils; but the wicked person is punished by such misfortune because he is corrupted by prosperity.
>
> “Since these things are so, whenever the good and the evil are afflicted alike, they are not therefore undistinguished because what both suffer is undistinguished. The dissimilarity of those who suffer remains even amid the similarity of their sufferings; and although they are under the same torture, virtue and vice are not the same. Just as under one fire gold glows and straw smokes, and under the same threshing-sledge the chaff is crushed and the grain purified, and just as olive dregs are not confused with oil because they are pressed out by the same weight, so one and the same force that falls upon them tests, purifies, and refines the good, but condemns, devastates, and destroys the wicked. Hence, amid the same affliction, the wicked curse and blaspheme God, while the good pray and praise him. The difference lies not in what is suffered but in who suffers it. For when shaken by the same motion, mud exhales a foul stench, while perfume gives off a pleasing fragrance.”
>
> Thus far Saint Augustine speaks with great elegance. In the following chapter he adds matters also pertinent to this passage: “What, then, did Christians suffer amid that devastation of things which, for those who considered it more faithfully, could not serve more greatly for their advancement?” He then explains the reasons why the good and the wicked are scourged alike. He develops this subject extensively in the following chapters as well.

Intermediate are things that can be directed toward either side according to the disposition and choice of the person who uses them—for example, wealth, power, honor, bodily strength, health, beauty, life itself, or death, poverty, bodily weakness, injuries, and other things of this kind.

**[Note: [Col. 0650D]]** This is a saying of Terence drawn from Plato: Things that are called goods among human beings—parents, a safe homeland, friends, birth, relatives, wealth—are, in themselves, just as the mind of the person who possesses them is. To the person who knows how to use them they are good; to the person who does not use them rightly they are evil.

According to the quality and disposition of the user, such things can contribute either to the good or to the evil. Wealth, for example, often contributes to the good, according to the Apostle, who commands the rich of this world to give freely, to share with those in need, and to lay up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that through these things they may attain true life (1 Timothy 6). According to the Gospel, wealth is also good for those who make friends for themselves from unrighteous mammon (Luke 16). Yet wealth is turned toward evil when it is amassed merely for hoarding or luxury and is not distributed for the needs of the poor.

That power and honor, bodily strength and health are intermediate and suitable for either direction is also readily shown by the fact that many saints in the Old Testament possessed all these things and are known to have been most pleasing to God while established in great wealth, the height of dignity, and bodily strength. Conversely, those who used these things badly and turned them into instruments of their wickedness were deservedly punished or destroyed, as the books of Kings frequently record.

That death and life are also intermediate is testified by the birth of Saint John and of Judas.

**[Note: [Col. 0650D–0651D]]** They are to be counted among the intermediate things, because in themselves they are neither good nor evil, but *ἀδιάφοροι*—“indifferent,” as the Greeks call them. Saint Bernard aptly says in his letter to Romanus (Letter 105):
>
> “I want you, even if you cannot escape death, at least not to fear it. The just person, though he does not avoid death, does not tremble before it. Indeed, if he is overtaken by death, he will be at rest” (Wisdom 4).
>
> “The just person dies, but securely, since his death is the end of the present life and the entrance into a better one.”
>
> He adds: “The death of the just is good because of rest, better because of renewal, and best because of security. But the death of sinners is most evil” (Psalm 33). Hear why it is most evil: it is bad in the loss of the world, worse in the separation from the flesh, and worst in the twofold torment of worms and fire.
>
> These words of Saint Bernard fit this passage well.

The life of one of them [John] benefited him so greatly that it is said to have brought joy at his birth to others also: “Many will rejoice at his birth” (Luke 1). Of the life of the other [Judas] it is said: “It would have been better for that man if he had not been born” (Matthew 26).

Of John’s death and the death of all the saints it is said: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Psalm 115). Of Judas and those like him: “The death of sinners is most evil” (Psalm 33).

That bodily weakness can sometimes be advantageous is shown by the blessedness of that poor ulcer-covered Lazarus. Although Scripture mentions no other merits of his virtues, simply because he endured poverty and bodily weakness with the greatest patience, he deserved by that alone to possess Abraham’s bosom in the most blessed lot (Luke 16).

Poverty, persecutions, and injuries, which in the opinion of the whole crowd are considered evils, are shown clearly to be useful and necessary by the fact that holy men not only never wished to avoid them but, either seeking them or enduring them courageously with the highest virtue, became friends of God and received the rewards of eternal life. The blessed Apostle gives voice to this when he says: “For this reason I am pleased with weaknesses, insults, necessities, persecutions, and distresses for Christ. For when I am weak, then I am strong, because power is perfected in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12).

Therefore those who are exalted by the greatest wealth, honors, and powers of this age should not be believed to have obtained from these things the principal good, which is defined as existing in virtues alone. They have obtained something intermediate, because these things are found to be useful and advantageous for the just who use them rightly and necessarily—for they produce an opportunity for good works and for fruits in the eternity of the future life—but for those who misuse their resources they are useless and disadvantageous, creating an opportunity for sin and death.

## CHAPTER IV. That no one can inflict evil on anyone unwillingly.

Holding firmly to these fixed and immovable distinctions, and knowing that nothing is good except virtue alone, which proceeds from the fear and love of God, and that nothing is evil except sin alone and separation from God, let us now carefully examine whether God has ever permitted evil to be inflicted upon his saints, either by himself or through anyone else. You will certainly find that this has nowhere happened.

**[Note: [Col. 0651D]]** This statement is repeated again in chapter 9. Saint Chrysostom expressed it in other words: “No one is harmed except by himself.” See the notes there.

For no one has ever been able to inflict the evil of sin upon another who was unwilling and resisting, except upon the one who alone received it into himself through the cowardice of his heart and his corrupt will.

Thus, when the devil wished to inflict this evil of sin upon blessed Job, after deploying all the devices of his wickedness, he not only stripped him of all his possessions but, after the extraordinarily grievous and unforeseen bereavement caused by the death of his seven sons, also loaded him with the worst of wounds from the crown of his head to the soles of his feet and with unbearable tortures.

**[Note: [Col. 0651D–0652D]]** Scripture testifies to this when it says: “In all these things Job did not sin with his lips, nor did he speak anything foolish against God” (Job 1). When even his wife urged him, unable to bear the violence of his grief, to say something against God in a complaining and blasphemous voice, he replied: “You are speaking as one of the foolish women speaks. If we have received good things from the hand of God, why should we not receive evil things?” (Job 2).

Yet the devil could not stain him with the blemish of sin, for he remained steadfast in everything and gave no assent to blasphemy.

## CHAPTER V. The objection: how God himself is said to create evils.

**Germanus:** We frequently read in the holy Scriptures that God created evils or inflicted them upon human beings. For example: “For there is no God besides me; I am the Lord, and there is no other, forming light and creating darkness, making peace and creating evils” (Isaiah 45). And again:

**[Note: [Col. 0652D]]** The Vulgate reading is: “Will there be evil in the city that the Lord has not done?” This means the evil of punishment, not the evil of guilt, as Saint Jerome teaches in his commentary on the passage: “The evil that the Lord does in the city is not opposed to virtue, but is affliction and torment. Concerning it we read: ‘Sufficient for the day is its own evil’ (Matthew 6), that is, tribulation and distress. And in the prophet we read: ‘I am God who made light and darkness, who make peace and create evils.’ Just as darkness is contrary to light and day, so war is contrary to peace; it is not evil in itself, but appears evil to those who endure it,” and so forth.

“If there is evil in the city that the Lord has not done” (Amos 3).

## CHAPTER VI. The answer to the question proposed.

**Theodore:** Divine Scripture sometimes uses the word “evils” improperly for afflictions, not because they are properly evil by their nature, but because they are felt as evil by those upon whom they are beneficially inflicted. Since divine judgment speaks to human beings, it must express itself in human words and according to human emotions.

A beneficial surgical incision or cauterization, which a physician mercifully applies to those whose bodies have become corrupted by the infection of ulcers, is considered evil by those who endure it. Neither is a spur pleasant to a horse, nor correction pleasant to a delinquent. All instruction also feels bitter at first to those being educated, as the Apostle says: “All discipline”

**[Note: [Col. 0652D–0653C]]** “Discipline” is understood as God’s correction. In Greek it is *παιδεία* (*paideia*), a word derived from *pais*, “child,” which properly signifies instruction joined with correction of the conduct and faults of the person being instructed, as in the education of children. Thus Saint Basil says at the beginning of his commentary on Proverbs:
>
> “Discipline is a kind of useful training which often cleanses the stains of vice through toil. At present it does not appear to be a source of joy but of sorrow; nevertheless, in the end it yields to those exercised by it a peaceful and salutary fruit. Just as small children, despising instruction because of the rods and blows that teachers and tutors customarily use, receive their lessons more attentively—and the word is not heard before the blows, while after the beating and pain, as though their ears had suddenly been opened, they receive the explanation and preserve it in memory—so it happens with those who hear divine commands and are negligent in keeping them. After discipline has been inflicted upon them by God, the divine commandments that had always been insistently impressed upon them are received as though they were falling into their ears for the first time.”

“All discipline at the present seems not to be joyful but sorrowful; afterward, however, it yields the most peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it” (Hebrews 12).

And, “The Lord disciplines the one whom he loves; he scourges every son whom he receives. For what son is there whom the Father does not discipline?” (the same passage and Proverbs 3).

**[Note: [Col. 0653C–0654C]]** These are Solomon’s words in Proverbs 3, quoted by the Apostle in Hebrews 12 according to the translation of the Septuagint, which nevertheless does not differ from the Vulgate except in the clause that follows: “but he scourges every son whom he receives.” Jerome translates this from the Hebrew as: “And as a father takes pleasure in a son.” These renderings, however, convey a meaning that is not very different. “He scourges every son whom he receives” differs little from “he disciplines, as a father does the son in whom he takes pleasure,” that is, whom he loves greatly.
>
> Moses says something similar in Deuteronomy 8. After recalling the afflictions of the people of Israel, he says: “So you may consider in your heart that as a man educates his son, so the Lord your God has educated you, that you might keep the commandments of the Lord your God,” and so forth.
>
> Proverbs 13 likewise says: “He who spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him diligently disciplines him.” Here “to educate” is used for “to correct,” just as “discipline” is used for correction, as stated above.
>
> Finally, Revelation 3 says: “Those whom I love, I rebuke and discipline.” Here “those whom” is used for “all whom,” for the Greek reads: *ἐγὼ ὅσους ἐὰν φιλῶ*—“I love all whomsoever I love.”

Thus evils are sometimes used for afflictions, as in the passage: “And the Lord repented of the evil that he had spoken of doing to them, and he did not do it” (Jeremiah 26). And again: “For you, Lord, are merciful and compassionate, patient and abundantly merciful, and repenting of evils” (Joel 2), that is, of the tribulations and hardships that you are compelled to inflict upon us according to the merits of our sins.

Knowing that these things are useful to some, another prophet, not begrudging their salvation but seeking their welfare, invokes them as follows:

**[Note: [Col. 0653B–0654C]]** Thus reads the Septuagint. The Vulgate version, however, has: “You have spared the nation, Lord; you have spared the nation—have you also been glorified?” Saint Jerome writes: “The evils that the Septuagint included are not found in the Hebrew. But because the passage above had said, ‘Therefore you brought in, destroyed, and carried away every male of theirs,’ they followed the same sense and added the word ‘evils’ on their own, so that those who are glorious on earth might be overwhelmed by double evils.”

“Add evils to them, Lord; add evils to the glorious of the earth.”

The Lord himself also says: “Behold, I will bring evils upon them” (Jeremiah 11), that is, pains and devastations by which, chastened in the present for their salvation, they may finally be compelled to return and hasten to me, whom they despised in times of prosperity.

Therefore we cannot define these as principal evils, for they benefit many toward the good and produce the causes of eternal joys.

To return, then, to the question proposed: all the things that our enemies or anyone else are thought to inflict upon us as evils should not be believed to be evils, but intermediate things. For they will not be found to be such as the one who inflicted them in a furious spirit thought them to be, but such as the one who endures them experiences them.

**[Note: [Col. 0654C–0654D]]** Saint Augustine, book 1 of *The City of God*, chapter 11: “A death preceded by a good life should not be considered evil. For nothing makes death evil except what follows death. Since Christians know that the death of the devout poor man amid the tongues of licking dogs was far better than that of the impious rich man in purple and fine linen, what did those dreadful forms of death harm the dead who had lived well?”

Lactantius, book 3 of the *Institutes*, chapter 19: “If someone asks us whether death is good or evil, we shall answer that its character depends upon the manner of life. For just as life itself is good if one lives virtuously and evil if one lives wickedly, so death must be judged according to the preceding acts of life. Thus, if life has been spent in the worship of God, death is not evil, because it has been transferred to immortality; otherwise it must be evil, because it leads to eternal punishments” (Luke 16).

Therefore, when death is inflicted upon a holy man, it should not be believed that evil has been inflicted upon him, but rather something intermediate. What is evil to a sinner becomes rest and release from evils to the just.

**[Note: [Col. 0654D]]** Saint Augustine reads this passage in the same way in his annotations on Job: “Death is rest for the man whose life is hidden,” either because it is hidden before God or because it is known to few. This should be understood of the death by which we die to the world. Such are Augustine’s words.

In the Vulgate edition, however, the words “death is rest for the man” are not found; it has only: “for the man whose way is hidden.” The Greek likewise reads: *οὗ ἡ ὁδὸς ἀπεκρύβη*—“whose way has been hidden.” Hence it is clear that the word “just” is an addition, and that the text should read: “whose way is hidden,” not “whose life is hidden.”

“For the just man death is rest, whose life is hidden” (Job 3).

Therefore the just man suffers no loss from this, since he has suffered nothing new. What was destined to come to him by the necessity of nature he received through the wickedness of his enemy, not without the reward of eternal life; and he paid the debt of human death, which must be rendered under an inexorable law, together with the abundant fruit of suffering and the reward of great recompense.

## CHAPTER VII. The question whether the person who inflicted death upon the just is guilty, when the just person receives a reward from death.

**Germanus:** If the just man who has been killed has not only suffered no evil but has also obtained the reward of his suffering, how can the one who did not harm him by inflicting death but benefited him be called guilty?

## CHAPTER VIII. The answer to the preceding question.

**Theodore:** We are discussing the nature of good and evil, or of what we have called intermediate, not the disposition of those who commit such acts. An impious or wicked person will not be exempt from punishment merely because his wickedness was unable to harm the just man.

The patience and virtue of the just person benefits not the one who inflicted death or punishment, but the one who patiently endured what was inflicted. Therefore the former will rightly be punished for the savage cruelty with which he wished to inflict evil, while the latter nevertheless suffered no evil, because by patiently enduring temptations and pains through the virtue of his soul, he made the things inflicted with an evil purpose contribute to the blessedness of a better condition and eternal life.

## CHAPTER IX. The example of blessed Job, tempted by the devil, and of the Lord, betrayed by Judas; and that both prosperity and adversity contribute to the salvation of the just.

The patience of Job did not acquire a reward for the devil, who made him more illustrious through his temptations, but for Job himself, who endured them manfully.

**[Note: [Col. 0655C]]** Saint Cyprian describes Job’s patience excellently in his book *On the Good of Patience*, as does Chrysostom in homily 28 on the First Epistle to the Corinthians.

Nor will Judas be granted immunity from eternal punishment because his betrayal contributed to the salvation of the human race. For it is not the outcome of the deed that must be considered, but the disposition of the one who performed it.

**[Note: [Col. 0655C–0656C]]** Saint Augustine explains this beautifully in his exposition of Psalm 93:
>
> “If we consider Judas’s act of handing over Christ and not the intention of the one who handed him over, Judas did what God the Father did, of whom it is written: ‘He did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all’ (Romans 8). Judas did what the Lord Christ himself did, of whom it is written: ‘He handed himself over for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant aroma.’ Again: ‘Christ loved his Church and handed himself over for her’ (Ephesians 5).
>
> “Nevertheless, we give thanks to God the Father, who did not spare his only Son but handed him over for us all; we give thanks to the Son himself, who handed himself over for us and thereby fulfilled the Father’s will. And we detest Judas, through whose deed God bestowed such a great benefit upon us, and rightly say: ‘The Lord repaid him according to his iniquity and destroyed him according to his wickedness.’
>
> “For Judas did not hand Christ over for us, but for the silver for which he sold him, although Christ’s handing over is our redemption. So also those who persecuted the martyrs, by persecuting them on earth, sent them into heaven. Though knowingly they inflicted the loss of the present life, unknowingly they conferred the gain of the future life. Yet all who persevered in unjust hatred of the just were repaid by the Lord according to their iniquities and destroyed according to their wickedness. For just as the goodness of the just harms the wicked, so the wickedness of the impious benefits the good.”
>
> A similar passage occurs in Augustine’s seventh tractate on the First Epistle of John: “The handing over was done by the Father, by the Son, and by Judas. What distinction, then, do you make among them? The Father and the Son did this in love; Judas did it in betrayal.” He concludes: “Different intentions make different deeds, although the matter itself is one and the same because of the different intentions.”
>
> Thus Augustine.

Therefore this definition must be guarded immovably in us: no one can have evil inflicted upon him by another except the one who has drawn it into himself through the cowardice and faintheartedness of his own heart.

**[Note: [Col. 0656C–0656D]]** Namely, the evil of sin, as he stated above, because no one sins unless willing. This is a celebrated teaching of the holy Fathers, especially of Saint John Chrysostom, although at first sight it appears paradoxical: that no one is harmed except by himself. To confirm it, while in exile and oppressed by many hardships, he wrote a special treatise, consoling both himself and his friends; it is such that, amid the many labors of so great a teacher, it alone could suffice to form the most complete Christian and to raise by consolation and fill with spiritual joy anyone submerged in an abyss of afflictions (Baronius, vol. V, A.D. 405). It was indeed the last offspring of so great a Father, and therefore most worthy always to be kept at hand, read over, and cherished.

Moreover, Boethius Severinus treated a similar subject excellently in his little book *The Consolation of Philosophy*. There is a commentary on it by a certain Thomas the Englishman, falsely ascribed to Saint Thomas Aquinas. Since there was a great similarity of sound between *Anglicus* (“the Englishman”) and *Angelicus* (“the Angelic”), it gradually came about through negligence and error that the writings of Thomas the Englishman were marked with the title of Thomas the Angelic, a title rightly attributed by theologians to Thomas Aquinas.

The blessed Apostle confirms the same statement in a single verse: “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God” (Romans 8).

By saying “all things work together for good,” he includes not only everything prosperous but equally everything that is considered adverse.

In another passage the same Apostle describes himself as having passed through these things when he says: “Through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left,” that is, “through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute; as deceivers and yet truthful; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet enriching many” (2 Corinthians 6), and so forth.

Everything considered prosperous and called of the right hand—the things that the holy Apostle designates by the terms “glory” and “good repute”—and everything considered adverse, which he clearly expresses by “dishonor” and “ill repute” and describes as belonging to the left, becomes for the perfect man a weapon of righteousness if he endures what is inflicted upon him with courage.

By fighting through these things, using the very things by which he seems to be attacked as weapons, and fortified by them like a bow, sword, and most powerful shield against those who inflict them, he gains the progress of patience and virtue and wins the most glorious triumph of steadfastness from the very missiles that are lethally launched against him.

He is neither lifted up by prosperity nor cast down by adversity, but always proceeds on a level road and royal way, never moved from that state of tranquility by joy arriving as though he were pushed to the right, nor again driven to the left when adversity presses in and sorrow prevails.

“For there is great peace for those who love your name, and there is no stumbling-block for them” (Psalm 118).

Of those who change with each circumstance according to its character and variety, it is said: “But the fool changes like the moon” (Ecclesiasticus 27).

Just as it is said of the perfect and wise: “All things work together for good for those who love God,” so it is declared of the weak and foolish:

**[Note: [Col. 0656D]]** Thus reads the Greek: *πάντα ἐναντία ἀνδρὶ ἄφρονι*—“Everything is adverse to the foolish man.” But the Latin and Vulgate translator has: “Nothing good will come to the deceitful son, but prosperous acts will belong to the wise servant, and his way will be made straight.”

“Everything is adverse to the foolish man”; for he makes no progress through prosperous circumstances, nor is he corrected by adverse ones.

The same virtue is required to endure sorrows courageously as to moderate prosperity; and it is certain that the person who is overcome in one of these two conditions can bear neither of them.

Nevertheless, a person can more easily be crushed by prosperity than by adversity. Adversity sometimes restrains and humbles even the unwilling and, through most salutary remorse, either makes them sin less or corrects them. Prosperity, however, raises the mind through soft and destructive flatteries and, making people secure through the success of their happiness, throws them down in a more grievous ruin.

## CHAPTER X. Of the virtue of the perfect man, who is figuratively called ambidextrous.

These, then, are those who are figuratively called in Holy Scripture **ἀμφοτεροδέξιοι**, that is, ambidextrous:

[Note: [Col. 0657C] Suidas says that ἀμφοτεροδέξιος, or “ambidextrous,” means one who has the left hand in place of the right, or one who uses the left as the right; it is also called ἀμφιδέξιος, in a contracted form. Among others, Gregory Nazianzen used this term in his funeral oration for Saint Basil, where he says that those who excelled either only in life or only in learning differed in no respect from one-eyed men; but those who had attained equal distinction in both respects were ἀμφιδέξιοι—that is, ambidextrous—and complete in every respect. [Col. 0657D] Budaeus writes in his Commentaries: “Among Plato’s works (Book VII of the Laws), ἀρτίποδες and ἀρτίχειρες are terms for those who use both feet and both hands equally, as do the ἀμφιδέξιοι, no limb having been weakened through disuse.”]

Thus Aoth is described in the Book of Judges as having been ambidextrous:

[Note: [Col. 0657D] He is named third among the judges of the people of Israel, after Judah. Concerning him, Judges III says: “The Lord raised up for them a savior named Ehud, son of Gera, son of Gemini, who used both hands as his right hand.” Hence he was called ἀμφοτεροδέξιος; Saint Jerome calls him ἀμφιδέξιος (Book I Against Jovinianus, chapter 17). He killed Eglon, the exceedingly fat king.]

“who used both hands as his right hand” (Judg. III).

We too can possess this virtue intellectually if we make both what is prosperous and considered “right,” and what is adverse and called “left,” belong to the right side through good and proper use, so that whatever may befall us becomes, according to the Apostle, “weapons of righteousness” (II Cor. VI).

For we plainly see that our inner person exists in two divisions and, so to speak, two hands:

[Note: [Col. 0657D] That is, the mind or soul. The expression is also frequently used in this sense by Paul.]

and no saint can be without this left hand, as we call it. Yet perfect virtue is discerned in this: that a person turns both hands into the right hand by using them well.

[Note: [Col. 0657D] Jerome writes something very similar in his commentary on the verse of Psalm XC: “A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand.” He says: “By him who dwells in the help of the Most High, a thousand shall fall at his side and ten thousand at his right hand. The right hand of the saint is named; the left is not named, but rather the side. Observe what is said: ‘And ten thousand at your right hand.’ How, then, had you said: ‘A thousand shall fall at your side’? When the right hand is named and the left is not, the side is named in place of the left. It could not rightly be that the just man should have a left hand. ‘If anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also’ (Matt. VI); he did not say, ‘and the left.’ For the one offered is not a left cheek, but another right cheek. Therefore I say plainly that the just man has two right hands. Hence also that Ehud who is mentioned in the Book of Judges is said to have two right hands, because he was just and killed that exceedingly fat king.” These are Jerome’s moral and tropological interpretations.]

To make what we are saying clearer, the holy man has a right hand—that is, spiritual successes—in which he stands when, fervent in spirit, he rules over all desires and passions; when, secure from every demonic assault, he rejects or cuts away the vices of the flesh without any labor or difficulty; when, raised above the earth, he regards all present and earthly things as empty smoke and a hollow shadow and despises them as things that will soon pass away; when, through an ecstasy of mind, he not only ardently desires future things but also beholds them more clearly; when he is more effectively nourished by spiritual contemplation; when the heavenly mysteries, opened to him, appear more brightly; when he sends his prayers to the Lord with greater purity and eagerness; and when, kindled by the ardor of the spirit, he passes with complete eagerness of soul toward invisible and eternal things, so that he no longer believes himself to remain in the flesh.

He likewise has a left hand when he is entangled in storms of temptation; when he is inflamed by the burning impulses of incitements toward carnal desires; when he is set ablaze by the fire of agitation toward the fury of anger; when he is assailed by the elevation of pride or vainglory; when he is weighed down by a sadness that produces death; when he is shaken by the devices and assaults of acedia; and when, all spiritual fervor having been withdrawn, he grows numb in a certain lukewarmness and irrational sorrow,

[Col. 0658B]

so that he is abandoned not only by upright and fervent thoughts, but also comes to dread the psalm, prayer, reading, and withdrawal into his cell alike, and all the instruments of virtue become repulsive through an intolerable and foul disgust. When the monk is assailed by these things, he should recognize that he is being pressed on his left side.

Whoever, therefore, in those things which we have said belong to the right side, is not at all lifted up by the intrusion of vainglory, and whoever fights manfully in those things which belong to the left side and does not fall through despair, but rather takes from adversity certain weapons of patience for the exercise of virtue—such a person uses both hands as his right hand. Having become victorious in both conditions, he will gain the palm of victory both over the left state and over the right.

We read that blessed Job merited such a condition. He was crowned through the right hand when, as a prosperous and wealthy father of seven sons, he continually offered sacrifices to the Lord for their purification, wishing to present them not so much as his own as received and entrusted to God:

[Note: [Col. 0658D] Some manuscripts read, “subject to God.” Dionysius reads “accepted” (Book X of the Institutes, chapter 6). Our reading is more correct because it is more common. By “received” understand “taken into one’s care or guardianship.” In former times, clients were called “received,” because patrons had received them under their protection, as we have noted elsewhere. Hence Saint Ambrose, Sermon 93: “The effective advocate’s nearness will be supplied in proportion as the faith of the one received has been devout.”]

when his door was open to every visitor; when he was the foot of the lame and the eye of the blind; when, from the fleeces of his sheep, the shoulders of the infirm were warmed; when he was a father to orphans and a husband to widows; and when he did not rejoice even in his heart at the ruin of his enemy (Job I).

Again, through the left side, he triumphed over adversity with a more exalted virtue: when, deprived in a single moment of seven sons, he was not crushed as a father by bitter mourning but, as a true servant of God, rejoiced in the will of his Creator (ibid.); when, from rich he became exceedingly poor, from wealthy naked, from strong diseased, and from renowned and glorious ignoble and despised, yet retained an unshaken strength of soul; and when, finally, deprived of all possessions and wealth, he became an inhabitant of a dungheap and, like a most severe executioner of his own body, scraped away the flowing discharge with a potsherd and, plunging his fingers into the depths of his wounds, removed clods of worms from every part of his limbs.

In all these things he did not fall into blasphemy through despair, nor did he murmur against his Creator in anything. On the contrary, not at all terrified by the weight and bitterness of his temptations, he tore off and cast away even the one garment that remained on his body from all his former possessions—the only thing that, because he wore it, could have been spared from the devil’s devastation—and added this voluntary nakedness to that inflicted by the most harsh [Lips. in margin: most dreadful] robber.

He also threw to his tormentor the hair of his head, the only remnant of his former glory that had remained untouched. By cutting away even what the raging enemy had left, he dances and exults against him in that heavenly utterance and taunts him:

“If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things? Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return there. The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job II).

I would rightly call Joseph ambidextrous as well. In prosperity he was more pleasing to his father, more religious toward his brothers, and more acceptable to God; in adversity he was chaste, faithful to his master, a most gentle prisoner, forgetful of injuries, beneficent toward his enemies, the envious, and—so far as lay in them—his murderers: toward his brothers he is found not only compassionate but also generous.

These men, then, and their like, are rightly called ambidextrous. They use both hands as their right hand, and, passing through those things which the Apostle enumerates, they say equally:

“Through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, through glory and dishonor, through evil report and good report” (II Cor. VI), and so forth.

[Col. 0659D]

Concerning this right and left, Solomon speaks in the person of the bride in the Song of Songs:

“His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song of Songs II).

Although she indicates that both are useful, she nevertheless places the left beneath her own head, because adverse conditions ought to be subject to the ruling part of the heart. They are useful only for this purpose: that, for a time, they may exercise and instruct us unto salvation and render the perfect steadfast in patience. But she desires the right hand, in the bridegroom’s saving embrace, to cling to her and be inseparably joined to her, cherishing and preserving her forever.

We too shall be ambidextrous when neither abundance nor poverty in present circumstances changes us; when the former does not drive us toward harmful indulgence or relaxation, nor the latter draw us toward despair and complaint; but when, giving thanks to God equally in both conditions, we receive an equal fruit from prosperity and adversity.

Such a person the true ambidextrous one, the Doctor of the Gentiles, testifies that he was, saying:

“I have learned to be self-sufficient in whatever circumstances I am. I know how to be humbled, and I know how to abound; everywhere and in all things I have been instructed both to be filled and to hunger, both to abound and to suffer want. I can do all things through him who strengthens me” (Philipp. IV).

## CHAPTER XI. On the twofold kind of temptations, which are inflicted in three ways

[Col. 0660B]

Therefore, although we have said that temptation is twofold—that is, arising either from prosperous or from adverse circumstances—we must nevertheless know that all human beings are tempted for three reasons:

[Note: [Col. 0659D] Namely, by God; for here he is speaking of the temptation which Scripture calls discipline, instruction, testing, correction, and chastisement. Its causes or purposes are here given as three, or rather four.]

most often for testing, sometimes for correction, and at times on account of the merits of their sins.

For testing, we read that blessed Abraham, like Job, and many of the saints endured countless tribulations. So too there is the passage spoken through Moses to the people in Deuteronomy:

“You shall remember the whole journey by which the Lord your God led you for forty years through the wilderness, that he might afflict and test you, and that what was in your heart might become known, whether you would keep his commandments or not” (Deut. VIII).

And there is the passage in the psalm:

“I tested you at the water of contradiction” (Ps. LXXX).

To Job also he says:

“Do you think that I spoke to you for any other reason than that you might appear just?”

For correction, he subjects his own righteous people to various temptations on account of certain small and lesser sins, or to humble the pride of their purity, so that he may burn away all the filth of their thoughts and, to use the prophet’s words, the dross which he sees to have congealed secretly within them. Thus he may send them into the future judgment as pure gold, permitting nothing to remain in them which the fire of judgment, searching them afterward, might find and purge through penal suffering (Isa. I).

In accordance with this is the saying:

“Many are the tribulations of the righteous” (Ps. XIII);

and:
