“My son, do not neglect the discipline of the Lord, nor grow weary when you are rebuked by him; for whom the Lord loves, he corrects, and he scourges every son whom he receives. For what son is there whom his father does not correct? But if you are without discipline, in which all share, then you are illegitimate and not sons” (Hebr. XII).

And in the Apocalypse:

“Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise” (Apoc. III).

To these people also, under the figure of Jerusalem, the word is addressed by God through Jeremiah:

“I will bring destruction upon all the nations among which I scattered you; but upon you I will not bring destruction. Rather, I will chastise you in judgment, so that you may not appear innocent to yourself” (Jerem. XXX).

For this salutary correction David prays, saying:

“Test me, Lord, and tempt me; burn my kidneys and my heart” (Ps. XXV).

[Note: [Col. 0661D] These are Jeremiah’s words, not Isaiah’s, although most manuscripts, according to Cuychius, read “Isaiah.” Dionysius, however, substitutes “Jeremiah” for “Isaiah.”]

Jeremiah too, understanding the benefit of this temptation, says:

“Correct me, Lord, but in judgment, and not in your anger” (Jerem. X).

And again:

“I will give thanks to you, Lord, because you were angry with me; your anger has turned away, and you have comforted me” (Isa. XII).

But on account of the merit of sins, the wound of temptation is inflicted, as when the Lord threatens that he will send wounds upon the people of Israel, saying:

“I will send the teeth of beasts against them, with the fury of those that drag themselves across the earth; and in vain I struck your children: you did not accept discipline” (Deut. XXXII).

Likewise in the Psalms:

“Many are the scourges of sinners” (Ps. XXXI).

And in the Gospel:

“Behold, you have been made well; now do not sin any more, lest something worse happen to you” (John V).

[Col. 0661B]

We also find a fourth reason, by which we know from the authority of Scripture that certain sufferings are inflicted on some people solely to manifest the glory and works of God, in accordance with the Gospel:

“Neither this man sinned nor his parents, but that the works of God might be manifested in him” (John IX).

And again:

“This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it” (John XI).

There are also other kinds of retribution by which some who have surpassed the limit of wickedness are struck in the present, as we read that Dathan and Abiron, and especially Korah, were condemned (Num. XVI). The same applies most particularly to those of whom the Apostle says:

“Therefore God gave them over to passions of dishonor and to a reprobate mind” (Rom. I),

which must be judged more severe than all other punishments.

Concerning them the Psalmist says:

“They are not in the labors of men, nor will they be scourged with men” (Ps. LXXI).

They do not deserve to be saved through the visitation of the Lord, nor to obtain healing through temporal wounds, because, in despair, they have handed themselves over to shamelessness, to the practice of every error and to uncleanness; and through hardness of heart and the habit and continual practice of sinning, they pass beyond the purification of this very brief age and the retribution of the present life.

To them also the divine word reproaches through the prophet:

“I overthrew you, as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you became like a brand snatched from the fire; yet even then you did not return to me, says the Lord” (Amos IV).

And Jeremiah says:

“I struck down and destroyed my people, yet they did not turn back from their ways” (Jerem. XV).

And again:

“You struck them, and they did not grieve; you consumed them, and they refused to accept discipline. They hardened their faces like rock; they refused to return” (Jerem. V).

Seeing that every medicine of this present time had been expended upon their healing in vain, the prophet, despairing in some manner of their salvation, cries out:

“The bellows have failed in the fire; the smelter has blown in vain. Your wickedness has not been consumed. Call them rejected silver, for the Lord has cast them away” (Jerem. VI).

The Lord likewise complains that he has applied the salutary purification of fire in vain to those who have become hardened in their crimes, speaking under the figure of Jerusalem, whose sin has solidified into deep rust:

“Set the bronze pot upon the coals empty, so that it may become hot and its bronze may melt, and its filth may be dissolved within it. It has been heated by great labor, yet its excessive rust has not gone out of it; not even through the fire has your detestable uncleanness been removed. I wanted to cleanse you, but you have not been cleansed from your filth” (Ezek. XXI).

Therefore, the most skillful physician, having exhausted all salutary treatments and seeing that no kind of remedy remained which could be applied to their illness, is, so to speak, overcome by the magnitude of their iniquities and compelled to withdraw from them his merciful correction. Thus he declares to them:

“I will no longer be angry with you, and my jealousy has departed from you” (Ezek. XVI).

But concerning others whose hearts have not been hardened by the frequency of their sins, and who do not require that exceedingly severe and, so to speak, caustic [Lips. in margin: chastising] medicine of fire,

[Note: [Col. 0661D] That is, harsh, piercing, austere. Thus, in Book X of the Institutes, chapter 5, he calls certain medicines “caustic”; the subject is treated there.]

it is said that the salutary instruction of the word is sufficient for their salvation:

[Note: [Col. 0661D] The Vulgate reads: “I will strike them according to the hearing of their assembly.” Ciaconius notes that in Origen, Homily 16 on Numbers, the text is corruptly read: “God terrifies in order to correct a man in the tribulation of hearing,” instead of “at the hearing of tribulation”; or, as the same author has it in Homily 1 on Ezekiel: “I will rebuke them in the hearing of their distress.”]

“I will correct them in the hearing of their tribulation” (Hos. VII, according to the Septuagint).

We are also aware of other causes of chastisements or retributions inflicted upon those who have committed the gravest offenses—not to expiate their crimes or erase the merits of their sins,

[Col. 0662C]

but to correct the living and inspire them with fear. We know that such punishments were inflicted upon Jeroboam son of Nebat, Baasha son of Ahijah, and Ahab and Jezebel, as the divine judgment declares:

“Behold, I will bring evil upon you, and I will cut off your posterity; I will destroy from Ahab every male, both bond and free, in Israel. I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat and like the house of Baasha son of Ahijah, because you have acted so as to provoke me to anger and have caused Israel to sin. The dogs shall eat Jezebel in the field of Jezreel. If Ahab dies in the city, the dogs shall eat him; but if he dies in the field, the birds of heaven shall eat him” (III Kings XXI).

And there is the declaration issued as a grave threat:

[Note: [Col. 0662D] This saying was not addressed to King Ahab, as this author seems to think when he connects it with the preceding material. Rather, it was addressed to the prophet who had been sent to Bethel to rebuke Jeroboam but was deceived by a false prophet and ate contrary to the Lord’s command; for this reason he was killed by a lion and given a foreign burial (III Kings XII).]

“Your corpse shall not be brought into the tomb of your fathers” (III Kings XIII).

[Col. 0662D]

This was not because the brief and momentary punishment would have been sufficient to purge either the extremely profane schemes of the man who first established the golden calves for the perpetual transgression of the people and their impious separation from the Lord, or the innumerable and utterly sacrilegious crimes of those men. Rather, it was so that all the others who, either through negligence or through complete disbelief in the future, were shaken only by consideration of present things might be struck with terror by the example of punishments that they feared.

They were also to recognize from this evidence that, in the presence of the majesty of the supreme God, there is no neglect of human affairs and daily governance, and to perceive more clearly that God is the retributor of all actions through the very things which they most terribly dreaded.

[Note: [Col. 0663C] Isidore of Pelusium wrote to the monk Orion in the same sense (Book I, Letter 181): “It was not unbelief or madness, most diligent man, that led the wisest Peter to put those who had sinned to death (Acts V), but rather the teaching of foreknowledge, which anticipated the many sins of human beings. For when they had just begun to sow the Gospel and immediately saw tares springing up, they wisely uprooted them at once, lest, growing together with the wheat, they should be reserved for burning in the future fire. In the same way, the divine Moses, seeing that the law had immediately been violated at its beginning, ordered the man who had gathered wood on the Sabbath to be buried under stones, even though the sin was small, writing that God himself had pronounced this judgment.” This is what Isidore says (Book VII of the Institutes, chapter 14). Elsewhere we have treated of the death of Ananias and Sapphira.]

We find, moreover, that some people have suffered the same sentence of immediate death for lighter offenses, as did those whom we have mentioned as having been authors of sacrilegious transgression—for example, the man who gathered wood on the Sabbath (Num. XV), and Ananias and Sapphira, who, through an error of faithlessness, had withheld a small portion of their property (Acts V):

[Col. 0663B]

not because the weight of their sins was equal, but because they were found to be presumptuous perpetrators of a new transgression and ought to provide the others with an example not only of sin but also of punishment and terror. Thus anyone who afterward attempted the same thing would know that, according to the same pattern by which those people had been condemned, the punishment would be exacted at the examination of the future judgment, even if the penalty were deferred in the present.

And because, in wishing to survey the kinds of temptations or retributions, we seem to have made some digression from the account we had begun—where we said that the perfect man always remains unmoved in both kinds of temptation—let us now return once more to that subject.

## CHAPTER XII. How the just man ought to resemble not wax but a diamond seal

[Col. 0663C]

Therefore the mind of the just man ought not to resemble wax or any other softer material, which always yields to the character of a seal and is shaped according to its form and image, retaining that impression within itself until another seal is impressed upon it and reshapes it. In this way, never remaining constant in its own nature, it is continually converted and transferred into the form of whatever is stamped upon it.

Rather, it ought to be like a certain diamond seal,

[Note: [Col. 0663D] That is, a seal made of diamond, whose hardness, according to Pliny (Natural History, Book XVII, chapter 4), is so great that it yields neither to iron nor to fire and never becomes hot. Hence arose the proverb by which we call anything hard, unconquerable, and impregnable “adamantine.” For the same reason Origen was called Adamantius, a surname bestowed because of the invincible power of the diamond, on account of his tireless nature in writing and reading (Saint Jerome, Letter 18).]

so that our mind, always guarding the inviolable figure of its own character, may stamp and transform everything that encounters it according to the quality of its own state, while it itself cannot be marked by any external assault.

## CHAPTER XIII. The question whether the mind can continually remain in one and the same condition

Germanus: Can our mind continually retain one state and always persist in the same condition?

## CHAPTER XIV. The answer to the questioner’s proposal

[Col. 0664B]

Theodore: According to the Apostle, a person must either be “renewed in the spirit of his mind” (Eph. IV) and advance day by day, continually reaching forward toward what lies ahead (Philipp. III), or, if he neglects this, it necessarily follows that he will turn backward and fall into a worse condition.

[Note: [Col. 0663D] This is a common passage concerning spiritual progress, which may be illuminated and confirmed by the sayings of several holy Fathers. Augustine, on Psalm LXIX, says: “However long we live here, however much we progress here, let no one say, ‘It is enough; I am righteous.’ Whoever says this has remained on the road and does not know how to arrive. Where he says, ‘It is enough,’ there he has stuck fast. Consider the Apostle, for whom it is not enough. ‘Brothers,’ he says, ‘I do not consider that I have apprehended’ (Philipp. III). And again he says: ‘If anyone thinks that he knows something, he does not yet know how he ought to know’ (I Cor. VIII). ‘Forgetting the things that are behind and stretching toward those that are ahead, I pursue according to my purpose the prize of the heavenly calling’ (Philipp. III). He is running, while you have stopped? He says that he is not yet perfect, while you boast of perfection?” Saint Leo the pope, Sermon 2 on Lent: “Our nature, while mortality still remains, is changeable, even when it is advanced toward the highest pursuits of virtue. Just as it can always have a point to which it may fall back, so it can always have a point to which it may rise. And this is the true righteousness of the perfect: never to presume that they are perfect, lest, ceasing to pursue a journey that is not yet complete, they fall into the danger of failing precisely where they have abandoned the desire to progress.” Saint Bernard, in one of his letters (Letter 255): “O monk, do you not wish to progress? No. Then do you wish to fail? Certainly not. What, then? ‘I want,’ you say, ‘to live in this way and remain where I have arrived; I do not permit myself to become worse, nor do I desire to become better.’ Then you want what cannot exist. For what stands still in this world? And certainly it is said especially of the human being: ‘He flees like a shadow and never remains in the same condition’ (Job XIV). See also the same author, Letter 341.”]

Therefore, in no way can the mind remain in one and the same condition, just as if someone tried to drive a ship upstream against the waters of a violent river by the force of his oars: he must either, by the strength of his arms, cut through the current’s force and climb toward the upper reaches, or, relaxing his hands, be carried back headlong by the descending stream.

Accordingly, this will be a clear sign of our decline if we realize that we have acquired nothing more. We should have no doubt that we have been recalled in every way to the rear on the day when we have not felt ourselves advancing toward higher things. For, as I have said, the human mind cannot continually remain in the same state, nor can anyone, while dwelling in this flesh, possess the summit of virtue in such a way as to remain unmoved.

Something must always either be added to or subtracted from virtue. No perfection can exist in any creature that is not subject to the condition of change, in accordance with what is written in the Book of blessed Job:

“What is man, that he should be spotless, and that one born of a woman should appear just? Behold, among his saints none is immutable, and the heavens are not clean in his sight” (Job XV).

We confess that God alone is immutable. To him alone the prayer of that holy prophet is addressed:

“But you are the same” (Ps. CI).

And he says of himself:

“I am God, and I do not change” (Malach. III),

because he alone is naturally always good, always full, and always perfect; nothing can ever be added to him, nor can anything be diminished.

Therefore we must continually stretch ourselves toward the pursuit of virtue with unremitting care and concern, and constantly occupy ourselves with exercises of this kind, lest, when progress ceases, decline immediately follow.

For, as we have said, the mind cannot remain in one and the same state—that is, it cannot neither receive an increase of virtue nor suffer a decrease. Not to acquire is to diminish, because the abandonment of the desire to progress is never free from the danger of turning back.

## CHAPTER XV. The loss involved in leaving one’s cell

Therefore one must preserve continual residence in one’s cell. For every time a person returns, he will waver and be disturbed in it as though he were a new inhabitant and a beginner, insofar as he has wandered away from it.

[Note: [Col. 0665B] You may learn even from this chapter how much frequent and unrestricted wandering by a monk, and excursions outside the monastery, harm spiritual progress and cause decline. Hence the frequent and proverbial saying among the Fathers: “What water is to fish, the cell is to monks” (16, question 1, chapter *Placuit*). For just as a fish cannot live long outside water, so a monk easily suffers the loss of spiritual life outside the monastery. The great Antony expressed the same thought in other words, according to Sozomen (Book I of the History, chapter 13): water is nourishment for fish, while solitude is an adornment for monks; fish lose their life when they touch the earth, and monks customarily lose the monastic life when they enter cities. Likewise, it is read in the Lives of the Fathers that when a certain brother had asked Abba Moses for a word, the old man said to him: “Go and sit in your cell. Your cell can teach you everything if you remain there. For just as a fish taken out of water immediately dies, so a monk perishes if he wishes to linger outside his cell.” Thus far the text. [Col. 0665D] For this reason the holy Fathers (Athanasius, Life of Saint Antony), and especially Saint Benedict (chapters 51 and 58 of the Rule), so strongly inculcate and commend stability of place to their monks. Hence the sacred canons also frequently and severely legislate against wandering monks (in Gratian, at the place cited above), concerning which more will be said elsewhere.]

For if the disposition of soul which he had acquired while remaining in his cell has been relaxed, he will be able to recover it again only with labor and pain. Having thus been led backward, he will not think about the progress he could have added had he not been driven from his cell; instead, he will rejoice if he finds that he has recovered the state from which he fell.

For just as lost and past time cannot be recalled, so neither can the benefits that have perished be restored. However much the mind’s renewed attention may accomplish afterward, it is the progress of the present day and the gain of the present time, not the recovery of profit once lost.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the mutability of the heavenly and celestial powers

[Col. 0666B]

Yet that the heavenly powers too are subject to mutability, as we have said, is declared by those who fell from their number through the fault of a corrupted will. Hence [Note: Angels may be understood to be of unchangeable nature, or naturally unchangeable, in two ways; in one sense the Fathers deny this, in another they affirm it. First, they may be called altogether unchangeable—that is, free from and incapable of every change. In this sense it is certain that neither angels nor any other creature is unchangeable and incorruptible: first, because by nature they depend upon God, and if he were to abandon them even for a moment, they would immediately fall into nothingness; and also because they are subject to other changes and movements, since they change in will, in knowledge, [Col. 0666C] and in place. For this reason the Fathers (Dionysius the Areopagite, *On the Divine Names*, ch. 4; Nazianzen, Oration 35) call them immortal or unchangeable not by nature but by grace. So too the Sixth Synod, art. 11; Ambrose, book III *On the Faith*; Jerome, *Against the Pelagians*, book II, ch. 3; and Damascene, book II *On the Orthodox Faith*, ch. 3. In another sense angels, like human souls, are called naturally unchangeable, immortal, and incorruptible because they possess no internal and intrinsic principle of their own corruption and destruction. Hence Saint Augustine frequently calls angels immortal substances (*City of God*, book XV, ch. 17).] those who persevere in the blessedness in which they were created should not therefore be thought to be of an unchangeable nature, because they have not likewise been corrupted in the opposite direction. For it is one thing to be of an unchangeable nature, and another not to be changed—through the diligence of virtue and the guardianship of goodness—by the grace of the unchangeable God. Whatever is acquired or maintained through diligence can also be lost through negligence. Therefore it is said: [Note: The Vulgate edition reads: “Do not call any man blessed before his death.” Ciaconius omitted this passage from his index of scriptural passages according to the Septuagint.] “Do not bless a man before his end” (Ecclus. XI), since each person is still [Note: This should be read as printed, as Ciaconius rightly observed; or, as other manuscripts have it, *in the arena of wrestling*, not *in the furnace*, as Dionysius has it, nor *in the figure*, *stemma*, or *stammate*, as others do. For *skamma* (σκάμμα) among the Greeks means the sand of the stadium, or the place in which athletes competed. It is so called from *skaptein* (σκάπτειν), “to dig,” because it was surrounded by a ditch and rampart, from which the contestants were not permitted to depart. The word is frequent in Greek authors, especially Chrysostom. Tertullian uses it metaphorically, as do most others, in his book *To the Martyrs*, addressing them thus (ch. 3): “Your trainer is Christ Jesus, who has anointed you with the Spirit and brought you forth into this arena.” Saint Jerome, Letter 61, *Against the Errors of John of Jerusalem*: “Why,” he says, “leaving the matters over which the battle is being fought, and departing from the arena and place of combat, do you linger over foreign and wholly unrelated disputes?” In the same author’s *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians*, ch. V, it is corruptly read: “Seeing many contend among themselves over the Scriptures and make the word of God an athletic *stemma*,” whereas it should plainly read *scamma*. It is equally corrupt in Saint Ambrose, book I *On Duties*, ch. 16: “Why do you desire to feast before the stadium is closed? The people are still watching; the athletes are still in the *stemma*”—for *scamma*—“and you already ask for food?” Elsewhere in Ambrose it is correctly read, as in *On Elijah and Fasting*, ch. 13: “In the arena, if someone lifts him from the ground, he is indeed deprived of the palm, but free from injury,” and ch. 21: “Once he has entered the arena, the wrestler must receive the dust.” [Col. 0666D] And again: “The wrestler is in the arena, and the dust in the stadium.” Paulinus, Letter 2 to Severus: “Do not, while we are in the arena, …”] placed in combat [Col. 0667A] and, so to speak, in the arena. Although he may usually conquer and frequently win the palms of victory, he cannot be secure from fear and uncertainty about the outcome. And therefore [Note: God alone is wholly and absolutely unchangeable, according to Malachi III: “I am the Lord, and I do not change”; and I Timothy VI: “Who alone possesses immortality.” For perfect immortality is complete unchangeability. Hence Saint Bernard, Sermon 81 on the *Song of Songs*: “True and complete immortality admits neither change nor end, since every change is in some measure an imitation of death. For everything that changes, when it passes from one mode of being to another, must in some sense die as what it is, so that what it is not may begin to be. But if there are as many deaths as changes, where is immortality?” In God, however, “there is no change, nor shadow of alteration” (James I; Thomas Aquinas, *Summa*, I, q. 9). God is also called alone unchangeable and immortal, namely, in himself and by his nature, since he is essentially life itself and possesses no principle of any change, whether internal or external; [Col. 0667D] angels and rational souls, however, possess these qualities only by participation and, as the Fathers say, are [Col. 0668B] immortal and incorruptible by grace, as was said above (Thomas Aquinas, *Summa*, I, q. 9).] God alone is called unchangeable [Note: For the reason that God is called alone unchangeable and immortal—namely, by essence—he is likewise called alone good by essence, because he is goodness itself. Hence Matthew XIX says: “There is one good, God”; and Luke XVIII: “No one is good except God alone,” namely, in himself and by nature.] or good, since one who possesses goodness naturally, not through the labor of diligent effort, cannot be anything other than good. Therefore no virtue can be possessed immovably by a human being; but, if it is to be held continually ready, it must always be guarded with the same diligence and industry by which it was acquired, [Note: Cnychius noted that these words are lacking in the older printed books, although, he says, they are found in eight manuscript codices and in Dionysius. They should therefore rightly be retained, since they are sound and appropriate.] and, what is more truly the case, guarded through the benefit of assisting grace.

## CHAPTER XVII. That no one collapses through a sudden fall

[Col. 0667B]

No one, however, should be thought to have fallen through a sudden collapse, but rather either to have been deceived at the beginning by a misguided formation, or, as the virtue of the soul gradually declined through prolonged carelessness of mind, to have fallen miserably as vices slowly increased through this process. [Note: The Vulgate and Clementine reading is: “Before destruction comes pride, and before a fall the spirit is exalted.” Saint Jerome, book III *Against Rufinus*, at the end, cites it as follows: “Before destruction comes insult, and before a fall evil thought.”] For “before destruction comes a fall, and before a fall an evil thought” (Prov. XVI). In the same way, a house never collapses into ruin from a sudden blow unless either an ancient defect in its foundation or the long negligence of its inhabitants has first weakened the roof’s supports, as tiny trickles of water gradually penetrate them [Col. 0668A]; and when, through longstanding neglect, these have been opened and collapsed to a greater extent, the storm of rains and showers then pours in abundantly. “Through slothfulness the beams will decay, and through the slackness of the hands the house will leak” (Eccles. X). Solomon describes the same thing as happening spiritually to the soul in other words: [Note: Saint Jerome, book I *Against Jovinianus*, cites it in this form, following the Septuagint, which paraphrastically explained the sense of the proverb. In Hebrew it reads: “A continual dripping on a rainy day and a contentious woman are alike.” Our translator renders it: “A leaking roof on a cold day and a quarrelsome woman are comparable.” More briefly, Proverbs XIX has: “A quarrelsome woman is a continually dripping roof.” Yet the Septuagint differs greatly here from both the Hebrew and our version. The Author has therefore truncated one part of the saying here and cited only the other, which serves his purpose.] “Drippings,” he says, “drive a man from his house on a winter’s day” (Prov. XXVII).

He therefore elegantly compared carelessness of mind to a house with a neglected roof. Through such carelessness, tiny drops of the passions first penetrate the soul; if they are neglected as small and insignificant, they corrupt the beams of the virtues, and afterward the rain of vices pours in with great force. Through this rain, “on a winter’s day”—that is, when the time of temptation arrives and the devil’s assault presses in—the mind will be driven from its dwelling among the virtues, in which it had once rested, retaining itself through watchful diligence as though in the house of its own possession.

Having learned these things, we received an immeasurable delight of spiritual nourishment, so that from this conference we were filled with greater joy of soul than previously we had been afflicted with sorrow over the death of the saints. For we were taught not only about the matters over which we had been uncertain, but also, through the question that had been posed, came to know those things that, because of the narrowness of our understanding, we had not even known how to inquire about.

# THE SEVENTH CONFERENCE, which is the first of Abbot Serenus  
## ON THE MOBILITY OF THE SOUL AND SPIRITUAL WICKEDNESSES

[Col. 0667]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0667A]

We think that we cannot satisfy our desire to introduce into the minds of earnest readers Abbot Serenus—a man of supreme holiness and continence, and a mirror of his own name [Note: The same account of Abbot Serenus, in the same words, is given in the *Lives of the Fathers*, book IV, ch. 50. From there Peter of Equilium also took it and reported it in his *Catalogue* (book III, ch. 148). Photius mentions both this Abbot Serenus—in his notice of Cassian; see the beginning of the work—whom he makes equal to Abbot Moses in manner of life and teaching, and this conference held with him, whose principal topics he briefly summarizes, listing it third after the two conferences of Moses. From this it may be inferred that these conferences had indeed been translated into Greek, as we have noted elsewhere.] whom, above all others, we have admired with singular veneration, in any other way than by attempting to insert his conferences into our little books.

In addition to all the virtues that shone forth through God’s grace not only in his actions and movements but even in his very face, he had received, through a particular gift, such an infusion of chastity that he did not feel himself troubled even in sleep by the natural impulses themselves. Since, however, he attained this outstanding purity of the flesh with the help of God’s grace, and since it seems to exceed the condition of human nature, I think it necessary first to explain how he reached it.

## CHAPTER II. A remarkable miracle concerning the purity of body that he attained, and the question of the aforementioned elder concerning the condition of our thoughts

[Col. 0669B]

This man, therefore, laboring tirelessly for the inward chastity of heart and soul in prayers by night and by day, and also in fasts and vigils, when he saw that he had obtained the desires of his prayers and that every heat of carnal desire had been extinguished in his heart, burned with a still greater thirst in his zeal for chastity, as though kindled by the sweetest taste of purity. He began to devote himself to more intense fasts and supplications, so that the mortification of this passion, which by God’s gift had been granted to his inner man, might extend also to the purity of the outer man, to the point that he would no longer be disturbed even by that simple and natural movement which is aroused even in infants and nursing children. [Col. 0669C] [Note: *Indepti* is printed for *adepti*, a usage familiar to Cassian, as we have noted elsewhere (Book VI of the *Institutes*, ch. 13).] Having experienced, that is, the gift which he knew he had obtained not through the merit of his labors but through God’s grace, he was moved with greater ardor to obtain this also. He believed that God could much more easily uproot from the very roots these goads of the flesh, which human skill too sometimes removes by certain drinks or medicines, or by cutting with iron, since God had bestowed as his gift that purity of spirit which is higher and which cannot be attained through human labor or effort.

While he persisted tirelessly in his initial petition with continual supplication and tears, an angel came to him in a nighttime vision and, as though opening his abdomen, tore from his viscera and cast away a certain fiery swelling of flesh [Note: A *struma* properly means a swelling, especially one affecting the neck, when certain glands formed from pus and blood arise around the throat: in French, *écrouelles* (Rhodian Collection of Antiquities, book X, ch. 26). Here it means a piece, fragment, or little lump of swollen and harmful flesh. By analogy Cicero speaks of the “swelling of the state,” meaning its plague or destruction. Thus in his speech *For Sextius*: “Those men heal the commonwealth who cut out some plague, as though it were a swelling of the state.”] and restored all his intestines to their places as they had been. “Behold,” he said, “the incentives of your flesh have been cut away, and know that today you have obtained [Note: A similar account is given of Saint Equitius by Saint Gregory, book I of the *Dialogues*, ch. 4: “When, in the time of his youth, the incentives of the flesh wearied him in a fierce struggle, the very pressures of his temptation made him more diligent in his devotion to prayer. When he sought a remedy for this matter from almighty God through continual prayers, one night, with an angel standing beside him, he saw himself made a eunuch; and in the vision it appeared that the angel cut away all the sexual organs from his body. From that time he was so free from temptation as though he had no sex in his body. Relying on this power through the help of almighty God, just as he had previously presided over men, he afterward began also to preside over women. Nevertheless, he never ceased warning his disciples not to trust themselves easily in this matter because of his example, and not to tempt a gift they had not received. A second example, not greatly different, of singular chastity and purity bestowed by divine and angelic assistance or ministry, is found in Saint Thomas Aquinas. When he drove a prostitute from his room with a brand seized from the fire, two angels bound his loins at night with a band—which is said still to exist at Vercelli—and as a result he was thereafter pricked by no goads of the flesh (Leander, *Life of Thomas*). To this pertains the prayer said by a priest who is about to celebrate Mass, when he takes the girdle among the sacred vestments: ‘Gird me, Lord, with the girdle of purity, and extinguish in me the heat of lust, so that the virtue of continence and chastity may remain in me.’] the perpetual purity of body that you faithfully requested.”

It is enough to have said this briefly about the grace of God that was specially attributed to this celebrated man. As for the virtues that he possessed in common with the other outstanding men, I think it superfluous to mention anything, lest this account, being especially concerned with his name, seem to deprive others of what has been uniquely praised in him.

Burning, therefore, with the greatest desire for his conference and instruction, we arranged to visit him during the days of Lent. [Note: Note the ancient observance of Lent, which the Author also mentions frequently elsewhere, as in Conference 10, ch. 2, and Conference 21, ch. 2 and following. The latter concerns the relaxation of the *Quinquagesima*, which follows Lent. We shall discuss more about it there (ch. 21 and following).] When he had asked us, in a very calm address, about the character of our thoughts and the condition of our inner man, and what benefit our residence in the desert for so long a time had brought us toward attaining its purity, we addressed him with the following complaints.

## CHAPTER III. Our answer concerning the mobility of the soul

The reckoning of time and our residence in solitude—which leads you to suppose that we ought to have attained perfection of the inner man—have brought us only this benefit: we have learned what we cannot be; they have not, however, made us what we strive to be. For we do not know that we have attained either the fixed stability of the purity we desire or any strength of firmness and knowledge, but only an increase of confusion and shame.

Indeed, since meditation upon every discipline is practiced and perfected through daily study for this purpose: that, advancing from tepid beginnings to certain and stable proficiency, it may begin to know what it formerly knew only obscurely or did not know at all, and, proceeding with a firm—so to speak—step in the quality of that discipline, may become perfect in it and practice it without any further difficulty, [Note: Cassian frankly acknowledges his imperfection and fragility. This is all the more an indication of modesty because, speaking in the singular number, he blames or criticizes only himself, not a companion or anyone else.] I find, on the contrary, that my labor in the pursuit of this purity has achieved only this: I know what I cannot be. From this I feel that nothing is brought to me except grief, with such contrition of heart that there is never a lack of material for tears; yet I do not cease to be what I ought not to be.

What good, therefore, has it done to learn what is supreme, if what has been recognized cannot be grasped? For when we feel that the direction of our heart is stretching toward the contemplation appointed for it, the mind, imperceptibly turned back from there, slips with an even stronger impulse into its former wanderings. Thus, occupied by daily distractions, it is continually carried away by countless captivities, so that we almost despair of the correction we desire, and this discipline seems futile.

For at every moment the soul wanders in slippery courses. When it is brought back to the fear of God or to spiritual contemplation, before it is established in that state it again vanishes more swiftly. When, as though awakened, we discover that it has strayed from its appointed purpose and wish to lead it back to that contemplation from which it had departed, binding it with the most tenacious intention of the heart as though with certain chains, it slips away in the very effort itself more quickly than an eel from the recesses of the mind.

For this reason, burning with concern over such daily practices, yet seeing that no strength of stability has come to our hearts from them, we are driven, broken by despair, to the opinion that these wanderings of the soul belong to the human race not through our fault but through a defect of nature.

## CHAPTER IV. The elder’s discussion concerning the condition and virtue of the soul

**Serenus:** It is a dangerous presumption, before matters have been rightly examined and a sure conclusion drawn, to propose and define something about the nature of any matter, and to form a conjecture from consideration of one’s own frailty, or to pronounce judgment about the condition and quality of the discipline itself or from the experience of others.

If someone ignorant of swimming, knowing from experience that the weight of his body cannot bear the fluid of the waters, wished to determine from his own incompetence that no one at all can be sustained in liquid elements while enclosed in solid flesh, his opinion should not for that reason be judged true merely because he appears to have offered it according to his own experience. For the clearest reasoning and the unquestionable evidence of the eyes prove that this is not only possible but also very easy for others.

Thus *nous* (νοῦς), that is, the mind, is defined as *aei kinētos kai poly kinētos* (ἀεὶ κινητὸς, καὶ πολὺ κινητὸς), that is, “always mobile and very mobile.” This too is written in the Wisdom that is called Solomon’s: *Gēinon oikēma barynei noun poly phrontizonta* (Γηίνον οἴκημα βαρύνει νοῦν πολὺ φροντίζοντα), that is, [Note: The text of the Vulgate edition reads: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks upon many things.” Ciaconius writes: “This passage in the Vatican manuscript of Cassian, as also in the Greek books of the Wisdom of Solomon IX, is read as follows: τὸ γεῶδες σκῆνος βρίθει νοῦν πολυφροντίδα. In the printed editions it is corruptly given as γήϊνον οἴκημα βαρύνει νοῦν πολὺ φροντίζοντα.” This is Ciaconius’s note. The Basel Greek edition omitted the passage, as did Dionysius. The manuscripts that I have been able to read are so corrupt and faulty that nothing certain can be obtained from them. Therefore, consulting the royal Bibles, I find it written thus: Φθαρτὸν γὰρ σῶμα βαρύνει ψυχὴν, καὶ βρίθει τὸ γεῶδες σκῆνος νοῦν πολυφροντίδα.] “The earthly dwelling weighs down the mind that thinks upon many things” (Wis. IX). (See Book VIII of the *Institutes*, ch. 9.)

According to the condition of its nature, therefore, the mind can never remain idle. Unless provision has been made for where it may exercise its movements and what may continually occupy it, it must wander through everything and fly about everywhere through its own mobility, until, having become accustomed through long exercise and prolonged practice to what you say you labor at in vain, it experiences and learns what materials it ought to prepare for its memory, around which it may direct its tireless flights, gaining strength by dwelling upon them. In this way it may become strong enough to drive out the suggestions of the enemy, by which it was being distracted, and to remain in the condition and quality it desires.

We must not, therefore, attribute this wandering of our heart either to human nature or to God its creator. For the statement of Scripture is true: “The Lord made man upright, but they sought many thoughts” [Note: Dionysius also reads it this way. Ciaconius, however, corrected it from the Greek to “many thoughts,” for the Greek has *logismous pollous* (λογισμοὺς πολλοὺς), and the Vulgate reading corresponds more closely: “I found only this, that God made man upright, and he has involved himself in innumerable questions.”] (Eccles. VII). [Note: See Cuychius’s seventh annotation at the end of the work.]

The quality of those thoughts therefore depends upon us. “A good thought,” he says, “draws near to those who know it, and a prudent man will find it.” Whatever is subject to our prudence and diligence so that it may be found, if it has not been found, must without doubt be attributed to our sloth or imprudence, not to a defect of nature.

The Psalmist also agrees with this meaning when he says: “Blessed is the man whose help is from you, Lord; he has arranged ascents in his heart” (Ps. LXXXIII). You see, therefore, that it lies within our power to arrange in our hearts either ascents—that is, thoughts reaching toward God—or descents, falling toward earthly and carnal things.

If these matters did not lie within our power, the Lord would not have rebuked the Pharisees: “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” (Matt. IX). Nor would he have commanded through the prophet: “Take away the evil of your thoughts from my eyes” (Isa. I); and: “How long will harmful thoughts remain in you?” (Jer. IV). Nor would their quality be demanded from us on the day of judgment, just as our deeds will be, with the Lord declaring through Isaiah: “Behold, I am coming to gather their works and their thoughts with all nations and tongues” (Isa. LXVI).

Nor, according to the blessed Apostle’s statement, would we deserve either to be condemned or defended by their testimony at that terrible and fearsome judgment, for he says: “Their thoughts accusing or even defending one another, on the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings, according to my gospel” (Rom. II).

## CHAPTER V. On the perfection of the soul assumed in the likeness of the evangelical centurion

[Note: Cassian uses the same expression in Conference 1, ch. 8, as noted there. Dionysius is somewhat clearer: “The perfect mind, therefore, is most beautifully represented by that evangelical centurion.” The evangelical centurion is the one whose outstanding faith and steadfastness Christ himself is recorded as having admired (Matt. VIII). His example is here proposed for monks to imitate, so that they too may become true and spiritual centurions. Below, Saint Paul is likewise called an evangelical centurion.]

The figure of the perfect mind, therefore, is most beautifully represented by that evangelical centurion, whose virtue and steadfastness were described in this figurative manner: he was not carried away by every thought that pressed upon him, but according to his judgment either admitted good thoughts or expelled contrary ones without difficulty. “For I too am a man placed under authority, having soldiers under me; and I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it” (Matt. VIII).

If we too, fighting manfully against disturbances and vices, can subject them to our authority and discernment, extinguish the passions warring in our flesh, bring the unstable cohort of our thoughts under the command of reason, and drive the fiercest crowds of hostile powers from the boundaries of our breast under the saving standard of the Lord’s cross, we shall, in proportion to the merits of such triumphs, be promoted to the rank of this spiritual centurion. We read that he was also mystically represented in Exodus through Moses: [Note: The Vulgate text reads: “Appoint from among them tribunes, centurions, and officers of fifty and tens” (Exod. XVIII), and so forth. Dionysius explains it: “Appoint for yourself chiliarchs, or tribunes, and centurions.” *Chiliarchos* or *chiliarches* in military usage means one who commands a thousand men; among the Romans this was called a military tribune, just as a centurion commanded one hundred infantrymen. As Josephus also reports, the military order among the Romans was that the soldiers came in the morning to the centurions, and the centurions to the tribunes—whom the Greeks call chiliarchs or chiliarches—to pay their respects.] “Appoint for yourself chiliarchs and centurions, commanders of fifty and commanders of tens” (Exod. XVIII).

Thus, raised to the summit of this dignity, we too shall possess the authority and power to command: we shall not be carried away by thoughts we do not want, but shall be able to dwell upon and cling to those in which we take spiritual delight. We shall command evil suggestions, “Go away,” and they will go away; but to good ones we shall say, “Come,” and they will come.

To our servant too—that is, to the body—we shall likewise impose what belongs to chastity and continence, and it will serve without contradiction. It will no longer stir up against us the goads of desire, but will offer complete service to the spirit.

Would you like to know what weapons this centurion has, and for what exercises of battle they are prepared? Hear the blessed Apostle proclaiming: “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God.” [Note: That is, through God, or through God’s help, they are so strong that they can destroy and tear down all the fortifications and devices of the prince of this world—that is, the devil.] He has stated what kind they are: not carnal or weak, but spiritual and powerful through God.

Then he goes on to indicate against whom they are to be exercised: “For the destruction of fortifications, cleansing thoughts, and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and taking every understanding captive into the obedience of Christ, and being ready to avenge every disobedience when your obedience has been fulfilled” (II Cor. X). Since it is necessary to examine these matters one by one, that task belongs to another time.

For now I wish only to disclose to you the kinds and properties of the weapons with which, if we wish to wage the Lord’s wars and serve among the evangelical centurions, we must also always go armed. “Take up,” he says, [Note: The Apostle enumerates five kinds of weapons to be assumed by the spiritual centurion and ascetic under the name of *panoplia*, that is, “full armor,” most of which are elegantly expounded here: (1) the shield of faith; (2) the breastplate of charity or righteousness; (3) the helmet, that is, the hope of salvation; (4) the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God; (5) footwear in the preparation of the Gospel of peace, that is, affections well mortified and thus arranged and prepared to run along the way of God’s commandments; and (6) the girdle or military belt, by which chastity is signified. “Stand therefore, having girded your loins” (see the note on Book XII of the *Institutes*, ch. 19).] “the shield of faith, with which you may extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one.”

Faith, therefore, is the shield which, receiving the fiery darts of lust, mortifies them through fear of the future judgment and belief in the heavenly kingdom.

“And the breastplate of charity,” he says (Eph. VI). Charity itself surrounds and protects the vital parts of our breast; placed against the deadly wounds of disturbances, it blunts the opposing blows and does not permit the devil’s darts to penetrate into our inner man. “It bears all things, suffers all things, endures all things” (I Cor. XIII).

“And the helmet of the hope of salvation.” The helmet is a protection for the head. Since Christ is our head, we must always fortify him with the hope of future goods as with an unconquerable helmet amid all temptations and persecutions, and above all preserve his faith unharmed and whole. A person mutilated in other members may be weak, yet it is possible for him somehow to survive; but without a head no one is granted even a brief extension of life.

“And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI). For it is sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart (Heb. IV)—dividing and cutting away whatever it finds in us that is carnal or earthly.

Whoever is armed with these weapons, always defended from the darts and ravages of his enemies, will not be carried away as a captive and subject, bound to the enemy’s land of thoughts by the chains of marauders. Nor will he hear the prophet say: “Why have you grown old in a foreign land?” (Baruch III). Rather, like a triumphant victor, he will remain in whatever region of thoughts he chooses.

Do you also wish to recognize the strength and power of this centurion, who carries these weapons—previously described as not carnal but powerful through God? Hear the king himself gathering strong men for spiritual warfare, [Note: Saint Cuychius observed a great variety of readings in manuscript copies. Some read: “By what selection he marks them”; others: “By what affection he marks them”; others: “By what means he marks them as chosen”; others: “How he marks them as chosen”; and finally others: “Who marks them as chosen.” Of all these, he says, the last seems best to him, and it most closely agrees with the reading of Plantin’s edition, which is noted in the margin here.] by which he may mark and approve them as chosen.

“Let the weak say, ‘I am strong’; and let the patient man be a fighter” (Joel III). You see, therefore, that no one can wage the Lord’s wars unless he is patient and weak—weak, undoubtedly, with the weakness in which our evangelical centurion spoke confidently: “When I am weak, then I am strong.” And again: “Power is made perfect in weakness” (II Cor. XII).

One of the prophets speaks of this weakness: “The one who is weak among you will be like the house of David.” [Col. 0675C] “The patient man also will fight these battles” (Zech. XII). It is that patience of which it is said: “You have need of patience, so that, having done the will of God, you may receive the reward” (Heb. X).

## CHAPTER VI. On perseverance in guarding the thoughts

[Col. 0676A]

We have also discovered through our own experience that we ought to and can cling to God, if we keep the pleasures mortified and the desires of this world cut off. We are taught this by those who speak confidently with the Lord and say: “My soul has clung after you” (Ps. LXII); and: “I have clung to your testimonies, Lord” (Ps. CXVIII); and: “But for me it is good to cling to God” (Ps. LXXII); and: “Whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit” (I Cor. VI).

We must not, therefore, exhausted by these wanderings of the soul, relax our devotion to this discipline. [Note: The Vulgate reading is: “He who works his land will be satisfied with bread; but he who follows idleness will be filled with poverty.” A similar statement occurs in Proverbs XII: “He who works his land will be satisfied with bread; but he who follows idleness is most foolish”; and in Ecclesiastes XX: “He who works his land will increase the heap of grain.” Venantius Fortunatus expressed the same thought poetically in this verse:]

“Who cultivates his own fields is accustomed to keep his granaries full.”

For whoever cultivates his own land will be satisfied with bread, but whoever pursues idleness will be filled with want (Prov. 28). Nor should we be broken by harmful despair in our resolve to maintain this discipline, because [Note: [Col. 0675D] Thus the Septuagint, as Ciaconius noted in his index. The received text reads: “In every work there will be abundance; but where words are many, there is often want” (Prov. 14).] “in every diligent undertaking there is abundance.” For “the one who is easygoing and without pain will be in want” (Prov. 14). And again: [Note: [Col. 0675D] The Vulgate edition reads: “The soul of the laborer labors for him, because his mouth has compelled him” (Prov. 16).] “A man labors amid hardships for himself, and does violence to his own destruction” (Prov. 16). Moreover, “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11). For no virtue is perfected without labor, nor is it possible for anyone to climb to that stability of mind which you desire without immense contrition of heart: “For man is born to labor” (Job 5). In order that he may attain “to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. 4), he must always be watchful with the greatest attentiveness and toil with unremitting concern. [Note: [Col. 0675D] That is, to the perfection and likeness of Christ of which he had spoken above.]

Yet no one will reach the fullness of that measure hereafter except one who has contemplated and been imbued with it in the present life, and who, while still situated in this age, has already tasted it in advance, having been designated Christ’s most precious member, [Note: [Col. 0675D] *Arrha*, or *arrhabo*, or, without aspiration, *arra* or *arrabo*, properly means something given as confirmation of a contract (Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book 27, chapter 2). [Col. 0676C] In French, *denier à Dieu*. The Author appears to allude to the Apostle’s words in Ephesians 1: “You were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance,” etc. (also 2 Cor. 1 and 5). There the Latin translator used *pignus* (“pledge”) for *arrhabo*, as Saint Jerome attests; likewise elsewhere, when he says that God has given the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts. There is, however, a difference between *pignus* and *arrhabo*: a *pignus* is given in a loan, whereas an *arrhabo* is given in a contract of purchase and sale, lease, or the like. Then the *pignus* is returned once the loan has been repaid; the earnest, however, is not returned once the price has been received, since it is itself part of the price (see Saint Thomas in his *Commentary*). Hence Saint Augustine also noted that some manuscripts read: “who is the earnest of our inheritance,” perhaps more accurately than “who is the pledge of our inheritance”; and that the Greek reads *arrhabon* (“earnest”), not *pignus* (“pledge”), as Irenaeus also read it in book 5, chapter 8. Nevertheless, because both terms are used for the certainty and security of a contract, the translator employed one for the other, *pignus* for *arrhabo*. In this sense, therefore, the Author calls the grace of the Holy Spirit and perseverance in the love of God the earnest of that bond—that is, union with Christ—which enables one to be joined to his body in this flesh. This grace is, as it were, the earnest and pledge of the future immortality and glory in which the saints will be perfectly united to the Lord Christ, as glorious members to a glorious head, and will receive the inheritance of eternal inheritance, to which they have been called and adopted. Of this glory Saint Jerome says (*Epistle* 60) that the saints have already received in this age its earnest and a small portion.] having possessed the earnest of that bond by which he may be joined to his body in this flesh, [Col. 0677A] desiring one thing alone, thirsting for one thing, directing continually toward that one thing not only all his actions but also his thoughts, so that what is said of the blessed way of life of the saints in the future [Note: [Col. 0677C] That is, imparted as an earnest, or in the manner of an earnest, or pledged. Thus Blessed Agnes says in Saint Ambrose’s *Life of Saint Agnes*: “My Lord Jesus Christ has pledged me to himself with his ring,” that is, he has bound, obligated, and betrothed me to himself.] he may already hold as pledged in the present, that is, [Note: [Col. 0677C] The meaning of this apostolic statement has been discussed elsewhere (*Institutes*, book 5, chapter 4), following Saint Jerome.] that God may be “all in all” for him.

## CHAPTER VII. An inquiry concerning the mind’s instability and the assault of the heavenly powers of wickedness

Germanus: Perhaps this volatility of the mind could be restrained to some degree if so great a number of adversaries, surrounding it, did not continually drive it toward what it does not wish—or rather toward whatever the very mobility of its nature also carries it. Since such innumerable, powerful, and terrifying enemies surround and whirl it about, we would believe that resistance to them was impossible for this especially fragile flesh, unless your statements encouraged us toward this conviction as though they were heavenly oracles.

## CHAPTER VIII. Serenus’ answer concerning God’s help and the power of free choice

Serenus: Those who have experienced the battles of the inner person cannot doubt that adversaries continually lie in wait for us. Yet we say that they oppose our progress in such a way that we should believe them to be merely instigators of evil, not also compel­lors. [Note: [Col. 0677C] *Incentores* (“instigators”) is better than *incensores*, as noted elsewhere. Demons are called instigators of evil, not impellers or compel­lors, because the devil can incite a person to sin or to consent to sin by persuading, enticing, flattering, and presenting pleasant things, says Saint Thomas (1–2, question 80, article 3); but he cannot compel anyone. We have discussed this matter more fully elsewhere (*Conferences*, 11.19). Photius also noted the same point among his comments on the chapters of this Conference, writing: “It is plainly impossible that the human mind should not be disturbed by demons, although it can never be compelled or necessarily forced to fall into evil; for it is ours either to drive away or to admit that disease and movement.”]

Otherwise, no human being could avoid any sin whatsoever that they wished to imprint upon our hearts, if they possessed as much power to compel as they do to suggest. [Lipsius, in the margin: “to implant.”] [Col. 0678A] Therefore, just as they have the opportunity to incite, so we have been granted the power to reject or the freedom to consent. Yet if we fear their power and assaults, let us set against them, in turn, God’s protection and assistance, of whom it is said: [Note: [Col. 0677D] Christ, who dwells in the hearts of the godly through grace, is greater and stronger than the devil, who rules in the world—that is, in worldly people—and is therefore called “the ruler of this world.” This is taught by the Gospel parable in Luke 11: “When a strong man armed guards his courtyard,” etc.] “Greater is he who is in us than he who is in the world” (1 John 4). His auxiliaries fight for us with a much more powerful force than the multitude of our adversaries wages war against us. For God is not only the suggester of good things but also their supporter and instigator; so much so [Note: [Col. 0677D] Hence the Church prays in one of its secret prayers: “That, in his mercy, he may also compel our rebellious wills to turn toward him” (Fourth Sunday after Pentecost). God does this while ordering all things gently: he does not compel or impose any force or necessity upon the will, but effectively persuades it, though gently, by enlightening the understanding, removing obstacles, instilling fear of divine judgment, eternal condemnation, and the punishments of hell, and by other means through which he knows how to make the unwilling, reluctant, and least of all intending it—even the rebellious—willing, ready, obedient, and eager to run. For, Saint Augustine says, the human will is so in God’s power that he makes it incline wherever and whenever he wishes; yet he does so gently and in the manner proper for God to act with a free will, so that he does not destroy freedom of choice. Thus God is said to draw people: “No one comes to me unless the Father draws him.” We also say, “He drew me over to his opinion”; and the Poet says, “Each person is drawn by his own pleasure.” More will be said on this subject elsewhere.] that he sometimes draws us to salvation even when we are unwilling and unaware.

It is therefore clear that no one can be deceived by the devil except one who has preferred to offer him the assent of his will. Ecclesiastes expressed this plainly in these words: “Because sentence against those who do evil is not executed quickly, therefore the heart of the children of men is filled within them to do evil” (chap. 8). [Col. 0678B] It is therefore evident that each person falls into sin because, when evil thoughts press upon him, he does not immediately oppose them with resistance. For, [Note: [Col. 0678C] Saint Gregory aptly compares the devil both to a lion and to an ant. Hence he calls him a *myrmicaleon*, as though composed of an ant and a lion: “Rightly,” he says (*Morals*, book 5, chapter 17), “he is called *myrmicaleon*, that is, lion and ant; for to ants he is a lion, and to winged creatures an ant: for the ancient enemy is strong against those who consent, but weak against those who resist. If assent is given to his suggestions, he cannot be endured as a lion; but if he is resisted, he is crushed like an ant. To some he is a lion, to others an ant, because carnal minds scarcely endure his cruelty, whereas spiritual minds trample his weakness beneath the foot of virtue.”] “resist him,” he says, “and he will flee from you” (James 4).

## CHAPTER IX. An inquiry concerning the conjunction of the soul and demons

Germanus: [Note: [Col. 0678D] Since the preceding chapter had stated that no one can be deceived by the devil unless he offers him his assent, Germanus objects that there sometimes appears to be such a great conjunction between souls and spirits, or demons, that the movements, gestures, and actions of the two can scarcely be distinguished from one another. This argument is presented more clearly and fully in chapter 11.] What, I ask, is this so undifferentiated and intermingled association of the soul with these wicked spirits, by which they can not merely be joined to it but united with it, address it imperceptibly, enter into it, and breathe into it whatever they wish; by which they can incite it to whatever pleases them, and see through and inspect its thoughts [Col. 0678C] and movements? How can such unity arise between them and the mind [Col. 0679A] that, without God’s grace, it is almost impossible to discern what proceeds from their incitement and what from our own will?

## CHAPTER X. Serenus’ answer concerning the manner in which unclean spirits are joined to human minds

Serenus: [Note: [Col. 0679A] An obscure answer to an obscure question. Both matters are clarified in what follows. A spirit is imperceptibly—that is, invisibly—joined to a spirit, namely a demon to a rational soul, when they exist together in the body of a possessed person and inhabit it; but the soul gives form to and vivifies the body, while the demon occupies, possesses, and moves it.] It is not surprising that spirit can be imperceptibly joined to spirit and exercise a hidden [Note: [Col. 0679B] “Persuading,” he says, not compelling or forcing, as stated above (chapter 8). The devil does this in two ways, as has also been noted elsewhere: either through the sensitive appetite, by stirring its passions toward illicit things, or through the imagination, by forming in it images that move a person toward evil.] power of persuasion toward whatever things it pleases. For there is between them a certain likeness and kinship of substance, as there is among human beings. Indeed, [Note: [Col. 0679B] That is, the definition of the soul may also be applied to those spirits; or, as Dionysius puts it more plainly, the definition given of the nature of the soul—that is, the rational soul—can also be applied to them in some fashion. They are intellectual and immortal substances, like the rational soul; but the soul is the form of the body and an imperfect substance, whereas good and evil angels are perfect substances and are not forms of bodies. Hence one of the errors attributed to the Origenists is that they believed souls to become angels and angels again to become souls, following the Platonists’ opinion (Jerome, letters 59 and 61; Augustine, *City of God*, book 9, chapter 11).] the definition that is taken from the nature of the soul is not unfittingly adapted also to the likeness of their substance.

But that they should be inserted into or united with one another mutually, so that each could be capable of the other, is altogether impossible. [Note: [Col. 0679C] That is, mutually or reciprocally; but it is evident that *intrinsecus* (“internally”) ought rather to be read. For the Author means only that human souls and spirits—that is, demons—are united in the possessed not intrinsically, that is, in substance, but by a certain proximity: they coexist and dwell together in one body, especially since they do not occupy space or mutually displace one another; not, however, intrinsically, as though they entered and flowed into one another. This belongs to God alone, as the following note explains more clearly.] [Note: [Col. 0679C] To enter into the mind, or human soul, and penetrate and pervade it thoroughly and intimately belongs to God alone, not to an angel or demon. This is the common opinion both of the ancient Fathers and of later theologians. Didymus treated it especially well in his books *On the Holy Spirit*, where he proves that the Holy Spirit is true God, consubstantial (*homoousios*, ὁμοούσιος) with the Father and the Son, because he truly inhabits the souls of the saints according to his very being and fills and occupies them with his divinity. In this sense they are said to be full of, or filled with, the Holy Spirit, since no creature can receive or enter the soul or mind of a human being according to its substance; this belongs to the Godhead alone (*On the Holy Spirit*, book 1, from the beginning). In book 3, near the end, he answers two arguments or examples that might be raised from Scripture against this teaching: the first concerns Ananias, to whom Peter is said in Acts 5 to have said, “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart, so that you should lie to the Holy Spirit?” For the Greek reads: ἐκπλήρωσεν τὴν καρδίαν σου (“he has filled your heart”), whereas our translator rendered it, “Why has Satan tempted your heart?” The second concerns Judas the betrayer, of whom John 13 says: “Satan entered into Judas, who was called Iscariot.” To both objections Didymus replies as follows: “In response to what is written, ‘Why has Satan filled your heart?’ it must be said that Satan fills someone’s mind and the ruling center of the heart not by entering into him and entering into his sense and, so to speak, into the sanctuary of his heart [Col. 0680A] (for this power belongs to the Trinity alone), but like a certain clever, wicked, deceitful, and fraudulent deceiver he draws the human soul into passions of wickedness through thoughts and incitements to the vices with which he himself is filled. Finally, Elymas the magician, the son of the devil, is described as existing according to wickedness and evil, full of every deceit and every malice, with Satan [Col. 0680B] his father turning this will of his, as though through the habit of vices, into his nature. Therefore the Apostle Paul, rebuking and reproving him, says: ‘O man full of all deceit and all malice, son of the devil, enemy of the justice of God’ (Acts 13)!” Because, being crafty and cunning, he had admitted into himself every deceit of fraud, he is called the devil’s son; because Satan filled his entire ruling faculty with fraud, wickedness, and every malice, so enticing and deceiving him that Satan himself was thought to have filled his soul and to dwell in it, having prepared him as his minister and servant for all the deceits of his perversity. Regarding the second example, namely that Satan had entered into Judas, this must be said: The devil observed through certain movements and signs of his actions toward which vices Judas’s heart was especially inclined. He discovered that Judas was open to the snares of avarice; and, having found the door of greed, he put into his mind how he might receive the money he desired and, by the opportunity for profit, become the betrayer of his master and Savior, exchanging silver for ownership and accepting from the Pharisees and Jews the price of his crime. [Col. 0680C] This opportunity for thought therefore gave Satan a place, so that, entering into his heart, he might fill it with the worst will. He entered, then, not according to substance but according to operation, because it belongs to an uncreated nature to enter into someone in such a way. Thus far Didymus, translated by Saint Jerome. Finally, he concludes as follows: “The devil does not, as some suppose, fill anyone by participation in nature or substance, nor does he become that person’s inhabitant; rather, through fraud, deception, and malice he is believed to dwell in the one whom he has filled.” This is what he says, along with other remarks that follow in the same vein.

Gennadius, or whoever was the author of the book *On the Dogmas of the Church*, final chapter (in volume 3 of Saint Augustine’s works), says: “We do not believe that demons, through energetic operation, enter the soul substantially, but that they are united to it by application and oppression. To enter into the mind belongs only to the one who created it.” The Venerable Bede, explaining the words “Why has Satan tempted your heart?” says: “It must be noted that nothing can fill the human mind substantially except the creative Trinity. Satan does fill someone’s heart, not by entering into it, but by drawing the mind toward an inclination to evil through a cunning and deceitful deception, through thought and the incitements of vices, with which he teems day and night. Thus Satan is said to have filled Ananias’s heart because he infused into him the poison of his own malice.”

Saint Bernard also agrees, in sermon 5 on the *Song of Songs*, where he says: “Know this: none of the created spirits can by itself be applied to our minds in such a way that, without any intermediary or instrument of our body or his own, it might be mixed with us and infused into us so that, through participation in it, we might become learned or teachers, good or better. No angel, no soul, is capable of me in this way, nor am I capable of any of them; nor do the angels receive one another in this way. Let this privilege, therefore, be reserved for the supreme and unbounded Spirit,” etc.

Finally, the scholastics, together with the Master of the Sentences (*Sentences*, book 2, distinction 8), attribute this entering into the human soul to God alone. From these authorities we understand [Col. 0681B] that entering into souls, or entering into minds, is one thing, while entering into or penetrating bodies is another. A demon can indeed enter bodies, with God’s permission, but not souls, except improperly and metaphorically, when through suggestion he leads someone into a mortal sin or keeps him impenitent in that condition. In this sense Satan is said to have entered into Judas, to have filled Ananias’s heart, and unclean spirits to dwell in a person and depart from him. Yet a demon does not enter the human body in such a way as to be united to it as its form, or to be in it as God is intimately and essentially present in the body—and in all things—by essence, presence, and power. Rather, the demon is there only as in a place, or as a mover in what it moves, or as a torturer in the same prison as the condemned person (Saint Thomas, *Summa*, part 1, question 6, article 3). [Col. 0681A] For this is properly attributed only to the Godhead, which alone is incorporeal and simple in nature.

## CHAPTER XI. An objection as to whether unclean spirits can be inserted into or united with the souls of those whom they have possessed

Germanus: We think that the following, which we see happening in those who are possessed, is sufficiently contrary to our reasoning: [Note: [Col. 0681C] Those possessed by the devil in body are called *arreptitii* in Latin, but in Greek *daemoniaci* or ἐνεργούμενοι (“those acted upon”), as though acted upon by a demon present and working within. For demons perform various remarkable acts in and through them, as experience shows: they disturb their inner and outer senses, impel their appetite in one direction or another, and use all their limbs and organs as they please, so as either to take away speech or hearing or to say through them whatever they wish. That these things are done by a demon dwelling within, rather than one situated outside the person, is clear both because in the Gospels the Savior is so often said, in healing the possessed, to have expelled demons by commanding them to depart from people, and because in the possessed there commonly occur things that cannot happen except through an indwelling demon, such as swellings and other phenomena seen in the possessed. Hence the common theological distinction between the obsessed and the possessed establishes this difference: in the latter, the demon is present as it sometimes was in statues of idols; the former, however, it merely torments, besieges, or accompanies from without.] when they are filled with unclean spirits, they speak and do things of which they are unaware. How, then, can we fail to believe that their souls are united with those spirits when we see their souls made, as it were, into the spirits’ instrument, abandoning their natural condition and passing over into the spirits’ movements and emotions, so that they now express not their own voices, gestures, and wills but those of the spirits?

## CHAPTER XII. Serenus’ answer concerning how unclean spirits exercise dominion over the possessed

Serenus: What you say happens in the possessed, when seized by unclean spirits they speak or do what they do not wish, or are compelled to utter what they do not know, is not contrary to our foregoing definition. [Note: [Col. 0681D] The possessed have just been discussed (in the preceding chapter); two kinds are distinguished here.] For it is certain that they do not all undergo this infusion of spirits in the same way. Some are so filled with them that they have no understanding of what they do or say; others know and later remember. This must not be understood as occurring through the infusion of an unclean spirit in such a way that it penetrates the substance of the soul itself and, being united to it and somehow clothed in it, sends speeches and words through the patient’s mouth. In no way should we believe that this can be done by them. For it is clearly perceived that this happens not through any diminution of the soul but through weakness of the body: when the unclean spirit sits upon those members in which the soul’s vigor resides, imposing upon them an unbearable and immense weight, it overwhelms and blocks the soul’s intellectual senses with the most dreadful darkness. We sometimes see the same thing happen through the effects of wine, fever, excessive cold, and other illnesses that come upon a person from outside. To prevent the devil, who had received power over Job’s flesh, from attempting to inflict this upon blessed Job, the Lord forbade him, saying: “Behold, I hand him over into your hands; only preserve his soul” (Job 2). [Note: [Col. 0681D] The Fathers understand “soul” both as bodily life and as soundness of mind. For the devil could have taken away from Job not only his life but also his mind—that is, the soundness of his mind—and his judgment, if God had permitted it; the command forbade both of these.] That is, do not make him merely insane: do not weaken the dwelling of his soul, invade his understanding, or wound the organ of reason through which he must resist you; nor overwhelm the understanding and wisdom of the one resisting you, [Note: [Col. 0682B] That is, with his mind alienated, driven into fury and madness, or completely suffocated. We learned above from Didymus that among the ancients the mind was called the ruling center of the heart; he calls the mind both the ruling center and the sanctuary of the heart. Origen, earlier than Didymus, says no less explicitly in homily 9 on Exodus: “That part which is the most precious of all within him can act within itself; some call it the ruling center of the heart, others the rational sense or intellectual substance, or whatever name may be given to that portion of us by which we are capable of God.” And in homily 2 on the *Song of Songs*, chapter 1, translated by Saint Jerome, on the words “He will dwell in the midst of my breasts,” he says: “Who is so blessed as to have the Word of God as a guest in the ruling center of the heart, in the midst of the breasts, in his chest?” Ciaconius rightly advises that the reading should be “in the ruling center of the heart.” Saint Jerome likewise reads it in book 1 *Against Jovinianus*, chapter 17: “My cousin is to me, and I to him; he will dwell in the midst of my breasts, in the ruling center of the heart, where the Word of God has a dwelling,” alluding to Origen’s words. The mind, or reason, appears to have been called the ruling center of the heart because, whereas the Platonists thought that the ruling part of the soul, which they called *to hegemonikon* (τὸ ἡγεμονικόν), was located in the brain, Christians instead thought it should be placed in the heart. Hence Jerome, in his letter to Fabiola, where he discusses the priestly garment, says: “The question is, where is the ruling center of the soul? Plato says, in the brain; Christ shows it to be in the heart. ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God’; and, ‘Out of the heart proceed evil thoughts’; and, ‘Why do you think evil in your hearts?’” (Matt. 5, 9, 15). Tertullian likewise teaches this in his book *On the Soul*, chapter 15; so do Theodoret in his third discourse *On Providence* and Gregory of Nyssa in his first discourse *On the Resurrection of Christ*.
