They call the ruling center *principatus*, or, in Tertullian’s term, *principalitas*, that is, the soul’s chief seat. Only Lactantius, in his book *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 16, leaves it uncertain whether the seat of the mind is in the heart or in the brain. Saint Jerome, however, expressly attacks this later view in the passage cited above; [Col. 0683A] and the sacred writings appear to agree more with the view that locates human thoughts in the heart or breast. Hence Saint Ambrose says in sermon 11 on Psalm 118: “Your heart is the fountainhead of your thoughts.” The same point is made by Lucretius, book 3:

“The judgment which we call spirit and mind;”

“And it is situated and fixed in the central region of the breast.”

Cicero also indicates in *Tusculan Disputations*, book 1, that those who used the expression “clear-minded” (*cordati*) held the same view; from this, he says, come the terms *excordes*, *vecordes*, and *concordes* (“heartless,” “mad,” and “of one heart”). Aristotle follows the same opinion in his book *On Sense and Sensibles*.] namely, suffocating the ruling center of his heart under your weight.

## CHAPTER XIII. That spirit cannot be penetrated by spirit, but only by God, who is incorporeal

[Col. 0683A]

[Note: [Col. 0683B] That is, although a demon, who is a spirit, enters into and possesses bodies, it does not therefore follow that he can also enter into and penetrate souls—as though the human soul, which is the form of the body, were more subtle than spirits, that is, than demons, who from time to time possess human beings. But this error once spread widely from the Platonic school.]

Nor, if a spirit is mingled with this thick and solid matter—that is, with flesh—which can happen very easily, is it therefore believed that he can likewise be so united with the soul, which is also a spirit, as to make it similarly receptive to his nature. This is possible only to the Trinity, which becomes the penetrator of the whole intellectual nature in such a way that it can not only encompass and surround it, but also enter into it and, as an incorporeal substance, be poured into it as into a body (see what was noted above on chapter 10).

For although we assert that there are certain spiritual natures, such as angels, archangels, and the other powers, and also our own soul—or at any rate this subtle air—

[Note: [Col. 0683B] The opinion was ancient and widespread, even among many orthodox writers, that angels, whether good or evil—that is, demons—are not wholly incorporeal but are endowed with bodies, either aerial or exceedingly subtle, an opinion received from the schools of the Platonists. Although Christians understood sufficiently from Scripture that angels are spirits and spiritual creatures, they did not nevertheless understand this as though they were entirely without matter and body; rather, they thought that they possessed bodies so thin and subtle that, in comparison with corporeal and perceptible things, they could be seen and rightly called incorporeal and spiritual. In the same way, winds are called “spirits of storms” (Psalm 148), even though wind is not wholly incorporeal, any more than air is. Thus taught Tertullian in *On the Veiling of Virgins*, Clement of Alexandria in book 3 of the *Stromata*, Basil in *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 16, Lactantius in book 2 of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 15, and Augustine both in many places in *The City of God* and in *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*. It is therefore not surprising that this Abbot Serenus too was imbued with this opinion.

As for rational souls, which he likewise seems to deny are incorporeal in the same way as angels, this was also Tertullian’s opinion (*On the Soul*)—or rather, as Saint Augustine calls it, his delirium—in book 2 of *On the Origin of the Soul*, chapter 5 (*On Heresies*).

Moreover, although that sort of opinion concerning angelic bodies might once have been tolerated, Saint Thomas rightly teaches that, both from the testimony of Scripture and from the common teaching of the holy Fathers and the whole Church, it is sufficiently and effectively demonstrated that angels and demons are wholly spiritual and incorporeal, and do not have bodies naturally united to them, whether aerial or of any other kind. Thus, although this has not been defined as a matter of Catholic faith, it nevertheless seems erroneous and rash to hold otherwise.

First, because the word “spirit” in Scripture is commonly understood to mean an incorporeal and immaterial substance, as in John 4, “God is spirit,” and in Mark 3, Acts 7 and 23, and Hebrews 1. Next, because the Lateran Council (*Firmiter*) says that God created both kinds of creatures from nothing, the spiritual and the corporeal, namely, the angelic and the worldly, where spiritual creation—that is, angelic creation—is clearly distinguished from corporeal creation.

Finally, because many, indeed most, of the Fathers, both Greek and Latin, agree in this opinion and unanimously teach that angels, both good and evil, are wholly incorporeal and free from matter. Among the Greeks: Dionysius the Areopagite, *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, chapter 2, and *On the Divine Names*, chapter 4; Gregory Nazianzen, *Oration 2, On Theology*; Chrysostom, *Homily 22 on Genesis*; and Damascene, book 2, chapter 3. Among the Latins, one authority may suffice for all, Saint Gregory, *Moralia*, book 4, chapter 9:

> God made two creatures capable of understanding him, namely, the angelic and the human; but one had a covering of flesh, whereas the other bore nothing weak from flesh. For an angel is spirit alone, while a human being is both spirit and flesh.

Thus Gregory. See also the same author, *Dialogues*, book 4, chapter 3.

It is nevertheless not implausible that those ancient writers who held a different opinion concerning the bodies of angels and demons, and attributed a corporeal substance to them, did not understand by “body” a true body endowed with quantity and bulk, but every substance composed in any manner whatsoever. On this account, that is corporeal which consists in some composition, and that is incorporeal which is free from every composition. In this sense God alone is truly called incorporeal, as Abbot Serenus adds shortly afterward, just as he is called alone immortal and invisible, since he is pure and utterly simple act, free from every composition as well as from change (see Sixtus of Siena, *Bibliotheca Sancta*, book 5, annotations 8 and 142, and book 6, annotation 31).

Compared with God, angels may rightly be called coarse, material, and corporeal—not because they possess a corporeal substance of which they are composed, but because they are so far removed from God’s simplicity and purity that, in comparison with him, they appear almost corporeal and material (Saint Thomas, *First Part*, question 3). The interval of perfection of nature and dignity between them and God is smaller than that between the earth and the highest heavenly spirit. In the former case, the comparison is between finite and finite; in the latter, between finite and infinite. Thus teach the Fathers.

Gregory, *Moralia*, book 2, chapter 3:

> Their knowledge, he says, is greatly expanded in comparison with our knowledge; yet in comparison with divine knowledge it is narrow. Likewise, their spirits are spirits in comparison with our bodies, but in comparison with the highest and uncircumscribed Spirit, they are body.

Damascene, in the passage cited above:

> An angel is called incorporeal and immaterial with respect to us. For everything compared with God, who alone is incorporeal, is found to be coarse and material; only the Godhead is truly immaterial and incorporeal.

Finally, Bernard, sermon 6 on the *Song of Songs*:

> Let us confidently ascribe to God alone, just as immortality, so also incorporeality, and so forth.

For the same reason, what is often read in Cassian and other Fathers concerning the corporeal nature of the human soul is suitably interpreted by some in this sense: the rational soul is called corporeal in comparison with God, just as angels are, because it is not free from every composition—at least from composition of act and potency, being and essence, substance and accidents, and so forth.]

must nevertheless by no means be considered incorporeal. For they have, in themselves, a body by which they subsist, although it is much more subtle than ours. They are bodies, according to the Apostle’s statement:

> “There are celestial bodies and terrestrial bodies” (1 Corinthians 15),

[Note: [Col. 0685B] The “animal body” is so called from the sensitive and vegetative parts of the soul, whose powers the body requires while we are alive. But the body will rise as a spiritual body, that is, incorruptible. The bodies of the righteous are called spiritual in a special sense, since they are endowed and adorned with the four qualities that theologians call the gifts of the risen body: impassibility, subtlety, agility, and brightness. But this contributes nothing to proving the corporeal substance of angels or souls.]

and again:

> “It is sown an animal body; it rises a spiritual body” (1 Corinthians 15).

From these statements it is clearly inferred that nothing is incorporeal except God alone. Therefore only he can be penetrable to all spiritual and intellectual substances, because he alone is wholly and everywhere and in all things, so that he sees and examines all human thoughts, all inward movements, and every hidden recess of the mind.

[Note: [Col. 0685B] The whole of Scripture testifies that God alone knows the hearts and thoughts of human beings. In addition to the passages cited here, see 1 Chronicles 28: “The Lord searches all hearts and understands every thought of the mind.” 2 Chronicles 6: “For you alone know the hearts of the children of men.” Job 10: “Behold, my witness is in heaven, and my testimony is on high.” Psalm 7: “God searches hearts and kidneys.” Isaiah 1: “Take away the evil of your thoughts from my eyes.” Jeremiah 17: “The heart of man is perverse and inscrutable; who can know it? I, the Lord, test the heart and search the kidneys.” There the human heart is called “perverse” not so much because it is evil as because it is hidden, concealed, and difficult to penetrate. Hence the Septuagint translators rendered it “deep beyond all things.” Romans 8: “He who searches hearts knows what the Spirit desires,” and similarly in many other places.]

Of him alone, therefore, the blessed Apostle declared:

[Note: [Col. 0685C] These words can be understood both of the uncreated Word of God—that is, the Son of God—and of the created word. Properly, however, in this passage “the word of God” is understood as the uncreated Word and Son of God, as Abbot Serenus and other Fathers explain it. This is the Word of which John 1 says, “In the beginning was the Word,” and 1 John 5 says, “The Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit,” and Revelation 19 says, “His name is the Word of God.” In these passages the Greek reads *logos* (λόγος), which translators render indifferently as “word” or “speech.” Ambrose therefore reads in book 4 of *On the Faith*, chapter 3: “For the Word of God is living,” and so forth.

Each word here has its own emphasis and force. The speech, or Word, of God is called living and effective because of its life-giving operation, and “more penetrating than any two-edged sword”—that is, a sword cutting on both sides—because God and the Son of God penetrate and pass through the innermost things by the vision of their knowledge, far more than a double-edged sword could penetrate. It reaches “to the division of soul and spirit”: by “soul” they understand the animal powers, or the sensitive part of the soul that we share with irrational animals; by “spirit,” the rational part or intellectual faculty. Thus Christ, the Word of God, reaches to the division of soul and spirit when he distinguishes animal from spiritual thoughts.

It also reaches “to the division of joints and marrow,” not because it divides joints from marrow, but because it examines and explores our external and internal realities. By “joints,” which are the external bindings of the limbs, he understands external works; by “marrow,” which lies hidden within, he understands inward thoughts. The following words explain this: “and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart”—that is, he knows and judges with complete precision not only what each person thinks in his heart, but also with what intention he thinks and wills.]

> “For the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart. And no creature is invisible in his sight, but all things are naked and open to his eyes” (Hebrews 4).

And blessed David says:

> “He who formed their hearts individually” (Psalm 32).

And again:

> “For he himself knows the secrets of the heart” (Psalm 33).

Job likewise says:

> “You alone know the hearts of the children of men.”

## CHAPTER XIV. The objection that demons must be believed to perceive human thoughts

Germanus: By the reasoning you give, these spirits cannot even observe our thoughts. We consider it very absurd to suppose this, since Scripture says:

[Note: [Col. 0686B] Saint Jerome on this passage: “The prince of this world and ruler of this darkness,” whom the Apostle also mentions in Ephesians 6, is now signified by Scripture. If he has entered our heart and the mind has received the wound of an evil thought, we must not willingly grant it a place, but fight against the worst thought and be freed from the greatest sin—namely, lest we complete the thought by an action; for it is one thing to sin in thought and another to sin in deed.

Shortly afterward he adds this translation by Symmachus: “If the spirit of the ruler rush upon you, do not leave your place, because chastity restrains many sins.” That is: if the devil has tickled your mind and stirred you to lust, do not follow the worst thought that flatters pleasure, but stand firm and rigid in the cold of chastity and extinguish the flame of pleasure.]

> “If the spirit of one who has power rises up against you” (Ecclesiastes 10).

And again:

[Note: [Col. 0686C] Saint Augustine, *Tractate 55 on John*: “If you ask what was sent into Judas’s heart, it was certainly this: that he should betray him. This sending is a spiritual suggestion, and it does not take place through the ear but through suggestion. For demonic suggestions are injected and mingled with human thoughts. It had therefore already been accomplished in Judas’s heart, through demonic insertion, that he should betray his master to the disciples.”]

> “When the devil had put into the heart of Simon Iscariot that he should betray the Lord” (John 13).

How, then, can it be believed that our thoughts are not open to them, when we feel that their seed arises for the most part from the fact that they themselves inject and incite them?

[Note: [Col. 0686C] Elsewhere, “origin.” For Abbot Moses, *Conference* 19, said that our thoughts have three origins, since they proceed from God, from the devil, and from ourselves. “From the devil,” he says, “the series of thoughts arises when he attempts to overthrow us both through the attraction of vices and through hidden snares, displaying evil as good with the subtlest cunning,” and so forth.]

[Note: [Col. 0686C] This is properly stated, as though he were saying “not entirely.” For not all thoughts, even wicked ones, arise from demonic insertion and suggestion. Saint Jerome, commenting on Matthew 15, “Out of the heart come evil thoughts,” rebukes those who think that all thoughts are injected by the devil and refuse to acknowledge that they arise from one’s own will.

Gennadius likewise says in *On Ecclesiastical Dogma*, chapter 82: “Not all our evil thoughts are always aroused by the devil’s prompting, but sometimes they emerge from the movement of our own free will.”

Thus the devil seemed rightly to complain to Saint Antony that Christians, especially monks, attributed all sins to him. For Antony, as Athanasius relates, said:

> “Once a demon knocked at the door of a monastery. When I went out, I saw a man of enormous height, with his head reaching to heaven. When I asked him who he was, he said, ‘I am Satan.’ And I said, ‘What are you seeking here?’ He replied, ‘Why do the monks unjustly accuse me? Why do all Christian peoples curse me?’ And I said, ‘They are right to do so, for they are frequently troubled by your snares.’ But he said, ‘I do nothing; they disturb one another. I have become wretched: behold, I now have no place, I possess no city, I have no weapons, and the name of Christ resounds through every province; even the solitudes are filled with choirs of monks. Let them guard and watch over themselves, and not tear me apart without cause or curse me unjustly.’”

Then, marveling joyfully at God’s grace, I spoke to him as follows:

> “I do not attribute so new and unheard-of a statement to your truth, for there is none. Since you are the father of deceit, you have been compelled to confess this without lying.”

This is what is found there.]

But so that it may be more certainly and distinctly clear what should be thought about this matter, Saint Thomas must be heard (*First Part of the Second Part*, question 80, article 4). Having proposed the question “Whether all human sins arise from the devil’s suggestion,” he answers:

> “It must be said that, occasionally and indirectly, the devil is the cause of all our sins, insofar as he led the first human being to sin. From that sin human nature was so corrupted that we are all inclined to sin, just as one might say that the cause of wood burning is the person who dried the wood, since it would consequently catch fire easily. But directly he is not the cause of all human sins, as though he persuaded us to commit each individual sin.

> Origen proves this in book 3 of *Peri Archon*, chapter 7, from the fact that even if the devil did not exist, human beings would still have an appetite for food, sexual intercourse, and similar things, and this appetite could be disordered; it would then be subject to free will.”

Thus Saint Thomas.]

## CHAPTER XV. The answer concerning what demons can and cannot do with human thoughts

Serenus: There is no doubt—

[Note: [Col. 0687B]

A very well-known question is discussed here: whether angels and demons know the thoughts of hearts. Although it is clear from what has been said that God alone enters into human minds, and that human thoughts and the counsels of hearts are open to him alone, it is nevertheless by no means easy to understand how those spiritual substances—or those spirits, exceedingly subtle and penetrating by nature—cannot perceive and penetrate our thoughts and affections, especially those which they themselves are said to inspire, suggest, and inject into us, since they seem to be prevented from doing so by no obstacle or impediment, either on their own side or on ours.

For an explanation of this matter and a fuller clarification of what Serenus discusses here, it must first be noted that there are two kinds of operations of the intellect and will. Some are natural, others free. Natural operations are determined toward one thing, or precede judgment and deliberation, such as first movements, thoughts, sudden affections, and involuntary wanderings. Free and voluntary operations arise from judgment and spontaneous will and are not determined toward one thing.

These two kinds of operations are related in such a way that free operations belong to a higher order than natural ones. Therefore, knowledge of natural operations does not entail knowledge of free operations insofar as they are free—that is, with respect to affirmation and denial, choice and avoidance, assent and dissent.

Second, it must be admitted that angels and demons can see our natural thoughts and affections, even those belonging to the higher and intellectual part—natural thoughts, that is, which precede reason and deliberation and are not properly human actions. Angels perfectly know all substances, their powers, and their natural acts, and this is not disputed. For nature’s action is naturally disposed to reveal itself; just as its substance cannot remain hidden, neither can its effects. But what is produced freely can likewise be freely concealed or revealed.

Third, it must be held as certain that neither angels nor demons, by their natural power, can know free and spontaneous thoughts and affections as they exist in the intellect and will, without some other manifestation.

First, because this is attributed to God as his peculiar prerogative, as was shown above from many passages of Scripture. To these may be added the Apostle’s statement in 1 Corinthians 2: “For who among human beings knows the things that belong to a human being, except the spirit of the human being that is in him?”

Saint Thomas, in his commentary, significantly notes that it says “who among human beings,” lest God also appear to be excluded from this knowledge, since he alone knows the secrets of the heart.

He says that the reason is clear why a human being cannot know what lies hidden in another’s heart: human knowledge is received through the senses. Therefore a human being cannot know what is in another’s heart except insofar as it is manifested through sensible signs, according to 1 Samuel 16: “A human being sees what appears outwardly, but God looks upon the heart.”

But neither a good nor an evil angel can know what lies hidden in the human heart except insofar as it is manifested through some effects. The reason can be taken from the Apostle’s own words: he says that the human spirit knows what lies hidden in the human heart because it is in the human being. But an angel, whether good or evil, does not enter into the human mind so as to be in the human heart and work inwardly within it. This belongs to God alone. Thus Saint Thomas.

Second, because the Fathers unanimously teach this and prove Christ’s divinity from his knowledge of hidden thoughts, so often manifested in the Gospel: Ambrose on Luke, chapter 5; Jerome on Jeremiah, chapter 17, and Matthew, chapter 9; Chrysostom, *Homily 30 on Matthew*; Cyril, book 2 on John; and others.

Third, by Saint Thomas’s fundamental argument (*First Part*, question 57, article 4):

> “The will of a rational creature is subject to God alone, and he alone can work upon it, as its principal object and ultimate end. Therefore those things that depend solely on the will, or that exist solely in the will, are known to God alone.”

Since our will can be moved inwardly by no one except God, and since the movement of the will is immediately subject to his command, the mind of the person thinking and willing can be known only to God and to that person himself.

Fourth, there is also the not-unpleasing account of John Climacus, in *The Ladder*, step 31. Speaking about discernment, he writes that monks sometimes deliberately deceived the demon by displaying one thing outwardly while entertaining another in their minds and thoughts:

> “Whoever conquers the vices wounds the demons; and by pretending to have vices, he deceives his enemies and remains unconquerable. One of the brothers was once subjected to disgrace. Although he had not been inwardly disturbed at all, he prayed secretly in his mind and began to lament amid the insults. By this feigned disturbance he most wisely concealed his tranquility.

> Another brother, although he had no desire at all for the first sitting, pretended most eagerly to desire it. But in what words shall I describe the chastity of the man who, entering a brothel as though for the purpose of sinning, brought the prostitute herself to repentance?

> Again, when someone living alone had brought a monk a bunch of grapes early in the morning and had then departed, the monk devoured it with great and sudden haste, without any appetite whatsoever, thereby indicating to the demons that he was enslaved to gluttony and mocking them.

> Another, having lost a few palm leaves, pretended throughout the day to be mourning.”

Climacus then adds this precaution:

> “They were extremely vigilant lest, while attempting to mock their enemies, they themselves should become more truly objects of mockery to them. For these are indeed the ones of whom the Apostle says: ‘As deceivers and yet truthful’” (2 Corinthians 6).

Finally, even pagans, guided by natural light, recognized and acknowledged that human thoughts are known to God alone and hidden from all others: Socrates in Xenophon, book 4; Apollonius of Tyana in his speech to Domitian; Julian the Apostate in Ammianus, book 25; and Pacuvius in Gellius, book 14, chapter 5.

Fourth, internal thoughts and affections of the mind can nevertheless be detected from outward signs—for example, from movement or alteration of the face or another bodily part, or from some other external sign. Angels and demons detect these much more skillfully and expertly than even the most skillful and experienced physicians, as Abbot Serenus teaches here, and other Fathers support him.

Saint Jerome, on Matthew 15:

> “The devil can be the assistant and inciter of evil thoughts, but he cannot be their author. If, however, he is always lying in wait and has inflamed the faint spark of our thoughts with his kindling, we must not suppose that he also searches the hidden things of the heart. Rather, he estimates from the body’s condition and gestures what we are pondering inwardly. For example, if he frequently sees us looking at a beautiful woman, he understands that the heart has been wounded by the dart of love.”

Saint Augustine, *On the Divination of Demons*, volume 3, chapter 5:

> “Sometimes they learn with complete ease not only the dispositions of human beings expressed in words, but also those conceived in thought, when certain signs are expressed by the body from the mind. From this they also foretell many future events, which seem marvelous to others who do not know the dispositions producing them.

> For just as a more agitated movement of the mind appears in the face, so that human beings too can perceive externally something of what is being done inwardly, it should not seem incredible that even subtler thoughts give certain signs through the body, signs that human beings cannot perceive with their duller senses but that demons can perceive with their keener ones.”

This Augustine seems in some way to retract in book 2 of *Retractions*, chapter 30, where he says:

> “I spoke of a very obscure matter with more confidence than I ought to have done. For it has been established by certain experiments that these things do come to the knowledge of demons. But whether those who are thinking give bodily signs perceptible to them but hidden from us, or whether they know these things by some other power, a spiritual one, can scarcely—or perhaps cannot at all—be discovered by human beings.”

Gennadius, in the passage cited above (*On Ecclesiastical Dogma*, final chapter):

> “We are certain that the devil does not see the inward thoughts of the soul, but we have learned by experience that he gathers them from bodily movements and from signs of affections. The secrets of the heart, however, are known only to him to whom it is said: ‘You alone know the hearts of the children of men’” (2 Chronicles 2).

Finally, Saint Thomas, following the ancient writers:

> “A thought is sometimes known not only through an external act but also through a change in the face, according to the Poet’s words: ‘How difficult it is not to betray one’s mind by one’s face!’ Physicians too can recognize certain affections of the mind through the pulse; much more so can angels, and even demons, since they assess such bodily changes with greater subtlety.”

Fifth, I add this final point: if God permits, a demon can so violently disturb and distract a person by injecting mental images that he can scarcely think of anything else or attend to anything other than what has been suggested to him. Thus the demon seems to divine what the person is then thinking. There are many testimonies and examples from the holy Fathers of this importunity and most troublesome assault.

Athanasius, the writer of Saint Antony’s *Life*, attests how frequent and importunate were the temptations of every kind that Antony experienced. Saint Jerome says of Hilarion:

> “The devil tickled his senses and suggested to his maturing body the customary fires of pleasures. Christ’s young recruit was compelled to think of what he did not know and to turn over in his mind the pageantry of a thing of which he had had no experience. Angry with himself and striking his breast with his fists, as though he could drive out thoughts by the blows of his hand,” and so forth.

The same Jerome says of himself in Letter 22, *On the Guarding of Virginity*, among other things:

> “How often, when I was established in the desert, in that vast solitude which, scorched by the sun’s heat, affords monks a dreadful habitation, did I imagine myself amid Roman delights! I, who through fear of Gehenna had condemned myself to such a prison, with only scorpions and wild beasts for companions, was often among bands of girls. My face was pale from fasting, yet my mind burned with desires in my chilled body; and before a man already dead to his own flesh, the fires of lust alone seethed. I remember joining day to night in crying out, nor did I cease striking my breast until, by the Lord’s rebuke, tranquillity returned.”

These and other passages occur there in Jerome, and will be cited more suitably elsewhere. There are similar examples in Palladius on Moses the Ethiopian; in Saint Gregory, *Dialogues*, book 2, chapter 2, concerning our most holy patriarch Benedict; and frequently in book 3 of the *Lives of the Fathers* and elsewhere.

But although, if God allows it, a demon can inject thoughts of this kind importunately, he cannot bring any compulsion or necessity upon the will. Nor can he have certain knowledge of the will’s assent or dissent, but only probable knowledge from outward signs, as has been said. God has not allowed him to exercise his powers in tempting as much as he would wish and could do, but only as much as human frailty can bear; and he never leaves it without sufficient aid. For, as the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 10: “God is faithful, who does not permit us to be tempted beyond what we can bear, but also provides with the temptation a favorable outcome,” that is, an increase of grace and assistance.]

that unclean spirits can discern the qualities of our thoughts, gathering them from sensible signs outwardly—that is, from our dispositions, words, and pursuits toward which they have observed us to be more strongly inclined. But they cannot approach those thoughts that have not yet emerged from the soul’s interior.

Even the thoughts they themselves inject—whether they have been received, and in what manner they have been received—they detect not through the nature of the soul itself, that is, through that inward movement hidden, as I may say, in its marrow, but from the movements and signs of the external person.

For example, when they have suggested gluttony, if they see a monk raise his eyes too inquisitively toward a window or toward the sun, or inquire too anxiously about the hour, they recognize that the desire for food has been received. If, while injecting fornication, they sense that he has patiently received the dart of lust, or see that he has been physically aroused, or at least has not sighed against the obscenity of the suggestion as he ought to have done, they understand that the dart of lust has been fixed in the soul’s innermost chambers.

If they apply incentives to sadness, anger, or rage, they discern whether these have taken possession of the heart from bodily gestures and perceptible agitation—when, for example, they observe him growl silently or sigh with some indignation, or notice that his face has changed with a certain pallor or redness. In this way they subtly discover to which vice a person is devoted.

They recognize with certainty that each of us takes pleasure in that vice at whose instigation they soon perceive, by some nod or movement of the body, that he has given his consent and agreement.

It is not surprising that these aerial powers detect such things, since we often see prudent men do the same: they recognize the condition of the inner person from the shape and expression, or the qualities, of the exterior person. How much more certainly, then, can these things be detected by those who, being spiritual natures, are unquestionably much subtler and more perceptive than human beings!

## CHAPTER XVI. An illustration showing how unclean spirits are taught to recognize human thoughts

[Col. 0691A]

[Note: [Col. 0691B] An exceedingly obscure and difficult comparison, for whose explanation one would almost have to summon Oedipus, or some petty thief of the kind under discussion. Dionysius’s paraphrase is somewhat clearer and more explicit. It reads as follows:

“Just as certain robbers and thieves, in houses into which they secretly enter, investigate the wealth of the inhabitants that they cannot see by scattering tiny grains of sand with their hands in the darkness of night, so that they may perceive the riches stored in the house by the ringing produced when the sand falls, and thus arrive at the most certain knowledge of the object or of whatever metal it may be through the sound elicited, so demons scatter wicked suggestions in our hearts, like tiny grains of sand, in order to investigate the treasure of our hearts when they see a bodily affection arise corresponding to the quality of the suggestions,” and so forth.]

For just as certain robbers, in the houses they wish to attack secretly, customarily investigate the hidden possessions of the inhabitants, carefully [*cauta*, “cautious”] scattering tiny grains of sand with their hands through the dreadful darkness of night, and detecting the concealed riches—which they cannot see—with a certain ringing or noise answering to the fall of the sand, and thus arriving at the most certain knowledge of the object or of any particular metal through the disclosure of a sound produced, so these beings too, in order to investigate the treasure of our heart, sprinkle harmful suggestions upon us as though they were grains of sand. When they see a bodily affection arise in accordance with their quality, they recognize, as though from a ringing emerging from the innermost chambers, what is hidden in the recesses of the inner person.

## CHAPTER XVII. That not every demon individually inflicts every passion upon human beings
We must understand, however, that not all demons inflict every kind of passion upon human beings, but that certain spirits lie in wait over particular vices: some take pleasure in uncleanness and the filth of lust; others in blasphemies; others devote themselves especially to anger and rage; others feed upon sadness; others are delighted by vainglory and pride. Each inserts into human hearts the vice in which it itself delights. Nor do they all impose their depravity at once, but each in turn, as opportunity is provided by the time, place, or disposition of the person who receives them.

[Note: [Col. 0691C] Dionysius the elucidator: Not all demons bring every kind of temptation or passion, but particular ones serve and pursue particular vices. For some delight in impurities, etc. The same is found in blessed Jerome’s *Letter to the Ephesians*, chapter VI: “For,” he says, “there are certain demons serving love affairs and love songs,” as the prophet also recalls when he says: ‘You have been seduced by the spirit of fornication.’ For they are said to have certain barbarous names as well” (as those whom the common people truly call sorcerers have often confessed), “as well as incantations, prayers, [Col. 0691D] various colors, and different kinds either of metals or of foods; when summoned to these, demons are said to attend and capture wretched souls. Others bring on anger, rages, and wars; others preside over enmities and stir up hatred among human beings.” Thus far blessed Jerome.

Moreover, we must remember what we noted elsewhere from blessed Thomas (*Book XII*, chapter 4): vices, or sins, are attributed to demons in two ways. “In one way,” he says, “according to guilt; in another, according to inclination. According to guilt, all sins can be found in demons, because by inducing human beings to every sin they incur the guilt of every sin. According to inclination, however, only those sins can be found in evil angels toward which a spiritual nature can be inclined; but a spiritual nature cannot be inclined toward goods proper to the body, etc.” From this he concludes that, according to inclination, no other sin can exist in demons than pride and envy, which are spiritual sins and from which the others derive.

[Col. 0692B] Blessed Augustine also confirms this in *The City of God*, XIV, chapter 3: “Even if the devil is a fornicator, or a drunkard, or guilty of some other evil of this kind belonging to the pleasures of the flesh, he cannot be called such, since he is also the secret persuader and instigator of such sins; yet he is supremely proud and envious. For who is more hostile than he to the saints? Who is found to be more contentious and vehement against them, and more jealous and envious?” Thus Augustine.

Therefore, when you read or hear here that some demons take pleasure in uncleanness and the filth of lust, others devote themselves especially to anger and rage, others feed on sadness, and so forth, do not understand this as though they themselves practice these things in themselves, or were inclined toward such vices and captured by their pleasure. Rather, understand it to mean that some take greater pleasure in harassing and tempting human beings through lust, others through anger, others through sadness, and others in other ways. It is likewise plausible that there are some who delight in making the people they possess mute or deaf; and others who, as blessed Jerome says, observe the changes of the moon in order to harass human beings and defame God’s creation.

This is gathered from Matthew XVII and Mark IX, where Christ says: “This kind of demon is not cast out except by fasting and prayer,” as though attributing this to their particular nature. From this diversity of temptations and harassments it also follows that they acquire different designations and names: one is called an unclean spirit, or a spirit of fornication; another, a spirit of pride; another, a spirit of dizziness; another, the father of lies; another, a murderer from the beginning, and so forth. They incline and incite more frequently and readily toward these vices. For the same reason, in Luke XI, the demon itself is called “mute.” But more on this below, in the following Conference.]

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### Germanus’s Question: Whether an Order and Regulated Alternation of Attack Is Maintained among the Demons

**Germanus:** Then must we believe that wickedness among them is ordered and, so to speak, disciplined, so that they observe some arrangement of alternation and conduct their attacks according to reason? For it is clear that neither measure nor order can exist except among the good and honorable, in accordance with that saying of Scripture: “You will seek wisdom among the wicked, and you will not find it” (Proverbs XIV, according to the Septuagint), and: “Our enemies are senseless” (Deuteronomy XXXII, according to the Septuagint). Also: “There is no wisdom, no strength, and no counsel among the impious” (Proverbs XXI, according to the Septuagint).

[Note: [Col. 0692D] Thus according to the Greek translation: ζητήσεις σοφίαν παρὰ κακοῖς, “You will seek wisdom among the wicked.” The Vulgate edition, however, reads: “The scoffer seeks wisdom and does not find it.”]

[Note: [Col. 0692D] The Vulgate: “Our enemies are our judges” (Deuteronomy XXXII). In some books, including certain copies of the Plantin edition, this testimony was incorrectly joined to the preceding one, which is cited from Proverbs, as Ciaconius noted.]

[Note: [Col. 0692D] The commonly printed edition reads: “There is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord.”]

## CHAPTER XIX  
### Serenus’s Answer: How the Assembly of Demons Maintains a Concerted Alternation in Its Attacks

[Col. 0693A]

**Serenus:** It is a settled truth that there is not perpetual agreement in every respect among the wicked, and that perfect harmony cannot endure even in those vices in which they commonly delight. For, as you have said, discipline and order can never be maintained in undisciplined matters. Nevertheless, in certain circumstances—when a common operation or necessity requires it, or when the prospect of some gain invites cooperation—they must lend one another a temporary agreement.

[Note: [Col. 0693B] That is, they must at least temporarily come to an understanding and agree among themselves, as thieves and brigands commonly agree with one another for the ruin and harm of others. For if Satan were divided against himself, how would his kingdom stand (Matthew XII)? On this subject blessed Thomas says (*First Part*, question 109, article 2): “The concord of demons, whereby some obey others, does not arise from friendship among them, but from their common wickedness, by which they hate human beings and oppose God’s justice. It is characteristic of wicked men to join themselves and submit themselves to those whom they see to be stronger, in order to carry out their own wickedness.” And in his response to the third argument: “Demons are not equal according to nature; hence there is in them a natural precedence, which does not occur among human beings, who are equal by nature.”

[Col. 0693C] “That inferiors are subjected to superiors is not for the good of the superiors, but rather for their evil; for since doing evil belongs supremely to misery, to preside in evil is to be more miserable.” Thus Saint Thomas.

From this we understand that among demons there are degrees of order—not according to grace or glory, but according to nature. Accordingly, some are superior and others inferior; some preside and dominate, others are subject and obey. Whatever order—whether of nature or of preeminence and superiority—they possessed before the Fall, they retain after the Fall, since their natural properties remained intact in the demons, as blessed Dionysius the Areopagite says (*On the Divine Names*, chapter 4).

But just as good angels willingly and cheerfully obey their superiors, so, conversely, evil demons obey their superiors like wicked slaves obeying harsh masters, or a weaker tyrant obeying a more powerful one: they do so unwillingly and only when subdued by evil. But more on this in the Eighth Conference.]

That this occurs in the warfare of spiritual wickedness is most clearly evident: they not only observe periods and alternations among themselves, but are also known to cling especially to certain places and to besiege them continually.

[Note: [Col. 0693B] Some places are more troubled than others and are habitually occupied and harassed by demons. This occurs not because of the nature or condition of the places, but according to God’s will and the demons’ choice, as Peter Thyraeus carefully teaches in a special book published on this subject, where he lists five or six kinds of such places (*On Troubled Places*, chapter 14 and following).

First are deserted and uncultivated solitudes. The prophet Isaiah seems to suggest this in chapter XXXIV, when he teaches that the deserted cities of Idumea will become dwellings of screech owls, demons, onocentaurs, and hairy creatures. John says the same in the Apocalypse, chapter XVIII, when he calls deserted Babylon a dwelling place of demons. So too the Evangelist Matthew, chapter IV, relates that Christ was tempted by the devil in the desert. The holy anchorites also often experienced this, as may be seen in the Life of Saint Antony by Athanasius, in the Life of Macarius of Egypt by Palladius, and in those of Paul and Hilarion by Jerome. Hence Jerome calls the desert fertile in monstrous animals. [Col. 0694B] Cyril, commenting on Isaiah XXXIV, says: “Evil spirits are said willingly to dwell in desert places.”

Second are damp and marshy places. This seems to be indicated in Luke XI, where the unclean spirit cast out from a person is said to find no rest in dry and waterless places and therefore to return to its former dwelling.

Third are underground caves, especially where metals and other necessities for human use are mined; hence the demons are called “metallic demons.” An example of this is found in the Life of Saint Theodore the Archimandrite in Surius, volume II.

Fourth are vast and spacious fortresses, or ancient and ruined buildings. Saint Antony also experienced this. As Saint Athanasius relates, after he had shut himself away for twenty years in a deserted fortress filled with serpents, he suffered the most severe harassment and attacks from demons. “For,” he says, “while many spent the night before his door, driven by the desire to see him and the eagerness to seek him, voices and tumult could be heard, like the cries of a mob saying against Antony: ‘Why do you intrude upon our dwelling places? What have you to do with the desert? Depart from foreign territory. You cannot live here or withstand our ambushes,’” and so forth.

Fifth are places distinguished by murders or other enormous sins. Palladius supplies examples of this in the *Lausiac History*. John the Deacon, in the Life of Blessed Gregory, also testifies that a certain estate belonging to Barbilian was infested by demons because of the crimes of its inhabitants, and that many inhabitants were killed by them.

Finally, Thyraeus adds the places of holy people, especially monks, whom demons especially envy and against whom they lie in wait. They inflict upon them whatever troubles they can, when God does not prevent them. He proves this from chapter 23 of this Conference, where he relates that formerly, in the very monasteries in which eight or ten monks lived, demons raged so violently and launched such frequent and visible attacks that the monks did not dare all sleep at night together. Instead, while some tasted sleep, others kept watch, devoting themselves to psalms, prayers, and readings. The same is evident from the Lives of the Holy Fathers Antony, Macarius, Benedict, and others.]

Since they must conduct their attacks through changing temptations and particular vices at particular times, this is plainly demonstrated by the fact that no one can at the same time be deceived by the vanity of vainglory and burned by the desire for fornication; nor can anyone be puffed up by the swelling of spiritual pride and at the same time be humbled by the abasement of carnal gluttony. Nor can someone be dissolved in foolish laughter and senseless merriment while at the same time being goaded by the stings of anger, or be overwhelmed by the sorrow of devouring sadness. Rather, each spirit must seize the mind one at a time for attack, so that when one has been defeated and departs, it yields the mind to another spirit to attack more fiercely; or, if it has proved victorious, it nonetheless hands the mind over to another to be similarly mocked.

## CHAPTER XX  
### That the Hostile Powers Are Not Equal in Strength, and That the Ability to Tempt Does Not Lie within Their Own Choice

[Col. 0694B]

We must also by no means be ignorant of the fact that the demons are not all of equal ferocity and desire, nor even of equal strength and wickedness.

[Note: [Col. 0694D] Blessed Antony’s statement agrees with this: “Their wickedness is diverse and distributed. Some have reached the highest summit of harmfulness; others, by comparison with the worse, appear gentler. All, according to the extent of their powers, have undertaken different battles against different causes.” Thus he himself.

Indeed, just as among the angels some surpass and excel others in gifts both of nature and of grace, so among demons some are more powerful by natural strength, more wicked in malice, and readier and fiercer in doing harm. This is taught by that Gospel parable in which the unclean spirit is said to take seven other spirits—meaning many—more wicked than itself, and the last state of that person becomes worse than the first (Matthew XII).

On this subject see an amusing example in Caesarius the Cistercian, *On Demons*, book V, chapter 36, where he shows that not all demons are equally evil and harmful. Palladius likewise relates in the Life of Paul the Simple that Saint Antony was unable to expel a certain chief demon—as he calls it—and sent it to Paul to be expelled. See chapter 31 of this Conference.]

Thus, for beginners and the weak, only weaker spirits are brought into combat; and once these spiritual wickednesses have been overcome, a stronger battle will always gradually follow against Christ’s athlete. For the difficulty of the struggle increases in proportion to the measure of human strength and progress.

No saint would in any way be sufficient to endure the wickedness of such and so many enemies, or to confront their ambushes, or even to withstand their cruelty and savagery, if the most merciful judge and [Note: [Col. 0695D] This expression was discussed elsewhere (*Book VI*, chapter 9). Tertullian also uses it when exhorting the martyrs (*To the Martyrs*, chapter 3): “You are about to enter a noble contest, in which God alone is the organizer of the contest, the Holy Spirit is the president of the athletic ground, the prize is the crown of eternity, and the citizenship of the angelic nature is in heaven, glory unto ages of ages. Accordingly, your presiding master is Christ Jesus, who anointed you with the Spirit and brought you into this arena,” etc. Rhenanus explains *agonothetes* as the one who organizes the contest with a prize set before the contestants; *xystarches* as the president of the *xystus*, that is, the place where athletes exercised during the winter; and *epistates* as the master of the athletes. See above, Conference 6, chapter 16. Saint Jerome says in Letter 28 to Lucinius: “Our organizer of the contest is not envious; nor does one person’s palm prepare disgrace for another. He desires all his athletes to be crowned.”]

Christ, the organizer and presiding judge of the contest, had not equalized the strength of the combatants, restrained and curbed their immoderate attacks, and brought about an escape through the temptation, so that we might be able to endure it.

[Col. 0695B]

[Note: [Col. 0696C] Thus he commonly reads *exitum*, “an escape,” because the Greek is ἔκβασιν, so that the meaning is: if temptation presses upon us, he will make it immediately depart, be overcome, and vanish. See the notes on Conference 3, chapter 17.]

## CHAPTER XXI  
### That the Demons Struggle with Human Beings Not Without Labor on Their Part

We believe that they do not carry on this struggle without labor on their part.

[Note: [Col. 0696D] At first sight this might seem to refer to bodily labor. Since he said above, in chapter 13, that demons are not altogether incorporeal but have a body, though much subtler than ours, it might seem consistent that in wrestling with us they labor and can be exhausted by bodily exertion. But since this struggle is spiritual, not bodily, and it has been amply demonstrated that demons are altogether incorporeal and spiritual, we can imagine no labor appropriate to demons other than one corresponding to their nature—that is, spiritual labor. He later interprets this as anxiety, sadness, pain, confusion, contrition, and so forth, which in demons are spiritual, not bodily, passions.]

For they too experience in their conflict a certain anxiety and sadness, especially when they have engaged stronger adversaries—that is, holy and perfect men. Otherwise it would no longer be conflict or wrestling, but merely a simple and, so to speak, effortless deception of human beings on their part.

And how could the Apostle’s statement stand: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this age, [Col. 0695C] against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians VI)? And again: “So I fight, not as one beating the air” (I Corinthians IX). And again: “I have fought the good fight” (II Timothy IV).

Where there is an agon—that is, a contest—and a struggle, a battle, or wrestling, there must necessarily be sweat, labor, and anxiety on both sides; and either pain and confusion must await them equally over their defeat, or joy must follow their victory. But when one wrestles with sweat while the other fights in leisure and security, and employs only his will, [Col. 0696A] according to his strength, to overthrow his adversary, this should not be called a battle, wrestling, or contest, but rather an unjust and irrational oppression by an attack.

Yet the demons plainly labor as well when they attack the human race. They sweat to prevail over each person and to gain the victory they desire; and the confusion [Col. 0696B] that would await us if we had been overthrown by them is turned back upon them, according to the saying: “The head of their encircling, the labor of their lips, will cover them” (Psalm CXL). And: “His pain will return upon his own head” (Psalm VII). And again: “Let the snare he does not know come upon him, and let the trap he has hidden seize him; and let him fall into the snare” (Psalm XXXIV)—namely, into the snare he devises in order to deceive human beings.

They therefore suffer no less themselves; and just as they overthrow us, so they too are overthrown. Nor do they depart defeated without confusion. Seeing these collapses and conflicts of the enemies—he who possessed the sound eyes of the inner person and daily perceived them rejoicing excessively at the ruin and downfall of individuals, while fearing that the same joy might befall him—prays to the Lord:

“Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death; lest my enemy ever say, ‘I have prevailed against him.’ Those who trouble me will rejoice if I am shaken” (Psalm XII).

And: “My God, let them not rejoice excessively over me; let them not say in their hearts, ‘Good, good, our soul!’ and let them not say, ‘We shall devour him’” (Psalm XXXIV). And: “They gnashed their teeth at me. Lord, when will you look upon this?” (the same Psalm). For he lies in wait secretly, like a lion in his den; he lies in wait to seize the [Col. 0696C] poor. And: “He seeks food for himself from God” (Psalm CIII).

When, after expending all their efforts, they are unable to achieve our deception, then, their labor having been frustrated, those who seek our souls to take them away must be confused and put to shame; those who devise evil against us must be clothed with confusion and disgrace (Psalm XXXIV). Jeremiah also says:

“Let them be put to shame, and let me not be put to shame; let them be terrified, and let me not be terrified. Bring upon them the anger of your wrath, and crush them with a double crushing” (Jeremiah XVII).

For no one doubts that, once they have been defeated by us, they are to be crushed with a double crushing: first, because while human beings sought holiness, the demons possessed it and lost it, and became the cause of human destruction; second, because spiritual substances were conquered by carnal and earthly beings.

Observing these ruins of the enemies and their own victories, each of the saints exclaims with joy:

“I will pursue my enemies and overtake them, and I will not turn back until they fail. I will crush them, and they will not be able to stand; they will fall beneath my feet” (Psalm XVII).

Against them the same Prophet also prays:

“Judge, O Lord, those who harm me; fight against those who fight against me. Take up arms and shield, and rise to help me. Draw out the sword and close the way against those who pursue me; say to my soul, ‘I am your salvation’” (Psalm XXXIV).

When we have conquered them, after all the passions have been subdued and extinguished, we shall deservedly hear that word of blessing:

“Let your hand be exalted over your enemies, and all your enemies shall perish” (Micah V).

[Note: [Col. 0697B] This may also be regarded as another paradox of this abbot: he thinks that all these sayings, both from the Psalms and from the Prophets, must be understood as spoken against demons rather than against human beings. Yet no one should doubt that they can be understood not only of demons—that is, invisible enemies—but also of visible and bodily enemies, as all interpreters understand and explain them. Nor does it follow from this, as the good abbot concludes, that we should not pray for our enemies or love them, but should even detest them. They are understood to have been spoken not from hatred and ill will, but rather from charity or at least [Col. 0697C] from zeal for justice in agreement with the divine will.

Such formulas of speech are exceedingly common in Scripture, especially in the Psalms and the Prophets. Their purpose is simply that God may restrain the impious, prevent them from heaping sins upon sins, from persisting in them, or from continuing to persecute the good; or that they may be punished with temporal penalties so that they may not perish eternally. As the Apostle says in I Corinthians X: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged; but when we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world.” Or else these are not so much imprecations as threats or predictions of the divine Spirit speaking through the mouths of the prophets and foretelling the punishments appointed for the wicked.]

Yet if, when we read or sing all these and similar passages inserted into the sacred books [Col. 0698A], we do not understand them to have been written against the spiritual wickednesses that lie in wait for us day and night, we shall derive from them not only no edification in gentleness and patience, but shall also conceive a certain dreadful disposition contrary to evangelical perfection. For we shall be taught not only not to pray for our enemies or love them, but shall also be provoked to detest them with implacable hatred, to curse them, and to pour out prayer against them without ceasing.

[Note: [Col. 0697C] To curse is the same as to speak evil. This occurs in three ways. First, declaratively, by indicating and explaining another’s evil, as in insult, mockery, and slander. Second, imperatively, by ordering evil to be inflicted upon another. Third, optatively, by wishing or invoking evil upon another.

“In the latter two ways,” says Saint Thomas, “in which evil is spoken either in the manner of a command or in the manner of a wish, something is lawful or unlawful for the same reason. If someone commands or wishes evil upon another insofar as it is evil, intending the evil itself, then cursing in either form is unlawful; and this is cursing in itself. But if someone commands or wishes evil upon another under the aspect of good, then it is lawful, and is not cursing in itself, but accidentally, because the speaker’s primary intention is directed not toward evil but toward good.

“Evil may be commanded or wished under the aspect of two kinds of good. Sometimes under the aspect of justice: thus a judge lawfully curses the person for whom he orders a just punishment to be inflicted. In this way the Church also curses by pronouncing an anathema. Likewise, the prophets in Scripture sometimes invoke evils upon sinners, as though conforming their will to divine justice, although these imprecations may also be understood as predictions.

“Sometimes evil is spoken under the aspect of usefulness—for example, when someone wishes a sinner to suffer an illness or some impediment, either so that he may become better himself or at least cease harming others.”

These words of Saint Thomas are fully sufficient to clarify this passage.

There is, however, an additional matter relevant here, reported by the blessed Gregory in book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter XV: a terrible example involving four monks who killed a bear that was serving a certain servant of God named Florentius. As a result, following his imprecation, they were struck by elephantiasis and died.

“Florentius,” Gregory says, “was terrified by what had happened and greatly feared that he had cursed the brothers in this way. Throughout the whole of his life he wept because his prayer had been heard, and he loudly called himself cruel and a murderer in their death. We believe that the almighty Lord did this so that a man of remarkable simplicity, however much he might be moved by grief, would not thereafter presume to hurl the dart of a curse.”

When Peter then asked, “Do we think it is a very serious matter if, perhaps, in the agitation of anger, we curse someone?” Gregory answered: “Why do you ask me whether this sin is serious, when Paul says: ‘Nor will the cursers possess the kingdom of God’” (I Corinthians V). “Consider, therefore, how serious the fault is which separates one from the kingdom of heavenly life.”

When Peter asked again, “What if someone hurls a word of cursing at his neighbor not out of malice, but through carelessness of speech?” Gregory replied: “If idle speech is condemned by the strict Judge, how much more harmful speech! Consider, therefore, how deserving of condemnation is the person who is not free from malice, if even speech that is devoid of beneficial goodness is punishable.”]

It is exceedingly wicked and profane to understand these holy men and friends of God as having spoken such things in that spirit. Before Christ’s coming, the law was not imposed upon them precisely because, transcending its commandments, they preferred to obey the evangelical precepts and strive toward apostolic [Col. 0698B] perfection, anticipating the dispensation of time.

## CHAPTER XXII  
### That the Power to Harm Does Not Lie within the Demons’ Own Choice

[Note: [Col. 0698D] Blessed Antony learned this first through repeated experience. He often and boldly challenged the demons with words such as these, exposing himself to them: “Here I am, Antony. I do not flee from your contests. Even if you make them greater, no one will separate me from the love of Christ.” He would sing:

“Though armies encamp against me, my heart will not fear” (Psalm XXVI).

And again: “If you had any strength, one of you would be enough for battle.” Likewise: “If you have any power, if the Lord has given you authority over me, here I am; devour what has been granted to you. But if you cannot, why do you strive in vain? The sign of the cross and faith in the Lord are an unconquerable wall for us.”

Finally, answering an objection below, he says: “But someone may say: Why, when the devil attacked blessed Job, did he bring his whole household to ruin? Why, after utterly scattering his possessions and overthrowing even the foundations of the walls, did he make one grave of his numerous offspring? Why did he finally strike Job himself with the novelty of a dreadful wound?

“Let the one who raises this objection hear the contrary answer: the devil could not do these things, but the Lord could, from whom power against us is given in two ways—either for glory, if we are being tested, or for punishment, if we sin. Rather, let him understand from this that the devil could not do anything even against one human being unless he had received power from the Lord. No one asks another for what belongs to his own jurisdiction.

“But why do I mention Job, whom the devil could not overcome even when he sought him? He could not exercise his own strength against Job’s cattle, sheep, or swine without God’s permission, as it is written in the Gospel: ‘The demons begged him, saying: If you cast us out from here, send us into the herd of swine’” (Matthew VIII). “How, then, could those who seek the death of swine, an image-bearing human being—an animal so dear to its Creator—pervert him by their own right?” Thus Saint Antony, as Athanasius relates in the Life of Saint Antony.

Later, again citing the confession of the devil himself, which we reported above, Antony exhorts and encourages the monks: “Here is the devil himself, who with his satellites practices such cunning, confessing that he can do nothing against Christians. Let Christians and monks therefore take care that, through their negligence, they do not provide strength to demons. For they customarily show themselves to us according to what they find us and our thoughts to be. If they find in our hearts the seed of an evil mind and fear, like thieves who occupy deserted places, they heap up the fears already begun and, cruelly pressing upon the unhappy soul, threaten it. But if we are cheerful in the Lord and inflamed by desire for future goods, if we always commit everything into God’s hands, none of the demons will be able to approach us for battle,” and so forth.

Blessed Augustine agrees with this in book VII of *The City of God*, chapter 35: “They cannot do what they are not permitted to do. They are permitted by the profound judgment of the supreme and just God, according to the merits of those whom it is just that they should merely afflict, or even subject and deceive.”

And in book II, the final chapter, *Against the Adversary of the Law*, he says: “Although Satan always desires to harm, he cannot harm anyone unless he has received power from the Almighty. What else is declared—not only in the Book of Job, but even more clearly in the Gospel—where the unclean spirits could not enter the swine unless the gracious Savior himself, when they asked, granted this to them, although he could have consigned them to the abyss? He wished to teach us something necessary: namely, that they have far less power to harm human beings by their own authority, since they could not even harm animals without permission.”

Blessed Gregory has similar statements in book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 21, and in book I of the *Moralia*, chapters 9 and following.]

That they do not have the power to harm any human being is clearly demonstrated by the example of blessed Job (Job II), where the enemy dares to tempt him no further than divine providence permits. The confession of those same spirits, recorded in the Gospel, also testifies to this when they say: “If you cast us out, send us into the herd of swine” (Matthew VIII).

They must be believed all the more unable, according to their own choice, to enter any human being created in the image of God, since they did not have power to enter even unclean and speechless animals without God’s permission.

Moreover, no one—not even the young men whom we see dwelling most steadfastly in this desert, but not even the perfect—could live alone in the desert surrounded by such armies of such enemies, if they possessed the power and freedom to harm or attack according to their own will. Our Lord and Savior’s declaration confirms this even more clearly, when he spoke to Pilate in the humility of the humanity he had assumed:

“You would have no power over me at all unless it had been given you from above” (John XIX).

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### On the Diminished Power of the Demons

[Col. 0700A]

It is nevertheless fully established for us, both by our own experience and by the report of the elders, that demons do not now possess the same power that they had in earlier times, at the very beginnings of the anchorites, when monks still lived only sparsely in the desert. For their ferocity was then so great that scarcely any but a few exceptionally steadfast and advanced in age could endure dwelling in solitude. Indeed,

> [Note: Here you see that even coenobia, or monasteries—that is, holy places cultivated by holy men—are sometimes harassed by demons, when God permits it, as was said above (Chapter 19). John the Deacon reports in his Life of Saint Gregory (Book IV, chapter 89) that monks in Rome, where Saint Gregory had his oratory, also endured very great troubles from demons. See other examples in Caesarius and Peter of Cluny (Caesarius, Book V; Peter of Cluny, Book I *On Miracles*, chapter 12).]

in the very coenobia where eight or ten of them lived, such was the violence of the demons, and so frequent and visible were their attacks, that they did not dare all to sleep at night at the same time. Instead, while some took a little sleep in turn, the others remained at their vigils, occupied with psalms, prayers,

[Col. 0700B]

or readings. And when the necessity of nature summoned those who were awake to sleep, the others were roused and similarly assigned to keep watch over those who were about to sleep. From this it cannot be doubted that there are only two possible explanations for the security or confidence now granted not only to us, who seem to have been strengthened to some degree by the experience of old age, but also to those younger in years: either

> [Note: A clear testimony from antiquity concerning the power and efficacy of the cross for routing and restraining demons. Innumerable examples of this exist from every age; we shall touch upon only a few, by way of illustrating this passage. Saint Basil, in his book *On the Holy Spirit* (chapter 1 and following), teaches that the apostolic tradition received in the Church was that the faithful, both in sacred matters and in other things which they blessed, should trace the sign of the cross with the hand, and that they should employ this most salutary remedy above all for driving away demons, using it in every circumstance. Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, says: “Do not be ashamed to confess the Crucified One; but let the seal of the cross be confidently impressed upon the forehead by your fingers, and let the cross be made in all other things: over the bread that is eaten, and over the cups that are drunk, on going out and coming in, before sleep, when lying down and rising, when walking and resting. This is a great protection, given freely to the poor, without labor for the sick, since this grace comes from God, as does the fear of demons; for this sign has triumphed over him. Display it boldly to him; for when they see the cross, they remember the Crucified One, and they fear him who crushed the heads of the dragon.” Thus Cyril, clearly drawing on the ancient practice of the faithful. Tertullian also speaks of it in *On the Soldier’s Crown* (chapters 3–4). Saint Nilus, writing to Olympiodorus the proconsul, advised that crosses should be painted in every bedroom and other dwelling-place (Second Council of Nicaea, article 4). The following verses of Prudentius also pertain here (*Cathemerinon*, hymn 6):

> The cross drives away every crime;  
> The darknesses flee the cross.

As for examples, Rufinus reports (*Book XI, chapter 29*) that in Alexandria each person painted the sign of the Lord’s cross on doorposts, entrances, windows, walls, and columns. Lactantius writes (Book IV, chapter 27) that, when a Christian who had marked his forehead with the cross was present, the pagan haruspices who sacrificed to the devil could not obtain oracles from him; and that this was often the principal reason for persecuting Christians. Epiphanius relates (*Heresy* 30) that a certain Joseph, not yet a Christian, expelled demons by the sign of the cross, and that after becoming a Christian he destroyed Jewish incantations by the same sign. Gregory of Nazianzus, in his First Oration against Julian, writes that Julian the Apostate, while invoking demons in a certain shrine, was terrified at their appearance, fortified himself with the sign of the cross, and immediately all the apparitions vanished (Theodoret, *History*, Book III, chapter 16). Saint Antony was terrifying to all demons by the sign of the cross alone, and against every terror he commanded the monks to be safe and secure by the sign of the cross alone. Saint Jerome gives the same testimony concerning Paul the Hermit and Hilarion. Daniel the Stylite everywhere carried the cross to drive away demons, “as an invincible weapon,” says Metaphrastes. By this same sign Saint Remigius extinguished a great fire kindled by the devil at Rheims, according to Hincmar; and Saint Vedastus abolished another magical work, driving away an apparition and, after liquid had been poured out, shining forth in a miracle, as Albinus Flaccus, the author of his Life, testifies. Finally, Theodoret, Book V, chapter 21, throughout his *Religious History*, and the blessed Gregory, Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 7, record many miracles performed by the sign of the cross, especially the expulsion of demons. (See Bellarmine, Book II *On Images*, chapter 29; Baronius, Volume I of the *Annals*, year 60.) If we wished to pursue and enumerate the examples and testimonies of later times,

[Col. 0702B]

there would be no end to the discussion. For the judgment of all the saints concerning this sign and trophy of our salvation has always been the same, and the experience of every age has likewise been the same.]

either the power of the cross, penetrating even the deserts and flashing everywhere through its grace, has blunted the demons’ wickedness, or our negligence has made them slower to attack us than formerly, since they disdain to engage us with the same determination with which they once raged against those most proven soldiers of Christ—using this strategy, namely, to strike us more cruelly with invisible temptations. For we see that some have fallen into such great tepidity that they must be encouraged even by milder admonitions, lest they abandon their cells and return to more destructive disturbances, becoming entangled, as wanderers and fugitives, in grosser vices, so to speak. It is believed to be a great gain from them if they can merely remain in solitude, even with whatever laziness, and the elders commonly tell them, as a great remedy:

> “Remain in your cells, and eat, drink, and sleep as much as you wish, provided only that you remain continually in them.”

## CHAPTER XXIV. How demons prepare an entrance into the bodies of those whom they are about to seize

> [Note: Similar statements are found in Saint Augustine, *City of God*, Book IV, chapter 34: “Demons cannot possess anyone unless they have deceived him by trickery.” And in Book X, chapter 22: “The hostile power conquers or subjugates no one except through fellowship in sin.” Again, in Sermon 197 *On Time*, he answers an objection there raised as follows: “Someone says: If the devil is bound, as he is, why does he still prevail? It is true, dearly beloved brothers, that he prevails greatly—but over the lukewarm and negligent, and over those who do not truly fear God, he exercises dominion. For he is bound like a dog fastened by chains, and he can bite no one except one who has joined himself to him in a deadly fellowship.” Thus Saint Augustine. Likewise, in Metaphrastes, on 1 February, when a demon was questioned by Triphon, a holy man, about why it had entered the daughter of the emperor Gordian, it replied that demons have power over those who perform works pleasing to them—such as, it said, the worship of images, blasphemies, adulteries, magic, envy, murder, and so forth. It should, however, be observed that such statements signify not what can happen and occasionally does happen, but what generally occurs. For in moral matters one considers not what happens rarely, but what commonly happens, as Aristotle teaches in the *Ethics*. Saint Augustine, therefore, like Abbot Serenus, intended to signify what usually and for the most part occurs: namely, that demons first possess people’s minds and thoughts, through mortal sin, before they penetrate and take possession of their bodies. Otherwise he would contradict himself, since it is clear from what follows that the souls of those whose bodies are possessed by demons are not always possessed by them, and that holy men and friends of God have sometimes, by God’s permission, been bodily possessed by a demon on account of a slight fault or even without fault.]

It is therefore clear that unclean spirits can enter those whose bodies they are about to possess only after they have first possessed their minds and thoughts. Once they have stripped them of the fear and remembrance of God, or of spiritual meditation, as though they had been disarmed of every divine defense and protection, they boldly attack them, knowing that they can then be easily conquered, and afterward presuming to establish a dwelling in them as in a possession handed over to them.

## CHAPTER XXV. That those possessed by vices are more pitiable than those possessed by demons themselves

Although it is agreed that those who do not appear to be bodily filled by demons are often harassed more grievously and violently, they are nevertheless possessed in a more destructive manner in spirit, being entangled in their vices or pleasures.

> [Note: *Suppleri* (“to be filled”), used here for *occuperi* (“to be occupied”), *corripi* (“to be seized”), or, if one prefers, *repleri* (“to be filled”), is frequent in Cassian (Book V of the *Institutes*, chapter 13).] For, according to the Apostle’s saying,

> [Note: We have treated this saying elsewhere.]

“By whatever anyone is overcome, by that he is enslaved” (II Peter 2). They suffer more hopelessly in this respect because, although they are the demons’ slaves, they recognize neither that they are being attacked by them nor that they endure their domination.

> [Note: It therefore happens, although more rarely, that someone is possessed by a demon not only on account of mortal sins but also on account of slight and venial faults, as was indicated above. This is demonstrated by the example of Abbot Moses in the following chapter, who was attacked and grievously tormented by a demon because of impatience and a harsh word. A similar case seems to be the one Saint Gregory relates in *Dialogues*, Book I, chapter 4, concerning a nun who was likewise seized by a demon because of a lesser fault of gluttony. “One day,” he says, “a woman devoted to God entered a garden and, seeing a lettuce, desired it. Forgetting to bless it with the sign of the cross, she eagerly bit into it, but was immediately seized by the devil and fell. While she was being tormented, word was quickly sent to Father Equitius, so that he might come swiftly and help her by praying. As soon as that father entered the garden, the devil who had seized her began to cry out from her mouth, as though making his defense: ‘What have I done? I was sitting there upon the lettuce; she came and bit me.’ Then the man of God, in great indignation, ordered him to depart and to have no place in the servant of almighty God; and he immediately departed and was unable to trouble her again.” Thus Gregory. Nor does the example of the woman whom a certain magician, by his magic and through the operation of a demon, had made mute and caused to appear to everyone who saw her as a mare rather than a woman seem unlike this. Saint Macarius of Egypt cured her by sprinkling blessed water and praying, and restored her to her former state. The man of God admonished her in these words: “Never abandon the Church; never abstain from communion in Christ’s sacraments. For this has happened to you because for five weeks now you have not approached the undefiled sacraments of our Savior.” Thus Palladius (*Lausiac History*, chapters 19 and 20).
