He assigns no other cause for this diabolical affliction and torment than the temporary interruption, through negligence, of sacred communion—which does not seem to have been more than a venial fault—just as in the case of the bite of the lettuce without the sign of the cross.]

Moreover, we know that those who have been bodily handed over to Satan, or even holy men afflicted with severe illnesses, have suffered for the lightest offenses, since divine mercy does not permit it to find in them even the slightest blemish or stain on the day of judgment. In the present life it burns away all the dross of their hearts, according to the judgment of the prophet—or rather, of God—in order to send them, like gold or silver refined by fire, into that eternity without need of any penal purification:

> “And I will refine your dross to purity, and I will remove all your tin; and after this you shall be called the city of the just, the faithful city” (Isaiah 1).

And again:

> “As silver and gold are tested in the furnace, so the Lord tests hearts” (Proverbs 27).

And again:

> “Gold and silver are tested by fire, but a person is tested in the furnace of humiliation” (Ecclesiastes 2).

And also:

> “For whom the Lord loves, he disciplines; and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12).

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the death of the deceived prophet and the illness of Abbot Paul, which he deserved for his correction

We clearly see this fulfilled in that prophet and man of God mentioned in the Third Book of Kings. On account of a single act of disobedience—which he had contracted not deliberately or through a fault of his own will, but through another person’s deception—he was immediately crushed by a lion, as Scripture relates:

> “He is a man of God, who was disobedient to the word of the Lord; and the Lord delivered him to the lion, and it crushed him according to the word of the Lord that he had spoken” (III Kings 15).

> [Note: Many miracles and most evident signs of divine providence shone forth here: first, that God wished the prophet to be killed by a lion on account of his disobedience and transgression of the divine command, although he had been deceived and misled by another prophet; second, that he wished to punish his fault with a temporal penalty, lest he punish him eternally; third, that the lion did not tear the prophet apart or devour him, but killed him—apparently, as Scripture suggests, by crushing his jaws or bones, or breaking his neck—without any other injury; fourth, that the same most ravenous beast restrained itself so completely that it tasted nothing of the corpse entrusted to it, nor shed or drank his blood; fifth, that, standing beside the body with the donkey, it guarded it until it was carried away; sixth, that it did not injure or drive away the donkey itself; seventh, that it neither frightened nor hindered those who came to remove the body, but departed once the body had been taken away. It is worthwhile here to hear blessed Gregory discussing both the prophet’s fault and his punishment. In Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 24, he says: “The man of God sent against Samaria, because he ate on the way in disobedience, was killed by a lion on that same journey. But it is immediately written that the lion stood beside the donkey and that the lion did not eat from the corpse. From this it is shown that the sin of disobedience was released in the very death, because the same lion that presumed to kill him while alive did not presume to touch him when dead. He who had dared to kill did not receive permission to eat from the corpse of the slain, because the man who had been culpable in life had, once his disobedience was punished, already been made just by death. Thus the lion that had first killed the sinner’s life afterward guarded the corpse of the just.” Thus Gregory.]

In this event, both the absolution of the present offense and of the unwary error, and the merits of the righteousness for which the Lord temporarily handed his prophet over to the tormentor, are shown by the predator’s very restraint and self-control, since the most ravenous beast dares taste nothing at all of the corpse entrusted to it.

A sufficiently clear and open confirmation of this same matter also occurred in our own times, in the case of Abbot Paul and Moses, who lived in that place of this solitude called Calamus.

> [Note: The matter of Abbot Paul was treated in Book X, chapters 24 and 25. Moses is treated in the same book and in Conferences 1 and 2, which bear his name.]

The former lived in the desert adjoining the city of Panephysi.

> [Note: Cassian speaks of Panephysi in Book IV, chapter 30.]

We know that this solitude was formerly flooded by extremely salty water. Whenever the north wind blew, the water, driven from the lagoons and spread over the neighboring lands, covered the entire surface of that region so completely that it made the ancient villages there—which had long been deserted by all their inhabitants for this very reason—appear like islands.

Here, then, Abbot Paul had advanced so greatly in purity of heart through the quiet of solitude and the silence of the desert that he could not bear to have before his eyes—not to mention a woman’s face—even the clothing of that sex. Once, as he was going with Abbot Archebius, a resident of the same solitude, to the cell of an elder, a woman happened by chance to meet them. Offended by her appearance, he fled back to his own monastery with such haste—abandoning the charitable duty of visitation which he had undertaken—that no one would have fled from the face of a lion or even the most savage dragon. He was not moved even by the shouts and prayers with which the aforementioned Abbot Archebius called him back and urged him to continue the journey they had begun, so that they might visit the elder as they had planned.

> [Note: We treated the same man in Book V, chapter 37. In Conference 11, chapter 2, there is also this splendid encomium of him: “The most blessed and eminent man, Bishop Archebius, who was taken from the company of the anchorites and appointed bishop of the town of Panephysi, guarded the discipline of solitude throughout his entire life with such strictness that he relaxed nothing of his former humility and did not flatter himself because of the honor bestowed upon him.”]

Although he did this out of zeal for chastity and ardor for purity, nevertheless, because he had presumed beyond what knowledge warranted, and because he had exceeded the bounds of proper discipline and sound discretion—for he believed that not only familiarity with women, which is truly harmful, but even the very appearance of that sex should be abhorred—he was immediately struck by such a correction that his entire body was paralyzed, and no member of it could perform its proper function. Not only his feet and hands, but also the movement of his tongue by which speech is expressed, and even his ears, lost the ability to hear, so that nothing more than an immobile and senseless figure remained in him of a human being.

> [Note: We have discussed this matter in Book V, chapter 37. Concerning the same man, Conference 11, chapter 2, contains this splendid encomium: “The most blessed and eminent man, Bishop Archebius, who was taken from the company of the anchorites and appointed bishop of the town of Panephysi, guarded the discipline of solitude throughout his entire life with such strictness that he relaxed nothing of his former humility and did not flatter himself because of the honor bestowed upon him.”]

He was reduced to such a condition that the diligence of men was entirely unable to care for his illness; only the attentiveness of women could minister to him. For when he had been carried to a monastery of holy virgins, food and drink—which he could not request even by a gesture—were put into his mouth by female service. The same attentiveness served him in fulfilling all the necessities of nature for nearly four years, that is, until the end of his life.

> [Note: Holy men often cured the sick with oil blessed, touched, or administered by them. Thus Saint Hilarion healed those bitten by serpents with oil, and by the same means raised two people from the dead, as Saint Jerome testifies (*Life of Hilarion*). Likewise, according to Palladius (*Lausiac History*, chapter 13), Abbot Benjamin healed anyone upon whom he laid his hands or to whom he gave oil that he had blessed: “And yet this man, who had been considered worthy of such grace, suffered from dropsy for eight months before his death, and his body became so swollen because of the pain that he seemed another Job. While he was suffering from this incurable disease, he healed others who were afflicted with every kind of illness.” This corresponds exactly to the example of Abbot Paul under discussion. A paralytic woman is also said to have been cured with oil by Saint Macarius, and a demoniac freed from a demon, according to the same Palladius. Abbot John likewise healed many with blessed oil. Theodoret reports the same about Abbot Aphraates and Simeon in his *History of the Holy Fathers*, chapters 8 and 26 (*Lausiac History*, chapters 20 and 43). Egyptian monks also cured a paralytic by anointing with oil, as Rufinus and Sozomen testify (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 4; Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 21). Finally, Abbot Machetes relates the following about himself in Cassian: “I also detested above all else blessing oil and giving it to petitioners, judging that this proceeded from great presumption of heart. Once many secular people suddenly surrounded me and so constrained me that I could in no way escape them unless they compelled me, by the greatest force and entreaty, to place my hand—after making the sign of the cross—upon the vessel they had brought. Thus, believing that they had obtained oil of blessing, they finally released me.” Thus he. Severus in the *Life of Saint Martin*, and others who wrote the deeds of the saints, frequently mention the same sanctification and use of oil for imparting health. It should be understood, however, that this kind of oil and anointing, although sanctified by some blessing, was very different from the sacrament of extreme unction, which is given in the Catholic Church to the sick, as Baronius rightly observes (see Baronius, Book I of the *Annals*, year 63). For it was not instituted to remit the sins of the sick and obtain invisible grace; rather, it was customary for any Christian to use it in Christ’s name, even upon someone alien to the faith, in order to confer bodily health. Such was plainly the oil which Tertullian says was customarily administered by the Christian Proculus for curing diseases (*To Scapula*, chapter 4). Baronius adds that such oil, like other substances prepared for human use, was customarily sanctified by prescribed prayers—for Clement’s *Constitutions* (Book VIII, chapter 35) also contains a written blessing of water and oil—so that it was sufficient to bless it merely with the sign of the cross, sanctify it in the name of the most holy Trinity, and apply it to the sick.]

Although all his limbs were so tightly bound by weakness that none of his joints retained lively movement or sensation, nevertheless such an abundance of virtue proceeded from him that whenever the sick were anointed with oil which had touched his body—more a corpse than a body,

> [Note: This means that it was not actually a corpse, for Paul was alive, but it was like a corpse, that is, almost dead from illness. Isidore says that *cadaver* is so called from *cadere*, “to fall,” because it can no longer stand (*Etymologies*, Book XI, chapter 2).]

they were immediately cured of every illness.

> [Note: Cassian frequently uses *valetudo* to mean illness or infirmity, as noted elsewhere.]

Thus, even to unbelievers, it became clearly and openly evident in connection with this illness of his that the weakness of all his limbs had been granted through the dispensation and love of the Lord, while the grace of healing was bestowed upon him through the power of the Holy Spirit as a testimony to his purity and a manifestation of his merits.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the temptation of Abbot Moses

The second man whom we said had lived in this desert was himself also an exceptional and incomparable man. Because of a single statement which he had uttered somewhat harshly while arguing against Abbot Macarius,

> [Note: See what we noted elsewhere (Book V, chapter 41) concerning the two holy Egyptian anchorites named Macarius, contemporaries of one another, one called the Egyptian and the other the Alexandrian. What is related here about Macarius seems to be understood of the Egyptian, whom Palladius and others write to have been distinguished by an extraordinary gift and power against demons.]

having been influenced by a certain opinion,

> [Note: It may indeed seem astonishing that a holy man was handed over to so savage a demon on account of a slight fault, and was attacked and deprived of his reason to such a degree that he shamefully put human excrement into his own mouth. But it will not seem so very astonishing if we consider that people are sometimes attacked and possessed by demons without any fault of their own, though not without great reasons belonging to divine providence (John Chrysostom, *On the Providence of God*). This is established by many examples and testimonies. First, Saint Jerome writes in Letter 25, concerning the death of Blesilla: “Why is it,” he says, “that infants of two or three years, and those still nursing at their mother’s breast, are often seized by demons, filled with leprosy, and consumed by jaundice?” He later adds: “These invisible matters must be left to the inscrutable judgment of the Most High.” Saint Augustine, *City of God*, Book XXII, chapter 22, says: “Against the manifold attacks of demons, who trusts in his innocence, since, lest anyone should trust in it, they sometimes torment even baptized infants, than whom nothing is more innocent, so that in them above all, by God’s permission, the lamentable misery of this life and the happiness desired in the next may be displayed.” Thus Augustine. There are also examples: first, the boy mentioned by Mark the Evangelist in chapter 9, who had suffered the demon’s most grievous torment from infancy, as his father confessed when the Lord questioned him; second, another boy whom Saint Macarius freed from a most savage demon, as Palladius testifies in the *Life of Macarius*; third, a girl of Toulouse from whom Saint Remigius expelled a demon at the request of blessed Benedict, concerning whom Hincmar writes in the *Life of Saint Remigius* (Book II, chapter 3); fourth, another boy mentioned in the *Life of Saint Bernard*; fifth, a five-year-old girl possessed by a demon at her father’s curse, as Caesarius relates (Book V, chapter 26). But lest anyone suppose that this happens only to boys or infants and not also to adults, Sulpicius (*Dialogue on the Virtues of Saint Martin*) relates the memorable example of a most holy anchorite, renowned for his virtue, who asked God and obtained permission for the devil to have power over him for five months, so that he might become like those whom he himself had cured—that is, so that his body might be afflicted for five months by a demon dwelling within him, to avoid the danger of pride or vainglory. Sulpicius, expressing his wonder and emphasizing the matter, adds: “That man of great power, that man renowned throughout the whole East for signs and virtues, to whose threshold crowds had once flocked, at whose doors the powers of this world had prostrated themselves, was seized by a demon, held in bonds, and suffered everything that the possessed ordinarily endure. At the end of the fifth month he was cleansed—not only of the demon but, what was more useful and desirable for him, of vanity.” Another example of the holy Abbot Alexander is found in the *Spiritual Meadow* (chapter 182). Shortly before his death, by God’s permission, he was seized by a demon and splendidly reproached it for its weakness: “You came in the evening,” he would say, “wretch. This is no great achievement, since I am bound in bed and cannot move: you have shown your weakness, most miserable one. For if you were powerful and strong, you ought to have approached me fifty or sixty years ago. I, strengthened by Christ who strengthens me, would have shown you your weakness, cast down your roaring, and broken your stiff and unbending neck. But now it is not my weakness; it is illness that weighs me down. Nevertheless, I give thanks to God, to whom, as I depart, I shall show the injury I have suffered from you: after so many years of labor and toil, you attacked me so savagely near my departure.” Saying these and many other things hour by hour, on the tenth day he peacefully gave up his spirit to the Lord Christ. So it is related there. Baronius also noted (Volume I of the *Annals*, year 32) that certain criminal women, although afterward repentant and entirely pleasing to God, and although they obtained forgiveness for their sins, were nevertheless accustomed to be harassed by demons with more bitter attacks. Anyone who reads, he says, the deeds of the penitent Pelagia, Mary of Egypt, and others will clearly understand this. Baronius says this while discussing Mary Magdalene and the question whether she was possessed by seven demons before or after the Lord’s anointing, as the Evangelist says.]

he was immediately handed over to so savage a demon that, filled by it, he put human excrement into his own mouth. The Lord showed that he had inflicted this scourge for the sake of purification, so that no stain even of a momentary offense might remain in him, by the speed of his cure and by the author of the remedy. For as soon as Abbot Macarius had humbled himself in prayer, the evil spirit was driven away from him and departed more quickly than words can say.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. That those who are handed over to unclean spirits should not be despised

From this it is clearly understood

> [Note: Saint John Chrysostom agrees with this. In the books he wrote *On Providence*, he likewise recognizes and commends divine providence in the fact that holier people are sometimes seized and tormented by demons, lest they fall into sins (Volume V). By this reasoning he also consoles a certain Theodore who was possessed by a demon. See Peter Thyraeus, *On Demoniacs*, chapter 32.]

that we ought not to abominate or despise those whom we see handed over to various temptations or to these spirits of wickedness. For we must hold firmly to two beliefs: first, that no one is ever tempted by them without God’s permission; second, that everything inflicted upon us by God, whether it appears presently sad or joyful, is imposed for our benefit by a most loving Father and most merciful Physician. Therefore they are humbled as people handed over to tutors, so that, when they depart from this world, they may either be transferred to the next life more purified or be punished with a lighter penalty. For, according to the Apostle,

> [Note: The Apostle Paul handed over a certain incestuous Corinthian to Satan, in First Corinthians, chapter 5. He also handed over Hymenaeus and Alexander, heretics and blasphemers, in First Timothy, chapter 1. To hand someone over to Satan—that is, to the devil—according to ecclesiastical usage and doctrine, as we noted elsewhere (*Institutes*, Book II, chapter 16), means nothing other than to cast him outside the Church by a sentence of excommunication, or to cut him off from the body of Christ. Since the kingdom of Christ is the Church, while the devil’s kingdom is outside the Church, it follows that one who is cast outside the Church of God is deprived of its special protection and is consequently exposed and handed over to demons, like wolves prowling outside Christ’s sheepfold. Chrysostom and Theodoret further report that in the primitive Church, when no other means existed for restraining rebels and keeping them in their duty, those who had been excommunicated and handed over to Satan were immediately seized by a demon and bodily tormented, God so disposing it: first, to confirm the power of the Church and of ecclesiastical prelates, conferred by Christ, over all demons and over all the power of the enemy (Matthew 10; Luke 9 and 10); and second, to restrain and subdue the obstinacy of the wicked. This is the proper and genuine meaning of the words “to hand over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh,” that is, for bodily mortification, torment, and suffering. In the present passage, however, Abbot Serenus seems to understand such handing over as the situation in which someone, sometimes because of a slight fault or even without fault, is attacked, seized, and bodily tormented by the devil, when God permits it, so that, purified by this torment, he may afterward become more cautious and holier, as may be gathered from what precedes.]

“they have been handed over in the present time to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (I Corinthians 5).

## CHAPTER XXIX. The objection why those who are tormented by unclean spirits are separated from the Lord’s communion

Germanus: How is it, then, that in our provinces we see not only that such people are despised or shunned by others, but also that they are perpetually kept away from the Lord’s communion, in accordance with that saying of the Gospel, “Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before swine” (Matthew 7), when, as you say, we ought to believe that the humiliation of this temptation is assigned to them for the sake of purification or benefit?

## CHAPTER XXX. Answer to the question proposed
Serenus: If we hold this opinion—or rather, this faith—which I set forth above, namely, that everything is done through the Lord and that all things are dispensed for the benefit of souls, then we shall not only in no way despise them, but shall also pray for them unceasingly as for our own members, and shall sympathize with them with all our inward being and the fullness of our affection. For “when one member suffers, all the members suffer with it” (I Cor. XII). We know that, without them—as our members—we cannot in any way be made complete, just as we read that even our predecessors could not attain the fullness of the promise without us, as the Apostle declares concerning them: “And all these, though approved by the testimony of faith, did not receive the promise, God having provided something better for us, so that they should not be made perfect without us” (Heb. XI).

[Note: Saint Thomas likewise teaches that communion in the Eucharist should not be denied to the possessed or demoniacs (III part, q. 80, art. 9, ad 1), and confirms this with the testimony of Cassian. The matter is also supported by Canon 3 of the Council of Orange (in Gratian, 26, q. 6, chapter *Qui recedunt*): “All works of piety are to be conferred upon the insane” (Sotus, *In 4 Sent.*, dist. 12, q. 1; Thyraeus, *De Daemon.*, part I, chapter 28). It is confirmed still more clearly by the example reported by Saint Prosper of Aquitaine in these words (*De Promiss. et Praedie. dimid. temp.*, chapter 6):

“In our own times, when Aspar, a man of consular rank, was governor at Carthage, who among the citizens of that region is unaware of the diabolical and monstrous sign that occurred there? A certain young Arab girl, wearing the habit of a servant of God, while bathing in a bathhouse, looked immodestly upon an image of Venus and, making herself like it, offered herself as a dwelling-place to the devil. At once that lion who goes about roaring found the one whom he sought. Taking possession of her throat, and allowing no food or drink to pass through it, the devil, for nearly seventy days and as many nights, imposed upon the vessel he had seized and possessed a fast for himself.

“When the girl’s parents hoped that this monstrosity might be removed after so many days, but could no longer endure the continual evil, they presented themselves with their daughter before a priest, faithfully reporting what had happened. The girl admitted only this: that in the middle of the night a certain bird appeared and poured something—I do not know what—into her mouth. Everyone was astonished to see that, despite such prolonged fasting, the girl showed no sign of emaciation: no pallor, wasting, or weakness; rather, she was robust in the vitality of her inward parts and the mass of her body.

“When the things being reported seemed incredible, after consultation in the monastery of the women, where the relics of Saint Stephen are kept, the priest entrusted the girl both to the superior and to the monastery. There she declared that the bird had appeared only on the first day and had rebuked her because, compelled neither by hunger nor by thirst, she had sought a place to which she was not permitted to approach. She remained in the monastery for two full weeks, taking no food or drink.

“It happened that the fifteenth Sunday dawned. The priest came with us so that the morning sacrifice might customarily be offered there, and the superior led the girl to the altar with the walk and appearance with which women flushed from food and drink commonly arrive. But when she prostrated herself before the altar, her cry of weeping, groans, and tears moved all who were present; through them the people begged the Lord to remove so great an evil.

“When the sacrifice had been completed, she received from the priest, among the others, a small particle of the body of the Lord dipped in the chalice. Yet after chewing for half an hour she could not swallow it, since the one of whom the Apostle says had not yet been driven out: ‘What concord is there between Christ and Belial?’ And again: ‘You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons; you cannot share in the table of the Lord and the table of demons’ (I Cor. X).

“Therefore, while the priest supported her face with his hand so that she would not spit out the holy sacrament, one of the deacons suggested that the bishop apply the saving chalice to her throat. When this had been done, at once the devil left the place that he had occupied, at the command of the Savior. The girl cried out that she had swallowed the Sacrament which she held in her mouth, with praise of the Redeemer.

“Then there was joy; then voices arose in praise of God, because, after eighty-two days, once the devil had been expelled, the girl had been rescued from the power of the enemy.”

Thus far Saint Prosper. However, although we have said that holy communion may be given to demoniacs, we do not mean that it should be given to all, or at every time, but only to those who retain possession of their mind and judgment, so that they can distinguish this food from other food and prepare themselves for it with devotion and reverence—and, indeed, at a time when the demons are not troubling them and no irreverence toward the Sacrament is feared (Peter Thyraeus, *De Daemoniacis*, chapter 28). Accordingly, when Blessed Dionysius says that this Sacrament should not be given to the possessed (*Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 3), Saint Thomas understands him to mean the unbaptized. See below Cuichius’s tenth annotation.]

We have never heard from our elders that the most holy communion was forbidden them. On the contrary, if it were possible, they judged that it ought to be imparted to them every day. For, contrary to the Gospel saying which you improperly apply to this matter, “Do not give what is holy to dogs,” we must believe that holy communion reaches them not as food for the demon, but rather for the cleansing and protection of body and soul. Once received by a person, it drives away the spirit that dwells in his members, or is recognized as lurking within them, like a consuming fire.

In this way we recently saw the abbot Andronicus cured, along with many others.

[Note: It is uncertain which Andronicus this abbot is discussing. There is, to be sure, the celebrated history of Andronicus and his wife Tharasia, both anchorites, whose memory is also famous in the Roman Martyrology on October 9. By mutual agreement they vowed continence, chose the anchoritic life, and lived it with great holiness under the discipline of Abbot Daniel, whom I believe to be the Daniel who debates in the fourth Conference in our Cassian. Whether he is the Andronicus mentioned here, however, I leave to the reader to judge.]

For the enemy will assault the possessed more and more when he sees him separated from heavenly medicine; and he will attack him all the more savagely and frequently the farther he perceives him to have been deprived of spiritual remedy.

## CHAPTER XXXI. That those are wretched who are not deemed worthy to be subjected to these temporal temptations

Moreover—

[Note: The sacred Scriptures repeatedly indicate this. They proclaim as happy and beloved of God those whom he chastises in this life, lest he punish them eternally; but they call unhappy and reprobate those with whom he is not angry. Thus, in Ezekiel XVI, he abandons them; in Psalm LXXX, he gives them over to the desires of their hearts; and in Hosea IV, he does not visit their sins.

In this connection the words of the author of II Maccabees VI are outstanding, though less commonly known. He says: “I beg those who will read this book not to be disheartened because of these adverse circumstances, but to consider that what happened was not for the destruction but for the correction of our race. For it is a sign of great kindness not to allow sinners to act according to their own will for a long time, but immediately to apply punishments. For the Lord does not wait patiently, as he does with other nations, to punish them when the day of judgment has come and their sins have reached their fullness; so also he has determined to deal with us, so that, when our sins have reached their limit, he may then take vengeance upon us. Therefore he never removes his mercy from us; while correcting his people through adversity, he does not abandon them.” Thus he.

Lactantius, in book V of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 23, following Seneca and citing him, speaks excellently to the same point: “If anyone wishes to know more fully why God allows wicked and unjust men to become powerful, happy, and rich, while he permits the pious to be humble, wretched, and poor, let him take up Seneca’s book entitled *Why Many Misfortunes Befall Good Men, Although Providence Exists*. In it he speaks at length—not with worldly ignorance, but wisely and almost divinely. ‘God,’ he says, ‘treats human beings as children; but he permits the corrupt and vicious to live luxuriously and delicately, because he does not consider them worthy of correction. The good, whom he loves, he chastises more often and trains through continual hardships for the practice of virtue; nor does he allow them to be corrupted and depraved by transient and mortal goods. Therefore no one ought to be surprised if we are often chastised by God for our sins. Rather, when we are shaken and oppressed, then above all we give thanks to our most indulgent Father, because he does not permit our corruption to proceed farther, but corrects it through blows and scourges. From this we understand that God cares for us: he is angry with us because we sin.’” Thus Lactantius, drawing from Seneca.

To these may be added that distinguished senator and philosopher Severinus Boethius, in book IV of *The Consolation of Philosophy*. There he splendidly teaches and proves that the wicked are more fortunate when they suffer punishment than if no penalty of justice restrains them; and, conversely, that they are far more wretched when they act with impunity than when they are punished by just retribution. This accords perfectly with the present passage.]

Those, therefore, are truly to be judged wretched and pitiable who, though they contaminate themselves with every crime and disgrace, not only display no visible sign of demonic affliction—

[Note: That is, of invasion, possession, or vexation. Cassian commonly uses *suppletio* in this sense, as he does other words of the same derivation: “to afflict,” “afflicted.”]

—but are not subjected to any temptation proportionate to their deeds, nor to any scourge of correction. They do not deserve the swift and ready medicine of the present time, because their hardness and impenitent heart, exceeding the punishment of this life, “stores up wrath for itself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the righteous judgment of God” (Rom. II), when “their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa. LXVI).

Against such people the prophet, as though distressed by the affliction of the saints, sees them subjected to various hardships and temptations, while sinners, not only without any scourge of humiliation, pass through the course of this world, but even rejoice in an abundance of riches and the highest prosperity in all things. Inflamed by intolerable zeal and the fervor of his spirit, he cries out:

“But my feet were almost moved; my steps nearly slipped, because I was zealous over the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners. For there is no regard for their death, and there is no strength in their affliction. They are not in the labor of men, and they shall not be scourged with men” (Ps. LXXII);

that is, in the future they will be punished with demons, because in the present they were not deemed worthy to be scourged with human beings in the lot and discipline of sons.

Jeremiah also, disputing with God about the prosperity of the wicked, although he openly professes that he in no way doubts the Lord’s justice—“You are indeed just, O Lord, if I dispute with you” (Jer. XII)—nevertheless, seeking the causes of so great an inequality, adds and says:

“Yet I shall speak justly to you. Why does the way of the wicked prosper? Why is it well with all who transgress and act wickedly? You have planted them, and they have taken root; they prosper and bear fruit. You are near their mouth, but far from their inward parts” (Jer. XII).

When the Lord, through the prophet, laments their ruin, diligently sending physicians and teachers for their healing, and in a certain sense calling them to a similar lament, he says:

“Suddenly Babylon has fallen and is shattered. Wail over her; take balm for her pain, if perhaps she may be healed” (Jer. LI).

The despairing angels, to whom the care of human salvation has been entrusted—or, certainly, the prophet speaking in the person of the apostles, spiritual men, and teachers who see the hardness of their minds and their impenitent heart—reply:

“We have healed Babylon, but she was not healed. Let us abandon her, and let us each go to his own land, because her judgment has reached the heavens and has been lifted up to the clouds” (ibid.).

Of the hopeless sickness of such people Isaiah speaks to Jerusalem in the person of God:

“From the sole of the foot even to the crown there is no health in her; wound and bruise and swollen sore are not bound up, nor treated with medicine, nor softened with oil” (Isa. I).

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the diversity of the pursuits and wills exercised among the powers of the air

[Note: He repeats here, in different words, what he taught above in Conference 17: not all demons inflict every kind of suffering upon human beings, but particular spirits cling to particular vices. Some take pleasure in filth and lust; others in blasphemies; others attack anger and rage more especially; others feed on sadness; others are soothed by vainglory and pride. Each inserts into human hearts the vice in which he himself delights. From this he concludes that, just as demons have various activities and desires, so they also have various kinds.

It should be noted that two classifications of demons are commonly assigned. One is based on the places where they remain and lie in wait for human beings; the other, on the vices to which they chiefly endeavor to drive and incite people.

According to the first classification, the ancients spoke of certain heavenly or aerial, aquatic, terrestrial, and subterranean demons (Caelius Rhodiginus, book II, chapter 4 and following; Ludovicus Vives). Thus Marcus, in Psellus’s book *On the Nature of Demons*, chapter 9. Thomas of Cantimpré distinguishes four classes (book II, chapter 57): “There are demons who remain in the waters, whom poets call Neptunes; others above the earth, whom they call incubi; others in the earth, as in mountain caves or forests, whom Augustine calls Drusii (*The City of God*, book X); others in the air, whom the Apostle calls ‘the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places’ (Eph. VI).” Thus he.

According to the second classification, Cassian distinguishes in book V of the *Institutes* and the following books, and likewise in Conference 5, spirits of gluttony, fornication, avarice, anger, sadness, acedia, vainglory, and pride. These names may refer both to the vices themselves and to the demons who cause and instigate them, as stated elsewhere.

The Author explains this classification in the present chapter. Much may also be seen on the subject in John Climacus, Steps 15 and 21. See Cuichius’s eleventh annotation.]

That there are as many pursuits among unclean spirits as among human beings is clearly demonstrated. For we find that some of them, whom the common people call Fauns—

[Note: Fauns or Satyrs were very famous among pagan writers, especially poets. Saint Augustine also mentions them in book XV of *The City of God*, chapter 23. He says that they were called Silvans because they were more frequently seen in forests and were worshiped as woodland or rustic gods.

Saint Jerome writes in the *Life of Paul the Hermit* that, as the blessed Anthony was traveling through a vast wilderness to visit Paul the Hermit, a Faun met him. Jerome describes him as follows: “In a rocky valley he saw a little man, not very large, with a hooked nose and a forehead roughened by horns; the lower part of his body ended in the feet of a goat. Nevertheless, the creature offered Anthony the fruit of palm trees for his journey, as though they were pledges of peace.” When Anthony learned this, he stopped and asked who he was. The creature replied: “I am mortal and one of the inhabitants of this desert, whom the pagan world, deceived by various errors, worships under the names Fauns, Satyrs, and incubi.”

Jerome then adds, to confirm the matter: “Lest anyone be troubled by unbelief, this event is attested under the emperor Constantine, with the whole world as witness. For a man of this kind was brought alive to Alexandria and provided a great spectacle for the people; afterward his lifeless corpse was brought to Antioch, preserved with salt so that the summer heat would not destroy it, in order that the emperor might see it.”

Thus Saint Jerome depicts the Faun as a man bearing many human characteristics, although in the same passage he calls him a wanton creature, a portent, and a beast. Marianus therefore concludes in his scholia that it was some monstrous species, especially since, after the whole world has now been traversed, no such human beings are found. Baronius appears to agree, believing that the story narrated by Jerome should be attributed to a miracle—as one often reads of many other animals, though lacking reason, which by reason of God’s command have appeared almost rational and have performed for holy men services such as human beings ordinarily perform (Baronius, volume III of the *Annals*, year 343).

Whatever may be the truth about the Faun who met Saint Anthony, it is more probable that those Fauns and Satyrs who, as stated above, were regarded by pagans as the divinities of forests were demons appearing in human form, but in a monstrous shape ending in that of a goat or donkey, and mocking human beings, as the Author suggests here. Scripture accordingly calls them hairy ones. Isaiah XIII says: “The hairy ones shall dance there.” As Saint Jerome notes there: “By ‘the hairy ones’ understand either incubi, or Satyrs, or certain woodland men whom some call murderous Fauns, or kinds of demons.”

Likewise, in chapter 34 of the same prophet: “Demons shall meet; the onocentaur and the hairy one shall cry out to one another.” The demons are thought to be called hairy ones for another reason as well: they commonly appear to their worshipers in the form of a shaggy and hairy goat. But enough about this.]

—it is evident that they are seducers and tricksters. They continually occupy certain places and roads, yet they do not take pleasure in tormenting those whom they are able to deceive as they pass by; rather, content with laughter and mockery, they seek to weary them instead of harming them.

[Note: This must be understood comparatively: that is, they do not take pleasure in it to the same degree as the others, who are more savage and cruel and are discussed below. It is more correct to say that all demons desire to inflict the gravest evils upon human beings and would actually inflict them if God permitted it.

Saint Anthony teaches, in Athanasius, that all demons harbor hostile hatred toward human beings—more grievous toward Christians, and most grievous toward monks and virgins dedicated to God—yet that each can harm people only insofar as God permits. When they are not permitted to do more, they rejoice in mocking and deceiving human beings, as stated here, or in driving them into at least some venial sin: idle looking or speaking, excessive laughter, distraction in prayer, drowsiness, and similar faults, into which even the very perfect are easily drawn. See Peter of Cluny, book I of the *Miracles*, chapter 17.]

Some merely spend the night troubling human beings with harmless oppressions.

[Note: By harmless oppressions I believe that nocturnal oppression is meant: the condition that obstructs the passage of the voice and breath and presses upon people who are resting or asleep as though under a great weight, almost suffocating them. The Greeks call it ἐφιάλτης (*ephialtēs*, Suidas, entry “Ephialtes”); the Latins call it an *incubus*, and the French a *cauchemar*. This oppression and suffocation commonly arises from overeating, indigestion, or a type of melancholic illness, although at times it is caused by demons. Hence they are also called incubi or incubones, apart from the obscene oppression and intercourse with witches and striges discussed by Saint Augustine in the cited passage. Thus this condition is sometimes a bodily illness, and at other times the bare and pure infestation or mockery of a demon.]

Others are so devoted to rage and savagery that they are not content merely to torment with savage dismemberment the bodies of those whom they have afflicted, but hasten to rush upon people passing at a distance and attack them with the most cruel slaughter.

[Note: Matthew VIII says: “When they had come into the region of the Gerasenes, two men possessed by demons met him, exceedingly fierce, so that no one could pass by that road.” Luke, speaking of only one of them, adds that he wore no clothing and did not remain in a house but in the tombs, expressing their savagery, because no one dared meet them or receive them into his house. Thus, excluded from ordinary human habitation, they withdrew into the tombs, which were vaulted chambers.]

Such were those described in the Gospel (Matt. VIII), because of whose fear no one dared any longer to pass along that road. There is no doubt that they and demons like them also delight in wars and bloodshed because of their insatiable ferocity.

We see that others infect the hearts of those whom they have seized with a kind of empty swelling. The common people call these Bacucei—

[Note: By Bacucei, or Bacutei, or, as the manuscripts read, Bacuci, he understands people seized by a particular kind of demon, the word having been imposed upon them by the populace in some barbarous language. Although the passage properly concerns demoniacs, as the words indicate, rather than demons considered separately or their properties, it is nevertheless not improbable that the same name was also customarily given to demons when they appeared separately and outside mortal bodies.

Thus Saint Augustine writes that there are certain demons whom the Gauls called Drusii (*The City of God*, book XV, chapter 23); these will be discussed below.]

—because, lifting themselves above the stature of the body, they now exalt themselves into certain proud postures and gestures, and now, as though leaning forward, lower themselves into a kind of calm and affable manner. Considering themselves illustrious and worthy of everyone’s notice, they sometimes show by bending the body that they are worshiping higher powers, and at other times believe that they themselves are being worshiped by others. They enact every movement by which genuine acts of service are performed either proudly or humbly.

[Note: What is said here of demoniacs—that is, of demons occupying human bodies—also applies to demons separated from bodies who nevertheless display themselves in human form. For they are also said to have appeared in the form of giants, dwarfs, or little men, as may be seen in the *Life of Saint Anthony* by Athanasius, in Palladius’s account of Macarius (*Lausiac History*, 20), and in Gregory the Great’s account of Benedict (*Dialogues*, II, chapter 4).]

Others we find to be not only eager for lies, but also to inspire blasphemies in human beings.

[Note: Hence it is called the spirit of blasphemy. Even holy and very devout people are at times afflicted by it, so that unwillingly they think concerning God and divine matters things which they neither believe in their heart nor, indeed, anything more strongly abhor. Palladius says of Evagrius (*Lausiac History*, 86): “At one time the spirit of blasphemy troubled him, and for forty days he did not go to bed,” etc.

John Climacus, Step 23, describes it thus: “For it is not just any enemy, but one more savage and grievous than all enemies. And what is harder is that it cannot readily be disclosed to a spiritual physician or laid bare by confession. Consequently, it has sometimes caused despair and distrust in very many, all their hope being consumed no otherwise than wood is consumed by a worm. This most wicked spirit, then, often blasphemes the Lord at the holy synaxis and at the very dreadful hour of the sacred mysteries, and blasphemes the sacred rites themselves as they are being performed. From this we plainly infer that it is not our soul that has spoken within us those impious and intolerable words, but the demon—the adversary of God and of every good thing—who was cast down from heaven, because there too, while exalting himself through pride, he was seen to hurl blasphemies and insults against God. For if those shameful and wicked words are mine, why, when I receive the heavenly gift, do I adore? How can I at once bless and curse?”

And a little later Climacus says: “That impious spirit not only blasphemes God and all divine things, but also speaks mentally within us certain most shameful and loathsome words, so that we may either abandon prayer or cast ourselves into despair. This evil and savage tyrant has cut off the prayer of very many, separated others from communion in the sacred mysteries, subdued others by fasting, and granted them no rest.” Again, further on, the same Climacus says: “This kind of demon is commonly wont to dwell in the minds of the simpler and purer, since such people are especially accustomed to be shaken and disturbed more violently than others. Yet we do not say that this happens to them properly through any pride, but through the envy and cunning of demons.”

Climacus says these and other things, and finally adds the example of a monk troubled by the spirit of blasphemy and healed by his spiritual father: “A certain zealous monk, when he had been troubled by it for twenty years, did not cease to mortify his flesh by fasts and vigils. But when he perceived that he had gained no benefit from this, he wrote down his disturbance and temptation on paper and offered it to a certain holy and most approved elder, prostrating himself on his face and unable to look at him. When the elder had read it, he smiled and, raising the brother up, said: ‘Place your hand, my son, upon my neck.’ When he had done so, the elder said to him: ‘Let this sin be upon my neck, brother, for however many years it has fought, or will fight, against you. But see to it that henceforth you make light of it and reckon it as nothing.’ By these words the brother was so strengthened that he did not leave the elder’s cell before this kind of affliction had disappeared.” Thus he.]

We ourselves are witnesses of this, having heard a demon openly confessing that he had produced the impiety of the sacrilegious doctrine of Arius and Eunomius.

[Note: These were prominent and notorious heresiarchs. The former chiefly attacked the divinity of the Son, the latter that of the Holy Spirit. Arius, a presbyter of Alexandria, taught that the Son of God was a creature and therefore neither co-eternal with nor ὁμοούσιος—that is, “consubstantial”—with the Father. He was condemned at the great Council of Nicaea. When he wished to enter a church, he was suddenly compelled by a movement of the bowels to withdraw to a public latrine, where he discharged his intestines and soul together with his excrement.

Eunomius, the disciple of Aëtius, asserted that the Son was unlike the Father in every respect, and that the Holy Spirit was unlike the Son, as Saint Augustine says (*On Heresies*, 45 and 60).]

We also clearly read in the Third Book of Kings that one of those same spirits openly proclaimed:

“I will go out and become a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets” (III Kings XXII; II Chronicles XVIII).

Concerning them the Apostle, reproving those who are deceived by them, says:

“They attend to seducing spirits and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy” (I Tim. IV, 1–2).

The Gospels also testify that there are other kinds of demons, namely, mute and deaf demons (Luke XI, VII; Mark IX).

[Note: Demons are called mute or deaf when they render mute or deaf those whom they possess, as was noted above. The demoniac whom the Lord healed in Luke XI was mute and deaf, but this was caused by the demon, which is therefore called mute and deaf. Palladius also reports in the *Life of Abbot Possidonius* (*Lausiac History*, 77) that a woman was deprived of the use of her tongue for six years by this kind of demon.]

[Note: The demon who appeared to Saint Anthony in the form of a black boy belonged to this class. Athanasius relates the story as follows:

“One day, when the devil saw that he was always repelled from his thoughts, he appeared in the form that was appropriate to him, gnashing his teeth and howling. He appeared as a hideous and black boy, threw himself at Anthony’s knees, and wept in a human voice, saying: ‘I have deceived many and misled very many; but now, as I have been defeated by the labor of the other saints, so I have also been defeated by yours.’

“When Anthony asked him who he was who spoke such things, he replied: ‘I am a friend of fornication. I have taken up many weapons of shamefulness against all young men; hence I am also called the spirit of fornication. How many intending to live chastely have I deceived! How many who were beginning cautiously have I persuaded to return to their former filth! I am the one on account of whom the prophet rebukes those who have fallen, saying: “You have been led astray by the spirit of fornication”; and truly, through me, they were overthrown. I am the one who has often tempted you, yet has always been repulsed.’

“When the soldier of Christ heard this, he gave thanks to God. Strengthened with greater boldness against the enemy, he said: ‘Then you are greatly contemptible and despicable, for both your darkness and your age are signs of weakness,’ and so forth.

“The demon called Asmodeus in Tobit VI and VIII also seems to have belonged to this class. He killed Sarah’s seven husbands on their first night, when they had been inflamed by lust and, shutting out the fear of God, rushed into carnal desire; the angel Raphael bound him and led him away into the desert.

“Such also were the demons whom Saint Augustine, in the cited passage, says the Gauls called Drusii, who were accustomed continually both to tempt and to effect this impurity.

“Such was the kind of demon that the Savior said could be cast out only by fasting and prayer (Luke XXII), by which carnal lust is especially restrained.

“Such also was the demon whom Cyprian—then a magician, later a saint—sent against the virgin Justina, as Gregory of Nazianzus relates in Oration 18. And such was the demon whom a young man from Gaza, using magical arts, buried beneath the threshold of a house in order to conquer another virgin. When Saint Hilarion asked it why it had not entered the young man himself, it replied: ‘Why should I enter one who already has my companion, the demon of Love?’ Saint Jerome relates this in the *Life of Hilarion*.

“Finally, such was the demon who aroused in a most chaste virgin a kind of frenzy and madness of love, as is recorded in the *Life of Saint Basil*. The same kind of demon inflicted the greatest carnal troubles upon Moses the Ethiopian and Evagrius, according to Palladius, and upon Hilarion himself, according to Jerome.”]

The prophet also mentions certain spirits as instigators of lust and sexual excess:

“The spirit of fornication deceived them, and they fornicated against their God” (Hos. IV).

[Note: This refers to the passage of the ninetieth Psalm: “From the arrow that flies by day; from the business that walks about in darkness; from the attack and the noonday demon.” Basil, Jerome, and others interpret this verse as referring to various kinds of demons. They call them nocturnal demons when they are accustomed chiefly to infest, tempt, or afflict human beings at night. Hence they are also called, in a particular sense, “the rulers of darkness” and “the power of darkness”; poets call them *lucifugi*, *tenebriones*, specters, larvae, shadows, and phantoms. Against them the Church sings, following Ambrose:

“May dreams depart far away,

And the phantoms of the night;

Restrain our enemy,

[the supplied text ends here]

That bodies may not be defiled. Diurnal and noonday demons are those especially accustomed to roam about or exercise their strength and attack people more fiercely by day and at noon; they do so both by spiritual temptation and assault, especially of lust and acedia—two sins which press most vehemently upon a person swollen and full with food, as Euthymius and Theodoret teach on this same psalm, and our Cassian, *Institutes*, Book X, chapter 2—and by bodily afflictions and annoyances, as may be seen in the *Life of Saint Antony* and elsewhere. Yet these things should not be understood as though demons depended on places or times, but because, by their own will and God’s permission, or at the command of higher spirits, they choose or are assigned these or those times more readily or frequently.

Scriptural authority likewise teaches of nocturnal as well as diurnal and noonday demons (Ps. 90). It would take very long, if we wished to search through all the volumes of Scripture and go through them one by one, to discuss their diversity: those designated by the prophet as onocentaurs, hairy creatures, sirens, lamiae, screech-owls, ostriches, and hedgehogs (Isa. 14); those called asps and basilisks in the Psalm (Ps. 90); those named lions, dragons, and scorpions in the Gospel (Luke 10; John 14); and those whom the Apostle calls “the ruler of this world,” “the rulers of the darkness of this age,” and “the spiritual forces of wickedness” (Eph. 6).

[Note: These and similar names are attributed to demons either commonly and indiscriminately to all of them, or specifically and particularly to certain ones. This is done for two reasons: first, metaphorically, insofar as they imitate the properties and wickedness of such animals or monsters, as will be explained below; second, because they are accustomed to assume such forms and make themselves visible in them, as is well known from the *Life of Saint Antony*, so often cited and to be cited in this connection.

“For,” as Athanasius says, “assuming the forms of beasts and serpents, they immediately filled the cell where the holy man lived with visions of lions, bulls, wolves, asps, serpents, scorpions, leopards, and bears. Each of these roared according to its own nature. The lion roared, wishing to kill; the bull threatened with bellowing and horns; the serpents resounded with hissing; the wolves gaped in their assault; the many-colored leopard indicated the varied cunning of its author. The faces of all were savage, their voices horrible, and their sound dreadful.”

Athanasius also reports that many other appearances of demons in various monstrous forms and shapes occurred to the same Antony. “Antony asserted,” he says, “that he had seen the devil in such a form as blessed Job came to know him when the Lord revealed him. His eyes were like the appearance of Lucifer; from his mouth proceeded blazing torches; his hair was scattered amid flames; smoke issued from his nostrils, as though from the heat of a furnace burning with coals; his breath was like live coals, while flame gathered from his mouth.”

At another time he saw a beast that presented a human face as far as the groin and from there ended in an ass.

The same Antony, according to Jerome (*Life of Paul the Hermit*), saw a man mingled with a horse, to which the poets’ imagination gave the name hippocentaur. Yet Saint Jerome doubts whether this was the devil, who had assumed that form in order to terrify him, or some monstrous animal, since the desert is accustomed to abound in such monsters.

Something similar is related by the same Jerome about Hilarion. While Hilarion was living in the desert, one night he began to hear the cries of infants, the bleating of sheep, the lowing of cattle, the weeping—as though of women—the roaring of lions, the murmur of an army, and again prodigious varieties of voices, so that, terrified by sound before sight, he gave way, and so forth.

There is likewise a similar account by blessed Gregory (*Dialogues*, Book III, chapter 4) concerning Datius, bishop of Milan. When Datius had entered at Corinth, for the purpose of lodging, a certain house abandoned by human beings and occupied by demons, the ancient enemy, while the man of God was resting in the silence of the dead of night, began to imitate with immense voices and great cries the roaring of lions, the bleating of sheep, the braying of asses, the hissing of serpents, the grunting of pigs, and the squeaking of mice.

Then Datius, suddenly roused by the voices of so many beasts, rose up in great anger and began to shout loudly against the ancient enemy, saying: “It has gone well for you, wretch! You are the one who said, ‘I shall set my throne toward the north, and I shall be like the Most High’” (Isa. 14). “Behold, through your pride you have become like pigs and mice; and you who improperly wished to imitate God, behold, as you deserve, you imitate beasts,” and so forth.

Here the reason is explicitly given why God permits demons to appear in the forms of such beasts or to imitate their voices: namely, for their greater confusion, disgrace, and humiliation of their pride.

Many other examples may be found in Peter of Cluny, Caesarius of Cîteaux, Thomas of Cantimpré, and other more recent writers (Peter of Cluny, *Book I on Miracles*; Caesarius, *Book on Demons*; Peter Thyræus, *On Apparitions of Spirits*, chapter 9; Delrio, *On Magic*, Book II, question 27).

We must not understand that these names were assigned to them by chance or accident. Rather, their ferocity and madness are distinguished by the significance of those beasts, which among us are either less harmful or more destructive; and because of the resemblance of their venomous wickedness, or of the dominion which a certain superiority of malice grants them among the other beasts or serpents, they too are called by those beasts’ names. Thus one, because of the violence of his fury and the madness of his ferocity, receives the designation “lion”; another, because of the deadly venom that kills before it is perceived, is called a “basilisk”; while another, because of the sluggishness of his wickedness, is given the name “onocentaur,” “hedgehog,” or “ostrich.”

## CHAPTER XXXIII  
### The question of how such a great difference among the wickednesses of the heavenly beings arose

**Germanus:** We do not, indeed, doubt that those orders which the Apostle enumerates also refer to these beings, since “our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this age, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6). Yet we wish to know where such a great difference among them came from, or how such great degrees of wickedness arose. Were they created for this purpose, so that they would receive these orders of wickedness and, in a certain way, serve in the army of this wickedness?

## CHAPTER XXXIV  
### Postponement of the answer to the question proposed

**Serenus:** Although your propositions steal away the entire time of our nightly rest from our eyes, so that we are in no way aware of the nearness of the approaching dawn and are urged to weave the words of this conversation insatiably until sunrise, nevertheless, since the resolution of the question proposed, once we begin to investigate it, will lead us into a vast and exceedingly deep sea of questions which the brevity of the present hour does not permit us to cross, I think it more convenient to reserve it for the investigation of the coming night. In this way, on the occasion of this question, I shall receive from your more eager conversation greater spiritual joy and richer fruit, and, with the Holy Spirit providing us favorable winds, we shall be able to penetrate more freely into the depths of the questions proposed.

Therefore, after tasting a little sleep, let us shake off the torpor that is creeping over our eyes, since the light is already near; and afterward, proceeding together to the church, [Note: To proceed to the church. For it was customary even among the ancient monks and anchorites to assemble at church on the Lord’s Day, as we noted long ago in the books of the *Institutes*. Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 31, speaking of the monks of Nitria, says: “They all come together in one place and hold an assembly on the first and last day. If anyone happens to be absent, it is clearly understood that he is unwillingly absent, prevented either by some affliction or by illness,” and so forth. Cassian likewise relates (*Conferences*, 18.15) that, in the very desert, on Sunday Paphnutius proceeded from his cell to the church with the other monks. See *Conference* 23.21, where more is said on this matter.]

since the solemnity of the Lord’s Day reminds us to do this, after the synaxis, [Note: We have also discussed the synaxis elsewhere (*Institutes*, Book II, chapter 10, and frequently in other places). Here it may be understood as the assembly or congregation of monks for prayer and the celebration of the divine praises in church on the Lord’s Day, or as the sacrifice of the Mass and the holy communion, which they were accustomed to receive on Sundays, as will be said in its proper place (*Conference* 23, final chapter).

Thus, in Palladius (*Lausiac History*, chapter 59), Abba Hellos once came to certain monks and, since it was Sunday, said to them: “Why did you not hold the synaxis today?” They replied: “Because the presbyter did not come.”

Among Greek writers, the verb *synagein* (συνάγειν), from which *synaxis* is derived, has two meanings. Sometimes it means to hold an assembly, or to gather the people into the church for a sacred purpose; at other times it means to admit someone to communion. This was observed by Jacques de Billy, Book I of *Sacred Observations*, chapter 40.]

when we return, let us share with doubled joy those things which the Lord, according to your desire, will have graciously granted for our common instruction.

# THE EIGHTH CONFERENCE  
## The second of Abbot Serenus  
### ON PRINCIPALITIES OR POWERS

[Col. 0719]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0719C]

When the activities required by the solemnity of the day had been completed and the congregation had been dismissed from the church, we returned to the old man’s cell and first refreshed ourselves with a very sumptuous meal.

For [Note: Concerning *muria*, Isidore says (*Etymologies*): “It is called *liquamen* because the little fish, dissolved in brine, liquefy (*liquant*; alternative reading: *linquant*, ‘leave’) the same liquid; its liquor is called *salsugo*, or *muria*.” Properly, however, *muria* is water mixed with salt and given a taste like that of the sea.” This is Isidore’s account. Ambrosius Calepinus makes it somewhat clearer: “*Muria* is a kind of sauce made from tuna fish. It is also called *salsugo*, that is, a liquid dissolved from salt, which we commonly call *salmuria*—in French, *saumure*.” Pliny, Book XXXI, chapter 8: “*Muria*, or *salsugo*, thickens, bites, attenuates, and dries.” Festus Pompeius, following Veranius, interprets *muria* as dirty salt, pounded in a mortar, put into an earthen jar, covered and sealed with gypsum, and baked in a furnace.]

in place of the *muria*, upon which a drop of oil was customarily poured and which was served with the daily refreshment, he mixed a small amount of sauce and poured over it somewhat more oil than usual.

For each person, when about to eat, drips that drop of oil every day for this reason—not so that he may derive from it some sweetness in his throat, since the amount is so small that it scarcely suffices to coat, or even to pass through, the passage of the throat and pharynx, but so that this practice may blunt the vainglory of the heart. That vainglory, on account of the stricter abstinence, habitually creeps in gently and secretly, and the drop dulls the goads of elation; for the more secretly abstinence itself is practiced, and the more it is accomplished with no human witness, the more subtly it does not cease to tempt the one who conceals it.

[Note: The older books read this way, and Dionysius agrees with them, as Cuychius observed. But other ancient manuscripts read: “He set before them three olives each, fried with salt.” This reading seems more plausible and convenient, and Lavardinus rendered it in French as follows: “Then he set before each of us three olives fried with salt.” Otherwise, the conjunction *and* would have had to be inserted for the sake of the sense. But why would salt be fried separately when *muria* was present, and was extremely salty?]

Then he set before us fried salt and three olives each, and afterward placed before us a basket containing [Note: *Cicer*, Greek *erebinthos* (ἐρέβινθος), is a kind of legume, concerning which Pliny writes in Book XVIII, chapter 12: “The nature of the chickpea is to grow with saltiness; therefore it burns the soil, and it can be sown only after being soaked the previous day.”]

fried chickpeas, which they call *trogalia* [Note: *Trogalia* (τρωγάλια), as Ciaconius observed, are called in Latin *bellaria*, that is, sweetmeats and delicacies for the palate, according to those who have written glossaries. But in the Scetian desert fried chickpeas served the monks in place of sweetmeats, and for that reason they called them *trogalia*.], of which we took only five grains each;

two *myxaria* [Note: *Myxaria* are plums smaller than Damascene plums, with a triangular stone inside. See Pliny, Book XIII, chapter 5, and Book XV, chapter 13, although there he calls them *myxae* and *myxa*, not *myxaria*.];

and one *carica* each [Note: *Caricas*, not *carycas* with a Greek *y*. For *caryca* is a condiment made from blood and various delicacies, as Suidas says; in Greek it is also called *karykeuma* (καρύκευμα) (Caelius Rhodiginus, Book XXVII, chapter 23). A *carica*, however, is a kind of fig peculiar to Syria. Pliny, Book XIII, chapter 5: “Syria has trees peculiar to itself among the varieties of figs, called *caricae*, and smaller figs of the same kind, which they call *cutanae*.” Cicero, *On Divination*, Book II: “When Marcus Crassus was embarking his army at Brundisium, someone in the harbor who was selling figs imported from Caunus kept shouting, ‘Cauneas!’”

Strabo, as Cuychius notes, testifies that this kind of fig grows abundantly in the region of Caria and that it derived its name from that region.

It is remarkable, moreover, that it is said here that each monk was allowed only one *carica*, and that exceeding this number was blameworthy, unless it is understood in conjunction with the other foods. For Saint Jerome, as a great miracle and an example of extraordinary abstinence, relates—even with an oath—that a certain monk barely lived on five *caricae* a day. “I call Jesus and his holy angels to witness,” he says (*Life of Paul the Hermit*), “that in that part of the desert which borders Syria and the Saracens, I saw monks, one of whom, shut away for thirty years, lived on barley bread and muddy water; another was sustained each day by five *caricae* in an old cistern, which the Syrians in their native language call a *cuba*.”

In the *Life of Hilarion* he writes that Hilarion likewise ate only fifteen *caricae*, and that only after sunset.

Here the reader should carefully consider the delicacies of the ancient monks—or rather, the courses and dishes with which the Author says that he and his companion Germanus were sumptuously refreshed as guests of Abbot Serenus. It will be useful to note them all briefly.

The first course was *muria*, which we commonly call *salmuria*. The second was a small amount of oil or sauce, scarcely enough to pass through the throat. The third was fried salt. The fourth was three olives each. The fifth was a few grains of fried chickpea. The sixth was two *myxaria*, that is, two plums each. The seventh was one *carica*, or fig, each.

Having seriously considered these matters, reflect on how great the difference is between those times and ours, and between their customs and ours. On this subject see Saint Bernard’s *Apology to Abbot William*, where, among other things, he exclaims:

> O how far we are from those who were monks in the days of Antony! When, out of charity, they visited one another from time to time, they received from one another the bread of souls with such eagerness that, completely forgetting bodily food, they spent most of the day with empty stomachs but not empty minds. And this was the proper order, when the more worthy part was served first. This was the highest discretion, when the greater part received more. This was true charity, when the souls for whose love Christ died were refreshed with such great care.
>
> But when we come together—as I may use the Apostle’s words—it is no longer to eat the Lord’s Supper (1 Cor. 11). No one seeks the heavenly bread; no one offers it. Nothing is said about the Scriptures or the salvation of souls; instead, trifles, laughter, and words are poured out upon the wind. During the meal, as much as the throat is nourished by dishes, so much are the ears nourished by gossip, to which one is so entirely attentive that one does not know one’s proper measure in eating.
>
> Meanwhile, dish is placed upon dish, and, in place of the meats from which they abstain, great bodies of fish are multiplied. When you have been satisfied with the earlier courses, if you touch the later ones, you will seem not yet to have tasted fish. Everything is prepared with such care and culinary skill that, after four or five courses have been devoured, the earlier ones do not hinder the later ones, nor does satiety diminish the appetite.

This is Bernard speaking of the Cluniacs, who nevertheless abstained from meat.]

For it was blameworthy in that desert for anyone to exceed this number.

When this refreshment was over, and we began to ask again for the promised resolution of the question, the old man said: “Put forward your question, the investigation of which we postponed until this hour.”

## CHAPTER II  
### The second proposition, concerning the diversity of the heavenly powers of wickedness

Then Germanus said:

**Germanus:** We ask, therefore, where such great variety among the powers opposed to humanity, and this diversity, came from. Blessed Paul enumerates them as follows:

[Col. 0721B]

> “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this age, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6).

And again:

> “Neither angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. 8).

Whence, then, has such hostile opposition, marked by so great a wickedness, arisen against us? Are we to believe that the Lord created these powers for this purpose, so that they might wage war against humanity according to these degrees and orders?

## CHAPTER III  
### The answer concerning the manifold nourishment of the holy Scriptures
Serenus: The authority of the divine Scriptures has spoken some things about those matters in which it wished to instruct us so lucidly and plainly even to those who lack intellectual acuity that not only are they obscured or veiled by no shadow of a more hidden meaning, but they do not even require the support of interpretation, displaying their meanings and judgments on the surface [Col. 0722B] of the wording and letter. Other things, however, are so covered and darkened by certain mysteries that, in examining and understanding them, they leave us an immense field for exercise and diligence. It is manifest that God arranged this for many [Note: [Col. 0722D] Other Fathers also give the same reasons why God willed Sacred Scripture to be obscure in many passages. St. Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, Book II, chapter 6: “The Holy Spirit,” he says, “with magnificent and salutary wisdom so fashioned the Sacred Scriptures that in their clearer passages he might meet our hunger, while through their obscurities he might cleanse away our distaste. For scarcely anything is drawn from those obscurities that is not found stated with complete clarity elsewhere.” St. Gregory, *Homily 6 on Ezekiel*: “This obscurity of the divine utterances is of great usefulness, because it exercises the understanding, so that it is enlarged through fatigue, and when exercised it grasps what, at leisure, it cannot grasp. It has also this still greater advantage: if the understanding of Sacred Scripture were open in every respect, it would become cheap; whereas in its more obscure passages it refreshes with so much greater sweetness the more laboriously the mind has sought it,” etc.] [Col. 0723A] reasons. First, lest the divine mysteries, having no veil of spiritual understanding drawn over them, be opened to all people—that is, to the faithful and the profane alike—with equal knowledge and awareness, and thus there be no difference in virtue and prudence between the idle and the diligent; then also so that, among the faithful themselves, while immense expanses of understanding are spread out before them, the sluggishness of the indolent might be exposed in some, and the eagerness and industry of the diligent demonstrated in others. [Note: [Col. 0723B] That is, among the faithful, or Christians. For this is a periphrasis for Christians handed down by the Apostle. Galatians VI: “Let us do good to all, but especially to the household of faith.” Christians are called the household of faith, according to Thomas, because they are united not only by similarity of nature but also by faith, charity, and grace, serving one Father and Lord in one household, which is the Church. Hence the same Apostle, Ephesians II: “You are no longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household.”] [Note: [Col. 0723B] St. Chrysostom, *Homily 40 on John*, and Rupert, Book I *On the Holy Spirit*, chapters 1 and 2, treat this same comparison excellently.] Therefore divine Scripture is very aptly compared to a rich and fertile field. Although it produces and brings forth many things that serve for human nourishment without any cooking by fire, some things, unless first softened and mellowed by the heat of flame so that they lay aside all the harshness of their rawness, [Col. 0724A] will be judged either unsuitable for human use or harmful. Other things are found to be so suitable for both kinds of use that, even uncooked, they do not displease or offend by their rawness, and yet, when cooked by the heat of fire, become more wholesome. Many things, too, are produced solely as food for irrational beasts and animals, whether wild creatures or birds, and are of no use at all for human nourishment; remaining in their own harshness, without any preparation by fire, they provide the beasts with life-sustaining fullness.

We see this principle sufficiently clearly contained in this most fertile paradise of the spiritual Scriptures, in which things are arranged in such a way [Note: [Col. 0723C] For the understanding of this passage and of almost the entire chapter—which is truly difficult and obscure, since it deals with the meanings of Scripture—it seems worthwhile to set down briefly a few observations concerning the same matters.

First, Scripture is assigned a twofold meaning—not because several meanings are found in every one of its parts or statements, but because it is characteristic of Scripture very often to contain two meanings: the literal or historical, and the spiritual or mystical. The Fathers commonly teach this, in the passages marked here in the margin and in many others (St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* I, question 10, article 3; Jerome, letter 48; Ambrose, Book I *On Penance*, chapter 15; Augustine, *On True Religion*, chapter 9, and *On Christian Doctrine*, Book II, chapter 3; Gregory, *Homily 9 on Ezekiel* and preface to *Job*).

Second, the literal meaning is that which the words immediately express, or which the author of Sacred Scripture, the Holy Spirit, first and immediately intended to signify [Col. 0723D] through words, whether proper and customary or metaphorical. The spiritual meaning is referred elsewhere than to what the words immediately present, or is signified remotely and mediately through the words, but proximately through the things themselves signified by the words. From this it follows that the literal meaning is twofold: proper or simple, and figurative, as Bellarmine teaches in Book III of *On the Word of God*, chapter 3. The simple meaning is expressed by words taken properly; the figurative by words taken improperly and figuratively, or transferred from their proper signification. There are as many kinds of this as there are kinds of figures among rhetoricians.

Third, more recent theologians distinguish the spiritual meaning into three kinds: allegorical, tropological, and anagogical. But these are not at issue in this chapter.

Fourth, the literal meaning is found in every part of Scripture, that is, in every statement of both the Old and the New Testament; the spiritual meaning is not found everywhere.
