For the literal meaning is primary and first intended by the Holy Spirit, the author, and it is [Col. 0724B] the foundation of the whole mystical meaning, as the Fathers teach: Jerome in the epitaph of Paula and in the preface to Isaiah; Augustine, *City of God* XV, chapter 27; Gregory, second homily on Ezekiel. The spiritual meaning is indeed found in both the Old and the New Testament, but not in every statement of either. For the words, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart,” etc., Deuteronomy XXVI and Matthew XXII, and similar commandments, have only one meaning, namely the literal, as Abbot Serenus rightly teaches here.

Fifth, the figurative meaning, which is elsewhere called metaphorical—because metaphor encompasses all figures and tropes—although it is in reality literal, genuine, and proper, since it is primarily and immediately intended and expressed by the author, is nevertheless sometimes called by the Fathers spiritual, mystical, allegorical, or symbolic, because it is not taken from the proper signification of the words, but from their figuratively and metaphorically transferred signification (Chrysostom, *Homily 30 on John*; Ambrose, Book V on Luke, the chapter on the sending of the disciples; Gregory, *Moralia* IV, [Col. 0724C] chapters 1 and 2).

Hence the Fathers teach that, where the letter fails, one must have recourse to the mystery. By “letter” they understand the literal and proper meaning; by “mystery,” or mystical meaning, the literal, figurative, and tropological meaning—as though they were saying that the words of Scripture are to be understood figuratively and tropically when they cannot be understood properly and simply. This is especially relevant to the clarification of this chapter. For in this way the abbot here takes the spiritual meaning, which he calls allegorical interpretation, first in the words: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke XII), etc. For according to the letter and the Savior’s intention, this is not properly understood of bodily loins, but of the loins of the mind; and likewise the lamps mean spiritual lamps, that is, virtues and examples of good works.

Similarly, “Whoever does not take up his cross daily,” etc. (Matthew X), is not understood literally of a material or wooden cross, as those simple monks understood it, but of a spiritual [Col. 0724D] and inward cross, that is, the mortification of the affections and the preparation of the soul—or its ready willingness—to undergo death and every affliction for Christ’s name and God’s glory. Likewise, “There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew XIX), is not understood of bodily castration, as Origen and others foolishly understood it, but of the spiritual kind, which is accomplished through a vow of perpetual continence.

Thus in such statements there is indeed a literal meaning, but it is not proper; it is figurative. The statement cited here in second place, “Whoever has no sword, let him sell his tunic and buy a sword” (Luke II), admits of a varied and manifold interpretation—not only spiritual, allegorical, or figurative, as the Author seems to suggest, but also literal and proper, as may be seen in the commentators (see the Golden Chain of St. Thomas and John Maldonatus).

Finally, Sacred Scripture sometimes [Col. 0725A] has several meanings under the same words, even literal and genuine ones. This is what Abbot Serenus finally teaches in this chapter, producing several passages of Scripture, both in this chapter and in the next: passages which, as he says, “are suitably, indeed necessarily, understood in both ways,” that is, both historically and allegorically. St. Thomas suggests the reason from St. Augustine, writing as follows [Col. 0725B] (*Summa Theologiae* I, question 1, article 10): “Since the literal meaning is that which the author intends—and the author of Sacred Scripture is God, who comprehends all things simultaneously in his intellect—it is not inappropriate,” as Augustine says in *Confessions* XII, chapter 31, “that even according to the literal meaning several meanings should exist in one passage of Scripture.” The same Augustine suggests another reason in Book III of *On Christian Doctrine*: “For what more abundantly and richly could have been divinely provided in the divine utterances than that the same words should be understood in several ways?” Here Augustine indicates that it belongs to the richness and fruitfulness, and therefore to the dignity, of Sacred Scripture that several meanings should be contained and concealed in the same words.

As for the passages of Scripture produced here, the first—“If anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also”—may be understood literally, as the words sound; but then it will not be a command, but advice: namely, that we offer the other cheek to one who strikes one of them, [Col. 0725C] for our humiliation and mortification, without any other cause requiring this of us. For if it were a command to be observed literally, Christ and the Apostle Paul (John XVIII; Acts XXIII) would certainly have observed it word for word. They did not, but, after being struck severely, answered those who struck them.

If, however, it is understood as a command, it must be understood as referring to the preparation or readiness of the mind, as St. Augustine teaches in Book II of *On the Sermon on the Mount*, chapter 36: we must always be mentally prepared to endure and forgive an injury rather than inflict or avenge one. Thus the things the Lord commands—offering the cheek, surrendering one’s cloak, going two miles—are stated hyperbolically, signifying only that everything should be endured rather than that vengeance or retaliation should be sought, in the manner we have explained elsewhere (*Institutes* VIII, treatise on Anger).

The second passage cited—“When they persecute you in this city, flee into [Col. 0725D] another”—apart from the literal and customary sense presented by the words, and about which St. Augustine speaks at length in letter 180, receives from Hilary another allegorical or figurative exposition in these words (*Canon 10 on Matthew*): “He urges flight from one place to another, because his preaching, first driven out of Judea, passes over to Greece; then, wearied by the sufferings of the apostles throughout the cities of Greece, it remains finally among all the nations.”] [Col. 0725A] some shine forth in the clear and evident signification of the letter, so that they require no higher interpretation, but, by the simple sound of the letter alone, abundantly feed and nourish their hearers, as in: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deuteronomy VI); and, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength” (ibid.).

Other things, unless they are refined through allegorical explanation and softened by the testing of spiritual fire, cannot in any way reach the nourishing food of the inner person without causing corruption; from their apprehension, injury rather than any benefit will follow. Such are: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke XII); and, “Whoever has no sword, let him sell his tunic and buy himself a sword” (Luke XXI); and, “Whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me” (Matthew X).

Certain of the strictest monks, who indeed possessed zeal for God but not according to knowledge, understood these words simply [Note: [Col. 0725D] It is remarkable that no memory of this matter survives in other writers earlier than Cassian, at least among those whom I have had the opportunity to consult. Nor is there any such account in Cardinal Baronius, a highly careful writer and critic of antiquities, throughout at least the first six or seven centuries, during which the event would have had to occur for Cassian to report it, since he did not reach the sixth century. Nevertheless, no one should regard it as doubtful or incredible, since it is established that those ancient monks, clinging too closely to the words of Scripture, fell through simplicity or ignorance into many other similar and more serious errors, several of which can be observed in Cassian (see *Conference* I, chapter 20): concerning footwear, as though forbidden by divine command, *Institutes* I, chapter 10; concerning permissible and praiseworthy lying, Book V, chapter 37, and *Conference* 17, chapter 8; concerning assigning human form and limbs to God, *Conference* 10, chapter 2 and following; concerning tempting God and voluntary self-killing, *Conference* 2, chapters 5 and 6; concerning self-castration or self-circumcision, *Conference* 2, chapter 8; concerning good will anticipating God’s grace, *Conference* 13, chapter 9 and following; concerning the observance of Lent, *Conference* 21, chapter 29, etc.

Indeed, St. Chrysostom, in a certain homily (*Homily on the Adoration of the Cross*, volume I), seems to have hinted at and incidentally refuted the same error of certain monks or others concerning the carrying of material and wooden crosses. In discussing Christ’s words (Matthew X; Luke IX), by which he commanded everyone to take up his cross, he teaches that they are to be understood not of a material but of a spiritual cross: “What does this word mean?” he asks. “That each of us should carry a piece of wood? Certainly not. For were all the martyrs who followed the Lord crucified with the Lord? Were all the virgins who, according to the Apocalypse, follow the Lamb of God crucified in order to follow him? Was the Apostle Paul crucified when he said, ‘Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world’” (Galatians VI; see Gretser, Book IV, *On the Holy Cross*, chapter 1)?

He says this so that you may understand that the cross is not a wooden instrument of execution, but the resolve of a life of virtue. Thus St. Chrysostom.

Nevertheless, lest that simplicity appear wholly to be condemned or despised when it proceeds from a devout zeal to imitate Christ and obey his commandments, since the Apostle says, “The foolishness of God is wiser than men,” and “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise” (1 Corinthians I), it will be worthwhile to record here the singular and memorable example of Nicholas the Pilgrim, a holy man and *staurophoros*, that is, a cross-bearer, concerning whom Peter of Equilinus relates as follows (*Catalogue of the Saints* V, chapter 78): [ [Col. 0726D] Matthew Raderus reports the same story in his book *On Simplicity*, final chapter.]

Nicholas, surnamed the Pilgrim, a confessor and by birth a Greek, flourished in the time of Pope Urban II. In his youthful years he led an angelic life in the monastery of St. Luke, situated in the regions of Scyros in Greece. When he had carefully heard the Lord’s commandments, which order us to take up the cross and follow the Lord, he seized not merely a spiritual but a bodily cross in his hands, left the monastery, and began to travel as a pilgrim so that he might follow Christ more freely.

Coming to Hydruntum, a city of Apulia, and staying there for some time, he went to Tarentum, where, after displaying certain miracles, he was held in reverence by the people. From there he came to the city of Trani. There, carrying a cross in his hands according to his custom, he gathered a multitude of boys. Going around the sacred places of the city with them, he never ceased crying, “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”), and urged the boys who followed him to cry out in the same way. To induce them to come to him every day and repeat this daily, he attracted the little boys with apples and fruits given to him.

Some citizens considered him insane, while others thought more highly of him and presumed in him the simplicity of a dove. For he wore very poor rags, walked barefoot, prayed without interruption, took no food each day before evening, and always ate only a little bread and drank water.

When his reputation reached the archbishop of Byzantium, the archbishop summoned him and asked why he went around the city crying out such things. The holy man immediately cited the Lord’s commandment concerning taking up the cross, which he had resolved to carry daily not only in spirit but in body. If the bishop denied him this in his diocese, he said, he would at once hasten to another town.

The prudent prelate, considering the holy confessor’s upright intention and dove-like simplicity, did not wish to forbid him from fulfilling his purpose; indeed, he asked him to come daily to his table to be refreshed. When Nicholas obeyed the archbishop’s instructions and traversed the city according to his custom, crying “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”) and carrying the cross with the boys, after a few days he was seized by fever and was nursed with the greatest devotion in the home of a certain noble citizen.

When he came to his final moments, he summoned his boys, handed his cross to them, and blessed them in the name of the Lord. Thus he surrendered his spirit to the Lord in peace, on the fourth day before the Nones of June. Immediately, the citizens flocked together to him unanimously, carried him to the church of Blessed Mary, and all, rushing forward in rivalry, reverently kissed his feet. Thus the body of Nicholas the Pilgrim was honorably buried by the archbishop and the people in that same church, where it shines forth through many signs. This is Peter of Equilinus, who also records several miracles performed through contact with the body. Baronius mentions the same Nicholas of Trani in volume eleven of his *Annals* (A.D. 1094, at the end).] [Col. 0726D] made wooden crosses for themselves and continually carried them around their shoulders. They brought not edification but laughter to everyone who saw them. [Col. 0727A]

Other things are so suitably and necessarily understood in both ways—that is, both historically and allegorically—that each explanation supplies the soul with life-giving nourishment. Such is: “If anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also” (Matthew V); and, “When they persecute you in this city, flee into another” (Matthew X); and, “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me” (Matthew X).

Scripture also produces hay for beasts, with which all its fields are filled: namely, the simple and pure narrative of historical reading. Through this, those who are simpler and less capable of perfect and complete reasoning—and to whom it is said, “You will save both human beings and beasts, O Lord” (Psalm XXXV)—are, according to the condition of their state and measure, made more vigorous and stronger for the work and labor of their present life. [Col. 0727B]

## CHAPTER IV  
### On the Twofold Meaning Concerning the Understanding of the Holy Scriptures

[Col. 0728A]

Therefore, concerning those things that have been brought forth with open explanation, we too may confidently define and boldly express our judgment. But those things that the divine Spirit inserted into the Holy Scriptures, reserving them for our meditation and exercise, wishing them to be gathered from certain indications and opinions, must be compared carefully and gradually, so that their assertion or confirmation may remain within the judgment of the person discussing or receiving them.

For sometimes, when different opinions are advanced concerning one matter, both may be judged reasonable and accepted either firmly or provisionally, that is, in such a way that neither full belief nor absolute rejection is assigned to them. The later opinion should not derogate from the earlier, since neither is found to conflict with the faith. An example is the statement [Note: [Col. 0727D] Among the questions about which one may doubt without endangering the faith, and follow either side without harm to the faith or derogation of the other side, he sets down two examples from Scripture: one concerning Elijah, the other concerning the abomination of desolation, which is discussed both in Daniel and in the Gospels.

As for Elijah, he seems to make the question problematic: whether the prophet Elijah is to come before the second advent of the Lord. God indeed promised that he would come, Malachi IV: “Behold, I send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes, and he will turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers.” But Christ seems to explain this passage of John the Baptist, and to identify him as the Elijah who was to be expected according to that prophecy. Therefore Elijah has already come in John, as is said here, and is not to come again or be expected. Thus, speaking of John the Baptist, Matthew XI says: “He is Elijah who is to come.” Again, and more explicitly, in Matthew XVII, when the disciples asked, “Why then do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?” he answered them: “Elijah indeed will come, and will restore all things; but I tell you that Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him,” etc.

From this answer it may reasonably be questioned of which Elijah the Lord is speaking: the true Elijah the Tishbite, who is believed to come before Christ’s second advent, or the mystical Elijah, that is, John the Baptist, the Lord’s forerunner, who is called Elijah in spirit because he came in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke I), before the Lord’s first advent. Jansenius admits (*Harmony of the Gospels*, chapter 77) that it may be understood of both.

Nevertheless, although there is some ambiguity in the Lord’s words, it was the constant judgment of the orthodox Fathers, and therefore the common opinion of Christians, that the prophet Elijah of whom the Fourth Book of Kings speaks will truly come before the day of judgment and Christ’s second advent. This is gathered from Scripture so clearly and plainly that it is not permissible to hold another opinion or call it into question without rashness.

First, it is evident that Malachi is speaking of the second advent when he says, “Before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes,” just as Joel II says: “The sun shall be turned into darkness before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes.” Hence all the Fathers commonly interpret Malachi’s words of the true Elijah and of the Lord’s second advent (Chrysostom, *Homily 4 on the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians*; Jerome on Matthew XVII; Augustine, *Tractate 4 on John*; Gregory, *Moralia* IX, chapter 4).

Second, the author of Ecclesiasticus, chapter XLVIII, writing about this Elijah and alluding to Malachi’s testimony, finally adds after other things: “Who is written in the judgments of the times, to calm the wrath of God, to reconcile the heart of the father to the son, and to restore the tribes of Jacob.”

Third, Christ says that Elijah will come in the future and restore all things, which cannot be understood of John. When he later says that Elijah has already come, he sufficiently shows that he is not speaking of the Elijah whom he had said would come, but of John the Baptist, who had already come in the spirit and power of Elijah. For the remaining arguments, see the commentators.] that Elijah came in John and will again come before Christ’s advent (Matthew XI); and [Note: [Col. 0728D] The other question that this abbot likewise places among matters that are problematic and probable on both sides seems to be, insofar as his words can be gathered, whether the abomination of desolation predicted by Daniel was fulfilled under King Antiochus, called Epiphanes; or under the emperor Titus, in the devastation of Jerusalem that followed Christ’s death immediately; or, finally, whether it is to be fulfilled under the persecution of Antichrist—or what precisely that abomination of desolation is. On this matter, see the various opinions in Jansenius, Maldonatus, and other commentators.] concerning the abomination of desolation: whether it stood in the holy place through the statue of Jupiter that we read was set up in the temple at Jerusalem, and whether it is again to stand in the Church through the advent of Antichrist (Daniel IX); and that all the things that follow in the Gospel (Matthew XXIV) are understood as having been fulfilled before the captivity of Jerusalem and as destined to be fulfilled at the end of this world. Of these opinions, neither attacks the other, nor does the later understanding nullify the earlier. [Col. 0729A]

## CHAPTER V  
### That the Proposed Question Should Be Accepted among Matters to Be Held Provisionally

And therefore, although the question you have proposed does not seem to have been sufficiently or frequently debated among people, nor to be open to the majority, and for this very reason what we shall put forward may perhaps seem ambiguous to some, we ought to temper our judgment in such a way that, since it prejudices nothing concerning the faith of the Trinity, it may be counted among those matters to be held provisionally. Yet this should not be an opinion gathered merely from suspicions and conjectures, but everything must be confirmed by clear testimonies of Scripture. [Col. 0730A]

## CHAPTER VI  
### That Nothing Evil Was Created by God

[Note: [Col. 0729B] St. Augustine often insists on this: that there is no evil nature, that is, no creature substantially evil, but that all things are good. All the authors of our religion agree with him, and they commonly execrate Marcion, Mani, and the other ancient heretics who invented two principles, as though there were two gods: one good, the author of good things; the other evil, the author of evils.]

Therefore, far be it from us to confess that God created anything that is substantially evil, since Scripture says: “Everything that God made is very good” (Genesis I). [Note: [Col. 0729C] These—the principalities and powers evil by their own nature—that is, the spirits concerning whose beginning, nature, condition, and fall the following question was proposed above (chapter 2): “Whence has such diversity of wicked spirits arisen? Is it to be believed that the Lord created those powers for this purpose, so that they might wage war against humanity under these ranks and orders?”

He answers that question first in this chapter, from the certain definition of faith and the authority of Scripture: all angels, or spirits, were created by God good, not evil; and they were not created for an evil end, namely, so that they would always persist in wickedness or urge human beings to sin. For God is not the author of evils, but everything he made is very good (Genesis I).

Moreover, it is confirmed by the authority of Scripture and the judgment of the holy Fathers that not only the blessed angels but also the demons were created in sanctifying grace—that is, grace that makes one pleasing to God. Scripture indicates this in Isaiah XIV: “How you have fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, who rose at dawn!” And in Ezekiel XVIII: “You were perfect from the day of your creation.” And again: “You were full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God.”

The Fathers confirm the same. St. Anthony, in Athanasius, says: “We must first fix this in our minds: God made nothing that is evil, nor did the beginnings of demons originate from his creation; that perversity is a fault of the will, not of nature. For, being good, since they were created by God, they fell from heaven to earth by their own free choice of mind, and there, in the filth of mire, they established impious forms of worship according to the will of the pagans, and they do not cease to stir up every evil, lest we take their former dwellings.”

St. Jerome, commenting on Hosea II, writes that the demons were created in great abundance of the Holy Spirit. St. Augustine, Book XII of *The City of God*, chapter 9: “We must beware,” he says, “lest the good will of the good angels be believed to be uncreated and co-eternal with God. For since they themselves were created, how can it be said that their will was not created? But since it was created, was it created together with them, or did they exist previously without it? If it was created together with them, there is no doubt that it was made by the one by whom they too were made; and as soon as they were made, they clung to the one by whom they were made, with the love with which they were made. Thus these were separated from the fellowship of the others because they remained in that same good will, while the others were changed by falling away from it—by an evil will, precisely in that they fell away from the good from which they would not have fallen had they truly willed otherwise.”] [Col. 0730C]

For if such beings were created by God, or made for this purpose—that they should occupy these ranks of wickedness and always be occupied with the deception and ruin of human beings—then, contrary to the sentence of the Scripture cited above, we would defame God as the creator and inventor of evils, as though he himself had created the worst wills and natures, creating them for this purpose: that, always persisting in wickedness, they could never pass over into the disposition of a good will.

This, then, is the explanation of this diversity that we have received through the tradition of the Fathers from the fountain of the Holy Scriptures.

## CHAPTER VII  
### On the Beginning of the Principalities, or Powers
[Note: [Col. 0730C] Besides this abbot, other distinguished authors, and almost all the Greeks, have also thought that the angels were created before this corporeal world. Hence St. Thomas (I, q. 61, art. 3) says that this is the opinion of the Greek doctors. Gregory Nazianzen, in Oration 42, says that God first conceived the angels and the heavenly powers, and that they were the work of his thought. Basil, Homily 1 on the Hexaemeron, says that spiritual and invisible natures, endowed above all with the power of reason, existed before the world. Damascene, in Book II, chapter 3 of *The Orthodox Faith*, commends the opinion of Gregory Nazianzen and professes to follow it. Among the Latins, St. Ambrose appears to hold the same view in Book I, chapter 5 of the *Hexaemeron*: “The angels,” he says, “dominions, and powers, although they began at some point, nevertheless already existed when this world was made.” St. Jerome, on chapter 1 of the Epistle to Titus, says: “Six thousand years of our time have not yet been completed, and what periods, and what beginnings of ages, must we suppose there were, during which the angels, thrones, dominions, and the other orders served God!” Finally, Isidore, Book I, chapter 12 of *The Highest Good*: “Before every creature of the world, the angels were created.” St. Augustine, however, in Book XI, chapter 33 of *The City of God*, leaves this question in the middle as doubtful and problematic: “Let no one doubt, nevertheless, that the holy angels in the exalted dwellings of heaven are not indeed coeternal with God, but are secure and certain of their own everlasting and true happiness.” Nevertheless, the opinion of the other Fathers, commonly received by theologians, is considered much more probable—indeed, almost certain—namely, that the angels were created on the first day together with heaven and earth (*Book I of the Decretals*, chapter *Firmiter*, title “On the Supreme Trinity and the Catholic Faith”). First, this is proved by the authority of Scripture. Genesis 1: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” (For this would not be true if he had created anything beforehand, says St. Thomas.) Likewise Exodus 20: “In six days the Lord made heaven and earth, and the sea, and all that is in them, and he rested on the seventh day.” Second, by the authority of the Lateran Council, where it is said: “From the beginning of time God created both creatures out of nothing, the spiritual and the corporeal, namely, the angelic and the earthly.” Third, by the authority of the Fathers who taught this: Epiphanius, Heresy 65; Augustine, Book XI, chapter 9 of *The City of God*; Theodoret, Question 3 on Genesis; Gregory, Book XXXII, chapter 10 of the *Moralia* (see Sixtus of Siena, Book V of the *Bibliotheca*, annotation 5). Although these authorities firmly confirm this opinion and render it more than probable, St. Thomas nevertheless piously and wisely warns that the contrary is not to be considered erroneous. “Especially,” he says, “because of the opinion of Gregory Nazianzen, whose authority in Christian teaching is so great that no one has ever dared to bring a charge against his statements, just as no one has against the teachings of Athanasius, as Jerome says.”]

No believer doubts that before the creation of this visible creature God made the spiritual and heavenly powers, which, precisely because they knew that they had been brought forth from nothing by the Creator’s gift for such a glorious happiness, continually gave him thanks and clung without ceasing to his praises. [Note: [Col. 0731C] Indeed, with due reverence for this abbot, we ought to hold that the angels are called God’s first work not because they existed before the constitution of this world, but because they were created on the first day together with heaven and in heaven, as befitted their dignity, as the noblest parts and creatures of the entire universe, just as the holy Fathers cited above held and proved.]

Nor should we suppose that God first began the origins of his creation and workmanship with the constitution of this world, as though during those preceding and innumerable ages he had been idle, without any providence or administration, and as though he were believed to have been solitary and deprived of every act of generosity because he had no one toward whom to exercise the benefits of his goodness. To think this of that immense, unoriginated, and incomprehensible majesty is altogether low and unfitting. The Lord himself says of those powers: [Note: [Col. 0731C] Thus indeed the Seventy Translators render the passage, and in this way Epiphanius and Augustine also cite it above; from this they likewise infer and prove that the angels were created on the first day. The Vulgate reading, however, is: “When the morning stars praised me together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy” (Job 38). From this it can only be inferred that the angels were created before humanity; on that point there is no controversy. Certainly St. Gregory, in Book XXVIII, chapter 14 of the *Moralia*, says that the angels are called “morning stars” because they were created at the very dawn of the first day.]

“When the stars were made together, all my angels praised me with a loud voice” (Job 38). [Note: [Col. 0731D] Epiphanius and Theodoret answer that the stars were created on the fourth day, as Scripture teaches. Therefore the angels, who had been created on the first day, could have been present at the creation of the stars and praise God in it.]

Those, therefore, who were present at the creation of the stars are most clearly shown to have been created before that beginning in which heaven and earth are said to have been made, since they are reported to have praised the Creator with a loud voice and in wonder on account of all those visible creatures, which they saw proceeding from nothing. [Note: [Col. 0731D] That first sentence of the Book of Genesis—“In the beginning God created heaven and earth”—is expounded in three ways, as St. Thomas teaches (I, q. 46, art. 3), in order to exclude three errors. Some held that the world had always existed and that time had no beginning; to exclude this, “In the beginning” is understood as “at the beginning of time.” Others held that there were two principles of creation, one of good things and another of evil things; to exclude this, “In the beginning” is understood as “in the Son.” For just as the effective principle is appropriated to the Father because of power, so the exemplary principle is appropriated to the Son because of wisdom (see Augustine, Book XII, chapter 23 of the *Confessions*). Others said that corporeal things were created by God through the mediation of spiritual creatures; to exclude this, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” is understood as “before all things.” For four things are posited as created together: the empyrean heaven, corporeal matter, understood by the name “earth,” time, and the angelic nature. Thus St. Thomas.]

Before, therefore, that temporal beginning which Moses sets forth and which, according to the historical—or rather Jewish—sense, signifies the age of this world (without prejudice, of course, to our interpretation by which we understand Christ to be the beginning of all things, in whom the Father created everything, according to the words of John 1: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made”), before that temporal beginning of Genesis, there is no doubt that God created all those heavenly powers and virtues. The Apostle, enumerating them in order, describes them as follows: [Note: [Col. 0732B] Far be it from us to suppose that during those earlier and innumerable ages—if one may speak in such terms—which preceded the world, God was idle, solitary, or deprived of every act of generosity throughout all eternity. We acknowledge in God eternal actions, which theologians call immanent—that is, remaining within God—and internal actions, which God contemplated, considered, and exercised within himself before the constitution of the world: for example, the eternal contemplation of his own divinity, attributes, and perfections; the eternal generation of the Son by the Father; the eternal procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son; the eternal counsel and decree concerning the creation and governance of the world, the incarnation and economy of the Son, the election and reprobation of angels and human beings, and everything pertaining to divine Providence. Occupied with these before the constitution of the world—if it is permissible to speak in this way—God certainly could not be called idle, solitary, or ungenerous. For the supreme generosity of the eternal Father was to communicate his essence to the Son and then, together with the Son, to communicate that same essence to the Holy Spirit, so that God would always be one in essence and three in persons. If this argument had any force, it would certainly conclude not merely that the angels preceded and were older than this world, but also that they were coeternal with God, lest we be forced to admit that God had been idle or solitary during the earlier and innumerable ages of eternity. Here, however, the Wise Man’s warning applies: “He who is a searcher of majesty will be overwhelmed by glory”; and the Apostle’s: “Do not be high-minded, but fear,” and, “Do not be wiser than you ought to be, but be wise unto sobriety” (Proverbs 25; Romans 12). For “who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” Nevertheless, it is worthwhile here to hear St. Augustine discussing this or a similar question, at greater length but very appropriately for clarifying this passage, in Book XI, chapter 12 of the *Confessions*: “Behold,” he says, “I answer the one who says: What was God doing before he made heaven and earth? I answer not with what someone is reported to have said in jest, evading the force of the question: ‘He was preparing hell for those who pry into mysteries.’ It is one thing to see, another to laugh. I do not answer that. I would rather answer, ‘I do not know,’ because I do not know, than with that answer which mocks the one who asked lofty questions and praises the one who gave a false reply. But I say to you, our God, creator of every creature: If by the name of heaven and earth every creature is understood, I boldly say that before God made heaven and earth, he was not making anything; for if he was making something, what was he making except a creature? And would that I knew everything I desire usefully to know in the same way that I know that he was making no creature before any creature was made! Or if some winged imagination wanders through images of past times and wonders that you, almighty, all-creating, all-sustaining God, the maker of heaven and earth, ceased from so great a work for innumerable ages before you made it—let it awaken and attend, for it wonders at what is false. For how could innumerable ages have passed which you had not made, since you are the author and creator of all ages? Or what times could there have been which were not created by you? Or how could they have passed if they had never existed? Since, therefore, you are the maker of all times, if there was any time before you made heaven and earth, why is it said that you were resting from your work? For you had made that very time; nor could times pass before you had made times. But if there was no time before heaven and earth, why ask what you were doing then? For there was no ‘then’ where there was no time; nor do you precede times in time, since otherwise you would not precede all times. You precede, rather, all past times by the height of your ever-present eternity, and surpass all future times because they are still future, and when they have come they will be past. But you are always the same, and your years shall not fail” (Psalm 101). “Your years neither go nor come.” Thus far St. Augustine, followed by what comes next. Two points in this passage deserve particular notice: first, that before heaven and earth God made absolutely nothing, yet was not idle, because it is one thing to make, which is to produce an external work, and another to act through an immanent action, as explained above; second, that before the creation of heaven and earth no age had passed, if “age” is taken properly, since it is a part or some span of time, and no time existed before the world. It is therefore inappropriate and foolish to ask what God was doing then—that is, during those earlier ages—and so forth.]

“For in Christ all things were created, those in heaven and those on earth, visible and invisible, whether angels or archangels, thrones or dominions, principalities or powers; all things were created through him and in him” (Colossians 1).

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Fall of the Devil and the Angels

[Note: [Col. 0733C] That is, concerning the entire multitude of angels or heavenly spirits, whose several orders the Apostle listed shortly beforehand; and concerning some of the principal ones—that is, those of the order of the principalities, or of the first orders of angels. For understanding this matter, it must first be noted that the holy Fathers, especially Dionysius the Areopagite and Gregory the Great (Dionysius, *Celestial Hierarchy*, chapter 6; Gregory, Homily 34 on the Gospels), distinguish three hierarchies of angels or spirits, and place three orders or choirs in each hierarchy. In each case the first order is the highest, the second intermediate, and the third lowest. In the first hierarchy, which is nearest to God, are the seraphim, cherubim, and thrones; in the second, dominions, virtues, and powers; in the third, principalities, archangels, and angels. St. Thomas discusses these extensively in the First Part, Question 108. Second, concerning the fall of the first angel, which is chiefly at issue here, there are two opinions. One is that of Damascene (Book II, chapter 3): the first angel to sin, who also caused the others to sin, belonged to the lowest hierarchy of angels and the lowest order of spirits. The other is that of St. Gregory, which the other Fathers and theologians commonly follow: the first fallen angel, represented by the name Lucifer, was the highest of the highest hierarchy and the first among the angels. St. Thomas expresses the same view in other words, saying that the highest angel among those who sinned was the highest among all angels. Elsewhere we have confirmed this opinion, following St. Gregory, with many arguments (Book XII of the *Institutes*, chapter 4), which it is worthwhile briefly to repeat here. Third, from this same opinion it may probably be inferred that some angels fell from every order of each heavenly hierarchy. First, because some human beings are taken from every angelic order for the restoration or completion of the angelic ruin, as St. Anthony teaches in Athanasius, Jerome in Book I, final chapter, on the Lamentations of Jeremiah, Augustine in chapter 29 of the *Enchiridion*, and Gregory in Homily 34 on the Gospels. Second, this further confirms freedom of choice, because in every rational or intellectual creature the will can bend toward evil. Third, we see the devil called a cherub in Ezekiel 28: “You are the anointed cherub who protects.” The Lord in Luke 11 calls Beelzebub the prince of demons, and the Apostle in Ephesians 6 calls demons “principalities and powers.” Also in 1 Corinthians 15: “When he has abolished every principality, power, and virtue.” Why, then, are they not called seraphim or thrones? St. Thomas gives the reason in these words (I, q. 63, art. 9): “In sacred Scripture the names of certain orders, such as seraphim and thrones, are not attributed to demons, because these names are taken from the ardor of charity and from the dwelling of God, which cannot coexist with mortal sin. The names cherubim, powers, and principalities are attributed to them because these names are taken from knowledge and power, which can be common to the good and the wicked.”]

The lamentation of Ezekiel or Isaiah most clearly teaches that some of these principal ones fell—that is, some of the spirits or principalities. Among them we recognize the prince of Tyre, or that Lucifer who rose at dawn, as lamented by them in sorrowful mourning. Concerning him the Lord says to Ezekiel:

[Note: [Col. 0734C] Among the other passages of Scripture that can admit several senses, including literal and proper senses, two are especially famous and commonly cited in this matter concerning the fall of the angels: one from Ezekiel and the other from Isaiah, both cited in this chapter. The passage from Ezekiel is chapter 28, which is understood as referring both to the king of Tyre and to the devil and his pride and fall, under the name and figure of the king of Tyre. The other is Isaiah 14, which the Fathers likewise explain indiscriminately as referring both to the king of Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar, and to Lucifer, the prince of demons. The Holy Spirit intermingled and tempered the speech about both in such a way that some things apply properly and historically, while others apply to the demons and those kings only improperly and figuratively, as St. Jerome noted (on Isaiah 4). As for the first passage, from which our Serenus proves that some principal spirits or principalities fell, defected from God, and were cast into the abyss, Tertullian, Book II, chapter 10 against Marcion; Cyril, Book III, chapter 29 on John; Jerome on Psalm 81; Augustine, Book XI, chapter 15 of *The City of God*; and Gregory, Books XXXIII, chapters 24 and 25 of the *Moralia*, interpret it as referring to the demon and prince of demons. Most interpreters likewise explain the other passage cited here from Isaiah 14—“How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose at dawn,” and so forth—as referring to the prince of demons, that is, the first transgressing angel, whose type was Nebuchadnezzar. St. Jerome admits that many things are said there about Lucifer that can be attributed to the king of Babylon only figuratively and hyperbolically, as the very words sufficiently indicate. This abbot, however, seems to understand Isaiah’s passage as referring to a different demon or prince of demons from the one mentioned above, apparently in order to prove that several among the principal ones—that is, among the higher orders, or from the order of principalities—fell. On this occasion he entitled this comparison “On Principalities or Powers.” But the Fathers unanimously refer both interpretations to one and the same devil, although nothing prevents the passages from being referred or adapted to different demons.]

“Son of man, raise a lamentation over the prince of Tyre, and say to him: Thus says the Lord God: You were the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God. Every precious stone was your covering: sardius, topaz, and jasper, chrysolite, onyx, and beryl, sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald. Gold was the work of your adornment, and your settings were prepared on the day when you were created. You were an outspread, protecting cherub, and I placed you upon God’s holy mountain; you walked in the midst of fiery stones. You were perfect in your ways from the day of your creation, until iniquity was found in you. In the abundance of your commerce your interior was filled with iniquity, and you sinned; and I cast you out from the mountain of God and destroyed you, O protecting cherub, from the midst of the fiery stones. Your heart was lifted up because of your beauty; you corrupted your wisdom because of your splendor. I cast you to the ground; I set you before kings, that they might look upon you. By the multitude of your iniquities and the iniquity of your commerce you profaned your sanctification” (Ezekiel 28).

Isaiah likewise speaks of another:

“How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose at dawn! You have fallen to the earth, you who wounded the nations, who said in your heart: ‘I will ascend into heaven; I will exalt my throne above the stars of God; I will sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High’” (Isaiah 14).

Yet Scripture does not say that they alone fell from that summit of blessed standing. It says [Note: [Col. 0735C] From this opinion St. Thomas infers that the first transgressing angel caused the others to sin—not by force, but by exhorting, persuading, and, as it were, flattering and entangling them with his tail. “The sign of this,” he says, “appears from the fact that all the demons are subjected to that supreme one,” as is evident from the Lord’s words in Matthew 25: “Depart, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.” For the order of divine justice is that whoever consents to another’s suggestion in guilt should be subjected to his power in punishment, according to 2 Peter 2: “By whatever a person is overcome, to that he is enslaved.” From the same opinion it may also be inferred that more angels stood and persevered in the good than defected and fell. For if the dragon—that is, the devil—dragged down only a third part, he therefore left two-thirds intact. This is also confirmed by Elisha’s statement in 2 Kings 6: “Those who are with us are more than those who are with them.” This is explained as referring to the good angels, who are with us to help us, and the evil ones, who oppose us. Thus St. Thomas (in the passage cited above, art. 9). Consistent with this is what is read in the *Lives of the Fathers*, from Rufinus (Book VI, little work 18): When Abba Moses was once being gravely assaulted by fornication, he went and told Abba Isidore. When Isidore had received him into his cell, he said to him, “Look toward the west.” Looking, he saw a multitude of demons, and they were confused and jostling one another as they attacked. Isidore said to him again, “Look toward the east.” He looked and saw an innumerable multitude of angels in glory. Abba Isidore then said: “These are those who have been sent to help us; those who rise in the west are the ones who attack us. Therefore, those who are with us are more numerous than those who are against us.” Giving thanks to God, Abba Moses took courage and returned to his cell.]

that the dragon dragged down with him a third of the stars (Revelation 12). One of the Apostles also says more explicitly that God “has kept the angels who did not preserve their principality but abandoned their dwelling in everlasting bonds under darkness for the judgment of the great day” (Jude, canonical Epistle). Likewise, what is said to us—“But you shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes” (Psalm 81)—what else does it signify than that many princes fell? From these indications [Note: [Col. 0736C] He assigns two causes for the diversity of orders among the demons: one on the basis of nature, or the natural distinction in which they were first created by God; the other on the basis of wickedness, through which some subsequently advance farther than others in evil. St. Thomas acknowledges the first cause (in the same passage); the second rests upon the teaching stated above, according to the opinion of the ancients, that some demons are more wicked and harmful than others (Conference 7, chapter 20).]

the reason for this diversity is gathered as follows: these distinctions of orders, which the opposing powers are said to possess in imitation of the holy and heavenly virtues, they either still retain from the degree of that former order in which each had been created, or, having been cast down from the heavenly realms, they have claimed among themselves, in the opposing realm, grades and titles of orders corresponding to those virtues which remain there, according to the measure of their wickedness in which each grew toward evil.

## CHAPTER IX. Objection: That the Devil’s Fall Began with the Deception of Eve

[Col. 0736B]

Germanus: Until now we had believed that the cause and beginning of the devil’s fall or transgression, by which he was cast down from the angelic station, had been specifically envy, when with jealous cunning he deceived Adam and Eve.

## CHAPTER X. Response Concerning the Beginning of the Devil’s Fall

Serenus: [Note: [Col. 0736C] In explaining this chapter, there seems scarcely any need to add anything to the critique of Dom. Cuychius, in which he has left almost every difficulty arising here explained no less learnedly than fully—especially since elsewhere (Book XII of the *Institutes*, chapter 14) it has been demonstrated sufficiently and more than sufficiently that the devil’s first sin was, and could only have been, pride. From pride there subsequently arose envy, the only vices that can properly befall a spiritual and intellectual creature.]

The reading of Genesis shows that this was not the beginning of his transgression or downfall. Before the deception of those human beings, Genesis believed him already marked with the name of the serpent, saying:

[Note: [Col. 0736D] It is certain that, according to the literal sense, these words are understood of a real serpent; nevertheless, this abbot interprets them here as referring to the devil, just as he subsequently refers the serpent’s curse not to the real serpent but to the devil. The serpent is called wiser, or more cunning, than all the beasts of the earth, not because it possessed the faculty of reason and understanding, as the Jewish Josephus seems to have thought (Book I of the *Antiquities*, chapter 1), but because it is an exceedingly crafty, treacherous, and deceitful animal and, as Diodorus of Tarsus says, an instrument especially suited to deception. It was therefore not without reason that the devil chose and assumed it above the other animals, in order to use it as an instrument for imitating human speech and deceiving the woman. Hence St. Augustine, Book XIV of *The City of God*, says: “The devil chose the serpent in the bodily paradise—where, together with those two human beings, male and female, the other earthly animals also lived, subject and harmless—an animal slippery and mobile in twisting coils, suited to his purpose, through which he might speak. By an angelic presence and a superior nature he subjected it to his spiritual wickedness and, using it as an instrument, spoke to the woman for the purpose of deception.” In Book XI, chapter 27 of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Augustine says that the devil was permitted to tempt through this animal alone so that the woman might understand that a poisonous animal could breathe forth nothing but poison.]

“Now the serpent was wiser—or, as the Hebrew books express it, more cunning—than all the beasts of the earth which the Lord God had made” (Genesis 3).

You understand, therefore, that before that deception of the first human being he had departed from angelic holiness, so that he deserved to be marked not only by the disgrace of this name but also to be preferred to the other beasts of the earth in the deceitfulness of wickedness. For Scripture would not have designated a good angel by such a name, nor would it have said of those who persevere in that blessedness, “The serpent was wiser than all the beasts of the earth.” This designation could in no way be applied to Gabriel or Michael; indeed, it would not suit any good human being. Therefore, most clearly, both the name “serpent” and the comparison with the beasts signify not the dignity of an angel but the disgrace of a transgressor. Finally, the material of envy and seduction by which he was driven to deceive the human being arose from the cause of his earlier fall: he saw that one newly formed from the mud of the earth was being summoned to that glory from which he remembered that he, one of the princes, had fallen. And therefore [Note: [Col. 0737C] See Cuychius’s thirteenth annotation, after the end of the work.]

his earlier fall, by which he fell through pride and by which he also deserved to be called a serpent, was followed by a second fall through envy. This found him still possessing something upright within himself, so that he could even share in a kind of conversation and counsel with the human being. [Note: [Col. 0737C] As stated, this abbot refers the Lord’s sentence by which he cursed the serpent not to the true and natural serpent but to the devil himself, who was speaking in the serpent. This was also the opinion of other Fathers: Augustine, Book XI, chapter 36 of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*; Bede; Rupert; Hugh of St. Victor; and many others in their treatment of that passage of Genesis. Others, however, have thought it more consistent with the narrative of Moses that the serpent’s curse, according to the historical sense, referred to the true serpent, but that according to the mystical sense—though this too was principally intended by God—it should be referred to the devil. The same applies to the narrative of the bronze serpent in Numbers 21, which pertains principally to Christ the Lord, as Christ himself interprets it (John 3), but allegorically; in the literal sense it concerns that bronze serpent which Moses raised in the desert.]

The Lord’s sentence therefore usefully cast him down to the lowest place, so that he would no longer, as before, walk proudly while gazing upon something lofty, but would crawl clinging to the ground and, humbled upon his belly, feed upon earthly vices and works. In this way he would thereafter reveal the hidden enemy and establish between him and the human being useful enmity and salutary discord, so that, while he was avoided as a harmful enemy, he could no longer injure humanity through fraudulent friendships.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Punishment of the One Who Deceives or Is Deceived

[Col. 0738B]

This should especially teach us to avoid evil counsels: although the author of the deception is punished with an appropriate penalty and condemnation, the one who is led astray is not exempt from punishment, even if his punishment is somewhat lighter than that of the one who was the author of the deception. [Note: [Col. 0737D] He identifies three degrees of punishment by which, as we read, the sins of Adam, Eve, and the serpent were differently punished by God. Rupert wrote excellently on this difference as well (Book II of *The Victory of the Word*, chapter 15): “Certainly,” he says, “he did not say to the woman, ‘Cursed are you,’ nor to the man, ‘Cursed are you,’ but only, ‘Cursed is the earth in your work.’ The curse of the earth is nothing other than the manifold and frequent affliction by which human beings are afflicted through various events arising from the earth, which had been seized and made worse. To the serpent alone he said, ‘Cursed are you.’ By this statement a firm and immutable sentence of eternal condemnation is to be understood. For although the wording appears capable of being understood of the living serpent, nevertheless the whole must be understood, and much more fully understood, of the serpent who is the devil. Otherwise, how could what was said to him—‘You shall walk upon your breast’—be regarded as a curse or punishment of a curse, since he had this by nature before the devil used him for the destruction of humanity? More properly, therefore, this was laid upon that ancient serpent as a curse: that he should walk upon his breast and eat earth all his days; that is, that he should seek and devour with insatiable hatred and an impenitent heart only those human beings who are so earthly that they neither desire nor look toward heaven. Thus he was given over to a depraved mind, so that, against his own intention, he would always further and assist God’s purpose concerning the elect while trying to hinder it. This is what it means for him to walk upon his breast. As for the woman and the man, whatever was said to them—including bodily death, which merciful God imposed when he said, ‘For you are dust, and to dust you shall return’—these are the words of one who reproves and desires to save, and who even then hedges the ways of the turned-away human being with thorns, so that at least affliction alone might give understanding to the ear and remind the human being of his condition, so that, humbled, he might be corrected and saved.” Thus Rupert.]

We see this expressed most fully here. Adam, who was deceived—or rather, to speak in the Apostle’s words (1 Timothy 2), who was not deceived but, yielding to the deceived woman, seems to have entered into a fatal consent—was condemned only to the sweat of his face and labor, which was imposed upon him not through his own curse but through the barrenness and curse of the earth. The woman, who had been the persuader in this matter, earned an increase of groans, pains, and sorrow, and was likewise bound under a perpetual yoke of subjection. But the serpent, who was the first instigator of this offense, was punished with an everlasting curse. Therefore we must avoid evil counsels with the greatest care and vigilance, because just as they punish the author, so they neither leave the deceived person free from sin nor exempt from punishment. [Note: [Col. 0738C] St. Augustine most aptly explains how Adam was or was not deceived in these words (Book XIV, chapter 11 of *The City of God*): “Just as Aaron did not consent when induced to make an idol for the erring people, but yielded under constraint; and it is not believable that Solomon thought in error that idols ought to be served, but that he was compelled to those sacrileges by feminine blandishments, so we must believe that Adam, one human being for one woman, husband for wife, did not believe his wife as though she were speaking the truth and was thus deceived into transgressing God’s law, but obeyed through the bond of companionship. For the Apostle did not say without reason, ‘Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived,’ unless because she accepted what the serpent said to her as though it were true, whereas he did not wish to be separated from his one companion or from fellowship in sin. Yet he was no less guilty, for he sinned knowingly and deliberately. Accordingly, the Apostle does not say, ‘He did not sin,’ but, ‘He was not deceived.’ For he plainly shows that Adam himself sinned when he says, ‘Through one man sin entered into the world.’ Those are intended to be understood as deceived who do not think that what they do is sin; but he knew. Otherwise, how would it be true that ‘Adam was not deceived’? Yet, inexperienced in divine severity, he could have been deceived into thinking that the offense would be venial. Thus, in the respect in which the woman was deceived, he was not deceived; but he was mistaken about how the deed he was going to commit ought to be judged, when he would say, ‘The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave me, and I ate.’ Therefore, although both were not deceived in believing, both were captured in sinning and entangled in the devil’s snares.” Thus far Augustine.]

## CHAPTER XII. On the Congestion of Demons and the Restlessness They Continually Exercise in This Air

[Col. 0740A]

[Note: [Col. 0739B] Three paradoxes are contained in this chapter, resting upon that false principle and foundation that demons are corporeal, or—as the scholastics put it—that they possess bodies naturally united to them, whether aerial or of some other subtler substance. We have shown above that this is erroneous and foreign to the truth.

The first paradox: that this lower air is crowded and compressed by the great number and density of demons. This would certainly follow if demons were corporeal, just as we see air thicken and condense from multiplied vapors into clouds. But whoever has learned from true Christian philosophy that angels and [Col. 0739C] demons are, in substance, wholly spiritual, incorporeal, and immaterial understands well enough that, properly speaking, the air cannot be condensed or compressed by them, however innumerable and infinite their multitude may be.

The second paradox: that God has therefore usefully withdrawn them from human sight. If they were corporeal, this could not happen without a miracle—and a perpetual one at that. Yet miracles ought not to be invented or multiplied without necessity or evident reason, as St. Augustine teaches in Book II of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*.

The third: otherwise, if demons flying about in the air were visible and could be seen, human beings would be thrown into intolerable terror and would perish; or at least they would daily become more wicked, corrupted by their continual examples and imitation, etc. This last point concerns the error of those who understood the passage in Genesis (Gen. VI), “The sons of God, seeing the daughters of men, that they were beautiful, took wives for themselves from all those whom they chose,” etc., of angels or spirits rather than of human beings. This will be treated below [Col. 0739D] (Chapters 10 and 21).

Once these errors or paradoxes have been excluded, we must hold as certain what theologians teach with great unanimity: that a vast multitude of demons continually remain and wander in this lower air, for the testing and exercise of human beings, until the day of judgment.

This is gathered first of all from the Apostle’s words in Ephesians VI: “Against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places.” That is, against spiritual wickednesses; “in the heavenly places,” because demons, who are spiritual and utterly wicked, dwell in this turbulent air near us, which is called heaven, as Peter Lombard explains.

Second, the Fathers explicitly teach the same. St. Jerome, commenting on that passage of the Apostle (Book II, distinction 6), says: “This is the opinion of all teachers: that this air, which divides heaven and earth and is called the void, is full of hostile powers.” And in chapter II of the same Epistle he says: “The prince of the power of the air, who is in this air, is understood to be the devil, who now works in the children of unbelief.” This does not mean that the devil and his satellites, who wander through this world and insinuate sins into human beings, can dwell in heaven, from which they fell because of their merits; rather, this air above us is called heaven, in accordance with the Savior’s saying, “Consider the birds of heaven,” etc. For it is clear that the birds do not fly through heaven but through the air, etc.

St. Anthony, as reported by Athanasius, says: “The command of the divine voice is that we guard our souls with unceasing vigilance, because we have enemies trained to overthrow us—namely, demons—against whom, according to the Apostle’s testimony, our struggle is without interruption. For he says: ‘Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers of this world, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.’ [Col. 0740C] A vast multitude of them traverses this air; a troop of enemies runs about not far from us.”

St. Augustine likewise says in Book III, chapter 10, of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis* that “this dark air is, as it were, a prison for demons until the time of judgment.” From this St. Thomas concludes that two places have been assigned to demons: one temporary, namely this dark air, until the day of judgment and the consummation of the age; the other everlasting, namely hell, after the day of judgment. For just as a place in the empyrean heaven has been assigned to the good angels on account of their blessedness, while on account of their ministry and assistance toward us they remain with us in this world, so also a place in hell has been appointed to demons on account of their damnation, while, for the sake of our exercise, they are in this dark air. Some of them, however, are even now in hell, tormenting those whom they have led into evil, just as some good angels are with holy souls in heaven.

Although some demons, having gone out from hell to tempt human beings, are found in the air, they nevertheless suffer the punishments of hell everywhere [Col. 0740D] and carry the fire of Gehenna with them, as the Gloss on the Third Epistle of James maintains. Wherever they go, as Strabo writes in his commentary on chapter III of the Epistle to the Philippians, they carry their punishments with them. Likewise, the glory of the good angels is not diminished because they are sent to help and guard us, since it is written: “Their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V).

Nevertheless, it should not altogether be denied that demons are punished and tormented less here than in hell, since they have here the power to wander through the world and harm human beings—a power they will not possess in hell, especially after the day of judgment. Hence Luke, in chapter VIII, writes that the demons begged Christ not to command them to go into the abyss.]

This air, then, which is spread between heaven and earth, is so crowded with a multitude of spirits. They do not fly through it in repose or idleness; and Providence has most usefully hidden and withdrawn them from human sight. Otherwise, either because of the terror of their assembling or because of the horror of their faces—into whatever forms they transform and change themselves at will whenever they please—human beings would be thrown into intolerable fear and would perish, wholly unable to behold such things with bodily eyes. Or else they would daily become more wicked, corrupted by their continual examples and imitation [Col. 0741A] of them. As a result, a harmful familiarity and pernicious union would arise between human beings and the unclean aerial powers. For the crimes now committed among human beings are concealed either by the barriers of walls, or by distance of place, or by a certain sense of shame. If people continually saw these things openly, they would be incited to an even greater madness of fury, since there would be no moment in which they could see those beings cease from such crimes—beings whom no bodily weariness, ordinary occupation, or concern for daily sustenance ever compels, as it sometimes compels us, even against our will, to desist from undertakings once begun.

## CHAPTER XIII. That the assaults which the angels direct against human beings they also turn against one another

[Col. 0741B]

For it is entirely certain that they also inflict upon one another the assaults with which they attack human beings. They likewise carry on, without ceasing, discord and conflict concerning certain nations which they have taken under their charge through a kind of familiar association in wickedness.

We read that this too was most clearly represented in the vision of the prophet Daniel, when the angel Gabriel said:

“Do not fear, Daniel, for from the first day on which you set your heart to understand and humbled yourself before your God, your words were heard, and I came because of your words. But the prince of the kingdom of the Persians resisted me for twenty-one days; and behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to my aid, and I remained there beside the king of the Persians. Now I have come to teach you what will happen to your people in the latter days” (Dan. X).

[Note: [Col. 0741B] There is an old and widespread question concerning the prince of Persia who, according to Daniel chapter X, is said to have resisted the archangel Gabriel, who was acting on behalf of the Jewish people, for twenty-one days: whether he was a good angel or an evil one, and what kind of contention and disagreement took place between them.

Benedictus Pererius treated this question carefully and at length in Book XII of his *Commentaries on Daniel*. I therefore refer the reader to him for a fuller treatment of the difficulty. For my part, I have thought it sufficient to bring together here a few summary observations explaining the passage.

1. The Fathers almost universally agree that the prince of Persia mentioned here was an angel, not a human being, and the sacred text itself sufficiently indicates this. The question, however, is whether he was a good angel or some demon from the order of principalities or another order.

The present Author—or Cassian, or rather Abbot Serenus, to whom Cassian attributes this conference and discussion—understood him to be an evil angel or evil spirit. Rupert, abbot of Tuitium, also seems to have followed this opinion. In Book IX of *The Victory of the Word* he writes:

“As for these princes of the Persians and Greeks, what kind they are, one of the outstanding teachers, St. Jerome, briefly indicates. ‘These,’ he says, ‘are the princes of whom Paul wrote: “We speak wisdom among the perfect, which none of the princes of this age knew; for if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory”’ (I Cor. II).

“Indeed, even if the authority of this teacher were lacking, a prudent reader would nevertheless have no doubt that those princes are to be understood as evil angels, namely those against whom the good princes had to fight—those who opposed the prayers of holy human beings and the embassy of the holy angels.

“If the devil is called by the Lord the prince of the world as a whole, who would doubt that he is prince over its parts? If the devil is the prince of the whole world, are not the princes of its parts—namely, the princes of the Persians and Greeks—rightly understood as evil powers serving the greater prince, the devil? For the Persians and Greeks were not worshipers of God; rather, they served the creature instead of the Creator. They worshiped not God but a demon in God’s place: the Persians, the sun, which they called Apollo; the Greeks, under the name or pretext of their wisdom, Minerva; and other nations, the monstrous beings of other demons. Each nation worshiped its own particular demon above the rest, while all alike, under the name of Jupiter, worshiped the prince of demons, the prince of the world, the devil, and prostrated themselves before their images to such evil spirits.

“Therefore, those whose gods they were may with still greater propriety be called their princes. Good princes are always in agreement with one another; but the wicked always resist the good, as far as they can, and are always at odds among themselves. There are always quarrels among them, because they are proud.”

Thus far Rupert. At the outset he cites St. Jerome as the author and patron of his opinion. Yet St. Jerome explained that passage of Daniel so ambiguously that nothing certain can be established concerning his view.

For he first says: “It seems to me that this prince of Persia is the angel to whom Persia has been entrusted.” Here he appears to understand a good angel. Afterwards, however, he adds what Rupert reported: “These are the princes of whom Paul speaks in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter II: ‘We speak wisdom among the perfect, which none of the princes of this age knew,’” etc. There the discussion is undoubtedly of evil angels, and Jerome seems to indicate that the prince of Persia belonged to their number.

Rupert himself also raises and answers several objections or difficulties that might be brought against this opinion, as follows:

“From where does an evil angel obtain the power to fight against and resist a good one? From the sins of human beings or peoples.

“Where does this battle between good and evil angels take place? In the field of justice, in the conflict of judgment, with God himself as spectator and judge.

“But how do good and evil angels fight among themselves? The evil angel fights by accusing; the good by defending. To the extent that the evil angel’s accusation is serious and true, the good angel’s defense is slow and weak.

“For example, the evil angel who was present in the kingdom of Assyria, where the ten tribes of Israel were led into captivity, accused them with the greatest force: they had never departed from the sins of Jeroboam; they had always had wicked and ungodly kings; finally, they had sinned obstinately and incorrigibly. Because this accusation was extremely grave, the defense before God of the good angel who had charge of those tribes was ineffective. Therefore those tribes were never freed from captivity.

“Likewise, the evil angel who was present among the Persians and is here called the prince of the kingdom of Persia strongly resisted the liberation of the tribe of Judah from captivity. He did this in four ways.

“First, by inciting and leading the Jews into the gravest crimes, so that before God they would become less worthy of liberation from captivity. Then by dissuading the Jews from returning to their homeland, exaggerating the advantages they certainly possessed in captivity and magnifying the evils and hardships they would suffer on their return, while minimizing the benefits they could hope for in returning home.

“Further, he alienated King Cyrus’s mind from the Jews, so that he would show them no favor when they returned to Judea and would in no way release those who remained with him, persuading him that this would greatly serve the safety, peace, security, and permanence of his empire.

“Moreover, he brought before God the gravest accusation against the Jews, setting forth their crimes, because of which, according to the law of divine justice, they ought in no way to be liberated.

“This was what the evil angel did against the tribe of Judah. His accusation, however, was grave, but not as effective as it had been against the tribes of Israel. Judah too had sinned, but not with the same obstinacy. It had had many kings who either repented, as Manasseh did, or were pious and just and corrected the people, as Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, and Josiah did.

“Therefore Gabriel says: ‘The prince of Persia resisted me.’ What must be supplied is: ‘But he could not resist me altogether,’ because your cause and the nature of your sin gave your prince Michael, who alone is my helper, room in all these matters to defend justly that you ought not to be held in perpetual captivity, since you have not departed from the Lord forever,” etc.]

Thus far what is taken from Rupert. Although it is somewhat lengthy, it seemed necessary for explaining this passage and will hardly be unwelcome to the diligent reader.

2. The second opinion, and one much more probable, is that both the princes of the Persians and of the Greeks named in the passage of Daniel were good angels who had been placed by God over those kingdoms and nations, and that the entire contention and dispute mentioned there between those princes, Gabriel, and Michael occurred among good angels alone.

The chief authorities for this opinion are St. Basil, Book III *Against Eunomius*; Theodoret, on chapter X of Daniel; and Gregory, Book XVII of the *Moralia*, chapter 7. It will be enough for our purpose to hear Gregory, who discusses the matter most appropriately:

“Here I would like to inquire: if perfect peace is maintained in the heights, what is meant by the words spoken to Daniel through the angel: ‘The prince of the kingdom of Persia resisted me for twenty-one days; and behold, Michael came to my aid, and now I shall return to fight against the princes of the kingdom of Persia’? Whom does he call the other princes of the nations, then, except angels who could have resisted him as he departed?

“What sort of peace, therefore, can there be in the heights if even among the angelic spirits a struggle of battle takes place, although they always stand before the sight of Truth? But because particular angelic ministries have been assigned for the governance of particular nations, when the conduct of those under them deserves the assistance of their respective ruling spirits, the spirits who preside over them are said to come against one another.

“The angel who spoke to Daniel is recognized as having been placed over the Jewish captives settled in Persia; Michael, on the other hand, is found to have been appointed over the Jews who remained in the land of Judea. Hence this same angel says to Daniel: ‘No one is my helper except Michael, your prince.’ And again: ‘Michael, one of the chief princes, came to my aid.’

“When he is said not to be present together with him but to come to his aid, it is plainly recognized that he presides over the people who were being held captive in another region.

“What, then, does it mean for the angel to say, ‘I came because of your words, but the prince of Persia resisted me,’ except that he is reporting his own works to those subject to him? It is as though he openly said to Daniel: ‘The merits of your prayers indeed require that your people be freed from the yoke of their captivity; but there is still something in that people that must be purified under Persian rule. Therefore the prince of Persia rightly opposes me in liberating them, although your prayers, together with the tears of those who were left in Judea, assist this liberation.’

“The angel therefore hears the prophet’s prayers, but the prince of Persia resists, because although the life of the righteous petitioner already demands the liberation of the people, the life of that same people still stands in opposition. Since those who had been led into captivity had not yet been fully purified, it was still just that the Persians should rule them.

“It is rightly said that the angels come against one another, because the merits of the nations entrusted to them are opposed to one another. For the exalted spirits who rule those same nations do not fight on behalf of those acting unjustly; rather, they examine their deeds with right judgment. When the guilt or righteousness of each nation is brought before the council of the supreme court, its appointed ruler is said to have prevailed or not prevailed in the contest.

“Yet the victory of all of them is one: the will of their Creator over them. While they always contemplate that will, they never desire what they cannot obtain.

“Job therefore rightly said: ‘He makes peace in the heights’” (Job XXV).

Thus far Gregory.

From this it follows:

3.
