Holy angels are said to disagree and fight with one another when, concerning the conflicting and mutually opposed merits of human beings, they consult divine Wisdom and await its decree, each presenting his own case on behalf of his side. They do not disagree with one another by an absolute act of will; rather, because God’s will and judgment have not yet been revealed to them, they set forth before God the differing merits or demerits of the peoples or persons over whom they preside and ask him for different outcomes.

As soon as God’s will and judgment have been revealed to them, all disagreement among them ceases. In complete harmony they all perceive and desire what they recognize to be consonant with the divine will.

So Pererius explains, and this is gathered from the words of St. Gregory just quoted and declared more accurately by St. Thomas (*First Part*, question 113, article 8).

Thus the prince of Persia—that is, the angel appointed as guardian of that kingdom—is said to have resisted Gabriel for twenty-one days. During all that time Gabriel was offering Daniel’s prayers to God and seeking, with Michael’s support, the liberation of the Jews from Babylonian captivity. The other angel, on the contrary, set forth the impiety, ingratitude, and other reasons and obstacles of the Jewish people by which he dissuaded that freedom and liberation.

For example, he might have argued that the Persians would receive great spiritual benefit from association and intercourse with the people living among them in Persia. The Persians could become proselytes and, through the example and exhortation of the Jews, be led to the religion and worship of the true God; they could be taught good morals and dissuaded from evil ones.

Certainly this reason seems more plausible than the claim that the prince of Persia, as a good angel, would have presented before God the impiety and ingratitude of the Jewish people, etc. That is rather the work of the devil or accuser than of a good angel, whose task is to wish and pray for the good of all and, insofar as it lies within him, to procure and advance everyone’s salvation.]

That prince of the kingdom of Persia must undoubtedly have been an opposing power favoring the Persian nation, which was hostile to the people of God. To obstruct the benefit which he saw was to be supplied by the archangel through the resolution of the question for which the prophet had entreated the Lord, he willingly threw himself in the way, so that the consolation of the saving angel might not reach Daniel more quickly and strengthen the people of God, over whom the archangel Gabriel presided.

[Note: [Col. 0744D] That is, the decision or settlement of the case and dispute concerning the freedom and deliverance of the Jews, over which Gabriel, the Jews’ patron, and the prince of Persia—that is, the angel set over that nation—were contending.]

Yet he says that even then he could not reach him because of the violence of that opposition; and that, unless the archangel Michael had come to his aid—meeting the prince of the kingdom of Persia, inserting and opposing himself in the latter’s struggle, and defending Gabriel against his attack—he would not have arrived to instruct the prophet until after twenty-one [Col. 0744A] days.

A little later the angel says:

“Do you know why I have come to you? And now I shall return to fight against the prince of Persia. When I was departing, the prince of the Greeks appeared, coming. Nevertheless, I shall tell you what is written in the writing of truth. And no one is my helper in all these matters except Michael, your prince” (ibid.).

And again:

“At that time Michael will arise, the great prince who stands for the sons of your people” (Dan. XXI).

We therefore read that another is likewise called the prince of the Greeks. Since he favored the nation subject to him, he evidently seemed to oppose both the people of Israel and the Persian nation. From this it is plainly evident that the opposing powers also exercise against one another the discords, conflicts, and hostilities which, at their instigation, the nations wage among themselves; that they rejoice in the victories of those nations or are tormented by their decline; and that for this reason they cannot remain in agreement among themselves, since each persistently contends in restless rivalry on behalf of those over whom he presides against the ruler of another nation.

## CHAPTER XIV. How it came about that spiritual wickednesses received the names of powers or principalities

We can therefore gather, in addition to the opinions explained above, and for an evident reason, that they are called principalities or powers because either they rule over and preside over different nations, or at least exercise their principalities over inferior spirits and demons [Col. 0745B]—of whom the Gospels also testify, by their own confession, that they are legions (Luke VIII).

They cannot be called dominions unless there are those over whom they exercise the authority of their dominion; nor can they be called powers or principalities unless there are those over whom they claim principality.

We find this also clearly indicated in the Gospel, when the Pharisees blasphemed: “By Beelzebub, the prince of demons, this man casts out demons” (Matt. XII). For we also read that they are called “the rulers of the darkness” (Eph. VI), and another is called “the prince of this world” (John XIV).

Yet the blessed Apostle asserts that these ranks will be abolished in the future, when all things have been subjected to Christ: “When he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father,” he says, “when he has abolished every principality, power, and dominion” (I Cor. XV).

This will happen in no other way than by removing from their authority those over whom, in this age, they are known to exercise powers, dominions, or principalities.

[Note: [Col. 0745B] This does not mean that demons received that principality and power from God; rather, they possess it because of the wickedness and ungodliness of those whom they command and rule, and who subject themselves to them through sin.

Hence St. Augustine, in Sermon 8 *On the Lord’s Words on the Mount*, explaining who the “rulers of the world” are whom the demons rule, says: “To prevent you from understanding wrongly, he explains what the world is whose rulers they are: ‘the rulers of the darkness of this world.’ What is the world? ‘Of this darkness.’ Over whom does he rule? Over his lovers and unbelievers, with whom the world is filled. The Apostle calls these people darkness.” Thus Augustine.

Moreover, since the devil is called by Christ the Lord “the prince of this world” (John XIV), and by the Apostle “the god and prince of this age” (I Cor. II) and “the ruler of this darkness” (Eph. VI), what wonder is it if his evil angelic ministers are called the princes and governors of various kingdoms, as we heard Rupert reason above?

It should also be added that some evil angels fell from every order of angels, as was stated above (Chapter 8). Therefore, just as God appointed good spirits from the order of principalities to preside over kingdoms and provinces, so there is no difficulty in saying that the devil likewise appoints certain beings from the orders of principalities, powers, and dominions to disturb, deceive, and corrupt the nations and peoples subject to different kingdoms and provinces.]

## CHAPTER XV. That the names of the holy and heavenly angelic powers, whether angels or archangels, were not given without reason

[Col. 0746B]

[Note: [Col. 0745D] The ancient manuscripts read: “For since the names of these orders are taken in a good sense,” etc. Ciaconius reads: “For since the names of these same orders belong to the good part,” etc. But this reading of Plantin, which is also supported by the paraphrase of Dionysius, seems both more correct and more common: “There is likewise no doubt that the same names of the orders were not imposed upon the good spirits without reason, and that they are names of offices, merits, or dignities,” etc.

From this paraphrase I conclude that the word *nam* (“for”) does not here have the force of a causal conjunction, but is used in place of *autem*, “but,” or *porro*, “moreover,” or some similar connective particle of distinction. The “good part” of the angels here means the good spirits upon whom these names were imposed because of the offices to which they are assigned by God, or because of their merits—that is, their good acts by which they earned greater glory—or because of the dignities by which they excel over others beneath them.]

For the names of these orders were given to the good part for a reason and cause, and that they are names of offices, merits, or dignities, no one can doubt.

Thus, because of the office of announcing, they are plainly called angels, that is, messengers. [Col. 0747A]

[Note: [Col. 0746C] “Angel” is the name not of a nature but of a ministry, as St. Jerome testifies. Hence Psalm CIII says: “Who makes his angels spirits”—that is, he makes those who are spirits by nature his angels by assigning them the office of announcing.

For the Greek word *angelos* (ἄγγελος), which is represented in Latin declension by *angelus*, is translated in Latin as “messenger,” says St. Augustine (Book XV of *The City of God*, chapter 23), along with Hilary (Book V *On the Trinity*) and Prosper (*Sentences*, 103). St. Gregory likewise says in the passage cited above:

“It should be known that the word ‘angel’ is the name of an office, not of a nature. For those spirits of the heavenly homeland are always spirits, but they cannot always be called angels, because they are angels only when something is announced through them.

“Hence the Psalmist says: ‘Who makes his angels spirits,’ as though he were plainly saying: ‘He makes those whom he always possesses as spirits into angels also, whenever he wishes.’”

Thus far Gregory.

This name is used in two ways: first, as a common designation for all spirits; second, as the proper name of the last and lowest order. Hence St. Thomas says:

“An angel is called a messenger. Therefore all heavenly spirits, insofar as they manifest divine things, are called angels. But the higher angels possess a certain excellence in this manifestation, from which the higher orders receive their names. The lowest order of angels adds no excellence beyond the common manifestation; therefore it is named from simple manifestation. In this way the common name remains proper to the lowest order, as Dionysius says in chapter 5 of the *Celestial Hierarchy*. Or it may be said that the lowest order is specifically called the order of angels because they announce things to us immediately.”]

It is therefore clear that they are called angels, that is, messengers, because of the office of announcing; and the propriety of the name itself shows that archangels are so called because they preside over the angels.

[Note: [Col. 0747B] According to Dionysius, archangels are intermediate between principalities and angels (Dionysius the Areopagite, *Celestial Hierarchy*, chapter 9). What is intermediate, when compared with one extreme, appears to be the other insofar as it participates in the nature of both: thus lukewarm water is cold in relation to hot water, but hot in relation to cold water.

So archangels are called, as it were, “prince-angels,” because in relation to angels they are princes, while in relation to principalities they are angels.

According to Gregory, however, they are called archangels because they rule only over the order of angels, as though they announced great things.

The archangel Michael nevertheless possesses this special distinction: he is called “Archangel” not because he belongs to the order of archangels, but because he is the head and prince of all the angels, raised up in the place of Lucifer. Hence he is also regarded as the protector of the Church of God (Molanus, Book III *On Sacred Images*, chapter 39).]

Dominions are so called because they exercise dominion over certain beings.

[Note: [Col. 0747C] This is the first order of the second hierarchy. Dionysius and Gregory agree on this point, although they assign different explanations for the name.

Dionysius says in chapter 8 of the *Celestial Hierarchy*: “I believe that the holy dominions, in a name full of mystery, signify a higher understanding, free from all servitude and from every kind of subjection, and in no way subjecting itself to any tyrannical dissimilarity,” etc.

Thus Dionysius derives the name from the internal perfection of this order, as stated.

Gregory, however, derives it from its external ministry: “They are called dominions,” he says, “because they also transcend the principalities by the height of their distinction. For to exercise principality is to be first among others; but to exercise dominion is also to possess those who are subject.”

Those angelic hosts, therefore, which excel by marvelous power are called dominions because the other orders are subjected to them in obedience.]

Principalities likewise receive their name because they have those over whom they are princes.

[Note: [Col. 0747D] This is the first order of the third hierarchy, according to Dionysius, though not according to Gregory. Dionysius places the virtues beneath the dominions and above the powers; he places the principalities beneath the powers and above the archangels.

Gregory, however, places the principalities between the dominions and the powers, and the virtues between the powers and the archangels.

He explains the name as follows: “Those are called principalities who preside even over the good spirits of the angels. While they arrange what must be done for those subject to them, they exercise principality over them in carrying out the divine ministries.” For the distinction among the terms dominions, powers, and principalities as applied to angels, see St. Thomas (*Question* 108, article 5, response to objection 3), if desired.]

And they are called seats or thrones because they are so closely joined to God and so domestic and familiar to him that the divine majesty peculiarly rests in them as upon a kind of seat, and in a certain manner reclines more firmly upon them.

[Note: [Col. 0748B] They are also called thrones, and complete the last order of the highest hierarchy. Dionysius says of them in chapter 7 of the *Celestial Hierarchy*:

“By the name of the highest and elevated seats we are taught that they are far removed from every lowly affection toward earthly things and are borne upward toward what is lofty with an inviolable zeal. Being distinguished from all lower things by continual attention and firmly and immovably established with all their powers around him who is truly exalted, they receive the divine advent without the hindrance of any disturbance; and, bearing God through their devotion to his service, they are always open to receive his splendors.”

Gregory, however, says: “Those hosts are called thrones over which almighty God always presides in exercising judgments. Since in Latin we call thrones *seats*, those who are filled with such an abundance of divine grace that the Lord sits in them and through them issues his judgments are called the thrones of God. Hence the Psalmist says: ‘You sit upon the throne, judging righteousness’” (Ps. IX).]

## CHAPTER XVI. On the subjection of demons, which they offer to their own principalities
[Note: [Col. 0748C] That there are certain demons who are higher and others lower has been indicated above (Chapter 8), and two grounds for this inequality and distinction were assigned. The first arises from their nature, which is not equal in all of them: some are more perfect than others, and therefore the lower must necessarily be governed by the higher and be subject to them [Col. 0748D]. The second arises from their malice and wickedness, which requires that a certain order and concord be maintained among them so that they may harm human beings, as the author taught in the preceding Conference (Chapter 9). Nor is this contradicted by the statement that in the underworld there is said to be no order, but everlasting horror (Job 9). There is indeed no order among them directed toward eternal blessedness or contributing anything to it; nevertheless, there is an order of power, which follows from their inequality of nature and which God, supremely good and great, has assigned to them for the exercise of the good and the tormenting of the wicked.]

That unclean spirits are ruled by more wicked powers and are subject to them is taught not only by those testimonies of Scripture that we read recorded in the Gospels as well, in the Lord’s response to the Pharisees’ slander:

> “If I cast out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons” (Matthew 12),

but also by many clear visions and experiences of the saints.

[Note: [Col. 0748D] You have this example in *The Lives of the Fathers*, book 4, chapter 54 of the new edition, and another similar one in book 5, booklet 5, as well as in Saint Gregory, *Dialogues*, book 3, chapter 7.]

For when one of our brothers was traveling in this solitude, and evening was already approaching, he found a certain cave and stopped there,

[Note: [Col. 0748D] That is, the evening office, or prayer, elsewhere called the evening solemnity; concerning it, see the note to book 2 of the *Institutes*, chapter 10. We now call it Vespers, together with Compline.]

wishing to celebrate the evening synaxis there. While he was chanting the psalms according to custom, the time of midnight passed. After the solemnity had ended, he sat down for a little while to refresh his weary body. Suddenly he began to see innumerable throngs of demons converging from every direction. Advancing in infinite density and in a very long procession, some went before their prince and others followed him.

At last the prince himself arrived, taller than all in stature and more terrifying in appearance. After setting up a throne, he sat upon a kind of very lofty tribunal and began carefully to examine the conduct of each one. Those who said that they had not yet been able to outwit their rivals he ordered to be driven from his presence as sluggish and cowardly, with disgrace and insult, reproaching them amid the roar of his fury for having spent so much time and labor in vain. But those who reported that they had deceived the persons entrusted to them, he sent away before all, with the highest praises, amid the rejoicing and applause of everyone, as the most glorious and courageous warriors, for the example of all.

Among these, a particularly wicked spirit arrived more joyfully, as though he were bringing a most splendid triumph. He identified a monk whom he knew very well and asserted that, after besieging him continuously for fifteen years, he had finally prevailed to the extent that he would overthrow him that very night through the ruin of fornication. For he had not only prompted him to commit the crime of sexual violation with a certain consecrated girl, but had also persuaded him to keep her for himself by right of marriage.

When immense joy had arisen among them at this report, the spirit was raised up with the highest praises by the prince of darkness, crowned with great acclamations, and departed.

When dawn came and the whole multitude of demons had vanished from sight, the brother doubted the unclean spirit’s assertion. He was even more angered that, with the deceitfulness habitual to him, the spirit had wished to mock him and brand an innocent brother with the crime of incest. Remembering the Gospel saying that the devil “did not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him; when he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own resources, because he is a liar and its father” (John 8),

[Note: [Col. 0749B] Pelusium was a town on the extreme coast of Egypt; the outermost mouth of the Nile, by which Egypt is bounded off from Asia, was therefore called Pelusium or Pelusiac. The Lord threatens it with a grave outpouring of his indignation in Ezekiel 30. There Saint Jerome writes: “I will pour out my indignation upon Sain,” which we render as Pelusium. It is called the strength of Egypt because it has a very safe harbor and maritime commerce is conducted there to the greatest extent. Hence the poet calls the lentil “Pelusiac,” not because this kind of legume grows there especially, but because it is brought there in great quantities from the Thebaid and all Egypt through the Nile’s gateway. Thus Jerome. That Isidore who was called Pelusiotes was born in this town. Distinguished for holiness and learning, he was a disciple of Saint John Chrysostom and, as stated elsewhere, our Cassian’s fellow student; he was also renowned among Greek ecclesiastical writers and lived in the time of Theodosius the Younger.]

he went to Pelusium, where he knew that the man whom the unclean spirit had claimed to have been overthrown was living. The brother was also very well known to him. When he sought him out, he discovered that on the very night when that most hideous demon had announced his fall to his troop or prince, the monk had abandoned his former monastery, gone to a village, and, after becoming involved with the girl in question, had fallen into a miserable ruin.

## CHAPTER XVII. That two angels always attend each human being

For,

[Note: [Col. 0749C] Among Catholics there is no doubt concerning the good angel. It has always been believed, not only through perpetual tradition but also on the basis of more than probable testimonies of Scripture, that each human being has a good angel as guardian, and that each is entrusted to that angel’s care. This is especially inferred from Matthew 18, where Christ, speaking of little ones, teaches that they must not be offended or despised, because “their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven.” By these words he clearly signified that even individual children, and likewise other human beings, have guardian angels appointed for them by God. Hence Saint Jerome exclaims at that passage: “Great is the dignity of souls, that each one has, from the beginning of its birth, an angel assigned to its protection.” He confirms the same point from another similar passage of Scripture, since in Acts 12, when the girl Rhoda announced that Peter was standing at the door, some thought that it was his angel—plainly from the common persuasion then held concerning angels as guardians of individual human beings.

The second part of the assertion, concerning an evil angel, has a very different and much lesser degree of certainty or probability: namely, that every human being has an evil angel or demon as a constant plotter or assailant. Nevertheless, this was a very ancient tradition, held not only by Christians but also by the Hebrews, as Maldonado notes on that passage of Matthew. The tradition is usually supported by ancient authors from the old book of *The Shepherd*, discussed below, which was once held in great esteem and authority, especially among the Greeks. Such authors include Origen, *Homily 10 on Luke*; Abbot Serenus here; Abbot Chaeremon, *Conference 13*, chapter 12; Gregory of Nyssa, *Life of Moses*; and finally Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book 2, distinction 11. Reason also seems to support them. For it is credible that the devil, the prince of demons, as God’s ape, imitates God in administering his kingdom: just as God assigns an angel to each human being, so the devil assigns a demon to each.

Nevertheless, most reject this opinion: first, because it has no solid foundation in Scripture, or, more precisely, among the Fathers (Ludovicus Vives on book 9 of *The City of God*, chapter 11; Coelius Rhodiginus, *Ancient Readings*, book 2, chapter 3); second, because this book, *The Shepherd*, is listed among the apocrypha not only by Saint Jerome in the *Galeated Prologue* but also by the holy Pope Gelasius; third, because Saint Prosper also censures Cassian under this heading (*Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*), on the ground that he attempted to confirm his opinion by the authority of a book regarded by Catholics as having no authority; and finally, because the opinion seems to favor the pagan error concerning two genii assigned to each person from birth, one good and the other evil. Concerning these, see Alexander of Alexandria, *Genialia*, book 6, chapter 4. See Cuychius’s fourteenth annotation.]

that two angels—that is, a good one and an evil one—are attached to each of us, Scripture testifies. Concerning the good angels, the Savior says:

> “Do not despise one of these little ones; for I tell you that their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18).

There is also the passage:

> “The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him, and he will deliver them” (Psalm 33).

Likewise, in the Acts of the Apostles it is said concerning Peter:

> “It is his angel” (Acts 12).

Concerning both angels, however,

[Note: [Col. 0750C] The author of this book, Hermes—or, as others prefer, Hermas—is believed to have been a disciple of the Apostle Paul (see below, Conference 13, chapter 12, and Conference 21, chapter 29). Concerning him Saint Jerome writes: “Hermas, whom the Apostle Paul mentions when writing to the Romans: ‘Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them.’ They assert that he was the author of the book called *The Shepherd*, which is also publicly read in certain churches of Greece. In truth, it is a useful book, and many ancient writers have used testimonies from it; but among the Latins it is almost unknown.” Thus Jerome. For the authority of this book, see Baronius, volume 2 of the *Annals*, under the year 159; Sixtus of Siena (*Bibliotheca*, book 2); Bellarmine (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*); and others—Pamelius on the *Creed*, Rufinus among the works of Cyprian, Possevinus in the *Sacred Apparatus*, and Saint Antoninus, part 2 of his *History*, title 15, section 7.

For a fuller illumination of this chapter, so that the reader may lack nothing, it seems appropriate to record here the annotation of Peter Maturus of the Society of Jesus, a theologian, on this passage of Cassian, as abridged by Saint Antoninus of Florence. It reads as follows:

“Cassian does not prove from that book alone, *The Shepherd*, that two angels—a good and an evil one—assist each human being, but also from several passages of sacred Scripture. Above all, to establish the assistance of the good angel and our guardian angel, he uses this most certain and truthful saying of Christ in Matthew 18: ‘See,’ he says, ‘that you do not despise one of these little ones; for I tell you that their angels always see the face of my Father.’ Saint Jerome likewise, in his commentary on this passage, concludes from it that an angel has been given to each of us from the beginning of our birth for our protection. Chrysostom does the same in Homily 60 on Matthew and Homily 3 on Colossians. The author of the *Imperfect Work* does the same in Homily 40. Theophylact, Oecumenius, Euthymius, Basil in book 3 *Against Eunomius*, Hilary in Canon 18 on Matthew, and many other ancient writers also use the passage in the same sense. All of them silence that most importunate mouth of Calvin, who, among the other ravings of his impiety, was not ashamed to ridicule this special guardianship of individual angels. Against him, see Fevardentius, book 1 *Against Heresies*, on the angels, heresy 3. Thus far he; from him we shall also draw other noteworthy matters below.”]

the book *The Shepherd* teaches most fully. If we also consider the one who attacked blessed Job, we shall be instructed most clearly that he was the one who was always lying in wait for him, yet had never been able to incite him to sin, and therefore had asked the Lord for power, as one who would be overcome not by Job’s virtue but by the Lord’s protection, since the Lord had always guarded him. Concerning Judas also it is said:

> “And let the devil stand at his right hand” (Psalm 108).

## CHAPTER XVIII. Confirms by the testimony of two philosophers the difference in wickedness found among evil spirits

We have learned much about the differences among demons through those two philosophers who had formerly and frequently experienced, by magical arts, both their weakness and their strength and savage wickedness.

[Note: [Col. 0751D] Saint Athanasius relates this story somewhat differently in his *Life of Antony*, concerning the Antony mentioned here. He says nothing about the demons’ sending and assault, but about demoniacs brought to Antony, whom he cured by impressing the sign of the cross upon their foreheads, while the philosophers watched in wonder, after he had held a lengthy disputation with them.]

For, despising blessed Antony as an unlearned and illiterate man, and wishing—if they could do him no greater harm—at least to disturb him in his cell by magical tricks and the deceptions of demons, they sent the most wicked spirits against him, driven to this attack by envy, because an immense crowd of people came to him daily as to a servant of God.

Sometimes he impressed the sign of the cross upon his breast and forehead; at other times he devoted himself fervently to prayer. The most savage demons did not even dare to approach him, but returned without any result to those who had sent them. The philosophers then sent others still more powerful in wickedness, yet these likewise spent the strength of their wickedness in vain and returned fruitlessly. They were sent again, now more powerful, against the victorious soldier of Christ, but they accomplished absolutely nothing.

Their plots, so numerous and so great, pursued with such magical art, achieved only this: they demonstrated most clearly that great power inheres in the Christian profession, against which such savage and powerful shades,

[Note: [Col. 0751D] We noted above that demons are often called by this name and by other synonyms in both profane and sacred authors (Conference 7, chapter 52). Yet “shades” was also used of the souls of the dead who sometimes appear to the living, as in Virgil:

> “The unhappy phantom, and the shade of Creusa  
> Appeared before his eyes, an image larger than life.”

]

which they believed could have darkened or obscured the sun and moon if directed against them,

[Note: [Col. 0752C] Most read *obducere*, “to cover over”; some, however, read *abducere*, “to lead away.” *Obducere* means “to darken” or “to cover,” or, as Dionysius explained, “to cover with a kind of mist,” just as Cicero wrote in the *Academica*: “To cast darkness over the clearest matters.” But if Cassian wrote *abducere* or *deducere*, rather than *obducere*, he seems to have imitated Virgil, who wrote:

> “By songs they can draw down the moon from heaven.”

For magical arts and incantations are at issue in both places, as Ciaconius correctly observes. Similar is the following passage of the same poet, concerning a woman who possessed power of the same kind:

> “By spells she promises to free the minds  
> Of those she wishes, and to inflict upon others  
> Harsh cares; to halt the water in rivers,  
> And turn the stars backward.”]

had been unable not only to harm him in the slightest but even to disturb him for a moment in his monastery.

## CHAPTER XIX. That demons have no power against human beings unless they have first besieged their minds

Filled with wonder at this, the two philosophers immediately went to Abbot Antony and disclosed the magnitude, causes, and hidden plots of their attacks, then promptly asked to become Christians.

When Antony asked them on what day the attack they had revealed had occurred, he declared that he had then been assaulted by the bitterest goads of thought. By this experience blessed Antony proved and confirmed the opinion that we stated yesterday in the Conference:

[Note: [Col. 0752C] We have indicated elsewhere how this should be understood (Conference 7, chapter 24).]

that demons can in no way invade anyone’s mind or body, nor have the power to rush entirely into anyone’s soul, unless they have first deprived it of all holy thoughts and rendered it empty and bare of spiritual contemplation.

It must nevertheless be understood

[Note: [Col. 0752D] Demons are subjected to human beings in two ways: namely, by divine authority and by diabolical authority. The divine authority—that is, the authority conferred and instituted by God—was given first to all the faithful, but especially to the apostles and disciples of Christ and their successors, the ministers of the Church. For Christ gave them power over unclean spirits, so that they might cast them out (Matthew 10; Mark 3; Luke 9). To the seventy-two disciples he said in Luke 10: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall harm you.” Hence the common exultation of those same disciples over this power and its effect: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name.”

Christ promised this same power not only to the apostles and disciples but to all believers—that is, to the Church generally and collectively—when he was about to ascend into heaven, in these words recorded in Mark 16: “These signs will accompany those who believe: In my name they will cast out demons,” and so forth. This promise concerns all the faithful of Christ—not because such power was communicated to each individual, but because it was communicated to those for whom it was appropriate to use it, whenever and for as long as it might be expedient for promoting God’s glory, for the common benefit of the Church, and for spreading and strengthening the faith.

Such power is of two kinds in the Church: private and public. Private power is bestowed upon certain holy people, as a testimony to their holiness, through a special gift and grace of God, which is called a freely given gift. It is well known that those holy fathers and anchorites, although private individuals—Antony, Hilarion, Paul the Simple, Macarius, and others—were distinguished by this gift. Hence Saint Jerome writes in the *Life of Hilarion*: “Hilarion was hiding on the island of Cyprus. Yet scarcely had twenty full days passed when, throughout the island, all who had unclean spirits began to cry out that Hilarion, the servant of God, had come and that they ought to hasten to him. Salamis, Curium, Lapetha, and the other cities all proclaimed this. Thus, within thirty days, or little more, nearly two hundred men and women gathered around him, all of whom were cured by him.” Thus Jerome.

The other power is public, and belongs only to the ministers of the Church. Among them is the order of exorcists, whose proper duty is to adjure demons and drive them out of bodies that are possessed or obsessed. On this subject Tertullian writes in *To Scapula*, chapter 2: “We do not merely reject demons; we also overcome them, expose them daily, and drive them out of human beings, as is known to very many.” Saint Cyprian writes to Demetrianus, proconsul of Africa: “Oh, if only you were willing to hear and see when they are adjured and tormented by us with spiritual lashes and the tortures of words, and are driven from possessed bodies; when, wailing and groaning with a human voice and feeling the lashes and blows through divine power, they confess that the Judge is coming! Come and learn that what we say is true.” Thus Saint Cyprian.

In the Fourth Council of Carthage (chapter 7), which Saint Augustine attended, the following is prescribed, among the other orders, concerning the ordination of an exorcist: “When an exorcist is ordained, he is to receive from the hand of the bishop a book in which the exorcisms are written, while the bishop says to him: ‘Receive this, commit it to memory, and have the power to lay hands upon one possessed by a demon—that is, one agitated by a demon—whether baptized or a catechumen.’” This ministry was then so much in use, as it is now, that Augustine even used it proverbially when recounting the evasions of the Donatists at the Conference of Carthage, by which they tried to prevent certain acts that would confound their schism from being read: “O great confusion,” he said, “though not a surprising one! For when would a demon have feared an exorcist as much as the Donatists feared that these things should be read?” For more concerning the order and antiquity of exorcists, see Baronius, volume 1 of the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 56.]

that unclean spirits obey human beings in two ways: either they are subjected to the holiness of the faithful by divine grace and power,

[Note: [Col. 0753D] The other method of subjecting demons, or commanding them, is what we have called diabolical power. Magicians and sorcerers, worshipers of demons, use it by invoking them, indeed by adoring and sacrificing to them, as is said here.

Here we should note, first, that magicians possess no power or strength over demons except through a pact or through the demons’ simulation. Consequently, they cannot force demons, against their will, to do or refrain from doing anything, except fictitiously and deceptively. For demons pretend to be compelled by magicians, whom they willingly obey and serve, so that they may entangle them and others still more deeply, and keep those already entangled in their snares, as Saint Augustine teaches in book 2 of *The City of God*, chapter 6.

Hence the excellent saying of a certain not obscure theologian: “The demon pretends to be captured in order to capture you; bound in order to bind you; subjected to your command in order to subject you to himself; confined by you in order finally to confine you; he pretends to be bound by your art to an image or stone in order to lead you, bound by the ropes of sins, to hell” (Alphonsus de Castro, book 1 *On the Just Punishment of Heretics*).

Moreover, since some demons are more powerful than others because they are higher, it follows that if a magician has a pact with a higher demon, he can, through that demon, who serves him by pact, compel lower demons and subject them to his service. Thus Apollonius the magician is said to have driven out demons, among his other marvels (Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius*). Saint Gregory, in book 1 of the *Dialogues*, chapter 10, also relates that a certain noble woman was freed from a demon by magical incantations, but afterward was occupied by an entire legion of demons. “By the wondrous judgment of almighty God,” he says, “while one demon was driven from her by the perverse art, a legion suddenly entered her; and from that moment she began to be shaken by as many movements and disturbed by as many voices and cries as there were spirits possessing her.”

For more on these matters, see Peter Thyraeus, Martin Delrio, and others who have written about demons and demoniacs.]

or, won over by the sacrifices of the impious or by certain incantations, they fawn upon human beings as intimate friends.

The Pharisees, deceived by this opinion, also thought that the Lord and Savior had commanded demons by this art. They said:

> “He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons” (Matthew 12),

following the custom by which they knew their own magicians or sorcerers, through invocation of that name and through the rites of sacrifices which they knew pleased and delighted him, to possess power over demons subject to him, as though over his household servants.

## CHAPTER XX. Question concerning the apostate angels who are said in Genesis to have had intercourse with the daughters of human beings

**Germanus:** Since the reading from Genesis was brought forward a little earlier concerning the dispensation, and appropriately reminded us of something we have always desired to learn, we now wish to ask about it at a suitable point:

[Note: [Col. 0754C] This difficulty arose in very ancient times from the differing translation and interpretation of the passage in Genesis 6: “When the sons of God saw the daughters of human beings, that they were beautiful, they took wives for themselves from all whom they chose.” And below: “Now giants were upon the earth in those days. For after the sons of God had gone in to the daughters of human beings, and they had borne children to them, these were the mighty men who were famous from of old.”

In this passage, the Septuagint translators, in the older edition followed by Philo the Jew, Eusebius, and others (Philo, *On Giants*; Josephus, *Antiquities*, book 1, chapter 5; Eusebius, *Evangelical Preparation*, book 5; Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, books 3 and 5), rendered “sons of God” as οἱ ἄγγελοι τοῦ Θεοῦ, “the angels of God,” as Saint Augustine also quotes it in book 14 of *The City of God*, chapter 23.

This incorrectly placed designation of “angels” generated the greatest difficulties and distracted people’s minds into various opinions and even errors. Some thought that “angels” meant holy angels, who at that time first sinned with women and were therefore expelled and banished from heaven. Thus Lactantius writes in book 2 of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 15: “When the number of human beings began to increase, God, foreseeing that the devil—whom from the beginning of the earth he had given power either to corrupt or to destroy the human beings he had made at the beginning—might accomplish this through his deceptions, sent angels to guard and cultivate the human race. Above all, he commanded them not to defile themselves with earthly contamination or lose the dignity of their heavenly substance. But while they lived among human beings, that most deceitful ruler of the earth gradually enticed them into vices by familiarity and polluted them through intercourse with women. Then, because of the sins into which they had plunged themselves, they were not received back into heaven but fell to earth. Thus the devil made them, from angels of God, his satellites and ministers.” See Lactantius.

Before him, Justin Martyr held the same opinion in both *Apologies*, as did Clement of Alexandria in books 3 and 5 of the *Stromata*, and finally Tertullian in several places (see Pamelius on the paradoxes of Tertullian). For this reason he calls them “deserting angels,” whom our Cassian calls “apostates.”

Others, however, thought that the apostate angels, or demons, had been cast down from heaven immediately after the world was created and that, having intercourse with women, they fathered giants. Thus Eusebius of Caesarea writes in book 2 of the *Evangelical Preparation*, whose words I omit for the sake of brevity.

Later, however, a more accurate edition of the Septuagint appeared, more closely conformed to the Hebrew text. In it the reading is not ἄγγελοι, “angels,” but υἱοὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ, “sons of God.” Ambrose and Augustine recognized this version as legitimate, and the Latin Vulgate, approved by the Council of Trent, followed it. From this every Catholic should understand that in this passage “sons of God” does not mean angels—that is, heavenly spirits—nor demons, but the sons and descendants of Seth, worshipers of the true God, just as our Serenus learnedly explains in the following chapter. We shall add more notes on this matter there.]

what, then, should be thought about those apostate angels who are said to have mingled with the daughters of human beings (Genesis 6)? We wish to know whether, according to the literal sense, this can befit a spiritual nature. We also wish to hear similarly who is to be understood as the father of the devil in that Gospel testimony you mentioned earlier:

> “For he is a liar, and its father” (John 8).

## CHAPTER XXI. The proposed question is answered
[Note: [Col. 0755D] See Cuychius’s fifteenth annotation.]

**Serenus:** You have proposed two considerable questions at once. I shall answer them, insofar as I can, in the same order in which you proposed them.

[Note: [Col. 0755D] This statement seems to me sufficiently clearly explained by Cuychius and not to require a fuller explanation. Nevertheless, if anyone desires further information, let him consult Abulensis on Genesis, chapter VI, question 6, and on Exodus, chapter VII, question 12; Sixtus of Siena, *Bibliotheca*, book V, annotations 73 and 77; and finally Father Martin Delrio, *On Magic*, book II, question 15. From the latter it will be sufficient here to note only two conclusions containing the summary decision and explanation of the question.

**First conclusion.** Demons, although incorporeal and spiritual, can assume the bodies of the dead, or newly form bodies for themselves out of air, tangible and resembling flesh; and in such bodies they can engage in sexual intercourse with women, as they are accustomed to do with witches (*striges*) and sorceresses (*sagae*); indeed, they can also beget offspring from such intercourse. This is the common opinion of the Fathers, theologians, and philosophers, confirmed by the experience of many centuries and nations.

**Second conclusion.** Nevertheless, demons cannot, by their own power and from their own substance, generate in the manner of human beings or animals—for example, through the power of their own seed, which they do not possess and cannot possess of themselves, since they lack all matter as well as a vegetative soul. This alone was intended by Saint Chrysostom, *Homily 22 on Genesis*; Cassianus, or Serenus, in this passage; and Philastrius, *Against Heresies*, chapter 108.]

In no way should we believe that spiritual beings can carnally have intercourse with women. But if this could at some time have happened literally, [Note: [Col. 0756C] Many authors attest that it happened repeatedly even before the time of Cassian and this Serenus, so that, on Saint Augustine’s testimony, it would be either impudent or insane to doubt the matter. Experience likewise confirms that it happened not only in those times but also in later periods and even in our own age, with the greatest certainty, evidence, and testimony, as has been said—not, indeed, so that a child might be born from intercourse with demons without the seed of a man, but through the borrowed seed of some man. Consequently, the one born from it should not be called the demon’s son, but the son of the man whose seed was received, as Saint Thomas teaches from Augustine (*First Part*, question 51, article 3, reply to objection 5; *On the Trinity*, book III, chapters 8 and 9).] how would we not even now see the same thing happening, and how would we likewise see some people conceived by demons being born of women without a man’s seed or intercourse?

[Note: [Col. 0756C] But from where is this established? Is it because unclean spirits are commonly so called? They are not called this because they are themselves unclean, or because they are affected by or take pleasure in unclean delights within themselves, or because they delight in intercourse; rather, they are so called because they incite human beings to unclean things, rejoice when God is offended by human beings, and when the human race is shamefully polluted by the filth of such lusts. This paradox, therefore, proceeds from the same principle and source as the other matters discussed above (chapter 12).]

Especially since it is certain that they take extraordinary pleasure in the filth of lust—pleasures which, without doubt, they would prefer to practice by themselves rather than through human beings, if that could in any way be accomplished. Ecclesiastes likewise declares the same thing [Col. 0756A] (chapter I): “What is that which has been? The same which is; and what is that which has been done? The same which shall be done;” and: “There is nothing new under the sun of which one can speak and say, ‘Behold, this is new’; it has already existed in the ages that were before us.”

But the question is resolved in the following manner. After the murder of the righteous Abel, so that the whole human race might not take its beginning from a fratricide and impious man, Seth was born in the place of his murdered brother; he was to succeed not only to the posterity but also to the righteousness and piety of his brother. His descendants, following their father’s righteousness, remained always separated from the society and union of that kindred which descended from the sacrilegious Cain, as the account of the genealogies plainly declares in these words (Genesis V): “Adam begot Seth, Seth begot Enos, Enos begot Cainan, and Cainan begot Malaleel, [Col. 0756B] Malaleel begot Jareth, Jareth begot Enoch, Enoch begot Methuselah, Methuselah begot Lamech, and Lamech begot Noah.”

The genealogy of Cain, likewise, is described as separate (Genesis IV): “Cain begot Enoch, Enoch begot Irad, Irad begot Maviael, Maviael begot [Note: [Col. 0756D] Methusael, not Methuselah; for this was a different man from Methuselah, who was descended from Seth and was mentioned above.] Methusael, Methusael begot Lamech, and Lamech begot Jubal.”

Thus that generation which descended from the line of the righteous Seth, [Note: [Col. 0756D] That is, associated with one another and joined in marriage, as Dionysius explains—namely, within the same family and line of Seth.] continually mingled within its own line and kinship, [Note: [Col. 0756D] Namely, Seth, the first father and ancestor of that family. True religion and worship of the true God remained in that family and line until its union with the offspring of Cain. Through the latter’s contagion, a change of religion and corruption of morals followed, which became the cause of the Flood. Moreover, Dionysius and others, followed by Ciaconius, read: “In the holiness of their fathers and ancestors,” and so forth.] endured for a long age in the holiness of its father and ancestor [Col. 0757A], entirely uninfected, of course, by the sacrileges and utter wickedness of that evil offspring, which retained within itself the seed of impiety, as though [Note: [Col. 0757C] By the name “ancestor” he seems to understand Cain himself, whose genealogy he set out shortly before, and from whom his descendants inherited impiety and idolatry as though by inheritance. Some manuscripts, with Dionysius, read: “As though by an ancient tradition.” Others, followed by Plantinus, read: “As though by an ancestral tradition,” as Cuychius noted.] inserted by an ancestral [or ancient] tradition.

Therefore, as long as this distinction between their generations continued among them, that seed of Seth, proceeding as it did from an excellent root, [Note: [Col. 0757C] The solution of the first question proposed by Germanus: When Genesis says that the sons of God went in to the daughters of men and that they bore giants, this should not be understood of angels, whether good or evil, as though they desired and experienced intercourse with women, but of the sons, or descendants, of Seth. They are called angels of God, or rather sons of God, because until that time they had persevered in the worship of the true God. They are said to have gone in to the daughters of men when they began to associate with the daughters of Cain and took them for marriage and intercourse.

It seems worthwhile, however, to hear Saint Augustine discuss the matter more subtly and accurately (*City of God*, book XV, chapter 23): “They were not angels of God in such a way that they were not human beings, as some suppose; Scripture itself clearly declares that they were undoubtedly human beings. For after it had first been stated that the angels, seeing the daughters of men, because they were beautiful, took wives for themselves from all whom they chose, it immediately added: ‘And the Lord God said: My spirit shall not remain in these men forever, because they are flesh.’ For by the Spirit of God they had been made angels of God and sons of God; but by turning toward lower things they are called human beings by nature, not by grace; they are also called flesh, deserters from the Spirit, and, by deserting, themselves deserted.

“The Seventy translators indeed called these beings both angels of God and sons of God; but not all manuscripts contain this reading, for some have only ‘sons of God.’ Aquila, however, the translator whom the Jews prefer to the others, translated not ‘angels of God’ or ‘sons of God,’ but ‘sons of gods.’ Both readings, however, are true. For they were sons of God, under whose father—the Father of their fathers—they were also brothers; and they were sons of gods, since they had been begotten by gods, with whom they themselves were also gods, according to the saying of the Psalm: ‘I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.’ It is rightly believed that the Seventy translators received the prophetic Spirit, so that if they altered anything by its authority and expressed what they translated differently from the original, no one would doubt that this too had been spoken by divine inspiration; although it is said to be ambiguous in the Hebrew, so that it could be translated both ‘sons of God’ and ‘sons of gods.’” Thus far Saint Augustine.]

on account of the merit of its holiness was called “the angels of God,” or, as different copies read, “the sons of God.” Conversely, those others, because of their own impiety or that of their fathers and because of their earthly works, were called “the sons of men.”

When, therefore, this useful and good separation still existed between them up to that time, the sons of Seth, who were sons of God, afterward saw the daughters of those born from Cain’s lineage. Inflamed by desire for their beauty, they took wives for themselves from among them. These women, pouring the wickedness of their fathers into their husbands, immediately corrupted them from that innate holiness and paternal simplicity.

To them, quite appropriately, that saying was addressed (Psalm LXXXI): “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High. But you shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes.”

Those men, too, [Note: [Col. 0758C] That is, they had fallen away from a complete knowledge of natural things.] fell away from that true discipline of natural philosophy which had been handed down to them by their ancestors. The first man, who immediately followed upon the establishment of all nature, had been able clearly to attain it and to transmit it to his descendants by sure reasoning.

For he had seen the infancy of the world itself, still tender, and, as it were, palpitating and raw. There had been infused into him not only such fullness of wisdom but also such a grace of prophecy, through that divine inspiration, that he gave names to all living creatures, the inhabitants of this still-primitive world (Genesis II). He could distinguish not only the fierceness and venom of every kind of beast and serpent, but also the powers of herbs, the natures of trees and stones, and the changes of seasons not yet experienced, so that he could effectively say (Wisdom VII):

[Note: [Col. 0758C] The most wise king Solomon speaks these words about himself, commemorating the singular gift of God bestowed upon him; the present Author applies them to Adam. Whether Adam or Solomon was wiser, and which of them could more truly appropriate these words, may be seen in Pererius, *Commentaries on Genesis*, book IV, question 3.]

“The Lord gave me true knowledge of the things that are, so that I might know the arrangement of the world, the powers of the elements, their beginning, end, and middle, the courses of the years and the dispositions of the stars, the natures of animals, the tempers of beasts, the force of spirits, and the thoughts of human beings; the differences of trees, the powers of roots, and the things that are hidden and those that are in plain sight I came to know.”

Receiving, therefore, this knowledge of all natures through the succession of generations by the paternal tradition of Seth, the seed of Seth exercised it, as long as it remained separated from the sacrilegious offspring, just as it had received it in holiness, both for the worship of God and for the usefulness of common life.

But when it had been mingled with the impious generation, it turned, under the instigation of demons, toward profane and harmful purposes what it had learned piously. [Note: [Col. 0758D] Hence the books of curious arts received their name. In the Greek text, βιβλοὶ περίεργοι—that is, “curious books”—we read in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter IX) that, when Paul was driving demons out of possessed bodies at Ephesus, many of those who had pursued curious practices—that is, who had practiced curious arts—brought their books and burned them before everyone. When their prices had been calculated, they found the sum to be fifty thousand denarii.]

It boldly established from it curious arts of sorcery, deceitful practices, and magical superstitions, teaching its descendants that, after abandoning the sacred worship of the divine name, they should worship either these elements, or fire, or demons of the air.

Although the resolution of the proposed question does not require it, nevertheless, since the occasion of this explanation has reminded us of it, I think that I should briefly indicate how this knowledge of curious things did not perish in the Flood but became known in succeeding ages.

According to what the ancient traditions relate, [Note: [Col. 0758D] Ham, also called Zoroaster or Zoraster, was the inventor and propagator of the magical art, under the instigation and instruction of a demon. Saint Clement discusses him in book IV of the *Recognitions*, where, speaking of the rebellious angels, he says [Col. 0759B] (see Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXX, chapter 1): “They taught human beings that demons could be compelled by certain arts to obey mortals; and, as though from some furnace and workshop of wickedness, they filled the whole world with the smoke of impiety after withdrawing the light of piety.”

For these and several other reasons the Flood was brought upon the world, and all who were upon the earth were destroyed, except Noah’s family. Noah survived with his three sons and their wives. One of them, named Ham, transmitted to one of his sons, called Misraim, from whom the peoples of the Egyptians, Babylonians, and Persians descended, the magical discipline that he had wrongly discovered. The peoples who then existed called him Zoroaster, admiring him as the first author of the magical art; many books on the subject are also known by his name. Thus writes Clement the pontiff.

Moreover, there was not one Zoroaster or Zoraster but several, as M. Delrio reports from Arnobius and others in book I of *On Magic* (chapter 3). The first was that Chaldean discussed here, Noah’s son, otherwise called Ham or Cham, the inventor of magic, whom Clement of Rome mentioned above. For this reason Egypt is often called the land of Ham in Sacred Scripture (Psalms CIV and CV), according to Saint Jerome in the *Hebrew Questions*.

The second was the Bactrian, or king of the Bactrians, who waged war against Ninus, king of the Assyrians, by whom he was both defeated and expelled from his kingdom; Suidas, however, seems to confuse him with the first. Pliny and the historian Justin discuss this same figure (Pliny, book XXX, chapter 1; Justin, book I; Clement, book I of the *Stromata*).

The third was a Pamphylian by birth, also called Erus, whom Clement of Alexandria discusses.

The fourth, finally, was an Armenian, the grandson of Hostanes.]

Ham, the son of Noah, who was infected with these superstitions, sacrilegious arts, and profane practices, knowing that he could not bring any written memorial of them into the ark, into which he was about to enter together with his righteous father and holy brothers, [Note: [Col. 0759D] These matters seem to have been taken from a tradition of the Hebrews that is not especially certain or authentic, since neither Saint Jerome nor any other ancient writer mentions them. Nevertheless, the author of the *Scholastic History* writes something similar (*On Genesis*, chapter XXXIX): “Ninus,” he says, “defeated Ham, who was still alive and reigning among the Bactrians—or, as others prefer, in Thrace—and who was called Zoroaster, the inventor of the magical art. He wrote this art, together with the seven liberal arts, upon fourteen columns: seven of bronze and seven of brick, against the twofold destruction of the world which he had heard was to come—one by water, the other by fire.”

That author appears to have imitated Josephus, who reports the same or similar matters concerning Seth and his descendants in these words (*Antiquities*, book I, chapter 4, from Rufinus’s translation): “They were the first to discover the discipline of heavenly things and their arrangement. And lest what they had discovered should disappear from human beings, or perish before coming to their knowledge, Adam, having foretold that the destruction of all things would come once through the power of fire and again through the force and multitude of waters, made two columns, one of stone and the other of brick. They wrote upon both whatever they had discovered, so that if the brick structure were destroyed by rains, the stone one, remaining, might provide human beings with the opportunity to learn and display what it contained inscribed upon it.”

Thus Josephus. The French poet Guillaume Sallustius expressed and adorned this history in a notable poem (*The Last Two Weeks*, final poem). Following such an example, but with perverse rivalry and ingenuity—for the children of this age are no less prudent, indeed more prudent, than the children of light—it is credible that that impious Ham, devoted to magical arts, impressed, engraved, and inscribed his wicked arts and profane inventions, as the present account says, upon sheets of various metals and upon the hardest stones, so that they might not perish in the Flood; and that after the Flood he taught them to his descendants and thus spread them throughout the world.]

engraved his wicked arts and profane inventions upon sheets of various metals, which could not be destroyed by the inundation of waters, and upon the hardest stones. After the Flood had passed, he searched for these objects with the same zeal with which he had hidden them, and transmitted to his descendants a seedbed of sacrilege and perpetual wickedness.

In this way, therefore, the popular belief that angels had handed down either sorceries or various arts to human beings was fulfilled in reality.

[Note: [Col. 0760C] From the abominable intercourse of the descendants of Seth and Enos, in whose families God was worshipped, with the descendants of Cain, who had long served idols, sprang giants—people of monstrous size and stature. From the union of people of such differing worship and religion, moreover, the knowledge of God was utterly extinguished (I Peter III), except in Noah’s family—that is, in the eight souls who were saved through the ark, namely, delivered from the Flood. Saint Augustine, however, teaches that giants also existed before the families of Seth and Cain were joined in marriage (*City of God*, book I, chapter 23).]

Accordingly, from those sons of Seth and daughters of Cain, as we have said, more wicked sons were begotten. They were extremely powerful hunters, exceedingly violent and savage men, and, because of the enormous size of their bodies or of their cruelty and wickedness, they were called giants (Genesis VI). They were the first to begin devastating neighboring peoples and practicing robbery among human beings, demanding their livelihood through plunder rather than being content with the sweat and labor of their work. Their crimes increased to such an extent that, unless the world were cleansed by the Flood, it could not otherwise be purified.

Thus, when the sons of Seth, instigated by lust, transgressed that command which had been observed for a very long time from the beginning of the world through natural instinct, it became necessary that it later be restored through the written law: “You shall not give your daughter in marriage to his son, nor take one of their daughters for your son, for they will seduce your hearts, so that you depart from your God, follow their gods, and serve them” (Deuteronomy VII).

## CHAPTER XXII. Objection: how the profane union of the descendants of Seth with the daughters of Cain could be charged against them before the prohibition of the law.

**Germanus:** They could rightly have been charged with the crime of transgressing this presumption of marriage if that command had been given to them. But since no ordinance had yet established any requirement to observe this separation, how could their intermingling of lineage be imputed to them as guilt, when it had been forbidden by no command?

[Note: [Col. 0760D] That is, to punish; “past offenses” means those committed before the law was enacted. A jurist expresses the same point in other words: “A law does not extend to past matters” (*Lex Legem*, Code, *On Laws*, book I, title 2 of the *Decretals*). This maxim is also expressed in canon law under the title *On Constitutions*, chapter 2: “Whenever something new is established, it ordinarily gives form to future matters in such a way that it does not condemn the past to loss, lest those who were ignorant incur harm before the prohibition, which afterward they rightly must endure once forbidden.” And in the final chapter of the same title: “Since it is certain that laws and constitutions give form to future affairs, they should not be applied to past acts unless provision is expressly made in them concerning the past.”

It is evident, moreover, that such statements or maxims are not understood of the eternal law, which is the very wisdom of God, or of the natural law [Col. 0761A], which is born in human beings with the very condition of their nature [Col. 0761B]—for crimes are not preceded by these laws in such a way that they can be punished—but of positive law, whether divine or human, which does not extend to past matters unless it expressly says so, even when the reason for the law preceded the law itself, as Doctor Navarrus says (*Relectio*, chapter “Si quando”). The reason for this has been stated above.]

For the law ordinarily condemns not past offenses but future ones.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Response: how, by the natural law, human beings were subject from the beginning to judgment or punishment.

[Col. 0761A]

Serenus: [Note: [Col. 0761B] “Naturally,” that is, in the very establishment of nature, or, as he says below, “from the beginning of creation and together with nature itself.”]

When God created humanity, he naturally implanted in human beings the entire knowledge of the law. If this knowledge had been preserved by humanity according to the Lord’s purpose, as it had begun to be, it would certainly not have been necessary for another law to be given, later promulgated in written form. For it would have been superfluous to offer from outside a remedy that still remained active within.

But [Note: [Col. 0761B] The law of nature impressed upon human minds, or written in human hearts—nothing other than the dictate of right reason, insofar as it teaches what each person ought to do or avoid—has been explained with great skill by Saint Thomas in these words (1–2, q. 94, a. 6):

“First, certain very general precepts belong to the natural law, and these are known to everyone; but there are also certain secondary and more particular precepts, which are, as it were, conclusions close to the principles. As regards those common principles, therefore, the natural law cannot in any way be wholly erased from human hearts. It can, however, be erased in a particular practical matter, insofar as reason is prevented from applying the common principle to a particular action, because of concupiscence or some other passion. As regards the other, secondary precepts, the natural law can be erased from human hearts, either because of evil persuasions or even because of depraved customs and corrupt habits. Thus, among some people, robbery was not regarded as sinful, nor even unnatural vices, as the Apostle also says in the Letter to the Romans.”

Thus Saint Thomas. From this it may be understood what Saint Augustine says in Book II, chapter 4, of the *Confessions*: “Your law is written in human hearts, and no iniquity indeed erases it.” Concerning this same law the Psalmist says: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Psalm 4). The Apostle likewise says of it in Romans 2: “The Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature the things of the law.” The Gloss says there: “Although they do not have the written law, they nevertheless have the natural law, by which each person understands and is conscious of what is good and what is evil.”]

because this law, as we have said, had already been thoroughly corrupted by the freedom and practice of sin, the severe rigor of the Mosaic law was added as the exactor, executor, and avenger of this knowledge, and, to speak in the very words of Scripture, as its helper, so that even through fear of present punishment the knowledge of natural goodness would not be completely extinguished, in accordance with the prophet’s saying:

[Note: [Col. 0761D] So it stands in the version of the Septuagint: “For he gave the law as a help” (*νόμον γὰρ ἐς βοήθειαν ἔδωκεν*). The Vulgate is more obscure: “To the law rather, and to the testimony” (Isaiah 8), that is, “you ought to turn.” By these words God warned the Jews always to keep his law before their eyes and never to allow its memory to fall from their minds.]

“He gave the law as a help” (Galatians 3),

[Note: [Col. 0761D] In Galatians 3: “The law was our pedagogue in Christ, so that we might be justified by faith. But when faith came, we are no longer under a pedagogue.” Saint Jerome elegantly explains this passage:

“A pedagogue,” he says, “is assigned to children, so that a wanton age may be restrained and hearts inclined toward vices may be held in check; while tender childhood is educated through study and, restrained by fear of punishment, prepared for the higher disciplines of philosophy and the governance of the state. Yet a pedagogue is not a teacher or a father; nor does the one being educated expect from the pedagogue an inheritance or knowledge. The pedagogue guards another man’s son, and, once that son has reached the lawful time for receiving his inheritance, the pedagogue will withdraw from him. Finally, the very name ‘pedagogue’ conveys this meaning: it is formed from the term for leading children, that is, conducting them.

“So also the law of Moses was imposed upon a wanton people like a stricter pedagogue, in order to guard them and prepare them for the faith that was to come. After that faith came and we believed in Christ, we are no longer under a pedagogue; the tutor and guardian withdraw from us, and, entering upon the lawful time of maturity, we are called true children of God,” and so forth.]

which, according to the Apostle, is also described as having been given to them as to children, as a pedagogue, instructing and guarding them so that they would not, through a kind of forgetfulness, depart from that discipline in which they had naturally been formed (Isaiah 8).

Now, the fact that all knowledge of the law was infused into humanity from the beginning of creation is clearly demonstrated by the following: [Note: [Col. 0762B] He shows by many examples that the precepts of the natural law were observed by the ancient fathers not only before the written law—that is, the Mosaic law—but even before the Flood.

The first example is righteous Abel, who by natural instinct and guidance understood that the best things ought to be offered to God. Therefore he offered from the firstborn of his flock and from their fat. God himself later declared this through the law given by Moses, when he commanded that the firstborn be offered to him (Exodus 13). He thus intended it to be understood that those things which many centuries later were prescribed and commanded to the Hebrews through the law of Moses had already been practiced from the beginning of the world among true worshipers of God (Chrysostom, Homily 24 on Genesis).

The second example is Noah, who, even under the law of nature and through natural knowledge, as is stated here, understood long before the Mosaic law which animals were unclean. Under the law of nature, however, those animals were considered unclean which it was not permitted to offer to God; under the Mosaic law, animals were called unclean which the Jews were forbidden to eat in Leviticus. It is plausible that these animals were also regarded as unclean in Noah’s time—not because they were considered unclean by nature, which was the error of the Manichaeans, but because of some figure or significance, whether allegorical or tropological. On this see Saint Thomas, 1–2, q. 102; 1–2, q. 103, art. 1.

Nevertheless, before the law of Moses the observance of these matters was not imposed upon human beings by any command of God or by what is called a positive law. Rather, it was introduced into custom and worship partly by God’s impulse, partly by the natural judgment of reason, and especially by the tradition of the ancestors.

The third example is Enoch, who is said to have walked with God (Genesis 5). This means nothing other than to walk in the way of the Lord, or in his commandments—that is, to live holily and blamelessly, to obey God’s will and commands, and, in short, to please God, just as the Septuagint translators rendered it: “Enoch pleased God.”

The fourth example is Shem and Japheth, the sons of Noah, who by natural light understood that their father’s nakedness ought not to be uncovered, indeed not even looked upon, before the law said: “You shall not uncover your father’s nakedness.”

The fifth example is Abraham, who by natural light sufficiently understood that the spoils recovered from the enemies of the people of the Pentapolis ought to be restored to their rightful owners, and that tithes were owed by natural right to priests.

The sixth example is Abraham himself and his nephew Lot, who are read to have practiced hospitality under the law of nature and to have offered their guests the duties of human kindness (Saint Thomas, 2–2, q. 87, a. 1, and *Quodlibet* 2, a. 8).

For the rest, let no one conclude from these examples that what certain Hebrew rabbis have reported is true: namely, that all the precepts of the Mosaic law were observed before the law by upright and pious worshipers of God. On the contrary, it is most certain that many things were permitted before the law of Moses which were later forbidden to the Jews by the law. Two examples alone will suffice, so that I do not become unnecessarily long by pursuing more.

The first is Genesis 9, where God granted Noah and his descendants permission to eat every animal without distinction (Pererius on Genesis 9). But the law of Moses ordered the Jews to abstain from many kinds of animals as unclean, in Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14.

The second is Genesis 29, where Jacob is read to have taken wives and at the same time possessed two sisters, Leah and Rachel. Yet the law of Moses forbade such a marriage to the Hebrews, in Leviticus 18.

Therefore, when Serenus says here that the holy worshipers of God observed the commandments of the law before the law, indeed before the Flood, this must not be understood of all the commandments or precepts generally, but chiefly of moral precepts—not of all of those either, but of many of them, especially the better-known and more general ones. This will become clearer later from the teaching of Saint Thomas.]

we know that all the saints observed the commandments of the law without reading them in writing, before the law, indeed before the Flood. For how could Abel (Genesis 4), before the law commanded it, have known that he ought to offer God a sacrifice from the firstborn of his sheep and from their fat, unless he had been taught this naturally by the law implanted within him?

How could Noah (Genesis 9) have distinguished which animal was clean and which unclean, when the legal command had not yet made this distinction,

[Note: [Col. 0763C] Here he calls “natural knowledge” what he shortly before called the law naturally implanted, or the natural law.

Natural knowledge can be understood in two ways. It may mean knowledge implanted in a human being from creation or birth; for whatever is possessed from birth is called natural. In this sense we are said by nature to be children of wrath, in Ephesians 2. But what is called natural in this sense is not opposed to what is supernatural, since both natural and supernatural gifts may be possessed from birth, as is well known (see Bellarmine, *On the Grace Given to the First Man*, chapter 5).

Accordingly, this natural knowledge does not exclude the higher and supernatural knowledge which those holy patriarchs possessed through divine revelation or inspiration before the written law.

Or “natural” may mean what is consonant with nature, since it does not destroy nature but perfects and adorns it. In this sense Saint Augustine teaches that the Apostle’s statement—“The Gentiles who do not have the law do by nature the things of the law”—is to be understood. But only the former interpretation is intended here, for the discussion concerns the natural law and natural knowledge as distinguished from the written, or Mosaic, law.

As to how Noah could have discerned through this natural knowledge which animals were clean and which unclean, when God commanded him to take seven pairs of every clean animal but two of every unclean animal (Genesis 7), Saint Thomas explains it as follows:

“The distinction between clean and unclean animals did not exist before the law with respect to eating, since it is said in Genesis 9: ‘Everything that moves and lives shall be food for you.’ It existed only with respect to the offering of sacrifices, because sacrifices were offered from certain specified animals. If there was some distinction among animals with respect to eating, this was not because eating them was considered unlawful, since no law forbade it, but because of abhorrence or custom. Thus, even now we see that some foods are considered disgusting in certain lands although they are eaten in others.”

These are the words of Saint Thomas, consistent with what was said above.]

unless he had been instructed by natural knowledge? From where did Enoch (Genesis 5) learn to walk with God, when he had received no illumination of the written law from anyone?

Where had Shem and Japheth read, “You shall not uncover your father’s nakedness” (Leviticus 18), so that they might walk backward and cover their father’s nakedness (Genesis 9)?

From where was Abraham warned to abstain from the spoils of the enemy that were offered to him, so that he would not obtain the reward for his labor (Genesis 18); or to pay tithes to the priest Melchizedek, which the Mosaic law commands (ibid., 14)?

From where did Abraham himself, and from where did Lot (Genesis 18, 19), humbly offer to passersby and strangers the duties of kindness and the washing of feet, before the commandment of the Gospel had shone forth?

[Note: [Col. 0764C] These matters are sufficiently clear and well known from the history of Job.]

From where did Job acquire such devotion of faith, such purity of chastity, such knowledge of humility, gentleness, mercy, and human kindness—such as we do not now see fulfilled even by those who know the Gospels by heart?
