[Note: [Col. 0764C] A similar passage of Saint Thomas helps to clarify this place. There he teaches that all moral precepts are in some way reducible to the natural law (1–2, q. 100, a. 1):

“Since moral precepts concern matters pertaining to good conduct, and since good conduct consists in what accords with reason, while every judgment of human reason is derived in some way from natural reason, it is necessary that all moral precepts belong to the natural law, though in different ways.

“Some things are such that the natural reason of every person immediately judges by itself that they ought to be done or not done—for example, ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and ‘You shall not kill’ and ‘You shall not steal.’ Such things belong absolutely to the natural law.

“Others are judged by the wise, through more subtle consideration of reason, to be matters that ought to be observed. These belong to the natural law in such a way that they nevertheless require instruction, by which those of lesser understanding are taught by the wiser—for example, ‘Rise before the gray head and honor the person of the old man,’ and similar matters.

“Still others require divine instruction for human reason to judge them; through this instruction we are taught about divine matters, as in: ‘You shall not make for yourself a graven image or any likeness,’ and ‘You shall not take the name of your God in vain.’

”Thus Saint Thomas.]

Which of the saints do we read to have violated any commandment of the law before the law?

Which of them did not observe: “Hear, Israel: The Lord your God is one Lord” (Deuteronomy 6)?

Which did not fulfill: “You shall not make for yourself a graven image, nor any likeness of what is in heaven, or on earth, or in the waters under the earth”?

Which of them did not observe: “Honor your father and your mother,” or the commandments that follow in the Decalogue: “You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness, you shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” (Exodus 20), and many other commandments far greater than these, which preceded not only the commandments of the law but even those of the Gospel?

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### That those who sinned before the Flood were justly punished

Thus we understand that from the beginning God created all things perfect, and that nothing needed to be added to his original ordering as though it were improvident or imperfect, nor did anything afterward need to be added to it, if everything had remained in the condition and arrangement in which he had created it.

And therefore we shall prove that God, by a just judgment, took action against those who sinned before the law, indeed before the Flood, because, [Note: [Col. 0765B] The author seems chiefly to have in view here the sons of Seth, who are said to have transgressed the natural law when they went in to the daughters of men—that is, when they took wives from the daughters of Cain, who were unbelieving and idolatrous. Reason and the natural law dictate that marriage should not be contracted with people of a different worship and religion, that is, with unbelievers, because of the danger of apostasy or defection into unbelief and idolatry. This was also repeatedly forbidden by the Mosaic law (Exodus 34; Deuteronomy 7). Hence Ezra the priest separated, dissolved, and broke up such marriages contracted by Jews with foreigners (1 Ezra 10). See Gratian, 28, q. 1, chapters “Cave” and “Sic enim.”] having transgressed the natural law, they deserved to be punished without any excuse.

[Note: [Col. 0765C] The Manichaeans and Marcionites blasphemed God as the author of the Old Testament, calling him an evil god and the prince of darkness, and mocked him with questions of this kind. See Epiphanius, Augustine, and others who wrote about heresies.]

Nor shall we fall into the blasphemies and slanders of those who, ignorant of this reasoning, disparage the God of the Old Testament and, deriding and mocking our faith, reply:

[Note: [Col. 0765C] Against such Manichaean quibbles and blasphemies, Saint Thomas assigns three reasons, gathered both from Scripture and from the Fathers, why the new law ought not to have been given from the beginning of the world:

“The first,” he says (1–2, q. 107, art. 3), “is that the new law, as has been said, is principally the grace of the Holy Spirit. This grace ought not to have been given abundantly before the obstacle of sin had been removed from the human race through the completed redemption by Christ. Hence it is said in John 7: ‘The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.’ The Apostle clearly assigns this reason in Romans 8, where, after speaking of the law of the Spirit of life, he adds: ‘God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and concerning sin, condemned sin in the flesh, so that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us.’

“The second reason can be taken from the perfection of the new law. Nothing is brought to perfection immediately at the beginning, but through a certain temporal order of succession; just as someone first becomes a child and afterward a man. The Apostle assigns this reason in Galatians 3: ‘The law was our pedagogue in Christ, so that we might be justified by faith; but when faith came, we are no longer under a pedagogue.’

“The third reason is that the new law is the law of grace. Therefore, it was first necessary for human beings to be left to themselves under the condition of the old law, so that, falling into sin and recognizing their weakness, they might recognize their need for grace. The Apostle assigns this reason in Romans 5, saying: ‘The law entered so that the offense might abound; but where the offense abounded, grace abounded still more.’

”Thus far Saint Thomas. Here the author chiefly has in view the second reason assigned above, which is derived from the perfection of the new law.]

“What then pleased our God, that after so many thousands of years he should wish to promulgate the law, allowing so many centuries to pass without a law? If afterward he discovered something better, it appears that at the beginning of the world he judged inferior or worse things to be good, and that later, as though taught by experience, he began to foresee what was more correct and to amend his original arrangements for the better. This cannot possibly accord with the immense foreknowledge [Lipsius in the margin: ‘wisdom’] of God; nor can such things be said of him without grave blasphemy by heretical madness.”

The Ecclesiast says:

[Note: [Col. 0766B] The Vulgate text is: “I have learned that all the works which God has made endure forever. We cannot add anything to them or take anything away from them, which God has made so that he may be feared” (Ecclesiastes 3, according to the Septuagint). The passage has been explained in more than one way by various authors. For the present passage, however, Saint Thomas’s explanation will suffice (1–2, q. 98, a. 2, ad 2):

“God’s works endure forever, because God made them in such a way that they should endure forever; and these are the things that are perfect. The old law, however, is rejected at the time of the perfection of grace, not as evil, but as weak and useless for that time. The Apostle says in Hebrews 7: ‘There is a rejection of the former commandment because of its weakness and ineffectiveness, for the law brought nothing to perfection.’ And in Galatians 3: ‘When faith has come, we are no longer under a pedagogue.’”]

“I have learned that all the things which God made from the beginning will themselves remain forever. Nothing can be added to them, and nothing can be taken away from them” (Ecclesiastes 3, according to the Septuagint).

And therefore, [Note: [Col. 0766C] See this statement of the Apostle explained elsewhere, *Conference* 21, chapter 8.] “The law was not made for the just, but for the unjust and disobedient, for the ungodly and sinners, for the wicked and defiled” (1 Timothy 1).

For the just, possessing a sound and unimpaired discipline of the natural and implanted law, had no need of this law, externally added and written in letters, which was given as a help to that natural law.

From this it is gathered with the clearest reasoning that this law written in letters ought not to have been given from the beginning, for it would have been superfluous while the natural law still stood and had not yet been wholly violated. Nor could evangelical perfection have been handed down before the observance of the law.

For they could not have heard: “If anyone strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also” (Matthew 5),

[Note: [Col. 0766C] The law of retaliation was given to the Jews in Exodus 21: “Eye for eye, tooth for tooth, foot for foot, burning for burning, wound for wound, bruise for bruise”—supply, “the one who injures another shall repay.” And in Leviticus: “Whoever inflicts a blemish on one of his fellow citizens, as he has done, so shall it be done to him: fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth; he shall restore it” (Leviticus 24 and Deuteronomy 19).

This law was imposed upon the Jews not for the sake of revenge, as the Pharisees wrongly interpreted it, but for the sake of justice, and for three reasons:

1. So that it might serve judges and magistrates as a rule to follow in punishing offenders, preventing them from exceeding or neglecting the proper measure of punishment, but making them punish the guilty in proportion to the injury inflicted (see Maldonado on this passage).

2. So that it might restrain people through fear of punishment from laying hands upon others, and prevent them from doing to others what they would not wish to suffer themselves.

3. To restrain the desire to pursue excessive vengeance, even in the case of a judge.

Thus Augustine says in Book 19, chapter 15, *Against Faustus*:

“Indeed, this was commanded in order to restrain the flames of hatred raging against one another and the immoderate impulses of human beings. For who is easily satisfied with returning no more vengeance than the injury he has received? Do we not see people who have been lightly injured plotting murder, thirsting for blood, and barely finding in the misfortunes of an enemy enough to satisfy them? Therefore, to this immoderate and unjust retaliation the law sets a just limit by instituting the punishment of retaliation: namely, that each person should receive such punishment as the injury he inflicted. This is not fuel but a boundary for fury, so that what had been subdued would not be kindled again, and what was already burning would not spread farther. A just vengeance has been imposed, which is justly owed to the one who has suffered the injury. What is owed may indeed be mercifully remitted, but it is not unjustly demanded again.”

Thus Augustine.

This explanation shows that the Jews, not content with the equality of retaliation, as is said here, often avenged injuries received with more severe punishments: for the lightest slap they returned deadly kicks—that is, heavy and dangerous blows of the feet—and wounds from weapons; for the smallest injuries they repaid the greatest. For one tooth they sought the lives of those who had struck them.]

who were not content to avenge their own injuries with the equality of retaliation, but returned deadly kicks and wounds from weapons for the lightest slap, and sought the lives of those who struck them for a single tooth.

Nor could it be said to them: “Love your enemies” (Matthew 5), since it was already considered a great benefit and advantage that they should love their friends, avoid their enemies, cease hating them alone, and not hasten to oppress or kill them.

## CHAPTER XXV  
### How the saying in the Gospel about the devil is to be understood: that he is a liar and the father of it

But as for what had troubled you concerning the devil, “that he is a liar and the father of it”—so that the Lord’s words (John 8) might appear to declare that both he himself and the father of it are liars—it is altogether absurd even to entertain such an opinion lightly.

[Note: [Col. 0767D] This is the second difficulty previously proposed by Germanus. Saint Augustine solves it in nearly the same way as Abbot Serenus here:

“Some,” he says (*Tractate 24 on John*), “have thought from these words that the devil has a father, and they have asked who the father of the devil is. This is the error of the Manichaeans. For not everyone who lies is the father of his lie. If you received a lie from someone else and repeated it, you have indeed lied, but you are not the father of the lie. But because he did not receive the lie from elsewhere—by that lie, like a serpent with poison, he killed the human being—he is the father of the lie, just as God is the Father of truth.”

From this we understand that the devil is called the father of the lie because he was its first author and inventor, and in a certain sense gave it birth, as the Fathers commonly explain.]

For, as we said shortly before, spirit does not beget spirit, just as soul cannot beget soul, although we do not doubt that the concretion of flesh comes together through human seed. The Apostle makes the matter clearer by distinguishing to which author each of the two substances—that is, flesh and soul—is to be attributed. He says:

“We had the fathers of our flesh as instructors, and we revered them; shall we not much more submit to the Father of spirits and live?” (Hebrews 12)

What could he have defined more clearly by this distinction, by declaring that human beings are the fathers of our flesh, while consistently expressing that God alone is the Father of souls?

[Note: [Col. 0768C] That rational souls are created by God alone and infused into human bodies at the very moment of generation, and that for this reason God is called the Father of spirits, or souls, is taught, besides Serenus here, by other Fathers who interpret this passage of the Apostle. See Saint Thomas in his commentary.]

Although even in the formation of this body the service alone is to be attributed to human beings, while the ultimate constitution belongs to God, the creator of all,

[Col. 0767C]

as David says: “Your hands made me and fashioned me” (Psalm 118).

And blessed Job says: “Did you not, as it were, milk me like milk, and coagulate me like cheese; you furnished me with bones and sinews?” (Job 10)

And the Lord says to Jeremiah: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you” (Jeremiah 1).

The Ecclesiast, carefully and appropriately gathering the nature and origin of both substances by examining the origin and beginning from which each proceeded, and considering the end toward which each strives, and discussing at the same time the separation of this body and soul, says:

“Before the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it” (Ecclesiastes 12).

What could he have said more plainly than that he declares the material of the flesh, which he called dust because it takes its beginning from human seed and appears to be sown through its service, to return again to the earth, as though taken from the earth; while the spirit, which is not generated through the union of the sexes but is specially bestowed by God alone, returns to its author?

This is also clearly expressed through the divine inbreathing by which God first gave life to Adam (Genesis 2).

[Note: [Col. 0768C] “He breathed into his face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul” (Genesis 2). The breath of life is understood here as the soul, breathed and infused by God together with the production or formation of the body.

Saint Thomas nevertheless warns that “to breathe into” should not be understood bodily. Rather, he says, “to breathe into” means to make a spirit.

Moreover, Moses, wishing to signify the creation of the rational soul and its infusion into Adam’s body, used the word “inbreathing,” or “blowing,” for three reasons:

1. According to Theodoret, so that it might be understood that the creation of a rational soul is as easy for God as it is for a human being to emit breath from his mouth.

2. So that we might infer from this that the rational soul is not drawn from the potentiality of matter, as the souls of brute animals are, but comes from outside, since it is created by God from nothing, and is therefore immaterial and immortal.

3. So that it might signify that the soul is created and infused into the body at the same time. For God creates it by infusing it, and infuses it by creating it, at the same moment of time, although in the order of nature the creation of the soul precedes its infusion (see Pererius on this passage).]

Accordingly, from these testimonies we clearly gather that no one can be called the Father of spirits except God alone, who makes them from nothing whenever he wills; human beings, however, are called only the fathers of our flesh.

Thus, insofar as the devil was created as either a spirit or a good angel, he had no father except God his creator. But when he had been lifted up by pride and had said in his heart, “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14), he became a liar and did not stand in the truth. Bringing forth a lie from the treasure of his own wickedness, he became not only a liar but also the father of the lie itself (John 8). Promising divinity to the human being and saying, “You will be like gods” (Genesis 3), he did not stand in the truth, but from the beginning became a murderer—either by bringing Adam into the condition of mortality or by killing Abel through his instigation, by the hand of his brother.

But now the dawn that follows concludes our discussion, completed through nearly two nights of labor, and has drawn the little boat of this conference from the deepest sea of questions into the safest harbor of silence, by the concise account of our rusticity.

In that depth, however, the farther the breath of the divine Spirit has led us inward, the more widely the immensity that lies before our eyes will continually open up; and, according to Solomon’s saying, “It will become farther from us than it was, and the deep depth—who will find it?” (Ecclesiastes 7)

Therefore let us beseech the Lord that either his fear or that charity which cannot fall may remain immovable within us, making us wise among human beings and always protecting us unharmed from the devil’s weapons.

With these guardians, it is impossible for anyone to fall into the snares of death. The difference between the perfect and the imperfect is this: in the perfect, charity is fixed and, so to speak, more mature; remaining more tenaciously, it guards them more firmly and makes it easier for them to persevere in holiness. In the imperfect, however, charity is bestowed as though more weakly and cools more easily; consequently, it compels them more quickly and more frequently to become entangled in the snares of sins.

When we heard these things, the discourse of this conference so inflamed us that, departing from the old man’s cell with greater ardor of mind than when we had entered, we thirsted for the fullness of his teaching.

## NINTH CONFERENCE  
### The first conference of Abbot Isaac: On Prayer

[Col. 0769]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0769B]

# On the Perpetual and Unceasing Continuity of Prayer

The *Conferences* of this elder, whom we now bring forward—Abbot Isaac—will, with the Lord’s favor, fulfill what was promised in the second book of the *Institutes* [Note: Thus it is stated in chapter 9 of that work: “Since the order of the *Institutes* has led us onward, in due sequence, to the rule of the canonical prayers—whose fuller treatment, although we reserve it for the *Conferences of the Elders*, we shall arrange there more fully when we begin to discuss their character or continuity in their own words,” and so forth. Here the reader should note what we stated at the beginning of this work: that the books of the *Institutes* are commonly called Cassian’s twelve books, which precede the *Conferences*, and that by this title the books of the *Institutes* are ordinarily distinguished from the books of the *Conferences*. As for their subject and purpose, Cassian himself indicates the difference in that passage: “For these little books”—namely, the *Institutes*—“will more suitably serve the observance of the outward person and the ordering of monasteries; but those other books will pertain rather to the discipline of the inner person, the perfection of the heart, and the life and teaching of the anchorites.” Thus far he.]concerning the perpetual and unceasing constancy of prayer.

When these matters had been explained, and when we had fulfilled the commands of the most blessed in memory, Pope Castor, as well as your desire [Note: On the designation “pope” and “most blessed,” see the note on the author’s first preface at the beginning of the work. Concerning Leontius, we added some observations to the first preface of the *Conferences*, where Cassian adorns him with the same title of honor, just as Faustus, bishop of Riez, does in the preface to his book *On Free Will*, where the inscription reads: “To the most blessed and most reverend Leontius, pope, Faustus”; and at the beginning of the letter: “Because of your pastoral concern, blessed Pope Leontius,” and so forth.

There is, however, great ambiguity, and the matter is difficult to explain, as to which Leontius is meant here. Three bishops of that name are found, all distinguished men, and all nearly contemporaries of one another and of our Cassian—or at least close to him in age—and all Gallicians: the bishops of Arles, Fréjus, and Bordeaux.

Jacques Sirmond, theologian of the Society of Jesus, asserts in his notes on Sidonius, against Savary’s opinion, that Sidonius Apollinaris’s third letter of Book VI was written to Leontius of Arles. “There are many things,” he says, “in Sidonius’s words which identify the man of Arles, such as his reference to the privilege of the place and to toga-clad men pleading there; and there is no doubt that the bishop of Arles at that time was Leontius. This is shown by the letters of Pope Hilary, from which we also learn that Leontius took possession of the see in the year 462, approximately ten years before Sidonius; further, by the Council of Arles mentioned by Faustus, over which that same Leontius presided; and by Ruricius’s fifteenth letter to Aeonius, in which he indicates that Aeonius succeeded Leontius, now dead.”

Thus Sirmond, confirming his view concerning Leontius of Arles with considerable plausibility.

The extremely careful historian Baronius, however, opposes him in two places, where he maintains that the Leontius to whom Sidonius writes was not the bishop of Arles but the bishop of Fréjus. First, after recalling, and largely quoting, under the year of Christ 445, Pope Leo’s letter against Hilary addressed to the bishops of Gaul in the province of Vienne (*Leo, Letter* 90), Baronius adds:

“The pontiff also added a warning to those same bishops not to impose a sentence of excommunication for a trivial cause; and he appointed Bishop Leontius so that future synods in that province might be held with his consent. That Leontius was the bishop of Fréjus in Gaul Narbonensis, a man famous for his reputation. To him there survives a letter of Sidonius Apollinaris, in which he honors him with these praises: ‘Our mediocrity in the age of our life, the period of our dignity, the privilege of our place, the praise of our learning, and the gift of your conscience are easily surpassed by you,’ and so forth. Sidonius addressed these words to Leontius when he was already bishop of Auvergne” (*Sidonius*, Book VI, Letter 3; Book VII, Letter 6). “He also mentions him in a letter to Basil.”

Thus Baronius.

Again, under the year of Christ 465, in the fifth year of Pope Hilary, he says:

“There survives a letter of Pope Hilary to Leontius, Veranus, and Victorius, bishops, to whom he delegates the investigation and restoration of the rights of the bishop of Embrun, metropolitan of the Maritime Alps. Leontius is placed first among the bishops to whom the case is entrusted. Although no mention is made of the church over which he presided, you should nevertheless recognize him as the very man praised by Hilary of Arles in his funeral oration for Saint Honoratus, his predecessor as bishop. I believe him to be the bishop of Fréjus to whom the letters of Sidonius Apollinaris are extant.

Hilary of Arles also mentions this same Leontius of Fréjus in the *Life of Saint Honoratus*, saying: ‘Accordingly, because of the excessive heat and fear of poisonous creatures, he sought an island lying not far beneath the Alpine ridge; besides the advantage of solitude, he was attracted by the neighborhood and bound by the affection of the holy and most blessed man in Christ, Bishop Leontius, although many tried to deter him from so novel an undertaking.’”

From this Baronius also teaches that Saint Honoratus, returning to his own people at Arles, first took up residence on the island of Lérins—which was infested with serpents—at the advice above all of Leontius, the neighboring bishop of Fréjus; and that, when the serpents withdrew, Honoratus built a church and monastery there and received those who had fled from the world in order to cultivate the monastic life.

As for what Baronius had said above concerning Sidonius’s letters to Leontius of Fréjus, he appears to have corrected it in the appendix to the *Annals* (Volume X), where, while praising Sirmond in opposition to himself and adopting his opinion, he names Caesarius of Arles—who, he says, occupied that see in the year of the Lord 524—as the successor of this Leontius, who succeeded Aeonius and was himself succeeded by Ravennius. It follows, therefore, that Leontius too was bishop of Arles.

These considerations make Savary’s note on that passage of Sidonius concerning Leontius of Fréjus extremely weak and uncertain. Savary says that Leontius “subscribed the Council of Lyons and Faustus’s letter against the presbyter Lucifer,” as is clear from Faustus’s letter to Lucifer at the end of *On Free Will*, and from Lucifer’s letter to Leontius and the others. He also identifies him with the hermit Cassian mentions in the first and ninth prefaces of the *Conferences*. Thus Savary interprets both of Cassian’s passages as referring to Leontius of Fréjus.

Finally, there was a third Leontius, of Bordeaux, later than the preceding two, as Sirmond noted (*ibid.*). Venantius Fortunatus mentions him in his poems (Books I and IV), as does Gregory of Tours in *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 65. From these sources Baronius gathers further information under the year of the Lord 566.

Here, indeed, reader, you may well be astonished at the instability or uncertainty of human judgment in so great a writer: the man whom Baronius had first judged to be bishop of Fréjus, and afterward bishop of Arles, to whom those letters of Sidonius were addressed, he finally, after changing his opinion once more, declares to have been bishop of Bordeaux.]

—or, most blessed Pope Leontius, and holy brother [Note: In the same way Cassian addresses him in the first preface, distinguishing him from Leontius in such a manner as to indicate that he was not a bishop but a monk or anchorite, when he dedicated these *Conferences* to him and added this commendation: “The other adopted the lofty practices of the anchorites, not, like some, undertaking to follow them by his own presumption; rather, having grasped, through the prompting of the Holy Spirit, the legitimate path of instruction almost before learning it, he preferred to be formed not so much by his own inventions as by their traditions.” Thus far he.

Nothing else concerning this Helladius presently occurs that could help establish the matter or provide some knowledge of him, except that in Saint Leo’s fifty-second letter, written to all the bishops of Gaul, Helladius is named among the others, and not among the least. One may conjecture that this is the very man in question, both from the chronology and from other indications. For it is credible that, because of the merit of his holiness, for which he is commended here, he was afterward advanced to the episcopate—namely, during the time of Saint Leo the pope. Cassian had already been asked by Leo, then archdeacon of the city of Rome, to write books against Nestorius concerning the Incarnation of the Lord, as Gennadius testifies (*Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, chapter 61). Cassian completed those books at Massilia, where he also ended his life, while Theodosius and Valentinian were reigning, after he had long since completed the books of the *Conferences*, as he himself testifies in the preface.

As for Cassian’s calling Helladius “brother,” it is uncertain whether he intended him to be the brother by birth of Leontius, or “brother” according to the common and ancient terminology of monks, or at least one bound to himself or to Leontius by fraternal affection.

Saint Helladius, or Elladius, bishop of Auxerre, is indeed mentioned in ecclesiastical records (*Roman Martyrology*, 8 May). He succeeded Valerian, held office during the reigns of the emperors Constantius and Constantine, and is listed by the records of Democharis as the fifth bishop of that see (*On the Sacred Mass*, Book II, chapter 19). But that man lived much earlier than Pope Leo and our Cassian.]

I believe that I have satisfied you, most blessed Pope Leontius and holy brother Helladius, by first excusing the work’s length. For although we were striving to touch upon many matters in a concise discourse and to pass over many others in silence, the work has been extended much further than we had planned. After a lengthy discussion had been prefaced concerning various institutions—which we preferred to abridge for the sake of brevity—blessed Isaac finally introduced the following words.

## Chapter II. The Words of Abbot Isaac Concerning the Nature of Prayer

The entire aim of the monk, and the perfection of his heart, tends toward continual and uninterrupted perseverance in prayer; and, insofar as human frailty permits, he strives toward unshakable tranquility of mind and perpetual purity. In order to possess this, we diligently seek and continually practice every labor of the body and every contrition of the spirit, and there is between the two a certain reciprocal and inseparable union.

For just as the whole structure of the virtues tends toward the perfection of prayer, so, unless all these things are bound and compacted together by prayer’s summit, they cannot in any way remain firm or stable. For just as this perpetual continuity of prayer and constant tranquility of which we speak cannot be acquired or perfected without the virtues, so neither can the virtues that prepare the way for it be completed without its continual practice.

Therefore, we shall neither be able to discuss rightly the affection [Lipsius, in the margin: “effect”] of prayer nor enter by a sudden discussion upon its principal end—which is accomplished through the labor of all the virtues—unless first everything that must either be cut away or prepared for its sake has been enumerated and examined in due order; and unless, following the discipline of the Gospel parable (Luke 14), we have reckoned up and carefully gathered in advance whatever pertains to the construction of that spiritual and most lofty tower [Note: Ciaconius, consulting manuscripts, reads: “After all the purgation of vices had been cleared away, and the fallen, dead rubble of the passions had been dug out,” and so forth. This reading certainly seems more genuine to me, as well as more common.

For what purpose would the phrase “after the fallen supports had been poured out” serve, or what meaning could it have? *Succidia*, or *succidium*, in Varro and other authors means nothing other than a mass of salted pork, preserved for necessary use; and the term is derived either from *succidere*, “to cut off whenever there is need,” or rather from the slaughter of pigs. Thus Varro, in *On Agriculture*, Book II, chapter 4, says that a farmer is lazy or extravagant if he hangs a *succidia* in the meat room obtained from a butcher rather than from his own farm.

*Rudera* are fragments of stones scattered throughout fields or mixed with earth. They are also called *succidua*, because they are inclined to fall, and *mortua*, “dead,” because they are useful for nothing. They are therefore customarily dug out and cleared away down to the living and solid earth, as is said here, so that foundations may safely be laid.

Hence a beautiful metaphor is taken and adapted to the laying of a spiritual foundation; this is explained more clearly in the following chapter. Moreover, everyone understands that *repurgium* is used here for “purification”; Cassian uses the same word in the following chapter.], which is to be raised by the labor of spiritual virtues.

Yet these preparations will be of no benefit, nor will they permit the lofty summits of perfection to be placed properly one upon another, unless every purgation of vices has first been cleared away, and the *succidia* and dead rubble of the passions have been poured out, and the strongest foundations of simplicity and humility have been laid upon the living—as they say—solid earth of our breast, or rather upon that evangelical rock. Upon these foundations the tower can be built by the labor of the spiritual virtues, firmly stabilized so that it may rise with confidence in its own strength to the highest summits of heaven.

For when it rests upon foundations of this kind, even if the most abundant rains of the passions pour down upon it, even if violent torrents of persecution strike it like a battering ram, even if the savage storm of hostile spirits rushes upon it and presses against it, the assault will not only fail to overthrow it, but will not even disturb it in any significant way.

## Chapter III. How Pure and Sincere Prayer Is Prepared

And therefore, if prayer is to be uttered with the fervor and purity with which it ought, the following things must be observed in every respect.

First, concern for carnal matters must be cut away altogether. Next, not only anxiety over any business or cause, but even its memory, must be completely excluded. Detraction, empty talk, or excessive talk, as well as buffoonery, must likewise be cut off. Above all, the disturbance of anger or sadness must be uprooted completely; the harmful tinder of carnal desire and love of money must be torn out by the roots.

When these and similar vices have thus been entirely expelled and cut away, and the purification we have mentioned—accomplished through the purity of simplicity and innocence—has preceded, the unshakable foundations of profound humility must first be laid [Note: Saint Gregory also says this in *Morals*, Book X, chapter 16:

“Before the times of prayer, one must always carefully examine whatever can be rejected in prayer. Often, while we are free from prayer, we turn over in our minds things that are impure or unlawful. But when the mind raises itself to the practice of prayer, it suffers the images of those things to rebound upon it, because it had previously pressed upon them willingly while idle.”

And further:

“Often we occupy ourselves willingly with worldly cares; and when afterward we devote ourselves to prayer, the mind is in no way lifted toward heavenly things, because the weight of earthly concern has plunged it into the depths.”], foundations capable of supporting the tower that is to enter the heavens. Then the structure of the spiritual virtues must be set upon them, and the mind must be restrained from every restless wandering and slippery distraction, so that gradually it may begin to rise toward the contemplation of God and spiritual vision.

For whatever our soul has conceived before the hour of prayer must necessarily present itself to us in prayer through the intrusion of memory. Therefore, if we wish to be found in a certain condition when we pray, we must prepare ourselves in that condition before the time of prayer.

The mind is formed in supplication according to its preceding state. When we fall down to seek peace, the image of those same actions, words, or thoughts plays before our eyes. It will either make us angry according to our previous disposition, or cause us grief, or make us reconsider former desires or causes; or it will strike us with the titillation of some silly remark or deed—something it is even shameful to mention—through foolish laughter; or it will make us flit back to our former distractions.

Therefore, whatever we do not want to intrude upon us while we pray, let us hasten to drive out beforehand from the hidden places of our breast, so that we may fulfill the Apostle’s command: [Note: These two statements provide the foundation for the following *Conference*, which is the second of Abbot Isaac. Its subject is taken from them: the continuity, or constant practice, of prayer. The matter will therefore be treated more conveniently there (*Conference* X, chapter 14).] “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5); and, “Lifting up holy hands in every place, without anger or disputation” (1 Timothy 2).

For we shall otherwise be unable to fulfill this command unless our mind, purified from every contagion of vice and devoted only to the virtues as though they were natural goods, feeds continually upon contemplation of almighty God.

## Chapter IV. The Mobility of the Soul Compared with a Feather or Small Wing [Another reading: “compared”]

Indeed, the soul is not inappropriately compared with a very fine feather or the lightest wing. If it has not been spoiled or soaked through by the corrupting effect of some external moisture, it is naturally lifted toward lofty and heavenly things by the mobility of its substance, with the assistance of the lightest breath.

But if it has been weighed down by a sprinkling or infusion of some moisture, it will not merely be carried by its natural mobility into any aerial flight; it will also be pressed down toward the lowest depths of the earth by the weight of the moisture it has absorbed.

So too our mind, if it has not been burdened by encroaching vices and worldly cares, or corrupted by the moisture of harmful lust, will be lifted by the natural benefit of its purity and raised toward the heights by the lightest breath of spiritual meditation. Abandoning lowly and earthly things, it will be transferred to heavenly and invisible realities.

For this reason we are rightly warned by the Lord’s commands: “See to it that your hearts are not weighed down with feasting, drunkenness, and worldly cares” (Luke 21). And therefore, if we want our prayers to penetrate not only the heavens but also what is above the heavens, let us take care to bring the mind, cleansed of all earthly vices and purified of every filth of the passions, to its natural elevation, so that its prayer may ascend to God without being weighed down by any burden of vice.

## Chapter V. The Causes by Which Our Mind Is Weighed Down

We should nevertheless note the causes by which the Lord indicated that the mind is weighed down. He did not mention adultery, fornication, murder, blasphemy, or robbery—things whose mortality and condemnability no one is ignorant of—but gluttony, drunkenness, and worldly cares or anxieties (Luke 21).

These are so little avoided or judged condemnable by anyone in this world that some people—even those who, shameful as it is to say, call themselves monks—become entangled in these very distractions as though they were harmless and useful. [Note: Namely, gluttony, drunkenness, and worldly cares or anxieties, in which monks sometimes become entangled.]

Although these three things, when committed literally, weigh down the soul, separate it from God, and press it down toward earthly things, avoiding them is nevertheless easy—especially for us, who are separated from all association with this world by such a long withdrawal, and who have absolutely no occasion to mingle with these visible cares, drunkennesses, and gluttonies.

But there is another spiritual gluttony and drunkenness that is more difficult to avoid, as well as a worldly care and anxiety that frequently entangles us even after we have perfectly renounced all our possessions and abstained from every kind of wine and banquet, and even while we are established in solitude. Concerning these the prophet says: [Note: In the royal Bibles this passage is read in Greek as follows: “Wake up, you who are drunk from your wine” (*eknēpsate hoi methyontes ex oinou autōn*); that is, “Awaken, you who are drunk from their wine,” or, as Jerome rendered it, “in your wine.”

Jerome nevertheless acknowledges that among the Septuagint the reading is: “And not from wine.” His words occur in his commentary on Joel, chapter 1, where he lists the various forms of spiritual drunkenness meant here in this way:

“Nothing intoxicates like mental disturbance. There is a drunkenness that leads to death. This is the detestable drunkenness. There is anger, which does not accomplish God’s righteousness, and which makes a person nearly incapable of controlling his mind, so that his lips tremble, his teeth chatter, and his face changes color.

“What shall I say of joy and pleasure, and especially of love, which blinds the eyes of the heart and permits the lover to think of nothing except what he loves? Is this not to be called drunkenness, when, because of a worthless prostitute and a shameful bodily member, the freedom of the soul bends toward servile caresses; when it prepares future wealth for pleasure through theft, crime, and perjury; and when, although everyone sees it, it thinks that it is not seen?

“Greed also blinds the mind of the person for whom nothing is enough, as do feminine fear and desire for sweet vices. Hence it is said to them: ‘Awaken and rouse yourselves, you who are drunk,’ not from wine—as is contained only in the Septuagint—but from every disturbance of vices.”

Thus Saint Jerome.

Cassian therefore followed here what he regarded as the genuine reading of the Septuagint, whereas the Vulgate reads: “Awaken, you drunkards, and weep and howl, all you who drink wine in sweetness, because it has perished from your mouth.”]

“Awaken,” he says, “you who are drunk, and not from wine” (Joel 1).

Another passage says: “Be stunned and astonished; stagger and totter; become drunk, and not from wine; be shaken, and not by drunkenness” (Isaiah 29).

The wine of this drunkenness and gluttony must consequently, according to the prophet, be the fury of dragons. Observe also from what root this wine proceeds: “Their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their branch from Gomorrah. Do you wish also to recognize the fruit of this vine and the sprout of its branch? Their grapes are grapes of gall; their cluster is bitterness to them” (Deuteronomy 32).

Unless we are cleansed from all vices and sober from the gluttony of every passion, without drunkenness from wine and without an abundance of banquets, our heart will be weighed down by a drunkenness and gluttony far more harmful.

For the fact that worldly cares can sometimes fall upon even us, who take part in none of the activities of this world, is clearly demonstrated by the rule of the elders. They defined everything that exceeds the necessity of daily sustenance and the unavoidable use of the body as belonging to worldly care and anxiety.

For example, if the work of earning one coin could meet the needs of our body, but we chose to extend ourselves through more intensive work and labor in order to acquire two or three coins; and [Note: This is an important passage concerning the frugality and moderation monks ought to practice, and the luxury and excess they ought to avoid, both in daily expenses and in clothing, cells, rooms, and dwellings.

As regards clothing, some monks greatly offend in this matter. Not content with one or two decent habits, they acquire and accumulate a large quantity of garments and equipment from every source. They cannot rest unless they somehow obtain five or six tunics, just as many robes, just as many cloaks, and as many other garments, so that they may have new and different changes of clothing for almost every week, not to say every day, although one or two sets would be more than sufficient.

In this matter they display great forgetfulness of, or negligence toward—if not contempt for—the Rule and their profession. The Rule says that two tunics and two cowls are sufficient for a monk (Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 55). And in all things the statement in the Acts of the Apostles must be considered: “It was distributed to each according to his need” (Acts 5), and no more.

They also disregard their profession, through which they embraced evangelical poverty, with which that luxury and abundance of garments are directly at odds, and which they solemnly promised to observe.

Hence the Council of Trent (Session 25, chapter 2, *On Regulars*) gravely decrees that superiors should permit religious to use movable goods—including, without doubt, clothing above all—in such a way that their possessions correspond to the state of poverty they have professed, and that there be nothing superfluous in them, while nothing necessary is denied them. If anyone is found to possess anything otherwise, he is to be deprived for two years of both active and passive voice, and is also to be punished according to the constitutions of his Rule and order (see chapters 7 and 55 of the Rule).

For more concerning the abuse and excess of clothing, see Turrecremata and Trithemius.]

although the covering of two tunics would be sufficient, one for night and one for day, we seek to become owners of three or four tunics [Note: Cuychius observed that in some manuscripts *Domini* is read in place of *nobis*, in others *Demum*, and in several manuscripts the word *Domini* has been deleted. He rightly rejected that deletion. Abbot Isaac means that although the covering of two tunics or robes is sufficient, we are nevertheless not content with these and seek, as explained above, to become possessors of three or four tunics.]

And although the dwelling of one or two cells would be sufficient, taking delight in worldly ambition and spaciousness, we construct four or five cells, themselves more elaborately adorned and more spacious than use requires [Note: That is, worldly ambition, as Dionysius explained.], displaying wherever we can the passion of worldly desire.

## Chapter VI. The Vision of an Elder Concerning the Restless Activity of a Brother

Clear experience has taught us that this does not happen without demonic prompting.

A certain highly esteemed elder was passing by the cell of a brother who suffered from the illness of mind we have described: he was constantly exhausting himself in daily distractions by building and repairing unnecessary things. From a distance the elder saw him crushing an extremely hard stone with a heavy hammer. He also saw an Ethiopian standing beside him, striking the stone together with him by joining and interlocking his hands with the blows of the hammer, and driving him to persist in that labor with burning torches [Note: We have already shown above, by many examples, that a demon commonly appears in the form of an Ethiopian (*Conference* II, chapter 13), and many other examples could be added.].

The elder stood there for a very long time, marveling either at the pressure exerted by so fierce a demon or at the deception of so great an illusion.

For when the brother, exhausted by excessive fatigue, wished to rest and bring the work to an end, he was nevertheless stirred by the prompting of that spirit to take up the hammer again and was driven not to abandon the purpose of the work he had begun. Thus, sustained without tiring by the same incitements, he did not feel the injury of so great a labor.

At last the elder, moved by such a dreadful demonic deception, turned aside to the brother’s cell. After greeting him, he said: “What, brother, is this work you are doing?”

The brother replied: “We are laboring against this extremely hard stone, and we have scarcely managed to crush it at last.”

The elder answered: “You have spoken well: ‘We have scarcely managed.’ For you were not alone when you were striking it. There was another with you whom you did not see. He stood beside you in this work, not so much as a helper as a most violent driver.”

Therefore, abstinence from those activities that we cannot undertake even if we wish, and contempt for those things whose desire would immediately make us blameworthy both before spiritual men and before worldly people, do not sufficiently prove that the disease of worldly ambition is absent from our minds [Note: In our earlier edition, through an error and great typographical carelessness, the word *non* was omitted here. Cuychius found the same defect in some older copies, as can be seen in his corrective notes. Once the word is removed, the resulting meaning becomes completely contrary to the truth and no less contrary to the author’s intention, as is clear to anyone who pays attention.

The true meaning is the one Dionysius Carthusianus clarified in his paraphrase—or rather through a clearer syntax and an orderly arrangement of the words, as grammarians call it—in this way:

“Abstinence from, or cessation of, those activities that we cannot carry out even if we wished to do so, and contempt for those things whose desire would make us blameworthy at first sight both in the presence of spiritual men and before worldly people, do not sufficiently show that the sin of worldly ambition is not present in our minds. Rather, this is shown when, with strict severity of mind, we reject even those things that lie within our power and that seem capable of being possessed with some degree of propriety.”

Thus Dionysius.

The French version of these *Conferences*, published by Jean Lavardin together with Dom Cuychius’s annotations, likewise agrees very well with this interpretation. Possevinus, however, does not mention this version in his apparatus among Lavardin’s works [Note: The author does not mention this translation.]. The French translator rendered the passage in his own language as follows:

“For this reason, not only abstinence from, or delay in, those affairs which we cannot carry out even if we wished; nor contempt and rejection of those things which, if we desired and coveted them, would immediately make us blameworthy both in the presence of spiritual men and before worldly people, sufficiently show that the sin of worldly ambition does not rest within our spirits; but rather, this is shown when, with strict severity of soul, we reject everything that lies within our power and that seems capable of being retained or possessed with some degree of propriety.”

Thus far the French translator.

It is clear that our speaker is here referring to the final words of the preceding chapter, where he had described the vice of ambition in certain monks as follows:

“Although the dwelling of one or two cells is sufficient, taking delight in worldly ambition and spaciousness, we construct four or five cells, and these more elaborately adorned and more spacious than use requires, displaying wherever we can the passion of worldly desire.”]

Rather, this is shown when even those things that lie within our power and seem to be permissible under some pretext of propriety are rejected with strict severity of mind.

And truly, these things that seem small and insignificant, and that we see admitted without concern by those who share our profession, weigh down the mind according to their character no less than the greater things that ordinarily intoxicate the minds of worldly people according to their condition, not allowing [alternative reading: “nor do they allow”] the monk, once earthly dregs have been set aside, to breathe freely toward God, upon whom his attention ought always to be fixed. For a monk must believe that even a slight separation from that highest good is present death and most destructive ruin.

When the mind has been established in such tranquility, freed from every bond of carnal passions, and its attention of heart has clung most firmly to that one and highest good, it will fulfill the Apostle’s command: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5); and, “Lifting up pure hands in every place, without anger or disputation” (1 Timothy 2).

Through this purity, with the mind, so to speak, absorbed and transformed from its earthly condition into spiritual and angelic likeness, whatever it receives within itself, whatever it considers, whatever it does, will be the purest and most sincere prayer.

## Chapter VII. Is It More Difficult to Guard Good Thoughts Than to Prepare Them?

[Col. 0779A]

Germanus: Would that we could possess the permanence of spiritual thoughts with the same ease with which we generally conceive their seeds.

[Col. 0779C] You may observe a notable example of this in Saint Augustine, especially throughout the eighth book of his *Confessions*, in which he describes the beginning of his conversion; compare this passage with chapters 17 and 18 of the first Conference, where the mobility of thoughts and the instability of the mind are discussed. For when they have been conceived in our heart either through the memory of Scripture, the recollection of some spiritual acts, or certainly the contemplation of heavenly mysteries, they quickly vanish through some imperceptible flight. And whenever our mind encounters other occasions for spiritual perceptions, with others creeping in, those thoughts too which had been grasped scatter in slippery movement, so that the soul, retaining no constancy of its own and possessing no firmness of holy thoughts by its own power, is believed to have conceived them accidentally rather than deliberately, even when it seems somehow to retain them. For how can their origin be attributed to our will when their persistence does not depend upon us? But lest, while investigating this question, we wander too far from the order of our discussion and delay too long the proposed exposition concerning the state of prayer, reserving this matter for its proper time, let us earnestly seek instruction about the character of prayer, especially since the blessed Apostle urges us never to cease from it, saying: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5). And therefore we first wish to be instructed concerning its character—that is, what prayer ought always to be when uttered—and then how we may possess or practise this same prayer, whatever its nature, without ceasing. For both daily experience and the course of your holiness demonstrate that it cannot be accomplished without great concentration of heart; you have defined the goal of the monk and the summit of all perfection as consisting in the completion of prayer.

## CHAPTER VIII. Isaac’s answer concerning the various kinds of prayer

Isaac: I believe that all the kinds of prayer cannot be comprehended without great contrition of heart, purity of spirit, and illumination by the Holy Spirit. For there are as many kinds as states and qualities can arise in one soul—or rather, in all souls. And therefore, although we know that, because of the dullness of our heart, we cannot discern all the kinds of prayer, nevertheless we shall attempt to arrange them as best we can, insofar as the modest measure of our experience has been able to attain.

[Col. 0779D] Prayer varies according to the varying disposition of the person praying. This is the first division of prayer, and an indefinite one, on the part of the subject.

For according to the measure of purity in which each mind advances, and according to the character of the state into which it is either inclined by circumstances or renewed through its own diligence, the mind itself is continually reshaped from moment to moment. It is therefore absolutely certain that no one can always utter prayers of a uniform character. Each person entreats differently when cheerful, differently when weighed down by sorrow or despair, differently when flourishing through spiritual successes, differently when oppressed by the mass of temptations; differently when seeking pardon for sins, differently when asking for the acquisition of grace or some virtue, or certainly when imploring the eradication of some vice; differently when pierced by consideration of hell and fear of the future judgment, differently when inflamed by hope and desire for future goods; differently when in necessities and dangers, differently when living in security and tranquillity; differently when enlightened by revelations of heavenly mysteries, differently when constrained by barrenness of virtues and dryness of spiritual perceptions.

## CHAPTER IX. On the fourfold kind of prayer

[Col. 0780C] Having thus arranged these matters concerning the character of prayer—not as fully as the greatness of the subject demands, but only as the pressure of time permits, or as the slightness of our intellect and the dullness of our heart are able to contain—there now confronts us the greater difficulty of explaining the kinds of prayer individually. The Apostle distinguished them in a fourfold manner, saying: “I exhort, therefore, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made” (1 Timothy 2).

[Col. 0779D] The Apostle’s words occur in the First Epistle to Timothy, chapter 2: “I exhort, therefore, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made,” and so forth. Similar are the words in Philippians 4: “In every prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.” By these words the Apostle is considered to have wished to distinguish four kinds or forms of prayer.

First, then, it should be noted that some consider the first three terms to be synonymous, employed and piled up together by the Apostle for greater emphasis and force of exhortation. Accordingly, they think that the Apostle did not intend by these words to indicate any division, but rather to impress the same matter through several synonymous expressions. Thus Theophylact, following Chrysostom.

The more common and probable opinion of the other Fathers, however, is that different kinds of prayer are designated by these words of the Apostle—as this abbot teaches—and that they are also distinguished in the Greek text. For first stands δεήσεις (*deēseis*), “supplications”; second, προσευχάς (*proseuchas*), “prayers”; third, ἐντεύξεις (*enteuxeis*), “intercessions.”

Second, since this division and distinction appears somewhat obscure, it is necessary to see briefly what the Fathers left written about it. Saint Hilary, writing on Psalm 140, says: “The Apostle signifies that there are four kinds of prayer when he writes to Timothy: ‘I exhort, therefore, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made.’ To supplicate belongs to our humility; to pray, to God’s magnificence; to ask, to faith; to give thanks, to confession and praise.”

Saint Ambrose, Book 6 of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 5: “Prayer,” he says, “ought to begin with the praise of God; then follows supplication, as the Apostle taught when he said: ‘I exhort that supplications and thanksgivings be made.’ The first prayer, therefore, ought to contain the praise of God, the second supplication, the third petition, and the fourth thanksgiving.” Here he places first the prayer that he calls the praise of God.

Saint Augustine, in Letter 59 to Paulinus, discusses these terms at length and refers the whole passage to the liturgy and the sacrifice of the Mass. He says that supplications belong to the prayers made in the Mass before the consecration; prayers belong to the time when the host is blessed and consecrated and broken for distribution—that is, from the consecration until communion. He says that petitions are the prayers by which the people are blessed. “For then,” he says, “the bishops—that is, overseers or pastors—as advocates, offer those entrusted to them—that is, the people committed to their care—to the most merciful compassion.” When these things have been completed and so great a sacrament has been received, thanksgiving concludes everything; the Apostle also commended it as the final element in these words.

Cassian, or Abbot Isaac, discusses this division at considerable length in this Conference and teaches, in summary, that by supplication is understood prayer for the remission of sins; by prayer, vows through which we offer something to God; by petition, or intercession, prayers that we pour out for the salvation of others; and by thanksgiving, praises of God for benefits received.

Saint Bernard, in his sermon “On the Four Ways of Praying” (Volume 1 among the sermons *On Various Matters*), understands supplication as the prayer of a sinner beginning repentance, who employs intercessors because he does not yet dare approach God personally; prayer as the petition of the penitent who asks God personally for pardon; petition as the prayer of the righteous person who asks for the kingdom of heaven and other necessities of salvation; and thanksgiving as the prayer of the perfect person who is certain that he has been heard.

It seems preferable, however, to hear him reason in his own words:

“There are some whom the consciousness of sin still terrifies and torments, since they have not yet received the power to resist—namely, when the Spirit of truth first shines upon them as they lie in the mire of sins, arouses them, makes them blush, and causes them to fear God, while they see the enormity of their crimes, the smallness of their merits, and, as it were, hell burning before them. They are terrified because they find no good in themselves and grasp from elsewhere what may cover them. Since, therefore, they fear—and rightly fear—to approach by themselves, they strive to supplicate as though through others. Such is the kind of prayer in which we commonly say: ‘Holy Peter, pray for us,’ and similar prayers.

“But when he has received the power of self-restraint, the one who is conscious of past offenses approaches confidently, seeking pardon for his sins and using the prayer that is the speech of our mouth, when he now speaks with his own mouth to his God. Hence it is that Mary Magdalene, although no less humble than that woman suffering from hemorrhage (Luke 7), nevertheless does not fear to approach in this way: she waters the feet with her tears, wipes them with her hair, anoints them with perfume, and kisses them with devoted lips (Luke 8). It is therefore sufficiently clear that she had already resolved in her heart to abstain from sin thereafter, and that the flow had, as it were, ceased.

“If you have now attained this, your first task is, while speaking to the Lord himself in prayer, to recall your years in the bitterness of your soul. Then, after persevering for some time in the laments of repentance and acquiring a certain cheerfulness and confidence in forgiveness, proceed to petitions, so that, secure as one received back into the Lord’s favor, you may dare to ask for yourself and your fellow servants what is fitting.

“As for the fourth kind of prayer, which is thanksgiving, I believe that very few attain it; and the rarer it is, the more precious. For he will find abundant grace with God who, according to God’s promise, is heard before he calls, and whose spirit bears witness to his spirit that he has from God, because his desire has been heard, so that he can now be certain that he should not pray but give thanks. Thus you have it in the raising of Lazarus, where the Lord, although he had previously prayed for nothing, says: ‘Father, I give you thanks because you have heard me’ (John 11).

“The first, therefore—that is, supplication—should be made with a bashful disposition. The second, which we have properly called prayer, should be made with a pure disposition, so that we neither conceal our sins nor flatter ourselves, knowing that each person finds grace with God if he is found to be a harsh judge of himself. The third, namely petition, seeks a generous disposition and breadth of confidence, as it is written: ‘Let him ask in faith, doubting nothing.’ The fourth, which is thanksgiving, ought to be filled with the fullest devotion and overflowing delight.”

Thus far the words of Saint Bernard, with many intervening passages omitted to avoid prolixity.

Saint Thomas, explaining this same division (*Summa theologiae* II-II, question 83, article 1), writes that three things are necessary in every prayer. First, the mind must be joined to God; this takes place through prayer, which is the elevation and ascent of the mind to God. Second, something must be requested from God; this takes place through petition. Third, some reason must be proposed for obtaining what is requested; and this reason, he says, is either on God’s side or on the petitioner’s side.

The first and principal reason for obtaining something on God’s side is his goodness, on account of which we ask to be heard, according to Daniel 9: “For your own sake, incline your ear, my God.” Another reason is the merit of Christ, which is also presented through supplication, the profoundly sacred appeal by which we say: “By your nativity, deliver us, O Lord.” The reason for obtaining something on the petitioner’s side is thanksgiving, because by giving thanks for benefits received we merit greater benefits, as is said in the collect.

Saint Thomas then explains that all these elements are found and observed in the collect for the Holy Trinity. When we say, “Almighty and eternal God,” that is prayer. When we add, “You have granted your servants, in the confession of the true faith, to acknowledge the glory of the eternal Trinity,” and so forth, that is thanksgiving. When we add, “Grant, we ask, that we may always be defended from every adversity by the steadfastness of the same faith,” that is petition. When we conclude, “Through our Lord Jesus Christ,” and so forth, that is supplication.

Saint Thomas then adds, referring to this passage of Cassian: “In the Conferences of the Fathers it is said that supplication is imploration for sins, prayer is made when we vow something to God, and petition when we ask for others. But the first is better.” Thus he himself.

[Col. 0781A] It must by no means be doubted, therefore, that these were divided by the Apostle in this manner, not without reason. First we must investigate what is signified by supplication, what by prayer, what by petition, and what by thanksgiving. Then we must inquire whether these four kinds are to be assumed equally by the person praying—that is, whether all are to be joined together in every supplication—or whether they are to be offered alternately and individually, so that at one time supplications, at another prayers, at another petitions or thanksgivings, should be uttered. Or perhaps one person ought to offer supplications and another thanksgivings to God, according to the measure of his age—that is, according to the degree in which each mind advances through the diligence of its intention.

## CHAPTER X. On the order of the kinds of prayer

[Col. 0782A] Therefore the properties of the nouns and verbs themselves must first be treated, and the difference between prayer, supplication, and petition must be examined. Then, similarly, it must be investigated whether they are to be offered individually or together.

[Col. 0782D] That is, whether these four conditions or parts of prayer occur and are required in every prayer, or whether they are found separately in different kinds or parts of prayer. The question is answered below, in chapter 15.

Third, it must be investigated whether the very order arranged by the Apostle’s authority teaches the hearer anything further, or whether this distinction should simply be accepted and regarded as having been arranged by him in such a manner without difference—which seems to me quite absurd. For we must not believe that the Holy Spirit spoke anything through the Apostle in passing or without reason. And therefore, in the order with which we began, let us review each point as the Lord grants.

## CHAPTER XI. On supplication

“I exhort, therefore, first of all, that supplications be made” (1 Timothy 2).

[Col. 0783B] Saint Augustine, in the passage cited above (Letter 59), reads *deprecationes*, “prayers of deprecation,” instead of *obsecrationes*, and distinguishes it from prayers or supplications in this way: “Many consider *precari* and *deprecari* to mean the same thing, and this has entirely prevailed in ordinary usage. But those who spoke Latin more precisely used *precationes* when wishing for good things and *deprecationes* when avoiding evils. For they said that *precari* meant to wish for good things by praying; *imprecari*, to wish evil, which is now commonly called cursing; and *deprecari*, to drive something away by praying.”

Supplication is imploration or petition for sins, by which each person, moved to compunction either for present or past offenses, begs forgiveness.

## CHAPTER XII. On prayer

Prayers are those by which we offer or vow something to God.

[Col. 0783B] Cassian appears to have read in the Apostle’s text εὐχάς (*euchas*), “vows,” whereas in the Greek text now current one does not read εὐχάς but προσευχάς (*proseuchas*), that is, “prayers.” Saint Augustine also approves and confirms this reading (in the passage cited above) in such a way as to refute Cassian’s contrary reading in these words:

“‘Prayers,’ which the Greek has as προσευχάς, are exceedingly difficult to distinguish from petitions or supplications. But since some manuscripts do not have *prayers* but *adorations*, because the Greek does not say εὐχάς but προσευχάς, I do not think that this was translated knowingly; for it is very well known that the Greeks call προσευχάς ‘prayers.’ Certainly it is one thing to pray and another to adore.”

And below, explaining the same distinction more clearly, he says:

“For the term which they call εὐχή Scripture rarely uses in such a way that it means prayer; rather, much more commonly and habitually it calls a vow εὐχή. But προσευχή, the word as it is used in the passage under discussion, it always calls prayer. Hence, as I said above, some learned men, considering the origin of the word, have wished to call προσευχή not ‘prayer’ but ‘adoration’; yet adoration is more properly called προσκύνησις. But because prayer is sometimes called εὐχή, προσευχή was taken to mean adoration.

“Moreover, if, as I have said, εὐχή is more commonly called a vow in Scripture, then, apart from the general name ‘prayer,’ that prayer is properly understood which we make toward a vow—that is, πρὸς εὐχήν. Everything offered to God is vowed, especially the offering of the holy altar.”

Thus far Saint Augustine.

Gregory of Nyssa explains the force and difference of both terms in nearly the same sense, in these words (*Oration 2 on the Lord’s Prayer*, Matthew 6):

“When you pray,” he says, “he did not say ὅταν εὔχησθε, that is, ‘when you make vows,’ but ὅταν προσεύχησθε, ‘when you pray,’ as though the duty pertaining to a vow ought already to have been performed before God is approached through prayer.

“But what is the difference between these terms with respect to their meaning? εὐχή, that is, a vow, is a promise of some thing that is dedicated in the name of piety and assigned to sacred purposes; προσευχή, however, that is, prayer, is a petition for good things offered to God with supplication.

“Since, therefore, we need confidence in order to speak freely when we approach God to ask for our benefits, the duty belonging to a vow must necessarily precede, so that, having performed the duty which ought to have been performed by us, we may then confidently ask God in return for a benefit. For this reason the Prophet says: ‘I will pay my vows to you, which my lips have uttered’ (Psalm 65). And: ‘Make vows and pay them to the Lord your God’ (Psalm 46).

“And shortly afterward: The Word therefore teaches us not to ask anything from God before we have offered him some gift that is acceptable and pleasing. One must vow first and then pray, just as one must sow before receiving fruits. Therefore we must first cast down the seeds of the vow, and then receive from those seeds the grown and ripened harvest, obtaining our reward through prayer. Since, as it were, conversation cannot be held with confidence unless access has been opened by a prior vow and gift, the vow must necessarily precede prayer.”

Thus Gregory of Nyssa.

From these words we understand why prayer, by which we ask for some good, is called προσευχή: a vow is called εὐχή, and those ask God for good things with confidence who have previously vowed some good to him.

So that the reader may not miss anything noted by others concerning this passage, I have decided to insert here, as I began to do above (Conference 8, chapter 17), the annotation of Peter Maturus, which agrees with what has already been said; I shall do the same in the following passages.

Thus he writes in his notes on Saint Antoninus (Title 15, chapter 2, section 8):

“The Greek word εὐχή, which Cassian has translated as ‘prayer,’ means *votum* in Latin, both among secular and sacred writers. Without bringing forward anything from external authors, this is clear from the following passages of Sacred Scripture:

Genesis 28: Καὶ ηὔξατο Ἰακὼβ εὐχὴν λέγων, that is: ‘And Jacob vowed a vow, saying.’

Genesis 31: Καὶ ηὔξω μοι εὐχήν, that is: ‘You vowed a vow to me.’

Leviticus 7: καὶ ἐὰν εὐχὴ ᾖ, ἢ ἑκούσιον θυσιάζῃ τὸ δῶρον αὐτοῦ, that is: ‘And if it is a vow, or if he offers his gift as a voluntary sacrifice.’

And similarly in many other places.

“By using ‘prayer’ for ‘vow,’ Cassian plainly shows that monks were already bound in that age by the three vows to which religious persons are bound today—especially obedience, when they prayed or vowed that, dead to all the acts of the world, they would serve the Lord with the full intention of their heart; poverty, when, rejecting all riches, they promised to cleave to the Lord in contrition of heart and poverty of spirit; and finally chastity, when they openly professed that they would offer the purest chastity of body and steadfast patience of mind.

“Thus the claim made by certain recent critics of monks—that those ancient leaders and followers of the religious life were not so free in this state of life that it was permitted them to depart from their purpose whenever they wished—is false.”

Thus he.

[Col. 0784A] For when the Greek says τὰς εὐχάς μου τῷ Κυρίῳ ἀποδώσω, the Latin reads: “I will pay my vows to the Lord” (Psalm 115). According to the proper meaning of the word, this could be expressed: “I will return my prayers to the Lord.”

What we read in Ecclesiastes—“If you have vowed a vow to God, do not delay in paying it” (Ecclesiastes 5)—is written simply in Greek as ἐὰν εὔξῃ εὐχὴν Κυρίῳ, that is:

[Col. 0784D] The Abbot interprets εὐχήν as “prayer,” but this is not in accordance with the mind and judgment of Saints Augustine and Gregory, as has just been seen. Saint Jerome, translating from the Septuagint, renders it: “If you have vowed anything to God, do not delay in paying it.” This is also the reading of the Vulgate.

“If you have prayed a prayer to the Lord, do not delay in paying it.”

This will be fulfilled by each of us in the following way. We pray when, renouncing this world, we promise that, dead to all worldly acts and conduct, we shall serve the Lord with the full intention of our heart. We pray when we promise, having despised secular honor and rejected earthly riches, to cleave to the Lord in complete contrition of heart and poverty of spirit. We pray when we promise that we shall perpetually offer the purest chastity of body or steadfast patience; or when we vow to uproot completely from our heart the roots of anger or of sorrow that produces death.

If, having been loosened by negligence and returning to our former vices, we fail to do these things, we shall be guilty of our prayers and vows, and it will be said to us: “It is better not to vow than to vow and not pay” (Ecclesiastes 5).

[Col. 0785D] Saint Jerome translates: “It is much better not to vow than, after vowing, not to fulfil one’s promises.” Or, from the Hebrew: “It is better not to vow than to vow and not pay.”

According to the Greek this can be said: “It is better not to pray than to pray and not pay.”

## CHAPTER XIII. On petition

[Col. 0785D] Saint Augustine reads “intercessions.” Writing back to Paulinus (Letter 59), he says:

“As for intercessions, since our manuscripts have them, I believe that you have placed ‘petitions’ according to your manuscripts. In these two expressions—that is, where some have translated ‘petitions’ and others ‘intercessions’—they wished to render by one word what the Greek has as ἐντεύξεις. And certainly you notice the issue. But you know that to intercede is one thing and to petition another. We do not usually say, ‘They petition in order to intercede,’ but ‘They intercede in order to petition.’ Nevertheless, because of the closeness of the terms, the word has been used whose very proximity supplies the meaning, and it should not be censured as though by a censor’s mark. It is also said of the Lord Jesus Christ himself that he intercedes for us (Romans 8). Does he intercede and not also petition? Indeed, because he petitions, ‘intercedes’ has been put in his place,” and so forth.

In the third place come petitions, which we also commonly utter for others when we are established in the fervor of the spirit: for our loved ones, or asking for the peace of the whole world; and, to express it in the Apostle’s own words, when we supplicate “for all people, for kings, and for all who are in high positions” (1 Timothy 2).

## CHAPTER XIV. On thanksgiving

[Col. 0786D] In Greek, εὐχαριστία derives from the verb εὐχαριστέω, which means “to give thanks” both in sacred and secular authors. Hence the sacrament of the altar is called the Eucharist, or otherwise the sacrament of thanksgiving, because through its offering and reception we give thanks to God for all his benefits toward us, and especially for this sacrament itself and its fruit.

In the fourth place, then, come thanksgivings, which the mind offers to God through ineffable transports, whether it recalls God’s past benefits, contemplates those present, or looks forward to what and how great God has prepared in the future for those who love him. With this same intention, further prayers are sometimes uttered, when our spirit, beholding with pure eyes the rewards of the saints reserved for the future, is impelled to pour out ineffable thanks to God with immense joy.

## CHAPTER XV. Whether the four kinds of prayer are necessary for everyone together, or individually and alternately

From these four kinds, although occasions for abundant supplications sometimes arise—for we know that very fervent and burning prayers frequently proceed both from the kind of supplication born of compunction for sins, and from the state of prayer that flows from the confidence of offerings and the fulfilment of vows through purity of conscience, and from petition, which proceeds from the ardor of charity, and from thanksgiving, which is generated by consideration of God’s benefits, greatness, and goodness—
