[Col. 0786D] That is, devout prayers, which below he calls “most fervent and burning prayers.” He is referring to Psalm 62: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness, and my mouth shall praise you with joyful lips.” Genebrard aptly says: “Marrow and fatness are symbols of grace and divine consolations. Let your grace satisfy my soul, and then my mouth shall celebrate you with joyful lips. God’s grace is the richest nourishment of souls; consolation, the most delicate.”

[Col. 0786A] —so that it is evident that all the kinds mentioned above are useful and necessary for everyone, and that in one and the same man a varying disposition may now utter pure and most fervent supplications of supplication, now of prayer, now of petition, nevertheless the first appears to belong more particularly to beginners, who are still stung and gnawed by the prick and memory of their vices; the second to those who already stand in spiritual progress and the desire for virtues with a certain elevation of mind; the third to those who, fulfilling their vows through their deeds, are also moved to intercede for others by consideration of their weakness and zeal for charity; the fourth to those who, with the thorn of a punitive conscience already torn from their hearts, now securely contemplate with the purest mind the Lord’s generosity and mercies—those which he either bestowed in the past, grants in the present, or prepares for the future—and are carried toward that burning prayer [alternative reading: ecstasy] which the mouths of human beings can neither comprehend nor express, rapt with the most fervent heart.

[Col. 0786B] Sometimes, however, the mind that advances toward the true disposition of purity and has already begun to take root in it is accustomed to conceive all these things together at once. Sweeping through them all like an incomprehensible and violently rushing flame, it pours out before God ineffable prayers of the purest vigor, which the Spirit himself, interceding with unutterable groanings, sends forth to God without our knowing. At that moment it conceives and pours out in supplication, ineffably, such a quantity as it could not, I will not say utter with its mouth, but not even recall in its own mind at another time.

And someone placed at any level may sometimes be found to utter pure and concentrated prayers. For even from that first and humble rank, which rests upon remembrance of the future judgment, one who still stands under the punishment of fear and dread of the examination may be so pierced at a given moment that he is filled with no less spiritual joy by the richness of supplication than the one who, surveying and passing through God’s generosity by the purity of his heart, is dissolved in ineffable joy and gladness. For, according to the Lord’s saying, he begins to love more because he recognizes that more has been forgiven him.

## CHAPTER XVI. That one must strive gradually toward these kinds of prayer

[Col. 0787A] Nevertheless, as we advance in life and attain perfection in virtue, we ought rather to seek those kinds of supplication that are poured out either from contemplation of future goods or from the ardor of charity—or, to speak more humbly and according to the measure of beginners, those generated by the acquisition of any virtues or the eradication of any vice. For we shall in no way be able to reach those more sublime kinds of supplication mentioned above unless our mind has gradually and step by step advanced through the ordered sequence of these petitions.

## CHAPTER XVII. That Christ made use of these four kinds of supplication

[Col. 0787B] The Lord also graciously initiated us into these four kinds of supplication by his own example, so that in this too he might fulfil what is said of him: “Jesus began both to do and to teach” (Acts 1).

[Col. 0787C] On this expression, see the annotation below on chapter 25 of this Conference.

[Col. 0787C] For he assumes the kind of supplication when he says: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26). Or that which is sung concerning him in the Psalms: “My God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” (Psalm 21), and other similar passages.

It is prayer when he says: “I have glorified you upon earth; I have finished the work which you gave me to do” (John 17). Or: “For them I sanctify myself, so that they too may be sanctified in truth” (ibid.).

It is petition when he says: “Father, those whom you have given me, I will that where I am they also may be with me, so that they may see my glory which you have given me” (ibid.). Or certainly when he says: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23).

It is thanksgiving when he says: “I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and have revealed them to little ones. Yes, Father, because this was pleasing before you” (Matthew 11). Or certainly when he says: “Father, I give you thanks because you have heard me; I knew, however, that you always hear me” (John 11).

Although our Lord distinguished these four kinds of supplication in his examples as to be offered individually and at different times, according to the order we have understood, he also repeatedly showed through his examples that they can all be contained together in a perfect supplication—namely, in the prayer that we read he poured out at great length near the end of the Gospel according to John. Since it would be lengthy to go through the whole of its text, a diligent investigator can learn from the sequence of the reading itself that this is so.

The Apostle also clearly expressed the same meaning in his Epistle to the Philippians, placing these four kinds of supplication in a somewhat altered order and showing that they should sometimes be offered within the fervor of a single supplication. He says:

[Col. 0787C] It should be noted here that “supplication,” “prayer,” and “thanksgiving” are expressed in Greek by the same words as in the Epistle to Timothy cited above; only the name for petition varies. For it is not ἐντεύξεις but αἰτήματα, which properly signifies “requests” or “petitions.” This indication seems to show that the Apostle wished here to explain what he had said elsewhere—namely, that ἐντεύξεις is better understood as “petitions” than as “intercessions,” as Cardinal Bellarmine observed.

[Col. 0788B] “But in every prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God” (Philippians 4). Through this he wished especially to instruct us that thanksgiving ought to be mingled with petition both in prayer and in supplication.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Lord’s Prayer
These forms of supplication are followed by a still higher and more exalted state, which is shaped by contemplation of God alone and by the ardor of charity. Through charity, the mind, dissolved in love for him and most intimately united to God, speaks with him as with its own father, in a special devotion.

[Note: This passage, and the dignity of its subject—namely, the Lord’s Prayer, whose explanation the Author is undertaking—seem to require that we record here some commendations by ancient Fathers and writers, by which they testify that it surpasses all other prayers, or forms of prayer, in: 1. authority; 2. brevity; 3. perfection; 4. order; 5. usefulness or efficacy; and finally, necessity.

1. It surpasses them in authority, because Christ himself both composed it and delivered and taught it with his own most holy mouth; hence it is also called the Lord’s Prayer. Tertullian says in *On Prayer*: “What wonder? God alone could teach how he wished to be prayed to. Therefore, the religious form of prayer was ordered by him; and, proceeding from his own Spirit, when it was then made living by being uttered from the divine mouth, it ascended to heaven by its own privilege, commending to the Father what the Son had taught.” Likewise Cyprian, in the special book he published on this prayer: “He who made us live also taught us to pray, so that when we speak to the Father in the prayer and supplication which the Son taught, we may more readily be heard.”

2. It also surpasses them in brevity. For, as Cyprian likewise observes, “It is the prayer which God taught, who by his instruction compressed all our prayer into a brief saving utterance.” This was foretold through the prophet Isaiah, when, filled with the Holy Spirit, he spoke of God’s majesty and mercy: “Completing and abbreviating the word in righteousness,” he says, “because God will make an abbreviated utterance throughout the whole world” (Isaiah 10). And Saint Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord*, sermon 28: “You see how brief the prayer is, and how full of every virtue.” And in sermon 182, *On Time*: “This prayer, in concise words and seven petitions, embraces every kind of prayer. Christ taught us to pray briefly, since he wishes to grant what is asked quickly.” Alexander of Hales, part IV, question 37: “By this brevity,” he says, “it is more easily understood, better retained, more frequently repeated, less wearisome to the one praying, and it suggests that one will be heard quickly; it implies that one should pray more with feeling than with the mouth, and it reproves the ignorant.”

3. It is more excellent in perfection, because it contains everything that we ought to ask from God. And, as Tertullian says (*ibid.*), it “has embraced not only the proper duties of prayer—the veneration of God and the petition of human beings—but almost the whole discourse of the Lord and the entire commemoration of his discipline, so that in truth a compendium of the whole Gospel is contained in this brief prayer.” Following Tertullian, the blessed Cyprian likewise says (*ibid.*): “What are the mysteries of the Lord’s Prayer, dearest brothers; how many and how great things have been gathered briefly into its utterance, yet are spiritually rich in power! Nothing at all has been omitted which is not contained in the abridgment of heavenly teaching in our prayers and supplications.” Finally, Saint Augustine, in his letter 121 to Proba (chapter 12): “If you run through the words of the holy prayers in their entirety, as I think, you will find nothing that this Lord’s Prayer does not contain and embrace.” And again: “Whatever other words we say, we say nothing other than what is set forth in this Lord’s Prayer, if we pray rightly and appropriately.”

4. It surpasses them in order, because, as Saint Thomas says, in the Lord’s Prayer we ask not only for everything that we may rightly desire, but also in the order in which it ought to be desired (II–II, question 83, article 9). For first we ask for what concerns God’s glory, then for what concerns our salvation; and among the latter, first for eternal things, then for temporal ones.

It also surpasses them in efficacy, or usefulness. “The Father recognizes the words of the Son when we pour out our prayer,” says Cyprian. “And since we have an Advocate with the Father for our sins, when we sinners petition for our offenses, we utter the words of our Advocate. For when he says, ‘Whatever you ask in my name, he will give you,’ how much more effectively do we obtain what we ask in Christ’s name if we ask with his own prayer?” Saint Augustine, homily 42 among the fifty: “We have hope of obtaining our case when such a Jurist has dictated our prayers for us, he who sits at the right hand of the Father. He is our Advocate, who is to come as our Judge” (Bellarminus, book I, *On Good Works*, chapter 4; Durantus, book II, *On the Rites of the Church*, chapter 46).

Finally, this prayer also excels in necessity. All Christians ought to know it and say it frequently. Saint Clement, book VII of the *Apostolic Constitutions* (chapter 25), instructs Christians to recite it three times a day. In canon 9 of the Fourth Council of Toledo, priests and the other clergy are commanded to say the Lord’s Prayer daily, since it is a daily prayer. Finally, the Council of Reims, chapter 2, states that no Christian may fail either to know the Lord’s Prayer by heart, to understand it, or to practice it frequently.]

He therefore instituted the formula of the Lord’s Prayer, saying, “Our Father” (Matthew 6), by which we confess in our own voice that the God and Lord of the universe is Father. By declaring ourselves transferred from a condition of servitude into the adoption of sons, we then add, “Who are in heaven” (ibid.), so that, with complete horror, we may avoid remembering the present life in which we dwell on this earth as something foreign and as that which separates us very far from our Father; rather, we may hasten with the greatest desire toward that region in which we confess that our Father dwells. Let us admit nothing of such a kind as would make us unworthy of this profession of ours and of the great nobility of this adoption, deprive us, as degenerates, of our paternal inheritance, or cause us to incur the anger of his justice and severity.

Having been advanced into this order and rank of sons, we shall burn with that continual devotion which belongs to good sons, so that now we may devote our entire affection not to our own interests but to the glory of our Father, saying to him, “Hallowed be your name” (ibid.). We testify that our desire and our joy are the glory of our Father, becoming imitators of him who said: “He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory; but he who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and there is no injustice in him” (John 7).

Finally, the Vessel of Election, filled with this affection, even wishes to become anathema from Christ, provided that a great multitude of his family may be gained for him, and that the salvation of the whole Israelite people may increase the glory of his Father.

[Note: How the Apostle could have wished to be anathema for his brothers, that is, for the Israelites, and Moses likewise to be erased from the book of life so that the sinful Jews might be forgiven, is explained by teachers in more than one way. Saint Jerome, in his letter to Algasia (Letter 113), takes “anathema” here to mean bodily death: “That anathema sometimes signifies killing can be proved by many testimonies of the Old Testament.” Yet this explanation is not approved by Chrysostom and others, and it seems opposed to what follows, where something more serious than bodily death appears to be signified by Christ; for no one would say that a person who died for his brothers was accursed by Christ. Others think that both the Apostle and Moses spoke hyperbolically in this way, to express their affection and love for the Jews.

For the one who had said shortly before (chapter 8), “I am certain that no creature will be able to separate me from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus,” would not immediately have wished actually to be separated from him. Rather, it is a hyperbolic expression, as Moses’ was also. Others finally reply that the Apostle did not simply wish to be anathema. For he does not say, “I wish to be anathema for my brothers,” but “I wished,” or, as others translate from the Greek, “I could wish”—as though, placed in an ecstasy and excess of love, he had said: “If it could happen and were permitted, I would desire to be separated from Christ for my own people.” This meaning almost coincides with the preceding one.

Similarly, Moses did not simply wish to be erased from the book of life. Rather, so that he might obtain what he was asking in its entirety, he added disjunctively to his petition something he knew God would not do. Thus, partly under the impulse of love, by which he desired good for his people, and partly through his singular confidence in God, by which he firmly believed that he himself would not be erased from the book of life, he spoke in such a way that the other thing he asked for on behalf of his people might be granted by God—as if someone were to say to a dearest friend: “Either grant this, or renounce our friendship.”]

For he securely wishes to perish for Christ who knows that no one can die for life (Romans 9). And again he says: “We rejoice when we are weak, but you are strong” (2 Corinthians 13). And what wonder if the Vessel of Election, for Christ’s glory and the conversion of his brothers and for the privilege of his people, wishes to become anathema from Christ,

[Note: The prophet did not wish to lie—for that is evil and sin in itself, and “we must not do evil so that good may come” (Romans 3). Rather, he wished that what he foretold might not come to pass, preferring to lack the prophetic spirit, by which he could not proclaim anything false, than actually to foresee and foretell the calamity and captivity of his people. Thus we commonly say: “Would that I were lying! Would that I were a false prophet!” This is a proverbial expression by which someone indicates that what he says will certainly happen, that he says it unwillingly, and that he wishes it were not so certain—not that he wishes to lie, but because he wishes that what he knows will happen would not happen.

Saint Jerome explains the passage in this way and likewise illuminates it with the Apostle’s words, as though the prophet were saying to the Jews: “Do not think that I wish to speak, or that I rejoice to proclaim what I see is going to happen. I myself would wish to be anathema for my brothers, who are Israelites. Would that I were speaking from my own imagination, and that I alone, counted among the false prophets, might perish, and that what I say were not true!” and so forth.]

while the prophet Micah also wished to become a liar and alien from the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, provided that the Jewish people might escape those blows and the destruction of captivity which he had foretold in his prophecy: “Would that I were not a man who has the spirit, and that I spoke rather a lie” (Micah 2).

Let us set aside the affection of that lawgiver who, even with his brothers destined to perish, did not refuse to perish, saying: “I beseech you, Lord: this people has committed a great sin; either forgive them this offense, or, if you do not, erase me from the book that you have written” (Exodus 32).

[Note: In this chapter he offers three explanations of the first petition, “Hallowed be your name.”

The first refers to the glory of God’s name, which we ask to become known, to be enlarged, and to be made illustrious by all and among all. Concerning this he said above: “We testify that our desire and our joy are the glory of our Father.” Following this interpretation, Saint Augustine, book II of *The Sermon on the Mount*, says: “We do not ask, ‘Hallowed be your name,’ as though God’s name were not holy, but that it may be held holy by human beings—that is, that it may become known to them in such a way that they do not consider anything holy which they fear offending more.”

The second explanation is that it may be hallowed in us—that is, that we may be holy or persevere in holiness. “For,” he says, “the sanctification of God is our perfection.” Tertullian and Saint Cyprian interpret it in this way. Yet this explanation appears less probable, because according to it this petition would seem to be the same as the third, since the Apostle says (1 Thessalonians 4): “For this is the will of God, your sanctification.”

The third explanation is that, through our good conduct and good works, God’s name may be hallowed and glorified by all. Christ taught this in other words in Matthew 5: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” And the Apostle Peter, in the second chapter of his First Letter: “Keep your conduct honorable among the nations, so that when they speak against you as evildoers, observing your good works, they may glorify God on the day of visitation.” Cyril, in catechesis 5, and Chrysostom, in his commentary on Matthew 6, explain the passage in this way.]

The statement “Hallowed be your name” may also suitably be understood in this way: “The sanctification of God is our perfection.” Thus, when we say to him, “Hallowed be your name,” we say this in other words: “Make us, Father, such that we may either deserve to understand how great your sanctification is, or to receive it—or at least so that you may appear holy in our spiritual conduct.” This is effectively fulfilled in us when people see our good works and glorify our Father who is in heaven (Matthew 5).

## CHAPTER XIX. On the statement, “Your kingdom come”

The second petition of the most pure mind earnestly desires that the kingdom of its Father should come immediately,

[Note: Some explain this petition as referring to the kingdom of God called the kingdom of grace, by which God is said to reign in the hearts and minds of the just through charity and grace, according to the saying in Luke 17: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Ambrose, book V, *On the Sacraments*, chapter 4; Rupert, on Matthew 6). But Bellarmine rejects and refutes this explanation with many arguments (*above*, chapter 6), chiefly because the kingdom of grace is nothing other than obedience to and observance of God’s law, or the carrying out of the divine will; therefore this petition would be confused with the third.

It is therefore better understood as referring to the kingdom of glory, or eternal happiness, which we ask to come to us—that is, to be granted after this life—in the way the Savior commanded us first to seek the kingdom of God. Hence Saint Augustine says to Proba (Letter 12, chapter 11): “We stir up our desire for that kingdom, so that it may come to us and we may reign in it.” The priest and poet Sedulius also splendidly portrayed this in the following verses (*Carmen*, book II):

> May that kingdom come at last—indeed, that kingdom  
> Free from death and without end, to which no periods of time  
> Succeed throughout the ages, because it knows not how to have time;  
> A continuous day without night, where Christ is prince,  
> Embracing his noble head with an everlasting crown,  
> And the victorious soldier rejoices, bearing rich rewards.]

or, in fact, that kingdom in which Christ daily reigns in the saints. This happens when, through the extinction of stinking vices, the devil’s dominion has been driven from our hearts, and God has begun to rule within us through the good fragrance of the virtues: when chastity has reigned after fornication was conquered, tranquility after rage was overcome, and humility after pride was trampled down.

Or certainly it means that kingdom which at the appointed time has been generally promised to all the perfect and sons of God, in which Christ will say to them: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25). With his gaze somehow fixed and his desires directed there, he awaits it and says to him: “Your kingdom come.” For by the testimony of his conscience he knows that, when it appears, he will immediately become a participant in it. No criminal will dare say or wish for this, because whoever knows that, at Christ’s coming, punishment rather than the palm and rewards due to his merits will immediately be repaid to him will not wish even to see the tribunal of the Judge.

## CHAPTER XX. On the statement, “Your will be done”

The third petition

[Note: He explains the third petition of the Lord’s Prayer in two ways.

First, we ask that God’s will be done on earth as it is in heaven—that is, that just as the holy angels in heaven obey God promptly, perfectly, and in all things, so human beings on earth may also obey him perfectly (Augustine, book II of *The Sermon on the Mount*, chapter 11, and Letter 121 to Proba).

Second, we ask that the will of God be fulfilled by which, according to the Apostle, he wishes all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2)—namely, insofar as it depends upon him and by what is called his antecedent will. Yet this explanation is too restricted and particular. For other explanations, see Bellarmine and others (Damascene, book II of *The Faith*, chapter 19).]

is the petition of sons: “Your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.” There can be no greater prayer than to desire that earthly things may deserve to be made equal to heavenly things. For what else is it to say, “Your will be done as in heaven and on earth,” than that human beings may be like angels, and that just as God’s will is fulfilled by them in heaven, so those who are on earth may do, not their own will, but his entire will?

No one will be able to say this from the heart except one who believes that God disposes all things that appear either adverse or favorable for our benefit, and that he is more provident and concerned for the salvation and welfare of his own than we ourselves are for ourselves.

Or it must be understood in another way: God’s will is the salvation of all, according to the blessed Paul’s statement: “He wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2). Concerning this will the prophet Isaiah also says in the person of God the Father: “And all my will,” he says, “shall be done” (Isaiah 46).

[Note: Theologians distinguish two kinds of God’s will: one is the will of sign, and the other the will of good pleasure (Saint Thomas, Part II, question 19, article 11). The will of sign consists in God’s commands and prohibitions, or in whatever God commands or forbids. Just as we call a king’s letters the king’s will, although they are rather its sign. The will of good pleasure is his true and inward will itself, by which God absolutely wills something to happen; and this will is always fulfilled.

The present passage from Isaiah is understood of this latter will, as is also the statement in Psalm 113: “All that the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth,” and in Esther 13: “There is no one who can resist your will.”

The Fathers agree, however, that in the third petition it is not the will of good pleasure but properly the will of sign that is signified. Hence Saint Cyprian says (*On Prayer*): “When we say, ‘Your will be done, as in heaven so on earth,’ we do not mean that God should do what he wills, but that we may be able to do what God wills. For who can resist God, so that he may not do what he wills?” And Augustine (Letter 121): “When we say, ‘Your will be done,’ and so forth, we ask him for that very obedience, so that his will may be done by us as it is done in heaven by his angels.”

Nevertheless, it must be admitted that this petition also refers in some way to the divine will of good pleasure, insofar as we ought in all things to subject and conform our own will and all our affections to the divine will; never to murmur against or criticize his good pleasure; but whatever he has determined concerning us, whatever calamity, whatever good or evil he sends upon us, to endure patiently and willingly and to say with Christ: “Not my will, but yours be done” (Matthew 26). And with blessed Job: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away. As it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1). Tertullian indicates this meaning in the passage cited above: “By saying this,” he says, “we forewarn ourselves to endure,” and so forth.]

Therefore, when we say to him, “Your will be done, as in heaven so on earth,” we pray to him in other words that, just as those who are in heaven are saved by knowing you, Father, so all who dwell on earth may likewise be saved.

## CHAPTER XXI. On supersubstantial, or daily, bread

Then,

[Note: In this petition the Author wishes “our bread” to be understood not as bodily bread but as spiritual bread, that is, the body of Christ. This can be gathered sufficiently both from the entire, though somewhat obscure, course of this chapter and from chapter 24. In this sense, too, most ancient authors, piously and religiously and in a manner suited to the practice of the Church, said that “our daily bread” is called the body of Christ: Tertullian and Cyprian, *On Prayer*; Ambrose, book V of *The Sacraments*, chapter 4; Jerome in his *Commentary*; Peter Chrysologus, sermon *On the Lord’s Prayer*.

For it is truly bread, since it descended from heaven; and it is daily because it is received and consumed every day—if not by individuals, at least by the whole Church in the name of all the faithful. It is also *epiousios* (ἐπιούσιος), that is, supersubstantial, because it is above all substances and surpasses all creatures in the sublimity of its majesty and sanctification, as it is explained here.

Others understood “daily bread” as the spiritual nourishment of the soul, namely, the word of God, which the mind needs every day and by which it is daily fed through meditation and the practice of God’s commandments, just as Christ said in John 4: “My food is to do the will of my Father,” and in John 6: “Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which endures unto eternal life.” Saint Augustine interprets it in this way in book II of *The Sermon on the Mount*.

On the other hand, there are those who think that nothing other than bodily bread is requested here, as Chrysostom does in his commentary on Matthew 6. But the best and truest explanation is that by “bread” both spiritual and bodily food are understood—that is, all the means necessary to preserve life, both of the soul and of the body (Maldonatus; Bellarmine, *above*; Leonard Lessius, *On the Institution*, book II, chapter 37).

But since the means of spiritual life—such as the sacraments, especially the sacrament of Christ’s body, as well as Christian doctrine and other things of that kind—are nobler and more necessary than the means of bodily life, it is fitting that the mind and intention of the one praying should first and chiefly tend toward spiritual bread, and secondarily toward bodily bread.

As for the word *epiousion* (ἐπιούσιον), interpreters explain it in various ways. Saint Jerome reads it as follows: “Give us today our supersubstantial bread.” And, supplying the reason why he translated it in this way, he says: “We rendered it ‘supersubstantial.’ In Greek we have *epiousion* (ἐπιούσιον), which the Seventy Translators very frequently translate by *periousion* (περιούσιον). We therefore examined the Hebrew, and wherever they rendered it *periousion*, we found *segullah*, which Symmachus translated as *exaireton* (ἐξαίρετον), that is, ‘special’ or ‘excellent,’ although in one passage he interpreted it as ‘particular.’

Therefore, when we ask God to grant us a particular or preeminent bread, we ask for the one who says: ‘I am the living bread that came down from heaven.’ In the Gospel called ‘according to the Hebrews,’ instead of ‘supersubstantial bread’ I found *machar*, which is said to mean ‘tomorrow,’ so that the meaning is: ‘Give us today our bread for tomorrow,’ that is, our future bread.

We can also understand ‘supersubstantial bread’ in another way: as that which is above all substances and surpasses all creatures.” Thus Saint Jerome explains three meanings of this petition.

Yet afterward he rejects the interpretation by which *epiousion* means “tomorrow”: “Because,” he says, “according to the Apostle’s statement, ‘Having food and clothing, with these let us be content,’ the saints concern themselves only with present food; hence the command that follows: ‘Do not be anxious about tomorrow.’”

Accordingly, according to Saint Jerome, the word *epiousios* (ἐπιούσιος) means either “supersubstantial,” or else “preeminent,” “particular,” or “excellent.”

Others interpret *epiousion* (ἐπιούσιον) not as “supersubstantial” but simply as “substantial,” that is, necessary for nourishing our substance. The ancient translator also had this meaning in view when he rendered it as “daily,” that is, the bread of which we need every day, just as all the ancient Latin authors read and explain it, whereas Saint Jerome translates it as “supersubstantial.”

Suidas embraces both meanings: “*Epiousios bread*,” he says, means “bread corresponding to our nature, or daily bread.” The Latins call it a *diarium*, that is, something necessary or appointed for each day. For we imitate little children who, setting out for school in the morning, first ask their father or mother for the portion of bread appointed for that day.]

“Give us today our *epiousion* bread” (ἐπιούσιον), that is, “our supersubstantial bread” (Matthew 6). Another Evangelist called it “daily” (Luke 11).

The former expression signifies the quality of its nobility and substance, namely, that it is above all substances and that the sublimity of its majesty and sanctification surpasses all creatures. The latter expresses its property in use and benefit. For when he says “daily,” he shows that without it we cannot possess spiritual life on any day.

When he says,

[Note: Saint Cyprian likewise interprets this as referring to the sacramental bread to be received daily (*On the Lord’s Prayer*): “We ask that this bread be given us daily, lest we who are in Christ and daily receive the Eucharist as food, through the intervention of some graver offense, while we are withheld from communion and do not communicate, be forbidden the heavenly bread and separated from Christ’s body.” And Saint Ambrose, book V of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 4: “If bread is daily, why do you receive it after a year, as the Greeks in the East are accustomed to do? Receive daily what may benefit you daily; live so that you may deserve to receive daily. Whoever does not deserve to receive daily does not deserve to receive after a year.” Thus Ambrose.

This daily custom of communion was apostolic, as Luke attests when he says in Acts 2: “They continued steadfastly in the teaching of the apostles and the fellowship of the breaking of bread.” And again, shortly afterward: “Daily also, continuing with one accord in the temple and breaking bread from house to house, they took food with gladness and simplicity of heart, praising God.”

This custom continued at Rome until the age of Saint Jerome, as he himself attests in his letter to Lucinius (Letter 28 and the *Apology to Pammachius*); and likewise at Milan until Saint Ambrose, as may be gathered from the final chapter of book IV of *On the Sacraments*; and in Africa until the times of Saint Augustine, as is clear from his Letter 118. But in the Eastern Church the custom of daily communion had long since ceased, as is clear both from Saint Ambrose’s words just cited and from Chrysostom, homily 61 to the people of Antioch and homily 17 on the Letter to the Hebrews. There he reports the various practices of some who communicated on feast days, during Advent, and in Lent; of others who did so only at Easter, or twice or three times a year; and of hermits who, from humility, did so once a year or every second year. For this reason the Fathers mentioned press not so much for daily communion as for worthy reception of the Eucharist.

Moreover, the case of laypeople—among whom most monks were formerly counted—is different from that of priests, especially religious priests, for whom it is particularly fitting, insofar as human frailty permits, to offer the sacrifice daily and to frequent that divine mystery than which nothing more pleasing to God, more salutary, or more religious can be performed. See the annotation to chapter 21, conference 23.]

“today,”

[Note: “Today” is understood in two ways. In one way it signifies precisely this day, as the Author understood it above. In another way it signifies the present time, namely, the period of this mortal life, as it is understood by the Apostle in Hebrews 3: “Exhort one another while it is called ‘today.’”]

he shows that it must be received every day, and that yesterday’s provision of it is not sufficient unless it has likewise been granted to us today. He reminds us that we must pour forth this prayer at every moment, because of our daily need: there is no day on which we do not need, by eating and receiving it, to strengthen the inner heart of our human being.

Although the word “today” may also be understood as referring to the present life, that is, while we dwell in this world, grant us this bread. For we know that it is to be granted in the future to those who have deserved it from you, but we ask you to bestow it upon us today, because unless one has deserved to receive it in this life, one will not be able to share in it in the next.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the statement, “Forgive us our debts”

And forgive us [Note: [Col. 0796B] By “our debts” in this passage are meant nothing other than our sins, by which we are bound to God as by a debt of money. Hence in Luke XI it is expressly said: “Forgive us our sins.” And in Matthew VI, explaining this petition, the Lord says: “For if you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins.” In the same sense those who have sinned against us or inflicted some injury upon us are called “our debtors.” For “debt,” says Tertullian (*On Prayer*, ch. 7), “is a figure of sin in Scripture, since it is likewise owed to judgment and exacted by it; nor does it escape the justice of exaction unless the exaction is remitted, as the master remitted the debt to that servant” (Matthew XVIII). Here “figure” is taken to mean “signification,” as Pamelius notes: that is, debt is called a figure of sin because in this passage, as also in Matthew XVIII, it signifies sin. But perhaps it is better to say that debt is a figure of sin because it is sin’s effect and offspring. For a double debt, or double guilt, is contracted through sin: guilt of fault and guilt of punishment; and we ask that both be forgiven us, that is, pardoned. In what follows the Greek reads παραπτώματα ὑμῶν, which properly means “your lapses.” For our sins are also true lapses, by which we slip and fall away from uprightness.] our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.

O ineffable mercy of God, who not only delivered to us a form of prayer, established for himself an acceptable discipline of our conduct, and, through the necessity of the formula he gave us and commanded us always to use in prayer, uprooted alike the roots of anger and sadness, but also grants those who pray an opportunity and opens to them a way by which they may induce God to pronounce a merciful and kindly judgment toward them; and in a certain sense granted them power by which we may temper the sentence of our Judge—constraining him to forgive our offenses by the example of our own forgiveness, when we say to him, “Forgive us as we also forgive.” Therefore [Note: [Col. 0796C] Understand this as applying provided that he does not omit the other things necessary for obtaining the forgiveness of sins. In this sense also that saying of the Savior—“For if you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will forgive you your offenses”—is not to be understood absolutely, as Saint Augustine warns (*The City of God*, Book XXI, chs. 22 and 27), but on the condition that the other things prescribed for this end are present, such as sorrow for sins, the intention not to sin, and so forth. Hence Augustine also reproves certain heretics who thought that even those who had lived wickedly until they closed the final day of this life had all their sins, whatever their kind and whatever their magnitude, forgiven daily through this prayer, provided only that they remembered to observe this: whenever those who had injured them by any sin asked their pardon, they should forgive them from the heart. To them he replies as follows:

“The daily prayer which the Lord himself taught—and for this reason it is called the Lord’s Prayer—does indeed blot out daily sins when it is said each day: ‘Forgive us our debts,’ provided that what follows is not merely said but also done: ‘As we also forgive our debtors.’ But it is said because sins are committed, not so that they may be committed because it is said. Through this prayer the Savior wished to show us that, however justly we live amid the darkness and weakness of this life, we are not without sins for whose forgiveness we ought to pray, and that we ought to forgive those who sin against us so that we too may be forgiven. The Lord therefore did not say, ‘If you forgive people their sins, your Father will also forgive you your sins,’ so that, trusting in this prayer, we might confidently commit daily crimes—whether through power by which we need not fear human laws, or through cunning by which we might deceive people themselves—but so that through it we might learn not to consider ourselves without sins, even if we were free from crimes,” and so forth.] whoever is indulgent toward his own debtors but not toward the debtors of his Lord will confidently ask forgiveness for his offenses, relying on this prayer. For some of us are accustomed—and this is the worse—to show ourselves peaceful and most merciful toward those offenses committed against God, even when they are serious crimes, while toward the debts arising from even our slightest offenses we prove harsh and inexorable exactors.

[Note: [Col. 0797B] “For if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive you your sins” (Matthew VI). This does not mean that God forgives our debts on this sole condition, that we forgive our debtors; rather, it means that unless we forgive others, he will not forgive us. It is therefore a necessary condition without which the forgiveness of sins is not obtained, but by itself it does not suffice. See Peter Chrysologus, sermons 68 and 71.]

Whoever, therefore, does not forgive from the heart a brother who has sinned against him will obtain by this supplication not pardon but condemnation, and by his own profession will ask to be judged more severely, saying, “Forgive me as I also have forgiven.” When this has been repaid to him according to his petition, what else will follow except that, by his own example, he be punished with implacable anger and an unforgiving sentence? Therefore, if we wish to be judged mercifully, we too must be merciful toward those who have sinned against us.

[Note: [Col. 0797C] This saying too must be understood according to what has been stated above, namely, in a negative rather than an affirmative sense. For God forgives us much more, much greater things, much more generously, and when we deserve it much less, than we either customarily forgive or are able to forgive our debtors. Yet he is said to forgive us as much as we forgive others because, if we do not forgive, he will not forgive us; and if we do forgive, he too will forgive us, provided that we perform the other necessary things. Thus, among others, Sedulius explains this condition poetically:

> We ask that all our debts be loosed:
>
> Let us likewise loose them; for the pledge of our own words
>
> Holds us bound by its manifest promise, and we are bound more heavily once released
>
> If we refuse to loose another’s chains.
>
> And the merciful Lord will begin by forgiving ten thousand talents,
>
> If he should find that we afflict a fellow servant
>
> Over a hundred denarii,
>
> And immediately hand him over to the torturers, and so forth.]

For we shall be forgiven as much as we forgive those who have harmed us by whatever malice. Fearing this, some people, [Col. 0798A] when this prayer is sung by the whole congregation in church, silently omit this passage,

[Note: [Col. 0797D] He notes the folly and presumption of certain people who, unwilling to pardon injuries, deliberately pass over those words in their prayer so as not to lie: “As we also forgive our debtors.” In doing so they deceive themselves. For even if they do not lie by omitting these words, they nevertheless ask in vain for their sins to be forgiven, since the Lord said so plainly: “If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your Father forgive you your sins.” Moreover, they lie when they recite the remaining parts of the Lord’s Prayer. For how can one truly say, “Our Father,” if one does not wish to be a son of God? Or, “Hallowed be your name,” if through that person God’s name is blasphemed or dishonored? Or, “Your kingdom come,” if that person fears nothing more than the Lord’s coming? Or, “Your will be done,” if that person always does his own will rather than God’s?]

so that they may not seem by their profession to bind rather than excuse themselves, not understanding that they vainly attempt to bring these quibbles before the Judge of all, who wished to show his suppliants how he will judge. For since he does not wish to be found harsh and inexorable toward us, he established the form of his judgment, so that, just as we wish to be judged by him, so we should judge our brothers if they have sinned against us, because “judgment without mercy will be shown to the one who has not shown mercy” (James II).

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### On the saying: “And do not lead us into temptation.”

Then follows,

[Note: [Col. 0798B] Saint Cyprian reads: “And do not permit us to be led into temptation.” Saint Augustine, in Book II, chapter 34, of *The Sermon on the Mount*, says: “The sixth petition: ‘And do not bring us into temptation.’ Some manuscripts have ‘lead us,’ which I think has the same meaning. For both have been translated from the one Greek expression, εἰσενέγκῃς. Many, however, say in prayer: ‘Do not permit us to be led into temptation,’ explaining how ‘lead us’ is to be understood. God does not lead a person into temptation by himself; rather, he permits the one whom he has abandoned to his own aidlessness to be led there, according to a most hidden order and according to merits. Often, too, for manifest reasons he judges a person worthy to be abandoned and permits him to be led into temptation.

“But to be led into temptation is one thing, and to be tempted another. No one can be approved without temptation, whether by himself or by another. We do not therefore pray that we may not be tempted, but that we may not be brought into temptation—just as someone who must be tested by fire does not pray that he may not come into contact with fire, but that he may not be burned. We are led into temptation when circumstances arise that we cannot endure.”

Thus Augustine plainly confirms the opinion of Cassian, or of Abbot Isaac, who teaches that to be tempted is one thing and to be led into temptation another; and that here we do not ask not to be tempted, but not to be overcome by temptation. Augustine himself, however, in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 6, thinks that we simply pray not to be tempted at all, especially by that temptation through which we are enticed to sin. For, mindful of our weakness and not trusting in ourselves, we prefer to be delivered from temptations and their dangers rather than exposed to them. Although temptation is sometimes useful, it is always dangerous because victory is uncertain and precarious. Therefore it is not only presumption to desire it, but also humility to avoid it and to ask God not to bring us into such a contest or permit us to be brought into it.

Nor do the Scriptures cited here to the contrary conflict with this. They prove only that temptation or affliction must be endured not merely courageously but also joyfully. Yet what is endured is not loved. Hence Augustine, *Confessions* X, chapter 28: “You command us to endure them, not to love them; no one loves what he endures, even if he loves to endure it. For although he rejoices that he endures it, he would nevertheless prefer that there were nothing for him to endure.”]

“And do not lead us into temptation.” Concerning this, a considerable question arises. For if we pray not to be permitted to be tempted, where will the virtue of steadfastness in us be tested, according to the saying: “Every person who has not been tempted has not been tested” (Ecclesiasticus XXXIV)? And again: “Blessed is the person who endures temptation” (James I). The meaning of “Do not lead us into temptation” is therefore not, “Do not ever permit us to be tempted,” but, “Do not permit us, once placed in temptation, to be overcome.”

Job was tempted, but he was not led into temptation. He did not ascribe folly to God, nor did he enter, with impious and blasphemous speech, into the will of the tempter toward which he was being dragged. Abraham was tempted, and Joseph was tempted, but neither was led into temptation, because neither gave consent to the tempter.

Finally, it follows:

[Note: [Col. 0799A] From this interpretation it appears that this abbot thought the entire final period of the Lord’s Prayer—“Do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil”—contained not two petitions but only one. Bellarmine rightly refutes this as contrary to the common opinion of both ancient and modern theologians, showing from the teaching of Saint Augustine (*On Good Works*, Book I, ch. 1) and others that the petition “But deliver us from evil” is distinct from the preceding “Do not lead us into temptation,” and consequently that the Lord’s Prayer contains seven petitions.

Moreover, most of the ancients understood “evil” to mean the devil, to whom the term “evil,” in Greek τὸν πονηρόν, properly applies by antonomasia, since he stands at the extreme degree of wickedness and cannot be recalled from it. Saint Cyprian, Augustine, and others, however, interpret “evil” as every evil thing. The Church seems to approve this meaning when, immediately after the Lord’s Prayer in the sacrifice of the Mass, it adds: “Deliver us, we beseech you, Lord, from all evils, past, present, and future.” Past evils are sins committed, for which we ask forgiveness; present evils are temptations, into which we ask not to be led; future evils are every impending evil, whether in this world or in the next, from which we ask to be delivered.

As for present evils—that is, the things we suffer in this world, such as illnesses, hunger, thirst, poverty, wars, and misfortunes—we ask to be delivered from them, but not absolutely; rather, under the Christian qualification, “If it should seem good to God,” or presupposing the preceding petition, “Your will be done,” as will be explained more fully below.]

“But deliver us from evil”—that is, do not permit us to be tempted by the devil beyond what we can bear, but with the temptation also provide a way out, so that we may be able to endure it (I Corinthians X).

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### That no other things should be requested than those contained in the form of the Lord’s Prayer alone

You see, then, what kind of measure and form of prayer has been proposed to us by the Judge himself, whom we are to entreat through it. It contains no petition for riches, no remembrance of dignities, no request for power or strength, no mention of bodily health or temporal life.

[Note: [Col. 0799C] In the same sense Isidore of Pelusium writes in a certain letter—namely Letter 281 of Book II—in Billius’s translation: “The prayer which the Lord taught his disciples contains nothing earthly, but everything heavenly and directed toward the benefit of the soul,” and so forth.

Yet this statement, if taken simply and literally, as though nothing perishable or temporal were asked of God in the Lord’s Prayer, must be judged entirely implausible, indeed paradoxical. Who would deny that temporal goods—especially those necessary to sustain life—are rightly asked and expected from God, the giver of every good? And since the Lord’s Prayer is completely full and perfect, as Saint Augustine teaches in Letter 121, who would doubt that it contains everything that can be asked of God? Finally, we showed above, according to the opinion of the Fathers, that by “daily bread” are understood all the supports necessary for both spiritual and bodily life.

Nevertheless, Abbot Isaac explained, or at least softened, his opinion in the words that follow, where he says: “Therefore whoever, neglecting eternal petitions, prefers to ask him for something transitory and perishable will inflict the greatest injury upon his magnificence and generosity,” and so forth. In this sense, then, we are forbidden to ask for temporal and transitory things while neglecting eternal things—that is, spiritual petitions—meaning that we are forbidden to prefer temporal and perishable things to spiritual and eternal ones, since we are commanded to seek first the kingdom of God, so that the rest may then be added to us.

Christ’s purpose was not to command us, through the Lord’s Prayer, to seek bread and temporal things—matters that are lowly and earthly and toward which we are naturally very inclined—but to teach us from whom, namely from God, the giver of all good things, and to what extent we ought to seek and request them.

It should be noted, moreover, from Saint Thomas (*Summa theologiae* II–II, question 83, articles 5 and 6), that there are three kinds of goods that may be requested from God. Some are spiritual, such as grace and virtues, forgiveness of sins, eternal life, and so forth. These are to be requested first and absolutely, as things desirable in themselves.

Others are temporal but necessary for sustaining life, concerning which the Apostle says: “Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content” (I Timothy VI). These are indeed requested absolutely, just as in the Lord’s Prayer we absolutely ask: “Give us this day our daily bread.” Yet they are not to be sought first and principally, in Saint Thomas’s words, as though we were to establish our end in them, but as aids by which we are helped to strive toward blessedness—inasmuch as bodily life is sustained by them and inasmuch as they serve us instrumentally for acts of virtue, as the Philosopher also says in the first book of the *Ethics* (ch. 8).

This is what Augustine says to Proba (*Letter* 121, ch. 6): whoever desires the sufficiency of life, and not more than that, desires it not improperly. It is not desired for its own sake, but for bodily health and for the fitting condition of a person, so that one may not be unbecoming to those among whom one must live honorably. These goods, therefore, when we have them, are to be retained; when we do not have them, we should pray to have them.

Third, there are temporal goods that are by no means necessary, such as riches, honors, bodily strength, sound health, long life, and so forth. Since these very often become a person’s ruin, they should not be requested absolutely, but under a tacit or explicit condition: if they are to be beneficial to us in the future. This is known to God alone. Hence, in asking for these things, the best practice is to pray that God may deal with us as he knows will be expedient for his glory and our salvation. This is substantially Saint Thomas’s teaching in article 6 of the question cited.

In the other article he confirms and explains the same doctrine as follows:

“Just as Marcus Valerius reports” (Book VII, ch. 1), “Socrates thought that nothing further should be requested from the immortal gods than that they grant good things, since they alone would know what was useful to each person. We, however, generally desire by our prayers what it would have been better not to obtain. This opinion is in some measure true with respect to those things that can have a bad outcome and that a person can use either well or badly. Thus riches, which—as is said in the same passage—have been the ruin of many; honors, which have destroyed very many; kingdoms, whose endings are often seen to be wretched; and splendid marriages, which sometimes overthrow entire households.

“Yet there are certain goods that a person cannot use badly and that cannot have a bad outcome. These are the things by which we are made blessed and by which we merit blessedness. The saints ask for these absolutely, according to the saying of Psalm LXXIX: ‘Show us your face, and we shall be saved.’ And again, Psalm CXVIII: ‘Lead me in the path of your commandments.’”

Thus far Saint Thomas. See the seventeenth annotation after the end of the work.]

For the Creator of eternity does not wish anything perishable, anything lowly, anything temporal to be implored from him. Therefore whoever, neglecting these eternal petitions, prefers to ask him for something transitory and perishable will inflict the greatest injury upon his magnificence and generosity, and through the baseness of his prayer will incur the displeasure rather than the favor of his Judge.

## CHAPTER XXV  
### On the character of the higher prayer

Although this prayer therefore seems to contain the fullness of every perfection, since it has either been initiated or established by the authority of the Lord himself,

[Note: [Col. 0801B] Thus he also said above, in chapter 17: “The Lord himself was willing, by his example, to initiate us into these four kinds of supplication.” Now *initiare* most often means to imbue with sacred things or to initiate into sacred rites; hence *initiatus*, “initiated,” that is, imbued with sacred things. The book of Ambrose, *On Those Who Are Initiated into the Mysteries*, uses the term in this sense (Volume IV).

At other times, however, as here, *initiare* means to begin, establish, or inaugurate. Sidonius, Book II, Letter 3, has *gratiae initiatae*, “grace begun” or “initiated.” Julius Firmicus, *Mathesis* Book II, ch. 5: “Spring is initiated when the sun has entered the first part of Aries.”]

it nevertheless advances those who belong to the household of God toward that more exalted state mentioned above, and leads them by a higher step to that fiery prayer known and experienced by very few—or rather, to speak more accurately, ineffable prayer. Transcending every human understanding, it is distinguished by no sound of the voice, not even by the movement of the tongue or by any utterance of words. Rather, the mind, illumined by the infusion of that heavenly light, does not express it in human and restricted phrases, but pours forth its gathered thoughts abundantly, as though from some most copious fountain, and ineffably belches them forth toward the Lord, uttering in that very brief moment as much as the tongue could not easily express and the mind, when it returns to itself, could not traverse.

The Lord likewise represented this state among the forms of supplication—those which he is described as having poured forth either alone while sitting on the mountain (Luke XXII) or in silence—when, placed in the agony of prayer, he also shed drops of blood in an incomparable example of intensity.

## CHAPTER XXVI  
### The spirit of prayer is stirred to fervor in various ways

Who could adequately explain the varieties, causes, and very origins

[Note: [Col. 0801C] Concerning compunction, one should first consider what it is, and then what its causes and origins are, as discussed here. We can learn both from several choice sayings and encomia of the holy Fathers, which, I hope, the reader will receive no less gladly than profitably.

Saint Augustine writes in *On the Spirit and the Soul*, chapter 50: “Meditation gives birth to knowledge, knowledge to compunction, compunction to devotion, and devotion perfects prayer.” Compunction is when, through consideration of one’s evils, the heart is touched by inward sorrow. Devotion is a pious and humble affection toward God: humble because of awareness of one’s own weakness, pious because of consideration of divine mercy.

Gregory, *Moralia* XXIII, chapter 21: “There are,” he says, “four conditions by which the soul of a righteous person is intensely moved to compunction: when it remembers its evils, considering where it was; when, fearing the sentence of God’s judgments and asking itself, it considers where it will be; when, carefully attending to the evils of the present life, it sorrowfully considers where it is; or when it contemplates the good things of the heavenly homeland and, because it has not yet attained them, mournfully sees where it is not.

“Paul remembered his evils and afflicted himself over the things in which he had been, when he said: ‘I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God’ (I Corinthians XIII). Again, carefully weighing divine judgment, he feared that his future state would be bad, saying: ‘I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be rejected’ (I Corinthians IX). Again, he weighed the evils of the present life when he said: ‘While we are in this body, we are away from the Lord’ (II Corinthians V); and, ‘I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin,’ and so forth.

“And again he considered the good things of the eternal homeland, saying: ‘Now we see through a mirror in a riddle, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I am known’ (I Corinthians XIII).” See the same Gregory, *Dialogues* III, chapter 33.

Saint Gregory also says in Homily 22 on Ezekiel: “One kind of compunction arises through fear, another through love, because it is one thing to flee punishments and another to desire rewards. Hence the Law also commands two altars to be made in the tabernacle (Exodus XXIV and XXX): one outer and one inner; one in the courtyard and one before the ark; one covered with bronze and the other clothed in gold. On the bronze altar flesh is burned, but on the golden altar spices are kindled. What does this mean, dearest brothers, that flesh is burned outside and spices inside, except what we see daily—that there are two kinds of compunction? Some still weep through fear, while others already lament through love,” and so forth.

Saint Bernard, in a certain sermon (*On the Way of Life*, sermon 10): “Compunction of heart is humility of mind arising from remembrance of sin and fear of judgment. That compunction is perfect which drives away from itself every pleasure in carnal things and fixes the mind’s attention entirely upon the contemplation of God. We read that there are two kinds of compunction: one by which, for God’s sake, the soul of each servant of God is moved, namely when it recalls the evils it has committed; and another when it sighs because of its desire for eternal life. The mind of a righteous person is pierced in four ways: by remembrance of sins, recollection of future punishments, consideration of this life’s pilgrimage, and desire for the heavenly homeland.”

This is Saint Bernard’s teaching. Here, reader, do not be greatly surprised that compunction is sometimes called twofold and sometimes fourfold. You will easily see, if you pay attention, that the fourfold kind can be reduced to the twofold. For just as the first two belong to one kind, which arises from fear, so the latter two belong to one kind, which arises from love and desire for the heavenly homeland.

These collected sayings of the Fathers concerning compunction seem sufficient for our present subject and purpose. Besides them, if anyone wishes to consult complete treatises on the same topic, let him read Chrysostom, who composed two elegant and highly worthwhile books on compunction of heart; and Saint Ephrem the Syrian, among whose works there are likewise four very beautiful homilies on compunction.]

of compunction by which the mind, inflamed and set ablaze, is stirred to pure and most fervent prayers? We shall present a few of them by way of example, insofar as we can at present recall them through the Lord’s illumination.

Sometimes a verse of any psalm has provided an occasion for fiery prayer while we were singing. At other times, the melodious modulation of a brother’s voice has roused our astonished minds to attentive supplication. We also know that the measured delivery and solemnity of the one chanting have contributed greatly to the fervor of those standing nearby; likewise, the exhortation of a perfected man and spiritual conversation have frequently raised the affection of those lying in prayer to abundant petitions.

We know also that the death of a brother or of any beloved person has drawn us no less powerfully into complete compunction. The remembrance of our tepidity and negligence has sometimes kindled within us a salutary fervor of spirit. In this way, there is no doubt that innumerable occasions exist through which, by God’s grace, the tepidity and drowsiness of our minds can be awakened.

## CHAPTER XXVII  
[Note: [Col. 0803B] Ciaconius titles this: “On the various qualities of compunction,” as do our manuscripts, followed by Dionysius and the Basel manuscript. It might also have been entitled “On the various effects of compunction.” For three plainly distinct effects of compunction, or fervent prayers, are explained here: sometimes a kind of cry bursts forth from an overflowing inner joy and exultation of heart; sometimes there is silence, silent groaning, and a kind of astonishment of the mind struck with wonder; sometimes there is an outpouring of tears, which is treated especially in what follows.]  
### On the different emotions of those who pray fervently

How, or in what ways, these compunctions themselves are brought forth from the innermost chambers of the soul is no less difficult to investigate. Frequently the fruit of most salutary compunction emerges through ineffable joy and spiritual gladness, so that it even bursts forth into certain cries under the immensity of an unbearable joy,

[Note: [Col. 0803C] From this it may be inferred that the cells of those ancient monks, even those living in solitude, were joined together or at least close to one another. Saint Jerome likewise attests this in Letter 22 to Eustochium, writing about the Egyptian coenobites: “They remain separate, but with their cells joined together.” Monks’ cells and small cells have often been discussed elsewhere as well (Book V of the *Institutes*, ch. 37, and Book X, ch. 3).]

and the joy of heart and magnitude of exultation penetrate into the cell of a neighbor. At other times the mind is hidden within the secrecy of profound silence with such great quiet that the astonishment of sudden illumination encloses every sound of the voice entirely; and the spirit, struck with wonder, either restrains all its senses inwardly or releases them, pouring forth its desires to God in inexpressible groans.

At other times the abundance and grief of compunction are so great

[Note: [Col. 0803C] For *repletur*, “is filled,” as Dionysius rendered it; this expression is very frequent in Cassian.]

that it cannot otherwise discharge them than by the evaporation of tears.

## CHAPTER XXVIII  
### Germanus asks why the outpouring of tears is not in our power

**Germanus:** My own smallness is not entirely unfamiliar with this emotion of compunction. Frequently, when tears have arisen from the remembrance of my sins, I have been so invigorated by that ineffable joy, as you described, when the Lord visited me, that the greatness of the joy itself seemed to tell me that I ought not to despair of their forgiveness. I consider no state more sublime than this, if its restoration lay within our own control.

Sometimes, wishing with all my strength to rouse myself to a similar compunction of tears, and setting all my errors and sins before my eyes,

[Note: [Col. 0803D] John Climacus treats this matter skillfully and appropriately in the seventh step of his *Ladder*, where he discusses this grace of compunction and the gift of tears no less devoutly than subtly:

“I have seen,” he says, “small drops, like blood, poured forth with labor. I have also seen springs flow without labor. Just as a creature sometimes generates movement from itself and sometimes receives it from elsewhere, so we must understand compunction as well. Whenever the soul, without our caring or laboring for it, is moved by the hidden force of compunction into tears and rests in weeping alone, let us run eagerly; for the Lord has come unbidden and, in his mercy, offers us the sponge of divine sorrow and the waters of devout tears, by which the crimes of our written bond may be erased. Guard it as the pupil of your eye until it departs of its own accord. For the power of such compunction is far greater than that which we have acquired through our own effort and labor.”]

I cannot recover that abundance of weeping. My eyes become hardened like an exceedingly hard flint, so that not a single drop of moisture at all drips from them. Therefore, to the extent that I rejoice when tears pour forth, to the same extent I grieve that, whenever I wish, I cannot regain them.

## CHAPTER XXIX  
### The answer concerning the diversity of spiritual tears
Isaac: [Note: [Col. 0803D] Saint Gregory, *Dialogues*, book III, chapter 34, establishes only two kinds both of compunction and of spiritual and salutary tears: one arising from fear, the other from love. “This,” he says, “is aptly represented by the fact that Aza, the daughter of Caleb, sitting upon a donkey, sighed. Her father said to her, ‘What do you want?’ She replied, ‘Give me a blessing: you have given me a southern land, dry and arid; add to it one with water.’ And her father gave her the upper springs and the lower springs” (Joshua 15). Aza sits upon the donkey because the soul presides over the irrational movements of its flesh. Sighing, she asks her father for watered land, because the grace of tears must be sought from our Creator with great groaning. There are some who have already received the gift of speaking freely on behalf of justice, protecting the oppressed, distributing their possessions to the needy, and possessing the fervor of faith, but who still do not have the grace of tears. They have, to be sure, a southern and arid land, but still need water; for, established in good works, in which they are great and fervent, they must nevertheless mourn the evils they previously committed, either through fear of punishment or through love of the heavenly kingdom. But because, as I have said, there are two kinds of compunction, her father gave her the upper springs [Col. 0804D] and the lower springs. The soul receives the upper springs when it afflicts itself with tears out of desire for the heavenly kingdom; it receives the lower springs when it dreads the punishments of hell with weeping.”

So Gregory. But Saint Bernard, in sermon 3 on the Epiphany, lists three kinds of pious tears, namely tears of devotion, repentance, and fraternal compassion, which are also expressed in this chapter:

“These,” he says, “are tears of devotion, in which one seeks not the remission of sins but the good pleasure of God the Father, when the spirit of adoption as sons descends upon us, bearing witness to our spirit that we are children of God, so that we seem to hear from heaven a honey-sweet voice, because God the Father truly takes pleasure in us. There is indeed no small difference between these tears of devotion, belonging to an age already mature and manly, and those which an early age poured forth amid the cries of infancy—tears, certainly, of repentance and confession. Yet far more excellent than both are other tears, into which the savor of wine is also infused [Col. 0805C] and which I would truly say are changed into wine: those which arise in the fervor of charity from the feeling of fraternal compassion, for which, even for a time, you seem to forget yourself in a sober kind of drunkenness.”]

Not every outpouring of tears proceeds from the same feeling or virtue. The weeping that flows when the thorn of sins pricks our heart is of one kind. Of it is said: “I am weary with my groaning; every night I wash my bed; I water my couch with my tears” (Psalm 6). And again: “Pour out tears like a torrent by day and by night, and do not give yourself rest, nor let the pupil of your eye be silent” (Lamentations 4).

Another kind arises from contemplation of eternal goods and desire for that future glory. From the intolerable joy and immense exultation of this longing, even more abundant fountains of tears burst forth, while our soul thirsts for God, the living fountain, saying: “When shall I come and appear before the face of God? My tears have been my bread day and night” (Psalm 41), while every day it cries out with wailing and lamentation: “Woe is me, for my sojourn has been prolonged; my soul has been a long-time inhabitant” (Psalm 119).

Tears of another kind flow without any consciousness of such crimes, but nevertheless from fear of Gehenna and remembrance of that dreadful judgment. Struck by its terror, the prophet prays to God: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person shall be justified in your sight” (Psalm 142).

There is also another kind of tears, produced not by one’s own conscience but by the hardness and sins of another. Thus Samuel wept for Saul (1 Samuel 15); and Jeremiah, in earlier times, is described as having wept for that city, Jerusalem, as is also the Lord in the Gospel (Luke 19). Jeremiah says: “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, that I may weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people?” (Jeremiah 9).

Or certainly such are the tears of which Psalm 101 sings: “For I ate ashes like bread, and I mingled my drink with weeping.” It is certain that these do not arise from the same feeling as those which emerge in Psalm 6 from the person of a penitent—“Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger,” and so forth—but from the anxieties, distress, and afflictions of this life, by which the righteous, placed in this world, are weighed down. This is clearly shown not only by the text of the psalm itself but also by its title (the title of Psalm 101), which is described in the person of that poor man of whom the Gospel says, “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5) [Col. 0806B]:

[Note: [Col. 0805C] The title is that of Psalm 101, which begins, “Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you.” All Hebrew, Greek, and Latin manuscripts have this title, though with some variation in wording. Saint Augustine reads: “The prayer of the needy, when he was distressed, and he poured out his prayer in the sight of the Lord.” Others have: “The prayer of the poor man when he is anxious, and he pours out his prayer in the sight of the Lord.” From this title the subject of the same psalm is derived. For this psalm is a sort of formula of prayer which any poor person, or anyone placed in affliction—indeed, any sinner made anxious by the prick of conscience, struck by fear of God, and longing to recover his grace and reconciliation—may use. Blessed Jerome seems to have understood this, when he writes in his Commentary that the prophet speaks in the person of a sinner. Truly, no one is poorer or more wretched than one who needs the grace of God. Hence the Church numbers this psalm among the seven penitential psalms.]

“The prayer of the poor man when he is distressed, and pours out his prayer before God.”

[Note: [Col. 0805D] It is also useful here to set down the very salutary admonitions of John Climacus, which agree with this passage. He says (*Step* 7): “Sometimes ungrateful tears of vainglory are mingled with grief according to God. We recognize that this happens piously and prudently when we see that we are mourning ourselves and yet acting wickedly. Compunction is properly sorrow of spirit, free from all exaltation, allowing itself no consolation whatsoever, and meditating hour by hour only upon its own dissolution, while awaiting the consolation of God, with which he visits humble monks, as one who awaits cold water. Whenever you detect pride or anger in those who seem to mourn according to God, know that their tears are not among those which salutary compunction produces. For, as he says, ‘What fellowship has light with darkness?’ (2 Corinthians 6). Adulterine compunction usually produces exaltation, whereas that which is praiseworthy and approved produces consolation. As fire ignites and consumes straw, so chaste tears consume all stains, both visible and invisible.

“Most of the Fathers define the nature of tears as something not readily apparent, exceedingly obscure, and extremely difficult to discover, especially in those who are beginners. Tears arise from many different causes: from nature, from God, from blameworthy affliction, and likewise from praiseworthy affliction; from vainglory, fornication, and love; from remembrance of death; and from many other sources. But when all these kinds of tears have been examined and recognized through divine fear, let us strive, through the continual remembrance of our own dissolution, to acquire tears that are utterly pure and free from every suspicion of deceit. For in them there is no suspicion of stolen exaltation, but great cleansing, progress in love of God, abolition of sin, and a most radiant and blessed repose, removed from all tumult of disturbance.

“It is neither new nor surprising that those who mourn should sometimes begin with the best tears and end with worse ones. But to be transferred from contrary or even natural tears to spiritual tears is both rare and truly worthy of praise. Those who are more inclined toward vainglory understand this problem most clearly. Do not trust the showers of your tears before you have been perfectly purified. For wine freshly pressed from the winepresses is not yet trustworthy. No one disputes that all the tears we shed according to God are wonderfully useful. But what their usefulness is, we shall recognize at the time of our departure.” Thus far this man of exceedingly profound and hidden doctrine.]

These tears, therefore, differ greatly from those wrung from dry eyes by an hardened heart. Although we believe that they are not entirely fruitless—for their emission is attempted with a good intention—this is especially true of those who have not yet been able either to attain perfect knowledge or to cleanse themselves completely from the stain of former or present vices.

## CHAPTER XXX

### That tears should not be drawn forth when they are not shed spontaneously

Yet by those who have already advanced into the disposition of the virtues, an outpouring of tears ought not to be extorted in this way. Nor should the weeping of the outward person be pursued with particular effort; even if such weeping is produced to some degree, it can never attain the abundance of spontaneous tears. Rather, by distracting the supplicant’s mind through its own efforts, it will humble it and drag it down, removing it from that heavenly elevation in which the astonished mind of one praying ought to remain steadfastly fixed. It will compel the mind, with the attention of its prayers relaxed, to fall sick over the sterile and forced drops of tears.

[Note: [Col. 0806D] Louis of Granada teaches this admirably in book II of *Prayer and Meditation*. Relevant here is what John Climacus writes, in the passage cited, about the grace of tears and the barrenness that can sometimes befall spiritual men. Taught by his own experience and that of others, and exceptionally practiced in such matters, he says:

“Sometimes tears themselves lift certain people into a lighter state; for this reason they are withdrawn from some by divine dispensation, so that, seeing themselves deprived of them and seeking them more earnestly, they may recognize their own misery and wear themselves down with groans, sorrow, grief of soul, profound sadness, and perplexity. All these can take the place of tears, if they are not themselves contemptuously regarded as worthless.

“Sometimes, if we observe carefully, we shall find the demons attempting something ridiculous in us. When we have been filled with food, they prick us with compunction; but when we have fasted, they harden us, so that, deceived by tears, we may expose ourselves to gluttony and indulgence, the parents of vices.
