We must not obey them, but do precisely the opposite.

“As I consider the power of compunction, I am astonished at how that which is called mourning and sorrow can inwardly contain joy and gladness, like honey and the honeycomb, when it is consumed. What, then, does this suggest to us? Surely that such compunction should be acknowledged as properly the gift of God.” Thus far he.]

## CHAPTER XXXI

### The saying of Abbot Antony concerning the state of prayer

And so that you may perceive the character of true prayer, I shall present to you not my own judgment but the saying of blessed Antony. We know that he sometimes persevered in prayer in such a way that, while he was frequently praying in the same ecstasy of mind, and the rising sun had begun to pour forth its light, we heard him cry out in the fervor of the spirit:

“What are you hindering me from, O sun, which are now rising for this purpose, to draw me away from the splendor of this true light?”

[Note: [Col. 0807C] This saying is not found in the *Life of Saint Antony* written by Athanasius, nor is the other saying later attributed to him. This is not very surprising, since it is sufficiently clear that Athanasius did not commit all Antony’s deeds and sayings to writing, but omitted many. For when Saint Jerome relates Antony’s meeting with Paul the first hermit (*Life of Paul the Hermit*), Athanasius does not mention it even in a word. This is doubtless because, as Jerome himself testifies, [Col. 0807D] Athanasius wrote Antony’s *Life* while Antony was still alive and brought it to Rome two years before Antony’s death, when he had been summoned by Pope Julius. At that time the episode concerning Paul, as well as many other deeds and sayings of Antony, had not yet occurred (Baronius, volume III of the *Annals*, note 343). Hence many other sayings of Antony are found both in the *Lives of the Fathers* and in Palladius and others which do not exist in Athanasius. We should not suppose that everything done or said, even during his own lifetime or earlier, came to his knowledge; nor was it necessary for him to mention everything that he did know.]

His is also the following heavenly and more-than-human saying concerning the end of prayer:

“Perfect prayer,” he says, “is not that in which the monk understands even that he is praying.”

[Note: [Col. 0807D] This refers to that kind and degree of perfection which belongs only to the holiest and most perfect persons, such as Antony: a state in which the mind is so raised and fixed upon God in prayer that it thinks of nothing apart from God. This is certainly the most perfect manner of praying; but whoever can receive it, let him receive it.]

And if we too dare, according to the measure of our weakness, to add something to this admirable saying, we shall offer signs of prayer being heard by the Lord, insofar as we have learned them through experience.

## CHAPTER XXXII

### The sign that prayer has been heard

When, as we pray, no hesitation has intervened and cast down the confidence of our petition through a kind of despair; if we sense, in the very outpouring of prayer, that we have obtained what we ask, [Note: [Col. 0808B] He says the same thing more clearly below (chapter 34): “No one should doubt that he will certainly not be heard when he has doubted that he will be heard.” For a proper understanding of this, two points must be noted. First, prayer does not require faith, or a settled conviction, by which we believe that we have obtained, or will obtain, what we ask. It requires only that we believe God to be supremely powerful, wise, kind, and faithful, and therefore able, knowing, and also willing to do what we ask, provided that we ask rightly.

“That it is not required that we believe with certainty that God will hear us is manifestly gathered from David’s prayer for his son (1 Samuel 22). For these words show that he did not believe with certainty that he would be heard: ‘Who knows whether the Lord may perhaps grant him to me?’ Likewise, when the Apostle prayed that the thorn of the flesh might be removed from him (1 Corinthians 12), he undoubtedly prayed with true faith; yet he did not believe that he would certainly obtain what he asked. Otherwise his faith would have been false, since he did not obtain what he requested, the Lord saying: ‘My grace is sufficient for you.’

“Nor does the universal Church pray in this manner for unbelievers and sinners, that they may be brought to faith and righteousness. For it does not believe with certainty that all unbelievers and sinners will be converted.

“Second, although faith by which we certainly believe that God will hear us is not required, trust is nevertheless required: we must confidently and unhesitatingly trust that, in his goodness, God will do what we ask, if it is expedient for the glory of God and our salvation. This is the condition the Lord sought in the paralytic to whom he said: ‘Take heart, son; your sins are forgiven’ (Matthew 9). The Apostle likewise requires it in Hebrews 2: ‘Let us approach his throne of grace with confidence.’ And James says in chapter 1: ‘Let him ask in faith, doubting nothing.’ ‘In faith,’ that is, with confidence of obtaining what we ask, says Saint Thomas (in his Commentary).

“By this reasoning, therefore, the abbot here teaches that a sure sign of being heard, or of obtaining what has been requested, is present when no hesitation intervenes as we pray and casts down the confidence of our petition through despair, but we sense that we have obtained what we ask in the very outpouring of prayer. That is, when during prayer we feel within our soul great confidence that we shall obtain what we ask. For when God does not hear, he does not infuse this kind of confidence; but when he determines to hear, he inspires a certain distinctive confidence and cheerfulness in the mind of the one praying, as each person occasionally experiences.]

we should not doubt that our prayers have effectively penetrated to God [Col. 0808B]. For a person will deserve to be heard and to obtain as much as he believes either that he is regarded by God or that God is able to grant what he asks.

[Note: [Col. 0808D] No one doubts that this saying is irrevocable and infallible, provided that the required conditions are present, most of which are explained below in chapter 34. For there is this distinction between God’s promises that affirm and those that deny: the negative promises are understood absolutely and without any exception, whereas the affirmative promises are never understood absolutely, but always with this general exception: unless something intervenes, or something similar.

“Thus Mark 16 says: ‘Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved’—supply, ‘if he possesses the other things that are necessary.’ But: ‘Whoever does not believe will be condemned.’ Therefore that saying and promise, ‘Whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you will receive it,’ and so forth, since it is affirmative, is not to be understood absolutely, but with this condition: if you ask rightly. Saint James indicates that this condition must be understood when he says: ‘You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly’ (James 4).]

For irrevocable is that saying of our Lord: “Whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you will receive it, and it will come to you” (Mark 11).

## CHAPTER XXXIII

### The objection that the foregoing confidence of being heard seems to belong only to the saints

Germanus: We believe that this confidence of being heard surely proceeds from purity of conscience. But how can we possess it, when our heart is still pricked by the thorn of sins and we have no merits to support us, by which we might confidently presume that our prayers will be heard?

## CHAPTER XXXIV

### The response concerning the various causes of being heard in prayer
Isaac: [Note: [Col. 0809C] The Author proceeds to explain by what means, considerations, and conditions we are more readily heard by God and obtain what we ask. Six conditions drawn from Sacred Scripture are listed here, which ordinarily make prayer effective and efficacious—that is, which assist in obtaining what is requested: fraternal charity, faith, perseverance, almsgiving, repentance, and the groaning of the afflicted. Although these conditions greatly assist in obtaining what is requested, especially when joined and operating together, they do not do so in such a way that their effect in obtaining it is infallible, certain, and perpetual. For there is no absolute promise of God by which we are made absolutely certain that we shall obtain what we have asked once those conditions are present, since the condition is always understood: “provided that the other requirements are present.” What those requirements are, the blessed Thomas explains in these words (II–II, q. 83, art. 13): “Four conditions,” he says, “are posited, when all of which concur a person always obtains what he asks: namely, that he ask for himself, for what is necessary for salvation, piously, and perseveringly.” It will be useful to explain these conditions here somewhat more fully.

The first condition, therefore, is that each person ask for himself. Even the saints are not always heard when they pray for others—namely, when those for whom they pray are unworthy to receive what is requested—as Saint Augustine teaches in Tractate 73 on John. He gathers this from the Lord’s words in John 16: “If you ask anything of the Father [Col. 0810B] in my name, he will give it to you.” “All the saints,” he says, “are heard for themselves; but they are not heard for everyone, whether friends, enemies, or any others, because it is not simply said, ‘He will give,’ but, ‘He will give to you.’”

The second condition is that what is requested be necessary or useful for salvation. Augustine likewise gathers this condition from the words “in my name.” “Whatever,” he says, “we ask contrary to the benefit of salvation, we do not ask in the name of the Savior. Yet he is the Savior not only when he does what we ask, but also when he does not do it, because by not doing what he sees to be requested against salvation, he shows himself all the more to be the Savior. A physician knows what the sick person asks for that is beneficial to his health and what he asks for against it; and therefore he does not do the will of one requesting harmful things, in order to bring about health. Accordingly, when we wish him to do whatever we ask, we must ask not simply, but in his name—that is, in the name of the Savior.” Thus far Augustine.

Yet this condition appears to be gathered still more effectively, as the Author gathers it, from John’s statement: “This is the confidence that we have toward God: that whatever we ask according to his will, he hears us” (1 John 5). Hence Augustine infers: “Therefore he commanded us to have full and undoubted confidence of being heard only concerning those things which accord not with our advantages or temporal consolations, but with the Lord’s will.” We are also commanded to include this in the Lord’s Prayer, saying, “Your will be done”—that is, not ours (see Bellarmine, Book I, *On Good Works*, chapter 9).

The third condition is that we ask and pray piously. According to Saint Thomas in the passage cited above, this piety includes five conditions: faith, hope, charity, humility, and devotion.

The fourth condition is that we pray perseveringly. Christ wished to impress this condition upon us through two parables: the one about the importunate friend asking his friend for bread in the middle of the night, in Luke 11; the other about the widow persistently troubling the unjust judge, in Luke 18. Nor did he intend anything else by the words, “It is necessary always to pray and never to grow weary,” as will be explained more fully in the following Conference.]

The Gospel or prophetic utterances testify that there are various causes of being heard, according to the diverse and varying condition of souls. You have the fruit of being heard marked out by the Lord’s voice in the agreement of two persons, according to this saying: “If two of you agree on earth about anything whatever they ask, it will be done for them by my Father, who is in heaven” (Matthew 18). You have another cause in the fullness of faith, which is compared to a mustard seed. “For if,” he says, “you have faith like a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ and it will move, and nothing will be impossible for you” (Matthew 17). You have another in the persistence of prayers, which the Lord’s discourse called importunity because of the tireless perseverance of the petitions: “Amen, I say to you: if he will not rise and give him as much as he needs because he is his friend, yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as much as he needs” (Luke 11). You have another in the fruit of almsgiving: “Enclose almsgiving,” he says, “in the heart of the poor, and it will itself pray for you in the time of tribulation” (Ecclesiasticus 29). You have another in the amendment of life and works of mercy, according to this saying: “Dissolve the bonds of wickedness; undo the bundles that oppress” (Isaiah 58). And shortly afterward, after the barrenness of an unfruitful fast has been rebuked: “Then,” he says, “you will call, and the Lord will answer you; you will cry out, and he will say, ‘Here I am’” (ibid.).

Sometimes even the excess of tribulations causes a person to be heard, according to this saying: “To the Lord, when I was afflicted, I cried, and he heard me” (Psalm 119). And again: “You shall not afflict the stranger; for if he cries out to me, I will hear him, because I am merciful” (Exodus 22).

You see, then, in how many ways the grace of being heard is obtained, so that no one may be broken by despair of conscience when seeking to obtain things that are salutary and eternal. For even if, in contemplating our wretchedness, I grant that we are entirely deprived of all the virtues mentioned above, and that we possess neither that praiseworthy agreement of two persons, nor that faith compared to a mustard seed, nor those works of piety that the prophet describes, can we not at least possess importunity, which is available to everyone who wishes to have it? Through importunity alone the Lord promises that he will give whatever is asked of him.

Therefore we must persist in prayer without the hesitation of unbelief, and we must not doubt that by the constancy of our prayers we shall obtain everything we ask for according to God. For the Lord, wishing to bestow eternal and heavenly things, exhorts us to constrain him in some sense by our importunity; he not only does not despise or reject us as importunate, but even invites and praises us, and most graciously promises that he will grant whatever they have steadfastly hoped for, saying: “Ask and you shall receive; seek and you shall find; knock and it shall be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and he who seeks finds, and to him who knocks it shall be opened” (Luke 11). And again: “Whatever you ask in prayer, believing, you shall receive, and nothing shall be impossible for you” (Matthew 21). Therefore, if all the causes of being heard mentioned above entirely fail us, let at least the urgency of importunity encourage us; it lies, without any difficulty either of merit or labor, within the power of anyone who wishes. Let no one who supplicates be at all doubtful that he will not be heard, once he has begun to doubt that he is being heard.

That the Lord must be supplicated without fatigue, we are also taught by the example of blessed Daniel. [Note: [Col. 0811B] Thus the archangel Gabriel addressed Daniel: “Do not be afraid, Daniel, for from the first day on which you set your heart to understand and humbled yourself before your God, your words were heard, and I came because of your words” (Daniel 10). Saint Jerome says there: “It is asked: If he was heard immediately, why was the angel not sent immediately, but his arrival to Daniel was delayed for twenty-one days? Clearly, the delay gave Daniel an opportunity to entreat God more intensely, so that, through desiring more earnestly by labor, he might also deserve to hear more through the angel’s revelation.”]

He was heard from the first day on which he began to pray, but he obtained the effect of his petition after the twenty-first day (Daniel 10). Therefore we too must not cease from the purpose of our prayers once we sense that we are being heard only slowly. [Note: [Col. 0811C] Saint Augustine, Sermon 5 on the Words of the Lord according to Matthew: “When he sometimes gives more slowly,” he says, “he commends his gifts; he does not deny them. Things long desired are obtained more sweetly, while things given quickly are held cheaply. Ask, seek, persist; by asking and seeking you grow, so that you may receive. God keeps for you what he does not wish to give quickly, so that you may learn to desire great things greatly” (see Saint Jerome on Habakkuk, chapter 1).]

We must not cease, I say, if we find that we are heard only after delay, [Col. 0812B] lest perhaps the grace of being heard be postponed by the Lord’s dispensation for a time. [Note: [Col. 0811C] Observe here one of the principal offices and ministries of angels toward us: to offer our prayers to divine goodness, to assist and commend them by their own prayers, to obtain divine benefits for us, and in a certain sense to bring those benefits to us. This is clear from many passages of Scripture.

Genesis 28: “Jacob saw in a dream a ladder standing on the earth, whose top touched heaven, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon it, and the Lord leaning upon the ladder.” Why this, unless—as the matter itself and Scripture indicate—they act as advocates for the human beings whom they serve and for the kingdoms and principalities over which they preside? Angels ascend in order to offer our prayers to God; they descend to bring us his benefits, obtained and secured for us.

Thus in Judges 13 we read that the angel who foretold Samson’s birth ascended into heaven in the flame of the burnt offering. This signifies that the angel in a certain sense carried into heaven, before the Lord’s presence, the sacrifice offered by Manoah in thanksgiving.

Moreover, in Tobit 12 the angel Raphael addresses him in these words: “When you prayed with tears and buried the dead, I offered your prayer to the Lord.” Then the Greek text continues: “I am Raphael, one of the seven holy angels who present the prayers of the saints to God.” This is confirmed by Acts 10, where the angel who entered to Cornelius as he was praying said: “Your prayers and your almsgiving have ascended as a memorial before God.” And below: “Your prayer has been heard, and your almsgiving has been remembered before God.” “They have been remembered,” he says—that is, by the angel himself. This explains the expression, “They have ascended.”

Prayers are said to ascend as a memorial before God when they are in a certain sense represented and recalled to the divine Majesty by holy spirits. But this is proved more clearly by Revelation 8, where it is said that an angel stood before the altar, holding a golden censer, and that much incense was given to him so that he might offer it with the prayers of all the saints upon the golden altar before God’s throne. “And the smoke of the incense,” it says, “ascended from the prayers of the saints from the angel’s hand before God.”

To this is added the authority of the Church, which prays in the sacred canon of the Mass: “We humbly beseech you, almighty God: command that these things”—namely, the priest’s vows and prayers and those of the whole people—“be carried by the hands of your holy angel to your sublime altar, in the presence of your divine Majesty,” and so forth. Commentators note that the angel is placed in the singular here on behalf of the plural.

Finally, the testimonies of the holy Fathers also contribute. Saint Augustine discusses not only that this occurs, but also why and how it occurs, in Letter 120. Explaining the twenty-first Psalm’s statement, “A future generation shall be announced to the Lord,” he adds:

“It does not say, ‘The Lord shall be announced to a future generation,’ but, ‘A future generation shall be announced to the Lord.’ This must not be understood as though something were announced to one who does not know it so that he may know it, but in the manner in which angels announce to him not only God’s benefits to us but also our prayers. For it is written in Tobit 12, in the Greek text, where the angel says to human beings, ‘I presented the memorial of your prayer’—not so that God might then know what we wish or what we need, for the Lord says, ‘Your Father knows what you need before you ask him’; but because a rational creature, in obeying God, necessarily refers temporal causes to eternal truth, whether by asking that something be done for him or by seeking guidance about what he should do. This is a pious disposition of mind, by which the creature itself is built up, not God instructed.”

Rupert, Book IX of *The Victory of the Word*, chapter 8: “We must know,” he says, “that the holy angels are God’s ministers between God and human beings, his servants; that we sing psalms and pray in their presence; and that they are always ready to offer the Church’s prayers to God.”

Saint Bernard, Sermon 7 on the *Song of Songs*: “We believe,” he says, “that the holy angels stand beside those who pray and offer prayers and vows to God, provided that they see pure hands lifted without anger or dispute.” And below he addresses the holy angels as follows: “Who will grant me through you, O benevolent princes, that my petitions may be made known before God? Not to God, to whom even a human thought confesses; but before God—that is, to those blessed powers and disembodied spirits who are with God.”]

Or perhaps an angel who has gone forth from the presence of the Almighty to bring us a divine benefit may be delayed by the devil’s resistance. [Note: [Col. 0813C] An angel is said to go forth from the presence of God, not because he departs from God’s knowledge, power, or presence—which is everywhere—or is deprived of the beatific vision, but because, after making supplication and intercession for us before God, he comes to us to bring or announce divine benefits. For, as the Apostle says, “Are they not all ministering spirits sent out for service, for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Hebrews 1).

Yet, as blessed Gregory says (Book II of the *Morals*, chapter 3), they do not go forth from the divine vision in such a way as to be deprived of the joys of inward contemplation. If, when going forth, they lost sight of the Creator, they could neither raise up those who lie prostrate nor announce truth to the ignorant; nor could they offer the blind the fountain of light which they themselves would lose upon departing.

In this, therefore, the angelic nature is distinguished from the condition of our nature: we are confined by place and restricted by the ignorance of blindness, whereas angelic spirits are indeed confined by place, but their knowledge is nevertheless extended incomparably far beyond ours. They are therefore both sent and present: because, being confined by place, they go forth; and because they are also present within, they never depart. Thus they always behold the Father’s face (Matthew 18), and yet they come to us, because they go forth to us by spiritual presence while preserving themselves there, through inward contemplation, from which they have departed. Thus Gregory.

How a good angel bringing us a divine benefit may nevertheless, as is stated here, sometimes be detained or delayed because the devil resists him—although it is certain that even the least good angel is more powerful than the highest evil angel, since, as Saint Thomas teaches (I, q. 109, art. 4), among angels the order of grace outweighs and prevails over the order of nature—Rupert briefly explains in these words (Book IX of *The Victory of the Word*, chapter 6):

“Whence does an evil angel derive the power to fight against a good angel and resist him? From the sins of human beings or peoples. Where does this battle between good and evil angels take place? On the field of justice, in the conflict of judgment, with God himself as spectator and judge. But how do good and evil angels fight one another? The evil angel fights by accusing; the good by defending. Insofar as the evil angel’s accusation is grave and true, the good angel’s defense is correspondingly delayed and weakened,” and so forth.]

If we should discover that we have ceased from the purpose of our petition, the angel who has gone forth from the presence of the Almighty to bring us the divine benefit cannot, it is certain, carry out the desire of the commission entrusted to him. This could undoubtedly have happened to the prophet mentioned above, had he not, through incomparable strength, prolonged the perseverance of his prayers until the twenty-first day.

Let us therefore not be broken by any despair of this confidence of faith when we do not clearly perceive that our prayer has been obtained, nor let us hesitate concerning the Lord’s promise, which says: “Whatever you ask in prayer, believing, you will receive” (Matthew 24).

We must recall the statement of blessed John the Evangelist, by which the uncertainty of this question is plainly resolved: “This is the confidence that we have toward God: that whatever we ask according to his will, he hears us” (1 John 5). [Col. 0813B] Therefore he commanded us to have full and undoubted confidence of being heard only concerning those things which accord not with our advantages or temporal consolations, but with the Lord’s will. We are also commanded to include this in the Lord’s Prayer, saying, “Your will be done” (Matthew 6)—that is, not ours.

For if we also remember the Apostle’s statement that “we do not know what we ought to pray for as we ought” (Romans 8), we understand that we sometimes ask for things contrary to our salvation, and that it is most beneficial for us when the one who sees our interests more rightly and more truly than we do denies us what we ask.

There is no doubt that this also happened to that teacher of the Gentiles, when he prayed that the angel of Satan might be taken away from him, although by the Lord’s will it had been assigned to strike him beneficially. He said: “For this I pleaded with the Lord three times, that it might depart from me; and he said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness’” (2 Corinthians 12).

The Lord also expressed this meaning when praying in the person of the assumed human nature, [Note: [Col. 0814C] That is, according to the human nature assumed by him, and representing it in prayer. For it was fitting for Christ to pray as man, not as God, since according to his divinity he is equal to the Father. He is not said to have prayed in the person of the assumed man as though there were in Christ one person of the Word and another of the assumed man, as the impious heresiarch Nestorius taught. Rather, he is said to have prayed in the person of the assumed man for the reason just given: because he prayed, and now prays, not as God but insofar as he is man, just as the Apostle says to the Hebrews 7: “He always lives to intercede for us” (see Saint Thomas, II–II, q. 83, art. 10, and Leonard Lessius, Book II *On Justice*, chapter 37).]

so that he might also provide us, as with everything else, an example of how to pray. Thus, when he prayed, he said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26). [Note: [Col. 0814D] Thus Pope Saint Agatho defined at the Sixth Ecumenical Council: “We proclaim two wills in Christ”—namely, the divine and the human—“not contrary to one another, as the impious heretics assert, but with his human will following, not resisting, but rather subject to, his divine and omnipotent will.” Thus there. On the complete harmony of these wills in Christ, consult the interpreters of the saying cited here from Matthew and the theologians commenting on the Master of the Sentences, Book III, distinction 17.]

His will certainly did not differ from the Father’s will. For he had come to save what had perished (Matthew 18) and to give his life as a ransom for many (Matthew 20). Of this he himself says: “No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10).

In his person, concerning the unity of his will, which he continually possessed with the Father, blessed David also sings in Psalm 39: “To do your will, my God, I desired.” We likewise read concerning the Father: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John 3). And concerning the Son we find: “He gave himself for our sins” (Galatians 2).

Just as it is reported of the Father, “He did not spare even his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Romans 8), so it is narrated of the Son, “He was offered because he himself willed it” (Isaiah 53). Thus the one will of the Father and the Son is signified in every respect, so that even in the mystery of the Lord’s resurrection their operation is shown not to have been discordant.

For just as the blessed Apostle proclaims that the Father effected his bodily resurrection, saying, “And God the Father, who raised him from the dead” (Galatians 1), so the Son declares that he will raise up the temple of his body: “Destroy this temple,” he says, “and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2).

Therefore, instructed by the Lord’s examples mentioned above, we too ought to conclude all our supplications with a similar prayer and always add this expression to all our petitions: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26).

It is sufficiently clear that the threefold number of prayers customarily celebrated in the gatherings of the brothers to conclude the synaxis cannot be observed by one who does not pray with an attentive mind. [Note: [Col. 0815A] The negating particle, which is missing here in the Plantin edition, has been restored from Dionysius and others. Dionysius the paraphrast renders the passage as follows: “Finally, it is sufficiently clear that the threefold prayer customarily made in the gatherings of the brothers to conclude the synaxis cannot be observed by one who does not pray with an attentive mind.” Many manuscripts, moreover, read: “The number of three prostrations,” and so forth, which amounts to the same thing.

The Author seems to have in view the passage in Matthew 26, where Christ is read to have prayed in the garden on his knees, saying the same words three times: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” In imitation of this, as can be gathered from the present passage, those monks used, before leaving the church or assembly—which he here calls the synaxis, after the office had been completed—to adore God with a threefold supplication and bending of the knees. The Author here admonishes that this be done with great devotion, attention, and reverence, as does Saint Benedict also (Rule, chapter 52): “When the Work of God is finished, let all depart in complete silence, and reverence be shown to God,” and so forth.]

# CHAPTER XXXV. On praying within one’s room with the door closed

First of all, [Note: [Col. 0815B] Two things must be observed here. First, that the command to enter one’s room and close the door should be referred not so much to a material room and door as to the room of the heart. Otherwise this Gospel saying would conflict with the Apostolic one: “I desire men to pray in every place, lifting pure hands” (1 Timothy 2).

Christ does not command us literally to enter a room and close the door in order to pray secretly. He merely forbids us to seek from our prayer the empty praise of human beings, and commands us to pray as though we were seen and heard by God alone. Besides this abbot, the holy Fathers likewise give this admonition.

Saint Jerome, commenting on Matthew, says: “Taken simply, this teaches the listener to avoid the vain glory of praying. But it seems to me that this command means rather that we should pray to the Lord with the thought of the heart enclosed and the lips compressed.” We read that Anna did this in the Book of Kings: “Only her lips moved, and her voice was not heard” (1 Kings 2).

Saint Augustine, Book II of *The Sermon on the Mount*, chapter 6: “He shows,” he says, “that he forbids the pursuit of that reward which fools desire, namely, to be praised by human beings. ‘But when you pray,’ he says, ‘enter into your rooms.’ What are these rooms except the hearts themselves, which are also signified in the Psalm when it says, ‘What you say in your hearts, and be contrite in your beds’” (Psalm 4)?

“And closing the doors, pray,” he says, “to your Father in secret. It is not enough to enter the rooms if the door remains open to intruders. Through that door, things outside intrude improperly and seek our interior spaces. By things outside we mean all temporal and visible things, which enter our thoughts through the door—that is, through bodily sense—and disturb those who are praying with a crowd of empty imaginings. The door must therefore be closed; that is, resistance must be offered to bodily sense, so that spiritual prayer may be directed to the Father. This prayer takes place in the innermost heart, where our Father is prayed to in secret.”

Saint Gregory, Book XXII of the *Morals*, chapter 18: “True petition,” he says, “does not consist in the sounds of the mouth but in the thoughts of the heart. Our words do not make the stronger voices before God’s most secret ears; our desires do. If we ask for eternal life with our mouth but do not desire it in our heart, while shouting we remain silent. But if we desire it from the heart, even when we are silent with our mouth, while silent we cry out.

Hence, in the wilderness, the people make a great noise, while Moses is silent amid the noise of words; yet, though silent, he is heard by the ear of divine mercy, when it is said, ‘Why do you cry out to me?’ (Exodus 14). Within, therefore, in desire, there is a secret cry that has not yet reached human ears, yet fills the hearing of the Creator.

Hence Anna went to the temple and was silent with her mouth, yet uttered so many voices of her desire. Hence in the Gospel the Lord says, ‘Enter into your room, and with the door closed pray to your Father in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you’ (Matthew 6). One asks in the room with the door closed when, though the mouth is silent, one pours forth the affection of the mind in the presence of heavenly mercy. The voice is heard in secret when one cries out silently through holy desires.

Thus the Psalmist rightly says: ‘The Lord has heard the desire of the poor; your ear has heard the preparation of their heart’ (Psalm 9).” Thus Gregory.

Second, it must be noted here that the subject is private prayer, not public prayer. The case of public prayer, or of the divine praises, which ought to be celebrated communally, is different. Saint Thomas explains this most appropriately in these words (II–II, q. 83, art. 12):

“There are two kinds of prayer: common and individual—that is, public and private. Common prayer is offered to God by the ministers of the Church in the name of the whole faithful people. Therefore such prayer must be made known to the entire people for whom it is offered; and this could not happen unless it were vocal. It was therefore reasonably instituted that the ministers of the Church should pronounce such prayers in a loud voice, so that they might come to everyone’s knowledge.

Individual prayer, however, is offered by an individual person who prays, whether for himself or for others. There is no necessity that such prayer be vocal. Nevertheless, a voice is added to such prayer for three reasons.

First, to arouse inward devotion, by which the mind of the one praying is lifted up to God. For through outward signs, whether of words or of certain actions, the human mind is moved according to apprehension and consequently according to affection. Hence Augustine says to Proba (Letter 121, chapter 9) that by words and other signs we more keenly rouse ourselves to increase holy desire. Therefore in individual prayer one should use words and such signs only insofar as they help to arouse the mind inwardly. If they distract or in any way hinder the mind, they should be abandoned. This happens especially in those whose minds are prepared for devotion without such signs. Thus Psalm 26 says, ‘My heart has spoken to you; my face has sought you.’ And it is written of Anna in 1 Kings 1 that she spoke in her heart.

Second, vocal prayer is added as the payment of a debt, so that a person may serve God according to the whole of what he has received from God—that is, not only with the mind but also with the body. This especially pertains to prayer insofar as it is a work of satisfaction. Hence Hosea 14 says, ‘Take away all iniquity and accept what is good, and we will repay the calves of our lips.’

Third, vocal prayer is added through a kind of overflow from the soul into the body arising from vehement affection, according to Psalm 15: ‘My heart rejoiced, and my tongue exulted.’” Thus far Saint Thomas.

Other Fathers teach the same concerning private prayers. Augustine, in chapter 5 of the Rule: “In the oratory no one should do anything except what it was made for and from which it received its name, so that if some people wish to pray outside the appointed hours, when they have leisure, they may not be hindered.” See Umbertus’s commentary there.

Likewise Saint Benedict, chapter 52 of the Rule: “When the Work of God is finished, let all depart in complete silence, and reverence be shown to God, so that a brother who perhaps wishes to pray privately may not be hindered by another’s misconduct. But if another wishes to pray more secretly, let him simply enter and pray, not in a loud voice, but with tears and attentiveness of heart,” and so forth.

Finally, Caesarius, cited by Turrecremata: “Above all,” he says (*Treatise 118 on the Rule*), “my brothers, whenever we devote ourselves to prayer, we must supplicate in silence and quiet, because whoever wishes to cry out in a loud voice appears to deprive all those standing near him of the fruit of prayer. Let only groans, sighs, or moans be heard. For our prayer ought to be like that which is recorded of Anna, the mother of blessed Samuel. It is written of her that she prayed weeping; only her lips moved, and her voice was not heard at all.”]

Therefore the Gospel command must be observed with particular care: that, entering our room and closing our door, we pray to our Father (Matthew 6). We fulfill it in this way.

We supplicate within our room when, removing our heart completely from the noise of all thoughts and anxieties, we secretly and familiarly present our prayers to the Lord. We pray with the door closed when, with our lips tightly shut and in complete silence, we supplicate the one who searches not voices but hearts.

We pray in secret when, with the heart alone and an attentive mind, we entrust our petitions to God alone, so that not even the hostile powers may be able to discover the character of our petition. Therefore we must pray in complete silence—not only so that we may not distract the brothers standing nearby with our whispers or cries and disturb the minds of those who are praying, but also so that our enemies themselves, who especially lie in wait for us while we pray, may remain unaware of the purpose of our petition.

Thus we shall fulfill the command: “From her who sleeps in your bosom, guard the doors of your mouth” (Micah 7). [Note: [Col. 0818B] “Do not suffer what Samson suffered from Delilah,” says Saint Jerome.]

# CHAPTER XXXVI. On the usefulness of brief and silent prayer

For this reason, [Note: [Col. 0818C] A passage worthy of note in commendation of brief and ejaculatory prayers, about which we have also spoken elsewhere (Book II of the *Institutes*, chapter 10). Through such prayers our heart is kindled as by sparks, and the heart of God is pierced as by arrows.

Concerning their frequent and familiar use among those monks, Saint Augustine writes to Proba (Letter 122): “The brothers in Egypt are said to have frequent prayers, but they are nevertheless very brief and, as it were, ejaculated in haste, lest that alertness which is greatly necessary to one who prays should vanish and grow dull through prolonged delays. By this they also sufficiently show that, just as this attentiveness should not be extended if it cannot endure, so, if it endures, it should not be broken too quickly.”]

we must pray frequently but briefly, lest, while we linger, the enemy who lies in wait should be able to insert something into our heart.

For this is the true sacrifice: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Psalm 50). This is the salutary offering; these are the pure libations; this is the sacrifice of justice (ibid.); this is the sacrifice of praise (Psalm 49); these are the true and rich victims; these are the marrow-filled burnt offerings (Psalm 65), which are offered with contrite and humbled hearts.

If we present them with the discipline and attentiveness of spirit that we have described, we shall be able to sing with effective power: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight; the lifting of my hands like the evening sacrifice” (Psalm 140).

The arrival of that hour and night also appropriately reminds us to offer this with devotion. Although many things may seem to have been said about it in proportion to our weakness, and although the Conference has been prolonged for a long time, we nevertheless believe that, given the sublimity and difficulty of the subject, very little has actually been discussed.

Struck with amazement rather than filled by these holy discourses, [Note: [Col. 0818C] That is, after the evening office or prayer had been completed.] and after celebrating the evening synaxis, we relaxed our limbs in sleep for a little while. At first light we departed to our quarters, intending to return again for a fuller discussion, rejoicing both in the acquisition of the instructions and in the assurance of the promises.

For we had sensed that those discussions had shown us only the excellence of prayer, while we had not yet fully grasped the order and power by which its persistence is either to be acquired or maintained.

# TENTH CONFERENCE, which is the second of Abbot Isaac, ON PRAYER

[Col. 0817]

# CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0817D]

Among these lofty institutions of the anchorites, which, with God’s favor in some measure, have been arranged in an unpolished style, the order of the narrative itself compels us to insert and weave in something that may seem like placing a blemish upon a beautiful body:

[Note: “Blemish” (*naevus*), according to Festus, is a distinctive mark on the body or a birthmark. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I: “But there is a blemish on the body; yet to him this seemed a light.” It is used metaphorically for any fault. Saint Ambrose, *On Duties*, book I, chapter 18: “the blemish of error.” Sidonius Apollinaris, book II of the letters, letter 5: “Weakened religion’s blemish.” Ausonius, in his *Epistles*, idyll 7: “We love our blemishes and scars.” Paulinus to Ausonius, letter 2: “Your favor toward me has never been stained even by the slightest blemish.” Cassian, *Conference* 7, chapter 25: “When divine mercy finds not even the slightest blemish or stain in them on that day of judgment.” Finally, it is commonly said that no body is so beautiful that it is without a blemish. The author therefore said that placing a blemish upon a beautiful body meant inserting a digression of sorts, foreign and irrelevant to the subject, and somewhat unpleasant and unwelcome.]

although I do not doubt that from this very matter no small instruction may be drawn concerning the image of almighty God that is read of in Genesis (Genesis I and II), and that it ought especially to be imparted to the more simple-minded, since so important a doctrine is at stake that ignorance of it cannot exist without grave blasphemy and harm to the catholic faith.

[Note: Here again the word “not” was omitted in the earlier edition; because of its absence, the sentence is made contrary and false, as is evident in itself.]

## CHAPTER II. On the custom of celebrating Easter in Egypt

[Note: The Paraphrast, in a rougher style and syntax, says: “This custom is observed in the region of Egypt by ancient institution: when the day of the Epiphanies has passed—the day which the priests of that province say is the day of Christ’s baptism, or of his birth according to the flesh, and hence they make one solemnity out of both events, not two, as is done in the regions of the West—then letters are sent,” and so forth. But he incorrectly adds, “Then therefore letters are sent,” as though this were a different period, whereas everyone can see that it is one sentence dependent upon the words, “This custom is observed,” namely, so that letters may be sent. Nor do I approve his having earlier substituted “institution” for “tradition.” For although tradition possesses the force of an institution, the word “tradition” nevertheless seems preferable to retain against the sectarians of our time, who do not know how to listen to ecclesiastical traditions and wholly reject or ridicule them. See Cuychius’s nineteenth annotation.]

[Note: This custom began with the great Council of Nicaea. Since it had been most sacredly decreed there that the feast of Easter was to be celebrated by all the faithful on one and the same day, and that day a Sunday, a question then began to be debated concerning the method of determining the day of Easter, so that it might be fixed and certain for everyone. Otherwise there was danger from the differing calculations of time adopted by different people: although all the faithful might celebrate Easter on a Sunday, they would nevertheless do so on different Sundays. Therefore, says Baronius (*Annals*, volume III, under the year 325), since it was universally recognized that from the most ancient period the Egyptians had claimed for themselves the particular knowledge of investigating the seasons of the year and the courses of the sun and moon, the holy synod decided to entrust this responsibility to Alexander, bishop of the Church of Alexandria. Taking with him men highly skilled in calculation, he diligently discharged the task entrusted to him.

The holy synod also decreed that the bishops who succeeded Alexander in the Church of Alexandria should retain this duty and office, so that they would first inform the bishops of the Roman Church on which day Easter ought to be celebrated each year, and through them all the other Churches would be notified. Hence Saint Leo, writing to the emperor Marcian (*Letter* 64), says: “Although the feast of Easter, which above all contains the sacrament of human salvation, must always be celebrated in the first month, it is nevertheless so changeable through the condition of the lunar cycle that the choice of the most sacred day is often uncertain; and from this it frequently happens—which must not happen—that the whole Church does not observe together what ought to be one and the same observance. The holy Fathers therefore strove to remove the occasion of this error, entrusting the entire responsibility to the bishop of Alexandria, since among the Egyptians the expertise of this calculation appeared to have been handed down from ancient times. By it the day on which the aforesaid solemnity would occur each year was reported to the apostolic see, and the notice contained in that document was circulated generally to the more distant Churches.” Thus Saint Leo.

The first Council of Arles also mentions this custom, chapter 1, as does Innocent I in his first letter to Aurelius. This custom long continued in the Alexandrian Church: the bishop of that see would issue what were called “paschal letters,” by which he first reminded the Roman pontiff of the day on which Easter was to be celebrated in the following year, so long as catholic bishops occupied that Church. This office was interrupted when bishops who were heresiarchs began to preside over the same Church, because the Catholics would not accept their letters. But let us proceed with explaining the text; the other matters related to this subject will thereby become clearer.]

Within the region of Egypt this custom is preserved by ancient tradition: when the day of the Epiphanies has passed

[Note: *Epiphania* is feminine singular, while *Epiphaniorum* is neuter plural, as here; likewise *Theophania* occurs in both genders and numbers, with the same meaning. One says “the feast of the Theophanies,” just as “of the Epiphanies,” among both Latins and Greeks. It is the day on which the birth of Christ was manifested, when he first began to be revealed to the Gentiles as the Magi worshiped him. Hence it is called *epiphaneia*, that is, “manifestation,” or *theophaneia*, that is, “manifestation or revelation of God,” although Gregory of Nazianzus calls the day on which the Lord Jesus Christ was born the Theophany.

Two noteworthy points are made here concerning the day of the Epiphany, or Epiphanies. First, as Baronius also observed, among the Egyptians the nativity of Christ and his baptism were customarily celebrated not in two ways—that is, on two distinct days, as happens in the Roman and Western Church—but on one and the same day, namely the sixth of January, the day on which we celebrate the Epiphany of the Lord, or the feast of the Three Kings. This is also clear from the homily of Blessed John Chrysostom on Luke II and from the preface to the paschal letter of Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria; it is therefore likely that Cassian took what he reports here from that source. Isidore also mentions this custom in book I of *Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 16, when discussing the feast of the Epiphany.

Saint Epiphanius likewise seems to have held this view when he writes in *Heresy* 51 that the Lord was born on the eleventh day of the month Tuli, which for us is the day of the Epiphany, but was baptized before the sixth of the Ides of November. Saint Jerome, however, refutes this opinion in his commentary on Ezekiel, book I, chapter 1, and asserts that the Lord was baptized on this very day, but not born on it: “Among the eastern peoples,” he says, “after the gathering of the crops and the treading of the winepresses, when the tithes were brought to the temple, October was the first month and January the fourth. The prophet adds the fifth day of the month in order to signify the baptism, in which the heavens were opened to Christ, and the day of the Epiphanies is venerated to this day—not, as some think, as the day of his birth in the flesh. At that time he was hidden and did not appear, which agrees with the present occasion, when it was said: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’” (Matthew III). Thus Jerome.

Following this opinion, the Western Church recalls on one and the same day, which it calls the Epiphany, the coming of the Magi, Christ’s baptism, and that first remarkable miracle when Christ changed water into wine. The rest of the Greeks, however, agree with the Latin Church in distinguishing the Lord’s birthday from the solemnity of the Epiphany, as is clear from Gregory of Nazianzus, in his oration on the Nativity of Christ, and from other Greek Fathers.

The second point reported here is that it was customary on the very day of the Epiphany, or Epiphanies, for a letter written by the patriarch of Alexandria to announce throughout all the Churches and monasteries—not only of Egypt but of the entire world—the beginning of Lent and the day of Easter. Baronius explains how this was done as follows: “Once it had first been learned from the letters of the bishop of Alexandria on which day of the year Easter was to be celebrated, and once this had been proclaimed to all the Churches in the name of the apostolic see on the sacred day of the Epiphany, deacons in each Church customarily announced it during the solemn celebration of Mass. Since the paschal letter was first customarily sent to Rome, to the Roman pontiff, from whom the other Churches were to receive it, on the day of the Epiphany of the Lord, it was necessary for the paschal letter to be written and sent by the deacons’ proclamation during the sacred rites not in the same year whose Easter it announced, but in the preceding year.” Thus Baronius.

Therefore, when it is said here that the letters of the Alexandrian pontiff were sent throughout all the Churches of Egypt, designating the beginning of Lent and the day of Easter, this should be understood to mean that it was done after the Roman pontiff had first been notified and his authorization received.]

(which the priests of that province define as either the day of the Lord’s baptism or of his birth according to the flesh, and therefore celebrate the solemnity of both sacraments not in two separate observances, as in the western provinces, but together under the festivity of this one day), let letters of the Alexandrian pontiff be sent throughout all the Churches of Egypt, by which the beginning of Lent and the day of Easter may be designated not only throughout all the cities but also throughout all the monasteries.

According to this custom, only a very few days after the previous conference had been held with Abba Isaac, the solemn letters of Theophilus, bishop of the aforesaid city, arrived. In them, together with the paschal announcement, he also discussed at length the foolish heresy of the Anthropomorphites.

[Note: Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, at first deserved well of the Church because he had vigorously fought against Origen and the Origenists. Later, because of the hatred and persecution he stirred up against John Chrysostom, he became hated by the Roman pontiff and by all good men. Toward the end of his life he came to his senses and, after ruling that Church for twenty-seven years, departed this life.

John of Damascus, book III *On Images*, reports the following about him from Isidore the Deacon: “Because of that sin”—namely, because he had forbidden the name of John Chrysostom to be recited in church—“Theophilus could not die until an image of Chrysostom was brought to him. When he had venerated it, he gave up his spirit.” In the *Lives of the Fathers* we read the following about the same man: “Theophilus, archbishop of holy memory, when he was about to die, said: ‘Blessed are you, Abba Arsenius, because you always kept this hour before your eyes.’”

This Theophilus was a contemporary and equal of Saint Jerome, as the letters they wrote to each other testify. He wrote three paschal and solemn letters, which Saint Jerome translated into Latin. They are useful and learned letters and survive in volume III of the *Library of the Holy Fathers. *Bellarmine, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.]

[Note: We have discussed elsewhere the Anthropomorphites—*Institutes*, book VIII, chapter 4—as heretics so called because they asserted that God possessed human form, human limbs, and a human body. They relied on two foundations drawn from sacred Scripture.

The first was that Scripture frequently attributes human limbs to God—head, eyes, face, arms, hands, and feet—and not only limbs but also human actions, passions, and emotions, such as seeing, hearing, repenting, rejoicing, sitting, and standing.

The second foundation, touched upon here, was that Scripture says that man was created in the image and likeness of God (Genesis I). Since man is corporeal, they concluded that God too must be corporeal.

Against them Theophilus accomplished what Gennadius, in complete agreement with Cassian, expresses as follows in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 33: “Theophilus, bishop of the city of Alexandria, wrote one large volume against Origen, and so forth. He also refuted at length the heretical Anthropomorphites, who say that God consists of human form and limbs, convicting and confuting them by the testimonies of the divine Scriptures. He showed that, according to the faith of the Fathers, God must be believed to be incorruptible and incorporeal, composed in no way whatsoever of the outlines of limbs, and therefore resembling nothing among created things in substance; nor had he given to any creature the incorruptibility, immutability, or incorporeality of his own nature,” and so forth. Thus Gennadius.

In the paschal letters of Theophilus themselves, however, which were translated into Latin by Saint Jerome, there is no mention whatsoever of the heretical Anthropomorphites, against whom Cassian, Gennadius, and likewise Sozomen, whom he will cite shortly, assert that he argued at length. Nor does Saint Jerome, who often mentions them, record that he wrote anything against them in those letters. From this it follows that Theophilus’s writings or letters against the Anthropomorphites were later than those translated by Saint Jerome, and that, apart from them, no other works of Theophilus now survive.]

He destroyed it by an abundant discourse. This was received with such bitterness, owing to the error of their simplicity, by almost the entire body of monks dwelling throughout the province of Egypt that, on the contrary, the greater part of the elders decided that the aforesaid pontiff, as though corrupted by a most grievous heresy, must be denounced by the whole body of the brotherhood. For he seemed to be attacking the teaching of Holy Scripture by denying that almighty God was formed by the composition of a human figure, whereas Scripture most plainly testifies that Adam was created in his image (Genesis I). Finally, those dwelling in the desert of Scetis, who surpassed all the monks in the monasteries of Egypt in perfection and knowledge, rejected this letter so thoroughly that, apart from Abba Paphnutius, the priest of our congregation, none of the other priests who presided over the three other churches in that same desert would permit it even to be read or recited at all in their assemblies.

## CHAPTER III. Serapion’s fall into the heresy of the Anthropomorphites

Among those held by this error was Serapion, a man of most ancient rigor and in every respect perfected in practical discipline. His ignorance concerning the doctrine just mentioned prejudiced all who held the true faith as greatly as he himself surpassed almost all the monks in either merit of life or length of years. When the holy priest Paphnutius could not bring him back to the path of right faith despite many exhortations, because this persuasion seemed novel to him and never before known or handed down by his predecessors, it happened that a deacon of the highest learning, named Photinus, came from Cappadocia, desiring to see the brothers dwelling in that desert.

[Note: I do not know who this Photinus was. Certainly he was not the heresiarch mentioned by Saint Jerome in the *Catalogue* and by Socrates, book II, chapter 3; nor was he the much earlier Photinus, bishop and martyr, who was the predecessor of Irenaeus. The latter is mentioned by the same Jerome in letter 84 and by Eusebius, book V, chapters 2 and 3. In John Moschus—or, if preferred, Sophronius—in the *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 127, a Photinus is mentioned who was abbot and bishop of Phari. Our Photinus, however, is said to have been not a bishop but merely a deacon, certainly a catholic man, exceptionally learned in the doctrine of the faith, and perhaps for that reason later advanced to the episcopate.]

Blessed Paphnutius received him with the greatest joy and, bringing him forward to confirm the faith contained in the letter of the aforesaid pontiff, asked him in the presence of all the brothers how all the catholic Churches of the East interpreted the statement in Genesis, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Genesis I).

Photinus explained that all the leaders of the Churches understood the image and likeness of God spiritually, not according to the humble, literal sound of the words. He established this with an abundance of speech and numerous testimonies from Scripture, showing that nothing of this kind could apply to that immeasurable, incomprehensible, and invisible majesty—nothing that could be circumscribed by human composition or likeness—for it is an incorporeal, uncompounded, and simple nature, which cannot be grasped by the eyes and likewise cannot be measured by the mind.

At last the old man, moved by the many and powerful arguments of the learned man, was drawn to the faith of catholic tradition. When his assent to this teaching had filled Abba Paphnutius and all of us with boundless joy—because the Lord had not allowed a man of such great antiquity and perfected in such great virtues, who had erred only through ignorance and the simplicity of rusticity, to deviate all the way to the end from the path of right faith—we rose together and poured out prayers to the Lord in thanksgiving.

[Note: Ciaconius and others read: “That anthropomorphic image of the deity”—*anthropomorphic*, that is, “having a human appearance,” or “fashioned in human form,” as explained above.]

But during the prayer the old man became so mentally distraught because he felt that the Anthropomorphite image of the Godhead, which he had been accustomed to place before himself in prayer, was being removed from his heart, that he suddenly burst into the most bitter tears and repeated sobs. Throwing himself upon the ground, he cried out with a mighty wail:

“Alas, wretched me! They have taken my God away from me, and I have no one whom I can now hold; I no longer know whom I should adore or address.”

[Note: Ciaconius and others read: “That anthropomorphic image of the deity.” *Anthropomorphic* means “representing a human appearance” or “fashioned in human form,” as explained above.]

Deeply moved by this, and with the force of the previous conference still abiding in our hearts, we returned to Abba Isaac. We looked directly at him and addressed him in these words.

## CHAPTER IV. On the return to Abba Isaac and the examination of the error into which the aforesaid old man had fallen

Although the novelty of the matter that had recently arisen, together with our desire to return to Your Blessedness concerning the preceding conference that had been arranged on the state of prayer, invited us to come to you while setting everything else aside, the exceedingly grave error of Abba Serapion also added something to this desire—an error conceived, as we believe, through the cunning of the most wicked demons.

We are cast down into no small despair when we consider that he has not only entirely lost, through this fault of ignorance, the great labors he commendably spent in this desert for fifty years, but has also incurred the danger of eternal death. We therefore desire first to learn from where and why such a serious error crept into him. Then we ask to be instructed how we may attain that quality of prayer concerning which you recently discoursed not only at length but also magnificently. For that wonderful conference achieved this much in us: it awakened astonishment in our minds, but did not show us how we might accomplish or apprehend it.

## CHAPTER V. Isaac’s reply concerning the origin of the heresy discussed above

**Isaac:** It is not surprising that a very simple man, who had never been thoroughly instructed concerning the substance and nature of divinity, could have remained until now—or, more truly, could have continued in his former error—and been deceived through the fault of rusticity and the habit of an ancient error.

This error is not imposed, as you suppose, by a recent deception of demons, but by ignorance inherited from former paganism. According to the practice of that error, by which demons were worshiped as composed in human form, people now likewise suppose that the incomprehensible and ineffable majesty of the true Godhead must be adored under the limitation of some image. They believe that they retain or possess nothing if they do not have before them some image that they can continually address while engaged in supplication, carry about in their minds, and keep always fixed before their eyes.

The following sentence is appropriately directed against this error: “And they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man” (Romans I).

[Note: Erasmus, in his annotations, reads the phrase in the ablative, “in likeness,” because the Greek has *en homoiōmati*—“in likeness.” He says that it is expressed as though one said, “through the assimilation of an image,” so that the sense is: “They exchanged the glory of God by fashioning images for themselves, by which they thought they represented the true God, who is incorporeal.”

Such were those against whom Paul argues in Acts XVII, taking the occasion from the inscription on an altar, “To an unknown god.” After much discussion he concludes: “Since we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the divine is like gold, silver, or stone, an image formed by the art and thought of man.” Thus Erasmus.

Although this commentary is good, it is not by the best author and should therefore not be valued highly—especially since the Greek interpreters, Chrysostom, Oecumenius, and Theophylact, interpret the passage in the same way as the Latins. They were not unaware that the preposition *en* is frequently used in place of *hōs*, “as,” especially when the accompanying verb requires it, as here.]

Jeremiah likewise says: “My people have exchanged their glory for an idol” (Jeremiah II).

Although this error became ingrained in the minds of some through the origin we have described, it nevertheless also took root in the minds of those who had never been contaminated by pagan superstition, through ignorance or rusticity and under the pretext of the testimony, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Genesis I). Thus the heresy called that of the Anthropomorphites emerged under the occasion of this detestable interpretation. It stubbornly maintains that the immeasurable and simple substance of divinity is composed according to our outlines and fashioned in human form.

[Note: They make a certain man named Audaeus the first author of this heresy; from him its adherents were called Audiani or Vadiani. Nicephorus, book XI, chapter 14, reports as follows: “At that time there was also a certain Audaeus, a Syrian by race and language, an inventor of new doctrines. When he had misunderstood the statement, ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness,’ he first supposed that God had human form and possessed bodily limbs, failing to understand sufficiently the meaning of sacred Scripture, which attributes the names of human parts to the works of the divine Majesty.” Thus he.

Theodoret, in question 20 on Genesis, refutes such heretics with this argument: “If God is thought to have a body like man’s because Scripture describes him as equipped and furnished with human limbs, by the same reasoning it would be concluded that man is not like God and was not made in his image and likeness. For Zechariah, chapter IV, describes God as having seven eyes, whereas we have only two; and in Psalm XC God is presented as having feathers and wings, which we lack. Scripture attributes many other things metaphorically to God which, if taken literally and measured by reality, would make God misshapen and monstrous, and utterly unlike man. The image of God must therefore not be sought in the human body but in the mind, which, like God, possesses and is capable of reason, counsel, and wisdom.” See Abulensis and Pererius in their commentaries on Genesis.]

Whoever has been instructed in catholic doctrine, however, will detest this as pagan blasphemy and will thus attain that most pure quality of prayer which not only will mingle no image of divinity or bodily outlines—something it is impious even to say—with his supplication, but will admit into himself no memory of any saying or deed, nor any appearance or form of any kind of image.

## CHAPTER VI. For what reasons Christ Jesus appears to each of us either humble or glorified

For according to the measure of its purity, as I said in the preceding conference (Conference 9, chapter 8), each mind is raised or formed in its prayer. It withdraws from contemplation of earthly and material things in proportion as the condition of its purity has advanced it and has caused Jesus to be perceived by the inner sight of the soul either as still humble, or as corporeal, or as coming glorified in the glory of his majesty.

[Note: He carefully distinguishes and morally interprets three classes of people who see Jesus, or three ways in which Jesus appears to human beings, as the title of the chapter says.

Some see Jesus only as corporeal or carnal—for example, the carnal Jews, who recognized Christ as nothing but flesh and a mere human being; or those who imagine God as carnal and corporeal, such as the Anthropomorphites discussed above; or the Arians, who asserted that Christ was nothing but flesh and a creature; or the Nestorians, who divided Christ, separating the person of the man from the person of the Word in Christ, and called Christ not God but *theophoros*, “God-bearing.”

Others see Jesus as humble, that is, as small or lowly—for example, the uneducated and imperfect Christians who consider only Christ’s humanity and his human works; or, as is said here, those occupied only with the external works of the active life, like Martha in the Gospel (Luke X), and those to whom the Apostle wrote: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians IV).

Finally, others see and contemplate Jesus as glorious. These constantly recall and meditate upon his divinity, glorification, and other divine and sublime mysteries: devout and perfect monks and contemplatives who, with Mary, choose the better part, which shall not be taken away from them.]

For they will not be able to behold Jesus coming in his kingdom, because they are still held, as it were, under that Jewish weakness and cannot say with the Apostle: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him” (II Corinthians V).

[Note: “According to the flesh,” that is, according to the carnal and visible presence of the body. “But now we no longer know him” means that we do not now honor him in that manner, as though he were present in a visible body.]

Only those with the purest eyes contemplate his divinity who, rising from humble and earthly works and thoughts, withdraw with him to the lofty mountain of solitude. Free from the tumult of all earthly thoughts and disturbances, and separated from the mixture of every vice, that mountain, exalted by the purest faith and the excellence of virtues, reveals the glory of his countenance and the image of his splendor to those who deserve to behold him with the pure sight of the soul.

Yet Jesus is also seen by those who dwell in cities, towns, and villages—that is, by those who live in active fellowship and are engaged in works—but not in the brightness in which he appeared to those who were able to climb with him the aforementioned mountain of virtues, namely Peter, James, and John (Matthew XVII).

Thus he appeared to Moses in the solitude (Exodus III) and spoke to Elijah (III Kings XVIII and XIX). Desiring to confirm this and leave us examples of perfect purity—and although he himself, as the inviolable source of holiness, had no external need of the aid of withdrawal or the benefit of solitude in order to attain purity, since the fullness of purity could not be stained by any defilement of crowds, nor could he who cleanses and sanctifies everything polluted be contaminated by human companionship—our Lord nevertheless withdrew alone to the mountain to pray (Matthew XIV).

Through this example of his withdrawal he instructed us that, if we too wish to appeal to God with a pure and undivided disposition of heart, we should likewise withdraw from every disturbance and confusion of the crowds. Thus, while dwelling in this body, we may fit ourselves, at least in part, into a likeness of that blessedness promised to the saints in the future, and God may be for us all things in all (I Corinthians XV).

## CHAPTER VII. In what the end and consummation of our prayers consist
Then the prayer of our Savior, which he prayed to the Father for his disciples, saying, “That the love with which you loved me may be in them, and they in us”; and again, “That they all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I in you, so that they too may be one in us” (John 17), will then be perfectly accomplished in us—when that perfect love of God, with which he first loved us (1 John 4), has also passed into the affection of our hearts. By this the Lord’s prayer, which we believe can in no way be made void, will have been fulfilled.

This will happen when all our love, all our desire, all our zeal, all our effort, all our thought—everything that we see, say, or hope for—will be God; and when that unity which now exists between the Father and the Son, and between the Son and the Father, has been infused into our perception and minds: that is, when, just as he loves us with a sincere, pure, and indissoluble love, we too are joined to him by a perpetual and inseparable love. Thus united to him, whatever we hope for, whatever we understand, and whatever we say will be God. I mean that we shall arrive at the end mentioned above, which the same Lord, in praying, desires to be fulfilled in us: “That they all may be one, just as we are one; I in them and you in me, so that they too may be perfected in unity” (John 17). And again: “Father, I desire that those whom you have given me may be where I am, and that they too may be with me” (ibid.).

[Note: “Solitary” means “monk.” Cassian so calls him throughout, especially in Books 9 and 10 of the *Institutes*. The Greeks call them ἡσυχασταί (*hesychasts*), that is, those who act quietly and peacefully, as Justinian writes in Novel 5. Jeremiah encompasses both designations in the verse that especially suits monks: “He shall sit alone and keep silent, because he shall lift himself above himself” (Lamentations 3). On this see more at *Conference* 19, chapter 8.]

This, then, must be the whole intention of the solitary: to deserve to possess in this body an image of the future blessedness, and in some manner to begin tasting in this little vessel a pledge of that heavenly way of life and glory.

[Note: On this pledge, or earnest, see the notes above at *Conference* 7, chapter 5.]

This is, I say, the goal of all perfection: that the mind, stripped daily of all carnal dross, may be raised to spiritual things, until its entire way of life and every movement of the heart become one continuous prayer.

[Note: Through this, the Gospel saying is truly fulfilled: “We ought always to pray and never lose heart” (Luke 18); and the apostolic command: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5). This conference was composed concerning the continuity and constancy of prayer, as is clear from the conclusion of the preceding conference and from the whole course of this one.]

## CHAPTER VIII. Question concerning the instruction in perfection by which we may attain to perpetual remembrance of God

**Germanus:** Our astonishment grows even greater at the wonder of that preceding conference, because of which we have returned here. For the more intensely the teaching of this discourse inflames us with desire for perfect blessedness, the more deeply we collapse into despair, not knowing how we can seek or obtain a discipline of such sublimity. Therefore, what we began turning over in prolonged meditation while in our cell, since it must perhaps be expressed in a rather talkative exposition, we ask you patiently to allow us to set forth. We know, indeed, that your blessedness is not usually offended by the foolishness of the weak; such things should be brought into the open precisely so that whatever is absurd in them may be corrected.

As far as our opinion extends, the perfection of any art or discipline must necessarily begin with certain gentle rudiments, being first instructed in easier and more elementary beginnings,

[Note: This is the familiar maxim: “In every art and science one must proceed from easier and more elementary principles to higher and more difficult ones” (Aristotle, *Physics* 1).]

so that, nourished by a kind of rational milk, it may gradually be brought up and grow, and thus ascend little by little and step by step from the lowest things to the highest. Once it has entered upon the clearer principles and, so to speak, the gates of the profession it has undertaken, it will consequently and without difficulty reach the more penetrating heights of perfection.

For how could a child pronounce simple combinations of syllables unless he had first carefully learned the forms of the letters? Or how could he acquire the skill of reading if he were not yet able to join together the short and very narrow outlines of words? And how could someone inadequately trained in grammatical learning attain either rhetorical eloquence or philosophical knowledge?

[Note: Hence Paul, writing to the Corinthians while they were still inexperienced and unskilled in faith and Christian teaching, says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal—as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (that is, simple and easy teaching, not solid food, meaning more advanced teaching concerning higher mysteries). “For you were not yet able; indeed, even now you are not able, for you are still carnal” (1 Corinthians 3). Likewise, to the Hebrews 5: “You have become people who need milk, not solid food. For everyone who partakes of milk is unacquainted with the word of righteousness, for he is an infant. But solid food belongs to the mature,” and so forth. Peter also says in his First Canonical Letter: “Like newborn infants, desire rational, guileless milk, so that by it you may grow toward salvation” (1 Peter 2).

The Gloss explains this as follows: “Seek the simpler rudiments of faith from the breasts of Mother Church,” that is, from the teachers of both Testaments. In the apostolic text, instead of *rationabiles* (“rational”), corrected Bibles now read *rationabile* (“rational”), as does the Greek τὸ λογικόν (*to logikon*). The Author seems to have had this in view here.

Thus Saint Jerome, commenting on Isaiah 55, says: “Milk signifies the innocence of little children.” This custom and type is still observed in the churches of the West, so that wine and milk are given to those reborn in Christ. Paul spoke of this milk when he said, “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food”; and Peter: “Like newborn infants, desire rational milk.” Elsewhere also, commenting on Jeremiah 32, Jerome teaches that the Hebrews were promised a land flowing with milk and honey because they were unable to receive solid food, but were nourished with the honey and milk of infancy.]

Therefore, just as in this discipline by which we are instructed to cling continually to God, I do not doubt that there are certain foundations of instruction. Once these have first been laid with the greatest firmness, the lofty heights of perfection may then be built upon them.
