We suspect that its beginnings are these, in a modest way: first, that we should know by what meditation God is held or contemplated. Then we must learn how we may steadfastly preserve this same material, whatever it is—which we do not doubt is also the summit of all perfection. For this reason we desire that some material for the memory, by which God may be conceived in the mind or held perpetually, be shown to us. If we keep it before our eyes, then, whenever we sense that we have slipped away from it, we shall have at hand something toward which we can immediately look and to which we can return, and we shall be able to take it up again without any delay caused by wandering or any difficulty of searching.

For it happens that, when we have wandered away from spiritual contemplations,

[Note: That is, when we have strayed and been drawn away from serious and spiritual thoughts and meditations, and so forth. Moreover, the variety of readings in different copies makes this passage obscure and ambiguous. The Plantinian edition, which we previously followed, reads below: “We seek that material which has been buried, by which we may be able to revive spiritual memory.” But our present, later reading, being more widespread, seems also more correct: in it, “which has been buried” refers not to spiritual memory but to the material. Dionysius’s paraphrase agrees more closely with this, in these words: “For it happens that, while we turn from spiritual contemplations to ourselves, we fall into a kind of deadly sleep; then, as though awakened, we seek the material which has been interrupted, by which we may revive spiritual memory,” and so forth.

The French translation of Jean Lavardin also agrees; I do not consider it inappropriate to consult it in such doubtful passages. It reads: “For it happens that when, wandering outside spiritual contemplations, we fall back into ourselves and begin to think about our affections and affairs, carried away as though by a deadly sleep, and when, as if awakened, we seek this material—which has been buried within us—by which we may revive spiritual memory, it happens, I say, that, delayed by the length of the search and inquiry, we are again thrown outside our attempt, effort, and means before we find it,” and so forth.]

and turn back to ourselves as though from a deadly sleep,

[Note: Dionysius omitted the little word *de*. The “deadly sleep” in this passage seems capable of being understood in two ways: first, as a sleep like that of Lethe, from the river Lethe—that is, deep and heavy; or as death-dealing, that is, deadly, harmful and destructive to the soul’s salvation.]

and, as if awakened, seek the material that has been buried, by which we may revive spiritual memory, we are delayed by the very slowness of the search. Before we find it, we fall back again from our effort, and before some spiritual vision is produced, the intention conceived in the heart vanishes.

It is sufficiently certain that this confusion happens to us because we do not firmly hold before our eyes something particular, as a kind of formula, to which the wandering mind may be recalled after many turns and various wanderings, and by which, after long shipwrecks, it may enter as though into a harbor of rest. Thus, because the mind is continually impeded by this ignorance and difficulty, it is always tossed about, wandering and, as it were, drunken, among different things. It does not even hold for long and firmly that spiritual thought which happens to occur to it more by chance than by deliberate effort, since it is always receiving one thing after another and does not perceive either their entry or their beginnings, nor likewise their end and departure.

## CHAPTER IX. Isaac’s response concerning the efficacy of understanding acquired through experience

**Isaac:** Your minute and subtle inquiry indicates that you are near to purity. No one could even ask about such matters—not to mention looking into and discerning them—unless diligent and effective activity of mind, together with vigilant concern, had advanced him to investigate the depths of these questions, and unless the continual pursuit of a disciplined life had, through experience, led him actually to attempt the thresholds of this purity and knock at its doors.

Therefore, since I see that you have not merely stood at the doors of that true prayer of which we are speaking [*Al.:* “not merely stand”], but have in some manner touched its inner chambers and interior recesses with the hands of experience, and are already almost touching certain of its members, I do not think I shall have to labor in order to lead you, who are already wandering, so to speak, within its hall, into its inner sanctuaries also, as far as the Lord directs. Nor will any obstacle of difficulty delay you from examining what must be shown.

For the person who wisely recognizes what he ought to seek is close to knowledge,

[Note: Aristotle says: “He who knows nothing doubts nothing.” Hence the Apostle: “If anyone thinks that he knows something, he has not yet known how he ought to know.” And Socrates, judged the wisest of the Greeks, said: “This I know: that I know nothing,” as Saint Jerome also reports in his letter to Paulinus.]

and the person who has begun to understand what he does not know is not far from knowledge.

Therefore I do not fear incurring a charge of betrayal or frivolity if I disclose what, in the preceding treatise, while discussing the perfection of prayer, I had withheld from the discussion. I think that, by God’s grace, the power of these things must already have been revealed to you, who are engaged in this exercise and pursuit, even without the assistance of my discourse.

## CHAPTER X. On the instruction in perpetual prayer

[Col. 0831B]

Therefore, in accordance with that method of instruction which you have wisely devised for teaching children—who cannot first receive the teaching of the alphabet, or recognize its lines, or trace its letters with an unafraid hand, unless

[Note: Ciaconius and others read: “which, by means of certain models and formulas,” and so forth. Here *typus* or *protypon* means a model of writing proposed for imitation.

On this occasion it will not be out of place to note the various and manifold ways of writing, or the materials adapted to writing, among the ancients before the invention of our paper. First, they wrote on wax, or on waxed tablets, including writing tablets such as are still circulated, with an instrument made of iron, bronze, or some other material, rather like a large needle. They called it a *stylus* or *graphium*. Hence we still call a manner of speaking a “style”; and the tablets were called *pugillares* because writing was done on them by pricking with a stylus.

If you seek ancient testimony concerning this, Pliny says in Book 1 of his Letters: “Nearby there were not a hunting spear or a lance, but a stylus and writing tablets: I was composing something and taking notes, so that although I returned with empty hands, I brought back tablets full of wax.” Saint Jerome, in Letter 7, elegantly and aptly describes how a little girl should be taught to write. Among other things he says: “When she begins to draw the stylus over the wax with a trembling hand, or when another’s hand is placed over hers, let the joints be guided; or let the letters be carved on a tablet, so that the traces enclosed by the grooves may be drawn along them and may not be able to wander outside.” Again, in Letter 20: “The trembling hand guides the wandering stylus through the curved paths of the wax.”

Second, they wrote on palm leaves. Varro, as quoted by Servius on *Aeneid* 6, says: “On palm leaves he sometimes wrote signs, sometimes words.”

Third, they wrote on the thinnest tree bark. The papyrus plant among the Egyptians was especially suited to this use, as noted elsewhere (*Conference* 3, final chapter). From its name we still call our paper—made from beaten linen—raw papyrus, because it serves us for the same purpose that papyrus once served the Egyptians.

Fourth, they wrote on parchment, or thin skins, which were first invented at Pergamum, and hence were called *pergamena*. Pliny, Book 7, chapter 11, says: “Cicero reported that Homer’s *Iliad*, a poem written on parchment, was contained in a nutshell.” Saint Jerome, in Letter 42 to Niceas, says: “Those uncultivated Italians whom Ennius calls the Cascos, who, as Cicero says in his *Rhetoric*, sought their livelihood in a savage manner, before the use of paper and parchment, exchanged letters either on tablets smoothed from wood or on the bark of trees. Hence they called those who carried such letters *tabellarii*, and writers *librarii*, from the books of trees.”

Fifth, there was finally an ancient custom of writing public records on rolls of lead, and private records on woven linen. Pliny mentions this in Book 13, chapter 11; so do Symmachus in Book 4, Letter 34, and Ausonius in Letter 23 to Paulinus. Hence the expression “linen books,” in Livy, Book 4. See also Trithemius, *On Polygraphy*.]

unless they first become accustomed to reproducing the forms of the letters by constant contemplation and daily imitation after certain models and formulas have been carefully impressed into wax—so you must be given the formula of this spiritual contemplation. You should always fix your gaze upon it with the greatest tenacity, learning either profitably to turn it over with unbroken constancy or, through its use and meditation, to ascend to higher contemplations.

This, then, is the formula of the discipline and prayer you seek. Every monk who is striving toward perpetual remembrance of God must become accustomed to meditate upon it with the unceasing movement of his heart, banishing every variety of thought. For he will not otherwise be able to retain it in any way unless he has been freed from all bodily cares and anxieties.

[Col. 0832B]

Just as this formula was handed down to us by a few survivors of the most ancient fathers, so we too disclose it only to the rarest persons, those who are truly thirsty.

Therefore, for possessing perpetual remembrance of God, this formula of devotion must be set continually before you:

> **God, come to my assistance;  
> Lord, make haste to help me.**

[Note: This is an outstanding and comprehensive commendation of that Davidic verse: “God, come to my assistance; Lord, make haste to help me.” Its manifold uses and benefits are explained with such abundance and brilliance of prayer that nothing seems capable of being added.

Thus Cassiodorus, in his exposition of the same psalm, says: “The eloquent Cassian, in the tenth conference, celebrates this passage with such honor, discussing its usefulness at such length, that monks do not begin anything they undertake without a triple repetition of this verse.” By repeating it with renewed praise, he proves its memory exceedingly useful.

Moreover, the learned Navarrus valued this teaching of Cassian, or of Abbot Isaac, so highly that he inserted almost the whole of this chapter into his commentary *On Prayer*, chapter 19. He begins as follows: “In order that we may continually remember God Almighty and become accustomed to continual prayer, especially mental and brief prayer, wherever we may be and whatever we may be doing, without impeding our activities, with great consolation and benefit to our souls, it is good to use that verse of the Psalmist: ‘God, come to my assistance,’ and so forth.” Thus Navarrus.

To summarize the substance of this teaching briefly: first, the verse repeatedly cited here serves to arouse every devout affection; hence the Author calls it a formula of devotion. Second, it serves to overcome or repel every temptation, and for this reason it is rightly called an impregnable wall, impenetrable armor, and a most heavily fortified shield. Third, it serves against every disorder of the soul: perverse inclinations, affections, the enticements and provocations of vices—especially carnal vices—and the dangers and occasions of sin. Fourth, it serves against nocturnal illusions and assaults of demons. Finally, it serves to preserve perpetual remembrance of God and to maintain constant and assiduous prayer easily and without weariness. See Bellarmine in the preface to this psalm.

Accordingly, it should be pronounced, turned over in mind and mouth, and repeated continually: in every place and time, by night and by day, in prosperity and adversity, in every spiritual undertaking, and in every temptation. Concerning the sign of the cross, which is commonly used with this verse, Tertullian says in *On the Soldier’s Crown*, chapter 3: “At every step forward and movement, at every entrance and exit, when we dress, put on shoes, bathe, sit at table, cross thresholds, enter bedrooms, or take our seats—whenever the circumstances of life engage us—we mark our foreheads with the sign of the cross.”

Finally, it is also worth noting, as greatly relevant to the commendation of this verse, that the canonical hours begin with it. Turrecrematus notes this in his commentary on chapter 8 of the Rule of Saint Benedict, in Book 5, chapter 2 of Durandus’s *Rationale*. There it says: “In wintertime, the verse being first recited: ‘God, come to my assistance; Lord, make haste to help me,’” and so forth.

Turrecrematus comments: “Because, as the Lord says in the Gospel of John 15, ‘Without me you can do nothing,’ the holy Father rightly arranges that the divine office should begin with devout prayer. According to the teaching handed down in the conferences of the Fathers, prayer must be poured forth with unceasing continuity at every moment, in prosperity and adversity: in prosperity, lest we be exalted; in adversity, so that we may be rescued. Moreover, since, according to the Apostle, everything must be done in the name of God (1 Corinthians 10), it is rightly begun with him.”

Likewise, the Gloss on Psalm 69, “God, come to my assistance,” says: “Note that this verse is recited at the beginning before all the hours, because whenever we ought to pray, the devil then strives especially that dying flies may spoil the sweetness of the ointment” (Ecclesiastes 10). Therefore, before everything else, we ask the Lord for help against his assault.

It should also be noted here that one can sin in three ways: in heart, in speech, and in deed. Therefore, as stated in the *Rationale of the Divine Offices*, the hours begin in three ways: Compline with “Restore us, O God our Savior,” against sin of the heart; the nocturnal hours with “O Lord, open my lips,” against sin of speech; and the other hours with “God, come to my assistance,” against sin of deed (Durandus, *Rationale*, Book 5, chapter 2).

Since sin of heart and sin of speech also contain an element of deed, however, “God, come to my assistance” is said at all hours, both nocturnal and diurnal. Monks, following the institution of Saint Father Benedict, say this first at the nocturnal hours: “God, come to my assistance,” and afterward, “Lord, open my lips,” because without God’s help neither the heart nor the lips can be opened to his praise. Thus Turrecrematus.

Moreover, Pope Gregory the Great, by papal authority, commanded that the same verse—which Saint Father Benedict had ordered to be placed first at the canonical hours in his monasteries—be placed before them by the whole Church, with the verses “Glory be to the Father” and “As it was in the beginning” added, as Arnold Wion of Monte Cassino writes in Book 5 of *The Tree of Life*, under Gregory.

Walafrid Strabo, in chapter 25 of *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, says concerning this same verse: “Certainly the Fathers of old seem to have established that the verse customarily said at the beginning of all offices, except the Mass—that is, ‘God, come to my assistance,’ and the rest—should precede not only all offices but also all actions. For invoking divine assistance at the beginning of every action makes both the constancy of asking and the power of obtaining easier. In the affairs of the dead and around the solemnity of the Lord’s Passion, however, the beginnings and endings of the offices are not made as in other cases, in order to signify sadness.”]

This verse has rightly been drawn from the whole instrument of Scripture. It embraces every affection that can arise in human nature and is suitably and appropriately adapted to every condition and every assault. It contains an invocation of God against every danger; it contains the humility of devout confession; it contains constant vigilance born of concern and fear; it contains recognition of one’s own frailty; confidence that one will be heard; and trust in present and ever-standing protection. For the person who continually invokes his protector is certain that he is always present.

It contains the ardor of love and charity; it contains awareness of ambushes and fear of enemies. Seeing himself surrounded by them day and night, the one who prays confesses that he cannot be delivered without the help of his defender.

For all who suffer from demonic assault, this verse is an impregnable wall, impenetrable armor, and a most strongly fortified shield. It does not allow those placed in acedia, anxiety of spirit, sadness, or depression under any thoughts whatever to despair of the remedies of salvation. It shows that the one whom they invoke continually observes their struggles and is not absent from those who beseech him.

It warns those established in spiritual success and gladness of heart not to become exalted or puffed up by their prosperous condition. It testifies that this condition cannot be retained without God the protector, since it asks him not only always but also quickly to come to its aid.

This verse, I say, is found necessary and useful for each one of us, whatever condition we inhabit. Whoever always and in everything desires to be helped shows that he needs God as helper not only in hard and sorrowful matters but equally in favorable and joyful ones: so that, just as God may rescue him from the former, he may cause him to remain in the latter, knowing in either case that human frailty cannot subsist without his assistance.

I am afflicted by the passion of gluttony and seek foods unknown to the desert; in the barren solitude the fragrances of royal dishes are brought before me, and I feel myself dragged most unwillingly toward their desires. Therefore I must say:

> **God, come to my assistance;  
> Lord, make haste to help me.**

I am urged to anticipate the appointed hour of eating, or I struggle with great pain of heart to preserve the proper and customary measure of restraint. With a groan I must proclaim:

> **God, come to my assistance;  
> Lord, make haste to help me.**

When fatigue of the stomach prevents me from undertaking the stricter fasts I need for combating the flesh, or dryness and constriction of the belly frighten me away, I must pray that my desire may be fulfilled, or at least that the heat of carnal desire may be quieted without the discipline of a stricter fast:

> **God, come to my assistance;  
> Lord, make haste to help me.**

When I approach food at the proper hour, as the appointed time suggests, I recoil from taking bread and am excluded by natural necessity from all eating, I must cry out with lamentation:

> **God, come to my assistance;  
> Lord, make haste to help me.**

When, wishing to persevere in reading for the sake of firmness of heart, an intervening headache prevents me, and at the third hour sleep strikes my face against the sacred page; when I am compelled either to exceed or to anticipate the time assigned for rest; when an overpowering weight of sleep causes me to interrupt even the canonical arrangement of the gathering and psalms, I must likewise proclaim:

> **God, come to my assistance;  
> Lord, make haste to help me.**

When sleep has been removed from my eyes and I find myself exhausted for many nights by diabolical nightmares, with every restoration of nocturnal rest driven from my eyelids, I must pray with sighs:

> **God, come to my assistance;  
> Lord, make haste to help me.**

While I am still engaged in the struggle, the tickling of the flesh suddenly pricks me and, through seductive pleasure, attempts to drag me, while sleeping, into consent. So that an alien fire, blazing up, may not burn the sweet-smelling flowers of chastity, I must cry out:

> **God, come to my assistance;  
> Lord, make haste to help me.**

When I feel the incentives of lust extinguished and the sexual heat in my members grown lukewarm, so that this virtue—or rather, this grace of God—may remain in me longer or forever, I must say attentively:

> **God, come to my assistance;  
> Lord, make haste to help me.**

When I am troubled by the goads of anger, love of money, or sadness, and am forced to interrupt the gentleness I have resolved upon and cherish, so that I may not be led into the bitterness of gall by the disturbance of fury, I must proclaim with the greatest groaning:

> **God, come to my assistance;  
> Lord, make haste to help me.**

When I am assailed by acedia, vainglory, and the elevation of pride, and my mind subtly delights in some thought concerning the negligence or lukewarmness of others, I must pray with complete contrition of heart, lest this destructive suggestion of the enemy prevail in me:

> **God, come to my assistance;  
> Lord, make haste to help me.**

When, after laying aside the swelling of pride, I have acquired through continual compunction of spirit the grace of humility and simplicity, I must proclaim with all my strength, lest again the foot of pride come upon me and the hand of the sinner move me (Psalm 35), and lest I be more grievously pierced by exultation over my victory:

> **God, come to my assistance;  
> Lord, make haste to help me.**

When I burn with innumerable and diverse wanderings of soul and with instability of heart, and cannot restrain the dispersions of my thoughts; when I cannot pour out my prayer without interruption, fantasy, and the recollection of empty images, words, and actions; when I feel myself so bound by the barrenness of this sterility that I sense no birth at all of spiritual perceptions—then, in order to deserve liberation from this desolation of spirit, from which I cannot free myself except through many groans and sighs, I must necessarily cry out:

> **God, come to my assistance;  
> Lord, make haste to help me.**

When I feel that, through the visitation of the Holy Spirit, I have again obtained direction of soul, stability of thoughts, and gladness of heart, together with ineffable joy and ecstasy of mind; when I perceive that I am overflowing with an abundance of spiritual perceptions and, through the Lord’s sudden illumination, receive the revelation of most sacred understandings previously entirely hidden from me, I must cry out earnestly and frequently, so that I may deserve to remain longer in these things:

> **God, come to my assistance;  
> Lord, make haste to help me.**

When I am harassed by the terrors of demons surrounding me at night and troubled by the phantasms of unclean spirits, and the very hope of salvation and life is taken from me by the horror of trembling, I shall flee to the saving harbor of this verse and cry out with all my strength:

> **God, come to my assistance;  
> Lord, make haste to help me.**

Again, when I have been restored by the Lord’s consolation and, animated by his arrival, feel myself surrounded as though by countless thousands of angels—so that I dare suddenly to seek out and challenge the conflicts of those whom previously I feared with deadly terror, whose touch, indeed whose proximity, I had felt with horror of mind and body—I must proclaim with all my strength, so that the vigor of this steadfastness may remain in me longer through God’s grace:

> **God, come to my assistance;  
> Lord, make haste to help me.**

The prayer of this verse must therefore be poured forth with unceasing constancy: in adversity, so that we may be rescued; in prosperity, so that we may be preserved and not become exalted. Let meditation on this verse revolve unbroken in your heart. Do not cease chanting it when you are engaged in any work or ministry, or when you are on a journey. Meditate upon it while sleeping, while eating, and in the final necessities of nature.

When this movement of the heart has become for you a salutary formula, it will not only preserve you unharmed from every assault of demons, but, cleansing you from every vice of earthly contamination, will lead you to those invisible, heavenly contemplations, and will raise you to that ineffable ardor of prayer experienced by very few.

Let sleep overtake you while you are meditating on this verse, until, formed by its ineffable practice, you become accustomed to chant it even in your sleep. Let it be the first thing to meet you when you awaken; let it anticipate all your thoughts as you become conscious; let it hand you over, rising from your bed, to the bending of your knees; and from there let it lead you onward to every work and action. Let it accompany you at all times.

You shall meditate upon it according to the legislator’s commands, while sitting in your house and walking on the road, while sleeping and rising. You shall write it on the threshold and doors of your mouth; you shall place it on the walls of your house and in the inner chambers of your heart, so that, when you kneel down for prayer, it may be for you a descending chant; and afterward, when you rise and proceed to all the necessities of life, it may become an upright and perpetual prayer.

## CHAPTER XI. On the perfection of prayer, to which one ascends through the foregoing instruction
Let the mind hold this formula unceasingly, until, strengthened by its uninterrupted use and constant meditation, it casts away and rejects the riches and abundant possessions of every thought; and thus, constrained by the poverty of this verse, it may readily attain that evangelical blessedness [Col. 0837A] which holds first place among the other beatitudes. “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). And thus, existing as an outstanding poor man through this sort of poverty, he fulfilled that prophetic utterance: “The poor and needy shall praise your name” (Ps. 73). Indeed, what poverty can be greater or holier than that of one who, recognizing that he has no protection and no strength of his own, asks daily assistance from another’s generosity; who understands that his life and substance are sustained at every moment by divine aid; who rightly professes himself to be the Lord’s beggar and daily cries out to him in supplication: “But I am a beggar and poor; O God, help me” (Ps. 39)?

And thus, ascending also to that manifold knowledge of God, with God himself enlightening him, let him thereafter begin to be nourished by higher and more sacred mysteries, according to what is said through the Prophet: “The high mountains are for the stags,

[Note: [Col. 0837C] Saint Jerome, in Letter 3, reads: “The rock is a refuge for the hares.” In place of this, he says, many read “for hedgehogs.” The hedgehog is a small animal, quick to flee, weighed down by thickets of spines. And in his letter to Sunia and Fretella (Letter 135): “The rock is a refuge for hedgehogs”; in Hebrew *sephanium* is written, and all rendered it as χοιρογρυλλίους (*choirogryllious*), a similarly sounding term. The Septuagint alone, interpreting them as hares, translated *tois lagōois*, that is, “the rock is a refuge for hares.” It should be understood that this is an animal no larger than a hedgehog, resembling a mouse and a bear; hence in Palestine it is called *ktomys*. This species is extremely abundant in those regions, and they habitually live in caves of rocks and hollows in the earth. Thus Jerome. Isidore, however, in Book 12 of the *Etymologies*, chapter 3, says: “The hedgehog, also called *herinaceus*, is an animal covered with spines, and is so called because it contracts itself when it closes itself within its spines, by which it is protected on every side against ambushes. For as soon as it senses anything, it first contracts itself and, turning into a ball, gathers itself back into its own weapons” (see Pliny, Book 8, chapter 37). This is his account.

Moreover, the monk is compared here to the hedgehog, or *herinaceus*, for various reasons: first, because of innocence and simplicity; second, because of the caution and natural prudence by which it seeks refuge in caves or holes in the rocks, or gathers and curls itself inward so that it may remain covered and protected on every side by its spines; third, because of humility or smallness. Saint Gregory, however, reasons quite differently about the hedgehog, its nature, and its significance in the *Pastoral Care* (Part 1, chapter 12), as may be seen there.]

“the rock is a refuge for hedgehogs” (Ps. 103). This is very appropriately fitted to the meaning we have explained, since whoever perseveres in simplicity and innocence, harming or troubling no one, content solely with his own simplicity, desires only to protect himself from the prey of those lying in wait for him—having become, as it were, a spiritual hedgehog—by being sheltered beneath the covering of that evangelical rock,

[Note: [Col. 0838C] He allegorically understands the evangelical rock as Christ. In its openings—that is, in his wounds—the spiritual hedgehog, namely the humble monk, has his refuge, asylum, and protection. Concerning this rock the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10). The Psalmist likewise says: “Blessed is he who shall take and dash your little ones against the rock” (Ps. 36). And the Bridegroom in the *Song of Songs*: “My dove in the clefts of the rock, in the hiding places of the wall” (Song 2). Finally, the evangelical saying: “He laid the foundation upon the rock” (Luke 6). The Fathers also repeatedly interpret the evangelical Rock—that is, Christ. Saint Basil, quoted by Saint Thomas in the *Catena aurea*, says: “To lay the foundation upon the rock means to lean upon the faith of Christ, so that one may remain immovable amid adversities, whether they arise through human or divine agency.”]

that is, fortified by the memory of the Lord’s Passion and by the unceasing meditation of the aforementioned verse, he avoids the snares of the hostile enemy. Concerning these spiritual hedgehogs it is also said in Proverbs: “And the hedgehogs are a weak people who made their houses in the rocks.”

[Note: [Col. 0838D] In the common text we read: “The little hares, a feeble people, who place their dwelling in the rock.”]

And indeed, what is weaker than a Christian, what more infirm than a monk, for whom not only is no vengeance for injuries permitted, but not even the slightest silent disturbance is allowed to arise within? But whoever, progressing from this state, possesses not only the simplicity of innocence but is also fortified by the virtue of discernment, becomes an exterminator of venomous serpents, has Satan crushed beneath his feet, and reaches the figure of the rational stag through the liveliness of his mind—he will feed upon the prophetic and apostolic mountains, that is, upon their loftiest and most exalted mysteries. Strengthened by their continual pasture, and taking into himself all the emotions of the Psalms, he will begin to chant them in such a way that he will draw them forth with profound compunction of heart not as compositions made by the Prophet, but as though produced by himself, or at least will regard them as having been addressed to his own person. He will recognize that their statements were not fulfilled only at that time through the Prophet or in the Prophet, but are daily enacted and fulfilled in him.

For then the divine Scriptures become clearer to us, and their veins and marrow are, in a sense, laid open, when our experience not only apprehends their meaning but also anticipates it, and the sense of their words is disclosed to us not through explanation but through proof. Receiving, then, the same disposition of heart by which each Psalm was chanted or written, we shall, as though becoming its authors, anticipate its meaning rather than follow it. That is, gathering first the power of the words and only afterward their knowledge, we shall, when their meditation comes upon us, in a sense recall what has happened within us or is happening through daily assaults: what our negligence has produced, what our diligence has sought out, what divine providence has bestowed, what the enemy’s instigation has fraudulently brought about, what slippery and subtle forgetfulness has taken away, what human frailty has introduced, or what imprudent ignorance has deceived us about.

For we find all these emotions expressed in the Psalms, so that, seeing what has befallen us as though in the purest mirror, we may recognize it more effectively; and thus,

[Note: [Col. 0838D] Ciaconius has this reading, I think, in the Lyon and Roman editions, and I believe with this meaning: “taught by effects as teachers,” as the proverb has it. This reading and meaning fit well with what precedes and follows. Most others, however, have: “instructed by the emotions as teachers.” Following them, the Paraphrast says: “Instructed by our own emotions as teachers, let us touch these things as though experienced, not as though heard,” and so forth; the French translator likewise rendered it literally.]

instructed by effects as teachers [Lipsius, in the margin: “by emotions”], let us touch them as accomplished realities, not as things merely heard; and not as matters committed to memory, but as though implanted in the very nature of things, let us bring them forth from the inward emotion of the heart. Thus we may penetrate their meaning not through the text of our reading but through preceding experience, and so our mind may attain that incorruption of prayer to which, in the preceding treatise, the order of the conference ascended, insofar as the Lord deigned to grant it (Conference 9, chapter 29). This prayer is occupied not only by the contemplation of any image, but is distinguished by no sequence of voice or words; rather, it is uttered through the ineffable ecstasy of the heart, by the mind’s fiery intention and the unconquerable liveliness of the spirit, while the mind, made external to all the senses and visible materials, pours itself out to God in unutterable groanings and sighs.

## CHAPTER XII  
### The question of how spiritual thoughts may be held immovably

Germanus: We think that you have expressed not only the teaching of the spiritual discipline which we requested, but the perfection itself, with sufficient clarity and precision. For what can be more perfect or more sublime than to embrace the memory of God in so concise a meditation, to withdraw, through the repetition of a single verse, from all the boundaries of visible things, and in a brief utterance, as it were, to enclose the affections of all prayers?

[Note: [Col. 0839C] The verse in question is: “O God, come to my assistance,” and so forth, concerning which see above, chapter 10.]

And therefore we still ask that one remaining matter be explained to us: how we may steadily retain this same verse which you have given us in place of a formula, so that, just as by God’s grace we have been freed from the foolishness of worldly thoughts, we may likewise hold every spiritual thought immovably.

## CHAPTER XIII  
### The mutability of thoughts

For whenever our mind has conceived the “chapter” of any Psalm,

[Note: [Col. 0839C] “Chapter” is taken here as the subject, or as the beginning or starting point, just as Saint Jerome also reads and explains the passage of Psalm 39 (in the *Hebrew Questions* and in Isaiah, chapter 29, and Ezekiel, chapter 2): “In the beginning, or chapter, of the book it is written of me,” that is, in the beginning of Genesis or in Holy Scripture, which is called one book. Dionysius, however, uses “chapter” here for a verse of a Psalm, and thus seems to understand any verse of any Psalm. I would not wish to reject this.]

it slips away imperceptibly, and the mind, unaware and astonished, turns to the text of another Scripture. When it begins to revolve that passage within itself, before it has fully examined it, the memory of another testimony arises and excludes meditation on the earlier subject. From that one it is transferred to another, as a further meditation enters in; and so the mind, continually moving from Psalm to Psalm, leaping from the text of the Gospel to the reading of the Apostle, and from that again descending to prophetic utterances, then carried off to various spiritual histories, is tossed unstable and wandering through the entire body of Scripture. It has no power at its own discretion either to reject or retain anything; nothing is brought to completion with full judgment and examination. It becomes merely a toucher and taster of spiritual meanings, not their producer or possessor.

[Note: [Col. 0839C] Saint Jerome also laments this instability and wandering of the mind in prayer in his *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*, representing in himself the person of irreverent men:

“‘I attend prayer,’ he says; ‘I would not pray if I did not believe. But if I truly believed, I would cleanse that heart by which God is seen; I would strike my breast with my hands; I would moisten my cheeks with tears; my body would shudder; my face would grow pale; I would lie at the feet of my Lord and drench them with weeping, wipe them with my hair, and cling to the solid trunk of the cross, nor would I let go until I obtained mercy. But now, very often during my prayer, I walk about through colonnades, or calculate interest, or, carried away by a shameful thought, even do things of which I should be ashamed to speak. Where is faith? Do we suppose that Jonah prayed in this way? Or the three children? Or Daniel among the lions? Or the thief upon the cross?’ Thus Saint Jerome.

Saint Hilarion also experienced this very thing, as the same Saint Jerome relates in the *Life of Hilarion*: “Once he was praying with his head fixed to the ground, and, as is natural to human beings, his mind, drawn away from prayer, was thinking about something else. A swift driver—the devil—leapt upon his back, struck his sides with his heels, and beat his neck with a whip. ‘Come on,’ he said, ‘why are you sleeping?’ Then, laughing from above, when he had become exhausted, he asked whether he wanted to receive barley. This is Jerome’s account.

For the wandering or distraction of the mind in prayer, one should also consult Turrecremata, who discusses the matter at considerable length in Treatise 77 on the Rule of Saint Benedict. Among other things he says:

“Notice that when the heart suffers wandering during prayers, it sometimes happens through human infirmity, sometimes through negligence, and sometimes deliberately. Although all of this is blameworthy, the third is more so than the second, and the second more than the first.

“There are also thoughts concerning certain necessary matters, as when some responsibility falls upon a person about which he must think. Concerning these Wisdom says: ‘Earthly thought depresses the mind occupied with many things’ (Wis. 9). Others are thoughts of vanity, concerning which the Psalmist says: ‘The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain.’ Others are thoughts of iniquity: ‘Perverse thoughts separate from God’ (Wis. 1). During prayers one must beware of the first, but more of the second, and most of the third.

“Some thoughts arise from the intrusion of demons; some from a preceding fault, as when someone is so distracted before prayer that, because of that circumstance, thoughts arise during prayer which impede him, just as they do in sleep; and some from a present fault, as when, while reciting the divine office, a person occupies himself with other matters. The first is bad, the second worse, and the third worst.

“Again, while praying, some useful thoughts arise concerning matters belonging to prayer—for example, when, because of a word occurring in prayer, someone thinks of something useful for composing a sermon or completing a prayer. Sometimes useful thoughts arise concerning matters unrelated to prayer; sometimes thoughts arise that are irrelevant and useless, or even harmful. The first have some excuse, the second less, and the third least. According, therefore, to the distinctions of thoughts just described, one can discern when a person ought to fear most for his conscience when he suffers wandering thoughts in prayer.”

This is Turrecremata’s account.

He then adds a salutary warning of Saint Bernard, directed to the same matter, in these words (Sermon 47 on the *Song of Songs*):

“Beloved, I exhort you always to attend purely and earnestly to the divine praises: purely, so that while you sing the Psalms you think of nothing other than what you are singing. I do not say merely that vain and idle thoughts must be avoided; those thoughts too must be avoided which, at that particular hour and in that particular place, the brothers responsible for the offices are frequently compelled to admit for the common necessity, as though by necessity. Nor, surely, would I advise you then to receive even those things which you may perhaps shortly before have read in a book while sitting in the cloister. They are beneficial, but you do not turn them over beneficially while singing the Psalms. For at that hour the Holy Spirit does not graciously receive whatever else you offer, neglecting what you ought to offer.” Thus Saint Bernard.]

And thus the mind, always mobile and wandering, is distracted in various directions even during the time of the communal office, like a drunken person, performing no duty appropriately. For example, while praying, it recalls a Psalm or some other reading; while singing, it meditates on something different from what the text of the Psalm itself contains; when reciting a reading, it wishes to do something or remembers something already done. In this way nothing is received or dismissed in an orderly or timely fashion, as though everything were being driven by random assaults; and it has no power either to retain what pleases it or to linger over it.

It is therefore necessary above all for us to know how we may properly carry out these spiritual offices, or at least how we may hold immovably this same verse which you have given us in place of a formula, so that the beginning and end of all our thoughts may not fluctuate in their own instability but may remain under our control.

## CHAPTER XIV  
### Isaac’s response: how stability of heart or of thoughts may be acquired

[Col. 0842A]

Isaac: Although, when we discussed the state of prayer earlier, I think sufficient expression was already given concerning this matter, nevertheless, since you ask that these things be repeated, I shall briefly explain the strengthening of the heart.

[Note: [Col. 0841B] Much similar material may be found in Saint Gregory, *Moralia*, Book 26, chapters 36–37, and in Saint Bernard, *On the Interior House*, chapter 54 and following.]

There are three things that make a wandering mind stable: vigils, meditation, and prayer. Their persistence and continual application provide the soul with stable firmness. Yet these things can in no way be attained unless, through the unremitting continuity of work dedicated not to avarice but to the sacred uses of the monastery, all anxieties and concerns of the present life have first been entirely renounced. Thus we may fulfill that apostolic command:

[Note: [Col. 0841B] This sentence contains and expresses the aim and subject of this conference, as its title also indicates: namely, the quality and constancy of prayer, whose explanation we have therefore postponed until now. Similar statements are found throughout Scripture: Psalm 33, “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth”; Ecclesiasticus 8, “Do not cease from praying always”; Luke 18, “We ought always to pray and never lose heart”; Luke 21, “Watch, praying at all times”; and the final chapter of Luke, “They were always in the temple, praising and blessing God.”

How these passages are to be understood is rightly questioned, since human frailty does not permit constant and uninterrupted prayer. I find several solutions and explanations of this difficulty.

First: one must pray always and without interruption, not because we can always be occupied in prayer, but because we must always either pray or do something good (Augustine on Psalm 33). For he always prays who always acts well, and he never ceases to pray who does not cease to do good, as the Ordinary Gloss says. Saint Thomas, explaining this more clearly (2–2, question 83, article 14), teaches that prayer ought to be constant, not in itself but according to its cause—that is, according to the affection or desire of charity from which prayer should proceed. This desire ought to be continuous in us, either actually or virtually. The power of this desire remains in everything we do from charity. We ought to do all things for the glory of God, as is said in 1 Corinthians 10. Hence Augustine says to Proba (Letter 121): “In faith itself and in charity, we always pray with uninterrupted desire.” But prayer considered in itself cannot be constant, since we must be occupied with other works. This is Saint Thomas’s teaching.

Yet such statements, and the command to pray expressed by them, do not seem capable of being understood solely of virtual prayer, or of the affection of charity and the desire for eternal life—which is presupposed in every good work—since they plainly require an actual act. For someone who never or very rarely prayed in fact would not be judged to have fulfilled this command, even if he retained that affection of charity.

Accordingly, Saint Augustine gives another interpretation in Book 1 of *On Heresies* (chapter 57), which Pope Nicholas I first reports and follows in his response to the inquiries of the Bulgarians (chapter 61). According to this interpretation, the person who is said to pray always and without interruption is one who does not omit the established times of prayer on any day. In this sense David said to Mephibosheth, in 2 Samuel, chapter 9: “You shall eat bread at my table always,” that is, daily, at the customary hours.

Thus Saint Jerome says in Letter 22 to Eustochium: “Although the Apostle commands us always to pray, and even sleep is prayer for the saints, nevertheless we ought to have appointed hours of prayer, so that if we should happen to be detained by some work, the appointed time itself may remind us of our duty.”

Likewise Saint Eligius, bishop of Noyon, says in Homily 11 on Holy Thursday (in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, volume 2): “Who can always pray and persist in prayers without weakness or interruption, so that he has no time either to take nourishment or to sleep? To whom, then, should it be said, ‘We ought always to pray and not lose heart,’ except to one who does not cease daily, at the canonical hours and according to the rite of ecclesiastical tradition, to praise and petition the Lord with the customary psalmody and prayers? And this is what the Psalmist says: ‘I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth’ (Ps. 33).” This is his statement. Bede reports virtually the same words in his commentary on Luke 18.

This interpretation is supported by the fact that Acts 12 says that, while Peter was being held in prison, “prayer was made without interruption by the Church for him.” And the Apostle writes to the Thessalonians: “We give thanks to God always for you, remembering you in our prayers without interruption” (1 Thess. 1). These words do not, however, exclude intervals of time for eating, sleeping, and fulfilling other duties of charity or nature.

The third opinion is that the words “always,” “at all times,” and “without interruption” are a kind of hyperbole, so that “to pray always” means to pray much and frequently, or to devote oneself to prayer, as Saint Benedict says (chapter 4 of the Rule), or as much as human frailty permits, as Saint Chrysostom says. Saint Athanasius seems to explain the apostolic command in this way when he writes of Saint Antony: *proseuchēto synechōs, mathōn hoti dei kat’ idian proseuchesthai adialeiptōs*—that is, “he prayed frequently, having learned that one ought to pray privately without interruption.”

The fourth and truest interpretation is that those words signify nothing other than that we must pray constantly and perseveringly. If we do not immediately obtain what we ask, we must not despair or lose heart—which is what “to fail” means in Luke 18. Rather, we must persist more and more, knock, and pray and ask again and again until, at least because of our persistence—that is, our importunity—we obtain what is beneficial for us. This is precisely what is signified by the parables of the widow persisting before the judge and of the friend asking importunately for three loaves. By their example Christ taught that we must devote ourselves to prayer not only at fixed hours but whenever an opportunity arises, both by night and by day.]

so that we may fulfill the apostolic command, “Pray without interruption.” For he prays very little who is accustomed to pray only during the time when he kneels. Indeed, he never prays who, even with knees bent, is distracted by any wandering of the heart. Therefore, if we wish to be found as people who pray, we must be such before the time of prayer. The mind must be shaped during the time of supplication by its preceding condition; while it prays, it is either raised toward heavenly things or dragged down toward earthly things according to the thoughts upon which it had dwelt before prayer.

Thus far Abbot Isaac had set forth for us, as we listened in amazement, the second conference on the quality of prayer. We greatly admired his teaching concerning the meditation of that aforementioned verse—which he had given beginners to retain as a kind of instruction—and earnestly desired to cultivate it. We had thought it concise and easy, but found it considerably more difficult to observe than the study by which we had previously wandered here and there through the whole of Scripture in varied meditation, without any bond of perseverance.

It is therefore clear that no one is excluded from perfection of heart through ignorance of letters, nor does rusticity hinder the attainment of purity of heart and soul. This perfection lies most concisely within the reach of everyone, provided that they preserve a sound and undivided intention of mind toward God through the constant meditation of this verse.

# PART TWO  
## Containing seven further conferences of the Fathers living in the Thebaid of Egypt

[Col. 0843]

## Preface  
### To Honoratus the Bishop and Eucherius

[Note: [Col. 0845D] That is, of the anchoritic life. Cassian and his companion Germanus learned these institutions and beginnings of the eremitical life from those Fathers and anchorites.]

that one of you, presiding over a great brotherhood in a monastery, desires your community—which is taught daily by the sight of your holy conduct—to be formed also by the precepts of those Fathers; while the other wished to be edified by the sight of those same men in the flesh and therefore went deep into Egypt, so that, leaving behind this province, as though numbed by the chill of Gaul, he might approach those lands more closely regarded by the Sun of Justice, overflowing with ripened fruits of virtue,

[Note: [Col. 0843C] Cassian instituted three orders or classes of conferences, as was mentioned above (in the first preface to the conferences), and prefixed to each class its own preface, as a kind of introductory and dedicatory letter. After the first class, dedicated to Helladius and Leontius, he now greets Honoratus and Eucherius, holy men known and familiar to him, in a new preface, and dedicates to them the second class—that is, the seven following conferences of three anchorites living in the solitude of the Thebaid.

Who these men were—Honoratus and Eucherius—I would not dare assert with certainty. Nevertheless, from the circumstances and conditions expressed here, I seem able to conclude with considerable probability that Honoratus was the bishop of Arles at that time, while Eucherius was not yet a bishop but was later made bishop of Lyon. Both were holy men, as Cassian calls them; both were Cassian’s contemporaries, active in Gaul or the regions of Gaul, and therefore more easily known to him because of their proximity.

That Eucherius was certainly not yet a bishop at the time when Cassian dedicated these conferences to him can be gathered sufficiently both from the inscription, in which only Honoratus is called bishop, and from the preface to the final seven conferences, where the author likewise declares that he dedicated these seven conferences to the blessed Bishop Honoratus and to the holy servant of Christ Eucherius.

There is no uncertainty concerning the holiness of either man, since the memory of Honoratus is celebrated in the Church on 17 February, and that of Eucherius on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December—that is, 16 November (see Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 63, and Isidore, *On the Life and Death of the Saints*, chapter 16).

It is equally clear that Saint Honoratus was first made abbot, then bishop, while nevertheless continuing to preside over his community of brothers, as is asserted here. For Eucherius himself says of Honoratus in the preface to Book 1 addressed to Salonius: “You were brought up by Father Honoratus—I mean that Honoratus who was first a teacher of the islands and afterward of the churches.” Eucherius says this because, before being placed over the Church of Arles, Saint Honoratus had presided as abbot over the famous monastery on the island of Lérins, or Lerina, which he had also founded.

Thus the same Eucherius, speaking of the congregation of Lérins, says: “It was worthy to have been founded by Honoratus, worthy to have received as Father one who, by the vigor of the apostolic spirit and the dignity of his countenance, shone forth in such great institutions.” Saint Eucherius also practiced the monastic life before his episcopate in that monastery of Lérins, as his book *In Praise of the Desert*—that is, of Lérins—testifies, in which he invites everyone to the desert of that island; Hilary likewise testifies to this in the *Life of Saint Honoratus*.

Finally, the chronology demonstrates that both men were Cassian’s contemporaries. Saint Honoratus presided over the Church of Arles, as Baronius notes in his annotations to the Martyrology, during the reigns of Theodosius the Younger and Valentinian III, while Coelestine and afterward Sixtus governed the Roman Church. It is known from Gennadius, Trithemius, and other authorities that Cassian flourished at Massilia during those same times.

Although Eucherius was somewhat younger, it is likewise established from the same sources that he lived in that period. Gennadius says that he collected certain short works of Cassian—works extended in eloquence but compressed in verbal expression—into a single volume, as well as other writings necessary both for ecclesiastical and monastic studies; and he died during the reigns of Valentinian and Marcian. This is Gennadius’s account.

That abridgment or revision of Cassian’s works by Eucherius no longer survives. When Cassian calls Honoratus and Eucherius “brothers,” this should not be understood as referring to nature, but either to office, or to monastic institution and profession, or to mutual charity and familiarity, or to age and shared life. Sidonius and other reliable authors likewise apply the name “brother” to contemporaries and those of the same age (Sidonius, Letter 5, Book 3, and Letter 1, Book 4).

More concerning Eucherius may be found in Baronius (volume 5, under the year of Christ 441, and in the Martyrology under 16 November), especially in the appendix to volume 7, under the year of Christ 529. There he corrects and retracts his earlier opinion, according to which he had previously thought that there was only one Eucherius, bishop of Lyon. He acknowledges instead that there were two Eucheriuses, both bishops: one, though it is not sufficiently certain of which church he was bishop, subscribed to the earlier Council of Orange; the other subscribed to the later Council of Orange, held approximately ninety-two years after the first. The latter was the bishop of Lyon, and to him he asserts that those homilies should be restored which have hitherto commonly circulated under the title of Eusebius of Emesa or Emissenus.]

[Col. 0845D] One of them, if I am not mistaken, was the monastery of Lérins, concerning whose praises Saint Eucherius composed a special book, as has been said. Founded by Saint Honoratus, mentioned above, on the island of Lérins or Lerina, it became famous throughout Gaul both for the number of its monks and for the strictness of its religious observance, so that it was almost a common refuge and training ground for all who renounced the world.

From this monastery emerged many bishops renowned for holiness and learning, some illustrious through their writings and others through miracles: Saint Honoratus, the first father and founder of the same monastery, as we have said; Saint Hilary, later archbishop of Arles; Eucherius of Lyon, of whom we are speaking; Caesarius of Arles; Lupus of Troyes; Vincent of Lérins, famous for his little book against heresies; Maximus and Faustus, both bishops of Riez; and others celebrated by Sidonius Apollinaris in his *Eucharistic Poem* to Faustus, where he says, among other things:

“How many mountains that level island  
has sent up to heaven.”

Caesarius imitated him in Homily 25: “Blessed and happy is the island of Lérins, which, although it appears small and level, is nevertheless known to have sent innumerable mountains up to heaven.” Mountains—that is, bishops and priests. For the monastery of Lérins was like a nursery of bishops (see Sidonius, Book 7, Letter 17, and Book 9, Letter 3, and Renatus Choppinus, *Monasticon*, Book 1, title 3).

Caesarius adds: “This is the place that nourishes exceptional monks and sends forth outstanding priests throughout all the provinces; as though it receives sons, it returns fathers, and those whom it nourishes as little ones, it returns as great men.” This is his account.

Lerina is an island adjoining the province of Narbonensis, opposite Antipolis (Pliny, *Natural History*, Book 3, chapter 5). Some mistakenly confuse it with another island similar in name and nearby in location. For there are two well-known islands in the Gallic Sea opposite the town of Antipolis in the province of Narbonensis: Lero and Lerinus, or Lerina. The former now bears the name of Saint Margaret, and the latter that of Saint Honoratus, who first laid the foundations of his monastery there. Sirmond thus annotated the passage in Sidonius.]

you, holy brothers Honoratus and Eucherius, so that one of you, presiding over a great monastery of brothers, desires his congregation—which is taught daily by the sight of your holy conduct—to be formed also by the precepts of those Fathers; while the other wished to be edified even by the sight of those men in the flesh and therefore penetrated into Egypt, so that, abandoning this province as though it were torpid from the cold of Gaul, he might approach those lands more closely regarded by the Sun of Justice, overflowing with ripened fruits of virtue,

[Note: [Col. 0846C] The following properties are attributed to the turtledove: first, like swallows, this bird seeks warmer places in winter and returns in spring, as Cicero testifies in Book 2 of *On Ends*, to which the present author refers; second, it is mute in winter and vocal in spring (Pliny, Book 10, chapter 35); third, it continually mourns and builds its nest in lofty trees, according to the following passage of Virgil (*Eclogues*):]

Nor did the most chaste turtledove cease to coo from the bronze-leaved elm.

[Note: 4. It practices conjugal chastity and remains widowed. Origen, *Homily I on the Song of Songs*, translated by St. Jerome, says: “They report this to be the nature of the turtledove: neither does the male take another female besides one, nor does the female tolerate more than one male; so that, if one of the pair is killed and the other survives, its love of intercourse dies together with its mate.” Jerome likewise writes in Book I *Against Jovinian*: “The turtledove, a most chaste bird, always dwelling in high places, is a type of the Savior. Let us read the naturalists, and we shall find this to be the nature of the turtledove: if it loses its mate, it does not join itself to another.”]

Like the most chaste turtledove, it would fly across. The virtue of charity necessarily compelled me to this, so that, while attending to the desire of one and also to the labor of the other, I might not avoid so abrupt a risk in writing, provided that authority might be added to the former among his sons and that the latter might be spared the necessity of so dangerous a voyage.

Accordingly, since neither the *Institutes of the Coenobia*, which we composed in twelve books for the blessed Bishop Castor, in such language as we were able, nor the ten *Conferences* of the Fathers dwelling in the Scetian desert, which we arranged as best we could at the command of the holy bishops Helladius and Leontius, have been able to satisfy your faith and fervor, I have now entrusted to you, for consecration, seven conferences of three Fathers dwelling in another desert—the first whom we saw—written in the same style, so that those matters concerning perfection which may perhaps have been treated more obscurely or omitted in our earlier works may be supplied.

If these, too, should not be able to satisfy the holy thirst of your zeal, seven further conferences, to be sent to the brothers who dwell on the islands of the Stoechades, will, I think, fulfill the desire of your fervor.

[Note: The Stoechades are three islands situated in the Gallic Sea, near the coast of Massilia. Pliny writes in *Natural History* III.5: “The three Stoechades, so called by the neighboring Massilians because of the order in which they lie, are also named individually: Proten and Messen, which is also called Pomponiana, and the third Hypola.” Isidore writes in *Etymologies* XIV: “The Stoechades are islands belonging to the Massilians, sixty thousand paces from the mainland, opposite the province of Narbonensis, where the river Rhône enters the sea.” Ennodius, in the *Life of Epiphanius*, joins the Stoechades with Lero and Lirino, mentioned above, as neighboring islands, in these words: “On his return he visited each of the holy settlements, the middle islands, the Stoechades, Lero, and Lirino itself, the level nurse of lofty mountains.”]

## ELEVENTH CONFERENCE

The first of Abbot Chaeremon, **On Perfection**

[Col. 0847]

### CHAPTER I

[Col. 0847B]

When we were dwelling in the Syrian coenobium, [Note: This was doubtless the Bethlehem coenobium, founded by St. Paula and enlarged and administered by St. Jerome (*Epitaph of Paula*), which surpassed the other monasteries of Syria in antiquity, dignity, number of monks, and holiness. Hence I believe it was called “the coenobium of Syria” in an antonomastic sense, because it was the foremost and principal monastery among those of Syria or Palestine. Cassian likewise says of it in *Institutes* III.4: “In our monastery, where our Lord Jesus Christ, born of a Virgin, graciously received the growth of human infancy, He also strengthened by His grace our own still tender and nursing infancy in religion.” Again, in chapter 5 of this conference: “At least this labor of so great a journey ought to obtain this: that we hastened here from the beginnings of the Bethlehem coenobium, out of desire for your instruction and love of our own progress.” Elsewhere also (*Institutes* IV.12 and *Conference* XVII.5) he calls it the cave in which “our Lord shone forth from the royal chamber of the Virgin’s womb.” That there were, besides this Bethlehem monastery, many other coenobia in Syria and Palestine is testified by St. Jerome in the *Life of Hilarion*.]

after the first beginnings of faith had been made and our progress had advanced to some degree, we began to desire the greater grace of perfection. We therefore decided at once to seek Egypt and, penetrating even into the remotest desert of the Thebaid, [Note: The Thebaid, or Thebais, as it has been called elsewhere, is a region of Egypt extending toward Ethiopia. It was formerly filled with monasteries and flourished with a great multitude of monks, as well as with the discipline and institutions of monastic life. We have learned this from Cassian, Palladius, Theodoret, Evagrius, Nicephorus, and also from the holy Fathers Jerome and Augustine, who wrote much about the inhabitants of the Thebaic desert and the manner of their monastic institution. Nor were the communities in those Thebaic monasteries composed only of Egyptians, Greeks, and Syrians; gatherings of Latins were also extremely frequent, as St. Jerome testifies. He translated into Latin the rules of monastic life written in Egyptian Greek by Pachomius, Theodore, and Orsiesius, so that they might also be useful to Latin monks remaining, as it were, on duty in that monastic province. Moreover, St. Antony, the father and propagator of monastic discipline, flourished in the Thebaid; from him innumerable leaders of monks arose, especially Ammon, Hilarion, Macarius, and others, through whom the monastic religion was spread throughout Asia and Africa. Isidore also lived in the Thebaid and governed a thousand monks. More will be said about him elsewhere (*Conference* XVIII.15).]

to visit the many holy men whose glory fame had spread throughout the world, if not in order to imitate them, at least in order to become acquainted with them.

Thus, after completing the voyage, we reached an Egyptian town called Thennesus. [Note: You will find nothing about the town of Thennesus either in Pliny or Ptolemy; nor is this surprising, since Pliny attributes two thousand notable towns to Egypt and Ptolemy eighteen hundred, although they mention by name only a very few of the more distinguished ones.]

Its inhabitants are so completely surrounded either by the sea or by salt marshes that, since they lack land, they devote themselves exclusively to commerce and acquire their wealth and possessions through maritime trade. Indeed, when they wish to construct buildings, they have no earth available unless it is brought by ship from a distant place.

### CHAPTER II  
### On Bishop Archebius

When we arrived, divine providence, favoring our desires, granted us the arrival of the most blessed and distinguished man, Bishop Archebius, [Note: We have discussed this Archebius elsewhere (*Institutes* V.37).] who had been taken from the company of anchorites and appointed bishop of the town of Panephysi. [Note: Concerning the Egyptian city of Panephysi, Ptolemy says only this in *Geography* IV: “Between the Busiritic and Bubastic rivers lies the nome and metropolis of Panephysis,” where “nome” means a district or prefecture. Pliny lists twelve such nomes, or prefectures of towns, in the Thebaid in *Natural History* V.9.]

Throughout his entire life he guarded the purpose of solitude with such strictness that he relaxed nothing of the tenor of his former humility and did not flatter himself because of the honor added to him. He did not testify that he had been chosen as suitable for this office; rather, he complained that he had been expelled from the discipline of anchoritism as unworthy, since, although he had spent thirty-seven years in it, he had not been able to attain the purity of so great a profession.

When he had received us piously and with the greatest kindness in the aforementioned Thennesus, where the election of the bishop had brought him, and had learned of our desire to seek holy Fathers even in the more remote parts of Egypt, he said:

“Come and see, for the time being, some old men dwelling not far from our monastery. Their antiquity already shines forth in their bodies, bent with age, and their holiness shines even in their appearance, so that the mere contemplation of them can impart great instruction to those who behold them. From them you may learn, not so much by words as by the example of their holy life, that which I grieve to have lost and am no longer able to transmit. I believe that this undertaking will somewhat relieve my poverty, if, while you seek that evangelical pearl (Matthew XIII) which I myself do not possess, I can at least show you where you may more conveniently purchase it.”

### CHAPTER III  
### Description of the Desert in Which Chaeremon, Nesteros, and Joseph Dwelt

[Col. 0850A]

Taking a staff and a bag—or, more accurately, a *paenula*, as is customary there for all monks setting out on a journey—[Note: Cassian discusses the staff and bag, or rather the *paenula*, among the clothing or equipment of Egyptian monks in *Institutes* I.8–9. “Their final garment,” he says, “is a goatskin, which is called the *melotes*, and a bag, and a staff. They carry these in imitation of those who prefigured the outlines of this profession in the Old Testament, namely the prophets Elijah and Elisha.” We have noted that *paenula* should preferably be read here. Cassian then explains the meaning of both. Of the *paenula* he says: “This garment of goatskin signifies that, after all wantonness of carnal passions has been put to death, they must stand in the utmost gravity of virtue, and that no wanton or heated remnant of former youthful and restless behavior should remain in their bodies.” Of the staff he says: “Its carrying spiritually warns them never to walk unarmed among so many barking dogs of vices and invisible beasts of spiritual wickedness, but to blunt their attacks with the sign of the cross,” and so forth.]

he himself served as our guide and led us to his own city, that is, Panephysi, as we proceeded along the road.

When the sea, after a sudden earthquake, crossed its former boundaries and occupied the land—or rather a very large part of the neighboring region, once exceedingly wealthy, since, as the story goes, food was supplied from it to the entire region—and when nearly all the villages had consequently collapsed, it covered the formerly fertile lands with salt marshes, so that they thought the words sung spiritually in the Psalm, “He turned rivers into a desert, and springs of water into thirst; a fruitful land into salt marsh, because of the wickedness of its inhabitants” (Psalm CVI), had been spoken literally about that region. [Note: The holy Fathers explain this passage spiritually, that is, allegorically, as referring to the fruitfulness of the Church and the barrenness of the Synagogue, or to the calling of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews—Basil, Jerome, Augustine, and Prosper. Jerome may speak for all in his commentary on Habakkuk III: “After the Lord came into the world, and that which He said in the Gospel was fulfilled—‘For judgment I have come into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind’ (Matthew XI)—then the land of Israel, from which rivers formerly flowed and watered the whole people of Judea, dried up, and its springs were stopped. But the whole world, which had been desert and barren and had not possessed the waters of the Lord’s preaching, was turned into pools of water; and as many teachers as it produced, so many springs did it have,” and so forth. Thus Jerome interprets that Psalm spiritually, as is said here.

Nevertheless, there is no doubt that the same words can be understood literally and according to the letter as referring to a real and external transformation by which God at times made rivers into a desert—that is, turned rivers into dry land, or dried them up and caused their channels to wither where they had previously flowed abundantly—and turned fruitful land into salt marsh, that is, into barren land such as land covered with salt, because of the wickedness and depravity of its inhabitants.

We have an example of this transformation in Genesis XIII, where it is said that Lot lifted up his eyes and saw all the land around the Jordan, which was everywhere watered before the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, like the paradise of the Lord. God then dried up this watered and fruitful land, like paradise, with sulfur and fire sent down from heaven and condemned it to everlasting barrenness, as we read in Genesis XIX.

St. Jerome further adds, in the passage cited above, the following words relevant here: “We read in the works of those who composed volumes on marvels, and of those who have brought down the Olympiads of Greece to our own memory, explaining what new event occurred in the world in each year, that among other things rivers burst forth through earthquakes which had not existed before; and again, others were swallowed up and perished. For all the veins of the earth, just as the blood in the human body, contain within themselves hidden waters, which are ruptured by the shaking of the earth and flow out as rivers.” Thus far St. Jerome.

Concerning these and similar changes—earthquakes, eruptions of the sea and rivers, islands arising from them, and lands swallowed up—which are discussed in this chapter, see Pliny, *Natural History* II.85.]

In these places, then, many towns, situated on higher mounds, stood out; after their inhabitants had been driven away, that flood made them like islands, which offer the desired solitude to the saints who withdraw from the world. In them dwelt three very ancient anchorites: Chaeremon, Nesteros, and Joseph.

[Note: Cassian assigns the seven following conferences to these three anchorites: three to Chaeremon, two to Nesteros, and two likewise to Joseph.]

### CHAPTER IV  
### On Abbot Chaeremon and His Excuse Concerning the Requested Instruction

Accordingly, the blessed Archebius preferred first to lead us to Chaeremon, [Note: Ciaconius advises that this name be written in this way because it is written in Greek as Χαιρεμών (*Chairemōn*). I am more inclined, however, to follow Suidas, who reads Χαιρήμων (*Chairēmōn*), so that the middle syllable is long, the Greek eta being changed, as usual, into a long Latin *e*. Palladius seems to refer to this Chaeremon in the *Lausiac History* 92, when he writes: “It happened in those days that Chaeremon the ascetic died while seated, and was found dead in his chair, holding work in his hands.” Three things are noted here: first, ἄσκησις (*askēsis*), that is, discipline or exercise, from which he is called an ascetic; second, extreme old age, on account of which Chaeremon was compelled to sit; third, his continual labor until the end of life, since he was found with his work in his hands.]

who was nearer to his monastery and older than the other two. For although he had passed the hundredth year of his life, still vigorous in spirit, his back had been so bent by age and constant prayer that, reduced as it were to his earliest infancy, he moved forward with his hands lowered and extended to the ground. [Note: We have discussed more fully elsewhere the longevity of these ancient monks and anchorites, who lived to and beyond a hundred years amid the greatest austerity of life (*Conference* III.1).]

As we observed both his remarkable face and his manner of walking—for although all his limbs had already become weak and deadened, he had by no means lost the strictness of his former discipline—and as we humbly requested speech and instruction, declaring that the desire for spiritual teaching alone had been the cause of our arrival, he sighed deeply and said:

“What instruction can I provide for you, when the weakness of old age has relaxed my former rigor and taken away even my confidence in speaking? How can I presume to teach what I myself do not do, or instruct another in what I recognize that I now practice less fully or less fervently? For this reason I have never permitted any younger man to live with me until this age, lest another’s discipline should be relaxed by my example. The authority of one who gives instruction will never be effective unless he has fixed it in the heart of the hearer by the accomplishment of his own works.”

### CHAPTER V  
### Our Reply to His Excuse

At this we were pierced by no small confusion and replied:

“Although the difficulty of this place, and even this solitary life itself, which strong youth could scarcely endure, ought to be sufficient for our entire instruction, and although these things instruct and humble us abundantly even without your speaking, we nevertheless ask you, after laying aside your silence for a little while, graciously to pour into us those teachings by which we may embrace the virtue that we see in you not so much through imitation as through admiration.

For even if our lukewarmness, once revealed to you, does not deserve to obtain what we seek, at least the labor of so great a journey ought to secure this: that we hastened here from the beginnings of the Bethlehem coenobium, out of desire for your instruction and love of our own progress.”

[Note: Concerning this, see above, chapter 1 of this conference, where it is called, in an antonomastic sense, “the coenobium of Syria,” because it surpassed the others.]

### CHAPTER VI  
### Abbot Chaeremon’s Proposition: That Vices Are Conquered in Three Ways

[Col. 0852A]

Then the blessed Chaeremon said:

“There are three things that cause people to abstain from vices: either fear of Gehenna or of present laws; or hope and desire for the kingdom of heaven; or affection for goodness itself and love of the virtues.

Fear is said to abhor the contagion of evil in this way: ‘The fear of the Lord hates wickedness’ (Proverbs VIII). Hope also excludes the assault of every vice: ‘None of those who hope in him shall offend’ (Psalm XXXIII). Love likewise does not fear the ruin caused by sins, because ‘love never falls’ (1 Corinthians XIII). [Note: The conjecture proposed in the earlier edition is not satisfactory—namely, that *Charitas numquam cadit* should be regarded as an error for *excidit*, as in the Vulgate reading of the Apostle. For *cadit* and *excidit* have the same meaning, and this author does not always preserve the precise words of Scripture. Indeed, he uses the same phrase in chapter 10 of this conference. Elsewhere (*Conference* I.11), however, he has *Charitas numquam excidet*, where the matter is explained: namely, how charity never falls or fails.]

And again: ‘Love covers a multitude of sins’ (1 Peter IV). Therefore the blessed Apostle, summing up the whole of salvation in the perfection of these three virtues, concludes: ‘Now there remain faith, hope, and love—these three’ (1 Corinthians XIII).”

[Note: The teaching of the Council of Trent, Session 6, in the decree on justification, chapter 6, aptly agrees with and corresponds to this passage.
