There the manner of preparation for justification is set forth as follows: “Sinners are disposed toward justification itself when, awakened and assisted by divine grace, they freely move toward God, conceiving faith through hearing and believing those things to be true which have been divinely revealed and promised—especially that the ungodly are justified by God through His grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus—and when, understanding themselves to be sinners, they turn from the fear of divine justice, by which they are beneficially shaken, to consider God’s mercy and rise into hope, trusting that God will be propitious toward them for Christ’s sake, and begin to love Him as the source of all justice,” and so forth.]

“For faith is what causes the contagion of vices to be avoided through fear of future judgment and punishments; hope, drawing our mind away from present things, despises all bodily pleasures in expectation of heavenly rewards; and love, kindling us through the ardor of the mind to love Christ and the fruit of spiritual virtues, makes us detest with complete hatred whatever is contrary to them.

Although these three seem to tend toward one end—for they all move us to abstain from unlawful things—they nevertheless differ from one another by great degrees of excellence. The two preceding ones properly belong to human beings who are striving toward progress but have not yet conceived an affection for the virtues. The third belongs especially to God and to those who have received within themselves the image and likeness of God. [Note: Here the author understands the image and likeness of God as the imitation of divine goodness, through which a human being is assimilated and made like God, as will be clear from what follows, especially chapters 9 and 10. Those, therefore, have received the image and likeness of God within themselves who imitate divine goodness and beneficence by doing good to all, both good and evil, friends and enemies—or who have attained the perfection of charity.]

“For He alone performs what is good without being moved by any fear or by the prospect of reward, but solely by an affection for goodness: ‘The Lord has made everything for Himself,’ as Solomon says (Proverbs XVI). For the sake of His own goodness He bestows every abundance of good things upon the worthy and the unworthy, because He can neither be wearied by injuries nor moved in a suffering way by human iniquities, always remaining perfect goodness and an unchangeable nature.”

### CHAPTER VII  
### By What Degrees One May Ascend to the Height of Charity, and What Stability It Possesses

If anyone is striving toward perfection, [Note: Three states or degrees of human beings in the spiritual life are distinguished. The first and lowest is the state of beginners, who are drawn toward good by servile fear and restrained from evil, according to the saying: “The wicked hate sin through fear of punishment.” The second is the state of those making progress, who are led by hope and desire for reward. The third is the state of the perfect, who are moved solely by love and charity, according to the saying: “The good hate sin through love of virtue.” These three states are also called the states of servants, hired laborers, and sons.]

he will ascend by progressive steps from that first degree of fear, which we have properly called servile, concerning which it is said, “When you have done everything, say: We are unprofitable servants” (Luke XVII), [Note: One must progress from servile fear to hope. Thus Augustine, explaining the Psalm verse, “The Lord is well pleased with those who fear Him, and with those who hope in His mercy” (Psalm CXLVI), says: “Judas the betrayer of Christ feared, but he did not hope in His mercy. Afterwards he repented that he had betrayed Christ. You feared well, but if only you had hoped in the mercy of Him whom you feared! He departed in despair and hanged himself. Therefore fear the Lord in such a way that you hope in His mercy. For you will appease Him if you hope in His mercy.”]

to the higher path of hope. He is then compared not to a servant but to a hired laborer, because he expects the wages of recompense and, as though secure concerning the forgiveness of sins and freedom from punishment, and conscious of his good works, appears to seek the reward of approval. Yet he has not been able to attain the affection of the son who, trusting in the generosity of his father’s indulgence, does not doubt that everything belonging to his father is his own.

Even that prodigal son, who had lost the name of son along with his father’s property, did not dare aspire to it, saying: “I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants” (Luke XV). After those pods of pigs, whose filling was denied him—that is, the filthy foods of vices—when he had returned to himself and, struck by salutary fear, had begun to loathe the uncleanness of pigs and dread the punishments of dreadful hunger, he, already made as it were a servant, also desired the state of a hired laborer, now thinking of his wages, and said: “How many hired servants in my father’s house have bread in abundance, while I perish here from hunger! I will arise and go to my father and say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me as one of your hired servants” (Luke XV). [Col. 0853A]

### CHAPTER VIII  
### How Greatly Those Who Turn Away from Vices through Affection for Charity Excel

But when the father ran to meet him at this humble cry of repentance, he received him with a greater tenderness than the son had expressed. Not content to grant him something lesser, he restored him without delay to the former dignity of sonship, after he had passed through both degrees. [Note: Namely, those of servants and hired laborers.]

We, too, must therefore hasten to ascend to the third degree, that of sons, who believe that everything belonging to the Father is their own. By ascending through the indissoluble grace of charity, may we deserve to receive the image and likeness of that heavenly Father and, in imitation of the true Son, proclaim: “Everything that the Father has is mine” (John XVI).

The blessed Apostle also declares this concerning us: “All things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas, whether the world or life or death, whether things present or things to come; all are yours” (1 Corinthians III).

The Savior’s commandments likewise urge us toward this likeness: [Note: “As” does not denote equality but similarity of qualities, and indeed a similarity of the kind that can exist between God and a human being, not the kind that exists between one human being and another. We cannot attain or equal the perfection that is in God, but we can imitate it. Hence the Fathers observed that Scripture designates not one but many kinds of perfection. Clement of Alexandria writes in Book IV of the *Stromata*: “I find that ‘perfect’ is understood in many ways, according to the one who conducts himself rightly in each virtue. Someone is therefore perfected and brought to completion as pious, religious, patient, continent, a worker, a martyr, or endowed with knowledge. But I do not know whether anyone is perfect in all things except Him alone who for our sake assumed humanity.”

St. Ambrose writes in Book III of *Duties* (chapter 2): “I read that Paul is perfect and not perfect. For after saying, ‘Not that I have already received or am already perfect, but I pursue, if I may apprehend,’ he immediately adds, ‘Therefore, whoever among us are perfect.’ For there are two forms of perfection: one having incomplete numbers, the other complete; one here, the other there; one according to human possibility, the other according to future perfection. But God is just in all things, wise in all things, perfect in all things.”

St. Jerome says nearly the same in Book I *Against the Pelagians* (chapter 5), discussing the same passage of the Apostle: “It is clear from this that there are two perfections in the sacred Scriptures, two kinds of righteousness, and two kinds of fear. The first perfection, incomparable truth, and perfect righteousness must be conformed to the virtues of God. The second is suited to our weakness, according to the Psalm: ‘No living person shall be justified in your sight’ (Psalm CXLII), and to that righteousness which is called perfect not by comparison but by God’s knowledge.”

Finally, Cassian writes below, reporting Abbot Chaeremon’s view, as follows (*Conference* XII.12): “According to the state and measure of each mind, divine Scripture calls the freedom of our will toward various degrees of perfection; for a single crown of perfection could not be set before everyone, since neither is everyone’s virtue, will, or fervor the same. Therefore divine speech has established, in a certain sense, different orders and different measures of perfection themselves. The variety of the evangelical beatitudes clearly demonstrates that this is so,” and so forth. See also St. Thomas, *Summa theologiae* II–II, question 184, article 2.]

“Be perfect,” He says, “as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matthew V).

For in those other states the affection for goodness can sometimes be interrupted, when the vigor of the mind is relaxed by some sluggishness, joy, or pleasure, or when either fear of present Gehenna or desire for future things is withdrawn. Yet those states provide a certain degree of progress, instructing us that, when we begin to avoid vices either through fear of punishments or through hope of rewards, we may pass to the degree of charity, because, as it is written, “There is no fear in charity, but perfect charity casts out fear, because fear has punishment. Whoever fears is not perfect in charity. Let us therefore love, because God first loved us” (1 John IV). [Col. 0855A]

[Note: The reference is specifically to servile fear. Augustine writes in his ninth treatise on the First Epistle of John: “Fear, as it were, prepares a place for charity. But when charity begins to dwell there, the fear that prepared the place is driven out. For as charity increases, fear decreases; and as charity becomes more inward, fear is driven outward. Greater charity, lesser fear; lesser charity, greater fear. But if there is no fear, there is no way for charity to enter. It is like sewing with linen thread through a bristle: the bristle enters first, but unless it comes out, the thread does not follow. Thus fear first occupies the mind, but fear does not remain there, because it entered in order to introduce charity. Once security has been established in the soul, what joy is ours, whether in this world or in the world to come?” Thus Augustine.

St. Thomas, moreover, in his commentary, distinguishes four kinds of fear of the Lord. First is servile fear, which is fear of Gehenna alone; second is initial fear, which is fear of Gehenna and of offending God; third is filial fear, which is fear of offending God alone; fourth is reverential fear, which is reverence alone toward the divine majesty. The first is not in charity, but prepares a place for it and finally introduces it, like a bristle or needle introducing thread, as Augustine says. The second is not in perfect charity, of which the Apostle speaks here. The third is greater in those who are more perfect, because it belongs to more perfect charity on the way, though not in the homeland. The fourth remains with the perfect charity of the homeland; concerning it, Psalm XVIII says: ‘The holy fear of the Lord endures forever.’]

“We shall therefore not be able to ascend to that true perfection in any other way than this: just as He first loved us for the sake of no other reason than our salvation, so we also must love Him for no other reason than His love alone.

Accordingly, we must strive to ascend with perfect ardor of mind from this fear to hope, from hope to the love of God and of the virtues themselves, so that, passing over into an affection for goodness itself, we may hold fast immovably to what is good, insofar as this is possible for human nature.”

### CHAPTER IX  
### That Charity Not Only Makes Sons from Servants but Also Bears the Image and Likeness of God

[Col. 0855B]

For there is a great difference between one who extinguishes within himself the fire of vices through fear of Gehenna or hope of future recompense, and one who, through the affection of divine charity, abhors wickedness and impurity themselves and possesses the good of purity solely from love and desire for chastity, no longer looking toward the promise of future reward but doing everything out of delight in the present good, and acting not from contemplation of punishments but from delight in virtues.

For this state cannot be corrupted, even when the testimony of all human beings has been removed, by taking advantage of an opportunity for sin, nor violated by the secret pleasures of thought, since one who holds the affection for virtue itself deep within does not merely refuse in his heart whatever is contrary to it, but detests it with the utmost horror. It is one thing for someone, delighted by a present good, to hate the contagion of vices and of the flesh; another to restrain unlawful desires with a view to future recompense; one thing to fear present loss, and another to dread future punishment. Finally, it is far greater not to wish to depart from the good because of the good itself than not to give consent to evils because of fear of evil. In the former there is voluntary goodness; in the latter, goodness is, as it were, compelled and violently wrung from one unwilling, either by fear of punishment or by desire for rewards.

For one who abstains from the allurements of vices through fear, once the obstacle of fear has been removed, will return again to what he loves; and therefore he will neither continually retain stability in the good nor ever cease from the struggle. [Col. 0856B] For where there is the disturbance of battles, there cannot fail to be the dangers of wounds as well. Anyone engaged in combat must, even if he is a warrior and frequently inflicts deadly wounds on his adversaries while fighting bravely, nevertheless sometimes be grazed by the enemy’s sword.

But one who, having overcome the assault of vices, already enjoys the security of peace and has passed into an affection for virtue itself will strive to retain the perpetual state of that good of which he is now wholly possessed, because he considers nothing more harmful than damage to inward chastity. For he judges nothing more dear or precious than present purity, to which either a harmful transgression of the virtues or the poisonous contagion of the vice itself is a grave punishment.

To such a person, I say, neither reverence for human presence will add anything to his uprightness, nor solitude diminish it; but, always and everywhere carrying with him [Note: The tranquillity and happiness of an innocent and blameless conscience, which the just and devout enjoy even in this life—as though they carried everywhere with them the most faithful, intimate, and sincere witness and judge of their actions, indeed even of their thoughts—is declared by Solomon in Proverbs, where he says: “A secure mind is a continual feast” (Prov. XV). And the Apostle says: “This is our glory, the testimony of our conscience, that we conducted ourselves in this world in simplicity of heart and sincerity before God” (I Cor. XII). The Fathers add their testimony. Saint Martial, in his letter to the people of Toulouse: “Those whose conscience is good have nothing to fear.” Jerome, Letter 47, On Avoiding Suspicious Companionship: “A good conscience,” he says, “flees the eyes of no one.” Augustine, on the Psalmist’s words, “God helps me” (Ps. LIII): “All the saints are helped by God, but inwardly, where no one sees.” For just as the conscience of the ungodly is a great punishment, so the conscience of the devout is a great joy; for “This is our glory,” the Apostle said, “the testimony of our conscience.” Bernard, in The Interior House, book I, chapter 22: “A good conscience is the title of religion, the temple of Solomon, the field of blessing, the garden of delights, the golden couch, the joy of angels, the ark of the covenant, the king’s treasure, the court of God, the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit, a book sealed and closed, to be opened on the day of judgment. Nothing is more pleasant, nothing safer, nothing richer than a good conscience: let the body weigh it down, let the world drag it, let the devil terrify it—it will remain secure. A good conscience will be secure when the body dies, secure when the soul is presented before God, secure when both are placed before the terrifying tribunal of the just Judge on the day of judgment.” Thus far the holy Fathers.

Pagan writers likewise agree with this view. Cicero, Tusculan Disputations, book II: “No theater is greater for virtue than conscience.” And in Cato: “The conscience of a life well lived and of many good deeds is most delightful.” And in his speech For Cluentius: “If throughout one’s life conscience has been the witness of the best counsels and deeds, we shall live with the highest honor and without any fear.” Seneca, Letter 43: “What good does it do to hide oneself and avoid the eyes and ears of human beings? A good conscience summons a crowd; an evil one is anxious and troubled even in solitude. If what you do is honorable, let everyone know it; if shameful, what does it matter that no one knows, when you know? Wretched man, if you despise this witness.”

Poets may also be added. Horace, in the Epistles (Epistle I):

> Let this be a wall of bronze:
>
> To be conscious of no guilt, and to grow pale at none.

But concerning an evil conscience, Juvenal, Satire 3:

> Whatever is committed by a wicked example displeases its author himself:
> this is the first punishment, that no guilty person is acquitted
> when he is his own judge.

And Cicero, For Roscius of Ameria: “Each person’s own fraud and his own error torment him most; each person’s own crime agitates him and drives him mad; his evil thoughts and the conscience of his mind terrify him. These are the constant and domestic Furies of the ungodly.” [Col. 0857D]

This is what they say about conscience—the judge, witness, and arbiter of good and evil actions and thoughts—which in Greek is called συντήρησις (*syntērēsis*, moral self-awareness). As Saint Jerome says (Commentary on Ezekiel, chapter I): “The spark of conscience in Cain’s breast was not extinguished even after he had been driven from paradise”; by it, though overcome by pleasures or rage, and sometimes deceived by the very semblance of reason, we feel that we are sinning.

Nevertheless, although conscience is itself the judge and arbiter of itself and of its own actions, it has a superior judge and arbiter—none other than God himself, who knows human hearts and understands all their thoughts. Hence the Apostle says in I Corinthians IV: “I am conscious of nothing against myself; yet by this I am not justified. For the one who judges me is the Lord.” And Augustine, Sermon 23, On the Words of the Lord: “Perhaps you find nothing in your conscience; he finds what he sees better.”

From this we understand that the testimony or judgment of a good conscience does indeed bring great joy and tranquillity of spirit, [Col. 0858B] but not infallible certainty. For we rejoice and glory not only in those things which we are certain that we possess or will possess, but also in those which we trust that we possess or hope that we will possess, although not without fear or apprehension concerning the contrary, as the common saying goes. Hence in the second Psalm we are commanded to exult with trembling. See more on this in Saint Bernard’s truly golden little book The Interior House and in the other work entitled On Conscience. See also the Council of Trent, session 6, chapter 9.] he strives especially to please that conscience, knowing that he can neither outwit, deceive, nor escape it.

## CHAPTER X  
### That the perfection of charity is to pray for one’s enemies, and by what sign it may be recognized that the soul has not yet been purified

If anyone, relying not on the labor of his own effort but on God’s help, should deserve to possess this state, he will begin to pass from the condition of slavery—in which there is fear—and from the mercenary desire for hope—in which what is sought is not so much the goodness of the giver as the reward of recompense—into the adoption of sons, where fear and desire no longer remain, but that charity which never fails endures continually (I Cor. XIII).

Concerning this fear and charity, the Lord, rebuking certain people, showed what was appropriate to each condition. [Note: Saint Jerome, commenting on this passage of Malachi, after many observations worthy of notice, says: “God, knowing the difference between a son and a servant, seeks glory from the son and fear from the servant. For the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” Thus we may pass from the fear of servants to the glory of sons.] “A son honors his father, and a servant fears his master. And if I am a Father, where is my honor? And if I am a Lord, where is my fear?” (Mal. I).

For one who is a servant must fear, because, knowing his master’s will, if he does not do it he will rightly be beaten with many blows (Luke XII). Through this charity, therefore, whoever has attained the image and likeness of God will now delight in the good will because of the good itself; and, possessing in some way an affection resembling patience and gentleness, he will thereafter grow angry at none of the faults of sinners, but rather will ask forgiveness for them, grieving and sympathizing with their weaknesses.

He will remember that he himself was attacked for so long by the goads of similar passions until he was saved by the Lord’s mercy; that he was not snatched from the assault of the flesh by his own efforts but saved by God’s protection; and that therefore mercy, not anger, ought to be shown to those who have gone astray. With complete tranquillity of heart he will sing to God the verse:

> You have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise (Ps. CXV).

And:

> Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell (Ps. XCIII).

Remaining in this humility of mind, [Col. 0858B] he will also be able [Note: Love of enemies is of two kinds: one general and common, the other special. The former belongs to a precept; the latter to counsel and perfection, as is said here. The precept is that we should not hate any human being, however hostile to us; that we should return evil to no one, wish evil upon no one, and embrace all people—especially Christians—with a general charity; that we should not exclude them from common prayers, almsgiving, and acts of kindness performed for everyone; and that we should at least assist them in extreme necessity. Counsel and perfection, however, require that we do good to them even outside necessity, greet them by name, address them familiarly, pray for them in a particular way, and help them by every means available to us.] to fulfill that evangelical commandment of perfection:

> Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you (Luke VI).

And thus [Note: Saint Augustine, Sermon 5, On Saint Stephen, aptly applies the following to this passage: “Great is the labor of loving enemies and pleading for persecutors; nor do we deny it, brothers: it is indeed no small labor in this world, but it will be a great reward in the future. For by loving an enemy, you become a friend of God; indeed, not merely a friend but also a son, as the Lord himself says: ‘Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven’ (Matt. V). If some rich person in this world wished to make you his adopted son, how would you serve him, what honors would you show him, and what harsh and sometimes even disgraceful insults from his servants and his service would you endure in order to reach his passing and fragile inheritance? What that person endures for the sake of earthly wealth, endure for the sake of eternal life.”] he will be able to attain the reward that follows, through which we shall not only bear the image and likeness of God but also be called sons of God:

> So that you may be sons, he says, of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Matt. V).

Blessed John, recognizing that he had attained this affection, says:

> So that we may have confidence on the day of judgment, because as he is, so are we in this world (I John IV). [Note: Saint Thomas, in his Commentary: “As he is full of charity, holy, and just, so are we,” as the Interlinear Gloss says. Here “as” does not indicate equality but a certain likeness. Through this confidence we imitate the perfection of his love in the world by loving friends and enemies, as he makes rain fall upon the just and the unjust.]

For in what respect can frail and weak human nature be as he is, unless, in imitation of God, it continually extends the tranquil charity of its heart toward the good and the evil, the just and the unjust? Thus it will act from an affection for the good because of the good itself, reaching that true adoption of the sons of God concerning which the same blessed Apostle declares:

[Note: There are various and diverse explanations of this statement. The first is: Everyone who has been born of God—that is, reborn through baptism from water and the Holy Spirit—does not sin, insofar as and to the extent that he has been born of God, and cannot sin, namely mortally (Jerome, book II Against Jovinian). The second is: He cannot sin so long as the seed of God—that is, charity infused through the Holy Spirit—remains in him. For as long as a person has charity, he does not sin mortally and cannot do so; yet he can absolutely sin and lose, indeed cast away, charity and commit mortal sin (Augustine, Tractate 5 on the Epistle of John). The third, from Saint Bernard (Sermon 1 on Septuagesima): “He who is born of God does not sin,” that is, one who is predestined does not remain in sin, because God preserves him so that he cannot perish—the heavenly generation, that is, God’s predestination, cannot be deceived.]

> Everyone who is born of God does not commit sin, because his seed is in him, and he cannot sin, because he is born of God (I John III).

And again:

> We know that everyone who is born of God does not sin, but the generation of God preserves him, and the evil one does not touch him (I John V).

This is to be understood not of every kind of sin, but [Note: That is, of mortal sins, in the manner in which Jerome and Augustine explain John’s statement. We have elsewhere noted, following Saint Thomas (I–II, question 85, article 3), that capital sins are called such in two ways. In one sense, “capital” derives from “head” in its proper meaning; accordingly, a sin or crime is called capital when it is punished by capital penalty, that is, death. In this sense every deadly sin is understood as capital, as in the present passage, because it brings death to the soul. In another sense, a capital vice is called such from “head” because the term metaphorically signifies the beginning or directing source of other things; thus a vice is called capital when several other vices arise from it. In this sense Gregory places seven capital vices (Moral Works XXXI, chapter 31), while Cassian places eight (Book V and Conference 5).] only of capital crimes.

Of these, whoever refuses to withdraw and cleanse himself is declared by the Apostle mentioned above, in another passage, not even to be one for whom prayer ought to be offered:

> Whoever knows that his brother is committing a sin not unto death, let him ask, and life will be given to him who sins not unto death.

[Note: The Apostle John distinguishes two kinds of sin: one, sin unto death; the other, sin not unto death. What precisely is sin unto death and sin not unto death, however, has been variously interpreted. Some understand sin unto death as every mortal sin, and sin not unto death as any venial sin. This is the interpretation of Abbot Chaeremon in this passage, supported also by the Ordinary Gloss and other authors. Yet the following seems to oppose this interpretation: “Whoever knows that his brother is committing a sin not unto death, let him ask, and life will be given to him who sins not unto death.” For one who sins venially does not lose the life of the soul, which consists in grace and charity; therefore life cannot be restored to him when he already possesses it. Moreover, the Church constantly prays for those who commit deadly sins, as Christ prayed for his crucifiers and Stephen for those who stoned him; and the Lord himself commanded: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. V). Therefore sin unto death is not identical with mortal sin as distinguished from venial sin, nor is sin not unto death identical with venial sin. Rather, among mortal sins one must seek a particular kind of sin that John calls sin unto death and distinguishes from sin not unto death. What that sin is remains disputed.

The Greeks understand sin unto death as μνησικακίαν (*mnēsikakian*), that is, a tenacious memory of injuries and an obstinate desire for revenge. So Oecumenius. Others understand it as sin against the Holy Spirit, especially opposition to acknowledged truth and envy of fraternal charity. Concerning this the Lord said in the Gospel: “Whoever speaks a word against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matt. XI). Others understand it as any very serious mortal sin, such as homicide, perjury, or sacrilege. Finally, others understand sin unto death as final impenitence, or mortal sin in which a person perseveres until death and the end of life. So Augustine, On Correction and Grace, chapter 12, and Gregory, Moral Works XVI, chapter 31.

Interpreters further note that John’s words, “I do not say that anyone should pray for it,” do not forbid or prohibit prayer for great and serious sinners, but merely indicate the difficulty of being heard and do not promise, on God’s part, certain acceptance and forgiveness—as though he were saying: “I endure, indeed I approve, your praying for all sinners; but I do not say, that is, I do not command, that anyone pray for those who sin unto death as though he were certain to be heard.” Accordingly, when the Church prays daily and offers the unbloody sacrifice for sinners of every kind, indeed for unbelievers, Jews, and heretics, it does nothing contrary to this teaching of John. Saint Augustine, however, and others say that one should not pray for those who die in mortal sin, that is, for the damned. But this is difficult to understand, since we cannot know another person’s conscience or the state of his soul, especially after death; whereas the Apostle says: “Whoever knows that his brother is sinning not unto death,” and so forth.]

> There is sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it (ibid.).

Concerning those sins which are declared not to be unto death—sins from which even those who faithfully serve Christ cannot be free, however carefully they guard themselves—it is said:

> If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us (I John I).

And again:

> If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us (ibid.).

For it is impossible for any of the saints not to fall into those minor sins which are committed through speech, through thought, through ignorance, through forgetfulness, through necessity, through intention, or through sudden surprise. Although these are distinct from the sin said to be unto death, they nevertheless cannot be free from guilt and blame.

When, therefore, someone has attained the affection for goodness and imitation of God mentioned above, then, clothed in the inward compassion of the Lord’s patience, he will likewise pray for his persecutors, saying:

> Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing (Luke XXIII).

But [Note: This is Saint Jerome’s statement, to be cited immediately below, expressed in nearly the same words.] it is an evident sign that the soul has not yet been purified of the dregs of vices when, in the case of another’s crimes, it does not grieve with merciful feeling but maintains the rigid censure of a judge.

For how can one who does not possess what the Apostle marked as capable of completing the fullness of the law attain perfection of heart?

> Bear one another’s burdens, he says, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ (Gal. VI).

Nor does such a person possess that virtue of charity which is not provoked, is not puffed up, thinks no evil, bears all things, and endures all things (I Cor. XIII).

> The righteous man has compassion on the souls of his animals [Lipsius, in the margin: “of his sinners”]; but the inward parts of the wicked are merciless (Prov. XII). [Note: Cuychius, Ciaconius, and others read this in that way. Dionysius and others, however, have “the souls of their sinners,” which I think is erroneous. Still others have “the souls of their animals,” and so forth. The Vulgate edition reads (Prov. XII): “The righteous man knows the souls of his beasts, but the inward parts of the wicked are cruel.”]

Therefore it is absolutely certain that the monk is subject to the same vices which he condemns in another with an unmerciful and inhuman severity.

> A stern king falls into evils; [Note: The Vulgate text reads: “Whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself cry out and not be heard.” Saint Jerome says concerning this: “This statement is to be understood generally, and not only of the poor or of one physically weak. For one who does not grieve over another’s crimes with an affection of mercy, but prefers to maintain the judgment of a critic, shows that he has not yet been purified of the dregs of vices and is not worthy to hear of divine mercy.”]

> and whoever closes his ears so as not to hear the weak will himself call, and there will be no one to hear him (Prov. XXI).

## CHAPTER XI  
### Germanus’s Question: Why he called the affection of fear and hope imperfect

**Germanus:** You have indeed spoken powerfully and magnificently about perfect charity toward God. Nevertheless, what troubles us is that, although you have preferred it with such praise, you said that fear of God and hope of eternal recompense are imperfect, whereas the Prophet seems to have thought something quite different about them, saying:

> Fear the Lord, all you his saints, for those who fear him lack nothing (Ps. XXXIII).

And again, when observing God’s ordinances, he admits that he has applied himself with a view to recompense:

> I inclined my heart to do your ordinances forever [Note: Jerome translated from the Hebrew: “Because of eternal recompense.” The first and proper reason why the mind ought to be applied to carrying out God’s commands is God himself, or God’s will and command—namely, because he wills and commands it—just as the primary reason why God should be loved is God himself, or his supreme goodness; hence we are commanded to love him for his own sake. A second reason is recompense, or hope of eternal recompense, which the abbot here calls mercenary because it looks to payment and personal advantage—not because it is vicious, but because it is less perfect than charity, by which God is loved for his own sake without regard to reward, as the following chapter explains.] because of recompense (Ps. CXVIII).

And the Apostle says:

> By faith, he says, Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to have the enjoyment of temporal sin, considering the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt (Heb. XI). For he was looking toward the reward.

[Note: These are the words of the Apostle in Hebrews XI. It is known from the account in Exodus that Moses was taken in, adopted, and raised by Pharaoh’s daughter. Saint Stephen confirms this in Acts VII, saying: “When he had been exposed, Pharaoh’s daughter took him up and raised him as her own son.” But when and how, once he had grown up—that is, reached adulthood and mature age—he denied, or, as the Greek has it, recoiled from and rejected, being called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, we read neither in Exodus nor in Josephus. Saint Thomas therefore interprets it as follows: He denied that he was her son, not in word but in deed, because against Pharaoh’s will he killed the Egyptian who was striking a Hebrew, and joined himself to the Hebrew people. So Saint Thomas.

Others, however, think that Moses denied it not only in deed but also in words, openly professing himself a worshiper of the true God and a member of the Hebrew people and religion. Josephus, Antiquities, chapter 6, relates how Moses, while still an infant and presented to Pharaoh by his daughter, threw down the diadem that Pharaoh had placed upon him and trampled it underfoot, thereby also denying or refusing to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter and heir to the kingdom—an act which it is reasonable to believe was performed under divine impulse and inspiration.]

How, then, should it be considered imperfect, when blessed David also boasts that he performed the Lord’s ordinances with a view to recompense, and when the lawgiver, looking toward future rewards, is said to have rejected adoption into royal dignity and preferred the most severe affliction to the treasures of Egypt?

## CHAPTER XII  
### Response concerning the diversity of perfections
Chaeremon: [Note: [Col. 0862C] The text is somewhat obscure; Dionysius’ paraphrase is a little clearer and reads as follows: “Sacred Scripture arouses and [Col. 0862D] encourages the freedom of our free will toward the various degrees of perfection, according to the measure, disposition, and condition of each mind,” etc.] According to the condition and measure of each person’s mind, divine Scripture calls forth the freedom of our will toward various degrees of perfection. For no single, uniform crown of perfection could be proposed to everyone, since neither is everyone endowed with the same virtue, will, or fervor. Accordingly, divine discourse has established, in a certain sense, different orders and different measures of perfection. [Note: [Col. 0862D] He touches upon the difference among the evangelical beatitudes—that is, those mentioned and proclaimed in the Gospel—and among the rewards promised to them when compared with one another. This difference of rewards, however, lies not so much in reality as in the words. Whether these matters are referred to the present life or to the future, they all concur and mutually embrace or follow one another. Yet, if one considers the force or emphasis of the words, the kingdom of heaven (which is promised to two beatitudes, the first and the eighth) denotes a greater reward than possession of the earth, whether earthly or heavenly; and so with the rest, as is explained here. Nor need one inquire why the Author here enumerates only six beatitudes and their [Col. 0863C] rewards, whereas Matthew mentions eight: it was enough for him to show by these examples that the degrees of perfection are diverse and unequal (which is the purpose and subject of this chapter), just as the degrees of the evangelical beatitudes and their promised rewards are diverse, as they are expressed in the Gospel. But it is fitting here to hear St. Thomas, who explains these matters more fully and accurately from the opinion of the ancient Fathers, as follows (I–II, q. 69, arts. 2 and 4):

“Concerning these rewards,” he says, “the expositors of Sacred Scripture have spoken in different ways. Some say that all these rewards belong to future blessedness, as Ambrose does in his commentary on Luke (in the chapter on the Beatitudes, vol. V). Augustine, however (Book I, On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount, ch. 9), says that they belong to the present life. Chrysostom, in his homilies (Homily 6 on Matthew), says that some of them belong to the future life and some to the present.

“For an understanding of this, one must consider that the hope of future blessedness may be in us for two reasons. First, because of some preparation or disposition for future blessedness, which is by way of merit; secondly, through a certain imperfect beginning of future blessedness in holy persons even in this life. For one has hope of a tree’s fruiting in one way when it is green with leaves, and in another when the first beginnings of fruit have already begun to appear. Thus, the things mentioned in the beatitudes as merits are certain preparations or dispositions for blessedness, whether perfect or begun; but the things set forth as rewards may be either perfect blessedness itself, and thus belong to the future life, or some beginning of blessedness, as it exists in perfect persons, and thus the rewards belong to the present life. For when someone begins to advance in the acts of virtues and gifts, one may hope that he will attain both the perfection of the way and the perfection of the homeland.” Thus St. Thomas.

In the other article he adds what also bears on [Col. 0864C] this passage: “The rewards stand in an additive relation to one another. For to possess the land of the kingdom of heaven is more than simply to have it: we have many things which we do not possess firmly and peacefully. To be consoled in the kingdom is also more than to have and possess it, for we possess many things with sorrow. To be filled is more than simply to be consoled, for fullness implies an abundance of consolation. Mercy, moreover, surpasses fullness, so that a person receives more than he has deserved or could have desired. Still greater is to see God, just as he is greater who at a king’s court not only dines but also sees the king’s face; and the king’s son has the highest dignity in the royal house.” Thus far the Angelic—indeed divine—Doctor, who considered and expounded that variety of beatitude and rewards, and their relation to one another, differently and more subtly than it is explained in this passage.]

This is clearly shown by the variety of the evangelical beatitudes as well. [Col. 0863A] Although those whose is the kingdom of heaven are called blessed, as are those who will possess the earth, those who will receive consolation, and those who will enjoy fullness (Matt. V), we nevertheless believe that there is a great difference between dwelling in the kingdom of heaven and possessing whatever land is meant by “the earth,” and between receiving consolation and the fullness and satisfaction of righteousness. There is also a great difference between those who will obtain mercy and those who will be deemed worthy to enjoy the most glorious vision of God. “One glory belongs to the sun, another to the moon, and another to the stars; for star differs from star in glory, and so also is the resurrection of the dead” (I Cor. XV).

Since, then, in this manner divine Scripture praises those who fear God and says, “Blessed are all who fear the Lord” (Ps. CXXVII), and thereby promises them complete blessedness, it nevertheless says again: “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment; and whoever fears is not perfect in love” (I John IV). Again, although serving God is glorious, and it is said, “Serve the Lord in fear” (Ps. II), and, “[Note: [Col. 0864C] St. Jerome also recognizes this reading; the Vulgate reading, however, is: ‘It is a small thing that you should be my servant’ (Isa. XLIX), etc.] It is a great thing for you to be called my servant” (Isa. XLIX), and, “Blessed is that servant whom, when his lord comes, he will find so acting” (Luke XII), nevertheless the apostles are told: “I will no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his lord is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John XV). And again: “You are my friends if you do what I command you” [Col. 0864A] (ibid.).

You therefore see that the degrees of perfection are different, and that the Lord calls us from high things to higher things, so that the one who has been blessed and made perfect in the fear of God, walking—as it is written—from strength to strength (Ps. LXXXIII), and ascending from one perfection to another, that is, from fear to hope, with an eager mind, may be invited to a still more blessed condition, which is love. And whoever is a faithful and prudent servant may pass into the fellowship of friendship and the adoption of sons. [Note: [Col. 0864D] The solution to the difficulty proposed: how could he have called the affections of fear and hope imperfect? They are imperfect in comparison with love, although in their own kind and degree they possess their own perfection. Yet one must not stop at them; rather, one must progress step by step from fear to hope and from hope to love. He said the same in chapter 7.]

According to this meaning, our own statement must also be understood—not that we declare contemplation of that everlasting punishment or of the most blessed recompense promised to the saints to be of no importance, but that, although these things are useful and introduce their followers to the beginnings of blessedness, love, in which there is fuller confidence and already perpetual joy, takes them from servile fear and mercenary hope, transfers them to the love of God and the adoption of sons, and in a certain sense makes those who are already perfect more perfect. “There are many dwelling places,” says the Savior, “in my Father’s house” (John XIV).

Although all the stars appear to be in the heavens, there is nevertheless a great difference between the brightness of the sun, the moon, the morning star, and the other stars. Therefore the blessed Apostle, preferring love not only to fear and hope but also to all the spiritual gifts that are regarded as great and wondrous, [Note: [Col. 0864D] St. Thomas explains in a few words why the Apostle called love a way (2–2, q. 24, art. 4): “We are called wayfarers because we are journeying toward God, who is the final end of our blessedness. On this way we make greater progress the closer we come to God; and we do not approach him by bodily steps but by the affections of the mind. Love brings about this nearness, because through it the mind is united to God. Therefore the Apostle calls love a way when he says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians XII: ‘I show you a still more excellent way.’”] declared love to be superior beyond measure to them all. For when he wished, after completing the whole catalogue of spiritual gifts, to describe the members of its virtues, he prefaced it in this way: “And I show you a still more excellent way.” “If I speak in the tongues of men and angels, and if I have prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so that I move mountains, and if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (I Cor. XII and XIII).

You see, therefore, that nothing more precious, nothing more perfect, nothing more exalted, and—as I may put it—nothing more enduring than love can be found. For whether prophecies will be abolished, tongues will cease, or knowledge will be destroyed, love will never fail (ibid.), and without it not only those most eminent kinds of spiritual gifts but even the glory of martyrdom itself is emptied of value.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the fear that arises from the greatness of love

Whoever, therefore, has been firmly established in the perfection of this love must necessarily ascend, by a still more excellent degree, to that higher fear of love [Note: [Col. 0865C] Filial fear, which is joined and kindred to perfect love: it fears not the punishment of sin but the offense of the loving Father, that is, God. It is also called chaste, holy, and reverential fear, and it endures forever, according to the words of the royal Psalmist: “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring forever and ever” (Ps. XVIII). In Greek, the reading is ἁγνὸς, that is, pure or chaste, not ἅγιος. Hence Augustine frequently calls it chaste fear (Treatise 9 on the Epistle of John), and distinguishes it from servile fear by a familiar example appropriate to this passage, concerning two women:

“Nothing,” he says, “can explain better the difference between the two fears than to imagine two married women, one of whom wishes to commit adultery but fears that her husband will condemn her. She fears her husband; but because she loves wickedness, she fears her husband for that reason. His presence is not welcome but burdensome to her; and if she is living wickedly, she fears that her husband may come. Such are those who fear the day of judgment.

“Imagine the other loving her husband and owing him chaste embraces, unwilling to defile herself with any adulterous impurity. She desires her husband’s presence. How, then, are these two fears distinguished? The one fears, and the other fears. Let them now be asked why they fear. The first will say, ‘I fear my husband, lest he come’; the second will say, ‘I fear my husband, lest he depart.’ The first will say, ‘I fear my husband, lest he condemn me’; the second will say, ‘I fear my husband, lest he abandon me.’

“Apply these things to the mind, and you will find the fear that love casts out, and the other chaste fear that endures forever and ever. Perfect love casts out that fear because that fear contains torment: the conscience of sins is tortured, and justification has not yet been accomplished. That fear pricks, but love enters and heals what fear wounds. Chaste fear, however, produces security in the mind.”

Such is Augustine’s account. See other examples in the same author, Sermon 18 on the Words of the Apostle.]

—which is generated not by dread of punishments or desire for rewards, but by the greatness of love. It is the fear by which a son reverently regards a most indulgent father, a brother his brother, a friend his friend, or a spouse the other spouse, with anxious affection: he fears not blows or insults, but even the slightest offense against love, and in all things, not only deeds but words, he is always filled with awed devotion, lest the warmth of that person’s love toward him grow even slightly cold.

The prophet Isaiah beautifully expressed the majesty of this fear when he said, [Note: [Col. 0866D] “The riches of salvation” means, in the Hebrew manner, true and salutary riches: wisdom and knowledge. But the fear of the Lord, chaste and filial, is a great treasure, because the riches of the virtues are stored and preserved in it as in a treasury.] “The riches of salvation are wisdom and knowledge; the fear of the Lord itself is his treasure” (Isa. XXXIII). He could not have expressed the dignity and merit of this fear more clearly than by saying that the riches of our salvation, which consist in true wisdom and knowledge of God, can be preserved only by the fear of the Lord.

The prophetic words therefore invite not sinners but the holy to this fear, as the Psalmist says: “Fear the Lord, all you his saints, for those who fear him lack nothing” (Ps. XXXIII). Whoever fears the Lord with this fear certainly lacks nothing for perfection. For the Apostle John plainly speaks of penal fear: “Whoever fears is not perfect in love, because fear has punishment” (John IV).

There is therefore a great difference between this fear, which lacks nothing and is the treasure of wisdom and knowledge, and that imperfect fear which is called the beginning of wisdom and which, containing punishment within itself, is driven from the hearts of the perfect by the fullness of love: “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear” (ibid.).

Indeed, if the beginning of wisdom consists in fear (Ps. CX), what will its perfection be except the love of Christ, which contains within itself that fear of perfect love and is no longer called the beginning but the treasure of wisdom and knowledge?

Accordingly, there are two degrees of fear. One belongs to beginners, that is, to those who are still under the yoke and terror of servitude; of it it is said: “The servant will fear his master” (Mal. I). And in the Gospel: “I do not call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing” (John XV). Therefore, he says, “the servant does not remain in the house forever” (John VIII). He trains us to pass from that penal fear to the fullest freedom of love and to confidence as God’s friends and sons.

Finally, the blessed Apostle, who had long before passed beyond that servile degree of fear through the power of the Lord’s love, looking down upon inferior things, professes that he has been enriched by greater gifts from the Lord: “For God,” he says, “has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power and love and sobriety” (II Tim. I).

He also exhorts those who burned with perfect love for that heavenly Father, and whom divine adoption had already made sons instead of servants, in these words: “For you have not received the spirit of servitude again in fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. VIII).

When the prophet described this sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, he also spoke of this fear, which [Note: [Col. 0866D] In addition to Ciaconius’ sufficiently accurate note on “the man of the Lord,” which the reader will find in its proper place, I shall add a few observations collected elsewhere concerning the same terminology.

First, the ancients are sometimes said to have called Christ “the man of the Lord” (The Master of the Sentences, book III, distinction 8, § M; St. Thomas, Part III, q. 16, art. 7; Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 31). Epiphanius frequently uses this expression in the Ancoratus, as does Augustine in Book LXXXIII of Questions, chapter 36, where he uses the same words as this abbot: “It must be urged that those good things should be awaited which were present in that man of the Lord.” Again: “Here the most excellent and unique example of the man of the Lord must be proposed: although he showed by so many miracles that he possessed such power over things, he rejected what the ignorant consider great goods and endured what they consider great evils.” He uses the expression in other places as well, especially in his exposition of the Psalms (Pss. I, IV, and VII). Bede also uses it in his exposition of I Kings I.

Yet this formula of speech later displeased Augustine, not without reason, and he retracted and corrected it in these words: “I do not see whether it is rightly said that Christ Jesus, who is the mediator between God and human beings, is ‘the man of the Lord.’ I read this expression among certain Catholic commentators, and wherever I used it, I would wish that I had not. Later I saw that it ought not to be said, although it could be defended in some way.” Thus Augustine indicates the reason for his retraction in three words: since Christ is truly and properly Lord, he should not be called “of the Lord” in a denominative sense. For “of the Lord” and “the Lord’s” refers to what belongs to the Lord, says St. Thomas, as in “the Lord’s will,” “the Lord’s hand,” or “the Lord’s passion.” Therefore Christ himself, who is Lord, should not be called “the man of the Lord”; but his flesh may be called “the Lord’s flesh,” just as his passion is called “the Lord’s passion.”

Hence it belongs to the Nestorian heresy to call Christ “the man of the Lord,” if the expression is understood strictly, since by this the claim that he is naturally Lord is denied. Nevertheless, St. Thomas teaches that the expression can be defended or excused in two ways, and Ciaconius reports the first. The other is this: “We may say that ‘of the Lord’ is predicated essentially in place of ‘Lord,’ as denominatives are sometimes taken substantially—for example, when we say ‘the divine essence’ or ‘the divine persons,’ which are nothing other than God himself. In this way ‘the man of the Lord’ means ‘the man who is God and Lord.’”]

there is no doubt descended upon that man of the Lord [Col. 0867A] according to the dispensation of the Incarnation—said: “The Spirit of the Lord will rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety.” Finally, as though introducing something especially distinguished, he added: “And the spirit of the fear of the Lord will fill him” (Isa. XI).

In this statement we must first observe carefully [Note: [Col. 0867D] St. Jerome observed something similar in his commentary on this same passage, although he turns it in another direction and toward another purpose. He writes:

“It must also be noted that the Spirit of the Lord—of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and strength, of knowledge and piety, and of the fear of the Lord—that is, the number seven, which are called the seven eyes in one stone in Zechariah (Zech. III)—rests upon the shoot and flower that arose from Jesse and therefore from the stock of David. But specifically the spirit of the fear of the Lord filled him for the sake of those who need the fear of the Lord, because they are little ones; perfect love casts it out.”

Thus St. Jerome refers this prophecy not so much to Christ as to Christ’s members, that is, to the Church, in which there are many more little ones—that is, imperfect people led by servile or initial fear—than there are perfect people. To signify this, the prophet used the word “will fill” for the gift of fear instead of “will rest,” which he had used for the other gifts. See St. Gregory, Homily 29 on Ezekiel.]

that he did not say, “The spirit of the fear of the Lord will rest upon him,” as he had said of the preceding gifts, but, “The spirit of the fear of the Lord will fill him.” For its abundance is so great that, once it has possessed someone by its power, it occupies not merely a part but the whole of the person’s mind. And rightly so. For fear is joined to love, which never fails; it not only fills the person but possesses the one it has seized with perpetual and inseparable continuance, undiminished by any delights of temporal joy or pleasure. This sometimes happens even to the fear that is cast out.

This, then, is the fear of perfection, with which that man of the Lord is said to have been filled. He had come not only to redeem the human race but also to provide the form and examples of perfection and virtue. The true Son of God, who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found (I Pet. II), could not possess that servile fear of punishments.

## CHAPTER XIV. Question concerning the consummation of chastity

[Col. 0868A]

Germanus: Since the discourse has dealt with the perfection of love, we also wish to inquire more freely into the end of chastity. We do not doubt that the lofty summit of love, by which—as has been explained thus far—we ascend to the image and likeness of God, cannot exist at all without the perfection of chastity. But we wish to be instructed whether its perpetuity can be attained in such a way that the slightest stirring of lust never assails the integrity of our heart, and that, while living as exiles in this body, we may be able never to be scorched by the heat of its impulses.

## CHAPTER XV. Postponement of the requested exposition

[Col. 0868B]

Chaeremon: It is indeed the height of blessedness and a singular merit continually either to learn or to teach this affection by which we cling to the Lord, so that meditation upon it, according to the Psalmist’s saying, may consume all the days and nights of our life (Ps. I), and may sustain our mind, insatiably hungry and thirsty for righteousness, by the continual rumination of this heavenly food.

But [Note: [Col. 0868C] Holy men generally called their body a beast of burden, a little donkey, or something similar, because the flesh, lacking reason in itself and resisting the spirit, thinks like cattle or beasts of burden only about food and drink, and longs solely for present pleasures belonging to it, looking toward nothing future.

Thus St. Hilarion, according to Jerome, became angry with himself and beat his chest with his fists, as though his hands could drive out his thoughts by slaughtering them: “I shall make you stop kicking, my little donkey. I shall not feed you with barley but with straw; I shall wear you out with hunger and thirst, so that you will think about food rather than wantonness.” Such was his saying.

Moreover, Jerome says that an animal of burden is so called from the fact that it helps (Book II against Jovinian). Thus the name “beast of burden” is not inappropriately applied also to our body, as the burden-bearing and assisting animal of the soul, since it ought to serve the rational soul—especially in carrying out acts of virtue—and obey it without resistance, bearing the burden imposed upon it in the manner of a beast of burden. Hence it is not without reason that it should be cared for and provided for as beasts of burden ordinarily are, though not indulged; this is what the Collator advises here.]

we must also care for the beast of burden of our body, in accordance with the most gracious providence of our Savior, so that it does not fail on the way. “The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. XXVI). Even now it must be cared for by the taking of a little food, so that, after it has been restored, the mind’s attention too may be applied more diligently to investigating the matters you desire.

## THE TWELFTH CONFERENCE, which is the second of Abbot Chaeremon. ON CHASTITY

[Col. 0869]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0869A]

When the meal had ended, and the food of instruction—which we desired—seemed to us more burdensome than pleasant, the old man perceived that we were immediately expecting the discourse he had promised and owed us. “I am pleased,” he said, “not only by the attentive eagerness of your minds to learn, but also by the orderly discipline of the question you have proposed. For you have indeed maintained a rational sequence in your inquiry.

It is necessary that the immense rewards of perfect and perpetual chastity should follow upon so lofty a fullness of love, and that there should be a corresponding joy in so equal a share of victory. For these two are bound together in such close fellowship that one cannot be possessed without the other.

Your proposal, therefore, has embraced the question whether [Note: [Col. 0869C] That is, the movement of lust. Paul’s statement teaches that desire is a kind of inward fire: “It is better to marry than to burn” (I Cor. VII). Likewise his other statement: “Take the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one” (Eph. VI). Hence the Fathers commonly call lust fire, flame, fuel, incentive, heat, or burning.

St. Ambrose, Book I on Repentance: “Lust is a fierce fire, and therefore we must not supply it with fuel for luxury. Lust is fed by banquets, nourished by sins, kindled by wine, and set aflame by drunkenness.”

St. Jerome, Letter 10 to Furia: “The burning arrows of the devil must be extinguished by the austerity of fasts and vigils.”] we might explain, by a similar discussion, whether that fire of desire, whose inward heat this flesh experiences as something implanted within it, can be entirely extinguished.

First, let us examine more carefully what the blessed Apostle understood by it: “Put to death,” he says, “your members that are upon the earth” (Col. III). Before we investigate anything else, let us determine what these members are that he commanded to be put to death. [Note: [Col. 0869C] Nor does the Lord Christ, when he likewise says, “If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you,” compel us to mutilate ourselves. These statements are understood metaphorically or hyperbolically, as commentators note (see John Maldonatus on Matthew V).

They are metaphorical if by the right eye and right hand we understand things especially dear and precious to us, which we ought rather to cast away from ourselves than to sin on their account. They are hyperbolical if we suppose the condition or exception “if it could or might be done,” as is customary in exaggerations. Christ signifies that we must suffer any loss rather than incur guilt, even to the point of cutting off our right eye or right hand if we could not otherwise avoid sin. But because we can always avoid sin, it is wrong for us to cut off any part of our body.]

For the blessed Apostle does not drive us by a cruel command to cut off hands, feet, or genital organs, but [Note: [Col. 0869D] The Apostle frequently calls the “body of sin” the old person, of whom he says: “Strip off the old person with his deeds.” This is the same as: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth.” For just as a human being, or a human body, consists of various members, so the old person, or body of sin, is joined together from various kinds of sins, like different members and actions.

The same Apostle immediately lists these members; they are explained individually and with a kind of spiritual anatomy in the following chapter. They are said to be “upon the earth,” that is, earthly or terrestrial, because such vices drag a person down toward the earth and turn him as far as possible away from God. Their mortification is discussed in chapter three.] he desires that the body of sin—which certainly consists of members—be destroyed as quickly as possible by the zeal of perfect holiness. Concerning this body he says elsewhere: “That the body of sin may be destroyed” (Rom. VI). He then explains what its destruction is: “so that we may no longer serve sin” (Rom. VII). With a lamentation he also asks to be freed from it, saying: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?”

## CHAPTER II. On the body of sin and its members
This body of sin is therefore shown to be constructed from many members of vices [Col. 0870C]; and whatever is sinned by deed, word, or thought [Col. 0871A] belongs to its component parts. These members are rightly said to be “upon the earth.” For those who employ their service cannot truthfully profess, “Our citizenship is in heaven.”

[Note: [Col. 0870C] The common division of sin into sin of the heart, of the mouth, and of deed is reported by St. Jerome in chapter 43 of Ezekiel, at the words: “For seven days you shall offer a goat for sin each day, and a calf, and a ram.” He says: “In the goat, the calf, and the ram, three general offenses are indicated, to which the whole human race is subject. For we sin either in thought, or in speech, or in deed. Thought is referred to the ram, since it is the first of all sins and from it the other two sins arise. The kid or goat refers to speech, which is always concerned with higher matters. Deeds, however, are properly assigned to the calf, since it is devoted to the plow, to labor, and to earthly works.” Thus Jerome. St. Augustine likewise says, to the same effect, against Faustus the Manichaean (Book II, chapter 27): “Sin is something done, said, or desired against the eternal law; and the eternal law is divine reason, or the will of God,” etc. This division of sin, however, is not the division of a genus into different species, but of the same species into different degrees, as St. Thomas teaches (I–II, question 62, article 7). “These three,” he says, “belong to one perfect and complete species of sin, since they proceed from the same motive. For an angry man, because he desires revenge, is first disturbed in his heart, second bursts into insulting words, and third proceeds to injurious actions; the same is evident in lust and in every other sin.]

In describing the members of this body in the present passage, the Apostle says: “Put to death, therefore, the members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is the service of idols” (Colossians III).

[Note: [Col. 0871C] St. Augustine, Book XI of *The City of God*, explaining why the Apostle calls greed the service of idols or images, says: “The perverse and greedy wish to enjoy money and to use God; for they do not spend money for God’s sake, but worship God for money’s sake. Although they acknowledge and revere God as the father of all things, nevertheless, because of the immoderate affection by which they cling to filthy money, they seem in reality and in deed to deny that he is the final end and highest good.” See elsewhere for more on this subject.]

[Note: [Col. 0871C] That is, he placed fornication first as a member of the body of sin. Here fornication signifies illicit intercourse, or the union of male and female, as the Author indicates.]

He therefore considered fornication, which is accomplished by carnal intercourse, to be introduced in the first place.

[Note: [Col. 0871C] The Author interprets “uncleanness” as every pollution, whether the emission of semen, even involuntary—as occurs during sleep—or otherwise, as is clear from his own words and from the testimonies he cites. Properly, however, the term refers to voluntary pollution, which the Apostle also calls “effeminacy.”]

He called uncleanness the second member. It sometimes steals upon a person, whether asleep or awake, without any contact with a woman, through the negligence of an unwatchful mind; and for that reason it is noted and forbidden in the Law. The Law not only deprived the unclean of participation in the sacred meats, but also commanded that they be separated from the assembly of the camp, lest by their contact they pollute holy things, saying:

[Note: [Col. 0871D] He cites this passage again, in the same words, in *Conference* 22, chapter 5. Ciaconius thinks one should read, “in which there is uncleanness,” so that the phrase refers rather to the person, whom he wished to be understood under the name “soul,” than to the soul itself. For the Greek is καὶ ἀκαθαρσία αὐτοῦ ἐπ᾽ αὐτῷ (*kai akatharsia autou ep’ autō*; Deuteronomy VII according to the Septuagint), that is, “and his uncleanness is upon him.” It is read in this way in Cyprian (*Sermon on the Lapsed*) and elsewhere. The Vulgate version, however, is slightly different, as we have indicated elsewhere.]

“Any soul that eats meat from the sacrifice of well-being—which belongs to the Lord—while uncleanness is upon it shall perish before the Lord; and whatever the unclean person touches shall be unclean” (Leviticus VII).

In Deuteronomy likewise: “If there is among you anyone who is unclean because of a nocturnal emission, he shall go outside the camp and shall not return until he has washed himself with water at evening; and after sunset he shall return to the camp” (Deuteronomy XXIII).

He then places lust as the third member of sin. It grows in the hidden recesses of the soul and can kindle something even without any bodily passion. It is undoubtedly called *libido* from that which gives pleasure.

[Note: [Col. 0871D] He appears to understand “lust” as an ugly and obscene thought, or as a pleasure hidden in the mind and not brought outward. Erasmus translated it as “effeminacy,” while others translated it as “disease,” meaning that foul obscenity which in Greek is called πάθος (*pathos*), from which those who suffered such disgraceful things were called *pathici*. St. Augustine, in Book XIV, chapter 16, of *The City of God*, takes it to mean every sexual act or pleasure: “Although there are lusts for many things, nevertheless, when lust is mentioned without specifying whose lust it is, the mind usually understands none other than that by which the obscene parts of the body are aroused. It claims for itself not only the whole body, and not merely the external body, but also what is within; it moves the whole person, joining and mingling the mind’s affection with the body’s appetite, so that there follows that pleasure than which there is no greater among bodily pleasures, and at the very moment when its climax is reached, almost the whole sharpness and, so to speak, vigilance of thought is overwhelmed.”]

After this, descending from the greater sins to the lesser, he introduces evil desire as the fourth member. This may refer not only to the passion of impurity mentioned above, but also generally to every harmful desire, which is merely the sickness of corrupted pleasure (*voluptatis*; Lipsius in the margin: *voluntatis*, “will”).

[Note: [Col. 0872C] Specifically, the desire prohibited by the express commandment of the Decalogue: desire for a sexual object, or desire for another man’s wife.]

The Lord says of it in the Gospel: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew V). It is indeed much more difficult to restrain the desire of a slippery mind when the occasion of enticing sights is presented to it. From this it is most clearly proved that, for perfection of purity, bodily chastity alone cannot suffice unless integrity of mind is also added to it.

After all these things, he identifies greed as the final member of that body and says:

[Note: [Col. 0872C] He interprets greed, as nearly all others do, according to the common meaning of the word, as desire for money or riches.

[Col. 0872D] St. Jerome, however, writing on chapter 5 of the Epistle to the Ephesians, where it says, “Fornication and every uncleanness, or greed, must not even be named among you,” argues that greed, called πλεονεξία (*pleonexia*) in Greek, should not be understood as the pursuit of money, as it commonly is, but as a certain insatiable desire for disgraceful pleasures: “What connection is there,” he says, “that among fornication, uncleanness, disgracefulness, foolish talk, and buffoonery he should have placed greed in the middle and, unusually, among them?”—that is, that he should have numbered it among the sins of lust. This argument appears to show that the word should be understood in the same way in the passage addressed to the Colossians that is being explained here.]

“Greed,” clearly indicating not only that the mind must be restrained from desiring what belongs to others, but also that one must magnanimously despise what one possesses.

This is what the multitude of believers is said to have done in the Acts of the Apostles: “The company of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one claimed that any of the things he possessed was his own, but everything was held in common. As many as were owners of lands or houses sold them, brought the proceeds of what they had sold, and laid them at the apostles’ feet. It was distributed to each according to need” (Acts IV).

And lest this perfection appear to belong only to a few, he testified that greed is the service of idols. Nor is this without reason. Whoever does not share with the needs of the poor and, with faithless tenacity, preserves his money while setting Christ’s commandments second, incurs the crime of idolatry: he prefers love of worldly matter to divine charity.

# Chapter III  
## On the Mortification of Fornication and Uncleanness

If, therefore, we have seen many people cast away their possessions for Christ in such a way that we can judge not only their ownership of money but also its desire to have been permanently cut out of their hearts, it follows that we should believe that the heat of fornication can likewise be extinguished.

[Note: [Col. 0873C] As we have noted elsewhere, he frequently uses *substantiae* to mean possessions or resources.]

[Note: [Col. 0873C] He explains what it means to put to death “our members that are upon the earth.” It is not enough merely to abstain from the vices listed above or no longer to commit them. Rather, their movements and desires, when they rise up, must be struck down immediately at the very threshold, like the little ones of Babylon, and dashed against the rock—that is, against Christ—and all their occasions must be avoided. We have discussed this matter frequently elsewhere. We do not put the members of sin to death perfectly and as fully as the Apostle requires if we do not also extinguish, as far as lies within us, the desires of the sins themselves, especially carnal sins, even when those desires are involuntary.]

For the Apostle would not have joined an impossible thing to a possible one; rather, knowing that both were possible, he decreed that both should be mortified in the same way (Colossians III).

And blessed Paul trusts that fornication, or uncleanness, can be rooted out from our members to such an extent that he declares not only that they must be put to death, but that they must not even be named among us: “Fornication,” he says, “and every uncleanness or greed must not even be named among you, nor filthiness, nor foolish talk, nor buffoonery, which is not fitting” (Ephesians V).

He also teaches that these things are equally harmful and drive us from the kingdom of God by an equal exclusion, saying: “Know this: no fornicator, or unclean person, or greedy person—which is the service of idols—has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (ibid.).

And again: “Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor idol-servants, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers shall possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians VI).

There should therefore be no doubt that the contagion of fornication and uncleanness can be removed from our members, since he has commanded that these be cut off in no other way than greed, foolish talk, buffooneries, drunkenness, and theft, whose removal is easy.

[Note: [Col. 0873D] That is, they must be put to death and restrained.]

# Chapter IV  
## That Human Effort Is Not Sufficient to Obtain the Purity of Chastity

[Col. 0874A]

We must nevertheless be certain that, although we undertake every rigorous practice of continence—namely, hunger and thirst, vigils, constant labor, and unceasing devotion to reading—we still cannot attain the enduring purity of chastity by the merit of these labors, unless, while continually toiling in them, we are taught by the instruction of experience that its incorruptibility is granted through the generosity of divine grace.

[Note: [Col. 0873D] Cassian repeatedly inculcates this in various places, especially in Book VI, chapter 6, of the *Institutes*: “Truly, since in all progress in virtue and in the struggle against every vice the grace and victory belong to the Lord, this is especially a peculiar benefit and special gift of God. The teaching of the Fathers and the experience of purification itself most clearly declare this to those who have deserved to possess it. In a certain sense, it is to leave the flesh while remaining in the body; and it is beyond nature, while enclosed in fragile flesh, not to feel the thorns of the flesh. Therefore it is impossible for a person to fly up by his own wings, so to speak, to so lofty and heavenly a reward, unless the Lord’s grace has drawn him from the mire of earth by the gift of chastity. See more on this in Book VI, chapters 5 and following.]
