For this reason alone, let each person recognize that he must persevere tirelessly in these exercises: so that, having obtained the Lord’s mercy through their affliction, he may deserve, by a divine gift, to be freed from the struggle of the flesh and from the domination of powerful vices—not so that he may confidently expect through them to acquire the inviolable bodily chastity he desires.

Let him be inflamed with as great a desire and love for acquiring chastity as the most greedy lover of money longs to satisfy his desire with the most impatient ardor, or as one consumed by the highest ambition for honors, or as one carried away by an intolerable love of a beautiful woman. Thus it will happen that, while we burn with insatiable desire for the permanence of purity, desirable food will be despised, necessary drink will be dreaded, and sleep itself, owed to nature, will be rejected.

Or at least the most treacherous deceiver of purity, its rival and adversary, will be caught with a startled and wary mind. Then each person, becoming every morning an examiner of his own integrity, will rejoice in the purity granted to him and will recognize that he has attained it not by his own effort or vigilance but through the Lord’s protection. He will understand that its continuance will remain joined to his body only as long as the Lord grants it by his mercy.

For whoever firmly maintains this faith will not, in his pride, rely upon his own virtue.

[Note: [Col. 0874C] That is, he will not applaud himself excessively or exult in himself because he has remained unpolluted for a long time. John Climacus confirms this judgment in Step 1, where, discussing pollution and its causes, he says: “Among those who are still beginners, bodily emission most often results from luxurious living; among those of intermediate attainment, it also results from elation of spirit; but among those who are closer to perfection, it generally results from condemning and proudly despising one’s neighbor.” And again below: “Some think and assert that these battles against us and the emission of obscene fluid are aroused solely because of food, but I have known people worn out by extreme illness and fasting most severely to be defiled by such a discharge. Once I asked a very suitable monk, adorned with discretion, what should be thought about these things, and that blessed man answered me with great clarity: ‘There is indeed one kind of emission of semen in sleep that comes from an abundance of food and from rest, and another that comes from pride—namely, when we have remained clean from this foul pollution for a longer time and are thereby lifted up into pride. It also often occurs when we judge and condemn our neighbor.’ Of these kinds, he says, two can occur even in the weak, and perhaps all of them. But if someone sees himself to be clean from all the causes mentioned above, he is blessed by such tranquility. If, however, he suffers this through the envy of demons, with God permitting it to happen for a time, it occurs so that through this affliction, which is without sin, he may safely possess the deepest humility.” Thus he.]

Nor, deceived by the pleasant security of long intervals free from obscene fluid, will he be relaxed, knowing that he will immediately be stained by the spray of the foulest pollution if divine protection withdraws from him even slightly. Therefore, for its permanence, he must keep watch with unceasing prayers, with complete contrition and humility of heart.

# Chapter V  
## On the Benefit Generated for Us by the Struggle Arising from the Heat of the Incitements

Do you wish to grasp clear evidence of the truth of what we are saying, by which you may both approve what has been stated and be taught that this bodily struggle—which is thought to be hostile and harmful to us—has been beneficially implanted in our members?

Consider, I ask, those who are eunuchs in body, and what cause makes them especially sluggish and lukewarm in the pursuit of virtues. Is it not because they believe that they are not exposed to the danger of corrupting chastity?

[Note: [Col. 0875C] Abbot Daniel gives the same example of spadones, or eunuchs, in *Conference* 4, chapter 17, in these words: “In those who are eunuchs in body, we generally find this tepidity of spirit because, as though freed from this carnal necessity, they think that they need neither the labor of bodily continence nor contrition of heart. Relaxed by this security, they never hasten either truly to seek or to possess perfection of heart or even purification from spiritual vices.” Thus he compares lukewarm and sluggish monks, languid and negligent in the pursuit of perfection, to eunuchs, who are inactive men. John Climacus writes to the same effect in the passage cited: “Some have called blessed those eunuchs who were born in such a condition, as though they had been freed from the most violent domination of the flesh. But I call those especially blessed who become eunuchs through daily struggle. For by reason, as by a sword, they habitually cut themselves off and mutilate themselves.”]

Let no one think that I have proposed this in such a way as to affirm that none of them can ever be found burning with complete renunciation. Rather, because they in a certain sense overcome their own nature, if any of them should strive with the utmost strictness of spirit toward the palm of the perfection set before him, the ardor and desire that have once kindled him will compel him to endure hunger, thirst, vigils, nakedness, and every bodily hardship—not merely patiently, but willingly.

[Note: [Col. 0875D] The Vulgate text is: “The soul of one who labors labors for himself, because his mouth has compelled him” (Proverbs XVI).]

“A man labors for himself in his sufferings and does violence to his destruction” (Proverbs XVI, according to the Septuagint).

And again:

[Note: [Col. 0876C] The Vulgate reading (Proverbs XVII) is: “A satisfied soul tramples the honeycomb, but to a hungry soul even bitter things seem sweet.” There is a striking hyperbole in the verb “trample,” meaning to abhor or disdain. This saying consists of two proverbial observations, well known from experience itself. Cajetan notes that it can be applied to everything that we strongly desire while deprived of it but quickly grow tired of once we have obtained it; Jansenius discusses this at length in the same passage.]

“To a hungry soul even bitter things seem sweet” (Proverbs XXVII).

For otherwise the desires for present things can neither be suppressed nor torn away unless other, wholesome desires are introduced in place of the harmful passions that we wish to cut off. The vitality of the mind cannot in any way continue without some affection of desire or fear, joy or sorrow, unless these same affections are changed toward what is good.

Therefore, if we wish to drive carnal desires from our hearts, let us immediately plant spiritual desires in their place, so that our mind, always bound to them, may have objects on which it can continually dwell and may reject the enticements of present and temporal joys.

When our mind, trained by daily exercises, has advanced to this condition, then, taught by experience, it will conceive the meaning of that verse which we all sing in the customary melody of psalmody, but whose power only a few who have experienced it perceive:

“I kept the Lord always before me, because he is at my right hand, so that I shall not be moved” (Psalm XV).

For only the person who has reached that purity of body and soul of which we are speaking effectively grasps the force and meaning of this song. He understands that at every moment he is preserved by the Lord from falling again into the same state, and that his right hands—that is, his holy works—are continually strengthened by him.

For the Lord always stands beside his saints, not on the left—for a holy man has nothing left, that is, nothing sinister, in him—but on the right. He is not seen by sinners and the impious, because they do not possess those right hands at which the Lord is accustomed to stand. They cannot say with the Prophet: “My eyes are always toward the Lord, for he will draw my feet out of the snare” (Psalm XXIV).

No one can truthfully profess this unless, judging everything in this world either harmful, or superfluous, or at least inferior to the highest virtues, he has fixed his entire gaze, all his zeal, and all his care upon the cultivation of his heart and the purity of chastity. Thus, with the mind refined by these exercises and polished by progress, he will attain perfect purity of body and soul.

[Note: [Col. 0876C] Similar statements are frequent in St. Jerome, as in his commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 41: “In a holy man, both sides are right, both are perfect.” In Ecclesiastes X: “The righteous man has no left; everything in him is right.” Again, on Matthew V: “When our right cheek has been struck, we are not commanded to offer the left, but the other one—that is, another right cheek. For the righteous man has no left.” In his commentary on Psalm XC: “The right hand of the holy man is mentioned; the left is not mentioned, but the side is named in place of the left. For it was not fitting that the righteous man should have a left. ‘Whoever strikes you,’ he says, ‘on your right cheek, offer him the other also.’ He did not say, ‘and the left.’ For the one offered is not the left, but the other right. Therefore I say simply that the righteous man has two right hands. Finally, Ehud, who is mentioned in the Book of Judges, is also said to have had two right hands because he was righteous, and he killed that very fat king” (Judges III).]

# Chapter VI  
## That Patience Extinguishes the Heat of Fornication

[Col. 0877A]

To the degree that a person advances in gentleness and patience of heart, he will advance in purity of body; and the farther he drives away the passion of anger, the more firmly he will retain chastity. No one will avoid the heat of the body unless he has first restrained the movements of the mind.

This is made perfectly clear by the beatitude praised by the mouth of our Savior: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matthew IX).

[Note: [Col. 0877C] St. Bernard likewise interprets “earth” as our flesh (Sermon 1 on the Feast of All Saints). We are said to possess it when, through the gift of continence, we keep it under our control and subject to the rule of reason: “By this earth,” he says, “I understand our body. If the soul wishes to possess it, if it desires to reign over its members, it must itself be meek and subject to its superior; for it will find its inferior such as it has shown itself to its superior. The creature is armed to avenge the injury done to its Creator. Therefore let the soul know that, when it finds its flesh rebellious against it, it too is less subject than it ought to be to the higher powers. Let it become gentle and humble itself under the powerful hand of God Most High; let it be subject to God and likewise to those prelates whom it must obey in his place, and it will immediately find its body obedient and subject.”]

We shall not possess our earth in any other way—that is, this earth of our rebellious body will not be subjected to our dominion—unless our mind has first been founded upon the gentleness of patience.

Nor can anyone suppress the battles of lust rising against his flesh unless he is first equipped with the weapons of meekness:

“The meek shall possess the earth, and they shall dwell upon it forever and ever.”

As I have said, the same Prophet teaches us in what follows in that psalm how we can obtain this earth: “Wait for the Lord and keep his way, and he will exalt you so that you may inherit the earth” (Psalm XXXVI).

It is therefore evident that no one can climb to the possession of this earth and hold it securely except those who, by the steadfast gentleness of patience, keeping the difficult ways and commandments of the Lord, have been lifted up by him from the mire of carnal passions.

The meek, therefore, shall possess the earth; and they will not merely possess it, but will also delight in the abundance of peace (ibid.). No one whose flesh is still stirred by the battles of desire will securely enjoy that peace.

For he must be harassed by the fiercest battles of demons, and, wounded by the fiery darts of lust, he will be cast down from possession of his earth until the Lord removes the battles to the boundaries of his land, breaks the bow, shatters the weapons, and burns the shields with fire (Psalm XLV)—namely, with that fire which the Lord came to cast upon the earth—and breaks the bows and weapons with which spiritual wickednesses, fighting against him day and night, pierced his heart with the fiery arrows of the passions.

Then, when the Lord has shattered his battles and freed him from every heat of incitement, he will reach that state of purity in which, having laid aside the shame with which he formerly dreaded himself—that is, his flesh—while it was under attack, he will begin to delight in it as in a most pure tabernacle.

“For evil shall not approach him, and the scourge shall not come near his tabernacle” (Psalm XC).

Thus, by the virtue of patience, he will attain that prophetic condition in which, by the merit of meekness, he will not only inherit his earth but also delight in the abundance of peace (Psalm XXXVI). Where the anxiety of combat still remains, there can be no abundance of peace. For it does not say, “They shall delight in peace,” but “in the abundance of peace.”

This clearly shows how exceedingly effective patience is as medicine for the heart, according to Solomon:

[Note: [Col. 0878D] In Greek: πραΰθυμος ἀνὴρ καρδίας ἰατρός (*praÿthymos anēr kardias iatros*), “A gentle man is a physician of the heart.” This saying is not expressed in the same way in the Vulgate edition; instead it has: “A sound heart is the life of the flesh” (Proverbs XIV). The Chaldean translator rendered it: “He who divides the anger of his heart is medicine to his flesh.”]

“A gentle man is a physician of the heart” (Proverbs XIV),

so that he may uproot not only anger, sadness, acedia, vainglory, and pride, but also the tinder of lust and of every vice alike.

[Note: [Col. 0878D] Thus in the Greek version of the Septuagint: ἐν μακροθυμίᾳ εὐοδία βασιλεῦσι (*en makrothymia euodia basileusi*), “In patience there is prosperity for kings.” The Vulgate translator rendered it: “By patience the ruler will be softened.” The Chaldean has: “In patience of spirit the ruler is refreshed.”]

“For kings,” says Solomon, “there is prosperity in long-suffering” (Proverbs XXV).

For the person who is always meek and tranquil is neither inflamed by the disturbance of anger, nor consumed by the anguish of acedia and sadness, nor stretched upon the rack of vainglory, nor lifted up by the swelling of pride.

“For there is great peace for those who love your name, and there is no stumbling-block for them” (Psalm CXVIII).

And therefore it is rightly declared:

“Better is the patient person than the strong, and the one who controls his anger than the conqueror of cities” (Proverbs XVI).

[Note: [Col. 0878D] The Vulgate text is: “Better is the patient man than the strong, and he who rules his spirit than one who conquers cities” (Proverbs XVI). The poet Ovid elegantly expressed this in the verse:

> Stronger is he who conquers himself than he who conquers the strongest walls.]

Until we deserve to possess this peace firmly and permanently, we must necessarily be tested by many struggles.

We must frequently repeat this verse with groaning and tears:

“I have become wretched and have been afflicted exceedingly; all day long I walked in sadness, because my loins are filled with illusions, and there is no health in my flesh because of your anger; there is no peace in my bones because of my folly” (Psalm XXXVII).

We shall lament these words appropriately and truthfully when, after a long period of bodily purity, hoping that we have altogether escaped carnal contagion, we again feel the goads of the flesh rise against us because of elation of heart, or when the impurity of our former pollution sprinkles us through the deception of dreams.

When someone begins to rejoice in a long-standing purity of heart and body, it is necessary that, while believing himself no longer able to fall away from that sincerity, he should in some way grow proud within himself and say:

“In my abundance I said, ‘I shall never be moved’” (Psalm XXIX).

But when, being beneficially left by the Lord [Lipsius in the margin: “left to himself,” or “suddenly left”], he feels the state of purity in which he trusted himself to be disturbed, and sees himself faltering in that spiritual progress, let him immediately return to the author of that integrity. Recognizing his weakness, let him confess and say:

“Lord, not in my own will but in yours, you gave strength to my beauty. You turned your face away from me, and I became troubled” (ibid.).

Let him also repeat the words of blessed Job:

“If I wash myself with snow-water, and my hands shine as though they were perfectly clean, yet you will plunge me into filth, and my garments will abhor me” (Job IX).

The person who stains himself with filth through his own fault, however, cannot say this to his Creator.

Until he reaches the perfect state of purity, he must therefore be repeatedly instructed through these fluctuations, until, strengthened by God’s grace in the purity he desires, he deserves effectively to say:

“I waited, waiting, for the Lord; and he inclined toward me and heard my prayer. He brought me out of the pit of misery and the mud of filth; he set my feet upon a rock and directed my steps” (Psalm XXXIX).

# Chapter VII  
## On the Differences and Degrees of Chastity
[Note: [Col. 0879C] This abbot distinguishes six degrees of chastity. Omitting, however, those that could be distinguished more subtly and particularly as intermediate between them, John Climacus establishes only three degrees or distinctions, which he calls beginning, middle, and end: “The beginning,” he says (*Step* 15), “of chastity is not to yield to filthy thoughts, and at intervals to be sprinkled simply and without any illusion of an image by that obscene fluid; the middle is to be disturbed by natural movements arising from the overfullness produced by food, without images, yet in such a way that they do not proceed as far as emission; but the end is to mortify the body, when filthy thoughts have already been put to death,” etc.

There is also the well-known and customary division of chastity handed down by St. Ambrose into virginal, widowed, and marital chastity: “We are taught,” he says (*On Widows*), “that chastity is a threefold virtue: one marital, another belonging to widowhood, and a third belonging to virginity. For we do not commend one in such a way as to exclude the others: each of these is appropriate to its own profession. In this consists the Church’s rich discipline: she has those whom she prefers, but not those whom she rejects—and may she never have any whom she must reject. Thus we commend virginity without rejecting widows; thus we honor widows while reserving their proper honor for marriage.”]

For there are many degrees of chastity by which one ascends to that inviolable purity. Although our virtue may be insufficient either to perceive or to express them as they deserve, nevertheless, since the order of our exposition requires it, we shall attempt to set them forth as best we can, according to the measure of our experience, reserving the more perfect matters for the perfect. Nor do we thereby prejudice those who, possessing a purer chastity through more ardent devotion, surpass others in insight as much as they exceed them in diligence.

Accordingly, although the six degrees are separated from one another by great differences of elevation, I shall distinguish the lofty summits of chastity in such a way as to pass over certain intermediate stages—which nevertheless are numerous—whose subtlety so eludes human perception that neither the mind can contemplate it nor the tongue express it. Through these stages the perfection of chastity itself gradually grows by daily progress. For just as earthly bodies imperceptibly increase from day to day and, without knowing it, are brought to their full form, so too the soul acquires strength and maturity in chastity.

The first degree of purity, therefore, is that a monk, while awake, should not be overthrown by carnal assault. The second is that his mind should not linger over lustful thoughts.

[Note: [Col. 0879D] How dangerous and destructive it is to linger over pleasurable or lustful thoughts and to nurture them in the mind—whence they are also called “deliberate” or “lingering” thoughts, from delay or lingering—has already been demonstrated often and in various places from the teaching of the holy Fathers. For the first corruption of chastity and purity, and the first fuel of lust, is precisely this lingering pleasure, which arises from thought or imagination of a sexual matter and is especially powerful in this sin, as the apostle James says: “Each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire. Then desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin,” etc. (James I).

For not only is external action distinguished from inward desire in the matter of which Christ says, “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew V); but the pleasure itself, called lingering and sexual, when the mind delights in an impure thought, is judged mortal even if the act itself is rejected.

St. Augustine teaches this clearly in Book XII of *On the Trinity* (chapter 12): “Nor indeed, when the mind takes pleasure in unlawful things through thought alone—not deciding that they should be done, but nevertheless willingly retaining and turning over what, as soon as it touched the mind, that is, the higher reason, ought to have been rejected—is it to be denied that there is sin.”

He plainly indicates that this is mortal sin in what follows: “For it cannot be said that, just as in those first two human beings each bore his own person, and therefore, if the woman alone had eaten the forbidden food, she alone would have been punished with death, so, in one human being, thought alone could be condemned for willingly feeding on unlawful pleasures from which it ought immediately to turn away, without deciding to do evil but still retaining them sweetly in memory, as though a woman could be condemned without a man. Far be it from us to believe this. Here there is one person, one human being, and the whole person will be condemned unless, through the grace of the Mediator, those sins of thought alone are forgiven—sins felt without the will to perform the act, but nevertheless with the will to delight the mind in such things.”

By these words he openly teaches that consent to pleasure is mortal sin, on account of which the whole person must be lost and condemned unless it is forgiven through the Mediator’s grace.

The same St. Gregory, in the *Pastoral Rule* (Part I, chapter 11), where he teaches that one who is defiled by such pleasures, even without an intention to act, is unfit to offer sacrifice to God or to cleanse the sins of others—that is, to obtain their forgiveness from God through intercession or satisfaction—as is clear from his words, indicates with sufficient clarity that the sin is mortal. It is better to hear him speaking in his own words:

“He is burdened who does not practice shameful behavior in deed, but is nevertheless weighed down in his mind by constant thought of it without restraint; who is not actually dragged as far as the abominable act, but whose mind delights in lustful pleasure without any obstacle of resistance. He is therefore burdened who, flowing with all his thoughts toward wantonness, carries the weight of shame in his heart; and although he does not practice evil in deed, is nevertheless not torn away from it in mind. Whoever, then, is overcome by any one of these vices is forbidden to offer loaves to the Lord; nor can one whose own sins still devastate him cleanse the sins of others—that is, obtain their forgiveness from God.”

This is St. Gregory’s teaching.

The grave and pointed saying of St. Jerome also belongs here: “Virginity is lost even in the mind.” Elsewhere (*Letter* 4) he teaches that the Egyptian monks labored so diligently at manual work not so much because of the necessities of life as for the salvation of the soul: “so that,” he says, “the mind might not wander among destructive thoughts.”

The following distinction of John Climacus, drawn from the Fathers, also belongs here:

“Most of the Fathers, especially those distinguished for discernment, define one thing as the first impulse, another as lingering in thought, another as consent, another as captivity, another as struggle, and another as what is called passion or disturbance in the soul. They say that the first impulse is a simple conception or image of anything whatsoever, newly injected into the heart. Lingering occurs when someone remains with that image, either with some passion or without passion. Consent is the assent and inclination of the soul toward that image with pleasure. Captivity is the violent carrying away of the unwilling heart, or its continual entrance into whatever matters and the destruction of our best condition. They define struggle as occurring when one fights with equal strength and each person is either overcome or conquers by his own choice.

They say that passion is that which has settled in the soul viciously for a longer period and, according to its habit, has brought the soul over into its own condition, so that the person runs toward it of his own accord and by his own will. Of all these degrees, the first is without sin; the second is not so, but involves some sin; the third is judged according to the condition of those who are fighting; and struggle is the cause either of a crown or of punishment. Captivity is judged one way during prayer and another way outside the time of prayer; likewise, it is judged differently when it occurs amid particular evil thoughts and when it occurs amid all evil thoughts. But passion, without any controversy, is subject either to worthy repentance or to future torment.”

Here Climacus uses the word “passion” in a much different sense from that in which theologians and philosophers commonly use it. By “passion” he understands a habit, or an inclination toward acts of lust, confirmed by use and custom, as is clear from his own description.

Finally, the definition of the Council of Trent should be added (Session 14, chapter 5), in these words:

“From these things it is gathered that penitents must enumerate in confession all mortal sins of which, after diligent examination of themselves, they are conscious, even if those sins are most hidden and have been committed only against the last two commandments of the Decalogue—sins which sometimes wound the soul more grievously and are more dangerous than those committed openly.”

A little later the Council says:

“Since all mortal sins, even sins of thought, make human beings children of wrath and enemies of God, it is necessary to seek forgiveness from God for all of them through an open and shamefaced confession. Therefore, while the faithful of Christ strive to confess all the sins that come to memory, they undoubtedly lay before divine mercy everything that must be acknowledged. But those who act otherwise and knowingly retain some sins offer nothing for remission by the priest to divine goodness. For if the sick person is ashamed to reveal a wound to the physician, what the physician does not know cannot be healed.”

The second degree is that the mind should not linger over lustful thoughts.

[Col. 0881A] The third is that one should not be moved to desire even slightly or delicately by the sight of a woman. The fourth is that, while awake, one should not experience even a simple movement of the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0882B] To what extent these matters and others like them are true, and how they should be understood, see the explanation at *Institutes*, Book VI, chapter 10.]

The fifth degree is that, when the memory of human generation is introduced either by the course of discussion or by the necessity of reading, the mind should not be touched by the subtlest assent to pleasurable action; rather, it should contemplate the matter with a calm and pure gaze as a simple work and a service necessarily contributed to the human race. It should conceive nothing more from its recollection than it would if it were considering in the mind the operation of the ribs or of any other workshop.

[Col. 0882A] The sixth degree of chastity is that one should not be deceived, even while asleep, by the seductive fantasies of women.

[Note: [Col. 0882B] Cassian says the same in *Institutes*, Book VI, chapter 10: “This will be the evident sign and full proof of perfect purity: that either no seductive image appears to us while we are resting and relaxed into sleep, or, if one does appear, it is unable to arouse any movement of desire. For although such agitation is by no means reckoned as the full guilt of sin, it is nevertheless not an indication of a mind that is already perfect, nor a manifestation that the vice has been thoroughly burned out, since this deception operates through such deceptive images.” And again, in chapter 22: “When the mind is still deceived while asleep by the vision of images, let it know that it has not yet been burned out to complete perfection in chastity.”]

Although we do not believe that this deception itself is subject to sin, it is nevertheless an indication that desire still lies hidden in the innermost parts.

[Note: [Col. 0882C] St. Basil, in *The Institutions of Monks* (chapter 23), after posing the question, “From what source do indecent and shameful nocturnal fantasies come to us?” answers as follows: “These things arise chiefly from the soul’s movements and unworthy and unsuitable actions during the day. For if the soul is free to dwell on God’s judgments, it is purified through meditation on the divine law and study of God’s word; and if it occupies itself there unceasingly, always seeking and examining, it will have such dreams also.”

Likewise, Cassian, in *Institutes*, Book VI, chapter 11, explaining from what vice nocturnal deception proceeds, says: “The quality of thoughts, which is guarded too carelessly amid the distractions of the day, is tested by the rest of night. Therefore, when such a deception occurs, it is not to be regarded as the fault of sleep, but as the negligence of the preceding time and the manifestation of a disease hidden within. The night did not first give birth to it; rather, the refreshment of sleep brought to the surface of the skin what had been hidden in the innermost fibers of the soul, exposing the hidden fevers of passions that we contracted by feeding on harmful thoughts throughout the entire day,” etc.

Gregory of Nyssa, in *On the Making of Man*, chapter 13, says: “There is also another kind of dream, formed according to the variety of each person’s character. For the nocturnal imaginations of a brave person are one kind, those of a fearful person another; the dreams of a temperate person are one kind, those of an intemperate person another. One kind of dream is presented to a person consumed by insatiable greed, another to a generous person during sleep. The mind does not shape these visions; rather, that part of the soul which is devoid of reason gives them form. For the things to which a person has accustomed himself through his daily pursuits are also represented in his dreams.”

Gregory Nazianzen, in his poem on his own life, says:

“For nightly visions bring back the cares of day.”

Pagan writers also agree. Plato, in the *Timaeus*, says that dreams are the vigils of sleepers, while hopes are the dreams of those who are awake, as St. Basil reports in Letter 19 to Nazianzen. Aristotle, in Book I of the *Ethics*, chapter 13, says that the dreams of good people are better and more peaceful, while those of bad people are troubled and dreadful. See more on this in Father Martin Delrio’s *Adagiales*, on Proverbs V, and in Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, chapter 3.]

It is nevertheless clear that this deception occurs in different ways. For each person is tempted during sleep according to the practice in which he was accustomed, while awake, to engage or to think. Those who have known carnal intercourse are deceived in one way; those who are inexperienced in intercourse with women are deceived in another. The latter, just as they are generally disturbed by simpler and purer dreams, can also be cleansed with more readily exercised diligence and less effort. The former, however, are deceived by dirtier and more explicit fantasies, until gradually, in proportion to the measure of chastity toward which each person strives, the mind—even when sunk in sleep—is turned toward hatred of that very thing which it had previously experienced as voluntary desire.

Then the promise made through the prophet to strong men as the highest reward for their labors may be granted to him by the Lord: “I will break bow, sword, and war from your land, and I will make you sleep securely” (Hosea II). Thus at last one may attain the purity of blessed Serenus and of the few men like him.

[Note: [Col. 0883C] Cassian discusses the exceptional purity and chastity of Abbot Serenus in *Conference* 7, chapters 1 and 2. Among other things he says of him: “The gift of chastity was infused into him by a singular grace to such a degree that, above all his other virtues—which shone forth by God’s grace not only in his bearing and conduct but even in his very face—he felt himself no longer disturbed even by the natural incentives themselves, not even in sleep.”]

I have separated this purity from the six degrees of chastity mentioned above because it can be possessed, and even believed in, only by the rarest of people. Moreover, what was specially bestowed upon him by the generosity of divine grace cannot be proposed as a general rule—namely, that our mind should be so shaped by the purity of chastity itself that, even when the natural movement of the flesh has died away, it should produce no obscene fluid at all.

I must not remain silent about the opinion of certain people concerning this bodily emission. They say that it does not occur to those who are asleep because it is produced by the deception of dreams, but rather because an excess of that fluid creates certain seductive images in the diseased heart.

[Note: [Col. 0883D] In addition to what has already been said on this matter, Abbot Theonas teaches from what causes pollution and nocturnal deception arise in *Conference* 22, entitled “On Nocturnal Deceptions.” St. Gregory likewise writes in response to the questions of Bishop Augustine as follows (*Question* 12):

“In nocturnal deception, discernment is extremely necessary, so that it may be carefully considered from what cause it occurs in the mind of the sleeper. Sometimes it arises from drunkenness, sometimes from an excess or weakness of nature, and sometimes from thought. When it arises from an excess or weakness of nature, this deception is not at all to be feared, because the mind, which has endured it unknowingly, is more to be pitied than blamed for having produced it. But when the appetite for food is carried beyond measure in taking nourishment, and the reservoirs of the humors are consequently burdened, the mind incurs some guilt because of this—not, however, to the point of being forbidden to receive the sacred mysteries or to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass, etc.

But if the deception of the sleeping person arises from a shameful thought entertained while awake, the mind’s guilt is evident. For he sees from what root that pollution proceeded: what he knowingly thought, he endured unknowingly. Yet one must consider whether the thought occurred as a suggestion, as pleasure, or, what is more serious, as consent to sin.”

This is Gregory’s teaching, with what follows more conveniently and suitably related elsewhere.]

Finally, they say that when that concretion is not disturbing a person, its deception likewise ceases, just as its flow does.

## CHAPTER VIII. That those without experience cannot discuss the nature of chastity and its effects

[Col. 0884A]

No one, however, can receive and test these matters, or determine with certain judgment whether they are possible or impossible, unless through long experience and purity of heart he has reached, under the direction of the Lord’s word, the boundaries between flesh and spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0884D] That is, unless, under the guidance of God’s word, he has reached the limits and boundaries of each, so as to know and preserve them, and has recognized what belongs properly, appropriately, and suitably to each.]

The blessed Apostle says of this: “The word of God is living and effective, sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (Hebrews IV).

And when he has been placed, so to speak, between the boundaries of these two, he will distinguish, as an inspector and judge, with a just balance, what is necessarily and unavoidably attributed to the human condition and what has been introduced by vicious habit and the carelessness of youth. Concerning their effects and nature, he will not accept false popular opinions; rather, weighing the measure of purity on the reliable scale of his own experience and with sound examination,

[Note: [Col. 0884D] He attacks the error of certain people who, when they incur pollution through their own negligence or fault, nevertheless attribute and impute it not to their own vice but to the weakness of nature, thereby doing no small injury to the Creator. Yet it is certain that nocturnal pollution can often occur in sleepers through weakness of nature or an excess of humors, without any fault, as was shown above from St. Gregory.]

he will not be deceived by the error of those who, defiled by more frequent discharges than nature compels through the fault of their negligence, complain about their natural condition. For it is clear that such people rather do violence to nature and extort from it a pollution that nature itself does not produce; yet they attribute their intemperance to the necessity of the flesh, or rather to its Creator, transferring their own faults to the disrepute of nature.

Concerning such people, Proverbs elegantly says: “The folly of a man corrupts his ways, but in his heart he blames God” (Proverbs XIX, according to the Septuagint).

[Note: [Col. 0884D] This saying occurs in the Greek not in chapter XVIII of Proverbs, as Ciaconius’s Lyon edition notes, but in chapter XIX, where the Vulgate reads: “The foolishness of man undermines his steps, and against the Lord his heart is inflamed.”]

Finally, if anyone wishes to detract from the credibility of this assertion of ours, I ask him not to dispute with us while holding a preconceived opinion, before he has undertaken the practices of this discipline. If, after observing for a few months the moderation by which it is taught, he will certainly be able to test the truth of what we have said.

It is useless, however, for anyone to argue about the end of any art or discipline if he has not first pursued with the utmost zeal and virtue everything that belongs to its completion. For example, suppose I assert that the likeness of honey can be produced from wheat, or that from wheat, as also from the seeds of radishes and flax, a very mild oil can be produced (see Pliny, Book XV, chapter 7; Book XX, chapter 4; and elsewhere). If someone entirely ignorant of such things were to stand before me, would he not loudly declare that this was contrary to nature and ridicule me as the author of an obvious lie?

If I produced countless witnesses who testified that they had seen, tasted, and made these things, and if I further explained the method and process by which those substances are transformed either into the richness of oil or the sweetness of honey, while he persisted in the obstinacy of his foolish conviction and denied that any sweetness or richness could be produced from those seeds, would not his irrational and stubborn argument deserve censure rather than the truth of my statement deserve ridicule—a truth supported by the weight of many faithful witnesses, by evident proofs, and, more than all these, by the testing of experience?

Therefore, whoever has reached that state of purity through constant attention of heart in which his mind, entirely freed from the tickling of this passion, causes his flesh during sleep to expel excess fluid as a natural surplus, will most certainly understand the condition and limits of nature. Thus, when he awakens and discovers that his flesh has been polluted after a long interval, without his knowledge or awareness, he will then truly attribute it to natural necessity.

He will undoubtedly have reached that state in which he is found the same at night as during the day, the same in bed as in prayer, the same when alone as when surrounded by crowds of people.

Finally, he will never see himself naked in such a way as to be ashamed to appear before human beings, nor will that unavoidable eye

[Dionysius adds: “of God”]

detect in him anything of the kind that he wishes to conceal from human sight.

[Note: [Col. 0885B] That is, naked. Concerning this exposure—whether of the naked body or its lascivious or curious inspection—which those who cultivate chastity and purity, especially religious persons, must avoid with the greatest care, hear St. Bernard, who discusses it no less seriously than piously and no less subtly than elegantly (*Treatise on the Order of Life*):

“To hear that something shameful has occurred is itself a matter of great embarrassment; but to see whether anything of this kind has occurred—what horror that involves! What displeases us in others: can it fail to displease us in ourselves? Nature itself teaches us no differently. It has perfectly unfolded all the parts of our body, both to provide for necessity and to adorn beauty; yet those parts which would be pleasing to look upon, in which the summit of beauty, as though placed in a citadel, and the grace of form and appearance of face stand out, and whose use is more readily available, it left exposed and open. But those parts in which there is a natural service of necessity, lest they offer a deformed spectacle of themselves, it partly corrected and concealed within the body itself and partly taught and urged us to cover.

Does nature itself, then, not become a teacher of modesty? Its modesty covered and concealed what it found hidden in the structure of our body. The craftsman of nature therefore showed such concern for our modesty, and guarded what is seemly and honorable in our body with such care, that he relegated certain channels and outlets of our bodily passages behind us and turned them away from our sight, lest the evacuation of the belly offend the eyes.

The Apostle speaks beautifully of this: ‘Those members of our body which seem weaker are necessary; and those members of the body which we consider less honorable, we surround with greater honor; and our unseemly parts have greater decorum’ (II Corinthians XII).

Indeed, by imitating nature, human ingenuity has increased this grace, so that we not only hide from our eyes what ought to be hidden, but also regard it as indecorous even to name the functions and signs of the members we have received to be hidden. If these parts are exposed by accident, modesty is confused; if deliberately, it is judged shamelessness.

Since, then, certain human members are so deformed that even naming them is a great indecency, how shameful and shameless are those who not only desire to look upon these secret parts of the body but deliberately touch them! I am ashamed and reluctant to recount the actions of those in whom sodomitical lust reigns, against whom God was so angered and whom, by his just judgment, he handed over to a debased mind, so that a male might practice shamefulness with a male.

Have they not become worse than the brute animals, which lack understanding? If Ham, who laughed at his father’s nakedness, was cursed in his son, with what curse will those be struck who are not ashamed, from a desire to sin, to uncover their own shame and that of others? If only they could see how greatly they offend God by such crimes!”

Thus far St. Bernard.

I think that for the same reason—namely, the dishonor and danger of nakedness—St. Jerome wrote to Laeta on the education of her daughter (*Letter* 7):

“I entirely disapprove of baths for a mature virgin, who ought to be ashamed of herself and cannot see herself naked. If she disciplines her body with vigils and fasts and subjects it to servitude; if she desires to extinguish the flame of lust and the incentives of a burning age by the coldness of continence; if she hastens to disfigure her natural beauty with deliberate squalor, why does she, on the contrary, rekindle those extinguished fires through the warmth of baths?”

The following words of the often-cited John Climacus also point in the same direction (*Step* 15):

“It is the devil’s custom to drive those who are engaged in the contest—that is, ascetics or monks—and who have chosen the solitary life, with the whole force of his wickedness, with every effort and skill, every temptation and trick, toward those vices that are contrary to nature, and to attack them all the more fiercely.

Hence those who never live with women and are not burned by any desire of that kind consider themselves blessed, wretchedly unaware that where one is engaged in the greater struggle, there is no need of the lesser. I think that those murderers—that is, the demons—and those most miserable beings customarily attack and destroy us miserable people most fiercely in matters contrary to nature for two reasons: because material for ruin is everywhere available and ready, and because a heavier punishment is owed for this crime.

He knows what was said in the *Lives of the Fathers* (Book V, booklet 8 of the new edition): that young man who had formerly ruled over wild asses was at last pitiably cast down and deceived by spiritual and exceedingly savage wild asses; and he who had previously been nourished by heavenly bread was finally deprived of so great and singular a gift. More remarkably still, our teacher Antony, lamenting most bitterly after his repentance, said: ‘A great pillar has fallen,’ without, however, revealing the nature of its fall.

For he knew very wisely that fornication could be committed bodily without the joining of one body to another. There is within us a kind of death and destructive ruin, which we always carry within us and with us, especially in youth; yet I have not dared to commit it to writing. For he restrained my hand who said (Ephesians V): ‘What some people do in secret, it is shameful even to speak of, write of, or hear.’

Thus Climacus, as was fitting, conceals rather than reveals the shameful matter under whatever obscurity of language he could devise. Let whoever reads understand, and whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.”

Moreover, to illustrate this passage with examples so as to produce a greater horror and detestation of this shamefulness, there is the outstanding example—worthy not so much of admiration as of imitation—of the singular modesty and chastity that Athanasius relates of St. Ammon, or Ammonius, the anchorite (*Life of St. Antony*):

“It was once necessary for him to cross the river called the Lycus, swollen by sudden floodwaters. He asked Theodore, who was with him, to withdraw a little from his sight, lest either should see the other’s body naked. Theodore withdrew; nevertheless, when Ammon wished to strip himself, he was ashamed. While he was considering the matter, divine power conveyed him to the opposite bank.”

Thus God provided both for chaste modesty and for chastity, and by a remarkable miracle showed how pleasing and acceptable these were to him. Conversely, St. Prosper teaches by the example of a certain girl, whom he relates was possessed by a demon for this reason, how displeasing to God is the exposure of bodily members, especially the genitals, and the curious or lascivious inspection of one’s own body or another’s:

“A certain young woman,” he says (*On the Half-Times*, chapter 6), “wearing the habit of a handmaid of God, while bathing in a bath, looked shamelessly at an image of Venus and at herself, comparing herself with it, and offered herself as a dwelling to the devil. Immediately that roaring lion who prowls about found what he sought. Occupying the passage of her throat, and allowing no food or drink to pass through it, for nearly seventy days and as many nights the devil kept a fast for himself in the vessel he had captured and possessed.”

This is St. Prosper. He then relates how the same girl was delivered from the demon, which we have mentioned above on another occasion.]

Then, when he begins continually to delight in the sweetest light of chastity, he will be able to say with the Prophet: “And night shall be illumination in my delights, for darkness shall not be darkened from you, and night shall be illuminated like the day; its darkness shall be as its light” (Hebrews IV; Psalm CXXXVIII).

Finally, since this appears to exceed the condition of human nature, the same prophet adds how he obtained it: “For you possessed my reins” (ibid.)—that is, “I did not merit this purity by my own diligence or virtue, but because you put to death the burning desire for lust implanted in my reins.”

## CHAPTER IX. The question whether, even while asleep, we can escape bodily movement

[Col. 0887B]

**Germanus:** We have experienced to some extent that perpetual purity of body can be possessed by those who are awake through the grace of God. We do not deny that, when the rigor and judgment of discipline resist it, the movement of the flesh can fail to occur in those who are awake. But we wish to be taught whether, while asleep, we can also be free from this disturbance.

For we do not believe that this is possible for two reasons. Although we cannot mention them without shame, nevertheless, since the necessity of this very remedy compels us, we ask you to receive with indulgence whatever may perhaps have been exposed with excessive frankness.

The first reason is that, when the mind’s strength is relaxed through the repose of sleep, the intrusion of that movement cannot possibly be guarded against. The second is that, when the accumulation of urine has continuously filled the capacity of the bladder with an internal flow of fluid while we are at rest, it arouses the languishing limbs; this happens by the same law even to children and eunuchs.

Thus, if the mind’s consent is not wounded by lustful pleasure, nevertheless the shamefulness of the bodily parts humbles it through embarrassment.

[Note: [Col. 0887D] Concerning the shamefulness and modesty of the genital members, and its cause, see, if you wish, St. Augustine, *City of God* XIV, chapter 19.]

## CHAPTER X. The answer: that a movement of the flesh occurring during sleep does not injure chastity
[Col. 0888B] **Chaeremon:** It is evident that you have not yet recognized the power of true chastity, since you believe that it is preserved among the wakeful only with the aid of austerity. Hence you suppose that integrity cannot be maintained by those who are asleep, as though the mind’s rigor had been relaxed. But chastity does not subsist, as you imagine, [Note: [Col. 0887D] “Austerity,” that is, strictness. Cassian uses the word frequently in this sense. But “through love of itself” means, I understand, love of chastity itself, which is lovable in its own right, in accordance with Cicero’s saying: “If virtue could be seen with the eyes, it would arouse in human minds an astonishing love of itself” (*On Duties*, I).] through the protection of austerity, but through love of itself and delight in its own purity.

[Note: [Col. 0887D] Cassian likewise taught that chastity is distinguished from continence in Book VI, chapter 4: “It is one thing,” he says, “to be continent—that is, ἐγκρατής [self-controlled]; another to be chaste and, so to speak, to pass over into a disposition of integrity or incorruption, which is called ἁγνόν [pure].” Saint Bernard agrees, writing in one place (*On the Words of Wisdom*, vol. II): “Note that it is one thing to be continent and another to be chaste. The luxurious and the chaste are opposites. It belongs to the luxurious to feel the movements [of desire] and to consent to those movements; to the chaste, neither to feel the movements nor to consent to them. The continent person stands in the middle, taking a share from both: having with the one the experience of feeling the movements, and with the other the refusal to consent to the movements,” and so forth.

It should also be noted from Saint Thomas (*Summa theologica* II-II, question 155, articles 1 and 2) that the term “continence” is understood in two ways. First, it signifies a virtue by which someone abstains from every venereal pleasure, as it is commonly understood in Sacred Scripture and among the holy Fathers; in this sense it does not differ from chastity. Thus theologians distinguish three degrees of continence: virginal, widowed, and marital, as was said above concerning chastity (chapter 7). Second, it signifies firmness of mind by which someone resists depraved desires that are vehement within him. In this sense the Philosopher understands continence in Book VII of the *Ethics* (questions 7 and following) and calls it ἐγκράτεια [self-control]. Saint Thomas says that continence is also understood in this way in the Conferences of the Fathers, undoubtedly with this passage in mind.

Saint Basil, in his *Longer Rules*, takes continence somewhat more broadly, so that it includes abstinence, temperance, and the other virtues that moderate the passions: “He who moderates all the affections of his soul, is not moved by the tickling of pleasures, and is firmly and steadfastly disposed against every depraved desire—he is perfectly continent.”]

For where some opposition of pleasure still resists chastity, the proper term is not chastity but continence. You see, then, that for those who have received the affection of chastity in their very marrow through God’s grace, the cessation of austerity when they sleep does not hinder them. [Note: [Col. 0888D] Dionysius the paraphraser omitted this. The apparent meaning is that the cessation or interruption during night sleep of the usual daytime austerity does not harm those who are asleep, nor does it harm their chastity when they experience movements of the flesh in dreams, since even while awake they unwillingly undergo such movements and impulses, as the Apostle testifies concerning himself in 2 Corinthians 12.

Accordingly, their austerity is called unreliable, because even while they are awake it does not immediately free them from every temptation of the flesh. Nevertheless, there is a great difference between a person who is awake and one who is asleep in such illusions and enticements of the flesh. The person who is awake possesses sound and free will and judgment; if he consents, he has no excuse. The person who is asleep, however, lacks the free use of reason and therefore can neither consent nor dissent, and consequently can do neither good nor evil. What a sleeping person does is therefore not imputed to him as guilt, just as what a madman or deranged person does is not imputed to him, says Saint Thomas (*Summa* I, question 8, article 8; II-II, question 154, article 5).

Hence Saint Prosper, *On the Contemplative Life* III, chapter 6: “The mind, usually affected carnally, takes pleasure in images even when they are absent; fixed upon them by excessive attention to an impure thought, it seems not to imagine that it is embracing images of bodies, but bodies themselves. Hence that bodily discharge which occurs without guilt in those who are asleep sometimes occurs through guilt in those who are awake. What happens in a sleeping person is one thing; what a waking person does is another. In the former, the fullness of bodily fluid is naturally expelled; in the latter, desire is shamefully made manifest. But this desire produces such a discharge in those who are awake when filthy conversation has stirred their impure appetite,” and so forth.]

This austerity is demonstrably unreliable even for those who are awake. For whatever is suppressed with effort grants the combatant temporary truces, but after the struggle it does not provide a lasting repose of security. Whatever, however, has been conquered by profound virtue and settled without any suspicion of disturbance grants the victor a continual firmness of peace.

Therefore, so long as we feel ourselves assailed by the movement of the flesh, let us recognize that we have not yet reached the heights of chastity. We remain under the weakness of continence, wearied by battles in which the outcome must always be uncertain. But you wished to establish that the movement of the flesh is unavoidable by pointing out that even eunuchs cannot be free from it after their genitals have been removed. It should be understood that they lack not the bodily heats and the passion of desire, [Col. 0889B] but only the power of procreative generation.

[Note: [Col. 0889D] Saint Basil discusses eunuchs at length in his book *On True Virginity*. There he condemns those eunuchs who castrated themselves in order to preserve chastity, as Origen did; and he shows that such castrated men, although incapable of sexual intercourse, are harassed and driven by stronger impulses of lust and are more inclined toward desire than others.

Saint Jerome agrees, writing in Book I *Against Jovinian*: “The castrated eunuch is cut off for a long and secure life of lust.” To this corresponds Solomon’s saying: “A eunuch embracing a virgin and sighing” (Proverbs 30), because he cannot satisfy his desire or fulfill in action what he ardently craves.]

Hence it is clear that even if they wish to attain the chastity toward which we strive, they must not relax their humility and contrition of heart or the austerity of continence, although one should certainly believe that they can attain chastity with less labor and effort.

## CHAPTER XI. On the great difference between chastity and continence

Therefore the perfection of chastity is distinguished from the laborious beginnings of continence by perpetual tranquility. This is the consummation of true chastity: it does not merely resist the movements of carnal desire but detests them with complete horror, and preserves its own constant and inviolate purity. [Note: [Col. 0890D] Elsewhere also (Institutes VI, chapters 15–16) Cassian maintains that the chastity designated by the Apostle is called sanctification and holiness. “This is the will of God, your sanctification” (1 Thessalonians 4); and, “Pursue peace with all people, and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Hebrews 12).]

Nor can it be anything other than holiness. This will happen when the flesh, having ceased to desire against the spirit, consents to its desires and virtue; and when they begin to be joined to one another by the firmest peace, so that, according to the psalmist’s saying, “brothers dwell together in unity” (Psalm 132), possessing the blessedness promised by the Lord, of which he says: “If two of you agree on earth about anything whatever that they ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18).

Whoever, therefore, has gone beyond the rank of that intellectual Jacob—that is, of the supplanter—will rise from the struggle of continence and the supplanting of vices to the merit of Israel, with the sinew of the thigh struck numb and the heart perpetually directed toward God. [Note: [Col. 0890D] We have discussed elsewhere the two names Jacob and Israel, and intellectual or intelligible Jacob. See also Book VII *On the Incarnation*, chapter 9.]

Blessed David also distinguished this order by a prophecy of the Holy Spirit. First he says: “God is known in Judah”—that is, in the soul that is still held beneath the confession of sins, for Judah is interpreted as “confession.” “In Israel,” however—that is, in the one who sees God, or, as some interpret it, “the most upright of God”—his name is not merely known but is great.

Then, calling us to higher things and wishing to show the very place in which the Lord delights, he says: “His place has been established in peace”—that is, not in the conflict of struggle and combat with vices, but in the peace of chastity and the perpetual tranquility of the heart.

If someone merits attaining this place of peace through the extinction of carnal passions, and then progresses from this stage and becomes spiritual Zion—that is, God’s watchtower—he will consequently also become the Lord’s dwelling place. [Note: [Col. 0890D] Saint Jerome likewise interprets this in Letter 29: “In Zion,” that is, “in the watchtower, in the sublimity of doctrines and virtues, in the soul of the believer.” Elsewhere he says: “Zion, which is interpreted as ‘watchtower,’ because it is situated on a mountain, is called a citadel; the rest of the city is called Jerusalem, which was formerly named Jebus and Salem.” Peter Berchorius discusses spiritual Zion learnedly and at length in his *Moral Dictionary*, where, among other meanings, he interprets Zion as religion or the religious life.]

For the Lord does not dwell in the struggle of continence but in the perpetual watchtower of virtues. There he no longer blunts or restrains the powers of the bows, but has broken them forever—the bows from which the flaming arrows of lust were once directed against us.

You see, then, that just as the Lord’s place is not in the struggle of continence but in the peace of chastity, so also his dwelling is in the watchtower and contemplation of the virtues. Hence the gates of Zion are rightly preferred to all the tents of Jacob: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob” (Psalm 86).

But since you assert that the movement of the flesh is unavoidable because urine, continually filling the bladder by its steady inflow, arouses even the limbs when they are at rest, it should be understood that, although this movement does not in the least prejudice true practitioners of purity in their attainment of it, since it is sometimes produced solely by this necessity and during sleep, nevertheless, when the limbs are aroused in this way, they are brought back to their proper repose by the command of chastity, so that they are calmed not only without any itching but even without the slightest recollection of desire.

Therefore, so that bodily law may agree with the law of the mind, excess must also be restrained in the drinking of water itself. In this way the daily accumulation of fluid, flowing into the limbs after they have first been dried out, will make the bodily movement that you consider unavoidable not only very rare but also slow, mild, and cool—so to speak, a fire that is cold—and will kindle a flame that gives off dew without the heat of any burning, like [Note: [Col. 0891C] A beautiful allegory drawn from Moses’ vision, of which Exodus 3 says: “The Lord appeared to Moses in a flame of fire from the midst of the bush, and he saw that the bush was burning but was not consumed. Moses said, ‘I will go and see this great sight, why the bush is not burned.’”] that astonishing vision of Moses, so that the bush of our flesh, surrounded by a harmless fire, is not burned (Exodus 3); or like the three young men whose furnace flame was dispersed by the spirit’s falling dew, so that not even the smell of fire touched their hair or their garments’ hems (Daniel 3); so that we may begin already in this body to possess what is promised to the saints through the prophet: “When you walk through fire, you shall not be burned, and the flame shall not consume you” (Isaiah 43).

## CHAPTER XII. On the wonders that God works especially in his saints

Great and truly marvelous are those things—known thoroughly to no human beings except those who have experienced them—which the Lord grants with ineffable generosity to his faithful while they still dwell in this vessel of corruption.

The prophet surveyed these things with the purity of his mind and, speaking both in his own person and in that of those who attain this condition and disposition, exclaimed: “Wonderful are your works, O Lord, and my soul knows them exceedingly well” (Psalm 138).

Otherwise, the prophet would appear to have said nothing new or great if these words were thought to have been spoken with some other disposition of heart or about other works of God. There is no human being, after all, who does not recognize that God’s works are wonderful simply from the greatness of creation itself.

But those things that he distributes among his saints in his daily working and pours forth abundantly with special generosity [Lipsius, margin: “magnificence”] are recognized by no one except the soul that enjoys them. In the secrecy of its conscience, that soul is their sole witness, so that it is unable not only to describe them in any language but even to grasp them through sense or thought when, departing from that fiery fervor, it falls back to these material and earthly perceptions.

[Note: [Col. 0891C] A most beautiful passage on the marvelous effectiveness of divine grace, especially in the transformation and renewal of a human being. We have a most weighty witness to this, indeed a splendid example, in Augustine. What he had experienced in his own conversion and the reforming of his life, he wished to make known to all for their common benefit.

“They held me back,” he says (*Confessions* VIII, 11), “the trifles of trifles and vanities of vanities, my ancient friends; they tugged at my fleshly garment and murmured: ‘Are you dismissing us? From this moment shall we no longer be with you forever?’” A little farther on: “They delayed me as I hesitated to tear myself away from them and leap over to where I was being called, while violent habit said to me: ‘Do you think you can live without these things?’”

Augustine was speaking of that struggle and great quarrel, as he himself calls it, between flesh and spirit. But once he had broken the bonds by which he was held and devoted himself with his whole soul to God’s service, so that he no longer sought either a wife or any hope in this world, what did he feel and experience within himself, and how greatly had he changed?

“How sweet it suddenly became for me,” he says (*Confessions* IX, 11), “to be free of the sweets of trifles; what I had feared to lose, I now rejoiced to dismiss! For you cast them out from me, you true and highest sweetness, and entered in their place, sweeter than every pleasure—not to flesh and blood, brighter than every light, more inward than every secret, higher than every honor, but not higher in those who exalt themselves.”

Saint Cyprian likewise testifies from his own experience (*Book II, Letter 2*), describing both conditions of his soul in these words:

“When I lay in darkness and blind night, and when I wavered upon the sea of the tossing world, wandering with uncertain steps and faltering feet, I thought it altogether difficult and hard, given my former habits, that what divine mercy promised me for my salvation could be accomplished: that a person could be born again, that, while the structure of the body remained, the human being could be changed in soul and mind.

“‘How can such a transformation be possible?’ I said. ‘How can what has been hardened either by the natural disposition of matter or by long-established habit through old age be suddenly and swiftly stripped away? These things have settled deeply, with roots penetrating far below. When will the person accustomed to sumptuous banquets and lavish feasts learn frugality? When will the person who has shone in gold and purple and been conspicuous in costly clothing put aside his way of life for the dress of an ordinary and simple person? The man surrounded by ranks of clients and honored by a large retinue of attendants considers it a punishment to be alone.

“‘Drunkenness must entice him, as it once did; pride inflate him, anger inflame him, greed disturb him, cruelty goad him, ambition delight him, lust plunge him headlong. These things I often considered within myself. For just as I was held entangled in many errors of my former life, from which I did not believe I could be freed, so I complied with the vices clinging to me and, despairing of better things, favored my evils as though they were already my own native possessions.

“‘But after the aid of the saving water had washed away the stain of my former life, and light from above poured itself into my cleansed and purified heart; after a second birth from heaven, by the breathing of the Spirit, had remade me as a new person, things that had been doubtful immediately began, in an astonishing manner, to become certain; closed things opened; dark things shone; what had previously seemed difficult became possible, and what had been thought impossible began to be accomplished.’”

Saint Cyprian writes these and many other elegant things. Every religious person can recognize the same things in himself and proclaim them concerning himself. For what baptism accomplished in Cyprian, religious profession accomplishes in us: through it we die to the world and our former life, are born to God and the spiritual life, and are transformed into a new creation. Hence Saint Bernard and other Fathers call religious profession “another baptism” (*On Precepts and Dispensations*).]

Who, on seeing within himself the insatiable gluttony of the belly and the costly, destructive extravagance of the appetite so restrained that he scarcely ever partakes of even scanty and worthless food, and then only reluctantly, would not marvel at the works of the Lord?

Who would not be astonished at the works of God after perceiving that the fire of lust, which he had formerly believed to be natural and virtually unquenchable, had grown so cool that he no longer felt himself stirred even by the simplest bodily movement?

How could anyone fail to tremble at the Lord’s power when he saw people once savage and ferocious—people who were provoked to the utmost madness of anger even by the gentlest services of their subjects—pass over into such gentleness that they are now moved by no injuries, and even rejoice with the greatest magnanimity when injuries are inflicted upon them?

Who, plainly, would not marvel at God’s works and proclaim with his whole affection: “For I have known that the Lord is great” (Psalm 134), when he has seen either himself or someone else changed from most rapacious to generous, from extravagant to self-controlled, from proud to humble, from delicate and soft to rough and austere, and willingly enduring the poverty and hardship of present circumstances?

These are truly the marvelous works of God, which the soul of the prophet and of those like him recognizes in stunned wonder through the vision of a marvelous contemplation.

These are the wonders that he has set upon the earth, which the same prophet, contemplating them, summons all peoples to behold, saying: “Come and see the works of God, who has set wonders upon the earth, removing wars to the ends of the earth. He will break the bow, shatter the weapons, and burn the shields with fire” (Psalm 45).

For what greater wonder could there be than that, in an exceedingly brief moment, the most rapacious tax collectors should become apostles, and savage persecutors become the most patient preachers of the Gospel, so that they propagated even by the shedding of their own blood the faith they had persecuted?

These are the works of God that the Son declares he performs daily together with the Father, saying: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5).

Concerning these works of God, blessed David sings in the Spirit: “Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, who alone does great wonders” (Psalm 71).

Concerning them also the prophet Amos says: “He who does all things and [Note: [Col. 0893C] The Vulgate reads: “Turning darkness into morning, and changing day into night” (Amos 5).] turns them and transforms them into the morning shadow of death” (Amos 5).

This is indeed “the transformation of the right hand of the Most High” (Psalm 76). Concerning this saving work of God the prophet prays to the Lord, saying: “Establish, O God, what you have worked in us” (Psalm 67).

And, to pass over those secret and hidden dispensations of God which the minds of all the saints perceive as being specially carried out within them at every moment, there is that heavenly infusion of spiritual joy by which the dejected mind is lifted up by the exhilaration of an unexpected gladness into those unknown ecstasies of the heart and into joys whose consolations are as ineffable as they are unheard of. Through them, we who sometimes lie sluggish and numb with profound torpor are awakened to the most fervent prayer as though from the deepest sleep.

This, I say, is the joy of which the blessed Apostle says: “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart” (1 Corinthians 2)—that is, into the heart of the person who, dulled by earthly vices, is still merely human and clings to human affections, perceiving nothing of these gifts of God.

Finally, the same Apostle, speaking both of himself and of those like him who had already withdrawn from the human manner of life, adds: “But God has revealed these things to us through his Spirit.”

[Note: [Col. 0893C] Concerning this, Saint Bernard writes on the Apostle’s words, “The kingdom of God is not food and drink” (Romans 14): “I shall speak of what the experienced person knows and the inexperienced person does not know; for the natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2). Do not all the hidden depths of our being often tremble as we pray, in remembrance of that joy which is in Jerusalem above, which is our mother (Galatians 4)? And does not a flood of tears pour over the faces of those who meditate? “If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand be forgotten; let my tongue cling to my palate if I do not remember you, if I do not set Jerusalem at the beginning of my joy” (Psalm 136). Truly at the beginning of joy, because its end is stored up there. The beginning of that joy which we sometimes feel here is a drop, a little droplet descending from that river whose streams gladden the city of God (Psalm 45).]

## CHAPTER XIII. That only those who experience it recognize the sweetness of chastity

[Note: [Col. 0894C] Saint Ephrem the Syrian speaks excellently of this sweetness and delight of chastity, as though transfixed by wonder at it:

“O chastity, mother of love and pattern of angelic life! O chastity, pure in heart, sweet in speech, and joyful in appearance! O chastity, who make human beings like angels! O chastity, tranquil harbor established in perfect peace and security! O chastity, who gladden the heart of the one who possesses you and attach wings to the soul for heavenly things! O chastity, who produce spiritual joy and remove sorrow! O chastity, who lessen the passions and free the mind from disturbances! O chastity, spiritual chariot carrying your possessor on high! O chastity, who bloom like a rose in the midst of the soul and body and fill the whole house with fragrance!”

The holy and ancient Father says these and many other things, almost carried outside himself by the sweetness and delight of chastity.]

In all these matters, therefore, the more the mind advances toward a subtler purity, the more sublimely it will contemplate God, and the more its inward wonder will increase, rather than its ability to speak or find words for narration.

For just as an inexperienced person cannot grasp in his mind the power of this joy, so the experienced person cannot explain it in speech. It is as though someone wished to describe the sweetness of honey in words to a person who had never tasted anything sweet: the person who had never experienced that flavor in his mouth would not receive its sweetness through his ears, nor could the other express in words the sweetness he had come to know through the pleasure of taste. Rather, drawn only by his own recognition of the sweetness, he must silently admire within himself the delight of the taste he has experienced.

In the same way, whoever merits reaching the condition of virtues described above, silently surveying all these things that the Lord works in his saints by a special grace, and inflamed by astonishment at the contemplation of them all, will cry out from the depths of his heart: “Wonderful are your works, O God, and my soul knows them exceedingly well” (Psalm 138).

This, then, is the marvelous work of God: that a human being who is carnal, while placed in the flesh, should reject carnal affections, maintain one disposition of soul amid such variety of circumstances and assaults, and remain immovable amid every change of events.

Endowed with this virtue, [Note: [Col. 0895B] I have not yet discovered who this old man was. Similar sayings concerning the preservation of patience in adversity are also found among pagan writers. Dionysius the tyrant, expelled from his kingdom and asked what benefit Plato and the study of philosophy had brought him, replied: “That I might endure so great a change of fortune with an even mind” (Diogenes Laertius VI; Aelian, *Various History* IX).

Diogenes, when someone asked what profit he gained from philosophy, replied: “If nothing else, certainly this: that I am prepared for every fortune.”

Finally, there is the story of a certain young man, whom Aelian describes in these words: “A certain young Eretrian had attended Zeno’s school for a long time for the sake of his education. When he returned, his father asked what wisdom he had learned. When he said that he would show him, his indignant father beat him. But he endured it modestly and patiently and said: ‘This is what I have learned: to endure my father’s anger with moderation.’”

So much for them. If that empty and artificial philosophy had such power among pagans, how much more powerful ought the true and evangelical wisdom of Christ to be among Christians, when he says: “Bless those who persecute and slander you; bless, and do not curse” (Matthew 5), and so forth. “If glass is so highly valued,” says blessed Jerome (*Letter 10 to Paulinus), “what value must be assigned to the most precious pearl?”]

a certain old man, when surrounded by crowds of unbelievers in Alexandria and assailed not only with curses but also with the gravest insults from those who attacked him, was asked mockingly: “What miracle has your Christ, whom you worship, performed?” He replied: “He has enabled me not to be shaken or offended by these insults, or by worse ones if you should inflict them.”

## CHAPTER XIV. Germanus’s question concerning the character of the discipline and the time in which chastity can be perfected
