**Germanus:** Since our amazement at this chastity—which is not human or earthly but plainly heavenly and angelic—has so suddenly overwhelmed us that it inspires the terror of despair more than it prompts our souls to seek it, we ask you to instruct us with a completely full discussion concerning the character of the discipline and the length of time within which it can be acquired or perfected. Thus we may both believe that it can be brought to completion and be encouraged to seek it after a period of time has been established.

For we judge it in some sense incomprehensible to those who remain in this flesh unless a definite order and path by which it can be reached are disclosed to us with certainty.

## CHAPTER XV. Chaeremon’s answer: within what period chastity can be acquired

[Col. 0896A]

**Chaeremon:** It is sufficiently presumptuous to define a fixed period for the completion of the chastity of which we are speaking, especially amid such diversity either of pleasures or of abilities. Even in these material arts and visible disciplines, it is not easy to determine such a period. According to the disposition of each person’s mind and the quality of his intelligence, people necessarily grasp them more quickly or more slowly.

Nevertheless, we can define with complete confidence the rule of discipline and the period within which its possibility may be recognized. Whoever, therefore, has withdrawn from all idle conversations, has been freed from every anger, anxiety, and worldly care, and has been content with only two [Note: [Col. 0895D] We have discussed *paxamacia*, or *paximacia*, extensively elsewhere (Institutes IV, chapter 14; Conferences II, chapters 11 and 19). It is therefore clear that a *paximacium* was a small loaf of about six ounces, and that the appointed amount of daily food—or the daily portion, as it is called—for the monks of Egypt was two *paximacia*, as is also indicated here. Yet the more perfect among them hardly ever used this measure, being content with much less, as is known of Hilarion, Antony, and others.

Suidas nevertheless argues that the word is Latin rather than Greek and signifies bread baked twice, writing of it as follows: παξαμὰς ὁ δίπυρος ἄρτος, ἐστὶ δὲ λέξις Ῥωμαϊκή—that is, “*paximas*, or *paxamacium* or *paxamadium*, is bread baked twice; it is a Roman, or Latin, word.” Saint Ephrem also mentions *paxamacia* in his treatise *On Virtue*, chapter 10.]

*paximacia* [Variant: *paxamacia*] as his daily food, has denied himself his fill of water, and has limited his sleep to a period of three hours—or, as others have established, four hours, he must nevertheless believe that he will attain chastity not through the merit of these labors or continence but through the Lord’s mercy, since without this faith all human effort is futile. He will recognize that the perfection of this state is not impossible for him within no more than [Note: [Col. 0896B] Dionysius: “within six months.” This passage, in which a six-month period is prescribed for acquiring chastity, appears to require the criticism found in the recently published *Life of Father Balthasar Alvarez*, a religious of the Society of Jesus. It says as follows (chapter 42):

“One must not prescribe to God the time of his visitations and mercies. Therefore a matter should be regarded with suspicion if someone establishes a general rule that whoever applies such and such diligence for so many years or months will receive from God such and such favor or degree of virtue. In this regard some criticize Cassian because he prescribed a period of time for attaining the perfection of chastity to one who applied the diligences he specifies there.

“For this depends not so much on human effort, method, or time, since it is the work of grace or of God’s special providence, who distributes to each person as he wills and when he wills. Therefore, in the exercise of virtue, it is extremely important for beginners to follow the ordinary and well-trodden path and to cooperate fervently on their part with God’s ordinary direction and grace, removing impediments and employing the prescribed means, while laying aside the cares and anxieties of pursuing progress by extraordinary paths. They should rightly entrust such progress to God’s providence, so that he may direct and arrange it according to his will and according to what is most beneficial, while they do not abandon their station until they hear: ‘Friend, move up higher’ (Luke 14).”

So much for that passage. Its author seems to have had in mind the grave and admonitory speech of Judith (Judith 8) to the rulers and people of Bethulia, who had in a sense prescribed a fixed time for God to provide aid: “What is this word by which Uzziah has agreed to surrender the city to the Assyrians if help does not come to you within five days? Who are you, that you put the Lord to the test? This is not a speech that will call forth mercy, but rather one that will provoke anger and kindle fury. You have set a time for the Lord’s mercy and appointed a day for him according to your own judgment,” and so forth.

That statement of the same Chaeremon, made at the beginning of this chapter, should therefore be retained: that it is presumptuous to define a fixed period for the completion of chastity, and so forth.]

six months.

Yet it is an evident sign of already approaching purity to begin not to expect it from the productivity of one’s own labor. For if each person truly grasps the force of that verse: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Psalm 126), it follows that he will neither become proud of the merits of his purity, understanding that he has obtained it not through his own diligence but through the Lord’s mercy, nor attack others with harsh severity, knowing that human virtue is nothing if divine virtue does not assist it.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the end and remedy of acquiring and preserving chastity
Therefore, for each one of us who struggles with all his strength against the spirit of fornication [Note: [Col. 0897C] Serapion likewise, in the fifth Conference, after saying that the extinction of temptations and assaults must be specially and continually sought from God, adds: “For it is impossible for anyone to merit triumph over any passion before he has understood that he cannot obtain it by the diligence or labor of his own struggle.” Climacus likewise, in the passage cited above: “Whoever wishes by his own effort to conquer or subdue his flesh runs in vain. Unless the Lord destroys the house of the flesh and builds the house of the soul, anyone who attempts to destroy it by fasting and keeping vigil labors in vain. Place before the eyes of the Lord the natural weakness of the flesh, and, humbled and acknowledging your own weakness, you will wholly receive the gift of chastity in your inmost being.”], the singular victory consists in not hoping for a remedy on the basis of the merit of his own effort. [Col. 0897B] Although this conviction may seem easy and plain to everyone, beginners possess it with no less difficulty than they attain perfection in chastity itself. For whenever some small measure of purity has smiled upon them, a certain subtle elation immediately steals into the secret places of their conscience, and they flatter themselves, believing that they have obtained it through the zeal of their own diligence. Consequently, once they have been somewhat stripped of that heavenly protection, they must be overwhelmed by those passions which divine power had extinguished, until experience teaches them that they cannot obtain the good of purity by their own strength and effort.

And, to conclude briefly our discussion of the end of complete chastity, which was composed through a long night of study, [Col. 0898A] gathering into one all that has been set out at length and in scattered form, this is the consummation of chastity: that no pleasure of lust should touch the vigilant monk; that, when he rests, no illusion of dreams should deceive him; but that, if an agitation of the flesh should steal upon him while he sleeps, through the negligence of his drowsing mind, then, just as it arose without any tickling of pleasure, so also it should subside without any bodily irritation. These are the things we have arranged concerning the end of chastity, as far as we could, not under the instruction of words but under the instruction of experience. [Note: [Col. 0898C] Thus also he said elsewhere (Conference 10, chapter 1): “Taught by the mastery of the affections or their effects.”]

Although I think that these things may perhaps be judged impossible by the idle and negligent, I am nevertheless certain that they will be recognized and approved by earnest and spiritual men. For there is as much difference between one human being and another as there is between the objects toward which their minds’ attention is directed, which are separated from one another by as great a distance as heaven from hell, or Christ from Belial, according to the saying of the Lord and Savior: “If anyone ministers to me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also shall my minister be” (John XII). And again: “Where your treasure is, there also shall your heart be” (Matthew VI).

Up to this point blessed Chaeremon had discussed the perfection of chastity and had concluded his admirable teaching on the highest purity in these words. He then urged us, who were astonished and anxious, that, since most of the night had already passed, we should not deprive our limbs, committed for a little while to rest, of the natural nourishment of sleep, lest the mind too, weakened by the torpor of the body, should lose the vigor of its holy purpose.

## THIRTEENTH CONFERENCE

The third conference of Abbot Chaeremon, ON THE PROTECTION OF GOD.

[Col. 0897]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0897C]

When, after having taken a little sleep, we returned to the morning synaxis [Note: [Col. 0897D] That is, to the morning assembly, at which they first performed the divine office; hence at the end of this chapter he calls it the solemn observance of prayers and psalms. Afterwards they discussed and conferred among themselves concerning divine and spiritual matters; hence such gatherings and assemblies were called “conferences,” as has been said elsewhere. This is clear both from most of these Conferences, which are reported as having taken place in the morning, that is, after the night’s rest, and from the Rule of Saint Pachomius, whose seventh article, according to Jerome’s translation, reads as follows: “In the morning, when the prayers have been completed in each house, they shall not immediately return to their cells, but shall confer among themselves on what they have heard the superiors discussing; and then they shall enter their sleeping quarters. The discussion by the superiors of the houses shall take place three times each week,” etc.], we found the old man, the abbot Chaeremon. [Col. 0898C] Germanus was greatly troubled by the scruple that, in the preceding discussion—whose force had instilled in us the deepest longing for a chastity unknown to us—[Note: [Col. 0898D]

He expressed the same point above, in the twelfth Conference, more than once and in different words. In chapter 15: “For if each person truly understands the force of that verse: ‘Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain’ (Psalm CXXV), it follows that he will not be lifted up by the merits of his purity, understanding that he obtained it not through his own diligence but through the Lord’s mercy,” etc. And in the following chapter: “For each one of us who struggles with all his strength against the spirit of fornication, the singular victory consists in not hoping for a remedy on the basis of the merit of his own effort.” And below: “Experience teaches them that they cannot obtain the good of purity by their own strength and effort.” The addition of this statement in the preceding Conference gave occasion to the present Conference, which the Author chose to title “On the Protection of God”; the reason for this will become clear from what follows.

This is that famous Conference on account of which Cassian not only acquired a bad reputation among Catholics and cast no slight stain upon his name and reputation, but also deserved the censorial condemnation of Pope Gelasius and came to be numbered among apocryphal authors, or among those whose writings are apocryphal, as we warned in our preface. For in this Conference, under the name of Abbot Chaeremon, he wrote about the grace of God and human free will in such a way that he seemed either to agree with Pelagius and the Pelagian heretics, or at least to favor them, and to undermine and weaken the teaching of Augustine, which had been approved by the Roman pontiffs and received by the universal Church.

For this reason, D. Prosper of Aquitaine, bishop of Riez, not only complained gravely about him in writing to Augustine himself—which Hilary, bishop of Arles, also did with the same zeal for defending the truth—but also published at that time a book against the “Collator,” directing the title “Collator” [Col. 0899C] not against Abbot Chaeremon, whom Cassian here introduces as speaking, but against Cassian himself. Whatever is faulty and erroneous in this Conference he ascribed not to Chaeremon but to Cassian, as its author.

But in order that these matters may become clearer and more certain, it will be useful here to hear more fully the most accurate writer of the Ecclesiastical Annals, Cardinal Baronius, as he narrates them. “In this year,” he says—namely, 433—“Saint Prosper opposed with powerful writings the Pelagian heresy, which was reviving in the West and spreading secretly. A dangerous war seemed to be arising in the Church, not from enemies, but from those who lived in the Church under the Catholic name, indeed, who seemed to have fought against the Pelagian errors with stronger weapons and with great praise. For who would beware of an enemy whom he had seen, while fighting in the ranks of the faithful, hurling missiles against the enemy? Something of this kind happened in the Church at that time.

“For when John Cassian, a priest of the Church of Massilia, had published an eloquent and very useful Commentary on the Incarnation of the Lord against Nestorius, and in the same volume had vehemently attacked Pelagius and the Pelagians as the first authors of that heresy, it seemed to some that it was regarded as a slanderous charge that Cassian himself should be accused of the Pelagian heresy by Catholic men such as Prosper and others. Accordingly, the Conferences of the Fathers were heedlessly read by the faithful without suspicion of error and without discrimination, since Cassian was considered a Catholic man whose entire work was thought to be Catholic. Thus they unknowingly became Pelagians, at least in that respect in which the powers of free will were proclaimed against grace.

“To meet these hidden evils, Saint Prosper composed a book against the Collator in that year. It is distinguished for its learning: it exposes the poisons and prepares an antidote against them.” Thus far Baronius [Col. 0900B] (volume V of the Annals, year 433).

In what respect Cassian seemed to approach Pelagianism or to favor the Pelagian heresy will be explained more fully in this treatise. I judged that D. Prosper’s book ought to be attached and appended at the end of this work, together with the annotations and censures of D. Cuychius and Peter Ciaconius, so that nothing might be lacking for the completion of the present work and so that the reader’s diligence, tranquility, and security might all be served. From it I shall conveniently extract, in summary form and in their appropriate places during the course of this Conference, many of the antidotes, inserting them as we proceed, so that the reader may have readily before his eyes the path by which to withdraw his foot from scandal or error, and may know, according to the Apostle, “to test everything and hold fast what is good” (1 Thessalonians V); or, as Isaiah says, may know “to reject evil and choose good” (Isaiah 7), lest he drink poison instead of milk and imbibe falsehood instead of truth.

I add in passing that this Conference of Cassian’s, printed separately in some places, was prohibited in the Roman Index. [Col. 0900C] Thus it is stated there in the appendix (Letter C): “Cassian of Constantinople, On Free Will, a Conference, printed at Haguenau by Johann Sicerus in 1528.”

As for Chaeremon, whom Cassian here introduces as disputing, let no one suppose that his sanctity or authority was formerly diminished because of this Conference, which is sprinkled with errors. His distinguished memory appropriately presented itself in the litanies instituted by Pope Gregory the Blessed (as reported by Arnoldus Wion, The Tree of Life, book V). There, among the holy monks and hermits, the principal authors or speakers of these Conferences are invoked under the same title of sanctity; among them is our Chaeremon, or Chaerimon, for this is how it appears there:

“Saint Paphnutius, pray for us. Saint Serene, pray for us. Saint Nesteros, pray for us. Saint Chaeremon, pray for us. [Col. 0900D] Saint Moses, pray for us. Saint Abraham, pray for us. Saint Isaac, pray for us.”

Since this solemn and public invocation, instituted and celebrated by so great a pontiff, Gregory the Great, and approved by the consent of the entire Church, establishes that this Chaeremon, together with the other anchorites who authored these Conferences, was regarded and counted by the Church among the saints, it is reasonable to say that this otherwise most holy man may at some time have held an erroneous opinion concerning the grace of God and human free will—if the account and Conference that Cassian attributes to him are genuine, as we suppose—but that he later came to his senses and corrected the error conceived through simplicity, after recognizing the truth and acquiring sounder doctrine, and that he remained in the true and Catholic understanding and judgment of the Church.]

## CHAPTER II

Objection: Why are the merits of virtues not attributed to the effort of the one who labors?

Then Germanus said:

“To the extent that we are almost,” he said, “if I may put it so, excluded from believing in the possibility of that most excellent height of virtue which was disclosed in the nighttime discussion, to that same extent—if I may say so with your permission—it seems absurd to us that the reward of labor, namely, the perfection of chastity, which is acquired through the persistence of one’s own sweat, should not be specially attributed to the effort of the one who labors. For it is unreasonable that, if we see a farmer applying unremitting zeal to the cultivation of the earth, we should not ascribe the harvest also to the effectiveness of his labor.”

## CHAPTER III

Answer: Without the help of God, not only can the perfection of chastity be achieved, but absolutely nothing good can be accomplished.

Chaeremon said:

“By the very example you have proposed, [Col. 0901A] it is more clearly demonstrated that the effort of one who labors can achieve nothing without the help of God. For even when the farmer has expended all his efforts in cultivating the fields, he cannot immediately attribute the yield of the crops and the abundance of the harvest to his own industry. He has often learned that his industry is fruitless unless suitable rains and the calm serenity of winter follow it.

“Thus we have often seen crops already grown and solidified in complete maturity snatched, as it were, from the hands of those who were holding them, and all that unbroken persistence of sweat contribute nothing to those who labored, because it was not directed by the Lord’s assistance. Therefore, just as divine mercy does not grant an abundance of crops to idle farmers who often fail to work their fields with the plow, so the sleepless anxiety of those who labor will be of no benefit unless the Lord’s mercy prospers it.

“Yet human pride must in no way attempt either to equal or to mingle itself with the grace of God, or seek to insert itself as a partner in God’s gifts by imagining that its labor is the author of divine generosity and boasting that the abundant yield of crops has corresponded to the merits of its industry. Let it consider and weigh with truthful examination that it could not even have expended the efforts which it applied, intent upon the desire for abundance, through its own strength, unless the Lord’s protection and mercy had strengthened it for every task of agriculture. Its will and power would likewise have been ineffective unless divine clemency had supplied the opportunity to complete the work—an opportunity that is sometimes taken away by excessive drought or excessive rain.

“For since the good of virtue [Lips. in the margin: “virtue is a good”], the health of the body, and the successful outcome of all works and actions are granted by the Lord, we must pray that what is written may not happen to him: that the heaven become bronze and the earth iron, and that what the locust leaves the caterpillar may eat, what the caterpillar leaves the grub may devour, and what the grub leaves the rust may consume (Joel I).

“Nor does the farmer’s labor need divine assistance only in this respect. He also needs it to avert unforeseen accidents. Even if the field has been enriched by the desired fertility of its fruits, he may not only be frustrated by the vain expectation of his hope, but may also be deprived of the abundance of the crops already gathered and stored either on the threshing floor or in the granary.

“From this it is manifestly gathered, [Note: [Col. 0901B] This is a true and Catholic doctrine, which D. Prosper also highly commends at the very beginning of his work, as a kind of preface (chapter 3). There, distinguishing truth from falsehood and giving his judgment concerning this Conference, he says: “Yet although at the beginning of the discussion it does not depart from the piety of truth and deserves to be honored with a just proclamation, it deviates from the rectitude with which it began through a headlong and oblique progress.” For, after comparing the farmer, whom he adapted as a figure of one who lives under grace and faith, and declaring his labor fruitless unless he were assisted in every respect by God, he introduced a thoroughly Catholic definition, saying: “From this it is manifestly gathered that not only the beginnings of actions but also of good thoughts are from God,” etc. Thus Saint Prosper; and again, near the end of his little work, when gathering together the principal definitions of this Conference, he places this same definition first, embracing it and confessing it to be Catholic. This assertion is a principal foundation of Catholic doctrine against the Pelagians. For after Cassian’s words, “He who begins what is good and carries it out,” there follows in Antoninus: “Therefore, if we are drawn, what we follow is not ours but his by whom we are drawn; but to resist and refuse to follow is ours.” Thus it stands there. Thus Augustine, On the Spirit and the Letter, chapter 34: “Certainly God works in a person even the will to believe, and his mercy anticipates us in all things; but to consent to God’s call or to dissent from it belongs to the will itself.” And in book II of On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, chapter 5: “God is called our helper; and he cannot help unless one freely attempts something, because God does not work our salvation in us as he does in lifeless stones, or in those whose nature he did not constitute with reason and will.” And in On Predestination and Grace, chapter 9: “God, distributing times and offices, ordained that we should take up the beginnings of good things through his call; but, having been called and enlightened, that we should recognize the ways of his commandments through the understanding of a good disposition, and freely choose either to follow them or to abandon them.” Prosper, book II of On the Calling of the Gentiles, chapter 26: “We believe and experience this more abundant grace to be so powerful that we in no way consider it violent. This was also defined by the Council of Trent, session 6, chapter 5 and canon 6.” Thus far in D. Antoninus, from Peter Maturus.]

They have hardened their necks; they would not return.’”

## CHAPTER IV

Objection: How is it said that the Gentiles possessed chastity without the grace of God?

Germanus said:

“To this view, whose piety we cannot abruptly reject, there seems to be an obstacle [Col. 0903B] in what tends toward the destruction of free will. [Note: [Col. 0903B] This is the old refrain or complaint of the Pelagians: once the necessity of grace is established, human free will is overthrown and destroyed. The Fathers, however, answer them in the opposite way: free will is not destroyed by grace but rather perfected, because what it cannot do by itself and through its own powers it receives through God’s grace so that it can do it.

Thus D. Jerome, in his letter to Ctesiphon against the Pelagians, responds elegantly to Pelagius’s maxim, “If I need the assistance of another, freedom is destroyed in me”: “To will and to run is mine; but this ‘mine,’ without God’s continual assistance, will not be mine.” And Augustine, letter 89: “Free will is freer in proportion as it is healthier; and it is healthier in proportion as it is more subject to divine mercy and grace.” And below: “Free will is not removed because it is helped; rather, it is helped because it is not removed. For whoever says to God, ‘Be my helper,’ confesses that he wishes to fulfill what God has commanded, but asks assistance from the one who commanded it, so that he may be able.”

The same, letter 105: “Those who think that free will is taken away from them if they admit that human beings cannot have even a good will without the help of God do not understand that they are not strengthening the human will, but driving it to move through empty spaces, rather than placing it in the Lord as upon a firm rock.” Prosper, Against the Collator, chapter 38: “We are not troubled by the foolish complaint of the proud, who claim that free will is taken away if the beginnings, progress, and perseverance in good things to the end are said to be gifts of God, since the aids of divine grace are the foundations of the human will.”]

“For since we see many among the Gentiles, who certainly do not merit the grace of divine assistance, shining not only with the virtues of frugality and patience, but—what is even more astonishing—with the virtues of chastity as well, how are we to believe that these virtues were bestowed upon them by God’s gift when the judgment of free will had been taken captive? After all, as far as we have learned either from the sequence of our reading or from the traditions of certain people, the followers of worldly wisdom, who were utterly ignorant not only of God’s grace but even of the true God himself, are said to have possessed the highest purity of chastity through the diligence of their own labor.” [Col. 0904A]

## CHAPTER V

Answer: The imaginary chastity of the philosophers.

Chaeremon said:

“I am pleased that, while you burn with the highest love of recognizing the truth, you have also proposed certain foolish arguments, through whose objection the virtue of the Catholic faith may appear more approved and, so to speak, more thoroughly tested. For what wise person would employ propositions so contradictory that, although yesterday you asserted that the heavenly purity of chastity could not be bestowed upon any mortal even through the grace of God, you now believe that the same purity was possessed by Gentiles through their own virtue?

“But since you are certainly raising these matters—as has been said—in your zeal to test the truth, pay attention to what we are to hold concerning them. First, [Note: [Col. 0903D] What is said here about chastity, D. Augustine establishes generally about the moral virtues. He holds that among philosophers and other Gentiles or unbelievers, however celebrated for virtue, there was no true virtue in the absolute and proper sense, but either simulated and shadowy virtue, or virtue that was merely begun and imperfect.

Thus he says in book XIX of The City of God, chapter 25: “However much the mind may seem laudably to rule the body, and reason the vices, if the mind and reason themselves do not serve God, as God himself has commanded that he be served, they in no way rightly rule the body and the vices. For how can the mind be mistress of the body and the vices when it does not know the true God and is not subject to his authority, but has been prostituted to the most vicious demons who corrupt it? Therefore, the virtues which it seems to possess, by which it rules the body and the vices, unless it refers them to God as the goal to be attained or held, are themselves vices rather than virtues. For although some then consider them true and honorable virtues when they are referred to themselves and sought for no other reason, even then they are inflated and proud, and therefore must be judged not virtues but vices.”

The same author, book IV Against Julian (chapter 3): “Far be it from us to say that true virtue exists in anyone unless he is just. But far be it from us to say that anyone is truly just unless he lives by faith. ‘The just shall live by faith’ (Romans I). Who among those who wish to be regarded as Christians, except the Pelagians alone, would call an unbeliever just, or call an impious person just, or call one enslaved to the devil just? Let him be Fabricius, let him be Fabius, let him be Scipio, let him be Regulus,” etc. And below: “Far be it from us to say that true virtues serve anyone except the one to whom and for whom we say, ‘God of virtues, convert us’ (Psalm LXXIX). Therefore, virtues that serve carnal pleasures, or any temporal advantages and profits, cannot be true at all. But those that wish to serve no one are not true either. For true virtues serve God in human beings, from whom they are given to human beings.”

Thus far D. Augustine on virtues in general. Concerning continence or chastity in particular, he teaches the same thing in the same place, writing among other things: “If the impious do not possess true justice, certainly they do not possess the other virtues that accompany and belong with it, because when the gifts of God are not referred to their own author, those who use them thereby become evil and unjust; and if they possess any, they do not possess them truly. Accordingly, neither is the continence or chastity of the impious true.”]

it must in no way be believed that the philosophers attained such chastity of soul as is required of us, for we are commanded that not only fornication but even impurity should not be named among us. They did possess a certain μερίδα, that is, a small portion of chastity—namely, restraint of the flesh—so that they restrained lust only from intercourse. But this inner, perfect, and perpetual purity of mind and body they were unable not merely to attain in practice, but even to conceive. [Note: [Col. 0904D] Ciaconius reads μερικήν, that is, partial, divided, or imperfect. The word is derived from μέρις, “a part” or “small portion”; μερική means divided, halved, or imperfect. Abbot John explains it in Conference 19, chapter 9: “But this is μερική, that is, not perfection consummated in every respect, but a part of perfection.”]

Finally, that most famous Socrates of theirs, [Note: [Col. 0905B] He was judged the wisest of the Greeks by the oracle of Apollo at Delphi. According to Augustine (City of God, book VIII, chapter 2), he is remembered as the first to turn all philosophy toward the correction and ordering of morals, whereas before him all men had devoted most of their effort to investigating physical, that is, natural, matters.] was not ashamed to confess this about himself, as they themselves celebrate it. For when a certain physiognomist, [Note: [Col. 0905B] A physiognomist, or physiognomon, is one who recognizes or conjectures a person’s morals, character, disposition, or inclination from the body and face. Such was Zopyrus, who made observations about Socrates. Cicero says of him in On Fate: “What of Socrates? Have we not read how Zopyrus, the physiognomist, marked him? He professed that he could thoroughly recognize the morals and natures of human beings from their bodies, eyes, faces, and foreheads.” Caelius Rhodiginus (book VI, chapter 2) says: “Physiognomy is that part of divination which conjectures the morals of human beings from the mouth and from the face, movement, and shape of all the bodily members. Concerning it, Aristotle and Adamantius [Origen] wrote, as did many other Latin and Greek authors” (Alexander ab Alexandro, book II of Genialia, chapter 19).] had said to him, [Note: [Col. 0905C] This reading of Ciaconius seemed more suitable and appropriate than that of Cuychius and others, ὄμματα παιδερασταί, “eyes of corrupters of boys.” The interjection O is understood, expressing mockery or reproach: “O eyes of a corrupter of boys!” Paederastes and paederastia are disgraceful terms, and the vice itself is even more disgraceful; Socrates was accused of it along with other philosophers and distinguished men. Hence Tertullian, in Apologeticus (chapter 46): “If they challenge us concerning chastity, I read part of the sentence pronounced by the Athenian court against Socrates, the corrupter of young men.” Seneca says something similar (On Tranquility of Mind, chapter 15): “Socrates was not ashamed to play with boys.” Concerning other corrupters of this kind and the disgrace attached to this vice, see, if desired, Caelius Rhodiginus, book XV, chapters 9 and 10.

D. Jerome likewise, discussing this vice in his commentary on Isaiah II, says: “The Greeks and Romans once suffered from this vice to such an extent that even the most distinguished philosophers of Greece publicly kept boys as lovers; and Hadrian, educated in the arts of philosophy, consecrated Antinous as a god and established a temple, sacrifices, and priests for him. From this, a city and region of Egypt received its name. Boys also stood among prostitutes in the brothels, exposed to public lust, until under the Emperor Constantine, when the Gospel of Christ shone forth, both the unbelief of all the nations and this shamefulness were destroyed.” Thus D. Jerome.

Prudentius too, in his poem Against Symmachus, the consul, reproaches Antinous, Hadrian’s Ganymede, in these same terms:

“What should I say of Antinous, placed in the heavenly seat?

Once the delight of that divine prince; him

Stripped of his manly lot in the purple lap,

The Ganymede of the god Hadrian,” etc.

Chrysostom also frequently repeats these things (Homily 27 on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians and Homily 66 to the people of Antioch). For this reason, and with this disgrace in view, the Apostle Paul, severely reproving such wise men of this age—that is, the Gentile philosophers—says that they were delivered over by God’s just judgment to dishonorable passions and to a reprobate mind, so that they did what is not fitting, males working shame with males and receiving in themselves the recompense which was due for their error (Romans I), etc. See also D. Cyprian, Letter 2 to Donatus.]

a physiognomist had said, “ὄμματα παιδεραστοῦ”—that is, “the eyes of a corrupter of boys”—and his disciples rushed upon the man, wishing to avenge the insult offered to their teacher, Socrates is said to have restrained their indignation with these words: “Παύσασθε ἑταῖροι, εἰμὶ γὰρ, ἀλλ᾽ ἀπέχω,” that is, “Stop, friends; for I am, but I restrain myself.”

It is therefore shown most clearly, not only by our assertion but also by their own confession, that they suppressed only the consummation of immodesty—that is, the shameful act of intercourse—by a forceful constraint; they did not, however, exclude the desire from their hearts or the pleasure of that passion. [Col. 0905B]

And with what horror must that saying of Diogenes be uttered? [Note: [Col. 0906B] As the saying goes, the lid is worthy of such a dish; the saying is worthy of such a philosopher. The disgrace of this Diogenes, the Cynic philosopher—called “Cynic” because of his doglike shamefulness and obscenity—is sufficiently well known. In addition to Plutarch and Laertius, see D. Augustine, City of God, book XIV, chapter 20. Since, according to Aristotle (Aristotle, Politics), each person judges matters in accordance with the disposition of his own mind, it is not surprising that a doglike man—indeed, more truly a dog than a philosopher—should have judged adultery, because it was offered freely, no more deserving of punishment than canine filth.] For what the philosopher of this world was not ashamed to put forward as something memorable [Col. 0906A] cannot be repeated by us without shame or heard without disgust.

For when someone was accused of adultery [Note: [Col. 0906C] That is, someone who was to be punished for the crime of adultery. That adultery was also punished by death among the Gentiles may be inferred from this passage (Alexander ab Alexandro, Genialia, book IV, chapter 1; Aulus Gellius, book X, chapter 23). It is more certainly established by the Julian Law on Adultery, which condemns adulterers and adulteresses to capital punishment. Among the Jews, the adulteress was ordered to be killed together with the adulterer (Leviticus XX and Deuteronomy XXII). Later, however, the custom was introduced that adulteresses should be buried under stones, as is clear from the history of Susanna (Daniel XIII) and of the woman caught in adultery (John VIII). Among Christians also adultery was punished by death, as is shown by a letter of D. Jerome concerning a woman struck seven times because of an accusation of adultery falsely brought against her and her husband (Letter 49). See also Cassiodorus, Various Letters (book I, letter 37; book V, letter 33; book IX, letter 18), and the edict of King Theodoric preserved by him.], he said, as they relate: “τὸ δωρεὰν πωλούμενον θανάτῳ μὴ ἀγόραζε,” that is, “Do not buy with death what is sold for free.”

It is therefore established that they did not even recognize as a virtue the true chastity that is sought from us. And so it is sufficiently certain that our circumcision, which is spiritual, can be possessed only as a gift of God, and that it exists only in those who serve God with complete contrition of spirit.

## CHAPTER VI

That without the grace of God we are able to carry out no strenuous efforts.

Although in many cases—indeed, in all cases—it can be shown that human beings always need God’s assistance [Col. 0906B], and that human weakness is utterly unable by itself, that is, without God’s help, to accomplish anything pertaining to salvation [Col. 0907A], this is demonstrated nowhere more clearly than in the acquisition and preservation of chastity.

[Note: [Col. 0906D] This is a pious and Catholic assertion, if understood in a sound and Catholic sense. But Cassian, or his interpreter Chaeremon, does not seem to have understood it in the sense conveyed by these words, as is clear from what we noted in Book XII of the *Institutes*, chapter 12 and following chapters, and will become still clearer from the next chapters of this Conference. The whole force lies in the word “perfect,” which he explains elsewhere (*Conference* 12, chapters 11 and 13) as obtaining the perfection of the virtues, or attaining the end or summit of perfection. By this expression he wished to signify—though not without a certain artifice—that a person can, by the powers of nature, or free will, and without God’s prevenient grace, begin or initiate something that pertains to obtaining justification, grace, and salvation; but cannot perfect it or bring it to the end of perfection without God’s special and supernatural assistance. Catholic truth, however, teaches that not only the progress, perfection, and completion of virtues and good works, but also their very beginning, initiation, desire, faith, and prayer, are gifts of God and depend upon God’s grace. In this consists nearly the whole controversy of Saint Prosper and the other Fathers against Cassian and his associates, the clergy of Massilia; it will be explained more fully as this Conference proceeds.]

For, leaving aside for the moment a discussion of the difficulty of its purity, let us briefly discuss its means. Who, I ask, however fervent in spirit, could sustain by his own strength the squalor of solitude, or dry bread—not merely daily hunger, but even satiety—without the support of human praise? Who could endure perpetual thirst for water without the Lord’s consolation? Who could deprive his eyes of that sweet and delightful morning sleep, and confine all refreshment of rest within a continuous observance of four hours? [Col. 0907C]

[Note: [Col. 0907C] Among the other means or instruments for acquiring perfect and consummate chastity, he listed this in the preceding Conference: “If he limits the repose of sleep to a period of three or—as others have determined—four hours.” [Col. 0907D] From this we infer that those holy anchorites and monks, lovers of perfect chastity, allowed themselves only three or four hours for sleep and rest. This is also understood from Cassian’s *Institutes*, Books II and III, where it is said that monks were not permitted to return to sleep after the night office and the morning Lauds; rather, they devoted the remainder of the night to prayer, meditation, or manual labor (*Institutes* II.13 and III.5). There were also some who allowed themselves not even an hour for sleep; hence they were called ἀκοίμητοι, that is, sleepless. Evagrius discusses them in his *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapters 19 and 20. Abba Arsenius, as recorded in the *Lives of the Fathers* (Book V, booklet 4 of the new edition), kept vigil all night; and when, toward morning, he wished to sleep because of nature’s necessity, he would say to sleep, “Come, wicked servant,” and would steal a little sleep while sitting, then immediately rise. More examples may be found in Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, in the accounts of Moses the Ethiopian, Macarius, and others. See Turrecremata on chapter 23 of Saint Benedict’s Rule, where he argues against sleepy monks.]

Who could sustain unremitting persistence in reading? Who could complete unrelenting diligence in work, seeking no advantage of present profit, without God’s grace? [Col. 0907B] Just as all these things cannot continually be desired by us without divine inspiration, so they cannot in any way be brought to completion without his assistance.

And to make these same points clearer to us, not only through the discipline of tested experience but also through definite indications and arguments: when we desire to accomplish many things that are useful, and the full ardor of desire and a perfect will are not lacking, does not some intervening weakness frustrate our conceived resolutions, so that the result does not support our purpose unless the power to complete it has been granted by the Lord’s mercy? Thus, although there is an innumerable multitude of those who faithfully desire to cling to the pursuit of the virtues, you will nevertheless find only a small number who are able to complete or endure these things. I shall pass over the fact that even when no weakness at all restrains us, the entire capacity to accomplish whatever we wish [Col. 0908A] does not lie within our power.

For we do not retain at our own discretion either the withdrawal into silence, the strictness of fasts, or the persistence of reading, even at a time when we are able to do so; rather, when certain circumstances arise, we are frequently drawn away, even very unwillingly, from salutary practices. Thus we must ask the Lord for the availability of a place or time in which we can practice these things. It is certainly established that what we can do is not sufficient for us unless the Lord also grants the opportunity to carry out those things that are in fact possible for us. Concerning this the Apostle says: “Because we wished to come to you both once and again, but Satan hindered us” (1 Thess. 2). Sometimes, therefore, we even perceive that we are usefully called away from these spiritual pursuits, so that when the direction of our course is interrupted against our will, and we grant some respite to the weakness of the flesh, we are preserved, even unwillingly, for salutary perseverance. Concerning this dispensation of God, the blessed Apostle says something similar: “For this reason I pleaded with the Lord three times that he might depart from me; and he said to me: My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor. 12). And again: “For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought” (Rom. 8).

## CHAPTER VII. On God’s Principal Purpose and His Daily Providence

God’s purpose—by which he did not make the human being to perish, but to live forever—remains immovable. When his goodness perceives that even the smallest spark of good will has shone forth in us, or when he himself has struck it out, as it were, from the hard flint of our heart, he cherishes and awakens it, strengthening it by his inspiration [Col. 0908C], wishing all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. 2).

[Note: [Col. 0908C] Here at last the Author begins to reveal his own mind, and the beginning of his error, which he explains more clearly in the following chapter. For what he here calls a “spark,” there he calls a certain “beginning” or “origin” of good will, where he treats the matter at greater length.]

[Note: [Col. 0908C] “Before our Savior God, who wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Tim. 2). This statement has received various interpretations. Saint Thomas gives three of them from the Fathers (*Summa Theologiae* I, question 39, article 6): “That word of the Apostle, that God wills all human beings to be saved, and so forth, can be understood in three ways. First, the distribution may be understood appropriately in this sense: God wills all human beings who are saved to be saved. This does not mean that there is any human being whom he does not will to be saved, but that no one is saved whom he does not will to be saved, as Augustine says (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, Book I, chapter 8). Second, it may be understood as a distribution by kinds of individuals, not of all individuals within each kind, in this sense: God wills human beings from every state to be saved—men and women, Jews and Gentiles, small and great—but not all from each individual state. Third, according to Damascene (*On the Faith*, Book II, chapter 9), it is understood of the antecedent will, not the consequent will. This distinction is not taken from the side of the divine will, in which there is nothing earlier or later, but from the side of the things willed.” [Col. 0909C] Thus far Saint Thomas, who then explains at greater length what the antecedent and consequent will are; the reader may consult him there.

Damascene’s teaching concerning God’s antecedent and consequent will is as follows: “It must be understood that God antecedently wills all to be saved and to possess his kingdom. For he did not form us in order to punish us, but, being good, in order to make us sharers in his goodness; yet he wills to punish sinners as the just one. The first will is therefore called antecedent and good pleasure, which he conceived in himself; the other is consequent and permission, having its cause from us.”

By his antecedent will, therefore, God wills all to be saved—that is, insofar as it depends upon him and on his part—because he created all for eternal blessedness and established and provides for all the means suitable to attaining it. By his consequent and absolute will, however, he wills to render to each person according to his works, whether reward or punishment, as the law of equity and justice requires. For the Lord is proclaimed not only merciful but also just.]

And again: “It is not the will of your Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish” (Matt. 18). And again: “God does not will the soul to perish, but devises plans, considering how the one who has been cast out may not utterly perish” [Lipsius in the margin: “deliberating, he considers”] (2 Sam. 14). God is truthful and does not lie when he solemnly declares: “As I live, says the Lord God, I do not will the death of the wicked, but that he should turn from his way and live” (Ezek. 33).

If he does not will one of the little ones to perish, how can he be thought, without grievous sacrilege, to will not universally that all, but only some in place of all, should be saved? [Col. 0909A] Therefore, whoever perishes, perishes against his will, while he daily cries out to each one of them: “Turn back from your evil ways, and why will you die, house of Israel?” (ibid.). And again: “How often I wished to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling” (Matt. 23). And again: “Why has this people in Jerusalem turned away with a stubborn turning? They hardened their faces [Lipsius in the margin: “necks”]; they were unwilling to return” (Jer. 8).

[Note: [Col. 0909D] This is not directed against the absolute will, which is called the will of good pleasure, concerning which it is said: “Whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth” (Ps. 134); and: “Who resists his will?” (Rom. 9). Rather, it is directed against the antecedent will, by which God is said to will all human beings to be saved, insofar as it depends upon him, because he prevents no one from salvation but invites and urges all toward it, as was said; or against the will of sign, because God has set before all his precepts and counsels by which he instructs and invites them to salvation. The will of sign is called the sign of his will, as are precepts and counsels; thus we call a prince’s letters his will, that is, the sign of his will.]

[Note: [Col. 0910C] These statements at first sight appear pious and Catholic, and they can serve to prove that sufficient help of grace is given to all human beings, at the appropriate time and place, by which they can be saved, according to the more probable opinion of theologians. Yet something lies hidden beneath the surface that pertains to Pelagianism, as can be gathered from what has been said.

The Pelagians, and those who secretly favored the Pelagians in Gaul, held that God’s grace was prepared for all human beings, provided that they themselves were willing to ask for and receive it; but they held that each person could, by the powers of free will and without any other prevenient grace, desire, invoke, and receive grace. Catholic teaching, on the other hand, is that no one can ask or invoke grace—or even think of doing so—unless, through God’s prevenient grace, he is stirred up and moved to ask, knock, and invoke. Therefore God’s grace and the movement of the Holy Spirit precede all our desires and every invocation of ours.

This was defined in the Council of Orange in these words (Canon 3): “If anyone says that God’s grace can be conferred through human invocation, but does not acknowledge that grace itself causes us to invoke it, he contradicts the prophet Isaiah, or the Apostle, who says the same thing: I was found by those who did not seek me; I openly appeared to those who did not ask for me” (Isa. 65; Rom. 10).]

God’s grace, then, is present daily. Since it wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, it calls everyone without exception, saying: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11). But if he calls not all universally, but only some, it follows that not all are burdened either by original or by actual sin; nor would the statement be true: “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God,” nor would death be believed to have passed through all human beings (Rom. 3).

All who perish perish so much against God’s will that God is not even said to have made death, as Scripture bears witness: “For God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living” (Wis. 1). Hence it is that, when we ask for things contrary to our good, our prayer is often heard either late or not at all; and, conversely, the Lord, like a most kindly physician, sometimes inflicts upon us—even when we are wholly unwilling—things that we believe to be contrary to us, usefully restraining and turning back our harmful purposes and deadly efforts from their destructive outcome, drawing those who hasten toward death back to salvation, and extracting the ignorant from the jaws of hell.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Grace of God and the Freedom of the Will

The divine word elegantly expressed this care and providence of his toward us through the prophet Hosea, under the figure of Jerusalem as a prostitute eagerly pursuing the worship of idols. When she says: “I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my water, my wool and my flax, my oil and my drink,” the divine condescension, consulting her salvation rather than her will, replies: “Behold, I will hedge her way with thorns; I will wall her in, and she will not find her paths. She will pursue her lovers and will not overtake them; she will seek them and will not find them. Then she will say: I will return to my first husband, because it was better for me then than it is now” (Hos. 2).

Again, he describes our defiance and contempt—by which, in a rebellious spirit, we disdain him when he invites us to return to salvation—through this comparison: “And I said: You will call me Father, and you will not cease to follow after me. But just as a woman despises her lover, so the house of Israel has despised me, says the Lord” (Jer. 3).

This is entirely fitting. Since he had compared Jerusalem to an adulterous woman leaving her husband, he also compared the love and perseverance of his kindness to the love of a husband who is deserted by his wife. The piety and love of God, which are always expended upon the human race, cannot be more aptly expressed by another comparison: God is never so overcome by any injuries that he withdraws from caring for our salvation, or, as though defeated by our iniquities, is recalled from his original purpose; rather, he resembles a man who loves a woman with ardent love, and the more he senses himself neglected by her, the more intensely he is inflamed with passionate zeal for her.

Divine protection, therefore, is always inseparably present with us. So great is the Creator’s piety toward his creature that he not only accompanies it but also precedes it with continual providence. The Prophet experienced this and openly confessed it to the Lord, saying: “My God, his mercy will come before me” (Ps. 58).

[Note: [Col. 0911A] This is the stumbling block and rock of offense; it is, I say, Cassian’s first and principal lapse and error. By it both he himself and the other presbyters of Massilia who, as is believed, were instructed by him, began to attack and criticize Saint Augustine’s doctrine of grace, promulgated against the Pelagians, and on this account stirred up great dissension and controversy in the Gallican Church.

To make the matter clearer and easier to understand—since the understanding of the rest of this Conference and discussion depends entirely upon it—I have thought it worthwhile first to explain briefly the subject of the disagreement that arose between Augustine and his disciples on the one hand, and Cassian, the Massilians, and the other Gauls on the other, concerning the necessity of grace and its cooperation with free will.

In this controversy Saint Augustine fought against two errors. First, he fought against the heretics Pelagius and Coelestius, who asserted the following concerning grace:

1. That a human being could, by the powers of nature alone, by the faculty of free will alone, and without special assistance—that is, without God’s prevenient grace and inward movement, excitation, and illumination—obtain the gift of faith and the grace of justification, observe [lacuna] the law, persevere in righteousness to the end, and finally merit eternal life;

2. That the special grace of Christ was useful only for accomplishing and obtaining these things more easily and successfully, but was not absolutely necessary;

3. That this grace was granted to us according to our merits—that is, according to works performed by our own powers—and was given to us by merit in strict justice.

Against these errors Saint Augustine and the other Fathers proved that Christian faith is a supernatural gift of God, and that no one can believe, be justified, observe the law, or attain salvation without God’s special assistance and prevenient, accompanying, and cooperating grace.

Second, Augustine disputed against another error, namely that of those whom Saint Prosper and Hilary call “the remnants of the Pelagians,” and who were commonly called Semi-Pelagians. As has been said, these were the clergy of Massilia in Gaul Narbonensis. Among them was Cassian, who had migrated from Palestine to Massilia, as we related from Gennadius and Trithemius in the Preface, and who possessed great renown and authority for his learning. He was regarded as the principal author of this teaching, as is clear both from Hilary’s and Prosper’s letters to Augustine (Augustine, volume VII), and from Prosper himself at the beginning of his book against the Collator, where, pointing out Cassian, he says: “We shall report chiefly the definitions of one man who, as there is no doubt, surpasses all those others in the study of the sacred Scriptures,” and so forth. (See below, after Saint Prosper’s book.)

Many bishops throughout Gaul followed their opinion. Pope Celestine wrote a letter to them in which he restrained the boldness of the Massilians and approved Augustine’s doctrine.

These men, therefore, being otherwise Catholic and religious, admitted against Pelagius that Christ’s grace—both external preaching and internal inspiration and illumination—was not merely useful but necessary for justification, perseverance, and the merit of eternal life. Unless our efforts were assisted by it, they held, we would not merely achieve with difficulty what we pursued, as the Pelagians maintained; rather, our efforts would be entirely useless and empty for obtaining justification and meriting eternal life. Up to this point they thought correctly.

But they added something erroneous and alien to the truth: that certain beginnings of good wills and affections could arise from us without any inward movement of Christ’s grace, and that, on account of these beginnings, God’s grace would subsequently be conferred upon us to advance such efforts and pious desires.

They therefore held that free will, by its own powers alone, could initiate any good work—at least by willing, striving, and desiring—and could, through this desire, obtain grace for completing it, by way of merit of suitability (*meritum de congruo*). Thus, a prayer proceeding from faith, according to Augustine’s opinion, is effective in obtaining the grace of justification and merits it by suitability.

For this reason they were rightly called not Pelagians but Semi-Pelagians: whereas Pelagius declared God’s grace necessary neither for beginning nor for completing a good work, they embraced the former part and rejected the latter as erroneous. Thus, in the question of the necessity of grace, they agreed with him only halfway.

From this error, admitted as a false foundation and evil first principle, it followed that they accepted many other absurd and paradoxical positions consistent with and consequent upon it: that the beginning of salvation comes from us; that God’s grace is the attendant of our will; that the assistance of grace is subject to human obedience; that God’s grace is sometimes preceded by our prayers; that a human being can in some way prepare himself to receive grace by the powers of nature alone; and similar opinions. All these are handed down by Chaeremon and gravely and sharply attacked by Saint Prosper throughout the remaining discussion, from this point to the end of the Conference.

From this also one can infer why Cassian titled this Conference not simply *On the Grace of God* but *On the Protection of God*: namely, because he judged that God’s grace was not simply necessary for awakening or initiating a good purpose in us, but for protecting—that is, preserving and advancing—it.

Having noted these points generally concerning the cause of Cassian and the Massilians, we must now examine and pursue the words of the text quoted above. The Collator first presupposes what was noted earlier: that a certain beginning or origin of good will can occasionally emerge from us without God’s help—that is, that a human being can, by the powers of nature alone, will or think something good.

This is directly contrary, first, to the Catholic statement that he himself had earlier placed as the foundation of the entire discussion and confirmed by the testimony of Scripture (chapter 3): “Not only the beginning of actions but also of good thoughts is from God, who inspires in us both the beginnings of holy will and the power and opportunity to carry out what we rightly desire—or have begun. Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” (James 1), and so forth.

Saint Prosper repeatedly sets this definition of his against him, and on this basis reproves him for levity and inconstancy, since he contradicts himself: having previously attributed everything to grace, he now assigns a part to free will.

Second, it is contrary to the manifest testimonies of Scripture, of which the chief are these: “No one can come to me unless my Father draws him” (John 6). “Without me you can do nothing” (John 3). “We are not sufficient to think anything of ourselves, as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Cor. 3). “He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion until the day of Christ” (Phil. 1). “For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure” (Phil. 2).

Third, this opinion is condemned as erroneous and heretical by the Council of Orange, convened by order of Pope Leo against the remnants of the Pelagians. Its seventh canon states: “If anyone affirms that by the strength of nature a person can think or choose any good pertaining to the salvation of eternal life, he is deceived by a heretical spirit, not understanding the voice of God in the Gospel: Without me you can do nothing (John 13); and the Apostle’s words: Not that we are capable of thinking anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God (Phil. 1).”

Fourth, it is condemned by the supreme pontiffs, especially by Celestine in that letter to the bishops of Gaul in which he imposed silence upon the Massilians. Among other things he says: “The will is prepared by the Lord, and, so that they may do something good, he himself touches the hearts of the faithful with paternal inspirations. For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the children of God” (Rom. 8). Thus we should not feel that our free will is absent, yet we should not doubt that his assistance is stronger in each movement of the human will toward good.

God works in human hearts and in free will itself in such a way that holy thought, pious counsel, and every movement of good will are from God, because through him we can do something good, and without him we can do nothing.

Fifth, it is also refuted by other Fathers, especially Augustine, Prosper, Fulgentius, and others. I omit their testimonies in order to avoid excessive length, especially since some will be brought forward below when appropriate.

Finally, there is the condemnation of the works of Cassian and of Faustus, bishop of Riez, at the Roman Council presided over by the holy pontiff Gelasius; it is found in Gratian’s *Decree*, distinction 16, chapter “Sancta Romana.” The works of Cassian—which otherwise contain many highly useful and salutary things—were counted among the apocrypha for no other reason than this opinion concerning good works pertaining to piety, which he maintained could be performed or initiated without the assistance of grace.

Hence Gennadius is exposed as manifestly false, a man of Massilian origin and stained with the Massilian taint. In order to excuse Cassian, he condemns and attacks Saint Prosper in these words: “I have read Prosper’s book against works whose author Cassian is suppressed by name; works that the Church of God approves as salutary, he brands as harmful” (Baronius, *Annals*, year 433).

Such was Gennadius, who, by condemning Prosper, acquits Cassian, and by acquitting Cassian, condemns Prosper—worthy of as much confidence in this matter as in many others: when he prefers Rufinus to Saint Jerome, a doctor who deserved so well of the Church; when he accuses Augustine of not escaping sin through excessive speech; when he praises the *eulogies* (εὐλογίαι) of Pelagius, which Saint Jerome declares in his *Dialogues against the Pelagians* to be full of heresies; when he commends the books of Faustus of Riez on grace and free will, which Peter Damian and other Eastern authorities anathematize; and in similar cases.]

When he has perceived in us some beginning of good will, he immediately enlightens and strengthens it, and urges it toward salvation, granting increase to what he himself either planted or has seen emerge through our effort. For he says: “Before they call, I will answer; while they are still speaking, I will hear” (Isa. 65). And again: “As soon as he hears the voice of your cry, he will answer you” (Isa. 30). He not only benevolently inspires holy desires, but also prepares opportunities for life and shows those who have gone astray the opportunity for good action and the direction of the way of salvation [Col. 0914A].

## CHAPTER IX. On the Power of Our Good Will and the Grace of God
Therefore [Note: [Col. 0913D] Here again St. Prosper accuses the Collator of contradiction: “He had said,” he remarks, “in regular fashion”—that is, according to the norm and rule of Catholic doctrine—“that the source not only of good actions but also of good thoughts is from God.” And lest this be understood as referring to instruction supplied externally, he had vigilantly added: “Who inspires in us both the beginning of holy will and the power and opportunity to carry out the things we rightly desire” [Col. 0914A]. Then he addresses the Collator as follows: “Catholic teacher, why do you abandon your profession? Why, leaving the most serene light of truth, do you descend into the smoky darkness of falsehood? Why, when you marvel that God gives to those who ask, seek, and knock, do you not ascribe this to the same grace by which it is desired? You see good endeavors and pious pursuits, and do you doubt that they are gifts of God?” and so forth.

Here first observe that Cassian is called “a Catholic teacher,” an outstanding title of honor [Col. 0914B], because, although he turned away from Catholic truth through error, he did not obstinately defend that error against the judgment of the Church. Indeed, it is entirely credible that he later retracted it and yielded to the truth, as we noted in the preface.

To make that contradiction clearer, Prosper shows that the Collator’s fiction and invention was, in a certain sense, a middle position and a third alternative between the Pelagian heresy and Catholic doctrine. According to Pelagius, the beginnings of good wills and thoughts come from us; according to Catholic truth, they come from the grace of God, which precedes and inspires; but according to the Collator, they sometimes come from us and sometimes from grace.

The Collator raises several objections and difficulties from Scripture, which seem to contradict one another, in order to prove that in some cases our will precedes grace, while in others it is preceded by grace. Accordingly, part of good thoughts and wills is to be attributed to free choice and part to grace, as though the Scriptures—which seem now to favor and commend one, now the other—could not otherwise be reconciled [Col. 0914C]. Yet since, according to the truth of the matter, grace cooperates with free choice in every good act, it is not surprising if Scripture sometimes commends free choice, but more often grace (Augustine, *Book II to Boniface*, chapter 8, and *On Grace*, chapter 5).

For, as St. Anselm says (*On the Harmony of Foreknowledge and Predestination*, chapter 3): “When Scripture says something in favor of grace, it does not altogether remove free choice; nor, when it speaks of free choice, does it exclude grace, as though grace alone or free choice alone were sufficient to save a human being,” and so forth. Thus certain Scriptural statements commend grace without excluding free choice; others, conversely, commend freedom without excluding grace, but presupposing it.

On this basis the objection is answered: God gives to those who ask, is found by those who seek, and opens to those who knock; but the very asking, seeking, and knocking come from the grace of God, because no one asks, seeks, or knocks unless preceded, roused, and assisted by God’s grace [Col. 0914D].

God is found by those who do not seek him, and so forth, not only because he calls and bends many who are profoundly alienated, resistant, and ungodly—as is well known from the calling of Paul, Matthew, and Magdalene—but also, generally, because he is found by those who do not seek him of themselves and on their own side, without God’s movement and call. This was also expressly defined at the Council of Orange, in words borrowed from Cassian, canon 6:

“If anyone says that mercy is divinely conferred upon us who believe, will, desire, strive, labor, keep watch, devote ourselves, ask, seek, and knock without the grace of God, but does not acknowledge that, through the infusion and inspiration of the Holy Spirit, it comes about in us that we believe, will, or are able to do all these things as we ought; and if he joins the assistance of grace to human humility and obedience, but does not admit that the gift of that same grace enables us to be obedient and humble, he resists the Apostle who says: ‘What do you have that you did not receive?’ and, ‘By the grace of God I am what I am’ (1 Cor. 4).”

A similar decree is found in the Council of Trent, in these words (Session 6, canon 3):

“If anyone says that without the prevenient inspiration of the Holy Spirit and his assistance a human being can believe, hope, love, or repent as he ought, so that the grace of justification may be bestowed upon him, let him be anathema.]

It is not easily discerned by human reason [Col. 0915A] how the Lord gives to those who ask, is found by those who seek, and opens to those who knock (Matt. 7), and yet is again found by those who do not seek him; how he appears openly among those who were not asking him, and all day long stretches out his hands to a people that does not believe in him and contradicts him (Isa. 65; Rom. 10); how he calls those who resist and are far away, draws the unwilling toward salvation, deprives those who desire to sin of the opportunity to fulfill their will, and in his kindness obstructs those rushing toward wickedness.

[Note: [Col. 0915B] This is the Collator’s second objection, whose principal force lies in the Apostle’s words: “It is not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. 3). The preceding material contributes little or nothing to the issue. For where did the Collator read—except among the Pelagians—that the whole of our salvation is attributed to our own choice, when Scripture says the opposite: “Your destruction is from yourself, Israel, but from me alone is your salvation” (Hos. 13)?

What does the promise about eating the fruits of the land have to do with grace and salvation? Gregory Nazianzen (Oration 31) and Chrysostom (in his commentary) explain the Apostle’s words in such a way that attaining grace and salvation is not the work of the one who wills and runs—that is, of the human being—alone, but of God who shows mercy, because the will is insufficient unless it is assisted by God’s grace.

Yet this explanation does not satisfy St. Augustine. “For,” he says, “if it is rightly said, ‘It is not of the human being who wills, but of God who shows mercy,’ because the human will alone does not accomplish it, why is it not also rightly said, conversely, ‘It is not of God who shows mercy, but of the human being who wills,’ because God’s mercy alone does not accomplish it?” No Christian will dare say this. Thus Augustine (*Enchiridion*, chapter 32).

Although, in running and willing, the human will cooperates with divine mercy, grace itself nevertheless holds the leadership and primacy. This explains why it is not said with equal propriety, “It is not of God who shows mercy, but of the human being who runs,” whereas it is rightly said, “It is not of the human being who wills, but of God who shows mercy.”

Therefore Augustine adds: “It remains that the statement, ‘It is not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy,’ is rightly understood to mean that everything is given to God, who both prepares the human will to be helped and helps it once prepared. For both are found in the sacred utterances: ‘His mercy shall go before me’ (Ps. 58), and, ‘His mercy shall follow me’ (Ps. 22). He goes before the unwilling, so that they may will; he follows the willing, lest they will in vain.”]

But who could easily understand how the whole of salvation is attributed to our own choice, when it is said, “If you are willing and will hear me, you shall eat the good things of the land” (Isa. 1), and how it is not of the one who wills or runs, but of God who shows mercy (Rom. 9)?

[Note: [Col. 0915D] The third objection. It is easily answered that God works in us both to will and to accomplish, because by his grace he makes us willing—that is, gives us a good purpose—and enables us to carry it out. Yet what is thus done remains our work, since it proceeds from our will consenting to and cooperating with divine grace.

Thus God works in us in such a way that we also cooperate with him. “We pray willingly,” says Prosper (*Chapter 38*); and yet, “God sent the Spirit into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. 8). We speak willingly; and yet, if what we say is pious, “it is not we who speak, but the Spirit of our Father who speaks in us” (Matt. 10). We willingly work out our salvation; and yet God himself works in us both the willing and the working (Phil. 2). We willingly love God and our neighbor; and yet love is from God, poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5).

We confess this concerning faith, endurance of sufferings, marital chastity, virginal continence, and every virtue without exception: if these had not been given to us, they would not be found in us.

To the further objections that follow, there is one answer already given above, and it is explained in the following chapter as well: certain passages affirm and commend the assistance of grace, while others affirm free human choice, because both are necessary for a good work, yet in such a way that the prior and more important roles are assigned to grace.

If God alone performed the things mentioned here, it would be pointless to say to human beings, “Draw near to God; make your ways straight; make yourselves a new heart; turn to God,” and so forth. And if human beings were sufficient for these things, it would be pointless to say, “Turn us, O God our Savior”; “Create a clean heart in me, O God”; “Direct my way in your sight,” and so forth.

Thus St. Prosper, *On the Calling of the Nations*, chapter 26: “The grace of God,” he says, “takes the principal place in every justification: persuading through exhortations, moving through examples, frightening through dangers, stimulating through miracles, giving understanding, inspiring counsel, and illuminating the heart itself and filling it with the affections of faith. Yet the human will is also joined to it, having been aroused by the aids mentioned above, so that it may cooperate worthily in the work within it and begin to exercise toward merit what it conceived through the heavenly seed as an inclination toward endeavor. If it fails, it attributes this to its own mutability; if it progresses, to the assistance of grace.

This assistance is supplied to all in countless ways, whether hidden or manifest. What many reject is due to their own wickedness; what many accept belongs both to divine grace and to human will.”]

What, moreover, is meant by the statement that God “will repay each person according to his works” (Rom. 2), and that “God is the one who works in you both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will” (Phil. 2), and that “this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast” (Eph. 2)?

What is meant by the statement, “Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you” (Ps. 5)? And by what he says elsewhere: “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6)?

What is meant by the statement [Note: [Col. 0916D] The Vulgate edition reads: “Make straight paths for your feet, and all your ways shall be established.”], “Make straight courses for your feet, and direct your ways” (Ps. 5)? And what is meant by what we say in prayer: “Direct my way in your sight”? And, “Perfect my steps in your paths, so that my footsteps may not be moved” (Ps. 16)?

What is meant by the command given to us again, “Make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit” (Ezek. 18), and by the promise: “I will give them a new heart, and I will place a new spirit within them; I will take away the heart of stone from their flesh and give them a heart of flesh, so that they may walk in my commandments and keep my judgments” (Ezek. 11)?

What is meant by the Lord’s command: “Wash your heart from wickedness, Jerusalem, so that you may be saved” (Jer. 4)? And what is meant by the Prophet’s request to the Lord: “Create a clean heart in me, O God”? And again: “You shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. 50)?

What is meant by what is said to us [Note: [Col. 0916D] See *Collation* 14, chapters 9 and 16, where this statement is likewise cited and explained.], “Illuminate yourselves with the light of knowledge” (Hos. 10)?

And what is meant by what is said of God, “He teaches human beings knowledge” (Ps. 93), and, “The Lord gives light to the blind” (Ps. 145)? Or certainly by what we say in prayer with the Prophet: “Illuminate my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death” (Ps. 12)—unless it is that [Note: [Col. 0917A] This is not to be understood as asserting equal powers in the two, as the Collator and the Massilians supposed. Prosper noted this in his letter to Augustine in these words:

“They produce testimonies in which the exhortation of divine Scripture incites human wills to obey: by free choice they either do what is commanded or neglect it. They think it follows that, since the transgressor is said not to have obeyed because he was unwilling, the faithful person likewise must be considered devoted because he was willing; and that each person has as much ability for good as for evil.
