They suppose that the mind can, with equal force, move itself toward vices or virtues: when it seeks good, God’s grace fosters it; when it pursues evil, just condemnation overtakes it.

But according to the declaration of the Council of Trent (Session 6, chapter 5, on justification), the beginning of justification in adults must be derived from the prevenient grace of God through Jesus Christ—that is, from his calling, by which they are called when they have no merits of their own. Those who had been turned away from God through sins are, through that grace which rouses and assists them, disposed to turn toward their own justification by freely assenting to and cooperating with the same grace.

Thus, when God touches the human heart through the illumination of the Holy Spirit, the person himself does not do absolutely nothing in receiving that inspiration, since he can also reject it; yet without the grace of God he cannot move himself by his free will toward righteousness before him.

Accordingly, when Scripture says, ‘Turn to me, and I will turn to you’ (Zech. 1; Joel 2), we are reminded of our freedom. When we respond, ‘Turn us, O Lord, toward you, and we shall be turned’ (Lam. 5), we confess that we are preceded by the grace of God.”]

In order to understand what the prevenient and rousing grace of God is—the grace from which the beginning of our salvation and justification must be derived, and which is chiefly at issue throughout this entire discussion—it seems altogether appropriate to set down here certain matters about grace and its divisions or subdivisions that are necessary to know.

First, then, it must be noted [Col. 0917C] that grace is here understood as a supernatural and freely given gift or benefit of God, bestowed for securing human salvation on the basis of Christ’s merits. Hence it is called the grace of Christ, or grace through Jesus Christ.

Romans 7 says: “Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ.” He did not simply say, “The grace of God,” but “through Jesus Christ.” More explicitly, Romans 3 says: “Being justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.”

The Apostle was not content to say, “Being justified freely by his grace,” but added, “through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus”—that is, through the merit of our Redeemer Jesus Christ—in order to signify that justification after Adam’s fall is given not only freely or gratuitously, but also to the undeserving and to sinners. In this way he distinguished the grace of Christ from the grace of God understood more generally, which was bestowed not on the basis of Christ’s merits but solely from God’s generosity, at creation, upon the angels and our first parents—not indeed upon the undeserving and sinful, but nevertheless upon those who were neither worthy nor deserving [Col. 0917D].

Second, leaving aside the other divisions of grace, which do not serve our purpose or discussion, two divisions of grace must be noted.

The first divides grace into habitual and actual grace. Habitual grace is a habit or certain quality infused into us by God and inhering in the soul, by which we are formally justified and are made righteous from sinners. Hence it is also called grace that makes one pleasing, the grace of justification, and righteousness—or justification itself.

The Council of Vienne under Clement V speaks of this grace; it is found in *Clementine* 1, *On the Supreme Trinity*, where the Council approves the opinion of those who say that, in baptism, the habit of grace and the virtues are infused into both infants and adults.

The Council of Trent, in Session 6, chapter 7, defines justification as not merely the remission of sins, but also the sanctification and renewal of the human being through the voluntary reception of grace and gifts. A little later in the same chapter it adds that, in justification itself, together with the remission of sins, faith, hope, and charity are infused and inhere in the soul. In canon 11 it defines the grace of justification as not merely God’s external favor, but also God’s charity poured into the heart and inhering in it.

Finally, the Roman Catechism, explaining the mind of that same Council in its treatment of the sacrament of baptism, says: “Grace is, as the Council of Trent decreed that all must believe under penalty of anathema, not only that by which the remission of sins takes place, but also a divine quality inhering in the soul, as it were a certain splendor and light that removes all the stains of our souls and makes them more beautiful and radiant” [Col. 0918B].

Actual grace, which is otherwise called the grace of special assistance, is nothing other than a divine movement, or a special assistance of God, by which a human being is moved and helped to perform supernatural acts. Such acts chiefly include believing, hoping, loving, and repenting as one ought, so that the grace of justification may be conferred upon us, as the Council of Trent taught, and before it the Councils of Milevis and Orange.

It is called a divine movement in order to distinguish it from habitual grace and from the other infused virtues and habits. For this grace, or special assistance, is not an infused habit or a quality inhering in us, but an action by which God moves a person to act well or works together with him.

It is called special assistance in order to distinguish it from the general assistance and concurrence by which God cooperates with a human being, as with other secondary causes, in his natural actions—that is, actions which do not exceed the powers of his nature, such as understanding and desiring human things.

For supernatural acts require a certain supernatural and special assistance by which the human being is raised above the capacity of nature. God alone can provide this, according to the words: “The Lord will give grace and glory” (Ps. 69).

There is frequent discussion of this actual grace in Scripture, in the councils, and among the Fathers. For what else do the words of John 6 mean—“No one can come to me unless my Father draws him”—and those of Lamentations 5—“Turn us, O Lord, toward you, and we shall be turned”—than actual grace from God?

Whatever the Council of Trent, the earlier councils, and St. Augustine so often teach about divine calling, inspiration, illumination, and the inner movement, anointing, instruction, and inclination of the will belongs to this actual grace.

Finally, as has been said, actual grace is chiefly at issue in this Collation. For the whole difficulty of the controversy and discussion consists in the necessity of grace for every good work, and in its harmony and concurrence with free human choice.

There was no dispute concerning habitual grace, but only concerning actual grace, or special assistance, between Augustine and his disciples on the one side and Pelagius and his followers or the Semipelagian supporters of Pelagius on the other.

Leaving aside habitual grace, actual grace is further divided into rousing and assisting grace.

Rousing grace, or assistance, is nothing other than an interior illumination and inspiration of the Holy Spirit, by which God knocks at the human heart and rouses it to turn—whether toward faith, repentance, love, or the performance of any other supernatural act.

This is established by the Council’s decree in Session 6, chapters 5 and 6, and chapters 3 and 4, where this assistance is variously called the prevenient inspiration of the Holy Spirit, rousing grace, the divine touch through the illumination of the Holy Spirit, and divine calling.

It is called rousing because it performs, as it were, the function of awakening our will from the sleep of sin or negligence. Just as awakening occurs without the sleeper’s consent, so rousing grace acts without our freedom. Hence it is also called prevenient, because it precedes all our free consent; and operating—or rather, in Augustine’s expression, that which God works in us without us—that is, without our free and deliberate consent.

Assisting grace, however, is the divine cooperation, direction, and protection—of which the title of this Collation speaks—by which we are helped both to choose and to will, and to do what God has inspired beforehand.

Hence it is also called cooperating and accompanying grace, because it works with us and accompanies our consent.

Thus Revelation 3 says: “I stand at the door and knock.” This signifies the first grace, prevenient and rousing. God is said to stand at the door and knock through holy inspiration—that is, through the illumination of the understanding and the movement of the will—which belongs to rousing grace.

The second grace, assisting and cooperating, which begins at the very moment when the person who has been roused freely responds to God calling him, is signified by these words: “If anyone opens the door, I will enter in to him and dine with him,” not alone, but “with him.”

Both graces are also signified by that prayer of the Church: “Going before our actions with your inspiration, we ask, O Lord, and following them with your assistance,” and so forth.

Finally, the Council of Trent includes both (Session 6, chapter 6), when, speaking of preparation for justification, it says: “They”—namely, adult sinners—“are disposed toward righteousness when, roused and assisted by divine grace, they conceive faith through hearing,” and so forth.

Catholics therefore acknowledge both graces as necessary for attaining justification and salvation; the Pelagians acknowledge neither; the Semipelagians acknowledge only the former in part, as has been shown.

So much for grace. Free choice will be discussed below (Chapter 10), insofar as seems sufficient for the present purpose.]

In all these things both the grace of God and the freedom of our choice are shown [Col. 0919A], and because a human being can sometimes, by his own movements, extend himself toward the desire for virtues, yet always needs to be assisted.

For no one enjoys health merely by willing it, nor is anyone freed from the illness of disease according to the desire of his own choice. What good does it do to have desired the grace of health, unless the Lord, who grants the use of life itself, also bestows the strength of soundness?

[Note: [Col. 0919D] Here again the Collator contradicts himself and destroys his own assertion; he misuses the Apostle’s words, as though the Apostle had possessed that willing—that is, good will—through the good of nature, that is, from natural ability, although he declares that his sufficiency comes from God, including the ability merely to think.]

But so that it may become clearer that even through the good of nature, which was granted through the Creator’s beneficence, the beginnings of good wills sometimes emerge—though, unless they are directed by the Lord, they cannot reach the completion of virtue—the Apostle bears witness, saying: “To will is present with me, but I do not find how to accomplish the good” (Rom. 7).

## CHAPTER X. On the weakness of free choice

For [Note: [Col. 0919D] Two things concerning free choice are presented here which must be held as matters of certain faith: first, its freedom in human beings even after sin; second, its weakness, or feebleness and inability, contracted from sin, to act well without the grace of God.

Two contrary errors directly oppose this doctrine: one of the Manichaeans, the other of the Pelagians. The Manichaeans removed free choice altogether; today the Lutherans and Calvinists follow them. The Pelagians, however, exalted it excessively and attributed more to it than to the grace of God.

For a more convenient understanding of these matters, certain points must be noted here.

1. In reality, free choice is nothing other than the rational or intellectual will, although its root and origin arise from the intellect and the complete use of reason. Hence it is commonly called the free choice of the will, or free will.

Thus Augustine says in the *Enchiridion* (chapter 105): “Either it is not the will, or it must be called free.” Damascene (*On the Orthodox Faith*, Book I, chapter 22) defines the will as a rational and free appetite. St. Bernard explains and proves this most extensively of all in his book *On the Harmony of Grace and Free Choice*.

The Greeks express this more briefly and significantly by saying αὐτεξούσιον (*autexousion*), meaning “having power over oneself,” or “being one’s own master,” and being lord of one’s own actions. Hence St. Jerome says in Book III *Against the Pelagians*: “What the Greeks call αὐτεξούσιον, we call free choice.”

To understand in what sense free choice is called free, a second distinction must be noted concerning the twofold division of freedom.

It is divided, first, into the freedom of nature, grace, and glory. This is St. Bernard’s division in the passage cited: “Three freedoms,” he says, “have been assigned to us: from sin, from misery, and from necessity. The last of these was given to us in the condition of nature. We are restored to the first by grace; the middle one is reserved for us in our heavenly homeland.

Let the first therefore be called the freedom of nature, the second the freedom of grace, and the third the freedom of life or glory. First, we were created as a noble creature of God in free will and voluntary freedom; second, we are restored to innocence as a new creation in Christ; third, we are raised to glory as a creature perfected in spirit.

The first freedom possesses much honor, the second very much virtue, and the final one the fullness of joy. Through the first we surpass the other animals; in the second we subdue the flesh; through the third we subject death.” Thus St. Bernard.

From this we understand that free choice is not named from the freedom of grace, which is freedom from sin, nor from the freedom of glory, which is freedom from misery, but from the freedom of nature.

This freedom is further divided into freedom from coercion and freedom from necessity. Freedom from coercion is a certain power by which the will cannot be forced. Freedom from necessity is the power by which the will can choose any one of several options and is not bound to any one of them by necessity.

Strictly speaking, free choice pertains to freedom from necessity, as has been said, not to freedom from coercion. A human being desires blessedness without coercion, yet not freely, because he desires it necessarily. Animals also necessarily desire food, without coercion, yet not freely, because they lack free choice.

Thus freedom from coercion is one thing, and freedom from necessity another.

Nor is it required that the will be free to choose either good or evil. Such freedom follows only from the different states of free choice. Its powers were one way in the state of innocence, another in the state of sin, another in the state of grace, and another in the state of glory.

The ability to choose evil should be called not a perfection but an imperfection of freedom. Consequently, it belongs neither to God nor to the angels nor to the blessed. Conversely, the ability to choose good does not belong to demons and the damned, although they possess free choice.

Thus Augustine, discussing the variation of free choice according to each person’s state (*City of God*, Book XXII, chapter 30), says: “They will not for that reason lack free choice, because they will not be able to take pleasure in sins. Rather, free choice will be more fully liberated from the pleasure of sin into an unwavering pleasure in not sinning.

The first free choice, which was given to human beings when they were first created upright, was able not to sin, but it was also able to sin. The final free choice, however, will be more powerful because it will not be able to sin,” and so forth.

With these premises and preliminaries established, two propositions must be set forth for the clarification of this chapter, indeed of the entire Collation and discussion concerning grace and free choice.

1. Adam was created by God with free choice, and in the state of innocence he was able to act well and badly.

Sacred Scripture bears witness to this most clearly. Ecclesiasticus 15 says: “God created human beings from the beginning and left them in the hand of their own counsel; he added his commandments and precepts,” and so forth.

The same is inferred from the words of Genesis 3: “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness, so that he may rule over the fish,” and so forth. The Fathers attribute the image of God in human beings, among other reasons, above all to freedom of choice.

Thus Damascene says in Book II *On the Orthodox Faith*, chapter 12: “That the human being is made in the image of God signifies that he is intellectual and possesses free choice, αὐτεξούσιον.

2. After the fall of the first human being, free choice, although weakened and wounded, was not lost or extinguished.

Leaving aside the countless authorities of sacred Scripture and the holy Fathers, which the reader may seek in Cardinal Bellarmine and other writers on controversies, it is enough for us to cite the definition of the Church expressed at the Council of Trent (Session 6, chapter 5). There it is first defined that human beings who had been turned away from God through sins are, through his rousing and assisting grace, disposed to turn toward their own justification by freely assenting to and cooperating with that same grace; so that, when God touches the human heart through the illumination of the Holy Spirit, the human being does not do absolutely nothing in receiving that inspiration—since he can also reject it—yet cannot, without the grace of God, move himself by his free will toward righteousness before him.

Again, canon 4 pronounces anathema upon anyone who says that the free choice of a human being, moved and roused by God, does not cooperate by assenting to God who rouses and calls him, so that he may dispose and prepare himself to obtain the grace of justification; or who says that it cannot dissent if it wishes, but is like something lifeless, doing absolutely nothing and remaining purely passive.

The following canon likewise strikes with the same anathema anyone who says that free choice was lost and extinguished after Adam’s sin, or that it is merely a name—or even a name without a reality.

These, as stated above, are the two articles of faith taught in this chapter concerning free human choice. Although they are true and confirmed by the most certain testimonies of Scripture, the conclusion which the Author intends to draw from them is nevertheless false: namely, that our choice is free in such a way that it possesses an equal or sufficient power for good and evil and does not need the assistance of grace except to perfect what it has begun, not to will and begin it. For the same Scriptures most certainly establish the necessity of grace for both.]

Divine Scripture confirms the freedom of our choice [Col. 0921A], saying: “Guard your heart with all vigilance” (Prov. 4). But the Apostle reveals its weakness when he says: “May the Lord guard your hearts and your understandings in Christ Jesus” (Phil. 4).

David declares the power of free choice, saying: “I inclined my heart to perform your justifications” (Ps. 118). Yet the same man, praying, teaches its weakness in similar fashion: “Incline my heart,” he says, “toward your testimonies and not toward avarice” (ibid.).

Solomon also says: “May he incline our hearts toward himself, so that we may walk in all his ways and keep his commandments, ceremonies, and judgments” (1 Kings 8).

The Psalmist indicates the power of our choice, saying: “Restrain your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit” (Ps. 33). Our prayer declares its weakness when we say: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of protection around my lips” (Ps. 140).

The capacity of our choice is declared by the Lord when it is said: “Loose the bonds from your neck, captive daughter of Zion” (Isa. 52). The Prophet sings of its fragility [the marginal reading has *denuntiat*, “announces”], saying: “The Lord sets free those who are bound” (Ps. 145). And, “You have broken my bonds; to you I shall sacrifice a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 115).

In the Gospel we heard the Lord inviting us to hasten to him through free choice: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11). But [Col. 0922A] the same Lord testifies to its weakness, saying: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6).

The Apostle stimulates our free choice, saying: “Run so as to obtain” (1 Cor. 9). But John the Baptist bears witness to its weakness when he says: “A human being cannot receive anything from himself unless it has been given to him from heaven” (John 3).

We are commanded to guard our souls carefully, as the Prophet says: “Guard your souls” (Jer. 17). But another Prophet proclaims in the same Spirit: “Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it keeps watch in vain” (Ps. 126).

The Apostle, writing to the Philippians in order to indicate their free choice, says: “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling” (Phil. 2). But to show its weakness he adds: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XI. Whether God’s grace follows or precedes our good will
And thus these matters are, in a certain sense, indiscriminately intermingled and confused,

[Note: [Col. 0922C] Among the Pelagians—or Semi-Pelagians—but not among Catholics, for whom it is accepted and beyond doubt that every beginning of a good will proceeds from God, as was shown above. Three errors and absurdities are committed here. First, they equally condemn and declare to be mistaken both those who, like Catholics, confess that a good will arises from God’s mercy, and those who, like the Pelagians, assert conversely that grace depends upon a good will. Second, both opinions are nevertheless decreed to be accepted, since an example and illustration of the one is presented in Matthew and Paul, and of the other in Zacchaeus and the thief—as though one good thing could be made and combined from two evils, or one truth from two falsehoods. Third, the examples proposed for the other party, namely, the erroneous and Pelagian party, are false and mistaken, as is clear from what follows.]

so that among many people the question of what depends upon what may be debated at length: namely, whether God has mercy upon us because we have furnished the beginning of a good will, or whether, because God has mercy, we attain the beginning of a good will. For many, investigating each of these alternatives and asserting them more strongly than is just, have become entangled in various errors contradictory to one another. If we say that the beginning of a good will belongs to us, what good will was there in the persecutor Paul, or in the tax collector Matthew, one of whom was absorbed in the bloodshed and punishments of the innocent, the other in public violence and extortion, yet was drawn to salvation? But if we say that the beginnings of a good will are always inspired by God’s grace,

[Note: [Col. 0923C] Prosper replies that both faith in Zacchaeus and piety in the thief were inspired by God, and that both were anticipated by a divine calling. For the one who illuminated the heart of Matthew the tax collector and of Paul, who was then persecuting the Church, also illuminated the heart of Zacchaeus and the heart of the thief crucified beside Christ. The Lord’s voice was not ineffectual when, addressing Zacchaeus, who was seeking to see who he was, he graciously said: “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must remain in your house.” And did he not prepare the heart of the man whose hospitality he chose?]

what are we to say about the faith of Zacchaeus, or about the piety of that thief on the cross, who, by their desire exerting a kind of force upon the heavenly kingdom, anticipated the special summons of their calling?

But if we attribute the completion of virtues and the execution of God’s commandments to our free choice,

[Col. 0923B] how do we pray: “Confirm, O God, what you have worked in us” (Psalm LXVII); and, “Direct the works of our hands over us” (Psalm LXXXIX)?

We know

[Note: [Col. 0923C] See Conference 24, chapter 17.]

that Balaam was hired to curse Israel (Numbers XXII), but we see that he was not permitted to curse when he desired to do so.

Abimelech is guarded lest, by touching Rebecca, he sin against God (Genesis XX).

Joseph is dragged away through the jealousy of his brothers, so that the descent of the children of Israel into Egypt might take place, and while they were plotting the murder of their brother, remedies for the future famine might be prepared. Joseph himself, recognized by his brothers, makes this clear when he says: “Do not be afraid, and do not let it seem harsh to you that you sold me in these regions; for the Lord sent me ahead of you for your salvation.” And below: “For the Lord sent me ahead, so that you might be preserved upon the earth and might have food for your survival. It was not by your plan, but by the will of God, that I was sent here; he made me as a father to Pharaoh, lord of his whole household, and ruler in the land of Egypt” (Genesis XLV).

And when, after their father’s death, his brothers were afraid, he removed their fearful suspicion, saying: “Do not be afraid; can we resist God’s will? You intended evil against me, but God turned it into good, so as to exalt me, as you now see, and to save many peoples” (Genesis L).

Blessed David likewise declares in an orderly fashion that this had then happened, in Psalm CIV, saying: “And he called a famine upon the land, and shattered every support of bread. He sent a man before them; Joseph was sold into slavery.”

These two things—namely, either the grace of God or free choice—seem indeed to be opposed to one another,

[Note: [Col. 0923C] Not, however, in such a way that in some people the will precedes grace, while in others grace precedes the will, but so that in everyone the will follows grace. Otherwise, if free choice is removed when it is preceded by grace, grace too is removed when it is preceded by free choice, and thus one or the other would be taken away from man. Concerning this passage, Peter Maturus, whom I have often cited, reported by D. Antoninus [Col. 0923D] above (Chapter III), made the following observation: “John Cassian, a hearer of Chrysostom, placing himself midway between those who, with the Catholics, affirm that we are preceded by the grace of God, and those who, with the Pelagians, assert that we precede the grace of God, taught that some people anticipate divine grace by their own will, while the wills of others are preceded by divine grace. Prosper, bishop of Riez, argued against this opinion of Cassian in a separate volume entitled On Free Choice.” Sixtus of Siena, *Bibliotheca*, book VI, annotation 183. Prosper’s opinion is confirmed by Augustine, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 2; *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book II, chapter 9; *On Predestination and Grace*, chapter 10; and *On the Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chapter 44; by Fulgentius, *On the Incarnation and Grace of Christ*, chapter 18; by D. Thomas, *Summa theologiae* I–II, question 109, article 6, and II–II, question 6, article 1; and by D. Antoninus himself, *Summa*, part IV, title 9, chapter 5, section 4, and chapter 6, section 1. This was also defined by the Council of Trent, session 6, chapter 5, and canon 3. The Second Council of Orange, canon 6, and the Council of Milevis, canon 5, had likewise established it earlier. Thus far the author himself.]

but both agree with each other, and from considerations of piety we conclude that we must accept both equally, lest, by taking one of them away from man, we appear to have exceeded the rule of ecclesiastical faith.

For when God sees that we are turning our will toward the good, he comes to meet us, directs us, and strengthens us. “As soon as he hears, he will answer you at the voice of your cry” (Isaiah XXX). And again: “Call upon me in the day of your tribulation, and I will deliver you, and you will glorify me” (Psalm XLIX). But if he perceives that we are unwilling or have grown lukewarm, he applies saving exhortations to our hearts, by which a good will is either restored or formed within us.

## CHAPTER XII. That a good will is neither always to be attributed to grace nor always to man.

[Col. 0924C] [Note: Several further absurdities may likewise be noted here. First, he ineptly adduces the example of Adam, who plainly was created by God upright and free from every fault, whereas the subject here is not free choice in the state of innocence and integral nature, but in the state of nature corrupted by Adam’s sin. The weakness, or feebleness, of free choice does not arise from the original establishment of nature, but was contracted through sin.

Second, the Collator reasons badly as follows: “If man cannot will the good from himself, then he lacks free choice.” The inference is denied. It is sufficient for freedom of choice that he can do this, provided that what must be presupposed is supplied—namely, the aids of divine grace, which are available to all, as he himself stated above (Chapter 8). Otherwise, by the same argument one would conclude that God’s grace is needed neither for beginning nor for completing, contrary to the Collator himself.

Third, he also improperly brings forward, to prove the freedom and capacity of choice, that passage from Genesis: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil” (Genesis III). It is as though the devil had truly foretold and promised something to Adam, and as though these words signified what Adam gained through sin, rather than what he lost. According to the common judgment of commentators—that is, interpreters—these words are considered to have been spoken ironically, so that it might be understood how great was the mockery and derision deserved by Adam, who not only failed to become what he wished to be, but did not even preserve what he had become. So D. Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book XI, chapter 39.

Fourth, the Author sinned in the very conclusion, because from a false understanding of Scripture he drew a false conclusion, saying: “Therefore, after his transgression, Adam conceived the knowledge of evil, which he had not possessed; but he did not lose the knowledge of good, which he had received.” Both claims are false, because Adam had learned from God’s warning how great an evil he ought to avoid, and, when he believed the devil, he forgot in what great good he had been established. So Prosper.

That conclusion could indeed have a true sense if it were understood of what is called experiential knowledge, by which, after his transgression, Adam learned through experience the distinction between the good that he had enjoyed before the fall and the evil that he incurred by sin. From that point he began to possess knowledge of good and evil. For this reason many teach that the tree was called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil from its outcome—namely, from what followed upon eating it. But the Author did not intend this sense, nor did D. Prosper, since it would not serve the argument.]

For one must not believe that God made man such that he should neither ever will nor be able to do good.

Otherwise, he did not grant him free choice, if he permitted him only to will and be able to do evil, while he granted him neither the will nor the ability to do good from himself. And how will that sentence of the Lord, pronounced after the transgression of the first man, stand: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil” (Genesis III)? He must not be thought to have previously been such as to be entirely ignorant of good; otherwise we must admit that he was formed like some irrational and senseless animal. That is entirely absurd and wholly alien to the Catholic faith.

Indeed, according to the judgment of the most wise Solomon, God made man upright—that is, so that he might continually enjoy only the knowledge of good—“but they themselves sought many inventions” (Ecclesiastes VII); for they became, as has been said, knowing good and evil.

Therefore, after his transgression, Adam conceived the knowledge of evil, which he had not possessed, but did not lose the knowledge of good, which he had received.

Finally, the Apostle’s statement most clearly declares that the human race did not lose the knowledge of good after the transgression. He says:

[Note: [Col. 0925C] The Fathers have transmitted two interpretations of this statement. Some explain it of Gentiles who had already been converted to the faith of Christ. So D. Ambrose in his *Commentaries*. Others explain it of Gentiles and unbelievers who, entirely ignorant of Christ, were guided solely by the natural light. So Chrysostom and the other Greek Fathers, and among the Latins Jerome, *To Algasiа* (Letter 151, question 8).

Augustine reports both interpretations in *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 28, but gives greater approval to the first. D. Prosper also seems to admit both interpretations in this passage; but neither of them supports the Collator, who concluded from it that knowledge of good—or the natural light—was sufficient in itself for right action, and consequently that the beginnings of virtues and good works could arise from us without the help of grace.

Not the first interpretation, because believers are not said to do what belongs to the law—that is, to observe the commandments of the law—“naturally,” meaning by the powers of nature, but, as Augustine explains, “naturally,” that is, with nature reformed and restored by grace (*Augustine, Against Julian*, book IV, chapter 3); or, as St. Thomas says, by the natural law and under the guidance of reason, though grace is not thereby excluded.

Nor the second interpretation, because although it may be admitted that Gentiles without faith and grace can perform some moral good and observe some commandments of the law, they cannot observe all of them, even in the substance of the work, since Scripture repeatedly teaches that observance of the law is to be attributed to God’s grace. Ezekiel XXXVI: “I will put my spirit within you, and I will make you walk in my commandments.”

The Apostle intended nothing else than that although the Gentiles were without the law—namely, the law written on tablets—they were not entirely without law. For when they sometimes act according to the dictate of reason, they show that they have the law of nature written in their hearts. Yet this law does not by itself suffice to make us love doing everything that we know ought to be done.

For, as D. Bernard aptly says (*On Grace and Free Choice*), it is not the same capacity to know what ought to be done and to do it, just as it is one thing to provide a guide for a blind man and another to provide a vehicle for the exhausted. And the poet says: “I see and approve better things; I follow worse ones.” Hence the servant who knows his master’s will but does not do it will be beaten with many blows (Luke XII). And the wise men of this age were rightly condemned because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God, but became futile in their reasoning, and so forth (Romans I).]

“For when Gentiles who do not have the law do by nature what belongs to the law, these, although they do not have the law, are a law for themselves. They show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness to them, and their thoughts accusing or even defending them among themselves, on the day when God will judge the hidden things of men” (Romans II).

In this sense the Lord also, through the prophet, rebukes the Jews for blindness that was not natural but voluntary, which they stubbornly inflicted upon themselves: “Hear, you deaf”; and, “Look, you blind, that you may see.”

“Who is deaf except my servant, and who is blind except the one to whom I sent my messengers?” (Isaiah XLII).

[Note: [Col. 0926D] But the deaf and blind are not rebuked and reproved in this way as though, by the capacity of nature, they could open their ears to hear or their eyes to see, since it is written: “The Lord enlightens the blind” (Psalm CXLV), and, “Morning by morning he awakens my ear” (Isaiah L); but because they refuse to admit and cooperate with divine illumination and opening, and persist in their blindness and deafness. Hence they are said to be blinded and hardened.]

And lest anyone perhaps be able to attribute this blindness of theirs to nature rather than to the will, elsewhere he says: “Bring out the blind people who have eyes, and the deaf who have ears” (Isaiah XLIII).

And again: “You have eyes,” he says, “and do not see; you have ears, and do not hear” (Ezekiel XIV).

The Lord also says in the Gospel: “Because they see and do not see, and hear and do not hear, nor understand” (Matthew XIII).

And the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled in them: “With hearing you will hear and will not understand; and seeing you will see and will not perceive. For the heart of this people has grown dull; they have heard heavily with their ears, and they have closed their eyes, lest they ever see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and be converted, and I heal them” (Isaiah VI).

[Note: [Col. 0926D] This assertion was answered shortly before, when he attributed not only the will of the good but also its possibility—that is, its capacity—to free choice, as though it were the same thing to be able, by natural judgment, to discern what is just and to perform and carry it out in action; to know what ought to be done and to do it; and as though this natural understanding were required of them so that, from that knowledge, they might carry out what is just.]

Finally, to indicate that the possibility of good was present in them, he rebukes the Pharisees: “Why, even of yourselves, do you not judge what is right?” (Luke XII).

[Col. 0927A] He would certainly not have said this to them unless he knew that by natural judgment they were able to discern what was equitable.

Therefore, we must take care not to refer all the merits of the saints to the Lord in such a way

[Note: [Col. 0927B] Rather, we must take care not to attribute some good to human nature in such a way that we do not refer all the merits of the saints to God. Thus Coelestine I defined in the letter cited above (Chapter 8), following the opinion of his predecessor Innocent: “All the zeal, all the works, and all the merits of the saints must be referred to the glory and praise of God, because no one pleases him [variant: “has pleased him”] except from what he himself has bestowed.”

The Council of Trent expressed this more clearly in these words (Session VI, chapter 16): “Although the sacred writings attribute so much to good works that Christ promises that whoever gives one of his least ones a cup of cold water will not be deprived of his reward (Matthew IX and X), and the Apostle testifies that our present momentary and light tribulation works in us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure (II Corinthians IV), nevertheless, let it be far from a Christian to trust or glory in himself rather than in the Lord, whose goodness toward all human beings is so great that he wills the merits that are his gifts to be regarded as theirs.” Thus the council.

Those final words are taken from Augustine’s Letter 105 and other passages.

Prosper, moreover, vehemently attacks this opinion of the Collator, declaring it Pelagian and blasphemous: “What,” he says, “could any disciple have defined more clearly or explicitly, in accordance with the invention of Pelagius and Coelestius? They say that God’s grace is given according to our merits and therefore [variant: “the same persons”] say that God’s grace is not given for individual acts. This man has enclosed both blasphemies within a single statement, saying that we must take care not to refer all the merits of the saints to God, lest we attribute to human nature anything except what is evil and perverse. He therefore wants there to be many merits proper to human beings, which were not bestowed by the generosity of grace, and to which certain gifts from above are owed as an increase to natural resources. He wants us not to receive God’s grace for individual acts, and consequently not always to pray for every good work, and so forth.”]

that we attribute to human nature nothing except what is evil and perverse.

In this matter we are refuted by the testimony of the most wise Solomon—or rather, of the Lord, whose words these are. For when he prayed after the temple had been completed, he said: “My father David had it in his heart to build a house for the name of the Lord God of Israel. And the Lord God said to David my father: ‘Because you had it in your heart to build a house for my name, you did well to have this in your mind; nevertheless, you will not build the house for my name’” (III Kings VIII).

[Note: [Col. 0927D] There can be no doubt that the king David’s thought, or plan and intention, of building the temple was good and inspired by God, since the work was in itself pious and honorable, and his intention was upright. Nor is it an obstacle that its accomplishment or execution was denied him for certain reasons and reserved for his son Solomon. For this is neither rare nor unusual, as Prosper proves by two examples, one taken from Scripture and the other from the practice and custom of the Church.

Scripture records that the Apostles, although they most ardently desired to preach the Gospel to all the nations, nevertheless were unable to speak the word in Asia; and when they attempted to go into Bithynia, they were prevented by the Spirit of Jesus (Acts XVI). Who could doubt that their good will was inspired by God, although he did not then wish it to be carried out?

So the Church’s will and pious desire are good when she prays daily for all her enemies—that is, for unbelievers—that they may be converted; yet she does not obtain this for many of them.

To these add two other similar examples. Abraham’s will was good when he wished to sacrifice his son in obedience to God, yet its execution was prevented (Genesis XXII). Likewise, the will of the Apostle Paul was good when he asked the Lord three times that the thorn in his flesh, which buffeted him, might be removed; yet he did not obtain this, since the Lord said: “My grace is sufficient for you” (II Corinthians XII).]

Therefore, is this thought and intention of King David to be called good and from God, or evil and from man? If that thought was good and from God, why is its result denied him by the one from whom it was inspired? But if it was evil and from man, why is it praised by the Lord?

It remains, therefore, that it should be believed to have been both good and from man. In the same way we can judge our own thoughts each day. For it was not granted only to David to think something good from himself, nor are we naturally denied the ability ever to conceive or think anything good.

[Note: [Col. 0928B] D. Prosper also refutes this opinion, although the holy Fathers frequently use it in another sense. St. Anthony, according to Athanasius (*Life of St. Anthony*), appears to mean by it the seeds of virtues naturally implanted in us, in an exhortation delivered to the brothers; so too Basil, *Homily 9 on the Hexaemeron*, and in greater detail in *The Longer Rules*, question 2.

Chrysostom admits the same thing more explicitly in *Homily 2 on the Epistle to the Ephesians*: “You see,” he says, “that by nature we have implanted within us the seeds of virtue; whatever belongs to wickedness is contrary to nature.”

Jerome says in his commentary on Galatians I: “Many people, without faith or the Gospel of Christ, act wisely or piously in some matters: they obey their parents, extend a hand to the needy, do not oppress their neighbors, and do not seize what belongs to others. For this very reason they become more liable to God’s judgment, because, possessing within themselves the beginnings of virtues and the seeds of God, they do not believe in him without whom they cannot exist.”

Damascene says in book III of *The Orthodox Faith*, chapter 14: “The virtues are natural, and naturally and equally present in all, although not all of us equally perform what belongs to nature.”

Yet these Fathers understood the seeds of virtues in a different and more proper sense than Cassian, whom Prosper is attacking. For if the seeds of virtues are taken properly, they are nothing other than the light of the practical intellect and the inclination of the will to pursue good and flee evil, as St. Thomas teaches, I–II, question 63, articles 1 and 2.

In this sense it is true that the seeds of virtues are present in every rational soul and remained even after sin; nor can they be entirely abolished in man, since they are certain first and immovable principles of practical reason, which D. Augustine, in book II of *On Free Choice of the Will*, calls the principles and lights of the virtues.

For just as in the speculative intellect nature has implanted certain principles that philosophers called axioms, or dignities and common maxims, which no one can deny—such as that a thing cannot both be and not be, that the whole is greater than its part, and so forth—so also in the practical intellect there are certain principles known to all. These are nothing other than certain judgments concerning human ends: that happiness is to be desired, that wisdom should be pursued, that one should live justly, that one should not do to another what one does not wish done to oneself, that worse things should be set aside for better ones, and similar principles.

St. Thomas, following Jerome and other ancient writers, calls such a judgment of the practical intellect *synderesis*. Others call it the summit or height of the mind, which always remains inviolate and uncorrupted, however much a person may be corrupted by false opinions and depraved affections.

Cassian, however, understood by the seeds of virtues the seeds of true piety—that is, good thoughts and pious desires, even the beginnings of faith and of other virtues, by which a person could prepare himself for grace and in view of which grace might be conferred upon him.

This is clearly inferred both from this passage, where he asserts that these seeds of virtues are naturally implanted in every soul in such a way that they do not need divine assistance except in order to reach the growth of perfection; and from the preceding material, especially chapter 9, where he says that from the good of nature, which was granted through the Creator’s beneficence, the beginnings of good wills sometimes emerge, although, unless they are directed by the Lord, they cannot reach the completion of the virtues.

Here it should be noted that the Pelagians and their supporters called the benefit of creation “grace” and concealed their heresy under this cloak. When pressed to acknowledge the necessity of God’s grace, they indeed confessed that without God’s grace we can do nothing; but they wanted free choice and natural gifts of that kind to be understood by the name of grace. Thus Pelagius craftily eluded the Council of Palestine, as Augustine testifies in Letter 105 and in *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 3.

Prosper refutes the Collator’s opinion concerning these seeds of virtues in the following words: “Therefore, when someone says that the seeds of virtues are naturally present in every soul without any work of grace, what is he laboring to show except that from these seeds certain sprouts of merits arise before the grace of God? That is, he wants to show and prove nothing other than that these seeds are certain merits in us that precede all the grace of Christ. See the rest in the same author.”]

Therefore, there can be no doubt that all the seeds of virtues are naturally present in the soul, implanted there through the Creator’s beneficence; but unless these seeds are awakened by God’s assistance, they cannot reach the growth of perfection. For, according to the blessed Apostle, “neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (I Corinthians III).

That free choice stands alongside man in either direction, even

[Note: [Col. 0929C] This was said from the book called *The Shepherd* in Conference 8, chapter 17; the testimony brought forward here by the Collator is dismissed by D. Prosper as having no authority (see Baronius, volume II of the *Annals*, under the year 159).]

the book called *The Shepherd* teaches most clearly. In it,

[Note: [Col. 0929D] Although I have discussed this opinion above to some extent (Conference 8, chapter 17), I nevertheless wish here to hear the distinguished theologian of this age, John Maldonatus, disputing about it: “It is also less certain among the authorities,” he says (*Commentary on Matthew XVIII*), “whether individual human beings have not only a good angel, by whom they are defended, but also an evil angel, by whom they are attacked.” Nevertheless, this too has been handed down by a most ancient tradition, not only among Christians but also among the Hebrews, as Rabbi Moses writes in book III of the *Guide of the Perplexed*, chapter 25.

The ancient writers commonly establish this tradition from the ancient book *The Shepherd* and from the Epistle of Barnabas, which we read was once held in great authority among Christians—for example, Origen, *Homily 10 on Luke* and *On First Principles*, book III, chapter 2; Cassian, Conference 8, chapter 15, and Conference 13, chapter 12; and Bede on Acts XII.

Gregory of Nyssa, in the *Life of Moses*, and the author of the *Imperfect Commentary*, Homily 5 on Matthew, confirm the same tradition.

Some trace of this matter may be observed in Scripture. For St. Paul says that an angel of Satan was given to him to buffet him (II Corinthians XII). Although this can be understood in other ways, it can also be understood in this manner, and it is credible that the devil, prince of demons, imitates God in administering his kingdom. Just as God appoints individual angels over individual human beings, so he sets individual demons against them.”

Thus Maldonatus, as appears, leans toward the affirmative side and more toward the opinion of this Author. John Durantus likewise follows and defends it in book II of *On the Rites of the Church*, chapter 13. See the *Sentences of the Master*, book II, distinction 11.

Nevertheless, many oppose this opinion, among them Cardinal Bellarmine (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*), whom the reader may consult.]

it is said that two angels adhere to each one of us, namely, a good one and an evil one; and that it lies within a person’s choice to select which one he will follow.

And for this reason free choice always remains in man, so that he can either

[Note: [Col. 0930C] In itself he can indeed neglect grace, but he cannot love except through the grace of God; that is, he can fall by himself, but cannot rise again by himself. “Easy is the descent to Avernus;

But to retrace one’s step and climb back to the upper air,”]

[Note: This is the work, this is the labor . . . says the poet (Virgil, *Aeneid* VI). And St. Bernard, in his book *On Grace*: “The fall of the sinner is not to be ascribed to the gift of free power, but to the fault of the will. Yet, although the fall arises from the will, it is not equally within the will to rise again: for although the will was given the ability to stand, so that it might not fall, it was not given the ability to rise again if it should fall. For no one can leave a pit as easily as he can fall into it.”]

to neglect or to love. For the Apostle would not have commanded, saying, “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling” (Philippians II), unless he knew that it could either be cultivated or neglected by us. But lest they should believe that they did not need divine assistance for the work of salvation, he adds: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, according to his good pleasure” (ibid.). And therefore, when admonishing Timothy, he says: “Do not neglect the grace of God which is in you” [Col. 0930A] (I Timothy IV). And again: “For this reason I remind you to stir up the grace of God which is in you” (II Timothy I).

Hence, when writing also to the Corinthians, he exhorts and warns them not to show themselves unworthy of the grace of God through fruitless works, saying: “And as fellow workers, we also urge you not to receive the grace of God in vain” (II Corinthians VI). Since Simon had undoubtedly received it in vain, the reception of saving grace did him no good. For he did not choose to obey the commands of blessed Peter, who said: “Repent of this wickedness of yours, and pray to God, if perhaps this thought of your heart may be forgiven you; for I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bondage of iniquity” (Acts VIII).

The mercy of the Lord therefore precedes the human will, concerning which it is said: “My God, his mercy will precede me” [Col. 0930B] (Psalm LVIII). And again, our will precedes the Lord when he delays and, in a certain sense, beneficially holds back, in order to test our free choice, as it is said: “And [Note: An unjust and foolish comparison is established here between the human will and divine grace, as though they possessed equal power, and as though what grace accomplishes in some cases, the will accomplishes by its own power in others; thus grace is now the forerunner, now the attendant of the will. But when the Psalmist says, “In the morning my prayer will precede you,” this should not be understood as though the will approaches him first, invoking him without being called, awakened, or preceded, as it is said: “No one can come to him unless the heavenly Father draws him” (John VI). And: “Who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid him?” (Romans VIII). Hence Augustine, explaining that verse, says: “Now ‘morning,’ after the night of unbelief and the darkness have passed. Your mercy preceded me, so that this morning might be mine. For how could I invoke him unless I believed? How could I believe unless I heard? But in order that I might believe what I had heard, he himself drew me; for, secretly, from the death of the heart, it was he himself—not any ordinary physician—who raised me up.” Thus Augustine. Metaphorically, however, our will or action is said to precede God when it invokes him more earnestly or more promptly than usual, implores his help more fervently, and, as though he were sleeping, rouses him with repeated and importunate cries, just as the apostles, when imperiled in the boat, cried out: “Lord, save us; we are perishing” (Matthew VIII; Psalm CXVIII). To precede in the morning therefore means to precede early, quickly, promptly; or, as another psalm says, “at dawn,” whether before dawn or at an untimely hour—that is, in the morning, before the proper time, in the dead of night. Or “morning” means when the light of grace shines forth and the darkness of unbelief and sin has been driven away, as St. Augustine explains.] my prayer will precede you” (Psalm [Col. 0931A] LXXXVII). And again: “I preceded the dawn and cried out, and my eyes anticipated you at daybreak” (Psalm CXVII).

He also calls and invites us when he says: “All day long I have stretched out my hands toward a people that does not believe in me and contradicts me” (Isaiah LXV). And he is invited by us when we say to him: “All day long I have stretched out my hands toward you” (Psalm LXXXVII). He awaits us, as it is said through the prophet: “Therefore [Note: God awaits us in order to have mercy upon us, not because he first investigates and observes in us good movements of our will, as the Collator said above (Chapters 8 and 9), nor because he ought to or can first be invoked by us without his preceding grace—for our awaiting and invoking him are themselves gifts of divine grace—but because he stands and knocks daily at the door of our heart. That is, he offers us his grace and, through external objects, benefits, exhortations, terrors, and dangers, as well as through internal inspirations, invites us to repentance and works of righteousness. Thus, if we hear his voice and open to him who knocks—that is, if we assent to his call—he enters us, remains with us, and dines with us (Revelation III), that is, he cooperates with us for salvation. Hence St. Jerome says: “Great is the clemency of God, that he should await our repentance; that, until we turn from our vices, he should restrain his powerful hand, lest he be compelled to strike.” Thus the Council of Orange, against the Massilians, explained how God does or does not await us: “If anyone contends that God awaits our will in order that we may be cleansed from sin, but does not confess that, in order that we may also desire to be cleansed, this desire is produced in us through the infusion and operation of the Holy Spirit, he resists that same Holy Spirit, who says through Solomon, ‘The will is prepared by the Lord’ (Proverbs VIII), and who is salutarily proclaimed by the Apostle: ‘It is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish’ (Philippians II), and so forth.”] the Lord awaits, that he may have mercy upon you” (Isaiah XXX), and he is awaited by us when we say: “Waiting, I waited for the Lord, and he looked upon me” (Psalm XXXIX). And: “I have awaited your salvation, O Lord” (Psalm CXVIII).

He strengthens us when he says: “And I instructed them and strengthened their arms, yet they devised evil against me” (Hosea VII). And he urges us to strengthen ourselves when he says: “Strengthen the feeble hands and fortify the weak knees” (Isaiah XXXV).

Jesus cries out: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John VII). The Prophet also cries out to him: “I have labored, crying out; my throat has become hoarse; my eyes have failed while I hoped in my God” (Psalm LXVIII).

The Lord seeks, saying: “I sought a man, and there was none; I called, and there was no one who answered” (Isaiah LXVI). And he himself is sought by the bride, who mournfully complains: [Note: In the Vulgate edition only the following words are found: “On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, and did not find him” (Song of Songs III).] “In my bed at night I sought him whom my soul loved; I sought him, and did not find him; I called him, and he did not answer me” (Song of Songs III).

## CHAPTER XIII. That human efforts cannot compensate for the grace of God

And so the grace of God always cooperates with our free choice for the good, and in all things assists, protects, and defends it, [Note: This has been rejected and refuted above. The argument added by the Author—that otherwise God would seem to confer his gifts upon those wholly asleep or given over to sluggish idleness—is entirely without force. For it is clear from the parable of the laborers (Matthew XX) that God calls, awakens, invites, and sends into the vineyard not only those who are sleeping, inactive, and idle—whom we call the first gratuitous gifts of God—but also enemies, rebels, contradictors, and very serious sinners. Isaiah LXV: “All day long I have stretched out my hands toward a people that does not believe and contradicts me.” Matthew XXIII: “How often I wanted to gather your children, and you were unwilling?” And there are six hundred other passages and examples of this kind in Scripture.] so that at times he may even demand or await from it certain efforts of good will, lest he seem to bestow his gifts upon one wholly asleep or dissolved in idle inactivity [Col. 0932B], seeking, in a certain manner, occasions whereby, once the torpor of human sloth has been shaken off, the generosity of his munificence may not appear irrational, while he imparts it under the guise of some desire and labor, [Note: In this way the Massilians attempted to evade the Apostle’s meaning. For when they said that the beginnings of good will and good works could arise from us and would suffice to obtain and merit the grace of God, at least by merit of suitability, the Fathers opposed to them the Apostle’s statement to the Romans XI: “But if by grace, then it is not by works; otherwise grace is no longer grace.” They replied that the grace of God remained gratuitous and was truly grace even if it were given on account of our labor and effort, because that labor was very slight and exceedingly small, and could not be compared with divine grace and generosity. But Augustine, Prosper, and the other defenders of grace prove not only against Pelagius that grace is not given on the basis of merits proportionate to the reward of free choice—for then grace would no longer be grace, since it would be given as though for an equal price, as is self-evident—but also show against the Semi-Pelagians and Massilians that grace is not given on the basis of merits of suitability arising from free choice. For then it would not be pure and absolute grace and mercy, since it would not be wholly gratuitous and undeserved, but rather a kind of reciprocal and remunerative gift, even if it were granted for slight labors and works. They therefore conclude, from those words of the Apostle, that every work of bare free choice is excluded if it can possess even the slightest character of merit, cause, or occasion on account of which God would either prepare his grace for us from eternity or bestow it in time. For if anything from us—that is, from the mere powers of free choice—whether the smallest merit or the smallest cause, preceded it, grace would not be wholly liberal and gratuitous, or bestowed from mercy, but would be conferred upon us as a repayment of gratitude. Such a reciprocal gift, as they call it, is not regarded even by human laws as a pure and gratuitous gift, as is found in the law *Aquilius Regulus*, *Digest*, “On Donations.” Thus Augustine, *To Boniface*, book II, chapter 8: “If, without the grace of God, the desire for good begins through us, that beginning itself will be a merit to which assistance comes as a debt, as though the grace of God were not freely given but bestowed because of our merit.” And in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 2, after recounting the opinion of those who said that the beginning of faith—that is, the very will to believe—could be possessed through the powers of nature, he adds: “There is therefore no departure from that opinion which Pelagius himself was compelled to condemn in the episcopal judgment at Palestine: that the grace of God is given according to our merits.” St. Fulgentius, *On the Incarnation and Grace of Christ*, chapter 12: “But if, according to their opinion, the will to believe is ours before the grace of God begins to help us, grace is unjustly called grace, because it is not freely given to human beings but repaid to a good will.” Finally, St. Prosper, *Against the Collator*, chapter 6: “How do you fail to see that you fall into that condemned error when, whether you wish it or not, you are proved to say that the grace of God is given according to our merits, since you affirm that some good work originating in human beings precedes, on account of which they obtain grace?” Nevertheless, it does not follow from this that every notion of merit must likewise be excluded from works performed through the preceding grace and faith of God, by which the sinner is prepared for justification. For that which is attributed to grace itself does not cease to be grace; nor does the Apostle speak of these works when he says: “If therefore by grace, then not by works,” but of those works performed by the sole powers of nature, with no grace presupposed. If grace were bestowed with regard to such works, it would certainly not be pure grace, but in some measure a remuneration owed, as has been said. But those works which, before justification, are performed through divine grace, inspiration, and special assistance, since they are gifts and effects of grace itself, may truly be called both impetratory and, in some way, meritorious, whether of a greater actual grace or of habitual grace, which is justification itself. Theologians call this merit *de congruo*, merit of suitability. Thus Augustine, Letter 105: “Nor is the remission of sins itself without some merit, if faith obtains it; for the faith by which that man said, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner,’ and descended justified, is not without merit—the merit of faith by which he was humbled. Nor does this conflict with the decree of the Council of Trent (Session 6, chapter 5), which says that the beginning of justification in adults must be derived from the preceding grace of God through Jesus Christ—that is, from his call, by which they are called when none of their merits exist, and so forth. For it is clear that the Council is speaking of works that precede the call itself or preceding grace; in these it teaches that there is no merit, neither merit of condignity, against the Pelagians, nor merit of suitability, against the Semi-Pelagians and Massilians.] and nevertheless the grace of God always remains gratuitous, since through certain small and slight efforts it bestows, with immeasurable generosity, so great a glory of immortality and such great gifts of everlasting blessedness. [Note: Similar points are found in Book XII of the *Institutes*, chapter 11.]

For it is not because faith had preceded in that thief on the cross that we should therefore declare that the blessed dwelling in paradise was not promised to him gratuitously (Luke XXIII); nor should we believe that David’s repentance—the one word by which he said, “I have sinned against the Lord” (II Samuel XII)—removed his two such serious crimes, rather than that the mercy of God did so, so that through the prophet Nathan he might merit to hear: “And the Lord has taken away your iniquity; you shall not die” (ibid.).

That he added murder to adultery was certainly the work of free choice; but that he was reproved through the prophet was the grace of divine favor. Again, that in his humiliation he acknowledged his sin was the work of his own freedom. But that within the briefest moment of time he obtained forgiveness for such great crimes was the gift of the merciful Lord.

And what shall we say of this very brief confession and the immeasurable greatness of the divine recompense, when it is easy to consider what the blessed Apostle declared, looking toward the greatness of the future reward, concerning his innumerable persecutions? “For this momentary and light tribulation of ours,” he says, “works in us, beyond all measure and beyond comparison, an eternal weight of glory” [Col. 0934A] (II Corinthians IV). Concerning this he also declares elsewhere with confidence, saying: “For the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Romans VIII).

However much human frailty may strive, therefore, it cannot be equal to the future recompense. Nor does it so diminish divine grace through its labors that grace does not always remain gratuitous. Hence that aforementioned Teacher of the Gentiles, although he testifies that he obtained the rank of apostle by the grace of God, saying, “By the grace of God I am what I am” (II Corinthians XV), nevertheless also declares that he responded to divine grace, saying: “And his grace in me was not fruitless, but I labored more abundantly than all of them and prevailed, [Note: “But the grace of God, the grace which is with me” [Greek: Ἀλλ᾽ ἡ χάρις τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἡ σὺν ἐμοί], with me, understood: “which is with me.” He did not say “which is in me,” but “which is with me,” to show that grace does not work alone but works together with us. Hence Augustine, *On Free Choice*, chapter 15: “Not I, however, but the grace of God with me”; that is, not I alone, but the grace of God with me. Therefore, neither grace alone nor he alone, but the grace of God with him.] not I, however, but the grace of God with me” (ibid.).

For when he says, “I labored,” he signifies the effort of his own free choice. [Col. 0934B] When he says, “not I, however, but the grace of God,” he displays the power of divine protection. When he says, “with me,” he declares that grace cooperated with him not while he was idle or secure, but while he was laboring and sweating.

## CHAPTER XIV. That God tests the power of the human will through his temptations.

This too we read that divine justice provided in the case of Job, its most tested athlete, when the devil demanded him for a special contest:

> [Note: [Col. 0934C] This chapter likewise contains three errors, consequences of those discussed above, and sufficiently refuted by Prosper. It will therefore be enough merely to point them out to the reader. The first error is that Job was for a time left to himself and deprived of God’s assistance, so that he might fight against the devil by his own strength and on his own initiative; consequently, his patience was to be attributed not to divine grace but to his natural freedom and strength. Among other objections, one may set against this the teaching of Abbot Paphnutius, or of Cassian himself, *Conferences* 3.17 and following. For that conference almost diametrically opposes this conference of Chaeremon. To the extent that this book exalts free will in comparison with grace, the other depresses it and subjects it to grace, teaching that it always needs God’s help; that the beginning of good will and its completion, faith, understanding, fear of the Lord, and finally endurance and victory over temptations come from God. He proves this by the Apostle’s words: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear, but with the temptation will also make a way out [or, as we have it, an outcome], so that you may be able to endure” (1 Cor. X). At last he concludes as follows (the final chapter): “By what we have set forth, we do not wish to remove man’s free will, but to prove that God’s help and grace are necessary to it every day and at every moment.”

> “The second error is that the faith of the centurion and of Abraham was tested and approved by God—not the faith that God himself had inspired, but the faith that they could display through the freedom of their will: ‘For,’ he says, ‘there would be no praise or merit if Christ had commended in him what he himself had given.’ But, besides what Saint Prosper adduces against this opinion, the contrary is also taught by Paphnutius’s words, *Conference* 3.16: ‘So completely did the Apostles perceive that everything pertaining to salvation had been bestowed upon them by the Lord that they even asked the Lord to grant them faith itself, saying: “Lord, increase our faith” (Luke XVII). They did not presume upon its fullness as proceeding from free will, but believed it would be conferred upon them by God’s gift.’

> “The third error, which nevertheless coincides with the preceding ones, is the claim that divine grace always summons the human will in such a way that it does not protect and defend it in every respect, so that it also makes it fight against spiritual enemies by its own efforts. So says the Collator. But the Fathers teach instead that no true temptation can be overcome by the powers of nature alone and without divine help, and they assert that the contrary is Pelagian. Thus the Council of Palestine, as reported by Augustine in Letter 106, presses Pelagius: ‘Let Pelagius confess that, when we fight against temptations and unlawful desires, although we also possess our own will in that struggle, our victory nevertheless proceeds not from it but from God’s help.’ Celestine I, in his letter to the bishops of Gaul, chapter 6, says: ‘No one, even if renewed by the grace of baptism, is capable of overcoming the devil’s snares and conquering the desires of the flesh unless, through God’s daily help, he receives perseverance in a good manner of life.’ Saint Augustine, *On the Perfection of Justice*, near the end, says: ‘Whoever denies that we ought to pray lest we enter into temptation’—and he denies it who maintains that God’s grace is not necessary to a person for avoiding sin, but that, once the law has been received, human will by itself is sufficient—‘I do not hesitate to say that such a person must be removed from the ears of all and anathematized by the mouth of all.’ Finally, Prosper, on this passage, after showing that the whole of holy Job’s victory was achieved through God’s help and grace, concludes: ‘Whoever, therefore, does not fail in tribulation should not doubt that he is helped by the one to whom the hearts of all the faithful cry out daily: “Do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil.”’]

If he had encountered the enemy not by his own strength but solely through God’s protecting grace, and had endured those manifold assaults and destructive trials, sought with all the enemy’s cruelty, supported solely by divine assistance and without any strength of his own patience, how could the devil not more justly have repeated against him that slanderous accusation which he had uttered earlier: “Does Job worship God for nothing? Have you not hedged him around, and his house and all his possessions on every side?”

> [Note: [Col. 0936B] The text is incorrectly quoted and corrupted by an even worse gloss. The Greek text has: “But send out your hand” (ἀλλὰ ἀπόστειλον τὴν χεῖρά σου). The Latin and the Vulgate correspond to it: “But stretch out your hand a little, and touch all that he possesses” (Job I), and so does the Chaldean paraphrase; all interpreters agree, except that some read *send* for *stretch out*, coming closer to the Greek verb. What, then, is meant by “Take away your hand” instead of “stretch out” or “send out your hand”? Does *take away* mean the same as *stretch out* or *send out*? Even if this is admitted, what relevance does it have here, where the subject is God’s grace? The passage treats it as though, in the sense of the narrative, taking away God’s protecting hand—that is, the external protection of God by which Job’s house and all his possessions were hedged around and fortified—were the same as taking away the assistance of grace, so that Job, deprived of it, would be forced to fight the devil by his own strength. Yet “there is no power upon earth that can be compared with him who was made so as to fear nothing” (Job XLI).]

“But take away your hand,” that is, “allow him to fight with me by his own strength, unless he blesses you to your face” (Job I).

But since the slanderous enemy does not dare to repeat any such complaint after the conflict, he confesses that he was overcome not by God’s strength but by Job’s—although we must not believe that God’s grace was wholly absent from him, since that grace granted the tempter such power to tempt:

> [Note: [Col. 0936C] Prosper more correctly says, as he notes: “How much strength to resist he knew that he had given him.” The correction of a single word would have tempered, with some moderation, the whole of that glory which he wished to assign to human powers, so that the marvelous patience shown amid such great affliction would be attributed both to God’s help and to the freedom of man’s will. See the rest.]

that grace, which had granted the tempter as much power to tempt as it knew him to have strength to resist, did not protect him from the enemy’s assault in such a way as to leave no place for human virtue, but merely ensured that the most violent enemy, by driving his soul into madness and depriving him of understanding, would not weigh him down with an unequal and unjust burden of combat.

That the Lord sometimes tests our faith so that it may become stronger or more glorious is taught us by the example of that evangelical centurion. The Lord certainly knew that he could cure the man’s servant by the power of his word, yet he preferred to offer his bodily presence, saying: “I will come and cure him.” But when the centurion surpassed this offer through the ardor of a more fervent faith and said: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word and my servant will be healed,” the Lord marvelled at him, praised him highly, and placed him before all those who had believed from the people of Israel, saying: “Amen I say to you, I have not found such faith in Israel” (Matt. VIII). For there would be no praise or merit if Christ had commended in him what he himself had given; otherwise he would have said: “I have not given such faith in Israel.”

We likewise read that divine justice exercised this testing of faith in that most illustrious patriarch when it is said: “And it came to pass after these words,”

> [Note: [Col. 0936D] Sometimes *to tempt* means to incite to sin, as in Acts V, 1 Corinthians VII, 1 Thessalonians III, James I, and elsewhere. In this sense the devil is said to tempt, and hence he is called Satan, that is, “tempter” (Saint Thomas, *Summa*, I, q. 114, a. 2). Wicked people also, as ministers of the devil, are accustomed to tempt others in this way; God never does so. For he is the tempter of no one toward evil, but himself tempts no one, as James I says.

> “At other times *to tempt* means to inquire and investigate for the purpose of acquiring knowledge, and both the devil and God are said to tempt human beings in this way. Yet God tempts differently from human beings and demons. They tempt in order to learn what they do not know; God tempts so that what he knows may also become known, as though he had learned it by investigation and experience—or so that those whom he tempts may come to know themselves, as Saint Augustine interprets it. Thus in Genesis XXII, Exodus XVI, Deuteronomy VIII and XIII, and frequently elsewhere.”]

“God tested Abraham” (Gen. XXII).

For he did not wish to test the faith that the Lord inspired in him, but the faith that, once called and enlightened, he was able to display before the Lord through freedom of will. Therefore his steadfastness in faith is rightly approved, and, when God’s grace came to his aid—the grace that had left him for a little while in order to test him—it is said to him: “Do not stretch out your hand against the boy, nor do anything to him; for now I know that you fear the Lord, and you have not spared your beloved son for my sake” (Gen. XXII).

That this kind of temptation may also occur to us as an occasion of meritorious testing is proclaimed clearly enough by the lawgiver in Deuteronomy: “If,” he says, “a prophet should arise among you, or one who says that he has seen a dream, and he announces a sign or portent, and what he has said comes to pass, and he says to you, ‘Let us go and serve foreign gods whom you do not know,’ you shall not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer, because the Lord your God is testing you, to determine whether you love him with all your heart and keep his commandments, or not” (Deut. XXIII).

What, then? When God has allowed this prophet or dreamer to arise, are we to believe that he will protect those whose faith he has decided to test in such a way that he leaves absolutely no place in their free will for them to fight the tempter by their own strength?
