> [Note: [Col. 0937C] An excellent answer is given below, by which the Collator refutes himself and contradicts himself: “So that, whether victorious, he may understand God’s grace, or, when overcome, his own weakness, and thus learn always to hope not in his own strength but in divine assistance, and continually to return to his protector.” So he himself says. But how can the victor understand and acknowledge God’s grace if he wins by his own strength and efforts, as is said there, and without grace? And why should he not be able to hope in his own strength if he understands that he possesses within himself an equal power of resistance, with God’s assistance and support excluded? See how these claims cohere.]

And why would it be necessary for those to be tempted whom he knows to be so weak and fragile that they could in no way resist the tempter by their own strength? Yet surely the Lord’s justice would not have permitted them to be tempted unless he knew that they possessed an equal power of resistance, by which, according to the judgment of equity, they could be judged either blameworthy or praiseworthy in both respects.

The same is true of the Apostle’s saying: “Therefore, whoever thinks that he stands, let him beware lest he fall. No temptation has overtaken you except a human one.”

> [Note: [Col. 0937C] This seems to be the reading required by Cassian’s interpretation, because the Greek has εἴληφεν, “has apprehended,” whereas the Latin translator appears to have read εἰληφέτω, “let it apprehend.” Cassian himself insists that the former is the correct reading in Book V, chapter 16 of the *Institutes*, as may be seen there. Nevertheless, the Vulgate edition is preferable; it is supported both by the authority of the holy Fathers and by the approval of the sacred Council of Trent, as we noted there.]

“But God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear, but with the temptation will also make a way out, so that you may be able to endure” (1 Cor. X).

When he says, “Whoever stands, let him beware lest he fall,” he makes free will vigilant; for he knew that, once grace had been received, it could stand through diligence or fall through negligence. But when he adds, “No temptation has overtaken you except a human one,” he reproves their weakness and instability, since their minds were not yet strong enough to be attacked by the storms of spiritual wickedness, against which he knew that he himself and those who were perfect fought daily. Of these he says to the Ephesians: “Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI).

But when he adds:

> [Note: [Col. 0937D] The Apostle does not mean that we are at some times tempted, or that we endure temptation by our own strength, as though this were a “human temptation” that does not exceed the powers of free will, as this author subtly interprets it. Rather, he means that God does not permit us to be tempted beyond the strength received through grace. There are also temptations that are more severe and prolonged than others—such as were experienced by the holiest men, Anthony, Hilarion, Jerome, and others—and to overcome and escape them a greater and more powerful grace and divine assistance are required. This assistance is not denied to one who does what lies within him according to the grace received.

> “Thus God is called faithful because he does not fail in his promises—that is, he does not fall short of the promised grace which he knows to be necessary for us to overcome every kind of temptation. Rather, with the temptation he provides a means of escape, that is, an increase of grace proportionate to the nature and severity of the temptation; or an escape, *ekbasin* (ἔκβασιν), that is, the ability to get out, as Saint Cyprian explains (*Testimonies* II.91).”]

“But God is faithful, who does not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear” (1 Cor. X),

the Lord does not thereby wish to prevent them from being tempted, but wishes to prevent them from being tempted beyond what they could endure. The former statement indicates the capacity of human free will; the latter displays the grace of the Lord, who regulates the struggles of temptation.

In all these matters, therefore, it is demonstrated that divine grace always incites the human will in such a way that it does not protect and defend it in every respect, but also makes it fight its spiritual enemies by its own efforts. In these struggles, the victor may recognize God’s grace, while the defeated may recognize his own weakness; and thus he may learn always to hope not in his own strength but in divine assistance, and continually to return to his protector.

And so that this may be confirmed not by our conjecture but by still clearer testimonies of Scripture, let us revisit what is read in Joshua:

> [Note: [Col. 0938C] This should not be understood as though the words quoted here were written in the Book of Joshua, also called Jesus son of Nave, since, as noted, they are taken from the Book of Judges. They occurred, however, in the person of Jesus son of Nave—that is, in Joshua’s time and under his rule. Although he had conquered other nations, God nevertheless did not wish these nations to be conquered by him, so that through them he might test—that is, prove and exercise—Israel, and so forth.

> “Moreover, the Book of Judges may in part be called the Book of Jesus son of Nave, or Joshua, since he was the first of the judges, and his final deeds, as well as his death and burial, are described in that same book. Hence Saint Jerome, *Against Helvidius* (chapter 2), says: ‘When the book that is called by his name was completed in the burial of Jesus, he is described again in the Book of Judges as though alive and rising again; and under a recapitulation (*anakephalaiosis*, ἀνακεφαλαίωσις) his deeds are proclaimed. We read: “Jesus sent the people away, and the children of Israel went, each to his inheritance, to possess the land. And the people served the Lord throughout all the days of Jesus,” and so forth. Immediately afterward it is added: “And Jesus son of Nave, the servant of the Lord, died at the age of one hundred and ten years” (Judg. II).’”]

“These nations,” he says, “the Lord allowed to remain and did not wish to destroy, so that he might test Israel through them, to see whether it would keep the commandments of the Lord its God and retain the practice of fighting against enemies” (Judg. III).

And, to compare something mortal with the incomparable clemency of our Creator—not as equal in kindness, but by some resemblance of indulgence:

> [Note: [Col. 0938D] Although this comparison seems very apt and agrees in many respects, it fails and limps in the point that is primary and most important here: the child’s strength and power to walk and work do not depend on the nurse, whereas the capacity and strength of our will and free choice to act and live well depend on God’s grace. The child’s powers are present in him by nature and grow with age.

> “Nevertheless, divine grace performs toward us the function of a nurse, indeed of a midwife as well, rendering the same services that a nurse renders to a little child. In this respect the comparison of divine grace with a nurse and midwife holds. Hence Job XXVI speaks of the serpent—that is, the devil—being brought forth by the hand of God acting as midwife, meaning that he is expelled from the hearts of the faithful. Elsewhere God compares himself to a mother, Isaiah LXVI: ‘As a mother comforts her children, so I will comfort you,’ and so forth. He also compares himself to an eagle flying and urging its young to fly (Deut. XXXII), and to a hen gathering her chicks beneath her wings (Matt. XXIII).”]

if a kind and attentive nurse carries a little child at her breast for a long time so that eventually she may teach him to walk, at first allowing him to crawl, then supporting him upright, as he leans on one foot and then the other, by the strength of her right hand; soon, when she has left him alone for a little while and sees him tottering, she immediately catches him, receives him as he sways, lifts him when he falls, and either prevents him from falling or, even allowing him to fall gently—[Lipsius, in the margin: “lightly”]—raises him after his fall; but when she has brought him to the strength of childhood, adolescence, or youth, she imposes certain weights and labors—not to crush him but to exercise him—and allows him to contend with his peers, how much more does that heavenly Father of all know whom he carries in the bosom of his grace, whom he exercises in virtue before him through the freedom of the will, and yet helps when he labors, hears when he calls, does not abandon when he seeks, and sometimes rescues from danger even when he is unaware of it!

## CHAPTER XV  
### On the manifold grace of callings

Through these considerations it is also clearly shown

> [Note: [Col. 0939C] This is the Apostle’s statement (Rom. XI): “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!” The Greek word means “inscrutable,” as Saint Augustine also reads it in *On Grace*, chapter 22. Chrysostom notes the emphasis of the word: “For they cannot merely be comprehended; they cannot even be searched out. Such is the depth of God’s judgments.”

> “‘Unsearchable’ is put negatively for “uninvestigable.” The Apostle alludes to Isaiah XI: ‘And there is no investigation of his way,’ as Saint Jerome notes there.

> “The manifold ways of divine calling which the author lists here, by which God draws human beings to salvation, were reduced to three classes by Abbot Paphnutius in *Conference* 3.3, where he says: ‘There are three orders of callings,’ and so forth; and then in the following chapter: ‘The first is from God, the second through a human being, the third from necessity,’ and so forth.”]

that the judgments of God are inscrutable and his ways unsearchable (Rom. XI), by which he draws the human race to salvation.

We can also confirm this through examples of evangelical callings. Andrew, Peter, and the other apostles, who were thinking nothing about the remedy of their salvation, he chose beforehand by the spontaneous graciousness of his grace (Matt. IV). Zacchaeus, who was faithfully stretching himself out toward the sight of the Lord and raising himself above the smallness of his stature by climbing a sycamore, he not only received but also honored with the blessing of dwelling with him (Luke XIX). Paul, unwilling and resisting, he drew to himself (Acts IX). Another man he commanded to cling to him inseparably, so that when he asked for a brief delay to bury his father, he did not grant it (Matt. VIII). To Cornelius, who was constantly devoted to prayers and almsgiving, the way of salvation was shown as though in return for his merits; through an angel’s visitation he was instructed to summon Peter and learn from him the words of salvation by which he and all his household would be saved (Acts X).

Thus that manifold wisdom of God distributes salvation to human beings through a varied and inscrutable kindness, and grants the grace of his generosity according to each person’s capacity, so that he also exercises the healings themselves not according to the uniform power of his majesty, but

> [Note: [Col. 0939D] This is a deceptive disjunctive proposition. According to the dialecticians, for it to be true it is sufficient that only one of its two members be true; nevertheless, it is introduced and proposed as though both were true—that is, as though in some people God found faith that he had not given, which is false and erroneous, while in others he found faith that he himself had bestowed, which is true and Catholic.

> “The entire difficulty of this chapter lies in the words ‘according to the measure of faith,’ and in similar words below: ‘God’s generosity itself is shaped according to the capacity of human faith.’ By these expressions he intended to signify that we can possess faith from ourselves, and consequently that faith should be counted among the goods of free will rather than among God’s gifts, as Prosper says; and that, according as each person possesses greater or lesser faith from himself, he receives greater or lesser grace from God.

> “This opinion appears to be supported by the statement in the evangelical parable that a man going abroad—by whom Christ is signified—distributed his gifts, or talents, to his servants, giving five to one, two to another, and one to another, ‘to each according to his own ability’ (Matt. XXV). The Pelagians interpreted this ‘own ability’ as each person’s faith, which, they said, must come from ourselves for it to be called each person’s own ability; according to its capacity or measure, God would bestow his grace upon us to a greater or lesser degree, as though faith itself were not also to be counted among the gifts of grace.

> “Saint Augustine had at one time also been involved in this error, as he himself confesses in several places (*Retractions* I.23 and *On Predestination* 3). But after gaining a clearer understanding of the matter, he corrected himself and, vigorously attacking the heresy of Pelagius, along with the other Fathers, taught by which testimonies of Scripture he had been recalled from that error.

> “The principal passages specifically confirming this truth are these: Matthew XXIX: ‘Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.’ John VI: ‘This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom the Father has sent.’ Ephesians II: ‘You have been saved by grace through faith, and this is not from you; for it is God’s gift, not from works, so that no one may boast.’ Philippians II: ‘To you it has been granted not only to believe in him,’ and so forth.

> “In addition to other arguments, the Fathers use this proof as especially effective: the Church prays for unbelievers that they may be converted to the faith, and for those same people, once converted to the faith, it gives thanks to God. Both actions are most certain arguments of divine grace.

> “The authority of the Council of Orange also supports this, in canons 5, 6, 7, and 8, where it is defined against the Pelagians and their remnants that ‘the beginning of faith itself and the very inclination to believe are God’s gift, just as the increase of faith is’; and those are condemned who say either that the beginning of faith is naturally present in us or that by the power of nature we can consent to evangelical preaching without the illumination and inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

> “The same Fathers explain this opinion more fully in the final chapter, asserting that we ought to believe that, through the sin of the first man, free will was so inclined and weakened that thereafter no one can believe in God unless divine grace and mercy have preceded him. They make the same point through various examples and testimonies of Scripture.

> “Following this teaching, the Fathers of the Council of Trent, session 6, canon 3, condemn with an anathema anyone who says that, without the preceding inspiration and assistance of the Holy Spirit, a human being can believe as one ought. This means nothing other than believing with Christian, or Catholic, faith—not with merely human faith or with any assent to divine matters that does not rest upon the first truth but upon experience or some human reasoning. Faith of this kind is also found in demons and unbelievers. For ‘the demons also believe and tremble,’ says Saint James (James II).

> “As for the phrase in the evangelical parable, ‘to each according to his own ability’ (Matt. XXV), Saint Jerome and Bede interpret it excellently as meaning the same as ‘according as each person prepares himself more or less to receive grace,’ with God’s grace preceding and assisting, as the Council of Trent teaches (session 6, chapters 5 and 6). This is an ecclesiastical dogma, though heretics resist it: the more each person prepares himself for justification with faith and love, the greater the grace of God infused into him—provided that this faith, love, and every other disposition are acknowledged to come from God’s gift and help, and are attributed to him.

> “Thus Saint Thomas responds to the objection drawn from the Gospel (II-II, q. 24, a. 3): ‘It must be said that the ability according to which God gives his gifts to each person is the preceding disposition or preparation, or the effort of the one receiving grace; but the Holy Spirit also precedes this disposition or effort, moving the human mind more or less according to his will,’ and so forth.”]

according to the measure of faith in which he finds each person, or as he himself has apportioned to each, he chooses to deal with them.

For the man who believed that Christ’s will alone would suffice to cleanse his leprosy, he cured by the assent of his will alone, saying: “I will; be cleansed” (Matt. VIII). To another, who begged him to come and raise his dead daughter by laying his hand upon her, he entered the man’s house and, in the very manner in which the man had hoped, granted what was requested (Matt. IX). To another, who believed that the fullness of salvation consisted in the preaching of his word and replied, “Only say the word and my servant will be healed” (Matt. IX), he restored weakened limbs to their former strength by the command of his word, saying: “Go, and as you have believed, so may it be done for you” (ibid.). To others who hoped for healing from touching the fringe of his garment, he generously bestowed gifts of health. When asked, he granted healing to the illnesses of some. To others he provided medicine spontaneously. He encouraged others to hope, saying: “Do you wish to be healed?” (John V). To others who did not hope, he brought help unasked. He examined the desires of some before satisfying their wishes, saying: “What do you wish me to do for you?” (Matt. XX). To another, who did not know the way by which he might obtain what he desired, he kindly showed it: “If you believe,” he said, “you will see the glory of God” (John XI).

Among others he poured out the power of healing so abundantly that the evangelist records of them: “And he healed all their sick” (Matt. XIV). But among others that immense abyss of Christ’s benefits was so closed that it is said: “And Jesus could not perform miracles among them because of their unbelief” (Matt. XIII).

Thus God’s generosity itself is shaped according to the capacity of human faith, so that to one he says: “According to your faith, let it be done to you” (Matt. IX); to another: “Go, and as you have believed, so may it be done for you” (Matt. VIII); to another: “Let it be done to you as you wish” (Matt. XV); and again to another: “Your faith has saved you” (Matt. IX).

## CHAPTER XVI  
### On the grace of God, which transcends the limitations of human faith

> [Note: [Col. 0941D] The Collator appears anxious and concerned lest his writings convict him of agreeing with Pelagius that God’s grace is given according to our merits, and consequently that grace is not grace—a position so absurd to the Fathers that, at the Council of Palestine, the first council held against Pelagius, Pelagius himself condemned it, though falsely and hypocritically.

> “He therefore attempts to excuse himself by a twofold subterfuge. First, he says that he did not claim that the whole of our salvation—which elsewhere he calls its perfection and completion—lies within the control of our faith, that is, in a faith which we could possess from ourselves, as though he attributed the entire business of salvation to free will; rather, he acknowledges that grace is altogether necessary for attaining perfection and salvation.

> “Second, he admits that this same grace often exceeds and surpasses the merit of our faith, as he demonstrates by several examples from Scripture.

> “But Prosper brings three objections against both excuses and shows that, whether he wishes it or not, the Collator falls into what he calls the profane opinion, that is, the dogma of Pelagius.

> “First, although he did not teach that perfection comes from us, he did teach that the beginning of salvation comes from us; and this is sufficient for grace to be said to be given according to our merits. For the beginning of salvation either means faith itself, since faith is the foundation and beginning of all justification, as the Fathers of Trent teach (session 6, chapter 8), or it means the inclination and desire for salvation by which we obtain the grace through which we are saved. Thus to say that the beginning of salvation comes from us is to say that we can merit the gift of faith and actually obtain faith by believing without the help of God’s grace; or that we can conceive a serious desire for salvation by which we may obtain and merit, at least by merit of suitability, the grace of justification, as has been said.

> “Second, he said that the centurion, whose faith was praised by the Lord’s voice (Matt. VIII), would have no praise or merit if God had commended in him what he himself had given. It follows that the whole merit consists in faith belonging to the person himself and not given by God.

> “Third, in the preceding chapter he expressly asserted that God bestows the grace of his generosity according to each person’s capacity. What else is this than saying that grace is given according to each person’s merits?”]

No one should suppose that we have brought these matters forward in order to assert that the whole of salvation lies within the control of our faith, according to the profane opinion of certain people who, assigning everything to free will, define God’s grace as distributed according to each person’s merit.

Rather, we declare with an entirely unequivocal judgment that God’s grace sometimes overflows and surpasses the limitations of human unbelief. We recall that this happened in the case of that evangelical royal official who, finding it easier to believe that his sick son could be healed than that a dead son could be raised, hastened to implore the Lord’s presence, saying: “Lord, come down before my son dies” (John IV).

Although Christ reproved his unbelief with these words: “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe” (John IV), he nevertheless exercised the grace of his divinity according to the weakness of the man’s faith. He did not, as the man had believed, drive away the deadly fever by his bodily presence, but by the word of his power, saying: “Go; your son lives” (ibid.).

We likewise read that the Lord poured out this superabundance of grace in the healing of the paralytic. When the man asked only for remedies for the illness by which his body had been paralyzed, the Lord first bestowed health upon his soul, saying: “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you” (Matt. IX).

After this, when the scribes did not believe that he could forgive human sins, he restored to strength even the man’s limbs, weakened by paralysis, by the word of his power, in order to confound their unbelief, saying: “Why do you think evil in your hearts? Which is easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? But so that you may know that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins”—then he said to the paralytic—“Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house” (ibid.).

Likewise, in the case of the man who had lain helpless for thirty-eight years beside the edge of the pool, hoping for healing from the movement of its water, he displayed the munificence of spontaneous generosity. Wishing to call him toward the means of salvation, he said to him: “Do you wish to be healed?” (John V). When the man complained of the lack of human assistance and said: “I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred,” the Lord, taking pity on his unbelief and ignorance, restored him to his former health—not by the way he had hoped, but by the mercy the Lord chose—saying: “Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house” (ibid.).

And what wonder is it if these things are reported as accomplished by the Lord’s power, when divine grace also worked similar deeds through his servants? As Peter and John were entering the temple, a man lame from his mother’s womb, who had no knowledge whatsoever of walking, asked them for alms. They did not give the worthless coins that the sick man requested, but bestowed the use of his feet; and they enriched him, who hoped for the comfort of a very small sum, with the rewards of unexpected health. Peter said: “Silver and gold I have none; but what I have, this I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, rise and walk” (Acts III).

## CHAPTER XVII  
### On the inscrutable dispensation of God
[Note: [Col. 0943C] This is the conclusion and, as it were, the summation of the preceding errors. For since he has hitherto taught that some are saved by the merits of nature and others by the grace of God—that is, that in some the beginning of salvation and grace arises from the powers of free choice, while in others it comes from God’s prevenient aid—it follows that there are two classes of people in the Church: one consisting of those who are saved willingly and spontaneously, and the other of those who, unwilling and thinking of nothing of the kind, are invited and dragged along. Consequently, Christ ought to be called not the Savior of all, but merely the receiver and helper of some. This is refuted by Saint Prosper with many arguments. On this occasion, since the matter has hitherto been deferred, it seems necessary here to warn the reader that from what has so far been argued it becomes clear that the most serious theologians rightly censure Peter Ciacon, the so-called scholiast of Cassian. While he favored Cassian more than was proper and strove to defend his teaching against error both in the books of the *Institutes* and in the *Collations*, he himself became entangled in the same snares of error, plainly conceding with Cassian that some beginning of grace and salvation comes from us. Thus, in his third proposition, where he admits that some detestation and sorrow for sin may arise from natural judgment and power alone and may constitute the beginning of justification, he likewise confesses that God is the receiver of some and the Savior of others, because he entirely precedes the latter, while he is preceded by the former (Gabriel Vásquez, *In Primam Partem*, disputation 91, chapter 11). In his second proposition he admits a certain remote disposition and preparation for grace arising from the good use and moral works of free choice, contrary to the common opinion of theologians; on this see Bellarmine, *De Gratia*, book VI, chapter 5. In his fifth proposition he openly admits that prayer—or some inclination and effort to pray—can be drawn from the good of nature, so that by it we may in some measure be made worthy of God’s grace and obtain it. These are precisely the positions of the Massilians, condemned by the supreme pontiffs, councils, and other Fathers, as is clear from what has been said. The diligent reader will observe these and other propositions collected by Ciacon from Cassian, written without sufficient caution and deserving no slight scrutiny; they have already been refuted sufficiently and more than sufficiently.]

Through these examples, then, which we have brought forward from the records of the Gospel, we can perceive most clearly that God provides for the salvation of the human race in diverse, innumerable, and inscrutable ways. He invites the course of some who are willing and thirsting to still greater fervor; while others, even unwilling and resistant, he compels, at one time assisting them so that what he has seen them profitably desire may be accomplished, and at another inspiring even the beginnings of the holy desire itself, granting either the beginning of a good work or perseverance in it.

Hence it is that in our prayers we proclaim the Lord not only our protector and Savior, but also our helper and receiver. In that he first calls us and, while we are ignorant and unwilling, draws us to salvation, he is our protector and Savior; but in that he is accustomed to bring aid to us when we strive, and to receive and fortify us when we flee, he is called our receiver and refuge.

Finally, as blessed Paul the Apostle pondered this manifold generosity of God’s dispensation in his mind, and saw himself plunged into a certain immeasurable and boundless sea of God’s goodness, he exclaimed: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments, and how unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord?” (Romans 11). Whoever believes that he can measure by human reason the depth of that immeasurable abyss will therefore attempt to empty the wonder of this knowledge, which so great and distinguished a teacher of the nations found terrifying. For whoever is confident that he can fully conceive or explain the dispensations of God by which he works salvation in human beings will undoubtedly, in profane boldness, declare that God’s judgments are scrutable and his ways traceable, thereby attacking the truth of the apostolic statement. The Lord himself also bears witness to this in these words addressed to them:

“For my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your ways my ways, says the Lord. For as the heavens are exalted above the earth, so are my ways exalted above your ways, and my thoughts above your thoughts” (Isaiah 55).

Thus, wishing to express through the movement of human affection this dispensation and love of his, which the Lord in tireless goodness deigns to bestow upon us, and finding in this creation no affection of charity to which he could more worthily compare it, he compared it with the tenderest heart of a loving mother. He uses this example because nothing dearer can be found in human nature, saying: “Can a woman forget her infant, so as not to have pity on the child of her womb?” (Isaiah 49). But not content with this comparison, he immediately surpasses it and adds: “And even if she should forget, yet I will not forget you” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XVIII

### The Definition of the Fathers: Free Choice Is Not Adequate for Salvation

From this it is gathered by evident reasoning that those who measure either the greatness of grace or the capacity of human choice not by loquacious words but under the guidance of experience understand that “the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, nor bread to the wise, nor riches to the prudent, nor grace to the learned; but one and the same Spirit works all these things, dividing to each one as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12).

And so it is confirmed by an unquestioning faith and, so to speak, tangible experience that God, like a most loving father and most benevolent physician, works all things in all people without distinction, as the Apostle says. At one time he inspires the beginnings of salvation and implants in each person the ardor of a good will; at another he grants the effect and completion of the work itself, and the perfection of virtues; at another he recalls even the unwilling and ignorant from a fall already imminent and a precipitous collapse; at another he presents occasions and opportunities for salvation, restraining sudden and violent impulses from destructive dispositions;

[Note: [Col. 0945D] Yet Saint Prosper does not mean this in such a way that, according to the new division proposed in the preceding chapter, Christ is the Savior of some and the receiver of others. Rather, Christ is everywhere both the receiver and the Savior of all the faithful. Hence in our prayers we proclaim him not, as the Collator said above, the protector and Savior of some and the helper and receiver of others, but the protector, Savior, helper, and receiver of all. But how could he say shortly before that God, like a most loving father and most benevolent physician, works all things in all people without distinction, according to the Apostle, if this distinction and difference that he himself devised is true—namely, that some are saved while others are merely received? How can God act without distinction if he deals and works so differently toward these and those? And since in the other benefits enumerated earlier everything is attributed entirely to God, why, in this final benefit, which is to save or to be the Savior—the benefit that concludes and contains all the others—is only a part assigned to him?]

He receives some who are willing and running toward him, while he drags others who are unwilling and resisting, compelling them toward a good will. Yet all this is not always granted to us while we resist or remain obstinately unwilling. And that the sum of our salvation is to be attributed not to the merit of our works but to heavenly grace, we are taught by the very words of the Lord:

“And you shall remember your ways and all your crimes by which you were defiled in them, and you shall be displeased with yourselves in your own sight because of all your wickednesses that you committed; and you shall know that I am the Lord, when I have done good to you for my name’s sake, not according to your evil ways or your most wicked crimes, house of Israel” (Ezekiel 20).

For this reason all the Catholic Fathers who learned the perfection of the heart define that it is a divine gift: first, that each person should be stirred to desire everything that is good, yet in such a way that free choice remains fully capable of either alternative; likewise, secondly, that it is the work of divine grace that the exercises of virtue mentioned above can be accomplished, but in such a way that the possibility of choice is not extinguished; and, thirdly, that it belongs to God’s gifts that the perseverance of acquired virtue be maintained, but in such a way that liberty, though bound, does not experience itself as captivity.

Thus God, the Lord of all, is to be believed to work all things in all people in such a way that he incites, protects, and strengthens, but does not take away the freedom of choice that he himself once granted. If something gathered by human argument and reasoning in a more subtle fashion seems to oppose this understanding, it should be avoided rather than proposed as a challenge to the destruction of faith. For we do not earn faith from understanding, but understanding from faith, as it is written: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah 7). For that God works all things in us, while everything is nevertheless ascribed to free choice, is expressed in the words addressed to it: “If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land” (Isaiah 1).

[Note: [Col. 0946D] If not fully, at least with moderation—just as the Apostle commands us to think soberly, not to think more highly than we ought (Romans 12)—I believe that what has been written and explained thus far in this *Collation* has made the matter clear to some extent. I hope no one will blame me for having written so freely and openly about the errors of our Collator, that is, Cassian, and for having exposed and refuted them when I ought rather to have concealed or excused them. Far be it from me, being more devoted to truth and the public good than to Cassian, to conceal that he was mistaken or to defend his mistakes, contrary to the faith and duty of an honest interpreter. Rather, I repeatedly profess and openly declare what I announced and avowed in my preface: “Cassian is my friend, but truth is a greater friend.” For error, when it is not resisted, is approved; and truth, when it is not defended at all, is suppressed, as Pope Innocent says (in Gratian, distinction 83). It is human to slip and err, but to persist in error is diabolical or heretical. Cassian, however, was always very far from that charge: he was always Catholic and regarded among Catholic authors, as even Saint Prosper himself, his bitterest opponent and adversary, bears witness (see more in our preface). What wonder, then, if, as a human being, he experienced something human and, in his excessive zeal for investigating truth, occasionally strayed from the path of truth—especially in matters so obscure and difficult, which at that time had not yet been defined and fully clarified by the Church? Should this either detract from his authority in his other writings or turn those devoted to religion and piety away from reading and studying him? Certainly not. Rather, it should kindle and inflame them all the more to embrace, read, and study him, since now that every error of his has been openly detected and the contrary truth made manifest, no danger or fear of deception remains to prevent anyone from safely and securely engaging with him and turning his pages back and forth, with antidotes and instructions everywhere ready and supplied for every encounter and occasion.

For, as Saint Jerome writes admirably to Augustine (Letter 97): “I have learned to offer this fear and honor only to the books of Scripture that are called canonical: I firmly believe that none of their authors erred in writing anything. But if I encounter in them something that seems contrary to the truth, I will not hesitate to conclude that either the codex is corrupt, or the interpreter has not grasped what was said, or I myself have not understood it.” As for other authors, however greatly they may excel in holiness and learning, I read them in such a way that I do not regard something as true merely because they thought it so, but because either through those canonical authors or by probable reasoning they have been able to persuade me that it does not depart from the truth. Thus Saint Jerome.

Elsewhere (Letter 76), he gives his judgment and advice in these words concerning ancient writers of this kind, whose writings are known to be sprinkled with certain errors: “I think that Origen should sometimes be read for his learning in the same way as Tertullian, Novatian, Arnobius, Apollinaris, and certain other ecclesiastical writers, both Greek and Latin: so that we may choose what is good in them and avoid what is contrary, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: ‘Test everything; hold fast what is good,’ and so forth.”

Thus Cassian should be read like any other Catholic author: whatever in him agrees with truth and piety, let us embrace; whatever is alien to them, let us reject; and let us destroy the poison of falsehood with the antidote of truth.

Moreover, since human dispositions are so varied, and the tastes—and, as it were, certain appetites (*orexeis*, ὀρέξεις)—of varied dispositions are also varied, so that what pleases one produces nausea and disgust in another, I certainly did not wish to fail to set before my readers, as before fellow guests at a banquet, another dish that may perhaps please them more than the difficult and obscure treatment of the preceding disputations. I mean the sound and Catholic teaching of Dionysius the Carthusian, a man no less distinguished for holiness than for learning, concerning the grace of God and the free choice of human beings. He gathered this teaching for the most part from the statements of Abbot Chaeremon, arranging it with such skill that, after removing and wiping away the errors, he presented it in its entirety as pure, orthodox, pious, and salutary. At the end of the eighteenth chapter he substituted and inserted it into the remainder of the *Collation*, as though it were spoken by Chaeremon himself, fulfilling here not the office of a paraphraser, as elsewhere, but that of a censor and corrector. Thus Dionysius continues Chaeremon’s *Collation* from chapter eighteen to the end.]

To the fullest extent, however, it cannot, in my judgment, be grasped by human understanding and reason.

## CHAPTER XIX

### The Catholic Teaching of Blessed Dionysius Richel, the Carthusian, Substituted by Him for the Preceding *Collation*

Divine protection is inseparably present with us, and so great is the Savior’s goodness toward his own creature that by his providence he not only accompanies it but continually goes before it. The Prophet experienced this and openly confessed it to the Lord: “My God, his mercy has gone before me” (Psalm 58).

He not only benevolently inspires holy desires, but also provides occasions for salvation and shows those who are wandering the opportunity for good actions and the direction of the saving way. Hence it happens that he is found by those who do not seek him, and appears openly among those who did not ask him; and all day long he stretches out his hands to a people that does not believe and contradicts him. He also calls those who resist and are far away, attracts the unwilling to salvation, takes away from those who wish to sin the opportunity to fulfill their desires, and benevolently resists those hastening toward evil, so that it is no longer a matter of the one who wills or the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy (Romans 9), who works in us both willing and accomplishing according to his good pleasure (Philippians 2). And this is not from ourselves: it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast (Ephesians 2).

For what does the Savior say? “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14). And again: “No one comes to me unless the Father draws him” (John 6). What, likewise, do we pray? “Direct my way in your sight” (Psalm 5), and: “Perfect my steps in your paths, so that my footsteps may not be moved” (Psalm 16). What, finally, does God promise? “I will give them a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within them. And I will take away the heart of stone from your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh, so that you may walk in my commandments, keep my judgments, and perform them” (Ezekiel 36).

And what is it that the Prophet himself asks from the Lord when he says: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Psalm 50)? And again: “You will wash me,” he says, “and I shall be whiter than snow” (ibid.). Likewise, what is meant by the statement concerning God: “He teaches human beings knowledge” (Psalm 94), and: “The Lord gives light to the blind” (Psalm 146)? Or by what we say in prayer with the Prophet: “Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death” (Psalm 12)? Is it not that all these things declare the grace of God, by which human beings always need to be helped by the Lord?

The Apostle reveals the weakness of free choice when he says: “May the Lord guard your hearts and your understanding” (Philippians 4). David teaches the same thing in prayer when he says: “Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to covetousness” (Psalm 118). Solomon likewise says: “May he incline our hearts to himself, so that we may walk in all his ways, keep his commandments and his ordinances” (1 Kings 8). Our own prayer confesses the weakness of free choice: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips” (Psalm 140).

Likewise the Prophet says: “The Lord releases those in chains; the Lord gives light to the blind” (Psalm 145). And again: “You have broken my bonds” (Psalm 115), and so forth. Likewise Christ says in John’s Gospel: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6). And the most blessed John the Baptist declares: “A human being cannot receive anything of himself unless it has been given to him from heaven” (John 3). Therefore the Prophet cries out in the Spirit: “Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it keeps watch in vain” (Psalm 126). And the Apostle says: “God is the one who works in us both willing and accomplishing according to his good pleasure” (Philippians 2).

Furthermore, if we attribute the completion of virtues and the carrying out of the commandments to our own choice, how do we pray: “Confirm, O God, what you have worked in us” (Psalm 57), and: “Direct the works of our hands over us” (Psalm 89)?

We know that Balaam was hired to curse the children of Israel, but we see that he was not permitted to do what he desired (Numbers 22). Abimelech was guarded so that he would not sin against the Lord by touching Rebecca (Genesis 21). Joseph was sold because of his brothers’ jealousy, so that the descent of the sons of Israel into Egypt might take place and provision might be made for the famine that would come while they were plotting Joseph’s death. Joseph himself discloses this when he says:

“Do not be afraid, and do not let it seem harsh to you that you sold me in these regions. For God sent me before you for your salvation” (Genesis 45).

And again:

“God sent me ahead so that you might be preserved upon the earth and might have food for your survival. It was not by your counsel but by God’s will that I was sent here; he made me like a father to Pharaoh, lord of all his household, and ruler throughout the whole land of Egypt” (ibid.).

And when, after the death of his father, he removed the suspicion of fear from his brothers, who were afraid, he said:

“Do not be afraid. Can we resist God’s will? You planned evil against me, but God turned it into good, so that he might exalt me, as you now see, and save many peoples” (Genesis 50).

David sings of this same event as an act of divine economy or dispensation in the Psalm: “He summoned famine upon the land and destroyed every support of bread. He sent a man before them; Joseph was sold as a slave” (Psalm 104).

Let us therefore establish the power and effectiveness of God’s grace, lest we seem to have exceeded the rule of ecclesiastical faith. The ecclesiastical rule is proclaimed by the Apostle: “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12). The ecclesiastical rule is: “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me has not been fruitless; rather, I labored more than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me” (1 Corinthians 15). And: “I obtained mercy so that I might be faithful” (1 Corinthians 7).

The ecclesiastical rule is: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing power may belong to God and not come from us” (2 Corinthians 4). The ecclesiastical rule is: “In nothing be terrified by your adversaries. This is for them a cause of destruction, but for you of salvation, and this is from God. For to you it has been granted through Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Philippians 1).

The ecclesiastical rule is: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For God is the one who works in you both willing and working according to his good pleasure” (Philippians 2). The ecclesiastical rule is: “Not that we are capable of thinking anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves; our sufficiency is from God” (2 Corinthians 3).

God confirms this rule when he says: “No one can come to me unless it has been given to him by my Father” (John 6). And: “Everything that the Father gives me will come to me” (ibid.). And: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15). And: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (ibid.). And: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and the one to whom he wishes to reveal him” (Matthew 11). And: “As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to those whom he wills” (John 5). And: “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 16).

By this rule the will is taken away from no human being, because the power of grace does not work in wills so that they cease to exist, but so that what is evil may become good, what is unbelieving may become faithful, and those who were darkness in themselves may become light in the Lord; so that what was dead may be brought to life, what lay fallen may be raised, and what had perished may be found. We believe that the grace of the Savior acts in precisely this way in all human beings who are rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of the Son of God’s love (Colossians 1), without exception of persons.

For, as the author of this *Collation* has reasonably defined, we say and defend that not only the beginning of good actions but also the beginning of good thoughts comes from God. He inspires in us the beginning of a good will and grants us the power and opportunity to carry out the things we rightly desire: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1). He both begins what is good and carries it out and brings it to completion in us. For when God sees that we have grown lukewarm, he introduces into our hearts salutary prayers [alternative reading: thoughts], by which a good will is restored in us.

There can be no doubt that the first human being was created upright and free from every fault, and that the nature of all human beings was created in him. He received free choice in such a way that, if he did not abandon the Lord who was helping him, what he had naturally received could have persevered in us because he willed it; and by the merit of perseverance he would have reached the same blessedness, so that he would neither have wished nor been able to fall into worse things.

But by that same free choice by which he remained good for as long as he willed, he departed from the law laid down for him. He did not fear the punishment of death when it was announced to him; he abandoned God and followed the devil, rebelling against the Lord his Savior and obeying the enemy and destroyer.

Adam existed, and in him we all existed. Adam perished, and from him all perished. Blessed Ambrose said this no less truly than Truth itself said: “The Son of Man came to seek and save what had perished” (Luke 19).

For in that universal ruin of human nature brought about by the transgression, neither substance nor will was taken away; rather, the light and beauty of the virtues were stripped from it by the deceit of the envious one. Once it had lost the things by which it could attain the eternal and imperishable incorruption of body and soul, what remained to it except what belongs to temporal life, which is wholly subject to condemnation and punishment?

For this reason those born in Adam must be reborn in Christ, lest anyone be found in that generation which perished. For if the descendants of Adam naturally acted in those virtues in which Adam was before sin, they would not be by nature children of wrath; they would not be darkness or under the power of darkness; they would not need the grace of the Savior, since they would not be good without purpose and would not be deprived of the reward of righteousness while possessing those goods whose loss caused our first parents to deserve exile from paradise.

But now, since no one can escape eternal death without the sacrament of rebirth, does not the singularity of this remedy make it perfectly clear into what profound evil the nature of the entire human race has been plunged by the transgression of the one in whom all sinned, and that they lost everything he lost?

The first man lost faith; he lost self-restraint; he lost charity. He was stripped of wisdom and understanding; he lacked counsel and fortitude. In impiously pursuing higher things, he was cast down from knowledge of the truth and the piety of obedience. Nor was even fear left to him, by which he might have avoided what was forbidden or feared punishment—he who had refrained from it through love of righteousness.

Free choice, then—that is, the spontaneous appetite for what pleased it—when it grew weary of using the good things it had received, and, as the safeguards of its salvation became cheap in its eyes, directed its diseased desire toward experiencing transgression, drank the poison of every vice, and drenched the whole nature of humanity with the drunkenness of its intemperance.

From that moment, before digesting the lethal crudity by eating the flesh of the Son of Man and drinking his blood, memory slipped, judgment went astray, one’s steps faltered, and the human being became in every way incapable of choosing and desiring the good from which he had voluntarily deprived himself. For just as he was able to fall without God’s impelling him, so he cannot rise without God’s raising him.

Lest we believe that we do not need divine help to perform the work of salvation, the Apostle says: “God is the one who works in us both willing and accomplishing according to his good pleasure” (Philippians 2). Therefore he also admonished Timothy: “Do not neglect the grace of God that is in you” (1 Timothy 4). And again: “For this reason I remind you to stir up the grace of God that is in you” (2 Timothy 1).

Writing also to the Corinthians, he urges them not to make themselves unworthy of the grace of God through unfruitful works, saying: “As fellow workers, we entreat you not to receive the grace of God in vain” (2 Corinthians 6). Because Simon had received it in vain, the reception of saving grace did him no good. For he did not take care to obey the command of the most holy Peter, who said: “Repent of this wickedness of yours and pray to God, if perhaps this thought of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity” (Acts 8).

The mercy of the Lord therefore precedes the will of the human being, according to what is written: “My God, his mercy has gone before me” (Psalm 58). Moreover, the Lord calls and invites us, as he says: “All day long I stretched out my hands to a people that did not believe and contradicted me” (Isaiah 65). God waits for us, as he speaks through the Prophet: “Therefore the Lord waits, that he may have mercy on you” (Isaiah 30). He strengthens us, according to what he says: “I instructed them and strengthened their arms, yet they devised evil against me” (Hosea 7). The Lord Jesus cries out: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7). The Lord seeks us, saying: “I sought, and there was no man; I called, and there was no one who answered” (Isaiah 52).

Thus the grace of God always cooperates with our choice for good, and in all things so helps and protects it that it always remains gratuitous, while with immeasurable generosity it grants small efforts the glory of such great immortality and such great gifts of everlasting happiness.

Was not the forgiveness of so many crimes, obtained by David in an extremely brief moment of time, a gift of the merciful God? Finally, what shall we say about David’s confession, so brief, and the immeasurable magnitude of the divine mercy and recompense, which is so incomparable? We know what the Apostle, looking toward the greatness of future blessedness, declared concerning his countless and most grievous persecutions:

“For this momentary and light affliction of ours is producing in us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure and beyond all comparison” (2 Corinthians 9).

And elsewhere he firmly confesses: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8).

Therefore, however much human frailty may strive and exert itself, it cannot be compared with the future recompense; nor can it so diminish the grace of the Creator through its labors that the grace would cease to remain gratuitous.

For this reason the teacher of the nations mentioned above, although he testifies that he received the rank of apostolate by the grace of God, saying, “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15), nevertheless affirms that he responded to and cooperated with divine grace, adding:

“And his grace toward me has not been fruitless; rather, I labored more abundantly than all of them. Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (ibid.).

When he says, “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me,” he displays the power of divine protection. When he says, “with me,” he testifies that God’s grace cooperated with him not while he was idle or secure, but while he was laboring and sweating.

Thus the Lord, wishing to express through the movement of human affection the dispensation of his goodness and the love that in tireless goodness he deigns to bestow upon us, and finding no charity in created things to which he could more worthily compare it, compared it with the tenderest heart of a mother. He uses this example because nothing dearer can be found in creation: “Can a woman forget her infant, so as not to have pity on the child of her womb? Yet even if she should forget, I will not forget you” (Isaiah 49).

From this it is gathered by evident reasoning that the sum of our salvation must be attributed to heavenly grace, not to the merits of our actions, with God speaking through the Prophet:

“You shall remember your ways and all your crimes, and you shall be displeased with yourselves because of your wickednesses; and you shall know that I am the Lord, when I have done good to you for my name’s sake, not according to your evil ways or your most wicked crimes, house of Israel” (Ezekiel 12).

Hence all the Catholic Fathers who have learned the perfection of the heart, not through empty disputation but through a worthy manner of life, affirm that this is the first work of the divine gift: that each person should approach the desire for everything good, yet in such a way that free choice remains fully capable of either alternative.

They declare that the second work of divine grace is that the aforementioned exercises of virtue may be accomplished, while the possibility of choice is not removed. Third, they testify that it belongs to grace that the acquired virtues be preserved with perseverance, but in such a way that liberty does not experience captivity.

Thus God, the Lord of all, is to be believed to work all things in all people in such a way that he incites, protects, and confirms, but does not take away the freedom that he once granted.

If anything gathered by human argument and reasoning seems cleverly to derogate from these principles, it should be avoided rather than proposed or urged toward the destruction of faith. For we do not earn faith from understanding, but understanding from faith, as it is written: “Unless you believe, you will not understand.” For, in my judgment, human reason cannot fully comprehend how God works all things in us while everything is nevertheless attributed to free choice, when the Lord says: “If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land” (Isaiah 1).

[Note: [Col. 0953A] Up to this point Dionysius has pursued this *Collation* in a Catholic manner, as though speaking in the person of Abbot Chaeremon. He is certainly deserving of great praise for having extracted and expressed gems from dung, or pure gold from mud—that is, true and Catholic teaching from false and erroneous material. John Lavardin likewise wisely and prudently judged in his French translation that this alone should be retained and expressed, with the rest omitted; he too deserves praise for not wishing to present doubtful or dangerous teaching in the vernacular to inexperienced or weak minds. Finally, Cassian, the narrator of this *Collation* as of the others, concludes chapter 18 in this way: “This food strengthened us, blessed Chaeremon, and enabled us not to feel the labor of such an impassable journey.” The food, of course, was spiritual, not bodily.]

## THE FOURTEENTH COLLATION

### The First of Abbot Nesteros: On Spiritual Knowledge

[Col. 0953]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0953B]

**Of the Promise** [Note: That is, of the promise recently published in the preface to these *Collations* in these words (Preface to Collation 11): “Now, so that the arrangement of our journey may also be understood, I have judged it fitting to dedicate to you the seven *Collations* of the three Fathers who lived in another desert and whom we first saw, written in the same style; by them those things which in our previous little works may perhaps have been treated more obscurely or omitted concerning perfection may be supplied.] our journey’s order requires that the instruction of the distinguished Abbot [Note: He was the second of the three anchorites whom the Author reported as living in the wilderness near Panephysis (*Collation* 11, chapter 3), with whom the following seven *Collations* were held. Two of these are attributed to Nesteros: this first one, on spiritual knowledge, and the later one, on divine gifts. Concerning Abbot Nesteron—for there he is called Nestero or Nesteron, not Nesteros as here—two examples of his virtues are related in the *Lives of the Fathers*. The first occurs in Book IV, chapter 8: “Abba Nesteron the Elder was walking in the desert with a certain brother, and when they saw a dragon they fled. The brother said to him, ‘And you, Father, are you afraid?’ The old man replied, ‘I am not afraid, my son; that is not the reason. But it is expedient. For I fled from the dragon because I had to flee from the spirit of vainglory.’” The second is in the same book, chapter 15: “The old man”—Abba Pastor—“asked Brother Nesteron, saying: ‘Abba Nesteron, how have you acquired this virtue, so that when some trouble [another reading: disturbance] arises in the monastery, you do not speak or put yourself in the middle of it?’ But he said nothing. When the old man questioned him at length, he said to him: ‘Forgive me, Abba. When I first entered the community, I said to myself, “You and the donkey must be one.” Just as the donkey is beaten and does not speak, suffers insult and does not answer, so must you be, as it is written in the psalm: “I have become like a beast of burden before you, and I am continually with you” (Psalm 72).’ Thus far the text.]

of Nesteros, a man eminent and of the highest knowledge in every respect, should follow. When he perceived that we had committed certain passages of the sacred Scriptures to memory and desired their meaning, he addressed us in these words:

“There are indeed many kinds of knowledge in this world, as many as there are varieties of arts and disciplines. But although all of them are either altogether useless or useful only for the advantages of the present life, there is nevertheless none that does not possess its own order and method of instruction, by which it can be attained by those who seek it. If, then, those arts are directed toward making themselves understood by definite and particular lines, how much more must the discipline and profession of our religion—which tends toward contemplating the mysteries of invisible things and seeks not the rewards of present gain but the recompense of eternal rewards—rest upon a definite order and method!”

[Note: Of the religious discipline and profession mentioned above. The common division of knowledge into speculative and practical knowledge was handed down by Aristotle (*Metaphysics*, Books I and VI). In view of this distinction, the Fathers likewise distinguish two lives, the active and the contemplative (Jerome, Book II on the *Lamentations of Jeremiah*). Saint Gregory says in Book VI, chapter 28 of the *Moralia*: “There are two lives in which Almighty God instructs us through sacred discourse, namely the active and the contemplative. Human life, as Saint Thomas teaches (*Summa theologica* II–II, question 179), is chiefly considered according to the operation of the intellect. That operation is concerned either with the investigation and knowledge of truth, which belongs to contemplation, or with external actions, which is called the active life. Everything living is shown to live through the operation most proper to it and toward which it is most strongly inclined: thus the life of plants is said to consist in being nourished and reproducing; that of animals, in sensing and moving; and that of human beings, in understanding and acting according to reason. Since some people devote themselves chiefly to the contemplation of truth, while others attend principally to external actions, human life is suitably divided into the active and the contemplative. Thus Saint Thomas. It is therefore clear that it is the same whether one speaks of two lives of human beings or of two kinds of knowledge. The subject of this *Collation* is not human knowledge in general, but, as the title teaches, spiritual knowledge—that is, knowledge of spiritual things joined with piety and charity—as will become clear from what follows. It is also numbered among the gifts of the Holy Spirit. ‘This is the knowledge of the saints,’ says Saint Thomas (*Summa theologica* II–II, question 10, article 3), ‘of which Wisdom 10 says: “The Lord led the just man by straight paths and gave him the knowledge of the saints.”’]

This knowledge has two forms. The first is practical—that is, active—and is perfected through the correction of conduct and the cleansing away of vices; the other is theoretical—that is, it consists in the contemplation of divine things and the knowledge of the most sacred meanings.

## CHAPTER II  
### The Way to Theoretical Knowledge

[Note: Saint Jerome calls it *theoretical* in his commentary on the *Lamentations of Jeremiah*. “There is,” he says, “one and only one theoretical life, that is, the contemplation of God, to which all the merits of justification and all the means of virtue are rightly subordinated.” Dionysius likewise reads *theoricam*, not *theoreticam*. Jerome also takes *theoricam* substantively, as Cassian does here with *theoreticen* (Book I, chapter 2). See also what we have noted elsewhere concerning *theorica* and *theoretica*.]

Whoever, therefore, wishes to reach theoretical knowledge [Note: Gregory, in the passage cited above (*Moralia* VI, chapter 28), explaining the words, “You will enter the grave in abundance” (Job 5), says: “The perfect man enters the grave in abundance, because he first gathers the works of the active life and afterward, through contemplation, hides the sense of the flesh, dead to this world, completely from it. Hence it is suitably added: ‘As a heap is gathered in its season.’ The time of action comes first, and that of contemplation last. Therefore everyone who is perfect must first exercise the mind in virtues and afterward store it in the granary of repose.” And below: “This is why Jacob served for Rachel and received Leah, and it is said to him: ‘It is not customary in our land to give the younger in marriage before the elder’ (Genesis 23). Rachel means ‘vision in principle,’ while Leah is said to mean ‘laboring.’ What is signified by Rachel if not the contemplative life, and by Leah if not the active life? In contemplation the principle, which is God, is sought; in action one labors under the heavy burden of necessities. Thus Rachel is beautiful but barren, while Leah is bleary-eyed but fruitful, because when the mind seeks leisure for contemplation it sees more but generates fewer children for God; when it turns toward the labor of preaching, it sees less but suffers more. After embracing Leah, Jacob reached Rachel, because everyone who is perfect is first joined to the active life for fruitfulness and afterward joined to the contemplative life for rest. Gregory has similar material in Homily 14 on Ezekiel, as does Isidore in Book III, chapter 15 of *On the Highest Good*. See also Saint Thomas, II–II, question 182, article 1, and Cajetan in the same place.]

must obtain practical knowledge first, with every effort and virtue. For practical knowledge can be possessed without theoretical knowledge, but theoretical knowledge cannot in any way be grasped without practical knowledge. There are certain degrees, ordered and distinct, by which human humility can ascend to what is sublime. If they follow one another in the manner we have described, one can reach the height that cannot be flown over once the first step has been removed. Therefore the person who does not avoid the contamination of vices strives in vain toward the sight of God:

“For the Spirit of God will flee deceit and will not dwell in a body subjected to sins” (Wisdom 1).

[Note: The order of the sacred text is inverted here. It reads as follows: “Wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul, nor dwell in a body subjected to sins. For the holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit and withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding” (Wisdom 1). The Septuagint reads: “The holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit and withdraw from foolish thoughts.”]

## CHAPTER III  
### That Practical Perfection Rests on Two Principles

[Note: The active life has two duties, or the active life consists in two things: the cleansing away of vices and the acquisition of virtues. The Psalmist expressed this in other words: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 36). These are the first precepts, or duties, of Christian righteousness.]

Practical perfection rests on two principles. The first is that the nature of every kind of vice and the means of its cure be understood. The second is that the order of the virtues be so discerned, and our mind so formed by their perfection, that it no longer serves them as though compelled and subjected to a kind of violent command, but delights in and is nourished by them as by a natural good, and ascends that difficult and narrow way with pleasure.

For how will one be able to attain either the knowledge of the virtues—which is the second step in practical discipline—or the mysteries of spiritual and heavenly things, which are found on the higher step of contemplation, if one has neither been able to understand the nature of one’s own vices nor attempted to uproot them? It will consequently be declared impossible for one who has not overcome the lower things to advance to the higher; and still less will anyone grasp what lies outside him who has been unable to understand what has been implanted within him.

Yet we must know that we must labor with a twofold exertion, both in driving out vices and in acquiring virtues. We are not guided to this by our own conjecture, but are thoroughly instructed by the statement of the one who alone knows the power and order of his office [Lipsius, in the margin: “work”]:

“Behold,” he says, “I have appointed you today over nations and over kingdoms, to uproot and destroy and ruin and demolish and build and plant” (Jeremiah 1).

[Note: Saint Jerome observes that the expression he added from the Hebrew, “to demolish,” or “to tear down,” is not found in the Septuagint. “It should be considered,” he says, “that four sorrowful things are followed by two joyful ones. For good things could not be built unless evil things had been destroyed, nor the best things planted unless the worst had been uprooted,” and so forth. The following poem of Boethius is relevant (*Consolation of Philosophy*, Book III, meter 1):

> Whoever wishes to sow a noble field  
> First frees the fields from thorns;  
> With the sickle he cuts away brambles and fern,  
> So that Ceres may advance laden with new grain.  
>   
> You also, while looking upon false goods, first  
> Begin to draw your neck back from the yoke;  
> Thereafter true things will enter the soul.]

In the expulsion of harmful things, therefore, he showed that four actions are necessary: to uproot, destroy, ruin, and demolish. In perfecting the virtues and acquiring what pertains to righteousness, only building and planting are required. Hence it is plainly evident that the passions ingrained in body and soul are more difficult to tear out and eradicate than it is to construct and plant spiritual virtues.

## CHAPTER IV  
### That the Active Life Is Directed toward Many Professions and Pursuits

[Note: The works of the active life, although numerous, can be reduced to three categories. The first includes those works that pertain to one’s own correction and perfection, such as works of penance, fasts, vigils, prayers, and so forth; these are chiefly at issue here. The second includes those which, not without merit on our part, concern the conversion of souls and the salvation of our neighbors, such as the works of mercy called spiritual works. Saint Gregory says of these (*Homily 14 on Ezekiel*): “The active life is to correct the one who is in error, to recall a proud neighbor to a humble life, to distribute to each person what is expedient as occasion allows,” and so forth. The third consists of those things which, along with one’s own advancement, are directed toward the temporal and bodily needs and uses of ourselves or others; these are called corporal works of mercy. The same statement of Gregory is understood of these as well: “To distribute to each person what is expedient as occasion allows, and to provide for those entrusted to us in such a way that they may be able to subsist.”]

This practical discipline, then, which, as has been said, rests on two principles, is divided among many professions and pursuits. [Note: Saint Thomas used this passage to prove and confirm the variety and diversity of religious communities, or religious orders. He writes as follows (*Summa theologica* II–II, question 148, article 2): “The religious state is ordered toward the perfection of charity, which extends to love of God and neighbor. The contemplative life, which desires to devote itself to God alone, directly pertains to love of God. The active life, which serves the needs of one’s neighbors, directly pertains to love of neighbor. And just as one loves one’s neighbor through charity for God’s sake, so the service rendered to one’s neighbors redounds to God, according to the saying in Matthew 25: ‘Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me.’ Therefore services rendered to one’s neighbors, insofar as they are referred to God, are called sacrifices, according to the final chapter of Hebrews: ‘Do not forget kindness and fellowship, for God is pleased with such sacrifices.’ Since it properly belongs to religion to offer sacrifice to God, it follows that certain religious communities are suitably ordered toward the works of the active life. Thus, in the *Collations of the Fathers*, Abbot Nesteros [Note: In some copies it is corruptly read “Abbot Nestor” or “Nestorius.”], distinguishing the various pursuits of religious communities, says: ‘Some place the whole aim of their purpose upon the solitude of the desert and purity of heart; some upon the formation of brothers and the care of coenobitic communities; some take delight in the service of a xenodochium, that is, hospitality.’”]

Some place the whole aim of their purpose upon the solitude of the desert and purity of heart. Thus we know that in former times Elijah and Elisha, and in our own time blessed Antony and other followers of the same purpose, clung most intimately to God through the silence of solitude. Some devoted all the concern of their effort to the formation of brothers and the vigilant care of coenobitic communities, as we recently remember Abbot [Note: Concerning him, Cassian speaks in Book V, chapters 27 and 28, and frequently elsewhere. The nineteenth *Collation*, inscribed under the name of Abbot John, also seems to belong to him, so far as one may infer from the circumstances. Many other famous anchorites of this name also existed, as may be seen in the *Lives of the Fathers*, Palladius, and others.]

John, who presided over a great coenobium in the vicinity of [Note: Ciaconius restored this name of the city, since previously it was read corruptly not only in ancient manuscripts but also in the Plantinian edition as “Thmuius” or “Thymus.” It was Θμοῦϊς, or Thmuis, a town of Egypt, according to Saint Jerome in his *Catalogue*. “Aristeas,” he says, “concerning the Egyptian city called Thmuis.” Again, in the same work, under Serapion: “Serapion of Θμοῦϊς, bishop, who on account of the elegance of his intellect earned the surname ‘the Scholastic,’” and so forth. The same city is mentioned in the Sibylline Oracles. Jerome also says that it was named from a goat, in Book II *Against Jovinianus*: “The cities among the Egyptians are likewise named from the names of animals: Leonto, Cyno, Lyco, Busiris, and Thmuis, which means ‘goat.’” And in his commentary on Isaiah 46: “Most towns among the Egyptians have names derived from beasts and animals: Κυνών, from a dog; Λεών, from a lion; Θμοῦϊς, in the Egyptian language, from a goat; Λυκών, from a wolf.” Thus Jerome. Baron also noted the following concerning this same city in his annotations to the *Martyrology* (21 March): “This city was situated in the province of Egypt called Schethi, which is often found under the name Scythia, after the eastern Scythians. Justin states in Book II of his *History* that the Egyptians had been defeated by the Scythians. That the city called Thmuis was in Schethi is clear from a letter of Saint Germanus, bishop of Capua, and the other legates to Pope Hormisdas, which we possess in manuscript. Concerning the monks of Schethi, or Scythia, it reads: ‘These men accuse the bishops of their province, among whom is Paternus, bishop of the city of Thmuis,’ and so forth. This is taken from Baron’s annotations.]

the city called Thmuis [Lipsius, in the margin: “in a neighboring city”], and we remember that several men of equal merit shone even through apostolic signs.

Some take delight in the pious service of a xenodochium and of receiving guests. [Note: A *xenodochium* is a guest-house or public hospice in which guests—that is, travellers—are received. Josephus and Hegesippus report that this kind of institution was first built at Jerusalem by Hyrcanus (*Antiquities* XIII, chapter 16; Hegesippus, Book I). At Constantinople a certain priest, Zoticus, founded a Roman xenodochium in the time of the emperor Constantine (Baronius, *Martyrology*, 31 December). Likewise, at Rome Saint Fabiola is said to have been the first to establish a *nosocomium*, that is, a hospice for the sick, and Saint Pammachius a xenodochium at the Roman port. Jerome says of Fabiola: “She was the first of all to establish a *nosocomium*, in which she gathered the sick from the streets and cared for the limbs of the wretched, wasted by disease and hunger.” Of Pammachius’s xenodochium he says in the same place: “The whole world has likewise heard of the xenodochium situated at the Roman port.” Palladius also mentions (*Lausiac History* VII) a xenodochium on Mount Nitria, over which monks presided. From these things the ancient institution of xenodochia may be observed; hence the hospitaller orders took their name.] Through this service we know that in former times the patriarchs Abraham and Lot pleased the Lord, and more recently blessed [Note: We have noted elsewhere that there were two Egyptian men named Macarius, famous for the praise of holiness and the practice of anchoritic life. One was called Alexandrian because, as Palladius writes (*Lausiac History*, chapter 29), he served as a priest in the Alexandrian church; the other was simply called Egyptian. The present passage seems to concern the former, or Macarius of Alexandria, since the circumstances mentioned here indicate that he presided over a xenodochium near Alexandria. Palladius also relates this notable example of his exceptional charity toward the sick and his remarkable abstinence: Once, when he desired to eat some fresh and very fine grapes that had been sent to him, he demonstrated his self-control by sending them to another suffering brother who also desired grapes. When that brother received them, he did the same thing, although he himself greatly desired to eat them.
