After the grapes had subsequently reached many brothers, and none had wished to eat them, the last person who received them sent them back to Macarius, as though giving him a great gift. After carefully investigating what had happened, Macarius marveled and gave thanks to God for their great self-restraint; he himself did not finally eat any of them. Thus far Palladius. The same story is also related in other words in the *Lives of the Fathers*.]

Macarius, a man of extraordinary gentleness and patience, who presided over a xenodochium [Col. 0959A] near Alexandria in such a way that he must be considered inferior to none of those who pursued the solitude of the desert. Some chose the care of the sick; others carried out the intercession offered for the wretched and oppressed; others devoted themselves to teaching or distributed alms to the poor. Among the great and eminent men, each flourished according to his own disposition and piety.

## CHAPTER V  
### Perseverance in the Profession Once Undertaken

Therefore it is useful and fitting for each person, according to the purpose he has chosen or the grace he has received, to hasten with the greatest zeal and diligence toward the perfection of the work he has undertaken. He should praise and admire the virtues of others, but in no way depart from the profession he once chose, knowing, according to the Apostle, that the Church is one body but has many members, and that it possesses gifts differing according to the grace given to us: prophecy according to the proportion of faith, ministry in serving, teaching in instruction, exhortation in exhorting, giving in generosity, presiding in diligence, and showing mercy with cheerfulness (Romans 12).

[Note: An excellent passage concerning transfer from one religious community to another and stability of place, which monks—especially Benedictines—explicitly profess according to the institution of their Rule (chapter 10). Saint Bernard writes the following about this in his work *On Precept and Dispensation*: “Let the covenant of stability”—that is, the vow—“from now on forbid every lax descent, contentious departure, wandering and inquisitive roaming, and all the frivolity of inconstancy. This does not apply, however, to the things that follow in the order of the profession, namely conversion of conduct and obedience, which are practiced according to the Rule. For if these cannot perhaps be obtained there, because of the wickedness and irreligiousness of those living together, I unquestionably advise a person, guided by the spirit of freedom, to move to another place where he will not be prevented from rendering to God the vows his lips have uttered. Certainly, concerning religious and well-ordered monasteries, no professed member, on my advice, should leave—even from a desire for a stricter life—or even with the permission of his superior. If, however, after leaving he finds and chooses something better, he should nevertheless not, on my advice, return to the inferior good that he had abandoned and despised in comparison with the better, especially if that better place seems to accord with his first profession. And shortly afterward: ‘Perhaps someone wishes to pass from the observances of the Cluniacs to the poverty of the Cistercians, choosing in preference to those customs a greater purity of the Rule. If he consults me, I do not advise it, unless he has properly secured the consent of his abbot. Why? First, because of the scandal to those whom he would abandon. Second, because it is not safe to leave certainties for uncertainties. Perhaps he can maintain the one but will not be able to maintain the other. Third, I suspect the fickleness by which people often reject, before testing, what they wish to do, being almost at the same moment both desirous of it and rejecting it, as lightly and irrationally as possible. We frequently find many such people, who scarcely remain one hour in a single intention and, driven by the breeze of fickleness, waver and change from place to place like drunken men, altering their judgment according to what they have experienced—or rather, wavering and agitated without judgment, presuming to form as many plans for themselves as places they visit; always desiring what they do not have and despising what they have.’ Thus Saint Bernard. If you desire more on this transfer, see Saint Thomas, II–II, question 189, article 8.]

For no members can claim for themselves the ministries of other members, since neither do eyes perform the service of hands nor noses that of ears. Therefore not all are apostles, not all prophets, not all teachers; not all possess gifts of healing, not all speak in tongues, and not all interpret.

## CHAPTER VI  
### The Instability of the Weak

[Col. 0960A]

Those who have not yet become firmly established in the profession they have undertaken are accustomed, when they hear certain people praised for different pursuits and virtues, to be so inflamed by their praise that they immediately long to imitate their discipline. In this, human weakness necessarily expends its efforts in vain. For it is impossible for one and the same person to shine simultaneously in all the virtues mentioned above.

[Note: For this reason Cassian, in Book V, chapter 4 of the *Institutes*, teaches on the authority of blessed Antony that a monk who, after adopting the coenobitic purpose—that is, the monastic or coenobitic profession—strives to attain the heights of more sublime perfection and reach the ark of the anchoritic life should not seek every kind of virtue from a single person, however eminent. “One,” he says, “is adorned with the flowers of knowledge; another is more strongly fortified by discernment; another is grounded in the gravity of patience; another is distinguished by humility, another by the virtue of continence; another is adorned by the grace of simplicity. One surpasses the others in greatness of spirit, another in mercy, another in vigils, another in silence, another in dedication to labor. Therefore the monk who wishes to gather spiritual honey, like a very prudent bee, should draw each virtue from those who possess it most intimately and carefully store it in the vessel of his breast. He should not investigate what anyone lacks, but should consider only what virtue that person possesses and diligently extract it. For if we wish to borrow all virtues from one person, examples suitable for imitation will either be difficult or certainly never be found.”]

If someone wishes to pursue all of them equally, he must fall into the situation that, while following them all, he achieves none of them completely; and he will suffer greater loss than gain from this change and variety. There are many roads by which one tends toward God. Therefore each person should complete, with an unchangeable determination of his course, the path he has once undertaken, so that he may be perfect in whatever profession he follows.

## CHAPTER VII  
### An Example of Chastity Showing That Not Everything Is to Be Imitated by Everyone

Apart from the loss with which, as we have said, a monk is struck when through instability of mind he wishes to pass to different pursuits, there is also a danger of death in the fact that things rightly done by some are sometimes presumed upon by others as a bad example; and what has turned out well for certain people is experienced as harmful by others.

To offer an example: suppose someone wished to imitate the virtue of that man whom Abbot John was accustomed to mention [Note: Concerning this, see above, chapter 6. For if he had meant another person, I think he would have distinguished him by some identifying mark.] not as a model for imitation but merely out of admiration.

A certain man came to the aforementioned old man in secular clothing and, after bringing him some of the first fruits of his crops, found there a man possessed by a most savage demon. The demon, despising the adjurations and commands of Abbot John, declared that he would never leave the body he had possessed at the old man’s command. But terrified by the newcomer, he departed with the most reverent proclamation of that man’s name.

The old man greatly admired such an evident grace [Note: See how great is the virtue and grace of chastity and virginal continence, which the demon could not endure even in a layman and peasant.] and was even more astonished because he saw him dressed in secular clothing. He began carefully to inquire into the order of his life and profession. When the man said that he was a layman and bound by marriage, blessed John considered the excellence of his virtue and grace and examined more attentively what his manner of life was.

[Note: A remarkable and rare example of piety in a peasant. Palladius relates similar things in the *Life of Abbot Paphnutius*. An analogous account concerning Saint Antony is given by an anonymous author in Book VII, chapter 15 of the new edition of the *Lives of the Fathers*.]

The man testified that he was a peasant who earned his living by the daily labor of his hands and was conscious of no good in himself except that he never went out in the morning to perform the work of the fields, nor returned home in the evening, without giving thanks in the church to God his benefactor for the sustenance of daily life. Nor did he ever take anything from his produce without first offering its first fruits and tithes to God. Nor did he ever drive his oxen across the boundary of another person’s field without first closing their mouths, so that his neighbor would not suffer even a small loss through his carelessness.

When these things also seemed to Abbot John inadequate in comparison with the greatness of the grace by which he saw that man surpassing him, and when he questioned and searched him to discover what it was that could be credited with such merits of grace, the man, compelled by the old man’s reverent and earnest inquiry, confessed that, although he had wished to profess the monastic life, he had been forced by the authority and command of his parents to take a wife eleven years earlier. He testified that, without anyone even now knowing it, he guarded her as a virgin, in place of a sister.

[Note: By this example the Fathers teach that married people may, by mutual consent, vow and preserve continence. Palladius gives a similar example of the monk Ammon, who, having unwillingly taken a wife, lived with her for eighteen years but treated her as a sister and preserved both himself and her as virgins. How pleasing this was to God is clearly shown by the fact that Saint Antony saw his soul being carried into heaven by angels with the greatest glory, as Athanasius relates in the *Life of Saint Antony*. Another similar account occurs in Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 32. He relates that when one of two spouses who had mutually preserved perpetual continence died, the other broke out in these words: “I give you thanks, almighty Creator, that just as you entrusted this girl to me undefiled and pure from every stain of pleasure, so I return her to you.” She, although dead, smiled and said: “Be silent, man of God, for it is not necessary to disclose our secret when no one has asked.”]

When the old man heard this, he was so moved by admiration that he openly exclaimed in the man’s presence:

“No wonder the demon who had despised him could not endure the presence of one whose virtue he himself would not dare to approach without danger—not only in the burning vigor of youth, but even now.”

Although Abbot John put this event forward [Lipsius, in the margin: “related it”] with the greatest admiration, he nevertheless did not encourage any monk to test it, knowing that many things rightly done by some had brought great destruction upon others who imitated them, and that not everyone can presume to use what the Lord has granted to a few as a special gift.

## CHAPTER VIII  
### On Spiritual Knowledge

But let us return to the exposition of the knowledge from which the beginning of this discourse was taken. As we said above, practical knowledge is directed toward many professions and pursuits. [Note: Here the abbot refers theoretical knowledge, or theoretical science, chiefly to the knowledge, understanding, and interpretation of the sacred Scriptures. He teaches that this is twofold: historical or literal, and mystical or spiritual. Historical understanding, or interpretation, is what the words of Scripture present first and immediately; mystical understanding is directed toward something other than what the words immediately signify. He teaches that these two senses are signified by the book written within and without, in Ezekiel 2 and Revelation 5. See *Collation* 8, chapter 3, and the notes there.]

Theoretical knowledge, however, is divided into two parts: historical interpretation and spiritual understanding. Therefore, when Solomon had enumerated the Church’s manifold grace, he added:

“For all who are with her are clothed doubly” (Proverbs 31).

[Note: The Greek manuscripts differ somewhat. They now read as follows: **Πάντες γὰρ οἱ παρ᾽ αὐτῇ ἐνδεδυμένοι εἰσί. Δίσσας χλαίνας ἐποίησε.** That is: “For all who are with her are clothed. She made double garments” (Proverbs 31). Cassian, however, seems to have read **δίσσως** instead of **δίσσας**, that is, “doubly” instead of “double.” The Vulgate reads: “For all her household are clothed in double garments.” Saint Jerome gives another interpretation of this sentence, very different from the one transmitted here, understanding the strong woman as the Catholic Church.]

Theologians usually assign three other mystical senses to Scripture: the allegorical, the tropological, and the anagogical. [Note: Saint Thomas, Part I, question 1; Sixtus of Siena, Book III of the *Bibliotheca sancta*; Bellarmine, Book III, chapter 3 of *On the Word of God*.] The allegorical sense is that which concerns Christ or the Church; the tropological sense concerns morals; and the anagogical sense concerns the future life or the Church triumphant. Thus four senses are assigned altogether, concerning which the following familiar verses are found:

> The letter teaches the events; allegory, what you should believe,
Moral: what you should do; anagoge: where you should tend.] The kinds of spiritual knowledge are tropology, allegory, and anagogy. Concerning these it is said in Proverbs:

[Note: [Col. 0962D] There is considerable variation among the versions concerning this passage. The Vulgate reads: “Behold, I have described it to you three times in [Col. 0963C] counsels and knowledge” (Prov. XXII). The Septuagint: “And do you yourself write them down for yourself three times, as counsel and understanding.” The Chaldean: “And behold, I have written them for you three times, in counsels and knowledge.” St. Jerome, in his letter to Hedibia, question 12, says: “It is prescribed, as Solomon says: ‘But you describe them three times in counsel and knowledge, so that you may answer with words of truth those who put questions to you.’” He interprets these words as follows:

“Threefold is the inscription and rule of the Scriptures in our heart: first, that we understand them according to the historical sense; second, according to tropology; third, according to spiritual understanding. In the historical sense, the order of the things written is preserved. In tropology, we rise from the letter to greater things, and whatever was done carnally among the former people we interpret in a moral sense and turn to the profit of our soul. In spiritual contemplation (θεωρία), we pass to higher things, leave earthly matters behind, and discuss the blessedness of the future and heavenly things,” and so forth.

And in chapter XVI of Ezekiel he says: “We are commanded to understand the words of truth—that is, the holy Scriptures—in three ways: [Col. 0963D] first according to the letter; second, in an intermediate way through tropology; third, in a loftier manner, so that we may recognize all that is mystical.”

Again, in chapter IV of Amos he says: “We must first understand Holy Scripture according to the letter, carrying out in ethics—that is, in practice—whatever has been commanded; second, according to allegory, that is, spiritual understanding; third, according to the blessedness of future things.” Thus far St. Jerome.

From this we understand that the Fathers did not always observe the distinction among the spiritual senses accurately, nor always express it by the terms mentioned above, as Cardinal Bellarmine noted in book III, chapter 3, On the Word of God. For in the passage cited from his letter to Hedibia, Jerome includes the allegorical sense under the name of tropological, while conversely, in chapter IV of Amos, he includes the tropological under the name of allegorical. In Ezekiel, however, under the third category, which he calls sublime and sacred understanding, he includes the allegorical and anagogical senses.]

“But you describe them for yourself three times, [Col. 0963A] according to the breadth of your heart” (Prov. XXII).

Thus the historical sense embraces knowledge of past and visible events, which the Apostle recapitulates as follows:

[Note: [Col. 0964C] Four senses are found in this statement of the Apostle: the historical sense in the words “Abraham had two sons”; the allegorical sense in “These are the two covenants,” and so forth; the tropological sense in “How then he who was born according to the flesh,” and so forth; and finally the anagogical sense in “But the Jerusalem above.”]

“For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and the other by a free woman; but the one who was by the slave woman was born according to the flesh, while the one by the free woman was born through the promise” (Gal. IV).

The allegorical sense concerns what follows, because things that truly happened are said to have prefigured the form of another covenant:

“For these,” he says, “are the two covenants: one indeed from Mount Sinai, generating slavery, which is Hagar—for Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, which corresponds to the Jerusalem that now exists, and is in slavery with her children.”

Anagogy, ascending from spiritual mysteries to certain higher [Col. 0963B] and more sacred secrets of heaven, is then presented by the Apostle:

“But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother. For it is written: ‘Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail; for the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband’” (ibid.).

Tropology is a moral explanation concerned with the amendment of life and practical instruction—for example, if we understand these same two covenants as practical and theoretical disciplines; or, again, if we take Jerusalem or Zion to mean the human soul, according to the words: “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion” (Ps. CXLVII).

Thus, if we wish, the four figures mentioned above converge into one [Col. 0964A], so that

[Note: [Col. 0964C] Another example of these four senses in the single word “Jerusalem.” Jerusalem is understood in Scripture in four ways: first, historically, as that famous city of the Jews; second, allegorically, as the Catholic Church; third, tropologically, as the faithful soul; fourth, anagogically, as eternal blessedness or the triumphant Church. Thus St. Jerome interprets the word in four ways (in chapter XLIX of Isaiah and in Ezekiel, chapter XVI), and Psalm CXLVII may be expounded according to this fourfold sense: “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem.”]

one and the same Jerusalem may be understood in four ways: historically, as the city of the Jews; allegorically, as the Church of Christ; anagogically, as that heavenly city of God which is the mother of us all; and tropologically, as the human soul, which the Lord frequently rebukes or praises under this name.

Concerning these four kinds of interpretation the Apostle says:

“Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, what benefit will I bring you unless I speak to you either in revelation, or in knowledge, or in prophecy, or in doctrine?” (1 Cor. XIV).

[Note: [Col. 0964C] St. Thomas distinguishes and explains these four senses differently in his Commentary:

“Whether the illumination of the mind for knowing concerns divine or earthly things, it is illumination. If it concerns divine things, this illumination belongs to the gift of wisdom. For the revelation of divine things belongs to this gift, since no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God (1 Cor. II); and therefore he says, ‘in revelation,’ by which the mind is illuminated for knowing divine things.

“Or the illumination concerns earthly things—not all earthly things, but only those that pertain to the building up of faith; and this belongs to the gift of knowledge. Therefore he says, ‘in knowledge,’ not the knowledge of geometry or astrology, since these do not pertain to the building up of faith, but the knowledge that belongs to the saints. Wisdom X says: ‘He gave him the knowledge of the saints.’

“Or it concerns future events; and this belongs to the gift of prophecy. Therefore he says, ‘or in prophecy,’ which Cassiodorus defines as follows (In the Prologue to the Psalms, chapter 1): ‘Prophecy is divine inspiration announcing future events with immovable truth.’

“Or it concerns moral actions; and this belongs to doctrine. Hence he says, ‘or in doctrine.’ Romans XII says: ‘The one who teaches, in teaching’; and Proverbs XIII: ‘Good doctrine will give grace.’”]

Revelation pertains to allegory, by which those things that the historical narrative conceals are disclosed through spiritual meaning and interpretation. For example, if we attempt to explain how [Col. 0964B] all our fathers were under the cloud, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and how all ate the same spiritual food and all drank the same spiritual drink from the rock that followed them—for the rock was Christ (1 Cor. X)—this explanation, compared with the prefiguration of the body and blood of Christ, which we receive daily, contains the nature of allegory.

The knowledge likewise mentioned by the Apostle is tropology, by which we discern through prudent examination all matters belonging to practical judgment, whether they are useful or honorable. Such is the passage in which we are commanded to judge among ourselves whether it is fitting for a woman to pray to God with her head [Col. 0965A] uncovered (1 Cor. XI). As stated, this mode of interpretation contains a moral meaning.

Likewise, prophecy, which the Apostle places third, signifies anagogy, by which speech is transferred to invisible and future things. Such is the passage:

“We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the others who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus. For this we say to you by the word of the Lord: we who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who have fallen asleep, because the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead who are in Christ will rise first” (1 Thess. IV).

This form of exhortation displays the figure of anagogy.

Doctrine [Col. 0965B] however, reveals the simple order of historical exposition, in which no deeper meaning is contained except what resounds in the words themselves. Such is the passage:

“For I delivered to you first of all what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he rose on the third day, and that he appeared to Cephas” (1 Cor. XV).

And:

“God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” (Gal. IV).

Or again:

“Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one” (Deut. VI).

## CHAPTER IX. How one advances from practical knowledge to spiritual knowledge

Therefore, if you are concerned to reach the light of spiritual knowledge—not through the fault of empty boasting, but for the sake of purification—first let yourselves be inflamed by desire [Col. 0965C] for that blessedness of which it is said:

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V);

so that [Col. 0966A] you may also attain to that of which the angel said to Daniel:

“But those who are learned shall shine like the splendor of the firmament, and those who instruct many in justice shall be like stars for everlasting eternities” (Dan. XII);

and also to that which another prophet says:

[Note: [Col. 0965C] The Vulgate reads: “Sow for yourselves in justice, and reap in the mouth of mercy; renew for yourselves the fallow ground. It is time to seek the Lord, when he comes, who will teach you the justice of God.” St. Jerome says: “In place of what we have rendered, ‘Reap in the mouth of mercy,’ the Septuagint translated, ‘Harvest the fruit of life’” (Hos. X).]

“Kindle for yourselves the light of knowledge while there is time” (Hos. X).

Since I recognize in you that diligence in reading, hasten with every effort to grasp as soon as possible the practical discipline—that is, the ethical discipline—in its entirety. Without this, the purity that we have called theoretical cannot be attained. Only those who have been perfected not by the words of other teachers but by the power of their own actions, after many rewards of works and labors, finally obtain it as though it were a prize.

For they acquire understanding not from meditation on the law, but from the fruit [Col. 0966B] of their works, and with the Psalmist they sing:

“From your commandments I have gained understanding” (Ps. CXVIII).

And, when all their passions have been refined away, they say confidently:

“I shall sing and understand in the immaculate way” (Ps. C).

For the one who sings understands what is being sung when he proceeds in the immaculate way with the step of a pure heart.

Therefore, if you wish to prepare in your hearts a sacred tabernacle for spiritual knowledge, cleanse yourselves from every contagion of vice and strip yourselves of the cares of the present age. For it is impossible for a soul occupied even by the slightest worldly distractions to obtain the gift of knowledge, or to become productive of spiritual meanings, or retentive of sacred readings.

Observe this first of all—and especially you,

[Note: [Col. 0965C] He is addressing John Cassian, who was still young, engaged in the beginnings of sacred study and instruction, and longing for knowledge of divine things. He earnestly commends silence to him as especially suitable and necessary. Who would believe that Cassian would have revealed this about himself and committed it to writing, unless he had judged it useful for the edification and instruction of younger monks? In the same way, St. Augustine, that eminent teacher of the Church, was not ashamed to recount and openly lament in the books of his Confessions the sins of his youth and his ignorance, for the glory of God, his own humiliation, and the benefit of others.

Moreover, the same law of silence was seriously commended to the monk Cassian—our Cassian, as I believe—as one who had formerly been his close companion, colleague, and fellow student under Chrysostom, by that most weighty and most holy man, Isidore of Pelusium (book I, letter 309 of the Billian edition). Isidore observed and restrained Cassian’s excessive talkativeness and intemperance of speech, especially during the very beginnings of his monastic life, writing to him as follows:

“I hear that you have fled this fleeting and corruption-bound life and hastened with all speed toward monastic discipline, yet meanwhile you possess a bold and insolent tongue and speak rashly. This is nothing other than constructing a strong wall inaccessible to enemies while leaving open to them a gate of entry. If you wish to preserve the wall free from every danger and to show yourself firm and strong against your enemies, keep your tongue under control as much as you can, since from it come sudden and immense falls.”

Thus far Isidore.

We may infer that Cassian profited greatly from this salutary admonition, thereafter kept his tongue under control, and imposed a great silence upon his mouth from what we have noted elsewhere: in almost all these Conferences he records only his companion Germanus as speaking with the Fathers, while he himself remained present and silent, listening to them and committing their words and answers to memory, later setting them down in written records.]

John, whose still more youthful age gives greater support [Col. 0966C] to preserving what I am about to say, lest the labor of your study and desire for reading be rendered fruitless by empty exaltation,

[Note: [Col. 0966C] This is a notable passage on the religious silence that all monks, especially the young and candidates for sacred learning, ought to cultivate and observe. It is certainly worthy of being expanded and illustrated with several sayings and examples of the holy Fathers bearing on the same subject, especially since, when mention and commendation of it occurred elsewhere, we transferred that treatment to this place.

As for the sayings of the Fathers, although innumerable examples could be cited, none is more suitable to this passage or more comprehensive than the teaching of our most holy Father Benedict. After describing and prescribing the rule of monastic obedience, he considered nothing more important than inviting his disciples—that is, the cenobites—to cultivate and love restraint and silence. He exhorts them as follows (chapter 6 of the Rule):

“Let us do what the prophet says: ‘I said, I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue. I have set a guard over my mouth; I was silent and was humbled, and I kept silent even from good things’” (Ps. XXXVIII).

Here the Prophet shows that if, on account of silence, a monk must sometimes refrain even from good speech, how much more must he cease from evil words because of the punishment of sin!

Commenting on these words, Turrecremata gives ten reasons why the gravity of silence and restraint should be especially dear to religious persons. Of these, it will be sufficient to note only four of the chief reasons, most closely suited to the passage under discussion.

“First,” he says, “because through silence a person avoids many sins that ordinarily arise from talkativeness.” St. Benedict gives this reason when he says: “For it is written: ‘In much speaking you will not escape sin’” (Prov. X).

Climacus, in The Ladder of Divine Ascent, step 11, which concerns talkativeness, says: “Talkativeness is a sure sign of ignorance, the gate of slander, the guide of buffoonery, the craftsman of lies, the desolation of compunction, the author or summons of acedia, the forerunner of sleep, the dissipation of attentive and fixed thought, and the destruction of vigilance. Therefore Ecclesiasticus X rightly says: ‘Whoever uses many words injures his own soul.’”

“The second reason is that silence is very appropriate to the state and condition of disciples, such as religious men, who continually exercise themselves in the school of virtue. For, as Sidonius says in letter 21, Pythagoras is reported to have taught newly arrived disciples the endurance of silence before showing them the doctrine of speech. And as Jerome says in his letter to Nepotian: ‘Hippocrates bound his disciples by oath before teaching them, compelled them to swear by his words, and exacted silence under oath.’”

St. Benedict gives this reason when he says: “For speaking and teaching befit the master, while silence and listening suit the disciple.”

“The third reason is that this seems to be demanded by the very name ‘religious,’ which derives from religare, ‘to bind,’ as blessed Augustine attests (On True Religion, chapter 55, and book I of the Retractions, chapter 13). Thus one should first strive to bind that member which most needs binding—namely, the tongue. Hence the Wise Man admonishes: ‘Make a balance for your words, and make straight the restraints of your mouth.’ And the most religious David prays: ‘Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth’” (Ps. CX), and so forth.

Blessed James, however, delivers a decisive judgment: “If anyone thinks himself religious while not restraining his tongue but deceiving his own heart, his religion is worthless” (James I).

For this reason a voice from heaven came to Arsenius as he was striving toward perfection and the religious life, saying: “Arsenius, flee, be silent, and keep still” (in The Lives of the Fathers).

“The fourth reason is that silence greatly assists and disposes one toward contemplation and conversation with God. Climacus, in the same place (step 11), says: ‘The devotee of silence draws near to God; continually attending upon him in the hidden place of the heart, he is illumined by him.’

“Lamentations III says: ‘It is good to await the salvation of God in silence.’ It continues: ‘He shall sit alone and keep silent, because he will rise above himself’—that is, above the human condition.”

These words seem to portray vividly the true cultivator of religious life and the true monk, that is, the solitary, as St. Jerome noted in his letter to Eustochium (letter 22).

Thus far the sayings and reasons concerning the silence of monks produced by Turrecremata.

Now, to turn to examples of the Fathers who observed silence most strictly in the religious life, whether eremitical or cenobitic: first, in The Lives of the Fathers, you have Paul the Simple, a disciple of St. Antony, who, because of a slip of the tongue—for he had asked whether Christ had lived before the prophets—imposed three years of silence upon his mouth; and Abbot Agathon, who learned to keep silent by placing a small stone in his mouth and remained silent for three years.

Pambo, or Pambus, the abbot, as recorded in the Tripartite History (book VIII, chapter 1), was unlettered and approached someone to be taught a psalm. When he heard the first verse of Psalm 38: “I said, I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue,” he would not allow the second verse to be heard, saying: “If I can fulfill this in practice, this one verse will be enough for me.” Much later, when he returned and was asked why he had delayed so long in going back to his teacher, he said that he had not yet perfected what he had learned.

Ammonius, according to Palladius (Lausiac History 48), the father of three thousand monks of Tabennesis, exercised them in such silence that they seemed to be in the desert, each secretly carrying out the rule of his own life.

Abbot Theonas, likewise according to Palladius (Lausiac History 50), a holy man shut up in a small dwelling, practiced silence for thirty years.

John the Silent, formerly a bishop and later a solitary, according to Cyril the monk, his contemporary, remained silent for forty-seven entire years, until the age of 104.

Severus Sulpicius, according to Blessed Jerome in his Catalogue of Illustrious Men, having been deceived by the Pelagians and recognizing the fault of talkativeness, maintained silence until death, so that he might completely remedy by silence the sin he had contracted through speaking.

St. Thomas Aquinas, the Angelic Doctor, cultivated silence so greatly in his youth, as we have noted elsewhere, that among his fellow students he acquired the name of the mute ox.

Albert the Great, however, having tested his exceptional intelligence in disputations and discerned where that silence was tending, said: “This ox will one day produce such a bellow that the sound of it will be heard throughout the world.”

Let these brief observations on silence suffice, for we are hastening to explain other matters.]

impose, as you show, the utmost silence upon your mouth [Col. 0967A]. For this is the first entrance into practical discipline:

“All the labor of man is in his mouth” (Eccles. VI);

and you should receive all the institutions and sayings of the elders with attentive heart and, as it were, silent mouth, carefully storing them in your breast and hastening rather to fulfill them than to teach them.

From the former, the destructive presumption of vainglory will sprout; from the latter, the fruit of spiritual knowledge.

Therefore, do not dare to say anything in the gathering of the elders unless either harmful ignorance compels you to ask about it, or the necessity of acquiring knowledge requires the question—like certain men distracted by love of empty glory who, in order to display their learning, pretend to ask about matters they know perfectly well.

For it is impossible for one who applies himself to the study [Col. 0967B] with the intention of acquiring human praise to obtain the gift of true knowledge.

For the one conquered by this passion

[Lips. in the margin: “bound by this passion”]

must [Col. 0968A] also be bound by other vices, especially pride, and thus, defeated in practical and ethical struggle, will by no means attain the spiritual knowledge that arises from it.

Be quick, then, in every respect to hear, but slow to speak (James I), lest what Solomon notes fall upon you:

[Note: [Col. 0968D] The Vulgate reads: “Have you seen a man swift in speaking? More hope is to be expected of a fool than of his correction” (Prov. XXIX). St. Jerome aptly applies this to the present passage: “The vice of folly is indeed serious, but talkativeness is no lighter. For it often happens that some ignorant person, even one unacquainted with letters themselves, accepts words of salutary correction more quickly than one endowed with an abundance of speech, who strives to put forward boastfully what he knows—or imagines he knows—rather than listen to the sayings of the wise.”]

“If you see a man swift in words, know that a fool has more hope than he” (Prov. XXIX).

Do not presume to teach anyone by words what you have not first done in practice. Our Lord himself established by his example the order we ought to observe, for it is said of him:

“Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts I).

Beware, therefore, lest, rushing ahead to teach before acting, you be counted among those of whom the Lord says to his disciples in the Gospel:

“Observe and do whatever they say [Col. 0968B] to you, but do not act according to their works; for they say and do not do. They bind heavy [Col. 0969A] and unbearable burdens and place them on people’s shoulders, but they themselves are unwilling to move them with a finger” (Matt. XXIII).

For if the one who loosens even one of the least commandments and teaches people thus is called least in the kingdom of heaven (Matt. V),

[Note: [Col. 0969B] St. Gregory, Homily 12 on the Gospels: “He dissolves the commandment and teaches who does not wish to fulfill in practice what he teaches. How, then, will he be called least in the kingdom who is not permitted to enter it in any way for this reason? What, then, is signified by this statement except the present Church, which is called the kingdom of heaven? In it, the teacher who has dissolved the commandment is called least, because when his life is despised, his preaching too is bound to be disregarded.”]

then surely the one who neglects many greater commandments and presumes to teach them will no longer be regarded as least in the kingdom of heaven, but will be considered greatest in the punishment of Gehenna.

Therefore, you must beware of being stirred to teach by the example of those who have acquired skill in disputation and fluency of speech. Because they can discuss whatever they wish elegantly and abundantly, they are believed by those who do not know how to distinguish its power and quality to possess spiritual knowledge.

For it is one thing to possess ease of mouth and polish of speech, and another to enter into the veins [Col. 0969B] and marrow of heavenly utterances and contemplate the profound and hidden mysteries with the purest eye of the heart. This cannot be obtained at all through human teaching or secular learning, but only through purity of mind illumined by the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER X. On acquiring the discipline of true knowledge

[Col. 0970A]

Therefore, if you wish to attain the true knowledge of Scripture, you must hasten to acquire first an immovable humility of heart, which will lead you, through the perfection of charity, not to the knowledge that puffs up but to that which illumines.

[Note: In the preceding chapter he said: “For it is impossible for a soul occupied by worldly distractions, even slight ones, to merit the gift of knowledge, or to become the generator of spiritual perceptions or the steadfast possessor of sacred readings” [Col. 0969B]. And again: “It is impossible for one who applies himself to reading with the intention of acquiring human praise to merit the gift of true knowledge” [Col. 0969C]. Again, in chapter 14: “It is impossible for an unclean soul, however intensely it may labor in persistent reading, to attain spiritual knowledge.” And in chapter 16: “No one in whom the inclination toward carnal passions—and especially fornication—still holds sway can possess spiritual knowledge.” How and in what sense such statements are true, when one sees many bad, indeed very wicked, men endowed with great knowledge of Scripture, has been explained elsewhere to some extent and is explained more fully below, in chapter 14. Yet it is worth adding here what the Reverend Father Pererius writes on this subject both eloquently and learnedly in book 15 of his Commentaries on Daniel [Col. 0969D]:

“They can indeed,” he says, “even if wicked, acquire considerable understanding of divine matters. For even amid the greatest crimes they often retain divine faith, which is like a certain light in the human mind for understanding sacred things to some degree; and knowledge of sacred letters is numbered among the freely given graces. Therefore it can also be bestowed upon criminal people. Yet such people understand divine matters, but not as they ought. For their knowledge is bare, barren, and unfruitful for them, since it lacks its principal effect and fruit. That effect is love of God, obedience, the healing of vices, correction of life, right formation of morals, eagerness to help as many people as possible and bring them to eternal salvation—in a word, earnest and constant exercise in cultivating every virtue and in pursuing honorable things.” Thus far Pererius.]

For it is impossible for an unclean mind to attain the gift of spiritual knowledge. Therefore, with every possible precaution, avoid allowing the study of reading to produce in you—not the light of knowledge, nor that perpetual glory promised through the illumination of teaching—but instruments of perdition born from the vanity of arrogance. Next, you must strive with all your might [Col. 0970B] to expel every earthly anxiety and thought,

[Note: Thus the blessed Jerome writes to Nepotianus (Letters 2 and 4): “Read the divine Scriptures frequently; indeed, let them never be put down from your hands.” And to the monk Rusticus: “Let the book never depart from your hand or your eyes. Learn the Psalter word for word; love knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh. Let books be written, so that the hand may work for food and the mind be satisfied by reading” [Col. 0969D–0970B]. And to Laeta, On the Education of a Daughter (Letter 7): “Let reading follow prayer, and prayer follow reading.” In his Letter to the Ephesians, chapter 5: “We must read Scripture with every diligence and meditate day and night on the law of the Lord, so that, like approved money-changers, we may know which coin is genuine and which counterfeit.”

The blessed Benedict likewise commends sacred reading to his monks in several places of his Rule (chapters 38, 42, and 43), commanding them to devote themselves to it at set hours, especially on Sundays and during Lent; and he places among the instruments of good works the willing hearing of sacred readings. See there the twelve benefits of sacred reading explained at length by Turrecremata [Col. 0970C], which Abbot Smaragdus summarized in fewer words as follows:

“Knowledge of sacred reading supplies its practitioners with sharpness of perception, multiplies understanding, dispels sluggishness, removes idleness, orders life, corrects morals, produces a salutary sigh, brings forth tears from a contrite heart, grants eloquence in speaking, promises eternal rewards to those who labor, increases spiritual riches, restrains idle talk and vanities, and kindles desire for Christ and the heavenly homeland. It must always be joined to prayer and always remain connected with it. For by prayers we are cleansed, but by readings we are instructed. Therefore whoever wishes always to be with God must pray frequently and read frequently. When we pray, we speak with God; when we read, God speaks with us. All progress, therefore, proceeds from reading, prayer, and meditation. What we do not know, we learn by reading; what we have learned, we preserve by meditation; and so that what we have preserved may be put into practice, we obtain it through prayer” (Bernard, Sermon 50 to his Sister).]

you should devote yourself constantly, or rather without interruption, to sacred reading, until continual meditation imbues your mind and, as it were, forms it into its own likeness,

[Note: These words refer to the Apostle’s statement in Hebrews 9: “The ark of the covenant covered on every side with gold, in which were a golden urn containing manna, and Aaron’s rod that had blossomed, and the tablets of the covenant” [Col. 0970D]. It is not the place here to investigate how the Apostle can say that the golden urn containing manna and Aaron’s rod were preserved in the ark of the covenant, when 3 Kings 8 says that there was nothing in the ark except the two stone tablets that Moses had placed there. It is enough that, according to the Apostle, these three things were at some time in the ark of the covenant; morally and tropologically they are here referred to the mind or soul of the true religious person, or of the perfect human being, just as Origen likewise referred that ark to the same subject:

“The golden ark,” he says, “in which are the tablets of the covenant, signifies, as I think, nothing other than our mind, in which we ought to have God’s law written” (Homily 11 on Numbers) [Col. 0971B]. This golden mind must be pure and precious, in which we always have God’s law written, as the Apostle says: “Written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of fleshly hearts,” and so forth (2 Corinthians 3).

But the blessed Gregory interprets these things particularly of prelates and rulers [Col. 0971C]. In their minds, as in the ark of the covenant, there must be knowledge of the divine law, represented by the tablets; the manna of sweetness, or gentleness; and the rod of discipline and severity:

“Gentleness must be mingled with severity, and something composed from both must be made, so that subjects are neither embittered by excessive harshness nor released into disorder by excessive kindness” (Book 20 of the Morals, chapter 6, and Letter Book 1, chapter 24). “This is precisely what the ark of the tabernacle signifies, in which, together with the tablets, there are also the rod and the manna; for when the knowledge of sacred Scripture is in the breast of the good shepherd, there must be both the rod of discipline and the manna of sweetness.”

For other meanings of the ark of the covenant, see Origen, book 3 on the Letter to the Romans; Ambrose, on the Letter to the Hebrews, chapter 9; Isidore, on Exodus, chapter 43; and Bernard, in a sermon on the Blessed Mary, volume 2.]

thereby making from it, in a certain way, an ark of the covenant, containing within itself the two stone tablets—that is, the perpetual firmness of the twofold Testament [Col. 0971A]; and also the golden urn, that is, a pure and sincere memory, which preserves within itself with unfailing tenacity the manna stored there, namely, the enduring and heavenly sweetness of spiritual perceptions and of that angelic bread; and also Aaron’s rod, that is, the saving standard of our supreme and true High Priest, Jesus Christ, ever putting forth leaves with the evergreen vitality of immortal memory. For this is the rod which, after being cut from the root of Jesse, revives more vigorously after having been mortified.

[Note: He alludes to what the Apostle adds in the same place: “And above it were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat” [Col. 0971C–D].]

All these things, moreover, are protected by two cherubim, that is, by the fullness of historical and spiritual knowledge.

[Note: The Fathers agree. Dionysius the Areopagite, On the Celestial Hierarchy, chapter 7: “Those who are skilled in the Hebrew language say that the holy seraphim signify burning or inflaming, but the cherubim signify a multitude of knowledge or an outpouring of wisdom.” The blessed Jerome, Letter 103: “Cherubim, which is interpreted as a multitude of knowledge,” and so forth. Gregory, Morals, book 33, chapter 25: “Cherub is interpreted as fullness of knowledge.” See also the same author, Homily 23 on the Gospels.]

For cherubim is interpreted as “a multitude of knowledge,” which will continually protect the mercy seat of God—that is, the peacefulness of your heart [Col. 0971B]—and overshadow it against all assaults of spiritual wickedness. Thus your mind, advanced not only into the ark of the divine covenant but also into the priestly kingdom, and in a certain way absorbed into spiritual disciplines through an undivided devotion to purity, will fulfill the priestly command prescribed by the Lawgiver in these words: “He shall not go out from the holy places, lest he pollute the sanctuary of his God” (Leviticus 21)—that is, his own heart, in which the Lord promises that he will dwell continually, saying: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (Leviticus 26; 2 Corinthians 6) [Col. 0972A].

For this reason, the succession of the sacred Scriptures must be carefully committed to memory and

[Note: That is, it must be read, examined, and meditated upon most frequently—namely, in the sense in which the words “Pray without ceasing” and Psalm 1, “And on his law he will meditate day and night,” and similar passages, are explained. The meaning is not that a just or religious person cannot be free from reading and meditating on the divine law even for a moment; rather, he must very frequently recall his mind to the precepts of the law, frequently devote himself to reading and prayer, and always be mindful of the divine law and of his own profession whenever anything arises that must be thought, said, or done—especially when there is danger that justice or religion might be violated. See above, Conference 10, chapter 4 [Col. 0971D–0972C].]

recalled without interruption. For the constancy of this meditation confers on us a twofold fruit. First, while the mind’s attention is occupied in reading and preparing the readings,

[Note: The blessed Ambrose says in a sermon (Sermon on the Lord’s Fast): “The reading of sacred letters is itself food that bestows eternal life and excludes from us the snares of diabolical temptation.” Chrysostom, Homily 25 on Genesis: “What sensible food does for increasing the body’s strength, the reading of the Bible does for the soul. For it is spiritual nourishment; it makes the soul strong and steadfast, not allowing it to be captured by absurd thoughts, but making it light and winged and transferring it, as it were, into heaven itself” [Col. 0972C–D].

This remedy was likewise suggested to the blessed Augustine, so that he might finally emerge from the mire of a luxurious life. For, as he himself relates in the Confessions (Book 8, chapter 12), when he had thrown himself down beneath a certain fig tree and was imploring divine grace with tears, he heard a voice saying, “Take up and read; take up and read.” He hurried back to the place where he had put down the Apostle’s book. “I seized it,” he says, “opened it, and read in silence the section on which my eyes first fell: ‘Not in feasting and drunkenness, not in bedrooms and impurities, not in strife and rivalry, but put on the Lord Jesus Christ’ (Romans 12), and, ‘Make no provision for the flesh in its desires.’ I did not wish to read further, nor was there any need. For as soon as the sentence ended, as though a light of security had been poured into my heart, all the darkness of doubt fled away.”]

it is necessary that it not be captured by any snares of harmful thoughts. Second, what we could not understand at the time with an attentive mind, while laboring to commit to memory what we had traversed through very frequent repetition, we later perceive more clearly when, withdrawn from the allurements of all activities and sights, and especially in silent meditation by night, we turn it over within ourselves. Thus the meaning of the most hidden passages, which while awake we had not grasped even by the faintest conjecture, is revealed to us while we are at rest and either immersed in the stupor of sleep [Col. 0972B] or sunk in slumber.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Various Meanings of the Divine Scriptures

As the renewal of our mind increases through this study, the appearance of the Scriptures will also begin to be renewed, and the beauty of their more sacred meaning will in some manner advance along with our own progress.

[Note: This is a physical axiom: “Whatever is in the recipient is in accordance with the mode of the recipient,” which may appropriately be applied here.]

For their appearance is adapted to the capacity of human understanding. To the carnal they will appear earthly, but to the spiritual they will appear divine, so that those to whom previously they seemed wrapped in certain dense mists [Col. 0973A] are unable either to grasp their subtlety or to endure their brightness. But in order that what we are attempting to establish may be made clearer by an example, it is enough to produce one testimony from the Law, through which we may show that all the heavenly commandments likewise extend to every class of human beings according to the measure of our condition. It is written in the Law: “You shall not commit fornication” (Exodus 20). A person still bound by the passions of carnal obscenities rightly observes this according to the plain sound of the letter. But one who has already withdrawn from that filthy act and impure desire

[Note: He identifies here four kinds of spiritual fornication. The first is idolatry; the second, every pagan superstition, including auguries and observances of days and times; the third, Jewish superstition in legal ceremonies; the fourth, heresy. He adds a fifth kind, general fornication, which is every sin by which someone turns away from God and turns toward a creature. Concerning this fornication, the blessed Augustine says in book 2 of the Confessions, chapter 6: “The soul commits fornication when it turns away from you and seeks outside you what it does not find pure and undiluted except when it returns to you.” And in his book Against Adimantus, chapter 7: “The fornication of the soul is a turning away from the fruitfulness of wisdom and a turning toward the conception of temporal allurements and corruptions” [Col. 0973C].]

must observe the same command spiritually, so that he withdraws not only from the rites of idols but also from every pagan superstition, from auguries, and from every observance of signs, days, and times [Col. 0973B]; or at least so that he does not become entangled in conjectures based on certain words or names that pollute the sincerity of our faith. Jerusalem is said to have been defiled by this fornication: “She fornicated upon every high hill and under every leafy tree” (Jeremiah 3). And the Lord again rebukes her through the prophet: “Let the astrologers of heaven stand and save you, those who observed the stars and calculated the months in order to announce from them what would happen to you” (Isaiah 47). Elsewhere, too, the Lord accuses them of this fornication, saying: “The spirit of fornication deceived them, and they fornicated against their God” (Hosea 4).

Whoever has withdrawn from this twofold fornication will have a third to avoid, which is contained in the superstition of the Law and of Judaism. Concerning these the Apostle says: “You observe days and months and seasons and years” (Galatians 4) [Col. 0973C]. And again: “Do not touch, do not taste, and do not make conjectures” (Colossians 2) [Col. 0974A]. There is no doubt that these words concern the superstitions of the Law. If someone falls into them, he is undoubtedly an adulterer who has departed from Christ and does not deserve to hear from the Apostle: “I betrothed you to one man, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11). Rather, the following words of the same Apostle will be addressed to him: “I fear, however, lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ Jesus” (ibid.).

If he has escaped the impurity of this fornication as well, he will have a fourth kind, committed through the adultery of heretical doctrine. Concerning it the blessed Apostle says: “I know that after my departure savage wolves will enter among you, not sparing the flock, and from among yourselves men will arise speaking perverse things in order to draw the disciples after them” (Acts 20). Whoever has been able to avoid this must beware lest he fall into the vice of fornication through a subtler sin, which consists in the wandering of thoughts. For every thought—not only an unclean one but even an idle one—that departs in the slightest degree from God is judged by the perfect man to be the most impure fornication.

## CHAPTER XII. An Inquiry into How One May Reach Forgetfulness of Secular Songs

Germanus: At first I was moved by these hidden matters to compunction, and then, groaning heavily, I said: “All these things that you have set forth so fully have increased my despair far more than I had previously endured. For, besides those general captivities of the soul,

[Note: That is, the innate and inborn weaknesses and miseries of both mind and body common to all human beings, by which the soul is bound, as though captive in a prison, within the body, and is oppressed and restrained as if by chains [Col. 0973C–D]. Lamenting these captivities of the soul within himself, the Apostle says: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” (Romans 7). The blessed Bernard summarized them in these few words (Sermon 5 on the Dedication): “What need is there to enumerate each of its miseries—how burdened with sins, clouded by darkness, ensnared by allurements, itching with desires, subject to passions, filled with illusions, always inclined to evil, prone toward every vice, and finally filled with every kind of confusion and ignorance?”]

which I do not doubt afflict all the weak from outside,

[Note: On the occasion of these words, one might ask whether it is advantageous for monks to study, or to have studied, the liberal disciplines—grammar, poetry, rhetoric, philosophy, and similar subjects. From this passage it appears that such study is considered not merely useless to a monk but harmful and dangerous, since it causes great hindrance to prayer and meditation, and consequently an impediment to salvation, when the mind is distracted in prayer by memories of histories, fables, poems, and so forth, and is called away from holier exercises and occupations by such phantasms, as the abbot Germanus here testifies from his own experience and grief [Col. 0974C].

To this is added the very weighty authority and memorable example of the blessed Jerome, who recalls that for this reason he suffered severe punishments from God. He had read Cicero too eagerly and too frequently, and he recounts the matter in this way in his letter to Eustochium (Letter 20) [Col. 0974D]:

“When many years ago I had cut myself off from home, parents, sister, relatives—and what was more difficult than these, from the habit of more sumptuous food—for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, and was going to Jerusalem as a soldier, I could not entirely do without the library that I had painstakingly and laboriously assembled for myself at Rome. Thus, wretched man that I was, I would fast in order to read Tully. After frequent vigils at night, after tears that the remembrance of my past sins drew from the depths of my entrails, Plautus would be taken up. If at times, returning to myself, I began to read the Prophets, their unpolished diction horrified me; and because my blind eyes could not see the light, I thought the fault lay not in my eyes but in the sun.

“While the ancient serpent was thus mocking me, toward the middle of Lent a fever penetrated my marrow and seized my exhausted body; and, without any rest—something almost incredible to say—it so consumed my unhappy limbs that I scarcely clung to my bones. Meanwhile, preparations were made for my funeral, and while the warmth of my living soul had already grown cold throughout the rest of my body, it alone still beat in my barely warm breast. Suddenly, carried away in spirit, I was dragged before the tribunal of the Judge. There was so much light there, and so great a radiance from the brightness of those standing around [Col. 0975A], that, thrown to the ground, I did not dare to look upward.

“Asked about my condition, I replied that I was a Christian. But the one presiding said: ‘You are lying. You are a Ciceronian, not a Christian. For where your treasure is, there also is your heart’ (Matthew 6). Immediately I fell silent; and amid the blows—for he had ordered me to be beaten—I was tormented more by the fire of conscience, as I recalled that verse: ‘But in hell who will confess you?’ (Psalm 6). I began to cry out and, wailing, to say: ‘Have mercy on me, Lord; have mercy on me.’ This cry echoed amid the lashes.

“At last those who stood by fell upon the knees of the presiding judge and begged him to pardon my youth and to grant a place for repentance to my error, exacting punishment thereafter if I should ever read books of pagan literature. Since I was constrained in such a critical moment and wished to promise even more, I began to swear and, calling upon his name, say: ‘Lord, if I ever possess secular books, if I ever read them, I have denied you.’ After these words of the oath I was released and returned to the world above. To the amazement of everyone, I opened my eyes, drenched in such a flood of tears that even those who did not believe were convinced by my grief.

“Nor had that been sleep or empty dreams by which we are often deceived. The tribunal before which I had lain bears witness; the terrible judgment that I had feared bears witness. May I never again fall into such an examination! I confess that I had bruised shoulders and that after waking I felt the blows; and thereafter I read divine books with as much zeal as I had previously read mortal ones.”

Thus far the blessed Jerome.

Some nevertheless doubt whether these things truly and literally happened to him, or only imaginatively in a dream—that is, whether Saint Jerome was really beaten and truly carried away to the tribunal of Christ. On this matter the Reverend Father Nicholas Serarius, an eminent theologian of the Society of Jesus, has an excellent discussion, adducing many arguments on both sides (Biblical Prolegomena, chapter 28). Certainly, anyone who attends to Jerome’s words can scarcely doubt that he is describing a genuinely true history. But whatever the case may be, this much must certainly be admitted: through that beating and scourging—if not real, then at least imaginary—the blessed Jerome was divinely warned of his duty and restrained from excessive devotion to and reading of Cicero and other pagan authors [Col. 0975B–C].

Nevertheless, despite these considerations, I say that it is exceedingly useful and honorable for all monks and religious persons to be instructed in the liberal disciplines, or to have been trained and cultivated in them from youth. This can be established for many reasons drawn from the sacred canons and examples of antiquity.

First, on account of the priesthood: all monks in our time are no longer counted among the laity, as they once were, but are ordered to be promoted at the appropriate time, once any legitimate impediment has ceased, to the clerical state and sacred orders, and finally to the priesthood. Thus Clement V, at the Council of Vienne, for the advancement of divine worship decreed that every monk, at the admonition of his abbot, should present himself for promotion to all the sacred orders, unless a legitimate excuse existed (Clement, “Ne in agro,” On the Status of Monks) [Col. 0975D].

If the Church requires some literary knowledge and learning, at least of the Latin language, even for the minor orders (Council of Trent, session 23, chapter 11, On Reform), and indeed entirely bars the illiterate from receiving them (in Gratian, Distinction 36, chapter “Illiteratos”), how much more must this be required in the higher orders, especially in the priesthood, lest one fall under the sentence that the Lord speaks through the prophet: “Because you have rejected knowledge, I will reject you, so that you shall not serve as priest to me” (Hosea 4).

And if we read that the Pachomian monks—who at that time were certainly laymen—were commanded that absolutely no one should be in the monastery who did not learn letters and retain something from the Scriptures (as article 80 of the Rule of Saint Pachomius states), how much more must this be decreed and observed in the dwellings and monasteries of monks who are, in any event, clerics!

Hence the pontiff adds in the same place: “So that the monks themselves may not lack a suitable opportunity to advance in knowledge, in each of their monasteries, wherever the resources for this are available, a suitable teacher shall be maintained who will diligently instruct them in the elementary sciences” (Council of Cologne, chapters 30 and 31) [Col. 0976A]. By “elementary sciences” he means grammar, logic, and philosophy, as Pope Benedict XII explained in his Benedictine constitution (Constitution of Benedict XII, under the title “On the School of Letters”), whose words we shall cite shortly (chapter 6).

Secondly, on account of theological study, which is especially commended to all monks and to which the inferior sciences are subordinate. Thus Pope Benedict, in the passage cited above:

> Since, he says, through the exercise of reading the pearl of knowledge is acquired, and through the study of sacred Scripture one more familiarly reaches knowledge of divine excellence, while through the recognition of human law the mind is made more reasonable and more certainly instructed in justice; therefore, desiring that men of this same order or religious institute, laboring in the Lord’s field, be instructed first in the elementary sciences and thereafter in the canonical sciences of divine and human law, and adhering to the constitution of Pope Clement V, our predecessor, issued concerning the instruction of monks in the sciences within the monasteries where they dwell, we firmly desire and command that it be observed. Moreover, we add and decree that henceforth in every cathedral church, monastery, priory, and other conventual and solemn place belonging to this order or religious institute where the resources for this are available, there shall be a teacher (see the chapter *Quia nonnullis*, concerning teachers) who shall instruct its monks in these elementary sciences, namely grammar, logic, and philosophy, etc.

To the same purpose is the decree of the Council of Trent (Session 5, chapter 1, on reform), by which it is established that theological instruction be provided in all monasteries.

Although, for some kind of theological study and for some reading and understanding of Scripture, it is by no means necessary to have previously learned profane sciences—rhetoric, philosophy, and other disciplines of that kind—no one will deny that they are necessary, or at least highly useful, for a more perfect and profitable study. This is what the holy Fathers, the doctors of the Church most skilled in Scripture, and the greatest theologians have taught, not merely by their example but also in their writings and authoritative statements.

The blessed Jerome, replying to a distinguished Roman orator who asked why he inserted examples from secular literature in his little works and, as the man put it, polluted the purity of the Church with pagan filth, explains at length the method and precedent by which he did so and approved of its being done. Among other things he writes (Letter 84):

> For who does not know that both in Moses and in the books of the Prophets certain things were taken from the books of the Gentiles, and that Solomon both proposed certain matters to the philosophers of Tyre and answered some of their questions? Hence, at the beginning of Proverbs (Prov. 1), he urges us to understand “the words of prudence, and the subtleties of sayings, parables, and obscure speech, the sayings of the wise, and riddles”—things that properly belong to dialecticians and philosophers.

But the Apostle Paul too made use of a verse by the poet Epimenides when he wrote to Titus:

> Κρῆτες ἀεὶ ψεῦσται, κακὰ θηρία, γαστέρες ἀργαί,

that is:

> Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies (Titus 1).

Callimachus later used the hemistich of this heroic verse. In another Epistle Paul inserts a senarius of Menander:

> Φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρηστὰ ὁμιλίαι κακαί,

that is:

> Evil conversations corrupt good morals (1 Cor. 15).

And when disputing before the Athenians in the Areopagus, he calls Aratus as a witness:

> For we are indeed his offspring (Acts 17),

which in Greek is:

> τοῦ γὰρ καὶ γένος ἐσμέν,

and is the closing clause of a heroic verse.

And, as though this were not enough, the leader of the Christian army and unconquered orator, pleading Christ’s cause, even twists an accidental inscription into an argument for the faith. For he had learned from the true David to wrest the sword from the hands of the enemy and cut off the head of the most arrogant Goliath with his own weapon (1 Sam. 17). He had read in Deuteronomy that the Lord commanded the head, eyebrows, all the hair, and the nails of a captive woman to be shaved or cut off, and that she was then to be taken in marriage (Deut. 21). What wonder, then, if I too wish to make secular wisdom, on account of the beauty of its eloquence and the beauty of its limbs, into an Israelite woman who is a servant and a captive? Whatever in her is dead—idolatry, pleasure, error, or lust—I either cut away or shave off; and from her I beget for the Lord of Hosts native-born servants, united to a most pure body.

Thus far the blessed Jerome.

Saint Augustine, in Book II of *On Christian Doctrine* (chapters 16 and following), teaches not only that philosophy is useful to the theologian, but also rhetoric, poetry, dialectic, politics, arithmetic, history, and, in general, whatever the Gentiles have discovered and handed down to memory in a manner consistent with reason, acute, and ingenious.

Cassiodorus, following Augustine, says in the *Institutes of Divine Readings*:

> Whatever is found in the divine Scriptures concerning such matters—the liberal arts and disciplines—is better understood through prior knowledge; for it is evident that, as though at the source, indications of these things were sown by the Spirit of wisdom, and that the teachers of secular literature afterward transferred them most prudently into their own systems.

In chapter 25 he commends cosmography; in chapters 26 and 27, grammar, rhetoric, dialectic, geometry, arithmetic, astronomy, and every other liberal discipline:

> For there is unquestionably, as our fathers also judged, a useful knowledge of these matters that ought not to be rejected, since you find it everywhere diffused through the sacred writings, as though in the source of a universal and perfect wisdom.

Again, in chapter 28:

> Many of our fathers, educated in such literature and remaining in the law of the Lord, attained true wisdom. Thus the blessed Augustine, as recorded in *On Christian Doctrine*, says: “Do we not see how much gold and silver and clothing Cyprian, the most eloquent teacher and most blessed martyr, carried away from Egypt? How much Lactantius? How much Victorinus, Optatus, and Hilary?” And, to say nothing of the living, how many innumerable Greeks?

So far Cassiodorus.

To these may be added the blessed Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine himself, and other Fathers who are known to have excelled in every branch of secular learning.

Moreover, is it not the case that in former times many monasteries, especially those of the Benedictines, appear to have been academies of learning and schools of sacred literature and of other disciplines? This was not because monasteries were originally established and founded chiefly for the purpose of conducting public literary studies within them, as heretics foolishly claim; rather, the studies flourished exceedingly in most well-ordered monasteries because they were joined to the pursuit of piety and religion (see Hieronymus Platus, Book II of *On the Good of the Religious State*, chapters 32 and 33). For many ages, when elsewhere they had been almost universally abandoned and held in contempt, they retained a seat and dwelling among the monks. From there they produced many outstanding men—pontiffs, teachers, and bishops distinguished for holiness and learning—as support and adornment for the Catholic Church, and raised them like burning lamps upon a lampstand,

> so that they might shine for all who are in the house of God

(Matt. 5; Luke 16).

The most authoritative witness to this is John Trithemius, Book I of *On the Illustrious Men of the Order of the Blessed Benedict*. Since his excellent account, though sufficiently lengthy, seemed worth using to illuminate this matter and make it more credible and clear, I shall quote the passage:

> From the beginning, he says, of our order until the time of the Emperor Henry IV, many very learned men flourished in it, as we shall explain in part, insofar as we are able, in the second book of this work. For while Saint Benedict was still alive, and the order was spreading through various regions of the earth, many noble and exceedingly well-educated young men submitted their necks to monastic discipline according to his Rule. They were regarded as highly skilled not only in the divine Scriptures but also in secular literature.
>
> Among them was that most illustrious senator Cassiodorus, a man learned in every field, who, after laying aside his senatorial dignity, became a cenobitic monk for the love of God.
>
> As time went on, the monks’ chief pursuit was Scripture, together with a continuous love of learning in every discipline of the liberal arts. Those who had come to conversion already educated usefully supplied the younger brothers with instruction in learning; nor could lesser age obstruct the desire for advancement, since it was governed by the authority of teachers.
>
> To give a few examples from among the many, let us consider Boniface and Rabanus, archbishops of Mainz, and also Bede the presbyter. Boniface, the first of these, was entrusted to a monastery in England while still a boy of five. There he advanced so greatly through constant study of Scripture that he came to be regarded as the teacher and apostle of the Germans. His elegant letters to various persons are still extant. There also remain various compositions in which the overflowing stream of his intellect poured forth the currents of sacred doctrine.
>
> Rabanus, who succeeded Boniface in the archbishopric as the sixth in succession, came as a boy to the monastery of Fulda for conversion. How far he advanced in knowledge of Scripture is almost infinitely attested by the volumes he composed. He was highly skilled not only in the exposition of sacred literature but also in every branch of human learning. His ability in poetry and verse is shown by his remarkable work on the holy Cross; the distinguished volume entitled *On the Universe* reveals how thoroughly he was trained in the histories of antiquity. His knowledge of rhetorical art is recognized as shining abundantly in his writings and letters.
>
> The monk and venerable presbyter Bede, known throughout the world, was entrusted by his parents to a monastery when he was seven years old. His works are praised throughout the entire Church.
>
> These most holy men and teachers, highly skilled in Scripture, learned everything they knew of scriptural knowledge in monasteries under the Rule of their order. They were not sent abroad to foreign peoples for the sake of learning, since they always had teachers of the liberal arts in their monasteries.
>
> I say nothing of the many other highly learned men who, entering the monastic life in childhood, shone forth in glory both for their learning and for their holiness. Great devotion burned within them; in their minds there blazed a commendable zeal for the discipline of the Rule, which never allowed them to be idle.
>
> Apart from the divine office, to which they all devoted themselves faithfully, the monks devoted the remainder of their time to the study of Scripture. Through it they were not only enlightened in understanding but also moved to compunction in their affections. In the holy practice of the monks there always flourished a love that called them from reading to vigilant prayer.
>
> Those who had devoted themselves more extensively to the sacred Scriptures applied themselves during free hours to study and exposition of them, preparing books and various treatises by which they daily stirred their brothers’ studies toward God. The other brothers, in accordance with what the Rule forbids, did not give themselves to idleness; after prayers they applied themselves directly to manual labor. Those who were capable wrote books, and they put into finished form the works issued by the teachers from their notes. Others skillfully joined together the written codices. No one’s hand was absent from this holy task; all rejoiced to be considered participants in the studies carried on in the expositions of Scripture.
>
> The younger brothers were also trained in scholastic disciplines, according to what suited each of them: some in grammar, others in orthography, some in rhetoric or dialectic; certain ones in music, arithmetic, and the art of computation; others in philosophy. Still others, already grounded in these subjects, were introduced to the theoretical study of Scripture. No room was given to idleness in the monasteries; each person devoted himself to his studies and labors.
>
> Thus many most holy and highly learned men, outstanding in every branch of scriptural knowledge, emerged with great praise for their own name and for their order.

This is what Trithemius says concerning the teachers of our order and the extraordinary study of the monks in ancient times, as the title of his chapter indicates.

Finally, there is a third reason: the various offices, whether spiritual or temporal, which monks must exercise both within and outside the monasteries.
