They cannot carry them out suitably, religiously, and prudently, as they ought, unless they are equipped and instructed with extensive and varied knowledge, experience, and practice in such matters—as is self-evident.

Who could govern others, teach, preach, hear confessions, or properly administer other ecclesiastical duties if he were uneducated or at least not moderately versed in letters? Who, on the other hand, could properly manage temporal affairs, conduct the business of a monastery, and administer its common goods correctly—which, by decree of the Council of Trent (Session 25, chapter 2, on religious orders), belongs exclusively to the officials—unless he possessed at least some knowledge and skill in arithmetic, politics, economics, and other disciplines of this sort?

Therefore superiors provide excellently for their monks and cenobites, and also deserve great credit for their monasteries, when they take care that these men be imbued from youth with such liberal sciences and trained, according to ancient custom, by the best and most learned teachers. Each is thereby made capable, according to his capacity, of undertaking in due time the spiritual or temporal duties assigned to him. Occupied either in reading or in another office and exercise, he carefully avoids idleness, than which nothing is more destructive in religious life, and advances daily more and more toward greater growth in piety and learning.

As for the objection formerly raised on the authority of Abbot Germanus, the difficulty or impediment that sometimes arises for those who pray or meditate from reading poets or histories—when the mind is distracted by remembering such matters—can easily be answered: it is abundantly compensated by many other advantages and benefits. Nor does it have such force that it can take away or obstruct the fruit of prayer or meditation except for those who willingly and deliberately consent to it.

Moreover, monks in our time ought not to devote themselves solely to contemplation, as solitary monks and anchorites once did. They must also engage in many works and exercises of the active life, according to the institution of each order and religious community, for which the assistance of these sciences is especially useful.

If, however, the study and consideration of better, more necessary, and more useful matters are disturbed by such profane subjects, one must certainly strive to erase and remove them from memory, as Abbot Nesteros wisely advises. But if they are restrained to their proper places and times and suitably employed for the glory of God, then, as is clear from what has been said, one should not seek to forget them.

In answer to the example of Saint Jerome, Serarius says that it was not the reading in Jerome of Cicero and Plautus, whom he expressly names there, nor the reading of other pagan authors, that was censured and corrected in Jerome—whether truly or imaginatively, through certain forms and phantasms of things—but the manner of his reading.

First, because he read these authors more eagerly, more frequently, and more carefully than the sacred writings, even though he had already renounced the world, sought solitude, and above all owed himself to God. Second, because, compared with these profane authors, he found the sacred writings distasteful and recoiled from the style of Scripture as though it were uncultivated and tasteless, as he himself admits.

A special [Col. 0975A] impediment to salvation is added because of that scanty acquaintance with literature which I seem to have just touched upon. In it, either a pedagogue’s [Col. 0976A] insistence or continuous application to reading so wore me down that now my mind, as though infected by poetic [Col. 0977A] songs, meditates even at prayer time—while I am singing psalms or entreating forgiveness for sins—on those trifles of fables and histories of wars with which it was imbued from early childhood in its first rudiments of study. Either an unseemly memory of poems intrudes, or an image, as if of heroes fighting, turns before my eyes; and the imagination of such phantasms, always mocking me, does not permit my mind to rise toward heavenly contemplations, so that it cannot be expelled even by daily tears.

## CHAPTER XIII. The answer: how we may erase their memory

**Nesteros:** From the very matter that gives rise to your greatest despair of purification,

[Note: [Col. 0980D] For contraries are cured by contraries, and one nail drives out another.]

a sufficiently prompt and effective remedy can arise, if you are willing to transfer to the reading and meditation of the spiritual Scriptures the same diligence and persistence that you say you formerly devoted to those secular studies. Your mind must remain occupied with those poems for as long as it takes, through similar zeal and assiduity, to seek out something within itself for recollection and to bring forth spiritual and divine things in place of those barren and earthly ones. Once it has conceived them deeply and profoundly and has been nourished by them, the former things can gradually be driven out or entirely erased.

The human mind cannot remain vacant of all thoughts. Therefore, until it has been occupied with spiritual studies, it must be entangled in the things it previously learned. For as long as it has nowhere to turn and no tireless activity in which to exercise itself, it must fall back upon the things with which it was imbued from childhood and continually revolve what it conceived through long habit and meditation.

Thus, so that this spiritual knowledge may be strengthened in you with perpetual solidity, and so that you may no longer enjoy it only temporarily, as those do who encounter it not through their own study but through another’s report and perceive it, so to speak, merely through an airy scent, but so that it may somehow be stored within your senses, examined, and grasped, you must observe this rule with complete care: even if you happen to hear things being presented in a conference that you know very well,

[Note: Let those who disdain or grow weary of sermons or exhortations they have often heard or already know take note of this. The following saying from the Acts of the Apostles applies to them: “The Athenians devoted themselves to nothing else except either saying or hearing something new” (Acts 17).]

you should not receive them disdainfully or weariedly merely because they are already familiar to you. Rather, you should entrust them to your heart with the eagerness with which words desirable for salvation ought continually to be poured into our ears or continually issued from our mouths.

For however frequently holy matters may be recounted, they will never produce weariness in a soul that thirsts for true knowledge. Instead, receiving them each day as though they were new and desired, the more frequently it has drunk them in, the more eagerly it will either hear or speak them. From their repetition it will gain confirmation of the knowledge it has acquired rather than any weariness from frequent conference.

For it is clearly a sign of a lukewarm and proud mind if it receives with distaste and negligence the medicine of salutary words, even when it has been administered with excessive regularity for its instruction.

[Note: On this statement, see what was noted above (*Conference* XII, chapter 5), and Saint Gregory, Book VII of the *Morals*, chapter 7.]

For a soul that is filled makes sport of honeycombs, but to a hungry soul even bitter things seem sweet (Prov. 27).

If, therefore, these things have been carefully received, stored in the recesses of the mind, and sealed in silence, then later, once they have been matured by the old age of understanding and patience, they will be brought forth from the vessel of your breast with great fragrance, like certain sweet-smelling wines that gladden the human heart. They will overflow like an unfailing spring from the veins of experience and the watered channels of the virtues, pouring forth continuous streams as though from a certain abyss of your heart.

In you will come to pass what is said in Proverbs to the man who has brought these things to completion in action:

[Note: Saint Jerome likewise reads this in chapter 32 of Ezekiel, according to the translation of the Septuagint. The Vulgate reading, however, is: “Drink water from your cistern, and streams from your well; let your springs flow out, and divide your waters in the streets” (Prov. 5). Explaining these words, Saint Gregory says in the *Pastoral Rule* (Part III, chapter 25): “A preacher drinks water from his own cistern when, returning to his heart, he first hears within himself what he says. He drinks the streams of his own well if he is watered by the irrigation of his own word. This is rightly followed by: ‘Let your springs flow out, and divide your waters in the streets.’ It is right that he should first drink himself and then flow toward others by preaching. To make springs flow outward is to pour the power of preaching into others externally; to divide waters in the streets is to distribute the divine words among a great multitude of hearers according to the quality of each one,” and so forth. See also Saint Ambrose, *On Paradise*, chapter 3.]

> Drink waters from your vessels, and let waters from the fountain of your wells overflow for you; let waters from your spring flow over, and let your waters pass into your streets (Prov. 5).

And, according to the prophet Isaiah, you will be like a watered garden and like a spring of waters whose waters do not fail. In you the ancient ruins will be rebuilt; you will raise up the foundations of generation after generation; and you will be called a builder of fences, turning aside the paths of iniquity (Isa. 58).

You will also receive the blessing that the same prophet promises:

> The Lord will no longer make your teacher fly away from you; your eyes will see your instructor, and your ears will hear a word behind you warning you: “This is the way; walk in it,” neither to the right nor to the left (Isa. 30).

And so it will come about that not only every direction and meditation of your heart, but also all the wanderings and movements of your thoughts, will be for you a holy and unceasing rumination upon the divine law.

## CHAPTER XIV. That an impure soul can neither impart nor receive spiritual knowledge

It is impossible, as we have already said, for anyone inexperienced in these matters either to recognize or to teach them. For one who is not even capable of receiving them, how can he be fit to impart them? Even if such men presume to teach something, their speech will undoubtedly reach only the ears of those who hear them; it will not be able to penetrate their hearts, exposed as it is by the inactivity of their deeds and the fruitlessness of their vanity, because it is drawn not from the treasure of a good conscience but from the empty presumption of self-display.

It is impossible for an impure soul, however assiduously it may labor in reading, to attain spiritual knowledge. No one pours some noble perfume, the finest honey, or any precious liquid into a foul and corrupted vessel. For a vessel once imbued with dreadful odors contaminates even the most fragrant myrum more readily than it can itself receive any of its sweetness or fragrance.

[Note: “Myrum,” says Ciaconius, or μύρον in Greek, means “perfume.” Perfumes were customarily made exceedingly fragrant and costly, as Saint John himself also testifies in the Gospel when he relates that Mary took a pound of costly spikenard perfume, anointed Jesus’ feet, and filled the house with the fragrance of the perfume. Hilary uses this word as a Latin term in his commentary on Psalm 132: “Aaron,” he says (chapter 12), “is anointed with myrum of confusion.” A little later he adds: “Thus this myrum extinguishes all foul odors.” Saint Jerome—or rather Rufinus—in the translation of Origen’s commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 5, has the following: “Or again, when he did not prevent the sinful woman from touching his feet, bathing them with tears, wiping them with her hair, or anointing them with myrum.” In the printed editions of Cassian, the reading was “the most fragrant myrrh,” or, more incorrectly, “the most fragrant myrrhum.” This is Ciaconius’s explanation, which we have followed in this correction.]

Thus the vessel of our breast, unless it has first been cleansed of every foul contagion of vice, will not deserve to receive that anointing of blessing of which the Prophet says:

> Like ointment upon the head, which runs down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, which runs down to the edge of his garment (Ps. 132);

nor will it preserve undefiled that spiritual knowledge and those words of Scripture that are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb (Ps. 18).

For what partnership is there between justice and iniquity? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness? What agreement does Christ have with Belial? (2 Cor. 6).

## CHAPTER XV. Objection that many impure people possess knowledge, while holy people do not

**Germanus:** This definition does not seem to us to be supported by truth or grounded in a probable argument. Since it is clear that all who either do not accept the faith of Christ at all or corrupt it through the impious perversity of their doctrines are impure in heart, how is it that many Jews and heretics, and even Catholics entangled in various vices, have attained a perfect knowledge of Scripture and boast of the greatness of spiritual doctrine? Conversely, how is it that an innumerable multitude of holy men, whose hearts have been cleansed from every contagion of sin, are content with the purity of simple faith—

[Lipsius, in the margin: “covered”]

—and remain ignorant of the mysteries of deeper knowledge? How, then, can this statement stand, which attributes spiritual knowledge solely to purity of heart?

## CHAPTER XVI. The answer: that evil people cannot possess true knowledge
Nesteros: He does not properly examine the definition of a virtue who does not carefully weigh every word of the proposition put forward. For we stated beforehand that such people possess only skill in disputation and elegance of expression; as for entering into the veins of Scripture and the mysteries [Col. 0983A] of spiritual meanings, they are unable to do so. [Col. 0983C]

[Note: Here he calls “true knowledge of God” what above he called “spiritual” knowledge—that is, knowledge joined with true piety and the grace of the Holy Spirit. This certainly cannot coexist with uncleanness of the flesh, or with filthiness and other similar vices, and is possessed only by true worshipers of God. To this pertains the teaching of Saint Thomas (2–2, q. 10, art. 3), by which he confers the gift of knowledge—which this Author calls spiritual knowledge—together with the gift of understanding, since both are gifts of the Holy Spirit in Isaiah: “Just as it was said,” he remarks, “of the gift of understanding, that not everyone who understands possesses the gift of understanding, but that the person who understands possesses it as though from a habit of grace, so also it must be understood of the gift of knowledge: only those possess the gift of knowledge who, through the infusion of grace, have right judgment concerning what is to be believed and done, so that in no respect do they depart from the rectitude of justice. And this is the knowledge of the saints, of which it is said in Wisdom 10: ‘The Lord led the just man by straight ways and gave him the knowledge of the saints.’”]

For true knowledge is possessed only by true worshipers of God; and certainly that people does not possess it of whom it is said: “Hear, foolish people, who have no heart, who have eyes and do not see, and ears and do not hear” (Jeremiah 5). And again: “Because you have rejected knowledge, I also will reject you, so that you shall not serve as my priest” (Hosea 4).

Since all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are said to be hidden in Christ (Colossians 3), how can one who has refused to find Christ, or who has blasphemed against him after finding him with sacrilegious mouth, or who has polluted the catholic faith with unclean deeds, be believed to have attained true knowledge? “For the Spirit of God’s discipline will flee from deceit, and will not dwell in a body subjected to sins” (Wisdom 1).

Therefore, one does not reach spiritual knowledge by any other route than the order which one of the prophets elegantly expressed, saying: “Sow for yourselves unto righteousness; reap the hope of life; enlighten for yourselves the light of knowledge” (Hosea 10). First, therefore, we must sow unto righteousness—that is, we must extend actual perfection through works of righteousness. Then we must reap the hope of life—that is, we must gather the fruits of spiritual virtues by driving out carnal vices. In this way we shall be able to enlighten for ourselves the light of knowledge.

The Psalmist likewise determines that this order must be observed, saying: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord; blessed are those who search out his testimonies” (Psalm 118). For he did not say first, “Blessed are those who search out his testimonies,” and then add, “Blessed are the undefiled in the way”; rather, he says first, “Blessed are the undefiled in the way,” thereby clearly showing that no one can rightly arrive at the searching out of God’s testimonies unless he first walks undefiled through an active way of life in the way of Christ.

These people, therefore, whom you mentioned, possess not the knowledge which the unclean cannot have, but pseudonymous—that is, falsely named—knowledge (τῆς ψευδωνύμου). [Note: Ψευδώνυμος is derived from ψευδής, that is, “false” or “lying,” and ὄνομα, “name.”] Concerning this the blessed Apostle says: “O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of words and oppositions of falsely named knowledge” (1 Timothy 6). In Greek it is said:

ἐκτρεπόμενος τὰς βεβήλους κενοφωνίας καὶ ἀντιβάσεις τῆς ψευδωνύμου γνώσεως.

That is: “avoiding profane empty talk and contradictions of falsely named knowledge.”

[Note: That is, “emptinesses” or “vanities of words,” as Chrysostom and Oecumenius read them. But our translator read καινοφωνίας, “novelties of words,” as did Saint Ambrose. Moreover, Ciaconius and others cite only the final words: ἀντιθέσεις τῆς ψευδωνύμου γνώσεως. Dionysius, as is his custom, omits the Greek.]

Concerning those who seem to acquire some semblance of knowledge, or concerning those who diligently devote themselves to reading the sacred books and memorizing Scripture but nevertheless do not abandon carnal vices, it is elegantly expressed in Proverbs: “As a golden earring in her nose, so is beauty in a badly behaved woman” (Proverbs 11).

[Note: Thus according to the Greek translation; the Vulgate has: “A golden ring in a swine’s snout is a beautiful woman who is a fool.” Saint Jerome gives three interpretations of this saying; the second is especially appropriate and suited to this passage: Whoever acquires the adornment of divine utterances through meditation but pursues it by living badly has a golden ring in his snout. Yet, after the manner of swine, he does not cease to turn up the earth, because what he has perceived through the fragrance of righteousness he has defiled by unclean action. Therefore such a soul is considered beautiful and foolish: beautiful through knowledge, because it is devoted to carnal allurements, but foolish through its conduct.]

For what does it profit anyone to attain the adornment of heavenly utterances and that most precious beauty of Scripture, if, by clinging to muddy works or thoughts, he breaks it as though turning over the most filthy earth, or pollutes it in the muddy wallows of his desires? It will happen that what is ordinarily an ornament to those who use it rightly will not only be unable to adorn such people, but will also become soiled with an even greater filth of mire.

“For praise is not beautiful from the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclesiasticus 15). To such a person the Prophet says: “Why do you recount my righteous deeds and take up my covenant in your mouth?” (Psalm 49).

Concerning such souls, who do not steadfastly possess the fear of the Lord—of which it is said, [Note: The Vulgate edition has: “The fear of the Lord is the discipline of wisdom.”] “The fear of the Lord is discipline and wisdom”—but nevertheless attempt to acquire the meaning of Scripture through their constant meditation upon it, Proverbs speaks very appropriately: [Note: The Vulgate has: “What does it profit a fool to possess riches, since he cannot buy wisdom?”] “Why should there be riches for a fool? For the senseless cannot possess wisdom” (Proverbs 15, according to the Septuagint).

Indeed, true and spiritual knowledge is so far removed from that secular learning which is polluted by the filth of carnal vices that we know it sometimes to have flourished wonderfully in certain people who were inarticulate and almost entirely uneducated. This is demonstrated most clearly in the apostles and in many holy men, who took delight not in the empty luxury of philosophers but were bowed down by the true fruits of spiritual knowledge.

[Col. 0985A] Of them it is also written in the Acts of the Apostles: “When they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and realized that they were unlettered and ordinary men, they marveled” (Acts 4).

Therefore, if you care to reach its unfading fragrance, strive first with every effort to obtain purity of chastity from the Lord. For no one in whom the inclination toward carnal passions—and especially fornication—still rules can possess spiritual knowledge.

“Wisdom will rest in a good heart, and whoever fears God will find knowledge with righteousness” (Proverbs 14).

The blessed Apostle also teaches that one reaches spiritual knowledge by the order which we have described. For when he wished not only to compose a catalogue of all his virtues but also to explain their order, showing which virtue should follow which and which should give birth to which, after some intervening words he said:

[Note: In these words the Apostle embraces four combinations, or conjunctions, of virtues: he joins fasting to vigils, knowledge to chastity, gentleness to endurance, and charity to the Holy Spirit, since indeed “charity is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit” (Romans 5), whose special and most proper gift it is.]

“By vigils, by chastity, by knowledge, by endurance, by gentleness, by the Holy Spirit, by sincere charity” (1 Corinthians 6).

In this conjunction of virtues he clearly intended to teach us to proceed from vigils and fasts to chastity, from chastity to knowledge, from knowledge to endurance, from endurance to gentleness, from gentleness to the Holy Spirit, and from the Holy Spirit to the rewards of sincere charity.

When you too, therefore, have reached spiritual knowledge by this discipline and in this order, you will undoubtedly possess—as we have said—not a barren or inert teaching but a living and fruitful one, and the seed of the saving word. When it has been entrusted by you to the hearts of those who hear, the following abundant rain of the Holy Spirit will make it fertile; and in accordance with what the prophet promised, “rain will be given to your seed wherever you sow it in the land, and the bread of the produce of your land will be most abundant and rich” (Isaiah 30).

## CHAPTER XVII. To whom the method of perfection should be disclosed

Beware [Note: He teaches that the mysteries of sacred doctrine and spiritual knowledge are not to be disclosed to unclean persons—that is, carnal or sensual persons—but to spiritual and chaste persons. “For the natural man does not receive the things that are of God.” Hence the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 2), says: “I could not speak to you as to spiritual persons, but as to carnal persons. As to little children in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food; for you were not yet able; indeed, even now you are not able, for you are still carnal.” And in Hebrews 5: “Everyone who partakes of milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness; but solid food is for the perfect, those who by practice have their senses exercised to distinguish good and evil.” Blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, Paul’s disciple, likewise earnestly impressed this teaching upon Timothy, also a disciple, at the beginning of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, in these words: “Take especial care not to divulge the holy things of the holy ones, nor allow them to be profaned by impure lights; rather, reverence them, never handing them about indiscriminately to the untrained, but secretly disclosing the understanding of holy things only to holy persons.”] [Col. 0985C] lest, when a more mature age has advanced you to the work of teaching, you—deceived by love of empty glory—indiscriminately thrust upon unclean people what you have learned through both reading and the labor of experience, and incur what the wisest Solomon forbade:

[Note: Μὴ προσαγάγῃς ἀσεβῆ νομῇ δικαίου (“Do not bring an impious person to the pasture of a righteous man”; Proverbs 24, according to the Septuagint). Thus the published and manuscript Greek books read it, and Lucifer of Calaris cites this testimony in precisely the same words in Book 1, On Not Associating with Heretics. But Saint Cyprian, Book 3 to Quirinus, chapter 55, does not seem to have read νομὴν, “pasture,” but μόνην, “dwelling” or “tabernacle.” For he cites it thus: “Do not bring the impious into the dwelling of the righteous.” Saint Jerome likewise has, in his Commentary on Micah: “Do not bring the impious into the tabernacle of the righteous.” But the Hebrew word is ambiguous and can mean either. Thus Ciaconius. The Vulgate reading, moreover, is: “Do not lie in wait and seek wickedness in the house of the righteous, nor destroy his repose” (Proverbs 19); the Chaldean version agrees closely: “Do not wickedly lie in wait for the dwelling of the righteous, nor cast down the house of his habitation.”]

“Do not bring the impious to the pastures of the righteous, and do not be deceived by the fullness of the belly; for delicacies are not fitting for a fool, [Col. 0986B] nor is wisdom needed where understanding is lacking” (Proverbs 19).

[Note: Vulgate: “Delicacies are not fitting for a fool.”]

For folly is rather led onward; because “a harsh servant will not be corrected by words. For if he understands, he will not obey” (Proverbs 29).

[Note: Ἄγεται, “is led,” not “is said,” as it was previously read incorrectly. The Vulgate text is: “A servant cannot be instructed by words, because he understands what you say and refuses to respond” (Proverbs 29). Saint Jerome says: “A servant is any sinner who understands correctly but, in the work of truth, refuses to respond without the discipline of the scourge.” Concerning such people Truth says: “That servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many blows” (Luke 12).]

And: “Say nothing in the ears of the imprudent, lest he mock your wise sayings” (Proverbs 23).

[Note: The Vulgate has: “Do not speak in the ears of fools, because they will despise the instruction of your discourse.”]

And: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine, lest they perhaps trample them under their feet and, turning, tear you to pieces” (Matthew 7).

[Note: Matthew 7: “Do not give what is holy to dogs.” Isidore of Pelusium (Book 1, Letter 143) says: “We are forbidden by divine command to throw pearls before swine—that is, before those who wallow in vicious affections and follow a swine-like way of life—lest they perhaps trample them under their feet, bringing insult to the divine majesty in their criminal pursuits.”]

Therefore, when concealing the mysteries of spiritual meanings from such people, you should effectively sing: “I have hidden your utterances in my heart, that I might not sin against you” (Psalm 118).

But perhaps you will say: To whom, then, should the mysteries of the divine Scriptures be dispensed? The wisest Solomon teaches you:

[Note: The Vulgate has: “Give strong drink to those who are grieving, and wine to those who are bitter of heart. Let them drink and forget their poverty, and remember their sorrow no more.” The commentary on this saying which he gives here was borrowed almost word for word by the abbot Nesteros—or Cassian himself—from Saint Jerome. Saint Jerome writes: “By strong drink and wine here he means the heavenly consolation of divine wisdom, which should be offered to those hearts that refuse to be consoled by earthly things and receive whatever comes in the present with a bitter spirit, clinging with their whole mind only to the heavenly joys they do not yet see, in accordance with him who said: ‘My soul refused to be consoled; I remembered God, and I was delighted’” (Psalm 76). Likewise: “Give strong drink to those who are grieving” (Proverbs 31), and so forth. “Pour abundantly into those who are weighed down by grief and sorrow on account of repentance for their former deeds the delight of spiritual knowledge, like wine that gladdens the human heart; and revive them with the intoxicating abundance of the saving word, lest, overwhelmed by the continual burden of grief and plunged into such despair, they be swallowed up by still greater sorrow.”]

“Give,” he says, “intoxication to those who are in sorrow, and wine to drink to those who are in pain,” so that they may forget their poverty and remember their sorrows no more” (Proverbs 31)—that is, pour abundantly into those who are weighed down by grief and sorrow because of repentance for their former deeds the delight of spiritual knowledge, like wine that gladdens the human heart (Psalm 103), and refresh them with the intoxicating abundance of the saving word, lest those who are overwhelmed by continual grief and deadly despair be swallowed up by still greater sorrow (2 Corinthians 2).

But concerning those who remain in tepidity and negligence, who are not pierced by any sorrow of heart, it is said:

“For the one who is complacent and without pain will be in poverty” (Proverbs 21).

[Note: Vulgate: “Every sluggard is always in poverty.”]

Therefore, with as much caution as you can, avoid becoming so detained by the love of empty glory that you cannot share in the condition of the man whom the prophet praises, “who has not given his money at interest” (Psalm 14).

[Col. 0987B] For everyone who dispenses the utterances of God—of which it is said, “The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances, silver tested by fire, proven upon the earth, purified sevenfold” (Psalm 11)—out of love of human praise lends his money at interest. He will deserve not only no rewards for this praise but also punishments. For this reason he preferred to squander the Lord’s money, so that he himself might obtain from it a temporal reward, rather than that the Lord, as it is written, should come and receive what is his with interest (Luke 19).

## CHAPTER XVIII. For what reasons spiritual teaching is unfruitful

[Col. 0987C] It is evident that the teaching of spiritual matters is rendered ineffective for two reasons.

[Note: The teaching of preaching is made empty and ineffective for two reasons: first, because of the preacher’s part or fault; second, because of the hearers’ guilt. See Saint Gregory, Homily 17 on the Gospels.]

For either the teacher, commending things he has not experienced, attempts to instruct the hearer with an empty sound of words; or else the wicked hearer, filled with vices, does not receive the holy and salutary teaching of a spiritual man because his heart is closed.

Concerning such people the prophet says:

[Note: In Isaiah it reads: “Blind the heart of this people.” But the Septuagint translated it: “The heart of this people has been blinded,” or “has been fattened.” They did this deliberately, so that Gentiles, reading these words in Isaiah, would not suppose that God was the author of this blinding. God is said to blind or harden not because he infuses blindness or hardness, but because he abandons the person who was first abandoned and does not supply the grace deprived of which a human being rushes headlong into many sins and is gradually hardened and blinded through his own vice and guilt.]

“The heart of this people has been blinded, and they have heard heavily with their ears, and they have closed their eyes, lest they ever see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them” (Isaiah 6).

## CHAPTER XIX. That even the unworthy often receive the grace of the saving word

[Col. 0988B]

[Note: Saint Gregory’s thirty-first book of the Moralia, chapter 35, offers an apt discussion for illuminating this passage: “Often a word is granted to the teacher because of the grace of the hearer, and often the discourse is withdrawn from the teacher because of the hearer’s fault. Therefore, when the teacher preaches abundantly, let him not exalt himself, lest perhaps his tongue be filled not on account of his own grace but on account of the hearer’s grace; and when the teacher speaks unfruitfully, let the hearer not become angry, lest perhaps the teacher’s tongue grow sluggish not because of his own rejection but because of the hearer’s rejection. For the sake of the hearer’s grace, a good word is given even to evil teachers, as the words of preaching could be supplied to the Pharisees, concerning whom it is written: ‘Therefore, whatever they tell you, observe and do; but do not act according to their works’ (Matthew 23). But because of the hearers’ rejection, the word is withdrawn even from good teachers, as when God says to Ezekiel concerning Israel: ‘I will make your tongue cling to the roof of your mouth, and you shall be mute, unable to act as one who reproves, because it is an exasperating house’ (Ezekiel 3). Sometimes the word of preaching is given on account of both groups; sometimes it is withdrawn on account of both. It is given on account of both when the divine voice says to Paul among the Corinthians: ‘Do not be afraid, but speak.’ And shortly afterward: ‘Because I have many people in this city.’ It is withdrawn on account of both when Eli the priest knew of his sons’ wicked conduct but did not exercise a voice of reproof worthy of the offense. Thus far Gregory, together with what follows.”]

Nevertheless, sometimes, through the generous liberality of our provider, God, who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2), it is granted that one who has shown himself unworthy of evangelical preaching through reprehensible conduct may obtain the grace of spiritual teaching for the salvation of many.

By what means, moreover, the charisms of healings are also granted by the Lord for the expulsion of demons, it is fitting that we explain in a similar discussion. We shall reserve it for the evening, when we rise for refreshment, since whatever is conveyed gradually and without excessive bodily exertion is always more effectively received in the heart.

## FIFTEENTH CONFERENCE, THE SECOND OF ABBOT NESTEROS  
### ON DIVINE CHARISMS

[Col. 0989]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0989A]

After [Note: The word *synaxis*, although used in various ways by the Fathers and possessing several meanings, as we have noted elsewhere (*Institutes*, Book II, chapter 26, and *Conference* 7, final chapter), nevertheless generally denotes in Cassian a meeting or gathering of monks for prayer and the singing and celebration of divine praises. The same is true in Saint Ephrem, in a certain letter to John the Monk, where he says: “Nor should you neglect your synaxis on the pretext of bodily needs.” And in the book *On Virtue*, chapter 5: “If you come forward before all the others to the synaxis and remain until it is concluded, let not your thoughts exalt you on this account,” and so forth. Thus he calls the evening synaxis the evening gathering for prayer, or prayer itself, the psalmody, or the evening office. See other notes on the same [Col. 0989B] word.] intent upon the promised discussion, we likewise took our seats on the *psiathia*, according to custom.

[Note: The *psiathia* and their twofold use among ancient monks have been discussed fully elsewhere (*Institutes*, Book IV, chapter 23, and *Conference* 1, final chapter).]

When we had maintained silence for a while out of respect for the old man, he anticipated our bashful silence with the following words:

[Note: *Charisma* means the same as grace or gratuitous gift. The word was adopted and retained by the Latins from the Apostle, in 1 Corinthians 12, where, speaking of the various gifts and graces of the Holy Spirit, he says: “Earnestly desire the better charisms.” Saint Thomas explains this as “the more excellent graces.” Tertullian, likewise expressing the same thought (*To His Wife*, Book I, chapter 3), says: “Let us be followers of the better gifts.”

Among theologians, however, *grace* does not mean every natural or spiritual benefit of God, in the sense in which the heretics known as Pelagians wished free will and other gifts of that kind to be understood by the term “grace,” as Saint Augustine testifies (*On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 3 and following). Rather, it means only God’s supernatural gifts and benefits—that is, those which surpass the capacity of nature and are freely bestowed by God even upon the undeserving [Col. 0989C] (see *Conference* 13, chapter 9).

Theologians distinguish two kinds of grace (Saint Thomas, *Summa*, I–II, question 111, articles 1 and 4). One is that by which the human person is himself united to God; this is called “grace that makes pleasing” (*gratia gratum faciens*), and it was discussed in the preceding conference. The other is that by which one person cooperates with another so that the latter may be brought back to God. Such a gift is called “grace freely given” (*gratia gratis data*), because it is granted to a person above the capacity of nature and beyond his merits. But since it is not given so that the person himself may be justified through it, but rather so that he may cooperate in another’s justification, it is not called grace that makes pleasing. Of this the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 12: “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good,” that is, for the benefit of others.

Since the gifts of grace freely given are various, and are elsewhere called *charisms*, as the Apostle teaches in these words: “There are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit,” and, “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good” (that is, spiritual but visible gifts are conferred so that they may be the sign and manifestation [Col. 0989D] of the invisible Spirit received): “To one, through the Spirit, is given the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, the grace of healings in one Spirit; to another, the working of mighty deeds; to another, prophecy; to another, the discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, the interpretation of speech.”

Nevertheless, in this conference, which is entitled *On Divine Charisms*, the subject is not all charisms or graces freely given indiscriminately, but specifically and particularly two: the grace of healings, or cures—that is, the grace of healing and curing illnesses—and the working of mighty deeds, that is, signs and miracles, as will become clear from what follows.

Why, then, does the Apostle distinguish the grace of healings from the working of mighty deeds or miracles, since healing itself is miraculous and takes place through divine power? Saint Thomas answers (*Summa*, II–II, question 178, articles 2 and 4) that the grace of healings is mentioned separately because through it a particular benefit is conferred upon a person, namely bodily health, in addition to the common benefit exhibited in all miracles, namely that people may be brought to the knowledge of God.

The Author later assigns three reasons, or a threefold rationale, for why such charisms are granted to some. The third reason, however, refers not so much to the true grace freely given—whether of healings or of miracles—as to a counterfeit and simulation, or a certain diabolical imitation, of such graces, which the devil works through his ministers, as will be explained more fully below.

Saint Thomas (*Commentary*) set forth both causes or reasons—that is, the first and the second—together with the distinction between the two graces, in these words:

“It belongs to grace that makes pleasing that the Holy Spirit dwell through it; this does not belong to grace freely given, but only that through it the Holy Spirit may be manifested, as the interior movement of the heart is manifested through the voice. The Holy Spirit is manifested through such graces in two ways. First, as dwelling in the Church, teaching and sanctifying it—for example, when a sinner, in whom the Holy Spirit does not dwell, performs miracles to show that the faith of the Church which he preaches is true. Hence Hebrews 2 says: ‘God bearing witness with signs and wonders and various distributions of the Holy Spirit.’ Second, the Holy Spirit is manifested through such grace as dwelling in the person to whom such graces are granted. Hence Acts 6 says that Stephen, ‘full of grace,’ performed many wonders and signs, and the one whom they chose was full of the Holy Spirit. In this way such graces are granted only to the saints.

“And lest this manifestation appear fruitless, he adds: ‘For the common good’—in which the purpose of these graces is indicated—either when the true doctrine of the Church is proved, and thus the faithful are strengthened and unbelievers converted, or when someone’s holiness is proposed to others as an example. Hence it is said below: ‘Seek for the building up of the Church, so that you may abound.’ And in chapter 10: ‘Not seeking what is useful to me, but what is useful to many, so that they may be saved.’”]

The preceding order of discussion has now reached the exposition of the nature of spiritual charisms, which, as we have learned from the tradition of our elders, is threefold.

The first cause of healings is when the grace of signs accompanies those chosen and righteous men on account of the merit of their holiness. It is clear that the Apostles and many saints performed signs and wonders according to the Lord’s command, who said: “Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons; you have received freely, give freely” (Matthew 10).

The second is when, for the edification of the Church—or of those who bring their sick to them, or of those who are to be healed—the power of healing proceeds even from sinners and the undeserving. Concerning such people the Savior says in the Gospel: “Many,” he says, “will say to me on that day: Lord, Lord,

[Note: Saint Jerome, commenting on this passage, says: “To prophesy, perform mighty deeds, and cast out demons is sometimes not the merit of the one who acts; rather, he does it through invocation of Christ’s name, or it is granted for the condemnation of those who invoke it and for the benefit of those who see and hear, so that although people may despise those performing signs, they may nevertheless honor God, at whose invocation many miracles are performed. Saul, Balaam, and Caiaphas also prophesied, without knowing what they were saying (1 Kings 10; Numbers 23; John 11); Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar learned future things through dreams (Genesis 41; Daniel 2); and in the Acts of the Apostles the Jewish sons of Sceva appeared to cast out demons (Acts 19). Judas the Apostle is also said to have performed many signs among the Apostles while possessing the mind of a betrayer.” Thus Saint Jerome. See below, chapter 6.]

did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty deeds?” And then I will declare to them: “I never knew you; depart from me, workers of iniquity” (Matthew 7).

Conversely, if faith is lacking in those who offer the sick or in the sick themselves, he does not allow even those to whom the gifts of healing have been granted to exercise the power of healing. Concerning this the evangelist Luke says: “And Jesus,” he says, “could not perform mighty deeds among them because of their unbelief” (Luke 4).

[Note: This is explained in two ways. First: “He could not,” that is, he did not wish to, because of their unbelief. Thus the brothers of Joseph are said to have been unable to speak peacefully with their brother because they hated him (Genesis 37), that is, they did not wish to. So also Christ says in John 7: “The world cannot hate you”—that is, it does not wish to hate you, since you have been purified. Second: “He could not,” that is, it was neither fitting nor becoming for him to do so, just as he said to the sons of Zebedee: “It is not mine to give you” (Matthew 20)—that is, “I do not wish to give it to you, because it is not yet appropriate for those who are carnal and worldly.”]

Hence the same Lord says: “There were many lepers in Israel under Elisha the prophet, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian” (Matthew 13).

[Note: This collusion and simulation by demons, through which they pretend to be compelled by magicians and to be violently expelled from possessed bodies by their commands, was discussed above (*Conference* 8, chapter 20). The Author mentions this mode not because it truly belongs to divine charisms and the supernatural gifts of healing and miracles discussed here—as is clear to everyone—but because it displays a certain resemblance and appearance of them. The devil imitates divine actions like an ape, as far as he can, but he cannot attain or equal them.

Accordingly, although both by himself and through his ministers, with God’s permission, he can perform many things which seem miraculous and wondrous to human beings (Saint Thomas, *Summa*, I, question 111, article 4; II–II, question 178, article 2), he cannot perform true miracles—that is, miracles surpassing the power of all natural things, such as raising the dead, giving sight to the blind, and the like—or absolute wonders, to which the words of the Psalm refer: “Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, who alone does wondrous things” (Psalm 71); and again: “Who alone does great wonders” (Psalm 135).

For example, a demon sometimes cures, through magicians and sorcerers, illnesses which appear to human beings—and truly are—incurable. Yet there is no miracle here, because the demon does nothing that surpasses the powers of all nature. Rather, he uses natural causes and means, applying active causes to passive ones, whose powers and capacities he knows much more accurately and perceptively than any highly experienced physician; or else he removes the causes of diseases which he himself secretly introduced. See Saint Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book III, chapters 7 and 10, and *The City of God*, Book X, chapter 16.]

The third mode of healing is counterfeited through the collusion and agency of demons. Thus, while a person bound by manifest crimes is believed, because of the admiration aroused by his signs, to be holy and a servant of God, imitation of his vices is also encouraged; and by this, when an opening for slander [Lipsius, in the margin: “hearing”] has been opened, the holiness of religion is disgraced. Or else the person who believes himself to possess the gifts of healing is brought down more severely because he has been lifted up by pride of heart.

This is why those who invoke the names of persons whom they know to possess neither merits of holiness nor any spiritual fruits pretend to be burned by their merits and to be driven from possessed bodies.

[Note: I now think that *uri* should not be understood as *urgeri*, as I supposed in the earlier edition, but properly as “to be burned,” since it is clear from the lives of many saints that demons possessing bodies have often cried out: “I am burning, I am burning,” and so forth. Energumens have also often been heard to say this. For just as demons are truly burned by fire, even bodily fire—that is, they suffer a kind of inward and spiritual burning in hell, according to the more probable opinion—so it is not improbable that, by God’s will, they are truly tormented and in some manner burned by the presence and power of the saints. See examples in Caesarius and Surius.]

Concerning such people, Deuteronomy says: “If a prophet has arisen in your midst,” it says, “or someone who claims to have seen a dream, and he has foretold a sign or wonder, and what he has said comes to pass, and he says to you: ‘Let us go and follow strange gods whom you do not know, and let us serve them,’ you shall not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer, because the Lord your God is testing you, so that it may become evident whether you love him or not, with all your heart and with all your soul” (Deuteronomy 14).

And in the Gospel: “False Christs and false prophets will arise,” he says,

[Note: The Apostle explains what the signs and wonders of Antichrist and his ministers will be when, speaking of Antichrist, he says that his coming will be “according to the working of Satan, with all power and signs and lying wonders” (2 Thessalonians 2).

They will be lies either because they will usually be imaginary and mere illusions. He will appear to raise the dead, heal the sick, and so forth, but this will be done deceptively and by trickery, as the miracles which Apollonius of Tyana and Simon Magus are once said to have performed. Or they will be lies because, even if some of them are genuinely performed, since they do not exceed the power of nature—for example, raising winds and storms, drawing fire from heaven, or suddenly curing the sick and infirm—nevertheless, as miracles of the kind Antichrist will boast of performing, they will be false and lying. True miracles surpass every natural power and therefore are accomplished by the power of God alone, who cannot be a witness to or approver of falsehood (see Saint Thomas, II–II, question 178, article 1).

Thus Augustine says (*City of God*, Book XX, chapter 19): “It is often questioned whether they are called signs and lying wonders because he will deceive mortal senses through phantasms, making what he does not do appear to have been done; or because, even if those wonders are genuine, they will lead those who believe to falsehood, since they do not know that they could have been performed by the devil’s power and will believe that they could have been performed only by divine power—especially when he will receive power such as he has never previously possessed.

“For when fire fell from heaven and in a single assault consumed the holy Job’s entire household together with his flocks, and when a whirlwind struck and overthrew the house and killed his children, these were not phantasms, although they were works of Satan, to whom God had given this power. Why, then, are these called wonders and signs of falsehood? That will become apparent at the time. But whatever the reason for the expression, they will deceive by signs and wonders those who deserve to be deceived, because, as the Apostle says, ‘they did not receive the love of the truth, so that they might be saved.’” Thus Augustine.]

and they will give great signs and wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led astray (Matthew 24).

## CHAPTER II  
### In Which It Is Explained How One Should Admire Holy Men

Therefore we should never admire those who pursue these things for the sake of such powers. Rather, we should examine whether they have been made perfect by the expulsion of every vice and the correction of their conduct. This is granted not on account of another person’s faith or because of a diversity of circumstances, but according to each person’s diligence, as God’s grace dispenses it.

[Note: That is, the grace discussed in the preceding conference, which is occupied with expelling vices and acquiring virtues, as was said there.]

For this practical knowledge, which the Apostle calls charity by another name (2 Corinthians 13), is placed by apostolic authority above all the tongues of human beings and angels, above the fullness of faith that can even move mountains, above all knowledge and prophecy, above the distribution of all possessions,

and finally even above glorious martyrdom. For after he had enumerated all the kinds of charisms and said: “To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another faith, to another the grace of healings, to another the working of mighty deeds” (1 Corinthians 22), and so forth, when he was about to speak of charity and show how he placed it above all charisms, observe briefly what he says: “And I show you a still more excellent way” (ibid.).

By this he clearly demonstrates that the summit of perfection and blessedness consists not in the performance of those wonders but in the purity of charity. And rightly so: all those things will be abolished and destroyed, whereas charity will remain forever.

[Note: The holy men mentioned here do not pursue miracles, called works of signs; rather, they avoid them as far as possible, unless compelled by necessity or charity. They do so for two reasons: first, because of the danger of display and empty glory; second, because of the danger of tempting God. Christ taught by his own example that both were to be avoided.

He avoided the first when he sometimes forbade the miracles he had performed to be made public, and when he immediately restrained the disciples who were rejoicing and boasting that even demons were subject to them, saying: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven,” namely because of pride; and he added: “Do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you; but rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10).

Likewise, when the scribes and Pharisees said: “Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you,” he replied: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it,” and so forth (Matthew 12 and 16). And when, by Pilate’s order, he was led to King Herod, who desired to see some sign performed by him, he gave him no answer, although Herod questioned him at length (Luke 23). He must unquestionably be understood to have acted thus because those people sought signs out of mere curiosity or vanity.

He avoided the second when he taught that it is tempting God to wish to perform a miracle without necessity or a just reason. Saint Augustine says in his second treatise on the Epistle of John: “Christ was tempted by Satan concerning a miracle when Satan said to him: ‘Throw yourself down, for it is written: He has commanded his angels concerning you, that they may receive you, lest you strike your foot against a stone.’ He resisted the tempter. For if he had performed a miracle, it would have appeared that he had either yielded or acted out of curiosity.

“He did perform miracles when he wished, as God, but as one healing the weak; for if he had done so then, it would have been thought that he merely wished to perform a miracle. But so that people would not think this, observe what he replied. And when such temptation comes to you, say the same thing: ‘Get behind me, Satan; for it is written: You shall not tempt the Lord your God’—that is, ‘If I do this, I shall tempt God.’

“This is what he wished you to say when the enemy suggests to you: ‘What sort of person are you? What sort of Christian? Have you just performed even one miracle? Have the dead risen at your prayers, or have you healed those suffering from fever? If you truly possessed any merit, you would perform some miracle.’ Answer and say: ‘It is written: You shall not tempt the Lord your God. Therefore I will not tempt God, as though I belonged to God if I performed a miracle and did not belong to him if I did not.’” Thus Augustine.]

The examples of Saint Anthony, recorded by Athanasius; of Hilarion, by Saint Jerome; of Macarius and others, by Palladius; and of Benedict, by Gregory, show how cautiously and with what difficulty the holy Fathers, instructed by Christ’s example, approached the performance of miracles, and how humbly they conducted themselves afterward.

Concerning Hilarion, Saint Jerome writes:

“In the sixty-third year of his life, when he saw a great monastery and a multitude of brothers living with him, and crowds of people bringing to him those afflicted with various diseases and unclean spirits, so that every kind of person filled the surrounding solitude, he wept daily and remembered his former way of life with an incredible longing. When the brothers asked him what was wrong and why he was wasting away, he replied: ‘I have returned to the world and have received my reward in my lifetime. Behold, the people of Palestine and the neighboring province think that I am a person of some importance.’”

Saint Augustine says that he restrained in himself the desire for miracles or signs, which from time to time troubles even perfect men, in these words:

“From you, my Lord God, to whom I owe humble and simple service, the enemy works against me with how many contrivances of suggestion, so that they may ask for some sign! But I beseech you, by our King and our country Jerusalem, simple and chaste, that just as this consent is far from me, so may it always be farther and farther removed” (*Confessions*, Book X, chapter 35).

Concerning our most holy legislator Benedict, Saint Gregory says:

“When a peasant who had lost his son cried out: ‘Give me back my son, give me back my son,’ and the brothers urged him to yield to the man’s request, the servant of God immediately became very sorrowful and said: ‘Go away, brothers, go away. These things are not ours but those of the holy Apostles. Why do you wish to lay burdens upon us which we cannot bear?’ But the man, driven by excessive grief, persisted in his request and swore that he would not leave unless Benedict raised his son. At last he obtained what he desired” (*Dialogues*, Book II, chapter 32).

You have two other examples in the *Lives of the Fathers*, concerning the anchorites Pimen and Bessarion. But if you will bear with it, reader, you will be glad to hear another story, no less pleasant than serious and relevant to monastic discipline, concerning two boys corrected and punished by an abbot because, through a miracle performed by their simplicity and innocence, they had provided an occasion for vainglory. Sulpicius Severus tells the story as follows:

“A certain solitary who had recently withdrawn to the desert and had built his hut no more than six miles from this monastery was sent bread by the abbot through two boys. The older was fifteen years old; the younger was twelve. As they were returning from there, a serpent of extraordinary size came toward them. At its approach they were not at all frightened. When it came to their feet as though enchanted by spells, it lowered its blue neck. One of the boys seized it by the hand, wrapped it in his cloak, and began to carry it. Then, entering the monastery like a victor, he placed the captured beast before the brothers, after unfastening his cloak, not without a swelling of boastfulness.

“But when the others praised the faith and courage of the children, the abbot, with deeper wisdom, lest their youthful age become insolent, restrained both with rods. He rebuked them severely for having disclosed what the Lord had worked through them, telling them that the deed had not been the work of their faith but of divine power. They should learn instead to serve God in humility, not to glory in signs and mighty deeds, because awareness of weakness was better than the vanity of virtues.” This is his account (*Dialogues*, Book I, chapter 9).]

For this reason we never saw these works of signs pursued by our Fathers. On the contrary, although they possessed them through the grace of the Holy Spirit, they never wished to exercise them unless perhaps extreme and unavoidable necessity compelled them.

## CHAPTER III  
### On the Dead Man Raised by Abbot Macarius

As we remember, a dead man was also raised by Abbot Macarius, who was the first to find a dwelling in the Scetian desert.

[Note: Elsewhere called the Scythian or Scetian desert; it has been discussed more fully in several places. Sozomen, in the passage cited above, writes that both Macariuses presided with the highest distinction over monasteries situated in the solitude of Scete and on the mountain there. Yet it is not surprising if this Egyptian elder was the first to discover a habitation there, as is said here. Palladius also writes (*Lausiac History*, XIX) that Macarius of Alexandria came to the Great Macarius, who was in Scete; and he adds a pleasant anecdote concerning Macarius’ name, its fine allusion, and the resulting benefit:

“Once, when both were about to cross the Nile, it happened that they boarded a very large ferry. Two tribunes, with great pomp and equipment, also boarded it. When the tribunes saw them clothed in old rags and sitting in a corner, they judged that humble and meager mode of life blessed. One of the tribunes said to them: ‘Blessed are you who mock the world.’ Macarius, who was urbane, replied: ‘We indeed have mocked the world; but the world mocks you. Know that you have said this not of your own accord, but prophetically. For we are both called Macarii, that is, blessed.’ The man was pierced by his words; when he came home, he took off his clothes, chose to live a solitary life, and gave many alms.” Thus there.

[Note: This miracle is also related by Palladius (in the passage cited above) and Nicephorus (Book IX, chapter 14), besides Sozomen cited above. The same story appears in Evagrius, or rather Rufinus, in the *Lives of the Fathers* (Book II, chapter 28), described at length but with some variation and distinction that it will be useful to note here. Speaking of Macarius, he says:

“They also said that on one occasion a certain Hieracite heretic came to him—a kind of heresy found in Egypt. By great skill in speaking this man disturbed many of the brothers dwelling in the desert, and he dared even in Macarius’ presence to assert the perversity of his faith. When the elder resisted and contradicted him, the man evaded his simpler words by crafty arguments. But when the saint saw the brothers’ faith endangered, he said: ‘What need is there for us to contend in words to the overthrow of our hearers? Let us go out to the tombs of the brothers who have preceded us in the Lord; and let everyone know that the faith of whichever of us the Lord grants to raise a dead man from the tomb is approved by God.’ This proposal pleased all the brothers present. They went to the tombs, and Macarius urged the Hieracite to call forth the dead man in the Lord’s name. But he said: ‘You, lord, who proposed it, call him first.’ Macarius prostrated himself in prayer before the Lord; when he had prayed sufficiently, he raised his eyes and said: ‘Lord, show which of us two holds the right faith by raising this dead man.’ Having said this, he called by name a brother who had recently been buried. When the man answered from the tomb, the brothers immediately approached, removed what had been laid upon him, and, after unbinding the wrappings with which he had been bound, brought him alive out of the tomb. When the Hieracite saw this, he was stunned and took to flight. All the brothers pursued him and drove him beyond the boundaries of that land.’ Thus Rufinus. Although his account agrees with our Author concerning the miracle of the dead man raised, it differs considerably in the rest of the narrative; let the reader judge which deserves greater credence.]

[Note: That Egyptian elder mentioned above (Sozomen, Book III, chapter 13). As can be gathered from Sozomen, who, while discussing the two Macariuses, explicitly and by name attributes the miracle narrated here to Macarius the Egyptian, assigning it to him on the basis of common report. He writes of him:

“Macarius the Egyptian is reported to have brought a dead man back to life, so that he could persuade a man who held the contrary opinion that there would be a resurrection of the dead. He lived for approximately ninety years, sixty of which he spent in the desert. As soon as, while still a young man, he devoted himself to the monastic and strict discipline, he excelled in it to such a degree that the monks called him *paidariogérōn* (παιδαριογέρων), that is, ‘a young man in the manner of an old man’ [or: ‘an aged child’], because he displayed an old man’s gravity. When he had reached his fortieth year, he was ordained a presbyter; the other was ordained a presbyter much later,” and so forth.

The memory of this Macarius is recorded in the ecclesiastical calendars on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February, in these words: “In Egypt, Saint Macarius, abbot, famous for the life and miracles of the blessed Anthony’s disciple” (*Roman Martyrology*). Gennadius also numbers him among ecclesiastical writers (*On Illustrious Men*, chapter 10), and in the *Lives of the Fathers* he is called the father of fifty thousand monks (Book I, *Life of Posthumius*, chapter 7).

As for the name, *Macharius* is also printed incorrectly in Plantin. It should be written without aspiration, as Ciaconius correctly noted. In Greek it is μακάριος (*makários*), a word meaning “blessed,” as is well known. See the following note.]

For when a certain heretic, who followed the perfidy of Eunomius,

[Note: Eunomius was an exceedingly wicked heresiarch, mentioned elsewhere as well (*Conference* 7, chapter 32). Under the emperor Valens, according to Suidas, he was a supporter of Arius, asserting not only with Arius that the Son of God was a creature, but also blasphemously maintaining that the Holy Spirit was a creature of the Son. Saint Basil and Didymus wrote distinguished works against him. The First Council of Constantinople, assembled against him and Macedonius, condemned both. See Baronius, volumes III and IV of the *Annals*.]

attempted by dialectical art to undermine the integrity of the Catholic faith and had already deceived a great multitude of people, the blessed Macarius, at the request of Catholic men who were deeply distressed by the ruin caused by so great a subversion, came to free the simplicity of all Egypt from the shipwreck of unbelief.

When the heretic attacked him with dialectical skill and attempted to lead him, ignorant of Aristotle, into its thorny thickets,

[Note: That is, the subtleties and sharp points of syllogisms and sophisms, pricking like thorns. The Author appears to have had in mind a passage of Saint Jerome in which, discussing the various errors of pagan philosophers and heretics, he says: “Since all their doctrines are cold and unable to fly, they find for themselves a seat and resting place among the thickets of Aristotle and Chrysippus” (*Commentary on Nahum*, chapter 3).

From this Eunomius derives the proposition: “What was born did not exist before it was born,” and so forth.]

the blessed Macarius, bringing his loquacity to an end with apostolic brevity [Lipsius, in the margin: “authority”], said:

“The kingdom of God is not in speech but in power. Let us therefore go to the tombs, invoke the name of the Lord over the first dead man we find, and, as it is written (2 Corinthians 4), demonstrate our faith by our works, so that the evidence of the true faith may be most clearly declared by his testimony, and that we may prove evident truth not through the empty disputation of words but through the power of signs and through that testimony which cannot deceive.”

When the heretic heard this, he was constrained by shame before the assembled crowd. For the moment he pretended to consent to the proposed condition and promised that he would be present the next day. But on the following day, while everyone was waiting and those most eager for the spectacle had gathered at the appointed place, he fled in terror from the consciousness of his unbelief and immediately departed from all Egypt.

When the blessed Macarius had waited for him until the ninth hour with the people and saw that he had avoided the challenge out of conscience, he took the crowd which had been led astray by him and went to the appointed tombs.

Now the bed of the Nile River has brought about the following Egyptian custom:

[Note: The Nile River in Egypt rises remarkably around the summer solstice, so greatly that, spreading across the whole of Egypt, it irrigates with its waters the land deprived of all rain and covers it with highly fertile mud. Concerning this overflowing of the Nile, its increase, and its causes, see Pliny, Book V, chapter 9.]

Since the entire breadth of the land is covered, for a considerable part of the year, as though by an immense sea, by the customary eruption of the waters, no one then has the opportunity to bury a human body until the waters have receded and their course has run its way,

[Note: This Egyptian custom—namely, preserving the bodies of the dead with pigments or aromatics, in order to repel decay and produce a pleasant smell—is reported by Herodotus, Book II; Diodorus Siculus, Book I; Plato in the *Phaedo*; Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book I; Pliny, Book XI, chapter 37, and Book XVI, chapter 11.

This rite was transferred from the Egyptians to the Jews through the patriarch Joseph. Thus Joseph commanded his physician-servants to embalm his father with aromatics. When they had fulfilled the command, forty days passed, for this was the custom of those who embalmed corpses (Genesis 50).

Likewise, we read that the body of Asa, king of Judah, was buried full of aromatics and ointments prepared by the art of the perfumers (2 Chronicles 16). The Evangelists also report that the same practice was observed in burying Christ’s body (Matthew 26; Mark 14; Luke 21; John 11 and 19). He himself had foretold that this would happen to him in these words: “She has performed a good work upon me; for in pouring this ointment upon my body, she has done it for my burial.” John reports its fulfillment: “Nicodemus came, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds. They took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with aromatics, as is the custom of the Jews in burying.”

Among the Gentiles also, both Greeks and Romans, this custom was practiced: the body of the deceased was first washed with water and then anointed. Concerning the Romans, the verses of Ennius are celebrated:

“Tarquinius’ body a good woman washed and anointed.”

Likewise Virgil, in Book VI of the *Aeneid*:

“Some bring warm water and bronze vessels boiling over the flames…”]

They prepare the body, wash it when cold, and anoint it. Hence those who anointed corpses and stuffed them with aromatics were called *pollinitores*. The Septuagint called them ἐνταφιαστάς (*entaphiastas*, “embalmers”). Concerning them, St Augustine says in Book I of his *Locutions on Genesis* (the final chapter):

“For they themselves do not bury—that is, consign bodies to the earth—which in Greek is not ἐνταφιάσαι (*entaphiasai*), but ἐντάψαι (*entapsai*). Those ἐνταφιασταί therefore perform the work that is done for bodies destined for burial, whether by seasoning, drying, wrapping, or binding them; and in this work the Egyptians excel.”

Thus Augustine. Moreover, among Christians this same custom has prevailed from the time of Christ’s example, especially in the burial of the bodies of holy men. Hence Tertullian says in his *Apologeticus* (chapter 24):

“Let the Sabaeans know that more of their costly and precious merchandise is squandered on the burial of Christians”—that is, that a greater quantity of incense and aromatics is consumed in burying corpses among Christians than in the sacrifices of the nations.

Prudentius likewise describes in the following verses what was customarily done in the Western churches when the bodies of the dead were clothed and anointed:

> Hence the greatest care  
> Is bestowed upon the tombs; hence  
> The final honor receives  
> The limbs released from life  
> And adorns the funeral procession.  
> It is customary to spread over them  
> Linen shining with bright whiteness;  
> And, sprinkled with myrrh,  
> The body is preserved by Sabaean medicine.

[Col. 0998C] St Gregory likewise states in his *Commentary on the Song of Songs* (chapter 11) that the bodies of the dead were seasoned with myrrh so that they would not decay. Finally, the Benedictine monk and historian Aimoinus reports that the bodies of the dead were carefully anointed and seasoned with aromatics, Book IV, chapter 33. See Onuphrius, *On the Rites of Burial*.

[Col. 0998C] but the bodies of the dead, embalmed with fragrant spices, are laid away in more elevated chambers.

[Note: [Col. 0998C] That is, in more elevated caves, removed from the danger of flooding. Among the Romans also, it was considered sacrilegious for the buried dead to “float”; indeed, if the remains of the buried were touched by the force of a river, it was permissible, after consulting the pontiff, to transfer them elsewhere. Book I of the *Codex*, “On Religious Places and Funeral Expenses.” Hence in former times uncultivated, rocky, and very arid fields were purchased by law for burying bodies; concerning this, see Cicero, *On the Laws*, Book II. Siculus Flaccus, *On the Conditions of Lands*, says: “In rocky and barren places, even in the midst of estates, they make tombs.” Sidonius Apollinaris, Book I, Letter 8, lists among the disadvantages of the soil of Ravenna: “The living thirst; the buried float.” Isidore, Book XV of the *Etymologies*, chapter 11: “Among our ancestors,” he says, “the powerful were buried either beneath mountains or in mountains.” From this arose the practice of building pyramids over corpses or placing enormous columns there. Lucan, Book VIII:

> And let the ashes of kings rest beneath a raised mountain.

Virgil, Book VI of the *Aeneid*:

> The pious Aeneas raises a tomb  
> Of enormous mass for the man, and beneath an artificial mountain  
> Places his arms, his oar, and his trumpet.

Moreover, it is equally clear that it was customary among both Egyptians and Jews to bury the dead in chambers or excavated, vaulted caves: first from Genesis, chapter 23, where Abraham is said to have purchased from Ephron the Hittite a double cave for burying his wife Sarah; and then from the Gospel, where Joseph is said to have placed Jesus’ body “in his own new tomb, which he had hewn out in the rock” (Matthew 27). That other Hebrews likewise customarily did the same, when their means allowed it, is shown by what St Epiphanius (*Heresies*, Book III) relates in these words:

“They lead the wretched young man after sunset to the nearby *tumbae*—for that is what they call tombs—namely, caves excavated and constructed in the rocks, and so forth.”

Such caves were called *cryptae* by the Romans; during the time of persecution, the bodies of martyrs were hidden in them. From these caves the bodies of the holy martyrs were brought forth, whose churches of the Society of Jesus have recently enriched our Belgium. See Baronius, *Martyrology*, under 3 January.]

For the soil of that land, drenched with perpetual intoxication, prevents the work of burial.

[Note: [Col. 0998C] Here *solum* is a noun, meaning “earth” or “soil.” The sentence should therefore be construed as follows: “The soil of that land, drenched with perpetual intoxication, prevents the work of burial,” as if he had said: “That land, perpetually drunk or waterlogged, prevents bodies from being buried there.” This also connects with what follows: “For if it receives any corpses”—supply, “the soil of that land.”]

For if it receives corpses that have been buried, it is compelled by the excessive force of the floods to vomit them back onto its surface. When, therefore, the blessed Macarius had stood beside a very ancient corpse, he said:

“O man, if that heretic son of perdition had come here with me, and, while he stood by, I had invoked the name of Christ my God and cried out, would you have risen before those who had almost been overthrown by his deception? Tell me.”

Then the man rose and replied in an assenting voice. The abbot Macarius asked him what he had once been, when he enjoyed this life, what age of mankind he had belonged to, and whether he had known the name of Christ at that time. He answered that he had lived under the most ancient kings and affirmed that in those times he had not even heard the name of Christ.

The abbot Macarius said to him again: “Sleep in peace with the others in your order, to be raised by Christ at the end of time.”

Thus this power and grace of his would perhaps always have remained hidden, insofar as it depended on him, unless the necessity of the entire province, which was in danger, and his complete devotion and sincere love toward Christ had compelled him to perform this miracle. What compelled him to do it was certainly not a desire for glory, but the love of Christ and the advantage of the entire people, as the reading from the Books of Kings also shows that the blessed Elijah did. He requested that fire descend purely from heaven upon the sacrifices placed there, in order to free the faith of the entire people, which was endangered by the tricks of the false prophets (3 Kings 18).

[Note: [Col. 0999C] He says “purely” because there was no fire placed beneath it. Dionysius, however, omitted this word. Others read: “He therefore devoutly requested fire to descend upon the sacrifices placed upon the pyre,” as Cuychius observed.]

## CHAPTER IV. On the miracle that Abbot Abraham performed on a woman’s breasts

[Note: [Col. 0999C] At first encounter with the name of this Abbot Abraham, I suspected that the holy hermit Abraham—or Abrahamius or Abramius—was meant here. Blessed Ephrem described his life in an elaborate discourse, and his memory is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology on 16 March. But after examining the matter more carefully, I easily recognized that the case was otherwise, and that another Abbot Abraham, or Abrahamius, is designated here. The former was a Syrian and a disciple of St Ephrem the Syrian, as Ephrem himself and others testify (St Ephrem, *Testament*; Sozomen, Book III, chapter 15; Nicephorus, Book IX, chapter 16); this one, however, was an Egyptian, as is manifestly gathered from this text. The former remained shut up in a cell for fifty years, as St Ephrem relates; this man came down from the desert of the Thebaid—which is called Upper Egypt—to Lower Egypt in order to reap, as is stated here. This man was surnamed παῖς (*pais*, “boy”) on account of his simplicity and innocence; the former was not. Finally, nothing is found in the fuller account of the acts of that Syrian Abraham, as narrated by Metaphrastes, concerning the miracles attributed here to this Egyptian Abraham. I therefore think that no other Abbot Abraham is to be understood here than the one to whom Cassian assigns the twenty-fourth and final Conference, entitled “On Mortification.” More about him will consequently be said there as it arises.]

What more should I relate about the deeds of Abbot Abraham, who was surnamed παῖς (*pais*), that is, “simple,” because of the simplicity and innocence of his character?

[Note: [Col. 1000B] Ciaconius and others have only: παῖς, “on account of simplicity and innocence.” In fact, παῖς properly signifies not “simple,” but “boy” or “servant,” as is sufficiently well known.
