Yet this name could have been given to the abbot because, on account of his simplicity and innocence, he appeared more like a child than a man; I suppose that he was imitating the Savior’s saying: “Unless you become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5).]

When, during the days of Quinquagesima, he had gone from the desert to Egypt for the purpose of reaping,

[Note: [Col. 1000C] Observe that in former times monks and hermits used to leave their cells or monasteries during the harvest season to reap the crops. Following their example, St Benedict piously admonishes his cenobites that, if the need of the place or poverty should require them to occupy themselves personally with gathering the crops, they should not be distressed: “For then they are truly monks, if they live by the work of their hands, as did our fathers and the apostles.” Here understand “Quinquagesima” as the entire period that we call Eastertide, as we have noted elsewhere. It is treated specifically in Conference 21, entitled “On the Remission of Quinquagesima” (see also Book III of the *Institutes*, chapter 11). But, you may ask, how could the Easter season—that is, the period before Pentecost—be suitable for reaping and appropriate for crops that were already ripe? It certainly could, since not only in Egypt but also in Palestine and other regions the harvest generally occurred in the month of May. For it is sufficiently established from Leviticus and Deuteronomy that among the Jews the harvest customarily took place between Passover and Pentecost (Leviticus 23; Deuteronomy 16). In Egypt, however, as Pliny says, “they sow every month, and wherever there are no summer rains, as in India and Ethiopia”; and elsewhere: “In Egypt barley is harvested in the sixth month after sowing, wheat in the seventh” (Pliny, Book XVII, chapter 18, and Book XVIII, chapter 7). Elsewhere he also writes that two harvests and two summers occur, with a winter midway between them (Book VI, chapter 17).]

and had been constrained by the tearful pleas of a certain woman who was carrying her little child, already wasted away and half-dead from lack of milk,

[Note: [Col. 1000D] *Seminex* means “half-dead,” “half-alive,” or “dying.” Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book I:

> And thus, with boiling water,  
> She softened some of his half-dead limbs.

Sidonius, Book I, Letter 7: “Augustan piety might even reward the half-dead man … with exile.”]

he gave her a cup of water to drink, having impressed upon it the sign of the cross. As soon as she drank it, her already completely dry breasts immediately and wondrously began to overflow with an abundance of milk.

## CHAPTER V. On the healing of a certain lame man, which he likewise performed

[Col. 1001A]

Or again, when he himself was proceeding to a village, he was surrounded by crowds of mockers. They jeered at him and pointed out a certain man whose contracted knee had deprived him of the use of his legs for many years, and who crawled about because of his long-standing weakness. They tested him, saying:

“Show us, Abbot Abraham, if you are a servant of God, and restore this man to his former health, so that we may believe that the name of Christ whom you worship is not vain.”

Then he immediately invoked the name of Christ, bent down, seized the man’s withered foot, and pulled it. At once, through the pulling, the dry and crooked knee was straightened, and the use of his legs, which his long infirmity had already caused him to forget, was restored. He departed joyfully.

## CHAPTER VI. That each person’s merit should not be judged by miracles

These men therefore claimed no credit for themselves on account of the power of such miracles, because they confessed that these things were performed not by their own merit but by the mercy of the Lord. In their admiration of miracles, they rejected human glory in the words of the apostles:

“Men and brothers, why do you marvel at this? Or why do you stare at us as though by our own power or authority we had made this man walk?” (Acts 3).

[Note: [Col. 1001B] Thus Paul and Barnabas, when the citizens of Lystra wished to offer them divine honors because they had healed a lame man, leaped into the crowd after tearing their garments and cried out: “Men, what are you doing? We also are mortal human beings like you,” and so forth (Acts 14).]

They held that no one should be praised for God’s gifts and miracles, but rather for the fruits of his own virtues, which are produced by the diligence of the mind and the excellence of his actions. For, as has already been said above (chapter 1),

[Note: [Col. 1001B] It has been established by many examples and authorities from Scripture that wicked people—that is, people bound by mortal guilt, though still believers—can cast out demons and perform other miracles signified by such powers, and that they have often done so. After the Lord had departed from Saul, Saul persecuted the innocent David; yet when he came among a band of prophets, the Spirit of the Lord came upon him and he prophesied with the other prophets (1 Samuel 19). Hence the proverb arose: “Is Saul also among the prophets?” (Matthew 10). Caiaphas, too, an impious man, prophesied, “because he was high priest that year” (John 11). Judas also performed miracles while he believed in Christ and adhered to him: for he received power together with the other apostles and rejoiced with them that demons were subject to him (Luke 10); and yet he was a thief and kept the money box (John 12).

And, as St Jerome seems to think, he was already then considering his betrayal in his mind. The same is clearly gathered from Christ’s words: “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons?’” and so forth (Matthew 7). He does not answer that they are lying or speaking falsely, as he would have answered if they had not truly prophesied, cast out demons, or performed true miracles; instead he says only: “I never knew you.” This means the knowledge of approval, as theologians call it.

Finally, Paul clearly shows that miracles can be performed by faith without charity when he says: “If I have all faith, so that I could move mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing,” and so forth (1 Corinthians 13). Hence this abbot rightly assigned above (chapter 1 of this Conference) a second cause of such signs or healings: “When, for the edification of the Church, or because of the faith of those who bring their sick to us, or of those who are to be healed, the power of healing proceeds even from sinners and the unworthy.”

But here he says something more: that people corrupt in mind and reprobate in matters of faith—that is, unbelievers, such as Jews, pagans, and heretics—often, that is, very frequently, cast out demons in the name of the Lord and perform very great miracles; and that at the end of the world they will say: “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name?” and so forth. This must indeed be understood soundly and, as the saying goes, with a grain of salt. For many examples establish that true miracles have also been performed through unbelieving people, as Chrysostom teaches (*Homily 25 on Matthew*) and Jerome teaches in his *Commentary on Matthew*. Balaam, for example, otherwise a false and unbelieving prophet, uttered a distinguished prophecy concerning Christ and his birth. And the Lord’s words, “Many will say on that day,” and so forth, can be referred not only to believers but also to unbelievers, as the same authorities testify.

Thus wicked and unbelieving people can sometimes, after invoking the name of Christ or divine power, cast out demons and perform other miracles, if God deigns to use their ministry or to cooperate with them as instruments, for their own benefit or that of others, or to manifest his glory and power—provided that they do not direct or presume to use this for confirming their own error or false doctrine, as was said above.

Thus even Julian the Apostate, by making the sign of the cross, suddenly drove away demons, as Gregory of Nazianzus testifies (*Oration 1 against Julian*), as do the *Ecclesiastical Histories* (Theodoret, Book III, chapter 3; Sozomen, Book V, chapter 2). Epiphanius (*Heresy 30*) also relates concerning Joseph, a Jewish man, that although he did not yet believe, he freed a demon-possessed man in the name of Jesus. Another Jew, mentioned by Gregory the Great (*Dialogues*, Book III, chapter 7), was lying in the temple of Apollo, where demons had gathered. When they discovered that he was signed with the cross, they immediately fled, crying: “Woe, woe! An empty vessel, but sealed.”

[Col. 1002C] Since true miracles are certain divine testimonies, according to the passage in Hebrews 2, “God also bearing witness with signs and wonders and various powers” (for God uses miracles as a seal, in testimony to and confirmation of the truth, just as kings and others use a seal affixed to letters to establish credibility), it is impossible for a Jew, a heretic, or any other unbeliever to perform a true miracle or cast out demons in order to establish and confirm falsehood—for the latter can also be counted among miracles.

It follows that neither heretics, whose sole concern is to establish and confirm the erroneous doctrine they profess, nor Antichrist and his false prophets and false apostles have ever performed, or will perform, any miracle—although heretics have often attempted to do so. Thus the Apostle rightly declared all the signs and wonders of Antichrist to be false or lying signs that would occur (1 Thessalonians 2). Concerning this, see above.

Yet one might object with the miracle of Paul, bishop of the Novatians, which Socrates relates in these words (Book VII, chapter 17):

“A certain Jewish impostor, pretending to be a Christian, had been baptized repeatedly; by this deception he had amassed a great deal of money. After he had fraudulently duped people from various sects and had no one left upon whom to impose, he finally came to Paul, bishop of the Novatians. He said that he was burning with a great desire to receive baptism and begged to obtain it through Paul’s hand.

“Paul approved his intention; but he said that he would not give him baptism until he had been instructed in the articles of faith and had spent several days in fasting. The Jew, compelled to fast against his will, pressed him insistently to grant him baptism.

“Since Paul did not wish to offend a man who was requesting baptism so earnestly by delaying him, he prepared the things necessary for baptism. After purchasing a white garment for him and ordering the baptismal basin to be filled with water, he led the Jew there in order to baptize him. But all the water, by a certain divine power that could not be seen or perceived by the eyes, suddenly disappeared.

“Since neither the bishop nor the others who were present carefully considered how this had happened, they supposed that the water had flowed out through a hole at the bottom of the basin, through which they customarily drained the water on other occasions. They therefore filled the baptismal basin again from the beginning, after carefully sealing all the holes in it. But when the Jew was led into the baptismal basin a second time, the water again completely vanished.

“Paul then said: ‘Man, either you are playing the part of an impostor, or you have received baptism without knowing it.’

“When many people had gathered there because of the miracle, someone happened to recognize the Jew by his face and had seen him baptized earlier by Atticus, bishop of Constantinople.”

This miracle was performed through Paul, the Novatian bishop. Thus far Socrates—and Socrates himself was a Novatian.

In response to this miracle being brought against him, Cardinal Bellarmine teaches that it was not a miracle of Novatian error but of true baptism. This, he says, is clear from the fact that Socrates immediately adds that the Jew was soon recognized as having already been baptized according to the Catholic rite by Atticus, bishop of Constantinople. Therefore, because God did not wish a baptism rightly received in the Church to be mocked, he did not permit the impostor Jew to be baptized a second time by a heretical bishop. Thus Bellarmine, *On the Marks of the Church*, chapter 14.

See more, if desired, in Baronius, volume four of the *Annals* (in the year of Christ 419, at the end). There he teaches that this account by Socrates, a Novatian, is not free from suspicion of falsehood. Finally, he concludes that the miracle—if it is believed to have been genuine—served rather to confirm Catholic truth than to glorify Paul’s merits, whom Socrates adorns with praise.

So much for them. But I thought it appropriate to add here, from Nicephorus, what they omitted and what agrees with this passage. After recounting the same story, he says:

“I have not related this incident merely in passing, but so that we may know that divine grace very often displays itself even among the unworthy, without thereby suffering any harm. Most worthy of admiration, however, is that grace which manifests itself in such varied ways through new events, both through the worthy and sometimes also, when necessity requires it, through the unworthy.”

This is what Nicephorus says. From what has been stated, it can easily be gathered to what extent these words are true or false. By “the unworthy,” he seems here to mean those whom we earlier called wicked and unbelieving. By “divine grace,” he means the grace of miracles, as is clear from what precedes.]

people corrupt in mind and reprobate in matters of faith cast out demons in the name of the Lord and perform very great miracles. When the apostles complained about these people and said, “Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we forbade him because he does not follow us,” Christ nevertheless replied to them at that time: “Do not forbid him; for whoever is not against you is for you” (Luke 9).

Yet he testifies that when they say at the end, “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name perform many miracles?” he will answer them: “I never knew you; depart from me, workers of iniquity” (Matthew 7).

And for this reason he also warns those to whom he himself has granted this glory of signs and miracles as a reward for holiness, so that they may not become proud of them, saying: “Do not rejoice because the demons are subject to you; rejoice rather because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10).

## CHAPTER VII. That the power of spiritual gifts consists not in miracles but in humility

[Col. 1004A]

Finally, the very author of all signs and miracles, when he summoned his disciples to be instructed in his teaching, clearly showed what his true and especially chosen followers ought to learn from him. “Come,” he says,

> [Note: A similar saying of St. Augustine’s is widely known and often repeated by preachers, in Sermon 10 *On the Words of the Lord*: “Learn from me—not to fashion the world, not to create all visible and invisible things, not to work miracles in the world itself and raise the dead, but: because I am meek and humble in heart” (*On Holy Virginity*, ch. 35). Elsewhere Augustine, reflecting on the same saying, exclaims in amazement: “Have all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden in you been reduced to this, that we should learn this great thing from you: that you are meek and humble in heart? Is it really so great a thing to be small, that it could not be learned at all unless it were done by you, who are so great? It certainly is; for the soul finds no rest otherwise, unless the restless swelling by which it was great in its own eyes—when it was not sound before you—has been dispersed,” and so forth. This is a most beautiful passage and well worth reading.]

“and learn from me”—certainly not how to drive out demons by heavenly power, not how to cleanse lepers, not how to give sight to the blind, not how to raise the dead. For even if I perform these things through some of my servants, human nature cannot intrude upon God’s praises, nor can the minister and servant claim any share for himself in what belongs to divine glory alone. “But you,” he says, “learn this from me, because I am meek and humble in heart” (Matthew 11).

For this is something that everyone can generally learn and practice.

> [Note: St. Augustine evades the pagans’ objection in this way: “Why,” they ask, “are the miracles which you proclaim to have happened not performed now?” I could indeed say that they were necessary before the world believed, in order that the world might believe. Whoever still seeks wonders in order to believe is himself a great wonder, since, while the world believes, he does not believe (*City of God*, book 22, ch. 8). He nevertheless adds, and in that entire chapter relates, many miracles of healings that occurred even in his own time, although they were not known to everyone, through the merits and prayers of the saints. And in *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 79: “For this reason,” he says, “these things are not granted to all the saints, lest the weak be deceived by a most harmful error, supposing that greater gifts are present in such deeds than in works of righteousness, by which eternal life is obtained.” St. Gregory, in *Homily 29 on the Gospels*, explaining Christ’s words, “These signs will accompany those who believe,” and so forth, asks: “My brothers, do you not believe because you do not perform these things? But these were necessary at the beginning of the Church. To make the multitude of believers grow in faith, it had to be nourished by miracles; for when we plant shrubs, we pour water upon them only until we see that they have become established in the soil; once they have taken root, the watering stops.” Hence Paul says: “Tongues are for a sign, not to believers but to unbelievers” (1 Corinthians 14). We have yet to consider more subtly these signs and miracles.

“For holy Church daily performs spiritually what it then performed bodily through the apostles. For when its priests, through the grace of exorcism, lay hands upon believers and repel the evil spirits that claim to dwell in their minds, what else are they doing but driving out demons? And when the faithful, having abandoned the worldly speech of their former life, give voice to the holy mysteries and, as far as they can, proclaim the praises and power of their Creator, what else are they doing but speaking in new tongues? When by their good exhortations they remove wickedness from the hearts of others, they take up serpents. And when they hear poisonous counsels but are not drawn into evil action, they drink what is deadly, yet it does them no harm. Whenever they see their neighbors weakened in good works, they hasten to their aid with all their strength and strengthen their lives by the example of their own conduct. When those neighbors falter in their own actions, what else do they do but lay hands upon the sick so that they may be well?

“These miracles are better insofar as they are more spiritual: through them it is not bodies but souls that are raised. Therefore, dearest brothers, if you wish, you perform these signs by God’s authority. For the life that those who perform the outward signs obtain cannot be gained through those signs. Those bodily miracles sometimes display holiness, but they do not produce it. These spiritual miracles, however, which take place in the mind, do not display the virtue of life but produce it. The wicked can possess the former; only the good can enjoy the latter. Do not, then, brothers, love signs that may be shared with the reprobate, but love the miracles of charity and piety that we have just mentioned. They are the safer precisely because they are hidden, and the reward they receive from the Lord is greater in proportion as their glory among human beings is less.”

Thus far St. Gregory.]

But the working of signs and miracles is neither always necessary nor granted to everyone.

> [Note: In a few words he has gathered together three praises of humility, and the principal ones at that:  
>   
> 1. That it is the mother and teacher of all virtues. Thus St. Gregory says in the twenty-third book of the *Moralia* (ch. 13): “True teaching strives both to speak of humility, which is the teacher of all and mother of the virtues, and to display it by living, so that among the disciples of truth it may express it more by deeds than by words.”  
>   
> 2. That it is the foundation of the heavenly and spiritual building. Apart from other passages that we have cited elsewhere, Chrysostom says in his *Homily on Genesis* (35): “Let us preserve moderation everywhere, and let us lay humility beneath our good works as a foundation, so that we may safely build the virtues upon it. For virtue is nothing unless it possesses humility joined to it. Whoever lays this foundation correctly will be able to raise the structure to whatever height he wishes. This is an unconquerable tower; it contains the whole building and does not permit it to be thrown down either by the violence of winds, the assault of rains, or the force of storms, but makes it inaccessible to every ambush and unconquerable, as though it had been fastened together from adamant.” St. Bernard expresses the same thought in his book *On Consideration*: “Humility is a most precious and good foundation; upon it the entire spiritual building is constructed and grows into a holy temple in the Lord.”  
>   
> 3. That it is the Savior’s own magnificent gift. Hence St. Gregory says in the thirty-fourth book of the *Moralia*: “How great is the power of humility, for the sole purpose of truly teaching which he who is immeasurably great became small even unto his passion.” And in the following chapter: “Just as pride is the clearest sign of the reprobate, so humility, conversely, is the sign of the elect. When it is recognized how each person relates to humility, it is discovered under which king he serves. For each person bears, as it were, a title of his work by which he readily shows under whose authority he serves.” St. Augustine has something similar in *The City of God*, book 14 (ch. 13), where he teaches that the two cities—namely, the city of God and the city of the devil, that is, the society of the righteous and the wicked—are chiefly distinguished from one another by these two marks, as by tokens: humility and pride.]

Humility, therefore, is the teacher of all virtues; it is the firmest foundation of the heavenly building; it is the Savior’s own magnificent gift. Whoever follows the meek Lord—not through the exaltation of signs but through the virtue of patience and humility—performs all the miracles that Christ performed without danger of conceit.

But whoever desires to command unclean spirits, grant gifts of healing to the sick, or display some wondrous sign before the people, even though he invokes Christ’s name in his exhibitions, is nevertheless alien to Christ, because he does not follow the teacher of humility with a humble mind.

For even when he was returning to the Father and, so to speak, drawing up a testament, he left this commandment to his disciples: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (John 13). Immediately he added: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” He did not say, “if you perform signs and miracles in the same way,” but “if you have worthy love for one another.” It is certain that only the meek and humble can preserve such love.

Therefore our elders never considered those monks to be good or free from the disease of vainglory who publicly professed themselves exorcists,

> [Note: *Exorkizō* (ἐξορκίζω), that is, “I adjure.” Hence exorcists are adjurers, who drive out unclean spirits from bodies that are afflicted or possessed by adjuring them in the Lord’s name. Concerning them St. Augustine says in *The City of God*, book 10 (ch. 22): “By true piety, the people of God drive out by exorcism the aerial power that is hostile and opposed to piety, not by appeasing it.” St. Jerome says that this is signified by the child who, in Isaiah, draws a serpent out of a rocky hole with his hand.

> It should also be noted that from the beginning there were two forms of power in the Church for driving out demons, and accordingly two classes of exorcists. One was communicated only to clergy or ecclesiastical persons through ecclesiastical ordination. Hence exorcist is called the third of the minor orders, an order certainly celebrated and frequently praised by the Fathers; from it they often establish the truth of our faith against its adversaries, as Justin in his *Dialogue with Trypho*, Tertullian in *To Scapula*, Lactantius in book 2 of the *Divine Institutes*, and Cyprian in his letter *To Demetrianus*. The other was also common to laypeople, that is, to those initiated into no order. This latter was itself twofold.

> The first was general, such as most of the faithful are known to have received in the very beginnings of the Church from Christ’s general promise: “These signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will drive out demons” (Mark 16). It remained in force in the Church as long as it seemed necessary for the propagation and confirmation of the faith. Hence Tertullian writes that demons were driven out even by soldiers and that parents were accustomed to exorcise their children (*On the Crown of the Soldier*, ch. 11; *On Idolatry*, ch. 11).

> The other was special: it was granted to certain people as a sign of exceptional holiness or for the edification of the Church, through a particular gift. The Apostle includes this gift among the other gifts of the Holy Spirit, or freely given graces, as we have said, under the gift of healings or the working of miracles (1 Corinthians 12). In this category many holy anchorites especially distinguished themselves, although they were laymen and consecrated by no ecclesiastical order; among them were Antony, Paul the Simple, Hilarion, and others.

> Such were the monks in question here. They repeatedly abused this gift and power of exorcising for display and empty glory. Although laymen, they publicly claimed the office of exorcists and freely exercised it before others in order to hunt after a reputation for holiness. Nothing prevents some of them from having been clerics and initiated into orders; for, conversely, holy men, as has been said, strongly avoided this practice unless compelled either by charity or by the persistence of those who entreated them, for the reasons explained above (ch. 2).

> Thus St. Benedict sent an energumen—a demonically afflicted person—who had been brought to him, to St. Remigius, as Hincmar records in his *Life*. Likewise, when St. Lawrence Justinian, patriarch of Venice, was asked to drive a demon out of a woman, he replied: “Do not ask me to do what I cannot do.” Gregory of Langres, himself a most holy bishop, answered in the same way, as Gregory of Tours testifies.]

and who, amid crowds of admirers, proclaimed with the most boastful display the gift that they had either deserved or presumed to possess. But it was all in vain.

> [Note: This saying is absent both from the Hebrew text and from the Greek Septuagint, as Father Delrio noted (*On Proverbs*). It is nevertheless cited by Clement of Alexandria in book 1 of the *Stromata* and by St. Augustine in book 3 *Against Cresconius*, chapter 9, in these words: “Whoever relies on falsehoods feeds the winds,” that is, becomes food for evil spirits. The prophet Hosea alluded to the same idea in chapter 12: “Ephraim feeds on wind and pursues the east wind; all day he multiplies lies and desolation.” St. Jerome interprets “to feed on wind” as “to deceive oneself with vain hope.” Rupertus explains it as being puffed up by the spirit of pride.]

“For whoever relies on lies will feed the winds; and that same person pursues flying birds” (Proverbs 10). Without doubt, what is said in Proverbs will happen to them:

> [Note: The Vulgate reads: “Clouds and wind, but no rain; so is a boastful man who does not fulfill his promises.” The Chaldean paraphrase is more consonant with it: “As the day of clouds and wind in which there is no rain, so is the man who boasts in a false gift.” St. Jerome teaches that this verse also contains what the Apostle says: “Having the appearance of piety but denying its power” (2 Timothy 3).]

“As winds and clouds and rains are most conspicuous, so is the man who boasts in a false gift” (Proverbs 25).

And therefore, if anyone has performed one of these things before us, he ought to be praiseworthy among us not because of our admiration for his signs but because of the adornment of his character. We must inquire not whether demons are subject to him, but whether he possesses the members of charity that the Apostle describes.

> [Note: Those words are: “Charity is patient, charity is kind,” and so forth (1 Corinthians 13). Fifteen functions of virtue are expressed there, and perfect charity is composed and completed as though by these members.]

## CHAPTER VIII  
### That it is more wondrous to drive vices from oneself than demons from another

> [Col. 1007B]

> [Note: In other words he expressed the same thought, concluding this conference as follows (last chapter): “For it is a greater virtue and a more sublime grace to extinguish the inward lust of the flesh than, by the Lord’s sign and the power of the Most High, to subdue the wickedness of demons rushing in from outside, or to drive them from possessed bodies by invoking the divine name.” The words that Abbot Chaeremon discussed concerning God’s wondrous works in his saints respond most aptly and harmoniously to this statement, in Conference 12, chapter 12. Among other things he says:

> “Who would not marvel at the Lord’s works in himself when he has seen the insatiable gluttony of the belly, and the costly and destructive luxury of the appetite, so restrained in himself that he scarcely ever takes even a small and most worthless amount of food? Who would not be astonished at God’s works when he has felt that fire of lust, which he formerly believed to be natural and almost unquenchable, grow so cool that he does not feel himself stirred even by the body’s simplest movement? How could anyone not tremble before the Lord’s power when he has seen men once savage and ferocious, who were provoked to the utmost frenzy of anger by even the gentlest obedience of their subjects, pass into such gentleness that they are now moved by no injuries and even rejoice with the greatest magnanimity when injuries are inflicted?

> “And again, in the following chapter: ‘This, then, is the wondrous work of God: for a human being made of flesh, while placed in the flesh, to reject carnal desires; and amid such variety of circumstances and assaults to preserve one disposition of soul, remaining unmoved amid every change of things that befall him.’”

> Thus far Chaeremon. Blessed Gregory writes similarly in book 3 of the *Dialogues*, chapter 17. There he also teaches that it is a greater miracle to convert a sinner by the word of preaching and the comfort of prayer than to raise a dead man in the flesh. See St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* I–II, question 111, article 5, and question 113, articles 9 and 10.]

And in truth, it is a greater miracle to eradicate the fuel of lust from one’s own flesh than to drive unclean spirits from the bodies of others. It is a more magnificent sign, by the power of patience, to restrain the savage movements of anger than to command the rulers of the air. It is more to expel from one’s own heart the most voracious diseases of sadness than to drive fevers and bodily illnesses from another person. Finally, in many respects it is a more splendid virtue and a more exalted achievement to heal the disorders of one’s own soul than those of another’s body.

> [Note: St. Gregory Nazianzen wrote with complete truth that a disease of the soul is more serious than one of the body to the extent that the soul is superior to the body. “The one,” he says elsewhere, “exists against the will; the other proceeds from the will. The one ends with this life; the other accompanies us when we depart from here. Finally, the one is worthy of pity; the other of hatred—at least among those who possess sound judgment.”]

For to the extent that the soul is more exalted than the flesh, its health is more excellent; and to the extent that its substance is more precious and superior, its ruin is likewise more serious and destructive.

## CHAPTER IX  
### How greatly integrity of life surpasses the working of signs

> [Col. 1008B]

And concerning those healings it is said to the most blessed Apostles:

> [Note: Cyril, quoted by St. Thomas in the *Golden Chain*, asks: “But why, Lord, do you not allow them to rejoice in the honors bestowed by you, when it is written: ‘In your name they will rejoice all day long’ (Psalm 88)?” But the Lord raises them to a greater joy. Hence he adds: “But rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” Thus Cyril.

> Christ therefore does not forbid the disciples to rejoice that demons were subject to them; this was a gift of God, and it is permissible to rejoice in it, provided both the gift itself and the joy are referred to its author. But he teaches that they should rejoice less in this than in the fact that their names were written in heaven. To have one’s name written in heaven means the same as to have it written in the book of life, as Scripture often expresses it in other words (Exodus 32; Psalm 68; Philippians 4; Acts 3).

> The theologians further teach (St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* I, question 24) that people are written in the book of life in two ways: either according to God’s eternal predestination, which cannot be deceived or changed; or according to each person’s present righteousness, which can change. Those written according to the first manner are never erased; those written according to the second may be erased and rewritten, according as the righteous now become unrighteous, and again the unrighteous become righteous.]

“Do not rejoice that the demons are subject to you” (Luke 10).

> [Note: This was emphasized above (ch. 6) in other words, where he says: “Holy men, when performing miracles, claimed nothing for themselves on account of the virtue of such wondrous deeds, because they confessed that these things were accomplished not by their own merit but by the Lord’s mercy, rejecting human glory in their admiration of signs with the words of the Apostles: ‘Men, brothers, why do you marvel at this, or why do you look at us as though by our own virtue or power we had made this man walk?’” (Acts 3).

> Peter used these words after healing, through invocation of the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, the man lame from his mother’s womb, while the people gathered around and were astonished at the miracle. Paul and Barnabas did and proclaimed the same thing among the people of Lystra (Acts 14), as we noted there.

> St. Athanasius confirms the same teaching in the *Life of Antony*, chapter 52, writing: “Did Antony heal by the command of his own power? Did he consider what he had done to be within his own ability? Demons yielded to prayers, not commands, and everything was always accomplished at the naming of Christ our God. Let no wise person attribute the wonder of healings to Antony, but to the Lord Jesus, who, displaying his customary benevolence toward his creatures, now also graciously exercised it through his chosen servant. Antony merely prayed, and the Lord granted everything on account of his way of life.” What Athanasius says here may be said of any other holy man who performs miracles.

> For a fuller understanding of this matter, observe the teaching of St. Thomas in these words (*Summa Theologiae* II–II, question 178, article 1): “It must be said that, just as prophecy extends to all things that can be known supernaturally, so the working of miracles extends to all things that can be done supernaturally. Their cause is the divine omnipotence, which cannot be communicated to any creature. It is therefore impossible that the principle of working miracles should be some habitual quality remaining in the soul. Nevertheless, it can happen that, just as the prophet’s mind is moved by divine inspiration to know something supernaturally, so the mind of one who works miracles is moved to do something to which there follows the effect of a miracle that God produces by his own power.

> “Sometimes this occurs after prayer, as when Peter raised Tabitha from the dead (Acts 9). Sometimes it occurs without a manifest prayer preceding it, but with God acting at the person’s command, as when Peter, by rebuking Ananias and Sapphira for their lies, delivered them over to death (Acts 5). Hence Gregory says in the second book of the *Dialogues* (ch. 30) that the saints sometimes display miracles by power, and sometimes by petition.

> “In either case, however, God is the principal agent. He uses instrumentally either the inward movement of the human being, or his speech, or some outward action, or even bodily contact with a dead body.”

> See Cajetan there. Thus, in Joshua 10, when Joshua said, as though with authority, “Sun, do not move against Gibeon,” it is subsequently added: “There has never been a day like it before or since, when the Lord obeyed the voice of a man.” Thus far St. Thomas.

> It is therefore clear how, according to Gregory, the saints sometimes perform miracles as though by authority and command, although it is established that all miracles are performed by divine power, as has been said. They are said to perform them by authority when, without an immediately preceding manifest prayer, they undertake the miracle at once by a mere command—such as Joshua when he stopped the sun, and Peter when he raised Tabitha, although Peter had first offered prayers; or St. Benedict, who, as Gregory relates above (ch. 31), freed a bound peasant from his chains by a mere glance.]

For it was not their power that performed these things, but the power of the Lord’s name when invoked. For this reason they are warned not to dare claim for themselves any blessedness or glory from this, which is accomplished solely by God’s power and might, but rather from that inner purity of life and heart by which they deserve to have their names inscribed in heaven.

## CHAPTER X  
### The revelation concerning the testing of perfect chastity

And in order to confirm what we have said, whether by the testimonies of the ancients or by divine oracles, let us present more appropriately, in his own words and through his own experience, what the blessed Paphnutius thought either about the admiration of signs or about the grace of purity—or rather, what he learned through an angel’s revelation.

> [Note: We have often discussed this matter, and have observed that, instead of *Pafnutius*, *Paphnutius* should be read, as it appears in the Plantin edition.]

For he had lived for many years under an exceptionally strict discipline, so that he believed himself entirely freed from the snares of carnal desire,

> [Col. 1010A]

because he felt that he had become superior to all the assaults of demons, with whom he had long and openly contended. When holy men arrived, he prepared for them the lentil dish that they call *athera*.

> [Note: On lentils, see the notes at chapter 20 of book 4 of the *Institutes*, or *Institutes for Renunciants*.]

> [Note: *Athēra* or *athara* (ἀθήρα or ἀθάρα), as Ciaconius noted, is according to Hesychius a certain food that the Egyptians make from wheat and milk. For Pliny it is rather a medicinal preparation. He writes: “We said that *olyra* is called *ariuca*; when cooked, it makes a medicine that the Egyptians call *athara*, very useful for infants; adults also smear it on themselves.” Dioscorides says almost the same in book 2, chapter 114.

> St. Augustine—not Jerome, as it was incorrectly printed—in his *Questions on Genesis*, commenting on chapter 45, “And he gave them provisions for the journey,” says: “The word *zeda*, which everyone here has translated with one voice as *episition* (ἐπισιτισμόν), that is, provisions or travel supplies, also occurs in the Psalter. For where our copies read, ‘Blessing I will bless her widow’ (Psalm 131), although in most manuscripts some read *thēran* (θήραν) instead of *widow*—that is, instead of *chēran* (χήραν)—the Hebrew has *zeda*, that is, ‘I will surely bless her provisions.’ Now *thēra* may signify hunting more readily than grain, although it is customary among the Egyptians also to call meal *thēra*, which they now corruptly call *atheran*. Thus Augustine—or whoever was the author of that book.]

When his hand was burned in the oven, as a flame passed over it in the usual manner, he was saddened by what had happened and began silently turning this over in his mind:

“Why does fire not remain at peace with me, when more savage battles with demons have yielded before me? Or how will that unquenchable fire, which examines all merits, allow me to pass through it on that dreadful day of judgment, when this small and temporal fire has not spared me externally?”

While he was burning with thoughts and sadness of this kind, a sudden sleep came upon him. An angel of the Lord appeared and said:

“Why are you sad, Paphnutius, because this earthly fire has not yet been pacified for you,

> [Note: The holy presbyter Ursinus also experienced this. Blessed Gregory relates the story in *Dialogues*, book 4, chapter 11. When Ursinus was seized by a severe fever and was already near death, his sister brought her ear close to his nostrils to discover whether any spirit still remained in him. With what little strength he could summon, he gathered his spirit, raised his voice, and cried out: “Go away from me, woman; the little fire still lives. Take away the straw.” Thus far his story.

> The following passage from the *Lives of the Fathers* points in the same direction (book 5, booklet 10): “They said of a certain old man that for fifty years he had neither eaten bread nor readily drunk water, and he said: ‘I have extinguished fornication, greed, and vainglory.’ When Abbot Abraham heard that he had said these things, he came to him and said: ‘Did you say this?’ And he replied: ‘Yes.’ Abbot Abraham said to him: ‘Behold, you enter your cell and find a woman lying on your mat; can you avoid thinking that she is a woman?’ He said: ‘No, but I resist my thought so that I may not touch that woman.’ Abbot Abraham said: ‘Then you have not killed fornication, for the passion itself lives, though it is bound.’

> “Again, if you are walking along the road and see stones, pieces of pottery, and gold lying among them, can you regard what you see as though it were stones?’ He replied: ‘No, but I resist my thought so that I may not pick them up.’ Abbot Abraham said: ‘Then the passion lives, but is bound.’

> “Abbot Abraham said again: ‘If you hear of two brothers, one of whom loves you and speaks well of you, while the other hates you and slanders you, and both come to you, do you receive them equally?’ He said: ‘No, but I force my soul to treat the one who hates me as well as the one who loves me.’ Abbot Abraham said: ‘Then the passions live, but they are in some manner restrained by holy men.’”

> This is reported somewhat roughly from a Greek author.]

while the agitation of carnal movements still remains in your members and has not yet been thoroughly burned away? As long as their roots live in your marrow, they will not permit this material fire to be peaceful toward you. You will not be able to experience it as harmless unless you have tested by these indications whether all your inward movements have been extinguished within yourself.

“Go and take hold of a naked and exceedingly beautiful virgin. If, while holding her, you feel that the tranquility of your heart remains unmoved and that your carnal passions remain at peace within you, then the gentle and harmless touch of this visible flame will also caress you, like the three youths in Babylon” (Daniel 3).

The old man, struck by such a revelation, did not expose himself to the danger of the divinely indicated test. Instead, he questioned his conscience and examined the purity of his heart. Concluding that the weight of his chastity did not yet equal the weight of this trial, he said:

“It is no wonder that, although the battles with unclean spirits have yielded to me, I still feel the burns of fire, which I had believed inferior to the fiercest battles with demons, raging against me. For it is a greater virtue and a more sublime grace to extinguish the inward lust of the flesh than to subdue, by the Lord’s sign and the power of the Most High, the wickedness of demons rushing in from outside, or to drive them from possessed bodies by invoking the divine name.”

> [Note: In the Lyon edition, *without the Lord* is printed very badly instead of *by the Lord’s sign*, as the other manuscripts and Dionysius the paraphrast have it, and as the truth of the matter requires. The Lord’s sign is the sign of the holy cross, which is customarily used in exorcisms and adjurations of demons through invocation of the divine name.]

Thus far Abbot Nesteros, completing his discourse on the true working of spiritual gifts. As we hurried to the cell of the old man Joseph, which was situated nearly six miles away, he continued to instruct us through his teaching.

# THE SIXTEENTH CONFERENCE, WHICH IS THE FIRST OF ABBOT JOSEPH: ON FRIENDSHIP

> [Col. 1011]

## CHAPTER I

> [Col. 1011C]

The blessed Joseph, whose practices and teachings are now to be disclosed, was one of the three whom we mentioned in the first conference.

> [Note: In the total sequence it is the eleventh; but it is the first of the ten conferences belonging to this second class, which were held with the three anchorites mentioned there: Chaeremon, Nesteros, and this Joseph.]

He was a man of very distinguished family and a leading citizen of his city in Egypt,

> [Note: See above, Conference 14, chapter 4, concerning this city.]

which is called Thmuis. He had been so carefully instructed not only in Egyptian but also in Greek eloquence that, whether speaking to us or to those who had no knowledge at all of Egyptian speech, he did not converse through an interpreter like the others, but argued most elegantly in person.

When he realized that we desired his instruction, he first asked whether we were biological brothers. When he heard from us that we were bound not by bodily but by spiritual brotherhood, and that from the beginning of our renunciation we had always been joined in inseparable fellowship—both in the pilgrimage that each of us had undertaken for the sake of spiritual warfare and in the discipline of the coenobium—he began his discourse as follows.

## CHAPTER II  
### The same old man’s discussion of the faithless kind of friendship
[Note: [Col. 1011C] Besides Aristotle, who enumerated three kinds of friendship [Col. 1011D] (Book VIII of the *Ethics*, chapter 3)—the pleasant, the useful, and the honorable—the ancient Fathers also described various kinds of friendship. Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, Book II, chapter 9, says: “We are taught that there is a threefold kind of friendship. The first kind, and the best and most excellent, is that which proceeds from virtue; for the affection that proceeds from reason is strong. The second, intermediate kind, proceeds from mutual recompense; this kind is suited to fellowship and communication, freely sharing with others and contributing to life. The third we call that which proceeds from habit.”

Saint Chrysostom, more clearly, in his commentary on the Epistle to the Colossians, says: “There are many causes from which friendship arises; and, to omit the shameful ones, [Col. 1012C] because they are evil, and bring forward only the good, some friendships are temporal, some natural, and some spiritual. Temporal friendships arise from a benefit, from sharing a table, a journey, the same craft, the same neighborhood, or other such things. Natural friendships are those of a father toward his son, a son toward his father, [Col. 1012D] a brother toward a brother, a grandson toward his grandfather, a mother toward her children, and a wife toward her husband. These indeed appear to be stronger than the others—appear, I say, because very often they are inferior to them. For in some cases friends have been seen to be more genuinely attached than brothers. Spiritual love, however, surpasses all the others, like a queen possessing dominion over her subjects and conspicuous in splendid attire. For nothing earthly gives rise to it, as happens with the others: it does not arise from habit, benefit, nature, or time, but descends from above, from heaven itself.” This is Chrysostom.

Augustine, Homily 38 among the fifty, says: “Consider what I say about friendship. There are friends [Col. 1013B] through a certain friendship which ought not even to be called friendship, produced as it is by an evil conscience. There are people who commit evil deeds together and therefore seem joined to one another. Apart from that, there is a kind of carnal friendship arising from the habit of living together, conversing, and spending time together, so that a person grieves when he is abandoned by his friend. This is the friendship of habit, not of reason. Even animals possess it. There is also a higher friendship, not of habit but of reason, by which we love a person because of faith and mutual goodwill.”

Cassiodorus likewise, in his book *On Friendship*, distinguishes many kinds of it according to the causes from which it proceeds: “The source and origin [Col. 1013C] of friendship is love, and love is, as it were, the genus in relation to the species. For although love often exists without friendship, friendship never exists without love. Love, then, sometimes derives its cause from the instinct of nature, sometimes from carnal impulse, sometimes from duty, sometimes from reason alone, and very often from reason and affection together.” Thus Cassiodorus, who afterward explains each member of this division at greater length.]

There are many kinds of friendship and companionship, [Col. 1013A] which bind the human race together in a fellowship of affection by various means. In some cases, a recommendation preceding acquaintance first led to intercourse, and afterward to friendship. In others, a certain contract, or [Note: [Col. 1013C] Dionysius’s paraphrase: “An agreement of what is given and received.” An agreement, or pact, is said to be the concurrence of two or more persons in the same decision, or consent, namely, to do or give something, as the text says in Book I of the *Digest*, *On Pacts*. Hence every contract is called a pact in the general sense. An agreement of what is given and received is a certain contract between giver and recipient by which they mutually bind themselves: if the recipient has spent less than he received, the remainder is to be returned to the giver; conversely, if he has spent more than he received, the excess is to be repaid to the recipient. Hence it is elsewhere called an account of expenditure and receipt, concerning which see the end of Book I, *The Buyer*, in the *Digest*, *On Pacts*. Hence also the account-books and records of what was given and received in Cicero’s speech *For Roscius the Comedian*, and Coelius Rhodiginus, Book XII, chapter 21.] an agreement of what was given and received, joined the bonds of affection. Others were tied by the bonds of friendship through the resemblance and sharing involved in business, military service, a craft, or a common discipline. Through this, even savage hearts are so softened toward one another that those who delight in brigandage in forests and mountains and take pleasure in the shedding of human blood embrace and cherish their accomplices in crime.

There is also another kind of affection, joined by the instinct of nature itself and the law of kinship, through which fellow tribesmen, spouses, parents, brothers, and children are naturally preferred to others. This is found not only in the human race but also in all birds and living creatures. For, impelled by natural affection, they protect and defend their chicks or cubs so strongly that they often do not hesitate to expose themselves to danger and death on their behalf. [Col. 1014A]

Finally, even those kinds of beasts, serpents, and birds which intolerable savagery and deadly venom separate and set apart from all others—such as [Note: [Col. 1013D] Some call the basilisk the “little king,” by an equivalent derivation. It is a kind of serpent which, according to Pliny (*Natural History*, Book VIII, chapter 2), is common in the deserts of Africa, no more than twelve fingers in length, with a white mark on its head like a diadem. By its hiss it puts all other serpents to flight. Unlike other serpents, it does not propel its body forward, but walks erect, raised from the middle, killing shrubs and grasses not only by touch but also by its breath.

The monoceros is an animal bearing a single horn; hence it is also called a unicorn (*Isidore, Etymologies*, Book XII, chapter 4). It nevertheless differs from the rhinoceros: the latter bears its horn on the nose, the former on the forehead. Pliny describes it as follows: “The fiercest beast is the monoceros, otherwise resembling a horse in body, with the head of a stag, the feet of an elephant, the tail of a boar, a deep bellow, and a single black horn projecting two cubits from the middle of its forehead. They say that this beast cannot be captured alive.” So he writes. The Fathers, however, generally confuse the monoceros with the rhinoceros (*Jerome’s commentary*, or rather Bede’s, on Job; Isidore, in the same place, chapter 13). For where we read in the Vulgate edition, Job 39, “Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve you?” some read, “Will the monoceros be willing to serve you?” Hence Saint Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XXXI: “This rhinoceros, which in Greek copies is also called monoceros, is said to possess such great strength that it cannot be captured by any skill of hunters,” and so forth.

The gryps, or griffin—whence *gryphes* or *gryphi* in the plural—is a winged quadruped. This species of beast is born in the Hyperborean mountains; in every respect it is like a lion, except that in its wings and face it resembles an eagle, and it is exceedingly hostile to horses (Pliny, Book X, chapter 40; Isidore, above). Hence Virgil says (*Eclogue* 8):

> Let griffins now be joined with horses.]

—basilisks, monoceroses, or griffins, although they are said to be harmful to all by their very appearance, nevertheless remain peaceful and harmless among themselves through the fellowship of their common origin and affection.

But just as all the kinds of affection we have mentioned are common to the wicked and the good, and even to wild beasts and serpents, so it is certain that they cannot continue permanently. For separation of place, temporal forgetfulness, and the interruption caused by a word, a cause, or business dealings frequently break them apart. Just as they are usually acquired through various associations of profit, lust, kinship, or other relationships, so they are dissolved when any occasion for separation intervenes.

## CHAPTER III. From what source indissoluble friendship arises

In all these kinds of friendship, then, [Note: [Col. 1014C] A description of true and perfect friendship, which consists in charity alone—or rather is Christian charity itself, insofar as it includes a certain mutual goodwill and communication, as Saint Thomas teaches (*Summa theologica*, II–II, question 23, article 5). It is called indissoluble and eternal, not because it cannot be lost, but because the person who possesses charity is so disposed toward God and neighbor that he does not wish to be separated from God by any temptation or occasion, nor to abandon his friend in adversity, although, because of the mutability of the human will, he can be led in the opposite direction.

Hence Solomon says: “He who is a friend loves at all times, and a brother is proved in distress” (Proverbs 17; see Delrio on the *Adagia*). Ecclesiasticus also ridicules the temporary friend: “There is a friend according to his season, and he will not remain in the day of trouble” (Ecclesiasticus 6). Saint Jerome says (*Epistle* 41): “Friendship which can cease was never true.” Chrysostom likewise (*Homily 61 on Matthew*): “Those who enter into friendship for perishable and unstable reasons cannot remain joined forever; contempt, loss of money, envy, ambition for glory, or some other such cause will dissolve their friendship and produce division. If its root were spiritual, no worldly thing could uproot it. Certainly that charity which is founded for Christ’s sake is firm, stable, and unconquered; it is shaken neither by slander, dangers, death, nor any other temporal thing. Therefore Paul also said: ‘Charity never fails’” (1 Corinthians 13). “For everything that destroys worldly friendships strengthens spiritual love.” Thus Chrysostom.]

there is one kind of charity that cannot be dissolved, joined neither by the favor of recommendation, nor by the magnitude of services or gifts, nor by any consideration of contract, nor by the necessity of nature, but solely by similarity of virtues. This, I say, is never severed by any circumstances. Not only can intervals of place or time not separate or destroy it; even death itself cannot tear it apart. This is true and unbroken affection, which grows through the mutual perfection and virtue of the friends. Once its covenant has been established, neither variation in desires nor contentious opposition of wills will break it.

Nevertheless, we know many who have undertaken this way and, although they were bound by the most ardent fellowship for the sake of Christ’s charity, were unable to preserve it perpetually and without interruption. For although they relied upon a good beginning in their fellowship, they did not maintain the undertaking they had begun with one and equal zeal. Their affection was therefore temporary, because it was preserved not by equal virtue in both but by the patience of one. Although one may retain it magnanimously and without fatigue, it must nevertheless be broken by the faintheartedness of the other. For however great the endurance of the strong may be by which the weaknesses of those who seek the health of perfection too lukewarmly are supported, the infirm themselves cannot bear it.

They have causes of agitation implanted within them, which do not allow them to remain quiet. Thus those who are afflicted by bodily illness are accustomed to attribute the disgust of their stomach and their infirmity to the negligence of cooks or attendants; and however solicitously their servants may attend them, they nevertheless ascribe to the healthy the causes of their agitation, not perceiving that these causes are present in themselves because of the defect of their health. [Col. 1016B]

Therefore, [Note: [Col. 1015B] For friendship to be firm, constant, and indissoluble, two things are required.

First, devotion to virtue. The first foundation of friendship must be laid in virtue. Saint Ambrose, *On Duties*, Book III, chapters 15 and 16: “He cannot be a friend to a man who has been unfaithful to God. Friendship is the guardian of piety.” Saint Jerome to Paulinus (*Epistle* 103): “That is the true bond, joined by the glue of Christ, which is brought about not by the advantage of domestic affairs, not merely by bodily presence, not by crafty and flattering adulation, but by the fear of God and devotion to the divine Scriptures.” Saint Augustine to Macedonius (*Epistle* 52; see more below, chapter 5): “No one can truly be a friend of a human being unless he has first been a friend of truth itself.”

Nor were the pagan philosophers unaware of this. Aristotle, in Book VIII of the *Ethics*, chapters 3 and 8, teaches that true and perfect friendship is that which is established solely for the sake of virtue, not advantage or pleasure. Laelius speaks thus in Cicero’s *On Friendship*: “This is my first conviction: friendship cannot exist except among the good.” By “good” he means those who conduct and live their lives so that their faithfulness, integrity, justice, and generosity are approved, and in whom there is no greed, lust, or recklessness. A little later he says: “Without virtue friendship cannot exist in any way.”

The second necessary element in friendship is a certain equality or parity of virtues. If virtue excels in one person and is lacking in another, friendship will easily be dissolved on that side, as this abbot demonstrates at length, in agreement with both the Fathers and the philosophers. Saint Ambrose, in the passage cited above, says: “Friendship is a teacher of equality, so that the superior presents himself as equal to the inferior, and the inferior to the superior. There cannot be friendship between unequal characters.” Saint Jerome, in his commentary on Micah, chapter 7: “Friendship either accepts equals or makes them. Where there is inequality—one person’s superiority and another’s subjection—there is not so much friendship as flattery.” Hence we also read elsewhere: “Let a friend be of the same soul.” And the Lyric poet, praying for his friend, says: “Preserve him as half of my soul.”

Aristotle, in the passage cited, says: “Perfect friendship is that in which good men endowed with equal virtue are joined and united to one another.” Finally, Cicero, whose book is *On Friendship*, entitled *Laelius*, says: “Just as those who are superior in friendship ought to make themselves equal to their inferiors, so inferiors ought not to allow themselves to be surpassed by their friends in talent, fortune, or rank. Unequal characters produce unequal pursuits, and their dissimilarity separates friendships. Nor can the good be friends with the wicked, or the wicked with the good, for any other reason than that the difference between their characters and pursuits is as great as it can possibly be.”

These are their views. From them a considerable difficulty clearly arises, since it seems to follow that true friendship can exist neither between us and God nor between unequal human beings—that is, between superiors and inferiors. Yet nothing could be more opposed to reason and truth. To resolve this difficulty, I have found the following points worth noting (see Gregory of Valencia).

First, two notable passages of Saint Thomas (*Summa theologica*, II–II, disputation 3, question 1) are especially suitable for clarifying this matter and for understanding the true nature and concept of friendship. The first concerns charity toward God, which holds the first place among all friendships and must be regarded as the rule and standard of the others:

“Charity,” he says (*Summa theologica*, II–II, question 65, article 5), “does not signify merely love of God, but also a certain friendship with him. This adds to love a mutual return of love, together with a certain mutual communication, as is said in Book VIII of the *Ethics*, chapters 2 and 3. That this pertains to charity is clear from what is said in 1 John 4: ‘Whoever remains in charity remains in God, and God in him.’ And in 1 Corinthians 1: ‘God is faithful, through whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son.’ This fellowship of a human being with God, which is a kind of familiar association with God, begins here in the present through grace, but will be perfected in the future through glory.”

The second passage noted here is as follows (*Summa theologica*, II–II, question 23, article 1): “According to the Philosopher, in Book VIII of the *Ethics*, not every love has the character of friendship, but only love accompanied by goodwill—that is, when we love someone in such a way that we wish him good. If we do not wish good to the things we love, but wish their good for ourselves, as when we are said to love wine, a horse, or something of that kind, this is not the love of friendship but a kind of desire. For it is ridiculous to say that someone has friendship with wine or a horse. Nor is goodwill alone sufficient for the nature of friendship; a certain mutual love is also required, because a friend is a friend to his friend. Such mutual goodwill is founded upon some form of communication.

“Since there is a certain communication between a human being and God, insofar as God communicates his blessedness to us, some friendship must be founded upon this communication. Of this communication it is said in 1 Corinthians 1: ‘God is faithful, through whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son.’ The love founded upon this communication is charity. It is therefore clear that charity is a certain friendship of the human being with God.”

Thus Saint Thomas.

From these passages Cajetan concludes that the name “friendship” implies or includes three conditions: goodwill; a return of goodwill, or reciprocal love; and communication, that is, participation in something—for example, blood relationship among kindred, military service among comrades-in-arms, or religion and profession among monks. He shows that these conditions are found especially in charity.

Second, when friendship is said to require equality or parity in virtue, this should not be understood as an absolute equality, called arithmetic equality, but as geometric or proportionate equality according to the persons involved, or according to each person’s state and condition. One kind of devotion to virtue and one degree of perfection are required in superiors, another in inferiors; one among religious, another among secular persons; one in the aged, another in the young. For friendship to be firm and stable, each friend must perform his duty with equal zeal in accordance with the proportion and condition of his state, namely, to cultivate virtue: a father as befits a father, a superior as befits a superior, a monk as befits a monk, and so forth (Aristotle, Book VIII of the *Ethics*, chapter 7). This is what Ambrose says in the passage cited above: that the superior ought to present himself as equal to the inferior, and the inferior to the superior. This abbot—or Cassianus in this passage—also teaches that the faithful and indissoluble union of friendship is founded solely upon parity of virtues.

This also concerns the Apostle’s exhortation, in which he urges both superiors and inferiors to anticipate one another in honor and to compete with one another in mutual offices of charity, kindness, and humility: “Be diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace,” and “be solicitous for one another,” since they are members of one another (Romans 12). He discusses this beautifully throughout chapter 12 of the First Epistle to the Corinthians, likewise in chapter 12 of the Epistle to the Romans, and in many other places.

Third, true friendship, like true repentance, can be understood in two ways. In one sense, friendship is called true when the true nature of friendship is found in it, just as we call Christ true God and true man, and call gold true when it is not counterfeit (Bonaventure, *Commentary on the Four Books of Sentences*, distinction 14). In this sense true friendship is opposed to false friendship, in which true love and the other conditions listed above are absent.

In another sense, friendship is called true when it is constant, perpetual, and uninterrupted, and when it attains its proper end—the end, namely, of eternal salvation, which true and sincere friendship ought to pursue. This is called both perfect friendship and the friendship of the perfect. In this sense it is said that true love never perishes. According to Solomon: “He who is a friend loves at all times” (Proverbs 17). This, however, is not true of the true friend and true friendship in the former sense. The same applies to Saint Jerome’s statement: “Friendship which can cease was never true.” Similar is the saying often quoted from Augustine’s book *On Friendship*: “Charity which can be abandoned was never true”—that is, perfect—although that book has no certain author and is not believed to have proceeded from Augustine (Bellarmine, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*).

From these considerations, I think, the difficulty has been resolved.]

this is, as we have said, the faithful and indissoluble union of friendship, founded solely upon parity of virtues. For the Lord makes [Note: [Col. 1017C] The Septuagint translated *monotropous* (Μονοτρόπους), that is, “people of one kind and way of life,” or, as others interpret it, “solitary people.” Saint Jerome says that the Hebrew reads: “The Lord makes monks dwell in a house.” Those who mock and attack the name of monks as something novel or recent—monk-scourgers and monk-fighters, sectarians—should have noted this antiquity. They themselves are “newly born and newly planted” (*neogennētoi kai neophytoi*, νεογέννητοι καὶ νεόφυτοι), that is, the most recent and novel of all, newly born and both new and innovators.

This does not conflict with what Saint Augustine writes in Treatise 97 on John: “Hospices and monasteries were afterward called by new names; nevertheless, the realities themselves existed before their names and are confirmed by the truth of religion.” As is clear from his preceding words, Augustine is speaking of the first Christians, and of the apostolic period, when the disciples were first called Christians at Antioch, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 11). At that time the terms “monks” and “monasteries” were not yet in use, at least not with such frequency. Yet the Apostles and their first disciples living at Jerusalem were in reality true monks, since they were the first to establish the monastic, or cenobitic, life, in which everything was held in common, as Acts 4 records.

Hence Saint Jerome, in his book *On Illustrious Men*, says of Philo that the first Church of believers in Christ was such as monks now strive and desire to be. Cassianus, Book II of the *Institutes*, chapter 5, asserts that the Egyptian monks received their first form of life from Saint Mark the Evangelist.

Nevertheless, it is plainly evident that the terms “monks” and “monasteries” were known and widespread in the Church even during the apostolic period or shortly afterward. This is clear both from Dionysius the Areopagite, who wrote a letter to Demophilus the monk (*Epistle* 8) and explains at length in his book *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* the form of monastic profession and discipline; and from Philo, who was even older than Dionysius and who, in his book *On the Contemplative Life of the Petitioners*, chapter 6, writes that among those Alexandrian Therapeutae each person had a sacred dwelling of his own, which was called a *monastērion* (μοναστήριον).

At this time, therefore, what Augustine says is true: hospices and monasteries were called by new names, although the reality itself had existed long before its names. Even in the Old Testament, the sons of the prophets and others are asserted by the Fathers to have been true monks, and to have been leaders and chiefs of monks. More will be said about these matters in Collation 18, where they are treated expressly.

For the present it is enough to have shown that the monastic institution is not recent but flourished from the beginning of the nascent Church, even if the name itself was not as old as the name “Christian.” Yet the name too was used in apostolic times, as Saint Jerome observed that it had been foretold in the Hebrew text.]

dwell in one household according to one way of life (Psalm 67). And [Col. 1018A] for this reason unbroken affection can remain only among those who have one purpose and one will, [Note: [Col. 1018C] A celebrated saying of Sallust (*Conspiracy of Catiline*), also used by many authors. Thus everyone, to signify their equal fellowship and purpose, declared that one mind and one soul were present in two bodies.

to wish and refuse the same things. If you too desire to preserve it inviolate, you must hasten, first expelling your vices, to mortify your own wills, and, with united zeal and purpose, diligently fulfill what the Prophet greatly delights in: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Psalm 132). This must be understood not locally but spiritually. It is of no benefit if people differing in character and purpose are joined in one dwelling; nor does it harm those established in equal virtue to be separated by distances of place. For before God it is the dwelling together of character, not of place, that unites brothers in a common dwelling. The integrity of peace can never be preserved where diversity of wills is found.

## CHAPTER IV. The question whether something useful should be accomplished even against a brother’s wish

[Col. 1019B]

**Germanus:** [Note: [Col. 1019B] A related question is found in Cicero (*On Friendship*) and Aulus Gellius (*Attic Nights*, Book I, chapter 3): whether one should ever do wrong for the sake of a friend. But this question has no place among Christians, much less among monks and religious, for whom the apostolic teaching is established that one must obey God rather than human beings (Acts 5), and that God scatters the bones of those who please human beings, because God has rejected them (Psalm 52).

Cicero also understood this well when he says: “There is no excuse for sin if you have sinned for the sake of a friend.” And again, in the same work: “Let this therefore be established as the first law of friendship: that we neither ask for shameful things nor do them when asked; for a shameful excuse is offered, both in other sins and especially if someone confesses that he acted against the commonwealth for the sake of a friend.” And after much else: “In such matters the stability of friendship can be confirmed, when people joined by goodwill first command the desires to which others are enslaved, then rejoice in equity and justice, and each undertakes everything on behalf of the other; neither will one ever ask the other for anything except what is honorable and right. Therefore there is a pernicious error in those who think that friendship grants license for every lust and sin. Friendship was given by nature as an ally of virtues, not as the companion of vices.”]

What, then, if one person wishes to accomplish something which he sees to be useful and salutary according to God, while another does not give his assent? Should it be carried out even against the brother’s wish, or should it be neglected according to his judgment?

## CHAPTER V. The answer: perpetual friendship cannot exist except among the perfect

[Col. 1020A]

**Joseph:** For this reason we said [Note: [Col. 1019C] He again commends and repeats the opinion of the elders, with the wording somewhat altered, in chapter 24: “Stable and unbroken charity cannot endure except among men of the same virtue and purpose.” He likewise concludes this collation as follows: “It is therefore the most certain opinion of the wisest men that true harmony and inseparable fellowship cannot endure except among men of corrected character and of the same virtue and purpose.”

This also pertains to the definition of friendship given by Cicero and highly commended by Saint Augustine. Writing to a certain Marcellinus, an old friend who had become a catechumen from paganism, Augustine says (*Epistle* 155): “You know how the Roman, the greatest authority in eloquence, Tully, defined friendship. He said—and said most sacredly and truthfully: ‘Friendship is the fullest agreement in human and divine matters, with goodwill and charity.’ But you, my dearest friend, once agreed with me in human matters; in divine matters, however, since at that time no virtue had yet shone upon me, our friendship was lame in the greater part of that definition. [Col. 1020B] It was agreement only in human matters, not also in divine matters, although joined with goodwill and charity,” and so forth.

“Thus, among those between whom there is no agreement in divine matters, there can be no complete and true agreement in human matters either. For the person who despises divine things must necessarily judge human things otherwise than he ought; and whoever does not love the one who made humanity will not know how to love a human being rightly.

“Therefore I do not say, ‘You are now more fully my friend, whereas formerly you were my friend in part’; rather, reason shows that you were not even my friend in part, since you did not then maintain true friendship with me even in human matters. “Since I hated my own soul, how could I possess a true friend who wished for me the things in which I myself was allowing myself to be an enemy to myself?

“Thanks, therefore, be to God, who at last deigned to make you my friend. For now we have agreement in human matters, joined with goodwill and charity, in Christ Jesus our Lord, our truest peace. He summed up all the divine proclamations in two commandments, saying: ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind; and you shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ On these two commandments the whole law and the prophets depend (Matthew 22).

“If you hold these two commandments most firmly with me, our friendship will be true and everlasting, and it will join not only us to one another but also both of us to the Lord himself.”

Thus Saint Augustine speaks about the true definition of friendship, no less elegantly than subtly. Although he speaks at length, I have judged that the passage ought to be recited in full for the understanding and clarification not only of this passage but of the whole of this collation and discussion concerning true friendship.]

that the full and perfect grace of friendship cannot continue except among perfect men of the same virtue, whom the same will and one purpose allow either never—or certainly only rarely—to think differently, or to disagree in matters pertaining to progress in the spiritual life. If they begin to seethe with impassioned disputes, it is clear that they were never harmonious according to the rule we have stated.

But since no one can begin with perfection unless he has begun from its foundation, and since you are asking not how great its magnitude is but how one may reach it, I think it necessary to disclose to you briefly its rule and a certain path by which your steps may be directed, so that you may more easily attain the good of patience and peace.

## CHAPTER VI. By what means an inviolable fellowship may be preserved

[Col. 1021A]

First [Note: [Col. 1021C] Eight means are handed down here by which true and perfect friendship may be initiated, preserved, and increased among monks.
