For ease of remembering them, they may be briefly summarized as follows: 1. to lay a firm and solid foundation in religious poverty, contempt for, and renunciation of temporal possessions; 2. for each person to cut back his own wishes, and to prefer obeying not his own decisions but those of his neighbor; 3. to know that everything, even what he considers necessary or useful, must be postponed to the good of charity and peace; 4. to beware of anger, which is the mother of discord; 5. to desire to heal and calm a brother’s anger against him, even when conceived without reason, just as much as his own; 6. to believe that he will depart from this world every day—something that destroys all vices generally and decisively; 7. even in opinions belonging to the realm of understanding, to avoid disputes; 8. never to trust his own judgment, but rather another’s.] The foundations of true friendship, therefore, lie in contempt for worldly substance and in disdain for all the possessions we have. For it is utterly unjust and impious if, after renouncing the world and all its vanity, the cheapest furniture that remains [Lips. in the margin: “is superfluous”] is preferred to the most precious love of a brother. The second principle is that each person should so cut back his own wishes that, not judging himself wise and prudent, he would rather obey the decisions of his neighbor than his own. The third is that he should know that everything, even what he considers useful and necessary, must be postponed to the good of charity and peace. The fourth is that he should believe that one must never become angry, whether for just or unjust reasons. The fifth is that he should desire to care for a brother’s anger against him, even when conceived without reason, in the same way as he would care for his own, knowing that another’s sadness is equally harmful to him, as though he himself were moved to anger against another, unless, insofar as it depends on him, he also drives that sadness from his brother’s mind. The final principle—which is unquestionably the general and decisive destruction of all vices—is that he should believe he will depart from this world every day. This conviction not only permits no sadness to remain in the heart, but also suppresses every impulse of all desires and sins. Whoever, therefore, holds to these principles will be unable either to endure or to inflict the bitterness of anger and discord.

When these things have ceased, as soon as [Note: [Col. 1021D] The devil—or greed, the root of all evils, the rival and enemy of charity, which he later calls [Col. 1022C] the first cause of quarrels. Cassiodorus aptly applies the following to this passage (On Friendship, chapter 1): “The friendship introduced by worldly greed is deceitful; it has nothing true, nothing secure, nothing stable. It loves a person’s goods, not the person; it measures love by profit; it embraces fortune in its wishes, not the individual. As the saying goes:

He is not a friend of the person, but of prosperity;

whom sweet fortune holds, bitter fortune drives away.”

And below: “Hear blessed Ambrose (On Duties, book III, final chapter): ‘Friendship is not tributary but generous: it is a virtue, not a profit; it is not won by money but by favor; it is not born and nourished through the conflict of battles, but through the mutual contest of goodwill,’ and so forth.] that rival of charity has gradually poured the poisons of sadness into the hearts of friends, it is inevitable that, through frequent quarrels and love gradually growing cold, he will eventually separate the hearts of lovers, long wounded. For one who proceeds along the path of the direction described above—who could ever be at odds with his friend, if he has cut out at the root the first cause of quarrels, which is usually generated from small matters and the cheapest possessions, claiming nothing as his own, and carefully preserves the unity of believers that we read about in the Acts of the Apostles with every virtue?

“Now the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and no one said that any of the things he possessed was his own; rather, everything was held in common among them” (Acts IV). How, then, could a seedbed of dissension arise in someone who serves not his own will but his brother’s, and who has become an imitator of his Lord and Creator, who, speaking in the person of the man he had assumed, said: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John V)? How could he kindle any fuel for contention who has resolved to yield [Lips. in the margin: “to trust”] concerning his understanding and judgment, not so much to his own decision as to his brother’s examination—according to his brother’s discretion either approving his own discoveries or rejecting them—and who completes that Gospel saying with the humility of a devout heart: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew XXVI)?

Or by what reasoning will he admit anything that might sadden his brother, who judges nothing more precious than the good of peace, never losing the memory of that saying of the Lord: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John XIII)? Through this spiritual mark Christ wished his flock of sheep to be recognized in this world and, so to speak, distinguished from all others by this character.

For what reason would someone either receive resentment into himself or allow the bitterness of sadness to remain in another, when his fundamental conviction is that there can be no just grounds for anger—which is harmful and unlawful—and that he cannot pray in the same way while his brother is angry with him, as though he himself were angry with his brother, always retaining humbly in his heart that command of the Lord and Savior:

“If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matthew V)?

For it will be of no benefit if you claim that you are not angry and believe that you are fulfilling the command: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger,” and, “Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment,” while, with an obstinate heart, you disdain another’s sadness, which you could have soothed by your gentleness. You will be punished in the same way for transgressing the Lord’s command. For the one who said that you must not be angry against another also said that another’s sadness must not be despised; because, before God, who wills all human beings to be saved, it makes no difference whether you destroy yourself or someone else.

[Note: [Col. 1022D] For the sense in which this and what follows should be understood, see our annotations on book VIII of the Institutes. He wisely says “irascibility,” not “anger.” Anger is often just and has just causes; irascibility does not, as was said in its proper place.]

[Note: [Col. 1023B] Thus Cassianus, Institutes, book VIII, chapter 13: “For the Lord common to all does not take such pleasure in our services that what he gains in one he loses in another, when sadness prevails. For in the loss of any one person he suffers a loss, since he desires and awaits the salvation of all his servants in the same way.”]

Indeed, one loss arises for him from the destruction of any individual; likewise, the one who rejoices in everyone’s ruin gains one profit, whether through your death or your brother’s. Finally, how could someone retain even the slightest sadness against his brother who believes that he is departing from this world every day—or rather, continually?

## CHAPTER VII. That nothing should be preferred to charity, nor anything postponed to anger

Just as nothing should be preferred to charity, so conversely nothing should be postponed to fury or irascibility. For everything, however useful and necessary it may seem, must nevertheless be rejected in order to avoid the disturbance of anger; and everything, even what is thought to be adverse, must be accepted and endured, [Note: [Col. 1023C] Saint Augustine, On the City of God: “So great is the good of peace that even in earthly and mortal affairs nothing is ordinarily heard with greater pleasure, nothing desired with greater longing, and nothing better can finally be found.” The same author—or whoever wrote To the Brothers in the Desert—says: “You ought to know, brothers, that there are certain things which are good but not pleasant, and certain things which are pleasant but not good. For example, fasts, vigils, bodily mortifications, and similar practices are good. They are good, but not pleasant, because the flesh does not delight in them but is harmed by them. Feasts and drunkenness are pleasant, but not good. O monk, you will scarcely be able to find in the present life something that is both good and pleasant. Do you nevertheless wish to find it? Pursue peace and embrace it. For it is the only virtue that possesses both goodness and pleasantness. It is that goodness which makes us dwell together in one manner of life, so that we may always desire to live and die together. O peace, serenity of mind, tranquility of spirit, bond of love, fellowship of charity! This is the highest happiness, which restrains wars, suppresses anger, calms the discordant, reconciles enemies, pleases everyone, and is desired by everyone. Blessed is the one who possesses you; accursed is the one who hates you and breaks you among human beings, for he is the Antichrist and the son of perdition.”]

so that the tranquility of love and peace may be preserved unharmed; for nothing should be considered more harmful than anger and sadness, nor anything more beneficial than charity.

## CHAPTER VIII. For what reasons does dissension arise among spiritual persons?

For just as that enemy quickly separates brothers who are still carnal and weak on account of cheap and earthly possessions, so [Note: [Col. 1023D] The salutary warning of Saint Gregory applies to these people: “Those who are at odds should be admonished so that they may know with certainty that, however great their virtues, they can in no way become spiritual if they neglect to be united with their neighbors in concord. For it is written: ‘The fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, and peace’” (Galatians V). “Whoever therefore does not care to preserve peace refuses to bear the fruit of the Spirit.” Hence Paul says: “While there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not carnal?” (1 Corinthians III). Again he says: “Pursue peace with everyone, and holiness” (Hebrews XII). And again, admonishing them, he says: “Be diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians III) (Gregory, Pastoral Care, part III, admonition 2).]

he also produces discord among spiritual persons through differences of understanding. From this, without doubt, arise verbal contentions and quarrels, which the Apostle condemns (Galatians V); consequently, the hostile and malicious enemy introduces divisions among brothers who ought to be united. True is that saying of the wisest Solomon:

[Note: [Col. 1024B] In Greek: μῖσος ἐγείρει νεῖκος. This can be translated in either of two ways. “Contention raises hatred,” as it is cited here, where μῖσος is in the accusative and νεῖκος in the nominative; or “hatred raises contention,” if the cases are reversed, as the Latin translator renders it: “Hatred raises quarrels, and charity covers all offenses” (Proverbs X).]

“Hatred raises contention, but friendship protects all who do not contend” (Proverbs X).

## CHAPTER IX. On cutting away even spiritual causes of discord

Therefore, in order to preserve perpetual and undivided charity, [Note: [Col. 1024C] The causes of disagreement and discord among brothers are of two kinds. Some are carnal, when disputes arise over “mine” and “yours,” that is, over external possessions, which this abbot calls “most useful” here—as they truly are when compared with spiritual and heavenly things—such as clothing, food, a more honored place, authority, dwelling, utensils, rights, and other conveniences. Others are spiritual, when debate arises over various questions, interpretations of Scripture, and other controversial matters belonging, as he says here, to the realm of understanding, because people cling to their own opinions beyond what is proper. For this reason Saint Gregory of Nazianzus delivered a splendid speech on the moderation to be observed in disputes, in which he says among other things (Oration 26): “What is most excellent in teaching? Peace. I will add: what is most useful. Conversely, what is most shameful and harmful? The separation of wills.” Saint Ambrose, On Duties, book I, chapter 22: “Speech is divided into familiar conversation and into discussion and debate concerning faith and justice. In both, care must be taken that there be no disturbance; rather, speech should be gentle, calm, full of goodwill and grace, without any insult. Let stubborn contention be absent from familiar conversation; for raising questions often produces more empty subtlety than usefulness. Let discussion be without anger, pleasantness without bitterness, admonition without harshness, and exhortation without offense.”]

it is of no benefit to have cut away the first cause of dissension, which usually arises from perishable and earthly things, and to have despised all carnal matters, permitting the brothers to share indiscriminately everything our use requires, unless we also cut away in the same way the second cause, which usually arises under the appearance of spiritual interpretations, and acquire in all things a humble understanding and harmonious wills.

## CHAPTER X. On the best examination of truth

I remember that, when my younger age was still urging me to remain in the company of the brothers, such an understanding was often introduced among us, whether in moral disciplines or in the sacred Scriptures, that we considered nothing more true or more reasonable than it. But when we gathered together and began to state our opinions, certain matters, examined in a common inquiry, were first identified by one of us as false and harmful; then, after being judged harmful by the common decision, they were condemned. Previously they had shone as though illuminated by light, having been infused by the devil to such a degree that they could easily have generated discord, unless the instruction of the elders, guarded like a divine oracle, had recalled us from every contention. By a kind of legal sanction they had prescribed that neither of us should trust his own judgment more than that of his brother, if he never wished to be deceived by the devil’s cunning.

[Note: [Col. 1024D] Here the fruit of spiritual conferences or conversations, as well as the custom and method ordinarily observed among the ancient monks, is explicitly displayed. On this, see also our annotation on Conference 2, chapter 2.]

## CHAPTER XI. That it is impossible for anyone who trusts his own judgment not to be deceived by the devil’s illusion

For it often proves true that saying of the Apostle: [Note: [Col. 1025C] Saint Gregory, Moralia, book XXXIII, chapter 22, on Job XLI: “Who will reveal the face of his garment?” Gregory says: “This Leviathan—that is, the devil—tempts religious minds in one way and those devoted to this world in another. To the wicked he openly presents the evils they desire; but, secretly lying in wait for the good, he deceives them under the appearance of holiness. To the former, as to his intimates, he insinuates himself more openly as wicked; but to the latter, as to strangers, he disguises himself under the pretext of a certain apparent honesty, so that what he cannot openly introduce into them he may insert covertly under the veil of a good action.”]

“For Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light” (2 Corinthians XI), so that he may deceitfully pour out the dark and foul mist of false understandings in place of the true light of knowledge [Lips. in the margin: “pour over”]. Unless these thoughts, received with a humble and gentle heart, are submitted to the examination of a most mature brother or a thoroughly tested elder, and, after careful scrutiny according to their judgment, are either rejected or accepted by us, we shall undoubtedly venerate in our thoughts the angel of darkness as an angel of light and suffer the gravest destruction.

[Note: [Col. 1025C] He calls the devil’s deception “destruction.” Thus Abbot Moses, Conference 2, chapter 10: “True discernment is acquired only through true humility. The first test of this humility will be whether everything—not only what is to be done but also what is thought—is submitted to the examination of the elders, so that no one, trusting his own judgment, may in every matter rely on their decisions, and may learn from their tradition what he ought to judge good or evil.” And in the following chapter: “The devil drags and leads a monk to death through no other fault so precipitously as when, after neglecting the advice of the elders, he persuades him to trust in his own judgment, decision, or teaching.” He gives there many examples of monks and hermits who, trusting too greatly in their own judgment, fell into grave and astonishing errors. Saint Dorotheus, sermon 19: “Since we are subject to many passions and depraved affections, we must not trust our own judgment at all. For when a standard or rule is crooked and bent, whatever is aligned according to it never becomes straight, but remains distorted.” Saint Benedict, chapter 3 of the Rule: “Let no one in the monastery follow the desire of his own heart.” Saint Bernard, sermons 2 and 3 on the Resurrection: “What greater pride can there be than for one person to prefer his own judgment to the judgment of the entire congregation, as though he alone possessed the Spirit of God?” And again: “There are two kinds of leprosy in the heart: one’s own will and one’s own counsel. Both kinds of leprosy are exceedingly evil, and all the more harmful the more inward they are.”]

No one who trusts his own judgment can escape this destruction unless, having become a lover and practitioner of true humility, he fulfills with complete contrition of heart what the Apostle earnestly urges:

“If there is any encouragement in Christ, any comfort from love, any participation in the Spirit, any affection and sympathy, complete my joy by being of the same mind, having the same love, being united in soul and intent on one purpose; doing nothing through contention or empty glory, but in humility considering one another superior to yourselves” (Philippians II);

and also:

“Outdo one another in showing honor” (Romans XII),

so that, as each person attributes greater knowledge and holiness to his companion, he may believe that the fullness of true discernment rests more in another’s judgment than in his own.

## CHAPTER XII. Why inferiors should not be despised in a conference

It often happens, whether through the devil’s illusion or through human error—for there is no one in this flesh who cannot be deceived as a human being—that even [Note: [Col. 1026C] For the same reason stated in the title of this chapter, Saint Benedict prescribes the following (chapter 3): Whenever anything important must be done in the monastery, the abbot is to call the entire congregation together, state what is under consideration, hear the advice of the brothers, deliberate privately, and do what he judges most useful. “We have said,” he explains, “that all should be called to the council because the Lord often reveals what is better to the younger.” He appears to have in view the Gospel saying: “I thank you, Father, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matthew XI); and the Apostle’s words (1 Corinthians XIV): “If something is revealed to one who is younger, let the elder be silent.” Hence Abbot Smaragdus, commenting on this same passage of the Rule: “Often, for the sake of humility, the Lord reveals to the younger what he conceals from the elder. For God is not a respecter of persons; but in every age, condition, sex, and nation, whoever fears him is acceptable to him” (Acts X); “and the Spirit blows where it wills” (John III), and he graciously grants the gift of wisdom. “For he did not distinguish age in Daniel and Samuel, but granted grace” (Daniel XIII; 1 Samuel III). “The understanding of a person is his gray hair, and an unsullied life is old age” (Wisdom II).]

sometimes the one who has the sharper intellect and greater knowledge conceives something false in his mind, while the one whose intellect is slower and whose merit is lesser perceives something more rightly and more truly. Therefore no one, however [variant: “of whatever”] endowed with knowledge, should persuade himself in his empty conceit that he has no need of another’s conference. For even if his judgment does not suffer the devil’s deception, he will not escape the more serious snares of self-exaltation and pride. Who could claim such independence without great ruin, when the Chosen Vessel, in whom Christ, as he himself declared, was speaking (2 Corinthians XIII), says that he went up to Jerusalem for no other reason than to confer in a private examination with his fellow apostles concerning the Gospel that, with the Lord revealing and cooperating, he preached to the Gentiles (Galatians II)? This shows that these precepts preserve not only unanimity and concord, but also ensure that all the hostile devil’s ambushes and the snares of his illusions need not be feared.

## CHAPTER XIII. That charity is not only a thing of God but also God

Finally, the virtue of charity is exalted to such a degree that blessed John the Apostle declares it to be not only a thing of God but also God, saying: “God is love; and whoever abides in love abides in God, and God abides in him” (1 John IV).

[Note: [Col. 1027B] To understand correctly how charity is both a thing of God—that is, God’s gift—and God, observe first that, according to the sacred Scriptures, not only the love by which we love God but also the love by which God loves us is called charity. “God demonstrates,” says the Apostle, “his charity in us,” or “toward us” (Romans V); and: “Because of his great charity with which God loved us” (Ephesians II). The statement Paul makes in Romans VIII—“Who will separate us from the charity of God?”—is understood by some as referring to the charity with which God loved us, and by others to the charity with which we love God. Both are rightly called God’s charity: the former because it is intimate to God, indeed God himself; the latter because it is bestowed and conferred by him. Hence it is both a thing and a gift of God.

Moreover, the very charity by which God is loved by us is distinguished by theologians into two kinds: uncreated charity, which is God himself, concerning which John says, “God is charity”; and created charity, of which Paul speaks when he says that it has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us (1 John IV). For it must be something other than the Holy Spirit whom the Spirit himself pours into our hearts.

The Master of the Sentences, Peter Lombard (Sentences, book I, distinction 17), because he was convinced from Scripture that the Holy Spirit is present and substantially dwells in the hearts of those whom he sanctifies, did not consider any habit of charity necessary. Indeed, he judged that there was no created charity to which the dignity commonly attributed to charity could belong: that whoever remains in charity remains in God and has God remaining in him; that charity transfers a person from death to life; that it makes people children of God, the temple of God, and members of Christ; that it joins a person most closely to God and makes one spirit with him. Since he thought these and similar attributes far exceeded the power and dignity of created charity, he removed the notion of created charity and taught that charity itself is the Holy Spirit, not some created habit like the habits of faith, hope, and the other virtues.

But this opinion of the Master has now been driven from the schools (Saint Thomas, II–II, question 23, article 2; Bellarmine, On Grace, book I, chapter 9), and it has certainly been established that the charity by which God is loved by us is a certain created and infused quality or habit, which is both a virtue and the mother of virtues, and which may most truly be called a thing or gift of God. For Saint Augustine, in his letter to Jerome, teaches that charity is a true and great virtue. And in On Nature and Grace, chapter 70, he says that charity begun in us is justice begun, charity advanced is justice advanced, and charity perfected is justice perfected. Yet these stages do not apply to uncreated charity, as is clear, nor is that justice ours by which we are properly and formally called and made just.

Saint Bernard therefore speaks most aptly in Letter 11 and at the end of On Loving God: “Charity is rightly called both God and God’s gift; for charity gives charity—the substantial gives the accidental.”]

For we perceive it to be so divine that we plainly recognize the Apostle’s statement taking effect in us: “The charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us” (Romans V). This is as though he were saying:

[Note: [Col. 1028B] “Hard is this saying, and who can hear it?” (John VI). He explains that statement of the Apostle—“The charity of God has been poured into our hearts”—in an exceedingly improper, not to say incongruous, way, κατακρητικῶς, as referring to uncreated charity. For who would speak, or willingly hear it spoken, that uncreated charity—that is, the Holy Spirit—is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us? Here there is manifest and gross tautology. Saint Augustine therefore gives a better explanation in On the Spirit and the Letter, chapter 32: “The charity of God is said to be poured into our hearts, not the charity by which he himself loves us, but that by which he makes us lovers of him; just as the justice of God is called that by which we are made just through his gift, and the salvation of the Lord that by which he made us safe, and the faith of Christ that by which he makes us faithful.”]

“God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us.”

And when we do not know what we ought to pray, he intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings. Whoever searches the hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because he intercedes for the saints according to God (Romans VIII).

[Note: [Col. 1028C] The Holy Spirit requests or intercedes for us—that is, he teaches us to request, as Saint Augustine explains (Tractate 6 on John and Letter 21). In the same way Christ said to the apostles: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking in you” (Matthew X). And the Apostle says: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Galatians IV), that is, causing us to cry out.]

## CHAPTER XIV. On the degrees of charity

It is possible for everyone to show that charity which is called ἀγάπη—love, affection, and charity among the Greeks—and concerning which the blessed Apostle says:

[Note: [Col. 1026D] Metaphrastes writes that the hermit Saint Arsenius, although exceedingly learned, nevertheless, in order to practice greater humility, was accustomed to seek and follow the advice of younger men even in minor matters. Likewise Saint Augustine, so great a teacher of the Church, possessed such humility that he showed himself ready to be taught and admonished even by the least person, as he wrote to Saint Jerome (Letter 15): “I repeatedly ask you to correct me confidently whenever you see that I need it. Although, according to the terms of honor now established by ecclesiastical usage, the episcopate is greater than the presbyterate, yet in many matters Augustine is less than Jerome, even though correction from anyone whatsoever, however lesser, should not be rejected or disdained.”]

however endowed with knowledge, should persuade himself in his empty conceit that he has no need of another’s conference. For even if his judgment does not suffer the devil’s deception, he will not escape the more serious snares of self-exaltation and pride. Who could claim such independence without great ruin, when the Chosen Vessel, in whom Christ, as he himself declared, was speaking (2 Corinthians XIII), says that he went up to Jerusalem for no other reason than to confer in a private examination with his fellow apostles concerning the Gospel that, with the Lord revealing and cooperating, he preached to the Gentiles (Galatians II)? This shows that these precepts preserve not only unanimity and concord, but also ensure that all the hostile devil’s ambushes and the snares of his illusions need not be feared.

## CHAPTER XIII. That charity is not only a thing of God but also God

Finally, the virtue of charity is exalted to such a degree that blessed John the Apostle declares it to be not only a thing of God but also God, saying: “God is love; and whoever abides in love abides in God, and God abides in him” (1 John IV).

[Note: [Col. 1027B] To understand correctly how charity is both a thing of God—that is, God’s gift—and God, observe first that, according to the sacred Scriptures, not only the love by which we love God but also the love by which God loves us is called charity. “God demonstrates,” says the Apostle, “his charity in us,” or “toward us” (Romans V); and: “Because of his great charity with which God loved us” (Ephesians II). The statement Paul makes in Romans VIII—“Who will separate us from the charity of God?”—is understood by some as referring to the charity with which God loved us, and by others to the charity with which we love God. Both are rightly called God’s charity: the former because it is intimate to God, indeed God himself; the latter because it is bestowed and conferred by him. Hence it is both a thing and a gift of God.

Moreover, the very charity by which God is loved by us is distinguished by theologians into two kinds: uncreated charity, which is God himself, concerning which John says, “God is charity”; and created charity, of which Paul speaks when he says that it has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us (1 John IV). For it must be something other than the Holy Spirit whom the Spirit himself pours into our hearts.

The Master of the Sentences, Peter Lombard (Sentences, book I, distinction 17), because he was convinced from Scripture that the Holy Spirit is present and substantially dwells in the hearts of those whom he sanctifies, did not consider any habit of charity necessary. Indeed, he judged that there was no created charity to which the dignity commonly attributed to charity could belong: that whoever remains in charity remains in God and has God remaining in him; that charity transfers a person from death to life; that it makes people children of God, the temple of God, and members of Christ; that it joins a person most closely to God and makes one spirit with him. Since he thought these and similar attributes far exceeded the power and dignity of created charity, he removed the notion of created charity and taught that charity itself is the Holy Spirit, not some created habit like the habits of faith, hope, and the other virtues.

But this opinion of the Master has now been driven from the schools (Saint Thomas, II–II, question 23, article 2; Bellarmine, On Grace, book I, chapter 9), and it has certainly been established that the charity by which God is loved by us is a certain created and infused quality or habit, which is both a virtue and the mother of virtues, and which may most truly be called a thing or gift of God. For Saint Augustine, in his letter to Jerome, teaches that charity is a true and great virtue. And in On Nature and Grace, chapter 70, he says that charity begun in us is justice begun, charity advanced is justice advanced, and charity perfected is justice perfected. Yet these stages do not apply to uncreated charity, as is clear, nor is that justice ours by which we are properly and formally called and made just.

Saint Bernard therefore speaks most aptly in Letter 11 and at the end of On Loving God: “Charity is rightly called both God and God’s gift; for charity gives charity—the substantial gives the accidental.”]

For we perceive it to be so divine that we plainly recognize the Apostle’s statement taking effect in us: “The charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us” (Romans V). This is as though he were saying:

[Note: [Col. 1028B] “Hard is this saying, and who can hear it?” (John VI). He explains that statement of the Apostle—“The charity of God has been poured into our hearts”—in an exceedingly improper, not to say incongruous, way, κατακρητικῶς, as referring to uncreated charity. For who would speak, or willingly hear it spoken, that uncreated charity—that is, the Holy Spirit—is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us? Here there is manifest and gross tautology. Saint Augustine therefore gives a better explanation in On the Spirit and the Letter, chapter 32: “The charity of God is said to be poured into our hearts, not the charity by which he himself loves us, but that by which he makes us lovers of him; just as the justice of God is called that by which we are made just through his gift, and the salvation of the Lord that by which he made us safe, and the faith of Christ that by which he makes us faithful.”]

“God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us.”

And when we do not know what we ought to pray, he intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings. Whoever searches the hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because he intercedes for the saints according to God (Romans VIII).

[Note: [Col. 1028C] The Holy Spirit requests or intercedes for us—that is, he teaches us to request, as Saint Augustine explains (Tractate 6 on John and Letter 21). In the same way Christ said to the apostles: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking in you” (Matthew X). And the Apostle says: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Galatians IV), that is, causing us to cry out.]

## CHAPTER XIV. On the degrees of charity

It is possible for everyone to show that charity which is called ἀγάπη—love, affection, and charity among the Greeks—and concerning which the blessed Apostle says: “Therefore, while we have time, let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith” (Galatians VI). It must be shown generally to everyone to such an extent that we are commanded by the Lord to extend it even to our enemies. For he says: “Love your enemies” (Matthew V).

[Note: [Col. 1028D] Among the Greeks, Ἀγάπη is called love, affection, and charity. Hence Tertullian (Apologeticus, chapter 3): “It is called agape, which among the Latins is dilectio.” And Saint Cyprian, book III to Quirinus: “Agape and brotherly love are to be practiced religiously and steadfastly.” Among ancient Christians, agape was a meal, or small banquet, at which the poor were entertained on Sundays and feast days. See Conference 24, chapter 12.]

[Note: [Col. 1028D] Διάθεσις has several meanings, of which the principal ones are affection or disposition, illness, condition, arrangement, and testament—also called διαθήκη. Here it is taken to mean an affection, inclination, or special love by which we embrace those who are closer to us more than others. It contains as many degrees as there are kinds and differences of relationships and connections, as is explained here.]

Διάθεσις, that is, affection, is shown to very few, namely, to those connected with us either by likeness of character or by fellowship in virtue, although even this disposition itself appears to contain considerable differences. Parents are loved in one way, spouses in another, brothers in another, and children in another; and even within these relationships there is great variation, nor is the affection of parents toward their children uniform.

This is also demonstrated by the example of the patriarch Jacob. Although he was the father of twelve sons and loved them all with paternal charity, he nevertheless loved Joseph with a more devoted affection, as Scripture plainly records concerning him: “His brothers were jealous of him, because their father loved him” (Genesis XXXVII). This does not mean that the just man and father did not love his other children very much, but that, because Joseph prefigured the Lord, Jacob clung to him with an affection that was in some way sweeter and more indulgent.

[Note: [Col. 1029C] Saint Jerome, Against Jovinianus, book I: “John,” he says, “one of the disciples, who is reported to have been the youngest among the apostles, and whom the faith of Christ had found a virgin, remained a virgin, and for that reason is loved more by the Lord and reclines upon Jesus’ breast. And Peter, who had had a wife, does not dare to ask, but asks him to inquire,” and so forth.]

We also read that this was most clearly indicated concerning John the Evangelist, when it is said of him: “The disciple whom Jesus loved” (John XIII). Certainly, he had likewise embraced the other eleven, chosen in the same way, with such particular love that he indicated this also by evangelical testimony, saying: “As I have loved you, you also love one another” (John XIII). Elsewhere it is said of them: “Loving his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end” (ibid.).

[Note: [Col. 1029C] This does not mean that he did not love the other apostles, or loved them less; rather, for the sake of a particular signification, or out of consideration for chastity and virginity, he showed his love toward John more than toward the others through external signs and familiar association.]

But this love for one individual did not express a lukewarmness of charity toward the other disciples; it expressed a more abundant superfluity of love toward him, which the privilege of virginity and incorruption of the flesh conferred upon him. For this reason it is marked as something higher, with a certain qualification: it is exalted not by comparison with hatred, but by the more abundant grace of overflowing love.

We read something similar in the person of the bride in the Song of Songs, where she says:

“Set charity in order in me” (Song of Songs II).

[Note: [Col. 1029D] So the Greek interpreters: Τάξατε ἐπ’ ἐμὲ ἀγάπην, which Saint Jerome also reads in his commentary on Ezekiel, chapter XLII. The Vulgate, however, has: “He has ordered charity in me.” This is how the Fathers commonly cite it. See Saint Bernard, Sermon 50 on the Song of Songs.]

This is truly ordered charity: it hates no one, yet loves some more by right of their merits; it loves everyone generally, yet selects from among them those whom it ought to embrace with special affection; and again, among those who are highest and most distinguished in love, it chooses certain ones whom it may exalt above the affection shown to the rest.

## CHAPTER XV. On those who strengthen either their own agitation or that of their brothers by concealment

Conversely, we know—would that we did not!—that some brothers are so obstinate and hard-hearted that, when they perceive either their own dispositions aroused against a brother or a brother’s disposition aroused against them, they withdraw from those whom they ought to have calmed by humble satisfaction and conversation, pretending to conceal the sadness of their own mind that has arisen from the indignation of either party’s agitation, and begin to chant certain verses of the Psalms.

[Note: [Col. 1029D] Against this illness Saint Benedict established and prescribed the following antidote: “If a brother is corrected for any, even the slightest, reason by the abbot or by any superior in any manner, or if he senses, however slightly, that the mind of any superior is angry or agitated against him, he should immediately, without delay, prostrate himself on the ground before that person’s feet, lying there to make satisfaction until the agitation has been healed by a blessing.”]

While they think that by this means they are soothing the bitterness conceived in their hearts, they increase it by insulting the other—something they could immediately have extinguished if they had been more anxious and humble, so that suitable contrition might heal their own hearts and soothe the dispositions of their brothers. In this way they caress and nourish the defect of their faintheartedness—or rather, of their pride—rather than uprooting the fuel of quarrels, forgetful of that command of the Lord:

“Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matthew V);

and:

“If you remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there at the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XVI. That when a brother harbors hostility against us, the Lord rejects the gifts of our prayers
Therefore God so greatly does not wish us to hold another’s sadness in contempt that, [Note: St. Gregory, in the *Pastoral Rule* (Part III, Admonition 23): “Those who are at variance must be admonished, so that they may know that, so long as they disagree with the charity owed to their neighbors, they offer no sacrifice of good work. For it is written: ‘If you offer your gift at the altar,’ etc. From this command it must be weighed whose offering is rejected, and how intolerable the fault is shown to be. For since all evils are washed away by the good deeds that follow, let us consider how great are the evils of discord, which, unless they are utterly extinguished, do not permit good to follow.” See the same author, *Dialogues*, Book IV, final chapter.] if a brother has anything against us, he neither accepts our gifts nor permits our prayers to be offered to him by us, until we have removed from his heart, by prompt satisfaction, the sadness that he has conceived—whether justly or unjustly.

[Note: St. Jerome expresses this in nearly the same way: “He did not say, ‘If you have anything against your brother,’ but, ‘If your brother has anything against you,’ so that the more demanding necessity of reconciliation might be imposed upon you.” Cassian explains and asserts the same more clearly in Book VIII, chapter 13: “Because we very often disregard brothers who have been injured and saddened, or at least despise them when they say that they have been offended through no fault of ours, the physician of souls and knower of hidden things, wishing to uproot occasions of anger from our hearts, commands us not only, if we have been injured, to forgive and be reconciled to our brothers, retaining no memory of injury or harm against them, but also, if we know that they have something against us, whether justly or unjustly, he similarly commands us to leave our gift,” etc. For how these things are to be understood, and to what extent we must be reconciled with a brother who has offended us before offering our gift, see the note in that same place.]

For he does not say, “If your brother has a genuine complaint against you, leave your gift there at the altar and go first to be reconciled to your brother”; rather, he says, “If you remember that your brother has something against you” (Matthew 5). That is, even if the matter by which your brother’s anger against you was aroused is slight and insignificant, and if it has suddenly come back to your memory, you should know that you ought not to offer the spiritual gifts of your prayers until, by kindly satisfaction, you have driven from your brother’s heart the sadness that arose from whatever cause.

If, then, the Gospel command requires us to make satisfaction even for a past and minor quarrel arising from trivial causes, what will become of us miserable people who stubbornly disregard recent and very serious causes of grievance committed through our own fault, and who, swollen with diabolical pride and ashamed to humble ourselves, deny that we are the authors of our brother’s sadness? In a rebellious spirit we disdain submission to the Lord’s commands and insist that they neither ought to be observed nor can be fulfilled. Thus, judging that he has commanded impossible or inappropriate things, we become, according to the Apostle, not doers but judges of the law (James 4).

## CHAPTER XVII. On those who think patience should be shown more toward secular people than toward brothers

This too ought to be mourned with what tears, that some brothers, when inflamed by an insult of any kind, if they are wearied by the entreaties of someone who wishes to calm the matter, proclaim immediately—when they hear that sadness against a brother must neither be conceived nor retained, according to what is written, “Whoever is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment” (Matthew 5), and, “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Ephesians 4)—“If some pagan or secular person had done this or said this, it ought rightly to have been endured. But who could tolerate a brother conscious of so grave a fault, or uttering such insolent abuse?”

As though patience were to be shown generally only toward unbelievers and sacrilegious persons, and anger against a Gentile were to be considered harmful while anger against a brother were useful, when in fact the stubborn agitation of a disturbed mind brings harm upon itself, no matter against whom it has been aroused.

What greater obstinacy—or rather, what greater folly—could there be than that, through the dullness of a brutish mind, someone cannot even distinguish the exact wording? For it is not said, “Everyone who is angry with a foreigner shall be liable to judgment,” which perhaps, according to their interpretation, could have allowed an exception in the case of companions in our faith and religious conversion. Rather, the Gospel deliberately expresses itself by saying, “Everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment” (Matthew 5).

[Note: By “the rule of truth” he means the truth of the matter itself, or the Gospel saying, “You are all brothers” (Matthew 22), etc. St. Jerome notes (*Against Helvidius*, chapter 8) that in the divine Scriptures people are called brothers in four ways: by nature, by nation, by kinship, and by affection. Again, brothers by affection are named in two ways: spiritually—or perhaps specifically—and commonly. “To avoid prolonging the matter,” he says, “I shall return to the final division: that people are called brothers by affection, which is divided into the spiritual and the common. Spiritually [or specifically], because all Christians are called brothers, as in: ‘Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell together in unity!’ And in another psalm the Savior says: ‘I will tell your name to my brothers,’ etc. Commonly, because all human beings, born from one father, are joined to one another by equal kinship: ‘Say to those who hate you, “You are our brothers,”’ etc. (John 20).” Thus far Jerome.]

Although, according to the rule of truth, we ought to regard every human being as a brother, nevertheless in this passage the term “brother” more particularly designates one who is faithful and shares our way of life, rather than a pagan.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On those who, while pretending to be patient, provoke their brothers to anger by silence

What shall we say of this? Sometimes we think ourselves patient because, when provoked, we disdain to answer; yet by bitter silence, or by mocking movements and gestures, we taunt our agitated brothers in such a way that we provoke them to anger more by our silent expression than swollen insults could have incited them. We consider ourselves entirely free from guilt before God because we have uttered nothing with our mouths that could have caused us to be marked or condemned in human judgment.

As though before God only words, and not especially the will, were held guilty; as though only the act of sin, and not also the desire and intention, were regarded as criminal; or as though judgment sought only what each person has done through speech, and not also what he has tried to do through silence.

For not only the character of the disturbance inflicted, but also the intention of the one who provokes it, belongs to the offense. Therefore our true Judge’s examination will inquire not how the quarrel was aroused, but through whose fault it blazed up.

[Note: This has been emended in the present edition, although Dionysius, together with the manuscripts, reads it differently (see column 6, chapter 9). “For the effect of the sin” is the result of the sin. The present reading fits better with what precedes, where he says: “As though before God only words, and not especially the will, were held guilty; and only the act of sin, and not also the desire and intention, were regarded as criminal.” For what is the disposition of sin but the will, desire, and intention of the sinner? The meaning is plainly what the words express: that God regards more the disposition or will of the sinner than the manner and sequence of the sinning, for “God looks upon the heart” (1 Samuel 16). To this, however, Dionysius’s paraphrase seems rather contrary: “For the effect of the sin must be considered, not merely the order of the deed.” See chapters 11 and 12, column 17.]

For what difference is there between someone killing his brother with his own sword and driving him to death by some deceit, when it is clear that he has destroyed him by his fraud or crime? It is not enough that a blind man has not been pushed headlong into danger by one’s own hand, if one is equally guilty who, though able to call back a man already leaning toward and close to the pit, has refused to do so. Nor is only the person guilty who has strangled someone with his own hand; so too is the one who prepared or placed the noose, or who, though able to remove it, refused to do so.

Thus it is of no benefit to remain silent if we claim silence for ourselves precisely so that what ought to have been done through insult we may do through silence, imitating certain gestures by which the person whom we ought to have cared for is inflamed to more vehement anger, while we are praised above all this for his harm and destruction. Surely a person is even more criminal for this very reason: that he has wanted to seek glory for himself through his brother’s ruin.

[Note: This is the evil and perverse silence in which someone, out of bitterness of spirit, contempt, or mockery of his neighbor, remains silent and does not deign to address or answer him, in order to irritate and provoke him more. St. Gregory speaks of such silence in Book V of the *Moralia* (chapter 31): “Sometimes anger, having disturbed the mind, imposes silence as though by judgment; and, because it does not express itself outwardly through the tongue, it burns more fiercely within. Thus an angry person withdraws his conversation from his neighbor and, by saying nothing, declares how estranged he is. Sometimes this severity of silence is practiced as a prudent disciplinary measure, provided that the rule of discernment is carefully preserved in the depths of the heart. But sometimes, while the inflamed mind is restrained from its usual conversation, with the passage of time it becomes entirely separated from love of its neighbor. More bitter goads enter the mind, and causes arise that exasperate it more severely; and the speck in the angry person’s eye becomes a beam when anger is changed into hatred. Often anger enclosed in the mind by silence boils more violently and forms silent, clamorous voices. It presents to itself words by which it may be exasperated and, as though sitting in judgment on the case, answers more harshly once exasperated. Thus it happens that the disturbed mind feels the greater tumult of its silence, and the closed flame of anger consumes it more severely.” Thus Gregory. Elsewhere it will be said that silence is an excellent remedy for suppressing and calming both one’s own anger and that of one’s neighbor.]

Such silence will therefore be equally harmful to both: for just as it increases sadness in the other’s heart, so it does not allow it to be extinguished in one’s own.

Against such people the prophet’s curse is very appropriately directed: “Woe to him who gives his friend drink, pouring out his gall and making him drunk, so that he may look upon his nakedness; he is filled with disgrace instead of glory” (Habakkuk 2).

The following passage also refers to such people: “Every brother who supplants will utterly supplant, and every friend will walk deceitfully; a man will mock his brother and will not speak the truth. For they have stretched out their tongue like a bow of falsehood and not of truth” (Jeremiah 9).

Often feigned patience kindles anger more sharply than speech, and malicious silence surpasses the harshest verbal insults; the wounds of enemies are more lightly endured than the deceitful flatteries of those who mock.

Of such people the prophet says: “His words are softer than oil, yet they are arrows” (Psalm 54).

And elsewhere:

[Note: St. Jerome translates: “The words of a whisperer seem simple, yet they reach the innermost parts of the heart” (Proverbs 26). A similar saying occurs in Proverbs 18: “The words of a double-tongued person seem simple, yet they reach to the innermost parts of the belly.”]

“The words of the crafty are smooth, but they strike the innermost parts of the belly” (Proverbs 26).

The following can also be elegantly applied to them: “With his mouth he speaks peace to his friend, but secretly he lays snares for him” (Jeremiah 9). Yet by these snares the deceiver is more deceived himself.

For, “He who prepares a net before the face of his friend surrounds his own feet with it; and he who digs a pit for his neighbor falls into it himself” (Proverbs 26).

[Note: The Vulgate text reads: “A man who speaks with flattering and deceitful words to his friend spreads a net for his feet” (Proverbs 29). St. Jerome notes that both readings can be explained: “for his feet” and “for his own feet,” owing to the ambiguity of the Greek verb περιβάλλει, which means both “to spread around” and “to surround.” It can therefore refer either to the person deceived—for “he who digs a pit for his neighbor falls into it”—or to the deceiver himself. Thus deceitful nets entangle not so much the person around whose feet they are spread as the person who spreads them. Thus St. Jerome.]

Finally, when a great multitude came with swords and clubs to seize the Lord, no murderer proved more cruel toward the author of our life than the man who, going before them all with the feigned honor of a greeting, imposed a kiss of deceitful love. To him the Lord said, “Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke 22). That is: Has the bitterness of your persecution and hatred assumed the appearance by which the sweetness of true love is expressed?

The prophet also more openly and forcefully magnifies the violence of this grief:

[Note: The evils inflicted by strangers cause less pain. But the torments we suffer from those whose affection we had presumed upon rage more fiercely within us, because, together with bodily harm, we are tortured by the loss of love, says Blessed Gregory (*Homily 35 on the Gospels*).]

“For if my enemy had reviled me, I could surely have endured it; and if one who hated me had spoken great things against me, I would surely have hidden myself from him. But you, a man of one mind with me, my guide and my acquaintance, who together with me enjoyed sweet food—we walked in the house of God in harmony” (Psalm 54).

## CHAPTER XIX. On those who fast out of indignation

[Col. 1034B]

There is another profane kind of sadness that would not deserve mention unless we knew that some brothers practice it. When they have been saddened or angered, they obstinately abstain even from food itself, so that—something we cannot say without shame—those who, when calm, claim that they cannot postpone eating until the sixth hour, or at most the ninth, when they have been filled with sadness or fury do not even notice fasts lasting two days, and sustain such exhaustion from hunger by the satisfaction of anger.

[Note: This is a phrase characteristic of Cassian, as we have often noted.]

In this they plainly incur the crime of sacrilege: they endure fasts that are to be offered specially to God alone for the humiliation of the heart and the cleansing of sins, but endure them instead because of diabolical pride.

[Note: Since sacrilege, in the general sense, is every abuse of a sacred thing or of something dedicated to the worship of God, a kind of sacrilege seems to be committed by one who abstains from food or fasts out of anger or indignation, because he offends God in the very practice by which he ought to worship him.]

This is as though they were presenting prayers and sacrifices not to God but to demons, and deserved to hear the Mosaic rebuke: “They sacrificed to demons and not to God, to gods whom they had not known” (Deuteronomy 32).

## CHAPTER XX. On the simulated patience of certain people who offer the other cheek to be struck

[Col. 1035A]

We are also aware of another kind of madness found in some brothers under the appearance of counterfeit patience. It is not enough for them to have stirred up quarrels unless they also provoke the one who incites them to strike them with goading words. Although they may have been touched by only a slight impulse, they offer another part of their body to be struck, as though by this they intended to fulfill the perfection of the commandment that says:

[Note: We said above that this saying does not contain an absolute command, but partly a command and partly counsel. The command is that we should rather turn the other cheek—that is, accept another injury—than avenge the one already received; or, as stated here, that we should not repay in kind, meaning an equal or similar injury, or return evil for evil; and that we should be inwardly ready to endure injuries whenever charity and God’s glory appear to require it. The counsel is that, even when neither charity nor God’s glory demands this of us, we may nevertheless, for the sake of mortification, carry these things out literally—not indeed by irritating or provoking our neighbor to inflict injury upon us, which is rightly criticized here, but by stirring up and strengthening ourselves to receive and endure it if it should be inflicted.]

“If anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also” (Matthew 5). They are entirely ignorant of the force and purpose of Scripture, for they think they are practicing evangelical patience through the vice of anger.

To eradicate this at the root, not only retaliation and the provocation of contention are forbidden, but we are also commanded to calm the fury of the one who strikes us by enduring a doubled injury.

## CHAPTER XXI. Germanus asks how those who obey Christ’s commands are deprived of evangelical perfection

Germanus: How can a person be reproached who, fulfilling the evangelical command, not only does not retaliate but is even prepared for the injury to be doubled?

## CHAPTER XXII. Joseph’s answer: Christ observes not only the deed but also the will

[Col. 1035C]

Joseph: As was said shortly before (Chapter 18), [Col. 1036A] we must consider not only the deed itself that is performed, but also the quality of the mind and the intention of the person performing it.

Therefore, if you weigh in the innermost examination of your heart with what disposition and feeling each action is performed, you will see that the virtue of patience and gentleness can by no means be fulfilled by the contrary spirit—that is, by impatience and fury.

Our Lord and Savior, instructing us in the profound virtue of patience and gentleness—not merely so that we may display it on our lips, but so that we may store it in the hidden recesses of our soul—gave us this pattern of evangelical perfection, saying: “If anyone strikes you on your right cheek,

[Note: This is the moral interpretation, also favored by St. Jerome in his commentary: “According to the mystical understanding,” he says, “when the right cheek has been struck, we are not commanded to offer the left, but the other—that is, the other right cheek; for the righteous person has no left cheek.”]

offer him the other also” (Matthew 5). “Other,” without doubt, means the right cheek. What other right cheek can be understood except the face, so to speak, of the inner person?

[Note: That is, readiness or preparation of spirit to receive and endure injuries. St. Augustine, in the place cited above, teaches that the Gospel saying about offering the cheek is to be understood in this way. See St. Thomas on chapter 12 of the Epistle to the Romans.]

Through this he wished utterly to uproot every source of anger from the deepest recesses of the soul: if your outward right cheek receives the assault of the striker, the inner person too should offer his right side to be struck through the assent of humility, sympathizing with the suffering of the outward person and, in a certain sense, yielding and submitting his body to the striker’s injury, so that the inner person may not be moved, even silently within, by the beating of the outward person.

[Note: The outward right cheek. Two excellent examples, entirely relevant to this passage and, I hope, useful to readers, come to mind. The first concerns Spiridion, bishop of Cyprus, who, as we read in his life (in Surius, December 14), once went to the emperor Constantius, by whom he had been summoned. He wore a cheap garment, held a palm staff in his hand, and had a clay vessel hanging from his neck; in short, he looked like a despised and insignificant man. As he entered the palace, a certain person considered it disgraceful that a man of such lowly appearance should enter the royal palace and insolently struck him across his sacred cheek. The holy man endured this patiently and also presented the other cheek to the striker with a ready spirit of endurance. The incident so shamed that insolent man that he immediately became his suppliant and begged forgiveness for his rash boldness. Spiridion willingly granted it and fatherly instructed him to restrain himself from inflicting injury. As a result, he was honored by leading men, who escorted him with the greatest reverence to the emperor.

The second example concerns St. Bernard (*Life*, Book III, chapter 6). A certain regular cleric came to Clairvaux and persistently insisted that he be received as a monk. When the holy Father advised him to return to his own church and refused to receive him, the man, like a madman, attacked him and struck his cheek, so violently that redness immediately followed the blow and swelling followed the redness. Those who were present were already rushing upon the sacrilegious man, but the servant of God forestalled them, crying out and adjuring them by the name of Christ not to touch him, but to lead him away carefully and look after him so that no one might harm him.]

You see, then, how far such people are from evangelical perfection, which teaches that patience is to be preserved not in words but in the inner tranquility of the heart. When something adverse occurs, it commands us to guard it in such a way that we not only keep ourselves free from the disturbance of anger, but also, by yielding to the injuries of those who have been agitated through their own fault,

[Note: That is, yielding to their injuries and patiently enduring them; or, as the Apostle says, “giving place to wrath”; or, as our paraphraser says, “humbling and submitting ourselves to those who have been agitated, we must compel their injuries to return to peacefulness, once their appetite for striking has been satisfied, conquering their fury by our gentleness,” etc. The passage alludes, though more obscurely, to Matthew’s saying: “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also” (Matthew 5). He teaches from Christ’s saying that the perfection of Christian and religious patience reaches the point that a person who has been struck, beaten with slaps or blows, patiently endures until the other person is at last satisfied with striking and becomes calm. Thus evil is conquered by good, as follows.]

we compel them to return to peacefulness once their appetite for violence has been satisfied, conquering their fury by our gentleness.

And in this way we shall also fulfill the Apostle’s saying: “Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good” (Romans 12).

[Note: St. Thomas excellently explains what it means to be conquered by evil or to conquer evil: “It is natural for a human being to wish to conquer an adversary and not be conquered by him. But something is conquered by another when it is drawn toward that other, just as water is conquered by fire when it is drawn toward the heat of fire. If, therefore, a good person, because of the evil inflicted upon him by someone, is drawn into doing evil to him, the good person is conquered by evil. But if, conversely, because of the benefit that the good person shows his persecutor, he draws him to love, the good person conquers evil.”]

It is entirely certain that this cannot be fulfilled by those who utter words of gentleness and humility with such a spirit and swelling pride that they not only fail to calm the fire of anger they have conceived, but cause it to blaze more fiercely both in themselves and in the sense of their agitated brother.

Even if they could somehow remain gentle and calm themselves, they would still gain no fruits of righteousness, claiming the glory of patience at the cost of their neighbor. In this they are altogether alien from that Apostolic charity which “does not seek its own” (1 Corinthians 13), but what belongs to others. Nor does it desire riches in such a way as to make profit for itself through its neighbor’s loss, or seek to acquire anything through another’s impoverishment.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That the strong and healthy person is the one who yields to another’s will

It must be understood generally that the stronger role belongs to the person who subjects his own will to his brother’s will, rather than to one who is found more stubborn in defending and maintaining his own determinations.

The one who supports and tolerates his neighbor takes the place of a healthy and robust person; the other takes the place of the weak and, in a certain sense, sick person. The latter must sometimes be gently handled and encouraged, so that, for the sake of his rest and peace, it may even be healthy to relax something of what is necessary.

In this, no one should think that he has diminished anything from his own perfection, even if, by condescending, he has lowered something of the strictness he had undertaken. On the contrary, he should know that he has gained much more through the good of patience and long-suffering.

For the Apostle commands: [Note: The Apostle’s words are Romans 15: “We who are stronger ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak and not please ourselves.” The Greek word is βαστάζειν, meaning “to carry” or “to bear on the shoulders,” as porters do, who are called βαστάζοντες in Greek. The Apostle expresses the same in other words: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6).]

“You who are strong, bear the weaknesses of the weak” (Romans 15); and, “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6).

A weak person never supports another weak person, nor can one who is similarly sick tolerate or heal the sick. Rather, the weak person is healed by one who is not himself subject to weakness. For rightly it is said to him: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4).

## CHAPTER XXIV. That the weak are injurious and cannot endure injuries

It must also be noted that the character of weak people is always such that they are ready and eager to inflict insults and engage in quarrels, while they themselves do not wish to be touched even by the suspicion of the slightest injury. Although they freely overstep all limits in hurling insolent abuse, they are unwilling to endure even the smallest and lightest offense.

[Note: Above, chapter 3: “This is the firm and indissoluble union of faithful friendship, founded solely upon equality in virtue.” And chapter 5: “The full and perfect grace of friendship cannot endure except among perfect men who share the same virtue.”]

Therefore, according to the previously cited judgment of the elders, stable and unbroken charity cannot last except among people of the same virtue and purpose.

[Note: As stated earlier (Chapter 3): “We know many who have entered upon this purpose”—that is, this manner of life—“who, though bound by the most fervent fellowship because of the charity of Christ, could not preserve it perpetually and without interruption. For although they relied upon a good beginning in their association, they did not maintain the purpose they had undertaken with one and equal zeal. There was between them a certain temporary affection, because it was preserved not by the equal virtue of both, but by the patience of one.”]

For it is necessary that such friendship eventually be severed, however carefully one of the parties may have guarded it.

## CHAPTER XXV. Germanus asks how the strong person can be one who does not always support the weak

Germanus: In what respect, then, can the patience of a perfect man be praiseworthy if he is unable always to tolerate the weak?

## CHAPTER XXVI. Joseph’s answer: the weak person does not allow himself to be supported

[Col. 1038C]

Joseph: I did not say that the virtue and patience of the strong and robust person must be overcome, but that the grave illness of the weak person, nourished by the support of the healthy one, may daily decline for the worse,

[Note: Cassiodorus speaks of these causes in his *Book on Friendship*, chapter 6: “There are four vices by which the noble dignity of friendship is often darkened: anger, instability, suspicion, and loquacity.” Elsewhere (chapters 17 and 28): “There are four things from which the separation of friends arises: affection, attachment, security, and pleasantness. It belongs to love to advise, provide for, and show benefits to a friend. Attachment concerns a certain pleasant and very sweet delight. Security concerns the sharing of every secret without fear or suspicion. Pleasantness concerns friendly, familiar, sweet, and gentle conversation about prosperity and adversity, useful and harmful things, and everything by which the human mind is affected.

“In these matters friendship suffers a separation. For although love remains in some form, that very sweet affection of love is withdrawn; security, through which one disclosed one’s secrets, perishes; and the pleasantness created by gentle conversation is disturbed. Love therefore remains, but the grace of familiarity is removed.

“Cicero—or Laelius in Cicero, in the passage cited above—says: ‘There is sometimes a kind of calamity in ending friendships, and it may be necessary. The vices of friends often break out against the friends themselves and against outsiders, whose disgrace nevertheless does not redound to their friends. Such friendships should therefore be cleansed by a relaxation of use and, as I have heard Cato say, should be unstitched rather than cut apart—unless some wholly intolerable injury has flared up, so that it is neither right nor honorable, nor possible, to avoid immediate estrangement and separation.

“But if some change in character or interests has occurred, as commonly happens, care must be taken lest it appear that not only friendship has been laid aside but enmity also taken up. Nothing is more shameful than to wage war against one with whom you have lived familiarly. Care must also be taken lest friendships turn into serious hostilities, from which quarrels, curses, and insults arise. Yet if these are bearable, they must be endured, and this honor must be paid to the old friendship: that the person who commits the fault, not the one who suffers the injury, should be in the wrong.’ Thus far Cicero. At least for the most part, these statements do not conflict with Christian philosophy.]

and generate causes by which either he himself should no longer be tolerated or, reasoning that the patience of his neighbor has become a reproach and deformity of his own impatience, he may at some point prefer to depart rather than always be supported by another’s magnanimity.

Therefore, for those who desire to preserve the affection of companionship inviolate, we judge that the following must above all be observed: first, when provoked by any injury, the monk must keep not only his lips but also the depths of his heart tranquil.

If he senses that these have been disturbed even slightly,

[Note: This is excellent advice, likewise commended by the holy Fathers: when provoked by abuse or another injury, we should restrain our tongue and preserve patience silently in our hearts. Thus the Church sings of the holy martyrs:

“They are struck with swords like sheep;

No murmur resounds, no complaint;

But with a silent heart, a conscience at peace,

The mind preserves its patience.”

St. Ambrose, *On Duties*, Book II, chapters 2 and following: “When someone abuses us, provokes us, incites us to violence, or summons us to a quarrel, then let us practice silence; then let us not be ashamed to become mute. For the sinner who provokes us and inflicts injury wishes to make us like himself.

“Finally, if you remain silent and pretend not to notice, he usually says: ‘Why are you silent? Speak, if you dare. But you do not dare; you are mute; I have made you speechless.’ If you remain silent, he is more deeply enraged: he considers himself defeated, mocked, passed over, and ridiculed. If you answer, he thinks himself superior because he has found an equal.

“If you remain silent, it will be said: ‘He abused this man, and this one disregarded him.’ If you return the insult, it will be said: ‘Both of them abused each other.’ Both are condemned; neither is acquitted. His purpose, therefore, is to provoke us, so that I may say and do things like him. But it is the part of the righteous person to disregard the matter, say nothing, preserve the fruit of a good conscience, and entrust himself more to the judgment of the good than to the insolence of the accuser,” etc.

St. Jerome reports in his letter to Eustochium that Paula of Rome used this same remedy during the quarrels of others: “Whenever,” he says, “an enemy became especially insolent and advanced as far as verbal quarrels, she would recite that verse of the Psalter: ‘When the sinner stood against me, I was silent and humbled myself; I was silent from good things,’ etc.” (Psalm 38).]

he should restrain himself entirely in silence and carefully observe what the Psalmist recalls: “I was troubled and did not speak” (Psalm 76).

And again: “I said, ‘I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue. I placed a guard over my mouth when the sinner stood against me. I was mute and humbled myself, and I was silent from good things’” (Psalm 38).

He should not consider only his present condition and utter what furious anger suggests in the moment or what an exasperated mind dictates. Rather, he should either recall the grace of former love or foresee in his mind the restoration of peace that is to be renewed, contemplating it even in the midst of agitation as though it were about to return immediately.

While he preserves himself for the sweetness of the harmony that will soon be restored, he will not feel the bitterness of the present quarrels. Thus he will answer only in ways by which, once charity has been restored, he cannot be made guilty by himself or reproved by another. In this way he will fulfill the prophetic saying: “In wrath, you will remember mercy” (Habakkuk 3).

## CHAPTER XXVII. How anger is to be restrained
Therefore we must restrain every movement of anger and govern it by discerning judgment, lest we be swept away by headlong fury into what Solomon condemns:

> “The fool gives full vent to his anger, but the wise person dispenses it by degrees” (Proverbs 29).

[Note: Ciaconius corrected the text in this way from the Greek and from Dionysius the Paraphrast, whereas the ancient manuscripts read: “The wicked gives full vent to all his anger.” The correction is supported by the Vulgate reading, which has: “The fool gives full vent to all his spirit; the wise person delays and reserves it for the future” (Proverbs 29). Saint Jerome also borrowed the explanation of this saying given here by the abbot. Saint Jerome writes: “The fool gives full vent to all his spirit”: driven by impatience, he acts so that his whole spirit is brought forth externally. For this reason disturbance more quickly casts him out, because no discipline of wisdom more quickly contains him. “But the wise person delays,” and so forth. For the person who has been injured does not desire to avenge himself immediately, because, even while enduring, he wishes to spare; nevertheless, he does not fail to understand that all things will be avenged at the final judgment. The ancient translation has the passage as follows: “The wicked gives full vent to all his anger, but the wise person distributes it by portions.” For the fool is inflamed toward revenge by the disturbance of anger, whereas the wise person gradually weakens and expels it through mature deliberation and restraint.]

That is, the fool is inflamed toward revenge by the disturbance of anger, whereas the wise person gradually weakens and expels it through mature deliberation and restraint. Likewise, there is what the Apostle says:

> “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to anger” (Romans 12).

[Note: In Greek, ἐκδικοῦντες, that is, “avenging,” specifically by one’s own authority. Our translator renders this as “defending,” and not incorrectly. In Scripture and in ecclesiastical usage, “to defend” is often used for “to avenge.” Thus Psalm 8 has: “that you may destroy the enemy and the avenger,” where Augustine reads “the defender.” Again, for the words in Revelation 6, “How long, Lord, will you not judge and avenge our blood?” the Church sings: “How long will you not defend our blood?” and so forth.]

That is, do not let anger drive you toward revenge, but:

[Note: Just as three kinds of anger may be considered when an injury is inflicted—the anger of the person inflicting it, the anger of the person suffering it, and the anger of God who is offended—so the Fathers interpret this saying in three ways. Regarding one’s own anger, the meaning is: “Give place to anger,” that is, let your anger quickly pass away and vanish, just as smoke immediately dissipates. Regarding another person’s anger: “Give place to anger,” that is, willingly yield to the angry person and endure his weakness, as the Apostle says elsewhere (Romans 15). The abbot Joseph gives this twofold interpretation here. Chrysostom and others, however, refer it to God’s anger and explain it thus: “Give place to anger,” namely, to divine anger; that is, leave vengeance and retribution to God. For the person who avenges himself does not permit or give place to divine anger, but anticipates and forestalls it.
