Hence the Apostle adds: “For it is written: ‘Vengeance is mine,’” and so forth—words understood as referring to God.]

> “Give place to anger.”

That is:

[Col. 1041A]

Let not your hearts be so confined by the straits of impatience and faintheartedness that, when the violent storm of agitation breaks upon them, they are unable to withstand it. Rather, be enlarged in your hearts, receiving the hostile waves of anger within the broad expanses of that charity which bears all things and endures all things (1 Corinthians 13). Thus, with your mind enlarged by the breadth of steadfastness and patience, let it contain within itself salutary recesses of deliberation, in which the most hideous smoke of anger may, as it were, be received, dispersed, and immediately vanish.

Or certainly it should be understood in this way: We give place to anger whenever, with a humble and tranquil mind, we yield to another person’s agitation and, in a certain sense, acknowledge ourselves worthy of any injury, submitting to raging impatience. But those who distort the meaning of apostolic perfection so far as to think that people give place to anger by withdrawing from the angry person seem to me not to cut off the fuel of dissension but to nourish it. Unless a neighbor’s anger is immediately overcome by humble satisfaction, the person who flees rather than defuses it provokes it further.

Similar, too, is what Solomon says:

[Note: The Vulgate text reads: “Do not be quick to anger, because anger rests in the lap of the fool.” These words do not forbid anger altogether; rather, they forbid being quick to anger—that is, according to Olympiodorus’s explanation, they forbid conceiving the evil disposition of anger in such a way that it passes into the heart’s affection. With the same distinction the Apostle Saint James says: “Let every person be quick to hear, but slow to speak and slow to anger” (James 1).]

> “Do not hasten in your spirit to become angry, because anger rests in the lap of fools” (Ecclesiastes 7);

and:

[Note: The Vulgate version reads: “What your eyes have seen, do not bring forth quickly in a quarrel, lest afterward you be unable to make amends when you have disgraced your friend.” In the royal Bibles the words “What your eyes have seen” are absent.]

> “Do not rush quickly into a quarrel, lest you regret it at the end” (Proverbs 25).

[Note: Saint Jerome imitates this interpretation in his treatment of that passage from Ecclesiastes. He writes: “He does not say, ‘Do not hasten to become angry’ as though he were permitting anger to be delayed; rather, he says, ‘Do not hasten in your spirit to become angry,’ because, when anger is postponed while it is still fresh and raging, it can more easily be removed once it has been calmed. And because anger, always joined to pride, desires revenge,” and so forth. Saint Jerome is plainly speaking there of evil and blameworthy anger, which the Wise Man says rests in the lap of the fool—that is, the desire for personal revenge, immoderate and furious anger, or quarrelling and irascibility, as here. Such anger is invariably vicious, and its delay is not approved when haste is condemned.]

For he does not condemn hastiness in quarrelling or anger in such a way as to approve their slowness. Likewise, we should accept the following:

[Note: The Vulgate reading is: “The fool immediately reveals his anger, but the prudent person conceals the injury.”]

> “The fool declares his anger at that very moment, but the astute person conceals his disgrace” (Proverbs 12).

For he does not decree that the shameful passion of anger must be concealed by wise people in such a way that, while condemning the speed of anger, he fails to forbid its delay. Rather, if anger breaks in through the necessity of human weakness, he judged that it should be concealed for this reason: so that, while it is wisely covered for the present, it may be destroyed forever. For this is the nature of anger: when delayed, it grows weak and perishes; when expressed, it blazes more and more.

Therefore our breasts must be widened and enlarged, lest, constricted by the narrowness of faintheartedness, they be filled with the turbulent surges of anger. Otherwise, with a narrow heart, we shall be unable to receive, according to the prophet, God’s exceedingly broad commandment, nor say with the prophet:

> “I ran along the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (Psalm 118).

For that steadfastness is wisdom, we are taught by the clearest testimonies of Scripture:

[Note: The Vulgate has: “The patient person is governed by much wisdom, but the impatient person exalts his foolishness.”]

> “The steadfast person is exceedingly abundant in prudence, but the fainthearted person is very foolish” (Proverbs 24).

For this reason Scripture recalls, concerning the one who laudably asked the Lord for the gift of wisdom:

> “And the Lord gave Solomon exceedingly great wisdom and understanding, and breadth of heart like the immeasurable sand of the sea” (1 Kings 4).

## CHAPTER XXVIII. That Friendships Entered into by Conspiracy Cannot Remain Firm

This too has very often been confirmed by many experiences: in no way can those who entered into a covenant of friendship through conspiracy preserve an unbroken harmony,

[Note: Dionysius’s paraphrase is: “Those who entered into a treaty of friendship with an oath.” This agrees sufficiently with what follows, where they are said to be made transgressors of their sacrament—that is, of their oath—or, as Dionysius likewise explains, of the pact they entered into.

It appears from this passage that at that time certain monks were accustomed to form among themselves private and particular associations and friendships, even employing an oath by which they pledged mutual fidelity and a closer familiarity and relationship. Hence they were called fellow-conspirators and conspirators. Saint Basil strongly condemns and detests this kind of friendship as harmful to religion and exposed to many dangers, and does so in more than one place (Sermons 1 and 2 on the Institution of Monasticism):

“In the common fellowship”—that is, among monks—“the law of charity absolutely does not permit friendships or associations to be formed separately. For it is entirely impossible that these affections, which incline more toward one side than toward another, should not greatly harm the common harmony of all. Therefore all must love one another equally, and the same measure of charity must be maintained toward the whole assembly of the brethren. If anyone is found who appears, for whatever reason, to love a brother monk, a relative, or anyone else with a greater inclination of mind, he must be corrected as one who injures public charity. For, by loving one person more than another, he readily shows that he considers the rest inferior in love.”

Again, elsewhere (Discourse 1 on the Love of God and Neighbor):

“Whoever holds one person dearer than the others in the community makes himself guilty, since he does not possess perfect charity. Therefore this individual affection must be kept far from every association and gathering, as though it were an indecent quarrel. For just as the former produces open enmities, so the latter generates envy and hostility.”

Again, in the Monastic Constitutions (chapter 30):

“The brethren ought to have mutual charity among themselves, but not in such a way that two or three form an association among themselves apart from the others. For this is not charity but sedition and division, and it is evidence of the wickedness of those who form such a group. If such people truly possessed the dignity of common discipline, they would undoubtedly maintain common and equal charity toward all. But if they voluntarily separate themselves from the others and form a group, this is a vicious reconciliation of friendship; it must be something different from the common institutions that unites them among themselves, and this is certainly nothing other than an innovation against the ancient stability of discipline.”

Thus far Saint Basil, who was exceedingly sharp and discerning in judging affections of this kind.

Moreover, Cassian, among the other institutions of the ancient monks, reports that such friendships, familiar gatherings, and private conversations were strictly forbidden and most severely punished among them:

“Each person carries out his work in such a way that, while reciting a psalm or any Scripture from memory, he gives neither opportunity nor time not only to harmful conspiracy or wicked counsels but even to idle conversations, his mouth and heart alike being occupied in spiritual meditation. With the greatest vigilance it is guarded that no one be found to have stood with another, especially younger monks [or: a younger monk], even for a moment, or to have withdrawn anywhere with him, or to have held hands with him. If anyone is found to have done anything contrary to the discipline of this rule, he will be pronounced guilty of no light offense as a disobedient person and transgressor of the commandments, and he will be unable to escape suspicion of conspiracy and wicked counsel. Unless he cleanses this offense by public penance in the presence of all the brothers assembled, none of them is permitted to take part in the brothers’ prayer.”

This is Cassian (Institutes, Book 2, chapter 13).

John Climacus likewise says, when discussing discernment in Step 26:

> “I have seen young men who loved one another with the purest love and according to God, yet, when they perceived that the consciences of others were being harmed by this, they agreed among themselves to distance themselves from one another for a time.”

Moved by these examples and arguments, Saint Benedict, too, in order to exclude such singular and disordered affections, used the same caution and discernment. In chapter 69 of the Rule he earnestly warns that no one, on any occasion, should presume to defend or, as it were, protect one monk against another in the monastery, even if they are joined by any degree of blood relationship. Nor should monks presume to do this in any way, because the gravest occasion for scandals can arise from it. If anyone transgresses this rule, he is to be restrained more severely.

Saint Bernard also vigorously attacks these corrupt associations and private factions of monks in Sermon 24 on the Song of Songs, where he vividly depicts and reproves the conduct and gatherings of such whisperers who conspire and murmur among themselves:

> “You may see them walking apart, meeting together, and sitting together; then immediately they loosen their shameless tongues into detestable whispering. They enter into familiarity for slander, united for discord. They reconcile among themselves the most hostile friendships, and an odious conference is celebrated with a common and harmonious affection for wickedness. Herod and Pilate once acted in the same way, of whom the Gospel relates (Luke 23) that they became friends on that day—that is, on the day of the Lord’s Passion. When people gather together in this way, they are not eating the Lord’s Supper; rather, they are offering and drinking the cup of demons, while their tongues carry the poison of others’ destruction and their ears willingly receive the death entering them.”

The Blessed Laurence Justinian, Venetian patriarch, agrees with all of this in his book On the Discipline and Perfection of Monastic Life. There he writes, among other things (chapter 10):

> “Private conversation must be forbidden in communities of the servants of Christ. Although it may not be reprehensible in any other respect, it cannot take place without scandalizing one’s neighbors.”

And below:

> “For in familiar and excessively frequent conversations, unless they are conducted cautiously, idle talk, buffoonery, detraction, and unrestrained laughter tend to become mingled; through these the mind is distracted, compunction is dissolved, grace is withdrawn, and one’s neighbor is badly edified.”

These are the teachings of the holy Fathers.

Moreover, within this category of corrupt association and friendship, monks undoubtedly sin most gravely when they conspire and enter into a conspiracy against their abbots or superiors, as Blessed Gregory writes in the Dialogues (Book 2, chapter 3) concerning those who conspired against the holy Father Benedict and gave him poison.

Accordingly, in the Council of Chalcedon a statute is recorded against conspirators and fellow-conspirators, as found in Gratian (Question 11, canon 1):

> “The crime of conspiracies and confederacies—which in Greek is called φρατρία, ‘brotherhood’ or ‘faction’—is certainly forbidden altogether even by public laws. It is all the more fitting that it be rejected from the holy Church of God, lest it occur there. If any clerics or monks are found conspiring or confederating, or forming any brotherhoods or factions against their bishops or against other clerics, they must altogether fall from their proper rank.”

[Col. 1044C]

Here it should be noted that, although the word φρατρία, or phratria, generally signifies any fellowship, association, gathering, sect, or tribe—for the Athenian people are said to have been divided into twelve tribes, and each tribe into three phratriae—here it is understood as a faction or sedition stirred up among brothers or monks. The same is true in Saint Ephrem’s Paraenesis 39, where he makes such factionalists say:

> “Let us be joined together in a brotherhood,”

and below:

> “Let us be strong for battles and brotherhoods—that is, factions—and contradictions.”

As for what was said above from Saint Basil—that the brothers ought to love one another equally and all embrace one another equally, and that anyone who loves one person more than the others is therefore guilty and injurious to public charity—these and similar statements should not trouble anyone. They are to be understood with respect to external conduct and familiarity, or with respect to the external and common signs and duties of friendship and charity, which must be shown equally—that is, impartially and indiscriminately—to all the brothers.

With respect to the inward affection of love and certain particular duties of charity—for example, particular prayers, sacrifices, and so forth—nothing prevents, and indeed it is consistent with reason, that some people should be loved and preferred more than others, either because they are better, or because they are closer to us, more dutiful, better known, more beneficent, and so forth, provided that the intention is upright, due measure is observed, and the scandal of others is avoided. See Saint Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* II–II, question 26, article 6 and following.]

—whether because they did not try to preserve it out of a desire for perfection or in obedience to the command of apostolic charity, but for earthly affection and through the necessity and bond of an agreement; or because that most cunning enemy, in order to make them transgressors of their oath, hastens them more quickly toward breaking the bonds of friendship.

[Note: This saying was treated above (chapters 35 and 24).]

Therefore the judgment of the wisest men is entirely certain: true harmony and undivided fellowship cannot endure except among men of reformed conduct who possess the same virtue and purpose.

Thus the blessed Joseph discussed friendship in a spiritual discourse and inspired us more ardently to preserve the perpetual charity of our fellowship.

# SEVENTEENTH CONFERENCE, WHICH IS THE SECOND OF ABBOT JOSEPH

## ON THE DETERMINING OF MATTERS

[Col. 1045]

## CHAPTER I

After the preceding conference had ended, and while the silence of the night had likewise set in,

[Note: This may be understood either of the natural silence of night, of which Virgil writes in Book 4 of the *Aeneid*:

> “It was night, and the weary bodies throughout the lands  
> were taking peaceful sleep; the forests and savage seas  
> had grown quiet, while the stars revolved in their mid-course;  
> when every field is silent, and the cattle and painted birds,  
> whatever creatures occupy the broad clear lakes  
> and whatever inhabit the rough country thick with brambles,  
> laid down in sleep beneath the silent night,  
> eased their cares and their hearts forgetful of toil.”

Ovid writes similarly in Book 10 of the *Metamorphoses*: “It was the time when all things are silent.”

Or—and this seems more probable—of the religious and regular silence that was strictly observed at night even among the ancient monks. Cassian discusses this in Book 2, chapter 15 of the *Institutes*, where he treats of the silence after the night office:

> “When the psalms have been finished and the daily assembly has ended, none of them dares either to remain even briefly or to speak with another,”

and so forth.

Following their example, Saint Benedict especially commends and prescribes nocturnal silence to his monks in chapter 42 of the Rule, entitled “That no one should speak after Compline”:

> “At all times the monks ought to devote themselves to silence, but especially during the hours of the night.”

A little later he adds:

> “Therefore, when all have gathered together, let them complete”—Turrecremata says, meaning the reading of the *Conferences*—“and from there let all enter Compline unanimously. After leaving Compline, no one is to have permission to speak any further.”

If anyone is found to have violated this rule of silence, he is to be subjected to a heavier punishment, except when the necessity of receiving guests arises or when the abbot happens to command something of someone. Even that, however, must be done with the utmost gravity, moderation, and propriety.

The observations of Smaragdus and Turrecremata on this passage should be noted. Smaragdus says:

> “We must be silent after Compline so that at Matins we may rightly say: ‘Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise’; that is, during the night hours we ask the Lord to open our lips, which he had closed under his protection at Compline.”

Elsewhere we read:

> “From the hour of Compline, when prayer is given for taking sleep, no one at all should presume to speak unless a grave necessity of the monastery demands it.”

Turrecremata says:

> “It should be considered that during the nighttime three things must be taken into account in which a breach of silence may be permitted: imminent danger, urgent necessity, and an intervening question from a superior.

“Imminent danger occurs, for example, if you see a fire burning: you may lawfully shout, ask for water, and do whatever else is appropriate.

“Urgent necessity may be either spiritual or bodily. Bodily necessity arises if you see a brother suddenly suffering from a dangerous illness: you may speak and help him. For regulations established for the sake of charity ought not to work against charity.

“Spiritual necessity arises if, in such a circumstance, a sick brother wishes to confess: you may hear him and speak with him about what is necessary.

“An inquiry from a superior occurs when he asks you about something so that you may answer him. Even this, however, must be done, as stated, with the utmost gravity, both by the prelate who asks and by the subject who answers.”

These are his words.

Saint Amalarius also agrees with them (Book 4 on Ecclesiastical Offices, chapter 6). Speaking of Compline, he says:

> “Among monks, this is observed according to the Rule of Saint Benedict: from that office they fortify the enclosure of their mouths and make them unavailable for conversation until they return again to their work.”

Amalarius appears to have had in mind the ancient custom of the Egyptian monks, who, according to Saint Basil in his letter on the solitary life, used to apply themselves to manual labor at sunrise, after the morning office had been completed. Cassian also repeatedly confirms this in the books of the *Institutes* (Books 2 and 3).]

When the silence of night had intervened, we had been led by the holy abbot Joseph to a secluded cell in a private place for the sake of rest. His words had kindled a kind of fire in our hearts, and we had spent the entire night sleepless. We left the cell, withdrew nearly one hundred paces from it, and sat down in a more remote place.

## CHAPTER II. The Pious Desire of Abbot Germanus to Make Progress Is Explained

[Col. 1046A]

Since the darkness of night also provided us with an opportunity for a private and familiar conversation, once we had sat down, Abbot Germanus, sighing heavily, said:

> “What are we to do?”

[Note: They considered themselves bound by an immense danger and a most wretched predicament. Distracted by a twofold concern and troubled by a double scruple, they did not know what to do or where to turn. On the one hand, an intense desire for perfection and spiritual progress urged them to remain longer among those holy anchorites, so that they might absorb more deeply their institutions and salutary teachings and advance daily more and more through their companionship and association, by worthy emulation and imitation.

On the other hand, they were greatly tormented by the scruple that, having been established in the Bethlehemite monastery, where they had professed monastic life and obedience, they had promised to return after three years in order to obtain more easily from their superiors permission to travel and visit the places of the holy Fathers. They had been released under that condition, which they had not sufficiently prudently understood or accepted. Since a considerable amount of time had already passed in this pilgrimage, they seemed unable to remain there any longer with a safe conscience and intact obedience. Thus they believed they had to return to their own monastery, though this would cause great harm to their progress and spiritual life.

In this anxiety, therefore, they did not know what counsel to adopt or in which direction to turn. Taking this occasion, Abbot Joseph composed the discussion of this conference to calm and instruct their minds. Cassian entitled it “On Determining Matters,” because the principal question asked and treated was whether it is lawful or expedient for a monk to determine, decide, establish, promise, pledge, or otherwise define something concerning his future actions, and whether, once such a determination or pledge has been made, he is necessarily bound to fulfill it. This is the status of the question around which the entire discussion turns. From this general thesis the discussion then proceeds to the particular case of Germanus and Cassian, which was the specific and immediate subject (see chapters 27 and following below).]

“For we see ourselves bound by an immense danger and an exceedingly wretched predicament. Reason itself, and the way of life of the saints, effectively teaches us what is more beneficial for our spiritual progress, yet the promise we gave to our elders does not permit us to choose what is advantageous. We could have been formed, through the examples of such great men, for a more perfect life and purpose, if the terms of our promise did not constrain us to hasten back to the monastery.

“But if we return, no further opportunity will be granted us to come back here. If, on the other hand, we remain here and prefer to fulfill our desire, what are we to do about the good faith of the promise that we know we made to our elders, when we promised them a very swift return so that we might be permitted, even in haste, to travel through the holy places and monasteries of this province?”

And while we were thus burning with anxiety, unable to discover what should be determined concerning the condition of our salvation, we could do nothing but testify by our sighs to the necessity of our most difficult situation, accusing the tenderness of our brow and our inborn modesty,

[Note: As Ciaconius observes, “tenderness of the brow” means in Cassian a certain rustic shyness by which people are often prevented from carrying out what they hope will be useful to them. Seneca writes in Book 1, Letter 2: “I know that there is a blush which suddenly spreads even over the most serious men.” It appears more strongly in young people, who possess both more heat and a tender brow; nevertheless, it touches veterans and old men as well, and nothing was softer than Pompey’s expression. Conversely, “hard brow” is used for shamelessness. Saint Jerome writes against the Pelagians: “So that the shamelessness of the hard-browed may be crushed.” Pliny uses “iron brow” in the same sense in the *Panegyric*: “Let them uselessly offer that bloodless and iron brow to be pierced by blows”; and Terence, in the *Eunuch*, uses “hard face” for “shameless.” Seneca likewise writes in Book 2, *That Injury Cannot Befall the Wise*, chapter 17: “If he was able to do this through hardness of face, having unlearned shame through constant abuse.” The same author speaks of “weakness of brow” in Book 2 of *On Benefits*: “There are many whom weakness of brow makes generous.”]

and lamenting that, weighed down by the burden of this modesty,

[Note: That is, weighed down by the burden or impediment of modesty. This reading flows better than that of others, who read “the burden of this matter.” Germanus complains that, because of excessive shame and modesty, they had not dared to ask their own community for a longer absence and greater freedom; or, as Dionysius explains more familiarly, they could not otherwise have resisted the pleas of their fellow monks who were trying to keep them back against their progress and purpose except by promising to return very soon.]

we could not otherwise have resisted the pleas of those who wished to retain us, even against our advantage and purpose, unless we had come here after promising to return very soon. We grieved that we were afflicted by that defect of shame of which it is said:

> “There is a shame that brings sin” (Ecclesiasticus 4).

[Note: Ecclesiasticus 4 reads: “There is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that brings glory and grace.”]

## CHAPTER III. Cassian’s Counsel and His Answer to Abbot Germanus’s Question

Then I said:

> “Let counsel—or rather, the authority of the elder to whom we ought to bring our anxieties—bring relief to our distress. Whatever he determines as his judgment, let it set an end to all our anxieties as though it were a divine and heavenly answer.”

Let us have no doubt that this is granted to us by the Lord through the mouth of this holy man, both because of his merit and because of our faith. For by his gift, those who believe have often received salutary counsel from the unworthy, and those who do not believe from the holy, with the Lord granting it either because of the merit of those who answer or because of the faith of those who consult.

When the holy Abbot Germanus received these words with such eagerness, as though I had uttered them not from myself but by the Lord’s inspiration, we waited a little for the elder’s arrival and for the hour of the nocturnal assembly, which was already approaching.

[Note: It may be inferred from this that they had a fixed and appointed hour for the nocturnal gathering and office. They would not have awaited its approach if it had not been fixed and certain. Cassian discusses this in Book 2, chapter 17 of the *Institutes*, and Saint Benedict in chapters 8 and 47.]

After we had welcomed him with the customary greeting, and the prescribed number of prayers and psalms had been completed, we again sat down, as was customary, on the same *psiathia* on which we had settled ourselves for rest.

[Note: The *psiathia* are discussed in Book 4, chapter 13 of the *Institutes* and frequently elsewhere. The word appears as *psiathus*, *psiathius*, and *psiathium*, and is often and interchangeably found in the *Lives of the Fathers* and of the ancient monks.]

## CHAPTER IV. Abbot Joseph’s Question and Our Answer Concerning the Origin of Our Anxiety

Then the venerable Joseph, observing that we were more downcast in spirit and inferring that this had happened to us for a reason, addressed us in the words of the patriarch Joseph:

[Note: In the Vulgate edition these are the patriarch Joseph’s words to Pharaoh’s cupbearer and baker, who were imprisoned with him and troubled by their dreams: “Why are your faces sadder today than usual?”]

> “Why are your faces sad today?”

[Col. 1048B]

We replied:

> “Unlike those ministers of Pharaoh who were imprisoned with him, we have not seen a dream for which there is no interpreter; rather, we have spent the night sleepless, and there is no one to lighten the burden of our anxieties unless the Lord removes them through your discernment.”

Then he, who in both name and merit might be compared with the patriarch Joseph, said:

> “Is not the healing of human thoughts from the Lord? Bring them into the open, for divine mercy is able, according to your faith, to provide them with a remedy through our counsel.”

## CHAPTER V. Abbot Germanus Explains Why We Would Prefer Either to Remain in Egypt or to Be Recalled to Syria

At this Germanus said:

> “We believed that, after being filled not only with spiritual joy but also with abundant progress through the sight of your blessedness, we would return to our monastery, and that after our return we would pursue, even if only through weak emulation, the things we had obtained through your instruction.

“This was also what compelled us to make a promise to our elders out of affection for them, since we believed that in that monastery we might in some measure imitate the sublimity of your life and teaching. Therefore, while we thought that all our joy would come from this, we are instead consumed by intolerable grief when we consider that we cannot obtain what we know is salutary for us by that course.

“Thus we are now constrained from both sides. If we wish to fulfill the promise that, compelled by our elders’ affection, we uttered, and that we made publicly before all the brothers in the cave in which our Lord shone forth from the palace of the virginal womb,

[Note: This cave, that is, the grotto in which our Lord was born, was discussed elsewhere (Book 4, chapter 12). The Bethlehemite monastery was near it; Cassian received the monastic habit there together with Germanus, as he himself testifies in several places.]

as he himself witnessed, we incur the greatest harm to our spiritual life. But if, forgetful of our promise, we remain in these regions and prefer the advantage of our perfection to that agreement, we fear the dangers of the broken and unfulfilled promise of falsehood.

“Nor can we relieve our anxiety by this counsel: that, once the condition of our promise has been fulfilled through a very swift return, we should quickly return again to these places. For although even a short delay is dangerous and harmful for those striving toward progress in spiritual matters and virtue, we would discharge our promised faith through a belated return,

[Note: That is, slowly, late, after a long delay. It is contrasted with the very early and very swift return mentioned here and by Dionysius.]

if we did not know that we would be bound irrevocably to our elders not only by affection but also by their authority, so that thereafter no opportunity whatsoever would be granted us to return to these places.”

## CHAPTER VI. Abbot Joseph Asks Whether Greater Progress Would Be Granted Us in Egypt Than in Syria

Then the blessed Joseph, after remaining silent for a little while, said:

> “Are you certain that greater progress in spiritual matters can be granted to you in this region?”

## CHAPTER VII. The Answer Concerning the Difference between the Institutions of the Two Provinces
Germanus: Although we ought also to give the greatest thanks to those who taught us [Note: [Col. 1049D] That is, from childhood: at the age when Cassian became a monk with his Germanus in that Bethlehemite monastery, as he himself testifies. Hence, in his preface to Castor he says: “What, from our childhood, while living among them and stirred on by their daily exhortations and examples, we either attempted to do or learned,” etc. And again, in the eleventh Conference, chap. 1: “When we were living in a monastery of Syria, after the first rudiments of faith, as our growth gradually increased, we began to desire a greater grace of perfection,” etc.] from childhood to attempt great things and, having given us a taste of the good, planted in our inward parts an outstanding thirst for perfection. Yet, if our judgment is to be trusted in anything, we make no comparison between these practices and those which we learned there—not to mention the incomparable purity of your way of life, which we believe is conferred upon you not only through the strictness of your mind and purpose, but also with the favoring assistance of the place itself. Therefore, we do not doubt that, in order to imitate the magnificence of your perfection, this teaching which is being delivered hurriedly cannot suffice for us unless we also receive the assistance of dwelling here, and unless the instruction of a long period, through daily formation, in some measure shakes off the torpor of our heart.

## CHAPTER VIII. That perfect men ought to define nothing absolutely; and whether they may rescind what has been defined without sin

Joseph: It is certainly sound and perfect, and wholly in keeping with our profession, that we effectively fulfill whatever we decide under some pledge. [Col. 1050B] For this reason a monk ought not to define anything abruptly, lest he either be compelled to fulfill what he rashly promised or, recalled by consideration of a more honorable perspective, prove himself a transgressor of his pledge. But since our present purpose is to discuss not so much a state of health as the cure of weakness, what you ought first to have undertaken is not the question; rather, sound counsel requires us to ask how you can escape from the reef of this perilous shipwreck. Since, then, no bond constrains us and no condition binds us, when a choice is proposed by comparison of secondary goods, what offers the greater advantage should be preferred; but when some adverse loss stands in the way, in comparing the harms [Note: [Col. 1050C] After these words, the Basel and Lyons editions insert the following: “As someone said: Of the greatest evils, choose the least.” Since we found this neither in our manuscripts nor in the paraphrase of Dionysius, we preferred, omitting it, to follow the Plantinian edition.] what entails the lighter losses should be sought. Accordingly, as your own statement has revealed, since an ill-considered pledge has brought you to the point where, whichever course you take, you must suffer the loss of some serious advantage, the power of choice should incline toward that side which either brings more tolerable losses or can more easily be expiated by the remedy of satisfaction. If, therefore, you believe that this stay will confer greater spiritual gains upon you than those which arose for you from life in that monastery, and if your pledge cannot be fulfilled without the loss of immense advantages, [Note: [Col. 1050D] That is, to commit a lie or fail to keep one’s promises. Here Abbot Joseph enters upon a discussion of lying, which he endeavors to prove, by many examples and authorities from Scripture, to be not only sometimes permissible but even praiseworthy and necessary, and this for two reasons or ends: (1) to avoid some great evil or procure some great good; (2) when one must lie out of humility, so that someone may conceal his virtues by a lie in order to avoid empty glory. He argues the first part of this position from chap. 12 through chap. 21, and the second from chap. 21 through chap. 25. This opinion was not held by this abbot alone, but by many ancient writers, as may be seen in the critique of Dom Cuychius (see toward the end of the volume), who treated this subject carefully, diligently examined and refuted all the arguments for this opinion cited in this Conference, and solidly confirmed the true and sound doctrine. I therefore consider it superfluous to linger longer over the same question, lest I seem either to be doing work already done or to claim for myself the writings of another. Only two or three points seem here to require annotation for greater clarity and explanation.

First, a lie is properly speech contrary to the speaker’s mind; to lie is to depart from, or speak contrary to, one’s mind; or, as the Master of the Sentences says (Book III, distinction 35), it occurs when someone, by signifying, declares something contrary to what he thinks in his heart, so that one thing is concealed in his breast and another is uttered by his tongue. This, says St. Augustine (Enchiridion, chaps. 18 and 22), is proper to the liar: for everyone who lies speaks contrary to what he thinks in his mind. By “speech,” however, everything used for signifying is understood, so that not only words but also gestures and every sign by which we signify something are included. For there are lies not only of words but also of actions, such as those consisting in hypocrisy and pretense. Nor is it required that what is said be false, since someone can lie even by speaking the truth, if he does not believe the very things he truthfully says to be as he states them. A lie is not so called because it does not correspond to the matter of which the speech is concerned, but because it does not at all correspond to the speaker’s mind or inward thought. Falsity and truth, however, are judged by conformity or nonconformity to the thing itself. Hence Augustine says in On Lying (ch. 3): “He lies who has one thing in mind and declares another by words or by any other signs.” Thus the liar is also said to have a double heart—that is, a double thought: one concerning the thing which he knows or believes to be true but does not disclose, and another concerning the thing which he presents in its place, knowing or believing it to be false. From this it follows that someone can say what is false without lying, if he believes it to be as he says, although it is not so; and that someone can speak the truth while lying, if he believes it to be false and declares it as true, although in reality it is as he declares. Thus Augustine. It also follows that someone who speaks the truth while believing it false is deceived and mistaken; whereas one who lies, insofar as it depends upon him, deceives, even if he has no explicit intention to deceive. Therefore it is not necessary to include an intention to deceive in the definition of a lie, since it is enough not to speak or signify contrary to one’s mind, and the essential character of a lie consists in this. Nevertheless, St. Augustine, in his book Against Lying (ch. 10), says that a lie is “a false signification with the will to deceive.” He did this because he wished the will to deceive to be understood in the very act by which someone signifies something other than what he holds in his heart. For if someone who speaks in this manner, insofar as it depends upon him, deceives, then the will to speak in this manner is a will to deceive; or, at least, as St. Thomas explains (2–2, q. 110, art. 1), the desire or will to deceive belongs not to the substance but to a certain perfection of the lie, just as an effect belongs to the perfection of its cause.

Second, although some ancient ecclesiastical writers, following Plato’s opinion, taught that it is sometimes permissible to lie, the true and sound doctrine is that every lie is, in itself, vicious sin and prohibited by divine law; consequently, it is always unlawful, and cannot be made lawful and guiltless by any pretext, intention, end, or dispensation. This doctrine has three primary and general foundations:

1. The authority of Sacred Scripture, which generally, absolutely, and very often condemns and prohibits every lie. The passages in Proverbs are perfectly clear: “The just man will detest a lying word” (Prov. XIII, XVII, XXX); “He who relies on lies feeds the winds” (Prov. X); “A lying word is not fitting for a ruler” (Prov. XVII); “Vanity and lying words keep far from me” (Prov. XXX). And in Exodus: “You shall flee from a lie” (Exod. XXIII). In Leviticus: “You shall not lie, nor shall each one deceive his neighbor” (Lev. XIX). In Ecclesiasticus: “Do not desire to utter every lie” (Ecclus. XIV); and, “Before all things, let a true word go before you” (Ecclus. XXXVII). In the Apostle: “Putting away lying, speak the truth, each one with his neighbor, because we are members of one another” (Eph. IV); and, “Do not lie to one another” (Col. III).

2. The authority of the holy Fathers, especially St. Augustine, who, both elsewhere and above all in two books—one On Lying and the other Against Lying—vigorously attacked as erroneous and false the position that lying is permissible. The other Fathers thereafter, as well as the scholastic theologians, subscribed to this position with the Master. Hence Gregory, in Book XVIII of the Moralia (ch. 2), says: “Every lie must be avoided with the greatest care, although sometimes a certain kind of lie may involve lesser guilt, as when someone lies in preserving another’s life. But because it is written, Wisdom I: ‘The mouth that lies kills the soul’; and Psalm V: ‘You will destroy all who speak lies,’ even this kind of lie perfect men greatly avoid, so that not even another’s life should be defended through their deception, lest they harm their own souls while striving to preserve another’s bodily life. Nevertheless, we readily believe that this very kind of sin is easily forgiven when piety itself, the mother of a good work, accompanies it.” Thus St. Gregory.

3. To this is added an evident argument drawn from the nature of the matter itself, which St. Augustine expressed in these words (Enchiridion, ch. 22): “Every lie must therefore be said to be a sin, because a human being ought to speak not only when he himself knows what is true, but also when he errs or is deceived, as human beings do, what he holds in his mind, whether it is true or is merely believed and is not true. Everyone who lies, however, speaks against what he thinks in his mind with the will to deceive. Words were instituted for this reason: not so that people might deceive one another through them, but so that they might bring their thoughts to one another’s knowledge. To use words for deception, rather than for what they were instituted, is a sin. Nor should any lie therefore be thought not to be a sin because we can sometimes benefit someone by lying. We can also benefit someone by stealing, if a poor person to whom something is given openly recognizes the advantage; yet no one would for that reason say that such theft is not a sin.”

Third, the Fathers who wrote otherwise about lying can be excused for two reasons: (1) they wrote at a time when nothing had yet been defined by the Church concerning this matter, and in it followed not the mind of the Church but the philosophy of Plato, who in Book II of the Republic teaches that lying should be used as a kind of medicine or seasoning; (2) they use the terms “lie” and “pretense” in a broader sense, and call even an amphibological statement—that is, one spoken with another sense, or limited by a tacit mental qualification or condition—a lie, so that one person understands something else and is deceived; and by “pretense” they also understand concealment. There is a close affinity and a slight difference among these terms and their meanings: falsity, lying, pretense, hypocrisy, dissimulation, amphibology, and the violation or withdrawal of one’s pledge or promise. These are sometimes confused.

Falsity, as stated, is the very disparity and discrepancy of words from the thing itself. A statement is called false when it declares the matter to be otherwise than it is. A lie is a false signification by words—that is, a discrepancy not always from the thing itself but from the mind of the speaker. Simulation, says St. Thomas (2–2, q. 111, art. 1), is a kind of lie in outward signs of actions. For just as lying consists in words, simulation consists in deeds. Hypocrisy is a species of simulation. For every hypocrisy is simulation, but not every simulation is hypocrisy—only that in which someone pretends to possess a holiness he does not have. Dissimulation is nothing other than the concealment of truth; it is in itself indifferent and implies no fault, and differs greatly from simulation and lying. For just as someone lies in words when he signifies what is not, but not when he remains silent about what is—which is sometimes permitted—so also someone lies and simulates in the matter itself when, through outward signs of actions or things, he signifies something that is not, but not when he omits signifying what is. Thus someone may conceal his sin without simulation. So St. Thomas.

To the same category belongs ambiguous or amphibological speech, when someone is not bound to speak or answer according to another person’s mind and understanding. Someone who uses amphibology or a tacit restriction does not lie, because he does not intend to say what is false or to speak contrary to his mind, but either to express his own mind in a way different from the way the other person understands it, or not to express it in its entirety but only in part.

Moreover, the correction or withdrawal of a pledge or agreement is not a lie and is not opposed to truth, but rather to faithfulness, as is well known (see St. Thomas, 2–2, q. 110, art. 2, ad 5). Properly speaking, someone who violates a pact or promise does not lie, because he does not speak contrary to his mind; it is otherwise if he makes a promise without intending to promise or carry it out. Accordingly, Abbot Joseph misuses the term “lie” here when he calls a change of counsel or of a pledge that has been made a lie, as Dom Cuychius learnedly explains. The reader should not fail to consult his critique of this passage together with Ciaconius’s annotation.] it is better for you to undergo the loss of lying or of an unfulfilled promise—something which, once it has passed, can neither itself be repeated nor by itself generate other sins—than to fall into that condition by which, as you say, a more tepid way of life inflicts upon you a daily and interminable loss. For an ill-considered decision may permissibly, indeed even [Note: [Col. 1053D] Gratian contains many chapters to this effect, such as Augustine’s: “It is great wisdom for a man to retract what he has spoken wrongly”; and Isidore’s: “In evil promises, break faith; in a shameful vow, change your resolution. For a promise fulfilled by wickedness is impious. An oath by which evil has been rashly promised is not to be observed.” Abbot Joseph teaches the same below in chap. 14.] laudably, be changed if it passes over to the healthier side; nor should it be regarded as a violation of constancy whenever a vicious pledge is corrected—that is, as an amendment of rashness. All these points can also be most clearly confirmed by testimonies from Scripture: it is useful and salutary to see how harmful it has been for many to cling to their own decisions, and conversely how beneficial it has been to abandon them.

## CHAPTER IX. That it is often—that is, sometimes—more useful to dissolve established decisions than to fulfill them

This is most clearly attested by the examples of the holy apostles Peter and Judas the betrayer. The former, because [Note: [Col. 1053D] Sophronius aptly relates this example in the Spiritual Meadow (chap. 216): “When I was in the holy city, a certain faithful man came to me and said: ‘Because a quarrel has arisen between my brother and me, and he is unwilling to be reconciled to me, speak with him and urge him to reconciliation.’ I gladly undertook this and met his brother, speaking with him about such matters as seemed to pertain to charity and concord. For the moment he appeared to comply with me. But afterward he said to me: ‘I cannot be reconciled, because I swore by the cross never again to be reconciled to him.’ Hearing this, I smiled and said to him: ‘Your oath has the same force as if you had said: “By your precious cross, O Christ, I will not observe your commandments, but will do the will of your enemy the devil.” For not only ought we not keep what we have resolved most wickedly, but we ought also to do the greatest penance and afflict ourselves for what we have determined against our salvation. For if Herod had repented, he would neither have kept the oath which he foolishly uttered nor ever committed that greatest crime, the beheading of Christ’s Forerunner.’ This is also confirmed by the opinion of Basil himself, drawn from the Gospel, when the Lord wished to wash the feet of the blessed apostle Peter: though Peter at first stubbornly resisted, he afterward changed his mind.” Thus he. See that opinion of St. Basil in the prologue to the Ethics. The statement of Pope Gelasius, cited by Gratian (as above, chapter “Beatus”), has the same bearing: “The blessed apostle Paul must not—far be it—be thought to have deceived or contradicted himself because, though he had promised that he would go to Spain, he was occupied by greater causes through divine disposition and could not fulfill what he had promised. So far as his own will was concerned, he declared what he had truly wished to accomplish. But with respect to the secret counsels of God—which, being human, he could not know in every respect, even though filled with God’s Spirit—he was forestalled by the heavenly disposition. Nor, because the blessed apostle Peter answered the Lord himself from an affection of divine reverence (John XIII), ‘You shall never wash my feet,’ must he—far be it—be thought to have deceived or not remained steadfast in his resolution, because he soon yielded to that same divine will and, compelled by the reasons of human salvation, willingly allowed to be done what he had said he would not do.”] he departed [Col. 1053B] from the judgment of his ill-considered decision when he had said, “You shall never wash my feet” (John XIII), earned the eternal fellowship of Christ and all the saints, whereas he would undoubtedly have been cut off from the grace of this blessedness if he had remained obstinate in his words. The latter, however, retaining the obstinacy of his pledge, was condemned to everlasting death, from which he would undoubtedly have been freed if he had preferred to be found one who abandoned his decision rather than one who persisted in it.

We are also taught this most plainly in the case of the two sons who, in the Gospel, are sent to work in the vineyard. One resisted his father’s command, while the other consented with an easy response (Matt. XXI). Yet the humble and obedient response did not benefit the latter, because in practice he refused to fulfill his father’s command; nor did the refusal of the command harm the former, because, after changing the determination expressed in his words, he fulfilled his father’s purpose by carrying out the work and laudably corrected what he had reprehensibly decided. [Note: [Col. 1054D] Christ proposed this parable in Matthew XXI: “A certain man had two sons, and approaching the first he said: Son, go today and work in my vineyard. But he answered: I will not. Yet afterward, moved by repentance, he went. Approaching the other, he said the same. But he answered: I am going, Lord; and he did not go. Which of the two did the father’s will?” They say to him: “The first.”]

Nor should the example of Herod, the bloodiest of kings, be omitted. He rashly maintained his oath [Note: [Col. 1054D] That is, his sworn promise. Herod, delighted by the dancing of Herodias’s daughter, promised her under oath that he would give her whatever she requested. But instructed by her mother, she said: “Give me here on a dish the head of John the Baptist” (Matt. XIV). From this rash oath followed evils and sins far greater than the oath itself: first, the death of the most innocent and holy Prophet, than whom, as even the Truth testifies, no one greater had arisen among those born of women; second, Herod became guilty of the most atrocious homicide. It would have been better for him to perjure himself than to keep his oath. “It is contrary to duty,” says Blessed Ambrose (Book I On Duties, chap. 50), “sometimes to fulfill a promise and preserve an oath, as Herod did, who swore that he would give Herodias’s daughter whatever she requested, and carried out the killing lest he deny his promise. Likewise, it would have been better for Jephthah to promise nothing of the kind than to fulfill his promise by parricide.” And Augustine (Sermon 11 on the Saints): “Herod, lest he offend God by perjury, offended God by his savagery.” A little later he adds the example of King David, who, having rashly sworn that he would kill Nabal, allowed himself to be entreated by Nabal’s wife Abigail and did not fulfill his oath. “He swore rashly,” Augustine says, “but in greater piety he did not fulfill his oath; indeed, he gave thanks for this, saying: ‘Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, who sent you today to meet me; and blessed are you, who kept me today from going to bloodshed and taking revenge with my own hand.’” Third, Herodias herself and her daughter also became guilty of the murder, because through her the daughter requested John’s head; indeed, all the guests were guilty, because, as Matthew says, the king wished his oath to be kept and carried out for the sake of those reclining at table with him. He therefore wished, as St. Jerome notes in his commentary, all his guests to be accomplices in his crime. Fourth, Ambrose says, “a spectacle was presented which even all barbarians are accustomed to shudder at. Amid food and banquets an edict for the completion of cruelty is issued. And from the banquet to the prison, from the prison to the banquet, the service of a deadly crime is carried about. How many crimes are contained in a single deed!” And St. Jerome says in his commentary: “We read in Roman history that Flaminius, a Roman commander, because he agreed to have a condemned criminal beheaded at a banquet for the sake of a little prostitute reclining beside him, who said she had never seen a man beheaded, was expelled by the censors from the senate-house, because he had mixed blood with the banquet and, for another’s pleasure, had provided the death even of a guilty man, so that lust and homicide might be joined together. How much more criminal were Herod and Herodias, and the girl who danced and, as the price of blood, requested the prophet’s head, so that she might have power over the tongue which condemned an unlawful marriage?” Thus St. Jerome. It should moreover be observed that Dionysius the Paraphrast omitted this example of Herod, for a reason I do not know, unless perhaps, because the matter concerned an oath, he wished to avoid appearing even outwardly to favor perjury. Yet it is certain that this oath could not in any way bind him to an unlawful act, and that carrying it out involved the crime of perjury more than failing to carry it out would have done, as has just been said. To lie—what is being considered here—is something very different from withdrawing or violating a promise or oath, as is clear from what has been said.] and became the bloodstained murderer of the Lord’s Forerunner, plunging himself, through his empty fear of perjury, into condemnation and the punishments of everlasting death (Matt. XIV).

The first principle is always to establish what is best. If matters turn out otherwise, the next best course is to change what has been established for the better and, so to speak, extend a helping right hand to our decisions when they have fallen. When the beginnings of a plan are not approved, prudence requires that they be repaired by adding a useful provision. If the first arrangement limps, let correction be applied to the second. In every matter, therefore, the outcome must be considered, and the course of our purpose directed according to it. If, when a healthier counsel has arisen, we see that this course is turning toward the worse, it is more right to remove an unsuitable arrangement and pass to a better judgment than, by clinging obstinately to established decisions, to bind ourselves to more serious sins.

## CHAPTER X. Our question concerning fear of the pledge made in the monastery of Syria

Germanus: As far as our desire is concerned, which we took up for the sake of spiritual benefit, we would wish to be built up by the continual presence of your companionship. For if we return to our monastery, it is certain that we shall not only fall away from so lofty a purpose but also, because of the mediocrity of that way of life, be shaken by many losses. Yet the following evangelical command strongly deters us: “Let your speech be: Yes, yes; no, no; whatever is more than these is from evil” (Matt. V). [Note: [Col. 1056C] Thus they interpreted Christ’s words in Matthew concerning the fulfillment of promises, as though the meaning were: What you have promised to do, do; what you have promised not to do, do not do. Paul likewise speaks in this manner in 2 Corinthians I: “Did I use fickleness? Or do I conceive according to the flesh, so that with me there is yes and no? But God is faithful, because our word which was among you is not yes and no.” Yet the proper and genuine meaning of Christ’s words concerns not swearing: that is, that we abstain from every form of oath except in cases of necessity, and use simple speech, a simple affirmation or denial, according as the truth stands. If you seek a fuller and more exact explanation of his meaning, see, among other interpreters, the decretal of Innocent III on Oaths (Book II of the Decretals, title “On Oaths,” chapter “Although Christ”), in which he teaches no less learnedly than clearly to what extent it is permitted or not permitted for a Christian to swear. Its final part, or conclusion, concerning religious persons is cited below (at chap. 27).] For we believe that no righteousness can compensate for the transgression of so great a commandment, and that what was begun with an evil beginning cannot rightly end well.

## CHAPTER XI. The answer: that the purpose of the person acting, not the outcome of the undertaking, must be considered

Joseph: In every matter, as we have said, it is not the course of the deed but the will of the person acting that must be examined; nor must one immediately ask what someone did, but with what intention he did it. [Note: [Col. 1056D] Elsewhere, in different words (Conference 16, chap. 18): “As though before God only words, and not chiefly the will, were held culpable, and only the deed, and not also the wish and purpose, were counted as a crime,” etc. And below: “The inclination of the sin, not the course of the act, must be considered.” Thus there. This is what is commonly said: the will is counted as the deed—namely, before God and in the court of conscience. The same point is again emphasized in the following chapter.] Thus we find some condemned for deeds from which good things afterward arose, and conversely others who reached the highest righteousness through reprehensible acts. The favorable outcome of an undertaking did not benefit the former, who, with a very evil purpose, did not intend to perform the good that followed but something contrary to it; nor did it harm the latter, who began reprehensibly but endured the necessity of a blameworthy beginning not out of contempt for God or an intention to sin, but with regard to a necessary and holy end.

## CHAPTER XII. That good outcomes did not benefit evil authors, nor did evil deeds harm the good

And, to clarify these same points by examples from the sacred Scriptures, what more salutary or useful remedy could have been procured for the whole world than the saving remedy of the Lord’s Passion? [Note: [Col. 1057C] Abbot Theodore taught the same thing in Conference 6, chap. 9: “For the patience of Job did not earn a reward for the devil, who made him more illustrious through his temptations, but for Job himself, who endured them manfully; nor will Judas be granted immunity from eternal punishment because his betrayal benefited the salvation of the human race. For it is not the outcome of the deed that must be considered, but the inclination of the person acting.” Here “outcome” has the same meaning as “course” above—that is, success or result.] Yet this not only did not benefit the betrayer, but even harmed him so greatly, through whose ministry it is shown to have been accomplished, that it is expressly declared of him: “It would have been better for that man if he had not been born” (Matt. XXVI). The fruit of his deed must not be assigned to him according to what happened, but according to what he wished to do or believed he would accomplish.

Again, what is more criminal than deceit and lying, even when committed against a stranger, not to mention against one’s own father? Yet Jacob the patriarch not only incurred no condemnation or reproach for these acts, but was also enriched with the perpetual inheritance of blessing (Gen. XXVII). Nor was this without reason: Jacob desired the blessing destined for the firstborn not out of greed for present gain but out of faith in an everlasting sanctification; whereas the other betrayed the Redeemer of all to death not for the sake of human salvation but through the crime of avarice. Therefore the outcome of their actions was assigned to each according to the determination of their minds and the purpose of their wills, since one did not intend fraud and the other did not intend salvation. For each person is justly repaid as a reward what he principally conceived in his mind, not what afterward emerged for good or ill contrary to the agent’s intention.

Accordingly, the most just Judge considered such a presumptuous liar excusable—indeed praiseworthy—because without it he could not have attained the blessing of the firstborn. [Note: [Col. 1057C] There Abbot Joseph excuses the patriarch Jacob on the ground that, desiring to obtain the blessing and being unable to obtain it by another means, he was, as it were, compelled to lie. This excuse is certainly weak and inadequate unless one understands Jacob to have been necessarily lying in order to obtain the blessing that was rightfully his. For on this basis he can certainly be excused, if not from every lie, at least from what is called a harmful lie, because it is contrary to justice and charity and therefore deadly. Nor does it matter that by this act he inflicted serious harm upon his brother, since he did what was just while exercising his right, from which Esau had stripped himself; hence he did him no injury, since there is no injury except against justice. St. Gregory says in the passage cited above: “Jacob did not steal the blessing of the firstborn by fraud; he received it as his due, having bought it from his brother by the price of a portion of lentils.”] Nor should what arose from a desire for blessing have been counted as a crime. Otherwise the patriarch would not only have been unjust toward his brother but also a deceiver of his father and a sacrilegious man, if, having another way by which he could reach the grace of that blessing, he had preferred this way, which was harmful and injurious to his brother. You see, therefore, that before God it is not the course of the deed but the determination of the mind that is examined. [Col. 1058B] With these matters thus established, let us return to the question proposed, on account of which all these preceding points have been introduced. First, I wish you to tell me for what reason you bound yourselves by the ties of that pledge.

## CHAPTER XIII. Our answer: what reason compelled us to make the oath of the pledge

Germanus: The first reason, as we said, was that we feared grieving our elders and resisting their commands. The second was that, if we should perceive from you—whether by sight or by hearing—anything perfect and magnificent, we believed, with very ill-considered confidence, that we would be able to practice it once we had returned to our monastery.

# CHAPTER XIV  
## The Elder’s Discussion: That the Order May Be Changed Without Guilt in the Action, Provided That the Result of a Good Endeavor Is Attained

[Col. 1059A]

**Joseph:** As we stated above, [Note: [Col. 1059C] The mind’s purpose—that is, intention—rewards a person, that is, makes him acceptable to God, and renders his work meritorious, in accordance with the saying in Matthew VI: “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light.” For, says Augustine (*On the Sermon on the Mount*, Book II, chapter 21), by “eye” we should understand our intention; and if it is pure and upright, all our works, which we perform according to it, are good. He called all these works “the whole body,” because the Apostle also calls certain works our members when he says: “Put to death your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness,” and so forth. Therefore, it is not what someone does that must be considered, but with what disposition he does it. Nevertheless, the same Augustine, in the book *Against Lying* (chapter 7), warns that this should be understood of works which are not evil in themselves, and which can be made good by an intention or purpose of mind. “It makes a very great difference,” he says, “for what reason, to what end, and with what intention something is done.” [Col. 1059D] But those things which are plainly sins must not be done under the pretext of any good cause, any supposedly good end, or any apparently good intention. For human actions which are not sins in themselves are sometimes good and sometimes evil, depending on whether they have good or bad causes: thus, to provide food for the poor is a good work if it is done out of mercy and with right faith; likewise, marital intercourse, when undertaken for procreation, is good if it is done with the intention that children may be begotten for regeneration (see Saint Bernard, *On the Precepts*, chapters 17 and 18). Such actions are good or evil according to their causes, because those very same actions, if they have evil causes, turn into sins—as when a poor person is fed for the sake of boasting; or intercourse with one’s wife is undertaken for the sake of lust; or children are begotten not to be nourished for God but for the devil. But when the actions themselves are sins, such as thefts, fornications, blasphemies, or other things of this kind, who would say that they should be done for good causes, so that they would either not be sins or, more absurdly, would be righteous sins? Who would say: “So that we may have something to give to the poor, let us steal from the rich,” or “Let us sell false testimony, especially if no innocent people are harmed by it, but rather the guilty are rescued from judges who would condemn them”? For through this sale of falsehood two good things would be accomplished: money would be obtained to feed a needy person, and the judge would be deceived so that a man would not be punished. These are Saint Augustine’s words, together with what follows in the same sense.] Thus the mind’s purpose either rewards or condemns a person, according to the saying: “While their thoughts accuse or even defend them among themselves, on the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings” (Romans II). And also: “I am coming to gather all their works and thoughts, together with all nations and tongues” (Isaiah LXVI).

Therefore, as I see it, you bound yourselves by this pledge because of your desire for perfection, believing that it could be attained by the order in which you now perceive that, when a fuller judgment has intervened, you cannot ascend to its heights. Consequently, whatever may have happened differently [Col. 1059B] from that arrangement does not prejudice the matter, provided that no subsequent divergence from that original purpose follows. For changing a tool is not abandoning the craft, nor does a traveler’s choice of a shorter and more direct road indicate laziness. So, in this matter also, the correction of an ill-considered plan must not be judged a transgression of the spiritual vow.

Whatever is accomplished out of love for God and devotion to piety—which has the promise of the life that now is and of the life to come (1 Timothy IV)—even if it seems to begin amid harsh and adverse circumstances, is worthy not only of no reproach but also of the highest praise. Therefore, an imprudent pledge does not prejudice the matter if, by whatever means, the goal alone—that is, the intended purpose of piety—is maintained. For we do everything for this reason: that we may be able to present a pure heart to God. [Col. 1059C] If its attainment is judged easier in these places, nothing [Col. 1060A] will be harmed by the alteration of the agreement that was forced from you will do you no harm, provided that the principal perfection of purity, for which your pledge was made, is acquired sooner in accordance with the Lord’s will.

This alteration cannot be judged a lie, but rather a prudent and salutary correction of an ill-considered decision. And, to add something from the realm of nature that may resolve the knot of the question before us, nature itself changes its works in us according to the counsel of the divine majesty. For we are transferred from infancy to boyhood, from boyhood to youth, and from youth into the further stages of old age. Thus our Creator’s work has brought us to completion through these changes, without any lie being attributed to our age.

In the same way, our inner person, weaned from the tender beginnings of its first instruction, advances through successive stages of life [Col. 1060B] and grows stronger at each one; thereafter, reaching the gray-haired maturity of understanding and “the perfect man, unto the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians IV), he lays aside the things that belonged to a child. Should he then be thought to have fallen into the variability of falsehood, rather than to have attained the fullness of perfection?

Thus the rudiments of the Old Testament are transferred, through the dispensation of God the Lawgiver, to the perfection of evangelical blessedness. Yet this should not be regarded as an alteration or divergence from the former decree, but as the fulfillment and greater culmination of higher and heavenly commandments; nor should the sacred promulgation be judged abolished, but elevated; not changed, but advanced. Hence our Lord says: “Do not think [Col. 1060C] that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets” (Matthew V); [Note: [Col. 1060C] How Christ can say that he did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it, although in reality he dissolved and abrogated it, is explained most beautifully by John Maldonatus (*Commentary on Matthew*, chapter V), following Saint Thomas (*Summa Theologiae* I–II, question 107, article 2). His words are these: “Christ fulfilled the precepts of the old law both by his works and by his teaching. By his works, because he wished to be circumcised and to observe the other legal practices that were to be observed at that time, in accordance with Galatians IV: ‘Made under the law.’ By his teaching he fulfilled the precepts of the law in three ways. First, by expressing the true meaning of the law, as is clear in the cases of murder and adultery, in whose prohibition the scribes and Pharisees understood only the external act to be forbidden. Therefore, the Lord fulfilled the law by showing that the interior acts of sin also fall under its prohibition. Second, the Lord fulfilled the precepts of the law by ordering how what the old law had established might be observed more safely. Thus the old law established that a person should not swear falsely; this is observed more safely if one entirely abstains from swearing, except in a case of necessity. Third, the Lord fulfilled the precepts of the law by adding certain counsels of perfection, as is evident in Matthew XIX, where, when the man says that he has observed the precepts of the old law, the Lord tells him: ‘One thing you lack: if you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have,’ and so forth.”] that is, not [Col. 1061A] to make the former things obsolete, but to bring imperfect things to perfection.

# CHAPTER XV  
## The Question Whether It Is Without Sin to Provide the Weak with an Occasion for Lying through Our Conscience

**Germanus:** As far as concerns the force of the arguments that have been arranged reasonably and prudently, the scruple regarding our pledge could have been driven from us without difficulty, if this had not deterred us most forcefully: that through these examples an occasion for lying may perhaps appear to be offered to the weaker, if they come to know that the faith of an agreement can in any way be dissolved. For this very thing is forbidden in such great and threatening words, the Prophet saying, [Note: [Col. 1061B] These and similar statements, according to the common interpretation, are understood not of every kind of lie, but only of a harmful lie (see below, chapter 18), especially one that is opposed to piety or religion. For just as truth is found chiefly in religious teaching, so, by antonomasia, that is called a lie which contradicts the truth of religion and the word of God.] “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Psalm V); and, “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wisdom I).

# CHAPTER XVI  
## The Answer: That the Truth of Scripture Must Not Be Changed Because of the Scandal of the Weak

[Col. 1061B]

**Joseph:** [Note: [Col. 1061C] Dionysius the paraphraser omitted this chapter and the three that follow (and Lavardinus followed him). In place of the teaching of this chapter—which seemed to contain some ambiguity and to open a way into the following discussion and defense of lying—he inserted the following clearer passage in the person of Abbot Joseph, responding to an objection made against him. He extracted only certain statements from the following chapter: “We stated these things about changing an imprudent promise, not in order to give or open a way or entrance to forbidden and harmful lies. We judged it more useful that, if an ill-considered decision should perhaps precede us, it be moderated by the later arrival of a healthier counsel; nor is it right for us to remain rigid and irrevocable in what we have once decided, if mature and prudent discernment should later discover something more correct.” For it is one thing to lie and another to alter decisions or promises maturely, and so forth. Dionysius then continues with the material found in chapter 19. Nevertheless, the teaching of this chapter, as it was produced by the Author, contains nothing alien to the truth, and it rightly teaches when scandal must be avoided and when it must be disregarded. A similar passage is found in Saint Gregory’s *Homily 7 on Ezekiel*, in these words: “In our good work, sometimes the scandal of our neighbor must be avoided, but sometimes it must be disregarded as nothing. We learned this from our own Author, who, when tribute was demanded from Peter, first proposed an example by which he answered that he owed nothing, saying: ‘From whom do the kings of the earth receive tribute or tax—from their own sons or from strangers?’ When he was told, ‘From strangers,’ he immediately replied: ‘Then the sons are free.’ But after showing that he was free, lest he perhaps cause anyone to stumble, he added: ‘Nevertheless, so that we may not scandalize them, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up; and when you have opened its mouth, you will find a stater. Take it and give it to them for me and for you’ (Matthew XVII). Again, when he had said that whatever enters the mouth does not defile a person, the disciples approached him and said: ‘Do you know that when the Pharisees heard this word they were scandalized?’ But he answered: ‘Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted. Leave them: they are blind guides of the blind’ (Matthew XV). Behold, the Teacher Truth, lest scandal arise in certain hearts where it ought not to arise, paid the tribute. Again, because he saw that scandal was arising in certain hearts against the truth, he allowed them to remain in their scandal. From this we must understand that, insofar as we can do so without sin, we ought to avoid causing scandal to our neighbors. But if scandal is taken from the truth, it is better to allow scandal to arise than to abandon the truth.” These words of Gregory may be seen explained more fully by Saint Thomas (*Summa Theologiae* II–II, question 43, article 7).]

Occasions and causes of destruction cannot be lacking for those who are destined to perish—or rather, for those who desire to perish. For the testimonies of Scripture must not be cast aside or completely scraped away from its body because they stimulate the perversity of heretics, harden the unbelief of Jews [Col. 1062A], or offend the pride of pagan wisdom. Rather, they must be believed piously, held firmly, and proclaimed according to the rule of truth.

Therefore, on account of another person’s unbelief, we must not reject the *oikonomiai*—that is, the dispensations—of the prophets and saints that Scripture records. If, while believing that we ought to accommodate ourselves to their weakness, we did so, we would defile ourselves not only with the charge of lying but also with that of sacrilege. Instead, as we have said, we must acknowledge these things according to their historical meaning and explain how they were piously accomplished.

Moreover, those who are perversely disposed will not thereby be prevented from lying if we labor either to deny altogether or to weaken through allegorical interpretations the truth of the things that we are about to proclaim or have already proclaimed. [Col. 1062B] For what harm will the authority of these testimonies do them, when the corruption of their will alone is sufficient?

# CHAPTER XVII  
## That the Saints Used Lying Venially, as Though It Were Hellebore

Accordingly, one must think of lying in this way, and use it in such a manner [Note: [Col. 1062C] I shall first set down here the words of Peter Maturus concerning this passage, lest anything escape the reader. “Plato,” he says, “used nearly the same comparison in Book III of *The Republic*, and Origen in Book VI of the *Stromata*. Nevertheless, although some of the sacred Doctors exist who permit a Christian man to lie on occasion, the preferable judgment is that of Augustine in *On Lying to Consentius*, chapter 5; *Against Lying*, chapter 2; and Letter 8 to Saint Jerome, as well as that of Saint Thomas in *Summa Theologiae* II–II, question 110, article 3, and in *Sentences* III, distinction 38, article 3. This judgment is also followed by Saint Antoninus below in this same section, and in Part II of his *Summa*, title 10, chapter 1, section 91: namely, that every lie—whether officious or playful—is a sin. Innocent III also supports this view in the *Decretals*, Book V, title 19, *On Usury*, chapter 4, where he says that Holy Scripture forbids anyone to lie for another person’s life. Besides the authors already named, see also Alfonso de Castro, *On Heresies*, under the word ‘Lying,’ and Sixtus of Siena, *Bibliotheca*, Book V, annotation 107.” These are the words of Peter Maturus.
