But now let us proceed to examine the text and its principal difficulties: “Lying is to be used as though the nature of hellebore were inherent in it.” That is, lying is sometimes to be used as hellebore is used. This is the first paradox, or first false and erroneous proposition, among those by which permission to lie is asserted and defended in this conference, which Lord Cuychius collected and arranged in order so that they might be more apparent to readers and more carefully avoided. Hellebore—or, as others prefer, *helleborum*—is an herb possessing remarkable purgative power, which the Latins call *veratrum*. The finest grows on the island of Anticyra, where it was also taken most safely for purging the brain, according to Pliny (Book XXV, chapter 5). Hence those who seemed to be of unsound mind were told to sail to Anticyra or drink hellebore. Among the Greeks, ἑλλεβορίζειν (*helleborizein*) is used for “to be insane,” and those who are unstable in mind or suffer from lightheadedness or vertigo are said to need hellebore, ἑλλεβόρῳ δεῖσθαι (*helleborō deisthai*), because the ancients believed that hellebore purged the brain and thereby cured madness. Hence Isidore (*Etymologies*, Book XVII, chapter 9): “The Romans,” he says, “call hellebore by another name, *veratrum*, because when taken it restores a disturbed mind to health.”] as though it possessed the nature of hellebore. [Col. 1063A] If it is taken when a deadly disease is imminent, it becomes beneficial; but taken without the necessity of extreme danger, it brings immediate death.

Thus we read that holy and highly approved men of God also used lying venially, as did [Note: [Col. 1063C] Rahab of Jericho used an officious lie when, ordered to hand over the Hebrew spies who had turned in to her, she replied: “I admit that they came to me, but I did not know where they were from. And when the gate was being closed in the darkness, they went out together; I do not know where they went,” and so forth (Joshua II). Comparing this lie with that of the Egyptian midwives, who, in order to save the Hebrew children from death, are said to have lied to Pharaoh, Saint Augustine explains his judgment concerning both in this way (*Against Lying*, chapter 15): “The fact that Scripture says that God did good to the Hebrew midwives and to Rahab the prostitute of Jericho did not occur because they lied, but because they showed mercy toward the people of God. It was not deception that was rewarded in them, but benevolence; goodness of mind, not the wickedness of the liar. For just as it would not be astonishing or absurd if God wished to forgive some evil deeds committed by them at an earlier time on account of later good deeds, so it is not astonishing that at one time and in one matter God, seeing both things—that is, the act done mercifully and the act done deceitfully—rewarded the good and, because of that good, forgave the evil. And later, after a lengthy discussion of both women, he concludes: ‘Therefore Rahab in Jericho, because she received God’s foreign guests in hospitality; because she was endangered by receiving them; because she believed in their God; because she carefully concealed them wherever she could; and because she gave them faithful advice about returning by another route, is praised as worthy of imitation by the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem. But the fact that she lied—even if something prophetic is intelligently understood there—cannot wisely be proposed for imitation. Although God honorably commemorated those good deeds, he mercifully forgave that evil.’ These words of Saint Augustine concerning Rahab’s lie are highly appropriate for explaining this passage and refuting the false assertion that lying may be used profitably and laudably.] Rahab (Joshua II), concerning whom Scripture records not only no memorial of virtues but also [Note: [Col. 1064C] Scripture mentions no other evidence of Rahab’s immorality except that both the history of Joshua and the Apostle in Hebrews XI and James in chapter II call her a prostitute. Nevertheless, Nicholas of Lyra maintains that she was not properly a prostitute but an innkeeper or hostess. See Maldonatus on Matthew I.] evidence of immorality. For such a lie—by which she preferred to conceal the spies rather than betray them—she deserved to be incorporated into the people of God by an eternal blessing.

If she had preferred to speak the truth or to secure the safety of her fellow citizens, there is no doubt that she would neither have escaped the impending destruction together with her entire household nor have deserved to be included among the authors of the Lord’s Nativity and counted in the catalog of the patriarchs, through the succession of her offspring, to bring forth the Savior of all.

Finally, Delilah (Judges XVI), who, concerned for the interests of her people, betrayed the truth she had discovered, received the return of perpetual destruction and left to everyone only the memory of her crime. [Col. 1063B]

Therefore, when some grave danger threatens because of a confession of the truth, refuges of lies may be accepted [Note: [Col. 1064D] Against this, the Apostle protests that evil must not be done so that good may result (Romans III). Blessed Job protests, saying: “Does God need our lie?” (Job XIII). The holy Fathers cited above also protest (chapter 8).], but in such a way that we may salutarily be stung by the guilt of a humbled conscience.

When no condition of extreme necessity is present, however, lying must be avoided with every precaution as something deadly. This is just as we said about drinking hellebore: it is beneficial if taken only when an unavoidable and deadly illness [Col. 1064A] threatens; but if it is taken when the body is sound and undisturbed, its pernicious power immediately advances to seize the vital organs.

This has been clearly demonstrated in the case of Rahab of Jericho (Joshua II) and the patriarch Jacob (Genesis XXVII). Neither could have escaped death by any means other than this remedy, nor could Jacob have attained the blessing of the firstborn. For God is not merely the examiner and judge of our words and actions; he is also the examiner of our purpose and intention. If he sees that something has been done or promised by someone for the sake of eternal salvation and in view of divine contemplation, even though it may seem harsh and unjust to human beings, he nevertheless, looking into the innermost disposition of the heart, judges not the sound of the words but the intention of the will, [Col. 1064B] because the end of the work and the disposition of the one who performs it must be considered. [Note: [Col. 1064D] He is referring to the examples of Rahab and Delilah cited above. But the Apostle Paul speaks very differently about Rahab: “By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with the unbelievers, having received the spies in peace” (Hebrews XI). By faith, he says—not by lying—and by a faith that was neither counterfeit nor dead, but living and working through charity, as Blessed James explains when he says: “Likewise, was not Rahab the prostitute justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out by another way?” (James II). Delilah, Samson’s wife, incurred the sin of everlasting death not because she confessed the truth, but because she treacherously betrayed her husband into the hands of his enemies (Judges XVI).] Thus, as was said above, some have been able to be justified even through lying, while others have incurred the sin of everlasting death through asserting the truth.

With that end in view, the patriarch Jacob (in the same passage) did not fear to disguise the hairy appearance of his brother’s body by wrapping himself in skins, and he laudably obeyed his mother when she urged him to this lie. For he saw that greater gains of blessing and righteousness would be conferred upon him through this than through observing simplicity. He did not doubt that the stain of this lie would immediately be washed away by an outpouring of his father’s blessing, and [Col. 1065A] that it would be swiftly consumed like a little cloud by the breath of the Holy Spirit; nor did he doubt that, through this deliberate simulation, richer rewards of merit would be granted him than through that innate truthfulness.

# CHAPTER XVIII  
## The Objection That Only Those Who Lived under the Law Used Lying with Impunity

**Germanus:** It is not surprising that these dispensations were employed more freely in the Old Testament, and that at times holy men lied venially, [Note: [Col. 1065B] Concerning this passage, Augustine’s familiar distinction of lying should be noted: officious, playful, and harmful lying. In this discussion, special attention must be given to this distinction. An officious lie is one told without injury to another, for someone’s safety or advantage. A playful lie is uttered solely from the desire to please or entertain. A harmful lie is one by which serious injury is inflicted upon someone. Of these three kinds of lies, it is clear from the nature of the term itself that only the harmful kind is deadly by its nature; the playful kind harms no one, and the officious kind even benefits someone, and therefore these are only venial. Hence Saint Augustine says in the *Enchiridion* (chapter XXII), in his exposition of the fifth psalm: “There are altogether two kinds of lies in which the fault is not great, though they are nevertheless not without fault: when we joke, or when we lie in order to benefit our neighbors.” Elsewhere (*Against Lying*, chapter 9), concluding his discussion of the officious lie, he says: “It is therefore a sin, but a venial one, which benevolence excuses.” Concerning such lies, which Scripture occasionally attributes to holy men, he makes this general statement: “When we read these things in the Holy Scriptures, we must not, merely because we believe that they were done, also believe that they ought to be done, lest, while indiscriminately following examples, we violate commandments.” And below: “It is clear that we must not transfer into our conduct everything we read as having been done by holy or righteous men; but from this also we must learn how widely applicable, and to whom, is the Apostle’s statement: ‘Brothers, if a person is overtaken in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness’” (Galatians VI).] even though we see that much greater things were permitted to them in the infancy of those times.

For why should it be surprising that blessed David, fleeing from Saul, when the priest Ahimelech questioned him, saying, “Why are you alone, and no one is with you?” answered: “The king commanded me concerning a matter, and said: ‘Let no one know the matter for which I have sent you; for I have also instructed the young men concerning such-and-such a place’” (1 Samuel XXI). And again: “If you have a spear or a sword here at hand, for I did not bring my sword or my weapons with me” (ibid.); for, he said, the king’s command pressed upon him.

Or consider this: when he was brought before Achish, king of Gath, he pretended to be insane and mad, altered his expression before them, collapsed into their hands, struck against [Col. 1066A] the door of the gate, and let his saliva run down into his beard. At the same time, they were lawfully enjoying groups of wives and concubines, and no sin was charged against them on that account. Moreover, [Note: [Col. 1066B] I do not sufficiently understand what Germanus means here. For waging wars and shedding the blood of enemies in a just war is no less lawful under the evangelical law than under the old law. But shedding human blood either by private authority or through personal recklessness was expressly forbidden even before the old law and the Decalogue, in Genesis IX: “Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed. For man was made in the image of God.” If he is referring to the law of retaliation, which commanded that an eye be repaid for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, and a wound for a wound (Exodus XXI, Leviticus XXIV, Matthew V), it is established that this law was given to judges and magistrates as a rule to follow in conducting trials and punishing crimes, not to private persons, to whom the contrary is stated in Leviticus XIX: “You shall not seek revenge, nor remember the injury done by your fellow citizens.”] they also frequently shed the blood of their enemies with their own hands, and this was believed to be not only irreproachable but even praiseworthy.

Now, with the Gospel shining forth, we see these things entirely forbidden, so that none of them can be committed without grave crime and sacrilege. Likewise, we believe that no lie, however piously concealed beneath a pretext, can be used by anyone—not merely lawfully, but not even venially—since the Lord says: “Let your speech be ‘Yes, yes,’ ‘No, no’; anything more than this is from evil” (Matthew V). The Apostle also agrees with this, saying: “Do not lie to one another” (Colossians III).

# CHAPTER XIX  
## The Answer: That the Permission to Lie—which Was Not Granted Even in the Old Testament—Was Nevertheless Used Venially by Many
Joseph: *[Note: [Col. 1066C] The plurality of wives simultaneously and at the same time, which the Greeks call polygamy, although it was neither desirable in itself nor consonant with the perfection and original institution of marriage—for which reason Lamech is rightly reproved (Gen. IV), since he first introduced it when he took two wives, or divided one flesh between two wives, as St. Jerome says—was nevertheless, after the Flood, when there were few human beings and human life had been greatly shortened, permitted by divine dispensation when the law of monogamy was abrogated or relaxed. Polygamy was granted to human beings both for the multiplication of the human race and for the propagation of the faithful people and divine worship, which remained in the single household of Abraham and thereafter in the Israelite people. Thus Abraham is read to have had three wives, Jacob four, and David many more. But when it is said here that freedom regarding wives and concubines was formerly permitted, this must not be understood as though holy men and patriarchs possessed mistresses and harlots, as heretics slanderously claim. Rather, within that plurality of wives, after the primary wife there was one or another woman who was admitted not merely to the marriage bed but to communion in all goods; these were called secondary and inferior wives, or concubines, although they were true and legitimate spouses and were indiscriminately called wives or concubines. Thus Hagar and Keturah are called Abraham’s concubines (Gen. XXV), and we read of David’s concubines (1 Kings XVI); and the Levite’s consort is called at one time a wife and at another a concubine (Judg. XIX). Moreover, once the human race had been sufficiently multiplied, the Lord Christ entirely abolished this license and freedom of polygamy, restoring and renewing the original law of monogamy inspired in our first parents, in Matthew XIX. He adduces three arguments from that primordial institution of marriage, as St. Jerome also observed. First, in the opening of Genesis it is said: “He made them male and female,” not “male and females,” but “male and female,” so that they might enter into the partnership of one spouse, says Jerome. Second, it is said: “For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife,” not “wives.” Third, it is said: “They shall be two in one flesh,” that is, “the two shall be one flesh”: two, he says, not more. Thus Christ, as though recalling by right of return and restoring in full the law of monogamy first instituted and later abrogated or relaxed, added: “I say to you, whoever divorces his wife, except on account of fornication, commits adultery.” The Fathers understood these words to exclude polygamy altogether. For, as Innocent III reasons in a decretal (*Extravagantes*, *On Divorce*, chapter *Gaudemus*): “If, after a wife has been dismissed, another may not lawfully be taken, then this is even more true while the first is retained.” From this it clearly appears that plurality in either sex, since they are not judged by unequal standards, is to be rejected in marriage. Thus the pontiff. (See also Sixtus of Siena, book VI, annotation 82.)]*

The freedom to have many wives and concubines, now that the end of the ages was at hand and the multiplication of the human race had been accomplished, was rightly to be cut away through evangelical perfection as no longer so necessary. For until Christ’s coming, it was necessary that the blessing of that primordial saying should remain in force: “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth” (Gen. I). Therefore it was altogether just that from that root of human fecundity—which, by the dispensation of time, had beneficially flourished in the synagogue—the flowers of angelic virginity should spring and the sweet-smelling fruits of continence be produced in the Church.

That lies had nevertheless been condemned even then is clearly shown by the entire text of the Old Testament, which says: “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Ps. V). And again: “Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be filled with gravel” (Prov. XX). The lawgiver himself says: “You shall flee from a lie” (Exod. XXIII).

*[Note: A lie is intrinsically evil, so that no necessity or dispensation can make it good. Aristotle also recognized this in Book IV, chapter 7 of the *Ethics*, saying that a lie is wicked and blameworthy in itself, whereas truth is beautiful and praiseworthy. A lie does indeed become pardonable or excusable in a necessity—a lie called officious—as in the case of David and others. But being excused is one thing and being approved another; what is certainly good and perfect needs no excuse, whereas what is imperfect and defective does.]*

But we have said that a lie was then used pardonably only when some necessity or salutary dispensation was joined to it, on account of which it ought not to be condemned. Such was the case you mentioned concerning King David (1 Kings XXI), when, fleeing Saul’s unjust pursuit, he used lying words before the priest Ahimelech—not with any intention of gaining something, nor from a desire to harm anyone, but merely to save himself from Saul’s most wicked persecution. He did not wish to stain his hands with the blood of the enemy king, a man so often delivered into his power by God, saying: “May God be gracious to me that I should not do this thing to my lord, the Lord’s anointed, and stretch out my hand against him, for he is the Lord’s anointed” (1 Kings XXIV).

And so, when necessity constrains us, we cannot entirely renounce those dispensations which we read that holy men in the Old Testament carried out either because of God’s will, because they prefigured spiritual mysteries, or for the salvation of certain persons. Indeed, we see that not even the apostles avoided them whenever consideration of some advantage required it. We shall defer these matters briefly for now; after first arranging what we still intend to bring forward from the Old Testament, we shall introduce them more appropriately, so that it may more readily be shown that just and holy men, in both the New and the Old Testaments, agreed entirely in these arrangements.

What shall we say about that pious deception of Hushai toward Absalom, undertaken for the safety of King David? It was advanced with the full intention of deceiving and misleading, and opposed the interests of the person offering the advice; yet it is approved by the testimony of divine Scripture, which says: “The Lord had ordained to defeat the counsel of Ahithophel, so that the Lord might bring evil upon Absalom” (2 Kings XVII).

*[Note: Hushai used not so much a pretense as a plausible and persuasive plan for the safety of King David; Absalom regarded it as wiser and safer than Ahithophel’s advice, and yet Absalom was deceived by that wisdom.]*

For that could not be reproved which was undertaken with right purpose and pious judgment on behalf of the just party, and which had been conceived as a religious deception for the safety and victory of one whose piety was pleasing to God.

What shall we say also about the deed of that woman who received those men whom the aforementioned Hushai had sent to King David, hid them in a well, and, spreading a covering over its mouth, pretended that she was roasting groats?

*[Note: The words of the text are: “As though she were drying groats.” Some interpret *ptisanas* as crushed wheat, others as hulled barley. On this subject see Pliny, Book XVIII, chapter 7, and Book XXII, chapter 25. In this deception, and in other similar examples, the duty of humanity is commended, not whatever lie may have been employed.]*

“After they had tasted a little water,” she said, “they passed on,” and by this fiction she rescued them from the hands of their pursuers (ibid.).

*[Note: St. Augustine answers such a question (*Against Lying*, chapter 17): “Let a person do even for the temporal salvation of human beings whatever he can. But when the matter has reached the point at which he cannot provide for such salvation except by sinning, let him consider that he has nothing left to do, once he sees that what remains is something he cannot rightly do.” And below (chapter 19), proposing the same or a similar question again in the person of those who defended lying: “How can people be rescued—people who, if they are deceived, are undoubtedly turned away from destruction, whether another’s or their own—if our human feeling does not incline us to lie? If the crowd of mortality, the crowd of weakness, will patiently hear me, I shall answer something on behalf of the cause of truth. Certainly pious, true, holy chastity exists only through virtue [another reading: truth], and whoever acts against it certainly acts against truth. Why, then, if those in danger cannot otherwise be helped, do I not commit adultery, which is contrary to truth precisely because it is contrary to chastity, while, in order to help one in danger, I tell a lie, which is most plainly contrary to truth itself? Why has chastity earned such favor among us, while truth has incurred offense, when all chastity derives from truth, and when truth dwells in the mind just as chastity of the body does?” And so forth.]*

Therefore, I ask you, answer me: what would you have done if a similar situation had now arisen for you, living under the Gospel? Would you have preferred to conceal them with a similar lie, saying in the same way, “They passed on after tasting a little water,” and thus fulfill what is commanded: “Rescue those who are being led away to death, and do not hold back from saving those being dragged to slaughter” (Prov. XXIV)? Or would you, by confessing the truth, have exposed those hiding to their executioners?

And where is the Apostle’s saying: “Let no one seek his own advantage, but that of another” (1 Cor. X)? And: “Love does not seek its own, but the things of others” (1 Cor. XIII)? And concerning himself: “I do not seek what is advantageous to me, but what is advantageous to many, so that they may be saved” (1 Cor. X).

For if we seek what is ours and stubbornly insist on retaining what is useful to us, then even in such necessities we must speak the truth and become guilty of another’s death. But if, placing what is salutary to others above our own advantage, we fulfill the apostolic command, then without doubt we must undergo the necessity of lying. Therefore we can possess neither the full inward compassion of charity nor seek what belongs to others according to apostolic discipline unless, relaxing somewhat what suits our strictness and perfection, we willingly stoop to the interests of others, and thus, with the Apostle, become weak to the weak so that we may win the weak (1 Cor. IX).

## CHAPTER XX. That the apostles too considered a lie commonly pardonable and truth harmful

Instructed by these examples, blessed James the Apostle and all the foremost leaders of that primitive Church likewise encouraged the Apostle Paul to descend to the devices of pretense for the weakness of the weak.

*[Note: St. Luke relates the history as follows (Acts XXI): “When we had come to Jerusalem, the brethren gladly received us. On the following day Paul went in with us to James, and all the elders were assembled. Having greeted them, he related in detail what God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry. When they heard it, they glorified God and said to him: ‘You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and all are zealous for the law. But they have heard concerning you that you teach apostasy from Moses to the Jews who are among the Gentiles, saying that they ought not to circumcise their children or walk according to the customs. What then is to be done? The multitude must certainly assemble, for they will hear that you have come. Therefore do what we tell you. We have four men who have a vow upon themselves. Take them, purify yourself with them, and bear the expense for them, so that they may shave their heads; and all will know that the things they have heard concerning you are false, and that you yourself also walk in observance of the law.’ Then Paul, taking the men, on the next day, after being purified with them, entered the Temple, announcing the completion of the days of purification, until the offering should be made for each one of them.” Thus far St. Luke.

Observe here that four legal rites and ceremonies prescribed for the consecration or sanctification of Nazirites are indicated (Num. VI). The first ceremony was the vow by which they publicly consecrated themselves to the Lord. The second was that they remained in the Temple praying for thirty days and meanwhile abstained from wine; this was called cleansing or purification. Third, when the time of purification was completed, an unblemished lamb was offered as a holocaust, a ewe for sin, and an unblemished ram as a peace offering. Finally, their heads were shaved, and the hair was burned together with the sacrifice of peace offerings. These ceremonies prescribed by the law, customarily performed not by just anyone but by the holier observers of the Mosaic law—that is, the Nazirites—the Apostle Paul, yielding to the counsel of the elders, undertook and observed in himself together with the other Jews, as Luke relates.

In this observance St. Jerome, as also this abbot, judges that Paul employed a certain pious pretense in order to avoid scandal to the weak who had believed from among the Jews. Thus Jerome says (Letter 89): “O Paul, I ask you again: why did you shave your head? Why did you perform barefoot rites from the ceremonies of the Jews? Why did you offer sacrifices, and why were victims sacrificed for you according to the law? You will surely answer: ‘So that those who believed from among the Jews might not be scandalized.’ You therefore pretended to be a Jew in order that you might win the Jews, and James and the other presbyters taught you this very pretense.”

But St. Augustine denies that Paul properly pretended; rather, he used the liberty of his conscience, by which he knew that legal ceremonies had not yet been so abrogated that their use, at least temporarily and until the promulgation of the Gospel, was forbidden. Thus, according to Augustine, it was not true pretense or hypocrisy, as this abbot speaks improperly, because Paul performed such rites not in order to deceive but to show that Jews were still free to observe legal rites, provided they did not place their hope of salvation in them.

For these matters to become clearer, it will help here to hear the opinion of St. Thomas (1–2, question 103) concerning the cessation of legal observances, and concerning Peter’s pretense, rebuked by Paul and disputed between the most eminent doctors of the Church, Jerome and Augustine—an opinion highly relevant to this treatise. Thus St. Thomas, commenting on Paul’s words to the Apostle Peter in the Epistle to the Galatians, “If you, being a Jew,” etc., says: “It must be known that no small controversy arose between Jerome and Augustine on the occasion of these words. As can plainly be gathered from their words, they seem to disagree on four points.

“First, concerning the time of the legal observances—when, namely, they ought to have been kept. Jerome distinguishes only two times, one before Christ’s Passion and the other after it. Thus Jerome holds that legal observances before Christ’s Passion were living, that is, retained their efficacy, insofar as original sin was removed through circumcision and God was appeased through sacrifices and victims. But after the Passion he says not merely that they were neither living nor dead, but, what is more, that they were deadly, and that whoever observed them after Christ’s Passion sinned mortally. Augustine, however, distinguishes three times: one before Christ’s Passion, and agrees with Jerome that at that time legal observances were living; another immediately after Christ’s Passion, before grace was promulgated, as in the early time of the apostles. In this time Augustine says that legal observances were dead, but not deadly to Jews converted to the faith, provided that in observing them they did not place their hope in them as though they were necessary to salvation. The third time is after the truth and grace of Christ have been promulgated; in this time he says that they are dead and deadly to all who observe them.

“Second, Jerome and Augustine disagree concerning the observance of legal rites by the apostles themselves. Jerome says that the apostles never observed legal rites in reality, but only with a certain pious pretense, lest they scandalize the Jews and impede their conversion. In this manner he says Paul pretended when he fulfilled the vow in the Temple at Jerusalem (Acts XXI), when he circumcised Timothy (Acts XVI), and when, admonished by James, he undertook certain legal observances (Acts XV). This pretense must be understood not to mean that they did not truly perform those acts, but that they did not do them as observers of the ceremonies of the law, but for other reasons. Augustine, however, says that the apostles observed these legal rites, not because they placed in them any force or hope of salvation, but because this was expedient both for the conversion of the Jews and for burying the Synagogue with honor, lest, if legal observances were immediately abolished and prohibited, they seem to be held on the same level and in the same place as Gentile rites and idolatry, as though they had not been instituted by God and good.

“Third, they disagree concerning Peter’s sin. Jerome says that Peter did not sin in the aforesaid pretense, because he did this from charity and not from any worldly fear. Augustine, however, says that Peter sinned, though venially, through indiscretion, by which he seemed to cling too much to the Jews in order to avoid scandal to them.

“Fourth, they disagree concerning Paul’s rebuke. Jerome says that Paul did not truly rebuke Peter, but did so by pretense, just as Peter observed the legal rites by pretense. Augustine rejects this, because Paul says in the canonical Epistle to the Galatians II—in which it is impious to believe that anything false occurs—that Peter was blameworthy. Thus it is true that Peter sinned, and that Paul truly, not by pretense, rebuked him.” This is St. Thomas, with some things abridged or omitted because of excessive length. If you desire more, reader, consult Baronius, who discusses this whole controversy very learnedly and accurately in the first volume of the *Annals*, and also Bellarmine, *On the Roman Pontiff*, book I, chapter 28.]*

They compelled him to purify himself according to the observance of the law, shave his head, and perform vows, considering the present loss arising from this hypocrisy as nothing, but looking instead to the gains that would result from his long-lasting preaching (Acts XXI). For the gain bestowed upon the Apostle Paul by this strict observance was not as great as the harm his swift death would have caused all the nations. That harm would undoubtedly have befallen the whole Church at that time had not this useful and salutary hypocrisy preserved him for evangelical preaching.

*[Note: St. Augustine (*Against Lying*, chapter 10) calls lies of the kind under discussion, like other sins whose consequences are offset by some advantage and which are therefore excused among human beings, “compensatory” sins: “In all our actions, compensatory sins especially trouble even good actions, so that they are not considered sins if they have such causes for which they are committed—causes in which it seems that one would sin more by not committing them. This has prevailed especially concerning lies in human opinion: such lies are not considered sins; indeed, they are believed to be rightly done whenever someone lies for the benefit of a person whom it is advantageous to deceive, or so as not to harm someone who appears likely to cause harm unless he is avoided by lies.”]*

At that time, then, one necessarily and pardonably accepts the harm of a lie when, as we have said, a greater loss threatens from confessing the truth, and the benefit we receive from the truth is not sufficient to offset the harms that would result.

The blessed Apostle also everywhere testifies, in other words, that he always maintained this same balance. For when he says:

*[Note: How the Apostle did this without pretense or lying, Augustine explains in the same work (chapter 12): “When Paul says, ‘I became all things to all people, that I might win all,’ he did so by showing compassion, not by lying. A person becomes as one whom he wishes to help when he helps with as much mercy as he would wish to be helped if he were in the same misery. Thus he becomes as that person—not because he deceives him, but because he considers himself as though he were in that person’s condition. For if, because he said, ‘To the Jews I became as a Jew; to those under the law, as one under the law,’ he is therefore to be thought to have falsely taken upon himself the sacraments of the old law, then he ought likewise to have taken upon himself pagan idolatry by lying, because he also said that he became as one without the law, in order to win those who were without the law. But he certainly did not do this. He did not sacrifice anywhere to idols or worship those images; rather, as a martyr of Christ, he freely displayed them as detestable and to be avoided.”]*

“I became as a Jew to the Jews, so that I might win the Jews; to those under the law, as though I were under the law”—although I myself was not under the law—“so that I might win those under the law; to those without the law, as though I were without the law”—although I was not without the law of God, but was in the law of Christ—“so that I might win those without the law; I became weak to the weak, so that I might win the weak; I became all things to all people, so that I might save all” (1 Cor. IX)—what else does he show than that he always accommodated himself to the weakness and measure of those being instructed, and relaxed something of the rigor of perfection, not holding to what strict severity seemed to demand, but preferring what the interests of the weak required?

And, investigating these same matters more attentively and recalling one by one the marks of the Apostle’s virtues, let someone ask how blessed Paul is proved to have adapted his role to everyone in every respect. Where did he become as a Jew to the Jews? Certainly there, where, guarding deep within his heart the statement he had announced to the Galatians—“Behold, I, Paul, say to you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. V)—he nevertheless assumed, in a certain manner, the appearance of Jewish superstition in the circumcision of Timothy.

And again, where did he become as one under the law to those who were under the law? Surely there, where James and all the elders of the Church, fearing that the multitude of believing Jews—or rather, of Christians who were Judaizing—might rush upon him, came to his aid in his peril through this plan and persuasion. They had accepted the faith of Christ while still adhering to the rites of the legal ceremonies. They said:

“You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and they are all zealous for the law. But they have heard about you that you teach the Jews who live among the Gentiles to abandon Moses, saying that they should not circumcise their children” (Acts XXI).

And below:

“Do therefore what we tell you. We have four men who have a vow upon themselves. Take these men and purify yourself with them, and pay their expenses so that they may shave their heads; and everyone will know that the things they have heard about you are false, but that you yourself walk in observance of the law” (ibid.).

Thus, for the salvation of those who were under the law, temporarily trampling upon the strictness of the judgment by which he had said, “Through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God” (Gal. II), he is compelled to shave his head, be purified according to the law, and offer vows in the Temple according to the Mosaic rite.

Do you also ask where, for the salvation of those who entirely ignored the law of the Lord, he became as though he himself were without the law and became without the law? Read in the Gentile city of Athens, where impiety flourished, the opening of his preaching:

“Passing by,” he says, “I saw your images and an altar on which was written, ‘To the unknown God’” (Acts XVII).

Having begun his discourse from their superstition, as though he himself too were without the law, he introduced the faith of Christ under the pretext of that profane inscription, saying:

“What therefore you worship without knowing, this I proclaim to you” (ibid.).

And shortly afterward, as though entirely ignorant of the divine law, he preferred to cite a verse of a pagan poet rather than a saying of Moses or Christ:

“As some of your own poets have said,” he says, “For we are indeed his offspring” (ibid.).

Having thus confronted them with their own testimonies, which they could not refute, and confirming truths from falsehoods, he added:

“Since therefore we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the divine nature is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and thought of man” (ibid.).

He became weak to the weak when, in accordance with indulgence rather than command, he allowed those who could not contain themselves to return to the same state (1 Cor. VII), or when, feeding the Corinthians with milk rather than solid food, he says that he was among them in weakness, fear, and great trembling (1 Cor. III).

He became all things to all people so that he might save all when he says:

“Let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat, and let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats” (Rom. XIV);

and:

“He who joins his virgin in marriage does well, and he who does not join her does better” (1 Cor. VII).

And elsewhere:

“Who is weak,” he says, “and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not burning?” (2 Cor. XI).

In this way he fulfilled what he had commanded the Corinthians:

“Be without offense to Jews and Greeks and the Church of Christ, just as I also please everyone in everything, not seeking what is advantageous to me, but what is advantageous to many, so that they may be saved” (1 Cor. X).

For it would certainly have been advantageous not to circumcise Timothy, not to shave his head, not to undertake Jewish purification, not to perform the barefoot rites, and not to offer legal vows.

*[Note: Among the Jews, *nudipedalia* were certain sacred rites, or public supplications, in which the people walked barefoot while imploring rain from God; Josephus discusses them in Book II of *The Jewish War*. They were also sometimes practiced among Christians (Coelius Rhodiginus, Book XV of the *Ancient Readings*, chapter 6). The present abbot appears to indicate that the same rite was observed, according to ancient tradition, in that Jewish purification and sanctification, although no mention of this ceremony appears in Numbers VI, where the rites of the Nazirites are discussed. Otherwise it is not apparent when the Apostle performed such barefoot rites in the Jewish manner, though St. Jerome also indicates this in the passage cited above. Again, in Book I *Against Jovinianus* (chapter 8), Jerome says: “The Apostle is often compelled to wish for things he does not wish for: he circumcised Timothy, shaved his own head, performed barefoot rites, grew his hair, and cut it at Cenchrea.” Tertullian also mentions the barefoot rites of pagans in his *Apology* (chapter 41).]*

But he did all these things while giving greater consideration to their salvation, because he did not seek what was advantageous to himself, but what was advantageous to many, so that they might be saved.

Although this was done with consideration for God:

*[Note: Rather, as is clear from what has been said, it was without simulation—unless you use “simulation” here and throughout in the sense of dissimulation or concealment of the truth. For Augustine says (*On Lying*, chapter 5): “Paul did not, as some think, circumcise Timothy or himself celebrate certain sacraments according to the Jewish rite merely as a pretense; rather, he did so from the liberty of his judgment, by which he preached that circumcision did not benefit Gentiles or harm Jews. Thus he judged that the former should not be bound to Jewish custom, nor the latter deterred from their ancestral practice. Hence his words are: ‘Was anyone called while circumcised? Let him not seek to remove the marks of circumcision. Was anyone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised. Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but keeping the commandments of God. Let each remain in the calling in which he was called.’ And below: ‘Although Timothy had been called in uncircumcision, because he was born of a Jewish mother and had to show his relatives, in order to win them, that he had not learned in Christian discipline to abominate the sacraments of the old law, he was circumcised by the Apostle. In this way he demonstrated to the Jews that the Gentiles did not refuse to receive those practices because they were evil or had been wickedly observed by their ancestors, but because, after the coming of so great a sacrament—which the whole of Scripture had brought forth through prophetic figures over such a long period—they were no longer necessary for salvation. Paul would also have circumcised Titus when the Jews pressed the matter, had not the false brethren who had infiltrated the community wished this to be done so that they would have something to spread about Paul—as though he had yielded to their claims, who preached that the hope of evangelical salvation lay in circumcision of the flesh and such observances, and maintained that Christ benefited no one without them; whereas Christ benefited not at all those who were circumcised with the intention of placing salvation there.””]*

Nevertheless it was not without a certain appearance of pretense. For he who had died to the law through the law of Christ so that he might live to God (Gal. II), and who had counted as loss the righteousness of the law in which he had lived blamelessly, regarding it as refuse in order to gain Christ (Phil. III), could not offer what belonged to the law with a true affection of heart. Nor may we believe that he who had said, “If I rebuild the things that I destroyed, I make myself a transgressor” (Gal. II), fell into the very thing he had condemned.

And so the matter itself that is done is considered less than the disposition of the person doing it; indeed, the truth is found to have harmed some, while a lie benefited them.

For when Doeg the Edomite complained before King Saul’s servants about David’s flight, saying:

“Will the son of Jesse give all of you fields and vineyards, and make all of you commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds, because you have all conspired against me and there is no one who informs me?” (1 Kings XXII),

what did he reveal except the truth when he said:

“I saw the son of Jesse at Nob with Ahimelech the priest, who consulted the Lord for him and gave him provisions; he also gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine” (ibid.)?

For that truth he deserved to be uprooted from the land of the living, and the Prophet says of him:

“Therefore God will destroy you forever; he will tear you away and remove you from your tent, and uproot you from the land of the living” (Ps. LI).

From that land, therefore, he is torn away by perpetual uprooting for having reported the truth, in which Rahab the prostitute (Josh. II) is planted together with her family because of a lie.

Likewise, we remember that Samson (Judg. XVI) concealed that day by a lie but most disastrously revealed it in truth to his impious wife. Truth incautiously disclosed brought deception upon him because he had neglected to observe the prophetic command: “Guard the doors of your mouth from her who sleeps in your bosom” (Mic. VII).

## CHAPTER XXI. Whether hidden continence ought to be disclosed without lying to those who ask, and whether what has once been refused should be accepted

To offer some examples from our own unavoidable and almost daily necessities—necessities which, however carefully we observe ourselves, we can never so guard against that we are not compelled to fall into them, willingly or unwillingly—what, I ask, should be done when, as we intend to postpone our meal, a brother arrives in the evening and asks whether we have eaten? Should the fast be concealed and the virtue of moderation hidden, or should it be disclosed by a profession of the truth?

*[Note: St. Augustine denies this: “For,” he says, “to conceal the truth is not the same thing as uttering a lie. Although everyone who lies wishes to conceal what is true, not everyone who wishes to conceal what is true lies. Often we conceal truths not by lying, but by remaining silent. The Lord did not lie when he said, ‘I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now’ (John XVI). He kept silent about truths; he did not speak falsehoods to those whom he judged less capable of hearing those truths. Therefore austerity of life—which the abbot here calls continence—is not to be concealed by a lie, but covered either by silence or by some ambiguity of speech, or, when appropriate, openly professed for God’s glory, not one’s own. Whoever does this certainly does not lose his reward, as the abbot incorrectly interprets it. See the following annotation.”]*

If we conceal it in order to fulfill the Lord’s command, “Do not appear to people to be fasting, but to your Father who is in secret” (Matt. VI), and again, “Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing” (ibid.), then we are certainly lying. If we disclose the virtue of continence, the evangelical sentence rightly strikes us: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (ibid.).

But if someone firmly refuses a cup offered by a brother, expressly denying that he will accept it, while the brother, rejoicing at his arrival, humbly begs him to drink it—would it be right for him to comply, even at the cost of his own effort, with a brother who has fallen to his knees and prostrated himself on the ground, believing that only through such acts of service could he fulfill the inward demands of charity? Or should he persist in the obstinacy of his words and his original resolve?

## CHAPTER XXII. The objection that continence ought indeed to be hidden, but that what has once been refused should not be accepted
Germanus: In that preceding example, at least, there is no doubt, as we believe, that it is preferable to conceal our ascetic discipline [Col. 1076A] rather than reveal it to those who inquire about it.

[Note: [Col. 1075D] Not, however, in such a way that, while avoiding arrogance, one abandons the truth, as St. Augustine says (*Tractate 43 on John*, chapter 2). And St. Gregory, in the twenty-sixth book of the *Moralia*: “They are imprudently humble who entangle themselves in a lie while avoiding arrogance; indeed, by lying they become proud, because they set themselves against the truth, which they abandon. For whoever, compelled by necessity, speaks truly about the good things in himself is joined all the more closely to humility because he is also joined to truth. Was Paul not humble when, out of zeal for the truth against the false apostles, he recounted so many mighty deeds concerning himself to his disciples? He would plainly have been an enemy of the truth if, by concealing his virtues, he had allowed the preachers of error to prevail” (see Climacus, step 12).]

And concerning matters of this kind we too admit that lying is unavoidable.

[Note: [Col. 1076D] Rather, one must maintain the opposite: that lying is never unavoidable. Because of these and similar erroneous and paradoxical statements scattered throughout this Conference, I read somewhere (in old manuscript codices) that this Conference of Abbot Joseph, together with the thirteenth Conference—which St. Prosper attacked—was condemned and rejected by the theology faculty of Paris.]

In the second case, however, no necessity compels us to lie: first, because we can return what is offered through the service of the brothers in such a way that we do not bind ourselves by any definitive declaration; and second, because, once we have refused, we can hold firmly to our decision.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The Answer: That Persistence in This Decision Is Unreasonable

Joseph: There is no doubt that these decisions belong to the monasteries in which, as you say, the beginnings of your renunciation were formed. Their leaders commonly place their own wishes before the refreshment of the brothers [Col. 1076B] and carry out with the greatest stubbornness whatever they have once conceived in their minds.

Our elders, however, whose faith was attested by the signs of apostolic virtues, and who conducted everything by judgment and spiritual discernment rather than by rigid obstinacy of mind, judged that those who accommodated themselves to the weaknesses of others gained much richer fruits than those who persisted in their own decisions. They declared it to be a higher virtue to conceal one’s ascetic discipline, when necessary, by the humble lie mentioned above, than to expose it by a proud declaration of the truth.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How Abbot Piammon Preferred to Conceal His Ascetic Discipline

[Col. 1076C]

Finally, after twenty-five years, Abbot Piammon accepted without hesitation a bunch of grapes and wine offered to him by a certain brother, and immediately tasted what had been placed before him contrary to his customary practice. He preferred to do this rather than reveal to everyone the virtue of his unknown abstinence.

[Note: [Col. 1076D] The Conference that follows—namely, the eighteenth, concerning the three kinds of monks—belongs to him; several further points about the same matter should be noted there.]

For if we also wish to consider what we remember our elders to have done without hesitation—those who used to present the remarkable deeds of their virtues, or their own actions that had necessarily to be brought forward for the instruction of the younger brothers in the Conference, under the names of other persons—what else can we judge concerning such things than that they were an open lie?

[Note: [Col. 1076D] A plainly frivolous argument, as Cuychius rightly says. Who would say that someone who speaks about himself in the third person is lying, if he mixes nothing false into his account? Was Christ therefore lying when he said, “The Son of Man will be handed over to the Gentiles to be mocked, scourged, and crucified”; and, “The Son of Man will come with great power and majesty,” and so forth? What could be more absurd than to say so?]

And would that we too possessed something worthy of being proposed to the younger brothers for the purpose of stimulating their faith! We certainly would not hesitate to follow such inventions of theirs. For it is better to lie under the cover of such a figure than, on account of an irrational observance of this truth, to conceal by inappropriate silence things that could have edified those listening; or, if they are truthfully spoken in our own person, to recount the harmful vanity of boasting.

The teacher of the Gentiles clearly instructed us in this as well by his own example. He preferred to relate the greatness of his revelations in the person of another, saying: “I know a man in Christ, whether in the body or outside the body I do not know—God knows—who was caught up to the third heaven; and I know that such a man was caught up into paradise and heard ineffable words, which it is not permitted for a human being to speak” (2 Corinthians 12).

## CHAPTER XXV. Scriptural Testimonies Concerning Changed Decisions

It is impossible for us to run briefly through everything. For who could be sufficient to enumerate almost all the holy patriarchs and the countless others who, some for the protection of life, some out of desire for a blessing, some for the concealment of a mystery, some out of zeal for God, and some for the examination of the truth, have, so to speak, taken up the defense of lying?

[Note: [Col. 1077C] It is very strange that this abbot should be so foolish as not to hesitate to attribute to the patriarchs, and even to the Apostles, not only the mark of lying but also its defense. Nothing is more alien to the truth than this. Yet one must be indulgent toward the simplicity of people of this kind.]

Just as all these examples cannot be enumerated, so they ought not all to be entirely passed over. For piety compelled blessed Joseph to bring a false accusation against his brothers, even invoking the safety of the king, when he said:

[Note: [Col. 1077C] Joseph knew that his brothers were not spies, and he had no doubt about this. Some interpret his words as having been spoken merely by way of testing and investigation, not as an assertion. But he brought this accusation against them in order to compel them to reveal the condition of their father and their uterine brother Benjamin, whom he loved uniquely. Josephus says this in *Antiquities*, book 2, chapter 3, and Sulpicius in *Sacred History*, book 1. Yet he did not accuse them unjustly or insultingly. Since he was acting publicly in the role of judge in Egypt, he could deal with them more severely according to judicial custom and, as one aware of the crime committed against him, publicly exact retribution from the accused. Nevertheless, he exacted far less than they deserved, because the matter was not being handled in a public court. We must therefore admit that it was a kind of officious lie—or something similar—not harmful because it was not unjust.

Yet St. Augustine appears to excuse him from every lie when he explains those words as follows (*Questions on Genesis*, question 168): “You are spies,” that is, “you are worthy of the punishment due to spies,” or “you are to be regarded as spies.” And, he says, Joseph added an oath to this statement because, if they had not spoken the truth, they would have been spies—that is, worthy of the punishment due to spies—although he knew that they were telling the truth. For no one is perjured if he says to someone whom he knows to be chaste, “If you committed this adultery of which you are accused, God condemns you”; and if he adds an oath to these words, he swears something entirely true. The condition is present in the words, “If you did it,” although he is certain that the person did not do it.

But someone may say: It is true that, if he committed adultery, God condemns him; but how is this statement true—“If you do not speak the truth, you are spies”—when even if they were lying, they would not be spies? This is what I meant when I said that it was expressed in this way: “You are spies,” that is, “you will rightly be considered spies because of your lie.” The verb “you are” can be used in the sense of “you will be regarded” or “you will be reckoned”; countless similar expressions demonstrate this. Thus the prophet Elijah says: “Whoever is answered by fire, he shall be God.” He will not in fact become God at that time, but he will then be regarded as God. So Augustine.]

“You are spies; you have come to inspect the unfortified parts of the land” (Genesis 42). And further: “Send one of your number,” he said, “and bring your brother here; but you shall be kept here until your words become evident—whether you speak the truth or not. Otherwise, by the life of Pharaoh, you are spies” (Genesis 42).

For if he had not terrified them by this merciful lie, he could neither have seen his father and brother again, nor have supported them amid such great dangers of famine, nor finally have cleansed their consciences from guilt for selling him. Therefore, it was not so reprehensible to inspire fear in his brothers by a lie as it was holy and praiseworthy, by means of a fabricated danger, to compel his enemies and sellers into salutary repentance.

Finally, when they were pressed by the odium of this very serious accusation, they were not broken by consciousness of the charge falsely brought against them, but by consciousness of their earlier crime. They said to one another: “We deserve these things, because we sinned against our brother; because we saw the anguish of his soul when he begged us and we did not listen to him. Therefore all this tribulation has come upon us” (ibid.).

This confession, as we believe, expiated their enormous crime not only before their brother, against whom they had sinned with impious cruelty, but also through a most salutary humility.

[Note: [Col. 1078D] No lie is recognized in Solomon’s judgment, because he spoke nothing contrary to his mind; nor was there properly speaking any simulation, since he wished to deceive no one. Rather, there was a most perceptive investigation of the maternal and natural affection, from which he wisely recognized and judged whose son the child in question was.]

What of Solomon, who, in his first judgment, revealed the wisdom he had received from God only by resorting to a lie? In order to draw out the truth that was concealed by the woman’s lie, he himself also employed the aid of a lie, devised with great cleverness, saying: “Bring me a sword, and divide the living child into two parts, and give half to one and half to the other” (1 Kings 3).

When this pretended cruelty moved the entrails of the true mother, while the woman who was not the mother praised it, he then pronounced, with the most perceptive judgment [alternative reading: indication] of the truth, that sentence which no one failed to believe had been inspired by God: “Give the living child to this woman,” he said, “and do not kill it; for she is its mother” (ibid.).

Accordingly, that we neither ought nor are able to carry out everything that we decide, whether in tranquility of mind or under agitation, is also taught more fully by other testimonies of Scripture. In them we frequently read that holy men, angels, and even almighty God himself changed what they had decided.

Thus blessed David, after making a decision under oath, said: “May God do these things to the enemies of David, and add these things, if I leave alive by morning any male belonging to Nabal” (1 Samuel 25).

[Note: [Col. 1079D] Concerning this rash oath of David and his salutary correction and withdrawal from it, Augustine says the following in the book often cited (*Against Lying*, chapter 9): “Because David swore that he would kill Nabal and did not do so out of a merciful consideration, are we therefore to say that he should be imitated, so that we rashly swear that we will do something which we later see ought not to be done? God forbid.”]

Immediately, when his wife Abigail intervened and pleaded on Nabal’s behalf, he abandoned his threats and softened his decision. He preferred to be judged a transgressor of his intention rather than to keep faith with his oath by carrying out cruelty, saying: “As the Lord lives, if you had not come quickly to meet me, Nabal would not have been left alive until the morning, not even a male” (ibid.).

Just as we judge that the rash ease with which he made that oath—a rashness proceeding from the agitation of a disturbed mind—is in no way to be imitated, so we decide that the remission and correction of a decision should be pursued.

The Chosen One, writing to the Corinthians, promised his return with an unconditional decision, saying: “I will come to you after I have passed through Macedonia; for I will pass through Macedonia, but I will remain with you, or even spend the winter, so that you may send me on my way wherever I go. For I do not wish to see you now only in passing, since I hope to remain with you for some time” (1 Corinthians 16).

He also recalls the matter in the second Epistle: “With this confidence I intended to come to you first, so that you might have a second favor, and through you to pass into Macedonia, and again from Macedonia to come to you, and to be sent on my way by you into Judea” (2 Corinthians 1).

But when a more salutary plan intervened, he most clearly confesses that he did not carry out what he had promised. “When I had this intention,” he says, “did I act with fickleness? Or do I make my plans according to the flesh, so that with me there is ‘yes and no’?” (ibid.).

Finally, he explains, even with an oath, why he preferred to retract his declared intention rather than bring sorrow upon his disciples by his arrival: “I call God as witness against my soul, that to spare you I did not come again to Corinth. For I decided this within myself: not to come to you again in sorrow” (2 Corinthians 1).

When the angels were about to enter Lot’s house in Sodom, they denied that they would enter, saying to him: “We will not enter, but will remain in the street” (Genesis 19).

[Note: [Col. 1079D] This abbot thinks that the angels used simulation or changed their decision. It is more probable, however, that they merely denied that they would enter at the first opportunity, that is, in response to this initial invitation, but not if they were pressed further. So Cajetan.]

Immediately, compelled by his entreaties, they changed their decision, as Scripture adds: “And Lot compelled them, and they turned in to him” (Genesis 19).

If they knew that they would turn in to him, then they refused the petitioner’s request by a simulated excuse; but if they were making a sincere excuse, they are clearly shown to have changed their decision.

We believe that the Holy Spirit inserted these examples into the sacred books for no other reason than to teach us by them not to persist stubbornly in our decisions, but to subject them to our judgment and to preserve our judgment free from every legal constraint, so that it may be ready to follow wherever a salutary plan calls it, and neither delay nor refuse to pass without hesitation to whatever a beneficial discernment has found to be more useful.

And to ascend to still more exalted examples: King Hezekiah was lying on his bed and suffering from a grave illness when the prophet Isaiah addressed him in God’s name, saying: “Thus says the Lord: Put your house in order, for you shall die and not live.” And, it says, “Hezekiah turned his face to the wall, prayed to the Lord, and said: ‘I beg you, Lord; remember, I pray, how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done what is good in your sight.’ And Hezekiah wept with great weeping” (Isaiah 38).

After this, the following was again said to him: “Return and say to Hezekiah, king of Judah: Thus says the Lord God of David your father: I have heard your prayer and seen your tears; and behold, I will add fifteen years to your days, and I will deliver you and this city from the hand of the king of Assyria; and I will protect this city for my sake and for the sake of David my servant” (ibid.).

[Note: [Col. 1079D] This abbot does everything possible to summon support for lying from every quarter. Not content with having made even the holiest men, and even angels, liars and patrons of lying, he comes close to teaching that God himself is a liar. The threatening declarations that he wrongly adduces in support of his opinion—by which God threatened Hezekiah with death, the Ninevites with the destruction of their city, and other sinners with various punishments that he nevertheless did not inflict—were not absolute but conditional, and should be understood under this or a similar condition: “unless they repent or implore God’s mercy.” God’s word is therefore not annulled, nor is God’s decision properly changed, when, after correction and repentance have followed, the threatened effect does not occur. God threatens not in order to carry out his threats, but rather so that, once human beings have been corrected and have repented, he may not carry them out. See more in the censure of Cuychius.]

What testimony could be clearer than this, by which the Lord, out of regard for mercy and compassion, preferred to cancel his own word and extend the life of the one who prayed by fifteen years beyond the appointed limit of death, rather than be found inexorable through the immutability of his decree?

He speaks similarly to the Ninevites in a divine pronouncement: “In three days Nineveh will be overthrown” (Jonah 3). Immediately, however, their repentance and fasting softened this threatening and abrupt sentence, and pious mercy inclined it toward the side of compassion.

If someone should claim that the Lord threatened the destruction of the city to them, as though he knew beforehand that they would convert, in order to provoke them to salutary repentance, it follows that those who preside over the brothers may, without being reproached for lying, threaten those who need correction with punishments even more severe than they will in fact impose, if necessary.

But if someone says that God revoked that severe sentence of his in consideration of their repentance, in accordance with what he says through Ezekiel—“If I say to the wicked, ‘You shall surely die,’ and he repents of his sin and does what is lawful and right, he shall surely live and shall not die” (Ezekiel 33)—then these examples teach us that we ought not to persist stubbornly in our decisions, but should soften a threat necessarily made through merciful compassion.

And lest it be believed that the Lord granted this only to the Ninevites in particular, he also declares generally through the prophet Jeremiah that he will do the same toward everyone and, when necessary, will undoubtedly change his decision according to our merits. He says: “Suddenly I will speak against a nation and against a kingdom, to uproot, destroy, and ruin it. If that nation turns from its evil concerning which I have spoken against it, I too will repent of the evil that I intended to do to it. And suddenly I will speak concerning a nation and a kingdom, to build and plant it. If it does evil in my sight, so that it does not hear my voice, I will repent of the good that I had said I would do to it” (Jeremiah 15).

He also says to Ezekiel: “Do not withhold the word, in case they listen and each one turns from his evil way, and I repent of the evil that I had intended to do to them because of the wickedness of their practices” (Jeremiah 26).

These testimonies show that we ought not to cling stubbornly to our decisions, but should moderate them by reason and judgment. We must always choose and prefer what is better and, without hesitation, pass over to whichever side has been judged more useful.

## CHAPTER XXVI. That Divine Clemency Neither Rewards nor Punishes Each Person According to the Immensity of Divine Foreknowledge, but According to Present Actions

That immeasurable judgment also teaches us above all that, although the end of each person is known to God before that person’s birth, he nevertheless dispenses everything in an orderly and generally rational way, adapting himself, in a manner of speaking, to human affections. He does not judge everything according to power or according to the ineffable knowledge of his foreknowledge, but according to people’s present actions; accordingly, he either rejects or attracts each person, and either pours out his grace daily or withdraws it.

The election of Saul also demonstrates that this is so (1 Samuel 10). Although God’s foreknowledge could not have been ignorant of Saul’s blameworthy end, God chose him from among the thousands of Israel and anointed him king, rewarding the merit of his present life in him and not taking into account the sin of his future transgression.

Thus, after Saul had become rejected, God is portrayed as though he were repenting of his choice, and as though he were complaining about him in human words and affections, saying:

[Note: [Col. 1081D] St. Gregory (*On 1 Kings 15*) asks: “Why is the Lord said to repent, when he is not believed to change in his affections?” But because supreme immutability speaks with mutable beings, when he is said to repent in their manner of speaking, the arrogance of the proud is shown to be displeasing to him. We usually repent when those to whom we have given honors or gifts repay us with evil. Therefore, because almighty God complains, in our manner of speaking, about the ingratitude of the proud king, he is said to repent of having bestowed royal dignity upon him. This is said of the proud as an increase of their great condemnation, because what they are is no longer for merit but for punishment, since they are not in the will of God. God’s repentance, therefore, is his not having the reprobate in his will, while he remembers the honors he bestowed upon them; it is his recognizing that those to whom he gave good things have used those good things badly. God indicates this repentance of his in other words through the prophet Malachi, saying to the Jews: “I have no pleasure in you, and I will not accept an offering from your hand” (chapter 1). See St. Ambrose, *On the Ark and Noah*, chapter 4; St. Augustine, *City of God*, book 15, chapter 25; and St. Thomas, part 1, question 19, article 7.]

“It repents me that I made Saul king, because he has abandoned me and has not fulfilled my words in action.” And again: “Nevertheless, Samuel mourned for Saul, because the Lord regretted that he had made Saul king over Israel” (1 Samuel 15).

Finally, since he had already carried this out in action [the text reads *hoc quoniam*; perhaps *quod jam*], the Lord later also declares through the prophet Ezekiel that he will deal with all human beings according to this daily judgment: “Even if I say to the righteous that he shall surely live, and, trusting in his righteousness, he commits iniquity, all his righteousnesses shall be forgotten, and he shall die in the iniquity he has committed. But if I say to the wicked, ‘You shall surely die,’ and he repents of his sin and does what is lawful and right, restores the pledge, returns what he has stolen, walks in the commandments of life, and does nothing unjust, he shall surely live and shall not die. None of the sins he committed shall be remembered against him” (Ezekiel 33).

Finally, when the Lord had turned away the sight of his mercy from the people whom he had adopted from among all nations because of their sudden transgression in making the calf, the lawgiver intervened on their behalf and cried out: “I beg you, Lord: this people has committed a great sin; they have made gods of gold. And now, if you will forgive their sin, forgive it; but if not, erase me from the book you have written.” The Lord answered him: “Whoever has sinned against me, him I will erase from my book” (Exodus 32).

David too, while complaining in prophetic spirit about Judas and the persecutors of Christ, said: “Let them be erased from the book of the living.” And because they did not deserve to attain salutary repentance for the guilt of so great a crime, he added: “And let them not be written among the righteous” (Psalm 68).

Finally, the prophetic force of this curse was plainly fulfilled in Judas himself: after completing the crime of betrayal, he hanged himself (Matthew 27), lest, if after the erasure of his name he had turned to repentance, he might once again deserve to be written among the righteous in heaven.

There is therefore no doubt that, at the time when Judas was chosen by Christ and received the rank of apostle, his name had been written in the book of the living, and that he had heard, together with the others: “Do not rejoice that the demons are subject to you; rejoice instead that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10).

But because he was corrupted by the plague of avarice and cast down from the heavenly inscription to earthly things, the prophet aptly says of him and those like him: “Lord, let all who abandon you be put to shame; let those who depart from you be written in the earth, because they have abandoned the Lord, the spring of living waters” (Jeremiah 17). And elsewhere: “They shall not be in the council of my people, nor shall they be written in the writing of the house of Israel, nor shall they enter the land of Israel” (Ezekiel 13).

## CHAPTER XXVII. That Holy Men Cannot Be Stubborn and Harsh

Nor should the usefulness of that command be left unmentioned: even if, prompted by anger or by any other passion, we have bound ourselves by some oath—

[Note: [Col. 1083B] That is, if we have obligated ourselves by a vow, oath, or promise. According to Festus, *sacramentum* means whatever is done after an oath has been given. Our author also uses the term in this sense. Hence the expression “military oath,” by which soldiers swore allegiance to the words of their commander.

Moreover, swearing without necessity is especially disgraceful for religious people and those who fear God, particularly when it arises from anger or another passion, as is said here. Hence St. Jerome, writing to Celantia (*Letter 14*): “Let your tongue be entirely unfamiliar with lying and swearing, and let your love of truth be so great in you that whatever you say you regard as sworn.” St. Augustine, who before his conversion had been inclined to swear, says of himself after reforming his life and aspiring to evangelical perfection (*Sermon 10 on the Saints*): “By fearing God, we have removed swearing from our mouth. Behold, we live among you. Who has ever heard us swear?” and so forth.

There is also an excellent document on this subject from Pope Innocent III in canon law, in which he admonishes and instructs certain monks in these words (*Book 2 of the Decretals*, chapter “Although Christ,” title “On Oaths”): “Although you ought to be perfect men, so that, as far as you can, you avoid the bond of an oath, nevertheless, wishing to provide for the security of your monastery, lest, through a lack of witnesses, it suffer injury to its rights, by this present document we grant you permission”—that is, we show that permission has been granted, as the gloss says—“to bear witness to the truth on its behalf.”

This is what the Pope says, along with other material cited above from the same chapter (at chapter 10).]

—even though no monk ought ever to do this—nevertheless, the cause of either matter must be weighed with a sound judgment of mind. The decision we have made must be compared with the one to which we are compelled to turn, and we must pass without hesitation to whichever is judged more just after the elders have considered the matter.

[Note: [Col. 1083C] That is, to change one’s decision even when it has been confirmed by a vow or oath. What follows shows that this should not be understood of the principal commandments necessary for salvation—that is, of the precepts and vows of religious life—but of certain bodily exercises, namely fasts, prayers, and other austerities, by which those monks used carelessly and imprudently to bind themselves from time to time by vow or oath.

Consequently, they later fell into great scruples and anguish of conscience when, because brothers or travelers arrived, or because some other necessity demanded it, they were compelled to relax some part of their austerity and thus appeared to be vow-breakers, perjurers, or excessively stubborn and inhuman.

In this matter they were plainly mistaken, because they did not understand that the obligation of a vow, oath, or any promise ceases for two reasons.

First, if the thing or action sworn or promised later becomes impossible for the person who swore or vowed it, or becomes unlawful because a superior forbids it (St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* II–II, question 89, article 7; Bede, homily 13; Gratian, *Decretum* 22, question 4, canon “If anything”). In such cases the venerable saying of Bede, cited by Gratian, applies: “If it should happen that we have rashly sworn to something whose observance tends toward a worse outcome, let us know that it must freely be changed by a more salutary counsel,” and so forth. This is what the abbot says here in other words: it is better for us to retract our statement than to suffer the loss of something more salutary and pious.

Second, the thing sworn or promised may not be evil in itself, but may nevertheless impede a greater good. For example, a monk may vow long and severe fasts, disciplines, sleeping on the ground, and so forth, through which he would become incapable and unfit to perform other duties that are more spiritual and salutary; or he may swear that he will go to church on a certain day, and then it may happen that a sick person needs his presence.

That promises and oaths of this kind either do not bind from the beginning or cease to bind later is shown by Bede’s words quoted above, since their observance tends toward a worse outcome when it excludes a greater good.

Such, it seems, was the pledge—or vow, or oath—by which Cassian and his Germanus had bound themselves to their superiors and brothers in the monastery at Bethlehem to return to the monastery within a fixed period. Nevertheless, following the instruction and teaching of Abbot Joseph, and as though confirmed by a divine oracle, they preferred to remain in Egypt and live and associate with those fathers and anchorites, until at last, after seven years had been completed, they went back to their own monastery and fulfilled their pledge.

This was the whole point of the abbot’s discussion and instruction in this Conference (see chapter 2 above): to teach them that they had not acted wisely or provided well for themselves when they had bound themselves so strictly to a fixed period, since by keeping that condition they would be prevented from pursuing a greater good—that is, spiritual progress, the pursuit of perfection, and more successful advancement.

He therefore concludes that they were not bound by a condition and decision of this kind, and that they could safely and with a clear conscience retract it or suitably interpret it according to *epieikeia* (ἐπιείκεια, equitable interpretation). At his urging, they did so.
