In this matter neither the adviser nor those who followed his advice seem blameworthy—except that, on this occasion, he turned aside into a defense and advocacy of lying, which was extraneous and unnecessary to the matter under discussion, and that he often took lying to mean a change of counsel or decision, as though to lie and to change one’s mind were the same thing. They are plainly very different, as is clear from what has been said.

This long and serious residence among the fellowship and community of the most holy monks [Col. 1084D] and anchorites—undoubtedly under the laws of obedience and regular discipline, and with no other purpose than to attain greater perfection—appeared to be a transition to a stricter religious life, from the coenobitic life to the eremitical one. Such a transition is approved by the holy Fathers and is also permitted by canon law, with the superiors’ permission, even if that permission has not been obtained, in the chapter “Although,” *On Regulars* (Book 3 of the Decretals).

They are especially supported by St. Bernard’s statement in *On Precept and Dispensation* (chapter 20), where he writes: “Certainly, in the case of religious and well-ordered monasteries, no professed member should leave, on my advice, even out of a desire for a stricter life, without the permission of his superior. Yet if, after leaving, he finds and chooses something better, then, still on my advice, he should not return to the inferior good that he had abandoned and despised in favor of the better—especially if that better state appears compatible with his original profession. Let him himself consider by what reasoning and intention he presumed to seek higher or stricter things; but, on my advice, he should not apostatize to lower or more relaxed things.” Thus Bernard.

From these considerations it may be inferred with sufficient probability that Cassian and Germanus, notwithstanding their profession and promise, could remain with those fathers in the desert and lead a religious life with them. This was the position and purpose of the entire discussion and Conference.]

For it is better for us to retract our statement than to suffer the loss of something more salutary and pious.

Finally, we do not remember that reasonable and approved fathers were ever harsh or irrevocable in decisions of this kind. Rather, just as wax is softened by the heat of the sun, so they were softened by reason and, when a more salutary counsel intervened, yielded without hesitation to the better course.

But whenever we saw people clinging stubbornly to their decisions, we always judged them unreasonable and lacking in discernment.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The Question: Whether the Statement “I Have Sworn and Determined,” and So Forth, Is Contrary to the Foregoing Opinion

Germanus: With regard to this argument, which has been set out clearly and at length, a monk ought to make no decision, lest he be found either a transgressor or stubborn. But where then do we place the Psalmist’s declaration: “I have sworn and determined to keep the judgments of your righteousness” (Psalm 118)?

For what else does it mean to swear and determine than to keep firmly what has been decided?

## CHAPTER XXIX. The Answer: In What Matters a Decision Must Be Held Firm, and in What Matters It Must Be Rescinded, If Necessary
Joseph: We do not make these decrees concerning the principal commandments, without which our salvation cannot possibly endure at all, but concerning those matters which we can relax or maintain without danger to our state: for example, an unrelaxed strictness of fasting; perpetual abstinence from wine or oil; completely restraining departure from one’s cell; uninterrupted constancy in reading or meditation—practices which, without damage to our profession and purpose, may both be undertaken whenever we wish and, when necessary, be omitted without blame. But concerning observance of those principal commandments, we must make the most steadfast determination; and for their sake, even death, if necessary, must not be avoided. For these are the matters about which one must say immovably, “I have sworn and determined.” This must be done for the preservation of charity, for whose sake everything must be despised, lest the goodness and perfection of its tranquility be stained. Likewise, one must swear for the purity of chastity; and we ought to do the same for faith, sobriety, and justice. All these must be maintained with unalterable perseverance, and to depart from them even slightly is damnable. [Col. 1085C]

[Note: This definition, or resolution, of the chapter should be carefully noted. It explains no less learnedly than piously in what matters and statements the saying cited above in chapter 27 applies: “It is better for us to pass beyond our own statement than to suffer the loss of something more salutary and pious.”]

[Note: You see that among the monks of old, violation of the vow of continence and of the other essential vows was judged damnable and mortal, no less than violation of the principal commandments of God. This is confirmed by another passage consistent with it, and no less serious concerning the obligation and violation of essential vows, in Book IV of the *Institutes*, chapter 33, in these words: “Just as immense glory is promised in the future to those who faithfully serve God and adhere to him according to the institution of the Rule, so the gravest punishments are prepared for those who have carried it out lukewarmly and negligently, and who have failed to offer it the corresponding fruits of holiness according to what they have professed, or according to what people believe them to be. For, according to the judgment of Scripture, it is better for anyone not to vow than to vow and not fulfill it. And, ‘Cursed is the one who performs God’s work negligently.’” Thus far the passage.]

As for those bodily exercises of which it is said that they are useful for a little while (1 Tim. 4), we must determine matters as we have said: if some more certain opportunity for piety should arise and advise that they be relaxed, we are bound by no law concerning them, but, leaving them aside, may freely proceed to more useful things. For in those bodily exercises there is no danger if they are abandoned for a time; but to turn away from the others even for a moment is deadly. [Col. 1086A]

### CHAPTER XXX

How matters entrusted in confidence should be concealed from others

This also must be attended to with similar caution: if perhaps some statement that you wish to remain hidden should slip from your mouth, the hearer should not be troubled by any injunctions of secrecy. It will remain more hidden if it is passed over carelessly and simply, because none of the brothers will be tormented by anxiety over its dissemination, thinking that some insignificant matter was uttered in passing conversation, and that it is all the less important because it was not commended to the hearer’s mind by a most cautious command of silence. For even if you bind his trust by some solemn oath, [Col. 1086B] you should have no doubt that he will disclose it all the sooner. The force of the devil’s attack against him will rise up more strongly, so that it may both distress or expose you and make him, as quickly as possible, a transgressor of his oath.

[Note: Therefore, according to this abbot’s judgment, it is not advisable to entrust one’s secrets or private matters to anyone under pledge and oath of silence, unless the seriousness or necessity of the matter recommends otherwise. On this subject, consult the treatise of Domingo de Soto, *On the Manner of Concealing a Secret*.]

### CHAPTER XXXI

Nothing should be determined concerning matters belonging to the practice of common life

[Col. 1086C] And therefore a monk should make no abrupt determination concerning those matters alone that pertain to bodily exercises, lest, by provoking the adversary to attack what he guards as though under the observance of a law, he be compelled to violate them sooner. For when each person, established under the grace of liberty, sets a law before himself, he binds himself with a ruinous servitude, so that what he could have undertaken lawfully—or even laudably, with thanksgiving—he may, if necessity should compel him, be forced to receive as a transgressor, together with the sin of violation. “For where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. 4).

[Note: Do. Cuychius rightly observed that from these words it may be inferred that Cassian adhered to Abbot Joseph’s opinion and assertion concerning the permissibility of lying, or at least incurred suspicion of the same error. Especially since, in Book VI of the *Institutes*, when writing about and praising Abbot Archebius, he says that he used “religious deception” and “a lie of charity” among the brothers—as though charity could be joined with lying, when, according to the Apostle, it “does nothing improperly, does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices with the truth” (1 Cor. 13), not with lying. Cassian is therefore not unjustly reproached by St. Prosper under the title of *Collator* on this very account (*Book against the Collators*, chapter 9).]

Confirmed by this instruction and teaching of the most blessed Joseph as though by a divine oracle, we preferred to remain in Egypt. Yet although thereafter we were somewhat unconcerned about our promise, when the number of seven years had been completed, we gladly fulfilled our pledge. For when we went out to our monastery at the time when we had confidence of obtaining permission to return to the desert, we first paid the elders our due honor; then we restored the former affection of those whose ardor of charity had not been at all softened by the most frequent letters of apology we had sent; and finally, when the thorn of our pledge had been entirely removed, and they too saw us off with joy, we returned to the seclusion of the Scetian desert. [Col. 1087A]

This work has labored, as our unskilled ability allowed, to present to you, holy brothers, the knowledge and teaching of illustrious Fathers. Even if our uncultivated speech has perhaps confused rather than arranged it, I ask that our rusticity not nullify the praise of distinguished men. For in the sight of our Judge it seemed safer for us to disclose the magnificence of this teaching even in uncultivated language than to remain silent; since, if the reader considers the sublimity of its meaning, the offense caused by our inexperience in speech cannot harm his progress, and our concern for usefulness is greater than our concern for praise. I knew well that in transcribing the sayings of holy men I was undertaking something both full of danger and poor in praise; but, as the saying goes, knowingly I put my foot into the snare, and I did not refuse to expose myself to a certain danger in the uncertain hope of benefiting others. I warn all into whose hands these little works may come that whatever in them is pleasing belongs to the Fathers, while whatever is displeasing belongs to us—all who love the life and teaching of the saints. [Col. 1088A]

## PART THREE

Containing the seven final Conferences of the Fathers dwelling in the regions of Further Egypt

### Preface

TO JOVINIAN, MINERVIUS, LEONTIUS, AND THEODORUS

[Col. 1087C] After, with the help of Christ’s grace, completing ten Conferences of the Fathers, which were arranged as best we could at the urging of the most blessed bishops Helladius and Leontius, I dedicated seven others to the blessed Bishop Honoratus and also to the holy servant of Christ, Eucherius. [Col. 1088C]

[Note: Thus most copies read; printed editions, however, have: “With the help of Christ’s grace having sent forth,” etc. The Paraphrast has: “Having completed ten Conferences,” etc.]

And now I have believed that an equal number should be assigned to you, holy brothers Jovinian, Minervius, Leontius, and Theodore. The last of you founded that holy and distinguished discipline of monasteries in the Gallic provinces upon the strictness of ancient virtues; the others, through your instruction, have encouraged monks not only to seek the coenobitic profession above all, but also to thirst for the sublimity of the anchoritic life. [Col. 1089A]

[Note: These four abbots and fathers of monks came from the Gallic regions and, if I am not mistaken, from the congregation of Lérins, as may be inferred from what follows.]

These Conferences have been woven together through the discussion of the supreme Fathers and have been so tempered in every respect that they may suit both professions—the professions through which you have caused not only the western regions but also the islands to flourish with the greatest companies of brothers. [Col. 1089B] That is, they may instruct more fully according to the condition of their places and state both those who still persevere in a praiseworthy congregation under obedience and those who, withdrawing not far from your monasteries, desire to pursue the discipline of anchorites. [Col. 1090A]

[Note: Namely, the Stoechades Islands, situated in the Gallic sea and near both Lérins and other islands, flourishing through the great number and holiness of their monks. The Author sent this third collection of Conferences to them, as he himself testifies in his preface to the eleventh Conference, addressing Bishop Honoratus and Eucherius as follows: “But if these writings cannot satisfy the holy thirst of your study, seven other Conferences, brothers, which are to be sent to the saints dwelling in the Stoechades Islands, will, I believe, fulfill the desire of your ardor.”]

The previous diligence of your labor has contributed this chief advantage to them: since they are already prepared and have been found engaged in the same exercises, they may more easily receive the precepts and institutions of the elders. [Col. 1090B]

[Note: This pious admonition and exhortation also accords with my own desire: that all monks should gladly and eagerly receive these Conferences, together with their authors—namely, the holy Fathers and anchorites—into their cells, and retain them there; that they should converse and speak with them daily, question them, and receive their answers; so that, instructed by them, they may proceed more eagerly and securely along the way of perfection shown and trodden by them. For what else are the Conferences of the Fathers, their institutions, and their life—says our own St. Benedict, their distinguished rival and imitator—than examples and instruments of virtue for monks who live and obey well? (*Rule*, final chapter).]

Receiving the authors of the Conferences themselves into their cells, together with the volumes of the Conferences, and conversing with them, as it were, through daily questions and answers, they should not seek this difficult and almost unknown path through their own inventions. Even in places where well-trodden paths and countless examples of those who preceded them are not lacking, the discipline of anchoritic life remains dangerous; they should therefore accustom themselves to grasp it rather through the instruction of those whom both ancient tradition and the diligence of long experience have trained in every respect.

## THE EIGHTEENTH CONFERENCE

Which is that of Abbot Piammon

On the three ancient kinds of monks and the fourth that has recently arisen

### CHAPTER I

How, coming to Diolcos, we were received by Abbot Piammon

[Col. 1089C]

After seeing and conversing with those three elders, whose Conferences, at the urging of our holy brother Eucherius, we have arranged as best we could, and since we ardently desired to visit the regions of Further Egypt, where a greater and more perfect number of saints moved about, we arrived at a village called Diolcos, situated near one of the seven mouths of the Nile. We were driven there not so much by the necessity of travel as by our desire for the saints who lived there. [Col. 1090C]

[Note: This village or town was mentioned elsewhere (*Institutes*, Book V, chapter 36); Sozomen and Nicephorus testify that Abbot Piammon was renowned there.]

For we had heard from the ancient Fathers that many famous monasteries had been established there. Immediately, therefore, as though undertaking a voyage of uncertain exploration, persuaded by the hope of greater profit, we set out. When, after wandering for a very long time, we directed our eyes in every direction toward those mountains conspicuous for the sublimity of their virtues, our first glance noticed Abbot Piammon, the senior of all the anchorites dwelling there and their priest, like a certain most exalted lighthouse. [Col. 1091A]

[Note: Cuychius advises that *Piammon*, not *Piamon*, should be read, following the Greek authors. This is the Piammon mentioned above, whose humility and diligence in concealing his own perfection and austerity were reported. Sozomen gives the following account of him (*Book VI*, chapter 29; Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 35): “At that time Piammon and John also presided over the most famous monasteries near Diolcos in Egypt; they performed the priesthood with the utmost care—for they were presbyters—and with the greatest reverence. It is related that once, while Piammon was celebrating the sacred rite, he saw an angel of God standing near the holy table and writing in a book the monks who were present, while erasing from it those who were absent.” Thus far his account.

But this same example is related somewhat more fully and accurately in the *Lives of the Fathers* in the following manner (*Book II*, chapter 32): “We saw a remarkable presbyter named Piammon, a man of complete humility and kindness, who also possessed the grace of revelations. Once, when he was offering sacrifice to the Lord, he saw an angel of God standing beside the altar and writing in a book held in his hands the name of each monk who approached the altar, while not writing the names of certain others. When the elder had carefully observed who those were whose names he had not written, after the sacred mysteries had been completed he called each of them aside and asked what sin they had secretly committed. By their confession he discovered that each of them was guilty of mortal sin. He then urged them to do penance and, prostrating himself with them before the Lord, wept day and night as though he himself were guilty of their sins. He remained with them in penance and tears until he again saw the same angel standing and writing the names of those who approached; and after writing everyone’s name, he then called those men also by their names and invited them to reconciliation at the altar.” Thus far the passage. But when the elder saw this, he understood that their repentance had been accepted, and so restored them all to the altar with complete rejoicing.

From this we understand that Cassian does not use “elder” and “presbyter” as identical terms, but understands “elder” as referring to age and “presbyter” to rank and the office of the priesthood, although *presbyteros* (πρεσβύτερος) means “elder” in Latin. From the same passage we may also infer that in former times many fathers and abbots of monks were accustomed to be presbyters and priests, ordained for the purpose of celebrating the Lord’s sacraments and administering them to others; this has been confirmed elsewhere by many other passages and examples.]

[Note: Pharos, as Cuychius notes, is a small oblong island near Egypt, opposite the mouths of the Nile, now joined to the mainland; it formed the harbor of Alexandria (Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 12). In that harbor, Strabo testifies, a huge tower was built on a very high rock to give light to sailors at night; the tower too was called a *pharos* from the island. Hence all such towers and devices that furnish light to those who are lost or in danger are called *pharoi* (φάροι), as though *phanoi* (φάνοι), because torches appear from them. Cassian therefore compares Abbot Piammon, on account of his outstanding gifts and virtues, to a most exalted Pharos. This is Cuychius’s account; Ciaconius says the same in other words.]

For this man, established like that evangelical city upon the summit of a high mountain (Matt. 5), immediately shone before our eyes. [Col. 1091B] We believed that his virtues and miracles—which, through him and under our own observation, divine grace bore witness to his merits—should be passed over, lest we exceed either the form of our purpose or the limits of this volume. For we promised to transmit not accounts of God’s miracles, but certain matters concerning the institutions and practices of the saints that it is possible to recall, so as to provide readers only with the necessary instruction for a perfect life, not a useless and superfluous admiration unaccompanied by any correction of vices.

When the blessed Piammon had received us with the greatest joy and refreshed us with suitable hospitality, he realized that we were not from the same region. He first carefully asked where and why we had come to Egypt; and when he learned that we had come there from a monastery in Syria because of our desire for perfection, he began as follows.

### CHAPTER II

How inexperienced monks should be instructed by the example of their elders

[Note: Abbot Moses used nearly the same argument in Conference 2, chapter 11: “Although all the arts and disciplines discovered by human ingenuity, which serve no purpose beyond the conveniences of this life, can be grasped with the hands and perceived with the eyes, nevertheless no one can properly master them without the instruction of a teacher; how foolish, then, to believe that this one discipline alone does not need a teacher,” etc. And St. Jerome says in Letter 103 to Paulinus: “I say nothing of grammarians, rhetoricians, philosophers, geometricians, dialecticians, musicians, astronomers, and so forth. Let me come to the lesser arts, those administered not so much by the tongue as by the hand: farmers, masons, workers in metal, cutters of wood, wool-workers, fullers, and all the others who manufacture various furnishings and humble articles cannot be without a teacher in what they seek.”]

Whoever among human beings desires to acquire mastery of any art, unless he devotes himself with every care and vigilance to the study of the discipline he wishes to know and observes the precepts and institutions of all the perfected masters of that craft or science, vainly hopes in empty wishes to attain the likeness of those whose care and diligence he refuses to imitate. [Col. 1091C]

[Note: “Sons,” not “son,” as was printed earlier. Piammon is addressing several people, as is clear from the end of this chapter and the beginning of the third.]

For we know that some have come to these places from your regions merely to visit the monasteries of the brothers for the sake of acquiring knowledge, not to accept the rules and institutions for which they had come here, nor to withdraw into cells and try to put into practice what they had learned either by sight or by tradition. Retaining the customs and pursuits with which they had been imbued, they were thought—as some are accustomed to reproach them—to have changed provinces not for the sake of their progress but out of the necessity of avoiding poverty. For, with the obstinacy of a stubborn mind, they could neither acquire any instruction nor even remain longer in these regions. Since they had changed neither the custom of fasting, nor the order of the psalms, nor finally even the style of their clothing, what else could they be thought to be pursuing in this region except the mere economies of their food?

### CHAPTER III

That younger monks should not scrutinize the precepts of their elders

Therefore, if, as we believe, the cause of God has drawn you here to emulate our knowledge, abandon completely all the institutions by which your beginnings were shaped there, and follow with the greatest humility whatever you see your elders doing or teaching. Nor should it disturb you, or draw you away and divert you from imitation, if for the present the reason or cause of some matter or action is not clear to you. For those who think well and simply about everything, and who faithfully imitate all that they see handed down or performed by their elders, will also acquire knowledge of all things through experience in practice. [Col. 1092C]

[Note: It is not for monks to scrutinize the commands or actions of their superiors, but to obey simply and without examination. Other Fathers taught the same. Basil says in the *Monastic Constitutions* (chapters 20 and 23): “Let monks obey their superior most willingly and not demand from him an account of what is imposed upon them, investigating his commands with excessive curiosity in no respect.” St. Jerome writes to the monk Rusticus (Letter 4): “Believe that whatever the superior of the monastery commands you is salutary, and do not judge the opinion of your elders. Your duty is to obey and fulfill what has been commanded, as Moses says (Deut. 17): ‘Hear, Israel, and be silent.’” Cassian writes in Book IV of the *Institutes* (chapters 10 and 41): “The Egyptian monks hasten to fulfill everything commanded by their superior, as though it had been issued from heaven by God, without any examination.” And St. Gregory says in Book II on the First Book of Kings (chapter 2): “Whoever has perfectly learned to obey does not know how to judge.”]

But whoever begins to be instructed by examination will never enter into the reason of truth, because the enemy, seeing him rely upon his own judgment rather than that of the Fathers, easily drives him so far that even those things which are most useful and salutary appear to him superfluous and harmful. Thus the crafty enemy mocks his presumption, until by stubbornly clinging to his irrational determinations he persuades himself that only what he has judged right and most just through the error of his own obstinacy is holy to him.

### CHAPTER IV

On the three kinds of monks that exist in Egypt

Therefore you ought first to recognize the order and origin of our profession—how and from where it descended. For one can pursue the discipline of the desired art more effectively and be stirred more ardently to practice it when one has recognized the dignity of its authors and founders. [Col. 1093B]

[Note: In this chapter he lists only three older kinds; he adds a fourth, more recent than these, below in chapter 8, though he does not name it here. Thus he establishes four kinds of monks. Hence the title prefixed to this Conference: “On the three ancient kinds of monks and the fourth that has recently arisen.”

St. Jerome, however, in his Letter to Eustochium (Letter 22), mentions only three kinds of monks in Egypt, from which it appears that the fourth had not yet arisen at that time, or was not yet well known: “There are,” he says, “three kinds of monks in Egypt: the first, the coenobites, whom they call *sauses* in their native language; we may call them those who live in common. The second are the anchorites, who live alone in the deserts and are so called because they have withdrawn far from human beings. The third kind is called *remoboth*, the worst and most negligent, and in our province it is either the only kind or the first.” Thus St. Jerome.

Following Cassian, as he commonly does, St. Benedict likewise designates four kinds of monks in chapter 1 of his Rule: first, coenobites; second, anchorites; third, sarabaites; fourth, gyrovagues. He briefly describes the character and institutions of each.

St. Augustine, moreover, in his book *On the Morals of the Church*, recognizes only two orders or kinds of monks properly and truly so called: one of anchorites or hermits, the other of coenobites. Cassian also discusses these in Book V of the *Institutes*, chapter 36. This opinion is indeed the truest. For that third kind mentioned by St. Jerome, and the third and fourth mentioned here by Piammon and by St. Benedict, are not truly kinds of monks, but rather monsters or specters of monks; nor are they true orders, but confusions, overturnings, and corruptions of religious life, as Bellarmine noted (*On Monks*, Book II, chapter 3).

The third kind is said to consist of those who live in coenobia but still retain some private possessions and do not obey their superiors in everything—an unmistakable corruption of coenobitic life. The fourth consists of those who pass from monasteries to the desert, not in order to live more holily but more freely, namely, after shaking off the yoke of superiors and of coenobitic laws. This is a corruption of the eremitical life. Hence these two are rightly called the two worst kinds of monks.

Isidore errs, however, in Book II of *On Divine Offices* (chapter 15), where he enumerates six kinds of monks: coenobites, hermits, anchorites, gyrovagues, circumcellions, and sarabaites. For anchorites and hermits are the same, just as circumcellions and gyrovagues are also the same, as will be clear from what follows.

Isidore does distinguish hermits from anchorites (Bellarmine, *On Monks*, Book II, chapter 3): “The former withdraw far from human beings and inhabit deserts and vast solitudes, in imitation, he says, of Elijah and John the Baptist, who penetrated the retreats of the wilderness; the latter, already perfected in coenobitic life, shut themselves up in cells removed from human sight, granting access to no one, and continue to live solely in divine contemplation—that is, in theoria.” But this distinction, which consists more in words than in reality, is not so substantial that it changes the species or kind of monastic life. Isidore does not, however, name the gyrovagues; he merely portrays their customs and pursuits, such as St. Benedict and the other Fathers attribute to gyrovagues.]

There are three kinds of monks in Egypt. Two of them are excellent; the third is lukewarm and must be avoided in every way. The first is that of the coenobites, who live together in a congregation and are governed by the judgment of a single elder. The greatest number of monks throughout Egypt belong to this kind. The second is that of the anchorites, who were first formed in coenobia and, having now been perfected in active life, chose the solitude of the desert. We too desire to share in this profession. The third is the reprehensible kind of the sarabaites. We shall discuss them individually and more fully in order.

You ought first, as we have said, to recognize the founders of these three professions. For from this very knowledge there may arise either hatred of the profession that must be avoided or desire for the one that must be followed, since each path necessarily draws its follower toward the end reached by its author and originator. [Col. 1094A]

### CHAPTER V

By whose authority the profession of the coenobites was established
Therefore, [Note: [Col. 1094C] The other Fathers likewise affirm this. Basil, in *Monastic Constitutions*, chapter 19, speaking of coenobites, says: “They are true and perfect imitators of our Liberator and of his institutions while he lived among us. For just as he gathered a choir of disciples, made everything common, and offered himself in common to the apostles, so they too, obeying their superior (provided that he correctly preserves the prescriptions of his way of life), imitate the manner of life of the apostles and of the Lord.” Chrysostom, in Homily 11 on the Acts, says that monks live as all the faithful in Jerusalem once lived at the beginning of the Church. And in Book III *Against the Detractors of the Monastic Life* he asserts that the apostles fulfilled what monks now fulfill. Jerome, in his *Catalogue*, says: “Philo, an Alexandrian by nationality, writing a book about the first Church of the evangelist Mark at Alexandria, speaks in praise of our people, stating that they existed not only there but also in many provinces, and calling their dwellings monasteries. From this it is evident that the first Church of those who believed in Christ was such as monks now strive and desire to be: nothing belonged privately to anyone; no one among them was rich, no one poor; inheritances were divided among the needy; they devoted themselves to prayer and psalms, as well as to instruction and continence. Luke reports that the first believers in Jerusalem were likewise such (Acts IV).” Cassian, *Institutes*, Book II, chapter 5, testifies that in the beginnings of the Church the monks at Alexandria received their rule of life from the blessed evangelist Mark, and that they not only retained those magnificent practices which we read that the primitive Church, or the crowds of believers, celebrated in the Acts of the Apostles—“The multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul,” and so forth—but also accumulated practices much more sublime. Augustine likewise (Sermons 1 and 2 *On the Common Life of the Clergy*), Isidore (*Etymologies*, Book VII, final chapter), and others do the same. Moreover, Turrecremata rightly observed (*Treatise 8 on the Rule of St. Benedict*) that this order of coenobites, in some respect, took its beginning from the companies of the prophets. “Hence,” he says, “Samuel is said to have first instituted assemblies of religious persons, continually singing psalms to the Lord, as the Master says in the *Historia Scholastica* concerning 1 Kings X: ‘You will meet a band of prophets coming down from the high place, with a psaltery before them.’” That the assembly of those prophets represented the persons of religious men is testified by Jerome in his letter to the monk Rusticus, where he says: “The sons of the prophets, whom we read of as monks in the Old Testament,” and so forth. As for the perfect form of the common life and renunciation of earthly possessions, this order of monks, this discipline of the coenobites, took its origin, as Cassian says, from the time of the apostolic preaching. Thus far Cassian.]

The discipline of the coenobites therefore took its origin from the time of the apostolic preaching. For such was the entire multitude of believers at Jerusalem, of which it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul; nor did anyone say that any of the things he possessed was his own, but everything was common to them. They sold their possessions and goods and distributed them to everyone according to each person’s need” (Acts IV). And again: “For there was not any needy person among them. For as many as owned fields or houses, selling them, brought the prices of the things they sold and laid them at the apostles’ feet. And distribution was made to each according to each person’s need” (ibid.). Such, I say, was the whole Church then, whereas now it is difficult to find even very few such persons in coenobia.

But after the departure of the apostles the multitude of believers began to grow lukewarm—especially that multitude which came together to the faith of Christ from foreign peoples and different nations. From these the apostles, on account of the rudiments of their faith and their deeply rooted pagan custom, demanded nothing more than that they abstain from sacrifices offered to idols, fornication, things strangled, and blood (Acts XV). When this liberty, which had been granted to the Gentiles because of the weakness of their initial belief, also began gradually to corrupt the perfection of that Church which existed at Jerusalem, and as the number of natives and newcomers increased daily while the fervor of that first faith grew cold, not only those who had gathered to the faith of Christ but even those who were leaders of the Church were released from that strictness.

For some, thinking that what they saw conceded to the Gentiles because of their weakness was also lawful for themselves, believed that they would suffer no harm if they followed the faith and confession of Christ together with their possessions and means. But those who still possessed the apostolic fervor, mindful of that former perfection, withdrew from their cities and from the company of those who believed that the negligence of a more relaxed way of life was permissible for themselves or for the Church of God. They began to live in suburban and more secluded places and privately and individually to practice what they remembered had been instituted generally by the apostles throughout the entire body of the Church. Thus this discipline, which we have mentioned, was formed: that of disciples who had separated themselves from their contagion.

Little by little, as time passed, these men withdrew from the crowds of believers and from the [Note: [Col. 1095C] Why monks are so called, and what the origin and etymology of this name may be, is reported variously by writers. Although the name “monk” is extremely common among all the Fathers, both Greek and Latin, it is not explained by all in the same way as to what it signifies (Bellarmine, *On Monks*, Book II, chapter 1). Most think it is derived from solitude, because μόνος (*monos*) means “alone” in Latin. St. Jerome appears to support this view in his letter to Heliodorus (Letter 1), where he says: “Interpret the word ‘monk,’ that is, your own name: what are you doing in a crowd, you who are alone?” And again, in his letter to Paulinus (Letter 13): “If you wish to be what you are called—that is, alone—what are you doing in cities, which certainly are not dwellings of the solitary but of the many?” Yet according to this reasoning and etymology, the name “monk” would properly apply only to hermits and anchorites, who lived alone in deserts, whereas the name and institution of monks are found in Dionysius the Areopagite, who preceded Paul the first Hermit by nearly three hundred years. Jerome himself, in his letter to Eustochium (Letter 22), wants the name “monk” to be common both to coenobites and to anchorites.

Others interpret “monks” as deriving from *monad*, that is, from unity or union. But this unity or union is again explained in two ways. For St. Augustine, explaining the verse of Psalm 132, “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity,” says: “These words of the Psalter, this sweet sound, this pleasing melody both in song and in understanding, also gave birth to monasteries. Stirred by this sound, the brothers desired to dwell together in unity. This verse was their trumpet. It sounded throughout the world, and those who were scattered were gathered together into one.” And below: “Why should we not call them monks, when the psalm says, ‘Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity’? For *monos* means ‘one’; not one in just any manner—for even in a crowd there is one—but one together with many. *Monos* cannot mean that, that is, alone; for *monos* is one alone. Those therefore who live together in such a way as to form one person, so that for them there is truly, as it is written, one soul and one heart—many bodies but not many souls, many bodies but not many hearts—are rightly called *monos*, that is, one alone. Hence also that one man was healed in the pool” (John V). Thus Augustine indicates by these words that “monk” signifies nothing other than a person living in such unity and community with others of the same institution that, together with them, he becomes as it were one person, one heart, and one soul, just as was said of the first Christians, who had one heart, one soul, and everything in common (Acts IV). But according to this interpretation the name “monk” would apply only to coenobites; indeed, it would signify nothing other than a coenobite, that is, one living communally with others.

There remains, therefore, the truest explanation of this word, which the abbot Piammon gives here: that they were called μοναχοί (*monachoi*) or μονάζοντες (*monazontes*) because they abstained from marriage and separated themselves from the company of their parents and from the society of this world, so that they might cleave to God alone through contemplation. The blessed Dionysius the Areopagite also confirms this in chapter 6 of *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, where he says that monks are so called because, having abandoned divisible things, they strive to please and unite themselves to the Monad—that is, to the divinity—alone. “Hence,” he says, “our holy teachers (the apostles) addressed them with divine names: some calling them *therapeutai*, that is, worshipers, because of their sincere service and worship of God; others calling them monks, from their undivided and singular life, by which, through holy combinations and gatherings of divisible affections into one, they are advanced toward a godlike and singular perfection.”

The canon of the Council of Nicaea, cited by Gratian (16, q. 1, c. 1), points in the same direction, in these words: “It pleased all those present at the holy synod of Nicaea that the conduct and life of monks, according to the etymology of the name, should differ from that of all others. For *monachus* in Greek is translated into Latin as ‘singular.’ Therefore a monk ought to act singularly in all things.” Thus far the canon. Elsewhere we have also noted, on the authority of St. Jerome, that the name “monk” is sanctioned and hallowed by the authority of Scripture.]

because they abstained from marriage and separated themselves from the company of their parents and from the society of this world, they were called monks or [Note: [Col. 1097A] Not *Monozantes*, as Plantinus printed it; for μονάζω (*monazo*) means “I live in solitude.” Basil frequently calls them by this name in the *Monastic Constitutions*. Related to these are the familiar names used among the Greek Fathers for monks: μονασταί (*monastai*), θεραπευταί (*therapeutai*), ἱκέται (*hiketai*), ἀσκηταί (*asketai*), φιλόσοφοι (*philosophoi*), ἀναχωρηταί (*anachoretai*), ἐρημοπολῖται (*eremopolitai*), ἡσυχασταί (*hesychastai*), κοινοβίοι (*koinobioi*) and κοινοβιῶται (*koinobiotai*), along with others of the same kind. They were called by different names according to the places in which they lived and the kind of stricter discipline they followed.]

Monazontes, from the strictness of a singular and solitary life. Hence it followed [Note: [Col. 1097A] Coenobites are so called from the common life, because they live together in a congregation and are governed by the judgment of one elder, as stated above in this same chapter. They are also called *synodites*, *syncellites*, and *cellulani* by Sidonius, with the same meaning; in common usage they are called cloistered and conventual persons. Concerning them there is the fifth novella of the emperor Justinian, which begins as follows: “The life of monastic conduct is so honorable, and knows so well how to commend to God the person who comes to it, that it wipes away every human stain and renders him pure, fitting for rational nature, active in many things according to the mind, and higher than human thoughts. If anyone is to be a perfect monk, he needs both instruction in the divine utterances and integrity of conduct, so that he may be made worthy of so great a transformation.” Thus far the novella. I have wished to cite these words here both for the commendation of the monastic life and for the salutary instruction of monks and coenobites.

St. Benedict says (*Rule*, chapter 1): “The first kind of monks is that of coenobites, that is, those who serve in a monastery under a rule or an abbot.” Here a disjunctive conjunction is used for a conjunctive one, as the commentators observe, so that the meaning is: “under a rule and an abbot.” Trithemius cites a similar example from canon law. Turrecremata adds that in this passage the name “abbot” should be understood to include any elder or father by whose judgment the others in the congregation are governed. For there are many religious houses living the coenobitic life in which the rulers are called not abbots but deans, provosts, priors, fathers, or superiors.

But this passage seems to require that we hear the illustrious Fathers Jerome and Augustine discussing the coenobites of their own time and their customs and institutions, so that coenobites, especially Benedictines, may behold themselves as in a mirror or model, compare their own customs with theirs, and, by contemplating them—as is fitting for monks of the same profession—either correct or more exactly order their own conduct.

Thus Jerome says (Letter 12): “Having therefore exterminated these as certain plagues (namely, those monks of the third kind), let us come to those who are more numerous and live in common, that is, those whom we have said are called coenobites. Their first bond of fellowship is to obey their superiors and to do whatever they command. They are divided into groups of ten and hundreds, so that one man presides over nine, and again the hundredth has ten superiors under him. They remain separate, but with their cells joined together. Until the ninth hour, as has been established, no one goes to another, except to the deans whom we mentioned, so that if anyone happens to be wavering in his thoughts, he may be consoled by their conversation.

After the ninth hour they all come together. Psalms resound, the Scriptures are recited according to custom, and when the prayers have been completed and all have taken their seats, the one whom they call the Father begins to speak. While he is speaking, such silence prevails that no one dares look at another or cough; the speaker’s praise is found in the tears of his listeners, and silent tears roll down their faces, while their grief does not even break out into sobs. But when he begins to announce the coming kingdom of Christ and the future blessedness and glory, you may see everyone, with restrained sighs and eyes lifted toward heaven, saying within himself: ‘Who will give me wings like a dove, and I will fly away and rest?’ (Psalm 54).

After this the assembly is dismissed, and each group of ten goes with its father to the table; they take turns serving week by week. There is no noise at meals, and no one speaks while eating. They live on bread, legumes, and vegetables seasoned only with salt. Only the old men receive wine. Meals are also often provided for the old and for the little ones, so that the weariness of some age may be supported and the beginning of another not be broken. Then they rise together, and after a hymn has been sung, they return to their stalls. There each person speaks with his companions until evening and says: ‘Did you see that man and that one? How much gravity there is in him, how much silence! How measured his walk!’ If they see someone sick, they console him; if someone is fervent in the love of God, they encourage him to pursue it.

Because at night each person keeps vigil in his cell outside the public prayers, they go around to the individual cells and carefully investigate what each person is doing by applying their ears. If they find someone slower than the others, they do not rebuke him; they pretend not to know what they have learned, visit him more often, and, by first beginning themselves, encourage him to pray more rather than compel him. The work of the day is set down and delivered by the dean to the steward, who each month gives an account to the father of all with great trembling. The foods, once prepared, are also tasted by him. And because no one is allowed to say, ‘I have no tunic, cloak, or mat woven of reeds,’ he regulates everything in such a way that no one asks for anything and no one lacks anything” (see Marianus’s scholium here).

“If someone begins to fall ill, he is transferred to a larger chamber and is restored by the service of so many elders that he does not long either for the luxuries of the cities or for a mother’s affection. On Sundays they devote themselves only to prayer and readings; indeed, they do this at all times after completing their tasks. Every day something is learned from the Scriptures. The fast of the whole year is uniform, except during Lent, when a stricter way of life alone is permitted. From Easter to Pentecost, suppers are changed into midday meals, both to satisfy ecclesiastical tradition and so that they may not burden the stomach with doubled food.”

Philo, an imitator of Platonic discourse (*On the Contemplative Life*), and Josephus—the Greek Livy—report that such persons existed in their account of the second Jewish captivity (*Antiquities*, XVIII.2; *Jewish War*, II.7).

Such is Jerome’s general account of the coenobites. Augustine, after discussing the anchorites and their austerity, says:

“If this exceeds our endurance, who would not admire and praise those who, having despised and abandoned the allurements of this world, gathered into a common, most chaste and holy life, spend their days together, living in prayers, readings, and discussions; puffed up by no pride, turbulent through no obstinacy, embittered by no envy, but modest, reserved, peaceful? They offer to God himself, from whom they have merited the ability to do so, a life most harmonious and wholly intent upon him, as a most acceptable gift.

“No one possesses anything as his own; no one is a burden to anyone. They work with their hands at things by which the body may be nourished and the mind may not be hindered from God. They hand over their work to those whom they call deans, because they preside over groups of ten, so that none of them need concern himself with his bodily care, whether regarding food, clothing, or anything else required by daily necessity or by illness, as health commonly changes.

“The deans, arranging everything with great care and providing whatever that life requires because of the weakness of the body, nevertheless themselves give an account to one whom they call the Father. These Fathers are not only most holy in their conduct but also outstanding in divine doctrine, eminent in all things. Without pride they advise those whom they call sons, possessing great authority in commanding and finding great willingness among them to obey.

“At the end of the day they come together from their several dwellings, while still fasting, to hear that Father. At least three thousand men gather around each Father; indeed, many more live under one. They listen with incredible eagerness and profound silence, expressing the emotions of their souls as the speaker’s discourse moves them—by groaning, by weeping, or by joy, but with restraint and without shouting.

“Afterward the body is restored as much as is permitted for health and well-being, each person restraining his desire lest it overflow, and being sparing even with the foods that are available and very cheap. Thus they abstain not only from meat and wine, for the sufficient subduing of lusts, but also from those foods that provoke the appetite of the belly and throat more vigorously because they seem to some people cleaner.

“Certainly, whatever exceeds necessary nourishment—for much remains over from manual labor and the restriction of meals—is distributed to the needy with as much care as though it had not been acquired by those who distribute it.”

Thus Augustine describes the way of life of the coenobites. Epiphanius has similar statements (*Against Heresies*, 80).

As for the coenobium, Isidore gives the etymology of the word in this way (*Etymologies*, Book XV, chapter 4): “A coenobium is a dwelling of many living together in common; for κοινόν (*koinon*) means ‘common’ in Greek.” Others describe it more fully as follows: “A coenobium is a place where a common life is led; for κοινός (*koinos*) means ‘common,’ and βίος (*bios*) means ‘life.’”

There are also other words commonly used among the Greeks to designate the dwellings of monks: μοναστήρια (*monasteria*) in Athanasius’s *Life of St. Antony*. Philo was the first to explain the meaning of this name (*On the Contemplative Life*) in these words: “For each person there is a sacred dwelling, which is called a sanctuary and monastery, in which, while they remain, the mysteries of the holy life are celebrated.” That is: “Each person has a sacred dwelling, which is called a monastery, in which those who remain celebrate the mysteries of the holy life.”

Gregory Nazianzen calls it μονή (*monē*), that is, as Philo says elsewhere, μοναυλία (*monaulía*), a secluded court or dwelling; and in his First Oration against Julian, ἁγνευτήριον (*hagneutērion*), that is, a sanctuary or shrine. Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, chapter 28, calls it ἀσκητήριον (*askētērion*); Theodoret, in Books VI and X of *The Therapeutics*, calls it ἀσκητῶν καταγωγή (*askētōn katagōgē*), that is, an inn or lodging of ascetics; and finally Suidas calls it φροντιστήριον (*phrontistērion*), that is, a school or assembly.]

so that, from their common fellowship, their cells and lodgings came to be called coenobia. This, therefore, was the sole and most ancient kind of monks. It was first not only in time but also in grace, and for many years it alone remained inviolate, lasting until the age of Abbot Paul [Note: [Col. 1099C] Before the time of Paul and Antony there were no monks other than coenobites. Instituted by the apostles, as has been said, they preceded the anchorites until that time—that is, until the end of the third century. There were indeed people before Antony who, through fear of persecution, abandoned the cities and lived either in the countryside or in hidden places, leading a life like that of angels. Eusebius reports that some of them were crowned with martyrdom (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book VI, chapter 34, and Book VIII, chapters 7 and following). Antony himself mentions some of them when, in his zeal for a purer life, he withdrew to a desert place and received from one of them his first rudiments of monastic instruction, as Athanasius testifies in his *Life of Antony*.

Yet they were not then counted among the order of monks or anchorites, because they followed no definite rule of life prescribed for themselves; rather, as Scripture says, “Everyone did what seemed right to him” (Judges XVII), that is, he lived according to his own custom and judgment.

Paul the Hermit died in the year of Christ 343, at the age of 113, having spent nearly one hundred years in the desert; shortly before his death he was known only to Antony. Antony, however, died in the year 358, after having lived more than 105 years (Baronius, volume III of the *Annals*). But more will be said of these matters in the following chapter.]

or Antony. Even now [Col. 1100A] we see traces of it remaining in strict coenobia.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Order and Origin of the Anchorites

From this number of the perfect—and, so to speak, from this most fruitful root—there afterward arose the flowers and fruits of the holy anchorites. [Note: [Col. 1100A] The author seems not to have used that disjunctive particle “or” rashly or by chance, but deliberately and cautiously, since many have disputed which of them was the first author or founder of the anchoritic life. Thus the blessed Jerome begins the *Life of Paul the Hermit*: “There has been much uncertainty as to which of the monks first began to inhabit the desert. Some, going farther back, took their beginning from blessed Elijah and John; of whom Elijah seems to us to have been more than a monk, and John to have begun to prophesy before he was born. Others (and the entire common people agree with this opinion) assert that Antony was the head of this way of life. This is true in part. For he was not so much the first of all as the one through whom everyone’s zeal was stimulated. Amathas and Macarius, Antony’s disciples—the former of whom buried his teacher’s body—even now assert that a certain Paul of Thebes was the founder of this undertaking; and in this we too agree with them, not so much in name as in opinion.” And below: “When blessed Paul had already been living a heavenly life on earth for 113 years, while Antony, a nonagenarian, was dwelling in another desert, a thought came into Antony’s mind, as he himself used to say: that no perfect monk had settled in the desert beyond him. But while he was resting during the night, it was revealed to him that there was another much better than he, whom he ought to go to see. At once, as daylight broke, the venerable old man, supporting his infirm limbs with a staff, began to set out, not knowing where he was going,” and so forth.

Elsewhere, speaking of anchorites, he says (Letter 22): “These men came out of the coenobium and, except for bread and salt, carry nothing else into the deserts. The author of this life was Paul, its illuminator Antony; and, if we ascend to earlier times, its founder was John the Baptist.” Thus Jerome.

Since it is established that Paul died long before Antony, having spent nearly one hundred years in the desert, as has been said, it follows that he led the anchoritic life before Antony and therefore deservedly may be called the first hermit or anchorite.

When the blessed Jerome says that Antony illuminated the anchoritic life, this should be understood in the sense that Antony himself first practiced that way of living—for he remained hidden in solitude for twenty years, as Athanasius testifies in the *Life of St. Antony*—but afterward, at God’s prompting, having gathered many brothers together and instructed them in the principles of the monastic life, he established the coenobitic life with them and founded many monasteries in different places.

Of these Athanasius writes: “There were monasteries on the mountain, like tents, filled with divine choirs singing psalms, reading, and praying. His discourse had kindled in the minds of all such ardor for fasting and vigils that, eagerly hoping for the future reward, they labored continually to show mutual love and mercy to the needy. They seemed to inhabit a vast region and a town separated from worldly society, full of piety and justice,” and so forth.

But afterward, and finally, Antony returned to the anchoritic life, although in the meantime he did not abandon care for his own people. By his example it happened, in a kind of reciprocal order, that anchorites produced coenobites and, conversely, coenobites produced anchorites—men who were permitted to live alone under the authority of an abbot or elder presiding over all, yet who remained bound by the bond of obedience. Nevertheless, there were also very holy men who, from their first entrance into the monastic life, sought the desert and followed a solitary life, such as Paul himself, of whom we are speaking.

Thus the eremitic, or anchoritic, life was first begun by Paul, but introduced, cultivated, illuminated by definite rules and institutions, and organized into a definite monastic order by Antony. For although Paul was the first of all to live in the desert, he had no disciples and was not known until shortly before his death, as has been said. Antony, however, had disciples who were both anchorites and coenobites. Therefore, just as he deserved to be called the restorer of the coenobitic life, so also he deserved to be called the founder and author of the anchoritic life—not so much because he preceded everyone as because through him everyone’s zeal was stimulated, as St. Jerome says. Accordingly, both may be called the first and founder of the eremitic life: Paul in respect of time, Antony in respect of teaching, as Bellarmine aptly says (*On Monks*, Book II, chapter 5).]

We know that the founders of this profession were those whom we mentioned shortly before, namely, Saint Paul and Antony. They did not seek the seclusion of solitude, as some do, because of cowardice or the disease of impatience, but out of a desire for higher progress and divine contemplation, although the former [Note: [Col. 1101C] Namely, Paul. For what occasion or necessity caused him to seek the desert, St. Jerome reports as follows:

“Under the persecutors Decius and Valerian, at the time when Cornelius at Rome and Cyprian at Carthage were condemned to a blessed death, a cruel storm devastated many Churches in Egypt and the Thebaid. At that time it was the desire of Christians to be struck down by the sword for Christ’s name; but the crafty enemy, seeking punishments that delayed death, wanted to slaughter souls rather than bodies. As Cyprian himself says, having suffered under him, those who wished to die were not permitted to be killed.”

And below:

“At the same time, when such things were happening in the Lower Thebaid, Paul was left, after the death of both his parents, with a sister already married, in possession of a rich inheritance. He was about fifteen years old, thoroughly educated in both Greek and Egyptian letters, gentle in disposition, and a great lover of God. When the storm of persecution thundered, he withdrew to a more remote and secluded estate.

“But what can you not compel mortal hearts to do,

Accursed hunger for gold!

His sister’s husband began to want to betray the man whom he ought to have hidden. Neither his wife’s tears, nor the bond of blood, nor God, who sees all things from above, recalled him from his crime. In addition, cruelty persisted, pretending to imitate piety. When the prudent young man understood this, he fled to the deserts of the mountains while awaiting the end of the persecution. He turned necessity into choice, advancing little by little, then stopping again, and repeating this many times. At last he found a rocky mountain, at whose base, not far away, was a large cave closed by a stone. When he removed it—for human curiosity eagerly seeks to discover what is hidden—he explored more eagerly and noticed inside a large vestibule. Above it the open sky spread out, while an ancient palm tree covered it with its broad branches and displayed a very clear spring. Its stream alone emerged outside, only to be immediately absorbed through a small opening by the same earth that had produced the waters.

“Having come to love this dwelling, as though it had been offered to him by God, he spent his entire life there in prayer and solitude. The palm supplied him with food and clothing.”

Thus far St. Jerome.]

although he is said to have entered the desert, during a time of persecution, in order to avoid the plots of his relatives. Thus from the discipline we have mentioned there arose another kind of perfection, whose followers are deservedly called anchorites, that is, withdrawers, because they were not content with the victory by which, among human beings, they had trampled upon the hidden snares of the devil; rather, desiring to engage demons in open battle and manifest conflict, they did not fear to penetrate the vast recesses of the desert, [Col. 1101B] [Note: [Col. 1102C] The holy Fathers call Elijah, Elisha, and John the Baptist hermits and founders of hermits: Basil in his letter to Chilo, Nazianzen in his *Apology* after his return from exile, Chrysostom in Homily 69 on Matthew, Jerome in Letter 13 to Paulinus and Letter 22 to Eustochium, Sozomen in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book I, chapter 12, and Isidore in Book II, chapter 5 of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*.]

imitating, that is, John the Baptist, who remained in the desert throughout his life; and also Elijah and Elisha, as well as those whom the Apostle mentions in this way: “They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, afflicted, tormented—of whom the world was not worthy—wandering in deserts, mountains, caves, and caverns of the earth” (Hebrews XI).

Concerning them also the Lord says figuratively to Job: [Note: [Col. 1102C] Gregory, *Morals*, Book XXXI, chapter 22: “The wild ass,” he says, “which dwells in solitude not incongruously signifies the life of those who, removed from worldly crowds, live apart. “Who,” he says [Lipsius in the margin: “however”], “released the wild ass, and loosed his bonds? He appointed his dwelling in the desert and his tents in the salt land, mocking the multitude of the city and hearing not the complaint of the taskmaster. He considered the mountains of his pasture and seeks every green thing” (Job XXXIX).

Likewise in the Psalms: “Let those who have been redeemed by the Lord say, whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy” (Psalm 106). And shortly afterward: “They wandered in the wilderness, in a waterless place [Lipsius in the margin: ‘dryness’]; they did not find the way to a city of habitation. Hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted within them. And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their distresses” (ibid.).

Jeremiah also describes them in this way: “Blessed is the man who has taken up his yoke from his youth; he will sit alone and be silent, because he has lifted himself above himself” (Lamentations III). And in feeling and practice they echo the Psalmist: “I have become like a pelican of the wilderness. I kept vigil and became like a solitary sparrow on the roof” (Psalm 101).

## CHAPTER VII. On the Origin and Way of Life of the Sarabaites
When the Christian religion rejoiced in these two professions of monks, but this order too had gradually begun to decline for the worse, there subsequently emerged that [Note: [Col. 1102D] The first kind, not of monks but of pseudo-monks. St. Jerome likewise speaks of it (Letter 22): “The third kind is what they call Remoboth, the most loathsome and neglected kind, and in our province either the only one or the first. They live together in pairs or threes, and no more, living according to their own judgment and authority; and from what they have worked for they contribute shares to a common fund, so that they may have common provisions, etc.” St. Benedict likewise says (Rule, ch. 1): “The third, and truly most loathsome, kind of monks is that of the Sarabaites, who are approved by no rule, tested by experience as gold in the furnace; rather, softened like lead, they are still, by their works, keeping faith with the world, and are known to lie to God by their tonsure. These live in pairs, or threes, or certainly singly, without a shepherd, shut up not in the Lord’s but in their own sheepfolds. The pleasure of their desires is their law, so that whatever they think or choose, they call holy, and whatever they do not wish, they consider unlawful.”] most detestable and faithless kind of monks—or rather, that harmful planting revived and took root, [Note: [Col. 1103B] Thus the venerable Bede, writing on the Acts of the Apostles, says that this most detestable kind of monks, called Sarabaites, arose from the example of Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5), who wished to retain something of their own under the appearance and profession of monastic life. St. Jerome, in his Letter 8 to Demetrias, says: “Ananias and Sapphira, timid stewards—or rather, double-hearted—and therefore condemned because, after their vow, they offered as though it were their own what they had vowed once for all to the one to whom it belonged, reserving for themselves a portion of property that was already alien.” Cassian, Institutes, Book VII, chapter 14: “Ananias and Sapphira, reserving a portion of what they possessed, were condemned to death by the apostolic word.” See there the notes concerning the death of Ananias and Sapphira.] which, sprouting through Ananias and Sapphira at the beginning of the Church, was cut down by the severity of the apostle Peter (Acts 5). Among monks it was judged detestable and accursed for so long, and was appropriated by no one thereafter, as long as fear of that exceedingly strict sentence remained implanted in the memory of the faithful. By it the blessed apostle did not allow the aforementioned originators of the new crime to be healed by repentance or by any act of satisfaction; rather, he cut down the most pernicious shoot by a swift death.

When that example—punished in Ananias and Sapphira by apostolic strictness—had gradually been withdrawn from people’s contemplation through prolonged negligence and the passage of time, this kind of Sarabaites emerged. Since they separated themselves from the communities of the coenobia and individually attended to their own needs, [Note: [Col. 1103C] St. Jerome says that this third kind was called Romoboth or Remoboth, a term which Marianus (in his scholia) conjectures to be Hebrew, not Egyptian, and believes to have been derived from their proud gait. It may therefore be that they were called Romoboth in Hebrew, but Sarabaites in the Egyptian language. Marianus seems supported by these words of St. Jerome (Letter 22): “Among these”—that is, the Remoboth—“everything is affected: loose sleeves, bulging boots, a rather coarse garment, frequent sighs, visits to virgins, disparagement of clerics,” etc. Isidore, treating of the same people (On Ecclesiastical Offices, Book II, ch. 15), gives them another name and portrays them in these colors: “The sixth kind of monks, itself most loathsome and neglected, sprang up through Ananias and Sapphira at the beginning of the Church and was cut off by the severity of the apostle Peter. Because they separate themselves from coenobitic discipline and seek their own free wills, they are called Sarabaites, or Renuitae, in the Egyptian language. For they set up cells for themselves and falsely call them monasteries; free from the authority of elders, they live by their own judgment, competing in labor, not to distribute to those in need, but to acquire money to store away; and, as St. Jerome says of them, as though it were a holy craft rather than a life.” These are Isidore’s words, drawn partly from St. Jerome and partly from his own sense and from that opinion concerning the six kinds of monks discussed above. From them we learn that Jerome’s Remoboth, Benedict’s Sarabaites, and Isidore’s Renuitae are the same people. Moreover, Renuitae seem to be named from refusing, as those who refuse or reject the yoke of monastic discipline. St. Odo, abbot of Cluny, interprets it thus when, lamenting himself and the monks of his own time, he says (Conference 3): “We wretches are not monks, as we are falsely called, but Sarabaites—that is, Renuitae—who have refused the yoke of regular discipline.” Thus that holy man judged himself with great humility. Nor would one be wrong to say that Sarabaites were named from the Hebrew word Saravim, meaning rebels, such as these pseudo-monks are, who will submit neither to a rule nor to superiors; or from the Greek σάραβος, an indecent word—see Suidas, if you wish. Perhaps for this reason this author calls this kind of monks “most detestable,” while Jerome and Benedict more properly call it “most loathsome,” that is, most foul and shameful; or, finally, from Sarah, Abraham’s wife, as also the Saracens, though this is an erroneous and falsely assumed derivation, since it is established that they derive their origin not from Sarah, mistress and free woman, but from Hagar, handmaid and slave. Therefore they should truly be called not Saracens but Hagarites and Ishmaelites, that is, sons of a slave man and a slave woman. In the same way, Benedict says, Sarabaites are approved by no rule having experience as its teacher. They falsely usurp the name of monks and are known to lie to God by their tonsure, as though free—or rather, as though having liberty as a cloak for malice (1 Peter 2)—while meanwhile they are the most wretched slaves and the vilest bondsmen of their own desires. The statement Jerome reports concerning the Saracens (Life of Hilarion) also suits them: that they worship Venus because of Lucifer—the star of Venus—to whose worship, he says, the Saracen nation is devoted. Likewise Benedict says of the Sarabaites, “softened into the nature of lead,” that is, effeminate and soft, for whom the pleasure of desires is law. But lest we linger too long over these trifles, let Caelius Rhodiginus finally close this note. Concerning Sarabaites among the Turks who act under the appearance of religion, he writes (Antiquarian Readings, Book XXVII, ch. 6): “In Egypt Sarabaites are priests of that name, generally dwelling in hollows of rocks, clad about with swine and bovine skins, girded with ropes in place of belts, barefoot and sprinkled with blood. When the festival of Tabernacles comes on, they emerge from their caves and make for Jerusalem; entering the temple, they make a display of want and abstinence, thrust themselves upon everyone, and even sharply pluck their beards, so that all may behold these things and think them men sent down from heaven and admire them, although beneath their skins they are always soaked in vices. Augustine therefore commands that they are not to be imitated, and the eloquent writer Jerome mentions them.” Thus he.] [Col. 1104A] they were called Sarabaites by the distinctive usage of the Egyptian language, arising from the number of those whom we have mentioned. They preferred to counterfeit evangelical perfection rather than truly embrace it, evidently provoked by rivalry with, or praise of, those who prefer the perfect nakedness of Christ to all the riches of the world.

These men, then, while attempting a virtue of the highest order with weak resolve—or while compelled by necessity to enter this profession—and while hastening merely to be counted by the name of monks without any zeal for their discipline, do not seek the discipline of coenobia at all. They do not submit to the judgment of the elders, nor, instructed by their traditions, learn to overcome their own wills; nor do they receive any rule of sound discernment through legitimate training. They renounce only outwardly—that is, before the eyes of men—or, under the privilege of this name, remain bound to the same occupations in their own dwellings. Alternatively, they build cells for themselves, call them monasteries, and remain in them under their own authority and liberty, in no way submitting to the evangelical commands. Their purpose, supposedly, is to avoid being occupied by any daily concern for food or by any distractions connected with household property.

This is completed without faithless hesitation only by those who, freed from all the resources of this world, have submitted themselves to the superiors of the coenobia so completely that they confess themselves masters of not even their own persons. But those who, avoiding the strictness of the coenobium as we have said, live two or three together in cells, are not content to be governed by the abbot’s care and authority. Their chief concern is to possess, once freed from the yoke of the elders, the liberty to exercise their own wills, to go out wherever they please, and to do whatever they desire. They spend even more time in daily work than those who live in coenobia, consuming days and nights in labor, but not with the same faith or purpose.

These men work not to submit the fruit of their labor to the steward’s judgment, but to acquire money that they may store away. Observe how great the difference is between them. The former, thinking nothing of tomorrow, offer to God the most pleasing fruits of their sweat. The latter, extending their faithless anxiety not merely into tomorrow but over periods of many years, believe either that God is deceitful or that he is powerless: that he either cannot or will not provide them with the promised sufficiency of daily food and clothing.

The former desire with all their prayers to possess ἀκτημοσύνην—that is, nakedness and poverty in all things—[Col. 1106A] whereas the latter desire to attain an abundance of every resource. [Note: [Col. 1105C] Ἀκτημοσύνη, as Ciaconius observes, means something more than poverty and want. Ἀκτήμων is one who possesses absolutely nothing, such as those Egyptian anchorites; κτῆσις, by contrast, is possession of some thing. Abbot John especially condemns possession in the solitary (Conference 19, chapter 6): “Although,” says Ciaconius, “in the editions printed up to now ἀλκῆς κρῆσις is corruptly read instead of κτῆσις.” Thus he.] For this reason they labor eagerly at their daily tasks, going beyond the established rule, so that whatever overflows from the monastery may, at the abbot’s discretion, be distributed to prisons, or [Note: [Col. 1105C] The xenodochium was discussed above (Conference 14, chapter 4). Just as a xenodochium is a lodging for strangers, so a nosocomium, in Greek νοσοκομεῖον, is a lodging for the sick or infirm, or a place where the sick are received and cared for. St. Jerome, in his Letter to Oceanus (Letter 30), says: “He distributed, squandered, and sold the wealth he could have possessed, and prepared the money thus gathered for the use of the poor. First of all he established a nosocomium, that is, a house for the sick, in which he might refresh the sick and the wretched limbs of those exhausted by illness and starvation.” Justinian too uses the term in law 16, “Illud,” and law 18, “Sancimus,” On Sacred Churches. In monasteries it is commonly called the infirmary, or infirmarium; we have noted more about it elsewhere (On Pachomius’ Rule, 5). Popes Innocent III, in the chapter “Cum ad monasterium” of On the Status of Monks, and Benedict XII in his constitution, chapter 26, also mention it, although the latter calls it infirmitorium. A related term is the institution called in Greek γεροντοκομεῖον, a place assigned to the elderly, mentioned by St. Gregory in Register, Book XI, chapter 16.] to a guesthouse, or a hospital, or the needy.

The latter seek to ensure that whatever remains from their daily gluttony either contributes to more lavish pleasure or is stored away through the vice of avarice. Finally, even if we grant that what they accumulate without the best intention can sometimes be distributed better than we have said, they still do not attain the merit of virtue and perfection.

For the former, while contributing such revenues to the monastery and renouncing them daily, continue in such profound humility of submission that they are deprived of authority over what they acquire by their own sweat, just as they are deprived of authority over themselves. By stripping themselves daily of the fruits of their labor, they continually renew the fervor of their first renunciation. The latter, however, become proud precisely because they give something to the poor, and every day fall headlong into ruin.

Patience and strict discipline make the former—who persevere so devotedly in the profession they once undertook—daily crucified and living martyrs, because they never fulfill their own wills. [Note: [Col. 1105D] The monastic life, joined as it is to the mortification of one’s own will and of carnal desires, is a spiritual crucifixion (on which Cassian, Institutes, Book IV, chapter 34, may be consulted) and a kind of martyrdom. Hence St. Jerome, in his epitaph of Paula to Eustochium (Letter [Col. 1106C] 27): “The Lord is your portion; and, that you may rejoice more, your mother has been crowned by a long martyrdom. For not only is the shedding of blood counted as confession, but the unblemished servitude of a devoted mind is also daily martyrdom.” Again, elsewhere (Letter 8): “Take up the shield of faith, the breastplate of righteousness, the helmet of salvation, and advance to battle. Chastity preserved has its own martyrdom.” St. Augustine, in his sermons for the season (Sermon 50), says: “Let no one say that in our times the struggles of martyrs cannot exist; our peace too has its martyrs. For, as we have often suggested, to restrain anger, flee lust, preserve justice, despise avarice, and humble pride is a large part of martyrdom.” St. Gregory, Homily 36 on the Gospels: “We can be martyrs without the sword, if we truly preserve patience in our hearts.”] Their sluggish self-will, however, plunges the latter alive into hell.
