These two kinds of monks, then, contend with one another in this province in almost equal numbers. In other regions, however, which the necessity of the Catholic faith compelled me to travel through, we learned that this third kind of Sarabaites is abundant and almost the only kind found there. [Note: [Col. 1106C] Lucius, after St. Athanasius, was bishop of the Arian party and held the Church of Alexandria until the emperor Theodosius expelled him. His monstrous crimes and outrages against the orthodox, especially against monks, are extensively recounted in a letter of Peter, bishop of Alexandria, preserved by Theodoret. Among other things it says: “As soon as the athletes of Christ whom we have mentioned arrived at Heliopolis, where everyone was devoted to superstition, these vigorous defenders of the Church, seized by divine zeal, were first thrown into custody. Then, beaten with blows, lacerated, and subjected to torture, they were sent to the mines at Pheno and Proconnesus; among them were many monks, etc.” Rufinus, an eyewitness to the same tragedy, since he was then living in Egypt, wrote the following about Lucius (Book II, chapters 3 and 4): “Then, after the flight and exile of citizens, after killings, tortures, and flames with which he had destroyed countless people, he turned the weapons of his fury against the monasteries, ravaged the desert, and declared war on those who lived in peace. He undertook to attack simultaneously three thousand men, or more, scattered throughout the entire desert in secluded and solitary dwellings; he sent an armed force of cavalry and infantry. He chose tribunes, prefects, and commanders of war as though he were going to fight against barbarians. When they arrived (see Platina, p. 4), they saw a new kind of war: the enemies offered their necks to the sword and said nothing except, ‘Friend, why have you come?’ At that time the fathers of the monks—men renowned for the merit of their life and antiquity—Macarius, Isidore, another Macarius, Heraclides, and Pambus, disciples of Antony, were living throughout Egypt and especially in the regions of the desert of Nitria. They were believed to share the life and conduct not of other mortals but of the angels above. I speak of what I saw with my own eyes and report the deeds of those whose sufferings I was privileged to share.” Thus Rufinus. St. Gregory Nazianzen, in his oration in praise of Heron (Oration 23), Socrates, Book IV, chapter 16 and following, Sozomen, Book VI, chapters 19 and 20, and Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 29, also discuss this very persecution inflicted on Catholics by Lucius, the Arian pseudo-bishop. The aforementioned Peter of Alexandria proclaimed the same slaughter of Catholics not only in writing but also orally at Rome, where he had taken refuge, displaying the bloodstained garments of those killed there; at this pitiable spectacle the city was moved to tears (Baronius, in the Martyrology, May 13). This too deserves remembrance: when Lucius the Arian was persecuting Catholics everywhere, monks performed miracles with these words: “In the name of Jesus, whom Lucius persecutes, rise and walk.” Rufinus records this in Book XI, chapter 4.] 

For in the time of Lucius, who was bishop of the Arian perfidy, under the rule of Valens, [Note: [Col. 1107D] As Ciaconius observes, diaconia here means a collection, or an offering of alms gathered and distributed to poor Christians. The Apostle uses this word in 2 Corinthians, chapter 9: περὶ μὲν τῆς διακονίας τῆς εἰς τοὺς ἁγίους περισσὸν ἐμοί ἐστι τὸ γράφειν ὑμῖν, which the Latin interpreter rendered: “Now concerning the ministry performed for the saints, it is superfluous for me to write to you.” Diaconia also means the administration or management of affairs belonging to monasteries, entrusted, as Cassian reports in Conference 21 (chapters 1, 8, and 9), by the vote of all the elders to the monk among them of most approved character. He also calls it dispensation in Institutes, Book V, chapter 40, where he says that the dispensation and management of the Church—that is, the congregation—were entrusted to Abbot John by the priest Paphnutius. Onuphrius gives another, related sense of diaconia in these words (Explanation of Ecclesiastical Terms): “Diaconiae were so called from deacons. They were public charitable houses for the poor, with attached oratories and chapels, where the Father of the diaconia, or deacon, supplied the needy with necessities. For deacons were ministers to the poor, the afflicted, widows, and orphans, and presided over these charitable houses. In ancient times the Roman Church assigned deacons to each district of the city, and they were called regional deacons, or deacons of this or that district. Later, when their chief use had fallen into disuse and the charitable houses had been destroyed through their neglect, their chapels or little shrines remained, retaining the name diaconiae; from these the cardinal deacons of the city of Rome afterward received their designation.” Thus he. Baronius explains these matters more fully in his notes to the Roman Martyrology (8 August).] [Note: [Col. 1107B] The emperor Valens was at first a Catholic, but was later led astray by the Arians and became the leader of the Arians. He stirred up severe persecutions against Catholics, especially bishops and monks. He also encouraged and intensified the cruelty of Lucius by a public edict which, as Socrates says (Book IV, chapter 17), ordered that all who held the faith of consubstantiality be expelled not only from Alexandria but from all Egypt. Indeed, the prefect was ordered to pursue everywhere with large forces all whom Lucius identified. At that time the monasteries in the desert were plundered, harassed, and cruelly attacked. Armed men assaulted unarmed men who could not even raise a hand to ward off a blow, and slew them in such a pitiable manner that the crimes committed against them cannot be explained in any form of speech. Thus Socrates. St. Jerome says the following about this persecution in his Chronicle (year 375): “Many monks were killed by tribunes and soldiers. For when Valens had issued a law that monks should serve in the army, he ordered those unwilling to do so to be killed with clubs.” Orosius says: “After the death of his brother, Valens, as though with the unrestrained boldness of liberty, issued a law that monks—that is, Christians who, abandoning the manifold activity of worldly affairs, devote themselves wholly to the one work of faith—should be compelled to military service. At that time the deserts and broad sands of Egypt, unknown to human habitation because of their thirst, barrenness, and the most dangerous abundance of serpents, had been filled by a great multitude of monks. Tribunes and soldiers were sent there; they dragged away the holy and true soldiers of God under another name of persecution, and there killed many ranks of saints.” Thus they write. From these accounts it is clear that under the emperor Valens monks were harassed in various ways: some were beaten with clubs and killed, some were dragged into military service, some were banished into exile, and others were assigned and deported to dig and excavate mines, as is said below.] while we were delivering a diaconia to our brethren—namely, to those who had been exiled to the mines of Pontus and Armenia because of their perseverance in the Catholic faith—[Note: [Col. 1108B] That is, condemned and deported to dig in the mines. This was one of the many forms of punishment by which martyrs, formerly sent either by pagans or heretics to particular places, were afflicted by continual labor in excavating and extracting metals and were kept in fetters, thus enduring a prolonged martyrdom. On this subject there is an outstanding letter of St. Cyprian (Letter 77), in which he praises at length the martyrs condemned to the mines, setting individual consolations against their individual torments in a beautiful antithesis. He summarizes those torments more or less in these words: “In the mines the body is not warmed by a bed or mattresses; exhausted limbs lie upon the ground, disfigured by filth and grime, without baths; there is little bread; clothing is lacking for those who are cold; the hair of the half-shaven head bristles, etc.” (See Baronius, in the Martyrology, February 16.) Tertullian calls those dreadful workshops “funereal factories” (Book On the Apparel of Women). We noted above, from the letter of Peter of Alexandria, that many Egyptian monks were tortured by that Lucius, the Arian pseudo-bishop, with this punishment. Legal scholars distinguish between someone condemned to the mines and someone condemned to mining labor. These were different kinds of penalties: condemnation to a mine and condemnation to mining work. The difference between the two punishments lay in the fetters. Those condemned to a mine, or to the mines, were burdened with heavier chains; those condemned to mining work with lighter ones. Christians were also condemned to other public works, such as digging sand, quarrying stone, and working in lime and sulfur mines, as their Acts testify.] [Note: [Col. 1108D] Pontus was discussed elsewhere (Institutes, Book V, chapter 32). Armenia is a region of Asia, also called Ararat and Aram in Sacred Scripture; upon its highest mountains Noah’s ark came to rest (Genesis 8). See Pliny, Book VI, chapter 9.] [Note: [Col. 1108D] Baronius, in volume IV of the Annals (year 372), charges this passage of Cassian with falsehood on the authority of Gregory Nazianzen (to Hellenius) and Basil (Letter 79), who state most explicitly that in their own time many monks and anchorites existed in Pontus. Possevinus also noted this concerning Cassian (Apparatus).] Although we saw the discipline of coenobia to be exceedingly rare in certain cities, we nevertheless discovered that among those people not even the name of anchorites was known.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the fourth kind of monks

[Col. 1109A]

There is certainly also [Note: [Col. 1109B] This fourth kind of monks, which the abbot here left anonymous or unnamed, St. Benedict called by its proper name gyrovagi, “wandering monks,” and depicted it in these terms (Rule, chapter 1): “The fourth kind is that of monks called gyrovagi, who throughout their entire lives lodge for three or four days at a time in the cells of different people throughout different provinces; always wandering and never stable, but always and everywhere serving their own pleasures and the enticements of the belly, and in every respect worse than the Sarabaites. Of whose most wretched manner of life it is better to be silent than to speak.” St. Augustine also seems to portray such monks, or rather pseudo-monks, in these words (On the Work of Monks, chapter 28): “The enemy of the human race has scattered everywhere so many hypocrites under the habit of monks, roaming through the provinces, sent nowhere, settled nowhere, standing nowhere, sitting nowhere. Some sell the relics of martyrs, if indeed they are relics of martyrs; others display their fringes and phylacteries; others falsely claim that they have heard that their parents or relatives are living in one region or another and that they are going to them; and from everyone they ask and demand either the expenses of profitable poverty or the price of pretended sanctity. Meanwhile, wherever they are caught in their evil deeds or become known in any way, your profession is blasphemed under the general name of monks—a profession so good and holy, which in Christ’s name we desire to flourish throughout all Africa, as it does throughout other lands.” St. Augustine also indicates, in his exposition of Psalm 132, that such monks were called gyrovagi and vagabonds by another name, circumcellions or circumcellites. Rebuking them and contrasting them with true monks, he says: “What need is there for our words to compare drunkards with the sober, rash men with the thoughtful, the raging with the simple, the wandering with the gathered? Yet they are accustomed to say, ‘What is the meaning of the name monks?’ How much better we say, ‘What is the meaning of the name circumcellions?’ But, they say, they are not called circumcellions. Perhaps we call them by a corrupted sound of the name; we shall tell you their complete name. Perhaps they are called circumcellions, not circellions. Clearly, if this is what they are called, let them explain what they are; for those are called circumcellions who wander around cells. They are accustomed to go here and there, having no fixed dwelling, and to do the things you know and the things they know, whether they wish it or not.” Thus Augustine. From this it is clear that Isidore is wrong to distinguish circumcellions from gyrovagi, since they were called circumcellions precisely because they wandered around cells, as Augustine says—and the name gyrovagi expresses the same thing sufficiently. Turrecrematus gives three reasons why St. Benedict calls gyrovagi worse than Sarabaites. First, he says, because Sarabaites build cells and remain firmly in them, whereas gyrovagi do not, but travel through different provinces like guests. Second, because, although Sarabaites are wicked, they nevertheless live from their own labor, while gyrovagi live from the labor of others; indeed, what has been acquired or gathered through much time and labor is consumed by them in a brief hour. Third, because, running through different places, they corrupt and ruin many by the example of their evil life. Before all these writers, St. Basil seems to have designated and pointed out the same gyrovagi in his Monastic Constitutions (chapter 9), where he says: “Those too must be avoided who repeatedly change their place and go now to these brothers, now to those, and, driven by restless impulse, occupy themselves continually in touring monasteries, and under the pretext of spiritual charity serve the lusts of the flesh. In their minds there is nothing firm, nothing solid, nothing suited to an ordered discipline, and finally nothing of prudence or gravity; on the contrary, the greatest curiosity, perversity of character, fickleness, thoughtlessness, deceit, hypocrisy, and flattery full of lying and crafty speech abound in them. For these men are rough in speech and intemperate in the belly,” etc.; there he describes their character more fully. Cardinal Peter of Ostia speaks of the same men in Letter 9 of Book V, in these words: “In the monastic order, those whom we see regularly remaining in cloisters under the abbot’s authority we consequently call monks; but those whom we see possessing what is their own, running indiscriminately here and there, freed from laws, and dissolving themselves according to the judgment of their own will, we judge worthy to be called not monks but rather gyrovagi.”] another, fourth kind, which we have recently seen emerge among those who flatter themselves with the appearance and image of anchorites. At the beginning of their course they seem, with a certain brief fervor, to seek the perfection of the coenobium; but soon growing lukewarm, they disdain to cut away their former habits and vices, are unwilling to endure longer the yoke of humility and patience, and disdain to be subject to the authority of the elders. They seek separate cells and desire to sit in solitude, so that, unprovoked by anyone, they may be judged by men to be patient, gentle, and humble.

This arrangement—or rather, this lukewarmness—once it has infected them, never permits them to approach perfection. [Note: [Col. 1110C] Cassian emphasizes this repeatedly in Institutes, Book VIII, chapter 17 (see also Conference 19, chapter 10, and Conference 5, chapter 4): “Whatever vices we have brought into the desert without curing them, we shall find covered over within us, not abolished. For solitude, just as it knows how to open the purest contemplation to those whose character has been corrected, so it is accustomed not only to preserve the vices of those who are less corrected but even to intensify them. A man seems patient and humble to himself only so long as he has no association with anyone; but he soon returns to his former nature when an occasion for any disturbance arises. For the vices that lay hidden immediately emerge; and, like unbridled horses, nourished by prolonged idleness, they burst more fiercely and savagely from their barriers, striving to destroy their own charioteer. For when human exercise and practice have ceased, our vices grow more wild if they have not previously been purged.” See similar and corresponding passages in St. Basil (Basil, Longer Rules, Question 7).] In this way their vices will not merely fail to be cut away; they will grow stronger for the worse, since, provoked by no one, they spread like a deadly and inward poison. The longer they are concealed, the more deeply they penetrate, producing an incurable disease in the sick person.

Because of the respect accorded to the solitary cell, no one now dares to rebuke the solitary’s vices—vices he has preferred to have ignored rather than cured. Virtues, however, are produced not by hiding vices but by conquering them.

## CHAPTER IX. The question: What is the difference between a coenobium and a monastery?

Germanus: Is there any difference between a coenobium and a monastery, or is the same thing understood by both names?

## CHAPTER X. The answer

[Col. 1111A]

Piammon: Although some customarily call monasteries coenobia without distinction, there is nevertheless this difference: monastery is the name of a lodging-place, signifying nothing more than the place—that is, the dwelling—of monks; coenobium, however, also designates the character and discipline of the profession itself. And [Note: [Col. 1111C] Philo and the interpreter cited above say the same thing (on chapter 5 of this Conference): “For each person there is a sacred dwelling, which they call a sanctuary or monastery.” If the words are taken strictly, just as the dwelling of one monk cannot be called a coenobium, since communal life belongs not to one but to many, so a coenobium cannot be called a monastery if monastery is derived from solitude and means the dwelling of one monk, as is said here. Nevertheless, these terms are commonly confused and taken as equivalent. Thus St. Benedict too (Rule, chapter 1) calls coenobites “monastic” monks. But if coenobites are the same as monastic monks, then coenobia and monasteries are likewise the same. Moreover, that coenobium was also a familiar term among pagan philosophers, and that they themselves sketched a kind of example of coenobitic life, is shown by Aulus Gellius (Attic Nights, Book I, chapter 9). Speaking of the discipline of the Pythagoreans, he says: “All those who had been received by Pythagoras into that fellowship of disciplines contributed to the common fund whatever each possessed in family property and money, and an inseparable society was formed, as though this were that ancient partnership which in both reality and word was called κοινόβιον.” Thus he.] a monastery may also be the dwelling of a single monk, but it cannot be called a coenobium unless there is the united communion of many co-dwellers living together. Monasteries are indeed also called those places in which communities of Sarabaites reside.

## CHAPTER XI. On true humility, and how the abbot Serapion exposed the false humility of a certain man

[Col. 1111B]

Since, therefore, I see that you have undertaken the beginnings of this profession from the best class of monks—that is, that from the praiseworthy training-ground of the coenobia you are striving toward the lofty heights of the anchoritic discipline—pursue with a genuine affection of heart the virtue of humility and patience, which I do not doubt you learned there. Do not imitate certain people by feigning it through a false abasement of words, or through affected and excessive bodily prostration in certain services.

This fiction of humility [Note: [Col. 1112C] He discusses this elsewhere more than once (Conferences 2.11 and 5.1); he is said to have presided over ten thousand monks.] was once elegantly ridiculed by Abbot Serapion. For when a certain man came to him displaying extreme self-abasement in dress and speech, and the old man, according to custom, urged him to gather himself for prayer [Al. “to offer prayer”], the man by no means agreeing [Col. 1111C] with the request, declared that he was so entangled in enormous crimes that he did not even deserve to breathe this common air. He also avoided sitting on the old man’s mat (*psiathium*) and sat instead on the ground.

When he showed even less willingness to submit to the washing of his feet, Abbot Serapion, after the meal had ended, began—at the prompting of the customary conference—to admonish him kindly and gently not to wander about everywhere in unstable frivolity, idle and without purpose, especially since he was a young man of such robust strength, but to remain in his cell and, according to the rule of the elders, prefer to support himself by his own work rather than by another’s generosity.

The Apostle Paul, in order not to fall into this situation—even though such provision was rightly owed him while he labored in the Gospel—nevertheless preferred to work day and night, so that by his own hands he might prepare daily sustenance either for himself or for those who served him but were unable to carry on their work (Acts 20).

At these words the man was so filled with sadness and grief that he could not conceal the bitterness he had conceived in his heart even from his face. The old man said to him:

“Until now, my son, you were loading yourself with the full weight of your crimes, without fearing that by confessing such atrocious offenses you would incur the stain of a bad reputation. Why, then, I ask, do I now see you so provoked by a simple little admonition of ours—which nevertheless contained not only no insult, but even an expression of edification [Col. 1112B] and affection—that you could not conceal your indignation even in your face or disguise it beneath a serene brow? Or perhaps, while you were humbling yourself, you were expecting to hear from my mouth the sentence, ‘The just man is first an accuser of himself’ (Proverbs 18)?

[Note: [Col. 1112C] Saint Ambrose, to Constantius (Letter 42, Book II): ‘Many possess the appearance of humility but do not possess its virtue; many display it outwardly but oppose it inwardly; they put it forward as a pretense, but deny it in truth; they refuse it to grace. For one person humiliates himself wickedly, while his inner parts are full of deceit; another submits himself excessively because of abundant humility. Therefore there is no humility unless it is without pretense and without fraud. That is true humility which possesses a devout sincerity of mind. Great is its virtue.’ And Jerome, to Caelantia (Letter 14): ‘Follow humility—not that which is displayed and feigned by bodily gesture or a broken tone of speech, but that which is expressed by a pure affection of heart. For it is one thing to possess virtue, another to possess the likeness of virtue,’ and so forth, as cited elsewhere.]

Accordingly, true humility of heart must be retained: it does not arise from affected bodily and verbal behavior, but from the innermost humiliation of the mind. It will then shine forth with the clearest signs of its patience, when a person does not himself broadcast crimes which others would not believe, but scorns accusations arrogantly brought against him by others and endures the injuries inflicted upon him with the gentle equanimity of his heart.

## CHAPTER XII. The question: how true patience can be acquired

[Col. 1112C]

**Germanus:** We wish to learn how this tranquility can be acquired or preserved, so that, just as we close the barriers of our mouths when silence is imposed upon us and restrain the license of speech, we may likewise guard the gentleness of our hearts. For sometimes, even when the tongue is restrained, the heart inwardly loses the condition of its peace. And therefore we think that no one can possess the good of meekness except by seclusion in a cell and by living in a solitary dwelling.

[Note: [Col. 1112D] That is, by solitude and withdrawal from others.]

## CHAPTER XIII. The response

[Col. 1113A]

**Piammon:** True patience and tranquility can neither be acquired nor preserved without profound humility of heart. If humility descends from this source, it will need neither the benefit of a cell nor the refuge of solitude. For it does not seek the protection of anything external; rather, it is supported inwardly by the power of humility—that is, of its origin and guardian.

But if we are stirred when someone provokes us, it is certain that the foundations of humility have not been firmly established within us. Therefore, at the assault of even a slight storm, our building is shaken by a ruinous disturbance. Patience would not be praiseworthy or admirable if, untouched by any arrows of the enemy, it merely retained its purpose of tranquility; [Col. 1113B] its excellence and glory consist in remaining immovable when storms of temptation rush upon it. For that in which it is thought to be harassed and broken is instead strengthened; and that in which it is thought to be blunted is sharpened all the more.

[Note: [Col. 1113C] Petrus Maturus, as quoted in these words by Saint Antoninus: ‘Patience is called in Greek, especially in the sacred books, ὑπομονή (*hypomonē*). Just as the name “patience” derives from the verb *patior*, “I suffer,” so *hypomonē* derives from *hypomenō*, which means “I remain beneath” and “I sustain.” Hence, Cassian reports that in this passage patience is so called from suffering and endurance.’]

No one is unaware that patience is so called from suffering and endurance. Therefore [Note: [Col. 1113D] Saint Gregory says: ‘Patience is to endure the evils of others with equanimity and not to be gnawed by any grief even against the one who inflicts the evils. For whoever bears the evils of his neighbor while nevertheless grieving silently and awaiting the time of deserved retribution does not display patience but merely makes a show of it. For it is written: “Charity is patient, it is kind” (1 Corinthians 13). It is patient so that it may tolerate the evils of others; it is kind so that it may love even those whom it bears.’]

It is therefore clear that no one can be called patient except one who endures without indignation everything that has been inflicted upon him. Thus Solomon rightly praises patience:

“Better is the patient man than the strong, and he who restrains his anger than he who captures a city” (Proverbs 16).

And again:

“The long-suffering man is rich in prudence, but the short-tempered man is exceedingly foolish” (Proverbs 14, according to the Septuagint).

When someone, overcome by an injury, is set ablaze by the fire of anger, we must not think that the severity of the insult inflicted was the cause of his sin. Rather, it was the manifestation of a hidden weakness, according to the Savior’s parable concerning the two houses: one founded upon rock and the other upon sand. He says that the torrents of rains, rivers, and storms rushed equally upon both; but the house founded upon the solidity of rock felt no harm at all from that violent impact, whereas the one constructed upon the unstable movement of sand immediately collapsed (Matthew 7). It is evident that the latter did not fall because it was struck by the flood of rains or torrents, but because it had been foolishly built upon sand.

A holy man does not differ from a sinner because he is not tempted in the same way, but because the holy man is not conquered even by a great assault, whereas the sinner is overcome even by a small temptation. Nor, as we have said, would the strength of any righteous person be praiseworthy if he conquered without being challenged, since victory cannot exist without the adversity of combat.

“Blessed is the man who endures temptation, because when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life which God has promised to those who love him” (James 1).

According to the Apostle Paul also, virtue is perfected not in leisure and pleasures but in weakness (2 Corinthians 12).

“For behold,” he says, “today I have made you a fortified city, an iron pillar, and a bronze wall over all the land: against the kings of Judah, its princes, its priests, and all the people of the land. They will wage war against you, but they will not prevail, because I am with you to rescue you, says the Lord Almighty” (Jeremiah 1).

## CHAPTER XIV. An example of the patience of a devout woman

I wish, therefore, to set before you at least two examples of this patience, [Note: [Col. 1113D] John Moschus recounts a similar example in *The Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 206.] one of a certain devout woman who pursued the virtue of patience with such eagerness that she not only did not avoid the assaults of temptations, but even procured occasions of trouble for herself, so that, being more frequently provoked, she would not yield.

While she was living in Alexandria, and though she was born of parents of no obscure rank, she served the Lord devoutly in a house left to her by her parents. She came to [Note: [Col. 1113D] Saint Athanasius, that great and divine man, whose creed is read in the churches (Jerome, *Catalogue*), bishop of Alexandria, outstanding in holiness and learning and a most vigorous defender of the Catholic faith against the Arians. For its defense he endured many plots from them and fled to Gaul to the Emperor Constantius. Returning from there with letters, and again driven into exile after Constantius’s death, he remained in hiding until the time of Jovian. After Jovian restored him to the governance of his church, he died in the year of the Lord 370, leaving and transmitting to posterity many distinguished monuments of his genius.] the bishop Athanasius, of blessed memory, and asked him to give her a widow to support, one who was maintained from ecclesiastical funds.

To express her request in her own words, she said: “Give me one of the sisters whom I may refresh.”

[Note: [Col. 1114D] That is, whom I may nourish or refresh. Niccolò Perotti says (*Book I*): ‘*Pausa* signifies the rest of something. The poet Actius says: “Rest for speaking has been given to us.” From this comes the verb *pauso*, “I rest,” and from it *repauso*, meaning “I take rest.” They are derived from the verb παύομαι, meaning “I cease from work” or “I rest.” Thus *repausem* is used actively in this passage, meaning “to refresh,” “to restore,” “to treat humanely,” and, as it were, to impose a pause—that is, an end—upon her labors. This is clear from the second request of the same woman, where she says, “So that you might order someone to be given to me whom I could refresh,” and so forth. Some, however, read: “In whom I may rest,” as Cuychius has noted.]

The bishop, therefore, praising the woman’s purpose because he saw her extremely ready for the work of mercy, ordered that a widow be chosen from among them who surpassed all the others in uprightness of conduct, dignity, and discipline. He did not want the recipient’s desire for generosity to be overcome by her own fault, nor did he want the woman seeking a reward in the needy person to suffer damage to her faith through offense at the other’s depraved behavior.

After the widow had been brought to her and the woman had served her in every way, she experienced her modesty and gentleness and saw herself honored at every moment by expressions of gratitude for her kindness. A few days later she returned to the bishop and said:

“I had asked you to order that someone be given to me whom I could refresh and whom I could serve with dutiful attentions.”

Since he still did not understand the woman’s purpose and desire, the bishop thought that her request had been neglected through the administrator’s evasiveness. While investigating the reason for the delay with no little agitation, he learned that a more respectable widow had been assigned to her than the others. He secretly ordered that the woman be given one who was worse than all the rest—one who surpassed all others dominated by these vices in anger, quarrelsomeness, violence [Lipsius, in the margin: “drunkenness”], loquacity, and even vanity.

When this widow had been found much more easily and the woman had begun to keep her in her house, serving her with the same care as the earlier widow, or even more diligently, the only gratitude she received in return for such service was to be continually subjected to undeserved injuries. She was harassed by constant insults and reproaches; the widow accused and cursed her with slanderous abuse because she had asked the bishop not to be given a woman for refreshment but rather for torture and humiliation, and because she had been transferred from rest to labor, rather than from labor to rest.

When the repeated quarrels advanced so far that the insolent woman did not even refrain from laying hands upon her, the devout woman redoubled the services of her humble obedience. She did not learn to overcome the raging woman by resisting her, but by submitting herself more humbly, so that, provoked by insults of every kind, she might soothe the madness of the one who abused her through the gentleness of kindness.

Having been fully strengthened by these exercises and attained the perfection of the patience she desired, she went to the bishop to offer thanks both for his judgment in choosing the widow and for the benefit of her training. According to her desire, he had at last provided her with a most worthy teacher of patience, by whose continual injuries she was strengthened every day, as though by the oil of a training-ground, until she reached the highest degree of endurance of spirit.

“At last,” she said, “you have given me someone whom I may refresh, for the earlier woman rather honored and refreshed me by her services.”

Let this suffice as an example from the female sex, so that through its remembrance we may not only be edified but also put to shame—those of us who cannot preserve patience unless we have been shut away, like wild beasts, in the cages of our cells.

## CHAPTER XV. An example of the patience of Abbot Paphnutius

Now let us disclose another example, that of Abbot Paphnutius, who always devoted himself with such zeal to the secluded places of that celebrated and everywhere renowned Scetian desert, where he is now a priest, that the other anchorites [Note: [Col. 1115D] We have noted elsewhere that Paphnutius was given the surnames Bubalus and Cephalas (Conference 3.1, which is titled under his name). Some, however, posit two different Paphnutiuses: one called Cephalas, about whom Palladius writes in chapter 91, and another surnamed Bubalus, the Scetian priest discussed here and also in the third Conference.] gave him the surname Bubalus, because, so to speak, by an inborn desire he always delighted in dwelling in solitude.

While he was still in his youth, he possessed such virtue and grace that even distinguished and eminent men of that time admired his gravity and immovable constancy. Although he was younger in age, they considered him equal to his elders on account of his virtues and thought that he should be enrolled in their order.

That envy which once stirred the hearts of Joseph’s brothers against the patriarch kindled one of the brothers with the fire of consuming jealousy. Wishing to disfigure Paphnutius’s beauty with some blemish and stain, this man devised the following form of malice: he waited for an opportunity when Paphnutius would be absent from his cell because he was going to church on Sunday.

He then secretly entered it and hid his own book among the woven palm strips [Note: [Col. 1116D] As Ciaconius notes, *plectae*, called Egyptian *sirae*, are straps or rods woven from palm, reed, or spartum; baskets, hampers, and similar objects are made from them. They are called *plectae* from the verb πλέκω, “I entwine” or “I weave.” Likewise, the Greeks interpret πλεκτὴν σειράν as “a woven cord.” The word is frequent in the *Lives of the Fathers*, where *flecta* is also found.] that he used to weave. Secure in the plot he had contrived, he himself also went to church as though his conscience were pure and innocent.

When the entire solemnity had been celebrated according to custom, he brought a complaint before the holy Isidore, who before this time and likewise before Paphnutius had been priest of the same desert. In the presence of all the brothers he asserted that his book had been stolen from his cell.

His complaint so disturbed everyone’s minds, especially the priest’s, that they did not know what first to suspect or what decision to make. As all were struck with the greatest astonishment at the novelty of such an unheard-of crime, the accuser who had reported the matter pressed them to keep everyone in the church and send chosen men to search each brother’s cell individually.

The priest assigned this task to three elders. Searching through all the sleeping quarters, they finally found the hidden book in Paphnutius’s cell among the palm strips which he [Col. 1116D] called *sirae*, exactly as the plotter had concealed it.

The investigators immediately brought it to the church and displayed it before everyone. Although Paphnutius was secure in the sincerity of his conscience, he nevertheless acted as though he acknowledged the crime of theft. He surrendered himself entirely to satisfaction and humbly asked for a place of penance. He was concerned for his modesty and sense of shame, lest, if he attempted to remove the stain of theft by his words, he should additionally be branded a liar, since no one suspected anything other than what had been found.

When he left the church, not so much cast down in spirit as trusting in God’s judgment, he shed continual tears in prayer, trebled his fasts, and prostrated himself with the deepest humility of mind even before human beings. For nearly two weeks he subjected himself to every contrition of body and spirit, so that on Saturday or Sunday morning he would hurry to the church—not to receive Holy Communion, but to prostrate himself on its threshold and humbly ask forgiveness.

But the witness and knower of all hidden things did not permit him to be further humbled by himself or defamed by others. For what the inventor of the crime—the wicked thief of his own deed and cunning defamer of another’s glory—had committed with no human witness, the devil, who had prompted the crime, made public.

Seized by a most savage demon, the man disclosed the whole hidden plot. The one who had devised the accusations and frauds was also their betrayer. He was tormented so severely and for so long by that unclean spirit that he could not be cleansed even by the prayers of the saints who were present there and who, by the merit of their divine gifts, commanded demons. Nor could even the singular grace of the priest Isidore drive out the most savage tormentor from him.

[Note: [Col. 1117C] I believe that he names him “priest” here and above in this chapter in order to distinguish him from Isidore, bishop of Nitria, whom Saint Jerome mentions in the *Epitaph for Paula* in these words (Letter 27): “When the holy and venerable bishop Isidore the confessor met her, together with innumerable crowds of monks,” and so forth. Theodoretus also writes that this man, along with Macarius and other fathers of the monks, was banished into exile under the tyranny of Lucius the Arian (Book IV, chapter 19). For this reason he deserved to be honored with the title “confessor,” by which no one in former times was accustomed to be called unless he had confessed the faith of Christ before the enemies of the faith when summoned to do so, as Baronius notes in the *Martyrology* (January 2).

But this Isidore, the priest and abbot discussed here, seems to be the man about whom Sozomenus writes in his account of the monks of Egypt: “At that time, among the monks, the most illustrious fathers were Isidore, Serapion, and Dioscorus. Isidore surrounded the monastery on every side with a wall and took careful measures to prevent any of those inside from leaving, while ensuring that they possessed all the necessities of life.” Palladius also writes in the *Lausiac History* 71 that the monks of this monastery were endowed with great holiness and the grace of miracles. This agrees sufficiently with the present passage, where the extraordinary grace of this Isidore is recalled.

Nevertheless, whether he is the Isidore praised by Socrates (Book VI, chapter 9), Rufinus (Book II, chapter 4), Sozomenus (Book VIII, chapter 12), and Evagrius (*Lives of the Fathers*), who is known to have lived at the same time with a great reputation for holiness, I would rather doubt than affirm, although I incline more toward the negative view. For that man later defected to the Origenists and, having become their defender and leader, obscured his former reputation. Saint Jerome discusses him in Letter 61 to Pammachius and Ctesiphon.

Another Isidore is also commemorated as famous for holiness of life, faith, and miracles; the Roman Martyrology commemorates him on January 15. Baronius, however, thinks that this man lived elsewhere rather than in Egypt.

Finally, the most distinguished Isidore in this class of monks by both reputation and name was that Isidore of Pelusium, a disciple of John Chrysostom and celebrated among Greek ecclesiastical writers, often cited in these notes. The Roman Martyrology commemorates him on February 4.]

For the Lord had granted such power to Isidore that no demoniac who was slow to recover was ever brought even to his threshold. Christ reserved this glory for the young Paphnutius: the one who was cleansed was purified solely through the prayers of the man whom he had plotted against. The envious enemy, who had thought he could detract from Paphnutius’s honor, proclaimed his name and thereby received both forgiveness for his offense and an end to his present punishment.

Thus, even in his youth, Paphnutius already displayed signs foreshadowing his future character. While still a boy, he traced certain outlines of that perfection which was later to be increased by maturity. If, therefore, we wish to reach the summit of his virtues, we must lay for ourselves foundations of such a beginning.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the perfection of patience
The account of this event was prompted by a twofold purpose. First, by weighing this man’s steadfastness and constancy, we may recognize that, although we are assailed by the enemy’s plots, our temptations are far smaller than his, and thus acquire a correspondingly greater disposition toward tranquility and patience. Second, we may hold firmly to the conclusion that we cannot be safe from the storms of temptation and the assaults of the devil if we place the whole defense of our patience and all our confidence not in the strength of our inner self, but in the enclosure of our cell, the retreat of solitude, the company of the saints, or the protection of anything external to us. Unless he strengthens our mind by the power of his protection who says in the Gospel, “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17), we vainly imagine that we can overcome the snares of the aerial enemy with the help of those living with us, avoid them by occupying particular places, or exclude them by the fortification of buildings.

For although Saint Paphnutius lacked none of these things, the tempter was nevertheless able to find an avenue of attack against him; nor did walls, the solitude of the desert, or the merits of so many saints assembled there drive that most wicked spirit away from him. But because the holy servant of God had fixed the hope of his heart not on external things but on God himself, the hidden judge of all things, he could not be shaken by the machinery of so great an assault.

And, on the other hand, did not the man whom envy drove to so great a crime also enjoy the advantage of solitude, the guidance of a more remote dwelling, and the company of the blessed abbot and presbyter Isidore and of other saints? Yet the devilish whirlwind, which found him upon the sand, not only struck him but also overturned his dwelling.

Let us not, therefore, seek our peace externally, nor imagine that another person’s patience can help cure the vices of our impatience. For just as the kingdom of God is within us (Luke 17), so “a man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Matthew 10). No one opposes me more than my own mind, which is truly my intimate and domestic companion. Therefore, if we are vigilant, we shall scarcely be harmed by enemies within. For wherever our own household members do not oppose us, there the kingdom of God is acquired through tranquility of mind.

If you examine the matter carefully, I cannot be harmed by another person, however malicious, unless I myself contend against him with an unpeaceful heart. If I am harmed, the fault lies not in another’s attack but in my own impatience. Just as heavy and solid food is beneficial to a healthy person but harmful to one who is sick, so it cannot harm the person who takes it unless the recipient’s weakness gives it strength to do harm.

If a similar temptation should ever arise among the brothers, let us by no means be shaken from the course of tranquility and open an avenue to the blasphemous slanders of worldly people. Nor should we be astonished that some perverse and detestable persons are found lurking among the number of holy men. For while we are trampled and crushed on the threshing floor of this world, it is necessary that chaff also be mixed among the choicest wheat and destined for everlasting fire.

> **Note:** This is a wise saying, celebrated both in Scripture and among the Fathers, by which we are taught that in the Church militant the wicked are mixed with the good, just as wheat and chaff are mixed in a heap before they are winnowed and cleansed. Thus Isidore says (*Etymologies* 17.1): “Some say that chaff is so called because it is winnowed with a winnowing shovel, so that the grain may be purified.” Hence Jeremiah 23: “What has straw in common with wheat?” says the Lord. The Apostle expressed the same thought in other words: “What partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? Or what fellowship has light with darkness?” (2 Corinthians 6). And in Matthew 3 and Luke 3 it is said of the Savior: “His winnowing shovel is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor; he will gather his wheat into the granary, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.” Here the threshing floor signifies the Church; the wheat, the elect, because they are fruitful, full, and weighty with virtues; while the chaff signifies the wicked and rejected, because they are fruitless, empty, and devoid of good works.

> Saint Jerome, *Against the Pelagians* 1: “In the Lord’s field, while the master of the household slept, the enemy sows weeds over the wheat; and, while we are unaware, the nocturnal sower inserts barren darnel and wild oats among the good grain. Therefore this parable of the evangelical master of the household is to be feared: he cleanses the threshing floor and, after storing the wheat in the granaries, leaves the chaff to be scattered by the winds and burned in the fires. Hence we also read in Jeremiah: ‘What has straw in common with grain?’ says the Lord (Jeremiah 23). Chaff is separated from grain at the consummation of the age. From this it is shown that, while we are in this mortal body, the chaff is mixed with the wheat.”

> Saint Augustine, in one of his sermons (*Sermon on Time* 22): “Brothers, we have often said, we say often, and as long as we live we must say that the Church of this present time possesses both chaff and wheat. Let no one seek to drive out the chaff before the time of winnowing,” and so forth.

> Saint Gregory, *Moralia* 34.5: “After the threshing of the present life, in which the wheat now groans beneath the chaff, the wheat and chaff are so separated by the winnowing shovel of the final judgment that neither does the chaff pass into the granary of the wheat, nor do the grains of the granary slip into the fire of the chaff.” These are the words of the holy Fathers.

Finally, if we recall either Satan among the angels, or Judas among the apostles, or Nicholas, the inventor of a most depraved heresy, among the deacons chosen by the apostles, it will not be surprising that the most wicked are found inserted among the order of the saints.

> **Note:** Concerning Nicholas the deacon, one of the first seven whom the apostles are said to have ordained (Acts 5), there are two opinions among the ancients. Most assert that he fell away from the Catholic Church and taught, among other extremely shameful errors, that fornication and every kind of lustful impurity were permissible. Thus Saint Jerome, following earlier writers—Tertullian (*On the Prescription Against Heretics*), Irenaeus, and Epiphanius—says (*Letter* 1): “Do you regard Peter? Consider Judas also. Do you admire Stephen? Look also at Nicholas, whom the Lord condemns in his Apocalypse (Revelation 1); he devised such shameful and abominable things that the heresy of the Nicolaitans arose from that root.” Again, in *Letter* 48 to the deacon Sabinianus: “Nicholas of Antioch, one of those formerly belonging to your order, is reported to have been the author of every impurity and of the heresy of the Nicolaitans.” Again, in the *Dialogue Against the Luciferians* 8: “Nicholas, one of the seven deacons, celebrating weddings day and night, dreamed of obscene intercourse, shameful even to hear of.” This is Saint Jerome’s account. The author here follows the same opinion.

> Others, however, teach the contrary: that Nicholas was a pious and holy man, while the Nicolaitans condemned in Revelation 2—who taught the practices reported by Jerome—were heretics falsely called Nicolaitans. They supposedly assumed that name falsely and boastfully, as heretics customarily do, so as to cloak their heresy under an honorable name, calling themselves Nicolaitans as though they were disciples of Nicholas. See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* 3.23.

For although some assert that this Nicholas was not the one chosen by the apostles for the work of ministry, they nevertheless cannot deny that he belonged to the number of disciples who were all manifestly then such and so perfect as we now scarcely find scarcely a few even in monasteries.

> **Note:** Saint Augustine, commenting on Psalm 132, says: “There are false monks as well. We know such men; but the pious brotherhood has not perished because of those who profess to be what they are not. For there are false monks just as there are false clerics and false believers. These three classes, my brothers, which we have sometimes commended to you, have their good members and their bad members. Of all three classes it is said: ‘Two will be in the field; one will be taken and one left; two will be in bed; one will be taken and one left; and two will be grinding at the mill; one will be taken and one left’ (Matthew 24).

> “Those in the field are the ones who govern the Church. Hence the Apostle says—and see whether he was not in the field—‘I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth’ (1 Corinthians 3). By those in bed he wished those to be understood who loved quiet—for by the bed he intended quietness—not mixing themselves with crowds or with the tumult of the human race, but serving God; and yet of these one is taken and one left. There are worthy people there and rejected people. Likewise, the two at the mill are designated by a feminine noun because he wished the common people to be understood. Why at the mill? Because they move about in this world, where the mill signifies the world, since this world turns like a millstone—woe to those whom it crushes. Thus the good believers move about there: one of them is consumed, the other taken,” and so forth.

> The same Augustine says elsewhere (*Letter* 127, cited by Gratian, *Decretum*, distinction 4): “However vigilant the discipline of my household may be, I am a human being and live among human beings. I do not dare to claim that my household is better than Noah’s ark, where nevertheless one reprobate was found among eight people (Genesis 9); or better than Abraham’s household, where it was said, ‘Cast out the slave woman and her son’ (Genesis 21); or better than Isaac’s household, to whom it was said concerning the twin brothers, ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated’ (Malachi 1); or better than Jacob’s own household, where a son defiled his father’s bed (Genesis 49); or better than David’s own household, where one son had intercourse with his sister and another rebelled against his father’s most holy gentleness (2 Samuel 13); or better than the household of the Apostle Paul, who, even if he lived among all good people, would not have said, ‘Outside there are conflicts, inside fears’ (2 Corinthians 7), nor, speaking of Timothy’s holiness and faith, ‘I have no one who is genuinely concerned for you. For they all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ’ (Philippians 2); or better than the household of the Lord Christ himself, in which eleven good men endured the treacherous and thieving Judas; or finally better than heaven, from which angels fell.

> “Yet I frankly confess to your charity before the Lord our God, who is witness over my soul, that from the time I began to serve God I have found it as difficult to find people better than those who have advanced in monasteries as I have found none worse than those who have fallen in monasteries. So much so that I think this is written in the Apocalypse: ‘Let the righteous become more righteous, and let the filthy become filthier still.’

> “Therefore, although we grieve over certain impurities, we are nevertheless consoled by the greater number of adornments. Do not, then, detest the winepress because of the dregs that offend your eyes; from that winepress the storehouses of the Lord are filled with the fruit of brighter oil.” Thus far Saint Augustine. Nothing could be more appropriate to this passage.

Let us not, therefore, set before ourselves the downfall of the brother mentioned above, who fell so grievously in that desert—a stain which he nevertheless afterwards washed away with immense tears of repentance—but rather the examples of the blessed Paphnutius. Let us not be destroyed by that man’s overthrow, whose ancient vice of envy was made worse by his affected religious profession. Instead, let us follow with all our strength the humility of this man, a humility that was not suddenly produced by the quiet of the desert, but that had been acquired among human beings and was perfected and cultivated in solitude.

> **Note:** The seven deacons chosen and ordained by the apostles, among whom was Nicholas, a proselyte from Antioch, are reported by Luke (Acts 6). He says: “Calling together the multitude of the disciples, the twelve apostles said: ‘It is not right that we should abandon the word of God and serve tables. Therefore, brothers, select from among yourselves seven men of good reputation, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this task,’” and so forth. Further on: “They chose Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit, and Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicholas, a proselyte from Antioch. They set them before the apostles, and after praying they laid their hands on them.”

> There are two ministries of deacons, from which they also received their name. For διάκονος (*diakonos*) means “minister” in Latin—not just any kind of minister, but one ready, prompt, and devoted to service. One ministry is spiritual and ecclesiastical: in sacred matters deacons serve bishops and priests according to their own rank and office. The foremost place in this category belongs to the ministry of the altar, concerning which Blessed Ignatius the Martyr says in his letter to the Trallians: “What are deacons except imitators of angelic virtues, who offer them—that is, the priests—a pure and blameless ministry, as Saint Stephen did for blessed James, Timothy and Linus for Paul, Anacletus and Clement for Peter,” and so forth.

> The deacon and poet Arator elegantly expressed the same point in his poem about the apostles:

> *The rights of ministry suited to sacred altars*  
> *They established in seven men, chosen from everywhere,*  
> *Whom it pleases us to call Levites: how splendidly*  
> *The hand of the Church began to shine,*  
> *That it might mix the cups of life*  
> *And present the liquid together with the blood of the Lamb!*

> The other ministry of deacons is temporal and political, or economic, though entirely profane and secular, as the sectarians maintain. Through it they distributed among the poor and widows the alms offered by the faithful at the time of the sacrifice and deposited in the church treasury; the term “widows” also includes other poor persons. Luke mentions only this ministry, since he was content to explain the occasion of their ordination: namely, the murmuring of the Greeks against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily ministry—that is, in the daily distribution of alms.

> Saint Leo likewise speaks of this ministry in his sermon on Saint Lawrence: “He excelled not only in the ministry of the Sacraments but also in the administration of the Church’s property.” From this office the administration and distribution of alms itself was called *diaconia*, a task customarily entrusted not only to deacons but also to others. We have discussed it above and shall discuss it again below. See Saint Gregory, *Letters* 9, indiction 4, letter 24.

> **Note:** A work of Hippolytus on the seventy disciples of Christ is reported by Jerome in his *Catalogue*. It testifies that the deacon Nicholas, a man proven in the Catholic faith, was advanced to higher orders and made bishop of Samaria by the apostles. Dorotheus agrees in his *Synopsis*.

**CHAPTER XVII. On the Evil of Envy**

It must certainly be understood that the disease of envy is more difficult to bring to a cure than the other vices.

> **Note:** The Fathers concur. Cyprian (*On Jealousy and Envy*) says: “Treatment is easier where the wound is apparent, and a visible wound is soon brought to health when a remedy is promptly applied. The wounds of jealousy are hidden and concealed, and those who shut themselves up with blind grief in the recesses of conscience admit no remedy or treatment from the physician.” And below: “To hate a happy man is a calamity without remedy.” Basil (*Homily* 11) says: “When the envious man is asked to disclose his disease, he is altogether afraid to accuse himself, retaining in the deepest recess of his heart the disease that burns and consumes his entrails. Thus he cannot find a physician or a medicine fit to drive it away, although books are filled with treatments for the sick.” Chrysostom, *To the People of Antioch* 53: “This disease is incurable, so that even when countless medicines are applied, it gives forth its own corruption.” Prosper, *On the Contemplative Life* 3.5: “Excellence of merit makes a person envied; the punishment of sin makes him envious. No remedy can be applied by man to one whose wound is hidden.” For the person whom it has once corrupted with the plague of its poison, I would almost say, is without remedy.

This is the very plague of which the prophet speaks figuratively: “Behold, I am sending among you venomous serpents, against which there is no enchantment, and they shall bite you” (Jeremiah 8).

The prophet therefore rightly compares the bite of envy with the deadly poison of the basilisk, through which that first author and prince of all poisons both perished and brought death. Before he became the destroyer of the one whom he envied, before he poured the poison of death into another, he destroyed himself.

“Through the devil’s envy death entered the world” (Wisdom 2), and those who belong to his party imitate him. For just as the one who was first corrupted by the plague of this evil admitted neither the remedy of repentance nor the soothing treatment of any cure, so those who have handed themselves over to be struck by the same bites exclude every aid of the holy enchanter. Since they are tormented not by the faults of others but by their prosperity, they are ashamed to reveal the truth itself and seek externally certain unnecessary and foolish causes of their offense. Because these causes are entirely false, there is only one cure: that the deadly poison they refuse to disclose remains hidden in their inmost parts.

> **Note:** He alludes to Psalm 57: “Like a deaf asp that stops its ears, which does not hear the voice of charmers or of a skillful enchanter.” This proverb is applied to those who refuse to hear people giving sound warnings and good advice, as envious people especially do. The Jews expressed this outwardly in reality when Stephen preached to them. Of them it is said: “Crying out with a loud voice, they stopped their ears” (Acts 7). Hence Augustine, commenting on the same psalm, says: “They were not deaf, but made themselves deaf. Since they did not have ears open in their hearts, the force of the word rushing through the ears of the flesh nevertheless compelled even the ears of their hearts; they closed the ears of their bodies and went to the stones. Behold deaf asps, harder than the stones with which they stoned their enchanter. They did not hear the voice of the enchanter, nor the medicine administered by the wise man.” Thus Augustine.

Elsewhere that Most Wise One aptly expressed their condition: “If a serpent bites without hissing, there is no advantage to the enchanter” (Ecclesiastes 10).

> **Note:** See what we have written elsewhere on this subject (*Collation* 2.2).

These are the silent bites to which alone the medicine of the wise brings no relief. This affliction is so incurable that kindness aggravates it, attentions inflate it, and gifts provoke it. For, as the same Solomon says:

> **Note:** The Septuagint translators read this as follows. Saint Jerome reads: “Envy is impatient.” The Vulgate reads: “Anger has no mercy, nor does fury when provoked; and who can withstand the force of an aroused spirit?”

“Envy tolerates nothing” (Proverbs 6).

For the more another person advances, whether through humble submission, the virtue of patience, or the praise of generosity, the more strongly the envious person is driven by the goads of envy; he desires nothing except the ruin or death of the one whom he envies.

Finally, the envy of those eleven patriarchs could not be softened by any submission of their innocent brother. Scripture says of them: “His brothers envied him because his father loved him, and they could not speak peacefully to him” (Genesis 37). Their envy, which could not endure any soothing from their brother’s obedience and submission and desired his death, could scarcely be satisfied except by the crime of selling their brother.

> **Note:** Envy is of two kinds, good and bad. Bad envy is also called “the envy of bitterness,” “the gall of bitterness,” and “the root of bitterness.” Saint Benedict says in the penultimate chapter of the *Rule*: “Just as there is a bad zeal of bitterness, which separates from God and leads to hell, so there is a good zeal, which separates from vices and leads to God and eternal life.” Concerning the envy of zeal, the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 3: “Since there is envy and contention among you, are you not carnal?” And Blessed James says: “Where there is envy and contention, there is instability and every evil work” (James 3).

It is therefore clear that envy is more pernicious than all the vices and more difficult to cleanse, since it is inflamed by the very remedies through which the others are extinguished. For example, the person who grieves over a loss inflicted upon him is cured by compensation through generosity; the person who is angered by an injury inflicted upon him is appeased by an act of humble satisfaction. But what can you do with someone who is offended precisely because he perceives you to be more humble and kinder? He is not inflamed by desire, which can be soothed by a reward; nor by the wound of an injury or the love of vengeance, which can be overcome by acts of kindness; he is provoked solely by another person’s success.

Who, in order to satisfy an envious person, would wish to fall away from good things, be deprived of prosperity, or become entangled in some calamity?

Therefore, so that the basilisk may not destroy with a single bite of this evil everything in us that is vigorous and, as it were, animated by the life-giving growth of the Holy Spirit, let us continually implore the divine aid, for nothing is impossible to God.

The other poisons of serpents—that is, carnal sins and vices, which human frailty contracts quickly but can also expel easily—leave some marks of their wounds in the flesh. Although the earthly body may swell most dangerously from them, nevertheless, if someone applies the remedy of theriac or the healing medicine of salutary words through a skilled enchanter of divine songs, the virulent affliction does not reach the soul’s everlasting death.

> **Note:** Concerning theriac, Ciaconius writes: “*Theriakē*—with ‘antidote’ understood—means any medicine effective against poisons. In particular, however, the name came to designate that famous preparation made from several simple ingredients and the flesh of vipers. It was called *theriakē*, as though one were to say, ‘made from venomous beasts.’ For among physicians *thēria* specifically means beasts that inflict poison by their bite or sting, especially vipers, from whose flesh that medicine is composed.” This is his account. See, if desired, further discussion in Pliny, *Natural History* 20, final chapter, and 29.1, and in Caelius Rhodiginus, *Ancient Readings* 6.16.

But the poison of envy, as though poured out by a serpent basilisk, excludes the very life of religion and faith before a wound is even felt in the body. For the person who, attacking no fault in his brother but only his good merit, blasphemously rises not against a human being but plainly against God, criticizes not the man’s fault but God’s judgments alone.

This, then, is that root of bitterness growing upward (Hebrews 12), which, rising toward heavenly things, extends its challenge in insult to the very author who bestows good upon humanity.

No one should be troubled by the fact that God threatens to send venomous serpents to bite those whom he is offended by their crimes (Jeremiah 8). For although it is certain that God cannot be the author of envy, it is nevertheless just and worthy of the divine judgment that, while good things are bestowed upon the humble and denied to the proud and rejected, envy should strike and consume those who, according to the Apostle, deserve to be handed over to a depraved mind—as though sent by God himself—according to the saying:

> “They provoked me to jealousy with what is no god,  
> and I will provoke them to jealousy with what is no nation” (Deuteronomy 32).

By this discussion the blessed Piammon inflamed more ardently our desire, with which we had begun to aspire from the elementary instruction of the coenobium to the second degree of the anchoritic life. From him we first received instruction in the beginnings of solitary dwelling, the knowledge of which we later acquired more fully in Scetis.

# THE NINETEENTH CONFERENCE

**That of Abbot John: On the End of the Coenobite and the Hermit**

# CHAPTER I

**On the Coenobium of Abbot Paul and the Patience of a Certain Brother**
A very few days later, drawn onward by a desire for more advanced instruction, we proceeded once again with the greatest eagerness of spirit to the coenobium of Abba Paul.

> **Note [Col. 1125A].** We have shown elsewhere that there were several anchorites of this name, famous for their holiness and nearly contemporaneous with one another (*Institutes*, Book X, chapter 24). Which Paul’s coenobium is meant here, anyone may conjecture, but, I believe, no one can determine—especially since the Author says that he went again to Abba Paul’s coenobium, indicating that he had previously been there, although so far I do not remember having read this anywhere in these Conferences. Cassian does indeed mention Abba Paul in Book X of the *Institutes*, in the penultimate and final chapters, saying that he returned to him to seek advice; but that Paul is said to have had a private cell there, not a coenobium or a community of monks. He also mentions another Abba Paul in *Conference* 7, chapter 26, whom he says lived in the desert adjoining the city of Panephysis; but there is no mention there of Paul’s coenobium. We must therefore suppose that the Paul meant here was the Libyan Paul, of whom Sozomen writes in Book VI, chapter 29: “Paul had his dwelling at Pherme, which is a mountain in Scetis; he had no fewer than five hundred disciples.” Nicephorus gives the same account in different words (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book XI, chapter 36): “Paul lived the monastic life at Pherme, which is a mountain in Scetis, having no more than five hundred monks.” In the margin one finds: “Paul, abbot of five hundred ascetics.” Some, however, confuse this Paul with the Paul who lived near Panephysis [Col. 1125C].

Although more than two hundred brothers were living there, nevertheless, in honor of the solemnity then being celebrated, an immense crowd of monks from other coenobia had also gathered.

> **Note [Col. 1125C].** This is indeed a considerable number, though small in comparison with other coenobia, in which at least three thousand monks lived under one abbot, as Saint Augustine testifies (*On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, chapter 31). We have spoken of this matter several times elsewhere.

For the anniversary of the death of the former abbot who had presided over that coenobium was being solemnly celebrated.

> **Note [Col. 1125C].** Observe the antiquity of anniversaries for the dead. Tertullian likewise writes about them in *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 3: “We make annual offerings on the appointed day for the dead and for birthdays.” Here he indicates two kinds of anniversaries: one for deceased believers and the other for birthdays, namely, those of the martyrs. In *On Monogamy*, chapter 10, he urges a wife’s duty toward her deceased husband in these words: “Let her pray for his soul, and meanwhile ask refreshment for him, and fellowship in the first resurrection, and make offerings on the yearly days of his falling asleep.” And in the *Exhortation to Chastity*: “Again and again make petition before God, for whose spirit you ask, for whom you render annual offerings.” Gregory of Nazianzus, in his tenth oration, concerning his brother Caesarius, says: “Offering yearly honors and commemorations,” and so forth. John of Damascus, in his sermon on the dead, writes that the memories of the departed were also celebrated with prayers on the anniversary day. Venerable Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, Book V, chapter 15: “They celebrated the memories of the dead with anniversary prayers, vigils, the praise of psalms, and Masses.” In Book III, chapter 2, he reports that at the cross which King Oswald had erected in England, the brothers of the Church of Hexham every year, on the day before the anniversary of Oswald’s death, continued through the night in vigils with abundant praise of psalms and were accustomed to offer the sacrifice of the sacred oblation for the salvation of his soul. See Onuphrius, *On the Rite of Burial*, chapter 10. Amalarius, *On the Offices of the Church*, Book III, final chapter: “The anniversary day is observed for the dead because we do not know how their condition is in the other life. Just as the anniversary of the saints is recalled to our memory in their honor for our benefit, so the anniversary of the dead is observed for their benefit and to fulfill our devotion, in the belief that we shall one day come to share in the company of the saints.” Durandus, *Rationale of the Divine Offices*, Book VII, chapter 35: “Some observe an anniversary for three reasons. First, so that the dead may pass from the years of calamity to the years of eternity, or to eternal life, which has no end and is like a year revolving upon itself; or because there is identity there and no variation is found. Second, because just as we celebrate the anniversary of the saints for their honor and our benefit, so we celebrate the anniversary of the dead for their benefit and our devotion. Third, the anniversary day is observed for the dead because, according to Augustine, we do not know what their condition is in the other life; and it is better that our benefit should remain to them than that it should be lacking.” Augustine, *On the Care to Be Had for the Dead*, final chapter; Gratian, *Decretum* 13, question 2, chapter “We Do Not Think.”

We mention this gathering for the following reason: we wish briefly to relate the patience of a certain brother, which shone forth under the presence of the entire congregation through his steadfast gentleness. For although the purpose of this work is directed elsewhere—namely, to set forth the sayings of Abba John, who, having abandoned the desert, had submitted himself to that coenobium with the utmost humility—we do not think it absurd to provide, without any circumlocution, a great edification for all who earnestly pursue virtue.

> **Note [Col. 1126C].** I believe this was not that John of Lycopolis who, filled with a prophetic spirit, foretold to the Emperor Theodosius his victories over the tyrants Maximus and Eugenius. Rufinus discusses him in Book II, chapter 1; Augustine, *City of God*, Book V, chapter 26; Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 43 and following; and Cassian, Book IV of the *Institutes*, chapter 23 and following, and again *Conference* 24, final chapter. That John is nowhere said to have passed from the eremitical life to the coenobitic life; rather, he is said to have died peacefully in the desert of the Thebaid, near Lyco, or Lycopolis. This must instead be another Abba John, whom we mentioned above on the authority of Sozomen (*Conference* 18, chapter 1), where he is said to have flourished with Abba Piammon near the city of Diolcos. Sozomen writes: “At that time Piammon and John presided over the most famous monasteries around Diolcos in Egypt. They discharged their priestly office with the greatest distinction—for they were presbyters—and with the highest reverence. God had granted John such power against illnesses and diseases that he healed many suffering from gout and those whose joints and limbs had been paralyzed.” This is Sozomen’s account. Palladius likewise writes in *Lausiac History*, chapter 73: “We also saw another man at Diolcos, named John, Father of monasteries, who likewise possessed great grace, the appearance of Abraham, and the beard of Aaron. He performed miracles and healings, and healed many paralytics and sufferers from gout.” Palladius says this after having discussed, in the preceding chapter, the presbyter Ammonas, whom Sozomen and others call Piammon. If, as reason suggests, we believe that Piammon, or Ammonas, is the same person in Sozomen, Palladius, and Cassian in the preceding Conference, where Cassian also records that he lived at Diolcos, it is consistent to conclude from the circumstances of place and the similarity of the narratives that John, to whom this Conference is attributed, was Piammon’s companion and contemporary. Cassian seems to have wished to imitate Sozomen, or Sozomen Cassian: for just as the former joined Abbots Piammon and John in his narrative, so Cassian placed one immediately after the other in these Conferences and introduced them in conversation. I also believe that he is the same John whom Cassian mentions in Book V of the *Institutes*, chapters 27 and 28, and likewise in *Conference* 14, chapters 4 and 7. It is no objection that there he is said to have been placed over a great coenobium and a multitude of brothers, just as Palladius calls him “Father of monasteries.” From this it follows that at that time he was a coenobite, not an anchorite—that is, he lived a common and coenobitic life, not a solitary one. But this John, with whom we are now concerned, is not said to have been superior or abbot of a coenobium; rather, after leaving the desert, he is said to have submitted himself with the utmost humility to Abba Paul’s coenobium and, while Paul was still alive, to have excelled among the other elders in singular virtue. For, as he himself testifies below, in chapter 3, he first became a coenobite and spent thirty years in the congregation of the coenobium. During that period it is believable that he had charge of many monks and monasteries, as the authors cited relate. Afterwards he withdrew into solitude, where he completed another twenty years in the anchoritic life. Finally, when he saw that some anchorites were falling away from their former fervor and austerity, he abandoned the desert, returned to the coenobium, and remained there. Thus he first passed from being a coenobite to an anchorite, and later was restored from being an anchorite to being a coenobite. Nevertheless, I do not deny, nor am I unaware, that many other holy anchorites and monks named John are listed both in the *Lives of the Fathers* and in the *Ecclesiastical Tables*. If anyone can show more plausibly that another John was the author of this Conference, I shall certainly not resist very strongly.]

In a vast courtyard, with that multitude of monks seated beneath the open sky in orderly ranks divided into groups of twelve, one of the brothers brought in the dish that had been assigned to him somewhat late. Taking advantage of this delay, the aforementioned Abba Paul, who was moving anxiously among the serving brothers, struck him with an outstretched hand, with his palm, in full view of everyone, so that the sound echoed even in the ears of those seated opposite, or at a considerable distance.

> **Note [Col. 1128C].** *Subdiale*, or *subdivale*: for one says both *sub dio* and *sub divo*, that is, beneath the open air and without a roof. Thus those monks and hermits of Egypt ate beneath the open sky; this is not very surprising, since they were safe from rain. For it is said that it never rains in Egypt, the land being watered and made fertile solely by the inundation of the Nile River. Pliny, Book V; Isidore, Book XIV, chapter 2.

He did this so that the young man’s patience might be displayed to all who were present and so that everyone who witnessed such a spectacle might be instructed by the example of his composure. How deliberate the elder’s action had been, the outcome proved. For the young man of memorable patience received it with such gentleness of spirit that not only did no word fall from his mouth, nor the slightest murmur appear in the silent movement of his lips, but even the modesty and tranquility of his face did not change, nor did its color alter in the least.
