This action seemed so astonishing not only to us, who had recently come from a monastery in Syria and had learned the virtue of this patience through examples so evident, but also to all who were not strangers to such practices, that through it even the greatest men received a special lesson: namely, that although a paternal correction had not disturbed his patience, not even the sight of so great a multitude had stained his face with any sign of shame.

## Chapter II. On the humility of Abba John

In this coenobium, then, we encountered a very old man named John. We judged that neither his words nor his humility, by which he surpassed all the saints, should be passed over in silence, knowing that he had flourished especially in this perfection. Humility is the mother of all virtues and the firmest foundation of the entire spiritual structure, yet it is completely absent from our institutions.

It is therefore no wonder that we cannot rise to the sublimity of those men who—not merely unable to remain under the discipline of a coenobium until old age—are content to endure the yoke of submission for scarcely two years before flying off immediately to the presumption of a harmful liberty.

> **Note [Col. 1128C].** Cassian is referring to himself and his companion Germanus, and seems to accuse them of a certain lightness or instability because they remained scarcely two years in that Bethlehem coenobium and, insufficiently tested and instructed in monastic discipline, flew off to foreign places where they would enjoy greater freedom and live almost according to their own will.

And even during that short time we submit ourselves to the authority of an elder only in some fashion, not according to the rule of strict discipline but according to the liberty of our own judgment, so that we seem not to be learning the fruit of patience but to be waiting for the time when we may obtain permission to act as we please.

When we had therefore seen this old man in Abba Paul’s coenobium, we first admired his age and the grace with which the man was endowed. Then, with our faces lowered toward the ground, we began to beg him to explain to us why, having abandoned the liberty of the desert and that exalted profession by which fame had celebrated him above the other men who followed the same way of life, he had preferred to submit to the yoke of a coenobium.

> **Note [Col. 1128C–D].** By the example and argument of this John, Saint Thomas teaches (*Summa theologica* II–II, question 189, article 8) that it is sometimes permissible to pass from a stricter religious life to a less strict one: “Someone may laudably pass from one religious order to another. First, through zeal for a more perfect religious life. Second, because a religious order has declined from its proper perfection—for example, if religious in a stricter order begin to live more negligently. In that case someone may laudably pass even to a lesser order, if it is better observed. Thus, in the Conferences of the Fathers, Abba John says of himself that he passed from the solitary life, which he had professed, to the lesser life of those who live in community, because the eremitical life had begun to decline and to be observed more loosely. Third, because of infirmity or weakness,” and so forth.

He, as though unequal to the anchoritic discipline and unworthy of the sublimity of so great a perfection, said that he had returned to the school of the younger men—if indeed he could even fulfill their practices according to the demands of their profession. When our persistent entreaty ruled out this humble answer, he finally began as follows.

## Chapter III. Abba John’s answer concerning why he had abandoned the desert

I do not merely reject or refuse the anchoritic discipline, which you marvel that I abandoned; rather, I embrace and accept it with every mark of reverence. After the thirty years that I had spent in the congregation of the coenobium,

> **Lipsius, in the margin:** *transieram* (“had passed through”) instead of *transeg eram* (“had spent”).

I rejoice that I completed another twenty years in it in such a way that among those who pursued it even moderately I was not altogether marked by sluggishness.

But because, once tasted, its purity was sometimes sullied by being interrupted with concern for bodily matters, it seemed more advantageous to return to the coenobium, so that the completion of the easier undertaking I had begun might proceed more readily, and there might be less danger in the difficulty of the higher profession I had presumed to undertake.

> **Note [Col. 1129B–C].** That is: it is better to be a devout coenobite than a bad or undevout anchorite. This comparison is the subject here. The statement is worth noting, since it gives the reason why one may sometimes pass from a stricter religious life, such as the eremitical or anchoritic life, to a less strict one, namely the coenobitic life, as was said above: specifically, because the stricter religious life has declined from its proper perfection and observance. For this reason Abba John says here that he passed from the desert to the coenobium: many of the hermits with whom he lived had at that time begun to fall away from their former fervor and continual contemplation and to live more loosely. He explains this more clearly in chapter 6.

For it is better to be found devout in a lesser profession than undevout in a greater one.

And therefore, if I should perhaps say something too elevated—or rather, something too free—I ask you to judge it not a fault of boasting but something drawn from my concern for your edification, because I do not think that anything of the truth should be withheld from you, who seek it so earnestly. I believe that some instruction can be given to you if, setting humility aside for a little while, I simply disclose the whole truth of my purpose. I trust that, among you, the freedom of my words will not incur the stigma of vainglory, nor, in my own conscience, will the suppression of truth incur the crime of falsehood.

## Chapter IV. The virtue of the aforementioned old man, which he practiced in the anchoritic discipline

If someone, delighted by the hidden places of the desert, was able to consign human society to oblivion and to say with Jeremiah, “You know that I did not desire the day of man” (Jeremiah 17:16),

> **Note [Col. 1129C–D].** Saint Jerome interprets “the day of man” either as the longer span of life or as the prosperous circumstances of this world. Others understand by “the day of man” human judgment, so that the meaning is: “I have not cared about the judgments of men,” as the Apostle says: “But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you, or by man’s day” (1 Corinthians 4:3)—that is, by human understanding, which is called “the day of man,” according to Saint Thomas in his commentary, or by human judgment. For, as Blessed Gregory says, *Moral Expositions*, Book I, chapter 20: “If the darkness of ignorance is without doubt the night of the heart, understanding is rightly called day.” Hence Paul also says: “One person judges one day to be better than another, while another judges every day alike” (Romans 14:5). It is as though he said plainly: one person understands certain things while leaving some aside, whereas another recognizes all things capable of being understood as they ought to be seen. So Gregory. The statement of Saint Jerome in Letter 26 is relevant here: “The first virtue of a monk is to despise the judgments of men and always to remember the Apostle’s saying: ‘If I were still trying to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ’” (Galatians 1:10). Others explain “the day of man” as the favor of men, which comes to the same thing. For since “day” may signify prosperity, just as “night” signifies adversity, “the day of man” means the approval, favor, and praise of men. Thus those anchorites and solitary monks could say with Jeremiah: “I did not desire the day of man”—that is, I did not seek the favor and praise of men, or even their companionship and intimacy.

I confess that, by the Lord’s grace, I either attained this or certainly strove to attain it. Thus, by the gracious gift of our Lord, I remember that I was frequently carried away in an ecstasy of this kind,

> **Note [Col. 1130C–D].** Dionysius gives the clearer construction: “I recall that I was frequently carried away into such raptures.” The “ecstasy of the mind,” which in Greek is *ekstasis* (ἔκστασις), is what is meant. Thus Saint Augustine often reads “in ecstasy” where the Psalms have “in an excess.” Writing on Psalm 67, he says: “Ecstasy is an excess of the mind. It sometimes occurs through fear, but at other times through a revelation and a separation of the mind from the bodily senses, so that what is to be shown may be shown to the spirit.” Saint Bernard, in his sermon on the *Song of Songs*, sermon 49, says: “There are two kinds of ecstasy in blessed contemplation: one in the understanding and the other in the affection; one in light and the other in fervor; one in knowledge and the other in devotion. A devout affection, a breast warmed by love, an infusion of holy devotion, and even a spirit filled with vehement zeal are not brought back from anywhere other than the wine-cellar. Whoever is granted to rise from prayer with an abundance of these things can speak truthfully, because ‘the King has brought me into the wine-cellar’” (Song of Songs 2:4). And elsewhere he says: “When the soul passes beyond itself—even if not beyond life, certainly beyond the sense of life—it is necessary that it no longer feel the temptation of life either. ‘Who will give me wings like a dove, and I will fly away and be at rest’” (Psalm 54:7). “Would that I might frequently fall into this death, so that I might escape the snares of death; that I might not feel the deadly allurements of a luxuriant life; that I might not be stunned by the sense of lust, the heat of greed, the goads of anger and impatience, or the anguish of anxieties and the burdens of cares. The soul dies the death of the righteous, so that no deceit may ensnare it and no wickedness delight it. It is a good death, which does not take life away but transfers it to something better.” These words of Saint Bernard harmonize beautifully with this passage. See more concerning ecstasy in Saint Thomas, I–II, question 8, article 3, and II–II, question 175.

so that I would forget that I was clothed in the burden of bodily frailty, and my mind would suddenly reject all external senses and be wholly exiled from all material things, so that neither my eyes nor my ears performed their proper functions. My spirit was so filled with divine meditations and spiritual contemplation

> **Note [Col. 1130D–1131C].** Those holy anchorites, occupied with spiritual joys and delights of the mind, partly forgot the body and bodily necessity. Thus Abba John did not remember in the evening whether he had eaten that day, and on the following day was uncertain whether he had broken his fast the previous day—that is, whether or not he had eaten. They also partly endured this bodily servitude with difficulty and therefore considered themselves happier the more rarely and briefly they could satisfy bodily necessity. Philo writes of those earliest Alexandrian monks: “Many, because of their eagerness for spiritual delights and contemplation, scarcely refreshed their bodies every fifth or sixth day.” Saint Athanasius likewise writes of Blessed Antony, who, whenever human nature compelled him to give his little body food or sleep, or to attend to some other bodily need, was overcome with extraordinary shame that such a small boundary of flesh should restrain so great a liberty of soul. For frequently, while sitting with the brothers, he would be distracted from the food placed before him by the memory of spiritual nourishment.

that often by evening I did not know whether I had eaten, and on the following day I was completely uncertain whether I had broken the previous day’s fast.

For this reason, the food for seven days—that is, seven pairs of *paximacia*—is placed separately on Saturday

> **Note [Col. 1131C].** There were two *paximatia*, or *paximacia*, assigned to each brother for his daily nourishment, as the ordinary measure or portion, according to the custom and rule of the elders, as has been stated more than once elsewhere.

in a *procherium*, that is, in a basket kept at hand, so that any omitted meal may not go unnoticed.

> **Note [Col. 1131C–D].** Cuychius notes that *procherium* means a basket or little hamper in which they stored the loaves. But since the Greek word *πρόχειρον* means whatever is at hand—for example, Plutarch calls *πρόχειρα σκεύη* vessels ready and necessary for use—Ciaconius plausibly conjectures that the reading should be *in prochiro*, an adjective meaning “in a hand-basket,” with a noun understood: “especially,” he says, “since there seems to be no etymological basis for *procherium* itself to contain the meaning ‘basket.’”

By this practice the error of that forgetfulness is also excluded, since the completed course of the week and the return of the solemnity of that day are indicated by the number of loaves having been used up. Thus the sacred festival day

> **Note [Col. 1131D].** Namely, Sunday, when they were accustomed to go together to church and receive the sacred Eucharist, as is stated in *Conference* 7, final chapter; *Conference* 18, chapter 15; and *Conference* 21, final chapter.

and the solemnity of the congregation cannot remain unknown to the solitary. Even if the ecstasy of mind mentioned above should happen to disturb this order, the amount of daily work, marking the number of days, nevertheless prevents error.

To pass over in silence the other virtues of the desert—for we are not dealing with their number and multitude, but with the end of solitude and the coenobium—I shall instead briefly explain the reasons why I preferred to leave it, which you also wished to learn. I shall touch briefly upon all those fruits of solitude that I have mentioned and that I would say must be set below more exalted merits in another respect.

## Chapter V. On the advantages of the desert

As long, then, as the small number of those who at that time lived in the desert, granting us liberty, allowed us to delight in the more expansive vastness of solitude, and as long as, in more remote places, we were very frequently carried away into those heavenly ecstasies,

> **Note [Col. 1131D–1132C].** See what we noted above concerning these matters. Richard of Saint Victor, *On Contemplation*, Book V, adds three ways by which someone is perfected in contemplation: through the expansion, elevation, or alienation of the mind. “The expansion of the mind,” he says, “occurs when the mind’s vision is spread more widely and sharpened more intensely, though it does not in any way exceed the limits of human effort. The elevation of the mind occurs when the liveliness of understanding, divinely illumined, transcends the boundaries of human effort, though it does not pass into alienation of the mind, so that what it sees is above itself and yet it does not wholly depart from its accustomed condition. The alienation of the mind occurs when the memory of present things slips away from the mind and, through a transformation brought about by divine action, it passes into a foreign condition, the lowest state of the soul with respect to human effort.” Those who deserve to be raised to the highest summit of this grace experience these three modes of contemplation. Thus far Richard.

and as long as the great influx of visiting brothers did not burden our senses with the strain of immense cares through the necessity of preparing hospitality, I pursued with insatiable desire and with all the ardor of my soul the tranquil solitude of the desert and that way of life which might be compared with the blessedness of angels.

But when, as I said, a greater number of brothers began to seek habitation in that solitude, and the liberty of the vast desert became constricted, this not only caused that fire of divine contemplation to grow cold but also hindered the mind in many ways with the bonds of bodily concerns. I chose to fulfill, as best I could, the purpose of this discipline rather than, in that exalted profession, become sluggish through the provision of bodily necessities.

Thus, even if that liberty and those spiritual ecstasies are denied me, I may nevertheless be consoled by completing the Gospel command, having utterly cast away concern for the following day; and whatever is taken from me of that contemplative sublimity may be compensated by this submission to obedience.

For it is wretched for someone to profess the discipline of any art or pursuit and yet not attain its perfection.

## Chapter VI. On the usefulness of the coenobium
Therefore [Note: [Col. 1132C] He touches upon several advantages of coenobitic life, on account of which he shows—quite properly and not without deliberation—that he returned to it. The first is freedom from and exemption from the cares and anxieties of procuring food, drink, and other necessities: for true coenobites leave this concern to their superiors and prelates, whereas solitaries must occupy and burden themselves with it. Hence St. Jerome, in that frequently cited letter to Eustochium, writes that the profession of poverty among the monks of his time was so strict that [Col. 1132D] no one was permitted even to ask for necessities; yet the diligence and vigilance of the superiors and leaders was so great that no one lacked anything necessary. “For,” he says, “no one is permitted to say: I have no tunic, no cloak, no mat woven from rushes; he regulates everything in such a way that no one asks for anything, and no one lacks anything.” Marianus, in his scholia, says: “Alternatively: so that no one asks for anything, and no one is without anything—that is, everyone has everything in abundance.” The interpreter (namely Erasmus) considers both readings false and immediately substitutes another in these words: “So that no one has what he might ask for.” Yet the first reading, which the majority of manuscripts contain, seems truer to me; and Jerome’s meaning is that no one asks for anything, since this is not permitted at all, while provision is made for everyone by the superiors of the monasteries in such a way that no one lacks anything. Thus Marianus. But with due respect to him, the other reading substituted by Erasmus seems to me not only easier and clearer, but also more genuine and appropriate: “so that no one has what he might ask for,” or, with correct syntax and word order, “no one has anything that he might ask for.” This follows immediately from what precedes: if the superior of the monastery regulates everything properly—that is, provides and takes thought for all necessities—none of the monks will have occasion to ask for anything. Nevertheless, Marianus’s reading can also be explained without incongruity so as to reach the same meaning, as follows: “No one asks for anything” (that is, requests something), “and no one lacks anything”—supply: a tunic, a cloak, and other necessities—the superior providing everything before it is requested. But this has been added only in passing, because of the obscurity of the passage. The second advantage is flight from *cenodoxy*, or vainglory, whose greatest danger threatens the solitary. Hence St. Jerome (Epistle 4): “In solitude,” he says, “pride easily creeps in; and if he has fasted for a little while and has not seen a human being, he thinks himself a person of some importance; and, forgetting who he is and whence and whither he came, inwardly in his heart and outwardly with his tongue he wanders.” The third advantage is the subjection and mortification of one’s own will, which he touches upon toward the end of this chapter. It will, however, be worthwhile to set down here more fully and extensively these and other advantages of coenobitic and communal life as St. Basil recounts them (in *The Longer Rules*, chapter 7). For, when the question was proposed whether it is more expedient for one who has decided to leave the world to live a solitary life apart from others, or rather with companions of the same counsel and purpose, he answers without hesitation as follows:

“I understand that it is more useful for many things if several live together in one and the same place. First, none of us is so sufficient in himself that he can adequately provide the things necessary for life; for in seeking these things we see that each in turn needs the assistance of others. This, namely, that we should in turn need one another’s services, was ordained by our Maker God for this purpose: that by exchanging duties among ourselves, by giving and receiving, we might have this reason for mutual union.

“Moreover, in withdrawing from others into this kind of life, there is also this disadvantage: no one easily understands that he is sinning, since he has no one from whom he may receive gentle and kindly admonition and correction. Thus the saying applies to him: ‘Woe to him who is alone; for when he falls, he has no one to lift him up’ (Ecclesiastes 4). There is also this further point: those who have gathered together in one place in greater numbers can simultaneously satisfy more commands. The opposite is true of one who is alone: while he carries out one task, he is hindered by another. For example, if he visits a sick person, he cannot receive a guest; nor can he retain his attention on a task if he is occupied with dividing and distributing the necessities of life for use—especially when the brothers must necessarily be detained for a longer time in carrying out these ministries.

“And if we are all called in one hope, are one body, and have Christ as our head, while each of us is in turn a member of the others, surely, unless we agree to this—that we should be joined and fitted together among ourselves in the Holy Spirit, after the likeness of one body, and that no one should establish for himself a life separated from communion with the others—how will we be able, amid such dispersal and, as it were, tearing apart, to provide mutual harmony and mutual services among the very members? For in such separation circumstances do not permit anyone to rejoice with one who rejoices or to sympathize with one who suffers, since separation makes one person entirely unaware even of the condition of the other.

“Furthermore, since no single person is capable of receiving all spiritual gifts, it comes about in a shared life that the gift peculiar to each becomes common also to the other companions: ‘To one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another faith, to another prophecy, to another the gift of healings,’ and so forth (1 Corinthians 12). Whoever possesses any one of these gifts possesses it no more for his own sake than for that of others. [Col. 1134A] Therefore, in a society of life, whatever spiritual efficacy exists in one person must pass through all together.

“Thus the person who lives apart from others perhaps possesses one particular gift; and he makes that very gift useless because he exercises nothing but keeps it buried within himself. Conversely, wherever the fellowship of many flourishes, each person enjoys what is his own, and likewise receives from what belongs to others as though it were his own.

“Add that this kind of solitary life is accompanied and beset by another danger besides those already mentioned: first and greatest, that the one who lives it may flatter himself as though he had already plainly attained perfection. Since he will have no one there who can judge what he does, he will imagine that he has performed everything to the fullest (see Jerome Platus, book 1, *On the Good of Religion*, chapter 39). From this it will follow that, since he has continually restrained and, as it were, enclosed within himself the disposition of soul he possesses toward virtue, he will neither understand what he lacks nor see any progress he makes in the virtues, since he has removed from himself on every side all material for exercising the commandments. For by what means will he give evidence of his humility if he has no one before whom he can declare himself humbler? What proof will he give of his compassion toward others, cut off as he is from the fellowship of many and having absolutely no dealings with anyone?”

These and more Basil presents rather obscurely, and the interpreter renders them too verbosely (see also Peter Damian, book 6, letter 12). Concerning the same comparison of coenobitic and solitary life, one may see Turrecremata treating the matter at length in his commentary on the Rule of blessed Benedict, where he begins as follows:

“Although both kinds of life, that of anchorites as well as that of coenobites, are praiseworthy, nevertheless the kind of life of coenobites seems to excel in three respects: in reward—and this after death; in security—and this in death; and in manifold benefit—and this in life.”

He then explains what these benefits are. Yet, so that these matters may be understood more accurately and clearly, since it has elsewhere been said that solitary and anchoritic life is more sublime and more perfect than common and coenobitic life, and since St. Augustine says in his book *On the Work of Monks* (chapter 23) that those are holier who, separated from the sight of human beings, allow no one access to them and live in great concentration upon prayers, it seems necessary to insert here the explanation and truly golden teaching of St. Thomas. Treating this question (*Summa theologica* II–II, question 188, article 8)—“Whether religious life among those living in community is more perfect than that of those leading a solitary life”—he answers in this manner:

“It must be said that solitude, like poverty itself, is not the very essence of perfection, but an instrument of perfection. Hence, in the *Conferences of the Fathers* (Conference 1, chapter 7), Abba Moses says that solitude is to be pursued for purity of heart, just as fasting and other things of this kind are.

“But it is manifest that solitude is not an instrument suited to action, but to contemplation, according to the saying of Hosea 2: ‘I will lead her into solitude and will speak to her heart.’ Hence it does not suit religious orders that are directed toward works of the active life, whether bodily or spiritual, except perhaps for a time, following the example of Christ, who, as it is said in Luke 6, went out alone onto the mountain to pray and spent the night in prayer to God. It does suit religious orders directed toward contemplation.

“It must nevertheless be considered that whatever is solitary ought to be sufficient unto itself. Now that is sufficient unto itself which lacks nothing belonging to the nature of perfection; and therefore solitude suits the contemplative person who has already reached perfection.

“This happens in two ways. In one way, through a purely divine gift, as is evident in John the Baptist, who was filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb; hence, while he was still a child, he was in the deserts, as is said in Luke 1. In another way, through the exercise of virtuous action, according to Hebrews 5: ‘Solid food belongs to the perfect, to those who through habit have their senses trained to distinguish good and evil.’

“For the exercise of this kind of activity, a person is helped by the society of others in two ways. First, as regards the intellect, so that he may be instructed in the things that are to be contemplated. Hence Jerome says to the monk Rusticus: ‘I would like you to have a sacred fellowship, and not teach yourself.’ Second, as regards the affections, so that harmful emotions may be restrained by the example and correction of others; for, as Gregory says in the *Moral Expositions*, book 30, chapter 23, commenting on the words ‘To whom he gave a gift in solitude’: ‘What benefit is bodily solitude if solitude of heart is lacking?’ [Col. 1135C] Therefore social life is necessary for the exercise of perfection.

“Solitude, however, suits those who are already perfect. Hence Jerome says to the monk Rusticus: ‘Do we condemn the solitary life? Certainly not, since we have often praised it. But we want soldiers of this kind to go forth from the training ground of monasteries—men whom the harsh beginnings of the desert will not frighten, who have given proof of their manner of life over a long period.’

“Therefore, just as what is already perfect excels that which is being exercised toward perfection, so the life of solitaries, if rightly undertaken, excels social life. But if such a life is undertaken without previous training, it is exceedingly dangerous, unless divine grace supplies what is acquired by exercise in others, as is evident in the blessed Anthony and Benedict.”

Thus far the Angelic Doctor—and wholly angelically. In his response to the fifth argument he also explains sharply and learnedly Aristotle’s statement in *Politics* 1, chapter 2: “The solitary person is either a beast or a god.” For if someone loves solitude because of impatience and harshness of spirit, or from despair, or from hatred of obedience and love of his own will, like those Sarabaites discussed in the preceding conference (chapter 7), he is like a beast; but if he seeks solitude so that he may be wholly free for divine contemplation and cling to it, then he becomes wholly divine and like God.

From these things it is clear which life excels the other and ought rather to be chosen, the eremitical or the coenobitic. For solitary life is superior in itself, if it is rightly undertaken by the perfect, for whom it is properly suited; but coenobitic life is more convenient and useful for most people, and more suitable for attaining perfection.]

I shall now briefly explain the great advantages I enjoy in this manner of life [Col. 1133A]. You may judge, from the account arranged here, whether the gains of that solitude can be compensated for by these benefits [Col. 1134A]; and from it one may also determine whether I preferred to be confined within these narrow limits of the coenobium out of distaste for, or out of desire for, that solitary purity [Col. 1135A].

In this manner of life, there is no provision for the day’s work, no preoccupation with selling or buying, no unavoidable annual anxiety about bread, no concern for bodily necessities—for not only one’s own needs but also those required for the use of the many who arrive must be prepared—and, finally, no arrogance arising from human praise, which, in God’s sight more polluted than all these things, often renders even the great labors of the desert fruitless.

But, leaving aside the waves of spiritual exaltation and the destructive dangers of *cenodoxy* in that anchoritic discipline, let us return to this general burden of all, namely, the common concern of preparing food. It has now so far exceeded the standard—not to mention that ancient rigor which knew nothing at all of the use of oil—that it has not been content even with the relaxation of our own time, in which [Note: [Col. 1135D] A *sextarius* is said to be one-sixth of a *congius*, a measure used by the ancients for both liquids and dry goods. It holds a pound and a half, or eighteen ounces—that is, two *cotylae*, which are also called *heminae*. For each *congius* contains six *sextarii*, while twelve *heminae* are equivalent to one *congius*, since two *heminae* complete a *sextarius*. Hence one *sextarius* of oil, which sufficed for a year to receive and feed guests, as is said here (Epiphanius, *On Weights and Measures*; Alexander of Alexandria, book 2, chapter 20). A *modius* is a kind of measure containing sixteen *sextarii*, according to Suidas twenty-six pounds and eight ounces; half of it is called a *semodius*. Lentils were discussed in book 4 of the *Institutes*, chapter 20.] the duties of all the year’s nourishment were fulfilled with one sextarius of oil and likewise one *modius* of lentils prepared for the use of visitors, whereas now the need for provisions can scarcely be met with a double or triple *modius* [Col. 1136A].

And in some people the force of this harmful relaxation has increased so greatly [Note: [Col. 1136B] Cassianus gives an example of this ancient frugality and marvelous abstinence observed among them in *Conference* 8, chapter 1, where he recalls that he and his brother were entertained by Abba Serenus with such delicacies:

“For instead of brine,” he says, “over which a drop of oil was usually poured and which was added to the daily meal, he mixed in a little fish sauce and poured over it somewhat more oil than usual. For everyone who is about to eat drips that drop of oil in every day—not so that he may perceive some sweetness of it in his throat, since the quantity is so small that it scarcely suffices even to touch, much less to pass through, the passage of the throat and jaws—but so that by this practice he may blunt the boasting of the heart which, because of stricter abstinence, habitually creeps in gently and secretly, and may dull the goads of pride. For the more secretly abstinence itself is practiced, and the less it is accomplished before human witnesses, the more subtly it never ceases to tempt the one who conceals it.” Thus far Cassianus, suitably applied to the understanding of this passage.] that, mixing vinegar with brine, they no longer add that single drop of oil which our predecessors, who pursued the practices of the desert with greater virtue of abstinence, were accustomed to pour in solely to repel *cenodoxy*, but [Note: [Col. 1136C] “For the sake of salts,” that is, for delicacies and luxurious fare. Thus these more lax and lukewarm monks, contrary to the custom of the ancients, used a double dish, and consumed two foods differing—or distinguished—from one another in their particular flavor, as is said here: namely, brine mixed with vinegar and sprinkled with a drop of oil, and cheese likewise covered with oil, enjoying both under the pleasure of a single flavor, namely that of oil [Col. 1136D]. The former of these, he says, could have sufficed for each meal along with *paximatia*, or loaves, specifically one pound in weight.] they break up Egyptian cheese “for the sake of salts” and pour over it more oil than necessary; and thus they consume under the pleasure of a single flavor two foods differing in their distinctive taste, foods which, taken separately and at different times, could have most agreeably refreshed the monks.

Indeed, the possession of material things—this use of *alkēs chrēsis* (ἀλκῆς χρῆσις) [Note: [Col. 1136D] *Alkē* (ἀλκή) properly signifies assistance, strength, or vigor; hence *alkēeis* (ἀλκήεις), “strong” or “vigorous.” Here it is used for the support of life: *chrēsis* (χρῆσις), that is, “use.” Ciaconius, moreover, reads only *ktēsis* (κτῆσις), a word signifying dominion and possession of something, opposed to *aktēmosynē* (ἀκτημοσύνη), that is, complete freedom from and lack of all possession, which monks profess, as stated above. The Basel edition and most manuscripts omit both Greek words.]—has so greatly increased that even a cloak, something I cannot mention without embarrassment [Note: [Col. 1136D] See the note on the cloak in book 5 of the *Institutes*, chapter 30. St. Jerome mentions it among other monastic garments in his letter to Eustochium and in the *Life of Hilarion*.], has begun to be kept by anchorites in their cells under the pretext of hospitality and receiving guests [Col. 1136B].

I shall say nothing of those matters by which the astonished soul, always intent upon spiritual contemplations, is burdened in a special way: the assembling of brothers, the duties of receiving and accompanying them, mutual visits, and the endless concern caused by various conversations and occupations. Even when the time comes in which these impediments appear to cease, expectation itself keeps the mind tense through the continual recurrence of its customary unrest [Col. 1137A].

Thus the freedom of anchoritic life, hindered by such bonds, does not reach, by an unobstructed ascent, that ineffable joyfulness of heart, and it loses the fruit of the eremitical profession. If that fruit is denied me now, situated as I am amid assembly and crowds, at least the repose of soul and tranquillity of heart, freed from all occupations, will not be lacking. Unless this too is available to those who dwell in solitude, they will indeed endure the labors of anchoritic life, but they will be deprived of its fruit, which is acquired only through a tranquil stability of mind [Col. 1137B].

Finally, even if, situated in the coenobium, something of that purity of heart is diminished for me, I shall be content with the compensation of the Gospel command alone—a command certainly not to be placed below all those fruits of the desert: namely, that I should think nothing of tomorrow and, subject to the abbot until the end, seem in some measure to imitate him of whom it is said: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Philippians 2); and that I may deserve humbly to say his words: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father” (John 6).

### CHAPTER VII. Inquiry concerning the fruit of the coenobium or of solitude

[Col. 1137C]

Germanus: Since it is clear that you have touched not merely upon the beginnings of both professions, as many have, but have climbed to their very summits, we wish to learn what the end of the coenobite and what the end of the hermit are. For no one can doubt that anyone could discuss these matters either more faithfully or more fully than one who, having attained both forms of perfection through long practice and experience as his teacher, can explain their merit and end with truthful instruction.

### CHAPTER VIII. Response

Joannes: I could have stated categorically that it is impossible for one and the same person to be perfect in both professions, were I not held back by the example of a very few. It is indeed a great thing to find someone consummate in either of them; how much more arduous it is to perfect both fully, and how nearly—as I may put it—impossible for a human being, is evident. Yet if this should ever occur, it cannot immediately be reduced to a general rule. For the universal rule must be proposed not on the basis of the smallest part—that is, from consideration of the few—but concerning those things that lie within the capacity of many, indeed of all [Col. 1138B]. But what is obtained only very rarely and by very few, and exceeds the possibility of ordinary virtue, as though granted beyond the condition and nature of human frailty, must be separated from general precepts and presented not so much as an example as a miracle. Therefore I shall briefly explain what you ask according to the modest measure of my understanding.

[Note: [Col. 1137C] St. Jerome bears witness to the following concerning the Egyptian coenobites and their imitators (Epistle 22): “Their first rule of association is to obey their superiors and to do whatever they command.” Cassianus, speaking of the prefect of novices in book 4 of the *Institutes*, chapter 8, says: “His principal concern and chief instruction will be this: that the younger man whom he has introduced may thereafter be able to ascend even to the heights of supreme perfection. He must first teach him to conquer his own wills; and, diligently and carefully exercising him in these matters, he will deliberately make a point of always commanding him to do what he perceives to be contrary to his spirit. For, instructed by many experiments, they teach that a monk, and especially a younger one, cannot even restrain the desire of his own pleasure unless he has first learned, through obedience, to mortify his own will” (see Conferences 3 and 4).]

The end of the coenobite is to mortify and crucify all his own wills, and, according to the saving command of evangelical perfection, to think nothing of tomorrow (Matthew 6). It is absolutely certain that this perfection can be fulfilled by no one except a coenobite. The prophet Isaiah describes and blesses such a man, praising him in these words:

[Note: [Col. 1137D] Citing this passage, Turrecremata says: “In this authority the Lord, through the prophet, describes the end or perfection of monastic or coenobitic discipline, and its fruit or reward. The end consists in three things. First, in turning away from sins by which rest is violated, designated by observance of the sabbath. Hence he says: ‘If you turn your foot away from the sabbath’—that is, if you do not violate rest of mind—which, as the Gloss says, is to be celebrated at all times. Second, in denial of one’s own will, when he says: ‘You shall not do your own will.’ Third, in restraining the tongue: ‘so that you do not speak a word,’ namely an evil word, against God or one’s neighbor [Col. 1138C]. He touches upon a twofold fruit of coenobitic life: one in the present, namely delight in divine consolations, when he says: ‘Then you shall delight in the Lord’; the other in the future life, namely the consolation of eternal happiness, when he says: ‘I will raise you above the heights of the earth, and I will feed you with the inheritance of Jacob your father.’”]

“If you turn your foot away from the sabbath, from doing your will on my holy day, and glorify him, while you do not follow your own ways, and your own will is not found, so that you speak a word, then you shall delight in the Lord, and I will raise you above the heights of the earth, and I will feed you with the inheritance of Jacob your father” (Isaiah 58). For the mouth of the Lord has spoken.

[Note: [Col. 1138C] Precisely so, and in almost the same words, St. Jerome speaks concerning the passage in Jeremiah: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth” (Lamentations 3):

“The perfection of Christ’s soldiers,” he says, “is to have the mind stripped of all earthly affairs, according to the saying of the Apostle: ‘No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs,’ and so forth (1 Timothy 6), and, insofar as human weakness permits, to unite it with Christ. The good hermits and monks who are bound by the vow of monastic discipline strive to imitate this form of life; but it is rare, and this perfection is granted by God to very few. For he is truly and not partially perfect who sustains with equal greatness of soul both the squalor of solitude in the desert and the weaknesses of the brothers in the coenobium. It is therefore difficult to find anyone consummate in every respect in both professions, since neither can the anchorite attain contempt and deprivation of material things, nor can the coenobite attain theoretical purity in its entirety.”

Thus St. Jerome, beautifully agreeing with the teaching of this abbot. The words of Dionysius the Areopagite also apply here (*Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 6), cited above (*Conference* 18, chapter 5), where he says that monks were called by the apostles from their undivided and singular life, which, through holy combinations and gatherings of divisible affections into one, advances toward divine unity and singular perfection [Col. 1139C]—that is, because, having abandoned divisible and temporal things, they strive to please the Monad, that is, the Divinity alone. In this sense, we said that the name “monk” properly belongs only to hermits and solitaries.]

But the perfection of the hermit is to have the mind stripped of all earthly things and, insofar as human weakness permits, to unite it with Christ. The prophet Jeremiah describes such a man when he says: “Blessed is the man who has borne the yoke from his youth;” [Note: [Col. 1139C] Ordinary Gloss: “With God, not mixed up with the turmoil of affairs and desires.”] “he will sit alone and be silent” [Note: [Col. 1139C] Gloss: “From all the clamor of the world.”], “because he has lifted himself above himself” [Note: [Col. 1139C] Gloss: “By despising earthly things and aspiring to heavenly things. For, Augustine says, by good desire we are lifted up to God.” Thus far the Gloss. It seems to me that three things are commended here in the monk: quiet of mind and body, signified by sitting alone; silence of the mouth, when it says, “and he will be silent”; and the pursuit of contemplation, by which he is raised above himself.] (Lamentations 3).

The Psalmist likewise says: “I have become like a pelican of the wilderness. I have watched, and have become like a sparrow alone upon the roof” (Psalm 101).

Unless each of them reaches the end which we have declared to belong to his respective profession, the one vainly seeks the discipline of the coenobium and the other that of anchoritic life. Neither has fulfilled the virtue of his profession.

### CHAPTER IX. On consummate and true perfection

[Note: [Col. 1139C] Ciaconius corrected this from the Vatican manuscripts, since previously most copies, including the Plantinian edition, erroneously read *meris* (μερὶς) or *meritikē* (μεριτική). The correct form is *merikos* (μερικός), “partial,” “halved,” or “imperfect.” Thus, in Conference 13, chapter 5, Abba Chaeremon teaches that the gentile philosophers possessed only a certain *merikē* (μερική) or *meris* (μερίς), that is, a small portion of chastity [Col. 1139D].]

But this is *merikē* (μερική), that is, a perfection not complete and consummate in all respects, but a part of perfection. Perfection is therefore rare and granted by God to very few. For he is truly and not partially perfect (the words of St. Jerome cited above) who sustains with equal greatness of soul both the squalor of solitude in the desert and the weaknesses of the brothers in the coenobium. It is therefore difficult to find anyone completely consummate in both professions, since the anchorite cannot attain *aktēmosynēn* (ἀκτημοσύνην), that is, contempt and deprivation of material things, nor can the coenobite attain [Note: [Col. 1139D] Here again *theorica* is used for *theoretica* in Cassianus, as also in St. Jerome, as mentioned above (*Conference* 1, chapter 2; *Conference* 14, chapter 2).] theoretical purity in its entirety, although I know that Abba Moses, Paphnutius, and the two Macarii possessed both perfectly.

They were so perfect in both professions that, although they withdrew beyond all the inhabitants of the desert and fed insatiably upon the secrecy of solitude, and, insofar as it depended upon them, by no means sought human company, they nevertheless endured the crowds and weaknesses of those who flocked to them in such a way that, when an innumerable multitude of brothers gathered around them for the sake of visitation or departure, they tolerated the almost continual disturbance of receiving them with immovable patience. One would have thought that throughout their entire lives they had learned or practiced nothing else than to serve the common needs of those who arrived. Thus it was uncertain to everyone in which profession their greater diligence was displayed: whether in that eremitical purity or in this communal life, and in which their greatness of soul was more wonderfully adapted [Col. 1140B].

### CHAPTER X. On those who seek the desert while imperfect

[Note: [Col. 1139D] St. Jerome seems to sketch such people, at least in certain features, in Epistle 4, to the monk Rusticus:

“Some,” he says, “with their shoulders raised high and croaking within themselves I know not what, and with their eyes fixed in astonishment upon the ground, weigh out swelling words, so that if you added a herald you would think that a prefecture was advancing. There are those who, through the dampness of their cells, immoderate fasts, weariness of solitude, and excessive reading—while these things resound in their ears by day and by night—are turned toward melancholy and need the remedies of Hippocrates more than our admonitions.”

Thus St. Jerome. Nor are those monks very different from them concerning whom Evagrius writes the following (*Ecclesiastical History*, book 1, chapter 21):

“Men and women hide themselves in a solitude boiling with heat; and, while only those members which serve natural necessity are covered, they expose the rest of the body naked to immense cold and burning heat from the sun, despising heat and cold alike. In addition, having completely rejected the foods on which human beings usually feed, they graze upon the earth; hence they are called *boskoi* (βόσκοι), that is, ‘feeders.’ From it alone they obtain their food, to such an extent that in time they become like beasts, since they differ from other human beings in bodily appearance and disposition of soul. And if by chance they see human beings, they immediately flee; and if anyone pursues them, they either escape by the swiftness of their feet or hide themselves in places concealed in the earth, which are exceedingly difficult to approach.”]

Some, however, become so savage through the prolonged silence of solitude that they utterly dread human society; and whenever, through a visit from the brothers, they withdraw even slightly from the secrecy of their retreat, they burn with conspicuous anguish of mind and evident signs of faintheartedness. This is especially accustomed to happen to those who, not perfectly trained in coenobia and not having their former vices thoroughly purged, transfer themselves to solitary life through an immature desire [Col. 1141A]. They are always imperfect and fragile in both respects, bending wherever the breeze of agitation drives them.

For just as they become impatiently heated by the company or interruption of the brothers, so, when they remain in solitude, they cannot endure the very desolation of the silence they have sought [Note: [Col. 1142D] That is, its duration, length, and burdensomeness.]. They do not even know the reason for which solitude ought to be desired or sought; instead, they think that the whole virtue and substance of this profession consists in avoiding the company of the brothers and merely shunning and detesting the sight of human beings.

[Note: [Col. 1140C] Hence St. Jerome writes in that same letter: “I want soldiers of this kind to go forth from the training ground of monasteries—men whom the harsh beginnings of the desert will not frighten, who have given proof of their manner of life over a long period; who have been the least of all, so that they might become the first of all; whom neither hunger nor satiety has ever overcome; who rejoice in poverty; whose clothing, speech, face, gait, and teaching are instruction in the virtues,” and so forth.

Cassianus, book 5 of the *Institutes*, chapter 36: “We hastened, urged on by the praise of all, to examine with a most discerning mind another order, considered more excellent, namely that of the anchorites. For these, after dwelling for a very long time in coenobia, and having been carefully instructed in every rule of patience and discernment, and having likewise acquired the virtues of humility and nakedness, and having almost completely destroyed the totality of their vices, enter the deepest recesses of the desert in order to engage in the most terrible battles with demons.

“And again, in book 8 of the *Institutes*, chapter 17: ‘The desert ought to be sought by those who are perfect and cleansed of every vice. They should enter it after their vices have been thoroughly burned away in the fellowship of the brothers—not as a refuge from faintheartedness, but for the sake of divine contemplation and the desire for a higher vision, which can be attained by the perfect only in solitude.’

“St. Benedict also (chapter 1 of the Rule) wisely shows who should be called true anchorites, and who should be judged suited and qualified for this kind of life: namely, those who have learned, not through the novice’s fervor of conversion (Turrecremata’s commentary), but through long experience in the monastery, to fight against the strongest and most cunning warrior, the devil, with the comfort of many—that is, with the assistance of others, such as the teaching, example, and prayers of the brothers—and who, well trained, are able, from the fraternal battle line—that is, from the congregation and fellowship of brother-combatants—to proceed to the single combat of the desert, already secure without consolation, and, with God’s help, to fight against the temptations of the flesh, the world, and the devil by their own hand or arm—that is, by their own virtue and strength.”

Here Turrecremata adduces the teaching of St. Thomas reported above (on chapter 6), in which he teaches whom solitary life suits and how dangerous it is for the unlearned, inexperienced, and not yet sufficiently practiced in spiritual warfare to undertake solitary and eremitical life.]

### CHAPTER XI. Inquiry concerning the remedy for those who quickly leave the coenobia

[Col. 1141B]

Germanus: What remedy, then, can be provided either for us or for others who share the same weakness and misery [Lipsius, in the margin: “measure”], who, only superficially trained in the cenobitic disciplines, began to desire dwelling in solitude before all vices had been expelled? Or by what means can we attain steadfastness of undisturbed mind and the immovable firmness of patience, when we have prematurely abandoned the very schools and training ground of this discipline—the monastery—in which our beginnings ought to have been fully instructed and perfected? How, then, while now living alone, shall we attain the perfection of endurance and patience? Or how will the conscience, which tests our inner movements, discover whether these virtues are present or absent in us, lest perhaps, because we are separated from human company and provoked by none of its irritations, we be deceived by a false estimate and believe that we possess immovable tranquillity of mind?

## CHAPTER XII. John’s reply: How a solitary can recognize his vices

Joannes: For those who sincerely seek medicine, remedies for healing cannot be lacking from that truest physician of souls—especially for those who have not despised their illnesses [Note: That is, the diseases and weaknesses of the soul. For, as has been said elsewhere, *valetudo* is an ambiguous term.] through despair or neglect, nor concealed the dangers of their wounds, nor rejected the medicine of repentance with presumptuous minds, but who, for the ailments contracted through ignorance, error, [Col. 1141D] or necessity, have at last fled to the heavenly physician with humility and caution.

Therefore we must understand that, if we withdraw into solitude or secluded places while our vices are not yet cured, only their effects are restrained; their inclinations are not extinguished. For the root of all sins, which has not been uprooted, lies hidden within us—indeed, it even spreads—and we discover that it is still alive in us by the following signs.

For example: When, living in solitude, we receive the arrival of brothers, or even their very brief stay, with a certain anxiety of our agitated spirit, let us know that the most vigorous fuel of impatience still exists within us. But when we hope for the arrival of some brother, and, if he is delayed for a little while by some necessity, silent indignation blames his excessive tardiness, and the anxiety of prolonged expectation disturbs our mind, then the examination of our conscience proves that the vices of anger and sadness still remain in us.

Likewise, if a brother asks us either for a book to read or for any other object to use, and his request saddens us, or our refusal repels him, there can be no doubt that we are still fettered by the snares of avarice, or love of money (*philargyria*).

If the recollection of a woman is brought before us either by a sudden thought or by the sequence of a sacred reading, and we feel ourselves struck by a certain stimulation through it, let us know that the heat of fornication has not yet been extinguished in our members.

But if even the slightest elation concerning the comparison between our own strictness and another’s laxity assails our mind, it is certain that we have been corrupted by the dreadful disease of pride.

When, therefore, we detect these signs of vices in our heart, let us plainly recognize that what is lacking in us is not the inclination toward sin, but only its effect. These passions, whenever we mingle again with human society, immediately emerging from the caverns of our senses, prove that they did not arise for the first time when they broke out, but were then at last revealed because they had long lain hidden.

Thus the solitary also detects, by certain signs, that the roots of each vice remain firmly planted within him—provided that he has sought not to display his purity before human beings, but to present it inviolate before the sight of Him from whom none of the heart’s secrets can remain hidden.

## CHAPTER XIII. The question: How one who entered solitude without purging his vices can be healed

Germanus: We have understood clearly and openly the arguments by which the signs of our weaknesses are gathered, and the method for distinguishing our illnesses—that is, how the vices concealed within us can be detected. Daily experience and the long-continued movements of our thoughts show us all these things exactly as they have been described.

It remains, then, that just as the proofs and causes of the illnesses have been disclosed to us in the clearest discourse, so also the remedy of healing should be shown. For no one can doubt that the one who has first discovered the causes and origins of evil illnesses, as the conscience of the sick bears witness, can most rightly discuss their remedies.

Thus, although your teaching has exposed the hidden wounds within us, so that we dare to hope for something even concerning their remedies—for such an evident disclosure of the illness promises hope of a cure—we nevertheless collapse once more in destructive despair. For since, as you say, the beginning of salvation is first acquired in communities, and no one can be healthy in solitude except those whom the medicine of monasteries has first healed, perhaps we who left the monastery imperfect will never be able to become perfect in the desert.

## CHAPTER XIV. John’s reply concerning their medicine

Joannes: For those concerned about the healing of their illnesses, a saving remedy cannot be lacking. Therefore, just as the signs of each vice are detected, so its remedies must also be sought.

For just as we have said that the vices of human society are not absent from solitaries, so we do not deny that the practices of virtue and the instruments of healing can also be available to all who are separated from human society.

When, therefore, each person has discovered by the signs mentioned above that he is being attacked by disturbances of impatience or anger, he should always exercise himself through opposing challenges [Note: As Blessed Gregory says (*Homily 35 on the Gospels*), “The darts that are foreseen strike less severely; and we bear the evils of the world more tolerably if we arm ourselves against them with the shield of foreknowledge.” For this reason Christ foretold future persecutions carefully, especially to the apostles, so that when they occurred they would neither be scandalized nor troubled. “I have told you these things,” he says, “so that you may not be scandalized: They will expel you from the synagogues,” and so forth (John 16). To the same point is directed St. Chrysostom’s homily *On Avarice*: “In prosperity,” he says, “expect adversity. In calm, expect the storm; in health, expect illness; in riches, expect poverty and beggary. Remember,” says Scripture (Ecclesiasticus 18), “the time of famine in the time of abundance, and beggary and want in the days of wealth. If you are disposed in this way, you will administer riches with great sobriety; and, should poverty occur, you will endure it most courageously. For an unexpected evil will disturb the mind when it occurs. But what was expected, if it happens, causes little disturbance.”], and, setting before himself various kinds of insults and losses as though inflicted upon him by another, accustom his mind to submit with perfect humility to everything that wickedness can inflict.

Frequently setting before himself every kind of hardship and intolerable treatment, he should continually meditate, with complete contrition of heart, on the gentleness with which he ought to meet them. Thus, looking toward the sufferings of all the saints and of the Lord himself, and declaring that every kind not only of insult but also of punishment is inferior to his merits, he will prepare himself to endure every kind of pain.

Whenever he is recalled by some invitation to gatherings of the brothers—a circumstance that can scarcely, or only rarely, occur to even the strictest inhabitants of the desert—and discovers that his mind has been silently disturbed even by trivial matters, he should immediately reproach himself, as a most severe censor of hidden movements, with those harsh kinds of insults by which he exercised himself daily in meditation toward perfect endurance. Rebuking and reproving himself, he should address himself as follows:

“Are you that good man, then, who, while exercising yourself in that training ground of your solitude, confidently presumed that you would overcome every evil with complete steadfastness? You who, when you had just proposed to yourself not only the greatest bitterness of insults but even intolerable punishments, believed yourself strong enough and immovable against every storm?

“How has that invincible patience of yours been pierced by the utterance of the lightest word? How has the slightest breeze shaken your house, which you had built, as you imagined, with such a massive structure upon that most solid rock?

“Where is that which, desiring war in peacetime and trusting in empty confidence, you proclaimed: ‘I am ready, and I am not disturbed’ (Psalm 118)? And with the prophet you often said: ‘Test me, Lord, and try me; burn my kidneys and my heart’ (Psalm 25); and, ‘Test me, Lord, and know my heart; question me and know my paths, and see whether there is any way of wickedness in me’ (Psalm 138)?

“How has the enormous equipment of your battle been terrified by the tiny shadow of an enemy?” [Lipsius, in the margin: “crushed.”]

Condemning himself in this way with the chastening of compunction, he should not allow the disturbance of his spirit to go unpunished. Instead, chastising his flesh with stricter correction through fasting and vigils, and torturing the fault of his fickleness with continual acts of abstinence, he should consume in solitude, through this fire of discipline, what he ought to have fully burned away in the life of the monastery.

To obtain continual and stable patience, this must be held firmly and immovably: since divine law forbids us not only to avenge injuries but even to remember them, we are not permitted, under the pretext of any loss or provocation, to be moved to anger.

For what more grievous loss could befall the soul than to be deprived, through the sudden blindness of agitation, of the brightness of the true and eternal light, and to withdraw from contemplation of Him who is meek and humble in heart?

What, I ask, is more harmful or more disgraceful than for someone to lose the judgment and rule of honesty and the discipline of right discernment, and, while sober and sound-minded, to commit acts that not even a drunken or senseless person could have committed without pardon?

Whoever weighs these and similar losses will easily scorn not only every kind of damage but also whatever insults and punishments the most cruel may inflict. He will judge nothing more ruinous than anger and nothing more precious than tranquillity of mind and the perpetual purity of his heart. For the sake of this purity, the advantages not only of bodily but also of apparently spiritual things must be despised if they cannot otherwise be acquired or perfected without disturbing this tranquillity.

## CHAPTER XV. The question: Whether chastity should be tested in the same way as the other passions

[Col. 1145A]

Germanus: Just as the remedy for the other wounds—anger, sadness, and impatience—has been shown through the presentation of contrary circumstances, so we wish to be taught what kind of cure should be applied against the spirit of fornication. That is, can the fire of desire likewise be extinguished by setting before us greater and more powerful sources of provocation, as in the other case? We consider this quite contrary to chastity, if the fuel of lust is not merely intensified within us but even touched upon by the mind’s passing glance.

## CHAPTER XVI. The reply: By what proofs it can be recognized

[Col. 1145B]

Joannes: Your shrewd question has anticipated the subject that would have followed our account even if you had remained silent. For this reason I have no doubt that it must be received effectively by your minds, since the keenness of your intellect has preceded our instruction.

The obscurity of any question is clarified without difficulty when the inquiry, anticipating its solution, goes ahead to the point where the answer must be led.

Accordingly, human company not only does no harm to the remedies for the vices mentioned above but contributes greatly to them. For the more frequently the causes of one’s impatience are exposed, and the more often they inflict the pain of compunction upon those who overcome them, the more rapid a recovery they provide for those who are suffering.

For this reason, even those who remain in solitude—although the fuel and material of provocations cannot arise from human beings—must deliberately recall those provocations, so that, while fighting against them through constant struggle of thought, a more immediate remedy may be supplied to us. [Lipsius, in the margin: “it” rather than “them.”]

[Note: Lust is conquered not by resisting but by fleeing. The Apostle indicates this when he says: “Flee fornication” (1 Corinthians 6). St. Thomas explains how this is to be understood: “It should be noted that the other vices are overcome by resistance, because the more a person considers and examines particular matters, the less he finds in them that gives pleasure, and the more he becomes anxious. But the vice of fornication is not overcome by resistance, because the more it is considered, the more it is inflamed. Rather, it is overcome by fleeing—that is, by completely avoiding unclean thoughts and every occasion of them—as it is said in Zechariah 2: ‘Flee from the land of the north, says the Lord.’

“St. Jerome explains this same teaching most beautifully. He aptly refutes the heretic Vigilantius, who reproached monks and solitaries as unwarlike and cowardly because they avoided the battle of lust by fleeing. Responding to Vigilantius’s objection, he says:

“‘Why do you go into the desert? Surely so that I may neither hear nor see you; so that I may not be moved by your fury or suffer your battles; so that the harlot’s eye may not capture me; so that a beautiful appearance may not lead me into unlawful embraces.

“‘You will reply: “This is not fighting but fleeing. Stand in the battle line; armed, resist your enemies, so that when you have conquered you may be crowned.”

“‘I confess my weakness. I do not want to fight in the hope of victory, lest at some time I lose the victory. If I flee, I have avoided the sword; if I stand, I must either conquer or fall. But why is it necessary to abandon certainties and pursue uncertainties? Death must be avoided either with a shield or with one’s feet.

“‘You who fight can both be overcome and conquer; when I flee, I do not conquer in that from which I flee, but I flee so that I may not be conquered. It is not safe to sleep beside a serpent. It may happen that it will not bite me, but it may also happen that at some time it will bite me.

“‘We call women mothers, sisters, and daughters, and are not ashamed to cover our vices with names of affection. What is a monk doing in the cells of women? What is the purpose of solitary and private conversations, and eyes that avoid witnesses? Holy love has no impatience.

“‘What we have said about lust, let us apply to avarice and to all the vices that are avoided through solitude. For this reason we avoid the crowds of cities, lest we be compelled to do what nature does not so much force us to do as our will.’”

This is Jerome’s statement. He seems to suggest a certain distinction between the vices John touches upon in the words: “Everything that is in the world is either the desire of the flesh, or the desire of the eyes”—that is, avarice—or “the pride of life” (1 John 4).

For we are impelled in some way by nature toward the desire of the flesh, or lust; toward the other vices we are impelled not so much by nature as by a will inclined toward them. Cassian also teaches this (Book 7 of the *Institutes*, chapters 1 and 5).

Nevertheless, we must avoid, insofar as it lies within us, the occasions and provocations of every vice, because things set before us move our faculties—especially objects of lust—and therefore must be avoided all the more.

Likewise Augustine says in one of his sermons: “That lust must be fled, as we urge, the Apostle Paul clearly demonstrates. Although he preached that all vices must be resisted, when he spoke against lust he did not say, ‘Resist,’ but, ‘Flee fornication.’ So also elsewhere in the divine Scriptures we read: ‘Do not look intently upon the face of a virgin, lest her appearance scandalize you’ (Ecclesiasticus 9).

“And blessed Joseph, so that he might escape the shameless woman, left behind the cloak by which he had been seized and fled. Therefore, against the assault of lust, seize flight if you wish to gain victory. Do not be ashamed to flee if you desire to obtain the palm of chastity.”

So Augustine.

Therefore, against lust one must fight in the manner of the Parthians—by fleeing and by turning one’s arrows back, as Virgil says (*Georgics* 3). Baptista Mantuanus expresses the point elegantly:

> Against this, beware of fighting; for to conquer is to be conquered:
>
> To conquer is to turn your back and carry your footsteps backward.

Against the spirit of fornication, however, the method is different and the situation is unlike the others. For just as bodily intercourse and proximity to the flesh of lust must be completely removed from the body, so its memory must be wholly removed from the mind.

It is exceedingly harmful for minds and hearts that are still weak and diseased to admit even the slightest recollection of this passion, so that sometimes even [Note: For this reason Cassian advises in Book 6 of the *Institutes*, chapter 13, that the first safeguard of chastity is this: when the memory of the female sex has slipped into our mind through the subtle cunning of the devil’s suggestion, we should immediately hasten to drive it from the recesses of our mind by introducing the recollection of our mother, our sisters, or certainly holy women, and so forth.

“For the same reason St. Jerome advises the monk Rusticus (Letter 4) not even to live with his mother: ‘Otherwise,’ he says, ‘you may either grieve her by refusing the delicate foods she brings, or, if you accept them, add oil to the fire, and among the company of girls see by day what you think about at night.’

“And in his book against Vigilantius he says: ‘A monk has the office not of a teacher but of one who mourns—one who mourns either for himself or for the world and awaits the coming of the Lord in fear; who, knowing his weakness and the fragile vessel he carries, fears to offend, lest he stumble, fall, and be shattered. For this reason he avoids the sight of women, especially young women, and is so strict with himself that he fears even what is safe.

“Possidius writes of St. Augustine (*Life of St. Augustine*, chapter 26): ‘No woman ever lived within his house; none remained there—not even his own sister, who, serving God as a widow, lived for a long time until the day of her death as superior of the handmaids of God. Nor did his uncle’s daughters or his brother’s daughters, who likewise served God, live there.’

“St. Gregory proposes this example of Augustine for imitation by clergy and monks in his letter to the defender Romanus (Book 7, Letter 39), writing among other things: ‘It is written that blessed Augustine did not agree even to live with his sister, saying: “Those who are with my sister are not my sisters.”’

“Therefore the caution of learned men ought to be a great instruction for us. It is the presumption of the heedless that what the strong fear, the less powerful should not fear.

“Augustine himself—or perhaps the author of the book *On the Singularity of the Clergy*—says elsewhere: ‘Chastity has drawn a formidable enemy, against which one must not merely resist but, with the reins cast aside, flee farther. Women must be fled no less because they appear religious; for the more religious they are, the more quickly they attract, and beneath the pretext of religion lies the snare of lust. Believe one who has experience; I speak as one who has experienced it: before God I do not lie. I have discovered cedars of Lebanon and leaders of flocks to have fallen under this plague—men whose fall I suspected no more than I suspected the shameful impurity of Ambrose or Jerome.’”

This is Augustine.

To these examples may be added that of Abba Arsenius. When a certain matron wished, out of devotion, to see him, he replied severely: “Do you not know that you are a woman, and that perfect men are seduced through women? Is it not enough for you to have heard of my deeds?”

She answered: “I do not wish to see your face; but pray for me.”

He replied: “I pray God that the memory of you may be erased from my heart.”

She departed groaning (*Lives of the Fathers*, Book 3, no. 65, and Book 5, booklet 2).

There is also the example of Abba Pior, reported by Palladius and Sozomen. When he went to his sister at the command of his abbot, in order to satisfy her persistent requests, he approached her door with his eyes closed and guided by another. He allowed himself to be seen by her, but did not himself see her; and, having been seen by her, he immediately departed (*Lausiac History*, chapter 87).]

under the recollection of holy women or through the story of sacred reading, the stimulus of harmful titillation is aroused.

For this reason our elders [Note: For this reason—namely, to avoid such thoughts—St. Prosper says (*On the Contemplative Life*, Book 3, chapter 6) that the ancients had decreed that young men should not read the book of Genesis, part of the prophet Ezekiel, or the Song of Songs, nor other such books in which the generations, deeds, and names of certain women are recorded.

“Read St. Jerome’s preface to his first commentary on Ezekiel and his letter to Paulinus concerning all the books of divine history.

“St. Benedict also seems to have had this passage of Cassian in mind in chapter 42 of his Rule. There, concerning books to be read or not read in the chapter after supper, he prescribes as follows: ‘As soon as they have risen from supper, let them all sit together in one place, and let one person read the Conferences or Lives of the Fathers, or certainly some other work that edifies the hearers, such as the ancient moral books—those of St. Gregory and others, for example—or homilies of holy teachers, which principally breathe the sweetness of devotion and contain instruction for edification,’ says Turrecrematus. ‘This has been rightly and most holily established, because from that reading the monks can draw material for edification and devotion, by which during the time of silence they may advance toward the heights of contemplation. The books of the Conferences and Lives of the Fathers have rightly been chosen for this purpose, because they contain the teaching of all perfection, edification, and holiness.’

“So far he.

“St. Benedict then adds: ‘But not the Heptaticum, nor the books of Kings,’ supplying the word ‘books.’ By *Heptaticum* he means what St. Jerome calls the *Heptateuch*, that is, the sevenfold collection of sacred books: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, and Judges, with Ruth as a kind of appendix; these are followed by the books of Kings.

“Just as the ancients called the five books of Moses the *Pentateuch*, so, joining together Joshua, Judges, and Ruth, they called them the *Octateuch*, as Cassiodorus does in chapter 1 of his *Divine Institutions*; and Greek authors, whose writings are read *εἰς τὴν ὀκτάτευχον*—‘concerning the Octateuch.’

“But since the Hebrews, as Jerome observes, combine the history of Ruth with Judges into one book, this led many to call it the *Heptateuch* instead of the *Octateuch*, as Jerome does in Letters 7 and 28. Apparently St. Benedict also does so in the passage just cited, where he calls it the *Heptaticum* instead of the *Heptateuch*.

“To return to this point: Benedict himself adds the reason why he advised that these books not be read at that hour, saying: ‘Because for weak understandings’—that is, for the unlearned, inexperienced, and those without knowledge of the Scriptures—‘it will not be useful to hear that Scripture at that hour’ (see Smaragdus at the same place).

“For the legal and historical books, since they are full of and concealed beneath many obscure figures and contain very profound mysteries, are not so suitable for simple monks to read, especially at that hour when the reading ought to be wholly edifying and filled with the simplicity of moral teaching, providing support for holy meditations—not various histories of wars, from which various phantasms could arise in those who are falling asleep. They may be read at other hours.

“Behold: he does not simply forbid the reading of the legal and historical books mentioned above (Turrecrematus), but forbids them only at that hour.”]

customarily pass over such readings with the greatest prudence in the presence of the younger men.

Certainly, for those who are most perfect and already consummated in the highest devotion to chastity, there can be no lack of tests by which they may examine themselves, through which the most perfect integrity of heart may be confirmed by an incorruptible judgment of conscience.

For a man who is completely perfected, there will also be a test of himself concerning this passion, in accordance with what has been said above: when he knows that he has already completely uprooted the roots of this illness, he may, if he wishes, admit some image that serves to test him, for the purpose of examining his chastity.

But those who are still less firm and perfect must in no way undertake this examination, so that they may entertain in their hearts the union with a woman and a kind of tender and gentle touching. For such a thing will be more harmful than beneficial to them.

What kind of test can such people obtain through this method, when the very thing being avoided is present in the test, and danger lies in the examination itself?

When, therefore, someone established in the most perfect virtue discovers that no assent of the mind and no movement of the flesh is aroused within him by enticing thoughts, he will receive the most certain evidence of his purity.
