Thus, exercising himself toward this firmness of purity, he will possess the good of chastity and incorruption not only in his mind, but, even if bodily contact with a woman should occur for some necessary reason, as sometimes happens, he will be wholly unaware of any sense of passion.

This is what Abba John said. [Note: We have noted elsewhere that monks in former times, since they fasted daily outside the season of Pentecost, normally did not take food before the ninth hour from sunrise—which for us is three o’clock in the afternoon—unless they broke their fast in order to practice hospitality.

“St. Jerome writes in his Letter 22 to Eustochium that this hour for breaking the fast was observed among the Egyptian cenobites, and Cassian confirms the same in Conference 21, chapter 23. Hence St. Benedict says in chapter 41: ‘On Wednesday and Friday let them fast until the ninth hour; on the other days let them dine at the sixth hour.’

“Prudentius also preserves a notable memory of this ancient and primitive observance—in which those who fasted abstained even from drink until the ninth hour—in this verse from the hymn *On the Crown*, hymn 10 (*περὶ στεφάνων*):

> The priest sees certain people from the crowd  
> Offering him a cup to taste.  
> “We are fasting,” he says; “I refuse the drink:  
> The ninth hour has not yet released the day.””]

When he sensed that the ninth-hour meal was approaching, he brought the conference to a close.

# THE TWENTIETH CONFERENCE, WHICH IS THAT OF ABBA PINUFIUS. ON THE END AND SATISFACTION OF REPENTANCE

[Col. 1149]

## CHAPTER I. On Abba Pinufius’s humility and his desire to remain hidden

In speaking of the teaching of the distinguished and singular man Abba Pinufius concerning the end of repentance, I seem to cut away a large part of the subject if, out of consideration for the reader’s weariness, I silently omit here the praise of his humility, which I touched upon briefly in the fourth book of the *Institutes* (chapter 30), entitled *On the Institution of Those Renouncing the World*. [Note: That is, the book entitled *On the Institutions of Those Renouncing the World*. Concerning the inscription or title of the fourth book, see the note there on chapter 1.]

This is especially so because many who do not know that little work might encounter the present account, and the authority of everything said would be weakened if the merit of the speaker were removed.

When Pinufius was abbot and priest, presiding over a great monastery not far from the Egyptian city of Panephysi, as stated there, the glory of his virtues and miracles had raised him so high throughout that entire province [Note: Ciaconius reads *Pynuphium*; the manuscript has *Pinofium*. Concerning him, see Cassian, *Institutes*, Book 4, chapters 30 and following.] that he already seemed to himself to have received, in the reward of human praise, payment for his labors.

Fearing that the emptiness of popular favor—which he especially detested—might deprive him of the fruit of the eternal reward, he secretly fled his monastery and hastened to the innermost retreats of the monks of Tabennesis [Note: The monks of Tabennesis, or Tabennesiots, were instituted by St. Pachomius; hence they were also called Pachomians or Pachumians. Concerning them, see Cassian, *Institutes*, Book 4, chapter 1, and St. Jerome’s preface to the Rule of Pachomius.]

There he chose not the solitude of the desert, nor the security of the solitary life—which even imperfect men sometimes pursue in proud presumption because they cannot endure the labor of obedience in monasteries—but preferred to be subjected to a very populous monastery.

Nevertheless, so that no indication of his identity might betray him, he put on secular clothing and, for many days, stood weeping before the doors, as is customary there. Throwing himself at everyone’s knees, he endured their prolonged contempt. To test his desire, they said that, now in extreme old age and driven, as it were, by want of bread, he had not sincerely sought the holiness of their way of life. At last he obtained admission.

There he was assigned to assist a young brother who had undertaken the cultivation of the garden. He fulfilled with such astonishment-inspiring humility not only everything that the superior ordered or that the care of the assigned work required, but also certain necessary tasks which the others avoided because of their unpleasantness. He completed these secretly through nocturnal labor, so that at dawn the whole community, admiring such useful work, remained unaware of its author.

After he had spent nearly three years there, rejoicing in the labors of the humiliating subjection he had desired, it happened that a certain brother known to him arrived from the regions of Egypt from which he had departed.

For a long time the brother hesitated to trust the promptness of his recognition because of the lowliness of Pinufius’s clothing and office. But after unmistakably investigating the matter, he threw himself at his knees. First he caused astonishment among all the brothers; then, when his name was revealed—the name whose reputation for exceptional holiness had spread even among them—he also caused them the pain of compunction, since they had assigned a man of such merit and priestly dignity to such humiliating tasks.

After Pinufius had been brought back to his monastery amid the honorable escort of the brothers, weeping profusely and blaming the envy of the devil, as though for a grave betrayal occasioned by his exposure, he remained there only a short time. Then he was again offended by the attentions paid to his honor and precedence. Secretly boarding a ship, he crossed over to Palestine in the province of Syria.

There, as though he were a beginner and novice, he was received into the monastery where we were living, and the abbot ordered him to reside in our cell. But even there the merit of his virtue could not long remain hidden. For when he was exposed by a similar betrayal and recalled to his monastery with great honor and praise, he was finally compelled to be what he was.

## CHAPTER II. On our arrival at Abba Pinufius’s monastery
Since, therefore, after no very long time the desire for holy instruction also compelled us to seek Egypt, we searched for him with the greatest eagerness and longing. He received us with such grace and humility that he honored us as his former fellow-cellmates—[Note: That is, cohabitants of the same cell, or those living together in the same cell. Sidonius uses *concellitae*; Ennodius, with the same meaning, uses *concellanei*. He calls them “former” here because above, near the end of the chapter, he said that Pinufius had been ordered to live with him in the same cell—namely, in the Bethlehem monastery—when he had been received there as though he were a beginner and novice. For understanding this, one should note the words of St. Jerome in the preface to the Rule of Pachomius: “In each monastery,” he says, “there are Fathers, stewards, weekly officers, ministers, and superiors of individual houses, so that in one house approximately forty brothers dwell, obeying the superior; and, according to the number of brothers, there are thirty or forty houses in one monastery. Three or four houses are joined into one tribe, so that they may either go together to their tasks or succeed one another in the weekly ministry in due order.” Thus brothers numbering approximately forty were called *syncellitae* because they lived together in one cell—or rather, in one house—and were subject to one superior. There were several cells in one house, however, in which either single monks, or certainly two or three together, lived, as St. Jerome states in his letter to Eustochium (Letter 22). Hence the Rule itself, article 7, clearly distinguishes cells from houses: “In each house,” it says, “when the prayers have ended, they shall not immediately return to their cells, but shall confer among themselves about what they have heard the superiors discussing,” and so forth. Later centuries and customs, moreover, came to regard the cohabitation of two or more brothers or monks in the same cell or chamber as neither expedient nor seemly; I remember that this was also noted elsewhere. Thus it is recorded that the Council of Tours decreed: “Nor shall monks be permitted to have common cells, where either two may remain or single cells may be assigned,” and so forth (Tours II, canon 10). The emperor Justinian, in his Novel (Novel 5, *Concerning Monks*), prescribed that monks should have one house, one common dining hall, and one dormitory, but separate chambers or cells: “Or if one house should not suffice for the multitude of monks,” he says, “they shall be distributed into two or more—not separately and by themselves, but in common, as witnesses to one another’s honesty and chastity; unless some of them, living in contemplation and perfection, lead a withdrawn life in solitude. Such men they customarily call anchorites and hesychasts, as though taken from the common life for better things.” These provisions were drawn both from other Fathers and from chapter 22 of the Rule of St. Benedict. The Cassinese monks added this statute: “According to modern custom, for the sake of propriety, so that the brothers may more freely devote themselves to prayers and other spiritual exercises, and so that curiosity may be avoided, the dormitory is divided into separate cells, and we assign each brother one cell, so that they sleep individually in individual cells.” This is their explanation of the chapter of the Rule that prescribes that the monks sleep one by one in separate beds.]

and gave us lodging even in the little cell that he had built at the far end of the garden. There, after he had delivered before all the brothers assembled in the synaxis instructions that were sufficiently difficult and lofty for a certain brother who was entering upon the Rule—instructions which, as we stated earlier, I have summarized as briefly as I could in the fourth book of the *Institutes* (chapter 32)—the heights of true renunciation appeared to us so incomprehensible and so marvelous that we believed our humility could in no way ascend to them. Accordingly, cast down by despair, and not concealing even in our faces the bitterness of our innermost thoughts, we returned to the blessed old man in great anxiety. When he immediately asked the reason for such sadness, Abbot Germanus answered with a deep groan:

## CHAPTER III. An inquiry concerning the end of repentance and the sign of satisfaction.

The more magnificent and sublime the discourse of your unfamiliar teaching has opened before us the arduous path of the loftiest renunciation, and, as though the darkness had been removed from our eyes, shown us its summit established in heaven, the greater is the weight of despair by which we are crushed. For when we measure its immensity against the smallness of our strength, and compare the excessive degradation of our slothfulness with the infinite height of the virtue displayed, we perceive that our perversity is not merely unable to advance toward it, but may even fall away from the position it now occupies. Oppressed, therefore, by the burdens of excessive despair, we are somehow slipping from the lowest places into still lower ones. Consequently, the one and singular remedy that can be applied to our wounds is that we learn something concerning the end of repentance, and especially concerning the sign of satisfaction, so that, assured of the remission of our former sins, we may also be encouraged to climb to the heights of the perfection described above.

## CHAPTER IV. Abbot Pinufius’s reply.

**Pinufius:** I take very great pleasure in the abundant fruits of your humility, which I also observed, with no inattentive consideration, when I received you as former inhabitants of that cell; and I rejoice greatly because you have received with such admiration what is perhaps commanded by us, the lowest of all Christians, with nothing more than freedom of speech, that—if I am not mistaken—you fulfill it no less earnestly than it was spoken by us. And since—as I remember—the diligence of your labor almost equals what we have said, you conceal the merit of your virtue as though no breath of what you practice daily had reached you. But because this itself is most worthy of the highest praise, that, like people still inexperienced, you testify that these institutions of the saints are unknown to you, let us briefly embrace, as best we can, what you earnestly request of us. For we must obey the command of your ancient friendship even beyond our ability and strength.

Accordingly, concerning the exhortation to repentance and its merit, many have published a great deal, not only orally but also in writing, showing how great its usefulness and grace are, so that, when God is offended by former crimes and inflicts so just a punishment for such offenses, repentance—as one may properly say—somehow resists him and, as it were, unwillingly, if I may put it so, holds back the right hand of the avenger. But I do not doubt that all this is so well known to you, either because of your supernatural wisdom or because of your unwearied devotion to sacred letters, that the first planting of your way of life has grown from it. In short, you are not asking anxiously about the nature of repentance, but about its end and the sign of satisfaction; with very perceptive questioning you investigate what others have left aside. Therefore, we shall strive to satisfy your desire with all possible brevity and concision.

## CHAPTER V. The manner of repentance and the evidence of having received indulgence.

[Note: Other Fathers define repentance in nearly the same way. Lactantius, *Institutes*, book VI, chapter 24: “To do penance,” he says, “is nothing other than to profess and affirm that one will sin no more.” And below: “For the person who repents of his deed understands his error; therefore the Greeks more aptly and significantly call it *metanoia* (μετάνοια), which we may call ‘recovery of the mind.’ For he recovers his mind, as it were, from madness, who is troubled by his error; he chastises himself for his folly and strengthens his mind for living more rightly.” Augustine, *Sermon 7 on Time*: “This is true repentance: when someone is so converted that he does not return; when he repents in such a way that he does not repeat the offense.” Gregory, *Homily 34 on the Gospels*: “To repent is to mourn past sins and not commit again the sins that must be mourned.” Isidore, *On the Supreme Good*, book II, chapter 16: “Isaiah says concerning sinners: ‘Wash yourselves; be clean.’ He is washed and clean who both mourns past sins and does not again commit what must be mourned. He is washed but not clean who mourns what he has done but does not abandon it, and who, after his tears, repeats what he had mourned.”

But so that these and similar statements may be rightly understood, one should note that, just as was said above concerning true friendship in Conference 16, the expression “true repentance” can be understood in two ways, as St. Bonaventure carefully observes in the fourth book of the *Sentences* (distinction 14). First, repentance is called true when the true character of repentance is found in it, just as we call gold true when it is not counterfeit; in this sense true repentance is opposed to false or feigned repentance. In another sense, repentance is called true when it brings a person to the ultimate end, namely eternal life. It is of this true, that is, perfect, repentance that the Fathers speak when they say that true repentance is to mourn past sins and not thereafter commit sins that ought to be mourned. Or they understand repentance as cessation from sins, at least in the penitent’s intention and purpose, just as the Fathers of Trent (Session 14, chapter 4) teach that contrition—which is the first act of repentance—is sorrow and detestation for a sin committed, together with the purpose of not sinning thereafter (see Session 6, chapter 14). Augustine’s, Isidore’s, and Abbot Pinufius’s words here also seem to be understood in this way.

It must, however, be held as certain—and this too is declared by the Fathers of Trent—that the word “repentance,” both in divine Scripture and among the holy Fathers, is used not merely for a change of mind or alteration of life, as heretics maintain, but for detestation and punishment of sins committed. The Council’s words are as follows (in the place cited above): “The holy synod declares that this contrition includes not only cessation from sin, the purpose and beginning of a new life, but also hatred of the old life, in accordance with the words: ‘Cast away from you all your transgressions by which you have transgressed, and make for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit’” (Ezekiel 18). Indeed, anyone who considers those cries of the saints—“Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you”; “I am weary with my groaning; every night I wash my bed” (Psalms 50 and 6); “I will remember my years before you in the bitterness of my soul” (Isaiah 38)—and others of this kind will easily understand that they arose from a vehement hatred of their former life and an intense detestation of their sins. Thus far the Council.]

The full and perfect definition of repentance is that we never again commit the sins for which we repent or by which our conscience is tormented. [Note: That is, the sign or evidence from which someone may conclude that he has fully and perfectly expiated his sins or satisfied for them, and consequently has obtained their pardon and indulgence. This is the end of repentance, the subject for which this Conference was established and entitled. For a sound understanding of this passage, one should not neglect the annotation of Peter Maturus (*Chronicle*, part II, chapter 2, title 15, §19) in St. Antoninus: “What is presented here,” he says, “concerning recognizing the absolution and remission of one’s sins may indeed be signs and conjectures of the absolution of sins, but they are not certain and necessary proofs by which a person can be brought to believe this with certainty. For it is the settled opinion of Catholics that no one can be certain, except through divine grace, with the certainty of faith that his sins have been forgiven. See Canisius, *Catechism*, chapter on Sins against the Holy Spirit, question 3; St. Thomas, *Summa* I–II, question 112, article 5; Soto, *On Nature and Grace*, book III, chapters 10–12; and Vega, *On Justification*, book IX. These confirm what was decreed in the Council of Trent, Session 6, chapter 9, and canons 12 and 13, as well as Sixtus of Siena, *Bibliotheca*, book VI, annotation 210.” Thus Peter Maturus. But see the fuller notes below.]

The sign of satisfaction and indulgence is also that we have driven the affections for those things out of our hearts. For let each person know that he is not yet absolved from his former sins so long as, while he is occupied with satisfaction and groaning, the image of the deeds he has committed—or of similar crimes—has appeared before his eyes, and their pleasure, or even their recollection, disturbs the secret places of his mind. Therefore, let the person who keeps vigil for the sake of satisfaction recognize that he has been absolved from his crimes and has received pardon for his former offenses when he no longer feels his heart touched even in imagination by the allurements of those same vices.

For this reason, a most truthful examiner of repentance and indulgence resides in our conscience; while we are still dwelling in this flesh, before the day of judgment and knowledge, he reveals to us the absolution of our guilt and discloses the end of satisfaction and the grace of remission. And to express these same matters more significantly, [Note: How can this be believed, when Ecclesiasticus says: “Do not be without fear concerning a pardoned sin” (Ecclesiasticus 5), and Solomon: “A person does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred” (Ecclesiastes 9)? It must be said that “believe” here means “trust,” and to rest quietly in this devout confidence. In the same way, “faith” is taken for “confidence” in Matthew 6: “If God so clothes the grass of the field, how much more you, O you of little faith!”; and in Matthew 16: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed,” and so forth; and in James 1: “Let him ask in faith, doubting nothing.”

But apart from revelation no one ought to presume or persuade himself, with certain faith or belief, that his sins have been forgiven. Besides the very clear authorities of divine Scripture, the Council of Trent also teaches this (Session 6, chapter 9), against the vain confidence of heretics, in these words: “Although it is necessary to believe that sins are neither remitted nor ever have been remitted except freely through the divine mercy on account of Christ, nevertheless no one ought to believe that his sins are remitted or have been remitted merely because he boasts of confidence and certainty concerning the remission of his sins and rests in that alone. For among heretics and schismatics this vain confidence, removed from all piety, can exist—or rather, in our time does exist—and is proclaimed with great contention against the Catholic Church.

“Nor should it be asserted that those who are almost justified must establish within themselves, without any doubt whatsoever, that they are justified; or that no one is absolved and justified from sins unless he certainly believes himself absolved and justified; or that absolution and justification are accomplished by faith alone—as though one who does not believe this were doubting God’s promises and the efficacy of Christ’s death and resurrection. For just as no devout person ought to doubt God’s mercy, Christ’s merit, or the power and efficacy of the Sacraments, so anyone, when he considers himself and his own weakness and indisposition, may fear and be apprehensive concerning his possession of grace, since no one can know with the certainty of faith—which cannot be subject to falsehood—that he has obtained God’s grace.” Thus the Council, and these points are also defined under anathema in canons 12 and 13 of the same session.

For the rest, you will find another answer below, in the response to the following question.]

Only then, therefore, should we believe that the contagion of our former vices has been remitted when the desires and passions for present pleasures have likewise been driven from our heart.

## CHAPTER VI. An inquiry whether sins ought to be remembered for the sake of compunction of heart.

**Germanus:** [Note: It is unknown whether this entire chapter was omitted from the previous edition through some error or negligence. Here Germanus presents the question, and Pinufius answers it in the following chapter. Since that response plainly presupposes this question, we judged it necessary to restore it to its proper place. Dionysius’s paraphrase also agrees with it.]

From what, then, can that holy and salutary humiliation and compunction arise which is described in the person of the penitent in these words: “I have made my sin known to you, and I have not concealed my iniquity; I said, ‘I will declare my iniquity against myself to the Lord’” (Psalm 31), so that we may also be worthy effectively to say what follows: “And you forgave the wickedness of my heart” (ibid.)? Or how, when we have prostrated ourselves in prayer, shall we be able to stir ourselves to the tears of confession through which we may deserve to obtain the forgiveness of our offenses, according to the words: “Every night I wash my bed; I water my couch with my tears” (Psalm 6), if we drive from our hearts the memory of our sins, which we are commanded, on the contrary, to preserve tenaciously, since the Lord says: “I will not remember your iniquities; but you, remember them” (Isaiah 43 according to the Septuagint)? For this reason, both when I am at work and when I am praying, I strive deliberately to recall to my mind the memory of my sins, so that, being more effectively inclined toward true humility and contrition of heart, I may dare to say with the Prophet: “See my humiliation and my labor, and forgive all my sins” (Psalm 25).

## CHAPTER VII. Abbot Pinufius’s response: how far the memory of former deeds should be retained.

[Note: Chrysostom, *On Compunction of Heart*, book I: “This alone is required of us,” he says, “that we always recall our evils to mind and keep the consciousness of our deeds before our eyes, so that we may plead with God for them, set Gehenna before our sight, and remember the angels who will run everywhere on the day of judgment,” and so forth. And in book II: “So much good is gained from frequently remembering one’s sin that we see even the Apostle Paul bringing forward matters that had already been abolished and erased. Although he had no present guilt, because he knew that the remembrance and mourning of sins benefit the soul, he also recalled sins committed in ignorance that the grace of baptism and confession of faith had erased.” And below: “We ought, therefore, to remember former offenses, even those for which we have obtained forgiveness, so that, seeing how great a debt God has remitted to us, we may love him more, conceive shame and embarrassment, and be moved to compunction of heart, considering that, unless his mercy had helped us, so great a burden of sins would undoubtedly have weighed us down in the lowest punishments and torments of hell.”

St. Augustine likewise used the recollection and commemoration of his sins to stir himself to compunction and devotion. He wrote the books of the *Confessions* on this subject, in which he recalled and reviewed in the bitterness of his soul the years of his former life and even the things he had done as a child. In this way it can happen that even the good and just may practice perpetual repentance for mortal sins until the end of life, as some formerly did. For this reason they shut themselves up in prisons, tombs, and monasteries, as in Climacus (*The Ladder*, step 5, which concerns exact repentance) and in the Lives of the Saints; others, like the Apostle Paul, fled to deserted places for the sake of practicing repentance, wandering about in sheepskins and goatskins, in poverty, distress, and affliction, in deserts, mountains, caves, and holes in the ground.]

What you have said concerning the remembrance of sins is indeed sufficiently useful and necessary, but it applies to those who are still practicing repentance, so that with continual contrition of heart they may proclaim: “I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Psalm 50); and also: “I will think upon my sin” (Psalm 37). While, therefore, we are practicing repentance and are still tormented by the memory of our vicious acts, it is necessary that a rain of tears, arising from confession of guilt, extinguish the fire of our conscience. But when, for someone fixed in this humility and contrition of spirit and persevering in labor and groaning, the memory of these things has fallen silent, and the thorn of conscience has been torn from the marrow of the soul by the grace of the merciful God, [Note: The same point is expressed in other words in chapter 5: “Then let the person who keeps vigil for the sake of satisfaction recognize that he has been absolved from his crimes and has received pardon for his former offenses,” and so forth.

At first sight this assertion might seem rightly to be numbered among the errors of Cassian, or of the *Conferences*, since it is certain that in this life no one can, without divine revelation, be certain and secure concerning the state of his soul and the forgiveness of his sins (Council of Trent, Session 6, chapters 9 and 16), as is clear from the third note on the same chapter, unless it can be excused by a benign interpretation—one which the author, although somewhat obscurely, suggests. I believe that Cuychius and Ciaconius noticed this as well, since in their observations and censures they did not address this statement, although elsewhere they examined such matters with great care.

Three points should be noted in this interpretation. First, the author is not speaking of absolute and infallible certainty, such as the certainty of demonstration among philosophers, which produces knowledge, or the certainty of Catholic faith, to which falsehood cannot be subject. He is speaking of moral and fiduciary certainty, which is inferred from certain signs and indications of true conversion, satisfaction, and remission of sins—signs discussed below—and which is inspired by God.

Second, when he removes from the truly penitent and justified person all remembrance of former crimes, he does not mean simple or bare recollection, remembrance, or apprehension of them. Someone may be absolved from sins and nevertheless be troubled by the memory of former sins. Rather, he means a seductive recollection or imagination joined with some affection and pleasure, especially as it occurs in sins of the flesh. Theologians commonly call this *delectatio morosa*, “deliberate pleasure.” So long as it remains in the mind and draws the reason toward itself, it is certain that a person does not possess perfect repentance and complete purity of conscience, which is the end of repentance and the subject of this Conference and discussion.

Third, the abbot is not speaking here of the truth or nature of repentance itself, as he insists at the beginning of this chapter, but of the end of repentance, as the title of this Conference indicates—that is, of the goal and perfection toward which repentance itself is directed. Repentance is then considered perfect and complete when someone, through works of repentance and satisfaction, has obtained the full pardon and remission of all sins, both as regards guilt and as regards punishment, since this is the end and goal of repentance, as stated above.

No one, however, can be wholly certain of this in the present life, except through a special divine revelation, as were those to whom the Lord said: “Your sins are forgiven,” or “Your sins have been forgiven” (Matthew 9; Luke 5 and 7). Indeed, it is not free from fault to investigate this matter more closely than is proper, as St. Gregory replied to a noblewoman from the imperial court who had earnestly asked him about it: “You have requested,” he says (*Letters*, book VI, letter 186), “a useless thing, for you ought not to become secure concerning your sins unless you are already unable, on the final day of your life, to mourn those same sins. Until that day comes, you should always fear your sins with suspicion and trembling, and wash them away with daily tears.

“Certainly the Apostle Paul had already ascended to the third heaven, had been carried into paradise, and had heard secret words that it is not lawful for a human being to speak (2 Corinthians 12); yet he still said in fear: ‘I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate’ (1 Corinthians 9). He still fears, though he is being led to heaven; and the person who still lives on earth already wishes not to fear. Consider, daughter, that security is usually the mother of negligence. Therefore, you ought not to possess in this life a security that would make you negligent. For it is written: ‘Blessed is the person who is always fearful’ (Proverbs 28); and again: ‘Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling’ (Psalm 2). During the brief time of this life, then, trembling must hold your mind, so that afterward it may rejoice forever in the joy of security.” Thus Gregory.

Although these matters stand as described, the Fathers nevertheless commonly point out, for the consolation of penitents, certain signs of true conversion and remission of sins, so that each person may infer from them what his condition is and may, as far as possible, recognize himself. These signs also provide the benefit of inflaming the penitent’s soul to desire and attain what he perhaps has not yet obtained in his reconciliation with God.

We can learn these signs from St. Basil and St. Bernard. St. Basil says as follows (*Shorter Rules*, question 269): A soul may be persuaded that it has been freed and cleansed from sins if someone notices in himself an affection like that of David, of whom it is said: “I hated iniquity and abhorred it” (Psalm 118). Second, a person may know that he has attained the Apostle’s command: “Put to death your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and avarice” (Colossians 3), so that he can truly say: “A crooked heart did not cling to me; I did not know the wicked person who turned away from me” (Psalm 100). Third, a person may understand that he possesses such an affection if he has imitated that remarkable and awe-inspiring mercy of holy men toward sinners, like David, of whom it is said: “I saw the transgressors, and I wasted away” (Psalm 118), and like the Apostle, who says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not inflamed?” (1 Corinthians 11). And below: “Whenever, therefore, a person notices that his mind is affected in this way toward either his own sins or the sins of others, then let him believe that he is free from sin.”

St. Bernard says as follows (*Sermon on the Four Ways of Prayer*): “But perhaps you ask how or by what means you can know whether you have obtained this indulgence. Divine goodness ordinarily arranges matters in this way, for the preservation of humility: the more someone progresses, the less he considers himself to have progressed.” And shortly afterward: “Then the Lord said to the paralytic: ‘Rise, take up your bed, and walk’ (Matthew 9). Therefore, if first you are already rising through desire for heavenly things; second, if you are taking up your bed, that is, lifting your body above earthly pleasures, so that your soul is no longer carried by its desires but rather governs it and carries it where it does not wish to go; third, if at last you are walking, forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward in desire and purpose toward advancement (Philippians 3), do not doubt that you have been healed. For you could not rise if the burden had not been lightened to some degree; nor could you take up your bed unless you had been more fully relieved of your burden; nor could you walk in the fervor of your way of life while weighed down by the heavy mass of sins.” Thus St. Bernard.]

It is certain that such a person has reached the end of satisfaction and the merits of indulgence and has been cleansed from the stain of every crime. Yet this forgetfulness is attained in no other way than through the obliteration of former vices and affections and through perfect and complete purity of heart. No one who has neglected to cleanse his vices through slothfulness or contempt undoubtedly attains this purity, except the person who, by continuing unceasingly in mournful groans and sighs, has burned away every stain of his former filth and has proclaimed to God through the strength and work of his soul: “I have made my sin known to you, and I have not concealed my iniquity” (Psalm 31); and “My tears have been my bread day and night” (Psalm 41). Thus he may subsequently deserve to hear: “Let your voice cease from weeping and your eyes from tears, for there is a reward for your work, says the Lord” (Jeremiah 31).

The following words of the Lord should likewise be addressed to him: “I have blotted out your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like a mist” (Isaiah 44). And again: “I am he who blots out your iniquities for my own sake, and I will remember your sins no more” (Isaiah 43). Then, freed from the cords of his sins by which everyone is bound (Proverbs 5), he will sing to the Lord with complete thanksgiving: “You have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise” (Psalm 115).

## CHAPTER VIII. That the expiation of sins can be attained in many ways.

After that general grace of baptism [Note: [Col. 1159B] Through this grace, namely, the full and perfect remission of all sins is conferred (Council of Trent, Session 5, chapter 5): full, because all sins, however numerous and heinous, are pardoned; perfect, because each one is completely remitted, without retaining any penalty to be paid in the future age. [Col. 1159C] Ezekiel foretold this grace of baptism in these words (chapter 36): “I will pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your impurities.” Commenting on this passage in his letter to Oceanus, Jerome says: “I will cleanse you from all your filth”; by saying “from all,” he omits nothing. In the same sense he adds that passage of Micah 7: “He will plunge our iniquities beneath, and will cast all our sins into the depth of the sea.”], and that most precious gift of martyrdom, which is obtained through the washing of blood [Note: [Col. 1159C] That martyrdom supplies the place of baptism for those who have not been reborn is a constant tradition of the Church, reported by Gratian (On Consecration, distinction 4, chapter “Baptism takes the place”); likewise, it is called the baptism of blood, and martyrs are said to be baptized in their own blood. Hence Augustine, *The City of God*, book 13, chapter 7: “Whoever dies for confessing Christ, even without having received the washing of regeneration, receives as much benefit for the remission of sins as if he had been cleansed in the sacred font of baptism. For he who said (John 3), ‘Unless someone is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven,’ made an exception for these persons in another sentence, where he said no less generally (Matthew 10), ‘Whoever confesses me before men, I too will confess him before my Father who is in heaven.’ And elsewhere (Luke 9), ‘Whoever loses his life for my sake will find it.’ Hence it is written (Psalm 115), ‘Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.’ For what is more precious than a death by which even all sins are forgiven and merits are increased more abundantly? For those who, being unable to postpone death, were baptized and departed this life with all their sins erased, do not possess as much merit as those who, although able to postpone death, did not postpone it because they preferred to end this life by confessing Christ rather than reach his baptism by denying him.” Thus Augustine. Likewise, Cyprian, in his letter to Jubaianus, says that catechumens who are martyrs are baptized with the most glorious and greatest baptism of blood, concerning which the Lord said in the Gospel that he had another baptism with which he was to be baptized (Luke 12). As Pamelius notes there, Cyprian took this doctrine of the baptism of blood from Tertullian’s book *On Baptism* (chapter 16), where he says: “There is indeed for us also a second washing, one and the same—that is, of blood—concerning which the Lord says, ‘I have a baptism with which I am to be baptized,’ although he had already been baptized.” And below: “This is the baptism that both represents the washing not received and restores the washing that was lost.” Fulgentius mentions this same baptism of blood in his book *On Faith to Peter* (chapter 3), as does the author of *On the Dogmas of the Church*, chapter 74, and Prosper, sentence 146. On the same subject, see Bernard at greater length in letter 77, and Gratian, *On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter “Baptism takes the place.”], there are many fruits of repentance through which one reaches the expiation of crimes [Note: [Col. 1160C] He calls them “fruits of repentance,” not the effects themselves of repentance, but penitential and satisfactory works, or whatever external signs by which genuine repentance of soul can be recognized, such as tears, fasts, confession of sins, and good works opposed to former sins. Of these it is said in Matthew 3: “Therefore produce worthy fruit of repentance.” Hence Ciaconius and others assign this title to the chapter: “On the various fruits of repentance.” Here he lists many kinds of such works, which are frequently commended in Scripture as highly useful means for propitiating God and obtaining forgiveness of sins—not because each one, by itself and separately, is sufficient for this purpose, but because they must be joined with and employed together with the other requirements, as stated elsewhere (*Conferences* 9, chapter 21). Among these, the principal place belongs to the sacrament of repentance and the reception of sacramental absolution, or the desire for it, which is included in conversion to God and contrition of heart.]. For eternal salvation is not promised only through that simple name “repentance,” of which the blessed apostle Peter says (Acts 3): “Repent and be converted, so that your sins may be blotted out.” John the Baptist, or the Lord himself, likewise says (Matthew 3 and 4): “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near.”

But the burden of sins is also overwhelmed through the affection of charity: “For charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4). Likewise, through the fruit of almsgiving, healing is provided for our wounds, because, just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin (Ecclesiasticus 3). In the same way, through the shedding of tears, the washing away of sins is obtained: “For every night I will wash my bed; I will water my couch with my tears.” Finally, he adds, showing that they had not been shed in vain: “Depart from me, all you who practice iniquity,” he says, “for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping” (Psalm 6).

The abolition of sins is also granted through confession of crimes: “I said,” he says, “I will declare my injustice against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the wickedness of my sin” (Psalm 31). And again: “Declare your iniquities first, so that you may be justified” (Isaiah 43). Through affliction of heart and body as well, forgiveness of the sins committed is likewise obtained. “Look,” he says, “upon my humility and my labor, and forgive all my sins” (Psalm 24).

Above all, it is obtained through amendment of conduct: “Remove,” he says, “the evil of your thoughts from my eyes; cease to act perversely; learn to do good; seek judgment; assist the oppressed; judge the orphan; defend the widow; and come and accuse me, says the Lord. And if your sins are like scarlet, they shall be made white like snow; and if they are red like crimson, they shall be white like wool” (Isaiah 1).

Sometimes forgiveness of sins is also obtained through the intercession of the saints. “Whoever knows that his brother is committing a sin not unto death, let him ask, and God will give life to him whose sin is not unto death” (1 John 5). And again: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him bring in the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him” (James 5).

Sometimes, too, the stain of vices is burned away through the merit of mercy and faith, according to the saying: “By mercy and faith sins are cleansed” (Proverbs 15). Frequently it is accomplished through the conversion and salvation of those who are saved by our admonitions and preaching. “For whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way saves his soul from death and covers a multitude of sins” (James 5).

Likewise, through our own indulgence and forgiveness, we arrive at the forgiveness of our crimes: “For if you forgive men their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your offenses” (Matthew 6).

[Note: [Col. 1161B] Saint Antoninus, following his customary method, pursued the summary of this chapter and thought that it should end at the close of this sentence. To prevent any opportunity for error from arising out of what was said above, he inserted his own opinion and explanation, which I have thought neither unwelcome nor useless to append here. Thus he writes (in *Chronicon*, part 2, chapter 2, title 1, section 19):

“It must certainly be understood in this way. For sin is sometimes called the guilt or offense itself, and sometimes the penalty owed for sin. As regards guilt, God alone forgives it principally and effectively. ‘I alone,’ he says through Isaiah (chapter 43), ‘blot out your iniquities.’ And Augustine says: ‘No one forgives sins except Christ, who is the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world’ (John 1), and so forth. *On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter ‘No one.’

“As regards the sinner, only contrition, through grace, has this effect, according to Ezekiel (chapter 18): ‘On whatever day the sinner is converted and groans, I will no longer remember all his iniquities,’ says the Lord. But as regards the temporal penalty owed for sins, all the practices mentioned above are effective for the remission of sins—that is, of the penalties owed for sins. This is to be understood when they are performed in a state of grace; for when performed in mortal sin, they do not have that effect, but serve dispositionally toward the remission of mortal sins—that is, so that through them a person may be disposed and prepared for grace and true contrition, as is said under *On Repentance*, distinction 5, chapter ‘False things.’

“And below he says, Pinuphius: ‘If shame holds you back and you are embarrassed to reveal these things before men, do not cease to confess them through continual supplication to him whom they cannot escape, and say to him (Psalm 50): “For I acknowledge my iniquity.”’ This too must be properly understood, because after the decree *Omnis utriusque sexus* (*On Repentance and Remission*), one must confess if one has access to a confessor and is able to do so. In the time of John Cassian, however, the question was held to be open—namely, whether confession had to be made to a priest, or whether this could be understood as public confession, which religious persons made for the sake of mortification.”

Thus far Saint Antoninus, explaining Cassian’s opinion in the scholastic manner. Peter Maturus, however, a man of mature judgment and distinguished learning, observed several points in this explanation that required a clearer and more precise account, which he appended in these words:

“Although Saint Antoninus interprets this chapter of Cassian in a highly pious manner, I have nevertheless thought it necessary to add certain things, so that the truth of the Catholic faith may shine forth more clearly. First, it is certain that God alone, by his own authority, possesses the power to forgive sin. But it is also acknowledged that the sacraments of the New Law, and the priests who administer them, confer grace and forgive sins as secondary and instrumental causes. After Saint Augustine (*Tractates on John*, 80, and book 19 *Against Faustus*, chapter 16), Saint Thomas teaches this in the third part, question 62, articles 1 and 4, and in book 4, distinction 1, question 1, article 4, and question 2; Saint Antoninus teaches it in the fourth part of the *Summa*, title 14, chapter 2, section 1; and Soto in book 4, distinction 1, question 3, article 1, and distinction 20, question 2, article 1. It was also defined at the Council of Florence in its teaching on the sacraments, and at Trent, Session 6, chapters 7 and 14, and canons 6, 7, and 8.

“As for what is added, that only contrition on the sinner’s part has the power to remit sin, this too is true; but it is necessary that the intention of confessing and making satisfaction accompany this contrition, as Saint Antoninus himself teaches in the third part of this work, chapter 7, section 3, and in the third part of the *Summa*, title 14, chapter 18, and as Soto teaches in book 4, distinction 1, question 1, article 1, and Cajetan in *Opusculum* 17. This too was defined by the Council of Trent, Session 6, chapter 14, and Session 14, chapter 4.

“When Saint Antoninus later adds that, after the decree *Omnis utriusque sexus*, confession became necessary, this must not be understood as though sacramental confession became necessary only from that time, or were then first instituted. It is of divine law, instituted by Christ, and has always been observed in the Church, as Saint Thomas indicates in the third part, question 64, article 2, and in the *Supplement*, question 6, article 2; Soto expressly proves it in book 4, distinction 18, question 1, article 1. It was defined at the Council of Trent, Session 7, canon 1, and Session 14, canon 3. See also Vega, *On Justification*, book 13, chapter 28.

“Moreover, that famous decretal did nothing other than establish the time at which Christ’s command was to be fulfilled. Just as it would be absurd to say that holy communion was instituted by that very decretal, although it established a time for receiving communion, so it is far from the truth to assert that sacramental confession was then instituted, although the time for confessing was determined there. This too was decreed by the Council of Trent, Session 14, chapter 5, and canon 8.

“Finally, when Saint Antoninus adds that in Cassian’s time this matter was considered open, this must not be understood of private confession to a priest. Among Catholics there was never any doubt that such confession was necessary for salvation. Rather, it must refer to public and almost theatrical confession, as Saint Antoninus himself says; Sozomen reports that this had shortly before been abolished at Constantinople by Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople (*Tripartite History*, book 9, chapter 36).

“Therefore, whatever heretics derive from Saint Chrysostom against the sacramental confession of sins must not be understood of private confession to a priest, but of public confession, made in the presence of the entire people, as Sixtus of Siena clearly teaches in book 5 of the *Bibliotheca*, annotation 175, and Vega in *On Justification*, book 13, chapter 29. Cassian’s words must likewise be understood of this same public confession, as the following words sufficiently indicate: ‘For God is accustomed both to heal without any public exposure of shame and to forgive sins without reproach.’ These things occur in the public disclosure of sins, not in private confession.”

Thus far Maturus’s note on Saint Antoninus, which nevertheless also applies to a sound understanding of this passage of Cassian. But see the rest in the following note.]

You see, therefore, how many avenues of mercy the Savior’s clemency has opened, so that no one who desires salvation may be broken by despair, when he sees himself invited to life by so many remedies.

If you claim that, because of bodily weakness, you cannot wipe away your sins through the affliction of fasting, nor can you say, “My knees have become weak from fasting, and my flesh has been changed because of the oil” (Psalm 108); “for I ate ashes as bread and mixed my drink with weeping” (Psalm 101), then redeem them through generous almsgiving. If you do not have anything to distribute to the needy—although no one is excluded from this work by want or poverty, since the widow’s two small coins are preferred to the great gifts of the rich (Luke 21), and the Lord promises to repay even a cup of cold water (Matthew 10)—you can certainly be cleansed through amendment of conduct without those gifts.

If you cannot attain perfection in the virtues by putting all vices to death, devote pious concern to the salvation of another. But if you complain that you are not suited to this ministry, you can cover sins through the affection of charity. If any weakness of mind makes you fragile in this as well, at least humbly implore through prayer and the intercession of the saints remedies for your wounds [the text reads *submissus*; *subnixus*, “supported,” is a variant].

Finally, who cannot humbly say: “I have made my sin known to you, and I have not hidden my injustice” (Psalm 31), so that through this confession he may also confidently add: “And you forgave the wickedness of my heart” (ibid.)?

[Note: [Col. 1163C] Similar statements are found frequently in Chrysostom, Cassian’s teacher and master, and heretics abuse them against sacramental confession. In Homily 2 on Psalm 50 he says: “Tell your sins, so that you may erase them. If you are ashamed to tell someone that you have sinned, tell them every day in your soul. I do not say that you should confess them to your fellow servant, but tell them to God, who heals them.” And in Homily 4, *On Lazarus*: “Why, then,” he says, “are you ashamed and embarrassed to confess your sins? Take care not to tell a man, lest he reproach you. For you do not confess to a fellow servant so that he may make it public; rather, you show your wounds to the one who is Lord and physician. He does not fail to know them even if you do not tell him,” and so forth.

These and similar statements of both Chrysostom and Cassian, however, are not to be understood of private and sacramental confession, in which a person confesses to a man not as a man but as God—that is, as God’s representative—but of the public and theatrical confession that was made publicly by those performing public penance. So Cuychius and Ciaconius note, following the Master of the Sentences in book 4, distinction 17. After saying that sins must first be confessed to God and then to a priest, he adds: “The statement of John Chrysostom cited above must not be understood as permitting anyone, if he has the opportunity, not to confess to a priest. Rather, when the crime is hidden, it is enough to say it to God alone through the priest, once; and what is hidden need not be made public before many people. This is what he indicated when he said: ‘I do not tell you to expose yourself publicly.’ For just as a public offense requires a public remedy, so a hidden offense is cleansed by secret confession and secret satisfaction. Nor is it necessary to confess again what we have once confessed to a priest; but with the tongue of the heart, not of the flesh, we must continually confess it before the true Judge.” Thus far his words.

Pinuphius is therefore speaking here of this internal confession, which must first be made to God. It does not, however, exclude external and sacramental confession; rather, it directs one toward it and includes and presupposes the desire or intention to make it.]

If shame holds you back and you are embarrassed to reveal these things before men, do not cease to confess them through continual supplication to him from whom they cannot be hidden, and say: “I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me; against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you” (Psalm 50). He is accustomed both to heal without making that shame public and to forgive sins without reproach.

After this remedy, so ready and certain, divine goodness has also bestowed upon us another still easier one, entrusting the help of the remedy itself to our own choice, so that we may presume upon the forgiveness of our crimes according to the disposition of our heart, saying to him: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6).

Whoever, therefore, desires to attain forgiveness of his crimes should strive to equip himself with these instruments and should not, through the obstinacy of a hardened heart, turn away from the saving remedy the fountain of such great mercy. For even if we do all these things, they will not be sufficient for the expiation of our crimes unless the Lord’s goodness and clemency erase them [Col. 1164B].

[Note: [Col. 1164C] This sentence has the same meaning and sense as other similar statements made and rejected in the thirteenth Conference (chapters 7, 8, 9, and 13). It should therefore either be interpreted and accepted in a sounder manner, or rejected along with those statements. It should be accepted if it is understood of the efforts of a justified person, and of one who works or repents through grace, having been stirred up by God’s prevenient grace; but it should be rejected if it is understood of the efforts or powers of free will alone, with prevenient and stirring grace excluded, since such efforts can contribute nothing by themselves toward grace and salvation. For Saint Bernard’s statement is entirely true: “The efforts of free will are empty if they are not helped, and worthless if they are not stirred up” (*On Grace and Free Will*).]

When he sees the religious efforts and services offered to him by us with humble hearts, he rewards even small and insignificant efforts with immense generosity, saying: “I am he, I am he who blots out your iniquities for my own sake, and I will no longer remember your sins” (Isaiah 45).

Whoever, then, has ascended to the state we have described will obtain the grace of satisfaction through daily fasts and the mortification of heart and body, because, as it is written, “without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness” (Hebrews 9). And not without reason. “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 15). Therefore, whoever wishes to restrain the sword of the spirit, which is the word of God, from the shedding of this blood will undoubtedly be punished by the curse of the prophet Jeremiah.

[Note: [Col. 1164C] Apart from the literal sense, which is not relevant here, this sentence is expounded by the Fathers in two tropological ways. In the first, which Cassian follows here, the person who prevents or withdraws his sword from blood is called accursed and hateful to God—that is, the person who does not strike down or cut away his enemies, evil affections, with the sword of mortification, but allows them to live and rule, and does not heed the Apostle’s admonition: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Colossians 3). Likewise: “Put to death your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and greed” (Galatians 2), and so forth. And again: “Not in feasting and drunkenness, not in bedrooms and shameful acts, not in contention and rivalry; but put on the Lord Jesus, and do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” (Romans 13).

The second interpretation concerns superiors who neglect to correct and punish the sins and transgressions of their subjects with the sword of discipline, indulgently tolerating or ignoring them. Thus Gregory the Great says in the *Pastoral Rule* (chapter 26): “If those who were not at all ignorant of the medical art saw a wound that needed cutting but nevertheless refused to cut it, they would certainly commit the sin of fraternal death through sheer sluggishness. Let those, therefore, who recognize wounds of the mind but neglect to heal them by cutting with words consider how great their guilt is.” Hence the prophet rightly says: “Cursed is the one who restrains his sword from blood” (Jeremiah 48). To restrain the sword from blood is to hold back the word of preaching from the slaughter of carnal life. Of this sword it is again said: “And my sword shall devour flesh” (Deuteronomy 32). Peter Damian likewise says (*Letters*, book 4, letter 3): “He restrains the sword from blood who neglects to punish the sins of wrongdoers.”]

For he says: “Cursed is the one who restrains his sword from blood” (Jeremiah 48). This is the sword that, by beneficially pouring out that harmful blood through which the matter of sins is animated, cuts away and severs whatever it finds in our members that has become compacted of flesh and earth. It makes those who have been put to death to vices live for God and flourish in spiritual virtues.

Then he will begin to weep no longer from remembrance of an old offense but from hope of future joys. Thinking not so much about past evils as about future goods, he will pour out tears not from sorrow over sins but from the gladness of that eternal happiness; and, forgetting what lies behind—that is, carnal vices—he will reach forward to what lies ahead, namely, spiritual gifts and virtues.

## CHAPTER IX. That forgetfulness of sin is useful for the perfect, and that the remembrance of shameful offenses should be avoided. [Col. 1165B]

But as for what you said shortly before, that you deliberately revisit the memory of past sins [Note: [Col. 1165C] Namely, the memory of past sins, as he said earlier. This is to be understood of carnal and sexual sins, as the title of this chapter also indicates, although the title varies somewhat among the authorities. Dionysius and Ciaconius have: “That forgetfulness of sin is useful for the perfect, and that the remembrance of crimes should be avoided.” Cuychius, following the Plantinian and Basel editions, has: “That forgetfulness of the progress is useful, and that the remembrance of crimes should be avoided.” Here *progress* appears to be redundant, since without it the sentence is clearer and complete: “That forgetfulness of sin is useful,” as though he were saying that this applies not to every sin but to crimes, as he immediately explains.

For *flagitia* properly denotes not every vice but especially sins of the flesh or of lust, because they are shameful, servile, and worthy of the lash. Thus Cicero says in the *Cato*: “Debaucheries, adulteries, and every such shameful offense are stirred up by no enticement other than pleasure”; and in book 2 of *On Ends* he calls lusts shameful (*flagitiosas*).

Such sins are conquered not by resisting them, as with other vices, but by fleeing them—that is, by completely excluding their memory and thought, as has often been said elsewhere (*Conference* 19, chapter 16), and as is clear from the whole context of this chapter. It is therefore not beneficial to revisit and turn over the memory of such past or long-committed sins, because the more they are considered and turned over in detail, the greater the enticement and stimulus—or at least the danger—they bring of vicious lust and pleasure, as Saint Thomas teaches in the passage recently cited on this subject.

Other Fathers who discuss the matter in these Conferences also confirm this teaching. The following passages especially deserve notice. Abbot Serapion says in *Conference* 5, chapter 4: “For those who strive after purity it is of the greatest benefit first to remove from themselves the very materials of these carnal passions, from which either the occasion or the memory of those same passions may be generated in a soul still sick. For a twofold illness requires a twofold cure. From the body, so that desire may not attempt to break out into action, the image and material must necessarily be removed; and for the soul, so that it may not even conceive it in thought, attentive meditation on Scripture, vigilant concern, and the removal of solitude should likewise be beneficially applied.”

Abbot John likewise says in *Conference* 19, chapter 16: “Against the spirit of fornication the method of struggle is different and the situation is unlike that of other vices. For just as the use of lust and proximity to the flesh must be removed from the body, so its memory must be utterly removed from the mind. It is exceedingly harmful to allow even the slightest recollection of this passion into breasts that are still weak and sick,” and so forth.

These statements do not conflict with what the author taught above, or what Abbot Pinuphius taught (*Conference* 20, chapter 7): that for those doing penance the remembrance of sins is not merely useful but necessary, so that with continual contrition of heart they may cry out: “For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Psalm 50), concerning which we noted several things there. The remembrance of sins is useful so that a person may mourn and punish the sins committed, but not in such a way that he lingers in their constant or prolonged thought, imagination, or mental rehearsal.

This applies especially to carnal sins, as stated, both with respect to perfect men, who have wiped away the stains of their former life through prolonged repentance, and with respect to the imperfect and weak, though for different reasons. For the imperfect, the remembrance of such sins is harmful, as is clear from what has been said, because of the fragility of corrupted nature and the danger of vicious pleasure. It is chiefly of such persons that the Apostle James speaks when he says: “Each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire” (James 1).

For the perfect, or those making progress, such remembrance is harmful when on this account they are drawn away from the sweetness of contemplation, the fervor and confidence of prayer, and other holier exercises. This seems especially to be what the abbot had in view in this chapter, and it is indicated by the title prefixed by Dionysius and others.]

This should not be done at all; indeed, even if the memory has forced its way in, it should immediately be expelled. For it greatly draws the mind away from the contemplation of purity, especially in one who lives in solitude, entangling it in the filth of this world and choking it with the stench of vices.

When you recall what you committed under the ruler of this age, whether through ignorance or through lust, let me grant you that no pleasure steals in while you are engaged in this thought; nevertheless, even the mere contagion of the old corruption must necessarily infect the mind with a foul stench and exclude the spiritual fragrance of the virtues—that is, the sweetness of a good odor.

When, therefore, the memory of past vices knocks at the mind, we must recoil from it in the same way that an honorable and serious man recoils if an immodest and shameless woman approaches him in public either in conversation or in embraces. Unless he quickly withdraws from her touch and refuses even the briefest delay in dishonorable conversation, he will not escape the mark of infamy and blame in the judgment of all who pass by, even if he rejects consent to the shameful pleasure.

So, when we have been drawn into such thoughts by a pestilential memory, we too must quickly withdraw from contemplating them and fulfill what Solomon commands:

[Note: [Col. 1167C] The Vulgate text reads: “Keep your way far from her, and do not approach the doors of her house” (Proverbs 5). Jerome has this on the passage: “The Apostle says, ‘Flee fornication’ (1 Corinthians 6), because the first remedy for this vice is to stay far from those whose presence either attracts or contributes to vice. It is also beneficial for weak hearers to be separated from listening to heretics.”]

“Go away,” he says [Lipsius has *go forth* in the margin]; “do not linger in her place, and do not fix your eyes upon her” (Proverbs 5), lest, when the angels see us entangled in filthy and shameful thoughts, they be unable to say of us as they pass by: “The blessing of the Lord be upon you; we have blessed you in the name of the Lord” (Psalm 128).

For it is impossible for the mind to linger upon good thoughts when the governing faculty of the heart has fallen toward shameful and earthly sights [Note: [Col. 1167C] That is, the mind or thought; see the note on *Conference* 7, chapter 12.].

For true is Solomon’s statement:

[Note: [Col. 1167C] The Vulgate version reads: “Your eyes will see strange women, and your heart will speak perverse things; and you will be like one sleeping in the midst of the sea, and like a drowsy pilot who has lost the rudder; and you will say: ‘They struck me, but I did not hurt; they dragged me, but I did not feel it.’” On this passage the venerable Bede says: “The voice of one struck and sleeping is expressed. The mind, sleeping away from vigilant care, is struck and does not suffer; for just as it does not foresee the evils that threaten, so it does not acknowledge those it has committed. He is dragged and feels nothing who is led by the enticements of vices but is not awakened to guard himself.

“He wishes to wake up so that he may find wine again; for although he is weighed down by the sleep of stupor and neglects to guard himself, he nevertheless strives to wake for the concerns of the world, so that he may always become drunk with pleasures. While he sleeps through what he ought to have watched over diligently, he seeks what he might rightly have slept through.” Thus far Bede.]

“When your eyes see a strange woman, then your mouth will speak perverse things, and you will lie as though in the heart of the sea, and like a pilot in a great storm. You will say: ‘They struck me, but I did not suffer; they mocked me, but I did not know it’” (Proverbs 23).

Once all thoughts have been abandoned—not only shameful thoughts but also all earthly thoughts—our mind’s attention must always be lifted toward heavenly things, according to the saying of our Savior: “Where I am,” he says, “there also will my servant be” (John 12).

It frequently happens that, while someone recalls with compassionate feeling either his own falls or those of others who are inexperienced, he himself is struck by the assent of a subtle, pleasure-giving dart; and what began under the appearance of piety ends in an obscene and harmful conclusion.

[Note: [Col. 1167D] This statement is cited in *Conference* 1, chapter 20, where we also made some observations.]

“For there are ways that seem right to men, but their ends lead into the depths of hell” (Proverbs 16).

Therefore we must strive to stir ourselves to laudable compunction through desire and longing for the virtues and the kingdom of heaven rather than through harmful recollections of vices. For a person must necessarily be choked by the most pestilential stench of a sewer for as long as he wishes either to stand above it or to stir up its filth.

## CHAPTER X. On the sign of satisfaction and forgetfulness of past crimes.

[Col. 1168A]

[Note: [Col. 1167D] Chapter 5: The indication of satisfaction and pardon is also to have expelled from our hearts affection for those things. For each person should know that he has not yet been freed from his former sins so long as the image of those things for which he groans, or of similar crimes, has appeared before his eyes while he is devoted to satisfaction and groans, and so long as not to say their enjoyment, but even their recollection, troubles his mind. And below: Then at last we should believe that the former contagions of vices have been forgiven us when the desires and passions of present pleasures have likewise been driven from our heart. How these words should be understood, see what is noted in the same place.]

Let us know, then, as we have often said, that we have finally made satisfaction for past sins when the very impulses and affections through which we committed the acts for which we must repent have been cut away from our hearts. Yet no one should believe that he can attain this who has not first, with all the fervor of his spirit, cut off the very causes and occasions on account of which he fell into those crimes. Thus, for example, if he has fallen into fornication or adultery through a ruinous intimacy with women, he must with the greatest haste avoid even the sight of them; or, if he has been inflamed by an abundance of wine and excessive feasting, he must punish unlawful gluttony with the utmost strictness. Again, if he has fallen into perjury, [Col. 1168B] theft, murder, or blasphemy after being corrupted by the desire for and love of money, he must cut away the alluring material of greed, which deceives him. If he is driven into the vice of anger by the passion of pride, he must tear out the fuel of arrogance by the supreme virtue of humility. Thus, in order that each sin may be extinguished, the cause and occasion through which or on account of which it was committed must first be cut away. By this remedy of healing one undoubtedly also reaches forgetfulness of the crimes committed.

## CHAPTER XI. We ought not to forget venial sins, but only mortal sins

But this definition of the aforementioned forgetfulness [Note: [Col. 1168C] That is, of mortal sins. From this chapter one may establish the distinction between mortal sin, which is called “crime,” and venial sin, or “offense,” a distinction that the heretics Pelagius and Jovinianus removed. Concerning this, St. Gregory, *Moralia* XXI (chapter 9), says: “This is the difference between sin and crime: every crime is a sin, but not every sin is a crime; and in this life many can be without crime, but no one can be without sins.” In this distinction between sins and crimes, it must be considered that some sins pollute the soul, whereas crimes destroy it. St. Augustine says nearly the same in the *Enchiridion* (chapter 64).] is established only with respect to capital crimes, which are also condemned by the Mosaic law; and just as the affections for these are rejected or consumed through a good manner of life, so repentance for them also reaches its end.

As for these lesser sins [Note: [Col. 1168D] The Fathers call these sins “venial,” by a certain allusion to Luke XII: “I tell you, you will not come out from there until you have paid even the last small coin.” By the “last small coin” the Fathers understand the very lightest sins, such as idle words, for which satisfaction will have to be made in the prison of purgatory unless they have been purged or remitted in this life. St. Jerome, on Matthew V: “This is what he means when he says: ‘You will not come out of prison until you have paid even the smallest sins.’” Augustine, *Sermon* 41 *On the Saints*: “In that passing fire of which the Apostle said, ‘He himself will be saved, yet so as through fire,’ not capital sins but lesser sins are purged.” And below: “Although we do not believe that these lesser sins can kill the soul, they nevertheless fill it, as it were, with pustules and with a dreadful scab, and make it so disfigured that they scarcely permit it—or permit it only with great confusion—to come to the embraces of that heavenly Bridegroom.”] among which the righteous person falls seven times, as it is written (Prov. XXIV), and rises again, repentance will never be lacking. For whether through ignorance, forgetfulness, thought, speech, surprise, necessity, or the weakness of the flesh, we frequently fall into them each day, unwillingly or willingly. On account of them David also, praying to the Lord, begs purification and pardon, saying: “Who can understand sins? Cleanse me from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others” (Ps. XVIII). And the Apostle says: “For I do not do the good that I wish, but the evil that I hate, that I do” (Rom. VII). Concerning these matters he also cried out in lamentation: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from the body of this death?” (Ibid.).

For we slip into these matters with such ease, as though by a law of nature, that however great the vigilance and watchfulness with which they are guarded against, [Col. 1169B] [Note: [Col. 1169B] St. Augustine, *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 36: “Except for the holy Virgin Mary, concerning whom, for the honor of the Lord, I wish to raise no question at all when sins are being discussed. For we know from this that she received a greater grace for conquering sin in every respect: she was worthy to conceive and give birth to him who is acknowledged to have had no sin. Therefore, excepting this Virgin, if we could gather all those holy people who lived here and ask them whether they were without sin, what do we think they would have answered except what the Apostle John says: ‘If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us’ (I John I).” Thus Augustine, whose opinion the Church confirmed at the Council of Trent (Session 6, chapter 22), with the following canon: “If anyone says that a person once justified can avoid throughout his entire life all sins, even venial sins, unless by a special privilege from God, as the Church holds concerning the Blessed Virgin, let him be anathema. More will have to be said about these matters in Conference 22, chapter 9, and Conference 23, chapters 6 and following.] these cannot be completely avoided. Indeed, concerning these matters one of the disciples whom Jesus loved, making a categorical pronouncement, says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and his word is not in us” (John I).

Therefore, for one who desires to reach the summit of perfection, it will not be enough to have reached the end of repentance—that is, to abstain from unlawful things—unless he also continually stretches himself forward with tireless effort in those virtues by which one reaches the indications of satisfaction. Nor will it be enough for anyone to have abstained from the most foul stains of crimes, which the Lord abhors, unless he also possesses that good fragrance of virtues in which the Lord delights, through purity of heart and the perfection of apostolic charity.

Thus far Abbot Pinufius has spoken about the indication of satisfaction and the end of repentance. Although he earnestly begged us to prefer remaining in his monastery, when he could not retain us—attracted as we were by the reputation of the Scythian desert—he sent us away.

# THE TWENTY-FIRST CONFERENCE, THE FIRST OF ABBOT THEONAS: ON THE REMISSION OF THE FIFTIETH DAY

[Col. 1169]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1169C]

Before we begin to unfold the words of this conference held with the eminent man Abbot Theonas [Note: [Col. 1169C] The abbot Theonas, or Theon, was discussed at Conference 2, chapter 11. Moved to compunction by his exhortation, Serapion disclosed the hidden vice of gluttony from which he suffered and was miraculously cured of that illness by him. Palladius discusses the same man in *The Lausiac History*, chapter 50, where he calls him a holy man, endowed with the gift of prophecy, and writes that he maintained silence for thirty years. He is also mentioned by Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 28, and by the *Tripartite History*, Book VIII, chapter 1. The three conferences immediately following are attributed to this Theonas: this first one, on the remission of the Fiftieth Day—that is, the relaxation of fasting during the paschal season, as we call it, up to Pentecost; the second, on nocturnal illusions; and the third, on the Apostle’s statement, “For I do not do the good that I wish,” etc.] I think it necessary briefly to touch upon the beginning of his conversion, because from this the merit of the man and the grace given to him will become more evident to the reader.

This man, then, while still very young, was bound by his parents’ care and authority with the bond of marriage. For while they religiously guarded his chastity and feared the uncertain fall of a slippery age, they believed that the impulses of youth should be forestalled by the lawful remedy of marriage. When, therefore, he had spent the period of one lustrum with his wife [Note: [Col. 1169D] For Isidore, a *lustrum* is *πενταετερίς* (*pentaeteris*), that is, a five-year period, which, he says, is said to be instituted every fifth year on account of the Olympiads—among the Romans, in place of the Olympiads. For at that time there were still consuls and still the era; the present reckoning did not yet exist. It is a five-year period. It is called this because, after the census had been conducted in the state, the city of Rome was purified. So he says.
