Varro, Book V: “*Lustrum* signifies a five-year period and is derived from *luendo*, that is, ‘paying,’ because taxes and tribute were paid every fifth year, or because communities were purified every five years.” Since, therefore, the census itself, or *lustrum*, took place every fifth year—the period during which the Roman magistracy of the censors lasted—the custom became established that by *lustrum* a period of five years was understood, what the Greeks call an Olympiad, that is, a five-year period. Hence Sidonius (Book IX, Letter 10) speaks of a *bilustre* period, which the scholiast interprets as ten years.] he came to Abbot John [Note: [Col. 1170D] I think this is the John mentioned above in Conference 18, which bears his name.] who at that time, chosen on account of the merit of his holiness, presided over the diaconia [Note: [Col. 1170D] Baronius teaches here (*Martyrology*, August 8) that *diaconia* should be understood as the administration or management of the monastery. Cassianus likewise calls this office *dispensatio* in Latin, in *Institutes* Book V, chapter 40. Yet it seems much more probable that it should be understood, as in Conference 18, chapter 7, and again below in chapters 8 and 9, as the collection or gathering of money and alms contributed by the people in the church on Sundays for the use of monks and other poor persons. The care and distribution of these funds were entrusted by the elders to a single monk chosen for that purpose, so that he could provide for the needs of the monks and hermits scattered throughout the desert, as well as for other needy or sick people. Hence he was also called the steward; today we call him the almoner. This is made sufficiently clear by the words that follow, where it is said: “When the aforementioned young man had come to the blessed John with devout zeal, bringing religious gifts among the other landowners who eagerly offered the old man tithes or firstfruits of their crops from their possessions,” etc. Such men were said to offer or bring the *diaconia*, or to preside over the *diaconia*—which amounted to distributing alms to the poor, or, as it is commonly said, presiding over the table of the poor. The first to exercise this office were the seven deacons instituted by the Apostles at Jerusalem on that occasion (Acts VI), and at Rome St. Lawrence, deacon and martyr, under Pope Sixtus; and, if one looks to more recent times, Titus the deacon, whom St. Prosper mentions in his *Chronicle* under the year A.D. 429 in these words: “Titus the deacon, a holy man distributing money to the poor at Rome, was killed.” See what is noted elsewhere about the *diaconia* (Conference 18, chapter 7).]

For no one is advanced to this rank by his own will or ambition; rather, it is the man whom the assembly of all the elders, on account of the precedence of his age and the testimony of his faith and virtues, has judged superior and more eminent than all the others.

When, then, the aforementioned young man had come to this blessed John with devout zeal, bringing religious gifts among the other landowners who eagerly offered the aforementioned elder tithes or firstfruits of their crops from their possessions, and when the old man saw that they had come to him with many gifts and wished to repay their devotion in kind, he began, according to the Apostle (I Cor. IX), to sow spiritual things for them, whose material gifts he was reaping. Finally, he began his exhortation as follows.

## CHAPTER II. Abbot John’s exhortation to Theonas and the others who came with him

[Col. 1171B]

“I am indeed delighted, dearest sons, by the pious generosity of your gifts, and I gladly embrace the devotion of this offering, whose distribution has been entrusted to me, because you faithfully offer your firstfruits and tithes, destined for the needs of the indigent, to the Lord as a sacrifice of good fragrance [Col. 1172A]. You believe, of course, that by this offering the fullness of the fruits and of all your possessions, from which you have made this offering to the Lord, will also be abundantly blessed, and that, in accordance with the faithfulness of his command, you yourselves will be enriched even in this age with a manifold abundance of every good thing:

[Note: [Col. 1171D] St. Jerome also cites this from the Greek in his commentary on Ezekiel XLV. The Vulgate reading is: “Honor the Lord with your substance, and give to the poor from the firstfruits of all your crops” (Prov. III). There Jerome says: “Many give much to the poor, but from another person’s substance and from crops that they have seized by force or fraud. Many give generously from what is their own, but by giving they do not honor the Lord, because they act for human approval and not out of love for the heavenly observer. Therefore, whoever desires the fruit of almsgiving to be profitable to him should give from his own possessions and for the honor of the Creator, so that human beings, who are his creation and have been made in his image, may be restored. We are commanded to honor the Lord not only from the substance of money that we extend to the poor, but also from the substance or fruits of every good work that we perform and of all the heavenly grace that we have received—that is, to seek his praise in everything, and not our own. The person also honors the Lord from his substance and from the firstfruits of his crops who attributes everything good that he does not to his own strength and merits but to heavenly grace, remembering the saying: ‘Without me you can do nothing’ (Matthew VI).]

“Honor God from your just labors, and offer him the first portion of the fruits of your righteousness, so that your granaries may be filled with an abundance of grain, and your winepresses may overflow with wine” (Prov. III).

By faithfully carrying out this devotion [Lipsius, in the margin: “taking up”], know that you have fulfilled the righteousness of the ancient law. Under that law, those who transgressed it inevitably incurred guilt, while those who fulfilled it could not reach the summit of perfection.”

## CHAPTER III. On the offering of tithes and firstfruits

[Col. 1172B]

“Tithes [Note: [Col. 1172C] In Numbers XVIII it is said of the Levites: ‘They shall possess nothing else, content with the offering of tithes, which I have set apart for their uses and necessities.’ This entire passage seems to have been taken from St. Jerome’s commentary on Ezekiel XLV, where he distinguishes four kinds of tithes. ‘The *δεκάδα*,’ he says, ‘that is, the tenth part of all crops, the people owed by law to the Levitical tribe. Again, from those tithes the Levites—that is, the lower order of ministers—gave a tenth to the priests, and this is called the *δευτεροδεκάδα*. There were also other tithes that each member of the people of Israel set aside in his granaries, so that he might eat them when he went to the temple in the city of Jerusalem and in the temple court, and might invite the priests and Levites to the banquets. There were still other tithes that they stored up for the poor, which in Greek are called *πτωχοδεκάδαι*.’ But the *primitiva*—that is, the firstfruits—which they offered from their crops were not defined by a fixed number; they were left to the discretion of the offerers. We have received the tradition of the Hebrews that this was not prescribed by law but established by the discretion of the teachers: those who gave most gave a fortieth part to the priests, while those who gave least gave a sixtieth; anything they wished could be offered between a fortieth and a sixtieth. Therefore, what was left uncertain in the Pentateuch is here specifically defined on account of the priests’ greed, so that they might not demand more from the people in the presentation of firstfruits—that is, so that they might offer a sixtieth part of what the earth produces.’ Thus Jerome.]

“According to the Lord’s command, were set apart for the uses of the Levites, while offerings and firstfruits were consecrated to the priests (Num. V and XVIII). This, however, was the rule for firstfruits: a fiftieth part of either crops or animals was to be provided for the service of the temple or priests (Num. III). The more lukewarm, reducing this amount faithlessly, paid a sixtieth part of their produce, while the more devout, increasing it, paid a fortieth part.” [Col. 1173A]

[Note: [Col. 1173B] “The law,” says the Apostle, “was not established for the just but for the unjust,” etc. (I Tim. I). Augustine teaches that the true meaning of this statement should be sought from other similar statements of the same Apostle, such as Romans VI: “You are not under the law but under grace”; chapter VII: “Now we have been released from the law, in which we were held”; and Galatians V: “If you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.” By these statements the Apostle does not mean that the just are not bound by laws or that they do not sin if they do not observe the law. Rather, they do not have the law over them as though it were hanging over their necks, frightening and threatening them with a scourge, as it does the unjust, who obey laws only from fear of punishment. The just do good out of love for righteousness and willingly; they would do so even if there were no law or if it threatened no punishment. Thus they are a law to themselves, showing that the work of the law is written in their hearts, as the Apostle says in Romans II. Therefore the law has no coercive force over them, as St. Thomas says (I–II, question 96, article 5, reply to objection 1), whereas it does over the unjust. The poet expressed the same idea elegantly in these verses:

> The good hate sin from love of virtue;  
> the wicked hate sin from fear of punishment.

For this reason the just are said to be in the law rather than under the law, as the same Apostle says of himself (I Cor. IX): “To those who are under the law I became as though I were under the law” (though I myself was not under the law), “and to those who were without the law I became as though I were without the law” (though I was not without God’s law, but was in Christ’s law).

In this sense St. Thomas (*Commentary* and I–II, question 93, article 6) explains that the law was not established for the just—that is, it was not imposed as a burden weighing upon them through fear and terror of punishment, or with coercive force, as was just said. But how the Apostle can say that the just are not under the law (Gal. V), he explains as follows:

“Those words of the Apostle can be understood in two ways. First, a person may be understood to be under the law when he submits unwillingly to the obligation of the law, as to a kind of burden. Thus the gloss says there that the person is under the law who abstains from evil works through fear of the punishment threatened by the law, and not through love of righteousness. In this sense spiritual persons are not under the law, because through charity, which the Holy Spirit has poured into their hearts, they willingly fulfill what belongs to the law.

“Second, it may be understood in the sense that the works of a person who is led by the Holy Spirit are called more properly the works of the Holy Spirit than the works of the person himself. Since, therefore, the Holy Spirit is not under the law, it follows that works of this kind, insofar as they are the works of the Holy Spirit, are not under the law.”]

For the just, for whom the law was not established, are shown not to be under the law in this way: they strive not only to fulfill the righteousness of the law but even to surpass it. Their devotion is greater than the legal command; while adding abundance to the observance of the precepts, it voluntarily adds what is beyond obligation. [Lipsius, in the margin: “willingly”]

## CHAPTER IV. That Abraham, David, and the other saints surpassed the commandments of the law

Thus we read that Abraham surpassed the commands of the future law when, after defeating the four kings, he refused entirely to touch any of the spoils of Sodom, which as victor were not unjustly owed to him and which the king himself, whose spoils he had recovered, humbly offered him. Calling upon the divine name, he proclaimed: “I raise my hand to the most high God, who made heaven and earth: if I take anything from all that is yours, from a thread to a sandal strap” (Gen. XIV).

Likewise we know that David surpassed the commandments of the law. When Moses commanded that retaliation be rendered to enemies, he not only failed to do this but also embraced those who persecuted him in love; he piously prayed to the Lord for them, even weeping bitterly, and avenged the slain. [Note: [Col. 1174C] Moses did not impose the law of retaliation upon individual private persons, as the scribes and Pharisees wrongly understood it, but only upon judges and magistrates, as has been said elsewhere (Conference 8, chapter 24). That is, in judging and punishing injuries inflicted upon one’s neighbor and brought before the court, they were to observe this rule and measure, punishing the guilty with retaliation: inflicting wound for wound, bruise for bruise, death for death, and taking eye for eye and tooth for tooth.]

We likewise prove that Elijah and Jeremiah were not under the law. Although they could have used marriage lawfully and without reproach, [Note: [Col. 1174C] St. Jerome also testifies that Elijah, Elisha, Jeremiah, and others in the Old Testament remained virgins, in his letter to Eustochium (Letter 22): “Elijah was a virgin, Elisha a virgin, the sons of the prophets were virgins. And to Jeremiah it is said: ‘And you shall not take a wife.’” In Book I *Against Jovinianus*, chapter 13, he rebukes Jovinianus for foolishly placing Elijah and Elisha in the catalog of married men. Cassianus also confirms this in *Institutes* Book VI, chapter 4.] they preferred nevertheless to remain virgins.

Likewise we read that Elisha and the other men of the same purpose surpassed the Mosaic commandments. Concerning them the Apostle says: “They went about in sheepskins, in goatskins, afflicted, oppressed, needy; the world was not worthy of them; they wandered in deserts and mountains, and in caves and caverns of the earth” (Heb. XI). [Note: [Col. 1174D] St. Jerome discusses these men in his letter to Paulinus (Letter 13). Counting them among the monks of the Old Testament, he says: “Among these are also the sons of Rechab, who did not drink wine or strong drink, who lived in tents, who are praised by God’s voice through Jeremiah, and to whom it is promised that a man from their line would not cease to stand before the Lord (Jer. XXXV). I think that this is also signified by the title of Psalm LXX: ‘Of the sons of Jonadab and of those who were first led into captivity.’ This is Jonadab the son of Rechab, who is written in the Book of Kings as having mounted a chariot with Jehu (IV Kings X). His sons are those who always lived in tents and who, finally, because of the invasion of the Chaldean army, were compelled to enter the city and are said to have endured this first captivity—after the freedom of the desert, they were enclosed in the city as in a prison.”]

What should I say about the sons of Jonadab, son of Rechab? When the prophet Jeremiah, at the Lord’s command, offered them wine, we read that they answered him: “We do not drink wine, because Jonadab, son of Rechab, our father, commanded us, saying: ‘You and your sons shall not drink wine forever; you shall not build a house, sow seed, or plant vineyards, nor shall you possess them, but you shall live in tents all your days’” (Jer. XXXV). Hence they also deserved to hear from the same prophet: “Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: There shall never fail to be a man from the line of Jonadab, son of Rechab, standing in my presence all the days” (Ibid.).

All these men, not content merely to offer tithes of their possessions but rejecting the possessions themselves, offered themselves and their souls to God instead. No human being can make any exchange for them, as the Lord declares in the Gospel: “What exchange will a man give for his soul?” (Matt. XVI).

## CHAPTER V. That those living under the grace of the Gospel ought to surpass the legal commandments
Therefore we must understand that we—by whom the legal commandment is no longer required, but to whom the evangelical proclamation daily resounds, “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything that you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19)—when we offer God tithes from our possessions, are still in some manner held under the burden of the Law and have not yet reached that evangelical height which, when obeyed, rewards its followers not only with the benefits of the present life but also with future rewards.

For the Law promised those who fulfilled it not the rewards of heavenly kingdoms but the comforts of this life, saying: “Whoever does these things shall live by them” (Lev. 18). But the Lord said to his disciples and apostles: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5); and, “Everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life” (Matt. 19).

And rightly so. For it is not so praiseworthy to abstain from what is unlawful as it is also to abstain from what is lawful, and not to use, out of reverence for him, those things which he permitted us to use because of our weakness. Therefore, if even those who faithfully offer the tithes of their fruits and serve the Lord’s earlier commandments are still unable to ascend to the evangelical summit, you can clearly see how far from it are those who do not even do this. For how will those who disdain to fulfill even the lesser commandments of the Law be able to share in evangelical grace?

The ease of these commandments is so strongly attested by the legislator’s authoritative words that a curse is even pronounced against those who do not fulfill them: “For cursed is everyone who does not remain in all the things written in the book of this law, to do them” (Deut. 27). Here, however, because of the excellence and sublimity of the commandments, it is said: “Whoever can accept it, let him accept it” (Matt. 19).

There, the violent compulsion of the lawgiver indicates the modest character of the precepts. “For I call heaven and earth to witness against you today,” he says, “that if you do not observe the commandments of the Lord your God, you will perish from the face of the earth” (Deut. 4). Here, the magnificence of the lofty commandments is signified by the very manner not so much of one commanding as of one exhorting: “If you wish to be perfect, do this or that” (Matt. 19).

There, Moses imposes an inescapable burden even upon those who refuse. Here, Paul comes to the aid of those who desire and hasten toward perfection. For what cannot be grasped universally by all because of its wondrous sublimity was not to be imposed as a general command—or, so to speak, canonically required of everyone—but rather all are invited by counsel and grace, so that those who are great may deservedly be crowned by the power of perfection, while those who are small and cannot fulfill the measure of the fullness of Christ, though they may seem to lie hidden beneath the brilliance of their superiors like stars, may nevertheless remain free from the darkness of the curses contained in the Law. Nor are they cast down by the disasters of present evils or punished with eternal torment.

[Note: This is a common discussion concerning the evangelical counsels, to which monks bind themselves voluntarily and freely and which are distinguished from commandments. Several commendations by the holy Fathers, agreeing with this passage, deserve notice here. Gregory Nazianzen, *Oration 1 Against Julian*: “Among our laws,” he says, “some impose the necessity of obedience and cannot be omitted without danger; others do not constrain by necessity but are left to choice and free will. Accordingly, they have this character: those who observe them are adorned with honor and rewards, while those who fulfill them less completely need fear no danger.”

Cyprian, *On the Habit of Virgins*: “The Lord does not command this, but exhorts; nor does he impose the yoke of necessity, since the freedom of the will remains unimpaired. But when he says that there are many dwellings with his Father, he points out the lodging of a better dwelling. You seek these better dwellings; by cutting off the desires of the flesh, you obtain in heaven the reward of greater grace.”

Ambrose, *On Widows*: “Those who fulfill the commandment,” he says, “can say: ‘We are useless servants; we have done what we were obliged to do’” (Luke 17). A virgin does not say this; neither does the one who sold his possessions and distributed them to the poor.

Jerome, *Book I Against Jovinian*: “The master of the contest offers a reward, invites to the race, holds in his hand the prize of virginity, displays the purest fountain, and cries out: ‘If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink.’ He does not say: ‘Whether you wish it or not, you must drink and run’; but, ‘Whoever wishes, whoever is able to run and drink—he will conquer, he will be satisfied.’ And for this reason Christ loves virgins more, because they freely offer what was not commanded them,” etc. (See the same author, *Epistle 12 to Eustochium*, chap. 8).]

Christ, therefore, does not constrain anyone to those lofty heights of virtue by the necessity of a commandment; rather, he summons them through the power of free will, through the usefulness of counsel, and kindles them with the desire for perfection. For where there is a commandment, there is necessity;

[Note: Theologians distinguish three kinds of necessity, just as they distinguish three kinds of freedom (Bellarmine, *On Monks*, book II, chap. 29).

The first is natural necessity, which is an absolute determination toward one thing; thus animals act by necessity. Opposed to this is freedom of choice, which exists in human beings.

The second is the necessity of compulsion, whether it is absolute compulsion—as when someone is forcibly dragged somewhere he does not wish to go—or moral and quasi-conditional compulsion: when someone does not wish to do something and does not do it willingly, yet does it under compulsion from some human or servile fear. The Apostle speaks of this necessity when he says, “Not from sadness or necessity.” And to Philemon: “So that your good may not be as though from necessity, but voluntary”—that is, not compelled or extorted against one’s will, but arising from one’s own affection.

The third is the necessity of obligation, whether it arises from a commandment or from a vow; opposed to this is freedom from such obligation. We are said to do freely what we are not bound to do, and necessarily what we are bound to do. Such necessity, however, does not exclude freedom of choice but presupposes it; nor does it diminish the goodness or merit of the work, but rather increases it.

Thus St. Augustine says in his letter to Armentarius, who was distressed over having made a vow of continence: “Do not regret that you made your vow; rather rejoice that you are no longer permitted to do what, to your detriment, would have been permitted. Happy is the necessity that compels us to better things.”

It is of this necessity that the abbot speaks here when he says, “Where there is a commandment, there is necessity.” For he is comparing the commandments of the Mosaic Law with the evangelical counsels, which are works of perfection and, as he calls them, lofty heights of virtue. For this reason, that necessity of a commandment ought not to have been imposed upon them, lest difficulty follow from such necessity—not indeed from the commandment in itself and by its nature, but from human vice and weakness, as happens in the observance of legal requirements.

What is said here—“Where there is necessity, there is difficulty; where there is difficulty, there is negligence,” and so forth—is indeed true of that necessity of compulsion which the Apostle calls “the spirit of slavery in fear” (Rom. 8), by which the Jews observed the commandments of the Law. It is not true, however, of the necessity of a commandment or vow, considered in itself and absolutely. It can happen—indeed, it ordinarily does happen—that what is done by commandment or vow is done more willingly and readily than what is done without a commandment or vow.

If some perform such things with sadness and difficulty, this occurs because of human perversity or weakness, not because of the nature of a commandment or vow. Nothing, therefore, can be concluded from this against the excellence and dignity of a vow, as though it were better or more meritorious to do something without a vow than by virtue of a vow. The contrary must be maintained, as St. Thomas teaches and explains for three reasons.

First, he says, to make a vow is an act of worship, which is the chief among the moral virtues. The work of a nobler virtue is better and more meritorious.

Second, one who vows something and fulfills it subjects himself more fully to God than one who merely does it. For he subjects himself to God not only with respect to the act but also with respect to his power, just as one gives more who gives a tree with its fruits than one who gives only the fruits, as Anselm says in *The Book of Similitudes* (chap. 84).

Third, through a vow the will is immovably confirmed in the good. To do something from a will confirmed in the good belongs to the perfection of virtue, as is clear from Aristotle in the second book of the *Ethics* (chap. 4). Just as to sin with a stubborn mind aggravates the sin and is called sin against the Holy Spirit, so St. Thomas teaches (*Summa Theologiae* II–II, q. 88, art. 6).]

Where there is a commandment, therefore, there is necessity; where there is necessity, there is difficulty; where there is difficulty, there is negligence; where there is negligence, there is sin; and where there is sin, consequently there is punishment. Those who observe the things to which they are compelled by the fixed severity of the Law merely escape the punishment threatened by it; they do not obtain a reward or recompense.

## CHAPTER VI. How the grace of the Gospel, as it grants the kingdoms of heaven to the perfect, so mercifully sustains the weak.

[Col. 1178A]

Thus,

[Note: Some manuscripts connect this chapter with the preceding ones. The printed editions separate it, as does Dionysius. Moreover, the teaching of this chapter is confirmed by St. Fulgentius on Matthew 24, where he says: “In these commandments”—that is, the evangelical ones—“as in most abundant dishes, such a spiritual abundance of heavenly delights overflows that in the word of God there is enough for the perfect to eat and enough also for the little one to suck. For there are there both the milky drink by which the tender infancy of believers is nourished, and the solid food by which the vigorous youth of the perfect may receive spiritual growth in holy virtue” (see Blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, *Letter to Titus*).]

As the evangelical word raises up the strong to sublime and exalted things, so it does not allow the weak to sink to the depths: granting indeed the fullness of blessedness to the perfect, but bestowing pardon upon frailty.

[Note: An obscure statement; and perhaps made still more obscure by Dionysius’s very paraphrase, which came into my hands rather corruptly printed, and reads as follows: “For the Law placed those who had fulfilled its commandments, as it were, in a certain middle position between the two deserts, separating them from the glory of the perfect by as much as it separates them from the condemnation of transgressors.” Nor does Lavardin seem to me to have grasped the meaning. It can be derived only from the preceding chapter, where the following antitheses, as it were, or contrasts and differences between the two laws, the old and the new, are set forth: the old law, a law of fear; the new law, a law of charity. The old law is low in its precepts—namely, the ceremonial ones, which the Apostle calls weak and beggarly elements and carnal ordinances [Col. 1178A]—severe and rigid in punishments and penalties, threats and curses; sparing and poor in rewards, since they are merely temporal and earthly (Gal. 4; Heb. 7). Conversely, the new law is exalted in its evangelical precepts and counsels, lavish and generous in heavenly and eternal rewards, gentle in imposing punishments and remitting sins, inviting rather than frightening, and granting peace, indulgence, and pardon to all penitents.

The old law weighs perfect and imperfect, strong and weak, in an equal balance, rewarding and punishing both alike; and thus places and leaves both in the middle position, as it is here called, of the two deserts—that is, of reward and punishment [Col. 1178B]—in an equal condition. But the new law always calls and advances the strong to higher things, while being indulgent toward the weak, rewarding the former with ampler prizes and decreeing to the latter rewards also proportionate to their merits. Thus, by as much as the old law separates from the condemnation of transgressors, by so much does it separate from the glory of the perfect: that is, the old law differs from the new in rewarding those who observe it as much as it differs in withholding punishment from transgressors. For as its precepts are low and slight, so too are its rewards; and as the punishments of transgressors are temporal and external, so too is the recompense of observers temporal and external, whereas under the new and evangelical law the case is the reverse.

Yet these matters seem to require fuller and more exact explanation from St. Thomas, who, treating of this difference between the Mosaic and evangelical laws, says: “It must be said that all the differences assigned between the new law and the old are understood according to perfect and imperfect. For the precepts of every law concern acts of virtue; but the imperfect, who do not yet possess the habit of virtue, are inclined to perform virtuous works differently from those who are perfected through the habit of virtue. Those who do not yet have the habit of virtue are inclined to perform works of virtue through some external cause, for example through the threat of punishments or the promise of certain external rewards, such as honor, riches, or the like. Therefore the old law, which was given to the imperfect—that is, to those who had not yet attained spiritual grace—was called a law of fear, insofar as it led men to observe its precepts through the threat of certain punishments; and it is said to have certain temporal promises.

“But those who possess virtue are inclined to perform virtuous acts for love of virtue, not on account of some external punishment or reward. Therefore the new law, whose principal element consists in spiritual grace itself infused into hearts, is called a law of love and is said to have spiritual and eternal promises, which [Col. 1178D] are the objects of virtue, especially of charity. For this reason the old law is also said to restrain the hand, not the mind: because one who abstains from sin through fear of punishment does not have his will simply withdraw from sin, as does the will of one who abstains from sin through love of justice. Therefore the new law, which is a law of love, is said to restrain the mind.

“Nevertheless, some in the state of the Old Testament possessed charity and the grace of the Holy Spirit, principally awaiting spiritual and eternal promises; in this respect they belonged to the new law. Likewise, even in the New Testament there are some carnal persons who have not yet attained the perfection of the new law and who had to be led, even in the New Testament, to works of virtue through fear [Col. 1179D] of punishments and through certain temporal promises. Although the old law gave precepts of charity, nevertheless through it the Holy Spirit was not given, by whom charity is poured into our hearts, as is said in Romans 3.” Thus St. Thomas; by whose words the teaching of this and the following chapters is wonderfully illustrated and made clear.]

For the Law placed those who fulfilled its commandments, as it were, in a certain middle position between the two deserts, separating them from the condemnation of transgressors by as much as it separates them from the glory of the perfect. How low and miserable that condition is, consider even from the state and comparison of the present life, in which it is judged most miserable if a person strives and labors only not to be regarded as guilty among honorable people, rather than also as wealthy, honorable, and glorious.

## CHAPTER VII. How it lies within our power whether we wish to remain under the grace of the Gospel or under the terror of the Law.

Therefore it lies within our power today whether we wish to remain under the grace of the Gospel or under the terror of the Law. For each person must necessarily be assigned to one side or the other according to the character of his action. For Christ’s grace receives those who go beyond [Col. 1179B] the Law; or else the Law holds back those who are inferior as its debtors and persons bound to it. For one guilty of neglecting the legal precepts will by no means be able to attain evangelical perfection, though he vainly boasts that he is a Christian and has been set free by the Lord’s grace.

For not only must that person be considered still under the Law who refuses to fulfill what the Law commands, but also the one who is content to observe only what the Law enjoins and by no means produces fruits worthy of Christ’s calling and grace. There it is not said, “You shall offer your tithes and firstfruits to the Lord your God,” but, “Go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Deut. 12; Matt. 19; Luke 9). There, because of the magnificence of perfection, not even the briefest interval of an hour is granted to the disciple who asks leave for his father’s burial, nor is the duty of human affection preferred to the power of divine love.

## CHAPTER VIII. How Theonas exhorted his wife to renounce the world as well.

Having heard these things, the blessed Theonas, inflamed with an inextinguishable desire for evangelical perfection, received the seed of the word in a fruitful heart and, as it were, deposited it in deep, cultivated furrows. He was especially humbled and compuncted because the elder had said that he had not merely failed to attain evangelical perfection but had scarcely fulfilled even the commandments of the Law itself.

[Col. 1180A]

For although he was accustomed to pay the tithes of his crops yearly to the diaconia,

[Note: On the diaconia, see above (chapter 1); and observe further here that tithes and firstfruits were formerly brought and offered by the people in the Church to the diaconia—that is, to the common table of the poor—from which both monks and other ministers of the Church received food, dispensed by the steward. The abbot Theonas is said in the following chapter to have exercised this office after the abbot Elias.]

he thought that he had not even heard of the requirement of firstfruits. Yet even if he had fulfilled this in the same manner, he humbly confessed that, according to the elder’s judgment, he was nevertheless still far from evangelical perfection.

He therefore returned home sad, afflicted with that sorrow which works steadfast repentance unto salvation; and, being no longer doubtful of his own resolve and determination, he turned all the concern and care of his mind toward his wife’s salvation. He began by similar exhortation to invite her to the desire with which he himself had been inflamed and, with tears by day and night, to urge her that conversion to a better life ought by no means to be delayed, because the vain hope of immature age would not forestall the necessity of sudden death, which carries off infants, boys, youths, and old people alike by the same lot.

## CHAPTER IX. How, when his wife did not consent, he hastened to the monastery.

[Note: This entire chapter, which relates the remarkable action of the abbot Theonas, who, leaving his wife even against her will and while she resisted, betook himself to the desert and monastic life, was learnedly and carefully examined and explained by D. Cuychius, [Col. 1180D] who refuted every reason alleged by Theonas himself in defense and approval of his divorce, so that it seems almost superfluous to add anything to his judgment. Yet I shall set down here Bellarmine’s opinion alone concerning this act. Having first proved from Scripture, then from the Fathers, and finally from the sacred decrees of popes and councils, that a ratified and consummated marriage is not dissolved by monastic profession, and that after consummation of marriage spouses may not vow continence or monastic life except by mutual consent, he answers this objection made from the example of Theonas: it is one of those deeds of saints which are to be admired, not imitated. For it must be believed that it was done through a special warning or inspiration of the Holy Spirit, outside the common order and law, since afterwards he shone forth with so many signs and virtues. Thus he. Ciaconius says almost the same in his annotation.]

And when his wife, though he persisted continually in entreaties of this kind, most stubbornly gave no assent and said that, in the flower of her age, she could not entirely abstain from marital consolation, and that consequently, if, abandoned by him, she committed any fault, it ought rather to be imputed to him who had broken the bonds of marriage, he replied as follows. After he had long set before her the condition of human nature, how fragile and uncertain it is, and how dangerous it is to remain longer entangled in carnal

[Col. 1180C]

desires and works, he added that no one may deprive himself of a good that he has come to know, and that it is more harmful to despise a goodness once known than not to love one that is unknown. Therefore, he said, he was already entangled in the guilt of prevarication if, having found gifts so splendid and heavenly, he preferred earthly and filthy things.

He said that the magnificence of perfection belongs to every age and every sex, and that all members of the Church are summoned to climb the height of lofty merits, the Apostle saying: “So run that you may obtain” (1 Cor. 9). The ready and eager ought not to stop because of the delays of the slow and sluggish, since it is more fitting that the idle be stirred by those running ahead than that those hastening be held back by those sitting still.

Therefore, he said, he had resolved and determined to renounce the world and die to the world so that he might live to God. And if he could not obtain this blessedness so as to pass with his companion into fellowship with Christ, he would rather be saved even with the loss of one member and enter the kingdom of heaven maimed, as it were, than be condemned with bodily soundness (Matt. 18).

He added also these words: “If Moses permitted wives to be dismissed because of hardness of heart (Deut. 24; Matt. 19), why should Christ not permit this for the desire of chastity? Especially since the same Lord, among the other affections—that is, for fathers, mothers, and children, to whom not only the Law (Exod. 20) but he himself (Matt. 15) had commanded every reverence to be shown—nevertheless decreed that, for his name and the desire for perfection, they must not merely be simply disregarded but even hated (Luke 14). He similarly joins the name of wives with them, saying: ‘And everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life’ (Matt. 19).

“He allows nothing to be compared with the perfection that he preaches, so that he even dissolves that bond of father and mother which, according to the Apostle, holds the first commandment with a promise: ‘Honor, that is, father and mother, which is the first commandment with a promise, that it may be well with

[Col. 1181C]

you and that you may be long-lived upon the earth’ (Eph. 6); and he commands it to be disregarded for love of himself (Matt. 19). Therefore, just as the evangelical word plainly condemns those who break the marriage bond when adultery has not intervened, so, for love of Christ and desire for chastity, it promises a hundredfold rewards to those who have rejected the carnal yoke.

“Therefore, if it is possible that, having at last accepted reason, you may be turned to this most desirable lot for me—namely, that, serving the Lord, we may together escape the punishment of Gehenna—I do not reject the affection of marriage; indeed, I embrace it with still greater love. For I acknowledge and honor my helper, assigned to me by the Lord’s decree; and I do not refuse to cleave to her in Christ by the unbroken bond of charity, nor do I separate from myself what the Lord joined to me by the law of my very first creation, provided that you too are what the Creator willed you to be.

“But if you are unwilling to be a helper but instead a deception; if you prefer to show yourself not an aid to me but an adversary, and think that the sacrament of marriage was conferred for this purpose—that, by defrauding yourself of the salvation now offered, you should moreover draw me away from discipleship of the Savior—I shall courageously embrace that saying spoken by the mouth of the abbot John, indeed of Christ, so that no carnal affection can tear me away from spiritual good: ‘For whoever does not hate father and mother and children and brothers and sisters and wife and fields, and even his own life, cannot be my disciple’ (Luke 14).”

When the woman’s purpose was not bent by these and similar words but remained in the same hardness of obstinacy, blessed Theonas said: “If I cannot draw you away from death, neither will you separate me from Christ. It is safer for me to have a divorce from a human being than from God.”

Therefore, with God’s grace assisting him, he at once undertook to carry out his resolution and did not allow the ardor of his desire to grow lukewarm through any delay. For immediately, stripped of all worldly property, he hastened to the monastery. There in a short time he shone with such splendor of holiness and humility that, when John of blessed memory departed from this life to the Lord,

[Note: Palladius mentions two abbots or anchorites named Elias in the *Lausiac History*: one in *Lausiac History* 51, of whom he says: “We saw another old man also in the desert of Antony, which is the metropolis of Thebes, named Elias, who was one hundred and ten years old. They said that the spirit of Elijah the prophet had rested upon him,” etc. Sozomen, book 6, chapter 28; Nicephorus, book 11, chapter 34; and Rufinus, book 2, chapter 12, speak of the same man. The other is in *Lausiac History* 111. But neither seems suited to this passage. For the former spent seventy years alone on a certain inaccessible mountain, so that, Palladius says, it was frightening even to see it. The latter lived in a cave in places of Palestine, not among Egyptian monks living a common life, as is the case with the person discussed here. The Author likewise mentions the abbot Elias in book 5 of the *Lives of the Fathers*, book 9. John Moschus also mentions another abbot Elias [Col. 1182D] in the *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 19.]

and likewise the holy Elias, a man who was not inferior to his predecessor,

[Note: A predecessor is so called because he has departed before and yielded his place to a successor, just as a successor succeeds a predecessor. So Sidonius, book 5, letter 16; Pope Celestine, letter 1, chapter 2; the Sixth Council of Carthage, canon 1; Cassiodorus, book 7, letter 2; Gregory of Tours, book 4, *On St. Martin*, chapter 7; and the Twelfth Council of Toledo, chapter 1.]

had similarly departed, Theonas was chosen third by the unanimous judgment of all and succeeded them in the administration of the diaconia

[Col. 1182C]

## CHAPTER X. Cassian explains why he has introduced this example.

[Note: These are Cassian’s words, not those of the abbot John, as the context shows, although at first sight it might seem otherwise. Cassian excuses himself for having recounted the example of the abbot Theonas, from which he might seem to intend to recommend marital divorces. He rejects that suspicion of himself, neither approving nor condemning the deed, but leaving it to the judgment of others.]

Let no one suppose that we have set these things forth to provoke marital divorces. We not only do not condemn marriage but, following the apostolic statement, say: “Marriage is honorable in all things, and the bed undefiled” (Heb. 13). Rather, we have done so in order faithfully to disclose to the reader the beginning of the conversion by which that great man was dedicated to God. From him I first ask this favor: whether the matter pleases or displeases him, let him grant that I am in no way open to calumny, and in this deed let him either praise or blame its author

[Col. 1183A].

But I, who have not expressed my own opinion on this matter but have embraced the history of the deed in a simple narrative, ought, fairly, to claim nothing for myself from the praise of those who approve this deed, and likewise not to be struck by the hostility of those who disapprove it. Let each person, therefore, as we have said, have his own judgment concerning it. But I warn him so to restrain the censure of his own examination that he may not think himself more just or holier than the divine judgment, which bestowed upon him even apostolic signs of virtues; not to mention the judgment of so many Fathers, by whom his deed was not merely not blamed, but plainly so highly praised that by election to the diaconia they preferred him to men of the highest and most exalted rank.

And I think that the judgment of so many spiritual men, uttered with God as its author [Lips. in the margin: *approved*], did not err, a judgment which was also confirmed by so great a wonder of signs, as has already been said above.

## CHAPTER XI. The question why, in Egypt, people do not fast throughout the days of Pentecost or bend their knees in prayer.

But now it is time to continue the order of the promised discussion. Accordingly, when Abbot Theonas had visited us during the days of the Quinquagesima, [Note: [Col. 1183A] We discussed the Quinquagesima in Book II of the *Institutes*, chapter 18, where, following the opinion of the ancients, we distinguished two Quinquagesimas: one of fasting and repentance before Easter, the other of joy and remission after Easter, namely from Easter Day until Pentecost; it is the latter that is under discussion here. It is called Quinquagesima, or in Greek *Pentecost*, because it comprises a period of fifty days. Thus St. Jerome, writing against Montanus and the Luciferians, said “throughout the whole Pentecost” (Letter 54, to Marcellus, and *Against the Luciferians*, chapter 4). Yet elsewhere (Letter 22, to Eustochium) he takes “Pentecost” not for the whole Quinquagesima, or period of fifty days, but, as is commonly done, for their endpoint or conclusion—that is, for the solemnity of Pentecost itself, or the coming of the Holy Spirit, which completes and concludes the Quinquagesima—according to the words of Acts 2: “When the days of Pentecost were completed.” Among other things, he writes as follows concerning the institutions of the Egyptian monks:

“The fast of the whole year is the same, except during Lent, when a stricter way of life is permitted. From Easter to Pentecost, evening meals are changed into midday meals, both to satisfy ecclesiastical tradition and not to burden the stomach with doubled food.”

Thus St. Jerome says: “From Easter to Pentecost, evening meals are changed into midday meals”; for before Easter—that is, during Lent—they ate only an evening meal without a midday meal, whereas after Easter until Pentecost they ate at midday without an evening meal, always content with a single meal unless they were compelled by the presence of guests to set the table more often. This change took place among them for two reasons. First, so that they might satisfy the Church’s tradition concerning the remission of the Quinquagesima, by relaxing to some extent that stricter fast which they had kept before Easter until evening, or at least until the ninth hour. Second, so that they would not excessively burden and weigh down the body, already weakened and enfeebled, with doubled food—that is, with two meals.

There is moreover a distinguished monument of this ancient monastic institution and observance in canon 13 of the Second Council of Tours, in these words:

“As for fasts, the ancient arrangements established by the monks shall be observed, so that from Easter until Quinquagesima [Col. 1183D] (that is, Pentecost), except during the Rogation days, a midday meal shall be prepared for the brothers every day. After Quinquagesima, let there be a strict fast throughout the entire week. Thereafter, until the Kalends of August, let them fast during the week on the second, fourth, and sixth days, except those who are constrained by some illness. In August, because the Masses of the saints are celebrated daily, let them have a midday meal. Throughout September and November, let them fast three times a week. From December until the Lord’s Nativity, let them fast every day. And because from the Lord’s Nativity until Epiphany there are festivals every day, they shall likewise eat a midday meal.” And shortly afterward: “After Epiphany, until Lent, let them fast three times a week.”

These passages show that various fasts of the monks were instituted according to the diversity of seasons, while the Quinquagesima, or Paschal season, was always excepted, as stated above (Book II of the *Institutes*, final chapter).]

When the evening solemnity of prayer had ended, we sat for a short while on the ground and began to inquire more carefully why among them such strict care was taken that no one throughout the entire Quinquagesima should either bend his knees in prayer or presume to fast until the ninth hour [Col. 1185A]—and we investigated this all the more diligently because we had never seen such a practice observed with such caution in the monasteries of Syria.

[Col. 1184A] Moreover, that those monks neither bent their knees in public prayer throughout all the days of the Quinquagesima nor presumed to fast until the ninth hour, as they commonly did at other times, was not peculiar to them but was commonly observed throughout the Church by ancient tradition: this is attested by many highly authoritative writers.

Tertullian, in Book *On the Crown of the Soldier* (chapter 3), says:

“We consider fasting, or worshiping on our knees, unlawful; from Easter until Pentecost we enjoy the same exemption.”

St. Jerome, in *Against the Luciferians* (as Rhenanus noted), seems to have imitated this passage of Tertullian, in these words (chapter 4):

“For many other practices that are observed in the Churches by tradition have claimed for themselves the authority of written law—for example, immersing the head three times in the font” [that is, threefold immersion in baptism]; “on Sunday and throughout the whole Pentecost, not worshiping on one’s knees” [that is, not praying with knees bent] “and relaxing the fast, along with many other practices not written down, which reasonable observance has claimed for itself.”

Again, concerning fasting, the same Jerome says in the preface to the Rule of St. Pachomius:

“Twice a week, on the fourth and sixth days, everyone fasts, except during Pentecost” [that is, as Tertullian puts it, from Easter until Pentecost, or, in Cassian’s phrase, throughout all the days of the Quinquagesima].

He also gives the reason for this tradition in the preface to his Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians:

“Pentecost is a time of joy and victory, when we do not bend our knees or bow down to the earth, but are lifted up with the Lord to the heights of heaven.”

St. Epiphanius, in his *Compendium of Church Teaching*, says:

“Throughout the whole year this fast is observed in the holy Catholic Church, namely on the fourth day and on the day before the Sabbath” [that is, Friday] “until the ninth hour, except during holy Pentecost—that is, throughout all fifty days, during which neither are knees bent nor is fasting prescribed.”

St. Ambrose, sermon 61, and in Gratian, Distinction 76, chapter *Scire*, says:

“During these fifty days there is for us a continual and uninterrupted festival, so that throughout this whole period we neither prescribe fasts for observance nor bend our knees to entreat God.”

St. Augustine likewise says in Letter 119:

“For this reason we relax fasts and pray standing, which is a sign of the resurrection. Hence this is also observed at the altar on all Sundays.”

Other Fathers teach the same: Maximus, bishop of Turin, in Homily 1 on Pentecost; Isidore, Book I of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 33; and Rabanus, Book II of *On the Instruction of Clergy*, chapter 41.

Finally, the whole reasoning of this abbot is directed toward explaining why that practice which he calls the remission of the Quinquagesima was instituted—that is, the relaxation of fasting during the Quinquagesima, or Paschal season.

These statements, however, should not be understood as though it were unlawful to fast during this period from private devotion, provided it is done without superstition, contempt, or scandal. St. Jerome expressly made this point in his letter to Lucinius Baeticus (Letter 28), also cited by Gratian in Distinction 76, final chapter:

“Would that we could fast at all times! We read that the Apostle Paul and the believers with him did so on the days of Pentecost and on the Lord’s Day in the Acts of the Apostles” (Acts 13). And below: “I do not say this because I think that one ought to fast on Sundays or remove the festival days spread across the fifty days; rather, let every province abound in its own understanding, and let it regard the precepts of the ancestors as apostolic laws.”

Isidore, also cited there (Book I of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 42), says:

“After Easter until Pentecost, although the observance of the Churches has relaxed the strictness of abstinence by means of midday meals, nevertheless, if any monks or clergy wish to fast, they should not be forbidden; for Antony, Paul, and the other ancient Fathers are read to have abstained in the desert even on these days and not to have relaxed their abstinence except on Sunday.”

Thus far he.

Someone may perhaps object to the foregoing: If, according to the judgment of the holy Fathers, fasting is relaxed and interrupted during the Quinquagesima—that is, from Easter Day until Pentecost inclusively—why then is there fasting on the vigil of Pentecost and during the Rogation days before the Lord’s Ascension?

I answer that the fast of the vigil of Pentecost does not derive from the primitive institution of the Church or from apostolic tradition, as do the fasts of the four seasons, but was introduced in later centuries through the pious custom and devotion of the faithful, and through reverence for so great a solemnity as the coming of the Holy Spirit. The Fathers consistently affirm that no fast was prescribed between Easter and Pentecost [Col. 1185D]. It is observed in the Church not so much to promote repentance and bodily affliction as to stimulate devotion and spiritual joy. Hence it is also called the fast of exultation and joy (St. Thomas, *Summa* II-II, question 147, article 5; Durandus, *Rationale*, Book VI, chapter 106).

Nevertheless, this custom is clearly very ancient. The Roman Order mentions this fast, and Alcuin and Amalarius frequently cite it in these words:

“On Saturday, at the vigil of Pentecost, everyone fasts.”

From this it is inferred that this is a custom of the universal Church, which has the force of law and precept, although otherwise there is no explicit precept concerning this fast, as St. Thomas also teaches, followed by Cajetan.

As for the three-day fast of the Rogation days, the common opinion is that this observance was not so much a matter of precept as of counsel, since it is clear from the foregoing that, according to the most ancient institution, no fasts were prescribed between Easter and Pentecost [Col. 1186B]. Nevertheless, if this fast is observed somewhere under the force of a precept, it should not be condemned. The custom of the Church should be observed in such matters, as Jerome says in his letter to Lucinius and Augustine in his letter to Casulanus.

Thus Bellarmine.

St. Augustine mentions the same institution and the three-day fast during the Rogation days in Sermon 173, *On the Season*, on the vigil of the Ascension; so does Sidonius in Book V, Letter 14, and Book VII, Letter 1. The same is found in canon 29 of the Council of Orléans, cited by Gratian under the chapter *Rogationes*, *On Consecration*, Distinction 3, and in those who wrote about ecclesiastical offices and rites: Gregory of Valencia, *II-II*, disputation and question 2; Bellarmine, Book II of *On Good Works*, chapter 21; Baronius, notes to the Martyrology, April 25; Alcuin, Book II; Amalarius, Book II, chapter 37; and Rabanus, Book II of *On the Instruction of Clergy*, chapter 40.]

## CHAPTER XII. The answer concerning the nature of things that are good, evil, or intermediate

To this Abbot Theonas began his speech as follows:

“It is indeed necessary for us to yield to the authority of the Fathers and to the custom of our ancestors, prolonged through so many years down to our own time, even when we do not perceive the reason for it; and to preserve it, as it was handed down from antiquity, with continual observance and reverence.

“But since you wish to know the causes and rationale of this matter, listen briefly to what we have learned from our elders concerning this institution. Yet before the authority of divine Scripture is brought forward, if it pleases you, let us say a little about the nature and character of fasting itself, so that the authority of Scripture that follows may confirm our discussion.

“Divine Wisdom, through Ecclesiastes, designated a proper time for every matter—that is, for all things, whether prosperous or considered adverse and sorrowful—saying:

‘There is a time for everything, and a time for every matter under heaven: a time to give birth and a time to die, a time to plant and a time to uproot what has been planted, a time to kill and a time to heal, a time to destroy and a time to build, a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance, a time to scatter stones and a time to gather stones, a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embraces, a time to acquire and a time to lose, a time to keep and a time to cast away, a time to tear apart and a time to mend, a time to be silent and a time to speak, a time to love and a time to hate, a time for war and a time for peace’ (Ecclesiastes 3).

And below: ‘Because there is a time,’ he says, ‘for every matter and every deed’ (ibid.).”

[Note: [Col. 1186C] Jerome translated this from the Hebrew. The Vulgate version is: “All things have their time, and all things pass in their appointed intervals under heaven: a time to be born, and a time to die,” and so forth (Ecclesiastes 3).]

“Therefore he did not define any of these things as perpetually good, except when one of them has been completed at an appropriate and suitable time. Thus the very things that now turn out well when done at the right time are found useless and harmful if undertaken at an unsuitable or improper time; [Note: [Col. 1186C] He distinguishes three classes of human things and actions. Some are good in themselves and intrinsically, so that they can never become evil, such as the virtues. Augustine defines virtue as ‘a good quality of the mind, which no one uses wrongly’ (Book III of *On Free Choice of the Will*, chapters 18 and 19). The author calls these principally good, or primary goods.

“Others, by contrast, are evil in themselves and intrinsically, so that they can never become good, such as lying, adultery, and so forth. These he likewise calls principally evil, or primary evils—not evil because they are prohibited, but prohibited because they are evil.

“Between these extremes are certain intermediate things, as it were indifferent matters. In this category he places abstinence, fasting, and the choice of foods. If these are performed at a suitable time and directed toward a good end—for example, the glory of God and the mortification of the flesh—they are good; if they are undertaken for an evil end, such as display or superstition, or at an inappropriate time or without moderation, they are evil. You have the same distinction in *Conference* 6, chapter 3.]

“except for those things that are principally good or evil in themselves [Note: [Col. 1186D] Because no one can use virtue wrongly, as Augustine says. St. Thomas, however, objects (I-II, question 55, article 4): ‘Whoever takes pride in something uses it wrongly; but many take pride in virtue. Augustine says in the Rule (chapter 3) that pride even lies in wait for good works so that they may perish. Therefore it is false that no one uses virtue wrongly.’

“St. Thomas replies that someone can use virtue wrongly as an object—for example, when he thinks wrongly about virtue, hates it, or takes pride in it—but not as the principle of use, that is, in such a way that the act of virtue itself is evil.] and can never be turned into their opposite, such as justice, prudence, fortitude, temperance, and the other virtues, or, conversely, the vices, whose definitions cannot fall into another category or be changed into one.

“But if some things can at times pass into either disposition, so that according to the character of those who use them they are found to be either good or evil, these are not judged absolutely according to their nature, but according to the disposition of the one performing them and the suitability of the time: they are sometimes useful and sometimes harmful.”

## CHAPTER XIII. What kind of good fasting is

“Accordingly, we must now ask what decision we ought to make concerning the condition of fasts: whether fasting itself is likewise good in the same way as justice, prudence, fortitude, or temperance, which, as we have said, cannot pass entirely into the opposite category; or whether it is something intermediate, which, when performed, can sometimes be beneficial, while when omitted it cannot always condemn; something whose performance is sometimes blameworthy and whose omission is sometimes praiseworthy.

“For if we include fasting in that definition of the virtues, so that abstinence from food is placed among the primary goods, then the consumption of food will certainly be evil and criminal. For whatever is contrary to a primary good must undoubtedly be regarded as a primary evil. Yet the authority of the holy Scriptures does not permit us to define it in this way. [Note: [Col. 1187B] This was the heresy and superstition of many heretics, who fasted or abstained from certain foods because they believed that those foods were by nature unclean and detestable and therefore unlawful and forbidden.

“Some said that the flesh of all animals was unclean: the Ebionites, according to Epiphanius, heresy 30; the Encratites, according to Augustine, heresy 25; the Eustathians, according to Socrates, Book II, chapter 33; the Priscillianists, according to Augustine, heresy 70; and the Apostolics, according to Bernard, Sermon 66 on the *Song of Songs*.

“Others declared not only flesh but also wine unclean and entirely to be avoided, such as the Manichaeans, according to Augustine, heresy 46.

“But Christians,” says Augustine (*Against Faustus*, Book XXX, chapter 5), “not heretics but Catholics, abstain not only from flesh but also from certain fruits of the earth in order to subdue the body and humble the soul from irrational impulses—not because they believe those things to be unclean, but for the sake of the soul. Some few do this always, while almost everyone does it on particular days and at particular times, as during Lent.”]

“For if we fast with such an understanding and intention that we believe sin is incurred by participation in food, we shall not only gain no fruits from our abstinence, but shall also incur, according to the Apostle, the greatest guilt and the crime of sacrilege by abstaining from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who have known the truth: ‘For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving’” (1 Timothy 4). [Note: [Col. 1187C] “In the last days,” says the Apostle, “some will depart from the faith, forbidding marriage and abstinence from foods that God created,” and so forth (1 Timothy 4). By these words the Apostle condemns certain heretics, especially the Marcionites and Manichaeans, whom he foresaw in the spirit as future in the last days—that is, in later or succeeding times—who would abstain from certain foods and teach that they should be avoided as intrinsically unclean and unlawful.

“Catholics do not act in this way when they abstain from certain foods out of temperance or to chastise the flesh. In this manner the first Christians established by St. Mark at Alexandria were accustomed to take food only in the evening and to abstain from flesh and wine, as Eusebius reports from Philo (Book II of *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 17), and Jerome in *On Philo*, chapter 75.

“St. Epiphanius, in the *Compendium of Doctrine*, testifies that there were people who voluntarily abstained from flesh throughout the whole year; but during Holy Week, or the Great Week preceding holy Easter, the entire Church traditionally persisted in the use of dry foods, which is called *xerophagy*. We have discussed this elsewhere (Book IV of the *Institutes*, chapter 21).

“St. Jerome likewise writes in his letter to Eustochium (Letter 22) that among the anchorites and Egyptian monks there were continual fasts throughout the whole year, except during Pentecost, as stated above, and perpetual abstinence from wine and flesh. Augustine teaches the same in Book I of *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, chapter 31, as do many other Fathers.”]

“For whoever thinks that something is unclean, to him it is unclean” (Romans 14); and therefore merely eating food condemns no one, unless something has been joined to it or subsequently followed it by which the person deserved condemnation.”

[Note: [Col. 1188C] “I know and am confident in the Lord Jesus,” says the Apostle, “that nothing is unclean through itself, except for the one who considers something to be unclean; for him it is unclean” (Romans 14). Here “unclean” means profane and impure. The Jews called anything unclean that they were not permitted to eat or touch.

“‘Nothing is unclean δι’ ἑαυτοῦ,’ Paul says—δι’ ἑαυτοῦ (with a rough breathing) meaning ‘through itself’—because nothing is unclean by nature. If, however, it is read δι’ αὐτοῦ, with a smooth breathing, as our translator reads it, it means ‘through him,’ namely the Lord Jesus, who purifies all things.” Hence Peter was told in Acts: ‘What God has purified, you must not call unclean’ (Acts 10).

“God purified all foods because he did not wish any food to be unclean for Christians, whereas many foods were unclean for the Jews on account of the symbolism and figure that Christ removed by fulfilling all figures, as St. Thomas says in his Commentary.

“Therefore Christians must abstain from no food as unclean, since it is neither unclean by nature, as the heretics claimed, nor by symbolic significance, as under the time of the old law. Nevertheless, if someone considers a food unclean and still eats it, it becomes unclean for him, according to the Apostle, because of his conscience. ‘To the one who considers something unclean, it is unclean’ (Romans 14), because he acts against his conscience, which, according to the theological maxim—although it may be erroneous—always binds. For ‘whatever is not from faith is sin,’ says the Apostle in the same passage. ‘Whatever is not from faith’ means whatever is done against one’s conscience and personal conviction. Here *faith* (*pistis*, πίστις) signifies conviction, as the Fathers teach and the context requires (St. Thomas, I-II, question 19, articles 5 and 6; Bellarmine, Book V of *On Grace and Free Will*, chapter 10).]

## CHAPTER XIV. That fasting is not a primary good

[Note: [Col. 1188D] The Paraphrast: “That fasting is something intermediate is proved from this: just as it justifies when observed, so it does not condemn when broken, unless perhaps,” and so forth. “Intermediate” means between things that are good in themselves and always, and things that are always and in themselves evil. Fasting is called intermediate because sometimes, when observed, it can be beneficial, while when omitted it cannot condemn; and because, as the author says in the preceding chapter, its performance is sometimes blameworthy. Fasting therefore does not condemn a person when it is broken or not observed—namely, lawfully and at a time permitted by the Church.]

“Thus it is most clearly shown to be intermediate also by this: just as it justifies when observed, so it does not condemn when broken, unless perhaps what is punished is the transgression of a precept rather than the consumption of food.

“A primary good must have no empty interval, so that no one may be without it, because the negligent person must fall into evil when it ceases. Nor is any time granted to a primary evil, because what is always harmful can never, once admitted, fail to cause harm or ever be changed into something praiseworthy. [Note: [Col. 1189D] What he calls a primary good or a primary evil was explained above (chapter 12).]

“Accordingly, those things for which we see established qualities and times, and which sanctify when observed without polluting when omitted, are clearly intermediate—for example, marriage, agriculture, wealth, withdrawal from solitude, vigils, reading sacred texts, meditation on books, and fasting itself, from which this discussion arose.

“Divine command, or the authority of the holy Scriptures, has not decreed that all these things must be obtained without interruption or observed continually, so that even a brief interruption would be sacrilegious. Whatever is imposed by command entails death if it is not fulfilled; whatever is recommended rather than commanded benefits when done but does not punish when left undone.

“And therefore our ancestors ordered and prudently directed us to perform all or at least some of these things with regard to the reason, place, manner, and time. If any of them is practiced appropriately, it is suitable and fitting; if inappropriately, it is clearly inept and harmful. [Note: [Col. 1189D] The observations we have made elsewhere more than once concerning the practice of hospitality and the relaxation of the regular fast for the sake of guests belong here.]

“If, at the arrival of a brother whom he ought to refresh with kindness, because he must refresh Christ, and embrace with the most gracious hospitality, someone wishes to preserve the strictness of the fast, does he not incur rather the crime of inhumanity than acquire praise or religious merit? Or if the exhaustion and weakness of the flesh demands restoration of strength through the reception of food, and someone refuses to relax the rigor of abstinence, should he not be judged a cruel murderer of his own body rather than a provider for his health?

“Likewise, when the time of a festival grants suitable nourishment from food and the necessary restoration of strength, if someone obstinately wishes to retain the rigid observance of fasts, he must be regarded as undisciplined and irrational rather than religious.

“The same things are also opposed to those who seek human praise through fasts and acquire a reputation for sanctity by the empty display of pallor. The Gospel declares that such people have received their reward in the present life (Matthew 6). The Lord also detests the fast of those whose fasting is condemned through the prophet. Speaking in their person, after they had complained, ‘Why have we fasted, and you have not looked upon us? We have humbled our souls, and you have not known it?’, he immediately revealed the reasons why they did not deserve to be heard:

“‘Behold, on the day of your fast your own will is found, and you demand payment from all your debtors. Behold, you fast for quarrels and strife, and strike with an impious fist. Do not fast as you have done until this day, so that your cry may be heard on high. Is this the fast that I have chosen: for a person to afflict his soul for a day? Is it to bow his head like a reed and spread sackcloth and ashes beneath him? Is this what you call a fast, and a day acceptable to the Lord?’” (Isaiah 58).

“Then he continues by teaching how the abstinence of one who fasts becomes acceptable, and clearly declares that fasting by itself cannot be beneficial unless it is accompanied by the causes that follow:

“‘Is not this the fast that I have chosen? Break the bonds of wickedness; undo the bundles that oppress. Set free those who have been crushed, and tear apart every burden. Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the poor and homeless into your house. When you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh. Then your light shall break forth like the morning, and your healing shall quickly arise; your righteousness shall go before you, and the glory of the Lord shall gather you. Then you shall call, and the Lord will answer; you shall cry, and he will say, “Here I am.”’” (ibid.).

“You see, therefore, that fasting is in no way judged by the Lord to be a primary good, since it becomes good and pleasing to God not by itself but through other works. On the other hand, because of accompanying circumstances it is judged not only useless but even hateful, as the Lord says: ‘When they fast, I will not hear their prayers’” (Jeremiah 14).

## CHAPTER XV. That things good by their own nature should not be practiced for the sake of intermediate things; rather, conversely, intermediate things should be undertaken in order to acquire things that are primarily good

“For mercy, patience, and charity, or those precepts of the virtues mentioned above in which the good is unquestionably primary, are not to be maintained for the sake of fasts, [Note: [Col. 1189D] Chrysostom, Homily 47 on Matthew: “I have said this not because fasting does not please me—I am accustomed to praise it highly—but because I grieve if, while neglecting the other virtues, you consider fasting sufficient for salvation. In the choir of the virtues it certainly occupies the last place. The chief virtues are charity, humility, and mercy.”

“And Jerome, to Caelantia: ‘What does it profit to make the body thin through abstinence if the soul swells with pride? What praise shall we deserve for the pallor of fasting if we are livid with envy? Then abstinence is excellent; then the chastisement of the body is beautiful and magnificent, when the soul is fasting from vices. Indeed, those who hold the virtue of abstinence wisely and with understanding afflict their flesh so that they may break the pride of the soul.’”]

“but rather fasts are to be practiced for the sake of those virtues. We must strive to acquire through fasts those virtues that are truly good, not to direct the practice of those virtues toward the goal of fasting.

“For this reason bodily affliction is useful; for this reason the medicine of hunger is to be applied to the body: so that through it we may reach charity, in which there is an immovable and perpetual good without any exception of time.

“For the discipline of medicine, goldsmithing, or the other arts that exist in this world is not practiced for the sake of the instruments belonging to the work, but rather the tools are prepared for the pursuit of the art. These instruments, just as they are useful to those skilled in the art, are superfluous to those who do not know its discipline. They are of great benefit to those who rely on their service to accomplish their work, but they can be of no benefit to those who, not knowing the purpose for which they were instituted, are content merely to possess them, because they place the whole value of their usefulness in retaining them rather than in completing the work. [Lipsius, in the margin: “their own.”]

“That, therefore, is supremely and primarily good for the sake of which intermediate things are done; the supreme good itself, however, is pursued not for another reason but solely because of its own goodness.”

## CHAPTER XVI. How the primary good is distinguished from other goods

“This primary good is distinguished from the other things that we have said are intermediate in the following ways: if it is good in itself and not through something else; if it is necessary for its own sake and not for the sake of something else; if it is immutably and always good, continually retaining its own character and never able to pass into the opposite; if its removal or cessation cannot fail to bring complete destruction; and if what is contrary to it is likewise a primary evil and can never pass into the good category.

“These definitions, by which the nature of primary goods is distinguished, cannot in any way be applied to fasting. For fasts are not good in themselves or necessary for their own sake; rather, they are beneficially practiced to acquire purity of heart and body, so that, when the sting of the flesh has been blunted, the peaceful mind may be reconciled with its Creator. Nor are they immutably and always good, since we are often not harmed by interrupting them; indeed, when practiced excessively and at an unsuitable time, they sometimes turn to the soul’s destruction.

“Nor is the primary evil that which appears opposed to fasting—namely, the naturally pleasant consumption of food—for this cannot be defined as evil unless intemperance, luxury, or some other vice follows. For [Note: [Col. 1191C] That is, food is not unclean in itself and by nature, as the Jews believed. It can nevertheless defile by reason of disobedience or intemperance in its consumption, or by reason of the scandal with which it is consumed. Thus eating flesh on a day of fasting defiles the soul; otherwise neither drunkenness nor gluttony would defile the soul, which not even a heretic would say.]

“‘It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what proceeds from the mouth—this defiles a person’” (Matthew 15).

“Therefore whoever does this primary good not for its own sake but for the sake of something else detracts from it and does not carry it out perfectly or without sin. Everything must be done for the sake of this good, while it itself is to be sought solely for its own sake.”

## CHAPTER XVII. The reason for and usefulness of fasting

“Therefore, while continually retaining this definition concerning the character of fasting, let us desire it with all the strength of our soul, yet recognize that it is suitable for us only when the consideration of time, quality, and measure is preserved in it.
