We should not fix the end of our hope in fasting itself, but use it to reach purity of heart and apostolic charity.

“From this it is evident that fasting, for which not only particular times have been established—times when it should either be practiced or omitted—but also a prescribed quality and measure, is not a primary good but something intermediate.

“Those things, however, that by the authority of a precept are either commanded as good or forbidden as harmful are never so subject to the exception of times that what is forbidden should sometimes be done or what is commanded sometimes omitted. [Note: [Col. 1191D] It is not without some difficulty to explain how it can be said that no measure is established for justice, patience, sobriety, chastity, and charity. Concerning charity, which is the mother and queen of all the virtues, Paula and Eustochium write to Marcella (Letter 17 among Jerome’s letters): “Charity has no measure.” St. Bernard likewise says in *On Loving God*: “The measure of loving God is to love without measure.”

“Conversely, there is the philosophical maxim that virtue consists in the mean. Jerome, in the *Epitaph for Paula*, commends the philosophers’ saying: μεσότης ἡ ἀρετὴ, κακία ὑπερβολὴ πέλεται—that is, “moderation is virtue; excess is vice.” As he says, we can express this in one brief sentence: “Nothing in excess” (see St. Thomas, I-II, question 64, articles 1 and 4).

“But the answer is easy: this abbot means nothing other than that no fixed measure is established for justice, patience, and the other virtues on the side of time. There is no time when we ought not to practice justice, patience, sobriety, chastity, and charity, and avoid the contrary vices. He had said the same thing in the preceding words, though in different terms, namely that these things are never so subject to the exception of times that what is forbidden should sometimes be done or what is commanded sometimes omitted.

“For he compares fasting, as an intermediate good, with the two extremes—namely the virtues and vices mentioned here. He teaches that the virtues must always and at every time be cultivated, and the vices always and at every time avoided, whereas fasting must be undertaken at appropriate times and with due measure and moderation; at other times it must be interrupted or relaxed, as happens during the Quinquagesima, which is the particular subject here.]

“For no fixed measure has been established for justice, patience, sobriety, chastity, or charity; nor has liberty ever been granted for injustice, impatience, rage, impurity, envy, or pride.”

## CHAPTER XVIII. That fasting is not always appropriate
Therefore, having prefaced this discussion with these remarks on the character of fasting, it seems necessary to add the authority of Holy Scripture, by which it may be more clearly established that fasting neither ought nor can be observed perpetually. In the Gospel, when the Pharisees were fasting together with the disciples of John the Baptist, while the apostles—as friends and table companions of that heavenly Bridegroom—not yet observing the practice of fasting, the disciples of John, who believed that they possessed the highest degree of righteousness through their fasts, since they were followers of one who was an outstanding preacher of repentance and who set an example before all peoples by refusing not only the various kinds of food provided for human use but even the ordinary eating of bread itself, complained to the Lord, saying: “Why do we and the Pharisees fast frequently, but your disciples do not fast?” (Mark 2).

In reply, the Lord clearly showed that fasting is not appropriate or necessary at every time, since on the occasion of some festival or when an opportunity for charity intervenes, permission for refreshment may be granted:

[Note: [Col. 1193C] Blessed Jerome writes aptly for the clarification of this passage as follows (Commentary on Matthew 9): “Some think that for this reason the fasts should be undertaken after the forty days of the Passion, although the immediate arrival of Pentecost and of the Holy Spirit indicates to us that it is a time of festivity. Taking this testimony as their occasion, Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla also observe a Quadragesima after Pentecost, because, once the Bridegroom has been taken away, the children of the Bridegroom ought to fast. The custom of the Church, however, approaches the Passion of the Lord and the Resurrection through humility of the flesh, so that by bodily fasting we may prepare ourselves for spiritual nourishment.” [Col. 1193D] Thus far Jerome, rebuking the folly of Montanus and the Montanists, who on the basis of this passage celebrated a Quadragesima after Pentecost, naturally interpreting the removal of the Lord and Bridegroom as his Ascension. The Catholic Church, better instructed by the Holy Spirit, understands by the removal of the Bridegroom the Passion and death of our Lord, and therefore institutes greater fasts at the time when it begins to commemorate the Lord’s Passion. Through these fasts, too, it prepares us for spiritual nourishment—that is, for the paschal refreshment and synaxis. For according to the reasoning of the Montanists, one would have to fast at all times except during the period before Christ ascended into heaven.]

“Can the children of the Bridegroom,” he said, “mourn as long as the Bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the Bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast” (ibid.).

[Note: [Col. 1193D] Namely: “Can the children of the Bridegroom fast as long as the Bridegroom is with them?” These words are properly understood to designate the season of Pentecost, during which Christ, after his Resurrection, remained with the disciples for forty days, appearing to them, eating with them, and speaking about the kingdom of God (Acts 1). Ten additional days had to be added to those days, because of the promise and expectation of the coming of the Holy Spirit; these were to be celebrated with equal solemnity and joy, as is explained below.]

Although he spoke these words before the Resurrection concerning his bodily presence, they properly indicate the season of Pentecost, during which, after the Resurrection, the joy of the Lord’s daily presence did not allow the disciples to fast while the Lord feasted with them for forty days.

## CHAPTER XIX. The question why fasting is relaxed throughout all fifty days

Germanus: Why, then, do we relax the severity of abstinence in our meals throughout the whole of Pentecost, when Christ plainly remained with his disciples for only forty days after the Resurrection?

## CHAPTER XX. The answer

[Col. 1193C]

Theonas: Your question deserves, not inappropriately, to recognize the reasoning of the most complete truth.

[Note: [Col. 1194C] Saint Ambrose speaks in nearly the same way: “The whole course of Pentecost is celebrated as the equivalent of the Lord’s Day, and all these days are reckoned as though they were Sundays. For the Resurrection is on Sunday. By rising on the Lord’s Day, the Savior returned to human beings, and after the Resurrection he remained with human beings throughout the whole of Pentecost. Therefore it was necessary that the festivity of those whose holiness was equal should also be equal. For the Lord arranged it so that, just as we mourned his Passion through the fasting of the Quadragesima, so we should rejoice in his Resurrection during the festivals of Pentecost.” Thus Ambrose.]

After the Ascension of our Savior, which took place on the fortieth day after his Resurrection, the apostles returned from the Mount of Olives, where he allowed himself to be seen as he went to the Father. As the reading from the Acts of the Apostles also testifies (chapter 1), they entered Jerusalem and are reported to have awaited the coming of the Holy Spirit for ten days. When these days had been completed, they received him with joy on the fiftieth day, and thus the number belonging to this festival was clearly fulfilled.

We also read that this number was figuratively prefigured in the Old Testament. There, after seven weeks had been completed, the priests were commanded to offer to the Lord the firstfruits of bread (Deut. 16). This is most truly shown to have been offered to the Lord through the preaching of the apostles, who are recorded as having preached to the people on that day: the true bread of firstfruits, brought forth through the institution of the new teaching, consecrated to the Lord the first Christian people from the Jews when five thousand men had been satisfied by the gift of its food.

[Col. 1194B]

For this reason, these ten days also must be celebrated with equal solemnity and joy together with the preceding forty. The tradition of this festival, handed down to us in the same form through apostolic men, must be maintained.

[Note: [Col. 1194D] This ancient tradition, received from the Fathers, has been sufficiently discussed above (chapter 11).]

For this reason, during these days people do not bend the knee in prayer, because bending the knee is an indication of repentance and mourning. Hence, throughout these days we also preserve the same solemnity as on the Lord’s Day, on which our predecessors handed down that neither fasting should be undertaken nor the knee bent, out of reverence for the Lord’s Resurrection.

## CHAPTER XXI. The question whether relaxing the fast’s abstinence harms bodily chastity

[Col. 1194C]

Germanus: Can this flesh, enticed by the unusual pleasures of so long a festival, fail to sprout something thorny from the tinder of the vices, even though it has been cut away, or can the mind, burdened with foods taken beyond its customary measure, fail to bend the strictness of its authority toward the servant body—especially since, in us, more vigorous youth can quickly drive the subjected limbs into rebellion if we presume either to consume our usual foods in greater abundance or, at any rate, to indulge more freely in unusual ones?

[Note: [Col. 1194D] “Thorny” (*sentuosum*), that is, literally “full of thorns,” is used metaphorically for something vicious. The phrase refers to the tinder of the vices, although it has been cut away—that is, the lust or desire of the flesh, previously subdued through prolonged abstinence. Saint Augustine also calls desire the tinder of sin (On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, book 1, final chapter), and the Council of Trent follows him when it says (Session 5, chapter 5): “This holy synod confesses and believes that concupiscence and the tinder of sin remain in those who have been baptized; since it has been left for the struggle, it cannot harm those who do not consent but resist manfully through the grace of Christ Jesus.” From these words it may be understood that it is, strictly speaking and *καταχρηστικῶς*—that is, improperly—said that this tinder has been cut away, since it remains in the reborn after baptism.]

[Col. 1195A]

## CHAPTER XXII. The answer concerning the preservation of the proper measure of continence

Theonas: If we weigh everything we do with the reasonable examination of the mind, and if, concerning the purity of our heart, we always consult not the judgment of others but our own conscience, it is certain that this interval of refreshment cannot rightly damage strictness, provided that, as has been said, the mind weighs with an equal balance the proper measure of indulgence and continence, and chastises equally both forms of excess.

[Col. 1195B]

It must distinguish, through true discretion, whether the weight of pleasures depresses our spirit or whether, on the contrary, the greater austerity of abstinence inclines the other—that is, the bodily—part, suppressing or supporting whichever portion it perceives to be either exalted or weighed down.

[Note: [Col. 1195C] Abbot Moses says similarly in Conference 2, chapter 16: “The good of discretion must be acquired with every effort through the virtue of humility, which can preserve us unharmed from either extreme. For there is an old saying: *ἀκρότητες ἰσότητες*, that is, ‘extremes are equal.’ Excessive fasting and gluttony arrive at one and the same end; and by the same loss, the monk is enveloped by the torpor of the deepest sleep through the excessive continuation of vigils. Whoever has been weakened through an excess of continence must necessarily be restored to that condition in which the negligent person is held through carelessness.” Thus he. See our notes there (see book 6 of the Institutes, final chapter).]

For our Lord wills nothing to be done for his worship and honor without the moderation of judgment, because “the honor of the king loves judgment” (Psalm 98). Therefore the wisest Solomon, warning us not to incline in either direction through a biased judgment, says: “Honor God with your just labors, and offer him a portion from the fruits of your righteousness” (Prov. 3).

[Note: [Col. 1195C] The same author says in Conference 20, chapter 5: “A most truthful examiner of repentance and judge of indulgence resides in our conscience. While we still dwell in this flesh, before the day of knowledge and judgment, he reveals to us the absolution of our guilt and opens the completion of satisfaction to the grace of forgiveness.” How this is to be understood is explained there.]

For an incorrupt and true judge resides in our conscience, and sometimes, concerning the state of our purity, while everyone else is in error, he alone is not deceived.

[Col. 1195C]

[Note: [Col. 1195D] Similar passages occur in book 5 of the Institutes, chapters 8, 9, and 22, and in Conferences 2, chapters 22 and 26. The sayings of the holy Fathers support the same teaching. Basil, in his book On True Virginity, says: “Just as it is grievous and dangerous to incline toward excess in food, so it is entirely unreasonable to wear out the body through excessive abstinence and render it useless. For abstaining from the pleasure of the palate is not desirable in itself, but because it contributes to the acquisition of virtue. If, however, through immoderate starvation, we neglect the purpose for which we choose abstinence from food, we act contrary to our intention. For once the instrument has been broken and crushed, we can neither cling to God through devotion to reading and prayer nor perform the human duty of kindness toward our brothers. Therefore care of the body is also necessary—not for its own sake, but so that we may use it in the service of philosophical pursuits, that is, of wisdom or contemplation.” Saint Jerome writes in his letter to Nepotian (Letter 2): “Impose upon yourself as much fasting as you can bear. Let your fasts be pure, chaste, simple, moderate, and not superstitious.” And to the monk Rusticus (Letter 4): “Let fasts be moderate, lest excessive fasting weaken the stomach and, demanding a greater replenishment, break out into indigestion, which is the parent of lust. Food that is moderate and temperate is beneficial both to flesh and soul.”]

For if the watchfulness of an attentive heart is preserved continually with every care and skill, how could we, with the judgment of our discretion in error, weigh the substance of our strength on an unjust scale, whether inflamed by a thoughtless desire for continence or enticed by a longing for excessive relaxation? Rather, placing the purity of the soul in one pan and the strength of the body in the other, we should weigh both by the judgment of conscience, so that we do not perversely incline toward either excessive strictness or excessive relaxation because of an excessive attachment to one of them, but lean more carefully toward the balance of equality.

Otherwise it may be said to us, whether on account of excessive relaxation or excessive strictness:

[Note: [Col. 1196C] This is according to the Greek translation of the Septuagint, which most of the Fathers followed. Among them is Augustine, The City of God, book 15, chapter 7: “In this admonition that God addressed to Cain, the statement, ‘If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned?’—since it is not clear why or from where it was said—has produced many interpretations through its obscurity, as each interpreter of the divine Scriptures attempts to express it according to the rule of faith. A sacrifice is rightly offered when it is offered to the true God, to whom alone sacrifice should be offered. But it is not rightly divided when the places, times, things offered, the one who offers, the one offered, or those to whom what has been offered is distributed for eating are not rightly distinguished; so that by ‘division’ we understand ‘discretion.’ This occurs whether something is offered where it ought not to be offered, or when it ought not to be offered, or when something is offered that ought not then but at another time to be offered, or when something is offered that ought never and nowhere to have been offered, or when a person keeps for himself the choicer items of a given kind rather than offering such items to God, or when a profane person—or anyone who ought not to do so—becomes a participant in what has been offered.” Thus Augustine. The Vulgate version of Saint Jerome, approved by the Council of Trent, reads: “If you act well, will you not receive? But if you act badly, sin will immediately be present at the door” (Gen. 4).]

“Have you not sinned if you offer rightly but do not divide rightly?” (Gen. 4, according to the Septuagint).

For we believe that we rightly offer to the Lord those victims of fasting that we inconsiderately tear from ourselves through the violent convulsion of our entrails. Yet he who loves mercy and judgment curses them, saying: “I am the Lord, loving judgment and hating robbery in a burnt offering” (Isa. 61).

He also condemns as fraudulent laborers those who, taking for the nourishment of the flesh and their own use the chief portion of their offering—that is, of their duties and actions—bring the remainder and the smallest portion to the Lord: “Cursed is the one who performs the work of the Lord deceitfully” (Jer. 48).

Therefore the Lord does not unjustly rebuke one who deceives himself by such an unjust examination, saying: “Nevertheless, the sons of men are vain; the sons of men are liars in the balances, so that they may deceive” (Psalm 61).

[Col. 1196C]

And therefore the blessed Apostle warns us, so that, retaining the safeguards of discretion, we may not be enticed to incline toward either side through excess, saying: “Your reasonable service” (Rom. 12).

[Col. 1197A]

The Lawgiver likewise forbids this, commanding: “A just balance and equal weights, a just measure and an equal sextarius” (Lev. 19). Solomon also pronounces a similar judgment on this matter:

[Note: [Col. 1197B] The Vulgate text reads: “A weight and a weight, a measure and a measure: both are abominable before God” (Prov. 20). The author gives here a threefold moral exposition of this sentence, from which Saint Jerome’s twofold exposition differs little. Jerome writes as follows: “A weight and a weight,” that is, a greater and a lesser; “a measure and a measure,” likewise a greater and a lesser—both are abominable before God. Leaders in the Church who live wickedly have these double measures in their houses, that is, in their consciences, because they themselves do not do the good that they command to others, and they do not cease to commit the evil that they condemn in their subordinates. “A weight and a weight, a measure and a measure”: hypocrites and heretics have them in their houses, that is, in their minds, in that they falsely claim to be clean in thought and pure in action while rejecting and despising others as filthy and sinful. As though by a deceitful balance and a double measure, they weigh their own conduct one way and that of their neighbors another; thus they are in both respects abominable before God. For the person who searches his own actions for what may be praised, but those of others for what may be blamed, has one weight in his house and another measure, pretending one thing in himself and another in his neighbor. The Lord therefore rightly abhors such a person, because insofar as he pleases himself without merit, he displeases the heavenly observer with equal justice. Saint Jerome expresses this elegantly; and when his words are compared with our text, they are found to agree with it completely.]

“A great weight and a small, and double measures, are both unclean before the Lord; and whoever does these things will be fettered by his own contrivances” (Prov. 20).

Accordingly, we must strive not only in the way we have mentioned but also in this way: not to have unjust weights in our hearts or double measures in the storehouses of our conscience. That is, we must not ourselves presume upon those practices that soften the rule of strictness through a more relaxed indulgence, while burdening those to whom we preach the word of the Lord with stricter commands and heavier weights than we ourselves are able to bear.

When we do this, what are we doing except weighing or measuring the grain and produce of the Lord’s commands with a double weight and measure? If we administer these things one way to ourselves and another way to our brothers, the Lord rightly rebukes us because we possess deceitful balances and double measures, according to Solomon’s saying: “A double weight is an abomination to the Lord, and a deceitful balance is not good in his sight” (ibid.).

We also clearly incur the guilt of a deceitful weight and a double measure if, out of a desire for human praise, we display before our brothers certain stricter practices that we customarily perform privately in our cells, seeking to appear more abstinent and holier before human eyes than before God. This disease must be not merely avoided but especially abhorred by us.

But meanwhile, having wandered somewhat farther from the question proposed, let us return to the same point from which we departed.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the time and measure of refreshment

[Col. 1198B]

Accordingly, the solemnity of the days mentioned above must be observed in such a way that the indulgence benefits rather than harms the care of body and soul, because neither does the joy of that festival know how to blunt the stings of the flesh, nor does that relentless adversary know how to be softened by reverence for days.

[Note: [Col. 1197C] It seems to me that this may be explained as referring to a threefold adversary: the devil, the flesh, and our conscience.

As for the devil, Dionysius explains it by this paraphrase of the passage: “The solemnity of the days mentioned above must be observed in such a way that the permitted relaxation benefits rather than harms the worship or progress of flesh and soul, because neither the stimulus of the flesh nor the devil is softened by the joy of any festival or by the honor paid to days.” Lavardinus also appears to follow him.

The Apostle Peter says of this adversary: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5). This adversary is harsh and cruel; no reverence for days softens him—that is, no reverence or religious observance of festivals touches him so that he might rest and cease to attack us or entice us to evil. Indeed, the more relaxed and unguarded he finds us, the more boldly and persistently he attacks us.

This may also be understood of the flesh, or of desire of the flesh, in the way that some interpret the Savior’s words in Matthew 5: “Be reconciled with your adversary quickly, while you are with him on the way,” and so forth (Athanasius, Question 62; Letter 80, book 1; Juvencus, in his poem).

In this passage, Isidore of Pelusium says, the adversary is divinely understood as bodily desire opposing the spirit. He calls the way the life that our race travels without any interruption. Finally, he calls agreement and goodwill toward the body the recognition of its rebellion, which must be perceived immediately, lest, if we submit to its commands and commit things unworthy of the heavenly calling, it hand us over to the Judge when he comes to gather our works and words and repay each according to his work. Thus he writes according to Bill’s translation.

This interpretation, however, may perhaps seem less suitable and fitting to this passage—not to speak of the evangelical text and meaning—because in this way the adversary would not be distinguished from the preceding expression, since this adversary would be the same as the thorns of the flesh. Therefore there would have been no need for the distinction. Nevertheless, it can truly also be said that this adversary, that is, the thorn of the flesh, is not softened by reverence for any days, meaning that it does not rest; it was troublesome even to blessed Paul at all times (1 Cor. 14).

The third interpretation, which I prefer, concerns the conscience, which accuses us as a most serious adversary. It cannot be softened, pacified, or made secure if it perceives that during the days of Pentecost or another solemnity we have used excessive license, intemperance, or relaxation that harms the worship or progress of body or soul, as was said above.

Concerning this adversary, who is also judge and avenger, he said above (chapter 22): “An incorrupt and true judge resides in our conscience, who sometimes, concerning the state of our purity, while everyone else is in error, alone is not deceived.” Elsewhere he calls the conscience the arbiter not only of our actions but also of our thoughts (Conference 11, chapter 9). Saint Jerome calls it “watchful keeping” (*syntērēsis*, συντήρησις); common usage calls it “synderesis.”

Saint Athanasius also interprets the Gospel passage in this way (Question 62, Matthew 5): “Conscience too is called an adversary. For it secretly reproves us in our heart, restrains us from evil, and, if we are disobedient, eventually brings us before God’s tribunal, where we shall pay the penalties both for grave sins and for those that are light and very small.”]

Therefore, so that the established custom of solemnity may be preserved even on festival days, and the most healthful measure of frugality may in no way be exceeded, it is sufficient to allow the indulgence of relaxation to proceed only so far that the food which was to have been taken at the ninth hour may be taken somewhat earlier—that is, at the sixth hour—because of the festival. [Note: [Col. 1199C] In the same way Abbot Moses teaches in Conference 2, chapter 26 how hospitality may be shown to visiting brothers without loss of the customary strictness and abstinence: “So that we may not be found blameworthy on either side, this practice should be retained by us: at the ninth hour, of the two paximacia [rusks] to which we are rightfully entitled as the canonical allowance, after taking one rusk, we reserve the other until evening in expectation of this; if any brother arrives, we consume it together with him, adding nothing further to the usual custom. By this arrangement a brother’s arrival, which ought to be most welcome to us, will in no way make us sad, since we render the offices of hospitality in such a way that we relax nothing of the rigor of continence.”]

This is to be done only on the condition that the customary quantity or quality of the food not be changed, lest the purity of the body or the integrity of the mind, acquired with greater care through the abstinence of the Quadragesima, perish through the relaxation of Pentecost, and lest it profit us nothing to have obtained through fasting what an excited satiety soon compels us to lose.

This is especially important because, through the well-known cunning of our enemy, he attacks the defense of our purity most particularly when he perceives that its guardianship has been relaxed by the celebration of a solemnity.

[Col. 1199C]

[Note: [Col. 1199C] Observe here, devout reader, the frugality and moderation to be used during the paschal season, or after the fast of the Quadragesima, and on the more solemn days, as is said here. Pope Innocent III seems to have taken account of this notable teaching when, among other provisions for monastic reform, he decreed as follows (chapter “Cum ad monasterium,” On the Status of Monks): “Nor should the community, on certain solemnities—as has sometimes been customary—go out with the abbot, leaving a few behind so that they may eat meat outside the refectory, since on those days especially regular discipline ought to be observed with greater care.”]

For this reason, we must provide with the utmost vigilance that the vigor of our mind never be weakened by seductive blandishments, lest, as has already been said above, we lose through the repose and security of Pentecost the purity of chastity acquired through the labor of the Quadragesima.

[Col. 1199B]

Therefore no addition at all should be allowed either in the quality or in the quantity of the food. Rather, even on the most festive days, we should similarly abstain from the foods whose restraint we practiced during the days of fasting for the sake of preserving complete chastity. Otherwise the joy of the festival, stirring up within us the most destructive battle of carnal incentives, may be turned into mourning, deprive us of that more excellent festival of the mind which rejoices in the joy of incorruption, and cause us, after the brief vanity of bodily joy, to lament for a long time in penitence the chastity of heart we have lost.

Indeed, we must strive so that the prophetic exhortation may not be directed to us in vain: “Celebrate your festivals, Judah, and fulfill your vows” (Nahum 1).

[Col. 1199C]

For if the continuity of continence is not altered by the solemnity inserted among the days, we shall continually enjoy spiritual festivals, and, while we cease from servile labor, “there shall be month after month and sabbath after sabbath” (Isaiah 66).

## CHAPTER XXIV. The question concerning the differing observance of the Quadragesima

Germanus: Why is the Quadragesima celebrated over six weeks, although in certain provinces a more zealous concern for religion seems perhaps to have added a seventh week, when neither number, with Sunday and Saturday subtracted, reaches the total of forty days? For only thirty-six days are contained in the weeks themselves.

[Note: [Col. 1199D] As has been shown elsewhere (Institutes, book 3, chapter 9), Easterners, or Greeks, excluded and subtracted Saturday from the fast of the Quadragesima, except Holy Saturday. On Saturdays they did not fast, but they nevertheless abstained from meat and eggs, as they also did on Sundays.

Saint Ambrose himself testifies that this was observed in the West in the Church of Milan in his time, writing in his book On Elijah and Fasting: “During the whole Quadragesima, except Saturday and Sunday, fasting is observed. This fast includes the Lord’s Pascha.”

Since among the Easterners Saturdays, together with Sundays, were excluded from fasting, while among the Latins only Sundays were excluded, it was necessary for the former to observe seven weeks of the Quadragesimal fast and for the latter only six, so that both might equally complete the number of thirty-six days. For the seventh week among the Easterners made up for the Saturdays, together with Holy Saturday. But more will be said about this below.]

## CHAPTER XXV. The answer to the question proposed, in which he also teaches that the fast of the Quadragesima comprises the tithe of the whole year

[Col. 1200B]

Theonas: Although the pious simplicity of some people removes the need to ask this question, nevertheless, since you scrutinize even matters that another person might have considered unworthy of inquiry, wishing to recognize the complete truth of our observance and its mystery, understand the very clear reasoning of this matter as well, so that you may more plainly approve that our predecessors handed down nothing irrational.

A general command was promulgated in the Mosaic Law for the whole people: “You shall offer your tithes and firstfruits to the Lord your God” (Exod. 22).

[Col. 1200C]

Thus, since we are commanded to offer the tithes of all our possessions and all our fruits, it is much more necessary that we offer the tithes of our own manner of life, human activity, and works. These are plainly fulfilled in the reckoning of the Quadragesima.

[Note: [Col. 1200C] This is one reason, among several others, why the Quadragesima, or Quadragesimal fast, was instituted: namely, so that through Quadragesimal abstinence we might offer to the Lord, as it were, the tithes of our life and works (see Bellarmine, On Good Works in Particular, book 2, chapter 16; Gregory, Homily 16 on the Gospels; Gratian, De Consecratione, distinction 5, chapter “Quadragesima”). Pope Gregory also expressed this reasoning in a sermon to the people: “From the present day”—that is, from the first Sunday of the Quadragesima, as Gratian reported—“until the joys of the paschal solemnity there are six weeks. Their days amount to forty-two; when the six Sundays are subtracted, no more than thirty-six days remain in abstinence. Since the year consists of three hundred and sixty-five days, while we afflict ourselves for thirty-six days, we give to God, as it were, the tithes of our year, so that, having lived for ourselves during the year we have received, we may mortify ourselves for our Creator through abstinence in his tithes. Therefore, dearest brothers, just as you are commanded in the Law to offer tithes of your possessions, so strive to offer tithes of your days.” Thus Gregory.

Isidore likewise imitates this passage of Cassian in book 1 of On Ecclesiastical Offices, chapter 36: “In the Mosaic Law it was generally commanded for the whole people to offer tithes and firstfruits to the Lord God. Thus, when this statement admonishes us to refer the beginnings of our intentions and the conclusions of our works to God’s grace, in the reckoning of the Quadragesima the full sum of these legal tithes is nevertheless completed. For the whole period of the year is tithed by the number thirty-six. After the Sundays, on which fasts are relaxed, are subtracted from the Quadragesima, we come to the church on these days as though for the tithes of the whole year and offer to God the work of our actions as a sacrifice of jubilation.”]

For the total number of all the days into which the year, revolving in its course, is enclosed is tithed by the number of thirty-six and a half days.

[Note: [Col. 1201C] “A half,” that is, with a half added—not “six by six,” as it is mistakenly given in Dionysius. For the tenth part of all the days of the year, according to the more exact reckoning, absolutely requires and comprises thirty-six and a half days (Durand, Rational of the Divine Offices, book 6, chapter 28; Gratian, De Consecratione, distinction 3, chapter “Sabbati”; Alcuin, On the Divine Office; Amalarius, chapter 26; Rabanus, On the Institution of the Clergy, book 2, chapter 38; Durand, cited above, chapter 78).

For if thirty-six is multiplied by ten, as Gregory and Isidore calculate less exactly, the result is only three hundred and sixty days; therefore five days remain, and these are equal to ten half-days. See the notable gloss in Gratian at the place cited above.]

In seven weeks, however, when Sundays and Saturdays are subtracted, thirty-five days remain assigned to fasting. But when that day of the vigils is added—the day on which the Saturday fast is prolonged until cockcrow, as Sunday dawns—not only is the number of thirty-six days completed, but, if the remaining portion of the night is included, the five days that seemed still to be lacking for the tithes are also supplied, and nothing at all is missing from the fullness of the total.

[Note: [Col. 1201D] That is, from the vigil of Pascha, or Holy Saturday. On that day not only the Romans but also the Greeks and Easterners customarily fasted, contrary to the usual practice concerning Saturdays, and celebrated vigils in the church until midnight on Sunday. Hence the Mass of that Saturday is not the Mass of the day but of the night, as nearly all who have written about ecclesiastical offices and ceremonies observe. The collect and preface of that same Mass sufficiently indicate this, since they mention the night, not the day.

For this reason Saint Jerome, in his commentary on Matthew 25, teaches that it is an apostolic tradition that on the day of the Paschal vigil the people may not be dismissed before midnight, as they await the coming of Christ; after that time has passed, they are to celebrate the feast day with confidence. Moreover, Vigilantius the heresiarch, as the same Jerome reports (Against Vigilantius, book 1, chapter 4), attacked and tried to diminish ecclesiastical nocturnal vigils—as an enemy of his own name—yet claimed that vigils should be held once a year, at the paschal solemnity. There is also a sermon of Saint Augustine on the Paschal Vigils, cited by Amalarius (book 1, chapter 16) in this connection.]

## CHAPTER XXVI. How we must also offer our firstfruits to the Lord

[Col. 1201B]

What [Note: [Col. 1202C] In order that we may satisfy, insofar as it is natural and pertains to conduct, the command cited above (Collation 3) concerning offering tithes and firstfruits to God, the abbot teaches here that, in addition to the tithes of the whole year—which, as we said, are paid through the Lenten fast—we must offer certain firstfruits, and indeed many of them, to God every day, and this in the first hours of the day, that is, in the morning, so that they may truly be called firstfruits.] shall I say about the firstfruits that it is certain are presented daily by all who faithfully serve Christ? For when, awakened from sleep and rising with an alertness renewed, as it were, after slumber, before they conceive in their hearts any movement of the senses or admit any memory or concern for household affairs, they consecrate the beginnings and first stirrings of their thoughts in divine holocausts, what do they pay, through the high priest Jesus Christ, for the use of this life and as an image of the daily resurrection, if not truly the firstfruits of their own produce?

And when awakened from sleep, they likewise offer God the sacrifice of their rejoicing: at the first movement of their tongue they invoke him, celebrate his name and praises together, and, first opening the barriers of their lips to sing hymns to him, sacrifice to God the services of their mouths. In the same manner they present to him the first offerings of their hands and feet, when, rising from their beds, they stand in prayer; before using the offices of their limbs for their own affairs, they take nothing away from their service, but direct their steps toward his honor and fix them upon his praise. Thus they pay the firstfruits of all their movements by extending their hands, bending their knees, and prostrating their whole body.

For we cannot fulfill elsewhere what is sung in the psalm: “I rose before dawn and cried out” (Psalm CXVIII); and, “My eyes went before the morning toward you, that I might meditate on your words” (ibid.); and, “In the morning my prayer shall go before you” (Psalm LXXXVII)—unless, after the rest of sleep, recalled into this light, as we said above, as if from darkness and an imagined [Note: [Col. 1202D] That is, an image of death:

“For what is sleep except the image of cold death?” says the poet (Juvenal).

Hence sleep is also often taken for death in Scripture, and the dead are said to sleep: “Our friend Lazarus sleeps”; yet he had spoken of his death (John XI): “We do not want you to be ignorant concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the rest who have no hope” (I Thessalonians IV).] death, we dare to presume upon nothing whatsoever from all the functions of mind and body for our own needs.

For there is no other one whom the prophet anticipated in the morning, nor whom we likewise ought to anticipate, except either ourselves—that is, our occupations, affections, and mortal cares, without which we cannot exist—or the enemy’s most subtle suggestions. While we are still at rest and submerged in sleep, he tries to introduce them through the phantasms of empty dreams, so that, as soon as we awaken, he may seize and entangle us with them, and, first plucking the rich flower of our firstfruits, take them for himself.

Therefore, we must take every precaution—if indeed we wish by our actions to fulfill the force of the verse mentioned above—that vigilant watchfulness may guard the first beginnings of our morning thoughts, lest some hasty presumption of the envious enemy [Note: [Col. 1203B] That is, of the devil, who envies us. Attaminare is used for contaminare, “to defile,” or contingere, “to touch.” Saint Ambrose frequently uses this verb; in him the passage of the Apostle in Colossians II also reads: “Do not touch, do not defile, do not taste,” things that lead to corruption by their very use.] touch and stain them, and cause our firstfruits, already regarded as worthless and common, to be rejected by the Lord. If he is not anticipated by us through vigilant watchfulness of mind, he will not cease daily to anticipate us with his deceptions, since he does not abandon the habit of his most wicked preemption.

And therefore, if we desire to offer God firstfruits pleasing and acceptable from the produce of our mind, we must devote no ordinary care to preserving all the senses of our body—especially in the morning hours—like sacred holocausts of the Lord, pure and untouched in every respect. Many even among secular people carefully maintain this kind of devotion. Rising before daylight or at dawn, they do not become entangled in the familiar and necessary activities of this world before hastening to the church and striving to consecrate the firstfruits of all their actions and works to the divine presence.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Why is Lent observed by most people for a differing number of days?

Moreover, concerning what you say—that Lent is celebrated in some provinces according to different custom, namely for six or seven weeks—one and the same principle and manner of fasting is enclosed within the differing observance of the weeks. [Note: [Col. 1203C] There is therefore no disagreement between the Latins and Greeks regarding the number of days, although there is regarding the number of weeks. Both observed thirty-six days of fasting during Lent. The Greeks, or Easterners, celebrated Lent over seven weeks because they excluded from the fast not only Sundays but also Saturdays, except Holy Saturday. The Latins, or Romans, fasted for only six weeks because they excluded from the Lenten fast only Sundays. Thus both agreed in the number of days, although they differed in the number of weeks. For just as thirty-six fasting days are found in six weeks when the Sundays are subtracted, so the same number of fasting days is contained in seven weeks when Sundays and Saturdays are subtracted, with the single exception of Easter Saturday.

Saint John Damascene teaches that the Greeks established the period of Lent as seven weeks in his booklet On Fasts, addressed to Cometas, where, on this subject, he cites the ancients: Saint Athanasius in the book of Solemn Sermons, Saint Basil in his sermon Against Drunkenness, Peter Martyr, patriarch of Jerusalem, and Anastasius of Antioch in the book he calls the Ὁδηγός, “Guide.” Socrates, and after him Sozomen (Socrates V.21; Sozomen VII.19), understand such Greeks to mean the people of Constantinople and the surrounding nations as far as Phoenicia. They add, however, that throughout Illyricum, western Greece, Libya, Egypt, and Palestine, an equal Lent consisting of six weeks was retained.] For those who prescribe an observance of six weeks believe that one must fast on Saturday as well. Thus they complete six fasts in a week, and, by repeating these six times, complete the same thirty-six days.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Why is it called Lent when one fasts for only thirty-six days?

There is therefore, as we have said, one principle and one manner of fasting, even though there appears to be a difference in the number of weeks. But when human negligence had obliterated the explanation of this matter, the period during which, as we have said, the annual tithes are offered to God through thirty-six half-fasts received the name of Lent. Perhaps it seemed that it ought to be designated by this word because Moses, Elijah, or our Lord Jesus Christ are said to have fasted for forty days.

To the mystery of this number may also appropriately be joined the forty years during which Israel dwelt in the wilderness, and likewise the forty stations by which it is described as having mystically traversed it. Perhaps the very tithe rightly received the name of Lent, as it were, from the practice of the tax office [Note: [Col. 1203D] Telonium, or teloneum, was a place where taxes were collected; among the Jews it was also called the tax collectors’ table, since the tax was usually money, which was customarily counted out upon a table. It was from this place that Matthew was suddenly changed from a tax collector into an apostle. Telonium was derived from the Greek word τέλος, which among other meanings signifies “tax.” Hence τελῶνες or τελῶναι, “tax collectors,” who were also called publicans because they exacted taxes. Concerning them, see Theodosius’s Canon of the Tax Office in Book III of On Remitting Debts, chapter 4. We read in Cassiodorus, Book V, Letter 39, of the tax-office payment and understand that it was paid to the Gothic kings (Jerome on Matthew IX; Suidas, entries τέλος and τελώνης; Budaeus in his commentary).] as the name of Lent. For just as that public exaction is commonly called the “fortieth,” from which as much profit is assigned to the king’s interests as the lawful “fortieth” tax is exacted from us by the King of all ages for the use of our life, so this may have received the name of Lent by analogy.

[Note: [Col. 1204C] Three probable explanations are suggested for why Lent was called by this name even at a time when the fast lasted not forty but only thirty-six days. The first explanation concerns the fact that, although the number forty was not complete, it was nevertheless thought appropriate to call it Lent because it fell only slightly short of that number; through this fast they professed that, according to their capacity, they wished to imitate the forty-day fasts of Christ, Moses, and Elijah. This was especially so because on Sundays also, although the fast was not full or complete, an imperfect and partial fast, as Tertullian calls it (Book On Fasting), was nevertheless observed everywhere—namely, abstinence from meat and from the other prohibited foods.

The second explanation is that the number forty is a symbol of penitence and affliction. Thus the forty years, and the forty—or, according to Jerome, forty-two—stations of the Israelite people in the wilderness prefigured this symbolism (Jerome on Jonah III and Ezekiel XXIX, and Letter 127 to Fabiola; Peter Damian, Book II, Letter 3). Saint Ambrose explained this reason more fully in Sermon 23 on Lent: “We read,” he says, “in the Old Testament (Deuteronomy III) that when holy Moses rescued the children of Israel from the yoke of Egyptian captivity in order to lead them into the promised land, he reached that land after forty-two days’ stations, and that he was granted as many periods of time as we rejoice to enjoy the promises made to us by the Savior. By the same number Moses reached rest through his stations as we hasten to heaven through fasts. For our fasts are certain stations by which, journeying spiritually, we walk in the virtues of the soul; through daily progress we draw nearer to the promised land,” and so forth.

The third explanation is that, just as among the Romans a certain portion of the revenues fell to the prince or emperor from the customary use of the tax office—Cicero, Against Verres, Act IV—that is, from the taxes, tithes, and other revenues of the Roman people which the publicans collected or offered for collection by selling the right to collect them for a price (whence they were also called decumani, from decumae or tithes), so this abstinence, like an annual tax that we pay to God, may have received the name of Lent by analogy.

A further and subtler explanation can likewise be gathered from Alcuin, Book On the Divine Office, chapter 8. There he also explains the reason for the name Septuagesima in these words: “It is the custom of the divine Scriptures that whenever any number has passed beyond a decade—for example, when it reaches the third monad [for so, I think, it should be read]—that number is not reckoned as belonging to the preceding decade, but to the one toward which it tends. Read the book of Genesis in the genealogy of the sons of Noah.” Thus, in the same way, we should understand the Lenten fast: since thirty-six days exceed the thirtieth, they are therefore said to belong to the fortieth and ought to be designated by that name.

From what has so far been said about the Lenten fast, several points especially worth noting and knowing may be gathered.

1. In the Catholic Church, throughout all ages, among both Greeks and Latins, the paschal fast was a fast of forty days, or approximately forty days—that is, thirty-six. For all the ancient councils and Fathers use the name Lent when commending the paschal fast (Bellarmine, Book II On Good Works, Part I, chapter 15; Council of Nicaea, canon 5; Council of Laodicea, canon 49; Ignatius, Letter to the Philippians; Origen, Homily 10 on Leviticus; Tertullian, Book II On Fasting; Basil, Oration 2 On Fasting). By the name Lent, however, nothing can be understood except a number of forty, or approximately forty.

2. Lent properly begins on the first Sunday of Lent, as the Micrologus observed in chapter 49. This is also gathered from Saint Ambrose, Gregory, Cassian, and others who write that Lent consists of forty-two days; when the six Sundays on which there is no fasting are subtracted, thirty-six fasting days remain. The same is clear both from the office of that Sunday and from the fact that formerly the Lenten fast was ended toward evening, now after the office of Vespers, whereas the fast of the four days preceding the first Sunday is commonly ended at the ninth hour, or after the office of None.

3. Although at the beginning the Lenten fast consisted of only thirty-six days, which were reckoned as the tithe of the whole year, as has been said, nevertheless, as Gratian cites from Gregory (De Consecratione, distinction 5, chapter “Quadragesima”), four days of the preceding week were added so that the sacred number of forty days might be fulfilled, the number consecrated by our Savior through his holy fast. These were Wednesday, which is marked as the beginning of the fast, the following Thursday, Friday, and Saturday. Yet there may also have been another reason for this institution: that, together with the tithe of the Lenten fast, we might offer something to God as firstfruits in the observance of these four days, and thus also fulfill in this way the natural commandment concerning the offering of tithes and firstfruits.

4. It is not sufficiently clear when or by whom these four days were first instituted as an addition to the forty-day fast, or in order to complete the number of forty days. For the holy Fathers explicitly state that the Lenten fast consists of forty days. From this it is understood that these four days before the first Sunday of Lent were already observed in most churches. Saint Augustine, Sermon 62 On Time, says: “With good reason we ought to keep the number of forty days, which we read was consecrated through the examples of Moses, Elijah, and Christ.” Saint Leo, Sermon 4 on Lent, says: “It was provided that a forty-day exercise should heal us in restoring purity of mind.” And in Sermon 5: “The apostolic institution is fulfilled by a forty-day fast.”

The same may be gathered from chapter 2 of the Council of Orange (in Burchard, Book XIII, chapter 9), whether this means the first or the second council, since it is certain that both were celebrated long before the time of Saint Gregory. There it is prescribed: “On Holy Saturday, that is, the vigil of Easter, the fast is not to be broken before the beginning of the night except by children or the sick; nor on Good Friday itself, since the Lord’s Supper, Good Friday, and Saturday pertain to those forty days”—that is, to the forty-day Lenten fast. It follows that these four days had already been added to Lent at that time, since they too belong to and complete the number of forty days. Consequently, the beginning of the Lenten fast must be Wednesday, since it is universally acknowledged that the law of fasting is suspended on Sundays.

Furthermore, the Council of Agde, celebrated around the year of our Lord 506, prescribes in chapter 9 that penitents, sprinkled with ashes and clothed in sackcloth, be expelled from the church by the bishop at the beginning of Lent. This seems to mean nothing other than Ash Wednesday itself, which we call the beginning of the fast. On that day, singers in former times used to sing in the church: “Let us change our garment for ashes and sackcloth; let us fast and weep before the Lord,” and so forth. This is also customarily sung at the same Wednesday in our own time; it is never read as having been used on Sunday, which the Fathers have always regarded as a day of rejoicing.

Finally, writers on ecclesiastical ceremonies and observances remember this addition as extremely ancient and received throughout the Church, at least the Latin Church, when treating of the beginning of the fast. Among them Amalarius Fortunatus says that these four days are to be guarded with devotion similar to that of the thirty-six days, and with equal abstinence—that is, with the observance of fasting—and that they are commended both by the authority of the holy Fathers and by reason itself. It is reasonable to understand the holy Fathers whom he names as not later than Saint Gregory himself, but rather as his contemporaries or predecessors.

To these may be added Alphonsus of Pisa, who writes in his Book On Penance, chapter 8: “It has always been the custom of the Roman Church to celebrate the Lenten fast from Ash Wednesday until the days of Easter; for within that period of time, excluding Sundays, the number forty remains.” It is therefore clear that the opinion of some—that Gregory added those four days of fasting before the first Sunday of Lent—is not true. There exist sermons of Saint Augustine, much earlier than Gregory, for Ash Wednesday and the three following days. Thus he, and much more besides.

Cardinal Bellarmine further notes that the addition of these four days varied somewhat. In the time of Saint Leo the four days were Monday, Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday; in the time of Saint Gregory they were Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, and Saturday, as they are observed now. This may have moved Gratian to think that these four days had been instituted by Saint Gregory. Yet he cites certain matters under Gregory’s name that are not found in Gregory, as Peter Maturus noted in his commentary on Saint Antoninus. More on these matters may be found in Turrecremata on chapter 49 of the Rule of Saint Benedict, and in Bellarmine, Book II On Good Works, chapter 15 and following, from which we have extracted some points in summary.]

Certainly, although this does not pertain to the question proposed, since an opportunity for narration has presented itself, I do not think even this should be passed over: our elders very frequently testified that in those days, above all, every kind of monk was attacked by the ancient custom of the hostile race and driven more fiercely to migrate from its dwelling places. They said that, in accordance with the likeness by which the Egyptians then oppressed the children of Israel with violent afflictions, the intellectual Egyptians now also strive to bend the true Israel—that is, the multitude of monks—with the harshest and muddiest labors, lest, leaving the land of Egypt through a rest pleasing to God, we should pass safely into the desert of the virtues.

Thus Pharaoh, roaring against us, says: “They are idle, and therefore they cry out, saying, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to the Lord our God.’ Let them be oppressed with labors, and let them be concerned with their works, and not be concerned with empty words” (Exodus V). For the vanity of the ungodly declares the holy sacrifice of the Lord—which is offered only in the desert of a free heart—to be the height of vanity. “Religion is an abomination to the sinner.”

## CHAPTER XXIX. How the perfect surpass the law of Lent

[Note: [Col. 1207C] It had seemed sufficient here to advise the reader to read and weigh carefully the annotations and censures of Dom. Cuychius, as well as those of Ciaconius, on this passage. But Cardinal Bellarmine’s opinion on this same passage aptly presents itself: it not only excuses Cassian—or rather Abbot Theonas—but asserts that he was very far from the error of the Begards, who taught that perfect men were not bound by laws of fasting. For the reader’s convenience and satisfaction, I have thought it proper to set down Bellarmine’s judgment here. Bellarmine therefore says (Book II, On Good Works, chapter 10): “With regard to Cassian, he was very far from the error of the Begards. There are three principal points that he teaches in that chapter. First, he affirms that righteous and perfect men are not subject to a coercive law, since they fast freely and cheerfully not only during Lent but throughout the whole year. Secondly, he adds that such perfect men, if there is cause to relax an imposed fast, can safely do so more readily than others who observe only the prescribed fasts, because they are certain, both in their own judgment and in that of others, that they relaxed their fast not for intemperance but solely for charity. Thirdly, he adds that those perfect men who fast throughout the whole year are not bound by the laws of fasting by which others are bound, since they offer God more than these laws command. In this third point, however, we do not think his opinion should be followed, both because a necessary offering ought not to be omitted on account of a voluntary offering, and because of the reason given a little earlier. For although those who are accustomed to fast for whole months do not need a fast of a few days to subdue the flesh, nevertheless the law is common and imposed upon all, and therefore does not cease to bind them as well.” Thus far Bellarmine. The Synod of Trent entirely supports this opinion (Session 6, canon 2), defining under anathema that a justified person, however perfect, is bound to observe the commandments of God and of the Church.]

Thus, the just and perfect person is not bound by the law of Lent; nor is he content with subjection to this slight canon, which the leaders of the churches established especially for those who, throughout the whole year, are entangled in pleasures or secular business (I Timothy I), so that, constrained by this sort of legal necessity, they might at least on these days be compelled to devote themselves to the Lord and dedicate to him the tithes of the days of their life, which they would otherwise devour in their entirety as fruits.

But the just, for whom there is no law, and who devote not merely that small portion—the tenth—but the whole of their lives to spiritual duties, are free from the obligation of legal tithes. Therefore, if an honorable and holy necessity comes upon them and constrains them, they dare to relax the fast without any dispute. [Note: [Col. 1208C] In Cassian, statio jejunii, “the station of the fast,” means the fast itself, as we have shown elsewhere (Institutes, Book V, chapter 24). Tertullian uses the word in the same way in the final section of his Book On Prayer, where he asks whether the station is dissolved by receiving the Eucharist; that is equivalent to asking whether the Eucharist is such food that, once it has been taken, the fast is considered dissolved.

In that ancient book, although apocryphal, entitled The Shepherd, Hermas, its author introduces the Shepherd speaking with him in this way: “Why have you come here so early?” I replied, “Because I have a station.” “What is a station?” he asked. And I said, “A fast.”

Saint Jerome likewise uses the term station in Book II Against Jovinianus, writing: “Saul, as it is written in the First Book of Kings, said, ‘Cursed is the man who eats bread before evening, until I take vengeance on my enemies.’ And all his people did not taste food.” So great was the authority of a station once dedicated to the Lord that Jonathan, who had brought about the victory, was detected by lot and could not avoid the charge of ignorance.] For those who have offered everything of theirs together with themselves to the Lord do not diminish the smallness of their tithes. [Lipsius in the margin: “because.”] But one who offers nothing voluntarily to God cannot do this without the gravest charge of fraud; necessity under the law inexcusably compels him to pay his tithes.

Therefore it is clearly proved that the servant of the law cannot be perfect if he merely avoids what is forbidden or carries out what is commanded. Rather, those are truly perfect who do not even use what the law permits. For this reason, when it is said of the Mosaic law, “The law brought nothing to perfection” (Hebrews VII), we nevertheless read that some of the saints in the Old Testament were perfect, because they transcended the command of the law and lived under evangelical perfection, knowing that “the law is not laid down for the just, but for the unjust and disobedient, for the ungodly and sinners, for the wicked and defiled” (I Timothy I).

[Note: [Col. 1208D] “Of itself,” understood. For the fact that certain holy and perfect people existed under the law was not achieved from the law or through the power of the law, but through the grace of Christ—that is, of the Messiah—in whom they believed, as the Apostle teaches repeatedly in his Epistles. The law merely prepared the way to grace and led them by the hand like a pedagogue. Hence John I says absolutely and by antithesis: “The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ,” not through Moses.]

## CHAPTER XXX. On the cause and beginning of Lent

[Note: [Col. 1208D] Although Ciaconius tries to defend this passage to some extent and rescue it from error and falsity, there are nevertheless two matters here that seem to me to deserve correction rather than excuse and defense.

First, the law concerning the observance of Lent was not promulgated by the apostles in the earliest beginnings of the Church, but was instituted later by priests—that is, bishops (Bellarmine, Book II On Good Works, chapter 14).

Second, in ancient times an equal and continuous fast was observed by all Christians in the primitive Church. But as devotion gradually grew cold and fasting began to be neglected by many, all the priests supposedly agreed that the Lenten fast should be imposed and established by fixed law. Yet this opinion is contradicted especially by the apostolic canon (Canon 68) and by the apostolic constitution on the observance of Lent, cited by Saint Clement (Clement, Book V of the Constitutions, chapter 13). It is also contradicted by the holy Fathers, who unanimously teach that the Lenten fast is an apostolic institution and tradition.

Thus Saint Jerome writes to Marcella: “We fast one Lent, according to the tradition of the apostles, at the fitting time throughout the year.” And Saint Leo says: “What, then, dearly beloved, is fitting for every Christian to do at all times must now be carried out with greater earnestness and devotion, so that the apostolic constitution may be fulfilled by a forty-day fast—not merely by sparing food, but especially by renouncing vices.”

Cardinal Bellarmine also shows that the foundation of this same opinion is false in these words: “Although it is credible that the apostles and certain others, just as they lived in common and practiced perpetual continence, likewise fasted either throughout the whole year or at least very frequently, nevertheless it is neither certain nor probable that all Christians fasted throughout the entire year. Nor should one in any way affirm that all Christians everywhere under the apostles led celibate and common lives. For among the Corinthians and in other Greek cities, as is clear from the letters of the Apostle Paul, many Christians had children and retained their own property. Hence collections were made among them on the first day of the week—that is, on Sunday—so that the poor might be supported by the alms of the rich; Cassian also teaches this in Book VII of the Institutes, chapter 17.

Moreover, in I Corinthians VII the Apostle admonishes the Corinthians to suspend marital relations for a time so that they may devote themselves to prayer; the Greeks add καὶ τῇ νηστείᾳ, that is, ‘and to fasting.’ They therefore did not customarily fast throughout the whole year. And in I Corinthians VIII he advises them to eat whatever is sold in the market. From this we conclude that they were also permitted to eat meat, from which those who fast abstain.”]

It must certainly be understood that this observance of Lent did not exist as long as the perfection of that primitive Church remained inviolate. Those who enclosed the whole year in an equal fast were not confined within the strict limits of fasts, bound by the necessity of this commandment or by something like a legal sanction. But when the multitude of believers, descending from that apostolic devotion, began daily to cling to its own possessions and no longer distribute them for the common use according to the apostles’ instructions (Acts IV), but, privately attending to its own expenditures, strove not merely to preserve but even to increase them (Acts V), being unwilling to be content with following the example of Ananias and Sapphira, then all the priests agreed that people bound by secular cares and almost—so to speak—ignorant of continence or compunction should be recalled to the holy work by a canonical imposition of fasts.

They were to be compelled, as it were, by the necessity of legal tithes—something that can indeed benefit the weak but cannot prejudice the perfect. Established under the grace of the Gospel, the perfect transcend the law through voluntary devotion, so that they may reach the blessedness of the apostolic saying: “Sin will not rule over you, for you are not under the law but under grace” (Romans VI). For sin truly cannot exercise dominion over one who rules his sinful affections.

## CHAPTER XXXI. The question: how should the Apostle’s statement “Sin will not rule over us” be understood?

Germanus: Since this apostolic statement cannot be false, and promises security not only to monks but generally to all Christians, it seems exceedingly obscure to us. For when it declares that all who believe in the Gospel are free and separated from the yoke and dominion of sin, how does the dominion of sins prevail in nearly all the baptized, according to the Lord’s statement: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John VIII)?

## CHAPTER XXXII. The answer: on the difference between grace and legal commandments
Theonas: Your inquiry has once again stirred up no small question for us. Although I know that its force cannot be conveyed or understood by the inexperienced, I shall nevertheless try, insofar as I can, to resolve and explain it briefly in words—provided that your understanding also follows what we say in practice. For whatever is learned not through instruction but through experience, just as it cannot be imparted by one without experience, so it cannot be conceived or retained in the mind except by one who has been formed by a similar zeal and training. Therefore I think it necessary first to investigate more carefully what the purpose or intention of the Law is, and what the discipline and perfection of grace are, so that from these we may subsequently recognize either the domination of sin or its expulsion.

Thus the Law principally commands that the marriage union be sought, saying:

> Blessed is he who has seed in Zion and householders in Jerusalem (Isaiah 31, according to the Septuagint);

and:

> Cursed is the barren woman who has not borne children.

[Note: This is how the Septuagint translated that passage of Isaiah where our version reads: “Whose fire is in Zion, and whose furnace is in Jerusalem.” Thus Saint Jerome also cites it in Letter 101 to Pammachius: “For that passage which we read in Isaiah, ‘Blessed is he who has seed in Zion and householders in Jerusalem,’ the Hebrews customarily mock when they hear it.” And in his Letter to Eustochium (Letter 22): “There was another kind of happiness under the old Law. There it is said: ‘Blessed is he who has seed in Zion and householders in Jerusalem’ (Isaiah 31; Psalm 127). And: ‘Cursed is the barren woman who did not bear’ (Deuteronomy 15). And: ‘Your children are like olive shoots around your table’ (Isaiah 56). And: ‘The promise of riches’ (Matthew 5). And: ‘There will be no weak person in your tribes’ (Luke 16). Now it is said to eunuchs: ‘Do not think yourself a dry tree’ (2 Corinthians 12). You have, in place of sons and daughters, an eternal dwelling in the heavenly places. Now the poor are blessed, and Lazarus is preferred to the rich man in purple. Now the one who is weak is stronger,” and so forth. These and other statements of Saint Jerome agree extremely well with the teaching of this chapter and several following chapters, in which the difference between grace and the commandments of the Law—that is, between the evangelical and Mosaic Laws—is discussed.]

By contrast, grace invites us to the purity and chastity of perpetual incorruption and blessed virginity:

> Blessed are the barren, those who have not borne children, and the breasts that have not nursed;

and:

> Whoever does not hate his father and mother and wife cannot be my disciple (Luke 14).

And the Apostle says:

> It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none (1 Corinthians 7).

The Law says:

> You shall not delay to offer your tithes and firstfruits (Exodus 22).

Grace says:

> If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have, and give to the poor (Matthew 19).

[Note: Indeed, it forbids every private individual from doing this on private authority, as was said elsewhere. Leviticus 19: “You shall not remember the injury done by your fellow citizens.” And Proverbs 12: “The ways of those who retain the memory of wrongdoing lead to death.” And what of the passage in our version of Deuteronomy: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Deuteronomy 32), which the Apostle rendered: “Vengeance belongs to me, and I will repay” (Romans 12)? Moreover, the fifth commandment of the Decalogue, “You shall not kill,” prohibits not only every harm that can be inflicted upon one’s neighbor’s body, but also the will to do harm. Hence Cassian himself elsewhere proves from these same Scriptures that the Old Law uproots anger not only in its effect but also in thought (Institutes, Book VIII, chapter 14). What else is this than prohibiting insults and injuries, or the retaliation for them and the desire for vengeance? Yet even in this respect there is a considerable difference between the old and the new Law. For that old law of retaliation restrained people merely through fear of punishment, lest they lay hands upon others, as Chrysostom observed. But Christ, the new legislator, wished us to be led to good action not by fear, like slaves, but by love, like sons: “For you have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you have received the spirit of adoption as sons of God” (Romans 4). And he taught us not only not to seek vengeance, but also patiently to endure injury—not merely to endure it, but to desire it and glory in it. Finally, he commands us to offer the other cheek to one who strikes us on one cheek, and to leave our cloak to one who wishes to take our tunic (Matthew 5). As the Apostle says [supply: “we glory”] not only “in the hope of the sons of God,” but also “in tribulations” (Romans 5).]

The Law of retaliation does not prohibit the vengeance of insults and injuries, saying:

> An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth (Exodus 21).

Grace wishes the repetition of injuries or blows that have been inflicted to be tested by our patience, and commands us to be prepared to endure a double loss:

> Whoever strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also; and to the one who wishes to bring you to court and take your tunic, leave him your cloak as well (Matthew 5).

[Note: Namely, the tunic and cloak, as was just said from the fifth chapter of Matthew.]

That law [Note: Not the Law itself, but the Pharisaic perversion of its interpretation, which Christ rejected and repudiated, saying: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall love your neighbor, and hate your enemy.’ But I say to you: love your enemies; do good to those who hate you; and pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven,” and so forth (Matthew 5).] says that enemies are to be hated (Leviticus 19); grace, on the contrary, declares that they are to be loved, so that we should always be considered bound to pray to God even for them (Matthew 5).

## CHAPTER XXXIII. That the precepts of the Gospel are lighter than those of the Law

Whoever, therefore, has ascended to this summit of evangelical perfection is certainly exalted above the whole Law by the merits of such great virtues. Despising as insignificant everything commanded through Moses, he recognizes himself as living entirely under the grace of the Savior, by whose assistance he understands that he has reached that most exalted state. Sin therefore does not rule in him, because the love of God, which has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Romans 5), excludes every affection for anything else. Such a person can neither desire what is forbidden nor despise what is commanded. His entire effort and desire are always directed toward divine love, and he is so little captured by the pleasure of base things that he does not even make use of things that have been permitted.

[Note: This entire passage seems sufficiently obscure that it may properly be assisted and clarified by the French translation of Lavardin, which runs as follows:

“Now, in the Mosaic Law, in which the obligations of faith and marriage are observed, it is impossible that the goads of carnal desire should not retain their vigor and strength, even though that same Law commands a man to limit himself, on the basis of his pledged faith, to one woman and wife. It is difficult for the fire to which fuel and nourishment are supplied to be so confined, enclosed, and restrained within the boundaries prescribed for marriage that, extending beyond them, it does not burn everything it touches. Although its object—that is, its wife—is always presented before it, so that it is not permitted to burn outwardly, nevertheless it burns even while it is restrained; for the will itself is guilty and blameworthy, and the habit of lying with one’s wife is quickly carried toward the excesses of adultery. But those whom the Savior’s grace has inflamed with the holy desire for an incorrupt life consume and destroy by the flames of divine charity all the thorns of carnal desires so completely that not even the hot and smoldering ashes of sins diminish in any way the refreshment of their purity and innocence. The slaves and servants of the Law therefore fall into illicit things by making use of what is licit or permitted. Those who share in grace, or who are ministers of the Gospel, when they despise what is licit and are unwilling in any way to use it, have no acquaintance with illicit things and have no part in them. Just as sin lives in one who loves marriage, so likewise it lives in one who is content merely to pay his tithes and firstfruits,” and so forth.

Thus far Lavardin’s interpretation, which is not unworthy of consideration and, I hope, will not be unwelcome to the reader.]

Under the Law, however, in which the rights of marriage are preserved, although the wandering of lust is restrained and bound to one woman alone, nevertheless the goads of carnal desire cannot fail to remain vigorous. It is difficult for a fire, to which fuel is deliberately supplied, to be enclosed within such fixed boundaries that, when it wanders beyond them, it does not burn whatever it touches. Even if its own object is always present to it in such a way that it is not allowed to flare up outwardly, nevertheless, while it is restrained, it still sets things ablaze, because the will itself [Al. pleasure] is blameworthy, and the habit of intercourse is carried toward the swiftest excesses of adultery.

But those whom the grace of the Savior has inflamed with a holy love of incorruption consume all the thorns of carnal desires by the fire of divine charity, so that not even the still-warm ember of vices diminishes the refreshment of integrity. The servants of the Law, therefore, slide from licit things into illicit ones through using what is permitted; those who share in grace, by despising what is licit, have no knowledge of illicit things.

Just as sin lives in one who loves marriage, so likewise it lives in one who is content merely to offer his tithes and firstfruits.

[Note: Ciaconius printed *redhibere* here; others, more clearly along with Dionysius, have *reddere* (“to return”); some manuscripts have *dare* (“to give”). Among jurists, however, *redhibere* means, as the jurist Ulpian says (in Book XXI, *On the Edict of the Aediles*), to cause the seller to have again what he sold. Since this was done by returning and restoring it, *redhibitio* came to be so called, as though it meant return and restoration to the original condition. For, as Festus says, that which has been returned is properly called *redhibitum*. Here, therefore, *redhibere* is used simply for “to return,” “to present,” or “to pay,” as also in Plautus, *Menaechmi*: “I return the purse to you safe, just as you gave it to me.” Cassian likewise uses the same word *redhibitio* in Book IV of the *Institutes*, chapter 4.]

For it is necessary that, while delaying or neglecting them, he should sin either in their quality, their quantity, or their daily distribution. For one who is commanded tirelessly to minister what belongs to him to those in need, however faithfully and devoutly he distributes it, can scarcely avoid frequently falling into the snares of sin.

But sin cannot rule over those who have not rejected the Lord’s counsel and who, perhaps giving all their possessions to the poor, follow the giver of heavenly grace after taking up their cross. For one who distributes the riches already consecrated to Christ, and money regarded as belonging to another, through pious giving, will not be gnawed by the faithless anxiety of preserving his livelihood; nor will mournful hesitation drive away the cheerfulness of almsgiving. For once he has offered everything to God, he scatters it as something belonging to another, without recalling his own needs or fearing a narrow means of subsistence. He is certain that, once he has reached the nakedness he desires, God will feed him even more surely than he feeds the birds of the air.
