By contrast, one who retains worldly substance and, constrained by the sanction of the ancient Law, distributes either tithes and firstfruits of his produce or a portion of his money, although he may extinguish the fire of his sins to a considerable degree by this dew of almsgiving, nevertheless—however generously he distributes his wealth—cannot completely free himself from the domination of sin, unless perhaps, through the grace of the Savior, he also lays aside, together with his possessions, the very desire to possess.

In the same way, whoever, at the command of the Law, chooses to exact an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth (Exodus 21), or prefers to hate his enemy, cannot fail to serve the bloody rule of sin.

[Note: This is not prescribed by the Law, but by the perverse interpretation of the Pharisees and scribes, as was said above. The gloss on Matthew 5 says: “It should be known that the words ‘You shall hate your enemy’ are not written anywhere in the whole body of the Law. But this is said with regard to the tradition of the scribes, who thought that it should be added because the Lord commanded the children of Israel to pursue their enemies and to wipe Amalek from beneath heaven” (Exodus 17).]

For while he wishes to avenge his injury through reciprocal retaliation, and while he preserves the bitterness of hatred against his enemies, he must always be inflamed by the disturbance of fury and anger.

But whoever lives under the illumination of evangelical grace, overcoming evil not by resisting but by enduring, willingly offers the other cheek to the one who strikes him on the right cheek; to the one who wishes to bring a lawsuit against him over his tunic, he relinquishes his cloak; and whoever loves his enemies and prays for those who slander him has thrown off the yoke of sin and broken its bonds (Matthew 5; Hebrews 7).

For he does not live under the Law, which does not destroy the seeds of sin. Hence the blessed Apostle not unreasonably says of it:

> The rejection of the preceding commandment occurs because of its weakness and uselessness; for the Law brought nothing to perfection.

And the Lord says through the prophet:

> I gave them commandments that were not good, and judgments in which they would not live.

[Note: Saint Thomas says that the Lord there speaks of the ceremonial precepts (1–2, question 98, article 1). These are called “not good” because they did not confer the grace by which people would be cleansed from sin, although through such observances they demonstrated themselves to be sinners. Hence it is expressly said: “And judgments in which they will not live” (Ezekiel 20), that is, through which they cannot obtain the life of grace. He adds afterward: “And I will defile them in their gifts,” that is, “I will show them to have been defiled.”]

But he lives under grace, which not only cuts off the branches of wickedness but completely uproots the very roots of the harmful will.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. How one may be proved to be under grace

Whoever, therefore, has made it his aim to hold fast to the perfection of evangelical teaching is established under grace and is not weighed down by the domination of sin. For this is what it means to be under grace: to fulfill what grace commands.

But whoever refuses to submit to the fullness of evangelical perfection should realize that, although he may appear to himself to be baptized and a monk, he is not under grace but is still hindered by the bonds of the Law and heavily burdened by the weight of sin. For it is the purpose of him who adopts by the grace of adoption all whom he has received not to destroy but to build upon;

[Note: Thus Christ declared at the beginning of his preaching: “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the prophets; I have not come to abolish but to fulfill” (Matthew 5). He fulfilled it not only by supplying the spirit of grace through which the Law is fulfilled by us, but also by confirming, interpreting more fully, and supplementing what had been expressed less clearly in the old Law, as is evident from the same passage. See Saint Thomas, 1–2, question 107, article 2.]

nor to annul but to fulfill the Mosaic enactments.

Some, being completely ignorant of this and neglecting the magnificence of Christ’s counsels and exhortations, are so released by the security of presumptuous liberty that they not only fail to approach Christ’s commands as difficult, but even despise those Mosaic commands that are like small matters for beginners and children, saying with the harmful liberty that the Apostle condemns:

> Let us sin, because we are not under the Law but under grace (Romans 6).

Whoever, therefore, is neither under grace, because he has not ascended to the summit of the Lord’s teaching, nor under the Law, because he does not accept even those small commandments of the Law, is oppressed by the twofold rule of sins. He thinks that he has received Christ’s grace for the sole purpose of becoming alienated from Christ through harmful liberty, falling into what the Apostle Peter warns us not to incur:

> Live as free people, and not as those who have freedom as a veil for wickedness (1 Peter 2).

The blessed Apostle Paul likewise says:

> You have been called to freedom, brothers (Galatians 5);

that is, you have been released from the domination of sin—but only so that you do not give freedom an opportunity for the flesh, that is, do not suppose that the abolition of the commandments of the Law is permission for vice.

The Apostle Paul teaches that this freedom exists nowhere except where the Lord dwells:

> The Lord is Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom (2 Corinthians 3).

Therefore I do not know whether I have been able to express and clarify the meaning of the blessed Apostle as those who have experienced it understand it. I know one thing most certainly: it is laid open even without anyone’s explanation to all who have perfectly mastered the practical discipline.

[Note: Abbot Nesteros describes this as follows in *Conference* 14, chapter 1: *praktikē* (πρακτική), that is, “active” or “practical,” which is perfected through the correction of conduct and the cleansing of vices. And in chapter 2: “Whoever therefore wishes to reach contemplation must necessarily acquire practical knowledge first, with every effort and virtue. For practical knowledge can indeed be possessed without contemplation, but contemplation cannot at all be grasped without practical knowledge.” In the following chapter he teaches that this practical discipline consists of two things: driving out vices and acquiring virtues.]

For they will not labor to understand through disputation what they have already learned by putting it into practice.

## CHAPTER XXXV. The question why, at times, when we are fasting, we are more sharply pressed by carnal impulses

[Col. 1215C]

Germanus: You have revealed with complete clarity a very obscure question, one that, as we think, is unknown even to many. We therefore beg you to add this also to our progress: explain carefully why, sometimes, when we are fasting more earnestly and are exhausted and weakened, more violent struggles of the body arise. For often, even after waking from sleep, when we discover that we have suffered the emission of bodily fluid,

[Note: What is meant by the contagion of bodily poison will be explained in the following Conference.]

we are so cast down by conscience that we do not even dare to rise confidently for prayer itself.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. The answer that this question should be reserved for the forthcoming Conference

Theonas: Your zeal, by which you desire to reach the way of perfection not superficially but principally and completely, tirelessly urges us to remain engaged in this discussion. For you are investigating not external chastity and manifest circumcision, but that which is hidden, carefully inquiring into it. You know that the fullness of perfection is not contained in this visible continence of the flesh, which can be possessed either through necessity or through hypocrisy even by unbelievers. Rather, you seek that voluntary and invisible purity of heart which the blessed Apostle proclaims in these words:

[Note: That is, it is not the one who openly and manifestly boasts that he is a Jew according to the flesh, but the one who confesses Christ in secret—that is, in heart and spirit—through faith, who is truly a Jew. Nor is that circumcision true which is manifest in the flesh—that is, not external circumcision of the flesh but spiritual circumcision of vices. Similarly, the person who externally displays himself as chaste and religious is not thereby immediately chaste and religious before God; rather, it is the person who is pure and chaste in secret—in heart and mind—whose praise comes not from human beings but from God (Romans 2).]

> For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is that circumcision which is outward in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit and not in the letter, whose praise is not from human beings but from God (Romans 2);

that is, from God alone, who searches the secrets of hearts.

Nevertheless, since it is impossible to satisfy your desire fully—the short period of night that remains is insufficient for investigating this extremely obscure question—I think it appropriate that it be postponed for the time being. These matters must be communicated gradually, both as they are brought forth by us and as they are received into your minds after the heart has been completely freed from the noise of every thought. Just as they must be investigated for the purification of conscience, so they cannot be handed down or assigned except by one who has experienced the gift of integrity. For the question is not what empty arguments of words assert, but what the inward faith of conscience and the greater force of truth impress upon us. Therefore, concerning the knowledge and teaching of this purification, nothing can be uttered except by one who has experienced it, nor can anything be transmitted except to one who ardently and earnestly loves that virtue itself, desiring to attain it not by the fruitless exercise of loquacity but by striving with all the powers of his soul for inward purity.

# THE TWENTY-SECOND CONFERENCE

The second conference of Abbot Theonas

## ON NOCTURNAL ILLUSIONS

[Col. 1217]

[Note: [Col. 1217C] [Col. 1217] This note is printed at the foot of column 1217, but its callout letter, a, does not appear in the text. It is likely that during these days Cassian, together with his Germanus, privately discussed among themselves, in their customary manner, the matters treated and debated in the preceding Conference, and committed them more carefully to memory, or even transmitted them in written records for the instruction and edification of later generations, as with the other material.]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1217A]

After approximately seven days had passed, once the solemnity of Pentecost had been completed, when, at the very beginning of the night—that is, after the evening synaxis—we had entered the cell of Saint Theonas, suspended in anticipation of the promised discussion, the cheerful old man addressed us first with a bright and friendly face:

“I was astonished,” he said, “that your most ardent zeal could have postponed the resolution of the proposed question for these seven days, and could have granted your debtor such a long delay, especially without his asking for it. Since your kindness has freely granted me so lengthy a respite, it is only right that I too should not delay in repaying what I owe. For the occupation of this interest is welcome: while it is being paid, it acquires greater increases; and it enriches not only the recipient but also diminishes nothing in the giver. The dispenser of spiritual things gathers a double profit. He gains not only from the progress of the one who listens but also from his own discussion, kindling himself no less toward the desire for perfection while instructing his hearer. Therefore your ardor is my progress, and your concern is my compunction. Indeed, I too would now be sluggish in mind and would not be considering in my heart anything of what you seek, unless your fervor and expectation had somehow awakened me, as I slept, to recollection of spiritual matters. Let us therefore bring forward the question, if you please, whose resolution we recently preferred to postpone because of the shortness of time.”

## CHAPTER II. Repetition of the question proposed: why greater abstinence is sometimes followed by a greater assault of the flesh

[Col. 1218A]

Your inquiry, if I am not mistaken, concerned this: why, when we fast more moderately, we are sometimes tickled by lighter goads of this flesh, while at other times, when we abstain more rigorously, with the body afflicted and exhausted, we are pressed by sharper impulses, so that, as your confession revealed, upon waking we find ourselves sprinkled with the discharge of natural fluids.

[Note: This means that we have suffered the contagion of bodily poison, that is, that we have been polluted, as he said above (Conference 18, chapter 31).]

## CHAPTER III. That bodily pollution arises from three causes

Our forebears have handed down three causes of this kind of disturbance, which bursts through the order of the appointed time by untimely excesses. It is caused either by an excessive accumulation of food, or by the mind’s negligence, or by the provocations of an enemy who mocks us.

First, therefore, the vice of gluttony—that is, voracity or greed for food—forces out this overflow of obscene fluid. For even when it pollutes the state of purity during a period of stricter abstinence,

[Note: Similar statements occur in Cassian, *Institutes*, Book V, chapter 9, Book VI, chapters 11 and 23, and *Conference* 12, chapter 7.]

it is not discharged from the present hunger, as you suppose, but from the excess of past satiety. What had congealed in the marrow through the excesses of voracity must necessarily be expelled through irritation or, at any rate, through ignorance, even when the body has been wasted away by a lengthy fast. Therefore one must abstain not only from more lavish meals, but must also practice equal restraint with regard to humbler foods. Indeed, even satiety from bread and water must be avoided, so that the bodily purity acquired in us may long endure and may in some fashion imitate the undefiled chastity of the spirit.

Yet we must confess that sometimes, even without any effort of the mind, whether because of the constitution of their bodies or the maturity of age, some people are soiled less frequently, or are not polluted by the discharge of this fluid. But one merit belongs to the person who obtains peace through inactive good fortune [Dionysius: “security”; Lipsius in the margin: “facility”], and another to the one who earns victory through glorious virtues. For the power of the latter, which conquers all vices, is worthy of wonder; whereas the former, whom the facility of goodness protects in his own inactivity, I would judge to be more deserving of security than of praise.

[Note: Cuychius records two readings here. One is: “I would rather say that he possesses security than praise,” which is the reading of the Basel manuscript. The other, from a manuscript and preferred by him, is: “I would rather judge him secure than worthy of praise,” namely, worthy of security. This is his own reading. We have followed it here, while omitting the supplement, which seemed entirely unnecessary. Dionysius the paraphraser expressed the passage as follows: “For the power [*poenitentia*—repentance, in place of *potentia*, power] of the one who conquers in this way by fighting is worthy of admiration as the conqueror of all vices. But the one whom the facility of goodness protects in his inactivity, I judge to be more properly called secure than praised.”]

[Note: Cassian says similarly in Book VI, chapter 11: “The quality of thoughts, which during the day is guarded less carefully amid distractions—that is, amid various occupations—is tested by the quiet of the night. Therefore, when some such illusion has intervened, it should not be attributed to the fault of sleep, but to negligence during the preceding period, and to the manifestation of a disease lying hidden within. The hour of night did not first give birth to it; rather, the refreshment of sleep brought to the surface of the skin what had been stored away in the innermost fibers of the soul, exposing the hidden fevers of passions that we had contracted by feeding upon harmful thoughts throughout the entire day.”]

The second cause of that impure discharge is this: if the mind, emptied of spiritual studies and exercises and not formed by the disciplines of the inner person, has through habitual and continuous torpor acquired a kind of stagnant sluggishness; or if, by failing to guard against the hostilities [Al.: impurities] of foul thoughts, it desires that sublime purity of heart so sluggishly that it believes the whole perfection of chastity to consist solely in the external chastisement of the body.

As a result of this error and negligence, it follows that not only does a manifold wandering of thoughts shamelessly and brazenly invade the mind’s secret place, but also that the seeds of all its former passions remain within it. As long as these lie hidden in its recesses, they disturb the sleeper with seductive phantasms, even when the body is disciplined by a severe fast. Through these phantasms, before the proper time has run its course, obscene fluids are drawn out—not now by the necessity of nature, but still through the deception of spiritual wickedness. If they cannot be completely restrained by the body’s emptiness, they are at least, with the help of God’s grace, reduced to the simple condition of a natural discharge rather than a pollution. Therefore, above all, the movements of the senses must be restrained, lest the mind, accustomed to such excesses, be drawn in sleep toward more shameful provocations of lust.

The third cause occurs when, through an orderly and careful discipline of continence, we desire to acquire perpetual purity of chastity through contrition of heart and body; but while making excellent provision for the well-being of flesh and spirit,

[Note: Against such infestations and demonic illusions the Church and devout minds have a customary evening prayer:

> May dreams depart far away,  
> and the phantasms of enemies;  
> restrain our enemy,  
> lest our bodies be polluted.

Likewise, in another hymn recited during Lent at Compline:

> May heavy sleep not rush upon us,  
> nor may the enemy carry us away,  
> nor may the flesh consent to him …]

May he make us guilty before you. Pope Saint Alexander, who was the fifth to occupy the chair after blessed Peter, ordained that water sanctified by priestly blessing should be kept in bedrooms to drive away the devil’s malice, lest he deceive us through dreams or phantasms.

There is, moreover, a remarkable matter which should not be passed over in silence: to remove this diabolical infestation and illusion, Saint Bernard suggests a remedy proven by experience:

“If an illusion happens to you during the night,” he says, “do not be distressed, but confess on the following day. If someone calls you to serve at Mass, excuse yourself cautiously before everyone by the customary sign, so that all may understand that you have suffered that pollution.”

Someone among us did this even when no one had called him to Mass, so that he might be more deeply ashamed; and he was freed from the temptation of the flesh to such an extent that afterward he scarcely experienced anything of the kind, suffering such an urge only once or twice a year.

Likewise, in the Life of Saint Malachy, chapter 47: When Saint Malachy the archbishop was offering the sacraments and a deacon approached him, he looked at him and groaned, because he sensed that something improper was concealed within him. After the sacrifice had been completed, he privately questioned him about his conscience, and the man confessed that he had been deceived by an illusion in a dream during the night. Saint Malachy imposed a penance upon him and said:

“You ought not to have ministered today, but should have withdrawn modestly, so that, cleansed by this humility, you might afterward minister more worthily.”

This is Saint Bernard’s account.] The envy of the most treacherous enemy so assails [the preceding subject]: while he attempts to cast down our confidence in conscience and humble us as though under some guilt, especially on those days when, with a greater claim to integrity, we desire to please the divine gaze alone—without any itching of the flesh, any consent of the mind, or even any illusion caused by a phantasm—he nevertheless pollutes us by the simple discharge of that fluid, in order to deter us from holy communion.

It is believed that, among certain beginners whose bodies have not yet been thinned by prolonged fasting, this illusion occurs through diabolical agency for the following reason: when the devil discovers that they are devoting themselves to more intense fasts, he overturns all their efforts by this stratagem. Thus, when they feel that they have not only made no progress toward bodily purity through stricter fasting but have even been more seriously polluted, they come to dread the strictness of abstinence—the teacher and nurse of incorruption and purity—as though it were an enemy. (See Book II of the *Institutes*, chapter 13, and Book VI, final chapter.)

Therefore, we must understand that we should not be cleansed from each individual vice merely because it occupies our senses through its own disturbances, but because it is not content to dominate alone, without the company of others; rather, once the harsher fellowship of all the vices has been admitted, it ravages the mind subject to it through multiplied captivity. [Note: See Book V of the *Institutes*, chapters 6, 10, 21, and 23, and *Conferences* 5, chapters 10 and 11.]

For this reason gluttony must be conquered, not only for its own sake—namely, lest it corrupt us through burdensome voracity—nor only lest it set us ablaze with the fire of carnal desire, but also lest it make us slaves to anger, fury, sadness, and all the other passions. For when food and drink are supplied to us either somewhat carelessly or somewhat late, if we are oppressed by the dominion of the appetite, it naturally follows that we are also goaded by the spurs of anger. Again, we cannot be soothed by pleasurable flavors without the plague of avarice, through whose excessive preparations luxury rejoices in great expenditure. Avarice, vainglory, pride, and the multitude of all the vices are joined together in indivisible companionship; thus, if any single vice begins to grow strong in us, it also fosters the growth of the others.

## CHAPTER IV. Question: Is it permissible for someone polluted by a nocturnal illusion to approach holy communion?

**Germanus:** By God’s dispensation, we believe that this question has been brought forward so that we may now dare confidently to inquire—prompted by the opportunity for discussion and by the orderly presentation of the matter itself—about what, because shame at asking restrained our confidence, we were never previously able to learn.

Therefore, if, at the time when it is proper to approach the holy mysteries, we should realize that we have been polluted by an illusion in a dream, should that salutary food be avoided?

[Note: Saint Augustine, bishop of the English, also proposed this same question, among others, to Saint Gregory in these words:

“I also ask whether, after an illusion that commonly occurs during sleep, one may receive the Lord’s body, or, if he is a priest, celebrate the sacred mysteries.”

Saint Gregory replied as follows, after giving the distinction cited above:

“When it has occurred through the natural excess or weakness of the body, this illusion is in no way to be feared, because the mind, which unknowingly endured it, should rather grieve that it suffered it than that it committed it.” [The passage appears corrupt, and a different reading is found in Gratian, Distinction 6, chapter *Testamentum*.]

“But when the appetite is carried beyond measure in taking food, and the receptacles of the humors are consequently burdened, the mind does incur some guilt; yet not to the point of forbidding the reception of the sacred mystery or the celebration of Mass, when perhaps a feast day requires it, or necessity itself compels the mystery to be offered because another priest is absent. If others are present who can perform the ministry, an illusion caused by overindulgence ought not to prevent reception of the sacred mystery; but, in my judgment, the person ought humbly to abstain from offering the sacred mystery, provided that an obscene imagination has not disturbed the mind of the sleeper.

For there are some in whom an illusion commonly arises in such a way that their mind, even while their body lies in sleep, is not defiled by imaginative images. In this matter it is shown that the mind itself is not then guilty but free according to its own judgment: although, while the body sleeps, it remembers having seen nothing, it nevertheless remembers, while the body is awake, that it fell into gluttony.

But if the illusion of the sleeper arises from an obscene thought entertained while awake, the mind’s guilt is evident. For he sees from what root that imagination proceeded: what he knowingly thought, he unknowingly endured.

Yet one must consider whether that thought occurred by suggestion, by delight, or—what is more serious—by consent to sin. Every sin is completed in three ways: by suggestion, delight, and consent. Suggestion comes through the devil, delight through the flesh, and consent through the spirit. Thus, when the serpent first suggested the fault, Eve, as flesh, was delighted, while Adam, as spirit, consented. Great discernment is therefore necessary, so that the mind may judge between suggestion, delight, and consent.

When the evil spirit suggests sin to the mind, if no delight in sin follows, sin has not in any way been committed. But when the flesh begins to take delight, sin begins to be born. If, after deliberation, one descends also to consent, then sin is understood to be completed. In suggestion, therefore, there is the seed of sin; in delight, its nourishment; in consent, its perfection.”

Thus far Saint Gregory. Explaining his teaching more concisely and clearly, Saint Thomas teaches that two things can be considered with regard to nocturnal pollution:

“One,” he says (*Third Part*, question 80, article 7), “by reason of which it necessarily prevents a person from receiving this sacrament; the other by reason of which it does not necessarily prevent him, but does so on grounds of propriety.

“Only mortal sin necessarily prevents a person from receiving this sacrament. Although nocturnal pollution, considered in itself, cannot be mortal sin, it nevertheless sometimes has mortal sin attached to it by reason of its cause. Therefore the cause of nocturnal pollution must be considered.” (See Dominicus a Soto, *In IV Sententiarum*, distinction 12, question 1, article 7.)

“Sometimes it arises from an external spiritual cause, namely, from the illusion of demons, who can stir up phantasms; pollution sometimes follows from the appearance of these phantasms. Sometimes pollution arises from an internal spiritual cause, namely, preceding thoughts. At other times it arises from an internal bodily cause: from excess, from weakness of nature, or even from an excess of food and drink.

“Each of these three causes can exist either without sin or with venial or mortal sin. If it exists without sin or with venial sin, it does not necessarily prevent reception; that is, the person who receives is not thereby guilty of the Lord’s body and blood. But if it is accompanied by mortal sin, it necessarily prevents reception.

“The illusion of demons sometimes arises from previous negligence in preparing oneself for devotion, which may be either mortal or venial sin. At other times it arises solely from the demons’ wickedness, since they wish to prevent a person from receiving this sacrament. Thus it is recorded in the *Conferences of the Fathers* that, when a certain brother suffered pollution every time there was a feast on which communion was to be received, the elders discovered that no prior cause had proceeded from him and decreed that he should not abstain from communion on that account; and the demonic illusion ceased.

“Similarly, preceding lascivious thoughts can sometimes be entirely without sin—for example, when someone is compelled to think about such matters for purposes of reading or discussion. If this occurs without lust or delight, the thoughts are not unclean but honorable, although pollution may follow from them, as is clear from the authority of Augustine cited above (*On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book XII, chapter 15).

“At other times preceding thoughts arise from lust and delight. If consent is present, there will be mortal sin; if consent is absent, the sin will be venial.

“Likewise, the bodily cause may sometimes be without sin, as when it results from weakness of nature. Thus some people, even while awake, suffer a discharge of semen without sin. Or it may result from an excess of nature: just as blood can flow without sin, so can semen, which according to the philosopher is an excess of blood (Aristotle, *On the Generation of Animals*, Book I, chapters 18 and 19).

“At other times it occurs with sin, as when it results from excess food and drink; and this too may be venial or mortal sin, although mortal sin occurs more frequently in connection with obscene thoughts, because consent is more easily given there, than in connection with the consumption of food and drink. Hence Gregory, writing to Augustine, bishop of the English, says that one should abstain from communion when the pollution arises from obscene thoughts, but not when it arises from excess food or drink, especially if necessity is present.

“Thus, from the cause of the pollution, it can be determined whether nocturnal pollution necessarily prevents reception of this sacrament.

“On grounds of propriety, however, it prevents reception for two reasons. One always occurs: a certain bodily uncleanness, with which, out of reverence for the sacrament, it is not fitting to approach the altar—for this reason those who wish to touch something sacred wash their hands—unless, perhaps, such uncleanness is permanent or prolonged, as with leprosy, a discharge of blood, or something similar.

“The other is a wandering of the mind that follows nocturnal pollution, especially when it occurs with an obscene imagination. Nevertheless, this impediment arising from propriety should be set aside in case of some necessity—for example, as Gregory says, when a feast day requires it, or necessity compels someone to perform the ministry because another priest is absent.”

This is Saint Thomas’s teaching. Nothing more exact or more lucid can be offered on this subject. Since it is especially suited to this passage and to the argument of nearly the entire conference, it seemed least appropriate to omit it.

The provisions found in the *Ceremonial of the Benedictine Congregation of Binsfeld* agree very well with these remarks; it will not be irrelevant or superfluous to reproduce them here as well. Thus, in the chapter concerning those deceived during nocturnal sleep, it says:

“Although nocturnal pollution occurs to many without any preceding fault of their own, nevertheless, because such an affliction commonly leaves behind a certain itching of the flesh and dullness of mind, while this condition persists in the sufferer it is fitting that he abstain from celebration or communion, even if, as stated, it has occurred without fault.

“On solemn feast days, however, or at particularly important times, whoever he may be, after prior confession and devout exercise to the extent possible, may, because of the public notice involved, approach confidently—with the permission of his prelate or confessor—either to celebrate or to receive communion.

“You should act similarly if, by office, you are required to celebrate Mass on the day when such an occurrence has happened to you.

“If someone suffers this discharge daily or with excessive frequency—as happens to some merely from thinking about, speaking of, or hearing about carnal vices in confession or elsewhere, even against their will and resistance and with abhorrence of the vice—he should not use this as a reason to celebrate less often or to deprive himself of holy communion. Rather, with the knowledge and approval of his prelate or confessor, and while being moved by the proper disposition, let him approach confidently.”

This was issued there by prudent and religious Fathers.]

## CHAPTER V. Answer: When does this affliction incur guilt for the person sleeping?

[Col. 1223A]

**Theonas:** With every possible diligence, insofar as it lies within us, we ought to strive to preserve the purity of unblemished chastity, especially at the time when we desire to stand before the venerable altars. With the most vigilant circumspection we must take care lest bodily integrity, guarded beforehand, be violated particularly on the night in which we prepare ourselves for communion at the saving banquet.

But if that most wicked enemy, in order to deprive us of the medicine of heavenly healing, deceives the guardianship of the sleeping mind—yet only in such a way that no blameworthy itching intervenes and no assent to pleasure pollutes it, but presents as an impediment to our sanctification a discharge expelled either by natural necessity or, certainly, through the devil’s assault without any sense of pleasure—then we can and ought confidently to approach the grace of the saving food.

But if this discharge has been produced by our own fault, we should examine our conscience and fear the Apostle’s words:

“Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a person first examine himself, and thus eat of the bread and drink of the cup.” (1 Corinthians 11.)

For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the Lord’s body—that is, failing entirely to distinguish that heavenly food from the lowliness of ordinary foods, and failing to judge it to be such that it may be received only with a pure mind or body.

Finally, he adds:

“For this reason many among you are weak and sick, and many are asleep.”

[Note: Here the abbot interprets the Apostle’s words—“For this reason many among you are weak and sick, and many are asleep”—as referring to spiritual weakness, or sickness of the soul, and likewise spiritual death, that is, mortal sin. Most Fathers, both Greek and Latin, interpret the words as referring instead to bodily illnesses and deaths inflicted by God, by which many among the Corinthians were punished in the primitive Church because of their unworthy reception of the Eucharist. Other examples of this matter may be found in Cyprian’s sermon *On the Lapsed*, in Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, and in Sophronius’s *Spiritual Meadow*.]

That is, he specifically says that spiritual weaknesses and deaths arise from this presumption. For many who presumptuously take it by an illicit use become weak in faith and feeble in mind, being entangled in the maladies of the passions; and they sleep in the sleep of sin, never rising from this deadly slumber through a salutary concern.

Then he continues:

“If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged.”

That is: if, whenever we were preceded by the wound of sin, we judged ourselves unworthy to receive the sacraments, we would certainly devote ourselves to correcting our condition through repentance, so that we might approach them worthily; and we would not, as unworthy persons, be chastised by the Lord with the most severe scourges of illness, so that, at least thus struck with remorse, we might return to the remedies for our wounds. Lest, having not been accounted worthy of the very brief correction of the present age, we be condemned in the future together with the sinners of this world.

The same is expressly commanded in Leviticus:

“Every clean person shall eat the flesh; but whoever eats of the flesh of the sacrifice of well-being, which belongs to the Lord, while uncleanness is upon him, that person shall perish before the Lord.” (Leviticus 2.)

[Note: Cassian also cited this passage in Book VI of the *Institutes*, chapter 8; see the notes there. Moreover, this sentence is not found in Leviticus 7 among the Septuagint, as it is cited here; but something similar appears in Leviticus 22: “Any person who approaches those things that have been consecrated while uncleanness is in him shall perish before the Lord.”]

In Deuteronomy, too, an unclean person is mystically separated in the same way from the spiritual camps:

[Note: Alluding to this passage, Saint Gregory says:

“The Testament of the old law calls a person polluted before the Lord and does not permit him to enter the Church until he has been washed with water, even until evening. The spiritual people, however—that is, the Christian people—understand this differently and regard as deceived, as though in a dream, the person who, tempted by uncleanness, is defiled in thought by empty images. He must be washed with water, so that he may cleanse the guilt of his thoughts with tears; and unless the fire of temptation has first departed, he should recognize himself as guilty, as it were, until evening.”

Gratian cites the passage in this way, although the original of Gregory has it somewhat differently.

Isidore likewise writes in the same sense:

“Nighttime sleep” (Commentary on Deuteronomy, chapter 20) “is a hidden temptation, through which something shameful is conceived in dark thought but is not completed through bodily action. Yet a person polluted by nighttime sleep is commanded to go outside the camp, because it is fitting that someone polluted by an unclean thought should consider himself unworthy of the fellowship of all the faithful. He should place the merit of his guilt before his eyes and despise himself in comparison with the esteem accorded to the good.

“To go outside the camp while polluted means that someone suffering from a shameful assault should despise himself when compared with those who practice continence. He washes with water toward evening when, recognizing his failing, he turns to the lamentation of repentance, so that with his tears he may wash away everything that secretly accuses his soul of defilement.

“But after sunset he should return to the camp, because, when the heat of temptation has cooled, he must once again take confidence in the good of the community. After the water, with the sun setting, he returns to the camp who, after the tears of repentance, when the flame of illicit thought has grown cold, is restored to confidence in the merits of the faithful, so that he no longer considers himself far from the others, rejoicing that he has been cleansed through the death of his inward burning.”

Thus far Isidore. Elsewhere he adds (*Book III of the Sentences*, chapter 6):

“Whoever is polluted by a nocturnal illusion, although he feels himself defiled without any recollection of his thoughts, should nevertheless attribute the fact that he was tempted to his own guilt, and immediately wipe away his uncleanness with tears.”]

“If there is among you a man who has been polluted by a nocturnal dream,” he says, “he shall go outside the camp and shall not return until he has washed with water toward evening. After sunset he shall return to the camp.” (Deuteronomy 20.)

## CHAPTER VI. That bodily pollution is sometimes free from guilt and occurs through the enemy’s agency is demonstrated by an example.

But in order that it may be demonstrated more clearly that this impurity is sometimes brought about by the machinations of the enemy:

[Note: [Col. 1225D] That is, that pollution is produced in dreams by the devil’s activity and deception. Thus below: “They discerned the hidden snares of diabolical plotting.” Also: “The entire spectacle of diabolical plotting was exposed.” Again: “He taught that the enemy’s machinations are to be driven back by crafty deception.” That pollution is sometimes produced by the devil in those who are sleeping is expressly taught by St. Thomas (3rd part, question 80, article 7): “Sometimes,” he says, “pollution proceeds from an external spiritual cause, namely, from the deception of demons, who are able to stir up phantasms; and from the appearance of these, pollution sometimes follows.” [Col. 1226B] Thomas of Cantimpré, book II, chapter 57: “By this worm the demons are signified, which appear to men at night in dreams and pollute and mock them with phantasmal visions.” He then adds an example concerning a monk whom a demon mocked by arousing pollution in him during sleep. “I remember,” he says, “having read something rather amusing about this. When a certain monk had approached a possessed man, with a large crowd standing around, the demon called out to him mockingly and said: ‘Come, brother, come—did I perhaps bring you a beautiful woman in your dreams this night?’ For, as the monk later confessed in confusion, he had been polluted in his sleep that night, but had not confessed it. Thus far he. See more on this at chapter 3 of this work.]

We knew a brother who, although he continually possessed chastity of heart and body, acquired with the greatest vigilance and humility, and although he was in no way troubled by nocturnal deceptions, nevertheless, whenever he had prepared himself to receive the Lord’s communion, was defiled in his sleep by an unclean discharge.

[Note: [Col. 1226C] This example was related by the above-cited St. Thomas. Something similar is read in the Life of the Blessed Peter of Morone, who, having been an anchorite, was created supreme pontiff and called Celestine V. After resigning the papacy and spending the rest of his life in solitude, he became famous for his virtues and miracles; from him the order of the Celestines also took its beginning and name. For, as Peter of Ailly relates, it happened that, out of reverence for the sacred mystery, he was greatly perplexed about what he ought to do when his body happened to be defiled by nocturnal pollution, although his exceptionally pure soul strove with all its strength to resist such impurity. When he asked religious brothers for counsel as to whether he should celebrate on that same day or refrain from celebrating, and there was no unanimity among them, some thinking one way and others another, his devout mind, wavering in doubt, turned to divine assistance. [Col. 1226D] And behold, Christ appeared to stand before him in a dream, resolving the perplexity of this doubt and instructing him through a parabolic comparison: if his donkey—that is, his brutish and irrational body—were, according to its innate habit, to commit its own impurity, his master—that is, his rational soul—who was alien to consent to the allurements of unclean flesh, ought not on that account to grow sluggish in ascending to heavenly things, that is, in contemplating divine realities or exercising the spiritual mysteries. Comforted by this vision, the servant of God recovered peace of mind and spiritual joy, understanding that, because of involuntary pollution of the flesh, contrary to the law of his mind, he ought not to abstain from communion in the divine sacrament. Thus far.]

Since he abstained fearfully from the most sacred mysteries for a long time, he finally brought this question to the elders, confident that through their healing counsel he would obtain a remedy for his struggle and distress. But when the spiritual physicians’ teaching examined the first cause of his illness,

[Col. 1226A]

which commonly results from excessive consumption of food, and they discovered that this was not present in the brother in question—and when it was clear that this deception did not arise from the fault of overeating, since the brother’s known strictness on the customary days on which the pollution occurred did not permit them to suppose any special exception—they immediately transferred their investigation to the second cause of this illness,

[Note: [Col. 1226D] That is, of illness or infirmity, as has often been said.]

examining whether perhaps, because of some fault of the soul, the flesh, exhausted by fasting, was being assailed by unclean deceptions. Even men of the strictest discipline are polluted by these when, slightly elated over the purity of their body, they fall through the vice of pride—namely, when they believe that they have obtained by human strength the outstanding gift of God, bodily chastity.

Accordingly, when he was asked whether he thought his own diligence so capable of this virtue that he had no need of divine assistance, he emphatically rejected this impious notion. He humbly affirmed that he could not have preserved bodily purity even on the other days unless he had been assisted in everything by divine grace. Then they immediately returned to the third cause, discerned the hidden snares of diabolical plotting, and, proving that the fault lay neither with his soul nor with his flesh, confidently judged that he ought to partake of the sacred feasts.

They feared that, if he persisted in this obstinacy

[Lipsius, in the margin: abstinence]

and were bound by the crafty snares of the evil enemy, he might be unable to participate in sanctification and in the body of Christ, and that through this fraud he might be deprived forever of the medicine of saving remedy. Once this had been done, the entire spectacle of diabolical plotting was exposed, so that immediately, through the protecting power of the Lord’s body, that former habit of deception ceased. In this the enemy’s deceit clearly appeared, and the judgment of the elders was at once set forth and confirmed: this most unclean discharge is generally brought about not by a fault of the soul,

[Col. 1227B]

but by the enemy’s crafty deception.

[Note: [Col. 1227C] He proposes several remedies against nocturnal deceptions and pollutions. The first is the mortification of every passion, or of every lustful desire; the second is abstinence, or restraint of the body and its members from every immodest act—which, according to the Apostle, is to crucify one’s flesh with its vices and desires (Galatians V); the third is the firm resolution and inward will of the human being, that is, of the soul, to abstain perpetually from every sexual pleasure, whether inward and spiritual or outward and bodily, and to devote oneself, pure and undefiled in body and spirit, to divine service. These, however, are general and more remote remedies. The nearer and more particular remedies are fervent and devout prayer, especially in the evening or also during the night; frequent reception of the sacraments of confession and the Eucharist; fasts and other exercises of mortification and repentance; avoidance of women, shameful objects, and images; devout and voluntary self-abasement and shame; and similar practices, of which much has often been said elsewhere. [Col. 1227D]]

Therefore, if we wish the deceptive imagination of dreams, which entices toward impure discharge, to be unknown either forever or at least for certain months—as I might say, according to the humbler, or ordinary, condition—then, after that faith by which it is fitting for us continually to hope especially in God’s grace for the gift of purity, we must restrain excess in food and drink.

For from their abundance such humors necessarily arise more readily. Since, once congealed, they cannot but be discharged and driven out by the law of nature itself, they emerge on the occasion of any kind of itching or deception. When the fullness of food has been reduced, it follows that these unclean discharges also develop more slowly. Thus, just as their discharge, so also the deception disturbs sleepers either more rarely or more subtly, because not only does the discharge arise from imagination, but imagination also arises from excessive discharge.

[Col. 1227C]

[Col. 1228A]

Therefore, if we wish to be freed from the allurements of these deceptions, we must strive with every virtue. First, having conquered the passion of fornication, we must ensure, according to the blessed Apostle, that sin does not reign in our mortal body so that we obey its desires (Romans VI). Second, once the body’s seductive movement itself has been completely quieted and put to sleep, we must not present our members to sin as weapons of iniquity (ibid.). Third, when our inner person too has been wholly and profoundly mortified with respect to that titillation of lust, we must present ourselves to God as those alive from the dead, and, having thus advanced, present our members to God no longer as weapons for lust, but as weapons of righteousness (ibid.).

When we have been firmly established in this purity of chastity,

[Col. 1228B]

sin will no longer rule over us. For we are not under the law, which, while commending the lawful rights of marriage, also nourishes and preserves in our inmost parts the ardor of him whose service accomplishes the work of unlawful fornication; but under grace, which, while suggesting the incorruption of virginity, also destroys the pleasure of this harmless and simple bodily movement, and even of lawful intercourse. Thus, when all the most impure fluids have been dried up,

[Note: [Col. 1227D] The Lord commends these in the Gospel, saying: “There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew XIX), that is, they have chosen and vowed perpetual continence, and by that vow have deprived themselves of the power to enjoy every sexual pleasure. St. Jerome likewise writes concerning them (Book I Against Jovinianus, chapter 7): “It is a great matter of faith, and a great matter of virtue, to be the purest temple of God, to offer oneself wholly as a dwelling for the Lord, and, according to the same Apostle, to be holy both in body and in spirit. These are the eunuchs who, thinking themselves a dry tree because of their barrenness, hear through Isaiah that a place in heaven has been prepared for them in place of sons and daughters. Their type is Ebed-melech in Jeremiah (Jeremiah XXXVIII), and the eunuch of the queen Candace in the Acts of the Apostles, who, because of the strength of his faith, obtained the name of man (Acts VIII). To these also Clement, successor of the Apostle Peter, whom the Apostle Paul mentions (Philippians IV), writes letters, composing almost his entire discourse on the purity of virginity.” Thus St. Jerome. Again, in his Commentary on Isaiah (Isaiah LVI), he says: “Ecclesiastical histories report that such was the eunuch whom Jesus loved exceedingly, John the Evangelist, who reclined upon Jesus’ breast; who, when Peter was walking more slowly, ran to the Lord, lifted up on the wings of virginity (John XIII and XXI); who, plunging himself into the secrets of the divine birth, dared to say what all the ages had not known: ‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God,’ and so forth (John I). Let every Jewish quibble therefore depart, and let it cease to expose itself to ridicule by opening the kingdoms of heaven to half-men, since chastity lies in the weakness of the body but in the will of the soul.”]

we shall deserve to possess that blessedness promised to the excellent and praiseworthy eunuchs proclaimed through Isaiah.

“For thus says the Lord: To the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, choose what I will, and hold fast my covenant, I will give in my house and within my walls a place and

[Col. 1228C]

a name better than sons and daughters.”

[Note: [Col. 1228D] That is, greater glory than that of the sons and daughters of God, as this abbot explains, understanding by them holy men in the Old Testament who were married and joined in wedlock; or the name of Christians, derived from the name of Christ, which is much better than the name of the sons of Abraham, in which the Jews chiefly gloried, saying: “We are Abraham’s offspring; we are Abraham’s sons.” Or, in the simple sense, “better and more honorable than sons and daughters,” that is, than having many children. This is also how the Seventy translators rendered it: “A notable place, better than sons and daughters” (τόπον ὀνομαστὸν κρείττω υἱῶν καὶ θυγατέρων).]

I will give them an everlasting name that shall not perish” (Isaiah LVI).

[Col. 1229A]

Who are these sons and daughters, above whom these eunuchs are so greatly preferred that they are said to receive a place and name better than theirs, unless they are those holy people who, remaining in the marital union in the Old Testament, deservedly attained adoption as sons of God through observance of the commandments?

And what is that name which is promised to them as something especially outstanding, in place of the highest reward, unless it is this—that we are reckoned by the name of Christ? Concerning this name the prophet says elsewhere: “I called my servants by another name; by it, whoever is blessed on earth shall be blessed in God. Amen. And whoever swears on earth shall swear in God. Amen” (Isaiah LXV). And again: “You shall be called by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord has named” (Isaiah LXII).

They, moreover, because of this purity of heart and body,

[Col. 1229B]

will also enjoy that distinctive and singular blessedness,

[Note: [Col. 1229C] St. Augustine, in his book On Holy Virginity, addressing and praising virgins, says among other things in chapter 29: “The rest of the multitude of the faithful, which cannot follow the Lamb for this purpose, will see you; it will see you and will not envy you; and, rejoicing with you, it will possess in you what it does not possess in itself. For it will not be able to sing that new song which is properly yours; yet it will be able to hear it and delight in your excellence. But you, who will both sing and hear it—for you will hear from yourselves what you sing—will rejoice more happily and reign more joyfully.” Thus Augustine. St. Gregory, imitating him in the Pastoral Rule (Part III, chapter 29), says: “To sing the song of the Lamb uniquely means to rejoice with him forever, above all the faithful, in the incorruption of the flesh. The other elect, however, can hear the song, although they cannot sing it, because through charity they rejoice in the exalted state of those others, even though they do not rise to their rewards.”]

so that they may continually sing that song which none of the other saints can sing, except these alone who follow the Lamb wherever he goes: “They are virgins, and they have not defiled themselves with women” (Revelation XIV).

Therefore, if we wish to attain this most sublime glory of virgins, let us cultivate incorruption of mind and spirit with every virtue, lest we fall into the number of those foolish virgins (Matthew XXV). Their virginity was not counted to them because they merely kept themselves free from carnal intercourse, and for this reason

[Note: [Col. 1229D] St. Jerome sharply reproves and censures such virgins, both male and female, in his letter to Eustochium on the preservation of virginity. Among other things he writes (Letter XXII): “Let us fear that prophecy, lest it also be fulfilled in us: ‘The good virgins shall fail’ (Amos VIII). Observe what he says: ‘The good virgins shall fail,’ because there are also evil virgins. ‘Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her,’ he says, ‘has already committed adultery with her in his heart’ (Matthew V). Virginity therefore also perishes in the mind. These are the evil virgins: virgins in the flesh, not in the spirit; foolish virgins who, having no oil, are shut out from the Bridegroom. But if even those who are virgins are not saved in the virginity of their bodies on account of other causes, what will become of those who have prostituted the members of Christ and changed the temple of the Holy Spirit into a brothel, and so forth.”]

they are called virgins, indeed, but foolish, because when the oil of inward purity fails in their vessels, the brightness and splendor of bodily virginity are extinguished. For the chastity of the outward person must necessarily be supplied and continually animated toward perseverance in perpetual incorruption by the cherishing warmth [Lipsius, in the margin: drink] and nourishment of inward purity.

Therefore those foolish virgins do not deserve to enter the glorious bridal chamber of the Bridegroom with the prudent virgins, because they did not preserve their spirit, soul, and body blameless on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Those are the true and incorrupt virgins of Christ; those are considered admirable and outstanding eunuchs—not those who fear to fornicate, but those who have no desire to do so; not those who merely restrain the reins of immodesty, but those who have also conquered the slightest titillation of the mind and the faintest impulses of lust, and have so weakened that sense of the flesh, so to speak,

[Col. 1230B]

that they are touched not only by no pleasure arising from its movement, but not even by the slightest titillation.

[Note: [Col. 1230C] “This,” says the abbot Chaeremon, “is the perfection of chastity” (Conferences XII, final chapter): “that no pleasure of lust should touch a monk who is awake, that no deception of dreams should mislead him while he is resting; but if, through the negligence of a dormant mind, a movement of the flesh should creep upon one who is sleeping, then, just as it arose without any stimulation of pleasure, so also it should subside without any bodily itching.”]

## CHAPTER VII. That no one should ever judge himself worthy of the Lord’s communion

We must therefore fortify our heart with so great a guard of humility that we hold this conviction with perpetual steadfastness of mind: that we can never attain such a degree of purification that, even if by God’s grace we have done everything mentioned above,

[Note: [Col. 1230C] The dignity of merit is one thing, and the dignity of disposition another. No one is so foolish as to believe himself worthy of communion with so great a Sacrament by the dignity of merit, as though this benefit were owed to his merits, or as though he had attained such purity and perfection of mind as the dignity and majesty of this Sacrament require. For everyone who is about to receive communion ought humbly to say with the centurion: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof,” and so forth (Matthew VIII). The dignity of disposition is the suitable and necessary preparation for sacred communion or for the offering of the unbloody sacrifice. Whoever possesses it is said to approach this Sacrament worthily; whoever lacks it, unworthily. Concerning this preparation, the Fathers of the Council of Trent delivered and defined the following (Session XIII, chapter 7): “If it is not fitting for anyone to approach any sacred functions except in a holy manner, certainly the more clearly a Christian understands the holiness and divinity of this heavenly Sacrament, the more carefully he ought to take care not to approach it without great reverence and holiness, especially since we read those fear-inspiring words of the Apostle: ‘He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord’ (1 Corinthians XI). Therefore, anyone wishing to receive communion must recall the command: ‘Let a person examine himself.’ Ecclesiastical practice declares that this examination is necessary, so that no one conscious of mortal sin, however contrite he may seem to himself, should approach the sacred Eucharist without prior sacramental confession. The holy synod decreed that this must always be observed by all Christians, including those priests whose office requires them to celebrate, provided that a confessor is available to them. If urgent necessity forces a priest to celebrate without prior confession, he must confess as soon as possible. Again, in the decree on what is to be observed and avoided in the celebration of Mass (Session XXII), they say: ‘Anyone can easily judge how great a care must be taken that the most sacred sacrifice of the Mass be celebrated with every form of religious worship and veneration, if he reflects that in sacred Scripture the one who performs God’s work negligently is called accursed (Jeremiah XLVIII). If we must necessarily admit that no other work so holy and divine can be undertaken by Christ’s faithful as this very awe-inspiring mystery, in which that life-giving victim by whom we have been reconciled to God the Father is daily sacrificed on the altar by priests, it is also sufficiently clear that every effort and diligence must be devoted to ensuring that it be performed with the greatest possible inward cleanliness and purity of heart, and with an outward appearance of devotion and piety.’ Thus far. [Col. 1232C] Cassiodorus also demonstrates that this was an ancient practice when, from Sozomen, he relates in Book VIII of the Tripartite History, chapter 1, the story of Dioscorus and Eulogius, most holy Egyptian monks and priests. “Dioscorus,” he says, “presided over no more than one hundred monks. Although he was a priest, when offering the sacrifices he exercised the utmost perfection, examining and carefully discerning those approaching the sacred mysteries, so that they might purify their minds and have no consciousness of any evil. He adds concerning Eulogius: ‘The priest Eulogius is said to have possessed foreknowledge of the thoughts of everyone who came to him, and he openly reproved their offenses and revealed whatever they had secretly thought. Those who had done something evil or conceived an evil plan he kept away from the altar, making known to them the sin they had committed; and, once they had been carefully purified, he received them again.’ Thus far.”]

we should nevertheless believe ourselves unworthy of communion with the sacred body.

First, because the majesty of that heavenly manna is so great that no one clothed in this earthly flesh receives its food by his own merit, but only from the Lord’s gratuitous generosity.

Second, because no one can be so vigilant amid the struggles of this world that the arrows of sins—whether rare or slight—do not strike him. For it is impossible not to sin either through ignorance, negligence, vanity, inadvertence, thought, necessity, or forgetfulness.

Even if someone should rise to such an exalted summit of virtues that, without boasting, he could cry out with the Apostle: “For me it is a very small matter that I should be judged by you or by a human tribunal; indeed, I do not even judge myself. For I am conscious of nothing against myself,” he must nevertheless know that he cannot be without sin.

For the same Teacher did not add this without reason:

[Col. 1231B]

“But by this I am not justified”—that is, if I have believed myself to be just, I will not immediately possess true glory; nor, because my conscience does not prick me with the accusation of any sin, am I therefore untouched by any stain. For many things remain hidden even from my conscience which, although unknown and obscure to me, are known and manifest to God.

Therefore he adds: “But the one who judges me is the Lord”—that is, from him alone, from whom the secrets of hearts are not hidden, will the true examination of judgment concerning me proceed.

## CHAPTER VIII. The objection of Abbot Germanus based on what has been said about receiving the sacred mysteries

Germanus: It was said above that only holy people ought to be participants in the heavenly Sacraments. Now it is added that it is impossible for a human being to be entirely free from sin. If, then, no one is free from guilt, no one is holy; and it follows that a person who lacks holiness cannot participate in Christ’s mysteries and ought not even to hope for the kingdom of heaven, which the Lord promises to the holy alone.

## CHAPTER IX. The response: many may be holy, but no one except Christ is without sin

Theonas: We cannot deny that there are many holy and righteous people, but there is a great difference between being holy and being immaculate. For it is one thing for someone to be holy—that is, consecrated to divine worship; Scripture testifies that this name is common not only to human beings, but also to places, vessels of the temple, and cauldrons. It is another thing to be without sin, which belongs uniquely to the majesty of our one Lord Jesus Christ. Concerning him the Apostle also declares, as something especially distinctive and singular: “He committed no sin” (1 Peter II).

He would assign him a sufficiently paltry and unworthy praise, unworthy of his glory, as though it were something incomparable and divine, if we too could pass our lives untouched by every sin.

Again, the Apostle says to the Hebrews: “For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who was tempted in every respect according to our likeness, without sin” (Hebrews IV).

[Note: [Col. 1232D] See the observations on this point in Conference V, chapter 5.]

If, then, such fellowship can exist between our earthly lowliness and that exalted and divine High Priest that we too may be tempted without any offense of sin, why does the Apostle, admiring this in him as something unique and singular,

[Lipsius, in the margin: accepting]

distinguish his merit from that of human beings by so great a separation?

He is therefore distinguished from all of us by this sole exception: it is established that we are not tempted without sin, whereas he was tempted without sin.

For what human being, however strong and warlike, is not generally exposed to the enemy’s arrows? Who, enclosed as though in impenetrable flesh, can enter such dangers of battle without danger? But he alone, “beautiful in appearance beyond the sons of men” (Psalm XLIV), assuming the condition of human death together with all the frailty of flesh, was never stained by the touch of any impurity.

## CHAPTER X. That the Son of God alone conquered the tempter without any wound of sin

[Note: [Col. 1232D] Abbot Serapion discussed Christ’s temptations in the same manner and almost the same words in Conference V, chapter 6; it would therefore be superfluous to make further notes about them.]

For he was tempted according to our likeness (Hebrews IV), first by the vice of gluttony, so that the crafty serpent might attempt to deceive him, when he was hungry, with the desire for food, in the same order in which he had formerly deceived Adam (Genesis III): “If you are the Son of God,” he said, “command that these stones become loaves of bread” (Matthew IV).

But he incurred no sin from this temptation. Although he possessed unquestionable power, he rejected the food which the architect of deception offered him, saying: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Deuteronomy VIII).

He was also tempted by vainglory according to our likeness, when it was said to him: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down” (Matthew IV). But he was not captured by the devil’s deceitful suggestion. Refuting the most vain seducer even by an appeal to Scripture, he said: “You shall not put the Lord your God to the test” (Deuteronomy VI).

He was also tempted by the swelling of pride according to our likeness, when the devil offered him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. But the tempter’s wickedness was mocked and rebuked. For he answered him: “Go away, Satan” (Matthew IV); “for it is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deuteronomy VI).

By these testimonies we are taught that we too must resist the enemy’s deceitful suggestions by the authority of Scripture.

[Note: [Col. 1233C] Just as our Savior scattered and drove away all the devil’s temptations by the protection of Scripture, or of the divine word, so the Apostle advised the Ephesians to use the same weapon against the temptations of the demon: “And take the helmet of salvation,” he says, “and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.” “It is not enough,” says blessed Gregory (Moral Works XIX, final chapter), “to resist temptations if one puts aside the sword of God’s word by living badly.” And St. Jerome, in his letter to Eustochium (Letter 22): “As soon,” he says, “as lust has tickled the senses, or the pleasing fire of pleasure has suffused us with its sweet warmth, let us burst into the cry: ‘The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what flesh can do to me’ (Psalm CXVII). Thus St. Anthony, according to Athanasius, opposed the temptations of demons as though with a weapon—the verse of the Psalmist: ‘The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me. The Lord is my helper, and I shall look down upon my enemies’ (Psalm CXVII). And this one: ‘Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered, and let those who hate him flee from his presence.’ Finally, Abbot Isaac, in Conference X, chapter 10, teaches that the verse of Psalm LXIX, ‘O God, come to my assistance; O Lord, make haste to help me,’ is a most powerful remedy for conquering every temptation. ‘For,’ he says, ‘it contains invocation of God against every danger; it contains the humility of devout confession; it contains vigilance in continual concern and fear; it contains consideration of one’s own weakness and confidence of being heard; it contains trust in present assistance, which is always standing by. This verse is an unconquerable wall, an impenetrable breastplate, and a most secure shield for all who suffer from demonic attacks.’ Thus far.]

Again, he was tempted by pride according to our likeness, so that the same contriver of snares might attempt to force upon him through human beings the kingdom which he had earlier rejected when it was offered by the devil. But without sin he mocked the snares of the tempter.

For when Jesus realized that they were about to come and seize him in order to make him king, he fled again by himself to the mountain (John VI).

He was tempted according to our likeness when he was scourged with whips, struck with blows, spattered with the horror of spittle, and finally endured the specially devised torments of the cross (Matthew XXVI). Yet never was he driven by any insults—or rather, not even by punishments—into the swelling of the slightest indignation, because, fixed upon the gibbet, he mercifully cried out: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII).

## CHAPTER XI. That Christ alone came in the likeness of sinful flesh
How, then, is this also to be understood: that the Apostle recalls that Christ came “in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Romans 8), if we too can possess flesh untouched by any stain of sin?

> **[Note: [Col. 1233D]** The Greek is ἐν ὁμοιώματι, “in likeness.” This is the reading followed here by the author, although the Vulgate has *in similitudinem*, “in the likeness.” Tertullian says that Christ is said to have come “in the likeness” or “into the likeness of sinful flesh” (On the Flesh of Christ, chapter 16), not because he received a likeness of flesh—as though he had an image of a body and not the reality—but because “the likeness of sinful flesh” is intended. Saint Thomas explains the matter more fully in his commentary on this passage: “ ‘Into the likeness of sinful flesh’ must not be understood as though he did not have true flesh, but only the likeness of flesh, as if it were phantom flesh, as the Manichaeans say; for the Lord himself says in Luke: ‘A spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have.’ Thus he does not merely say ‘into the likeness of flesh,’ but ‘into the likeness of sinful flesh.’ For he did not have sinful flesh—that is, flesh conceived in sin and subject to sin—because his flesh was conceived by the Holy Spirit, who takes away sin. Matthew 1: ‘For that which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit.’ But he had the likeness of sinful flesh—that is, flesh like sinful flesh—in that it was capable of suffering. For human flesh before sin was not subject to suffering.” Thus Saint Thomas.]**

For this also is mentioned as something singular in the case of him who alone is without sin: “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Galatians 4). Since he assumed the true and complete substance of human flesh, he is to be understood to have assumed not sin itself in it, but the likeness of sin. The likeness, therefore, is not to be referred to the reality of the flesh,

> **[Note: [Col. 1234C]** This concerns Marcion, the heresiarch, against whom Tertullian wrote his book *On the Flesh of Christ*, and the Manichaeans, against whom Saint Augustine wrote *On Heresies* and elsewhere, as well as the Priscillianists, against whom Pope Saint Leo wrote Letter 93. These heretics, wrongly interpreting the Apostle’s words and explaining them in the manner of sophists—in the terminology of dialecticians—said that Christ had assumed not true flesh but phantom flesh, referring the “likeness of sinful flesh” to the flesh itself and not to sin. Against them Tertullian says in Book 5 of *Against Marcion*: “It would be no great thing if the Spirit of God restored flesh; but if flesh, while it is flesh, is like sinful flesh, yet is not of sin. Thus the likeness belongs to the designation of sin, not to a falsehood concerning the substance. For he would not have added ‘of sin’ if he wished the likeness of substance to be understood, so as to deny its reality. He would have mentioned flesh alone, and not also sin. But by constructing the phrase ‘sinful flesh,’ he both confirmed the substance—that is, flesh—and referred the likeness to the defect of the substance, that is, to sin.”]**

according to the wicked interpretation of certain heretics, but to the image of sin. In him there was indeed true flesh, but without sin, and therefore like sinful flesh. The former belongs to the truth of human substance; the latter, to vices and conduct.

[Col. 1235A] He had the likeness of sinful flesh when, as though ignorant and concerned about food, he asked, “How many loaves do you have?” (Mark 6). Yet just as his flesh was in no way subject to sin, so his soul was not subject to ignorance. Indeed, the evangelist immediately adds: “But he said this to test him; for he himself knew what he was going to do” (John 6).

He had flesh like sinful flesh when, as though thirsty, he asked a Samaritan woman for a drink; yet it was not stained by the filth of sin, because, on the contrary, the woman was moved to ask for living water, which would never allow her to thirst, but would become in her “a spring of water welling up to eternal life” (John 4).

He possessed the reality of this flesh when he slept in the boat; but lest those sailing with him should likewise be deceived by the likeness of sin, he rose and commanded the winds and the sea, and “there was a great calm” (Matthew 8).

He seemed to be subject to sin, as all are, when it was said of him: “If this man were a prophet, he would surely know who and what sort of woman this is who touches him, for she is a sinner.” Yet he did not possess the reality of sin, because, rebuking the Pharisee’s blasphemous thought, he immediately forgave the woman’s sins (Luke 7).

He was thought to bear sinful flesh like the rest when, as though placed in mortal danger and struck with fear at the punishments threatening him, he prayed: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26), and, “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (ibid.). But that sorrow knew no contagion of sin, because the author of life could not fear death. For he says: “No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10).

## CHAPTER XII  
### That all the just and holy were not in the likeness but in the reality of sin

In this respect, therefore, the man who was born of the Virgin is separated by a great distinction from all who are produced by the union of the two sexes. For while all of us bear in our flesh not the likeness but the reality of sin, he assumed not the reality of sin but its likeness, together with the assumption of true flesh.

Although the Pharisees had very clearly remembered what had been written about him by the prophet Isaiah—“He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (Isaiah 53)—nevertheless they were so deceived by the likeness of sinful flesh that they said: “Behold, a glutton and a wine-drinker, a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (Matthew 11). And to the man who had been healed of blindness: “Give glory to God; we know that this man is a sinner” (John 9). And to Pilate: “If he were not a sinner, we would not have handed him over to you” (John 18).

Whoever, therefore, dares to claim for himself, through the crime of blasphemy and pride, equality in this matter—which is singular and proper to Christ alone—will necessarily say that he possesses the likeness of sinful flesh and not the reality of sin.

## CHAPTER XIII  
### That the sins of the saints are not so serious as to deprive them of merit or the name of holiness

Moreover,

> **[Note: [Col. 1235C]** The Council of Trent subscribes to this teaching of the holy Fathers in these words (Session 6, chapter 11): “Although in this mortal life even the holy and just sometimes fall into lesser and daily sins, which are also called venial, they nevertheless do not thereby cease to be just. For the just rightly, humbly, and truthfully say: ‘Forgive us our debts.’ Hence the just themselves ought to feel all the more bound to walk in the way of justice, since, having been freed from sin and made servants of God, they may progress through Jesus Christ by living soberly, justly, and devoutly,” etc. See Collation 20, final chapter, and Collation 23, chapters 6 and following. Nevertheless, from these and similar statements—which generally assert that all human beings, however just and holy, are not free from sin, except Christ the Lord, who is not merely man but true God and man, and therefore ἀναμάρτητος, that is, impeccable—the Virgin Mary, Mother of God, must also be excepted. The holy Fathers teach that, by a singular privilege of God, she remained free and exempt from every sin throughout her life. Thus Saint Augustine says in *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 36: “Except for the holy Virgin Mary, concerning whom, because of the honor due to the Lord, I wish no question at all to be raised when sin is discussed,” etc. The Council of Trent likewise, while denying that a person once justified can avoid all sins, even venial sins, throughout his entire life, added this exception (Session 6, canon 23): “Unless by a special privilege of God, as the Church holds concerning the blessed Virgin.”]**

Scripture plainly declares that just and holy men are not free from fault, saying:

> **[Note: [Col. 1236C]** Bede—or whoever wrote the commentary on this passage—says almost the same things as this abbot: “How is the just man called just when he is said to fall, that is, to sin? Unless he is speaking of lesser and daily sins, without which no just person could exist in this life.
