For through ignorance, forgetfulness, thought, speech, inadvertence, necessity, and the weakness of the flesh, we frequently incur guilt each day, whether unwillingly or willingly; yet the just man rises again, because he is just, and the fall arising from human weakness does not prejudice his justice. Hence, when speaking of the fall of the just man, he does not add ‘into evil.’ For although what they fall into is evil, they nevertheless quickly rise again, so that they cannot remain in the evil into which they have fallen. But concerning the reprobate he says: ‘The wicked will fall into evil,’ because, when the wicked fall—or, more seriously, when they collapse, as Scripture says, that is, when they commit capital crimes—they consent to their fall with such delight that they disdain to be lifted from it by repentance.” Thus far the passage.]**

“Seven times the just man falls and rises again” (Proverbs 24). For what else is falling than sinning? Yet although he is said to fall seven times, he is nevertheless pronounced just, and the fall resulting from human weakness does not prejudice his justice, because there is a great difference between the fall of the just man and that of the sinful man.

It is one thing to commit mortal sin, and another to be anticipated by a thought that is not free from sin; to offend through the error of ignorance or forgetfulness; to stumble through the ease of idle speech;

> **[Note: [Col. 1236D]** To hesitate for a point or moment in the theory of faith occurs in two ways. First, it may occur with firm and deliberate assent, when someone freely and intentionally chooses to doubt and remain doubtful about an article of faith—for example, whether purgatory exists—and refuses to assent and believe firmly. This is a mortal sin. For, as Pope Stephen says (*Extra*, “On Heretics,” chapter 1): “The doubtful in faith is an unbeliever.” Saint Bernard likewise says: “Faith admits no ambiguity; if it has ambiguity, it is not faith.” Such unbelief or doubt concerning faith can occur in a point or moment of time, since the assent of the will does not depend on duration; and if it is voluntary, it is mortal, no less than deliberate pleasure in sin, even when it lasts only a moment, according to all authorities (Saint Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* II-II, question 10, article 7; Cajetan on that passage; Major, Book 3, distinction 25; Panormitanus on chapter 1, “On Heretics”; Melchior Cano, *On Theological Places*, Book 12, chapter 9). In another way, a person may waver concerning faith without full consent: through inadvertence or involuntary hesitation, through negligence in rejecting doubt, or through a certain weakness or feebleness of faith, of which it was said to Peter: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matthew 14). In that case doubt does not remove faith altogether, but indicates faith that is slight and imperfect. It is of such hesitation in the theory of faith that the abbot is speaking here when he counts it among venial faults, as the very words sufficiently indicate: “to hesitate at a point in the theory of faith,” that is, to waver lightly and imperfectly.]**

or to be shaken by some subtle tickling of vainglory; or through natural necessity to withdraw for a while from the highest perfection. These, then, are the seven kinds of falls in which the saint, although he sometimes falls, nevertheless does not cease to be just. Although they may seem light and small, they nevertheless make it impossible for him to be without sin. For he has reasons to practice daily repentance, truly ask forgiveness, and pray continually for his sins, saying: “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6).

To prove by the clearest examples that some saints have erred and yet have not departed from their justice, what else must we believe that the most blessed and foremost of the apostles, Peter, was except a saint—especially at the time when the Lord said to him:

“Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16).

What could be more glorious than this praise of the Lord? What could be more exalted than this power and blessedness? Yet shortly afterward, when, in ignorance of the mystery of the Passion, he unwittingly opposed so great a benefit [Lips. in margin: *utilitatis*, “benefit”] for the human race, saying, “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall never happen to you,” he deserved to hear: “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling-block to me, because you do not understand the things of God but those of men” (ibid.).

> **[Note: [Col. 1237C]** “The very Equity”—that is, the very Truth, namely Christ the Lord, who says of himself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 12). There is emphasis in the word “Equity,” as though he were saying: “The most equitable Lord and Judge—indeed, Equity and Truth itself.”]**

When this Equity rebuked him in these words,

> **[Note: [Col. 1237C]** The phrase is obscure and should be resolved as follows: “He must altogether be understood to have fallen when rebuked by the Lord, and yet to have remained in holiness and justice.” A double negative is equivalent to an affirmation. But the question arises: how did Peter fall—that is, sin—when he said, “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall never happen to you” (Matthew 16)? To resolve this question and clarify the passage, it will be sufficient to set out here the opinions of two ancient Fathers and doctors of the Church and oppose them to the perverse interpretation of the heretics. By these highly insolent words, indeed, they rebuke Peter for that reason and, as far as lies in them, disparage and deride his faith, as though he had foolishly wished to turn Christ back from the death on which our salvation depended. Chrysostom and Jerome, however, speak of Peter in a far different spirit and with far different moderation: just as shortly before, in professing Christ to be the Son of the living God, he had displayed a faith in him singular above the other apostles, so now he displayed a greater love toward that same Christ; and, if he sinned at all, he sinned through ignorance and imprudence. [Col. 1238B] To establish this more fully, it will be better to hear the Fathers themselves speak in their own words. Thus Chrysostom says (*Homily 45 on Matthew*): “What is this, that Peter, who had received the Father’s revelation, fell so quickly and became unstable? But we say that it is not surprising if he was ignorant of this, since he had not yet received revelation concerning the Passion. For by revelation he had learned that Christ was the Son of the living God; but the mystery of the Cross and Resurrection had not yet been revealed to him. Therefore Christ, showing that he had to come to the Passion, rebuked Peter,” etc. Saint Jerome says in his *Commentary on Matthew* (see also his Letter to Algasia, question 3): “We have often said that Peter had an exceedingly ardent and very great love for the Lord and Savior. Therefore, after his confession, in which he had said, ‘You are Christ, the Son of the living God,’ and after the Savior’s reward, which he had heard, ‘Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah,’ etc., he suddenly hears from the Lord that he must go to Jerusalem and there suffer many things from the elders, scribes, and chief priests, be killed, and rise on the third day. He wishes—that is, thinks—his confession to be destroyed, and does not think it possible that the Son of God should be killed. He therefore takes him aside in his affection, or leads him away privately, lest he seem to rebuke his master in the presence of his fellow disciples; and he began to rebuke him with the affection of one who loves and wishes well, saying: ‘Far be it from you, Lord.’ Or, as the Greek has it more aptly, ἱλέως σοι, Κύριε, οὐ μὴ ἔσται σοι τοῦτο: that is, ‘Be propitious to yourself, Lord; this shall not happen to you.’ It cannot happen, nor can my ears accept that the Son of God should be put to death. To him the Lord, turning, said: ‘Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling-block to me.’ *Satan* means adversary or opponent: ‘Because,’ he says, ‘you speak things contrary to my will, you ought to be called an adversary.’ Many think that it was not Peter who was rebuked, but the hostile spirit—that is, the devil—who was suggesting these words to the Apostle. But to me this apostolic error, arising from an affection of piety, will never seem an instigation of the devil. ‘Get behind me, Satan.’ To the devil it is said: ‘Get behind me’ (Matthew 4); Peter hears: ‘Get behind me’: that is, follow my judgment, because you do not understand the things of God but those of men. It is my will, and that of my Father—whose will I came to do—that I should die for the salvation of humankind; you, considering only your own will, do not wish the grain to fall so that it may bear much fruit.” Thus far Saint Jerome. From these words we learn that Peter was called *Satan* by Christ, not as the devil’s proper name, but in the common sense of adversary, because he opposed Christ, who wished to die for humankind’s salvation, and unwittingly and imprudently obstructed so great a benefit for the human race, as this abbot says. But why did Christ rebuke him so sharply? Maldonatus answers (*Commentary on Matthew* 16): “Not so much because Peter’s fault, if indeed there was one, deserved it, as because the greatness of the matter under discussion did.” Jansenius says (*Harmony of the Gospels*, 66): “He now loved the Lord imprudently and without discernment. For he ought to have considered that he whom he had confessed to be the Son of God could do or say nothing deserving rebuke; and likewise to have reflected that the Lord had said it had to happen thus, and therefore had seemed good to the Father. But the vehemence of a love not yet perfect, but still excessively human, prevented him from considering these things.”]**

must we believe that, by these words, he had not fallen at all, or that he had not remained in holiness and justice?

And what of the time when he is plainly not to be denied to have suffered a fall, when, with the fear of his persecutors imminent, he was compelled three times to deny the Lord? Yet immediately afterward, when repentance followed,

> **[Note: [Col. 1239C]** Certainly not. For who could deny or doubt that Peter fell gravely and suffered ruin when he denied Christ? Nevertheless, some have thought that, when Peter denied Christ, he either did not sin or at least did not lie, but spoke ambiguously while preserving the truth. They said that he was not lying when he denied knowing Christ as man—meaning merely as man—while he knew him as true God. Saint Jerome seems to have noted them in these words in his commentary on Matthew 26: “I know that certain people, out of pious affection for the apostle Peter, have interpreted this passage in such a way as to say that Peter did not deny God but man, and that the meaning was: ‘I do not know the man, because I know God.’ The prudent reader understands how frivolous this is. They defend the Apostle in such a way as to make God guilty of lying. For if he did not deny him, then the Lord lied when he said: ‘Amen I say to you, this night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.’ Observe what he says: ‘You will deny me,’ not ‘the man.’ ” Thus Jerome. But why, you may ask, does the author adduce this example, which seems rather contrary to the purpose and argument of this chapter, in which he teaches that the saints and just are not free in this life from venial and daily faults, when it is clear that Peter’s denial was not a light and venial fault but an extremely grave one? I answer that, since he had mentioned Peter’s lesser fault and had proved his point by it, it would have been easy for someone to object with another fault of Peter’s, much more serious, namely his denial of Christ. In answer to this objection, he teaches by Peter’s example that saints and just persons sometimes fall and sin gravely, but rise again immediately after their fall, when God places his hand beneath them—that is, supplies the help of his grace and mercifully raises them up. Thus, although they may for a time fall away from justice and holiness, they are not thereby entirely erased from the roll of the just, because through repentance, at least final repentance, they return to justice and recover the merits of their preceding good works. This is what the Psalmist says: “When the just man falls, he will not be shattered”—that is, he will not perish forever or be rejected by God like a vessel that has been broken and smashed. He is speaking of the elect, whom God leads to the kingdom by infallible grace: “Those whom he predestined, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified.”]**

by washing away the stain of so great a crime with the bitterest tears, he did not lose the merit of holiness and justice (Matthew 26).

Concerning him, therefore, and the holy men like him, we must also understand what David sings:

“The steps of a man are directed by the Lord, and he delights greatly in his way. When he falls, he will not be shattered, because the Lord supports him with his hand” (Psalm 36).

For whose steps are directed by the Lord, if not those of the just man? Yet of this very man it is said: “When he falls, he will not be shattered.” What does “when he falls” mean except “when he incurs the fall of some sin”? “He will not be shattered,” he says—that is, he will not long be oppressed by the assault of sin. Although for the moment he may seem struck down, he is raised by the divine help that he implores, and by a speedy resurrection does not lose the stability of justice. Or even if for the moment he commits some fault through the weakness of the flesh, the Lord’s supporting hand will restore him.

The holy man does not cease to be holy after his fall when he recognizes that he cannot be justified by confidence in his own works and believes that he can be freed from so many bonds of sin only by the grace of the Lord. With the Apostle he does not cease to cry out: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from the body of this death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7).

## CHAPTER XIV  
### How the Apostle’s saying is to be understood: “For I do not do the good that I want”

When the Apostle Paul recognized that the immeasurable abyss of purity could not be penetrated by man while the surges of his thoughts resisted it, and after being tossed about for a long time as though through the deep, he had said:

“For I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I hate, that I do” (Romans 7).

And again:

“If I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me. For I delight in the law of God according to the inner man; but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin which is in my members” (ibid.).

Having perceived both his own frailty and that of nature itself, and terrified by the immensity of so vast an abyss, he fled to the safest harbor of divine assistance. As though despairing from the natural weakness of his mortality, oppressed by the burdens of a shipwrecked vessel, he asked from him for whom nothing is impossible the remedies of shipwreck, crying out with a kind of miserable lamentation:

> **[Note: [Col. 1240D]** “Body of death,” says Jerome (*Book 1 of the Apology against Rufinus*, chapter 6), “he calls that which is subject to vices, diseases, disturbances, and death until it rises with Christ in glory, and until the fragile clay is hardened by the heat of the Holy Spirit into the most solid pottery, changing its glory but not its nature.” Thus Jerome. Yet the genitive in this expression may also be referred to death itself, so that the sense is: “Who will free me from the body of this death,” that is, from the body in which, even against my will, I experience this kind of death.]**

“Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from the body of this death?” (ibid.).

Immediately, however, he confidently added the deliverance that he had despaired of obtaining from the weakness of nature, but presumed upon from God’s kindness:

> **[Note: [Col. 1240D]** There is a double reading among the Greeks. Some read χάρις τῷ Θεῷ, “thanks be to God,” as Chrysostom does (*Homily 13*) and Jerome (*Letter 151, question 8, to Algasia*). Others read χάρις τοῦ Θεοῦ, “the grace of God,” in the genitive: that is, “the grace of God will free me,” not the law of Moses and not the powers of nature. Our translator rendered it in this latter way.]**

“The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XV  
### Germanus objects that the Apostle said these things in the person of sinners

[Col. 1241A]

**Germanus:** Many determine that this apostolic passage must be understood in such a way that they affirm that he spoke not in his own person but in the person of sinners—namely, those who wish to abstain from bodily allurements and pleasures but, bound by their former vices and captivated by the delight of carnal passions, cannot restrain themselves, because,

> **[Note: [Col. 1241B]** How difficult it is to cure a habitual or deeply rooted custom of vice is shown, beyond the other testimonies of Scripture, by the well-known saying of Jeremiah, in which he rebukes the deeply rooted wickedness of the Jews: “Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? Then you also can do good, having learned evil” (Jeremiah 13). “It was established,” says Jerome in that place, “not by nature but by excessive habit and love of sinning, so that it seems to have been transformed into nature.” And in his Letter to Laeta on the education of a daughter he says: “What inexperienced minds have absorbed is eradicated with difficulty. A new vessel long retains both the taste and the smell with which it was first filled.” Basil discusses the same matter at length in his *Longer Rules*, chapter 6: “A habit strengthened by age commonly acquires the force of nature.” Chrysostom says in his commentary on 2 Corinthians 4: “Great is the tyranny of habit, so great that it compels in the same way as nature.” Finally, Saint Augustine, having experienced this difficulty in himself, explained it at length in the account of his conversion. Thus, among other things, he says in Book 7, chapter 5, of the *Confessions*: “I was bound not by another’s iron but by my own iron will. The enemy held my will, and from it he had made a chain for me and bound me; for from a perverse will comes lust, and when lust is served it becomes habit, and when habit is not resisted it becomes necessity.” Bede says the following about Zacchaeus in his commentary on Luke 15: “He sought to see the Savior entering Jericho, but could not because of the crowd. He desired to share in the grace that the Savior brought to the world, but the deeply rooted habit of vices hindered him from reaching his desire. For the same crowd of harmful habit that rebuked the blind man who cried out, so that he would not ask for light, also delayed the tax collector who looked up, so that he might not see Jesus.”]**

they are oppressed by the deeply rooted habit of vices, as by the harsh domination of a kind of tyranny, and cannot breathe freely into the liberty of chastity.

For how could what the blessed Apostle says apply to him, when it is certain that he reached the highest summit of all perfection: “For I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I hate, that I do”? And also what he adds: “If I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me”? Or even this: “I delight in the law of God according to the inner man; but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin which is in my members” (Romans 7).

How, then, can these things be fitted to the person of the Apostle? What good was there that he could not accomplish? Conversely, what evil was there that, unwillingly and hating it, he nevertheless committed under compulsion from nature? To what law of sin could the chosen vessel, in whom Christ the Lord spoke, be led captive? He had taken captive every disobedience and every height that exalted itself against God (2 Corinthians 10), and he confidently proclaimed of himself:

“I have fought the good fight; I have completed the course; I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of justice, which the Lord, the just judge, will give me on that day” (2 Timothy 4).

## CHAPTER XVI  
### Postponement of the question proposed

**Theonas:** As I enter the safest harbor of silence, you are trying once again to recall me to the immeasurable sea of this most profound question. But, having embraced the opportunity for a secure anchorage, we shall meanwhile, with the course of so long a conference completed, cast the anchor of silence, so that tomorrow, provided no force of the storm intervenes, after testing the breath of a favorable wind, we may spread the sails of discussion.

# TWENTY-THIRD CONFERENCE

The third conference of the abbot Theonas, **On Willing the Good and Doing the Evil**

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 1241D]

With daylight having returned, when the old man was compelled by Germanus’s persistent insistence to probe the abyss of the apostolic question [Note: [Col. 1241D] By “the abyss of the apostolic question,” or, as he said above (Collation 21, final chapter), “the immense ocean of a most profound question,” he hyperbolically denotes the quite difficult and obscure question concerning the Apostle’s words in Romans VII, recently proposed by Germanus and reserved for this conference. Its substance is this: whether the Apostle speaks there in the person of sinners, as Germanus maintained, or in his own person and that of those like himself, that is, the righteous. Or, in other words: whether he speaks of impious people, established in a state of sin and carnal; or rather of the righteous, reborn through grace and spiritual, such as Paul was. This question, however, is not as difficult and profound as it appeared to this abbot. For St. Augustine teaches, and after him St. Thomas, that the Apostle’s words can be expounded in either way; nor do either side lack ancient and approved authors and defenders. Chrysostom, Theophylact [Col. 1243B], and others on this passage advanced the former exposition, as did Augustine himself in Book I, chapter 1, to Simplicianus. They hold that the Apostle speaks not of himself and righteous people like himself, but assumes the person of impious people who are led by the concupiscence of the flesh and dragged into many shameful deeds; or, what is the same thing, that he intended to express in himself the state of humankind placed under sin and not restored by grace. Hence he says: “For I know that the law is spiritual; but I am carnal, sold under sin” [Col. 1243C] (Rom. VII). St. Jerome also seems to favor this view in Daniel III, where he says: “Just as those three youths placed in the furnace spoke thus in the person of the people: ‘We have sinned and acted wickedly in departing from you,’ etc., so the Apostle’s words must be understood: ‘For I do not do what I will; but I do what I do not will.’” And likewise the rest written in the same passage. But the other exposition later pleased Augustine more, in Book II, chapter 1, of his Retractions, and throughout his books against the Pelagians. St. Anselm, Thomas, and later interpreters also approved it more, as does this Theonas; accordingly it is better for us to adhere to it. Yet, to satisfy the reader as far as possible and make this view clearer, the arguments advanced above to the contrary by Germanus must be answered (the preceding Collation, penultimate chapter): “How,” he asks, “can what he says be applicable to the blessed Apostle, who certainly attained the summit of all perfection: ‘For I do not do the good that I will; but I do the evil that I hate’ [Col. 1243D]? And also what follows: ‘But if I do what I do not will, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me.’ And likewise this: ‘For I delight in the law of God according to the inner man; but I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin which is in my members.’ In what respect, then, can these things be fitted to the Apostle’s person? For what good is there that he could not fulfill? Conversely, what evil is it that, though unwilling and hating it, he nevertheless committed against his will under nature’s compulsion? Under what law of sin could the vessel of election, in whom Christ the Lord spoke, be carried away captive?” Thus far Germanus. To answer these arguments briefly—for a fuller discussion and explanation must be sought from the interpreters—it should be noted that the Apostle here treats of involuntary movements of concupiscence [Col. 1244B], which spring from Adam’s sin in nature corrupted and vitiated, and which even holy and perfect people experience unwillingly in this life. For this is what the Apostle says: “I do not do the good that I will,” because I will not to feel concupiscence, not to experience its movements, yet I cannot attain this. “But I do the evil that I hate,” namely, to feel concupiscence. Augustine says (Against Two Letters of the Pelagians, chapter 10) that when he said he “does” this, he meant not by consenting affection [Col. 1244C], but by the very movement of concupiscence. Thus, the good which the Apostle could not fulfill in this life was to experience no movement of concupiscence; and the evil which he affirms that he does, though unwilling and hating it, is to feel concupiscence. Although this is evil, because it is a kind of disease and defect of corrupted nature, it is not sin properly so called if the consent of reason is absent. Yet the Apostle sometimes calls it sin because it is the cause and fuel of sin, as the Council of Trent teaches and explains (Session 5, Decree on Original Sin). Accordingly, when the Apostle adds, “But if I do what I do not will, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me,” he means: if I feel concupiscence according to the flesh, though I detest it in my mind, it is not my work but the work of sin—that is, of concupiscence—which comes from sin and inclines toward sin. But to Germanus’s third objection, concerning the law of the members that takes captive, or leads captive into [Col. 1244D] the law of sin—something which does not seem applicable to the Apostle—St. Augustine replies that it is called “taking captive,” that is, attempting to take captive, or taking captive according to the flesh, not according to the mind (On Marriage and Concupiscence, chapter 30). These matters will be explained more fully in chapters 11 and following.], he spoke as follows:

> “The testimonies by which you endeavor to prove that the Apostle Paul spoke not in his own person but in the person of sinners—‘For I do not do the good that I will, but I do the evil that I hate’; or again, ‘But if I do what I do not will, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in my members’; or what follows, ‘For I delight in the law of God according to the inner man, but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin that is in my members’ (Rom. VII)—plainly demonstrate the contrary: that these statements cannot in any way apply to the persons of sinners, but belong only to the perfect, and are fitting only to the holiness of those who follow the apostles’ merits.

> “For how could this apply to the persons of sinners: ‘For I do not do the good that I will, but I do the evil that I hate’? Nor indeed this: ‘But if I do what I do not will, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me’? For which of the guilty defiles himself unwillingly with adulteries and fornications? Who, against his will, lays an ambush for his neighbor? Who is compelled by unavoidable necessity to destroy a man by false testimony, to deceive by theft, to covet another’s possessions, or to shed blood?

> “Moreover, as it is written—[Note: The Vulgate text reads: ‘Every thought of the human heart is intent upon evil at all times’ (Gen. VI). From the Hebrew: ‘The formation of the human heart is only evil.’ This is a hyperbolical expression, referring only to the wicked of that period, just as the Psalmist’s statement does: ‘All have turned aside; together they have become worthless,’ etc. (Ps. XIII). For it is certain that Noah there, as here David and the other righteous and upright people, must be excepted.]—the human race has been diligently intent upon wickedness from its youth (Gen. VII according to the Septuagint). For all who burn with love of vice desire so ardently to accomplish what they crave that they even seek out opportunities for committing crimes with vigilant care; and, boasting of their disgrace and heap of offenses, they acquire for themselves, according to the judgment of the rebuking Apostle (Phil. III), a kind of praise from their shame.

> “The prophet Jeremiah likewise declares that they not only commit their crimes unwillingly, or with their hearts and bodies at rest, but that they labor with such strenuous efforts to bring them to completion that they sweat over accomplishing them and are not recalled from their deadly appetite for crime even by formidable difficulties, saying: ‘They have labored to commit iniquity’ (Jer. IX).

> “Who could say that this applies to sinners: ‘Thus I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin’ (Rom. VII), when it is evident that they serve God neither in mind nor in flesh? Or how can those who sin in body serve God in mind, when the flesh conceives the seedbed of vices in the heart, and the very author of both natures declares that the source and origin of sins proceed from there? ‘From the heart,’ he says (Matt. XV), ‘come evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, thefts,’ and other things of this kind.

[Note: [Col. 1244D] On the several laws distinguished by the Apostle in that passage, see below at chapter 11 of this conference.]

> “Therefore it is plainly shown that this cannot possibly be understood of the persons of sinners, who not only do not hate evil but actually love it, and who serve God neither in mind nor in flesh to such an extent that they sin in mind before they sin in body, and are overtaken by the sin of their thoughts before they fulfill the desire of the flesh.”

## CHAPTER II  
### He teaches that the Apostles possessed many good things, but possessed the perfection of goodness only in wish and desire.

[Col. 1245A]

It remains, therefore, that we measure the force of the meaning from the speaker’s innermost disposition, and determine what the blessed Apostle called good and what he pronounced evil in comparison with it, not by the bare signification of the words, but with the same perspective with which he spoke. We must also investigate his meaning according to its dignity and merit.

For then shall we be able to comprehend statements inspired by God according to their purpose and intention, when, weighing the condition and merit of those by whom they were uttered, we take on an equivalent disposition—not in words but in experience. For according to the quality of that disposition, all meanings are either conceived or expressed.

Let us therefore examine more carefully what the principal good was that the Apostle could not perfect even when he wished to do so. [Note: In order to clarify this passage, besides what Dom. Cuychius has noted, it may also be useful to observe that, according to Augustine, there are three kinds of goods in a human being, which he calls great, intermediate, and least (On Free Choice of the Will, II.19). Least goods are those without which one can live rightly, such as health, strength, bodily appearance, eloquence, knowledge, and the like. Intermediate goods are those without which one cannot live rightly, such as the powers and faculties of the soul, especially the will and the intellect. Great and greatest goods are those by which one lives rightly and which no one uses badly, such as the virtues of the soul and the gifts of the Holy Spirit. No one can use these badly as principles of action, although one can use them badly as objects—for example, if someone takes pride in virtue, as was noted above from St. Thomas. If this abbot is speaking of the first and second kinds of goods when he says that the blessed Apostle and other righteous people possessed many goods by nature, there is no difficulty, since such goods are natural and do not surpass the powers of nature. If, however, he is speaking of the third kind, as appears from the words that follow, Cuychius explains how this should be judged true or false.]

For we know many good things which we cannot deny that the blessed Apostle and all men of his merit both possessed by nature and acquired through grace. Chastity is good, continence praiseworthy, prudence admirable, humanity [humility] generous, sobriety watchful, temperance moderate, mercy devout, and justice holy. There is no doubt that all these qualities were so full and perfect in the Apostle Paul and his companions that religion was taught by them more through the example of their virtues than through words.

What is more, they were always consumed by constant care for all the churches (II Cor. II) and by unceasing anxiety. What a great good of mercy this is, and what perfection: to burn for those who cause scandal and to become weak with those who are weak!

Since, then, the Apostle abounded in such gifts, we shall not be able to recognize what good he lacked in perfection unless we enter into the disposition in which he himself spoke. All the virtues we have said that he possessed, although they are like splendid and precious gems, nevertheless, if they are compared with that famous and singularly precious pearl which the Gospel merchant sought and desired to purchase by selling everything he possessed (Matt. XIII), their worth becomes so diminished and despised that, once they have been sold without hesitation, possession of that one good enriches the seller of innumerable goods. [Note: This refers to the Gospel parable (Matt. XIII), in which the good merchant is said to sell everything in order to buy one pearl of the highest value. The word is *margarita*, and also *margaritum* in the neuter gender. Hence Tertullian, On the Pallium, V: ‘A pearl, precious even in its name, has been drawn out.’ Elsewhere (To the Martyrs, IV) he uses this as a proverbial expression: ‘So much for glass? How much for a true pearl?’ St. Jerome imitates this (Letter to Paulinus): ‘If glass is worth so much,’ he says, ‘how much is a precious pearl?’ The saying signifies the greatest inequality: pearls—also called *uniones*—have the highest value among gems, whereas glass is extremely cheap, though it can imitate pearls and deceive the inexperienced.]

## CHAPTER III  
### What the true good is which the Apostle testifies that he cannot perfect.

[Col. 1246B]

What, then, is the one thing so incomparably superior to those many and such great goods that, once all else has been despised and rejected, it alone ought to be possessed? Surely it is that best portion whose greatness and permanence the Lord praised when Mary preferred it to the duties of receiving and showing hospitality that she had set aside:

> “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things; but few things are necessary—or even one. Mary has chosen the best portion, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke X). [Note: See the explanation of this in Collation I, chapter 8, and St. Thomas, II–II, question 182, article 1.]

There is therefore one and only one *theoria*, that is, contemplation of God, to which all the merits of justification and every exercise of virtue are rightly subordinated. All those qualities which we said shone forth in the Apostle Paul are not only good and useful but also great and excellent. [Note: These same words, together with what precedes, are found in St. Augustine, Sermon 43, On Time.]

Yet just as the metal tin, which was considered useful and valuable, becomes worthless when silver is contemplated, and silver itself loses its value again in comparison with gold; and as gold itself is despised when compared with gems, while the multitude of gems, however remarkable, is surpassed by the radiance of a single pearl—so all those merits of holiness, although they are not only good and useful for the present but also obtain the gift of eternity, will nevertheless be judged cheap and, so to speak, saleable when compared with the merits of divine contemplation.

And to confirm this same comparison by the authority of Scripture, does not Scripture generally pronounce concerning all things created by God, saying, “And behold, everything that God had made was very good” (Gen. I)? And again, “All the works of God are good in their time” (Ecclus. XXXIX)?

These things, then, which in the present are pronounced not merely good but very good—with the added qualification—are truly useful to us who dwell in this world for the purposes of life, for the healing of the body, or for some other benefit unknown to us. They are also very good in that they enable us to perceive, through the things that have been made, the invisible things of God from the creation of the world, and to contemplate his eternal power and divinity (Rom. I) through the immense and orderly construction of the world and the continued existence of everything within it.

Nevertheless, none of these things will retain the name of good if they are compared with that future age, where there is no alteration of goods and no corruption of true blessedness to be feared. The blessedness of that world is described thus: “The light of the moon shall be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, like the light of seven days” (Isa. III).

These great, excellent, striking, and marvelous things, therefore, if compared with the future promises received by faith, will immediately appear vanity, as David says:

> “They will all grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. CI).

Therefore, because nothing is stable in itself, nothing immutable, and nothing good except the deity alone, while all creatures attain the blessedness of eternity or immutability not through their own nature but through participation in and grace from their Creator, they cannot retain for themselves the merit of goodness that belongs to their Creator.

## CHAPTER IV  
### Human goodness and justice are not good when compared with divine goodness and justice.

If we wish to support the reasoning of this position with still clearer testimonies, do we not read in the Gospel that many things are called good: a good tree, a good treasure, a good man, and a good servant, because, as it says, “A good tree cannot bear evil fruit,” and “A good man brings good things out of the good treasure of his heart,” and, “Well done, good and faithful servant” (Matt. VII, XII, XV; Luke XVIII)?

Although there is no doubt that all these are good in themselves, if we turn our attention to the goodness of God, none of them will be called good, since the Lord says, “No one is good except God alone” (Mark X). [Note: That is, good by nature, as was said above (chapter 3). For God’s essence is goodness itself. All other things are good through participation in God, as Blessed Dionysius the Areopagite teaches in On the Divine Names, chapter 4: ‘Just as this sun illuminates everything not by thought or choice but simply by what it is, and all things in proportion to their capacity receive a share of its light, so that supreme good, surpassing the sun—as an indistinct image is surpassed by its original form—by its very substance pours forth rays of the whole of goodness upon all things that exist, according to each one’s capacity.’ Thus Dionysius. See there the notable commentary of St. Thomas Aquinas.]

In view of him, even the apostles themselves, who by the excellence of their election had surpassed the goodness of the human race in many ways, are called evil, since the Lord speaks to them as follows: “If you, then, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give the good Spirit to those who ask him” (Matt. VII)!

Finally, just as our goodness is changed into evil when viewed in relation to the goodness above, so our justice, when compared with divine justice, is reckoned like a menstruous cloth, as the prophet Isaiah says:

> “All our righteousnesses are like a menstruous cloth” (Isa. LXIV). [Note: These words are applied to the author’s purpose rather improperly. Isaiah is not speaking in his own person but in the person of the people, nor is he speaking of the works of the righteous, especially Christian righteous people; rather, he is speaking of the works of the impious Jews, as is clear from the text. Nor does he refer to all their works, as though everything they did were sin, but only to those works which they regarded as righteousnesses—such as sacrifices, new moons, and other Jewish ceremonies in which they placed their confidence. The prophet, on the contrary, says that these were like a menstruous cloth, than which nothing is more unclean, because they were not performed with right intention or as they ought to have been. Hence the Lord also says through Isaiah: ‘Do not continue to offer sacrifice in vain; incense is an abomination to me. Your new moons and your feasts my soul has hated.’ From this it is clear how impiously and foolishly Lutherans infer from this passage that every work of a Christian, even of a righteous Christian, is sin. If those words are sometimes applied by accommodation to the righteous and their works, they should not be understood as though all the works of the righteous were unclean and sinful, as those blabberers claim. Rather, they are understood either by comparison with divine justice, beside which human justice is reckoned like a menstruous cloth, as explained here; or because certain evil works, many defects, and negligences are occasionally mixed with good works. These are light and daily sins, which, although they do not remove the praise and merit of justice, nevertheless diminish and somewhat stain it, and thus make it in some degree resemble a menstruous cloth. Bellarmine responds to the heretics’ argument from this same passage as follows (On Monks, II.13): ‘To the third point I reply with Jerome in the same place that the prophet is speaking in the person of the gravest sinners, who, if they performed any good works, at least morally speaking, polluted them by the mixture of many crimes. We, however, are not speaking of sinners but of the righteous when we say that people can keep the law—and thus be righteous—and even do more; nor do we admit that all the works of a sinner are necessarily sins. For Isaiah does not compare the works of sinners with filth, but with a dirty cloth in which there are clean parts and stained parts.’ These words of his shed considerable light on the meaning of that statement.]

Moreover, even the life-giving precepts of the law itself—which is said to have been ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator (Gal. III), and of which the same Apostle says, “Therefore the law is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good” (Rom. VII)—if compared with evangelical perfection, are declared by the divine oracle to be not good at all. For he says:

> “I gave them statutes that were not good, and judgments in which they shall not live” (Ezek. XX). [Note: This statement is explained somewhat elsewhere (Collation XXI, chapter 33).]

The Apostle likewise declares that, in the light of the New Testament, the glory of the law is so eclipsed that, compared with the radiance of the Gospel, he pronounces it not to have been glorified, saying:

> “For what was glorified has not been glorified in this respect, because of the surpassing glory” (II Cor. III). [Note: The Apostle’s words in the Vulgate are somewhat obscure: ‘For what was glorified has not been glorified in this respect because of the surpassing glory’ (II Cor. III). The meaning is: what shone forth—that is, the law, which was glorified in the lawgiver Moses—was not truly glorified in this respect, that is, in comparison with the evangelical law, because of the latter’s surpassing glory.]

Scripture preserves the same comparison in the opposite direction as well, namely, in balancing the merits of sinners, so that it justifies those who are much less impious by comparison with worse people, saying: “Sodom has been justified in comparison with you.” And again: “What has your sister Sodom done?” And: “Israel, the apostate, justified her soul in comparison with Judah, the transgressor” (Ezek. XVI).

Thus, too, the merits of all the virtues mentioned above, although good and precious in themselves, are darkened by comparison with the radiance of contemplation. For although many saints are occupied with good works, they are nevertheless engaged in earthly pursuits, which draw them away from and delay them in contemplation of that supreme good.

[Note: A similar and fully lucid passage agreeing with this is found in St. Jerome, Against the Pelagians, I.6: ‘What is surprising,’ he says, ‘if, in comparison among the saints, some are better and others inferior, when the contrary may also be understood in comparison among sinners? To Jerusalem, which had been pierced by many wounds of sin, it is said: “Sodom has been justified in comparison with you.” Not that Sodom is righteous in itself—for it has fallen into eternal ashes and hears through Ezekiel: “Sodom shall be restored to her former state” (Ezek. XVI)—but because, in comparison with the more criminal Jerusalem, she appears righteous. For Jerusalem killed the Son of God, whereas Sodom, because of the abundance of bread and the greatness of luxury, exceeded the limit of lust. The publican in the Gospel, who beat his breast (Luke XVIII), as though it were a treasury of evil thoughts, and who, because of consciousness of his sins, did not dare raise his eyes, becomes more righteous by comparison with the proud Pharisee. Tamar, too, disguising herself as a prostitute, deceives Judah and merits hearing the judgment of the man who was deceived: “Tamar is more righteous than I” (Gen. XXXVIII). From all these examples it is established not only that human beings are in no way perfect in comparison with the divine majesty, but that not even angels and other human beings who have climbed the heights of virtue are so, and so forth.’]

## CHAPTER V  
### That no one can remain continually intent upon that supreme good.

[Note: [Col. 1250B] In summary: can anyone engaged in the works of the active life at the same time be free for contemplation? Germanus asked almost the same question in Book I, Chapter 12: “Who, enclosed in fragile flesh, can remain so constantly attached to this θεωρία [contemplation] that he never thinks about a brother’s arrival, visiting the sick, manual labor, or at least showing kindness to strangers or visitors? Finally, who is not interrupted by the provision or care of the body itself?” To him Abbot Moses replied (Conference 1, Chapter 13): “To cling continually to God and to be inseparably joined to his contemplation, as you say, is impossible for a person enclosed in the fragility of this flesh. But we must know where we ought to fix the intention of our mind and toward what goal we should always recall the gaze of our soul,” etc.

Moreover, for a fuller clarification of this passage, the teaching of St. Thomas seems entirely necessary (2.2, question 182, article 3), where he asks and explains whether the contemplative life is impeded by the active life—which is the subject of this chapter. “It must be said,” he writes, “that the active life can be considered in two ways. First, with regard to the study and exercise of external actions; and in this respect it is obvious that the active life impedes the contemplative, insofar as it is impossible for anyone simultaneously to be occupied with external actions and to devote himself to divine contemplation. Second, the active life can be considered with regard to its ordering and disciplining the soul’s interior passions. In this respect the active life assists contemplation, which is impeded by the disorder of the interior passions.” Hence Gregory says in the sixth book of the *Moralia* (Chapter 27): “When some desire to hold the summit of contemplation, let them first test themselves in the field through the exercise of works, so that they may carefully know whether they now inflict no evil upon their neighbors, whether they bear with equanimity the evils inflicted by their neighbors, whether their mind is not dissolved in joy by temporal goods offered to them, and whether it is not wounded by excessive grief when those goods are withdrawn. Then let them consider whether, when they return inwardly to themselves and search out spiritual things, they do not drag along with them the shadows of temporal things, or perhaps drive away with the hand of discernment those shadows that they have brought with them.” Thus the exercise of the active life contributes to the contemplative life by quieting the interior passions, from which the phantasms arise that impede contemplation. So St. Thomas.]

For who, rescuing the helpless from the hand of one stronger than he, and the needy and poor from those who plunder them; who, crushing the jaws of the wicked and wresting spoils from between their teeth, can in the very work of intercession behold the glory of the divine majesty with a tranquil mind [Lipsius, in the margin: “receive”]? Who, distributing food to the poor or welcoming crowds of visitors with benevolent kindness, can at that moment, when his mind is anxiously occupied with his brothers’ needs, contemplate the immensity of heavenly blessedness; and when shaken by the distresses and cares of the present life, behold the state of the future age with his heart lifted above earthly contamination?

Therefore blessed David, defining this alone as man’s good, desires to cling continually to God, saying: “But it is good for me to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord God” (Psalm 72). Ecclesiastes likewise declares that no righteous person can accomplish this without fault: “For there is not a just person on earth who does good and does not sin” (Ecclesiastes 7).

For who, however distinguished among all the just and holy, bound by the chains of this body, should be believed ever to have possessed this supreme good in such a way that, never departing from divine contemplation, he was thought to have been distracted from him who alone is good by earthly thoughts for not even a brief moment; who never took any thought for food, clothing, or other bodily necessities; who was never concerned about receiving brothers, changing his dwelling, or building his cell; who never desired any human assistance; or who, harassed by the barrenness of poverty, never incurred the sentence of the Lord’s rebuke: “Do not be anxious about your life, what you shall eat, nor about your body, what you shall wear” (Matthew 6)?

Finally, we confidently assert that even the apostle Paul himself, who had surpassed the labors of all the saints in the multitude of his sufferings, could not fulfill this. He himself bears witness in the Acts of the Apostles to his disciples: “You yourselves know that these hands provided what was necessary for me and for those who were with me” (Acts 20). Or when writing to the Thessalonians, he testifies that he worked “in labor and weariness, night and day” (2 Thessalonians 3). Although these labors prepared great rewards of merit for him, nevertheless his mind, however holy and exalted, could not avoid being drawn away at times from that heavenly contemplation by the demands of earthly work.

Finally, when he saw himself being enriched by such and so many fruits, and weighed in his heart the good of contemplation—placing, as it were, on one scale the progress gained through so many labors and on the other the delight of divine contemplation—and after his breast had been subjected to a long inward examination,

[Note: [Col. 1251C] This saying of St. Augustine fits this passage beautifully (*City of God*, Book 19, chapter 19): “The love of truth seeks holy leisure; the necessity of love undertakes just business. If no one imposes this burden, one must devote oneself to receiving and contemplating the truth. But if it is imposed, it must be undertaken because of the necessity of love. Even then, however, the delight of truth must not altogether be abandoned, lest that sweetness be removed and this necessity overwhelm us.” Thus Augustine. (See St. Thomas, 2.2, question 182, article 1.)

A notable text of Innocent III in Canon Law points in the same direction, expressed in these words (*Extra*, “On Regulars,” chapter *Licet*): “Let this rule always be observed inviolably: no one, without the permission of the Roman pontiff, may presume on any pretext to abandon the episcopate”—that is, the bishopric—“for just as the greater good is preferred to the lesser good, so the common good is preferred to the particular good.” In this case, therefore, doctrine is rightly preferred to silence, solicitude to contemplation, and labor to repose. To signify this, the only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, was not born according to the flesh from Rachel but from Leah (Genesis 29); nor is he said to have been received into his house by Mary, but by Martha (Matthew 1). So says the pontiff.]

while on one side he was delighted by the immense rewards of his labors, and on the other the desire for union and inseparable fellowship with Christ invited him even to the dissolution of the flesh, he finally cried out anxiously:

[Note: [Col. 1251D] That is: “I am driven by a divided desire in both directions, and I do not know which of the two I should prefer. On the one hand, I desire to be dissolved through death and to be with Christ, which—if I consider only my own advantage—is much better for me; but on the other hand, remaining in the flesh is necessary for your sake, that is, I consider my life and presence necessary for you, for your progress and the joy of faith.”]

“I do not know what to choose; I am hard pressed between the two. I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, for that is much better; but to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake” (Philippians 1).

## CHAPTER VI. How intensely the Apostle thirsted for the salvation of his brothers

Although he had preferred the excellence of this good in many ways even to all the fruits of his preaching, nevertheless, he subordinates contemplation to charity, without which no one can win the Lord’s favor; and for the sake of those to whom, like a nurse, he was still giving milk from the breasts of the Gospel,

[Note: [Col. 1252C] “For it is much better,” he says—that is, more pleasant and desirable for me—“to be dissolved and to be with Christ; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Philippians 1). The divine Apostle is rightly to be admired, says Theodoret, because for the sake of human salvation he preferred a life joined to many labors and dangers.]

he does not refuse separation from Christ, harmful to himself but necessary for others. For he is compelled to choose this course above all by that extraordinary virtue of devotion, through which, for the salvation of his brothers, he would have wished, if it were possible, even to incur the final evil of anathema.

[Note: [Col. 1252C] In addition to what we have written elsewhere on this saying of the Apostle (Conference 9, chapter 18), it should be noted from St. Thomas (2.2, question 182, article 2) that the contemplative life, in itself and absolutely speaking, has greater merit than the active life. Hence Gregory says in Homily 3 on Ezekiel: “The contemplative life is greater in merit than the active, because the active labors in the exercise of present work, in which it is necessary to assist one’s neighbors; but the contemplative already tastes inwardly the rest that is to come, namely, in the contemplation of God.” Nevertheless, it can happen that someone merits more through works of the active life than another through works of the contemplative life—for example, if, because of an abundance of divine love, in order that God’s will might be fulfilled and for his glory, a person sometimes endures separation from the sweetness of divine contemplation; just as the Apostle said in Romans 9: “I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers.” Explaining this, Chrysostom says in Book 1 of *On Compunction*: “The love of Christ had so completely overwhelmed his mind that even what was dearer to him than all else—to be with Christ—he would once more despise, because this was pleasing to Christ.”]

“For I could wish,” he says, “that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites” (Romans 9). That is: “I would be willing to be consigned not only to temporal punishments but also to everlasting punishments, provided that, if it were possible, all human beings might enjoy fellowship with Christ.” For I am certain that the salvation of all is more useful both to Christ and to me than my own.

## CHAPTER VII. That those who believe themselves immune from every sin are like people with bleary eyes

This supreme good, then—that is, to enjoy the sight of God and cling continually to Christ—the Apostle desires to attain perfectly by being dissolved from the body (Philippians 1), for this body, subject to decay and obstructed by many necessities of its weakness, cannot avoid being torn away from fellowship with Christ.

[Note: [Col. 1253C] St. Bernard, in Sermon 5 on the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary, enumerates three impediments to contemplation in these words: “There are three things,” he says, “that confuse the eye of the understanding and exclude it from contemplation of the true light: namely, the darkness of sins, the recollection of those sins, and concern for earthly actions.”

The prophet lamented that he was disturbed in the first way when he said: “My strength has failed me, and even the light of my eyes is not with me” (Psalm 37). For when we are deprived of the light of righteousness, we find nothing except the darkness of our sins.

He felt himself burdened in the second way when he said: “I turned in my distress, while the thorn was fixed in me” (Psalm 31), namely, the recollection of sins.

In the third way he complains of being occupied when he says: “For I ate ashes like bread” (Psalm 101), that is, the ashes of action instead of the bread of contemplation.

Whoever, therefore, wishes to direct the eye of the mind toward divine contemplation must certainly strive first to cleanse it of this threefold impediment. If anyone attempts to do so, let him know that a threefold remedy will correspond to the threefold disease. The first is cured by confession, the second by prayer, and the third by repose. Thus Bernard.

St. Thomas offers another impediment (2.2, question 180, article 2): the violence of the passions. “There are two things,” he says, “that impede the act of contemplation: the violence of passion, by which the soul’s attention is drawn away from intelligible things toward sensible things, and the external tumult of occupations.”]

For it is impossible even for a mind stretched by such frequent cares and hindered by such troublesome and varied anxieties always to enjoy the divine vision. What study of the saints could be so persistent, what purpose so arduous, that the crafty tempter could not at some time mock it? Who has pursued the seclusion of solitude so earnestly and avoided the company of all mortals so completely that he has never slipped into superfluous thoughts, or fallen away from the contemplation of God—which alone is truly good—through the sight of things or the occupation of earthly activities? Who could ever retain such fervor of spirit that he would not sometimes, carried away by slippery thoughts even during the very concentration of prayer, suddenly fall from heavenly things to earthly ones?

Who among us, to pass over the other periods of wandering, does not even at the moment when, praying to God, he raises his mind to sublime things, collapse through a kind of stupor and thereby, even unwillingly, offend in the very act through which he hoped to obtain pardon for his sins? Who, I say, is so practiced [Lipsius, in the margin: “so well exercised”] and watchful that, while singing a psalm to God, his mind is never drawn away from its meaning?

Who is so familiar with God and so closely joined to him that he can rejoice in having carried out even for a single day the apostolic command by which he orders us to pray without ceasing (1 Thessalonians 5)?

Although all this may seem light and almost unrelated to sin to certain people entangled in grosser vices, nevertheless to those who understand the good of perfection even the multitude of the smallest matters is exceedingly burdensome. Suppose, for example, that we place in a large house, cluttered with many tools, vessels, and bundles, two people entering together: one with a sound and penetrating power of sight, the other whose eyesight has been clouded by bleary vision. Would not the person whose sight was dull for seeing everything judge that there was nothing there except cupboards, beds, benches, stalls, and whatever presents itself not so much to the eyes of one examining it as to the hands of one groping? By contrast, the other, who with the clear strength of his eyes had searched out even hidden things, would declare that many minute objects were present—so many that they could scarcely be counted—and that, if gathered into a single heap, their number would equal or perhaps surpass the size of the few things the first person had touched?

[Note: [Col. 1254C] The prophets were formerly called “Seers.” 1 Samuel 9 says: “Formerly in Israel, when anyone went to consult God, he spoke thus: ‘Come, let us go to the Seer.’ For the one who is now called a prophet was formerly called a Seer.”

St. Jerome explains the reason for this name in these words (Letter 103 to Paulinus): “They were called prophets, or Seers, because they saw him whom the others did not see. Abraham saw his day and rejoiced” (John 8). “The heavens were opened to Ezekiel, while they were closed to the sinful people,” etc. (Ezekiel 1).

The Author seems to allude to this designation when he here calls holy and perfect men “Seers,” as it were by antonomasia, because they observe and scrutinize in themselves even the smallest and lightest defects, which the inexperienced and imperfect pass over without noticing.

So also St. Gregory (*On 1 Kings*, chapter 9): “A Seer is one who also looks upon inward things, which the mind of carnal people does not attend to. Hence it is said of the holy living creatures: ‘They were full of eyes all around and within’” (Ezekiel 1). “They are watchful in outward things and provident inwardly.” In contrast, the Lord rebukes the presumption of carnal teachers in the Gospel: “If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit.”]

Thus the holy—and, so to speak, “Seers”—whose pursuit is perfection, astutely detect in themselves even those things that the darkened sight of our mind does not perceive, and condemn them most sharply. Consequently, those who, as our negligence would have it, have not even stained the brightness of a pure conscience with a slight blemish of sin may nevertheless seem to themselves to be covered with many stains if not the wickedness of a vain thought has crept into the chambers of the mind, then at least the recollection of the psalm that should be recited has diverted the attention of the person praying during the time of prayer.

[Note: [Col. 1254D] St. Benedict reasons similarly concerning reverence in prayer (Chapter 20 of the Rule): “If we wish to make some request of powerful people, we do not presume to do so without humility and reverence; how much more, then, must we beseech the Lord God of all things with complete humility and devoted purity! And let us know that we are heard not through a multitude of words but through purity of heart and compunction of tears.” See Turrecremata.]

For, they say, if when we make a request of an important human being—not, I say, for our life and salvation but even for some financial advantage—we fix the whole attention of mind and body upon him and anxiously await his nod, fearing greatly lest some inept or unsuitable word should turn away the mercy of the one listening; and then, if while we are standing in the marketplace or before the tribunals of secular judges, with an adversary also standing opposite us, a cough, throat-clearing, laughter, yawning, or sleep should overtake us in the middle of our plea and conflict, with what ruinous accusation would our most vigilant enemy stir up the severity of the judge against us?

How much more, when we plead with him who knows all hidden things because of the danger of impending eternal death, especially when the cunning tempter and accuser is likewise present, must the mercy of the judge be entreated with concentrated and watchful prayer?

Nor is it unjust that the person who pours out a prayer to the Lord and suddenly departs from his sight—as though from the eyes of one who neither sees nor hears—by following the vanity of an evil thought, should be charged not only with a light sin but even with a very grave offense of impiety.

[Note: [Col. 1255B] Namely, through voluntary and deliberate wandering, concerning which the Lord sharply reproved the people of Israel through the prophet Isaiah, saying: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah 29).

On this subject St. Cyprian, in *On the Lord’s Prayer*, discusses the matter gravely and with equal appropriateness to this passage: “When we stand at prayer, dearest brothers, we ought to watch and devote ourselves to prayer with our whole heart. Every carnal and worldly thought must depart, and at that time the mind must think of nothing except the very thing for which it prays.

“For this reason the priest, after the preface preceding the prayer, prepares the minds of the brothers by saying, ‘Lift up your hearts,’ so that when the people answer, ‘We have them with the Lord,’ they may be reminded that they ought to think of nothing other than the Lord. The breast must be closed against the adversary and opened to God alone; for during prayer it must not allow God’s enemy to approach. He frequently creeps in and penetrates us, and, subtly deceiving us, draws our prayers away from God, so that we have one thing in our heart and another on our lips, when it is sincere concentration that ought to pray—not the sound of the voice but the mind and understanding.

“What indifference, then, is it to be distracted and carried away by foolish and profane thoughts while you are entreating the Lord, as though there were something else you ought to think about more than what you are saying in conversation with God? How do you ask to be heard by God when you do not hear yourself? Do you wish God to remember you when you pray, although you yourself do not remember yourself? This is not to guard against the enemy at all; this is, when you pray to God, to offend God’s majesty through negligence; this is to keep watch with the eyes while sleeping in the heart, when a Christian ought, even while sleeping with the eyes, to keep watch in the heart, as it is written in the person of the Church speaking in the Song of Songs: ‘I sleep, but my heart is awake’ (Song of Songs 5).

“Therefore the Apostle admonishes us carefully and cautiously, saying: ‘Persist in prayer, watching in it’ (Colossians 4), teaching and showing that those who ask things of God can obtain what they request when God sees them keeping watch in prayer.”

Thus St. Cyprian. On these words of the holy doctor and martyr, cited by Gratian (*On Consecration*, distinction 1, chapter *Quando*), the learned Navarrus published a sufficiently extensive and useful commentary entitled *On Prayer and the Canonical Hours*.]

[Col. 1256A] having followed the vanity of an evil thought [Lipsius, in the margin: “secure in the vanity of an evil thought”].

But those who cover the eyes of their heart with the thick veil of vices and, according to the Savior’s saying, “seeing do not see, and hearing do not hear, nor understand” (Matthew 13), scarcely contemplate even those things that are great and capital crimes in the recesses of their breast. They cannot, with cleansed eyes, observe any stealthy intrusions of thoughts, nor those slippery and hidden irritations within them that prick the mind by a fine and subtle suggestion, nor the captivities of their soul. Rather, always wandering in shameless thoughts, they do not know how to grieve when they are distracted from that contemplation which is unique, nor do they have anything over which to grieve as lost—for they open their minds at will to the thoughts that assail them and have nothing firmly established as their principal concern, nothing that they desire with their whole being.

This cause certainly plunges us into such error: because,

[Note: [Col. 1255D] Thus reads Cuychius, and St. Jerome also uses this word in the preface to Book 4 of his *Commentary on Jeremiah*, interpreting it similarly as “freedom from sin.” But Ciaconius reads ἀναμάρτητον, which is almost the same if τὸ ἀναμάρτητον is taken substantivally, as it is taken in Chapter 21, the final chapter of this Conference, where the question is whether it is possible for human nature to possess τὸ ἀναμάρτητον.

Among the Latins, if one considers the reality, “innocence” and “to be innocent,” or “to be without sin”—which is properly expressed by ἀναμάρτητον—amount to the same thing. For ἁμαρτία, or ἁμάρτημα, means “sin”; hence ἀναμάρτητος means “empty of” or “free from fault and sin.”

However, I do not approve of, nor does it fit this passage, the way Ciaconius translates ἀναμάρτητον as “impeccability.” He says that ἀναμάρτητον means “impeccability” or “impeccance,” as though impeccability and impeccance were the same: the former meaning inability to sin, and the latter meaning not sinning, or being without sin. In Latin, the better terms are “innocence,” “integrity,” or “freedom from fault.”

Everyone can see that these differ greatly, just as “being unable to sin,” or “being impeccable,” differs greatly from “being able not to sin”; and “being unable to die,” which means being absolutely immortal, differs from “being able not to die,” as Adam could in the state of innocence.

Nor do Scripture or the Fathers understand the word ἀναμάρτητον in that way. In John 8, Scripture says: Ὁ ἀναμάρτητος ὑμῶν, that is, “the one among you who is without sin,” as we have it—not “the one who is impeccable.”

St. Jerome, in his letter to Ctesiphon, rebuking the Pelagians and their supporters, says: “Let them be ashamed of their leaders and associates, who say that a person can be without sin if he wishes, which the Greeks call ἀναμάρτητον. And because the Churches throughout the East cannot tolerate this, they pretend to say ‘without sin’ but do not dare to say ἀναμάρτητον—as though ‘without sin’ meant one thing and ἀναμάρτητον another, and as though the Latin expression had not rendered the Greek phrase, which among them is composed of two words, by two words.” Thus St. Jerome interprets ἀναμάρτητον not as “impeccable” but as “not sinning,” or “free from sin and innocent,” and, as he himself says, by the two words “without sin.”

Likewise Elias of Crete, the Greek scholiast on Gregory of Nazianzus, says in Oration 3: “A human being was created ἀναμάρτητος, that is, free from sin; but ἀναμάρτητος does not mean that sin cannot fall upon him, but that sinning is not part of his nature; rather, it lies in his choice. Thus, with the help of divine grace, he can remain and advance in goodness, and likewise, with God’s permission, because of the freedom of his will, he can turn away from the good,” etc.

Moreover, it is clear that this passage is not concerned with those who boast of being impeccable, but with those who think themselves holy and perfect because they do not commit more serious—or, as he calls them, capital—crimes, while meanwhile paying no attention to lesser ones. He therefore says that they do not know the virtue of ἀναμαρτησία, or ἀναμάρτητον, that is, impeccance.

Finally, Cassian himself interprets τὸ ἀναμάρτητον in no other way than as impeccance, not impeccability, as can be seen in Chapters 20 and 21 of this Conference.

Let it therefore be granted that, by the force of the word, ἀναμάρτητος might perhaps not improperly be translated “impeccable,” that is, one who not only has not sinned but who cannot sin, as Christ the Lord can never sin. But that is not the meaning here, nor in St. Jerome, despite the false attribution made to him by the Greek Lexicon.

Enough, then, on these matters. In elucidating them, it is unfortunate that we have received no assistance from manuscripts or older printed editions, since they either omit the Greek altogether, as Dionysius the Paraphrast does, or express it so faultily and corruptly that nothing certain can be obtained from them here.]

because we entirely fail to understand the virtue of ἀναμαρτησία, that is, impeccance,

[Col. 1257A] we suppose that we can incur no guilt at all from these idle and slippery excursions of thought. Stunned by dullness and, as it were, struck blind, we contemplate nothing in ourselves except capital crimes, and believe that only those things must be avoided which are condemned even by the severity of secular laws. If we perceive ourselves to be free, even slightly, from such things, we immediately suppose that no sin is present in us.

Consequently, excluded from the number of the Seers, because we do not see the minutiae of the many impurities heaped up within us, we are not pierced by salutary compunction if an illness of sadness interrupts our understanding; nor do we grieve when struck by the subtle suggestion of vainglory; nor do we weep over a prayer uttered too slowly or too lukewarmly; nor do we reckon it as guilt if, while we are singing psalms or praying, something other than the prayer or psalm itself occurs to us.

Nor do we shudder at the fact that many things which we are ashamed to say or do before human beings we are not ashamed even briefly to conceive in our heart, although we know that they are open to the divine gaze. Nor do we cleanse the pollution of shameful dreams with a plentiful washing of tears.

Nor do we mourn that, even in the pious act of almsgiving, when we assist our brothers’ needs or distribute food to the poor, the serenity of our cheerfulness is clouded by greedy hesitation. Nor do we believe that we have suffered any loss when, abandoning the memory of God, we think about temporal and bodily things, so that Solomon’s saying applies to us:

[Note: [Col. 1257D] The Vulgate text reads: “They struck me, but I did not suffer; they dragged me, and I did not feel it” (Proverbs 23). “When shall I awake, and again find wine?” See what we noted above from the commentary of St. Jerome or Bede. St. Gregory has nearly the same in the *Pastoral Rule* (Part 3, chapter 33).]

“They struck me, but I did not suffer; they mocked me, but I knew nothing” (Proverbs 23).

## CHAPTER VIII. Very few recognize the foulness and magnitude of sins

[Col. 1258A]

On the other hand,

[Note: [Col. 1257D] When vices are at the extremes of conduct, while virtue lies in the middle, he now sets against the first extreme—which he explained in the preceding chapter, namely, that some people, confident in their holiness and perfection, neglect to avoid and correct lesser sins—a second extreme. In this second extreme, some people are excessively scrupulous and anxious, making an elephant out of a gnat: that is, they are excessively distressed and consumed with grief over the smallest and lightest defects; and if they are diverted even slightly from the taste of contemplation and spiritual sweetness, they become despondent and think themselves abandoned by God.]

those who place the whole summit of their pleasure, joy, and blessedness solely in the contemplation of divine and spiritual things, when they are unwillingly drawn away from it even slightly by violent thoughts, punish what is almost a kind of sacrilege in themselves with the present vengeance of repentance. Mourning that they have preferred the basest creature toward which the gaze of their mind has been diverted to its Creator, I might almost say that they charge themselves with the crime of impiety. And although they turn the eyes of their heart with the greatest eagerness toward the contemplation of the splendor of divine glory, nevertheless, unable to endure even the briefest darkness of carnal thoughts, they curse whatever draws the mind’s sight away from that true light.

Finally, when blessed John the Apostle wished to instill this disposition in everyone, he said: “Little children, do not love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of God is not in him, because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life; it is not from the Father but from the world. And the world passes away, and its desire; but whoever does the will of God remains forever” (1 John 2).

The saints therefore disdain all the things with which this world is occupied. Yet it is impossible that no human being even now—except our Lord and Savior—

[Note: [Col. 1258C] This exception also includes his most holy mother, the Virgin Mary, though with a great distinction between the two. Christ the Lord was impeccable by nature, as God, and by the hypostatic union, as man. Mary, however, was fortified and preserved from every sin by a special grace and singular privilege, so that she never sinned through love of any worldly thing, as was proved above (Conference 22, chapter 13).]

should have so restrained the natural wandering of the mind, always fixed in the contemplation of God, that he never sinned by being carried away by the delight of any worldly thing. Scripture says:

[Note: [Col. 1258D] The Vulgate reading is as follows (Job 25): “Behold, even the moon does not shine, and the stars are not clean in his sight; how much less man, who is rottenness, and the son of man, who is a worm!” “In his sight” means “in comparison with him,” says Augustine (in his notes on Job).]

“The stars themselves are not clean in his sight” (Job 25). And again:

[Note: [Col. 1258D] So read the Greek interpreters: Εἰ κατὰ ἁγίων οὐ πιστεύει, οὐρανὸς δέ οὐ καθαρὸς ἐναντίον αὐτοῦ, “If he does not trust in his saints, and heaven is not pure before him.”

St. Augustine likewise has: “If there is no faith in his saints,” or, as others read, “if there is no one faithful,” “and heaven is not clean before him.”
