The Vulgate edition, which the Author here also admits to be more accurate, reads: “Behold, among his saints no one is immutable, and the heavens are not clean in his sight,” etc.

A similar statement occurs in Job 4: “Can a human being be justified in comparison with God, or can a man be purer than his Maker? Behold, those who serve him are not steadfast, and in his angels he finds perversity.”

The Greek reads: “If he does not trust his servants, and against his angels he has devised something crooked.” St. Jerome reads instead: “And against his angels he has devised something perverse.” Augustine has: “If he does not trust his servants, and finds something perverse against his angels.”

It seems that this abbot has confused the two passages and fused one statement out of the two.]

“If he does not trust in his saints, and finds perversity in his angels”—or, as the more accurate translation has it: “Behold, among his saints no one is immutable, and the heavens are not clean in his sight” (Job 15).

## CHAPTER IX. To depart from God is a harmful and present destruction

Rightly, then, the saints, who retain the memory of God steadfastly and are borne along in suspended motion as though walking on lines stretched high above,

[Note: [Col. 1259C] Σχοινοβάτης, in Latin *funambulus*, is one who runs or walks for sport along stretched ropes—which he here calls “lines stretched high above”—like a tightrope walker. It is formed from σχοῖνος, “rope,” and βαίνω, “I walk.”

Among the Romans, Messala Corvinus was the first to use *funambulus* for the person whom the Greeks call σχοινοβάτης, as Ciaconius notes. Juvenal, in Satire 3, writes the following about Nero and his performances:]

Augur, tightrope walker, physician, magician—he knows everything. Caelius, in his eighth book of letters to Cicero, said *schoenobaticam facere*, that is, to practice that art. Pliny, in Book VIII of his *Natural History*, speaks of elephants that were tightrope walkers [Col. 1259D], and there is also a very amusing letter by Lipsius concerning them, which I remember reading many years ago.] I would compare them to tightrope walkers, commonly called *funambuli*, who, placing the whole safety of their lives upon the extremely narrow path of that rope, have no doubt that they will immediately suffer a terrible death if their foot should deviate even slightly through stumbling, or if they should go beyond the limits of that life-preserving straight course.

While, by a marvelous art, they attempt to make their aerial steps across empty space [Col. 1259B], if they do not preserve that narrow path for their feet with careful and vigilant control, the earth—which for everyone is, as it were, the natural base and the firmest and most solid foundation—becomes for them an immediate and evident cause of destruction: not because its nature changes, but because they plunge upon it under the precipitous weight of their flesh.

So too, that tireless goodness of God and His immutable substance injures no one in itself; but when we turn away from what is highest and strive toward what is lowest, we bring death upon ourselves. Indeed, the very turning away becomes death to the one who turns away. “Woe to them,” He says, “for they have departed from me. They shall be laid waste, because they have transgressed against me” (Hosea VII). And again: “Woe to them when I depart from them” (Hosea IX). “Your wickedness shall rebuke you, and your apostasy shall reprove you. Know and see that it is evil and bitter for you to have abandoned the Lord your God” (Jeremiah II).

> **Note [Col. 1259D].** “His own iniquities ensnare the wicked man, and he is bound by the cords of his sins,” says the Vulgate version (Proverbs V). Saint Jerome, commenting on Ezekiel IV, on the words “Behold, I have surrounded you with bonds,” says: “Some are the Lord’s bonds, by which we are bound for salvation; others are the devil’s, by which he had bound the woman in the Gospel for eighteen years; hence each person is bound by the cords of his sins.” The Lord loosens these bonds in the figure of the resurrected Lazarus, who had lain bound in the tomb with bandages and strips of cloth (Luke XIII). See the same author on Isaiah V.

For each person is bound by the cords of his own sins (Proverbs V). To such people this rebuke is appropriately directed by the Lord:

> **[Col. 1260A]** “Behold,” He says, “all you who kindle a fire, who gird yourselves with flames: walk in the light of your fire and in the flames that you have kindled” (Isaiah L).

And again:

> **Note [Col. 1260C].** Thus according to the Greek text of the Septuagint. The Vulgate, however, has: “He who speaks lies shall not escape” (Proverbs XIX).

> “He who kindles wickedness,” He says, “shall perish by it” (Proverbs V).

## CHAPTER X. That those who strive toward perfection are humbled in truth and always recognize that they need God’s grace

> **Note [Col. 1260C].** Ciaconius noted this briefly; it seemed worthwhile to state it somewhat more explicitly. The four succeeding chapters—including this one—through the end of the thirteenth chapter occur, in exactly the same words and in a continuous passage, under Saint Augustine’s name among his sermons for the liturgical year, Sermon 47. Either Augustine borrowed from Cassian, or—as I think more likely—Cassian borrowed from Augustine, or someone inserted this passage here or there from the works of one of them. I leave it to others to judge which explanation is most probable. Certainly Cassian was Augustine’s contemporary or lived near his time, as is clear both from Saint Prosper’s book against the *Collator* and from his other writings addressed to Augustine, as well as from the chronology and sequence of events.]

Since the saints therefore perceive each day that they are heavily burdened by the weight of earthly thought, falling from that sublimity of mind and being involuntarily—or rather, even without knowing it—brought under the law of sin and death, and, to pass over everything else, being drawn away from the presence of God even by those good and just, yet earthly, works that I mentioned above, they certainly have reasons to sigh continually toward God. They have reasons, being humbled and contrite in truth,

> **Note [Col. 1260D].** How holy and perfect men declare themselves sinners—not merely in words but also in feeling, that is, sincerely, from the heart, and without pretense—and indeed declare themselves very grave sinners, as Saint Francis was accustomed to say of himself, is explained in Book XII of the *Institutes*, chapter 15.

to pronounce themselves sinners not merely in words but in feeling, and, continually asking forgiveness truthfully for everything into which they daily fall when overcome by the weakness of the flesh, to pour out genuine tears of repentance without ceasing. For they see that they remain enveloped, even to the very end of their lives, in the same struggles by which they are continually afflicted with sorrow, and that they cannot offer even their prayers without anxious thoughts.

Having therefore experienced that, because of the burden of the flesh, they cannot attain the desired end by human strength, nor be joined, according to the desire of their heart, to that supreme and highest good, but are carried away captive from its contemplation toward worldly things, they hasten to the grace of God, who justifies the ungodly, and proclaim with the Apostle:

> **[Col. 1260B]** “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans VII).

For they feel that they cannot accomplish the good that they desire, but that they continually encounter the evil that they do not desire and hate—that is, the movements of their thoughts and concern for bodily matters.

## CHAPTER XI. Explanation of the statement: “For I delight in the law of God according to the inner man,” and so forth

And

> **Note [Col. 1261A].** Following the Apostle’s example and imitation, who speaks of himself and of those like him, the just and holy, in this way: “For I delight in the law of God according to the inner man; but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin that is in my members” (Romans VII). Here it must be noted that the Apostle distinguishes four laws: the law of God and the corresponding law of the mind, both of which draw a person toward good; and, in addition, the law of sin and the law of our flesh, or members, which proceeds from it and is mutually connected with it, dragging us toward evil. The first two pertain to the higher part of the human being, or to the inner man; the latter two to the outer part of the human being, or to the senses and the flesh. The law of God and the law of the mind have great affinity and agreement with one another, for through the law of the mind a person is subjected to the law of God. Likewise, there is great agreement between the latter two, for through the law of the flesh or of the members—which is otherwise called flesh, concupiscence, sensuality, or the tinder of sin—a person is subjected to the law of sin. See Jerome, *Questions to Algasi[a],* question 8; Damascene, Book IV of *The Orthodox Faith*, chapter 23; and Augustine, Sermon 5 on the Words of the Apostle.

> **[Col. 1261C]** Moreover, the law of sin is opposed to the law of God, just as the law of the flesh or of the members is opposed to the law of the mind. Although the law of God coincides with the law of the mind, just as the law of the members coincides with the law of sin, there is nevertheless some distinction between them: they differ as cause and effect. The law of God is God’s own ordinance, commanding good and prohibiting evil. The law of the mind is a certain impression of God and a participation in the eternal law implanted in the human mind, as though written on the fleshly tablets of the heart, as the Apostle says (II Corinthians III); it is also called our conscience and *synderesis*. “The suggestion of the evil one,” says Damascene—that is, the law of sin—“coming upon the members of the flesh, itself introduces this into us.” For, once we had voluntarily transgressed God’s law and admitted the evil one’s suggestion, we gave him entry and handed ourselves over to sin; hence our body is readily led toward it. Thus the odor and sensation of sin are said to adhere to our body—that is, bodily concupiscence and pleasure—as a law in the members of our flesh.

> Therefore the law of the mind, that is, conscience, delights in the law of God, that is, in the commandment, which it desires. But the law of sin, that is, the devil’s suggestion, through the law that is in the members—that is, through the concupiscence, inclination, and movement of the flesh—and through the irrational part of the soul, wages war against the law of my mind, that is, against my conscience. Thus Damascene.

> Concupiscence is called a law for two reasons, according to Saint Thomas in his commentary on this passage. First, because of similar effects: just as the law leads one to do good, so the tinder of sin leads one to sin. Second, by comparison with its cause. Since the tinder of sin is a certain punishment for sin, it has a twofold cause. One is sin itself, which has acquired dominion over the sinner and imposed a law upon him, just as a master imposed a law upon a conquered servant. The other cause of the tinder is God, who imposed this punishment upon the sinful person so that his lower powers would not obey his reason. See Saint Augustine, Book XIV of *The City of God*, chapter 15 and following.

> **[Col. 1262A]** Accordingly, the very disobedience of the lower powers, which is called the tinder of sin, is called a law insofar as it was introduced by the law of divine justice, like the sentence of a just Judge, which has the force of law, according to I Kings XXX: “And this became an ordinance from that day onward, and a statute, and as a law in Israel to this day.”

> **[Col. 1262B]** Although in reality the law of the flesh and the law of sin are the same, and both exist in the flesh and in the members, the Apostle speaks as though they were different, because of the different reasons for the two designations, when he says: “I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin that is in my members” (Romans VII). Concupiscence is called the law of sin because it proceeds from sin and leads to sin, as was said elsewhere (*Conference* IV); and just as the law of the mind is the rule of right conduct, so concupiscence is the rule of sinning.

> It is called the law of the flesh or of the members because it exists in the flesh or the members, that is, in the sensory appetite. In its origin, Saint Thomas says, it is located in the flesh, but it is diffused throughout all the members; therefore the Apostle says, “in my members.” Hence the same Apostle says in Romans VI: “Just as you presented your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity for iniquity,” and so forth.

> This law has two effects in a human being. First, it resists reason; with regard to this he says, “warring against the law of my mind,” that is, against the law of Moses, which is called the law of the mind insofar as it agrees with the mind, that is, with reason; or against the natural law, which is called the law of the mind because it is naturally implanted in the mind, according to Romans II: “They show the work of the law written in their hearts.” Of this opposition it is said in Galatians V: “The flesh desires against the spirit.”

> The second effect is that it reduces a person to slavery. Hence the Apostle adds: “And making me captive” (or “leading me captive,” according to another reading) “to the law of sin that is in my members,” that is, in myself. The law of sin makes a person captive in two ways: first, by consent and action, it makes the sinner captive; second, in one who is under grace, it does so with respect to the movement of concupiscence. Of this captivity it is said in the Psalm: “When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion.” Thus Saint Thomas in his commentary on Psalm CXXV.]

they do indeed delight in the law of God according to the inner man, who, transcending all visible things, strives always to be united with God alone. But they see another law in their members (Romans VII), that is, implanted in the nature of the human condition, which wars against the law of their mind and drags their senses captive under the violent law of sin, compelling them, after abandoning that principal good, to submit to earthly thought.

Although this may appear necessary and useful to the body when it is undertaken as part of the orderly fulfillment of some religious necessity, nevertheless, when compared with that good whose contemplation delights all the saints, it is judged by them to be evil and to be avoided, because through it they are in some way—even if only for a short time—withdrawn from the joy of that perfect blessedness.

For truly it is the law of sin that the transgression of its author introduced into the human race, through the guilt of the one against whom the sentence of the most just Judge was pronounced:

> **Note [Col. 1262D].** Saint Jerome gives this interpretation in his *Hebrew Questions*, and the Septuagint translators rendered it in the same way. Jerome interprets “works” not as the cultivation of the soil but as sins; for, he says, that is how it appears in the Hebrew, and Aquila does not differ, saying: “Cursed is the ground because of you.” The Vulgate version has: “Cursed is the earth in your work; in labors you shall eat from it all the days of your life; it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Genesis III). Saint Jerome also follows this version in chapter III of his commentary on Zechariah.

> Here the words receive both a tropological and an allegorical interpretation. The tropological meaning lies in the thorns and thistles of evil thoughts sprouting from the cursed earth, that is, from our corrupted nature, and likewise in the sweat of the face, that is, in labor and the mind’s attentive exertion, as explained below. The allegory lies in the bread, which he interprets as heavenly and spiritual bread. For in the following chapter he reasons as though the words “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” must be understood not of ordinary bread but of heavenly bread: “For,” he says, “the rich, as we see, eat that ordinary bread without any sweat of their face.” Yet this argument has more subtlety than solidity. Those words do not refer to every individual human being, but to many, and especially to Adam himself, or to the human race collectively.]

> **[Col. 1263A]** “Cursed is the earth in your works; it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you, and in the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Genesis III).

This, I say, is the law implanted in all mortal members, which wars against the law of our mind and keeps it from the divine contemplation. The cursed earth in our works, after the knowledge of good and evil, began to produce thorns and thistles of thought; their prickles choke the native seeds of the virtues, so that we cannot eat without the sweat of our face the bread that came down from heaven and strengthens the human heart.

> **Note [Col. 1263B].** It is unclear whether he means sacramental and Eucharistic bread here, that is, the body of Christ in the sacrament, of which he himself says: “For the bread of God is that which comes down from heaven and gives life to the world” (John VI). The worthy and frequent reception and communion of this bread are discussed both in this and in the preceding conference (*Conference* 22, chapter 7, and below, chapter 21); or does he mean spiritual bread, that is, sacred doctrine, which is food for the soul, concerning whose continual meditation and remembrance—which constitute a certain spiritual eating and refreshment—this conference speaks repeatedly?

> Both kinds of bread are discussed in that discourse in John VI, according to Augustine’s interpretation (Book III of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 16), and the statement “Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which endures unto eternal life” (John VI) is properly understood of the same bread. Both are also heavenly bread, and both must be received in the sweat of the face, that is, with attentive concentration of heart, as the Author explains.

> The sacramental bread was prefigured in the paschal lamb, which was commanded to be eaten with wild lettuce (Exodus XII). Wild lettuce, Saint Gregory says, is exceedingly bitter (Homily 22 on the Gospels). The flesh of the lamb must therefore be eaten with wild lettuce, so that when we receive the body of the Redeemer, we may afflict ourselves with tears for our sins, so that the bitterness of repentance may wipe away from the stomach of the mind the corrupt moisture of life. Thus Gregory speaks of sacramental bread.

> The bread of sacred doctrine and the understanding of heavenly mysteries, however, are received only with great labor, study, and difficulty. Saint Augustine also interprets the Lord’s statement in this sense when commenting on Psalm LXXVII: “Everything,” he says, “has been so covered and closed that even if, with His help, we can reach something from which we may be healthfully nourished, nevertheless we eat our bread in the sweat of our face and pay the penalty of the ancient sentence through the labor not only of the body but also of the heart.”]

## CHAPTER XII. Explanation of the statement: “But we know that the law is spiritual,” and what follows

> **Note [Col. 1263D].** This law commands us to eat, in the sweat of our face—that is, with the attentive concentration of our heart—that true bread, whether sacramental or spiritual, which came down from heaven. Here he takes “law” to mean that sentence of divine condemnation spoken to Adam and his descendants: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread,” which, he says, is called spiritual by the Apostle. By this interpretation, which is scarcely suitable or plausible, he confuses the Apostle’s words with the words of Genesis, adapting both to his own meaning and purpose.

> **[Col. 1264A]** For the Apostle is not speaking of that divine sentence, much less of the law of sin and of the members, when he says: “We know that the law is spiritual” (Romans VII), but specifically of the law of God and of the commandment of the Decalogue, “You shall not covet”; or of the law of the mind, which agrees and corresponds with the divine law, as stated above.]

Therefore the entire human race is universally subjected to this law, without exception. For no one, however holy, receives the bread mentioned above without the sweat of his face and the attentive concentration of his heart. But many rich people, as we see, eat this ordinary bread without any sweat of their face.

The blessed Apostle also asserts that this law is spiritual, saying: “We know that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal, sold under sin” (Romans VII). Spiritual indeed is this law, which commands us to eat in the sweat of our face that true bread which came down from heaven; but that sale under sin made us carnal.

> **Note [Col. 1264B].** The Apostle speaks of this in the person of the human race fallen in Adam: “But I am carnal, sold under sin,” that is, reduced under the tyranny of sin; I am its slave, like a purchased servant of sin, because “whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John VIII).

> Or, if it is referred to the person of the Apostle himself and of the just, as it was said above that it may be so referred: “I am carnal,” that is, according to the nature corrupted in Adam, inclined to desire the things of the flesh. “Sold under sin,” that is, sold by Adam, through the sweetness of temporal pleasure as the price, into the slavery and yoke of sin—that is, of concupiscence—which, even against my will, causes sinful and vicious movements to boil up within me.

> For the Apostle does not call himself carnal because he walks according to the flesh, since he expressly denies that shortly afterward, but because he is not wholly spiritual, as he will be after the resurrection and as he desired to be. Saint Augustine explains this beautifully in these words (Sermon 5 on the Words of the Apostle):

> **[Col. 1264C]** “The Apostle is carnal, although he said to others, ‘You who are spiritual, instruct such a one in the spirit of gentleness’ (Galatians VI). He addresses others as spiritual, while he himself is carnal?”

> And below he answers:

> “Although not according to the mind, certainly according to the flesh. He is spiritual because he lives according to the spirit; yet, as long as he remains partly in mortal flesh, the same person is both spiritual and carnal. Behold the spiritual person: ‘With my mind I serve the law of God.’ Behold the carnal person: ‘With the flesh I serve the law of sin.’ Is the same person therefore both spiritual and carnal? Precisely so, for as long as he lives here, that is his condition.

> “Do not be surprised, whoever you are, whoever yields and consents to carnal desires—whether you think them good because they satisfy the fullness of lust, or whether you already see them to be evil but nevertheless yield to them, consent to them, follow where they lead, and carry out what they wickedly suggest. You are wholly carnal; whoever you are who is such, you are wholly carnal.

> “But if you desire what the law forbids when it says, ‘You shall not covet,’ and nevertheless keep another commandment that the law likewise gives, ‘Do not follow your desires’ (Ecclesiasticus XVIII), then in mind you are spiritual, in flesh carnal. For it is one thing not to covet, and another not to follow one’s desires. Not to covet at all belongs to the perfect; not to follow one’s desires belongs to one who is fighting, struggling, and laboring. When will victory come? When death is swallowed up in victory (I Corinthians XV). Then there will be the voice of one who triumphs, not the sweat of one who fights.

> “When will that voice of the triumphant be heard? When this corruptible nature has put on incorruption and this mortal nature has put on immortality.”

> These and other statements of Saint Augustine concern the same subject.]

That sale under sin, then, made us carnal. Whose was this, and whose sin was it? Without doubt, Adam’s, by whose transgression and, so to speak, ruinous bargain and fraudulent exchange we were sold.

He, deceived by the serpent’s persuasion, consigned all his offspring, sold off through the taking of the forbidden food, to the yoke of perpetual slavery. For it is customary between buyer and seller that one who wishes to surrender himself to another’s ownership receives some price from his buyer in exchange for the loss of his own freedom and his permanent enslavement.

We see this completed most clearly between Adam and the serpent. Adam, receiving from the serpent the price of his freedom in the eating of the forbidden tree, departed from his natural liberty and preferred to surrender himself perpetually into the service of the one from whom he had obtained the deadly price of the forbidden fruit. Bound thereafter by this condition, he not unjustly subjected all the offspring of his posterity to perpetual servitude under the very one whose slave he had become. For what else can a slave marriage produce but slaves?

What then? Did this crafty and cunning buyer seize from the true and legitimate Lord the right of dominion? Not so. For the true Lord did not so lose the power of His dominion over all God’s own possession through the deceit of a single fraud; rather, He restrains even that buyer,

> **Note [Col. 1265B].** By God’s “possession” he means the human being created in God’s image and assigned and reserved, as it were, for God’s particular lot and treasure. Saint Thomas will illuminate this passage (*Summa Theologiae* III, question 48, article 4) through an argument he proposes and its solution, so that it may be understood to what extent the human being was handed over to the devil and in a certain sense sold to him, and through Christ’s passion redeemed and liberated from the devil’s right and dominion.

> “No one buys or redeems what has not ceased to be his own; but human beings never ceased to be God’s, according to Psalm XXIII: ‘The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it.’ Therefore it seems that Christ did not redeem us through His passion.”

> He answers: “A human being is said to be God’s in two ways. In one way, insofar as he is subject to God’s power; and in this way a human being never ceased to be God’s, according to Daniel IV: ‘The Most High rules in the kingdom of human beings and gives it to whomever He wishes.’ In another way, through the union of charity with Him, according to Romans VIII: ‘If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Him.’

> “In the first way, therefore, a human being never ceased to be God’s; in the second way, he ceased to be God’s through sin. Thus, insofar as he was freed from sin when Christ, by suffering, made satisfaction, he is said to have been redeemed through Christ’s passion.

> “If you object further that no redemption was necessary, since the devil had deceived the human being by fraud and therefore possessed him unjustly, so that the human being ought not to have been redeemed by a price but seized by force—for no one ought to benefit from his own fraud or deceit—Saint Thomas replies that although, insofar as it depended on him, the devil unjustly held under slavery the human being whom he had deceived by fraud, it was nevertheless just for the human being to suffer this: God permitted it with respect to guilt and ordained it with respect to punishment. Therefore, on God’s part, justice required that the human being be redeemed, though not on the devil’s part.”

> Saint Bernard argues in the same sense against Peter Abelard (*Letter* 190):

> **[Col. 1265D]** “Let them learn that the devil had not merely power over human beings but also a just claim, so that consequently they may see that the Son of God came in the flesh to liberate human beings. Yet although we call the devil’s power just, we do not call his will just. Hence it was not the devil, who invaded; not the human being, who deserved it; but the just Lord, who exposed him. For no one is called just or unjust on account of power, but on account of will.

> “This, then, was a certain right of the devil over the human being—not acquired lawfully but wickedly usurped, yet justly permitted. Thus the human being was held captive justly, although that justice existed neither in the human being nor in the devil, but in God.”

> Thus Bernard.]

although he was an apostate and rebel,

> **Note [Col. 1265D].** That is, the devil. He used *refuga* for *transfuga*, meaning an apostate, as Tertullian often does (*Against Marcion* I and II, chapter 10), and Prudentius in *On the Crown*, as Ulpian does in the law “Aut Dominum,” concerning punishments: “Those who desert from the mines are condemned from one mine to another.” The form *refugum* is nevertheless found in that sermon of Saint Augustine mentioned above.

Thus the human being is said to have been sold not by another but by himself, and not to anyone other than the devil, as buyer—but a faithless and fraudulent buyer.]

yet restrained him under the yoke of slavery. But because the Creator had granted all rational creatures freedom of choice, He ought not to force back into their innate freedom those who had sold themselves unlawfully through transgression born of ravenous desire.

For whatever is contrary to goodness and equity is repugnant to the Author of justice and mercy. It would have been evil if He had withdrawn the gift of the freedom He had granted; unjust if, by His power, He had oppressed and taken captive a free human being and had not allowed him to exercise the privilege of the freedom he had received,

> **Note [Col. 1266B].** Cuychius reads this way on the basis of manuscripts on which he placed great reliance. Augustine has in that sermon: “He would not have allowed him to exercise the privilege of the freedom he had received.” Ciaconius, however, has: “He would not have allowed him to exercise the *pontificium* of the freedom he had received.”

> On this occasion he noted the following concerning *pontificium*: *Pontificium* is frequently used for “power” in the imperial constitutions, as in the Theodosian Code, Book XV, title “On the Catholic Faith,” chapter 3: “Nor should the power and authority to obtain the churches thereafter be granted to them,” and in the same book, title “On Heretics,” chapter 13: “Therefore all who have claimed either the power or the office of these professions.”

> Aulus Gellius, Book I, chapter 13, likewise has: “For there are not a few who, once they have fixed their opinion on one side, and once a matter has been settled and decided by the person whose business and authority it was, have by no means thought that anything should be done contrary to his command.”

> Arnobius, too, in Book II *Against the Pagans*, reads as follows in the *Vatican Codex*: “For just as particular gods have particular guardianships, permissions, and powers among you, and you do not ask any one of them for what is not within his power and permission, so it belongs to Christ alone, by His *pontificium*, to give souls salvation and confer upon them the spirit of immortality.”

> The other Arnobius, in his exposition of Psalm LXXIII, speaking of those who sat at the gate, says: “At the gates, therefore, they receive the *pontificium* of judging and rebuking.”

> Thus also the Church sings of Saint Peter: “O God, who, by giving the keys of the heavenly kingdom to Your blessed apostle Peter, entrusted to him the *pontificium* of binding and loosing souls,” and so forth.

> To Ciaconius’s notes I would add the following excerpts from Baronius (*Martyrology*, April 9):

> **[Col. 1266D]** “*Pontificium* means a certain right and power to do something. That this is the proper meaning of the word can easily be demonstrated from numerous monuments of ancient writings, such as Book I, *On Maternal Property*, of the Theodosian Code, where these words are found: ‘Let them remain under the power and dominion of their parents, so that they may have the *pontificium* of enjoyment, while permission to alienate is denied them.’

> “Likewise, in Book I, chapter ‘What Things May Not Be Exported,’ Coelius Rhodiginus, according to the ancient reading, has: ‘No one shall have the *pontificium* of transferring wine, oil, and fish sauce to foreign lands.’

> “Pope Gelasius writes to the bishops of Dardania: ‘It is sufficiently clear that Acacius had no *pontificium* for dissolving the judgment of the Apostolic See without its knowledge.’

> “Juretus collects many other passages, both from the letters of Symmachus and from various rescripts of emperors, in his notes on Symmachus’s twenty-seventh letter in Book VII.

> “All these usages agree, then, in showing that *pontifex* was derived from the ability to act, and *pontificium* from the right itself, that is, the power to act. Both words subsequently passed, with their proper meaning, into the usage of the Christian religion, so that bishops came to be called *pontifices*, and the divinely granted right itself came to be called *pontificium*.”]

of the freedom he had received, whose salvation He then reserved for future ages, so that the fullness of the appointed time might be completed in due order.

For it was necessary that his offspring should remain under this condition for as long as it took for the grace of the former Lord to restore them, once freed from their original bonds, to their ancient state of liberty by the price of His blood. Though He could have saved them even then by an impulse of mercy, He did not wish to do so, because justice did not permit Him to violate the sanction of His decree.

> **Note [Col. 1267C].** That is, the decree by which God had determined from eternity to free the human being through the way of justice and satisfaction, not through the way of power alone or mercy alone. Once this decree is presupposed, the following scriptural statements are understood: “It was necessary that Christ should suffer and thus enter into His glory” (Luke XXIV); “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone” (John XII); “If this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, let Your will be done” (Matthew XXVI). The Apostle Peter likewise says (Acts II) that Christ was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and so forth.

> “But apart from this decree, by the same power with which God created the human being just and free, He could have restored him immediately, by a mere act of His will, when he had fallen and become disfigured, driving his enemy the devil far away. Since He was supreme Lord and bound by no laws of a superior, He could have set aside the rigor of justice and embraced a plan based solely on His mercy—especially in abolishing those sins that had been committed against His own majesty, since everyone has it in his power to forgive sins directed specifically against himself. On this matter see Saint Thomas, Part III, question 46, article 6.

> “But once that decree by which He willed justice to be satisfied had been fixed, one of two things was necessary: either the guilty human being had to be condemned, or an equivalent price or punishment had to be paid for his liberation. > “The equity of God therefore did not permit the sanction of this divine decree to be violated. That is, the decree of justice concerning the punishment to be undergone for sin could not be annulled. Yet God could have made a decree based not on justice but on mercy. Nor did He consider justice alone in the work of human redemption; rather, He wonderfully reconciled both justice and mercy.

> “Justice was present because He did not leave sin unpunished; mercy was present because the Judge Himself transferred the punishment of sin from the guilty person to Himself. > “He imposed the punishment through justice, but changed the person through mercy. Justice said: ‘I require punishment for sin.’ Mercy said: ‘I do not reject punishment, but I change the person and take the punishment upon myself.’

> “Thus it came to pass that in the work of human redemption and reconciliation, mercy and truth—or, what is the same thing, justice and peace—which at first glance may appear opposed, since one forgives while the other punishes, were wonderfully reconciled and acted together, meeting one another in a certain sense and greeting one another, as it were, with mutual kisses.

> **[Col. 1268D]** “Saint Bernard discusses this matter most beautifully in Sermon 1 on the Annunciation. See the passage.”]

For justice did not permit Him to violate the sanction of His decree.

Do you wish to know the cause of your sale? Hear your Redeemer Himself proclaiming most clearly through the prophet Isaiah:

> “Who is this bill of divorce of your mother with which I dismissed her? Or who is my creditor, to whom I sold you? Behold, you were sold because of your iniquities, and in your crimes I dismissed your mother” (Isaiah L).

Do you also wish to recognize clearly why He did not wish to redeem you, who had been subjected to the yoke of slavery, by the power of His might? Hear what He added to the preceding words, in which He reproaches these same servants of sin for the cause of their voluntary sale:

## CHAPTER XIII. Explanation of the statement: “I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh”

Therefore, since that first curse of God made us carnal and condemned us to thorns and thistles, and since our Father sold us under such an unjust bargain that we cannot do the good we wish to do—for, torn away from the memory of the supreme God, we are compelled to think about the things belonging to human frailty; and while we burn with love of purity, we are often, even against our will, pierced by natural impulses which we would most deeply wish to ignore—[Note: [Col. 1268D] “I know,” says the Apostle, “that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh” (Rom. 7). Here he uses “flesh” not for one part of the human being, which we usually call the body or flesh and which is distinguished from the soul, but for the carnal soul, or for the whole human being insofar as he is carnal—that is, insofar as he has been propagated from Adam and sprinkled with the contagion of sin. The sentence is similar to that in Genesis: “The sense and thought of the human heart are inclined toward evil” (Gen. 8).] we know that good does not dwell in our flesh (Rom. 7)—that is, the perpetual and uninterrupted tranquility of the contemplation and purity of which we have spoken.

[Col. 1268B] But this most grievous and disastrous separation has taken place within us: although we wish to serve the law of God with the mind, and certainly never wish to turn our gaze away from the divine brightness, yet, surrounded by carnal darkness, we are compelled by a certain law of sin to be dragged away from what we know to be good—namely, toward earthly cares and thoughts—falling from that height of mind to which the law of sin, that is, that sentence of God, not unjustly condemned us, the sentence which the first sinner incurred. Hence the blessed Apostle, while he most openly confesses that he, or all the saints, are constrained by the unavoidable necessity of this sin, nevertheless boldly declares that none of them is thereby condemned, saying: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death” (Rom. 6)—that is, by daily grace Christ frees all his saints from this law of sin and death, into which they are continually compelled to fall, even against their will, when they beseech the Lord [Note: [Col. 1269B] Ciaconius has corrected this, since previously it read: “When he asks the Lord to absolve him from the remission of his debts” [sic]. See the note at the end of chapter 10. Moreover, the discourse attributed to Saint Augustine extends this far, comprising the four chapters already traversed.] to remit their debts.

[Note: [Col. 1269B] He therefore supplies the following syllogism, which can be formulated thus: It has been proved above that the Apostle is speaking in his own person and in the person of those like him; but such persons are not sinners or unjust and impious people; therefore the Apostle did not speak in the person of sinners, as Germanus maintained, but in the person of the just. Saint Augustine shows that this interpretation pleased him more in *Against Julian*, chapter 11, although he had previously held a different view, as stated above: “But as for your assertion,” he says, “that I understand the Apostle’s words—when he says, ‘I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh,’ and the rest up to the point where he says, ‘Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?’—in a way different from how the entire passage ought to be understood, you attribute too much to me without knowing it. For I was neither the only one nor the first to understand this passage in the manner in which your heresy is overthrown, as it ought truly to be understood. Indeed, I had earlier understood it differently, as certain writings of mine from that period also testify. For it did not seem to me that the Apostle could be saying of himself, ‘I am carnal,’ when he was spiritual, or that he was being led captive under the law of sin which was in his members. But afterward I yielded to better and more discerning interpreters—or rather, as must be confessed, to the truth itself—so that I might see in those words of the Apostle the groaning of the saints who struggle against carnal desires. Although they are spiritual in mind, they are still rightly understood to be carnal in this corruptible body, which weighs down the soul; they will be spiritual in body when the animal body has been sown and the spiritual body rises again (1 Cor. 15). They are also rightly understood to be captive in that part which is subject to the movements of desires to which they do not consent. Thus it came about that I understood these things as Hilary, Gregory, Ambrose, and the other holy and renowned teachers of the Church understood them: they believed that the Apostle himself had vigorously fought against the carnal desires which he did not wish to have and yet did have, and that he had borne witness in these words to that very struggle of his.” This is Augustine’s statement; nothing more suitable or more fitting could have been brought forward for clarifying this passage and the whole discussion.] You see, therefore, that the blessed Apostle uttered this sentence not in the person of sinners, but in the person of those who are truly holy and perfect, [Note: [Col. 1270B] Here Saint Augustine must again be heard (*Sermon 5 on the Words of the Apostle*), since the whole discussion of this Conference turns on this statement of the Apostle. He speaks thus in the person of the Apostle: “Now, while the conflict with death is raging, I do not do what I will: in part spiritual, in part carnal; spiritual in the better part, carnal in the lower part. I am still fighting; I have not yet conquered. It is a great thing for me not to be conquered. I do not do what I will, but what I hate, that I do. What do you do? I desire. Although I do not consent to desire, although I do not follow my desires, nevertheless I still desire; and assuredly I myself am even in that very part. For I am not one person in the mind and another in the flesh. But what, then, am I myself? For I am in the mind and I am in the flesh. There are not two contrary natures, but from both there is one human being, because there is one God by whom the human being was made. Therefore I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but the law of sin with my flesh: with my mind I do not consent to the law of sin, yet I would not have any law of sin in my members. Therefore, because I would not have it and yet it is there, I do not do what I will, because I desire and do not will; I do not do what I will, but what I hate, that I do. What do I hate? Desiring. I hate to desire, and yet I do it in the flesh, not in the mind. What I hate, that I do. But if I do what I do not will, I consent to the law, because it is good. You would consent to the law if you did what you willed; if you do what the law hates, how do you consent to the law? Certainly, if I do what I do not will, I consent to the law, because it is good. How? What does the law command? ‘You shall not desire.’ What do I will? Not to desire. In willing what the law wills, I consent to the law, because it is good. If the law said, ‘You shall not desire,’ and I wished to desire, I would not consent to the law and would be wholly opposed to it by that perversity of will. What now? What do you say, O law? ‘You shall not desire.’ And I do not wish to desire; thus I do not will what you do not will. Therefore I consent, because I do not will what you do not will. My weakness does not fulfill the law, but my will praises the law.” Thus far Saint Augustine, elegantly and acutely, in the person of the Apostle and of similar just persons struggling in this life against the movements of the flesh, as has been said.] “For I do not do the good that I wish, but I do the evil that I hate” (Rom. 7). And: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XIV. Objection that the Apostle’s statement, “For I do not do the good that I wish,” seems applicable neither to unbelievers nor to the saints

[Col. 1269B]

Germanus: We say that this cannot properly apply either to those who are entangled in capital crimes, or to the Apostle and those who have advanced to his measure; rather, we judge that it must be understood specifically of those who, after receiving the grace of God and recognizing the truth, wish to abstain from carnal vices but are dragged back toward their accustomed desire for the passions by an ancient habit, which dominates their members with the force of a natural law. For the practice and frequency of sinning become, as it were, a natural law which, implanted in the members of human weakness, seizes and carries captive toward vices those whose soul has not yet been fully trained by the pursuit of the virtues, but whose chastity is still, so to speak, raw and tender. Subjecting them to death under the ancient law, it delivers them to the yoke of reigning sin, not allowing them to attain the good purity they love, but rather compelling them to practice the evil they abhor.

## CHAPTER XV. Reply to the objection proposed

Theonas: Your opinion is making considerable progress. For you yourselves have already begun to assert that this cannot at all be true of those who are altogether sinners, but properly applies to those who strive to abstain from carnal vices. Since you have now separated these people from the number of sinners, it follows that you must gradually insert them into the company of the faithful and the saints. What kinds of sins do you say that such people can commit, if, after baptismal grace, they become involved in them but are then freed again through the daily grace of Christ? Or concerning what body of death are we to believe that the Apostle said, “Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7)?

Is it not clear—as truth has compelled you yourselves to confess—that he is speaking not of those members of capital crimes through which the penalty of eternal death is earned, namely, murder, fornication, adultery, drunkenness, theft, and robbery, but of that body mentioned above, which is daily aided by Christ’s grace? For whoever, after baptism and knowledge of God, has fallen into that body of death [Note: [Col. 1271D] By “body of death” here he understands the state of sin, which consists, as it were, of many members constituted by capital crimes, as is clear from what precedes. He teaches that the Apostle was not speaking of this body of death when he said, “Wretched man that I am; who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7), but of the law of sin and death—that is, the inclination to sin or the fuel of sin, as has often been stated (see Conference 12, chapter 1). This inclination is also present in the just and causes them difficulty; hence they desire to be freed from it. Thus, in this and the following chapter, he distinguishes two bodies: the body of death and the body of sin.] should know that he will be cleansed not by the daily grace of God—that is, by the easy remission which our Lord, when entreated, habitually grants our errors at every moment—but either by prolonged affliction of repentance and penal sorrow, or certainly by being consigned for these things to the punishments of eternal fire in the future, as the same Apostle declares: “Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6).

Or what is this law warring in our members, which fights against the law of our mind and, when we resist, leads us captive under the law of sin and death, making us serve it in the flesh while nevertheless permitting us to serve the law of God in the mind? For I do not think that the law of sin here designates crimes, or that this can be understood of the crimes mentioned above. If someone commits them, he does not serve the law of God in his mind; indeed, he must first depart from it in spirit before committing any of them in the flesh. For what is it to serve the law of sin except to fulfill what sin commands? What kind of sin, then, is it by which such holiness and perfection should feel themselves taken captive, while nevertheless trusting that they will be freed by Christ’s grace, saying, “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7)?

What law in our members will you maintain to be present which draws us away from the law of God and, taking us captive under the law of sin, makes us wretched rather than guilty, so that we are not consigned to eternal punishments, but, as though a joy of blessedness had been interrupted, sigh for it and seek a helper to draw us back to it, crying out with the Apostle, “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?” [Col. 1271D] For what else is being led captive under the law of sin than to remain in the effect and practice of sin?

Or what other principal good can be identified which the saints cannot fulfill, except that good in comparison with which, as we said above, all other goods are not goods at all? [Note: [Col. 1272D] The same point was made above, chapter 2.] Indeed, we know that there are many goods in this world, especially chastity, self-restraint, mercy, moderation, and piety; but all these cannot equal that supreme good, and they can be perfected not only by the apostles but even by ordinary people. Those by whom they have not been fulfilled are either punished with eternal punishment or, as stated above, freed through the great labor of repentance, not through Christ’s daily grace.

It remains, therefore, that we rightly acknowledge this statement of the Apostle to be applicable only to the persons of the saints, who, falling daily into that law of sin—not of crimes—which we have described, confident of their state of salvation, are not thrown headlong into wrongdoing but, as has often been said, are cast down from divine contemplation into the misery of bodily thoughts and are frequently deprived of the good of true blessedness. For if they felt themselves bound by this law of their members to daily crimes, they would complain not about the loss of happiness but about their innocence; and the Apostle Paul would not say, “Wretched man that I am,” but, “Impure or wicked man that I am.” Nor would he wish to be freed from the body of death—that is, from the mortal condition—but from the shameful deeds and crimes of this flesh.

But because he felt himself captive through the condition of human frailty—that is, drawn away into carnal anxieties and cares, which the law of sin and death produces—he groaned over this law of sin, into which he had fallen against his will, and immediately turned back to Christ, being saved by the most present redemption of his grace. Therefore, whatever the law of sin, which naturally produces thorns and thistles of mortal thoughts and cares, has caused to sprout in the soil of the Apostle’s heart, the law of grace immediately uproots. For he says: “The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death” (Rom. 8).

## CHAPTER XVI. What the body of sin and death is

This, then, is the unavoidable body of death into which all the perfect—those who have tasted how sweet the Lord is—fall back daily, experiencing with the prophet how evil and bitter it is for them to depart from the Lord their God (Jer. 2). This is the body of death which draws them back from heavenly contemplation and leads them toward earthly things; which makes them, while singing psalms and prostrate in prayer, review uselessly human forms, conversations, business affairs, or actions.

This is the body of death which prevents those who emulate angelic holiness and wish to cling continually to the Lord from finding the perfection of this good, because the body of death resists it. Instead, they do the evil they do not wish—that is, their minds are carried even toward things that do not contribute to the progress and perfection of the virtues.

Finally, to make clear that the blessed Apostle said this about the saints, the perfect, and those like them, he points to himself, as it were, by touching and designating himself, and immediately adds: “So then I myself” (Rom. 7) [Col. 1273A]—that is, “I who utter these things disclose the hidden places of my own conscience, not another’s.” The Apostle commonly uses this form of expression when he wishes to designate himself specifically, as in: “I myself, Paul, appeal to you by the meekness and gentleness of Christ” (2 Cor. 10); and again: “Unless it was that I myself did not burden you” (ibid. 12); and again: “But be it so, I myself did not burden you” (ibid.); and elsewhere: “I myself, Paul, say to you: if you are circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you” (Gal. 5). And to the Romans: “For I myself could wish to be accursed from Christ for the sake of my brothers” (Rom. 9).

It can also reasonably be understood in this way, as spoken more explicitly and emphatically: “So then I myself” (Rom. 7)—that is, “I whom you know to be an apostle of Christ, whom you all revere [Note: [Col. 1273C] *Suspicientia*, that is, reverence and admiration; from the verb *suspicere*, meaning “to look upward.” We admire the person whom, as though placed above us, we look up to.] and admire, whom you believe to be supreme and perfect, and in whom Christ speaks—although with the mind I serve the law of God, yet with the flesh I confess that I serve the law of sin. That is, through the tension of the human condition I sometimes fall from heavenly things to earthly ones, and the height of my mind slips down toward the cares of lowly matters. Through this law of sin I feel myself taken captive at every moment, so that, although I persevere with an unwavering desire in the law of God, I nevertheless feel that I can escape the force of this captivity in no way unless I always flee to the grace of the Savior.”

## CHAPTER XVII. That all the saints truly confessed themselves to be unclean and sinners

And therefore, all the saints, pierced by daily sighs on account of this frailty of their nature, while they examine the variety of their thoughts and the hidden recesses and depths of their conscience, humbly cry out: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. 142). And also: [Note: [Col. 1273C] The Vulgate edition reads: “Who can say: ‘My heart is clean; I am pure from sin’?” (Prov. 20). Saint Jerome observes: “Notice that he does not say, ‘Who can have a clean heart and be pure from sin?’ but, ‘Who can say: “My heart is clean; I am pure from sin”?’ For there are people who, by the generosity of divine grace, can, according to the human measure, possess purity both of heart and of deed. Hence the Lord’s saying: ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God’ (Matt. 5). And in the psalm: ‘Who will ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who will stand in his holy place? The innocent in hands and pure in heart’ (Ps. 23). For if no one has a pure heart and no one is free from sin, it necessarily follows that no one ascends the mountain of the Lord and no human being stands in his holy place. But since it is certain that many will ascend the mountain of the Lord and stand in his holy place, it remains that there are many who are pure in heart and, according to the measure of human possibility, free from sin. Nevertheless, no one declares himself pure in heart and free from sin without presumption. For it is foolish boasting to vaunt one’s own praise, and presumptuous for anyone to glory in his innocence or righteousness.”] “Who will glory in having a pure heart, or who will have confidence that he is clean from sin?” (Prov. 20). And again: “There is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin” (Eccles. 7). [Note: [Col. 1273D] That is, one who always does good in such a way that he never sins; or, as he explains below, no one on this earth has ever been or can ever be found so holy, so diligent, and so attentive that he can cling continually to that true and singular good without feeling himself daily drawn away from it and falling into sin.] Thus they understood human righteousness to be weak, imperfect, and always unworthy of God’s mercy. One of them, whose iniquities and sins God cleansed by sending a burning coal of his word from the altar, after that marvelous contemplation of God, after seeing the exalted seraphim and receiving revelation of heavenly mysteries, says: [Note: [Col. 1274C] The prophet’s complete statement is: “Woe is me, because I was silent; for I am a man of unclean lips,” and so forth. Saint Jerome explains these words in two ways. “Isaiah,” he says, “according to the Septuagint interpreters, testifies that he was pierced, saying: ‘Wretched am I, because I have been pierced,’ not on account of other crimes, but because he had unclean lips. Happy is the conscience that has sinned only in speech—not through its own fault, but because it was polluted by association with a people whose lips were unclean, with whom he was often compelled to speak. This shows that it is harmful to live among sinners. ‘Whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it’ (Eccles. 13). But because in the Hebrew we read, ‘Woe is me, because I was silent,’ the prophet laments that he was not worthy to praise the Lord of Sabaoth together with the seraphim, whom we understand to be angelic powers. He did not dare to praise the Lord because he had unclean lips, because he lived among a sinful people. Or it should certainly be understood thus: ‘Because I was silent,’ and did not boldly rebuke the wicked king Uzziah, therefore my lips are unclean, and I do not dare to sing the Lord’s praises with the angels, lest it be said to me: ‘Why do you recount my statutes and take my covenant upon your mouth?’ (Ps. 49), for ‘praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner’ (Eccles. 15). We say this not to teach that Isaiah was such a person, but because, in humility, he confesses himself unworthy of God’s praise on account of his unclean lips alone.] “Woe is me, for I am a man of polluted lips, and I dwell among a people having polluted lips” (Isa. 6).

As I think, he would perhaps not even then have perceived the uncleanness of his lips had he not been granted, through the contemplation of God, to recognize true perfection and complete purity. In contemplating it, he suddenly recognized in himself a pollution previously unknown to him. For when he says, “Woe is me, for I am a man of polluted lips,” the following words show that he is confessing this about the pollution of his own lips, not that of the people: “And I dwell among a people having polluted lips.”

But even when, in prayer, he confesses the uncleanness of sinners as though it were universal, he includes not only the wicked but also the people of the just in a general supplication, saying: “Behold, you were angry, and we sinned; in these we have always been, and we shall be saved” [Note: [Col. 1274D] See what we noted above on this interpretation, which the present author adapts to his own meaning, whereas according to the prophet’s intention it should be referred only to the impious and wicked Jews, as stated above (chapter 4).]—“we have become as an unclean person, all of us, and all our righteousnesses are like a menstrual cloth” (Isa. 64).

I ask: what could be clearer than this statement, in which the prophet embraces not one but all our righteousnesses and, considering everything that is judged unclean or horrible, prefers to compare them to a menstrual cloth because he could find nothing dirtier or more impure in human conduct?

## CHAPTER XVIII. That even the just and the saints are not without sin

It is therefore useless to oppose the edge of a thorny objection to the most manifest truth, as you said shortly before: “If no one is without sin, no one is holy; and if no one is holy, no one will be saved.” The knot of this question can be untied by the prophet’s testimony. “Behold,” he says, “you were angry, and we sinned” (Isa. 64)—that is, when, through the pride of our heart or our negligence, you withdrew us from your help, the abyss immediately swallowed us up in sins; just as if someone were to say to the splendid element of the sun, “Behold, you have set,” and immediately a dark obscurity covered us.

Yet here, although this saint says that he has sinned—and not merely sinned, but also remained continually in those sins—he does not utterly despair of salvation, but adds: “We have always been in them, and we shall be saved.” I shall compare this statement, “Behold, you were angry, and we sinned,” with the Apostle’s: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7). Again, what the prophet adds, “We have always been in them, and we shall be saved,” corresponds to the Apostle’s subsequent words: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

Likewise, this statement of the same prophet—“Woe is me, for I am a man of polluted lips, and I dwell among a people having polluted lips” (Isa. 6)—seems to express the meaning of the words cited above: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?” And what follows in the prophet—“And behold, one of the seraphim flew to me, and in his hand was a burning coal, or a stone, which he had taken from the altar with tongs; and he touched my mouth and said: ‘Behold, I have touched your lips, and your iniquity will be taken away, and your sin will be cleansed’” (ibid.)—is such that it seems to have been spoken by Paul’s mouth when he says: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

You see, therefore, how all the saints, not so much in the person of the people as in their own person, truly confess themselves to be sinners, yet by no means despair of their salvation. Rather, they place their confidence in the fullness of justification which, because of the condition of human frailty, they distrust their ability to attain by their own power, relying instead on the grace and mercy of the Lord.

## CHAPTER XIX. He demonstrates from the form of the Lord’s Prayer that no one lives without sin

[Col. 1276A]

No one [Note: [Col. 1275D] Understand this with the exception stated above, namely Christ the Savior and the Virgin Mother of God. Just as the Fathers exempt her from the general statements of Scripture that deny that a human being can live without sin, so it must also be said that she was exempt from the obligation to recite the words of the Lord’s Prayer in her own person. Rather, she recited them for the whole assembly of the faithful, among whom many—and, apart from her, all—were sinners; and this was her singular privilege.] in this life, however holy, is free from the debts of sins; even the teaching of the Savior instructs us in this. When he handed his disciples the form of perfect prayer, among the other sublime and most sacred commands—which, since they were given only to the holy and perfect, cannot apply to the wicked and unbelieving—he commanded that this be inserted: “And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6).

[Note: [Col. 1275D] From this petition of the Lord’s Prayer, the Fathers derive two ecclesiastical doctrines consistent with this passage. The first is that all human beings, however just and holy, are not free from sins in this life, since all must say to God daily: “Forgive us our debts.” Among others, Tertullian and Cyprian teach this in their books on prayer. The second, which follows from the first, is that there are certain venial sins which, by their nature, do not make a person an enemy of God and can coexist with grace, charity, and righteousness. Accordingly, although the just are not free from these sins, they are nevertheless not denied to be just, as is stated at the end of this chapter.]

If, therefore, this prayer is truly uttered by the saints, as we must unquestionably believe, who could be found so stubborn and presumptuous, so uplifted by the proud fury of the devil, that, declaring himself to be without sin, he would believe himself superior not only to the apostles but even accuse the Savior himself of ignorance or vanity—as though he either did not know that some could be free from debts, or had taught them in vain although he knew that they did not need the remedy of this prayer?

But since all the saints, observing the commands of their king, say every day, “Forgive us our debts,” then, if they speak the truth, no one is truly free from guilt; and if they deceive, it is equally true that they are not free from the sin of falsehood. Hence even that most wise Ecclesiastes, mentally surveying all human actions and pursuits, declares without exception: “There is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin” (Eccles. 7)—that is, no one on this earth has ever been or can ever be found so holy, so diligent, and so attentive that he can cling continually to that true and singular good without feeling himself daily drawn away from it and falling into sin. Yet although he is declared unable to be free from fault, he is not thereby denied to be just.

## CHAPTER XX. That even at the very time of prayer it is scarcely possible to avoid sin

Whoever, therefore, attributes τὸ ἀναμάρτητον—that is, impeccancy—to human nature [Note: [Col. 1276D] He says *impeccancy*, not *impeccability*, as Ciaconius explained above (chapter 7).] should contend with us not by empty words but by the testimony and proof of his conscience; and only then should he declare himself to be without sin when he has perceived that he has not been torn away from this supreme good. Indeed, whoever examines his conscience and finds that he has celebrated even one synaxis [Note: [Col. 1276D] That is, an assembly, prayer, or communion, as noted elsewhere.] without any interruption by word, deed, or thought should declare himself to be without sin.

Since we confess that the swift flight of the human mind through all these idle and superfluous matters [Note: [Col. 1277B] See the seventh Conference, which concerns the instability of the soul and calls this the winged wandering of the human mind. Elsewhere (Conference 24, chapter 24) it is called the mind’s many-willed vanity and slippery wanderings; see also Saint Bernard, *On the Interior House*, chapter 54 and following.] cannot be avoided, we consequently confess that we are truly not without sin. For however watchfully each person strives to guard his heart, he will never guard it according to the desire of his spirit while the condition of the flesh resists. The more the human mind has progressed and reached a purer clarity of contemplation, the more unclean it will see itself when it looks into the mirror of its own purity; for when the mind extends itself toward a higher vision and, looking toward greater things than those it presently accomplishes, desires them, it must always regard the things in which it remains as lower and more contemptible.

## CHAPTER XXI. Although we acknowledge that we are not without sin, we nevertheless ought not to withdraw from the Lord’s communion

[Col. 1277B]

Much indeed does a clearer vision disclose, and an irreproachable life produces for itself a greater grief over reproach; the correction of one’s conduct and attentive striving after virtues multiply groans and sighs. For no one can be content with the degree to which he has advanced; and the purer a person’s mind has become, the more, seeing himself as defiled, he finds reasons for humility rather than exaltation. The more swiftly he has pressed toward higher things, the more clearly he foresees how much remains for him to pursue.

Finally, that distinguished apostle whom Jesus loved, reclining upon His breast, uttered this saying as though from the Lord’s own heart: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1). Therefore, when we say that we have no sin, having no truth—that is, Christ—in us, what else do we accomplish except to prove by this very profession that we are not merely sinners but criminals and impious persons?

Lastly, if we wish to investigate more truly whether it is possible for human nature to possess τὸ ἀναμάρτητον—that is, impeccability—where could we learn this more clearly than from those who have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires, and for whom the world has truly been crucified (Galatians 5, 6)? Although they have not merely uprooted all vices from their hearts but have also striven to exclude the memory and thoughts of sins, nevertheless they faithfully confess every day that they are not free from the stain of sin for even a single hour.

[Note: From this passage and what follows we learn plainly that the ancient monks, even those living in the deserts, and laymen—that is, persons not initiated into sacred orders, as most people of that period were, as has often been said—were accustomed to receive Communion at least every Sunday. This may be gathered from many other passages of Cassian (Book 3 of the *Institutes*, chapter 2; *Conference* 7, final chapter; *Conference* 18, chapter 15; *Conference* 22, chapter 15), where they are said to have assembled in church on Saturdays and Sundays according to Eastern custom, and to have celebrated and completed the sacred mysteries, one of them serving as priest and the others ministering.

Palladius also reports this in his account of Pachomius (*Lausiac History*, 38). Among the other rules of the Tabennesiot monks, dictated by an angel, he records this prescription as well: “When they enter for Communion with Christ on Saturday and Sunday, let them loosen their belts, remove their sheepskins, and enter wearing only the cuculla.” Sozomenus (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book 3, chapter 13) and Nicephorus (Book 9, chapter 14) likewise attest this.

The rule of Pachomius, rendered into Latin by Saint Jerome, says in article 5: “On the Lord’s Day, at the assembly in which the offering is to be offered.” Here “assembly” means a gathering for prayer and sacrifice in the church, otherwise called a *synaxis*.

Likewise, Palladius writes (*Lausiac History*, 59): “Once, when it was Sunday, Abba Helles, or Hellas, came to certain monks and said to them: ‘Why did you not hold the synaxis today?’ They replied: ‘Because the presbyter did not come,’” and so forth. From this it may be inferred that the absence of the customary observance was an unusual occurrence for them. Indeed, offended by this, Helles miraculously crossed a great river carried by a crocodile, in order to summon a priest from another region (Sozomenus, Book 6, chapter 28; Cassiodorus, *Tripartite History*, Book 8, chapter 1; Nicephorus, Book 11, chapter 34).

Saint Basil also testifies that anchorites, or monks living in solitude and separately from others, when they could not assemble at church, were accustomed from time to time—when a priest or minister was absent—to keep the sacred Eucharist in their private cells, to be received by their own hands on appointed days. This practice was also permitted to other Christians, even laymen, especially during times of persecution, when they were not free to assemble at church and celebrate the synaxis whenever they wished. This is clear from Tertullian (*To His Wife*, Book 1), Cyprian (*On the Lapsed*), and others (Gregory Nazianzen, *Oration in Praise of Gorgonia*; Jerome, *Apology for the Books Against Jovinian*). Indeed, it is reported by the holy Fathers that the same practice continued for some time even after peace had been restored to the Church under Christian and Catholic emperors.

Saint Basil, cited by Baronius to establish this point (*Roman Martyrology*, August 15), says in his letter to Caesaria Patricia on the reception of the Sacraments: “All who live the monastic life in the deserts, when no priest is present, keep Communion at home and, when they have it there, receive it by themselves,” and so forth. Numerous examples of the same practice are also found both in the *Lives of the Fathers* and in Sophronius’s *Spiritual Meadow*.

As for cenobitic monks, Saint Benedict likewise indicates rather clearly in his Rule (chapter 38) that they were accustomed to receive Holy Communion every Sunday. Speaking of the weekly reader, he says: “The one who is to read for the whole week shall enter” —that is, to read—“and, after Mass and Communion, shall ask everyone to pray for him,” and so forth. Turrecremata explains that this means after the Communion of the brothers (*ibid.*), which ordinarily took place after Mass, or at the principal Mass. See also the Cassinese commentary.

Saint Benedict adds below: “The weekly server, however, shall receive the mixed portion”—that is, bread with drink, as the same Turrecremata explains—“before he begins to read, on account of Holy Communion.” His interpreter Smaragdus says: “He says ‘on account of Holy Communion’ so that, having taken something from it, he may not spit it out in his saliva.” Thus far Smaragdus.

Here the great caution and foresight of the pious Father Benedict shines forth, out of reverence for the most holy Sacrament received on that day, namely Sunday: lest something of it should perhaps be expelled by spitting and expectoration, which tend to occur more frequently on an empty stomach, while the reader is reading.

But we must now examine what, in later centuries, the supreme pontiffs decreed concerning the celebration of Mass and Communion among monks. First, Clement V, in the Council of Vienne, solemnly decreed (*Clementine Constitutions*, “Ne in agro,” concerning the status of monks) that, every month, both within monasteries and outside them, every monk individually and all monks collectively, without any excuse being admitted, should approach confession at least once, and that in the first Sunday of every month they should always receive Communion in their monasteries—unless there should be some reason which they did not delay to disclose to the abbot, prior, or penitentiaries of the monasteries, in whose judgment they should either abstain or approach.

Thus Clement the pontiff. Following in his footsteps, his successor Benedict XII confirmed and expanded the same constitution concerning Benedictines, both priests and non-priests, in these words (*Benedictine Constitution*, chapter 27):

“Moreover, we admonish all priors, administrators, and monks of that order or religious institute who are in priestly orders and reside within their churches, monasteries, or other conventual places, that each of them strive to celebrate Mass two or three times”—but those who are in priories or other non-conventual places, or in schools, or elsewhere, “at least once a week, if not more frequently, subject to propriety and due devotion. Nevertheless, those who preside over conventual places shall celebrate the principal conventual Masses there on solemn feasts.

“Others, however, who are not priests, shall confess at least every week, if not more frequently, and every month, in accordance with the constitution of the aforesaid predecessor Clement promulgated in the aforementioned Council of Vienne, approach Communion: those, namely, who are within churches, monasteries, or other conventual places, at the high altar; but those who are outside them, wherever it shall seem more proper to them—unless they abstain for a reasonable cause and with the permission of their superiors or confessors. If they negligently omit this, they shall be severely reproved by those same superiors and, nevertheless, duly punished.

“By this, however, we do not intend in any way to derogate from the statutes or customs of the churches, monasteries, or places mentioned above, where it is observed that they should confess, celebrate, or receive Communion more frequently.”

See the Council of Trent, session 25, chapter 10, concerning religious.

Thus the pontiff. Although he prescribes for non-priest monks only monthly Communion—namely, on the first Sunday of each month—he nevertheless indicates clearly enough that he desires and urges more frequent Communion, just as he does confession, which in most well-ordered monasteries is customary and regular every week. This is indicated both by the expressions “if not more frequently” and “more frequently,” and by the clause of the constitution cited above, in which he declares that he does not intend in any way to derogate from the statutes and customs of monasteries where non-priest monks are accustomed to receive Communion every Sunday. Consequently, it is understood that he approves such practices altogether and leaves them in force and validity.

To this is finally added the authority of the sacred Council of Trent (session 23, chapter 13, concerning reform), which admonishes subdeacons and deacons that, at least on Sundays and solemn feast days, when they have ministered at the altar, they should receive Holy Communion. If this is to be observed by secular clerics, it ought much more to be observed by regulars and religious.]

Nevertheless, we ought not on that account to suspend ourselves from the Lord’s Communion because we acknowledge that we are sinners. Rather, we should hasten to it more and more eagerly, both for the healing of the soul and for the purification of the spirit—yet with such humility of mind and faith that, judging ourselves unworthy to receive so great a grace, we seek remedies instead for our wounds.
