Otherwise, not even annual Communion should rightly be presumed, as some do who live in monasteries and measure the dignity, sanctification, and benefit of the heavenly Sacraments in such a way that they think only holy and immaculate persons ought to presume to receive them, rather than receiving them so that through their participation they may make us holy and pure.

Such persons in fact incur a greater presumption of arrogance than the one they seem to themselves to avoid, because whenever they receive the Sacraments they judge themselves worthy to receive them.

For it is far more just that, with this humility of heart by which we believe and confess that we can never receive those sacred mysteries as something merited by us, we presume to receive them every Sunday as a remedy for our sicknesses, than that, elated by the vain persuasion of our hearts, we should believe ourselves worthy to receive them even after a year.

[Note: “To receive them” (*participio*) means “by participation,” as above. Those who thought that they would communicate more worthily and devoutly if they postponed it for a year seem to be noted by Saint Ambrose in these words (*On the Sacraments*, Book 5, chapter 4): “If it is daily bread, why do you receive it after a year, as the Greeks in the East are accustomed to do? Receive daily what benefits you daily. Live so that you may deserve to receive it daily.”

These words apply to other believers, and much more to religious, priests, and prelates, for whom nothing can be more fitting or appropriate than to offer God a daily sacrifice. This may be learned from Saint Gregory, who, in Homily 37 and in Book 4 of the *Dialogues*, chapter 56, particularly praises a certain bishop named Cassius because he offered daily sacrifices to God, so that scarcely a day of his life passed without his offering a sacrifice of appeasement to almighty God. He then adds how great was the preparation of soul and devotion with which Cassius did this.

It is also reported that Saint Thomas Aquinas, as a memorable example to later generations, celebrated Mass every day and assisted at the celebration of Mass by others (Garzon, in his *Life*). See other examples in Antonius Demochares, *On the Sacrifice of the Mass*.]

Therefore, so that we may understand these things and retain them fruitfully, let us earnestly implore the Lord’s mercy to assist us in bringing them to completion. They are not learned, as other human arts are, by some method of words that precedes them, but rather by action and experience leading the way. Moreover, unless they are frequently examined and polished through conferences with spiritual men, and carefully tested through instruction and daily experience, they either grow stale through negligence or perish through idle forgetfulness.

## THE TWENTY-FOURTH CONFERENCE

The third of Abbot Abraham. On Mortification.

[Col. 1279]

### CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 1279D]

This twenty-fourth conference of Abbot Abraham is brought forth, with Christ’s favor, bringing to a close all the traditions of the elders.

[Note: I think that this is the Abbot Abraham whose notable encomium appears in Conference 15, chapters 4 and 5, where two miracles of healing performed by him are related. There too he is said to have been called παῖς, that is, “boy,” on account of his simplicity and innocence; and I have there shown by many indications and arguments that he was different from Saint Abraham, or Abramius, the Syrian, whose life and deeds the blessed Ephrem wrote.

But I am uncertain whether he was Abraham, or rather Abramius, the Egyptian, of whom Palladius records only this (*Lausiac History*, 105): “There was a certain Abramius, an Egyptian by birth, who lived an exceedingly harsh and wholly rustic life in the desert. His mind having been wounded by an untimely delusion, he came to the church and contended with the presbyters, saying: ‘I was ordained priest by Christ at night; receive me as a priest.’ When the Fathers had removed him from the solitude and led him to a less rigorous and more ordinary manner of life, they cured him of his pride by bringing him to recognize his own weakness and that he had been mocked by demons.” Thus Palladius.

There was another Saint Abraham of Auvergne, concerning whom Sidonius Apollinaris published a notable poem (Book 7, chapter 17); Gregory of Tours mentions him (*History*, Book 2, chapter 21), as does the Roman Martyrology, 17 Kalends of July. Finally, Theodoret mentions two other anchorites called Abraham (*History*, Book 4, chapter 26; *Religious History*, chapter 17). But these are not under discussion here.] When it has been completed through your prayers, we believe that we shall be released from the obligations of all our promises, in mystical correspondence with the number of those twenty-four elders who are said in the holy Apocalypse (Revelation 3) to offer their crowns to the Lamb.

[Note: That is, the authors, presenters, or interlocutors of these twenty-four conferences. They are called twenty-four elders, by allusion to the twenty-four elders seen by John in the Apocalypse, not according to the number of persons but of conferences. For not one conference is assigned to each: some receive two and others even three. Thus, as to the number of persons, only fifteen anchorites are named in these conferences: first, Abbot Moses, to whom belong the first conference, on the monk’s purpose or end, and the second, on discernment; second, Paphnutius, to whom belongs the third, on the three renunciations; third, Daniel, to whom belongs the fourth, on the desire of flesh and spirit; fourth, Serapion, to whom belongs the fifth, on the eight principal vices; fifth, Theodorus, to whom belongs the sixth, on the death of the saints; sixth, Serenus, to whom belong the seventh, on the mobility of the soul and spiritual wickednesses, and the eighth, on principalities or powers; seventh, Isaac, to whom belong the ninth, on prayer, and the tenth, on continual prayer; eighth, Chaeremon, to whom belong the eleventh, on perfection, the twelfth, on chastity, and the thirteenth, on God’s protection; ninth, Nesteros, to whom belong the fourteenth, on spiritual knowledge, and the fifteenth, on divine charisms; tenth, Joseph, to whom belong the sixteenth, on friendship, and the seventeenth, on making decisions; eleventh, Piammon, to whom belongs the eighteenth, on the three kinds of monks; twelfth, John, to whom belongs the nineteenth, on the end of the cenobite and hermit; thirteenth, Pinufius, to whom belongs the twentieth, on the end of repentance and the proof of satisfaction; fourteenth, Theonas, to whom belong the twenty-first, on the remission of Pentecost, the twenty-second, on nocturnal illusions, and the twenty-third, on the Apostle’s saying, “For I do not do the good that I will,” etc.; and fifteenth, Abbot Abraham, to whom the twenty-fourth and final conference, on mortification, is assigned. Hence it is clear that there are many more conferences than interlocutors.]

If, therefore, these twenty-four elders of ours should have been crowned because of the merit of their instruction, whatever glory there may be, they will lay it at the feet of the Lamb who was sacrificed for the salvation of the world. For He has deigned to grant both to them such an outstanding understanding and to us whatever sort of discourse we possess, by which so great a depth might be made worthy of pursuit, for the honor of His name.

And the merits of the gift must necessarily be referred to the author of all good things, to whom the greater the repayment, the more is owed through that very repayment.

Accordingly, we brought to this Abraham, in anxious confession, the struggle against our thoughts, because we were being pressed by daily anxieties to return to our province and to revisit our parents.

[Note: By “parents,” although strictly speaking father and mother are meant, jurists, according to Festus, also understand a grandfather and great-grandfather, as well as other higher ancestors of either sex. Indeed, we find that the term was extended even to any blood relatives. This usage is found, however, only among those who spoke less correctly as the purity of the Latin language was already declining; the Gauls observe the same usage in their vernacular. There is therefore nothing to prevent the word from being understood in that way here.

How dangerous it is for monks to go out rashly or without necessity to visit their parents or relatives according to the flesh, the monk Malchus learned through his own loss and experience. Saint Jerome recorded his life in writing. Although the abbot advised him against it, Malchus left the monastery to visit his homeland and parents and fell into the hands of barbarians, by whom he was carried off and abducted and thereafter endured many hardships and difficulties. It is a familiar and instructive story (*Works of Saint Jerome*, volume 1).

A contrary and memorable example of Abba Pior is reported by Sozomenus in these words (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book 6, chapter 29):

“When Pior had decided from the beginning of his adolescence to consecrate himself to the monastic life, at the very moment when he left his father’s house for this reason, he promised God that thereafter he would never again look upon any member of his family. After fifty years, his sister learned that he was still alive. Since, overcome by immense joy at such an unexpected report, she was almost stunned, she could not rest until she had seen her brother with her own eyes. The bishop of that place, moved with compassion for her—an aged woman who lamented and implored assistance in this matter—wrote to the superiors of the monks living in the desert and asked them to send Pior to him.

When ordered to go, Pior set out, since he could not oppose them. He therefore came to his homeland with one companion, stood before the doors of his father’s house, and gave a sign that he had arrived. When he sensed the doors creaking, he called his sister by name with his eyes closed and said: ‘I am Pior, your brother. Come, look at me as much as you wish.’

She was greatly delighted by this and gave thanks to God. But after praying near the doors, he returned to the place where he lived.”

Such is Sozomenus’s account, in which many lessons about antiquity and monastic discipline are contained.

First, the monks and anchorites living in solitude, together with their fathers and abbots—that is, their superiors—obeyed the bishop of that place when he issued commands and showed themselves subject to him. This is sanctioned by many canons and decrees collected by Gratian (16, question 1; and 18, question 2).

Second, although those anchorites lived alone and separately in remote cells and places, they nevertheless had superiors and prefects, whose districts were divided by fixed boundaries and territorial limits, just as religious today have their provincials and visitors. They rendered obedience to these superiors, often assembled with them, consulted them about doubtful matters, listened to them preaching or disputing, and, when they were priests, received the sacraments from them at appointed times. This is well known from many passages in Cassian and from the *Lives of the Fathers*.

Third, Pior, a solitary living an especially austere life, was ordered after fifty years to go to his homeland and satisfy his sister’s desire. He set out in obedience to his superiors. Yet he did not undertake the journey alone, but took one companion with him. This was customary among the Tabennesiot, or Pachomian, monks, who were not to go outside except in pairs, as the Rule prescribes: “No one is to be sent outside alone for any business unless another has been joined to him.”

Saint Augustine likewise prescribed the same rule for his regular clerics in these words (chapters 28 and 29 of the Rule): “Let them not go anywhere they must go with fewer than two or three. And the one who has some necessity of going somewhere must go with those whom the superior orders him to accompany.”

Fourth, Pior made himself visible to his sister without looking at her, judging it foreign to a monk to take pleasure in the sight even of his parents. After praying, he immediately departed from the place; so far was he from entering his father’s house, resting there briefly, or even refreshing his body.

It is also fitting to add Saint Jerome’s astute saying, consistent with these teachings (*Letter 1, to Heliodorus*): “No prophet is accepted in his own country” (Luke 4), nor can a monk be perfect there; but to be unwilling to be perfect is to sin.]

For we were continually driven by the daily urgings of our hearts to return and visit our parents. From this arose for us the greatest occasion of desire: we remembered that our parents were endowed with such religious devotion and piety that we would in no way put our own way of life before them. We constantly revolved this thought in our minds: that we would gain greater progress from their constant company, and that we would not be occupied by any concern for bodily things or by any distraction involved in providing our food, since they would abundantly and gladly supply everything necessary for us.

[Note: That is, supplying us with everything we needed. See below, chapter 11 and following.]

Moreover, we nourished our minds with the hope of empty pleasures, believing that we would reap the greatest benefit from the conversion of many people who, as though guided by our example and exhortations, would be directed onto the path of salvation.

In addition, the locations where our ancestors had possessed property were vividly pictured before our eyes, together with the pleasant beauty of the regions, extending over the agreeable and suitable spaces of solitude, so that the secluded places of the forests might not only delight a monk but also provide great advantages for sustaining life.

When we had simply disclosed all these thoughts to the aforementioned elder in accordance with the testimony of our conscience, and had declared with floods of tears that we could no longer endure the force of these assaults unless God’s grace came to our aid through his remedy, he remained silent and hesitated for a long time. At last, sighing heavily, he replied as follows.

### CHAPTER TWO

How the Elder Exposed Our Errors
You have not yet renounced worldly desires. [Note: [Col. 1283C] From these words one may infer why Cassian entitled this conference “On Mortification”: namely, because Abba Abraham took this opportunity to speak about mortifying the affections and desires by which, as they had previously made clear, they were still held and greatly troubled; and because he earnestly commended to them this mortification of passions or affections, especially those directed toward parents, blood relatives, and worldly things. Among others, John Buzaeus, a theologian of the Society of Jesus, treats this mortification excellently in his very select and useful *Panarium, or Antidote of Vices* [Col. 1283D]. For the reader’s convenience, and because it is necessary here, I have thought it worthwhile to extract the following brief passage:

“First,” he says (under the word *Immortification*), “consider what it properly means to mortify the passions of the soul, and you will easily understand what it means for them to remain unmortified. You mortify them when you subdue disturbances of the soul—for example, anger or hatred—as soon as they arise; when you restrain the flesh’s inclination toward excessive food or drink; when you willingly subject your own judgment and will to another’s. For just as a man who has been killed or is dead, even if he is subjected to insults or praises, gives no indication of sorrow or joy, so a truly mortified person, even if he is subjected to many hardships or injuries, displays no sign of anger or impatience; indeed, he sometimes derives great pleasure from them.

“But you will mortify those passions most perfectly if you restrain the desires of the flesh and the senses not only in unlawful things—that is, in those things forbidden by divine or human law—but also in lawful things, so that you withdraw something from lawful food, drink, sleep, bed, recreation, and other bodily comforts, as is proper to all religious persons and other servants of God. Concerning these matters, Blessed Augustine wrote in his book *On Faith to Peter* as follows (ch. 3, 14, 42):

“‘The humble servants of Christ, who desire to serve their Lord without hindrance and without the harm of sinful thought, do not seek marriage at all, and abstain from meat and wine insofar as bodily health permits—not because it is a sin either to have a wife or to consume wine or meat, but because they pursue the practices of a purer life and wish to chastise their bodies.’ [Col. 1284C]

“And Saint Gregory, in the fourth book of the *Dialogues* (ch. 11), speaking of a certain holy priest who, in order to preserve chastity, refused access even to devout and religious women, says: ‘Holy men have this characteristic: they are always far from unlawful things, and often cut themselves off even from lawful things.’

“Thus, the disease of unmortification afflicts the person who readily obeys and indulges the passions of his soul and the desires of his flesh, whether in unlawful or lawful matters.”

So he writes. If the devout reader trusts me, let him consult the rest in Buzaeus himself; he will not regret having done so.

Moreover, concerning the mortification of carnal affections toward parents and blood relatives—the subject treated specifically and particularly in this conference—you have a notable example in Cassian, *Institutes*, book V, chapter 29, in the monk and elder Machetes. When letters from his father and mother, as well as from many friends in the province of Pontus, had once been sent to him, he received the large bundle of letters and, after turning the matter over within himself for a long time, said:

“‘What a cause for thoughts these letters’ reading will be to me! They will drive me either to empty joy or to unprofitable sadness. For how many days will the recollection of those who wrote them turn my mind away from the contemplation to which I have devoted myself!’”

As he pondered these things in his heart, he decided not only not to open any letter, but not even to untie the bundle, lest, by reading the names of those who had written or recalling their faces, he should cease from the attentiveness of his spirit. Thus, just as he had received it bound, he handed it over to be burned, saying: “Go, thoughts of my homeland; burn together, and do not try any longer to call me back to the things from which I have fled.” [Note: This is found there.]

The weakness of your thoughts shows that you have not yet mortified your former desires. For just as the wandering of your desires reveals the idleness of your hearts, so you endure this exile and separation from your parents only in the body, whereas you ought rather to have undertaken them in your minds. All these things would already have been buried and utterly torn from your hearts if you had begun to understand either the rationale of renunciation itself or the fundamental reason for the solitude in which we live.

Therefore, I perceive that you are suffering from that sickness of idleness which is described in Proverbs in these words: [Note: [Col. 1284D] The same sentence is quoted from the Septuagint version in book X of the *Institutes*, chapter 21. In its place the Vulgate has: “The sluggard wills and wills not” (Prov. 23). On this point Saint Jerome, or Bede, aptly remarks in relation to this passage: “He is rightly designated by the name of sluggard who wishes to reign with the Lord but not to suffer with him: rewards delight him when they are promised, but struggles terrify him when they are commanded. Concerning him James says: ‘A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways’ (Jas. 1). And the son of Sirach says: ‘Woe to the sinner who enters the land by two paths’ (Sir. 2).”]

“Every idle person is in his desires,” and again: “Desires kill the sluggard” (Prov. 21).

The advantages of bodily comforts that you have praised could also have been available to us, if we had believed them suitable to our purpose, or if we had judged that such pleasure from pleasant surroundings could yield us a benefit equal to that which is gained from the squalor of this region and the mortification of the body.

Nor are we so deprived of the comfort of our parents that there would be no one willing and glad to support us from his own possessions—unless that saying of the Savior came to mind and excluded everything belonging to the nourishment of this flesh: “Whoever does not leave or hate father and mother, sons and brothers, cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14).

And even if we were deprived of our parents’ assistance, surely the services of the powerful of this world could not be lacking. They would gladly supply our needs with the greatest generosity and with every expression of gratitude. Supported by their munificence, we would be free from the anxiety of procuring food—unless that prophetic curse greatly deterred us: “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man” (Jer. 17); and, “Do not put your trust in princes” (Ps. 145).

We could even have situated our cells beside the channel of the Nile and had water at our doors, [Note: [Col. 1285B] Thus those holy Egyptian hermits and monks, although they could have established their dwellings either along the banks of the Nile or in other more convenient places where they could draw the water needed for their use nearby, nevertheless, out of a desire to mortify and discipline the body, preferred to choose dry, waterless places farther from the rivers for their habitation. Thus they were compelled to fetch water from a greater distance and carry it on their shoulders to their cells or monasteries.

Palladius records the following among the other austerities of Abba Moses: “After this, he devised for himself another way of practicing an austere life. This champion of Satan—for he fought against him in various ways—would go out at night to the cells of monks who had grown old in their labors and could no longer carry water for themselves. Taking their jars, he filled them with water without their knowledge. For in those places water is at a fixed distance: for some it is two stones [a distance measure], for others five, and for others half [the measure is uncertain].”

Sozomen, recounting the same event, explains these final words as follows (book VI, chapter 29): “It was a very laborious task, for the place from which they drew water was ten stadia away from some, twenty from others, and more than thirty from still others.”

Finally, Cassian says in book V of the *Institutes*, chapter 36: “They are constrained by such a scarcity of water that they distribute it with the care and scrupulousness with which no one among the most frugal preserves and spares even a quantity of the most precious wine. For they bring it from the channel of the aforementioned river for their necessary uses over a distance of three thousand paces, or more; and this interval, divided by sandy mountains, is made twice as arduous by the extreme difficulty of the labor.” So he writes. The extent of merit and reward before God that they gained by this voluntary labor is shown in this example from the *Lives of the Fathers* (book V, tract 7): “A certain elder lived in the desert, and water was twelve miles from his cell. Once, as he went to draw water, he became exhausted and said, ‘Why must I endure this labor? I will come and live near this water.’ Having said this, he turned and saw someone following him and counting his footsteps. He asked him, ‘Who are you?’ He replied, ‘I am an angel of the Lord, sent to count your footsteps and give you a reward.’ When the elder heard this, strengthened in spirit and made readier, he placed his cell still farther from that water.” This is found there.]

—and thus would not have been compelled to carry it on our shoulders for four thousand of our paces—unless the blessed Apostle, making us tireless in enduring this labor, continually encouraged us with these words: “Each person will receive his own reward according to his labor” (1 Cor. 3).

We also know that there are in our own regions pleasant and secluded places where an abundance of fruit, the beauty of gardens, or the fertility of the land could provide for our food with very little bodily labor—unless we feared that reproach directed in the Gospel against the rich man: “You received your consolation during your lifetime” (Luke 16). [Note: [Col. 1286B] Saint Jerome makes the same point in book II of *Against Jovinianus* (ch. 7). After demonstrating at length that solitude is especially suited and necessary for contemplation, he says:

“Many philosophers, moved by these considerations, abandoned the crowds of the cities and the suburban gardens, where irrigated fields, the leafy crowns of trees, the chirping of birds, the mirror of a spring, the murmuring stream, and many other delights for the eyes and ears might soften the soul’s strength through luxury and abundance, and violate its chastity. For it is useless frequently to look upon things by which one has at some time been captured and to expose oneself to experiences from which it is difficult to abstain.

“The Pythagoreans too, avoiding such company, were accustomed to live in solitude and deserted places. The Platonists and Stoics likewise spent time in temples and porticoes, so that, reminded by the holiness of a more august dwelling, they might think of nothing but the virtues. Plato himself, although wealthy, and although Diogenes trampled his couches with muddy feet, chose, so that he might devote himself to philosophy, a villa of the Academy far from the city, not merely deserted but also pestilential. In this way, through the anxiety and constant presence of illnesses, the assaults of lust might be broken, and his disciples might experience no other pleasure than that arising from the things they were learning.

“We read that some people put out their own eyes, lest through their sight they should be drawn away from the contemplation of philosophy. Hence that Crates of Thebes, throwing a considerable weight of gold into the sea, said: ‘Begone, perish, evil desires! I will drown you, lest I myself be drowned by you.’

“If anyone thinks that he can enjoy an abundance of food and drink and yet remain devoted to wisdom—that is, both live amid luxuries and not be held by the vices of luxury—he deceives himself. For if, when removed from these things, we are often captured by the allurements of nature and compelled to desire what we do not possess, how much more so when we imagine ourselves free while surrounded by the nets of pleasure!

“Our sense perceives what it sees, hears, smells, tastes, and touches, and it is drawn toward the desire for the thing whose pleasure captures it. The mind sees what the mind hears, and we can neither hear nor see anything unless our senses are attentive to the things we see and hear.”

This is Saint Jerome’s elegant and most appropriate teaching, which all religious and contemplative persons should carefully consider.]

But we have despised all those things, and rejected every pleasure of this world. We take delight only in these squalid conditions and prefer the terrible wasteland of this solitude to every luxury. We do not compare the riches of any fertile soil with this bitterness of the sands, for we pursue not the temporal gains of the body but the eternal benefits of the spirit.

For it is not enough for a monk to have renounced once—that is, at the beginning of his conversion, to have despised present things—unless he continues to renounce them every day. Until the end of this life we must say with the prophet: “You know that I have not desired the day of man” (Jer. 17).

Hence also the Lord says in the Gospel: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me” (Luke 9).

## Chapter III. On the character of places that should be sought by anchorites

[Col. 1287B] Therefore, the person who maintains vigilant concern for the purity of the inner man should seek places that do not distract his mind toward the cultivation of the land through the fruitfulness of their soil, nor disturb him from the fixed and immovable station of his cell, nor compel him to go out for some work under the open sky. [Note: [Col. 1287B] He teaches what sort of places solitary and contemplative persons should choose: secluded places, remote from human crowds. See Bellarmine, book II *On Monks*, chapter 39. Since the end of the solitary life is the contemplation of God and heavenly things, as is clear from Conference 19, which concerns the end of the eremitical and coenobitic life, while the best means to contemplation is to have a collected and tranquil mind, solitude certainly serves this purpose above all. It keeps far away every disturbance from things by which the mind could be distracted.

For this reason our Lord and Savior, when he wished to pray, used to withdraw into the mountains and the desert, as the Evangelist testifies (Luke 5). Likewise, when God wished to speak with Moses, he commanded him to ascend the summit of the mountain alone and enter the darkness (Exod. 24), so that he might see nothing that could draw his mind away from God. Indeed, Saint Jerome writes in the passage cited above that this is so true that, for this reason, many philosophers, following nature’s guidance, chose deserted, uncultivated, and even physically harmful and unhealthy places in which to philosophize and contemplate; and some even put out their own eyes.

Elsewhere he writes (*On the Hebrew Places*) that hermits’ cells were customarily situated on level ground in valleys surrounded by steep and precipitous mountains, so that the more humbly their bodies were weighed down, the more loftily their minds might be raised.

The following saying of the Poet also bears on this:

“Songs seek the retreat and leisure of the one who writes them.”

This may be said of every intellectual pursuit and contemplation.]

Thus, with their thoughts poured out into the open, they would scatter every direction of the mind and the most subtle focus of its purpose in different directions. Such things can be avoided or perceived by no one, however concerned and vigilant, except one who continually confines his mind and body within the enclosure of walls. In this way, like an excellent fisherman providing for himself by the apostolic art, he may, in the depths of his most tranquil heart, catch—attentive and motionless—the shoals of thoughts swimming there; and, as though carefully surveying the depths from a projecting rock, he may distinguish with prudent discernment which thoughts a person ought to draw toward himself for salvation, and which, like evil and harmful fish, he ought to disregard and reject.

## Chapter IV. What kinds of work should be chosen by solitaries
In this way, then, each person who continually perseveres in this watchfulness will effectively fulfill what is expressed clearly enough through the prophet Habakkuk:

> “I will stand upon my watch, and I will set my foot upon the fortress, and I will contemplate, that I may see what he will say to me, and what I shall answer to him who reproves me” (Habakkuk 2).

[Note: [Col. 1287D] The Vulgate version reads: “I will stand upon my watch, and I will set my foot upon the fortress, and I will contemplate, that I may see what is said to me, and what I shall answer to him who reproves me.”]

How great the labor and difficulty of this may be is demonstrated most clearly by the experience of those who dwell in that desert of Calamus or Porphyrion.

[Note: [Col. 1287D] Calamus, or Porphyrion, was a place of solitude in Egypt where Paul the Hermit lived. Cassian also mentions it in Book 10 of the *Institutes*, chapter 24; likewise in Conference 3, chapter 5, and Conference 7, chapter 26.]

For although they are separated from all cities and human dwellings by a greater expanse of solitude than the desert of Scetis—for they scarcely reach the privacy of their cells after penetrating the vast wilderness for seven or even eight stages—

[Note: [Col. 1288B] That is, after a journey of seven or eight days, as explained elsewhere (*Institutes*, Book 10, chapter 24). Thus Athanasius says in the *Life of Saint Antony* (chapter 54): “To the first station from Alexandria, which is called Chaereum…”]

nevertheless, because they are devoted to agriculture, they are by no means confined within enclosures.

[Note: [Col. 1288B] So that religious enclosed communities may better recognize the antiquity and sanctity of their cloister and monastic enclosure, it has seemed worthwhile, and highly consonant with our purpose, to record on the occasion of this passage some noteworthy matters concerning them. First: the Latin Fathers (Cassian here excepted) and also councils very frequently use the terms *claustrum* [cloister] and *clausura* [enclosure] in the same meaning and use now current among monks. I shall briefly touch on certain more select passages bearing on moral instruction. Pope Eugenius II, I think, cited by Gratian (16, q. 1, c. *Placuit*, 2): “It has pleased our common council that no monk, for earthly gain, presume by most impious daring to leave the monastery. Let the monk be content with his cloister”; and the rest cited below. Alexander II likewise in Gratian (ibid., c. *Juxta*): “In accordance with the tenor of the excellent Council of Chalcedon, we command monks, according to the Rule of St. Benedict (ch. 8), to remain within the cloister; we forbid them to roam through villages, castles, and cities, and decree that they cease altogether from preaching to the people—unless perhaps someone concerned for his soul’s salvation should wish to consult them within the cloister in order to assume their habit” (see the notes on Conference 24, ch. 14). Innocent III, in that solemn decree, *Cum ad monasterium*, on the condition of monks (Decretals, Book III, title 10): “In the oratory, refectory, and dormitory, continuous silence shall always be observed; likewise in the cloister, at specified hours and places, according to the ancient custom of the monastery laudably observed.” Clement V also mentions it in his Clementine *Ne in agro*. The Council of Mainz, ch. 20: “A monastery ought so to be established that all necessities are provided within the monastery, so that monks, clerics, or girls have no need to wander outside, because this is wholly detrimental to their souls.” Likewise, the aforesaid envoys (that is, delegates or visitors), together with the bishops, shall inspect the buildings of monasteries in various places, to see whether they are suitable and fittingly arranged for the holy profession, and whether they have a strong enclosure in which the souls of those dwelling there may be saved under canonical or regular discipline. The Rule for nuns attributed to St. Jerome (ch. 22): “In the choir of the church appointed for divine praises, in the dormitory, dining-room, cloister, and chapter house, it is not fitting to speak at any time, except what belongs to the purposes for which those places are appointed in the praises of God, so that both time and place may proclaim the holiness of your religious life.” St. Eucherius of Lyons, in a homily to monks: “Our profession in cloisters requires of us that we continually resist our own desires and reprobate wills, and also every impetuosity of carnality and acedia. It is certain that unless we strive daily to fulfill these things and manfully to uproot daily all passions and disobediences, we become far worse in the cloister than we were in the world, and our last state becomes worse than our first.” St. Bernard, in a sermon (*On the Feast of St. Nicholas*, vol. I): “Truly the cloister is paradise. Here are the verdant meadows of the Scriptures; the flowing abundance of tears, which heavenly love distils from the purest affections; here are the most upright trees, the choirs of saints, and none that does not rejoice in abundant fruitfulness,” etc. In Peter the Venerable (*Miracles*, Book I, ch. 13), a monk, when the devil under the guise of an abbot urged him to flee, replied: “I can by no means leave here, because both the prerogative of the cloister and the enclosure of the monastery forbid it, and the multitude of brothers surrounds me.” Then the devil said: “Nor, while you remain here, can I help you in anything. But contrive by any means to cross the bounds of the monastery; once you have done so, I shall immediately be there,” etc. Elsewhere (ch. 17) he records that the monastery of Cluny had two cloisters, a greater and a lesser. Again, in another chapter (ch. 15), among the monastery workshops which the devil could not enter, hindered, as it seemed, by his bulk, he names the chapter house (which is usually in the cloister), then the refectory and dormitory. To these may be added Hugh of Saint Victor (vol. II), who has a notable treatise on the cloister of the soul. Taking occasion from this, he lists twelve abuses of the monastic cloister, which it has seemed not irrelevant to our purpose to set down here: “There are twelve abuses of the cloister by which the entire substance of religion is corrupted: a negligent superior, a disobedient disciple, an idle young man, an obstinate old man, a courtly monk, a litigious monk, costly clothing, exquisite food, noise in the cloister, quarrelling in chapter, disorder in choir, and irreverence at the altar.” Thus Hugh, in imitation of the martyr St. Cyprian, or whatever author is credited with the book *On the Twelve Abuses of This Age*, as the gloss on the said Clementine *Ne in agro* notes. Moreover, sacred canons mention cloisters not only of monks but also of canons or regular clerics, who, after the manner of monks, used a common cloister, refectory, and dormitory, and lived so regularly that their manner of life did not seem inferior to the monastic [Col. 1289D] (see Peter Damian, Book I, epistle 16). Thus the Council of Mainz (ch. 9, vol. III of the Councils, and in Gratian, distinction 32), held under Charlemagne, decrees: “In all things, so far as human frailty permits, we decree that canonical clerics live canonically, observing the teaching of Holy Scripture and the instructions of the holy Fathers, and that they presume to do nothing disorderly without the permission of their bishop or their master. In each bishopric they shall eat and sleep together, remain in their own cloister, and every day at the first hour in the morning come to reading and hear what is commanded them” (see John Molanus, Book I, *On Canons*, ch. 13), etc. To the same purpose is the decree of the Synod of Tours (ch. 23): “We have determined that canons and clerics of cities living in episcopal residences shall dwell in cloisters, all sleep together in one dormitory, and take refreshment together in one refectory, that they may more readily attend the celebration of the canonical hours and be admonished and instructed concerning their life and conduct.” Likewise, the Synod of Aachen (ch. 117) requires the provost of the clergy to surround the cloisters in which they are to live canonically with strong fortifications on every side, so that absolutely no entrance or exit is open except through the gate; inside there must also be dormitories, refectories, cellars, and other dwellings necessary for the shared use of the brethren. Finally, Gratian includes the decree of Leo IX in these words (Causa 12, q. 1): “It is necessary that cloisters be established beside churches, in which clerics may devote themselves to ecclesiastical disciplines. Thus all shall have one refectory and dormitory, and the other workshops necessary for clerical use.” So far the holy Fathers and earlier councils adduced in commendation of the monastic cloister and enclosure, besides whom many further testimonies might be brought from the Council of Trent and elsewhere. From all these it is manifestly clear that the cloister of which we speak is understood in two ways: first, as the whole monastery, from the time when monasteries began to be surrounded and enclosed with walls or a boundary-wall and enclosure was imposed upon monks; concerning this, below. For, as Isidore says (*Etymologies*, Book XV, ch. 6), cloisters are so called because they are shut. For the same reason the bounds by which a monastery is enclosed and fortified are called its precincts. Secondly, it means a part of the monastery, surrounded—as is customary—by a quadrangular circuit of walls, from which even women are excluded, subject to a special enclosure and silence, and dedicated to the brothers’ quiet and contemplation; it is distinguished, as is known, from the oratory or church, refectory, and dormitory. Secondly, the excellent observation of William Durand, bishop of Mende, concerning the cloister, its significance, and its institution, should not be passed over: “The cloister,” he says, “as Richard, bishop of Cremona, says in the *Mitrale*, took its origin from the watch-posts and guards of the Levites around the tabernacle, or from the court of the priests, or from Solomon’s portico at the Temple. For the Lord commanded Moses not to number the Levites with the common multitude, but to appoint them over the tabernacle of testimony to carry and guard it” (Durand, *Rationale*, Book I, ch. 1). Because of this command of the Lord, while the divine mysteries are celebrated, clerics ought to stand in church separated from laypeople. Hence the Council of Mainz, *Extra*, *De vita et honestate clericorum*, ch. 1, decreed that the part separated from the altar by railings be open only to chanting clerics. Further, as the Temple signifies the triumphant Church, so the cloister signifies the heavenly paradise, where there will be one and the same heart in God’s love and will, where all things will be held in common; for what anyone has less of in himself, he will rejoice to have in another, because God will be all in all (1 Cor. VI). Therefore regulars dwelling unanimously in the cloister rise to God’s service, leave secular things behind, and lead a common life in all things. The diversity of workshops and offices in the cloister is the diversity of dwellings with diversity of rewards in the kingdom: ‘For in my Father’s kingdom are many dwellings,’ says the Lord (John IV). Morally, however, the cloister is the soul’s contemplation, where it withdraws, is separated from the crowd of carnal thoughts, and meditates on heavenly things alone. In this cloister are four sides: contempt of self, contempt of the world, love of God, and love of neighbor. Each side has its own row of columns. Contempt of self has humility of mind, affliction of the flesh, humble speech, and the like. The base of all the columns is patience. In this cloister the diversity of workshops is the diversity of virtues; the chapter house is the secret place of the heart; the refectory, love of holy meditation; the cellar, sacred Scripture; the dormitory, a clean conscience; the oratory, an unstained life; the garden of trees and herbs, a collection of virtues; the well of living waters, the irrigation of gifts which here mitigate thirst and in the future extinguish it wholly. Such are the teachings about the cloister and its parts handed down by that pious and learned man, who deserved very well of cloistered religious; would that, God granting, they might follow them. Finally, in connection with this passage there occur matters to be noted and briefly explained which Doctor Navarrus treats more fully in that excellent Commentary *On Regulars*, that is, religious. The first is that the enclosure of religious orders was introduced and imposed not by natural or divine law, as some think, but only by human and positive law. Not by natural law, because they are not bound to it by any precept self-evident in itself or inferred from self-evident principles. Not by divine law, because no command concerning the enclosure of a monastery occurs in all Scripture; nor by a mixture of both, both because then there could never be permission to leave and because all regulars would then be equal to Carthusians and all bound to equal enclosure, which is plainly false. Nor does it object that every regular expressly or implicitly vows stability of place, as is expressly found in the Rule of St. Benedict (ch. 58). For it is one thing to vow stability, another to vow enclosure or confinement. Stability means nothing other than perseverance in one’s profession and state of religion under the obedience due to superiors according to the Rule; it does not necessarily include perpetual enclosure or a promise never to leave the precincts of the monastery, unless this follows from the special institute of a particular order. Navarrus’s second point is that monastic or religious enclosure originated with the earliest monks or anchorites, before the founders of the four principal Rules, commonly called those of Basil, Augustine, Benedict, and Francis; later it was more fully and expressly prescribed and strengthened by the general Council of Nicaea, of which Pope Eugenius speaks in the chapter *Placuit* cited above; by Chalcedon, of which Alexander II speaks in ch. *Juxta*, in the same Causa and question in Gratian; and by the Council of Tarragona, in ch. *Monachi*, also reported there, which forbids monks to leave the monastery, even for its own benefit, without the permission or command of the abbot. That such enclosure had its beginning and origin with the first monks and anchorites, even before the Rules of the holy Fathers just mentioned, may be proved: (1) from Philo the Jew (*On the Contemplative Life*) and Eusebius of Caesarea (Book II, *History*, ch. 116), who, concerning the Alexandrian Therapeutae, or the first monks instituted by St. Mark the Evangelist at Alexandria, record among other things that each of them was accustomed, in his own cell or little dwelling, which they called *semneia* (σεμνεῖα) or *monasteria* (μοναστήρια), to devote himself continuously for the six days of the week to reading and contemplation, not going outside, indeed not even looking outside; but on the seventh day, that is Sunday, to assemble in a common gathering and sit down in fitting dress according to age, etc. (2) From the Rule of St. Pachomius (arts. 3, 30–34, 36, 82), who was plainly older even than Basil, and which contains many articles concerning this enclosure of the monks and nuns of Tabennesi [though Navarrus does not seem to have counted this Rule among the four principal ones, nor is it named by other canonists], especially art. 47: “No one shall have permission either to walk about in the monastery or to proceed outside the monastery wall unless he has asked the superior and that superior has granted it.” And art. 72: “Let no one go outside, let no one speak [supply: outside], let no one remain [outside], except by command of the superior.” These words express the truest definition and description of monastic enclosure, even according to Navarrus. (3) From the example of Abbot Isidore and other ancient Fathers (Sozomen, Book VI, ch. 28; Palladius, ch. 71). Rufinus says of Isidore (*Lives of the Fathers*, Book II, ch. 17): “We saw also in the Thebaid the very famous monastery of Isidore, enclosed by very extensive spaces and surrounded by a wall, in which ample dwellings were provided for the men living there. Within were many wells, irrigated gardens, every kind of fruit tree and tree of paradise, and whatever was necessary for use supplied sufficiently, indeed abundantly, so that none of the monks dwelling within had any need to go outside to seek anything. A grave elderly man, chosen among the foremost, sat at the gate. His duty was to receive newcomers on this condition: those who entered could not thereafter go out. If, therefore, it pleased someone to enter once, the law stood immovably; but, more admirably, not the necessity of law but the blessedness and perfection of life retained those who had entered.” This he relates more copiously and accurately than others who report the same thing (Sozomen, Book VI, ch. 21; Nicephorus, Book XI, ch. 34; Cassiodorus, *Tripartite History*, Book VIII, ch. 1 ff.). (4) Finally, to omit other examples, it may sufficiently be inferred from this passage of Cassian that among Egyptian anchorites and monks too some kind of cloister and enclosure had been observed from ancient custom and ancestral institution, since he says that some of them continually remained hidden in their cells, while others were not at all restrained and enclosed by such cloisters, as will be clearer below. The third point is that this common enclosure, established and confirmed by common law, was also received and approved by those four Fathers of the principal Rules and the later founders of other orders, and endured by their own enactments and institutes in every religious order, though not equally among all, but stricter in some, as among the Carthusians, whose enclosure seems a kind of perpetual prison and may not without reason be compared with that monastery of penitents called the prison, of which John Climacus speaks in step 5 of his *Ladder*. Hence Baptista Mantuanus: ‘Hence eternal silences in Carthusian cloisters.’ In others it is less strict. For, besides the testimonies set forth above concerning the cloister and its antiquity, to prove this from the individual Rules as well, St. Basil, father of Greek monks, frequently inculcates and commends monastic stability and enclosure: first, in the *Longer Rules*, ch. 36, concerning those who withdraw from the society of the other brethren; also ch. 44, concerning whom it ought to be permitted to travel from home abroad; in the *Shorter Rules*, question 120, ‘May one depart anywhere without first seeking leave from the superior?’ Answer: No; and this is a sign of great pride and presumption; in the *Monastic Constitutions*, ch. 8, entitled ‘That a monk ought neither frequently nor rashly to leave the monastery’; and in the following chapter, where he teaches that those wandering and vagabond monks are to be avoided who repeatedly and unsteadily change place, now joining these brethren, now those, etc. Navarrus proves that St. Augustine likewise imposed this enclosure on regular clerics or canons, because, he says, the Rule of Augustine plainly signifies it, though it is the most lenient of all, according to ch. *Quod Dei timorem*, *De statu monachorum*: both at its beginning, where it presupposes that his canons must be established in a monastery, gathered into one body, and be in one house; in calling their dwelling a monastery eight times; and in commanding in ch. 10: ‘Let them not go to the baths, or wherever it is necessary to go, in fewer than two or three; and one who needs to go somewhere must go with those whom the superior commands him to go with.’ Likewise by that passage in ch. 8: ‘When you go out, walk together; when you have arrived where you are going, stand together’; and by Hugh’s apt remark on the said ch. 10, ‘he must go with those whom the superior commands him to go with,’ namely, so that the superior may provide for the person’s safety and the virtue of obedience may be preserved in the subject. Thus Navarrus on the Rule of St. Augustine. Further, no fewer or less important supports for monastic enclosure are found in the Rule of our most holy Father Benedict. First, when it expressly prescribes that stability be professed in the profession itself (ch. 58): ‘The one to be received,’ it says, ‘shall promise in the oratory before all concerning his stability, knowing that it is established by law that from that day he is not permitted to leave the monastery or shake his neck free from beneath the yoke of the Rule,’ etc. For although enclosure is not necessarily included in the notion of stability, as has been said, it is referred to it insofar as it is contained under religious obedience, or insofar as it is lawfully imposed and prescribed according to the Rule. Thus St. Bernard, epistle 7: ‘Show yourself so stable in place that you do not disdain to be subject to the abbot; so obey the abbot as a subject that you do not lose stability of place.’ And Turrecremata on that passage of the Rule: ‘By stability the monk is understood to be bound not to abandon monastic life in any way, nor to leave the monastery without necessity and the authority of his superior.’ Secondly, when it makes such careful provision concerning the monastery’s doorkeeper or porter in ch. 67: ‘At the gate of the monastery let a wise old man be placed, who knows how to receive and give an answer. He should have a cell beside the gate, so that those arriving always find him present,’ etc. Thirdly, when it adds in the same place, doubtless imitating the Isidore mentioned above: ‘If possible, the monastery ought to be so constructed that all necessities—water, mill, garden, bakery, or various crafts—are carried on within the monastery, so that monks have no need to wander outside, because this is wholly detrimental to their souls.’ Fourthly, when, in the next chapter, speaking of brethren going on a journey, it says: ‘Brethren who are to be sent on the road should commend themselves to the prayer of all the brethren or of the abbot.’ And below: ‘Let no one presume to tell others whatever he has seen or heard outside the monastery, because it is very destructive. If anyone presumes to do so, let him be subject to regular punishment. Likewise anyone who presumes to leave the cloisters of the monastery, or to go anywhere, or to do anything, however small, without the abbot’s command.’ The same purpose is served by what Rule ch. 51 establishes concerning brethren travelling not very far: ‘Brethren who go out on any errand and expect to return to the monastery that same day must not presume to eat outside, even if they are earnestly invited by anyone, unless perhaps their abbot commands them,’ etc. To these may be added St. Bernard, a distinguished imitator of St. Benedict, whose notable saying is: ‘Monasteries are rightly compared to ponds, where fish, as it were imprisoned, have no freedom to wander’ (*Sermon on St. Andrew*). Finally, the last Rule of St. Francis, confirmed by Honorius III and numbered among the approved Rules, did not omit this law and prescription of enclosure, since it decrees that even permission to preach and to go out to convert unbelievers must be sought from ministers and superiors (chs. 9, 12). But enough has now been said concerning the cloister and enclosure of monks. For the enclosure of nuns, see Navarrus in the place cited above.]

When they come to these squalid places in which we dwell, or to those Scytiotic regions,

[Note: [Col. 1294C] Three of the more celebrated deserts, or solitudes, frequented by those anchorites are designated here: Calamus, otherwise called Porphyrion; the Thebaid, or Thebaïs; and Scetis, or Scetic, or Scytiotic, as it is called here. In these places there were various monastic institutions and different ways of life among the anchorites and monks. Some remained almost constantly within their cells and enclosed there, except on the days when they had to go out to the assembly or church; they maintained perpetual silence and devoted themselves privately, at fixed hours and times, to prayer, meditation, reading, and manual labor. Others, although living in deserts and secluded places, were not so strictly or continually confined within their enclosures and cells as is stated here; rather, they often went out to cities and other places, and even devoted themselves in season to agriculture, gathering fruit, and harvesting grain, thereby procuring food both for themselves and for others, since most of them were laymen and occupied with no other functions, as has been said elsewhere and is evident both from this passage and from others frequently noted.]

They are so tormented by such violent surges of thought and such great anxiety of mind that, like inexperienced men who have never even lightly undergone the exercises of solitude, they cannot endure the confinement of the cell or the silence of repose. Immediately shaken out of them, they are thrown into confusion like men unaccustomed and newly initiated.

For they have not learned, through continual watchfulness and persevering concentration, to quiet the movements of the inner person or to confront the storms of their thoughts. Every day, sweating over their open-air labors, they move about all day beneath the empty sky—not only in body but also in mind—and scatter their thoughts everywhere into the open along with the mobility of their bodies. Consequently, they perceive the fickle emptiness of their minds and cannot restrain its slippery wanderings. Unable to endure compunction of spirit, they regard the continual duration of their silence as intolerable; and, though tireless in arduous rural labor, they are overcome by idleness and wearied by the length of their repose.

## CHAPTER V  
### That anxiety of heart is burdened rather than relieved by bodily wandering

Nor is it surprising if someone sitting in his cell, as though within a very narrow enclosure, is suffocated by a multitude of anxieties when his collected thoughts burst forth from the prison of his dwelling and immediately rush in different directions like unbridled horses.

But when, for the moment, they wander away from their own stalls, a certain brief or melancholy consolation is at once obtained. When, however, the body returns to its own cell and the whole crowd of thoughts again rushes back, as it were, to its proper seat, the very habit of its long-established license arouses still more grievous goads.

Thus those who are not yet able—or are unwilling—to resist the impulses of their own desires, when acedia attacks their unaccustomed hearts with greater violence and they become distressed within the cell, will, if they grant themselves the freedom to go out frequently by relaxing the strictness of the rule, bring upon themselves through this supposed remedy a sharper disease. It is like those who think that they can extinguish the force of internal fevers by drinking the coldest water, although it is certainly clear that the fire is thereby kindled rather than calmed, since that momentary relief is followed by a much heavier affliction.

## CHAPTER VI  
### He demonstrates by an illustration how a monk ought to guard his thoughts

For this reason, the whole attention of the monk must always be fixed upon one thing, and the beginnings and circuits of all his thoughts must be energetically recalled to that same point—that is, to the memory of God.

It is as though someone wishing to enclose the vault of an apse above were continually to draw the line of its most subtle center around it, and, according to the most certain rule, to bring together the entire equality of its circular form and the discipline of its construction.

[Note: [Col. 1294D] Concerning *abside* or *apside*, I approve Ciaconius’s annotation, which I neither wish to deprive of its proper credit nor to withhold from the reader, while adding whatever else occurs to me from other sources. “Absis,” he says, “in Greek ἀψίς, signifies a vault or arch. Dio.: ἀψίστε τροπαιοφόρος ᾠκοδομήθη, that is, ‘a vault, or triumphal arch, was erected.’ Saint Jerome, in his commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians, Book 2: ‘Did he pass through and transcend the circles of the heavens, which philosophers call spheres, and stand at the summit of the vault of heaven—or, to use the very word, the apse?’ It also signifies a dome or chamber constructed in the form of a hemisphere. For Hesychius and Suidas report that ἀψίδες means καμάρας, ‘chambers.’ Pliny uses the word several times in Book 2 for the orbits of the planets. Cassian, in this passage, accordingly says ‘the chamber of the apse,’ just as elsewhere (Book 5 of the *Institutes*, chapter 24, and Conference 21, chapter 29) he says ‘the station of fasting,’ where *station* means the same as fasting, just as *apse* means chamber. Thus Ciaconius.

“Isidore calls it *absida* (*Etymologies*, Book 15, chapter 8): ‘Absida, in Greek speech, is translated into Latin as “bright,” because, having received light, it shines back through the arch.’ But whether we should say *absidam* or *absidem*, some learned men consider the form of the word ambiguous. Caelius Rhodiginus, Book 28: ‘The Greeks call *absides* what the Latins call arches customarily raised for emperors. The vaults of bridges are also designated by the same name.’ Onuphrius (*Antiquae Lectiones*, chapter 10), in his explanation of ecclesiastical terms: ‘An apse, or *apsis*, is the curvature of a wheel—that is, the wood extending over the wheels and supporting the ladders, or the part in which the spokes are fixed, or the wooden circumference of a wheel. In this sense others aspirate the initial letter and say *hapsis*, from ἅπτειν, “to touch,” because, when the wheel turns, that part touches the earth. By this name the curvature of a vault, and sometimes the entire vault, is also signified. Hence ecclesiastical writers call what we call the tribune of churches a *hapsis*. Thus Onuphrius.”]

But whoever attempts to complete it without examining that midpoint, however great his confidence in skill or talent, cannot preserve the equality of its circuit without error. Nor can he perceive merely by sight how much he has taken away through his mistake from the beauty of its true circular form, unless he continually returns to that standard of truth and, correcting the inner and outer circumference of his work according to its judgment, confines a structure of such lofty magnitude by the rule of a single point.

So too, unless our mind continually revolves the love of the Lord alone, fixed immovably like a center, through every moment of our works and undertakings, and with the trustworthy compass—as I might call it—of love either fits together or rejects the quality of all thoughts, it will in no way construct with reliable skill the structure of that spiritual craft of which Paul is the architect.

[Note: [Col. 1296D] “According to the grace of God that was given to me, like a wise architect I laid a foundation,” says the Apostle. See Saint Thomas in his Commentary.]

Nor will it possess the beauty of that house which blessed David, desiring to offer it to the Lord in his heart, says he loved: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells” (Psalm 25). Rather, it will foolishly raise up in its heart a house unbecoming and unworthy of the Holy Spirit, one destined immediately to collapse; and instead of being glorified by the hospitality of its blessed inhabitant, it will be mournfully crushed beneath the ruin of its own construction.

## CHAPTER VII  
### The question why the close habitation of relatives was thought harmful to us, although it did not harm those living in Egypt

[Col. 1295C]

Germanus: The kind of work that can be practiced within the cell is prescribed by a sufficiently useful and necessary discipline. Indeed, not only has the usefulness of this practice often been demonstrated to us, founded as it is upon the example of your blessedness and imitation of apostolic virtues, but our own experience has also borne witness to it.

But it is not sufficiently clear why the proximity of relatives, which you yourselves have not rejected too severely, ought to be avoided by us so greatly. For we see that you, proceeding irreproachably along the whole path of perfection, not only remain in your own regions but have not withdrawn far from certain of your villages. Why, then, should what is not harmful to you be considered opposed to us?

## CHAPTER VIII  
### The answer: that not everything is suitable for everyone
Abraham: Sometimes we see examples of evils arising from good things. For if someone undertakes the same actions without the same disposition and purpose, or with a different virtue, he certainly incurs a snare of deception and death precisely where others acquire the fruits of eternal life. That strong-handed boy, matched in combat against that most warlike giant, would likewise undoubtedly have suffered this fate if he had been dressed in Saul’s manly [Lipsius, in the margin: “mighty”] and very powerful armor; and the weapons by which a more robust age would have struck down countless enemy troops could have brought him certain destruction at the outset, unless by prudent discernment he had chosen kinds of arms suited to his youth and had been armed against that most terrifying enemy not with the breastplate and shield with which he saw the others equipped, but with the weapons with which he himself was able to fight (1 Samuel XVII).

[Note: The words of the sacred history (1 Samuel XVII): “Saul clothed David in his own garments, placed a bronze helmet upon his head, and clothed him with a breastplate. David therefore girded on his sword over his garment and began to try whether, armed, he could walk; for he had no experience. And David said to Saul: ‘I cannot walk in this way, because I have not used it.’ And he took them off and took his staff, which he always had in his hands,” etc. By this example, and by other most beautiful arguments and comparisons, the Author teaches here that not everything is suitable for everyone, and that each person must measure his own strength, lest he rashly and without deliberation undertake something which he is unable to accomplish.]

Therefore each of us ought first to weigh carefully the measure of his own strength and, according to that measure, undertake whatever discipline he wishes; for although all disciplines are useful, not all can be suitable for everyone. We do not, merely because withdrawal (*anachōrēsis*) is good, judge it suitable for everyone. Many find it not only unfruitful but even harmful. Nor, merely because we rightly profess the institution of coenobitic monasteries and the care of the brethren to be holy and praiseworthy, do we therefore think that everyone should pursue it.

The fruit of the hospice, too, is exceedingly abundant, but it cannot be sought by everyone without injury to patience. First, then, the practices of your region and of this one must be weighed against each other; next, the strength of individuals—acquired through the continual practice either of virtues or of vices—must be carefully balanced against it on different scales. For it can happen that what is arduous and impossible for a person of one nation has, through an ingrained custom, in some way become nature for others. Thus certain peoples, separated by immense differences in climate, endure great force of cold or the heat of the sun without bodily covering; yet others who have not experienced that harshness of climate cannot withstand it, however strong they may be.

So you, who with the utmost exertion of mind and body are trying, at least in this region, to oppose in many respects what is almost the nature of your homeland, should carefully consider whether in those sluggish regions—as the report has it—and, so to speak, bound by the cold of excessive unbelief, you can sustain this “nakedness,” as I may call it. For the ancient practice of holy conduct has implanted this strength of purpose in our people in a manner almost natural. If you see yourselves equal to their steadfastness and virtue, you ought likewise not to flee the proximity of your parents and brethren.

## CHAPTER IX. The mortification of Abbot Apollo

That you may be able to measure the extent of your strength with a suitable assessment and a strict test, I shall briefly relate to you an action of a certain old man, namely Abbot Apollo, so that, if the innermost examination of your heart judges you not inferior to his purpose and virtue, you may undertake residence in your homeland and proximity to your parents without loss of progress or danger to your profession—confident that the severity of this humility, which in this province not only your will but also the necessity of your pilgrimage forces upon you, cannot be overcome by affection for relatives or by the pleasures of places.

[Note: This has been discussed elsewhere (Conferences 2.13). Palladius uses the same word as indeclinable: “We saw,” he says, “in the desert a man named Apollo, who had monasteries upon a mountain. He was father of about five hundred monks, and was very famous and celebrated in the Thebaid; his works were great, and through him the Lord performed great deeds and many remarkable signs, and so forth.” Sozomen, speaking of the monks living in the Thebaid, says: “Among their number was also Apollo, who lived in the Thebaid. When he began to reach manhood, he devoted himself to the monastic life. After living in the desert for about forty years, he was commanded by a divine oracle to occupy a cave at the foot of a certain mountain, near places inhabited by human beings. Because of the multitude of his miracles, he soon acquired great renown and presided over very many monks. For he employed disciplines so useful for life that he attracted many,” and so forth (Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 29; Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 34; Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 25).]

When his brother came to this old man in the dead of night, begging him to leave his monastery for a short while and help pull out an ox which, as he lamentably reported, was stuck at a distance in marshy mud—for he could by no means extract it alone—Abbot Apollo, after the man had pleaded persistently, said:

“Why did you not ask our younger brother, whom, as you passed by, you had nearer to you than me?”

The man, thinking that Apollo had forgotten that his brother had long ago been buried and that, through excessive continence and prolonged solitude, he had become almost deranged, replied: “How could I call upon one who died fifteen years ago and had already been buried?”

Abbot Apollo said:

[Note: This saying is also famous in canon law: “Monks are dead to the world,” especially in the decree of Pope Eugenius preserved by Gratian (2, question 7, chapters *Placuit* and *Nullus*, and 26, question 1, chapter *Placuit*, and chapter *Sunt nonnulli*), where it says: “Let a monk be content with his cloister, because just as a fish without water lacks life, so a monk without a monastery does. Let him therefore sit in solitude and be silent, because he is dead to the world but lives to God.” Cassian likewise confirms the same point through the likeness of a crucified man in Book IV of the *Institutes*, chapter 34: “Renunciation,” he says, “is nothing other than a sign of the cross and of mortification. Therefore know”—he addresses the monk who has made his profession—“that from this day you are dead to this world, to its actions and desires; and that, according to the Apostle, you are crucified to this world and this world to you. Consider, therefore, the conditions of the cross, under whose sacrament you must henceforth live in this light; for you no longer live, but he lives in you who was crucified for you,” and so forth. And in the following chapter: “Thus,” he says, “we who are crucified by the fear of the Lord ought to be dead to all these things—that is, not only to bodily vices but also to the elements themselves.” See Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 83, where Abbot Serapion proved by a remarkable example—whether one capable of imitation, I do not know—that a certain nun was not truly dead to the world, as she claimed.]

“Do you not know, then, that I too died to this world twenty years ago, and that I can no longer offer you from the tomb of this cell any assistance concerning the condition of the present life? Christ does not permit me to relax even slightly from the purpose of the mortification I have undertaken in order to pull out your ox—not even for the briefest interval, since he did not grant a delay for the burial of one’s father (Luke VII), although that burial could certainly have been performed much more quickly, honorably, and religiously.”

Examine, then, now the secrets of your hearts, and wisely judge whether you too can continually preserve such severity of mind while living near your parents. When you have found yourselves to be like him in this mortification of spirit, then know that the proximity of your parents and brethren likewise will not be harmful to you: that is, although they are close at hand, you should regard yourselves as dead to them, so that you neither permit them to be comforted by your consolations nor allow yourselves to be released by their services.

## CHAPTER X. The question whether it harms a monk if his parents supply him with what he needs

Germanus: On this point you have plainly left no room for further uncertainty. We are indeed certain that we cannot practice in their vicinity either the poverty of our present condition or these daily barefoot exercises.

[Note: On what “barefoot exercises” (*nudipedalia*) are, see Conference 17.20 (see Molanus, *On Paintings*, chapter 82). From this passage it may also be inferred that those monks went barefoot and practiced barefoot exercises. We have discussed this elsewhere as well (Book I of the *Institutes*, chapter 10).]

Nor could we provide there, even with similar labor, what is necessary for food, as here we are compelled to bring water upon our shoulders from three miles away. Neither our own sense of shame nor theirs would permit us to do these things openly before them.

But what harm would it do to our purpose if, with them supplying everything, we—entirely freed from the anxiety of procuring food—devoted ourselves only to reading and prayer, so that, once the labor by which we are now distracted had been removed, we might keep more earnestly at spiritual pursuits?

## CHAPTER XI. A response drawn from the judgment of the blessed Antony

Abraham: I shall set before you on this matter not my own judgment but that of the blessed Antony. He refuted the negligence of a certain brother who, in the lethargy you describe, was sunk in sluggishness, and in doing so cut through the knot of your proposal.

A certain man came, as I have said, to the man mentioned above and declared that the anachoretic discipline was not at all worthy of admiration. He pronounced it a greater virtue if someone practiced what belongs to perfection among human beings than if he did so while living in the desert. The blessed Antony asked him where he himself lived.

When the man replied that he lived near his parents and, because they provided for him, was freed from every care and anxiety of daily [Lipsius, in the margin: “prolonged”] labor, and boasted that he devoted himself continually to reading and prayer alone, without that distraction of spirit, the blessed Antony again said:

“Tell me, son, whether you grieve over their losses or misfortunes and likewise rejoice over their prosperity.”

He confessed that he shared in both experiences. The old man said to him:

“Know that in the future age you will also be reckoned according to the lot of those with whom in this life you are shaken either by profit or loss, by joy or sorrow.”

Nor was the blessed Antony content with this judgment. He entered upon a still broader field of discussion, saying:

“This way of life and this exceedingly tepid condition harm you not only through the loss I have mentioned—although you yourself do not perceive it, saying, in a manner echoing that proverb of Solomon [Proverbs XXIII], ‘They struck me, but I was not hurt; they mocked me, but I did not know it,’ or what is said in the prophet [Hosea VII], ‘Strangers have devoured his strength, and he did not know it’—namely, because by changing your mind each day according to the variety of events, they continually drag you down to earthly things.

“They also deprive you of the fruit of your hands and of the just reward of your own labor, since, by supporting you through their provision, they do not permit you, according to the rule of the blessed Apostle, to prepare your daily sustenance with your own hands. When he delivered his final commands to the leaders of the Church of Ephesus, although occupied with the holy work of preaching the Gospel, he recalls that he supplied not only himself but also those who were hindered by necessary services in his ministry, saying: ‘You yourselves know that these hands ministered to my needs and to those who were with me’ (Acts XX).

“Yet, to show that he did this as a model for our usefulness, he says elsewhere: ‘We were not idle among you, nor did we eat anyone’s bread without paying for it, but in labor and toil we worked night and day, so that we might not burden any of you—not because we lacked the right, but in order to give you an example for imitation’ (2 Thessalonians III).”

## CHAPTER XII. The usefulness of work and the harm of idleness

And so, even though the support of our parents was not lacking, we preferred this nakedness to all resources. We chose to prepare our daily bodily nourishment by our own sweat rather than to be sustained by the secure provision of our parents, preferring this most laborious poverty to the idle meditation on Scripture and the unproductive persistence in reading that you praise.

We would unquestionably pursue that way most willingly if apostolic authority had handed it down as more useful by its own examples, or if the salutary institutions of the elders had established it as such. But know that you suffer no less a loss from this than from the one we mentioned above: for although you possess a healthy and robust body, you are sustained by another’s alms, which have rightly been assigned only to the weak.

For, apart from that one class of monks who, according to the Apostle’s command, live by the daily labor of their hands, the entire human race expects *agape* from another’s work.

[Note: *Agape* derives its name from charity. For among the Greeks *agapē* (ἀγάπη) means “love” or “charity,” from the verb *agapaō* (ἀγαπάω), “I love” or “I cherish.” Among ancient and Christian writers this word is used in two ways, generally and specifically. In the general sense it means the duty of charity, or almsgiving and assistance bestowed upon one’s neighbors, especially the poor, as in Tertullian’s *To the Martyrs*: “Let us compare the way of life in the world with that of the prison: if the spirit gains more in prison than the flesh loses, indeed, the flesh does not lose what is proper to it through the care of the Church and the *agape* of the brethren”—that is, even martyrs confined in prison are not deprived of what is necessary for bodily sustenance through the care and concern of the Church and the *agape* of the brethren, namely, the alms of the faithful.

“So also the blessed Cyprian, Book III of the *Testimonies*, chapter 3: ‘The *agape* and brotherly love must be practiced religiously and firmly.’ And Abbot Joseph, Conference 16.14: ‘This charity, which is called *agape*, can be shown by everyone.’ Hence the frequent expression in Saint Ephrem, ‘to make *agapes*’ (ἀγάπας ποιεῖν). It was a phrase among the ancient Christians when they entertained one another at a meal: they would say that they were making charity together, meaning that they were eating food together. This manner of speaking is also used by Italians and other nations and languages.
