“It is in this sense that *agape* is understood here, when it is said that whoever does not live according to the Apostle’s command—mentioned elsewhere [Book X of the *Institutes*]—by the daily labor of his hands awaits the *agape* of another’s work. To await the *agape* of another’s work is the same as being sustained by another’s alms, as he said above. In this sense he says that even the kings of the world are sustained by *agape*, that is, by the help and support of others.

“Elsewhere *agape* is used more narrowly for a small dinner or sacred banquet which wealthy Christians in the primitive Church, especially on solemn days, offered charitably to the poor. The blessed Clement testifies that this began in the time of the Apostles in his letter to James, the brother of the Lord. Hence the Apostle Jude also used the same word in his Catholic Epistle; the Latin translator rendered ἐν ταῖς ἀγάπαις ὑμῶν as *in your charities* (Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 39), meaning ‘at the banquets which you provide for the refreshment of the poor.’

“Tertullian describes this kind of dinner or banquet more fully in these words: ‘Our dining room alone is criticized; our dinner makes its own explanation by its name. It is called *agape*, which among the Greeks means love. However great the expense, it is gain to spend in the name of piety, since by this refreshment we also help the needy. If the reason for the banquet is honorable, judge the rest of its order from that reason and determine what belongs to the duty of religion. It admits nothing disgraceful, nothing immodest. No one reclines before prayer has been tasted beforehand. Food is eaten only in the quantity hunger can contain; drink only in the quantity useful to the chaste. They are so satisfied that they remember they must worship God even during the night; they converse as people who know that God is listening,’ and so forth.

“In the Council of Gangra, held in the time of Constantine against despisers of such *agapes*, this decree is recorded: ‘If anyone despises those who faithfully provide *agapes*, that is, banquets for the poor, and summon the brethren for God’s honor, and refuses to participate in such invitations, let him be anathema.’

“The blessed Augustine, Book XX against Faustus, chapter 20, says: ‘Our *agapes* feed the poor, whether with grain or with meat.’ Since in the time of the blessed Jerome certain wealthy widows did these things more for boasting and display than for charity and piety, Jerome rebuked them in his letter to Eustochium: ‘When they extend a hand to the needy, they sound a trumpet; when they invite someone to an *agape*, a herald is hired.’ Thus the blessed Jerome alludes to Matthew VI: ‘When you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues.’

“More on this may be found in Baronius, first volume of the *Annals* (Year 57), where he teaches that such *agapes* were ordinarily celebrated for three reasons. In their place came what we today call the table of the poor; we have noted above that it was also formerly called by another name, a *diaconia* (Conference 21.1 and 8).]

Accordingly, not only those who boast of themselves, or of their parents’ resources, or of their servants’ labor, or of the produce of their estates, but even the kings of this world are certainly sustained by *agape*. The definition of our predecessors finally declares: “Whatever is spent on the necessity of daily food, if it has not been produced and obtained by the work of our hands, must be referred to *agape*.” This accords with the Apostle, who strictly forbids aid from another’s generosity to the idle: “If anyone does not work, neither let him eat” (2 Thessalonians III).

The blessed Antony used these words against a certain man and also instructed us through the example of his teaching, so that we might avoid the most dangerous flatteries of our parents, the *agape* of all who supply what is necessary for food, and even every pleasure afforded by a pleasant dwelling. We should prefer to all the resources of this world the barren sands, bitter by nature, and regions scorched by a salty inundation and therefore subject to the right and dominion of no human being. Thus we would avoid not only the crowds of people by means of an impassable solitude, but also the temptation arising from the fertility of the soil to become absorbed in any kind of cultivation, through which the mind, distracted from its principal watchfulness over the heart, would be rendered sterile for spiritual pursuits.

## CHAPTER XIII. The story composed by Abbot Macarius about the barber’s earnings, for recognizing the devil’s deceptions

Since you are confident that you can also save others and are hastening to revisit your homeland in hope of greater profit, hear as well a story of Abbot Macarius, most delightfully and suitably fashioned, which he offered as a remedy through a most timely narrative to a man burning with desires similar to yours.

[Note: The matter concerning the Macarii has been discussed up to this point.]

“There was,” he said, “in a certain city a very skilled barber who, charging three denarii for shaving each person, acquired a small and cheap payment for his work and from this same amount obtained each day what was necessary for his support. After all his bodily needs had been met, he put one hundred denarii into his purse each day.

[Note: On the denarius and the solidus, which are mentioned here, see Book IV of the *Institutes*, chapter 14, and Book V, chapter 38.]

“But when he had continually amassed this income, he heard that in a certain distant city each person paid the barber one solidus. When he learned this, he said: ‘How long shall I be content with this poverty, laboriously seeking a payment of three denarii, when I can go there and gather wealth from an enormous income in solidi?’

“Accordingly, he immediately took the tools of his trade and, spending on the journey everything he had saved here over a long period, reached that highly profitable city with great labor. On the very day he entered, he received from each person the payment for his work according to what he had heard. Seeing toward evening that he had collected a large number of solidi, he happily went to the market to buy the food necessary for his refreshment.

“But when he began to purchase it at the high price of solidi, he spent on his very meager sustenance all the solidi he had acquired and brought home not even a single denarius of profit. When he saw that his earnings were being consumed day after day, so that he not only saved nothing but could scarcely meet even the necessity of daily subsistence, he reflected to himself and said:

“‘I shall return to my own city and resume that very small income from which, after all my bodily needs had been met, a daily surplus provided me with something that could accumulate for the support of my old age. Though it seemed small and slight, it nevertheless produced a considerable sum through continual increase. That profit in coins was more profitable for me than this imaginary profit in solidi, from which nothing remains for me to store away, and by which scarcely even the necessity of daily food is sustained.

“‘Therefore it is better for us to pursue with unbroken constancy this very small fruit of solitude, which no worldly cares, no worldly distractions, no exaltation of vainglory and vanity can gnaw away, and which no anxieties of daily necessity can diminish. For “a little with justice is better than great riches of sinners” (Psalm XXXVI).’”

[Note: The Vulgate edition reads: “Better is a handful with rest than both hands full with labor and affliction of spirit” (Ecclesiastes IV). Compare the similar passage in Proverbs XVI: “Better is a little with justice than many fruits with iniquity.”]

“Indeed, according to Solomon’s judgment, one handful with rest is better than two handfuls with labor and presumption of spirit” (Ecclesiastes IV).

All the weak are necessarily entangled in such deceptions and losses when, while still uncertain even about their own salvation, they themselves continue to need the instruction and teaching of another.

[Note: This refers to what Germanus had said above (chapter 1): “Moreover, we nourished our spirit with the hope of empty joys, believing that we would receive a very great fruit from the conversion of many, who would supposedly be directed toward the way of salvation by our example and exhortations.” The abbot calls this a diabolical deception, and rightly so. The blessed Bernard, in Sermon 64 on the *Song of Songs*, on the words “Catch us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards” (Song of Songs II), teaches that this is a most dangerous temptation. Like a little fox, it repeatedly deceives monks who are otherwise making progress and demolishes and overturns their spiritual advancement. He depicts it excellently in these words:

“Evil powers—that is, demons—do not dare openly to oppose the holier pursuits of those who are making progress, but they usually lie in ambush secretly, like certain deceitful little foxes: in appearance, virtues; in reality, vices. How many people entering upon the paths of life, advancing toward better things, progressing and advancing safely and confidently along the paths of righteousness, have I experienced being shamefully tripped up by the fraud of these foxes and, too late, lamenting that the fruits of their virtues had been strangled within them!

“I saw a man running well. Then came a thought—why should it not have been a little fox?—saying: ‘What a great good this is, which I alone enjoy! If I were in my homeland, I could certainly share it with my brothers, relatives, acquaintances, and friends. They love me and would readily listen to my advice. Why this waste? I shall go there and save many of them, and myself as well. There is no need to fear a change of place. For while I do good, what difference does it make where I am? Indeed, would it not certainly be better there, where I shall live more fruitfully?’

“What more need be said? He goes, and the wretched man perishes—not so much an exile returning to his homeland as a dog returning to its vomit. The unhappy man lost himself and gained none of his own. There is one little fox: that deceptive hope he had of gaining his relatives.

“You too can find or notice in yourself, by yourself, other similar foxes, one after another, if you do not neglect to do so. But do you want me to show you one more? Sometimes, when a person who is making good progress feels that something of heavenly grace has been more abundantly sprinkled upon him, the desire to preach enters his mind—not, indeed, to parents and relatives, in accordance with the words, ‘I did not immediately consult flesh and blood’ (Galatians I), but as though more purely, more fruitfully, and more powerfully, everywhere to strangers and to everyone.

“Be very cautious. He fears incurring the prophetic curse: ‘Let him who has received grain in secret hide it among the peoples’ (Proverbs XI), and acting contrary to the Gospel by failing to preach upon the housetops what he has heard in the ear (Matthew X). It is a fox, and more harmful than the former because it comes more secretly. But I shall catch it for you.

“Moses first says: ‘You shall not plow with the firstborn of an ox’ (Deuteronomy XV). Paul, interpreting this, says: ‘Not a novice, lest, being lifted up with pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil’ (1 Timothy III). And again: ‘No one takes this honor upon himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was’ (Hebrews V). He himself also says: ‘How shall they preach unless they are sent?’ (Romans X).

“We know that the duty of a monk is not to teach but to mourn. From these and similar passages I weave a net for myself and catch the fox, lest it destroy the vineyard. From these things it is clear and certain that public preaching is not suitable for a monk, is not expedient for a novice, and is not permitted to one who has not been sent. And how great a destruction of conscience it is to violate all three of these conditions!

“Therefore, whatever such a suggestion may be in the mind—whether it is your own thought or an impulse introduced by an evil angel—recognize the deceitful little fox, that is, evil under the appearance of good.”

This is what the blessed Bernard says. Similar material may be found in Cassian, Book XI of the *Institutes*, chapters 14 and 15, where he treats the vice of vainglory, by which monks are repeatedly urged to preach.

To this may be added the well-known saying of the blessed Jerome, which the blessed Bernard also had in mind: “The office of a monk is not that of a teacher but of one who mourns, so that he may mourn either himself or the world and await with fear the coming of the Lord” (in Gratian, 16, question 1).

However, none of these statements is intended, nor should they be understood, as though the office of holy preaching were either unlawful for monks or foreign to their institution—provided that it is undertaken and exercised properly and lawfully. For, as Gratian correctly responds to these and similar testimonies of the holy Fathers, either the Fathers are speaking of monks who were not clerics but laymen, who are often mentioned as being forbidden by law to preach; or they distinguish between clerics and monks according to the proper office and state of each, and show what is suitable to each according to his proper office.

For one thing is appropriate to a monk insofar as he is a monk, and another insofar as he is a cleric. Insofar as he is a monk, his office is to mourn his own sins and those of others; insofar as he is a cleric, it is to teach and feed the people. Thus Gratian writes (Distinction 23, chapter *Mulier*, and 16, question 1, chapter *Adjicimus*).

Or, according to others, the Fathers forbid monks to wander outside their monasteries on their own authority—or rather, in their rashness—under the pretext of preaching or of another office. They forbid them, without the authority of bishops and lawful formation, ecclesiastical commission, or another concession of the law, to seek or usurp the task of preaching or other ministries pertaining to the care of souls.

Finally, they intend to teach that a monk should not desire or seek the office of preaching, but should undertake it only at the command of a superior and by lawful calling or mission, and that in both accepting and exercising it he should carefully avoid that little fox of vainglory. Its characteristic, according to the blessed Augustine (Rule, chapter 4), is to lie in wait for every good work, especially works of honor performed publicly, so that they may perish, whereas every other form of iniquity operates in evil works so that they may be done. See the blessed Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, Part I, chapter 7, Part III, chapter 26, and Homily 2 on Ezekiel.

Thus the blessed Bernard explains himself when he says: “Public preaching is not suitable for a monk”—namely, with respect to his state and monastic profession; “it is not expedient for a novice or neophyte”—that is, on account of age, learning, and perfection, because of the danger of presumptuous vanity; “nor is it permitted to one who has not been sent”—that is, one who has not been lawfully called and appointed to that office (Bernard, as cited above). Gratian gathers many praises of the holy Fathers and decrees of supreme pontiffs and councils in support of this position.

Among them is the statement of Pope Boniface (Cause 16, question 1, chapter *Sunt nonnulli*), which applies especially to the Benedictines:

“Some people, supported by no doctrine and inflamed by an exceedingly bold zeal of bitterness rather than of love, assert that monks, because they are dead to the world and live to God, are unworthy of the power of the priestly office. But they are entirely mistaken. For the blessed Benedict, the gracious teacher of monks, in no way prohibited this; he merely decreed that they should be free from secular affairs. This is commanded with the greatest force not only to monks but also to canons by apostolic documents and the institutions of the holy Fathers. We, instructed by the examples of so many Fathers, believe that, with God working through them, priest-monks can worthily perform the office of binding and loosing, if they should worthily be elevated to this ministry.”

This is the Pope’s statement. From it the blessed Thomas concludes (2–2, question 187, article 1) that monks and other religious persons may not, by reason of their state, preach, teach, baptize, absolve, or perform similar acts, because the religious state does not give them authority to do these things. Nevertheless, they can perform them if they receive ordination and ordinary jurisdiction, or through a commission or privilege such as has been granted to the mendicant orders with respect to confession and preaching.]

All who are exceedingly weak, being still uncertain even about their own salvation and themselves still needing another’s instruction and training, are necessarily entangled in such deceptions and losses when they are urged by diabolical deceptions to convert and govern others; even if they are able to gain some profit from the conversion of certain people, they lose whatever they have acquired through their impatience and undisciplined conduct.

What the prophet Haggai describes will happen to them: “He who gathers wages puts them into a pierced purse” (Haggai I). Indeed, the person who loses through the intemperance of his heart and the daily distraction of his mind whatever he seems to acquire through the conversion of others stores his profits in a pierced purse.

Thus it will happen that, while they believe they can obtain greater profits by instructing others, they will also be deprived of their own correction.

[Note: The Vulgate edition reads: “There is one who is as rich though he possesses nothing, and one who is as poor though he has great riches” (Proverbs XIII).]

“For there are those who present themselves as rich while possessing nothing, and those who humble themselves amid great riches” (Proverbs XIII).

[Note: The Vulgate text reads: “Better is the poor man who is sufficient for himself than the glorious man who lacks bread.” Bede explains it as follows: “Better is the unlearned and simple man who, practicing the good things he knows, merits life in heaven than one who, distinguished by knowledge of Scripture or even performing the office of teacher, lacks the bread of love, that is, charity.”]

“Better is a man who serves himself in lowliness than one who acquires dignity for himself and lacks bread” (Proverbs XII).

## CHAPTER XIV. The question of how the error of such thoughts crept into us

Germanus: Your discussion, through sufficiently appropriate comparisons, has clearly revealed the errors of our thoughts. We likewise wish to recognize their causes and cures, and we equally desire to be taught how this deception came upon us. For no one can doubt that no one is able to apply remedies to serious illnesses unless he has first identified the origins of the diseases themselves.

## CHAPTER XV. A response concerning the threefold movement of the soul
Abraham: There is one source and beginning of all vices; but according to the quality of that part—or, so to speak, that member—which has been corrupted in the soul, it takes on different names for its passions and disorders. This is sometimes demonstrated also by the example of bodily diseases: although they have one cause, they are nevertheless distinguished into different kinds of illness according to the character of the bodily members they have affected. For when the force of a harmful humor has besieged the citadel of the body, that is, the head, it produces the condition of headache [*cephalalgia*].  

[Note: [Col. 1305C] *Cephalalgia* is pain of the head: for κεφαλή means “head,” and ἀλγέω, “I suffer pain.” Aristotle in the *Problems*: κεφαλαλγία, τὸ κεφαλῆς ἄλγημα, “headache, the pain of the head.”]

But when it has penetrated the ears or eyes, [Col. 1306B] it turns into the disease of earache or ophthalmia:

[Note: [Col. 1305C] Ciaconius restored *in otalgicum* from the Vatican manuscripts; it had also been omitted in the Plantinian edition, although both sense and the text required it, and Dionysius likewise did not omit it, since mention had been made of the ears and eyes. For *otalgic* disease concerns the ears, and *ophthalmic* disease the eyes. An otalgic disease is one that causes pain in the ears: for ὦτα means “ears,” and ἀλγέω, “I suffer pain”; hence ὠταλγικός. Ophthalmic disease, on the other hand, is disease or pain of the eyes.]

when it has spread through the various joints as far as the extremities of the hands, the condition is called articular disease and [*chiragra*]:

[Note: [Col. 1305C] *Chiragra* is pain of the hands, which is also called articular disease because it afflicts the joints of the hands. Hence *chirager* or *chiragric*, one who suffers from chiragra.]

but when it has flowed down to the extremities of the feet, it is called *podagra*, the name having been changed:

[Note: [Col. 1305C] A sufficiently well-known disease of the feet, especially afflicting old men, the wealthy, and the idle, and exceedingly difficult to cure. Hence Ovid, *Ex Ponto* II:

[Col. 1305D] “Medicine does not know how to loosen the knotted gout.”

Pliny says of podagra (*Book* XXVI, chapter 10): “Podagra is a foreign disease. For if it had existed in Italy from ancient times, it would have found a Latin name. For while people at Rome lived by sweating, working, and exercising their strength, Rome did not know this illness.” See Cassiodorus, *Variae* X, letter 29; Sidonius, *Letters* III, letter 13, and X, letter 29. St. Jerome also lists podagra among the illnesses and afflictions of old age (*Preface to Book II of the Commentary on Amos*), as does Aristotle, *History of Animals* VIII, chapter 22.]

Thus one and the same origin of the harmful humor is distinguished by as many names as portions of the body it has seized. In the same way, passing from visible things to invisible, let us believe that the force of each vice exists in the parts—or, so to speak, the members—of our soul. Since the wisest authorities define it as possessing a threefold faculty,

[Note: [Col. 1305D] Pythagoras, according to Suidas, said that the human soul is divided into three parts: νοῦν, φρενάς, καὶ θυμόν, “mind, understanding, and spirit.” In the *Timaeus*, Plato compared the two non-rational faculties of the soul—that is, anger and desire—to a pair of horses, and reason to a charioteer. Following Aristotle, the ancient theologians Gregory of Nyssa, John Damascene, and, after them, St. Thomas, posit in man, besides the rational and higher part of the soul, which consists in reason and will, a twofold appetite: one which they call the concupiscible, and the other the irascible appetite (Aristotle, *Politics* I; Gregory of Nyssa, *Philosophy* IV, chapter 81; Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith* II, chapter 12; St. Thomas, *Summa theologica* I, question 81, articles 2 and 3).

Although these appetites are shared by man and brute animals, they nevertheless differ greatly in man and in brutes. In man, although they are not rational in themselves, they nevertheless obey reason and can and ought to be governed by it—not, as those authors say, despotically and by absolute domination, but politically and civilly. Accordingly, the things which this Author attributes to them ought not so much to be called vices as certain natural passions or inclinations, which we can use well or badly, except insofar as they resist reason or draw it obliquely toward their own objects. On this subject see St. Thomas, *Summa* I–II, questions 22 and following.]

then it is necessary that either its λογικόν—that is, its rational part—or its θυμικόν—that is, its irascible part—or its ἐπιθυμητικόν—that is, its concupiscible part—be corrupted by some assault.

[Note: [Col. 1306C] Ciaconius restored the expression “the tripartite virtue or faculty of the rational soul” in Greek from the Vatican manuscripts. We have willingly followed him, and all the more willingly because St. Jerome left these same faculties or powers expressed by the same Greek terms—though he added a fourth—when, among the various interpretations transmitted by different authors concerning the four living creatures in Ezekiel (chapter I), he also reports this one:

“Many, following Plato, refer the rational, irascible, and concupiscible parts of the soul—which he calls λογικόν, θυμικόν, and ἐπιθυμητικόν—to man, lion, and calf respectively. They place reason, knowledge, understanding, judgment, and the same virtue and wisdom in the citadel of the brain; savageness, anger, and violence in the lion, which resides in the gall; and lust, luxury, and desire for every pleasure in the liver, that is, in the calf, which clings to the works of the earth. They posit a fourth element, which is above and outside these three, which the Greeks call συντήρησις, ‘preservation’—the spark of conscience—which was not extinguished even in Cain’s breast after he had been expelled from paradise,” and so forth.

Thus Jerome draws upon Platonic doctrine; from it those terms originated.]

When, therefore, the force of a harmful passion has occupied one of these affections, the vice is also given a name according to its cause. For if the plague of vices infects the rational part, it will produce the vices of vainglory, self-exaltation, envy, pride, presumption, contentiousness, and heresy. If it wounds the irascible faculty, it will give birth to fury, impatience, sadness, acedia, faintheartedness, and cruelty. If it corrupts the concupiscible part, it will produce gluttony, fornication, love of money, avarice, and harmful earthly desires.

## CHAPTER XVI  
### That the corrupted rational part of the soul must be cured first

[Col. 1307B]

Therefore, if you wish to recognize the source and origin of this vice, know that the rational portion of your mind and soul has been corrupted, from which the vices either of presumption or of vainglory commonly sprout. Accordingly, this first member of the soul, so to speak, must be cured by sound judgment and the virtue of humility. While it is corrupted, you not only believe that you have already reached the summit of perfection, but also that you are able to teach others, and you judge yourselves sufficient and qualified to instruct the rest. Through the vainglorious exaltation revealed by your confession, you are carried away into the wandering of vanity [Lipsius, in the margin: “into vanity”]. You will thereafter be able to cut these things away without difficulty if, as I said, founded upon the humility of true discernment, you learn through contrition of mind how laborious and difficult it is for each of us to save his soul. In the innermost feeling of your hearts, recognize not merely that you are far removed from that presumption of teaching, but also that you still need the help of a teacher.

## CHAPTER XVII  
### That the weaker part of the soul is the first to succumb to diabolical temptations

Apply, then,

[Note: [Col. 1307C] Clearly to the higher and rational part, of which he said above: “Know that the rational portion of your mind and soul has been corrupted”—namely, by the vice of vainglory and empty glory, through which they aspired to teach others.]

to this member or part of your soul, which we have specifically said is wounded, the remedy of true humility. Since this part is, so far as appears, weaker in you than the other powers of the soul, it is necessary that it be the first to succumb to diabolical assault. Just as, when certain injuries arise—whether produced accidentally by labor or by corruption of the air—it commonly happens in human bodies that the parts which are weak are the first to yield and succumb to such circumstances; and when the disease has settled more particularly in them, it infects the other parts of the body also with the same plague; so likewise, when the pestilential breath of vices is, as it were, blowing upon the soul of each one of us, that passion must chiefly be attacked in which its more tender and weaker portion does not resist the enemy’s powerful assaults with sufficient strength, and through which, because its guard is careless, it opens an easier entrance to betrayal and risks captivity.

Thus Balaam

[Note: [Col. 1307D] The avaricious prophet Balaam, concerning whom St. Jerome writes in the *Hebrew Questions* on Genesis, chapter 22: “That divine Balaam, whom the Hebrews say is called Elihu in the Book of Job, was at first a holy man and prophet of God; afterward, through disobedience and desire for gifts, while he wished to curse Israel, he was called by the name of a diviner. This Balaam was hired by Balak, king of Moab, for payment to curse the Israelites. When, against his own will, the Spirit of God impelled him to bless them, he nevertheless, prompted by avarice, gave King Balak this counsel: that he should send the most beautiful Moabite women into the camp of Israel, to provoke the people of God to lust and idolatry. For he said that in this way God, angered against his people, would favor King Balak and destroy the Israelites.

“Therefore Moses, in Numbers XXXI, was exceedingly angry because the Israelites had preserved the women of the Midianites unharmed: ‘Why have you spared the women? Are they not the ones who deceived the children of Israel at the suggestion of Balaam, and caused them to transgress against the Lord in the matter of Phogor, so that the people were struck?’ And in Revelation II the angel—that is, the bishop—of Pergamum is charged, among other things: ‘You have there those who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling-block before the children of Israel, to eat and to commit fornication.’

“Augustine, however, says (*Questions on Numbers*, question 63) that Scripture did not state that this wicked counsel was given so that women would be placed before them as a temptation, through whom they would commit fornication not only bodily but also spiritually by worshiping an idol; yet it is evident that this happened, since it is mentioned here. Augustine’s view is highly probable. For when Balaam saw that he could not curse the Israelites, he said to Balak, in order at least to gratify the king in some fashion while bidding him farewell: ‘Nevertheless, as I go to my people, I will give you counsel as to what your people shall do to this people at the end of time’ (Numbers XXIV). Moses, however, passed over this counsel there, and later expressed it when a similar occasion and danger arose.”]

reasoned with certainty that the people of God could be deceived. He advised that, on the side where he knew the children of Israel to be weak, harmful snares should be laid for them, not doubting that, when an opportunity involving women was offered, they would immediately fall into the ruin of fornication, because he knew that the concupiscible parts of their souls had been corrupted (Numbers XXIV and XXXI).

In the same way, therefore, spiritual wickednesses assail each one of us with crafty malice, constructing treacherous snares especially for those affections of the soul which they perceive to be diseased. For example, when they see that the rational parts of our soul have been corrupted, they try to deceive us by the same method through which Scripture records that King Ahab was deceived by those Syrians who said: “We know that the kings of Israel are merciful. Let us therefore put sackcloth on our loins and cords on our heads, and go out to the king of Israel; and we shall say: ‘Your servant Ben-hadad says: Let my soul live.’” To them he replied, moved not by true piety but by the empty praise of mercy: “If he is still alive, he is my brother” (III Kings XX).

By this example they also cause us, deceived through the error of that rational part, to incur God’s displeasure precisely where we believed we should gain a reward and receive the recompense of piety. Thus the same reproach is directed at us: “Because you have let go from your hand a man worthy of death, your soul shall be for his soul, and your people for his people” (ibid.).

Or when the unclean spirit says, “I will go out, and I will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets” (III Kings XXII), he unquestionably sets a snare of deception and death through the rational affection, which he knew to be open to deadly treachery. In the same way, the most cunning enemy impelled Herod, through the irascible part of his soul, to that slaughter of so many infants, because he knew that this part in him was especially corrupted (Matthew II).

The same spirit also supposed this of our Lord:

[Note: [Col. 1309C] On these matters see *Conferences* V, chapters 4 and 6, and again *Conference* XXII, chapter 10. St. Bernard discusses the same subjects in sermon 6 on the psalm “He who dwells.”]

when he tempted him in those three affections of the soul in which he knew the whole human race to be taken captive, yet accomplished nothing through his crafty assaults. He attacked the concupiscible part of his mind, saying: “Command that these stones become loaves of bread” (Matthew IV). He attacked the irascible part when he tried to incite him to seek the power of the present age and the kingdoms of this world. He attacked the rational part when he said: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down” (ibid.). In none of these attempts did his deception accomplish anything, because he found nothing corrupted in him according to the conjecture he had formed through his false supposition. Therefore no part of his soul consented when attacked by the enemy’s snares. For he says: “Behold, the prince of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John XIV).

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### Question: Whether we should be withdrawn to our homeland by a useful desire for a more secluded solitude  
### [Alternative: “a desire for greater silence”]

[Col. 1309C]

Germanus: Among the various kinds of our illusions and errors—which, as your blessedness sees with the discerning gaze of an attentive mind, had inflamed us with an empty promise of spiritual advantages toward a desire for our homeland—this was also, or rather this was the principal cause: that, when we are sometimes visited by the brothers, we cannot remain in uninterrupted solitude and prolonged silence according to our desire. Consequently, the course and measure of our daily abstinence, which we always wish to maintain unbroken for the chastisement of the body, must be interrupted when some brothers arrive. We are convinced that this could never happen in our province, where it is possible to find either no one, or certainly only very rarely, who follows this profession.

## CHAPTER XIX  
### Response: That God wills perfect men, even when hidden in the most remote solitudes, to be visited by others

Abraham: It is a sign of irrational and inconsiderate severity—or rather of the greatest tepidity—not to wish to be visited by people at all.

[Note: [Col. 1309C] We judged that *velle* should be restored altogether from Dionysius’s paraphrase, by which the meaning is made easier and more readily understood. For this is irrational and indiscreet severity, and a sign of great tepidity, or rather lukewarmness rather than fervor and perfection, when someone is so attached to his quiet and solitude that he wishes neither to see anyone nor to be seen or visited by anyone, even when charity demands or advises it, and refuses even the approach or conversation of holy brothers or religious men—as some people are obstinate or excessively scrupulous.]

For one who proceeds with excessively slow steps along the path he has undertaken, and lives according to the former man, it is fitting that no one should come to him—not even, I do not say the saints, but any human being.

[Note: [Col. 1309D] The passage is obscure in itself and has been made more obscure by variant readings. Some read *according to the inner man*, where there is no intelligible sense (so Ciaconius). For how can someone who walks with slow steps on the road of salvation live according to the inner man? Cuychius therefore rightly judged from the manuscripts that it should be read *according to the former man*, for which Dionysius has *according to the former or old man*.

The meaning is this: whoever proceeds with excessively slow steps in the religious and austere life which he has chosen and undertaken—that is, conducts himself negligently and lukewarmly—makes little or no progress, and lives according to the former man, that is, according to the custom of his former worldly way of life. Such are those of whom St. Jerome says (*Letter* 14): “I have seen some who, after renouncing the world, changed nothing of their former way of life except their clothing and the profession of their words, not their conduct.”

Such a person does not deserve to be visited not only by the saints but even by other human beings, because he can be useful to no one by his example or conversation. But whoever burns with true charity desires to benefit all, to care for the salvation of all, and to promote it as far as he can; and wherever an opportunity is given, he takes care to do so. Therefore he deserves to be approached and visited by everyone.]

But if you burn with a true and perfect love of our Lord, and follow God—who is certainly love (I John IV)—with the full fervor of the spirit, then, even if you flee to whatever inaccessible places, it is necessary that people visit those places. The closer the fire of divine love makes you to God, the greater will be the crowd of holy brothers that flows to you.

For, according to the Lord’s saying, “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden.” [Note: [Col. 1310D] The Vulgate text reads: “Whoever glorifies me, I will glorify him; but those who despise me shall be ignoble.”]

“For those who love me,” says the Lord, “I will glorify; but those who despise me shall be ignoble” (I Kings II; Matthew V).

Nevertheless, you must recognize that this is the devil’s most subtle cunning, this his most hidden pit, into which he casts the miserable and unwary: while promising them greater things, he steals from them the necessary profit of their daily life. He persuades them that more hidden and more extensive solitudes ought to be sought, painting them in their hearts as though they were planted with marvelous delights. He even fabricates unknown places—places which exist nowhere at all—as though they were known and prepared, already owed to our possession and to be acquired without any difficulty. He falsely represents the people of that region as tractable and ready to follow the way of salvation, so that, while promising richer fruits for the soul there, he fraudulently deprives us of present gains.

For when someone, through this empty hope, has been separated from the salutary companionship of the elders and deprived of everything he had vainly pictured in his heart, he will awaken as though from the deepest sleep and, coming to consciousness, find none of the things he had dreamed. Thus the devil entangles him in greater necessities of this life and in inextricable snares, and eventually does not even allow him to breathe toward the things he himself had promised. He binds him no longer to those rare and spiritual visits of the brothers which he had formerly avoided, but to the daily intrusions of worldly people, and never permits him to return even to the moderate quiet and discipline of the anchorite life.

## CHAPTER XX  
### That relaxation is useful when brothers arrive

[Col. 1311B]

Although that interval of relaxation and kindness which customarily occurs at the arrival of brothers may seem to you burdensome and something to be avoided, nevertheless attend patiently for a little while to how useful and healthful it is both for your body and for your spirit.

[Note: [Col. 1311B] Cassian says the same in *Institutes* III, chapter 11: “Every weariness is always endured more equably, and labor is undertaken without distaste, if some change is introduced into it, or any alteration whatever in the work.” And below, in chapter 21: “A small and brief relaxation, unless it occasionally lightens and relaxes the rigor of its concentration through some remission, will become weakened by unremitting strictness and will be unable, when necessity demands, to obey the strength of the spirit.”

Other Fathers plainly agree. St. Ambrose, otherwise a severe censor of morals, says in *On Virginity* III: “What you wish to do at length, do not do it at every moment.” He adds that farmers should be imitated, since they do not always sow their fields with the same seed, and sometimes allow them to rest so that they may become more fertile.

Augustine, *On Music* II, chapter 4: “I want you at last to spare yourself and allow your mind to go forth into the open air; for it is fitting for a wise man occasionally to relax the attention directed toward the things he is doing.”

Gregory, *Moral Commentary* XXVIII, chapter 10: “Often virtue is lost when it is held indiscreetly; and when it is interrupted with discretion, it is held more firmly. Nor is it surprising if we understand in incorporeal things what we see happening in corporeal things. Through use, the bow is bent, so that at the proper time it may be drawn with advantage. But if it receives no period of leisure and relaxation, it loses through the very habit of tension its power to strike. Thus virtue is sometimes preserved in exercise when, through discretion, it is temporarily set aside, so that it may strike vices more vigorously afterward, precisely because it prudently refrains from striking for a time.”]

It often happens—not to novices and the weak alone, but also to the most experienced and perfect—that unless the direction and judgment of their minds have been softened by certain intervals of relief and variation, they fall either into spiritual tepidity or at least into a harmful bodily condition. Therefore, when frequent visits from the brothers occur, prudent and perfect men must not merely endure them patiently but also embrace them gladly.

First, such visits provoke us to desire the secrets of solitude ever more eagerly; for, because it is in some measure believed to interrupt our course, it preserves us indefatigable and continuous. If our progress were never slowed by some obstacle, it could not continue with tireless speed all the way to the end.

In addition, they permit, with the benefit of human kindness, the body to be restored, conferring on us greater gains with a most agreeable relaxation of the body than those which might have been acquired through the fatigue of abstinence. On this matter I shall briefly indicate an especially apt comparison made familiar by an ancient story.

## CHAPTER XXI  
### The same point demonstrated by the authority of St. John the Evangelist

It is related

[Note: [Col. 1311D] It is strange that Baronius and other earlier historians—Metaphrastes, Abdias, Prochorus, Baronius in volumes I and II of the *Annals*, and Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* III, chapter 13—make not even a word of this story or apophthegm when writing about John the Evangelist. More surprising still, reader, is the fact that when Baronius relates that story—or, rather, not a fable in the sense of an empty or false tale, but a true account of a lost young man restored to repentance by John—under the year of Christ 98, and after producing John Chrysostom’s testimony concerning the same story, he immediately adds: “Cassian and many others cite this same story,” while in the margin he refers to this passage, Cassian’s *Conference* XXIV, chapter 21, as though the story related by Cassian in that chapter were the same as the one Baronius has just told, although it has nothing similar and in no way suits the subject of this passage. Thus the good Homer has nodded here, using one story in place of another; and it is no wonder if writers far inferior to so great an author sometimes nod.

But behold, kindly reader, this very story was recently expressed and published in elegant verse by my dearest brother, Father Angelinus Gazaeus, a priest of the Society of Jesus, among other works of his truly pious and truly cheerful character. Since it is worthy of remembrance, and since it offers you pleasure and refreshment after matters so serious and weighty, I have thought it worthwhile to append it here. He himself thus follows no author other than Cassian:

“What you long wish to do, sometimes do not do.

The enervated mind creeps toward its tasks,

Unless a companion’s leisure gives it support.

Among serious duties, playful things too must be admitted—

Honorable things, decorous things. There is great value

In the interval by which rest follows labor

And labor in turn follows rest.

The Evangelist made this clear in word

And festive in deed, the keeper of a sacred heart,

Who had wholly floated in God and reclined upon him.

While he governed Ephesus as bishop, a partridge,

Tame from its tender claws, was raised in his house.

When he had freed himself from weighty business,

He would gently call it to him, offering the bird

Now food, now drink, and smoothing

The level surface of its feathered back.

If sleep crept upon it, he allowed the most peaceful creature

To fall asleep in the warmth of his lap.

[Col. 1312D] And after several passages inserted more for poetic charm and grace than for the history itself:

Perhaps John was taking from the bird

The leisure of midday,

When some lightweight fellow, newly come from the forest,

A hunter appeared before him, still foul with mud.

A thorny branch had marked his face

With many a scratch; a hare hung from his back,

A quiver at his side, and his right hand carried a bow,

Whose loosened horns and slackened string,

As though commanded to sleep, were free from the notches.

He had long been eager to look upon the father of Zebedee

And, if permitted, to speak with him.

He sees, therefore, what is not particularly pleasing to see,

And, with an ugly grin like an angry sow,

He cries out: ‘What do I see? Is this the man of whom fame speaks?

Is this holiness? Have we come to him

For this? So easily does an old man waste his time?

Does so great an old man not return

More profit from his golden hours?’

‘Restrain your words, my son,’ says John.

‘Come, tell me: why do you carry a loosened bow in your right hand?’

‘Why?’ he replies. ‘If the moon-like curve of the threatening bow were unceasing, its string would very soon lose its tension and, deprived of the force of its strength, it would become feeble; nor would it be possible to shoot an arrow or aim it where one wished.’

[Col. 1313B] Here the holy man entangles him in his own snares.

‘Why, then, are you now so astonished

To see an old man taking his ease,

Whose mind, after great deeds and serious cares

Performed at home and abroad, must grow numb

Unless it is allowed to draw new strength

From the lap of rest? And, as you see, I am drawing it.

If, when you wish it, leisure is sometimes granted,

If rest is given to tired bows, why should leisure

And rest not also be given to tired limbs?’

Thus spoke the elder, and the hunter, properly instructed

By the bow, departed. Experience and the matter itself demand it:

A mind dulled by the stiffness of unremitting rigor

Grows slack; hence it longs to play through the open air

And to go forth freely, as puppies do

After they have long rolled and tumbled around

A spinning spit, whether rich in roasted meat

Or laden with birds. Once they have gained free reins

And an open orchard, they leap joyfully across the grass,

Drawing in fresh breath and a renewed mind.

What you always dare to do, you shall not always do.”

[Col. 1313C] Thus far my brother, most aptly imitating Cassian in his iambics.

Moreover, St. Thomas confirms his conclusion by this example (*Summa* II–II, question 168, article 2), teaching that playful activities are sometimes fitting even for serious men. There is a certain kind of moderation which the Philosopher calls εὐτραπελία, which we may render in Latin as *jucunditas*, “pleasantness”; it imposes the measure of reason upon games and jokes, or preserves decorum in playful activities. Hence εὐτράπελος is one who knows how to turn certain words and actions, at an appropriate time and with due moderation, toward the recreation of the mind (Leonard Lessius, *On Justice* IV, chapter 4; Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* IV, chapter 8).

That such activities are sometimes lawful even for serious and religious men is proved by St. Thomas as follows. Just as a person needs bodily rest for the restoration of the body, since he cannot labor continuously because his strength is finite and proportioned to definite labors, so it is also with the soul, whose strength too is finite and proportioned to determinate operations. Just as bodily fatigue is relieved by bodily rest, so animal fatigue must also be relieved by rest for the soul. The rest of the soul, however, is pleasure; therefore a remedy against animal fatigue is supplied through some pleasure, the attention being interrupted for a time so that one may return to the pursuit of reason.

As we read in the *Conferences of the Fathers*, when certain people were scandalized because they found the blessed John the Evangelist playing with his disciples, he is said to have instructed one of them who was carrying a bow to draw an arrow. After he had done this several times, John asked whether he could continue doing so without interruption. The man replied that if he did so continuously, the bow would break. Therefore blessed John added that the human mind would likewise break if it were never relaxed from its concentration.

Such words or actions, in which nothing is sought except the pleasure of the soul, are called [Col. 1314A] playful or jocular. It is therefore necessary to use such things occasionally, as a kind of rest for the soul. This is what the Philosopher says in the fourth book of the *Ethics*: that in the conduct of this life there is a certain rest accompanied by play.

Thus St. Thomas wonderfully illuminates this passage of Cassian, although he reports the teaching of blessed John somewhat differently; the matter is nevertheless the same. He adds three conditions which must be observed in such jokes and games, and these conditions also help to clarify this passage.

The first is that the pleasure described above must not be sought in shameful or harmful actions or words. Hence Cicero, *On Duties* I: “Just as we do not grant children unrestricted permission to play, but only that which is not alien to honorable actions, so in play itself some light of a good character should shine.” Then, explaining which kinds of jokes must be avoided, he adds: “There are altogether two kinds of joking: one is base, wanton, disgraceful, and obscene; the other is elegant, civilized, ingenious, and witty.”

The second condition is that we must not be excessive in playful activity: “lest,” he says, “the seriousness of the soul be wholly dissolved.” Hence Ambrose, *On Duties* I, chapter 20: “Let us beware lest, while wishing to relax the mind, we dissolve the entire harmony and concord of good works.” And Cicero: “The manner of joking itself ought to be neither excessive nor immoderate, but refined and witty.” Again: “It is permissible to use play and joking, but as with sleep and rest, only when we have fulfilled our serious and weighty duties.”

The third is that, as in all human actions, circumstances must be taken into account, so that the play suits the person, time, and place and is properly ordered according to the other circumstances—in other words, that it be worthy of the time and of the person, as Tully says in the same passage.

Thus far St. Thomas.

Hincmarus also remembers this same apophthegm of blessed John the Evangelist in his *Life of St. Remigius*, in Surius. St. Antony likewise used it on a similar occasion, as is related in the *Lives of the Fathers* (Book V, section 10):

“When certain brothers came to him to consult him about their fantasies and visions, a hunter arrived and saw the abbot rejoicing with the brothers, and this displeased him. Wishing to show him that one must sometimes accommodate oneself to the brothers, the elder said to him: ‘Put an arrow in your bow and draw it.’ He did so. Then he said: ‘Draw again,’ and he drew it. Again he said to him: ‘Draw farther,’ and he drew it. The hunter said to him: ‘If I draw beyond measure, the bow will break.’ Abbot Antony said to him: ‘So it is in the work of God: if we stretch the brothers beyond measure, they quickly grow weak. It is therefore useful now and again to relax their rigor.’ When the hunter heard this, he was moved to compunction and departed greatly benefited by the old man’s speech, while the brothers returned to their place strengthened.”

This is what is found there.

To the same point belongs what Nicephorus writes about Macarius of Alexandria (*Book* IX, chapter 14), following other historians (Suidas, under “Macarius”), in these words:

“Macarius of Alexandria, though equal to the Egyptian in all other respects, differed from him in this one matter: cheerful and pleasant in conversation, civilized and fond of witty sayings, he led young men toward the study and practice of piety.”]

It is said that the most blessed evangelist John, while gently stroking a partridge with his hands, suddenly saw a certain man approaching him in hunting attire. The man was astonished that one of such reputation and fame should stoop to amusements so small and humble.

“You are John, then,” he said, “the man whose distinguished and celebrated reputation has aroused in me too a great desire to know you? Why, then, are you occupied with such lowly amusements?”

Blessed John replied: “What is it that your hand is carrying?”

“A bow,” he said.

“And why,” said John, [Col. 1314A] “do you not always carry it stretched and drawn?”

He replied:

[Note: [Col. 1314D] Hence Horace says (*Odes* II):

“Nor does Apollo

Always keep his bow drawn.”

See above the statement of St. Gregory, which applies especially to this point (in the notes on chapter 20).]

“It is not advisable, lest through its continual bending the strength of its stiffness should weaken and perish; and when it is necessary to direct stronger arrows against some wild beast, the more violent stroke should be impossible because the bow has lost its rigidity through excessive continuous tension.”

“Nor should this brief and minor relaxation of ours offend you, young man,” said blessed John. “Unless it occasionally relieves and relaxes the rigor of its concentration through some measure of remission, this relaxation, growing slack through unremitting strictness, will not be able, when necessity demands, to comply with the strength of the spirit.”

## CHAPTER XXII  
### Question: How should the saying in the Gospel be understood: “My yoke is easy, and my burden is light”?

Germanus: Since you have supplied us with remedies against every kind of illusion, and since, by God’s granting, the devil’s snares by which we were shaken have been exposed through your teaching, we likewise ask that you explain to us what is said in the Gospel: “My yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11). For this seems quite contrary to that prophetic statement: “Because of the words of your lips I have kept hard ways” (Psalm 16). The Apostle, too, says: “All who wish to live devoutly in Christ will suffer persecution” (2 Timothy 3). But whatever is harsh and filled with persecutions can be neither light nor easy.

[Note: The Fathers raise—or at least imply—the same question and difficulty, and solve and explain it in various ways. Saint Jerome, commenting on the passage in Matthew 11, “For my yoke is easy,” and so forth. Saint Augustine, *Sermon 9 on the Words of the Lord*: “It seems strange to some, dearest brothers, when they hear the Lord say, ‘Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you’ (Matthew 11); ‘Take my yoke upon you,’ and so forth; and when they consider that those who have taken up that yoke with an unflinching neck and received that burden upon their most gentle shoulders are driven and exercised by such great difficulties in this world that they seem to have been called not from labor to rest, but from rest to labor—especially since the Apostle says: ‘All who wish to live devoutly in Christ will suffer persecution’ (2 Timothy 3). Someone therefore says: How is the yoke light and the burden light, since bearing that yoke and burden is nothing other than living devoutly in Christ? And how is it said, ‘Come to me, you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you’? Why is it not rather said, ‘Come, you who are at leisure, so that you may labor’? For he found even those who were idle and hired them for the vineyard, that they might bear the heat of the day.” And below he replies: “But surely the Holy Spirit is present, renewing the outward person day by day amid his corruption; and, once spiritual rest has been tasted in the abundance of God’s delights and in the hope of future blessedness, he sweetens all present things and lightens everything harsh and burdensome. People allow themselves to be cut and burned so that pains which are not eternal, though sometimes longer-lasting, may be bought off at the price of more severe pains from an ulcer. What storms or punishments do merchants endure in order to acquire future riches? Yet those who do not love these things suffer the same burdens as harsh; those who love them suffer the same things, but not as burdens. Love makes every savage and monstrous thing entirely easy, almost nothing. How much more easily, then, does charity accomplish for true blessedness what desire, as far as it could, accomplished for misery!”

Gregory, *Homily 17 on Ezekiel*: “If one reaches God through charity, and Truth itself says, ‘Enter through the narrow gate’ (Matthew 7), while I hear the Psalmist again saying, ‘Because of the words of your lips I have kept hard ways’ (Psalm 16), and in the Gospel the Lord says, ‘For my yoke is easy and my burden is light’ (Matthew 11), how then is charity broad, if the gate is narrow? Or how is the yoke easy and the burden light, if the ways that are kept according to God’s commandments are hard? But Truth itself quickly resolves this question for us, because God’s way is narrow for beginners but broad for those already living perfectly. The things we set before the spirit in opposition to its customary habits are hard; nevertheless, God’s burden is light once we have begun to bear it, so that, out of love for him, persecution itself becomes pleasing, and every suffering [Al. ‘affection’] endured for him comes with sweetness of mind. Thus even the holy apostles rejoiced when they endured scourging for the Lord. The narrow gate itself therefore becomes broad for those who love; the hard ways themselves become spiritually gentle and level for those who run along them, while the mind knows that in return for temporal pains it will receive eternal joys. And it begins to love the very thing by which it is afflicted.”]

**CHAPTER XXIII. Response, with an exposition of the statement**

Abraham: We shall easily prove by the evidence of experience itself that the statement of our Lord and Savior is wholly true, if we undertake the path of perfection lawfully and according to Christ’s will; if, putting all our desires to death and cutting away our harmful inclinations, we not only allow nothing of this world’s substance to remain for us [Lipsius, in the margin: “we recognize”]—through which, whenever it pleases him, the enemy would certainly find the power to ravage and tear us apart—but also realize that we are not masters even of ourselves, fulfilling in truth the Apostle’s saying: “I live, yet it is no longer I; Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2).

For what could be burdensome, what could be harsh, to one who has received Christ’s yoke with his whole mind; who, grounded in true humility and always looking toward the Lord, rejoices in every injury inflicted upon him, saying: “For this reason I am pleased with weaknesses, sufferings, and hardships for Christ; for when I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Corinthians 12)? What loss in a familiar possession, I ask, could torment one who, gloriously stripped of everything, voluntarily rejects all the resources of this world for Christ’s sake, and regards all its desires as dung, “that he may gain Christ” (Philippians 3), dismissing and rejecting the heat of every loss through meditation on that Gospel command: “For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul? Or what exchange can a man give for his soul?” (Matthew 16)?

Over the loss of what, then, will one grieve who knows that everything which can be taken away by others is not his, proclaiming with unconquerable strength: “We brought nothing into this world; beyond doubt, neither can we take anything from it” (1 Timothy 6)? By what necessity of poverty will the strength of one be overcome who does not know how to possess a purse for the road, money in his belt, or a garment for the seasons (Matthew 10), but glories with the Apostle “in many fasts, in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness” (2 Corinthians 11)?

What labor, what command of an elder so arduous, could disturb the peace of his heart who, having no will of his own, meets everything commanded him not only patiently but gladly, and, following the example of our Savior, seeks not his own will but that of the Father, saying to his Father: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26)? By what injuries, by what persecution, will he be terrified—or rather, what punishment could fail to be pleasing to one who, always exulting with the apostles amid every blow, desires to be found worthy to suffer disgrace for Christ’s name (Acts 5)?

**CHAPTER XXIV. Why the Lord’s yoke is felt as bitter and his burden as heavy**

That Christ’s yoke seems to us, by contrast, neither light nor easy should more rightly be attributed to our obstinacy. Cast down by distrust and unbelief, we perversely resist the command—or rather, the counsel—of him who says: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell, or give away, everything you possess, and come, follow me” (Matthew 19), stubbornly clinging to the material resources of earthly possessions. Since the devil holds our minds bound by the chains of these things, what remains except that, whenever he wishes to separate us from spiritual joys, he makes us sad through their diminution and loss?

He works through crafty deceptions so that, when the sweetness of that yoke and the lightness of its burden have been made heavy for us by the depravity of vicious desire, he may continually torment us with the scourges of worldly cares, entangling us in the bonds of the very possessions and substance that we reserve for rest and consolation, fashioning from ourselves that by which we are to be torn apart.

[Note: Our Translator: “The iniquities of the wicked ensnare him, and he is bound with the cords of his sins.”]

“For each person is bound by the cords of his sins” (Proverbs 5), hearing the prophet say: “Behold, all of you who kindle a fire, who gird yourselves with flames: walk in the light of your fire and in the flames that you have kindled” (Isaiah 50). Through these things, as Solomon bears witness, “by the very things through which each person sins, by those he is punished” (Wisdom 11). The pleasures we use are themselves our torment; the amusements and delights of this flesh are turned back upon their author in place of executioners. For one who is supported by his former possessions and wealth cannot receive either complete humility of heart or the full mortification of harmful desires [Lipsius, in the margin: “pleasures”].

With these instruments of virtue providing their support, all the hardships of the present life and every loss the enemy can inflict are endured not only with the greatest patience but also with the greatest joy. Yet, as they again exult in these things, such a dangerous self-exaltation grows that we are wounded by deadly blows of impatience at even the slightest insult, and the prophet Jeremiah’s words are spoken to us:

“Now what have you to do with the way of Egypt, to drink turbid water? And what have you to do with the way of Assyria, to drink the water of the river? Your wickedness will rebuke you, and your apostasy will reproach you. Know and see how evil and bitter it is for you to have abandoned the Lord your God and to have no fear of me within you, says the Lord” (Jeremiah 2).

What, then, does it mean that the wondrous sweetness of the Lord’s yoke is felt as bitter, except that the bitterness of our apostasy corrupts it? What does it mean that the divinely bestowed burden, so delightfully light, becomes heavy, except that we scorn through rebellious presumption the one by whom we were sustained? Scripture plainly bears witness to this very point, saying:

[Note: This passage was restored by Ciaconius; previously it had been read with faulty punctuation: “For if they walked in straight paths, they would certainly have found paths of justice. Light are we,” and so forth. The Greek reads as follows: “For if they walked in good ways, they would certainly have found easy ways of justice.” But Cassianus seems to have read, instead of *tribous agathas* (τριβοὺς ἀγαθὰς, “good ways”), *tribous orthas* (τριβοὺς ὀρθὰς, “straight ways”) or *eutheias* (εὐθείας, “direct ways”). Thus Ciaconius. Saint Jerome supports him in his letter to Caelantia, where he recalls and quotes this passage as follows: “The path of justice is found to be easy” (Proverbs 2). In the Vulgate edition, however, nothing of the sort is found.]

“For if they walked in straight paths, they would certainly have found easy paths of justice” (Proverbs 2, according to the Septuagint).

We, we plainly are the ones who roughen the Lord’s straight and level paths with the crooked and jagged rocks of our desires. Madly abandoning the royal road, paved with apostolic and prophetic stones and made level by the footsteps of all the saints and of the Lord himself, we pursue every crooked and thorny route. Blinded by the enticements of present pleasures, we crawl along the dark, obstructed paths amid the thorns of vices, our legs torn and that nuptial garment ripped apart—not only to be pierced by the sharpest spines of the brambles but also to be wounded by the bites of poisonous serpents and scorpions lurking there.

[Note: The Vulgate reads: “Weapons and swords are on the perverse way; but he who guards his soul withdraws far from them” (Proverbs 22). The Venerable Bede says: “This must be understood in two ways. The perverse are always armed to harm their neighbors by word or wicked deed, and the vengeance of divine judgment is always prepared and awaits them. But whoever seeks to preserve his soul eternally flees far from such weapons and swords, both restraining his mind and hand from harming his neighbors and taking careful precautions lest he be struck by the stern Judge’s punishment.”]

“For there are thorns and snares on crooked ways; but he who fears the Lord will keep away from them” (Proverbs 22).

Of such people the Lord also says through the prophet: “My people have forgotten me, sacrificing in vain and stumbling on their ways, on the paths of the age, so that they might walk along an untrodden road” (Jeremiah 18).

[Note: Vulgate text: “The ways of the slothful are like a hedge of thorns, but the way of the righteous is without stumbling” (Proverbs 15). Bede says: “He calls those people slothful who are reluctant to practice righteousness. When they desire the Lord’s way, the suspicions born of their fears prick them like opposing hedges that block the way.”]

“For, according to Solomon’s statement, the ways of those who do nothing are strewn with thorns, but the ways of the strong are worn smooth” (Proverbs 15). Thus, having strayed from the royal road, they will not be able to reach that capital city toward which our course must always be directed without deviation.

Ecclesiastes also expressed this clearly enough:

“The labor of fools will afflict those who do not know how to go to the city” (Ecclesiastes 10)—that heavenly Jerusalem, namely, “which is the mother of us all” (Galatians 4).

[Note: Vulgate: “The labor of fools will afflict those who do not know how to go to the city” (Ecclesiastes 10). “Read Plato,” says Jerome; “review Aristotle’s subtleties; examine Zeno and Carneades more carefully, and you will prove the truth of the statement: ‘The labor of fools will afflict them.’ They indeed sought the truth with every effort; but because they had no guide or leader on the journey, and thought that they could grasp wisdom through human senses, they did not reach the city, of which it is said in the Psalm: ‘Lord, in your city you will destroy their image’ (Psalm 72).”]

**CHAPTER XXV. What benefit temptations confer upon us**

Whoever truly renounces this world and takes Christ’s yoke upon himself, learning from him through daily training in injuries that he is meek and humble of heart (Matthew 11), will remain steadfast amid every temptation, and everything will “work together for his good” (Romans 8).

“For the words of God,” according to the prophet Micah, “are good for him who walks uprightly” (Micah 2). And again: “The ways of the Lord are right, and the just walk in them; but transgressors will fall in them” (Hosea 14).

Thus the Savior’s grace, benevolent toward us, has won us greater and more excellent rewards of praise through the struggle of temptations than if it had removed every necessity of combat from us. For it is a sign of a loftier and more excellent virtue to remain steadfast when surrounded by sufferings and hardships, and, while everything rages against one, to persevere confidently and fearlessly in God’s protection; to be girded, as though with weapons, by the armor of unconquered virtue against human assaults; to triumph most gloriously over impatience; and in a certain sense to acquire virtue through weakness, because “virtue is perfected in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12).

“For behold,” says the Lord, “I have made you an iron pillar and a bronze wall over all the land, against the kings of Judah, its princes, and all the people of the land. They will fight against you, but they will not prevail, because I am with you to deliver you,” says the Lord (Jeremiah 1).

Therefore, according to the true teaching of the Lord, the royal road is pleasant and easy, although it may be felt as hard and rough. Those who serve devoutly and faithfully, once they have taken the Lord’s yoke upon themselves and learned from him that he is meek and humble of heart (Matthew 11), will, as it were, lay down the burden of earthly passions and, by the Lord’s gift, find not labor but rest for their souls, as he himself testified through the prophet Jeremiah:

“Stand upon the ways and see, and ask about the ancient paths, which is the good way, and walk in it; then you will find refreshment for your souls” (Jeremiah 6).

For them crooked things will immediately become straight and rough things level paths (Isaiah 40); tasting, they will see how sweet the Lord is (Psalm 33); and hearing Christ proclaim in the Gospel, “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11), once the burdens of their vices have been laid down, they will understand what follows: “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (ibid.).

[Note: The difficulty—“How is the Lord’s yoke easy and his burden light?”—has a simple and brief solution: it is easy if it is held and borne according to his law, but heavy and difficult if borne otherwise. This results not from its nature and condition but from our vice, as is explained here.]

The Lord’s way therefore contains refreshment if it is held according to his law. But we are the ones who procure pains and torments for ourselves through turbulent exertions, preferring to pursue the crooked and perverse ways of this world even at the greatest risk and difficulty.

When in this way we have made the Lord’s yoke heavy and harsh for ourselves, we then blasphemously complain either about the yoke itself or about the harshness and severity of Christ who imposes it, according to the saying:

[Note: On this statement, see *Conference* 12, chapter 8.]

“The folly of man corrupts his ways, and in his heart he blames God.” And according to the prophet Haggai, when we say, “The Lord’s way is not straight,” the Lord rightly replies to us: “Is my way not straight? Are not your ways rather crooked?” (Ezekiel 18).

Indeed, if you compare the shining flower of virginity and the sweet-smelling purity of chastity with the foul and stinking mire of lust; the quiet and security of monks with the dangers and hardships in which the people of the world are entangled; and the rest of our poverty with the gnawing sorrows and sleepless cares of the rich, in which they are consumed day and night without escaping the greatest danger to life, you will very easily prove that Christ’s yoke is most sweet and his burden exceedingly light.

**CHAPTER XXVI. How a hundredfold is promised in this world to those who renounce everything perfectly**
Therefore, too, there is that recompense of rewards which the Lord promised in this life a hundredfold to those who renounce perfectly, saying:

> “And everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name’s sake…”

[Note: [Col. 1319D] St. Bernard speaks most aptly of this promise of Christ: “These are the words,” he says (*On the Declaration: ‘Behold, we have left all things’), “which persuaded the whole world to despise the world and persuaded human beings to embrace voluntary poverty. These are the words that fill monasteries with monks and deserts with hermits. These, I say, are the words that strip Egypt and plunder its finest vessels; this is the living and effective word, turning souls through a blessed rivalry in holiness and through the faithful promise of truth.”]

> “And everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name’s sake shall receive a hundredfold in the present, and shall possess eternal life” (Matthew 19).

[Note: [Col. 1319D] Christ promised two things to those who leave their possessions or their loved ones for the kingdom of God: namely, a hundredfold return and eternal life. That these are distinct and cannot be referred to the same thing, so that the latter part is an explanation and clarification of the former, is clear from Mark and Luke (Mark 10; Luke 18), who indicate that the former part belongs to the present age, the latter to the future—just as this abbot also explains it—although this distinction is not found in Matthew. Mark expressed the same meaning more fully, with a double negation:

> “There is no one who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or children, or fields for my sake and for the Gospel, who will not receive a hundred times as much now, in this present time, and in the age to come eternal life.”

Luke likewise has this, except that instead of “a hundred times as much,” or “a hundredfold,” he has “many more,” thereby indicating that the number one hundred is used for an indefinite multitude, just as a determinate number is often used in Scripture for an indeterminate one.

This hundredfold return can be understood in two ways: first, in quantity and number; second, in estimation and value. This abbot both approves and embraces both explanations, and in both senses asserts that a hundredfold will be repaid to those who have left their own people or possessions for Christ. They will receive not only things better, more precious, and more exalted, but also “a hundred times as much,” as Mark has it—that is, things infinitely more numerous, multiplied in number, and increased to a hundredfold or more, and in the same categories of things.

St. Jerome, however, seems to exclude the former explanation when he writes concerning that passage in Matthew:

> “Taking occasion from this saying, certain people introduce a thousand years after the resurrection, saying that then a hundredfold of all the things we have abandoned, together with eternal life, will be returned to us. They do not understand that, if the recompense is fitting in other matters, shamefulness appears in the case of wives: that one who has left one wife for the Lord should receive a hundred in the future. The meaning, therefore, is this: Whoever has left carnal things for the Savior will receive spiritual things; and, in comparison with their worth, these will be as though a small number were compared with a hundred. Hence the Apostle says—he who had left only one house and the small fields of one province—‘As having nothing, yet possessing everything’ (2 Corinthians 6).”

Thus far St. Jerome. His explanation is true, but does not exclude the other. For the evangelist Mark says that the one who has left his possessions will receive not merely a hundredfold in this present time, but also explains in what things he will receive it:

> “Houses,” he says, “and brothers, and sisters, and mothers, and children, and fields” (Mark 10).

Accordingly, this abbot, following Origen and other ancient interpreters, is not wrong to interpret the hundredfold received in this age as meaning that, for one father, mother, or brother, one receives a hundred, and likewise in the other cases: either because charity among Christians makes everything, in a certain sense, common—as is explained here—or because Christ ought to be everything to us: father, mother, brother, sister, spouse, house, and possession. He himself taught this when, stretching out his hands toward his disciples, he said:

> “Behold my mother and my brothers; for whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, and sister, and mother” (Matthew 12).

St. Gregory offers another, somewhat different explanation in Homily 18 on Ezekiel, in these words:

> “The number one hundred signifies great perfection, as is said of the elect: ‘Everyone who leaves house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life.’ No holy person, however, abandons earthly things in order to possess them more abundantly in this world; for whoever leaves earth because of earthly desire does not leave earth but desires it. Nor will the one who leaves one wife receive a hundred; rather, perfection is signified by the number one hundred. Whoever, for God’s name, despises temporal and earthly things receives perfection of mind even here, so that he no longer desires what he has despised, and in the age to come reaches the glory of eternal life.

> “Thus he receives a hundredfold what he gave: he receives the spirit of perfection and no longer needs earthly things, even if he does not possess them. But the person who is poor is in need of what he does not have. Yet whoever, though lacking, does not desire to possess is rich. Poverty consists in want of mind, not in the quantity of possessions. For one who is content in poverty is not poor.”

Thus St. Gregory.]
