He will receive a hundredfold in the present and will possess eternal life (Matthew 19). This is rightly and most truly accepted in the same sense, without any disturbance to the faith.

[Col. 1322A] For many, seizing upon this saying as an opportunity [Lips. in margin: “occasion”] and understanding it crudely,

[Note: [Col. 1321D] A little earlier we heard from Jerome that, long ago, taking occasion from that evangelical saying—as is also found here—certain people introduced a thousand years after the resurrection, saying that a hundredfold of all the things we had abandoned would be returned. St. Augustine, however, indicates that the occasion of their error (*City of God* 10.7) arose from a wrong understanding of the words of the Apocalypse, where it is said that the saints will reign with Christ for a thousand years after the first resurrection (Revelation 20).

From this they inferred that, after the resurrection of bodies, Christ would return to this world and reign here with the saints for a thousand years, in complete peace and happiness, as in a golden age of the sort described by the poets or even foretold by Isaiah and the Sibyl. From this fiction of a thousand years they were called in Greek χιλιασταί (*chilistaí*), and in Latin *Milliarii* or *Millenarii*.

The author of this opinion is said to have been Papias, bishop of Hierapolis, who lived in the time of the apostles. Concerning him St. Jerome writes in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*:

> “Papias is said to have published a Jewish *deuterosis* (δευτέρωσιν) concerning a thousand years; Irenaeus, Apollinarius, and the others followed him, saying that after the resurrection the Lord would reign in the flesh with the saints.”

Tertullian also, in his book *On the Hope of the Faithful*, and Victorinus of Pettau and Lactantius were led by this opinion. Jerome adds Justin Martyr and Sulpicius Severus in the dialogue to which he gave the name *Gallus*.

Tertullian’s words, in which he explains this view more fully, are as follows:

> “We confess that a kingdom has been promised to us on earth, but before heaven and in another state: after the resurrection, for a thousand years, in the divinely built city of Jerusalem brought down from heaven—which the Apostle also indicates as our mother above (Galatians 4), and, declaring that our *πολίτευμα*, that is, our citizenship, is in heaven (Philippians 3), assigns it to some heavenly city. Ezekiel knows this city, and the Apostle John saw it” (Ezekiel 48; Revelation 21).

So much for Tertullian.

This opinion was tolerated by the Church for some time out of reverence for and respect toward so many men, both most holy and most learned, who had held it. Hence St. Jerome—although he repeatedly attacks and ridicules it as empty and fabulous, indeed sometimes assailing it sharply—says that he does not dare condemn it:

> “Because many ecclesiastical men and martyrs have said these things; let each person abound in his own understanding, and let everything be reserved for the judgment of the Lord.”

So wrote St. Jerome, at a time when it appears that nothing had yet been defined by the Church concerning the matter.

Shortly afterward, however, when Apollinaris the heresiarch attempted to establish this opinion concerning the millennium and to defend it with all his strength, even to establish it as a Catholic dogma, the zeal of the Church and of the holy Fathers immediately blazed against him and the other Millenarians, so that they attacked the heresy and its patron more fiercely—especially since he added other impieties to the opinion. He said that human beings would be resurrected for circumcision, that Sabbaths were to be observed as in former times, that a material temple would be built, and that Jewish sacrifices would be offered; indeed, he even maintained that people would devote themselves to shameful pleasures.

Accordingly, at about that time, this opinion concerning the millennium, like Apollinaris’s other erroneous opinions, is believed to have been condemned by Pope Damasus, according to Baronius (*Martyrology*, February 22).

As for the passage in the Apocalypse from which the occasion of this error arose, St. Augustine (*City of God* 20.7) interprets the first resurrection as the resurrection of souls, which is also acknowledged in the Scriptures, and the second as that of bodies. As for the thousand years, he says:

> “The thousand years, as far as occurs to me, can be understood in two ways. Either because this event takes place in the final thousand years—that is, in the sixth millennium of years, as on the sixth day, the latter part of which is now passing; and then there will follow a sabbath without evening, namely, the rest of the saints, which has no end. Thus he may have called the final part of this millennium, as of a day, which will remain until the end of the age, ‘a thousand years,’ according to that manner of speaking in which a part is signified by the whole.

> “Or certainly he used ‘a thousand years’ for all the years of this age, so that the fullness of time itself might be signified by a perfect number. For the number one thousand is the square of the number ten. Ten multiplied by ten makes one hundred, which is already a square figure, though plane. But to make it rise in height and become solid, ten is again multiplied by ten, producing one thousand.

> “Moreover, if one hundred is sometimes used in some manner to signify the whole—as in the promise made by the Lord to the one who leaves everything and follows him: ‘He will receive a hundredfold in this age’—and as the Apostle, explaining it in a certain way, says, ‘As having nothing, yet possessing everything’ (2 Corinthians 6), because it had already been said: ‘The whole world is the wealth of a faithful person,’ how much more is one thousand used for the whole, since it contains the solidity of the square of ten?

> “Hence neither is this passage of the Psalm better understood: ‘He remembered his covenant forever, the word that he commanded for a thousand generations’ (Psalm 104), that is, for all generations.”

So far Augustine.]

These people affirm that, during that thousand-year period, all these things are to be restored carnally to the saints, although they admit that the age which they say will come after the resurrection cannot be understood as the present age.

It is therefore much more credible and much clearer that anyone who, at Christ’s urging, has despised some worldly attachment or possession receives even in this life a hundredfold more gracious love from the brothers and companions of his way of life, who are joined to him by a spiritual bond.

For it is clear that the affection which joins parents and children, brothers and sisters, spouses and relatives—whether through the bond of marriage or the necessity of blood relationship—is very brief and fragile. Finally, even good and devout children, when they have grown up, are sometimes excluded from their parents’ homes and possessions; the fellowship of marriage is sometimes broken even for an honorable reason; and contentious division destroys the affection of brothers.

Monks alone preserve the unity of perpetual union, and possess everything without distinction. They believe that everything belonging to their brothers is theirs, and that everything belonging to them is their brothers’. If, therefore, this love is granted to those affections by which people are joined through carnal charity, it is certainly a hundredfold sweeter and more sublime.

[Note: [Col. 1323C] “Marital continence” here does not mean marital chastity, as distinguished from virginal and widowed chastity—namely, the restraint by which married people remain within the limits and laws of marriage. Rather, it means abstinence by married persons from the marital act, as is clear from the words that follow, for this continence is contrasted with sexual intercourse. Many married people have practiced such continence either before or after the consummation of marriage.

For examples of the former—those who vowed and maintained continence after contracting marriage—see Bellarmine, *On Monks* 2.38. For examples of the latter—those who vowed continence by mutual consent after consummating marriage—see the same work, chapter 37. I omit what the Apostle advises married people: that, by mutual consent, they abstain for a time, in order to devote themselves to prayer and fasting (1 Corinthians 7).

The meaning of these words, therefore, is that married people who abstain from the marital act will experience greater sweetness and pleasure of mind than those who enjoy that act. For, as St. Gregory says (*Homily on the Gospels* 36), this is the difference between bodily and spiritual pleasures: bodily pleasures, when they are not possessed, kindle a painful desire; but when they are eagerly consumed, satiety immediately turns the one eating toward disgust. Spiritual pleasures, by contrast, are distasteful when they are not possessed; when they are possessed, they are desired; and the more they are eaten, the more they are hungered for, while the hungry person eats them all the more.]

Certainly, even in marital continence, a sweetness a hundredfold greater will be received than that which sexual intercourse previously supplied to the spouses.

In place of the joy someone formerly had in possessing one field and one house, he will enjoy a hundredfold greater delight in the wealth of possessions when, adopted as a son of God, he possesses as his own everything belonging to the eternal Father, and in affection and power, in imitation of the true Son, proclaims:

> “Everything that the Father has is mine” (John 15).

He will no longer succeed everywhere with the painful anxiety of division and concern, but securely and joyfully as though among his own possessions, hearing the Apostle daily proclaim to him:

> “All things are yours, whether the world, or things present, or things to come” (1 Corinthians 3).

And from Solomon:

> “The whole world is the wealth of a faithful man” (Proverbs 17 according to the Septuagint).

[Note: [Col. 1324C] The Greek reads: Τοῦ πιστοῦ ὅλος ὁ κόσμος τῶν χρημάτων, “The whole world is the wealth of the faithful man.” St. Jerome writes to Paulinus (Letter 103): “For one who believes, the whole world is wealth.” The same saying is frequently cited by the Fathers, from Proverbs 17, although it is not found in this form in the Vulgate edition.]

You therefore have this hundredfold recompense expressed in the greatness of its merit and in the distinction of a quality so incomparable.

For if, in place of a definite weight of bronze, iron, or some other cheap metal, someone returned the same weight in gold, would he not seem to have repaid more than a hundredfold? So, when spiritual joy and the delight of the most precious charity are repaid in place of the contempt of earthly pleasures and affections, even if the number itself is one hundred, the quality is nevertheless greater and more excellent than a hundredfold.

And, to make this clearer through repeated examples: formerly I possessed a wife in the passion of fragile desire; now I possess this same woman in the honor of sanctification and in true love of Christ. The woman is one, but the merit of charity has increased a hundredfold.

If, in place of the disturbance of anger and fury, you set perpetual gentleness of patience; in place of the anguish of anxiety and agitation, the quiet of security; in place of the fruitless and painful sadness of this world, the fruit of salutary sorrow; and in place of the emptiness of temporal joy, the abundance of spiritual gladness, you will see a hundredfold recompense in the exchange of these affections [Lips. in margin: “in comparison with these affections”].

And if the merits of the opposing virtues are compared with the brief and slippery pleasure of each vice, multiplied joy will show that these merits are a hundredfold better.

[Note: [Col. 1324C] These are the words of St. Jerome, *Against Jovinianus* 1.1, where, comparing virginity with marriage and widowhood, and at the same time explaining the evangelical saying concerning the threefold fruit, he writes:

> “Although the hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold fruit arise from one land and one seed, there is nevertheless a great difference in number. Thirty refers to marriage, for the very joining of the fingers, as though embracing one another in a gentle union and binding themselves together, depicts a husband and wife. Sixty refers to widows, because they are placed in distress and tribulation; hence they are represented by the upper finger being bent downward. The number one hundred—please, careful reader, attend closely—is transferred from the left hand to the right. It forms a circle with the same fingers, but not the same hand, by which married women and widows are represented on the left, and expresses the crown of virginity.”

So far Jerome, alluding to the custom of the ancients, who counted and expressed numbers by various flexions of the fingers, as is also evident from Plutarch’s *Problems*. Hence Tertullian calls the movements of the fingers used for calculation *supputatory gestures*.

This explanation is aptly echoed in the ecclesiastical hymn sung about St. John the Baptist, where three crowns and the three evangelical fruits are assigned to the three classes or degrees of human beings already mentioned, in these verses:

> “Garlands three times ten crown others,  
> > Increased by further growth.”

These are the married, living chastely. The first crown and first evangelical fruit, namely the thirtyfold, is marital chastity. The same verse continues:

> “Garlands doubled crown some.”

That is, doubled garlands crown those who practice continence, namely widows and widowers, because the second crown and second fruit, the sixtyfold, is assigned to widowhood as twice thirty, the marital chastity.

Then follows:

> “Garlands increased threefold by a hundredfold fruit  
> > Adorn you, holy one.”

They adorn you, O John the Baptist, and virgins like you, because the third and supreme crown, and the hundredfold fruit, is assigned to virginal chastity.

Nor should St. Gregory’s commentary be omitted here (*Apologia*, chapter 19). Interpreting the parable of the sower differently, but using the same allusion and comparison as St. Jerome (*Homily 17 on Ezekiel*), he writes as follows:

> “Since God gave sinful humanity a law written in ten commandments, and six times ten rises to sixty, perfection in good works is rightly signified by sixty cubits. The Lord also clearly indicates this in the Gospel. When he explained the parable of the sower, he said: ‘Another seed fell on good soil and produced fruit, rising and growing; and it yielded one thirtyfold, one sixtyfold, and one hundredfold’ (Mark 4).

> “The good earth yields thirty when the mind has conceived the perfection of faith, which is in the Trinity. It yields sixty when it has perfectly produced works of a good life. It yields one hundred when it has advanced to the contemplation of eternal life. Our left hand is the present life; the right hand is the life to come. The contemplation of eternal life is rightly signified by the number one hundred, because when, after counting thirty and sixty, we arrive at the hundredth number, the number one hundred passes to the right hand.

> “Faith and works are still on the left, because, while we remain here, we believe what we do not see and work in order to see. But when the mind has raised itself to the contemplation of eternal life, the counting has, as it were, reached the right hand.”

So far St. Gregory.

A little book among the works of Venerable Bede embraces this entire art of counting on the fingers; it is entitled *On Calculation, or Speech by Means of the Gesture of the Fingers*. From it it will suffice to note only those things that properly concern the understanding of this passage and of what has been said.

Bede therefore begins his calculation from the left hand and proceeds to ten:

> “When you say ten, place the nail of your index finger in the middle of your thumb. When you say thirty, join the nails of your index finger and thumb in a gentle embrace. When you say sixty, carefully encircle the bent thumb with the curved index finger.”

[Col. 1326C] After explaining the other cardinal numbers, which were expressed in various ways on the left hand up to ninety, he then turns to the right hand and adds:

> “When you signify one hundred, use the same gesture by which you showed ten on the left.”

From these words it must be inferred how the number one hundred, or the hundredth, was transferred from the left hand to the right: namely, because they counted on the fingers of the left hand up to one hundred, and at one hundred passed to the right. This also explains why, as Jerome says, thirty refers to marriage, sixty to widows, and one hundred—which is the first number on the right—to virginity.

Marriage is said to be signified by thirty because, with that number, the thumb and index finger are joined through gentle and soft contact, like spouses kissing and joining themselves. Widowhood and the distress of widows are expressed by the bending of the index finger over the thumb. The crown of virgins, signified by the number one hundred, is expressed on the right hand by the circle formed when the nail of the index finger is fixed in the middle of the thumb, like a crown.

[Col. 1326D] That one hundred and the numbers that follow it were customarily counted on the right hand is also taught by these verses of the satirical poet Juvenal (*Satires* 10), where, concerning Nestor, whom Homer reports to have lived three hundred years—that is, three human ages—he sings:

> “Happy indeed is he who through so many ages  
> > Delayed death and now counts his years on his right hand.”

Sidonius, imitating him while praising Faustus and indicating his great age as though he were a centenarian, says:

> “Since your years have now been counted by your right hand” (Book 9, Letter 9).]

For the number one hundred is transferred from the left hand to the right; and although it appears to retain the same figure in the counting of the fingers, it nevertheless grows enormously in the magnitude of its quantity. Thus it will happen that we who seemed to bear the form of a goat on the left will, once transferred to the right, attain the merit of a sheep.

Let us now turn to the quantity of those things which Christ restores to us in this age in return for contempt of the world and of other advantages, especially according to the Gospel of Mark, which says:

> “There is no one who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or mother, or children, or fields for my sake and for the Gospel, who will not receive a hundred times as much now in this present time—houses, brothers and sisters, mothers, children, and fields”—

[Note: [Col. 1326D] This is how it appears in Mark in the words quoted above. From them it is also understood that the hundredfold recompense is to be referred to the present age, not to the future, in which there will be no persecution.]

> “with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life” (Mark 10).

Whoever, for Christ’s name, abandons the affection of one father, mother, or child and passes into sincere love for all who serve Christ will receive a hundredfold the number of brothers and parents. In place of one, he will find so many fathers and brothers bound to him by a more fervent and excellent affection.

He will also be enriched by a multiplied possession of houses and fields: whoever has rejected one house for the love of Christ will possess countless monastic dwellings as his own, succeeding in any part of the world as though exercising the rights of his own house.

For how does he not receive a hundredfold—or, if it is permissible to add something to the saying of our Lord, more than a hundredfold—who abandons the unfaithful and coerced services of ten or twenty servants and is supported by the voluntary service of so many freeborn and noble people?

You yourselves have been able to prove this through your own experience. After leaving behind individual fathers, mothers, and houses, wherever in the world you have entered, you acquire countless fathers, mothers, and brothers, as well as houses, fields, and most faithful servants, without any labor of anxiety. They humbly receive you as their own lords, embrace and cherish you, and honor you through their services.

But, I say, they will rightly and confidently enjoy this ministry of the saints who first, through voluntary devotion, have subjected themselves and all that is theirs to the service of brotherhood. For, according to the Lord’s saying, they will freely receive what they themselves have previously given to others.

Whoever has not earlier, in sincere humility, offered these services to his companions—how will he patiently permit others to offer them to him, when he understands that he is burdened rather than comforted by their service, preferring to receive the service of his brothers rather than to render it?

All these things, however, he will receive not with relaxed security or idle enjoyment, but, according to the word of the Lord, “with persecutions,” that is, with the pressures of this present age and the greatest anguish of suffering. For, as that wisest man testifies:

[Note: [Col. 1327C] The complete sentence is rendered in Latin by the Septuagint as follows: “In every diligent person there is abundance, but the one who is gentle and without pain will be in poverty.” The Vulgate has instead: “In every work there will be abundance, but where there are many words, there is often poverty” (Proverbs 14).]

> “The one who is gentle and without pain will be in poverty” (Proverbs 14 according to the Septuagint).

For the kingdom of heaven is seized not by the idle, the lax, the delicate, or the pampered, but by the violent.

Who, then, are these violent ones? Those who inflict a noble violence not upon others but upon their own desires [Lips. in margin: “pleasures”], who, through a praiseworthy plundering, deprive themselves of every pleasure of present things and are proclaimed by the Lord’s voice to be eminent plunderers, violently invading the kingdom of heaven through such a seizure.

For, according to the Lord’s saying:

> “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew 11).

These indeed are the praiseworthy violent, who do violence to their own destruction.

For, as it is written:

> “A man labors for himself in sufferings and does violence to his own destruction” (Proverbs 16).

Our destruction is the pleasure of the present life—or, to say it more explicitly, the carrying out of our desires and wills. If someone removes and mortifies these from his soul, he certainly does a glorious and profitable violence to his own destruction, denying it only those most delightful desires which the divine word frequently censures through the prophet, saying:

> “For in the days of your fasting your will is found” (Isaiah 58).

And again:

> “If you turn your foot away from the Sabbath, from doing your will on my holy day, and glorify it by not doing your ways, and your will is not found so that you may speak a word…” (ibid.).

To this the Prophet immediately adds how great a blessedness is promised:

> “Then you will delight in the Lord, and I will raise you above the heights of the earth, and I will feed you with the inheritance of Jacob your father; for the mouth of the Lord has spoken” (ibid.).

For this reason our Lord and Savior, to provide us with a model for cutting off our own wills, said:

> “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6).

And again:

> “Not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26).

This virtue is exercised especially by those who live in monasteries and are governed by the authority of an elder. They do nothing at all according to their own judgment, but their will depends upon the will of the abbot.

Finally, to bring this discourse to a close: do not those who faithfully serve Christ also most clearly receive in this respect a hundredfold grace, when they are honored by the highest rulers? Although they themselves do not seek human glory, they nevertheless become venerable, even amid the pressures of persecution, to all judges and authorities. Their lowliness might perhaps have been despised even by ordinary people because of the obscurity of their birth or the condition of servitude, had they remained in secular life.

Through the military service of Christ, however, no one will dare to insult their status or reproach their obscure origin. Rather, through those very reproaches of the lowest condition by which others are shamed and dishonored, Christ’s servants are more gloriously ennobled.

[Note: [Col. 1327D] These matters should be compared with what Cassian writes consistently concerning this John in Book 4 of the *Institutes*, chapter 23. There, among the other hermits and elders whose virtues he recalls and praises, he places this abbot John first. He says that John lived near Lyco, a town of the Thebaid, and that, because of the virtue of his obedience, he was raised to the grace of prophecy and became so renowned throughout the whole world that even the kings of this world were rightly made illustrious through him.

For, while he lived in the farthest regions of the Thebaid, the emperor did not dare undertake war against powerful tyrants before being encouraged by John’s oracles and replies. Trusting in them as though they had been delivered from heaven, he returned from wars that seemed hopeless with triumphs over the battles and the enemy. So much for that passage.]

We can demonstrate this more clearly in the case of Abbot John, who lives in the desert adjoining the town of Lyco. Born of very obscure ancestors, he became so admired for Christ’s name by almost the whole human race that even the rulers of present affairs—those who hold the reins of this world and of the empire and inspire fear in all the powerful and in kings themselves—venerated him as a lord. Seeking his oracles from regions so distant, they entrusted to his prayers and merits the summit and stability of their empire and the outcome of their wars.

Blessed Abraham discussed these matters concerning either the origin or the remedy of our deception. He exposed, as it were before our eyes, the snares of the thoughts which the devil had implanted, and kindled in us a desire for true mortification. We believe that many will be inflamed by this, even though all these matters have been arranged in an unadorned style of speech.

Although the burning thoughts of the greatest Fathers may have been covered by the tepid ash of our language, we nevertheless think that the coldness of many can be warmed if they wish, by removing the ashes of the words, to stir up the vitality of the thoughts lying hidden within.

But I did not, O holy brothers, send forth this fire—which the Lord came to cast upon the earth and which he greatly desires to burn (Luke 12)—with a spirit of presumption, as though I intended to kindle your already fervent purpose by adding this heat. Rather, I sent it so that you might possess greater authority among your sons when the teachings of the greatest and most ancient Fathers confirm what you yourselves teach them not through the dead sound of words but through living example.

It remains that, after having been tossed about until now in a most dangerous storm, the spiritual breeze of your prayers may escort me to the safest harbor of silence.

[Note: [Col. 1328D] Other manuscripts read: “Now may the protection of your prayers preserve me in the safest harbor of silence. May this also happen to me. Amen.”]

[Note: [Col. 1327] In the Lipsian edition, certain short works relating to Cassian’s *Conferences* are placed here: namely, Prosper’s book *Against the Collator*, his letter to Augustine, Pope Celestine’s letter on behalf of Prosper, and the canons of the Second Council of Orange from the time of Leo the Great. Since, in our universal library, each praised author’s work should be presented in its more appropriate place, it will be enough to remind you, benevolent reader, to consult below the works of Prosper of Aquitaine, Celestine, and Leo the Great, when you wish. EDD.]
